en: Preface to the Newly Translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* of the Great Zhou,
Composed by the Celestial Emperor, Golden-Wheel Sage-Spirit Sovereign.

I have heard that at the very beginning of the creative transformation, when the Way of Heaven had not yet been differentiated, and at the inception of the patterns of the tortoise and dragon, when the culture of humanity first emerged—

From its initial establishment, although eighteen thousand years have passed, all have been brought together within this bounded realm; yet how could the seventy-two sovereigns have known the meaning of the boundless?
Consequently, people were deluded regarding the Four Patiences (*catur-kṣānti*), wandering in saṃsāra through the six destinies (*ṣad-gati*);

families were entangled by the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), drowning in the depths of the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*). Then, when Vulture Peak stood westward and the Elephant Vehicle drove eastward, the Sun of Wisdom and the Dharma...
The King transcends the four great elements and gazes loftily upon the sky; as a Tamer, he surpasses the ten stages to abide in supreme honor.
He encompasses the Iron Ring Mountains and compresses or extends aeons (*kalpas*). As for his essence, it is neither born nor extinguished; as for its characteristics, it neither departs nor arrives.
The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute his practice; compassion, joy, and equanimity are his four immeasurables.

The Dharma-measure guides the mind; the power of its skillful means is inconceivable. The capacities of those to be transformed are manifold and diverse, merging with the vast void to constitute the measure—how could they ever be exhausted by calculation?
Entering the subtlest regions as tiny as a mustard seed, they cannot be described by names or words.
That which is beyond all designation can only be called the Great Enlightenment. I, the Emperor, having planted causes in past kalpas, have been fortunate enough to inherit [this legacy].
The Buddha’s prophecy concerning the descent of the Golden Sage (Śākyamuni) was first manifested in the verses of the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* before the Jade Throne;

later, upon examining the texts of the *Ratnavarṣa-sūtra*, the blessings resulting from accumulated merit gathered upon this humble person. Consequently, the earth was leveled and the heavens were perfected;

the rivers became clear and the seas were tranquil. Extraordinary portents and rare auspicious signs arrived daily and were recorded monthly, while the sacred texts of the *Bhūrja-leaf* also reached us in due time.

Throughout the year, envoys have crossed oceans and deserts to present the full array of precious offerings; through perilous journeys and deep waters, their words have been conveyed across multiple translations.
This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vehicle, is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and the ocean of the Tathāgata’s nature.
Those who gaze upon it cannot discern its ultimate destination; those who draw from it rarely fathom its boundless limits.
The resolve of those in training and those beyond training is severed from all seeking; how could they hope to hear or receive [the teachings of] the Two Vehicles or Three Vehicles?
The traces adorned by the most supreme *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom) are already flourishing, and the causes of the vows and practices of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī are now fulfilled.

Within a single phrase, the boundlessness of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) is encompassed; within a single hair-tip, world-systems (*kṣetra*) are placed without any crowding. Thus it began in the kingdom of Magadha.
The conditions for this wondrous assembly have arisen, and thus the Hall of Universal Radiance has spread the principles of quiescent extinction.
Reflecting upon these profound meanings, their translation dates back to the Jin dynasty; over six dynasties have passed, and nearly four hundred years have elapsed.

Yet, of this single scripture, only some thirty thousand words have been obtained—merely half the pearl revealed, with the full treasure still unexamined. I have heard that the Sanskrit original was previously held in the kingdom of Khotan.

An envoy was dispatched from the Central Capital to welcome [the scriptures], which have now arrived at this nearby region. Having beheld these hundreds of thousands of wondrous verses, I have now opened these one hundred thousand authentic texts.

On the first day of the month of Guxi (the third lunar month) in the year of Yimwei, the first year of the Zhengsheng era, specifically on the fourteenth day, the eighth day of the Xinsi cycle, I personally received the editorial revisions and respectfully translated them at Dapiankong Monastery.

Wén subsequently attained the flowing essence of the nectar of immortality, as had been prefigured in his dream on the evening of Gengshen; later, during the hour of Renshu, he was drenched by a copious rain.
Thus, the gateway to the *dharmatā* (true reality) was opened, perfectly corresponding to the grace of the single flavor.

On the eighth day of the tenth month, Jichou, of the second year of the Shènglì era—the cyclical year Jihai—beginning from Renwu—he completed the task of transcribing this work, thereby augmenting the ocean of his nature.

Its waves broaden the domain of the Dharma-realm; this Mahāyāna Sudden Teaching universally covers the infinite, and these profound and extensive true expositions reach far across all conscious beings.

How could one have thought that in the final five hundred years, we would suddenly encounter the words from the Golden Mouth, and that within this Sahā world, the secrets of the pearl casket would be revealed?
It is hoped that these shall be propagated throughout the sands of the universe and expounded across the realms of dust, so that all may share in them.

The two luminaries hang forever high, spreading eternally throughout the ten directions; upon first beholding these precious verses, joy overflows my spiritual mind, and as I recite their profound essence three times, delight fills my body and spirit.

Although there is neither speech nor demonstration, for this principle accords with the gate of non-duality, yet it is through words that words are revealed, thereby elucidating the meaning of the great trichiliocosm. I have thus composed this humble work and hereby inscribe this preface.
Preface to the Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Composed by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇa Huìyán by Imperial Decree.
The true source of the Dharma-realm is a profound ocean of ten layers of treasuries; from it surges the King of Flowers, whose essence embodies the myriad virtues.

Through this practice, the bodies and lands are clearly manifested as mutually contained within reflections; cause and effect interpenetrate, and wisdom and compassion shine forth in mutual brilliance within the numinous and true.

Tracing their origin to the absence of self-nature, the wondrous light is like golden waves shimmering with images, or illusory births appearing simultaneously like the myriad waters dividing their forms.

This is truly because one momentarily follows the clarity and brilliance of a single illumination, only to suddenly lose sight of the thousandfold radiance of perfect reflection—thus returning [to the source].
Recognizing that the manifestation of creation arises from the essence of mind— like clouds appearing in the vast void— and that the movement of saṃsāra is stirred by the mind—
like waves rocking upon the jade ocean— I, Vairocana Tathāgata, out of compassion for those who slumber in delusion, have spread a cloud-body throughout all phenomena,
sat at the site of enlightenment within all-knowledge, and attained perfect awakening; thus I speak this Great Vaipulya Buddha-Flower [Sūtra].
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* encompasses the realm of Jambudvīpa and unifies the adornments of the *Avataṃsaka*:

the celestial deities are arrayed like stars across the five stages, while the ocean of lands in the ten directions is mirrored therein; within the carved palaces and azure halls, boundless weary beings find refuge, and upon the jade trees and golden terraces, Buddha-sons as numerous as motes of dust are born.
Before even a single thought has shifted from the lotus seat, the nine heavens—

Arising together from the thunderous voice, divine light opens the Dharma-gates of the ten assemblies, and precious moisture nourishes the three cycles of cause and effect; thus, at the beginning of this sutra,
the World-Rulers assemble like clouds and with one mind silently request instruction, posing thirty-seven questions that fully set forth the gates of essence, function, cause, and effect—
this is the ultimate pinnacle of the great masterwork of this entire scripture, which takes the concealment of the body as its essence and the ocean of practice as its function.

Taking the arising of function from essence to sever habitual tendencies as the cause, and the total embodiment of function to exhaust habitual tendencies as the fruit—within which the meaning of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) manifests through the mutual revelation of mind and object—the interpenetration of cause and fruit and the identity of essence and function are clarified. Thus, when one clarifies the arising of function from essence by contemplating the Dharma from the perspective of the mind, the spiritual powers of the Bodhisattva emerge;
when one clarifies function by proclaiming the voice from the perspective of the objective realm, [the same is realized].
In its entirety, the Buddha’s spiritual powers and all the wondrous gateways collectively answer this question.

Now, as for the Dharma, it has no fixed tenet upon which people may rely; thus, the fruits and causes of the ancient Buddhas are manifested to provide present-day beings with a basis for realization and faith.
Therefore, at the first assembly, when the World-Honored One’s radiance illuminated his white teeth and the oceanic multitude gathered like clouds, he revealed the fruit. Next, the jade...

That the sons of the Buddha are born from within the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the tuft of hair between the eyebrows) demonstrates the cause; that later, Samantabhadra receives the majestic power to proclaim the Flower Treasury Ocean (*Ghanavyūha*) demonstrates the perfection of the fruit through the cause.
Yet, when sealed by Vairocana, it clarifies that the fruit and cause of the ancient Buddhas provide a comprehensive answer to the preceding dharmas.

Furthermore, because the ocean of wisdom has no inherent nature, the cause is formed through the awakening to delusion as ordinary beings; once one realizes that the source of delusion is fundamentally void, [one attains liberation].
Because one perceives the Buddha through the ordinary mind, the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance takes the fruit of Buddhahood as the cause for faith within the ordinary mind.
At the third assembly on Mount Wondrous Peak, the characteristics of the ordinary mind are exhausted, and one abides as a Buddha.

At the fourth assembly in the Yāma Heaven, one follows wisdom through function to accomplish the practice of Buddhahood. At the fifth assembly in Tuṣita Heaven, wisdom and practice mutually penetrate to accomplish the dedication of merit toward Buddhahood. This constitutes the sixth assembly.
At the seventh assembly, in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the stage of Buddhahood where self and others are of one essence;

at the eighth assembly, in the Flower of Wisdom and Conduct purified through the three dhyānas, the manifestation of Buddhahood; at the ninth assembly, in the Universal Radiance Hall, the appearance of the Buddha as the fruition of his own causes;

at the tenth assembly, in the Universal Radiance Hall, the perfect integration of cause and effect as the eternal practice of Samantabhadra; and at the eleventh assembly, in the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, all positions are equally enlightened.
Together they manifest the Dharma-realm; this is the general response to the preceding teaching regarding the cause and effect of generating the bodhicitta.

Next, fearing that one might become confused regarding the cultivation of progress and fail to exhaust the delusions of the thousand gates, [the text] explains how, through constant practice, the wisdom and compassion of the ten thousand practices are perfected.

Thus, Sudhana is presented as a specific model of conduct: he first encounters Mañjuśrī as the cause of faith in Buddha-wisdom, and then travels south to seek various spiritual friends as the practice of setting forth.
By practicing to enter the Hall of Maitreya, when practice is exhausted and the fruit is realized, one again beholds Mañjuśrī;

thus cause and effect are simultaneous, and one immediately perceives the original conduct of Samantabhadra within the Dharma-realm. This reveals the complete cycle of cause and effect for the gate of practicing the Way.

Indeed, the profound mystery of the three cycles and ten assemblies points toward the ultimate aim of the thirty-seven meanings; even if one were to write this single gateway of the Dharma with an ocean of ink, it would remain inexhaustible.

The two vehicles of the provisional teachings are inexhaustible; even those who examine their limits find them unfathomable. Therefore, this teaching was not compiled by Śaṅkaraśaila, but was instead collected by Mañjuśrī.

It consists of three sections: one section contains as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms, one section contains as many chapters as there are atoms in a four-continent world system, and one section contains four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred and eight [verses].
This work consists of one hundred verses and twelve hundred chapters, totaling one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight sections.
It was hidden within the Dragon Treasury (Nāga-kośa) and had not yet been disseminated in Jambudvīpa until five hundred years after the passing of the True Dharma.

Then, the fourteenth patriarch, Nāgārjuna, employed his spiritual power upon the Ocean Treasury; observing that the first two sections were beyond the reach of worldly people, he recited the latter portion.
The various sections were transmitted to the Five Indies and spread for a thousand years before finally reaching China. During the early Eastern Jin dynasty, it was first translated;

subsequently, during the Tang dynasty, it was again brought forth as "Heavenly Descent" and "Nectar. In the Kaiyuan era of the Xuanzong reign, there was a reclusive scholar named Li Tongxuan in Taiyuan, who was a peer to Vimalakīrti across the ages.
With a divine insight that transcended the mundane world, he cultivated his sentiments within the teachings of Śākyamuni. Consequently, upon reading the *Avataṃsaka*, he...

The *Yanyi shu* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) laments: "The Great Teaching spreads its fragrance and many schools have produced elaborate compositions; laboring over texts until one's hair turns white, how can one find leisure for further cultivation?
Thus, [the author] exhausted the true exegesis of eighty fascicles and summarized the profound treatises of forty volumes.

By night he wielded his divine pen, radiating the auspicious light of his jade-like teeth; by day he explored the obscure and profound, moved by the celestial boy’s provision of meals, as he magnificently proclaimed the Teaching."

The *Hai lüe yìtiān dàzhōng zǎi wúzhū yǒu gāosēng zhì* (A Comprehensive Record of Eminent Monks Without Omissions, Compiled from Various Sources) contains such a wealth of material that it is difficult for later students to fathom its profundity as they seek its contents.
Consequently, I have combined the essential meanings of the sūtras and śāstras so that they may complement one another.

Yet, as these categories of meaning are vast and complex, and my own wisdom and research remain incomplete, I have ventured to consult various scholars while traveling among the clouds and waters. Having humbly examined their guiding insights, I now venture to inscribe this upon these tablets.
Having meticulously organized these [teachings] and briefly cataloged the sūtras and śāstras to highlight and integrate their doctrines and principles, the meaning becomes lucid and the text refined;
thus, one need not rely on a lion throne to embrace the volumes, for spiritual radiance and wisdom are spontaneously awakened. Why labor at Vulture Peak to seek a teacher?
This complete collection consists of one hundred and twenty fascicles. It was compiled by Baoen Guangjiao Daochang Zhengjue Konghui.
The Chan Master Yong’an has transmitted the ancestral seal of the mind and tasted the flavor of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

Having heard from afar of the Imperial Decree to open the seal with gold and propagate it for the broad benefit of wisdom, he respectfully received this mandate to compose a preface to the True Text. He has thus briefly set forth its general outline;

though he deeply regrets that his own writing lacks elegant refinement, he hopes that it may long illuminate the Sun of the Buddha, shining together with the two luminaries to eternally assist the Golden Wheel.
The two celestial spheres of the sun and moon revolve in vast distance; at this time, in the year of Qiandé, the *dingmǎo* year, on the full moon day of the month of Ruībīn,
I have composed the Preface to the Combined Commentary on the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty.

How distant and vast is antiquity! The Great Primal (*tài-sù*) existed prior to the chaotic nebula (*hún-tún*). To speak of its existence would be beyond discourse; the Dao is the beginning of the single life of all things.
The son of a great Confucian scholar returned from bathing at the banks of the Yi River. The sage of Zhou was as brilliant as a star; his joy lay in the music of the former kings.

Dao’an attained realization of the capacity of the Great Void; he manifested the Dharma-realm within a single speck of dust. He weeded out the beginning and the end, utterly eradicating birth and cessation.
Even the Great Void cannot equal his measure. That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is still but a provisional name;
it is eternally functional yet eternally non-abiding. To exist while not being existent—this is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. It was certainly not compiled by Arhats, nor is it of the Lesser Vehicle.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in its Great Original Version, as transmitted by the sages, can only be known and seen by a Buddha.
The Middle Original Version can be known by Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*). The Small Original Version consists of one hundred thousand verses;

of these, what has been transmitted today comprises only forty-five thousand plus some verses, which is the present eighty-fascicle scripture. (This is according to what is stated in the *Huayan jing zuanling ji*). Scripture.
It is said that this sutra does not fall into the hands of those of the Two Vehicles; if there are ordinary persons lacking the Great Mind, this Dharma-gate shall immediately perish.

This sutra contains the meanings of the Ten Mysteries and Six Phases (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*); it is like binding together various strands of silk, or like the celestial net and heavenly jewels, where each successive layer has its own systematic order.

To discuss the subject, one need only raise a single instance, and then ten thousand categories will simultaneously converge; the ocean of meaning, though a thousandfold in its distinctions, shines with brilliant splendor.

They are distributed like stars, taking dependent origination as their primary theme and the nature of the *dharmadhātu* as their central tenet. The *dharmakāya*, along with the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, are simultaneous;

essence and function are distinct yet possess no dual characteristics. They take the *Avataṃsaka* as their path of travel, the *bodhicitta* as their home, and the myriad virtues and myriad practices as their household vocation.
They take Mañjuśrī as the seed-wisdom and Samantabhadra as the flowers of practice. [Vairocana...]
Vairocana is the body of fruition, taking the forty-two stages as his retinue. When unfolded, they pervade the entire Dharma-realm;

when rolled up, the myriad phenomena converge within a single hair-tip on the vast ocean. Although it is said that they are so numerous, even if they enter a speck of dust or a hair, there is still room to spare.

Thus, the integrated and the sequential interpenetrate; principle and phenomenon mutually inform one another. Sequentiality is integrated and integration is sequential, as the primary and the attendant manifest together. As it is said: [the text continues with verses].
The single golden staff that is broken is many; as the gold of the broken staff is many, it is also one.

Contemplating a single object, the four dharma-realms manifest perfectly and instantaneously. Upon first ascending the first stage (*bhūmi*), the wondrous meanings of a hundred gates gather in continuous succession.

One proceeds toward the realization of the seventh stage, where the effortful application finally ceases. As the power of concentration deepens on the eighth stage, the arising of wisdom likewise depends upon all [dharmas].
The Buddha’s wind-sail having been set, he proceeded spontaneously and effortlessly, his momentum unceasing until he reached the stage of Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā*).

Within that assembly, those of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*) had not yet traveled there; they did not see Samantabhadra before the Buddha, nor did the ten great śrāvakas of Great Wisdom behold the sublime events at Jetavana.

This was truly because their initial resolve was small and their great vows were not yet perfected, remaining within the realms of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha*).
Only when these two delusions are exhausted will one manifest before [the Buddha]. This Dharma of the sutra is the *dharmadhātu*, without beginning and without end;

the Buddha-body is neither existent nor non-existent, neither accomplished nor unaccomplished. Great wisdom is without cessation and without birth, eternally taking the benefiting of others as its foundation.

Through the two hundred great questions of Universal Wisdom (*Samantabhadra*) and the two thousand dharma-answers of Universal Good (*Samantabhadra*), the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), appearing and disappearing, expanding and contracting with sovereign freedom.

(The Sūtra says: "It is as if a person, through their transformative mind, were to manifest a Buddha; whether that manifestation appears or not, there is no difference. All Buddhas, whether they have attained Bodhi or not, are without distinction.
Sudhana attained the Way in a single lifetime; six thousand bhikṣus realized wisdom without passing through many kalpas.
The white ox-cart was about to awaken, thereby transcending the Mahāyāna; in the presence of the Golden World, the wisdom of Mañjuśrī was fully realized.
The Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood in a mere instant; upon seeing the Buddha’s radiance at Mount Wutai, she ascended to perfect enlightenment in her first stage of realization.
This is simply following the perfect view; as for grasping gradual cultivation, sudden awakening occurs in a single moment, like a cow eating fatty grass.
Between the regions of Xing and Dai during the Great Tang, there was an elder surnamed Li named Tongxuan, who was in truth a man of extraordinary character.
No one knew where he came from; he composed this treatise in forty fascicles.

An account concerning him states that while he was carrying the sutra down from a cliff, after he began writing, gods and humans constantly provided him with food until the treatise was finished. He also passed away during his lifetime.
After his death, people obtained a draft copy of the work, which they transcribed and circulated. The principles elucidated in this treatise accord with those of the commentaries by various masters.

The meaning [of this scripture] differs slightly from others; it contains ten locations and ten assemblies. Examining the text of the *Yingluo jing* (the two-fascicle *Yingluo jing*), its wondrous text consists of forty chapters.
Since the text was spoken in the Third Dhyāna, and ten times ten constitutes a perfect number, how could there be only thirty-nine chapters?
I suspect that some portions were lost during the translation of the Sanskrit original.
Now, as I examine the scriptures and seek their meaning, it appears they are like flowers strung together and the flow of ambrosial dew;

yet, since the Sage has long been gone, who can provide further proof? On the path of a hundred thousand [verses], who is able to go back and inspect them? It is like the Master Sheng who endured death, or Qingbian who left behind his body;
only by cross-referencing them can one know where the true meaning lies. How could the three assemblies in the Hall of Universal Radiance have failed to achieve this?

Third, although Zhi Ning did not personally witness the assembly at the eastern side of the city of Puṇḍravardhana where Sudhana’s merit was perfected, he relied upon what has been widely transmitted among people regarding the composition of this treatise.
Upon examining this discourse, it seems he has somewhat grasped its general meaning.
Now, seeing that the gentlemen of this land who delight in the good find it difficult to harmonize the treatise with the sūtras, Zhi Ning, disregarding his own decline, [offers this explanation].
I, Mai, am devoid of talent and unable to do much; I shall now compose a commentary on the treatise appended beneath the sutra, so that future readers may not waste their efforts.
As soon as the sutra is opened, one shall find the treatise therein. I prostrate before all Buddhas, Vairocana, and all holy sages;
may you deign to grant your protection. From the eighth fascicle onward, the commentary will be integrated into the sutra, with the treatise and the sutra presented together.

It consists of one hundred and twenty fascicles; I hope that all discerning scholars will not find this strange. There is a commentary consisting of seven fascicles that was not included in the original annotations;
it has now been transcribed and appended at the beginning.
The Biography of Li Zhang (the Elder), the Master of the Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Li Zhang’s name was Tongxuan; his origins are not well known. When anyone inquired about his ancestry, he would simply say, "Cangzhou."

In the third month on the day of the full moon in the twenty-seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, I traveled with staff in hand and carrying my book-casket to the village of Daxian, located forty li west of Yuxian in Taiyuan.
There lived a man named Gao Shanu, who honored virtue and admired scholars, receiving guests without weariness.
The Elder went directly to his door; Shanu gazed intently at his divine countenance and knew him to be extraordinary.
His provisions were eventually exhausted; he performed prostrations with bowed head and requested permission to return to his place of retreat for the summer rains.

Each morning, he consumed only ten jujubes and a single small cake made of cypress leaves, about the size of a spoon. From then on, he did not associate with outsiders, remaining alone in his chamber.

Holding his brush and facing his paper, he never let a moment pass in idleness. This continued for three years, until one day he left the mountain and went southward five or six li to a place called Shan-nu.
He went to the ancient Buddha hall of the Ma family and constructed an earthen cell beside it, where he dwelt in quietude and silence for ten years.
Later, he again packed his scriptures and books and departed along the road. After traveling more than twenty li, he arrived at the manor of the Han family—this is the present-day village of Guange.
Suddenly, he encountered a tiger blocking the path; it lay prostrate and submissive, as if waiting for something. Long... [text ends]
The man said to him, "I am about to compose a treatise to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; you may accompany me to select a place for us to dwell.
Having finished speaking, the tiger rose up. The elder slowly stroked it, then hung the bag he was carrying upon the tiger’s back and let it choose its own resting place.
Thereupon, the tiger looked toward the foothills of Mount Shenfu and descended directly for more than thirty li, arriving at a spot where—
He crouched down before the earthen niche, and the elder immediately gathered his bag and placed it inside. The tiger looked back repeatedly, then tucked its tail and departed.
The niche was polished and bright, perfectly circular, and measured several *zhang* in circumference; it existed naturally and was not the product of human labor.
Originally there were no springs or streams around the niche, yet on the very evening the elder first arrived, a violent wind and thunder arose.

He uprooted an ancient pine tree over three hundred feet high; at dawn, beneath the roots of the tree, it transformed into a pond several fathoms deep, spanning more than fifty paces in circumference.
Its sweetness surpassed auspicious dew, and its color outshone lapis lazuli.
People of the time called it "The Elder’s Spring," which remains clear and bright to this day, never increasing or decreasing. During the *tiānyáng* year, one may pray to it.

It must have been on the evening when the Elder composed this treatise that his mind exhausted the profound mysteries and his mouth emitted white light that illuminated the interior of the grotto, serving as a substitute for lamps and candles. After he had resided in the mountains, two women suddenly appeared;

their beauty was peerless in the world, both were of marriageable age, and they were both dressed in coarse cloth garments with white turbans covering their heads. As for their surnames, residences, or origins, there was nothing at all known of them.
He would say, "I shall constantly draw water for the Elder, burn incense, and provide paper and ink.

From the hours of Māra and Cīna (dawn), he would invariably prepare pure offerings of sweet delicacies, fully prepared, and place them before the Elder. Once the fast was concluded, he would remove the vessels, leaving no trace of where they had been.
This continued for five years without a single lapse. When he was about to complete his treatise, he suddenly ceased these activities. According to the old records of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:

It is transmitted that when the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin dynasty was translating scriptures at the Temple of General Xie in Jiangdu, two youths dressed in blue robes suddenly emerged from the pond in the courtyard to attend upon a foreign monk. They burned incense and replenished the water jars, never leaving his side.
As evening approached, they would invariably return and hide back into the pond; this occurred every day as a regular occurrence. And...
Upon completing the translation, he wrote it out with purity and remained silent without a trace. The Elder’s spiritual resonance was such that his circumstances accorded with those of the past.
The Elder stood seven chi and two cun tall; his eyebrows were broad, his eyes bright, his lips crimson, and his face plump and purple-hued.

His long beard was lush and flourishing, his arms were long, straight, and well-proportioned, and his hair was a deep violet color with the tips of the strands curling to the right. His physical form was peerless, his demeanor exceptionally extraordinary, and his features possessed a most sublime beauty.
There was nothing he lacked; he wore a crown of birch bark upon his head and draped himself in hempen robes with a long skirt and wide sleeves, leaving his waist unbound as he walked.

He never wore leather girdles and usually went barefoot, refusing to engage in the formalities of welcoming guests. He lived in a state of expansive freedom among gods and men, unconstrained by any restrictions.
One day, he left the mountains to visit an old friend in the village, arriving just as the local people had gathered their clans to perform music together.

The elder addressed them all, saying, "May you dwell in peace; I am about to return home. The assembly then ceased their music and, looking at one another in alarm and distress, were all filled with deep sorrow.
They assumed the elder would return to Cangzhou, and shedding tears, they spoke with one voice, earnestly entreating him to remain.
The elder said, "Even if I were to live for a hundred years, I must eventually depart. Thereupon, the entire assembly escorted him back.
When he entered the mountains and reached the location of the niche, he spoke to them again, saying: "Coming and going are simply the constant nature of things;
you may each return home. Before the assembly had even turned their heels, mountain mists rose up on all sides and the landscape became indistinguishable.

All those traveling on the road were struck with wonder and astonishment. The next day, the Elder (Changzou) led his followers up the mountain to pay their respects, but they saw only his dignified and solemn countenance.
He had already passed away while seated within his shrine-casket. It was the twenty-eighth day of the third month, and he was ninety-six years of age.
A giant serpent coiled outside the casket, its eyes wide and its mouth agape, such that no one could approach it.
The assembly then offered their sincere prayers and vows, saying: "We now wish to collect the entire body of the Elder for interment; we pray that you will conceal your majestic spirit."
Upon arriving at the site of the snake’s death, he restrained his physical form so that it did not manifest;

the elders wept as they carried the remains to select a location on the northern slope of a great mountain, where they piled stones to form a tomb. This was intended to be a place of enduring purity, situated within the Śītavana Āraṇya on Mount Shenfu;
this is the present-day Fangshan. On the day the Elder passed away into concealment and when the tomb was completed, clouds and mist gathered and spread across the cliffs.
The valley shook and quaked as two white cranes wailed mournfully in the sky, and two deer called out to one another throughout the night;

other birds and beasts filled the mountains with their cries of grief. The people of the villages and countryside followed one another in changing their attire to mourn, following and yearning for him as if they had lost their own lord.
Whenever a fast was observed, clouds would rise from his tomb; this occurred thus for seven times seven days, which is truly extraordinary for an elder.
In former times, every year at the end of the third month, a pure assembly for the sages and worthies of the ten directions was regularly established;

women were not permitted to prepare the food, ensuring that every matter was performed with sincere devotion. Even such things as dates, pits, and rice-washings were not allowed to be discarded lightly;
once the fast was completed, these were given to dogs and pigs so they might be shared by all. This kind of assembly has been followed down to the present day without ever having been discontinued.

[Treatise]: Now, the root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source; the stream of conscious beings takes the Dharma-body as its essence.

It is simply because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because perceptions shift that the essence becomes distinct. When one reaches the fundamental source, emotions perish and knowledge [of reality] emerges.
The essence of the mind is now united with this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which clarifies the primordial limit of sentient beings and reveals the source of the fruition of all Buddhas.
As for its being the "root," it cannot be accomplished through effort; as for its being the "source," it cannot be attained through practice.
When effort ceases, the root is exhausted; when practice is ended, the source is perfected. This source and root are devoid of functional capacity, yet they follow along [with phenomena].

The one who possesses mastery over conditions is this very Vairocana. Taking his fundamental nature as primary, his wisdom accords with the faculties [of beings], and he delivers all things through great compassion;
it is for this reason that he is so named. Relying on this foundation, he establishes his teachings so that their grace flows abundantly throughout the dharma-realm to moisten all living beings.
Thereupon, he takes up a station within the four heavens and manifests the eight phases of his life at the site of enlightenment.

yet it contains the ten directions without obstructing the ocean of wisdom. Thus, the fruition and virtues are distinctively differentiated.
The gateway of the five stages eternally abides in the Hall of Dharma, demonstrating the practice of advancement atop the nine heavens;

Like many mirrors reflecting various forms without mutual hindrance, or like a thousand lamps sharing a single room, this sutra encompasses them all.

its hundreds of billions of wondrous words collectively extol the ocean-like conduct of the Buddha-flower. Through the ten bodies and ten assemblies, it expounds the dharma-gates of "ten times ten";

and Section Eleven clarifies the beginning and end of the assembly’s teachings.
First, the classification of schools based on the teachings is clarified.

Now, when the Tathāgata realizes the essence of the Way, he accords with the true source; through the two gates of principle and phenomena, the one and the many penetrate each other, and his realm of wisdom is perfectly tranquil—what dharma is not encompassed?
It is only because vessels differ that their modes and regulations vary; because capacities differ, there are gradual and sudden approaches from beginning to end.
He establishes teachings according to what is appropriate, with the Great and Small Vehicles being entirely distinct, and the timing of cause and effect being either protracted or brief.
The manifested Buddhas and their original bodies differ in the means they employ for instruction; the lands they inhabit vary in purity and defilement, and in increase and decrease;
and the stages, fruits, causes, and capacities of beings naturally differ. Those who have newly begun their studies are often unacquainted with the traces of the teachings;

clinging to provisional means as if they were ultimate reality, they remain deluded and fail to progress in their cultivation. If one does not comprehensively present the various schools, there will be no way to discern their respective benefits and harms, nor to clarify such delusions.
Those who are hindered—now I shall briefly distinguish ten dharmas to clarify and expound the teachings, so that students may know their fundamental principles:
shifting from the provisional to the real so as not to be hindered in their practice, and swiftly realizing Bodhi. First, the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna takes the conditioned as its principle.
Second, the Bodhisattva-śīla takes both the conditioned and the unconditioned (the real) as its principle, revealing them together. Third...

The fourth [treatise] takes the Prajñā teachings as its basis, establishing the revelation of emptiness as the manifestation of reality as its central tenet; the fifth takes the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* as its basis, establishing that which is neither empty nor existent as its central tenet;
the sixth takes the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as its basis, establishing the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two forms of selflessness as its central tenet;
and the seventh takes the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* as its basis, establishing the inconceivable through the harmonious integration of the two views of defilement and purity as its central tenet.

The seventh, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, takes the transformation of provisional means into the ultimate reality as its central theme. The eighth, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, takes the protection of the True Dharma as its central theme.
The ninth, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, clarifies Buddha-nature as its central theme. The tenth is named the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
by the name of this sūtra, it signifies that the causal perfection of the fundamental wisdom and compassion of all Buddhas is complete.

The fruit is the fulfillment of the single and the many, wherein phenomena and reality mutually penetrate throughout the *dharmadhātu*, and the dependent origination of principle and fact is sovereign and unimpeded;
thus, the Buddha Vehicle is established as the primary tenet. The above sections concerning the tenets all inherit the fundamental doctrines established by former masters.
Although there may be slight differences in increase or decrease due to individual perspectives, the general meaning and terminology are largely similar, as in the West.
The various virtues of this region and other directions each established their own religious traditions, which shall be further clarified later.

First, regarding the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna, for those who take the conditioned as their fundamental principle, it was taught by the Tathāgata when he first addressed ordinary people engaged in the creation of karma, stating:
"This should be done; this should not be done. To abandon [what is improper] is good; not to abandon it is unwholesome.
Establishing the teaching in this manner is not for the sake of [attaining] ultimate reality;

rather, such teachings are provisionally established based on the false imaginings of ordinary people regarding various evils, in order to restrain them and cause them to be reborn among humans and devas. Therefore, the preface to the *Prātimokṣa* states:
"If one desires to be born in the heavens or among humans, one should always protect the feet of the precepts and not allow them to be impaired."

Sentient beings perform conditioned actions that are illusory and unreal; because they have not truly attained [liberation], they are born among humans or devas, which is impermanent, illusory, and unreal.
Since they have not yet attained the Dharma-body or Wisdom-body, these are not considered truly existent entities.

Rather, they are established as provisional tenets based on conventional perception (*saṃvṛti-satya*), serving as the guiding principles and teachings within the Hīnayāna. This is not the case for upholding the precepts according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, as the Sūtra says:

"Is the body the holy life (*brahmacarya*)? Are the four modes of deportment of bodily action, or even the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, the ten assemblies, the seven prohibitions, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*), and the sacrificial altar (*maṇḍala*) the holy life? Thus one should contemplate with precision.
For one who seeks the holy life, it is found to be utterly unattainable; therefore, it is called the "pure holy life," as explained in the *Brahmacaryavarga*. Thus it is said.
The pure practitioner is named "one who upholds the Buddha-nature precepts" because they attain the Dharma-body of the Buddha;

even at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), they realize perfect awakening. Because they uphold the Buddha-nature precepts, their substance is equal to that of the Buddha, and their affairs are equal in principle.
They merge with the true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, in upholding the precepts, they do not perceive a self that can uphold the precepts, nor do they perceive another.
If one’s body possesses broken precepts, this is neither the conduct of an ordinary person nor the conduct of a noble sage.
One does not perceive within oneself the arousal of the bodhicitta, nor does one perceive the Buddhas attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.

Whether good or evil, if even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended, it is not called bodhi and is not called pure conduct. One should contemplate in this way: such intrinsic morality (*śīla*) is itself the Dharma.
The body is the Dharma-body, which is the wisdom of the Tathāgata; the wisdom of the Tathāgata is itself perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, it differs from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) because it is free from grasping and rejecting.
Second, regarding the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Bodhisattva Precepts, the thesis is that both the provisional and the ultimate are demonstrated together:
for those among ordinary beings who possess the great resolve, delight in practicing compassion, and aspire to seek the fruit of Buddhahood,

the Tathāgata taught that Vairocana Buddha is the primary body (mūlakāya) and the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis are the transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya), thereby causing them to attain [enlightenment] instantaneously.

Because consciousness returns to its source, the Sutra says: "In this way, thousands of billions [of beings], each accompanied by a multitude as numerous as motes of dust, come together to my presence.
It further says: "If a person receives the Buddha's precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas; being equal in rank to Great Enlightenment, they are truly children of the Buddhas.
Because this constitutes the nature-precepts (prakṛti-śīla), it is the True Vehicle; this is indeed the Great [Vehicle]."
The mind reveals the nature of the Dharmakāya and its precepts instantaneously to sentient beings; those of inferior capacity receive the gradual teaching.
Thus, through these two approaches for the two types of faculties, thousands of billions of beings—each as numerous as motes of dust—are individually received and all come together to my presence.

Clearly abandoning the provisional to embrace the real constitutes the teaching of the truly existent; because this teaching within the [Lotus] Sūtra instantaneously reveals both the provisional and the real, it is not the same as the Hīnayāna.
Taking the preceding [teaching] as impermanent and the subsequent as also impermanent, it serves merely to cause birth among humans and devas;

nevertheless, it establishes the doctrine of real existence, which differs from what is taught by Vairocana in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. According to this sūtra, the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) comes to its own original body only after having transformed those to be converted according to their respective capacities.
In contrast, the school of the Perfect Teaching (Eṇkyō) immediately reveals the original body all at once.
In this Dharma-realm, the great wisdom of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) manifests both cause and effect, as well as principle and phenomena, simultaneously.
Furthermore, the dimensions of the worlds described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* differ from the measurements of the lotus flowers in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*;
their breadth and narrowness are entirely distinct, as will be explained in detail below.
Third, regarding the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā, which takes the elucidation of emptiness to reveal reality as its primary tenet:

when the Tathāgata first taught the vehicles of the two *yānas* for ordinary beings among humans and devas, those beings were attached to both phenomena and principle as being real and were unable to leave behind their obscurations;
therefore, he taught the doctrine of emptiness to shatter what they were attached to. Thus, within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, eighteen kinds of emptiness are taught for the sake of the world.
The Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, the three periods of time, and all else are entirely empty; emptiness itself is also empty, as explained at length in the sūtras.

This means that ignorance, the various obstacles, and the karma thereof are all emptied away. When ignorance is completely exhausted, obstacles and karma are found to have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and nirvāṇa naturally manifests.
This is true existence and is not called the "School of Emptiness" (*śūnyavāda*); nevertheless, it is [regarded as] true existence.
The teaching gates explained therein often involve arising and ceasing, and thus cannot yet be considered perfect.
In contrast, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* fully manifests the marks and signs of retribution and adornment, being able to be both empty and real.

Within its own sections and chapters, ten times ten bodhisattvas and others interlace their respective characteristics, such that the principles of emptiness and existence do not proceed in isolation. Furthermore, through universality...
Worthy Mañjuśrī, the upper and lower realms interpenetrate, principle and phenomena mutually penetrate, and they reflect one another.

Throughout this entire scripture, each chapter penetrates the others and every phrase interlinks with the rest. Within a single chapter, the forty chapters of the sutra are all contained within a single word;
when the hundred thousand verses are unified, the one is formed, and when the one is dissolved, all is dissolved into the one.
All things are destroyed because their nature is equal, their time is equal, and their activity is equal; therefore, as with these various forms of equality, the teaching of the Dharma is also equal.
Because of such equality, one attains Buddhahood now in the same way as the Buddhas of the three periods of time attain Buddhahood.

This is because there are no three periods of time and because there is no time. It is not like that other teaching, which posits distinct times for formation and destruction, and thus establishes a sequence of cause and effect.

Therefore, the fourth [treatise], the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, is for those who hold the position that it is neither empty nor existent; after the Tathāgata had taught the doctrine of existence and the doctrine of emptiness,
he taught this single division of the scripture as the synthesis of the two views of existence and non-existence, establishing it as "not empty."
Regarding the absence of [intrinsic] existence, it is taught that the nine consciousnesses are pure and undefiled consciousnesses, like a torrential stream from which many waves arise;
for just as those waves depend upon water, the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses all depend upon the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
Thus, just as those waves depend upon water, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*: "It is like..."
If the conditions for the arising of a single reflection appear before a well-polished mirror surface, only one reflection arises;

if the conditions for two or many reflections appear, many reflections arise. Yet this mirror surface does not transform into those reflections, nor can any undergoing, ceasing, or exhaustion be perceived therein.
This clarifies that the ninth pure consciousness is the support for the five, six, seven, and eight consciousnesses.
It is also said that although such a bodhisattva relies upon and is established by means of the wisdom of the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*),
the intent of this sutra is to clarify that within the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), the essence of consciousness is fundamentally nothing other than true wisdom.
This is like waves arising from a torrential stream without ever departing from the substance of water, or like a clear mirror depending upon its own pure substance.
Being free from conceptual discrimination, it contains manifold images; while not obstructing existence, it is eternally non-existent.

Thus, the marks of consciousness manifested by one’s own mind do not depart from the fundamental essence. These image-marks manifested by the non-constructive, pure wisdom are entirely devoid of attachment to self and other, internal and external, and so forth.
Functioning in accordance with wisdom, they are without conceptual discrimination, thereby destroying the fetters of both existence and emptiness.
Because it is neither empty nor existent, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states in verse: "The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle;
Containing all seeds, it is like a torrential stream. I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self.

Regarding the phrase "the ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle," this draws those ordinary beings toward the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti*), which is not the same [as their current state].
The two vehicles and the Bodhisattvas who have newly begun their gradual training differ from ordinary beings in that they have destroyed marks and realized emptiness;

yet, because they are still bound by reality, they differ from [the ultimate state] and thus it is not empty and not non-existent. What dharma is not empty? It is wisdom, which can accord with conditions to illuminate capacities and benefit sentient beings.
What dharma is not existent? It is that when wisdom correctly accords with conditions, there are no intrinsic natures or characteristics. Therefore, it is non-existent.
Because it involves arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is for this reason called "not empty.
Although this sutra is thus, it causes one to know that emptiness and existence are non-dual within the sphere of mind-consciousness; however, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this.
It merely manifests the original body, the fundamental wisdom of the single reality of the Dharma-realm—the essence and function of the Buddha—thereby merging true nature with its characteristics.
The ocean of the Dharma-recompense is directly revealed for those of the highest faculties as the Buddha-fruit;

taking the single true Dharma-realm of original wisdom as the gate for opening, showing, awakening, and entering, it does not concern itself with the dharmas such as consciousness that arise following delusion.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra appears in the world to show and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s wisdom, enabling them to attain purity.

Therefore, [the Buddha] does not permit those of other vehicles—whether two or three, or the persons of the three vehicles—to know or understand the Dharma of the characteristics of the Buddha-nature.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The various meanings of natures and characteristics, I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know these matters; Śāriputra, pratyekabuddhas, and those who have attained non-retrogression..."

Bodhisattvas are entirely unable to know this, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* brings together those who study the provisional teachings of the three vehicles to return to the true Dharma-realm of the Buddha-vehicle.
Thus, while the "three chariots" before the gate represent the acceptance of provisional vehicles, the "white ox on the open ground" clarifies the virtue of the ultimate reality.
For this reason, there is a partial correspondence between the meaning and intent herein and that of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The dragon girl is the very vehicle—the white ox-vehicle—upon which she rides, and she has attained the same realization as Sudhana;

therefore, the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* directly reveals the fundamental essence through the gate of the Dharmadhātu Buddha-fruit, directly bestowing it upon ordinary beings of superior faculties to enable their awakening and entry.
This is unlike the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, which establishes [the stages] as five, six, seven, eight, or nine.
The provisional gate of the designation of consciousness, as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, provisionally establishes the ninth ādāna-vijñāna;

there are different approaches for those of the two vehicles who have long been weary of birth and death, cultivating emptiness to extinguish consciousness and directly proceeding toward empty quiescence.
Furthermore, at the second turning, the teachings such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* were spoken in order to turn back those of the two vehicles and to guide the bodhisattvas who learn gradually.
It is frequently taught that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) refutes existence (*bhāva*), taking the six *pāramitās* as the vehicle for practice.

Within this, although those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) may slightly turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna and gradually study as Bodhisattvas, their delight in emptiness increases and excels. For those provisional Bodhisattvas, this serves as an initial door of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa-mukha*).
It is only slightly similar to the initial door of counteractive treatment of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), differing in only one respect.
This stage involves the further development of compassion and the superior realization of principles such as the dharmakāya, buddha-nature, and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*),
yet it takes the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its vehicle and the six *pāramitās* as its formal practice. Initially, it employs remedial gates similar to those of the two vehicles—
such as the contemplations on impermanence, impurity, white bones, and atoms— before entering the contemplation of emptiness, which is identical to that of the two vehicles.

The Bodhisattva who has entered cessation retains his birth through the contemplations of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, thereby subduing the notions of self and phenomena so that they do not increase.

Since the primordial state is not yet the Dharmakāya, the Buddha-nature, or the fundamental wisdom—because his vision is not yet truly authentic—he takes pleasure in emptiness and increases its cultivation.
For this reason, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* skillfully establishes the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as distinct entities external [to the six].

The teaching that the nine consciousnesses constitute the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*)—referring to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses because they take the pure consciousness as their support—is not yet directly stated to be the eighth seed-consciousness as the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is because those disciples fear the accumulation of suffering;
if it were said that the seeds of karma are eternally true, they would be terrified and find it difficult to believe. Therefore, for the time being, this provisional arrangement is established.
The ninth *ādāna-vijñāna* is established as the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) so that the nature of consciousness may not be extinguished and may grow into great enlightenment.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Even while not yet possessing the Buddha-dharmas, one does not extinguish sensation (*vedanā*) nor does one realize [nirvana] through grasping.
Since sensation is not extinguished, perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so. This is taught directly for those whose faculties are matured, as in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The seeds of karma of the eighth consciousness constitute the *tathāgatagarbha*, as will be further clarified below. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The category of afflictions (*kleśa*) is the seed of the Tathāgata," and so forth. Now, among those who cultivate the path, there are diverse types and distinct approaches;
their understandings and practices differ in a thousand ways and myriad variations. Apart from the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), there are four different grades within the Bodhisattva vehicle.
1. Bodhisattvas who cultivate emptiness and non-self; 2. Bodhisattvas who gradually perceive the Buddha-nature; 3. Bodhisattvas who suddenly perceive the Buddha-nature;

4. Bodhisattvas who, by means of the Tathāgata’s intrinsically pure wisdom, employ the preparatory practices of the five stages to give rise to differentiated wisdom, fulfill the conduct of Samantabhadra, and perfect great compassion—ultimately remaining within the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
This briefly indicates the names and categories of the gates to the fruit of Buddhahood throughout the ten directions; these will be explained in detail below as taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

There is a class of bodhisattvas who, even after practicing the six *pāramitās* for hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of kalpas, do not give birth into the family of the Buddhas and are thus called "bodhisattvas by designation.
A comprehensive discussion of this appears in the text below, based on the fact that although they see the Buddhas...
One whose nature has not yet been manifested and whose intellectual activities are still merely nominal is called a "provisional bodhisattva.

As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which takes the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness as its core tenets—that sūtra was preached by the Tathāgata on Mount Laṅkā in the Southern Sea; he descended from this mountain and passed through Rāvaṇa’s palace.
That Yakṣa King and the Bodhisattva Maitreya, riding upon a flower palace, came to invite the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma on this mountain.
This mountain is steep and lofty; looking down from it, one sees the great ocean, and it has no gates or entrances.

Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are able to ascend; thus it symbolizes that the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground can only be ascended by those who possess neither cultivation nor realization.

Furthermore, looking down upon the great ocean symbolizes that the ocean of the mind is fundamentally pure from the beginning; yet, driven by the winds of external objects, the waves of consciousness surge and fluctuate.

To clarify that when one penetrates the nature of objects, the ocean of the mind is naturally still, and when both mind and objects are quiescent, there is nothing that is not illuminated—just as when there is no wind over the great ocean, the sun, moon, and the constellations appear with brilliant clarity—such is the intended meaning of that sutra.

This is because it is taught directly for Bodhisattvas whose faculties are matured, so that they may suddenly realize that the seed-consciousness and karmic consciousness are the Tathāgatagarbha—thereby distinguishing them from those of the Two Vehicles who extinguish consciousness and tend toward quiescence; and also because it is taught to distinguish them from Bodhisattvas practicing Prajñā who delight in emptiness and increase their attachment to it.
Thus, by directly clarifying that the essential nature of consciousness is entirely true, it immediately becomes the function of wisdom, just as in that [preceding] case.
When the great ocean is windless, its reflections become even clearer; the dharma-gate of the ocean-like mind is likewise so.

Upon realizing the truth, consciousness becomes wisdom. This sutra differs from the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* in its distinct establishment of nine consciousnesses, which serves to guide those of initial capacity by gradually causing them to retain their afflictions to grow toward great bodhi, rather than allowing their minds to plant seeds in emptiness.
One must not allow the mind to become like a rotten seed. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* serves as the initial gateway for entering into the delusions;
the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* directly reveal the fundamental reality of those delusions.

The *Laṅkāvatāra* clarifies that the eight consciousnesses are the Tathāgatagarbha, while the *Vimalakīrti* contemplates the true mark of the body, noting that the contemplation of the Buddha is likewise so. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* are largely identical.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* differs slightly from these two [other] sections; it is not like the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The Buddha-body and its spheres of activity (*viṣaya*) are vastly different in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It is taught that the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* was spoken by the Nirmāṇakāya;
its sphere of activity is a mountain peak within an impure land (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*), and the dharma-gate taught there concerns the sphere of consciousness (*vijñāna-viṣaya*).

Regarding the true dialogue, Mahāmati Bodhisattva is the primary figure; the manifested transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) clarifies the teaching as a provisional means, while the Great Wisdom (mahāprajñā) discusses the discernment [of reality] according to the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The Buddha-body is the fundamental reality of the Dharma-recompense (*dharmasambhoga*) realm;
the dwelling place is the Flower Treasury World (*puṣpasaṃbhava*); and the dharma-gate is the Dharmadhātu of the Buddha-fruit. Thus, the dialogue proceeds with the Dharmadhātu as its gateway.
This is precisely the wondrous function of the wisdom of principle and phenomena of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;

it is the mutual fusion of cause and effect within the five stages of practice, wherein the ten lands and ten bodies are thoroughly penetrated and mutually enter one another. As for discussing their identity or difference, they cannot yet be fully described here and must await further detailed exposition according to the stages in the subsequent text.

Sixth, regarding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which takes the inconceivable as its central theme: there are ten points of distinction between the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Avataṃsaka*, while one point is identical.

First, the distinction in the adornment of the pure land; second, the distinction between the various marks of the Buddha-body and the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) versus the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body);

third, the distinction between inconceivable virtues and supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); fourth, the distinction in the dharma-gates established according to the faculties of beings; fifth, the various... [text fragment ends]
1. The assembly that gathered to hear the Dharma is distinct; 2. The establishment of the teaching and the arrangement of the Dharma-gates are distinct;

3. The construction of the practice by the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti is distinct; 4. The locations where the Dharma-gates were expounded are distinct; 5. The retinues of those who constantly followed the Buddha are distinct; 6.
The entrustment of the Dharma-treasury and its circulation are distinct. First, the Dharma-gate of the expedient means for entering the Path is largely the same.
First, regarding the distinctions in the adornments of the pure lands: as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*,
when the Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe, the trichiliocosm was adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels,
such that the great assembly marveled at it, just like the Land Adorned with Immeasurable Merit-Jewels of the Buddha Ratnavyūha.
It was unprecedented that they all saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers,

yet had not yet spoken of such matters as the infinite adornments of Buddha-fields within a single mote of dust, as described in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the realm of the ten Buddhas,
Vairocana, and each of the ten Lotus Treasury World-Oceans, wherein every world-ocean contains the infinite.

The oceans of worlds are layered and mutually inclusive; within a single atom, there are inexhaustible oceans of worlds, wherein the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the realms of sentient beings interpenetrate one another without obstruction.
Adorned with myriad jewels, they are like light and like shadows, as extensively described in the sutras—not merely referring solely to the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
Regarding the distinctions between the marks of the two Buddha-bodies—the *saṃbhoga-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya*—which adorn and purify the realms:
it is said that this *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* was spoken by a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

As for the Buddha who speaks the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he possesses ninety-seven marks of a Great Man, as well as [marks] equal in number to the atoms within the oceans of the ten Flower Treasury World-Systems (*daśa-puṣpa-garbha-loka-dhātu-samudra-paramāṇurajaḥ-samāna*).

These are the marks of the true recompense as taught by the Tathāgata. Regarding the distinctions among the three inconceivable virtues and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
a Bodhisattva’s supernormal power can place the high and vast Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed;
it can take the waters of the four great oceans and enter them into a single pore; and within a small room, it can accommodate thirty-two thousand [beings].
Each of the thousand lion thrones was eighty-four thousand yojanas high;

with eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and a hundred thousand devas and humans, Vimalakīrti placed the entire assembly upon the palm of his right hand and carried them to the Āmra garden.
Furthermore, with his hand, he severed and brought the Buddha-land of Abhirati from the eastern quarter to this world.

Manifesting such supernatural transformations as sending [the assembly] back to their original places before the great multitude, he displayed these matters for the sake of the provisional practitioners—the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles.

Why is this? Because for the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, whose realization of the Path is not yet ultimate and who have not yet extinguished the distinction between self and other, all manifested supernatural transformations appear according to what is perceived by their respective faculties.
The distinctions of coming and going, as well as their measures and limits, are for the time being a manifestation of the Sage’s intention;

by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he transforms and gives rise to those of lesser faculties so that they may gradually progress. This is not due to the power of the natural law (*dharmatā*);

thus, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, because the nature of phenomena is such through the power of the fundamental reality (*dharmatā-bala*), one is able to contain the ten directions within a single atom.
All Buddha-fields and sentient-being fields are entirely contained within a single mote of dust; the world is not small, nor is the mote of dust large.
This is likewise true for every single mote of dust throughout all the worlds of the ten directions, just as it is described in the sutras:
that a Bodhisattva may attain equal and perfect enlightenment within the body of a single small sentient being and extensively deliver all beings.
One should know that small sentient beings, being ignorant and unaware, perceive the Buddha through provisional teachings because he guides those of inferior faculties;

thus they see the Buddha outside themselves and observe his manifestation of supernatural powers as coming and going. However, within the teaching of ultimate reality, by means of one's own original enlightenment, one awakens to the fundamental mind, wherein the nature and characteristics of body and mind are no different from those of the Buddha, and there are no views of internal or external, nor of coming and going.
Therefore, although the Buddha Vairocana does not move from his original place, his body sits pervasively in all places of practice;

and although the assemblies gathered from the ten directions do not move from their original places, they follow the transformations as they go. Thus, there is neither coming nor going, nor is it brought about by supernatural power.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because such is the nature of the Dharma. In the Sūtra, it is frequently stated that [this occurs] "by the supernatural power of the Buddha."
As for the power of the Dharma being thus: by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Buddha is extolled as supreme because the Dharma is thus;
yet when one extols his fundamental virtues, there is no transformation whatsoever. In every buddha-field, the body, mind, nature, and characteristics rely upon the source and do not follow delusion;
thus, all environments—whether large or small—are like light and like shadows, mutually reflecting and penetrating one another, pervading everywhere.

Throughout the ten directions, there is ultimately no coming or going, and no boundaries whatsoever; thus, within every single sentient being’s body and all its pores, the ten directions are fully pervaded.
This differs from the provisional teachings, which employ supernatural powers to divide space, come and go, and carry things back and forth, thereby giving rise to such false perceptions.
These actions contravene the fundamental Dharma-body, obstructing true Bodhi and the wisdom of original enlightenment.

Therefore, after the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti had manifested these supernatural transformations, he proceeded to expound the teaching of ultimate reality. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Contemplate the true mark of the body;
contemplate the Buddha in the same way. I contemplate the Tathāgata as not coming from the past, not going to the future, and not abiding in the present.
This is explained in detail in the "Akṣobhyavyūha" chapter. Therefore, those who delight in the provisional teachings and limited views [should turn toward this].

If one desires to attract Bodhisattvas of inferior capacity through extraordinary means, one should employ coarse, provisional teachings to guide them and inspire a joyful inclination toward study before imparting the gateway of ultimate reality.

One must not mistake these transformative expedients for the truth, for this would perpetually obscure the eye of wisdom. By recognizing the provisional as leading toward the real, one enters the gateway of the Dharma-realm;
yet, conditioned dharmas are difficult to perfect, and while non-action follows conditions, there is no agent to accomplish it—thus, the labor of an agent is in vain.

Merit is not contrived, but is spontaneously accomplished through following conditions; this is the merit of non-merit. Merit is not wasted; this is the merit of having merit. Yet all such merit is impermanent;
though accumulated through cultivation over many kalpas, it ultimately ends in decay and ruin.

It is not as good as the single thought-moment of the arising of non-arising through conditions, which transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles and the dualistic views of those four types of practitioners. As for the various Dharma gates established according to individual capacities: [the text continues with the description of these].
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra addresses those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) faculties, causing them to turn their merit toward Bodhi and enter the Mahāyāna;
furthermore, it addresses those within the Mahāyāna who are stalled in the realm of purity—Bodhisattvas whose compassion and wisdom are not yet perfected—urging them to advance in their practice.

This is illustrated by the assembly of Bodhisattvas from the World of Universal Fragrance who, desiring to return to their own land, requested the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to grant them a small portion of the Dharma.

The Tathāgata, observing through his faculties that those bodhisattvas were lingering in the Pure Land with inferior resolve regarding compassion and wisdom, preached the Dharma for them to train in the gates of liberation concerning the finite and the infinite. As the subsequent passage states:

"Without departing from great kindness and without abandoning great compassion, they deeply give rise to the mind of omniscience and do not neglect it; they teach and transform sentient beings, never becoming weary."
One should not grow weary of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), but constantly mindfully practice them in accordance with the teachings.

One should regard all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as if they were hell, and view the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as if it were a pleasure garden. Upon seeing those who come seeking help, one should regard them as a virtuous teacher. This is explained in detail in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.

That sūtra addresses those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and the three vehicles (*bodhisattva*) whose compassion and wisdom are not yet perfected, instructing them to gradually cultivate and increase their compassion.
Wisdom does not immediately and suddenly reveal the Buddha-gate; it does not immediately declare that those at the initial stage of the Ten Abidings have already attained perfect enlightenment;
nor does it immediately display its vast and wondrous matters, for all things possess their respective limits and gradations.

Fifth, as for the various assemblies who come to hear the Dharma and are distinguished from one another, they are like the assemblies present in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, with the exception of Mañjuśrī and Maitreya.

The assembly of great bodhisattvas such as Śāriputra, along with the shadow-like śrāvakas and other external guests, constitutes the entire assembly of those who follow the provisional teachings within the three vehicles.

Among them, even those bodhisattvas born in various realms of existence who have come together as companions all desire to perfect the provisional studies of the three vehicles, gradually causing them to progress until they reach fulfillment. This has not yet been fully explained.
The fundamental vehicle of all Buddhas is as described in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra: all those who have gathered here are riding the Tathāgata-vehicle.
Possessing the fruit-virtues of Buddha-wisdom, their own essence is the Dharmakāya, which fully embodies the practices of Samantabhadra.

They manifest as reflections throughout the ocean of lands in the ten directions at all sites of enlightenment, returning to perfect the original Dharma ridden by the Tathāgatas; there is not a single one among them who belongs to the three vehicles.
Regarding the capacities of sentient beings, there are those of the three vehicles; yet they are like the blind and the deaf—ignorant and unaware.
They are like a blind person facing the sun and moon, or a deaf person listening to celestial music.

They are like a person impoverished by karma encountering a treasury of heavenly jewels, or like one of great merit dwelling in hell, or like a hungry ghost standing on the shore of the great ocean. III.
For those who have not yet exhausted the power of the vehicle’s path and have not yet turned their minds, they constantly dwell within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, the sphere of all Buddhas;

sharing the same virtues and the same bodies as the Buddhas, they ultimately cannot believe, being unaware and unknowing, and thus seek a vision of the Buddha elsewhere, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas..."
Even if one has practiced the six pāramitās throughout other kalpas and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
if one has not heard this Dharma-door of the inconceivable qualities of the Tathāgata— or even if one has heard it at some time, yet does not believe,
understand, comply with, or enter into it— one cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because such a person is unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.
One should know that the assembly hearing the Dharma here is entirely distinct from the assembly in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
