The inhabitants of this Sahā world have not yet transcended their dualistic attachments, whereas the followers in the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyuha) realm remain fully within the dichotomy of defilement and purity. One should know that such types as these have not yet attained true insight;

though they maintain the purity of a single direction and are called "bodhisattvas," their realization of the Path is not yet perfected. Such individuals do not yet possess comprehensive understanding.
Although the Buddha’s mind possesses the aspiration for Bodhi, his will remains attached to dwelling in a pure land;

thus, he is far removed from the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body. Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra states that even those non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, cannot know [the Buddha].
This is just as in the Avataṃsaka-sūtra, where the assembly’s own bodies and the Buddha’s body are without distinction.

The distinctness of individual wisdom and the non-differentiation from the Buddha-wisdom; the nature and characteristics containing one another; the unity and multiplicity, the same and the different, all residing within the ocean of the Dharma-realm;

manifesting as the waters of wisdom that show themselves as fish and dragons; dwelling in the great mansion of Nirvana; appearing as yin and yang to transform sentient beings; the freedom of principal and attendant;
their mutual reflection and interpenetration; the merging of teacher and disciple; and the thorough penetration of cause and effect—all these are [the manifestations of this reality].
Regarding such a multitude, there are six ways in which the teachings are established and the dharma-gates distinguished.

Specifically, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* employs the householder Vimalakīrti to manifest a small measure of inconceivable supernatural transformations (*abhijñā-vikurvaṇa*) to cause those of the two vehicles to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].

Furthermore, while dwelling within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), he manifests physical illness to make known that defilement and purity are non-dual. Moreover, it represents the greatness of the Bodhisattva.
The *Baijing pusa* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) fully expounds the gate of non-duality and establishes the contemplation of samādhi and prajñā;
because its application of wisdom clarifies the most essential dharma of non-seeking, it says: "Those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek among all dharmas.

However, it does not yet resemble the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which fully expounds the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the similarities and differences in the aspects, causes, and effects of the five stages and six stages:
the name "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti) indicates that he manifested entry into birth-and-death out of great compassion, displaying the conduct of illness;
whereas in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Vairocana manifests entry into birth-and-death through great compassion to display the conduct of attaining perfect enlightenment, thereby manifesting great wisdom.
Regarding the distinctions in the locations where the eight Dharma-gates were expounded for the sake of transcending the world:
the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* was taught in the Āmra Garden at Vaiśālī and in the chamber of Vimalakīrti;
the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was taught in the Bodhimanda at Magadha, as well as in all worlds and within all atoms; and the *Navama-nityānubaddha-sūtra* [was taught] following the Buddha.
Regarding the distinction between the assemblies: when the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* was preached, the Śrāvakas were the assembly that constantly followed the Buddha, numbering only five hundred.
When the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was preached, the assembly consisted entirely of Mahābodhisattvas of the One Vehicle who constantly follow the Buddha;

they number as many as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, and constitute an assembly that fully embodies the essence and function of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī. Thus, there are ten such distinctions.

Regarding the specific transmission for the circulation of the Dharma-treasury entrusted [to others], it is stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, in the chapter on the Entrustment (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), where the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Maitreya, I now entrust to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, which I have accumulated over immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas; therefore, by means of that very..."
Regarding the entrustment of this sutra to those who have already become Bodhisattvas and are born into the family of the Buddha:

in the "Tathāgatotpatti-parivarta" (Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the entrustment for its circulation consists of handing over the Dharma of this very sutra to ordinary beings at the stage of the initial resolve who are just able to perceive the Path and are born into the family of the Buddha. Why is this so? Because this sutra is difficult to enter; it is permitted only for those capable of realizing it.
Because it is through self-realization that one is truly capable of explaining [the teachings], the manifestation of the three vehicles is merely provisional.

This is because all dharmas obtained through the holy ones' exhortation to practice and realization have not yet reached ultimate reality, and all who preach these dharmas have likewise not yet attained reality.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "This treasure of a sūtra does not enter the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the Dharma King, the Tathāgata."
True sons are born into the family of the Tathāgata and plant the seeds of the Tathāgata; those who cultivate all roots of goodness are the sons of the Buddha.
If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. Question:
If one calculates the true sons of the Buddha, they are as inexhaustible and boundless as the worlds of the ten directions; even the atoms within those worlds cannot measure them.
Question: Why need one worry about this sutra if there are no true sons [to uphold it], such that it would simply vanish and perish? Answer:
The intent of this sutra is to entrust it to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), so that they may awaken and enter this Dharma-gate;

it causes them to be born into the Buddha-family and to propagate the teaching so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. Thus, ordinary beings are enabled to enter the realm of reality. If it were entrusted only to those...

For great bodhisattvas and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); for the noble ones (*ārya*), it is self-evident that there are no ordinary beings among those who train.
If within the path of an ordinary being the seed of the Buddha (*buddha-gotra*) were severed, this sutra would perish;

for this reason, [the Buddha] entrusts it to ordinary beings to practice, rather than to those great bodhisattvas of former times who have already entered the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). This is because their skillful means for entering the path are identical.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "One who seeks the Dharma should have no seeking toward any phenomena;

even contemplating the true mark of the body, one contemplates the Buddha in the same way. I contemplate the Tathāgata as not coming from the past, not going to the future, and currently having no abiding.
Such passages constitute the initial gateways of contemplative wisdom, which are roughly identical to the entry points for the practice of entering the Path.
The sequential rules and procedures are entirely distinct and extensive, as explained in detail below.

Regarding the seventh point—that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* takes the integration of the provisional into the real as its central tenet—this scripture leads those of the three capacities to return to the true teaching of the One Vehicle;
it draws together all streams to return to the great ocean and gathers the three branches back into the source.

The Dharma Master Enzō and other former great virtuous ones maintained that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* constitutes the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), because it was not taught in common with the Three Vehicles;
whereas they held that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* constitutes the shared teaching of the One Vehicle, because it was heard in common by those of the Three Vehicles.

Examining this principle, one finds that these two approaches are consistent: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* leads those of provisional capacity back to the Truth, while the *Avataṃsaka* [reveals] that very Truth.

The Great Root is shown all at once, yet it is received directly; although the name "One Vehicle" is uniform, the matters of its application are largely the same, while its formal models (vidhi) possess many differences.
Now, wishing to enumerate them exhaustively, the details are too vast to encompass fully; thus, ten categories are briefly presented to provide a framework for understanding.
These ten categories are: first, the distinction of the Teacher; second, the distinction of the emission of light; third, the distinction of the land; fourth... [and so forth].
1. Requesting the Dharma Lord to separately elaborate on the adornments of the five great assemblies; 2. Separately elaborating on the true and manifested bodies within the six introductory sections;
3. Listing the assembly separately; 4. The Dragon Girl transforming her body to become a Buddha separately; 5. The separate location of the land where the Dragon Girl becomes a Buddha; 6.
The six thousand followers separately generating the aspiration for enlightenment; 7. Receiving the distant prediction from the various Śrāvakas separately; 8. The Principal Teacher.
Other teachers say that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was spoken by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha;

furthermore, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who had entered parinirvāṇa in the past, came to testify to and authenticate this sutra, as do all Buddhas of the three periods of time who proclaim it together.
This is not the case with the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, for its presiding teacher is Vairocana himself; as he is the presiding teacher, he is thus the Dharmakāya and Sambhogakāya.
The True Body of Wisdom and Principle is adorned with a body possessing the ocean-like merit of immeasurable marks;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time are of one and the same limit, appearing simultaneously within a single Dharma-realm, their retributive marks layered and profound without obstruction.
Since they are not of the three periods of time, there is one and the same limit throughout past and present: the Buddhas of old are not of the past, and the Buddhas of today do not newly emerge.
Because the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is equal in essence and characteristics, and because principle and phenomena are not distinct, the Original Buddha thus spoke this Dharma;
because the great root is received instantaneously, it is not a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).

Therefore, unlike the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where an ancient Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna appears while the present Buddha emerges to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*, for these reasons he is called the "Teaching Lord" (*śāstṛ*).

Regarding the distinction between the two types of radiating light: although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of emitting light from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*), the realms illuminated by this resultant light are said to be only eighteen thousand lands, all appearing like gold. Thus, they remain limited and do not accord with that which is boundless, immeasurable, and inexhaustible;
consequently, it manifests only the resultant dharma (*phala-dharma*) and does not manifest the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). In contrast, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*...

The table of the teachings, practices, causes, and effects of the various sections of the scriptures reveals that the light of the Dharma is complete from beginning to end; this shall be further clarified later.

Regarding the distinctions between the three lands: when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he transformed the world three times to make it a pure land, moved the devas and humans to other lands, and subsequently established the assembly gathered from other directions within this transformed realm of impurity.
When he causes this Sahā world to become a pure land by preaching the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this very Sahā world is itself the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmakośa-lokadhātu*).
Each and every world mutually contains one another; as the sutra says:
"Each and every world fills the ten directions, and the ten directions enter into one without remainder; worlds neither increase nor decrease, possessing incomparable merit."
Therefore, it is further said that when the Buddhas attain enlightenment within the body of a single small sentient being, they transform immeasurable multitudes therein;
yet that small sentient being neither knows nor perceives this, precisely because ordinary beings and sages share the same essence and possess no shifting characteristics.
Within a speck of dust, self and other are of one essence, which differs from the assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where humans and devas undergo shifting transformations.
The clarification of the pure lands here is intended for those with provisional capacities, who distinguish between self and other and establish such distinctions based on their obstructed views;
therefore, it is now clarified that the buddha-fields are distinct. Fourth, regarding the distinction of the Dharma masters:
at the time of preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Dharma master was Śāriputra, who served as the leader of the exhortation; whereas for the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*...

After some time, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the bodhisattvas according to their respective positions to each expound the Dharma-gate of their own station as the primary teaching of the Dharma.
The Buddha manifested the fruit-dharma, taking the fruit as the cause to give rise to the practice of great compassion;

because the essence of the fruit of fundamental wisdom is spontaneously accomplished, there is nothing that is not spoken through speechlessness. This is because the practice of great compassion proceeds from the root of non-action.
Because fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) arises, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the stage of the cause; they teach the dharmas of the Buddha-fruit to awaken sentient beings.

The *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* consists of worldly numerical dharmas that are vast and immeasurable; only the Buddha reaches their ultimate limit, for they do not belong to the causal or resultant gates within the five stages.
Therefore, these are internal dharmagates of the Buddha’s own station, spoken by the Buddha himself in accordance with [the capacity of beings].

The "Chapter on the Merit of Excellent Radiance" (*Svābhāvikakāya-hetu-phala-svayam-bhūta*) is a dharma-gate in which the Tathāgata himself subsequently explains the power of the *dharmatā* of the Buddha-dharma—the constant radiance of merit and wisdom—which does not belong to the characteristics or causes and effects within the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*).
Therefore, the Buddha himself also explained this to clarify that there are no two delusions (*moha*) in the fruit of Buddhahood. Excluding [these], [the remaining]...
Aside from these two chapters, all the remaining thirty-eight chapters are dharma-gates concerning the aspects of practice within the five stages;

therefore, the Buddha did not speak them himself, but instead had the bodhisattvas within their respective stages—such as those of the ten faiths, ten abidings, and ten practices—speak for themselves, while the Buddha merely emitted light to symbolize them. As for the light he emitted to symbolize the Dharma:
These matters shall be explained in detail later. When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is preached, there are no śrāvakas or small-scale bodhisattvas acting as the masters who request the Dharma;
rather, it is the great bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood who mutually question and answer one another to establish the characteristics of the practices of the Buddha-fruit dharmas.
This is for the sake of those with great faculties, so that they may directly receive the Buddha-fruit all at once.
The cause is the cause because it takes the fruit as its cause; the effect is the effect because it takes the cause as its effect.

This can be seen by contemplating various seeds through the power of concentration and wisdom. Therefore, what is now stated regarding the request for the Dharma Master to separately adorn the five great assemblies with true and manifested forms is as follows:
it is like the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, which purifies and adorns the trichiliocosm.
The various transformed assemblies are also strictly adorned and completely fill [the space]; all the Buddhas who come likewise declare these to be transformations.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this; rather, it possesses ten locations and ten assemblies where the multitudes completely fill the ten directions without shifting from their original places, yet they pervade the Dharma-realm.
Each individual physical form, every pore of the body, and the lands and realms are layered upon one another, containing within them Bodhisattvas and Buddhas.
Bodies interpenetrate one another, and beings of diverse classes are likewise entirely unimpeded; bodies and lands interpenetrate like shadows containing one another.
The assembly that gathers does not destroy the Dharma-body, yet it conforms to the marks and signs;

the Dharma-body and its marks and signs are of a single limit without distinction—form itself is the complete reality, for there is no transformation. This differs from other teachings which speak of transformation and speak of reality as distinct.

Because there are instances where they are gathered together, the present mention of a "great assembly" (mahāparṣad) distinguishes it from those cases. Among the six introductory sections (*nidāna*), the specific enumeration of the assembly is as follows:
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly, first the assembly of śrāvakas is listed, numbering twelve thousand people;
next, Mahāprajāpatī with her retinue of six thousand people is listed—these are the six thousand [nuns] who were her maternal aunt.
Next, Yaśodharā Bhikṣuṇī is listed; she was the wife of the Buddha when he was a prince.
When the Buddha was a prince, he had three wives: the first was named Gopī, the second Yaśodharā, and the third Manorathā.
Gopī represents the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), of the Bodhisattva Sudhana.

Because the joy of the Dharma of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is capable of bestowing compassion, it serves as the benefit for sentient beings through the Dharma; the joy of the Dharma that gladdens body and mind is the meaning of "wife.
Next, the eighty thousand bodhisattvas are listed together; next, the various devas, nāgas, ghosts, and so forth are listed.
However, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this: it first lists the chief bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, without mentioning [the others].
Following the attendants arranged in succession, after the assembly of Vajrapāṇi deities, there are fifty-five categories of various classes of deities,
nāgas, and devas; each category has its own distinct following, with each following consisting of as many members as there are atoms in a Buddha-world,
or some followings are simply said to be immeasurable— this applies generally to the first assembly.

The assembly at the site of enlightenment consists of fifty-five groups; these shall be further clarified in the subsequent discussion of the general meaning regarding the assemblies of the ten sessions.
As for the ocean-like assembly of Buddha-bodies within the boundless *dharmadhātu*, each and every body contains all others in a manifold manner without limit.
A single body takes the entire *dharmadhātu* as its measure, encompassing the realms of both self and others.
When the entire dharma-realm perishes, it is one's own body that pervades everywhere; the emotional attachments and dualistic views of subject and object are severed. To speak of this briefly:
after the listing of the assemblies in these ten sessions, it shall be further clarified. From the first session through the eighth, the name "śrāvaka" is never heard;
it is only within the ninth session that the three groups of bhikṣus first appear, and their specific characteristics are explained upon reaching that stage.

Regarding the specific case of the seven dragon girls transforming their bodies to become Buddhas, as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*, they transformed from female bodies and perfected the practices of a Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood in the southern region within a single kṣaṇa. This is not the case in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

rather, it simply requires that one be free from deluded views so that great wisdom becomes ever more luminous, whereby the essence of the myriad dharmas is realized as true and devoid of transformation.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Śāriputra said to the goddess, "For what reason do you not transform this female body?
The goddess replied to Śāriputra, "For twelve years I have sought the mark of a woman and could not find it at all;
how then could I transform anything? It is as the daughter of Aṇḍhika said to Śāriputra: 'From the birth of a son, I became a daughter.'"
Knowing that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is inherently thus, what is there to be transformed? As described in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
in the section concerning the spiritual friends of the youth Sudhana, each of the fifty-three individuals— including Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, monks, nuns,
elders, youths, laywomen, maidens, sages, and non-Buddhists— possesses their own distinct qualities.
The Bodhisattva’s practice inherently possesses the Buddha-dharma; according to the various sentient beings who perceive his body differently, he does not say that there is any transformation.
If one observes with the Dharma-eye, nothing mundane is not true; if one observes with the worldly flesh-eye, nothing true is not mundane.

By means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, for those of the three capacities who have not yet exhausted their views regarding the provisional teachings, it causes them to establish the seeds of faith. And so forth.
By swiftly transforming this female form into Buddhahood and causing such a marvelous event to arise, one only then awakens the mind and proceeds toward true knowledge and vision;
unable to abide in their original dharma, they give rise to roots of goodness. This clarifies that, for the time being, the three provisional means are led back to the single reality;
furthermore, it shatters the fixed attachment to kalpas and the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, so that one may realize, in a single instant, the original nature of the three periods of time.

The single limit, being without beginning or end, is called the equality of the Dharma; it tears asunder the net of views of the three vehicles and dismantles the thatched huts of the bodhisattvas, causing them to return to the gate of the Dharma-realm and enter the true abode of the Buddha.

Thus, the dragon girl’s attainment of Buddhahood clearly demonstrates that it does not require long cultivation over past eons, as her age is but eight years; furthermore, it signifies that even now, one need not rely on old learning to undergo transformation.
The female stage does not exceed a single kṣaṇa; one fully accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood without a hair’s breadth of deficiency.
The Dharma-nature is thus: its own essence is timeless, yet through provisional learning, the three faculties create separation for themselves.

Deluded regarding the reality of phenomena, they conversely claim it is a transformation, unaware that their own fundamental essence is such as this. Remaining entirely within the house, they still harbor lingering views—how can this be?
Pointing far beyond the boundaries of the world, the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* declares that this view does not depart from concentration;

yet it remains at odds with the ultimate, and only when the view is discarded can one return to the original dwelling. How could it be otherwise now? To extinguish the karma of various views merely brings about the toil and hardship of many kalpas before one finally turns back.

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies in its "Gate of the Dharmadhātu’s Dependent Origination," although the single reality of ordinary beings and sages exists, a separation persists as long as views remain.

In this very state, when ordinary sentiments vanish, one is called a Buddha; arising in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), whether bowing or rising, advancing or retreating, contracting or extending, or practicing humility and reverence—all are the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
There is not a single dharma that possesses a characteristic subject to transformation, nor is there anything characterized by birth, abiding, or cessation.

Therefore, this is not the same as the Dragon Girl’s transformation of her body to become a Buddha. As for the distinction regarding the land where the eight dragon girls became Buddhas, it is as follows: [The text continues with the description of that specific buddha-field.]

Regarding the statement that the "Stainless World" (Amala-loka) lies in the south and is not this Sahā world: the commentary explains that because the mind has attained arhatship (*arhat*), it is called "stainless" (*amala*);
because it correctly accords with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), it is designated as the south.

Since north represents correctness, and since south represents illumination and emptiness—furthermore, among the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*), the trigram *Li* corresponds to the mind, and the mind is empty and non-substantial.

Thus, it is clear that this remains based on the supplementary directions of the secular Eight Trigrams (Ba Gua). Although those directions lack the specific name of the "Eight Trigrams," their method is one and the same.
Therefore, while the principle is thus, since there is principle, there must also be phenomena; consequently, there must still be a nation to which the multitude can turn for refuge.
If one dwells elsewhere in the south, then self and others, as well as this side and that side, would remain separated.

This is because [the teaching] follows the three vehicles to gradually guide those with provisional capacities toward faith and understanding, so that they may eventually return to the Buddha-vehicle;

thus, it is for the sake of the three vehicles. Furthermore, because the force of remaining attachments is difficult to destroy, and because there are still those who have partially turned their minds but whose feelings of self and other are not yet severed, this is not the same as the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, where self and other are mutually penetrating in every single atom and each instant penetrates the essence of the Dharma-realm.
Because this is the gateway of Indra’s Net dwelling within the realm of dust,

it is now said that the lands inhabited by the nine thousand six hundred distinct assemblies who have separately resolved their minds are as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*: when the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood,
the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas of the Sahā world all saw from afar the Dragon Girl attain Buddhahood and universally benefit [all beings].
At that time, the assembly of devas and humans were greatly delighted in heart by this teaching of the Dharma and all paid them remote homage.

Furthermore, in the Sahā world below, three thousand sentient beings dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, and three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Jñatikauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly silently accepted this with faith.
Although the Bodhisattva Zhiji (Jñānākara) turned back Śāriputra to act as a wise man, he remained within the current of delusion to benefit and enlighten the ignorant;
thus he was dispatched to provide instruction and practice for the sake of ordinary learners, establishing a standard for them to follow.

Since the multitude in this Sahā world all pay remote homage, these six thousand who have resolved their minds are not yet extinguished, yet they merely conform to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Because one has not yet attained the Bodhi of the universal gate of the Dharma-realm— the primordial awakening in which self and others are of one essence—
for this reason, there is a prostration from afar. This is not the case for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
which is the realm of the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Treasury-body and the Universal Vision Dharma-gate, adorned with the Indrāla-jāla (Indra’s net).
The swirling ocean-seas of the Dharma-gates are simultaneously realized as a single, wondrous wisdom;

because this is the realization of all through one realization and the severance of all through one severance, within one's own body there exist the oceans of Buddha-lands adorned by the ten bodies of the Buddhas.
Within the body of the Buddha, the phenomena of the worlds of the ten directions are hiddenly manifest within the realm of one's own body, layer upon layer.
It is just as when many streams flow toward the great ocean: although they have not yet entered the sea, their moistening nature does not differ;
once they enter the great ocean, they all share the same salty taste. All sentient beings are also like this.
Though there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, the Buddha-ocean from which they originally arise is fundamentally no different. How is it stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
The assembly of this Sahā world pays distant homage; the ritual procedures for these matters differ entirely from those in the *Avataṃsaka*.

For instance, within the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, the six thousand members of the assembly have their ten eyes suddenly become more luminous, five hundred youths realize the ten bodies in a single lifetime, and all the other members of the assembly do likewise.
When Sudhana travels south to seek his spiritual friends, he attains the fruit of Buddhahood.

Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, having already perfected [their realization], re-enter the oceanic whirlpools of Samantabhadra’s body; in this gateway of universal penetration, principle and phenomena are fully present and co-extensive, such that there is no dharma that is not manifested.
Since the Dharma-realm is situated within every dust mote, how could there be any distance for which to offer prostrations?

Therefore, it is now said that among the assembly of six thousand, those who have resolved their minds are distinguished from the ten [bodhisattvas], and that the Śrāvakas receive distant predictions of their future enlightenment.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, although the dragon girl was suddenly sealed within the timeless gateway of the Dharma-realm, fully manifesting the fruit of Buddhahood, those of the three vehicles who follow provisional teachings—despite possessing a mind of faith and compliance—have not yet discarded their lingering habits;

they cannot realize it instantaneously, but must ascend [to enlightenment] only after many kalpas, and thus receive a distant prediction. This differs from the *Avataṃsaka*, where delusion is precisely the state of being an ordinary person, and awakening is the state of being a Buddha.
If this Buddha were to have any remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he would employ his Buddha-knowledge and insight (*jñāna-darśana*) to treat them;

were it not for this Buddha-knowledge and insight, they could only be suppressed (*vinīta*) but would not enter the swift current of the Buddha’s stream, requiring many distant kalpas before entry is possible.
This is because those at the initial stage of the Three Vehicles have inferior faculties of faith (*śraddhendriya*), and thus cannot escape the many entanglements of their fetters and cages.

Those who are attached to birth and death, though seeking transcendence, possess inferior faculties and remain stagnant or regress. Therefore, the Tathāgata employs such contemplations as those of birth,
old age, sickness, death, impermanence, impurity, and momentary destruction— wherein things do not abide even for a single thought-moment—
to cause them to observe these truths, engender revulsion, and through that revulsion, achieve a state of mind that dwells equally amidst both the pure and the defiled.

Within the teachings of transformation, for the sake of those with such faculties, although the Tathāgata exhorts them to cultivate compassion and wisdom in order to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he nevertheless points to the Pure Land as being located in another direction.
This is because the discriminative views of those of the three vehicles have not yet been extinguished;
seeing this Sahā world as perpetually defiled, he speaks of the cause and the fruit to shatter their doubts and temporarily transforms it into a pure land.
Withdrawing his supernormal powers, he returned to the impure realm; for the seals of the Three Vehicles' teachings have their own explicit texts.

Thus, through this contemplation of impermanence, the habitual tendencies of the intellect are difficult to turn back. Although the Dragon Girl was suddenly shown the Buddha-vehicle, despite her faith she could not immediately realize it.
For this reason, those who received predictions within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly all received the Dharma of distant kalpas.
Fahua gradually led [the teachings] back to the Avataṃsaka; at that time, he directly transmitted [the teaching that] one who resolves their mind [to attain enlightenment] is immediately a Buddha.
For this reason, the modes of practice differ. Within this single division of the scripture, there are two gates: the One Vehicle and the Tathāgata Vehicle.
The direct path to the site of enlightenment is the Tathāgata Vehicle, which is precisely the One Vehicle, as in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra (Xianshou).
The chapter states: "Among all the various classes of sentient beings in the world, those who seek the Śrāvaka vehicle are few;
those who seek the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are even fewer; and those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare.

Yet, while it is still relatively easy for those who seek the Mahāyāna to do so, it is exceedingly difficult to have faith in this Dharma. Furthermore, a sutra says: "If there are sentient beings whose minds are weary and submerged..."

For them, he teaches the path of the śrāvaka to bring about liberation from all suffering. Furthermore, for those sentient beings whose minds possess a slight degree of clarity and acuity, he teaches the Dharma of causes and conditions so that they may attain the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, for those sentient beings who delight in training in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion to extensively benefit other beings, he teaches the path of the bodhisattva. Furthermore, for those sentient beings who are resolute...
Delighting in great matters, he turns the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma to expound the path of the One Vehicle;

this is the meaning of the division into four vehicles within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Just as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the three carriages before the gate merely demonstrate the provisional gate, whereas the white ox in the open field clarifies the true teaching.
In the Buddha-vehicle, there is only one, neither two nor three. Nor are there two or three.
The provisional teachings outside the gate clearly reveal the reality of the open-air teaching;

while the four vehicles are brought into accord, the two teachings share a common purpose, yet their ritual manifestations (*vyavahāra*) each have their own distinctions. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Only this one fact is real; the other two are not true. Based on this single passage, it appears that three vehicles are established; however, when considering their ultimate accord, they actually constitute four.
That "the Dharma is solely this one reality" refers to the reality of the Buddha-vehicle; the other two refer to the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, which encompasses both Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
Since these latter two share a similar aversion to suffering, they serve as a model for one another and can clearly reflect each other like two dragons.
In a single kṣaṇa, the two dragon girls sealed the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the nature [of enlightenment] proceeds from the ordinary person to the sage without shifting even a hair’s breadth;
this is roughly identical to the Dharma-gate of entering the Way through understanding and practice as exemplified by the youth Sudhana.

That Sudhana attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime does not depart from the limit of a single kṣaṇa, wherein he realized the nature of the three periods of time as entirely equal throughout past and present; this is likewise identical to the Dragon Girl’s transformation of her body in a single kṣaṇa.
The practice of attaining Buddhahood is completed all at once; everything is designated according to the fundamental Dharma, for such is the nature of the Dharma.

As for the establishment of "aeons" (*kalpa*), this is merely the conceptual dust of sentient beings' minds. When Sudhana realizes this, it is called "one lifetime," because when the aeons of the three periods of time have already been exhausted, what further birth could there be?
Therefore, it is called "one lifetime. All other provisional arrangements of ten different types are as previously described.

The discussion on the transformation of the dragon girl’s body and the non-transformation of Sudhana—wherein there is a difference in terms of "transforming" versus "not transforming"—is hereby concluded.

[Commentary]: The eighth, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, takes the protection of the True Dharma as its primary theme because this sūtra is established within the "Jewel Enclosure" (*ratnavyūha*) in the realm of desire, situated below the form realm, to assemble all humans and devas from both the upper and lower realms.
The devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, and the eight classes of spirits—including nāgas—as well as the bodhisattvas from other directions, all gathered at the Jewel Monastery.
Among the various spirits, there were some who did not go; the Four Heavenly Kings pursued them with glowing iron wheels, compelling them to proceed to the Buddha’s presence.
There, the Tathāgata commanded that they all protect the True Dharma. Among the Māra kings, there was only one...
A certain Māra did not obey the Buddha’s command, vowing that he would only give rise to the bodhicitta once all sentient beings had attained Buddhahood.
(The text below this point is suspected of being incomplete.)
Regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which takes the Buddha-nature as its central tenet, there are ten points of distinction from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

These ten points of distinction are as follows: first, the difference in the location where the teaching was given; second, the difference in the adornments of the realm and the transformation-retribution bodies;

third, the difference in the assemblies of those who gathered for the great congregations; fourth, the difference in the wheel of Dharma established; fifth, the difference in the multitudes who came [to hear the teaching].
1. The distinction between hearing the Dharma; 2. The distinction between the pure and impure lands of retribution; 3. The distinction between the provisional and real aspects of the Buddha-body;

4. The distinction between the rules for birth and nirvana; 5. The distinction between the modes of instruction and practice; 6. The distinction between acting as a friend and a model from the very beginning.
Regarding the first point: it is like the grass called "fatty" found on the Snowy Mountains; if a cow eats it, she obtains only *sarpis* (clarified butter).
There is no distinction of color—such as blue, yellow, red, white, or black—in the location where the Dharma is taught;

however, it is said that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was taught between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Āriravati River in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, whereas the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught at the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha, beneath the precious Bodhi tree. Thus it is spoken.
Regarding the distinctions within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), there are two types: the adornment of the objective field and the transformation of retribution.
As it is said, when this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was being taught, the auspicious and blessed site of the twin *śāla* trees measured thirty-two *yojanas* in length and breadth;
the great assembly filled its entirety without any empty space. At that time, boundless multitudes of bodhisattvas from the four directions, together with their retinues...
The place where he sat was as small as the point of a needle or the tip of an awl;
yet, from the ten directions, great bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-worlds as vast as those atoms all gathered there. Furthermore, the text states:
"At that time, by the Buddha's spiritual power, the ground of this trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple, with no hills or ravines remaining."
The sand, soil, pebbles, stones, thorns, and poisonous weeds were adorned with various jewels, just like the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha Amitāyus in the western quarter.

This entire great assembly saw all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as motes of dust—as clearly as one sees one's own reflection in a bright mirror; their vision of these Buddha-lands was likewise so. Furthermore, below...

The twin *śāla* trees suddenly turned white, as extensively described in the sūtras. As it is said regarding the time when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached, there were ten lotus-treasury world-oceans;

furthermore, within the twenty tiers from top to bottom, in the very lowest tier, it is briefly stated that there are as many vast lands as there are atoms in a Buddha-world, and within each of these surrounding lands, there are ten Buddhas.
There are as many minor kingdoms as there are atoms in a buddha-field serving as its retinue, each increasing tenfold over the preceding one.

Thus, within this Lotus Treasury World, the ground is made of vajra, and the trees, terraces, towers, pavilions, halls, ponds, and oceans are all adorned with various jewels, just as described in the sutra.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Magadha.
In the land of Aranya-dharma at the site of enlightenment, he first attained perfect awakening;
its ground was firm, composed of vajra, adorned with exquisite jewel wheels and various precious flowers, and beautified by pure maṇi gems.
Thus, the infinite oceans of all forms and appearances were manifested, continuing downward until reaching the inconceivable [splendors] of all buddha-fields.

The discussion regarding all the adornments contained within the kalpa, which have been manifested and revealed over the course of the two middle pages of this scripture, is an extolling of all the adornments of the Buddha’s realm.

Furthermore, the detailed exposition of these very adornments in the subsequent "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" (*Huazang shijie pin*) constitutes the adornment of the Tathāgata’s own body through his true retribution; it is not like this [worldly] [adornment].
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, by means of the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he temporarily transforms [the assembly] to make it pure for the sake of sentient beings.
The reason for this is that the assembly gathered for this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* consists of a mixture of the various faculties of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

If it were not sustained by the Buddha’s supernormal power, there would be no way for them to see [the truth] on their own. This is unlike the *Avataṃsaka*, where the faculties of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) are pure and the assembly is without admixture.
Because the śrāvakas differ in their faculties, they originally do not see [the Buddha] within the assembly;

although this is so according to the sūtras, there are still instances where, through the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), as mentioned later in the text regarding "the power of the Dharma being thus," the term "supernormal" (*shen*) refers to the *arhat* (one who has attained truth), and is not identical to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
It is by temporarily enabling them to see that it is termed "supernormal. One should know that this is like the lotus flower.
The adornments of the treasury, the fundamental clarity, the true recompense, and the nirvana of supernatural power are but temporary, provisional manifestations.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* infers that the Buddha’s pure land lies to the west, beyond thirty-two lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and not in this location;
thus, it is clearly known that this is a transformation and not a reality. Therefore, the assemblies gathered for the three great convocations...
Others say that all those gathered for this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* consist of the multitudes of the human and celestial lineages of the three vehicles;
with the exception of the great bodhisattvas, all the rest have come because they remember the Tathāgata,
their eyes filled with tears as they carry fragrant firewood, lamenting in bitter sorrow and longing to serve the Buddha-sun— all such as these are [the assembly].
The assembly that has gathered here is precisely that which is worthy of hearing of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
with the exception of those bodhisattvas of the Single Vehicle who have entered the Buddha-wisdom and similar groups, all others are to be understood by this same principle.

As for the assembly that has come from afar as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, they are entirely bodhisattvas within the fruit-stage of Buddhahood inside the ocean of nature-wisdom; they are purely of the Single Vehicle, and there are no other types of persons.
The assembly of devas all shared the same root as they entered the stream of the Buddha’s wisdom and became endowed with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Within this first assembly, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, all born from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness.
This "ocean of roots of goodness" is precisely the ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; it is that which gives birth to all things through great wisdom.
The Buddha takes the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body as his root; all that arises from it is otherwise entirely comprised of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

These various practices, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until entry into the ocean of Buddha-wisdom, are provisionally categorized according to their shallow or deep stages of cultivation across the six positions:
the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten bhūmis, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

The distinctions between the characteristics [of these assemblies] are as follows: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* assembly includes the three vehicles and collectively gathers the seeds of goodness of humans and devas;
yet those of the three vehicles in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* assembly do not partake in that gathering, and even if they were within the assembly, they would be like the deaf who do not hear.
One should know that the assembly of the three vehicles—bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, humans, and devas—in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is not the same as that of the *Avataṃsaka*.
This refers to the assembly of Bodhisattvas within the stage of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Those who, from their initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), rank equal to the Buddha’s stage, enter the stream of the Buddha’s wisdom, and share the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, are true sons of the Buddha.

Fourth, regarding the distinctions between the principal and the attendant in the turning of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) established therein: at the beginning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s exhortation, it is Kāśyapa Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrī.
The Bodhisattvas Siṃhanāda and Śāriputra were the leaders who requested the establishment of the Dharma as a standard;
Māra Pāpīyān was the one who requested the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa;
and those who were the leaders in establishing the Dharma in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* were Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Bodhiruci, Dharmamati, Guṇakara, Vajradhvaja, and Vajramati.
Because the ten peaks, ten wisdoms, ten forests, ten banners, and ten treasuries— such as those in the *Guhyagarbha* and other tantras—
are established by great bodhisattvas within the state of the Buddha’s fruition as the dharma-gate of the five stages of the Buddha’s fruition;

and because these stages are themselves the Buddha and the Buddha is himself these stages, it is clear that the Buddha’s fruition is present within each stage, just as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Establishing the Dharma protocols through question and answer, all these Bodhisattvas are the assembly of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions and this land;
they have all penetrated the true source of the divine and their wisdom is equal to the Dharma-realm.

They manifest throughout the ten directions—coming without coming and going without going—and are designated as such according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), not due to any actual movement of coming or going, even within a single atom.
Thereupon, infinite clouds of bodies manifest within a single pore inconceivable oceans of marks; this is so throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the Dharma-realm.
In every place, they suddenly appear without coming from anywhere, and suddenly vanish without going anywhere.
At all places and at all times, within the bodies, forms, and spheres of experience of sentient beings, [they are thus manifested].
Mountains, rivers, great oceans, and the empty space of the ten directions manifest forms and images with sovereign mastery over existence and non-existence, in infinite and ever-receding layers;

all such beings are the assembly of great Bodhisattvas. Therefore, they differ from the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa and the Śrāvaka Śāriputra in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, who were born into human families and manifested the status of ordinary beings to guide those of the Three Vehicles.
Those of such dispositions, seeing the Buddha enter nirvāṇa, were moved by grief so that tears flowed down to fill their eyes; they came together for this assembly.

Among those gathered who heard the Dharma, there were those distinguished as śrāvakas, followers of the two vehicles, and provisional-vehicle bodhisattvas who practice various contemplative exercises (*vipaśyanā*) yet have not abandoned the obstacles of attachment, who delight in and cling to all conditioned activities, and who grasp at the characteristics of those activities. This *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* [was taught] for them.
Regarding these modes of activity, those who are deluded do not realize that the Dharma-body is without action, without realization, and without cultivation, being the primordial self-nature itself.

Because they establish the realization of enlightenment and nirvana through the duality of subject and object—claiming that it arises through practice and cultivation, or is manifested through cultivation—the Tathāgata, for the sake of such individuals, has taught in this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased..."

That which has already been stilled and extinguished is bliss; yet the wholesome practices one performs and that which can realize bodhi are phenomena subject to arising, while the nirvāṇa realized is a phenomenon subject to cessation. Since the mind thus dwells upon the duality of subject and object, and the processes of arising and ceasing do not cease, one becomes obstructed by the true principle because these processes of arising and ceasing do not cease. Therefore, within this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and that which can realize [them]— [The remainder of the passage continues: —are all empty and non-existent. Because they are empty and non-existent, they are ultimately ungraspable. Because they are ungraspable, they are called "nirvāṇa. This is why the Tathāgata speaks of the "Great Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflection, like a city of the gandharvas, and like a transformed body. Because they are like illusions and so forth, they are ultimately ungraspable. Because they are ungraspable, they are called "nirvāṇa. This is why the Tathāgata speaks of the "Great Nirvāṇa. For this reason, the Tathāgata conceals his body and does not appear, and when all subject and object—the mind—is exhausted, it is called Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*). In the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles, there may still be a subject [of realization].
All that is cultivated and realized is therefore called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*);
because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is devoid of subject and object. Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Cunda said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"Do not say that the Tathāgata is the same as conditioned phenomena. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī spoke thus because he knew [the truth].
To speak without knowing is to say that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
If one were to say that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena, then one could not say that he is the Sovereign Dharma King among humans and devas within the triple world.
Therefore, the Mahāparinirvāṇa enables those of the three vehicles to know that all conditioned phenomena are bodhi, and that what is realized and what realizes it are nirvāṇa.
All that arises is impermanent; that which was originally non-existent does not undergo cessation. To have no practice and no cultivation is called Great Nirvāṇa;

this is called Perfect Quiescence (Parinirvāṇa). Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* causes those of the three vehicles who delight in attachment to practice to abandon such practice and cultivation, so that they may realize that there is nothing to be realized through practice and nothing to be cultivated. This is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha’s land of recompense (*vipākabhūmi*) is indicated as being located to the west, beyond lands equal in number to the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers;

this is the land of recompense of Śākyamuni for those of the three vehicles who study through provisional means, whose defilement and purity have not yet been extinguished, and who perceive this Sahā world as foul, evil, and impure.
Consequently, the Tathāgata provisionally points to this land of recompense as being in the west. This is distinct from the *Avataṃsaka*’s teaching of ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
This Dharma-gate reveals that this Sahā world is pure and stainless, and that the worlds of the ten directions are pure and flawless;
for in the case of Bodhisattvas of the definitive teaching, both defilement and purity are exhausted, and thus their sphere of experience is purely clean.

However, because Bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching perceive impurity even in places that are naturally free from defilement and purity, it is indicated that the Land of Reward is located in the West, where the bodies of the seven Buddhas are provisional.
Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real: as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks are provisional, whereas the true reality of parinirvāṇa is real.

In reality, principle and phenomena are non-dual; without destroying the *dharmakāya*, one follows the ocean of marks, which is infinite and inexhaustible.
Thus, mark is identical to nature, retribution is identical to principle, and it is like light and its shadow—sovereign and unimpeded.

Moreover, within this sutra, apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, there are three types of Bodhisattva vehicles which encompass those two vehicles.
For the sake of the five vehicles, including humans and devas, the five precepts and ten wholesome actions are taken together to constitute six and seven vehicles.
