The Monk Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou, Tang Dynasty, Compiled the Sūtras and Combined the Treatises.
[Treatise] Second: Clarifying the Distinctions Based on the Teachings and the Vehicles. Now, the Great Awakened One appeared in the world, manifesting true wisdom and sovereign mastery.

His Dharma-body is boundless and equalizes all classes of beings by sharing its same essence. Adapting to the capacities of vessels, he manifests forms and bestows teachings in accordance with their faculties. As it is said:
An echo in an empty valley arises when struck and forms sound; the valley’s resonance is without intention and has no fixed location, yet it responds universally according to conditions.
The Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings is likewise so: by conforming to one's own faculties and conditions, one obtains the Dharma of one's own mind;
as these faculties expand, one brings them to maturity. He demonstrates the principle of impermanence to establish his teaching in response to beings.
When the sick are given medicine, the illness is cured and the medicine is discarded in a single thought-moment; yet the rain of immeasurable Dharma falls, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
As the manifested form-body appears, the Dharma is inexhaustible and the teachings of the various schools are endless. Without beginning or end, it is fully equipped for all faculties;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings, there are distinctions of their own respective stages. Thus, for example, the teaching of Vairocana is without beginning.
Being without end, his nature is without direction, without interruption, and without cessation;

according to the capacities and types of beings, he manifests birth in a womb, renunciation of the world, and the preaching of the Dharma from beginning to end, including his entry into quiescent *nirvāṇa*. Yet, in reality, the Tathāgata has never been thus.
Indeed, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also states: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, an immeasurable number of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed."
Because the perfect wisdom of the ocean of nature makes a single thought-moment identical to immeasurable kalpas, how could such perfect wisdom have before or after?
This sutra says that by entering the samādhi of the limit of the kṣaṇa, one manifests initial birth and nirvana.
Furthermore, as in this sutra, the son of the Tuṣita Heaven was already at the third birth and the tenth stage, yet even in his second birth above, he still followed [the path] from evil.

While on the way, he was graced by a light that illuminated his body; he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven and attained the Samādhi of Leaving the City, whereby he beheld the Tathāgata dwelling upon the ground of vajra-jewels, manifesting as a great Bodhisattva who had just entered his mother’s womb in Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra states: "When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa and the great fires consuming all, my land..."
Regarding the distinction between the earlier and later teachings of the Peaceful and Secure [School], there is none;

rather, they are established according to the practices and teachings of the ten ancient masters, which are both identical and distinct within a single period. These may be taken as models, and the rest may be understood by analogy.
First, Bodhiruci of the Later Wei established the "Single-Sound Teaching" (*ekasvara-dharma*). Second, Paramārtha Tripiṭaka Master of the Chen Dynasty...
Third, Guangtong Lushi of the Northern Wei established the theory of two simultaneous teachings;
fourth, Dayan Fashi of the Qi dynasty established the theory of four types of teachings; fifth, Hushen Fashi established the theory of five types of teachings;
sixth, during the Chen dynasty, Master Sengzhi of Mount Nanyue, Zhiyi, and others established the theory of four simultaneous teachings.
Seventh, Dharma Master Wonhyo of Silla in the East Sea during the Tang Dynasty composed a commentary on this sutra and established four teachings;
eighth, Dharma Master Jizang of the Tang Dynasty established three types of teachings; ninth, Dharma Master Yun of Guangzhai Temple during the Liang Dynasty established four teachings;
tenth, Dharma Master Yin of Jiangnan during the Tang Dynasty established two teachings.
First, regarding the theory established by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei Dynasty concerning the "Single-Sound Teaching" (*ekasvara-dharma*):

this asserts that all sacred teachings are exclusively the Tathāgata’s single, perfect sound-teaching (*ekasvara-dharma*). It is only because [beings] differ according to their faculties (*indriya*) that various distinctions arise.

As the sutras state regarding the moisture provided by a single rain, and as the scripture says: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single sound, yet sentient beings each receive it according to their own kind."
Regarding the second point, Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Chen Dynasty, established two teachings: first, the gradual, and second, the sudden.
The gradual teaching refers to that which is established for Bodhisattvas of gradual awakening, who primarily arise from the Small Vehicle;

it possesses the teachings of the Three Vehicles and includes such sūtras as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. As for the sudden teaching, it refers to that which is established for those of direct, sudden capacity, who do not arise from the Small Vehicle.
Only the Bodhisattva Vehicle is so called; thus it is named "Sudden," which refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The Great Master Huiyuan also held this same view.
Third, during the Later Wei dynasty, the Vinaya Master Guangtong, following the teachings of the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhatāra, established three types of teaching:
first, the Gradual; second, the Sudden; and third, the Perfect. Regarding the intent of Master Guang’s explanation: for those whose faculties are matured...
First, within a single dharma, all dharmas are fully expounded—teachings such as permanence and impermanence, emptiness and non-emptiness, and so forth;
because everything is taught completely without further gradual stages, it is called "Sudden.
Second, for those of superior capacity who partially accord with the Buddha’s realm, it explains the Tathāgata’s liberation, unimpededness, and the ultimate, perfected fruit-virtue.
Because it is the Dharma-gate of the Sovereign Secret, it is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which is established above the two previous teachings as the fourth teaching.
During the Qi dynasty, Master Dayan established four teachings: first, the Teaching of Causes and Conditions (*yinyuanjiao*), referring to the Sarvāstivāda and other Hinayana schools;
second, the Teaching of Provisional Names (*jiamingjiao*), referring to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the Sautrāntika school; third, the [Teaching of] Reality... [text fragment].
The "Real Teaching" (*shijiao*) refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, which explain the principle of emptiness and clarify that all things are unreal, and so forth.

The "True Doctrine Teaching" (*zhendaojiao*) refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the principle of the true nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the establishment of the five teachings by the Fifth Dharma Master Hushen:
within the aforementioned four teachings, he takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) as the "True Teaching," namely the *Nirvāṇa*.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the teaching on the fifth dharma-realm; that is, it elucidates the gate of the sovereign and unimpeded dharma-realm.
This is the sixth [point]. During the Southern Qi dynasty, Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue, Master Zhiyi, and others established the Fourfold Teaching:
first, the Tripiṭaka Teaching, also called the Hīnayāna Teaching, as the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "One must not associate with those of the Hīnayāna."
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, scholars of the Tripiṭaka maintain that the Hīnayāna constitutes the Tripiṭaka while the Mahāyāna constitutes the Mahāyāna-piṭaka.

These two names refer to the "Shared Teaching" (*sāmānya-dharma*) and are also called the "Gradual Teaching. This means that within the Mahāyāna sūtras, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are universally expounded, and the three faculties (*trividha-indriya*) are fully provided for.

Furthermore, in the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, stages such as the "Dry Wisdom Stage" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) are common to all three vehicles; these are the three names [of this teaching].

The Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) is also called the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*); this refers to those Dharma-gates and principles taught in the Mahāyāna sūtras that do not apply to the Hīnayāna.
Fourth is the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*), also called the Secret Teaching (*mi-mi-jiao*);

it teaches the Dharma-gate of the unimpeded interpenetration wherein the Dharma-realm is sovereign, complete, and perfect—wherein the one is all and all is one. *Huá* (Flower) [is the name of the scripture].

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others are examples of this. Seventh, the Master Wonhyo of Silla (Haidong) in the Tang Dynasty composed a commentary on this sūtra, which also establishes four teachings:
first, the distinct teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the teaching of the Four Truths and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*;
second, the common teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the Prajñā teachings and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; third... [text continues].
The classification of teachings according to the three vehicles is found in such scriptures as the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* (瓔珞經) and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* (梵網經).

The fourth is the complete teaching of the one vehicle (*ekayāna*), such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the teachings of Samantabhadra. Regarding these four, they are explained in detail in the eighth fascicle of that commentary.
During the Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Jizang established three types of teachings: first, the Wheel of the Fundamental Dharma, which is the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

The first teaching, which expounds the two branches and the wheel of the Dharma at its culmination—namely, the equality of the three vehicles—is the "Wheel of the Dharma that Subsumes the Branches into the Root" as taught later.
This refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where forty years after [the initial preaching], the teaching of "turning the three into one" was proclaimed.
Regarding the four teachings established by Master Yun of Guangzhai Temple during the Liang dynasty, it is said that they are as set forth in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The three carts at the gate constitute the Three Vehicles, while the great white ox-cart bestowed upon them in the four-way intersection constitutes the Fourth Vehicle;
this is because the ox-carts at the gate are identical to the sheep and deer carts in that neither can actually be obtained.

Were it otherwise, when the elder led his sons out from within the house, he would have said, "These three carts are located outside the gate," rather than waiting for the sons to emerge before bestowing them.
If one already possesses a carriage upon entering the house, why would one seek out the specific carriage previously pointed out and fail to find it, only to seek it again later?
Therefore, we know that this is a provisional teaching, identical in nature to the [teachings of the] sheep and deer carts.

Because this is a skillful means (*upāya*) taught through the provisional doctrine of the Mahāyāna, a detailed explanation is provided as found in the tenth fascicle of the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) by Yan of the Tang dynasty in Jiangnan.
The Dharma Master establishes two teachings: first, the *Śākyamuni Sūtra* named the "Teaching of Flexibility," because it is taught according to the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings;
second, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the teaching of the ten bodies of Vairocana. That Dharma Master’s establishment of these two teachings briefly comprises four distinctions:
first, the distinction of the principal [teacher], meaning that while the former was spoken by the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) Śākyamuni, this [latter] is [the teaching of] Vairocana.

There are four distinctions regarding this teaching: first, the distinction of the two locations; that is, while the former was taught by the Ten Bodies upon seats of trees and grass in the Sahā world, this sutra is taught in the Lotus Treasury World upon seats of jewel-trees and gold. Second, the distinction of the three assemblies;

that is, while the former was taught to śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, this is taught exclusively to bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage. Third, the distinction of the [audience]... Fourth, the distinction of the teaching... [The text continues with further distinctions].

"Others" refers to those who maintain that this essential treatise was spoken specifically for the eastern region, whereas it is taught universally throughout the ten directions, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The above interpretations by these ten masters all rely on the collection of points of agreement and difference compiled by the Dharma Master Jizang of the present Tang Dynasty;
each represents a distinct school, and all were men of exceptional talent whose wisdom surpassed their contemporaries.
To unify the teachings of the worthy and the sagely and to illuminate the bright lamp of the Buddha-sun, one must not add criticisms of right or wrong to his name.
Rather, one should simply know to look up with reverence at his lofty intent.

Just as the two masters Sengsi and Huizhi have already ascended to the hall, and Master Yuncong spreads the rain of Dharma beneath the Flower Court, awakening to the spirit of Vulture Peak this very evening, his Dharma-eye becomes even more clear as he ascends.
The stage of fruition is attained in this present age, while the Way is equal to that of antiquity.
Just as the Buddha spoke of the "inner," "outer," and "intermediate" [realms], he immediately entered meditative absorption. Subsequently, five hundred arhats each interpreted these words.

After the Buddha emerged from absorption, they all asked the World-Honored One whose interpretation accorded with his own intention. The Buddha said, "None of them accord with my intention. When the people questioned the Buddha further:
"If this does not accord with the Buddha's intent, would it not constitute an offense against the Buddha? The Buddha said:

"Although it is not my own intention, each [teaching] accords with correct principle and is fit to serve as sacred instruction; thus there is merit and no offense. Moreover, what these various virtuous ones have taught each possesses scriptural authority.
Now, in the Tang Dynasty, Master Zang inherited the teachings of Master Yan and served as his disciple; in establishing his system of instruction, he possesses profound reason."
One may also set forth its underlying intent in five stages: first, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teaching; third, the Final teaching; fourth, the Sudden teaching;
and fifth, the Perfect teaching. The first, the Hīnayāna, is easily understood. Regarding the second, the Initial teaching:

according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, this is established as the teaching of the third period, which uniformly maintains that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles will both fail to attain Buddhahood. Now, these [positions] are synthesized as follows:
First, this teaching does not exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma; therefore, it is established as the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Third, the Final Teaching holds that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles who lack the Buddha-nature, as well as the icchantikas, shall all eventually attain Buddhahood;
yet even this does not exhaust the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna, and is thus established as the Final Teaching. However, both of these aforementioned teachings—the Initial and the Final—are...

The gradual teaching consists of progressively cultivating and accomplishing [the path] according to the stages (*bhūmi*), whereas the sudden teaching is established as such because it teaches that the mere non-arising of a single thought-moment is itself called "Buddha," rather than proceeding through the stages sequentially. As stated in the *Sāṃkhyāvikrīḍita-sūtra*:
"One who has attained the true nature of all phenomena does not proceed from one stage to another. And as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: [One who has attained the true nature of all phenomena...]
It is asked: "What is the sequence from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the eighth stage, and even unto the stage of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?

Furthermore, in the 'Chapter on the Ten Stages' below, it is said that the ten stages are like the tracks of birds in the sky; how can any distinction be found? This is explained in detail in such works as the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra*.
Regarding the fivefold perfect teaching (*pañca-pariniṣpanna-yāna*): one stage is all stages, and all stages are one stage.
Because it is a single stage, the fulfillment of the mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-citta*) subsumes the six stages and the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
Based on the *Samantabhadra* Dharma-realm and the infinitely interpenetrating net (*jāla*), where the principal and its attendants are fully present, it is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Master Fazang harmonized these points by citing such scriptures as this; furthermore, Master Śīlabhadra of the Western Regions inherited the lineage of Maitreya from afar.
Asaṅga, Sthiramati, and Nanda, following closely upon his footsteps, established three types of teaching based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other treatises.

They maintain that when the Buddha first taught the Hīnayāna dharma in the Deer Park, although he spoke of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), he had not yet taught the truth of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
therefore, these scriptures, such as the four Āgamas, are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). As for the second period, although it was based on...

Although the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) was explained as the emptiness of all phenomena, the principles of dependent origination (*paratantra*), perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*), and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) had not yet been taught;
therefore, those teachings such as the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras are also not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

It is only during the third period that, in accordance with the correct principles of the Mahāyāna, the three natures, the three absences of nature, and the two truths of consciousness-only were fully expounded.

Now, for the sake of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), one should understand the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other such texts. Furthermore, these three stages each have three meanings: first, the capacity of the audience; second, the teaching spoken;

and third, the principle revealed. Regarding the first stage: it encompasses only the Śrāvakas, teaches only the Hīnayāna, and reveals only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Regarding the second stage:
it encompasses only the Bodhisattvas, teaches only the Mahāyāna, and reveals both types of emptiness (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*). Regarding the third stage: it universally encompasses all [beings].
The "Teaching for Those of Sharp Faculties" (*Tīkṣṇendriya-vinaya*) explains all vehicles and fully reveals both emptiness and existence;

therefore, because the first two [teachings] each lack completeness in their principles for gathering sentient beings, they are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Because the latter teaching gathers all without exception, and because its teachings are complete and its principles are perfect, it is of definitive meaning.
Furthermore, the Master Jñānaprabha inherited the lineage of Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna from afar, and received the transmission of Āryadeva in his immediate vicinity.
Bhāviveka, relying on sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and treatises such as the *Madhyamaka*, also establishes three teachings:

first, at the Deer Park, for those of inferior faculties, the Buddha taught the Hīnayāna, clarifying that both mind and objects exist; second, during the middle period, for those of middling faculties, he taught the Mahāyāna of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), clarifying the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) in which objects are empty while the mind exists; [this was] because of their faculties...
Because they were still inferior and had not yet been able to fully enter the equal and true emptiness, this teaching was given.
During the third period, for those of superior faculties, the signless Mahāyāna was taught, elucidating that both mind and objects are empty, equal, and of one flavor as the definitive meaning.
Furthermore, these three periods may also be explained through three meanings; first, regarding the inclusion of beginners: during the first period, only [those of such capacity] were included.

1. Regarding the capacities of beings (*pudgala-yāna*), the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles; this is because this school maintains that one portion of those in the two vehicles does not proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood.

3. Regarding the [capacities] of Bodhisattvas alone, they encompass both the gradual and sudden approaches, for all those in the two vehicles ultimately proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood and have no other path.
2. Regarding the teachings (*śāsana*): first, the Small Vehicle is taught; second, the common [teachings] are taught; third, [the Mahayana].
Regarding the subsequent exposition of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in three stages as a means of revealing the principle:

first, in order to refute the spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*) of non-Buddhists, it is taught that phenomena produced through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) are definitively real. Second, in order to gradually refute the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), those who cling to the reality of conditioned production are taught that these very conditioned phenomena are merely conventional existents (*prajñaptisat*), because they are terrified of this ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and thus still maintain the notion of conventional existence.

As for the method of guiding [beings], it is taught that at a later time, within the ultimate Mahāyāna, this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself the equality of the single flavor of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which does not obstruct the two truths.

Therefore, the "Dharma-characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) Mahāyāna, with its notion of "attainment" and so forth, belongs to the second teaching and is not the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This sequence of the three teachings is as explained by the Master Jñānaprabha.

It is said that this is the tradition of the Western Land (India); in establishing their teachings, each school has its own path, all of which expound the sacred doctrine within their respective regions.
I respectfully reflect upon these lofty principles and cannot presume to judge them all at once.

However, having personally investigated the profound mysteries of the sacred teachings, I have used my limited perspective to describe my thoughts and present them to future scholars. Based on the essential tenets of these teachings, I shall briefly establish ten [points].
The general purport of the teachings throughout the beginning and end of the Buddha’s appearance in the world consists of ten stages. What are these ten?

First, during the initial period, he taught the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) of purely affirmative doctrine (*sattvavāda*). Second, during the second period, he taught the Prajñāpāramitā, which refutes existence and clarifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Third, during the third period, he taught the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, which reconciles emptiness and existence to clarify the doctrine of neither non-emptiness nor non-existence. Fourth, during the fourth period...

The fifth period: preaching the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which clarifies the teaching that the provisional is identical to the real; the sixth period: preaching the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, which clarifies the teaching that the conventional is eternally real;
the seventh period: preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which clarifies the teaching of drawing back the provisional to return to the real; the eighth period:
preaching the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which causes those of the three vehicles to abandon the provisional and turn toward the real; [the ninth period: preaching the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In a single instant, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* comprehensively encompasses the ten periods of time in their perfect fusion, without beginning, end, before, or after.
It universally includes the ninth teaching, the "Common and Uncommon," and the tenth teaching, the "Uncommon and Common.

Regarding the first period, the teaching of the Small Vehicle that exclusively affirms existence, it was taught for the sake of ordinary beings who are bound by and attached to worldly phenomena, regarding them as truly existent. Following [their capacities]...
The dust of form (rūpa) gives rise to various unwholesome states; because of these unwholesome states, one falls into the realms of suffering.

Consequently, one must again take the Dharma as a bridle for that mind, using precepts to guard and restrain all that is unwholesome. Therefore, it is called "purely consisting of formal instruction" (vijñapti).

Within the Hīnayāna, it is further taught that there is also the nature of non-manifestation (avijñapti), moral discipline (śīla), and so forth, which generally pervade its essence; however, these are applied according to the capacities of individual faculties and their specific circumstances.
It is the same as with the Bodhisattva precepts. As the sutra says: "If a person receives the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.

This is also discussed in terms of the *dharmatā-śīla* (intrinsic precepts). Furthermore, it says: "In this way, thousands of billions [of emanations] each lead hosts as numerous as motes of dust, all coming together to my presence.

This means that first, through the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), they transform and guide those in the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) stage; subsequently, they cause them to return [to the ultimate source].

Regarding the Dharmakāya and the true reward-body (*vipākaphala-kāya*), for those of superior faculties, the phenomena and principle of the Dharmakāya serve as the basis simultaneously because they are the fundamental ground.
At the second stage, the teaching of Prajñā—which refutes existence and clarifies emptiness—is taught;

since it explains the substantial existence of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) to establish a model and discipline the body, speech, and mind so that one may abide in wholesome dharmas, it first teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) before proceeding further.

The teaching of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) breaks their attachments and gradually leads toward the *dharmakāya*; this is the third period, in which the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* was taught as a synthesis of the teachings on emptiness and existence.
This serves to reconcile the preceding two teachings of emptiness and existence so that those with extremist views do not remain stuck in the gates of either emptiness or existence.
It is the teaching of neither non-emptiness nor existence, intended for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who have extinguished consciousness.

Realizing quiescence and abiding in quiescence, one is free from [discursive] cognition; for the sake of turning away from that, the ninth *ādāna-vijñāna* is provisionally taught as the "purely immaculate consciousness.
The five, six, seven, and eight consciousnesses always rely upon this ninth consciousness as their support.

Ordinary fools, failing to understand this, falsely grasp it as a self, just as the torrential flow of water does not exist apart from the substance of water itself, nor do the waves exist apart from the water.

Because the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses always rely upon the pure consciousness (amalavijñāna) as their support—just as water serves as the support for waves—the mind of the two vehicles is gradually turned back, and they realize that these consciousnesses are perfected as wisdom. Why are nine consciousnesses established as the pure consciousness?

It is because those of the two vehicles have long harbored fear toward the seeds of karma within the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses throughout saṃsāra; [the ninth consciousness is established] lest they find it difficult to overcome such fears.

Trusting in skillful means within the cycle of birth and death, one establishes a pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) distinct from the seeds [of the other consciousnesses], gradually drawing it forth with the intention of causing delusions to remain unextinguished, so that compassion and wisdom may gradually arise. As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"In this way, although these bodhisattvas rely on the abiding of phenomena, they take wisdom as their support to gradually cause the view of emptiness to reach the point where consciousness is transformed into wisdom."
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, spoken during the fourth period, describes the teaching that the conventional is itself the ultimate.

As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states directly for those with the capacity of the Mahāyāna roots: it teaches that the eighth consciousness, the seed-consciousness of karma, is named the *tathāgatagarbha*-consciousness.

Furthermore, it says: "That which apprehends characteristics is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not apprehend characteristics is called wisdom (*jñāna*). Moreover, the sūtra speaks of the *ālayavijñāna*.

The ocean, though abiding in its own realm, is moved by the wind; likewise, this sutra directly addresses the seeds of karma from ignorance through the gateway of clear wisdom, clarifying that the nature of clarity and ignorance is non-dual. The *Awakening of Faith* also teaches this.

Although this teaching explains that the seeds of karma from ignorance are perfected as wisdom, it is still rare for one to transcend the mundane, as they have not yet manifested the state of being free from entanglements. This is the fifth explanation.
Regarding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it clarifies that the teaching which reveals the eternal truth within the conventional is the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*.
This is because within this sūtra, the śrāvakas of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles are not regarded as those who truly know the Dharma.
Consequently, the ten great disciples remained silent at Vaiśālī, and Maitreya and Prabhāvyūha ceased their eloquent discourse at the Dharma assembly; this sūtra thus refutes what preceded it.
Among the four types of teachings, for Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas whose defilement and purity have not yet been integrated, there is a constant aspiration to transcend the mundane;

thus, by manifesting in the body of a layperson through the "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti), he clarifies that the mundane is itself the eternal reality, thereby subverting the notion of a fixed pure appearance.

Because they constantly harbor the duality of defilement and purity, it is said that the "body of existence" (*satkāya*) constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata, and ignorance and craving constitute the lineage, so as to cause those of the three vehicles to... [attain realization].
When the mind of various pure marks has perished, one leaves the mundane and enters the entanglements; it is only when there is equality and non-obstruction that one clearly realizes true virtue.
Because there is a real school, it manifests the retribution of the Pure Land, such as the land manifested when the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe.

For those of the three vehicles whose faculties are inferior, they rely on the Buddha’s spiritual powers and faith to communicate; thus, while the inferior land may vanish, it is not something realized through one's own self-attestation.
Therefore, as for the remaining points, they have already been explained in the previous judgment of the divisions of the teachings within the *Zongmen* (School of Principles).
Consequently, this *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* clarifies the teaching that the conventional is eternally true;

thus, it takes Mañjuśrī as the Dharma-body and Vimalakīrti as the manifestation of conduct while entangled in the world. Taking the Dharma-body as the essence and conduct as the function, this scripture thereby...

The mutual inquiry between essence and function regarding the self-characteristics [of phenomena] is intended for those who delight in the study of the three vehicles, who seek the principle of suchness and emptiness, and who, wearying of the provisional and cultivating the real, require many lifetimes of accumulated practice to achieve Buddhahood; it causes them to return to the Dharma-realm where nature and characteristics, principle and phenomena, and cause and effect are simultaneous.
As for the similarities and differences of this sutra, the classification of teachings and the determination of its school have already been fully explained in the section on the sixth period.
In preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the Buddha] guides those of provisional capacity toward the teaching of ultimate reality:

he explains that for Arhats who accord with emptiness and meet with quiescence, and for Pratyekabuddhas who accord with the twelve links of dependent origination, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. By clarifying that the six sense faculties, consciousness, name-and-form, mind, and objects—these three categories—are by their very nature unborn, he shows that for these two types of persons, both mental consciousness and the karma of the three realms are extinguished.

Furthermore, those who possess wisdom and compassion do not give rise [to such views], as they analyze phenomena to clarify emptiness; using emptiness to destroy delusions, they aspire to be born in a pure land.

Even Bodhisattvas who intentionally retain their afflictions to moisten rebirth do not fully realize that the ignorance and various delusions of all sentient beings arise from the fundamental nature-purity of all Tathāgatas—the universal radiance of wisdom, which is neither center nor periphery.
There are various false views, such as those regarding pure lands and defiled lands, or one’s own Buddha and other Buddhas, involving attachment and aversion that do not accord with ultimate truth.

To lead these three faculties back to fundamental wisdom, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is employed to make known that the nature of ignorance and birth-and-death is fundamentally only the essence of wisdom;
its intrinsic nature is inherently undefiled. It is only that delusion and awakening differ, yet there is no [duality] therein.
The two natures are symbolized by the image of the lotus flower, for they lead those of the three faculties back to their original source. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"The characteristics of the world are clearly seen as eternally abiding, identical and such. This was already explained in the section on the classification of teachings and the differentiation of schools.

Seventh, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was preached, it caused all followers of the three vehicles to abandon the provisional and turn toward the true teaching; this was for the sake of the remaining three vehicles.

In the teachings, in order to censure pride and to address lack of faith, it was said that there are sentient beings without the nature [for Buddhahood] who ultimately will not attain Buddhahood, so as to inspire faith and encourage them to practice.
In this sutra, however, it is clarified that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and are no different from the Buddhas;
it is only because they are shrouded by ignorance that they do not see it. The former [teaching] served as three provisional means.

The final section is the reality; it concerns the cultivation of provisional *tathatā* within the Three Vehicles and the fulfillment of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* through the teaching of emptiness.

This constitutes the initial gateway for seeing one's nature (*prakṛti*). Within this context, the dialogue between the Buddha and Kāśyapa Bodhisattva also harmonizes with the principle established when the Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment and taught the Dharma-gate of the *dharmadhātu* to the great bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are other points of commonality and distinction that have already been judged in the previous section on the classification of teachings and the establishment of schools.
It was stated therein that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is the gateway for the three vehicles to abandon the provisional and realize the real, wherein the marks are exhausted and the nature is seen;

the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*), however, is the gateway for abandoning the provisional and realizing the real wisdom—the realm of phenomena where principle and fact, and essence and appearance, arise in mutual dependence. Both of these two sūtras are thus [identical in this regard].
Among these three vehicles, the teaching of the sixth period is spoken solely for the sake of those transformed through the gate of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mukha*);
because it distinguishes the sequence of time, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is categorized as the teaching of the seventh period. However, its realm of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*) has no succession;

it is the time of both past and present. The eighth is the time of preaching the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which, within a single instant (*kṣaṇa*), universally encompasses the three periods of time and the ten [directions].
Regarding the teaching of the world’s perfect interfusion (*jagat-saṃvṛti-yuga-naddha*), as the sutras state:
"Entering the samādhi of the limit of a single kṣaṇa, descending from heaven, taking birth, manifesting the eight phases of enlightenment, and entering nirvana—all occur without the passage of time.

This is because one relies on the fundamental nature of principle and wisdom (*dharmatā-prajñā*), which is inherently devoid of time; it is not a provisional reliance upon the basis. Therefore, this is called "entering," yet it does not exist within the fundamental dharma-nature itself.
Entering and emerging from samādhi according to the rules of transformation, he employs skillful means;
yet one must not cling to words as being without meaning, nor allow his traces of transformation to become stagnant, lest all classes of beings find no place of refuge.

Therefore, the wise do not follow his words when they say that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, alone enters the samādhi of the limit of a single kṣaṇa, for all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should abide within the Dharma.
The ocean of the body and wisdom, equal in number to all sentient beings, possesses various gates of samādhi that correspond to the perceptions of sentient beings;
one should know that these gates of samādhi of the Tathāgata are fundamentally without entering or exiting. The teaching-gate of this sutra is without beginning and without end;

it is the nature and characteristics of the Buddha’s true retributive fruit-virtue, perfectly encompassing and complete. If one seeks its head or tail, or its length and measure, [one will find none].
From beginning to end, this path is cut off; it encompasses all teachings and all practices, as well as all worldly realms and all modes of understanding.
Based upon the fundamental source, it constitutes a dharma-gate that is simultaneous and of a single limit, for its essence is thus from the outset.
It subsumes the times of the three periods into a single limit—a single moment of time—just as all rivers flow back to the ocean; thus does this Dharma emerge.
The external, separate arising of emotional cognition is entirely a provisional gate and not an ultimate teaching.

Such a dharma-gate would exist neither if a Buddha were not born into the world nor in his parinirvāṇa, because it relies on the fundamental Dharma, which is non-emotional in its instruction. That which relies on the fundamental Dharma has no entering or exiting;
that which relies on provisional learning speaks of appearing in the world and entering parinirvāṇa from the initial generation of the bodhicitta.
The beginning of the Ten Abodes, by the power of samādhi, suddenly seals the three realms as the single limit of the three periods of time;
all dharmas are of one flavor, the flavor of liberation and nirvana, eternally quiescent and extinguished. There is no further beginning or end;

cause and effect are a single limit; all natures are one nature; all wisdoms are one wisdom; all marks are one mark; all practices are one practice; the three periods of time are a single thought-moment.

To possess such mastery and unimpededness regarding phenomena spanning the three, ten, and even infinite eons—this Dharma-gate of the sutra is called the eternally turning wheel of Dharma, being without beginning and without end.
Therefore, this teaching of the sutra is established according to the fundamental reality to accommodate those of great capacity;
it relies on the single limit of the fundamental nature (*ekānta*) and does not establish beginning or end, for it is seen as neither false nor deceptive.
Entering into one [totality] and attaining the remainder as the single limit of the *dharmadhātu* is not like the provisional teachings, for their vision is not yet exhaustive.
Entering into the remainder and attaining one as the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is unimpeded: it is like a perfect sphere having no fixed direction;
like a bright mirror reflecting all at once; like space being without partition; like an echo having no support; like a shadow being unobstructed; and like a manifested person.
This Dharma-gate that has arisen encompasses the beginning and end as a single limit;
it is perfect, unobstructed, without formation or destruction, without emergence or disappearance, and constantly turns the Wheel of Dharma.

If a person can fully realize this Dharma-gate, the Buddha-wisdom, self-arisen wisdom, and teacherless wisdom will manifest before them, for this Dharma is without emergence or disappearance. Thus it returns.
By means of the wisdom of naturalness, which is without arising or ceasing, one is able to attain this for oneself; it cannot be attained through intellectual calculation or discursive thought.
All provisional teachings and Dharma-gates are contained therein and are expounded simultaneously.
Since all provisional teachings do not transcend the Dharma-realm—which is devoid of the three periods of time—they each rely on their own views, resulting in infinite differences.

The teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) was spoken at the time of attaining initial perfect enlightenment; if understood according to conventional sentiment, it was spoken at the very first moment of becoming a Buddha;
if understood according to wisdom, it is said to have no beginning or end. Ninth, regarding the common and uncommon teachings:

this refers to the various Mahāyāna sūtras, wherein humans, devas, and those of the three vehicles hear them together, yet the benefits they receive are each distinct. Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within a single pore...
Regarding the measurements of space and the distinctions in the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas within a single atom, as well as the differences in the understanding of sentient beings—
another sutra states that a Bodhisattva may attain equal and perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma within the body of a single small sentient being,
delivering immeasurable beings, yet this small sentient being neither knows nor perceives it; this is because [the Buddha] constantly dwells together with sentient beings.

Furthermore, since those of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles together abide within the ocean of the Buddha’s body and mind, there is fundamentally no distinction between their bodies and minds;

yet, they differ individually in whether they see the Buddha or do not see the Buddha, hear the Dharma or do not hear the Dharma, and in their degrees of liberation, knowledge, and vision, as well as their experiences of suffering and pleasure.
For this reason, it is called the "teaching of the common and the uncommon. Moreover, a sutra says: "Entering the limit of the *kṣaṇa*."
The manifestation of samādhi— descending from Tuṣita Heaven into the mother’s womb, appearing in the world, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvāṇa—
occurs within a timelessness wherein all sentient beings, each according to their own capacity, perceive the beginning, middle, and end;
and within a single sound of the Dharma, they each attain for themselves the path of devas and humans, the Hīnayāna, the Mahāyāna, or the Buddha-yāna.
Although the fruits attained by each are different, and the Buddhas they see, the kalpas in which they dwell, and the lengths of their lifespans vary individually,
in reality the nature of the Tathāgata is without fabrication, without birth, and without cessation. Because this unconditioned dharma-nature is intrinsically pure through its stainless,
white, and pristine wisdom, and because it is fundamentally identical in essence to all sentient beings, it is called "the multitude" (saṃgha).
Those who are born shall see and hear that which does not contradict their own thoughts; this is the wisdom of the *dharmatā*.
Since the wisdom of the *dharmatā* is fundamentally without a creator and is sovereign, it can accord with those thoughts so that they never miss their proper time.

Thus, they share the same Dharma as the Buddhas, the same wisdom, the same time, the same body, the same mind, and the same vehicle; yet, in terms of knowledge, vision, and liberation, each remains distinct.

Regarding the "shared" (sādhāraṇa) and "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) teachings: it is like the case where five hundred śrāvakas were together in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, yet they were as if deaf and blind; such is the matter. Tenth, regarding the "unshared shared teaching":
it is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where bodhisattvas from the ten directions have gathered in clouds, and the lands from which the Buddhas and their realms have come are each different.
While each individual hears the Dharma through common sounds according to their respective capacities, they collectively hear the Dharma and obtain benefits that are both shared and distinct.

Furthermore, within the assembly—consisting of devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, and non-humans—each with their own particular differences, all equally hear the Dharma-gate of the fruition-merit of Vairocana, possessing both shared and distinct qualities with sovereign mastery. This is also the case for the other three vehicles.
In this manner, the unique and shared teachings may be understood by analogy.
These ten teachings are all the Tathāgata’s instantaneous sealing—within a single moment and with a single sound—of the fundamental dharma-realm, like echoes responding to voices;
they differ according to the gradual or sudden capacities of the various sentient beings. Therefore, for the sake of a complete enumeration, they are now briefly divided into ten.
The various teaching methods are employed to manifest the distinctions between progressive cultivation and the practice of understanding.

As for the aforementioned ten periods of teaching, they are all spoken by the Tathāgata in a single moment from the ocean of wisdom that is free from the three periods of time; yet, due to the faculties and hearing of sentient beings, the distinctions of Great and Small Vehicles, as well as temporal divisions, arise from their own respective faculties.
Third, clarifying the distinctions in the teachings and their meanings:
Now, the Great Hero of the triple world, the Arhat, is tranquil and silent; his body and mind, as well as their nature and characteristics, are entirely devoid of purposeful action.

Nevertheless, through the arousal of great compassion from his essential nature, he is of one substance with the Dharma; following non-conceptual wisdom, he gives rise to teachings in accordance with conditions, like a single rain falling everywhere.

Nourishment, capacity, birth, and function each differ; there are cases where names are identical yet meanings are distinct (such as the ten stages of the gradual teaching versus the ten stages of the perfect teaching), or where words differ yet the meaning is the same (all dharma-gates throughout the worlds of the ten directions are dharma-gates of the Four Noble Truths). There are instances where principle and phenomenon diverge, or where essence and function penetrate one another;
whether sudden, gradual, or immediate, or perfect—dharmas do not manifest of their own accord, but are established according to faculties and teachings. When the faculties are weak...

If the Dharma is narrow while the vessel is broad, the Way remains incomplete; thus, it must accord with what is appropriate for each being, with the magnitude of the teaching varying according to their perception.

Sometimes, they understand differently despite identical words; at other times, they arrive at the same realization despite different languages. One should match the capacity of those to be guided and provide teachings according to the occasion.

Some may delight in the carriage at the gate, while others abandon it for the vehicle that travels upon the open ground. This applies both to those of the highest caliber and to those who progress gradually.

This brief exposition of the ten dharmas and their distinct principles is intended so that those who have newly begun their studies shall not be hindered by provisional means or obstructed from the ultimate reality.
These ten gates are: first, the distinction between the appearance of the Buddha-sun and the teacher;

second, the distinction between the manifestation of light as a symbol of the Dharma and its manifested signs; third, the distinction between the principal and the attendant regarding the subject matter of the questions and answers; fourth, the causes indicated...

1. The distinction of the fulfillment of the perfect fruit; 2. the distinction of the practices performed in each of the five stages; 3. the distinction of the six levels that cause Sudhana to realize the Dharma;
4. the distinction of the various dharmas taught in the six stages; 5. the distinction between the principle and the phenomena of the dharma-gates bestowed; 6.
the distinction of the fruits attained by the various followers of the three vehicles; 7. the distinction in the transmission and circulation of the entrusted treasury of the Dharma.
Regarding the distinction of the primary Buddha who appeared as the Teacher of this teaching: this teaching takes Vairocana as its Teacher.
In Sanskrit, *vi* means "various" and *rōcana* means "light that shines everywhere.
Furthermore, *vi* signifies "pervasive," meaning that with various lights of great wisdom, he illuminates the faculties and capacities of all sentient beings; this is precisely what is meant here.
The Dharma-body is designated by the names of compassion and wisdom; in the provisional teachings, it is referred to by its clan name as "Muni," which means "Silent One.
This is merely a praise for the essence of the Dharma being without speech or discourse.

As for wisdom and compassion, they possess only the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, and thus do not fully embody the ocean of infinite marks. Furthermore, this refers to one who has shaved off beard and hair, and is not [the ultimate reality].
Because the Buddha wears a flower crown, he is the same as those who have left the mundane world through the Three Vehicles;
yet he is not the same as them, for in this teaching, the mundane is identical to the ultimate truth, with no distinction between entering and emerging [from it].

For instance, the Tathāgata Vairocana, by way of general outline, possesses seventy-nine kinds of marks of a Great Man, including a flower crown upon his head that is fully adorned, along with the thirty-two [major] marks.

The King of Jewels manifests immeasurable varieties of adornments: his hands are graced with rings and bracelets, and his neck is draped with strings of pearls and necklaces, as extensively described in the sutras;
within each of these marks and secondary signs, there are inexhaustible characteristics.
Regarding the second point, the distinctions in the manifestations of light that symbolize the Dharma:

excluding the lights emitted from among the ninety-seven marks within the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," and also excluding the lights emitted by the Yāma devas and others, we shall now discuss directly the lights that symbolize the Dharma.
From beginning to end, there are eleven such lights, each of which symbolizes both cause and fruit.
Next, regarding the stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds,
the characteristics of their practice are without confusion; they differ from other teaching Buddhas who may emit many rays of light,
or a single ray without the ten, or whose entire body emits light without sequence, or who emit the light of the fruit without the cause.

Alternatively, there are cases where causes are emitted but no fruits follow, such as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which directly emits the fruit-light from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) without the causal light of the wheel-mark on the soles of the feet (*pāda-tala-cakra*).

This is like the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, in which the Buddha emits light from the wheel-mark on his soles and simultaneously emits light from his entire body; at that moment, he universally encompasses the causes and fruits of the Three Vehicles. Directly.

From below upward, light is emitted to form a gradual progression; from the ordinary person toward the sage, after the accumulation of practice over many kalpas has reached fulfillment, one finally achieves the fruit of merit.

This differs from the present sutra, where light is emitted from the fruit to establish the cause, and through the cause, the fruit is realized—the cause and fruit being a single, indestructible unity.
Regarding the foremost stage of progressive cultivation, first, ten [rays] are emitted from between the teeth.

The first [light] is the "Adornment of the Dharma Realm through All Paths of Radiance," which, upon his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, informs the multitudes throughout the ten directions to assemble;
this is as extensively explained in the sutra, for it constitutes the light that adorns the gathering of the assembly.
Second, he emits from between his eyebrows the "Fruit-light" which enters into the wheels of his feet; this serves as the beginning for generating faith by taking the fruit as the cause.
Third, thereafter, light rays corresponding to the fruits attained are emitted from the wheels on the soles of the feet to illuminate the Golden World.
The Buddha Akṣobhya is a fruition-Buddha and is also the essence of the fundamental Vajra-wisdom;
Mañjuśrī is the initial aspiration as well as the fundamental Dharma realized since the attainment of ultimate fruition.
The body becomes the mother of wisdom; as that light of the fruit from between the eyebrows enters the wheel of the feet, this is the use of the fruit to produce the cause.
Then, the light of the fruit that entered from beneath the wheel of the feet emerges again to illuminate the Golden World;

this is the Immovable Wisdom Buddha, which is the use of the cause to produce the fruit. Thus, the use of the fruit to produce the cause and the use of the cause to produce the fruit are shown simultaneously.
The gateway for accomplishing the first stage of faith is established by means of the ten bodhisattvas, such as Jñānottara (Wisdom Chief) and others, to constitute the stage of faith;

the characteristics of this stage will be explained in detail later. Furthermore, when the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" was taught, [the assembly] ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru, where the Tathāgata emitted light from the tip of his toe to illuminate the beginning of setting forth and the initial realization of the Path.
By the power of samādhi, one abides at the summit of the Dharma; from the preceding stage of faith, one enters the realization of reality.

The "Mount Sumeru" illustrates that through the cessation of thought (śamatha), wisdom becomes luminous. It is only by entering the essential concentration within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the noble ones that one can truly realize this luminosity of wisdom.
Therefore, from the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages downward, they share a common designation and are all called "wisdom."
Fifth, the Tathāgata ascends to the Yāma Heaven and emits light from his upturned feet to illuminate and thereby perfect the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).
Because this heaven is detached from the terrestrial realm, it is said to represent the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā-bhūmi*); it symbolizes that practice arises based upon emptiness.
This represents the Dharma by means of illumination: having first realized the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, one initiates the myriad practices. Sixth, he ascends...
In the "Chapter on the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," the Tathāgata emits light from his knees and expounds the Ten Dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) to signify this celestial realm.
Because within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) there is the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*dharmārtha-avyāghāta*), it is called the first dedication.

While the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena occurs not only at this specific stage of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), the terminology of the sequential stages must be employed according to the Dharma.
It is established that within each stage of the actual substance, all [qualities] are fully present. "Knee" (*jānu*) signifies the mastery of bending, extending, and revolving;

thus, it expresses the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It symbolizes mastery over the ultimate and the conventional, and the mastery of attaining both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through the perfection of wisdom and compassion.
In the seventh [heaven], the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), [the light] is emitted from between the eyebrows.
The radiance of the fruit-virtue of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark explains the stages of the ten bhūmis;

because it marks the conclusion of the causal and resultant positions of the bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis, it manifests as this deity. Since this transformation lacks a mind of its own, it arises in dependence upon others (*paratantra*).

This signifies that the bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis manifest transformations solely for the sake of what sentient beings require for their edification, yet these transformations themselves are devoid of karmic activity. Furthermore, this occurs at the boundary of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because it is free from desire, it is identical to the dharma-gate of the fourth dhyāna and the transcendence of the triple world;
because it differs from the Small Vehicle’s cultivation of birth-attained nirvāṇa to exit the delusions of the triple world;

and because it differs from the provisional teaching’s bodhisattvas who achieve the ten stages within the fourth dhyāna; furthermore, it proceeds from Tuṣita Heaven, bypassing Nirmāṇarati Heaven, to reach Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
The Lord Īśvara represents the dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*; therefore, there is no need for sequential progression.
The four *dhyānas* of the upper realms are likewise present within this assembly; they arrive without coming and reach without going, and are seen without moving.
Thus, all the heavens of the upper and lower realms reside therein, and the worlds of the ten directions are entirely contained within a single pore. This is merely a symbolic representation.
The stages of the Dharma descend in this manner; in reality, there is no up or down, nor self or other, nor coming and going.
At the assembly of the Flower Samādhi of Samantabhadra Buddha on the eleventh stage, it was taught in the Third Dhyāna Heaven, though the text there is incomplete.

In the eighth chapter, the "Appearance of the Tathāgata," taught in the Universal Radiance Hall, the Tathāgata emits a ray of light from between his eyebrows to anoint the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, thereby clarifying [the meaning].

Having concluded the stage of Equal Enlightenment within the Third Dhyāna at the end of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and having completed the presentation of the fundamental teachings on the modes and patterns of practice, the causes and effects were fully perfected. Once the establishment of the teaching was finished, he subsequently appeared;
yet, since the Dharma-gate had not yet been preached, what could his appearance be called? Furthermore, regarding the *Lokanātha-sūkṣma*...
In the "Chapter on Adornment," the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment appears, giving rise to the cultivation of the five stages through the arousal of confident faith;

once these five stages have culminated in Buddhahood, the fruit manifests spontaneously. Subsequently, in the "Chapter on Manifestation," it clarifies how one's own realization and cultivation of the fruit reach their consummation, manifesting as the Dharma-body itself is perceived;
furthermore, it elucidates the progression from beginning to end within the essence of the Buddha-dharmadhātu.
The Gate of the Sequential Stages of the Various Positions, from beginning to end, is eternally manifest as the primordial single limit, without before or after.
Light is emitted to consecrate the crown of Mañjuśrī; with the light of the fruit, the fruit-dharma is consecrated.
Since Mañjuśrī is the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body of the Buddha, it is intended that Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra be made to coexist.
Through their mutual inquiry and response, the beginning and end of the five stages, as well as the essence and function of cause and effect, are thoroughly integrated.
Thus, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, says in the Sūtra: "Who is the eldest son of the Buddha? Whom shall I now question?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata emits light from his mouth to irrigate the mouth of Samantabhadra; ninthly, light is emitted from the mouth of the Tathāgata to irrigate [the mouth of] Samantabhadra.

The light within the mouth of the Sage’s mouth is the light of the Buddha-dharma; it is intended that Samantabhadra shall explain, through his wisdom of differentiation, the Dharma-gate of the fruits and virtues of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
It was only after Mañjuśrī perceived the Buddha emitting this light that he knew where to inquire about the Dharma.
Since the holy wisdom is fundamentally self-knowing, it is now perfected by means of the seal of the Buddha-dharma, so that in the future it may be established. This is therefore...

Having emitted light nine times to establish the rules for the beginning and end of this single sutra and to synthesize the gates of cause, effect, essence, and function of the preceding five positions, these three persons are never separated from one another from beginning to end;
thus, it is clarified that the Tathāgata is the fruition of the two, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. In the tenth [chapter], once again at the Jeta Grove...

Internally, he again emits the light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows; since the causes and effects of the five aforementioned stages have already been perfected, he now employs these resultant dharmas to benefit sentient beings.

Thus, in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, he causes ordinary people among gods and humans, six thousand bhikṣus, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, and five hundred youths and maidens [to attain realization].
He causes all to attain the Way and become Buddhas within this Dharma-gate; further extensive meanings shall be clarified later.
From this point upward, ten times light is emitted, each expressing a specific meaning according to its own measure.
Because the emission of light in this sutra fully manifests the perfection of virtue, it is complete in its ten aspects, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, unlike the transformation-buddhas.
When emitting light while preaching a single section of a sutra, he may emit light once, or perhaps from his entire body;
such as has never occurred before. Within this sutra, each and every quality is fully perfected from beginning to end, and these qualities are ten in number.
It speaks of ten because the ten is a perfect number, signifying that the ten perfected qualities are inexhaustible.
Regarding the third section on the distinctions between the primary and secondary subjects of the questions and answers:

this explains the general characteristics and complete virtues of the essential meaning of the doctrines and the substance and function of the questions and answers within this single division of the sutra. There are three [figures]: first, the Buddha; second, Mañjuśrī;
and third, Samantabhadra. The Buddha represents the fruit-virtue (*phala-guṇa*), which is ineffable, beyond description, unconditionable, and unattainable.
One may realize the cause alone and attain the fruit; thus, one naturally attains the stage of Mañjuśrī’s causal state.

One may speak of this by means of the fruit-virtues of the *dharmakāya* to exhort the practice of Samantabhadra’s self-conduct, so that one may perform those practices until the ocean of conduct fills the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, these three virtues are employed for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings. Mañjuśrī has thus completed the praise of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the *dharmakāya*.
The Worthy One (Bhadrapāla) perfects the practice and virtue of differentiated wisdom;
all Buddhas rely upon these two venerable ones as their teachers and models to be able to achieve the ultimate fruit of Great Bodhi.

Some say that Samantabhadra is the eldest son, because he establishes the practice and brings it to fulfillment for the sake of sentient beings; others say that Mañjuśrī is the younger son, because he initiates [the path].
The initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is the head of the realization of the *dharmakāya*, fundamental wisdom, and Buddha-nature;

it is the first realization of the *dharmakāya*, fundamental wisdom, and Buddha-nature because it is the birthplace of the noble nature and wisdom of all Buddhas, and because it is the beginning of the illumination for those who are still in their infancy.
It is the "Youngest Son" (*kumāra*) in the Northeast, which corresponds to the *gen* hexagram; *gen* represents the Youngest Son and is also [the mountain].
The mountain consists of stone located between the directions of Chou and Yin; it represents the first light of dawn when darkness has already vanished but the sunlight has not yet fully manifested.
As the beginning of "Opening the Ignorant," it signifies the initial mind of the Ten Abodes, the first vision of the Path.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī is pointed out as being on Mount Qingliang in the northeast. Furthermore, this refers to the geographical position within the realm of this Jambudvīpa continent.
Furthermore, the Dharma is entrusted to the world so that it may be easily understood. Moreover, a sutra states:

"In all places, Mañjuśrī is the manifestation of the pervasive Dharmakāya. Also, ten Buddha-field-microdust worlds to the east, there is a Golden World where Mañjuśrī resides; thus, Mañjuśrīs are present throughout the ten directions.
When arriving in the Golden World (*Suvarṇabhāsa-lokadhātu*), gold appears white; its essence is yellow while its appearance is white.

That which is white in essence yet yellow in appearance clarifies that the Buddha-nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is wisdom. Its essence is pure, white, and clean; it does not belong to form or shape, and body and mind are unstained.
This whiteness is not like the whiteness of worldly colors; the Buddha-nature of the Dharma-body is without mind and without body.
Spontaneous and unconditioned, with objects of perception naturally pure and each thing devoid of mind, there is only non-reliant wisdom, which is termed "pure white.
When Bodhisattvas realize such a nature and such a body of wisdom, they are all yellow in color;
yellow is the color of auspicious merit, representing the harmony that arises when greed and hatred are absent—the virtue of benefiting beings through wisdom and compassion.
The Sūtra states that the Arhats and Bodhisattvas are all of a true golden color;
thus, when it says that Mañjuśrī comes from the Golden World, it clarifies that the Dharma in all places is truly real, signifying the One True Dharma-realm.
As for Samantabhadra being the eldest son, his position is in the east, the卯 (mao) position, which corresponds to the hexagram Zhen. Zhen represents the eldest son and is...
The head is the foremost; it is the Azure Dragon, representing auspiciousness and the springtime birth. It marks the beginning of establishing the Dharma rules.
Both worldly and Buddhist teachings take the East as the primary starting point to symbolize the rising sun, which illuminates all things so that everything becomes clearly manifest.
Because it is capable of performing tasks and being applied according to conditions, and because Samantabhadra is the foremost of all practices, [the East is thus established].
As the eldest son, Avalokiteśvara is the foremost of those who embody compassion;
he resides on the western slope of Mount Vajra and expounds the *Maitrī-karuṇā-sūtra*. The west corresponds to the hour of You (酉), which is the trigram Dui.

Dui represents metal, the White Tiger, misfortune and peril, and the autumnal killing-force (*qiusha*); therefore, the compassionate Avalokiteśvara presides over the performance of deeds in unwholesome places.
Compassion (*maitrī*) is Avalokiteśvara. Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara—these three dharmas are the common practice of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Within the seventh stage of "Great Compassion" among the Ten Dedications of Good Wealth Bodhisattva, they serve as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The broader meaning of this shall be further clarified later. Since the Buddha-dharma is wordless, it employs worldly phenomena to represent its meaning through metaphorical events.
All that possesses verbal expression is merely worldly dharma. If there were no words, how could the unenlightened be initiated?

For this reason, the three virtues of the Buddha—Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara—are employed as mutual leaders and companions to establish the Dharma rules for the primary purpose of transforming and benefiting sentient beings. The Buddha encompasses all fruits; Mañjuśrī encompasses all wisdom.
The causal and resultant dharmakāya of all practices, the primordial wisdom of Samantabhadra,
encompasses all distinctions of causal and resultant bodies of practice; for this reason, it is said that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are the teachers of all Buddhas,
or that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are the youngest son and the eldest son, such that these three mutually constitute a single dharma-realm.
This is the relationship between essence and function: Mañjuśrī represents the gate of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya at the very beginning of the path of seeing;
Samantabhadra represents the gate of the practice of conduct following the initial path of seeing; and the Buddha represents the non-acting essence within these two matters.
Therefore, by means of Mañjuśrī’s Dharmakāya, this entire body of teaching is encompassed, as it is the Dharmakāya that is the subject of the discourse.

Wisdom is fully equipped for all sentient beings; the initial gateway to the Path is universally encompassed by Samantabhadra within this single division of the teaching, which explains the various gateways of the practice of wisdom.
When the practice of the Dharma is fully perfected for all sentient beings, it is called Buddhahood.
Within the Buddha’s teachings, there is nothing that does not represent this; as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha conceals his physical form.
It does not manifest the realization attained by the youth of the Snowy Mountains in the past— that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing—
nor does it exclusively represent the *dharmakāya* and *nirvāṇa*, because these are devoid of conditioned activity. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sought the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā* and fulfilled the six *pāramitās*, yet he did not yet possess the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*.

The ten pāramitās, such as skillful means (*upāya*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), are intended solely to attract those of the lesser capacity among śrāvakas and devas who are not yet able to hear of the pāramitās of skillful means, power, knowledge, and so forth. Within the [standard] six pāramitās,
the absence of the pāramitā of skillful means is because that small capacity is not yet able to practice the pāramitā of skillful means— which operates even upon what is not the path.

Why is it so? It is because of fear and affection. Furthermore, in those scriptures, there are many *śrāvakas* who engage in dialogue with the Buddha, rather than great *bodhisattvas*. Even if there are *bodhisattvas*, they are not Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra.
Even if there is Mañjuśrī, if Samantabhadra is absent, it indicates that his practices are not yet complete; even if Samantabhadra is present...
The absence of Mañjuśrī clarifies that one has not yet seen the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya;
even if Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were present, their failure to engage in mutual dialogue indicates that the principle and phenomena have not been fully penetrated.

Furthermore, it does not mention "Mañjuśrī everywhere" or "Samantabhadra’s practice of all deeds within every atom," because these refer to the transformative Buddhas acting as the interlocutors themselves.
The respondent [teaches] that there are only causes and effects, requiring three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* [of practice]; this is for the sake of guiding those of inferior capacity.

[The present teaching] does not yet speak of cause and effect being simultaneous, nor of the perfect fusion of principle and phenomena (*li-shi yuanrong*), nor that the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) is itself Buddha, nor that there is no limit of before or after, nor that the entire *dharmadhātu* is instantaneously and completely realized, nor that both the ultimate and conventional truths are equally real—these are the points by which they differ in application.
Among all the teachings spoken by the various transformation Buddhas, none are equal to this sutra.
All other teachings are provisional expedients designed to lead those of various faculties to come here to this great ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*, to enter the realm of the single truth of Vairocana.
By means of the emptiness-contemplation of the three vehicles, one subdues manifest ignorance, so that the roots of arising and ceasing do not arise.

Because fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) has not yet fully developed the wisdom of differentiation (*pravicaya-jñāna*), one feels joy in being born in other lands and feels aversion toward this Sahā world;
even if one were to remain here, it is said that this is "retaining delusions" (*kleśa-avasthāpana*).

Furthermore, within this sutra, the youth Sudhana, by practicing the characteristics of the dharma-gates of the five stages throughout the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), has fully perfected his practice; therefore, these ten abodes inherently contain [all stages].
The practice-gates of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) manifest the fulfillment of the virtues and functions of this Dharma, and thus differ from the practices of other teachings.
For example, when the youth of the Snowy Mountains met a single spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he attained a single Dharma-gate; Sadāprarudita was likewise so.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the brief indication that a dragon girl attains Buddhahood merely points toward the south; it does not mean that [the south] is not the Dharma-realm itself.
Because he is perfected, he distinguishes between the small and the great while responding to questions; yet the principal teacher is the Transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya).

He establishes transformations in defiled lands to make them pure, though these are not actual pure lands. Furthermore, he moves humans and devas to other lands, yet this process is not yet finalized for either side.
If one were to say that there is a sutra distinct from other sutras, the matter would be so vast that it would be difficult to bring to a conclusion.
