The fourth section, "The Perfection of Causes and the Fulfillment of Results," distinguishes the three different aspects of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhaphala*). First, the fruit of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-phala*), which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) alone, transcending words and ceasing all practice.

Second, the fruit of the fulfillment of cultivation through the accumulation of practices. Third, [the fruit of] the ultimate realization of the path. (Note: The third aspect is implied by the structure of the commentary but not explicitly labeled in the provided fragment; the focus here is on the first two.)

After many kalpas of accomplishing merit, one finally achieves the fruit. At the time of the three initial awakenings of the mind, during the first stage of the Ten Abidings, the essence and function follow conditions.
The fruit thus achieved is initially beyond words and transcends practice; it is the Dharmakāya, the unconditioned fruit.

This refers to such scriptures as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which speak of the hidden body not manifesting and all phenomena coming to rest. Furthermore, it says that even rākṣasas [attain this].

The Śrāvaka youth says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing; once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) is bliss.
This is the fruit of non-action (*anabhisamskāra-phala*), because he does not possess the practice [of the bodhisattva path].

Second, as for those who clarify the fruit after many kalpas of accumulating and perfecting practice through cultivation—this refers to the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) which speaks of accomplishing the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of practice through the cultivation of conduct.

The fulfillment of the fruit of Buddhahood is precisely this: because one fails to realize that the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are fundamentally the wisdom of the *dharmakāya*, one becomes weary of them and uses the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana*) to suppress the active afflictions (*kleśa*).

By aspiring toward a separate gate of purity, one proceeds from the ordinary stage through the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) to newly realize the fruit of functioning in accordance with conditions; this is the "Flower."

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is it. At the culmination of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one attains the samādhi of skillful means (*upāya-samādhi*) to realize that the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are fundamentally the wisdom and compassion of reality (*dharmatā*).
Thus, one fully possesses the essence and function of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, which is the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, regarding the Buddhas encountered throughout the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas within the causal teachings and practices bestowed by the transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), as well as their definitive sutras:
Merit is always cultivated through practice; for a hundred kalpas one cultivates the karma of the marks and signs. By making offerings to the Lamp-Burning Buddha, one obtains radiance;
by not killing, one obtains longevity; by practicing generosity, one obtains wealth and resources; by practicing patience, one obtains physical excellence.

Each cause and effect corresponds in a manner that is perfectly analogous. Furthermore, only by applying various counteractive dharma-gates can one realize the nature and attain Buddhahood, just as a flower blooms.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is not like that; it is the dharma-gate of sudden realization of the Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment. Body, mind, nature, and characteristics are fundamentally only the substance of dharmas;

It is for this purpose that the Sages’ teachings differ—whether gradual or complete—so as to accord with the various faculties and capacities of beings. Thus it is.
The scriptural teachings present the Perfect Vehicle (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa) all at once for those of the highest of high capacities who are fit to receive it;
even those who are not yet so fit must joyfully cultivate it, for its ultimate flow leads them to dwell forever within this ocean.
Therefore, unlike other teachings where cause precedes effect, in this teaching cause and effect are simultaneous, as they cannot be separated within the ocean of the wisdom of *dharmatā*.
Because [the object] is attained, it is non-attainable; within this state of non-attainability, cause and effect are simultaneous and free from obstruction.
If cause and effect were attainable, they would necessarily have a sequence of before and after. That which is attained is entirely impermanent and is not the ultimate teaching.

If the cause were prior and the effect posterior, the cause itself would not be established, and thus the effect would also be destroyed. Such is the nature of phenomena born of conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Because there would be continuity, it would follow that there is annihilation; because self and other would not be established, just as when counting one coin one does not count the subsequent coin, if there were no "second," even the "one" would not be established. If moments do not continue into one another, the momentary fruit is destroyed;
if many eons do not continue, the causality across many eons is destroyed. This must await the time of counting the subsequent coin.
The same applies to the initial establishment of cause and effect: they are only established when there is an uninterrupted succession within a single moment.
If that were so, then just as when counting two coins simultaneously, where there is neither before nor after, what would constitute "one" and "two"?

Or, like holding up two fingers, which could be either cause or effect? Just as with the two fingers, depending on the point at which the mind counts them, one becomes the cause and the subsequent one the effect.
If the fruit were such that there is a prior and a subsequent, there must also be an interval between them;

yet if there is an interval, the relationship of cause and effect cannot be established. If they were simultaneous, it would be like two fingers held upright—neither prior nor subsequent—so who could be the cause and who the effect?
Thus, it would also fail to be established. This is as stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra regarding the simultaneity of cause and effect.

For this reason, this sutra does not establish the three preliminary worthy stages (*pūrvayoga-ārya*) and the ten levels of faith as being fully contained within [the ten stages].
The practice gates serve as the ground for this sutra because they precede the stage of seeing the path;

furthermore, during the intermediate period of the third-period teaching, one merely harmonized and integrated existence and non-existence, yet the practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—where principle and phenomena mutually encompass one another—were not yet perfected.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* expounds the dharma-gates of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages.
At that time, because the Buddhas of the ten directions all came together to grant their seal of approval, and because all Buddha-lands collectively expound this gate,
and because the thirteen types of signs manifest the ultimate reality, the sūtras of the Three Vehicles merely speak of ten stages (*bhūmi*) to encompass sentient beings,
yet this does not exhaust them; therefore, these are the provisional designations and provisional wisdoms within the three kinds of ten stages.
Because one practices the ten stages (bhūmis) based on provisional *tathatā*. Why is this so? It is because these eleven stages constitute the rank of a Buddha;
yet within the rank of a Buddha, there still remain obstructions. This clarifies that prior to the eleventh stage, the fundamental wisdom of true reality (*tattva-jñāna*) has not yet been attained.
If the wisdom of true reality were complete [from the beginning], how could there be the eleven types of grossness (*dausthulya*) in the eleven stages? Since they do indeed exist...

Coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) is not itself the ground; within each ground, there is Buddha-wisdom which functions as cause and fruit. Therefore, this sutra provisionally harmonizes existence and non-existence in a gradual manner so that one does not dwell in stagnation.
It is taught because it has not yet fully manifested the vast function of the wisdom of principle and phenomena, such as that of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
As stated in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayaguhya-sūtra* (Renwang jing), the practice gates of the five stages and ten grounds are established, progressing gradually from the level of an ordinary person.

Through the accumulation of practice over many lifetimes, one cultivates a provisional *tathatā*. Furthermore, there are scriptural teachings stating that afflictions are suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and realized through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) upon entering the stages;
or that one must intentionally retain afflictions without severing them, requiring three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood.
Such teachings are all provisionally established for those with provisional faculties and are not the ultimate truth; they belong only to the realm of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha.
These explanations are all intended to guide those of middling and inferior faculties; they do not represent the ultimate truth, though the rest may be inferred accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding the Buddha-fruit aspired to by followers of the Two Vehicles who turn their minds toward the provisional teachings, as well as the Buddha-fruit aspired to by Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings after completing an *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, they seek only the retributive fruit of a Buddha within a trichiliocosm.
One does not rejoice in the retributive fruits of the ten Buddhas' realms— the infinite realms of Vairocana throughout the ten directions—
as one rejoices in the Buddha-fruit within the superior understanding of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
An ordinary person possesses, within the mind of deep resolve, the joy of aspiring to cultivate the realm of the ten-fold body of Vairocana.
This vast, boundless, and profoundly mysterious wondrous realm is not the same as the realms of the Buddhas of the provisional teachings,
which all establish fixed divisions and limits; this is because those [provisional teachings] are established provisionally for those whose faculties are narrow and not yet broad,
such as the delineation of the stages of abandoning afflictions across the ten bhūmis in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, wherein the first bhūmi serves as the antidote.

The afflictions, karma, and birth of the miserable realms constitute the obscuration in the second bhūmi; the obscuration of the manifestation of subtle transgressions is countered in the third bhūmi;
the obscuration of desire and greed is countered in the fourth bhūmi; the obscuration of attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma is countered in the fifth bhūmi;
and the obscuration of exclusively turning one's back on either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa is countered in the fifth bhūmi.
The obstacle in the sixth bhūmi is the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse signs; the obstacle in the seventh bhūmi is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle signs;
the obstacle in the eighth bhūmi is the obstacle of effort regarding the signless and the unconditioned, as well as the lack of mastery over signs;
the obstacle in the ninth bhūmi is the obstacle regarding skillfulness in all aspects.
The obstacle of not attaining mastery over speech is the obstacle to be remedied within the tenth bhūmi;

it is the obstacle to the realization of the perfectly complete dharmakāya. Son of good family, this śamatha and vipaśyanā, in the stage of the Tathāgata, remedy the extremely subtle and most extremely subtle afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
However, within the stage of the initial resolve among the three grades of worthies prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to suddenly realize the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit,
which universally seals all positions— the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment— just as when a seal is pressed,
the patterns are fully manifest without beginning or end; thus, at the very moment of the initial resolve, one suddenly seals the three [bodies].

The realms of ignorance thus become the ocean of Buddha-wisdom; by the single seal of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, Wisdom-body, and Great Compassion, the world is instantaneously sealed as the Dharma-realm.

Because its great function is without before or after, and because the nature of phenomena is such, this differs from the provisional teachings which are established outside the [ultimate] reality, merely leading those of the three capacities to return to the one reality.

Regarding the fifth gate, the progressive cultivation of gradually perceiving the Buddha-nature, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) perceive the nature only partially, and even those at the tenth stage have not yet attained full clarity.

The *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna* states that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages attain a partial vision of the Dharma-body and manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment through transformation. As that treatise explains, this is due to their vows.
Since that which is produced by power is the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*) and not a true retribution (*vipāka*), it constitutes the gradual vision of Buddha-nature.
This is entirely the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) of the principle of gradual induction through successive stages; it is not the Perfect [Teaching].

For such cases, from the initial stage of the Abiding in Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) onwards, the realization of the Buddha-fruit is not fixed within the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Why? As in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
The Sūtra records that the butcher Guang'e (Broad Forehead) will attain Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa;

if even an icchantika who has merely first resolved to attain enlightenment possesses the merit to transcend kalpas, how much more so for one who fully possesses the faculty of faith and is further able to perceive a small portion of their nature—how could there be a separation by incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)?
There are those of virtue in the world who explain that the butcher Guang'e was merely a manifested being.

This is merely to pander to human sentiments without fully comprehending the Buddha’s intent. Since [the Buddha] gradually leads through skillful means toward the ultimate reality, how could he allow people to be captivated by their own attachments and cause them to deviate from the fundamental truth?

It is only when one is gradually led to such that the Dragon Girl and Sudhana attain Buddhahood within a single thought-moment that the true teaching is established; whereas the three vehicles represent limited views that merely contemplate over a long period of time.
The essence of things is fundamentally empty; sighing in admiration and yearning is but binding oneself without a rope—how can there be an end to this?
Previously, three kinds of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) were briefly explained. Furthermore, when evaluated according to the meaning of the sūtras, there are six kinds of ten stages:

as there are three kinds of ten stages within the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, so too are there three kinds of ten stages within the ultimate teachings, such as those in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.

In these three sections of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) taught therein are mostly established through the provisional gate of *tathatā* (suchness) to constitute the characteristics of the ten stages;
this is the threefold set of ten stages within the provisional teachings.

Fourth, as for the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there it is said that Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten abodes see their nature (*dharmatā*) to a small degree, whereas those at the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) [see it fully].

The stage where the realization of nature (*dharmatā*) is not yet perfectly clear is explained as taking Buddha-nature as the vehicle; it involves partial cultivation and partial realization across the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), specifically the fifth stage.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—which likens a cow eating the fatty grass of the Snowy Mountains to obtaining pure *sarpis* (clarified butter)—explains the realization of the Buddha-stage itself.
Thus, this constitutes the five kinds of ten stages; this teaching is common to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Because at the initial arousal of the mind one’s resolve accords with the perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas, the sixth [category] consists of the One Vehicle and the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).

As taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the gates of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are doubly profound and inexhaustible; by means of these, the Ten Stages are established. These constitute the six kinds of Ten Stages.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—such as the account of the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant—are all instances of guiding those of provisional capacity toward the teaching of ultimate reality.

Therefore, the realm of the Buddha-fruit as aspired to by Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles and ten stages consists merely of aspiring to the fruit of the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (recompense Buddha) within a trichiliocosm;
thus, this is the third type of *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body) within the True Teaching (*śāstric* or *tathatā-vāda*), and not the actual *saṃbhoga-kāya*.
Regarding these three types of transformation bodies: the first is the Buddha’s transformation body that manifests in various forms for sentient beings.
The two types of *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation bodies) refer to the Buddhas manifested within a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*) and the twenty-eight heavens;
the three types of *nirmāṇakāya* refer to the Buddhas manifested throughout the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
The *sambhogakāya* (recompense body) consists of the ten bodies of Vairocana, whose mutual essences penetrate one another in a realm of profound mystery, its magnitude equaling the *dharmadhātu*.
Furthermore, even down to the finest atom, within every atom, all are equal to the *dharmadhātu*, as explained in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Since the teachings of the Three Vehicles are provisional, and the dharma-gates and the realms of the Buddha’s retribution have not yet been taught as ultimate reality, they are termed "shared teachings" (*sādhāraṇa-deśanā*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Three Vehicles share the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Second, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*...

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) taught in the Sūtra were spoken directly for the sake of Bodhisattvas such as Gāmbhīrāvabhāsa, Pṛthubuddhi, and Viśuddhamati, who acted as questioners and interlocutors; they were not intended for Śrāvakas as questioners or interlocutors.
This was done so that the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* might redirect those who delight in emptiness and have become excessively attached to it, as found in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, toward these [stages].

Sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana* merely mention the names of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) without describing the stages prior to them—the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*), or the four stages of provisioning (*catur-sambhāra*).
Only the third [scripture], the *Ratnarājasūtra*, fully presents the dharma-gate of the practices and characteristics of all five stages.

Thus, in these provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), what is described as the "three worthies" (*tri-kṣānti*) and "ten sages" (*daśabhūmi*) is for the most part entirely an exposition of the conventional and the ultimate.

As one gradually refines [the mind] in successive stages, only then does the Buddha-nature become manifest; only then can one speak of mounting the Tathāgata-vehicle and proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Thus we know that the provisional teachings are not the ultimate truth, and that the sequence of stages (*bhūmi*) taught therein is not yet real.

Within the fourth, the Tathāgata-vehicle, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, those in the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) see the nature only partially, while even Bodhisattvas in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) have not yet fully realized it.

Those who are fully and clearly awakened are like the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, who, by virtue of their power of aspiration, are able to manifest Buddhahood through the eight phases [of a Buddha's life];

they belong to this same category. Although they have not yet reached full perfection, because they possess the power of having seen even a small portion of the nature (*dharmatā*), their capacity is such that it is comparable to a crown prince who, due to specific causes and conditions, is empowered by his father, the King.
Because he succeeds to the sovereign governance as a true son of this King, because his power is capable of such [attainment], because he has partially seen his nature,

and because he is a true son of the Tathāgata born into the Buddha-family— unlike those of other teachings who rely on provisional *tathatā* and provisional wisdom and only claim to be "born into the Buddha-family" upon reaching the first stage— it is clear that the power of his vision of nature is truly superior to others.

According to our school, this is the case even for a small portion; how much more so for those who have fully attained the fifth stage—the luminous and perfect teaching—wherein the wisdom that realizes the essence of the Way in a single thought-moment is identical to the Buddha, because the essence of ignorance is realized as being entirely identical to wisdom. As the Sūtra says: "When one is perfected, all are perfected;
when one is destroyed, all are destroyed. This shall be explained extensively later. These are called the five kinds of ten stages. This is it.

The sequential aspects of the four types of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are largely the same, with minor differences, within the gate of converting those of inferior and middling faculties and the gate of receiving birth;
however, regarding the gate of the fundamental Dharma teaching, among the provisional teachings, the three kinds of provisionally established *tathatā* serve as contemplative wisdom,
and the gradual and sudden two gates are fully established upon the essence of the Buddha-nature of the *dharmakāya*.
It is distinct in that, according to the provisional teachings, although one proceeds from the first bhūmi to counteract the afflictions,
karmic actions, and birth-related defilements of the evil destinies, up through the seventh bhūmi where one counters the manifestation of subtle signs—

yet these still constitute obstacles such that the wisdom of signlessness (animitta-jñāna) is not yet fully sovereign; it is only upon reaching the eighth bhūmi that there is signlessness and non-conceptualization without effortful application (anābhoga).
Furthermore, because one has not yet attained mastery even regarding the effortful cultivation of signs (*nimitta*), there are obstructions at every stage (*bhūmi*) due to this lack of mastery,
as previously explained according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* regarding the sequence of abandoning afflictions through the stages.
Just as the ten stages within the Three Vehicles are definitively established, one abandons afflictions through such successive gradations over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
The cultivation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred *kalpas* is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other texts within the section on the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
The sequential establishment of the stages (*bhūmi*) has already been clarified above. As the *Banyè yīngluò jīng* (*Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*) states:

"A Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes wears a copper-jewel necklace and becomes a son of the hundred-fold merit of a copper-wheel-turning king; taking them as his retinue, he is born in a single Buddha-field to receive the Buddha’s teachings and practices."
Teaching the ten practices of the bodhisattvas of two worlds, he is born as a silver-wheel-turning king with five hundred sons of merit as his retinue, wearing a silver-jewel necklace;
he receives instruction and performs transformations within the lands of three Buddhas.

Teaching the ten dedications of the bodhisattvas of three worlds, he is born as a golden-wheel-turning king with a thousand sons of merit as his retinue, wearing a diamond-jewel necklace; he enters the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
In the realm where all sentient beings within the four continents are transformed, those on the first bhūmi wear necklaces of a hundred jewels;
on the second bhūmi, a thousand jewels; on the third, ten thousand jewels; and on the fourth bhūmi, bodhisattvas wear necklaces of incalculable jewels.
Thus, from the first through the tenth bhūmi, the jewel necklaces gradually increase in scale, extending even to the tenth and eleventh bhūmis.

The Buddha, the King of Dharma, and the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) together possess fifteen types of universal monarch (*cakravartin*) positions, as explained extensively in the *Sūtra on the Necklace of Jewels* (*Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*).

It further states that the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness subdue the coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms; their coarse karmic paths (*karmapatha*), coarse continuities (*saṃtati*), and fruits do not arise.

Furthermore, through the Joyful Patience (*pramuditā-kṣānti*) of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they subdue the three [types of] karmic paths, and through the Patience of Detachment (*vairāgya-kṣānti*), they abandon rebirth in the hells.
The Path of Karma of the hungry ghosts and animals is subdued by the patience of clarity; the Path of Karma of the six heavens is subdued by the patience of the flame;
the Path of Karma of various views is subdued by the supreme patience; the Path of Karma of doubt and views is subdued by the patience of manifestation;

the Path of Karma of causes is subdued by the patience of non-arising; the Path of Karma of the cause of form is subdued by the immovable patience; and the Path of Karma of the cause of mind is subdued by the light patience.

Through the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*), one subdues the two paths of karma consisting of mental and physical habits; through the stainless patience (*vimala-kṣānti*), one subdues the path of karma that is the fruit of habituation.
Since the habits have already been eliminated previously, yet the fruit does not perish, the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) among the Buddha-sons are termed "subduing and severing.
From the stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) upward, one both subdues and severs all afflictions. When the patience of awakening (*bodhi-kṣānti*) manifests, it is one within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
All ignorance is suddenly severed without remainder. Thus, the above has explained the eleven kinds of patience (*kṣānti*).

The Bodhisattva of the Three Firmnesses (*tri-dṛḍha*) employs these to eliminate the coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, as well as to subdue and sever them. The commentary explains that the "Three Firmnesses" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Worthies (*tri-piṭaka*), namely the three stages prior to the [ten] grounds: the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*). Furthermore, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (The Jewel Garland) states: ... [text continues] ... The commentary further explains that the "Three Firmnesses" are the three stages of the worthies: the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences. These are the three positions prior to the grounds. Furthermore, the *Ratna-*.

The *Luo jing* (Luo-pin jing) states: "O Son of the Buddha, at the first stage (*bhūmi*), in a single thought-moment, the wisdom of the signless *dharmakāya* achieves ten million *asaṃkhyeya* merits, simultaneously illuminating the two truths; every thought is quiescent within the stream of the Dharma.

One cannot fathom these two kinds of *dharmakāya* with the consciousness of an ordinary person. The commentary explains that the "two bodies" are: first, the *dharmatākāya* (Dharmata-body); second, [the *nirmāṇakāya*].
The response to those who speak of the "flow of the dharma-nature" regarding the transformation body is as follows:

Since a bodhisattva of the first bhūmi spontaneously reaches the stage of Buddhahood within the flow of the wisdom of dharma-nature, there is nothing to be cultivated or contrived; how much more so for those of the second and third bhūmis?

Furthermore, a sūtra states that when bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness prior to the bhūmis enter the rank of the noble ones, they abide solely within the flow of dharma-nature, wherein every thought-moment is quiescent.
Spontaneously flowing into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment, O Son of the Buddha, even the names of the three stages of worthiness and the ten bhūmis are without name and without form;
they exist only as provisional manifestations. According to the dharma-methods of the ancient Buddhas, there are names for the ten bhūmis.
This sutra is precisely that which, after the teaching of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, further instructs those of the three vehicles during a subsequent period.
At the beginning, beneath the Bodhi tree when first attaining Buddhahood, I briefly recounted the Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Within this *Necklace Sūtra*, it is stated that I once expounded the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhāsa*), and later taught the Ten Abodes (*Daśabhūmi*) in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
now I shall again briefly explain them as they are extensively set forth in that sūtra, following its sequence.
Regarding the Dharma-gate Sūtra on the Eleven Stages taught within the Third Dhyāna after the Ten Stages: this scripture did not come from the Western Regions.

It states: "O Son of the Buddha, I previously gathered the assembly of the Eight Dhyānas within the Third Dhyāna and spoke one million billion verses concerning the Bodhisattva in his last birth entering the Buddha-flower Samādhi; now I have spoken it in brief."

The meaning of this single verse opens the minds of sentient beings; you should receive and uphold it. Furthermore, according to the *Ākāśagarbha-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), regarding the section on the Dharma-characteristics of severing delusions through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the *Sūtra* says:
"O Son of the Buddha, those in the preceding three stages of worthiness (*sādhaka*) suppress the ignorance of the three realms and thereby eliminate coarse karma.
Why is this? At the time of receiving birth, they take goodness as the causal seed. The commentary explains: "The three worthies..."
When a bodhisattva first receives the wisdom of the dharma-nature and is born into the family of the Buddhas, their compassion increases and becomes preeminent.
Because they regard all sentient beings within the three realms collectively as their own children, they vow never to abandon them.

Out of compassion, and because the karma for being born into the three realms has been moistened by their mercy, they take birth within the three realms. Furthermore, a sutra states: "In order to moisten karma, one undergoes the fruits of the future."
Therefore, it is called "the function of cessation. The commentary explains: because there is no creation of new karma within the three realms, it is termed the function of cessation.

Furthermore, a sutra says: "yet the function of non-interruption of craving [remains]. The commentary explains: although the karma of the three realms has perished, the compassionate karma of taking birth is not lost. A sutra says:
"There are eleven types of persons who likewise subdue the karmic fruits of the three realms within the Dharma-realm. The commentary explains: ten...
Regarding the "one person," there are eleven individuals when the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) are combined. Furthermore, a sutra states:

"From the first stage up to the seventh stage, the karmic fruits of the three realms are all suppressed and exhausted without remainder; it is at the eighth stage that they are completely ended. The commentary explains: "Prior to the seventh stage, [the afflictions] are suppressed and exhausted;
at the eighth stage, they are said to be 'exhausted according with the Dharma' (*dharmatā-kṣaya*). From this point upward, [the Bodhisattva] manifests [various deeds].

Because the Buddha manifests the birth in the royal palace, renunciation, attainment of the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and parinirvāṇa throughout all realms of emanation-buddhas, he has no attachment to offspring;
this is the retribution of the three realms, wherein only the habit-energy of ignorance remains. The commentary explains:

although one in the eighth stage, the Stage of Manifest Presence, dwells in effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) and delivers sentient beings, one has no perception of sentient beings. This is the seventh stage.

Prior to this, compassion was superior; from the eighth stage onward, the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*) manifests, and thus wisdom is superior. Although there is no further taking of birth, the Buddha spontaneously delivers beings;
it is not that he lacks the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for affection toward the Dharma. It is only at the stage of Buddhahood that these are finally exhausted.

By the power of his original vows, he manifests through transformational birth (*nirmāṇa-ja*). Therefore, when I previously spoke in the celestial realms of the meaning of "birth" and "non-birth," I referred to the Buddha as one who is born through karma and one who is born through transformation.
Within the stage of the Son of the Sage, there are two kinds of karma: first, the karma of wisdom (*prajñā-karma*), which is the wisdom of signlessness and non-arising;
because the mind takes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as its object, it arises without illumination—this is called the karma of wisdom. Second, the karma of merit (*guṇa-karma*);
because true wisdom produces a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of conditioned, untainted accumulations within the realm of existence, it is called the karma of merit. From...

From the first stage of the Sages upward, they manifest birth through transformation; because it is a transformation, they do not create new karma, yet by the power of their vows, they abide for hundreds or thousands of kalpas.
These births through transformation are all explained according to the *Bunyō-kyō* (Sutra of the Necklace of Fundamental Karma).
This is precisely what is taught within the Perfect Teaching (*Eṇ-gyō*), which possesses both the sudden and gradual gates. Regarding the sudden gate, this sutra says: "Three..."
The worthy Bodhisattva immediately enters the stage of the Sages and flows within the stream of the Dharma-nature, proceeding spontaneously toward the ocean of Buddhahood without further effort.
As for those who progress gradually, they sever delusions through successive stages of cultivation;

according to this *Ratnavyuha-sūtra*, the three grades of worthies and the ten abodes constitute entry into the flow of the Dharma-nature, which differs from the provisional teachings where the path is first seen at the first ground, with the subduing of afflictions occurring prior to that realization.

If one considers the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmika*), regarding the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), it does not state that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) must wait until they have become a sage (*ārya*) before practicing;
that scripture itself contains explicit clarifications. Furthermore, to clarify the matter of advancing and retreating, the *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states:
"O Son of the Buddha, whether one retreats or advances, [the aspiration] is generated within all the dharmas of ordinary persons prior to the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*)."
Among those sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who study and practice the Buddha-dharma with a mind of faith and signs within the bodhicitta,
there are those whose roots of goodness belong to the stage of regression. These good sons, having practiced for one kalpa, two kalpas,

or even up to ten kalpas while cultivating the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and entering the ten abodes (*vihāra*), may, from the beginning up to the sixth abode, if they cultivate the sixth *pāramitā*...

If the correct contemplation of the *pāramitās* manifests before them and they further encounter the protection and mindfulness of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they advance to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) and abide permanently in non-retrogression. Prior to this seventh stage, one is termed "subject to retrogression.
If a son of the Buddha does not retrogress, he enters the sixth stage, the *prajñā*, and practices within emptiness and selflessness.
That which is without person and without master is ultimately unborn and ultimately enters the state of Buddhahood.
O Son of the Buddha, if one does not encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), then for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even ten kalpas, one may regress from the Bodhi-mind—
just as eighty thousand among my assembly in the first gathering regressed, or like the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra and King Dharmamati.
Śāriputra and others, wishing to enter the seventh stage, encountered adverse conditions therein;
consequently, they regressed into the unwholesome evils of ordinary worldlings and were no longer called persons of the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*).

They fell back into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), where for one kalpa, ten kalpas, or even up to a thousand kalpas, they committed great false views and the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), performing every kind of evil.
Question: According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one who hears even the two characters "eternal" (*nitya*) shall not fall into hell for seven kalpas;

and according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, even if one hears the name of the Tathāgata or his teachings but does not give rise to faith or understanding, it can still form a seed that will inevitably lead to liberation and the attainment of Buddhahood.
For what reason, then, is it said here that this occurs only from the sixth stage of mind (*cittasthiti*) onward?
It is said that those at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may still regress; this point may be reconciled by explaining it as follows:
within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) has not yet been perfected. Failing to realize what has not been attained, they give rise to arrogance (*māna*).

Because they do not draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and do not revere the worthy and good, their indolence leads them to remain long among humans and devas, where evil karma arises and enables the accomplishment of the great earth [of saṃsāra].
If one possesses even a single moment of faith, is free from arrogance, and constantly seeks superior friends, then this fault will not occur.

In the provisional teachings, those in the sixth stage of mind may still experience regression; however, in the ultimate teachings, those who remain stagnant are exhorted to advance in their practice.
Śāriputra is an example of such a manifestation of a śrāvaka, not a real śrāvaka; all such skillful means are for the purpose of delivering beings.
Sentient beings are urged to advance according to the provisional teachings, wherein the sixth stage of mind (*citta-sthiti*) may be said to involve actual regression.
Why is this? Because within the provisional teachings, those prior to the stages—namely, the three levels of worthiness (*śaikṣa*)—have not yet seen the Path;
all the practices they cultivate are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and all their ignorance is merely suppressed. If their effort is not firm, they will give rise to regression.
If one subdues [the afflictions] with power, they will not be lost, just as the venom of a snake cannot arise due to the power of a mantra.
Within the Buddha-dharma, one plants the seed of faith, remains humble and free from pride, and respects the virtuous;
toward those who are evil, one always maintains compassion and patience; and toward those who surpass oneself, one seeks out what has not yet been heard and receives the teachings already heard.

Practicing the supreme Dharma without forgetting anything, relying on the teachings to eliminate all falsehoods, and constantly striving without rest upon the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—such is the natural law for those born as humans;
since it is fitting that things be thus, why need one worry about falling back?
The above five types of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) correspond to the three types of ten stages within the provisional teachings.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there are only ten stages (*bhūmi*), where the eighth is named the Stage of the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa-bhūmi*) and the ninth is named the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*).

Although the names of the ten stages differ slightly from those in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and although the names of the ten stages in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* are the same [as those in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*],
from the first stage through the eleventh stage, there are eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Regarding the twenty-two types of ignorance, these two sections of the sutras mention only the ten stages (*bhūmi*), omitting entirely the four types of provisions (*sambhāra*) prior to the stages.

Although the *Ratnarājasamādhi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) speaks of the ten levels of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences—the four provisions prior to the stages—it treats the ten levels of faith as the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and the ten abidings as the inner ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*). Thus, it does not [explicitly]...

Within the same Real Teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*), at the initial stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one immediately ascends to the nature of the sages (*āryatva*), with a substance equal to that of all Buddhas.

Among the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), if one does not believe that one’s own body and the Buddha-body are non-dual in terms of cause and effect, true faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) will not be established.
Therefore, the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta* states: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know that within his own mind there is [the Tathāgata]."
In every thought-moment, there are the Buddhas of the ten directions attaining equal and right enlightenment and turning the wheel of the true Dharma.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-mind and one’s own mind are non-dual. Only such a mind of faith can be called "faith.
How much more so for those in the stage of the Ten Abidings; if they do not realize this mind, how can they be said to abide? For this reason, [it is taught].
Therefore, abiding in the Buddha-abode is what is called "abiding"; thus, upon the initial arousal of the mind, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, in the provisional teachings, when the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are explained, there are no Buddhas from other directions who preach the Dharma with the same name, nor do Buddhas bearing the same name come to bear witness, as this would signify the identity of cause and fruit. For these reasons, [the stages are as they are].
Furthermore, since all the teaching gates are provisional establishments for the sake of guiding sentient beings of lesser capacity,

those with wisdom should not stagnate within them, but should instead rejoice in ascending further. Therefore, when the Dharma-gates of the five stages and ten grounds were being taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,

specifically when the Bodhisattva Dharmamati entered meditative concentration within the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*) intending to expound the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes, [the time] passed.
From beyond a thousand Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions, there came Buddhas named Dharmamati, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-worlds;

they touched the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati with their hands, praised him with their verbal activity, and bestowed thirteen kinds of empowerment through the power of Dharmamati’s wisdom.
When they were expounding the merits of the stages of the ten practices, the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma entered into meditative concentration.
Just as they were passing beyond ten thousand Buddha-worlds, there came Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-worlds,
all named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), together with thirteen kinds of Guṇakūṭa Bodhisattvas and others, who spoke on the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). At that time,
from beyond one million Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, there came Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within one million Buddha-worlds.
The "Coming [Buddha] of the same name Vajradhvaja" also consists of thirteen types; adding the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are likewise the same.
The fact that the names of the Buddha and the Bodhisattva are identical clarifies that cause and effect are the same, as will be explained extensively later.
This *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; it is an exposition of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which is the section on the ten stages within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Regarding the section on "Explaining the Meaning," the textual meaning applies to both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle. Among those who provide explanations therein, most explain the meaning of the Three Vehicles;
few understand the meaning of the One Vehicle. This is because the intellectual understanding of the principles of the One Vehicle is beyond their reach.
Even if there were those who attempted to understand it through intellectual speculation, their web of doubt would not be removed, as they would merely be relying on faith in the Buddha’s words.

Because this is what can be known by those who have severed their self-doubt, who have long remained in non-conceptualization without weariness toward suffering, who do not stagnate in quiescence, and who have realized the permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
therefore, the five kinds of ten stages and the three kinds [of ten stages] are provisional, while the remaining two kinds of ten stages constitute the teaching of ultimate reality.
For this reason, the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "The Way and Dharma of the Ancient Buddhas..."

To transform sentient beings, these ten stages (bhūmis) have been established; one should know that although the names of the ten stages are the same in the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, the skillful means employed and the resulting practices and understandings of sentient beings are entirely different.

This is because, as explained in this very place, there has not yet been a common seal of certification where Buddhas of the same name together establish the causal and resultant realization. Sixth, it clarifies the principle of the sudden realization of Buddha-nature.

Regarding the gate of the perfect integration of wisdom and the myriad practices: as described in the first assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs," the Tathāgata emits light from between his teeth, and again emits the light of the fruit and virtue of the Middle Way from between his eyebrows;
he further causes Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to enter samādhi and preach the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of Worlds" and the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World."
In the "Vairocana Chapter," the fruits of the Buddhas' teachings are explained so that beings may conceive a sense of love and joy;
once such love and joy have been generated, in the second assembly, Mañjuśrī is commissioned to speak on the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Names" and the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, light is emitted from the wheel between his two feet, and this light surpasses the [limits of] ten Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions.
Outside each world-system as numerous as motes of dust, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields who all came to assemble.

Furthermore, he spoke the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry for Clarification," the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," and the "Chapter on Worthy Leader," which are the gates for accomplishing the ten levels of faith.
The light from beneath the two wheels on his feet serves as the ultimate illumination for entering faith; thus, faith is taken as the cause.
Faith is the most foundational; therefore, this is because the light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows has been emitted.
As stated previously in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs," when the Tathāgata emitted light from between his eyebrows, it entered the wheels of his two feet.

This was intended to clarify that by raising up the functional power of the Buddha’s fruit-attainment to establish the stage of faith, all those in training (śaikṣas) return to faith in the functional power of the fruit-dharma to establish the beginning [of the path].
Because they have entered the gates of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), for this reason, from each of the ten directions, there come bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
they all come from worlds of the ten colors and from the presence of the Tathāgatas of the ten wisdoms.
Since the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute the beginning of entry into the Way, the bodhisattvas who have thus come are all called "Heads" (*mūrdhan*).
The ten worlds of form refer to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), where the bodhisattva has not yet achieved the realization of true proof and remains a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).

Although they believe in the fruit-virtues of the Buddha-realm, they have not yet departed from the dust of form; thus, they take form as their land. The ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) bodhisattvas possess the perfect clarity of both principle and phenomena (*li-shi*);

they take flowers as their land because they have newly emerged from the mundane stage, with principle and phenomena blossoming like flowers. As for the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) bodhisattvas... [text continues].
The Bodhisattva’s excellent discernment and awakened wisdom are perfectly luminous; taking wisdom as his kingdom, he proceeds through the ten dedications and the ten stages.
Taking wondrous function and mastery as his kingdom, he takes the Dharma as his kingdom, arriving from the dharma-gates of his respective positions.
It is not for the sake of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—that he enters the state of noble wisdom, having already transcended these obstacles at the stage of the ten faiths.

The Bodhisattvas within these positions have all come from the presence of the Buddhas of the Ten Wisdoms—namely, the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, the Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom, the Buddha of Liberation Wisdom, and so forth. These Buddhas of the Ten Wisdoms take wisdom as their fruit-virtue;

because they establish faith through the fruit within the stage of the Ten Faiths, they are called "clearly coming from the fruit. Because they take the fruit as the cause, [they are established in this way].
If one does not take the fruit as the object of faith, there would be nothing to believe in; thus, faith would have no basis.
For what reason is Mañjuśrī the leader? It is because Mañjuśrī is the master who initiates all [beings];
it is because all Buddhas of the ten directions take Mañjuśrī of Wondrous Virtue as the foremost in inspiring the mind of faith. This is to manifest [this truth].
Because it manifests the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the *dharmakāya*, Mañjuśrī is always taken as the stage of faith preceding the fruit;
because Samantabhadra clarifies that this is the differentiated wisdom (*pravicaya-jñāna*) as the practice following the fruit,
Sudhana first beheld Mañjuśrī as the gate of faith and later beheld Maitreya as the stage of Buddhahood, and finally saw his own body enter into Samantabhadra.
The body is the fruit of Buddhahood; subsequently, Mañjuśrī is the younger son and Samantabhadra is the eldest son. These two sages are a unified embodiment and are thus named "Buddha.
Mañjuśrī is the wondrous wisdom of the *dharmakāya*, while Samantabhadra is the virtue perfected through myriad practices;
because their essence and function are sovereign, they are named "Buddha. Mañjuśrī is the younger son because he represents the realization of the *dharmakāya* through faith.

Because fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) is the first-born, and because one is able to give birth to the Buddha-family by first realizing the Dharma-body of fundamental wisdom, Samantabhadra is the eldest son.

This is because he relies on fundamental wisdom to initiate practice, and through the differentiation of wisdom, he masters the various perfections (*pāramitā*) that constitute the laws of the Buddha-family;
thus, he constantly establishes the laws of the Buddha-family through the gate of practice.

In managing the affairs of the Buddha’s household, those who serve as interlocutors within the various sutras are predominantly Mañjuśrī when the responses clarify the gateway of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*);
they are predominantly Samantabhadra when the responses discuss their practice (*caryā*).
This serves to manifest that Mañjuśrī, riding upon a lion, symbolizes the initial realization of the fundamental source of the Dharma-body and Buddha-nature.
Because wisdom is the steed that cuts through delusions, Samantabhadra rides a fragrant elephant; this king represents the orderly progression of practice as his majestic virtue.

Furthermore, because Mañjuśrī constantly dwells in the Eastern World of Golden Color at the abode of Akṣobhya Buddha, it is to clarify that gold is white in color and capable of being free from defilement;
"golden color" represents the Dharmakāya, and "immovable" signifies its unshakable nature.
The wise one, relying on the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-nature body, gives rise to the function of wisdom;
because this is immovable, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva always dwells in the presence of the Buddha Ratnavīrya-tejo-rāja in the East.

This clarifies that the myriad practices are "jewels," and by means of these practices, one achieves "majestic virtue. If one possesses these practices, one attains mastery through the body of the Dharma-jewel. Its majesty...
Virtue, fearlessness, and sovereignty constitute kingship; if one does not possess these practices, one will always have cause for fear.
Even if one occupies a high position, one cannot be considered a true king because of this underlying fear.

As for being together with Mañjuśrī in the eastern direction, it is because the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, as well as principle and phenomena, essence and function, are fundamentally one and fundamentally non-dual. Furthermore...
Mañjuśrī resides on Mount Qingliang in the northeast because he corresponds to the hexagram Gen. Gen represents the "youngest son" and occupies the northeast;

thus, Gen is the youngest son, the unenlightened child, and Mañjuśrī. He constantly transforms ordinary beings by initiating their enlightenment, revealing their inherent nature and primordial wisdom at the very beginning.
Furthermore, he dwells together with Samantabhadra in the eastern position of the卯 (Mao) trigram.

The hour of the Rabbit corresponds to the Trigram Zhen, which represents the eldest son. It is also like the sun rising in the east; the spring yang initiates sprouting, such that there is nothing that does not grow and nothing that is not illuminated.
This symbolizes the simultaneous penetration of principle and wisdom, a single essence without duality.

Just as when the sun rises in the east there is nothing it does not illuminate, and when the spring yang initiates sprouting there is nothing that does not grow, so too does the fundamental wisdom distinguish [all things].
Distinct wisdom has no separate essence or function because it gives rise to the myriad practices;

therefore, Zi (rat) represents the stage of Buddhahood, Chou (niu) represents the stage of faith, Yin (yin) represents the ten abidings, Mao (mao) represents the ten practices, Chen (chen) represents the ten dedications, Si (si) represents the ten stages, Wu (wu) represents the stage of Equal Enlightenment, and Wei (wei) represents the darkening and brightening [of the moon] as one enters the mundane world to transform the deluded in common with them.
Shen (shen), You (you), Xu (xu), and Hai (hai) represent that which is acted upon.

Because of such transformations, the principles of the Dharma are thus established; as the Dharma is thus consistent, the hexagrams of the *I Ching* have Kan for the ruler, Li for the minister, Zhen for the high chancellor, and You for the supreme general.

The east is the Azure Dragon, the west is the White Tiger, the front is the Vermilion Bird, and the rear is the Black Tortoise. The Azure Dragon signifies auspicious celebration, while the White Tiger signifies misfortune and harm. The Vermilion Bird...
Because the Dark Warrior (Xuánwǔ) represents clarity and because black represents the profound, the Tathāgata governs the *Kǎn* trigram to manifest illumination.
Samantabhadra presides over the marks of wisdom and the myriad practices; Avalokiteśvara is the foremost of great compassion, acting as the supreme general who subdues calamity and peril;
Mañjuśrī is the foremost for awakening the ignorant, constantly serving as the teacher who receives those with faith. These embodiments intersect and harmonize to maintain the world.
The Dharma of the Buddha causes all sentient beings to abide in the Middle Way, wherein they dwell in a nature of tranquility and harmony, using wisdom and compassion to benefit all things.
For this reason, their bodies are entirely golden, their eyes and hair are deep blue-black, and their skin is white with a yellowish luster;
this is the harmonious breath of the Arhats. They are the form of the formless and the color of the colorless. If one considers their essence...
In application, each and every Bodhisattva fully possesses wisdom and virtue without limit; according to the sequence of their dharmas, Mañjuśrī is always established as the foremost leader of faith.

Now, while provisionally establishing the East and West gates based on the North and South, if one discusses their mutual resonance and profound mystery, both directions together possess ten [attributes]. As a sutra says: "In all places, there is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva."
The *Sarvatrānugata-suvarṇavarṇa-lokadhātu-sarvatrānugata-mañjuśrī-acalabuddhi-buddha-sūtra* states:
"The Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm and universally appears before all sentient beings;
it fills all those who are vessels capable of receiving transformation. Therefore, [the Buddha] dwells here beneath this Bodhi tree, amidst as many atoms as there are in all Buddha-fields."
In that many Buddhas seated within a single pore, there are immeasurable assemblies of Bodhisattvas, each of whom expounds the practices of Samantabhadra in their entirety.
Thus, one direction is equivalent to the ten directions in their inexhaustibility; a single atom is equivalent to the infinite ocean of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*).
Now, regarding these various manifestations of the transformative ritual, both general and specific, what stage of realization does "the ten faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*) signify?
One definitely accomplishes the gateway of the Ten Faiths, as stated in the "Chapter on the Radiance of Awakening" within the Ten Faiths:
"In all places throughout the ten directions, Mañjuśrī expounds the Dharma-gate of all places throughout the ten directions,
praising the Buddha’s ten kinds of fruits and virtues to establish the stage of faith," just as it is taught in the "Chapter on the Radiance of Awakening."
Furthermore, for those who have given rise to the faculty of faith, it causes them to become even more clear and pure.
Mañjuśrī again asked ten questions of the Bodhisattvas such as Daśaśīrṣa, concerning the mind not knowing karma and karma not knowing the mind, and so forth.

These ten questions caused those who had given rise to faith to observe themselves through contemplation, making their realization increasingly profound and firm. As the Sūtra says: "All dharmas are without functional activity and possess no intrinsic nature."
Therefore, all those things do not know one another; they serve as metaphors for how water flows, fire blazes, wind arises, and the earth produces [things], yet none of these know one another.
Furthermore, the subsequent verse says: "When one analytically contemplates the internal body, who herein is the 'self'?
If one can understand in this way, one realizes the existence and non-existence of the self. Thus it is said in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā*.

The gate of the contemplative practice of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) accomplished by the Bodhisattva Śrī-mukha is fully explained as described in the "Chapter on the Clarification of Questions" (*Pṛcchā-vibhāga*).

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Śrī-mukha," it is taught that from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one takes faith as the foremost and resolutely seeks the fruit of the Great Bodhi of the Buddha;
thus, from the ground of an ordinary person, one believes that the Mind of Non-discriminating Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from one's own mind.
Because of wisdom, yet because one is deluded by ignorance, there is no duality between ignorance and the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions from the very beginning.
Therefore, from the stage of an ordinary person, one should believe that the fundamental wisdom of the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from one's own.
Why is this? Because they are all the same Dharma-nature body and the same fundamental wisdom, just like a tree.
From a single branch grow many branches, leaves, and so forth; because of causes and conditions, formation and disintegration occur differently upon the same tree branch.
Therefore, from the stage of an ordinary person, I have been able to fully practice the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because I recall that since beginningless time, I have been swept along in the current of the ocean of suffering.
If one still performs even those matters that are of minor benefit, how much more so now for those matters that are truly beneficial?

How could a Bodhisattva not undertake the myriad practices for the salvation of sentient beings? From the stage of an ordinary person, one should believe that all Buddhas of the ten directions arise from samādhi;
I, too, shall surely attain it. Why is this? Because the samādhis of all Buddhas arise from the Tathāgata himself.
I too possess the nature born of skillful means—the naturally pure essence of the Tathāgata—which is equal to that of the Buddhas.
From the stage of an ordinary person, I have believed that I shall likewise attain all the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Why is this?
Because while the supernatural powers of the Buddhas rely upon true wisdom (*jñāna*), within my own reliance on the wisdom of true nature (*dharmatā-jñāna*), they do not exist.
When afflictions and ignorance are transformed into wisdom, all karmic activities cease; there remains only wisdom and compassion, which transform beings with sovereign mastery.
From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes that the Buddha’s wisdom is something I too shall attain.

Why? Because all Buddhas have come from the state of being ordinary persons. From the stage of an ordinary person, one believes in the Buddha’s great compassion, which universally covers all; I too [shall attain it].

"How shall I attain this? For what reason? Because the great compassion of all Buddhas arises from great vows, and I, like the Buddhas, have likewise made great vows. How shall I attain mastery? For what reason?

Because the mastery of all Buddhas—within the gateways of the Dharma arising from their nature, through their wisdom-body and dharma-body—enters the realm of sentient beings without being stained by them."

Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom arises from the nature that is not separate from the self of all the sensory faculties amidst the dust of the world, one begins from the stage of an ordinary person by generating the mind through faith;
after practicing meritorious deeds throughout inexhaustible kalpas, when the stages are fulfilled and equalized with those of the Buddhas, not even a single thought is shifted.
Why is this? Because the three periods of time have no temporal duration. Thus it begins from the ordinary person’s stage of faith and understanding.
Ultimately reaching the stage of Buddhahood, those who have developed the ten kinds of faith as described above will certainly be able to achieve the gateway of the ten faiths;
they shall abide in the seeds of firmness and never regress.
Furthermore, among these ten faiths, Mañjuśrī and the ten Chief Bodhisattvas, such as Buddhasimha and others, have all come from the worlds of the ten colors.
That which is called the Golden World signifies that [the teaching] comes from within the fundamentally pure Dharma; it clarifies that faith relies upon the fundamental faith.
That which is the World of Wondrous Colors signifies that faith arises through the sovereign and wondrous function of relying on both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
That which is the Lotus-Colored World signifies that one is able to believe by relying on practice; for the lotus represents the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*).

The world of *Campaka* flower color symbolizes that faith arises from the colors of merit and blessing through the nature of great compassion, wisdom, and the harmony of the Middle Way; among the five colors, yellow is supreme.
This is the color of the Arhats (*Arhat*), as well as the color of the Central Palace. Because it represents the color of the Middle Way, this flower is yellow.

Because this Bodhisattva of faithful mind has come from the world of the True Correspondence (Yingzhen), which is the color of the harmony between wisdom and compassion, the world of the Utpala Flower color represents that its flowers are reddish-yellow and possess a purple-flame fragrance;
this signifies that through both the single practice and all practices, one is able to generate faith whether purely or mixedly. The world of Jewel Color represents wisdom.

Because the practice of the Dharma of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is accomplished through faith and is thus worthy of esteem, the world of vajra-color symbolizes the generation of faith through the virtues of the Buddha-fruit;
because it is able to decisively sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), the world of sapphire-color resembles crystal and symbolizes that the essence of faith is fundamentally pure;
and the world of equal-color symbolizes that faith in the *dharmadhātu* is impartial.
Because they are equal and non-dual, these ten worlds of form are all dharma-gates of faith for Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths;
they all emerge from the dharma-gate of self-confidence, and are therefore said to come from such worlds.
Below this is the original Buddha whom they serve, namely: Akṣayamati-buddha (Immovable Wisdom Buddha), Asaṅga-jñāna-buddha (Unobstructed Wisdom Buddha), and Vimukti-buddha (Liberation Buddha).
These ten Wisdom-Buddhas (*jñāna-buddha*) are precisely the Buddhas within the fruit of Buddhahood. They clearly manifest one's own wisdom by taking the Buddha’s fruit-wisdom as its cause;
for it is shown that faith cannot be established without the fruit of Buddhahood as its cause.

Thus, during the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), [the Bodhisattva] ascends to the summit of Mount Sumeru and emits hundreds of thousands of wondrously colored rays of light from the tips of his two toes.
The ten stages of faith prior to the [ten] abodes are symbolized by the emission of light from the thousand-spoked wheels beneath the two feet in the Hall of Universal Radiance;

this signifies that the stage of faith belongs to ordinary beings who have not yet departed from the level of worldlings. The light emanating from beneath the feet symbolizes taking faith as the beginning, as its position is the lowest.
Now, explaining the ascent to the summit of Mount Sumeru for the ten abodes clarifies the nature of these ten abodes.
Because the beginner realizes the summit of the Dharma, they ascend from the earth to the limit where characteristics are exhausted;
because they reach the summit of the King of Mountains, the station of the Dharma King, it is clarified that *śamatha* (calm abiding) is the mountain.

As for entering reality and realizing that which is not [merely] *śamatha*, the emission of hundreds of thousands of rays of wondrous colors from the tips of the two feet serves to clarify the "feet."
*Gen* (Mounting) represents the fingers of the hands and feet; the first [line] takes up the Sage’s Way, which is not merely a lack of illumination, but signifies the beginning of treading upon it.

It marks the initial stage of following, the position of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) at the level of the Ten Faiths. Its ultimate beginning lies at the commencement of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*).

Treading thus from the very start upon the sacred tracks of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, one uses the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to universally contemplate all realms of both ordinary and sagely beings, wherein their nature and characteristics are non-dual.
Because there is no obstructive form that is not wondrous, it is called "light. As the *Bunyō-kyōraku-kyō* (Sutra of the Garland of Original Karma) says:
"By practicing the Dharma of the Three Worthies and entering the Dharma-stream of the stage of the Sages, mind after mind is quiescent, naturally flowing into the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment.
However, the meaning of this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is not so; when consciousness ceases, time perishes, and the objects of the senses are suddenly severed. Only...
In the realm of true wisdom, a single thought-moment illuminates all five stages simultaneously;
because the fruit of Buddhahood is taken entirely as the cause, even if an ordinary person dwells for a hundred years or many kalpas, they do not see the slightest shift in their own views.

They do not see that they will become a Buddha, nor do they see that they have already become a Buddha, nor do they see that they are currently becoming a Buddha—this is the state of the Ten Abidings.
Since the dharma-position is thus, what further birth could there be that does not achieve Buddhahood? What further birth could there be that achieves perfect enlightenment?
This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the gate of the fundamental Dharma-realm, the great ancestral abode where all Buddhas dwell, and the ultimate destination to which all Buddha-sons return.
Those of the transformation bodies and provisional vehicles all reside outside of it. If...

As for "entering," there is one entry into the entirety of True Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Within this stage, the Bodhisattva in the first dwelling of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*) enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*) through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because they directly share the same physical, mental, and cognitive characteristics as the Tathāgata, they suddenly seal all five stages (*pañcavihāra*);
their modes of practice are entirely contained therein. It is like holding a bright mirror that universally reflects all forms; such is the Dharma of this sutra.
The principle of the gate is thus: all that is praised and spoken of should be known in this way and understood with faith in this way.

As for the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm, it is perfect and without beginning or end; within a single thought-moment, years, months, and the cycles of darkness and light are layered and inexhaustible.
Within a single hair-tip, the realm of the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings have boundless forms and characteristics; when one is accomplished, all are accomplished.
"One destruction, all destructions. Within these ten stages of abiding (*daśabhūmi*), there are ten bodhisattvas;
those below share the same name, "Root of Wisdom" (*prajñāmūla*). Their original lands are all called "Flower"; they come from ten Flower-lands.
The Buddhas they originally served are all named "Moon. The commentary states: "In this stage, one realizes it for oneself."

Truly discerning the good and simplifying the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*). When principle and phenomena arise simultaneously, it blossoms like a flower;
taking the opening of the Dharma-gates as its dwelling place, one attains the Dharma and eliminates affliction, becoming as cool as the moon.
This is named the Buddha whom one originally serves. These designations collectively represent the Dharma-gates realized within the stages of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*); they are no empty names.
The Sūtra also says: At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Skillful Means.

By the power of this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields, all bearing the same name: Dharmamati.
He appeared before them all and bestowed thirteen kinds of empowerments upon the Bodhisattva Dharmamati. Regarding these thirteen empowerments:

the empowerment of verbal action consisted of praising him with the words, "Excellent! Excellent! The empowerment of physical action consisted of stroking the crown of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati’s head with his hand.
The empowerment of the wisdom of knowledge is stated in the sutra as follows: he immediately granted the Bodhisattva Dharmamati ten kinds of unimpeded wisdom.
And that the light of the Tathāgata of this land shines upon their bodies— this is the thirteenth [mark].

Qián (qù yán qiè). Bō (běi mò qiè). Chì (chǐ yīn). Wù (wǔ gù qiè). Chú (zhí yú qiè). Jiāo (jǔ qiáo qiè).
Jī (gǔ xī qiè). Cè (chǔ gé qiè). Juān (gǔ xuán qiè). Zé (chí gé qiè). Jùn (zǐ jùn qiè). Xiáng (sì yáng qiè). Méng (mò gēng qiè).

The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Expanded and Vast Teachings, Scroll Five.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Layman of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty: A Concordance of Sutras and Treatises. [Treatise]:
The reason why the Buddhas of the ten directions are given the same name, "Wisdom" (Hui), is that through this Dharma of the Ten Abodes, they have realized the stage of sainthood;
as their flow of Dharma has already entered the great ocean of the Dharma-realm, they share with the Buddhas entry into the wisdom of the saintly stage. Therefore, the Buddha and the Dharma...
The Bodhisattvas share the same names to signify that the dharmas they represent are identical; furthermore, it clarifies that the causes and effects of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are equal.
Since the fruit-virtues of the Buddha-stage constitute the cause for the Bodhisattvas, and the essence of cause and fruit is not different, they are spoken of by the same names.
When these ten stages were taught, [the Buddha] ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru, where there are six chapters of sutra that together form ten.
The characteristics of the practice of the Dharma-gates consist of: (1) the Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru; (2) the Chapter on Verses of Praise;
(3) the Chapter on the Ten Abodes; (4) the Chapter on Holy Conduct; (5) the Chapter on the Merit of First Generating the Bodhicitta; and (6) the Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma.
By studying and entering into the Dharma-gates of understanding and practice according to these six chapters of the sutra, one will certainly be able to accomplish the Dharma of the Ten Abodes.
Abiding in the gate, one is born into the lineage of the Buddhas and enters the family of the Tathāgatas, becoming a true son of the Buddha;

this differs from the provisional teachings where it is said that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) merely begins to be born into the Buddha-family, or where it is said that Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ pūjyāḥ*) attain Buddhahood through their vows.

This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* discusses directly the stage of actual realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) without relying on vows; thus, for this teaching-gate, all [stages] are subsumed as being simultaneous and of one time.
In the ultimate single Dharma-realm, there is no differentiated thought; the sentiments of before and after are severed, and the nature of ordinary beings and sages is one.

One should not engage in conceptual calculations, but should instead perceive it through the gate of the non-conceptual, non-active Dharma-realm. If one establishes views based on emotional attachments, they cannot be trusted.
Even if faith were to arise, it would be a matter of trusting the Buddha’s words from afar rather than being one's own vision. If it were one's own vision, [it would be true].

When insentient things are free from conceptualization and the mind is extinguished, one merges with principle; when wisdom is darkly unified with the object, one then knows that the nature of the myriad realms is mutually pervasive.
If it were not thus, the mind would constantly oscillate between this and that, competing with likes and dislikes, and how could defilement and purity ever cease?

If one can truly claim that the nature is extinguished, then the gate of the profound mystery of the Dharma-realm will spontaneously open, and the one and the many, the pure and the mixed, will be mastered with sovereign ease.

Encompassing both the general and the specific, one attains perfect mastery and sovereignty in the methods for benefiting sentient beings; being well-versed in the various faculties, one brings benefit to all according to their capacities.
