Those who respectfully receive and draw near to such a person are all treated as friends, just as when [the Buddha] ascended to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven and preached the "Chapter on the Ten Practices," or as when the Tathāgata emitted hundreds of thousands of rays from the two soles of his feet.

With wondrous forms and radiant light as its manifest support, one establishes practice based upon emptiness; only then can one attain mastery over both principle and phenomena, clarifying the stage of the Ten Abidings.
At the stage of the Ten Practices, one realizes the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya;

it is only through the unimpeded fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya that one can perform the myriad practices, and these practices themselves are likewise unimpeded. If one does not perceive the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, then the myriad practices performed will not be realized.
All these belong to the causes and effects of humans and devas; they are all tainted merits subject to arising and ceasing.

Using the self-wisdom of the *dharmakāya* to treat all delusions, and using the compassion of the myriad practices to save sentient beings, the *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya* employ non-conceptual great compassion (*anabhisaṃskāra-mahākaruṇā*) instantaneously and all at once.
Although this is provisionally associated with the characteristics of the seventh stage where compassion increases and the eighth stage where wisdom increases.
This "Dharma-realm Gate" of the *Avataṃsaka* encompasses all stages within the first stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
Because in this initial gate of the Ten Abodes, the stage is identical to the Buddha-fruit as the single essence and function of the Dharma-realm;

and because within a single stage, the ten *pāramitās* and the various sets of ten dharmas are fully present—when illuminated by the "Gate of the Profound Mystery of All Dharmas," this can be seen. This, then, is the comprehensive totality.
The Dharma Gate of the Tathāgatagarbha-body and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Ocean-like World-Whirlpools: This is like the sun and moon shining upon those who are blind;
it is not the fault of the sun and moon. One should instead reproach oneself and follow virtue, regarding them with the highest reverence.
To observe the Tathāgatagarbha-body through concentration and wisdom is to realize that this very body is the Dharmakāya, the ocean of all merit and wisdom.

Because there is nothing that does not abide within it, it is called a "repository" (garbha). If one does not perceive the Dharma-body, all merit, wisdom, great compassion, and great pity will fail to be accomplished;
they would all belong to the whirlpools of the world-ocean of birth and death. Within these, compassion and wisdom observe the various capacities of beings, which are winding and crooked;
the bodies, lands, and karmas extend through the mundane and reach into the profound. Sentient beings are multilayered, and their various karmas are each distinct.
Because compassion universally saves all faculties without exception, it is called a "vortex" (*samudra-āvarta*). A vortex signifies a profound eddy.

Just as this, within the state of the Buddha-fruit, when a Bodhisattva enters the gateway of the Dharma-realm, they encompass the karmic activities of the infinite, layered faculties of sentient beings;
thus, they lack any thought of departing from the world and are forever submerged in the swirling currents of the great ocean of birth and death.
Because they emerge and submerge [within one another], these ten stages of practice (*caryā*) are identical to the practices of Samantabhadra;

the preceding ten abodes (*vihāra*) are identical to the fundamental, signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) of the Dharma-body of Mañjuśrī. These two persons are of a single essence, acting as both master and attendant to one another.

The intermediate non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) constitutes the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, the three bodies are one, provisionally established across five stages to guide ordinary beings and those who are deluded.
If there are ordinary beings who, having fulfilled their faith and resolved their minds, attain the three bodies at the beginning of the ten stages,
they realize that Mañjuśrī is the Dharma-body of the Buddha, Samantabhadra is the practice-body of the Buddha, and non-active wisdom is the fruition-body of the Buddha. With the signless,
wondrous wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body as their precursor, they first preach and subsequently realize it.
The three bodies are simultaneously and inherently united with the Dharma in this way; it is impossible to discard one.

If one were to discard Mañjuśrī while retaining Samantabhadra, all the gates of practice would belong to the outflows (*āsrava*). If one were to discard Samantabhadra while retaining Mañjuśrī, the realized quiescent concentration would be that of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

If one were to discard the Buddha while retaining Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, [it would be untenable], for "Buddha" carries the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*); there could be no such thing as non-awakening. Therefore...
For this reason, one cannot discard any one of these three types of persons; if one were discarded, the triad would not be established.
Therefore, within the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, these three types of persons do not depart from one another from beginning to end.

Because the gates of the teaching have not yet reached ultimate reality, they are all collectively manifestations of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), provisionally following after those of lesser faculties. Thus, the provisional teaching is briefly applied, awaiting their maturation before finally leading them toward the ultimate.
In truth, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, all things gradually transition toward the ultimate teaching (*yāna*).

In this very sūtra, the initial stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) is identical to the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), and the stage of equal enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
One attains both the beginning and the end, with these positions mutually interpenetrating; within a single position, one attains fifty dharma-gates through their mutual integration.
Because they are thoroughly penetrated, within each and every stage, the meanings of the two thousand five hundred general and specific dharmas appear simultaneously;

this continues even unto the inexhaustible stages. The characteristics of progressive cultivation through these successive levels are not abandoned as they gradually become unified in a single moment, nor is this gradual process abandoned within that single moment.
Within these ten stages of practice, for each of the ten directions, there is one Great [Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattvas came to where the Buddha was, each leading a multitude of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, and they gathered there.
The names of the ten principal Bodhisattvas were all identical, being called "Forest Root" (Linben);

the names of the lands from which they originally came were all identical, being called "Wisdom Root" (Huiben); and the names of the Buddhas whom they had served were all identical, being called... [name of Buddha].
On each of the ten eyes are ten principal bodhisattvas, all of whom share the same name, "Lín-lín" (Forest-Forest). Each possesses five virtues: first, the virtue of establishing [the foundation];

second, the virtue of non-arising, wherein the body, roots, trunk, branches, and twigs mutually give rise to one another; third, the virtue of accomplishing benefit through flowers, leaves, and fruits;
fourth, the virtue of providing coolness by obstructing the heat of the sun; and fifth, the virtue of being inhabited by humans, devas, birds, and beasts.
As for the phrase "the place where spirits and deities return, what is this virtue? it refers to the establishment of a forest.
This virtue is like a great forest within which dragon deities dwell, which cannot be broken by great winds from without; were it not so, it could not be established as a lofty and prominent grove.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage possesses the dragon of great wisdom within, which is constantly sustained by great compassion.
Divine, he naturally guards the realm; the realm itself is quiescent. Without external objects of form, the winds of heterodox and deviant doctrines are shattered by wisdom.
Being free from the duality of subject and object, he establishes the myriad practices and shares them equally with all sentient beings.
Because he constantly acts for their benefit, he establishes these virtues. Second, what are called the body, the roots, and the trunk?

Branches and twigs depend upon one another to arise; yet, because they lack the quality of intrinsic arising, if one seeks within the trunk, branches, and twigs of the tree for the nature of that which produces and that which is produced, each is found to be unobtainable. They are merely phenomena born of conditions (*pratyaya-ja*).
Since the conditions themselves have nothing produced, they are fundamentally non-arising; yet this non-arising is itself arising. To clarify this state, [the Buddha addressed] the Bodhisattva.
Because the gates of the practices one undertakes are inexhaustible, and because the primordial wisdom of the *dharmakāya* serves as the precursor, one constantly performs the myriad practices;
yet, within the body and its objects, neither the agent of practice nor the object of practice can be found. One practices solely because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such.
Third, what are the virtues of the flowers, leaves, fruits, and seeds that bring about benefit? It is like a forest where flowers bloom.
Its leaves bring joy and delight to those who behold them; they can shield against the heat and provide refreshing coolness.

Its fruits nourish sentient beings, satisfying all who suffer from hunger and thirst. This illustrates that the Bodhisattva of this stage constantly practices the ten thousand deeds, bringing joy to the sight of gods and humans;
he spreads the leaves of great compassion far and wide, causing others to draw near him without abandoning him, and bestows great generosity.

The fruit of wisdom is such that it suffices the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and causes all sentient beings to be fully satisfied; only when this original vow is fulfilled does it come to an end.
Fourth, what is the virtue of being cool amidst the blazing heat of obstacles? It is said to be like a forest: whoever returns to it shall all escape the heat and obtain the joy of coolness.
To clarify the nature of this forest—it is entirely devoid of mind—so too is the Bodhisattva who has reached this stage the refuge for all.
As for "reliance," according to their respective faculties and natures, all attain the coolness of the fundamental nature; being without a [discriminating] mind, there is neither benefit nor harm.

Fifth, as for "the place where spirits and deities resort": this refers to the virtue of having excellent, lush forests where many people gather to harvest, many dragons dwell, and various birds congregate.
It clarifies that a Bodhisattva in this stage is likewise so, establishing the forest of the myriad practices (*sādhana*).
It is where all people turn for refuge to gather its manifold virtues; it is the dwelling place of dragons and spirits who always pay respect;
it is where birds and beasts turn for refuge to be free from fear. Furthermore, "forest" (*vana*) carries many meanings because the bodhisattva at this stage establishes numerous practices.
Moreover, because the practices are numerous, the merits are likewise numerous; that is to say, through the Dharma-body, compassion, and wisdom, one performs various deeds and accumulates merits.
Because it is like a forest, for this reason the lower names of the Bodhisattvas are all collectively called "Forest.
Why are the original lands from which they come all collectively called "Wisdom"?

Ordinary people name the land where they reside a "country," whereas these Bodhisattvas of this stage name their own and others' peaceful sustenance through concentration, wisdom, and liberation "Country."
In establishing a nation, all are made to leave suffering; this is what is called a "nation.
A nation inhabited by earth, water, fire, and wind is a reflection of the karma of sentient beings and is not real.

Therefore, the Dharma-body, wisdom, and liberation are the nation that is the eternally abiding essence of all Bodhisattvas, not a nation produced by the illusions of karma. For this reason, the Bodhisattva, by means of...

Wisdom is the country; furthermore, because the Bodhisattvas at this stage establish the myriad practices and, through their practice and understanding, benefit sentient beings—wherein their conduct is capable of shared participation (*samānārthatā*) and their wisdom is capable of establishing teachings to bring benefit and joy to humans and devas—the place they inhabit is called a "country.
Why are the Buddhas whom they originally serve all given the same name, "Eye"? This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* uses phenomena to symbolize the Dharma, for its...
The name "Buddha" is so called because he has realized that which is to be realized and because he abides in the state of the Dharma thus realized;

for this stage of Bodhisattva, who benefits sentient beings through practice and is well able to observe their faculties, who accords with the Dharma according to those faculties and delivers them without missing the proper time, he is called an "Eye.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva’s skillful..."
Having entered this samādhi through contemplation, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions,
there appear before him as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, all named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merits).
They bestow upon the Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa the thirteen kinds of augmentations previously described, just as they do for a Buddha at the stage of fruition.

Within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body, compassion and wisdom are always manifest; the gates of concentration and wisdom should always be fully possessed—what need is there to enter formal meditative absorption?
The Buddhas come to bestow their empowerment and establish teachings for the sake of all Bodhisattvas to deliver sentient beings, forming essential rules for accomplishment.

It is said that the Buddha’s spiritual power attributes excellence to the Honored One; yet while the essence of the Dharma-realm is uniform and equal, such distinctions are made for the purpose of the transformative ritual.

Therefore, it is necessary to maintain the relationship between teacher and disciple as a matter of pedagogical method (*vyavahāra*). One enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to contemplate the Dharma, and only upon emerging from absorption does one preach.

"Samādhi" is defined as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), which induces correct understanding and is thus termed "virtuous reflection" (*samyak-manasikāra*). Within the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), one transcends a thousand Buddha-worlds;
within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), one transcends ten thousand Buddha-worlds—these signify the expansion of one's rank and the manifestation of the pedagogical method.
The patterns of their conduct, the features of their brows and eyes, and their dharmic attributes are thus identical; yet their true nature fills the ten directions.

That the Buddhas coming from other directions and the Bodhisattvas who have entered samādhi share the same name, "Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha" (Forest of Merits), clarifies that cause and effect are equal and that their dharma-knowledge is of one kind; it is because these Buddhas coming from elsewhere and the Bodhisattvas who have entered samādhi bear the same name.
The thirteen kinds of empowerment are: first, empowerment by speech; second, empowerment by hand through the touching of the crown of the head; third, the bestowal of the ten kinds of wisdom;
and fourth, the illumination of his body by the light of the Tathāgata of this realm. Empowerment by speech signifies that the Dharma is not erroneous.

Empowerment by hand through the touching of the crown of the head signifies the union of the marks of the Dharmakāya—wisdom, compassion, knowledge, vision, and liberation. Furthermore, the touching of the crown of the head signifies consolation.
Regarding the phrase "in accord with the ten knowledges" (*daśajñāna-samprayukta*): it is called "in accord" because the wisdom of the Bodhisattva is equal to the fruit of Buddhahood;
furthermore, it is called "the Buddha is in accord" because he attributes his virtues to others, being humble and free from pride.

In the sūtras, these terms are all used because such is the nature of the Dharma, because they arise from one's own roots of goodness, and because they are the conventional rules of the transformative teachings (*nirmāṇa-vinaya*). This is why these words exist.
The stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi-prasthāna*) consists of four chapters of the sutra that together establish the gateway of its methodological principles:
(1) "Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven," (2) "Verses of Praise in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven," (3) "The Ten Practices," and (4) "The Chapter on the Inexhaustible Storehouse.
All the dharma-gates contained within the gateway of the Ten Practices should be practiced in accordance with these four chapters of the sutra.
The principles and phenomena are all fully complete. As it was said when the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" was taught:
for what reason did [the Buddha] ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven? For what reason did the Tathāgata emit light from between his two knees?

For what reason were the names of the leading Bodhisattvas all identical, being called "Dhvaja" (Banner)? From what land did they come, and why were the names of those lands all identical, being called "Sudarśana" (Wonderful)?
The Buddhas whom I have served in the past all share the same name; they are called "Dharmadhvaja.

As for the Tuṣita Heaven, because it occupies the middle position between the upper and lower regions of the Desire Realm, it is like the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, which is entirely subsumed under Śakra.
Likewise, the summit of Mount Sumeru is entirely comprised within the domain of a single heaven. The Yāma Heaven is named the Second Heaven, and the [Heaven of] the Four Kings is the Fourth Heaven.
The King, Śakra Devānām Indra, the realm of Sumeru, and the Yāma Heaven; above these are the celestial abodes (*antarikṣavāsin*).
In order, there are the Tuṣita Heaven below, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven above, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven situated between them.
Because these heavens occupy the central position within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is here that the assembly of the Dharma and the assembly of affairs convene.

The turning of the Way toward phenomena and the turning of phenomena toward principle constitute the gate of the wondrous function of wisdom and compassion, wherein principle and phenomena are unimpeded;

therefore, it is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*). Now, at the beginning of the Ten Abodes, principle and phenomena have been inherently united from the start and do not only come into existence through dedication in subsequent stages.
However, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, one must maintain the formal rules of the Dharma, beginning from the very first aspiration.
After the mind has become established, within the subsequent five stages, the principle and phenomena are fundamentally and naturally dedicated;

now, within this third stage, one dedicates each of the preceding ten abodes and ten practices, and because these individual dharma-positions are explained without obstruction, it is named the "Stage of Dedication" (pariṇāmanā).
It does not reside in the third [stage] alone, for it universally harmonizes all positions and is thus called dedication. This is because it relies upon phenomena to manifest the Dharma. Therefore...
When this deva spoke of the ten dedications, light was emitted from the Tathāgata’s knees; this was because there is nothing more sovereign than the knees for revolving, bending, and extending.

Thus, light in the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas was emitted from his knees to symbolize the unimpeded mastery over both principle and phenomena, and over nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, as well as the sovereign freedom of rolling up and unfolding. Furthermore, it is also for this reason.

The phenomena manifested herein—this specific portion of the scripture consisting of names, objects, locations, bodily forms, designations, and the emission of light—are all the self-realized Dharma-gates that are manifested.
Within this stage, the foremost Bodhisattvas are called "Banners" and "Lamps";
these Bodhisattvas of the Ten Dedication Practices possess mastery over wisdom and compassion, capable of destroying [the afflictions of] both themselves and others.
The afflictions and karma within the cycle of birth and death can establish all manner of virtues; this is termed a "banner" (*dhvaja*).

A banner signifies the meaning of establishing virtue without wavering, the meaning of subduing enemies, the meaning of destruction, and the meaning of firmness. It is the banner of the Dharma established by supreme wisdom, erected upon the foundation of great compassion;
it is firm, crushing the mountains of pride, traversing the jewel path, and resting upon the lotus throne to achieve wondrous enlightenment. Therefore:

The Bodhisattva at this stage is called a "Banner" (*dhvaja*), because through immovable and effortless wisdom and compassion, they are able to shatter the cycle of birth and death for both themselves and others. Furthermore,
because the teachings of this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* hold that the fruit of Buddhahood is present within each stage— the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the ten grounds—
this Bodhisattva at this stage is able to establish supreme virtues while remaining constantly within the realm of birth and death, bound by their vow.
To deliver all inexhaustible sentient beings while one’s wisdom remains free from timidity or fear is called the "Banner" (Dhvaja);
because this wisdom realizes the non-existence of ignorance, it is impossible for there to be any sense of longing or aversion.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), if there should be a beggar who asks for all manner of wealth and treasures, even exhausting everything in the world—including one's own body or life—whatever exists in the world shall be given.
To have a mind that is entirely joyful and unshakable is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*); "banner" carries the meaning of being unshakable.
There are two kinds of giving: first, giving through the Dharma; second, giving through material things. Giving through the Dharma means bestowing the Dharma upon others;
because there is no sense of "mine," all thoughts are absent, and this is called giving through the Dharma. Giving through material things means bestowing physical objects.
Sentient beings have no stinginess regarding what they seek in terms of body, life, or wealth;

the Bodhisattva in this stage practices two kinds of giving, constantly and without weariness, as explained extensively in the section on the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). What is the land from which [the light] comes?
It is named "Subtle Radiance" (*Sūkṣma-prabhāsa*). The Bodhisattva in this stage possesses the wondrous application of wisdom, which, through its sovereign and subtle functioning, remains unimpeded.
The faults of existence and non-existence, as well as various views, measures, limitations, and obstructions, are termed "realms" (*kṣetra*). What is the fundamental object of service?
It is the Buddhas who share the same name as "Banner" (*dhvaja*), identical in title to oneself. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage has perfected wondrous function;

in terms of principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, the essence of this stage is equal to that of the Buddha. It is likewise the same as the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) previously mentioned.
The status and the causal body of the Buddha with whom one serves are equal in each stage; such is the case at every level.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared [Buddhas] as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields.
The number of Buddhas was all identical in name, each being named Vajradhvaja, who appeared before him; it was just as previously described with thirteen kinds of empowerments.

Then, addressing the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, he said: "By the Buddha’s spiritual power"—this attributes the virtue to the Honored One, expressing the respect of a disciple toward his teacher—"he entered the Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom"; this refers to the samādhi of equal entry. Entering this samādhi induces its arising.
The light of immeasurable teachings takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as its essence and differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) as the light of the teachings.
This wisdom, which accords with the faculties [of beings] and bestows benefit, is the light capable of destroying darkness;

it is the teaching because it can destroy delusion, giving rise to clear understanding and opening the sun of wisdom for all sentient beings, so that the dense clouds and dark nights of those beings [may be dispelled].

Because it can resolve delusions, it enables the blind and the deaf to open their eyes and ears; because it can cause the mountains of false pride to collapse entirely, the light of the teaching is thus inconceivable.
In the preceding ten stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha entered the Samādhi of Excellent Contemplation;
in these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja enters the Light of Wisdom.
In this samādhi, the five stages are clarified through their successive expansion, with the characteristics of the eyebrows, eyes, and conduct made manifest.
While the preceding stage clarifies the initial skillful contemplation, this stage clarifies the mastery of wondrous function, wherein the light of the teaching shines far and wide.

Where the preceding stage surpassed the dust-motes of ten thousand Buddha-fields, this stage surpasses the world-systems of the dust-motes of one hundred thousand Buddha-fields; beyond these lie one hundred thousand Buddhas.
Even as Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a world-system arrive, they clarify the stages of the five positions as gates for progressive cultivation;

all involve the transcendence of deluded emotions through entry into the gate of Samādhi and Prajñā. Only when one illuminates both principle and phenomenon with the "Twofold Mystery" can confusion be resolved;
one must not hastily judge or give rise to overweening pride. Regarding the thirteen empowerments: the first ten consist of praising with words and stroking the crown of the head with the hand.
When the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja bestow upon him these ten kinds of wisdom, the Tathāgata of this land illuminates his body with light;
as for the thirteen empowerments, praising him with words is to clarify that the one who expounds the Dharma and the Dharma itself are not erroneous.
Rubbing the crown of his head signifies that the one who expounds the Dharma has attained union with the Buddha-wisdom, thereby granting him wisdom.

This clarifies that the speaker of the Dharma is identical to the Buddha’s wisdom; thus, the fact that the Tathāgata of this land illuminates his body clarifies that he is united with the Buddha’s light of teaching.
Furthermore, it is because the light awakens and touches him that he is permitted to preach the Dharma. Thirteenth, regarding the addition of the mental faculty:
it is intended to eliminate doubts in future generations, establish the Dharma, and inspire faith; such is the actual substance of the treatise.

In all cases, the Buddhas establish their names and manifest their bodies according to the fundamental dharmas of each of the five stages of practice, serving as models for sentient beings to emulate and learn from, thereby enabling them to awaken and enter [the Way].

Since the Buddhas have established these teachings, those who study them will certainly not find them in vain; this is why they are given the same names. These are the Ten Abodes and the Ten Practices.

The middle section has already been explained. Within this stage, there are three chapters: "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," "Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," and "The Ten Dedications. These three chapters of the sutra constitute this single stage.

As for the methods, applications, and rules of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications, those who study them should follow these established principles, just as it was taught during the exposition of the "Ten Grounds" chapter.
For what reason does he not ascend sequentially from Tuṣita Heaven to Nirmāṇarati Heaven? For what reason does he bypass Nirmāṇarati Heaven to ascend to Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven?
This is to clarify that the merit of the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages is vast and expansive, encompassing objects of perception that transcend sequential order;
furthermore, it clarifies that the wondrous functions of the ten stages are boundless, such that their accumulated merits manifest spontaneously.
Regarding the place where he dwells, he must also possess mastery; thus, like those gods, he is called "Vasavartin" (Mastery-Attainer).

Furthermore, it is clarified that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, because they accord with the essence of reality, have no mind and no self-mind, yet their transformations arise for the sake of sentient beings.
Because their great compassionate wisdom arises from others, their transformative virtues resemble those gods. Since this place serves as a manifestation of such virtues, for this reason—

The Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) were taught in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), because their merit is superior to that of the preceding stages and thus must transcend them in sequence;
secondly, because they manifest mastery over emanating for the sake of sentient beings, the Ten Stages were taught in this celestial realm.
Just as the stage of Samantabhadra and others is the rank of awakening, [the assembly] gathered from the third dhyāna heaven and the eight dhyāna heavens to enter the Buddha-flower Samādhi.
I have expounded one hundred trillion verses; the text of this single assembly is so vast that it cannot be transmitted or maintained in the world.
Such "transcending intermediate stages" is doubling [the merit] at each step prior to the Buddha-flower, which is the practice of the Buddhas.

Entering the Samādhi of Buddha-practice is the practice of Samantabhadra within the Dharma-realm. For what reason are there the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences?
Among the four assemblies, why are only ten leading bodhisattvas mentioned?
Within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), why are thirty-seven bodhisattvas mentioned who all share the same name, "Treasury" (*kośa*)?
Why is the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra alone named "Moon"? In this single division of the teaching, each bodhisattva [attains] the fruit of Buddhahood.
The equality of merit is manifested by the fact that Buddhas from the ten directions and Bodhisattvas who have entered meditative concentration share the same names;

this signifies that within their respective stages, the Bodhisattvas' realization and entry are equal to those of the Buddhas, such that cause and fruit are similar, thereby forming a model for emulation.
Nevertheless, within the six and five stages, there are no lack of gradations; the principles of identity and difference interweave and diverge, capable of reflecting one another in subtle variation.

The pure, the mixed, the identical, the distinct, the formative, and the disintegrating can be understood by applying the gates of the six characteristics—totality, particularity, identity, difference, formation, and destruction.

Regarding these six gates, each single gate contains all six, which mutually interpenetrate. The six characteristics are: first, the gate of totality; second, the gate of particularity; third, the gate of identity; fourth, the gate of difference;
fifth, the gate of formation; and sixth, the gate of destruction. The meaning of these six gates is such that within a single gate, all six are fully present, acting as one another's counterparts.
First, the pure and the mixed may not be discarded; the same applies to the ten layers of profound meaning (*shichong xuan yi*).
Although this text is extensive and appears in a separate edition, it shall for now be consulted as a reflection [of the core teaching].

As for the dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they are established within a separate section to explain their modes of practice (*lakṣaṇa*) at the level of hierarchical progression. These ten stages constitute the final teaching of the fruit of the Middle Way; therefore—
In the preceding stage, light was emitted from above the knees; in this stage, the Tathāgata emits a pure radiance from between his eyebrows called "Flame-Light of Bodhisattva Power.
These hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays constitute its retinue.

This light from between the eyebrows signifies the meaning of the culmination of the fruit of the Middle Way. This light from between the eyebrows first appeared during the initial assembly of the Tathāgata.
In the Chapter on Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇaparivarta*), the Tathāgata emits from between his eyebrows a light of the merit of fruition that enters into the wheels beneath his feet;
by means of the fruit, he causes the cause to be established, thereby causing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to manifest the merit of the Buddha’s fruition so that [beings] may develop faith and delight.
Once such delight has arisen, he then expounds the gate of faith. Immediately within the Chapter on Awakening to Light (*Prabhābodhiparivarta*), [the light] again issues forth from beneath both feet.
From within the wheel, he first emits light from between his eyebrows; this light of fruition and virtue enters and illuminates the Golden World.
Thus, through the Buddha Akṣobhya-jñāna, the stage of faith is established. Subsequently, when he was about to expound the "Ten Abodes" chapter, he ascended the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Then, in the "Verses of Praise" chapter, he emitted light from the tips of the Tathāgata’s two toes, following in sequence.
When about to expound the "Chapter on the Ten Practices," light was emitted from between the Tathāgata’s two feet during the "Chapter on Verses of Praise.
When about to expound the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications," light was emitted from the Tathāgata’s knees.
Now, as he expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages, light of the Buddha-fruit of the Middle Way is again emitted from the space between his eyebrows within this first assembly.
At the end, one returns to the beginning; this is the ultimate limit of the fruit. Within the three vehicles, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) differ;
their modes of practice are entirely distinct. Bodhisattvas on the ten stages have not yet clearly realized the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

In the first assembly, the Tathāgata emitted from between his eyebrows the light of the Buddha-fruit, named "The Universal Illumination of the Wisdom-Light of All Bodhisattvas, the Treasury of the Ten Directions."
Because this light causes Bodhisattvas to enter the gate of the Buddha’s fruit-virtues, it subsequently emits the light of fruition to cause them to enter that fruition;
for the causal practice and the fruition are similar in their joyful cultivation. As the Sūtra says:

"At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to enable the great assembly of all Bodhisattvas to attain the supernatural power of the Tathāgata’s boundless realm, emitted [light] from between his eyebrows."
The light is named "The Universal Radiance of the Wisdom of All Bodhisattvas, the Treasury Illumining the Ten Directions.

Its form is like a cloud of jewel-colored lamps. This light, named "The Universal Radiance of the Treasury Illumining the Ten Directions," illuminates this treasury of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), wherein each and every stage pervades the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of empty space, [manifesting] the merit, wisdom, and great compassion.

In this *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra*, these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constitute the concluding and re-initiating section within the first assembly concerning the gates accomplished by the bodhisattvas sent by the Tathāgata.
This is because they resemble the emission of light from between the eyebrows and because the locations of the light-emission are similar.
Previously, in the first assembly, the light emitted was like a cloud of jewel-colored lamps; now, in these ten stages, the light emitted...

The light is named "Flame of the Bodhisattva’s Power. Because the causes and effects of the preceding and succeeding lights are similar, and because the emergence of the lamp’s flame is similar [to the light], the previous emission of light was named "Bodhisattva Wisdom Light Universally Illuminating the Treasuries of the Ten Directions";
this clarifies that the Tathāgata awakens the wisdom of bodhisattvas, causing all bodhisattvas to reach this tenth [stage].
Regarding the "Grounds," within this chapter on the Ten Grounds, the light emitted by the Tathāgata is named "The Radiance of the Power of the Bodhisattva.

This signifies that the power of the Bodhisattva’s own strength has reached its ultimate limit as they ascend through the ten grounds. The preceding light was the initial unfolding, while the subsequent radiance represents the power of one's own strength.
Because of this power of one's own strength, one arrives at the place where the Tathāgata first unfolded [the Dharma], thereby aligning with the Buddha’s original intent for the first time.
Because they ultimately resemble one another, this gate of the final fruition of the Middle Way within these ten stages is clarified;

since the end penetrates back to the beginning, the preceding light presents the fruition to encourage practice, while the subsequent emission of light from the ten stages represents the cultivation of oneself until reaching that fruition.
Therefore, the light is named "the Power of the Bodhisattva," for the power of a bodhisattva’s own diligent cultivation is a power of non-retrogression and indefatigability.

Because one is able to cultivate and reach this tenth stage—the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm treasury (dharmadhātu-garbha)—through the power of diligence, the Bodhisattva is therefore called a "treasury" (*garbha*).
A "treasury" means that which contains and gathers within it a mass of virtues without omission. This Dharma-realm, in its essential nature, is pure and untainted;
as a gateway to the Dharma, its substance encompasses the entire Dharma-realm, containing all great wisdom and great compassion.
Because of all these merits, they give rise to clouds of myriad practices that universally rain down the Dharma-rain to moisten sentient beings;
for this reason, the Bodhisattvas at this stage are called "Treasury" (Kośa) according to such a dharma-name.

Within this stage, there are thirty-seven Bodhisattvas who share the same name, "Treasury," in order to clarify the ultimate fruit of this dharma-gate of the ten stages and to distinguish and know its true meaning.
Because the Path assists the Path, thirty-seven factors are established; these are the thirty-seven dharma-gates for the accomplishment of a Bodhisattva, as they are not the ultimate fruit.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth, all that the Bodhisattva practices is an auxiliary path and not the true station.
This is intended to clarify that what is practiced is an auxiliary path, whereas non-abiding and non-practice constitute abiding in reality (*tathatā*).

Because its own essence is termed the "correct fruit," if one considers the stage of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), the Bodhisattva—by means of the fundamental wisdom of the signless nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-niḥsvabhāva-mūla-jñāna*) which does not depart from the essence of non-action—performs all myriad practices; thus, the cause and effect of the Bodhisattva and the Buddha are fundamentally equal in essence.
This is provided that one excludes the Buddha-fruit, which is effortless and unconditioned, once the Bodhisattva’s correct preparatory application (*prayoga*) has already been undertaken.

Taken together, these are collectively named "Aids to the Path" (*bodhipakṣa*). Since movement and stillness are unimpeded, and since the primary and auxiliary aspects have from the beginning been non-different, this is a single Dharma-gate.
One must distinguish between the features—the essence and its function—yet in their perfect quiescence, the primary and auxiliary are entirely identical.
This is the gate of "total difference and total identity," which can be understood by reflecting upon it through the gate of "repeated profundity. Thus one hears the Dharma never heard before.

If one does not doubt this, [one realizes that] total difference and total identity are difficult to comprehend within the realm of reality. For both Buddhas and ordinary beings each possess their own distinct existence, this is the meaning of "total difference";
thus, the two views would perpetually persist. If they were entirely identical, one would become stagnant in quiescence.
In the path of perfect interfusion, principle and phenomena do not obstruct one another. If the Dharma-gate were to be divided into two directions, it would be merely the dharma of ordinary beings.
The unification of the one body is the Dharma of the Two Vehicles; however, because principle and phenomena are sovereign, the Way lies within them.
To dwell the mind upon them is to extinguish them; thus, it is neither possible to harbor them in the mind nor is it possible not to do so.
This auxiliary practice of the path is non-dual in essence with the gate of the unconditioned fruit and virtue of right wisdom; as such, its internal regulations and rules must not be transgressed.

They are not undifferentiated, because their essence and function cannot be considered entirely separate; nor can they be entirely identical, for that which is entirely identical would constitute an entire separation, and that which is entirely separate would constitute an entire identity.
Without entire separation there is no entire identity, and without entire identity there is no entire separation.
To be deluded regarding these two gates of identity and difference is for wisdom to lack sovereignty, as in the case of Bodhisattva Vimukticandra. III.
Seventeen [bodhisattvas] share the same name, "Treasury" (Kośa), while the thirty-seventh bodhisattva alone is named "Liberation Moon" (Vimukticandra). Why is this?
Those who share the name "Treasury" collectively represent the assembly of fellow practitioners within the primary and auxiliary teachings of the ten stages (daśabhūmi);
these thirty-seven [bodhisattvas] constitute the retinue, whereas Liberation Moon alone is their leader.
Because Śāriputra alone was the companion of the Light and not a member of the assembly of the Dharma, he was given a distinct title as the "guest" and "host.
There must be an invitation and the posing of difficult questions regarding the Dharma of the Ten Stages, so that the true Dharma may be heard in the present and future lives without doubt.
Such is the meaning of the sutra; it should be understood in this way. Therefore, this Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages is itself liberation.
Vimalacandra requested the Dharma for the assembly, and Vajragarbha Bodhisattva expounded the Dharma for the assembly; the foregoing may be understood as above.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom.
[This refers to] the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja entering the Great Wisdom of a Bodhisattva during the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Regarding the Samādhi of Radiant Light: now, at this tenth stage, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha enters the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Great Wisdom Radiance.
Because the wisdom of the Bodhisattva in this stage increases in brilliance, its wondrous function of discernment becomes increasingly luminous, further augmenting his insight.
This is because the Dharma-gates of the successive stages of the levels increase in excellence; however, as for all other [stages]...
Having entered this samādhi through the power of non-abiding wisdom, immediately in each of the ten directions,
beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten billion buddha-fields, there appeared before him ten billion buddhas— each named Vajragarbha— as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields.
These buddhas then empowered the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha with thirteen kinds of dharmas.
1. To praise and exhort the Buddhas of the twenty directions with speech; 2. To possess a body that cannot be eclipsed by others; 3. To possess unimpeded eloquence in joyful exposition; 4.
To possess pure wisdom that skillfully discerns all things; 5. To possess the power of excellent mindfulness that never forgets;
6. To possess clear and penetrating wisdom that is well-determined; 7. To go everywhere to awaken sentient beings.
1. The arising of wisdom; 2. the attainment of the path; 3. mastery of powers; 4. the Tathāgata’s fearlessnesses; 5.
the analytical discernment of all dharmas by the Omniscient One, together with eloquence and wisdom;
6. the supreme adornment of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas; 7. being touched by the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Thirteen: Regarding this Tathāgata of this land, his light illuminates their bodies and he bestows mental empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon them.

This is intended to cause those of future generations to sever their doubts, establish the Dharma, and give rise to faith. As stated in the sūtra, he praises and exhorts them with words, granting permission to speak without hesitation;
he comforts them by stroking their heads with his hand, signifying the granting of wisdom. Furthermore, as to why they share the same name, it clarifies the "Golden" [nature].
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha has realized the causes and effects of the Dharma in a manner similar to that realized by the Buddha;
just as the five stages of Bodhisattvas and the Buddha’s causes and effects are equal, they are all sealed with the same name, "Buddha.

This establishes the Dharma so that the assembly present and future generations may have no doubts. Furthermore, the Tathāgata of this land shines his light upon his body, constituting the thirteenth kind of empowerment.
Regarding the realm of Samantabhadra within the state of Perfect Enlightenment, according to the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avalambana-sūtra*, it is said to be taught in the Third Dhyāna;
however, the extant text is incomplete and cannot be fully reconciled.

The *Mūla-karman-sūtra* explains that after the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was concluded, he transformed the assembly of the Three Vehicles, and subsequently, once again at the site of Bodhi, briefly expounded that very sūtra once more.
There is a clear textual authority for these five stages of the teaching according to their sequential order; here, I shall briefly explain them first.

Later, within the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, I will further clarify the rules of conduct between teacher and disciple, the specific characteristics of practice, and the ways in which the Bodhisattvas of the five stages seek spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and benefit sentient beings, as well as each of the dharma-gates of the successive stages (*bhūmi*).

The distinct characteristics [of these teachings] are explained according to the text; only then can one understand the brief summary of the gate of the distinctions between the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The teachings, practices, seals, and creeds of the ten stages of the three vehicles are entirely distinct from top to bottom; by reading and contemplating them, this may be seen.

The ten stages of the three vehicles do not resemble those of this *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, which is the gate of the Buddha’s vehicle within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The sequence of the dharma-gates in this sūtra is fivefold.
The stages, the six positions, and the gates of practice all take the fruits and virtues realized by the Bodhisattvas themselves as their own personal titles;
this is just as in the stage of the ten faiths there are the ten "Heads" Bodhisattvas such as Śrīgarbha (Jue-shou),

in the stage of the ten abidings there are the ten "Wisdoms" Bodhisattvas such as Dharmamati (Fa-hui), and in the stage of the ten practices there are the ten "Forests" Bodhisattvas such as Guṇakūṭa (Gongde-lin).
As previously described, all these are named after the intrinsic realization of the fundamental dharma within their respective positions;
the lands from which they come are all led by fundamental wisdom to benefit sentient beings, and the wisdom that contemplates faculties and extinguishes delusions is designated as "the Fundamental.
The Buddhas whom they serve appear before them within their respective positions, with identical names throughout the ten directions.

The thirteen kinds of augmentations confirm the manifestation of the identity of cause and effect; the names are identical yet encompass both the general and the particular, penetrating through time and eons, mutually fusing in an inexhaustible manner.
The profound mysteries of one and many interpenetrate one another, such that all dharmas are like Indra’s net—identical and distinct, layered and layered, without obstruction.
Within the Three Vehicles, this seal does not exist among the three stages of worthiness or the ten bhūmis.
The characteristics of faith and practice are entirely distinct; those who truly cultivate the path must understand the provisional and the ultimate, lest they stagnate in their efforts.
To stagnate in the provisional while being deluded regarding the ultimate leads to much vain toil over many kalpas.
Regarding the sixth stage, which causes Sudhana to realize the Dharma in its particularity, it is as described in the sutra from the second assembly, the *Prabhāsa* [Assembly].
From the wheels on the two feet of the Tathāgata, light rays were emitted from the category of awakening,

illuminating hundreds of thousands of nayutas of trichiliocosms, and even all worlds throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive dharma-realm— immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, unequaled, incalculable, unfathomable, and unspeakable. 4.
The realms above and below were likewise thus; the light shone upon all places, reaching the Golden World in every direction.

Therein, the ten Bodhisattvas of the Ten Heads—Jñānottara, Cakṣuruttara, and the others—each accompanied by as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, arrived simultaneously, each proclaiming a single verse.
Such are the ten dharmas that together constitute the Dharma-gate of the Stage of Faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

Just as the youth Sudhana, having seen Mañjuśrī to the east of the city of Awakening (*Bodhagaya*) and heard various teachings, gave rise to faith, he now returns to emulate the Stage of Faith described previously, which was established by the ten Bodhisattvas headed by Mañjuśrī and Buddhabhadra. This is the third assembly, the Ascent.
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, ten bodhisattvas, including Dharmamati and others, each expounded a dharma-gate,
collectively corresponding to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as when the youth Sudhana traveled south to the summit of Mount Meghaśrī,

where he beheld the bhikṣu Meghadatta and the other ten spiritual friends; this is consistent with the previous scripture concerning the ascent to the summit of Mount Sumeru by Dharmamati and the other nine.
In the fourth assembly of the *Daśabhūmika-dharmamukha* spoken by the Bodhisattva Prajñā, within the Sudarśana Palace of the Yāma Heaven,
ten forest-dwelling bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha and others, each expounded one dharma to collectively form the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices.
This is like the youth Sudhana, who traveled south to the country of Trayastriṃśa and met the bhikṣu Sudarśana, followed by the other nine virtuous teachers.
The consciousness returns as previously explained in the sutra through the discourse of Guṇakusuma and others on the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*),
wherein each practice is practiced in turn. In the fifth assembly, while ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven palace, the ten Banner Bodhisattvas,
beginning with Vajradhvaja, each expound one dharma, together forming the ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) gates, just as [described] for Sudhana’s journey to the south.
Traveling to the vast country of Mahāvyūha, Sudhana sequentially inquires of each of his spiritual friends— beginning with the elder Utpalabhūti and the other ten virtuous friends—
regarding the ten methods of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) as taught by the ten *dhvajāgra* bodhisattvas,
such as Vajradhvaja, in the preceding scripture; this constitutes the sixth assembly, wherein he ascends to the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

The Bodhisattvas, such as Vajragarbha and others, expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) just as when the youth Sudhana arrived here in Jambudvīpa at the city of Kapilavastu before the night goddess Vasanti and the ten subsequent spiritual friends;

this was exactly as previously described in the sutra regarding the exposition of the Ten Stages by the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
In the seventh assembly of the *Bhūmi-dharmaparyāya*, where Sudhana inquires of his friends one by one regarding their practices,
he ascends to the third dhyāna and expounds for the assembly of the eight dhyānas all the dharmaparyāyas concerning the bodhisattva in his final birth who has entered the Buddha-flower samādhi.
This includes the stages of the eleven bhūmis and the state of universal equality (*samyaksambodhi*), such as the realm of Samantabhadra, just as when Sudhana arrived [at the presence of Maitreya].

Lady Māyā and the ten subsequent spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are explained again here as in the previous *Sūtra of the Necklaces* (*Mālā-sūtra*), concerning the sequential dharma-gates of the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, the realm of Samantabhadra.

As Sudhana inquires of his friends one by one, he emulates their practices and carries them out, thereby fulfilling the subsequent eighth assembly: the dharma-gate of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).
When he first attained perfect enlightenment within the Bodhimaṇḍa, he spoke as follows,
just as when the youth Sudhana reached the Great Adorned Garden and Vast Multi-storied Pavilion named Vairocana-alaṃkāra-garbha in the country of Samudrakaccha, where he met the Bodhisattva Maitreya;
this refers to the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who represents the perfection of the Buddha-fruit for Sudhana, as described in the aforementioned sutra.
The Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment for the first time within the Bodhimaṇḍa;

and as for the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Thirty-seven Tathāgatas," according to the sutra, the section preceding the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" is the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra," while the section following the "Chapter on the Appearance" is the "Chapter on Leaving the World. Furthermore, it was the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra who spoke [to] Sudhana.

One by one, following this example, they return from the previous five stages—the stage of Māyādevī and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—to achieve self-perfected awakening by riding upon the conduct of Samantabhadra and appear in the world;
they then use the conduct of Samantabhadra to guide sentient beings so that they may leave the world behind. Sudhana the youth likewise follows this example, proceeding from Maitreya.

When the Bodhisattva subsequently sees his own body enter into the body of Samantabhadra, it clarifies that he has perfected the practices of the Samantabhadra of his own vehicle, attained self-enlightenment, and appeared in the world.
By constantly guiding sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra, he causes them to transcend the mundane world.
That he sees his own body enter the body of Samantabhadra clarifies that his practice is fulfilled and identical to that of Samantabhadra; this is the Dharma.

Because they are similar and of one and the same substance, as in the "Chapter on Manifestation," the light from the Tathāgata’s own ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure between his brows) is poured onto Mañjuśrī’s crown, and the light from his mouth is poured onto Samantabhadra’s mouth, so that these two persons may engage in mutual question and answer.
This clarifies how cause and effect, principle and phenomena, penetrate and enter one another; for by means of these two persons, the substance of principle and phenomena [is revealed].
Because one attains the fruit of Buddhahood through two gates, one appears in the world;
just as when the youth Sudhana went to the abode of Maitreya, Maitreya Bodhisattva caused Sudhana to see his original spiritual friend, Mañjuśrī.
Having heard this, while Sudhana was still in the midst of recollecting it, he heard the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and immediately entered the state of non-arising.
By means of the samādhi-gate of measure, he immediately beholds his own body entering the body of Samantabhadra and the pavilion of Maitreya;
he perceives the events of the three periods of time as being present in the current moment. This is because Sudhana’s merit has reached its ultimate limit and his fruition is perfected;
thus, Maitreya Bodhisattva brings him into this assembly to establish a dharma-prototype, so that future learners may develop faith and understanding, and realize entry into the truth.
In the *Avikalpapraveśa-sūtra*, there are only the Dharma-gates, yet no one has sought to study them;
therefore, it causes Sudhana to inquire of his friends so that he may practice each and every path according to the rules of the aforementioned sutras.

If the Dharma were merely bestowed in vain, there would still be fear that one might remain confused regarding its practice; thus, it causes Sudhana to practice through practice, so as to enable future learners [to do the same].

Without obstruction, Maitreya causes Sudhana to see Mañjuśrī again; he clearly perceives that the Dharma-body, the fundamental essence, and the root-wisdom serve as the cause for seeing Maitreya Bodhisattva, while Sudhana’s own reliance on the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body serves as the fruit.
Furthermore, by means of the practices of Samantabhadra performed by all the spiritual benefactors, he sees Maitreya as the fulfillment of his own Buddhahood.
Later, upon entering the Dharma-realm of the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*), one sees for oneself that one’s own body has entered the body of Samantabhadra.
Although one has attained perfect enlightenment, one constantly benefits sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra.

This clearly shows that Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya—the three Buddhas representing the fruition—are from beginning to end in one place; this signifies that their path penetrates both cause and fruit, and that the way of these three is that of the ancient Buddhas.
This Great Capital is the source and the ultimate limit of all dharmas. For those who are deluded or enlightened, it is the place where the original state is fully attained.
Those who are deluded sink of their own accord into saṃsāra; yet the Way and Dharma of the Ancient Buddha have always been thus from the beginning.
Therefore, it is not a dharma of arising and ceasing; it is unconditioned and non-active. Both those who cultivate it and those who are negligent are alike "makers" [of karma].
Therefore, one who delights in tranquility should not be negligent, nor should one revert to being entangled by one's own emotions, thereby deviating from the nature of the sages.
For this reason, those who cultivate the Path should skillfully observe themselves through the power of concentration and wisdom, and must not become stagnant in their practice.

Seventh, regarding the distinctions among the assemblies of bodhisattvas at the six stages: for instance, within the provisional teachings, the sequence of the bodhisattva stages is explained such that only the conventional *tathatā* (true thusness) is said to serve as cause and fruit.

Consequently, during the three stages of worthiness prior to the [first] bhūmi, one has not yet attained direct realization; it is only within the first bhūmi that one realizes one *tathatā*, and through the ten bhūmis, one realizes ten *tathatās*.

Only after realizing the ten true suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) can one first see the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); prior to that realization of true suchness, it is further stated that there are "obstructions to the ten true suchnesses.

Since true suchness can function as an obstruction, it is clear that within the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), what is established is a "provisional true suchness" rather than the fundamental true suchness.
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) thus described, the followers of the three vehicles hear them together; as for the śrāvaka practitioners:
The gods all assemble here for this sutra; it is not otherwise. Among the six stages of the fruit-stage Bodhisattvas, each stage possesses ten [Bodhisattvas].
Furthermore, within each of these positions, the names of the ten Bodhisattvas below are identical;

they have each come from the ten directions with Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields to the presence of the Buddha. Within the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), they are all collectively named.
The leaders at the beginning are named the "First Awakening" (Bodhimukha) and the "First Name" (Nāmanmukha); there are ten such leading Bodhisattvas.

From the very inception of the arising of faith, there is a passage concerning Mañjuśrī from all directions regarding the land from which he comes—the Golden World—and the Buddha whom he originally served, both of whom are titled Immovable Wisdom (Acalamati).
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, phenomena are used to manifest the Dharma; there is not a single thing that does not do so.
The "Golden World" (*Suvarṇabhāsa*) that symbolizes the Dharma-gate refers to the white dharmas; gold being white in color signifies that the essence of the Dharmakāya is luminous.
The Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalajñāna-buddha*) signifies the non-active nature of wisdom within the Dharmakāya;
this is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Mañjuśrī is the causal factor that realizes [this], while the Immovable Wisdom Buddha is that which is realized.
Regarding this fruit, I now present this cause and effect as being of identical substance and non-dual in function, thereby establishing the initial gateway of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).
This causes those who possess faith to believe that the fruit becomes the cause, and to cultivate the dharmas of the fruit so as to establish the stage of cause.

Upon the very first thought of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), one immediately attains perfect enlightenment; thus, the fundamental wisdom of realized fruition serves as the cause. For this reason, [this is so].

The scripture below states: "By means of slight expedient means, one swiftly attains Bodhi. This differs from the provisional teachings, where Bodhi is considered identical to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thus established as the "attainer" and the "attained.
Within a single thought-moment, when there is neither subject nor object, and the state where both subject and object are exhausted is reached, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This also differs from the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), which merely extinguishes subject and object; here, one realizes that subject and object are fundamentally non-existent.
Because it moves, this is the abiding of the *dharmatā*; thus, both movement and stillness are equal, for they are the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is neither movement nor stillness.
Fools, failing to understand this, abandon movement and seek stillness; this constitutes great suffering. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Thoroughly penetrating the emptiness of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) is the meaning of suffering. This is because those of the *Hīnayāna* possess longing and aversion.
This refers to the arising of suffering. Because of this, the ten bodhisattvas beginning with Mañjuśrī manifest the fruit-virtues to awaken sentient beings.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "By means of the Buddha’s wisdom, he shows and awakens sentient beings so that they may attain purity.
For this reason, the ten bodhisattvas beginning with Bodhyagras (Jue-shou) are all named after the Buddhas from whom they originally received their teachings.
All are given the same name, "Wisdom"—namely, the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, the Buddha of Unimpeded Wisdom, the Buddha of Liberating Wisdom, and so forth.
These ten Wisdom Tathāgatas all manifest from that which they have come from: the Fundamental Wisdom.
The place from which they come is the wisdom of one’s own body; that from which they come is the cause. This clarifies that the fruit comes from the Fundamental Wisdom as its cause.

It is just as taking the entirety of gold to fashion bracelets and armlets, taking the entirety of the Buddha-body to become a bodhisattva, and taking the entirety of the Buddha-fruit to constitute one's own self;
now, returning by means of the fundamental wisdom of one's own Buddha-nature constitutes the initial realization.
All sentient beings are entirely like this; that those who have come from the presence of the Buddha represent the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*).
Sudden realization of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), identical in essence and function to that of a Buddha, constitutes the initial awakening;
taking this correct awakening as the cause for the first realization, the ten-headed Bodhisattvas manifest the cause arising from the fruit.
Subsequently, within the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), there are the ten wisdom Bodhisattvas, namely: Dharmamati Bodhisattva, Sarvamatī Bodhisattva, and Viśeṣamati Bodhisattva.
The ten bodhisattvas, such as Sāradhvaja and others, each arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field.
The Buddhas from whose lands they came—the Buddhas whom they originally served—were the ten Moon Buddhas:
namely, Viśeṣacandra, Akṣayacandra, Acalacandra, and so forth. These ten Moon Buddhas represent the wisdom of the fruition-dharma.
The ten wisdoms (*prajñā*) represented by these bodhisattvas signify the cause; furthermore, they signify that the cause arises from the fruit.

Since the Buddha is likened to the moon, it represents how, within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), one first realizes the merit of the fruit: because the heat of ignorance is removed, the nature is cool and refreshing.
For this reason, the merit of the fruit is represented as being cool, and thus the Buddha is named "Moon-like. This stage marks the initial realization of that fruit.
Therefore, it returns to being identical with the essence of cool serenity. As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva Dharmamati entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means.

By the power of this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields, all bearing the same name: Dharmamati."
The Bodhisattva Puxian Fahui (Universal Manifestation of Dharma-Wisdom) offers words of consolation and praise, saying "Excellent!

This statement that there are "a thousand" Buddhas is because each and every Buddha fills the ten directions; thus, it differs from the provisional teachings which limit the number of Buddhas and distinguish between this and that land.
This clarifies that within this stage, at the very moment the mind is first awakened, cause and effect are mutually perfected as a non-differentiated essence.

Therefore, although the names of the Bodhisattva and the Buddha are identical, it is because the Bodhisattva Dharmamati acts as the seal (*mudrā*) for cause and effect as a single entity that the Buddha’s name is the same as his own; this signifies that all who have realized the Path are likewise so.

Among the ten preceding faiths, Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalamati-buddha*) is the Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); here, within these ten abodes (*vihāra*), the name of the Buddha-fruit is "Moon."
This refers to the fruit obtained through progressive cultivation according to each stage; as for cause and effect, it is the cause and effect of that which is beyond cause and effect.
It is designated as "cause and effect" only by virtue of having no basis of dependence. It differs from the externalists who, out of emotional bias, deny cause and effect;
it differs from the ordinary beings of the human and celestial realms who are bound by and established in cause and effect. These two are not the same.
Such is the cause and fruit of Buddhahood. Within this stage, at the very beginning of the first of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*), one realizes this "cause-and-fruit that is not cause-and-fruit.
Therefore, at the moment of the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), one is already a Buddha.

Thus, within this stage, the Bodhisattva Anuttara-prajñā (Unsurpassed Wisdom) says in verse: "Ordinary beings lack awakening and understanding; the Buddha causes them to abide in the True Dharma. All phenomena are..."
Abiding thus, one realizes that this vision is not a body, yet speaks of a body; it does not arise, yet manifests arising; there is neither body nor vision—this is the unsurpassed body of the Buddha.
Question: For what reason, within the preceding stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), did the ten Bodhisattvas not enter samādhi before preaching the Dharma?
Furthermore, why was there no Buddha named Jñānottara (Awakening Chief) who addressed them?

Question: Why is it that within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enters samādhi and begins to preach the Dharma, and why do thousands of Buddhas—as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world—bear the same name as Dharmamati, all being called Dharmamati, and come to offer consolation and praise?

Furthermore, why is it that these signs did not exist during the preceding stage of the ten faiths (*śraddhā*)? What is the reason for this? Answer: It is because... [The text continues with the explanation.]
The stage of faith merely demonstrates the dharmas of the fruit; because cause and fruit are presented together, it serves only to engender faith and has not yet attained actual realization.

Therefore, one does not enter samādhi at this stage. Because one enters the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) to attain true realization, for this reason one must enter samādhi before being able to realize truly.
This is done so that one may accord with the principle of realizing the Dharma together with all sentient beings, thereby attaining correct realization.
Because the fruition and its merit are identical in name, the Buddhas come to seal them as the single flavor of cause and effect;

therefore, during the preceding stage of faith, one merely establishes faith but has not yet attained direct realization. For this reason, one does not enter samādhi, nor do Buddhas of identical names come to seal the single flavor of cause and effect—one should know it thus, believe and understand it thus. After these thousand Buddhas, there follow ten thousand Buddhas.
This clarifies the characteristics of advancing in practice;

as in the "Ten Practices" chapter, when the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation, and having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields, all bearing the same name: [Śākyamuni].
The Buddha appeared before Guṇakāśyapa and offered words of praise and consolation.
Because the cause and effect were identical to those of his previous station, the name of the Buddha was the same as the name of the Bodhisattva;

for the two entities—the Bodhisattva as cause and the Buddha as effect—were identical in their merit. Therefore, the names were the same. The lands from which these ten forest-Bodhisattvas originally came were all named [Guṇakāśyapa].

The ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Prajñāguṇakānana, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, came from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in the ten directions.
The names of those worlds were: Priyaprajñā, Dhvajaprajñā, Ratnaprajñā, and so forth—these ten wisdom-worlds.

The Buddhas whom this world has served from the beginning—namely, the Buddha Constant Abiding Eye, the Buddha Unsurpassed Eye, the Buddha Non-Abiding Eye, and so forth, these ten Eye-Buddhas—were asked:
"For what reason, among the first ten stages (*bhūmi*), do the Buddhas all share the same name, Dharmamati?
Why is the number of Buddha-fields cited as being equal to the dust motes of a thousand [fields], and why is it that the Bodhisattvas who come also exceed a thousand worlds?"
The worlds from which they come outside the realm are all named "Flower," and the Buddhas they originally served are all named "Moon.
Why is it that within these ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), the lands from which they originally came are all named "Wisdom," and the Buddhas they originally served are all named "Eye"?
What is the intention behind this? The answer is: because in the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*), one first departs from the state of an ordinary person.
Because the realization of the virtues of the fruit begins from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the lands are all named "Flower" (*puṣpa*);
because they are the dwelling place of the Buddha where the Buddha’s own wisdom first blossoms; because one realizes the Buddha-wisdom and is born for the first time into the family of all Buddhas;

and because the names of the Buddhas are all alike as "Moon" (*candra*) to signify that one has attained the coolness of the Dharma like the moon—these constitute the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*).
Throughout the beginning and end of this, the Buddha is entirely true both internally and externally; the land is named after the Dharma, and the Buddha is titled by the Dharma.
In the preceding stage, one first realizes [this truth] to represent it as the cool clarity of the moon; in this stage, having attained ultimate reality, it is purely called the "Eye.
This "Eye" is the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*). Within this practice, the Dharma-eye is perfectly clear and bright, responding to the capacities of sentient beings.
Because they illuminate the mundane world to bring about the perfection of virtue, the numbers increase gradually from thousands to tens of thousands;

this clarifies that the Dharmadhātu is perfectly luminous, neither increasing nor decreasing. However, because Bodhisattvas at the stage of Buddhahood employ skillful means to guide and receive ordinary beings, causing them to progress toward excellence, all of these are the Tathāgata’s secret intentional skillful means, just as in the case of the names of Buddhas.

In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Sound*, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Sūryacandraprabha, specifically increased his reverence and performed three prostrations with added gravity, stating that "those who extinguish their names of sin" do so because the Tathāgata uses skillful means to lead the minds of ordinary beings and inspire their resolve.
How could it be said that while the essence of all Buddhas is of one flavor, there are differences in their merits? Now, regarding the various [aspects] within the state of Buddhahood...

The stages and spheres established by Bodhisattvas expand and increase in such a gradual sequence that they speak of a thousand Buddha-worlds, ten thousand Buddha-worlds, and even until the end of all numbers.
Within each individual number, the essence and the dependent origination mutually penetrate;

within each individual number, the beginning and the end mutually enter one another without any limit of before or after. This is due to the secret intention and skillful means of all Buddhas, which is like... [as follows:]
When ten coins lose one coin, all ten are entirely without attachment; when ten coins are complete, they constitute all numbers.
Because they arise simultaneously like an echo responding to a sound, one attains the beginning and immediately attains the end.

Since their nature is equal, their time is equal, and they arise simultaneously through dependent origination, the dharma-gate for establishing the objective realm herein is thus [established]. (The following portion appears to be missing the text on the Ten Dedications.)

[Treatise] A Bodhisattva of the First Ground [Prathamabhūmi], through the King of the Illuminating Gates of Many Hundreds of Dharmas, transforms many hundreds of Buddha-worlds. A Bodhisattva of the Second Ground...
When Bodhisattvas transform thousands of Buddha-worlds by means of the King of Dharma-Light Gateways, this differs from the provisional teachings which maintain that there are actual limitations.
As with the aforementioned numbers of phenomena, they mutually penetrate one another;
it is like a person drawing hundreds of thousands of divisions as numerous as atoms in the air with their finger, and then erasing them all with their hand—yet within that space, nothing remains.
There is increase and decrease because they are measured by the mind; thus one perceives that space has an increase and decrease in number. This sutra is also like this:

the increase and decrease in the dharma-gates for establishing the stages of all bodhisattvas is likewise so. It is for the sake of accomplishing all sentient beings and causing them to advance in practice.
If everything were uniform and level, there would be no intention to advance—this is the case for ordinary people (pṛthagjana).
