There is no mind of deliberate cultivation; one awakens the aspiration to cultivate until reaching the state of non-cultivation, only then realizing that the myriad dharmas are without cultivation.
Yet, in the true teaching, the Bodhisattva attains all by attaining one, for within the essence of the Dharma there is neither before nor after.
It is like the net of Indra, where light and shadows interpenetrate and reflect one another, devoid of any limit of before or after. It is also like...
A hundred thousand jewel mirrors face a wondrous image together; within each mirror, the reflected images interpenetrate one another, their forms and colors level and even.

This is because, just as the various Bodhisattvas in the stage of Buddhahood arise from the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya by nature, so too, when first realizing the mind during the ten stages (*bhūmi*), all dharma-gates and realms are entirely based upon that source.
Since both essence and function are universally encompassed and thoroughly penetrated, they are equalized by means of the nature itself;

because they are equalized at that very moment, there are no further unequal dharmas remaining, for nothing else can be different. Unlike the provisional teachings where emotional obstructions have not yet been eliminated, and from the first through the ninth stages where the Buddha-nature has not yet been seen—such that the established stages all possess limitations and are considered "not yet attained"—[in this teaching, such distinctions do not exist].
Because one perceives that the Buddha-nature has the provisional *tathatā* as an obstruction, the sutra says: "The distinctions between the ten stages are like bird tracks in the sky.
Thus, the dharmas of these stages—whether provisionally established as increasing or decreasing—are taught in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
For one who realizes the Way, the ultimate and the conventional are immediately one and true; since all is true, there are no provisional dharmas at all.
One might hold a view of increase or decrease regarding this Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), treating it as equivalent to the Gradual [teachings];

however, all the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and various spirits in the ocean-like congregations described in this sutra are all bodhisattvas of the ocean-like assembly at the stage of Buddhahood.
They are not ordinary beings; rather, those who are made to enter [the path] are identical to the sages. Thus, it clarifies the subduing and transforming power of Vairocana.
Because the realms and so forth pervade all sentient beings, they are all the assembly of the stage of Buddhahood, acting as the principal and retinue through their transformative manifestations.
Thus, this assembly of the stage of resultant virtue gathers together to form the Dharma for the instruction and awakening of sentient beings.
After the formation of this Dharma, in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, Mañjuśrī brings forth this Dharma-gate of resultant virtue outside the assembly at Jetavana.
Traveling south, Śāriputra set out for the city of Bodhimaṇḍa to bring benefit and happiness to humanity.
On the road, six thousand bhikṣus attained the realization of the ten ears and ten eyes. In the eastern part of the city of Bodhimaṇḍa, he met Sudhana and sought out all his spiritual friends;
there were five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, and five hundred youths who had perfected the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
The five hundred maidens were all like the text of the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*; they cannot be described individually, for the entire assembly was likewise so.

If one lacks the karmic affinity, one will not hear them at all—just as the Arhats and bhikṣus in the Jeta Grove did not hear or see the Tathāgata preaching this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, even though they were in the same assembly as the five groups of followers.
Those who heard this Dharma together with Mañjuśrī are all of those who have attained realization;

therefore, the Sūtra says that this scripture does not fall into the hands of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), for even those who possess deep faith surpass the followers of the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, let alone those who are able to realize it.
Thus, in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) of this Sūtra, it says: "All classes of sentient beings in the world..."
Those who seek the Śrāvaka vehicle are few; those who seek the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are even fewer; and those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare.
While it is still relatively easy for one who seeks the Mahāyāna to have faith, it is exceedingly difficult to believe this Dharma.
Therefore, you should know that this assembly gathered like an ocean is not composed of ordinary worldlings, but consists entirely of devas and bodhisattvas at the stage of fruition.
The assembly was formed to establish this teaching; it was first revealed through the conversion of Mañjuśrī at Bodhimaṇḍa.

This teaching was intended to bring benefit and happiness to the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa. The group of five, including Sudhana, collectively represents those who have truly attained this Dharma.
The remaining meanings are as previously explained. Thus, the fact that the assembled multitude consists exclusively of bodhisattvas at the stage of fruition serves to clarify this point.
The fruition, virtue, and function are fully perfected for those of the highest capacity; there are no provisional teachings here.
Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, as well as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, devas, humans, and ordinary beings—such multitudes of causes and effects—have gathered in this assembly.

As for the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, they do not participate in this multitude from the first stage up to the ninth stage, let alone ordinary beings. Why is this? Because while they practice the six pāramitās, they do so with [attachment].
Regarding the ten *pāramitās*, because they achieve the merit of the fruit of the Path over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they differ from this teaching,
wherein all times are realized simultaneously and are not comprised within the non-sentient. Thus,

those who resolved their minds on the road where six thousand bhikṣus traveled southward from the Jeta Grove assembly with Mañjuśrī— this clarifies that even *śrāvakas* are permitted to possess the most supreme [attainment].

Their faculties were capable of entering this Most Excellent Vehicle; furthermore, those six thousand bhikṣus had all newly gone forth under Śāriputra and had not yet rejoiced in the minor fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
Because their faculties were sharp, they were able to give rise to the resolve and enter this stream of the stage.
Had they already attained the minor fruits, it would have been difficult for them to turn back suddenly; Śāriputra himself was merely a shadow and an echo of the Buddha’s voice.
To hear what is not the voice of a śrāvaka is to have already ascended to the rank of Buddha and entered the stream to connect with ordinary beings;

for this reason, the assembly gathered for this sutra differs from that of the provisional teachings. Even if a transformation Buddha were present, an assembly consisting solely of bodhisattvas without any followers of the Small Vehicle would still differ from this teaching. Why is this? Because there are certain teachings that state [enlightenment] is accomplished through causes alone.
The Buddha does not practice the five stages, nor do the characteristics and essence of these five stages differ as previously described;
thus, by this analogy, there is no one who is the same. Since the Dharma is not the same, the assembly is entirely distinct.
Furthermore, among all those present in this sutra, there are ten kinds of shared dharmas that distinguish this assembly from those present in other sutras.
1. Identical physical bodies; 2. Identical two dharma-bodies; 3. Identical fundamental wisdom; 4. Identical stages of compassionate wisdom; 5.
Identical turning of the wheel of Dharma through speech; 6. Identical places of origin; 7. Identical dharmas accomplished; 8.

Identical causes and effects with the Buddha; 9. Identical as teacher and disciple in service to the Buddha; 10. Identical in the perfection of the land of the reward body. 11. Identical in intention.
Regarding the doubt concerning the benefit obtained and the identity of the physical body (*rūpakāya*):

"Identity" refers to how, among the bodhisattvas of the five stages, those who come from each of the ten directions—each group consisting of as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields—all possess golden bodies with deep blue-black eyes and hair. Their physical bodies are similar to those of the bodhisattvas of their respective stages, just like the gods.
The eight classes of beings are similar to one another because they clearly realize the same Dharma; thus, their retributions are also identical.

For example, although there were fifty-five distinct categories within the first assembly, this was due to differences in the gates of illumination and practice used for gathering and transforming beings.
Nevertheless, their modes of conduct, physical forms, and Dharma-gates—these fifty-five divisions—interpenetrate one another, such that a single practice constitutes many practices.

Because it is similar that many practices become one practice, one body becomes many bodies, and many bodies become one body, the ten locations and ten assemblies in the preceding and following sections are likewise so.

As for the identity of the two dharma-bodies and fundamental wisdom: all the oceans of assemblies within the ten locations and ten assemblies are identical to the Tathāgata’s dharma-nature body and fundamental wisdom; therefore, even if there were new [assemblies], they would be the same.

When those who are ordinary beings studying to enter the assembly see or hear the Buddha-dharma, they all realize entry in a single instant because it is identical to the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-nature body;
thus, there is no one among those entering the assembly who hears or sees the Dharma without possessing the same wisdom as the Buddha’s body.
Consequently, the five hundred arhats within the assembly neither saw nor heard, neither knew nor perceived [the teaching].

This great assembly and the Dharma-gate taught herein differ from the provisional teachings; Bodhisattvas, those of the One Vehicle, and the eight classes of gods and humans gather together to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, obtaining benefits that are entirely distinct [from those of other vehicles]. Regarding the identity of the three—compassion, wisdom, and the Dharma-body:

the fundamental wisdom and the differentiated wisdom of the Dharma-body are identical in essence with compassion, for understanding and practice are unified; thus, they are [manifested as] Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Because the fruit of the Buddha’s wisdom is, from beginning to end, a single dharma—just as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that among the Three Jewels, the Buddha is the Buddha-jewel, Mañjuśrī is the Dharma-jewel, and Samantabhadra is the Saṅgha-jewel—this is the ancient law of all Buddhas past and present.
Therefore, if they are unified, all are identical in being the fundamental source; thus, it is not something created, nor is it subject to arising or perishing.
Regarding the fourfold identity of the wheel of Dharma through verbal expression, as stated in the sutra: Bodhisattvas from five directions each arrive from the ten directions;
in each direction, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields who come to this assembly. This is the case for all worlds in the ten directions.
At one time, they gather like clouds, and with different mouths but a single voice, the oceans of assemblies from the ten directions act simultaneously.
The recitation of the verses is identical in wording and terminology, exactly matching one another without any difference;
because their wisdom is the same, their practice is the same, and the Dharma-gates they teach are the same, this is uniform throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Unlike other sutras where the various understandings and practices differ such that some attain and others do not, here the assemblies of Bodhisattvas from each of the five stages come from the same places.
As for those who have gathered here from the five stages of bodhisattvas, they have arrived from every place throughout the ten directions;
furthermore, every single bodhisattva within the worlds of the ten directions and even within a single mote of dust dwells together.

Because the dharmadhātu is their very substance, all notions of self and other, this and that, far and near, have been exhausted; thus, they do not at all depart from a single mote of dust, being as they have been from the beginning.

Because there is no entry [into the ultimate], they do not resemble the provisional teachings; having reached this stage with the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* yet unfulfilled and various views not yet extinguished, they each return to their original lands.
Furthermore, it has not yet been discussed that even a single mote of dust encompasses the perfect Dharma-realm.

Since both the pervasive and the transformative are limited, all are said to be supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) rather than the fundamental dharma. Thus, the ten dharmas accomplished in the sixth stage are identical.
Because the gates of practice for Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes and the five or six stages are established identically throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
because the Buddhas of the past and present in all worlds of the ten directions share this same Dharma;

because cause and effect are shown instantaneously within a single kṣaṇa, as that Dharma is fundamentally without before or after; and because this is not like the provisional teachings where cause precedes and effect follows—[this constitutes] the tenth [point].
It is only upon reaching the final stage that one first realizes the nature of the mind; those bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, even if one were to attain Buddhahood before the stages, this would be attributed to the power of their vows rather than their fundamental dharma.

Alternatively, it may be attributed to bodhisattvas on the stages who lead ordinary beings to initiate superior practices; it does not refer to the fact that the fundamental dharma is inherently Buddha-nature. This is the *Avataṃsaka*.

The Dharma bestowed by this Sūtra discusses directly the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the Buddha’s own vehicle gate (*svayāna-mukha*), without discussing provisional teachings that open the gates of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) over many kalpas. It directly clarifies that sentient beings’ original self-nature has no creator;
because its nature is fundamentally the true Buddha-wisdom of the primordial *dharmadhātu*, it is taken as the vehicle to be mounted. Seventh, [it is] with the Buddha.

Since cause and effect are identical, and because the Dharmakāya and Jñānakāya of Mañjuśrī, the resultant virtues of all Buddhas, and the practice-gate of Samantabhadra are fundamentally one Dharma, all these oceans of assemblies are likewise identical to it.

Therefore, at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening; at that single kṣaṇa, all obtain this Dharma—this does not preclude [the occurrence of] the kṣaṇa.
If there were something obtained at another time apart from the limit, it would not be the fundamental dharma itself.

Therefore, if anyone within the Buddha-dharma perceives the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment as having a duration measured by kalpas, or as being restricted by place, their faith is not yet perfected;
let alone the paths of cultivation and seeing. For this reason, those who cultivate the path should not allow themselves to be deluded by such worldly attachments.
To falsely claim that one cultivates the Way while still transmigrating through birth and death without cessation is a matter of worldly sentiment, not the Buddha-Dharma.
Therefore, all those who have come to this assembly are equal in rank to the stage of Buddhahood; they shall all attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is because, by relying on the Dharma of fundamental wisdom, all who see, hear, awaken to, or enter into it are identical to the stage of Buddhahood. (8)
Serving the Buddha as teacher and disciple is like the reflections in Indra’s net, where they mutually penetrate one another;
thus, within this ocean of the Dharma-realm of the ten assemblies, Bodhisattvas are present at the abodes of all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm.

By serving all Buddhas, they establish the gate of reverence between teacher and disciple, for they are able to accord with the reverence between teacher and disciple in the fruit of Buddhahood without ever losing it.
Unlike the provisional teachings, which distinguish between self and other Buddhas, and thus involve going to the abodes of those Buddhas and returning to one's own land;
this teaching is not like that, for it does not shift from its original location nor employ supernatural powers, but rather remains eternally pervasive by relying on its fundamental dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the service of the various Buddhas, it is able to accord with both the universal and the particular. Ninth, the retribution body is perfected and its land is identical [to the Buddhas].

Because one gives rise to faith by means of the true Dharma and cultivates the practice, which is both constant and pervasive throughout the body, the wisdom of the Dharma-body (dharmajñāna) manifests such that both the person and the environment are perfected;
this is because a single perfection is identical to the fulfillment of all.

Because the wisdom of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna) ultimately encompasses all dimensions, whether great or small, it serves as the basis for the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body, such that the primary and secondary retributions are likewise equal.

Regarding those who share the same doubts and obtain the same benefits: as in the first assembly, fifty-five groups simultaneously shared the same doubts and thoughts, and together requested the Tathāgata to emit light to manifest the fruit and virtue;
they were simultaneously benefited, each group attaining one dharma. Once one person had attained the dharmas of all the others, it was thus for all nine assemblies that followed.
The ten types of shared dharmas mentioned above have no resemblance whatsoever to other teachings;
this fundamental wisdom, this fundamental dharma, at its fundamental time and fundamental place, consists of the practice-gates of the six stages of the ancient Buddhas.
The great ocean-like assembly fills the void and exists within every atom, layer upon layer in this manner, gathering simultaneously as described in this Great Sūtra.
From beginning to end, this ocean-like assembly has all achieved and manifested the gates of cause and effect for the Buddhas across the five stages and six positions that the Tathāgata rides;
not a single person among them has attained the fruits of the Three Vehicles.

This is because, through this Dharma, those at the initial mind of the Ten Abidings possess both essence and function equal to the Buddha, relying on the Dharma of fundamental wisdom, and thus neither increase nor decrease with respect to the Dharma.
The essential nature of benefiting sentient beings spontaneously across the ten locations and ten assemblies, along with the characteristics of the gathered multitudes,

can only be analyzed by explaining the meaning according to the text. Eighth, regarding the distinction between principle and phenomena within the dharma-gates bestowed, as stated in the provisional teachings of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, there exists...

The teaching that "sentient beings possess Buddha-nature while insentient things lack it," such that all grasses and trees cannot attain the Way or turn the wheel of Dharma—as found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—is the ultimate teaching that transcends conceptual sentiment (*vīta-rāga*).

This is not like the provisional teachings of the transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*). Regarding the teachings for ordinary beings, as exemplified by the ten forest Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakāśa (Virtue Forest) Bodhisattva, from whom they have come: [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the distinction between the ultimate truth of the *Avataṃsaka* and the provisional teachings of the *Vaipulya* or *Nirvāṇa* traditions concerning the capacity for Buddhahood.]
Each realm is also called "wisdom," and all objective spheres are collectively termed the "essence of wisdom.
Why is this so? Because there is neither sentient being nor non-sentient thing. This is because there are no two views;
it is the sphere of the single true wisdom where there is neither one who attains Buddhahood nor one who does not. Now, as for "sentient" and "non-sentient," these are merely based upon karma.
To say that one who has attained Buddhahood does not belong to the realm of karma is incorrect; for if one does not belong to the realm of karma, they would be neither sentient nor insentient.
How, then, can one calculate whether there is attainment of Buddhahood or non-attainment of Buddhahood regarding phenomena that transcend sentience?
That which is "sentient" and that which is "insentient" are categories subsumed under karma, not the liberation of a Buddha. How could one possibly [apply such distinctions] to the latter?
Based on my own mental calculations, I have made such a divination regarding the sentient and the non-sentient, and whether things are accomplished or not:
as stated in the sutras, all these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure;
the world-characteristic is eternally abiding, and all dharmas abide in their own dharma-position. Is this path for the sake of sentient beings and non-sentient things? Or is it not?
The essential meaning within this Avataṃsaka Sūtra is that fundamentally there are no ordinary beings or sages, and neither the animate nor the inanimate;
the entire true Dharma-body constitutes the single realm of Buddha-wisdom, with nothing else remaining. Do not use the conceptual measures of an ordinary person to falsely attempt to gauge it.
If one persists in such emotional calculations, one will see sentient beings attaining Buddhahood while seeing insentient things as unable to attain Buddhahood. This is...

Those who cling to their own karma and understand it in such a way will never attain Buddhahood. As for the statement that the principle of nature (*dharmatā*) pervades all insentient things yet sentient beings do not equally attain Buddhahood:

this is because they have not seen the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), do not rely on true wisdom, and have not realized that the various marks of the world are primordially and eternally abiding;
rather, they perceive only the arising and ceasing produced by the transformations of emotional consciousness.

To falsely deliberate upon these characteristics and claim that "sentient" and "insentient" are merely conventional designations while asserting that only the underlying principle (*li*) exists is incorrect.

For instance, regarding the attainment of Buddhahood—how could there be a Buddha existing apart from this principle? If the principle itself is the Buddha, then within this principle, the characteristics of the sentient and the insentient are fundamentally non-different;
how then could the categories of "sentient" and "insentient" be established based on deluded perception? As it is with the Buddha...
Sentient beings who are insentient should not be able to attain Buddhahood; yet if there are those who achieve Great Bodhi, it is because they do not rely on these two views.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings the provisional back to the one reality, stating:

"The meanings of the various natures and characteristics—I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know this matter. This applies to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
Those who study the provisional teachings of these three vehicles are collectively unable to understand this in its full extent, as detailed in that sutra.

For example, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is taught that both sentient and non-sentient beings are all the objective realm of wisdom; all mountains, rivers, trees, and forests can manifest the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and preach the Dharma.
These are identical to the Buddha-body in their capacity to manifest both identity and distinction.
While the Unobstructed Buddha dwells in the world, maintaining and establishing his sovereign, adorned realm with its various distinct arrays,
within each and every state of adornment of that wondrous land— within even a single mote of dust— the ocean of lands appears in successive layers;
the Buddha’s bodies are inexhaustible, and from the pores of each Buddha-body, there likewise appear...
Furthermore, within such realms, the myriad Buddha-bodies are inexhaustible, mutually penetrating one another;

they can be identical and yet distinct, entirely the same and yet entirely different. Pure and impure lands are without obstruction or hindrance, regardless of whether they consist of sentient or insentient beings.
Therefore, it is now said that the gates of teaching bestowed are distinct; moreover, within the provisional teachings, various practices take precedence.

The fruit of Buddhahood occurs after the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Within this teaching, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Buddha-fruit is realized first, while the wisdom of differentiation (*pravicaya-jñāna*) serves as its mutual support;
thus, the aspects of cause and effect are simultaneously and instantaneously penetrated without temporal sequence.
When one is perfected, all are perfected; when one is destroyed, all are destroyed—unlike other teachings, where one stage is cultivated at a time.
Because the stages are equal in nature, equal in time, equal in practice, and equal in wisdom, one should cultivate concentration and wisdom and observe them with discerning intelligence,
rather than relying on emotional or intellectual interpretations. Ninth,
regarding the distinction between [this teaching] and the attainment of fruits by the three vehicles, as explained in the sutras, it is for the sake of those who are śrāvakas.
The teaching of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; the teaching of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is for all Bodhisattvas;

and the teaching of the Six Pāramitās is what should be practiced now. This Flower Ornament Sūtra (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*) also teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, yet it differs from the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvakas, as is extensively clarified in the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," where all are established as the Four Noble Truths.

The illumination of the origin and nature of suffering and its accumulation is fundamentally the primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); it differs from the three vehicles because it is free from longing for the former and aversion toward the latter.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage practice the contemplation of the ten truths (*daśa-satya*), they perceive that all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions are expounding the Dharma-wheel of the Four Truths;
however, these differ only according to the various types of sounds [of sentient beings]. This is like the worldly teachings of Confucius and Laozi, which all serve as means of governance.
The dharmas for sentient beings are always the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths; however, according to the capacities of their vessels, the teachings bestowed differ in depth and breadth.
Whether it be the exposition of the twelve divisions of the scriptures or the recitation of mantras, all are subsumed within the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Śrāvakas, following only their own individual faculties, receive a portion of the teaching for severing suffering—just as in the Small Vehicle, one severs [the afflictions].

The nature of suffering is as extensively explained in the various schools of the Hīnayāna; here, we shall discuss it briefly in terms of the general characteristics of the goal and the place where the fruit is realized across the four vehicles.
Śrāvakas, contemplating the two truths of suffering and its origin, give rise to profound revulsion and weariness.

They practice contemplations such as impermanence, impurity, the white bone, and the reduction to dust, knowing that the body is empty and quiescent. Following this wisdom of the dharma of emptiness and quiescence, they extinguish the body.
The non-arising of delusion is called cessation; this state of cessation is termed *nirvāṇa*.

Even if one were to arise from emptiness, there would subsequently be no faults such as the three poisons of the world. This is because, prior to entering the Path, one cultivates various contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) to subdue [afflictions], just as one uses a mantra to subdue a venomous snake.
Furthermore, by cultivating the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one realizes that the nature of the mind is originally extinguished.
Because there is no self by virtue of this dharma of the non-self of persons, the three poisons are empty and karma is not produced.
Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, compassion and wisdom never depart from this practice; that which does not depart from this is ultimately identical to emptiness.

When the mind of compassion suddenly ceases, it is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). To extinguish and subdue all sufferings is called the Truth of Cessation. By means of this Truth of Cessation, it is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "For example, it is like a person who is intoxicated; only after the alcohol has worn off does he regain consciousness.

The realization of the Dharma is likewise: having attained the supreme body of a Buddha through such means as these, those who do not rely on the Buddha's wisdom but instead cultivate exclusively the concentration of emptiness recognize their error from this point onward, turn their minds toward the correct path, and are able to attain the Buddha-body, just as the sūtra describes those who achieve eternal cessation."
Because they are attached to stagnant quiescence, they are exhorted to practice early rather than seeking eternal extinction; for the nirvāṇa produced through cultivation is not eternal extinction.
This is a point of reconciliation found within the Mahāyāna sūtras themselves; for instance, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra contains no such passage [as that of the Śrāvakas].
As for those of the pratyekabuddha lineage, they know that the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is fundamentally without reality.
Knowing that their own essence is entirely empty, they realize that both body and mind are inherently devoid of a master.

Since body and mind lack a master, their nature is eternally without self (*anātman*). Because there is no self, ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished; with the extinction of ignorance, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are extinguished.

They dwell in solitary awakening, roaming freely according to their nature. Because they differ from the *śrāvakas*, they do not pursue [mere] quiescence; because they differ from the *bodhisattvas*, they have no [conceptual] existence.
Because his compassion and wisdom do not incline toward mere quiescence, he is superior to the śrāvakas; because he is able to uphold the Dharma, he is not inferior to the śrāvakas.
Although a śrāvaka may hear the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Buddha and be able to proclaim them, they have not personally realized them.
As Vimalakīrti rebuked him, such a person cannot preach the Dharma of the true mark with a mind that still functions in terms of arising and ceasing.

The bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings—those who have newly turned away from the two vehicles and lesser bodhisattvas who have not yet fully possessed the wisdom of great compassion—are exemplified by those in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and similar texts.
These works speak only of the six pāramitās to inspire those of lesser faculties and lead them to develop wisdom;
because such practitioners are biased toward the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and remain stagnant in a lack of wisdom, these texts teach only the six pāramitās.

Because their faculties are inferior, those who have attained the "honey" stage still fear birth and death; it has not yet been taught that the seven, eight, nine, or ten *pāramitās* constitute the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*).
Because they fulfill great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they are able to transport and deliver others while remaining within birth and death.
As stated in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), ordinary beings outside and inside the stages of holiness cultivate the six *pāramitās* and become six kinds of persons.
The four pāramitās beginning with patience (*kṣānti*) are all [included in] the four types of wheel-turning kings;
by practicing the ten pāramitās across the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), they can accomplish the ten kinds of celestial kingship.

Furthermore, according to other sūtras, for those of the gradual and sudden vehicles who train in their respective capacities, although they cultivate the ten pāramitās, they do so while cultivating compassion and wisdom (*karuṇā-prajñā*).
By means of the contemplation of provisional *tathatā*, one contemplates all phenomena as being, from the very beginning, inherently quiescent, non-transmigrating, and unchanging;
through this contemplation, one breaks the dualistic attachments to emptiness and existence and accomplishes the Dharma-gate of neither arising nor ceasing.

However, because those from the first up to the ninth stage have not yet clarified their Buddha-nature, they cultivate that provisional wisdom, which consequently becomes an obstruction—as previously explained.
The teaching of such sutras is for those of the highest faculties, who are shown instantaneously the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
At the very first moment its initial arousal, they are identical to the Buddha’s wisdom upon the stage of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*).

This is the meaning of [the passage] concerning Sudhana attaining the "light of the wisdom of all Buddhas" on the summit of Mount Meghaśrī. Because one relies upon the dharma of fundamental wisdom, there is nothing that is not [attained].

Because cultivation is primordial and there are no obstructions, compassion and wisdom are spontaneously accomplished without effort. Following conditions within the six realms, nothing is not the Dharma-realm;
realizing that the self-nature of dependently arisen phenomena is eternally true, there is no further need for cultivation or action. All thoughts and deliberations arise from wisdom;
one simply knows how to spontaneously manifest a physical body to preach the Dharma according to the capacity of beings, like an echo responding to a sound.
Although the *dharmakāya* is eternally quiescent while constantly abiding within the stream of birth and death, its essence does not shift even after passing through many kalpas;
entering death and being born is neither perishing nor arising. Because it accords with conditions through the power of great compassion and wisdom, the Dharma must be thus;
its nature is free from sorrow and affliction, and it does not abide in the cultivation of realization. Because the Dharma is thus, the Dragon Girl and Sudhana together clarify this principle.
This Dharma is difficult to believe; those of the Three Vehicles fold their hands and defer from afar, claiming that this is a transformation-body and not a human being.
They speak of the *saṃghī* [kalpa] as established according to worldly sentiment; how could they believe this gate of timeless wisdom?

Therefore, the Sūtra says that "to be able to believe this Dharma is extremely difficult"—this refers precisely to such matters. Even if one were to practice with diligent effort and austerity for many kalpas, [it would still be difficult].
If one seeks attainment, striving to lengthen or shorten, to do this or that, to create or destroy, and even sacrificing body and life, how could there ever be a time of attaining Buddhahood?
How much better it would be to enter the realm of Buddha-wisdom and practice from the very first thought;
would this not save effort and avoid wasting one's labor? For this reason, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are expedient [teachings].
The teaching for bodhisattvas— that the non-true understanding of the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
and the realm of true wisdom regarding *tathatā* and the *dharmakāya*, as well as all practices performed according to wisdom across the various stages (*bhūmi*),

are all expedient means of Vairocana to lead practitioners toward this ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*’s reality and cause them to return to the fundamental Dharma— is such that no subject-object duality arises in what is enacted through wisdom.
The mind accomplishes all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) entirely; it does not resemble the various teachings that apply distinct remedies on the stages (*bhūmi*).

Rather, at the very end of the stage of ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the initial position of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), one spontaneously realizes that the fundamentally wise realm of the intermingled *dharmadhātu* is such that ordinary beings and sages are no different, and the entire substance is the absolute truth, wherein one perceives neither sentient beings nor insentient things, and neither existence nor non-existence.
The nature [of phenomena] is thus bound and obstructed, such that they do not arise according to their own nature, as described in the sūtras.
When a Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment and appears in the world, he perceives all sentient beings with his own wisdom as having attained equal and perfect enlightenment;

he is free from the sentiments of good and evil, and their natures and characteristics are no different. Although he delivers sentient beings, there are none who are delivered—this is what is called [the ultimate reality].
Because it plants all the roots of goodness for the marks of a Tathāgata, this Dharma is entrusted for circulation;
its depth and shallowness differ entirely from those of the three vehicles. It is not heard by those of the provisional Mahāyāna, the two vehicles, or those of the human and celestial realms;
rather, it flows only for those of the most superior faculties—namely, the Bodhisattvas who aspire to the causal and resultant stages of Buddhahood.

One can hear that within the aforementioned four vehicles there are clear proofs; since the vehicles thus ridden are distinct and the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is entirely different, their depths and shallows are completely separated by a single name.

Furthermore, as stated in the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage cultivate ten kinds of contemplations on the Four Truths, while Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage cultivate ten kinds [of contemplations].
The twelve links of dependent origination differ from those of the three vehicles’ four truths and twelve links of dependent origination.
The tenth [section] clarifies the specific manner in which the entrusted Dharma-treasury is to be circulated, as stated in the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate was not taught by the Tathāgata for other sentient beings; it was taught only for those who are intent upon the Great [Vehicle]."

This Dharma-gate of the sutra is taught solely for those who ride the Bodhisattva vehicle—that is, for those who ride the inconceivable Bodhisattva vehicle—and it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the children of the Buddha.

It is, for example, like the seven treasures possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King; it is because of these treasures that the Wheel-Turning King is manifested, yet these treasures [do not belong to others].

They shall fall into the hands of other sentient beings, with the sole exception of a crown prince born of the first queen who is fully endowed with the marks of a noble universal monarch (*cakravartin*);

for if such a king lacks this son possessed of all virtues, immediately after his death, these various jewels will all vanish and perish within seven days. O Son of the Buddha, this sutra is likewise a precious jewel.

It is likewise thus: it shall not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for those true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and have planted the roots of goodness that produce the marks of a Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, if there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. Why is this? Because all those of the two vehicles...
If one does not even hear this sutra, how much less can one receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, analyze, or explain it?

Only bodhisattvas are able to do so. Therefore, when a bodhisattva hears this Dharma-gate, they should rejoice greatly and, with a heart of reverence, respectfully receive and uphold it upon their heads.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has faith and delight in this sutra will swiftly [attain...]
Because one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is explained that "being born into the family of the Tathāgata" means:
one personally awakens to the fact that the fundamental wisdom of one's own *dharmakāya* is equal in essence and characteristics to the true nature of the Buddha;

being devoid of self-nature and flavor, it is indistinguishably merged with the *dharmadhātu*. When all notions of self and other are exhausted, only the Buddha’s wisdom remains, penetrating clearly through the ten directions, for there is no self-nature.
To be without dependence and without the nature of birth-and-death is called being born into the family of the Buddha.
By virtue of the power of innate, effortless, and impartial compassion and wisdom, one upholds and glorifies the True Dharma and governs sentient beings.

According to what is appropriate for each, one subdues them with the Dharma, causing all sentient beings to eliminate the karma of birth-and-death; thus, all dharmas of peace and happiness are entirely [attained].
To delight in this is called upholding the Dharma of the Buddha’s household; it is also called planting the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata.

The commentary explains: to realize that the nature of the Buddha’s Dharmakāya is identical to the Dharma-realm and identical to the Buddha’s compassion and wisdom, and thus to practice with faith such that principle and phenomena are not distinct and nature and characteristics are equal—those who study in this manner plant the marks of a Tathāgata and accord with the goodness of the Buddha.
The faculties [of those addressed by] provisional teachings differ; they are entrusted to the three vehicles—śrāvakas and bodhisattvas—and are commonly circulated among them.
Furthermore, the teachings of the three vehicles are mostly entrusted to various sages and to ordinary beings who have not yet been born into the Buddha-family.
This sutra, however, is entrusted solely to ordinary beings of the supreme great mind who seek only the inconceivable vehicle of the Tathāgata and are thus born into the Buddha-family.
If ordinary beings without the great resolve were to seek this Dharma-gate and be born into the family of the Tathāgata, this sutra would surely perish. Why is this?
Because this sutra is difficult to believe; even if there were holy teachings, ordinary beings would not believe them or realize them, and thus this sutra would perish.
If it were not for such an entrustment to ordinary beings so that they may be born into the Buddha-family, the noble-rank bodhisattvas [would not have this opportunity].
When there are Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-worlds, why worry about the disappearance of this sutra?
You should know that such is the intention of the Tathāgatas: to cause ordinary beings to give rise to faith and practice so that they may be born into the family of the Buddhas.
One should not think that one has already attained the rank of a Buddha; rather, all bodhisattvas and all practitioners should understand it in this way. For what reason?

The teachings of the Three Vehicles were mostly entrusted to various noble ones (āryas) to ensure their circulation, as well as to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who have not yet been born into the Buddha-family.
This was because the Dharma of the Three Vehicles had not yet emerged from the dust of the sensory world and its principles were not yet manifest;

thus, it was easy for them to believe and understand. Therefore, both ordinary beings and noble ones were made to praise [the teachings] together so that the teaching might circulate and the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) would not be severed.

Because the measure of ordinary cognition does not accord with this—wherein the final moment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) is itself Buddhahood—for this reason, the teachings of the Three Vehicles provisionally lead beings forward gradually;
since they have not yet transcended the dust of the sensory objects, it takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before one attains Buddhahood.

Because these teachings that conform to worldly sentiments are easy for the faculties of beings to believe, they are praised by both the ordinary and the sages and are thus universally propagated, unlike [the sudden teaching].

The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the wisdom of differentiation (*prabheda-jñāna*), as well as the teachings on great kindness and great compassion of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the *Avataṃsaka*, transcend the dust of emotional attachments and are profound and difficult to believe. Therefore, they must await entry into the stage of realization at the rank of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), being born into the Buddha-family as a true son of the Buddha, for them to be propagated.
If there are only the holy words but no one who enters into realization, it cannot be called [the true transmission].
If the circulation [of the teaching] consists merely of the discourse of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) without anyone entering into realization, it cannot be called "circulation.

This is because one's own Dharma is not yet clear, and the state of doubt remains; since the darkness of both self and others has not been dispelled, one is unable to definitively know the Buddha’s intention.
For this reason, one must wait until one enters into realization and becomes identical to the wisdom-mind of all Buddhas before one can definitively know it.
Because it is the gateway to Buddhism, for this reason, entrusting it to great-minded ordinary beings who have entered realization is what constitutes its initial circulation;
merely hearing it without internalizing it does not constitute circulation.
Fourth, clarifying the identity and difference of attaining Buddhahood:

The wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) is vast and empty, encompassing the myriad phenomena to form its physical frame. Since the myriad phenomena have no form, they share the same substance as the wisdom-body.

When one deviates from the true marks, they are separated; when one attains the fundamental source, their forms are identical. It is solely because of straying from the fundamental and differing in appearance that transformation occurs.
The manifestations are each distinct: some see his form emaciated as he reclines upon a bed of grass beneath the Bodhi tree with his humble body;
some see him in the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*) amidst the wondrous appearance of a lotus flower; some see him dwelling under a precious Bodhi tree in a pure land to achieve perfection;
some see him practicing through distant eons; some see him attaining realization in a single instant; and some see the fulfillment of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The ocean of marks is boundless; sometimes one sees the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) with its divided bodies fully endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Such diverse forms and strange appearances pervade all sentient beings, whose emotional faculties differ in ten thousand ways and a thousand variations—how could words ever fully describe them?

For now, focusing on those shared by humans and devas, and categorized according to the provisional and real aspects of the four vehicles, we shall briefly compose ten gates to clarify the differences in the attainment of enlightenment.

For the sake of inspiring faith in the spiritually immature, removing their doubts, causing them to recognize the fundamental nature, and leading them to abandon provisional attachments while aspiring toward supreme virtues, there are ten sections:

first, the distinction of the Buddha-body; second, the distinction of the time of attaining Buddhahood; third, the distinction of the Bodhi tree; fourth, the distinction of the seat upon which he sits;
fifth, the distinction of the assembly dwelling with him; sixth, the distinction of the manifested marks; seventh... [and so forth].
Section Eight: The Distinction of Turning the Wheel of Dharma; Section Nine: The Distinction of the Places Where the Wheel of Dharma is Turned;

Section Ten: The Distinction of the Adornments of the Great Assembly; Section One: The Distinction of the Dharmas Received. Regarding the distinction of the body of the Buddha upon attaining enlightenment:
this body of Vairocana Buddha, as described in the sutra, possesses ninety-seven kinds of marks as well as an inexhaustible body of marks; it is not merely thirty.
Regarding the second point, the body endowed with the two marks and eighty minor characteristics: the distinction regarding the time of attaining Buddhahood is as follows.

In the provisional teachings, it is held that after the Buddha’s birth, he immediately leaves the city to renounce the world and attains perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; this is taken as the timing.
However, in the case of Vairocana Buddha, which represents the ultimate reality, it is not so; rather, the Tathāgata establishes his manifestation in this manner.
The manifestation of attaining Buddhahood through renunciation as a means to deliver sentient beings of the three vehicles should be viewed in this way;
it is not like the "Ocean of the True Dharma Realm" described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed. This is precisely the turning of those followers of the three vehicles toward the ultimate reality.

This treatise discusses how this Buddha Vairocana, having attained great enlightenment (mahābodhi) based upon the fundamental dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), likewise relies upon that same fundamental dharma-realm—which is without beginning or end, neither appearing nor disappearing, neither arising nor perishing, and devoid of temporal divisions. As this sutra states:
"The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa. This is the definitive teaching. Furthermore, he wears a flower upon his crown.
The crown is fundamentally not for those who have left the household life and lacks all eight characteristics [of a Buddha’s birth].

If there is anyone who can know that the Tathāgata neither emerges nor vanishes, neither becomes nor perishes, they will know that the Tathāgata eternally dwells in the world and eternally turns the wheel of Dharma;
this is precisely Vairocana appearing in the world, descending from the Tuṣita Heaven to enter the womb.
The turning of the wheel of Dharma and the entry into nirvāṇa within the mother’s womb do not exceed the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
While that deity has not yet descended from the womb and he has not yet emerged from it, he has already entered nirvāṇa; all matters of the dharmas are thus completely concluded.

Regarding the third point, the distinction concerning the Bodhi tree: among the three vehicles, the Buddha-path tree is seen as a wooden tree, its height and proportions corresponding to those of humans.
In this interim, within the One Vehicle, the tree under which the Tathāgata attains enlightenment is a precious tree,
lofty and exceptionally sublime, like the tree manifested within the body of Vajragarbha; it is one hundred triple-thousand great thousand-world systems in height,
and its circumference is thirteen thousand great thousand-world systems, its great significance pervading all places.

Therefore, regarding the distinction of the seat occupied in the fourth [section]: in the Three Vehicles, the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) attains enlightenment by discarding honor and nobility to rely upon a grass mat;
in this One Vehicle, the Original Body (mūlakāya) attains enlightenment seated upon a precious lotus lion-throne, adorned with exquisite jewels and endowed with all manner of ornaments.
Regarding the distinction of the fifth, the Great Assembly: it is for the sake of Vairocana Buddha.
The entire assembly surrounding [the Buddha] consists entirely of the multitudes such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, as well as those who have newly resolved their minds;

they are all members of the Dharma-realm assembly seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, and not the assembly of those of the three vehicles who study expediently, seeking the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas out of weariness with suffering, or those bodhisattvas who seek birth in a pure land out of attachment to pleasure. Even if there were any voice...

If one hears this yet the multitude’s minds have not yet turned back—as if deaf, not hearing, not knowing, and not seeing—this is because they are not the assembly that attained the fruit after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas following the previous sutra;

rather, it is the assembly for whom wisdom is perfected over many kalpas as a single limit, with no time of before or after. Sixth, regarding the distinction of the manifested marks, it is as follows:
In the provisional teachings, this refers to being born in Tuṣita Heaven, descending as a spirit, entering the womb, and so forth—the eight phases of attaining the Way.
In the One Vehicle teaching, it refers to taking the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya at the initial stage of the first resolve (prathamacittotpāda-vihāra) as true awakening.

Here, emotional attachments to beginning and end are severed; one perceives neither the passage of time nor its lack of passage. Without deviating from the present moment, one accumulates merit and attains realization.

The Buddha is entirely devoid of any temporal transition or change; his true self-nature constantly turns the wheel of Dharma, unlike the provisional teachings which involve matters such as the eight signs [of death].

He may sit upon the Jewel King throne in the realm of Maheśvara, or take the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system as his field of retribution—such are the dimensions he establishes through his skillful means.
Those who are restricted by limited measures merely guide sentient beings through the transformative rituals of gradual cultivation to broaden their minds;

this is not yet the ultimate reality of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Such a wondrous gateway to the *dharmadhātu* of the *Avataṃsaka*, which—by way of division—is comprised of ten Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust within the Lotus Treasury Sea of Worlds, reflecting one another in infinite layers, serves to clarify how inexhaustible Buddha-lands mutually penetrate one another.
Each and every Buddha-field fills the ten directions; as many lands as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields are all infinite and unobstructed.
Body and land correspond to one another, such that there is no appearance of coming or going between "this" and "that.

This differs from the three vehicles, which, for the sake of those with inferior faculties, provisionally establish limited measures of body and land. Such is the ocean-like manifestation of Vairocana; even a single atom [contains this].
It is not that the ten directions are separated from his pores, nor is there any deficiency in his ocean of lands.

Those who manifest the three vehicles are like fireflies whose light cannot be compared to the illuminating power of the sun and moon; their lapis lazuli is difficult to liken to the pure virtue of the maṇi jewel.
This is not because of the Buddha himself, but solely because the vessels [of sentient beings] are inferior. Thus, the seventh turning of the wheel of Dharma is distinct.
The manifested Buddhas turn the wheel of the Dharma of the three vehicles, while Vairocana turns the wheel of the Dharma of the one vehicle.
The "one vehicle" refers to the Buddha-vehicle; as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-vehicle is only one, there is no second, nor is there a third;
it is only through provisional verbal expressions that sentient beings are guided, until they mount the Tathāgata-vehicle and proceed directly to the Way."

This assembly is a Lotus Sūtra gathering intended to lead those of the three vehicles toward the ultimate reality, as previously explained in the section on the classification of teachings according to their schools.
It is solely for the sake of those with the dispositions of the three vehicles that the teaching of the three vehicles is expounded based upon their original dispositions.

To claim that the account of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant is merely a provisional transformation (a *nirmāṇa*) and thus constitutes a slander of the teaching that does not accord with the Buddha’s intent is incorrect.
The original intent of the Buddha was to enable the dragon girl to attain Buddhahood in a single instant as the fundamental Dharma;
since the Dharma itself is timeless, the moment of realization is the very essence of reality. To claim instead that this was merely an expedient transformation—alas, what a tragedy!
What can be done about it? Instead of expecting nectar, one has received poison; instead of taking precious jade, one has called it mere dust and soil. How can this be true?
Regarding that which is empty as being empty, and that which is empty as being real—may future sages refrain from following the dharma-gates of former worthies and ancient saints.
May all universally bestow their instructions; according to capacities, the provisional and the real follow paths that are not of one kind. This is deeply worthy of long reflection.

One who is fully conversant with the Buddha’s intent, clearly understands the provisional and the real, and transmits the teachings in accordance with them without obstructing any faculties, may bring both the provisional and the real to salvation; such a person alone is fit to lead others.
If the small [vehicle] returns to the great assembly and the holy ones grant their approval, then the real shall be established as the empty;

the Buddha will not be displeased, and one may rely on the transmitted teachings of the school to bring benefit and happiness to humans and devas, so that gold and jade may shine brilliantly and none shall sink into oblivion.

Therefore, the Buddha Vairocana preached the Buddha-vehicle, while the transformation Buddhas preached the three vehicles; within these teachings, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras represent the gradual [teachings].

The gate of gradually leading through provisional means toward the ultimate reality is exemplified by the parable of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant and the metaphor of the snow-mountain fat grass—such as when a cow eats it and produces only pure *sarpis* (clarified butter)—all of which serve to partially indicate what is not yet fully revealed.
Only this *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra possesses the complete gate that fully demonstrates the individual characteristics of cause, condition, retribution, and fruition; therefore, [it is supreme].

Now, regarding the "turning of the wheel of Dharma" and the "distinctions of the locations for turning the wheel of Dharma" as the eighth section: within the provisional teachings, the transformation Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma;
some say it is at the Deer Park, others say it is at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, and so forth, all of which have specific locations where they come and go between higher and lower realms.
This sutra, however, concerns ten locations and ten assemblies, as well as the Buddha-lands and Buddha-bodies within all atoms.

Layer upon layer, infinitely and inexhaustibly turning the wheel of Dharma—neither going nor coming, neither emerging nor submerging—at the sites of the ten assemblies, which shall be further clarified later;

all are said to be "not departing from the site of enlightenment while ascending to all places," as the *Sūtra* itself fully explains. Regarding the specific adornments of the ninth great assembly, they are now described.
At the time of this sutra’s teaching, the holy assemblies and great-minded beings from the ten directions gathered simultaneously in ten locations among devas and humans.
There were none among them who possessed a fixed nature in the three vehicles or had not yet turned their minds [toward enlightenment];

even those present in the assembly who did not belong to that stream were included. Furthermore, the members of each of these ten assemblies came from the ten directions, and for each direction from which they arrived, it is said:

There were assemblies of beings as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields who gathered together; in each successive stage and ground, they increased tenfold, hundredfold, and thousandfold to manifest inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, in each and every assembly, the multitudes pervaded the entire dharma-realm, layer upon layer, reflecting one another like images in light;
even within a single speck of dust, there were further layers of assemblies, and within each atom, there were further assemblies.

All these assemblies are equal to the Dharma-realm and empty space; even within the body of a single small sentient being, they manifest the ocean-like multitude of Perfectly Enlightened Ones, turning the wheel of the True Dharma in layers upon layers. Yet those sentient beings do not know or perceive this.
Such assemblies are all the bodies and lands of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whose nature pervades all places. All such assemblies...

Because it pervades all places, it does not resemble the assemblies of transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) within the Three Vehicles, which all have specific locations, limits, and boundaries, and involve coming and going;
this is because those [assemblies] are for the sake of beings with inferior faculties and are not the Buddha himself. However, the specific dharma-gate bestowed in the tenth stage is as follows:
according to the provisional teachings, one may gradually cultivate impermanence, suffering, and emptiness starting from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Disgusted with old age, sickness, and death, one cultivates the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths; therein, the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are regarded as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the two truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are regarded as ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). One contemplates that suffering and its origin are truly suffering, thereby giving rise to a profound sense of weary detachment and seeking the pursuit of nirvana.
Through contemplations such as impermanence, impurity, and the white bones, one contemplates those atoms until they are fully realized.

Through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), suffering and its origin are fundamentally non-existent; consciousness ceases and wisdom perishes. Taking emptiness as the realization, one first brings suffering to an end.

Only thereafter does one preach the Mahāyāna Dharma to cause them to turn their minds toward practicing the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), gradually giving rise to compassion and wisdom.
Alternatively, for those who possess the Mahāyāna bodhisattva lineage, their contemplative practice serves as an antidote that resembles [the goal].

Those of the Hīnayāna lineage possess compassion and delight in practicing the various pāramitās; they do not realize emptiness prematurely, but rather retain their afflictions to benefit sentient beings, cultivating contemplations such as the dharma-emptiness (dharma-nairātmya).
Alternatively, there are Mahāyāna bodhisattvas of the single-seed lineage who practice both the provisional and the true thusness (tathatā) all at once;
through the preparatory application of the gate of provisional thusness for subduing [afflictions], they traverse the ten stages over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

"Only upon seeing one's nature does one first become a Buddha. Some teachings state that Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages prior to the stages (bhūmi) suppress ignorance through the power of contemplation;
others state that upon reaching the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) on the stages, they see it.

Yet other teachings state that the Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages partially perceive the Dharma-body. All such explanations are entirely what is taught in the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, like these flowers.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is not like that; it directly bestows the fundamental Dharmakāya—the very essence of the Dharma-realm—upon those of the highest capacity.
It suddenly causes the ocean of wisdom of the ancient Buddhas, which has been obscured by ignorance, to manifest through the samādhi of skillful means.
It entirely confers the fruit of Buddhahood upon the initial mind of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) in a single thought-moment and at one time.

Within the single gateway of the ultimate Dharma-realm, the myriad practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—both principle and phenomena—are gathered instantaneously; there is no further measure of emotion or intellect.

Expanding and contracting, extending and shortening, they do not abandon conformity with worldly conventions, yet the distinctions of time, eons, and the years and days of the three periods of existence remain clearly present.
Thus, while those years and eons do not themselves shift, both the permanent and the impermanent are simultaneously manifest.

The nature of phenomena is neither produced nor destroyed; one understands the Truth of Suffering in this way: from the beginning, the Noble Truths have never possessed suffering, nor is there any nirvāṇa.
If one has such faith and understanding, and enters into realization accordingly, as the Sūtra says:

"By means of a small portion of skillful means, one swiftly attains Bodhi. Thus, through the gateway of the illusion of wisdom, one magically manifests a body equal in extent to the realm of sentient beings.
To engage in the affairs of sentient beings is to employ the gate of unimpeded mindfulness; to understand the faculties of sentient beings is to employ the gate of being a teacher and model;
to establish rules and regulations is to employ the gate of all arts and skills; to instruct and admonish sentient beings is to employ the gate of the field of practice that is without dependence;
for phenomena to be without attachment is to employ the gate of non-thought; and to think without attachment is to employ the light of pure wisdom.
The gate of illumination constantly shines, unimpededly establishing all dharmas to deliver sentient beings;
by means of the gate of inexhaustible marks, one does not destroy the form-body; by means of the gate of truthful vow-speech, whatever is spoken is true and real;
by means of the gate of illusory abiding, one dwells eternally in the world to bring sentient beings to the liberation of their faculties—these ten dharmas are thus.
The gateways of spiritual friends within the stage of Equal Enlightenment of the youth Sudhana,

which cause all practitioners to suddenly cultivate and enter the conduct that benefits and pacifies sentient beings through these ten dharmas, and the dharma-gate of liberation that excellently abides in the world,
are by no means like the methods of the Three Vehicles that involve revulsion toward suffering and its origin, and seeking joy in cessation and the path.
Nor is it a matter of lingering in delusions, delighting in emptiness, or emerging from the bonds of existence to separately seek a pure land.
Fifth, the distinctions in perceiving the Buddha are clarified:

for while the nature and characteristics of the Buddha’s body are a single, undifferentiated entity, the capacities of sentient beings are manifold, and their perceptions vary according to their faculties; thus, their mental dispositions differ.
When one perceives through conceptualization, views become severed, and the body stands in isolation; yet as shadows arise and emotions remain, the Buddha appears distinct from the Buddha.
Because the Buddha accords with these emotions, he deviates from the true mind. When emotions are exhausted and vanish, the Wisdom Body manifests spontaneously according to conditions.
Whether moving or still, all is true. To be in accord with this is what is called Vairocana Buddha. Vairocana means "various" or "manifold."

The light shines universally. Through the compassionate wisdom of the Dharmakāya, it manifests signs and employs the radiance of teaching to accord with the various faculties, appearing in forms according to their dispositions.

Because sentient beings deviate from the true nature, they perceive these signs differently, seeing distinct Buddhas. However, when essence and function are integrated, this is fundamentally the single wisdom-body of Vairocana.
One may only return to the truth and abandon the false; one must not remain attached to the false while claiming to have transcended it.
To briefly establish ten categories for the distinctions in perceiving the Buddha, so that those who have begun to believe may turn their minds toward them:
first, humans perceive the Buddha as possessing only the thirty-two primary marks; second, the devas perceive the Buddha as possessing only the eighty secondary signs;
third, the nāgas perceive the Buddha either as humans do or see him as... [text fragment].
1. As a great dragon king; other animals likewise perceive him as such. 2. The four classes of rishis see the Buddha only as a rishi. 3.
Other non-Buddhists see the Buddha as being of their own kind. 4. The eight classes of divine beings see the Buddha as their sovereign.
5. Those of the Hīnayāna see the Buddha as a great śrāvaka. 6. Those who are pratyekabuddhas see...
In the nine provisional teachings for Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas see the Buddha merely as the lord of a trichiliocosm,
with his merit and wisdom pervading that trichiliocosm. In the eleven vehicles of teaching,
Bodhisattvas see the Buddha as the lord of the Dharma-realm, presiding over a Lotus Treasury World-Ocean containing as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
The full text states: "Ten Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms of dust within the Lotus Treasury World" is mentioned to clarify that there is an inexhaustible, comprehensive integration of all lands;
for the oceans of marks of inexhaustibility are layered upon one another, with merit and wisdom filling all lands.

Thus, the ten aforementioned different ways of seeing the Buddha all arise from the differences in faith and aspiration at the time of generating the bodhicitta; it is by virtue of this faith and aspiration...

Because of these powers, the ways in which one perceives the Buddha differ; therefore, you should know that those who resolve their minds do so by giving rise to a vast mind, believing in the vast teachings, making vast vows, practicing vast deeds, and entering into vast wisdom.
By thus benefiting and bringing accomplishment to inexhaustible sentient beings, they shall swiftly achieve Bodhi, with their vows, merit, and wisdom all becoming perfectly complete.
If one does not proceed in this way, one will ultimately fail to achieve great bodhi; the labor will be great while the merit will be meager.
How much better it would be to go directly into the fundamental wisdom of all-knowledge!
Sixth, clarifying the timing for expounding the teaching.
Now, having realized the source of the Way—the awakened mind—which is empty and still, his wisdom is perfected; beginning and end throughout the three periods of time are both exhausted.

He unifies the myriad phenomena as being simultaneously existent and non-existent, blending past and future, and merging the present with antiquity. Vast and open, there is only the spirit; tranquil and serene, he responds to true feelings.

When attachment ceases, wisdom is established; when conceptualization is severed, compassion remains. His perfect voice spreads afar, benefiting beings according to their faculties, like a single rain that nourishes all universally.

The hundred flowers all attain [their blooming] simultaneously, like an echo in a valley that forms sound upon being struck; thus, all capacities receive benefit according to their wisdom, yet without intentional mind.

In a single kṣaṇa there is no limit—how could there be distinctions between past and present? Briefly relying on the provisional and the real, ten types of teachings are established, differing in their temporal sequence and duration.
The first is as stated in the *Mahābala-sūtra*: during the first seven days after the Buddha’s initial attainment of enlightenment.
First, having reflected thus, he immediately preached the Dharma at the Deer Park;

second, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, when the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths in the Deer Park, immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, up to the mind of a pratyekabuddha and the mind of great bodhi;
third, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, after twenty-one days, he went to the Deer Park.

The fourth [account] regarding the preaching of the Dharma is as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, which state that the Dharma was preached after six or seven days.
The fifth is as stated in the *Udānavarga-vṛtti* and the *Udāna-varga*, which state that the Dharma was preached after seven times seven days (forty-nine days).

The sixth is as stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which states that the Dharma was preached after eight times seven days (fifty-six days). The seventh is as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states it was after five times seven days (thirty-five days).
8. Regarding the timing of the preaching of the Dharma, according to the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra*, one year passed before the Dharma was preached. 9.

According to the judgment of Master Zang of the present Tang Dynasty, it was determined that after the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment for exactly two weeks, he then preached the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
10. Regarding the "Penetrating the Profundity" (*Tongxuan*), we now follow this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; as for the gateway of the *dharmadhātu*, we do not rely on [other] teachings.

The aforementioned discourse is as follows: this sutra takes as its primary tenet the fundamental reality of the Great Compassion of Principle and Phenomena, which is the self-substance and function of the original wisdom-nature of the Dharma-realm;

it does not rely on explanations based on emotional measures or temporal divisions. It exhausts all views of past and present, constantly turning the Wheel of Dharma without beginning or end, for the nature of phenomena is thus.
As explained above, this is entirely based upon the individual's own vision at the moment of the faculties.
These divisions are not like the Tathāgata’s distinctions; the essence of the Tathāgata’s fundamental dharma-wisdom admits no established temporal divisions.
Whenever one causes the mind to believe and resolve that the dharma-realm is timeless, that is precisely the time of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma.
When emotions cease and the mind is exhausted, those of sharp faculties act spontaneously—this is the time of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood and turning of the wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, if one’s mind persists in establishing views and claims that the Tathāgata appeared in the world at such a time and preached the Dharma at such a time, this is entirely based on personal bias rather than the Buddha’s vision. Such is the teaching-gate of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
it is a gate without beginning or end, and one must not follow personal sentiment to arbitrarily establish temporal divisions. This sutra is precisely [this].
Regarding "timelessness" as being all time, it is taught according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which says:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed. Since this measure is fundamentally non-existent, by what means could one know the time for preaching the Dharma?
All of these are the single function of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, his single perfect sound, occurring at a single moment; they are without time.
This is the time for preaching the Dharma.
Seventh, clarifying the provisional and the real regarding the Pure Land:
For the vast ocean of wisdom is so immense that its shores cannot be fathomed, and the profound source of truth is so expansive that it is rarely fully grasped.

Upon examining its boundaries, the essence and characteristics of the Vairocana Dharma-realm encompass as many vast and spiritual gateways as grains of sand on the Ganges, wherein purity and impurity interpenetrate infinitely.
It is simply that according to the differing objects perceived through the functions of one's own cultivation, the sacred teachings appear contradictory;

these variations arise because they are not fixed according to the faculties [of beings]. Thus, the provisional may distinguish a Pure Land in another realm, or point to the impure world of Sahā as such.
In some places, this location is presented as a provisional manifestation (*upāya*), while the upper direction is shown as the ultimate retribution body (*vipākaphala-kāya*);
Mañjuśrī’s residence is in the eastern land of the Golden World, yet he comes here, and Avalokiteśvara dwells in the western land of Sukhāvatī, yet he arrives here.

Thus, these various provisional manifestations differ, leaving those who have newly begun their faith without a point of reliance. Now, by briefly synthesizing these various approaches, I shall enable them [to understand].
