The Foundation for the Initial Practice: An Agreement in Ten Sections to Establish a Guide. First, the Pure Land of Amitābha;
Second, the Pure Land of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*; Third, the Pure Land of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*;
Fourth, the Pure Land of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*; Fifth, the Pure Land of the Māheśvara Heaven; Sixth, [the Pure Land] within the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The Pure Land indicated in the seventh [section], the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the land was transformed three times; the eighth, the Pure Land indicated in the assembly on Vulture Peak;
the ninth, the Mind-Only Pure Land; and the tenth, the Pure Land where Vairocana resides—these first four refer to the Pure Land of Amitābha.
This is for the sake of those ordinary beings who grasp at signs and have not yet attained faith in the Dharma.

By focusing one's mindfulness on the true principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and maintaining this contemplation without shifting from moment to moment, and because of such single-minded sincerity, the mind becomes purified in its various aspects and one attains birth in the Pure Land;

this is the provisional, not yet ultimate, method. Second, regarding the Pure Land described in the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, it is intended for those sentient beings who have not yet believed in the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena and who delight in wondrous forms and appearances, so as to lead them [to the path].

Third, regarding the Pure Land in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra: because one gives rise to the thought of that Buddha-land through the accomplishment of the visualization of his physical form, this is a provisional [land] and not the ultimate reality;
it is a land manifested for a time through the Buddha’s supernatural power by pressing the earth with his toe, which then vanishes.

This is the land of true retribution (*vipāka-kṣetra*), though its extent—whether broad or narrow—is not yet fully described; thus, while real, it is not yet extensive. Fourth, the Brahmajāla Sūtra...
Regarding those who purify the Buddha-land, although it is said that there is one great Flower-King with a thousand petals,
and upon each petal there are ten billion transformation Buddhas who convert sentient beings throughout ten billion four-continent worlds,

those thousand petals and the Flower-King itself are shown as the retributive realm (vipākabhūmi) in divided portions because the vision of the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles is not yet extensive; thus, it has not yet reached full perfection.
This provisional, yet not yet ultimate, fifth pure land of Maheśvara is where the Tathāgata sits upon a precious lotus throne and attains equal and perfect enlightenment as his true recompense;
whereas his attainment of perfect enlightenment here in the Bodhimaṇḍa of Magadha in this Jambudvīpa is a transformation. This [latter] constitutes the provisional teaching of the three vehicles.

Those who have not yet transcended the distinction between defilement and purity say that this Jambudvīpa and the six heavens above it belong to the tainted realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-sāsrava*), while Maheśvara in the higher realms is untainted (*anāsrava*);

thus, their minds still harbor the duality of defilement and purity, and this is a provisional teaching rather than a definitive one. This refers to the "purity" indicated in the sixth *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Regarding the "land," some say that the Tathāgata possesses a true recompense pure land located to the west, beyond thirty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* buddha-lands;
this is spoken by those of the provisional teaching of the Three Vehicles who have not yet eliminated the distinction between defilement and purity.
They claim that these three thousandfold great thousand-world systems are entirely impure lands, and thus they provisionally infer that the Tathāgata’s realm of recompense is a pure land.

The seventh point, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, states that the three transformations of the pure land in the West are a provisional teaching for those of the Three Vehicles whose notions of defilement and purity have not yet been extinguished;
it says that various humans and devas are moved and placed in another land, which is provisional and not ultimate.
The eighth point concerns the pure land indicated at the assembly on Vulture Peak, which is intended to lead those within the Three Vehicles [to the ultimate truth].
For Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who have not yet extinguished the distinction between defilement and purity, this land is known as impure yet eternally pure;

though the various assemblies may believe this, they are unable to see for themselves that it is real and not provisional. Those who believe but have not yet seen the ninth stage—the Pure Land of Mind-Only—must realize through self-verification that their own mind is, in its very essence, devoid of a mind-substance;
it is solely true wisdom, beyond the conceptualization of purity or impurity. This is called [the realization of] suchness.

Truly following one's own nature with a mind free from hindrance, and devoid of greed, anger, and delusion, while employing great compassion and wisdom to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings—this is the true Pure Land.
Because one is pure oneself, one teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they, too, may become pure.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "According to the purity of one’s mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-land. If you wish to obtain a pure land, you should purify your own mind."
The pure land where the tenth mind, Vairocana, dwells is precisely the Lotus Buddha-land within ten buddha-fields as numerous as atoms of dust;
it encompasses both the pure and the impure, yet is neither impure nor pure, and is devoid of the characteristics of high and low, this and that, or self and other.
Each and every buddha-field fills the entire dharma-realm without any mutual obstruction or separation. To speak briefly, there are ten buddhas.

The lands as numerous as motes of dust are known to be inexhaustible Buddha-lands; they do not emerge from a single mote because there is neither large nor small, and because no limits or measures are established.
Taking the Dharma as the boundary, it is unrestricted by the characteristics of edges or horizons;
the pure and mixed forms and images are layered upon one another—this is the land of true retribution, not a provisional gathering.

[Treatise] Part Eight: Clarifying the Sphere of Conversion and Transformation.
The realm of the Buddha is boundless, yet it appears differently according to the various capacities of sentient beings; its perceived breadth or narrowness varies with their dispositions.
It is not that the Tathāgata has apportioned these realms into fixed measures. When one’s disposition is subtle, the realm appears narrow; when one’s capacity is vast, the realm appears wide.

If one’s wisdom accords with the true source, the Buddha-realm pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. Thus, some may see Jambudvīpa as the scope of his transformation, while others may see the four continents...
The Continents serve to ferry living beings: some perceive his manifested form filling the great trichiliocosm, while others perceive his reward body within the ten oceans.

Thus, the various types of vessels are of ten thousand kinds, and the established teachings differ by a thousand variations and myriad distinctions. For those who have recently begun their studies, upon what can they rely?
I shall briefly indicate five gates to recognize the provisional and the real, so that they may abandon the various branches and return to the root.

Returning to the source from the branches, may you swiftly realize Bodhi without delay or hindrance. First, the Buddha-realm as perceived by humans; second, the Buddha-realm as perceived by the devas;
third, the Buddha-realm as perceived by those of the Two Vehicles; fourth, the Buddha-realm as perceived by Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings;
fifth, the Buddha-realm as perceived by Bodhisattvas of the definitive teachings. First: the Buddha as perceived by humans.
Those who see the Buddha in the second heaven, the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*), perceive only one Jambudvīpa of sentient beings being transformed;

this is because they see only their own realm, and their vision of the Buddha is likewise according to the breadth or narrowness of what they themselves perceive. Thus, those such as Śakra, Brahmā, and the various heavenly kings are at the stage of a Bodhisattva;
it is precisely by relying on this Bodhisattva stage that the Buddhas they perceive and the realms they transform and guide are assigned.
The breadth or narrowness of the realms cannot be relied upon according to the views of ordinary beings;

for instance, those such as the devas and humans—such as Śakra—are actually bodhisattvas at the second stage (*bhūmi*), and even those who gradually ascend to the rank of Brahmā-deva-rāja are bodhisattvas at the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
At times, by means of the Buddha’s temporary supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) to mature sentient beings, he also causes them to appear among the devas and humans.

Because ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and even lesser bodhisattvas can all perceive the realm of the Buddha’s land of recompense, it is as described in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe and manifested a pure land.
Furthermore, at times, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he enables humans and devas to see one another; this is as described in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.

It is said that within this supreme site of the Jewel Monastery (*ratnārāma*), the great assembly of humans and devas from the Desire Realm above and the Form Realm below are all gathered therein, as described in that sutra.
Regarding the third point, concerning the sphere of the Arhats among the two vehicles who see the Buddha’s activity of gathering and transforming beings:

it is like a great Arhat who, through the power of his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), is able to see the Buddha gathering and transforming beings throughout the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

This is the realm [of such practitioners]. For example, Aniruddha said: "With my divine eye, I see the trichiliocosm of Śākyamuni Buddha’s land as clearly as looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of my hand. For a lesser arhat, this vision is not fixed;
sometimes they may see the Buddha gathering and transforming beings throughout a single Jambudvīpa. This is achieved through long-standing submissiveness to patience (*kṣānti*).

The power to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is also called "severing the fetters" even when one has not yet attained the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Likewise, the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*) and miraculous manifestations is likewise termed such even before they are fully realized.

This is comparable to how, according to the sequence of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), Arhats may perceive the Buddha’s activity of gathering and transforming beings throughout the four continents and the realms above the threefold world (*traidhātuka*).

A detailed exposition of this is found within the various schools of the Lesser Vehicle. Fourth, as for the Bodhisattvas of the Provisional Teaching (*neyārtha*) perceiving the Buddha: [text continues].
Regarding the spheres of conversion and guidance: in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one perceives the sphere of a hundred Buddhas; in the second stage, a thousand Buddhas;
and in the third stage, ten thousand Buddhas, increasing progressively as taught in the Mahāyāna teachings of the Three Vehicles.

As for the sphere of conversion and guidance perceived by a Bodhisattva of the fifth [stage] according to the True Teaching (*saddharma-śāsana*), a Bodhisattva of the first stage immediately perceives many hundreds and many thousands of Buddhas. Thus it is.
The "inexhaustible hundred" does not mean a hundred of one hundred; rather, because a Bodhisattva of the Second Ground sees many thousands of Buddhas and so forth, these are "inexhaustible thousands.
Thus, for a Bodhisattva of the Third Ground, it is said to be "many tens of millions" and so on.
According to the definitive teaching, Bodhisattvas of all grounds see [the Buddhas] equally, like the net of Indra, as do the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (Tri-kṣānti).
It is likewise not merely that the lotus-womb world-systems (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, serve as the objective realm of retribution;

rather, the entire Dharma-realm and empty space are universally equal. At the very moment the beginner of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) first perceives the Path, they are already free from the perception of "large" or "small," because they perceive the entire manifested realm of the Buddhas as being identical to the Dharma-realm, without differentiating between large and small within the context of the sequential arrangement (*pratipatti*).
Regarding the stages and ranks as they descend, this scripture clarifies the meaning of "fulfillment" by stating that at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one sees the realms of many hundreds of Buddhas;
this is not like the "single hundred" of the three vehicles. This "many hundreds" is equivalent to an inexhaustible number.

Thus, while the Buddha who teaches according to the three vehicles is said to encompass one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*), the Buddha of retribution (*vipākabuddha*) is said to encompass [all].
Transforming a thousand billion four-continent worlds into a single realm of retribution for Śākyamuni—
as described in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the sphere of Vairocana’s transformative guidance— one provisionally establishes a single great Lotus Treasury World-Ocean,
vast and boundless, equal to the Dharma-realm and empty space; this is done solely for the sake of transformation.
For the sake of sentient beings, the shapes and forms are described in detail so as to cause their minds to expand and open, thereby overcoming their narrow and inferior mentalities.
Within this great lotus flower, it is stated in general that there are world-systems numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
however, as the written teachings are limited, only one hundred and eleven world-systems are established here.
In the center are eleven world-systems, each with twenty tiers of lotus-receptacle worlds above and below.
Within the very lowest tier, there is a central world surrounded by as many vast worlds as there are atoms in a Buddha-world;
the second tier above that contains as many worlds as there are atoms in two Buddha-worlds; and the third tier above that contains three... [as many worlds as there are atoms in three Buddha-worlds].
These eleven world-systems, numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-world, are all likewise arranged from bottom to top,
each successively increasing in scale; within the uppermost stratum, there are fully twenty world-systems,
as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-world, each being a vast realm surrounded by as many minor realms as there are atoms within ten Buddha-worlds.
Surrounding those eleven sets of twenty-fold world-systems, there are one hundred sets of single-fold world-systems encircling the eleven sets of twenty-fold world-systems.
Outside these one hundred sets of world-systems, near the Diamond Mountains (Vajra-parvata),
there are further ten sets of four-fold world-systems, within which the lands and realms are layered upon one another.
Within [the Vajra Mountain], as described above, it encircles the aforementioned world-systems and so forth,
abiding distributed like the net of Indra. The Tathāgata’s emanations pervade all within these various world-oceans—
pure and impure, uniform and mixed— wherein the number of world-systems, as taught in the Three Vehicles, is threefold.
From a thousand great trichiliocosms up to as many as the sands of one Ganges River constitutes a single world-system;

from such world-systems up to as many as the sands of a Ganges River constitutes a single world-ocean; from such world-oceans up to as many as the sands of a Ganges River constitutes a single world-lineage.
These worlds described in this sutra are all counted by the number of atoms in two Buddha-fields. Two Buddha-field atoms...
From the dust motes of three buddha-fields, multiplying in this manner until reaching the twenty buddha-field dust motes within the highest stratum,

and counting all such worlds throughout the vertical axis, a total of two hundred and ten buddha-field dust motes of vast fields constitutes a single world-system (*lokadhātu-vīja*); its number is not limited by the sands of the Ganges.
Among the three vehicles, the *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges) is frequently taken as the measure;
however, in this sutra, the dust motes of one buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra-rajas*) and ten buddha-fields are consistently taken to represent the inexhaustible.

By thus expanding the scale, it causes sentient beings who are narrow-minded and inferior to realize the scope of the Buddha’s transformative guidance and to resolve upon *bodhicitta*. This is the Buddha’s transformative guidance.
Within each and every atom of the objective realm, the realms are equal to the Dharma-realm and the void-realm;
it is not said that they transform only the trichiliocosm alone, for therein the principles are manifested. This will be explained extensively later in the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World."
The Ninth: Clarifying the Extension and Contraction of Cause and Effect.
The Dharma-realm is perfectly quiescent, without beginning and without end; its principle and wisdom are like empty space, neither cause nor effect.

It is only for the sake of sentient beings that provisional measures are established and names are temporarily attached. When deluded sentiment ceases and these measures are exhausted, what could be called "that which establishes"? A name cannot establish itself.
Giving originally arises from measure; when measure ceases and sentiment is exhausted, names also become inherently true.
Now, by means of the true name that is nameless, we speak of the true fruit that is fruitless; by means of the true teaching that is unspeakable, we speak of the true cause that is causeless.
Those who have merely begun to enlighten themselves must not remain stuck on their names, and those who are just starting their studies must not discard their [conventional] practices.
To speak of names is to establish them; when speech ceases, the names vanish. When conditions arise, they do so according to their nature; when phenomena arise, they do so according to their causes.
If there are no conditions, they cease, and only the phenomena themselves perish. These phenomena do not cognize one another by nature.
Now, to discuss cause and effect and their duration is like bird tracks in the sky or the son of a barren woman; it is spoken of only for the sake of sentient beings.
Sentient beings possess both folly and wisdom; according to their minds, they perceive delusion with varying degrees of slowness or speed.

Just as splitting bamboo or climbing a ladder are called different "capacities" (mārga), so too do these types differ in the duration of their progress. This difference in extension or brevity does not mean that the sun and moon have assigned specific time periods for them;

rather, the teaching does not manifest of its own accord, but arises because of the capacity [of the recipient]. The teaching responds to the faculties, and when there are faculties, the teaching is produced. Now, based upon these faculties...
Establishing these ten gates regarding the causes and effects of temporal extension and brevity is intended to enable beginners and later students to be free from doubt.
First, attaining the fruit of Arhatship through the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu) ordination in the Hīnayāna; second, attaining the fruit of Arhatship in one lifetime in the Hīnayāna;
third, attaining the fruit of Arhatship in three lifetimes in the Hīnayāna; fourth, [attaining it] in sixty [lifetimes] in the Hīnayāna...
1. Attaining the fruit of Arhatship within a single *kalpa*; 2. The fifth [category], the Pratyekabuddha who attains the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood after four births; 3.

The sixth, the Pratyekabuddha who attains the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood after a long period of one hundred *kalpas*; 4. The seventh, the Bodhisattva relying on the provisional teaching who is certain to attain the fruit of Buddhahood after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
5. The eighth, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the realization of the convergence of the three vehicles through the true teaching.

Returning to the One causes the Dragon Girl to attain Buddhahood in a single kṣaṇa, thereby subverting those sūtras of the Three Vehicles which state that one only attains Buddhahood after many kalpas;
the ninth [chapter] of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states that the Devaputra of Tuṣita attained the fruit of the Ten Stages in three lifetimes;
and the tenth [chapter] concerns the Bodhisattva Sudhana attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime—all such accounts as mentioned above pertain to the Three Vehicles and...

The teachings of the One Vehicle, based on the faculties and capacities of beings, have been expounded in various ways; each according to its own specific section of doctrine possesses its own internal consistency.

Now, wishing to extensively cite these various meanings, the textual passages would become too numerous. Since faculties are of ten thousand varieties and the teachings differ according to those faculties, I shall now briefly divide them into ten general categories.
By understanding the differences in the duration required to attain the fruit, one may come to know the provisional nature of the teachings.
In truth, one does not linger in the unreal but mounts the vehicle to enter the gate of reality, swiftly attaining the Buddha-way.

As the Dragon Girl shattered the fixed kalpas of the Three Vehicles to realize the gate of reality in a single kṣaṇa; as the Nirvāṇa Sūtra records that the butcher Pūraṇa shall attain Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa;
and as it declares that even icchantikas possess the nature for enlightenment, thereby expounding the merit of transcending the three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.
The Devaputra of Tuṣita, hearing of the supreme power of the One Vehicle teaching, gave rise to faith;
yet because he had not practiced it, even though he entered hell, he was able to plant the seeds [of enlightenment].

Upon receiving the light that touched his body, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven and ascended to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), just as described in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Minor Marks. This is one such example.
The purpose is to cause one to believe in that which these Buddhas ride upon; because it is difficult to believe, once belief is established, it will certainly become the seed.

Through the internal perfuming of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), one will inevitably attain Buddhahood. Even if one is temporarily attached to pleasure, upon encountering suffering, one shall immediately practice.

Upon reaching the stage of the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi-prathama-citta*), one is equal to the tenth ground and shall never again regress, just as in the case of Sudhana throughout his single lifetime.
One who attains Buddhahood is clear regarding the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); at the limit of a single kṣaṇa, emotions vanish and conceptualizations are exhausted.

In the three periods of time, there is but a single thought-moment, and nothing further arises; this is called "birth in one life" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*). One does not grasp at the existence of emotions to establish the birth of temporal divisions such as kalpas.
Since such non-arising is itself the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "birth in one life," which is identical to the original state of birth.
When the Dragon Girl, in a single kṣaṇa, reaches the point where emotion is exhausted and the self is extinguished, she is called a Buddha.
The tenth chapter clarifies the beginning and end of the teaching:
the World-Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, pervades and illumines the entire Dharma-realm; his wisdom encompasses all things, encompassing both the ordinary and the sage.
The principle and phenomena are mutually integrated, and essence and function interpenetrate;
thus, the sublime scriptures of forty chapters are woven together from beginning to end, and the wondrous words of one million verses reflect one another from front to back.

The ten locations and ten assemblies are as layered as Indra’s net, and the ten lands and ten bodies are like mirror-images that interpenetrate; if one gate is raised, all gates are simultaneously present.
When a single chapter is expounded, all chapters are simultaneously signaled; when the Tree of Enlightenment first takes form, the nine heavens arrive together.
At the Universal Radiance Assembly, all ten sites are ascended at once; there is no discrepancy between past and present, and the old and the new do not depart from a single thought-moment.

Within a single stage, the gates of the five stages are distinguished; within a single practice, the ocean-gates of the Dharma-realm, as numerous as atoms, are established, resting upon the essence of the Dharma-realm.
Establishing the principles for instructing the world, the teaching on the fruition of virtue and the nature of equality is set forth to guide and inspire sentient beings.

Mañjuśrī praises and elucidates the essence of the Dharma, while Samantabhadra brings the cultivation of conduct to completion; thus, the light of their compassion and wisdom intermingles, causing the precious moisture to flourish like clouds throughout the Dharmadhātu.
Within this "Dharmadhātu Chapter," it further directs Sudhana to practice again in emulation of this entire scripture.

Each and every practice of their modes of conduct, the Bodhisattvas’ protocols for receiving and delivering sentient beings, the successive stages of each, the aspiration for advancement, the distinctions between teachers and disciples, and the detailed presentation of the rules—these have been set forth so that the ignorant may easily understand and students do not labor in vain.
If one’s single thought accords with the Way, one immediately transcends eternal kalpas; herein, ten sections are divided.
The Dharma, by way of its concise principles and the various aspects of its teaching-body, is briefly understood through its constituent divisions:

First, elucidating Vairocana’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment; Second, elucidating the manifestation of the fruit and exhorting to practice; Third, elucidating the perfection of the development of faith; Fourth, elucidating the entry into the realization of reality;
Fifth, elucidating the arousal of the resolve and the cultivation of practice; Sixth, elucidating the integration of principle and phenomena.
The seventh [chapter] clarifies mutual interpenetration; the eighth clarifies the virtues perfected through the cultivation of the aggregates in accordance with conditions;
the ninth clarifies the completion of the stages of cause and effect; and the tenth clarifies enabling ordinary beings to realize the truth.
First, regarding the clarification of Vairocana’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment: this refers to the first chapter of the sutra, "The Sublime Array of the World-Ruler.

As for the term "initial attainment of perfect enlightenment," it means that through his own body and mind, he has realized all phenomena of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—as equal within a single thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*).
Within this single thought-moment, there is no distinction between long and short durations; yet, even within this single thought-moment, he does not fail to manifest for sentient beings.

The knowledge of the long and short kalpas of the three periods of time, as well as the knowledge of seeing the various distinctions among sentient beings—as described in the sūtras—enters the three periods of time without coming or going. Thus, there are ten kinds of knowledge fully set forth in the sūtras.
In this manner, the forty chapters of the sūtra, including those preceding and following, are all [attained] at the single moment of first attaining perfect enlightenment.
At that limit, by means of the Samādhi-gate of the Dharma-realm Ocean Wisdom Seal, one simultaneously and instantaneously seals the body, color, speech, and sounds to proclaim all Buddha-dharmas;

these are universally proclaimed and disseminated throughout the oceans of lands within every atom, as well as their entry into Nirvāṇa—without shifting for even a moment, a single limit, or a single nature—all because such is the nature of the Dharma. Thus it was for the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future.
Past and present are thus unified within a single moment; according to the various sentient beings, differentiated teachings are manifested.
That past and present penetrate one another is called "the beginning. That the Dharma accords with suchness is called "accomplishment.
That it accords with suchness and is not produced by the mind is called "right wisdom. To realize this principle is called "enlightenment. This sutra was [translated] during the Jin dynasty.
The original translation consisted of thirty-four chapters; now, during the Tang Dynasty, it has been retranslated as thirty-nine chapters.

Furthermore, examining the *Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-mūla-karma-sūtra*, it says: "O Son of the Buddha, I previously expounded the ten stages of the path (*daśabhūmi*) in the Sixth Heaven to transform devas and humans;
I now briefly open up the minds of sentient beings for you all to receive and practice. Moreover, the subsequent text states:
O Son of the Buddha, the mind of the forty-first stage is called the "Mind Entering the Dharma Realm. Furthermore, as stated in the following passage:

"O Son of the Buddha, previously, while in the third dhyāna, I assembled the assembly of the eight dhyānas and spoke one hundred trillion verses concerning the Bodhisattva in his final birth entering the Buddha-flower Samādhi. Now, I shall briefly explain the meaning of a single verse from that."
"Open the minds of sentient beings! You should receive and uphold this chapter. This chapter follows immediately after the "Ten Stages" (Daśabhūmi) chapter;

it constitutes the eleventh stage, the position of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi). As for the title of this chapter, it is called the "Buddha-flower Chapter" (*Buddhāvatamsaka*), following the principle of naming according to its content.
Furthermore, the text below states: "O Sons of the Buddha, formerly when I was here beneath this tree preaching the Ocean of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-sāgara*), there were eighty thousand..."
Because the Bodhisattva Vimala has manifested his body as a Buddha, he now briefly reveals for this great assembly the sphere of practice for the fruit of Buddhahood.
You should receive it with the highest reverence, just as the *Necklace of Fundamental Karma* (*Mūlakarma-kaṇṭhikā-sūtra*) does;

that is to say, having finished expounding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he transforms the multitudes of the three vehicles and leads them to come before the Bodhi tree, where he recounts in detail, one by one, the time of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
The Dharma-gates of the five stages of the *Avataṃsaka* as explained herein are fully set forth in that sutra;
however, this version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* lacks eleven stages and one chapter. Only by collating this with that [original] can the correct sequence be known.
Those who hear this in the future need not harbor doubts; they need only consult that sutra to discern the truth. Now, within the third dhyāna...
The "Chapter on the Buddha-Flower of the Eleven Stages" consists, in total, of ten locations, ten assemblies, and forty chapters;

all were taught simultaneously in a single moment at the time of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment through the Ocean-Seal Dharma-gate (*sāgaramudrā-dharmaparyāya*), because the fundamental Dharma has no sequence of before or after.
Since it serves as the root of the Dharma, he employed his original body and original wisdom.
Because it reveals the fundamental Dharma, there is no such thing as a "repeated assembly" in the Hall of Universal Radiance or the three assemblies;

for these are not considered repeated assemblies in the sense of a finite succession. Since the ocean-gate of the Dharma-realm subsumes all three periods of time within a single thought-moment, the preceding and succeeding moments are simultaneously one and the same time. Furthermore, there is no going there to assemble again or returning here to enter.

This is because, by means of the Sea-Seal Gate (*sāgaramudrā-dvāra*) that confronts the manifested form-body (*rūpakāya*) through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), all things are revealed simultaneously.
As for what is now called the "triple assembly in successive layers at the Hall of Universal Radiance" (*samantaprabhā-prāsāda*), this is not merely a sequential process;
rather, it is the dharma of instantaneous, simultaneous sealing (*ekakṣaṇa-sadyas-mudraṇa*). As the Sūtra says: "Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata expounds boundless sūtras."

The Ocean [Assembly] merely uses the categories of dharma-gates as symbols to represent the Dharma; thus, the names of the Bodhisattvas are distinct, yet they are not a multitude that has come first or later.
Within the ocean of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one must not conceive of before and after through emotional conceptualization, for that would contradict the fundamental Dharma.
As for the manifestation of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment, this is for the sake of sentient beings, and it does not [occur]... [in the ultimate sense].

This fundamental teaching spans the three periods of time; this is to clarify that the fundamental teaching cannot be derived from its secondary aspects. Since the carriage has already overturned in the past, one must change the course in the future;
one should not simply take the virtues of former masters as a model for imitation. Upon examining the intent of the sutra, there is no mention of a "repeated assembly.
While the arrangement of the dharma-gate through literary expression may appear to have a sense of repetition, this is not observed when considering the chapter structure.

The general purport of the middle section is always to describe the wisdom that encompasses the preceding and following [sections], as well as a single time, a single limit, and a single dharma-realm through its methods of teaching.
As stated in both the "Ten Samādhis" chapter and the "Leaving the World" chapter: "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in the country of Magadha, in the Bodhimanda, having just attained perfect enlightenment, in the Hall of Universal Radiance."
Regarding the entry into the Samādhi of the Momentary Limit (*kṣaṇakoṭi-samādhi*): it is merely a distinction in the names of Bodhisattvas according to their respective stages of Dharma;

it is not that the Tathāgata has departed and returned. Because the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-garbha*) is the essence of the resultant wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-phala-jñāna*), at this single moment, principle and phenomena are brought together, inseparable from the gate of non-constructive concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*). This is because the ten gates of concentration are the Dharma-realm itself.
Because the essence [of the teaching] is such, the practices of Samantabhadra are the functioning of the Dharma-realm; this is precisely the "Chapter on Leaving the World.
To comprehend these two chapters as being inseparable from the great mansion of the fruition-virtue in the Universal Radiance Hall is the fundamental locus of wisdom.
Thus, these three successive expositions are, in total, a single exposition of one place, one time, one Dharma-realm, and one assembly; they are not like... [as previously stated].
What is perceived by the mind—whether preceding or succeeding, coming or going—pervades the other nine assemblies;
all are unified within a single assembly, a single moment, a single dharma-realm, and a single ocean of wisdom.

In this dharma-gate of the multilayered simultaneous manifestation and concealment without obstruction or hindrance, we now, within this single dharma-realm, rely upon the modes of practice and skillful means according to one's cultivation, using provisional locations to symbolize and distinguish the teachings.
Regarding those ten locations and ten assemblies: first, the Bodhimaṇḍa, the first assembly; second, the Universal Radiance Hall, the second assembly;
third, ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru, the third assembly; fourth, ascending to the Yāma Heaven, the fourth assembly;
fifth, ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven, the fifth assembly; sixth, ascending to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the sixth assembly; seventh...
The seventh assembly is in the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna; the eighth assembly is at the Jeta Grove (Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma);
the ninth assembly is at the Great Stūpa to the east of the City of Awakening (Bodhigaya);

the tenth assembly is throughout all lands, atoms, and all spaces within the Dharmadhātu—these are called the ten assemblies in ten locations. This sutra is the assembly held within the Universal Radiance Hall (Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala).

The dharma-gates of the five stages and six positions, the sublime principles of the ten concentrations, the beginning and end of Samantabhadra’s myriad practices, and the essence and function [of these]—
all ten locations and ten assemblies are contained within the Hall of Universal Radiance. Within this abode of the fruition-dwelling,
where the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled in the single true dharma-realm, the worlds of the ten directions are entirely encompassed as one dharma, one place, and one time.
In terms of essence and function, the integration of the branches back into the root cannot be divided into separate accounts of three assemblies involving coming and going;
nor can one allow the dust of one's own subjective sentiments to obscure the true teaching. Furthermore, within this sutra, all phenomena are characterized by the number ten as their perfect count;
thus, one cannot merely speak of seven locations and nine assemblies. Again, he asked: "For what reason does it reach..."

Regarding the seventh assembly, which gathers the assemblies of the eight heavens up to the third dhyāna to expound the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*), why does it not extend to the fourth dhyāna heaven?
The answer is: because the fourth dhyāna heavens follow a sequential order as the locus of the Buddha’s fruition (*buddha-phala*);
thus, when the Buddha truly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it universally encompasses all four dhyānas.
The worlds of the ten directions are entirely a single Universal Radiance Hall, the abode of the Dharma-realm and the capital of retribution;

there is no longer any mark of coming or going, advancing or practicing that can be found. This clarifies that the mental characteristics of the Buddha’s four dhyānas have no dependence and no place for practice;
therefore, there is no coming or going. Sentiment is severed, and the response to reality is identical to the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, this fourth dhyāna of the Buddha, which was spent beneath the Bodhi tree as if in an āraṇya hermitage,

and the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā), which is his original dwelling— the retributive abode— are explained through these three points. By recounting the cause and effect from beginning to end,
it clarifies that from the very moment he first attained Buddhahood, he has never been separate from the essence of bodhi, the ocean of fundamental wisdom.
In this manner, the gate of the perfect fusion in which beginning and end, cause and effect, become a single point is harmonized across six locations within this sutra:
two instances in the section on "Manifesting the Fruit and Exhorting Practice," and four instances in the section on "Having Already Believed and Practicing.
The first is as follows: in the first assembly, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the Tathāgata-garbha-body.
The "Obscuration" [section] uses the Dharma-gate of the Vortex of the World-Ocean to reveal the source of the Buddha:
the Dharma-realm of the Ten Lotus Treasury World-Oceans, which is the gate of the beginning and end of cause and effect and the retribution attained therein.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is its practice, and the Tathāgata’s Treasury-Body is its essence; this clarifies that by entering the essence through its function, principle and phenomena are thoroughly penetrated. Second is Vairocana.
Regarding the seat upon which Vairocana sits and all its adornments, these also clarify that cause and effect, beginning and end, essence and function, are mutually penetrating;
thus, Vairocana Buddha himself is taken as the fruition of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).

Taking the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of all phenomena as the essence of the seat, and the myriad practices of Samantabhadra as the function of its adornment—by means of all these articles of adornment, [the mandala is perfected].
Furthermore, from among the various ornaments at the doors and windows of Luntai, a multitude of bodhisattvas emerged, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds,
who rained down jewels as offerings to the Buddha. This clearly illustrates that the fruit-virtue of the Tathāgata eternally dwells upon the seat of the emptiness of all dharmas,
while the wondrous functions of Samantabhadra’s myriad practices eternally evoke the adornments of the environment, wherein principle and phenomena are unified.

Because the essence and function of cause and effect constantly benefit one another, and because within the gate of practicing through faith there is the "Gate of the Fourfold Harmonization of Cause and Effect as Non-dual," namely:
the three proclamations of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment in the Hall of Universal Radiance, which subsumes the derivative back into the fundamental;

the single realm of the ultimate limit of reality (*dharmadhātu*) is the first harmonization; and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called "suchness" (the second). These constitute the four harmonizations.

In the "Chapter on the Manifestation," the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to drench the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head and emits light from his mouth to drench the mouth of Samantabhadra, so that these two may engage in mutual dialogue to explain the gateway of the Buddha’s manifestation—the fruition and virtue.

Herein, Mañjuśrī represents the essence of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while Samantabhadra represents the clarity of practice (*caryā*); through their union, essence and function are thoroughly integrated.
Therefore, "Buddha" as it occurs in the phrase "penetrating this place" refers to the Buddha of the First Assembly, clarifying that he attained Buddhahood through his own self-power.
Within the context of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*), "Buddha" clarifies what is reached through the Bodhisattva’s own power.

Because of the Buddha of the First Assembly, one gives rise to faith and diligence in what is to be cultivated; because one cultivates with faith and diligence, that which is reached is through one's own power.
Because it is the fruit of Buddhahood, and since one’s own fruit of Buddhahood is no different from that which was previously believed,

within the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Tathāgata, by means of the *siṃha-vijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s stretch samādhi), has raised the causes and fruits of the five stages to guide and benefit humans and devas.
Furthermore, within the pavilion of Maitreya, the four Sudhana youths harmonize the beginning and end of the causes of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
The fruition and Maitreya Bodhisattva’s beginning and end— cause and effect— are entirely of one boundary, for their essence and function are thoroughly pervasive.

Thus, they harmonize with the two previous locations of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and Vairocana Buddha within the "Gate of Universal Encouragement to Practice through Manifesting the Fruition," as well as with the subsequent "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter in the Hall of Universal Radiance, and the locations of the Jetavana Garden and Maitreya’s Tower.
The four entrances of the pavilion together constitute the six entrances; this is the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of essence and function, cause and effect, within a single limit.

Therefore, the name of Maitreya’s pavilion is the "Vairocana-Adorned Treasury" (*Vairocanavyūha-garbha*), which is identical in meaning to the name of the samādhi entered by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in the first assembly, namely the "Tathāgata-garbha. Thus, the names in the earlier and later sections are essentially the same.

Therefore, by simply taking the categories and contextual implications of the scriptural text and investigating and cross-referencing them, it can be seen that the Tathāgata’s harmonious integration constitutes a single time and a single limit (*ekakṣaṇa*).
From the abode of fundamental wisdom at the limit of a single instant (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*), there arises both parinirvāṇa and remaining permanently in the world to turn the wheel of the true Dharma;
all of this occurs without deficiency in the single moment when perfect enlightenment is attained.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going. This Sūtra consists of ten locations and ten assemblies, comprising forty chapters.
Within nine of these assemblies, the gathered multitudes total three hundred and forty-two kinds of congregations;
furthermore, the nine kinds of congregations from the single assembly in the third dhyāna are also included in this number. Such is...
The assembly each said that there were as many [Buddhas] as atoms in a Buddha-world, or some said ten Buddha-worlds;

thus the entire multitude gathered simultaneously at the very moment of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, like a great ocean pervading the ten directions, mutually reflecting one another without obstruction or hindrance. If one were to take the tenth...
The assembly of all lands and world-systems, within atoms, in space, and throughout the dharma-realm; those present in every such assembly— namely, the worlds of the ten directions,
the void of space, the dharma-realm, and even within a single mote of dust, as well as the ocean-like assemblies within the pores and hair-follicles of the bodies of all sentient beings—
extending infinitely and endlessly in ever-deepening layers throughout the ten directions without interval.

The ocean-like assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is eternally thus: the three periods of time are a single thought-moment, and all past and present are identical with the limit of the present moment.
Past and future, throughout inexhaustible kalpas, are simultaneously and without deficiency realized as the attainment of perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment.
Such is the nature of time; whether one attains Buddhahood or not, the dharma of time remains thus.
The second section, which clarifies the fruit and exhorts practice, consists of five chapters of the sutra:

the "Manifestation of Signs" (Rulai xianxiang pin), the "Samādhi of Samantabhadra" (Puxian sanmei pin), the "Accomplishment of the World" (Shijie chengjiu pin), the "Flower Adornment World" (Huayan shijie pin), and the "Vairocana" (Biluzhena pin).
In the "Manifestation of Signs" chapter, light is emitted from between the many teeth in the Tathāgata’s mouth, and by means of that light...
With a voice of medium pitch, he announced to the assembly throughout the ten directions, commanding them all to gather.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, as the eldest son of the Buddha, administered the laws of the Buddha’s household and entered the Buddha-samādhi. He extolled the meritorious virtues of the Buddha’s fruition so that the assembly would feel reverence and love, giving rise to faith, joy, and practice.
The Tathāgata, within his own person and seat, manifested the gates of cause, effect, substance, and function, so that the entire assembly might fully understand them.
The Buddha’s own body is the Great Wisdom Body of the Dharma-realm; his various ornaments are the retributive fruits of the practices of Samantabhadra;

and all phenomena being empty constitute his seat and body. By means of these three dharmas held in perfect equilibrium, he gives rise to the gates of compassion and wisdom, manifesting and awakening sentient beings without beginning or end—this is what is called the Buddha, the Tathāgata. Furthermore, from between his eyebrows...
From within the *ūrṇā-kośa*, he emitted a light named "The Radiance of the Wisdom of All Bodhisattvas Universally Illuminating the Treasuries of the Worlds of the Ten Directions.

Its form was like a cloud of jewel-colored lamps that, having universally illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, circled the Buddha to the right and entered beneath his feet, then emerged from within the *ūrṇā-kośa* between his brows. From this, ten Buddhas appeared in the world.
A multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, sat together upon a single lotus throne before that Buddha and further praised the profound realm of the Buddha.
This clarifies that cause and effect are non-dual. The light entering beneath the soles of the feet signifies that the fruit brings about the cause.
As for the light from between the eyebrows, it is the light of the fruit of the wisdom of the ten stages; its entry now into the soles of the Buddha’s feet [signifies this].
When the fruit arises from the cause at the stage of the Ten Faiths, this light again issues forth from the wheels on the soles of the feet.
Upon reaching the stage of the Ten Abidings, it next emerges from the tips of the toes. Within the stage of the Ten Practices, it issues from the tops of the ankles.

Within the stage of the Ten Dedications, it emerges from above the knees. Within the stage of the Ten Grounds, it returns to the space between the eyebrows; having thus completed the cycle, it begins once more.
The initial light of the hair-circle (ūrṇā-kośa) is the fruit-light of the ten stages; that from which bodhisattvas emerge therein is their causal practice.
This clarifies that the cause emerges from the fruit. These five preceding chapters of the sutra demonstrate the virtues of the Buddha’s fruition, so as to inspire faith and joy in the assembly.
Third, the clarification of the perfection of the mind of faith refers to the six chapters of the sutra within the second assembly:

the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas," the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," the "Chapter on Radiant Enlightenment," the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Wisdom," the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," and the "Chapter on Worthy Leader.
These six chapters together constitute one stage of the ten faiths, namely, the first stage.
Chapter on the Arrival and Names: Believing that the names of the Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions differ according to where they are born.

Chapter on the Four Noble Truths: Believing and knowing that the names and designations of the Dharma-gates in the worlds of the ten directions, though diverse, all take the Four Noble Truths as their foundation.
Chapter on the Illumination of Light: Knowing that the light originates from the fruit and enters beneath the Buddha’s feet.
Now, from beneath his feet, he emits the light of those fruits to establish the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). 1.

In the "Chapter on the Questions and Clarifications of the Four Bodhisattvas," it concerns the Dharma-gate asked by the Bodhisattva Śraddhā. 2. In the "Chapter on the Five Pure Practices," it clarifies that the pure practices of the Bodhisattva Śraddhā arise from the power of great vows. 3.
In the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla*), it clarifies that one knows the attainment of Buddhahood takes faith as its foremost priority; thus, one must have faith in these six [chapters].
These six chapters of the sūtra, which together constitute the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), were taught within the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabha-kuṭāgāra*).

Since this Hall is the fundamental abode where the fruition of the Buddha’s wisdom—the result of the perfection of his retributive merit—resides, it is from within it that the dharma-gate of the stage of faith is expounded.
This is to clarify that by speaking of the fruition, one establishes faith; once faith in the qualities of the fruition has been established, from this point onward, until...
From the "Ten Grounds" and "Eleven Grounds" chapters up to the "Buddha Flower" chapter, it is finally clarified that entering the Way involves the progressive cultivation of the five stages.
The distinctions between the completion and the stages, as well as the universal penetration, constitute the transition from cause to fruit without any temporal interval;
therefore, all ten Buddhas—beginning with the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom—are taken as the gates of faith, which in turn [serve as...]

Because the fundamental unmoving wisdom Buddha (Akṣobhya-jñāna-buddha) of one’s own mind serves as the essential substance and function of the assembly, the fourth [section] clarifies the entry into true realization:

from the third assembly, ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru, light is emitted from the tips of the Tathāgata’s two toes, within which six chapters of sutra are preached; this constitutes the first ascent to Mount Sumeru.
Chapter Two: The Summit of Mount Sumeru; Chapter Thirty: Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru;
Chapter Four: The Abodes; Chapter Five: Brahma Conduct; Chapter Six: The Merit of First Generating the Bodhicitta; Chapter Seven: Elucidation of the Dharma.
Among these six chapters of the sutra, the two chapters—the Summit of Mount Sumeru and the Verses of Praise—are like the reception and praise offered by Śakra and the devas.

The arrival [of the Buddha] and the praise of his merits and the excellence of his abode; the ten chapters on the stages (*bhūmi*), the chapter on pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), the chapter on the merit of the initial resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), and the chapter on the illumination of the Dharma—these four sutra chapters clarify the gateway to the Dharma first realized.

Abiding where the Buddhas abide, born into the family of the Buddhas, and sharing the same nature of wisdom as the Buddhas, one’s merit, practice, understanding, principle, and wisdom become like those of a Buddha from the very moment of the initial resolve.
That he emits light from the tips of his two big toes upon attaining perfect enlightenment signifies the beginning of his setting forth to realize the Dharma-gate;
that he ascends to the summit of Mount Sumeru signifies that, having previously relied on faith, he now ascends to the summit of the mountain of the Ten Abodes,
the King of Dharma, reaching the stage where wisdom-illumination is unimpeded, just as one reaches the ultimate limit of appearances atop a high mountain.

Furthermore, "mountain" symbolizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is capable of giving rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). From this point onward, one acts spontaneously according to the Dharma without effort; from beginning to end, one is a Buddha.
One does not become fully endowed with the "effortless necklace" (*anābhoga-maṇi-hāra*) merely by means of the eight stages. The *Wúgōng yīngluò jīng* (Sutra on the Effortless Necklace) states:

"The Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages reach Buddhahood spontaneously within the 'Flowing Water of the Dharma. The initial water and the final water are of a single nature. This 'water' refers to the Buddha as cause and the Buddha as fruit."
Because the Buddha is of one nature, there is no beginning, middle, or end within him; because there is no interval between thoughts, he relies upon the fundamental dharma.
Thus, there is no thought that can create an interval, and the cause and effect are finalized within a single moment of correspondence.

Because it is the Buddha of a single moment of correspondence, one does not speak of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) or the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), nor of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); these marks, signs, and powers are obtained from this very state of perfect enlightenment. If one realizes this perfection...

Awakening means not being attached to any marks; because one is constantly in accord with the path of awakening, the various marks and signs of excellence manifest through transformation and arrive spontaneously without being sought.
Even when one reaches the final stage of merit and wisdom, the three periods of time are simultaneous, as there is no separation between moments of thought.
Fifth, regarding the practitioner who initiates practice: from the fourth assembly, they ascend to the Yāma Heaven to [behold] the Tathāgata.
From between his two feet, he emitted light and preached the Sūtra in Four Chapters: (1) The Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven;
(2) The Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven; (3) The Chapter on the Ten Practices; and (4) The Chapter on the Inexhaustible Treasury.
Within this assembly, the two chapters—the Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven and the Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Yāma Heaven—were [spoken by] those devas.

The two chapters of the *Sūtra*, "Welcoming the Buddha" and "Praising the Buddha’s Merits and the Excellence of His Abode," as well as the "Ten Practices" and "Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries," clarify that from the wisdom-body one is endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra;

through the perfection of both compassion and wisdom, and the gates of both principle and practice, the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—are accomplished, such that merit and wisdom are inexhaustible. This stage proceeds from above the two feet of the Tathāgata.

The emission of light and the ascent to the Yāma Heaven for the purpose of teaching clarify that, from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the limit of the ultimate reality (*dharmadhātu*), one realizes the Buddha’s Wisdom Body;
then, descending to the Yāma Heaven, one gives rise to the gateway of the ten thousand practices of Samantabhadra based on the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
Thus, the locations are used to represent the Dharma so that it may be easily understood, just as those various devas are separated from the earth's surface.
Therefore, this heaven dwells supported by space, illustrating that the ten practices proceed in reliance upon the emptiness of the fundamental wisdom-dharma.

Sixth, to clarify the mutual interpenetration of principle and phenomena: from the fifth assembly, [the Buddha] ascends to the Tuṣita Heaven palace and emits light from his knee to expound the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) in three chapters of the sutra. First, ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven palace.
The first two chapters, "Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace" and "Dedication," consist of the preceding two sections of the sutra:
the former describes how the various devas welcome and praise the Tathāgata, extolling the Buddha’s virtues as well as the excellence of his dwelling place;
the latter is the formal exposition of the dharma-gate of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). As for dedication, it causes all phenomena and activities to enter [into the ultimate].

By principle, the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are subsumed within the preceding ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*); because the principle and phenomena are mutually unimpeded, they are called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).
The first ten abodes are the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Dharmakāya, while the subsequent ten practices are the myriad deeds of Samantabhadra;
that these two persons’ essence and function penetrate one another is termed "dedication. As for the light emitted from above the knees:
Because it clarifies that phenomena and principle are freely extended or withdrawn, it is like a person’s knee, for bending, stretching, and rotating all depend upon the knee.

Why is this stage taught in the Tuṣita Heaven? It is to clarify that this heaven occupies a central position within the Desire Realm, and furthermore, because it is the center among the five stages, five locations, and five assemblies of the heavens. Below it...
Above the two assemblies of Śakra’s palace and the Yāma heaven, there are the two assembly sites of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) and the third dhyāna;

thus, among these five assemblies, this heavenly realm is situated in the middle. Therefore, it is said that the ten dedications cause one to abide in the middle, where the fundamental wisdom of the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle and the various differentiated wisdoms are equally integrated with wisdom and compassion, thereby harmonizing the principles and facts.
Because the Path abides in the manifestation of phenomena, it is necessary to explain the gateway of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) at this location.

Seventh, regarding the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the aggregates: from the sixth assembly, [the Buddha] ascends to the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and emits a light from between the eyebrows of the Tathāgata named "Flame-Light of Bodhisattva Power. This light is identical to that of the first assembly.

Because the light emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows returns to its original place after it has finished its course, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (The Scripture on the Ten Stages) is taught.
Why is there no chapter on "Ascending to the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven" and no chapter of "Verses of Praise"?

It is to clarify that the fruit of the ten stages culminates in abiding within the palace of the fundamental Dharma, which eternally pervades all things; thus, the function is complete and the practice reaches its ultimate limit.
There is no further advancement up to the third dhyāna; this is also the case for the worlds of the ten directions.

This is to signify that the fruit is consummated and the wisdom of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is perfected, such that there is no further cultivation. Because the Buddhas of the ten directions are always present before one, they do not come newly, nor is there any need for praise.
Thus, these gates of the ten stages pertain only to the ten abidings (daśavihāra), the ten practices (daśacaryā), and the ten dedications (daśapariṇāmanā).

Having accumulated merit within the intermediate aggregates until they are fully matured, one abides nowhere further, yet accomplishes spontaneously; thus, one naturally brings all dharmas to fulfillment.
For what reason is the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages taught in this celestial realm? It is because this heaven is a transformation produced by others upon which one relies to achieve one's own bliss;
therefore, it is named the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). This is its stage.
Because Bodhisattvas rely upon sentient beings, they practice compassion and wisdom, giving rise to clouds of various practices and raining down the rain of all dharmas;
they take this as their joy, yet they have no thought of a self, nor do they form the marks of performing various practices, because they abide in the manifestation of the Dharma.

Therefore, it is necessary to speak of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmi) in this location. According to the explanation of Master Zang, when this chapter was being taught, there were three additions and five requests.
Examining the intent of the sutra, it is shown that the Buddhas possess thirteen kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Vimukticandra, and the other bodhisattvas have four levels of request. Regarding the thirteen kinds of empowerment:

first, the Buddhas of the ten directions who bear the same name manifest their bodies and praise and comfort him with words, causing him to preach the Dharma; furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow upon him the ten kinds of wisdom and...
1. The power of the roots of goodness of the eyes; 2. The power of superior wisdom; 3. The power of the Dharma; 4.
The power of the Buddhas of the ten directions placing their hands upon the crown of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva’s head, granting him permission to preach the Dharma; 5.

The Tathāgata Vairocana emitting light from between his eyebrows that illuminates the body of Vajragarbha, and within that light, proclaiming verses to exhort him to preach the Dharma—these are called the thirteen.

Commending with words and offering consolation constitutes the empowerment of verbal action (*vākkarman*); bestowing the ten kinds of knowledge constitutes the empowerment of the action of wisdom (*jñānakarman*);

rubbing the crown of the head with the hand constitutes the empowerment of physical action (*kāyakarman*); and the light radiating from between the eyebrows and the preaching of the Dharma within that light constitute the empowerment of the power of the Dharma (*dharmabala*).

Taken together, these—consisting of commendation with words, the ten knowledges, the hand-rubbing of the crown, and the illumination of the body—constitute the four empowerments in their entirety, totaling thirteen types.
Regarding the four requests: first, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra raised the doubts of the great assembly and requested Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, who declined and did not speak;
second, Vimukticandra requested again, and Vajragarbha declined once more; third, Vimukticandra requested for a third time;
and fourth, all the great Bodhisattvas simultaneously made a collective request—thus there are four requests in total. It is not yet known what the three empowerments (adhiṣṭhāna) are.

Regarding the five requests: from where do they originate? If one takes only the actions of body, speech, and mind as the three empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then this would conflict with the fact that the light from between the eyebrows illuminates the body of Vajragarbha and that he preaches the Dharma through the empowerment of light; thus, there would be additional empowerments.
If, however, one takes only the verbal praise of the Buddhas of the ten directions as the five requests, then [this is appropriate] because the status of a Buddha is most venerable.
Within the established rules, it is not appropriate to make such a request; for this reason, there are thirteen types in total.

Although the four types of requests and the ten types of cognitive activities (*jñāna-karma*) do not differ in their essential nature as wisdom, they constitute distinct analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) because they do not confuse the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).

Consequently, when they are employed, each functions separately and cannot be taken as identical simply because they belong to the same category, for within that single category there are distinctions.
The thirteen types of additional empowerments, each distinct, and the fourfold repeated requests for the meaning of the transcendent leap have already been explained.
Regarding the eighth [topic], "Unimpeded according to Conditions": at the seventh assembly, the eight classes of beings from the third dhyāna heaven gathered.

It is taught that a Bodhisattva in their final birth before Buddhahood enters the Buddha-flower Samādhi and, within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) among the eleven stages, expounds the Dharma-gate of Samantabhadra.
Having completed the ten stages, it clarifies the conclusion of the path of self-benefit;

within the stage of Equal Enlightenment, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra, universally manifesting entry into the mundane world and pervading the entire Dharma-realm. These practice-gates are layered and extensive, reaching throughout the void.

The ocean of lands within emptiness and even within a single atom, layer upon layer without obstruction, ultimately equal to the *dharmadhātu* and as vast as space—this is called the conduct of Samantabhadra within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As for the "Buddha-flower Samādhi," "flower" refers to the conduct;
it signifies that which is capable of being contemplated, which blossoms to evoke the realization of the fruit. This constitutes the conduct of the Buddha.

Regarding the "Dharma-gate of the Buddha": "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*). It clarifies the practice of Equal Awakening (*samyak-sambodhi*) throughout the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*), clarifying that after the tenth stage, the attainment of Buddhahood is completed, and subsequently, the practice of awakening is perfected in the eleventh stage; therefore, it is named the "Flower of the Dharma-gate of the Buddha. Regarding "Samādhi":

the fundamental substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the Great Quiescence Dharma-gate. When the delusions of both concentration and distraction are exhausted, it is called "fundamental quiescence"; by means of this concentration...
Therefore, the practice of the gateway of Samantabhadra’s conduct and all samādhis constitute its essential body.

Thus, in that celestial realm, for the sake of the assembly of those in the eight dhyānas of the form and formless realms, he taught one million billion verses on the gate of the *buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi* entered by a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). It is because a Bodhisattva at this stage enters the Buddha [samādhi]...
The Flower Dharma-gate clearly elucidates the entry into the mundane world to extensively benefit all sentient beings; because it is sovereign, it is named "Unimpeded Accordance with Conditions.
This stage clarifies that the practice of the Dharma-realm is universal. Why is it taught in that celestial realm?
It is because in that celestial realm, sorrow and suffering have vanished, and only the bliss of samādhi remains; this is to clarify the meditative concentration of the Bodhisattva of this stage.
To disrupt deluded emotions and eliminate them, one relies solely on wisdom and compassion to benefit sentient beings and bring them joy; thus, the Dharma is manifested through these locations.

It is at these locations that the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*) is taught. The details regarding the stages and the gates of practice are as extensively explained in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (瓔珞經).
This section corresponds to the text of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, though the current passage is not yet complete.
The ninth section, clarifying the conclusion of the stages of cause and effect, includes:

the Chapter on the Ten Samādhis, the Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers, the Chapter on the Ten Endurances, the Chapter on the Incalculable [Aeon], the Chapter on the Lifespan, the Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas, the Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas, the Chapter on the Ocean-like Marks of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies, the Chapter on the Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiant Light, and the Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra. As for...
The chapters from "Manifestation" (*Āvartaṇa*) to "Transcending the World" (*Lokottara*) constitute these twelve chapters of the sutra. Why is this so?

Because from the "Ten Samādhis" (*Daśa-vyūha*) chapter to the "Transcending the World" chapter, they comprehensively encompass the five stages, the ten bhūmis, and the Buddha-stage, as well as the gates of cause and effect from beginning to end regarding the myriad practices of Samantabhadra;

thus, from the "Ten Samādhis" chapter to the "Transcending the World" chapter, [the sequence] is thoroughly established from beginning to end. Therefore, the "Ten Samādhis" chapter and... [text ends].
At the beginning of both the second chapter of the *Lokadhātu-parivarta* and the first assembly,
it is stated that the Buddha had "just attained perfect enlightenment" in the *āraṇyaka-dharma-bodhimaṇḍa* in the kingdom of Magadha; however,
the statement that he was "entering the *kṣaṇānta-sarvabuddhasamādhi* in the Hall of Universal Radiance" is not [the case for those two assemblies].

The reason for returning to this assembly is solely because the two chapters, "The Ten Determinations" and "Transcending the World," constitute the gate of essence and function that pervades both the beginning and the end.
Thus, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, the Tathāgata again recounts [the teachings] according to those dharma-gates;
the differences in the names of the bodhisattva assemblies do not mean that they departed and have returned once more, but rather relate to the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications.
The teachings for the tenth and eleventh stages are expounded all at once throughout the various celestial realms;
the intent of these two chapters is to clarify that the essence and function of the Buddha’s cause and effect gates penetrate from beginning to end.
Since the substance of the Ten Samādhis is Mañjuśrī and the Dharma of Transcending the World is Samantabhadra, the Tathāgata emits light within the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter.

Because it is the gate through which the causes and effects of these two persons are harmonized and mutually penetrate, light is emitted from between the eyebrows to enter the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head,

and light is emitted from the mouth to enter the mouth of Samantabhadra, so that principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) may question and answer one another, thereby expounding the gate of the Buddha-fruit.

This gate of the Buddha-fruit resides entirely within the interval between the fundamental wisdom and the differentiated wisdom of these two persons, through the union of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
By the power of illumination, these twelve chapters of the sutra can be seen as a single, simultaneous assembly;

they collectively bring together the six stages and eleven grounds to enter the hall of universal light—the fundamental wisdom—and the great mansion of the fruits and virtues, which is the gateway to the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, the "Ten Samādhis" chapter and the "Transcending the World" chapter both recount the first and second [stages] of what preceded.
When this sutra was being preached, it was as if a hundred thousand precious mirrors were placed in the sky and a single Buddha image was placed upon the ground,
surrounded and adorned by a multitude of bodhisattvas; within those hundred thousand precious mirrors,
the images appeared all at once, and the reflections in each individual mirror interpenetrated one another without any coming or going.

The coming is likewise so; at the moment of initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, the heavens, the human realm, and the lands of the ten directions appear simultaneously and instantaneously, interpenetrating one another without any coming or going.
Therefore, the words, sounds, phrases, and meanings of all parties completely merge with one another, being entirely devoid of coming or going.
Do not consider this a reunion, nor should you form worldly conceptual attachments regarding it. Do not do so.

The intention for repeated encounters throughout the course of practice has already been described; however, as matters require deliberation, this is explained again here at the conclusion of the sutra.
One must understand that from beginning to end, the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta* clarifies the gateway to the culmination of the five stages and eleven grounds.
For this reason, it serves as the means for the circulation of the entire sutra from its inception to its conclusion.

The entrustment (*parindanā*) is contained within both: the *Samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna* (Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Conduct) appearing before the *Prādurbhāva* (Chapter on Manifestation) clarifies the practice for cultivating one’s own Buddha-fruit;
the *Lokottara* (Chapter on Transcending the World) appearing after the *Prādurbhāva* clarifies the conduct for benefiting sentient beings after attaining one’s own Buddha-fruit.
These clarify the practices of great compassion and wisdom performed after the realization of the Buddha-fruit, as well as the various habitual tendencies.
Although the totality of the ten thousand practices of Samantabhadra are performed, they are untainted by the world; this is called the "Chapter on Leaving the World.

The preceding section on the practices of Samantabhadra prior to attaining the Buddha-fruit clarifies that which one personally rides, as well as the exhortation for others to study for the sake of the Buddha-fruit.

The subsequent section on the practices of Samantabhadra indicates that once one's own Buddha-fruit is finalized, the stage after fruition consists purely of benefiting others; it is through this that [one is able to...]

The non-interruption of the Three Jewels, the ten penetrations (*daśābhijñā*), and the ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*) are also the ten concentrations (*daśasamādhi*) that pervade the five stages, their essence penetrating from beginning to end.
"Penetration" (*tong*) signifies the meaning of universal penetration and clarity. "Patience" (*ren*) refers to the gateway of the patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*).
"Asaṃkhyeya" clarifies the gateway of numerical quantity. "Life-span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) clarifies the life-span of the Buddha according to the person, the bodhisattva, and their place of abiding.
This clarifies that the sphere of activity for which Bodhisattvas act—namely, their transformation, guidance, and maintenance—is eternally present and indestructible.

The "Inconceivable Dharma" clarifies that the Tathāgata’s methods of transformation and his sovereign regulations are not known by those of the Two Vehicles or the provisional learners of the Three Vehicles.
The "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" clarifies the ten oceans of worlds and the ten... [etc.]

The "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks" (Rūpakāya-lakṣaṇānuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta) clarifies that Vairocana possesses ninety-seven kinds of marks and as many minor marks as there are atoms in the ten Flower Treasury worlds;

the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" (Samantabhadra-caryā-parivarta) clarifies the advancement toward the fruit through cultivation after having received benefit from the illumination of that radiance.
The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" is for the purpose of clarifying the stage of the final appearance of the cause-and-effect of the five stages of bodhisattvas through their own power;
