the "Chapter on Ultimate Transcendence of the World" is for the purpose of clarifying that after the fruit of Buddhahood, there is exclusively the benefit of others.
Thus, the thirty-nine chapters above comprise six stages; having completed the stages of cause and effect of the five stages, the benefit extends to all devas and... [the text continues].

In the *Śrīdevīparivarta-dharmadhātupraveśa-ekadharmaparyāya-sūtra*, after the Tathāgata entered the *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* and returned to expound the five stages of the Buddha-fruit to benefit the human realm,
the preceding summary concludes the Dharma-gates concerning the causes and fruits of the Buddha-stage within the first assembly,
the second assembly, and up to the seventh assembly of the eleven stages. The eighth assembly takes place at the Jeta Grove.
This shall be further explained later.
The tenth clarifies that those ordinary beings who have attained actual realization follow from the eighth assembly to within the Jeta Grove,
where the Tathāgata enters the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s stretch samādhi), and again manifests the fruits and virtues of the *dharmadhātu* throughout all worlds.
Five hundred śrāvakas, including Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, who had given birth to faith and joy and attained realization of the Buddha’s true reality,
manifested as if they had not heard [the teaching]. They were joined by those of the two vehicles— some with faith and some without— who were like the fifty-five assemblies in the first chapter,
as well as the ten chief bodhisattvas such as Jñānottara, the ten forest-dwelling bodhisattvas such as Guṇakusuma, and the ten banner-bearing bodhisattvas such as Vajradhvaja.
The thirty-seven Bodhisattvas of the Treasury, such as the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha and others, each gathered with a multitude of Bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields;
thus, according to their respective stages, they multiplied in number to manifest these various positions, enabling devas, humans, and ordinary beings to attain this Dharma-gate.
Within this assembly, six thousand bhikṣus were clearly seen to be ordinary beings.
Now, regarding Mañjuśrī, he suddenly clarified the ten ears and ten eyes; although this assembly was on the road, their state of mind did not depart from the Buddha’s assembly.
Their resolve while on the road serves to manifest progressive cultivation, rather than being either identical to or separate from that Buddha’s assembly.
This extends even to the ninth assembly at the east of the city of Vārāṇasī, where there were ten thousand dragon hosts and five hundred [others].
Five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred youths, and five hundred maidens were all ordinary beings who had equally realized the stage of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is now said that they caused ordinary beings to truly realize [the fruit].
At the site of the great stupa of the past Buddha to the east of the city of Jāṅgala, in the ninth assembly, Mañjuśrī preached the *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*.
The innumerable brahmins and nāgas attained birth in the human realm; ten thousand nāgas resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta;

and the five groups of beings in the City of Enlightenment all ascended together to the fruit of Buddhahood. Although Sudhana alone is cited as the leader, he is counted among the full number of five hundred, for the principle applies equally to all.
The number five hundred represents the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), and the number six thousand represents the six stages (*ṣaḍ-avasthā*).

Faith is also present therein; the "ten thousand dragons" represent the gateway of the ten thousand practices. Thus, not a single thing is established in vain, as all serve to symbolize the Dharma-gates.

The site of the great stūpa-temples of the Buddhas of the past serves as the assembly hall for this purpose, clarifying that the tracks of the path of ancient Buddhas and present Buddhas are no different, being identical to the singular goodness within the Tathāgata’s own assembly.
The Tenth Assembly: On the Return to Further Inquiry of Wealth-South and the Clarification of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Gathering and Transforming Sentient Beings.
This assembly encompasses all lands, atoms, spaces, and the dharma-realm;
these ten assemblies pervade all lands, atoms, spaces, the dharma-realm, the bodies of sentient beings, and the pores of their skin.

Because within this [Dharmadhātu] there are successively, layer upon layer, inexhaustible ocean-like assemblies of Tathāgatas, so it is with those who possess faith and understanding, as well as those who have newly resolved to attain awakening and enter into this Dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit of the Dharmadhātu:
they are like the cub of a lion king at the moment of its birth; although it is not yet able to equal the power, majesty, and sovereign mastery of its father, the lion king.
Thus, just as the lion’s form is entirely without distinction from that of all other beasts, yet all beasts stand in awe of it;
so too is it with those who cultivate faith, understanding, and initial realization within this Flower Garland Sūtra’s dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit:
they are able to believe that the nature and characteristics of their own body and mind are, in their entirety, identical to the self-substance of all Buddhas’ fruition, which is eternally true.

Because this is the fundamental great wisdom, and because those who realize and enter it share the gateway to the Buddha-fruit of all Tathāgatas, it is fundamentally without cultivation or construction;
its own essence is entirely Buddha. By means of this true gateway, one perfects the preparatory practice and cultivates the myriad distinct practices, which are eternally without beginning or end.
Although the power and function of this single true fruition-virtue have not yet reached the capacity of a Buddha, this is what is called the "seed."

The seed of the Buddha resides within the field of the body; taking faith as the beginning, those who enter through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom—at the very moment of their initial resolve, at the head of the ten stages—have already entered the wisdom of the Buddha. This is what is meant by being born into the family of the Buddha and becoming a true son of the Buddha;
because they have become one with the Buddha’s wisdom, they are fully endowed with all the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, one immediately transcends those three vehicles and attains the supernatural powers of a Bodhisattva on the ninth stage and beyond;

this vision is beyond the reach of the knowledge of all followers of the three vehicles, devas, and non-Buddhist practitioners. For this reason, those of capable faculties should single-mindedly practice and uphold it.
Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Phonetic Transcriptions: Pī (pronounced as in *pǔ jí*). Xūn (pronounced as in *xǔ yún*). Zhè (pronounced as in *zhí liè*). Yòu (pronounced as in *yǔ jiǔ*). Yàn (pronounced as in *yú qiàn*).
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament Scripture, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Lay Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, combining the various scriptures into a single treatise:
Chapter One, Part One, of the *Lokeshvararaja-vyuha* (The Array of the World-Ruling Sovereigns).
[Treatise] I prostrate to the pure ocean of the ten directions, the true retribution of the Dharma-realm, Vairocana, and the six stages of cause and effect.
This Vajra-phrase of the perfection of the fruit and virtue of the pure wheel of Dharma-gates taught by the great ocean-like assembly of all Bodhisattvas,
Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra— I now explain this subtle and wondrous scripture, desiring to bring vast benefit to all sentient beings.
May all the holy ones grant their protection, so that there may be no hindrance regarding these Dharma-gates, and that all who see or hear them may attain [realization].
The great benefits are all identical to the pure ocean of Vairocana.

Now, in expounding the teachings and propagating the sutras, one must distinguish four points: first, the long-term structural analysis of the sutra’s intent; second, clarifying the primary purport of the sutra;
third, elucidating its doctrinal essence; and fourth, providing a general enumeration of the assemblies.
To outline the general meaning of this scripture, it is briefly divided into ten sections: first, clarifying the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment;

second, clarifying the exhortation to practice by citing the fruit; third, clarifying the establishment of faith through the fruit; fourth, clarifying the entry into the realization of reality; fifth, clarifying the arousal of practice and cultivation;
sixth, clarifying the mutual integration of wisdom and compassion; seventh, clarifying the accomplishment of virtues through the cultivation of the aggregates; eighth... [and so forth].
1. Clarifying mastery over the welfare of sentient beings; 2. Clarifying the various worthies and their assigned stations; 3. Clarifying how ordinary beings are led to actual realization. 1.
Clarifying the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment refers to the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of World Rulers. 2.

Presenting the fruit to encourage practice refers to the five chapters of scripture beginning from the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" down to the "Chapter on Vairocana," as well as the "Chapter on World Rulers."
The "Chapter on Sublime Adornment" (Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra) cites the fruits accomplished by the Buddha to cause people to cultivate the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).
Those who attain faith through these fruits consist of the six chapters of the sutra from the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Name" (*Buddhanāma*) down to the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla*).
Furthermore, this also inclusively takes the preceding "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruler" (*Lokendrarāja-suvarṇaprabhāsa*); thus, it is based upon ten Buddhas of Wisdom.
The fruit of one’s own mind is headed by the Buddha Immovable Wisdom (Aksobhya-jñāna), clarifying that the wisdom of one’s own mind is unmoved by the nature of conceptual differentiation;

this constitutes the fourth entry into reality. As for the "Realization," it consists of the six chapters from the "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru" chapter onwards, which take the Ten Abodes as their essence, because one dwells in the house of the Buddha’s wisdom and is born therein. Fifth is the "Setting Forth."
The four chapters of scripture from "The Bodhisattva Descends from the Palace of Yāma Heaven" onwards take the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) as their essence,

because they constitute the practice of the Buddha's conduct. The three chapters of scripture from "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace" onwards take the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) as their essence,
because they perfect the integration of the ultimate and conventional truths to achieve great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Seventh, regarding the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the aggregates (*skandha-bhāvanā-siddha-guṇa*): from the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) among the ten stages of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, one aggregate is cultivated;
this is because the first three dharmas have been brought to mastery through habitual practice. Eighth, regarding mastery in benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-vaśitā*):

from the "Ten Samādhis" chapter (*daśa-samādhi-paṭala*) onwards, up to the "Universal Good Conduct" chapter (*Samantabhadra-caryā-paṭala*), these twelve chapters of the sutra collectively constitute the ten stages.
The middle aggregate of virtue, merit, and accomplishment—when the practices for the benefit of sentient beings are fulfilled—is then called the perfection of the Dharma-practice (*dharmacaryā*).
From beginning to end, the Buddha’s unconditioned essence does not shift by even a hair’s breadth or a single thought.

This is because he takes the nature of the perfectly luminous great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* as the initial stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) during the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), and thus has no thoughts at any time; for the three periods of time have no inherent nature.

Because they are integrated as one at all times, this is not something known by ordinary consciousness, but is realized only through wisdom. Ninth, regarding those who "entrust themselves to positions":
this refers to the aforementioned six stages of the Bodhisattvas, as well as the chapter on the appearance of Buddhas in the world;
these all emerge through skillful means from within the realm of the great wisdom of the ocean of nature, entrusting themselves to various positions to constitute the ten levels of faith.

The dharma-gate of the eleven stages— the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, plus the stage of Equal Enlightenment— causes ordinary beings to believe in, enter, emulate, and study them,
so that they do not become confused regarding these matters. The "Ten Clarifications" cause those ordinary beings who have attained actual realization to establish the six stages,
beginning with the ten faiths, within the nature of the Dharma-realm, so that they do not depart from the progressive cultivation of skillful means.
The essence and its function are not mutually exclusive; through skillful means, his wisdom becomes ever more sublime while his conduct becomes ever more humble.

As he pursues the roots of practice until they are perfected, it is called "progressive cultivation. According to his capacity and capability, he establishes various stages; according to each stage, he knows the practice so as not to be deluded regarding cause and effect.

This enables the student to clearly understand both the general and the specific, achieving success based on the stages without stagnating at the beginning; thus, one does not depart from the initial ground.
Therefore, as in the following passage, the assembly of Śraddhācūḍa (Good Wealth) and others—namely the upāsakas, upāsikās, boys, and girls—are each listed as five hundred;
since there are ten stages for each of the five positions of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground, they collectively total five hundred.
This is also consistent with the six thousand bhikṣus mentioned in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*.

The summary concludes by stating that six thousand ten thousand dragons—representing the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*)—all of whom were ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), attained the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) because they believed in this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the sphere of the Buddha-fruit’s wisdom (*buddha-phala-jñāna-gocara*).
Thus, it is said that ordinary beings have truly realized [the truth]. This concludes the ten long sections explaining the intent of the scripture; herein follows the detailed exposition.

It is only upon reaching this section that the meaning becomes clear: because the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm" (Fajie yipin) universally encompasses the preceding forty chapters of the sutra—since it is the total dharma realm—and because it clarifies that the dharmas of the three periods of time are the total dharma realm;
for this Chapter on the Dharma Realm is the fruit of all Buddhas and all sentient beings. Within this entire sutra, there are [altogether... in total.
The Meaning of the Pervasive Perfection of the Fivefold Cause and Effect: 1. Demonstrating the pervasive perfection of the causes and conditions for attaining perfect enlightenment:

This refers to the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Ruler" (*Lokendrarājavyūha*), which extends through the following five chapters of the sutra. 2. The pervasive perfection of the causes and conditions for the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) and subsequent cultivation:

This refers to the six chapters beginning from the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Name" (*Buddhanāman*), which extend through the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmana*).

Within the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, twenty chapters constitute the pervasive totality of the essence of the three concentrations (*tri-samādhi*): namely, the chapters on the ten concentrations, the ten supernormal powers (*daśābhijñā*), and the ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*).

Four chapters constitute the pervasive totality of the ocean of the four practices (*catur-caryā-sāgara*): namely, the "Universal Good Conduct" chapter (*Samantabhadra-caryā*) and the "Transcending the World" chapter (*Lokātīta*).

Five chapters constitute the pervasive totality of the inconceivable ocean of great perfect wisdom of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-acintya-mahāpariniṣpanna-jñāna-sāgara*): namely, the "Dharma-realm" chapter (*Dharmadhātu*).
Because these five meanings are all-pervasive, this single scripture is divided into five chapters; the fact that each chapter begins with "At that time,
the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha" as its opening indicates that these five dharmas are,
at one and the same time, within one dharma-realm, at one momentary limit, and constitute the single essence and function of all Buddhas.
The single common dharma is that cause and effect are all-pervasive, perfect, and complete, devoid of the meaning of sequence or priority;
all Buddhas are thus. Such a dharma does not depart from the ten meditative concentrations (*daśa-vyūha-samādhi*);
from the moment of descending as a spirit into the womb to manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood and entering *nirvāṇa*, it does not depart from a single kṣaṇa, nor is there any further shifting.
By means of this single section of the scripture, there are five stages for each [of these]. At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha;
in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" alone, he fully elucidated the general essence and purport of this entire scripture:

that the Great Perfectly Round Wisdom of the Single Dharmadhātu possesses these five kinds of pervasive causes and effects, which are cultivated through progressive practice beginning from the initial stage of faith.

The beginning and end of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the causes and effects, and the perfection of the myriad practices ultimately do not transcend the essence of the ten concentrations and the nature that is timeless.
In both ordinary beings and sages, this is uniformly so from the very beginning. Due to the deluded conceptualization of sentient beings, the measure of time arises accordingly;

because of such deluded conceptualization, birth and old age come to exist. If one were to give rise to notions of extension or brevity within the gateway of the fundamental *dharmadhātu*, [it would be a delusion].
All that is seen is merely one's own deluded perception; it is not truly existent.

Thus, by being deluded regarding the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature and violating the dharma-gate of primordial timelessness and wisdom, when one gives rise to perceptions that chase after emotions and follow delusions, the lengthening or shortening of eons does not constitute the seeds of faith within the Buddha’s True Dharma.
One should know that such a person, even if they practice and transcend the three realms, [remains bound].

Because they do not yet possess the seed for attaining Buddhahood as a fruit, these are the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the provisional teachings who possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, even those bodhisattvas of non-retrogression cannot know this:

that "non-retrogression" refers to emerging from birth and death, whereas [the former] does not achieve non-retrogression while remaining within birth and death; furthermore, they can only rely upon emptiness.

Observing that one enters the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the first bhūmi by subduing the active afflictions (*kleśa*), it is not yet the attainment of fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*) through reaching fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and seeing non-retrogression.
Thus, the Path of Seeing of the three vehicles consists entirely of bodhisattvas with the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*);
none of them have, at the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment, attained the great perfect mirror-like wisdom of the fundamental dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the three types of non-regressive mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) attained by those dwelling in the middle [stages] who have become Buddhas throughout the ten directions:

the first, second, and third stages are called the mind-made body of the bliss of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-sukha-manomaya-kāya*); the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are called the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva-avabodha-manomaya-kāya*);
and the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the mind-made body that is spontaneously born of its own kind and is free from effortful activity (*nikāya-sahaja-anābhoga-manomaya-kāya*).

These three kinds of mind-made bodies of Bodhisattvas are all like a thatched hut provisionally established as a skillful means outside the great gate of the ocean of wisdom of the Great Perfectly Round Dharma-realm, so that these sons may temporarily escape the calamity of the fire. As stated in the latter part of this sutra:
"The śrāvakas in the assembly were as if deaf and blind; even if the Bodhisattvas endowed with the six supernormal powers heard [the teaching]..."
This sūtra cannot produce faith in those who, as clearly explained in the scripture, have followed their own conceptual reckonings since beginningless time;

even if they were to produce faith in the Buddha-dharma, it would arise merely according to their own sentiments. Because such faith is deluded regarding the realm of one’s own wisdom, there is no realization of actual wisdom through which true faith and practice could arise.
If one does not turn the mind [toward enlightenment], one will ultimately fail to become a Buddha. Even if one were to...
They transform and guide sentient beings, enabling them to attain the seeds of the Three Vehicles as well as those of humans and devas; yet they dwell only in a single pure land,
lacking the great vision of boundless wisdom that is equal in measure to the vast Dharma-realm and pervades the infinite space of the lands within the dust-motes of the ten directions,
manifesting physical bodies to meet all sentient beings according to their faculties and leading them through the Three Vehicles without partiality.
It merely says that one sees the realm of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system;

as stated in this sutra, there are oceans of worlds, natures of worlds, and seeds of worlds, all of which are profoundly deep and vast, equal to the dharma-realm and empty space, as fully explained in the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World.
Just as within the Three Vehicles, even if one were to see the Tathāgata’s body with its thirty-two marks and eighty...

Even if one were to extensively describe the ten kinds of marks and eighty-four thousand secondary characteristics, one would not see the Tathāgata’s body, which is equal to the atoms of ten buddha-fields.
Those of the three vehicles merely see the Tathāgata’s manifestations filling the trichiliocosm;
they do not see the Tathāgata’s manifestations filling as many infinite buddha-fields as there are atoms.
The practices of those who follow the three vehicles are all finite in their scope;
they do not perceive that within every single atom of the dharma-realm there are infinite dharmas, nor that the practices of Samantabhadra interpenetrate one another without obstruction.
Second, to clarify the essential purport of the sutra, there are six points: first, clarifying the essential purport of the sutra; second, which collection (piṭaka) this sutra is subsumed under;
third, distinguishing its introductory section (nidāna); fourth, determining its main body (śarīra); fifth, clarifying to whom this sutra was entrusted;
and sixth, clarifying where this sutra circulates. First, regarding the clarification of the essential purport of the sutra: this sutra...
It is named the Vairocana Great Wisdom Dharmadhātu Original True Body, the Perfect Union of Quiescence and Function, the Dharma-fruit of Nature and Characteristics Unimpeded.
Taking as its primary tenet that which the Buddha himself rides, it is as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Riding this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, this sūtra states: "For those who joyfully seek the fruit of Buddhahood, I preach the most supreme [vehicle]."

The Vehicle of the Superior, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Inconceivable Vehicle, and so forth, are intended to cause those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment to aspire to the vast;
thus they shall again attain the fruit of such great wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is unified with one’s own wisdom as non-dual.
Therefore, the essential purport of this sutra is profoundly deep and difficult to believe; yet for those who do believe, it surpasses all other forms of support.

The merit obtained by serving Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields throughout the entire span of an eon is not equal to that of one who, having personally attained it, believes in this gate of the Tathāgata’s realm of great wisdom and the fruition of Buddhahood within this sutra;
the merit of such belief surpasses the former. As the verses in the latter part of the "Bhadrapāla Chapter" state: "There is one who, with his hand..."
To remain suspended in mid-air for an entire eon over ten Buddha-fields while performing such deeds is not considered difficult;

however, to have faith in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult. To bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon as many sentient beings as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields for the duration of an eon does not surpass the merit of one who has faith in this Dharma; such a person is most supreme. [As numerous as] the atoms in ten Buddha-fields...
If one were to serve all those who come for an entire eon, the merit of one who can recite and uphold this chapter would be far superior to that.
Furthermore, a previous verse states: "Among all the beings in all worlds, few desire the vehicle of the Śrāvakas;
those seeking Pratyekabuddhahood are even fewer; and those who aspire to the Mahāyāna are exceedingly rare. Those who aspire to the Great [Vehicle] are truly rare.

It is still relatively easy for those who ride the vehicles [of the three yānas] to believe this Dharma, but it is doubly more difficult; to clarify the profound intent of this sūtra is extremely difficult to believe.

For those who practice the contemplation of emptiness, those who have ceased delusion, those who practice dhyāna while still harboring notions of defilement and purity, and for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas with the six supernormal powers who have not yet turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], there is no such portion. As stated in the subsequent passage of the sūtra: "Suppose there were..."

Even if a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas and attains the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), they are still called a "provisional name" bodhisattva and not a true bodhisattva.

Should such a person hear this sutra and yet fail to believe or enter into it—as was the case with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—this is likewise for the purpose of turning those of the three vehicles toward the One Vehicle; thus, it turns them away from their respective gates.
The three outer vehicles are expedient means used to lead the sons back to the true gate of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and dharma-realm;
they serve to shatter the reliance upon those desks and tables, thereby enabling them to attain the Tathāgata’s wisdom of non-reliance and original sovereignty.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the teaching of the sudden [awakening] for those of superior faculties, delivered at the very moment of attaining perfect enlightenment, which is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Sūtra was spoken for the sake of those turning back from the three vehicles during the forty years following the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

Furthermore, the Buddha-vehicle and the three vehicles were taught simultaneously and collectively; however, according to individual faculties, they naturally correspond to specific distinctions within the Dharma-gate of a single sound.
While the meanings of the general and the particular arise, their true essence is such that there is never a time when they can be made sequential, as in the Lotus Sūtra.
The Sūtra says: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle; there is no second, nor is there a third.
It is only by means of provisional names that sentient beings are guided. It further says: "This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true.
Regarding these "other two," they refer to the three vehicles as being [provisional] in contrast to the gateway shared by all Buddhas of the ten directions, which is taken as the reality.

The remaining two are merely provisional designations and not yet true; because they are the "remaining two," when contrasted with the one reality, all provisional teachings constitute the "remaining two.
This is because the *Lotus Sūtra* criticizes the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and those of the three vehicles for all being unable to believe in the One Vehicle Dharma.
Thus, even though provisional-vehicle bodhisattvas possess a partial seeking [for the truth], [they remain within the category of the remaining two].
Because the bodhicitta still fears birth and death, one attains non-retrogression by being free from defilement;

however, this is not yet called "true" non-retrogression in which defilement and purity are equal. This includes Bodhisattvas who, through the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness, find increasing delight in emptiness;

those who, through the contemplation of provisional True Suchness, are consistently free from the entanglements; and all other Bodhisattvas who possess both longing and aversion, as well as the desire to be born in a Pure Land.

The assembly is all able to leave birth and death, transcend the entanglements, and neither retreat nor enter [the mundane], for they abide in the ocean-nature of the Dharma-realm, the single truth that is free from the gates of longing or aversion.
In light of this Buddha-vehicle, both those who delight in birth and death and those who loathe birth and death are equally subject to regression.
By contemplating emptiness to increase excellence, they cultivate the gate of the provisional True Suchness and practice the six *pāramitās* to attain the six [perfections].
The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are the non-retrogression that transcends birth and death; they are not the non-retrogression within the single nature of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras state that Bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers do not hear or believe in this scripture.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says: "Suppose there were a Bodhisattva who recited and chanted the eight..."
To explain the fourteen thousand treasuries of the Dharma for others and attain the six supernormal powers is not yet considered difficult;
however, to even briefly read this sutra is what is truly difficult. This realm of wisdom alone contradicts what the intellect habitually understands, and is therefore extremely hard to believe.

The faith and understanding of the three vehicles accord with what the mind delights in. Why is this? Because it is taught that the fruit of Buddhahood is already present within the three stages of the path of cultivation.
Following this, it is taught that the Buddha’s pure land lies in another direction, whereas this Sahā world is a defiled land.
Those who cultivate bodhi grow weary of defilement and aspire to true bliss, thus seeking rebirth in a pure land.

As for those bodhisattvas who remain in the world, their so-called "retention of afflictions to moisten birth" for the sake of saving sentient beings does not arise from the inherent power of the fundamental wisdom of dharmatā. Rather, it is through the power of mastery.
For this reason, such teachings for bodhisattvas are all in accordance with worldly sentiments; because these dharmas are easy to believe, they do not accord with what is taught in this sutra.

Entering the fruit of Buddhahood does not exceed a single kṣaṇa; it is only by distinguishing between delusion and awakening that "immeasurable kalpas" are spoken of, yet in total, not even a moment is displaced.
Thus, it is said that from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) at the very first vision of the Path, cause and effect are simultaneous.
One does not perceive the prior limit nor the subsequent limit; one does not see the time before attaining Buddhahood, nor the time of attaining Perfect Enlightenment;

one does not see the severance of afflictions, nor the realization of Bodhi. Ultimately, there is no movement whatsoever. Through moment-to-moment cultivation, the fifty stages are fulfilled, and all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) is entirely perfected.
Whether in terms of the general or the specific, the same or the different, or formation and disintegration—all are simultaneously sovereign and yet non-existent.

Because it is seen through the lens of worldly conditions, it is difficult to believe. As for that which is believed, it is as stated in the latter part of the sutra regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths:
in the Golden World, there is the Buddha Immovable Wisdom, whose chief Bodhisattva is named Mañjuśrī—translated here as "Wondrous Virtue.
He is called "Golden" because he is pure, bright, and stainless; this is the principle of the Dharmakāya.

The Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati*) is the wisdom within the principle (*tattva*). Because it is equally shared by the bodies of all ordinary beings and sages, it is said to be "in all places.
Mañjuśrī, in every place is the Golden World, and in every place is the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom.
Those who now have faith should believe that their own mind is the nature of non-abiding, and understand this through sublime wisdom.
"Detachment" refers to Mañjuśrī himself, who possesses sovereign discernment regarding the subtle principle of non-substantiality within the state where the mind has no dependence or abiding.
Because there is no non-substantiality that can be moved, he is named the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*).

Since the wisdom and phenomena of the Buddhas are non-dual and their wondrous function is sovereign, he is therefore titled the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue (*Mañjuśrī*). For this reason, all Buddhas arise from this faith; thus he is so named.
Mañjuśrī is the mother of all Buddhas of the ten directions; he is also called the Youthful Bodhisattva because faith is the birth of all.
When the mind of faith is perfected, it is sealed by the power of wisdom that observes through concentration and insight.

This mutual accord, corresponding in a single thought-moment, is called the initial mind of the Ten Abodes, wherein one immediately attains perfect enlightenment upon taking up the capacity for practice.
The place of practice is called Samantabhadra; taking the wondrous wisdom that has no basis of reliance, it is called Wondrous Virtue (*Guṇarāja*).

Taking the wisdom that is skillfully able to discern and know the faculties, it is named Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalajñāna-buddha*). To be in accord with oneself is called Right Enlightenment (*Samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, the place of faith is called the Mind of Faith (*Śraddhā-citta*); being in accord with oneself is called the Abiding Mind (*Vihāra-citta*). As for...
Because one abides in the dwelling-place of the Buddhas through the liberation of sublime wisdom, wherein all marks are exhausted and phenomena are unborn;
if there were a Buddha existing outside of the mind, it would not be called "faithful mind," but rather one would be termed a person of false views.

All Buddhas are identical with one’s own mind, and all sentient beings are identical with one’s own nature. Since this nature has no dependence, its essence is without differentiation; wisdom is of a single nature.

One should know it thus; by means of this wondrous wisdom of identical essence, one should believe and understand it to be like the minds of all Buddhas and the minds of all sentient beings, without deceiving oneself. Therefore, the primary intent of this sutra is established for the sake of sentient beings with the Great Mind;
it is the gateway through which the Buddhas themselves travel, a wondrous scripture of the One Vehicle, and the principle of the Dharma-realm.
Because sentient beings of great resolve enter the Buddha’s fundamental great wisdom and the fruit of Buddhahood, they accord with the principle of truth in a single thought;
as their wisdom manifests simultaneously, they are immediately Buddhas. Since this is the principle of the *dharmadhātu*, it is seen as being without beginning, middle, or end.

Therefore, for those of inferior understanding belonging to the three vehicles, who would otherwise hear that one attains the fruit of Buddhahood only after three incalculable eons, it is appropriate to explain [this teaching] to them.
The Pure Land of Akṣobhya is located in another direction, whereas this Sahā world is a defiled land;

therefore, within the Lotus Sūtra, for the sake of turning those with inferior understanding of the three vehicles away [from their limited views], it clarifies that even a dragon girl—who is not a fit vessel—can attain Buddhahood in an instant.

This demonstrates that the vastness of faith is not a provisional device, but is the teaching of reality itself. Because the practice of this teaching of reality is not circuitous or stagnant, [it leads directly to fruition].
The statement that the dragon girl was only eight years old indicates that she began her studies in this present life and did not study them previously;

that she was a female animal indicates that she did not cultivate this through past accumulations. This clarifies that the Dharma-gate she now believes in is direct in principle and free from obstruction;

thus, the essence of the Dharma-realm is not encompassed by the three periods of time. In a single thought-moment, she responds to reality, the sentiments of the three periods are exhausted, and wisdom is without [duality].

Since appearing and disappearing is itself the fruit of Buddhahood, the Sūtra says that for the sake of sentient beings of inferior understanding, he manifests deeds such as the eight signs of passing away.

Regarding the passage where the entire assembly in the Sahā world sees the Dragon Girl go to the Stainless World in the south and attain Buddhahood, the commentary explains that "the south" signifies clarity and correctness, as it presides over the element of fire (*tejas*); and fire represents...
"Clarity" refers to the sun; "voidness and non-existence" means being free from defilement.

That the multitude sees it from afar indicates that those who study the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles have faith but have not yet realized it for themselves; hence, it is said they see it from afar.

Since the Dharma-realm is the single truth in which self and other mutually penetrate, if one were to personally attain it, how could it be called seeing from afar? This sutra enables Sudhana to attain [realization] in a single lifetime.

The Buddha explained that "one birth" refers to the point after one has given rise to faith from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when the initial mind of the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*) accords with non-arising (*anutpāda*).
This is to be born by the power of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, not born through karma.

Although this will be explained extensively in the text, for now I shall briefly clarify the ultimate aim of the fundamental principle of this sutra. Who among the profoundly learned gentlemen would dare to [dispute] the gateways to the fruit of Buddhahood?
Contemplate this. Second, as for what treasury (piṭaka) this sutra is subsumed under:
this sutra is named the Vairocana Dharmadhātu Treasury and is subsumed therein because it universally illumines the ocean of the dharmadhātu and completely contains all dharma-gates.

Furthermore, this sutra is not permitted to be categorized among the provisional teachings of the transformation Buddhas of the three vehicles, nor is it within the scope of the knowledge and understanding of ordinary sentient beings.

Therefore, within the teachings of the Transformation Buddha, the assembly of Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles cannot understand the Dharma-gate of the Reward Buddha that is the One True Dharma-realm;
they know only the distinct dharmas of the Three Vehicles. Thus, these Bodhisattvas perceive only the trichiliocosm as the single realm of a Reward Buddha;
it is for this reason that there are thousands of billions of Śākyamunis.
Because it is an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), one does not understand this Dharma-gate taught by the Reward Buddha (*saṃbhogabuddha*) within the true reward-dharmadhātu of this One Vehicle.

Therefore, this sutra is titled the *Vairocana*; it is subsumed within the ocean of wisdom of the fruit of Buddhahood in the dharmadhātu, and is not the same as that which is included in the provisional Bodhisattva-piṭaka within the teachings of the emanation Buddhas of the Three Vehicles. Thus, below...
In the "Chapter on the Dharma-realm of Letters," it is said that the name of the pavilion where Maitreya resides is the "Vairocana-Adorned Treasury.

Once Sudhana has entered it, he sees only the infinite treasuries of the Buddhas' Dharma, the gateways of practice, and the marks of retribution—all adorned with inexhaustible signs of merit, each numbering as many as incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*.
This is precisely based upon Vairocana... [as described in detail in the sutra].

The palaces and towers wherein one dwells, which are obtained as the retribution for practicing the various teachings and practices taught by that Buddha, are formed according to the causes and effects of practicing the *dharmadhātu-garbha* (Dharma-realm treasury). This is because even the causes and effects of the adornments obtained as the retribution of all Buddhas are likewise so.
"Treasury" (*garbha*) has the meaning of containment; it contains all phenomena of the *dharmadhātu*.

Because the dharmas of causes and effects within the gates are all inexhaustible, the sutras of the Three Vehicles frequently use the sands of the Ganges as a standard of measure for the number of dharma-gates to establish their vast and great meaning.

Furthermore, the sutras of this One Vehicle frequently use the motes of dust in a single Buddha-field, or those in ten Buddha-fields, up to the motes of dust in immeasurable Buddha-fields, as the standard of measure for the number of dharmas. Moreover—
The characteristics of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles may consist of one, two, three, up to seven, eight, nine, or ten as their numerical count.
In this sutra’s dharma-gate, each individual element is complete with the number ten, thereby clarifying that the dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit is perfect and full.
Since the names and meanings [of these teachings] differ in their breadth and narrowness, the Dharma-treasuries must necessarily be distinct. Therefore, this sutra is the Vairocana...

That which is contained in this treasury is not subsumed under the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the three vehicles; therefore, this sūtra constantly takes the Buddha-fruit as the track for progressive cultivation.
It is because one cultivates the specific wisdom of the ancient traces of the Buddha’s fundamental great wisdom.

If it were otherwise than the ancient traces of the Buddha, there would be no meaning of attaining Buddhahood through progressive cultivation; it would merely be like the three vehicles, which at best avoid a single portion [of suffering].

The coarse suffering of birth and death is not that which relies upon the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom; rather, it is through the ancient traces of practice that one accords with the cultivation of the Buddha Vehicle.
Therefore, this sutra is included within the treasury of Vairocana and is not subsumed under the treasuries of the three vehicles of bodhisattvas.
The introductory section (*nidāna*) of the *Tri-sarvajñatā-vibhāga-sūtra* is divided into two gates: first, that which encompasses the entire treatise;

second, the specific introductory section for each chapter. Regarding the first, that which encompasses the entire treatise, it refers to the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruler" (*Lokendra-vyūha*).
Regarding the second, the specific introductory section for each chapter, as in the sūtra, within each chapter and within each assembly, there is always the phrase: "At that time... (*atha khalu*).

In this manner, he introduces the meaning within each chapter; furthermore, throughout this entire sutra, the location where the World-Honored One dwelt at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is introduced five times from beginning to end. To the question of why it is so, the answer is given:
from the very first, in the first fascicle, it says, "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha, at the beginning of the dawn."

The place where he attained Buddhahood was within an araṇya; furthermore, in the second assembly, at that time the World-Honored One was in the Bodhimanda of the Araṇya-dharma in the kingdom of Magadha, having just attained perfect enlightenment.

Without departing from this original site, he proceeded to his abode of retribution, dwelling therein in the Hall of Universal Radiance—this being the fruition of the practice of wisdom and principle.
Having attained this, one’s dwelling is shared with the world; when the realization of the *araṇya* is reached, one then arrives at the residence.
From this point onward, ascending to the celestial palaces, it is said that without leaving one's original location, the body sits pervasively in all places of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Alternatively, it is said that one ascends to such heavens; though ascending to the heavens and manifesting in various ranks for further cultivation, one does not depart from one's original location.

The principle of the dharma-realm is elucidated because the wondrous principle of the dharma-nature is devoid of coming and going or internal and external, and because the essence of great wisdom is inherently all-pervasive.
Accordingly, at the beginning of the fortieth fascicle, in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, it is further stated:
"At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, within the *āraṇya-dharma-bodhimaṇḍa*, having just attained perfect enlightenment in the Universal Radiance."
The "Illumination Palace" enters the Samādhi of the Limit of the Instant (*kṣaṇāntika-samādhi*).

Because the Dharma-body of the Dharma-realm takes concentration as its essence and lacks the nature of the three periods of time, the descent from Tuṣita Heaven, the entry into Nirvāṇa, and the forty-nine years of dwelling in the world turning all wheels of the Dharma do not, in total, transcend the limit of a single instant. It is by means of this samādhi that one first attains perfect penetration.

In the end, these are not of the three periods of time or of antiquity and modernity; therefore, they are described in this way to summarize that all Buddhas of the past, present, and future attain Buddhahood simultaneously, and the birth and death of sentient beings likewise does not shift by even a single moment.
It is only because sentient beings falsely calculate the length of years and ages that, as the Buddha has taught, there is "birth" and "death."

All of these occur without the passage of time; therefore, the Sūtra says: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas—neither going nor coming, and likewise without abiding.
Thus, by thoroughly knowing the events of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the Ten Powers.
This chapter of the Sūtra comprehensively encompasses the beginning, end, and intermediate stages, fully elucidating the nature that is devoid of past, future, present, antiquity, or modernity.
From the stage of an ordinary person, one suddenly sees the Way upon a single thought-moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment;

then, through the progressive cultivation of the five stages—the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground—one attains Buddhahood, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvana, all without shifting by even a single kṣaṇa.
Because this reveals the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering [the truth] through the gateway of the Dharma-realm, it clarifies the Real Teaching (Shikyo).
Because the Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle’s Dharma-realm is such that it is elucidated by means of the names of samādhis,
this chapter collectively presents this fundamental Dharma-realm of the Single Vehicle— the gate of quiescent function— wherein the beginning and end are one and the same,

and there is no distinction between origin and conclusion or temporal sequence; thus, it serves as the introduction to the "Chapter on Attaining Buddhahood," and the subsequent "Chapter on Leaving the World" follows in the same manner in its exposition.
From the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment up to the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsa*) refers to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra entering the Buddha-flower Samādhi.
"Buddha-flower" signifies the Buddha-activities cultivated; "samādhi" clarifies that the essence and function are unimpeded in their quiescence.

This is identical to the previous description regarding the location, clarifying that the substance and function of cultivating Buddha-activities are without beginning or end, being eternally constant.

Perfection is the absence of the three periods of time. This chapter clarifies that through the cultivation of Samantabhadra’s practices, one returns to the great wisdom of the essence of the Dharma-realm, which constantly accompanies all activities and completely encompasses the three periods of time without ever departing from the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
Thus, it is clarified that these various practices are themselves the essence and function of the Dharma-realm; therefore, this entire exposition demonstrates that time does not shift.
Nor does it shift location, because the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) has no center or periphery;

the various practices cultivated therein are always equal, like a single moment, for there is neither increase nor decrease across the three periods of time, and no coming or going. Next, regarding the entry into the *Dharmadhātuparivarta*, it says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One was in the city of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in the Anāthapiṇḍada Park. This citation indicates the actual location.
The vehicle of the Tathāgata, as taught by the Master, penetrates from beginning to end;
throughout the heavens, the human realm, and the worlds of the ten directions, it takes the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as its essence, for this is not a false or illusory essence.

Because sentient beings follow delusion and fail to realize this, within this chapter, the inconceivable essence of the dharma-realm throughout the heavens, the human realm, and the worlds of the ten directions is presented in its entirety.
Because its quiescent function is sovereign, it causes sentient beings to awaken to and enter [this state].

Therefore, this chapter is expounded by the Tathāgata solely through inconceivable spiritual power (*acintya-rddhi*) without relying on oral speech. This clarifies that the totality of the mundane world is both true and divine, for there is no coming or going;

it clarifies that the *dharmadhātu* universally encompasses all before and after as being fundamentally a single limit (*ekānta*). Thus, there is no need for [the teaching] to be identical [to worldly conventions].

The description of the Bodhimaṇḍa is provided because enlightenment (*bodhi*) is identical to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); since the preceding assemblies were all contained within this assembly of the Dharma-realm, it is described in this manner.

The essence and function of the ten assemblies are all comprehensively encompassed by this chapter as the fundamental matrix (*mātṛkā*) of the single substance, single nature, single time, and single wisdom. Thus, these five sections describe the initial realization of perfect enlightenment.
The "Awakened One" (Jue) generally clarifies that this Dharma-realm is simultaneous and devoid of before or after; thus, within this single scripture,

the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord," the "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas," the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," and the "Chapter on Leaving the World" all recount the events repeatedly from the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment up to the "Entering the Dharma-realm" chapter in the Hall of Universal Radiance, mentioning only the Anāthapiṇḍada.
The general purport of these five chapters of the sūtra consists of five kinds of Buddha-fruits that are all-pervasive;
they encompass the other chapters as their essential meaning, and for this reason they are recounted again.

It is solely because these five kinds of all-pervasive dharmadhātu cause and effect are fully manifested in a single kṣaṇa, and because all stages are subsumed within them, that they constitute the dharmadhātu.
Because it is the fruit of great wisdom, there are five sections whose titles are similar;
however, only the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter specifically mentions the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden. What are these five kinds of all-pervasive cause and effect?

First, the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruler" clarifies the initial attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood as being all-pervasive; the sutra states that without leaving his original location, his body pervades everywhere.

The "Chapter on the Names of the Two Buddhas Seated at All Sites of Enlightenment" explains within the Hall of Universal Radiance the Dharma-gate of the names of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its lands.

This assembly, which establishes transformation and benefits all beings, universally pervades the teaching of the six chapters of the sutra that accomplish the stage of faith and the fruit of Buddhahood.
This clarifies how the mind of faith universally pervades; as for the "Chapter on the Thirty Samādhis," it is as follows:

Entering the Samādhi of the Limit of the Instant (*kṣaṇāntika-samādhi*), by means of this samādhi, one universally encompasses this sutra as well as the inexhaustible kalpas of the three periods of time;

all are, in total, a single moment. From the beginning, it has been thus: it accords with and corresponds to the Buddha-way, manifesting its fundamental dharma, attaining Buddhahood, preaching the Dharma, and the timing of entering parinirvāṇa, without any shifting or change. This clarifies the greatness of the Buddha.
The nature of wisdom is inherently quiescent in its essence, yet its function is pervasive;

even when entering nirvana, remaining in the world for forty-nine years, dwelling in the mother’s womb, or not yet having descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, it remains so because the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is by nature devoid of coming and going, or past and present.
This is clarified in the "Chapter on Detachment from the World" (Caturtho laukikavibhāga).

Taking the great wisdom of the inherently quiescent and settled nature of the dharma-realm as the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice clarifies that the pervasive and all-encompassing "Buddha-flower" consists of awakened practice; "samādhi" is the essence of original awakening.

The "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-realm" elucidates the great wisdom of the fundamental essence of the dharma-realm—the fruit of Buddhahood—which pervades everywhere. These five types constitute pervasion.
In total, taking the Dharma-realm as its essence, this is a teaching of universal pervasiveness; these five modes of pervasion encompass all stages and all distinctions.

Fearing that people might not understand and thus lose the intended meaning, the titles are presented in five locations throughout this scripture, linking the preceding and following sections to demonstrate that this sutra takes the Dharma-realm as its foundation.
The essence is fundamentally without sequence, for there is no distinction between beginning and end, or the length of time in the middle;
it is like a royal seal that stamps everything simultaneously, forming characters without before or after. By means of the jewel-seal of the Dharma-realm, all stages are universally sealed;

however, this merely clarifies that while the five ranks, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and so forth differ in their progressive cultivation and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), their fundamental nature is without [distinction].

The principle of the mutual integration of the ten mysteries and six aspects—differentiation through the general and the particular, sameness and difference, and formation and disintegration—is self-evident.
These six characters represent the meaning of dependent origination; as three pairs of six characters, they encompass all phenomena:

first, the pair of the general and the particular; second, the pair of sameness and difference; third, the pair of formation and disintegration. They are fundamentally inseparable and cannot be discarded.
To retain one and reject the other is impossible; to establish both or to abandon both is likewise impossible.

All views—such as those of annihilationism and eternalism, arising and ceasing, or the extremes and the middle—are merely the limited measures of the deluded mind that fail to realize the self-nature of phenomena as dependently arisen.
This can only be understood through the power of non-conceptual, correct wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*); that which is known through conceptual thought is merely the level of faith. This is...
A Bodhisattva of the first stage observes that although all conditioned phenomena (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the world arise simultaneously, they are not reckoned as co-existent;

and although they collectively possess their individual distinctions, they all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). One cannot reckon these phenomena as being both existent and non-existent, nor as neither existent nor non-existent; the same applies to the other two pairs [of opposites].
All such things—existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, both and neither, permanence and impermanence—are merely what the mind conceives.
Just as all dependently arisen phenomena are like echoes in space— fundamentally unconditioned yet producing sound in response to objects—
and just as one skilled at divining with stalks or tortoise shells is without thought or effort, neither a ghost nor a spirit,

yet can respond to conditions to know all things and inform others of past and present good and ill fortune as clearly as looking at their own palms— one should know in this way, acting in accordance with the Dharma.

Dependent origination is not as it is conceived by the mind. Whether regarding the categories of unity and multiplicity, the general and the particular, or all modes of similarity and difference, as well as all processes of formation and disintegration—none of these can be reckoned as being prior or posterior, simultaneous, or otherwise. The same principle applies to the gateways of the *dharmadhātu*:

they are likewise neither prior nor posterior, neither existent nor non-existent, neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous, and neither ceasing nor persisting; for all such conceptions belong to the realm of mental fabrication. Thus, they are all [empty].
The nature-arising of great compassion and great unconditioned vows accords with the dependent origination of phenomena and is termed "unconditioned wisdom.
Because it is neither old nor new, the establishment of the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma and the arising and ceasing [of beings] are all unconditioned.

Thus, the understandings of coming and going as being either old or new are all due to the sovereign power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing; although they differ from those of the two vehicles, they are nonetheless [the same].
In the realization of quiescent cessation, where emotions have perished, wisdom immediately gives rise to great vows to benefit all sentient beings;

yet, while there is no thought of aspiration, one benefits beings through great kindness and great compassion without any thought of attachment. Although entering the cycle of birth and death, one does not sink into the mire;
although abiding in nirvana, one tirelessly enters and benefits the worlds of the ten directions—all of these are [the manifestations of such wisdom].

The Tathāgata’s powers of wisdom—being without intrinsic nature, without dependence, and without activity—cannot be construed through the intellectual interpretations of the past, future, or present, nor of antiquity or modernity.
Regarding the establishment of the primary teaching, there are three kinds of primary teachings: first, the primary teaching according to stages;
second, the primary teaching according to chapters; and third, the primary teaching of the great essence. First, as for the primary teaching according to stages, there are ten...
Regarding the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten transferences, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage, each has its own primary teaching (*zhengzong*).
The ten faiths take the Buddha’s fundamental unmoving wisdom as their primary teaching.

The ten abidings take the wondrous wisdom of the rational essence and the fruit-virtue of the Tathāgata—the wisdom of realizing entry into the Dharma-realm—as their primary teaching. The ten practices take the Buddha’s fundamental... [text truncated]

Taking the arousal of wisdom and the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct as the primary vehicle for cultivation, one employs the ten dedications to harmonize principle and wisdom, thereby giving rise to great vows that perfect both truth and conventionality.
This ensures that wisdom, principle, and great compassion are balanced and impartial, taking the integration of stillness and activity as the primary vehicle for the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
By accumulating the practice of compassion and wisdom, one brings this training to habitual mastery and ultimate fulfillment.

To take the "Eleventh Ground of the True Lineage" (*zhengzong*), the "Universal Worthy Conduct" (*Puxian xing*), and so forth—which flow from the sentiments of sentient beings and fill the ocean of the Dharma-realm—to serve as the primary teaching for benefiting living beings according to their capacities, constitutes the "Primary Teaching According to the Stages" (*suwei zhengzong*).

Second, regarding the individual chapters within the forty sections of this specific body of teachings, each chapter possesses its own primary teaching according to its respective title; these are collectively [designated as such].
This can be understood through three points: first, taking the general essence of the primary teaching as the orthodox tradition;

second, taking the Buddha-fruit of the One Vehicle—whose nature is the *dharmadhātu* of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom, transcending past and present, and whose essence and function are perfected—as the orthodox tradition;

and third, constantly using this orthodox tradition of the Buddha-fruit as the basis for revealing, instructing, awakening, and entering, thereby causing [the practitioner] to cultivate, habituate, and achieve mastery. Furthermore, [it is said:]...
Within the forty chapters of this sutra, the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" constitutes the primary teaching, while the remaining chapters serve as its accompaniments.

It is because the Buddhas of the ten directions take the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*— which is formed from their own minds' discernment of afflictions into all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñā*)—
as their vehicle to achieve perfect enlightenment, that these fundamental afflictions are not [the concern] of the three vehicles.

Because it is that which is to be known, the two vehicles merely suppress it so that it does not arise; however, the Bodhisattva, through the contemplation of emptiness, subdues it such that it no longer manifests.
This is explained at length in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*. All sentient beings take the gateway of the *dharmadhātu* as the means for opening, showing, awakening to, and entering [the truth];
thus, the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata is clearly revealed as being non-dual and in accord with the discriminative minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, because one possesses mastery over the *dharmadhātu*, by this principle, the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) immediately achieves perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

By means of the dharma-gates of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāma*), and the eleven stages (*ekādaśabhūmi*), one cultivates and habituates [the mind] until wisdom and compassion are perfected;
furthermore, these do not depart from the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*-wisdom of the initial mind. It is solely through this dharma that [this is accomplished].

The essence and function of the wisdom of the realms have no basis or dwelling; this gate remedies all habitual delusions. As delusions thin and wisdom becomes bright, these qualities become increasingly distinguished.
One need only employ the illumination of concentration and wisdom so that all phenomena of body and mind—both internal and external—are without dependence, without root, and without foundation.
Greed, anger, and ignorance gradually diminish, while the wisdom of the Buddhas gradually increases and clarifies, resulting in the joy of the Dharma.
Delighting in this is not craving for worldly pleasures; this is the gradual unfolding within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which has neither beginning nor end.
Fifth, as for to whom the Dharma-gate of this sutra is entrusted: the Dharma of this sutra is entrusted to ordinary beings of great resolve (*mahācitta*).

The sutra says: "The Dharma of this sutra does not enter the hands of other sentient beings. The commentary explains that "other sentient beings" refers to those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and outsiders (*bāhya*).
As for those who delight in the paths of humans and devas, or those who seek supramundane happiness—why is this?

Because this sutra does not permit even bodhisattvas of the three vehicles who possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) to give rise to faith upon hearing this sutra, let alone those of the two vehicles, humans, devas, or non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
As the sutra says: "Except for those born into the family of the Tathāgata, the true sons of the Dharma King"—that is, those of great resolve.

Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are able to give rise to faith and enter into realization, they are born into the family of the Buddha; it is not said that they have already been born into the family of the Buddha.
As for the great Bodhisattvas, they constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Ordinary beings who lack the Great Mind (the resolve for awakening) do not qualify as being entrusted with the teaching, nor do they qualify as its transmitters, because there is no one to believe and no one to realize and enter into it. Thus says the Sūtra.

If it is said that "this sutra will perish if this son does not exist," the explanation is as follows: it means that this sutra will perish if there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who believe and realize it.

If it were not so, since there are already great bodhisattvas born into the family of the Buddha who are as numerous as the atoms within the oceans of immeasurable Buddha-worlds, why would the Tathāgata need to concern himself with this?
When this sutra is about to perish, one should no longer think of the assembly of great bodhisattvas who have already been born into the Buddha-family as being those to be mindful of;
rather, one should know that ordinary beings of great resolve—who have not yet entered the ranks of the noble ones—are the ones to be mindful of.

This is because it should be known that this sutra is entrusted to ordinary beings of great resolve, as stated in the "Chapter on Manifestation. Sixth, regarding the locations where this sutra circulates: this sutra flows...
Generally, the section on the movement of the earth, the raining of flowers, and the offerings of the bodhisattvas occurs at the end of each chapter;
however, the section on the entrustment and circulation is found in the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter rather than at the very end of the sutra.
This is because this chapter constitutes the conclusion of the sutra, and it serves as the summary of the five stages of the bodhisattvas across the thirty-seven chapters.
Because this meaning concludes the section on the practice-gate of the five ranks of cause and effect, at the end of this sutra, as in the second chapter,
"Manifesting Signs," from the beginning of the sixth fascicle previously cited, the Tathāgata emits light from between his teeth,

causing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to expound upon the causes and effects of sentient beings and the causes and effects of the Tathāgata. Regarding the causes and effects of the Tathāgata, it refers to the world.
Through the retribution of his attainment, he adorns the land and emits light from between his eyebrows, causing Mañjuśrī, Bodhiruci, Bhadramukha,

and others to expound the gateway of the Ten Faiths; subsequently, from the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" through the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," he expounds the dharmas of the Ten Abidings,
the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, the Ten Grounds, the Eleventh Ground, the Ten Samādhis, and the Ten Supernatural Powers.
In the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) within the *Thirty-Six Chapters Sūtra*, there is one chapter preached in the third dhyāna;
although the extant text is incomplete, its total number is thirty-seven chapters.

Including the preceding and following sections, there are forty chapters in all, culminating in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," which marks the end of the beginning and conclusion of the causes and effects of the five stages.

Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," the method of manifestation is shown to represent the fulfillment of the causes and effects across the five stages from beginning to end;
thus, the light from between the eyebrows is poured onto the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and the light from his mouth is poured into the mouth of Samantabhadra,

so that these two— representing essence and function, cause and effect— interrogate and respond with one another, taking Mañjuśrī as the essence of the *dharmadhātu* and Samantabhadra as its function.

The two sages constitute the essence and function of the Dharma-realm; alternatively, Mañjuśrī serves as the cause and Samantabhadra as the fruit, or the two may serve as cause and fruit for one another.
Throughout this section of the scripture, these two sages are consistently used to symbolize essence and function, or cause and fruit.
This has been the case for all Buddhas of the past and present, who all rely upon these traces to clarify the principles of cause, effect, and spiritual cultivation.
Because of these benefits, the Tathāgata emits the light of fruition and the light of oral teaching from his mouth to empower these two Great Beings;

this clarifies the beginning and end of the five-stage teaching gate. The light from the mouth signifies the meaning of entrustment and the meaning of circulation, so that the practice of the teaching may circulate;
the light from the hair-tuft between the eyebrows signifies the meaning of fruition, as he emits the light of fruition to perform the entrustment.
Mañjuśrī causes Mañjuśrī to pose the questions regarding the fruit-dharma, while Samantabhadra explains the appearance of the Buddha; this constitutes the circulation [of the teaching].

Within this chapter, the entrustment and circulation are fully explained. Furthermore, through metaphors such as the prince of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) possessing the auspicious marks of a king and clearly capable of governing the royal throne, the text clarifies that it is only upon reaching this chapter that [the Buddha] is revealed as the appearance of the Tathāgata.

The "Chapter on Transcending the World" at the end of this volume is the gateway for training worldly beings through the practice of Samantabhadra’s altruism after the Buddha has realized his own fruition.
Prior to the fruition of the eleven stages, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra with both self-benefit and benefit for others;

subsequent to the fruition of the eleven stages, the conduct of Samantabhadra consists solely of benefiting others, as explained previously in the seven volumes of the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).

[Omission] Having already explained [the preceding], it is as follows: the "Chapter on the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-paṭala*) encompasses the entire body of the teaching as a whole within the gateway of the Dharma-realm.
That which is situated in the Jeta Grove clarifies that the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) is itself the Dharma-realm; that the nature of sentient beings is itself the inconceivable;
and that the discrimination of sentient beings is itself the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Thus, it clarifies [the teaching] in terms of the world of sentient beings.
Because this Dharma-realm is inconceivable.
