The thirteen and a half lines of this sutra (two hundred and twenty-six words) are divided into four sections according to their meaning: first, enumerating the number of the assembly; second, using positions to symbolize the Dharma;

third, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; and fourth, listing the numbers while praising their divine virtues. Regarding the first section, enumerating the number of the assembly:
the first line clarifies that the divine assembly is the Way, for its nature is equal to that of all Buddhas and its wisdom is identical [to theirs].
Because Truth follows the conduct of Samantabhadra and protects the world, it is called "Divine Protection" (*devatā-rakṣā*); thus, it is said that the True Dharma is protected.

Second, regarding the manifestation of the Dharma through practice: this refers to the second stage within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the Stage of Refining the Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its primary focus.
Since the meaning of "discipline" (*śīla*) is that of protection, the Dharma-body is designated as the essence of discipline; thus, it is called "True."

The Bodhisattva Vajrapūrvāmbudhicandraprabha-mahāvidyārāja, whose name means "Unbreakable," is the first among the ten stages of abiding (*daśabhūmi*), namely the stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-bhūmi*).
The meaning of this is as already explained in the preceding section. Within this assembly, there are ten divine beings.

Second is the Dharma-gate of the Stage of Purifying the Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*); its presiding deity is named Vajradhara, because his nature is that of the precepts (*śīla*) for the purpose of protection.

As for the "Rigid Deity" (Kangshen), that which grasps and maintains [the precepts] without transgression is called "Grasping" (Zhi); its wisdom corresponding to the ultimate truth is designated as "Deity" (Shen).
Regarding the three explanations of these names and their correlation with practice: this assembly of deities takes the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) as its essence.
The names of the ten deities are precisely the names of the ten *pāramitās* that correspond to the substance of the precepts; each deity represents one [of these].
This is the Dāna-pāramitā gate within the Śīla-pāramitā of the Vajrapāṇi deity Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the foremost and most wondrous form of the one-practice.
Because he accomplishes dāna through natural precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) and thereby invokes a wondrous form, and because the dharma-emptiness destroys delusion, he is named Nārāyaṇa;
this signifies the meaning of indestructibility. This stage clarifies that by upholding the natural precepts, one attains [this state].
"Destroyer of the attachment to the body" means the meaning of being indestructible; "Vajra-holder" means the meaning of being unbreakable.

The second [deity], the Vajra-holding God of the Swift Banner, takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)—the primary nature of discipline and its intermediate forms—as his essence. Because his light of discipline is without flaw, he is named the Sun-Disk (*sūryamaṇḍala*).
One who sees him is a worthy one (*arhat*). Because his own and others' delusions are exhausted, he is called the "Swift Banner."
Having no divergent thoughts in the mind is called "holding" (*dhṛti*); being indestructible is termed "vajra"; being truly sovereign is termed "divine" (*deva*).
Because wisdom constitutes divinity, he is the Vajradhara Deva of the Flower-Light of the Three Sumerus;

he presides over the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) and the *kṣānti-pāramitā* (perfection of patience). As for the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*), his name is the Exalted Sumeru.
Because they adorn practitioners with patience, all who see them rejoice; they are called "Flower. Because observing this breaks down arrogance, they are called "Light.
Because their patient mind never falters, it is named "Grasping the Dharma-nature. Because their patience is like a vajra, their wisdom knows all phenomena without conceptual thought;
they are called "Divine. They are the Lord of the Four Pure Cloud-Sounds Vajra-Holders.
Within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) treads upon the conventional while remaining eternally true; this is called "Purity.

To expound the Dharma without weariness and to moisten all sentient beings is termed "Cloud-Sound" (*megha-svara*). Hearing the Dharma and shattering delusions is named "Vajra-Wisdom" (*vajra-jñāna*).
To know all phenomena without acting is designated as "Divine" (*divya*). The five sense faculties are exquisite, and he holds the Vajra.
Within the divine lord’s perfection of precepts (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) constitutes meditative concentration without thought.

Because the six sense faculties function in accordance with wisdom, it is called "the exquisite refinement of the faculties. Because they function while remaining eternally quiescent, it is termed "grasping without thought.
Because this state can be broken through, it is designated as "vajra. Furthermore, because this wisdom of non-thought can destroy the delusions of both self and others, it is called "gold."

1. The Vajra of Steadfast Tranquility: His wisdom is immovable, and his correct insight functions accordingly; he is thus designated as a "spiritual power" (*śakti*). 2. The Vajra of the Radiance of the Six Objects of Delight:
He is the lord of wisdom, for he is able to destroy darkness. 3. The Vajra of the Thunderous Sound of the Great Tree: He presides over the seventh gate of great compassion.
"Tree" signifies the sense of providing shelter and shade; he clarifies the gateway of the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*) to provide shelter and shade for sentient beings.
Thus, the eighth, Lion-King Radiance, is the master of the perfection of aspiration;

he gives rise to effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) and possesses mastery like a lion king, for he is able to shatter the various heterodox arguments of non-Buddhists. The ninth, Honey-Flame Victorious Eye, is the master of the perfection of power;
through the mastery of the Dharma, he flows secretly in accordance with others’ activities, sometimes appearing as a heterodox teacher of false doctrines.
Because one breaks through what binds them by means of "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*), this stage is the position of the Great Dharma Master.
Generally, among the five sets of five hundred *pāramitā* gates within the nine *pāramitās*, the ninth in each is the position of the Dharma Master.
The ninth of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra*), such as the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of Sudhana in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.

In the ninth stage of the Dharma Master within the [Avataṃsaka] Sūtra, he manifests as the Brahmin Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, entering among the non-Buddhists by performing such acts as the "five heats" (*pañcatapana*), climbing the mountain of blades, and entering the mass of fire. This is called the "Secret Flame" (*Guhyajvāla*);

because he employs the same activities as others while remaining hidden, he establishes teachings to shatter ignorance, hence it is named "Secret Flame. Because he knows the faculties of beings, it is named "Victorious Eye" (*Jitākṣa*). (The tenth is the Lotus Stage.)
The Vajradhara deity named Flower-Light Maṇi-Bun presides over the perfection of wisdom within the perfection of ethical discipline.

He is like the spiritual friend known as the Girl named Compassionate Conduct, encountered by Sudhana during his tenth stage, the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), who attained true realization without actualizing [nirvana] while remaining in the secular world; she was untainted and named Lotus of Great Wisdom, who knew the faculties [of beings].
This is named the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). Ascending to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), it is called the Maṇi-Topknot (*maṇicūḍa*). "Maṇi" here translates as the "Stainless Jewel.
This is the second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground (*caryā-viśodhana-vihāra*). Within this, there are the ten dwellings and the ten *pāramitās* with their primary and attendant practices;
these ten dwellings, with their primary and attendant myriad practices, are designated as the ten Vajradharas, whose names are all derived from their respective stages of practice.

The reason for establishing these names is to clarify that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each single stage contains ten; thus, each stage contains one hundred [sub-stages], and this applies to all five positions.
They are sequentially assigned according to their names and meanings, and the correspondence with the Dharma is exactly as it should be.

Regarding the fourth [stage], from the passage "possessing Buddha-fields" onwards, there are seven lines of sūtra text that enumerate and praise its virtues through two gates, as can be understood from the text itself.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were body-retinue spirits as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world, namely: the Body-Retinue Spirits Adorned with Flower Topknots; the Body-Retinue Spirits Illuminating the Ten Directions;
the Body-Retinue Spirits Subduing with Oceanic Sounds; the Body-Retinue Spirits with Pure Flower-Adorned Topknots;
the Body-Retinue Spirits of Immeasurable Dignified Manner; the Body-Retinue Spirits Adorned with Supreme Light; and the Body-Retinue Spirits of Pure Light and Fragrant Clouds.
The deities of the body-guarding host, the deities of the body-universal-manifestation-gathering host,
the deities of the body-immovable-light host— these and others were their leaders; they were as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world,
all of whom had in the past fulfilled great vows and had made offerings to and served all Buddhas.
[Treatise] The third [stage], the Stage of Practice (*caryā-pratipatti*) among the Ten Stages (*daśa-vihāra*), consists of six and a half lines of scripture (one hundred and thirteen words).
Its meaning is divided into four parts: 1. Enumeration; 2. Assigning stages to manifest the Dharma; 3. Explaining the names and correlating them with practice; 4.
Reaffirming the number and praising its spiritual virtues. First, regarding the enumeration: as mentioned above, this is the second [stage]. Regarding the assignment of stages...

Regarding the "positions that symbolize the dharmas": these ten groups of body-deities (kāya-devatās) take up positions to symbolize the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Because they achieve the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*), they exercise mastery in benefiting sentient beings amidst birth and death; thus, they are called "deities" (*devatā*).
In the subsequent section on the praise of their virtues, it is clarified that they have fulfilled great vows and are skilled in making offerings to and serving all Buddhas throughout the past.
In the past, by means of a mind of harmonious patience, you served all sentient beings, causing them to attain Buddhahood;
because the essence of the Buddhas and sentient beings is non-dual, you have already become all Buddhas. Why, then, would you need to rely upon their offerings?
With infinite bodies and infinite multitudes of offerings, you serve and make offerings to all sentient beings at all times.

To cause them to attain Buddhahood is the meaning of "harmonious patience" (調忍) and the meaning of the "multitude of bodies" (身眾). This third explanation of the names correlates them with the practitioner:
these ten deities are the ten *pāramitās* within the *kṣānti-pāramitā*; thus, it clarifies that each individual practice pervades all practices.
The first is the Deity of the Multitude of Bodies Adorned with Flower Topknots (*Puṣpakūṭa-śobhana-kāyagaṇa-devatā*), who presides over patience (*kṣānti*).
Within the *pāramitās*, this is the gate of the *dāna-pāramitā*. It clarifies that patience (*kṣānti*) serves as the flower-crest;
by receiving this as its retribution, it adorns the ornament upon the crown of the head. Thus, "the multitude of bodies" refers to practicing *dāna* within the stage of patience.

It clarifies that with a multitude of clouds of bodies and a multitude of ornaments, one pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* to serve, make offerings to, and extensively benefit sentient beings. Therefore, it is called "divine."
Because this wisdom follows the practice of patience with mastery, it is termed "divine" (*śubha*). These ten *pāramitās* take patience as their essence.
Regarding the two lights illuminating the ten directions and the body of the various deities: these deities preside over the *śīla-pāramitā* within the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

In this stage, the essence of the precepts is the patience toward the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*). It is clarified that when patience and the precepts are perfectly luminous, those who behold them rejoice.
The deity named *Dharmaprītidhṛtikṣāntiprabha* (Light of the Patience of Joy in the Dharma) is called "Illuminating the Ten Directions.

As explained previously regarding the deities of the body-mass, the deity who subdues the body-mass through the sound of the three oceans (*Trisamudra-ghoṣa*) presides over the patience within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Thus, the one named Ocean-Sound (*Samudra-ghoṣa*) hears the sounds of all good and evil, praise and blame, as vast and numerous as the tides of the ocean.
That sounds do not give rise to sorrow or joy is the meaning of "subduing"; this constitutes "patience.

Furthermore, because one’s own voice is like the sound of the ocean tide, knowing the proper time to teach and transform sentient beings so that no opportunity is lost, [the goddesses] adorn their hair-knots with four kinds of pure flowers.
These are the deities presiding over the perfection of diligence within the perfection of patience, for they advance through the patience of the Dharma.
It is called "Pure" because its progressive practice is worthy of observation; it is called "Flower" because its causal practice invites the fruit to adorn the topknot.

This clarifies that diligence is the foremost of the long path; therefore, it uses flowers to adorn the crown. Regarding the five immeasurables, the majestic deportment, the body, and the various spirit-lords:
within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) manifests according to the faculties.

The Dharma is named the "Immeasurable," for its movements and stillness are eternally quiescent; this is called "Dignified Bearing" (*īryāpatha*). Walking, standing, sitting, and reclining never depart from the essence of meditative concentration;
this is called "Dignified Bearing. Sixth, the Supreme Radiance Adorning the Body: the various deities preside over wisdom, which illuminates both self and others;
thus, with the light of concentration and wisdom, they shine upon the mind and its objects to adorn the Dharma-body. Seventh.

The seventh assembly of deities is named Pure Radiance Fragrant Clouds. Their bodies are manifestations of spiritual brilliance, and they employ the skillful means of great compassion, being unrestrained by either defilement or purity.

They are called Pure Radiance because their compassionate embrace covers all beings; they are called Fragrant Clouds because their speech accords with the Dharma and delights the hearts of the multitude.
They are known as Luminous Rain because the rain of their precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation moistens all sentient beings.
This is the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcāṅga-dharmakāya). Regarding the eighth [point], the various deities who guard and sustain the body possess brilliant wisdom;

because they sustain all sentient beings in accordance with their great vows, one dwells in the eight stages (bhūmi) through these five positions. Within the eighth position, the wisdom of effortlessness (anābhoga-jñāna) is clarified;
once this effort is perfected, one receives the empowerment upon the crown of the head (abhiṣeka) by the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions. These...

Because the Buddha sustains and upholds all meanings, he attains the ninth power—the perfection of the Dharma-power of the Sovereign of Dharma—which universally manifests as the body that gathers and encompasses all spiritual deities.

It is called "universally manifesting and gathering" because he universally manifests among all ninety-six kinds of heterodox currents and all sentient beings, acting in identical conduct with them; this refers to the case of Jvalanāmukha.
The Brahmins and others constitute the assembly of deities of the ten immovable luminous bodies.
The tenth perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) is named "Immovable Light" (*acala-prabhā*), and it is also called the "Immovable Light" (*acala-prabha*) in the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Furthermore, within this stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one of the ten perfections is clarified; the final four numerical summaries and the praise of its virtues are as can be understood from the text.
The ten pāramitās mentioned above take patience as their essence; this clarifies that one attains the wisdom of immovability when faced with good or evil, and with slander or praise.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there are foot-walking goddesses (pādavikṣepa-devīs) as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world, namely, the foot-walking goddess named Ratnamudrāhastā.

The footstep-moving spirit Lotus-Radiance, the footstep-moving spirit Pure Flower Topknot, the footstep-moving spirit Gathering All Who See Well, the footstep-moving spirit Wondrous Jewel Star Banner,
the footstep-moving spirit Delighting in Uttering Wondrous Sounds, the footstep-moving spirit Sandalwood Tree Radiance, the footstep-moving spirit Lotus Light,
the footstep-moving spirit Subtle and Wondrous Radiance, and the footstep-moving spirit Accumulated Wondrous Flowers.

Caryādevī was the foremost among them; numbering as many as the atoms in a Buddha-world, they had all, throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, attended upon and followed the Tathāgatas without ever abandoning them.
[Treatise] In the fourth section, there are six and a half lines of sūtra (one hundred and eleven words), the meaning of which is divided into four parts:

first, listing the number of the assembly; second, using positions to symbolize the Dharma; third, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; and fourth, concluding the count and praising their virtues.
Regarding the first, listing the number of the assembly: as in the first line, the total number is enumerated. Second, using positions to symbolize the Dharma: these ten...
The "Divinity of Sufficient Practice" represents the stage of "Noble Birth" (*janmaja*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), where the primary quality is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
As stated in the subsequent section on praising virtues, the meaning of this vigor is that throughout immeasurable kalpas, one draws near to the Tathāgata and follows him without abandoning him.
To clarify that the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) serves as the essence of this practice, one employs these dharmic practices to adorn the Dharma.
The term "Kramapracāra" (Foot-Traveler) expresses the meaning of diligent exertion; because he is fully endowed with all practices, he is named the Kramapracāra Deva.
"Deva" refers to the wisdom that follows these practices. This is the first explanation of the name, which correlates it with the practitioner.
The Kramapracāra Deva, Jewel-Seal Hand and Foot, presides over the gate of the *dāna-pāramitā* within the *vīrya-pāramitā*, clarifying the seal of the wisdom of the Dharma-jewel.
Because they practice the conduct of diligence to attract and guide sentient beings, their hands signify the meaning of "drawing forth.

As for the foot-attendant spirit Lotus Light, it clarifies that within the stage of "Birth in a Noble Lineage" and the perfection of vigor, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is such that one constantly dwells in the ocean of birth and death like a lotus flower, unsullied by it; thus, those who see them give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
She is named Kramitāloka (Light-Step). This signifies the meaning of practicing diligence without weariness;
because her wisdom is sovereign, she is titled a "Divine One" (*devī*). She is the foot-step goddess of the Threefold Pure Flower Topknot (*Tripariśuddha-puṣpa-keśa*).

Regarding "diligence," within the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the stainlessness of the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*) is called "pure. Patience brings about its corresponding fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), which is the *Avataṃsaka*.
The crown ornament signifies the meaning of patience as a flower garland. The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) signify the feet;
the deity presiding over the practice of the perfections is diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Within the perfection of diligence, the inclusion of all views is the meaning of diligence.
To constantly restrain the sense faculties so that views do not arise is the absence of unwholesome views; this is the fifth wondrous jewel, the Star Banner Foot (*pañca-ratna-tārakadhvaja-pāda*).
The practice of the deity presiding over the Dhyāna-pāramitā gate takes sublime principle as its meditation; therefore, it is called the "Sublime Jewel. "Jewel" (ratna) refers to the Way.
Because one knows delusion through the practice, it is named the "Star Banner" (Tārakadhvaja). The myriad practices are like stars;

because they do not depart from the essence of dhyāna and all possess illumination, and because one knows the faculties clearly to destroy delusion according to those faculties, it is termed a "star. This is the stage.

Taking diligence as the essence of dhyāna, and through dhyāna being able to manifest wisdom, one is able to know phenomena; because one returns to the skillful knowledge of phenomena, it is called a "star.
The banner represents concentration. Regarding the six joys of emitting sublime sounds, the feet and the walking deity preside over the perfection of wisdom.
As for "joyfully emitting sublime sounds," it means that because diligence constitutes the essence of wisdom, one always delights in it.
Because he preaches the Dharma for the sake of others, the footstep-following spirit Seven Sandalwood Trees is the master of the seventh perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
Because he accomplishes the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he is named after fragrant trees to signify the meaning of compassionate shelter and protection.
"Light" signifies the meaning of illuminating and guiding sentient beings. The footstep-following spirit Eight Lotus Light is the master of wisdom (*prajñā*).
9. The station of the Dharma King of the Sovereign Power of the Practice of Subtle Radiance, because great vows benefit sentient beings without being defiled;
10. The station of the Sovereign Power of the Practice of Accumulating Exquisite Flowers, because one accumulates all teachings through wisdom, just as flowers are strung together.

"Binding the garland so it does not scatter" refers to the teaching and transformation of sentient beings. The ten *pāramitās* mentioned above all take the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor) as their essential substance;
within each stage, there are both common and specific meanings, which can be understood by reflecting upon them—they must not be treated with a one-size-fits-all standard.
The fourfold enumeration and the praise of virtues are to be understood according to the text.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within a buddha-world who were maṇḍala-deities,
namely: the maṇḍala-deity Pure Adornment Banner, the maṇḍala-deity Sumeru Jewel Light, the maṇḍala-deity Thunder Sound Banner Mark,
the maṇḍala-deity Rain of Flowers Sublime Eye, the maṇḍala-deity Flower Garland Radiant Topknot, the maṇḍala-deity Rain of Jewel Adornments, and the maṇḍala-deity Courageous Fragrant Eye.
The Dharma-site deity Vajra-Colored Clouds, the Dharma-site deity Lotus Radiance, the Dharma-site deity Sublime Illumination,
and others such as these were their leaders; numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-world,
they had all encountered immeasurable Buddhas in the past and fulfilled their vows by extensively making offerings.
[Treatise] The fifth section consists of six and a half lines of scripture (one hundred thirteen words). Its meaning is divided into four parts: first, enumerating the number of the assembly;
second, using a specific position to symbolize the Dharma; third, explaining the names and correlating them with the Dharma; fourth, concluding with the enumeration and praising their virtues.

First, regarding the enumeration of the assembly: as stated above, this is the first line. Second, regarding using a position to symbolize the Dharma: this particular position symbolizes completeness.
In the stage of Abiding in Skillful Means (*upāya-sthiti*), the ten *pāramitās* have the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as their essence.

This clarifies that the "field" (*kṣetra*) refers to the meaning of removing the impurities of the aggregates (*skandha-kalaṅka*); because it is explained that *dhyāna* can treat the aggregates, it is like a worldly field.

Furthermore, this clarifies that through the purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the defiled grasping of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses is purified, thereby manifesting *prajñā*, which opens up sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) for the discernment of principles.

Because it is the fundamental reality of the essence of wisdom, it takes the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as its field and substance, the *prajñā-pāramitā* as its human effort, and the myriad practices of Samantabhadra as the vehicle for transport.

It reaches the Palace of Universal Radiance Wisdom within the Dharma-realm as its great capital residence, and takes all manner of various wisdoms as its great treasury. Within this, there are ten [aspects].
Regarding the deities: one deity represents one *pāramitā* as a mode of benefiting oneself and benefiting others. Third, the explanation of names and their correspondence to the dharmas:
the first is the Dharma-Field Deity Pure Adornment Banner (*Vimala-vyūha-dhvaja-kṣetra-devatā*).

She primarily possesses skillful means and dwells within the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, yet through the gateway of the *dāna-pāramitā*, she takes the essence of the concentration of *dharmatā* as her giving; thus, she is named "Pure."
Furthermore, because the essence of concentration (*samādhi*) is without deficiency, the myriad practices are its banner of adornment;
"banner" signifies the meaning of the immovability of the essence of concentration. Taking the naturelessness of the *dharmatā* as that which is mounted upon, it is called the "Path.

Because the meditative concentration of naturelessness can cure the aggregates (*skandhas*) that serve as its basis, it is called the "Field. "Spirit" (*shen*) refers to that which exists within the state of non-reliance and naturelessness.
Great wisdom is that which, through non-conceptualization and non-action, and being formless and without substance, knows all phenomena as they are coextensive with the Dharma-realm;
this is what is called "spiritual power" (*śakti*). Second is the Way-Place Spirit of the Jewel Light of Mount Sumeru.

Because "Mount Sumeru" signifies loftiness and eminence, and "Jewel Light" signifies stainlessness, and because one causes those who see the mundane world to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment by means of the light of the precepts, [he is so named].
Dhyāna-samādhi transcends emotional consciousness through the observance of precepts; this is the meaning of "Sumeru. Because samādhi is free from delusion, it is the meaning of "stainless.

Because samādhi can give rise to the radiant light of the jewel of wisdom, it is the meaning of "thunder. The presiding deity of the site of enlightenment, Trailokya-ghoṣa-dhvaja-lakṣaṇa, presides over the perfection of dhyāna within the perfection of patience.
She clarifies that the sounds of praise and blame are like thunder, and thus one possesses the patience of the Dharma.
The Dharma-protector of the Bodhimanda named Moving Banner Mark is explained as before; because each of the ten pāramitās possesses its own respective bodhimanda ritual within the five stages.
The Dharma-protector of the Bodhimanda named Flower-Rain Wondrous Eye presides over the pāramitā of vigor within the pāramitā of dhyāna;
she clarifies that the Dharma-body is the essence of samādhi, and that the myriad practices arise based upon the essence of samādhi.
Vigor is called "Raining Flowers," which is the meaning of vigor; because it is certain to give rise to wisdom, it is called "Sublime Eye.

Because one practices with the Dharma-eye to benefit sentient beings through flowers without weariness, this is vigor. The five-flower garland of radiant hair is the presiding deity of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) who presides over the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Within the perfection of meditation, the perfection of meditation consists in the fact that the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu* is immovable.

Arising from stillness, one practices meditative cultivation to transform all distracted thoughts; this is called the "Flower Garland. Because concentration can give rise to wisdom, it is named "Light.
Because practice invites its fruit to adorn the crown of the head, it is given this name. Furthermore, these ten pāramitās are all "Crown Dharmas" (mūrdha-dharma). Why is this so?
It is because at the initial moment of the first stage of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi), [one attains them].
Because one proceeds from the Gate once and forth to the fruit of Buddhahood, there is no beginning, middle, or end;

because one initiates superior progress from the fruit of Buddhahood, [this is] the sixth, the Goddess of the Bodhimanda Adorned with Rain of Jewels, whose presiding perfection is Prajñāpāramitā, for wisdom can rain down the jewels of the Dharma.
The seventh is the Goddess of the Bodhimanda Fragrant Eye of Valor, whose presiding perfection is Upāyapāramitā; this stage is that of Maitrī (loving-kindness).

Because he dwells perpetually in birth and death out of compassion, he is named "The Valiant. Because he gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of loving-kindness, he is named "Fragrant Eyes" (*Gandhākṣa*);

because he views sentient beings with the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body—consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—and thereby uproots suffering and bestows happiness, he is thus called "Fragrant Eyes. [He is] the divine being of the Eight Vajra-Colored Cloud *Mārga-dhātu*.
The eighth is the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), which acts as a cloud of aspirations to cover all sentient beings;
because this stage possesses effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) capable of destroying heterodox currents, it is called the "Vajra-Variegated Cloud.
The ninth is the Lotus Radiance Bodhimanda Lord, whose power is the perfection of strength (*bala-pāramitā*); this is the station of the Dharma King.
The world is like a lotus flower; he preaches the Dharma as its radiance. Thus, the ten wondrous lights illuminate the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

The presiding deity of this stage is Wisdom-Pāramitā. Because one knows the faculties [of beings] through great wisdom, it is named "Wondrous Light. Because knowing the faculties destroys delusions, it is called "Illumination.
The above ten pāramitās all have the dhyāna-pāramitā as their essence. (Four points conclude the enumeration and praise.)
Their virtues may be understood from the text.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were city-ruling goddesses as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world, namely:

the City-Ruling Goddess Jewel-Peak Radiance, the City-Ruling Goddess Exquisite Adornment of Palaces, the City-Ruling Goddess Pure Joyful Jewels, and the City-Ruling Goddess Freedom from Sorrow and Purity.
The city goddess Flower Lamp Flame Eye, the city goddess Manifesting the Banner of Flames,
the city goddess Abundant Merit Radiance, the city goddess Pure Radiance, the city goddess Fragrant Topknot Adornment,
the city goddess Wondrous Jewel Radiance, and others such as these, numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-world, all [stood] there.
The palace where the Tathāgata Immeasurable-Inconceivable-Aeon-Adorned-Pure resides.
[Treatise] The sixth stage, the Abode of Right Mind, has the Perfection of Wisdom as its essence;
ten city-guardian deities preside over this Perfection of Wisdom, wherein are contained ten perfections. Within this, there are six and a half lines of scripture.

(One hundred and thirteen words) The meaning is divided into four parts: first, enumerating the number of the assembly; second, using their positions to symbolize the Dharma; third, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; fourth, concluding the enumeration and praising their virtues.
1. Enumerating the number of the assembly: As in the first practice, this is the [initial] group. 2. Using their positions to symbolize the Dharma:

By means of these divine hosts, they symbolize the "Abiding in the Right Mind," wherein the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness is manifested, clearly showing the skillful guarding of the mind.
The city is named Rectitude of Mind (*Saddharmacitta*). It is like the sixth spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the youth Sudhana.
He dwells in silent stillness at the side of the path of practice; when mindfulness is established, he sits upright and motionless.

As his inhalations and exhalations cease, he emerges from the navel of an asura with knees extended, manifests a celestial body, and from the crown of his head, he issues forth all Buddhas and the like.

With vast clouds of bodies pervading the entire Dharma-realm, they teach and transform sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding the stage of the Right-Minded Abode (*samyaktva-citta-vihāra*) within the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), the *Sūtra* states:
"When this Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, his mind remains fixed and unmoving.

This clarifies the Right-Minded Abode, as it involves skillfully guarding the city of the mind; thus, the City-Ruling Deity (*puram-dhara-devatā*) is employed as a metaphorical representation of this stage of Right Mind.

Third, the explanation of the name in relation to the practice: The presiding deity of the city, Jewel Peak Radiance (*Ratnaśikharaprabhā*), presides over the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
She is named Jewel Peak Radiance because she extensively bestows [benefits] upon all sentient beings through the wondrous wisdom of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
her radiance extends as far as the peaks of mountains until it reaches the limit where all characteristics of space (*ākāśa*) are exhausted. Thus is she explained.
Because the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena reaches the limit where all marks are exhausted, one employs the wondrous wisdom of signlessness to extensively bestow it upon sentient beings;
thus, one is named the "Lord of Illumination. Because one possesses mastery over the wisdom of emptiness, one is called the "Lord of the City.

Because one possesses mastery over both emptiness and existence, and does not conjoin with nor separate from nirvana and saṃsāra, it is called a "city. Furthermore, because one bestows the wisdom of phenomena upon others—
Because it is joined with the outflows of sensual desire, it is called a city. The primary deity of this city is the Palace of Sublime Adornment.

Taking wisdom as the means to benefit sentient beings, it takes the precepts as its essential body; taking sublime wisdom as the palace and the governance of people as the hall, it uses the myriad practices as adornments.
Furthermore, it takes the correct wisdom of the Bodhisattvas as the sublime adornment and great loving-kindness and great compassion as the palace.
The palace has no discursive thought as its sovereign; the wondrous wisdom of signlessness governs principle and reality, and thus it is known as "divine.
Here, sharp wisdom serves as the sovereign, and precepts serve as the protection. To protect all sentient beings is the meaning of the city.
The Lord of the City of the Treasure of Pure Joy presides over the perfection of wisdom within the perfection of patience.
The *Pāramitā* clarifies that because one achieves patience (*kṣānti*) through the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), it is called "pure joy" (*viśuddhaprīti*);
since patience is itself joy, and since the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*) is itself named a "jewel" (*ratna*), it clarifies that the ability to endure is a jewel.
From this point downward, the four assemblies of deities are to be assigned their positions according to the preceding pattern. As the scriptural text is vast, it cannot be explained item by item.
To summarize the principle: although there are lords of the mandala, lords of the city, and lords of the earth, they are all female deities.
Because they manifest compassion, in their true essence they are neither male nor female; they merely appear according to circumstances.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were earth-deity kings as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world, namely: the Earth-deity King Universal Virtue Pure Flower,
the Earth-deity King Firm Merit Adornment, the Earth-deity King Exquisite Flower Adorned Tree, the Earth-deity King Universally Scattering All Jewels,
the Earth-deity King Pure Eyes Observing the Seasons, the Earth-deity King Exquisite Color Supreme Eye, and the Earth-deity King Fragrant Hair Emitting Light.
The Earth-Ruling Goddess Pleasing Sound, the Earth-Ruling Goddess Wondrous Flower Swirling Topknot,
the Earth-Ruling Goddess Vajra-Adorned Body, and others such as these were the leaders; they were as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-world,
all of whom had in the past made profound and solemn vows to always draw near to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and to cultivate meritorious deeds together with them.
[Treatise] The seventh is the Sovereign Earth Deity (comprising seven lines and one hundred and seventeen words).

Because she presides over the ten *pāramitās* within the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), which is the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*), each of these is assigned ten divine names.

Here, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) serves as the substance of the earth, capable of generating all myriad practices; its divine nature consists of wisdom, principle, compassion, and loving-kindness, being without limit.
Because they retreat from movement, their great compassion is like the earth, nourishing all things.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable mountain deities, namely: the Mountain Deity Jewel-Peak Blooming-Flower; the Mountain Deity Flower-Forest Wondrous-Crest;
the Mountain Deity High-Banner Universal-Illumination; the Mountain Deity Dust-Free Pure-Crest; and the Mountain Deity Light-Radiance.
The mountain deities presiding over the ten directions— namely, the Mountain Deity Great Power Radiance, the Mountain Deity Universal Victory of Majestic Light,
the Mountain Deity Subtle and Secret Light-Wheel, the Mountain Deity Universal Eye Manifest Vision, and the Mountain Deity Vajra Secret Eye—
headed by these and others, were immeasurable in number; they had all attained the pure eye regarding all phenomena.

[Treatise] The eighth presiding mountain deity (six lines of scripture, ninety-eight words): This refers to the mountain of the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of vows and practices during the stage of the Youthful (kumārabhūmi).
"Immovable" signifies the meaning of loftiness and supremacy; "deity" signifies the essence of wisdom, the realization of truth, and sovereign clarity.
This summarizes the eighth stage, the eighth practice, the eighth dedication, and the eighth ground as being entirely effortless (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Because this wisdom is immovable like a mountain, it is symbolized by the mountain deities;
the ten deities therein represent the ten pāramitās of this stage, which are also called "wisdom" because they transcend the world and are as lofty and supreme as a mountain.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were an inconceivable number of forest-dwelling spirits (*vanavasin*), namely: the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Spreading Flowers Like Clouds;
the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Raising Stems and Radiating Light; the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Producing Sprouts and Emitting Splendor;

the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Auspicious Pure Master; the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Hanging Canopy of Flame-Treasury; the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Pure Radiance; and the Forest-Dwelling Spirit named Pleasing Thunder-Sound.
The forest deity Light and Fragrance Pervading, the forest deity Wondrous Light Shining Backward, the forest deity Flavor of Flower-Fruit Light,
and others such as these were the leaders; they were inconceivable in number, and each possessed immeasurable, lovely radiance.
[Treatise] The ninth, the Lord of the Forest Deity (six lines of sutra text, one hundred and eleven characters):

This is the rank of the Dharma Master, who dwells in the power of the Bodhisattva and practices the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), expounding the Dharma like a vast forest that provides abundant shade and protection.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable medicinal goddesses, namely: the medicinal goddess Śrīpati,
the medicinal goddess Candanavana, the medicinal goddess Vimalaprabhā, the medicinal goddess Viśrutayaśas, the medicinal goddess Romaprabhā,
the medicinal goddess Samantaviśuddhi, the medicinal goddess Mahānādābhinirghoṣa, and the medicinal goddess Sūryābhibhava-dhvaja.
The Lord Medicine King Spirit beholds the ten directions; the Medicine-Benefiting Vitality and Clarifying the Eyes Spirit;
with such spirits as these as their leaders, they are immeasurable in number, and their nature is free from defilement, benevolent and compassionate, protecting and aiding all beings.
[Treatise] The tenth, the Yakṣa Lord of Medicines (comprising five lines and ninety-five characters of scripture), clarifies the wisdom-pāramitā of the Lord of the Abode of Consecration.
Among the ten yakṣa lords of the wisdom-pāramitās, this section elucidates the wisdom that is able to know the faculties [of beings] and the medicinal dharmas;
the fourth praise of its virtues may be understood according to the text.

The above section, from the Bodhisattva Sāgaramanoratha-prabhāsa-mahāvyūha up to this Medicine King Goddess, concludes the hundred *pāramitās* within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of wisdom among the five ranks of the Tathāgata’s assembly. The multitude of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) should be understood as follows:
one must know that all the arrangements in this entire scripture are, in their totality, Dharma-gates; they are by no means in vain.

Since every single matter and every single word constitutes the method for entering through faith, cultivation, and awakening within the five stages, they serve as the gateways to the expedient means for entering the Dharma.
This clarifies the manner in which the fruit of Buddhahood enters the Dharma, benefits others, and provides universal protection;

thus, those who enter it are said to have their nascent [nature] merged with wisdom, which is termed "spirit" (*shen*), and by this they also provide universal protection and nourishment for all beings.
Because they are born [as such], they are blessed by the divine to benefit all beings;

because they dwell in mastery through their practice, they are like devas, and because they transform and benefit the various devas, they manifest the reception of celestial retribution throughout the ten directions and the three realms.
Furthermore, through the gate of dedication, they take on forms similar to asuras and enter the various ghost realms, thereby manifesting sovereignty like that of a king.
