Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Commentary on the Scripture of the Array of the World-Ruling Lords*, Fascicle One, Part Five. [Commentary:
The third section, from the Deity of Agricultural Cultivation down to the Deity of Day, comprises these ten groups of divine beings.

Regarding the cause and effect of the practice of the Dharma-gate for benefiting sentient beings, the deity who presides over crops serves as the symbol, because these practices serve as the provisions for growth.
Just as in the world one uses grain crops as provisions to nourish the conditioned body, so too in the Buddha-dharma,
one uses the practice of the ten *pāramitās* as provisions to nourish the *dharmakāya*, thereby gradually eliminating worldly habitual tendencies.

Subtly transcending worldly habitual tendencies, having accomplished great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great wisdom—just as explained in the stage of provisioning (*sambhāra-avasthā*) according to the Three Vehicles, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute the four types of provisioning prior to the Path;

from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward constitutes the preparatory practice for the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). For Bodhisattvas prior to the grounds of the Three Vehicles, this requires one great *kalpa*.
Having cultivated conditioned and out-flowing practices throughout *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one realizes the Path of Seeing at the first stage (*bhūmi*).

As described in this sutra, throughout the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one fully believes that the nature and characteristics of one’s own mind are non-different from the great wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

At the initial moment of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), by the power of cultivating the Samādhi of Skillful Means, one sees the Path; this begins from the Abode of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*) and extends upward.

The various stages of abiding (*vihāra*) are collectively designated as the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). The ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are collectively designated as the stage of application (*prayoga*) and the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*).
This is because the equipment and application advance together with the cause of Buddhahood;

they are called "application" because they are equal to the fruit of Buddhahood, and they are called "equipment" because they utilize the conduct of Samantabhadra to bring the fulfillment of compassionate vows to completion, beginning from the first of the ten abidings.

The dharmakāya realized by the mind, its nature of wisdom and principle, the fruit, the provisions, and the conduct of Samantabhadra do not belong to the conditioned and impermanent realms of humans or devas.

From the initial generation of the bodhicitta, one progresses through the five stages of cultivation toward the fruit of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya—the nature of wisdom and principle—and the fruit of the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Within the single true dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*), these elements serve as mutual provisions for one another, transcending the duality of "one" and "two."

Since neither is established as such, it is simply that a single defiled mind and a single pure mind arise; therefore, one adorns practice with the fruit of the Buddha’s wisdom and insight, and adorns the fruit with practice.

Thus, it is called the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* (The Flower Ornament of the Buddha). Consequently, throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) that follow, all the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow upon the Bodhisattvas entering these stages names identical to their own.
The "conferment of empowerment by touching the crown of the head with wisdom" refers to the wisdom that is identical in essence [to the Buddha].

While Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles are mostly reborn in the pure lands of other directions, and there are distinct Bodhisattva pure lands above the Four Dhyānas, even if such a land were situated within the Desire Realm, it would be said that they remain there to moisten their births through the power of compassionate vows while retaining their afflictions (*kleśa*). This is not the case for the dharma-gate of this sutra, which rides upon the Tathāgata’s *dharmadhātu*.

From the initial stage of generating the bodhicitta, one mounts [this vehicle] by means of the fruit of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom-dharmakāya-nature and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct, which universally pervades birth-and-death and stillness, unifying principle and phenomena, and advancing universally through the functional application of the dharma-realm body.

Because this treats residual habits and because phenomena have no prior or subsequent sequence, attachments to "new" and so forth do not exist; thus it is not like the separate teachings of the three vehicles, which speak of other directions.

There is another pure land; the "retention of delusions" refers to the *sāṃbhava* (this Sahā world). The preparatory practice (*prayoga*) occurs at the very beginning of the first stage (*bhūmi*), while the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) pertain to the five stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences. Since there is no fruit of Buddhahood within these [five] stages, it is clear that the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the ten stages is not yet truly suchness.
This sutra states that within the ten levels of faith, one has self-confidence that within one's own mind there are ten...
The ten kinds of worlds that constitute the fruit of Buddhahood are, namely, the Golden World, the World of Wondrous Colors, the Lotus-Color World, and so forth;
these ten colored worlds correspond to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). Because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the Buddha-realm that is the object of faith is "form" (*rūpa*).
The Buddha who is the original object of service is Akṣobhyajñāna (Immovable Wisdom) and Asaṅgajñāna (Unimpeded Wisdom).

The Buddha’s wisdom of liberation—the Buddha is thus these ten kinds of wisdom. Because the fruits of the ten kinds of wisdom of one's own mind are taken as the names of the ten kinds of Buddha-fruit, one ultimately realizes and cultivates the state of fulfillment of all Buddhas to accomplish this wisdom;
it is not different from this wisdom. Apart from these ten stages of faith, [one does so] with a mind subject to arising and ceasing.
Faith in the ten wisdoms of the ten material worlds, from the Tathāgata up to the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages,
equal enlightenment, and the eleventh stage— altogether comprising fifty instances of cause and effect—

all take the conduct of Samantabhadra as the cause and the nature of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya, wisdom, and principle as the fruit; or rather, these may be mutually integrated to support and stimulate one another.
Within these two types of five stages of cause and effect, there are one hundred layers of Buddha’s cause and effect in total.
Taking all five original stages together, each has five layers of cause and five layers of effect, totaling one hundred and ten layers of cause and effect.
For example, the Buddha’s cause and effect within the Ten Abodes stage is the Indraloka (Indra-flower) world.
In the Padma-flower World and the Jewel-flower World, there are Buddhas named Viśiṣṭacandra, Akṣayacandra, and Acyutacandra;
thus, in these ten flower-worlds, there are ten Buddhas all sharing the name "Candra.
These Buddhas take the Bodhisattvas of Dharma-Wisdom and the other nine Wisdom-Bodhisattvas as their fruit of Buddhahood, and they practice the conduct of Samantabhadra.

For this reason, by means of these ten stages (*bhūmi*), through the power of entering the *upāya-samādhi*, one realizes the Dharma-body and the wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) through direct verification.
Because the world is named "Flower" and the fruit is manifested through the blossoming of flowers, all the Buddha-fruits thus manifested are called "Moon.
This is to clarify that within the ten stages, the wondrous wisdom of the Dharma-body first appears before one without obstruction.

Because one attains the coolness of the Buddha’s Dharma-body from the heat of affliction— like the moon— the place where delusions are eliminated through the realization of the Path is designated as the name of the Buddha,
while the place where the mind is awakened is designated as the world-system. For example,

the *Indra-kusuma* (which is translated here as "Flower of the Sovereign") signifies that upon first entering the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), one is born into the family of the Buddhas and is able to provide for sentient beings.
The "Dharma Lord" (Dharmasvāmin) is thus [referred to as] the *pāṭala* flower, which is the red lotus (*raktapadma*).

This signifies the meaning of the ground of the *Prabhākārī-bhūmi* (the Luminous Stage), where one progresses through cultivation toward ever-increasing excellence, shining brilliantly and blooming in a manner worthy of contemplation.

In summary, these names—such as Buddha, the Buddha-land, the world-system, and Bodhisattva—are all established according to the causes and conditions of entering the Path at each respective stage; they do not exist externally, but collectively clarify one's own practice.
The practices are as follows: within the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), there are ten worlds of wisdom and ten names of Buddhas, all of which are termed "Eye" (*cakṣus*).
These constitute the Buddha-fruit; the Ten Forests of Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakānanavatī, constitute the causal practices.
This may be understood according to the sutra through the subsequent ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) and ten stages (*bhūmi*); it is only upon reaching these stages that they become clearly manifest.

To state the essential point: the ten Buddhas of their respective positions constitute the fruit of the fundamental position, while the ten Bodhisattvas of their respective positions constitute the cause of practice for those respective positions.

Thus, in this first assembly, the Tathāgata serves as the fruit of the five positions, while Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the various deities serve as the causes of practice for the five positions. Furthermore...
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the various devas and spirits take the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of Vairocana as the causal basis for initiating their practice,
and they regard their own bodies of practice as the fruit of the Buddha’s differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Thus, they take the wisdom-fruit of the Buddha-nature as the cause, because the body currently engaged in practice is itself the nature-fruit of the unity of principle and wisdom.

Because they are mutually cause and effect and mutually essence and function, the divine heavens, in their praise of virtue, first praise the Buddha’s virtues and subsequently praise themselves for sharing the same wisdom and the same virtue as the Buddha.
This serves as a model for entering the Dharma, so that all practitioners who are deluded are ordinary beings, while those who awaken are Buddhas;
therefore, one should advance simultaneously in both wisdom and compassion, just like the youth Sudhana.
In the first stage of the ten practices of the Son, the land inhabited by the spiritual friend of the Practice of Joy is named the Land of the Three Eyes.

This is identical to the worlds inhabited by Bodhisattvas of the ten practices, such as the World of Close Wisdom (*Pratibhāna*), the World of Banner Wisdom (*Dhvaja-prajñā*), the World of Jewel Wisdom (*Ratna-prajñā*), and so forth—these being the ten worlds of wisdom. As for the "Three Eyes," the first is Mahā... [text fragment].

The two types of *prajñā*, the two liberations, and the three *dharmakāyas* are likewise constituted by the three eyes—the eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*), the eye of insight (*prajñācakṣus*), and the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
This is like the world-symbol [a circle within a circle] or the three eyes on the face of the celestial king Maheśvara.
Because all Buddha-dharmas do not depart from this great wisdom, great insight, and *dharmakāya*, these constitute the meaning of the "World of Ten Insights."
Penetrating these three eyes, this corresponds to the first stage among Sudhana’s ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
In this land, the name of the bhikṣu spiritual friend is Sudarśana; he occupies the rank of the ten practices. The Buddhas there are named Nityapradīptanetra and Anabhibhūtanetra;
he is called Sudarśana because he possesses the three eyes. Within the ten practices, he acts through wisdom.
Because he knows the faculties of sentient beings and acts in accordance with them, the Buddha is called the "Eye" and the "Good Spiritual Friend," named "Excellent Vision.
His hair is deep blue-black, his skin is golden, and his halo extends one fathom; his marks and signs are like those of a Buddha.
This clarifies that the causal practice of the three eyes within the ten practices is itself the Buddha. The passage concerning the practitioner walking in the forest clarifies this point.

Because the dense forest of the myriad practices provides shade and protection for sentient beings, it is like the ten "forests" of bodhisattvas in the stage of the Ten Practices—namely, the bodhisattvas Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha (Forest of Merit), Prajñākāraṇḍavyūha (Forest of Wisdom), Jayakāraṇḍavyūha (Forest of Victory), and so forth.

Among Sudhana’s teachers during the Ten Practices, the one who serves as the locus of practice for the tenth stage is a bhikṣu; he dwells in a forest and practices walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), as described in the following text.
In the middle [section], the ten forest bodhisattvas such as Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha serve as the objects of practice.
Now, within this first assembly, the deity of the Harvest (Sasya-devī) serves as the provisions for the ten practices of the Buddha-fruit;

because these provisions cause sentient beings to enter the stage of Buddhahood, and because the bodhisattvas on the path of seeing and the path of accumulation increase their great compassion, thus, in this first assembly, the five stages of the Buddha-fruit and—
Following the second and third assemblies, the various bodhisattvas advance through the five stages (*pañca-vastu*), and the youth Sudhana demonstrates the practice of these five stages;

as their preceding and succeeding phases intersect and their essential structures correspond, they collectively clarify that the fruit of Buddhahood and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct mutually support one another in essence and function, remaining no different from beginning to end. For this reason, within the five stages, there are fifty kinds of provisions (*sambhāra*).
The fifty kinds of provisions for the Buddha-fruit act as mutual primary and secondary factors, mutual cause and effect, and mutual essence and function.
Thus, the nature-fruit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and principle constantly sustains the practice of Samantabhadra so that it remains untainted;
the practice of Samantabhadra constantly sustains the nature-fruit of the Tathāgata so that it may reach perfection. If either compassion or wisdom were abandoned, nothing would be accomplished.

The gates of practice consist of the causes and effects of humans and devas; if one attains that which transcends the world, it consists of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles, as well as the Bodhisattvas of the supramundane Pure Land who retain afflictions to moisten their rebirths.

These are not the dharmatā of the principle-wisdom of the world and its transcendence, nor the spontaneous, perfect fusion of great compassion, movement and stillness, and defilement and purity—such is the tenth [gate].

The practice and the provisions for the fruit of Buddhahood are like the gourd and its flower; both arise together, and the flower and fruit mutually support one another so that they function with effortless mastery.
This is because the practice of the principle-wisdom is naturally all-pervasive.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable field-protecting deities (*kṣetrapāla*), namely: the field-protecting deity Subtle-Supreme-Taste; the field-protecting deity Seasonal-Flower-Pure-Light;
the field-protecting deity Vigor-Strength-Valiant; the field-protecting deity Increasing-Essential-Vitality; the field-protecting deity Universal-Root-Fruit-Producing-Crop;
the field-protecting deity Wondrously-Adorned-Ring-Tuft; and the field-protecting deity Moistening-Pure-Flower. They all assembled.
Led by the field-protecting deity Sovereign of Wondrous Fragrance, the field-protecting deity Delightful to Behold,
and the field-protecting deity Stainless Pure Radiance, there were immeasurable such deities as these, all of whom had attained the accomplishment of great joy.

[Treatise] Regarding this section on the Lord of Crops (six lines of text, ninety-eight words), the meaning is divided into four parts: first, enumerating the number of the assembly; second, using their positions to symbolize the Dharma;
third, explaining the names and correlating them with their practices; fourth, concluding with the enumeration and praising of their virtues.
First, regarding the enumeration of the assembly: as stated in the first line, "First... Second, regarding using their positions to symbolize the Dharma: by means of the Lord...

The "Deity of Cultivation" (*kṛṣi-devatā*) represents the ten stages of practice within the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). Regarding the three explanations of the names and their correlation with the practices:
the "Deity of Cultivation of Soft and Exquisite Flavor" presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within the stage of Joyful Practice (*pramuditā-caryā*).

Within this perfection of giving, there are two meanings: first, the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*); second, the gift of material things (*āmiṣa-dāna*). As for the gift of Dharma, it refers to seeing those who come seeking the Dharma.
Because it brings joy without satiety, it is called the "supremely soft and delicious flavor.

Because it sustains people with the flavor of the Dharma, causing their minds to be tamed, this second matter of *dāna* refers to the deity who presides over cultivation; he belongs to the lineage of Hou Ji, the deity of grain.

Because he blesses the five grains through divine power so that they produce supreme flavors to nourish and benefit all living beings, [he is present] throughout the worlds of the ten directions, in every place.

The deity named *Kālapuṣpa-viśuddhaprabha-sasyādhipati* is none other than the one who practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) within the joyful practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Known as "One Who Knows the Faculties and Practices in Accordance with Them," he is called *Kālapuṣpa* because he causes the natural precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) to blossom;
he is named *Viśuddhaprabha* because he causes the flowers of the five worldly grains to flourish according to their season and bestows radiance upon them.
Because it is pure and fully blossomed, the power of the three colors is heroic and vigorous. The deity who presides over the harvest, within the *dānapāramitā*, clarifies the *kṣāntipāramitā*.
Having accomplished the merit of the patience toward dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), it is named "heroic.

Because one has attained the fruit of the patience that accords with reality (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), one obtains physical power and strength to adorn the body. Among all powers, the power of wind is supreme; among all practices, the power of patience is supreme.
Because he cannot be moved by the eight winds, and because he is able to practice accordingly and achieve patience, he is named "Valiant and Courageous.
He is like the third of the ten practices of Sudhana, the Upāsikā Guṇavatī, whose practice clarifies patience as the fruit among all practices;
therefore, he is named "Complete. He increases the fourfold vital energy and presides over the spirits of the crops; he presides over *dānapāramitā*.

Within the *pāramitās*, the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of diligence) utilizes the power of diligence as a provision, the power of the Dharma, and the powers of great loving-kindness and great compassion to transform sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death without weariness or fatigue. Because it seeks nothing for itself, it is called "increasing the vital energy.
It is represented by the deity who presides over crops, for without the power of diligence, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cannot be accomplished.
Regarding the fifth, the Universal Root-Fruit Bestowing Harvest Deity presides over the *dhyāna-pāramitā* within the *dāna-pāramitā*.
Taking the *dharmatā* as *dhyāna*, it gives birth to the myriad practices; the wondrous wisdom of principle and knowledge is called the "Universal Root-Fruit.
Because the *dharmatā*-principle *dhyāna* gives birth to wisdom and the myriad practices, it is both root and fruit, clarifying that the root arises from the fruit.

Because the root and the branches are not different, and because the fruit of Buddhahood and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practices mutually support one another, it is clarified that roots arise from the fruit and the fruit is supported by the roots.
In the sixfold subtle adornment, the Ringlet-Topknot Sovereign presides over the cultivation of the field, and the Sovereign of Generosity presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

Within this, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) clarifies that one adorns practice with sublime wisdom, while practice in turn adorns wisdom; thus, practice and wisdom mutually adorn one another.
Intending to benefit sentient beings, one uses the *āveṇika-phala* (the fruit of attraction) to form a ring for the topknot, thereby adorning the head;

this is the "topknot hanging like a ring," which clarifies that understanding and practice are perfected. Seventh, the deity who presides over moistening and pure flowers and rules over the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) is the deity of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*); in this stage, it clarifies the accomplishment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), acting as moisture.
Because the practice of benefiting others purifies the marshes, it causes others to understand and cause the flowers of the Dharma to bloom;

therefore, this constitutes the gateway of skillful means within the *dāna-pāramitā*. Because it brings about great compassion, it is the eighth of the ten practices, wherein the deity who presides over the harvest and the excellent fragrance accomplishes the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* within the *dāna-pāramitā*, being identical to the eighth [stage].
Because the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, which is the effortless wisdom of the stages, is fully accomplished;

and because through pure wisdom one knows the faculties and establishes teachings based upon those faculties, thereby accomplishing the wondrous fragrance of the perfections of morality, concentration, and wisdom;

as for the "nine views," it refers to the deity who loves and delights in cultivation, who presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within the power-perfection (*bala-pāramitā*), and who clarifies the rank of the Dharma-master in the accomplishment of preaching.

The Dharma benefits sentient beings because all who see or hear it find joy in it; tenth, the purity of the light free from defilement, presided over by the deity Chief of Crop-Growing, represents the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) within the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), for through wisdom one is able to leave behind the defilements of both self and others.

The consecration of all dharmas is identical to the stage of consecration found among the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Fourth, the number of verses concluding with a praise of virtues is as follows:
The names may be understood as above. These ten presiding deities of agriculture are all from within the *dāna-pāramitā* of the *pramuditā-bhūmi* (the Stage of Joy).
They are designated by names formed from their practices; the subsequent cases follow this same principle, with the rules as stated above.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable river-governing deities, namely: the River-Governing Deity Universal Emission of Swift Currents; the River-Governing Deity Universal Purity of Springs and Streams;
the River-Governing Deity Dust-Free Pure Eyes; the River-Governing Deity Universal Roar in the Ten Directions;

the River-Governing Deity Protector and Savior of Sentient Beings; the River-Governing Deity Heatless Pure Radiance; the River-Governing Deity Universal Generation of Joy; and the River-Governing Deity Vast...
The River Deity Virtuous Victorious Banner, the River Deity Light Illuminating All Worlds, the River Deity Oceanic Virtue Radiance, and others such as these were their leaders;
they were infinite in number, all diligently applying their minds to benefit sentient beings.

[Treatise] The twentieth is the Lord River Deity (consisting of six lines of scripture and ninety-eight words). This is the first of the ten *pāramitās* within the practice of the *śīla-pāramitā* of the Beneficial Conduct;
it is the Lord River Deity who Universally Releases the Swift Current. Among the ten practices within the *śīla-pāramitā*, this corresponds to the *dāna-pāramitā*.
If one considers the matter in this way, it is like the example of Mencius’s mother.

It is also like the episode of the Good Friend (kalyāṇamitra) in the "Beneficial Conduct" (upakāra-caryā) chapter of the *Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*, where ten thousand youths, headed by the son of a Śakra, play at gathering sand on a riverbank.
Because the river serves as the primary object for the manifestation of the essence of the precepts (śīla-dhātu), it is beneficial;

thus, in this first assembly, the River Goddess (nadī-devatā) acts as the embodiment of the precepts, being similar in nature to the preceding and succeeding sections, universally emitting a swift current.
The second is the River-God of the Universal Purity of Springs and Streams, who responds to the seeds of the One Vehicle.
The third is the God of Good Dharmas for the Three Vehicles, Humans, and Devas, etc.

Regarding the deities from the Perfection of Morality within the Ten Practices downward, their names and titles may be understood by correlating them with the meanings of the names according to their respective stages of practice, as previously explained.

Regarding the essence of the precepts within the Ten Practices: it is like the sons of the Śakra-devānām-indra who, through their skillful arts—such as the methods of calculation, the signs of physiognomy, the five elements, yin and yang, and other techniques for benefiting others—take these as the essence of the precepts within the Ten Practices.
Therefore, they are named the "Universally Pure Springs and Streams. If it were not thus, the practices would not be fulfilled; hence, it clarifies the human and celestial realms.
Furthermore, to transform beings through the three vehicles as a whole and to benefit them with skillful means is the meaning of "Universal Purity.
[Sūtra] Moreover, there were immeasurable ocean-ruling spirits, namely: the ocean-ruling spirit named Manifesting Jewel Light; the ocean-ruling spirit named Accomplishing the Vajra Banner;
the ocean-ruling spirit named Far Removed from Dust and Defilement; the ocean-ruling spirit named Universal Water Palace; and the auspicious...
The ocean-deity Jewel-Moon Sovereign, the ocean-deity Exquisite Flower Dragon-Crest Sovereign, the ocean-deity Universal Sustainer Light-Taste Sovereign,
the ocean-deity Jewel-Flame Flower-Light Sovereign, the ocean-deity Vajra Exquisite Crest Sovereign, the ocean-deity Ocean-Tide Thunder-Sound Sovereign,
and others such as these as their leaders— numbering in the infinite, they were all filled with the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s merit.
Filling his entire body.

[Treatise] The third is the Lord of the Ocean Devas (six lines of text, one hundred and two words). This clarifies the absence of opposition and explains the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Just as the ocean can receive all streams, so too is there no opposition. There are ten aspects to being the lord of the perfection of patience.
This "Ocean God" (Sāgara-deva) refers to the ten *pāramitās* within the *kṣānti-pāramitā*. Each should be understood according to its name, with their meanings assigned as previously detailed.
The general significance is that, among these ten practices, patience (*kṣānti*) takes the great compassion of the *dharmatā* as its essential body;
therefore, it is like the ocean which contains moisture and receives its tributary streams, being able to accommodate all the heights of ignorance.
Because the currents of pride and birth-and-death are all transformed into the current of the Dharma without obstruction, it is called the "Practice of Non-Contradiction.
Within this Practice of Non-Contradiction, as exemplified by the youth Sudhana, there is a city in the south named Sāgarāmukha.
There dwells a laywoman (upāsikā) named Paripūrṇa, who wears plain white garments and lets her hair hang loose; she possesses a countenance of loving-kindness and forbearance.
It completes the perfection of patience; because there is no practice that is not encompassed, it is called the "Ocean-Complete" (Samudra-sampūrṇa).

As for the goddess Samudra-devī, she is compassionate, gentle, and soft in her conduct, and she is able to endure with a mind like the ocean. Being fully endowed with merit and wisdom, she benefits all sentient beings;
therefore, patience is the fruition among the myriad practices, for it can accommodate all streams.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable water-lord spirits (*udakadevatā*), namely: the water-lord spirit named Universal Cloud-Banner Arising, the water-lord spirit named Ocean Tide-Cloud Sound,
the water-lord spirit named Wondrous Color Wheel Topknot, the water-lord spirit named Skillful Whirlpool, the water-lord spirit named Stainless Fragrance Accumulation,
the water-lord spirit named Merit Bridge Radiant Sound, the water-lord spirit named Contentment Sovereignty, and the water-lord spirit named Purity.
Led by the water deity Joyful and Virtuous Sound, the water deity Universal Manifestation of Majestic Light, and the water deity Roaring Sound Pervading the Ocean,
there were immeasurable numbers of such deities who constantly and diligently protected all sentient beings for their benefit.

[Treatise] The fourth Lord of Water Deities (six lines of sūtra, one hundred and two words) clarifies the practice of being unbending and unyielding as the mastery of the *pāramitā* of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

It is explained that just as the substance of water can cleanse all impurities, so too the Bodhisattva in this stage, using the water of the *dharmatā*, constantly exerts diligence to teach and transform sentient beings; knowing each one’s faculties (*indriya*), he benefits them without ever yielding.
Stirring the mind like water that moistens all things, it benefits them according to their nature so that each finds its proper place without any internal yielding or distortion.
These ten water deities represent the ten pāramitās within the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

They clarify that the myriad practices are like water in their shared function of moistening and giving life; each is assigned its meaning according to its respective name, and one should always [contemplate] them in this way.

In the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), vigor (*vīrya*) constitutes the essence, just as in the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) the gate of vigor takes joy in diligently contemplating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as its essence.
Within these ten practices, the gate of vigor takes benefiting others in the world by moistening sentient beings through one's conduct as its essence.

In each stage, that which corresponds to the primary practice of that specific stage constitutes the essence; the remaining nine [practices] serve as the essence of the primary practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
Because one cannot understand [the stages] exclusively as being distinct from one another, their essence and meaning should not be viewed in that way.

As in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* regarding the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) within the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are fused, and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is made even and spontaneous.
Thus, in these five stages, attaining one entails all five being simultaneously present and equal; yet, because they arise through the ripening of habitual practice, there must be a sequence.
Although a sequence is established, because the essence of the wisdom of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-jñāna) is without priority or posteriority, there is no before, after, or middle;

the sequence is of one nature without differentiation. Within this state where identity and difference cannot be conceptually constructed as prior or subsequent, if one speaks according to reality, it is like a single drop of water entering the waters of the great ocean within the stage of the first resolve (prathamacittotpāda-vihāra).
Within the ocean-like essence of the universal totality, all dragons, fish, and precious treasuries are contained therein.

For the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, the methods of the teaching-net and the fishing-trap must be fully prepared; recording them upon bamboo and silk in written registers is like the arising of successive meanings.
One who clarifies the Way through clear discernment is like holding a precious mirror, universally facing the myriad things.

The ten stages of the elephant clarify that through the perfection of habitual practice, one reaches the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), wherein mastery is attained and activity pervades the Dharma-realm.
If one were to establish only the single stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*), it would merely clarify the initial merit of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, if one were to establish only the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), there would be only the supramundane mind; thus, the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmana*) are added to give rise to clouds of great vows, thereby causing [the practitioner] to proceed.

When compassion, wisdom, and the myriad practices are perfected through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one merely accumulates merit and virtue; yet, to ensure that these become habitual, one must complete the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*).

Therein, one enters the mundane world with sovereign conduct, universally benefiting others according to the Dharma and clearly spreading the net of the teachings so that students have a place of refuge.
If one does not resolve their mind in this way, what else can be done?
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were countless fire-governing deities (*tejorājadevatā*), namely: the fire-governing deity Universal Radiant Flame Treasury,
the fire-governing deity Universal Assembly of Light Banner, the fire-governing deity Great Light Universally Illuminating, the fire-governing deity Myriad Wondrous Palaces,
the fire-governing deity Inexhaustible Light Topknot, the fire-governing deity Various Flames Eyes, and the fire-governing deity Ten Directions Palace Like Mount Sumeru.
The Fire God Sovereign of Majestic Radiance, the Fire God Sovereign of Light Dispelling Darkness, the Fire God Sovereign of Cloud-Sound Lightning—
these and others as their leaders, beyond all calculation, were all able to manifest various kinds of light,
causing the burning afflictions of all sentient beings to be extinguished.

[Treatise] The fifth is the Lord Fire God (comprising six lines of verse and one hundred ten words). This clarifies that the practice of non-delusion and non-confusion is the primary practice of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
Within this, the ten deities clarify the *dhyāna-pāramitā*; therein, the ten *pāramitās* all take the meditative states (*dhyāna*) of the ten stages as their essential body of practice.
This clarifies that universal wisdom illuminates while remaining eternally quiescent; thus, the Lord Fire God is taken [as the representative].

The essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is quiescence yet constant illumination; it is the constant principle within phenomena, and its compassionate wisdom and illuminating function are unimpeded.
Therefore, the Fire Deity is taken as the essence of concentration. If considered in terms of worldly affairs, he is the Southern Deity of Fire (*Jātavedas*);
if considered in terms of persons, it is the human mind, for it is the mind that is detached from [deluded] dharmas; and if considered in terms of dharmas, it is emptiness.
This wisdom is like the sun when it is external; it is like the eyes when it is within one's own body; it is the Middle Way when it pertains to the methods of practice.

It is the Correct, the Illuminating, the Void, and the Wisdom that illumines all existence. It is the Hall of Universal Radiance. Since this is a goddess, the reason why the youth Sudhana travels south is as follows: [Note:

The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the *Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*, specifically concerning the goddess Māyādevī (or a similar deity) and her location in the "Hall of Universal Radiance" (*Samantāvabhāsa-prāsāda*).]

It is for this reason that it is clarified that there is no deluded or confused activity; because the fire deity is able to destroy darkness, because it does not cause confusion, and because there is no obstruction of darkness—this section establishes the meditative concentration (samādhi) by way of its function.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable wind-ruling spirits (*vāyu-devaputra*), namely: the wind-ruling spirit Unobstructed Radiance,
the wind-ruling spirit Universal Manifestation of Valor, the wind-ruling spirit Cloud Banner Shaker, the wind-ruling spirit Pure Light Adornment,
the wind-ruling spirit Power to Dry Up Water, the wind-ruling spirit Great Roar Pervading All, and the wind-ruling spirit Tree-Tip Hanging Topknot.
Led by the wind spirit Unobstructed Conduct, the wind spirit Sovereign of Various Palaces, and the wind spirit Great Light Universally Illuminating,
there were immeasurable numbers of such spirits as these, all of whom diligently dispelled and extinguished the mind of self-conceit (*māna*).
[Treatise] The sixth is the Lord Wind Deity (six lines of scripture, ninety-eight words). It clarifies that the practice of goodness has the *prajñāpāramitā* as its essence.
The ten wind deities represent the ten *pāramitās* within the *prajñāpāramitā*.

In the mundane world, this corresponds to the period between the hours of the Dragon (*chén*) and the Snake (*sì*), and is the deity of the *Xùn* trigram; as she is a female deity, she serves as the principle of the Dharma.
It is also for the purpose of speech and instruction, such as the fourth hexagram of the Qian cycle in the *Zhou Yi*, where Xun is above and Kun is below, called Guan.
The *Yi* says: "Wind blowing over the earth allows one to observe its image.

When a gentleman establishes policies and teachings and the multitude follows and takes them as their model, it can be observed through this principle; therefore, Xun represents wind and instruction. This clarifies the sixth [hexagram].
The perfection of wisdom is accomplished through the teachings and transformations of Subhūti; this is called the practice of Subhūti.

Furthermore, during the hours of Chén and Sì, the Tathāgata takes this as the rule for fasting and precepts to clarify the junctures of good and ill fortune, bringing the completion of virtue to its conclusion.
Upon reaching Wǔ, all phenomena become correct. Above, it coincides with the Jiǎo (Pleiades) lunar mansion. The Jiǎo...
It serves as the Lord of the Celestial Gate; monks, nuns, and Daoists dwell within it, clearly establishing the teachings to form a gateway for all manner of goodness.

All social transformations and moral influences arise from this. The elephant uses its mouth as the Celestial Gate to inhale and exhale the vital energies (*vāyu*) that constitute governance and instruction;
thus, wisdom is taken as the spirit. Furthermore, it spreads forth flowers and brings forth fruit, giving rise to all things.
It is called "the practice of the Well-Appearing" because it is able to sustain, create, and destroy world-systems. As stated later in this sutra:
"The ocean has four kinds of winds: first, the 'Accumulating' wind, which can gather various jewels, representing the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
second, the 'Creating' wind, which can produce various jewels, representing the All-Accomplishing Wisdom; third, the 'Discriminating' wind, which can select..."
The four kinds of wisdom—the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation of the Radiance of All Jewels and the Wisdom of Equality—are able to disperse [all things];

therefore, these four wisdoms are taken as the Wind Deity (*vāyu-devatā*). Because they can manifest mastery over phenomena, the Wind Deity serves as the representation of the skillful manifestation of the *Sudṛśa* (Well-Appearing) realm. Thus, this sixth wisdom-dharma is the Wind Deity of Wisdom, which skillfully manifests.
Because all dharmas and practices are entirely sovereign, the fruit of Buddhahood is assigned to the sixth stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
This corresponds to the Southeast, where the Buddha’s name is Ultimate Wisdom (*Akṣayajñāna*). The Southeast is the direction of *Xun* (Swell).

In the *Xun* hexagram, *Xun* represents the Wind deity; furthermore, the *Yi Jing* states that *Xun* represents speech. Thus, by borrowing the object [the wind] to symbolize the dharma, one uses the Wind deity to represent it.
Because wisdom can skillfully manifest all phenomena (*dharma*), "direction" (*fang*) refers to phenomena; yet the Great Elephant takes up these phenomena without fixed direction.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable space-ruling spirits (*ākāśa-deva*), namely: the Space-ruling Spirit Pure Light Universally Illuminating, and the Space-ruling Spirit Universal Travel in the Profound.
The Ākāśadevatā Vastuśrī, the Ākāśadevatā Śivavāyu, the Ākāśadevatā Vighnavinivartanavyūhasthitā,
the Ākāśadevatā Vipulagatimaṇicūḍā, the Ākāśadevatā Asaṅgaprabhārciḥ, the Ākāśadevatā Asaṅgavijayasampannabala,
the Ākāśadevatā Vimalaprabhā, the Ākāśadevatā Gambhīrasvararuta, and the Ākāśadevatā Daśadigvyāptaprabhā.
With these as their leaders, their number was immeasurable; their minds were all free from defilement, vast, bright, and pure.

[Treatise] The sixth is the Lord of the Sky Devas (six lines of sūtra, ninety-eight words). This clarifies the practice of non-attachment, which masters the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) and establishes the gateway of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because they initiate practice through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they teach and transform, gathering in and embracing all sentient beings.

It is called "expedient means" and thus named "the practice of non-attachment. Within this, among the various divine powers and the *pāramitās* of expedient means, the ten *pāramitās* take the emptiness of all phenomena as their essence;
because they take wisdom as their divine power, there is nothing to which they are attached.
Since the emptiness of all phenomena can give rise to compassion and wisdom, these myriad practices are themselves non-attachment.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable directional lords (*dikpati*), namely: the Directional Lord Pervading All, the Directional Lord Universally Manifesting Radiance,
the Directional Lord Adorned with Luminous Conduct, the Directional Lord Moving Everywhere Without Obstruction,
the Directional Lord Permanently Severing Delusion, the Directional Lord Wandering Throughout the Pure Void, the Directional Lord Great Cloud Banner Sound, and the Directional Lord [Crest].
The presiding deity of the direction of Unconfused Eyes, the presiding deity of the direction of Universal Observation of the World’s Lords,

the presiding deity of the direction of Pervasive Roaming, and others such as these were their leaders; they were infinite in number, and through skillful means, they universally emitted radiance that constantly illuminated the ten directions in an uninterrupted succession.
[Treatise] The eighth, the Lord of the Directions (six lines of verse, one hundred and six characters): It clarifies that the practice which is difficult to attain is the function of wisdom;
because merit is difficult to accomplish without effort, it takes the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) as the essential nature of wisdom. Being pure, it uses aspiration to guard it;
by recollecting its original vow, it draws forth wisdom to give rise to practice, causing that practice to be all-pervasive, so that one neither dwells in nirvāṇa nor dwells in [saṃsāra].
Within this cycle of birth and death, there are ten spiritual deities (*śrāmaṇa*) who correspond to the ten *pāramitās*. Here, "method" (*dharma*) refers to the ten *pāramitās* themselves.
By means of the eighth practice, the Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*) is accomplished; through wisdom, one establishes the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.

This Great Wisdom constitutes the spiritual deities, collectively comprising the deities of the four cardinal directions—East (*zhen*), North (*kan*), West (*dui*), and South (*li*)—as well as the intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir.
This is because they collectively manifest the wisdom of non-activity, which perfectly encompasses all.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable night goddesses, namely: the night goddess Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā (Universal Virtue Pure Light), the night goddess Priyanayanalokanātha (Joyful Eye World-Protector), the night goddess Lokarakṣasattvavīrya (Guardian of the World’s Vitality), the night goddess Śāntasvarasāgara (Ocean of Silent Sound), and the night goddess Samantadarśinī (Universally Manifesting).
The auspicious Night Goddess Śrīmatī, the Night Goddess Sarvavṛkṣaprasavā, the Night Goddess Samantaparipālanī, the Night Goddess Ratiśīlā,
the Night Goddess Nityapramuditendriyā, the Night Goddess Viśuddhapuṇyasambhavā—
these and others were the leaders, numbering in the infinite, all of whom diligently practiced and took delight in the Dharma.
[Treatise] The ninth night goddess (consisting of six lines of verse and ninety-eight words) is named *Saddharmacāriprabhākarī* (She Who Illuminates the Practice of the True Dharma).
Having perfected the power of the *pāramitās* through the majesty of the Dharma King, she constantly dwells within the long night of birth and death, illuminating the world with the Dharma;
therefore, she is named *Saddharmacāri*. Among these ten goddesses who possess the majesty of the *pāramitās*, there are ten *pāramitās*.

Madhu is a goddess; because she is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the youth Sudhana, this clarifies that the essence of the practice of this stage penetrates the dharmas of all ten stages.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there are immeasurable Daytime Goddesses (*divā-devī*), namely: the Daytime Goddess Manifesting Palaces (*prāsādadarśana*), and the Daytime Goddess Initiating Wisdom (*prajñāsamutthāpana*).
The Day-God Fragrance Sovereign, the Day-God Joyful Supreme Adornment Sovereign, the Day-God Exquisite Light of Incense and Flowers Sovereign,
the Day-God Universal Gathering of Wondrous Medicines Sovereign, the Day-God Joyfully Creating the Eye of Delight Sovereign, the Day-God Universally Manifesting in All Directions Sovereign,
the Day-God Great Compassionate Radiance Sovereign, the Day-God Illumination of the Roots of Goodness Sovereign, and the Day-God Exquisite Flower Garland Sovereign.

With these as their leaders, they are infinite in number; all are able to give rise to faith and understanding in the Sublime Dharma, and together they constantly exert themselves in adorning their palaces.
[Treatise] The tenth is the Lord of the Day Deity (six lines of scripture, one hundred and six words), who clarifies true practice and presides over the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Among these, within the ten divine wisdom-pāramitās, the ten pāramitās are named "Masters" because they are constantly illuminated by the sun of wisdom;
their wisdom is unconditioned yet responds to the myriad phenomena, and thus they are called "divine.
Regarding the statement that they all together diligently adorn the palace: through wisdom, they universally pervade and transform sentient beings, thereby establishing the Dharma-palace.

Compassion serves as the palace and wisdom as the hall; because the palace and hall of compassion and wisdom for accomplishing sentient beings mutually benefit one another, the section above concludes the explanation of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*).
Fourth, from the Asura King to the Sun Deity, there are ten assemblies therein to symbolize the ten [stages].
Why is it that dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is thus? It is because the asuras dwell within the great ocean yet do not sink; their bodies remain manifest.
Likewise, through the ten dedications, one brings together the ultimate and the conventional (*saṃvṛti-paramārtha*), remaining constantly within the great ocean of birth and death without sinking.

While the preceding stages of the ten abidings (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) merely cultivated supramundane compassion and wisdom, here one increases them by means of dedication, turning toward the truth and entering into it.

The worldly convention holds that because one has perfected the compassion and wisdom for abiding in the world, the ten assemblies—such as the asuras and others—are used to symbolize the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Just as one does not drown while in the great ocean, this indicates that a bodhisattva in this stage, through the mind of great compassion, attains true realization yet does not realize it [as a final limit];
thus, while conforming to the conventional world, they remain untainted by it, exercising mastery in benefiting sentient beings.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable asura kings, namely: Rāhu Asura King, Vemacitra Asura King,
Kuśalamāyāvidhi Asura King, Mahāparivāra Asura King, Mahābala Asura King, Samantaprabha Asura King, and Dṛḍhacaryā-suvyūha Asura King.
The Asura King Vast Cause, the Asura King Appearance of Supreme Virtue,
the Asura King Wondrous Melodious Voice, and others such as these were their leaders; they were infinite in number,
and all had already applied themselves with diligence to subdue their pride and all afflictions.
[Treatise] First, regarding the initial section on the assembly of the Asura Kings (consisting of six lines and one hundred and eight words), the meaning is divided into four parts:

1. Stating the number of the assembly; 2. Using their positions to symbolize the Dharma; 3. Explaining the names and correlating them with practices; 4. Summarizing the numbers and praising their virtues.
Regarding the first, stating the number of the assembly: as in the first line... Second, using their positions to symbolize the Dharma: [referring to] the Asuras...
The *Luo-wei* (Vajra) stage represents the dedication "Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings. To clarify this first dedication:
although the asuras dwell within the great ocean, they are not submerged by its waters; yet, though they share the same realm as the devas, they lack the sublime bliss of the heavens.
Likewise, bodhisattvas at this stage dwell within birth and death, yet they do not exist within birth and death. Five.

Although one dwells in the bliss of nirvāṇa, because it lacks the bliss of quiescence within nirvāṇa itself, it is called the "Dedication to Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
Furthermore, as stated in the "Chapter on the Dharma-realm": "He accomplishes the Tathāgata’s eminence that transcends the world, like a king of the asuras.
Moreover, "king" has the meaning of sovereignty; this clarifies that the bodhisattva at this stage [is sovereign] regarding nirvāṇa.
Because they have attained mastery within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); furthermore, *asura* is also called *asu-ra*. *Asu* means "non-existent" (*na asti*) and *ra* means "to roam.
It is also said to mean "sublime" (*miao*) and *ra* means "playful" (*xi*). As explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are called "Non-Gods" (*asura*).

Although they are included within the realm of the gods (*deva-gati*), because they are largely characterized by deceit and guile and lack the sublime bliss of the gods, they are likened to this state.
The Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion and skillful means involves ten thousand deeds that may appear like flattery or deceit, and may seem like the cycle of birth and death;
yet they contain no pleasure of the five desires of humans or devas, nor do they possess the joy of eternal abiding, nirvana, or the world-transcending tranquility of cessation.

This refers to the gate of the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) within the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*). The old translation [of this term] was unnecessary, and its previous rendering was erroneous. Some call it *vī*.
Because Māyā’s mother was originally born from an egg, she is called an "inferior deva. As the Āgama Sūtras state:
"At the beginning of the kalpa, when the world was first formed, a deva from the Ābhāsvara Heaven came down into the ocean to bathe.

When the water touched his body, he emitted semen that fell into the water and transformed into a fleshy egg. After eight thousand years, a daughter was born from it, her body as large as Mount Sumeru."
There were nine hundred and ninety heads, each with a thousand eyes;
there were nine hundred and ninety mouths, each with four fangs from which fire issued like thunderbolts. He had fourteen hands and nine hundred and ninety feet.
Floating and sporting upon the sea, he drew water into his body, where it produced a fleshy egg. After eight thousand years, Vemacitra was born from it.
The body has nine heads, each head possessing a thousand eyes; from its mouths water flows forth, and it has nine hundred and ninety hands and eight feet.

Its form is four times larger than Mount Sumeru. It feeds exclusively on mud and lotus roots, and it even contends with the devas, as described at length in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*. Furthermore, there are five abodes of the asuras.
First, among the mountains of various jewels upon the earth, it is said that two hundred thousand *yojanas* below Mount Sumeru,
descending into the great ocean, there is an Asura king named Rāhu— translated here as "Obstruction"—
who is able to block the light of the sun and moon with his hands and leads immeasurable hosts. From this point, descending further by another twenty-one thousand *yojanas*, [there is...]
Ten *yojana*s away is an asura king named Śūra, who also leads a great multitude.
Four times twenty-one thousand *yojana*s further is an asura king named Puṣpamāla, who likewise leads various hosts.
A fifth [king], exceeding that number, is named Vemacitra—this means "Resounding Height"—who is the father of Śacī; Śacī is...

When Vaiśravaṇa, the father-in-law of Śakra Devendra, whose body was like Mount Sumeru, fought with Śakra Devendra, he emerged from the midst of the ocean and cried out in a loud voice, "I am Vemacitra! I am Vemacitra!
At that time, the mountains and peaks of Jambudvīpa shook all at once; it is also called Kūṭāgāra because there is light within it.
Because he dwells within the city of Light (Vairocana), he is sometimes included within the celestial realm (*devagati*).

According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, based on the *Abhidharma*, he is included within the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*). Furthermore, Vemacitra is translated as "Various Affairs" (*nānātva-vastu*);
alternatively, *vema* means "pervading space" and *citra* means "various ornaments. This refers to when this asura was at war with Śakra.

Various military accoutrements and ceremonial insignia were arrayed in the air; what was formerly called "Resounding Height" (Xiǎnggāo) or "Dwelling in the Depths" (Jiǔjū) is not this [state], for according to the Tang dynasty rites, Dharma Masters and others translated it as being subsumed under the fourth evil realm (*durgati*).
As indicated in the sūtras by the ten types of *asura* kings, this represents the stages of advancement and cultivation used to clarify the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the bodhisattva.
"Penetrating downward as if dwelling in the great ocean and reaching its bottom; the body emerges from the great ocean":

this clarifies that the Bodhisattva does not sink into the evil realms, for they are able to abandon self-conceit. By means of the True encompassing the Conventional, the True and the Conventional are perfectly interfused; thus, while dwelling in the sea of suffering, one constantly emerges. This stage is used to represent the Dharma-gate of Dedication (pariṇāmanā). Third, the explanation of the name and its correlation with the practitioner's practice: (1) [Note: The provided text appears to be a commentary on the "Ten Stages" (Daśabhūmi), specifically the ninth stage, the "Cloud of Dharma" (Dharmameghā). The passage explains the significance of the Bodhisattva’s mastery over the ocean-like depths of reality and their transcendence of the mundane through the integration of the ultimate and conventional truths.]
The Rāhu Asura King clarifies the *dāna-pāramitā* gate within the tenth dedication (*daśama-pariṇāmanā*) of the *Dāna-pāramitā*.
Within this dedication, the ten *pāramitās* are used to symbolize the Dharma through specific events; here, the Asura is taken to clarify these ten dedications.
These ten dedications take great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) as the very essence of the ten perfections.
The mind that seeks self-benefit resembles the abode of the asuras: from the bottom, their bodies extend down into the sea; from the top, half of their bodies emerge above it.
This is a general clarification of how phenomena are manifested through concrete events so that the Dharma may be easily understood;

thus, it resembles the function of the gate of great compassion, wherein each and every door of liberation within this stage is purely characterized by great wisdom, great compassion, and great vows that penetrate both the ultimate and the conventional truths.
Regarding "having a body like Rāhu": this is translated as "one who can obstruct light.

Because a Bodhisattva in this stage enters the realms of birth and death with a mind of great compassion to manifest the emptiness of the Great Dharma and obstruct the various evil destinies, [he is compared to Rāhu].
Second, regarding King Vemacitra of the Asuras, which illustrates the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) within the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*): *Vemacitra* means...
This is called "Resonant High Brilliance" because, through the sounds of great compassion and great vows, one pledges to deliver those in the three realms and six paths;

thus, compassion and vows constitute the essence of the precepts (*śīla*). "King" signifies the meaning of sovereignty, for within the ocean of suffering, one moves with mastery whether sinking or floating.
"Three Skillful Illusory Arts" refers to the King of the Asuras, who clarifies the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), clarifying this stage of bodhi...
Although Śakra dwells within the great ocean of birth and death, he constantly attains the patience that all things are like illusions;
thus, the Great Four Kings, the Asura Lords, preside over the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), for they universally gather sentient beings through the myriad practices.
The Five Great Powerful Asura Kings manifest the power of the great meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), remaining within the ocean of suffering yet...
Sixth, because he is free from suffering, the Asura King Universal Illumination possesses the light of clear wisdom that gathers and transforms sentient beings universally;

seventh, because he is adorned with the skillful means of great compassion, the Asura King Adorned with Firm and Wondrous Conduct possesses the light of great compassion and skillful means as his adornment;
eighth, because his wisdom is increased and clarified by its causes, the Asura King Vast Cause-Wisdom [possesses the light of primordial wisdom].

The vow to benefit sentient beings serves as the cause; because one attains the further clarification of wisdom within the eighth stage, one must always keep in mind the great vows made at the time of first generating the bodhicitta, thereby enabling the liberation of all beings.

Ninth is the appearance of supreme qualities, the King of Asuras, who occupies the rank of the Dharma Master and accomplishes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). Tenth is the Wondrous Beautiful Voice.
The Asura King is one who has attained the stage of clear wisdom and possesses a wondrous voice for skillfully expounding the Dharma;

thus, the fourfold enumeration of his praised virtues may be understood according to the text. The ten *pāramitās* mentioned above are all the knowledge of the ultimate truth within the conventional, which is unified within the nature of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
These ten perfections take great compassion as their essence; therefore, they rely upon it.

This matter reveals that the Dharma resides in the analogy of the asuras: it shows how a bodhisattva dwells within the ocean of birth and death yet reaches its bottom, never sinking into the midst of that ocean of birth and death.
Therefore, the subsequent text establishes the Tathāgata as one who eminently transcends the world, like the King of Asuras.
Furthermore, the Ten Abodes and the Ten Practices clarify the wisdom of penetration; those who have attained such truth are designated as [Arhats].
The ten divine stages and the ten bhūmis are all represented by the ten kings, clarifying that through the increase of habitual practice, mastery is attained;
the further extensive meaning will be clarified in the Chapter on the Ten Dedications (Daśapariṇāmanā-parivarta).

[For] all sentient beings.
[Treatise: The second section (consisting of seven lines of verse and one hundred twenty-two words) clarifies the "unbreakable dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).

It elucidates how, by means of the wisdom of ultimate truth, one simultaneously embraces and benefits sentient beings, thereby manifesting the precept of great compassion; for it realizes that the conventional nature and the ultimate truth are non-dual.
The name *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma) is its meaning; the name of this sutra, *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka*, is likewise its meaning.
Because it gives rise to the myriad practices through the wisdom of principle, great compassion, and the inherently pure awakening of the dharma-realm, it is titled the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*.
It clarifies that bodhisattvas [attain realization] through the great wisdom of the dharma-nature.
Great compassion that does not abandon the worldly flow through acting in concert with others is called "water"; being endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra is called the "lotus";
because awakening and practice mutually support one another, it is called the "wondrous Dharma. Therefore, it is named the "indestructible dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).
Its true nature is without deficiency, and its flowing into the conventional world is called "indestructible clarity. It is the bodhi of no-nature and the wisdom of non-abiding. From itself...
Therefore, the Garuḍa King is now used as a metaphorical device to reveal this; he is the Golden-Winged Bird (*suparṇin*). Within this section of the text, the meaning is divided into four parts:

first, citing the number of the assembly; second, using positions to symbolize the Dharma; third, explaining the names and correlating them with practices; fourth, concluding the count and praising their virtues.
First, regarding the citation of the number of the assembly, it may be understood as in the initial stage of practice. Second...
Regarding the symbolic representation of the Dharma through metaphorical positions:

by entrusting the matter to the position of the King of Garuḍas, it clarifies the meaning of diligently rescuing others—just as one observes with pure eyes a dragon whose life is ending upon the great ocean and seizes it with both wings.
As stated in the Dharmadhātu-parivarta: "May I constantly vow to deliver all sentient beings, uprooting them from the ocean of existence, like a Garuḍa."
O King, this "Golden-Winged Bird King" manifests the Bodhisattva of the Ten Dedications, who constantly soars above the great ocean of birth and death;

with the eye of the pure wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, he observes sentient beings whose faculties are mature and seizes them with the two wings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, establishing them upon the shore of self-nature-pure *nirvāṇa*. This is *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Taking the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the essence of *śamatha* and the wisdom of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niḥsvabhāva-jñāna*) as the essence of *vipaśyanā*, there are no two distinct entities of subject and object.
Because the primary precept—the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)—is pure, it is like the great ocean that does not harbor a corpse;
likewise, the precepts of great compassion and great wisdom do not harbor the dualistic views of defilement and purity regarding humans, devas, or the three vehicles.
Because he dies upon these corpses, the distance between the two wings of this *garuḍa* king is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names and their correlation with the practices: the *Garūḍarāja Mahāvega* (Great Swift Power) clarifies the *dāna-pāramitā* within the *śīla-pāramitā*;
it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage, through the arising of great compassion by nature, enters the ocean of birth and death.

To deliver sentient beings whose faculties are matured, by the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one reaches the shore of the Buddha-fruit and *nirvāṇa* in the duration of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
This is to clarify that within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, a single thought-moment is not bound by the three periods of time—past, present, or future.
Therefore, the analogy of the *garuḍa* seizing a dragon is used; just as one with swift power seizes [its prey] with the *garuḍa*.
When the dragon, in a single moment of thought, draws its body into the sea, it emerges from the water before the waves have even closed together;
this is called the power of swiftness. Therefore, in the subsequent passage praising his virtues, it says:

"He is well able to rescue and gather in all sentient beings, delivering them from the ocean of birth and death. A Bodhisattva who has attained the Way is also like this, observing with concentration and wisdom.

Power arises from the edge of the great ocean of ignorance; by binding the long and short thoughts, one responds to the truth in a single thought-moment, seeing the past, present, and future of the three periods of time all at once.
Seeing the Way is thus, and cultivating the Way is thus; this is called the non-duality of the initial aspiration and its ultimate fulfillment.
Such an aspiration is more difficult than the former [stages], yet it clarifies that the initial mind of the ten abidings proceeds from the state of an ordinary person.

Now, the fact that a single thought-moment responds to reality is difficult; it is not because the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood is difficult, for when one reaches the ultimate, it is no different from the initial mind.
This clarifies that the Dharma is not different [from the mind], wisdom is not different, and time does not shift.

Because this clarifies the essence and function of the Dharma-realm, it can be seen by illuminating it with concentration and wisdom; yet if one approaches it with emotional conceptualization, it is immediately [obscured].
From "The deluded" onwards, one may understand the four concluding summaries by correlating the various *pāramitās* with their names and meanings as they appear in the text.
The praise of virtues may be understood according to the text.

[Sutra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable Kinnara kings, namely: the Kinnara King Good Wisdom Radiance; the Kinnara King... [and so forth].
The Kinnara King Wondrous Flower Banner, the Kinnara King Various Adornments, the Kinnara King Delightful Roar,

the Kinnara King Subtle and Wondrous Flower Banner, and the Kinnara King Power to Shake the Earth.
King Nara subdued the hosts of evil beings, with the Kinnara King and others as their leaders;
they were immeasurable in number, all of them diligent and energetic, contemplating all phenomena with minds constantly joyful and sporting in sovereign ease.
[Treatise] The third section, the King of Kinnaras (consisting of seven lines and one hundred and seventeen words), clarifies the dedication of all Buddhas.

It shows that because all Buddhas abide within birth and death, they take the gate of *dharmakṣānti* (patience regarding phenomena) as the sovereign of the myriad practices, so that all sentient beings may attain the unsurpassed Dharma-bliss of Bodhi; thus, it is figuratively expressed through the Kinnara.
The King of the Rākṣasas, here translated as "Doubting Spirit" (Yíshén), is also the presiding deity of the practice. He appears human but has horns upon his head and a mouth like that of an ox;
when people see him, they all doubt whether he is a human or a non-human. Therefore, he is called the Doubting Spirit.

A Bodhisattva at this stage, having perfected the mind of great compassion through the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) and by the power of the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*), is born into the six realms of existence to practice in common with those beings.
When people see this person benefiting others, they all doubt whether he is an ordinary person or a sage. If he were an ordinary person, his wisdom would be like that of a Buddha;
if he were a worthy sage, his conduct would be identical to that of an ordinary person. Therefore, the spirit is invoked to manifest his practice.

This spirit can act as the master of deeds and the master of celestial play; through the gate of the *kṣānti-pāramitā* (perfection of patience), it takes patience as the master of the ten thousand practices.
If there is no patience (*kṣānti*), the myriad practices (*sādhana*) will not be accomplished; therefore, patience is the sovereign of all practices.

Within this, the four meanings should be understood by analogy with what was stated above. As for the ten deities of doubt, one may observe how the ten *pāramitās* are assigned to the ten names according to their respective meanings;
these belong to the category of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable mahoraga kings, namely: the mahoraga king Good Wisdom (Suvijñāna), the mahoraga king Pure Majestic Sound (Vimala-garjita-ghoṣa),
the mahoraga king Victorious Wisdom Adorned Topknot (Jaya-prajñā-vyūha-cūḍa), the mahoraga king Lord of Wondrous Eyes (Cakṣur-indra),
the mahoraga king Lamp Banner to Whom All Turn (Pradīpa-dhvaja-sarva-gati-gata), and the mahoraga king Most Victorious (Parama-jaya).
The mahoraga king Prabhāketu, the mahoraga king Siṃhakukṣi, the mahoraga king Citravyūhaghoṣa, the mahoraga king Sumerudṛḍha, the mahoraga king Priyakāntaprabha,
and others such as these were their leaders; they were immeasurable in number, and all had diligently practiced.
Through vast skillful means, they cause all sentient beings to forever sever the net of ignorance.
[Treatise] The fourth is the Mahoraga King (eight lines of text, one hundred thirty-one words). This is translated as "Great Python" (*mahoraga*), or also as "Great-Bellied Raga.
*Raga* means "one who moves by chest and belly. He presides over the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) and moves by chest and belly.
This clarifies that those who seek the benefit of the Dharma prostrate themselves, abandoning pride and practicing humility and respect;
this is the meaning of diligence. It clarifies the dedication that reaches all places: there is no place among the six realms and four modes of birth where it does not enter.

This refers to the protection of the *kṣetrapāla* (temple guardian deity), for they are able to protect the Dharma. As stated in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" [Chapter on the Realm of Reality]: "Seeing the Buddha, one rejoices," and so forth.

He personally paid homage to the Mahoraga King; herein, the ten kings illustrate the ten pāramitās within the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), each of which may be understood by correlating its name with its meaning.

This assembly also clarifies that skillful means (*upāya*) are identical to the attachments of sentient beings, illustrating how Bodhisattvas dwell in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) practicing together with them to bring about their liberation.
The net of craving is as described below in the section on praising virtues, where one practices vast skillful means to cause all sentient beings to forever sever the net of ignorance.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable yakṣa kings, namely: the yakṣa king Vaiśravaṇa, the yakṣa king Sovereign Sound (Vaiśvāsvara), and so forth.
The Yakṣa King Śaktidhara, the Yakṣa King Mahāprajña, the Yakṣa King Jvālākṣa,
the Yakṣa King Vajranetra, the Yakṣa King Vikrātabhuja, the Yakṣa King Śūraprativīryasainyapramardin,

Their number is immeasurable, and they all diligently protect all sentient beings.
[Treatise] The fifth Yakṣa King (five lines and a half; ninety-one characters) clarifies the inexhaustible treasury of merit dedicated by the Master of Dedication, the Perfection of Dhyāna.
Through the power of meditative concentration, this Yakṣa protects the minds of all sentient beings, causing their minds...
Because he does not falsely acquire a great treasury of merit, the yakṣa—here translated as "suffering existence" (kùhuó)—is also named "Discerning Clarity" (sìchá míng).
Through the gate of dhyāna, he guards and discerns the "suffering existence" mind of all sentient beings, ensuring that the mind does not stray.
As the Dharmadhātu-parivarta states: "Always diligently guarding the various yakṣa kings of sentient beings," and so forth; these are the ten other kings.
Within the dhyāna-pāramitā, the ten pāramitās may be understood by assigning their names and meanings according to their respective stages.
Furthermore, the yakṣa lord Vaiśravaṇa derives his name from being the master of the Vaiśravaṇas;
he leads the host of yakṣas and resides on the northern face of Mount Sumeru.
