the Nāga King Meghasvaraghoṣaketu, the Nāga King Jvālāmukhasāgaraprabha, the Nāga King Samantocchrayameghaketu,
the Nāga King Takṣaka, the Nāga King Anantapada, the Nāga King Viśuddhavarṇa, and the Nāga King Samantavāhanamahānirghoṣa.
With King Anavatapta Nāgarāja as their leader, there were an immeasurable number of such beings who all diligently raised clouds and spread rain,
causing the heat and afflictions of all sentient beings to be extinguished.
[Treatise] Sixth (five lines and a half; ninety-two characters). The Nāga King Virūpākṣa also derives his name from those under his jurisdiction.
As the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, he presides over the hosts of nāgas on the western side of Mount Sumeru.
Furthermore, there is Pūtana, who presides over the spirits of feverish diseases. This Nāga King presides over the illumination of the *anuloma-dṛḍha-pariṇāmanā*.
If the gates of the *pāramitās* are like a dragon roaming through the sky— able to appear and disappear, and raining down moisture to nourish sentient beings—
and because the sovereign wisdom of *prajñā-śūnyatā* rains down the rain of all dharmas to benefit sentient beings across both existence and non-existence,
they are represented by the dragon. As for Virūpākṣa, it is fully called Virūpākṣa, and is also translated as "Diverse Speech."
The "Lord" (nātha) was formerly called "Ugly-Eyed" (*Vikṛtākṣa*); the new name "Vi" signifies "various," while "lu" signifies "color.

"Pāhakhcha" signifies the "eye-faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya*). It means that the eye-faculty is adorned with various colors, and all views are adorned with various wisdoms so that one sees without attachment.
There are five kinds of *nāgas*: first, elephant-shaped; second, snake-shaped; third, horse-shaped... [and so forth].
1. The form of a fish; 2. The form of a frog. First, the Nāga King Supratiṣṭhita, who is the lord of all elephant-shaped nāgas;
second, the Nāga King Nanda—translated here as "Joy"—who is the lord of all snake-shaped nāgas;
third, the Nāga King Nābhadatta—translated here as "Free from Heat and Affliction," also named "Cool"—who is the lord of all horse-shaped [nāgas].
O Dragon Lord, this one dragon king is far removed from three kinds of afflictions of the dragons: first, hot sand does not fall upon his head;
second, he does not engage in sexual desire in the form of a snake; third, he has no fear of the *garuḍa* bird. Furthermore, there is yet another suffering:
when the wind blows away his precious robes, his body is exposed, giving rise to pain. Only this dragon king is exempt from such distress.
Therefore it is said that "Pure Coolness" relies upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. This Dragon King is a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage (*saptamī-bhūmi*).
The fourth is the Dragon King Vāsuki (Pāruṇa), which in Chinese means "Water Heaven," who is the lord of all fish-shaped dragons.

The fifth is the Dragon King Mānasvāti, also named Mānasa, which in Chinese means "Compassionate Heart"; because of his compassionate heart, the wind does not rustle the branches when it blows, and the rain...
Abhaṅga-kūṭa is also named "Attained the Intention" (*Iṣṭārtha*), and is also called *Mana*, which means "High Intention.
Because this dragon possesses majestic power (*mahānubhāva*), he is named "High Intention. He is the lord of all frogs-shaped dragons, as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"When dragons first take birth, when they sleep, when they are angry, and when they engage in desire—during these four times..."
They are unable to transform their forms at other times, yet they are able to transform them in all other circumstances; this is how it is with dragon kings within the context of the Three Vehicles.
As for dragon kings within this One Vehicle, their virtues consist entirely of Great Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of the Buddha-fruit of the inconceivable vehicle;
for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they universally manifest themselves throughout all realms of existence.
Now, within this assembly, the body celebrates the Buddha’s appearance in the world to repay his original vows;
it assumes a provisional station to symbolize the Dharma, as in this very sutra, where the Naga King Virūpākṣa attains the liberation door of extinguishing all the naga realms of blazing fire.
To clarify this stage, the dragon of Prajñā-wisdom constantly roams within the emptiness of phenomena through various means.
By establishing various nets of teaching through language, this is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) within the tenth stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
O Dragon King Sāgara, this ocean is the liberation door of being able, in a single thought-moment, to transform one's own dragon form and manifest as the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings;
it clarifies that this is the attainment of the retribution of great compassion and ethical discipline upon entering the ocean of birth and death.
Through the power of vows and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), these ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) fundamentally constitute the practice of compassion and vows.
The Dragon King Cloud-Sound Banner (*Meghasvara-dhvaja*) attained the liberation door of proclaiming the ocean of the Buddha’s boundless names with a pure voice throughout all realms of existence.
This clarifies that patience brings forth renown; thus one obtains such benefits.
In the *Fen zhong* (Section on Divisions), the Dragon King Takṣaka is extensively explained as follows: "Takṣa" means "the one who is harmed," and "ka" means "the one who harms.
This refers to the fact that when this dragon becomes enraged, his mere gaze causes humans and animals to meet their end.
As for the older translation "Many-Tongued Dragon" (*Duoshe Long*), it was so called because of his excessive speech; thus, he is termed "Many-Tongued."
It is not because there are many tongues in his mouth that he is so described; rather, it signifies his progress in cultivation.
This is the sixth *prajñāpāramitā* gate, for he skillfully expounds many teachings and is thus called "many-tongued. He assumes this dragon position as a metaphorical manifestation of the Dharma.
The following sections should be understood by correlating names and meanings according to the above pattern. Thus, these ten dragon kings represent the ten [stages].
In the dedication, the *prajñāpāramitā* serves as the essence, representing wisdom that wanders in emptiness and rains down the Dharma with mastery.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable kumbhāṇḍa kings, namely: the Kumbhāṇḍa King Vardhana, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Nāgendra, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Suvyūhita-dhvaja, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Samantopakāracaryā, and the Kumbhāṇḍa King Ati...
The Kumbhāṇḍa King Bhīṣaṇa, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Surucirakṣa, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Uccagati, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Vikrātabhuja, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Anantaviśuddhapuṣpanetra,
the Kumbhāṇḍa King Vipuladevavaktrāsuranetra— these and others were their leaders, and their number was incalculable.
All measure their diligent cultivation of the unimpeded dharma-gate and emit great radiance.

[Treatise] The seventh [section] (consisting of six lines and a half of scripture, totaling one hundred twelve words) concerns the dedication that accords with all sentient beings, presided over by the King of Kumbhāṇḍas;
it clarifies how the Bodhisattva of this stage achieves great compassion, enters universally into all paths, and extends kindness.
To benefit sentient beings is to encounter those possessed by malevolent spirits who consume their vital essence; these are also called "winter melon ghosts" (*tenggua gui*).
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, such evil beings have names like these. Toward them as well, the Bodhisattva accords with them accordingly;
therefore, this is called the dedication that accords equally with all sentient beings, extending even to entering everywhere into the hells.
This deity is the King of the Southern Quarter who leads two classes of beings: first, the *kumbhāṇḍas*, and second, the *piśācas*.
As for these *kumbhāṇḍas*, their scrotums are as large as winter melons; when walking, they lift them onto their shoulders, and when sitting, they squat upon them.
The "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" states: "One should constantly and diligently strive to eliminate all those in the realm of hungry ghosts."

The Kumbhāṇḍa kings clearly manifest passionate craving and seeking, like hungry ghosts; yet the Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion exhaustively employ their powers to follow them, severing all craving and seeking.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable Gandharva kings, namely: the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the Gandharva King Vṛkṣaprabha.
The Gandharva King Pure Eyes; the Gandharva King Flower Crown; the Gandharva King Universal Sound; the Gandharva King Delightfully Moving Sublime Eyes;
the Gandharva King Sublime Sound Lion Banner; the Gandharva King Universally Radiating Jewel Light;
the Gandharva King Vajra Tree Flower Banner; and the Gandharva King Delightfully Manifesting Everywhere.

The Gandharva King Śobhana and others such as these were the leaders; they were immeasurable in number, all of whom had developed profound faith and understanding in the Great Dharma, cherishing it with joy and affection, and diligently practicing it without weariness.

[Treatise] The eighth [dedication] (consisting of six and a half lines and one hundred twelve words) is the Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*). It employs the Gandharva King as a metaphor for the Dharma;
"Gandharva" here means "Seeker of Fragrance," referring to those who seek their sustenance by making music wherever there is fragrance.

By relying on this event, it symbolizes the aspect of the stage of True Suchness: that Bodhisattvas constantly [abide in] the True Suchness Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through the precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation.
The fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body of liberation-knowledge and vision—which is free from defilement—delights sentient beings and causes them to cherish it;
therefore, the subsequent text says: "All [beings] give rise to deep faith and understanding in the Great Dharma, joyfully cherishing and respecting it, practicing with diligence without weariness.
The *Dharmadhātu-praveśa-parivarta* states: "Constantly causing sentient beings to increase in joy, O Gandharva King."
Because the meaning is to gladden sentient beings with the Dharma, within this stage the ten kings clarify the perfection of vows;
herein, the wisdom of this stage increases, and by establishing teachings according to the faculties [of beings], it gladdens sentient beings and causes them to rejoice.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable Moon Devas, namely: the Moon Deva, the Flower-King-Tuft-Luminous Deva,
the Multitude-of-Exquisite-Pure-Luminosity Deva, the Peaceful-and-Joyful-World-Mind Deva, the Tree-King-Eye-Luminosity Deva, the Manifestation-of-Pure-Light Deva,
the Universal-Wandering-Immovable-Light Deva, and the Sovereign-of-the-Constellations-King Deva.
The Devaputra Śuddhabuddhi, the Devaputra Candrama, the Devaputra Mahātejaḥprabhāsa, and others such as these were their leaders;
they were immeasurable in number, and all were diligently manifesting the jewel of the minds of sentient beings.

[Treatise] Ninth (five lines and a half; ninety-two characters): The Dedication of Liberation Unbound and Unattached. This relies on the phenomenon of the Moon Deity (*Candradeva*) to manifest the Perfection of Power (*bala-pāramitā*).

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unbound and unattached, like empty space, wisdom illuminates sentient beings, purifying the heat of their afflictions and enabling them to attain the coolness of the Dharma. Within this [section], there are ten Moon Deities.
The ten *pāramitās* within the *balapāramitā* may be understood by correlating them with their respective names and meanings.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable Sun Devas (*sūryadevaputra*), namely:
the Sun Deva, the Flame-Eyed Deva, the Sumeru-Light Deva, the Dreadful and Venerable Banner Deva, the Stainless Jewel-Adorned Deva, and the Valiant Non-Retrogressive Deva.
The sons— such as the Devaputra Subhūṣitasragprabha, the Devaputra Jayadhvaja-prabhāsa, the Devaputra Ratnaśikhara-samantaprabha,
the Devaputra Prabhāsanetra, the Devaputra Jitaguṇa, and the Devaputra Samantaprabha— were the leaders among them;
they were immeasurable in number, all of whom diligently practiced for the benefit of sentient beings and increased their roots of goodness.
[Treatise] The tenth [dedication], consisting of six lines and ninety-nine words, is the dedication of entering the infinite dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

This is illustrated by means of the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*) as a symbolic event, clarifying that among the ten dedications, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is like the sun situated in space, looking down from above to illuminate the myriad phenomena.
While its position is high, its merit benefits those below; the Bodhisattva of this stage is likewise, for their wisdom is exceedingly lofty.
His practice descends further and further, penetrating through humans, devas, spirits, ghosts, those of external paths and heterodox practices,
animals, and down to the hells, such that all share in his practice. Just as the sun and moon have their forms above but their efficacy below,
illuminating both good and evil, so too within the ten days of the Son of Heaven of Wisdom, each of the ten *pāramitās* is fully realized.
The names and meanings are assigned accordingly, with the *prajñāpāramitā* (perfection of wisdom) always serving as its essential substance.
The above assignment of the ten kings to the ten *pāramitās* within the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) is concluded.

Just as in the ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten Dedications, and even up to the ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), one may grasp the general principle by taking the *pāramitā* appropriate to each respective stage. Thus, one obtains a single consistent pattern.
Regarding this, one does not know its specific course; as for the two positions of the sun and moon, their shapes and elevations are as described in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*:
the moon is forty thousand *yojanas* from the earth and forty *yojanas* in diameter.

Its two surfaces are composed of crystal and white silver, which revolve and reflect one another, thus causing its waning and waxing. This treatise explains it in this manner. However, [the following] has not yet been stated.
One may take this as a definitive basis; however, for those who rely on the scriptural teachings as their guide, according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, above that moon there is a city.
This city is square, measuring one thousand nine hundred and sixty *li* on each side, with its height and depth being the same.
It is composed of two parts of celestial gold and one part of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*). From a distance it appears circular, and the sons of gods [residing there] live for five hundred years.
The descendants succeed one another for the duration of a kalpa. When the sun and moon are near each other, their light and shadow reflect upon one another, resulting in waning and waxing;
this can be taken as the fixed rule. The city is fifty yojanas wide, square, measuring two thousand forty li on each side, and its height and depth are likewise the same.
The city is made of pure gold and adorned with the seven treasures. The king’s throne is twenty li away, and his lifespan is that of his son.
The Sun and Moon Devas, by virtue of being sustained by the wind, circumambulate Mount Sumeru;
these Sun and Moon Devas are all governed by the Four Heavenly Kings. This above has been explained primarily according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

Thus, the Sun and Moon Devas represent the gateway of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) that perfect the practice of great compassionate vows, clarifying that compassion and wisdom are without dependence.
It constantly takes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) as its essence, universally illuminating according to the faculties [of beings] without any deliberate effort;
it accomplishes benefit for the myriad existences through effortless wisdom that accords with the sun.
Fifth, from the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven downward to the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) Heavenly King, within this there is...
Regarding the ten great celestial kings who clarify the causes and effects of benefiting sentient beings through the ten stages:
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there are immeasurable kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, namely:
Śakra Indrāyaṇa Devendra, Samantaghoṣeśvararāja Devendra, Maitreyanetra-ratna-śikhara Devendra, Ratnārci-dhvaja-kīrti Devendra, and Janman...
The celestial kings headed by Ratiśikha, Priyadarśana-smṛti, Sumeru-jaya-ghoṣa, Smṛtisiddhi,
Priyadarśana-vimala-padma-prabha, Jñānasūrya-netra, and Vaśitā-prabhāsa-bodhana, were immeasurable in number; all of them diligently exerted themselves.
The Vast Karma of All Worlds.

[Treatise] From the first, the thirty-three gods (*Trāyastriṃśa*), the ten great heavenly kings (six lines of verse, one hundred and seven characters), entrusting the events to signify the meaning of the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*), which is divided into four parts:
first, listing the names and titles of the heavenly kings; second, using their stations to signify...
I. The Dharma; II. Explaining the Names; III. Correlating with Practice; IV. Summarizing the Number; V. Praising the Virtues. 1.
As for citing the names of the celestial kings, it is as the sutra says: "namely, the celestial king Śakrendra and so forth—the names of the ten great celestial kings.
2. As for using these positions to symbolize the Dharma, it means entrusting this heaven to represent that a Bodhisattva on the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) has attained joy.
At this stage, one attains the joy of the Dharma; because there is no attachment to the five worldly desires or other such fetters, this bliss is solely the bliss of the Dharma.

For this reason, one experiences abundant rapture and profound contentment, much like a worldly person who has newly been born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and enjoys celestial delights, or like one who has ascended a mountain peak and reached the limit of the signless (*animitta*).

The body merges with emptiness; this clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage ascends from the conditioned nature of the habitual tendencies of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications to this position of the first bhūmi at the juncture of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Because a portion of the habitual tendencies is exhausted, the summit of Mount Sumeru and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are used as metaphors for this stage to facilitate understanding. (10)

Abiding in the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) is metaphorically represented as being like a divine spirit; the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are metaphorically represented as being like a king;

and these ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are metaphorically represented as being like the light of heaven. One should understand that their progressive cultivation and gradual familiarization with the sublime are encompassed by the three pairs of six characters through the gates of totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration. They are likewise encompassed by the ten mysteries (*daśa-mithuna*). Thus it is.
Regarding the distinctions in progressive cultivation, in a single moment, neither identity nor difference can be grasped as they appear to the ordinary mind;
this may be seen by reflecting according to the principle. Furthermore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The stage of the practicing lineage possesses a copper wheel over two continents;
the silver wheel over three; the nature lineage, the path lineage, and the stage of firm virtue possess the seven treasures of a universal monarch with a golden wheel over four."
At the beginning of the world, a Bodhisattva of the first stage is the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and a Bodhisattva of the second stage is the King of the Yāma Heaven;
thus, their stations are successively assigned to correspond [to these realms]. It is clear that their merit and wisdom are so preeminent that worldly pleasures cannot be compared to them.
To speak in truth, they are embraced by the compassion and wisdom of the Bodhisattvas, such that wherever they are born throughout the six realms, they do not abandon even the most minute [beings].

They flow forth for the sake of benefiting all classes of sentient beings; because the *dharmatā* is sovereign, they are metaphorically designated as being like gods or kings to signify the meaning of sovereignty. They do not delight in worldly pleasures, and this is what is signified.
As stated in the later sections of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, bodhisattvas on the first stage (*bhūmi*) frequently act as kings of Jambudvīpa; now, these ten great celestial kings [are likewise].
This is merely to indicate that the progressive cultivation of the Dharma does not depart from a single kṣaṇa, yet gradually becomes increasingly sublime.

Furthermore, this heaven is named the Heaven of the Wondrous High (Sumeru). This mountain is situated in the great ocean; it rises eighty million yojanas above the water and extends eighty million yojanas deep into the water.
It is composed of four precious substances: its northern face is of gold, its southern face is of lapis lazuli, and its western [face is of silver].
Facing the east, its surface is made of crystal and its form is like a waist-drum; upon it are four tiers where the Four Heavenly Kings each dwell according to their respective directions.
On the summit of the mountain are four peaks, and on each peak reside eight heavenly kings, each with their own retinue.
At the center of the summit dwells Śakra, adorned with all manner of precious jewels; for these reasons, it is named Sumeru (the Wondrous High).

It is also called Mount Sumeru and is also called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; this is translated as "The Heaven of the Sovereign," so named because Śakra is able to act as the Lord of Devas, and thus the name is derived from its presiding deity.
Below it are seven successive layers of oceans, each surrounded by distinct mountains of gold.
The Garuḍas can fly there in seven days before finally reaching the golden mountains. There are heavens inhabited there, all of which belong to the Four Heavenly Kings.
Regarding those beings in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) who are governed by the King [of Gods]: their bodies are one yojana in height;
their garments are two yojanas in length and one yojana in width, weighing six *zhū*; their lifespan is one thousand years.
One day and night there is equivalent to one hundred years in the human realm; thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year.
The above is based on the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises on the three natures, which state that this Heavenly King has five names:
first, Śakra; second, Śakradevendra; third, Kauśika; fourth, Śakro Devānām Indraḥ;
and fifth, Indra. This is the name for the Lord of Devas. To speak fully, it is Śakrendra. Regarding "Śakra": this...
The name "Hundred" refers to the prior cause; by establishing one hundred *anantara* (unrestricted) assemblies, one attains the status of a Heavenly Lord (*devendra*).

This corresponds to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) within the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). The ten heavenly kings below this are to be understood as the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) within the perfection of giving, each assigned according to its respective name and meaning.
The textual assignments for these four sections may be seen as previously described.
Knowing that the phenomena of this stage— the Bodhisattva’s contemplative practice as an antidote— consist of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and the unreality of worldly dharmas,

all of which arise from the twelve links of dependent origination and are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics, he accomplishes the dharma of equanimity regarding his body, life, and wealth. Thus, through faith and compliance with all the Buddha-dharmas,
he practices and first remedies the coarse karma of stinginess in the desire realm by cultivating the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

For Bodhisattvas on the sixth stage who have not yet fully understood dependent origination, the twelve links of dependent origination are clarified through the analogy of repeatedly smelting true gold in fire; this illustrates the remedy for the obstacle of stinginess.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable Suyāma Heavenly Kings, namely: the Heavenly King Sucintita-kāla, the Heavenly King Priya-darśana-prabhāsa,
the Heavenly King Akṣaya-jñāna-guṇa-dhvaja, the Heavenly King Su-vikurvaṇa-sudarśana, the Heavenly King Dhāraṇī-mahāprabha,
the Heavenly King Acintya-jñāna, the Heavenly King Cakra-nābhi, and the Heavenly King Arciḥ-prabhāsa.
The King Radiant Light (*Prabhāsa*), the Heavenly King Universal Observer (*Samantadarśin*), the Heavenly King of Great Renown (*Mahāyaśas*), and others such as these were their leaders;
they were immeasurable in number, all of whom diligently cultivated vast roots of goodness and were ever content in mind.

[Treatise] Second, there are furthermore immeasurable Suyāma Heavenly Kings (occupying five lines and ninety-five characters of scripture). By means of this event, it symbolizes the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*);
because these devas are separated from the earth’s surface, they dwell in the void and possess various wondrous pleasures.

This stage corresponds to the Bodhisattva whose perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) has increased and excelled; possessing the sublime joy of the Dharma, they abide by means of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Because it constitutes the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*), one gradually advances and becomes detached from the worldly fetters of the preceding stage;

thus, in this first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) is predominant, while the pure precepts of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) in their highest degree are predominant. This stage is called "Stainless" (*vimalā*).

In the first stage, Mount Sumeru’s summit is metaphorically linked to the world of humans, sharing the same worldly realm; in this stage, however, the celestial abodes of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) are metaphorically linked to the transcendence of the world.
The first stage is called "Stainless" because it is free from worldly defilements;

it is likened to refined gold that has not yet been treated with medicinal salts, but which becomes increasingly bright and pure through repeated exposure to fire. In this stage, the refining of the true gold is further enhanced by the addition of alum;
taking the precepts as the alum, the essence of gold remains non-dual, and the precepts serve as the antidote to craving within the desire realm.
The coarse obstacles such as desire and so forth are polished and refined by means of the medicinal dharmas of the Dharma-body, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the great vows,
the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, the ten perfections, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, thereby rendering wisdom and compassion sovereign.
Thus, the Yāma Heaven— here translated as the "Time-Division Heaven"— is so named because this heaven has no sun.
The light of the Moon Deity naturally illuminates itself, making no distinction between day and night; one knows the divisions of day and night only by the opening and closing of the lotuses.
The bodies of the gods here are two yojanas in height, and their garments are four yojanas long and two yojanas wide, weighing three *zhu*.
Their lifespan is two thousand years, and the calculation of days, months, and years is double that of the previous heaven. This is the King of that Heaven.

There are ten classes of celestial beings; this clearly illustrates that within these precepts of *pāramitā*, the ten *pāramitās* are each assigned according to their respective stages and meanings, as can be understood by correlating them.
In this stage, one cultivates the supreme ten wholesome precepts (*daśakuśala-śīla*) to remedy the coarse afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) active in the desire realm.
Only upon cultivating the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) in the third stage will the afflictions of the three realms no longer arise.
Coming to this house, they share the same nature as the Tathāgata.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there are inconceivable numbers of Tuṣita Heaven kings, namely:
the King Saṃtuṣita, the King Nandisāgarajaṭa, the King Varaguṇadhvaja, the King Śāntaprabha, and the King Priyadarśana.
Led by such celestial kings as Sunetra (Wondrous Eye), Ratnaśikhara-vimalacandra (Jewel Peak Pure Moon),
Paramavikrāntabalavega (Supreme Valiant Power), Vajrasuprabha (Vajra Wondrous Light), Jyotirvicitradhvaja (Constellation Adorned Banner),
and Priyadarśanavyūha (Lovely Adornment), they were an inconceivable number who all diligently remembered and upheld the names of all Buddhas.
[Commentary]:
Thirdly, there is the inconceivable Tushita Heavenly King (six lines of text, one hundred words). This relies on the event to symbolize the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
This is called the Heaven of Contentment (*santuṣita-deva*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that this is the Bodhisattva in his final existence (*carama-bhavika*).

Regarding this teaching, according to the *Sūtra on the Original Action of the Garland* (*Ārya-śrī-māyopama-sūtra*), it is only upon reaching the eleventh stage, the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi-bhūmi*), that one is called a "One-Life-to-Enlightenment" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*) and is designated as being in their final body (*carama-deha*). This is assigned to the third dhyāna.

These Devaputras of the Heaven of Contentment who serve as the final bodies for Bodhisattvas therein are all Tathāgatas who, through timely skillful means, have established the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.

It cannot be definitively established. The preceding stage clarifies that through the ten supreme wholesome precepts (*daśa-kuśala-śīla*), one is free from the stains of the coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) currently active in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Therefore, in this stage, the Bodhisattva, by means of the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), purifies the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the desire realm;
having mastered the mind that transcends the three realms, it is like the skillful smelting of gold. Through such refinement, it is not [fixed].
When even a fraction of a *zhu* or *liang* is lost, one turns toward ever-greater clarity and purity.

One refines this with the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), contemplates it with the Dharma-eye, and applies it through practice without deficiency in the fundamental method. Thus, it becomes increasingly clear and pure.

One cultivates concentration (*samādhi*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to remedy the obstacle of desire, and cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*) in the higher realms to remedy the obstacle to concentration. Such remedial application is precisely as in the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva, abiding in the first dhyāna of the form realm, cultivates the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination to remedy the obstacles to meditative concentration.
By practicing the skillful means of conforming to the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, he remains unstained by attachment; this is the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).
Its essence is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Within this, the ten great celestial kings represent the ten perfections within the perfection of patience; these are the deities.
Their height is four *yojanas*; their robes are eight *yojanas* long and four *yojanas* wide; their lifespan is four thousand years.
The measurements of days, months, and years are all double those of the preceding heaven. Those who wish to be born among these gods of Contentment (*Tuṣita*) should cultivate three dharmas:

namely, ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). If one cultivates only ethical discipline and generosity (*dāna*), one will be born in other heavens where there is universal negligence (*pramāda*).
In the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, however, this is not so, for its celestial essence consists of all-pervading wisdom.

[Sūtra] Furthermore, there are immeasurable kings of the Heaven of Delightful Transformation (Nirmāṇarati), namely: the King of Good Transformation (Sunirmita), the King of Silent Sound-Light (Śāntasvaraprabha), the King of Radiance of Transformative Power (Vikurvaṇabala-prabha), the King Lord of Adornments (Vyūhādhipati), the King Light of Mindfulness (Smṛtiprabha), and the Supreme...
The Celestial King Cloud Sound, the Celestial King Most Victorious Light of Wondrousness, the Celestial King Radiant Crest of Sublime Light,
the Celestial King Accomplished Joyful Wisdom, the Celestial King Flower-Light Crest, and the Celestial King Universally Beholding the Ten Directions—
these and others were their leaders, numbering immeasurably; all were diligently subduing all sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation.
[Treatise] The fourth is the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven (consisting of five lines and ninety-seven words). By means of an event, it symbolizes the Bodhisattva of the Arciṣmatī Bhūmi.
Taking the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) as the means of contemplation, he takes equanimity (*upekṣā*) as his essence.

Because of his original vows and because the nature of dharmas is thus, he does not abandon the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings, adorning them through the gates of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The Noble Wisdom Karma (Sudharmakarma) uses the transformation and benefit of all sentient beings as its own joy;

just as this celestial realm constantly delights itself through transformations, it is also called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*). Since there are no external objects apart from the mind, they arise from the transformation of the mind.
This indicates that for Bodhisattvas in this stage, from the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*) onward, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) is manifested before the mind.

Because there is no external object to serve as the basis for further cultivation, one employs the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) as auxiliary gateways to the Path to counteract the obstacles of false views pertaining to this heaven and the three realms.

By refining and polishing the ground of the mind to adorn the work of wisdom so that it becomes luminous and pure, one intends to teach and transform all sentient beings, taking this as one's own joy; therefore, it is called the "Blazing Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī*) stage.
As stated in the *Bodhisattva-śiṅgala-mūla-karma-sūtra*: "1. The Bodhisattva of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is named 'Flowing Against the Stream' (*pratikūla-srota*);
2. The Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*) is named 'Flow of the Path' (*mārga-srota*); 3. The Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*) is named 'Entering the Stream' (*srotāpanna*);
4. The Fourth Stage is *Srotāpanna*; 5. The Fifth Stage is *Sakṛdāgāmin*; 6. The Sixth Stage is *Anāgāmin*; 7. The Seventh Stage is *Arhat*; 8. The Eighth Stage is Transformation."
The nine stages of transforming birth and death are the stage of wondrous goodness of wisdom; the tenth stage is the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the *Śrī-guṇavyūha-sūtra* states that Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes enter the flow of the Dharma and spontaneously reach Buddhahood.
Thus, within each of the five positions—the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage—of this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, [the same applies].

Each [of these stages] has ten levels. Taking the conduct of Samantabhadra as the cause for the fruit of Buddhahood, at the stage of the Ten Faiths, the mind comes to believe that the nature of one's own mind’s discrimination is the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, the Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom, and so forth—these ten fruits of Buddhahood are collectively the wisdom of one's own mind;
only then is it called "faith. In this way, one reconciles many various similarities and differences according to one's faith.

To discern distinctions such as kinship and estrangement based merely on one's own specific school while practicing the gates of cultivation is to rely on the gates of the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and disintegration;
yet these are all universally encompassed and perfectly interfused within the single moment (*kṣaṇa*), which is the meaning of "pervasive penetration.
If one were to seek understanding by extending time, it would violate the principle of the Dharma-realm. Within this assembly of celestial kings, there are ten celestial kings.
All these are the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), each to be understood by assigning them according to their respective names and meanings;

this stage always takes the pāramitā of diligence as its essence. It is likened to refining pure gold into ornamental vessels, and it is said that through the clear cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) as a counteractive measure against the delusions of the three realms, diligence acts as an adornment.
Due to the habitual tendencies of their karma, the bodies of these devas are eight yojanas in height; their garments are sixteen yojanas long and eight yojanas wide;
their lifespan is eight thousand years, measured by the days and months of the preceding heaven; their clothing weighs one *zhu*;
they consume the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*); and the praise of their virtues and other details may be understood as before.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were countless kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, namely: King Sovereign Attainment,
King Wondrous Eye Lord, King Wondrous Crown Banner, King Courageous Wisdom, King Wondrous Sound Phrase,
King Wondrous Light Banner, King Tranquil Realm Gate, King Wondrous Wheel Adornment Banner, and King Flower Pistil Wisdom.
The Lord of the Heaven of Sovereignty, Indra, the King of Sublime Adornment and Radiant Light, and others such as these were the leaders;
they were immeasurable in number, and all had diligently practiced the great Dharma-gate of the skillful means of mastery.

[Treatise] Fifth, there are furthermore countless kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven (occupying five lines and ninety-seven characters of scripture). This uses a concrete event to symbolize the "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*) stage.
It indicates that because this heaven is at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it clarifies that the objects of the bodhisattva’s desires are difficult to transcend;
hence it is called the Difficult to Conquer stage. It clarifies that from the fifth stage onward, the bodhisattva has not yet [fully mastered] the objects of the five desires.
Because they have attained complete mastery and merely contemplate the power of the practice of the various *pāramitās*, they do not sink into them;

yet, because they have not yet attained the effortless flow of mastery characteristic of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), the Bodhisattvas at this stage cultivate the contemplation of the ten truths (*daśatattva*) to remedy the habitual tendencies of the afflictions and cognitive obstructions regarding the defilement and purity of the three realms. Consequently, they attain the gateway to the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-kalā-vidyā*). Five.

Only when clearly manifesting this celestial realm and treating it with the cultivation of the ten-fold contemplation on truth (*daśa-tattva-vipaśyanā*) does one transcend it; otherwise, it becomes a demonic realm (*māra-gocara*).
Because one cannot attain mastery over the karmic habits of defilement and purity within the three realms, it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" stage (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
At this level, the Bodhisattva constantly takes the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) as the essence of their contemplation, while Māra Pāpīyān dwells within this celestial realm.
To cultivate the contemplation of the ten truths is itself the stage of a Bodhisattva; those who do not cultivate this contemplation belong to the retinue of Māra.
Furthermore, this heaven is named Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Mastery over Others' Emanations), because it takes the emanations of others as its own pleasure.

Likewise, a Bodhisattva at this stage constantly teaches and transforms sentient beings, taking the attainment of happiness by others as his own happiness. This is like grinding gold with mother-of-pearl.

To illustrate this, the ten truths are used as the mother-of-pearl inlay; therein, the ten great celestial kings clarify the ten pāramitās within the dhyāna-pāramitā, which can be understood by correlating them with the meanings of their respective names.
The bodies of these devas are sixteen yojanas in height, their robes are thirty-two yojanas in length, and their lifespans in years and months are all double those of the preceding [heaven].
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were incalculable Great Brahmā Kings, namely: King Śikhin, King Prajñāprabha,
King Su-prajñāprabhāsa, King Samanta-megha-ghoṣa, King Lokeśvara-vaśavarti-ghoṣa,
King Śāntaprabhā-netra, King Prabhā-samanta-daśadik, King Nirmāṇa-ghoṣa, and King Prabhābhāsvara.
The Celestial King Resplendent, the Celestial King Ocean-Sound Pleasing to the Mind, and others such as these were their leaders;
they were beyond counting, all endowed with great compassion and pity for sentient beings, emitting light that shone everywhere to bring them happiness.
[Treatise] Sixth, there are again incalculable Great Brahmā Kings (this section contains five lines and a half of text, ninety-six characters).

It clarifies that on the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), by means of the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), one attains the supernormal powers of cessation (*nirodha-abhijñā*) and the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa-mukha*).

Wisdom increases and becomes luminous, eliminating the obstacle of being deluded regarding reality while clinging to the bliss of tranquility in the First Dhyāna; it clarifies that [the practitioner] remains within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Cultivating meditative concentration within the realms (*dhātu*) is like that of a Bodhisattva of the third stage.
When the mind becomes defiled while cultivating wisdom within the realm of dhyāna, one immediately subdues it with the Dharma so as not to obstruct the true nature that is without dependence;
therefore, though constantly dwelling within the three realms, one does not abide therein. He is named Śikhin Devendra; according to the new translation, this is based on *Brahmavasu*, which means:

Purity and tranquility are attained through the first dhyāna; because there are no women in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and because one is free from the defilements of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are called "Brahma-bodies" (brahmakāya) because they are tranquil through the departure from desire.
Furthermore, according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, they are called "Brahma" because they speak with the Brahma-voice among the Brahma-multitude. Moreover, as for *Śikhin*, it is also called "Holder."
His hair is styled in a topknot, or as some say, a spiral topknot (*śikhā-jaṭā*), or as others call it, a "flame-summit" (*agni-mūrdhan*), because this heaven is reached by the calamity of fire.
Those who have cultivated and attained the first dhyāna are born in this heaven. This Heavenly King utters the great Brahma-sound (*brahma-svara*) among the assembly of Brahmas;
each of the devas thinks to themselves, "He is speaking only with me. He possesses supreme sovereignty within the great trichiliocosm, and his countenance is like that of a youth.
The body of this being is the color of white silver and measures half a yojana in height; his garments are golden in color, and he has no male or female form.
He takes the joy of dhyāna as food and has a lifespan of one kalpa. This is according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

It is said that at this stage, one attains the ten kinds of contemplation on dependent origination in both direct and reverse order, which is illustrated by the metaphor of polishing true gold with *vaiḍūrya* gems until it becomes increasingly bright and pure.
The ten gates of emptiness-concentration are the Vaiḍūrya jewel; "vai" means radiance.
The Bodhisattva in this stage represents the twelvefold dependent origination through ten types of contemplation and the ten emptiness-samādhis.
Just as one uses clear and pure Vaiḍūrya to polish wisdom until it becomes increasingly bright and pure, one contemplates ignorance and brings it to its fundamental root.
Fundamental wisdom further clarifies and purifies [the mind]; within this, there are ten Great Brahma Kings who illustrate the ten *pāramitās* within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Each may be understood by correlating its name with its meaning as previously assigned.

This sixth ground (*bhūmi*) and sixth dwelling (*vihāra*), etc., collectively clarify the transcendence of the karma of the three realms, the manifestation of quiescence, and the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Mastery over emptiness is exemplified by the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja within the Ten Abodes;

it is exemplified by the night goddess named Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥprabha in the sixth stage of the Ten Stages. Generally, these are represented by the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) encountered by Sudhana.
The seventh stage clarifies the entry into the world through shared activity (*samānārthatā*), as described below.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable kings of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, namely: King Lovely and Delightful Light,
King Pure Sublime Light, King Sovereign Sound, King Supreme Mindfulness and Wisdom, King Lovely and Delightful Pure Sublime Sound,
King Sound of Excellent Contemplation, King Universal Sound Illuminating Everywhere, and King Profound Light.
The Heavenly King Sound, the Heavenly King Stainless Adornment Light, the Heavenly King Supreme Pure Light, and others such as these served as their leaders;
they were immeasurable in number, and all dwelt in the vast, tranquil, joyful, and unimpeded Dharma-gate.
[Treatise] Seventh, there is again the King of the Immeasurable Light-Sound Heaven (five lines and a half of scripture, ninety-eight words).

It clarifies that the Stage of Far-Reaching Practice (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*) is like the second *dhyāna* heaven: as the first *dhyāna* eliminates sorrow and the second *dhyāna* eliminates suffering, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage has brought all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) to an end, perfected great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and fulfilled the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ) are constantly manifest; having already transcended one's own suffering through impermanence, one delivers others from suffering.

Regarding the two obstacles of affliction and knowledge (kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa), this stage is passed through. It is like pure gold adorned with various exquisite jewels, becoming even more sublime and brilliant;
taking the Dharma-body as the substance of the gold, the myriad practices of compassion and wisdom are perfected as the exquisite ornaments.
The jewels mutually adorn one another, for they constantly teach through the net of practice and universally transform all sentient beings with light;

thus, this deva has already extinguished sorrow and suffering. Because his mind is pure, light is produced from his mouth as he speaks, using this illumination to clarify the teaching-light that dispels darkness for the Bodhisattvas at this stage.
Within this [heaven], there are ten Great Light-Sound Heavens (*Mahāprabhāsvara*) to illustrate this.
Within the *upāya-pāramitā*, the ten *pāramitās* can be understood by assigning their respective meanings according to their names.
The bodies of the devas here are two *yojanas* in height, and their lifespan is two *kalpas*. When the calamity of water reaches this heaven, [the beings there pass away].
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there were immeasurable kings of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
namely: King Viśuddhayaśas, King Jyeṣṭhadarśana, King Śāntaguṇa, King Merusvara, King Viśuddhasmṛtinetra,
King Priyadarśanajyotirviśeṣaprabha, King Lokendrapati, King Arciṣpati, and King Sukha.
The Celestial King who Contemplates the Dharma, the Celestial King Banner of Transformations, the Celestial King Sublime Adornment of the Sound of Constellations,

and others such as these were their leaders; they were immeasurable in number, all of whom were already securely established in the vast Dharma-gates and diligently performed acts of benefit for all worlds.

[Treatise] Eighth, there are furthermore immeasurable Śubhakṛtsna devas (six lines of text, one hundred and six characters). This clarifies that for a Bodhisattva on the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), sorrow and suffering have already ceased, and there remains only the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*).
For a Bodhisattva at this stage, active effort (*prayoga*) has already reached its end, and there remains only the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-prīti*).
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of this joy of the Dharma only cease at the beginning of the tenth ground. When the wind-disaster (*vāyu-saṃvartanī*) reaches this heaven...
Because the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) stirs their nature, for Bodhisattvas at this stage, although non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) has manifested,

there still remains the pure habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) toward the knowledge of the bliss of the dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-sukha*). Only through the threefold empowerment and sevenfold exhortation of all Buddhas,
causing them to remember their original vows, do they finally act in accordance with that wisdom to extensively benefit sentient beings and deliver them throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

This limitation is the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teaching to provide protection; it is at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta that compassion and wisdom are perfectly integrated.
It is not only at this stage that there is the function of protecting against stagnation in purity; rather, within the principle that "the one is all," protection is present.
Considering that all matters are fully contained within the seventh bhūmi, how could the fruit of Buddhahood be known only in the eighth bhūmi?

Even seeing this, one has not yet reached the end; rather, through the mutual fusion of the Ten Mysteries and Six Penetrations, one must not interpret the essence of the Dharma-realm as having a sequence of before and after.
That which ordinary people delusively conceive as immeasurable kalpas is, in fact, merely the absence of beginning or end within the Dharma-realm.

This stage involves refining true gold to create the precious crown for the Human King (Cakravartin) and the crowns for his ministers—this serves as an illustration surpassing all others to clarify the Eighth Stage.
Because the wisdom of the functional nature of the stages (*bhūmi*) is superior and effortless, the ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are perfected upon the tenth stage;
the ocean-like practice of Samantabhadra is fulfilled upon the eleventh stage.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, there are immeasurable kings of the Bṛhatphala Heaven, namely, the King of Heaven named *Dharmābhiratilokadhvajaprabha*.
The Celestial King Ocean of Pure Adornments, the Celestial King Light of Supreme Wisdom, the Celestial King Banner of Sovereign Wisdom,
the Celestial King Delighting in Tranquility, the Celestial King Universal Wisdom Eye, the Celestial King Wisdom Light of Excellent Seed,
the Celestial King Stainless Tranquil Light, and the Celestial King Vast Pure Light— such as these...
They serve as leaders, their number being immeasurable; there are none who do not take the dharma of tranquility as their palace and dwell therein.

[Treatise] Ninth: Furthermore, there are immeasurable devas of the Vast Fruit Heaven (six lines of scripture, one hundred and two words), which clarify the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
In this fourth dhyāna, there is no inhalation or exhalation of breath, and it is not affected by the three calamities.
Furthermore, these ten heavens—as described in the "Praise of Virtues"—all take the dharma-gate of tranquility as their palaces, manifesting the adornments of the Good Wisdom (Sādhumatī) bhūmi;
they teach and transform sentient beings through hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya *mīlani* gates and palaces of the dharma-treasure.
One is able to use a single utterance to preach various dharmas for all sentient beings;
being without mind, thought, or consciousness, one serves as a great Dharma Master, fully endowed with the illumination of wisdom and the Dharma.
Just as this deva is able to produce speech without the thinking or consciousness of the lower realms, yet possesses the consciousness of the form realm, and so forth.

In the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (Āsaṃjñisattva), there is always subtle consciousness; if perception and consciousness were entirely exhausted, it would not be subsumed under the karma of the three realms.
Therefore, this stage is illustrated by the metaphor of refined gold used for a Universal Monarch’s (Cakravartin) crown, which cannot be surpassed by the crowns of any minor kings;
likewise, the jewel-crown of wisdom of a Bodhisattva in this stage cannot be surpassed by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages.
Within this [realm], there are ten celestial kings; among the ten pāramitās of the *prabhāva-pāramitā*, each may be understood by being assigned according to its respective name and meaning.
The bodies, garments, and lifespans of these devas are all double those of the preceding heavens.
Bodhisattvas in this stage always take the Dharma-palace as their place of rest. Because their merit and virtue are vast and great, it is called "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*).
[The Sūtra] says: Furthermore, there were countless kings of the Mahāśvara devas, namely:
the Deva King Subhavyūha-samudra, the Deva King Īśvara-yaśas-prabha, the Deva King Viśuddha-guṇa-netra, the Deva King Priya-rucira-mahāmati, and the Deva King Acala.
The Heavenly King Sovereign of Light, the Heavenly King Sublime Adornment Eye, the Heavenly King Light of Excellent Contemplation,
the Heavenly King Great Wisdom of Delightful Beauty, the Heavenly King Universal Sound Adorned Banner, the Heavenly King Radiance of Fame of Utmost Diligence,
and others such as these were the leaders; they were beyond measure, all diligently observing the dharma of signlessness.
[The Bodhisattva] practices equanimity.
[Treatise]: The tenth Great Lord of Heaven (Maheśvara), [comprising six lines and one hundred and two words], represents the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

As indicated below in the "Praise of Virtues," it shows that in this station, one diligently observes the signless (*animitta*) dharma and practices with equanimity. This clarifies the nature of this stage.
The Wisdom of Signlessness is accomplished as stated in the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avataṃsaka-sūtra*:

"The Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-piṭaka*) are able to subdue the coarse karma and the coarse continuity of results within the three realms. From the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, they both subdue and sever [these].

From the Eighth Ground onward, because the causes of form, the superior causes of karma, and the objective conditions of dharmas—the habitual tendencies of clinging to dharmas—have been eliminated, it is clear that there still remains the perception of objects."

Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of clinging to dharmas still persist as they have not yet been fully matured, from the ninth stage onward, the internal mind is superior due to its karma, and the internal mind itself takes the habitual tendencies of clinging to dharmas as its object.
Thus, at the ninth stage, there are internal mental states that take the habitual tendencies of clinging to dharmas as their objects;

therefore, at the tenth stage, the two tendencies of mind and form are simultaneously exhausted in their entirety, and it is only at the eleventh stage that one attains [liberation] within the dual objects of mind and境 (the objective field).

Because of unimpeded mastery, from the eighth to the tenth bhūmi, within the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), one contemplates the true Dharma and the internal and external habitual tendencies of grasping are extinguished;

yet, in the eleventh bhūmi, the gate of Samantabhadra is not yet fully mastered, as evidenced by the fact that when seeking Samantabhadra in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*), he is not seen.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that beyond the ninth heaven, there is...
There is another class of Bodhisattva-devas of the Ten Stages named Maheśvara. These devas have eight arms, three eyes, and ride white oxen;
in a single thought-moment, they know the number of raindrops falling throughout the trichiliocosm.

This is a skillful means established by the Bodhisattvas to lead others forward, employing phenomena to symbolize the Dharma and encompassing the realms of transformative guidance, which gradually increase in excellence.
Therefore, one should aspire to the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle, where principle and phenomena are co-participatory;
within a single atom, the Buddha-lands and the realms of humans and devas exist together, and the bodies and pores of sentient beings enter one another like shadows.

Those who cultivate the truth must know this as it truly is, and not follow the traces of transformation; they must accord with the Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment, wherein the one and the many are mutually inclusive.
The gate of the mutual identity of all phenomena within different aspects; the gate of sovereign mastery; the gate of the realm of Indra’s net;

the gate of the subtle containment and establishment of phenomena; the gate of the simultaneous attainment of the secret and the manifest; the gate of the distinct formation of the ten periods of time;

the gate of the unimpeded interpenetration of principal and attendant elements; the gate of generating understanding by relying on things to manifest dharmas; and the gate of the revolving of the mind-only.

The Gate of Skillful Accomplishment encompasses these ten gates of mystery because they accord with principle. The aforementioned positions of the divine beings are merely within the gate of benefiting sentient beings;

they rely on phenomena to manifest the Dharma so that it may be easily understood. For example, although the Tathāgata is not in reality a king of oxen, a king of dragons, or a king of elephants, he relies on these phenomena to manifest [the truth] so that understanding may arise. This is done in view of the place where one attains the Way.
That wisdom is formless and unconditioned, yet it is able to know all that exists; this is what constitutes the Divine (shen).

Because this divine nature accompanies one's actions to bless living beings, such action is not in vain. Because this wisdom constantly abides within the triple world without being defiled by its purity or impurity, it possesses sovereign mastery.
It takes up a station like a king, employing unhindered transformation in every direction, and its blessings surpass those of all classes of beings as it assumes its station.
That they are of the same nature follows from the fact that their pervasive arising is not in vain; thus, there is no hindrance to the fact that both identity and difference can represent reality.
