Regarding the name "Flower Treasury" (*Huāzàng*) and the three explanations of why the Flower Treasury World is obtained as a retribution:

from the initial stage of faith up to the eighth ground (*bhūmi*), one has constantly maintained non-retrogression from bodhi through the power of great vows and the ocean of *pāramitās*, while teaching and benefiting all sentient beings; upon reaching the eighth ground, one is capable of benefiting others at will.
One should know that the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is the fruition produced by the perfection of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

Just as the world of sentient beings is sustained by the winds of the karma of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the world of the Tathāgata is sustained by the winds of wisdom through the power of great vows.
This is because wisdom can follow the vow, and the vow can bring wisdom to fulfillment; thus, it is again sustained by the Dharma-body of the great vow.
That which is realized through wisdom constitutes the substance of the wind-wheel; yet, if it were not for the Dharma-body, all conditioned phenomena would be merely composite.
If there were no aspiration, the Dharma-body would lack intrinsic nature and could not manifest itself, let alone manifest for others.

Only by taking these three factors as conditions can one be fit to benefit sentient beings, remaining unimpeded in either emptiness or existence. When the cultivation of merit reaches maturity, one acts spontaneously.
Benefit is attained without effort; moreover, taking the primary cause as the foremost, one should take the great vow as the head.

One should maintain all phenomena by using the wind of the wisdom of the great vow as the basis for maintaining those objects. Therefore, in the subsequent text of this chapter, it says that "the exquisite mani-jewel flowers are scattered everywhere, abiding in mid-air through the power of former vows.
All the adornments of this Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) are entirely [the result of] this.
The wind-circle above supports all objects; arising fundamentally from the root of various meritorious actions and vows, it uses that original cause to sustain all effects.
By means of this perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), one is able to accomplish the ocean of all perfections (*pāramitā*).

Because the original cause is thus, cause and effect mutually sustain one another. This is now [discussed] in relation to the eighth stage and the time of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

Within the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), the ten perfections constitute ten kinds of wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) that serve to support the ten kinds of all-encompassing adornments above them.
Because the perfection of aspiration interpenetrates with the natures of the others, it can support all the adornments obtained as the retribution for various practices;
these are like the very lowest wind-circle, which is called "Equilibrium" (*samatā*), and this is the perfection of aspiration.
Because it is obtained as the retribution for the *dāna-pāramitā* within the *pāramitās*, one is able to uphold all the blazing jewel-flames and adornments above;
furthermore, this is born from the retribution of the giving of Dharma-wealth and wisdom through the gate of *dāna* within the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā*.
Thus, cause and effect mutually sustain one another and penetrate each other; phenomena are not obtained in vain, and causes are never wasted.
Next, following this principle, one should apply the ten-fold dharma-gate of the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* to correspond with these.
Because the ten kinds of wind-circles sustain the results of cause and effect, they are like the wind of deluded karma in the world of sentient beings, which dwells at the very bottom;
above it, they support the water-limit, the vajra-earth, and the mountains, causing them to abide securely. This is as explained by the Bodhisattva Xuan Guang.
The formation of celestial bodies and their movements, which do not fall away, are the retributive attainment of the essence of the Lotus Treasury, which is the Dharma-body;
the palace is the retributive attainment of the wisdom-essence that follows all conduct without dependence or abiding, and which universally nurtures through great compassion;
the pavilion is the retributive attainment of the wisdom-illumination that observes faculties and accords with compassion to save sentient beings; its ground is adamantine.
The retributive attainment of the Dharmakāya of equal self-nature consists solely of all the adornments therein;
those adorned with vajras are all the retributive attainment of the Dharmakāya’s accompanying conduct.

Those adorned with maṇi jewels are all the retributive attainment of the Dharmakāya’s accomplishment of the essence of precepts and its accompanying conduct. The Vajra Cakravāḍa Mountains are precisely the precept of great compassion.

The attainment of adornments of various flowers as the retribution for the karma of protection is because it is the retribution for the blossoming of manifold virtues through the ten practices (*daśapāramitā*) that benefit sentient beings.
The attainment of adornments of jewel-trees is because it is the retribution for establishing practice to benefit sentient beings and providing shelter and shade for all conscious beings;
this is as described in the section on the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), such as the ten bodhisattvas beginning with Guṇakusuma-vyūha (Guṇakusuma-śrī).
All those named "Forest" are so called because they provide covering and shade through their growth.

As for the adornment of the lion throne, it is established as the wheel of Dharma in accordance with wisdom by means of the Dharma-body, being the fruition of past deeds; thus, it is described briefly in this manner.
Furthermore, were one to explain the causes of such karmic retribution in detail, they could not be fully exhausted, for no retribution is obtained in vain, but all has its source.
If one does not know the cause, how can one cultivate the fruit? Therefore, at the beginning of this chapter, it says:

"This Flower Bank Adorned World-Ocean is that which was purified through the cultivation of world-ocean-microdust-numbered great vows by Vairocana Tathāgata in the presence of each of the buddhas within world-ocean-microdust-numbered buddha-fields in the past."
Regarding "purifying with solemnity," it is said that "vows" constitute practice; furthermore, because [the goal] is accomplished through vows, it is stated below:

"The practices of Samantabhadra’s ground of wisdom are all accomplished as every kind of adornment, from which they emerge. This is like the reward obtained for the karma of great compassion, which is the Fragrant Water Sea.
The Fragrant Water River is the reward obtained for the practice of progressive cultivation, as in the case of Mañjuśrī mentioned in the passage below.
Benefit constantly follows the assembly; therein, the Dharma is generally indicated by means of names. Thus, seeing the name, one knows the practice;
as it is with this Flower Treasury World-Ocean, seeing the fruit allows one to know the cause. One must not separately cite other sutras to come and verify this.
Only when one sees the name and immediately knows the Dharma, and sees the fruit and immediately knows the cause, can one truly understand the underlying intent of this sutra. The rest is as follows.
The gateways of the characteristics of the teachings in other sutras mostly do not correspond with this sutra.
While other sutras speak of the "Truth of Suffering," this sutra speaks of the "Noble Truth of Suffering"—thus, the meaning is more complete.

Other sutras explain the Four Noble Truths, whereas this sutra explains ten kinds of noble truths as well as the ten and twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If these were explained in their infinite variations, they could not be fully set forth here at once.
Because this meaning pertains to the correlation of cause and effect, one cannot cite other teachings to correlate them with the text of this sutra.
This sutra reveals that names signify practice and knowledge, while the resulting consciousness serves as the cause for the factors; as the text states regarding Mañjuśrī’s constant retinue:
"The goddess presiding over the directions, who is skilled in the rituals of the ten directions, eliminates the darkness of ignorance; the Night Goddess, Single-Minded."
The deities who illuminate the Buddha-sun without indolence are prime examples of this. This is the essential nature of the resultant attainment within the Flower Treasury World;
in brief, it consists of the Dharma-body of great vows, great wisdom, myriad practices, and great kindness and compassion.
Through these five things, they bring fulfillment throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm, even unto the interior of a single atom or hair-tip.
The conduct of all sentient beings throughout the ocean of重重 (repeatedly layered) buddha-fields is entirely equal and beneficial;
reaching the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), one acts with effortless spontaneity, naturally and constantly pervading all things, taking this as its essence.

Therefore, it is not the realm of those who cling to quiescent stillness for their own peace, nor of those among humans and devas who seek the fruits of happiness for themselves; nor is it the realm of bodhisattvas who delight in being born in pure lands (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Because this pure land is the realm (*dhātu*), even if bodhisattvas there practice the six *pāramitās* and attain the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*), they are still unable to give rise to faith;
therefore, it takes the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*—the wisdom of differentiation—as its basis, causing them to generate faith, diligence, and cultivation.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the shape of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*Kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusea*): by means of inexhaustible greatness...
May the wind-wheel support the water of great compassion, from which arise the flowers of boundless conduct;

because the space of the *dharmatā* can contain myriad objects without obstruction, even as they overlap, upon that water there arises a single great lotus flower that pervades the empty *dharmadhātu*, named "Various Stamen-Flame Banner.
This signifies the arising of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the practice of differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*) through the performance of differentiated conduct.
Within the lotus flowers of the *Keśara-gandha-dhvaja*, atop the *Sūryamaṇi-rāja* jewels, there are great Cakravāḍa mountains.
As the Sūtra says, "upon the *Sūryamaṇi-rāja* lotuses," this merely means that within the flowers there are jewels named *maṇi-rāja*;
it does not mean there are separate flowers. The forests and trees composed of various jewels, the fragrant waters, and the exquisite blossoms in full bloom are described in the Sūtra itself.
The *Sūtra* itself describes how that ground is composed of the inner-earth vajra, adorned with a profusion of various jewels interspersed throughout;
it further states that upon this ground are countless fragrant oceans of water, whose bottoms consist of various jewels, as detailed in the sūtra.
Outside each of these fragrant oceans, there are fragrances [as numerous] as the atoms of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*).
The river flows clockwise, encircling from the south toward the east in succession, as if forming the six auspicious marks (ṣaḍ-aṅga) on the right;
the adornments of this river are described in detail in the sūtra itself.
Within each of the unspeakably many seas of fragrant water, there resides a single world-system (*lokadhātu-vīja*). These world-systems are identical [in nature].
The realm inhabited by the flowing [waters] is called "various" (*nānā*), which refers to categories. As the former masters explained:

"When the number of three-thousand great thousandfold world systems reaches as many as the sands of the Ganges, it constitutes one 'ocean of worlds. When the number of oceans of worlds reaches as many as the sands of the Ganges, it constitutes one 'nature of worlds' (*jagat-dhātu*).
When the number of natures of worlds reaches as many as the sands of the Ganges, it constitutes one 'species of worlds' (*jagat-jāti*). Within this context, "world" refers to...
There are world-systems numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; within each of these seas of fragrant water, there is one such world-system.
As briefly mentioned in the sutra regarding the world-systems, that which is at the very center of all is the sea of fragrant water named "Boundless Light of Wondrous Flowers";
this name is given to signify the sublime function of the Middle Way’s wisdom and compassion.
This is the ocean of fragrant water located at the center within the great lotus called Various Stalks of Fragrance Banners atop the wind-circle.
Within this ocean emerges a great lotus named Adorned with All-Fragrant Mani Kings;
it contains a world-system that dwells therein, named Blazing Jewel Radiance Universally Illuminating the Ten Directions.
In this world-system, there are twenty tiers of worlds stacked vertically, each separated from the next by a distance equal to the number of atoms in a buddha-field.
This Sahā world is located in the thirteenth tier, specifically at the very bottom;
it is surrounded on all sides by a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a buddha-field. The tier immediately above it contains a number of worlds equal to the atoms in two buddha-fields.
The uppermost layer is surrounded on all sides by worlds numbering as many as the atoms in three Buddha-fields;
each successive layer increases by one, up to twenty layers in total, which are surrounded by worlds numbering as many as the atoms in twenty Buddha-fields.
Thus revolving around the center, there are eleven world-systems in total, each having twenty layers above and below.
The distances between them are similar; beyond these eleven world-systems, extending all around to the Cakravāḍa mountains,
there are another one hundred world-systems arranged according to the directions— ten in each direction—
aligned in straight rows facing their respective quarters and situated near the perimeter of the Cakravāḍa mountains, with ten world-systems encircling each [central] system.
Although the number of tiers from top to bottom consists of only four layers, the distance between each successive layer is extremely vast;

every third tier is level with this Sahā world. Regarding the uppermost tier, some say it is separated by a distance equal to the dust motes of seven Buddha-fields, while the second tier from the top is said to be separated from the one below it by a distance equal to the dust motes of ten Buddha-fields. Thus, these four tiers are calculated.
The world-systems, including the central eleven sets of twenty-fold world-systems, are equal in height;
these ten sets of world-systems adjacent to the Cakravāḍa Mountains consist of four layers each, while for the remaining ninety sets of world-systems, the number of layers is not mentioned.
To speak briefly, there are eleven sets of world-systems at the center of the world-systems.
Surrounding each world-system seed are one hundred world-system seeds; together, there are one hundred and eleven world-system seeds, arranged like the net of Indra.

In total, these comprise world-system seeds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, all situated upon a great lotus flower known as the Banner of Various Kinds of Filament Fragrance.
Above these, various seas of fragrant water each produce lotus flowers, upon which the various world-systems each abide.
Upon those great flowers, there are further distinct flowers where [the worlds] reside; this constitutes the second tier, arranged and abiding atop these individual lotuses.
Beneath all is a wind-wheel with atoms as numerous as Mount Sumeru that supports them.
The various adornments upon them, as well as the successive worlds supported above them, abide in space like the sun, moon, and many stars, sustained by wind.
For the extensive details, one should consult the text of the sutra itself; were I to cite them at length here, the writing would become too cumbersome, so I fear you might not see the full picture.
To briefly present the essential framework and speak of it in general terms, five [aspects] correspond to the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).
Regarding the establishment of the ocean of realms as belonging to causes: Now, effects do not arise of themselves, but are obtained from causes.
As the Sūtra says: "The vast clouds of vows pervade the Dharma-realm; throughout all kalpas, they transform all sentient beings.

The practices on the ground of Samantabhadra’s wisdom are all perfected, and all adornments emerge from this. As the Sūtra summarizes, these are as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
The enumeration of world-systems clarifies that the sphere of Samantabhadra’s practice of gathering and transforming beings pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
this is precisely the sphere of the conduct and realization attained as retribution by the assembly within the seat and the assembly between the eyebrows.

This collectively presents the sphere of the perfect and all-encompassing fruition and practice; therein, it merely mentions the assembly of Buddha-worlds as numerous as atoms in contrast to the "unspeakable."
The number of Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms is a brief enumeration; this [following] is the detailed enumeration.

For example, when speaking of the conduct of Samantabhadra, one merely says "ten thousand practices"—this is a brief statement intended to signify his inexhaustible practices that are equal to the Dharma-realm.

Thus, these two layers [of enumeration] present the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices within the fruit, just as [the light from] the space between the eyebrows of the assembly within the seat [is described].
The assembly [abides] within this Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, consisting of unspeakably many world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field,
distributed like Indra’s net amidst various stamens of great lotus flowers bearing banners of fragrance;
this is the realm obtained through the fulfillment of the fruition of birth, encompassed by those very practices of the fruit, which is not [explicitly] present here in the sutra.
To state the general number, one cites only the central eleven world-systems;
from top to bottom, there are twenty tiers, each separated by a distance equal to the atoms within a single Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).

Each of the worlds in the lowest tier is surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in a Buddha-field. Within this [central system], the second tier above it is described as "two Buddha-fields."
Surrounding the world-system on all sides, the third tier above it is likewise surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in three Buddha-fields;
proceeding upward tier by tier, adding one [set] at each level until reaching the highest tier,
the central space is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in twenty Buddha-fields.

All eleven world-systems are entirely like this; this clarifies that within the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), there are eleven realms attained as retribution through the progressive cultivation and gathering of beings via the practice-gates of the eleven stages.
The statement that there are twenty layers—ten above and ten below—gradually expanding, clarifies that within the practice-gates of the eleven stages, each stage contains two.
The emphasis on cause and effect indicates that throughout the progressive cultivation of each stage (*bhūmi*), there is both a primary fruit and a consistent fruit.
Among these twenty stages, all the names of the Buddhas are those of Buddhas who represent the causes and fruits of further advancement.
All the worlds are the spheres of transformation according to each respective stage; this clarifies the cultivation and the gathering of beings through the progression of the eleven stages.
Because the fruit of Buddhahood descends through successive stages, one may observe that each is assigned according to its respective level.

Apart from these eleven worlds, the separate enumeration of one hundred world-systems surrounding them clarifies that the practices of the ten *pāramitās*, which encompass and transform beings within these eleven stages, pervade the entire Dharmadhātu within the Cakravāḍa mountains; this is further arranged according to the sequence of the directions.
Each [of these] has ten, totaling one hundred, which signifies that they completely fill the realms as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.

The presence of ten world-systems surrounding the perimeter of the Vajra Rim Mountains, with four tiers stacked vertically, signifies that the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are pervasive throughout the eleven stages (*bhūmi*). The remaining ninety world-systems signify... [the remainder of the ten stages].

The reason the "types" (*jāti*) are not specified as being numerous is to clarify that they consist merely of the ten *pāramitās*. Within these ten, there are a hundred [subdivisions] which encompass the spheres of those to be converted.
Thus, this constitutes one complete set of cause and effect. As for the remaining ten sets of fourfold worlds, they are assigned to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Furthermore, another assignment is made by taking the eleven world-systems centered on the middle [world] and including their periphery.
From the surrounding [worlds] up to the Vajra-cakravāḍa mountains, there are one hundred world-systems in total;
these comprise one hundred and eleven world-systems, which are distributed across the five stages of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground.
Each stage possesses its own Buddha-causes and -fruits, totaling one hundred fundamental texts for these five stages. From the beginning, these have existed inherently within them.
There are ten layers of cause and effect based on the five positions (*pañca-avasthā*), with two layers of cause and effect within each position, thus making ten.
These constitute the basis for the five positions, as the Buddha’s cause and effect serve as the progressive cultivation within those five positions.
Thus, in this first assembly, the five positions and the Buddha-fruit together total one hundred and ten; furthermore, there is one additional world-system.

This seed is established as the "one" because it functions as the one that pervades all within the context of the Buddha-stage; for if this single stage did not exist, the various stages would not be established.
Furthermore, it clarifies that all dependently originated phenomena must necessarily possess a "one," for only then can the phenomena of dependent origination be fully realized.
For example, when the numbers one, three, five, seven, and nine act as conditions for ten, if two, four, six, and eight were omitted [the sequence would fail].
Because it is a complete set of ten, it is a perfect number that cannot be increased or decreased.

Since the Buddha-dharma and worldly phenomena are similar, just as the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days all take one, three, five, seven, and nine as their fundamental principle, they constitute the inexhaustible nature of dependent origination; for the one and the many mutually penetrate one another, clarifying that the "one" is not [a singular entity].
Because it is simultaneous and lacks before, after, or middle, it is "one"; because it does not act as "one" by means of itself, it is "many";

because the many do not act as "one" by means of themselves, it is "many. Thus, the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are established through the harmonious union of one and many, wherein they are spontaneously accomplished through mastery over one and many and the effortless manifestation of their characteristics. This is like the conventional phenomena where one represents the Yang and two represents the Yin.
Yang moves and Yin follows; they cannot act on their own. If Yin were to act on its own, then Heaven and Earth would be estranged from one another, clouds would not rise, and rain would not fall.
It is because the Yin and Yang of the primary and the attendant move and rest in mutual accord, acting as both primary and attendant to one another, that they form the conditions for arising.
If there are two yangs, there is a deficiency; if there are two yins, there is a separation. Because these cannot achieve mutual completion, it is for this reason that the Tathāgata appears.
The worldly mind aims at benefiting sentient beings; because it does not truly conform to worldly conventions, its actions are without contrivance and its virtues are without seeking to save.

Thus, the Buddha remains the Buddha and sentient beings remain sentient beings. If one were to establish dharmic rules for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, then the Buddha would be a manifestation of yang-virtue, while the teachings established would be yin.
For this reason, this sutra is named the "Perfect Teaching" (Yuanjiao) and is the place where the Buddha dwells.
The single line of the *Kan* (Khan/Kan) hexagram establishes the teaching by taking the *Kan* as the teacher;
therefore, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra clearly establishes the teaching for the benefit of sentient beings through the causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of phenomena.

Because one must be sovereign and unimpeded regarding dependent origination, one hundred and eleven world-systems are cited to correspond to the five stages of cause and effect, totaling one hundred [stages].

The tenfold gate of gathering the retribution of birth and sustenance constitutes one world-seed; it clarifies that the Buddha-stage serves as the manifold basis for the five stages and all practices.

Thus, it is like the Bodhisattva Viśvāghoṣa among the assembly at the ūrṇā-kośa, sitting alone upon a lotus pedestal, while the various Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are represented by the flower filaments, clarifying the relationship between the principal and the retinue.
Because the aspects of the one and the many are mutually identical, when observed through concentration and wisdom, one can see that ten below constitute one;

this clarifies the Dharma of the Benevolent One, wherein the phenomena correspond to eleven. Now, by establishing eleven worlds within these eleven, the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*) is revealed;
through the fourfold world-systems, the methods of the ten *pāramitās* and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are clarified.

Thus, the "Great Intent" (*Mahāmati*) section clarifies the assembly within the preceding seat and the assembly at the ūrṇā-kośa (the space between the eyebrows), thereby elucidating the practices they perform.

This "Flower Treasury World" (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*) clarifies the environmental fruits obtained as retribution for those practices. Within this, the various classes of worlds clarify the principle of the *dharmadhātu*:
that sentient beings, though dwelling together in one place, have distinct objective spheres (*viṣaya*). This is explained by way of the logic of the *dharmadhātu*.

The wisdom of the ultimate and conventional truths is not distinct; the sixfold explanation of the Vairocanagarbha World being pure and impure without obstruction means that it is the practice performed by the Buddha, for his practice pervades both the Dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings. Since this practice is all-pervasive, the resultant support (āśraya-phala) obtained from it is likewise all-pervasive.
However, those whose karma is not in accord with one another may dwell together in the same place yet remain unseen, just as in the case of spirits and deities.
The realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati) shares the same location as humans, yet humans cannot see them. As a sutra says:
"For example, two devas constantly follow a human body; the devas always see the human, but the human does not see the devas.

This sutra demonstrates that the Buddha’s activity pervades both the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *āśrita*), which differs from the approach of the Three Vehicles that seek the Pure Land in another direction and thus involve coming and going.
Its characteristics are such that for those of small minds and inferior faculties, he thus establishes a net of teachings;
therefore, those who ultimately seek the mind of great enlightenment must still return to this gate of non-duality and give rise to practices and vows that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Seventh, regarding how the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) perfectly encompasses the karmic environments of the three periods of time: this flower...
The Ocean of Treasuries clarifies this teaching by showing that a single thought-moment encompasses the three periods of time; thus, a single thought-moment is non-thought.
Non-thought is the absence of the three periods of time and all phenomena of past and present, thereby clarifying that the Dharmakāya is non-thought.
All sentient beings' deluded thoughts regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time and many kalpas do not depart from within non-thought. It is by virtue of this principle [that this is so].
Therefore, all the adorned realms within this Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) can manifest the karmic activities of all Buddhas;
the causes and effects of the deeds performed by sentient beings throughout the three periods of time are all manifested therein— whether past karma is manifested in the future,
future karma is manifested in the past, or the karma of both past and future is manifested in the present.

Alternatively, present karma appears within the past and future, just as hundreds of thousands of clear mirrors are suspended on all four sides so that their front and back images penetrate one another.

Because it is the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu* and is timeless, the karmas of the three periods of time are falsely conceptualized as suddenly appearing within this timeless reality. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time..."
The *Anāgamana-sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha, you should contemplate the majestic spiritual power of the world-systems (*kṣetra-vyūha*).
All future lands shall be seen as if in a dream; all the oceans of past lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear within a single land like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*);
and all Buddhas of the three periods of time, together with their lands, [appear] within one..."
Within the entire array of world-systems, one perceives everything. The Master of the Treatise states in verse: "The three times have no temporal existence;

they are falsely conceptualized as phenomena of the three times. Because true reality is free from discursive thought, a single moment manifests the three times. Since the three times have no temporal existence, there is not even a single moment;
attachment to the phenomena of the three times is entirely manifested within the realization of timelessness, whereby one thoroughly penetrates the dharma of timelessness."
Attaining Perfect Enlightenment in a Single Thought: Eight Explanations of the Original Emptiness of the Buddha-land.
Regarding the object of focus for the arising of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang Shijie*), what is the focal object? The mental focus of the mind is fourfold:

first, to clarify that although those of the Two Vehicles have attained liberation from the coarse karma of the triple world, they lack merit and wisdom, do not benefit sentient beings, and remain stalled in *nirvāṇa*; second, to... [text fragment ends].
Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles have the obstacle of delighting in birth in pure lands where pure appearances constantly persist;
thus, regarding the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), their cognition of defilement and purity is not in accordance with principle, and because their minds dwell upon pure lands, they lack mastery.

It is not so for this [Dharmakāya] Dharma, which possesses the freedom to manifest or conceal at will; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and manifesting supreme merit, it is endowed with ten thousand variations of marks and radiance.
It clearly illuminates so that the minds of sentient beings have no grasping or attachment;
like illusory clouds dispersing, not a single thing remains, and there is nothing to be attained because its binding conditions no longer persist. Third, regarding the emptiness of all phenomena:

sentient beings regard the principle of the emptiness and signlessness of phenomena as nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), claiming that emptiness lacks merit and wisdom, and thus they do not delight in contemplating emptiness but instead enjoy grasping.
For those bound by the fetters of signs who remain attached to objects and cannot achieve liberation from karma, the manifested fruits of merit— the primary and secondary bodies—
cause them to contemplate emptiness and the emptiness of phenomena, thereby dispelling ignorance and accomplishing meritorious karma.
These four points collectively serve as the measure and model for the vast scope of vows, practices, merit, and wisdom manifested for all practitioners of the three vehicles and all ordinary beings.
Because its emulation and study are free from biased attachment, the Sūtra says: "The lands of all Buddhas are like empty space—unequaled, unborn, and without marks;
yet, by the power of their original vows to universally adorn and purify them for the benefit of sentient beings, they abide therein.
Ninth, as for why the Flower Treasury World (Huāzàng Shìjiè) is able to manifest and conceal itself with sovereign mastery: it is because it arises from the emptiness of all phenomena.
Because this principle manifests according to wisdom, one attains mastery over concealment and appearance.

If even worldly dragons and ghosts, who possess the three poisons, are still able to conceal and appear at will, how much more so for the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), which exhausts all three poisons and is pure, clear intelligence?
It cannot fail to exercise mastery over concealment and appearance. This is like Sudhana entering Maitreya’s pavilion, where, through the power of samādhi, he perceives all manner of adornments.
Ghanavyūha arose from samādhi and suddenly vanished; not a single sign remained. Sudhana said, "Where has this array gone?
Maitreya replied, "It has gone to where it came from. Sudhana asked, "From where did it come?
He replied, "It came from the wisdom and supernormal powers of the Bodhisattva; it abides by the wisdom and spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, and thus has no going."
The locus itself has no place of abiding; it is neither accumulated nor permanent, but is utterly remote from all things.
Furthermore, it is like a magician who performs various illusory feats: they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
Although there is no coming or going, by the power of illusion, those adorned phenomena are clearly visible. This [reality] is also like that: it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Although there is no coming or going, through the power of the inconceivable wisdom of illusion resulting from habitual practice, and by the power of past great vows, it appears in this way;
the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) is likewise.

Through the power of the Tathāgata’s great vow and wisdom, and the power of the intrinsic emptiness and lack of self-nature of the dharmatā, its manifestation and concealment are sovereign; if one follows the Dharma...

In the nature of reality, all myriad phenomena are entirely non-existent; yet through the power of wisdom that accords with vows, all characteristics manifest in accordance with conditions. Their appearance and disappearance follow circumstances, and there is no creator at all.
It is simply because the principle of wisdom is inherently endowed with inconceivable efficacy and inconceivable transformations that they manifest freely.
Ordinary beings cling to this as being produced by an agent, which constitutes the obscuration of ignorance; yet since such an agent does not exist, these attachments vanish.

The function of wisdom is sovereign: it accords with the Dharmakāya such that the myriad phenomena are simultaneously quiescent; it follows the function of wisdom such that the myriad phenomena are simultaneously born.
Following great compassion, it constantly dwells within birth and death, yet following the principle-wisdom, birth and death are eternally true.

Through these three matters, the myriad modes of manifestation and concealment do not depart from the single true wisdom; the hundredfold transformations of the means of conversion follow ten principles. This is the explanation of the text and its meaning.
This chapter of the sutra is divided into twelve sections.
[Sutra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this Flower Bank Adorned World-Ocean was, in the past, by Vairocana Tathāgata, throughout as many eons as there are atoms in a world-ocean..."
When practicing the bodhisattva path, in each eon, they draw near to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds;
at the site of each Buddha, they purify and cultivate as many great vows as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, thereby adorning and purifying them.
O Children of the Buddha, this Flower Treasury Adorned Ocean of Worlds is supported by wind-circles as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru; its most [excellent]...
The lower wind-circle is named Equal Abiding; it can support all the blazing jewel-flames and adornments above it.
Next above that, the wind-circle is named Producing Various Jewel Adornments; it can support the King of Mani Banners of Pure Radiance above it.
Next above that, the wind-circle is named Jewel Splendor; it can support all the jewel-bells above it.
The upper wind-circle is named Equal Flame; it can support the sun-light-marked maṇi-king wheel above it.
The next wind-circle is named Various Universal Adornments; it can support the light-wheel flower above it.
The next wind-circle is named Universal Purity; it can support the lion-throne of all-flame-flowers above it. Above that is the wind-circle...
The wind-circle named Renown Pervading the Ten Directions supports the [world-system] above it, which consists of all kingly jewel banners;
the wind-circle above that, named Radiance of All Jewels, supports the [world-system] above it, which consists of all kingly mani-tree flowers;
the wind-circle above that, named Swift Universal Support, supports the [world-system] above it, which consists of all fragrant mani-Sumeru clouds; and the wind-circle above that—
O sons of the Buddha, there are clouds of various palaces for wandering and all kinds of jewel-colored fragrant terraces that can support them.
Among the wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru, the one at the very top is named "Treasury of Supreme Majestic Radiance.
It supports the fragrant water ocean called "Universal Light Mani Adornment. Within this fragrant water ocean, there is a great lotus flower named...

The Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, characterized by various radiant filaments, fragrant banners, and flowers, dwells therein, surrounded on all four sides by level, pure, and firm adamantine wheel-mountains; the oceans of land and the various trees each have their distinct divisions.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, relied upon the Buddha’s spiritual power and surveyed the ten [directions].
Then he spoke these verses:
"Because the World-Honored One cultivated pure deeds in the presence of as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust throughout all realms of existence,
he has attained this Ocean of Worlds, the Flower Treasury Adorned, which radiates various kinds of jewel-lights."

A vast cloud of compassion pervades all; having sacrificed bodies as numerous as the atoms of immeasurable lands through the power of practice over oceans of past eons, this world is now free from all defilement.
Emitting great light that abides throughout space, it is held by the power of the wind and remains unshakable.
The Buddha-treasury mani jewels are universally adorned; By the Tathāgata’s power of vows, they are made pure.
Mani flowers from the wondrous treasury are scattered everywhere, Abiding in the sky through the power of past vows.
Various oceans of firm and solid adornments, Clouds of light hang down, filling the ten directions.
From within all the mani-jewels emerge clouds of Bodhisattvas, who travel everywhere throughout the ten directions;
their blazing light forms wheels of radiant flames adorned with exquisite flowers. They flow through the entire Dharma-realm without exception, emitting pure light from within every jewel;
that light shines universally upon the ocean of sentient beings.
Pervading all the lands of the ten directions, he causes all beings to emerge from suffering and turn toward Bodhi;
as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-realm, from his pores there issue forth emanated forms such as Brahmā,
Śakra, and Cakravartin kings, as well as all sentient beings and all Buddhas.

He manifests light equal to the Dharma-realm; within that light, he proclaims the names of all Buddhas, employing various skillful means to demonstrate their taming of beings. He universally responds to the minds of all without exception.
Within every single atom of the Flower Treasury World, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm.
Buddhas of Jewel Light appear like gathering clouds;
this is the Tathāgata’s sovereign great vow-cloud pervading the Dharma-realm. Through all kalpas, they transform sentient beings;
the practices of Samantabhadra’s ground of wisdom are fully perfected, and all adornments emerge from this.
[Treatise] First, from the passage beginning "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... and extending through twenty-four lines of prose and twenty lines of verse,
it is explained how the Buddha, by virtue of his past causes— practicing the bodhisattva path and cultivating the power of pure great vows—
attained as a karmic reward a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) that supports the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpa-garbha-loka-dhātu*) along with its various adornments.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this Flower Bank Array World-Ocean rests upon a lotus flower of the Sun-Jewel King atop the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains.
Its body is made of sandalwood and maṇi-jewels; its peaks are made of majestic and powerful jewel-kings; and its circular rim is formed of exquisite fragrance maṇi-jewels."
Established by the Vajra-treasury, it is entirely filled with flowing streams of fragrant water;

amidst them are forests of various jewels, wondrous flowers in full bloom, and fragrant herbs carpeting the ground. It is adorned everywhere with great pearls and filled at every turn with various fragrant blossoms.
Nets of *maṇi* gems hang down and cover it all around. Such arrays of exquisite adornments are as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, and empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The great oceans of worlds are without limit; The jewel wheels are pure, with every kind of color.”
All its adornments are utterly wondrous; it arises through the spiritual power of the Tathāgata,
adorned with wheels of mani-jewels, wheels of exquisite incense, and wheels of pearl lamp-flames made of various sublime gems, and it rests securely within a pure wheel-enclosure.
With a treasury of firm maṇi jewels, adorned with Jāmbūnada gold,
it radiates light and flames throughout the ten directions; transparent within and without,
it is utterly pure, composed of vajra-maṇi, and further rains down various exquisite maṇi treasures.
Its precious essences are wondrous and manifold; it radiates pure light, universally majestic and beautiful.
Fragrant waters flow in streams of infinite colors, scattering various flowers, jewels, and sandalwood.
Myriad lotuses bloom in competition like spread-out robes, and rare herbs grow in profusion, all exquisitely fragrant.
Immeasurable jewel trees universally adorn [the realm], their blossoms opening and their filaments emerging in blazing colors;
various named garments are within them, and clouds of light shine everywhere, ever perfect.
Immeasurable and boundless great bodhisattvas hold canopies and burn incense, filling the entire dharma-realm.
They emit all manner of wondrous sounds, universally turning the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata;
formed from the powdered jewels of mani-trees, each individual jewel-particle manifests radiance,
wherein the pure body of Vairocana enters in its entirety, allowing all to see him.
Within all manner of adornments, the Buddha’s body appears;
With infinite forms and countless colors, it pervades everywhere throughout the ten directions. The sentient beings thus transformed are likewise limitless;
From all these adornments, wondrous sounds emerge, Proclaiming the wheel of the Tathāgata’s original vows.
[Verse: All the oceans of pure lands throughout the ten directions, the Buddha’s sovereign power causes to be pervaded entirely.

[Treatise: From "At that time" below, there are eight and a half lines of prose and twenty lines of verse which clarify the praise of the Jewel-Encircling Mountains atop the lotuses, complete with all manner of adornments produced by the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, within this world-ocean, all the great earth within the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains is entirely composed of vajra;
it is firm, adorned, indestructible, pure, level, and without high or low places, with wheels made of maṇi jewels and treasuries of various precious gems."
Various maṇi jewels in the diverse forms of all sentient beings were interspersed as adornments;
powdered masses of various jewels were strewn about, and portions of lotus-fragrance-treasury maṇis were placed therein.
All manner of ornaments filled the space like clouds, and the maṇi jewels were embellished with all the adornments found in the Buddha-lands of the three periods of time.
He perceived that the entire realm of the Tathāgata was manifested like the net of Indra, within which the sons of the Buddha were arrayed.
Within this ocean of worlds, there were adornments as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions by the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority and said:
He spoke in verse:
"That ground is level and utterly pure, Abiding firmly and indestructible.
It is adorned everywhere with mani-jewels, With various precious gems interspersed therein."
The ground of vajra is most delightful, adorned with precious wheels and jeweled nets;
lotuses are spread upon it, all perfectly complete. Exquisite garments cover it entirely and pervade everywhere;
bodhisattvas’ celestial crowns and jeweled necklaces are all spread upon the ground as beautiful ornaments.
Sandalwood and mani-jewels are scattered everywhere, all emitting pure and wondrous light;
Precious flower-blossoms send forth flames that radiate sublime brilliance, Their radiant flames like clouds illuminating all things.
These exquisite flowers and various jewels are scattered, Universally covering the earth as a magnificent adornment.
Dense clouds arise and spread, filling the ten directions; Vast and great radiance is without end.
Reaching everywhere throughout all lands of the ten directions, They proclaim the Tathāgata’s nectar-like Dharma.
Within the wish-fulfilling jewels of all Buddhas’ vows, Boundless and vast eons are universally manifested.
The deeds performed in the past by those of supreme wisdom are such that within these jewels,
no ground is seen that does not contain mani-gems; all Buddha-fields enter into every single atom of those various Buddha-fields, and all lands likewise enter therein.
The Flower Treasury World-realm, adorned with exquisite jewels, Is where Bodhisattvas travel throughout the ten directions,
Proclaiming the great vows of the Mahāsattvas; This is the power of mastery at the site of enlightenment,
A ground adorned with wondrous mani-jewels, Radiating pure light and complete with every ornament.
Pervading the Dharma-realm as vast as space, the power of the Buddha manifests spontaneously in this way;
those who cultivate the vows of Samantabhadra and enter the realm of the Buddha—
only those of great wisdom can know such miraculous transformations within this ocean of lands.
[Commentary] From "At that time" onwards, the ten and a half lines of sūtra and twenty lines of verse praise the level ground within the Cakravāḍa mountains,
which is composed of vajra, replete with various jewels interspersed throughout its surface, and adorned with nets of flowers.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, within the great earth of this world-ocean, there are incalculable numbers of fragrant water seas—as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields.
Their bottoms are adorned with all manner of wonderful jewels; their shores are adorned with exquisite fragrant *maṇi* gems; and they are made of *Vairocana-maṇi-rāja* jewels."
That net reflects the fragrant waters, which are transparent and possess the colors of all manner of jewels;

it is filled with various precious flowers spread out upon its surface, while fine sandalwood powder settles as sediment beneath. It emanates the sounds of the Buddha’s speech and radiates jewel-light;
boundless bodhisattvas hold various canopies and manifest supernatural powers, such that all the adornments of every world appear therein.
In the center appear ten jeweled stairways arranged in rows, surrounded on all sides by ten-jeweled railings;
there are lotus flowers as numerous as the atoms within the four continents, adorned with every kind of jewel, blooming upon the waters;
and there are unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of ten-jeweled morality-banners, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, draped with robes made of every kind of jewel.
There were banners with bell-nets as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, possessing infinite colors and forms; pavilions of precious flowers numbering hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas;
cities of hundreds of jewels and lotuses; groves of various precious trees as numerous as the atoms within the four continents, with nets made of jewel-flame mani-gems;
and sandalwood incense as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with mani-gems of radiant flames representing the speech and sounds of all Buddhas.
Inexpressible hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of walls made of various jewels completely surrounded [the assembly],
adorning it everywhere. At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, observed the Ten Powers by the power of the Buddha and spoke in verse:
Upon the great earth within this world-system, there is a sea of fragrant water,
adorned with maṇi jewels and purified by the distribution of exquisite gems;
it is established upon an indestructible foundation of diamond and has shores formed by heaps of fragrant-treasury maṇis, while wheels of sun-flame pearls are spread across it like clouds.
Auspicious lotus jewels form their necklaces; everywhere they are adorned, pure and stainless.
The fragrant waters are clear and still, possessing all colors; precious flowers swirl and spread, emitting brilliant light.
Resounding sounds shake far and near; through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the wondrous Dharma is proclaimed.
The steps and stairways are adorned with various jewels, further embellished with mani-gems as inlays;

the surrounding railings are entirely made of precious gems. Nets of lotus beads are spread like clouds, and rows of mani-jewel trees stand in formation, their blossoms and filaments in full bloom with radiant, blazing light.
Various musical sounds are constantly played in competition;
by the Buddha’s supernormal power, such various wonderful jewel *puṇḍarīka* flowers are spread out as adornments upon the fragrant water seas.
Fragrant flames and radiant light never cease for a moment, vast and perfect, pervading everywhere.
Luminous jewel banners are ever blazing, And exquisite robes hang down as ornamental adornments.
Nets of mani-bells proclaim the sounds of the Dharma, Causing all who hear them to advance toward Buddha-wisdom.
Exquisite jewel lotuses form the city walls, Resplendent and polished with multicolored mani-gems.
Pearl cloud-shadows spread across the four quarters; thus adorned, the walls of the fragrant water-ocean encircle it on all sides.
Multi-storied pavilions face one another, arrayed upon it, with immeasurable light perpetually blazing; such is the ocean of various pure adornments.
In the past, Vairocana Purified and adorned various oceans of lands;
Thus vast and boundless, All are the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
[Treatise] 4. From "At that time" onwards, sixteen and a half lines of prose and twenty lines of verse clarify the Vajra.
The jewel ground contains various seas of fragrant water, with various jewels for their floor and exquisite incense adorning the shores, complete with all manner of ornaments.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, each of these seas of fragrant water is encircled by as many rivers of fragrant water as there are atoms in four continents, all spiraling to the right and entirely made of gold."

Its banks are composed of adamantine pure-light maṇi-jewels, adorned with clouds of precious light-colored radiance appearing from all Buddhas, as well as the various sounds and voices of all sentient beings.
From every place where the river forms eddies, the diverse forms and characteristics of the causal practices cultivated by all Buddhas emerge.
Nets of maṇi-jewels and clusters of bells made of various treasures adorn it.
All the adornments of the oceans of worlds appear within it, covered above by clouds of *maṇi* jewels.

These clouds universally manifest the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa-lokadhātu*), Vairocana, and the emanated Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as all the supernatural deeds of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, they produce sublime sounds that extol the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time; from their fragrant waters, there is always...
Emanating clouds of light-flames from all jewels in an uninterrupted succession— were they to be described in detail,
each river would possess adornments as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds— at that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning,
surveyed the ten directions by the Buddha’s spiritual power and spoke in verse:
Pure fragrant streams fill the great river; its banks are made of wondrous vajra-jewels.
Jeweled dust is spread across the ground as a circular carpet, and various ornaments are all exquisite and precious.
Rows of jeweled staircases form a wonderful adornment, and the surrounding railings are entirely magnificent and beautiful.
With pearls as their core, they are adorned with various flowers; diverse necklaces and garlands hang down together.
With the pure colors of fragrant waters and jewel-light, they constantly emit mani-gems that flow forth in rapid competition.
As the various flowers sway with the waves, they all play musical sounds proclaiming the wondrous Dharma.
Fine sandalwood is ground into a paste, and all manner of exquisite jewels swirl together in eddies;
clouds of fragrant essence spread through the midst, emitting flames and flowing scents that pervade everywhere.
Within the river, various wonderful jewels are produced, all radiating light with blazing colors.
Its light spreads shadows to form a dais and throne, complete with canopies of flowers and strings of pearls;
within the sovereign maṇi jewel appears the Buddha’s body, its radiance universally illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
This serves as the wheel that adorns the ground, where fragrant waters reflect with clarity and are ever full.
A net of mani-jewels with bells of gold, Covering the entire Fragrant River, it proclaims the Buddha’s voice;
It fully expounds all paths to enlightenment And the sublime practices of Samantabhadra.
The jewel-shore is utterly pure, Constantly emitting the sounds of the Tathāgata’s original vows.
The past practices of all Buddhas are universally proclaimed by their voices so that all may see them;
from every place where the rivers swirl, Bodhisattvas constantly emerge like clouds,
proceeding to vast buddha-fields until they completely fill the entire dharma-realm.
[Verse] The King of Pure Jewels is spread like clouds, Completely covering all rivers of fragrance.
These jewels are equal to the mark between the Buddha’s eyebrows, Vividly manifesting the reflections of all Buddhas.
[Treatise] 5. From "At that time" onwards, twelve and a half lines of prose and twenty lines of verse clarify the various fragrances.
The ocean is filled with various fragrant rivers; the beds and banks of these rivers are adorned with all manner of ornaments and wind to the right around the ocean.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, the lands between these fragrant rivers are all adorned with various exquisite jewels, each one as numerous as the atoms within four continents."
Countless *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, adorned with jewels as numerous as the atoms of a world-system, completely filled the surroundings;

each was surrounded by rows of jewel-trees as numerous as the atoms of four continents, from every single tree constantly issuing clouds of all manner of adornments, while *maṇi-rāja* gems shone amidst them, and various flowers and fragrances filled every place. These were the trees.
Furthermore, they emitted subtle and wondrous sounds proclaiming the great vows cultivated by all Tathāgatas throughout all kalpas;
they also scattered various kinds of sovereign maṇi-jewel kings that filled the entire ground— namely, the lotus-wheel sovereign maṇi-jewel king,
the fragrant flame-light cloud sovereign maṇi-jewel king, and variously adorned sovereign maṇi-jewel kings manifesting the inconceivable.
There are oceans of worlds such as these: the Adorned Color Maṇi-Jewel King, the Sunlight-Radiant Garment Treasury Maṇi-Jewel King,
the Pervasively Hanging Light-Network Cloud Maṇi-Jewel King, the Manifesting All Buddhas’ Spiritual Transformations Maṇi-Jewel King,
and the Manifesting the Ocean of Karmic Retributions of All Sentient Beings Maṇi-Jewel King.
In every space between the rivers of fragrant water, numbering as many as atoms, each was fully endowed with such adornments.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, observed the ten directions by the Buddha’s spiritual power and spoke in verse:
The ground is level and utterly pure, adorned with true gold and mani jewels;
rows of trees cast their shade over it, their towering trunks and drooping branches gathering like clouds.
These branches are magnificently embellished with wondrous gems, and the flames of their blossoms form wheels of light that radiate in all directions.
Maṇi fruits spread out like clouds, universally causing them to be constantly seen throughout the ten directions;
maṇis are spread upon the ground, filling it entirely, further adorned with various flowers and precious powders.
Furthermore, palaces are made of maṇi, wherein the reflections of all sentient beings appear.
The maṇi-kings, images of all Buddhas, are scattered everywhere across the ground, reaching every place;
thus they blaze brilliantly throughout the ten directions, and within each and every atom, all Buddhas are seen.
Wondrous jewels are beautifully distributed as adornments, interspersed with nets of pearl lamps.
In every place there are mani-wheels, Each manifesting the supernatural powers of the Buddhas;
Adorned with various jewels, they emit great light, Within which all manner of transformation-Buddhas appear.
Each one travels everywhere without exception, Universally expounding the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
The exquisite maṇi jewel *puṇḍarīka* flowers fill every body of water;
their various blossoms are each distinct, all manifesting an inexhaustible radiance.
All the adornments existing throughout the three periods of time are clearly revealed within the maṇi fruits.
The essential nature is unborn and cannot be grasped; this is the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
Within all the adornments of this ground, the vast body of the Tathāgata appears everywhere;
yet it neither comes nor goes, for the Buddha’s past vows cause all to behold it.
Within every single atom of this ground, All the Buddha-sons practice the path;
Each perceives the lands they are destined to attain in the future, All of which are pure according to their respective inclinations.
[Treatise] Sixth: From "At that time" onwards, fifteen and a half lines of prose and twenty verses clarify the two [aspects of] the Fragrant River.
The level ground was adorned with trees, flowers, fruits, and various wonders, including *puṇḍarīka* flowers—these being translated as "hundred-petaled white lotuses.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones..."

The adornments of the ocean of realms are inconceivable. Why is this? O Sons of the Buddha, every single sphere within this Flower Bank Array Ocean of Worlds is adorned by pure merits as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, received the Buddha’s spiritual power and contemplated...
Observing the ten directions, he spoke these verses:
"In every place within this ocean of world-systems, All are adorned with various jewels;
Blazing flames rise into the sky like spreading clouds, Their light penetrating and constantly pervading all."
The mani-jewels emit clouds without end, In which the reflections of the Buddhas of the ten directions appear;
Their supernatural transformations never cease for a moment.
All Bodhisattvas have gathered here together, And all the mani-jewels proclaim the Buddha’s voice— A voice of wondrous beauty, inconceivable.
The deeds performed by Vairocana in the past are constantly heard and seen within these jewels;
the Honored One of Pervasive Pure Radiance appears as reflected images within every ornament,
surrounded by a multitude of manifested transformation bodies, pervading all oceans of lands.
All emanated Buddhas are like illusions; though one seeks their place of origin, it cannot be found.

By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha’s realm, such manifestations of the Tathāgata’s sovereign supernatural powers appear throughout all lands, pervading every world-system in the ten directions.
By means of this pure adornment of the ocean of lands, all things are seen within the jewels;
all the various transformations existing throughout the ten directions are like images in a mirror,
produced solely through the power of the Tathāgata’s past conduct, his spiritual penetrations, and his vows.
If there are those who can cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra, Entering the ocean of the Bodhisattvas' supreme wisdom,
They can universally manifest their bodies within every single atom,
Purifying all buddha-fields throughout inconceivable billions of great eons, And drawing near to all Tathāgatas.
Just as all beings act, they are able to manifest within a single instant all Buddha-lands like space— ineffable, unborn, and without marks—
universally adorning and purifying them for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, abiding therein by the power of their original vows.

[Treatise] From "At that time" (line 7) onwards, five lines of prose and twenty lines of verse collectively conclude and offer a general eulogy for the infinite merits and adornments of this ocean-like world-system of the Tathāgata.
The Combined Commentary on the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Flower Adornment Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-one.

The Treatise composed by Li Tongxuan, Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan of the Tang Dynasty;
