its Buddha is named Universally Illuminating Throughout the Dharma Realm.
[Treatise] These eleven [categories], including the tenth, are collectively enumerated in this tenth fascicle as one hundred world-systems surrounding a central area.
Eleven world-systems are arrayed in twenty tiers around the center;
ten of these world-systems are situated near the Cakravāḍa Mountains, while four tiers—high and low—are positioned above and below these eleven central world-systems.
The world-systems that are similar in type are separated by an extremely vast distance;
as for the remaining ninety world-systems, their numerical count is not stated, though there are one hundred and eleven world-systems in total.
The intended meaning therein has already been explained as before.

[Sūtra] "O Sons of the Buddha, within these ten unspeakably many buddha-field-microdust numbers of fragrant water oceans, there are ten unspeakably many world-systems, each as numerous as the microdusts of a buddha-field.
All of them rest upon lotus flowers adorned with mani-jewel king banners that manifest the forms of all bodhisattvas; they are each individually adorned without interruption."
They emit clouds of various jewel-colored radiances that cover their respective surfaces;

they possess various ornaments, various distinctions of eons, various appearances of Buddhas, various oceans of Dharma teachings, various sentient beings pervading and filling them, various universal entries into the ten directions, and each is sustained by the spiritual power of all Buddhas. This one...
Within a single world-system seed, all worlds rest upon various adornments, abiding in mutual connection to form a world-net;
these are established throughout the Flower Bank Adornment World-Ocean in all their diverse distinctions.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, received the Buddha’s majestic power and spoke in verse:
The Flower Treasury World-Ocean is equal to the Dharma-realm without distinction; its adornments are utterly pure, abiding in the void.
Within this world-ocean, the types of lands are inconceivable, each sovereign and distinct, without any confusion. This is the Flower Treasury World-Ocean.
The world-systems are well-arranged, with diverse forms and various adornments; their manifold characteristics differ from one another.
The transformation-sounds of all Buddhas take these various things as their essence.
According to the power of karma, they manifest the wondrous adornments of world-systems, such as Mount Sumeru, mountain cities, nets, whirlpools, and circular enclosures.
Vast lotuses bloom, each surrounded by others; In the forms of mountain banners, towers, and revolving wheels, as well as vajra shapes— Such are these inconceivable, vast world-systems.
The great ocean of world-systems has the luster of pearls and nets of light, Inconceivable; such are these world-systems.
All dwell within lotuses; in each and every world-system, inconceivable nets of light manifest myriad lands throughout the oceans of the ten directions.
All the ornaments of every world-system enter therein, and one perceives them all universally and without end.

The arrays of lands are inconceivable, and the worlds are boundless; all these various wonderful adornments arise through the power of the Great Sage. Within every array of lands, the worlds are inconceivable:
some are forming, some are decaying, and some have already been destroyed, just like the leaves in a forest.
There is arising and there is falling away; within such world-systems, worlds undergo formation and destruction.
Just as various kinds of fruits differ depending on a forest, so too do various sentient beings dwell depending on the variety of world-systems.
Just as seeds are distinct, the fruits they produce are each different.
Due to the differences in the power of karma, the realms of sentient beings are not the same.
Just as the jewel-king of the mind reflects all colors according to the mind, because the minds of sentient beings are pure, they are able to see pure lands.
It is like a great dragon king who raises clouds that pervade the void; such is the power of the Buddha’s vows.
The arising of all lands is like the magical arts of a sorcerer, capable of manifesting various phenomena;
because of the power of sentient beings' karma, lands are inconceivable.
Just as a multitude of painted images are produced by a painter, so too are all these buddha-fields created by the painter that is the mind.
The bodies of sentient beings differ, arising according to the distinctions of their minds; likewise, the various kinds of lands do not all fail to arise from karma.
Just as one sees a guide appearing in various distinct forms according to the mental activities of sentient beings, so too does one see all the realms of lands throughout the limits of all worlds.
A pervasive net of lotuses, with various distinct features, Is adorned in total purity.

Those nets of lotuses Are established within the nets of buddha-fields; With various kinds of adornments and the dwellings of various sentient beings, There are some buddha-lands That are treacherous, harsh, and uneven.
Due to the afflictions of sentient beings, such views arise therein; the immeasurable varieties of realms, both defiled and pure, arise according to the minds of sentient beings.
Sustained by the power of the Bodhisattvas, there are some buddha-fields that are both defiled and pure, arising through the force of karma.
The lands transformed by the Bodhisattvas emit radiant light; composed of stainless jewels, they are adorned with various exquisite ornaments. The Buddhas cause them all to be purified.
Within each and every world-system, though inconceivable eons of conflagration occur and what appears is ruined and decayed, those places remain eternally firm and solid.
Through the karmic power of sentient beings, many buddha-fields are produced;
they rest upon and abide by the wind-circle and the water-circle. Such is the nature of worlds:
though seen in various ways, they are in reality neither born nor destroyed, moment after moment of thought.
Born in immeasurable lands, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they see all realms— some pure and stainless,
some composed of earth, their substance exceedingly hard and rigid, dark and devoid of light, the dwelling place of those who perform evil deeds;
some realms are composed of diamond, yet filled with defilement, great sorrow, and terror.
Suffering is abundant while joy is meager; it is the dwelling place of those with little merit.
Some are fashioned of iron, others made of red copper. The rocky mountains are perilous and fearsome;
the world-system is filled with evildoers and hells. Sentient beings suffer without rescue, forever remaining in the midst of darkness.
Scorched by the blazing ocean of flames, or again there are those among the animals with various hideous forms;
due to their own evil karma, they constantly undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
Or one sees those in the realm of Yama, tormented and oppressed by hunger and thirst, ascending great mountains of fire and undergoing most grievous suffering.
There are various buddha-fields composed of the seven precious jewels;

these diverse palaces are obtained through pure karma. You should observe the world, wherein humans and devas achieve the fruits of pure karma and experience happiness at all times, even within every single pore.
Inconceivable billions of lands are adorned with various marks; never cramped or narrow, sentient beings therein each experience according to their own karma.

These worlds are of infinite kinds; within them, through grasping and attachment, they give rise to suffering and pleasure that differ from one another. There are lands formed of many jewels, which constantly radiate boundless light.
The wondrous lotus of the Vajra is adorned, pure and stainless; there is a realm whose essence is light, abiding upon a wheel of radiance.
With the fragrance of golden sandalwood, clouds of flames illuminate everywhere.
There is a realm formed by lunar discs, where fragrant garments are spread all around within a single lotus.
Bodhisattvas fill them all; some lands are composed of various jewels, their forms and colors free from all defilement, like the net of Śakra, with light constantly shining.
Some lands have fragrance as their substance, or consist of diamond flowers, or take the form of the reflected light of *maṇi* gems; when observed, they are exceedingly pure.
There are inconceivable lands accomplished by revolving flowers, filled with emanation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of universal radiance;
There are pure lands where all are flower-trees with wondrous branches arrayed as sites of enlightenment, shaded by clouds of mani-jewels; There are lands illuminated by pure light.
Some are formed of vajra-flowers; some are the emanated voices of Buddhas. Infinite arrays form a net; some lands are like Bodhisattvas.
Some are like exquisite maṇi-jewel crowns; some have the shape of thrones.
From these emanations, light rays issue forth; some are sandalwood powder, And some are the light from between the eyebrows.
Or from sounds within the Buddha’s light, this wondrous land is formed.
Some see the pure land adorned with a single ray of light; others see many adornments, all of which are marvelous and extraordinary.
Some use the sublime objects of ten lands as ornaments; others use those from a thousand lands.
All things serve as adornments— whether through the objects of billions of lands— adorned within a single realm with various differing features,
all appearing like reflections. Inexpressible numbers of land-objects adorn a single field,
each emitting its own radiance, arising through the power of the Tathāgata’s vows.
There are some lands purified by the power of vows; within all their adornments, one universally beholds oceans of realms.

For those who cultivate the vows of Samantabhadra, whatever pure lands are attained—the adornments of the realms throughout the three times—all appear therein. O Son of the Buddha, you should observe this!
By the majestic spiritual power of this world-system, may all future lands be seen in their entirety, like a dream; likewise,
the oceans of past lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions shall all appear as manifestations within a single land,
just like magical illusions— along with all the Buddhas of the three periods of time and their respective lands.

Within a single world-system, one perceives everything; The spiritual powers of all Buddhas manifest within a single atom, and all sentient beings therein are clearly seen in their various forms, like reflections without reality.
Or there may be many worlds, their shapes like the great ocean, Or like Mount Sumeru.
The worlds are inconceivable; there are lands well-established, Their forms like Indra’s net or like the shape of forest groves.
Buddhas fill them all, Some taking the form of jewel wheels, others the shape of lotuses, Complete with eight corners and manifold ornaments, Every variety entirely pure.
Some are shaped like a seat, or else they have three corners; some are like the city walls of Kharaka, or like the body of Brahmā;
some are like the topknot of the Lord of Devas; some are like a half-moon, or like Mount Maṇi;
some are shaped like the orb of the sun, or there are worlds with various other forms.
They are like whirlpools in the ocean of fragrance, or they form circles of light; some were purified and adorned by the Buddha in the past, while others take the shape of wheels or nets.
Some have the form of altars, some resemble the ūrṇā-kośa, the uṣṇīṣa, or the broad, long eyes of a Buddha. Some are like the hands of a Buddha, and some are like vajra-wands.
Some are shaped like Mount Jvālāmukha; Bodhisattvas pervade them all. Some are shaped like lions, or like sea shells;
with immeasurable varieties of forms and characteristics, their essential natures each differ.
Within a single world-system, the shapes of worlds are inexhaustible; all arise through the power of the Buddha’s vows.
Protected and mindful, they dwell in peace; some remain for one eon in a buddha-field, others for ten eons, or even beyond a hundred thousand, as numerous as the atoms within a land.
Some perceive the formation and destruction of fields within a single eon, while others perceive immeasurable, incalculable, and even inconceivable numbers.
In some lands there is a Buddha; in some lands there is no Buddha. In some there is but a single Buddha;

in others, there are immeasurable Buddhas. If a land has no Buddha, a Buddha from another world-system manifests through transformation, coming to perform all manner of wondrous deeds, passing away from heaven and descending into a spirit.
Abiding in the womb and being born, Subduing Māra and attaining perfect enlightenment,
Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings, Manifesting various forms— To turn the sublime wheel of Dharma,
responding entirely to their faculties and desires, In every single Buddha-field, A single Buddha appears in the world.
Having spent billions of years expounding the unsurpassed Dharma, beings who are not vessels for the Dharma are unable to see the Buddhas.
Yet, for those whose hearts find joy in it, they see them everywhere—in every single land, a Buddha appears in the world; thus, there are Buddhas in all lands.

Within these inconceivable billions of lands, each and every Buddha manifests immeasurable miraculous transformations that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, taming the ocean of sentient beings. There are realms without light, shrouded in darkness and filled with many terrors;
their painful touch is like swords and blades, bringing bitter anguish to all who behold them.
Some have the light of various devas; some have the light of palaces; or the light of the sun and moon—such networks of lands are inconceivable.

Some lands possess their own radiance; or trees emit pure light where there is never any suffering or affliction, due to the power of the merit of sentient beings; or some have the light of mountains.
Some are illuminated by the light of mani-jewels, Or by the light of lamps; All are due to the power of the karma of sentient beings.
Some are illuminated by the light of the Buddhas, With Bodhisattvas filling them.
There are lotuses with the color of blazing flames, most magnificent and beautiful; Some lands are illuminated by the light of flowers, And some are illuminated by fragrant waters.
Incense for anointing, incense for burning, and illumination— All arise through the power of pure vows.
Some illuminate with the light of clouds, the light of mani-shells, Or the light of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
They can proclaim delightful sounds, or illuminate with the light of jewels, Or with the flames of vajra; their pure voices can resound afar.

Wherever it goes, there is no suffering; Whether it be the light of mani-jewels, The light of ornaments, or the radiance of the site of enlightenment, It shines brilliantly within the great assemblies.
The Buddha emits a great light, and transformation Buddhas fill its midst; That light shines everywhere, touching and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
There are buddha-fields most terrifying, where the sounds of wailing and great suffering resound;
their voices are so acutely agonizing that those who hear them give rise to revulsion and fear.
In the realms of hell-beings, animals, and the domain of Yama—this turbid and evil world—there constantly arise sounds of sorrow and pain. Or there may be lands within which...
They constantly produce delightful sounds that please the mind and accord with the teachings; this is obtained through pure karma.
In some lands, one constantly hears the voice of Śakra, or the voice of Brahmā, or the voices of all the lords of the world.
Furthermore, in some buddha-fields, wondrous sounds emerge from within the clouds.
The mani-trees of the jewel-ocean, And the pervasive sounds of music;
Within the perfect halos of all Buddhas, Emanated voices that never cease, And the wondrous voices of Bodhisattvas, Heard throughout the lands of the ten directions, In inconceivable realms;
The sound of universally turning the Wheel of Dharma, The voice produced from the ocean of vows.
Cultivating sublime voices, all Buddhas of the three periods of time give birth to names for all worlds, fully endowed with them;

their voices are inexhaustible. In some lands, one hears the voice of the power of all Buddhas, as well as the stages, the perfections, and the immeasurables—they expound all such dharmas in this way.
By the power of Samantabhadra’s vows, he proclaims wondrous sounds across billions of lands;
those sounds, like the roll of thunder, endure for kalpas without end. In pure buddha-fields throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions, there is nowhere these sounds are not heard.

[Treatise] The final section of the twelfth fascicle of the *Sūtra* provides a comprehensive verse summary of all the preceding world-oceans—whether pure or defiled, homogeneous or mixed—which abide within space without obstructing one another. All these arise through the power of karma.

As the scriptural text is vast and extensive, it is not possible to provide a detailed structural analysis; furthermore, the profusion of sentences and phrases would otherwise hinder [the understanding].
The essential meaning, flavor, and general purport of this work have already been briefly outlined; the remaining extensive meanings are fully contained within the scriptural text itself.

Unlike minor sūtras, which require the citation of many external texts to adorn their meaning, this great compendium of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) finds that the meanings of other sūtras do not largely correspond with it, as its intent differs from those of the Three Vehicles.
The entirety of this distinct scripture cannot be categorized as such; these ten volumes above clarify three instances where the fruit is raised:
first, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment and the assembly within the seat raised the Buddha’s fruit of practice to clarify the Buddha’s self-realization;
second, the assembly at the ūrṇā-kośa (between the eyebrows) raised the Buddha’s fruit of the Middle Way practice for the sake of all those who have not yet believed.

The Causes for Producing Faith: The three sections on the Flower Treasury World-Ocean clarify the fruits obtained as the retribution for the practices performed by the assembly seated before [the Buddha] and the assembly within his brow.
In essence, this answers the previous thirty-seven questions by means of the fruit of the Buddha’s retributive karma;
by seeing the fruit, one knows the cause, so that future students may emulate such practice accordingly.
Such practices and vows result in such rewards.

the Sūtra-collation and Treatise-merger compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou of the Tang Dynasty; Chapter Six: Vairocana.
[Treatise] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, the intent of the chapter’s introduction; second, the explanation of the chapter’s title;
and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text. Regarding the first, the intent of the chapter’s introduction:

The preceding five chapters have presented the fruit of Vairocana Buddha in the present world, yet there may be a fear that this will not inspire faith. Why is this? Because in the past... [text ends].
What has become of those ancient traces today? By citing the past to corroborate the present, it is shown that the Way is not erroneous;
furthermore, by clarifying that the Dharma of all Buddhas across the three periods of time is similar throughout the ages, it ensures that those who achieve faith will have no doubts.
Regarding the title of this chapter, the "Vairocana Chapter," it is named after its primary subject (the *upādāya-saṃjñā*): it clarifies the citation of ancient Buddhas.
The title of this chapter is established based on the current faith and likewise takes the Buddha’s name as its designation. "Vicitra" (Vi) means "various," and "Cakṣuṣa" (Che-na) means "light.
This signifies that through the light of various teachings and practices established by the compassion and wisdom of the Dharmakāya, the karmic darkness of sentient beings is shattered.
Question: Are the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present one and the same, or are they different? Answer: Are they one or are they different? Why [ask such a question]?
That which is thus is the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body; the ninety-seven marks of a great man, great loving-kindness, great compassion, wisdom, and liberation—these are identical.
That each and every sentient being resolves their mind to attain Buddhahood is distinct.

Furthermore, that all the Buddhas of the immeasurable three periods of time all achieve Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, without any distinction between before and after, is identical; yet even so, it is not...
Within a single thought-moment, one destroys [the notion of] seeing immeasurable sentient beings across the temporal measures of the three periods;
this is understood through the ten mysteries and the meaning of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*). As the Sūtra says: "The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body;
likewise, their single body, single wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are also thus. Third, regarding the interpretation according to the text: in this one...
In this chapter of the sutra, the long section consists of fifteen segments of text. Within these fifteen segments, there are four instances of Buddhas appearing in the world;
these collectively clarify that Vairocana is the single name, which varies according to the conditions of each world and is not a difference in the Buddha’s actual name.
In the subsequent "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas" of this sutra, each individual Buddha [is detailed].
All names—whether those corresponding to the Dharma-realm, the realm of sentient beings, or those arising according to conditions, including every name in the world—are the names of all Buddhas.

This is because the virtues of the Tathāgata pervade all phenomena; just as empty space pervades and contains all things without exception, so too do the names of all sentient beings enter into the names of the Buddha, for there is nothing that is not pure.
Furthermore, it is like a fragrance called "Elephant-Treasury" (Gajagarbha) that arises from the battle of nāgas;
when a single pellet of this is burned, it remains potent for seven days, causing a rain of gold to fall. Those whose bodies are moistened by it all become golden in color.
In the same way, all names and designations that enter into the name of the Buddha are likewise entirely pure. Thus, the name of the Buddha pervades all things.
Because he illuminates the names of all worlds, he is first named Vairocana;
with the light of various teachings and practices, he shines universally upon all things, illuminating them with the eye of Dharma. This long treatise consists of fifteen sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, in the distant past, beyond world-microdust numbers of kalpas, and even twice that number, there was an ocean of worlds named Universal Gate Pure Radiance (*Samanta-mukha-viśuddha-prabhā*).
Within this ocean of worlds, there was a world named Supreme Sound (*Jaya-ghoṣa*), which rested upon an ocean of mani-flower nets and was supported by Mount Sumeru."
Worlds as numerous as the atoms of a mountain serve as its retinue; their shape is perfectly circular, and their ground is endowed with immeasurable adornments.
They are surrounded by three hundred tiers of wheels of various precious trees and encircled by mountain ranges, all covered above by clouds of every kind of jewel.
Pure and stainless, they shine with radiant light, and their cities and palaces are like Mount Sumeru draped in celestial robes.
Clothing and food arrived according to their thoughts; that eon was named "Various Adornments.
[Treatise] First: from "At that time" onwards, this section of eight lines of scripture clarifies how Samantabhadra addresses the assembly, intending to expound the Dharma.
Within this section, it is further divided into eleven parts: first, citing the number of eons through which the ancient Buddhas had passed.
1. Listing the names of ancient oceans of worlds; 2. Listing the specific names of individual worlds within those oceans of worlds;
3. Listing the bases upon which the worlds rest; 4. Listing the number of surrounding retinues of worlds; 5. Listing the shapes of the worlds; 6.
Listing the adornments upon the ground of the worlds; 7. Listing the jewel trees of the worlds.
Furthermore, the ninefold succession of the Cakravāḍa mountain ranges; the cities, towns, and palaces throughout the world;

the food, drink, clothing, and other necessities that appear for the people of the world according to their thoughts; and the names of the kalpas—all these and more are fully provided within the text itself and need not be further explained here.
[Sūtra] "O Sons of the Buddha, in that world of Supreme Sound (Ghoṣavatī), there is a sea of fragrant water named Pure Radiance (Vimalaprabhā).

Within that sea, there emerges a great lotus-mountain named Universal Adornment Banner of Flower Flames (Puṣpajvālā-samantavyūha-dhvaja), surrounded on all sides by railings made of ten kinds of jewels.
Upon that mountain is a great forest named Maṇi-flower Branch Wheel (Maṇipuṣpa-śākhā-cakra)."

Infinite pavilions of flowers and infinite jeweled terraces were arranged in every direction; infinite banners of exquisite incense and infinite banners of jewel-mountains stood towering and supremely adorned.
Infinite precious *puṇḍarīka* lotuses flourished everywhere, while infinite nets of fragrant *maṇi* lotuses hung down on all sides.
The sounds of music were harmonious and pleasing, and clouds of fragrance shone forth in countless numbers.
Each is surrounded by immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* cities, within which dwell various classes of sentient beings.
[Treatise] From the passage beginning "O sons of the Buddha" below, there are eight lines and a half of scripture; the major significance therein is divided as follows:
1. Clarifying the fragrant water ocean and enumerating its name within the world-system *Prabhāsa-ghoṣa*;
2. Clarifying that within the ocean there appears a flower-mountain shaped like Mount Sumeru; 3. Clarifying the adornments upon the mountain, which number fourteen; 4.
Clarifying that upon the mountain there is a great forest and enumerating the name of that forest; 5. Enumerating the five kinds of immeasurables upon the mountain.
The first section describes the adornments of the various matters; the second describes the countless cities upon the mountain peaks, which are difficult to record;
the third describes the cohabitation of various classes of sentient beings. As for the term *pundarīka*, it means "white lotus flower.
This preceding passage is self-evident and need not be further explained.

[Sūtra] "O Sons of the Buddha, to the east of this grove there is a great city named Jvālāprabhā, the capital of the King of Men, surrounded by a perimeter of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of cities.
It is established from pure and wondrous jewels; it measures seven thousand yojanas in both length and breadth.
Its walls, towers, battlements, and defensive works are all made of the seven treasures, and they are all lofty, magnificent, and adorned with sevenfold [enclosures]."
The precious moats were filled with fragrant water, and *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses—composed entirely of various jewels—were distributed everywhere as ornamental decorations.
Seven rows of precious *tāla* trees surrounded the palaces and towers, all of which were adorned with various precious substances;
diverse exquisite nets were spread over them, and they were anointed with fragrant ointments.
Scattered flowers were fragrant and brilliant within it; there were hundreds of billions of nayutas of gates, all adorned with jewels.
Before each gate stood forty-nine jeweled śīla-banners arranged in successive rows.
Furthermore, hundreds of billions of groves and gardens surrounded it on all sides, and within them were various kinds of *maṇi* trees of miscellaneous fragrances, their scents wafting everywhere.
Its fragrance permeates everywhere, and the harmonious songs of its birds bring joy to all who hear them.

Among all the inhabitants of this great city, there are none who do not possess the supernormal power of karmic fruition, traveling through the air at will with a gait like that of the devas; whatever they desire arrives as soon as it is thought of.
To the south of this city is a celestial city named Tree-Flower Adornment (*Vṛkṣapuṣpavyūha*), which is situated to its right and spirals clockwise.
The great dragon city is named Ultimate; next is the yakṣa city named Supreme Vajra Banner;
next is the gandharva city named Wondrous Palace; next is the asura city named Jewel Wheel;
next is the garuḍa city named Adorned with Wondrous Jewels; and next is the Brahmā king city named Various Wondrous Adornments.
Adorned in this manner were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of such cities;
each of these cities was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of pavilions, each of which possessed immeasurable adornments.
[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, nineteen lines and a half of the sūtra clarify the city of Eḍakavatī.
Within this section, the meaning is divided into eleven parts: 1) stating the name of the city; 2) stating the residence of the human king; 3) stating that it is surrounded by various cities;
4) clarifying that the substance of the city is composed of various jewels; 5) clarifying the dimensions of the city's breadth and width; 6) clarifying... [text continues].
The city walls and fortifications were all magnificent and grandly adorned. Regarding the seven bright cities, the various matters of their upper and lower sections were likewise adorned.

As for the term *lǔ* (rampart), according to the phonetic and semantic commentary, it refers to a defensive structure atop a city wall; that which protrudes forward at the front is called a *dík* (battlement);

that which is decorated, lofty, and superior is called *chóng* (lofty); and that which is beautiful and worthy of being beheld is called *lì* (magnificent). Below the city walls, there are long moats, deep and wide.
Those [walls] are called *hāo* (moats), and those [ditches] are called *qiàn* (trenches). The *utpala* flower—here translated as "blue flower"—has a root resembling a lotus root;
its leaves are narrow and long, small and rounded at the base, gradually tapering to a point at the tip like the eye of a Buddha. Thus, its floral stalk has no thorns.
According to the passage praising the Buddha, "His eyes are pure, long, and wide, like the blue lotus," this refers precisely to the petals of the blue lotus.
*Utpala* (also *padma*) is translated here as the red lotus; its stalks have thorns.
*Kuvalaya* has thorny stalks, or it is said to be a flower that is either red or white;
when its petals have not yet fully opened, their tips are somewhat short and its shape is like a withered bud. *Puṇḍarīka* is the white lotus. *Ratnatāla*.
As for the trees (some say they are *aśoka* trees, though this remains uncertain as it has not yet been verified by examining the texts), they surround [the city] in seven tiers.

In matters of the Dharma, the numbers one, three, five, seven, and nine are used, following the principle of the Yang (odd) numbers. *Śīla* is translated here as "Pure Jewel Banner" (the above adornments collectively constitute the various jewels).

In the eighth description, the inhabitants dwell within the city; in the ninth description, people attain supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) as the retribution of their karma, such that whatever they think of arrives immediately.

The city of Daśāloka is surrounded on four sides by seven kinds of mixed cities inhabited by devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and other such beings, as well as the city of Saṃyuta and the city of Apramāṇavyūha.
A question was asked: "Among these, one kind consists of humans who are neither devas, nāgas, nor spirits;
how is it that their karmic retribution, supernatural powers, clothing, food, and drink arrive according to their thoughts? Furthermore, regarding their dwellings..."
By what karma is this magnificent and superior environment adorned with jewels obtained as a karmic retribution? He replied:
"Because the cause is vast, the karmic retribution is vast; because the cause is magnificent and superior, the dwelling place of the karmic retribution is magnificent and superior.
He asked: "What constitutes the cause that is vast and magnificent? He replied: "It is because of past causes regarding this Vairocana..."
That Dharma-realm wisdom arises from the essence and function of the gate of non-abiding, which is by nature pure;

thus one generates faith and cultivates the power of resolute belief, constantly believing that self and others, ordinary beings and sages, are of one body. Because one equally realizes the wisdom of the future, it has no place of abiding;
because there is no self and no "mine," the mind and its objects are equal and non-dual. Since there is no "mine," all things [are as such].
Ordinary beings and sages are fundamentally nothing but the Dharma-realm, which is by nature unconditioned and devoid of arising or ceasing.
Abiding in the truth, they abide nowhere; their mental wisdom is identical to that of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
This abiding nature is the true Dharma-realm, wherein all discrimination is the fundamental unmoving wisdom of all Buddhas—ordinary beings and sages are one in this single reality.
Because this wisdom fully trusts that one’s own mind is the seed of Buddhahood and omniscience,
one does not have a separate mind that believes in a Buddha outside of the mind, nor does one perceive the appearance of a Buddha within one's own mind;
thus, while trusting in such a dharma, because one’s own power is as yet insufficient, this person attains all [qualities] among human beings.
By this power of faith, the Victorious Reward (Vipāka-jina) returns to dwell together with Vairocana Buddha in his realm;
he constantly manifests the supernormal powers of spiritual penetration and dwells among the devas.

All those who reside in every city—the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and others—are all co-participants in this Dharma, having given rise to faith and understanding within it; therefore, by means of this faith...
Because they have attained such supreme, wondrous, and vast fruits of retribution—both the primary body and its environment—due to their high and exalted merit, [the Sūtra says]:
"O Sons of the Buddha, within this Great Forest of the Jewel Flower Branch Wheel, there is a site of enlightenment named Jewel Flower Universal Illumination (*Ratnapuṣpa-samantāvabhāsa*).
It is adorned with the distribution of various great jewels, and wheels of *maṇi* flowers fill it, blooming everywhere. Thus it is said.
Incense and lamps possess the colors of various jewels, and clouds of radiant flames spread everywhere;
nets of light universally illuminate all manner of adornments, which constantly produce exquisite jewels, and amidst all kinds of music, refined sounds are perpetually played.

The Sovereign Maṇi Jewel manifests the body of a Bodhisattva, and various wonderful flowers pervade the ten directions. Before that site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is a great ocean named Fragrant Maṇi-Vajra.
There emerged a great lotus named Flower-Petal-Flame-Wheel; its flower was vast, measuring ten billion yojanas in extent.

Its stalk, leaves, filaments, and pedestal were all composed of wondrous jewels. It was surrounded by ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of lotuses, which constantly emitted light and perpetually produced sublime sounds that pervaded the ten directions.

[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are nine lines of scripture that clarify the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) within the grove of flowering branches, as well as its vast and magnificent adornments;
this grove is adorned with various flowers and is constantly filled with the sounds of music.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, in the first kalpa of that world Suprabha, there appeared ten Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru.
The first of these Buddhas was named Sarvaguṇaparvatasumerusuprabhamegha.
O Sons of the Buddha, you should know that one hundred years before that Buddha was about to appear, this Maṇipuṣpa...
In the Great Forest of Branch-Wheels, all adornments were universally pure;
that is to say, inconceivable clouds of jewel-flames issued forth, emitting sounds of praise for the Buddha’s merits and proclaiming the voices of countless Buddhas;

light was extended and nets were spread, completely covering the palaces and towers of the ten directions which illuminated one another; and the radiance of precious flowers surged upward to form clouds, from which further [emanations] issued forth.
The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara spoke of the vast roots of goodness practiced by all sentient beings in their past lives;
he spoke of the names of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; he spoke of the ultimate path of vows and practices cultivated by all bodhisattvas;
and he spoke of the various expressions used by all Tathāgatas in turning the sublime wheel of Dharma. Manifesting such signs of adornment as these, he revealed the Tathāgata.
When he appears in the world, all the kings within that world, seeing these signs, will have their roots of goodness matured;
desiring to see the Buddha, they shall come to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, the following twelve and a half lines of scripture clarify the appearance of Buddhas during the first eon.
The number of these manifestations is set forth together with the names of the initial Buddhas and the portents that first appeared in the Great Forest of Flower Branches.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha Sarvaguṇaparvatameruśrīmegha suddenly appeared within a great lotus at his site of enlightenment;
his body pervaded everywhere, equal to the true Dharma-realm, manifesting throughout all buddha-fields.
He is born in all places of enlightenment and goes to them all; he is endowed with boundless, wondrous colors and is utterly pure, such that no one in any world can outshine him.
He possesses the marks of various jewels, each distinct and luminous;
the images of all palaces appear within him, and all sentient beings are able to see them with their own eyes. Boundless transformation Buddhas emerge from his body in various colors.

His light filled the world-systems as he manifested his body and sat upon a seat atop the summit of Mount Sumeru in the Great Forest of Mani Flower Branch Wheels within the Pure Radiance Fragrant Water Ocean Adorned with Flower Flames; likewise,
on all sixty-eight thousand billion Sumeru mountain summits in the world-system of Supreme Sound, he appeared as well.

[The Sūtra says: "He sat down with his body [in the lotus]. [The Commentary states: From "At that time" onwards, there are nine lines and a half of sūtra text clarifying how the first Buddha suddenly appeared within the lotus, as well as describing how the Buddha’s body pervasively sat in all dharma-realm bodhimaṇḍas and was seen by all sentient beings, and so forth.
The interlocutor asked: "For what reason does this Buddha manifest through the transformation of a lotus, while Śākyamuni appears from the womb of his mother?
He replied: "It is according to what is seen by their respective faculties that he appears from the womb. Only those sentient beings of inferior understanding see him thus from a womb;
it is like what is said in the *Lokottara-parivarta*: 'He appears from the womb for the sake of sentient beings of inferior understanding. He should [appear] with a great faculty."
All sentient beings saw the lotus flower appear.
[Sūtra] At that time, that Buddha immediately emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows;
this light was named "Sound of Arousing All Roots of Goodness," and it had as its retinue as many rays of light as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, filling all ten directions.
In whatever lands there may be sentient beings who are ready to be tamed, as soon as their light touches them, they spontaneously awaken;
the heat of their delusions is stilled, the net of their hindrances is torn asunder, the mountains of their obstructions are crushed, and their defilements are purified.

They give rise to great faith and understanding, produce supreme roots of goodness, and forever leave behind all hardships and terrors; they extinguish all physical and mental suffering and distress. Thus it begins.

When they perceived that the Buddha’s mind was directed toward omniscience, the lords of all worlds, together with their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands, were awakened by the light of the Buddha;
thus, they all went to where the Buddha was and prostrated themselves at his feet.
[Treatise] From "At that time" onwards, the following eight lines of scripture clarify the initial appearance of the Buddha, his emission of light, and his gathering of the assembly,
as well as the virtues of the light and the arrival of the great multitude.
[Sūtra] "O sons of the Buddha, within that Great City of Blazing Radiance there is a king named Priyadarśana-Sujñāna (Joyful Vision and Good Wisdom), who governs a hundred trillion nayutas of cities.
He has thirty-seven thousand wives and court ladies, with Puṇyamaṅgala (Auspicious Fortune) as their chief;
he has five hundred princes [according to another version, twenty-five thousand], with Mahātejas (Great Splendor) as their chief. Great Splendor.
The Crown Prince had ten thousand consorts, with Wondrous Vision as the foremost.
At that time, having seen the Buddha’s radiance, by the power of the roots of goodness he had previously cultivated, the Crown Prince Mahātejas immediately realized ten kinds of Dharma-gates.
What are these ten? They are: realizing the samādhi of the wheel of merits of all Buddhas; realizing the first... [text continues].
The *Sarvabuddhadharmapraveśamukha-dhāraṇī* realizes the vast treasury of skillful means;
the *Prajñāpāramitā* realizes the great adornment of subduing all sentient beings; Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) realizes the universal cloud-sound;
Great Pity (*mahākaruṇā*) realizes the supreme mind that gives rise to boundless merit; and Great Joy (*mahāmuditā*) realizes the authentic awakening to all things.
Having attained the great equanimity of the Dharma, the vast treasury of the equality of skillful means,
the great supernormal power of increasing the strength of faith and understanding, and the great vow that universally enters the gate of eloquence and the light of all-knowledge,
at that time Prince Great Radiance, having obtained such illumination of the Dharma, by the Buddha’s majestic power surveyed the entire assembly.
He spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One sits at the site of enlightenment, Pure and of great radiance.
Like a thousand suns rising, he shines universally throughout the realm of space. Only once in immeasurable billions of kalpas Does a Guide appear in the world."
The Buddha has now appeared in the world, the one whom all gaze upon and revere.
Behold the Buddha’s radiance and the inconceivable emanated Buddhas; within every palace, he dwells in tranquil meditative absorption.
Behold the Buddha’s supernormal powers: from his pores issue clouds of flames that illuminate the world.
The light is inexhaustible; you should contemplate the Buddha’s body.
A net of light, utterly pure, manifests forms equal in number to all things, Pervading the ten directions. His wondrous voice fills the world;
all who hear it rejoice. In accordance with the languages of all sentient beings, He praises the virtues of the Buddha.
Wherever the World-Honored One’s light shines, all sentient beings find peace and happiness;

their suffering is entirely extinguished, and their hearts give rise to great joy. Beholding the assembly of Bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions, they all release clouds of mani-jewels and, appearing before the Buddha, offer praise with sublime voices from the site of enlightenment.
That voice is exceedingly deep and far-reaching, capable of extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings. This is the Buddha’s spiritual power;
all pay him reverence, their hearts filled with great joy, as they together gaze up at the Dharma King before the World-Honored One.
[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify the Great City of Radiance.
There was a human king named King *Priyadarśana-Sujñāna* who, together with his retinue, assembled and described the majestic light of the Crown Prince.
By means of his own roots of goodness, he beheld the Buddha’s radiance and attained ten kinds of Dharma-gates, as fully explained in the sutra. [The final three...]

The "Verses Clarifying Majestic Radiance" (*Gāthā-vibhāsita-tejorāja*) praises the Buddha; within these ten verses, the Buddha’s virtues and how those virtues benefit sentient beings may be understood according to the text.
[Sūtra] When the Crown Prince Mahātejorāja spoke these verses, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, his voice...
When King Sukhadarśana-Buddhimat of the world-system Samantavijitasvara heard these verses, his heart was filled with great joy;
he looked upon his retinue and spoke these verses:
"You should quickly convene The assembly of all the kings, As well as the princes and the great ministers."
The city governors and officials shall proclaim throughout the city: "Quickly strike the great drums and assemble all people;
let us all go together to see the Buddha. At every crossroads, let precious bells be rung;
together with wives, children, and kinsmen, let us all go to behold the Tathāgata."
All cities and fortresses should be made entirely pure; everywhere erect sublime and wondrous banners adorned with mani-jewels.
Let jeweled canopies be spread with various nets, and let music like clouds be arrayed and prepared in the void, filling every place so that all roads are solemnly purified.
A universal rain of exquisite garments, And handkerchiefs for your precious chariot;
Together with me, we shall behold the Buddha, each according to our own power.
A universal rain of ornaments, All spread like clouds, filling the void of space; Incense-flame lotus canopies, And half-moon jewel tassels.

And countless exquisite garments—you all should rain these down. The supreme maṇi wheels from the fragrant waters upon Mount Sumeru, And pure sandalwood—these you should all rain down, filling the sky.
Various precious flowers and necklaces, adorned, pure, and stainless, As well as maṇi lamps, you should likewise rain down.
[Verse: He caused them all to abide in space, And they all turned toward the Buddha;
With hearts filled with great joy, Together with their wives, children, and retinues, They went to see the World-Honored One.
[Treatise: From "O Sons of the Buddhas" onwards, there are two and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the Radiant One (Prabhāsa) spoke these verses on behalf of the Buddha.
The sound of his supernatural power was heard everywhere; when the King, his father, heard it, he rejoiced and spoke these verses.
Within these eleven lines of verse, it is clarified that King Śubhavyūha commanded the assembly to gather and ordered the preparation of the ritual requisites.
[Sūtra] At that time, King Priyadarśana-Sujñāna was accompanied by thirty-seven thousand queens and court ladies headed by Puṇyamaṅgala;
five hundred princes headed by Mahātejas; sixty thousand ministers headed by Jñānabala;
and a retinue of seven hundred and seventy billion nayutas of followers, both preceding and following him.
Surrounded [by his retinue], he emerged from the Great City of Blazing Radiance; by the power of the king, the entire assembly ascended into the air and proceeded there.
Various articles of offering filled the void as they reached the presence of the Buddha, whereupon they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
Furthermore, the Celestial King Banner of Skillful Transformation of the Wondrous Flower City was present, together with a retinue of ten billion nayutas.
Furthermore, there was the Dragon King Pure Light (Vimalaprabha) from the City of Ultimate Perfection, together with his retinue of twenty-five billion;
the Yakṣa King Fierce and Powerful (Pracaṇḍavikrama) from the City of the Victorious Vajra Banner, together with his retinue of seven hundred and seventy million;
the Gandharva King Joyful Sight (Priyadarśana) from the City of Stainless Radiance, together with his retinue of nine hundred and seventy million; and furthermore, the [King] of Wondrous...
In the city of Wheel-Purity, the Asura King Saṃjñāna was present together with five billion eight hundred million followers;
in the city of Wondrous Adornment, the Garuḍa King Daśadigcara was present together with ninety-nine thousand followers;
and in the city of Playful Joy, the Kiṃnara King Vajraśrī was present together with one billion eight hundred million followers.
Furthermore, there was the Mahoraga King Ratnakīrtidhvaja of the city Vajradhvaja, together with a retinue of three hundred billion nayutas;
and the Brahma King Varasundaravyūha of the city Viśuddhavyūha, together with a retinue of eighteen billion.
Thus, all the kings residing within these hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of great cities, along with—
The entire retinue went together to the place of the Tathāgata Sarvaguṇasumeru-jaya-megha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and sat to one side. At that time, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, that Tathāgata, within the ocean-like assembly of the site of enlightenment,
preached the *Sūtra on the Universal Collection of the Sovereign Dharmas of All Buddhas of the Three Times*.
With sūtras as numerous as the atoms in a world-system as its retinue, it brings benefit to all according to the inclinations of sentient beings.

The light of wisdom wherein all phenomena enter and abide within the initial bodhicitta;

the light of wisdom that clearly knows the ocean of the accomplishment of the adornments of the definitive understanding of all Buddhas; and the light of wisdom that clearly knows the manifestation of boundless Buddhas within the Dharma-realm.

Having heard the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma, I have attained the light of wisdom; by means of this, I behold the deeds performed by the World-Honored One in the past.

In all places of birth, including the distinctions of names and bodies, as well as the offerings made to the Buddhas—all such things I see entirely, as they were in the presence of the Buddhas of the past.

purifying the oceans of lands by relinquishing their own bodies—vast and boundless.

Through the power of Samantabhadra’s great vows, Within the ocean of all Buddhas, They practice immeasurable deeds.

As I shall be like the World-Honored One, I will extensively purify the oceans of all lands, Cultivating the practices of bodhi through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
