[Treatise] The second assembly consists of six chapters of scripture that clarify the gate of bodhisattva faith; within this particular assembly:

There are three parts: the introductory section (*nidāna*), the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), and the dissemination (*parīndanā*). From the beginning of the twelfth fascicle, from the words "At that time" (*atha khalu*) onwards, there are four and a half lines of scripture;
this constitutes the introductory section. From here down to the "Chapter on Worthy Chief" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) is the main exposition section.

At the end of the "Chapter on Worthy Chief," there are three and a half lines of scripture; this is the dissemination section. [The seventh chapter is] the "Chapter on the Names and Titles of the Tathāgatas" (*Tathāgatasya nāma-saṃkhyā-parivarta*).
From this point downward, up to the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (Bhadrapāla-parivarta), is the third major section.

Within this, the fruit establishes faith by showing that one's own mind is Buddha. In this segment, there are approximately six dharmas that establish faith in the fruit of Buddhahood, thereby causing those who believe to enter the fruit of Buddhahood.
First, the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas" (Tathāgatagunajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa) causes faith.
1. The Chapter on the Mind: To cause those with faith to know that the Buddha’s name pervades all worlds, for it is known that the nature of names is empty and detached.
2. The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths: To cause those with faith to personally realize that the truth of suffering in all worlds is itself the Noble Truth, so that they do not seek elsewhere.
3. The Chapter on the Awakening of Radiant Light: To cause those with faith to awaken through the radiant light of their own minds.
He illuminates all worlds throughout the inexhaustible great trichiliocosm, the universal realm of the Buddhas, and he himself is likewise equal [to them].
As his mind follows the light, each ray illuminates; thus, subject and object merge as one, and the distinction between internal and external perception vanishes.

Having first illuminated the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, he next returns to the eastern direction as the starting point, and the light reaches thirteen thousand [worlds] in the east.
The light illuminates a thousandfold great trichiliocosm, and likewise ten successive layers in each of the ten directions, circling them all around and illuminating the ten directions perfectly.
Body and mind are of one nature, unimpeded and all-pervasive, identical to the realm of the Buddha.
One should observe in this way with every mental application, and subsequently seal it with the samādhi of signless skillful means, entering therein.
At the initial stage of the Ten Abodes, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and becomes a true son of the Tathāgata, the Dharma-King of Wisdom.
Just as a single ray of light shines everywhere, as clearly explained in the sutras, one must not think that the Buddha’s light has no share in oneself;
rather, one should use the light of one's own mind to awaken the mind like the Buddha’s light, so that it may perfectly illumine the Dharma-realm.
4. Chapter on the Clarification of Questions: The Dharma-gate for those with faith to believe in; 5. Chapter on Pure Conduct:
For those with faith, it establishes that when Bodhisattvas first resolve their minds, they take the making of great vows as primary;

furthermore, it enables those with faith to turn back their beginningless deluded thoughts to form an ocean of wisdom characterized by the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; 6. Chapter on Worthy Leaders.
This chapter instructs those with faith to believe in the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that transforms boundlessly and attains great mastery, as well as the merit of faith;
these six dharmas are called "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*). When one contemplates these six dharmas in accordance with practice, it is termed "faith.
All ten Tathāgatas of Wisdom, such as the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati*), are one's own mind.
The fruit has immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) as its essence and the other wisdoms as its function; this will be explained clearly below.
Mañjuśrī, Bodhiruci, Prathamacittotpādika, Daśaśiras, and the other bodhisattvas are the bodies of those who practice faith.
From this chapter down to the "Chapter on Bhadramukha," these six chapters constitute the second major section within this entire sutra.

Third is the gate of establishing faith through the fruition. To clarify that at the first assembly, the Buddha’s fruition was presented to encourage the cultivation of faith, it is said that "this is what all Buddhas have attained.
This second assembly establishes faith through the fruition by showing that one's own mind is the Buddha, for it is not different from the Buddha of fruition;
this will be clarified in the text itself. What preceded it was the already-attained fruition of Buddhahood, which is now employed to encourage cultivation.

This passage cites the names of Buddhas as the fruit of cultivation; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single name that is not a Buddha-name, for the essential nature of names is itself liberation.

It is only because they accord with the diverse ways in which sentient beings hear them that this clarifies how the names of the Buddhas are all-pervasive, thereby demonstrating that one is unattached to any name whatsoever. This constitutes the commentary on this chapter.

This chapter consists of three sections: first, explaining the purpose of this chapter; second, explaining the title of the chapter; and third, explaining the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the explanation of the purpose of this chapter:

it clarifies that while the first assembly previously explained only the Tathāgata’s body of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and his wisdom that gathers and sustains sentient beings, it did not explain the breadth or narrowness of the Tathāgata’s name in gathering and sustaining sentient beings. This second assembly now addresses that.
The "Hall of Universal Radiance" (Pǔguāngmíng Diàn) is where the names and titles of the Buddha-fruit that encompass all beings are clarified; therefore, this chapter must appear here.

Furthermore, it is necessary for this chapter to appear so as to cite the names of the Buddha-fruit and cause sentient beings to develop faith and understanding. In the previous assembly, the pervasiveness of the body and wisdom was clarified;
in this assembly, it is clarified that both the name-body and the wisdom are equally pervasive. Thus, although the World Rulers asked in the first assembly, [the answer had not yet been fully given].
This chapter provides the answer to the preceding questions, intended to inspire faith in the minds of those who have yet to attain it.

It causes one to believe that the Buddha’s name-body and wisdom pervade the entire Dharma-realm, benefiting sentient beings according to their capacities, illuminating the mundane world, and shattering delusions;

thus, it is established as the Hall of Universal Radiance. This hall is named in accordance with its virtues, and its virtues are manifested through the hall itself. For these reasons, this chapter must appear here.

Within these Buddha-name titles, there are approximately five conditions by which the names are established: first, the name is established based on the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that is the very essence of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
second, the name is established based on the Tathāgata’s own virtues as he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment;

third, the name is established based on the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*) for benefiting sentient beings; and fourth, [the name is established] based on the progressive cultivation of the stages.
He attains Buddhahood under the name Tathāgata Sīmanta (Four Illuminations), taking as his causal condition the various inclinations and capacities of all sentient beings;
this is the fifth [point]. Regarding the equality of the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*, he takes all phenomena collectively as the causal condition for his Buddha-name;

this is the first [point]. To attain the Buddha-name by means of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that is the very self-substance of the *dharmadhātu* is, for example, like the Immovable Wisdom (*Acalajñāna*).
The Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom, the Buddha of Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness—these are the names of the ten Buddhas of wisdom.
By applying these ten names upon the fundamental wisdom of this dharma-realm, one establishes the ten kinds of power of faith.

Only when reaching this stage does the broad meaning and general intent become clear: to cause sentient beings to realize that their own fundamental ignorance is, in its essence, nothing other than Suchness.
First, the Fundamental Great Wisdom brings all sentient beings to the sudden realization of their original nature and causes them to suddenly become Buddhas.
Second, regarding the Tathāgata’s manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment and the establishment of his own titles:

this refers to the ten common titles shared by all Buddhas of the ten directions who manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, namely: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; furthermore, Vairocana...
That is the collective name for the Great Wisdom Light that illuminates various phenomena and various sentient beings;

thus, "Vairocana" means "Universal Illumination. Regarding the Tathāgata of the Threefold Knowledge (*trividyā*), his skillful means for benefiting sentient beings consist of progressing through stages and cultivating conditions to achieve Buddhahood, which is illustrated by the following ten roots.

The Buddha of Original Immovable Wisdom, having established the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), enumerates ten lunar months; the names of the Buddhas below are all identical and designated as "Moon" (*candra*) to establish the ten abodes (*vihāra*).
This clarifies that one has newly realized the Dharma-body and attained the mind of original wisdom, thereby achieving coolness and clarity.

It is because the Bodhisattva of this stage accords with principle, delusions vanish, and they attain the wisdom of the Dharma-nature that they achieve this coolness; thus, it is described from the perspective of their own realization.
The method for increasing [the roots of goodness] is to attain the name of a Buddha within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). Within this stage, ten Buddhas named "Eye" appear;

their names are all identical, designated as "Eye" or "Clarity. Because the Ten Practices utilize wisdom to know the faculties of beings and thereby benefit and sustain them, the Buddhas' names are "Eye";
because they skillfully know the nature of the faculties, these names are established based on the benefits attained by themselves, and thus they are called Buddhas.
In the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), ten names of the wondrous Buddhas are all uniformly titled "Wondrous" (*miao*) and "Luminous" (*ming*).
This is because within the stage of the Ten Dedications, as the Bodhisattva’s progressive cultivation matures and wondrous wisdom manifests before them, the Buddhas are thus named "Wondrous.
The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are likewise "Wondrous. Above this, it clarifies that from the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward, one relies on self-confidence and the discernment of one's own mind.
This wisdom is fundamentally one and the same as the immovable fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas; thus, one establishes faith.
To perceive phenomena outside of mind does not constitute faith. From this point of faith onward, through the power of samādhi, one accords with principle and merges with the source;
this is termed the Ten Abodes. The Buddha-names assigned to these stages are all "Moon," which refers to the stage of cultivation.
The Dharma attained by persons to achieve the title of Buddha is established through five stages (*pañca-sthāna*).
There are fifty Buddha-names, fifty causes, and fifty fruits; because each stage possesses both cause and fruit, this constitutes one hundred layers of cause and fruit.
Within these five fundamental stages, there are originally five causes and five fruits, thus forming one hundred and ten layers.

The dharma-gate of cause and effect is not different from the essence of the Dharma-realm, and the dharmas believed in during the ten stages of faith are not different from the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha who serves as the basis for cultivation and progress through the various stages.
To explain this extensively according to such a broad intent, it will be fully elucidated below in the fundamental positions;
this is called "cultivating and progressing according to the stages" to achieve the title of a Buddha. Thus, the Fourth Illumination Tathāgata [is attained].
Those who attain the name of Buddha according to the faculties and inclinations of all sentient beings—
manifesting forms such as physical bodies corresponding to the realms of sentient beings as Buddhas, devas, spirits, lords, humans,
or immortals throughout the entire realm of sentient beings so that no sentient being commits evil— all of this is ultimately beyond the measurement of one's own ordinary, mundane mind.

Furthermore, it is because the names of the Buddhas pervade the five vidyā-dhātus and the essence and function of the dharma-dhātu are equal, such that all dharmas are collectively termed "Buddha-names.
This is because all dharmas and their designations are inherently devoid of self-nature;
since the inherent self-nature of all dharmas is the nature of the dharma-dhātu, and the nature of the dharma-dhātu is the Buddha-name.

Therefore, since all phenomena (*dharmas*) and their designations are the names of the Buddha, the Tathāgata has attained Buddhahood by means of these very phenomena whose intrinsic nature is devoid of self-nature.
Desiring to extensively cite scriptural passages to substantiate this meaning, the text of this teaching becomes so vast that its words are prolix;
for those whose karmic roots are obscured, it is difficult to understand. Thus, one should rely solely upon the preceding portion of this sūtra.

Because those who practice in accordance with the lower [teachings] find it easy to understand, just as the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are also taught within the Three Vehicles, I now wish to cause those of the Three Vehicles to turn their minds.

By pointing to this Golden World and Akṣobhya Buddha, I intend to lead them to directly recognize that this is their own mind—the discerning wisdom that is fundamentally unmoving. This is the meaning of the text.
Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of one’s own mind that skillfully discerns the signless;
Bodhisattvas such as Buddhasena and Sāgarabuddhidhara are the principle-wisdom perceived within the sphere of one’s own mind according to their respective faith and understanding.

Why would those of the three vehicles who have not yet turned their minds toward [Mahāyāna] certainly not believe this? Because it was established for them that [the path] requires three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Because one shall attain Buddhahood after the kalpa has passed, one merely acknowledges oneself and one's own mind as being entirely those of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

One simply believes that the Buddha possesses the Immovable Wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) and so forth, yet lacks self-confidence regarding one’s own mind being the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha, which is no different from the Buddha.
For this reason, within this Dharma-realm vehicle (*dharmadhātu-yāna*), one does not achieve [realization] by means of the Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
To have faith in this sutra, one should have such direct faith as follows:

the nature of the conceptualization of one’s own mind is the fundamental unmoving wisdom-buddha within the nature of the dharma-realm; the golden world is the principle of the non-defilement of one’s own mind;
and Mañjuśrī is the sublime, discerning, wondrous wisdom of one’s own mind, the foremost in awakening and the foremost in vision.

These Bodhisattvas, following within the mind of faith, manifest the principle and wisdom (*dharmatā-jñāna*); by means of the cause of faith, they accord with the fruit-dharmas of all Buddhas without the slightest error, thereby perfecting the mind of faith.

From this faith onward, they advance through cultivation by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), passing through the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage, over the course of days, months, years, kalpas, and time.
When one realizes that the dharma-realm is without transition— remaining as it was, unmoving like the Buddha of Original Wisdom, and forming the ocean of all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā)—

and understands that the cause and effect of teaching and transforming sentient beings do not shift across time and that the kalpas do not change, only then does true faith arise. If one posits that the fixed, real body throughout the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas is that of an ordinary person,

and perceives a separation between the paths of the ordinary and the sage such that time and kalpas shift and change, and that there is something external to the mind, [one has not yet attained this faith].
The Buddha does not achieve faith; as stated above, there are these five kinds of different names and titles for the Buddha.
Question: What is the difference between a "name" (ming) and a "title" (hao)? Answer: There are two aspects regarding their identity and distinction. What are the two?

First, concerning those born of parents who are young and lack virtue, they are addressed by a simple designation; this is called a "name. Second, when one possesses virtue, the name is applied in accordance with that virtue. This is called a "title."

Establishing names means that those names which may be honored and invoked are called "titles" (*abhidhāna*); these titles are such that inferior persons are not permitted to invoke them, whereas other names are those that inferior persons are permitted to invoke.
Therefore, despite the distinction between having virtue and lacking virtue, they are all collectively subsumed under the category of "names," as they are encompassed by the term *nāma*.
If one considers this sutra’s treatment of Buddha-names, it is entirely based on the Dharma. Regarding the Dharma...

The establishment of these virtues differs from worldly nomenclature. Third, regarding the interpretation of the meaning according to the text, the meaning within this section is divided into two parts:

first, a general outline of the intent of the thirty-two chapters of the sutra; and second, a specific analysis of the intent of the individual chapter on the third dhyāna, which describes eleven stages.
Regarding the first, the general outline of the thirty-two chapters: [End of segment]

From this point, from the second assembly, the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas," following the twenty-eight questions raised by the World Rulers (*Lokendra*), up until the subsequent "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata"—this entire section concerning the causes and effects of what was asked by the World Rulers consists of thirty-two chapters of scripture.
Since these are the answers to the twenty-eight questions, they proceed from the "Universal... [chapter].
The palace where the Buddha-fruit retribution of the *Prabhāsa-jñāna-dharmadhātu* resides is named after the fruit of Buddhahood itself;

it further presents the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths through which the Buddha-fruit practices to teach and transform sentient beings, and it presents the fundamental essence of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, the name of the Buddha Akṣobhya-jñāna.
Thus, one completes faith and cultivation until reaching that "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata."
The thirty-two chapters of this sutra constitute the ultimate culmination of the causes and effects of the practice of faith and progress.
From the "Universal Radiance Wisdom Hall" chapter up to the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter, it clarifies that the causes and effects of this practice of faith and progress are non-dual;
furthermore, it elucidates how one gives rise to faith based upon the fruit-virtues of initial perfect enlightenment.
In the subsequent "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it is clarified that within the Dharma-realm there is no time that can create separation; thus,
it is shown that within the essence of the Dharma-realm, although ordinary beings perceive through deluded vision as if beginning their practice of faith and progress over immeasurable eons,
those who initiate practice based upon the Truth (the True) and cultivate it through the five stages of the path of practice do so without ever being displaced by time.
Therefore, when one has not yet given rise to faith and is practicing, one constantly thinks that the Buddhas of the past attained Buddhahood long ago,

having already passed through immeasurable kalpas; yet, by the power of right faith, one then perceives those immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions who attained Buddhahood immeasurable kalpas ago as attaining Buddhahood simultaneously with oneself, for there is no sequence of before or after.

For this reason, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, it was as if an ordinary person today were first to resolve upon bodhicitta, initiate practice, and cultivate the path until their own practice was fulfilled;

yet, from the very moment he first appeared having attained perfect enlightenment, he never departed from the Tathāgata’s original state, because the fundamental dharma-realm is originally without temporal measure. Therefore, the sutra says:

To say that faith and mind are ultimately not distinct means that because the nature of the Dharma-realm has no distinction between the three periods of time, there is no distinction in terms of the three temporal periods;
because there is no time, there is no distinction; and because wisdom is without distinction, there is no distinction.

This is because it is not different from the essence of the Buddha Akṣobhya-jñāna; thus, the function of wondrous wisdom is without distinction and not different from the skillful discernment of Mañjuśrī.

Because of the selection of sublime wisdom, there is no distinction in practice; from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one does not differ from the ten *pāramitās* as one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Because of great compassion, there is no distinction in constant teaching and transformation. Because of the great vows, there is no distinction in never abandoning sentient beings.
Because of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), there is no distinction in the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*). (30)
The seven factors of enlightenment have no distinction because these ten kinds [of faith] have no distinction; thus it is said that "the initial resolve and the ultimate end are not two.
Therefore, the initial resolve is difficult to clarify, for it is difficult for one who has entered these ten kinds of faith and understanding.
If one believes that outside of their own mind there is another Buddha who attains the Way while they themselves are an ordinary person, this is merely worldly sentiment.
If one merely measures this [teaching] without regarding faith or the practice of progress, one will simply follow the long current of birth and death, constantly caught in the net of views;
how great is the suffering! Therefore, as in the second assembly and the first assembly, it clarifies the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment;
furthermore, following the thirty-two chapters after the *Tathāgatotpatti-sambhava-parivarta*, the *Tathāgatotpatti-sambhava-parivarta* again clarifies the beginning.

The practitioner who ultimately believes and advances in their cultivation manifests simultaneously with the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because they clarify that the entire dharma-realm is fundamentally simultaneous.
Just as holding a precious mirror facing all reflected images, it illuminates and manifests them all at once without before or after;
thus, within the fundamental Buddha-wisdom realm of the dharma-realm, all phenomena manifest instantaneously, and one must not employ the deluded mind.
Because the measure and the means of measurement are understood as preceding and succeeding one another, there is a single basis:

the Buddha who first attained perfect enlightenment within the realm of Maitreya’s pavilion during the first assembly; the Buddha in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Buddha" who exhorts practice by citing the fruit;
and the Buddha who clarifies the causal practices of the five stages of advancement for all bodhisattvas, culminating in the Immovable Wisdom (*acalajñāna*) within the stage of faith.

Because it is addressed in relation to the Buddha, [the interlocutor] asks: "For what reason are the various chapters on the bodhisattvas spoken by others, while only the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* and the *Anuvyañjana-parivarta* are spoken by the Buddha himself? The answer is:

Just as there are the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of a bodhisattva and the afflictions and ignorance of the five stages, so too, within the stage of a Tathāgata, the inconceivable assembly of bodhisattvas is used to represent the completion of the bodhisattvas of the five stages.
The dharma-gate of the self-manifestation of stages in their proper order is exemplified by bodhisattvas such as the Ten Wisdoms, the Ten Forests, the Ten Banners, and the Ten Treasuries.

Within the stage of Buddhahood, there is the ignorance regarding dharmas; it is the Tathāgata himself who speaks of these incalculable chapters, such as the Chapter on the Minor Marks and the Chapter on the Excellent Signs. From this ignorance within the stage of Buddhahood, one finally attains resolution upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood itself.
Because these two are delusions, the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is only brought to an end at the stage of Buddhahood, as stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
This is because a portion of the teaching’s net is similar for the three vehicles, yet it does not permit the two vehicles or the bodhisattvas of the Pure Land to sever it;
they only attain the fundamental wisdom by realizing that this ignorance is the failure to understand [the ultimate]. Therefore, this is the teaching of the One Vehicle.
Taking the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom as the mind of faith, all these practices and realizations of various dharmas differ from this sutra;
therefore, this teaching clarifies that one should contemplate the initial mind and the ultimate mind as being entirely exhaustive, because within the Dharma-realm there are no three periods of time.
Furthermore, the three vehicles require the completion of fixed *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, which are the paths of progress for the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.

The stages beyond the ground (*bhūmi*), the stage of application (*prayoga-bhūmi*), and the first four stages of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) leading up to the fruition of Buddhahood are definitively fulfilled over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), as has already been clarified previously.
Why is it that in this sutra the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are presented as the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the stage of application, and the provisions all at once?

It is because the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* serves as the provision for those practices; these practices are sustained by the *dharmadhātu*, which remains untainted, and thus the provisions for practice are themselves the *dharmadhātu*.

The essence of wisdom is made clear through the habituation and maturation of practice; for it is from the ordinary state that one first perceives the nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and principle (*jñāna-dharmatā*).
Furthermore, within these five stages, each stage of cultivation possesses its own Buddha-fruit, which is established with distinct names according to the specific point of habitual practice.
In the teachings of the Three Vehicles, although there is a progression from the preceding stage toward the subsequent stage, there is only the fruit of a bodhisattva, not that of a Buddha.
Because it is the fruit, this Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm is extensively elucidated at the stage of the final arrival;

its exposition does not extend even for immeasurable eons, nor is it abbreviated within a single kṣaṇa. Only those who are deluded falsely construct interpretations of length and brevity, extension and contraction;
thus, they do not accord with the mind of the Arhat. From this point, starting from the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas," [the text continues].

From the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" up to the end, there are thirty-two chapters of sutra that detail the causes and effects of progressive cultivation through the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage.

Because the beginning is identical to the end and the end is identical to the beginning within this non-dual position, it is like the great royal road; its Dharma is eternally thus, neither old nor new.
As for the essence, it is as stated in the verse by Mañjuśrī: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons;
there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the ten powers.
Regarding the two sections within this chapter, they are further divided into four parts within this chapter itself.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest retreat (araṇya-dharma-bodhimaṇḍa), having just attained perfect awakening.
He sat upon the lion throne of the Lotus Treasury within the Hall of Universal Radiance;

his wondrous realization was fully perfected, the two paths were forever severed, he had penetrated the dharma of signlessness, dwelt in the dwelling of the Buddhas, attained the equanimity of the Buddhas, and reached the state of non-obstruction.
They were established in the unimpeded practice of the transformable Dharma and dwelt in the inconceivable state of universally beholding the three periods of time.
Together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields—all of whom were in their final birth before enlightenment—they had gathered from all directions.
They universally and skillfully observed the realms of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the world-realm, the realm of nirvana, and the fruits of all karmic actions.

[The text covers] the sequence of mental activities as retribution, and all words and meanings pertaining to the mundane and supramundane, the conditioned and unconditioned, and the past, present, and future. [Treatise:
First, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, there are eight lines and a half of scripture that clarify the praise of virtues and the gathering of the assembly.
The text is divided into two parts: first, a praise of the Tathāgata’s virtues; second, a praise of the virtues of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Within the first part, from the words "At that time" onwards, these two lines of scripture constitute the introduction (*nidāna*).

They describe the original location where [the Buddha] first attained enlightenment and the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantāvabhāsa-maṇḍala*), clarifying that these two places are not different so as to show that he has not moved from his original site.
Because the body sits pervasively throughout all places within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it constitutes the essence of the *bodhimaṇḍa*.

Because its essence is the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it constitutes the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*). Because this is the capital where the retribution-body of the Dharma-realm resides, and because the two essences of Dharma and retribution are identical in their nature and characteristics—the single truth in which beginning and end, cause and effect, are fundamentally non-different—it is for this reason that the ancient [teachings] are recounted once more.
The human commentator says that because they are situated near one another, it is necessary to recount them again; however, this is not the intended meaning of the Sūtra.
Furthermore, he says that seeing the Buddha dwelling in the open air, the dragon constructed the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantābhāsakūṭa*); this interpretation is also incorrect.

Even if such an event occurred, it would be a teaching pertaining to the Three Vehicles. Moreover, he says that the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River, whereas the Universal Radiance Hall is [elsewhere].

It is three *li* away to the southeast of the Bodhimaṇḍa. This clarifies that the Bodhimaṇḍa is the *āraṇya*, the place where the Way was attained, while the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-garbha*) is the dwelling of retribution.

Throughout this one section of the sutra, from the beginning up to the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," the phrase "At that time, the Buddha was... appears five times in succession; its intent clarifies that the dwelling place is the Dharma itself.
The realms, the bodies of the Tathāgatas, and the adornments of their palaces are all the fundamental wisdom of non-duality, which is the essential nature and characteristic of the Dharma-realm;
thus, the intent of the five perfections was already described in the previous assembly.

From the passage "Since his wondrous awakening is complete" down to "universally seeing the three periods of time," there are two and a half lines of scripture that constitute the formal praise of the Buddha’s virtues. The phrase "wondrous awakening is complete" clarifies this point.
Because the ten knowledges are all-pervasive and sovereign, the two modes of activity are forever severed;

this is because the two modes of activity regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) have been exhausted, and because one has realized the signless (*animitta*) dharma such that grasping and rejecting are ended.

One dwells in the Buddha-dwelling because one abides in the *dharmadhātu* shared by all Buddhas of the three periods—past, present, and future—through great wisdom and great compassion. Furthermore, [this is] like the Tathāgata and the [Buddhas of] the ten directions... the third...
The Buddhas of the world abide in five kinds of universal pervasiveness: first, the universal pervasiveness of manifesting perfect enlightenment, as in the first assembly at the Bodhimanda;
second, the universal pervasiveness of the adornments of the environment and the physical body, as well as their names and titles, as in the second assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance;
third, the universal pervasiveness of the essence of meditative concentration, as in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter; fourth... [text continues]
The universal pervasiveness of the teachings on Samantabhadra’s conduct is the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokātikrama-parivarta*);
the inconceivable, wondrous, and unimpeded wisdom-function that perfectly fulfills the five dharma-realms is the "Dharma-realm Chapter" (*Dharmadhātu-parivarta*).
Because these five kinds [of qualities] universally pervade all Buddhas, it is called "dwelling in what the Buddhas dwell in. For this reason, within this single [chapter],...
The sūtras of this section establish the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*). At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha;

only the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" differs slightly, clarifying the profound interpenetration and universal pervasiveness that does not depart from a single location, a single essence of bodhi, a single dharmadhātu, and a single fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), because at that one time there is no sequence of before or after.
Fearing that the meaning of the sūtra text might be lost, the five perfections are recounted again to clarify it.

Lest later students be confused regarding these matters, he clarifies that these five [aspects] are all-pervasive, collectively demonstrating that the single limit (ekānta) has neither before nor after;

that within a single momentary limit there is no duality of thought-moments; and that the turning of the Wheel of Dharma throughout forty-nine years—from the time he had not yet descended from Tuṣita Heaven, to when he had not yet emerged from his mother’s womb, until he had already entered Nirvāṇa—is never separate from the Buddha.
"Equality" means that because principle and phenomena are non-dual, one reaches the state of non-obstruction.

"The dharma that cannot be overturned" clarifies that the Buddha constantly dwells within birth and death without being displaced by karma, and furthermore, is able to overturn the dharma of non-displacement.

"Unimpeded in conduct" clarifies that within birth and death, the Buddha is always able to act in common with others (*sāmānārthya*), for the ultimate and the conventional do not obstruct one another; thus, it is established as "non-obstruction."

"Those who contemplate" refers to those who have perfected the Buddha-way through their practice and have reached the ultimate state where all activity is effortless and spontaneous in benefiting sentient beings;

because they possess mastery of wisdom, they cannot be measured by thought, reflection, or consciousness. "Universally seeing the three periods of time" means that their eye of wisdom is fully perfected;

it does not mean seeing the affairs of sentient beings within the three periods of time from within the three periods of time themselves. From [the point of] being granted [the vision of] ten Buddha-fields as small as a speck of dust...

"Accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of dust," and so on down to "in the past, present, and future"—within this, there are four lines of scripture praising the virtues of the bodhisattvas who are accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields.

This clarifies that their retinue is perfect, pervading the ocean of the Dharma-realm. "Accompanied" means arriving simultaneously, for they have neither coming nor going; there is none who is not [thus].
All of them are those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), for they are all Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

Because they attain the fruit of Buddhahood only after reaching the stage of Universal Good (*Samantabhadra*) within the position of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti*)—wherein the path is fully matured and merit is perfected—they are called "those in their final birth.

This is as explained in the *Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Jeweled Necklace* (*Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*). Furthermore, from the initial dwelling of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*) onward, they are also called "Bodhisattvas in their final birth."
Because one first perceives the nature and manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), seeing no prior or subsequent limits to its arising, it is called "the single life.
The *Śrī-kaṇṭha-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness, within the stream of the Dharma, spontaneously proceed to Buddhahood;

they all come together from other directions. The phrase "coming together from other directions" distinguishes them from the original assembly, indicating that these are not the established members [of the current gathering].
Without coming, they arrive; without going, they pervade. Furthermore, the previous assembly elucidated the fruit to encourage practice and inspire faith in the Buddha-fruit of others.
Now, in this second assembly, it is clarified that through the understanding and practice of the Buddha-fruit of others, one perfects the path of self-mind’s own realization and faith.
This is called "coming together from other quarters," meaning they all come from within the prior faith in the Buddha-fruit.
Those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) were already clear in their faith and understanding during the first assembly;
having reached this assembly, they fulfill their faith and enter the stage [of realization], thereby attaining Buddhahood—just as in the cases of the dragon girl, Sudhana, and others.

For this reason, those who have come from other directions are all members of the "one-life" assembly; this is precisely what is meant by the expression "entering the Dharma," signifying that they have come from other directions.

Furthermore, "delusion" is termed "other directions," while "awakening" is termed "coming. Having universally and skillfully observed the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the world-realm, and the nirvana-realm—this concludes the three lines of scripture praising those who have come.

This is because one skillfully observes that these three kinds of realms are non-dual in nature; thus, one knows that sentient beings follow along with afflictions and karma, and one also knows the bodhisattvas.
The afflictions, karmic activities, and other matters pertaining to each stage are as explained in the sutra.

[Sutra] At that time, the bodhisattvas reflected thus: "If the World-Honored One takes pity on us, we pray that he will, according to our wishes, reveal the Buddha-fields, the Buddha-abodes, the adornments of the Buddha-fields, the Dharma-nature of the Buddhas, the purity of the Buddha-fields, and what is spoken by the Buddhas."
The Buddha of the Dharma-realm, the Buddha of the essential nature of the Buddha-field, the Buddha of the majestic power of the Buddha-field, and the Buddha of the accomplishment of Great Bodhi—

just as all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in all worlds throughout the ten directions, act for the sake of bringing all bodhisattvas to fulfillment, for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never severed,
for the sake of protecting and succoring all sentient beings, and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to forever leave behind all afflictions.
Therefore, because they fully comprehend all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), expound all dharmas, purify all defilements,
forever sever the web of doubt, uproot all longing and expectation, and destroy all bases of attachment,
they speak of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten treasuries, ten stages, and ten... of the Bodhisattvas.
May they attain the ten concentrations, the ten penetrations, and the ten summits; and may they expound the stage of the Tathāgata, the realm of the Tathāgata, the spiritual power of the Tathāgata,
the conduct of the Tathāgata, the powers of the Tathāgata, the fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata, the samādhis of the Tathāgata, the supernormal knowledges of the Tathāgata,
the masteries of the Tathāgata, the unimpededness of the Tathāgata, as well as the eye of the Tathāgata, the ear of the Tathāgata, the nose of the Tathāgata, and the tongue of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata of the Future Body, the Tathāgata of the Tathāgata’s Intention, the Tathāgata of Eloquence, the Tathāgata of Wisdom, and the Buddha-World-Honored One of Supreme Vows— may he also speak for me. [Treatise] Second,
at the time of the section on the Great Assembly Requesting the Dharma, after the various Bodhisattvas had formed this reflection, [the following ten points were set forth].
Within these four and a half lines of scripture, there are thirty-two questions concerning the meaning, which are divided into two parts:

first, there are four questions asking about the four kinds of Buddha-fields; second, following the passage on accomplishing the great bodhicitta and being exhorted by the Buddhas of the ten directions, there are twenty-eight questions that generally inquire about the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the stages (*bhūmi*), the Buddha-eye, the Buddha-ear, and so forth.
These thirty-two questions continue until the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter, where they are answered as clearly detailed in the sūtra.
A question is raised: "The questions posed by the World Rulers (*Lokendra*) in the first assembly are largely similar in meaning to these, differing only in their degree of detail;
why, then, are the same questions asked again in this second assembly? The answer is: "In the previous assembly..."
In this assembly, the World Lord asks about the fruit of Buddhahood to encourage practice and to inspire faith in what is attained through the Buddha;

this is because one must have confidence in oneself—that one's own body and mind are the Buddha—and enter the stages of cultivation. Therefore, it is necessary to ask again regarding the preceding stage, which was the entry into samādhi by Samantabhadra as he manifested the fruit.
This present assembly, however, clarifies Mañjuśrī’s arising as the beginning of entering into faith, thereby clarifying the ordinary person.

Now, the initial stage of faith is for those whose faith is superficial; therefore, they do not enter meditative concentration. It is only from the Ten Abodes onwards that it is clarified that Bodhisattvas of this stage enter concentration, and it is then that the teaching begins.
For this reason, although the underlying principles of the previous inquiry are largely the same, they differ because the conditions and capacities of the audience vary.
In the previous assembly, one believed in the attainment [of Buddhahood] by other Buddhas; in this assembly, one enters into faith through one's own practice.

The ancients said that the previous assembly was for requesting [teachings], while the meaning of this assembly is for inquiry; otherwise, both the preceding and succeeding assemblies are fundamentally requests.
Since it is a request, it is therefore an inquiry. Thus, there is only a slight difference between this being an exhortation to practice and entering the Dharma for oneself.
As was raised in the previous assembly regarding the Tathāgata’s fulfillment of the path of cultivation and the past Buddhas who have already attained the Way:
This second assembly presents the fruit of perfected practice—the fundamental wisdom common to all Buddhas of the ten directions and shared by both ordinary beings and sages.
This refers to the Golden World existing everywhere, the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom existing everywhere, the Ten Wisdom Buddhas, and so forth;
it clarifies that all Buddhas and sentient beings equally possess this Immovable Wisdom.
The "Golden Color" is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*); it is called "color" because it arises and ceases in accordance with the mind of faith.
It is represented by the ten colored worlds; this is one of the four kinds of Buddha-fields asked about in this assembly.
It is the Buddha-field wherein all Buddhas and all sentient beings dwell together, and for that reason, it is "one."
The fundamental wisdom of all ordinary beings and sages is raised up so that all sentient beings may believe that their own minds are the wisdom in which the Buddhas abide;
for it is from this faith that all Buddhas arise, and it is from this too that all ordinary beings arise.
Regarding the two adornments—the nature of the Buddha-dharma and the Buddha-field—they are as described in the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, the Ten Dedications, and the Ten... [Bhūmis].
On each of the eleven stages, there are ten Buddha names corresponding to their respective positions;

it is for this reason that one gives rise to faith based on the fundamental wisdom of one's own mind and proceeds with practice, adorning the various *pāramitās* according to each stage and each action.

This is done so that the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body may be brought to maturity through such adornment. Furthermore, by employing the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body to adorn the myriad practices, [one fulfills them].
Because their conduct is free from attachment, it is called the adornment of the Buddha-nature and the Buddha-field; these three purities constitute the nature of the Dharma taught by the Buddhas.
Regarding the Buddha-field as the Tathāgata’s manifestation of perfect enlightenment and turning of the wheel of Dharma, these four constitute its essential nature.

As for the Buddha-field as the majestic power of the Buddha, this refers to the manifestation of supernatural powers appearing in accordance with the faculties of beings; this clarifies that the latter two types of Buddha-fields follow from this.

Because one has attained maturity through the practice of generating faith in the two previous Buddha-fields, by this principle one should know that the Buddhas of the ten directions all emerge together through this single path. Thus should it be known; thus should it be believed and understood.
By attaining such belief and understanding, one achieves the same realization as that which is believed by all Buddhas; he who attains this faith— [The original text concludes here.]
As stated in the "Chapter on the Wise" (Bhadrapāla), it is superior to lifting the trichiliocosm with one's hands and remaining suspended in mid-air for an eon,
because this clarifies the difficulty of such faith; it is also superior to the merit of making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of the worlds of the ten directions for an eon—
none of these compare to such faith as described below in the twenty [verses].

The *Aṣṭapraśna-sūtra* provides its own answers; those points whose meaning is obscure and difficult to clarify are explained here, while those whose meaning is manifest can be understood according to the text.

Among these thirty-two questions, some are found in the *Daśābhisamaya-daśottara-śikhara-sūtra*, yet there one finds only the ten penetrations (*daśābhisamaya*) and the ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*), with neither the name "Unseen Peak" (*adṛṣṭa-śikhara*) nor the ten peaks (*daśa-śikhara*). May the Buddha, the World-Honored One, likewise [elucidate this].
"For my sake, O Bodhisattvas, explain these two phrases as a formal request. From this point onward, the Tathāgata, through his supernormal power, raises the Dharma to provide a manifest response.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the various Bodhisattvas, manifested his spiritual power for each according to their kind.

Having manifested his supernatural powers, he traveled eastward past as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields to a world named Golden, where the Buddha was named Immovable Wisdom (*Acalajñāna*).

In that world, there was a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated and immediately...
In the east, he manifested a lion throne of lotus-treasury and sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
To the south, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, there is a world named Wondrous Color; its Buddha is named Unobstructed Wisdom.
There, a bodhisattva named Chief of Awakening, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he paid homage and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the southern direction, whereupon he sat cross-legged.
To the west, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world named Lotus Color;
its Buddha was named Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness. There was a bodhisattva there named Chief of Wealth, together with as many [bodhisattvas] as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.

The Bodhisattvas arrived together at the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, they paid homage and immediately manifested lion-thrones of lotus-treasury in the western direction, whereupon they sat cross-legged.

To the north, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, there is a world named Campaka-flower-color, where the Buddha is named Dignified Wisdom. There, a Bodhisattva named Jewel-Head [was present].
Accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, they came together to the place where the Buddha was.
Upon arrival, they prostrated and immediately manifested lion thrones of lotus-treasury in the northern direction, whereupon they sat cross-legged.
To the northeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there is a world named Utpalavarṇa, and its Buddha is named Prabhāsa.
The Wisdom-Knower perceived that there was a bodhisattva named Guṇarāja (Virtue-Head) who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated and immediately manifested a lion throne of lotus-treasury in the northeast, upon which he sat cross-legged.
To the southeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world...
The world-realm is named Golden Color and the Buddha’s name is Ultimate Wisdom.
There was a bodhisattva there named Eye Chief (*Akṣimati*), who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddhas were.
Having arrived, he prostrated and immediately manifested a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury in the southeast and sat cross-legged. To the southwest, beyond ten buddha-fields...
In worlds as numerous as atoms, there is a world named Ratnavarṇa where the Buddha is named Jyeṣṭhajñāna.
There, a bodhisattva named Vīryottama, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they paid their respects and immediately manifested a lion throne of lotus-treasury in the southwest, upon which they sat cross-legged.
To the northwest, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there is a world named Vajra-Color;

its Buddha is named Sovereign Wisdom. There dwells a bodhisattva named Dharma-Head, who, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they paid their respects and immediately manifested a lotus flower in the northwest.
Seated cross-legged upon a lion throne made of jewels, there was a world below, ten buddha-field atoms of worlds away, named Vaidūrya-varṇa;

its Buddha was named Brahmajñāna. There was a bodhisattva there named Jñānaśrī, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they paid their respects and remained below.

Just as he was transforming [the ground] into a lion throne of the Lotus Treasury and sitting cross-legged upon it, from above, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world named Equal Color and a Buddha named Observing Wisdom.

There was a bodhisattva there named Worthy Leader (*Bhadrapāla*) who, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to the place where the Buddha was. Upon arriving, they...
Having paid homage, he immediately manifested a Lion Throne of the Lotus Treasury in the space above and sat upon it in the full lotus posture.

[Treatise] Third: From the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One, having known the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas," the following forty-one lines of scripture clarify the section on the Tathāgata’s manifestation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Within this section, the meaning is divided into two parts.

I. Clarifying the Manifestation of Dharmas According to Species; II. Clarifying [the Stages] Based on Initial Faith. Regarding the first, "Manifestation of Dharmas According to Species," there are two parts:
1. Within the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), each class of Bodhisattva manifests ten kinds of Buddha-stages;

within the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the Eleventh Ground (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*), there are respectively names for the fruits of Buddhahood corresponding to each stage.

The "Titles" (hào) refer to how, in accordance with all lands and all classes of sentient beings throughout the world-systems, various different names are manifested, such as the names of the Buddhas spoken of by Mañjuśrī in the following passage; this is the second [category], concerning those who possess faith.
That is to say, this present chapter and the entire section as a whole are for the sake of faith; within this faith, one has comprehensive faith in the five [aspects].
Only when the mind is free from obstruction regarding cause and effect within these stages can one truly practice cultivation, as taught in the scriptures.
For example, it is like a person traveling a perilous road five hundred *yojanas* in length who first learns of its obstructions and clear passages before proceeding;
this is analogous to a Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths who, within the stage of faith, first understands the progress and obstacles of the five stages of advancement.
One defends [the mind] with the practice of vows and guards it with faith, because the nature of one's own mind’s discrimination is fundamentally the immovable wisdom-body of all Buddhas;
thus, one guards against false views and the external grasping of other objects.

Because deluded consciousness, according to its stages, scatters and moves, obstructing true wisdom, one guards it with the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. According to the stages, [one abides in] the eighth stage...
The eighth dedication of the eight practices obstructs the wisdom of the eighth stage by causing stagnation in quiescence;

therefore, it is guarded against by the one hundred and forty great vows. Because it obstructs true non-conceptual great compassion by creating an attachment to the cycle of birth and death, it is guarded against by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the contemplations of the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as the fourteen truths.

One contemplates the ten and twelve links of dependent origination; one guards against [defilements] by means of the ten *pāramitās* because there is a fear that benefiting sentient beings may not be vast and extensive.

One guards against [defilements] by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), because there is a fear that seeking the fruit of one's own happiness and teaching sentient beings may not be thorough or widespread.
Thus, one gives rise to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), augmented by great vows, great compassion, and great... [wisdom].

Out of compassion, one does not abandon those in the evil realms, the hells, humans, or devas, but is born everywhere among them to prevent their own attachment to pleasure and to avoid violating the bodhicitta through the notion of "attainment.
For this reason, the mind of the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā) universally permeates all five stages and is entirely constituted by faith.
If one’s self-confidence is thorough and penetrating, there is no dharma sought that cannot be attained; however, if there is a doubting mind...
If one does not eliminate [doubts], how can faith be established? Thus, in this chapter, the gateway of the Buddha-fruit is presented;

in the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (Xian-shou pin), the Buddha’s supernormal powers and the deeds he performed throughout his career are presented so that those with initial faith may attain thorough conviction. Therefore, it is first called "the stage of faith.
Now, this entire scripture suddenly presents the causes and fruits of the five stages, with the gateway of the Buddha-fruit constituting the whole.
Faith: Having already entered the stage of practice through general faith, one only then begins to be free from delusion regarding the principle and its wisdom (*li-zhi*).
It is like a person preparing food; only when the five flavors have all matured at once does one begin to eat it.

From the first moment of eating until the meal is finished, the five flavors are eaten together, and throughout, the flavors do not depart from these five. This clarifies the cause and effect of the five stages; the ten faiths collectively illustrate this.

Time does not shift its fundamental nature; because the three periods [past, present, and future] are one and the same limit, the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood is never separate from the dharmas of the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
This can be understood through metaphors such as painting a portrait according to a model.
Within this section on the Dharma-gate of manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), there are forty-one lines of scripture in total, which are divided into eleven segments. First: "At that time..."

The World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas had already descended, clarified in the following one and a half lines of scripture how the Tathāgata knows the thoughts of the assembly and manifests dharmas through supernormal powers.

From "In the east, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are motes of dust" onwards, for thirty-nine and a half lines of scripture, it generally clarifies the gathering of bodhisattvas from the ten directions; since each direction has its own specific measure, there is no need for further elaboration.
Furthermore, within this assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten directions, the exposition is divided into eleven sections:
first, citing the directions of the buddha-fields; second, citing the distance of the buddha-fields; third, citing the names and forms of the worlds; fourth, citing the names of the Buddhas;
fifth, citing the names of the principal bodhisattvas; sixth, clarifying the number of the great assembly; and seventh, clarifying the [qualities] of the great assembly.
1. Having arrived, they pay their respects. 2. The eight types of luminous seats according to the directions for transformation. 3. The names and categories of the seats. 4.
The great assembly ascending the seats and taking their places. First: Regarding the Buddha’s direction. He is in the East.

The East corresponds to the hexagram *Zhèn* (Thunder), to the spring season of birth and growth, to the first illumination, to the eldest son, to the head, to the foremost, to the Azure Dragon, and to auspiciousness.
In every direction to the east and in every direction to the south, one merely takes up their dharmas; the rest is to be inferred by analogy with these two.
Regarding the mention of the distance and proximity of Buddha-fields: beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields to the east, there are four meanings:
first, to clarify that "ten" is a perfect number, thereby demonstrating that the distances near and far are inexhaustible; second, to inspire faith.
First, it is to know that the realm of the Buddha is vast and expansive, causing one's own mind to become broad and magnanimous;

second, it is to realize that the Buddha-realm is all-pervasive, like images reflected in a mirror, mutually interpenetrating without obstruction; fourth, it is for those who have not yet given rise to faith, using the metaphor of the dust motes of ten Buddha-lands to illustrate how they remain lost in delusion;
and because the ten types of ignorance have not been reached, their own obstructions prevent the Buddha-realm from appearing before them.
Raising up a speck of dust serves to represent delusion; thus, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni’s Pure Land lies beyond thirty-two worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to the west.
This is entirely a numerical expression for representing the Dharma, as has already been explained in the commentary.
When it says here that [the Tathāgata] comes from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms of ten Buddha-lands, it clarifies that he is separated by ten levels of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Within ignorance, each individual instance of ignorance possesses immeasurable karmic latencies and habitual tendencies, with primary and secondary factors mutually perfuming one another;
these afflictions exceed the number of atoms in the worlds, their limits unknown, as they are able to obstruct the realm of wisdom.

Therefore, it is said that they exist "beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields. As for the term "coming," it clarifies that one enters faith from delusion; hence, it is designated as "coming."

The statement that there is a Buddha in that world named Acalamati (Immovable Wisdom) is intended to clarify that the Buddha Acalamati is the fundamental wisdom common to all ordinary beings and sages throughout the ten directions; because one can give rise to faith in this wisdom, he is designated as "coming here.
This Buddha Acalamati is eternally inherent within all sentient beings—if one were to grasp it...

To follow along with delusion is to be obscured by the dust of the sensory realm without end; yet if one awakens for even a single thought-moment, realizing that these appearances are identical to purity, they are like empty space.
It is only because of following delusion that we speak of "the external" in reference to the place of awakening;

yet in reality, the Buddha-field is fundamentally without distance, nor are there obstructions such as internal or external, nor is there coming or going. Boundless Buddha-fields do not transcend a single pore or a minute speck of dust.
The manifest expression is intended to convey the meaning to those far and near; because it causes the minds of those with initial faith to become vast, it says that they "come from that world.
Furthermore, to clarify the transition from delusion to awakening, it says that they "have come.
The mention of the Buddha named "Immovable Wisdom" clarifies that this refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the believer themselves; because they possess this wisdom, all [phenomena]...

Because sentient beings are able to give rise to the bodhicitta, they utilize the essence of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to comprehend the nature of delusion and transcend the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).
Thus, by transcending that realm of delusion, they are said to "come. As the *Awakening of Faith* states regarding the "mark of inconceivable activity":
"By relying on the purity of wisdom, one is able to produce all kinds of supreme and wondrous realms, namely, the immeasurable [realms]."
The characteristics of merit are eternally uninterrupted; they accord naturally with the faculties of sentient beings, appearing in various ways so that benefit may be obtained.
Furthermore, it is said that non-enlightenment arises based upon original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
It is also said that suffering and pleasure arise based upon wisdom (*jñāna*). As extensively clarified in the *Awakening of Faith*, the meaning is that all sentient beings [possess this nature].
Because one is deluded regarding fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and thus encounters the phenomena of worldly suffering and pleasure, wisdom is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Because it does not perceive [the truth] according to conditions, the karma of suffering and pleasure arises; yet because wisdom is without intrinsic nature, only when one is entangled by suffering can one then realize for oneself that the fundamental is without intrinsic nature, all conditions are without intrinsic nature, and all phenomena are inherently quiescent. If one does not perceive suffering at this time, then by means of non-existence...
Because of their nature, they do not collectively know whether there is existence or non-existence of nature;

just as a person falls because of the ground and rises because of the ground, all sentient beings fall because of the fundamental wisdom of their own minds and arise because of the fundamental wisdom of their own minds.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, within this sūtra of the One Vehicle, suddenly reveals the original Dharma.
In the Golden World, the luminous Dharmakāya is pure, white, and unstained, suddenly manifesting fundamental wisdom;
this is named the Buddha Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati-jñāna*). The sudden manifestation of Mañjuśrī is the wisdom of sublime discernment of one’s own mind.
The remaining nine worlds, with their nine Wisdom Buddhas and nine Bodhisattvas, represent the progressive stages of practice according to the faith and understanding of one’s own mind.
Because the cultivation of the superior Dharma-body and Wisdom-body follows various synonymous designations,

from this point one enters the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) based on the self-awakening of the Buddha of the originally unmoving wisdom within one’s own mind; thereupon, one initiates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages,
and the eleventh stage, further cultivating the Dharma-body, Wisdom-body, great vows, and great kindness and compassion.
It encompasses the four immeasurables, the ten perfections, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

from the very moment of the initial resolve, these are based upon the fundamental dharma-body and the essence of the originally unmoving wisdom. Through their mutual integration of compassionate vows, they serve as resources for the myriad practices.
The dharma-body serves as a resource for the practices, ensuring they remain untainted; the practices serve as a resource for the dharma-body, ensuring it reaches full maturity.
Within each of the five stages, ten fruits of Buddhahood and ten bodhisattvas are established respectively.
These names are designated based on the fruits of Buddhahood and the bodhisattva practices attained through one’s own cultivation during the progressive advancement through the stages;

they are not the names of other Buddhas or other bodhisattvas. Their names are established according to the fruits of Buddhahood realized through wisdom and according to the fruits of their respective practices throughout the five stages.

The causes and effects of each of these [stages] are fifty each, totaling one hundred; together with the five fundamental stages, there are five sets of cause and effect, totaling one hundred and ten dharma-gates of the city.
Therefore, this answers the previous question of the Bodhisattva regarding the four kinds of Buddha-fields:
the Buddhas dwelling in the Buddha-fields, the adornment of the Buddha-fields, and the pure nature of the Buddha-fields. From this point onward...

Regarding the two Buddha-fields mentioned above— wherein one attains the manifestation of perfect enlightenment and the sovereign spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) of a Buddha-field within the Buddha-field of the Buddha of Majestic Virtue (*Buddha-vaideha*)—
the questions posed by the World Rulers (*Lokendra*) in the previous assembly concern the causes and effects of the mastery attained by that other Vairocana Buddha.
These questions posed by the Bodhisattvas in this second assembly concern the Buddha-fields of those who are practitioners themselves.

From this point onward, up until the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," these five stages represent the culmination of the bodhisattva’s practice through the power of their own application (*prayoga*). This chapter clarifies the cause and effect of advancing through faith;
whereas the "Chapter on the Appearance" clarifies the cause and effect of reaching the ultimate limit of the stage of cultivation. Thus far...

Because one gives rise to faith, diligence, and practice upon the Buddha-wisdom that is the root of one’s own mind, this Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) is the ground for all Buddhas and all sentient beings.

It is by means of this wisdom that one acts as a sentient being, and it is by means of this wisdom that one attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Furthermore, when following delusion to act as a sentient being, within the six...
Throughout the realms of gods, humans, and the evil destinies, there are always [manifestations] corresponding to the retributive fruits of sentient beings' environments and bodies;

these vary according to the coarseness or subtlety of their karma. By means of this wisdom, at the time of awakening, one achieves the fruits of the three vehicles as well as the perfect Buddha-fruit of the One Vehicle within the Dharma-realm, including the wondrous retributions of both environment and body. If this wisdom were lacking, [such attainment would not occur].
Originally, it is neither empty space, nor sentient beings, nor the Buddhas. Therefore, it is asked:

"If all sentient beings inherently possess immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*), why do they not spontaneously realize the true, eternal, and pure state? Why do they instead follow along with defilement? The answer is:
"It is because all sentient beings give rise to the three realms by means of this very wisdom; it is because this wisdom lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) that [they are unable to realize it]."

To know for oneself that these dharmas—whether wisdom or non-wisdom, good or evil, suffering or pleasure—are the essence of wisdom, yet lack intrinsic nature and manifest only in accordance with conditions;
just as an empty valley’s echo forms sounds in response to objects, so too does wisdom lacking intrinsic nature merely respond to conditions through discrimination.
Because of this discrimination, delusion and craving arise; because of delusion and craving, the sickness of "mine" arises, and the notion of "self" is produced.
Because it clings to self and others, it gives rise to the grasping of karma; thus it is called *manas*. Because *manas* grasps, it is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Due to the seeds of consciousness, birth and death continue in succession. Because of birth and death, the various sufferings are immeasurable.
Since suffering is immeasurable, one seeks the path that leads away from suffering; yet those who are deluded do not recognize suffering.
Those who are unable to resolve their minds to recognize suffering and seek the Truth do so because their fundamental wisdom encounters the conditions of suffering;

only through encountering the conditions of suffering can one recognize it, for without encountering the conditions of suffering, one cannot recognize it. Because one recognizes the conditions of suffering, one is then able to resolve the mind to seek the Unsurpassed Way.
Bodhisattvas with the spiritual lineage (gotra), having already recognized suffering in previous lives, resolve their minds and develop faith and understanding.
Those of strong potential, though they may receive the fruits of happiness among humans and devas, are still able to resolve their minds to seek the Unsurpassed Way.

Therefore, when wisdom follows delusion, it is called consciousness; when wisdom follows awakening, it is called wisdom. Just as a person falls because of the ground and rises because of the ground, so too, when it follows delusion, it is named consciousness; when it follows awakening, it is named wisdom while remaining within the bonds of existence (*saṃsāra*).
What is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) exists within awakening as what is called "wisdom" (jñāna). Wisdom and consciousness originally have no names of their own;

they are established only in accordance with delusion and enlightenment. Therefore, one must not calculate them in terms of permanence or annihilation. This wisdom and this consciousness are merely named according to delusion and enlightenment.
If one seeks their beginning or end, it is like seeking tracks in the sky, or like seeking a person within a shadow.
Because one can never find a place where a self dwells within the body, such characteristics of location—whether new, long, or short—are absent.
Thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) have no beginning or end. When one attains *bodhi*, ignorance is not extinguished; why?
Because it is fundamentally non-existent and therefore has nothing further to be extinguished. If one follows along with ignorance at that time, [it does not arise].
The movement of wisdom is also not extinguished because it is fundamentally non-existent; thus, there is nothing further to be extinguished.

It is only when one follows after the objects of perception—form, sound, smell, and so forth—that it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). It is only when one knows suffering and gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment that it is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Since these are merely designated according to conditions, their essence has neither beginning nor end. Contemplate this as being like an echo in a valley.
