Third, regarding the naming of the world as "Golden": this is to clarify that the substance of gold is pure white.
The metaphor of "being unstained when lifted up" illustrates the Dharma-body, for its essence is devoid of nature and free from defilement;
it is like the gold of the West in the world, which is white in color. Its substance is white, yet it manifests a brilliant yellow.

The *Arhat* (True Reality) Bodhisattva internally accords with the White Dharma while externally manifesting the Yellow Aspect. This yellow is the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of the *Arhat*. As Master Xu Fu said, among the five colors—*189*
Yellow is the foremost [color]; the human face is like the color of a cucumber. Within it lies the *Sūtra on the Practice of the Sages*.
It says that Arhats and Bodhisattvas are all of true golden color. Furthermore, regarding the clarification of the Golden World, it clarifies the stage of faith:
although one believes that one's own mind is the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, pure and originally unstained, this belief is itself subject to arising and ceasing.

Because it is a mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*), it is both form and mind. The reason the eastern direction is cited as the primary one is to clarify that the east is the first illumination and the source from which all things arise and are stirred;
thus, it is taken to symbolize the Dharma. This serves as an analogy for the beginning of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
While directions are ultimately without fixed location, this citation of the direction merely uses the phenomenon to illustrate the principle and to manifest its essence.

Because it is used as such, it is like the king of oxen or the king of dragons; how much more so regarding the virtues of the Buddha. A question is asked: Since the eastern direction represents the Dharma, why is it used as a metaphor for the very beginning of the ten stages of faith?

Furthermore, while the position of gold is in the west, why is the eastern direction designated as the Golden World to represent the Dharmakāya, manifesting the fundamental wisdom as the Immovable Wisdom? Answer: The eastern direction is taken to represent the Dharmakāya because it signifies the initial arising of the mind. Just as the rising sun first appears in the east, so too does the Bodhicitta first emerge there. As for the designation of the world as "Golden," it is because the Dharmakāya is of the nature of pure gold, and this manifests that the fundamental wisdom is the Immovable Wisdom. Thus, by using the east to symbolize the Dharma, it serves as a metaphor for the commencement of the ten stages of faith. As for the location of gold being in the west, this refers to the stage of fruition; however, since the essence of gold is unchanging, it is used here to signify that although the stages of practice progress from the east toward the west, the fundamental wisdom remains eternally unmoving. Therefore, the golden world in the east is established to represent the Dharmakāya and to reveal that the fundamental wisdom is the Immovable Wisdom.

It is said: This question clearly elucidates the principle as explained in the sutras. Taking faith as the womb, one reaches the stage of the Ten Abodes, which is called being "born into the Buddha-family.

Now, the reason the eastern direction is designated as the Golden World is to clarify that gold corresponds to the first month [of gestation], the embryo [is formed] in the second month, the shape [is completed] in the third month, birth occurs in the fourth month [the Earthly Branch of Si], and nourishment occurs in the fifth month [the Earthly Branch of Wu].

In the fifth month one is capped, in the sixth month one wears the ceremonial girdle; in the seventh month there is the mutual relationship [of the parents], and in the eighth month the king [the fetus] becomes manifest.

Because the ten faiths are like a fetus, they are symbolized by the golden womb of the eastern direction; subsequently, the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir are used to symbolize the progressive cultivation and increasing excellence of the ten stages of faith.
Thus, this chapter uses phenomena to illustrate principles (*toshi-kōji*) so that they may be easily understood.
Mañjuśrī said: "World-Honored One, when you were formerly a bodhisattva, you attained accomplishment through various discourses, skillful means, stages, and positions;
you also caused sentient beings to know and see in this way, and thus preached the Dharma for them.
Later scholars, observing with wisdom, have all declared that these were merely explanations of general directions intended to symbolize the Dharma."
One should know that seeking fish by means of a net does not mean the fish is the net; yet, without a net, the fish likewise cannot be obtained.
Therefore, when one reflects through the principle of meaning, the ultimate truth is established as faith. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "In every place is the Golden World;
in every place is the Buddha Immovable Wisdom; in every place is Mañjuśrī. This clarifies the Dharma.
Because it pervades all phenomena and the bodies and minds of all sentient beings, it is the Universal Immovable Wisdom Buddha;
because it is the universal Mañjuśrī, one should know and believe it in this way.

It should be understood that the Golden World is named as such because it is the principle believed by those of faithful mind; furthermore, it is precisely because of this faith that it returns [to its source].

When one’s retribution for past deeds results in birth that is free from defilement and a dwelling place that is free from attachment, this is precisely what is meant by the Western World of Lotus Colors; it is like the World of Golden Color.
These examples—such as the Southern World of Wondrous Colors and the Western World of Lotus Colors—represent the excellence of advancing through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
For this reason, within these there are ten causes and ten fruits. As for the ten fruits, they are the ten Wisdom-Buddhas.
As for the ten causes, they are the ten Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī and Buddhamati. These are the causes of practice;
the benefits gained within the causes are themselves the fruits within the causes—namely, the ten Wisdom-Buddhas such as Akṣobhya-jñāna. These are the ten [World-Honored Ones].
The realms are the Dharma-gates to be cultivated. Fourth, regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name: the name of the Buddha is Akṣayamati (Immovable Wisdom).
This clarifies that the fundamental essence of wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings is now first invoked to establish the initial stage of faith.
This explains the answer to the previous question concerning where the Buddha dwells and his Buddha-field; the remaining nine Wisdom Buddhas are all included therein.

From this fundamental Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*), the name "progressive cultivation" arises; it does not belong to another, for all Buddhas of the ten directions share this same name as a trace of their manifestation.
By giving rise to faith and advancing in practice, one passes through the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) to attain the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*), the majestic power of the Buddha, and the majestic power of the Buddha-fields: these are the Tathāgatas.
This refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the remaining meanings have already been explained as before. Fifth, regarding the mention of the names of the preeminent bodhisattvas:
the name Mañjuśrī signifies the sublime wisdom that discriminates phenomena within the non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Because all Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment by discerning the correct from the erroneous through this very wisdom, he is titled "Mañju" (Wen).
She is truly the teacher of all Buddhas of the ten directions and is also called the Mother of Buddhas, for it is said that all Buddhas are born from this wondrous wisdom.
If one lacks this wisdom, even if one cultivates liberation, one will only attain the vehicles of the Two Vehicles or be reborn in a Pure Land;
such a Bodhisattva does not ride the Tathāgata Vehicle to achieve perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one must ride upon this.

The essence of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*), the sublime prajñā of Mañjuśrī, and the wondrous principle of the Dharma-body—this great wisdom proceeds from the stage of faith through the five ranks (*pañca-vastu*) without ever departing from the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom and the sublime prajñā of Mañjuśrī; thus one attains perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, it is called the Tathāgata-vehicle, the inconceivable vehicle, the most supreme vehicle, and the unsurpassed vehicle, by which one attains perfect enlightenment.
Because he has awakened, Mañjuśrī is also called the "Youngest Son" or the "Child.

This is because all Buddhas are born into the family of the Buddhas for the first time through this wondrous wisdom that skillfully knows the True Dharma; therefore, he is called the Child Bodhisattva.
Even after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, Mañjuśrī will still remain in the world, and when his future work of transformation is complete, [he will likewise pass away].
The teaching of the Three Vehicles states that he entered nirvana upon the summit of Mount Gandhamādana;
however, this sutra says that Mañjuśrī is present in all places, clarifying that he is equally shared by all sentient beings everywhere.
Now, at the beginning of this sutra’s instruction on faith, its name is cited to clarify that one who possesses faith believes in the wondrous nature of their own mind.
The wisdom that discerns is identical in this regard; it does not deviate from ancient traces.

This is the fundamental, wondrous wisdom of all Buddhas and sentient beings, which is shared equally by both ordinary and sagely beings without any difference in nature. It is like the great king’s highway;
its principle is eternally thus. All the various sutras currently extant that have Mañjuśrī as the primary interlocutor are [based upon this].
The gates of the wondrous wisdom of the Dharmakāya are elucidated by making Samantabhadra the primary interlocutor;

this clarifies that the essence and function of the myriad practices of wondrous wisdom are such that these two Bodhisattvas serve as the gateway for the wondrous application of the principle and wisdom of all Buddhas and their myriad practices.
Based upon these dharma-gates, they establish their respective names and manifest as Buddhas to benefit sentient beings.

Because they have been born [into this teaching], all sentient beings who have resolved their minds [toward enlightenment] practice together and possess the conduct of benefiting both self and others as their constant model. Now, regarding the reason why it is established within the teachings that Mañjuśrī and ten thousand bodhisattvas dwell therein at Mount Qingliang in the northeast, there are three meanings: first, * It serves as a place for those who have not yet resolved their minds to resolve them; * It serves as a place for those who have already resolved their minds to cultivate their practice; * It serves as a place for those who have already attained realization to manifest their spiritual powers. Furthermore, there are two reasons why he specifically dwells in this location: first, to manifest his great compassion by dwelling in a remote and difficult-to-reach place; second, to manifest his great wisdom by dwelling in a place where the Dharma flourishes. Furthermore, there are two reasons why he specifically dwells with ten thousand bodhisattvas: first, to manifest the power of his great vow by gathering a vast assembly; second, to manifest the power of his great merit by being surrounded by a multitude of holy ones. Furthermore, there are two reasons why he specifically dwells on a mountain: first, to manifest his great compassion by dwelling in a secluded place; second, to manifest his great wisdom by dwelling in a high and exalted place. To cause all sentient beings in this realm to have a joyful mind that pursues roots of goodness without interruption—this is the second clarity, that Bodhisattvas always abide in the world.
The third is the clarity of manifesting the Dharma according to direction, showing that the Dharma is easy to understand; thus, the first two gates may be understood.
Regarding the third, manifesting the Dharma according to direction, the explanation of the northeast refers to taking this single region of Jambudvīpa as the object.

This Mount Qingliang is located in the northeast; according to the scriptures, it is situated within the land of Zhendan, also called Jintina, which means "Contemplation" (*Sītuí*), so named because the people of that country engage in much reflection and deliberation—it is none other than the present-day Han country.
In representing the Dharma, the northeast corresponds to the hexagram Gen (*Gèn*), which signifies stillness and obstruction.

therefore, he resembles Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, who constantly inspires ordinary beings to enter right faith and causes the light of wondrous wisdom to arise in the ignorant who have first seen the Path.
Furthermore, because it is like reaching the summit of a mountain where all characteristics are exhausted, the illumination is as if at the very beginning.

Those who enter into right faith first believe in the emptiness of all phenomena; because they are able to believe in the emptiness of phenomena, wondrous wisdom arises. The month of Chou (the second month) is like the initial faith;
Yi (the third month) is like the initial realization of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); Mao, Chen, and Si represent progressive cultivation; Wu represents the Middle Way;
Wei, Shen, You, Xu, and Hai represent benefiting sentient beings through the same activities (*samānārthatā*); and Zi represents the stage of the Teacher.
The hexagram Kǎn represents the sovereign and the teacher; dwelling in simplicity, it establishes models and formulates laws to benefit living beings.
Therefore, it corresponds to the north, the position of the sovereign and the teacher, the honored one who dwells therein to govern by means of manifesting clarity.

Regarding the Lotus-Treasury Lion-Throne, within this section the meaning is divided into three parts: first, the lotus signifies the meaning of being unstained;
this is obtained as the retributive fruit of relying on the Dharma and practicing accordingly.

Because the nature of the practice of the Dharmakāya is unstained by the world, it can cause the fruits of wisdom and principle to blossom and become increasingly bright and pure; thus, it clarifies the relationship between cause and effect.
Because it causes the provisions to become fully matured, it clarifies the matter of the blooming and unfolding of the *padma* (lotus) as an adornment;

because the dharmas are worthy of contemplation, one practices by means of these dharmas, thereby invoking this retribution of the lotus flower as a seat. Regarding the "Two Treasuries" (*pitaka*), they carry the meaning of "containing.

This clarifies that the Dharmakāya, with its wisdom and principle, dwells in the world and benefits sentient beings according to their conduct, universally containing all dharmas for the sake of universal benefit.
That which gathers all manifold merits is called a "treasury" (*kośa*). It is named "Lion" (*siṃha*) by way of a dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*):
because he dwells in the world with a body of great wisdom and the non-arising and non-ceasing nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he benefits sentient beings and is fearless regarding birth and death;
furthermore, through the light of correct wisdom and the fearlessness of eloquence, he is free from the five fears and so forth. As it is said: [as in the verse]...
The Lion also [addresses] the great assembly; they ascend and sit upon their seats.

They take the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the substance of the seat, clarifying that because one accords with the substance of the Dharma-realm from the state of an ordinary person, it is through the practice of faith and diligence that faith is perfected.
This is the fruit-seat of all the Buddhas of the ten directions; it clarifies that initial faith is the sudden realization of the Buddha-fruit.
It is because one practices the Dharma oneself that faith is truly established. This section is further divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the breadth and narrowness of the seat; second, clarifying how the Bodhisattva sits upon it.
Regarding the first, the breadth and narrowness of the seat, as stated in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta": "That lion throne encompasses the entire Dharmadhātu," as clearly explained in the full text.
The general meaning is that because the nature of the mind is without dependence and lacks a fixed, chaotic substance, it is taken as the substance of the seat.

Second, to clarify how the Bodhisattva sits: it is said that he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). To unify the various conditions of the world into a single Dharma-realm is called "binding" (*parya*);
to designate many conditions by means of a single Dharma is called "kneeling" (*ṅka*). Furthermore, it is "binding."
Sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) is the mark of a tranquil and unmoving deportment;
therefore, this stage presides over the ten *pāramitās* within the *dāna-pāramitā*. Regarding the second [direction], the south and below, there are approximately four lines of scripture.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī, the Mother of Awakening, initiates enlightenment by causing one to believe, thereby guiding the faculties toward awakening.
To the east of the city, Sudhana entered the Way and advanced in his cultivation; he then traveled south to visit various spiritual friends.

This indicates that the south represents the ultimate, the sun, illumination, and the principle of emptiness (ākāśa). Therefore, when making offerings to the Buddha, one always says "Namo Ming" (Homage to Illumination);
the south is emptiness. However, the principle of emptiness is the meaning of the south, and it is present in all places.
In the South, the mere initial arising of faith is itself the meaning of the East in all places.

Therefore, while the Four Noble Truths are assigned to the East and West—Suffering and Accumulation—and the South and North—Cessation and the Path—the Dharma has no fixed location. When sentient beings receive its transformation, they give rise to understanding and faith;
were it otherwise, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) would be difficult to clarify. As stated later in this chapter: "The World-Honored One..."

he also taught the Dharma so that sentient beings might gain such knowledge and vision, as described in detail in the sutras.

Second, regarding the enumeration of the distance of the Buddha-fields: it says "the number of atoms in ten Buddha-fields," the meaning of which is as explained previously.
The commentary states: "The external entry into the Dharma" means "to come. 3. Third, regarding the naming of the world's color: it is named "Wondrous Color."

Second, because the stage of faith gradually increases and becomes sublime, it surpasses the preceding stages of faith; because one realizes that phenomena are empty and non-existent, the phenomena themselves are inherently sublime.

Thus, the four Buddhas are called "Unimpeded Wisdom. This clarifies that through the essence of Immovable Wisdom, one advances in the cultivation of faith, whereby wisdom increases and becomes unimpeded.
This collectively clarifies that the Buddhas of the stage of faith are one's own mind, and not something external.
Because the Buddha-mind, the sentient-being mind, and one’s own mind are collectively a single mind, a single nature, a single dharma-realm, and a single wisdom, faith is first established.
Fifth, as for the naming of the leading Bodhisattvas: he is named Awakening Head (Jue-shou), for he is enlightened by means of Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom;
he is able to skillfully discern the correct from the deviant and can awaken himself, and thus he also awakens others to that which he has awakened to.
Because the Dharma can awaken others, what is it that the Bodhisattva in this stage awakens to? Within this stage, there are three aspects of awakening:
first, awakening to the fact that one’s own body and mind are fundamentally the Dharma-realm, pure and unstained, just as in the previously described Golden World;
second, awakening to the nature of the discrimination of one’s own body and mind, which is fundamentally devoid of subject and object and is from the beginning suchness.
The Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna’s threefold awakening to his own mind—the sublime wisdom that skillfully discriminates between the correct and the erroneous—is Mañjuśrī.
At the initial stage of faith, he awakens to these three dharmas and is thus named Awakening Head (Jue-shou).
This clarifies that within the state of faith, the practice of skillful awakening is called the Bodhisattva Awakening Head; one must, in general, recognize this as being one's own.
The dharma-gate of practice is established only through faith; therefore, if one relies on the faith of others while lacking it within oneself, it cannot be called true faith.
Sixth, regarding the number of the great assembly, there are ten [assemblies] as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-fields, the meaning of which is as explained in the initial commentary.

Seventh, regarding the great assembly having arrived and paid homage, this is as can be known. Eighth, regarding the transformation seats according to their respective directions, this is as can be known from the preceding [text].

Ninth, the clarification of the names of the seats: the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne is so named because it clarifies that through the accomplishment of entering faith, one is able to be fearless amidst birth and death;
it is designated by its primary referent (the *tatpuruṣa* compound). Other meanings are as explained previously.
Tenth, the clarification of the great assembly ascending the seats and sitting: the meaning is as explained previously. The presiding figure of this stage is Precept-Wave (*Śīlataraṅga*).
The *pāramitā* is the leader and the other nine are its companions. Third, regarding the passage of four lines beginning with "Beyond ten buddha-lands as numerous as atoms" in the west:
therein, the ten dharmas are as previously explained. First, it cites the direction of the buddha-land, which is the west;
second, it cites the distance of the buddha-land, the meaning of which is explained as before; third, it cites the name and color of the world-system.

This is called "Lotus-Colored" (*padmavarṇā*) to clarify that within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one's progressive cultivation becomes increasingly superior; because the mind is unstained like a lotus, it is called "lotus-colored.
Furthermore, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of the stage of faith uses the mind and body to contemplate emptiness and the path of non-substantiality.
Fourth, regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name: the Buddha’s name is "Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness.
Because the West is gold, the White Tiger, slaughter, darkness, inauspiciousness, and the Truth of Suffering, the Buddha’s name is "Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness.
This signifies that in the stage of Clear Faith, one advances in practice and the wisdom of cultivation increases and excels.
Therefore, they are able to destroy the darkness of both themselves and others. Fifth, as for the naming of the Bodhisattvas who serve as leaders:
the one named Vasumitra (Wealth-Leader) is designated thus because, in the stage of "Clear Faith," he possesses superior Dharma-wealth to benefit sentient beings.

This is precisely the name for his own practice and his benefiting of sentient beings within the third faith. The Buddha’s title represents the wisdom of self-awakening, while the Bodhisattva represents self... [text ends]
The practice of wisdom generally clarifies that awakening and conduct advance together; other gates may be understood as already explained previously.

This section on the primary *pāramitā* of patience contains ten *pāramitās*. Below this, after passing worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields toward the north, there are four lines of scripture.
These ten gates are as described above: first, one cites the direction of a Buddha-field.
This refers to the two Buddhas of the northern direction; the distance between their Buddha-fields is as previously explained in the third section.
Regarding the names and colors of these worlds: the name is *Campaka-flower-color*. This flower is yellow.

It signifies that through the further development of the fourth stage of faith, one blossoms and attains the fruit, thereby obtaining the color of the Middle Way. Yellow is the most supreme among the five colors.
The color yellow is the color of the Central Palace and represents the qi of auspicious fortune; it clarifies that the inner mind is pure white while the external manifestation appears as yellow.
As the Sūtra says, "The Arhats and Bodhisattvas are all of true golden color," clarifying that this faithful mind is joyful, serene, pure, and unstained.
When the harmonious qi of blessings responds and the fruit of the Way unfolds, it is called the world. Therefore—
The world is the color of the *campaka* flower; those who raise their voices four times to recite the Buddha’s name, the Buddha’s title is *Viniyatakrama-jñāna* (Wisdom of Dignified Conduct).

The north corresponds to the *kan* trigram; it represents the teacher and the sovereign. Because the sovereign possesses virtue yet occupies a dark position while engaging with ordinary beings, he acts as a teacher.
The Buddha’s title, *Viniyatakrama-jñāna*, clarifies that the fourth stage of faith has increased and excelled, serving as the guiding standard.

Fan (範) receives and guides the ordinary and the ignorant, clarifying majestic deportment through wisdom; because he takes the dignified composure of wisdom as the appearance of a teacher, the names of the five leading Bodhisattvas are mentioned.
"Jewel Head" (寶首) is named thus because he serves as a teacher and model, benefiting sentient beings with the Dharma-treasure;
the remaining meanings are as previously explained. This stage presides over the gate of diligence, wherein [it encompasses] the ten perfections.
From the fifth line of the *Pāramitā* section below the northeast, the following four lines of scripture are divided into ten points as previously explained.

First, regarding the indication of the direction: it is stated that the northeast corresponds to the hexagram Gen (艮), representing the "young male," the "childlike ignorant," the "beginning of illumination," and the "clear dawn.
Second, regarding the meaning of the distance of the Buddha-fields, it is as explained in the initial commentary. Third...
Regarding the manifestation of the world’s name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): its name is *Utpalavarṇa* (Lotus-Color).

This is the image of the blue lotus; it is the fifth stage of pure faith. Because its color and fragrance are unstained, it blossoms and brings forth fruition, like the dawn position in the clear morning.
Fourth, regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name: the name of the Buddha is *Vairocanaprabhāsa-jñāna* (Wisdom-Image of Radiant Clarity); this is the fifth faith.
The mind becomes increasingly preeminent, like the appearance of the clear dawn at the position of Gen (艮).
Thus, one takes the Buddha whom one personally trusts as the primary designation, rather than any other Buddha. Fifth, regarding the naming of the leading Bodhisattvas:

the name "Guṇamukha" (功德首) is used because in the preceding stage, "Ratnamukha" (寶首) was designated, which refers to benefiting sentient beings through the Dharma-jewel; this present stage, however, refers to both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The merit and other meanings are as previously explained. In this stage, the ten *pāramitās* within the Dhyāna-gate are governed by the hexagram Gen (艮), which signifies "stopping.
Therefore, from the sixth [hexagram] in the southeast and below, approximately four lines of scripture apply; the ten meanings therein are as before.
First, regarding the direction of the Buddha: this refers to the southeast. This is the hexagram Xun (巽); Xun represents wind and...

Instruction, when applied to affairs, is a method; when applied to persons, it is an exposition. Like a superior person who expounds instruction to benefit others, the *I Ching* has clear and manifest teachings:
"The superior person establishes instruction to enlighten the ignorant. To follow this is like wind blowing over grass—it is the meaning of "accordance.
This is like the hexagram *Guan*, where the *I Ching* says: "Wind blowing over the earth forms the image of *Guan*; thus the superior person, possessing virtue, establishes governance."
It instructs all people to believe and comply, for just as wind blowing upon grass cannot fail to cause it to bend, the hexagram Xùn represents the multitude and signifies belief and compliance.

Furthermore, among the four great elements, the power of wind is supreme; heaven and earth rely upon it to be sustained, humans rely upon it to be born, and the sun and moon rely upon it for their movement.
Moreover, this clarifies that wind has the meaning of being able to sift out the foul and select the pure.
Therefore, it is for the purpose of teaching; this teaching is able to eliminate what is non-virtuous and select what is virtuous by instructing the ignorant and deluded.

For this reason, the position of the hexagram Xùn (巽) is in the southeast; its *jiā-chén* (earthly branch) holds the position of Chǒu. Chǒu is the position of Gèn (艮), which represents the "Youngest Son," the "Childish Ignorant," and "Brightness.

Xùn is Wind; it transforms and educates the childish ignorant, causing them to attain enlightenment. Thus, the temporal cycle (*chén*) of the Tathāgata’s Dharma corresponds to the months of Chén and Sì.
The period between [the hours of] *chen* and *si* is for the purpose of fasting and purification; during this time, the celestial mansion *Jiǎo* (the Horn) is positioned above.

*Jiǎo* is the Gate of Heaven (*Tiānmén*), presiding over monks, nuns, and Daoist masters—it is the gate to all that is wholesome. It clarifies wisdom and discourse, for it is the gate to all that is wholesome.
Therefore, the meaning of this is immeasurable and difficult to explain in full; I shall speak of it only briefly. Hereafter...
The wise examine it through the Dharma, scrutinize it, and contemplate it; because its meaning is profoundly subtle, two points are raised:

first, the meaning of the distance and proximity of Buddha-fields as explained previously; second, the names and forms of the worlds—here the world is named "Golden" (*Suvarṇa*) to clarify that the initial, primary stage of faith is like a fetus, and thus the Eastern direction is taken as the "Golden Womb" (*Suvarṇagarbha*).

The position indicates the initial stage of faith and understanding; now, by progressing through cultivation to the sixth stage of faith, it clarifies that the mind of faith becomes increasingly superior.
Therefore, gold arising from within oneself represents this faith; as the faith becomes even more brilliant, pure, and clear, it arises.
Thus, the golden world in the southeast represents the fourth month, where gold arises from within oneself, signifying faith.
The mind becomes increasingly clear, pure, and superior; it excels in the discernment of all phenomena and is able to expound the teachings and transform others through its conduct.
This serves as a manifestation of the gateway to wisdom. Fourth, regarding the raising of the Buddha’s name: the Buddha is named Ultimate Wisdom-Light (*paryanta-jñāna-prabhā*).
As one's faith increases, one is well able to use the teachings to discern the correct from the erroneous, reaching ultimate wisdom. Furthermore—
Xun represents wind; in terms of accomplishment, it is "fang," where *fang* signifies method (*dharma*). In the Sage, it accomplishes the principle of pure clarity through skillful discernment;
in speech, it accomplishes eloquence; in transformation, it accomplishes teaching; in the common person, it accomplishes folly;

and in wisdom, it accomplishes insight. It accomplishes the virtue of detachment; it is red and constitutes patterned ornament; it accomplishes the virtue of Dui; as gold first produced, it is pure white.
The trigram Dui represents metal, the mouth, and the ability to speak. Because it can explain the pure and ultimate principle, the Buddha is titled the Buddha of Ultimate Wisdom (*niṣṭhā-jñāna*).

Fifth, as for the naming of the foremost bodhisattvas: the name "Eye Chief" (*Akṣimati*) signifies that through the sixth stage of faith, one excels in skillfully distinguishing between the correct and the false; thus, the path becomes clearly manifest, and right view is free from delusion.
Taking "Eye" as the primary image, its position corresponds to the Xun hexagram in the southeast; its *xiāochén* (earthly branch) is Chou, and its location is Wind.

Above it lies the Ji (Scorpion) lunar mansion, clarifying that Ji signifies the meaning of "winnowing" or "discernment. Furthermore, Ji presides over the position of Yin, which governs initial illumination.
This sixth stage of faith takes Prajñā-pāramitā as its lord, employing definitive wisdom to illuminate this principle.
Because it skillfully discriminates between the correct and the deviant, causing the luminous wisdom of oneself and others to arise, it is named "Mukha" (The Head).
"Mukha" carries the meaning of excellent vision and clear discernment; the remaining meanings are as explained above.

To the southeast of this is the realm of Mingjiuxingdingzhengxi-zhi (The Boundary Between Auspiciousness and Misfortune, Certainty and Deviance), where all matters reach completion at the hour of the horse (wu). The hour of the horse is the Dharma-gate of Constant Illumination; this is the place of the youth Sudhana.
Traveling south, one consults friends regarding the Way of Emptiness, Non-action, and Eternal Illumination; this is the wondrous function of non-intervention.

Therefore, in the ritual protocols between ruler and minister, teacher and disciple, and father and son, the minister faces south while the ruler faces north—this is the governance of rectitude and clarity, the eternally constant Way of non-action and non-activity.
The south corresponds to the trigram Li; because Li is empty in its center, it represents emptiness and non-being.
It is the sun and the light; within the body it is the eyes, and in the mind it is the essence. Therefore, the *Zhouyi* says: "Li (the trigram for fire) represents the mind.
Indeed, phenomena have no place of abiding, and phenomena are unattainable; yet phenomena are not separate from the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Now, the Tathāgata uses these directional metaphors to manifest the Dharma, so that those who are still in their ignorance may easily understand.
Therefore, if one were not to manifest [the teaching] in this way to inspire faith, upon what could the instruction of the unenlightened rely?
All methods of verbal expression rely on phenomena (*dharma*) to reveal the image; thus, for those who grasp the essential meaning alone, both the phenomenon and the image are true.

Whether through speech or silence, all accord with this state, which takes the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) as its primary lord and the other nine perfections as its companions. This is the seventh [position], in the southwest.
From "In that direction" (*fang yi xia*) down to approximately four lines of the sūtra, there are ten points therein as previously mentioned: 1. First, regarding the direction of the Buddha:
it is in the southwest, between the *shen* and *wei* palaces, which constitutes the position of *Kun*.

*Kun* represents earth, faithfulness and compliance, tranquility, the bearing of all things, the nurturing of life, and perfection. 2. Second, regarding the distance of the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).

The meaning is as explained previously. Regarding the third mention of the name and form of the world, it is called "Jewel Color" (Ratnavarṇa) to clarify that this seventh stage of faith is the accomplishment of the gate of compassion through the perfection of skillful means; thus, it relies upon this position of the Earth (Kun) to serve as its mother.
This clarifies that one constantly nurtures and gives birth [to beings] with a compassionate heart, just like a mother; therefore, one benefits people by means of the Dharma-jewel.

The world is named "Jewel Radiance" (*Ratnaprabhāsa*); it benefits sentient beings through the Dharma-jewel. This world takes radiance as its essence and accomplishes the karma of benefiting sentient beings through the Dharma-jewel.
Because one has come from that world to be born here and experience the resulting fruit, it is manifested; since the manifest karma and the manifest Dharma are both like jewels, this is so.
Fourth, regarding the citation of the Buddha’s name: the Buddha’s name is "Supreme Wisdom Radiance" (*Varajñānaprabhāsa*); this is faith.

Because he abides in the stage where the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is preeminent, governing the multitude and causing people to believe and comply, the Buddha is named "Supreme Wisdom" (*Jñānavara*).

Furthermore, because his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is perfected like an earthen image, and because he bears the burden of sentient beings and nourishes all things like the great earth, he is named "Supreme Wisdom.
Fifth, as for the naming of the foremost bodhisattvas, he is named "Foremost in Diligence" (*Vīryottama*).
To clarify that great compassion is preeminent—like a mother among the assembly who benefits sentient beings with a mind free from weariness—it is called the "Foremost of Diligence.
The rest is as before. This stage presides over the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*), while the other nine serve as its companions.
From the eighth [direction], the northwest, and below, there are four lines of scripture; within them, the ten meanings are as previously explained. To cite one example of the Buddha’s directions:
In the northwest is the hexagram Qian; Qian represents metal, firmness, and strength, and it represents the father.

Second, the meaning of the distance and proximity of the Buddha-fields is explained as before. Third, regarding the name and color of the world: its name is "Vajra" (Diamond), and its color is "Bright.
This indicates that this stage of faith is the eighth, the *pāramitā* of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), because of its great power of firm solidity; therefore, it is called "Vajra-color."
Entrusting this position of *qian* (heaven) signifies metal and firmness; furthermore, because wisdom (*jñāna*) increases and excels, the fourth [section] cites the name of the Buddha.
The Buddha’s name is Sovereign Wisdom-Light (*svatantra-jñāna-āloka*). This eighth stage of faith corresponds to the wisdom of the eighth *bhūmi*, wherein wisdom increases and becomes sovereign;
thus it takes the image of *qian* as heaven and as the father, signifying the meaning of sovereign wisdom-light.
Fifth, as for citing the names of the leading Bodhisattvas, "Dharma-Head" (Dharmottara) is named here because wisdom increases and excels at this stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*);

because he benefits sentient beings through the Dharma, he is called "Dharma-Head. Other meanings are as explained previously. This stage primarily emphasizes the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
From the ninth section below, there are approximately four lines of scripture; within them, the ten meanings are as before. First, the citation of the Buddha:
Regarding the directions: that which is below is the lowest part, the limit of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). This wind is extremely firm and dense;
even if a mighty warrior were to strike it downward with a diamond wheel (*vajra-cakra*), the diamond would shatter into fine dust while the wind-circle remains undamaged.
Because of its firm density, it is able to support the world-system. This illustrates the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

This is the ninth power: the perfection of faith. One should believe in the accomplishment of the dharma-power of the nine abodes and nine stages, teaching and transforming sentient beings while bearing the burden of all things with a mind as firm as the wind and incapable of being harmed.
Second, regarding the distance between buddha-fields, its meaning is as explained before. Third, regarding the names and colors of the worlds: their name is *vaidūrya* color; this jewel possesses...
Regarding blue, yellow, red, and white: here, among these colors, "white" refers to that which is like the clarity of water;
because the wind of spiritual brilliance (*prajñā*) can distinguish the impure, it carries the meaning of "pure white. Furthermore, it takes the wondrous wisdom of the *dharmakāya* as supreme.
Fourth, regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name: the Buddha’s name is "Brahma-Wisdom-Bright-Wisdom Wind," which carries the meaning of purity. "Brahma" (梵) is translated here as...
This stage is pure and luminous because its progressive cultivation increases in excellence; through the application of great white-purity wisdom, it benefits both oneself and others.
Fifth, as for the naming of the Bodhisattva who heads this stage, he is named Jñānaketu (Wisdom-Topknot). This clarifies that the ninth *pāramitā*, power (*bala*), is realized.

Having achieved the faith and sublime wisdom of the nine stages (*navavihāra*) and the nine grounds (*navabhūmi*), he benefits sentient beings through wisdom; thus, he is called "The Topknot. Furthermore, below...
"Square" (fang) signifies the meaning of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the meaning of tranquil stillness, and the meaning of humility; it is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

"Above" (shang) signifies the meaning of contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), because it is like the sun and moon situated in space illuminating all things. Other meanings are as previously explained.
In this stage, the primary power is the *pāramitā* of the Dharma Master. Regarding the tenth "Above," the four lines of scripture that follow may be cited here.
The ten meanings within are as previously explained. First, regarding the indication of the Buddha’s direction:

by pointing to the upper region, it clarifies that the sun, moon, and myriad stars abide in space and illuminate all phenomena, which serves as an analogy for wisdom (*jñāna*). Abiding in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) while illuminating the various faculties (*indriya*), this represents the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Second, regarding the indication of the distance of the lands: the meaning is as previously interpreted. Third, [the indication of]...

Regarding "the world as name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): it is called "equal form" (*samarūpa*) because it represents the emptiness and signlessness of the upper realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), which is the equality [of reality].
For those with faith, the mind of dharma-emptiness manifests before them; because the feeling of dharma-emptiness is present, it is therefore termed "form.
Fourth, regarding the invocation of the Buddha’s name: the name of the Buddha is "Observing Wisdom" (*vipaśyanājñāna*), which serves as the illumination above.

Just as when the sun, moon, and stars appear in the void and illuminate all phenomena below, those with clear faith perceive through wisdom that the bodies and minds of both self and others have no intrinsic nature, being like the void;

and just as reflections of light have no substantial essence, they are therefore called the Wisdom of Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). Fifth, regarding the naming of the Bodhisattvas who are the leaders: their names are—

For the sake of the Worthy Head and for the sake of Clear Illumination, these ten kinds of worlds, the names of the Buddhas, and the names of the Bodhisattvas are all the wondrous principles perceived by the wisdom of one’s own mind. What is termed "world" is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena;
what is termed "Buddha" is wisdom itself; and what is termed "Bodhisattva" is the practice enacted by that wisdom. All of these are simply following what is seen and following what is practiced.
Through the cultivation and establishment of these ten dharmas, one attains them; thus, being named "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*), one possesses the aforementioned worlds, whether distant or near.
When it says "the dust-motes of ten Buddha-fields," this clarifies that the Buddha-fields are mutually inclusive in layers, like reflections in light.
For those who are deluded, the obstacles of the mind are boundless; therefore, the dust-motes of the fields are cited as a measure of distance for the sake of awakening.
Thus, inexhaustible Buddha-fields exist within the pores of one's own body, layer upon layer like reflections;

yet, because of delusion, one says they are far away in other lands. For one who has attained awakening, the names of persons and dharmas are spoken of as coming from distant lands in other directions.

This generally clarifies that the designations of "far" and "near" are applied to the states of delusion and awakening; it is not that such distinctions exist within the Buddha-field of the Dharma-realm.
Regarding matters both distant and near, the multitude of Bodhisattvas who have come here is said to be as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields.

This refers to those with the mind of faith who are able to believe in the conduct and wisdom of Samantabhadra; according to their faculties and desires, they engage in inexhaustible and ever-receding Bodhisattva practices that pervade all lands to teach and transform sentient beings, thereby completing this number. Having already attained such faith, their bodies are determined to be capable of acting accordingly.
Because of these practices and for this reason, the fact that Bodhisattvas in the ten directions each cite as many [Buddhas] as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields is precisely this meaning.
It clarifies that the practice of each and every Bodhisattva is inexhaustible and repeatedly fills all lands to teach and transform sentient beings;
thus it should be known and thus it should be believed and understood. This concludes the response to the previous section on "Adornment."
[They] adorn the Buddha-nature, the Buddha-fields, the Buddha-abodes, the Buddha-fields, and so forth.

[Sūtra]: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas and spoke these words: "These bodhisattvas are truly rare! O Sons of the Buddha!"

The buddha-fields are inconceivable; the Buddhas’ dwelling, the adornment of the buddha-fields, the dharma-nature of the buddha-fields, the purity of the buddha-fields, the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma, the appearance of the Buddhas, and the Buddhas’ attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are all inconceivable.
Why is this? O Sons of the Buddha, because all Buddhas in all worlds of the ten directions know all things.
Sentient beings have diverse inclinations and desires; according to what is appropriate for each, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to subdue them.

In this manner, extending even to the limits of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, O sons of the Buddha, within this Sahā world and its four continents, the Tathāgata manifests various bodies, various names, various physical forms, various heights and statures, various lifespans, and various locations.
O Sons of the Buddha, through various faculties, various places of birth, various verbal activities, and various observations,
the Tathāgata causes all sentient beings to each individually know and see him;
within these four continents, he may be named Sarvārthasiddha, or Pūrṇacandra, or Siṃhanāda, or Śākyamuni, or...
The seventh sage may see Vairocana, or he may be named Gautama, or named the Great Śramaṇa, or named the Most Victorious, or named the Guide;
such names as these number ten thousand. He causes all sentient beings to individually know and see him.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the east of this four-continent world system, there is another world named Well-Protected Tathāgata.
In that realm, there are ten thousand such names— some called Vajra, some called Īśvara,
some called Prajñāvat, some called Durjaya, some called Megharāja, some called Araṇa, some called Adhipati,
some called Hṛṣṭacitta, some called Asama, and some called Vādachedaka— and they cause all sentient beings to perceive them individually.
"Know, O sons of the Buddha, that to the south of these four continents, there is a world named Durdharṣa.

There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: sometimes he is called Śakra, sometimes Ratnayaśas, sometimes Vimala, sometimes Satyavādin, sometimes Vinetṛ, sometimes Prāmodyasampanna, sometimes Mahāyaśas, sometimes Hitakara, or..."
"Boundless," or "Supreme," and so forth—ten thousand such names cause all sentient beings to perceive and know each of the Buddhas individually.
Sons of the Buddha, to the west of this four-continent world system, there is another world named *Priyabuddhi*.
There, the Tathāgata is known as *Varuṇadeva*, or *Priyadarśana*, or *Vijayendra*, or *Vinītadeva*, and so on.
He is named True Wisdom, or Ultimate Attainment, or Joy, or Dharma-Wisdom, or One Who Has Accomplished What Was to Be Done, or Well-Abiding;
such names as these number ten thousand. He causes all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the north of this four-continent world system, there is a world named Possessing Lions, where the Tathāgata resides.
There, he was known by such names as Mahāmuni, Tapasvin, Lokapūjita, Uttamakeda, Sarvajña, Sumati, Viśuddha, Elāpattra, Anuttaradāna, and Taponiṣpanna;
these and others numbered ten thousand, and they caused all the multitudes [to rejoice].
O sons of the Buddha, each of you should individually know and see this: to the northeast of these four continents, there is a world named *Vipaśyana* (Wondrous Observation).

There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: some call him *Māradamana* (Subduer of Māra), some call him *Siddhi* (Accomplishment), some call him *Vyupaśama* (Cessation), some call him *Bhadradeva* (Worthy Deva), some call him *Vītarāga* (Free from Greed), some call him *Jñānavara* (Excellent Wisdom), some call him *Samacitta* (Equal Mind), and some call him *An...* [the text is incomplete].
He is named Victorious, or Wisdom Sound, or Hard to Appear, and so forth; ten thousand such names cause all sentient beings to each individually know and see him.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the southeast of this four-continent world system, there is another world named Joyful Delight.
There, the Tathāgata is named Utmost Majestic, or Mass of Radiance, or...

He is named Universal Knowledge, or Secret, or Liberation, or Abiding in Nature, or Practicing According to the Dharma, or King of the Pure Eye, or Great Valor, or Power of Diligence; such names as these number ten thousand.
He causes all sentient beings to individually know and see him. O Sons of the Buddha, this is in the southwest of these four continents.
Next, there is a world named Suṣaṃhata; there the Tathāgata is called either Sthita, or Jñānarāja, or Paripūrṇa, or Acala, or Sunetra, or Śikhararāja,
or Vaśitāghoṣa, or Sarvadada, or Dhṛtarsabha, or Vijayameru, and so forth.
There are ten thousand such [worlds], causing all sentient beings to individually know and see them.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the northwest of these four continents, there is another world named *Sudharmā*. There, the Tathāgata is known by various names:
sometimes he is called *Samantagata*, sometimes *Arciṣmat*, sometimes *Maṇicūḍa*, sometimes *Smaraṇīya*, sometimes *Anuttarārtha*, and sometimes *Nitya*.

He who is named Joyful Delight, or Purity of Nature, or Perfect Radiance, or Long Arms, or Abiding in the Source—there are ten thousand such names—and he causes all sentient beings to perceive and know him individually.
O Sons of the Buddha, beneath this four-continent world, in the direction below, there is a world named Flame-Wisdom; there, the Tathāgata is named Accumulation of Virtue.
The faculties are also called the Lion’s Mark, or Sharp Wisdom, or Golden Radiance, or All-Knowing,
or Ultimate Sound, or Benefactor, or Reaching the Culmination, or True Deva, or Universal Excellence;
such names as these number ten thousand, causing each and every sentient being to perceive them individually.
Sons of the Buddha, know that from this four-continent world system, proceeding upward, there is a world named Dharanimati.

There, the Tathāgata is known by various names: sometimes as Prajñāvat, sometimes as Viśuddhavadana, sometimes as Bodhimati, sometimes as Agraja, sometimes as Carya-vyūha, sometimes as Prāmodyasamudgata, sometimes as Manasparipūrṇa, and sometimes as Samṛddha.
Fire may be called "observing the precepts" or "the single path," and so forth; such names number in the tens of thousands, causing all sentient beings to each individually know and see them.

O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world there are ten billion sets of four continents, and within these there are hundreds of billions of various names for the Tathāgatas, causing all sentient beings to each individually know and see the Buddhas.
Son, to the east of this Sahā world, there is another world named Guhyaviniścaya.
There, the Tathāgata is called either Samatā, or Viśeṣa, or Āśvāsana, or Arthāvabodha-mati,
or Śrutajñāna, or Satyavākya, or Vaśitāprāpta, or Uttamadeha, or Mahāvikrama.
Some call him the Wisdom Equal to None; there are hundreds of billions of such various names and epithets by which all sentient beings individually know and see [the Buddha].
O Sons of the Buddha, to the south of this Sahā world, there is another world called Abundant Overflow.
There, the Tathāgata is called Original Nature, or Diligent Mind, or Unsurpassed Honored One, or Great.
Jñānolkā (Wisdom Torch), also known as Anāśrita (Without Support), or Prabhāgarbha (Treasury of Light), or Prajñāgarbha (Treasury of Wisdom), or Puṇyagarbha (Treasury of Merit),
or Devātideva (God of Gods), or Maheśvara (Great Sovereign)— by means of these and billions of other such various names,
he causes all sentient beings to individually know and see him. O Sons of the Buddha, next to the west of this Sahā world...
There is a world named Vimala (Stainless), where the Tathāgata is known as Manomaya (Mind-made), or Jñānagati (Gone by Knowledge), or Mūlasthita (Abiding in the Root),

or Bandhanamocaka (Liberator from Bonds), or Arthaprativedha (Penetrating Meaning), or Priyavikalpa (Delighting in Discernment), or Varadarśana (Supreme Vision), or Vinayacaryā (Conduct of Discipline),
or Bahuduḥkhacaryā (Practice of Many Sufferings), or Balasampanna (Endowed with Power). As it is there, so it is elsewhere.
These hundreds of billions of various names cause all sentient beings to each individually know and see [the Buddha].
O sons of the Buddha, to the north of this Sahā world, there is another world called Abhirati (Abundant Joy).
There, the Tathāgata is known by such names as Campaka-flower-colored, or Sun-treasury, or Well-abiding, or Manifesting Supernatural Powers, or Nature.
Transcendent One— sometimes named Sun of Wisdom, sometimes named Unobstructed, sometimes named Manifestation like the Moon,
sometimes named Swift Wind, or sometimes named Pure Body— by means of such hundreds of billions of various names,
he causes all sentient beings to know and see each of the Buddhas individually. Sons of the Buddha, to the northeast of this Sahā world, there is another world named...
He grasps the hundred [names] of the Tathāgata in that regard—

whether they be called "Permanently Free from Suffering," "Universally Liberated," "Great Treasure Trove," "Wisdom of Liberation," "Treasury of the Past," "Jewel Radiance," "Transcending the World," "Unobstructed Ground," "Treasury of Pure Faith," or "Immovable Mind"— and so forth.
"O Sons of the Buddha, by means of hundreds of millions of various names, I cause all sentient beings to know and see each of the Buddhas individually.
To the southeast of this Sahā world, there is another world called Ānanda (Beneficial).

There, the Tathāgata is named Prabhāsvara (Manifesting Light), or Samantajñāna (Exhaustive Wisdom), or Manojña-ghoṣa (Beautiful Voice), or Uttama-indriya (Supreme Faculty), or Vyūha-vitāna (Adorned Canopy)."
It is called the Faculty of Diligence, or Reaching the Further Shore of Discernment, or Supreme Concentration, or Discerning Speech, or the Ocean of Wisdom;
by such hundreds of billions of various names, it causes all sentient beings to each individually know and see [the Buddha].
O Sons of the Buddha, to the southwest of this Sahā world, there is another world named...
Rarely does a Tathāgata appear there, whether named Munīndra, or Sarvaratnavat, or Lokavimukti,
or Samantajñānamūla, or Varavākya, or Vibhaktadarśin, or Indravasitā, or Maharṣiśāstṛ, or Karmapradarśaka, or Vajrasimha, or any such [name].
O sons of the Buddha, by means of billions of various names, I cause all sentient beings to know and see each of the Buddhas individually.
To the northwest of this Sahā world, there is another world named *Ānanda* (Joy).

There, the Tathāgata is called *Puṣpasaṃcaya* (Cluster of Wondrous Flowers), or *Candanacchattra* (Sandalwood Canopy), or *Padmagarbha* (Lotus Treasury), or *Sarvadharmasamatikrānta* (Transcending All Dharmas), or...
It is named Dharma-Jewel, or Rebirth, or Pure and Sublime Canopy, or Vast Eye, or Possessing Wholesome Dharmas, or Solemn Mindfulness of the Dharma, or Net-Treasury;
by such hundreds of billions of various names, it causes all sentient beings to individually know and see [it]. O Sons of the Buddha, next below this Sahā world...
In a world-system named Guanyue (Gate-Pillar), the Tathāgata there is known by various names: sometimes he is called Initiating Flame,
sometimes Subduing Poison, sometimes Śakra’s Bow, sometimes Abode of Impermanence, sometimes Awakening to the Source,
sometimes Severing Growth, sometimes Great Swift Speed, sometimes Constant Joyful Giving, sometimes Discerning the Path, or sometimes Destroyer.
Prostrating to these and hundreds of billions of other such various names, may all sentient beings individually know and see them.
O sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world, immediately above, there is a world named Vibration-Sound (Jinyin).
There, the Tathāgata is called either Courageous Banner (Yongmengdang), or Immeasurable Jewel (Wuliangbao), or Delight in Great Giving (Le dashi), or Celestial (Tian).
The Light is also named Auspicious Arising, or Transcending Boundaries, or Lord of All, or Non-retrogressive Wheel, or Free from All Evils, or Omniscience;
there are billions of such various names, causing all sentient beings to each individually know and see them.
O Sons of the Buddha, as it is in this Sahā world, so it is in the eastern direction.
In hundreds of thousands of billions of countless, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable,
and unspeakable worlds throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, the names of the Tathāgatas are various and different;
it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, just as it was in the past, O World-Honored One.
When he was a bodhisattva, he brought beings to maturity through various discourses, various languages, various sounds, various karmas,
various retributions, various places, various skillful means, various faculties, various inclinations, and various stages;
he also taught the Dharma so that sentient beings might gain such knowledge and vision.
[Treatise] Fourth: From the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī... down to the end of the chapter, this section clarifies the division on the Exposition of the Dharma.
Within this division, the meaning is further divided into seven parts: first, from "Mañjuśrī" down to two lines of scripture, which clarifies Mañjuśrī’s observation of the assembly;
second, from "O Sons of the Buddha" down to three lines of scripture, which clarifies the praise...

3. "The four kinds of Buddha-fields are inconceivable. Why is this? The following two and a half lines of scripture clarify how the Buddhas establish the Dharma according to the faculties [of beings] to subdue them.

4. "O Sons of the Buddha," the following three and a half lines of scripture cite the Buddha’s bodily activities—such as name, form, appearance, and the length of his lifespan—as the methods for transforming the multitudes according to their faculties.
"Because they have been born," [it is said]. Below this, the names of the Buddhas are enumerated. First, the names of the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*) in this world-system are mentioned;
next, those of the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*); and finally, those that pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*. These names differ:

first ten thousand are cited, then gradually increasing until they reach an immeasurable number. "Ten thousand" is the primary unit of enumeration, intended ultimately to clarify the names of the Buddhas.
6. Because it universally encompasses all names, it causes all sentient beings to understand that all names are equal, pure, and free from discrimination between the good and the bad;

thus, from this point down to the end of the chapter—specifically the four lines of sutra beginning with "O sons of the Buddha"—this serves as a general conclusion for both this world and other directions. 7. Thus, O World-Honored One... [and so on].
The final three and a half lines of the sutra cite the causes practiced by the World-Honored One in the past, which he now expounds for the sake of the assembly.
This concludes the response to the four types of Buddha-fields and their pervasive names among the twenty-eight preceding questions.
Hereafter, in the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths, it clarifies how the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
This Dharma gate does not depart from the meaning of the Four Noble Truths;

furthermore, this "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata" does not merely discuss the pervasiveness of the names, but rather indicates that the Tathāgata’s actions of body, speech, and mind are all entirely pervasive.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva summarizes this point concisely, as stated previously in the text: "O sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, in the Sahā world..."
The various bodies, names, colors, and marks of all the four continents in the world systems are explained at length as in the sutra;
this clarifies that this chapter provides a comprehensive answer regarding how the Tathāgata’s activities of body, speech, and mind are entirely pervasive.

From this point in the text, Mañjuśrī raises the question of how the ocean-like fruition of the Buddha’s body, speech, and so forth is universally pervasive, in order to cause [the assembly] to realize it.
The assembly, having gained confidence in their own bodies as being identical to the three karmas of the Buddha, enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s nature and equal the wisdom of the Tathāgata;

from setting out and advancing through the practice of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage, up until the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter, this constitutes one complete cycle of cause and effect. This "Chapter on the Names" marks the very beginning of that initial entry.
The fact that the name is pervasive and all-encompassing means that all names are, in their totality, the manifestation of the fruit of one’s own Buddhahood;
for this is the fruit of having fulfilled the practice of one’s own self-cultivation.

Thus, the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to drench the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, causing him to inquire about the Dharma of the manifested fruit, and emits light from his mouth to drench the mouth of Samantabhadra.

By causing [the Buddha] to speak of the virtues of the fruit of Buddhahood, the cause and effect of one's own practice are first clearly elucidated; thus, the wondrous practices of wisdom and principle of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are shown to be identical in essence.

Although the "Chapter on Leaving the World" and the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm" appear later, because they are arranged according to the characteristics of the written text, they seem to have a sequence of before and after;
yet in reality, all of them are mutually interpenetrating and thoroughly pervasive throughout the Dharma. Therefore, they are all one and the same.
Because it is the single, perfected Dharma, as in the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, this one section of the sutra constitutes its great essence;

it is the fundamental source of all ordinary beings and sages. In the first assembly, faith in the Buddha-fruit was established by taking the Tathāgata and Samantabhadra as the primary figures, thereby clarifying faith in the fruit already attained as a Buddha and the fruit already practiced. Now, through entry...

Entering the gate of faith and practice for oneself consists precisely of taking the name of Mañjuśrī, the name of the Tathāgata, and the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths as the causes and effects of what is to be believed; this clarifies that one practices and studies by means of the Dharma-gate of wondrous wisdom and through names and phrases.
Question: For what reason does the Tathāgata not himself proclaim his own teaching? What is the purpose of delegating [this task]?

The Light-Commander Bodhisattva replied: "The Tathāgata’s intention was to have a bodhisattva of the corresponding stage speak the dharma-gate of that same stage, so that those who practice and study may understand the respective limits and find it easy to comprehend.
Mañjuśrī constantly acts as the cause for the faith of all Buddhas and all sentient beings, becoming the fundamental mother of wondrous wisdom; Samantabhadra..."
Sā always acts as the cause for all Buddhas and sentient beings to practice;
through these two persons, they achieve the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*) and the ocean of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samudra*).

Let these two persons question one another to explain the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," clarifying the beginning and end of the causes and effects of this practitioner, and the perfection of its preceding and succeeding conditions.

Because the nature of the fruit, the wisdom of the fruit, the practice of the fruit, and the characteristics of the fruit are thoroughly one in essence, it is clarified that from this chapter through to the "Chapter on Manifestation," the two practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—the cause and fruit of faith—reach the fulfillment of the stage of cultivation such that essence and function are thoroughly integrated.
This is so that future learners may easily understand them; thus, as there are two chapters where the Tathāgata himself has already spoken previously.
The exposition concludes; these two delusions regarding the fruit of Buddhahood are clarified only upon reaching Buddhahood.

[Commentary] Within this chapter, the meaning is divided into three parts: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the chapter...

Regarding the intent of the introduction, there are three parts; first, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. As for the explanation of the title of the chapter: *satya* (truth) means the sense of reality.
It clarifies that the Tathāgata has taught four kinds of real meanings so as to inspire faith and understanding in all sentient beings.
Question: Why are more than these not taught, but only four? Answer: Because these four types of truths encompass all [others]; this is taught for the sake of clarity.
All that pertains to the mundane world does not transcend suffering and its accumulation; all that pertains to the supramundane does not transcend cessation and the path.
The total exhaustion of all sufferings is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); the total exhaustion of *nirvāṇa* is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

While the *nirvāṇa* of the three vehicles can all be attained, this Great *Nirvāṇa* has nothing further remaining to be attained, and thus it is called the Truth of the Path. Because the two vehicles proceed [toward their respective goals]...
The Bodhisattva Jì (Śāntideva) states that bodhisattvas are mostly born in pure lands (*śuddhāvāsakṣetra*), yet he further suggests that these pure lands exist elsewhere in other directions.

He also says that because bodhisattvas intentionally retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten their rebirths, if they did not intentionally retain these afflictions, they would necessarily attain the realization of *nirvāṇa* or be born in a pure land in another direction. Therefore, the *nirvāṇa* of the three vehicles is all attainable. Furthermore, [he says]:
The Buddha who attained perfect enlightenment under a wooden tree on a grass seat in Jambudvīpa is an *nirmāṇa*-buddha;

the Buddha atop a red lotus in the Akaniṣṭha heaven above is a *vipāka*-buddha. Because both involve the feelings of aversion and aspiration, the Three Vehicles speak of the Four Noble Truths—aversion toward suffering and its origin, and aspiration for cessation and the path—calling this the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths. This One Vehicle sutra speaks of four [truths].
The Noble Truths are their ultimate reality. Why is this? Because one realizes the true nature of suffering and is thus free from longing or aversion;

because there is no other direction, no separate Buddha-field, and no distinct pure land; and because there is no path of cultivation involving longing or aversion toward saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, defilement, or purity.
As for the path of cultivation, it is to abide in accordance with the Dharma and to practice the path in accordance with the Dharma.
Free from aversion, non-attachment, non-delight, and non-grasping— just as the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has no nature of coming or going and no nature of abiding,
so too do the body, the pores of the skin, the mind, and all objects accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). To have such faith and understanding and to cultivate the path in this manner—
for this reason, the One Vehicle and the Four Noble Truths, and the Three Vehicles and the Four Truths, each have their respective distinctions.

There are those with faith and understanding who recognize that the Tathāgata’s establishment of teachings based on the faculties [of beings] and skillful means is not something that ordinary persons can formulate.
Just as practitioners today simply act according to the power of their own faith and understanding within their respective positions, this cannot be generalized as a fixed rule.

For example, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the sake of śrāvakas and the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for the sake of pratyekabuddhas.
To explain the six *pāramitās* for the sake of the bodhisattvas is likewise the Tathāgata’s teaching according to the occasion.

As stated in the "Ten Stages" chapter of this sutra: a bodhisattva on the fifth stage practices ten kinds of contemplation on the truths (*satya-darśana*), taking the four noble truths as their essence;

a bodhisattva on the sixth stage practices ten kinds of contemplation on the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). This is the Tathāgata’s progressive teaching according to the respective stages.

Regarding the essential points of the method of cultivation, it is said in summary that these Four Noble Truths and the Dharma-gate of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are such that all noble ones and all ordinary beings who give rise to a mind of faith and joy toward the Buddha-Dharma, yet whose path is not yet perfected, all— from their initial aspiration—
contemplate the suffering of themselves and others; thus they resolve upon Bodhicitta and joyfully seek the methods of the Path, relying solely on the Great and Small Vehicles.

Although the superior and inferior [teachings] differ, with the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination being distinct, the meaning of the Four Truths encompasses all mundane phenomena without exception.

This is because the Tathāgata’s verbal activity in preaching the Dharma is all-pervasive; thus, the reason the *Sūtra of the Necklace* (Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-nirdeśa) establishes the ninefold vehicle (*navayāna*) dharma-gates is to clarify that the three vehicles are used in combination, with the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination each [having its specific application].
Regarding the nine vehicles that attain the distinctions of the Way: first, the Śrāvaka-vehicle; second, the Śrāvaka-Pratyekabuddha-vehicle;

and third, the Śrāvaka-Bodhisattva-vehicle. These three vehicles alike contemplate the Four Noble Truths and the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, yet each attains the Way differently.
Within these three vehicles, there are respectively three types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which together constitute the nine supernormal powers.

In this inconceivable vehicle of the Dharma-realm, there are ten vehicles in total within the path of liberation, all of which attain the ultimate end and are free from the sufferings of the three realms.
All other gateways to the paths are merely the phenomena of birth and death belonging to the mundane world of humans and devas;
even if one attains a small measure of happiness therein, one ultimately does not escape the root of suffering. Although the Three Vehicles do emerge from the three realms, their paths—
Since this has not yet reached the true and ultimate fruit of the Buddha-vehicle, there are two explanations for the purpose of this chapter’s arrival.

First, to clarify that while the preceding "Chapter on Names and Titles" explains how the Tathāgata’s bodily karma manifests different names and titles according to various regions, this chapter explains how the Tathāgata’s vocal karma manifests the teaching of the Dharma according to various regions without departing from the Four Noble Truths; therefore, this chapter must follow.
Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: within this chapter of the sūtra, there are twelve sections in total.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha..."

The Noble Truth of Suffering is, in this Sahā world, called "sin," or "affliction," or "transformation," or "conditioning," or "accumulation," or "thorn," or "dependence on the faculties," or "deception," or "the seat of an ulcer," or "the conduct of fools.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering is, in this Sahā world—

Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha, this Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is in this world of Vaśavartin sometimes called "bondage," sometimes "destruction," sometimes "the meaning of attachment," sometimes "deluded conceptualization," sometimes "entering," sometimes "certainty," sometimes "a net," sometimes "proliferation," sometimes "concomitance," and sometimes "the root of inversion.
In this world of Vaśavartin, it is also called "non-contention."

It is called "freedom from dust," "tranquility," "signlessness," "non-perishing," "absence of self-nature," "unobstructedness," "cessation," "the reality of essence," or "abiding in its own nature. O Sons of the Buddha,
in this Sahā world, the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering is called the "One Vehicle" or "the Goal."

"Quiescence," or "Guidance," or "Ultimate Non-discrimination," or "Equanimity," or "Laying Down the Burden," or "Having No Destination," or "Conforming to the Noble Intent," or "The Practice of the Rishis," or "The Ten Treasuries"— O Sons of the Buddhas,
in this Sahā world, the Four Noble Truths are taught in these and other such ways numbering four hundred billion and ten thousand.
O Sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of Suffering in this Sahā world is,
in the world-system called Guhyavākya, known as the Root of Seeking,
or Non-Transcendence, or the Basis of Bondage, or Doing What Should Not Be Done, or Universal Quarreling, or Analysis.
They are all called "powerless," or "basis of action," or "extreme suffering," or "agitation," or "shaped objects.
O Sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering is, in the world-system of Guhyadēśanā,
called "conforming to birth-and-death," or "attachment," or "burning," or "transmigration," or "the root of decay."
It is called "the continuity of all existences," or "evil conduct," or "attachment," or "the source of illness," or "the enumeration of parts.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is, in the world-system of Guhyadṛśa,
called "the Ultimate Truth," or "liberation," or "praiseworthy," or "peaceful," or "the excellent entrance."
It is called "Subduer," or "A Portion," or "Blameless," or "Free from Greed," or "Certainty.
What the Sons of the Buddha call the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering is, in the world-system of Guhyadṛśa,
called "Fierce General," or "Superior Practice," or "Transcendence," or "Skillful Means," or "Equal Eye," or...
"Free from extremes," "thoroughly awakened," "grasping," "supreme eye," or "observing the directions"—

these and other such four hundred billion ten-thousand names for the Four Noble Truths are taught by the Buddhas' sons in the world of Guhyadṛśa (Secret Vision) to tame all sentient beings according to their respective minds.
O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world, that which is called the Noble Truth of Suffering..."

"Truths" (satya), O Sons of the Buddha, refers to what is called "terror," or "fragmentation," or "that which is loathsome," or "that which must be attended to," or "transformation," or "invoking enmity," or "that which can deceive and seize," or "difficult to deal with," or "false discrimination," or "possessing power" within that most excellent world. Thus it is said.
O sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering is, in that most excellent world,
