Chapter Nine:
The Section on Radiant Awakening.
[Treatise] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, explaining the title of the chapter; second, explaining the purpose for which the chapter appears;
and third, explaining the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the explanation of the title: This chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment" (*Guangming jue pin*).
It is so named because it clarifies the cause [of enlightenment], wherein the Tathāgata emits light from beneath his feet—within the ten faiths—to illuminate the ten directions. First...
It is said that from one trichiliocosm, they increase sequentially through thirteen trichiliocosms until reaching the ineffable dharma-realm and space-realm;
this is to clarify inexhaustibility, so that those with faith may understand that the mind-ground is vast,
inexhaustible, and unobstructed, equal to the dharma-realm and space-realm, thereby clarifying the wisdom of their own *dharmakāya*.
Because their bodies, vows, and practices are also equal, they awaken the mind of faith through the illumination of light and cause it to engage in cultivation.

For this reason, it is called the "Chapter on the Practice of Radiant Awakening. When each practitioner follows the light to contemplate and observe the ten directions, the observing mind itself is exhausted;
thus, they become one in essence with the Dharma-body and enter the initial stage of the Ten Abidings.

Those with faith should, one by one, contemplate the inner mind and the spatial dimensions according to the light of these clouds of jewel-colored lamps, causing the mind and its objects to be entirely without interior, exterior, or middle;
only then can they enter the Samādhi of Expedient Means and enter the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes.
If one does not perform this contemplation of the radiance of jewel colors, one will not accomplish the ocean of all Samantabhadra’s vows.
The divine powers, supernatural faculties, and the great functions of all Buddhas are entirely non-dual. Regarding the intent of this second chapter, "Explanation":
within this second assembly, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, the ten stages of faith are taught to clarify how ordinary beings realize the Buddha-fruit through their own minds.
This follows from the previous "Chapter on the Names and Titles of the Tathāgatas," which raised the subject by citing the eyes, ears, nose, and other faculties of the Buddha’s body.
The tongue and so forth, as well as the names and titles, pervade throughout the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths, clarifying the Tathāgata’s vocal karma and his practice of preaching the Dharma.
This practice of universal pervasiveness collectively clarifies the universal nature of the Buddha-fruit.

It causes this chapter to radiate the light of the Tathāgata’s teachings and practices for those at the stage of faith, awakening all beings and causing those with faith to have self-confidence, such that their own minds realize the realm of wisdom and their physical conduct becomes manifest.
Pervading everywhere refers to the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom in all places, Mañjuśrī in all places, and the ten Bodhisattvas such as Saṃcodana, Sāradvatīputra, and Vasumitra in all places;

this clarifies that for one who possesses faith, the names of their own physical, verbal, and mental activities pervade everywhere just as the Buddha does. Therefore, this chapter must be presented here to clarify this point.
The ten Wisdom Buddhas above, beginning with Akṣobhya-jñāna Buddha, are the fruits of faith within one’s own mind;
they are one’s own wisdom, fundamentally identical to that of the Buddhas. Mañjuśrī is the wisdom of the sublime principle of one’s own mind.
The remaining nine are practice. The ten colored worlds are the phenomena perceived. (3) Explanation according to the text.
Regarding the meaning: [Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from the wheels on the soles of his two feet, illuminating this trichiliocosm—
ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Pūrvavidehas, ten billion Aparagoyānīs, and ten billion Uttarakurus.
There are ten billion oceans of Uttarakuru, ten billion Cakravāḍa mountain ranges, ten billion bodhisattvas taking birth,
ten billion bodhisattvas leaving the household life, ten billion Tathāgatas attaining perfect enlightenment, ten billion Tathāgatas turning the wheel of Dharma,
ten billion Tathāgatas entering parinirvāṇa, ten billion Sumeru kings of mountains, ten billion assemblies of the Four Heavenly Kings, and ten billion [assemblies of] devas.
The thirty-three heavens, ten billion Yāma heavens, ten billion Tuṣita heavens, ten billion Nirmāṇarati heavens,
ten billion Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, ten billion Brahmakāyika heavens, ten billion Ābhāsvara heavens, ten billion Śubhakṛtsna heavens,

In this place, one sees the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury,
surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; likewise, in each of the ten billion Jambudvīpas,

ten billion Tathāgatas are also seated in this manner, all through the spiritual power of the Buddha, with a great Bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by [their own retinue].
Accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, they came together to the place where the Buddha was.

Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bodhiśrī Bodhisattva, Dhanaśrī Bodhisattva, Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva, Guṇaśrī Bodhisattva, Netraśrī Bodhisattva, Vīryaśrī Bodhisattva, Dharmaśrī Bodhisattva, Jñānaśrī Bodhisattva, and Bhadraśrī Bodhisattva.
"Sā" refers to the lands from which these bodhisattvas have come: namely, the Golden World, the World of Sublime Color, the Lotus-Color World,
the Campaka-Flower-Color World, the Utpala-Flower-Color World, the Gold-Color World, the Jewel-Color World,
the Vajra-Color World, the Crystal-Color World, and the World of Equal Color.
These bodhisattvas each cultivated the pure conduct of brahmacarya in the presence of various Buddhas, namely:

Buddha Immovable Wisdom, Buddha Unobstructed Wisdom, Buddha Wisdom of Liberation, Buddha Wisdom of Dignified Conduct, Buddha Wisdom of Radiant Marks, Buddha Ultimate Wisdom, Buddha Supreme Wisdom, Buddha Sovereign Wisdom, Buddha Brahma Wisdom, and Buddha Observing Wisdom. At that time, Mañjuśrī was present in all these places.
The Bodhisattvas, headed by Mañjuśrī, each simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of the Buddha.

[Treatise] From the initial passage "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, there are twenty-four and a half lines of scripture. Within this, the major significance is divided into five parts:
first, identifying the source from which the light emanates; second, identifying the distance and range of the realms illuminated by the light.

1. First, regarding the source from which the light emerges: the Sūtra states, "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from beneath the wheels on his two feet. 2. Third, all the assemblies of ten billion bodhisattvas gathered together from every location.

4. Fourth, in every buddha-field, the Buddhas of Fundamental Wisdom appeared. 5. Fifth, in every location, Mañjuśrī simultaneously uttered verses with one voice. 1. First, regarding the source from which the light emerges:
the Sūtra states, "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from beneath the wheels on his two feet."
This light is that which the Tathāgata emitted from between his eyebrows during the first assembly,
named "The Universal Illumination of the Treasury of the Ten Directions through the Wisdom-Light of All Bodhisattvas. This light serves to teach and transform the bodhisattvas of the ten directions,

establishing them in the sequence of the Dharma-gates of the ten stages of faith and the five positions and ten bhūmis, so that they may progress according to their respective stages and cause their wisdom to blossom.
The eye accomplishes an immeasurable ocean of merit and wisdom; therefore, it is named the "Treasury Illuminating the Ten Directions.

Furthermore, "treasury" (garbha) has two meanings: first, because the roots of goodness of sentient beings are capable of receiving this Dharma, it is called a treasury—just as Mañjuśrī praised Sudhana, saying, "Excellent, O Treasury of Merit, that you have come to my presence!"
The two great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom of the Dharmakāya are collectively termed the "Treasury" (garbha).

This radiance constantly illuminates the Dharma-realm of the ten directions for those sentient beings possessing roots of goodness, enabling them to accomplish the great Bodhicitta and the treasury that benefits sentient beings through great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom; such is the light emitted from the wheels on the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet.

It is explained that after the light from between the eyebrows in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" had already illuminated the ten directions, that light returned and entered beneath the Buddha’s feet.
This was because he wished to employ the fruit-light of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to bring the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) to completion;
therefore, in this chapter, he again emits that same light which had previously entered beneath the Tathāgata’s feet during the first assembly.
The accomplishment of the ten faiths is like the light emitted from the wheels beneath the feet of the Tathāgata; this is because it is the light entered within the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs.
Thus, the emission of light from beneath the feet clarifies that the initial stage of faith is accomplished through the fruit.
Just as in the stage of the ten abodes, the emission of light from the tips of the Tathāgata’s toes clarifies the beginning of the departure toward entry into the holy state.
Because it marks the beginning of the stage of the Arhat (Yijing’s *Yingzhen*), it is the birthplace of the great wisdom of all Buddhas.

Thus, in the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), light is emitted from the tops of the feet; in the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), light is emitted from the knees; and in the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), light is emitted from between the eyebrows.
Ending and then beginning again, one returns to the original fruit: first using the fruit to establish the cause, and through the cultivation of the cause, attaining the fruit.
The essence reaches its ultimate, the function is perfected, and the position is at its peak; from beginning to end, it does not shift, yet the supreme state becomes even more manifest.

Now, light is emitted from the two wheels on the soles of the feet because the fruit establishes faith; thus, throughout the course of cultivation, one constantly cultivates the essence of the fruit so that its habitual practice may reach maturity.
In this way, light is emitted from between the eyebrows and from the wheels beneath the feet.
Light is emitted from the tips of the fingers, light is emitted from the tops of the feet, light is emitted from the knees, and light is emitted from between the eyebrows.
In the "Chapter on Manifestation," it further states that light is emitted from between the eyebrows, named the "Tathāgata’s Light of Manifestation.

These six instances of emitting light collectively clarify the accomplishment of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*). Thus, there are eleven [stages].
The practice of cultivation according to the Dharma-gate of the Causes and Effects of the Grounds (Bhūmi) concludes here; therefore, the Dharmadhātu Chapter follows.

Furthermore, the emission of light from between the eyebrows signifies that this entire section of the sutra—comprising the cultivation through the five stages of a Bodhisattva and the fundamental Dharma realized upon the appearance of a Tathāgata—has the total Dharmadhātu as its essence. Thus, it clarifies that the single chapter on the Dharmadhātu represents the past and present.
Because it is the beginning and end of all future Buddhas; because it is the eternal Dharma; because it is the constant Way of the Dharma, which is inconceivable;
because it is the beginning and end of all sentient beings; and because it is the fundamental essence of all dharmas.
Second, regarding the illumination of the distant and the near by light: first, it illuminates the realm of the trichiliocosm; next, it illuminates the ten [directions].
From one hundred thousand up to ten billion, even to the unspeakably many. Question: Why is it that they do not illuminate all at once, but rather proceed through a gradual sequence?
Answer: Although it occurs within a single moment, it is presented as a gradual sequence because within the *dharmadhātu* there is no before or after.
This gradual sequence exists for the sake of cultivating superior progress and increasing excellence within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Third, [it is shown] in all places.
1. That ten billion assemblies of bodhisattvas gather together simultaneously clarifies that one’s own faith and practice are all-pervasive. 2.

The mention of the Buddha-worlds in all places and the Tathāgatas of the Ten Wisdoms clarifies that for one who possesses faith, the fruits of their own wisdom and virtue are all-pervasive. 3. That Mañjuśrī speaks verses simultaneously in all places clarifies...
Regarding those with faith, their own wondrous wisdom explains that the Dharma is all-pervasive, universally clarifying that it is inherently one's own and not a phenomenon from another.

From the very beginning, they have such self-confidence; thus, the ten-colored worlds, the ten wisdom Tathāgatas, and the ten-headed Bodhisattvas are all one’s own fruition-practices and the great wisdom of the pervasive nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because faith is established through these myriad practices being all-pervasive, from this point onward—
The practice throughout the five stages does not depart from this. Therefore, the initial resolve and the ultimate consummation are not two different things;
such an initial resolve is more difficult than any prior resolve. Because one first seeks to deliver others before having delivered oneself, I pay homage to the initial resolve.
This initial resolve makes one a teacher of devas and humans, surpassing both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, just as described in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
The *Bàn jīng* (P’an-jing) states that it is difficult for those who proceed from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to enter the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).

This is because ordinary beings generally identify themselves as such and are unwilling to recognize their own mind as the immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*). Therefore, it is difficult to enter the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*).

Once the ten stages of faith are perfected, one spontaneously reaches the first stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), namely, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), and continues until the ultimate realization.

Because it culminates in the fruit of Buddhahood—just as in the Three Vehicles one cultivates the ten minds of faith over ten thousand kalpas—in this teaching, the Dharma-realm of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is taken as the essence of the teaching.
Consequently, one attains realization immediately upon being capable of seeing reality, regardless of the duration of kalpas;
those such as the assembly of two thousand from the City of Enlightenment, with Sudhana at their head, are examples of those who set out on this path.
The assembly of six thousand bhikṣus was likewise composed entirely of those with sharp and keen wisdom, the most extraordinary among humanity;
upon hearing but once, they attained great understanding. Humble, forgiving, benevolent, and compassionate, they sought exclusively the Great Way to benefit all living beings.

They were all individuals who, having fulfilled their faith throughout a lifetime, had resolved their minds and entered the stages of realization. If you do not believe that your own mind is fundamentally the unmoving wisdom, [you will not realize this].
If a Buddha were to drift and sink through eternal kalpas, how could he benefit others or rescue sentient beings?
As stated in the sūtras, it is impossible for one who is himself bound to untie the bonds of another. Therefore, there are two ways of generating the resolve [for awakening]:

first, the generation of the resolve through the cultivation of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), which consists solely in cultivating the ten stages of faith and understanding; this is as described above regarding the ten wisdoms and the ten heads of the Tathāgata.

The Bodhisattva, having fulfilled these two types of faith, gives rise to the aspiration at the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which is called the "Stage of Initial Aspiration" (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*).
Thus, the ten wisdoms of the Bodhisattva and the ten months of the Buddha constitute their cause and fruit.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning explained within this section on the verses, it is divided into two parts: first, the explicit account of Mañjuśrī reciting ten verses to praise the Tathāgata’s ten [qualities].
Planting roots of virtue causes those with faith to increase their understanding and resolve. Second, clarifying the nature of faith:
the ground of the mind expands, and its radiance gradually increases. "Its radiance gradually increases" clarifies that faith progressively becomes superior, as can be understood from the text.
One should contemplate each object illuminated by the light with the mind, allowing the mind to proceed without obstruction in every direction throughout the ten [directions].

When one has thus universally contemplated the ten directions and perceives that only the observing mind remains, one further contemplates this observing mind and finds it to be neither internal nor external;
thus, with the ten directions being unimpeded, one enters the initial stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
From this point onward, following the verses spoken by Mañjuśrī, the ten kinds of virtues of the Tathāgata are praised, causing the faith of practitioners to gradually expand and broaden.
[Sūtra] If one sees the Perfectly Awakened One, liberated and free from all outflows, unattached to anything in the world—
that person does not yet possess the eye of the path of realization. If one knows the Tathāgata, that his essential marks are non-existent,
and through cultivation attains clear understanding, this person will swiftly become a Buddha and be able to see this world.
His mind does not waver, and it is likewise with respect to the Buddha’s body.
One who shall become a supreme knower—if their mind realizes the equality of the Buddha and the Dharma, and the two notions do not appear before them—shall tread upon the inconceivable stage.
If one sees the Buddha and one's own body abiding in equality, [one attains this].
Without dwelling and without entering anywhere, one shall become a rare-to-be-met being.
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise without number;
if one can know them thus, one shall become a Great Muni who transcends all views of both the mundane and the supramundane, and is able to skillfully know the Dharma.
One shall become a great radiance; if, regarding omniscience, one gives rise to the mind of dedication and perceives that the mind is unarisen, one shall obtain great renown.
Since sentient beings have neither arising nor destruction, if one attains such wisdom, one shall accomplish the unsurpassed path.
Within one, understand the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, understand the one. By comprehending their mutual arising, one shall attain fearlessness.
[Treatise] From the beginning, these ten verses of praise extol the qualities of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which is devoid of intrinsic nature.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond this world and illuminated ten Buddha-lands in the eastern direction;
it was likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
In each and every one of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens; everything contained therein became clearly manifest, just as here.
There, he saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, and in each of these, ten billion Tathāgatas were likewise seated.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions, there appeared a great bodhisattva.
Each one arrived at the place where the Buddha was together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
These great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they came were the Golden World and others;
and the Buddhas whom they had originally served were the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was present in every location.
Simultaneously, before each Buddha, they uttered these verses with one voice:
Sentient beings lack wisdom and are wounded by the poison of the thorn of craving. For their sake, one seeks awakening;
such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma. One universally perceives all phenomena and abandons both extremes.
Having realized the Way, he never regresses; he turns this peerless wheel.
For inconceivable eons, he has diligently cultivated all practices to deliver all sentient beings. This is the power of the Great Sage;
the Guide has subdued the hosts of Māras. Valiant and invincible, he expounds the wondrous meaning within his radiance.
Out of compassion, it is thus: with that mind of wisdom, he shatters all obstacles of affliction;
in a single thought-moment, he perceives all things—this is the Buddha’s spiritual power.
He beats the drum of the True Dharma to awaken the lands of the ten directions, causing them all to turn toward Bodhi; such is his sovereign power.
Without destroying the boundless realm, they travel through billions of lands; unattached to existence, they are as sovereign as the Buddhas.
Like the Buddhas, who are like space, ultimately and eternally pure, they rejoice in mindfulness.
Those whose vows are fully perfected dwell within each and every hell.
Having passed through immeasurable kalpas for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they are able to endure such suffering and do not begrudge their own bodies or lives;
constantly protecting all Buddha-dharmas, free from the notion of self, disciplined and supple,
they are able to attain the Way of the Tathāgata.
[Treatise] Twenty verses in praise of the Tathāgata’s virtue of great compassion, for the sake of causing sentient beings to seek the bodhicitta.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond ten worlds and illuminated a hundred worlds in the eastern direction, as well as the southern, western, and northern directions.
The four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir were likewise so;
in all those worlds, there appeared clearly ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens, and everything within them was manifest.
In each and every Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a Lotus Treasury Lion Throne, as numerous as the atoms of ten Buddha-fields.

Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas, and through the supernatural power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, to the place where the Buddha was.
These great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others; the lands they had come from were the Golden World and so forth. Their original [names] were...
The Buddhas whom they serve are Akṣobhyajñāna Tathāgata and others;
at that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in each of all those places simultaneously uttered these verses before his respective Buddha.
The Buddha has realized that all phenomena are like illusions, Pervading all things with unobstructed penetration. With a pure mind free from all attachments, he tames all living beings;
Some see him at his initial birth, His wondrous form like a mountain of gold, dwelling in his final body, Forever acting as the moon among men. Or some see him when he is walking in meditation.
Possessing immeasurable merit, skilled in both mindfulness and wisdom, with the lion-like stride of a Great Being or eyes of deep blue, he surveys the ten directions.
At times he manifests playful laughter to accord with sentient beings, or he utters the lion’s roar; his supreme and peerless body is thus beheld.
Manifesting his final birth, everything he speaks is nothing but truth.
Some see him renounce the world and liberate himself from all bonds, cultivating the practices of the Buddhas; others constantly delight in contemplating cessation (nirvāṇa).
Or they see him sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), awakening to all phenomena and reaching the further shore of merit.

The darkness of delusion and afflictions are exhausted; Or one sees the Supreme Being, Endowed with a heart of great compassion, turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, Delivering immeasurable sentient beings.
Or one sees the Lion’s Roar, whose majestic radiance is most extraordinary, Transcending all worlds, With peerless power of supernormal faculties.
[Verse: Or one may see the mind in tranquility, like a worldly lamp forever extinguished; thus, in the ten directions, he manifests various supernatural powers.
[Treatise: These thirty verses of verse praise the Tathāgata’s virtue of realizing that all phenomena are like illusions, and his manifestation of a body in accordance with conditions.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond a hundred worlds and illuminated a thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Within each of those individual worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens; everything therein was clearly manifested. Within each of those [worlds]...
Throughout Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata was seen seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury,
surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields; and through the supernatural power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions,
a great Bodhisattva arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, each accompanied by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
The great bodhisattvas— such as Mañjuśrī and others— the lands from which they had come— such as the Golden World—
and the Buddhas whom they had originally served— such as the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom— at that time,
each Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in every location simultaneously uttered these verses before their respective Buddhas.
The Buddha has attained unexcelled penetration into the profound Dharma; though sentient beings cannot comprehend it, he reveals it step by step.

Since the nature of the self never existed and what belongs to the self is likewise empty and quiescent, how is it that the Tathāgatas possess bodies? O practitioners of luminous conduct, [explain this].
Innumerable and peerless, you cannot find any worldly cause or measure that can surpass you;
the Buddha is not composed of the worldly aggregates, elements, or sense bases of birth and death.
Because he cannot be established by means of numerical categories, he is called the Lion among Men. His nature is fundamentally empty and tranquil, liberated both internally and externally.

Free from all deluded thoughts, such is the peerless Dharma: its essential nature is eternally unmoving, without self, and without coming or going; yet it can awaken to the world and bring infinite beings to complete subdual.
Always delighting in the contemplation of quiescence, it is of a single mark without duality, and its mind neither increases nor decreases.
Manifesting immeasurable spiritual powers, yet not acting for the sake of sentient beings;
though he understands the workings of karmic retribution and causal conditions without obstruction, the Dharma of the Sugata is thus:
while various sentient beings transmigrate throughout the ten directions, the Tathāgata makes no discriminations, yet delivers infinite multitudes.

The Buddhas are of true golden color; They do not exist, yet they pervade all realms of existence. In accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings' minds, They preach the Dharma of quiescent extinction.
[Treatise] These forty verses of praise extol the Tathāgata for revealing the profound qualities of the Dharma to the assembly.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond a thousand worlds and illuminated ten thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
In each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens; everything therein was clearly manifested. In each of those [worlds]...
Throughout the entire Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury,
surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; and through the supernatural power of the Buddha,
from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving before the Buddha.
As for those great bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they came, such as the Golden World;
and the Buddhas whom they originally served, such as the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom—at that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses before each Buddha.
One should perform such deeds as these: Arouse the mind of great compassion To rescue and protect all sentient beings, Forever delivering them from the realms of humans and devas;
Such deeds should be performed. Always maintain faith and joy in the Buddha With a mind that never regresses;
Draw near to all Tathāgatas; Such deeds should be performed. Be resolved to delight in the virtues of the Buddha.
With a mind that never regresses, abiding in cool and clear wisdom, one should perform this practice in all modes of conduct.
Constantly recollecting the Buddha’s virtues, day and night without even a moment’s interruption, one should perform this practice.
Contemplating the boundless three periods of time, one should study those virtues of the Buddha.
With a mind that is ever free from weariness, one should perform such deeds; Contemplating the body according to its true nature, all things are utterly quiescent.
Free from attachment to self or non-self, one should perform such deeds;
Observing the minds of sentient beings with equanimity, one does not give rise to any conceptual discriminations, And enters the realm of ultimate reality.

Such deeds should be performed: lifting up all boundless realms; drinking from all oceans—such deeds should be performed through the great power of supernatural knowledge and wisdom. Such deeds should be performed:
contemplating the characteristics of form and the formless in all lands, knowing them all completely—such deeds should be performed.
The dust motes of the lands of the ten directions— If each mote were a Buddha, One could know their number entirely;
Such deeds as these should be performed.
[Treatise] There are ten kinds of verses in fifty lines praising the Buddha’s virtue of protecting and saving sentient beings, intended to encourage those who cultivate the mind.
Because karma must be performed.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light pervaded ten thousand worlds and shone throughout a hundred thousand worlds in the east;
likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. In each of those worlds, there were ten billion...
From Jambudvīpa up to the hundred billion Akaniṣṭha heavens, everything therein was clearly manifested.
Within each of those Jambudvīpas, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury, surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of ten Buddha-fields;
all this was due to the spiritual power of the Buddha, such that in each of the ten directions...
Each of these great bodhisattvas came to the place where the Buddha was, accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
These great bodhisattvas included Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come included the Golden World and others;
and the Buddhas whom they had originally served included the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others. At that time, Mañjuśrī was present in every location.
The Bodhisattvas, headed by Mañjuśrī, each simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of the Buddha:

"To perceive the Teacher of Men, the Tamer, By means of his majestic power, physical form, or lineage— This is the distorted vision of a diseased eye; Such a person cannot know the most supreme Dharma."

The physical form, marks, and characteristics of the Tathāgata— No one in all the worlds can fathom them, even if they were to deliberate for a hundred billion nayutas of kalpas. His physical marks and majestic virtue become ever more boundless;
The Tathāgata does not take these marks as his essence, But is rather the markless dharma of quiescent extinction.
The physical marks and majestic deportment are all fully perfected; According to the inclinations of the world, all may behold them.
The Buddha-dharma is subtle and wondrous, beyond measure; No speech whatsoever can reach it.
It is neither a composite nor non-composite; Its essential nature is quiescent and devoid of all signs.
The Buddha’s body is unborn and transcends conceptual proliferation;
it is not a phenomenon consisting of a collection of aggregates, yet it attains the power of mastery and is seen with certainty. Its sphere of activity is fearless and beyond the path of words;
body and mind are entirely equal, both internally and externally liberated, abiding in right mindfulness for eternal kalpas.
Free from attachment and unbound, with a mind pure and luminous, their conduct is untainted;
their eye of wisdom is all-pervading, bringing vast benefit to sentient beings.
From one body they become infinite, and from the infinite they return to one; thoroughly understanding all worlds, they manifest forms everywhere.

This body has no origin, nor does it have any accumulation. Because sentient beings engage in conceptual discrimination, they perceive the various bodies of the Buddha. The mind discriminates the world; this mind is non-existent.
The Tathāgata knows this dharma, and thus he perceives the body of the Buddha.
[Treatise] Sixty-five verses in gāthā praise the Tathāgata’s virtue of the signless mark (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*),
for all who behold him are able to see it.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond hundreds of thousands of worlds and illuminated a million worlds in the eastern direction, as well as those in the south and west.
In the north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, it was likewise so;
in each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens, all of which appeared clearly.
Within each of those Jambudvīpas, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury, surrounded by ten Buddhas.

Surrounded by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, all through the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
These great bodhisattvas were Mañjuśrī and others; the lands they had come from were called the Golden World.
The Buddhas who were originally served by the realms and so forth were the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others;
at that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in each of all those places simultaneously uttered these verses before his respective Buddha:
The Tathāgata is most sovereign, transcending the world and without dependence; Possessing all merits, he brings liberation from all states of existence.
Untainted and unattached, without conceptualization and without a basis for reliance, his essential nature is immeasurable.
All who behold him offer praise; his radiance is universally pure.
All worldly burdens are completely cleansed; unmoving, one is free from the two extremes. This is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If one perceives the Tathāgata with body and mind free from discrimination, then regarding all phenomena, one will forever transcend all doubts and obstructions.
Throughout all worlds, everywhere he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Without intrinsic nature and nothing that undergoes transformation, the Teacher has taught this through skillful means. Regarding all phenomena, there is no doubt;
all conceptual proliferation is forever severed. Without giving rise to a discriminating mind, one thus recollects the Buddha’s bodhi and thoroughly understands the distinct nature of phenomena.
One does not cling to verbal expressions; therein is neither unity nor multiplicity.
This is called following the Buddha’s teaching: Among the many, there is no single nature; In the one, there is likewise no multiplicity.
Thus abandoning both, One universally enters the Buddha’s merit. Sentient beings and their lands— All are utterly quiescent;
Without dependence and without discrimination, One is able to enter the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Sentient beings and their lands— Neither identity nor difference can be found. One who observes thus with skill Is said to know the meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
[Commentary] These seventy verses of verse praise the Tathāgata’s independent and sovereign virtues, which are endowed with all merits. They cause [beings] to...
Because those with faith practice and study.
