[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond one million worlds and illuminated one hundred million worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens; everything contained therein became clearly manifest.
In each and every Jambudvīpa, they saw a Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury,
surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; and by the spiritual power of the Buddha,
from each of the ten directions, there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
The great bodhisattvas present with the Buddha— such as Mañjuśrī and others— the lands from which they had come— such as the Golden World and others—
and the Buddhas whom they had originally served— such as the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others— at that time, in every location,
each of the Mañjuśrī Bodhisattvas simultaneously uttered these verses before their respective Buddhas:
With wisdom peerless and dharmas boundless, Transcending the ocean of all existences to reach the other shore;
Your lifespan and radiance are both beyond compare— These merits belong to the power of skillful means.
All Buddha-dharmas are clearly understood, And you constantly contemplate the three periods of time without weariness.

Though they engage with objects, they do not discriminate; this inconceivable one, through the power of skillful means, delights in contemplating sentient beings while maintaining the notion of non-arising.
Universally beholding all realms of existence, they maintain the notion of no realms;
ever abiding in meditative stillness, their minds are unattached. This is the power of skillful means of unimpeded wisdom.
Skillfully penetrating all phenomena, they diligently cultivate the path to nirvāṇa with right mindfulness;

delighting in liberation and free from discord, these people of tranquil extinction possess the power of skillful means to exhort others toward the Buddha’s bodhi, leading them toward omniscience that accords with the dharma-realm.
Skillfully transforming sentient beings so they enter the Truths—this is the power of skillful means of abiding in the Buddha-mind.

Entering into all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, with vast wisdom that is unimpeded, one has reached the perfection of conduct in all places; this is the power of cultivating mastery in skillful means.
Constantly abiding in nirvāṇa like space, manifesting transformations according to the mind without exception;
this relies on the signless as its very sign, the skillful power of those who have reached the difficult-to-reach.
Day and night, sun and moon, years and eons—the signs of the world’s beginning, end, formation, and destruction.

Thus recollecting, they fully comprehend; at this time, through the power of the skillful means of numerical knowledge, they fully know all sentient beings who undergo birth and death, as well as all names—whether material or immaterial, with perception or without perception.
This dwelling is the power of inconceivable skillful means.
All that is spoken throughout the past, present, and future worlds, he understands and knows;
he realizes that the three periods of time are entirely equal. Such is his incomparable power of skillful means and wisdom.
[Commentary: These eight verses of twenty lines praise the Tathāgata’s virtues of wisdom and skillful means, causing those with faith to rejoice.
Because they study and practice.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond one hundred million worlds and illuminated ten billion worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion [Buddhas].
From Jambudvīpa up to the hundred billion Akaniṣṭha heavens, everything therein was clearly manifested.
Within each and every Jambudvīpa, the Tathāgata was seen sitting upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury, surrounded by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields;
all of this, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, occurred in each of the ten directions.
Each of these great bodhisattvas came to the place where the Buddha was, accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
These great bodhisattvas included Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come included the Golden World and others;
and the Buddhas whom they had originally served included the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others. At that time, in every location, Mañjuśrī...
The Bodhisattvas, headed by Mañjuśrī, each simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of the Buddha:
"We have practiced all manner of vast ascetic austerities, Diligent day and night without weariness or indolence.
Having crossed over that which is difficult to cross, we let out the lion’s roar; To universally transform sentient beings—this is our practice."
Sentient beings wander in the ocean of craving, Enmeshed in the net of ignorance and oppressed by great sorrow;
The Benevolent One, through his courageous valor, has severed them all— He vows likewise to act thus for their sake.
Those in the world are heedless, attached to the five desires, Suffering manifold pains through unreal conceptualization.
Practicing the Buddha’s teachings while constantly gathering the mind, Vowing to deliver these beings—this is their practice.
Sentient beings cling to a self and enter the cycle of birth and death; One cannot find its limit even by seeking it.
Universally serving the Tathāgatas and attaining the wondrous Dharma, Proclaiming it for their sake—this is their practice.

Sentient beings, having no protector, are entangled by illness; Constantly sinking into the evil realms, they give rise to the three poisons, which burn with fierce flames like a great conflagration. To deliver them with a pure mind is their practice.
Sentient beings are deluded and lose the right path; They constantly travel along deviant ways and enter the dark abode.
To kindle the great lamp of the True Dharma for them, And to provide eternal illumination—this is their practice.
Sentient beings drift and drown in the ocean of existence, In boundless sorrow and hardship where no footing can be found;
To launch for them the great ship of the Dharma, Causing all to cross over to the other shore—this is their practice.

Sentient beings, lacking knowledge, do not see the fundamental; Deluded, ignorant, and frantic amidst perilous difficulties, The Buddha takes pity on them and builds the bridge of Dharma, Causing them to ascend through right mindfulness—this is his practice.
Seeing all sentient beings in perilous paths, Constantly oppressed by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.
Cultivating immeasurable and boundless skillful means, with the vow to deliver all beings—this is their practice.
Hearing the Dharma and believing with understanding, free from doubt, they realize the emptiness and quiescence of nature without fear.
Adapting to forms throughout the six realms across the ten directions, they universally instruct the deluded masses—this is their practice.
[Treatise] These nine verses of twenty lines praise the Tathāgata’s virtue of vast asceticism and diligence,
so that those with faith may practice accordingly.
[Sūtra] At that time, the light passed beyond ten billion worlds and shone throughout one hundred billion and one thousand billion worlds in the eastern direction.
Worlds numbering one hundred thousand koṭis, worlds numbering ten billion koṭis, worlds numbering one hundred nayutas of koṭis,
worlds numbering one thousand nayutas of koṭis, and worlds numbering one hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis—
thus, they are infinite, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable.
In all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm—in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—it is likewise so.
Within each and every one of those worlds, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens;
everything therein is clearly manifested, and within each and every Jambudvīpa, all [of this] is seen.
The Tathāgata sat upon the lion throne of the Lotus Treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, who approached the presence of the Buddha. These great bodhisattvas were, namely, Mañjuśrī...
As for the lands from which Mañjuśrī and the others had come— such as the Golden World— and the Buddhas they originally served—
such as the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom— at that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattvas in every location simultaneously uttered these verses before their respective Buddhas.
In a single thought, universally observe immeasurable eons— Neither going nor coming, and likewise no abiding.
Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, One transcends all expedient means and accomplishes the ten powers.
With a good reputation matchless throughout the ten directions, Forever free from all hardships, one is always joyful.
They travel everywhere throughout all lands, extensively proclaiming this Dharma;
for the benefit of sentient beings, they make offerings to the Buddhas and obtain corresponding fruits according to their intentions.
They fully understand all phenomena in accordance with reality, manifesting spiritual powers throughout the ten directions.
From the first making offerings to the Buddhas with a mind of gentleness and patience, entering deep meditative concentration to contemplate the nature of phenomena,
universally exhorting sentient beings to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind, and seeking the Dharma throughout the ten directions with undifferentiated intent—
by these means, one swiftly accomplishes the unsurpassed fruit, so that the cultivation of merit may be brought to fulfillment.
Having utterly eliminated both the marks of existence and non-existence, such a person has true vision regarding the Buddha.
Traveling everywhere to all lands throughout the ten directions, they extensively proclaim the sublime Dharma to bring about benefit and welfare.
Abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without wavering, this person’s merit is equal to that of the Buddha.
The sublime wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata— All of it consists of the factors of enlightenment.
If one can hear this and awaken to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), Such a person constantly sees the Buddha;
Yet they do not see the Ten Powers as being empty or illusory; Though seeing, it is not seeing, like a blind man beholding.
Those who grasp at distinguishing marks do not see the Buddha; Only by being ultimately free from attachment can one see him.
Sentient beings differ according to their various karmas, Yet the Buddha’s body is unimpeded, pervading the ten directions.
Just as it is impossible to exhaustively see them, The same is true for seeing the Buddha.
Just as there are immeasurable lands in space, Neither coming nor going,
pervading the ten directions, Arising, abiding, and perishing without any support— The Buddha pervades empty space in just this way.

[Commentary] These ten and twenty verses of verse praise the Tathāgata’s true nature, which is devoid of the three periods of time, possesses merit, and is free from dualistic characteristics, pervading everywhere.

Because it causes all those with faith to practice and study, the above ten verses spoken by Mañjuśrī praise the ten virtues of the Buddha to inspire faith in those who have it, causing them to give rise to faith and advance in practice.

This "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance" sets forth the dharmas of the Buddha-fruit so that those with faith may correctly enter into faith themselves, their faith becoming identical to the fruit of all Buddhas.
The Dharma does not shift; the Dharmakāya is immovable. The Bodhisattva practice of Wisdom pervades and encompasses the entire body.
From antiquity to the present, there has never been another dharma. The single nature of ordinary beings and sages is identical in its lack of inherent nature or flavor.

The flavor of the great vows, great kindness, great compassion, and great wisdom—of Mañjuśrī’s wondrous prajñā and Samantabhadra’s myriad practices—is, in its entirety, the unified essence and function of movement and stillness.
Therefore, practicing with such faith, one advances simultaneously from the initial generation of the bodhicitta;

within this stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one establishes the four hundred and ten great vows to accomplish the practices of the Great Compassion, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*), and the Knowledge-body (*vidyākāya*) all at once.
Thus, the Dharma-body is the ten material worlds, and the Wisdom-body is the ten Wisdom-Buddhas.
This body of wisdom is Mañjuśrī; this great compassion is the fulfillment of the one hundred and forty great vows.
All the dharmas mentioned above are this very Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance, into which one enters with faith.
Just as in the Chapter on the Inquiry into Wisdom (*Prajñāparipṛcchā*), once one has entered into faith, the rules for question and answer establish that faith.
Because they are accomplished through the practice of power, it is asked: "For what reason are all the gates of the Ten Faiths established as the teaching of Mañjuśrī?
He replied: "It is to clarify that Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions, which skillfully discriminates between the correct and the false.
Once the correct and the false are determined, one then practices through conduct; this is precisely what is called the conduct of Samantabhadra. This sequence is naturally so."

It is clearly stated that this Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta is so named because he attained his name through the practice [of the stages] due to having first initiated the aspiration and entered the beginning of faith.

Question: Among the dharmas of the five positions (*pañca-avasthā*), it is taught that a Bodhisattva enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) before speaking; why then is it not taught that one enters absorption at the position of faith (*śraddhā-avasthā*)? Answer:
Faith is the faith of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) characterized by a mind of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-citta*); it has not yet entered [the state beyond such fluctuations].

Because it is realized, there is no fixed state; for the five stages are the essence of entry into the principle and wisdom of true non-action, which is manifested not through the absence of thought but cannot be sought among sentient beings—therefore, one must enter meditative concentration.

Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Luminosity [Śāstra] In order to explain this chapter, it is divided into three sections: first, an explanation of the title; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;

and third, an explanation of the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the explanation of the title: it is established to perfect the ten kinds of roots of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and to extend them.

Because the ten kinds of illumination of the Dharma were inquired about through the mutual relationship of principal and attendant among the various powers of faith, Mañjuśrī, Bodhiruci, and others, this is titled the "Chapter on the Illumination of Inquiry.

Second, regarding the intent of the chapter’s arrival: in the preceding chapter, light was emitted from the wheels beneath the Tathāgata’s feet to awaken [beings] to the far and near reaches of the Buddha-realm that is illuminated, causing those with faith to contemplate each of them individually.
It is because it causes the mind to act without obstruction, becoming vast and equal to the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praised the Buddha’s ten virtues with ten verses and exhorted those with faith to practice;
therefore, this "Chapter on Clarifying the Questions" is intended to clarify the correct practice of those with the ten levels of faith and to sever their doubts—hence the existence of this chapter.
Regarding the third section, "Explaining the Meaning According to the Text": Within this passage of the present chapter, there are eleven sections of scripture.
These clearly show how Mañjuśrī, Buddhasvabhāva, and the other ten bodhisattvas act as mutual leaders and companions, each inquiring about ten kinds of illumination of the Dharma.

Each is addressed by the name of a bodhisattva, which directly represents the practice of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Furthermore, Mañjuśrī returns to using these names [to explain their significance].

In the following section, they consult one another; ten bodhisattvas each respond with verses concerning their own methods of practice, so that those with faith may rely upon them for emulation and study. The ten questions and ten verses are as follows below;
the final paragraph concludes that all ten directions are likewise the same.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment: "O Son of the Buddha, the nature of the mind is one;

how is it that various distinctions are perceived—namely, rebirth in good or evil realms, the completeness or deficiency of the faculties, similarities and differences in birth, beauty or ugliness, and the disparity between suffering and pleasure? Furthermore, karma does not know the mind, and the mind does not know karma."

Feeling does not know its retribution, and retribution does not know feeling; the mind does not know feeling, and feeling does not know the mind; the cause does not know the condition, and the condition does not know the cause;
wisdom does not know its object, and the object does not know wisdom. At that time, the Bodhisattva Chief of Awakening answered in verse:
The Benevolent One now asks about this meaning in order to awaken the ignorant masses. I shall answer according to its true nature;
you, O Benevolent One, should listen attentively. All phenomena lack functional activity and possess no intrinsic nature;
therefore, they are all entirely incapable of knowing one another, just like the waters in a river.
Rapid currents rush and flow together, yet each is unaware of the others; all phenomena are likewise so.
They are also like a great mass of fire, where fierce flames break out simultaneously, yet each is unaware of the others;
all phenomena are likewise so. Furthermore, they are like a long wind that arises, fanning and stirring everything it encounters.

Each is unaware of the others; all phenomena are likewise so. Furthermore, just as the various elements of earth dwell in mutual dependence upon one another, each being unaware of the others, so too are all phenomena.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and the various sense faculties— by means of these, there is constant transmigration.
Yet there is no one who can transform it; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally unborn.

It manifests as having birth, yet within this there is no one who manifests, nor is there any object manifested. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sensory faculties are entirely empty and devoid of self-nature; they exist only through the conceptual discrimination of the deluded mind.
When one observes according to reality, all things are found to be without intrinsic nature.
This vision by the inconceivable Dharma-eye is not erroneous. Whether real or unreal, whether false or not false, mundane or supramundane—all exist only as conventional designations.
[Treatise] First, the six lines of scripture beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...

constitute the twenty questions posed by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva regarding the causes and effects of good and evil; these consist of either one word per question or one phrase per question, totaling twenty questions.
Following this, the eleven lines of verse are the initial response given by Bodhisattva Śirṣabuddhi.
The first verse praises the person who asks the question and exhorts [the audience] to listen; the subsequent ten verses answer the question regarding the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī skillfully asked about the mutual unknowing of the causes and effects of good and evil in the world and how karma can bring these to fruition.
Bodhisattva Vijñānakāya then answered with the truth of the mutual unknowing of phenomena.
It is simply that those who are deluded regarding the Truth create karma for themselves; those who know the Truth realize that all karma is itself the Truth.
The final verse clarifies the total disappearance of both truth and delusion by employing both analogies and doctrinal explanations, as is fully evident in the text itself.

One may contemplate this and see it for oneself; since the phrasing follows the logic and the principles are manifest, there is no need for further explanation here. Within these eleven verses, the meaning is as follows:
This is divided into three parts: (1) the meaning of the verses; (2) the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva"; and (3) the correlation with the causes and fruits according to the stages.
Regarding the meaning of the verses: these eleven lines constitute one verse. The first line praises the questioner and exhorts the audience to listen;
the subsequent ten lines each individually clarify the subject matter. The first line of this section is a verse on the non-activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*) of phenomena.

Regarding the next line on the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*): it provides an analogy based on the fact that flowing water does not know itself; one should understand this according to the underlying intent without the trouble of further sub-classification.

As for the second explanation of the name "Bodhisattva": it means one who possesses clear awakening. Although the substance of karma within the flow of birth and death follows along with that stream, its fundamental nature is eternally true and without such wandering.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind always know things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*), and thus do not wander.
Because it is the nature of birth and death, there is neither falsehood nor reality;
yet, because the Dharma of true wisdom—free from greed, hatred, and delusion—is called "true," such a teaching is proclaimed for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called the Great Way-mind that awakens oneself and awakens others. As for these sentient beings, they take this very ignorance as their substance...

Regarding the cause and effect of karma, one awakens oneself and awakens others to the realization that the self-nature of the Dharma-realm is the ultimate truth in which both the true and the false have vanished;
this is called "Chief of Awakening" (*Bodhimukha*). Because one first believes in this Dharma, it is named "Chief.

This clarifies that at the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one has complete faith in the entirety of one's own eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the entire being of all sentient beings.
Because both truth and falsehood have perished, there is only the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom;
therefore, the ten wisdoms of the Tathāgata Acalamati Buddha are taken as one's own fruition within the stage of the Ten Faiths.
The ten colored worlds—such as the Golden World, the World of Sublime Colors, and the Lotus-Colored World—are the principles to be believed within these Ten Faiths, [as taught by] Mañjuśrī.
The ten bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī, Vajramati, and Vasumati, represent the practice of the Ten Faiths;
they are named according to their practices, as each bodhisattva’s name is established based on their emulation of specific practices and understandings.
The same applies to the bodhisattvas listed below. The world is named "Exquisite Color" (Miaose), which is precisely the principle realized by the bodhisattva Vajramati.
The Buddha of Unobstructed Wisdom (*asaṅga-jñāna*) is precisely the Buddha-fruit cultivated by the stage of Awakening Head (*bodhi-mūrdhan*);

through this faith, one clarifies that the two aspects of truth and falsehood regarding the causes and effects of all karma have both vanished, for it is the unimpeded function of wisdom. Third, as for the correspondence between cause and effect according to each stage:
one always takes the Buddha of the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom of one’s own mind as the cause of faith, and proceeds with advancement.
The Buddha who has cultivated and attained this unimpeded wisdom is a Buddha according to his respective stage of fruition;

this is based solely on the questions and answers, as well as the names of the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas and the forms and characteristics of their worlds. The underlying meaning and principle are naturally clear;
there is no need for doubt.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Vasumitra Bodhisattva: "O Son of the Buddha, all sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings.

How is it that the Tathāgata, according to their time, their lifespan, their bodies, their conduct, their understanding, their speech, their mental inclinations, their skillful means, and their reflections..."
When he observes how to manifest his body among such sentient beings to teach and discipline them, the Bodhisattva Vasumukha replies in verse:
"This is the domain of those who delight in tranquility and possess great learning; I shall proclaim it for your sake."
O Benevolent One, you should now listen and receive this: Analyze and contemplate the internal body. Who herein is "I"?
If one can understand in this way, One will realize the existence or non-existence of the self. This body is a provisional designation;
its dwelling place has no fixed location. One who clearly understands this body Will have no attachment toward it.

By observing the body well, one clearly sees all things; knowing that all phenomena are empty and false, one does not give rise to mental discrimination. From whom does life arise? And by whom does it perish?
It is like a whirling firebrand: its beginning and end cannot be known. Only the wise are able to observe this.
All that exists is impermanent; all phenomena are empty and selfless.
Forever free from all marks, the manifold retributions arise according to karma. Like a dream, they are not real;
in every thought-moment they constantly perish and decay, just as the preceding is like the succeeding. Of all the phenomena perceived by the world, the mind alone is the sovereign.
Grasping at various characteristics according to one's understanding is inverted and not in accordance with reality.
All the discourses spoken in the world are mere conceptual constructions; there has never been a single dharma that can enter the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
By the power of the perceiving subject and the perceived object, various dharmas arise, yet they perish swiftly without pausing for even a moment.
[Commentary] Second, the five lines of scripture beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...
are Mañjuśrī’s questions to Dhanika Bodhisattva concerning the Tathāgata’s ten kinds of skillful means as timely dharmas. First:

Raising the point that "non-sentient beings" refers to the essence of karma being purely true as answered by Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment (*Bodhimukha*), he then asks why the Tathāgata’s ten kinds of timely transformations exist.
Bodhisattva Chief of Wealth (*Dhanamukha*) answers from the perspective of reality to establish faith, explaining that "timeliness" is provisional.
This meaning is fully elucidated in the following ten stanzas of the Ten Practices; herein lies the significance of these ten stanzas.
This is divided into three sections: (1) the meaning of the verses; (2) the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva"; and (3) the correlation with the causes and fruits according to the stages.
Regarding the meaning of the verses in this section: among these ten verses on the practices, each practice is treated in one verse.

In the first verse, the initial two lines praise the Dharma that was asked about as being beyond the capacity of those who are not great vessels, and as being the domain of those who possess extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

Regarding the next two lines, "Now, as you have asked, I shall explain" and "I urge you to listen," the following nine lines of verse constitute Vasumitra’s response based on reality, as clearly elucidated in the text.

As for the second explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name: because he will, as described in the subsequent verses, skillfully master the wealth of the Dharma—both its conventional and ultimate aspects—and bestow it as a gift upon sentient beings, he is named Vasumitra (Wealth-Head). By means of the ten... [ten powers/paramitas].
The initial practice of benefiting sentient beings through the wealth of the Dharma within the mind of faith is called the "World of Lotus Color.
This clarifies that within this faith, one benefits sentient beings with the noble wealth of the Dharma, causing both self and others to be free from defiled attachment;
thus the world is named "Lotus Color," signifying the dispelling of delusion by bestowing the Dharma upon others.

The perfection of wisdom is named the "Wisdom that Extinguishes Darkness," for the Buddha’s Radiance is inherently possessed within the faith of this stage as the principle, practice, and wisdom of cause and effect.
Thus, Vasumitra (Wealth Chief) represents the practice of this stage; the subsequent examples follow suit.
Regarding the threefold correspondence to the causes and effects of each stage: one always takes the fundamental non-moving wisdom-Buddha of one's own mind as Mañjuśrī.
The cause of faith is the cultivation of practice that attains the wisdom of liberation; the Buddha is the foremost wealth of this wisdom.
Since the Bodhisattva is the fruit of the conduct corresponding to each stage, the Buddha is the fruit of wisdom, and the others are to be understood by analogy in this manner.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva:
"O Son of the Buddha, all sentient beings equally possess the four great elements, which are without self and without what belongs to a self.

How is it then that there is the experience of suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, internal excellence and external excellence, little or much sensation, or the receiving of retribution in the present life or in future lives? For such is the nature of dharmas."
When there was neither beauty nor ugliness within the realm, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśīrṣa replied in verse:
"According to the actions one performs, Such is the retribution that arises.
The Buddhas have taught that there is no agent— Just as in a clear, bright mirror, Whatever object is reflected therein."
Manifestations differ from one another, and the nature of karma is likewise.
Just as fields and seeds do not know one another, yet they naturally give rise to growth, so too is the nature of karma.
Furthermore, it is like a skilled illusionist at a crossroads who manifests a multitude of forms and appearances.
The nature of karma is also like this: It is like a wooden mechanical man Who can produce various sounds;
Therein is neither self nor non-self. The nature of karma is also like this.
It is also like various kinds of birds That emerge from their eggs; Their voices are each different. The nature of karma is also like this.
Just as within the womb all the sense faculties are fully formed, yet their physical form has no place from which it comes—so too is the nature of karma.
Furthermore, just as the various kinds of suffering experienced in hell have no point of origin—so too is the nature of karma. It is like a wheel-turning monarch.
The attainment of the seven supreme jewels has no place from which they come; the nature of karma is likewise.
Furthermore, as when all worlds are consumed by a great fire, this fire has no place from which it comes;
the nature of karma is likewise.
[Treatise] Third: From "At that time" onwards, the four lines and a half of sūtra constitute Mañjuśrī’s questioning of Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva.
First, he generally states that all sentient beings equally possess the four great elements and are without self or what belongs to a self. Following the question "How so?
and below, there are ten questions regarding the dharma of the causes and effects of karma. Below that, there are ten lines of verse [spoken by] Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva.
In response to the ten preceding questions, the first part clarifies that the entire essence is non-conceptual;

the second clarifies that the excellence or deficiency of the karma one receives arises from one's practice, as explained in detail in the sutra. The general meaning is that when one realizes the essence, karma ceases; when one is deluded regarding the truth, karma arises.
Within these ten verses on practice, the exposition is divided into three sections: first, an analysis of the intent of the verses; second, an explanation of the name "Bodhisattva."

Regarding the meaning of the verse in the section on the correspondence between cause and fruit according to their respective positions: the first two lines praise the karmic retribution arising from practice;
the next two lines praise the essential nature of karma as fundamentally real and originally non-existent, as taught by all Buddhas.
The following nine lines—one verse per line—cite metaphors to reveal the Dharma, demonstrating that in the realization of the Dharma, there is no karma within the Dharma, and no Dharma within karma.

Second, regarding the difference in practice, it may be understood from the text. Second, as for the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva," this clarifies that at this stage of faith, one realizes that karma is itself the essence of the Dharma;
thus, there is no longer any phenomenon called "karma. Because one benefits others by means of this Dharma-treasure, making faith the foremost, he is named "Jewel-Head" (Ratnamati).
This clarifies that he belongs to the northern direction and occupies the rank of a teacher (*ācārya*), by virtue of his majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Because he follows the rules for the benefit of sentient beings, the Buddha is named Venerable Dignity Wisdom (*Vaiyāvṛtya-jñāna*). His world is named Campaka Flower;
this flower is yellow and radiant, representing the color of the merit of benefiting sentient beings.

Yellow is the vapor of auspicious fortune that corresponds internally to pure whiteness while externally manifesting as a yellow appearance; thus, the Tathāgata, as the teacher of devas and humans, wears robes.

The black robes correspond to the Northern Kan (Water) trigram; thus, internally they accord with the principle of being pure and unstained, while externally they manifest a yellow appearance to clarify the benefit of living beings.
Taking the auspicious mark of purity and non-defilement as the name for the world, they provide the virtuous conduct and ritual order to benefit sentient beings.
The Buddha’s title is "The Buddha of Dignified Manner and Wisdom," who constantly benefits living beings through the Treasure of the Dharma.
The nature of the perfected karma is truly named "Jewel Head" (Ratnaśrī) Bodhisattva;

this is the title for the principle and wisdom of cause and effect regarding the Dharma attained by the fourth stage of faith. Question: Why is the North designated as the Teacher and the Sovereign? Answer:
Water nourishes all things like a teacher, and water flows toward the lowlands like a sovereign. One who acts as a teacher or a sovereign does so out of compassion for the ignorant.
To rescue the deluded and cause them to attain enlightenment; furthermore, in the North, Kan represents the lower position.

That which takes the form of a sovereign or a teacher constantly employs conduct of humility and submissiveness to cause sentient beings to take refuge in it, benefiting them with the Way and nourishing them with its moisture.
Therefore, the noble person always remains humble and occupies a lower position to rescue things and bring forth illumination. For this reason, Kan of the North is so designated.

My lord, you are my teacher. The Great Way has no corners; we merely take its meaning to manifest virtue. Thus, the remaining positions have already been explained in the "Chapter on Names and Titles.

Since one Buddha’s name pervades the ten directions, this [text] uses the various directions to symbolize the Dharma. This is like the *Zhou Yi*, the hexagram *Tai* (Threatening), where Qian is below and Kun is above:
the first nine-line line reads, "Pulling up the thatch-grass by its roots," signifying that the grass is pure white and supple.
Weaken its roots; it is as sweet as a gentleman of virtue. Like the *máoh* grass—supple, pure white, sweet, and harmonious—it can be drawn forth and joined, much like taking office.
Yet, while the *máoh* is not itself a gentleman, it is used as a metaphor for one;

likewise, this particular region is not the Buddha, but it is used as a metaphor for the Dharma to enable one to know the Dharma. The wisdom of the Buddha is without dependence, yet it relies upon things.
What is called "wisdom" has no fixed direction, for it establishes directions through the Dharma; it is not a direction such as east, west, south, or north as perceived by the ordinary mind.
Thus, the three pairings correspond to their respective positions in the sequence of cause and effect:

one always takes the Buddha of the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom of one's own mind as the beginning (the cause of faith), and through progressive cultivation, attains the Buddha of the Wisdom of Majestic Dignity as the fourth (the perfection of vigor).
This is the fruit among the *pāramitās*.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Śrīkūṭa Bodhisattva: "O Son of the Buddha, the reality realized by the Tathāgata is but a single dharma;
why then does he speak of immeasurable dharmas, manifesting in immeasurable lands and transforming immeasurable beings?"
They manifested immeasurable sounds, displayed immeasurable bodies, knew immeasurable minds, and revealed immeasurable supernormal powers;

they were able to universally shake immeasurable worlds, manifest immeasurable and sublime adornments, and display boundless varieties of realms, yet within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), these marks of differentiation are all unobtainable. At that time, the Bodhisattva Virtue Chief (*Guṇasāgaraprabha*)...
The verse in response says:
The meaning asked by the Son of the Buddha Is profound and difficult to comprehend. The wise are able to know this:
The constant and blissful qualities of the Buddha Are like the nature of the earth, which is one, Yet sentient beings each dwell upon it separately.
The earth has no thought of oneness or difference; such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as the nature of fire is one yet can burn all things, and the flames have no discrimination, such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, just as the great ocean is one, though its waves are ten thousandfold and diverse, the water itself has no various distinctions.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: it is like the nature of the wind, which can blow upon all things yet the wind has not a single thought of difference. The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus.
It is also like a great cloud and thunder that rains everywhere upon all lands; there is no distinction among the drops of rain. The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus.
Just as the single element of earth Can produce various kinds of sprouts, So too are the qualities of all Buddhas;

Like the sun when free from the veil of clouds, Shining universally throughout the ten directions, Its radiance has no difference in nature— So too are the qualities of all Buddhas; And like the moon in the sky.
There is nothing in the world that is not seen; it is not that the moon travels to those places. Such is the nature of the Buddhas’ Dharma:
just as the Great Brahmā King manifests his presence throughout the three thousandfold world-system, yet his body remains without distinction, such is the nature of the Buddhas’ Dharma.
[Treatise] The fourth section, from "At that time" onwards, consists of six lines of scripture in which Mañjuśrī asks Guṇākara Bodhisattva about the single dharma realized by the Tathāgata.
Following this, there are ten questions as clearly set forth in the text.
Below that, there are ten lines of verse in which Guṇākara Bodhisattva provides the answer. Within the meaning of these verses, the exposition is divided into three parts.
I. An outline of the meaning of the verses; II. An explanation of the name "Bodhisattva"; III. A correlation of cause and effect according to the stages.

Regarding the first, the outline of the meaning of the verses: within these ten verses on practice, the first verse praises the profound nature of the subject asked about, which is known only by wisdom.
The subsequent nine verses clarify their general significance one by one, as clearly set forth in the text itself. This concludes the outline.

The myriad phenomena are not different from the single Dharma-realm; one practices immeasurable Dharma-gates within this single Dharma-realm, yet these immeasurable Dharma-gates are themselves the nature of the single Dharma-realm.
One should not be obstructed by the one such that it becomes many, nor should one be obstructed by the many such that they become one.

Contemplate this according to the *Ten Profound Meanings* (Shi xuanyan yi) and perceive it through the wisdom of non-abiding. Second, regarding the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name, it refers to their name and virtue.
"Head" (śu) signifies that this stage does not depart from the single nature of the Dharma-realm;
by eliminating delusion, craving, and all afflictions while constantly cultivating all merits, it is named "Virtuous Head.
That the world is named "Blue Lotus" clarifies that this fifth stage of faith is the perfection of dhyāna (meditation), and thus the mind is pure and without [defilement].
Because it is free from the defilements of greed, craving, and delusion, this is the Buddha of the northeast named Mingxiang Zhiming (Wisdom of the Appearance of Light).
This stage is the fruit of progressive cultivation; because one attains the purity of the Dharma-mind, it is like the appearance of light between the hours of *yīn* and *chǒu* in the position of Gèn.
Therefore, the Buddha is named Mingxiang Zhiming. This direction is used to symbolize the dharma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), hence it is the east.
The north is Gen; Gen represents the mountain, which symbolizes the meaning of stillness and immobility. This is the definition of Chan (meditation).

Therefore, regarding the correspondence of the three positions to cause and effect: one always takes the Buddha of the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom of one’s own mind as the cause of faith, and through diligent cultivation, attains the Buddha of the Wisdom of the Manifestation of Light as the fruit.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Mūrdhaja Bodhisattva:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s field of merit is equal and without distinction;

why then do we see differences in the fruits of sentient beings' giving—namely, various colors, various forms, various families, various faculties, various wealth, various masters, and various retinues?"
While [the Buddha] was dwelling amidst various official positions, various merits, and various wisdoms, his mind remained equanimous toward them all without any discriminatory thought;
at that time, the Bodhisattva Mūrdhaja replied with a verse:
Just as from a single great earth, various sprouts grow according to their seeds, so too is the Buddha-field of merit; toward it there is neither enmity nor affection.
Furthermore, just as water is of a single taste, yet appears different due to the vessels that contain it, so too is the Buddha-field of merit;
it differs only because of the minds of sentient beings, like a skillful magician.
The Buddha’s field of merit is thus: it causes the multitude to rejoice, making all sentient beings respectful and delighted, just like a wise and talented king who brings joy to the great assembly.
It causes all beings to dwell in peace and happiness; it is like a pure, bright mirror that reflects images according to their forms.
The Buddha-field is thus: according to one’s mind, one obtains manifold rewards.
Just as the *keta* medicine can cure all poisons, the Buddha-field is thus.
It extinguishes the afflictions of all troubles, just as when the sun rises, it illuminates the world; the Buddha-field is thus.
Dispelling all darkness like the pure, full moon, the Buddha’s field of merit likewise shines universally upon the great earth,
equal in all places. Just as the Vairambha wind causes the great earth to tremble,
so too does the Buddha’s field of merit move the beings within the three realms of existence.
Just as a great fire that arises Can burn all things, So does the Buddha-field of merit Burn all conditioned phenomena.
[Treatise] Fifth: From "At that time" onwards, the five lines and a half of sūtra constitute Mañjuśrī’s question to the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
The Tathāgata’s field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is equal and without distinction; that is to say, the ten questions below are as explained in the sutra.

The ten verses below represent the answers given by the Honored Head (Maitreya) according to the three gates, following the same format as the preceding section. Regarding the meaning of these verses:
each of these ten verses corresponds to one question. The purport of these verses is to answer the previous inquiries concerning the Buddha’s field of merit.

Regarding this, why is it that the retributions for the fruit of giving differ? There are two meanings to this difference: first, clarifying that the Buddha’s own field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) differs;
second, clarifying that the field of merit to which sentient beings give differs. First, regarding "clarifying that the Buddha’s own field of merit differs":
this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s body has eyes, hair, and eyebrows of deep blue-black, a golden-colored body, crimson lips, and a pure white [countenance].

The colors of the teeth upon one’s body each differ; the myriad variations in the adornments of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) collectively clarify that within the principle and wisdom of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), all things are inherently present.

Because immeasurable merits are fundamentally possessed within the principle and wisdom of the *dharmatā*, there are adornments obtained as the retribution for following practice, such as the ninety-seven marks of the Tathāgata’s body.
The marks of a Great Man are the essence of the wisdom-body of the Dharma-kāya, which is inherently possessed;

therefore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) as adornments of merit, for these are obtained as the retribution of his conduct. Just as the adamantine ground (*vajra-bhūmi*) within the external environment and its inhabitants is obtained as the retribution of the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), so too is the world adorned with jewel-trees obtained as the retribution of the Reward Body (*vipāka-kāya*). This is the Dharma... [text ends].

The nature following conduct results in the retribution of obtaining the dependent environment of palaces and towers; this is the Dharma-nature’s great wisdom following great compassion to nurture and sustain sentient beings.
Through the karma of superior retribution, one obtains the lion throne; this is the Dharma-nature following wisdom to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Through the retribution of following conduct, one obtains the Lotus Treasury World; this is the Dharma-nature following conduct to teach and transform sentient beings.
The fragrant ocean obtained as a result of the nature of defilement is the retribution for the practice of following the *dharmatā* with a mind of great compassion to benefit others through humility;
the rightward whirlpools of the fragrant rivers are obtained as the retribution for practicing in accordance with the *dharmatā* to teach and transform sentient beings;

and the totality is never separate from the *dharmatā*, being obtained as the retribution for the practice of great wisdom. Within each and every one of these practices, there are immeasurable [qualities].

The practice gates act as mutual principal and companions, thereby adorning both the environment and the physical body; within each and every state of existence, there are infinite similarities and differences.
This is observing the cause to know the fruit, by which one understands that, in general, they are all of one nature, differing only according to their respective functions.
Second, regarding the fact that the fruits and retributions of sentient beings' offerings to the field of merit differ: this...
This arises from differences in the weight of the mind, whether one possesses wisdom or lacks it, and whether one is humble or haughty;
thus, what is sought differs, though it is fundamentally one mind that varies according to its application. Second, regarding the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva":

the term "Sattva" (目首) signifies the head or leader, indicating that this stage lies between the directions of southeast and the time between the *chén* and *sì* hours, resembling how the eye of wisdom gradually rises as one advances in practice with this faith.
Skillfully knowing the causes and effects of the field of merit and so forth is called "the Head of the Eyes.

Therefore, the Tathāgata always takes the hours of the morning (Chen and Si) as the standard for observing the fast and precepts; this has already been explained previously in the "Chapter on Names and Titles," and one should understand it by referring to that.
Third, regarding the correspondence between cause and effect: one takes the Buddha of the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom within one's own mind as the cause, and this stage is the ultimate consummation.
Wisdom is the fruit of further cultivation.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Dharmakṣema Bodhisattva: "O Son of the Buddha, the Buddha’s teaching is one;
why is it that when sentient beings attain vision of it, they do not immediately sever all the bonds of affliction and thereby achieve liberation?"

Apart from this, there is no distinction between the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor between the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, ignorance, craving, or existence; such is the Buddha’s teaching regarding sentient beings, whether it brings them benefit or not.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīrapramardin replied in verse:
O Son of the Buddha, listen well; I shall now answer you according to reality.
Some attain swift liberation, while others find it difficult to escape.
If you wish to eliminate immeasurable faults and evils, you should within the Buddha-dharma always exert yourself with courageous diligence, like a tiny spark of fire.
Just as damp firewood is quickly extinguished, so too it is with those who are indolent within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Like one drilling for fire who repeatedly stops before the flame appears—the intensity of the fire ceases accordingly—so too it is with the indolent.
It is like a person holding a sun-crystal who does not use a substance to catch its reflection.
Fire can never be obtained; so it is with the indolent. Just as when the blazing sun shines upon a child who closes its eyes, one wonders why it does not see—so it is with the indolent.
Like a person without hands or feet, who wishes to shoot arrows of mere straw and pierce the entire great earth.
So too it is with the indolent: as if one were to take a single hair-tip to drain the waters of the great ocean until they are utterly dried up, so too it is with the indolent.
Or again, as if the fire at the end of an eon were to arise and one wished to extinguish it with a little water, so too it is with the indolent within the Buddha’s teaching and discipline.
Just as one might see the void Sitting upright and unmoving, Yet say it leaps everywhere—so too is it with those who are indolent.
[Treatise] Sixth: From "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards, the five lines and a half of scripture constitute Mañjuśrī’s question.
Regarding how one may perceive the "Diligent Chief" (Ghoṣadatta) school of Buddhism: there are differences such as whether afflictions (*kleśa*) have been severed or not.
However, from the ten questions below, there are ten verses of verse-lineage which constitute the response given by the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta.
Among these, there are three sections as previously categorized. As for the meaning of the first of these ten verses: [The first verse follows...]

The first line exhorts one to listen; the next line of verse exhorts one to diligently practice the hearing of the Dharma. The eight lines following this clearly reprove one's indolence as explained in the text.
Second, regarding the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name: he is named "Diligent Chief" (*Kusumaśirṣa*) to clarify the preceding objective.

"Chief" indicates the excellence of the field of merit and its causes and effects. The Buddha’s name is "Ultimate Wisdom" (*Anantajñāna*); at this stage, one must necessarily apply oneself with diligence.

Because one practices this, it is called the Buddha "Diligence Chief" (*Vīraśiras*); because one diligently cultivates supreme progress for the sake of attaining the fruit of supreme wisdom (*anuttara-jñāna*), it is called the Buddha "Supreme Wisdom" (*Jñānavara*).
Third, regarding the correspondence of cause and effect according to their respective stages:
again, the original Buddha "Immovable Wisdom" (*Acalajñāna*) serves as the cause, while the Buddha "Supreme Wisdom" serves as the fruit of progressive cultivation.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Dharmottara Bodhisattva:
"O Son of the Buddha, as the Buddha has taught, if there are sentient beings who receive and uphold the True Dharma, they are all able to eliminate and sever all afflictions.
For what reason, then, are there those who receive and uphold the True Dharma yet do not sever them—those who follow greed, hatred, and delusion; who follow pride, concealment, and anger?"
"Regret, envy, stinginess, deceit, and flattery—driven by the power of these, there is no mind free from them that can receive and uphold the Dharma.
For what reason, furthermore, do various afflictions arise within the mental formations? At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmottara answered in verse:
Sons of the Buddha, listen well to the true meaning of what you have asked. One cannot enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata through mere erudition alone.
It is like a person being swept away by water; though fearing drowning, they die of thirst.
So it is with one who does not practice the Dharma despite possessing much learning. It is also like a person who prepares a sumptuous meal.
One who starves oneself and does not eat, yet does not practice the Dharma, is like one who is learned in this way:
though a person may possess excellent prescriptions and medicines, they cannot cure their own illness. One who does not practice the Dharma, despite being much-learned, is just like this.
It is like a person counting another’s treasures, while having not even half a coin for themselves.
One who does not practice the Dharma, though they may be widely learned, is just like this:
it is as if one were born into a royal palace yet suffers from hunger and cold; one who does not practice the Dharma, though they may be widely learned, is just like this.
It is like a deaf person playing music: they please others but do not hear it themselves; so it is for one who does not practice the Dharma.
So too is it with much learning: like a blind man painting various images, he shows them to others but does not see them himself;
one who does not practice the Dharma, though possessing much learning, is just like this.
Like a sea captain who dies at sea, one who does not practice the Dharma, though possessing much learning, is just like this.
Just as one standing at a crossroads might speak at length of various excellent matters, yet possesses no actual virtue within;
so too is it when one does not practice.
[Treatise] The six lines of scripture beginning with "At that time" (the seventh section) are the opening of Mañjuśrī’s inquiry into the Dharma, just as was done by the Buddha.
It is said that if there are sentient beings who uphold the True Dharma, they are all able to eliminate and sever all afflictions (*kleśa*).
For what reason, then, are there those who uphold the True Dharma yet do not sever them? Within this, there are eleven questions, as clearly explained in the text.
Among these, there are ten verses which constitute the response of Dharmottara regarding the meaning of the three gates, as in the previous section.
It seems that within these ten verses of practice, the first line exhorts one to listen; the second line praises the ability to inquire;

the next two lines reprove those who possess much learning but do not practice; and the remaining nine verses—one verse for each—reprove those whose minds lack concentration despite their learning, such that they cannot sever the afflictions, as clearly explained in the text. Second, the explanation of *bodhi* (enlightenment).

Regarding the name "Dharma-Head" (*Dharmottara*): it signifies that within the long night of ignorance and delusion in the northwestern direction between the constellations of Shu and Hai, one is able to benefit oneself and others through the True Dharma, seeking this exclusively without slackening;
thus, he is named Dharma-Head. Regarding the world being named "Vajra": because of its firm vigor and lack of indolence, this world is entrusted to the West.
In the north is the Qian hexagram; Qian represents firmness and strength. The Buddha is named the Buddha of Sovereign Wisdom (Zìzài Zhì).

Because one attains realization through diligent self-observation and reaches the ultimate principle such that karmic activity ceases, he is called the Buddha of Sovereign Wisdom. Regarding the third correspondence of cause and effect according to their respective positions:
taking the Buddha of Original Immovable Wisdom within one's own mind as the cause, one advances in practice to attain the Buddha of Sovereign Wisdom as the fruit.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī: "O Son of the Buddha, within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is the foremost.

For what reason does the Tathāgata sometimes praise giving for the sake of sentient beings, or praise ethical discipline, or praise patience, or praise diligence, or praise meditative concentration, or praise wisdom, or again praise..."
When it was said that one cannot attain liberation or achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of only a single dharma, but rather through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), the Bodhisattva Jñānaśīri replied in verse:
The Son of the Buddha is most rare, Able to know the minds of sentient beings. Listen well now as I explain the meaning of what you have asked:
In the past and future ages, And among the present Guides, there has never been one Who attained the Way by teaching even a single dharma. The Buddha knows the minds of sentient beings.
The dispositions of beings differ from one another; according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, he teaches the Dharma in this way:
to the stingy, he praises giving; to those who violate the precepts, he praises morality;
to the wrathful, he praises patience; to the indolent, he praises diligence; to the distracted, he praises meditative concentration; and to the ignorant, he praises wisdom.
One who lacks benevolence praises loving-kindness; one prone to anger and harm praises great compassion;
one who is sorrowful praises sympathetic joy; and one with a crooked mind praises equanimity. By practicing in this successive order, one gradually fulfills all the Buddha-dharmas.
It is just as one first establishes a foundation and afterwards constructs a palace; so too it is with giving and ethical discipline.
The various practices of the Bodhisattvas are like the construction of city walls;
Patience and diligence are likewise used to protect the multitude of beings, just as they guard all Bodhisattvas.
Just as a powerful king is looked up to by the entire realm, so too are concentration and wisdom that upon which the Bodhisattvas rely.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King Is able to bestow all happiness, So too do the four immeasurables Bestow happiness upon all bodhisattvas.
[Treatise] Eighth: From "At that time" onwards, there are five lines of scripture; this is Mañjuśrī’s questioning of Jñānottara regarding the Tathāgata.
There is one single dharma through which liberation is attained; furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is foremost.

Why, then, are generosity and the other perfections praised? In total, there are ten questions. Their general meaning clarifies that the ten *pāramitās* and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are ultimately without intrinsic nature;
what need is there to employ them? Below, there are ten verses [composed by] the Bodhisattva Jñānacūḍa.
Answer: As clearly explained in the text, among these three sections, the first follows the meaning of the previous chapter. Regarding the intent of the verses:
within these ten verses, the first verse praises the questioner and exhorts the listeners;

the subsequent nine verses—one verse per section—explain, as detailed in the text, the meaning of Mañjuśrī’s response, clarifying that the various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) dispel afflictions according to individual faculties.
If one does not practice and study, the bodhi of non-nature will not be realized; this can be understood from the clear illustrations and analogies provided in the verses.
One must simply rely on the Dharma to treat whatever illness arises, just as when a mound of earth is removed, the path naturally becomes unobstructed.
Once one's own illness has been eliminated, one then administers the medicine to others; thus, the medicine and the prescription are never abandoned. (Two interpretations.)
The name of this Bodhisattva is Jñānaśīra (Wisdom-Head). By means of clear wisdom, he knows the faculties [of beings] and skillfully bestows the medicine of the Dharma.

Through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), he administers them according to where illnesses arise and increase, causing them to be taken. He manifests the unconditioned nature of bodhi and gradually causes them to rely upon it.

His original name was Jñānaśrī. This world below is called Prabhāsvarā, which means "Radiant," because through the ten gates of the pāramitās—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and so forth—it is like the earth in its ability to give rise to and produce all pure and white dharmas.
This world is named Vaidūrya, which is the color of white crystal; the Buddha’s name is Brahmajñāna, which means "Wisdom of the Pure One."
The mind is like the great earth, bearing all things while remaining eternally tranquil and pure; thus, "Brahman" (梵) signifies purity.

Thirdly, regarding the correspondence of cause and effect according to their respective stages: taking the Buddha of one's own inherently unmoving wisdom as the cause, and attaining the tranquility of mental wisdom through progressive cultivation as the result, represents the fact that the essence of the ground is tranquil and still.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha: "O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, attain liberation through only a single path.

Why is it that we now see all the various matters within the Buddha-fields as being diverse and different—namely, the world-systems, the realms of sentient beings, the preaching of the Dharma, the methods of discipline, the lifespans, and the radiance?"
The assemblies of those with supernormal powers, their methods of instruction, and the duration of their abiding each have their distinctions;
yet there is none who does not possess all Buddha-dharmas and thereby attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha answered in verse:
The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is ever thus: The Dharma-King possesses but this one Dharma.
All those who are unimpeded take the single path to transcend birth and death. The bodies of all Buddhas are but this one Dharma-body;
Their single mind and single wisdom, And likewise their powers and fearlessnesses, Are as they were when originally seeking Bodhi.
By whatever mind one dedicates [merit], such a buddha-field is attained;
the assembly there conversely teaches the Dharma, and all the adornments of every buddha-field are perfectly complete.
According to the different conducts of sentient beings, they perceive these things differently: the buddha-fields, the buddha-bodies, the assemblies, and the spoken teachings.

Thus, the dharmas of all Buddhas cannot be seen by sentient beings; yet those whose minds are already purified and whose vows are fully perfected—such wise and realized persons are then able to behold them.
According to the inclinations of sentient beings' minds and the power of their karmic fruits, they perceive these various distinctions.
By the majestic power of this Buddha, the buddha-fields are without distinction;
there is neither aversion nor attachment, yet they appear differently according to the minds of sentient beings.
Thus, what is seen in the world varies for each individual; it is not the fault of the Tathāgatas, the Great Sages.
In all worlds, those who are to be transformed, Constantly see the Heroes among Men;
Such is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
[Treatise] Ninth: From "At that time" onwards, this is the section where Mañjuśrī asks Śrībhadra about the single path of all Buddhas.
Having thus attained liberation, why is it that we now see such various differences? Regarding this, there are ten questions below and ten lines of verse below;
these are the answers given by Bhadrapāla. Within them, there are three sections as in the previous category. The meaning of the verses in these ten lines is as follows:
the first two lines praise the Dharma King as being unique—possessing a single dharma, a single body, and a single wisdom.
The general meaning of the following eight lines of verse consists of four points:

first, praising the differentiation of Buddha-fields as being accomplished by the fundamental mind of dedication, thereby clarifying that dedication accords with the faculties [of beings] to benefit them; second, that both body and land, as well as the methods of teaching, all accord with their faculties;
third, clarifying that the realm of the Buddhas' own retributive fruit is not seen through the causes of practice; fourth, [the remaining point].

The various distinctions among the multitudes arise entirely from the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings; they appear differently according to one's own mind, not because there is any difference in the Buddha.
Fourth, regarding the two explanations for the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) being able to manifest dharmas according to the faculties [of beings]:

first, it is called "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*), which clarifies that by attaining these ten kinds of faith, one believes in the meritorious virtues of the Buddha-fruit and [realizes them] within oneself.

The essence of the mind is thoroughly familiar with the good; having penetrated all doubts, obstructions, and openings, one enters the stage of the Worthy (Śaikṣa), and is thus named "Worthy Head" (Śrī-mukha).

This refers to the higher stages. The intent is to clarify that within this stage of Faith, both the mental wisdom and its objects are entirely like empty space—therein nothing is not contained, and there is no obstruction whatsoever.
Because these are the virtues of a worthy and benevolent person, he is named "Worthy Head. Furthermore, the name of the world is...
The equality of form is luminosity; since the body and mind are united with space above, the world is named Equality of Form.
The Buddha’s title is Wisdom of Contemplative Luminosity (*Vipaśyanā-jñāna-āloka*).

Because he is well able to contemplate all phenomena through the gateway of the emptiness of his own mind, seeing them as entirely empty and free from attachment, he is thus named the Buddha of Contemplative Wisdom. This is the third correspondence.

Regarding the cause and effect according to the stages: taking the Buddha of Fundamental Nature-Emptiness and Non-conceptual Immovable Wisdom as the cause, and through progressive cultivation reaching the Buddha of the Observational Wisdom of Dharma-Emptiness as the fruit;

this clarifies that Immovable Wisdom is the essence (*tattva*) and the Buddha of Observational Wisdom is the function (*vṛtti*), thus manifesting the perfection of essence and function, and the unity of cause and fruit.
Because of this meaning, it is further taught that the Tathāgata’s single body, single mind, and single wisdom-dharma-gate clarify the correspondence between the fruit and the cause;
from beginning to end, they are non-dual, for all are fundamentally rooted in the One. Question:
Why does the first verse state, "The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is ever thus"? Answer: It is because Mañjuśrī is the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Moving wisdom (*citta-jñāna*) is the essence, while Mañjuśrī is the function;
by means of this gate of the essence and function of the fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings, it serves as the essence and function of cause and effect for all those with faith.
Thus, by relying upon the source, until the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit is reached, it remains no different from the cause, because its nature is non-dual. Only then—

The names "initially resolved mind" (*prathamacittotpāda*) and "ultimate mind" (*niṣṭhācitta*) are not distinct; this is to clarify that these ten stages of faith are difficult to resolve, difficult to believe in, and difficult to enter.
Upon hearing this, everyone says, "I am but an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); how could I possibly attain Buddhahood?

Therefore, it is said that even one who possesses a small measure of faith is immediately praised for their spiritual powers and supernatural abilities. For this reason, you should know that for the time being, one must proceed in this manner.
Only when one possesses right faith does one begin to apply the power of right faith and right view through diligent practice, cultivating according to the Dharma.

As ignorance is gradually thinned away, the light of liberating wisdom increases; based on the depth of the Dharma realized within oneself, supernormal powers and spiritual qualities will naturally follow.
Since one has not yet attained even this faith, how can one seek supernormal powers? As for the statement that it occurs "gradually," it is not [as you imply].
Within the single moment, the single dharma-nature, and the single wisdom—amidst that which is without dependence or abiding and is non-apprehensible—one gradually proceeds.
Because the principles of the ten mysteries and six characteristics are perfected within the dharma-nature, there is neither gradual nor sudden;

however, because beginningless ignorance has been habitually cultivated and thoroughly ingrained, it is difficult to suddenly bring about an accord with this principle, and thus there is a "gradual" progression.
That which is "gradual" is so called because it ultimately lacks such measures as beginning or end, extension or brevity, long or short; thus it is named "gradual.
