Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìníng of Kāiyuán Monastery in Fúzhōu during the Táng Dynasty, Collating the Sūtras and Synthesizing the Treatises, Part Ten of the Remainder of the "Chapter on the Questions of the Bodhisattvas Clarifying Wisdom" [Sūtra]:
At that time, the various bodhisattvas addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, as for what we have understood..."
Having each spoken thus, they said: "We pray only that the Benevolent One, by means of your wondrous eloquence, will expound upon the entire domain of the Tathāgata:
what is the Buddha’s domain? What is the cause of the Buddha’s domain? What is the transcendence of the Buddha’s domain?
What is the entry into the Buddha’s domain? What is the wisdom of the Buddha’s domain?"
"What is this Dharma that is the Buddha’s realm? What is taught as the Buddha’s realm?
What is known as the Buddha’s realm? What is realized as the Buddha’s realm? What is manifested as the Buddha’s realm?
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva answered in verse:
The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space; though all sentient beings enter it, in truth there is nothing entered.
The Tathāgata’s profound realm—its victorious and wondrous causes—could not be fully expounded even in billions of eons, for they correspond to the wisdom of their respective minds.
Inducing all to increase their merit, thus they deliver sentient beings;
Into the realms of all Buddhas and all the lands of the world, they enter them all.
The body of wisdom has no form and cannot be seen by them; The wisdom of all Buddhas is sovereign, unimpeded throughout the three times.
Such is the sphere of wisdom, equal and like space; the realm of phenomena and the realm of sentient beings are ultimately without distinction—this is all fully understood.
This is the domain of the Tathāgata: within all worlds, all sounds whatsoever are comprehended by the Buddha’s wisdom.
It is without conceptual differentiation, Not that which can be known by consciousness, Nor is it the domain of the mind;
its nature is fundamentally pure. It reveals itself to all living beings:
Neither karma nor affliction, Without substance and without a place of abiding, Without illumination and without a sphere of activity, It moves through the world with equanimity.
The minds of all sentient beings Pervasively exist throughout the three periods of time; In a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata Comprehends them all with perfect clarity.
[Treatise] The tenth section, from "At that time" onwards, clarifies the passage where the various bodhisattvas collectively question Mañjuśrī. (11)
The ten verses beginning with "Planting the Buddha-realm" constitute Mañjuśrī’s response. Regarding this, there are three sections as in the previous classification;

the meaning of these ten verses is such that each verse corresponds to one [point], and since the meaning of the verses themselves fully answers the preceding questions, there is no need for further explanation. Second, as for the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name: his name is Mañjuśrī.

"Mañjuśrī" is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*); because he possesses wondrous wisdom that skillfully discriminates between the correct and the false with sovereign mastery, he is called "Wondrous Virtue.
This corresponds to the position of the East, the hour of the Rabbit (*mǎo*). It clarifies that the Rabbit presides over the East and the *Zhèn* hexagram;

*Zhèn* represents thunder, movement, and the beginning of awakening from hibernation and the emergence of life. Thus, it clarifies that this wondrous wisdom is the beginning of the movement and emergence of the mind of faith.

Therefore, it is also said that the Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth (Sudhana) was manifested so that all Buddhas might clarify how the ten stages of faith and understanding arise from this wisdom, and so that they might fulfill the ocean-like sea of all vows and practices for enlightenment.

As for the world being named "Golden," it clarifies that by citing the fruit [of Buddhahood], the essence of the cause is revealed as pure, white, and unstained; furthermore, it signifies the two months within the golden womb.
Because the ten stages of faith constitute the sacred embryo, in every place there is a Golden World;

because the wisdom of Mañjuśrī—the luminous, essence-less, pure insight—is omnipresent, the Buddha’s name is Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati*). Since ignorance is fundamentally empty and lacks a substantial entity that could be moved, it is named Immovable Wisdom.
Therein exists only the responsive cognition of phenomena according to conditions and the cognition of faculties according to the capacity of the vessel.
The resonance of the response has no location or physical form; it can be named "wisdom" because there is nothing to be grasped or rejected, and thus it is called "immovable.
Third, regarding the correspondence between cause and effect within their respective positions: wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cause and immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) is the fruit;
yet they also function as cause and effect for one another. If one considers that wondrous wisdom skillfully discriminates phenomena to manifest wisdom, then...

Taking wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) as the cause and immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) as the fruit; if one considers that wisdom arises from wisdom, then immovable wisdom is the cause and wondrous wisdom—Mañjuśrī—is the fruit.

Thus, whether taken individually or collectively, wisdom and insight are both the cause and the fruit, clarifying that essence and function are one true reality, non-dual in their dharma-nature. Furthermore, both wisdom and insight are, in their totality, neither cause nor fruit.

Because the fruit is the essence itself, being without beginning or end, and because it is obtained by relying upon [this] abiding, it is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*—a sovereign knowledge and vision that cannot be attained through worldly analogies of cause and effect.
Thus, from the time Mañjuśrī first gave rise to faith in Akṣobhya Buddha until the final limit of his faith, he never departed from this. Therefore...
Even when he reaches the fulfillment of his own practice and manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment, he does not depart from this;
thus, it is clarified that by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, he instructs and awakens sentient beings, desiring to lead them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

As for this "Buddha’s knowledge and vision," it refers to Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom and the Immovable Wisdom Buddha (Aksobhya-jñāna-buddha). This is the Buddha who is shared equally by both ordinary beings and sages.
[This] causes ordinary beings to awaken and enter [the truth].

[Sūtra]: At that time, within this Sahā world, there were all the various distinctions of dharmas among sentient beings, distinctions of karma, distinctions of worlds, distinctions of bodies, distinctions of faculties, distinctions of births, and distinctions of the fruits of upholding the precepts.
The distinctions in the fruits of violating the precepts and the distinctions in the fruits of the lands were all clearly manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Thus, in the east— extending across hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas, and being innumerable, immeasurable, boundless,
incomparable, uncountable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable— all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space...

All the distinctions among the dharmas of sentient beings within the world-system, up to the distinctions among the fruits of the lands, are all clearly manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power;
the same is true for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

[Treatise] 11. From "At that time" onwards, there are eight lines of sūtra which collectively enumerate the nine kinds of distinctions within the Sahā world, as well as all the distinctions throughout the ten directions;
all of these are clearly manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power, as can be understood from the text.
Above, this has merely followed the questions posed by Mañjuśrī and the respective stages of the bodhisattvas.
Based on the verses spoken by Satadharma, their underlying intent and principles are naturally clear; furthermore, by means of the names of worlds, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas,
one knows that the causes and effects of progressive cultivation are all contained within the previously mentioned four kinds of Buddha-fields—
the Pure Dharma-nature Adorned Fields— specifically the Golden World and the Buddha Immovable Wisdom among them.
The remaining nine worlds within the Buddha-field where [the Bodhisattvas] dwell, along with the nine Wisdom-Buddhas, constitute the Adorned Dharma-nature Buddha-field;
from the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) onward, these are all the Buddha-fields of the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter, which demonstrate the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
The Pure Buddha-fields are the Buddha-fields of the "Four Noble Truths" chapter. The general purport of this single chapter consists of six points, the first being the Bodhisattva.
First, names are used to represent conduct; second, the colors of the world are used to represent the principles attained; third, the names of Buddhas are used to represent the wisdom attained;
fourth, the directions and regions are used to represent the dharmas attained; fifth, these establish the practices performed during the ten stages of faith;
sixth, the similarities and differences in the cultivation of the ten stages of faith are clarified as already described above. Thus it should be understood.
Chapter Eleven: On Pure Conduct (*Śīla-viśuddhi*).
In explaining this chapter, the treatise employs a fourfold analytical framework: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;
third, the explanation of its central tenets and scope; and fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the text. Regarding the first, the explanation of the title: what is it?
Therefore, this is titled the "Chapter on Pure Conduct. Because beginningless views, ignorance, greed, hatred, delusion,

and craving have now been overturned by the arousal of the bodhicitta, faith and joy in the True Dharma, and the sudden transformation of all views into great vows and the gateway of great compassion—
if one were to merely counteract these with the three emptinesses and non-correspondence without generating great kindness and great compassion, one could not achieve success.
Because one wishes to practice the conduct of Samantabhadra, one must travel a long road; yet there is no way to go without feet.

Likewise, one who wishes to practice great compassion, enter the gate of Samantabhadra, and fulfill the conduct that pervades the Dharma-realm, must remain free from error regarding all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Thus, one accomplishes the adornment of the myriad practices by diligently cultivating these one hundred and forty gates of great vows. Thereupon, at once—
Within the ocean of birth and death, all conditioned activities of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are entirely purified because one enters the conduct of Samantabhadra;
therefore, it is called "Pure Conduct. If one lacks this vow, even if one were to sever the afflictions, that would merely be the practice of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
Even if one were a bodhisattva [without this vow], one would only be born in a pure land. By means of these one hundred and forty great vows, one can suddenly [attain]...
Second, because purifying all practices of affliction (*kleśa*) results in the accomplishment of the practices of Samantabhadra’s Dharma-realm, it is called "purifying practice.
Because adorning all worldly practices with this great vow constitutes the universal site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) within the entire Dharma-realm, it is called "purifying practice.
Because these various views bring about the perfection of great roots of goodness, it is called "purifying practice. II.

Regarding the purpose of this chapter’s introduction: it is to clarify that while the preceding "Chapter on Clarifying" (*Viniścaya*) establishes the understanding of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), this chapter establishes the practice of those ten faiths;
therefore, this chapter must follow. Furthermore, until the practices for the fruition are perfected, one does not depart from these great vows;
thus, there are three [points] regarding the core intent of this chapter. As for the title, "Jñānaśrī" (Wisdom Chief) is... [the following portion is missing].
In the world-system called Pāṇḍaravarṇa, the Buddha is named Brahmajñānaprabha.
All the Buddhas take the fundamental essence of the Dharma—the pure, unstained wisdom—as the questioner;
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva takes the excellent, discerning, and wondrous wisdom of all the Buddhas as the master who expounds the Dharma. By means of all...
The gateway to the fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas skillfully serves as the master and attendant for the dialogue on the gateway of the one hundred and forty great vows,
thereby perfecting the inexhaustible ocean of practices of Samantabhadra’s Dharma-realm— namely, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages,
and the eleventh stage— and inquires into its subtlety with primordial pure wisdom.
The wisdom discourse explains that the one hundred and forty gates of pure vows are used to purify, within the six stages beginning with pure faith,
the active manifestations of defiled and pure ignorance, the dharma-grasping of the seven stages, the habitual tendencies of dharma-grasping from the first through the tenth stages,
and the two delusions of the Buddha-stage— all at once. Within this mind of faith, one must not allow for partial attachment, using these vows as a safeguard.
Because it causes the quiescent and the functional to be unimpeded, these various Buddhas, through the gateway of their primordially pure wisdom and sublime insight,
expound one hundred and forty great vows; taking the prevention of the two obstacles of defilement and purity as their primary purpose,
they accord with each stage throughout the six positions, including the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage.
Within the six stages of affliction on the path of cultivation, there are twenty [afflictions] in each stage; thus, across the six stages, there are one hundred and twenty fundamental afflictions.
Furthermore, because the ten root ignorance-afflictions all arise from the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there are twenty [associated with them].

Including these, along with the defiled and purified afflictions that accompany the progress through each stage, there are a total of one hundred and forty. To prevent these, [the following is taught].

By giving rise to one hundred and forty vows to remove obstacles, this practitioner is enabled to achieve the perfect integration of principle and phenomena from the very first stage of the mind of faith.
Thus, the one who possesses faith realizes that the essence of these vows is without deficiency;

through the wisdom of subtle discernment—the fundamental pure wisdom of one's own mind—both movement and stillness are equally true, for there is no partial cultivation. Therefore, within the Flower Treasury World (Huazang Shijie), there is that which resembles... [the text continues].
It is supported by wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Meru; that which is above it is all manner of adornments.

Because great vows act as wind-circles, they are able to sustain the myriad practices, for practices summon their fruits. Thus, through the power of vows, the causes are firmly maintained, and the resultant wind-circles obtained through retribution support the world-systems.
Furthermore, it is said: "All such adornments of the Flower Treasury World arise from the power of Samantabhadra’s vows."
Because there is no aspiration, practice cannot be accomplished; thus, adornment does not manifest, and one fails to elicit the inexhaustible fruits of reliance and retribution.
For this reason, within supreme faith, the Dharma-nature, compassion, wisdom, sublime insight, and the myriad practices all rely upon the Buddha for their existence as they are cultivated.
One must not conceive of them as existing separately; if one were to separate from the Buddha and claim that there is a self-dharma [existing independently], [it would be a delusion].

Without accomplishing faith, one does not accomplish the ten kinds of resolute conviction, nor does one accomplish spiritual practice. Even if one exerts oneself in ascetic practices with diligence, this is false diligence;
though one may toil through many kalpas to be born among humans and devas, a single moment of greed or anger will at once consume it all.
Therefore, the subsequent text of this chapter says: "Abiding in the Way of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, [one acts] in accordance with sentient beings."
Abiding constantly without abandoning [the practice], one is able to thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are;
severing all evil and perfecting all virtues, one shall become like Samantabhadra, supreme in form and appearance, with all practices and vows fully accomplished.
The above clarifies the essential purpose; the intent is to clarify that by dedicating all grasped mental objects, distinctions of mind, and karmic actions, they are all transformed into vows.
Regarding the commentary on the text and its meaning according to the fourfold method of Samantabhadra’s Gate, the meaning herein is divided into two sections:
first, the general intent of this chapter; second, the word-by-word explanation.
As for the first section, the text and meaning of this chapter are divided into fourteen segments.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, how does a bodhisattva attain faultless conduct of body, speech, and mind? How does he attain non-harming conduct of body, speech, and mind?
How does he attain indestructible conduct of body, speech, and mind? How does he attain unbreakable conduct of body, speech, and mind?"
How does one attain non-regressive activity of body, speech, and mind? How does one attain unshakable activity of body, speech, and mind?
How does one attain superior activity of body, speech, and mind? How does one attain pure activity of body, speech, and mind?
How does one attain activity of body, speech, and mind preceded by wisdom?
[Treatise] From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānottara" onwards, there are ten questions in total concerning how one attains faultless actions of body,
speech, and mind; within these ten questions, there are one hundred and ten questions in total regarding the three types of worldly karma, as can be understood from the following.
[Sūtra] How does one obtain fulfillment of birthplace, fulfillment of lineage, fulfillment of family, fulfillment of physical form,
fulfillment of marks, fulfillment of mindfulness, fulfillment of wisdom, fulfillment of conduct, fulfillment of fearlessness, and fulfillment of awakening?
[Śāstra] Regarding the second [topic], "How is birth-endowment produced? among the ten types of endowment, the first is *jāti-sampad* (endowment of lineage), which has two meanings:
first, worldly, which refers to being born into a noble family as one's lineage;

second, supramundane, which refers to being born into the family of the Buddhas and possessing the Buddha-lineage (*gotra*), such that physical marks, mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth, are all those of a Buddha.
Because the household is not of the world.
[Sūtra] What is meant by attaining supreme wisdom, foremost wisdom, highest wisdom, most excellent wisdom,
immeasurable wisdom, incalculable wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, peerless wisdom, unfathomable wisdom, and ineffable wisdom?
[Treatise] 3. Regarding the question "How is it that... and so forth: the ten kinds of wisdom are all supramundane, superior wisdoms, as can be understood from the text.

[Sūtra] How does one obtain the power of the cause, the power of aspiration, the power of skillful means, the power of conditions, the power of the object of focus, the power of the faculties, and the power of investigation?
The power of *śamatha*, the power of *vipaśyanā*, and the power of contemplation.

[Treatise] Regarding the question "What are the four? and so forth, among the ten kinds of powers, the first is the power of the cause, which refers to the spontaneous ability to generate the power of great bodhicitta throughout successive lifetimes.
The power of aspiration refers to the resolve and delight in the mind of great bodhicitta.

Regarding the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*): because one has not fallen away from it, one awakens oneself well through great vows without expending effort, and is likewise able to awaken others, saving labor and avoiding detours.

Regarding the power of conditions (*pratyaya-bala*) and the power of the object (*ālambana-bala*): because one does not forget the objective support (*ālambana*) nor the subject that perceives it (*ālambaka*), one constantly gives rise to great vows.
Regarding the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*): because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the great vows are not lost.
The power of observation consists of the power of discernment (*vipaśyanā*), the power of calm abiding (*śamatha*), and the power of insight (*vipaśyanā*) acting together with calm abiding;

both are mastered whether they proceed in tandem, or whether calm abiding precedes insight, or insight precedes calm abiding, or whether calm abiding and insight are simultaneous, or insight and calm abiding are simultaneous—all of these are mastered. The power of reflection consists of not losing the correct principle.

Because wisdom is constantly present. [Sūtra] What is skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding the sense bases, skillfulness regarding dependent origination, skillfulness regarding the desire realm, skillfulness regarding the form realm,
skillfulness regarding the formless realm, skillfulness regarding the past, skillfulness regarding the future, and skillfulness regarding the present?
Skillful. [Treatise:
Regarding the ten questions beginning with "What are the five," they inquire about the ten types of skillfulness.

First, skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) clarifies that while arising together with the five aggregates of the world, one does not cling to them. Skillfulness regarding the realms (*dhātu-kauśalya*) concerns the eighteen [elements].
Skill in the elements and the factors arising within the three realms: regarding the "place" (*sthāna*), the three realms and the six destinies constitute the place;

regarding the "non-place" (*asthāna*), meditative concentrations and liberations constitute the non-place. Though he does not depart from either the place or the non-place, he remains unstained by them.
Skill in dependent origination: he does not destroy the twelve links of dependent origination in the world, yet he is neither bound by nor defiled by their entanglements.
One who is skilled in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm acts in concert with those in the three realms without attachment.
One who is skilled in the past, future, and present is autonomous regarding the mutual interpenetration of the three periods of time:
because one can dwell in a past eon within a present or future eon, and dwell in a present eon within a past eon. Thus, one is sovereign throughout the three times.

[Sūtra] What is the thorough cultivation of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the joy factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment,
the concentration factor of enlightenment, the equanimity factor of enlightenment, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?

[Treatise] 6. Regarding the ten questions beginning with "What is it that... and so forth, the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the three emptinesses (*trividhaśūnyatā*) may be understood according to the text.

[Sūtra] What is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), as well as the perfection of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
Compassion, joy, and equanimity.

[Treatise] Regarding the seven questions beginning with "How is it that... and so forth, the ten questions concerning the six perfections and the four immeasurables are to be understood according to the text.

[Sūtra] How does one obtain the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma in the past, future, and present, and the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*)?

The power of knowledge of others' faculties, the power of knowledge of various elements, the power of knowledge of various inclinations, the power of knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations,

the power of knowledge of the defilement and purification of meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, the power of knowledge of recollecting past lives, the power of unobstructed divine vision,
and the power of knowledge of the eradication of all latent tendencies.
[Treatise]: Regarding the passage beginning with "What are the eight," the questions concerning the Buddha’s ten powers (daśabala) may be understood according to the text.
[Sūtra]: How is it that one always receives the protection of the kings of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, human kings, and Brahmā kings?
"Protecting, honoring, and making offerings.

[Treatise]: From "What are the nine... onwards, ten questions are posed regarding how these ten kings protect this vidyā-mantra, and how they are drawn to pay homage through the reach of its vows and practices.
[Sūtra] How can one become a support, a rescue, a refuge, a destination, a torch, a light,
an illumination, a guide, a supreme guide, and a universal guide for all sentient beings?

[Treatise] Regarding the ten questions beginning with "What is it that... and so forth: it can be understood from the text that these ask how one is able to serve as a refuge, teacher, and guide for sentient beings.
[Sūtra] How is it that among all sentient beings, one is the foremost, the great, the superior, the most excellent, and...
"Exquisite, most exquisite, supreme, unsurpassed, peerless, and equal to the unequaled.
[Treatise] Regarding the eleven questions beginning with "How is it that...": the question "How is he the most excellent and most exquisite among all sentient beings?
may be understood according to the text.
[Sūtra] At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed Jñānacakra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, son of the Buddha!
Desiring to bring great benefit and great peace to many, out of compassion for the world and for the sake of the welfare and happiness of devas and humans, you have asked about this meaning.
Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas skillfully employ their minds, they will obtain all supreme and wondrous merits."
May your virtue be unimpeded regarding the Buddha-dharma; may you abide in the path of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
may you dwell among sentient beings without ever abandoning them; may you fully penetrate the true nature of all phenomena; may you sever all evil and be endowed with every excellence;
and may you, like Samantabhadra, possess the most supreme physical form and fulfill all practices and vows in their entirety.
There is no Dharma that is not sovereign; as the second teacher for sentient beings, O Son of the Buddha, how should one apply the mind so as to be able to obtain all supreme and wondrous merits?
[Treatise] From "At that time" onwards, up to "supreme and wondrous merits," there are eight lines and a half of scripture.
[The section on] Mañjuśrī’s one hundred and ten questions and the praise for the excellent questioning of Jñānottara.
[Sūtra]: O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva is at home, they should wish that all beings realize the emptiness of the nature of the household and be freed from its oppressions;
when serving their parents with filial piety, they should wish that all beings serve the Buddhas well and protect and nourish all their wives and children; when in assemblies...

May all sentient beings regard enemies and kin with equanimity and forever be free from attachment; should they encounter the five desires, may they wish that all beings extract the arrows of desire and attain ultimate peace and security.
In gatherings for music and entertainment, may they wish that all beings find joy in the Dharma and realize that such pleasures are not real.
Should they dwell in palaces, may they wish that all beings enter the ground of the noble ones and forever eliminate defiled desires and attachments.
When adorning oneself with necklaces, one should wish that all beings cast off all artificial ornaments and reach the realm of reality.

When ascending a multi-storied pavilion, one should wish that all beings ascend the tower of the True Dharma and perceive all things clearly. When practicing giving, one should wish that all beings be able to relinquish everything, their minds free from attachment.
When gathering in a great assembly, one should wish that all beings abandon the phenomena of worldly congregation and achieve [the state of non-congregation].
When encountering all-knowledge amidst hardships and calamities, may all beings attain mastery of their will, so that their actions are unimpeded;
when leaving the household life, may all beings attain the unimpeded renunciation of the homeless life and achieve liberation of mind;
when entering a monastery, may all beings expound various dharmas without discord or contention; when approaching teachers, great or small, may all beings become skillful...

When serving teachers and elders, practicing the wholesome Dharma, and requesting ordination, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the dharma of non-retrogression and have minds free from obstruction.
When casting off secular clothing, one should wish that all sentient beings diligently cultivate roots of goodness and abandon all yokes of sin.
When shaving off hair and beard, one should wish that all sentient beings forever leave afflictions behind and reach ultimate quiescence. When donning the kashaya robes, one should...

May all sentient beings have minds free from defilement and be endowed with the Way of the Great Sage; when they truly renounce the world, may they vow that all sentient beings likewise renounce the world as the Buddha did to rescue and protect all.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may they vow that all sentient beings perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and give rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may they vow that all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom becoming like the ocean.
When returning to the Sangha, one should wish that all beings govern the great assembly without any hindrance.

When receiving and studying the precepts, one should wish that all beings skillfully learn the precepts and commit no evil. When receiving the instructions of the ācārya, one should wish that all beings be fully endowed with dignified deportment and that their conduct be true and real.
When receiving the instructions of the upādhyāya, one should wish that all beings enter the wisdom of non-arising and reach [the ultimate].
When receiving full ordination without reliance on a formal assembly, one should wish that all sentient beings be endowed with all skillful means and attain the most supreme Dharma.
When entering a hall or building, one should wish that all sentient beings ascend the unsurpassed hall and abide therein immovably.

When spreading out a bed or seat, one should wish that all sentient beings unfold and manifest wholesome dharmas and perceive the true mark. When sitting upright with the body straight, one should wish that all sentient beings sit [in the same manner].

When sitting cross-legged at the seat of enlightenment with a mind free from attachment, one should wish that all sentient beings have roots of goodness firmly established and attain the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
When practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one should wish that all sentient beings subdue their minds through concentration until nothing remains.
When practicing insight (*vipaśyanā*), one should wish that all sentient beings perceive reality as it is and forever be free from conflict. When rising from the cross-legged posture, one should...

May all sentient beings contemplate that all conditioned phenomena ultimately dissolve and perish. When setting their feet down, may they wish that sentient beings attain liberation of mind and abide immovably.
When lifting their feet, may they wish that sentient beings emerge from the ocean of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
When putting on their lower garments, may they wish that sentient beings clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and be fully possessed of shame and remorse.
When tying one's belt, one should wish that sentient beings restrain their roots of goodness so they are not lost or scattered.

When putting on the upper garment, one should wish that sentient beings obtain supreme roots of goodness and reach the further shore of the Dharma. When donning the saṃghāṭī robe, one should wish that sentient beings enter the foremost stage and attain the state of immovability.
When holding a willow twig in hand, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the wondrous Dharma and reach its ultimate depths.
When finishing the act of chewing the tooth-stick, one should wish that all sentient beings have minds that are harmonized and pure, devouring all afflictions.
When voiding excrement or urine, one should wish that all sentient beings cast away greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.

When concluding the task and approaching water, one should wish that all sentient beings swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma. When washing away physical impurities, one should wish that all sentient beings be purified.
When washing one's hands with water that is pure, supple, and ultimately stainless, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
When washing one’s face with water, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the gates of the pure Dharma, forever free from defilement.
When holding a *khakkhara* staff, one should wish that all sentient beings establish great assemblies of giving and demonstrate the path of reality. When holding an alms bowl, one should...
May all sentient beings become accomplished vessels for the Dharma, receiving the offerings of devas and humans, and setting out upon the path toward enlightenment.

When setting out upon the path, may all sentient beings advance toward the conduct of the Buddhas and enter the state of non-reliance. While traveling on the road, may all sentient beings be able to practice the Buddha-way and head toward the Dharma of no-remainder.
As they proceed along the way, may all sentient beings tread upon the pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) with minds free from obstruction, seeing clearly.
When seeing an ascending path, one should wish that all beings forever transcend the triple world with minds free from cowardice;
when seeing a downward path, one should wish that all beings have humble minds and long cultivate the roots of Buddha-virtue;

when seeing a crooked path, one should wish that all beings abandon improper paths and forever eliminate evil views; when seeing a straight path, one should wish that all beings have upright minds and no... [deceit].
Seeing a road with dust from flattery and deceit, one should wish that all beings remain far removed from defilement and attain the pure Dharma.
Seeing a road free of dust, one should wish that all beings always practice great compassion and that their minds be moistened with kindness.

Seeing a perilous path, one should wish that all beings abide in the realm of the True Dharma and be freed from all calamities of transgression. Seeing a great assembly, one should wish that all beings preach...
When encountering all things in profound harmony, one should wish that all beings be free from the mind of self-contention and harbor no anger or resentment.
When seeing a great pillar, one should wish that all beings be worthy of the veneration of gods and humans.
When seeing a high mountain, one should wish that all beings have roots of goodness so transcendent that none can reach their summit. When seeing a thorny tree, one should...

May all sentient beings swiftly cut away the thorns of the three poisons. When seeing the lush foliage of trees, may they wish that all sentient beings take meditative concentration and liberation as their shade.
When seeing flowers bloom, may they wish that all sentient beings manifest the dharma of supernatural powers and so forth, like blossoming flowers.
When seeing the flowers upon the trees, may they wish that all sentient beings possess the various marks, like those flowers, complete with the thirty-two signs of a great man.
Upon seeing fruit, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the most supreme Dharma and realize the path to Bodhi.
Upon seeing a great river, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the stream of the Dharma and flow into the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.

Upon seeing a marsh or pond, one should wish that all sentient beings swiftly awaken to the single-flavored Dharma of all Buddhas. Upon seeing a pool, one should wish that all sentient beings fulfill their verbal karma and become skillful.
When able to expound the teaching, if one sees a well being drawn from, one should wish that all sentient beings be endowed with eloquence to expound all dharmas;
if one sees a spring gushing forth, one should wish that all sentient beings increase their roots of goodness through skillful means without exhaustion;

if one sees a bridge or a path, one should wish that all sentient beings extensively deliver all beings, just like a bridge; if one sees flowing water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain...
When wishing to wash away the stains of delusion, one should wish that all sentient beings cultivate the garden of insight and cultivation;
when seeing the grove of sorrowlessness, one should wish that all sentient beings forever leave behind craving and attachment, and give rise to neither sorrow nor fear;

when seeing a park or garden, one should wish that all sentient beings diligently practice all deeds to advance toward the Bodhi of the Buddha; when seeing a person adorned with ornaments, one should...
When seeing those adorned with the thirty-two marks, may all sentient beings vow to adorn themselves with these very marks.
When seeing those without adornment, may they vow that all sentient beings abandon all finery and ornaments, and be fully endowed with the dhūta practices.

When seeing those who delight in and are attached to worldly things, may they vow that all sentient beings find joy in the Dharma alone, loving it without ever forsaking it. When seeing those who have no such attachment, may they vow that all sentient beings find no pleasure in the affairs of the conditioned world.
Seeing people who are joyful, one should wish that all beings may always attain peace and happiness and joyfully make offerings to the Buddhas.
Seeing people who are suffering, one should wish that all beings may obtain fundamental wisdom and extinguish all their afflictions.

Seeing people who are not ill, one should wish that all beings may enter into true wisdom and forever be free from sickness and distress. Seeing people who are ill, one should wish that all beings may realize the emptiness and stillness of the body and be detached from it.
Upon seeing those who dispute the Dharma, one should wish that sentient beings always give rise to pure faith in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Upon seeing those who are physically unattractive, one should wish that sentient beings do not give rise to attachment toward unwholesome things.

Upon seeing those who repay kindness, one should wish that sentient beings be able to recognize the grace and virtue of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Upon seeing those who betray kindness, one should wish that sentient beings...
When encountering wicked people who do not repay kindness, one should wish that all beings become harmonious, gentle, and tranquil, ultimately reaching the supreme state.

When seeing śramaṇas, one should wish that all beings forever maintain the Brahma-conduct and remain free from all evil. When seeing brahmins, one should wish that all beings eternally uphold the Brahma-conduct and depart from all evils.
When seeing practitioners of asceticism, one should wish that all beings rely upon the practice of austerity until they reach the ultimate goal. When seeing those of steadfast conduct...
When seeing sentient beings who firmly maintain their resolve and conduct without abandoning the Buddha-way, may they don armor;

may they vow that all sentient beings shall always wear the armor of goodness and advance toward the Teacherless Dharma. When seeing those without armor or weapons, may they vow that all sentient beings shall forever be free from all unwholesome karma.
When seeing those engaged in debate, may they vow that all sentient beings shall be able to utterly subdue all heterodox arguments. When seeing... [the text ends here].
When encountering one who lives by right livelihood, one should wish that all beings attain a pure livelihood and do not feign dignified deportment.
When seeing a king, one should wish that all beings become Dharma-kings and constantly turn the wheel of the True Dharma.

When seeing a prince, one should wish that all beings be born through transformation from the Dharma and become children of the Buddha. When seeing an elder, one should wish that all beings be skillfully able to discern and judge with clarity.
When practicing unwholesome dharmas, if one sees a high minister, one should wish that all beings always maintain right mindfulness and practice all manner of goodness.
If one sees a city wall, one should wish that all beings attain a firm and stable body and mind, never yielding to anything.

If one sees a royal capital, one should wish that all beings gather their merits together and their minds are ever joyful. When seeing a place of forest thickets, one should wish that all beings... [respond appropriately].
When being praised and looked up to by devas and humans, may all beings enter the profound Dharma-realm with minds free from obstruction.
When entering the gates of people's homes to beg for food, may all beings enter the gates of all Buddha-dharmas.
Having entered their houses, may all beings attain entry into the Buddha-vehicle, which is equal throughout the three periods of time, and never abandon those they see.

May sentient beings never abandon the supreme dharmas of merit; upon seeing one who is able to practice renunciation, may they vow that all sentient beings forever attain liberation from the sufferings of the three evil realms.
Upon seeing an empty bowl, may they vow that the minds of all sentient beings be pure and empty of afflictions.
Upon seeing a full bowl, may they vow that all sentient beings be fully endowed with and perfected in all wholesome dharmas.
When receiving respect, one should wish that all beings respectfully practice all Buddha-dharmas. When not receiving respect, one should wish that all beings do not practice any unwholesome dharmas.
Upon seeing those who possess a sense of shame and modesty, one should wish that all beings be endowed with the practice of shame and modesty and guard their sense faculties.
Upon seeing those who lack shame and modesty, one should wish that all beings abandon such shamelessness and abide [in virtue].
With great compassion, if one obtains fine food, one should wish that all sentient beings may fulfill their aspirations and be free from covetous desire;
if one obtains coarse food, one should wish that all sentient beings may obtain the flavor of all samādhis;

if one obtains soft and tender food, one should wish that all sentient beings be permeated by great compassion and have minds that are supple and gentle; if one obtains rough and astringent food, one should wish that all sentient beings... [have] minds...

Being free from attachment and severing worldly craving, when eating food, one should wish that all sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their nourishment and be filled with the delight of the Dharma.
When tasting flavors, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the supreme flavor of the Buddhas and be satisfied by the nectar of immortality.
When the meal is finished, one should wish that all sentient beings have accomplished all that was to be done and be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas. When preaching the Dharma, one should wish...

May all sentient beings attain inexhaustible eloquence to widely proclaim the essentials of the Dharma. When leaving the house, may they aspire that all sentient beings enter deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom and forever transcend the triple world.
When entering water, may they aspire that all sentient beings enter into all-knowledge and realize the equality of the three periods of time.
When bathing their bodies, may they aspire that all sentient beings have no defilement in body or mind, becoming pure and radiant within and without.
During the heat of summer, may all sentient beings abandon all afflictions until they are entirely exhausted.
At the onset of the cool season when the heat has subsided, may all sentient beings realize the unsurpassed Dharma and attain ultimate purity and coolness.

When reciting the sutras, may all sentient beings follow what the Buddha has taught, attaining dhāraṇī so as not to forget. If they should behold a Buddha, may all sentient beings obtain the unobstructed eye and see.
When contemplating all Buddhas with true insight, one should wish that all sentient beings be as upright, handsome, and magnificent as Samantabhadra.
When seeing a Buddha stupa, one should wish that all sentient beings respect others as they do a stupa, receiving offerings and reverence from devas and humans.

When viewing a stupa with a reverent mind, one should wish that all sentient beings be gazed upon and prostrated to by both devas and humans at their stupas. When [viewing] a stupa, one should wish that all sentient beings... [one]... one.

When all devas and humans are unable to see the crown of one’s head, as one circumambulates the stupa to the right, one should wish that sentient beings act without opposition and achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
When circumambulating the stupa three times, one should wish that sentient beings diligently seek the Buddha-way with minds free from weariness.
When praising the merits of the Buddha, one should wish that sentient beings be fully endowed with all virtues, their praises being inexhaustible. When praising the Buddha’s marks and signs...

May all sentient beings achieve the Buddha-body and realize the signless Dharma. When washing their feet, may they vow that all sentient beings be endowed with the power of the divine feet, so that their movements are unimpeded.
When sleeping or resting at the proper time, may they vow that all sentient beings attain peace and stability of body and that their minds are free from agitation.
Upon first awakening from sleep, may they vow that all sentient beings awaken to all-knowledge and survey the ten directions.
[Treatise] Following the section "The thirteen sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, while at home," there are one hundred and forty great vows that answer the preceding questions.
These are intended for Bodhisattvas of the ten levels of faith to constantly apply to their minds, thereby purifying their conduct of body,
speech, and mind, as clearly elucidated in the text.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, if Bodhisattvas apply their minds in this way, they will attain all supreme and wondrous merits,
which cannot be shaken by any of the world’s devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, asuras,
or by any of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

[Treatise] Regarding the fourteen lowest sons of the Buddha: if Bodhisattvas possess the three practices as clarified in the sutras and act in accordance with the teachings, they will obtain their supreme benefits.

Thus far, these one hundred and forty kinds of worldly phenomena have been suddenly transformed into one hundred and forty kinds of great vows, used to establish the mind of practice within the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
Although this is a conditioned mind, it is capable of accomplishing the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the five subsequent positions;

the ocean of wisdom, principle, and great compassion, as well as the subsequent entry into the ocean of myriad practices, are all made possible by the superior power of these one hundred and forty great vows as their dominant condition. Therefore, if a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind lacks these...
May all the liberations cultivated through my vows result in the practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

even if these bodhisattvas are born only in pure lands and lack the conditions for attaining buddhahood, may those who have resolved their minds within this teaching ultimately realize that these conditioned phenomena are suchness,
thereby perfecting their wisdom and insight.

Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on the Worthy Head (Bhadramukha), Part One [Treatise] In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to five sections: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;
third, an elucidation of the central theme and intent of the chapter; fourth, an explanation of the regression and stabilization of faith; and fifth, an exegesis of the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter: Why is it named "Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha*)? It is because the name "Bodhisattva" is established based on his practice;
and the name of the chapter is established based on the Dharma and the practices taught by that Bodhisattva.

He is called "Worthy Leader" because he possesses clear faith and understanding in the causes and effects of the Tathāgata, and because his mental activities and conduct are pliant, harmonious, and compliant within the five stages of Samantabhadra’s practice-gates.

One who possesses an upright and profound mind, maintains right mindfulness, delights in accumulating roots of goodness, and constantly thinks of benefiting sentient beings is called "Worthy" (Bhadra).

One in whom the Dharma-realm is suddenly manifested from the state of an ordinary person, such that the cause and fruit, wisdom and prajñā of all Buddhas appear simultaneously, is called "Foremost" (Śrī).
These names are established according to the Master's [Fa-zang’s] understanding and practice; this "Worthy Foremost" (Xianshou) refers to the Buddha-fruit.

Because Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are the foremost of those who practice the conduct of the ocean [of virtues], being the foremost in faith regarding the Buddha’s cause and effect, wisdom and principle, and the perfection of the dharma-realm through understanding and practice without beginning or end;

and because they are the initial leaders for those who bring about the fruit-conduct of the Buddha’s Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra through faith—thus, this is titled the "Chapter on the Foremost" (*Śirṣaka-parivarta*). Regarding the second explanation of the purpose of this chapter: it is...

From the second assembly onwards, the five preceding chapters have only clarified the dharma-gates practiced by bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), as well as the one hundred and forty vows and other such dharmas.

This present chapter is presented because it clarifies the vastness of the merit of the practices and vows performed toward the fruit of Buddhahood—which is the object of aspiration within the ten stages of faith—and the conduct undertaken therein. Third, the essential purpose (*abhiprāya*) is explained.
This clarifies that having already given rise to the ten types of faith, one attains blessings and gains benefit; this is the primary thesis.

Fourth, regarding the meaning of "retrogression and abiding" within faith, there are two senses: first, the Three Vehicles, and second, the One Vehicle. Regarding the Three Vehicles, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, there are three kinds of arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*):
first, the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith, wherein the roots of goodness continue uninterrupted for ten thousand kalpas.
Regarding the second point, "reaching the stage of non-retrogression": this refers to generating the mind through the practice of understanding and conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*).

One may generate the mind by following the instructions of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or out of one's own great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), or by wishing to protect the True Dharma when it is about to perish. As the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* states:
"When such faith is perfected, one enters the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and never again regresses; this is called abiding within the lineage of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the primary cause, the two types mentioned previously constitute the non-retrogressive arousal of the mind. As for the third, the arousal of the mind through realization:

if there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha and receive offerings from him, they may give rise to the seeds of humans and devas or the seeds of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Even if they seek the Mahāyāna, their faculties...
Thus, they are not fixed, sometimes advancing and sometimes retreating. This is because their own roots of goodness are slight and they rely on others to arouse the mind;
or because they have been led to arouse the mind by means of the Two Vehicles; or because their practice of understanding and conduct is unreal.

Consequently, they all experience attainment and realization, as well as abandonment and grasping, remaining generally in a state of regression. Furthermore, as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "If a person practices..."
Because all wholesome dharmas naturally accord with the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena, the skillful means (*upāya*) are briefly explained as being of four kinds.

First is the fundamental skillful means of practice: it consists of contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn and free from false views, thereby not abiding in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
and contemplating that all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, such that the retribution of karma is never lost.

First, through the cultivation of great compassion and the accumulation of merit, one gathers and transforms sentient beings while not abiding in nirvana, because this accords with the non-arising nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Second, the ability to cease [unwholesome states] through skillful means: by means of shame, remorse, and repentance, one can cease all unwholesome dharmas so that they do not increase, thereby acceding to the nature of phenomena and remaining free from all faults. Third, the arousal of roots of goodness and their increase.
"Long-term skillful means" refers to diligently making offerings, prostrating to, praising, rejoicing in, and requesting the Buddhas of the Triple Gem.
Because of a heart of love and respect and a heart of profound sincerity, one's faith increases, thereby enabling one to aspire to the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, because one is protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one can eliminate karmic obstacles and ensure that one's roots of goodness do not regress.
Fourth is the skillful means of the equality of great vows, which accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) by being free from the obscuration of delusion;
that is to say, the vow to transform and deliver all sentient beings without exception throughout the future,
leading them all to ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder, because it accords with the nature of phenomena, which is vast, pervasive across all sentient beings, equal, and non-dual.
Because they contemplate the ultimate quiescence of both self and others, and because Bodhisattvas give rise to such a mind, they attain a partial vision of the Dharmakāya.
By virtue of this vision of the Dharmakāya, they are able to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment according to their vow-power to benefit sentient beings.
Nevertheless, these Bodhisattvas are not yet designated as the Dharmakāya, because throughout their immeasurable past lives...

Regarding the influx of out-flowing karma (*āsrava-karma*) which has not yet been decisively severed, it corresponds to subtle suffering according to its arising, as explained at length in that treatise.

Calculating even a small portion of this, one attains the vision of the Dharma-body; this is the Bodhisattva who has fulfilled the stage of faith (*śraddhā-paripūrṇa*) and entered the first stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).
The above constitutes the third vehicle’s arousal of the tenfold mind of faith, the fulfillment of that mind, and the entry into the initial stage of the ten abidings.
Above the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), one attains Buddhahood through the power of vows.

Regarding those who resolve their minds according to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as in this sutra, at the moment of the initial resolution of mind during the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), they manifest the fruit of the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment within the first assembly.

Through the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), they accord with the infinitely layered and inexhaustible pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, which are as numerous as the atoms of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Arising from the fruits of practice, one gives rise to faith; by believing in the fruits attained by all other Buddhas—specifically the fruit of the Tathāgata’s perfected retribution and the fruits of practice in the Second Assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance—one personally enters and practices with confidence.
The ten colored worlds, such as the Golden World, clarify the principle of self-awakening, namely the Ten [Buddhas] beginning with Acala-jñāna Buddha (the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom).
That "Wisdom Tathāgata" clarifies that what one believes is the Buddha-wisdom of one's own mind;

Mañjuśrī clarifies that the sublime wisdom of the discernment within one's own mental consciousness is identical in essence and function to all Buddhas of the past, present, and future, without the slightest discrepancy—this alone is called "faith. From this faith, one takes up the name of the Buddha.
The Chapter on the Ten Directions clarifies that the titles of the Buddha-fruit—the manifestation of perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions—pervade everywhere;

the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths clarifies that the Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time pervade the realm of sentient beings, with their names varying according to those realms;
and the Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment clarifies that the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-light universally illumines the entire Dharma-realm.
There is no end to those who are caused to give rise to faith; by observing them through observation, one causes the mind to become vast and expansive like the realm of a Buddha.

Thus, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination," the ten kinds of practices performed by a bodhisattva of the ten levels of faith are explained as the very practices one cultivates for oneself.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Pure Practices" contains the one hundred and forty great vows, which are precisely these ten.
The great vows generated at the stage of the position of faith constitute the gateway of great compassion and fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra;

this "Chapter on the Head of the Wise" elucidates the inexhaustible merits of the Buddha-fruit as rejoiced in by the ten levels of faith, clarifying the initial generation of these ten levels of faith.
It is taught that the merit of reciting and upholding this chapter surpasses the merit of making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields.
If this is so for a single eon, how much more so when one cultivates and refines [the practice] according to one's own understanding and conduct?

Thus, at the very moment the initial mind is generated within the first stage of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is the natural law that the body pervades the ten directions and manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

Although this is clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Merit of Generating the Mind" within the context of the Ten Stages, the details are extensive and have not been cited here; the reasons for this are manifold.
This clarifies that the ten faith-minds of this sutra are generated solely by means of the inconceivable vehicle of the dharma-realm and the vehicle of omniscience;
they are generated without relying on the Buddha, without relying on the Buddha-dharma, without relying on the bodhisattva-dharma,
without relying on the śrāvaka-dharma or the pratyekabuddha-dharma, without relying on worldly dharmas, and without relying on supramundane dharmas.
That mind is simply without dependence; it generates the bodhicitta solely by means of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

It does not generate the bodhicitta as the three vehicles do, which rely upon external objects; nor does it generate the bodhicitta based on the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
nor does it generate the bodhicitta based on the existence of the fruit of Buddhahood within the present or the three periods of time.

Because of this meaning, those who enter this faith shall never fall back. Therefore, even for those whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet matured, there is no falling back from their temporary mindfulness of faith or their state of abiding; this constitutes right faith.
One’s own body and mind are entirely the *dharmadhātu*, for Buddhas possess no nature of self or other. Thus, because the Buddhas of the ten directions are... [no difference].

By relying on the gateways of the adornments of the wisdom-abiding and illusion-abiding [samādhis], and so forth, one attains such faith and understanding as follows: that the Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and the nature of phenomena are eternally pervasive throughout the ten directions;

that the form-bodies appear like reflections facing one another because they are identical to one's own body, because they are fundamentally non-dual, and because their essence is without distinction;
and that the wisdom-bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions are like reflections and their speech is like echoes. Thus one shall attain it.
I who now believe that one attains Buddhahood likewise know and believe and resolve it thus: How could there be any regression?
The entire body and the whole mind—every single realm—is entirely the Dharma-realm;
the essence and function, principle and wisdom of the One True Dharma-body abide nowhere. If the body and mind have something upon which they rely, cast off that reliance.
Abiding thus, one attains the non-retrogression that realizes the body and mind are fundamentally without dependence or dwelling and fundamentally unattainable;
that all linguistic discrimination is like an echo in space, produced without effort through conditions as objects give rise to sound, fundamentally without dependence or dwelling.
To give rise to faith and understanding in such a Dharma is itself non-retrogression, and it is upon this basis of reliance that one gives rise [to the aspiration for enlightenment].
The mind, when it releases what has been attained and the locus of its attachment, immediately undergoes regression. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Those who have realized the arousal of the mind mostly abide in a state of regression, because they possess something attained that can be realized.
For this reason, one should ride upon this inconceivable vehicle—the vehicle of omniscience that has no basis for abiding—and arouse the bodhicitta; once set forth, it does not [regress].
If there is regression, it is solely because one’s faith has not been perfected; because one perceives attainability within the Buddha’s teachings and the vehicle of the Tathāgata;
because one engages in acceptance and rejection; and because faith has not yet been established, one does not enter the stream of faith. Furthermore, this sutra states:
"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six perfections..."

Even those who possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and are endowed with the *pāramitās*, if they have not yet heard this *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, are still called "provisional bodhisattvas" and are not true bodhisattvas. Even if they should hear it, they do not believe or enter into it, as described in detail in the sūtra.
As the verse in this chapter says: "Among all the multitudes of living beings in all worlds, few desire to seek the state of a śrāvaka."
Those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha are even fewer; those who set out for the Mahāyāna are extremely rare to encounter.
While setting out for the Mahāyāna is still considered relatively easy, being able to have faith in this Dharma is many times more difficult. Furthermore, as the verse below states:
"To take up ten Buddha-fields with one's hands and remain suspended in mid-air for an entire kalpa—such an act is not yet difficult; to be able to have faith [in this Dharma] is far more so."
This Dharma is even more difficult to transcend; it is difficult to believe, yet one who can believe in it possesses true faith and is certain not to regress.

Furthermore, as stated in this sutra by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "Even if one merely hears the names of the Tathāgatas and the Dharma-gates they teach, and though hearing them does not believe, one can still establish the seed of Vajra-wisdom—just as a person who consumes a small amount of vajra."

The analogy is as follows: if one considers it from the perspective of distant causes, there is no overall regression; however, if one considers it from the perspective of the causes for attaining Buddhahood in the present life, this refers to those who have not yet attained faith.

[Sūtra] At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had spoken on the great merit of the pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion, he wished to reveal the merit of the bodhicitta;
therefore, he questioned the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha in verse, saying:
I have now, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, Expounded the pure practices cultivated by the Buddha in the past;
You, O Benevolent One, should likewise within this assembly Proclaim and expound upon the supreme merits of such cultivation.
[Commentary] First, the two lines of scripture beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī... and the two lines of verse are spoken by Mañjuśrī.
The section on the Merit of Generating the Bodhicitta, requested by Mañjuśrī.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied in verse.
[Treatise] Second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied in verse" onwards, there are seven hundred and ten [verses].

These six lines of verse constitute the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla’s response; they clarify the final three and a half lines of the sutra and represent the section on the verses being granted approval by all the Buddhas.
[Sūtra] Excellent, O virtuous one! You should listen attentively: Those merits are immeasurable.
I now speak but a small portion according to my ability, like a single drop of water from the great ocean.
If there is a bodhisattva who first resolves their mind and vows to realize the Buddha’s bodhi, the merit of that person is boundless; it cannot be measured and has no equal.

How much more so for immeasurable and boundless eons— The merits of fully cultivating the stages and the perfections, Which all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions Together praise without being able to exhaust them.
Such are these boundless great merits; I shall now speak but a small portion of them.
Just as the space traversed by a bird’s feet, Or like a single atom of the great earth. [Commentary:

Thirdly, from the verse beginning “Excellent! O virtuous one, you should listen attentively” and continuing for eight lines, the vastness and immeasurability of the merit of generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) are clarified;
it is explained according to one's capacity that this is only a slight description, divided [into sections] to clarify that the *bodhicitta* cannot be fully encompassed.
Because it is the ultimate measure, its merit shall likewise be such.
[Sūtra] When a bodhisattva resolves their mind to seek awakening, it is not without cause nor without condition;
by generating pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, they thereby give rise to the vast mind.
Seeking neither the five desires nor royal rank, Nor wealth, personal pleasure, or great renown,
But solely for the eternal extinction of the suffering of sentient beings, And for the benefit of the world, they resolve their minds.
Constantly wishing to bring benefit and happiness to all beings, They adorn the buddha-fields and make offerings to the Buddhas.
"Upholding the True Dharma and cultivating all wisdoms, they resolve their minds for the sake of realizing Bodhi.
[Commentary: From "The four types of bodhisattvas resolve their minds to seek Bodhi" onwards, these six lines of verse clarify the section on the causes for the initial resolution of the mind.
[Scripture] With a profound mind of faith and understanding, always pure, they revere and honor all Buddhas;
they do likewise for the Dharma and the Saṅgha. With sincere devotion they make offerings and resolve their minds upon it;
they have deep faith in the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma, and they also believe in the path practiced by the sons of the Buddha.
And having faith in the unsurpassed Great Bodhi— this initial resolve of the bodhisattva, born of faith,
is the primordial source of the Way and the mother of all merit. It nurtures all wholesome dharmas, cuts through the net of doubt,
and brings one out from the current of craving, revealing the unsurpassed path to Nirvana.
Faith is unstained and turbidless, purifying the mind; it eradicates arrogance and is the root of reverence.
It is also the foremost treasure within the Dharma-treasury. Faith serves as the pure hand that receives all practices;
through faith one can bestow wisdom with a heart free from stinginess. Faith enables one to enter the Buddha-dharma with joy.
Faith can increase the merit of wisdom; faith can surely lead one to the stage of the Tathāgata.
Faith causes the faculties to be pure, clear, and sharp; the power of faith is firm and indestructible.
Faith can forever extinguish the root of afflictions; faith can single-mindedly direct one toward the virtues of the Buddha.
Faith is unattached to sense objects; It distances one from all hardships and attains the ease of being free from them.
Faith can transcend the paths of all Māras, Revealing the unsurpassed path of liberation.
Faith is the indestructible seed of merit; Faith can cause the Bodhi tree to grow.
Faith can increase the most supreme wisdom; faith can manifest all Buddhas.
Therefore, I shall explain according to the sequence of practice. Such supreme devotion through faith is extremely difficult to find;
it is like a wondrous wish-fulfilling jewel existing within the entire world.
