[Sūtra] All Tathāgatas together proclaim that the karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable.
The transformations of the various nāgas and the sovereign power of the Buddhas, as well as the inconceivable spiritual might of the bodhisattvas—
though one might wish to demonstrate these through metaphors, no metaphor exists that can truly illustrate them.
Nevertheless, those of wise and discerning intellect may understand their meaning by means of metaphors.
The minds of the śrāvakas abide in the eight liberations; all their manifestations are sovereign.
They can manifest many bodies from a single body, and again manifest a single body from many bodies.
Entering the fire-samādhi within the void, they walk, stand, sit, and lie down entirely in space.
Water flows from the upper body and fire from the lower; Fire flows from the upper body and water from the lower.
Thus, within a single thought-moment, They exercise various kinds of mastery in boundless measure.
Yet, lacking great compassion, They do not seek the path of the Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.
If they can still manifest such inconceivable deeds, how much more so their power of great benefit and mastery?
Like the sun and moon traveling through the void, their reflections pervade the ten directions;
in the waters of springs, ponds, marshes, and vessels, as well as in rivers, seas, and all precious waters, there is nowhere they do not appear.
The physical forms of the Bodhisattvas are likewise so; they manifest universally throughout the ten directions in an inconceivable manner.
These are all the sovereign dharmas of samādhi, which only a Tathāgata can fully realize and comprehend.
They are like the reflections of the fourfold army in clear water; each is distinct and separate, without confusion or admixture.
Swords, halberds, bows, and arrows are of many kinds; armor, helmets, chariots, and carriages are of no single sort.

According to their various characteristics and differences, there is none that does not appear within the water, yet the water itself is fundamentally without discrimination. The samādhi of the Bodhisattva is also like this.
In the ocean there is a deity named Good Sound; His voice universally accords with the speech of all sentient beings in the sea, And he clearly articulates it all, causing them all to rejoice.
Although that deity possesses greed, anger, and delusion, He is still able to skillfully understand all sounds.
How much more so, given the power of mastery over dhāraṇīs—how could one not cause the multitude to rejoice?
There was a woman named Prajñā (Eloquence), born through her parents' prayers to the gods;
if there are those who abandon evil and delight in the truth, may wondrous eloquence enter their bodies and arise within them.
If those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion can still provide eloquence by following [the teachings],
how much more so for a bodhisattva endowed with wisdom— who could not bring benefit to sentient beings?
Just as a magician who knows the illusory arts can manifest all manner of infinite things.
In an instant, he manifests days, months, and years; He displays cities, abundance, and great peace and joy.

If a magician, though possessing greed, hatred, and delusion, Can still delight the world through his illusory power, How much more so the power of meditative concentration and liberation— How could it fail to bring joy to all beings?
When the devas and asuras were at war, the asuras were defeated and fled;
their weapons, chariots, carriages, and followers all hid away at once so that they could no longer be seen.
Yet those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion are still able to manifest inconceivable transformations.
How much more so for one who dwells in the dharmas of supernatural powers and fearlessness—how could such a person not manifest sovereign mastery?

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, possesses an elephant-king; when he knows the Lord of Heaven intends to travel, he spontaneously transforms himself into thirty-two heads, each with six tusks fully complete.
Upon each tusk are seven pools of water, Pure, fragrant, and overflowing with clarity.
Within each of these pure pools, There are seven lotus flowers, exquisitely adorned.
Upon each of those adorned lotuses, There are seven celestial jade maidens.
Accompanied by skilled musicians playing various instruments, he enjoys himself together with Śakra.

That elephant may further cast off its original form and transform itself so that its deportment and movements are entirely equal to those of the devas; such is his power of supernatural manifestation.
If those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion can still manifest these various supernatural powers,
how much more so those who are fully endowed with the wisdom of skillful means? Though they may not yet have mastery over all meditative concentrations,
they manifest transformation bodies like those of the asuras, treading upon the adamantine foundation to stand amidst the ocean.
The seawater, though exceedingly deep, reaches only half his height; his head stands level with Mount Sumeru.

If those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can still manifest such great supernormal powers, how much more so for the Lamp that Illumines the World, who subdues the enemies of Māra—could he lack sovereign and majestic spiritual power?
When the gods and asuras were engaged in battle, Śakra’s supernatural power was inconceivable;
according to the number of the asura hosts, he manifested bodies equal to theirs to confront them.
Then the asuras thought: "Śakra Devānām Indra is coming toward us."
He will surely bind my body with fivefold fetters, Because of which that host is utterly distressed.

Śakra manifests his body with a thousand eyes; Holding a vajra from which flames erupt, clad in armor and bearing weapons, he is most majestic and awe-inspiring. When the asuras behold him, they all retreat in submission.
If even one with the power of such slight merit can thus destroy great enemies,
how much more so for the Savior of All? Among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, who possess the fullness of merit yet lack sovereign mastery,
there is a celestial drum that arises from the karmic retribution of their heavenly deeds.
Knowing that the hosts of devas are indulging in negligence, this sound spontaneously issues forth from the sky:
"All five desires are entirely impermanent; their nature is as false and hollow as a mass of foam on water.
All conditioned things are like dreams, like mirages, and also like floating clouds or the moon reflected in water."
Heedlessness is an enemy and a source of suffering; it is not the path to the Deathless, but the track of birth and death.
If one engages in various heedless acts, one enters the mouth of the great fish of death.
It is the root of all the sufferings in the world, which all noble ones loathe and detest.
The qualities of the five desires are by nature subject to decay; you should take delight in the true Dharma.
Hearing these words, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three all ascended together to the Hall of Good Dharma.
There, Śakra preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to them all, causing them to accord with tranquility and eliminate craving.
That voice is formless and invisible, yet it can still benefit the hosts of devas;
how much more so when the physical body manifests according to their mental inclinations—how could it fail to deliver all living beings?
When the devas and asuras are engaged in battle, the power of the devas' merit is preeminent.
The celestial drum resounded, proclaiming to the assembly: "You all should not feel sorrow or fear.
When the devas heard this proclamation, they all cast off their grief and dread, and their strength increased.
At that time, the heart of the asura trembled with terror, and the troops he led all retreated in flight.
The wondrous samādhi of ambrosia is like a celestial drum, Constantly producing the tranquil sound that subdues Māra;
With great compassion and pity, it rescues all, Universally causing sentient beings to extinguish their afflictions.
Like Śakra, it universally responds to all the goddesses, Numbering ninety-two nayutas.
Causing each of them to think in their own mind: "The Heavenly King alone is sporting with me.
Just as his body appears universally among the celestial maidens, so too is it within the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).
Able to manifest supernatural powers in a single thought-moment, he reaches before them all and preaches the Dharma for them.
Śakra possesses greed, hatred, and delusion, yet he is able to cause all his retinue to rejoice;
how much more so could one with great skillful means and supernatural powers not delight all others?
The six heavenly kings of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations have attained mastery within the realm of desire.
With karma, afflictions, and suffering as their skeletal lattice, they bind all ordinary beings.
Since those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can still exercise mastery over sentient beings,
how much more so could one endowed with the ten kinds of sovereign power not cause the multitudes to act in concert?
The Great Brahmā King of the trichiliocosm, Able to manifest his body and sit upon every dwelling place of the Brahmā heavens, He proclaims the subtle and wondrous Brahmā-sounds;
Abiding within the worldly path of Brahmā, His meditative concentrations and supernormal powers are as he wishes.
How much more so for those who have transcended the world and possess the unsurpassed state— those who are not yet masters of dhyāna and liberation,
such as Maheśvara, though they possess mastery over wisdom; who, when the great oceanic dragon kings send down rain,
can distinguish and count every single drop, discerning them all within a single thought-moment.
Having diligently practiced and studied for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you have attained this wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi;
why then do you not, within a single thought-moment, universally know the minds of all sentient beings?
The karmic retributions of sentient beings are inconceivable, yet by the power of a great wind, you raise up the world.
The great ocean, the various mountains, and the celestial palaces; The radiance of myriad jewels and the seeds of all things;
It can also raise clouds and send down great rain, And it can also disperse and extinguish all vapors;
It can also bring to maturity all grains, And it can bring peace and happiness to all living beings.
The wind cannot learn the *pāramitās*, nor can it learn the various merits of the Buddhas;
yet it still accomplishes inconceivable deeds. How much more so for one who has fulfilled all vows!

Whether the various sounds of men and women, or the voices of all birds and beasts— *Note: This verse is a poetic illustration of how the natural world manifests the power of the Dharma, even without conscious cultivation, let alone those who have perfected their aspirations.*
The sounds of great oceans, rivers, and thunder— All can please the minds of sentient beings;
How much more so when one knows the nature of sound is like an echo,
Attaining unimpeded and wondrous eloquence to preach the Dharma in universal response to sentient beings, Yet being unable to cause the world to rejoice?
The ocean possesses a rare and extraordinary quality:
it can serve as a seal of equality for all beings, for treasures, and for flowing rivers; it universally encompasses all without refusal.
Those who possess inexhaustible meditative concentration and liberation are likewise sealed by this seal of equality.
Having universally practiced all sublime deeds of merit and wisdom without weariness,
When the Great Ocean Dragon King sports, he attains mastery over all places;
He raises clouds that pervade the four continents, And those clouds are adorned with various colors.
The sixth is the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations; there, the color of the clouds is like refined gold.
In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, they are the color of red pearls; in Tuṣita Heaven, the color of frost and snow;
in the Yāma Heaven, the color of lapis lazuli; and in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the color of agate.
On the heavens of the Four Great Kings, it is the color of beryl; Upon the waters of the great ocean, it is the color of diamond;
Among the kinnaras, it is the color of exquisite fragrance; In the abodes of the nāgas, it is the color of the lotus;
In the dwellings of the yakṣas, it is the color of the white goose; Among the asuras, it is the color of mountain rock.
In Uttarakuru, it has the color of golden flames; in Jambudvīpa, it is the color of blue jewels;
in the other two continents, it is adorned with various ornaments. It appears according to the inclinations of beings.
Furthermore, in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, it flashes like lightning in the clouds, like the light of the sun.
In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, it is like moonlight; In the Tuṣita Heaven, it is Jāmbūnada gold;
In the Yāma Heaven, it is the color of white jade and snow; In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it is the color of golden flames;
In the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, it is the color of various jewels; Within the great ocean, it is the color of red pearls.
The realm of the kiṃnaras is the color of lapis lazuli; the abode of the nāga kings is the color of precious jewels;
the dwelling place of the yakṣas is the color of crystal; among the asuras it is the color of agate;
the region of Uttarakuru is the color of fire-pearls; and within Jambudvīpa it is the color of indranīla.
The other two continents are adorned with various ornaments; their colors and forms are like clouds, and their lightning is likewise.
In Paranirmita-vaśavartin, there is the sound of thunder; in Nirmāṇarati, the sound of celestial drums;
in Tuṣita, the sound of singing; and in Yāma, the voices of celestial maidens.
In that realm of the Thirty-three Gods, it is like the various sounds of the kinnaras;
among the world-protecting Four Kings and their devas, it is like the music produced by the gandharvas;
it is like the sound of two mountains colliding in the ocean, or the sound of flutes and pipes among the kinnaras.
In the cities of the nāgas, there is the sound of the kalaviṅka; in the abodes of the yakṣas, the voice of the nāga maidens;
among the asuras, the sound of celestial drums; and in the human realm, the roar of the ocean tide.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, a rain of exquisite fragrances falls, adorned with various kinds of flowers.
In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, there falls rain of tāla flowers, māndārava flowers, and fragrant incense;
in the Tuṣita Heaven, there falls rain of maṇi jewels, adorned with every kind of precious ornament.
The jewel in the topknot is like the light of the moon, and the exquisite garments are the color of pure gold.
In the Yāma heaven, there falls rain of banners, streamers, and parasols; Flower garlands, ointments, and exquisite ornaments;
Cloths of the finest quality, the color of red pearls; As well as various kinds of music and song;
The wish-fulfilling jewels of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; And solid black aloeswood and sandalwood incense.
Saffron, *kīra*, *tamāla*, and other exquisite flowers fall mixed with fragrant water;
within the cities of the World-Protectors, delicious food falls, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, increasing strength.
Furthermore, inconceivable multitudes of wondrous jewels rain down—all these are the works of the dragon kings.
Furthermore, within that great ocean, rain falls incessantly like the axle of a chariot;
it rains down inexhaustible treasuries of great jewels, and also rains down various kinds of ornamental gems.
In the realm of the kinnaras, there falls a rain of necklaces, lotus flowers of many colors, garments, and jewels.
Bālīśaka and mālatī incense, with every kind of musical sound fully provided;
in the cities of the nāgas, red pearls rain down; within the cities of the yakṣas, radiant maṇi-jewels;
among the asuras, weapons rain down, subduing all enemies.
In Uttarakuru, necklaces rain down; likewise, immeasurable and most exquisite flowers rain down in the two continents of Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī.
In Jambudvīpa, pure water rains down—subtle, refreshing, and always according to the season.
They nurture all flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs, And bring to maturity all crops and vegetation.
Such immeasurable and wondrous adornments— Various clouds, lightning, and thunderous rains—
the Dragon Kings can produce with sovereign mastery, Yet their bodies remain unmoving and free from conceptual discrimination.
Even those who dwell within the ocean of worlds can manifest such inconceivable power;
how much more so for those who have entered the ocean of Dharma and are endowed with merit—how could they not perform great spiritual transformations?
The gates of liberation of those bodhisattvas cannot be revealed by any analogy whatsoever.
"Now, by means of these various parables, I have briefly explained his sovereign power.
[Commentary: From "Eleven. Following what was spoken together by the Tathāgatas" onwards, there are one hundred and fifty-eight stanzas clarifying the section on "Exemplification through Parables."
[Sūtra] Supreme wisdom, vast wisdom, True wisdom, boundless wisdom, Victorious wisdom, and preeminent wisdom— This Dharma gate has now been proclaimed.
This Dharma is rare and most extraordinary; If anyone, having heard it, can accept it with patience, [they shall attain liberation].
To be able to believe, to accept, and to proclaim it—such deeds are exceedingly difficult.
Among all the ordinary people in the world, those who believe in this Dharma are extremely rare.
If one diligently cultivates pure merit, then by the power of past causes, one may come to believe.
Among all the multitudes of living beings in all worlds, few desire to seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha are even fewer still. Those who set out upon the Mahāyāna are extremely rare to encounter;
yet those who do so are still considered easy to find compared to those who can truly believe in this Dharma, for such people are many times more difficult to find.
How much more so for one who upholds and recites it, explains it to others, and practices according to the Dharma with true understanding!

To take upon one's head the three-thousandfold world system for an entire eon without the body moving—such an act is not considered difficult; rather, it is truly difficult to have faith in this Dharma.
To hold ten buddha-fields in one's hands And remain suspended in mid-air for an entire kalpa— Such an achievement is not yet difficult;
To be able to believe in this Dharma is truly difficult.
[Treatise] From the twelfth verse, "From the first wisdom, the vast wisdom," below, there are fourteen verses of gāthās that clarify [the meaning].
The Section on the Difficulty of Belief in the Buddha’s Wisdom, in which one desires to know it oneself through faith.
[Sūtra] If one were to bestow all articles of pleasure upon beings as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an eon, the merit thereof would not be supreme;
one who believes in this Dharma is the most supreme.
If one were to serve Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields for an entire eon,
yet if one can recite and uphold this chapter, that merit would be most excellent, surpassing the former.
[Commentary] From the verse beginning with "From those as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields," there are four lines of verse that clarify the faith and understanding.
[Those who] delight in upholding [this teaching] shall obtain their share of merit.
[Sūtra]: When the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha had finished speaking these verses, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways;
the palaces of Māra were obscured, the evil realms were stilled, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before him, each stroking his head with their right hand.
From their crowns, they praised with one voice, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You have well expounded this Dharma;
we all rejoice in it.
[Treatise] At the fourteenth stage, the passage of three and a half lines beginning with the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla clarifies the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
Regarding the section on "The Dharma-gate Taught Inspiring the Buddhas of the Ten Directions to Confer Authorization by Touching the Crown," it is divided into two parts.

As for the exegesis according to the text, the meaning is already clearly elucidated within the text itself, so there is no need for further explanation. Only those points that are obscure, hidden, or difficult to understand shall now be resolved.
Having previously provided a general clarification on how faith is established through the fruition, we now enter the realization of reality. This is like ascending to the Heaven of Śakra.

Master Gao states that the "Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes" constitutes the introductory section; the "Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru" is the introduction, while the remaining five chapters of the sutra constitute the main exposition section;
and the final three chapters, ending with the shaking of the earth and the raining of flowers, constitute the dissemination section.
Chapter Thirteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru [Śāstra] Within these ten stages of abiding (*daśabhūmi*), there are six chapters of the sūtra: first, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru";
second, "Verses of Praise on the Summit"; third, "The Stages of Abiding"; fourth, "Brahmacarya"; fifth, "The Merit of Arousing the Mind"; and sixth, "Clarification."
The six chapters on the Dharma thus together constitute the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*). To explain the meaning of this chapter, it is divided into three parts:

first, explaining the purpose for which the chapter has come; second, representing the Dharma through its location; and third, explaining the meaning according to the text. Regarding the first, explaining the purpose for which the chapter has come:
it clarifies that previously, in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-prāsāda*) upon the ground of the human realm, the mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) was accomplished.

Having concluded this, at the summit of this Wondrous Peak, it clarifies the ascent from the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) into the ten abodes (*vihāra*), thereby entering the [bodhisattva] positions;
for this reason, this chapter must follow. Second, regarding the use of place to symbolize the Dharma:

it clarifies that this mountain rises eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the water, within the seven concentric golden wheel-encircling mountains and the seven great oceans, and its length and breadth are equal.
It is likewise composed of four precious substances: gold on the eastern side, white silver on the western, lapis lazuli on the southern, and agate on the northern.
Upon it are four peaks, each with eight subsidiary peaks; these constitute thirty-two celestial hosts.
The central peak is named Sumeru, the "Wondrous High," where Śakra, the Lord of Devas, dwells atop it within his precious palace. Together, these constitute the third heaven, that of Śakra Devendra.
The thirteen heavens are collectively presided over by Śakra. Śakra has four names: first, Śakro Devendra;
second, Kauśika; third, Śakradevendra; and fourth, Indra. He is called Mahendra (Great Lord) because he is capable of acting as the sovereign for all the devas.
This Mount Sumeru is composed of the four precious substances, and the various devas [dwell there].
Because its precious palaces are magnificently adorned above, it is called Mount Wonderful Peak (Miaofengshan). Beyond this mountain are seven ranges of golden mountains and seven great oceans;
their vast extent is such that the distance between the two wings of a Golden-Winged Bird (Garuḍa) spans three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li*.
It can fly with such speed that in a single flap of its wings it covers ten million nine thousand *li*, doing so for seven days and seven nights.
Upon reaching its summit, one finds that the mountain stands in the midst of the great ocean, shaped like a waist-drum and rising loftily and steeply;

it cannot be ascended by climbing with hands and feet. It serves as a monument for this Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes, marking the initial birth into the family of Tathāgata-wisdom as a true son of the Buddha; it must not be sought through conceptualizations of arising and ceasing.
Because it is attained through investigation, extensive learning, and the mental apprehension of objects, it is compared to Mount Sumeru to serve as an illustration for future generations to emulate;
for "mountain" signifies the meaning of lofty excellence. This tenth stage is like that mountain because it dwells in the Dharma-body where the Buddhas abide, which is a wondrous ocean of wisdom;
thus, it represents the meaning of supramundane loftiness and excellence. As for Mount Sumeru:
The meaning of immovability is the dwelling place of the various devas; the meaning of wondrous bliss is the meaning of adornment.

When a Bodhisattva of this stage, through the samādhi of skillful means, remains serenely unmoving—without thought, without mind, neither withdrawing nor grasping, resting in natural composure—this is called conforming to the principle of equality and merging with the Dharmakāya.
Suddenly, wondrous wisdom arises from this samādhi, beginningless [in its continuity].

Having attained nothing at all through the total non-apprehension of ignorance, they abide in the sublime wisdom of the Buddhas; being entirely without dependence, they attain the wondrous joy of the Dharma.
Adorned with wisdom, they transcend all mundane views and fully comprehend every subtle and wondrous scripture of liberation taught by the Buddhas.
Because they have been born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the ignorance of the three realms is extinguished all at once and instantaneously.
Only the afflictions of habitual tendencies are gradually subdued by means of the Dharma, as stated in the "Ten Stages" chapter:

"O Son of the Buddha, the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva is vast, equal to the Dharma-realm and empty space; O Son of the Buddha, this is because the Bodhisattva dwells in the household of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, as stated in the "Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving the Mind": "One should know that such a person is..."
To be equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time is to be equal to the realm of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
it is to be equal to the merit of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. To attain the ultimate equality of the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies is true wisdom;
at the very moment the thought of enlightenment is first produced, one becomes [the refuge] for all beings in the ten directions.
The Buddhas collectively praise this, even to the point of shaking all worlds and manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood within all worlds,
as explained extensively in the text; it cannot be equated with the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles,

which state that bodhisattvas of the three stages prior to the grounds (the *pūrvayoga*) suppress the active manifestation of ignorance, while those on the grounds attain the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Because the dharma-teachings of this sutra arise from the fundamental immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas, and because one generates the mind of awakening by mounting the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvajña-jñāna-yāna*), one is able to share the same wisdom as the Tathāgata within these ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*).
Thus, it is not the same as the three vehicles (*triyāna*); rather, it merely employs the contemplation of the three emptinesses (*tri-śūnyatā*) for the sake of temporary subduing.
Those who give rise to the bodhicitta within this sutra do so by originating from the Buddha’s Immovable Wisdom (*acalajñāna*).

Should there remain residual habits, they are further treated with the Wisdom of Non-Abiding (*anāśrayasthitijñāna*). This is because it is fundamentally the Original Wisdom (*mūlajñāna*), which takes non-subjugation and non-severance as its essence;
it is the function of primordial quiescence (*prakṛtiśānti*), wherein there is no substance to be severed and nothing to be subjugated. Thus, its mastery is autonomous.
If one practices samādhi through natural spontaneity (*anābhoga*), because it is pure by nature, there is neither gathering nor subduing;
because it is naturally pure, even when practicing analytical discernment, one follows the spontaneous wisdom that functions according to circumstances, being without grasping or rejecting.

Thus, through spontaneous dharmas, one disciplines and transforms habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) so that they accord with the principle-wisdom (*jñāna*), causing their cultivation to increase in clarity until it is like that of a Buddha.

Because he vows to act in accordance with worldly affairs and grows in great compassion without emerging or submerging—since the single reality of mind and object is without emergence or submergence—he is represented in the sutras by figures such as the Asura Kings, using the metaphor of being within the great ocean without emerging or submerging.
Question: For what reason does he not ascend to the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings?
Having transcended [the realm of the Four Great Kings], he arrived at the palace of Śakra, who replied: "The Four Great Kings dwell on the side of Mount Sumeru;
this is not a place where one can manifest the summit of the Dharma. It is here that the ultimate marks appear, where one dwells in the adornment of wisdom and does not regress.
Thus, the youth Sudhana attained at Mount Sumeru the gate of the light of wisdom for recollecting all Buddhas.
Because they share this same stage, other cases may be understood by analogy: using a mountain to symbolize the traces of transcending sensory objects does not mean one must actually climb it;
entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata and being capable of leading the assembly does not mean one must become Śakra.
Third, in the explanation of the meaning according to the text, the meaning is divided into three parts: first, the general outline.
First, the second section clarifies that the Tathāgata’s bodily activities are all-pervasive, as the following sutra states:

"In all worlds throughout the ten directions, it is likewise so. This clarifies that the Tathāgata is seen ascending the summit of Mount Sumeru in all the wondrous peaks throughout the ten directions.
Third, the explanation of the meaning according to the text.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority (*ṛddhi-anubhāva*), in every single Jambudvīpa within the four continents of all worlds in the ten directions, the Tathāgata was seen sitting beneath a tree. In each place, there were bodhisattvas who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, expounded the Dharma;
none of them failed to think, "I am always in the presence of the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One did not depart from any of them.
When he rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and ascended Mount Sumeru toward the palace of Śakra, King Śakra,

seeing the Buddha approaching from afar before the Palace of Sublime Victory (Vaijayanta), immediately used his supernormal powers to adorn this palace and established upon it a lion throne called the Universal Radiance Treasury.
This throne was composed entirely of exquisite jewels, featuring ten thousand tiers of steps, and was most supremely adorned.
A net worth a thousand pieces of gold covered its surface; ten thousand kinds of canopies and ten thousand kinds of parasols were arranged in rows all around;
ten thousand silken fabrics served as hanging streamers; ten thousand pearl tassels were interlaced everywhere; ten thousand garments were spread upon the seat;
and ten thousand deva-sons and ten thousand Brahmā kings surrounded it from front and back with ten thousand rays of light.
To illuminate [the assembly], Śakra, Lord of Devas, at that time prepared a seat for the Tathāgata;
then, bowing with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddha, he spoke these words: "Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata! Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
We pray only that you will compassionately deign to dwell in this palace. Thereupon, the World-Honored One accepted his invitation and entered.
In the Sudharmā Hall, as well as in all the worlds of the ten directions, it was likewise.
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the musical sounds within the palaces naturally ceased;
Śakra then recalled the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke these verses:
Kāśyapa Tathāgata, endowed with great compassion, Is the most supreme among all auspicious things;
That Buddha once entered this hall, Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Kanakamuni saw without obstruction, He is the most supreme among all auspicious things.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Kālakubja, like a mountain of gold, is the unsurpassed among all that is auspicious;
that Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was free from the three stains; among all auspicious things, he was supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Śikhin Tathāgata was free from conceptual discrimination; among all auspicious things, he was supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was like the full moon, the supreme among all that is auspicious.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Puṣya, who has realized the ultimate truth, is the most supreme among all that is auspicious;
that Buddha once entered this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
Tiṣya Tathāgata, whose eloquence is unimpeded, is the most supreme among all that is auspicious.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Buddha Padmottara, pure and stainless, supreme among all that is auspicious, That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Great Radiance of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara is the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
Thus, in this world-system, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, praised ten Buddhas with verses.
The Śakra-devānām-indras of the worlds in the ten directions all likewise praised the Buddha’s merits in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Palace of Sublime Victory and sat cross-legged;
suddenly, this palace became vast and spacious, just like the dwellings of the celestial hosts, and so it was throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

[Treatise] Regarding the division of this chapter into ten sections: First, from the passage beginning with "At that time" (爾時) for three lines of scripture, it clarifies how the Buddha’s spiritual power universally manifests throughout the ten directions.
Second, from the passage beginning with "At that time" for one and a half lines of scripture, it clarifies how the Buddha, without departing from beneath the Bodhi tree, ascends to Mount Sumeru.
From "The Palace of Śakra" down to "Śakra, the Lord of Devas, having descended [from his seat] for about seven lines of scripture," it clarifies that Śakra saw the Buddha approaching from afar,
prepared the palace, arranged the seats, and bowed four times with palms joined. From "having descended" down to "Śakra invited the Buddha into the palace" (five sections),
and from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to the three phrases of scripture, these constitute the ten [aspects] of the Tathāgata.

The three phrases of the sutra beginning with "At that time, having accepted the invitation, he entered the hall" from "In all worlds of the sixty directions" and below conclude that the assemblies from the ten directions were gathered here in this same manner.

The one and a half lines of sutra beginning with "At that time, Śakra" clarify that through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the music ceased of its own accord. The four phrases beginning with "He then recollected" clarify [the following].
Śakra, reflecting upon his own past roots of goodness, spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha.

From "Having come here to this world" (*jagat*) down to the two and a half lines of scripture below, the text concludes this section by praising the Buddha in verse; the same applies throughout the ten directions.
From "At that time" (*atha khalu*) down to approximately two lines of scripture, it clarifies that the Tathāgata sat upon his seat, and that the hall was vast and expansive.
Being broad-minded, one should harmonize with those throughout the ten directions who likewise provide word-by-word commentary on this text.

As for the phrase "not departing from the Bodhi tree," it clarifies that the essence of Bodhi has no coming or going, nor distance or proximity, and thus there is neither a place to depart from nor a place to arrive at.

Furthermore, because the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body has no interior or exterior and its substance is all-pervasive; and because the Dharma-realm is neither large nor small, not even a single hair-tip or a single speck of dust.
Because they are mutually compatible; because mind and objects are non-dual, lacking center, periphery, or spatial location;
and because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, being eternally perfected as both one and many. Regarding the fact that Śakra saw the Buddha approaching from afar, there are two meanings:

first, the literal event; second, the symbolic representation of the Dharma. As for the literal event, it demonstrates that although the Tathāgata possesses the nature of neither coming nor going, he manifests coming and going.

Regarding the phrase "seeing from afar the two manifest dharmas" (*dvaya-vijñapti*): it clarifies that Śakra manifested this appearance because he had not yet realized that the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*) is all-pervasive and of one essence with the mind.

Therefore, it is said that he saw the Buddha coming from afar. Furthermore, "seeing from afar" refers to faith and understanding, while "the Buddha coming" refers to entering the stage [of realization] within one's own mind. Thereupon, Śakra employed his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) to adorn this hall.
This also has two meanings: first, the actual matter; second, the manifestation of the Dharma. The matter can be understood [as follows].

Regarding the second, the manifestation of the Dharma, it refers to one’s own preparatory application (*prayoga*). As for "installing [him] upon the Universal Radiance Lion Throne," this also has two meanings:

first, regarding the positioning of the throne; second, regarding the sovereign Indra’s own capacity and roots of virtue. Regarding the first, the positioning of the throne, it refers to this [context].

The stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) is the stage of the Dharma; because within these ten abodes one attains the treasury of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas and achieves mastery and fearlessness regarding all phenomena, this seat is established.
Thus, just as in the stage of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), one manifests a precious lotus lion-throne within the Yāma Heaven palace—this refers to the practice.
Abiding in all states of birth and death, one practices the ten thousand deeds with great compassion;
because the essence of wisdom and principle attains freedom from defilement, for this reason, one takes the lotus flower as a seat.

Abiding within this stage of the Ten Dwellings (*daśavihāra*), because one has attained the light of wisdom of all Buddhas which universally illumines the myriad dharmas, one is established in the Treasury of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhāsa-garbha*).
Regarding the lion throne: within these ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the throne is established with ten thousand tiers;
within the ten practices (*caryā*), it is manifested as a lion throne of one million tiers.

This indicates that for those at the initial stage of entering the ten abodes, [the state] is like being atop Mount Sumeru while still connected to the earth-dwelling realm, clarifying that the mind still has something to grasp, and that they have first encountered the truth through faith.
For this reason, as the retribution of the Dharma, the lion throne must be established.

Furthermore, because the Samādhi of Expedient Means is that which establishes it, within the stage of the Ten Practices—where the wondrous wisdom of principle and intellect has been perfected based on the stage of the Ten Abidings—one transforms that throne through its wondrous function; moreover, the practice is established from the standpoint of emptiness.
Furthermore, regarding the location, it is said that the seats of the gods dwelling in the void of the Yāma Heaven consist of ten thousand tiers and even a million tiers;
this also clarifies the manner of ascending and progressing through the various levels of the Śakra-devendra palace and the Yāma Heaven.
If one truly enters the flow of Dharma-wisdom, not a speck of dust shall escape, yet it pervades the oceans of all lands; such is the extent of those seats.

The ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are adorned with various heights and depths, each differing according to its respective position; one should understand this by analogy.
That the adornments upon these seats are all "ten thousand" in number clarifies that they are obtained as the retribution for the ten thousand practices (*daśasahasra-caryā*).

As for the "ten thousand golden nets," this refers to the capacity to use the net of the teachings and practices to filter out the karmic fruits and retributions of sentient beings; thus there are ten thousand kinds.

The "canopy" (*vitāna*) signifies the meaning of nurturing and raising; it is so called because it is obtained as the fruit of the practice of protecting and nurturing sentient beings by acting as a Buddha, a deity, or a powerful yakṣa in all places. The "ten thousand kinds of parasols" signify the meaning of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
they are so called because they are the fruit of covering and nurturing all sentient beings with a mind of great compassion.
Obtaining ten thousand pieces of fine silk signifies that within a single practice one carries out inexhaustible differentiated practices,
and within a single word or sound one possesses differentiated teachings— all of which are results clearly visible and worthy of contemplation.

The ten thousand pearl necklaces signify the result of the universal pervasiveness of the ten thousand practices, adorning the realm of wisdom to transform and benefit sentient beings without ceasing.
This is because one has attained such that within each and every atom there exists the inexhaustible body of Samantabhadra.
The ten thousand garments represent the fruit of having nurtured all sentient beings through gentleness and patience throughout the ocean of all births and deaths.
The ten thousand devaputras clarify those who are able to practice the ten thousand practices. The ten thousand Brahmā kings clarify...
Because wisdom is sovereign within their practice, the ten thousand rays of light shine forth;
this clarifies that the radiance of wisdom can shatter the long night of delusion for both oneself and others, bringing about great illumination.

All of the above constitutes the adornment formed by the fruit-virtues and functions of this stage, intended to cause bodhisattvas who have resolved to enter this stage to recognize the fruit through their causal practice.
Because he was free from doubt, from the passage beginning "having bowed" onwards, it clarifies that Śakra paid homage to the Tathāgata and requested the Buddha to enter his palace;
this illustrates his clarity of conduct and humble behavior. The Tathāgata’s acceptance of the request illustrates entering the dwelling through faith, as can be understood from the text.
Second, regarding Śakra’s own virtues, the final section clarifies that Śakra has attained the power of past mindfulness (*pūrvajātismara*) with respect to the past.

Regarding the verses spoken in praise of the Buddha by those who have planted roots of goodness under him, it is clarified that through the power of samādhi, they personally perceive that the essential nature of their own body and mind is identical to that of the Buddhas of the past and present, due to their wisdom and roots of goodness.

The ten Buddhas mentioned below represent the functional application of this stage, which unites with the past. Within these verses, there are twenty lines, with two lines constituting a single verse; this is the first.
The two verses praising Kāśyapa Buddha state that "Kāśyapa" means "Drinking Light" (飲光);
this is his clan name, so called because his bodily radiance was so extraordinary that it could "drink up" the light of the devas, the sun, the moon, and others, causing them all to disappear.
The next two verses praise Kanakamuni Buddha; he is correctly called "Kanakamuni," which means "Golden Sage" (拘那牟尼). "Kana" refers to...
"Na" (那) here means "gold"; "Muni" (牟尼) refers to the Buddha. He is designated by the name "Golden One.
The next two lines praise Kālakodra (迦羅鳩馱), fully called Kālakocunda Buddha (迦羅鳩村馱佛), which means "one who has already severed what ought to be severed.
The next two lines praise Viśvabhū (毗舍浮), which means "pervading all sovereignty. The next two lines... [text ends]
The praise of Śikhin Buddha is correctly rendered as Śikhiṇa, which means "Wearing a Topknot" or alternatively "Having Hair.
Next, two lines praise Vipaśyin Buddha, which means "Pure Vision," or alternatively "Supreme Vision," or "Diverse Vision.
Next, two lines praise Puṣya Buddha, correctly rendered as Puṣya, which means "Flourishing. Next, two lines praise [the next Buddha].
The Buddha Tiṣya is correctly called Tiṣya; this means "One Who Speaks the Dharma to Deliver Others. The following two lines praise the Buddha Padmottara;
*padma* is correctly called *potalaka*, which refers to the red lotus. The following two lines praise the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
The former two Buddhas are those of the present Bhadrakalpa, while the latter seven Buddhas are those of the past.
Within this eon, the Buddha first entered the gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) through clarity; thus, the laws of past and present converge in clarity.
Because the Dharma of ancient Buddhas and the Dharma of the present Buddha are not different, those who enter this stage meet in common without distinction.
Therefore, "Auspicious" is said because this mountain peak is praised as a place of merit and goodness. "Clearly Ascending" refers to the power of *samādhi*.
With body and mind unmoving like the King of Mountains, he unites with the wisdom of all Buddhas of the past and present;
thus, in this ninth [chapter], within this world-system, there are four sections of sutra text below the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the meaning of which is divided into four parts:
first, citing this world to praise the Buddha’s merits; second, summarizing that it is likewise in the ten directions; third... [er].

First, it clarifies that the Tathāgata entered the hall and ascended the throne to sit. Second, it clarifies that the hall suddenly became vast and expansive, universally accommodating the dwellings of all the devas.
This clarifies that, based on the Tathāgata’s virtue of being without self or other, he naturally caused the great assembly to see this;
it clarifies that he causes the great assembly to enter the stage [of realization] and become identical to this. The above explains "ascending the lion's seat."

The "Chapter on Maitreya" concludes. This section, in brief, clarifies that when one correctly enters meditative absorption through the power of samādhi, the body and mind become utterly serene, corresponding to the nature of the *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm) such that there is no distinction between interior and exterior; the luminosity is brilliant and penetrating.

This signifies the sudden expansion of vastness, as well as the meaning of the Lion Throne within the Universal Radiance Treasury. The manifestation of wisdom is the meaning of the Buddhas' arrival. Each and every [point]...
Thus, in practicing according to the principle, one must not merely follow words and names.
[Sūtra] Chapter Fourteen: Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru.
[Treatise] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed by means of four sections: first, the explanation of the title of the chapter; second, the explanation of the chapter...
The intent of the coming [of this section] is threefold: first, it brings together the meaning of these ten chapters on the Six Stages (*ṣaḍbhūmi*) of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*;
second, it follows the text to explain the meaning; third, regarding the explanation of the chapter titles:

the ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Dharmamati, each use verses to praise the method of cultivation appropriate to their own respective stages, thereby inspiring faith so that the final bodhisattva may emulate them.
Because of this realization and entry [into the truth], this chapter is titled "The Chapter on Verses of Praise" (*Gāthā-stotra-parivarta*).

It clarifies that all Buddhas of the past and present assemble here in this Hall of Wisdom and Palace of Compassion; it shows that the very self of the Buddhas of the past and present is identical to the Buddhas of the future, for their path is in harmony with that of the ancient Buddhas.
Second, regarding the purpose of the chapter’s introduction: it clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] has already ascended Mount Sumeru to the abode of Śakra.
This chapter, which praises the Buddha in verse, clarifies the stages of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

It describes how Bodhisattvas at each respective stage use verses to praise the Dharma-gates of that stage, so that those with faith may enter these stages; therefore, this chapter must appear here. First, it praises the Buddhas of the past;
next, it praises the Buddhas of the present; as for the Buddhas of the future, they are those who will enter these very stages.

This is so; therefore, it is not said in the sutra that the ten future Buddhas are past Buddhas, nor that Rucika is a present Buddha, nor that those who have newly entered the stage of practice are future Buddhas.

The intention behind the three assemblies within the Ten Abodes on the summit of Mount Sumeru, where the six chapters of the sutra were preached, is as follows: first, the "Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru" clarifies faith.
1. The Chapter on Ascending to the Summit of the Two Sumerus explains the verses of praise for the dharmas of the respective stages and exhorts the principle of ascending progress.
2. The Chapter on the Ten Abodes explains the practices to be performed within each stage. 3.
The Chapter on Brahma-Conduct explains the nature of signless precepts maintained throughout the ten abodes as a whole. 4. The Chapter on Arousing the Mind...
The "Chapter on Merit" clarifies the magnitude of the merit obtained through the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The sixth, the "Chapter on Dharmas," clarifies the dharmas of the respective stages as one ascends toward the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*).

These six chapters clarify the causes and fruits of the practice within the respective stages, as well as the causes for advancing toward the ten practices. [This concludes] the section on the exegesis according to the text.
Furthermore, it is divided into two parts: first, a general outline of the meaning of one chapter of the sutra; second, an exegesis of the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first, the general outline of the meaning of one chapter of the sutra, the content is divided into eleven sections.

[Sūtra] At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came one Great Bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, arriving from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred buddha-fields.
Their names were: Dharmamati Bodhisattva, Sarvamati Bodhisattva, and Vijayamati Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sa-guṇa-jñāna, the Bodhisattva Vīrya-jñāna, the Bodhisattva Su-jñāna, the Bodhisattva Jñāna,
the Bodhisattva Tattva-jñāna, the Bodhisattva Anuttara-jñāna, and the Bodhisattva Dṛḍha-jñāna came from their respective lands,
namely: the world-system Indrarāja-puṣpa, the world-system Padma-puṣpa, the world-system Ratna-puṣpa, and the world-system Utpala-puṣpa.
In the worlds of Vajrapuṣpa, Supuṣpagandha, Manojñapuṣpa, Aruṇapuṣpa,
Nārāyaṇapuṣpa, and Gaganapuṣpa, they each cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of Buddhas,
namely: the Buddha Viśeṣacandra, Akṣayacandra, Acalacandra, Anilacandra, and Jalacandra.
The Buddhas Candrabuddhi, Vimukticandra, Anuttaracandra, Jyotiścandra, Viśuddhacandra, and Vimalacandra—
having approached the presence of the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and each, according to the direction from which they had come,
miraculously manifested a lion throne of the Vairocanagarbha, sat upon those thrones in the full lotus posture. Thus it was.
In all worlds, including those upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, Bodhisattvas likewise gathered;
in all such worlds, the names of those Bodhisattvas, their respective worlds, and the names of their Buddhas were entirely identical and without distinction.

At that time, from his two great toes, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrous-colored light, which universally illuminated all worlds throughout the ten directions.
On the summit of Mount Mi, within the palace of Śakra, the Buddha and the great assembly were all manifest.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:

[Treatise] First, from the passage "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" (*tasmimś ca samaye buddhānubhāvena*) onwards, there are nineteen lines and a half of scripture that clarify how the Buddha, through his spiritual power, caused the assembly to gather.
Within this section, these nineteen lines and a half are further divided into seven parts.
First, from "At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" for five lines and a half, it clarifies the arrival of the bodhisattvas.
The three lines and a half of scripture following "Having gathered the lands from which they came" clarify the names of the worlds of the bodhisattvas.
The three lines of scripture following "Having each purified the brahma-conduct in the presence of a Buddha" clarify the Buddhas whom they originally served.
The two lines of scripture following "These bodhisattvas having arrived at the place of the Buddha" clarify that they have come to transform [others].
5. Sitting in the seat, the text below these two lines of scripture clarifies that the Bodhisattvas in all worlds throughout the ten directions are likewise so.

6. At that time, from the Buddha’s toes, light was emitted, illuminating all places including the palaces of Śakra; this is clarified in the two and a half lines of scripture beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One," specifically regarding the ten wheels of faith beneath his feet.

Regarding the emission of light within these ten stages (*bhūmi*): light is emitted from the tips of the toes during the stage of "Excellence in Progression" (*viśeṣagamana*) among the ten practices (*caryā*);

from the insteps during the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*); and from the hair-tuft between the eyebrows during the ten grounds (*bhūmi*). This light symbolizes the advancement through the stages of the Dharma;
it is the very same light emitted from the hair-tuft between the eyebrows in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" (*nimittavyūha*) of the first assembly, representing the fruit.
Regarding the phrase "the light from the toe-nails of the one who has attained the stage of entering through faith": this light clearly illuminates those who have entered this stage of abiding;
it signifies the initial entry into the noble state within the palace of body, mind, and wisdom, which is why light is emitted from the tips of the toes.

(7) From this point forward, the single line of scripture clarifies that the Bodhisattva Dharmamati speaks verses in praise of the Buddha; the remaining meanings may be understood according to the text.
If one understands the intent of the structural outline (*ko-wen*), one will fully comprehend its meaning.
Just as when the Bodhisattvas first assemble, their names, the worlds from which they come, and the Buddhas they originally served are all collectively presented;

by correlating these with the dharmas and dharma-gates appropriate to each stage, one can finally perceive the meaning of the causes and effects. Furthermore, from the perspective of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, this represents the practice cultivated within this specific stage.
Based on the Tathāgata’s wisdom as it is attained, the world is given the name Indrasumanā World.
This refers to the extraordinary Dharma practiced; the Buddha is the Moon of the Initial Resolve.
Within this stage of the Abiding of Initial Resolve, regarding the fruit of the Dharma practiced, "Indra" means "Capable Lord," and "sumanā" (flower) signifies "blossoming" or "manifestation."

Regarding the meaning of "fruit" (*phala*): because a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind within these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is able to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood throughout all worlds in the ten directions, that world is named "Capable Sovereign" (*Iśvara*).

This is because they are able to manifest as a sovereign leader for all sentient beings, and because through the flowers of their practice, they are able to cause the fruits of wisdom in themselves and others to blossom. As the Sūtra says:

The fact that each is accompanied by Bodhisattvas named Dharma Wisdom (*Dharmamati*) as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field clarifies that their wisdom, understanding, practice, awakening, and universal knowledge pertain to this very realm;

for since one realizes that all things are of the same nature as one’s own mind, when one is deluded, all are deluded, and when one awakens, all awaken. This clarifies that it is only those who are to be delivered who are themselves deluded.
Because they have attained liberation and their wisdom is all-pervasive, it is said that they come from worlds outside as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields.
This clarifies "delusion" by referring to "outside the lands," and "liberation" by referring to "coming.

Since delusion consists of the vast and manifold obscurations of ignorance, it is compared to the number of atoms in a world; whereas because the practice of awakening and liberation is vast and manifold, it is described in this way.
This is also compared to the dust of the world; wisdom and ignorance are similar, differing only in that they are separated by delusion and enlightenment.
Therefore, the latter part of this sutra says: "There is a scripture as vast as a trichiliocosm contained within the body of a tiny sentient being"—this is its meaning.
Regarding the Buddha's name "Extraordinary Moon" (*Viśiṣṭacandra*): "extraordinary" (*viśiṣṭa*) means...

"Victorious" (*jaya*) means "extraordinary"; "moon" (*candra*) means "cooling. When a Bodhisattva who has entered this stage is born into and dwells within the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the beginningless heat of ignorance and afflictions, as well as the blazing fires of the evil realms, are all extinguished at once.
Only the Tathāgata’s wisdom remains, radiant and cool like the moon; therefore, it is called "bright" (*prabha*). This is the brief explanation.
When the Bodhisattva first enters the Truth, being able to shatter the feverish delusions of affliction, he establishes for himself the name of his own Buddha-fruit.

Subsequently, through the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), as he ascends and progresses through these stages, the names of the Bodhisattvas and the names of their Buddha-worlds each differ according to their respective positions.
Among these, the names of the Buddha-fruits within the ten practices all share the same name.

Regarding this being established as the "eye" and the "faculty of knowledge," names are assigned according to the specific capacities for benefiting sentient beings within the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).

Among the names of the Buddha-fruit, all are designated as "Wondrous" (*miao*), because they represent the sovereign and wondrous function of benefiting sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death;
these are only fully clarified upon reaching that stage. Furthermore, it is said that the ten Bodhisattvas, such as Dharmamati and others who have come from the ten directions...

The phrase "the assembly of bodhisattvas each purify their brahma-conduct in the presence of the Buddha" means that the wisdom of the dharma-body within their own minds is able to purify afflictions and is as cool as the moon; thus, it is named "each purifying brahma-conduct in the presence of the Buddha.
Here, "brahma" (梵) signifies purity. This indicates that for the bodhisattvas at this stage, sublime wisdom manifests before them, and all practices take this as their essence.
Because it is inherently pure, its essence is the wisdom of the *dharmatā* that functions according to the Dharma; because it is without arising or ceasing, it is luminous.
Taking this essence—without arising or ceasing—as the locus, one thereby manifests the Buddha-fruit of one's own mind.

Therefore, those who have resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment] should, by means of such skillful means, manifest it for themselves through a concentration that is effortless, thought-free, and in accord with the nature of reality.
The Buddha-gate of the self-mind’s lack of intrinsic nature is precisely that which remains unstained by afflictions;
this is named the Buddha Viśeṣacandra. According to the direction from which he came, he manifested a lion throne of the Vairocana-treasury for each.
This is the position of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, marking the beginning of the entry into the stages in the eastern quarter.
At the very beginning of dispelling darkness, it is like the sun first rising in the east; because it is able to dispel darkness, it is designated by a worldly name as "extraordinary" (*viśiṣṭa*).
Because the light of wisdom can dispel the long night of delusion and darkness for oneself and others from time immemorial, the fruit of Buddhahood is likewise named "extraordinary.
From the moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], Buddhas are already [the refuge] for devas and humans.
The Master [states] that this world is named "Flower of the Capable Lord" (*Nengzhu-hua*);
the seat upon which his transformation-activity is performed is named the "Vairocana-treasury Lion-throne. This is the seat of the Buddha-fruition. To clarify:
*Vairocana* means "light," and *Cana* means "pervasive. Thus, it clarifies that the pervasive seat transforms all beginningless ignorance and afflictions into one.

The Lion, who has attained fearlessness—the gate of sovereign liberation that transforms the entire treasury of the light of great wisdom into the Dharma-realm by universally illuminating all states of mind—is so named through an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).

As for "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*), it is called such because one gathers delusive thoughts to constitute true wisdom; therefore, it is the sitting in the full lotus posture. This [concludes the section].
Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the ten bodhisattvas share the same sequence as Sudhana:
beginning with the initial entry into faith atop Mount Wonderful Peak, followed by the ten stages starting from the Bhikṣu Meghashri down to the Maiden Maitrāyaṇī;
their dharma-gates are similar, and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva clarifies the initial arousal of the mind of faith.
In this sutra, the teachings and practices are harmonized so that later students may easily understand them;

therefore, only the teachings are expounded, for those who practice find it difficult to comprehend. For this reason, in the first assembly, the Buddha’s fruition and the divine beings are presented to demonstrate entry into the Dharma and to encourage cultivation, clarifying that each and every thing is identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
In the second assembly, there is the exhortation to give rise to faith and understanding through the gate of faith established by the Buddha Immovable Wisdom (*Acalamati*).

Following this, the teaching on entering the stages and progressing in practice is explained; that is, the dharma-gates of the ten faiths, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage.
Within the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, Sudhana is cited as one who can practice these five stages, thereby illustrating the practice.
This is because it makes [the meaning] fully manifest so that it may be easily understood; otherwise, even if one sees the teachings being put into practice, one would still remain confused.

Therefore, in this single section of the sutra, the virtuous practitioner fully manifests each aspect—cause and effect, principle and wisdom, teaching and practice—so that those who cultivate the path may emulate and study them without error.
Thus, these ten stages (*bhūmi*) mark the beginning of entering the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Because the mind, together with the subsequent ten practices, ten dedications, ten stages, and the eleventh stage, constitutes the fruit of perfect enlightenment, it is like a person who has lived for a hundred years yet considers their firstborn to be the eldest;
or as when a man fathers ten sons, the firstborn is considered the eldest.
*The Combined Commentary on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, Scroll Thirty-One.
