Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Treatise on the Sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen, "Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru," Part Two.
[Treatise]: Second, the world of the Bodhisattva Sarvajñāna is named Padmapuspa; the Buddha’s title is Ananta.
Regarding this meaning, the interpretation is divided into five parts: first, the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva"; second, the explanation of the name of the world;
third, the explanation of the title for progressing toward the fruit of Buddhahood according to the stages; fourth, the explanation of the substance of his seat;
and fifth, the determination of the direction from which he has come. First, as for the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva," he is so named because he accords with the stages.
In the course of this progressive cultivation, one realizes that all phenomena (dharma) are without substance and without intrinsic nature;

because this is not a state of deluded attachment, it constitutes the second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground (*viśuddhabhūmi*). Within the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the ten perfections are practiced, for the essence of ethical discipline is defined as the fact that all phenomena lack both defilement and purity. Thus, these stages of the ten dwellings are described in the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*).
Second, regarding the two explanations of the name of the world: the reason the world is named *padma* (波頭摩華) is that this translates as "red lotus flower.

This signifies that the characteristics of the precepts are unstained while abiding in the world; they blaze forth and blossom in splendor, adorning the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*) and manifesting a fruit worthy of contemplation.
Third, regarding the explanation of the title of the Buddha’s fruition attained through progressive cultivation according to one's stage: the Buddha...
The title "Inexhaustible Moon" is the name of a bodhisattva; as for the fruit of Buddhahood, it is likewise titled "Inexhaustible Moon," because cause and effect are similar.
This clarifies that "All-Wisdom" (Sarvajñā) refers to one who has attained the wisdom of all Buddhas through practice.
The world is the dharma that is practiced, and the fruit of Buddhahood is that which is attained within the stages of the Grounds (*bhūmi*).
The fruit [of this practice] is explained as being able to cool all afflictions (*kleśa*). The essence of the four seats has already been explained previously.
Regarding the fifth, the direction from which they come: these are the assembly of the South. This signifies that the South is the position of detachment (*virāga*);

it signifies the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); it signifies the meaning of literary expression; and it signifies the brilliant splendor of the color red, like the sun positioned directly to the south.
Because its meaning is that of perfect illumination which shines upon the myriad phenomena, the Bodhisattva is named Sarvajñāna (All-Wisdom) and the world is named Raktapadma (Red Lotus);
the Buddha’s name is Anantacandra (Inexhaustible Moon). This refers to when the youth Sudhana saw the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha and saw the Buddha preach the *Samantanetra-sūtra*;
by reflecting upon its meaning, one will surely understand it clearly for oneself. Third is the Bodhisattva Vijñānagati (Supreme Wisdom).

The meaning is divided into four parts: first, clarifying the name of the Bodhisattva; second, clarifying the land in which he dwells; third, clarifying the title of the Buddha-fruit according to the stages;
and fourth, clarifying the direction from which he has come. Regarding the first, clarifying the name of the Bodhisattva:

he is named "Victorious Wisdom" (*Jñānavijaya*) because, as he advances through the successive stages, his cultivation becomes increasingly clear and pure; he does not shift a single dharma, yet he surpasses the preceding stages.

Therefore, regarding the second point, the explanation of the name of the world: it is called the "World of Jewel Flowers" (*Ratnapuṣpa*) because, having already attained the wisdom of all Buddhas through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one is able to practice the conduct of patience by means of the essence of the Path.
"Flowers" here signify "conduct"; it clarifies that the Dharma-body of wisdom is adorned by the conduct of patience. Thirdly, this explains the title of the Buddha’s fruition.
The reason the Buddha is named Immovable Moon (Acalacandra) is that, having attained the principle and perfected the practice, he has reached the state where mind and objects cannot be moved;
thus, it clarifies his capacity for endurance (*kṣānti*). "Moon" signifies coolness. Regarding the four directions from which [the assembly] comes, this refers to the assembly of the West.
The West is associated with autumn, with killing, and with the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); it is the station of compassion.
In the middle, as in the section on the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), Sudhana sees Avalokiteśvara to the west of Vajra Mountain.
This represents the position of "Killing" (*vadhasthāna*)—a place of manifold sufferings—to signify the cultivation of compassion and patience.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Jñānavikrama (Victorious Wisdom) and the world is named Ratnakusuma; the Buddha is named Acalacandra (Immovable Moon), which collectively clarifies the attainment.
Because the power and function of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) are superior, this is the meaning of the "Jewel Flower" (*ratna-puṣpa*);

this is the remedial dharma for the stage of practice (*caryā-vihāra*). This refers to Sudhana seeing the Bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita and attaining the Dharma-gate of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-dharmamukha*) through his ability to endure.
Regarding the fourth Bodhisattva, named Guṇamati, within this subject matter it is divided into four parts: first—
First, it clarifies the name of the Bodhisattva; second, it clarifies the name of the world; third, it clarifies the title of the Buddha’s fruition;
and fourth, it clarifies the direction from which [the Bodhisattva] comes. Regarding the first point, clarifying the name of the Bodhisattva: why is he named Guṇamati (Virtue-Wisdom)?

Because in this stage he cultivates the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), zealously practicing for the benefit of others and extensively aiding sentient beings, thereby attracting manifold merits, by which his name is established.
Regarding the name of the world, it is called "Utpala" (優鉢羅華), which in this language means "blue lotus.
Among all varieties of lotuses, this flower is the most excellent. It is so named because, among all practices, diligence is the most supreme;
and because this flower serves as the dharma-body for those who dwell there. Thus, all myriad practices take this as their merit—this is the third illumination.

The title of "Buddha-fruit" is so named because it represents the wind and moon; the Buddha clarifies the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), being free from pride and indolence, attaining Buddhahood in a single thought as swiftly as the wind.

Furthermore, he clarifies that diligent contemplation and the illumination of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) are like the wind, which can eliminate the defilements and impurities of ignorance, blowing away both fragrance and stench just as the wind clears and cools all things.
Therefore, the direction from which the Four Clarities (Sīmānta) originate is this very region;

as for the northern direction, it is the position of the *kan* trigram, which signifies blackness, ignorance, and the meaning of worldly peril and banditry. Furthermore, it is the station of the teacher and the sovereign.
For these reasons, by means of the *pāramitā* of diligence (*vīrya*), one assiduously cultivates beneficial practices to shatter delusion and depart from darkness.
To cause one to swiftly attain Buddhahood, the Bodhisattva is named Guṇamati;
the world is named Blue Lotus, and his Buddha-name is Vāyu-candra (Wind-Moon).
Because wind can purify all defilements, the above constitutes the remedial dharma-gate within the stage of "Noble Birth. This corresponds to the fourth spiritual friend of Sudhana.

The Elder Kātyāyana has finished expounding the Dharma-gate of the syllable *vṛ* (wheel), which clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) so that those who are ignorant and dark may attain supramundane bliss.
As for the fifth Bodhisattva, named Vīryamati, regarding this meaning, four points are as before;
he is called Vīryamati because this stage is characterized by being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya*) and abiding in diligent application.
The name is established because one cultivates the gates of expedient concentration (*upāya-samādhi*) to manifest profound wisdom;

furthermore, within a single practice, immeasurable practices are contained, such that the name "diligence" (*vīrya*) arises within the state of concentration, and the name "merit" (*guṇa*) arises above diligence, thereby clarifying that while various practices are employed, a single practice contains immeasurable practices. Second.

The world named Vajrapuṣpa takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the essence of dhyāna; it gives rise to wondrous wisdom that discriminates between the correct and the false without being destroyed—this is the meaning of "vajra" (diamond).
As for "puṣpa" (flower), it refers to conduct, because it represents the wondrous function of clearly discerning through concentration and wisdom.
The fruit of the three Buddhas is named Jalam-candra (Water-moon); this takes meditative concentration as its essence, for it is capable of purification and is cool and refreshing.
Because it can manifest myriad images like water, the direction from which the Four Clarities (*sīmā*) originate is the northeast.
The northeast is the position of *Gen* (艮). It represents mountains, rocks, and gate-towers; it represents childhood and the initial dawn of illumination;
it represents loftiness and clarity, as well as stillness and cessation. This clarifies that the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) pervades all positions. All... [text continues]
Practicing cultivation and advancement, he opened the way for enlightenment and clarified the feverish heat of delusion;
because it is the beginning and end of the process of progressive cultivation, it is "Mounting" (*gen*); because it is the beginning and end of the year, it is "The Beginning" (*sho*);

because it clarifies cessation, the Bodhisattva is named *Vīryamati* (Wisdom of Diligence), the world is named *Vajrapuṣpa* (Diamond Flower), and the Buddha is named *Jalamati* (Water Moon). This is Sudhana.
Fifth, the Good Friend, the Elder Vimukta, who presides over the gate of dhyāna, manifests within his own body ten buddha-fields as numerous as atoms;

all these buddha-lands of the ten directions, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, are entirely contained within his body, because he clearly realizes that the essence of dhyāna is all-pervasive. Sixth is the Bodhisattva Sumati.

The four meanings are as before. First, regarding the clarification of the Bodhisattva’s name: it clarifies that because this "Abiding in the Right Mind" cultivates the gateway of wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattva is named "Excellent Wisdom" (*Sudhīmat*). Second, regarding the world of "Exquisite Fragrance and Flowers":
this clarifies that through the fragrance and flowers of wondrously functioning wisdom, the fruits of Buddhahood for oneself and others blossom; it clarifies the teaching of wisdom.
Because they perceive the meaning of incense and flowers, three Buddhas are named Moon of Liberation (*Vimukticandra*), clarifying that their wondrous wisdom clearly liberates both mind and objects.
Fourth, to clarify the direction from which they come: these are the assembly from the southeast. The southeast is the position of *Xun*;
*Xun* represents wind and teaching, and is associated with speech. Taking this position as a metaphor, it signifies excellence in wisdom.
Because he preaches the sublime Dharma to transform and liberate sentient beings, the Bodhisattva is named Sudhīmat (Excellent Wisdom) and the world is named Sugandhakusuma (Sublime Fragrant Flower);

his fruit of Buddhahood is named Vimukticandra (Moon of Liberation). This corresponds to the stage of the Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja (Ocean Banner), the sixth station of Sudhana, wherein body and mind are tranquil and free from inhalation and exhalation, as emanated bodies issue forth from his own person to pervade the entire Dharmadhātu.

The seventh stage, named "Wisdom," is attained through mastery over the sovereign functioning of quiescence and the attainment of the supernormal powers of cessation. The four meanings are as explained previously.
First, explaining why the bodhisattva is named "Wisdom": it clarifies that this irreversible dwelling is the seventh, which perfects the gateway of great compassion;
it is only by bringing wisdom to full completion that one can skillfully enter the cycle of birth and death in accordance with worldly convention.

Regarding the name of the second world, *Manojñakusuma* (Pleasant Flower): because he possesses wisdom while remaining within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), he accords with the six realms of existence to benefit sentient beings through shared activities (*samānārthatā*).
Knowing their faculties, he gladdens worldly beings and causes them all to enter the joy of the Dharma, free from sorrow;
therefore, it is named Pleasant Flower. Third, regarding the Buddha’s title *Anuttara-candra* (Unsurpassed Moon): this clarifies that among all practices, compassion (*karuṇā*) is supreme.
Because he is the foremost, because he brings benefit and liberation to sentient beings, and because he is the most supreme, he is named Anuttara-candra (Moon of No Superior).

As for the direction from which he comes, it is the southwest; this is the position of Kun (Earth), representing faith and compliance, the mother, the earth, and the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*). With great compassion as his mother, he enters into all sentient beings.

Because he shares the same realm of birth and death as all sentient beings and teaches them so that they may believe, comply with, and enter the True Dharma, the Bodhisattva is named Prajñāloka (Wisdom-Light) and the world is named Manojñakusuma (Pleasant Flower); the Buddha is named Anuttara-candra (Unsurpassed Moon).
This is the seventh spiritual friend for Sudhana, the laywoman Śreṣṭhidāraka (Venerable Householder), which in this language is called—
Because Pūrṇapraṇidhāna fulfills the vows of sentient beings through the practice of great compassion, he is like this;

furthermore, as he represents the position of compassion for his mother in the southwest of this region, the eighth [stage], the Bodhisattva Tattvabuddhi, has four meanings as previously stated. First, regarding the name of the Bodhisattva:
because he practices the perfection of *praṇidhāna* (vows) within this eighth stage, the Stage of Youth (*kumārabhūmi*), by means of reality (*tattva*).
Because wisdom does not mislead sentient beings, it is the second [point]. To clarify the name of the world:
the world is named Aruṇapuṣpa (A-lu-na-hua), which translates as "Red Lotus. This flower is clearly distinguished as red and white;

because its red color is predominant, this stage is the eighth *vihāra* (dwelling), the stage where wisdom increases. It clarifies that through great wisdom, one follows the practice of compassion according to one's vows, thereby unifying wisdom and compassion.
It is perfected like a red lotus; the white and red colors clearly represent wisdom (*jñāna*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), respectively.

Therefore, the world is named "Red Lotus," signifying that while abiding in saṃsāra through true wisdom, one remains untainted—just as a lotus in water blooms with its white and red petals and can be clearly beheld. The Buddha of this stage is named "Star-Moon" for this reason.
Because True Wisdom shines brightly, clearly knowing the faculties and capacities while discerning their distinctions, the Buddha is titled "Star-Moon" (*Tārācandra*);
this signifies that he clearly manifests and distinguishes the various root-natures of sentient beings. Fourth, as for the direction from which he comes:
it is the northwest, which corresponds to the trigram *Qian*, to the Father, to firmness and hardness, to Heaven, and to the white and pure circle; it is able to manifest all colors.

Abiding therein for this reason, the Bodhisattva is named *Tathatājñāna* (True Wisdom), the world is named *Raktotpala* (Red Lotus), and the Buddha is named *Jyotir-maṇḍala-samantaprabha-vidyā-cakravartin* (The All-Illuminating Great Wisdom of the Constellation Moon).

He is able to manifest the distinctions among the faculties and capacities of sentient beings, just as the sky clearly reveals various phenomena and objects. This is the eighth spiritual friend encountered by Sudhana, a rishi.
Vimuktaśroṇa (Vimu-gu-sha) means "One Whose Utterances Are Terrifying. This refers to the Sage of Luminous True Wisdom who has perfected clarity;

it signifies that the wisdom of this stage increases and is untainted. Furthermore, it signifies that having attained wisdom, he transforms those with false views by appearing to conform to their errors.
Regarding the ninth stage, the Bodhisattva Anuttara-mati (Unsurpassed Wisdom), the four meanings are as before: first, the clarification of bodhi...
Regarding the name "Sa" (薩): because this stage is the dwelling of the Dharma Prince of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) who skillfully expounds the Dharma, it is called "Unsurpassed Wisdom.

Regarding the names of the two worlds: as for why the world is named *Naradapuṣpa*, *Nara* here means "person," and *Dha* means "to hold"; thus, because the fragrance of this flower is pure and exquisite, it is [named after] a person.

Wearing this sash signifies that a Bodhisattva of this stage, through skillfully expounding the wondrous Dharma, causes those who hear it to obtain the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body—consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Because all people uphold, recite, and wear it, the world is named Naradapuṣpa-trividyā.
For what reason is the Buddha of this stage named Vimalacandra? [Because he is like the pure moon.]
Because the Bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, he is a great Dharma-preacher; because he is able to purify the afflictions of both himself and others, the Buddha names him "Pure Moon.
As for the direction from which he comes—that is the lower direction—its assembly represents those of the lower direction.

Since the lower direction is characterized by the vajra, water, and the wind-wheel, which are able to sustain the world, it symbolizes that the Bodhisattva of this stage is skilled in eloquently expounding the sublime.
The Dharma can sustain the world’s norms and principles, causing people to emulate and learn them;
for this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Anuttara-mati (Unsurpassed Wisdom), the world is named Nārada-puṣpa, and the Buddha is named Viśuddha-candra (Pure Moon).
At this stage, he is like Sudhana seeing the Brahmin Jvalanānta ascending the mountain of blades and entering the mass of fire, as all devas and humans who come to see him do.

All of these attain the Way and depart; this clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom is identical to [the methods of] heterodoxy, for he gathers those of various other paths and causes them to enter right view.
Regarding the tenth stage, the Bodhisattva of Firm Wisdom (*Dṛḍhamati*), there are four points as before:
first, it clarifies why the Bodhisattva is named "Firm Wisdom," because this stage is the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) where one dwells in the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
First, it is named for its ability to firmly benefit all sentient beings.
Second, the two worlds are named "Flowers in Space" because the sun of wisdom illuminates both the mundane and supramundane realms, such that there is ultimately no abiding or reliance;
this is why they are so named. Third, the reason the Buddha is titled "Moon of Clarity" is that at this stage, great wisdom is perfected.
His name is derived from the fact that his brilliance universally illuminates the world such that there is nothing not clearly perceived.

As for the direction from which he comes, it is the direction above. "Above" refers to the realm of space, the sun, moon, and stars, which symbolize great wisdom that is non-reliant—neither relying on emptiness nor on existence—and which clearly carves out the myriad phenomena like the sun, moon, and stars. For this reason, the Bodhisattva is so named.
In the world-system Sthira-mati, there is a land named Gaganakusuma and a Buddha named Vimalaprabhācandra.
At this stage, Sudhana visits the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, the maiden named Maitrāyaṇī. As for this daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, she is one whose wisdom and compassion are perfected;
having completed the first of these ten stages, she is born into the family of the Buddhas, wherein the ten stages are harmoniously integrated.

The union of Dharma, compassion, and wisdom is finally perfected. From the initial stage of the first *bhūmi*, one is born into the family of the Buddhas by cultivating wisdom and practicing compassion;
thus, just as the Princess practiced compassion throughout the ten stages until it was fully realized, at the beginning of the eleventh stage, one employs compassion to cultivate wisdom.
This is the Buddha-mother Māyā, who through her illusory power gives birth to all Buddhas. The Buddha is Great Wisdom, and the Mother is Great Compassion.
The broad meaning and ultimate textual clarification are as follows; they may be understood through the ten sections of verse according to the text.

First, having explained the faults based on the preceding topical outline: the names of the Bodhisattvas, the names of the worlds, and the ten fruits of Buddhahood are all, within these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), titles for the causes and effects of progressive cultivation according to their respective positions. These are designated in accordance with the various directions to symbolize the Dharma.
The names are established according to their inclusion in the [respective] categories, as can be understood from the assignments provided above.
[Sūtra] The Buddha emits pure radiance, through which all are seen: the Teacher of the World resides within the Sublime Palace atop the King of Mountains, Sumeru;
all the Śakra-devānām-indras entreat the Buddha to enter their palaces.
With ten sublime verses, they praised all the Tathāgatas.
All the bodhisattvas present within those great assemblies had come from the ten directions; having manifested seats, they sat down peacefully.
All the bodhisattvas in those assemblies bore names identical to our own, and the worlds from which they came—
The names are likewise so; the World-Honored Ones of their original lands all share these same titles.
Each, at the site of their respective Buddha, has purely cultivated the supreme practice.
O Son of the Buddha, you should observe the Tathāgata’s power of mastery: throughout all Jambudvīpas, it is said that the Buddha is present therein.
We now behold the Buddha, Abiding upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; In all ten directions it is likewise so.

By the sovereign power of the Tathāgata, In every single world-system, Those who have resolved their minds to seek the path of the Buddha, And who cultivate the practices of enlightenment based on such vows— The Buddha, by means of various bodies, [manifests before them].
Wandering throughout all worlds, unimpeded within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is none who can measure you;
your light of wisdom shines eternally and universally, extinguishing all darkness in the world. Since you are peerless in every respect, how could you be measured or known?
[Treatise] From the point where the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, having received the majestic power [of the Buddha], spoke these verses downward for ten lines,
this section clarifies the Bodhisattva Dharmamati’s praise of the Buddha’s emission of light and the gathering of the assembly.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvajñāna, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to constantly behold the Tathāgata for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, If one does not contemplate the Savior of the World in accordance with the true meaning,
That person grasps at various signs, Only increasing the net of delusion and confusion."
Bound within the prison of birth and death, blind and ignorant, they do not see the Buddha. One should contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent;

just as their characteristics of arising and ceasing are merely spoken of by way of conventional designation, so too are all phenomena without arising and all phenomena without cessation. If one can understand in this way, [one attains liberation].
The Buddhas are ever manifest before one; the nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Without grasping and without seeing, the emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha—beyond the reach of thought or deliberation.
If one knows that the essential nature of all phenomena is thus, such a person will not be defiled or attached by afflictions.
Ordinary beings perceive all phenomena And revolve solely according to their marks.

Not understanding that phenomena are signless, they do not see the Buddha; The Muni is beyond the three times, Perfectly endowed with all marks, Abiding in non-abiding, Pervasive yet unmoving. Thus I contemplate all phenomena.
All have attained clear understanding; now they behold the Tathāgata.
There is no doubt whatsoever regarding the Dharma-wisdom previously taught by the Tathāgata concerning the true nature of reality.
From that, I have understood that Bodhi is inconceivable.

[Treatise] From "At that time" onwards, it clarifies how Sarvajñā (All-Wisdom) Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, spoke ten verses of verse-prose to praise the signless Dharma as the reality.
[Sūtra] At that time, Sarvajñā Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata’s great wisdom is rare and without equal; All the worlds cannot fathom it through thought.
Ordinary people observe falsely, Grasping at signs in an improper manner.
The Buddha is free from all signs; He cannot be seen by those who are deluded and ignorant.
Falsely grasping at the characteristics of the five aggregates, one fails to understand their true nature. Such a person does not see the Buddha;
yet, by thoroughly knowing that all phenomena have no inherent existence, one who thus understands the nature of dharmas sees Vairocana.
Because of the preceding five aggregates, the subsequent aggregates arise in succession.
By understanding this nature, one perceives the Buddha, who is inconceivable.
Just as a jewel in the dark cannot be seen without a lamp, so too, if the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even the wise cannot understand it.
It is like having a cataract in the eye: one does not see pure and wondrous forms; thus it is with the impure mind.
One does not see the Buddhas’ dharmas, Just as the bright, pure sun cannot be seen by the blind.

Those who lack the mind of wisdom Will never see the Buddhas. If one can remove the cataracts of the eyes And abandon the perception of forms, Not seeing any dharmas at all, Then one attains the vision of the Tathāgata.
All-Wise One, you first proclaimed The Dharma of the Buddhas’ Bodhi; From you I heard it, and thus I beheld Vairocana.
[Treatise] 4. From "At that time" onwards, it clarifies how the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom (Jñānavara) spoke ten verses of praise to lament the delusion of ordinary beings.
The true nature of the five aggregates is understood only through human explanation.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
All phenomena lack true reality, yet people falsely grasp at the appearance of true reality.
For this reason, all ordinary beings wander in the prison of birth and death. Regarding the teachings expressed through words, those of small intelligence falsely discriminate;
thus, obstacles arise. Failing to understand one's own mind, they are unable to comprehend their own minds.
How can one know the right path? It is through perverted wisdom that all evils increase;
failing to see the emptiness of all phenomena, one constantly undergoes the suffering of birth and death.
Because such a person has not yet attained the pure Dharma-eye, I myself underwent manifold sufferings in the past, due to my failure to see the Buddha.
Therefore, one should purify the Dharma-eye to observe what ought to be seen.
If one attains the vision of the Buddha, yet the mind grasps at nothing, such a person is truly able to see.
If one sees the true Dharma as the Buddha knows it, they are called a person of great wisdom; such a person possesses the pure eye.

One who is able to observe the world thus: "Non-seeing is itself seeing"—one who sees all phenomena as such has no [substantial] seeing at all. The nature of all phenomena is neither born nor extinguished.
How marvelous! The Great Teacher, who has awakened by himself and is able to awaken others.
The Victorious Wisdom has already explained the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata; having heard it from him, we are able to know the true nature of the Buddha.
[Treatise] Fifth: At that time, Guṇamati spoke ten verses in the *daṇḍaka* meter to clarify the false grasping of phenomena as being real.
[The Characteristics.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramatī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"If one dwells in conceptual discrimination, Then the pure eye is destroyed, And delusion and false views increase."

One never sees the Buddhas if one can understand false dharmas; Knowing that delusion is fundamentally true, as it is and without inversion, Seeing the Buddha is then purity. Where there is seeing, there is defilement;
this is not yet seeing. To be far removed from all views— In this way, one truly sees the Buddha.
The conventional language of the world is the false discrimination of sentient beings.
To know that all in the world is unborn is to truly see the world. If one sees by seeing the world, then what is seen is the mark of the world;
as it truly is, equal and without difference. This is called one who sees truly. If one sees with such equality and lack of difference, [one is a true seer].
Not discriminating among phenomena, this vision is free from all delusions. It is the outflow-free mastery revealed by the Buddhas.
All phenomena that are conceptually constructed are entirely unattainable, for their nature is pure;
the nature of phenomena is fundamentally pure, like space, devoid of characteristics.
Nothing at all can be spoken; the wise contemplate it thus. Free from the notion of "dharmas," they take no delight in any phenomena. There is nothing here to be cultivated.
One who can see the Great Muni as described by Guṇamati— this one is called a seer of the Buddha. This is the nature of all conditioned activities.
"The Essential Nature is Utterly Quiescent.
[Treatise] Sixth: At that time, Vīramati spoke ten verses of practice to praise how the self-nature of all phenomena is beyond seeing, and how false views lead to delusion regarding reality.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Suprajñā, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"How marvelous! The great heroes, the immeasurable Tathāgatas, Whose stainless minds are liberated—having crossed over themselves, they can deliver others.
I behold the Lamp of the World, who perceives reality without inversion."
As seen by those who have accumulated wisdom over immeasurable eons, all the activities of ordinary beings inevitably and swiftly reach exhaustion;
yet their nature is like space. Therefore, it is said that there is no exhaustion;
even this teaching of non-exhaustion is itself nothing taught, for its intrinsic nature is inexhaustible.
One attains the inconceivable exhaustion; within that which is taught as inexhaustible, there is no sentient being to be found, for the nature of sentient beings is thus.
Then one sees the Great Renowned One; non-seeing is called seeing, and non-arising is called sentient beings.
Whether it be seeing or sentient beings, one thoroughly understands them to be without intrinsic nature.
The capacity to see, the object seen, and the seer—all these are completely dispelled.

One who understands this true Dharma without destroying it knows the Buddha. If a person knows the Buddha and the Dharma taught by the Buddha, they can illuminate the world, just as the Buddha Vairocana, the Perfectly Awakened One, has excellently revealed.
The path of purity of the single dharma— The Great Being of diligence and wisdom Expounds immeasurable dharmas,
whether existent or non-existent; All such perceptions are extinguished, And thus one is able to see the Buddha abiding in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
[Treatise] At that time, the Bodhisattva Śubhamati spoke ten verses of practice to praise the Dharma that no sentient beings can be exhausted,
which is free from the two views of existence and non-existence.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñāna, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses:
Upon hearing the most supreme teaching, the light of wisdom immediately arose within me; it universally illumines the realms of the ten directions, and I see all Buddhas therein.
Within this, there is not the slightest thing; there is only the existence of provisional names.
To reckon that there is a self or a person is to enter a perilous path—this is the way of ordinary people who cling to grasping.
One who calculates the body as being substantially real cannot grasp the Tathāgata; such a person will ultimately never see him.
One who lacks the eye of wisdom cannot perceive the Buddha. For immeasurable eons, they will wander through the ocean of birth and death.
Where there is contention, there is said to be birth and death; where there is no contention, that is nirvāṇa.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—both are unattainable. If one pursues inverted names and grasps at these two dharmas, this person does not accord with reality;
not knowing the sublime path of the sages, they conceive such notions as:
"This is the Buddha," "This is the Most Victorious. These are inversions, not the true meaning.
One cannot see the Perfectly Awakened One by means of knowing this substantial entity;

rather, one sees the Honored One of Perfect Awakening through the mark of the quiescent *tathatā*. Transcending the path of language, the real mark cannot be revealed by words that speak of all phenomena.
Only through equality can one see it; as the Dharma is, so too is the Buddha.
The Perfectly Awakened One, regarding the past, the future, and the present, has forever severed the root of conceptual discrimination;
therefore, he is called a Buddha.
[Commentary] At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñāna spoke these ten verses of practice to praise that which transcends verbal expression and is the True Reality.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhūtamatī, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Better to undergo the sufferings of hell Than to receive immeasurable bliss Without hearing the names of the Buddhas. Therefore, in the past, I endured suffering for incalculable kalpas."
Wandering through birth and death, they do not hear the name of the Buddha; Regarding phenomena without inversion, they realize them as they truly are.
Free from all signs of composite aggregation, this is called unsurpassed awakening.
The present is not a composite; the past and future are likewise so. All phenomena are signless.
This is the true body of the Buddha; if one can contemplate in this way, then one sees the profound meaning of all phenomena—the true characteristic of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
Seeing reality as it truly is, and not seeing what is unreal as real, through such ultimate understanding, one is therefore called a Buddha.
The Buddha-dharma cannot be awakened to; realizing this is called awakening to the Dharma. All Buddhas cultivate in this way:
not a single dharma can be apprehended. Knowing that through the one there is the many, and knowing that through the many there is the one, all dharmas have no basis;
they arise merely from combination, with neither an agent nor an object of action.
Arising solely from the perception of karma—how is it known to be thus?
Because nothing else exists apart from this, all phenomena are without abiding; no fixed location can be found. The Buddhas dwell herein, ultimately unshakable.
[Treatise] At that time, the Bodhisattva Real Wisdom spoke ten verses of practice to praise the nature of all phenomena as being without conjunction or dispersion.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Unsurpassed Wisdom, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Unsurpassed Mahāsattva, who has distanced himself from the notion of sentient beings—because there is no one who can surpass him, he is called "Unsurpassed.
This is the state attained by all Buddhas: it is without action and without discrimination;
the coarse does not exist, and the subtle is likewise so. This is the sphere of activity of all Buddhas.
Within this there is no number; the Perfectly Awakened One is far removed from number.
This is the true Dharma of the Buddha; the light of the Tathāgata shines everywhere, extinguishing all darkness.
This light neither has illumination nor lacks illumination; it is unattached to phenomena, without thought, and without defilement.
Without abiding and without location, not destroying the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), herein there is neither duality nor even unity.
For those of great wisdom who see well, they abide skillfully according to reality;
in non-duality there is no duality, and even that non-duality is absent—the entire triple world is empty.
This is what all Buddhas see, yet ordinary beings lack awakening and understanding. The Buddha causes them to abide in the True Dharma;
all phenomena have no place of abiding. Awakening to this, one sees one’s own body: it is not a body, yet it is called a body;
it does not arise, yet it manifests as arising; without body and without seeing— this is the unsurpassed body of the Buddha.
Thus has the Wisdom of Reality spoken of the nature of the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas;
whoever hears this Dharma shall obtain the pure eye.
[Commentary: At that time, the Unsurpassed Wisdom spoke these ten verses of practice to praise the undifferentiated essence of the Dharma-body attained by the Buddha.
This is not included in the numerical categories.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"How magnificent is the Great Radiance! O valiant and unsurpassed Hero, For the sake of benefiting all deluded beings..."

Yet he has arisen in the world; with a heart of great compassion, the Buddha universally observes all sentient beings dwelling within the three realms of existence, revolving and undergoing manifold sufferings.
Except for the Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One endowed with virtue and the Great Teacher, there is no one among all devas and humans who can provide rescue and protection.
If Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the like did not appear in the world, there would be no sentient being who could obtain peace and happiness.

When the Tathāgatas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assembly of noble sages appear in the world, they are able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings; thus, those who behold the Tathāgata [attain this].
To attain great and wholesome benefit, one hears the Buddha’s name and gives rise to faith; this is a stūpa for the world.
We have seen the World-Honored One, and to attain great benefit, we have heard such a sublime Dharma.
All shall surely achieve the path of Buddhahood. By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, all bodhisattvas of the past—
Having attained the eye of pure wisdom, they fully comprehend the realm of all Buddhas;

now beholding Vairocana, their pure faith increases further. The Buddha-wisdom is boundless, and its exposition can never be exhausted—by the Bodhisattvas such as Jñānasamudgata and myself, Dṛḍhamati, throughout countless billions of kalpas.
[The Sūtra says: "Even speaking could not exhaust it.
[The Commentary says: At that time, Dṛḍhamati spoke ten verses in praise of the Buddha’s great compassion in appearing in the world for the benefit of others.
Above, these ten bodhisattvas each spoke ten verses on the practices to harmonize and enter the teachings of the stages, so as to transform body and mind.
All such reckonings are without basis; free from biased attachment, one dwells in that which the Buddhas dwell.
Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes.
[Treatise] In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to five sections: first, the explanation of the title of the chapter; second, the explanation of the chapter...

The intent of the coming [of this chapter] is as follows: First, the essential purport of the "Chapter on the Threefold Clarification" (*Trividha-vyākaraṇa-parivarta*): it is a compendium of four points concerning the sequence of severing delusions.

Second, the sequential explanation of the meaning according to the text: 1. Explaining the title of the chapter: This chapter expounds ten types of abiding gates (*vihāra-mukha*), and is therefore titled the "Chapter on the Ten Abidings" (*Daśa-vihāra-parivarta*).
2. Clarifying the intent of the chapter’s arrival: Since the preceding chapter was a gate of verse-praise and exhortation to practice, this chapter elucidates the actual [practice].
Raising up the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), this chapter must therefore come forth. Those who attain the ten stages give birth to the great wisdom of all Buddhas;
by dwelling and entering this position, they never again fall back, and for this reason it is called "dwelling" (*bhūmi*).

As for the essential purport of the "Chapter on the Three Clarities" (*trividyā*): it clarifies that this chapter explains the ten kinds of dwellings and the twenty kinds of causal practices for progressive cultivation.
The "True Main Body" (Zhengzong) further abides in that which the Buddha abides in, thereby clarifying the True Main Body.

Within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), each possesses two kinds of cause and effect. Within each respective stage, the first presentation of the ten dharmas constitutes the superior conditions for aspiring toward [the goal], while the subsequent presentation of the ten dharmas constitutes the fruit of cultivation within that specific stage, as clearly elucidated in the text.
Regarding the sequence for severing delusions during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as explained in the fourth assembly:

within these three stages—the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-bhūmi*), the Stage of Preparing the Ground (*caryāpratipatti-bhūmi*), and the Stage of Cultivation (*caryā-bhūmi*)—it is clarified that one collectively cultivates the supramundane mind to shatter the fetters of all mundane afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for these mundane afflictions, they are as described in the verses spoken by Sudhana, concerning the root afflictions.

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*), there are ten; as for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are six in total. As for the ten types of root afflictions: first, desire (*kāma*); second, form (*rūpa*);

third, formlessness (*ārūpya*)—these are the fundamental points of bondage within the three realms; fourth, pride (*māna*); fifth, the various destinies (*gati*); sixth, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); seventh, delusion (*moha*);
eighth, greed (*lobha*); ninth, anger (*dveṣa*); tenth, the Māra of the mind (*citta-māra*). These constitute the ten. Furthermore, regarding the secondary...
Afflictions, in total, are of six kinds: first, flattery; second, deception; third, doubt; fourth, stinginess; fifth, envy;

and sixth, arrogance. Sudhana’s verse says: The three realms of existence constitute the city walls, pride serves as the ramparts, the various destinies are the gates, the waters of craving form the moats, and ignorance acts as the dark canopy.
Greed and hatred blaze like fire, while Māra the King presides over it all.
When a ruler is immature, relying on craving as his bridle and reins, with deceit and guile as his bit, and with doubt obscuring his eyes, he enters into various false views;
because of stinginess, envy, and arrogance, he falls into the three evil realms.
This refers to what arises within the internal mind, not to the view of a self-identity, extreme views, view-grasping, precept-and-vow-grasping, or false views within the internal mind.

When all views are perfected as wisdom, they are themselves liberation. Because the essence of the teaching of this One Vehicle concerns only the realization that ignorance constitutes the functioning of great wisdom, and because one employs all views to exercise mastery, the five [wrong] views are not discussed here.
As stated in the passage concerning the stage of the Ten Faiths, when Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Dharmottara about the eleven kinds of afflictions, he said: "What are they?"
These eleven are: first, greed; second, anger; third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, concealment; sixth, resentment; seventh, enmity; eighth, jealousy;

ninth, stinginess; tenth, deception; and eleventh, flattery. As in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, these afflictions—such as the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination—are addressed here within the context of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), specifically during the stage of initial resolve, the stage of purifying the ground, and the stage of cultivation.
The three abidings are simultaneously and instantaneously established as fundamental wisdom;
this is like Sudhana on Mount Supratiṣṭhita seeing the bhikṣu Meghaśrī and attaining the gate of the light of the wisdom of all Buddhas,
whereby he immediately eliminates the aforementioned worldly afflictive hindrances and achieves the light of the Buddha-wisdom, just as Sudhana did on Mount Supratiṣṭhita.
The eye of faith is clear and pure, and the light of wisdom shines radiantly as one universally contemplates all realms, free from all obstructions.
This is the first stage, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve. In the second ocean-gate, the land of *Samudramegha*, one beholds the Bhikṣu *Samudramegha*.

By removing delusions regarding the mind and phenomena through the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, one becomes free from obstructions; thus, one sees a Buddha appear within the ocean, preaching the Universal [Dharma].

The *Cakṣur-sūtra* clearly reveals that the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within oneself and others constitutes the ocean of great wisdom; this is the meaning of "Buddha.

Since both mind and phenomena are entirely encompassed by the *sūtra*, one clearly attains the Buddha-wisdom previously mentioned and contemplates the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination to generate the ocean of great wisdom.
Because mind and phenomena are universally pervasive and sovereign, this is the stage of "Purifying the Ground" (*bhūmi-pariśodhana*), by means of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Because he governs them so as to bring them to the stage of Tathāgata-wisdom, in the third land, Sāgaratīra, he beheld the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita.
Having removed the obstacle of mental objects being unclear and impure, he attained the bodhisattva liberation door of unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid*).

He was able to clearly perceive the faculties, karmic actions, and conduct of all sentient beings, as well as their deaths and rebirths in this and other lives—all of which he saw with perfect clarity. This is the dwelling of his practice.
Within these three modes of abiding, it is clarified that one attains mastery over the mind by emerging from its entanglements; thus, through the ten levels of faith,

one universally illuminates with the light of the pure wisdom-eye of self-confidence, believing that all the delusions of discrimination within the triple world are fundamentally the Immovable Wisdom Buddha,
who, within the stage of the first resolve, possesses the power of sovereign and decisive understanding.
Contemplating the objective realm, one becomes free from all hindrances and attains realization by entering the initial mind of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

Through progressive cultivation according to the stages, fifty sequential dharma-gates of the Buddha-fruit are established as skillful means; all of these take Immovable Wisdom (*acalajñāna*) as their fundamental basis.

Thus far, the first stage, the Abode of Initial Aspiration (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*), the Abode of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmiparikarmavihāra*), and the Abode of Practice (*caryāpratipattivihaara*) have been clarified, wherein the ten [aspects] are attained.
In the third dwelling, the mind that emerges from the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) is superior to the [previous] seven;
thus, the first three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of Sudhana are all *bhikṣus*, clearly indicating that these represent the modes of practice within the stages of the first three dwellings.

In the fourth, the Dwelling of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*), it clarifies the remedies for worldly conventions and the obstacles of lack of mastery amidst the bustle of birth and death, thereby causing one to... [attain] self-mastery.
In this regard, it is as when Sudhana, while at a marketplace, saw the elder Megha preach the *Akṣarāvalī-sūtra*;

this signifies that within the bustling marketplace of birth and death, there is constant quiescence. In each and every syllable, the "one" and the "many" are perfectly complete, their mutual essences forming one another, just like a wheel.
Furthermore, it is like the jewel-net of Śakra, where each element acts as a condition for the others, reflecting one another.
Within each single character, which penetrates through all layers, there are inexhaustible words and phrases;

these constitute the worldly bodies of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, *vyañjana-kāya*) that guide those who have not yet studied, thereby establishing the rules of the teachings. By means of the worldly layman Megha, his conduct is perfected so that he may give rise to the supramundane mind.
Thereafter, one must clarify the nature of all phenomena—the worldly and the tranquil, the dependent origination of causes and conditions, and the nature of birth and death.
The meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing, as well as all worldly names and principles, and the mutual accomplishment of the speech of all sentient beings,
is like that of the ancient Fuxi and others. Fifth, the stage of being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya*) counteracts the views of self and body within the ultimate and conventional truths,
enabling mastery over the realm of great wisdom and destroying lack of mastery.
Because of this removal of obstacles, just as Sudhana saw the elder Vimokṣa enter the samādhi called "Universally Gathering All Buddha-fields with Boundless Dhāraṇīs," wherein oceans of Buddha-lands,
as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, each appearing in the ten directions,
were all manifested within his body; this clearly illustrates that the bodies of all sentient beings universally contain [all things].

The essence and characteristics of infinite Buddha-fields are unimpeded, clarifying that the forms of the ultimate and conventional truths are all like light and shadows, mutually accommodating one another because there is neither center nor periphery.

Because it seeks to bring about the liberation of the nature of the sixty-two views and all infinite views, the sixth stage, the Abode of the Right Mind (*samyaktva-nyāma*), counteracts the obstacle of wisdom being unable to freely manifest its quiescence and activity; this is as follows:
Sudhana saw the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja seated in the full lotus posture beside his place for walking meditation;

he was free from inhalation and exhalation and devoid of distinct thoughts or perceptions. From every part of his body, transformation bodies issued forth like clouds, extensively covering and pervading the ten directions according to how they were perceived by sentient beings. This demonstrates that his quiescence and activity are unimpeded. Thus it is said.
The preceding section generally clarifies that the convergence of the mundane and the supramundane leads to liberation.

Following this, the four *pāramitās* enter into worldly conduct and practice compassion so as to achieve mastery. In the seventh stage, the "Irreversible," one counters the obstacle regarding the non-perfection of mastery in gathering sentient beings through the concurrent practice of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*), thereby bringing it to perfection. It is just as follows:
In the Universal Adornment Garden, Sudhana saw the laywoman Śrīprabhā, who said to him:
"I have eighty-four thousand nayutas of companions and followers who always dwell in this garden,
clearly practicing the perfection of skillful means within the stage of great compassion, equal in number to all the eighty-four thousand unspeakable multitudes."
Regarding the shared activity of teaching and benefiting that gives rise to afflictions, the *Sūtra* states:

"Other sentient beings who dwell in this garden also all universally attain the stage of non-retrogression. This clarifies that those who practice compassion and wisdom act in the same manner as these.
Eighth, the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*) counteracts the entanglements of habitual tendencies toward worldly activities; it is the wisdom that does not [cling to] remaining habits.
Because it purifies obscurations and renders them pure, it is like Sudhana seeing the seer Vimalacitra, who represents great wisdom that is clean and unstained.

That the laywoman Śrīprabhā’s dwelling place shares the same name as the seer’s—both being located at the seashore—clarifies that this compassion and wisdom are of one essence, unstained and unpolluted. If...

If one cultivates wisdom following compassion, there remains a mind stained by habitual tendencies toward objects; this refers precisely to the union of the seventh and eighth stages as a single culmination.

If, however, one practices compassion following wisdom such that no stained habits remain, this is exemplified by the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, the maiden Maitrāyaṇī; one should reflect upon this to perceive its meaning. This is the ninth [point].
The stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra*) counteracts the obstacle of lack of mastery in teaching the Dharma, thereby bringing about such mastery;

it is just as when Sudhana saw the Brahmin Śroṇa (Vīraśakti) ascending the mountain of blades and entering the mass of fire to practice asceticism, such that all who came—whether devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, or non-humans—without exception obtained benefit. This is the tenth, the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
Abiding in the antidote that purifies the obstacle to the mastery of compassion and wisdom, one attains purity;

this is like Sudhana seeing the princess Maitrāyaṇī, daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, because she possesses mastery over wisdom. As for her being a "woman," it symbolizes acting in concert with others through compassion while remaining untainted by habitual tendencies;
thus, her clear wisdom is perfected as she dwells in the world out of compassion. This is identical [to the previous case].
Because these matters are devoid of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the ten aforementioned types of remedies— within a single thought-moment,
at the time of first generating the bodhicitta, within a single practice, and within a single instant— are free from the limits of before and after.
These remedies for the ten types of obstructive dharmas are perfected within a single dharma, a single mind, a single wisdom, and a single practice as ten inexhaustible dharmas.
All gates take the Buddha of the Immovable Wisdom of One’s Own Mind as their essence;

because within the performance of Dharma-activities these ten kinds of inexhaustible Dharma-gates are fully present, and because there is mastery over their identity and difference, unity and multiplicity, these ten kinds serve as remedies that simultaneously bring about mastery over habitual tendencies.
This is not like the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, which are directed toward sentient beings of inferior understanding.
Maintaining the nature of the three periods of time within the world, it is taught that the fruit of Buddhahood lies beyond three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
By means of the seeds of discrimination arising from the fundamental ignorance of one's own mind, one immediately becomes the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*).

Taking the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu* as the gates for entering through faith and diligence, one progresses from faith to the stages of entry, practicing until the ten [stages] are completed.
Abiding in the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage, one never departs from the fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha.

Without departing from a single moment, a single thought, a single dharma, or a single practice, there exist boundless, immeasurable, unspeakable, and ineffable Dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms within the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. Why is this? Because it arises from...

Because one must have faith and diligence to awaken to and enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the fundamental immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*), and because the nature of phenomena is such that it accords with this, it is like the Dragon Girl who attained Buddhahood in an instant, or Sudhana who attained the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Since the Dharma-realm is without intrinsic nature and without birth, "one lifetime" does not refer to a life subject to extension or contraction; for the essence of the Dharma-realm is devoid of any measurable duration.
Because it shortens the long and removes the distinctions of past, present, and future, all those with faith should understand it thus:

attaining Buddhahood now is simultaneous with the attainment of Buddhahood by all Buddhas of the past and future, because the essence of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* is without distinction of time.
It is like a single drop of water entering the great ocean; it becomes one with the great ocean, without any sense of new or old.
Because of the water, one departs from emotional attachments and only then perceives what is not consciousness; the mind knows it as such.

Within the Three Vehicles, even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes still undergo the segmented birth-and-death of the triple world. They cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to counteract the obstacle of the icchantika’s lack of faith.

Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices partially cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and practice deeds for the benefit of self and others to counteract the obstacle of the śrāvaka.

Hearing this, the Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ten Dedications practices the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-darśana*) and accomplishes the power of the great compassionate vow (*mahākaruṇā-praṇidhāna-bala*).
By manifesting forms within the six realms of existence to transform sentient beings, they counteract the obstacle of the Pratyekabuddha who seeks only self-deliverance.

This clarifies that among the three vehicles, the Bodhisattvas of the thirty minds counteract the three types of obstacles prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*); however, while they eliminate the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), they have not yet eliminated the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) sever their residual habits (*vāsanā*). Because a Bodhisattva of the first stage perceives the *tathatā* (suchness) of their own Buddha-nature, it is called the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
From the second stage through the seventh stage is the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), wherein one still practices with effortful application (*sābhisamskāra*).
From the eighth stage through the tenth stage is called the stage of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-mārga*), which does not require [effortful application].

Because they function spontaneously until the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood; furthermore, among the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) within the Three Vehicles, the first is the stage of the single lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), which corresponds to the ten gates of understanding;

the second is the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), which refers to the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); the third is the stage of joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*), which is the first ground (*bhūmi*);
the fourth is the stage of superior morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*), which is the second ground; and the fifth is the stage of superior wisdom (*adhijñāna-vihāra*), which is the third ground.
The fourth stage is the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the six realms; the fifth stage is the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the seven truths;
the sixth stage is the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with the eightfold dependent origination;
the seventh stage is the signless dwelling with effort and application; and the eighth stage is the signless dwelling without effort or application.
The first stage is the dwelling of the eleven non-obstructions; the nine stages are the dwelling of the twelve supreme bodhi; and the tenth stage is likewise as follows:

among the three vehicles, the bodhisattvas of the three levels of worthiness prior to the stages attain the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), while those in the ten stages and the Buddha stage attain the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, when compared with the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, [these correspond respectively to] the arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and the pure-land bodhisattvas.

Always employing the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) to suppress the active manifestations of the ten afflictions (*daśa-ānuśaya*) so that they do not arise—because one has not yet recognized the affliction of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*)—one still does not recognize [it]. How, then, can it be called the "severing of afflictions"?

One merely suppresses their active manifestations so they do not arise, thereby attaining the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) and undergoing the transformation-death (*parināma-maraṇa*) beyond the three realms. Such is the bodhisattva.
By practicing the six *pāramitās*, one attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); in both merit and supernormal power, these surpass those of humans and devas.

However, because this is not the cultivation of the gateway to the *dharmadhātu* of the Buddha-fruit, it remains outside that gate. The three vehicles—the chariots, the grass huts, and the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—differ from the bodhisattvas in their virtues.
While they transcend the triple world and practice the six supernormal powers, their names [and qualities] are distinct.

Because the fruits and retributions of the merit from practicing the six *pāramitās* are not identical, the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles who possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) do not hear or believe this *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*.
As this sūtra says: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable *nayuta* kalpas, practiced the six *pāramitās* and attained the six [supernormal powers]..."
Even those with supernormal powers who have not yet heard this Flower Ornament (Avataṃsaka) Sūtra are called "provisional bodhisattvas" and are not true bodhisattvas;
even if they should hear it, they do not believe or enter into it. It is the same as with the Lotus Sūtra. Regarding the three kinds of mind-made bodies within the Three Vehicles:
the first, second, and third stages are called the "mind-made body of the joy of the dharma" (dharmābhirati-manomaya-kāya) due to their meditative attainments (samāpatti).
The body [attained] on the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and eighth stages is called the "Mind-made Body that Awakens to the Self-nature of Dharmas.
The body [attained] on the third, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages is called the "Mind-made Body that is Innately Born according to its Type and is Effortless.

If one were to cite extensively from the various teachings of the Three Vehicles regarding these points—such as their own clear explanations, their syntheses, and their specific antidotes—one would find nothing at all corresponding to this One Vehicle teaching.

Taking the path of the three vehicles as its fundamental basis, the affliction of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is present within all Buddhas as their immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*), and it is likewise inherent in all sentient beings.
It is only because the essence of wisdom is without intrinsic nature and without dependence that it cannot realize itself;
it realizes itself only by encountering conditions (*pratyaya*). What is meant by "encountering conditions"? There are three ways of encountering conditions.
First, one may encounter suffering as a condition for awakening the mind; only when meeting with suffering can one resolve to seek enlightenment. Second, one may encounter happiness as a condition;

having long dwelt among humans and devas, one’s inner mind becomes clear and wise, and upon realizing that the fruits of worldly pleasure are impermanent within the cycle of birth and death, one finally seeks the Truth.

Third, by seeing the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle, one is able to resolve to seek the Buddha’s seed-wisdom; thus, by uniting these three conditions, one draws near to the Right Path.
A virtuous spiritual friend is one who can personally realize that the root of ignorance is fundamentally Buddha-wisdom; this is the same for all three vehicles.

However, because the depth of their aspirations differs, they each have distinct approaches: they generate faith based upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and enter into awakening by means of that fundamental wisdom.
Since they do not depart from fundamental wisdom, even at the stage of the first resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), the five stages are simultaneously perfected. Although...
The gate of the stages of practice for the ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground—its rules for progressive cultivation are like a king’s precious seal;

with a single seal there is no discrepancy. With the seal of the great wisdom of the one mind, all dharmas of the beginningless three periods of time are sealed as being simultaneously present. The wisdom-seal universally pervades all boundless dharmas, such that wisdom is equal to them all.
The Buddha, therefore, by means of his wisdom, is equal to the minds of all sentient beings; by means of his wisdom, he is equal to all phenomena;
by means of his wisdom, there is no center or periphery, interior or exterior, nor the three periods of time, long or short, near or far;

because his wisdom exceeds the measure of empty space, just as worldly empty space has nothing that can be known, so too does non-conceptual wisdom, within a single thought-moment, possess the power of discernment.
Because this dharma-gate transcends space and all other phenomena, the Sūtra states: "All of space may yet be measured, but the Dharma taught by the Buddhas cannot be measured.

For this reason, through the essence and function of the fundamental ignorance of one's own mind, one perceives that the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) shares the same single nature as all Buddhas and all sentient beings.
Sharing the same objective realm and the same ocean of wisdom, because one has thus set out from the very beginning to dwell in the family of the Buddha’s *jñāna*,
the moment the mind is first resolved, one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood throughout the ten directions,

as clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Merit of the First Resolve. For this reason, among these ten stages (*bhūmi*), those who enter the stage of the first resolve— *prathamacittotpādavihāra*— [attain this].
Abiding within the sphere of the ocean of great compassion and wisdom of all Buddhas means abiding through the simultaneous cultivation of the five stages;
because from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) through the tenth stage (*daśama-bhūmi*), one does not depart from the sphere of the wisdom of a single Buddha.

Thus, the names of the stages (*bhūmi*) are established merely to clarify the distinctions of superior and inferior based on the degree of ripening and habitual cultivation; they are within the essence of wisdom and are not objects of the conceptual mind of the three periods of time.
Because it is subsumed [within a single moment], it is like the Dragon Girl who, in a single instant, completed the three lifetimes of Samantabhadra’s conduct and attained the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is also as stated in the verses of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas;
there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the affairs of the three periods of time, one transcends all expedient means."
The *Daśabala-saṃsiddhi-śāstra* clearly explains that the attainment of Buddhahood through the three vehicles over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is a provisional, expedient teaching.
This teaching, based on the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), does not speak of attaining Buddhahood through the power of vows and so forth;

even if one practices by means of the power of vows, it still refers to attaining Buddhahood according to ultimate reality, and does not speak of attaining it temporarily through the power of vows. Therefore, one should know that from...
Among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), a bodhisattva who has first entered the initial stage practices all five positions as the common basis for the ten abodes;

this is because the characteristics of the ten abodes universally encompass the dharmas of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), and the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Thus, within the ten abodes, the seventh and eighth abodes further cultivate compassion and wisdom; the ninth abode is the stage of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka*); and within the tenth abode, compassion and wisdom are perfected.
Because the aspects of these five stages are thus similar, as in the case of Sudhana’s ten abodes where each spiritual friend’s realm of wisdom is entirely infinite,

yet for the sake of establishing the gates of practice through the five stages— which are fully endowed with the supreme dharmas of the Dharmakāya’s great wisdom and great compassion and possess inexhaustibility— all are in truth but one mind and one wisdom.

At one time, wisdom and its like pervade the path of practice; therefore, those who give rise to faith and advance in cultivation must not form views of the three periods of time—near or far, extended or compressed—within the realm of great wisdom.

To do so would be to contravene the realm of wisdom and lose the original realm of great wisdom. Because they pursue emotional consciousness, they revolve according to appearances; thus, this fourth [section] of the assembly severs [this error].
The sequence for abandoning delusions through these five stages is as follows: it is like space, which has no temporal duration; like a perfect mirror, which reflects all things instantaneously;
like a *maṇi* jewel, which can assume the colors of its surroundings; and like a single drop of water that, upon entering the great ocean, becomes identical and non-dual with it.
By means of the perfect mirror of great wisdom, all actions are universally reflected and none fail to be accomplished.
Because it is the great function of non-action, and because there is no single moment within the three periods of time.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Skillful Means.

By the power of this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name, Dharmamati. They appeared before him and addressed him.
The Bodhisattva Prajñā said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are able to enter this bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means.
Son of good family, all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields, together empower you with their spiritual power.
Furthermore, it is through the power of the past vows and majestic spiritual authority of the Tathāgata Vairocana."
By the power of yourself and the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, you have entered this samādhi so that you may preach the Dharma for the sake of increasing the Buddha-wisdom,

for the sake of penetrating deeply into the dharma-realm, for the sake of thoroughly understanding the realm of sentient beings, for the sake of entering without obstruction, for the sake of acting without hindrance,
for the sake of attaining peerless skillful means, for the sake of entering the nature of all-knowledge, and for the sake of awakening to all dharmas.
Therefore, know that because he understands all faculties and is able to uphold and expound all dharmas— namely, by initiating the ten stages of dwelling of the bodhisattvas—
son of good family, you should now, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, expound this Dharma. At that time,
the Buddhas immediately bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dharmamati unimpeded wisdom, non-attached wisdom, uninterrupted wisdom, and wisdom free from delusion.
There is no wisdom of difference, no wisdom of loss, no immeasurable wisdom, no surpassable wisdom, no weary wisdom, and no wisdom that can be taken away. Why is this?

Because the nature of the Dharma is such through the power of this samādhi. At that time, each of the Buddhas extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati immediately arose from his concentration and addressed the Bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas..."
The dwelling place is vast, equal to the dharma-realm and empty space; O Son of the Buddha, I shall now explain how that Bodhisattva dwells in the house of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
[Treatise] First: from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati... onwards, up to "...I shall now explain how that Bodhisattva dwells."
This section, consisting of nineteen and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the stage where the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and is empowered by all Buddhas.
Within it, there are eleven main points: first, the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s name; second, the clarification of the purpose for entering *samādhi*;
third, the elucidation of the power of that *samādhi*; and fourth, the manifestation of the Buddhas of the ten directions appearing before him to bestow the Dharma.
1. Wisdom is identical [to the Buddhas], termed the Five Sciences; the Buddhas of the Ten Directions grant their power, and they share a common faculty.
2. It is brought about by the power of the past vows of Vairocana Tathāgata. 3. It is because the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, through the power of his own roots of goodness, is able to enter samādhi.

4. This clarifies the causes and conditions for entering meditative concentration. 5. This clarifies that the Buddhas of the Ten Directions bestow the ten types of knowledge. 6. This clarifies [the result].
Dharmamati emerges from meditative absorption and expounds ten gates of dwelling. First, regarding the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva":
as in the stage of the ten faiths, those below [the bodhisattvas] are all collectively named "Foremost" (Śreṣṭha); this is to clarify that within the stage of faith, faith is taken as the foremost.
In these ten stages of dwelling, because they have already been born into the family of the wisdom of all Buddhas, those below are all collectively named [Bodhisattva].
This constitutes wisdom and illumination; entering the stream of the noble Dharma, one attains the Buddha’s wisdom and shares in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Skillfully distinguishing the correct from the false and harmonizing with the True Dharma is what is called "Dharma-wisdom. If one cannot personally accord with the wisdom and knowledge-vision of the Buddhas, then because one's own delusions have not yet been clarified, how could one distinguish false views?

Because this stage is able to accord with the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas, one attains all those Buddhas of identical name, Dharma-wisdom (Dharmamati), who appear before one as a seal of authentication to determine the expression of the truth.

Because it is identical to the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions, secondly, to clarify the intent of entering samādhi: for instance, within the stage of the ten faiths, it is first generated...
When one extinguishes the mind and believes that all that belongs to one's own mind— namely, the mind capable of conceptual discrimination that has existed since beginningless time—
is itself the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha, yet lacks the expedient means of samādhi to unify its essence and function,
for this reason, the ten worlds within the stage of the Ten Faiths are all termed "form," because the Ten Faiths have not yet entered [the true path].
Because the stream of the dharma-nature is believed and understood by means of a mind subject to arising and ceasing, ten worlds are designated as "form.

Within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), through the samādhi of skillful means, one is able to manifest the wisdom of the non-arising and non-ceasing of one's own essence, free from the states of dullness and agitation;
therefore, all practitioners on the path of cultivation first rely upon understanding through hearing.
Following faith and entry, one accords with the fundamental through non-conceptualization, because the fundamental wisdom is originally without activity;
