therefore, it is necessary to enter samādhi. Because the power of the defiled habits of攀緣 (pān-luán, *ālambana*) must be purified, the unconditioned true wisdom (*anabhisamskāra-bhūta-jñāna*) only then manifests clearly.
For this reason, it is necessary to enter samādhi. Third, as for what is called "correct samādhi" (*samyak-samādhi*), it refers generally to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Right concentration, right concentration: it is without sinking or agitation; it has no thought toward an object of focus; nor is there any grasping, suppressing, or extinguishing of the mind.
It is without longing and without aversion, being natural and free from volition. It accords with principle without being produced as wisdom, for it is self-luminous.
This is called skillful means; this is called the immeasurable. Because it purifies immeasurable deluded thoughts, it cannot be [grasped].
Because it is known through the measure and deliberation of the mind, it is called the "Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means. Third, "zheng" (正) means correctness;
"mei" (昧) refers to samādhi. This indicates that while emotional consciousness is obscured, correct wisdom is inherently luminous.

Just as the samādhis of the Form Realm and Formless Realm are attained by ceasing thought and deliberation, the samādhis of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are cultivated through the contemplation of revulsion.
As an antidote to this, those who delight in contemplating emptiness may extinguish their compassion and wisdom, taking nirvana as their pleasure;
such are the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who contemplate emptiness while practicing the six perfections, thereby departing from the root of suffering to be born in a pure land.

Even if some remain in this realm, claiming they "retain afflictions" to transform sentient beings, this is not the natural law (*dharmatā*), for there is no coming or going. Thus, [the true path] is in accord with reality.
Regarding this meaning, as for the samādhi of skillful means (*upāya-samādhi*):

because all sentient beings are deluded regarding the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*, and because sensual desires arise from them, one manifests original wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) through a non-conceptualizing mind.

Thus, taking the pure essence of the fundamental concentration (*maula-samādhi*) to purify these deluded emotions is what is called "skillful means"; it is not something falsely established separately outside of reality.

This samādhi is named "Expedient Means" (*upāya*). For example, just as the water-clearing jewel can purify turbid water, appearing as the condition for the manifestation of the originally pure water through the purity of the gem, yet it is not that the jewel itself can produce the pure water; so too is this Samādhi of Expedient Means.
It serves as the condition for manifesting the attainment of the originally non-active, self-pure wisdom through the non-activity of all phenomena.
Because of the power of wisdom, it is called "skillful means. However, all causes and effects belonging to devas, humans, non-Buddhists, and the three vehicles involve intentional action;
that which is produced thereby has a location and has karmic retribution, with various distinctions such as breadth and narrowness, or purity and defilement.
In contrast, within this Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s One Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka*, one dwells in non-abiding and non-action.
The Dharma-gate of Nature is such that its arising is spontaneously non-reliant; it is the wisdom of non-abiding mind, a mind-born illusory body that accords with the true Dharma-realm.
Before all sentient beings, it manifests a physical body, yet its essential nature has no coming or going.
Furthermore, it does not perform acts of supernatural power or transformation, and yet it universally appears throughout the three periods of time as one.
All karmic fruits exist within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), yet they do not abide in the three periods of time.
Regarding the views of distance, proximity, and the moment—whatever samādhis, wisdom, vows, and practices are performed in this sutra, they are all the functioning of principle and wisdom;
they are not dharmas of contrived cultivation involving attachment or aversion. This is the [nature of] the three vidyās and samādhi.
Regarding power (*bala*), there are five kinds: first, the power of the certainty that the essence of the body is pure and its aspiration is all-pervasive;

second, the power of the certainty that one can manifest wisdom equal to that of a Buddha; third, the power of the certainty that one can manifest bodily marks and names identical to those of a Buddha before one’s eyes;

fourth, the power of the certainty that one can accord with what a Buddha knows and sees, thereby obtaining the shared empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas; fifth, the power of the certainty that one can be born within suchness (*tathatā*).

To come home as a true son of the Buddha and dwell in the power of the Buddha’s wisdom means that by means of the essence of this non-active concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*), one is able to purify all desires.

This pervasive power is such that the deluded mind and body, being identical to empty space, are without interior or exterior and pervade the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, these two concentrations are able to manifest wisdom.

Those who share the Buddha’s power possess the meditative concentration of non-action (*anabhisamskāra-samādhi*), because they are able to manifest spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) that is inherently free from activity.

Since all sentient beings are fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom, yet their minds are obstructed by the arising of conditions for the five desires due to delusion regarding objects,
they take the cultivation of the meditative concentration of non-action as the skillful means (*upāya*), whereby the Buddha-wisdom and spontaneous wisdom are then realized.
Regarding the power of the three samādhis to manifest identically with the Buddha’s body, marks, and name:
it is because through the samādhi of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one realizes that one's own dharma-body and wisdom-body are non-active, pure, and stainless;
and because they are united with the dharma-body and wisdom of all Buddhas. Therefore, [the light reaches] as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions.
They appear before him with the same name, Dharma Wisdom (Dharmamati), because they have attained accord with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through wisdom;
therefore, their names are all identical to the Buddha’s own, being called Dharma Wisdom.

The phrase "the number of which is equal to the atoms within a thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions" clarifies that as one advances in practice according to the stages, wisdom becomes all-pervasive, ascending and descending.
In the tenth verse of this [chapter], it says "the dust motes of ten *buddhakṣetra*s," while in the tenth stage of the *daśabhūmi-pariṇāmanā*, it says "the dust motes of a million *buddhakṣetra*s.
This is to manifest the advancement of wisdom. When contrasted with the state of delusion, there are unspeakably many *buddhakṣetra*-dust motes of afflictions;
when contrasted with the state of awakening, there are unspeakably many *buddhakṣetra*-dust motes of Buddha-lands and Buddha-wisdom.
Wisdom. Through the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), one can accord with what the Buddhas know and see, thereby attaining the power of the Buddhas' empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
There are seven aspects of this empowerment by the Buddhas: first, the empowerment of the same name, which causes one to have no doubts;

second, the empowerment of verbal praise, which causes those who enter the stages to have peace of mind; third, the empowerment of Vairocana and his disciples, which manifests the fundamental [nature].
1. By the power of past vows, they are sustained by the four spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) and meet with their original teachers, because they share the same fundamental spiritual powers and wisdom; 2.

By the power of the sustenance of their own roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), they manifest their fundamental wisdom through the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) cultivated by their own skillful means; 3.

They attain the Buddhas of the ten directions who bear the same name, all of whom bestow upon them the sustenance of the ten kinds of power of knowledge (*jñānabala*), so that they may preach the Dharma equally with all Tathāgatas.

Because they come to expound the unimpeded [wisdom], they obtain the seventh [support]: the Buddhas of the ten directions bestowing their hands upon their crowns to empower them, reaching the pinnacle of the Buddhas' knowledge and vision, and granting approval that they are not mistaken. Thus, there are these seven kinds of empowerment.
Fifth, they are certain to be born into the family of the Tathāgata as true sons of the Buddha, dwelling in the power of the Buddha’s wisdom. This is because...
Because the essence of the unconditioned samādhi reveals that one’s fundamental wisdom is identical to the liberating wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten stages of the Bodhisattva dwelling wherein all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have spoken, will speak, and are now speaking.
What are these ten? They are: the stage of the initial resolve, the stage of purifying the ground, and the stage of cultivation.
The Dwelling of Birth in Nobility, the Dwelling of Endowment with Expedient Means, the Dwelling of Rectitude of Mind, the Dwelling of Non-retrogression, the Dwelling of the Youthful,
the Dwelling of the Dharma Prince, and the Dwelling of Empowerment— these are called the ten dwellings of Bodhisattvas as taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
[Treatise] Second, following the emergence from meditative absorption, the section clarifying the ten names and categories of the stages (*vihāra*) is as can be seen in the text.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Resolute Resolve? This Bodhisattva beholds the physical form and appearance of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
Possessing a majestic and perfect physical form that is pleasing for all to behold and difficult to encounter, and endowed with great power— whether by witnessing their supernormal powers,
hearing their prophetic declarations, listening to their instructions, seeing sentient beings undergoing intense suffering,
or hearing of the vast Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata— one awakens the mind of bodhi and seeks omniscience.

[Treatise] The third section, consisting of ten dharmas that clarify the correct explanation of the causes for generating the resolve [for awakening], refers to such things as seeing the Buddha’s physical form and its majestic beauty,
or hearing his instructions and admonitions, and so forth.
[Sūtra] This bodhisattva arouses the mind by taking ten kinds of difficult-to-attain dharmas as objects. What are these ten? They are: knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible;
knowledge of the retribution of good and evil karma; knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties; knowledge of the distinctions among various inclinations;
knowledge of the distinctions among various elements; knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; and knowledge of the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis.
The unimpeded knowledge of past lives, the unimpeded knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge that the outflows of the three periods of time are universally exhausted—these are the ten.
Sons of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas. What are these ten? They are: diligently making offerings to the Buddhas;
delighting in dwelling within birth and death to lead the world; causing the removal of evil karma; constantly practicing instruction and exhortation through the supreme and wondrous Dharma.
Through the merit of training in the unsurpassed Dharma, they are born before all Buddhas and are constantly sustained by their compassionate guidance.
They skillfully expound the samādhi of tranquility and praise the transcendence of the cycle of birth and death, acting as a place of refuge for sentient beings suffering in saṃsāra. Why is this?
It is because they desire to cause the bodhisattva’s mind toward the Buddha-dharma to increase and expand, so that whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately [realize for themselves].
Because his understanding is not dependent on the instruction of others, the Son of the Buddha asks: "What is the Bodhisattva's Dwelling in the Cultivation of the Ground?
How does this Bodhisattva give rise to ten kinds of mind toward all sentient beings? What are these ten? They are:

the mind of benefit, the mind of great compassion, the mind of peace and happiness, the mind of stable abiding, the mind of pity, the mind of gathering, the mind of protection, the mind of regarding them as oneself, and the mind of regarding them as a teacher."
O sons of the Buddha, these ten qualities constitute the mind of a Teacher. What are these ten dharmas that a bodhisattva should be encouraged to study?

They are as follows: reciting and practicing what has been heard; dwelling in seclusion and tranquility; drawing near to virtuous friends; speaking with a harmonious and pleasant countenance; always knowing the proper time for speech;
having no timidity or fear in the heart; thoroughly understanding the meaning; practicing in accordance with the Dharma; remaining free from delusion and confusion; and abiding securely.

Why is it called "Immovable"? It is because it causes Bodhisattvas to increase their great compassion toward all sentient beings, such that whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others. Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s practice-abiding?
By means of ten kinds of practices, the Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena. What are these ten? They are as follows: contemplating all...
All phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are empty;
all phenomena are without self; all phenomena are without agency; all phenomena are without flavor; all phenomena do not correspond to their names; all phenomena have no location;
all phenomena are free from conceptual discrimination; all phenomena lack solidity—these are the ten. Sons of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be exhorted [to realize them].
One studies ten dharmas. What are these ten? They are: observing the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the world-realm;
observing the earth-element, water-element, fire-element, and wind-element; and observing the desire-realm, form-realm, and formless-realm. Why is this?

It is because one wishes to cause the bodhisattva’s wisdom to be clear and lucid, so that whatever Dharma is heard is immediately understood through self-awakening, without depending on the instruction of others.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of Noble Birth?
This Bodhisattva is born from the holy teachings and accomplishes ten dharmas. What are these ten? They are: never regressing; generating profound pure faith toward all Buddhas;
skillfully examining phenomena; understanding sentient beings, lands, worlds, karmic actions, retributions, birth and death, and nirvāṇa.
P’an, these are the ten; O sons of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.
What are the ten? They are: to thoroughly understand all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present; to cultivate all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present;
to bring to perfection all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present; and to thoroughly understand everything.
The equality of all Buddhas: why is this? It is because they desire to cause [beings] to progress toward equanimity of mind throughout the three periods of time;

whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others. Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of skillful means?
It is that the roots of goodness cultivated by this Bodhisattva dwelling therein are all for the sake of rescuing, protecting, and benefiting all sentient beings.
To benefit all sentient beings, to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, to have compassion for all sentient beings, to deliver all sentient beings,
to cause all sentient beings to be free from all calamities and disasters, to cause all sentient beings to emerge from the suffering of birth and death,
to cause all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith, and to cause all sentient beings to attain complete subduing and transformation.
"O Son of the Buddha, all sentient beings shall realize nirvana; this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.

What are these ten? They are: knowing that sentient beings are boundless, knowing that sentient beings are immeasurable, knowing that sentient beings are innumerable, knowing that sentient beings are inconceivable, knowing that sentient beings have immeasurable forms, knowing that sentient beings are unfathomable, [and knowing] sentient beings..."
He knows that sentient beings have no activity, he knows that sentient beings possess nothing, and he knows that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature. Why is this?

It is because he wishes to cause their minds to turn toward further excellence, so that they remain unstained by attachment; whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without relying on the instruction of others.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Right Mind (*samyakcittavihāra*)? This Bodhisattva—

Hearing ten kinds of teachings, one’s mind remains concentrated and unshakable. What are these ten? They are as follows: hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha, one’s mind remains concentrated and unshakable regarding the Buddha-dharma;
hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma, one’s mind remains concentrated and unshakable regarding the Buddha-dharma;
hearing praise or disparagement of bodhisattvas, one’s mind remains concentrated and unshakable regarding the Buddha-dharma; hearing praise or disparagement of... [bodhisattvas].
The Dharma practiced by a bodhisattva is such that their mind remains fixed and unshakable within the Buddha-dharma when hearing it said that sentient beings are finite or infinite;
their mind remains fixed and unshakable within the Buddha-dharma when hearing it said that sentient beings are defiled or undefiled;
and their mind remains fixed and unshakable within the Buddha-dharma when hearing it said that sentient beings are easy to deliver or difficult to deliver.
Hearing it said that the dharma-realm is finite or infinite, his mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing it said that the dharma-realm undergoes formation or destruction, his mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma;

hearing it said that the dharma-realm exists or does not exist, his mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma. These are the ten, O Son of the Buddha; this bodhisattva should joyfully study them.
What are the ten dharmas? They are as follows: all dharmas are signless; all dharmas are without essence;
all dharmas are not to be cultivated; all dharmas are non-existent; all dharmas are without reality; all dharmas are empty; all dharmas are without intrinsic nature;
all dharmas are like illusions; all dharmas are like dreams; all dharmas are without differentiation.

For what reason? It is because he wishes to cause his mind to advance further, so that he may attain the non-retrogressive patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), such that whatever Dharma he hears, he immediately understands it for himself without relying on the instruction of others. Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Non-Retrogression?
This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings and remains firm and non-retrogressive. What are these ten? They are as follows:
Hearing that there is a Buddha or no Buddha, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma; hearing that there is the Dharma or no Dharma, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there is a bodhisattva or no bodhisattva, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there is the practice of a bodhisattva or no practice of a bodhisattva, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma; hearing that there is...

When a bodhisattva practices the cultivation of renunciation, they do not waver in their resolve toward the Buddha-dharma whether hearing that there were buddhas in the past or that there were no buddhas in the past;
they do not waver in their resolve toward the Buddha-dharma whether hearing that there will be buddhas in the future or that there will be no buddhas in the future;
and they do not waver in their resolve toward the Buddha-dharma when hearing that there are buddhas in the present.

Not regressing in one’s mind regarding the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma upon hearing that the Buddha’s wisdom is finite; not regressing in one’s mind regarding the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma upon hearing that the Buddha’s wisdom is infinite;
not regressing in one’s mind regarding the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma upon hearing that the three periods of time have a single characteristic;

and not regressing in one’s mind regarding the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma upon hearing that the three periods of time do not have a single characteristic—these, O Son of the Buddha, are the ten [resolutions]. This Bodhisattva should be encouraged to study these ten kinds of vastness.
What are the ten aspects of the Dharma? They are: teaching the one as the many, and teaching the many as the one; the text following the meaning, and the meaning following the text;
non-existence as existence, and existence as non-existence; the signless as the sign, and the sign as the signless;
and non-nature as nature, and nature as non-nature. Why is this? It is because they desire to cause others to progress and to become skillful in all phenomena.
Having attained renunciation, one understands the Dharma as it is heard through one's own insight, without depending on the instruction of others.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of the Youthful (kumārabhūta)? This Bodhisattva dwells in ten kinds of activities. What are these ten? They are:
faultless conduct of body, faultless conduct of speech, faultless conduct of mind; taking birth at will; and knowing the various desires of sentient beings.
Knowing the various inclinations of sentient beings; knowing the various realms of sentient beings; knowing the various karmas of sentient beings;
knowing the formation and destruction of worlds; and possessing mastery of the supernormal power of spiritual travel such that one's conduct is unimpeded—these are the ten.
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten? They are: knowing all buddha-fields and shaking all buddha-fields... [and so forth].
Upholding all buddha-fields, observing all buddha-fields, visiting all buddha-fields,
traveling through countless worlds, receiving countless Buddha-dharmas, manifesting bodies of sovereign transformation, emitting vast and pervasive sounds,
and serving and making offerings to countless Buddhas in a single kṣaṇa— for what reason? It is because one desires to cause further progress in...

Because they are able to attain skillfulness regarding all phenomena and immediately understand through their own insight whatever Dharma they hear, without depending on the instruction of others, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Abode of the Dharma Prince?
In this Bodhisattva abode, one skillfully knows ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten? They are:
skillfully knowing the births of all sentient beings; skillfully knowing the manifestation of all afflictions; [and so forth].
Knowing the continuity of habitual tendencies; skillfully knowing the expedient means of practice; skillfully knowing immeasurable dharmas; skillfully understanding all modes of conduct;
skillfully knowing the distinctions between worlds; skillfully knowing the events of the past and future limits; skillfully knowing how to expound the conventional truth;
and skillfully knowing how to expound the ultimate truth—these, O Son of the Buddha, are the ten things in which this bodhisattva should be encouraged to train.

What are the ten types of dharmas? They are as follows: skillfulness in the station of the Dharma King, the regulations of the station of the Dharma King, the palace of the station of the Dharma King, the entry into the station of the Dharma King, the examination of the station of the Dharma King, the consecration of the station of the Dharma King, the empowerment of the station of the Dharma King, the fearlessness of the station of the Dharma King, the repose of the station of the Dharma King, and the praise of the station of the Dharma King. Why is this? It is because one desires to cause [them] to progress.
With a mind free from hindrance, whatever Dharma he hears, he immediately understands it for himself without relying on the instruction of others.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Consecration? This Bodhisattva attains the accomplishment of ten kinds of knowledge.
What are these ten? They are: shaking countless worlds, illuminating countless worlds, and sustaining countless worlds.
He travels to countless worlds, adorns and purifies countless worlds, reveals the Dharma to countless sentient beings, observes countless sentient beings,
knows the faculties of countless sentient beings, causes countless sentient beings to enter the path,
and subdues countless sentient beings. These, O sons of the Buddha, are the tenfold manifestations of the body and bodily karma of this Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers.
The wisdom of the past, the wisdom of the future, and the wisdom of the present;
the wisdom that accomplishes the Buddha-land, the mind-realm, and the object-realm—all these are unknowable, such that even the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-Princes cannot know them.

Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva should be encouraged to study the ten kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas. What are the ten? They are: the wisdom of the three periods of time, the wisdom of the Buddha-dharmas, and the wisdom of the Dharma...
The unimpeded wisdom of the realms; the wisdom of the boundlessness of the dharma-realm; the wisdom that fills all worlds; the wisdom that universally illumines all worlds;
the wisdom that sustains all worlds; the wisdom that knows all sentient beings; the wisdom that knows all phenomena;
and the wisdom that knows the infinite Buddhas. Why is this? It is because one desires to cause the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) to increase and flourish.
Because upon hearing the Dharma, one attains self-awakening and understanding without depending on the instruction of others.

[Treatise] The fourth section contains ten dharmas of illumination. These concern the ten kinds of supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata, which serve as the objects of focus for the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*), as well as the ten dharmas pertaining to this stage.
Including those up to the end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there are a total of two hundred dharma-gates.
Together they constitute the stages of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*); within each abode there are twenty dharma-gates.

Ten dharmas establish the gates of the respective stage, and ten dharmas serve as the practices for advancement. The scriptural text provides these in full, so there is no need for further explanation;
one should simply understand their respective proportions and practice accordingly.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the supernatural power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways—namely, shaking, universal shaking, and so forth; rising, universal rising, and so forth;
surging, universal surging, and so forth; quaking, universal quaking, and so forth; roaring, universal roaring, and so forth; and crashing, universal crashing, and so forth.

A rain of celestial wondrous flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial flower garlands, celestial blended perfumes, celestial precious robes, celestial jewel-clouds, and celestial ornaments fell;
celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, emitting celestial radiance and sublime sounds.
Thus, upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, above the palace of Śakra, he preached the Dharma of the Ten Abodes and manifested various divine transformations.
The transformations of all worlds throughout the ten directions were likewise.

Furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions, there came to this place as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, filling the ten directions and speaking these words: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Buddha!"
We have taught this Dharma; we all share the same name, Dharmamati, and the lands from which we come are all named Dharmamegha.

The Tathāgatas in those lands are all named Saddharmaprabhāsa. The Buddhas from whom we came also taught the Ten Abodes, as well as the assemblies, retinues, phrases, and principles—all of which are exactly like this, without any increase or decrease. O Son of the Buddha, we have come here by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
"Entering this assembly, I shall bear witness for you; as it is in this assembly, so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions as far as the Dharma-realm and spoke in verse:
[Treatise] Fifth: Clarifying the Manifestation of the Dharma-Teaching’s Majestic Power and the Earthquake that Shakes the Great Earth.
This section is divided into six parts: 1. Clarifying the six types and eighteen modes of the earth's shaking; 2. Clarifying the ten kinds of celestial offerings from the rain; 3.

A summary clarifying that the same teaching is proclaimed throughout the ten directions; 4. Clarifying the majestic resonance of the ten directions reaching both far and near; 5. Clarifying the ten... [text ends].

Now, bodhisattvas bearing the same name all come to bear witness. Sixth, this clarifies that the fruit of the Buddhas of the ten directions is called the "Sublime Dharma," which clarifies that this Dharma is spoken from sublime wisdom.
[Sūtra] One beholds the most supreme, subtle, and wondrous body, its marks and signs perfectly complete and majestic.
Thus, with such profound respect and recognizing how difficult it is to encounter [a Buddha], the Bodhisattva, through courageous initial resolve,

beholds peerless great supernormal powers; hearing the teachings on the reading of minds and the instructions regarding the immeasurable sufferings of beings in the various realms of existence, the Bodhisattva thereby gives rise to this initial resolve.
I have heard that the Tathāgatas, the Universally Victorious Honored Ones, have fully accomplished all merits;
like space, they are free from discrimination. By this, the Bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind [of enlightenment].
The causes and effects of the three periods of time are called "possible" (sthāna), while our own inherent nature is called "impossible" (asthāna).
Desiring to fully comprehend the true meaning, the bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of awakening;
desiring to fully comprehend, without exception, all wholesome and unwholesome karmas throughout the past, future, and present worlds, the bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of awakening.
All dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis— whether defiled, pure, or of infinite varieties—
they fully understand their entry, abiding, and emergence. By means of this initial resolve, the Bodhisattva,
according to the sharp or dull faculties of all sentient beings, exerts such various powers of diligence.

Desiring to fully comprehend and discern them all— The various understandings of all sentient beings, And the differences in their respective inclinations— A Bodhisattva, for this reason, first generates the mind of awakening.
Desiring to fully know such immeasurable things— A Bodhisattva, for this reason, first generates the mind of awakening.
The various realms of sentient beings are each distinct;
All worlds are immeasurable, yet they desire to fully know their essential nature. By means of this, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind;
Every single path of conditioned phenomena has its respective destination.
Desiring to fully understand their true nature, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind;
All sentient beings in every world, drifting with their karma without a moment’s rest,
Desiring to obtain the divine eye to see them all clearly, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
Whatever existed in past lives— such as their essential nature and suchlike characteristics—
if one wishes to fully understand those former abodes (*pūrvanivāsa*), the Bodhisattva generates this initial resolve.
[He likewise seeks to know] all the fetters and delusions of sentient beings, their continuous manifestation, and their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Desiring to fully comprehend them to the ultimate limit, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
following the various ways in which sentient beings are established, and all their diverse discourses and paths of speech,
he desires to know them all according to worldly convention— this is why the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
All phenomena are beyond verbal expression; their nature is empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Desiring to fully comprehend this true meaning, the bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
Desiring to cause all lands in the ten directions to tremble and to overturn all the great oceans, he thus first resolves his mind.
Possessing the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
wishing to emit light from a single pore, it universally illumines immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions,
awakening all beings within each ray of light— the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
Wishing to place all inconceivable Buddha-fields within the palm of one's hand without them moving,
and understanding that all things are like illusions and transformations, the Bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of enlightenment;
wishing to place the sentient beings of immeasurable lands upon the tip of a single hair without any crowding.
Fully knowing that there is no person and no self, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of awakening;
wishing to take a single hair-tip to drop the waters of the ocean,
they desire to exhaust all great oceans and fully discern their respective quantities— the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of awakening.
All inconceivable world-systems, Could be ground to dust until none remained;
If one were to discern them all according to their number, The Bodhisattva, through this, first generates the mind.
Throughout immeasurable eons of the past and future, Regarding the signs of the formation and destruction of all worlds—
Desiring to fully comprehend and exhaustively master [all things], the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
desiring to know, without exception, the teachings of all Tathāgatas of the three times,
as well as all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
All immeasurable and boundless worlds, wishing to lift them all up with a single hair,
and to fully know them according to their essential forms and characteristics— by this, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind.
All immeasurable and innumerable Cakravāḍa mountains, wishing to cause them all to enter into a single pore.
Knowing all things according to their magnitude, the Bodhisattva, by means of this initial resolve,
desires to universally expound throughout the ten directions in a single sublime voice that accords with the various types of beings,
causing them all to be pure, clear, and fully understood; it is by means of this that the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind.
The linguistic conventions of all sentient beings— To expound them in a single word without exception;
Desiring to fully understand their intrinsic nature, The Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
There is no worldly sound or speech they do not produce, Causing all to understand and realize nirvana.
Desiring to obtain such a wondrous faculty of the tongue, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
desiring to cause all worlds throughout the ten directions— those undergoing formation and destruction—
to be seen and fully known as arising from conceptual discrimination, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, immeasurable Tathāgatas completely fill them;
desiring to fully understand their Buddha-dharma, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind [of enlightenment],
manifesting various transformations of immeasurable bodies, as numerous as the atoms within all worlds.
Desiring to fully comprehend all that arises from the mind, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the awakening mind;
Desiring to know, in a single thought-moment, the infinite and innumerable Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present worlds, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the awakening mind.
If one were to fully expound upon even a single phrase of the Dharma, it would not be exhausted for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
yet its words and meanings would each remain distinct; by means of this, the Bodhisattva first resolves their mind,
[observing] all sentient beings throughout the ten directions according to their characteristics of wandering through birth and death.
Desiring to clearly comprehend all in a single thought-moment, the bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment;
desiring to universally reach the ten directions with body, speech, and mental action without obstruction,
and to thoroughly know that the three times are entirely empty and quiescent, the bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
Once a bodhisattva has thus resolved their mind, they should be sent to the lands of the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Tathāgatas; by this means, they shall not regress,
for the bodhisattva courageously seeks the Buddha-way, dwelling within birth and death without weariness.
Praising them for their sake so that they may practice accordingly, he causes them thus to have no regression.
In immeasurable lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he acts as the honored lord within them all;
to the bodhisattvas he speaks in this way, thereby causing them not to regress.
The most excellent, supreme, and foremost, the profound, subtle, and pure Dharma—
I exhort you, O Bodhisattvas, to preach and bestow it upon others; Teaching thus, one leaves behind all afflictions,
for there is none equal to such a one in all the world, A state that is unshakable and cannot be overcome.
For those bodhisattvas, he constantly offers praise; such is his teaching that they do not regress.
The Buddha is the Lord of Great Power in the world, endowed with all virtues;
he causes all bodhisattvas to abide therein, and by this teaching, he acts as the Supreme Man.
He has gone to and approached all the infinite and boundless Buddhas,
always receiving their protection; thus instructed by them, he never regresses,
and he fully expounds all peaceful samādhis without exception.
For those bodhisattvas, he speaks thus, so as to cause them not to regress;

he crushes the wheel of birth and death within all states of existence and turns the pure, wondrous wheel of Dharma, remaining unattached to any world. For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he speaks thus.

For all sentient beings fallen into evil realms, Bound and oppressed by immeasurable, heavy sufferings, He acts as their refuge and place of reliance; For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he speaks thus:
"This is the Bodhisattva’s dwelling of the Initial Resolve," Single-mindedly aspiring to seek the Unsurpassed Way.
Just as I have taught this Dharma of instruction, so too do all Buddhas;
The second stage, the Dwelling of Refining the Ground, Bodhisattva, Should give rise to such a mind:
"May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions Be made to fully accord with the teachings of the Tathāgata."
With a mind of great compassion for their benefit and happiness, Abiding in a mind of pity that gathers them in,
A mind that protects sentient beings as oneself, A mind that regards them as teachers and guides—
Having established such sublime and wondrous minds, One should next cause them to recite and study to seek extensive learning.
Always delighting in tranquility and right reflection, Associating with all spiritual friends,
speaking with a pleasant voice free from harshness, Speaking always with awareness of the proper time and without fear,
Thoroughly understanding the meaning and acting according to the Dharma, One remains far removed from delusion and confusion, the mind unmoving.
This is the initial training in the conduct of awakening; those who can practice this conduct are true children of the Buddha.
I shall now explain what they ought to practice; thus should the children of the Buddha train with diligence.
This is the third bodhisattva stage of practice: one should diligently investigate it by relying upon the Buddha’s teaching.
All phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty; They lack a self or a person, and are devoid of activity.

All phenomena are not to be delighted in; They do not exist as names, they have no location, They are without discrimination and lack true reality. One who contemplates in this way is called a bodhisattva.
Next, cause them to observe the realm of sentient beings, And likewise exhort them to observe the dharma-realm;
Exhaustively and without exception, one should everywhere exhort them to observe The various worlds of the ten directions,
as well as space, And all that exists of earth, water, fire, and wind.
The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm— Exhort them all to observe these realms,
examining each one in its distinctions And its essential nature until they have fully mastered them;
Teaching them thus to practice with diligence— This is what is called a true son of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva in the fourth stage, the Dwelling of Noble Birth, is born from the various holy teachings;
having realized that all existents are non-existent, they transcend those phenomena and give rise to faith in the Dharma-realm.
Their faith in the Buddha is firm and indestructible, as they contemplate the quiescence of all phenomena with a mind securely settled.
He thoroughly understands all sentient beings, That their essential nature is illusory and lacks reality;
The worlds, lands, karma, and its retribution, Birth-and-death and nirvana are all likewise.
O Son of the Buddha, one who contemplates phenomena thus Is born directly from the Buddha and is called a Son of the Buddha.
Having thoroughly understood and perfected the accumulation of all the Buddha-dharmas throughout the past, future, and present worlds, one trains in this manner until reaching the ultimate,
whereby one is able to observe all Tathāgatas of the three times as entirely equal.
Various distinctions cannot be found; one who contemplates thus penetrates the three periods of time.
As for those whom I praise and extol, these are the merits of the four abodes.
If one can diligently practice according to the Dharma, one will swiftly achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.
From this fifth stage, the bodhisattvas are said to dwell in the perfection of skillful means;
they enter deeply into immeasurable and subtle expedients.
The various merits cultivated by these bodhisattvas, who give rise to ultimate virtuous deeds, are all for the sake of rescuing and protecting all living beings.
Dedicated solely to their benefit and happiness, Out of constant compassion, you lead them to liberation;
To remove all hardships for every world, You draw them forth from existence and bring them joy.
One by one, you tame them without exception, Causing them all to possess virtue and turn toward Nirvāṇa.
All sentient beings are boundless— immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable,
and beyond all calculation; those who hear and receive such a Dharma as this from the Tathāgata are the true sons of the Buddha in this fifth stage,
who have perfected skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
The Honored One of Great Wisdom and All Virtues has thus revealed this Dharma.

This is the sixth stage, the Perfect Abiding of the Right Mind: Without delusion regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena, one contemplates with right mindfulness, free from conceptual construction; Neither gods nor humans are able to disturb such a one.
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma, Of Bodhisattvas and their practiced deeds,
Whether sentient beings are finite or infinite, Whether they are defiled or undefiled, whether they are easy or difficult to deliver,
Whether the dharma-realm is large or small, or subject to formation and destruction— Whether things exist or do not exist, the mind remains unmoved.
Regarding the past, future, and present, one should always maintain firm resolve through attentive reflection and contemplation:
that all phenomena are signless, without substance, without intrinsic nature, empty, and devoid of reality;
like illusions and dreams, they are free from conceptual discrimination. One should always delight in hearing such meanings.
The seventh stage is the Bodhisattva of Non-retrogression. Regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bodhisattva practices—
whether they exist or do not exist, whether they emerge or do not emerge— even upon hearing such teachings,
there is no retrogression or wavering concerning all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, whether they exist or do not exist.
The Buddha’s wisdom is either finite or infinite; the three times have a single characteristic, and various characteristics are one, while that which is one is many.
As the phrasing follows the meaning and the meaning follows the phrasing, all such things are established through mutual interdependence; this should be explained to those who do not regress.
Whether phenomena possess characteristics or lack characteristics, whether phenomena possess intrinsic nature or lack intrinsic nature—
having heard these various distinctions and their mutual relations, this person attains the ultimate eighth Bodhisattva stage,
the Youthful (Kumārabhūta), and becomes fully endowed with the conduct of body, speech, and mind.
All-pure and free from all faults, you attain mastery over taking birth at will;
You know the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, And their various differing understandings and all their phenomena,
As well as the signs of formation and destruction of the lands in the ten directions.
Having attained swift and wondrous supernormal powers,
they go at will to all places to hear the Dharma in the presence of all Buddhas; praising their practice without weariness,
they thoroughly understand all Buddha-fields, shaking them, sustaining them, and observing them.
Transcending immeasurable Buddha-lands, they travel through world-systems in infinite *asaṃkhyeya* numbers, inquiring about all dharmas.
They possess mastery over whatever bodies they wish to assume, and their skillful speech and sounds reach everywhere; they serve countless Buddhas.
The Ninth Bodhisattva Stage: The Prince’s Abode. He is able to perceive the differences in the births of sentient beings;
he knows all afflictions and habitual tendencies without exception. He thoroughly understands the skillful means of their practice and the distinct postures and manners of all phenomena.
He perceives the differences among worlds and the preceding limits of desire.
Just as they thoroughly understand all conventional and ultimate truths without exception,
so too do they skillfully establish the abodes of the Dharma King; wherever those abodes and all their respective phenomena may be,
whether entering the palace of the Dharma King or observing what is seen therein.
The empowerment rites possessed by the Dharma King, The spiritual power of his sustaining grace that dispels all fear,
His private chambers and his praises— By these instructions he exhorted the Prince;
Thus he taught him exhaustively, Causing his mind to be free from any attachment.
Having realized this and cultivated right mindfulness, all Buddhas appear before one.
As a true son of the Buddha who has received the tenth consecration, one fulfills the supreme, foremost Dharma;
one is able to shake countless worlds throughout the ten directions, and one’s light shines everywhere.
The Abbot goes forth, yet remains without remainder; Pure and adorned, he is fully endowed with all qualities.
He reveals the teachings to sentient beings beyond measure, Observing and knowing their faculties to the very end.
His resolve to tame them is likewise boundless, Causing them all to advance toward Great Enlightenment.
They observe the entire realm of phenomena and travel to all lands throughout the ten directions;
their bodies and the deeds performed by those bodies, as well as their supernatural transformations, are difficult to fathom.
Regarding the various realms of the Buddha-lands of the three periods of time, even a prince cannot fully comprehend them.
The wisdom of all-seeing ones regarding the three periods of time; The wisdom that clearly understands all Buddha-dharmas;
The wisdom of the unimpeded and boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); The wisdom that fills all worlds;
The wisdom that illuminates and sustains the worlds; The wisdom that thoroughly knows the various dharmas of sentient beings.
And knowing the boundless wisdom of perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata explains it for them all so that they may fully realize it.
Thus, these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are all born from the transformation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
according to their respective meritorious practices, no devas or humans can fathom them.
In the past, future, and present ages, those who have resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood are boundless;
they fill all the lands of the ten directions, and there are none who shall not attain omniscience.
All lands are without limit, and the same is true for the worlds, sentient beings, and phenomena.
The afflictions, karma, mental inclinations, and individual differences—based upon these, the thought of enlightenment first arises as the single-minded seeking of the Buddha-way.
Even worldly beings and those of the two vehicles cannot know this; how much less can they know the remaining meritorious practices?
All the worlds throughout the ten directions, One can lift them all with a single hair;
Only those sons of the Buddha can know this, As they advance toward the wisdom-practice of the Tathāgata.
All the great oceans throughout the ten directions, One can exhaust them entirely by dripping them away with the tip of a hair.
That person can know this son of the Buddha— The meritorious deeds cultivated in a single thought-moment;
Even if all worlds were ground into dust, They could distinguish and know their number;
Only such a person as this can see The path traversed by these bodhisattvas.
The Buddhas of the ten directions— past, future, and present— along with all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas,
With various kinds of sublime eloquence, reveal and explain the merit of first generating the bodhicitta;
That merit is immeasurable, filling the entire realm of sentient beings.
The multitude of sages together could not exhaustively describe it, much less the other various sublime practices.
[Commentary: The sixth section clarifies how Dharmamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, speaks in verse to praise the Dharma.
Within this segment, there are a total of two hundred lines of verse used to praise the two hundred dharma-gates within the ten stages (*bhūmi*); the text is complete in itself.

There is no need for further explanation. As for "dwelling like one who has received the consecration" (*abhiṣeka*): it is like taking pure water and pouring it from the crown of the head so that it flows down over the entire body.

In this same way, a Bodhisattva in this stage, by means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*—which is a substance without center or periphery and equal to the realm of empty space—manifests bodies appropriate to all sentient beings as they appear before them, raining down the rain of Dharma simultaneously and equally upon all, such that there is none who does not receive it.

Because of this infusion [of empowerment], it is called the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*); furthermore, when one ascends to this stage, the Buddhas of the ten directions pour water upon one's crown, and for this reason it is also named the Stage of Empowerment.
*The Compendium of the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 33.

Phonetic Transcriptions: Duó (dú huó qiè) Xiè (jiè yīn) Jiè (jiè yīn) Zhí (zhí zhì qiè) Jù (qú lì qiè) Lián (lì yán qiè) Pò (bǎi yīn) Ài (niǎo jiè qiè) Jì (qí jì qiè) Chán (zhí lián qiè) Huì (hū jí qiè) Zī (zǐ sī qiè) Qǐn (qī rěn qiè) Guǎng (gǔ měng)
Qiē (qīe). Xìn (xǔjīn qiè). Mǐn (mǐn yīn). Diào (túdiao qiè). Mào (same as 皃). Jì (zàixì qiè). Xiá (hújiǎ qiè).
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Four.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Layman of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty; A Concordance of Scriptural Commentaries, Chapter Sixteen: Brahma-Carya.

[Commentary] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the chapter [content]; third, a summary of the essential meaning. First, regarding the explanation of the title: "Brahma-Carya" (梵行) means "pure conduct. It refers to the practice of the eightfold path that leads to the cessation of suffering and the attainment of Nirvana. It is called "pure" because it is free from the defilements of the three poisons and the eight worldly winds. It is called "conduct" (*carya*) because it is the practice undertaken by those seeking liberation. This chapter explains the various aspects of such pure conduct. Thus, it is titled "The Chapter on Brahma-Carya. Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter content... [text continues]
Regarding the threefold intention for this coming [section], the first part explains the title of the chapter. Why is it called the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-varga*)?
"Pure" (*brahma*) here means "clean. It is so called because through pure conduct one benefits sentient beings;
by constantly dwelling in the world and practicing all dharmas of conduct, one transforms and benefits sentient beings. When no conduct can be apprehended, then there is no conduct that is not pure.
Therefore, it is called the "Brahma-faring" (brahmacarya). Furthermore, with respect to the one who asks the question, it is termed "right mindfulness.
Mindfulness that is free from [conceptual] thought is called right mindfulness; practicing in accordance with non-thought is called right mindfulness-practice.

When both thought and mindfulness are entirely absent, using this to benefit sentient beings is called the "Sovereign of the Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-deva). Because the heavens possess compassion, they are called "Heavenly Sons" (devaputra). Furthermore, with respect to the one who...

The person who speaks it is called "Dharma-wisdom" (*dharmaprajñā*); that which follows non-thought is called "Dharma"; that which uses Dharma to distinguish from emotion is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*);
when emotions arise and deviate from principle, it is called "non-Dharma-wisdom"; when wisdom penetrates principle and emotions perish, it is called "Dharma-wisdom.
Now, taking the inquiring subject, the person who expounds the Dharma, and the Dharma being expounded together, they are collectively termed "Pure Conduct" (*viśuddhacaryā*).
Regarding the second section, "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Principle of Equal Distribution Chapter by Chapter," the intent for the arrival of this chapter is as follows:
Since the preceding chapter elucidated the gate of abiding in the Buddha’s non-abiding, one must now practice the practice of non-practice. Therefore, this chapter must follow.
Abiding in non-abiding is called the Buddha’s abiding; through the practice of non-practice, one benefits the multitude of beings who are themselves no-beings.

Birth is termed "pure conduct"; therefore, this chapter must be introduced here. Thirdly, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text, this single chapter of the sūtra is analyzed by means of seven topical sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Devaputra Samprajanya addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, how do the assemblies of bodhisattvas in all worlds,
having donned the dyed robes and left the household life in reliance upon the teaching of the Tathāgata,
attain the purity of the brahmacarya and proceed from the stage of a bodhisattva to the path of unsurpassed bodhi?"
[Treatise] First, the three lines of sūtra beginning with "At that time" constitute the section on the request made by the Devaputra Samprajanya.

[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), he should take ten dharmas as objects of focus and observe them through mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Namely: the body and bodily action; speech and vocal action; and the mind and mental action."
The Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, and Precepts.

[Treatise]: From the second section on Dharmamati Bodhisattva down to "the Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, and Precepts," for two and a half lines of scripture, he formally presents ten dharmas as the objects of contemplation.
[Sūtra] One should contemplate in this way: "Is the body itself the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or is it even the precepts that are the holy life?
If the body were the holy life, one should know that the holy life would then be non-virtuous, contrary to the Dharma, turbid, foul-smelling, impure, loathsome, antagonistic, and defiled."

Then it would be a corpse, and it would be a swarm of worms. If bodily action were the holy life (*brahmacarya*), then the holy life would consist merely in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, looking to the left and right, bending, stretching, bowing, and raising oneself.

If speech were the holy life, then the holy life would consist merely in sounds, breath, the lips, tongue, throat, and palate, and the processes of exhaling and inhaling, restraining and releasing, high and low, clear and dull. [This applies] to vocal action.
This holy life (*brahmacarya*)— the holy life that consists of rising, moving about, inquiring after one's health,
brief exposition, detailed exposition, parables, direct exposition, praise, censure, formal establishment, conventional discourse, and clear elucidation— if the mind were the holy life,
then the holy life would be awakening (*vitarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), discrimination, various kinds of discrimination, mindfulness, and the seeds.
Various recollections, these are mental formations; these various mental formations are like a magical illusion, like sleep, or like a dream.

If mental action constitutes the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should know that the holy life is merely conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Cold and heat, hunger and thirst, suffering and pleasure, sorrow and joy—if the Buddha were the holy life, would form (*rūpa*) be the Buddha?
Would feeling (*vedanā*) be the Buddha? Would perception (*saṃjñā*) be the Buddha? Or would mental formations (*saṃskāra*) be the Buddha?

Is it the Buddha’s *ālaya-vijñāna* that is the Buddha? Is it his marks (*lakṣaṇa*) that are the Buddha? Is it his beauty that is the Buddha? Is it his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that are the Buddha?

Is it his karmic activities that are the Buddha? Or is it his retribution (*vipāka*) that is the Buddha? As for those dharmas that constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*), is it their tranquility (*śānti*) that is the Dharma?
Is it *nirvāṇa* that is the Dharma? Is it non-arising (*anutpāda*) that is the Dharma? Is it non-origination (*anabhinirvṛtti*) that is the Dharma? It is not...
Is this Dharma that which is free from conceptual discrimination? Is this Dharma that which has no sphere of activity? Is this Dharma that which is not accumulated?

Is this Dharma that which does not conform [to conditions]? Is this Dharma that which is non-apprehendable? If the Sangha consists of those who practice the holy life, is the Sangha those who are stream-enterers-in-training?
Is the Sangha those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry? Is the Sangha those who are once-returners-in-training? Is the Sangha those who have attained the fruit of once-returning...?

Is the fruit of the Once-Returner the Saṅgha? Is the candidate for the fruit of the Non-Returner the Saṅgha? Is the fruit of the Non-Returner the Saṅgha? Is the candidate for the fruit of Arhatship the Saṅgha?
Is the fruit of Arhatship the Saṅgha? Are the three knowledges (trividyā) the Saṅgha? Are the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) the Saṅgha?
If the precepts constitute the holy life (brahmacarya), are the ordination platform and its precincts the precepts? Is the inquiry into purity the precepts? Is the instruction [the precepts]?
"Are the deportments the precepts? Is the triple recitation of the *karmavācanā* the precepts? Is the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) the precepts? Is the instructor (*ācārya*) the precepts?
Is shaving the hair the precepts? Is wearing the saffron robe the precepts? Is begging for food the precepts? Is right livelihood the precepts?
Having observed in this way, [he reflected:]...
[Treatise] From "Third, one should contemplate in this way" down to "having contemplated in this way," comprising twenty-six and a half lines of scripture,
is the section on the method of contemplation for correct practice.
[Sūtra] Regarding the body, there is nothing to be grasped; regarding cultivation, there is nothing to which one clings; regarding phenomena (*dharma*), there is no abiding.
The past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present is empty and quiescent. There is no agent who performs karma, nor is there any recipient of its retribution.
This world does not shift, and that world does not change. Within this, what dharma is called the "holy life" (*brahmacarya*)? From where does the holy life come?
To whom does it belong? What is its essence? By whom is it made? Is it conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Is it form (*rūpa*) or non-form? Is it feeling (*vedanā*) or non-feeling? Is it perception (*saṃjñā*) or non-perception? Is it mental formations (*saṃskāra*) or non-formation?
Is it consciousness (*vijñāna*) or non-consciousness? When one observes in this way, the dharmas of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) are not to be found; thus ends the third [section].
Because all worldly dharmas are empty and quiescent, because the mind has no grasping or attachment, because the mind has no obstructions, because one's conduct is non-dual,
because skillful means are sovereign, because one receives the signless dharma, because one contemplates the signless dharma, because one knows the equality of the Buddha-dharmas,
and because one is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas— this is called the pure brahma-conduct.

[Treatise] Fourth: From "having nothing to grasp regarding the body" down to "it is called pure brahmacarya," there are ten lines of sutra within which one universally contemplates the three periods of time;
therein, the body, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness, as well as the Buddha-dharmas, are all equal, fully possessing all the divisions of the Buddha-dharmas.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, one should cultivate ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten? They are: knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible;

knowledge of the retribution of karma in the past, present, and future; knowledge of all meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis; knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings; knowledge of various inclinations; knowledge of various elements;
knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; unimpeded knowledge of the divine eye; and unimpeded knowledge of recollecting past lives.
The wisdom that eternally severs habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

[Treatise: Regarding the fifth section, from "Furthermore, one should cultivate ten kinds of dharmas" down to "the wisdom that eternally severs habitual tendencies," three and a half lines of scripture therein correctly set forth the ten powers of the Tathāgata for the purpose of cultivation.
[Sūtra] One should examine each of the Tathāgata’s ten powers one by one; within each power, there are immeasurable meanings that should all be inquired about.
Having heard them, one should give rise to great compassion and observe sentient beings without abandoning them.
One should contemplate all dharmas without rest and practice the unsurpassed deed without seeking karmic retribution.
[Treatise] The sixth section, from "Regarding the Ten Powers of the Tathāgata" down to "Not Seeking Retribution," contains three scriptural passages that exhort the practice of the Ten Powers,
followed by a section on resolving doubts through inquiry and the arising of great compassion.
[Sūtra] To thoroughly understand that objects of perception are like illusions, like dreams, like shadows, like echoes, and like magical transformations—
if Bodhisattvas can accord with such contemplative practice, they will not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena;
all Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before them, and at the very moment of their first resolve, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Knowing that all phenomena are the very nature of mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom without depending on another for awakening.

From the passage in the seventh chapter of the *Śāstra* beginning with "having thoroughly understood the objects" and extending for four and a half lines of scripture, this clarifies the section on the final attainment of benefit through the realization that phenomena are like illusions, leading to the stage of Buddhahood.
Thus, by relying on the aforementioned contemplative practices, one brings the actions of body, speech, and mind to completion.

In the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the precepts, within form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and regarding the two views of self and what belongs to self across the three periods of time—whether distant or near—all is utterly non-existent.

Furthermore, there is neither the observing mind nor the observed object; the mind does not sink nor does it become agitated, it neither arises nor ceases. It accords with principle and is free from thought.
It is through this that the ten powers of the Tathāgata’s wisdom are manifested. Indeed, the Buddha’s wisdom is not profound; it is only because of the deluded mind that it appears so.
When one pursues appearances, the mind is impaired; when the One Body is hidden, wisdom is obscured. When wisdom manifests, it is not distant;

when wisdom manifests, attachments and hindrances completely vanish, and the ten directions become vast and open. Thus, one dwells freely within the mundane dust without being diminished, and pervades empty space without becoming great.
To exhaust its traces, there is not even a hair’s breadth of extension across the ten directions; yet to give rise to its function, it does not go beyond a single *kṣaṇa*.
The activities of the body pervade everywhere like space and are inexhaustible. If one clings to their existence, then the oceans of all lands manifest forms in infinite layers;
if one sets them aside as non-existent, the myriad realms cannot be perceived in their essence.
By knowing through non-conceptualization and non-deliberation, all phenomena are accomplished without being created or performed; this is knowledge that transcends birth and death.

Their resolve cannot be shifted by suffering or pleasure, nor can their nature be altered. If one does not accord with principle, one cannot know through emotional conceptualization, nor can one attain it by extinguishing the mind.
It is by means of this that the Tathāgata established the teaching of pure practice to contemplate the exhaustion of all phenomena.
When the True Dharma first flourishes, all views perish; when Buddha-wisdom subsequently arises, it is known that these views have perished.

Wisdom should be understood as attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta and being fully endowed with the body of wisdom, realized without depending on another;
therefore, later students should practice according to the Dharma and must not sink into the flow of delusion by chasing after sensory objects for kalpas on end.
Furthermore, if one wishes to explain its higher meaning, one must consider that an abundance of words may obstruct the principle and confuse later students.

The mind merely accords naturally with the extent of the sūtras as described above, exactly as they are; thus, that which is called "pure conduct" (*śuddhacaryā*) consists of the one hundred and forty vows.
In the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one accomplishes worldly knowledge and views through these vows, taking them as pure conduct.
In this stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), because the essence of conduct is non-conditioned and without self-nature, it is termed "purity."
By practicing these pure deeds, one accomplishes the function of wisdom;

this chapter on Pure Deeds establishes the Buddha-fruit of the initial aspiration within the Ten Abodes, and it also serves as the Buddha-fruit for the subsequent Ten Practices, Ten Transferences, and Ten Grounds.
Because these practices of non-substantiality are pure, all practices are thereby purified.
Because purity leads to the purity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), wisdom becomes pure; because wisdom is pure, the mind becomes pure; because the mind is pure, all dharmas become pure.
The purity of all dharmas is called the purity of the *dharmadhātu*; the purity of the *dharmadhātu* is the purity of sentient beings;
and the purity of sentient beings is the purity of the Buddha-land. To practice this equality of dharmas is what is called "pure conduct."

Chapter Seventeen: On the Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment [Treatise] The merit of one who has first resolved for enlightenment is difficult to measure; it is equal to the entirety of empty space and has no peer to which it can be compared.

Even if all the atoms within the dust of the lands were ground to nothingness, there would still be no way to repay its worth. Empty space merely illustrates the greatness of signlessness (*animitta*).
The atoms of all lands merely manifest the vastness of physical obstruction; how could they compare to the sphere of the merit and wisdom of the Bodhicitta?

That wisdom, in a single kṣaṇa, fills the ten directions with manifestations like clouds, wherein the wondrous images of Indra’s net interpenetrate one another in layers of light and shadow, each universally pervading through a single word and sound.
The teaching of the Dharma-realm for all sentient beings is like rain falling upon them, bringing the joy of mental coolness;
such is its merit. Its wondrous marks and adornments share the same substance as the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

At the moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, one abides equally with the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout an ocean of inexhaustible eons, yet within a single instant, time is both extended and contracted.
It is similar to how a small stream entering the great ocean becomes equal to the great ocean because the substance of the water is not different;
likewise, when a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment, they enter the stream of the great wisdom of all Buddhas and become equal to the Buddhas' merits.
Thus, there is no difference in duration between the initial entry and the ultimate state, for their wisdom is one and the same. This constitutes the vow.
Because their vow to deliver all sentient beings so that they may all attain Buddhahood is equal; and because,
just as if the worlds of the ten directions were ground into dust and within each particle there were immeasurable Buddha-fields and immeasurable sentient beings,
the great wisdom-body of the bodhicitta, in a single kṣaṇa, makes offerings to all Buddhas throughout the dust of all those fields.
He transforms sentient beings simultaneously and universally, solely through the power of wisdom, because the nature of phenomena is such and because his wisdom is all-pervasive;

yet he does not form any conceptualization of performing supernatural transformations. This is because the resolve and aspiration of a Bodhisattva who has first awakened the mind are vast, equal to the realm of Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings, and are without limit; therefore, this is what is praised at the beginning of this chapter.
To generate the bodhicitta by means of these ten kinds of merit— vast, immeasurable, incomparable, and beyond analogy—
is to generate the mind by way of the vehicle of the fundamental, immovable, great wisdom of this Buddha-fruit, the inconceivable *dharmadhātu*.
Such a person is like the crown prince of a universal monarch at the moment of his birth, fully endowed with royal marks, or like the cub of a lion king.
His majestic power is similar to that of his father because his physical form is no different;

just as when a bodhisattva first resolves upon bodhicitta, he is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-lineage, and at that time, what he knows through wisdom is no different from that of a Buddha.

Because he perceives that the kalpas of the three periods of time have neither extension nor contraction, it is no different from the perception of a Buddha. His aspiration and delight are vast, for he teaches and transforms sentient beings.
Because they are not different from the Buddha, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they mount the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience;
without departing from the limit of a single instant (*kṣaṇa*), they attain perfect awakening and transform sentient beings.

Because they are not different from the Buddha, even those who provisionally establish the three vehicles in accordance with worldly sentiments and teach that Buddhahood is attained over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* will ultimately turn their minds and enter this realm of omniscience.
Only by means of the *dhātu* (element) and the vehicle (*yāna*) can one attain Buddhahood;

as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this refers to the teaching that the three vehicles are subsumed within the realm of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), such as the case of the dragon girl who attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime at the moment of an instant.
All sentient beings must collectively awaken to this Dharma in order to attain Buddhahood; they must not grasp after the Tathāgata [as an external object].
Within the Three Vehicles, these are words of expedient means that accord with worldly conventions because the nature of phenomena is such. As stated later in this chapter:
"As soon as a bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, they are immediately praised by all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
they are then able to preach the Dharma and teach and subdue all sentient beings throughout all worlds."
This extends even to the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood and so forth, as extensively described in the subsequent sections of this chapter.

Within this chapter, the prose section consists of forty segments of scripture in total. There are two hundred and forty-two lines of verse praising the merits of bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*). The text follows below; it will now be explained by way of summary.

The analysis by way of three gates: first, explaining the title of the chapter; second, explaining the purpose for the chapter’s inclusion; third, explaining the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter:

this chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Merit of the Initial Arising of the Resolve" (*Prathamacittotpāda-guṇa-parivarta*). "Initial" (*prathama*) refers to the very first arising of the resolve, which is designated as such because it has no precedent in the past.

As for "arising of the resolve" (*cittotpāda*), it should be understood as the arising of the mind through wisdom. As for "merit" (*guṇa*), it refers to the body [of merit]. Thus, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of the Initial Arising of the Resolve."
The exhaustion of all extreme views is called "mind"; accomplishing great fruits without effort is called "merit" (*guǒ*);
benefiting all beings without seeking a reward in return while naturally attaining the adornment of boundless sublime marks is called "virtue" (*dé*).
Furthermore, the universal pervasiveness of merit and wisdom is called "merit," while the thorough mastery of all matters is called "virtue. These constitute the categories [of these qualities].
Section Two: An Equitable Exposition of the Doctrinal Meaning. Regarding the explanation of the intent behind the arrival of this chapter:
since the preceding chapter already established the merit of pure conduct, this chapter elucidates the boundless virtues within that very purity of conduct; therefore, this chapter must follow.
Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, it is further divided into two sections: first, a general outline of the sutra’s intent; second, [the detailed analysis].

Regarding the first major section of this sutra, which explains the liberation according to the text, the meaning of the scripture from the beginning, "At that time," down to the end of the chapter is divided into forty sections.
[Sutra] At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva first resolves upon bodhicitta..."
As for the measure of the merit obtained by this mind:
