[The Treatise] states that from "At that time" down to "what is its measure? there is one line and a half of sūtra text; this is the section on the Deva King’s request to bear witness to the merit of generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said: "This meaning is extremely profound; it is difficult to explain, difficult to know, difficult to discern, difficult to believe and understand, difficult to realize, difficult to practice, difficult to penetrate, difficult to contemplate, difficult to measure, and difficult to enter.
Nevertheless, I shall, by relying on the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, explain it for you."

[Treatise] From the words "The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said" down to "I shall explain it for you," three and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on the permission to explain the ten kinds of profound and difficult-to-know merits of the initial generation of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*).

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were someone who, for the duration of one kalpa, provided all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings in as many incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*) as exist in the eastern direction; and thereafter, taught them to purely uphold the five precepts.

The same would apply to the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir. O Son of the Buddha, what do you think? How great would the merit of this person be?"
"Would it not be much? The Deva-son said: "O Son of the Buddha, the merit of this person can only be known by a Buddha;
all others are unable to measure it.
[Treatise] From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "unable to measure it," these five lines clarify the merit of a single individual.
[He] provides for the sentient beings of one asaṃkhyeya world in each of the ten directions and causes them to purely uphold the five precepts;
let us take up but a portion of this merit, vast and immeasurable.
[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said: "O Son of the Buddha, compared to the merit of a bodhisattva’s initial resolve for awakening, the merit of this person..."
A hundredth part does not equal it; a thousandth part does not equal it; a hundred-thousandth part does not equal it;

likewise, a billionth part, a ten-billionth part, a hundred-billionth part, a ten-trillionth part, a nayuta-billionth part, a hundred-nayuta-billionth part, a thousand-nayuta-billionth part, a hundred-thousand-nayuta-billionth part, nor can any number, fraction, kalā, or calculation equal it.
Even a fraction, a portion, or even a *upaniṣad* (a minute part) thereof would not equal it.

[Treatise] From the passage "The Bodhisattva Dharmamati" down to "would not equal even a fraction," five lines and a half of scripture clarify that all the vast merits of previous offerings cannot be compared to the merit of the initial resolve for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
The section on the incomparable near analogy clearly explains that the offerings made by such persons cannot be measured;

it is like taking a *kalā* (a minute fraction) to compare the great with the small. It is not like the analogy of cutting the hair from a person's body into one hundred parts, for the merit previously performed by those people does not equal even one part of a hair among the one hundred parts of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind upon enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "a portion the size of a hair-tip" (*vālāgra-mātra*) and also "a fraction of a *upaniṣad*":
this refers to a minute, proximate, and similar portion of infinite roots of goodness that cannot be compared by means of anything finite; the rest is self-evident from the text itself.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, let this analogy be set aside for a moment. Suppose there were a person who, for a hundred kalpas, provided all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings throughout ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the ten directions; and after that, taught them to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action;
and after a thousand kalpas of such offerings, taught them to abide in the four dhyānas; and after a hundred thousand kalpas of such teaching...
Abiding in the four immeasurable minds for a billion eons, he taught [beings] to abide in the four formless absorptions for ten billion eons;
he taught them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry for a thousand billion eons, in the fruit of once-returning for a hundred thousand billion eons,
in the fruit of non-returning for a nayuta of billions of eons, and in the fruit of arhatship for...
“Buddha-son, suppose there were a person who, for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of kalpas, taught others to abide in the path of the pratyekabuddhas.
What do you think, Buddha-son? Would the merit of this person be great? The Deva-son said, “Buddha-son, the merit of this person can only be known by the Buddha.”
[Commentary] From "The five sons of the Buddha" down to "Only a Buddha can know," there are ten sūtra passages that clarify this. First, taking up the aforementioned vast portion of merit, it says:
"Those who abide in the ten paths of wholesome action—three of body, four of speech, and three of mind—are those born as gods in the desire realm.
As for 'superior wholesome [action]' which transcends the world, it refers to the karma of the form realm consisting of the four dhyānas. First.
The first dhyāna eliminates sorrow; the second dhyāna eliminates suffering; the third dhyāna eliminates joy; and the fourth dhyāna is solely tranquility.
What is taught regarding abiding in the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) refers to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

What is taught regarding abiding in the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*) refers to the formless realm concentrations. The above constitutes the wholesome karma (*kuśala-karma*) within the three realms. What is taught regarding abiding in the *śū*... [text ends]

The fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) refers to having first severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), abandoned the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), and for the first time attained the nature of a noble one (*āryatva*).

Because they have entered the stream of the noble practice, they are called "one who has entered the stream. Regarding the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner), this is translated as "one who returns once.

This means that although these noble ones have severed six grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because three remaining grades have not yet been severed, [they must return once].
Because a noble one (ārya) returns once more to birth in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), it is called the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin).

As for the abiding in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin)—this is translated as "not returning"—it means that having exhausted the nine grades of afflictions (kleśa) of the desire realm, one will not return from this [form realm] to take birth in the desire realm;
therefore, it is called "non-returning. Among these ten proclivities (anuśaya), doubt cannot yet be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Clearly understanding that one does not enter the fruit of Arhatship due to the ten afflictions (*kleśa*):

first, the five sharp afflictions—(1) the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), (2) extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), (3) clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), (4) clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and (5) false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);

and subsequently, the five dull afflictions—(6) greed (*rāga*), (7) hatred (*pratigha*), (8) delusion (*moha*), (9) pride (*māna*), and (10) doubt (*vicikitsā*)—these five dull afflictions are capable of causing delusion.

Regarding these ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) that accompany [the mind], the first five—the sharp proclivities—are suppressed and do not arise after the *srotāpanna* has realized the truths (*satyadarśana*).
As for the latter five—the dull proclivities—the *sakṛdāgāmin* attenuates greed, hatred, and delusion;

they have severed the six types of afflictions of the desire realm, and while they do not [sever] the greed of the formless realm, their hatred, delusion, pride, and the three types of subtle and thin [afflictions] manifest only in a faint and attenuated manner.

Because non-arising is not of the nature of a seed, it is absent; thus, for the two upper realms, there is no retribution. Furthermore, because hatred has been suppressed through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it does not manifest.
For the two fruits of *srota-āpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin*, there is a sense of wearying revulsion that prevents [defilements] from increasing, and they constantly seek the mind of world-transcendence.
Because of this, the seeds for sinking into the three realms are not formed. The *anāgāmin* causes [them] to be weary...

In the state of eternal cessation, there remains only doubt regarding the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*). Because one has not clearly realized the Path of Vision, one cannot immediately transcend the karmic fruits of the three realms.

Since for an Arhat there is no longer any doubt regarding the Path of Vision and the karmic fruits of the three realms are exhausted all at once, when compared to the preceding three fruits, although nine categories of afflictions have been severed, only doubt remains; thus it cannot be said that the afflictions have been "severed."
The affliction of ignorance regarding the truths (*satyājñāna*) is collectively termed "subjugation through aversion" (*vidūṣaṇa-prahāṇa*) rather than "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, while Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas merely delight in the pure lands of the supramundane, and Bodhisattvas as well as those Bodhisattvas who practice the contemplation of emptiness merely delight in supramundane conduct, all these [practitioners] who cultivate the six *pāramitās* are only subduing the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of ignorance; it cannot be called [complete] abandonment.
To permanently sever the afflictions, one temporarily uses the contemplation of emptiness to subdue ignorance that fails to realize [the nature of reality].
Since ignorance has been non-moving wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) from the very beginning, this failure to realize the root is subdued by emptiness so that it does not arise.
Even up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), although one attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and so forth, these are not yet called the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
In the practice of generating the ten contemplations on True Suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth, one severs the ten kinds of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).

Because one realizes that the root of ignorance is fundamentally the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and because its great functioning is eternally quiescent, within the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) regarding the Buddha-fruit, one generates the resolve based upon that fruit.
At the moment of first generating the resolve, one penetrates the fact that fundamental ignorance is itself fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*amala-jñāna*).

The Dharma-gate of the Great Application of the Wisdom of Differentiation, which is perfected upon the initial resolve and is the vehicle shared by all Buddhas, is called "Riding the Vehicle of All-Knowledge.
If one's wisdom, compassion, vows, and practices do not resemble those of a Buddha even by a hair’s breadth, then faith in the Buddha will not be established;
how much less could one abide where the Buddhas abide or be born into the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience) of the Tathāgata?
Born into the household as a true son of the Buddha, one accomplishes all the works of the Buddhas;

through wisdom it is not different, through vows and practice it is equal, through great compassion it is not different, and through infinite realms it is not different—there is no difference between the distinctions of past and future kalpas and a single thought-moment.
One should thus perceive this through the illumination of samādhi and prajñā; this is called the correct reliance upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The good spiritual friend relies on fundamental wisdom to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment as described in the following passage:

"A bodhisattva who has just aroused the aspiration can manifest their body attaining buddhahood throughout the ten directions because, at the moment of first arousing the aspiration, they have mounted the Tathāgata’s inconceivable vehicle of all-knowledge,
attained the Buddha’s seed-wisdom, been born into the family of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm, and mounted one portion of the Buddha’s wisdom."
The power of the great compassion of wisdom can thus manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in bodily form, as the following verse states:
"Though a bodhisattva has not yet realized the ten powers of a Buddha, they have no doubt regarding them;

within a single pore, they universally manifest immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions. This collectively clarifies the virtues of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind toward enlightenment.
Just as a crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch exercises provisional authority over the royal administration and attains a degree of sovereignty similar to that of his father,
so too does one obtain a portion of the Tathāgata’s power, wisdom, and majesty.
[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said: "O Son of the Buddha, the merit of this person does not equal even a hundredth part,
nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a single *upaniṣad* part of the merit of a Bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment."

[Treatise] From the words "The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said" down to "it does not even equal one or two lines and a half," the sūtra clarifies the section on the analogy that the previously mentioned merits cannot be compared to the merit of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*).
[Sūtra] For what reason, O Son of the Buddha, do all Buddhas, when first generating the thought of enlightenment,
not do so merely for the sake of providing all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings throughout ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the ten directions for a hundred kalpas,
or even for hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* of *koṭi* kalpas; nor do they do so merely for the sake of instructing that many [beings]?

They resolve upon the Bodhicitta in order to cause sentient beings to practice the path of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions; to teach them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments;
to teach them to obtain the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and the path of the Pratyekabuddha;
to ensure that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never severed; and to fulfill it.
Because they pervade all worlds; because they seek to deliver and liberate all sentient beings in all worlds;
because they fully know the formation and destruction of all worlds; because they fully know the defilement and purity of sentient beings in all worlds;
because they fully know the intrinsic purity of all worlds; and because they fully know the inclinations and joys of the minds of all sentient beings.
It is for the sake of thoroughly knowing all habitual tendencies of affliction; for the sake of thoroughly knowing the death and rebirth of all sentient beings;
for the sake of thoroughly knowing the faculties and skillful means of all sentient beings; for the sake of thoroughly knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings;
for the sake of thoroughly knowing the wisdom of all sentient beings regarding the three periods of time; and for the sake of thoroughly knowing the equality of the spheres of all Buddhas.
Therefore, they give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.

[Treatise] Why? From "Why? down to "the mind of unsurpassed bodhi," fourteen and a half lines of scripture clarify that a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind gives rise to an infinite mind in order to teach and transform all sentient beings.
[This] cuts off the lineage of the Buddhas.
[Sūtra]: "O Son of the Buddha, setting aside this metaphor, suppose there were a person who, in a single thought-moment, could pass beyond incalculable worlds to the east;
and if they continued to do so in every successive thought-moment for as many incalculable eons as there are worlds, there would be no one capable [of reaching the end]."
Suppose one were to know the limit of that [distance], and there were a second person who, in a single moment of thought,

could pass through as many worlds as the first person passed through in *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; and if, in this manner, they continued in succession for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until reaching the tenth person—
likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below— O Son of the Buddha, throughout these ten directions, all...
Suppose there were one hundred people, each passing through such worlds as described, and it were possible to know the limit of all those worlds.

[Treatise] Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, setting aside this analogy, from "and so forth" down to "it would be possible to know the limit," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify the section on the analogy for the vastness of the limit of swift travel that can be known.
[Sūtra] When a bodhisattva first resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, no one is able to know the limit of their roots of goodness.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, it is because the bodhisattva does not set a fixed limit;
rather, they resolve upon *bodhicitta* solely for the purpose of attaining knowledge of that many worlds, and for the purpose of thoroughly knowing the worlds of the ten directions.
The arousal of the bodhicitta consists in the desire to thoroughly understand that the wondrous world is itself the coarse world, and the coarse world is itself the wondrous world;
that the upward-facing world is itself the downward-facing world, and the downward-facing world is itself the upward-facing world;
that the small world is itself the great world, and the great world is itself the small world; and [the narrow world is itself] the vast world.
That which is a narrow world is itself a broad world; one world is itself unspeakably many worlds, and unspeakably many worlds are themselves one world.
Unspeakably many worlds enter into one world, and one world enters into unspeakably many worlds.
A defiled world is itself a pure world, and a pure world is itself a defiled world.
The world is itself a defiled world; one wishes to know the distinct natures of all worlds within a single hair-tip, and the single-natured essence of a single hair-tip within all worlds;
one wishes to know how all worlds arise from within a single world, and the essence-less nature of all worlds; and one wishes to know all of this with a single thought-moment.
They resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because they penetrate all vast worlds without obstruction.
[Treatise] From the nine bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, down to those who possess the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, there may be fifteen [sections].
The Chapter on the Infinite and Difficult-to-Know Realm of Worlds Known by Bodhisattvas Who Have First Produced the Thought of Enlightenment, from the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.

[Sūtra] Son of the Buddha, furthermore, setting aside this analogy, suppose there were a person who, in a single moment of thought, could know the number of eons of formation and destruction in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds in the eastern direction;
and if they were to continue doing so in every thought-moment for as many incalculable eons as there are in those worlds—through all these eons...

There is no one capable of knowing its limit; even if there were a second person who, in a single instant, could know the number of eons known by the former person over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)—and so it is explained in detail up to the tenth person in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—it would still be the same, O Son of the Buddha.
These incalculable worlds of the ten directions are thus formed.
The limits of the number of *saṃvarta-kalpas* (aeons of destruction) can be known.
[Śāstra]: "O sons of the Buddha, setting aside this analogy... and so on, down to "...the limits can be known.

These six lines and a half of scripture clarify that, for the time being, the number of kalpas of formation and destruction is taken up for swift understanding; it is possible to know the vast extent of these divisions.

[Sūtra] No one is able to know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness of a bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? It is because the bodhisattva does not set a limit;
rather, they aspire for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to fully know the number of kalpas of formation and destruction of all worlds.
One generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because of knowing the formation and destruction of all worlds without exception;
that is to say, knowing that long eons and short eons are equal, short eons and long eons are equal,
one eon and countless eons are equal, countless eons and one eon are equal, and eons with Buddhas and...

The eon without Buddhas is equal to the eon with Buddhas; the single eon of one Buddha contains unspeakably many Buddhas, and within unspeakably many Buddha-eons there is one Buddha. Finite eons are equal to infinite eons;
infinite eons are equal to finite eons; eons with an end are equal to eons without an end. There is no...
The exhaustion of kalpas and the non-exhaustion of kalpas are equal and ineffable; an ineffable kalpa is equal to a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is equal to an ineffable kalpa.
All kalpas enter into what is not a kalpa, and what is not a kalpa enters into all kalpas.
This is for the purpose of desiring to fully know, within a single thought-moment, the formation and destruction kalpas of all worlds throughout the past, future, and present.
To resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called the great vow-adornment of the initial generation of the mind,
which fully understands the supernormal knowledge of all kalpas.
[Treatise] From the eleventh point, "the bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind," down to "fully understanding the supernormal knowledge of all kalpas."
