"Excellent, excellent, Dharmamati! That you are now able to expound this Dharma—ten thousand buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms of dust in each of the ten directions, and the Buddhas therein, likewise expound this Dharma; all Buddhas speak thus."

[Treatise] The thirty-seven [sections], from "At that time, in the ten directions" downwards, consist of four and a half lines of sūtra text clarifying how Buddhas of identical names from the ten directions come to appear before him,
praising and approving his dharma, and how these are of the same category as those in the ten directions— namely,
Buddhas each passing through as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in ten thousand worlds, all named Dharmamati, who come to appear before him.
"Being one with the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions" clarifies that this is the union with the wisdom of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions;

"the dust motes of ten thousand Buddha-fields" clarifies the magnitude of ascending practice, which awakens the deluded and realizes the Dharma; and "the ten faiths, ten abidings, hundred practices, and ten thousand perfections" clarify the names of the ascending stages for perceiving the truths and awakening from delusion regarding the Dharma.
[Sūtra] "When you preached this Dharma, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields resolved upon bodhicitta;

we now bestow upon them all the prediction that, in a future age beyond a thousand unspeakably many boundless kalpas, within a single kalpa, they shall all attain Buddhahood and appear in the world, all bearing the same name: Tathāgata Pure Mind Abiding."
We shall all protect and uphold this Dharma, which distinguishes each and every world,
so that all bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it may now hear it in its entirety.
[Śāstra] 38. From the passage "When you preach this Dharma... down to "...all shall hear it," there are five scriptural passages that clearly explain this.

At the time of preaching this Dharma, in each of the ten directions, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields, Bodhisattvas resolve their minds [for enlightenment] and receive predictions of enlightenment;
as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields resolve their minds and receive predictions, exceeding a thousand *nirabhilāpya* (unspeakable) numbers.

The predictions of attaining Buddhahood throughout these kalpas all share the same name, "Pure Mind" (*viśuddhacitta*), because they clearly realize that the total purity of such dharma-gates spanning unspeakably many thousands of kalpas is thus. Therefore, the Buddha is named Pure Mind;
it is not a substantial reality as perceived by ordinary beings, nor is it a kalpa of vast duration. This generally clarifies the state of this stage according to delusion and awakening.
The name of the Dharma does not exist as a fixed duration of kalpas as perceived by deluded minds.
From this point until the end of the chapter, the text is self-evident; it contains the eulogies exactly as they appear in the scripture.
[Sūtra] Just as in this Sahā world, upon the summit of Mount Sumeru in the four continents, such a Dharma was taught so that all sentient beings,
having heard it, were transformed; so too in the ten directions, throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas—
countless, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, and unspeakable— all [beings] were likewise transformed.
In all worlds throughout the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, this Dharma is also taught to transform sentient beings;

those who preach it are all named Dharmamati (Dharma-Wisdom). This is all due to the spiritual power of the Buddhas, the power of the World-Honored One’s original vows, for the purpose of manifesting the Buddha-dharma, for the purpose of universally illuminating with the light of wisdom, for the purpose of expounding the true meaning, and in order to...
He teaches such a Dharma for the sake of realizing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), for the sake of causing the entire assembly to rejoice,

for the desire to reveal the causes of the Buddha-dharma, for the sake of attaining equality with all Buddhas, and for the sake of understanding that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is without duality.

[Treatise] Thirty-nine: Following this description of the Sahā world, down to the exposition of such Dharma, there are nine lines and a half of sūtra text clarifying the section on the simultaneous preaching of the persons who teach the Dharma and the Dharma-gates in the ten directions.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati universally surveyed all the assemblies in the lands of the ten directions throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, desiring to bring all sentient beings to complete fulfillment;
desiring to thoroughly purify all karmic fruits and retributions; desiring to fully reveal and manifest the pure Dharma-realm;
desiring to completely uproot the foundations of all defiled杂染 (zhá rǎn) [defilements]; and desiring to cause them all to increase...
Because of their vast faith and understanding; because they desire to cause all to know the faculties of immeasurable sentient beings;
because they desire to cause all to know the equality of the dharmas of the three periods of time; because they desire to cause all to observe the realm of nirvāṇa;
and because they desire to increase their own pure roots of goodness, they, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, spoke these verses:

[Treatise] At that time, from the passage beginning with "Dharmamati" down to the recitation of the verses, there are six and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section where the Bodhisattva Dharmamati contemplates the phenomena that serve as objects of desire and praises them in verse.
Below this, the verse text consists of two hundred and forty-two lines. One verse comprises four lines; these verses consist of sixty segments in total. When calculated altogether:
There are two hundred and forty lines; the final two lines summarize the meaning of the verses and offer praise and exhortation for the arousal of the bodhicitta.

The first one hundred and sixty-eight lines constitute the general praise of the five stages from the attainment of the Buddha-fruit back to the beginning, as well as the various dharmas such as faith.
They clarify that the one who first arouses the mind possesses an aspiration and wisdom that encompass all the wisdom of all Buddhas.
The essence, nature, and function of virtue are first perfected at the stage of a Bodhisattva who has just resolved their mind for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika-bodhisattva*).

It is precisely here that the state of the newly resolved mind and the mind [of reality] are shown to be non-dual. If one’s aspiration and delight differ even by a hair’s breadth from the practice of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, compassion, wisdom, and vows, one cannot be called a Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind for enlightenment.

[Scripture] For the benefit of the world, they have resolved upon the Great Mind; their minds pervade all sentient beings, lands, and the phenomena of the three periods of time throughout the ten directions.
Reaching the ultimate limit of the ocean of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is equal to empty space and the Dharma-realm—encompassing every single world in existence.
Just as all Buddhas have gone forth, so too has he resolved his mind without turning back;
with compassionate thoughts, he never for a moment abandons sentient beings. Free from all affliction and harm, he universally benefits them;
his radiance illuminates the world as a place of refuge, and his protection and mindfulness throughout the ten directions are inconceivable.
Entering all lands throughout the ten directions, Manifesting every form and appearance,
With merit and wisdom as vast and boundless as the Buddha’s, Cultivating causes in accordance with reality,
free from attachment; Some worlds dwell upright, some sideways, or inverted, Coarse, subtle, vast, and of infinite varieties.
Once a Bodhisattva has given rise to the supreme mind, they are able to travel everywhere without obstruction;
their sublime practices are unspeakable, for they diligently cultivate them without dwelling anywhere.
Seeing all Buddhas, they always rejoice, universally entering the profound ocean of the Dharma.
Out of compassion for all beings in the five realms of existence, you cause them to remove defilements and become universally pure;
you perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas so that it is never severed, and you utterly destroy the palaces of Māra without remainder.
Having already abided in the equanimity of the Tathāgata, you have skillfully cultivated the subtle path of expedient means.
Giving rise to faith in the realm of the Buddha, Receiving the Buddha’s empowerment with a mind free from attachment;
Mindful of the debt of gratitude owed to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, With a mind like a vajra, indestructible,
One is able to clearly illuminate the conduct of the Buddha And naturally cultivate the practices of Bodhi.
The various distinctions among the realms of existence are immeasurable; Karmic fruits and minds are likewise not one.
Even down to the diverse differences in faculties and natures, A single arousal of the Great Mind clearly perceives them all.
That mind is vast, equal to the Dharma-realm, Without support and unchanging, like space.

They proceed toward the Buddha’s wisdom without grasping; They realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are free from discrimination, knowing the minds of sentient beings as being without birth;

They thoroughly understand all phenomena as being without the notion of "phenomena," and though they universally discern them, they are without discrimination; They travel to billions of nayutas of lands.
The wondrous Dharma-treasury of immeasurable Buddhas— Observing it in accordance with reality, they are able to enter it entirely;
Knowing the faculties and conduct of all beings without exception, They reach such a state as the World-Honored One,
Constantly in accord with pure great vows, Delighting in making offerings to the Tathāgata without ever regressing.
Those seen by humans and devas never tire of beholding them; they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Their minds are pure and without dependence; though they contemplate the profound Dharma, they do not grasp it.
Thus they reflect for immeasurable eons, remaining unattached throughout the three periods of time.
Their minds are firm and difficult to restrain or discourage; they advance toward the Bodhi of the Buddha without obstruction.

With the resolve to seek the wondrous Way, they eliminate delusion and confusion; they traverse the entire Dharma-realm without weariness, knowing that the nature of all speech and phenomena is quiescent.
They enter only into True Suchness (*tathatā*), transcending all divergent interpretations.
They contemplate all the realms of the Buddhas in accordance with reality; Mastery of the three periods of time brings unimpeded mind.
As soon as Bodhisattvas give rise to the vast and great resolve, They are able to travel everywhere to the lands of the ten directions.
The Dharma gates are immeasurable and beyond description; The light of wisdom shines universally, making all clearly understood.
Great compassion that widely delivers others is most peerless;
A heart of loving-kindness is all-pervasive, equal to space, Yet it makes no discrimination among sentient beings. Thus pure, you wander through the world;
All sentient beings in the ten directions are fully comforted, And everything you do is entirely true.
Always with a pure mind, never speaking falsely, Constantly protected by the empowerment of all Buddhas,
Recalling everything of the past and discerning all that is to come,
He enters universally into the worlds of the ten directions To deliver sentient beings and lead them to liberation.
The Bodhisattva is endowed with the light of wondrous wisdom, Thoroughly understanding dependent origination without doubt;
All delusions are completely severed, And thus he traverses the Dharma-realm,
Shattering all the palaces of the Māra kings, While the cataracts of sentient beings are entirely extinguished.
Free from all conceptualization, the mind is unmoving; Thoroughly understanding the realm of the Tathāgata, the net of doubts regarding the three times is entirely removed.
Having given rise to pure faith toward the Tathāgata, through that faith one attains immovable wisdom; Because wisdom is purified, one realizes the ultimate reality.
To cause sentient beings to attain liberation, you exhaustively benefit them until the end of time;

for long periods you exert yourself with tireless mind. You endure even the hells with equanimity, being fully endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom, and you thoroughly understand the faculties and desires of all beings.
There is no karmic action that he does not perceive; according to their inclinations, he expounds the Dharma for them.
Fully understanding that all things are empty and selfless, he never abandons sentient beings with thoughts of loving-kindness.
With a single, subtle voice of great compassion, he enters everywhere throughout the world to proclaim it.
Emitting great light of various colors, it universally illuminates all sentient beings, dispelling all darkness.
Within this light, Bodhisattvas sit upon lotus flowers, expounding the pure Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
Upon the tip of a single hair, they manifest myriad lands, filled entirely with great Bodhisattvas.
The wisdom of those in the assembly differs from one another, yet all are able to clearly understand the minds of sentient beings.
Throughout the unspeakable worlds of the ten directions, they travel in a single thought-moment, leaving nothing unexhausted.
They benefit sentient beings and make offerings to the Buddhas, inquiring about profound meanings in the presence of all the Buddhas.
Regarding all Tathāgatas as one’s father, one cultivates the practices of awakening for the benefit of sentient beings;
through skillful wisdom, one penetrates the treasury of the Dharma, enters the realm of profound knowledge without attachment,
and, contemplating in accordance with reality, expounds the Dharma-realm, which remains inexhaustible throughout immeasurable eons.
Though wisdom skillfully enters that which has no location, it is without weariness or attachment;
born within the family of the Buddhas of the three times, one realizes the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body and manifests all manner of forms for the sake of all living beings,
just as a master illusionist can create anything at all.
Sometimes they manifest the initial cultivation of sublime practices;
Sometimes they manifest birth, renunciation, and the attainment of enlightenment beneath the tree; Or they manifest parinirvāṇa for the sake of sentient beings.
These rare dharmas in which Bodhisattvas dwell Are the domain of Buddhas alone, not that of the Two Vehicles.
Body, speech, and thought are all already eliminated, yet they can manifest in various ways according to what is appropriate.
The various Buddha-dharmas attained by Bodhisattvas cause sentient beings to fall into madness through their contemplation;
yet their wisdom enters the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) with an unimpeded mind, universally manifesting the sovereign power of the Tathāgatas.
In this world, there is none equal to you; how much less could there be one who excels in superior practice?
Although you have not yet fully perfected all-encompassing wisdom, you have already attained the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
Abiding in the ultimate path of the One Vehicle, you have deeply entered the subtle, supreme Dharma.
Skillfully knowing the proper and improper times for sentient beings, you manifest supernatural powers for their benefit,
dividing your body to pervade all buddha-fields. Emitting pure light to dispel the darkness of the world,
you are like a dragon king raising great clouds, raining down wondrous moisture everywhere until all is fully saturated.
Observing sentient beings as like illusions and dreams, they constantly transmigrate due to the power of karma;
with great compassion, they rescue and deliver them all. For their sake, he preaches the unconditioned nature of pure dharmas;
the Buddha’s power is likewise immeasurable, just as empty space has no bounds.
To cause sentient beings to attain liberation, He diligently practiced for billions of eons without weariness.
Contemplating various kinds of wondrous merits, He skillfully cultivated the unsurpassed, foremost deeds.
Never abandoning any of the supreme practices, He focused his mind exclusively on generating all-encompassing wisdom.
Manifesting infinite bodies from a single body, pervading all worlds;
With a pure mind free from discrimination, such is the inconceivable power of a single thought-moment.
Without discriminating among any worlds, one remains free from conceptual construction regarding all phenomena.
Though they contemplate all phenomena, they do not grasp them; They constantly rescue sentient beings, yet there are none who are saved.
The entire world is nothing but conceptualization; Within it, various distinctions arise.
Knowing that the realm of conceptualization is perilous and deep, They manifest supernatural powers to deliver and liberate them.
Just as a master illusionist possesses sovereign power, so too is the miraculous transformation of the Bodhisattva;
their body pervades the Dharma-realm and all of space, appearing to the minds of sentient beings such that there is nowhere it is not seen.
It is free from both subject and object, and from the duality of defilement and purity, with nothing to be grasped.
Whether bound or liberated, all knowledge is forgotten; I only pray that all sentient beings may be granted universal happiness.
All worlds exist solely through the power of conceptualization; entering by means of wisdom, the mind is fearless.
Contemplating all phenomena in this same way, one seeks them throughout the three times and finds them unobtainable.
Able to enter the past and exhaust its limit, able to enter the future and exhaust its limit,
and able to enter all places in the present, they constantly and diligently observe that nothing exists,
conforming to the dharma of nirvāṇa and cessation, abiding in non-contention and without dependence.
The mind is equal to the limit of reality, peerless; Single-mindedly directed toward Bodhi, it never regresses.
Cultivating all supreme practices without retreat or fear, It dwells securely in Bodhi, unshakable.
Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the world— Throughout the entire realm of phenomena, all are clearly understood.
Desiring to attain the most supreme and foremost path, To become a king of liberation through omniscience,
One should swiftly give rise to the bodhicitta, Which forever exhausts all outflows and benefits all beings;
The bodhicitta is pure, And its vast merit is unspeakable.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I shall now proclaim: You noble ones should listen well!

If all immeasurable worlds were reduced to dust, Within each and every mote of dust are immeasurable lands, And within them are immeasurable Buddhas, All of whom can be clearly seen without any grasping.
Skillfully knowing that sentient beings have no notion of birth, Skillfully knowing that speech has no notion of speaking;
Their minds are unimpeded throughout all worlds, Fully and skillfully understanding all things without attachment.
Their minds are as vast as space, Completely penetrating and clearly understanding the events of the three periods of time.
All doubts and delusions are utterly extinguished; With right contemplation of the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing to grasp.
To the infinite lands of the ten directions, They travel in a single thought-moment with a mind free from attachment.
Thoroughly penetrating the manifold sufferings of the world, They all abide in the true reality-limit of non-arising.
He goes to all the assemblies of immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas to pay his respects;
always acting as their leader, he questions the Tathāgatas regarding the various vows and practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas.
His mind constantly recollects the Buddhas of the ten directions, yet remains without dependence and without grasping.
Constantly exhorting sentient beings to plant roots of goodness, He adorns the lands, making them pure.
Regarding all realms of rebirth within the three existences, He observes them all with unimpeded eyes;
All habitual tendencies, faculties, and understandings— Infinite and boundless, he clearly perceives them all.
He fully understands the inclinations and joys of the minds of all sentient beings, and accordingly preaches the Dharma to them as is appropriate.
He penetrates all aspects of defilement and purity, causing them to cultivate and refine themselves so that they enter the Path.
In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva is able to enter immeasurable and innumerable samādhis.
Within that state, they thoroughly understand and master both conceptual cognition and its objects;
having attained this vast wisdom, these Bodhisattvas swiftly advance toward enlightenment without obstruction.
Desiring to benefit all living beings, they proclaim the Dharma of the Great Beings everywhere.
They skillfully know the long and short kalpas of the world, as well as the months, half-months, days, and nights;
they perceive the distinct natures of various lands as equal, always observing with diligence and without negligence.
They travel everywhere to all worlds throughout the ten directions, yet they grasp at no particular location.
He completely purifies the buddha-fields without exception, yet never gives rise to pure conceptualizations regarding sentient beings,
whether in terms of what is possible or impossible, or the distinctions in the retributions of various karmas;
by contemplating in accordance with these, he enters the powers of a Buddha and fully understands them all.
The various natures of all worlds, their various modes of conduct,
and those dwelling in the three faculties— superior, middling, and inferior— all such things he observes;
he clearly perceives their purity and impurity, their diverse inclinations, and their superior, inferior, and middling qualities.
The conduct of all sentient beings wherever they go, The continuity of the three realms of existence— all these can be explained.
The various meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, And how the causes of defilement and purity arise differently,
As well as the distinctions between past suffering and joy— By cultivating the power of the Buddha, one can perceive them all.
Sentient beings’ karma and delusions continue them through the various realms of existence; by severing these realms, one attains quiescence.
The various outflows (*āsrava*) never arise again, and their habitual seeds are fully understood.
The Tathāgata has eradicated all afflictions; the light of his great wisdom illuminates the world.
Although Bodhisattvas have not yet realized the ten powers of a Buddha, they harbor no doubts regarding them;
within a single pore, they universally manifest the infinite lands of the ten directions—
whether defiled or pure— and are able to fully comprehend all the various karmic actions therein.
Within a single atom are immeasurable lands, With immeasurable Buddhas and their sons;
Each land is distinct without confusion, All clearly seen as one within that single [atom].
Within a single pore, one sees the ten directions, All the worlds throughout the entirety of space.
There is not a single place empty of Buddhas; thus all these Buddha-fields are entirely pure.

Within a single pore, one sees Buddha-fields, and further sees all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, each differing in their six destinies. Day and night, month and season, there is bondage and liberation.
Thus, these Bodhisattvas of great wisdom, with single-minded devotion, aspire toward the station of the Dharma King;
dwelling in the presence of the Buddhas, they contemplate in accordance with reality and attain boundless, great joy.
These Bodhisattvas manifest immeasurable billions of emanations to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Their supernormal powers and transformations are peerless; they are able to abide in all places where Buddhas have traveled.
They have probed and admired the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, and they savor every treasury of the Dharma.
Having seen the Buddhas and heard the Dharma, they practice with diligence, their hearts filled with joy like those who have drunk nectar.
Having already attained the supreme samādhi of the Tathāgata, They skillfully enter all dharmas,
their wisdom increasing and their faith as immovable as Mount Sumeru. Universally becoming treasuries of merit for all living beings,
Their hearts of compassion vast and pervasive toward all sentient beings, May they all swiftly accomplish all-encompassing wisdom.
Always without attachment and without a place of reliance, Free from all afflictions and having attained mastery,
you have compassion for sentient beings with vast wisdom. Universally gathering all as if they were yourself,
you know that all is empty, signless, and lacks true reality, Yet you act with a mind that never slackens or retreats.
The measure of the merit of a bodhisattva’s resolve Cannot be exhausted by praise for billions of eons;
For it brings forth all Tathāgatas And bestows peace and happiness upon pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas.
To all sentient beings throughout the lands of the ten directions, They grant security for immeasurable eons.
Exhorting others to uphold the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths, And further dwelling in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and various meditative states;
Bestowing peace and happiness for many eons, Causing them to sever all afflictions and become arhats—
Though such a mass of merit may be immeasurable, It cannot compare to the virtue of generating the bodhicitta.

[Treatise] By means of these one hundred and sixty-eight lines of the first verse, there is a general praise of the causes and effects of the six stages beginning with faith, as well as a general praise of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue;
this serves as a teaching on the similarities between the Dharma and [the qualities of] those who have first resolved to attain enlightenment.
[The Sūtra] further teaches billions of beings to become pratyekabuddhas, causing them to attain the subtle path of non-contentious conduct (*araṇā-vihāra*).
Yet, when compared with the bodhicitta, no calculation or metaphor can reach it;
a single thought-moment can surpass as many buddha-fields as there are atoms, and thus it persists for immeasurable kalpas.
The number of these lands may still be measured, But the merit of generating the mind of enlightenment cannot be known.
All the eons of the past, future, and present May be infinite in their measure;
Yet even these eons may be reckoned, While the merit of generating the mind remains unfathomable.
With the bodhicitta pervading the ten directions, there is no conceptualization that is not known;
in a single thought-moment, one clearly understands the three periods of time for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
Regarding all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one desires to understand their skillful means and the conduct of their minds.
Even if the limits of empty space could be measured, the merit of generating the resolve for enlightenment is difficult to fathom.

The Bodhisattva’s vows are equal to the ten directions; with a heart of universal compassion, they cause all living beings to cultivate and achieve the merits of Buddhahood. Therefore, its power is without bound.
The desires, understandings, and inclinations of sentient beings, And their various faculties, skillful means, and modes of conduct—
All these he fully knows within a single thought-moment. With the mind of omniscient wisdom, equal toward all,
He perceives the afflictions and karma of all sentient beings, And how the continuity of the three realms of existence never ceases for even a moment.
The limits of these [worlds] may still be known, But the merit of generating the mind of awakening is inconceivable.
Generating the mind can bring one away from karma and afflictions, And allow for the offering to all Tathāgatas.
Once karma and delusions are abandoned and the continuum severed, One attains liberation throughout the three periods of time.
In a single thought-moment, one makes offerings to boundless Buddhas And likewise to countless sentient beings, All with incense, flowers, and exquisite garlands;
With precious banners, pennants, canopies, and superior robes;
With fine food, precious seats, and places for walking meditation; With various palaces, all exquisitely adorned.
The Vairocana wondrous jewel, the wish-fulfilling maṇi radiating light—
If one maintains such offerings in every thought-moment, Though the mass of merit of that person may be vast and unspeakable for immeasurable kalpas,
It does not equal the greatness of the merit of generating the resolve [for enlightenment].
The various analogies that have been taught Cannot equal the bodhicitta;
For all the Honored Ones among men of the three times Are born from the arousal of this mind.
This arousal of the mind is unimpeded and limitless; One cannot find its measure, even if one sought it.
I vow that the wisdom of all-knowledge shall certainly be accomplished; May all sentient beings be forever delivered.
The resolve to attain enlightenment is as vast as space, And the arising of all merits is equal to the Dharma-realm.
One's conduct is universally pervasive and without distinction, Forever free from all attachments, equal to the Buddhas.
There is no dharma-gate they do not enter; they are able to go to all lands;
they fully penetrate the realm of all-knowledge; they accomplish all merits and virtues;
their capacity for relinquishment is ever-continuous; they purify all categories of precepts without attachment.
Endowed with supreme and great merit, Always diligent and never regressing,
Entering deep meditative concentration and constant reflection, In harmony with vast wisdom—
This is the most excellent stage of the Bodhisattva, From which all paths of Samantabhadra arise.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time Without exception protect and mind those who have first resolved for enlightenment;
Through samādhis, dhāraṇīs, And the adornments of supernatural transformations, they do so together.
The sentient beings of the ten directions are immeasurable, And the worlds and empty space are likewise.
The resolve of the mind is immeasurable, exceeding even that; Therefore, it can give birth to the Bodhicitta of all Buddhas.
It is the root of the ten powers, And likewise the root of the four analytical knowledges and the fearlessnesses;
Even the eighteen unique qualities are thus— There is nothing that does not arise from the resolve of the mind.
The physical forms of all Buddhas, adorned with marks and signs, as well as their equal and wondrous Dharma-body;
the wisdom that is unattached and worthy of offerings—all these are attained through the arousal of the bodhicitta.
So too are the vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, and the bliss of the various dhyānas and samādhis of the Form Realm.
And all the samādhis of the formless realm— All these take the initial resolve as their foundation.
The sovereign bliss of all humans and devas, As well as the various pleasures of the different realms of existence,
And the manifold joys of the faculties, powers, and roots of progress— None of these fail to arise from that first resolve.
By giving rise to the vast mind through its causes, one is able to practice the six perfections;

One exhorts all sentient beings to practice right conduct, And within the three realms, abides in peace and bliss, possessing the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom of ultimate reality; All sublime deeds are thus fully revealed.
He is able to cause immeasurable sentient beings to sever all delusions and karma and head toward nirvana;
his light of wisdom is like the pure sun, his fulfillment of all practices is like the full moon,
his constant abundance of merit is like the vast ocean, and he is stainless and unimpeded like space.
Universally manifesting boundless vows of merit, Bestowing all happiness upon every sentient being;
Following these vows throughout the limits of the future, Constantly and diligently practicing to deliver all beings.
These immeasurable great vows are inconceivable— May they cause all sentient beings to be completely purified.

Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-reliance—through the power of their vows, they clearly manifest that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like space. All things are quiescent and entirely equal;
though these gateways to the Dharma are innumerable and ineffable, they teach them to sentient beings without attachment.
The Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions all together praise this initial resolve;
adorned with immeasurable virtues, it enables one to reach the other shore, equal to a Buddha.
Even if one were to speak of its merits for as many eons as there are sentient beings, they could not be fully exhausted.

Abiding in the vast dwelling of the Tathāgata, where no phenomenon within the three realms can serve as a metaphor—those who wish to know all the Buddha-dharmas should swiftly resolve upon the bodhicitta.
This mind is the most supreme among all merits; one will certainly attain the unobstructed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The mental activities of sentient beings may be counted, And likewise the atoms within all lands;
Even the limits of empty space might be measured, But the merit of generating the mind of enlightenment can never be fathomed.
It gives birth to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, And brings to fulfillment every happiness in the world.
Increasing all supreme virtues, Forever severing all doubts and delusions,
Revealing all wondrous realms, Completely eliminating all obstacles,
Accomplishing all pure buddha-fields, And giving birth to the wisdom of all Tathāgatas.

If you wish to behold all Buddhas of the ten directions, If you wish to bestow an inexhaustible treasury of merit, And if you wish to extinguish all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, You should swiftly resolve to attain Bodhicitta. [Commentary]:
Thereafter, the seventy-four stanzas begin as a reiteration of the preceding forty sections, wherein the cultivation and measurement of the resolve for enlightenment are compared.
The vast magnitude of the merit of the mind is clearly elucidated in the text; one should understand the four lines and one verse of praise according to the text by analogy with this.

Thus, having calculated the merit of the initial generation of the bodhicitta, suppose one were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure to infinite sentient beings throughout a realm as boundless as space, causing them all to attain human status.
The celestial superior joys further instruct one to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, as well as pratyekabuddhahood and the supramundane bodhi of the three vehicles;
yet, although such realms of space and the beings to be delivered are equal,
they do not cause the beings being transformed to attain Buddhahood, nor can they be compared to the initial resolve for the vehicle within this teaching.
The Tathāgata’s great wisdom is equal to that practiced by all Buddhas because he universally transforms sentient beings so that they all attain Buddhahood;

for this reason, he gives rise to the bodhicitta. Although the scope of the realms cited here is equal in its breadth and narrowness, it cannot serve as a valid comparison because the transformed sentient beings are not equal in terms of whether they attain Buddhahood or not. Therefore, the subsequent text of this chapter states:
It is said that a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind does not have even the slightest attainment regarding the three times—
namely, whether it be the Buddhas or the Buddha-dharmas, the bodhisattvas or the bodhisattva-dharmas,
the pratyekabuddhas or the pratyekabuddha-dharmas, or the śrāvakas or the śrāvaka-dharmas— and so forth, as explained at length in the sūtra; they seek only omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
With a mind that has no attachment toward any realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one gives rise to the bodhicitta. Briefly stated, there are four aspects to this dharma of bodhi:
first, the bodhi of the *śrāvaka*; second, the bodhi of the *pratyekabuddha*; third, the bodhi of the provisional-vehicle bodhisattva;
and fourth, the fruit of buddhahood of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) bodhisattva. The first three are all supramundane bodhis, whereas the fruit of buddhahood is...

This refers to the Dharma-body, great wisdom, and great compassion; because the true and conventional, the myriad practices, and the Dharma-realm are the perfection of Bodhi, there is no coming or going.

Although the Bodhi of the Three Vehicles contemplates the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, they do not yet know the actual substance of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination—not only do the Two Vehicles not know it, but [they do not know] the Bodhi of the three kinds of mind-made bodies.

Even those at the stage of a Bodhisattva who have ascended to the ten bhūmis are still unable to fully know [the ultimate truth]; it is only the Bodhisattva of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) who, through wisdom, comes to know it.
This is clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Bhūmis," though here it shall be stated briefly and in general terms.

Within the three vehicles, [practitioners] contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as the twelve links of dependent origination and the practice of the six pāramitās; these Bodhisattvas merely feel weary of suffering and aspire toward the Truth.
Only when seeking supramundane great compassion does a Bodhisattva of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) speak of "retaining delusions to moisten birth.

Such a Bodhisattva contemplates the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination through wisdom: ignorance is itself wisdom, and the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is itself the noble truth (*āryasatya*).

Because there is no distinction between bondage and liberation within the nature of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, this sutra names these the Noble Truth of Suffering and the Noble Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). Thus it is said.
The ten noble truths and the twelve links of dependent origination are, in their totality, the self-nature of the dharma-realm—unbound and unliberated, the dependent origination of sovereign freedom.

They are not called ignorance, nor are they called the truth of suffering. To contemplate all phenomena in this manner is what is called the wisdom of the single-vehicle dharma-realm dependent origination: sovereignty in compassion, arising according to the nature of conditions, the eye of all things.
The ears, nose, tongue, and body are all, without exception, the gate of the Dharma-realm’s dependent origination and sovereign mastery;

it is through this that all Buddhas possess their knowledge, vision, spiritual powers, and divine strength. Yet, these are manifested solely by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the contemplative observation of the various *pāramitās*.
Therefore, students should practice in this manner and, having done so, enter into awakening accordingly.
The four lines of the following verse are fully contained within the text itself; there is no need for further explanation.
Let the wise, in accordance with the words, offer praise so as to inspire the resolve of the assembly.
This concludes the eighteenth chapter, "The Exposition of the Dharma."
[Treatise] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;
and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. First, regarding the explanation of the title:

this chapter is intended to clarify the merits of the previous chapters—the "Ascent to the Summit of Mount Sumeru," the "Verses of Praise," the "Ten Abodes," and the "Brahma-conduct"—as well as the merit of the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Five Chapters on the Qualities of Virtue: having already resolved upon Bodhicitta, one attains vast merit through this diligence and wisdom.
The Dharma questioned here has two meanings: first, it causes the mind regarding the five preceding chapters of Dharma to become even more luminous;

second, it causes the practices to be undertaken in the subsequent chapters to become increasingly clear and manifest. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Luminosity of Dharma" (Ming-fa-pin), signifying the ascent of clarity.
Because it concerns the methods for progressing through the preceding and succeeding stages, the Bodhisattva Vīryamati requested the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"May all great vows be fully satisfied and may the vast treasury of all bodhisattvas be attained.
This clarifies that the dharmas previously obtained are made even more luminous, while subsequent progress is rendered clear; this is the cultivation of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

Regarding the second section, the "Explanation of the Chapter," which follows the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) that nourish the fundamental position: the intent of its arrival and its title are as previously stated.
The third part, the "Exegesis Following the Text," is divided into two sections: first, an outline of the sutra’s meaning; second, the word-by-word explanation.
Regarding the first, the outline of the sutra’s meaning, it is divided into three parts. First: "At that time... [and so forth].
The following prose section consists of thirty-three and a half lines of scripture;
the verse section consists of fifty-five and a half lines, clarifying the second part, "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Vīryamati Requesting the Dharma. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati...
[the following six lines of scripture clarify] the third part, "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Dharmamati Granting Permission to Speak. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...
From "Mahāsattva" down to the end of the chapter, the verses collectively clarify the section on the Exposition of the True Dharma (*bhūta-dharmadeśanā-vibhāga*).
This section is divided into two parts: first, the general meaning of this passage of the sutra;
second, the word-by-word commentary on its meaning. Regarding the first part, the general meaning of this passage of the sutra, it is categorized as follows:
This consists of three sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramati addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first resolves to seek omniscience, they accomplish such immeasurable merit and are endowed with great adornment."
Having ascended the vehicle of omniscience, entered the stage of the Bodhisattvas' correct position, abandoned all worldly dharmas, and attained the supramundane dharmas of the Buddhas,
they are embraced by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and are certain to reach the ultimate state of unsurpassed enlightenment.
How should those Bodhisattvas practice within the Buddha's teaching so that all Tathāgatas may give rise to joy?
Entering into all the abodes where bodhisattvas dwell, they bring all great practices to complete purity;

they cause all great vows to be fully satisfied and obtain the vast treasury of all bodhisattvas. According to those who are to be transformed, they constantly preach the Dharma, never abandoning the practice of the pāramitās.
All sentient beings they keep in mind are caused to attain liberation, thereby perpetuating the lineage of the Triple Gem.

"O Son of the Buddha, by what skillful means can those bodhisattvas ensure that this Dharma is brought to full perfection without ever severing their roots of goodness? Please, out of compassion, explain this for us;
there is none in this great assembly who does not long to hear it."

[Treatise] First, from "At that time" onwards, up to "there were none who did not delight in hearing," there are twelve lines of sūtra text clarifying the section on the Dharma-gate of the Initial Request made by the Bodhisattva Vīramati. Second, regarding the word-by-word commentary:
as for "at that time," "at" (爾) here means "when this Dharma was being preached. As for "the Bodhisattva Vīramati," in terms of...
The establishment of this stage through preparatory practice is termed "the universal application of the ten kinds of wisdom.
To bring about the advancement of this stage, one must rely upon the power of diligence (*vīrya*). Wisdom has the meaning of illuminating, while diligence has the meaning of non-conceptualization.
When the wisdom of non-conceptualization illuminates the activity of effort, that which is fundamentally non-existent as an activity becomes manifest in its myriad forms.
The Dharma is fundamentally pure from the beginning; that all phenomena are inherently pure is what is called "purity" (*śubha*).

One should know that the absence of artifice and wisdom, which responds to the faculties to benefit sentient beings, is what is called "progress" (*vīrya*); this refers to the designation for progress in cultivation within the stage of realization.

As for "Bodhisattva," it is as commonly explained. Regarding the Bodhisattva Pure Dharma Wisdom (*Śukladharmaprajñā*): "pure" (*śukla*) means luminous; luminosity refers to names and phrases, which express its [meaning].
The phrase "ascending the vehicle of omniscience" clarifies that one has entered this stage.

Because a bodhisattva at this stage mounts the vehicle of omniscience, is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and enters the Buddha’s seed-wisdom, they become a son of the Buddha and are constantly sustained by the protection of all Buddhas.
Therefore, it is said that their wisdom is in accord with clarity, making them capable of providing benefit; thus, they are said to be "gathered."
Regarding the statement "obtaining the vast treasury of all bodhisattvas," this refers to the ten treasuries,

such as the treasury of wisdom and the treasury of compassion found within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (The Ten Stages). Regarding the phrase "by what means," and so forth, these refer to the ten sets of ten dharma-gates within the actual exposition.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, just as all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly and diligently cultivate the practice of eliminating all the darkness of ignorance,
subduing Māra and his enemies, restraining all heterodox teachers, forever cleansing all defilements of the mind,
being fully able to accomplish all roots of goodness, eternally emerging from all evil destinies and difficulties, and purifying all great wisdom;

The accomplishment of the spheres of all bodhisattva stages, the pāramitās, dhāraṇīs, samādhis, the six supernormal powers, the three types of clear knowledge, and the four fearlessnesses; the adornment of all buddha-fields with pure merits;
the fulfillment of the marks and signs of excellence, as well as the conduct of body, speech, and mind; and the thorough knowledge of the powers of all buddha-tathāgatas.
The domain of activity of the fearlessnesses, the unique Buddha-dharmas, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); for the sake of maturing all sentient beings,
taking up Buddha-fields according to their inclinations, teaching the Dharma as is appropriate according to their faculties and the time,
performing various immeasurable and vast Buddha-deeds, as well as other immeasurable dharmas of merit, practices, paths, and all [other qualities].
Their spheres of activity are entirely perfected, swiftly becoming equal to the merits of the Tathāgatas; they are able to protect, reveal,
and expound the treasury of Dharma accumulated by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas over hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
such that no māras or non-Buddhists can obstruct or destroy it, and they uphold the True Dharma without end.
When preaching the Dharma throughout all worlds, the celestial kings, dragon kings, yakṣa kings, gandharva kings,
asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoraga kings, human kings, Brahmā kings,
and the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, all provide protection; they honor and make offerings to him with reverence, and together they perform the consecration.
His crown is constantly protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; all Bodhisattvas likewise love and revere him.

Having attained the power of roots of goodness, he increases pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and expounds the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma. Upholding the True Dharma, he adorns himself with it.
I pray that you will fully explain the successive stages of practice for all Bodhisattvas.

[Treatise] Second, furthermore, from "As all... down to "the sequence of practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas," twenty-one lines of scripture are expounded to clarify the diligence and wisdom of the Bodhisattva, as well as the specific practices to be cultivated at each stage and the benefits thereby obtained;
this is followed by an earnest exhortation to protect the Dharma. Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they are [summarized as] the body.

The supernormal power of penetrating the heavens, the supernormal power of the divine ear, the supernormal power of the divine eye, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, and the supernormal power of the body:
at a single moment, the body follows the function of wisdom to pervade the ten directions, manifesting physical bodies in response to beings and universally responding according to their faculties.
As for the supernormal power of the divine ear, the faculty of the ear constantly hears all sounds throughout the ten directions. As for the supernormal power of the divine eye...

The faculty of the eye constantly perceives all coarse and subtle forms throughout the ten directions; the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna) enables one’s wisdom to know, according to the three periods of time, the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings, as well as their performed actions and the causes and effects thereof;

and the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (paracittajñāna) enables one to know, in a single thought-moment, the mental inclinations and desires of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) consists of universally knowing all phenomena through wisdom, being free from passion, and not following the heart of delusion and attachment.
Furthermore, this sutra speaks of ten kinds of supernormal powers as explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernormal Powers. Regarding the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*):

first, the knowledge of past lives; second, the divine eye; third, the exhaustion of outflows—these are called the three types of clear knowledge. Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*): first, the fearlessness of possessing all-knowledge...

The fearlessness regarding the destruction of the two outflows (āsrava-kṣaya-vaiśāradya), the third fearlessness regarding the teaching on the obstacles to the path (antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya), and the fourth fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path leading to the end of suffering (nairyāṇika-pratipad-vaiśāradya).
As for the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), these are the "Ocean of the Marks of the Ten Bodies" from this sutra. Regarding the powers and fearlessnesses, these are the ten powers (daśabala):

first, the power of the possible and the impossible (sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala); second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration (dhyāna-bala); fourth, the power of the faculties (indriya-bala); fifth, the power of resolve (chanda-bala); sixth, the power of disposition (gotra-bala).

The power of [the knowledge of] all paths leading to every destination (sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala) is the seventh; the power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala) is the eighth; the power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-jñāna-bala) is the ninth; and the power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna-bala) is the tenth.

These constitute the thirteen [powers]. That which is called the "world" (*loka*) refers to the ripening of karma; to have thorough comprehension (*parijñā*) of this is called "knowing the non-existent.

To skillfully know the causes and effects of the karma of sentient beings, with a mind concentrated and immovable like the king of mountains (*śailarāja*), is the first chapter on the categories of the faculties (*indriya*)—superior, middling, and inferior.
The various distinctions of lower sensual pleasures, the diverse natures and categories of all worldly realms,
the differing paths of all dharmas, the thorough knowledge of past lives, the karma of the three periods of time, the divine eye unimpeded throughout the ten directions,

the comprehension of all conceptualizations, the fulfillment of the mind throughout the ten directions, the absence of defilement, and constant stainlessness— through these ten kinds, one attains mastery.
These are called the eighteen unique qualities of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness: first, no fault in the Buddha’s body;
second, no fault in his speech; third, no fault in his mindfulness; fourth, no fault in his perception; fifth, his mind is never unsettled and is always in samādhi;
sixth, he has no relinquishing without prior awareness; seventh, his aspiration does not diminish; eighth, his diligence...
10. No loss of the nine recollections; 11. no decrease in wisdom; 12. no decrease in liberation; 13.
no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; 14. bodily action follows wisdom; 15. verbal action follows wisdom;
16. mental action follows wisdom; 17. unimpeded knowledge of the past through wisdom.
Seventeenth, the matter of unimpeded knowledge of the future through wisdom; eighteenth, the matter of unimpeded knowledge of the present through wisdom.

Regarding "his speech is without fault," it means it is perfectly accordant with the sublime. Regarding "his speech is without deficiency," it means that he never forgets the wholesome dharmas he has practiced.
As for "the one of all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*), it refers to the one of manifold knowledge and inexhaustible knowledge.
This clarifies that because the wisdom of discernment is inexhaustible, as in the section on "Guarding," there are two meanings:
first, it clarifies that a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment guards the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas and is able to expound it for others;
second, they obtain the protection of celestial kings, yakṣa kings, Tathāgatas, Dharma-kings, and so forth.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramatī, wishing to restate its meaning, spoke these verses.
[Śāstra] From "At that time" onwards, the third section— comprising approximately one line of sūtra— clarifies the portion where Vīramatī restates her request for the Dharma using verses.
[Sūtra] The one of great renown is skilled at expounding The dharmas of merit accomplished by bodhisattvas;
He has deeply entered boundless and vast practices, And is endowed with pure, teacherless wisdom.
If there is a bodhisattva who first resolves their mind, They shall accomplish the vehicle of merit and wisdom.
Entering the stage of transcendence beyond the world, one universally attains the dharmas of perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, how does one within the Buddha’s teaching cultivate with firm diligence so that it ever increases in excellence,
causing all Tathāgatas to rejoice, and swiftly entering the ground where the Buddhas abide?

Their conduct is pure and their vows are all fulfilled; having attained the vast treasury of wisdom, they are ever able to preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Their minds rely on nothing and are free from attachment;
they skillfully practice all the bodhisattva pāramitās without any deficiency or diminution.
May all sentient beings you have in mind be fully delivered; May you always uphold the seed of the Buddha so that it is never severed.
May your actions be firm and not in vain, So that all merits may be perfected and liberation attained, Just as practiced by all the Victorious Ones. I pray that you will proclaim that path of purity.
Forever destroying all the darkness of ignorance, Subduing the hosts of Māras and non-Buddhists,
Completely washing away all defilements, One draws near to the Tathāgata’s great wisdom,
Forever leaving behind the perilous difficulties of the evil realms, And purifying the sublime sphere of great knowledge.
Having attained the power of the wondrous Way, you are equal to the Most Honored Ones;
all merits and virtues are fully accomplished, and you have realized the Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom.
Abiding in immeasurable lands, you preach the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings and perform vast Buddha-works.

How does one attain all the wondrous paths? How does one expound the Tathāgata’s treasury of the True Dharma, Constantly able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, Incapable of being surpassed and without equal?
How does one become fearless like a lion, With conduct as pure as the full moon?
How does one cultivate the Buddha’s virtues so that they are like a lotus flower, unstained by water?
[Treatise] In the section consisting of the repeated request in verse, there are twenty-two lines of verse.
The first two lines praise the Master who is able to preach the Dharma; the following twenty lines consist of two lines per verse. Of these, the first two lines praise the initial aspiration.
The first two verses explain how the Bodhisattva’s mind, wisdom, and merit transcend the world to obtain benefit; the next two verses exhort the practice of spiritual advancement;
the following two verses clarify the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā) that saves sentient beings without attachment;

the subsequent two verses clarify that all practices are without deficiency, benefiting living beings so that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted; and the final two verses clarify the nature of steadfast merit.
The next two verses clarify the path for dispelling darkness and subduing Māra, which is the most weighty exhortation to preach the Dharma of renunciation;
the following two verses clarify the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and likewise exhort that it be preached;
the subsequent two verses clarify how the Tathāgata’s Dharma is to be expounded; and the final two verses clarify [the manner of its exposition].
"How can one cause those who have first resolved their minds to be fearless like lions and unattached like lotuses?
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati addressed the Bodhisattva Vīryamati, saying: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You now desire to bring great benefit, great peace and happiness, and great welfare to many, out of compassion for the world and its devas."

Furthermore, when someone asks such a Bodhisattva about the pure conduct they have cultivated—asking, "O Son of the Buddha, you abide in the true Dharma, have aroused great diligence, and having increased it without regression, you have attained liberation;
you are able to ask such a question"—listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. Now, relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, I shall explain this for you.
[The Sūtra] speaks of only a small portion [of this].

[Treatise: Second, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati... and following, there are six lines of sūtra that clarify the section in which the Bodhisattva Dharmamati consents to speak.
Within this section, the praise for the person capable of asking the question may be understood according to the text.

Within the third section, the Section on Correct Exposition (*samyag-deśanā-bhāga*), there are further two divisions: first, a general outline of the sūtra’s meaning; second, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.

Regarding the first, the general outline of the sūtra’s meaning: from the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva who has already resolved upon the mind of omniscience" down to the end of the chapter, it is divided into twenty sections.

[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has resolved upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), they should abandon the darkness of delusion and apply themselves with diligence to guard it so as not to become negligent.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten dharmas in which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides that are called "non-negligence. What are these ten?
First, the upholding and protection of the various precepts; second, the distancing from ignorance and the purification of bodhi.
Third, the mind is joyful and upright, being free from all flattery and deception; fourth, one diligently cultivates roots of goodness without ever regressing;
fifth, one constantly and skillfully reflects upon the mind one has generated; sixth, one does not delight in associating with any ordinary persons, whether lay or ordained;
seventh, one cultivates various wholesome deeds without seeking worldly rewards. Eighth...
1. To be forever free from the practices of the two vehicles and to practice the bodhisattva path; 9. To delight in cultivating all manner of goodness so that it is never interrupted;
10. To constantly and skillfully observe the power of one’s own mental continuum. Sons of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas practice these ten dharmas, they are said to dwell in heedfulness.
[Treatise] First, from "the foremost son of the Buddha" onwards to "dwelling in heedfulness," there are ten scriptural passages clarifying the section on dwelling in the ten kinds of heedful dharmas.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in heedfulness, they attain ten kinds of purity.

What are these ten? First, acting according to what one has taught; second, the accomplishment of mindfulness and wisdom; third, dwelling in profound meditative concentration, neither sinking nor becoming agitated;
fourth, delighting in seeking the Buddha-dharma without weariness; fifth, according to the Dharma as it was heard...
Sixth, through the full development of rational investigation, one gives rise to skillful wisdom;
seventh, by entering deep meditative concentration, one attains the supernormal powers of a Buddha; eighth, the mind is equanimous, free from high and low;

ninth, toward all sentient beings—whether of superior, middling, or inferior classes—the mind is without obstruction, benefiting them equally like the great earth; tenth, when seeing sentient beings...
Even when they have only once resolved to attain bodhicitta, they honor and serve them as if they were their preceptors;
tenth, toward their ordination preceptors, ācāryas, all bodhisattvas, spiritual friends, and Dharma masters, they always give rise to respect, serve them, and make offerings.
O Son of the Buddha, these are called the ten kinds of purity for a bodhisattva dwelling in heedfulness.

[Treatise] Second, from "the sons of the Buddha" downwards to the ten kinds of purity, there are ten and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the section on attaining the ten pure dharmas by abiding in non-negligence. Regarding the second part, the word-by-word commentary:
among the twenty sections concerning Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the Main Exposition, I shall follow the meaning of the sūtra text where the words are implicit.
The passages in the scripture that are obscure can be explained; those that are self-evident are already complete as they appear in the text, so there is no need for further commentary.

For instance, regarding the passage "deeply entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), neither sinking nor excited": "neither sinking" means being free from the extinction-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the Śrāvakas, and also being free from the dhyānas of quiescence belonging to the two upper realms;
it is like the first *dhyāna* of the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), which extinguishes the sorrow and anxiety of the lower Desire Realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
When one attains a portion of non-arising pliancy and tranquility, yet still possesses craving for the desire realm while having a craving for tranquility, the calamity of water will arrive.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The moisture of conceptualization can produce the internal and external water element; because craving serves as the moisture, the great water element arrives.
Just as the second dhyāna of the form realm can extinguish the sorrow and suffering of the desire realm, [so too does this state].

When one has attained a portion of pliancy and tranquility, yet still possesses applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) while taking a tranquil object as a focus, the fire disaster reaches there;

this is like the third dhyāna. When there is no applied or sustained thought, but there is the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*), the wind disaster reaches there due to the movement of the mind’s joy;
this is like the fourth dhyāna, where body and mind are stilled and one is free from inhalation and exhalation, as well as the movement of joy.
Furthermore, they are not subject to the three calamities; their sublime form-bodies alone remain, as pure and radiant as white silver, with robes like gold.
Those in the fourth dhyāna have bodies twenty *li* long and robes forty *li* long; those in the lower three dhyānas decrease by half successively.
This has already been explained in the first assembly. Thus, these four dhyānas all serve to still and quiet the mind.

One considers that the stages of the formless realm—up to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—are all means of breaking through and ascending so that thoughts do not arise and one abides in tranquil concentration.

Thus, by breaking down the tranquility of the form realm, one brings about the emptiness and consciousness of the formless realm; furthermore, by breaking down the consciousness that perceives emptiness as being empty itself, it is called "emptiness of emptiness."

The concentration of the sphere of consciousness further breaks the view that consciousness is empty; it is also called the concentration of nothingness. This concentration of nothingness further breaks the mind of nothingness;
this state where even the thought of "non-thought" is absent is called the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus, all meditations cultivated in the higher realms involve deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*), maintaining intentional effort, subduing the mind, and preventing [distractions]; they are not states of spontaneity.
The nature of non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) is free from both depression and agitation; it is called the "tranquil function" of true wisdom and is the samādhi of acting without acting.
For example, the meditative concentration of the desire realm is called "agitation" because it clings to the five desires; the concentrations of the form and formless realms are called "depression";
and the concentrations of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are called "depression in emptiness. The Bodhisattva’s practice of the six *pāramitās* gives rise to [this samādhi].
In the Pure Land, these are termed *auddhatya* (restlessness). Thus, the concentrations (*samādhi*) of the three vehicles all possess the stains of *laya* (sinking) and *auddhatya*;

because they have not yet eliminated the views [of self] and lack true joy or revulsion, the concentrations of the two vehicles, though free from the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of the triple world, are merely antidotes that suppress and extinguish them through aversion. They lack the capacity to give rise to the notion, "I am born."
Those who do not give rise to compassion and wisdom, nor dwell in the meditative concentrations of cessation, even if a drum were beaten upon their heads, they would neither hear nor know it;
those who transform fire to burn the segmented body of their parents enter the cycle of *pariṇāmi-śīti* (transformative birth and death).

Such are the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who, having severed delusions, do not discriminate among phenomena, as their mental momentum is similar [to that of the Buddha]. Or there may be a *śrāvaka* who attains [realization] through the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The Way is thus: the paths attained by those of the three vehicles—Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pure Land Bodhisattvas—through their contemplative practices, are all supramundane.

These three vehicles function interchangeably, collectively constituting the essential substance of the nine vehicles. As summarized in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, they subdue the afflictions of the triple world so that they do not arise;
they attain the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and are free from the death and rebirth of the segmented cycle, attaining instead the transformation [body].
Birth and death are subject to change and are not the state of the Arhat; rather, one acts with mastery through wisdom, free from the duality of entering and emerging.
This essence of acting through wisdom to respond to sentient beings and provide them with ceaseless benefit and happiness is as extensively taught in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

For this reason, within the form realm, the formless realm, and the meditations of the three vehicles, there is both subsidence and agitation, just as in the Mahāyāna, where Bodhisattvas intentionally retain afflictions to moisten their rebirths.

Prior to the Path, one establishes the thirty minds of the Bodhisattva—the stages of the Habitual Nature (*śīkṣā-bhūmi*), the Nature of Essence (*gotra-bhūmi*), and the Nature of the Path (*mārga-bhūmi*)—before finally entering the Holy Nature (*ārya-bhūmi*).

These involve the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*), the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), the contemplation of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), and the names and characteristics of their corresponding aspects.
If one intends to encompass and transform realms and perceive the number of Buddhas, they are produced by the mind (*manomaya*).
The causes and fruits of attaining Buddhahood through the body of wisdom and the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) are entirely different.

For this reason, the meditative concentration cultivated by a Bodhisattva who intentionally retains afflictions to moisten rebirth is characterized by both laxity (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).

This is because they have only attained the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) and have not yet attained the body born of Tathāgata-wisdom; thus, they attain their respective categories only upon reaching the seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth stages.

Bodhisattvas who possess the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) born of innate non-conceptual attention have merely attained the contemplation of emptiness regarding the afflictions within the three realms;
they have subdued the active manifestations so that they do not arise, and thus possess mastery over the mind-made body.

However, because they have not yet entered the household of the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor have they developed habitual proficiency within that omniscience, [they are not yet fully liberated].

Regarding what is called "attaining Buddhahood," it is definitively said to require the completion of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. As for the realm of Buddhas perceived [by bodhisattvas], a bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) merely speaks of making offerings to and transforming a hundred Buddha-worlds, and attains only the "Gate of Illumination of a Hundred Dharmas" (*śata-dharma-prakāśa-mukha*).

In contrast, according to this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is named "Bodhi" because they have initially generated the Tathāgata’s mind of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākāra-jñatā-citta*).

One should hold the mind as it was at the moment of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), being born into the great wisdom-house of the all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas.
At the time of that initial resolve, one attains perfect enlightenment because the all-encompassing knowledge of all Buddhas and one's own wisdom are one and the same;
thus, Buddhahood is realized without passing even a single *kṣaṇa*, for the realm of wisdom is not subject to temporal extension.
Because it is concise, the scope of its transformation and guidance pervades as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms;

furthermore, the merit and function of the wisdom and clarity of hundreds of Buddhas are inexhaustible, infinite, and infinitely layered. This is still spoken in terms of progressive cultivation according to the stages, yet in principle, one is all and all is one, being infinite.
For example, among the ten stages, a Bodhisattva of the first stage makes offerings to many [Buddhas].

Although "hundreds of Buddhas" and "many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" numerically do not depart from the category of "hundreds," "many hundreds" implies the limitless, whereas a single hundred is merely comparable;
therefore, each and every dharma—such as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four means of integration, the four immeasurable minds, and the ten perfections—is entirely limitless.
For this reason, the concentrated karma cultivated by Bodhisattvas in these ten stages is...
This concludes the explanation of abiding in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without sinking or agitation, pertaining to both mundane and supramundane states of *samādhi*.
As for the statement that one who has entered deeply into meditative concentration attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Buddha:

these include the supernormal powers of the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as well as those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The supernormal powers of the form and formless realms are the karmic retribution of the purification of mental conceptions and perceptions through meditative absorption.
Regarding the attainment of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): the supernormal powers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) rely upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas, attained through the previously cultivated pure lands, consist of the power of purified intention (*āśaya-viśuddhi*), such as the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).

As stated in this sutra, those who enter profound meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and attain the supernormal powers of a Buddha do so because the mind accords with reality (*tattva*); fundamentally, there is no entering or emerging, and its essence is neither still nor disturbed.

The nature of non-constructive activity is spontaneously true according to principle; neither arising nor being suppressed, this truth of principle accords with wisdom and is naturally pervasive throughout the three times and the ten directions.
At once, it universally responds by manifesting form-bodies (rūpakāya) according to the needs of beings, transforming the multitudes through the application of wisdom.
Yet there is no coming or going, nor is there any transformation; this is called the Buddha’s supernatural power (ṛddhi), a wisdom that has no dependence.
The substance of form and color has no nature of coming or going; its nature is inherently all-pervasive and is not subsumed within the three periods of time.

Yet, it is able to universally respond to the phenomena of the three periods—this is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Therefore, a sutra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods without coming or going.
This is because the three periods are falsely established by the sentiments of sentient beings; they do not truly exist. Thus, the essence of wisdom is non-existent.
That physical form acts without deliberate effort yet responds to all classes of beings is called "spiritual power" (*shen*).
That it perfectly fills the ten directions, knowing no phenomena and perceiving nothing without its roots, is called "penetration" (*tong*).

1. Constantly practicing diligence without indolence; 2. Being well able to dwell securely in the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata;
