The Sūtra clarifies that by practicing these ten dharmas, one swiftly enters the various stages (*bhūmi*). As the Sūtra states:

"There are ten kinds of dharmas that cause all bodhisattvas to swiftly enter the various stages. This clarifies that although one is at the stage of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one universally knows the dharmas of all the stages, practices, dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and grounds; for the one is all, and the all is one.

Because they are one, cause is identical to effect; because they are identical, they are like the case where the youth Sudhana, having seen Maitreya Bodhisattva, was then led by Maitreya to see Mañjuśrī again.
This clarifies that cause and effect are neither different nor separate. Therefore, this [path] is also like this:
from the stage of first generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) to the stage of Buddhahood, one advances simultaneously in a single thought-moment, yet it is not...

Because within a single thought-moment one attains the realization of perfect enlightenment, such that the causes and effects of Buddhahood as well as the practices of a Bodhisattva are all fully perfected;
this is similar to the cases of Sudhana and the Dragon Girl, who attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime or without passing even a single kṣaṇa through three lifetimes.
Thus, when it is said that "one attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime," it clarifies that the present life—this body of segmented birth from parents—is the basis for faith.
When the mind and the vision of the Path arise through cultivation, one abandons the body of segmented birth and enters into the birth of transformation; this is called "one birth.
Furthermore, it does not transcend the limit of the moment (*kṣaṇa*). It is devoid of past and future, devoid of the nature of segmentation, and devoid of the nature of transformation.

Since all phenomena are like illusions and like transformations, they are neither arising nor ceasing, and they lack the three periods of time. By means of this, one abides in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Because one universally cultivates all stages and all grounds, one penetrates all phenomena as a whole; at once, with respect to the quantity or brevity of a single dharma, one possesses sovereign and unimpeded mastery that does not transcend the limit of a single *kṣaṇa*.
Since the nature of dharmas is thus, if one casts aside deluded sentiments and observes with wisdom, it can be seen.
As the Sūtra says: "To be of the same essential nature as all Buddhas of the three periods of time" refers to the Dharma.
The body and wisdom are identical; the vast eons of the three periods of time are identical within a single thought-moment;
and the practices of Samantabhadra and all Buddhas of the three periods of time are identical in the perfection of great wisdom and great compassion.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas first dwell in the stages,

Having thoroughly observed and known that all phenomena are solely one’s own mind and are without attachment, and having thus realized this, they enter the bodhisattva stages and are able to dwell securely therein. O Son of the Buddha, those bodhisattvas reflect as follows:
"We ought to swiftly enter the various stages. Why is this? Because if we dwell within each stage, we shall accomplish [the qualities] as they truly are."
Having fully perfected these vast merits, one gradually enters the stage of Buddhahood; having dwelt in the stage of Buddhahood, one is able to perform boundless and vast Buddha-activities.
Therefore, one should constantly and diligently practice without rest or weariness, adorning oneself with great merit and entering the stage of a Bodhisattva.

[Sūtra] That is to say: knowing their actions, knowing their causes and conditions, knowing their mental activities, and knowing their inclinations—[the Buddha] teaches the meditation on impurity to those with much lustful desire;
teaches great compassion to those with much anger; instructs those with much delusion to diligently observe [the nature of things];
and for those with equal parts of the three poisons, he teaches the Dharma-gate of accomplishing supreme wisdom; and for those who delight in birth and death...

For those who speak of the three sufferings, if they are attached to a place of dwelling, he speaks of the emptiness and stillness of that place; for those whose minds are indolent, he speaks of great diligence;
for those who harbor pride, he speaks of the equality of all dharmas; for those full of flattery and deception, he speaks of the Bodhisattva whose mind is upright and sincere;
for those who delight in tranquility, he extensively expounds the Dharma so that they may achieve the state of a Bodhisattva—in this way, he acts according to what is appropriate for each.
When preaching the Dharma, his words and phrases are interconnected and their meanings are free from error;
he contemplates the sequence of phenomena and distinguishes right from wrong with wisdom, definitively ascertaining that they do not violate the seal of the Dharma.

He establishes boundless gateways of practice in successive order, causing all sentient beings to sever all doubts, skillfully discerning their faculties, entering the teaching of the Tathāgata, and realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Dharma is equal, severing all craving for phenomena and eliminating all attachments; constantly mindful of all Buddhas without ever abandoning them from the heart;
understanding that the essential nature of sound is equality, the mind remains unattached to all verbal expressions;
skillfully employing parables without contradiction so that all may attain awakening; and the universal manifestation of the bodies of equal wisdom by all Buddhas according to the needs of beings.
When the Bodhisattva thus expounds the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, he personally cultivates and increases their welfare and benefit,
never abandoning the perfections, and fully adorning the path of the pāramitās.

They give rise to a mind that is equanimous and unwavering, like the great earth which can support all things;

being without attachment to the objects of the five desires, one is able to fully accomplish all successive meditative concentrations.

Constantly maintaining right reflection, one neither dwells nor departs, yet is able to extinguish all afflictions, give birth to immeasurable gateways of samādhi, and achieve boundless great spiritual powers.
By means of supernormal powers, one enters various *samādhis* in both forward and reverse order; through a single gate of *samādhi*, one enters infinite gates of *samādhi*.

Fully knowing the spheres of all *samādhis*, one does not contradict the seals of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*) regarding all *samādhis* and *samāpattis*, and is able to swiftly enter the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). This is the purification of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Having heard the Dharma from all Buddhas, they receive and uphold it; they attend upon spiritual friends without weariness and always delight in hearing the Dharma without satiety.
According to what they have heard and received, they contemplate it in accordance with reality, enter true samādhi, and remain free from all deviant views.

Skillfully observing all phenomena, they obtain the seal of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-mudrā*), fully understand the effortless path (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the Tathāgata, and ride upon the wisdom of the universal gate (*samantamukha-prajñā*).
Entering the gateway of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one attains eternal rest; this is the purification of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One manifests all worldly activities to teach and transform sentient beings without weariness, appearing in forms according to their inclinations.
In all actions, there is no defilement or attachment; one may manifest as an ordinary person or as a noble one.

The practices performed by these people may manifest as birth and death or as nirvāṇa; they are skillfully able to observe all that is done and manifest all manner of adornments, yet remain free from attachment.

They enter universally into all realms of existence to deliver and liberate the multitudes—this is the ability to purify the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) and to fully accomplish the adornment of all sentient beings.
They make offerings to all Buddhas throughout all worlds; they fully penetrate the dharma of non-obstruction;
they fully practice deeds that pervade the entire dharma-realm; their bodies dwell eternally through all future kalpas; their wisdom fully knows all mental activities;
they fully awaken to the cycles of transmigration and its cessation; they manifest in all lands; and they fully realize the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is the ability to purify the perfection of aspiration, because it possesses the power of profound resolve free from all defilement;
because it possesses the power of deep faith that cannot be overcome; because it possesses the power of great compassion that never gives rise to weariness;

because it possesses the power of great loving-kindness whose conduct is impartial; because it possesses the power of dhāraṇī, being able to maintain all meanings through skillful means; and because it possesses eloquence.
Because it causes all sentient beings to rejoice and be fully satisfied; because it possesses the adornment of the power of the *pāramitās* for the sake of the Great Vehicle;
because it possesses the power of great vows that are never interrupted; because it possesses the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) that give rise to the immeasurable;

and because it possesses the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) so that they may believe, understand, and receive [the teaching]—this is what enables one to purify the *pāramitā* of power and to know desire.
The practitioner knows those who practice with hatred, knows those who practice with delusion, and knows those who practice with equal parts [of the defilements].

The practitioner knows those on the stages of training; in a single thought-moment, they know the practices of infinite sentient beings, they know the minds of infinite sentient beings, they know the reality of all phenomena, and they universally awaken to the gates of the Dharma-realm through the powers of all Tathāgatas. This is that which can purify.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva thus purifies the *pāramitās*, fulfills the *pāramitās*,
and does not abandon the *pāramitās* while abiding within the Greatly Adorned Bodhisattva Vehicle,
he teaches the Dharma to all sentient beings according to their inclinations, causing them to increase their pure karma and attain liberation from falling [into lower realms].

For those in the evil realms, he teaches them to resolve their minds toward awakening; for those in times of hardship, he causes them to exert diligent vigor; for sentient beings with much greed, he shows them the dharma of non-greed;
for sentient beings with much anger, he causes them to practice equanimity; for sentient beings attached to views, he explains dependent origination;
for sentient beings in the desire realm, he teaches them to abandon desire, ill-will, and unwholesome dharmas; and for sentient beings in the form realm, he proclaims for them the *Vibhaṅga*.

For those beings of the formless realm who practice *vipaśyanā*, he proclaims subtle and wondrous wisdom; for those of the two vehicles who teach the practice of tranquility, and for those who delight in the Mahāyāna, he explains the vast adornment of the ten powers. He then taught the Dharma extensively to those who were capable of being transformed. Having attained the stage of non-retrogression, he was able to subdue all Māras and heretics. "I shall deliver them through various Dharma-gates according to their respective needs"—
the Bodhisattva who possesses such wisdom is able extensively to deliver all sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha,
the Bodhisattva who possesses such wisdom ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed.

[Treatise] Thirteenth: From "At that time" down to "causing the seeds of the Triple Gem to never be severed," fifty-two and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on the practice of the ten *pāramitās* to benefit sentient beings and their respective antidotes.

The scripture states: "Regarding those in the successive meditative concentrations (*anupūrva-samādhi*), the Bodhisattva is able to enter the formless [attainments] through the four dhyānas of the form realm in succession."

Bodhisattvas of the four dhyānas in the form realm are all able to enter them in regular order or by skipping stages (ultra-interval entry) and emerge from them, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the section on cremation:

entering the third dhyāna from the first dhyāna and emerging; entering the sphere of infinite space from the third dhyāna and emerging; entering the sphere of nothingness from the sphere of infinite space and emerging;

and entering the sphere of consciousness from the sphere of nothingness and emerging. Such are the ultra-interval entries and such are the sequential entries, as set forth in this sūtra’s "Dharma Net."

Entering meditative absorption in one direction and arising in the ten directions, or entering absorption in the ten directions and arising in one direction, and so forth, are all as explained in the stage of the Ten Faiths.
Regarding the "Seal of Wisdom of Samāpatti," this clarifies that stillness and function arise together;

it seals all myriad phenomena such that they are clearly understood without exception, like the myriad images appearing within the waters of the great ocean, where pure wisdom universally seals all as one.
To thoroughly understand all phenomena such that there is neither subject nor object, and no agent—this is what the Sūtra means when it says:
"One who enters true samādhi is free from the three realms and the three vehicles, as well as defilement and purity, sinking and agitation.

To be free from all deviant views refers to the two views of existence and non-existence, as well as internal and external views, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
From the beginning up to the sixty-two views—those who hold these sixty-two views calculate four views regarding all phenomena:
first, permanence; second, impermanence; third, both permanent and impermanent; and fourth, neither permanent nor impermanent.
There are four such views for each of the five aggregates, totaling twenty. Furthermore, there are these same four views applied to the five aggregates of the three periods of time.
Combined, these constitute sixty root views; together with the two fundamental views, they form the sixty-two views. All deviant views do not depart from these.

As the Sūtra says: "Those who skillfully contemplate all phenomena and attain the Seal of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā) use the Great Wisdom Seal—characterized by non-action, non-reliance, and signlessness—to seal all myriad dharmas.
They realize that arising is merely the arising of dharmas, and that there is no ignorance or conceptualization regarding the three periods of time."

The renowned Seal of Reality (bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā) and the Wisdom of the Universal Gateway (samantamukhaprajñā) refer to the wisdom that universally knows the various faculties of sentient beings, the wisdom of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), and the wisdom of the various distinctions [of these].
For the sake of sentient beings in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) who abide in meditative concentration, it teaches them to give rise to contemplation;
it teaches the cultivation of the signless contemplation (animittadhyāna) as the subtle wisdom that does not accord with [conceptual] signs.
Because it is for their benefit.
[Sūtra] Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas teach all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta, they are thus able to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted.
Because they constantly expound the treasury of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they are thus able to ensure that the lineage of the Dharma...
By unceasingly upholding the teachings of the Dharma without contradiction, they ensure that the lineage of the Saṃgha is never interrupted.
Furthermore, by being able to fully praise all great vows, they ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted.

By analytically expounding the gateway of causes and conditions, they ensure that the lineage of the Dharma is never interrupted. They constantly and diligently cultivate the six principles of harmonious respect.

Therefore, they are able to ensure that the lineage of the Saṃgha is not interrupted. Furthermore, by sowing the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings, they are able to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha is not interrupted.
By upholding the True Dharma without begrudging their own bodies or lives, they are able to ensure that the lineage of the Dharma is not interrupted.
By presiding over the great assembly without weariness, they are able to ensure that the lineage of the Saṃgha is not interrupted. Moreover—
Furthermore, regarding all the teachings spoken and the precepts established by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they uphold them all completely, never abandoning them in mind;
therefore, they are able to ensure that the lineages of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are never severed. In this way, the Bodhisattva perpetuates and honors the Three Jewels;
all their actions are free from fault, and whatever they do is dedicated toward the benefit of all beings.
Because the gates of wisdom are thus, the three karmas are all free from flaw or blemish.

Being free from flaw and blemish, whatever manifold virtues they perform and whatever practices they carry out to teach and transform sentient beings—expounding the Dharma according to their needs—even for a single thought-moment, there is no error;
all are in accord with skillful means and wisdom, and all are directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) without being in vain. This is the Bodhisattva.
Thus, by practicing wholesome dharmas, one is at every moment fully endowed with the ten kinds of adornment.

[Treatise] Regarding the fourteenth section, from "For what reason? down to "at every moment fully endowed with the ten kinds of adornment," there are eighteen lines of scripture that clarify the section on ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed, consisting of the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-samagrī*).
The Dharma consists of six factors—first, body; second, speech; third, mind; fourth, precepts; fifth, giving; and sixth, view—which are called the six dharmas of harmonious respect.

To sow the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings is to reveal the bodhi-wisdom of principle and knowledge to all sentient beings, and to serve as a superior condition for even the slightest roots of goodness.
[Sūtra] What are the ten? They are: first, the adornment of the body, because one manifests it according to the needs of sentient beings to be disciplined;
second, the adornment of speech, because one cuts off all doubts and causes everyone to rejoice;
third, the adornment of the mind, because one enters all samādhis within a single thought-moment; fourth, the adornment of the Buddha-field, because it is entirely pure and free from all afflictions.

The adornment of radiance, because it emits boundless light that universally illuminates all sentient beings; the adornment of the assembly, because it universally gathers the assembly and causes them all to rejoice;
the adornment of supernormal powers, because it manifests with sovereign mastery according to the minds of sentient beings;
the adornment of the correct teaching, because it is able to gather all those who are wise; and the adornment of the stage of nirvāṇa, because it is accomplished in a single place.
Because the Path pervades the ten directions without exception, he skillfully explains its adornments, preaching the Dharma according to place, time, and the faculties of beings.

When a Bodhisattva has accomplished such adornments, his actions of body, speech, and mind in every thought-moment never go to waste, as they are all dedicated toward the gateway of omniscience. If there are sentient beings who see this Bodhisattva...
Sā, you should know that there is likewise no one who passes away in vain, for they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether they hear the name, make offerings, dwell together, recollect, follow [the teacher] into homelessness,
hear the teaching of the Dharma, rejoice in roots of goodness, give rise to reverence from afar, or even merely extol and praise the name.
All these beings shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. O Son of the Buddha, it is like a medicine named "Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*);

when sentient beings see it, all their poisons are eliminated. In the same way, when Bodhisattvas accomplish this Dharma, if sentient beings behold them, all the poisons of their afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished and wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) increase. O Son of the Buddha, [this is the power of] the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Bodhisattva dwelling within this Dharma diligently practices it, extinguishing the darkness of ignorance with the light of wisdom;
subduing the armies of Māra through the power of compassion; restraining all non-Buddhists through the power of great wisdom and merit;
eliminating all mental impurities and afflictions through the adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*); and accumulating all roots of goodness through the power of diligence. With purity...
Through the power of all roots of goodness in the Buddha-fields, they remain far removed from all hardships of the evil realms;

through the power of non-attachment, they purify the sphere of wisdom; and through the power of skillful means and wisdom, they bring forth all the bodhisattva stages, the pāramitās, the samādhis, the six supernormal powers, the three types of clairvoyance, and the four fearlessnesses, causing them all to be completely pure by means of everything.
The power of the wholesome dharmas is fully developed, filling all the pure lands of the Buddhas with boundless marks and signs, and the body, speech, and mind are complete with adornments.
Through the power of observation by means of mastery in wisdom, one knows that the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-dharmas of all Tathāgatas are entirely equal.
By the power of vast wisdom, one thoroughly understands the realm of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
By the power of his past vows, he manifests Buddha-lands according to those who are to be transformed, turns the Great Wheel of Dharma, and delivers immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
[Treatise] Fifteenth: What are the ten [qualities], from "and so forth" down to "delivering immeasurable and boundless sentient beings"?
There are thirty lines of sūtra that clarify how ten kinds of adornments cause those who see them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], ensuring they do not pass through this stage in vain;

these have already been explained previously, as in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" (*Daśābhijñāparivarta*), where the ten supernatural powers are fully elucidated according to the sūtra.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas diligently cultivate this Dharma, they gradually accomplish all the practices of a Bodhisattva,
even attaining equality with all Buddhas; they become great Dharma-preachers in boundless worlds,
protecting and upholding the True Dharma, being remembered and guarded by all Buddhas, receiving and maintaining the vast treasury of the Dharma, and attaining [the state of] non-...

With unhindered eloquence, they enter deeply into the Dharma gates; amidst great assemblies in boundless worlds, they manifest their bodies according to the diverse types of beings, endowed with perfect physical forms that are most excellent and peerless. With unhindered eloquence, they skillfully expound the profound Dharma;
because their voices are perfect and skillfully distributed, they enable those who hear them to enter the gate of inexhaustible wisdom.
Knowing the mental activities and afflictions of all sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for them;
because the sounds and voices he utters are fully pure, he can expound the teaching with a single voice, causing all to give rise to joy.

Because his body is upright and possesses great majestic power, no one can surpass him when he sits amidst the assembly. Because he well understands the minds of the multitude, he is able to manifest his body everywhere.
Because he skillfully expounds the Dharma, his voice is unimpeded; because he has attained mastery over the mind, he skillfully expounds the Great Dharma that cannot be thwarted;
because he has attained fearlessness, his mind is free from timidity; because he has mastery over the Dharma, none can surpass him;
because he has mastery over wisdom, none can defeat him; and because he has mastery over the *prajñāpāramitā*, the characteristics of the Dharma he expounds are as follows:
Because of mastery over eloquence that is free from contradiction, they preach the Dharma according to the inclinations of others in an uninterrupted succession;
because of mastery over dhāraṇīs, they definitively reveal the true nature of all phenomena through mastery over eloquence;
and because of mastery over great compassion, they diligently instruct sentient beings with a mind free from weariness.
Because his great compassion is sovereign, he emits radiance that subtly gladdens the hearts of all beings.
Thus seated upon a high and vast lion throne, this Bodhisattva expounds the Great Dharma;

with the exception of the Tathāgata and those great Bodhisattvas of supreme vows and wisdom, no other sentient being is able to surpass him, none can behold the crown of his head, and none can outshine him. Desiring to...
It is impossible that they could be made to retreat or be disheartened by difficult questions. O Son of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has attained such sovereign power—[The Commentary:
From "O Sixteenth Son of the Buddha" down to "such sovereign power," there are twenty-three [sections].
The *Caryā-sūtra* clarifies that when a bodhisattva first attains the mind [of enlightenment], they obtain a dharma equal to that of a Buddha and are capable of being a great Dharma-master.
[Sūtra]: Suppose there were sentient beings, one by one, filling a vast and great bodhimaṇḍa as numerous as the measure of unspeakable worlds.
The majestic power, radiance, and physical forms of all sentient beings were like those of the Bodhisattva Sovereign of the Trichiliocosm;
as soon as he manifested his body here, he was able to completely outshine this great assembly. With great compassion, he pacified their timidity;
with profound wisdom, he examined their inclinations and desires; and with fearless eloquence, he preached the Dharma for them, enabling all to [attain realization].
They give rise to joy. Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, it is because these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have accomplished the wheel of immeasurable wisdom;
they have accomplished immeasurable skillful discernment; they have accomplished the power of vast and correct mindfulness;
they have accomplished inexhaustible skillful intelligence; they have accomplished the dhāraṇī that definitively realizes the true mark of all phenomena; they have accomplished the... [infinite]...
Because of the ultimate bodhicitta, they achieve unerring and wondrous eloquence;

because of attaining profound faith and understanding through the empowerment of all Buddhas, they achieve the power of wisdom that universally enters the assemblies and places of enlightenment of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and because of knowing that all Buddhas of the three periods of time share one and the same nature, they achieve a pure mind.
Because they possess the wisdom of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and the wisdom of the great vows of all Bodhisattvas,
they are able to act as great Dharma masters to expound the treasury of the true Dharma of all Buddhas and to protect and uphold it.
[Treatise] Seventeenth: Suppose there were an unspeakably vast *bodhimaṇḍa* world-system;

from this point downward, up to the section on "protecting and upholding the Dharma," there are thirteen lines and a half of scripture clarifying the stage of fearlessness in the assembly, mastery in preaching the Dharma, and the body being unobscured by others.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, wishing to restate its meaning, received the Buddha’s spiritual power and spoke these verses.
[Śāstra] From "At that time" onwards, the following one line of sūtra clarifies the section where Dharmamati praises the Dharma in verse.

[Sūtra] With the mind abiding in bodhi, one accumulates all merits; Always being heedful, one plants firm wisdom, and with right mindfulness, the mind never forgets. All Buddhas of the ten directions rejoice;
With a firm resolve for the Dharma, one exerts oneself diligently, Without reliance on the world and without fear of retreat.
Entering the profound Dharma through the practice of non-contention, all the Buddhas of the ten directions rejoice;
once the Buddhas have rejoiced, he fortifies his diligence and practices the dharmas of merit, wisdom, and the aids to the Path.
Entering the various stages (*bhūmi*), he purifies all his conduct and fulfills the vows spoken by the Tathāgata.

Thus practicing, one attains the sublime Dharma; having attained the Dharma, one bestows it upon all beings according to their inclinations and faculties, expounding it for them in a manner that accords with what is appropriate.
When a bodhisattva expounds the Dharma for others, they do not abandon their own practice of the perfections.
Having already perfected the path of the pāramitās, they constantly rescue all sentient beings from the ocean of existence;
day and night they practice with diligence and without weariness, ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed.
All the pure and white dharmas they practice are entirely dedicated toward the stage of the Tathāgata.
The various virtuous deeds cultivated by Bodhisattvas are universally for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment,
causing them to shatter darkness and extinguish afflictions; by subduing the armies of Māra and attaining perfect enlightenment,
they thus practice until they obtain the Buddha-wisdom and enter deeply into the Tathāgata’s treasury of the True Dharma.
Acting as a great Dharma Master, you expound the wondrous Dharma, Like nectar that is sprinkled everywhere;
With compassion and pity for all, you know the mental activities of sentient beings without exception.
According to their inclinations, you reveal and elucidate The infinite and boundless teachings of the Buddhas.
In his advancing and halting he is as calm and slow as an elephant king; In his courage and fearlessness he is like a lion;
Unmoving as a mountain, his wisdom is like the ocean; He is also like a great rain that dispels all heat.
[Commentary] Nineteenth: Thus, in praising the Dharma with verses, there are twenty lines of verse, with two lines forming each stanza.
The verses are as they appear in the text; their meaning is self-evident and is praised according to the words.
[Sūtra] When the Bodhisattva Dharmamati had spoken these verses, the Tathāgata rejoiced and the great assembly practiced them accordingly.

[Treatise] The twentieth section, the final line of the sutra, clarifies the "Chapter on the Great Assembly Hearing the Dharma with Joy and Practicing It in Accordance," the fourth assembly, which expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices in the Yāma Heaven.
This assembly, wherein [the Buddha] ascends to the Yāma Heaven, constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From the "Verse of Praise" (*Gāthā-stotra*) onwards is the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*). The shaking of the earth and the arising of offerings constitute the dissemination (*prabhāva*).
General Exposition. Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven.
[Treatise] In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed by means of three sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the chapter... [text continues].
Regarding the intent of the coming [of this chapter], there are three parts; first, the explanation of the title of the chapter. Why is it called the "Palace of the Yāma Heaven"?
It is because the location is used to symbolize the Dharma. This heaven is named the "Time-Portion Heaven" (*Kāmadhātu-deva*);

as this heaven has neither sun nor moon, nor the alternation of darkness and light, but takes the opening of the lotus flowers as day and their closing as night, it is therefore called the Time-Portion Heaven. Thus, it serves as a symbolic representation.
In the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices, one must know the proper time to respond to and transform sentient beings; therefore, it is essential not to fail to recognize the timing.
Thus, the divisions of time are used to represent the knowledge of faculties (*indriya*) and to correspond to the sūtras, for one must not act with a single-minded rigidity.

One must discern whether a person belongs to the lineage of humans and devas, or to the lineages of the two vehicles, the three vehicles, or the one vehicle, so that one may know by which roots of goodness they can be guided and led.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Yāma-deva) represents the practice that must be performed with knowledge of the proper timing;
Mount Sumeru represents the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi), clarifying that one ascends from faith, leaving behind the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana);

it further represents the initial ascent to the summit of the Dharma within the stages of the Ten Abodes, reaching the point where characteristics are exhausted; and it also represents the central position of Mount Sumeru within the great [cosmos].
Rising eighty-four thousand yojanas above the sea cannot be achieved by climbing with hands and feet;
thus, it is clear that the first stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) is not reached through the攀緣 (*ālambana*) of intentional seeking or meditative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*).

It is because there is no thought—being utterly vast and unconditioned—that wisdom responds to the myriad dharmas; only when one is without dependence can one ascend. These are the ten practices (*daśacaryā*).
The station of Yāma dwells clearly supported by emptiness and is not connected with the human realm;

the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are likewise so, for they act according to the dharma of emptiness and benefit worldly beings when the time is right. Therefore, it is represented by being situated in this heaven.
In Tuṣita Heaven, the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are taught to clarify that its location is among the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, this heaven clarifies the contentment found in celestial bliss; it serves as a symbol for the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), which employ correct wisdom to engage with the mundane world for the benefit of living beings through the gateway of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), thereby providing aid to all while remaining free from craving or seeking regarding any sensory objects. This heaven is established as the symbolic representation for this stage.
As for the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) upon ascending to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*): it signifies transcendence.
Passing beyond the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*) to manifest at the limit of the desire realm signifies mastery over the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Ascending from the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations to the summit of the desire realm signifies that the mind of transformation has reached the limit of desire; thus, one ascends to the third dhyāna to preach the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* Dharma-gate.
This clarifies that the practices of Samantabhadra are fulfilled, signifying that through the joy of these practices, one brings infinite sentient beings to joy. Furthermore—
The manifestation of the fourth dhyāna as the stage of Buddhahood is established here in this manner merely to represent the progression and regression of practice;
however, each instance of its principle and wisdom is all-pervasive and devoid of coming or going.
For this reason, it is said that without departing from the Bodhimanda or the Hall of Universal Radiance, one ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, and other heavens.
The third dhyāna surpasses the first and second dhyānas because its stages are twice as superior; this particular assembly has not yet appeared in previous texts.

This is the *Sūtra on the Original Karma of the Garland* (*Śrī-mālā-deśanā-sūtra*), in which the Tathāgata, leading the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, speaks at the foot of the Bodhi tree regarding how he first attained perfect enlightenment beneath this very tree in the past and preached the Dharma.
Because the *Dhātu-sūtra* enumerates each stage sequentially up to the third dhyāna, this [section] concerns the Yāma Heaven.

Regarding the purpose of the second chapter, "The Explanation of the Ten Practices" (*Daśa-caryā-vyākhyāna*): the preceding section clarified the advancement through the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) by ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru;
this section clarifies the advancement through the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) by reaching the Yāma Heaven. Consequently, this chapter follows in sequence.
Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the text, the major significance therein is divided into two parts: first, a general outline of the sūtra’s meaning;
second, the word-by-word explanation.
[Sūtra] At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, in each of the four continents within every world-system throughout the ten directions...
In Jambudvīpa and upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, all saw the Tathāgata dwelling amidst the assemblies;
those bodhisattvas, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, all preached the Dharma, each thinking that they were constantly in the presence of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not leave the foot of any of the bodhi trees or the summit of Mount Sumeru, yet he appeared before them.
In the Palace of the Yāma Heaven, within the Hall of Jewel Adornments, the King of the Yāma Heaven saw the Buddha approaching from afar;
he immediately employed his supernatural powers to manifest within that hall a lion throne of precious lotus-womb,
adorned with one million tiers, encircled by one million golden nets, and draped with one million canopies of flowers and one million canopies of garlands.

A million incense canopies and a million jewel canopies covered it from above; likewise, a million flower canopies, garland canopies, incense canopies, and jewel canopies were arranged in rows all around.

A million rays of light shone forth in illumination, while a million kings of the Yāma Heaven prostrated themselves in reverent worship, a million Brahmā kings leaped for joy, and a million bodhisattvas raised their voices in praise.
A hundred thousand celestial musical instruments were played, each producing a continuous succession of a hundred thousand kinds of Dharma sounds;
there were clouds of a hundred thousand kinds of flowers, clouds of a hundred thousand kinds of garlands, clouds of a hundred thousand kinds of ornaments, clouds of a hundred thousand kinds of robes,
and clouds of a hundred thousand kinds of mani-jewels, all surrounding and completely covering [the assembly], radiating brilliant light born from a hundred thousand kinds of roots of goodness.
It is sustained by the protection of ten million buddhas; it increases ten million kinds of merit;
it is purified by ten million kinds of profound resolve and ten million kinds of vows; it is brought forth by ten million kinds of practices;
it is established by ten million kinds of dharmas; and it manifests through ten million kinds of supernormal powers, constantly producing ten million [transformations].

When he manifested all phenomena through various sounds and voices, that celestial king prepared a seat and, bowing his body with palms joined in reverence and respect toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed the Buddha, saying: "Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata!
Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! We pray only that you will take pity on us and dwell in this palace. Then the Buddha accepted the invitation.
As it was in this palace of jewels, so it was in all the ten directions.
At that time, the Heavenly King, recollecting the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas, spoke these verses by the power of the Buddha’s majesty:
The Tathāgata Yaśas, renowned throughout the ten directions, Is the most supreme among all auspicious things;
he once entered this maṇi palace, And for this reason, this place is the most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Ratnarāja, the Lamp of the World, Is the most supreme among all auspicious things.
He once entered this pure hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Suvimalanetra beholds it without obstruction; among all that is auspicious, it is supreme.
He once entered this adorned hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara illuminates the world; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
He once entered this most excellent palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata benefits the world; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
He once entered this stainless palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Suprabuddha, who has no teacher and is supreme among all that is auspicious, Once entered this precious incense palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Jitendriya, the Lamp of the World, supreme among all auspicious things—he once entered this Hall of Exquisite Fragrance;

therefore, this place is most auspicious. The Tathāgata Anihata, the Bull among Orators, supreme among all auspicious things—[he once entered this Hall of Exquisite Fragrance; therefore, this place is most auspicious].
He once entered this Hall of the Universal Eye; therefore, this place is most auspicious and unsurpassed.
The Tathāgata, endowed with all virtues, is the supreme among all that is auspicious;
he once entered this Hall of Excellent Adornment; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Duṣkaracaryā benefits the world; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
He once entered this Hall of Universal Adornment; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In this world-system, the King of the Yāma Heaven, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, recollects the merits of the Buddhas of the past.
The celestial kings of the Yāma heaven throughout the worlds of the ten directions likewise all extolled the Buddha’s merits in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Palace Adorned with Maṇi Jewels and sat cross-legged upon a lion throne within a treasury of precious lotuses.
Suddenly, this palace became vast and spacious, as expansive as the dwellings of all those heavenly hosts.
The worlds of the ten directions are all likewise so.
[Treatise] Regarding the first major structural division of the meaning of this sūtra: within these forty-nine lines of scripture comprising this chapter, they are divided into ten sections.
The first begins from "At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata" and extends down to "constantly facing."

The Buddha has three and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the Tathāgata is seen simultaneously by all in the ten directions without leaving his original location, which is divided into two parts:

first, from "At that time" onwards until the "Palace of Precious Adornments," comprising approximately two lines of scripture, clarifies that without leaving the Universal Radiance Hall at every site of enlightenment throughout the ten directions, he ascends to the Yāma Heaven; second, the section beginning with "At that time in the Yāma... [is the third part].
From the time the Heavenly King had prepared his seat down to the point where the Heavenly King,

seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, adorned his seat through transformation and paid homage— this section spanning one folio and four lines and a half clarifies the timing. From the time the Heavenly King turned toward the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, down to his arrival at this palace— this section spanning two folios and two lines and a half clarifies the Heavenly King’s [actions].
The King invited the Buddha to enter the hall and ascend the seat; this is divided into five sections. After the Buddha accepted the invitation, [the narrative] down to the end is also like this;
there may be one line of sutra clarifying that the Tathāgata’s acceptance of the invitation universally applies to all ten directions. This constitutes the sixth section.
At that time, from the passage beginning with "The Heavenly Kings" down to one and a half lines of sutra, it clarifies how the Heavenly Kings recalled their past causes.

The section on praising the Buddha in verse consists of seven parts. Within the verses, there are twenty lines of verse that praise the ten Tathāgatas who have previously entered this celestial palace.

This constitutes the eighth part. From "In this world" below, down to the praise of the Buddha’s merits, there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how the ten directions likewise praised the Buddha at one and the same time. This constitutes the ninth part. At that time, the World-Honored One...
From this point downward, the two and a half lines of sūtra clarify how the Tathāgata accepted the invitation to enter the hall, which was vast and spacious;
this section is repeated in the same manner for all ten directions. This concludes the summary of the ten directions being identical in this respect.
Regarding the second part, the exegesis of the text according to its phrasing: first, from "At that time" down to "constantly facing."

Because the Buddha’s radiance constantly and universally pervades all places throughout the ten directions without increase or decrease, it is said that he does not depart from the summit of Mount Sumeru at the Bodhi tree to ascend to the Yāma Heaven; this clarifies that his wisdom pervades all places while he manifests his body without coming or going.
Thus, "seeing the Buddha approaching from afar" clarifies the transition from the stage of the Ten Abidings toward the stage of the Ten Practices.

Therefore, the transformation of the seat by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) clarifies that the basis of practice is established through wisdom that relies upon emptiness, wherein neither subject nor object exists;
thus, the seat symbolizes practice. It is called the "Lotus" because it represents non-conceptual practice (*anabhisaṃskāra-caryā*) that achieves freedom from all defilement and attachment.
"Treasury" (*kośa*) has the meaning of containment; it clarifies that the practice of non-practice contains and stores all virtues.
The lion symbolizes fearlessness; because one dwells within birth and death with the wisdom and principle of non-action (*wuwei*), one is fearless.

Thus, this "belonging-to-the-master" compound is designated as the seat. The term "one million tiers" clarifies the stages of progression through the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten thousand [thousand] practices, and the one million [practices], illustrating the ascending levels according to their respective positions. As for the "one million golden nets forming an interlaced lattice," it signifies...
This stage clarifies that one transforms sentient beings through the net of practice and the net of teaching; therefore, this constitutes the fruit of reliance obtained as retribution.
The "ten abodes," "ten thousand," and "one million" of the ten practices clarify ascending progress.

The flower garlands, fragrant jewels, and four kinds of canopies clarify that one gathers in and encompasses sentient beings through the skillful means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Furthermore, there are the four kinds of canopies.

It is revealed that because he covers and protects sentient beings with the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he illuminates them with a million rays of light;
it is revealed that because he observes their faculties with the eye of wisdom and gathers them in through transformation, he is the "Lord of Heaven," whose conduct is sovereign;
"reverently prostrating" signifies that his practice is free from pride; and "the Brahmā King leaping for joy" signifies purity.
"Practicing for the benefit of sentient beings" means that upon seeing those who beg, one rejoices without weariness.

"Praised by a million bodhisattvas" clarifies that through practice one rescues all things, causing the multitude of sages to rejoice and offer praise. "The music of celestial instruments plays" clarifies the fruit summoned by being skillful in preaching the Dharma.
"The four kinds of clouds cover the mundane world with compassion" refers to what was previously called a "canopy."
The "four kinds of clouds" are explained as being so named because they cover and nurture according to the size of the vessels [of sentient beings];
likewise, the "maṇi clouds" are so named because they illuminate and bestow benefits according to the capacity of the faculties.

The phrase "produced from ten million roots of goodness" indicates that all the aforementioned adornments are produced by the roots of goodness within the course of practice; thus, when practice is able to benefit others and accumulate merit, one attains the state of all Buddhas.
"Having been adorned by the protection of all merits," and so forth, may be understood according to the text. Regarding the phrase "Welcome, Sugata":
"Sugata" means one who has well extinguished all evils, sufferings, and calamities; "Gata" means one who has crossed over sentient beings and is free from bondage.

When the Buddha accepted the invitation and ascended the seat, it clarifies that he was advancing upward and entering the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). The above [sections] are viewed in relation to the Buddha’s own virtues throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the statement "From the All-Pervasive One, now performing ascent and descent," this refers generally to the progress, cultivation, advancement, and regression of sentient beings.

Within these twenty verses, the ten Buddhas are praised for having previously entered this hall; this clarifies that the principle and wisdom of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*) entered now are no different from those of antiquity.
These ten Tathāgatas are titles established according to the advancement achieved through their respective practices.
The ascent to the summit of Mount Sumeru during the stage of the Ten Abodes, as well as the names of the ten Tathāgatas, likewise correspond to the stages and accord with ancient titles;
this clarifies that the Dharma entered is no different across all Buddhas of the past and present.

Thus, within the stage of the Ten Abodes, when Śakra, Lord of Devas, sees the Buddha approaching from afar atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, he immediately prepares the Universal Radiance Hall within his palace.

The lion throne of the Treasury of Illumination clarifies that, at the very beginning of entering into the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one is established within the Universal Radiance Treasury by means of the gateway of the Samādhi of Skillful Means; this is because it clarifies that the treasury of the Dharma-realm is illuminated by wisdom.
Thus, at the stage of these ten practices, the Heavenly King of the Time-Interval sees the Buddha approaching from afar and transforms himself into jewels.

The "Lotus Lion Throne" clarifies that by means of the flowers of practice, one establishes the net of the teaching to filter all sentient beings and cause them to enter the treasury of the Tathāgata’s realm of wisdom; thus, the lotus symbolizes the meaning of non-attachment in practice.
The "Transformation Throne" clarifies the essence of practice, which is established upon the Dharma-body of emptiness through the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). So it is said.

It is performed as an emanation. By means of what is expressed here, the final five lines of the sutra conclude that the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously praise the Tathāgata’s entry into the hall;

that the hall encompasses all, like the abode of heaven, clarifies that by entering the stage and ascending through one's own wisdom, one attains vast capacity, and only then does one come to know the realm of the Buddha.
*The Combined Commentary on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Thirty-Six.

Phonetic Transcriptions: Pí (pronounced as *pí*). Juàn (pronounced as *qú juǎn*). Qū (pronounced as *qiū yú*). Chuǎn (pronounced as *chāng ruǎn*). Shěn (pronounced as *shì rěn*). Tuì (pronounced as *tā nèi*). Lì (pronounced as *lì zhì*).
Qiè (hú jiā qiè). Xiá (hú jiā qiè). Diàn (dīng niàn qiè). Lóng (lì zhòng qiè). Hù (pronounced as the sound hù). Cuò (qī gè qiè).
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament Scripture, Fascicle Thirty-Seven.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tōngxuan, a Layman of Fāngshān in Tàiyuán during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, Collating the Sūtras and Composing the Commentary, Chapter Twenty:
Verses of Praise in the Night-Wandering Heaven Palace (Yāma-deva-rāja-bhavana-gāthā-stotra-parivarta).
[Commentary] In order to explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, an explanation of the chapter title; second, an explanation of the chapter [content].
Regarding the threefold intention for the coming [of this chapter], the first part, the explanation of the title of the chapter:
it clarifies that having ascended to the palace of the Yāma Heaven, the Dharma of the Ten Practices is being taught.

In this chapter, the assembly of ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Guṇakusuma, each uses verses to collectively praise the Dharma of their respective stages; therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Verses of Praise."

Second, regarding the purpose for the arrival of this chapter on "Explanation": it clarifies that before one intends to explain the dharma of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), it is first necessary to offer a general praise in verse of the causal and resultant dharma-gates within those ten practices; therefore, this chapter must arrive.

If these causal and resultant dharmas of the practices were not first presented, upon what would the ten practices depend for their accomplishment? Third, regarding the word-by-word explanation of the meaning: in this [chapter]...
Within this chapter, there is a twofold analysis: first, a general outline of the meaning of the sutra; second, an explanation following the text.
Regarding the first, the general outline of the meaning of the sutra, it is divided into five sections.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from worlds outside as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions arrived together with a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, and Bodhisattva Forest of Victory.

The Bodhisattva Forest of Fearlessness, the Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Modesty, the Bodhisattva Forest of Diligence, the Bodhisattva Forest of Power, the Bodhisattva Forest of Practice, the Bodhisattva Forest of Awakening, and the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom. These are the lands from which these bodhisattvas have come:
namely, the world of Kind Wisdom, the world of Banner Wisdom, the world of Jewel Wisdom, the world of Supreme Wisdom, and the world of Lamp Wisdom.
In the world of Wisdom, the world of Vajra-Wisdom, the world of Peaceful Wisdom, the world of Solar Wisdom, the world of Pure Wisdom, and the world of Brahma-Wisdom—
these bodhisattvas each cultivated the pure conduct of brahmacarya in the presence of Buddhas, namely: the Buddha Constantly Abiding Eye,
the Buddha Unsurpassed Eye, the Buddha Non-Abiding Eye, the Buddha Immovable Eye, the Buddha Celestial Eye, and the Buddha Liberation.
The Buddha Netra, the Buddha Netravicārin, the Buddha Netraprabhāsa, the Buddha Netrottama, and the Buddha Nīlanetra—
when these bodhisattvas had arrived at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and, facing their respective directions,
each miraculously manifested a lion throne made of maṇi-jewels; upon these thrones, they sat cross-legged.

[Treatise] First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha" down to "sat cross-legged," there are thirteen and a half lines of scripture which clarify the section on the gathering of the ten bodhisattvas,
such as Guṇakusuma (Forest of Merits), according to their respective stages, as well as their own practices and the causes and fruits of the Buddhas.
Second, regarding the interpretation of the meaning according to the text, within this section the meaning is divided as follows:
This consists of three parts: first, the explanation of the name "Bodhisattva" and its correlation with the causes and effects of progressive cultivation according to the stages;
second, the explanation of the meaning of the distance between buddha-lands; and third, the explanation of how Bodhisattvas each share the same name while pervading everywhere.

Regarding the first—explaining the name "Bodhisattva" and its correlation with the causes and effects of progressive cultivation according to the stages—there are approximately ten types of cause and effect.
Regarding the first, the Bodhisattva Guṇakānanarāja (King of the Forest of Virtues):

because he has been born into the family of Buddha-wisdom within the stage of the Ten Abodes, his names are Dharmamati (Dharma-Wisdom) and Arthamati (Wealth-Wisdom), among others. This stage clarifies that through the practice of wisdom, the two retributions of merit and wisdom become vast and manifold;
thus, it is named after a "forest" (*kānana*). Furthermore, "forest" carries the meanings of being vast and manifold, providing shelter and shade, and being well-ordered.
The meaning of "adornment" (*vyūha*) is that the trunk, branches, twigs, flowers, leaves, and fruits mutually support one another.
This clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattvas at the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) who adorn the branches of the myriad practices with the wisdom of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva-prajñā*).

Taking great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their leaves, they provide shade and shelter to gather in and transform all sentient beings, causing the flowers and fruits of enlightenment for both self and others to fully blossom and ripen. It is like a river or marshland...
Just as various birds flock to a forest, so do many people rely on one who practices [the path]. For this reason, the ten practices of a bodhisattva are designated by the name "Forest.
This corresponds to the gate of the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) presided over by the practice of Joy (*pramuditā*).

It is like the first spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) named Sudarśana in the section on the ten practices of Sudhana, who was walking to and fro within a forest; it is just like that. The name of the country is...
Regarding the "three eyes": at this stage, the fruition of Buddhahood is designated as the "eye.

As for the land named "Intimate Wisdom" (*Sākhya*), it clarifies that these ten practices are produced directly from the Buddha’s wisdom as their cause, and they also constantly act as a source of intimacy for all sentient beings.
The fruition of Buddhahood is designated as the "Eternally Abiding Eye," for the Buddha is born directly from the Buddha’s wisdom.
Therefore, because all faculties of knowledge are sharpened for the mundane, they directly cause one to attain the eye of wisdom that perceives the eternal abiding;

thus it clarifies that one spontaneously attains the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom. Furthermore, because benefiting sentient beings also causes others to attain the eye of wisdom, it clarifies that the wisdom of observing faculties and benefiting beings through the Tathāgata’s wisdom is precisely the fruit of Buddhahood in its own stage. This is the merit.

The Forest of Virtue (Śīlavana) represents the person who practices the conduct to be manifested; the World of Intimate Wisdom (Pratyakṣajñāna-loka) is the cause of the wisdom practiced in that stage;
and the Buddha Constantly Abiding Eye (Nityapratyakṣa-buddha) is the fruit of knowing the faculties and insights in that stage.
Being in correspondence with fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), he is named the Buddha Constantly Abiding Eye. Second is the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom (Prajñāvana), who possesses clear intelligence.

Wisdom is like a vast forest because it possesses manifold meanings; therefore, this is the practice of benefiting others. By means of wisdom, one benefits all sentient beings so that they do not become deluded.
One practices the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), for at this stage, wisdom constitutes the essence of ethical discipline.
This is as in the case of the spiritual friend Śakradeva-kumāra among the Ten Practices of the youth Sudhana, who practiced the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline.
The *pāramitā* of wisdom employs the methods of calculation, mutual signs, and seals to establish the auspicious and inauspicious locations of villages, camps, cities, and towns;
this is because it is wisdom. Among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the Dharma-body serves as the essence of the precepts, while within these ten practices, wisdom serves as the essence of the precepts.
Therefore, the world-realm "Banner of Wisdom" is the cause of the practice undertaken through wisdom.
Because the essence of the precepts does not waver within the cycle of birth and death, the Buddha of Unsurpassed Vision is the fruit of what is practiced;
for he knows the faculties [of beings] with the eye of wisdom, as none other is superior. Third is the Bodhisattva Forest of Victory:

this is the master of the practice of non-opposition, presiding over the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Among all practices, the practice of patience is foremost; there is no [practice] prior to it.
Because patience does not constitute [the completion of] practice, he is titled the Bodhisattva Vanavāsin (Forest-Dweller).
Just as the youth Sudhana, within this stage, has a spiritual friend who is an upāsikā named Samantaguptā;

she fully embodies the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and subsumes all practices, with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity all contained therein. This clarifies that the upāsikā represents the practice of kindness and compassion.

Furthermore, wearing plain clothing and disheveling the hair represents the state of practicing restraint and patience; having four doors open in his single chamber symbolizes the Four Means of Integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) for the compassionate nurturing of sentient beings.
The ten thousand female attendants signify the perfection of the ten thousand practices (*daśasāhasra-pratipatti*).

Using a single small vessel to provide inexhaustible wisdom represents the abandonment of arrogance and self-exaltation, as well as the boundlessness of the Four Means of Integration; thus, each point is made clear.
Because the *pāramitās* mutually contain and function within one another, the Bodhisattva Śreṇika is one who practices these practices;
the world-realm Ratnamati is the Dharma that is cultivated therein. It is clarified that patience (*kṣānti*) is the treasure among all practices because it is worthy of honor and value;
thus, the Buddha Aniketacakṣus is the fruit of Buddhahood within patience itself. This clarifies that although one practices the conduct of patience, [one does not abide therein].
This is the fourth fearlessness: the Bodhisattva Forest of Constant Practice. He clearly practices constant diligence;
thus, within birth and death, he benefits humans and devas, which is his fearlessness. He presides over conduct that is never yielding or discouraged.

By means of wisdom, he knows the proper time, knows the Dharma, and knows the faculties of beings. He does not falter in his service to others nor does he stagnate in his achievements; therefore, he is like Sudhana.
The wise layman, the Good Spiritual Friend (kalyāṇamitra), is the Good Spiritual Friend within this stage.
Because he benefits sentient beings through his wisdom, he acts without yielding or discouragement; thus, he dwells in the city of Mahodaya, which signifies the meaning of diligence.
His presence in the markets and thoroughfares signifies that his benefit is vast, manifold, and limitless; therefore, one should maintain focused mindfulness for even a brief moment.
Because of the application of mental attention (*manasikāra*), one gazes upward at empty space; whatever things are required to benefit sentient beings all descend from that emptiness.
This is because clear wisdom is like space, as it should accord with the mindfulness of wisdom; thus, emptiness is the foundation of wisdom, for wisdom is not different from emptiness.
Therefore, when contemplating emptiness, objects appear in accordance with wisdom. Consequently, emptiness is the root of all phenomena.
This contemplation clarifies that all merits arise collectively from the wisdom of emptiness;
the Bodhisattva Fearless Forest (*Abhayavana*) is one who practices the conduct of this stage; the World of Supreme Wisdom (*Jñānavara*) is the method of cultivation for this stage;
and the Buddha Immovable Eye (*Acalanetra*) is the fruit of Buddhahood within this stage. Thus, it clarifies the stage of diligence, which does not change according to external objects.
Therefore, the Buddha is named "Immovable Eye" because he is unmoved by sense objects; this is called the fifth perfection, diligence.
The Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse is the master of conduct free from delusion and confusion. He practices dhyāna endowed with shame and remorse;
through dhyāna-concentration, wisdom is generated, and thus he practices conduct free from delusion and confusion, just like his spiritual friend Ratnacūḍa.
The Elder is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) within this stage. While in the midst of the marketplace, he is clear in his conduct and possesses the essence of meditative concentration;
though amidst clamor, he is ever tranquil. Taking Sudhana by the hand, he leads him to his residence—this signifies clear guidance and reception.
He guides and receives [Sudhana] within the marketplace of birth and death to lead him toward the fruit of wisdom; thus, through clarity, one contemplates the fruit to know its cause.
That dwelling is adorned with jewels, consisting of ten stories and eight gates; the courtyard has eight gates and the pavilion has ten stories.
The eight gates clarify the Eightfold Noble Path, and the ten-story pavilion represents the retribution of the ten *pāramitās*, corresponding exactly to the practice of the ten degrees.
Arranged from bottom to top, they naturally possess their own laws, which will be clarified in the text below. This is based on the essence of *dhyāna*.
The Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse (*Hrī-apatrāpya-vana*) who gathers all myriad practices is the person who cultivates practice at this stage.
The Lamp-Wisdom World (*Dīpa-prajñā-loka*) is the dharma that is practiced; because concentration can give rise to the illumination of wisdom that shines upon things, the world is named "Lamp.
The Buddha of Heavenly Eye (*Divya-cakṣus-buddha*) is the fruit of Buddhahood at this stage; because concentration can purify all the faculties (*indriya*), [he is so named].
The sixth is the Bodhisattva Forest of Diligence, whose name is Buddha Celestial Eye. This is the gate of the Perfection of Wisdom belonging to the Lord of the Practice of Good Manifestation.
Because he benefits all sentient beings by means of the Perfection of Wisdom and the skillful manifestation of all practices, he is named Forest of Diligence.
Just as with Sudhana, the spiritual friend in this stage is the Elder Universal Eye, who clearly manifests the initial salvation.
After giving away his body and life, he next bestowed food and drink and subsequently preached the Dharma to each according to their faculties, so that they achieved clear wisdom;
thus, the Forest of Diligence (*Vīryavana*) is the practitioner, while the World of Vajra-Wisdom (*Vajrajñānaloka*) is the Dharma of practice.
Because clear wisdom destroys afflictions, it is called "vajra," and the Buddha of the Eye of Liberation is the Buddha of this stage.
The Bodhisattva Phala-saptama-bala-vana (Fruit Seventh Power Forest) is the master of unattached practice and the light of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
By means of skillful means, he dwells in the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, conforming to their conduct and flowing along with them while remaining unattached in the world;

thus he accomplishes the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and for this reason he is called "Power Forest. Because he enters the mundane world through truth and remains undefiled by the fetters (*saṃyojana*), he is named "Power Forest. As it is said:
Sudhana, at this stage, the spiritual friend is named King Never-Weary. To practice great compassion, he manifests his own body to perform various unwholesome acts;
he then transforms his own body again to pursue, seize, punish, or even sever the life-force of those who must be disciplined through suffering.
He does so to cause sentient beings to truly fear and abandon evil, and to protect sentient beings with love, never abandoning them.
The Bodhisattva named Forest of the Power of Insatiable Resolve is the person who practices these deeds; the World of Peaceful Wisdom (*Anurāga-buddhi*) is the Dharma that is cultivated;
and the Buddha named Eye of Thorough Certainty (*Suviniścita-cakṣus*) is the fruit of this stage.

Because this stage constitutes the gateway to the accomplishment of great compassion, it is called the World of Peaceful Wisdom (*Anurāga-loka*); the name of the Buddha is derived from his bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings.
The One with the Eye of Thorough Discernment (Viniścita-cakṣus) knows with precise discernment which dharma should be used to transform sentient beings, and thus only then proceeds to subdue them.
The Bodhisattva Forest of the Eighth Practice is the master of the practice that is "difficult to attain.
Because this stage of wisdom is difficult to ascend, it is called "difficult to attain" yet "capable of being attained," just like the youth Sudhana.

In this stage, the King of Spiritual Friends is named Great Light; he is the eighth wisdom that fulfills great vows according to the inclinations of sentient beings, performing vast benefit by universally bestowing upon all beings the requisites for worldly happiness and the jewel of omniscience.
The Bodhisattva who can practice these deeds is Forest of Conduct, and the world where he cultivates them is Solar Wisdom.
The essence of wisdom in this stage increases and becomes luminous; the world is named Sun-Wisdom-Luminous-Phase-Eye, and the Buddha is the Sun-Wisdom-Luminous-Phase-Eye Buddha.
This is the fruit of this stage, and because the essence of wisdom in this stage increases and becomes luminous, the name of the Buddha-fruit is the Sun-Wisdom-Luminous-Phase-Eye Buddha.

The ninth is the Bodhisattva Forest-of-Awakening (Jue-lin). This is the power of the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-caryā*), namely the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). As in the case of Sudhana, this is the goodness of this stage.
The laywoman (upāsikā) named Wisdom Immovable is the ninth stage of the Dharma Master. Why is she in a female body?
It is because when one occupies the stage of a Dharma Master who is learned in the fields of knowledge, one must be chaste, compassionate, and gentle; thus, she is represented by a woman.

Since this woman first resolved her mind [on enlightenment], it has been as many eons as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa; from the time she first resolved her mind, not a single thought of the five [desires] has arisen in her heart.
The desire for clear, pure, compassionate, and gentle thoughts—these are the virtues of a Dharma teacher.
For this reason, this Bodhisattva is named Jue Lin Zhu (Forest of Awakening Sovereign). The *pāramitā* of Forest of Awakening is the person who practices the practice;
the World of Pure Wisdom is the method of cultivation; and the Buddha Most Supreme Eye is that which is cultivated.
Because the fruit is purified by wisdom, the Buddha is called the Supreme Eye. The tenth stage, the Forest of Wisdom, is so named because the Bodhisattva practices true wisdom;
thus, it presides over the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). This correspondence between name and position can be understood through the example of Sudhana:
at this stage, his spiritual friend is a renunciant non-Buddhist ascetic named Viśvāmitra, who has attained mastery over the knowledge of wisdom.
One who can harmonize with false views and encompass all such views is the realm of the Three Thousand Worlds;
the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths are those for whom I act as the Forest of Wisdom Bodhisattva. The World of Brahma-Wisdom is the Dharma to be cultivated;
the Buddha Azure-Eyed Eye is the fruit of this stage; and "Azure" refers to the Ten Practices.

Because wisdom is the ultimate fulfillment of oneness and the pinnacle of luminous, pure illumination, the second explanation concerns the meaning of the distance and proximity of buddha-fields (*kṣetra*).

The Sūtra says: "From each of the ten directions, accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, they come from worlds beyond lands as numerous as the atoms within one hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions."
Regarding the assembly, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* speaks of "the atoms of a hundred buddha-fields," while this text refers to "one hundred thousand.

This clarifies the expansion of ascending wisdom: the deluded mind and its various objects are measured by the quantity of atoms (*rajas*), and the abode of deluded attachment is termed a "land" (*kṣetra*).
As the mind turns according to objects, these are called "various lands"; when external attachment is extinguished, it is called "wisdom."
The name "Bodhisattva" (Coming-to-know Wisdom) signifies that their wisdom pervades all realms without anything it does not reach; thus they are so titled. This applies to each and every Bodhisattva.
Taken collectively, this clarifies that while the mind is deluded, its wisdom reaches everywhere. Third, the explanation of why each is individually called a "Bodhisattva" who pervades all:
this clarifies that when the mind is deluded, it is obscured by various objects and sensory fields; because ignorance is vast and manifold, when the mind awakens, its wisdom penetrates all.
Since the All-Knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) that pervades the distant oceans of lands does not differ in its vision, each respective name and title is universally pervasive.
When deluded, there is no object that is not confused; once awakened, there is no object that is not known.

These Bodhisattvas then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet to show their reverence. As they ascended the seat, the transformation-seat of the *maṇi* treasury appeared, representing the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
Abiding in birth and death while transforming sentient beings, their conduct is eternally stainless; thus, the "mani seat" refers to the jewel free from defilement (*vimala-ratna*).

"Treasury" (*kośa*) carries the meaning of containment or storage, and "lion" (*siṃha*) signifies fearlessness. This clarifies that while ordinary conduct is subject to defilement, the conduct of the sages is stainless.
Since the term "lion" is established based on its primary referent (*adhipati-nirukti*), it collectively elucidates the wisdom and virtue of the practitioner.
The Method of Practice.
[Sūtra] Just as the bodhisattvas from the Yāma Heaven have come to gather in this world, so it is in all worlds;
the names of the Tathāgatas in those worlds and among those bodhisattvas are all identical and without distinction.

[Treatise] Second: From this world downward, as far as the "all are equal and without distinction," this section of the sūtra describes, in two parallel passages, the gathering of bodhisattvas from all the worlds of the ten directions.

[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the tops of his two feet hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light of wondrous colors, which universally illumined all worlds throughout the ten directions;
within the palaces of the Yāma Heaven, the Buddhas and their great assemblies were all clearly manifested.
[Treatise] Third: From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "there was none who did not see it," these two lines of scripture clarify the section on the location where the light was emitted.
Regarding the passage "at that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light from his two feet":

the light emitted from the wheels on the soles of the feet pertains to the Ten Faiths, while the light emitted from the tips of the toes pertains to the Ten Abidings. These constitute the ten [points].
Regarding the "middle of the practice," this refers to the soles of the feet; it signifies ascending through the stages in successive order.

It represents the light of the Dharma, wherein ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, and a billion wondrously colored lights collectively signify ascending through the stages.
Generally, from the soles of the feet, the tips of the toes, and up to the tops of the feet, all do not depart from the practice being performed.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakaraṇḍa, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.
[Śāstra] Fourth, from this point in the prose section onwards, there are ten segments of verses;
these constitute the section on the exposition of the method of contemplation by the Bodhisattva Guṇakaraṇḍa, wherein each of the ten forest-Bodhisattvas speaks for themselves.
The dharmas practiced in their respective positions are formed into a single practice by means of these ten dharmas.
