Thus, within each individual practice, all ten practices are fully present. Each is designated according to its specific position within the practitioner's own path;
the meaning found beneath these names is precisely the dharma that is praised, as is clearly elucidated in the full text.
[Sūtra] The Buddha emits a great radiance, Universally illuminating the ten directions. All see the Honored One among gods and humans, Whose penetration is without obstruction.
The Buddha sits within the Yāma Heaven palace, Pervading the realms of the ten directions.
This matter is most extraordinary, Rarely encountered in the world. O Suyāma, King of Devas!
I praise the ten Tathāgatas as they appear in this assembly; it is the same in all places.
Those hosts of bodhisattvas all bear names identical to our own. Throughout the ten directions, in every place, they proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma;
the worlds from which they come and their respective names are likewise no different.
Each, in the presence of their respective Buddhas, Purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The names of all those Tathāgatas were likewise identical, And their lands were all abundant and blissful. Their spiritual powers were entirely sovereign throughout the ten directions;
In every place, all said, "The Buddha is here," Or saw him dwelling among humans.
Some see the Tathāgata dwelling peacefully throughout all celestial palaces and all lands;

we now behold the Buddha residing within this heavenly palace. Because he formerly made the vow for bodhicitta to pervade the worlds of the ten directions, the inconceivable power of the Buddha’s majesty fills them all.
Far removed from worldly attachments, Endowed with boundless virtues, He has thus attained supernormal powers;
There are no sentient beings who do not see him. Wandering through the realms of the ten directions, Like space, he encounters no obstruction.
A single body, yet infinite bodies— His characteristics cannot be apprehended. The Buddha’s merits are boundless.
How can it be measured or known? It neither dwells nor departs; it universally enters the Dharma-realm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Great Teacher of the World, the Stainless and Unsurpassed Honored One, is difficult to encounter even in inconceivable eons.
Now the Buddha emits a great radiance; throughout the world there is none who does not see it.
For the sake of the multitude, he extensively expounds the Dharma to benefit all living beings as the Tathāgata appears in the world.
To dispel the darkness of ignorance for the world, such is the Lamp of the World.

Rare and difficult to behold, having already cultivated giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he illuminates the world with these.
The Tathāgata is without equal; one cannot find anyone to compare with him.
Failing to understand the reality of phenomena, no one is able to perceive it;
The Buddha’s body and his sovereign spiritual powers are inconceivable— Neither going nor coming, yet he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If there are those who can see or hear him, That Pure Teacher of Gods and Humans, They shall forever emerge from all evil realms.
Having abandoned all suffering for immeasurable and incalculable eons, one cannot know this meaning by practicing the conduct of enlightenment; one cannot attain Buddhahood thereby.
Even if one were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas for inconceivable eons, if one can know this meaning, one’s merit will surpass that.
Even if one were to fill immeasurable lands with rare jewels and offer them all to the Buddhas, one could not know this meaning;
until this is known, enlightenment will not be attained.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jayavana, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
Just as in the first month of summer, The sky is pure and free from the veil of clouds, The brilliant sun radiates its splendor, Pervading the ten directions without exception;
Its light is immeasurable and boundless, Such that none can fathom or know it.
If this is so even for those with eyes, How much more so for those who are blind? So too it is with all Buddhas.
The merit is boundless, throughout inconceivable eons; No one can distinguish or know it.
All phenomena have no place from which they come, Nor is there any agent who creates them.
There is nothing from which they arise that can be distinguished; All phenomena have no coming, And therefore, they have no birth.
Because arising does not exist, cessation is likewise unattainable; all phenomena are without arising and, furthermore, without cessation. One who can understand in this way sees the Tathāgata;
because all phenomena are without arising, their intrinsic nature is non-existent—thus one should know through such discernment.
This person has realized the profound meaning because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
there is no one who can fully comprehend it, for such an understanding of phenomena is ultimately beyond comprehension.
Although they manifest in various lands by speaking of birth, they understand the true nature of those lands, and their minds remain undeluded.
"The nature of the world and its lands— observing them all as they truly are, if one can know this,
one well explains all meanings. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Forest of Fearlessness, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata’s vast body is ultimately coextensive with the dharma-realm; without leaving this seat, it pervades all places.
If one hears such a teaching and reverently believes and delights in it, they will forever leave behind the three evil realms and all sufferings and hardships, even as they travel through all worlds.
Immeasurable and incalculable, those who desire to hear with a focused mind— such as the sovereign powers of the Tathāgata and these various Buddha-dharmas,
which are unsurpassed enlightenment— if they wish even briefly to hear them, none shall be able to obtain them;
yet if there were anyone in the past who had faith in such Buddha-dharmas, [they would attain them].
Having already become a Honored One among two-legged beings, you act as a lamp for the world.
If there are those who shall hear of the Tathāgata’s power of mastery, and having heard it, are able to give rise to faith, they too shall attain Buddhahood.
If there are those in the present who can believe in this Buddha-dharma, they likewise shall achieve perfect enlightenment.
Teaching the Dharma with fearlessness for immeasurable and incalculable eons—this Dharma is extremely difficult to encounter.
If there are those who hear it, know that this is through the power of their original vows.
If there are those who can receive and uphold these teachings of the Buddhas, and having upheld them, proclaim them widely, such a person shall attain Buddhahood.
How much more so for one who is diligent and energetic, whose firm mind never abandons [the path]; you should know that such a person will certainly achieve bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Shame and Remorse, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
If a person hears this rare and sovereign Dharma, they can give rise to a heart of joy and swiftly eliminate the net of doubt.
The One of All-Knowledge and All-Vision has himself spoken these words:
"The Tathāgata knows all; therefore, he is inconceivable. There is nothing that proceeds from ignorance."
And thus wisdom arises; yet the world remains perpetually in darkness.
Therefore, nothing can arise that is like form or non-form; these two are not one.
Wisdom and ignorance are likewise distinct in their essential natures, just as the characterized and the uncharacterized, or saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Discriminations are each distinct; wisdom and non-wisdom are likewise so. When the world first comes into being, it has no characteristic of decay;

wisdom and non-wisdom are also thus. These two characteristics do not exist at one time, just as the initial mind of a bodhisattva does not coexist with a subsequent mind; wisdom and non-wisdom are also thus.
Two minds do not exist simultaneously, just as the various groups of consciousnesses are each without mutual conjunction;
so too is wisdom and the lack of wisdom—ultimately there is no conjunction.
Just as the agada medicine can neutralize all poisons, so too does wisdom neutralize the lack of wisdom.
The Tathāgata has no superior, nor is there anyone equal to him; none can compare with him, and therefore he is difficult to encounter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryavana, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
All phenomena are without distinction, and there is no one who can know them; only Buddhas and Buddhas know them, for their wisdom is ultimate.
Just as gold and the color of gold have no difference in their nature, so too do dharma and non-dharma;
their essential nature is without variation, whether they be sentient beings or non-sentient beings.

Both are devoid of reality; such is the nature of all phenomena. In true meaning, neither exists, just as in the future age there is no characteristic of the past. All phenomena are likewise devoid of any characteristic whatsoever;
just as the characteristics of arising and ceasing, all various [appearances] are not real.
All phenomena are likewise thus; their intrinsic nature does not exist. At the time of teaching, there are two kinds [of discourse]:
that nirvāṇa cannot be grasped. All phenomena are likewise thus; yet through conceptual differentiation, distinctions appear.
Just as based on the objects being counted, there arises the act of counting, so too does that nature not exist.
Thus one understands phenomena, like the method of calculation, increasing from one to immeasurable numbers;
yet phenomena have no intrinsic nature, for their distinctions arise from wisdom.
Just as the world at the end of the kalpa of conflagration comes to an end while space remains undestroyed, so too is the Buddha’s wisdom.
"Just as sentient beings in the ten directions Each grasp at the characteristics of empty space, So too are all phenomena;
the world falsely discriminates them.
Then, the Bodhisattva Power Forest (Balakānan), receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The realms of all sentient beings Are entirely within the three periods of time.
All sentient beings of the three periods Dwell entirely within the five aggregates (*skandhas*). The aggregates have karma as their basis; Karma has the mind as its basis.
The phenomena of the mind are like illusions, And the world is likewise so. The world is not created by itself.
Nor is it created by another, yet its formation occurs; likewise, its destruction occurs.
Although the world has its formation, and although the world has its destruction, one who thoroughly understands the world should not speak of these two. What is the world? And what is not the world?
The mundane and the non-mundane are merely distinctions of names. The phenomena of the five aggregates throughout the three times are called "the mundane";
their cessation is the "non-mundane. Since these are thus merely conventional designations, how can one speak of the aggregates?
What is the nature of the aggregates? The nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished.
Therefore, it is said that there is no arising; when one analyzes these aggregates, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished—this is the meaning of "non-arising.
Since sentient beings are thus, so too are the Buddhas. Both the Buddhas and the Buddha-dharmas have no self-nature whatsoever.
One who can know all these phenomena as they truly are, without inversion— the All-Knowing and All-Seeing One is always present before them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest-Walker, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
Just as all the elements of earth throughout the realms of the ten directions, though lacking any inherent nature, are omnipresent and nowhere absent—so too is the body of the Buddha.
It pervades all worlds with various forms and appearances, yet it has no fixed abode and no place from which it comes; it exists solely through the power of karma.
They are called "sentient beings," yet they are not separate from sentient beings. While karma can be apprehended, the nature of karma is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
That upon which sentient beings rely universally produces all manner of forms and appearances, yet these have no place of origin.
Such various forms and appearances—the power of karma is inconceivable.
Thoroughly understanding its root, one sees nothing therein. The Buddha-body is likewise; it is inconceivable and unattainable.
Although various forms and marks appear everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, the body is not the Buddha, nor is the Buddha the body; rather, the Dharma alone constitutes the body.
One who penetrates all phenomena and is able to see the Buddha-body, pure as the nature of reality (dharmatā), has no doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha-dharma.
If one sees that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like nirvāṇa, this is seeing the Tathāgata; ultimately, there is nothing in which to abide.
If one cultivates right mindfulness and clearly perceives the Perfectly Awakened One, being without signs and without discrimination—
this is called a Dharma Prince. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Forest of Awakening, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
For example, like a skilled painter who distributes various pigments, falsely grasping at diverse appearances;
yet the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) have no differentiation, and within the primary elements there is no form (*rūpa*).
Within form there are no primary elements, nor is it apart from the primary elements that form can be found; likewise, within the mind there are no painted images.
Within the painted image there is no mind, yet it does not exist apart from the mind; though the painted image can be perceived, that mind never dwells therein.
It is immeasurable and inconceivable, manifesting all forms while each remains mutually unaware of the others.
It is like a skilled painter who cannot know his own mind.
Yet it is through the mind that all things are painted; the nature of all phenomena is thus. The mind is like a master painter, capable of painting all worlds;
from it, the five aggregates entirely arise. There is no phenomenon that it does not create.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. One should know that the Buddha and the mind are one.

Their essential nature is entirely inexhaustible. If a person understands the movements of the mind, Which universally constructs all worlds, That person then sees the Buddha, Having realized the true nature of the Buddha.
The mind does not abide in the body, Nor does the body abide in the mind; Yet they are able to perform the work of a Buddha, With a mastery never before seen.
If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm as being entirely created by the mind alone.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
That which is grasped cannot be grasped; that which is seen cannot be seen;
that which is heard cannot be heard. The single mind is inconceivable. Whether finite or infinite, both are ungraspable.
If there is anyone who wishes to grasp it, they will ultimately find nothing to be obtained. One should not speak what ought not to be spoken.
This is to deceive oneself; one's own task will not be accomplished, nor will one cause the assembly to rejoice.
Yet, should one wish to praise the Tathāgata’s boundless and wondrous form-body, even throughout countless eons, none could fully describe it.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, which can manifest all colors.

Though formless, they manifest forms; the Buddhas are also like this. Furthermore, just as the pure void is not form and cannot be seen, yet manifests all forms, yet no one can see the void— the Buddhas are also like this:
they universally manifest immeasurable forms, yet these are not within the sphere of the mind.
No one at all can behold it; though one hears the voice of the Tathāgata, that sound is not the Tathāgata, yet it is not apart from sound.
One who can know the Perfectly Awakened One knows that Bodhi has no coming or going and is free from all conceptual discrimination.
How, then, within this, could one say that they are able to see it?
The Buddhas have no dharma; how could the Buddha have any teaching? It is only in accordance with their own minds that they say such a dharma is taught.
[Treatise] From the fifth verse onwards, there are ten sections of scripture clarifying each of the ten stages within the ten practices.

The section on the causes and effects of the Dharma-gate of Self-Cultivation is concluded above; from here on, the meaning according to each name shall be praised, and one may understand that the dharmas practiced in their respective positions are reached through the names—thus the dharmas may be known.
Chapter Twenty-One: The Ten Practices (Daśabhūmika).
[Treatise] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to three sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;

and third, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. First, regarding the explanation of the title: this chapter primarily expounds ten types of practice gates, and is therefore titled "The Chapter on the Ten Practices.
Second, regarding the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion: [this is placed here because] in this Yāma Heaven...
According to the intention of Master Miyamoto, the "Chapter on the Ten Practices" (Daśabhūmika) describes this heaven as follows: the lotus flowers open to signify day and close to signify night;
the light of this heaven illuminates itself, and although there are neither sun nor moon, day and night are distinguished by observing the opening and closing of the lotuses.
This is called the Heaven of Time-Divisions (*Kāmadhātu*). "Yāma" is a Sanskrit term. Such is the stage of the Bodhisattva.
Knowing when the minds of sentient beings are ready to be awakened, one should guide and receive them at the appropriate time;

for those who are not yet ready to be delivered, one creates the causal conditions for their deliverance, using this locus to manifest it. Therefore, it is at this locus that the ten types of practice-gates are taught.
While the preceding two chapters have clarified the arrival at this celestial realm and its praise, this present chapter specifically explains the ten [practices].
Because this is the section on the Gates of Practice (*caryā-mukha*), this chapter must follow to clarify the preceding Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).
While those ten abodes still rely upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, these ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) rely upon space; this represents the practice of non-attachment.

Third, in the detailed explanation according to the text, it is divided into two parts: first, a general outline of the meaning of the sūtra; second, a word-by-word commentary. First, the general outline of the sūtra.
It is my view that this single chapter of the Sūtra is divided into fourteen sections.

First, from "At that time" onwards until "This constitutes ten [sections]," spanning twenty-five lines of scripture, clarifies how the Buddhas named Guṇakusuma (Virtue Forest) collectively empower Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma to correctly expound the Ten Practices.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards until the... [end of fragment].
The first, the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*), is elucidated in forty-three lines of verse within the *Sūtra of the Correct Teaching*.
This is the third Dharma-gate concerning the practice of joy, starting from "O Son of the Buddha" down to the second, the Practice of Benefiting Others (*sahitārtha-caryā*).
This is clarified in forty-two lines of verse. Thus, these [two] practices, taken together as one chapter from beginning to end, comprise fourteen sections of verse throughout the sūtra.
The final two sections of the prose portion consist of: first, the section on the earth shaking and the offering;
second, the section where Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha (Gongde lin) observes the assembly and speaks in verse; and third, the section of two hundred and two lines of verse praising the Dharma.

These two chapters, both upper and lower, comprise fourteen sections in total, as they are already naturally divided according to their own structural limits; there is no need for further detailed sub-sectioning.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakara, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi of "Excellent Contemplation. Having entered this samādhi,
beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him ten thousand buddhas—
each as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields— all named Guṇakara, who addressed Guṇakara.
The Bodhisattva said, "Excellent, son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to enter this Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation.
Good son, this is because all the Buddhas of the same name, as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions, are collectively bestowing their empowerment upon you;
it is also due to the power of the vows and the majestic spiritual authority of the Tathāgata Vairocana from the past, as well as the merit of the assembly of Bodhisattvas."
The faculties and powers cause you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma for the sake of increasing Buddha-wisdom, for the sake of penetrating deeply into the dharma-realm,
for the sake of thoroughly understanding the realm of sentient beings, for the sake of unimpeded entry, for the sake of unobstructed conduct,
for the sake of attaining immeasurable skillful means, for the sake of encompassing the nature of all-knowledge, and for the sake of awakening to all dharmas— thus you should know.
Because they possess all faculties and are able to uphold and expound all dharmas— namely, by initiating the ten kinds of bodhisattva practices—
good son, you should now, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, expound this Dharma. At that time,
the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha unimpeded wisdom, non-attached wisdom, uninterrupted wisdom, and teacherless wisdom.
It is the wisdom of non-delusion, the wisdom of non-differentiation, the wisdom of non-loss, the immeasurable wisdom, the unsurpassed wisdom, the unwearied wisdom, and the unassailable wisdom.
Why is this? Because the nature of the Dharma is such through the power of this samādhi.

At that time, each of the Buddhas extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the head of Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha; thereupon, Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha arose from his concentration and addressed the bodhisattvas.
"Sā" means "Son of the Buddha. The conduct of Bodhisattvas is inconceivable and is equal to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the Buddhas of the three periods of time and practice accordingly.
Son of the Buddha, what is the conduct of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of conduct for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding what the Buddha has proclaimed, what are these eleven? First, the practice of joy; second, the practice of benefiting others;

third, the practice of non-opposition; fourth, the practice of being unyielding; fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion; sixth, the practice of excellent manifestation; seventh, the practice of non-attachment;
eighth, the practice that is difficult to attain; ninth, the practice of wholesome dharmas; tenth, the practice of truth... [The text continues with the eleventh.]
The practice of these constitutes the ten [stages].

[Treatise]: From the first section, "At that time," down to "this constitutes the ten," twenty-five lines of scripture clarify how the Buddhas of the same name, Forest of Merit (Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha), collectively empower the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit to correctly expound the division of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
In this section, there is a fourfold analysis: first, explaining the name of the samādhi; second, explaining the number of Buddhas with the same name;
third, explaining why all the Buddhas enter this meditative concentration together and why the Bodhisattvas share the same name;

and fourth, explaining how the Buddhas with the same name come to bestow their empowerment. Regarding the first, explaining the name of the samādhi: why is it called the "Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation"? It is because...

The ignorant claim that "detachment" is merely another name for the meditative concentration free from dullness and agitation; furthermore, within the context of dhyāna-concentration, there are four types of dhyāna:
first, the dhyāna practiced by foolish worldlings; second, the dhyāna of examining meanings; third, the dhyāna of mindfulness of true suchness; and fourth, the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
What is now called the "samādhi of skillful contemplation" refers to the dhyāna of examining meanings, as it is intended to definitively ascertain the Dharma.
One must skillfully observe and contemplate with right mindfulness to establish this Dharma-gate as a standard for future learners; therefore,
the second section clarifies the number of Buddhas sharing the same name by citing Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-fields,
all named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), thereby clarifying that if one is deluded regarding mind and objects, ignorance is no different from the infinite atoms of those fields.
If one thoroughly realizes the source of the mind, its wisdom and merit will be equal to those of the ten directions and inexhaustible.

Third, the reason why this is given the same name as the Bodhisattvas who have entered meditative concentration is that their own single mind is profoundly enlightened and indistinguishable from the merit and wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
Now, when this Bodhisattva enters this gate of concentration, they enter into accord with all Buddhas.

Because their merit and wisdom are identical, they attain the same title; because their wisdom, understanding, and practice are identical to those of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and because their merit, virtue, and qualities are identical, the fourth [point] concerns the Buddhas of the same title who come to bestow empowerment.
There are six kinds of such empowerment: first, empowerment by verbal praise, because they are praised and extolled in words; second, the empowerment of Vairocana’s vows.
1. Because the power of past vows is augmented; 2. Because the power of the three Vairocanas is augmented by the seal of the Buddha’s spiritual power; 3.

Because the roots of goodness of the assembly of Bodhisattvas are augmented by the shared roots of goodness; 4. Because the Buddhas augment wisdom, whereby one attains the ten kinds of unimpeded knowledge; 5.
Because the Buddhas augment [the practitioner] by placing their hands upon his head, comforting him and granting permission to preach the Dharma.
Therefore, the following section clarifies that Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha arises from meditative concentration and correctly expounds ten types of practice-entrances;
as shown below, these ten types of practice take the ten pāramitās as their essence.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Practice of Joy? O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva acts as a great donor;
of all things he possesses, he is able to give with wisdom. His mind is equanimous, free from regret or stinginess.
He does not look for karmic retribution, nor does he seek fame or reputation, nor does he crave gain and offerings. He does so solely to rescue and protect all sentient beings and to gather them in.
To receive all sentient beings and benefit all sentient beings; to learn the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas; to recollect the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas;
to delight in the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas; to purify the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas;
to increase the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas; and to maintain the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas.

Manifesting the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas and expounding those original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, they cause all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate this practice, they cause all sentient beings to rejoice and find delight;
and by the power of their vows, they take rebirth in whatever lands there may be where poverty and deprivation exist.

Though he is noble, wealthy, and possesses inexhaustible treasures, suppose that in every moment of thought there come to the Bodhisattva’s presence immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who say:
"O Benevolent One, we are impoverished and have nothing to sustain us; we are emaciated by hunger and suffering, and our lives are on the verge of ending.
We pray only that you will compassionately bestow upon us the flesh of your own body so that we may eat it and preserve our lives."
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately gave to them, causing them to rejoice and their hearts to be satisfied.
Thus, when immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings came to beg, the Bodhisattva never experienced any retreat or discouragement;
rather, his heart of compassion increased all the more. Seeing that these sentient beings all came to beg, the Bodhisattva felt even greater joy.
He joyfully forms this thought: "I have attained a great benefit; these sentient beings are my field of merit and my virtuous friends.
Without being sought or requested, they have come to instruct me in entering the Buddha-dharma. I should now practice and study in such a way as not to contradict the minds of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, he forms this thought: "May what I have done, what I am currently doing, and what I shall do in the future..."
By means of all roots of goodness I have cultivated, may I, in the future, receive a vast body among all sentient beings in all worlds;
with the flesh of this body, may I satisfy all sentient beings suffering from hunger.
Even if there were but a single small sentient being who had not yet attained full satisfaction, may I not relinquish my life, and may the flesh cut from my body never be exhausted.
By this root of goodness, may I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and realize Great Nirvāṇa;

and may all sentient beings who eat my flesh likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, obtain the wisdom of equality, be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, extensively perform the works of a Buddha, and even enter into Nirvāṇa without remainder. If but a single being...
"Only when my mind is no longer dissatisfied shall I finally realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this way, the Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a living soul, the notion of a life-principle, various notions, the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of a human, the notion of a man (*manava*), the notion of an agent, and the notion of an experiencer; he contemplates only phenomena (*dharma*).
When one contemplates that the realms of sentient beings are boundless, and that all phenomena are empty,
non-existent, signless, without substance, without location, without basis,
and unconditioned, one perceives neither oneself, nor the gift, nor the recipient, nor the field of merit, nor karma, nor retribution, nor fruit.

When the great fruit does not perceive the small fruit, at that time the Bodhisattva contemplates the bodies received by all sentient beings of the past, future, and present, which immediately perish and disintegrate;
he then forms this thought: "How strange! Sentient beings are deluded and devoid of wisdom;
within birth and death they receive countless bodies that are precarious, fragile, and unstable, quickly returning to destruction—whether already destroyed or currently being so."

If this body were subject to destruction, and if one cannot seek a firm body by means of this non-firm body, I shall thoroughly study all that the Buddhas have studied, realize all-knowledge, and know all dharmas;

for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the equality of the three periods of time, accord with the unbreakable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which is quiescent, and cause them to forever attain peace and happiness. Buddha.
This is called the first practice of joy of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Within the first practice of joy, the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving) constitutes its essence; it consists of forty-three lines of scripture divided into five sections:
1. From "O Son of the Buddha, what is the practice of joy? down to "causing all... [to be accomplished].

Regarding the joy and delight of sentient beings, nine and a half lines of the sūtra clarify the section on practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and training in the practices cultivated by the Buddha.

From "In whatever regions there are places of poverty" down to "not contravening the minds of any sentient beings," ten and a half lines of the sūtra clarify that a bodhisattva at this stage perceives those in poverty and...
Regarding the vow to be born into those wealthy and noble families, one completely relinquishes wealth, resources, and even one's own life to benefit others;

this is divided into three parts. Furthermore, from the point where he forms such a thought down to the attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is a passage of eight lines and a half in the sūtra that clarifies how a bodhisattva, during an era of famine, manifests a vast body and sacrifices it to relieve the destitute. Fourth, the bodhisattva.

From this point downward, until the passage "not perceiving a great fruit nor a small fruit," there are six lines and a half of sutra that clearly explain the true state of the *pudgala* who is without ideation (*asaṃjñin*).
This term "ideation of repeatedly taking up a course of existence" (*punaḥ-punar-gati-grahaṇa-saṃjñā*) refers to the notion of being a youth (*māṇava*), also called a "scholar-child" (*maṇava*).
The meaning is that one does not discriminate between good and evil, or between old and young.
From "He gives all these five [senses] away" at that time, down to the first section on the Joyful Practice (*pramuditā-caryā*),

which consists of seven and a half lines of scripture, it clarifies the portion concerning observing sentient beings as lacking solidity and seeking for oneself a solid body so that they may dwell in eternal peace and security.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s practice of benefiting others?
This Bodhisattva upholds pure precepts and is without attachment to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects.
He likewise proclaims this to sentient beings, seeking neither power, nor lineage, nor wealth, nor physical beauty, nor royal status."
All these are entirely without attachment; they simply uphold the pure precepts and form this thought:

"By upholding the pure precepts, I shall surely abandon all entanglements, greedy cravings, burning afflictions, the oppression of various difficulties, slanders, and turbidity, and attain the equal and true Dharma praised by the Buddhas.
When a Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva, thus upholds the pure precepts, regarding even a single...
Suppose, at midday, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great evil Māras were to approach the Bodhisattva,
each bringing immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of celestial maidens—
all skilled in the arts of the five desires, elegant and beautiful enough to bewitch the hearts of men, and carrying various kinds of precious playthings.
When they come seeking to delude and disturb the bodhisattva’s resolve for the path, the bodhisattva then reflects: "These five desires are dharmas that obstruct the path;
they even hinder unsurpassed bodhi. Therefore, he does not give rise to a single thought of desire, and his mind remains pure like that of a Buddha.
He employs skillful means only to teach and transform sentient beings, yet he never abandons the mind of omniscience.

O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva will not, for the sake of desire, afflict even a single sentient being; rather, they would sooner give up their own body and life than ever perform an act that afflicts a sentient being.
Since the moment the bodhisattva first beheld the Buddha, they have never given rise to a single thought of lustful desire, let alone engaging in such acts.
It is simply impossible for them to engage in such acts. At that time, the bodhisattva only acts as follows:
He reflects: "All sentient beings, throughout the long night, have conceived thoughts of the five desires, have turned toward the five desires, and have become greedily attached to them;
their minds are resolutely immersed and submerged in them, following along with their currents so that they find no self-mastery.
I should now cause these Māras, these celestial maidens, and all sentient beings to abide in the unsurpassed precepts and to abide in purity."

Having already established ourselves in the resolve for omniscience without ever turning back, we shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and even enter into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Why is this? Because this is the task we ought to perform;
we should follow the Buddhas in such training. Having trained in this way, we shall abandon all evil conduct and, realizing our own ignorance, [strive to overcome it].
Wisdom enters into all Buddha-dharmas and explains them for the sake of sentient beings to eliminate their inversions;
yet it knows that there are no inversions apart from sentient beings, nor are there sentient beings apart from inversions.
Sentient beings do not exist within inversions, nor do inversions exist within sentient beings. Furthermore, inversion is not the sentient being, nor is the sentient being the inversion.
Inversion is neither an internal phenomenon nor an external phenomenon; sentient beings are neither an internal phenomenon nor an external phenomenon.
All phenomena are false and unreal, arising and ceasing rapidly, lacking any solidity.
They are like dreams, shadows, illusions, and transformations that deceive the foolish. One who understands in this way is able to awaken to all phenomena.
Practicing the penetration of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, one realizes the Buddha-bodhi; having attained liberation oneself, one enables others to attain liberation;

having attained deliverance oneself, one enables others to attain deliverance; having attained self-mastery, one enables others to attain self-mastery; having attained tranquility oneself, one enables others to attain tranquility;

having attained peace and security oneself, one enables others to attain peace and security; having become free from defilement oneself, one enables others to become free from defilement; having become pure oneself, one enables others to become pure...
Pure in their own nirvāṇa, they lead others to nirvāṇa; happy themselves, they bring happiness to others.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva further reflects: "I shall follow all Tathāgatas, abandon all worldly conduct, and fulfill all the qualities of a Buddha.
Abiding in the state of supreme equanimity, I shall regard all sentient beings with impartiality, clearly penetrating the realm of reality, and remain free from [attachment]."
O Son of the Buddha, when one has severed all faults, abandoned all conceptual constructions, relinquished all attachments, and is skillful in renunciation,
with a mind that constantly dwells in unsurpassed, ineffable, independent, immovable, immeasurable, boundless, inexhaustible, and formless profound wisdom—
this is called the second Beneficial Practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

[Treatise] In the second [section], the Practice of Benefiting Others (*anugraha-caryā*), which has the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its essence, there are forty-two practices.
These are divided into five segments: first, from "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting others?
down to "attaining the equal and true Dharma praised by the Buddhas," there are six and a half lines of scripture that clarify the objective realm of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

"Not being attached" is divided into two parts. First, from "When the sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, thus maintain pure precepts" down to "the mind of omniscience," there are eight lines of sūtra explaining that Māra’s generals and celestial maidens cannot delude or disturb them.
Second, from "Sons of the Buddha" down to "nirvāṇa without remainder," there are eight and a half lines of sūtra explaining that the bodhisattva does not [cling] to the five desires.

The section on "Afflicting Sentient Beings" is divided into four parts. Why is this? From here down to "causing others to attain happiness," there are thirteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify how one must first discipline oneself well before being able to preach the Dharma so that others may attain happiness. This constitutes the fifth section.
From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the practice of benefiting others," there are six lines of scripture that clarify attaining liberation from worldly conduct and entering into the profound.
The Section on Wisdom.
[Sūtra] Son of the Buddha, what is the non-opposing conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? This bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dharma of patience;
he is humble and respectful, neither harming himself, nor harming others, nor harming both; he does not grasp for himself, nor from others...
They do not grasp, they do not grasp at both, they are not attached to themselves, not attached to others, and not attached to both; nor do they crave fame, reputation, profit, or offerings.

They only maintain this thought: "I shall always preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may leave behind all evils and sever greed, hatred, delusion, arrogance, hypocrisy, stinginess, envy, flattery, and deception, causing them to dwell constantly in patience, gentleness, and harmony, O Son of the Buddha."
When a bodhisattva has accomplished such a dharma of patience, even if there should come to their presence hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of sentient beings,
and each single being were to manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of mouths,
and each mouth were to utter hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of words— namely, those that are unbearable— [the bodhisattva would remain unmoved].
They address them with words that are unpleasant, not words of the Dharma, disagreeable, unlovely, not virtuous,
not the speech of noble wisdom, not associated with the noble ones, not frequented by the noble ones— words deeply loathsome and unfit to be heard—
and with such speech they revile and insult the Bodhisattva; furthermore, each of these sentient beings individually possesses hundreds of thousands [of such insults].

With billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of hands, each hand holding hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of weapons, they oppressed and harmed the Bodhisattva; thus it continued for asankhyeya kalpas without ceasing.
When the Bodhisattva encountered such extreme agony that the hairs on his body stood on end and his life was about to be severed, he thought to himself:

Because of this, if my mind were to become agitated, I would not be self-subdued, not self-guarded, not self-clarified, not self-cultivated, not correctly concentrated, not tranquil, not cherishing myself, and would give rise to attachment;
how then could I cause the minds of others to attain purity? At that time, the Bodhisattva further thought: "From [the beginningless]..."
From the beginning of the kalpa, he has dwelt in birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction. Reflecting thus, he earnestly exhorts himself to purify his mind and attain joy;
skillfully disciplining and regulating himself, he is able to abide securely within the Buddha-dharma. He further causes other sentient beings to likewise attain this Dharma.
Furthermore, he reflects that this body is empty and quiescent, devoid of self or what belongs to a self, and possesses nothing at all.
In true reality, emptiness is non-dual; whether it be suffering or pleasure, nothing exists, for all phenomena are empty.
I shall understand this and explain it extensively for others, so that all sentient beings may eliminate these views.

Therefore, although I now encounter bitter poison, I should endure it for the sake of compassionately regarding sentient beings, for the benefit of sentient beings, and for the peace and happiness of sentient beings.
Because of being born [into this world], because of compassion for sentient beings, because of gathering in sentient beings, because of not abandoning sentient beings,
because of having attained awakening oneself, because of causing others to awaken, because of the non-retrogression of the mind, and because of proceeding toward the Buddha-way—
this is called the third practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Practice of Non-Contradiction.
[Treatise] The third, the practice of non-opposing conduct, has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence. It consists of thirty practices, which are divided into three sections:

(1) from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "patience that is gentle and harmonious," there are five and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on patience that does not harm oneself or others and is gentle and harmonious;
(2) from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "causing the minds of others... [is the second section].
The attainment of purity is clarified in thirteen and a half lines of scripture concerning the section on the Bodhisattva’s endurance of harm to body and speech;

this begins from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... and extends to "...the practice of non-opposition," comprising ten and a half lines of scripture which clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of patience through the contemplation of emptiness.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, what is the unyielding practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva cultivates various forms of diligence, namely:

foremost diligence, great diligence, superior diligence, distinguished diligence, most excellent diligence, most wondrous diligence, supreme diligence, unsurpassed diligence, unequaled diligence, and universal diligence.
His nature of progress is free from the three poisons; his nature is free from arrogance; his nature does not conceal [faults]; his nature is free from stinginess and envy;
his nature is free from flattery and deception. Possessing self-shame and self-reproach, he never practices diligence for the sake of troubling even a single sentient being;
rather, he practices diligence solely for the sake of severing all afflictions, and he practices diligence solely for the sake of uprooting the source of all delusions.
He practices diligence solely for the sake of eliminating all habitual tendencies; he practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the realms of all sentient beings;
he practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the death and rebirth of all sentient beings;
he practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the afflictions of all sentient beings; he practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the one...
He practices diligence because he seeks to delight the minds of all sentient beings; he practices diligence solely to know the spheres of experience of all sentient beings;
he practices diligence solely to know the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings;
he practices diligence solely to know the mental activities of all sentient beings; and he practices diligence solely to know all phenomena.
One practices diligence for the sake of the realms; one practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the fundamental nature of all Buddha-dharmas;
one practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the equality of all Buddha-dharmas; one practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the equality of the three periods of time;
and one practices diligence solely for the sake of attaining the light of wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas.
They practice diligence solely for the sake of realizing the wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the single true mark of all Buddha-dharmas; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the boundless limits of all Buddha-dharmas;
and they practice diligence solely for the sake of attaining the vast, definitive skillfulness of all Buddha-dharmas.
Out of wisdom, he practices diligence solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge that discerns and explains the meanings of all phrases of the Buddha-dharma;
out of wisdom, he practices diligence, O Son of the Buddha, so that once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has accomplished such diligent practice, even if someone were to say:
"Could you, for the sake of all sentient beings in countless worlds, with each single [being]..."
Because of this birth, you shall undergo all manner of sufferings in the Avīci Hell for incalculable kalpas;
yet, you shall cause each and every one of those sentient beings to encounter the appearance in the world of innumerable Buddhas.
Because they have seen the Buddhas, they shall fully experience all kinds of bliss until they enter the Nirvana without remainder, at which point you yourself shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Can you do this? He replied, "I can. Furthermore, suppose someone were to say: "There are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* great oceans;
you should exhaust them by dripping from them with the tip of a single hair. There are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds; you should grind them all to dust.
If one were to count each of those drops and each of those particles of dust, could one know their total number? [He replied,] "Yes, for the multitude."
Having been born [in such realms], they have suffered uninterrupted pain for so many kalpas throughout every moment of thought.

Yet, the Bodhisattva’s practice does not give rise to even a single thought of regret upon hearing these words; rather, his joy and exultation increase all the more, and he deeply congratulates himself on having attained great and wholesome benefit.
"By my power, I shall cause those sentient beings to be forever liberated from all suffering."
By means of these skillful means, he causes all sentient beings in all worlds to eventually attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
this is called the fourth practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Practice of Invincibility.
[Treatise] The fourth, the practice of being unbending, has the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) as its essence.
It consists of thirty-seven and a half lines of verse, which are divided into three sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "for the sake of the phrases and meanings of all Buddha-dharmas," there are twenty-two and a half lines of verse clarifying that the Bodhisattva does not seek worldly benefits.
For the sake of seeking the Buddha’s omniscience, the section on the practice of diligence is divided into two parts. First, from "The sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas...
down to the response "I am able," there are six lines of sūtra that clarify how Bodhisattvas enter the hells for the sake of sentient beings without complaining of weariness.
This section is further divided into three parts: first, from "Even if there were someone... down to the "practice of being unbending."

There is a passage of eight lines and a half of sūtra clarifying the section on how Bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, do not decline the toil of undergoing suffering over many kalpas.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s practice free from delusion and confusion? This Bodhisattva accomplishes..."
With right mindfulness, the mind is undistracted, firm and immovable, supremely pure, vast, immeasurable, and free from delusion.
By means of this right mindfulness, one skillfully understands all worldly languages and can maintain the verbal expressions of all supramundane dharmas—
namely, the ability to maintain the verbal expressions of material and non-material dharmas, and the ability to maintain the establishment of the self-nature of matter.

Regarding the verbal expression of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, up to the verbal expression that establishes and sustains the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—his mind is free from delusion or confusion;
in this world, his mind is free from delusion or confusion regarding death here and birth there; his mind is free from delusion or confusion regarding entering and emerging from the womb;

his mind is free from delusion or confusion regarding the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); his mind is free from delusion or confusion regarding serving spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); and he diligently cultivates the Buddha...
The mind of the Dharma is free from delusion and confusion; one perceives the works of Māra with a mind free from delusion and confusion;
one is free from the activities of Māra with a mind free from delusion and confusion; and one practices the bodhisattva path for unspeakable eons with a mind free from delusion and confusion.
This bodhisattva accomplishes such immeasurable right mindfulness, having learned well from all Buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The Dharma heard by consciousness is as follows: the profound Dharma, the vast Dharma, the Dharma of adornment, the Dharma of various adornments, the Dharma that expounds various bodies of names,
phrases, and syllables, the Dharma of the adornment of bodhisattvas, the unsurpassed Dharma of the light of the Buddha’s spiritual power,
the Dharma of pure certainty and resolute understanding, and the Dharma of non-attachment to all worldly phenomena.
He discerns all worldly dharmas, the vast and great dharmas, and is free from the cataracts of delusion;
he illuminates all dharmas of sentient beings, both the common dharmas of all worlds and the uncommon dharmas.
Having heard such supreme dharmas of Bodhisattva wisdom and the sovereign dharmas of omniscience, his mind remains neither forgetful nor lost for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

He constantly maintains mindfulness without interruption. Why is this? Because when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates various practices throughout immeasurable kalpas, he never disturbs or confuses a single sentient being so as to cause them to lose right mindfulness, nor does he destroy the True Dharma or sever their roots of goodness;
for his mind constantly increases and expands toward vast wisdom. Furthermore, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in various ways...
Sounds cannot delude or disturb this bodhisattva— namely, sounds that are loud and high-pitched, coarse and turbid, extremely terrifying, pleasant, unpleasant,
noisy enough to distract the auditory consciousness, or those that impair the six sense faculties.
Even if such immeasurable and innumerable good and evil sounds were to fill incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* eons, this bodhisattva would remain undisturbed upon hearing them.
Throughout the realms, there has never been a single moment of mental distraction; that is to say, mindfulness is undisturbed, the objective sphere is undisturbed, samādhi is undisturbed,
entry into the profound Dharma is undisturbed, the practice of the bodhisattva path is undisturbed, the arousal of the bodhicitta is undisturbed, the recollection of all Buddhas is undisturbed,
the contemplation of the true Dharma is undisturbed, the wisdom for transforming sentient beings is undisturbed, and purification is undisturbed.

Because the wisdom of sentient beings is undisturbed, they decisively comprehend the profound meaning; because they are undisturbed, they do not commit evil deeds and thus have no obstruction of karma;
because they do not give rise to afflictions, they have no obstruction of afflictions; because they do not treat the Dharma with contempt, they have no obstruction of pride regarding the Dharma;
and because they do not slander the True Dharma, they have no obstruction of retribution. O Son of the Buddha, such are the sounds as described above.
Each fills incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka-dhātu*), never ceasing throughout immeasurable and innumerable eons (*apramāṇa-saṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
While they are able to disrupt and disorder all the faculties (*indriya*) of the body and mind of sentient beings, they cannot disturb the mind of this bodhisattva.
When this bodhisattva enters into samādhi and dwells in the noble Dharma (*āryadharma*), they contemplate and observe all sounds, thoroughly understanding them.
Having well understood the nature of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of sounds, and having heard this, one does not give rise to desire, does not arouse anger, and does not lose mindfulness;
one skillfully grasps their characteristics without becoming stained or attached.
One knows that all sounds are non-existent, truly unattainable, without an agent, and without a fundamental limit, being identical with the *dharmadhātu*.
Being thus equal and without distinction, these bodhisattvas accomplish the tranquil conduct of body, speech, and mind;
they never regress from omniscience; they skillfully enter all gateways of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); they know that all samādhis share a single essential nature;
they understand that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without limit; they attain the true wisdom of all phenomena; and they attain liberation from sound.
By attaining the Samādhi of Profound Sound, he gains incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) gates to various samādhis and increases his immeasurable, vast, and great compassion.
At that time, in a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva attains countless hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
hearing such sounds, his mind is not confused or disturbed, and he causes those samādhis to gradually expand further. He forms this thought: "I shall cause even a single..."

When all sentient beings dwell securely in unsurpassed, pure mindfulness, attain non-retrogression regarding omniscience, and ultimately achieve *nirvāṇa* without remainder—this is called the fifth practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: being free from delusion and confusion.
[Treatise] The fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion, takes the *dhyānapāramitā* as its essence. It consists of forty-nine lines of verse, divided into six sections.

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "cultivating the bodhisattva practice with a mind free from delusion and confusion," there are ten lines of verse clarifying the section on following birth and death through right mindfulness to benefit sentient beings without confusion. Second...

This Bodhisattva, from the point "having brought this down to the mind" (*cittam adhaḥ kṛtvā*) until "there is no interruption in constant recollection," has nine lines of sūtra that clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s hearing, retention, and right mindfulness being undisturbed. Why is this? From the point "already...

until "never for even a single thought-moment has the mind been distracted," there are seven and a half lines of sūtra that clarify [the practice] of right mindfulness regarding pleasant and unpleasant sounds.

The section on non-distraction has four parts: first, "right mindfulness being undistracted," down to "and cannot destroy this bodhisattva’s mind," which clarifies the eight and a half lines of sūtra concerning the practice of hearing the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings without any remaining obstacles;
second, "the bodhisattva enters into samādhi," down to "are equal and without distinction," which clarifies contemplation through five lines of sūtra.
The section on the "Absence of Substance in Sound" and the "Endurance" consists of six parts; thus, after the Bodhisattva has accomplished such tranquil conduct of body,
speech, and mind, down to the conduct free from delusion and confusion, nine sections of sutra clarify that the purity of body, speech,
and mind enables entry into all phenomena without departing from their single nature.
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Seven.
