A Combined Commentary on the Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one, Part Two:
“The Bodhisattva’s Good Manifestation. [Sūtra] Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s good manifestation? This refers to the purity of the bodhisattva’s physical karma.
With purity of verbal karma and purity of mental karma, they dwell in non-apprehension and demonstrate non-apprehension.
Because they know that the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are all non-existent and without falsehood, they are without bondage.

Whatever they manifest is without intrinsic nature and without dependence; dwelling in the mind as it truly is, they know the immeasurable nature of the mind and know the self-nature of all phenomena.

The nature is without attainment and without marks; it is profoundly deep and difficult to enter or abide in. Abiding in the true station of *tathatā* and the *dharmatā*, it is born through skillful means yet is free from karmic retribution;
it is neither arising nor ceasing. It abides in the realm of *nirvāṇa*, abides in the nature of tranquility, and abides in the reality of the nature of non-nature.
It is cut off from the path of language and transcends all worlds; having no basis, it enters the state beyond differentiation.
There is no other dharma of bondage; he enters the supreme wisdom of the true dharma, which is not something that can be understood by any worldly beings, but is a supramundane dharma.
This is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means for manifesting the appearance of birth.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva reflects thus: "All sentient beings have non-existence as their nature; all dharmas are without..."
To act for the sake of all lands characterized by the mark of signlessness; to realize that all three periods of time are merely verbal expressions;

to understand that all verbal expressions have no basis within phenomena; and that all phenomena likewise have no basis within verbal expressions—when a bodhisattva understands all phenomena in this way, they are all profoundly deep, and all worlds are...
All Buddha-dharmas are entirely quiescent, without any increase; the Buddha-dharmas are not different from worldly dharmas, and worldly dharmas are not different from Buddha-dharmas.
There is no confusion between Buddha-dharmas and worldly dharmas, nor is there any distinction between them.
Having realized that the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu* is equal, they universally enter the three periods of time and never abandon the Great Bodhicitta, remaining forever constant.

When the mind of a bodhisattva who has regressed toward maturing sentient beings turns back once more toward increasing great compassion and becoming a place of reliance for all sentient beings, that bodhisattva then further reflects: "If I do not mature sentient beings, who shall mature them?
If I do not discipline sentient beings, who shall discipline them? If I do not teach and transform sentient beings, who shall teach and transform them?"
"I have transformed myself, yet who shall awaken the sentient beings who do not awaken? I am pure, yet who shall purify the sentient beings who are not pure?
This is what is appropriate for me; this is what I ought to do. Furthermore, he reflects:
"If I were to understand this profound Dharma by myself alone, I would attain liberation in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as a solitary individual."
All sentient beings are blind and sightless, entering great perilous paths and being entangled by various afflictions;
like those with grave illnesses who constantly suffer pain, they dwell in the prison of craving and cannot escape on their own.
They do not leave the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama; they cannot extinguish suffering, they do not abandon evil karma, and they always abide in the darkness of ignorance.
Seeing that sentient beings in the cycle of birth and death have not attained liberation and dwell amidst the eight difficulties,
their minds shrouded by various defilements and attachments, and deluded by false views so that they do not practice the right path—
the Bodhisattva contemplates all such beings and thinks: "If these sentient beings are neither yet matured nor tamed, I shall leave them behind and take up [others]."
To realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not what I should do; rather, I should first transform sentient beings.

Throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons, I shall first bring to maturity those who have not yet matured while practicing the bodhisattva path, and first subdue those who have not yet been subdued. While this bodhisattva dwells in this practice, all the devas, māras, and brahmās—
Should any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or anyone in the world— including gandharvas and asuras— behold [this], dwell with it even for a moment,
revere, respect, serve, and make offerings to it, or even briefly hear of it and have it once pass through their minds,
such actions shall not be in vain; they will certainly and surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the sixth practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Practice of Good Manifestation (*sādhumatī*).
[Treatise] The sixth practice, the Practice of Good Manifestation, takes the Prajñāpāramitā as its essence. It consists of forty and a half lines of scripture, which are divided into four sections.
The first section, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*putra*) onwards, up to the "characteristics of manifesting birth through skillful means," comprises ten lines.
The first half of the sutra clearly explains that birth is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), demonstrating the skillful means (*upāya*) of manifesting birth; this is divided into two parts.

From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to "acting as a place of reliance for all sentient beings," ten lines of the sutra clarify how the Bodhisattva, having realized that the mind, objects, and all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and without support, teaches and transforms sentient beings while acting as their place of reliance.

The section for the three Bodhisattvas, from "At that time" down to "not practicing the right path," consists of eleven lines of scripture clarifying the stage of mindfulness in saving sentient beings.

The section for the four Bodhisattvas, from "Thus observing all sentient beings" down to "practicing well," consists of nine lines of scripture clarifying the stage where the saving of sentient beings is not yet complete and one does not personally realize *nirvāṇa*.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the unattached practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva, with an unattached mind, is able in every thought-moment to enter incalculable worlds and to purify incalculable worlds.
Regarding all these worlds, his mind remains unattached as he proceeds to the presence of incalculable Tathāgatas to pay them homage."
One should pay homage, serve, and make offerings with incalculable flowers, incalculable perfumes, incalculable garlands,
incalculable ointments, powdered incense, robes, precious jewels, banners, flags, and exquisite parasols— each of these various ornaments being incalculable in number— as an offering.
Such offerings are made for the sake of the ultimate unconditioned dharma and for the sake of abiding therein.
Because they contemplate the inconceivable Dharma, in every thought-moment they see countless Buddhas;
yet toward these Buddhas their minds have no attachment, they have no attachment to the Buddha-fields, and they have no attachment to the marks and signs of the Buddhas.

They see the radiance of the Buddhas and hear them preach the Dharma without any attachment, nor do they have any attachment toward the multitudes of worlds, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, they listen to the Buddha-dharma without attachment; having heard it, their minds give rise to joy, and their resolve and power become vast, such that they are able to embrace and practice all the bodhisattva deeds, yet they remain without attachment even to the Buddha-dharma.
These bodhisattvas, throughout unspeakable eons, behold unspeakable numbers of Buddhas appearing in the world; at the site of each and every Buddha, they serve and make offerings to them all.

Even throughout unspeakable eons, their minds never grow weary or satisfied; yet, seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and beholding the majestic adornments of the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, they remain entirely without attachment. Even when seeing impure worlds, they feel no aversion. Why is this?
Because these Bodhisattvas observe according to the nature of all Buddha-dharmas; within the Buddha-dharmas, there is neither defilement nor purity, neither darkness nor light.
He clearly realizes that there is no difference, no unity, no reality, no falsehood, no security, no peril, no right path, and no wrong path.
Thus, the Bodhisattva deeply penetrates the dharma-realm to teach and transform sentient beings, yet he gives rise to no attachment toward those beings;
he upholds all dharmas, yet he gives rise to no attachment toward those dharmas; he resolves upon bodhicitta and abides in the Buddha-nature.
Abiding in the dwelling of the Buddhas, one gives rise to no attachment; though there is verbal expression, the mind has no attachment to such expressions.
Entering the realms of sentient beings, the mind has no attachment to those realms. One understands samādhi, being able to enter and abide within it, yet the mind has no attachment to that samādhi.
One proceeds to the immeasurable Buddha-lands, whether entering them or...
If, while dwelling therein, one’s mind is unattached to the Buddha-field, and when departing there is no lingering attachment,
then because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus able to be without attachment, their mind is unobstructed regarding the Buddha-dharma;
they realize the Buddha’s bodhi, realize the Dharma-vinaya, dwell in the Buddha’s true teaching, and practice the bodhisattva conduct while abiding in bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Saṃcintya reflected upon the dharma of the bodhisattva’s liberation:

his mind was unstained by the bodhisattva’s dwelling place, he had no attachment to the bodhisattva’s conduct, he purified the bodhisattva path, and he received the prediction of enlightenment. Having received the prediction, he thought:
"Ordinary people are foolish, ignorant, without knowledge, without vision, without faith, without understanding, and lack wise practice."
Stubborn, dull-witted, and greedily attached, they wander through birth and death, seeking neither to see the Buddha nor to follow the guidance of the enlightened.
Disbelieving in the Tamer, they are deluded and erring, entering perilous paths; they do not revere the King of Ten Powers, nor do they recognize the kindness of the Bodhisattvas.

Clinging to their dwellings, they hear of the emptiness of all phenomena and are greatly terrified in their hearts. They distance themselves from the True Dharma and abide in false teachings, abandoning the noble path.

To enter the perilous path while abandoning the Buddha’s intent and following the intent of Māra, stubbornly clinging to existence within the various realms of rebirth—when a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings in this way, they increase their great compassion and give rise to all roots of goodness without attachment.
At that time, the bodhisattva further reflects: "For the sake of even a single sentient being, I shall [remain] throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
In each and every realm throughout the world-systems, for unspeakably unspeakable eons, they teach and bring to maturity beings;
as they do for a single sentient being, so it is for all sentient beings alike, never becoming weary or discouraged by this, nor abandoning them to depart elsewhere.
Furthermore, using a hair-tip to measure the entirety of the Dharma-realm, within the space of a single hair-tip, they exhaustively [manifest] that which is unspeakable.
For unspeakable eons, they teach and discipline all sentient beings;
at each and every hair-tip, they do likewise, continuing even until not for the duration of a single finger-snap do they harbor attachment to a self or give rise to notions of "I" and "mine.
At each and every hair-tip, throughout all future kalpas, they practice the bodhisattva path without clinging to a body.

They do not cling to dharmas, they do not cling to thoughts, they do not cling to vows, they do not cling to samādhis, they do not cling to contemplation, they do not cling to meditative stillness, they do not cling to objective spheres, they do not cling to the teaching and taming of sentient beings, and furthermore, they do not cling to entering the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva forms this thought: "I should contemplate all dharma-realms as being like illusions, just as the Buddhas do."
The practice of Bodhisattvas is like a shadow; the Dharma taught by Buddhas is like an echo; all worlds are like transformations, sustained by the power of karmic retribution;
differentiated bodies are like illusions, arising from the power of their conduct; all sentient beings are like the mind, due to its various defilements;
and all phenomena are like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), being unchanging. Furthermore, he thought to himself: "I..."
Throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm, they practice the bodhisattva path in lands of the ten directions;
in every thought-moment, they clearly comprehend all Buddha-dharmas, and with right mindfulness present before them, they remain free from grasping or attachment.

Thus observing the non-self of the body and seeing the unimpeded nature of the Buddhas, they expound various teachings to transform sentient beings, causing them to give rise to [faith] within the Buddha-dharma.
With immeasurable joy, pure faith, and a heart that protects all beings without weariness— because he is free from weariness—
he goes to every world where there are sentient beings who are not yet perfected or tamed,
and there he skillfully transforms and delivers those beings through various sounds, various karmas, various attachments, and various acts of giving.
They manifest various combinations, various cycles of transmigration, various activities, various objective realms, various births, and various deaths;

yet, by means of their great vows, they abide within these conditions to teach and transform beings, ensuring that their minds do not waver or regress, nor do they give rise to a single thought of defiled attachment.
Why is this? Because they have attained non-attachment and non-clinging.
Because it relies upon this, one’s own benefit and the benefit of others are purified and fulfilled; this is called the seventh practice of non-attachment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
[Śāstra] The seventh practice of non-attachment has the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) as its essence, and consists of sixty-five practices.

The sūtra is divided into six sections: 1. From "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "yet there is no attachment even to the Buddha-dharma," twelve and a half lines of sūtra clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s adornment and purification of Buddha-fields, making offerings to all Buddhas, and having a mind free from attachment.
2. From "This Bodhisattva" down to "because he is able to be thus without attachment," there are ten [lines].
The *Wuxing jing* (Sūtra on the Five Practices) clarifies the method for a Bodhisattva’s tireless service to the Buddha and its constant practice without attachment, dividing it into three parts:
from "having no obstacles in one's mind regarding the Buddha-dharma" down to "having no attachment to any roots of goodness," there are eleven [sections].

The *Yixing jing* (Sūtra on the One Practice) clarifies observing the suffering of sentient beings and the long development of great compassion, dividing it into four [parts]. The *Puxian*... [text truncated]

Section Five: From "At one time" down to "For what reason? there are ten lines and a half of sūtra text clarifying that Bodhisattvas constantly abide in birth-and-death to teach and transform sentient beings without attachment.

Section Six: From "The five Bodhisattvas having had this thought" down to "their minds are without weariness," there are nine lines of sūtra text clarifying the teaching and transformation of sentient beings through the contemplation of phenomena as being like illusions. Section Seven: [The section on] Non-attachment.

From the passage beginning with "Because of weariness" down to "the practice of non-attachment," seven and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings who have not yet been tamed, goes to be born among them.
[Sūtra] Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s practice that is difficult to attain? This Bodhisattva accomplishes what is difficult.
These are the roots of goodness that are difficult to subdue, the most excellent roots of goodness, the indestructible roots of goodness,
the unsurpassable roots of goodness, the inconceivable roots of goodness, the inexhaustible roots of goodness, the roots of goodness with sovereign power,
the roots of goodness with great majesty, and the roots of goodness that share the same nature as all Buddhas. When this bodhisattva cultivates these various practices within the Buddha-dharma...
They have attained the most supreme resolve regarding the Buddha’s enlightenment and have attained a vast resolve regarding the vows of Bodhisattvas;
they never cease throughout all kalpas, their minds never wearying; they do not give rise to revulsion toward any suffering;
they cannot be moved by any demons; they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; and they fully practice all the ascetic austerities of Bodhisattvas.
Cultivating the bodhisattva practices with diligent and tireless effort, they never retreat from their Mahāyāna vows.

Having established themselves in these difficult-to-attain practices, in every moment of thought they can turn back the cycle of birth and death for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas without abandoning their great bodhisattva vows.
If there are sentient beings who serve and make offerings to them, or even those who merely see or hear of them, [they all] in the *A*... [attain liberation].
Having attained non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, although this bodhisattva realizes that sentient beings do not exist,
they do not abandon the realm of all sentient beings. They are like a boatman who dwells neither on this shore nor on the other shore,
nor in the middle of the stream, yet is able to ferry sentient beings from this shore to the other shore by means of coming and going.
Because there is no rest, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: he does not abide in saṃsāra, nor does he abide in nirvāṇa;

yet, without abiding in the middle stream of saṃsāra, he is able to ferry sentient beings from this shore to the other shore, establishing them in a place of security, fearlessness, and freedom from sorrow and affliction. Furthermore, he does not harbor any attachment toward the category of sentient beings.
To abandon one sentient being while not abandoning many sentient beings, or to not abandon many sentient beings while abandoning one sentient being;
neither increasing the realm of sentient beings nor decreasing the realm of sentient beings, neither giving birth to the realm of sentient beings nor extinguishing the realm of sentient beings,

neither exhausting the realm of sentient beings nor extending the realm of sentient beings, and neither discriminating the realm of sentient beings nor viewing the realm of sentient beings as dual— why is this so?
Therefore, the Bodhisattva enters deeply into the realm of sentient beings as he does the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm are not two;
in this non-dual dharma, there is no increase and no decrease, no arising and no ceasing, no existence and no non-existence, no grasping, no reliance, and no attachment.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva understands that all phenomena and the dharma-realm are non-dual. Thus, the Bodhisattva is like...
Therefore, by means of skillful expedients, they enter the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and abide in the signless (*animitta*), adorning their bodies with pure marks.

They realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), yet they are able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena. Without grasping at sentient beings, they are able to know the number of sentient beings;
without being attached to worlds, they manifest their bodies in Buddha-fields; and without discriminating between phenomena, they are skilled in...
Entering deeply into the Buddha-dharma and thoroughly penetrating its principles, they extensively expound the verbal teachings;

understanding all phenomena as being free from desire and reaching the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), they do not sever the bodhisattva path nor retreat from bodhisattva conduct. They constantly and diligently cultivate inexhaustible practices and enter with mastery into the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It is like drilling wood to produce fire; once the fire is produced, its applications are infinite.
The Bodhisattva Ajita (Unconquered) thus brings sentient beings to maturity; his work is inexhaustible, and he dwells eternally in the world without ceasing.

He is neither ultimate nor non-ultimate, neither grasping nor non-grasping, neither dependent nor independent, neither worldly phenomena nor Buddha-dharma, neither an ordinary person nor one who has attained the fruit. It is difficult for a bodhisattva to achieve such a state.

When the mind practices the bodhisattva conduct, it does not speak of the Dharma of the two vehicles, nor does it speak of the Buddha-dharma; it does not speak of the mundane, nor does it speak of mundane dharmas;
it does not speak of sentient beings, nor does it speak of the absence of sentient beings; it does not speak of defilement, nor does it speak of purity. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are without stain and without grasping, neither turning forward nor retreating. Regarding the bodhisattva...
When practicing within such a dharma that is tranquil, subtle, profound, and supreme, one likewise does not give rise to the thought:
"I am currently practicing this path," "I have practiced this path," or "I shall practice this path.

One does not cling to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*), nor to the internal world, the external world, or the internal-external world; rather, all great vows, the *pāramitās*, and all phenomena [are understood as they truly are].

There is no attachment. Why is this? Within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is no dharma named "proceeding toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas" or "proceeding toward the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas";
there is no dharma named "proceeding toward the vehicle of the bodhisattvas" or "proceeding toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)";

there is no dharma named "proceeding toward the realm of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-dhātu)"; and there is no dharma named "proceeding toward defilement," "proceeding toward purity," "proceeding toward saṃsāra," or "proceeding toward nirvāṇa."

Why is this? Because all phenomena are neither dual nor non-dual. For example, just as space cannot be found—whether sought in the past, future, or present—within the ten directions, yet it is not that space does not exist;
so too, a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as being unfindable, yet it is not that all phenomena do not exist.
Thus, they are as they truly are, without difference, and they do not lose their functional efficacy.

They demonstrate the practice of all bodhisattva deeds without abandoning their great vows; they tame sentient beings, turn the wheel of the true Dharma, and do not destroy cause and effect, nor do they contradict the wondrous Dharma of equality.
They are equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, never severing the lineage of the Buddhas and never destroying the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
They penetrate deeply into the Dharma with inexhaustible eloquence; upon hearing the Dharma, they remain unattached, reaching the ultimate state.
They are well able to expound the profound depths of the Dharma; their minds are fearless; they do not abandon the dwelling of the Buddhas;
they do not contravene worldly laws; they manifest universally throughout the world yet remain unattached to the world.

Thus, these Bodhisattvas achieve rare wisdom and cultivate all practices, pulling sentient beings out from the three evil realms, teaching and taming them, and establishing them within the three periods of time.
Within the Buddha-way, one remains unshakable and further reflects: "The sentient beings of the world do not know how to repay kindness;
they instead harbor mutual enmity, are attached to false views, and are deluded, inverted, foolish, and ignorant.
Lacking wisdom and faith, they follow evil companions, giving rise to various forms of unwholesome insight. They are completely filled with craving, ignorance, and all manner of afflictions."

If the world were filled with those who know gratitude, possess intelligence and wisdom, and are good spiritual friends—those very places where I practice the bodhisattva path—I would not practice the bodhisattva path therein. Why?
Because toward sentient beings I have neither favoritism nor aversion, and I harbor no expectations; I do not seek even a single thread, a single hair’s breadth, or a single word of praise.

With these words, throughout all future kalpas, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices never for even a single thought-moment for their own sake, but solely desiring to deliver all sentient beings, causing them to become pure and forever attain liberation. Why is this?

For those who act as enlightened guides among sentient beings, the Dharma dictates that it must be so; they neither grasp nor seek anything for themselves, but practice the bodhisattva path solely for the sake of sentient beings.
The Way causes them to reach the secure further shore and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this is called the eighth difficult-to-attain practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

[Treatise] The eighth, the stage of difficult-to-attain practice (*durjayā*), has the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) as its essence and consists of seventy practices, which are divided into six sections:

1. From "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "the single nature of wholesome roots" (*ekasvabhāva-kuśalamūla*), there are four lines of verse that clarify the ten wholesome roots within this stage;
2. From "this Bodhisattva" down to "attaining non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*), there are eight [lines].
The section clarifying that there is no weariness in practicing for half a verse regarding suffering is divided into three parts:

first, from "This bodhisattva, having realized that sentient beings do not exist" down to "For what reason?"; second, the ten verses of practice clarifying the non-abandonment and non-attachment to the realm of sentient beings;
third, from "The bodhisattva has deeply entered the realm of sentient beings" down to "Not attaining the fruit," which consists of thirteen and a half verses.

The Sūtra clarifies that Bodhisattvas enter the realm of sentient beings without attachment yet without abandoning them, constantly manifesting their bodies within the world to deliver sentient beings;
this is the section for five Bodhisattvas who have thus achieved [their realization].

From here down to "without attachment to the world," nineteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on the mastery of teaching the Dharma through non-teaching for six Bodhisattvas. As it says:

From here below, down to the eighth section, "The Difficult-to-Attain Practice," there are fourteen and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the section on practicing the bodhisattva path without seeking karmic retribution.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of wholesome dharmas? This bodhisattva, for the sake of all..."
Because they have established a pool of the Dharma for cooling the world— including its devas, humans, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and gandharvas—

upholding the True Dharma so as not to sever the lineage of the Buddhas, and having attained the *dhāraṇī* of pure radiance; because they preach the Dharma and receive predictions with inexhaustible eloquence,
and having attained the *dhāraṇī* of the complete meaning, their analytical discernment of meaning is inexhaustible, whereby they attain awakening.

Because of the *dhāraṇī* of true dharmas, they attain inexhaustible eloquence regarding the Dharma; because of the *dhāraṇī* of the analysis of words and etymological explanations, they attain inexhaustible eloquence regarding language;
because of the *dhāraṇī* of the gate of unimpeded access to boundless phrases, inexhaustible meanings, and inexhaustible principles, they attain inexhaustible unimpeded eloquence;
and because their heads are consecrated by the *dhāraṇī* of the Buddha’s empowerment, they attain inexhaustible eloquence of joy.

Because of the *dhāraṇī* gate of awakening not through others, one attains inexhaustible radiance and eloquence; because of the *dhāraṇī* gate of identical eloquence, one attains inexhaustible identical eloquence;
because of the *dhāraṇī* gate of etymological interpretation within the various bodies of meaning, phrases, and syllables, one attains inexhaustible interpretive eloquence;
and because of the *dhāraṇī* of the boundless revolution, one attains boundless eloquence.
Exhausting this bodhisattva’s firm great compassion to universally gather all sentient beings, they manifest golden bodies throughout the trichiliocosm to perform Buddha-works;
according to the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all beings, they use their broad and long tongues to manifest immeasurable sounds within a single voice,
preaching the Dharma at the appropriate time to cause all to rejoice— even if there were those who were [otherwise] impossible...
He speaks of the various karmic retributions as countless sentient beings gather together in one place;

that assembly is so vast it fills unspeakably many worlds. Within that assembly, the Bodhisattva sits, and every single being therein possesses unspeakably many *asaṃkhyeya* mouths, each of which can produce hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* sounds simultaneously.

At that time, the Bodhisattva is able, within a single thought-moment, to receive and respond to the various distinct voices and different questions of all those present, thereby eliminating their doubts and perplexities;
as it is in one assembly, so it is likewise in assemblies as numerous as the unspeakably many.
Furthermore, suppose that from every single hair-tip, in every thought-moment, there were produced unspeakably many...
It may be said that at every single hair-tip within this assembly of the site of enlightenment, it is likewise so throughout all future kalpas;

though those kalpas may come to an end, the assembly never ends. Within each moment of thought, this Bodhisattva is able to receive and comprehend the various words and diverse questions of all these assemblies, without fear, without timidity, and without doubt.

Without error, one forms this thought: "Even if all sentient beings were to come together and question me with such verbal actions, I would expound the Dharma for them without interruption or exhaustion, causing them all to rejoice and abide in the wholesome paths;
furthermore, I would enable them to skillfully understand all speech and discourse, preaching various teachings for sentient beings while remaining without any discrimination regarding words."
Even if unspeakably many varieties of words and phrases were used to pose difficult questions, they would all be comprehended in a single thought-moment and answered in a single voice,
universally causing awakening without exception; for they have attained the consecration of omniscience,
have attained the treasury of non-obstruction, and have attained the perfect radiance of all dharmas, being fully endowed with everything.

O Son of the Buddha, because of this wisdom of wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, having established himself in the practice of wholesome dharmas, is able to purify himself and also universally benefit all sentient beings through the skillful means of non-attachment;
yet he does not perceive any sentient being who attains liberation. Just as it is in this trichiliocosm, so it is even up to...
It is unspeakable that he transforms his body into golden color, becomes endowed with wondrous sounds, and performs the work of a Buddha without obstruction regarding all phenomena.
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes ten kinds of bodies, namely:
the body that enters the boundless Dharma-realm, which is non-destination because it extinguishes all worlds; the body that enters the... [the rest of the text follows].
It is the body that arises throughout all realms of existence within the boundless Dharma-realm; it is the non-arising body because it abides in the equality of the non-arisen Dharma;
it is the non-ceasing body because all expressions of cessation are unattainable; it is the non-substantial body because it attains suchness;
it is the non-false body because it manifests in accordance with conditions; it is the non-transmigrating body because it is free from dying here and being born there; it is the indestructible body.

Because the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is indestructible, it is the body of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇakāya*); because the pathways of speech throughout the three periods of time are severed, it is the body without characteristics (*alakṣaṇakāya*);
and because it is well able to discern the characteristics of phenomena, the Bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of bodies.

For the sake of all sentient beings, they serve as a shelter and nurture all roots of goodness; for the sake of all sentient beings, they act as a savior, causing them to attain great peace and security.
Therefore, they act as a refuge for all sentient beings, providing them with a great place of reliance;
they act as guides for all sentient beings, enabling them to attain unsurpassed liberation; they act as teachers for all sentient beings, leading them into the true Dharma;
they act as lamps for all sentient beings, causing them to clearly perceive the retribution of karma; they act as light for all sentient beings...
Because it illuminates the profound and wondrous Dharma, it serves as a torch for all three periods of time; because it causes the realization of the true Dharma, it serves as a light for all worlds;
because it causes entry into the Ground of Radiance, it serves as a clear manifestation of the Tathāgata’s sovereign power for all realms of existence.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s ninth practice of the wholesome Dharma.
The Bodhisattva dwells securely in this practice to serve as a cooling pool of Dharma for all sentient beings, for it is able to exhaustively reach the source of all Buddha-dharmas.
[Treatise] The ninth, the Practice of Wholesome Dharmas, has the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its essence; within this section, it is divided into...
Section Five: From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the *dhāraṇī* of revolving," there are twelve lines of scripture clarifying the division on the inexhaustible eloquence (*ananta-pratibhāna*).

This is divided into two parts. First, from "This Bodhisattva" down to "is likewise in all respects," there are nine and a half lines of scripture clarifying the division on the unimpeded eloquence of manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood throughout the great trichiliocosm. Third, furthermore... [text ends].

Next, from here down to "and performs the work of a Buddha," there are sixteen lines and a half of sūtra text clarifying the section on manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood by showing the body at a single hair-tip site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), as well as at all inexhaustible hair-tip sites and unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms.
This is divided into four parts for the sons of the Buddha. From "this bodhisattva" down to "is well able to observe the characteristics of phenomena" [is the first part].
There are six lines and a half of sūtra that clarify the ten kinds of mastery; having thus accomplished these ten kinds of bodies, the five bodhisattvas [attain] the source of all Buddha-dharmas.
Thereafter, there are ten lines and a half of sūtra that clarify the stage of being the locus of reliance for all sentient beings.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, what is the true practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva? This Bodhisattva accomplishes the foremost speech of truth;

as he speaks, so he acts, and as he acts, so he speaks. This Bodhisattva studies the true speech of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, enters the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and becomes equal to the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Having attained the non-dual speech of the Buddhas of the three periods of time and following the training of the Tathāgatas, this Bodhisattva achieves the perfection of wisdom.

He accomplishes the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible regarding sentient beings; the knowledge of the karmic retributions of the past, future, and present; the knowledge of the sharpness and dullness of the faculties;

the knowledge of various realms; the knowledge of various inclinations; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; and the [knowledge of] the meditative concentrations, liberations, and... [the threefold gateways].
He possesses the knowledge of the arising and non-arising of ignorance, defilement, and purity; the knowledge of recollecting past lives in all worlds; the knowledge of the divine eye;
and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, yet he does not abandon any of the bodhisattva practices. Why is this?
Because he desires to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to become completely pure. Furthermore, this bodhisattva gives rise to such a superior resolve: "If I do not..."
If all sentient beings were to abide in the unsurpassed path of liberation while I first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it would contradict my original vow; this is what ought not to be.
Therefore, I must first cause all sentient beings to attain unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa without remainder, and only then become a Buddha. Why is this so? Because... [it is not].
Sentient beings requested me to resolve my mind [on enlightenment], yet I have spontaneously become their uninvited friend;
wishing first to cause all sentient beings to fulfill their roots of goodness and achieve all-knowledge, I am therefore the most excellent.
Because I do not cling to any world, I am the most supreme. Because I abide in the stage of the unsurpassed Tamer, I am free from cataracts and liberated.
Because sentient beings are boundless, I have fulfilled my original vow; because my original vow has been accomplished, I am well-versed in skillful transformations;

because I am adorned with the merits of a bodhisattva, I am a true refuge; and because I am sustained by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not abandon his original vow, thereby attaining entry into the adornment of supreme wisdom to benefit all beings.
They cause all who are born to be fully satisfied, so that according to their original vows, they all attain ultimate fulfillment.
Within all phenomena, they possess sovereign wisdom, causing all sentient beings to universally attain purity. Moment by moment, they travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
moment by moment, they visit unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands; and moment by moment, they see unspeakably [unspeakable numbers of Buddhas].
It is unspeakable how all Buddhas and their adorned, pure lands manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgatas,
pervading the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space; yet this Bodhisattva manifests infinite bodies that universally enter the world without any dependence,
and within those bodies manifests all lands, all sentient beings, and all phenomena as one.

All Buddhas [know this]; these Bodhisattvas know the various conceptions, various desires, various understandings, various karmic retributions, and various roots of goodness of sentient beings, and manifest their bodies accordingly to subdue them.

They contemplate all Bodhisattvas as being like illusions, all phenomena as being like transformations, the appearance of a Buddha in the world as being like a shadow, and all worlds as being like dreams.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the inexhaustible treasury of the body of meaning and the body of letters, who possess mastery over right mindfulness,

who have definitively realized and thoroughly understood all phenomena with supreme wisdom, who enter all samādhis, and who abide in the true nature of reality on the stage of non-duality and single essence,
practice such tranquility through the cultivation of great compassion for all sentient beings who are attached to duality.
By means of the Dharma of cessation, they attain the ten powers of a Buddha and enter the Indra-net Dharma-realm;
they achieve the Tathāgata’s unimpeded liberation and let out the great lion’s roar among men; they attain fearlessness and are able to turn the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma;
they attain wisdom-liberation and thoroughly understand all worldly realms, severing the revolving stream of birth and death.
Entering the great ocean of wisdom to protect and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time for the sake of all sentient beings,
and reaching the ultimate source of the reality-mark of the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas— once Bodhisattvas abide in this practice of truth, all those in the world,
including devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, and asuras, who draw near to them, [shall find...]
To cause all to attain awakening, joy, and purity is called the tenth true practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] The tenth true practice has the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) as its essence. Within this section, it is divided into three parts.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards until "causing all to be purified," there are ten lines of sūtra that clarify this.
The Bodhisattva on this stage trains in the truthful body, speech, and wisdom of all Buddhas of the three times and attains a portion of the ten kinds of Buddha-wisdom.

This is divided into two parts. From the passage beginning "This bodhisattva, having further generated such a superior resolve" down to the end of the Dharma-realm and the space-realm, there are sixteen lines and a half of scripture clarifying how, through the power of his vows, he teaches and transforms sentient beings without yet taking up full enlightenment.
Third, from this point down to the tenth stage, the Stage of True Practice (*bhūmi*), seventeen lines of scripture clarify the section on the mastery of containing all lands within one's own body,
knowing the faculties of beings, and benefiting living beings.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions shook in six ways—namely, shaking, universal shaking, and total universal shaking; rising, universal rising, and total universal rising; leaping, universal leaping, and total universal leaping;
trembling, universal trembling, and total universal trembling; roaring, universal roaring, and total universal roaring; and crashing, universal crashing, and total universal crashing.
Raining down exquisite celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial powdered incense, celestial garlands, celestial robes, celestial jewels, and celestial ornaments;

playing celestial music, emitting celestial radiance, and proclaiming the subtle and wondrous voices of the devas—just as these supernatural transformations were manifested while the Dharma of the Ten Practices was being taught in the Yāma Heaven palace of this world, so it was likewise in all the worlds of the ten directions. Furthermore...

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there came a multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, who filled the ten directions.
They addressed the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, excellent, excellent! You are truly able to expound upon the practices of all bodhisattvas."
In all those worlds that share the same name as this—Guṇakānanā—and which are all called Guṇadhvaja, the Tathāgatas therein all share the same name as this one, Samantaguṇa.

In our Buddha-fields as well, we have preached this Dharma; the assemblies, the retinues, the terminology, and the underlying principles are exactly like this, without any increase or decrease. O Son of the Buddha, we have all come here sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power.
"Having entered this assembly, I shall bear witness for you; it is likewise throughout all the worlds of the ten directions.
[Treatise] From here on, within the section concerning the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship, there are fifteen lines of scripture. The meaning is divided into three parts:
first, from "At that time" down to "the subtle and wonderful sounds of the heavens," there are five and a half lines of scripture clarifying the shaking of the earth.

The section on "Arising Offerings" is divided into two parts. From "In this world" down to "all are likewise," there is one and a half lines of scripture that clarify how it is the same throughout the ten directions.

This is divided into three parts. Furthermore, from "By the Buddha's spiritual power" down to "the worlds of the ten directions are all likewise," there are eight lines of scripture that clarify the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma of the ten directions.

The assembly gathers for the section on the realization of the fruit: outside worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields, all named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merits), in order to clarify that the ten practices are universally pervasive;
the Buddha’s name is Samantaguṇa (Universal Merit) in order to clarify that this universal pervasiveness of the ten practices is itself merit.
The pervasiveness of virtue is precisely the fruit attained within this stage, for it is the merit summoned by the pervasiveness of practice;

thus, the Buddha is titled "Universal Merit. To cite a number equal to the atoms of more than one hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions indicates that the dharmas reached by clear wisdom are likewise vast, as is the measure of the gate of clear practice—this is the Buddha-fruit.

The "Vastness of Merit" and the subsequent ten practices are categorized according to the ten *pāramitās* as the *Śengjin Jing* (Sutra on Advancement), which is already clearly detailed therein and need not be further explained.
These ten practices, taken as a whole, constitute a single moment of consciousness—a gateway of practice devoid of before or after.
One must not harbor views of temporal sequence or duration; rather, all must be understood through the essence and function of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
This constitutes the gateway to the cultivation of progress.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, universally surveyed all the assemblies throughout the ten directions,
extending to the entire Dharma-realm, desiring that the lineage of the Buddhas not be severed and desiring that the lineage of the Bodhisattvas be purified.
Therefore, they desire to cause the lineage of aspiration not to regress; they desire to cause the lineage of practice to continue perpetually;
they desire to cause the lineages of the three periods of time to be entirely equal; they desire to encompass the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they desire to open and expound upon all the roots of goodness that have been planted; they desire to observe all faculties; and they desire to resolve afflictions.
Because it is produced by the mental activities of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and because one desires to illuminate all the *bodhi* of the Buddhas, a verse is spoken.
[Treatise]: As it is said in the verses praising the Dharma, there are seven lines of sutra that clarify the non-interruption of the ten kinds of lineage (*gotra*);
thus, the verse reiterates this: "As far as the *dharmadhātu*. Here, "as far as" (*yāvat*) means "reaching" (*prāpti*); it means reaching the *dharmadhātu*.
[Sūtra] With a single mind, I pay reverent homage to the Honored One of Ten Powers,
whose stainless and pure vision perceives realms profound and far-reaching, beyond compare, who abides within the Way like empty space.
Those most supreme among humans in the past, Of immeasurable merit,
unattached, Courageous, foremost, and peerless— Those who have left the dust behind travel this path;
Now, throughout the lands of the ten directions, They are well able to expound the ultimate truth.
Free from all faults and most pure, those who are without reliance travel this path;
All future lions among men will travel everywhere throughout the dharma-realm.
Having already given rise to the great compassion of all Buddhas, those benefactors travel this path.
The peerless Honored Ones of the three times naturally extinguish the darkness of ignorance;
in all phenomena they are equal. Those of great power who practice this path universally perceive immeasurable and boundless realms, including all states of existence and all destinies.
Having seen this, their minds do not engage in discrimination; those who are unshakable travel this path.

They clearly understand all that exists within the dharma-realm, and in the ultimate truth, they are most pure, having forever destroyed hatred, pride, and delusion. Those possessed of such merit travel this path.
They skillfully discern all sentient beings and enter entirely into the true nature of the dharma-realm;
they awaken spontaneously without depending on others.
Those empty ones travel this path, exhausting all empty lands throughout every realm, going everywhere to preach the Dharma and extensively employ parables.
The purity described cannot be destroyed; that supreme Muni practices this path with full perfection, firm and non-retrogressive.
Having accomplished the venerable and most excellent Dharma, through inexhaustible power of aspiration he reaches the further shore. This is the path traveled by those who have practiced well.
He can know and see, without exception, all infinite and boundless stages, their vast and profound,
wondrous realms; he clearly understands every word and meaning of the path traveled by that Lion of Debaters, and he utterly subdues all opposing arguments.
Having attained certainty in the Dharma and being free from all doubt, that Great Muni follows this path;

having distanced himself from all worldly faults and afflictions, he universally bestows peace and happiness upon all sentient beings and acts as an incomparable, peerless guide. That one of supreme virtue traverses this very path.
Constantly bestowing the gift of fearlessness upon sentient beings, causing all to rejoice;
their minds are pure and free from defilement. That peerless one practices this path;
their mental karma is pure and perfectly disciplined, free from all conceptual proliferation and verbal faults.
With majestic light perfected and revered by all, that most excellent one follows this path;
entering the true meaning, they reach the further shore. Abiding in the state of merit, their mind is eternally tranquil;
protected by the Buddhas’ mindfulness, they are never forgotten. Those who have extinguished existence follow this path.

Distant from the self and free from affliction, he constantly proclaims the True Dharma with a great voice that pervades all lands throughout the ten directions. That peerless one practices this path;
his perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is already fulfilled, and he is adorned with the marks and signs of a hundred merits.
All sentient beings who see them rejoice; those of supreme wisdom practice this path.
The ground of knowledge is profoundly deep and difficult to enter;
yet they are able to dwell their minds well with sublime wisdom, ultimately unshakable. Those of steadfast conduct practice this path.
They are able to enter all that exists within the dharma-realm; wherever they enter, they reach ultimate perfection.

Their supernormal powers are sovereign and all-encompassing. Those peerless Great Munis who practice this path of the light of Dharma diligently cultivate samādhi, which is free from dualistic characteristics.
With the mind always in meditative concentration and delighting in tranquility, those who see all universally traverse this path;
they penetrate subtle and vast lands, each distinct from the other,
fully understanding them according to their respective realms— those kings of the mountain of wisdom traverse this path.
The mind is ever luminous and pure, free from all defilements; Within the three realms, there is no attachment.
Upholding all precepts, they reach the further shore; These pure-minded ones practice this path.
Their wisdom is boundless and ineffable, Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Skillfully training and dwelling therein, those of adamantine wisdom traverse this path—
the realm of all Buddhas of the three times— entering it with wisdom so thoroughly and universally that they never for a moment give rise to weariness; such supreme beings traverse this path.
Skillfully able to discern the Dharma of the ten powers, Thoroughly knowing all paths leading to every destination,

With unimpeded mastery over the body of karmic action, That one of meritorious body practices this path throughout The infinite and boundless realms of the ten directions; All sentient beings therein—
I shall protect and never forsake them; those fearless ones who practice this path,
diligently cultivating all the Buddha-dharmas, with minds always vigorous and untiring,
purifying all worlds— those great dragon kings travel this path.

Knowing that the faculties of sentient beings are not the same, and that their inclinations and understandings are immeasurably diverse, they clearly penetrate all various realms. Those who enter universally travel this path;
to the infinite lands of the worlds in the ten directions, they go to take birth in them all, beyond all counting.
Never for a single moment did they give rise to weariness; those who rejoice travel this path.
Universally emitting immeasurable light from their distinct nets, they illuminate all worlds.
Wherever that light shines, it enters into the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); these of excellent wisdom travel this path.
Shaking the lands of the ten directions—countless billions of nayutas—he causes no sentient being to feel alarm or fear.
This is the path traversed by the Benefactor of the World;
he is well-versed in all methods of language and has reached the ultimate perfection in answering difficult questions and engaging in debate.
The wise and discerning know all things; this is the path traveled by those who are fearless.

Skillfully understanding the various lands—whether inverted or upright—they contemplate and analyze them to reach the ultimate, causing all beings to dwell upon the ground of the inexhaustible; this is the path traveled by those of supreme wisdom.
With immeasurable merits numbering in the nayutas, he has practiced all the perfections (pāramitās) for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way. This teacher of the world’s great treatises,
whose conduct is inexhaustible, possesses the foremost eloquence and roars the lion’s roar.
Universally causing all sentient beings to reach the other shore—this is the path traveled by those of pure mind.

It is the foremost dharma for the Buddhas’ consecration; having received this dharma, their crowns are consecrated and their minds dwell perpetually in the gateway of the True Dharma. Those of vast mind travel this path.
All sentient beings are immeasurably diverse; Thoroughly understanding their minds, they pervade them all.
Resolutely upholding the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, They are like Mount Sumeru as they practice this path.
Within each and every word and phrase, They universally manifest immeasurable sounds.
Causing those sentient beings to understand according to their kind—this is the path of unimpeded vision.
All dharmas of written characters and spoken language, wisdom skillfully enters them all without discrimination, abiding in the realm of reality;
this is the path traveled by those who have realized the nature of vision.

Abiding securely in the profound great ocean of Dharma, they are well able to seal and determine all phenomena, having realized the true gateway of the signlessness of dharmas. This is the path traveled by those who see reality;
they visit every single buddha-field throughout immeasurable and boundless eons.
Observing and contemplating without a moment’s pause—this is the path traveled by those who are untiring.
The various names of immeasurable and countless Tathāgatas, each distinct from the others, they clearly perceive all upon a single hair-tip; this is the path traveled by those of pure merit.
Upon the tip of a single hair, one sees all Buddhas, Their number being immeasurable and beyond description;

All realms of reality are likewise so. These sons of the Buddha, practicing this path, Throughout immeasurable, boundless, and countless eons, Perceive them all clearly within a single thought-moment.
Knowing that length and brevity have no fixed characteristic—this is the path of practice for those on the way of liberation;

it enables those who see it not to pass in vain. All plant the seeds of causes and conditions within the Buddha-dharma, yet their minds remain unattached to what they do. Such is the path practiced by those Most Victorious Ones.
For *nayuta* eons he constantly encounters Buddhas, Never for a single thought-moment does weariness arise;
His heart’s joy increases ever further. This is the path traversed by Akṣayamati (Amoghadarśin);
Throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, He has observed the realms of all sentient beings.
Never before have I seen a single sentient being who, like this steadfast man,
has practiced the path that cultivates an infinite treasury of merit and wisdom;
who universally acts as a cool pond of merit to benefit all living beings— that foremost person now walks this path.
All the various categories within the dharma-realm, Pervading space, beyond measure—
To know that they all abide in verbal expression Is the path traveled by this lion’s roar.
Within each and every samādhi, One universally enters countless samādhis.
He has reached the most profound and subtle depths of all Dharma gates; this one of the lunar disc has traversed this path, diligently cultivating the power of patience to reach the other shore.
Able to endure the most supreme dharma of quiescent extinction, his mind is equanimous and unshakable—this is the path traversed by those of boundless wisdom.
In a single world, at a single seat, their bodies remain unmoving and eternally tranquil,
yet they manifest their forms everywhere; those of boundless bodies practice this path,
causing all infinite and boundless lands to enter together into a single atom.
Universally encompassing all without obstruction, he whose boundless thoughts and conduct have mastered this path understands what is possible and what is impossible;
he is able to enter universally into all bases of power and achieves the supreme powers of the Tathāgata— this is the path traversed by that foremost power.
Throughout the past, future, and present, he fully understands with wisdom all the immeasurable and boundless karmic retributions;
this is the path traveled by those who possess thorough realization.
Having mastered the world’s proper and improper times, he tames all sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.
Complying with all that is appropriate without fail—this is the path traveled by those who have thoroughly understood.
Skillfully guarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, they always cause their practice to accord with the Dharma.
Free from all grasping and attachment, they subdue the hosts of Māras; this is the path traveled by those whose minds possess wisdom.
Having attained skillfulness regarding all phenomena, they are able to enter the state of equality that is suchness;
their eloquence in proclaiming the Dharma is inexhaustible. These practitioners of the Buddha-way have already perfected this gateway of dhāraṇī;
they are well-established in the treasury of non-obstruction.
Thoroughly penetrating all realms of phenomena, this is the path traveled by those who have entered deeply;
All Buddhas of the three times are entirely equal to them in mind and identical in wisdom;
Of one nature and one characteristic, without distinction—this is the path traveled by those of unimpeded lineage.
Having already torn away the film of all ignorance, They have entered deeply into the vast ocean of wisdom;
Universally bestowing the pure eye upon all sentient beings, This is the path traveled by those with eyes.
Having perfected the qualities of all Teachers, Their miraculous powers are equal and their conduct non-dual.
Attaining the sovereign power of the Tathāgata, this is the path traveled by those who have practiced well;
they roam throughout all worlds, universally raining down the boundless rain of the sublime Dharma,
causing all to attain definitive understanding of its meaning— this is the path traveled by those in the Cloud of Dharma stage.
One who can give rise to pure faith in the Buddha’s wisdom and liberation, never regressing,
and through that faith develop the faculty of wisdom— this is the path traveled by those who learn well;
such a one can, in a single thought-moment, fully comprehend all sentient beings without exception.
Having realized the nature of the minds of those sentient beings, they reach the realm of phenomena—the path traversed by those who have attained the absence of intrinsic nature.
To all the infinite lands throughout the dharma-realm, they are able to manifest emanations without number;
their bodies are most wondrous and peerless, transcending all comparison. This is the path traversed by those of incomparable conduct.
The Buddha-fields are boundless and beyond numbering, Within which dwell immeasurable Buddhas;
To all of them the Bodhisattvas appear before them, Approaching, making offerings, and engendering respect.
A Bodhisattva is able, with but a single body, To enter into samādhi and remain in tranquil concentration.
They cause one to see their bodies as infinite in number, each arising from samādhi;
The dwelling place of these Bodhisattvas is most profound and wondrous, And their conduct and deeds transcend all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Their minds are pure and always joyful, Able to cause all sentient beings to rejoice.
The various faculties and their skillful means are each distinct;
with wisdom, he clearly perceives them all and understands that these faculties have no basis.
He is able to skillfully distinguish the path for those who are difficult to tame through his skillful means, attaining mastery over all phenomena.
The worlds of the ten directions are each different, yet within them all they perform the work of Buddhas;

their faculties are subtle and their conduct likewise, as they can extensively preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings—who among those who hear it would not rejoice? Such is the path traversed within this void.
The eye of wisdom is pure and peerless, clearly seeing all phenomena as they are;
with such skillful discernment of wisdom, this is the path traveled by the Peerless One.
May all the inexhaustible and vast merit [accrued thereby] bring all spiritual practices to ultimate completion.
Causing all sentient beings to be entirely pure— this peerless one practices this path and universally exhorts others to cultivate it,
establishing the factors that assist the Way. Causing them all to dwell securely on the stage of skillful means,
he delivers countless sentient beings, yet never for a moment gives rise to the notion of "sentient beings."
Observing all capacities and conditions, he first protects their minds so that no strife arises;
he universally shows sentient beings the place of peace and security.
This is the path traversed by those of skillful means, who have accomplished the supreme, foremost wisdom and are endowed with immeasurable and boundless knowledge.
Fearless among the fourfold assembly, this is the path traversed by the wisdom of skillful means.
Able to enter universally into all worlds and all phenomena, attaining mastery therein,
they likewise enter into all assemblies to deliver countless sentient beings.
Throughout all lands in the ten directions, he beats the great Dharma drum to awaken all sentient beings;
as the supreme and unsurpassed master of Dharma-giving, this Immortal One practices this path,
sitting upright in the full lotus posture, filling immeasurable realms throughout the ten directions.
Yet his body remains unconfined; this is the path traversed by the Dharmakāya.
Within a single meaning and a single phrase, he can expound immeasurable and boundless teachings, the limits of which cannot be found; this is the path traversed by infinite wisdom.
Having well trained in the liberation of the Buddhas, They have attained Buddha-wisdom without obstruction;

Accomplishing fearlessness, they are heroes of the world. This is the path traveled by those of skillful means, Who thoroughly know the oceans of worlds in the ten directions, And also know the oceans of all Buddha-lands.
He fully understands the ocean of wisdom and the ocean of Dharma; all sentient beings who behold him rejoice.
He manifests entering the womb and his first birth, or he manifests attaining perfect enlightenment at the site of awakening;
thus he causes the world to see these things—all this is the path traversed by this Boundless One.
Within immeasurable billions of lands, he manifests his body entering nirvana;
yet in truth, he does not abandon his vows to return to quiescence. This Heroic Debater’s path is firm and subtle;
this wondrous single body is equal to the Buddha, without distinction.
According to the various different perceptions of all sentient beings, The path traversed by those of the single true body is the dharma-realm,
equal and without distinction; It is fully endowed with immeasurable and boundless meanings,
wherein one contemplates the single characteristic with an unmoving mind— This is the path traversed by the wise ones of the three periods of time.
Regarding all sentient beings and the Buddha-dharma, they establish and sustain them to ultimate perfection.
Possessing the power of retention equal to that of a Buddha, these supreme holders traverse this path;
their supernormal powers are unimpeded like those of a Buddha, and their divine eye is unobstructed and most pure.
The faculty of hearing is unimpeded, excellently perceiving all sounds;
this one possesses in full all supernatural powers that proceed from such unimpeded intent.
According to their wisdom, they achieve complete accomplishment, thoroughly knowing all things without peer; this is the path traveled by these wise and noble ones.
His mind is in right concentration, unwavering; his wisdom is vast and boundless.
He has clearly mastered all spheres of experience and has reached the further shore of all merits—the path traversed by all seers.
He is able to deliver sentient beings according to their respective order.
Their minds are ultimately never satiated; this is the path traversed by those who are ever-diligent.
All the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time—they know and see them all;
born from the lineage of the Tathāgatas, these sons of the Buddhas practice this path.
Having already perfected speech that accords with truth, they skillfully subdue discordant discourse;
always able to advance toward the Buddha’s Bodhi, this is the path traveled by those of boundless wisdom.
A single light shines forth, illuminating without limit, pervading all the lands throughout the ten directions.
Universally causing the world to attain great illumination—this is the path traversed by those who destroy darkness.
According to what is appropriate for manifestation, one should make offerings;
appearing as the pure body of a Tathāgata to teach and transform hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings, the adornment of Buddha-fields is likewise so.
To cause all sentient beings to transcend the world, They cultivate every sublime practice;
This conduct is vast and boundless— How could there be anyone able to know it?
Even if one were to manifest unspeakable numbers of bodies, Equal in extent to the dharma-realm and empty space.
Together they all extol his virtues, which could not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
the Bodhisattva’s merit is boundless, and he is fully endowed with all practices.
Even if immeasurable and infinite Buddhas were to speak for immeasurable kalpas, they could never finish describing them.

How much less could the gods and humans of the world, nor all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, ever reach the ultimate end in praising and extolling [the Buddha] throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas? [Treatise:
