Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, the *Lijing Hेलुन* (Compendium of Scriptural Exegesis), Chapter Twenty-Two: The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of this chapter, there are three sections as previously stated. First, concerning the explanation of the title: this treatise sets forth ten [inexhaustible treasuries].

The second explanation clarifies the purpose of this chapter: since the ten kinds of practice have already been explained in this stage, these ten inexhaustible treasuries (akṣaya-kośa) establish the dharmas of the aforementioned ten practices so as to render them inexhaustible;
they establish the dharmas of the subsequent ten dedications (pariṇāmanā) so as to cause one to progress toward them, ensuring that the gates of practice do not become obstructed. Therefore...
Regarding the intended meaning of this chapter as divided into three long sections, it is categorized into two gates: first, the intended meaning of the long sectioned scripture;
second, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. First, concerning the intended meaning of the long sectioned scripture:
within this single chapter of the scripture, there are eleven total segments of text corresponding to the titles of the ten *piṭakas*, as follows.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakanda addressed the other Bodhisattvas, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of treasuries (kośa) possessed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have spoken, will speak, and are now speaking. What are these ten?

They are: the treasury of faith, the treasury of ethical discipline, the treasury of shame, the treasury of remorse, the treasury of learning, the treasury of generosity, the treasury of wisdom, and the treasury of mindfulness."
The treasury of retention, the treasury of the Dharma, and the treasury of eloquence—these are the ten, O Son of the Buddha. What is the treasury of faith of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
This bodhisattva has faith that all phenomena are empty; faith that all phenomena are signless; faith that all phenomena are wishless;
faith that all phenomena are unconditioned; faith that all phenomena are non-conceptual; and faith that all phenomena are without basis.
They believe that all dharmas are immeasurable; they believe that all dharmas are unsurpassed; they believe that all dharmas are difficult to transcend;

and they believe that all dharmas are unarisen. If a bodhisattva can thus accord with all dharmas and give rise to pure faith, then upon hearing that the teachings of all Buddhas are inconceivable, their mind will not be cowed; and upon hearing that all Buddhas are... [incomparable].
His mind is not cowed when hearing that the realm of sentient beings is inconceivable; his mind is not cowed when hearing that the dharma-realm is inconceivable;
his mind is not cowed when hearing that the realm of empty space is inconceivable;
his mind is not cowed when hearing that the realm of nirvana is inconceivable; his mind is not cowed when hearing that the past world is inconceivable.
The mind of deliberation is not timid when hearing of the inconceivable future world;
the mind is not timid when hearing of the inconceivable present world; the mind is not timid when hearing of the inconceivable entry into all kalpas.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva possesses single-minded, firm faith in the Buddhas and knows the wisdom of the Buddhas.

In each and every one of the infinite and inexhaustible, immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable Buddhas who have already attained, are now attaining, or will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
those who have already appeared in the world, are now appearing, or will appear in the world; and those who have already entered *nirvāṇa*, are now entering, or will enter *nirvāṇa*. Those Buddhas...
Wisdom neither increases nor decreases, neither arises nor ceases, neither advances nor recedes, neither approaches nor retreats; it is without knowing and without abandoning.
When this bodhisattva enters the wisdom of the Buddha, they achieve boundless and inexhaustible faith.
Having attained this faith, their mind does not regress, their mind is not distracted, it cannot be destroyed, it is free from attachment, and it always possesses its fundamental root.
To accord with the noble ones, to dwell in the household of the Tathāgatas, to protect and sustain the lineage of all Buddhas, to increase the faith and understanding of all bodhisattvas,
to accord with the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, and to give birth to the skillful means of all Buddhas—
this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Treasury of Faith. When a bodhisattva dwells in this Treasury of Faith, they are then able to hear and retain [the teachings].
"All the Buddha-dharmas are taught for the sake of sentient beings so that they may all attain awakening.

[Treatise]: From the first section, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa" down to "taught for the sake of sentient beings so that they may all attain awakening," there are twenty-eight and a half lines of scripture that correctly enumerate the names of the ten inexhaustible treasuries.
Furthermore, the ten kinds of faith in the Dharma are presented; within this section, they are further divided into six parts:
First, from "At that time, Guṇakusuma" down to "this constitutes the tenth," fourteen lines of scripture clarify the section on the formal exposition of the names of the ten treasuries (daśakośa).
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "giving rise to pure faith," five and a half lines of scripture clarify the initial presentation.

The section on the ten kinds of faith in the Dharma is divided into three parts: first, from "having heard that the Buddha-dharmas are inconceivable" down to "for what reason," there are seven and a half lines of sūtra explaining how hearing the Dharma gives rise to faith; second, from "this bodhisattva" down to "without ignorance and without abandonment," there are five and a half lines of sūtra explaining how one does not become timid regarding the Dharma;
third, [the remaining portion]; fourth, from this point onward, there are five and a half lines of sūtra explaining the knowledge of all things.
The Buddha’s appearance in the world and entry into *nirvāṇa*—the division of taking up and discarding without distance or proximity—is fivefold.

From "this bodhisattva, having entered the wisdom of the Buddha" down to "the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas," there are four and a half lines of scripture clarifying the entry into this treasury of faith;

being born into the family of the Buddha and conforming to the skillful means of the roots of goodness of all Buddhas constitutes the sixth division. This is called the Bodhisattva [having already attained].
The following one and a half lines of scripture clarify the concluding summary of the section on the ability to expound the Dharma through the perfection of faith;
this faith refers to the faith within the stage of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), for Mañjuśrī, Buddhamati, and the others represent the faith of the stage of the ten faiths (*daśaśraddhā*).

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of precepts of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva? This Bodhisattva accomplishes the precept of universal benefit; the precept of non-acceptance; the precept of non-abiding;
the precept of freedom from regret; the precept of freedom from contention; the precept of non-affliction; the precept of freedom from impurity;
the precept of freedom from covetous seeking; the precept of freedom from transgression; and the precept of non-violation. What is meant by 'universal'?"
Regarding the precept of benefiting others: this bodhisattva upholds pure precepts primarily for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
What is meant by "not receiving the precepts"? This bodhisattva does not receive or practice any of the various precepts of external paths;
rather, being naturally diligent, they uphold the equal and pure precepts of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the three periods of time. What is meant by "not abiding in the precepts"?
When a bodhisattva upholds the precepts, the mind does not dwell in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Why is this? Because they uphold the precepts without seeking rebirth in those realms. What is meant by "precepts without regret"?
This bodhisattva constantly dwells in a state of mind free from regret. Why is this? Because they do not commit grave offenses and do not practice deceit or hypocrisy.

Because he does not break the pure precepts, how is it that he possesses the precept of non-contention? This bodhisattva does not reject what was previously established, nor does he innovate new rules;
his mind always conforms to and inclines toward the precepts of nirvāṇa. He fully receives and maintains them without any transgression.
He does not trouble other sentient beings by means of his observance of the precepts so as to cause them suffering; rather, he wishes for all to have a mind of constant joy.

Regarding the observance of the precepts, what constitutes the precept of non-harming? This bodhisattva does not, for the sake of the training in precepts, practice incantations or prepare medicinal formulas to harm sentient beings;
rather, they observe the precepts solely for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings.
What constitutes the precept of non-mixture? This bodhisattva does not cling to extreme views nor maintain mixed precepts, but observes only...
Regarding the precept of upholding renunciation through dependent origination: what is the precept of being free from craving?
It is when this bodhisattva does not manifest unusual signs to display their own virtues, but rather upholds the precepts solely for the sake of fulfilling the dharma of renunciation.
What is the precept of being free from fault? It is when this bodhisattva does not become arrogant by saying, "I uphold the precepts," nor do they look down upon those who have broken the precepts.
To disparage others merely to cause them shame is to hold the precepts with a single-minded focus. What constitutes the absence of transgression in the precepts?
This bodhisattva permanently abandons killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter;
they possess and fully uphold the ten types of wholesome karma. When this bodhisattva maintains these untransgressed precepts:
One should form this thought: "All sentient beings who violate the pure precepts do so due to perversion;
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know by what causes and conditions sentient beings give rise to perversion and violate the pure precepts.
I shall attain unexcelled bodhi and extensively preach the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may be free from perversion. This is called a Bodhisattva.
The second treasury of precepts of the Mahāsattva.
[Treatise]: Regarding the section from "What is the second treasury of bodhisattva precepts for the sons of the Buddha?
down to "this is called the second treasury of precepts of the bodhisattva," there are twenty-eight and a half lines of sūtra within this passage, which is further divided.

Regarding the section from "A single son of the Buddha" down to "no violation of the precepts," there are three and a half lines of scripture that clarify the formal enumeration of the ten names of the precepts;

this is divided into two parts. From "What are they? down to "ten kinds of wholesome karma," there are twenty-one lines of scripture that clarify the formal exposition of the observance and violation of these ten kinds of precepts; this is divided into three parts. [In this section,] the Bodhisattva maintains these...
In the second treasury of precepts, four and a half lines of sūtra clarify the section on how these ten practices of a bodhisattva’s observance of morality are free from violation:
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of moral shame of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? This bodhisattva recollects the past..."
Feeling shame for all the evils one has committed, that bodhisattva reflects within his own mind:
"Since beginningless time, I and all sentient beings have been each other’s fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, sons, and daughters;
because we were possessed of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, flattery, deceit, and all other afflictions, we have harmed one another and oppressed one another."

They plunder, commit adultery, inflict injury, and kill; there is no evil they do not create. All sentient beings are likewise thus, fully committing all manner of evils through their various afflictions.
For this reason, each does not revere, respect, obey, humble themselves before, instruct, or protect one another;
instead, they mutually slaughter and harm each other, becoming enemies to one another.
I reflect upon myself and all sentient beings of the past, future, and present who practice the gradual-lessening dharma;
there are no Buddhas of the three times who do not know and see this. If I do not now sever this conduct of shamelessness, the Buddhas of the three times will likewise behold me.
How could I continue to act without ceasing? This is utterly unacceptable. Therefore, I should single-mindedly sever it.
To realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment and to extensively expound the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s third treasury of shame.
[Treatise] From "O Son of the Buddha" below down to the third section on the treasury of shame (*hrī-kośa*), there are thirteen and a half lines of sūtra.

Within this passage, it is further divided into two parts: first, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "should exclusively and with focused mind abandon [it]," there are twelve lines of sūtra clarifying the abandonment of shameless conduct (*āhrīkya*) and the possession of the conduct of shame (*hrī*); this is further divided into two, with one and a half lines.
The Sūtra clarifies the section on being fully endowed with shame (*hrī*) and skillfully preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s sense of shame (*apatrāpya*)? This Bodhisattva reflects with self-reproach:
'In the past, I have greedily sought after various objects of the five desires without ever feeling satisfied; because of this, my greed, anger, and delusion have increased.'"
"I should no longer engage in such actions as these afflictions; furthermore, I reflect that sentient beings, lacking wisdom, give rise to various afflictions and fully practice unwholesome dharmas.
They do not show mutual respect or honor, even going so far as to become enemies and adversaries to one another.
They commit every kind of evil without exception, and having done so, they rejoice, pursue it, and praise it."
Blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, one knows nothing and sees nothing;
entering the mother’s womb to receive birth, one forms a body of filth that ultimately reaches the stage of white hair and wrinkled face.
One who possesses wisdom observes that this is merely an impure phenomenon born from lust, which all Buddhas of the three periods have fully known and seen. If I were still to practice this even now—
To act otherwise would be to deceive the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

therefore, I shall practice shame and quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and extensively preach the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings—this is called the fourth treasury of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the Treasury of Shame.
[Treatise] Regarding the section from "O Son of the Buddha" (buddhaputra) onwards to "this is called the bodhisattva’s treasury of shame," there are twelve lines of scripture.

Within this, the general meaning is further divided into three parts: 1. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "furthermore practices these matters," there are three lines of scripture clarifying the first aspect:
self-reflecting on how one has long harbored greed for the objects of the five desires since beginningless time. 2. [The second part follows. 3. [The third part follows.]

Furthermore, having formed this thought, down to "I shall practice conscientiousness" (*hrī*), there are seven lines of sutra that clarify how sentient beings are deluded and act as mutual enemies for the sake of the five desires; the Bodhisattva, knowing this, should sever [these bonds] himself.
Following "swiftly attaining bodhi," there are one and a half lines of sutra that skillfully explain the truth to sentient beings.
Section on the Dharma.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s treasury of hearing?
It is when this Bodhisattva knows that because this exists, that exists; because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this arises, that arises.
Through the cessation of this, that ceases. These are mundane phenomena, supramundane phenomena, conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, determinate phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena.
What is it that, through the existence of this, that exists? It is that through the existence of ignorance, volitional formations exist.
What is it that, through the non-existence of this, that does not exist? It is that through the non-existence of consciousness... [and so forth].
Therefore, name-and-form [arise]. What is it that arises? It is because this thing arises that that thing arises; namely, because craving arises, suffering arises. What is it that ceases?
It is because this thing ceases that that thing ceases; namely, because existence ceases, birth ceases. What are mundane phenomena?
They are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. What are supramundane phenomena? They are ethical discipline and meditative concentration.

Regarding the liberation through wisdom and the knowledge and vision of liberation: what are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are the realms of sentient beings within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)? They are space, nirvāṇa, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the abiding nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). What are determinate phenomena (*vyākṛta-dharma*)? They are the Four Noble Truths. The four...

The fruits of śrāmaṇya, the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga). What are the indeterminate dharmas?
They are: the world is finite, the world is infinite, the world is both finite and infinite, and the world is neither finite nor infinite.
The world is eternal; the world is non-eternal; the world is both eternal and non-eternal; the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata exists; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata does not exist; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist;
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist. The self and sentient beings exist; the self and sentient beings do not exist.
Do I and sentient beings exist, or do they not exist? Are I and sentient beings neither existent nor non-existent?
How many Tathāgatas entered parinirvāṇa in the past, and how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas entered parinirvāṇa?

How many Tathāgatas, how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and how many sentient beings will there be in the future? How many Buddhas currently abide, and how many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are there now?
How many sentient beings does the Buddha abide with? In what manner do they abide? Which Tathāgata appeared first?
Which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas appeared first? Which sentient beings appeared first? Which Tathāgata appeared last?
Which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas appeared last? Which sentient beings appeared last? What dharma was at the very beginning?
The Dharma is supreme. Regarding the world: from where does it come? Where does it go? What exists within it?
How many worlds are formed? How many worlds are destroyed? From where do worlds come? Where do they go?
What is the initial limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*)? What is the final limit of birth and death? These are called the indeterminate dharmas (*avyākṛta-dharma*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
He forms this thought: "All sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death lack extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) and are unable to comprehend these all-encompassing dharmas.

I shall now resolve my mind to uphold the treasury of extensive learning, realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and expound the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is called the fifth [perfection] of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Extensive Learning.
The Treasury of Hearing.
[Treatise] From the fifth "Son of the Buddha" downward, up to the "Treasury of Hearing," thirty-four lines and a half of sūtra clarify the Treasury of Hearing;
within this section, it is further divided into three parts: first, from "Son of the Buddha" downward to the "unconditioned dharmas" (avyākṛta-dharma).
There are four sections of sūtra that clarify the division between the existence and non-existence of ten matters. What are they?

From "These matters exist" down to "This is called the indeterminate dharma," there are twenty-six and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the formal exposition of the existence and non-existence of the ten kinds of matters.

First, from the perspective of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is taught that because ignorance exists, formations exist; because consciousness does not exist, [formations do not exist].

Because name-and-form arise from craving, suffering arises; because existence ceases, birth ceases. Regarding these four matters above—consciousness and craving—both arise from the false conceptualizations of ignorance regarding all forms of existence (*bhava*).
Now, realizing that the root of existence is non-existent, the twelve links of dependent origination cease.
The cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination does not mean that existence is produced by wisdom or that existence is extinguished by wisdom; it simply means removing the illness.
That wisdom is without dependence, without form, and unconditioned, yet it is spiritually pervasive throughout all phenomena; it manifests without thought and is accomplished without action.
Those who study it must first perfect the practice of the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* before they can realize this single principle.

The ten subsequent methods are presented in their entirety according to the complete teachings of the Sage, detailing the various interpretations regarding the counteractive measures for the correspondence between consciousness and its objects, as explained below in accordance with the text.

Having completed the section on the three Bodhisattvas possessing clear wisdom, the following four lines of the sūtra clarify the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of all sentient beings who lack the wisdom of extensive learning;
this is the section on his seeking the treasury of extensive learning and extensively preaching the Dharma for them.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of giving of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva practices ten kinds of giving, namely:

giving by apportioning, exhaustive giving, internal giving, external giving, internal-and-external giving, universal giving, giving of the past, giving of the future, giving of the present, and ultimate giving.
O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva’s giving by apportioning?
This bodhisattva is by nature compassionate and fond of practicing wise giving. If he obtains delicious food, he does not consume it alone;
he must first give it to sentient beings before he himself eats. This applies to all things he receives. When he eats, he reflects thus:
"Within my body dwell eighty thousand families of worms who depend upon me for their existence. May my body’s fullness and pleasure benefit them."
"I shall satisfy my own hunger and suffering, for they too suffer from hunger. Now, as I partake of this food and drink that I possess, may all sentient beings everywhere obtain full satisfaction.
For the sake of giving to them, I eat this myself, not craving its flavor. Furthermore, he reflects:
"Throughout the long night, out of attachment to my body, I have accepted food and drink merely to satisfy it; now [I shall do otherwise]."
By giving this food as a gift to sentient beings, may I forever sever all craving and attachment toward my own body; this is called "the gift of partial reduction.

What is the "exhaustive gift" of a bodhisattva? O Son of the Buddha, if this bodhisattva obtains various superior flavors of food and drink, perfumes, flowers, clothing, and articles of livelihood, and were he to enjoy them himself, he would live in peace and longevity; yet if he were to set them aside...
If one gives to others, one will suffer poverty, misery, and an early death. At such times, there may be someone who comes and says, "Whatever you currently possess, you must give it all to me.

The Bodhisattva reflects: "Since beginningless time, because of hunger, I have lost my body countless times, yet I have never been able to benefit sentient beings even by so much as a hair’s breadth to obtain any wholesome merit. Now, I too—"

One should be as one was in the past when relinquishing one's life; therefore, for the benefit of sentient beings, one should give away everything one possesses according to their needs, even unto the exhaustion of one's life without any regret—this is called the "exhaustive giving.
What is the internal giving of a Bodhisattva? O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva, being in the prime of youth, handsome and beautiful, with fragrant flowers...
Adorning his body with garments, he was first consecrated to the rank of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin); possessing the seven treasures, he ruled over the four continents.
At that time, someone came and addressed the King, saying: "Great King, you should know that I am now aged and infirm, afflicted by a grave illness;
I am solitary and exhausted, and my death will not be long delayed. If I might obtain from the King’s body some blood, flesh, head, or eyes—"

"The marrow is my very life; I must surely hope for its survival. I only pray that Your Majesty will not further deliberate or have any lingering hesitation, but look upon me with compassion and grant it to me. At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"Now this body of mine shall inevitably die; there is no benefit whatsoever [in keeping it]. It is fitting that I should quickly give it up at this moment to save sentient beings. Having reflected thus, he spoke.
To give with a mind free from regret is called internal giving (*adhyātma-dāna*). What is the external giving (*bāhya-dāna*) of a Bodhisattva?

O Son of the Buddha, suppose this Bodhisattva is in the prime of his youth, possessed of a beautiful complexion and endowed with all the marks of excellence; he adorns his body with famous flowers and superior garments.

Having just received the consecration to the rank of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), he possesses the seven treasures and rules over the four continents. At that time, someone might come and say to him:

The king said, "I am now impoverished and oppressed by manifold sufferings; I only pray that you, out of benevolence and compassion, will take pity on me and relinquish this royal throne to provide for me.
I shall then govern it and enjoy the blessings of kingship. At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"All prosperity must inevitably decline; when the time of decline comes, one can no longer bring further benefit."
"Sentient beings, I should now fulfill their wishes according to what they seek. Having formed this thought, he immediately bestows them upon them without any regret;
this is called external giving. What is the internal and external giving of a Bodhisattva?
Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva, as previously described, occupies the station of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), endowed with the seven treasures and ruling over the four continents—
Then, someone came and addressed him, saying: "I have long occupied this position of a Wheel-Turning King, yet I have never attained it.
I only pray that Your Majesty will relinquish it to me, and that you yourself shall become my minister. At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"My body, my wealth, and even my royal throne are all impermanent phenomena subject to decay and destruction."
Now, when one is in the prime of youth and possesses the wealth of the world, and a beggar appears before them, they should think:

"I must seek the firm dharma through that which is not firm," and having formed this thought, they immediately bestow it—even to the point of personally and diligently performing menial labor without any regret in their heart.
This is called the giving of both internal and external things. What is the universal giving of a bodhisattva? O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva is also as described above.
It is said that when a Wheel-Turning King, endowed with the seven treasures, ruled over the four continents, there were immeasurable impoverished people who came before him and spoke thus:
"Great King, your fame is heard throughout the ten directions; we have come here out of admiration for your reputation.
We each now have a specific request; we pray that you will universally bestow your compassion so that our wishes may be fulfilled."

At that time, when various poor people beg from that great king for his kingdom, or his wife and children, or his hands, feet, blood, flesh, heart, lungs, head, eyes, marrow, or brain, the Bodhisattva then forms this thought in his mind:
"All unions of affection must inevitably end in separation; yet these things bring no benefit to sentient beings. I now desire to renounce all craving forever."
With love, [the Bodhisattva] reflects: "All these things must inevitably disperse; let them fulfill the wishes of sentient beings.
Having formed this thought, they give everything away with a heart free from regret, and they do not give rise to weariness or contempt for sentient beings.
This is called "giving all. What is the past giving of a Bodhisattva? When this Bodhisattva hears of all the merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past...

Having heard this, Virtue does not become attached; he thoroughly realizes that things do not exist, does not give rise to conceptual discrimination, and neither craves nor relishes them, nor does he seek to grasp them.

He has no dependence or reliance, seeing all phenomena as like dreams, lacking any solidity. Regarding all roots of goodness, he does not give rise to the notion of existence, nor does he rely upon them;
rather, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings who cling to grasping, he expounds them in order to bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity.
Furthermore, it is said that one observes all past phenomena and seeks them throughout the ten directions, finding them entirely unobtainable.
Having formed this thought, one ultimately relinquishes all past phenomena; this is called "past giving. What is the "future giving" of a bodhisattva?
This bodhisattva hears of the practices cultivated by future Buddhas and, having thoroughly understood that they do not exist, does not grasp at them.
They do not differentiate among signs, nor do they delight in being reborn in the various Buddha-fields; they neither savor nor cling to them, nor do they give rise to aversion.
They do not dedicate their roots of goodness toward those realms, nor do they allow their roots of goodness to regress because of them.

Rather, they constantly and diligently practice without ever abandoning them, desiring only to gather in sentient beings by means of those very objects, teaching them the truth to bring them to maturity.
The Buddha-dharma is thus: this Dharma has no location, nor is it without a location; it is neither internal nor external, neither near nor far.
Furthermore, one should reflect: if a phenomenon does not exist, it cannot but be relinquished; this is called "future giving. What is the "present giving" of a bodhisattva?
This bodhisattva hears [the teachings] from the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the Brahmā Heaven, Brahmakāyika Heaven, Brahmapurohita Heaven, Brahmakāyika-sabhāgata Heaven, Mahābrahmā Heaven; Ābhāsvara Heaven, Parīttābha Heaven, Apramāṇābha Heaven, Ābhāsvara-sabhāgata Heaven;
Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, Parīttaśubha Heaven, Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, Śubhakṛtsna-sabhāgata Heaven; Bṛhatphala Heaven, Parīttabṛhatphala Heaven, Apramāṇa... [Heaven].

Having heard that the gods of the Vast Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*), the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*), the Unafflicted Heaven (*Avṛha*), the Heatless Heaven (*Atapa*), the Good-to-See Heaven (*Sudṛśa*), the Good-Appearing Heaven (*Sudarśana*),

and the Ultimate Form Heaven (*Akaniṣṭha*), as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, possess such perfected merit— and having heard this, their minds are neither deluded nor submerged, neither gathered nor dispersed,
but simply contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being like dreams, unreal, and devoid of craving— this is for the sake of sentient beings.

To abandon the states of woe, to cultivate the bodhisattva path with a mind free from conceptual discrimination, and to expound the teachings for the sake of accomplishing the Buddha-dharma—this is called the gift of the present. What is the ultimate gift of a bodhisattva?
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were immeasurable sentient beings, some of whom lacked eyes, some lacked ears, and others lacked noses, tongues, or hands.
He came to where the Bodhisattva was and said to him, "My body is of meager fortune, its faculties incomplete;
I only pray that you, out of compassion, will employ skillful means to relinquish what you possess so as to make me whole. Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva immediately gave it to him.
Even if, because of this, his faculties remained incomplete for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he did not give rise to even a single thought of regret.

Regretting and grieving, one should simply observe the body: from its initial entry into the womb as an impure and minute form, through the stages of the embryo and the development of the sense organs, and finally its birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Furthermore, one observes that this body has no true reality; it is devoid of shame and modesty, not a thing of the noble ones, foul and unclean, held together by joints and smeared with blood and flesh, with nine orifices constantly flowing, loathed and despised by others. Thus [one contemplates].
Having observed this, he does not give rise to even a single thought of attachment, but further reflects: "This body is precarious and fragile, possessing no solidity;
how could I now give rise to longing and attachment? I should fulfill their wishes by bestowing it upon them.
By acting in this way, I shall guide all sentient beings so that they do not produce craving for body or mind, and may they all attain [liberation]."
The accomplishment of the body of pure wisdom is called ultimate giving; this is the sixth treasury of giving of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] From "the sixth son of the Buddha" down to "the treasury of giving," there are ninety-three lines of sūtra text in this section.

Within this, it is further divided into two parts: first, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "dividing and distributing the gifts," there are three and a half lines of scripture that clarify the ten types of gift-treasuries as a whole;

second, from "This Bodhisattva" onwards until "this is called the sixth gift-treasury of the Bodhisattva," which provides a general exposition of the aforementioned ten types of gift-treasuries, thereby clarifying the principle of these ten types of giving.
The details are fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva knows form as it truly is; knows the arising of form as it truly is;
knows the cessation of form as it truly is; and knows the path leading to the cessation of form as it truly is. He likewise knows feeling, perception,..."

One knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they really are; one knows the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as it really is; one knows the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as it really is;
one knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as it really is.

One knows ignorance as it really is; one knows the arising of ignorance as it really is; one knows the cessation of ignorance as it really is; one knows the path leading to the cessation of ignorance as it really is. One knows craving as it really is.
He knows craving as it really is; he knows the cessation of craving as it really is; he knows the path leading to the cessation of craving as it really is.

He knows the śrāvaka as it really is; he knows the dharma of the śrāvaka as it really is; he knows the arising of the śrāvaka as it really is; he knows the nirvāṇa of the śrāvaka as it really is. He knows the pratyekabuddha as it really is;
he knows the dharma of the pratyekabuddha as it really is; he knows the arising of the pratyekabuddha as it really is.
He awakens to nirvāṇa as it truly is; he knows the bodhisattva as it truly is; he knows the bodhisattva-dharmas as they truly are;
he knows the accumulation of the bodhisattva as it truly is; he knows the nirvāṇa of the bodhisattva as it truly is. How does he know?

He knows that all things are produced from the causes and conditions of karma and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); they are entirely false, empty, and without reality; they are not-self and lack solidity.

There is not even a slight phenomenon that can be established such that one might wish sentient beings to know its true nature; yet, for the sake of explaining it extensively, what is it that is taught?

It is taught that all phenomena are indestructible. What phenomena are indestructible? Form is indestructible; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are indestructible; ignorance is indestructible; the teachings of the śrāvakas, the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, and the teachings of the bodhisattvas are indestructible.
It is indestructible. Why? Because all phenomena are without action, without an agent, without verbal expression, and without location;
they are neither born nor arisen, neither given nor taken, without movement or transition, and without activity.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes such an immeasurable treasury of wisdom, they understand all phenomena through slight means, attaining natural clarity and penetration without depending on others.
Realizing that this treasury of inexhaustible wisdom is so called because it possesses ten kinds of inexhaustibility—what are these ten?
They are: the inexhaustibility of skill in extensive learning; the inexhaustibility of attending upon spiritual friends;
the inexhaustibility of skillfully discerning words and meanings; the inexhaustibility of entering the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and by means of a single flavor...
Because the adornment of wisdom is inexhaustible; because the mind that accumulates all merit and virtue is never weary and thus inexhaustible;
because entering all *dhāraṇī* gates is inexhaustible; because being able to discern the languages and sounds of all sentient beings is inexhaustible;
because being able to sever the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings is inexhaustible; [it] constitutes a single [unity].

Because they manifest all the spiritual powers of all Buddhas to teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings, causing their practice to continue without interruption and never be exhausted—this is the tenth.
This is the seventh treasury of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
those who abide in this treasury attain inexhaustible wisdom and are universally able to awaken all sentient beings.
[Treatise] From "The seventh son of the Buddha" down to "awakening all sentient beings," there are thirty lines of sūtra.
Within this section, it is further divided into five parts: first, from "The seventh son of the Buddha" down to "nirvāṇa, knowing them as they truly are," there are eleven lines of sūtra;
herein, he first cites the knowledge of mundane and supramundane dharmas according to their reality, including both the roots and the branches.
Regarding the section on the "aggregation of characteristics," there are two parts. From "How is this known?

down to "extensively proclaimed," there are three lines of sutra that collectively present the preceding phenomena as arising from conditions and being fundamentally non-existent, explaining them in three divisions.
From "What is it? down to "not realized through another," there are six lines of sutra that correctly explain the preceding [aggregates of] feeling, perception, and formations.
The section on the equality of non-substantiality regarding formation and destruction consists of four parts;

from "This treasury of wisdom" onwards, up to "this constitutes the eighteen aspects," the sūtra clarifies the section on the ten inexhaustibles; and from the following one and a half lines, it clarifies the section on attaining the Dharma and skillful exposition.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of mindfulness of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva abandons delusion and confusion, attaining perfect mindfulness.
He recollects one birth, two births, and even ten, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births;
he recollects eons of formation, eons of destruction, eons of both formation and destruction, and eons that are neither formation nor destruction.
Whether it be one kalpa of destruction, or one kalpa of formation and destruction, or hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas,
up to immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unmeasurable, unspeakable,
and even unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, [one may] recollect the name of a single Buddha, and so on, up to unspeakably unspeakable [kalpas].

Reciting the names of unspeakably many Buddhas; reciting the accounts of one Buddha’s appearance in the world and his bestowing of predictions, up to the accounts of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas appearing in the world and bestowing predictions;

reciting the sūtras of one Buddha’s appearance in the world, up to the sūtras of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas appearing in the world—just as with the sūtras, so too with the geyas and the predictions.
The same applies to the *gāthā*, *nidāna*, *udāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*.
Likewise, one recollects a single assembly, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of assemblies;

one recollects the exposition of a single dharma, up to the exposition of an unspeakably unspeakable number of dharmas; and one recollects the various natures of a single faculty, up to [the various natures of] all faculties.
Recalling the various natures of one faculty from among unspeakably unspeakable faculties, and so forth,
up to the various natures of one affliction from among unspeakably unspeakable afflictions;
and so forth, up to the various natures of one samādhi from among unspeakably unspeakable samādhis.
Regarding the various natures of the unspeakably unspeakable samādhis, this mindfulness has ten aspects, namely:

mindfulness of tranquility, mindfulness of purity, mindfulness of non-turbidity, mindfulness of lucidity, mindfulness of being free from dust, mindfulness of being free from various kinds of dust, mindfulness of being free from defilement, mindfulness of radiance, mindfulness of being lovely and delightful, and mindfulness of being boundless and unimpeded. When a bodhisattva dwells in these modes of mindfulness, [they attain] the first...
No one in all the worlds can disturb them; no heterodox arguments can move them; their roots of goodness from past lives have all attained purification;
they are unstained by worldly dharmas; they cannot be destroyed by any Māras or non-Buddhists;
they undergo rebirth in successive bodies without any loss of memory; and they preach the Dharma inexhaustibly throughout all worlds in the past, present, and future.
Dwelling together with sentient beings in the interim without ever committing a fault, entering the assemblies and places of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Buddhas without obstruction,
and being able to draw near to all Buddhas— this is called the eighth treasury of mindfulness of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] From the eighth son of the Buddha down to the "Recollection Treasury" (*smṛti-garbha*), there are twenty-seven lines of scripture.

Within this, the general meaning is further divided into two parts: First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the various natures of the unspeakable samādhi," there are eighteen lines of scripture which clarify the attainment of infinite right mindfulness regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*). Second, this mindfulness has ten aspects.

Having planted [the seeds], down to the eighth stage, the *Nidāna-saṃgraha* contains nine lines of sūtra clarifying the attainment of the ten right mindfulnesses (*daśa-samyak-smṛti*) at the time of being without fault regarding all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), these are: *Geya*, here translated as "should be recited";
*Gāthā*, here translated as "chanting"; *Nidāna*, here translated as "sūtras on causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-sūtra*); and *Udāna*...
This is called the "Unasked Spontaneous Declaration.

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Retention-Treasury? This Bodhisattva retains the words, phrases, and meanings of the sūtras spoken by all Buddhas without any loss or forgetfulness;
he retains them in a single lifetime, and even for as long as an ineffable number of kalpas."
One cannot describe how holding the name of a single Buddha— even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas—
sustains one for a single eon, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons; nor how holding a single Buddha’s prophecy—
even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas’ prophecies— sustains one for a single sūtra, even up to [unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sūtras].
He maintains one assembly from among unspeakably many assemblies, up to maintaining unspeakably unspeakable numbers of assemblies;
he expounds one teaching from among unspeakably unspeakable teachings, up to expounding unspeakably unspeakable numbers of teachings;

he maintains one faculty with its infinite varieties of natures, up to maintaining unspeakably unspeakable numbers of faculties with their infinite varieties of natures; he maintains one affliction...

The various natures of afflictions, up to unspeakably unspeakable varieties of afflictions, sustain the various natures of a single samādhi, up to unspeakably unspeakable varieties of samādhis. O Son of the Buddha, this Treasury of Sustenance is boundless;
it is difficult to fill, difficult to reach its bottom, difficult to approach, and cannot be overcome by any immeasurable [forces].
Inexhaustible and possessing great majestic power, this is the realm of the Buddhas; only a Buddha can fully comprehend it.
This is called the ninth treasury-holding of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Regarding the fourteen lines of scripture beginning with "The ninth son of the Buddha," the general meaning therein is further divided as follows:

From "O Son of the Buddha" downwards to "the unspeakable samādhis of various natures," there are eleven and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the infinite division of hearing and retaining all dharmas. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards,
there are three lines of sūtra clarifying that the infinite dharmas spoken by the bodhisattvas in this stage can only be fully understood by the Buddha.
This is called the Section on the Treasury of Retention.

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the treasury of eloquence of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? This bodhisattva possesses profound wisdom and thoroughly understands the true nature of reality (dharmatā);
he extensively expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, never contradicting the sūtras of any of the Buddhas."
He preaches one category of Dharma, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of categories of Dharma;
he speaks the name of one Buddha, up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of Buddhas' names;
likewise, he speaks of one world, one Buddha's prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), one sūtra, one assembly, the exposition of one Dharma, and the immeasurable varieties of a single faculty.
The single nature of the lineage is explained as having immeasurable varieties;
the single samādhi is explained as having immeasurable varieties, up to the point where the unspeakably unspeakable samādhis are explained as having immeasurable varieties.
This may be explained in a single day, or in a fortnight, a month, a hundred years, a thousand years, a hundred thousand years, or for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas.
Whether one speaks for a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand kalpas, or a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas;
whether for countless, immeasurable, or even unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—the number of kalpas may be exhausted, but the meaning of a single word or a single phrase cannot be fully exhausted.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has accomplished ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries, and having accomplished these treasuries...
The *dhāraṇī-door that encompasses all phenomena* manifests before him, with one million *asaṃkhyeya* *dhāraṇīs* as its retinue.
Having attained this *dhāraṇī*, he extensively expounds the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings through the light of the Dharma.
When he preaches the Dharma, his broad and long tongue emits wondrous sounds that fill the entirety of the ten directions.
In accordance with the faculties and natures of beings throughout the world, he causes them all to be fully satisfied and their hearts to rejoice;

he eliminates all the entanglements and defilements of affliction, skillfully enters into all sounds, speech, words, and letters of eloquence, and ensures that the seed of the Buddha is never severed among all sentient beings, maintaining a continuous succession of pure minds. Furthermore, by means of the light of the Dharma, he expounds the teaching without end.
He does not experience weariness because this bodhisattva has accomplished a body that exhausts empty space, pervades the Dharma-realm, and is boundless.
This is the tenth treasury of eloquence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
This treasury is inexhaustible, undivided, uninterrupted, unceasing, immutable, unobstructed, non-retrogressive, profoundly deep, bottomless, and difficult to fathom.
One attains entry into the gate that universally enters all Buddha-dharmas.
[Treatise] The section beginning with "The tenth son of the Buddha" consists of twenty-four lines of scripture; within it, the meaning is further divided into three parts.
First, from "The son of the Buddha" down to "For what reason," there are twelve lines of scripture which clarify...
This section on the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible treasury of eloquence (*pratibhāna-kośa*) is divided into two parts.

From the passage beginning "this bodhisattva, having accomplished the ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries" down to the tenth, the treasury of eloquence, there are ten lines of sūtra that clarify the correct exposition of the ten kinds of treasuries of eloquence.
This is further divided into three sections; the first consists of two lines of sūtra that clarify the boundlessness of the treasury of eloquence.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, these ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries possess ten kinds of inexhaustible dharmas that cause all Bodhisattvas to ultimately achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
What are these ten? They are: because they benefit all sentient beings; because they are skillfully dedicated through original vows;
because they are uninterrupted throughout all kalpas; and because they awaken the minds of all within the entirety of the realm of empty space.
Because it is infinite; because it dedicates toward the conditioned without attachment; because in a single thought-moment its sphere encompasses the inexhaustibility of all phenomena;
because the mind of great vows is immutable; because it skillfully grasps all *dhāraṇīs*; because it is protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
and because it understands that all phenomena are like illusions—these are the ten kinds of inexhaustible dharmas that are able to...
[It] causes all that is done by all worlds to attain the ultimate, inexhaustible great treasury.
[Treatise: Within the tenth section, eight lines of scripture clarify the general presentation of the ten preceding treasuries as the stage of the subsequent dharma-gate of dedication;
these ten kinds of treasuries are categorized to bring the ten practices of one's own station (*svabhāga-pratipatti*) to full completion.
Therefore, it also accomplishes the ten subsequent *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) dharma-gates; thus it is the same for each stage.
The above concludes the explanation of the ten *caryā* (conduct) dharma-gates. *The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 39.

Chapter Twenty-Three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
[Treatise] The fifth assembly, held in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*). This chapter provides the introduction to this assembly.
Regarding the division into the Exposition and the Dissemination: from this point, the initial ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven palace constitutes the Introductory Section;

the two chapters following it constitute the Exposition Section; and within those two chapters, the passage up to the shaking of the earth and the offering of worship constitutes the Dissemination Section.
The Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications is taught in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; within this stage, there are three chapters of the sutra in common.
Regarding the first of these stages, from the initial ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, there are three meanings as previously explained.
As for the explanation of the title of this chapter: it is named after the destination reached by the ascent. "Tuṣita Heaven" translates here as the "Heaven of Joyful Contentment.
Second, regarding the explanation of the intent behind the chapter: it clarifies that the two stages of the ten abodes and the ten practices [are completed] by means of...

Manifesting the supramundane, he has already accomplished the karma of Tathāgata wisdom; now, in this heaven, by clarifying the path for those who follow the vision of the Way, he accomplishes the karma of the Tathāgata’s great compassion for dwelling in the world to benefit sentient beings.

He brings together and harmonizes the mundane and the supramundane through the Dharma-gate of non-duality and non-identity. For this reason, this chapter must appear here; it is the initial opening of the gate of great compassion.

In the stage of Mind, one advances through cultivation by means of true wisdom while maintaining compassion; herein there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority across the ten abidings and ten practices.
Wisdom is cultivated concurrently with these stages, yet the supramundane mind is still predominant. In comparison to this position, Great Compassion is the locus of principle and wisdom;
though the supramundane mind ultimately returns to enter the cycle of birth and death, it is the compassion born of wisdom that nurtures Great Compassion throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, because [the merit] becomes even more profound and vast, within the dharma-representation of Sudhana’s ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are nine goddesses from the first stage onward, and one Gopā.
She represents the wife of the Prince when he was the Buddha-voice; she symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*).

Since the ten stages have already been completed, the "dharma-joy" (*dharmaprīti*) is the meaning of the wife. Therefore, the question is asked: why is this explained in the context of these celestial realms?

The Dharma of Dedication replied: "As explained on the summit of Mount Sumeru, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) clarify how one enters the abode of the Buddha and dwells upon the summit of the Buddha’s wisdom without ever regressing.
On the Yāma Heaven, the ten practices (*caryā*) were taught to signify that practice relies upon the emptiness of phenomena and is entirely free from attachment.
Here, in this Tuṣita Palace, it is shown that although one has not yet departed from the desire realm,"
Abiding in the gate of great compassion, they always practice contentment regarding the objects of desire, remaining unstained by them;

yet, for the sole purpose of benefiting sentient beings, they dwell within the world. Furthermore, as these devas reside within the five heavens above Mount Sumeru in the realm of desire, they employ wisdom and compassion in conjunction so that neither becomes one-sided, just as the Four Heavenly Kings still rely upon [the earth].
Because Śakra is the lord, it is for this reason that the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are taught in this heaven.

They clarify the harmonization of the ultimate and the conventional to achieve the excellence of great compassion; one dwells within saṃsāra without abandoning nirvāṇa, and this is called "dedication.

From the initial stage of the first resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*) until the conclusion of these stages of harmonization, because one attains its name exclusively at the end, it is therefore called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).
This is intended to represent the advancement of the Dharma through its locations;

furthermore, because wisdom and compassion are eternally pervasive and there is no coming or going, nor center or periphery, it merely clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s birth is represented by these locations.
Since his fruit and practice are perfected within this heaven, it clarifies the initial arising of the Tathāgata’s wisdom upon the first generation of the bodhicitta.
The family [of practitioners] practices the gate of great compassion through the wisdom of the Buddha; this is precisely the fulfillment of the fruit of the Tathāgata.

Because the fruit is eternally fulfilled and the practice is eternally performed, and because the characteristics of this fruit and practice are adorned, it is called the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* (Flower Adornment of the Buddha).
Based upon these ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences, the three dharmas further perfect their functional efficacy within the eleventh stage.

Furthermore, there is no separate formal establishment [of a ritual], because when the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are explained within the context of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), no further distinct ritual acts or offerings are performed;
rather, it is simply for the purpose of nurturing the great wisdom, great compassion, and great mercy of this stage so that they become profoundly firm and perfected.
Therefore, these are called the "Ten Stages. Third, regarding the word-by-word explanation, this meaning is further divided as follows:

This assembly consists of two parts; first, the general outline of the five stages of the assembly as a whole, which includes all those such as the various kings and bodhisattvas mentioned below—this constitutes one long section outlining the intent of the sūtra.
Second, the word-by-word commentary. Regarding the first, the long outline of the sūtra's intent:
from the beginning until the end of the sūtra, it is divided into eleven sections. The first is "At that time, the Buddha’s spiritual... [and so forth].

From the passage beginning with "By the power of... down to "...are all exactly equal," there are seven and a half pages of scripture that clarify the section on the King of Tuṣita Heaven seeing the Buddha approaching from afar and, together with the assembly of devas, arranging and adorning the seats; this is further divided into seven segments.
[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, in every Jambudvīpa within each of the four continents across all worlds in the ten directions,
everyone saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree; in each place, there were bodhisattvas who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual strength,
expounded the Dharma, such that none failed to think, "I am always in the presence of the Buddha."
[Treatise] First, from "At that time" onwards, up to the section on "Constantly Facing the Buddha," which consists of three lines of scripture,

elucidates the part concerning the constant perfection of the body of wisdom. Regarding the interpretation of the meaning according to the text within this "Chapter on Ascending to Tuṣita Heaven," the statement that "all worlds in the ten directions always face the Buddha" clarifies that the perfect wisdom is omnipresent.
[Sūtra] At that time, by means of his supernatural power, the World-Honored One, without departing from beneath this Bodhi tree,
nor from the summit of Mount Sumeru, nor from the palace of the Yāma Heaven, proceeded to the Palace Adorned with All Wondrous Jewels in the Tuṣita Heaven.

[Treatise] Second: From "At that time, the World-Honored One... down to "...the Hall of Wondrous Jewel Adornment," approximately two lines of scripture clarify that the Tathāgata’s great wisdom is all-pervasive and responds to conditions such that what is seen involves neither coming nor going. The explanation of this meaning is as follows:
"Without departing from the Bodhi tree, he ascends to the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens" refers to the wisdom of bodhi.
The essence of its nature is fundamentally without dependence or abiding; it pervades the ten directions, yet its nature cannot be apprehended as past, future, or present.
It has no place of residence and no transition or change; it is neither moving nor quiescent, and is without any deliberate activity.

Nevertheless, in accordance with the faculties [of beings], it manifests physical bodies before all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, transforming and delivering them as appropriate.
[Sūtra] At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, immediately prepared a lion throne of *maṇi*-treasury within his palace.
This lion throne was composed of all manner of celestial, exquisite jewels;

it was obtained through the roots of goodness cultivated in past practices and manifested by the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of *asaṃkhyeya* supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas.
Born from the roots of goodness, arisen from all the pure dharmas of the Tathāgatas, and adorned by the power of boundless merit, this retribution of pure karma is indestructible.
Those who behold it rejoice with never-ending satisfaction; it is a supramundane dharma, untainted by the world.
All sentient beings come to observe it, yet none are able to fathom its wondrous subtlety.
Excellent.
[Treatise]: In the third period, having seen from afar the Buddha approaching, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven descended;

there are seven lines of scripture explaining that no one is able to fully exhaust his wondrous excellence, which clarify the arrangement of seats within the Heavenly Palace and the distribution of their meanings.

At that time, when the King of Tuṣita Heaven saw the Buddha approaching from afar, this corresponds to the ten stages of practice (*daśa-prayoga*) preceding the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

His entering the hall and arranging the precious throne corresponds to the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), wherein, through the samādhi of skillful means, he manifests the flow of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; thus, upon the seat itself, there is the establishment of the ten [stages].

Regarding the practice itself, it takes the formless *dharmakāya* as the essence of the practice. As for the seat, it is said that a precious lotus treasury (*ratnapadmagarbha*) is manifested to represent the locus of the practice;
because [the practitioner] remains unstained by the world, just like a lotus, this seat is established within these ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*).

To accomplish great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in engaging with the mundane world, the seat is said to be "spread. "Spreading" carries the meaning of "opening up" or "unfolding," which represents great compassion.
He enters the mundane world to cause the flowers of manifold virtues to bloom and to reach the wondrous fruit of Bodhi;

furthermore, "to spread" (fu) signifies to establish, meaning that out of great compassion he enters the mundane world to establish the Dharma for the benefit of living beings, rather than seeking the supramundane Dharma for himself.
As for the *maṇi* nature of the seat, it clarifies that through great compassion he constantly dwells within birth and death without being defiled.
The lion throne named "Stainless Jewel" (*vimala-maṇi*) signifies the meaning of sovereignty, for the Tathāgata is the Lord of Fearlessness.
That it is composed of all the exquisite jewels of the heavens clarifies that it is obtained as the fruition of wondrous wisdom, principle, compassion, and the myriad practices.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "It is obtained through the cultivation of roots of goodness in the past."

That which is manifested by the spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of all Tathāgatas clarifies that the merit, wisdom, and myriad practices (*caryā*) of all Buddhas are not different from one's own Buddha-power;
because within the principle-wisdom of one's own mind, one shares the same merit and wisdom as all Buddhas,
and because their wisdom and practices are identical, it is said to be "immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas."
That which is born from the roots of goodness alone clarifies that within the dedication [of merit], the practices of merit, wisdom, and great compassion are all-encompassing;

this is the retribution [for such practice]. It is stated in general that this seat’s adornment is born from incalculable and limitless roots of goodness and arises from the pure dharmas of all Tathāgatas.
This clarifies that through wisdom one initiates practice such that there is no dharma that is not pure. The remainder is self-evident according to the text.
From this point down to the end of the first section, there are one hundred and ninety-eight and a half lines of scripture;
within these, one hundred eighty-four million billion kinds of various adorned jewel thrones and jewel grounds completely fill the void of space.
Furthermore, there are one hundred eighty million billion kinds of various bodhisattvas, and...

with palms joined in contemplation, they offered hymns of praise and held banners, while the assembly adorned the precious ground and filled the entirety of space. Furthermore, it was purified and beautified by ten hundred trillion roots of goodness.
