Chapter Twenty-three, Part Two: The Ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
[Sūtra] At that time, by the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority and as the outflow of his past roots of goodness, it was inconceivable...
By the power of his sovereign mastery, all the devas and devakanyās within the Tuṣita palace saw the Buddha from afar as if he were before their very eyes;
they simultaneously gave rise to this thought: "The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter.
Now that we have seen him—the One Endowed with All-Knowledge, the Unobstructed in Dharma, the Perfectly Awakened One"—thus did they reflect and thus did they contemplate.
He observed that the entire assembly simultaneously went out to welcome the Tathāgata,
each carrying celestial robes filled with all kinds of flowers, all kinds of incense, all kinds of jewels,
all kinds of ornaments, all kinds of celestial sandalwood powder, all kinds of celestial aloeswood powder, and all kinds of celestial exquisite jewel powder.
All the celestial incense and flowers were profusely displayed, and all the celestial *mandārava* flowers were scattered as offerings to the Buddha.
Hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* devas from Tuṣita heaven remained in the air;
they all gave rise to minds directed toward the realm of wisdom before the Buddha, burning every kind of incense so that its fragrance formed clouds, adorning the void.
Furthermore, Ākāśa gave rise to a heart of joy toward the Buddha and rained down clouds of all kinds of celestial flowers to adorn the void;
he gave rise to a heart of reverence toward the Buddha and rained down clouds of all kinds of celestial canopies to adorn the void;
he gave rise to a heart of worship toward the Buddha and scattered clouds of all kinds of celestial garlands to adorn the void; and toward the Buddha, he produced...
With a mind of resolute faith, they spread an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) net of gold that completely covers space; from all its jeweled bells, wondrous sounds constantly emerge.

Furthermore, generating a mind toward the Buddha as the most supreme field of merit, they adorn space with incalculable canopies and rain down clouds of all manner of necklaces without interruption. Moreover, generating deep faith toward the Buddha, they, by means of an incalculable...
The palaces of the various devas in the *saṃghāṭa* [heaven] adorned the void, and all celestial music produced sublime sounds.
Furthermore, they conceived the thought that the Buddha was the most supreme and rare encounter;

with clouds of celestial garments of immeasurable colors, they adorned the void and rained down incomparable, manifold, and exquisite robes. Moreover, they gave rise to immeasurable joy and exultation toward the Buddha.
With hearts leaping with joy, they adorned the void with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) celestial jeweled crowns, raining down immeasurable celestial crowns that formed vast clouds;
furthermore, giving rise to a heart of rapture toward the Buddha, they adorned the void with incalculable jewels of various colors,
raining down clouds of all manner of necklaces without interruption for hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas*.

The *saṃghī* devaputras all conceived pure faith toward the Buddha; they scattered countless varieties of celestial flowers of various colors and burned countless varieties of celestial incense of various colors as offerings to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, giving rise to a mind of great adornment and transformation before the Buddha, they held countless varieties of celestial sandalwood powder of various colors and respectfully scattered it over the Tathāgata. Moreover, at that time—
With hearts of joy and exultation toward the Buddha, they followed the Tathāgata holding countless canopies of various colors;
furthermore, with minds of superior resolve toward the Buddha, they spread countless celestial robes of various colors made of precious jewels upon the road as an offering to the Tathāgata;
moreover, with pure hearts toward the Buddha, they held countless celestial jewels of various colors.

They welcomed the Tathāgata with victory banners; furthermore, they gave rise to a mind of supreme joy in the presence of the Buddha and offered countless celestial ornaments of various colors to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they gave birth to indestructible faith in the presence of the Buddha and offered countless celestial jewel-garlands to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they gave birth to incomparable joy in the presence of the Buddha and held [countless... to offer to the Tathāgata.
Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of devaputras made offerings to the Tathāgata with various colored celestial jewel banners;
with minds that were disciplined, tranquil, and free from negligence, they offered countless varieties of celestial music producing sublime sounds to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of [devas] who previously resided in Tuṣita...

He was followed by a multitude of bodhisattvas from his palace, who had arisen from the Dharma that transcends the three realms, from conduct free from all afflictions, from a mind that is all-pervasive and unimpeded, from profound and skillful means, from immeasurable and vast wisdom, and from the increase of inconceivable roots of goodness born of firm and pure faith. They arose... [A]rhat.
With a mind that has accomplished offerings through the skillful transformations of the *Saṃghāṭa*, manifested by the Dharma-gate of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and sealed by it,
they made offerings to the Buddha with things surpassing all the offering implements of the devas;
they offered all jeweled canopies born from the *pāramitās* and all flowers born from the pure understanding of all Buddha-realms.
All garments produced by the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
all nets of bells produced by the adamantine dharma-mind of non-obstruction; all solid fragrances produced by the mind that realizes all phenomena are like illusions;
and all exquisite jeweled thrones for the Buddhas produced by the mind of the Tathāgata’s seat that pervades all Buddha-realms—these were used to make offerings to the Buddhas.
All jeweled banners produced by the mind of indefatigable resolve; all jeweled palaces where Buddhas abide, produced by the joyful mind that understands all phenomena are like dreams;
clouds of all jeweled lotuses produced by roots of goodness free from attachment and roots of goodness of non-arising;
clouds of all solid fragrances; clouds of all flowers of infinite colors; and all various kinds [of offerings].
Clouds of exquisite garments, clouds of all-pervasive and pure sandalwood incense, clouds of all manner of exquisitely adorned jewel canopies,
clouds of all types of burning incense, clouds of all exquisite garlands, and clouds of all pure ornaments— all these,
surpassing the offerings of the various devas, pervaded the entire Dharma-realm and were offered to the Buddha by those bodhisattvas.
From each and every body, there emerged unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, who completely filled the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Their minds were equal to those of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;

arising from the dharma that is free from inversion, they were empowered by the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgatas to reveal to sentient beings the tools of peace and security, fully endowed with the unspeakable.
Through names, phrases, and syllables, they universally enter into all immeasurable dharmas; from within the seeds of all *dhāraṇīs*, they give birth to an inexhaustible treasury of eloquence.

With a mind free from fear, they give rise to great joy, and through unspeakably immeasurable and inexhaustible praises of the Dharma as it truly is, they praise the Tathāgata without ever becoming weary.

[Treatise] Third: From "At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata" down to "praising the Tathāgata’s insatiability," this section of the sutra clarifies how the various devas welcomed the Buddha;
each saw the Buddha approaching from afar as if he were right before their eyes, and they paid homage to the Buddha and presented offerings.
To explain the meaning of this passage, it is divided into five sections. First, it is said: "Seeing the Buddha approach from afar" clarifies...
Because one initiates dedication toward great compassion and great vows based on the preceding ten practices, it is as if [the Tathāgata] were before one's eyes;

this clarifies that one is never separated from fundamental wisdom and is in constant union with it. As the subsequent passage states: "Seeing the Tathāgata endowed with all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā), this clarifies that one is in perfect accord with the Buddha’s wisdom and true awakening.
Regarding the phrase "one who is unimpeded in the Dharma and perfectly awakened," this clarifies that one has merged with the Buddha’s wisdom and true awakening. As it says:

Having completed this reflection, the following four lines concern the stage of correct entry (*samyak-praveśa*). Therefore, each [line] describes making offerings by placing them within celestial robes;
the subsequent ten types of offerings clarify the preceding section on making offerings through bodily emanations, thereby manifesting the arousal of vows.
This section clarifies that filling [the vessels] with robes represents the completion of physical conduct. Within this single segment on presenting offerings, there are sixty-five lines.

The Sūtra provides a fivefold analysis: first, from the passage "At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power" down to "simultaneously welcoming the Tathāgata," there are five lines and a half of sūtra text clarifying the section on how the various devas, through the Buddha’s spiritual power and their own roots of goodness, behold the Buddha from afar, accord with the Buddha’s wisdom, and welcome him;
this section is divided into two parts, each using celestial robes.

From "down to making offerings to the Buddha," there are four lines of scripture clarifying the section on how the various devas take fragrant flowers in their robes and scatter them as an offering to the Buddha;
this consists of ten types of offerings to an assembly of three hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* beings.
From "down to raining down clouds of all manner of necklaces without interruption," there are sixteen lines of scripture clarifying [this].
The various devas each offered clouds of offerings arising from their own minds as a portion of this section of ten kinds of offerings;
after [the description of] four hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* assemblies of offerings, down to the celestial music producing sublime sounds,
there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify and present these ten kinds of held and scattered offerings made to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha divided [the assembly] into five hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* groups, down to those who are "insatiable" (*atṛpta*),

wherein twenty-five chapters of sutras clarify how the bodhisattvas who have long resided in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace produce their resultant supports through the practice of the various *pāramitās* as offerings.
This section concerning the seventeen kinds of offerings refers to those who "have long resided."

Regarding the preparatory stage for those newly arriving at the fundamental position, among these seventeen kinds of offerings, the *vitāna* (canopy) is first presented because this stage involves entering the bodhisattva practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Great compassion is placed at the forefront, with all the *pāramitās* simultaneously serving as its supporting adornments;
"wisdom" carries the meaning of blossoming, while the "canopy" carries the meaning of encompassing.

The robes signify the meaning of patience; the bell-nets signify the teaching of the Dharma; and the mind being like an illusion signifies the meaning of firmness, because there is no substantial entity that can be created or destroyed.
Other points should be understood by analogy according to their names and meanings.
This third section contains thirty kinds of hundreds of thousands of millions of offerings. At the end, there is a host of Bodhisattvas who previously resided in celestial palaces.
The seventeen kinds of offerings arise from the various practices of the pāramitās; they arise from the wisdom of the Dharmakāya and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

As clearly explained in the text, they surpass the offerings of the devas because those are conditioned results obtained through retribution, whereas these arise from the non-active gate of the Dharma-realm and transcend emotional conceptualization.
[Sūtra] At that time, all the devas and the assembly of bodhisattvas beheld the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— the inconceivable hero among men— whose body was immeasurable and beyond reckoning,
manifesting inconceivable and diverse miraculous transformations that caused the hearts of countless sentient beings to rejoice greatly, pervading the entirety of the realm of empty space.
The entire dharma-realm is adorned with the adornments of the Buddhas, causing all sentient beings to dwell securely in roots of goodness;
it manifests the immeasurable spiritual powers of all Buddhas, transcending the path of all speech and languages, and is revered by all great Bodhisattvas;
according to those who are to be transformed, it causes them all to rejoice and abide in the vastness of the Buddhas.
The roots of goodness of his physical merit are entirely purified; his physical form is supreme and cannot be eclipsed by any other;

the realm of his wisdom is inexhaustible; he is born from incomparable samādhi; his body is boundless, dwelling pervasively within the bodies of all sentient beings, causing immeasurable beings to experience great joy, and [establishing] the lineage of omniscience for all.
They dwell uninterruptedly in the ultimate abode of all Buddhas, are born into the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
cause incalculable sentient beings to attain pure faith and understanding, bring to fulfillment the wisdom of all Bodhisattvas, gladden their faculties,
and universally cover the void and the dharma-realm with the clouds of Dharma, teaching and transforming them without exception according to the capacities of sentient beings.
They cause all hearts to be fully satisfied and establish them in non-conceptual wisdom that transcends all sentient beings;
they cause them to attain omniscience and emit great radiance, manifesting the roots of goodness from past lives;
they cause all to universally give rise to the vast mind, and establish all sentient beings in the indestructible wisdom of Samantabhadra, dwelling everywhere.
The lands of all sentient beings arise from the non-regressive True Dharma and abide within the universal, equal Dharma-realm;
clearly understanding the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, they manifest unspeakably,
unspeakably many varieties of distinct Tathāgata bodies that cannot be fully extolled by worldly speech, yet are able to cause all beings to constantly keep them in mind.

The Buddha fills the Dharma-realm and extensively delivers all sentient beings; according to their initial aspiration and what they desire to benefit from, he bestows the Dharma as a gift to bring them under his transformative influence, purifying their faith and practice.

He manifests an inconceivable physical body, observing the minds of sentient beings with non-attachment and abiding in unimpeded dwelling. Having attained the ten powers of a Buddha, he is free from all obstructions, and his mind is eternally tranquil.
Abiding in concentration never distracted, they are well able to expound the true meaning of various phrases and sentences;
they are able to penetrate deeply into the boundless ocean of wisdom and give birth to an immeasurable treasury of merit and insight.

Constantly illuminating the Dharma-realm with the sun of the Buddha, they always manifest according to the power of their original vows and never sink away. They dwell eternally within the Dharma-realm, abiding in the presence of the Buddhas.
Abiding without change, they are entirely unattached to "self" or "what belongs to self. Abiding in supramundane dharmas, they are untainted by worldly dharmas.
They raise the banner of wisdom over all worlds; their wisdom is vast, transcending the world and remaining unstained by it.
They pull forth all sentient beings from the mire, establishing them on the ground of supreme wisdom. All...

They benefit sentient beings with merit and virtue without exhaustion; they thoroughly understand all the wisdom of bodhisattvas and, with resolute faith and inclination, shall surely attain perfect enlightenment.

Through great compassion, they manifest unspeakably infinite Buddha-bodies adorned with various ornaments, proclaiming immeasurable teachings with wondrous voices to satisfy the minds of sentient beings according to their inclinations. As for their passing away...
From now until the end of time, their minds shall remain ever pure, causing all sentient beings to not cling to sensory realms;
they shall constantly receive predictions of enlightenment from all Bodhisattvas, entering the lineage of the Buddhas, being born into the Buddha-family, and receiving the Buddha-consecration.
They shall eternally travel throughout the ten directions without rest, yet remain without attachment to anything, being able to [pervade] the entire Dharma-realm and all Buddha-lands.
He travels everywhere to the minds of all sentient beings, understanding them all without exception.

Possessing all merit, he is pure and transcendent, dwelling neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, yet he appears throughout the world like a reflection. With the moon of wisdom, he universally illumines the dharma-realm;
he thoroughly realizes that all things are ultimately ungraspable, and through wisdom he constantly knows all worlds to be like illusions, like reflections, and like dreams.
Just as all transformations have the mind as their intrinsic nature, so do they abide.

According to the differences in the karmic retributions of sentient beings, the variations in their mental inclinations, and the distinctness of their faculties, the Buddha-body manifests accordingly.
The Tathāgata constantly takes countless sentient beings as his object of focus and teaches that the world arises entirely from conditions, knowing that the characteristics of all phenomena are thus.

The signless is but a single characteristic, the very root of wisdom. Desiring to cause sentient beings to depart from all attachments to signs, he manifests the nature and characteristics of all worlds while acting within them; for their sake, he reveals unexcelled bodhi.
Desiring to rescue and protect all sentient beings, he appears in the world to reveal the Buddha-way, so that they may behold the Tathāgata.
Taking the physical marks as objects of focus, one diligently practices mindfulness to eliminate the signs of worldly afflictions.
Cultivating the conduct of awakening with an undistracted mind, one attains complete perfection in all the gateways of the Mahāyāna.
One is able to observe the roots of goodness in all sentient beings and never allows them to perish, while maintaining pure karmic retribution and wisdom.

Clearly understanding and universally entering the three periods of time, forever free from all worldly discrimination, they emit webs of light that universally illuminate all worlds in the ten directions, filling them all without exception;
their physical bodies possess wondrous marks and signs such that those who see them never tire of doing so;
through great merit, wisdom, and spiritual powers, they give rise to the various practices of Bodhisattvas and attain mastery over the spheres of the various faculties.
Having perfectly accomplished all the deeds of a Buddha and then vanished, he was able to skillfully reveal the path of omniscience throughout the past, present, and future.
He caused a universal rain of immeasurable *dhāraṇīs* to fall upon all bodhisattvas, causing them to give rise to vast aspiration and joy, so that they might uphold, practice,
and perfect all the qualities of the Buddhas— perfect, blazing, and boundless.
His body was adorned with exquisite forms, such that there was no one in all the worlds who did not behold him.
He was forever free from all obstructive dharmas and had attained purity regarding the true meaning of all phenomena.

Having attained mastery over the qualities of merit, he was a Great Dharma King who shone universally like the sun; as a field of merit for the world, he possessed great majestic power and virtue. In a single...
He manifests transformation bodies throughout all worlds and emits the light of wisdom to bring all beings to enlightenment.

Desiring to let sentient beings know that the Buddha is endowed with boundless merit, he assumes his station by binding a non-obstructive silken ribbon upon his crown. He guides and instructs in accordance with worldly expedients;
with the hand of wisdom, he comforts sentient beings as a Great Physician King who skillfully cures all ailments. (1)
He is able to travel everywhere throughout all the infinite lands of the world-systems without ever resting;

with the pure eye of wisdom, free from all obscurations and veils, he perceives clearly all things. Toward sentient beings who have committed unwholesome and evil deeds, he employs various means of discipline to lead them into the Path.
He perfectly grasps the appropriate timing for this work without ceasing; and whenever sentient beings give rise to a mind of equanimity, [he likewise acts accordingly].

In order to manifest the equality of karmic retribution according to their mental inclinations and the fruits of their karma, they appear in the form of Buddhas and display various miraculous transformations, preaching the Dharma so that beings may realize and understand it, attain the wisdom of the Dharma, experience great joy, and have their faculties leap with exultation.
Seeing immeasurable Buddhas, they give rise to profound and heavy faith, generate all roots of goodness, and never again regress. 1.

All sentient beings, bound by their karma, slumber long within birth and death; when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he is able to awaken them and comfort their minds so that they are free from sorrow and fear.
If any should behold him, he causes them all to realize and enter the wisdom of the meaning of non-reliance.

His wisdom is skillful and thoroughly penetrates all realms; it is adorned with excellence such that nothing can eclipse it. It is a mountain of wisdom and the sprout of the Dharma. All... [omitted] ...are fully perfected.
Having attained purity, they manifest either as bodhisattvas or as the bodies of Buddhas, leading all sentient beings to the stage free from affliction.
Adorned with immeasurable merits and accomplished through karmic practices, they appear in the world;
there is nothing among the adornments and purities of all Buddhas that is not achieved through the karma of omniscience. They constantly maintain their original vows.
Having abandoned the world, he acts as a steadfast and virtuous friend to all sentient beings; possessing the supreme, pure, and stainless light, he enables all beings to behold him directly.
Through his spiritual power, the Buddha constantly follows and never abandons the infinite and boundless beings within the six realms of existence.
He causes all those who have planted similar roots of goodness in the past to become purified within these six realms.
Not abandoning their original vows, they do not deceive any sentient beings; through skillful means of wholesome dharmas, they gather them all in and cause them to cultivate pure karma.

They shatter all the conflicts and strifes of Māras, and from the realm of non-obstruction, they emerge as the Great Powerful and Most Victorious Sun-Treasury, appearing as reflections within the realm of the pure mind without any hindrance.
There is no one in all the worlds who does not behold him; he extensively bestows various dharmas upon sentient beings.
The Buddha is a treasury of boundless radiance, with all powers and wisdom fully perfected.

He constantly illuminates all sentient beings with great light, causing them to fulfill their aspirations according to their wishes. Free from all enmity and opposition, he is the supreme field of merit for all sentient beings.
He is the common refuge for all; whatever gifts are bestowed, he causes them all to be purified.
He causes even those who practice minor virtuous deeds to receive immeasurable merit and leads them all to enter the stage of inexhaustible wisdom.

He is the master who plants roots of goodness for all sentient beings and the supreme fertile field from which the merit of all sentient beings arises. His wisdom is profoundly deep and his skillful means are vast.
Skillfully able to rescue all from the sufferings of the three evil realms; thus believing and understanding, thus observing,
thus entering the abyss of wisdom, thus roaming the ocean of merit, thus universally reaching the wisdom of space,
thus knowing the field of blessings for sentient beings, thus bringing right mindfulness to presence and observing in this manner.

Thus one contemplates the Buddha’s various karmic marks and signs; thus one contemplates the Buddha universally manifesting throughout the world; thus one contemplates the Buddha’s sovereign mastery of supernormal powers.
At that time, the great assembly saw that from every single pore of the Tathāgata’s body there issued forth hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light.
Each ray of light possessed *asaṃkhyeya* colors and *asaṃkhyeya* purities.
This incalculable illumination causes incalculable multitudes to observe, incalculable multitudes to rejoice, incalculable multitudes to experience happiness,
incalculable multitudes to increase their profound faith, incalculable multitudes to purify their aspirations,
incalculable multitudes to cool their faculties, and incalculable multitudes to cultivate reverence and respect.
[Commentary] Fourth: From the passage beginning "At that time, all the devas and bodhisattvas, down to the incalculable multitude,
paid respectful homage" (one hundred and six lines of scripture), this section of the sūtra clarifies how the devas and bodhisattvas witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural transformations,
which benefited sentient beings, filling the ten directions and pervading everywhere without limit.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of these passages is fully elucidated in the sūtra.
[Sūtra] At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha’s body emitting hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable great radiances;
each and every radiance possessed inconceivable colors and inconceivable illuminations, shining in an inconceivable manner.
The boundless realm of phenomena, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, produces a great and wondrous sound;
this sound proclaims hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable hymns of praise that transcend all worldly speech and are accomplished by supramundane roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable, subtle, and exquisite adornments within the hundred...
Even if one were to praise them for inconceivable billions of nayutas of kalpas, they could never be exhausted; all are born from the inexhaustible sovereignty of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, he manifests unspeakably many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, appearing in the world to lead all sentient beings into the gateway of wisdom and to understand the most profound meaning. He also manifests unspeakably many Buddhas, Tathāgatas...
There are transformations that exhaustively pervade the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, causing all worlds to be equally pure;
all such manifestations arise from the unobstructed omniscience in which the Tathāgata abides, and they also arise from the inconceivable, supreme virtues cultivated by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable, wondrous jewel-lights.
This radiance arises from the roots of goodness produced by great vows of the past; because he once made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas and cultivated pure conduct without negligence;
because the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) has been generated without obstruction through the cultivation of roots of goodness;
in order to manifest the power of the Tathāgata as vast and pervasive; in order to sever the doubts of all sentient beings; and in order to cause all to behold the Tathāgata.
Therefore, in order to cause immeasurable sentient beings to abide in roots of goodness; to manifest the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata so that they cannot be eclipsed or surpassed;
to cause all sentient beings to universally enter the ultimate ocean;
to cause the bodhisattva assemblies in all buddha-lands to gather together; and to reveal and demonstrate the inconceivable Buddha-dharma.
[Commentary] Fifth:

From "At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha’s body" down to "the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the Buddhas," this section clarifies the portion concerning the Tathāgata’s bodily radiance universally illuminating the infinite.
Within this section, there are twenty lines of scripture divided into seven parts: 1.
From "At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha’s body" down to "the boundless realm of phenomena" (two and a half lines), which clarifies the section on the realm of the Buddha’s light.
2. From "By the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "accomplished by worldly and supramundane roots of goodness," [which constitutes] two [parts].
The third section, "The Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power Manifesting Sublime Sounds and Verses of Praise," consists of three parts.

From "Again manifesting hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas" down to "the place of birth of mastery," there are two and a half lines of scripture clarifying the fourth section, "The Tathāgata Manifesting the Adornments of His Own Retribution Body. From "Again manifesting the unspeakable" down to "extremely... [the text continues].
5. The section clarifying that the appearance of the inexhaustible Buddhas is manifested through a single line and a half of the sūtra concerning the profound meaning;

6. The section clarifying that the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers (ṛddhi) pervade everywhere through transformation is manifested from "furthermore, the unspeakable... down to "equally pure" in one line and a half of the sūtra;
7. The section [beginning with] "in this way... down to "produced by inconceivable supreme virtues."
One line and a half of the sūtra clarify that what was previously manifested is the portion produced by the Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom and merit; this constitutes seven [sections].

Furthermore, from "again manifesting hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas" down to "the Dharma-gates of the Buddha," there are eight lines of sūtra clarifying the Tathāgata’s manifestation of inconceivable, wondrous jewel-flames and the manifestation of his own accumulation of roots of goodness to assemble the great assembly; this constitutes seven [sections].

The textual meaning within this section is inherently complete; the intent of this section clarifies that the Tathāgata manifests his own realm in order to cause those who dedicate their merit to enter into it through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
[Sūtra] At that time, the Tathāgata, with great compassion universally covering all, manifested all the adornments of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), desiring to cause [beings] not to...
One may say that among the sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya worlds, those who have not yet developed faith cause to develop it;
those who have already developed faith cause to increase it; those who have already increased it cause to become purified; those who have already become purified cause to reach maturity;
and those who have already reached maturity cause their minds to be tamed, as they contemplate the profound Dharma and become endowed with immeasurable light of wisdom.
They clearly give rise to the immeasurable and vast mind of *sarvajñā* (omniscience), never regressing;

they do not contravene the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and do not fear the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Realizing the principle of ultimate truth, they fulfill all practices of the *pāramitās*.
Their supramundane roots of goodness are entirely purified, like those of Samantabhadra; they attain the mastery of a Buddha, leave the realm of Māra, and enter into the state of all Buddhas.

Having thoroughly understood the profound Dharma, they attain inconceivable wisdom; their vows for the Mahāyāna never regress, and they constantly behold all Buddhas without ever being separated from them.
Having accomplished realized knowledge and realized immeasurable dharmas, they are endowed with the power of the treasury of boundless merit.
They give rise to a heart of joy and enter the stage of non-doubt; free from evil and pure, they rely upon the vision of omniscience to perceive all phenomena.
Moving, they enter the assemblies of all bodhisattvas and are constantly born into the families of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
World-Honored One, these manifested adornments are all accomplished through the roots of goodness accumulated in the past;
they are revealed in order to discipline all sentient beings, to manifest the great majestic power of the Tathāgata, and to illuminate the treasury of unimpeded wisdom.
Therefore, because the Tathāgata’s boundless, supreme virtues are most brilliantly radiant; because he displays the inconceivable great supernormal transformations of the Tathāgata;
because by means of his power of supernatural faculties he manifests the Buddha-body in all realms of existence;
because he displays the infinite boundaries of the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations; and because his original vows have been entirely fulfilled—he thus reveals [himself].
Because they come with courageous wisdom that can travel everywhere; because they attain sovereignty over all phenomena and become Dharma Kings;
because they give birth to all gateways of wisdom; because they manifest the pure body of a Tathāgata; because they further manifest a body most sublime and excellent;
because they demonstrate the realization of the equal Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; and because they reveal the treasury of the purity of roots of goodness.
Therefore, it is displayed because its supreme and wondrous form has nothing in the world to serve as a simile;
it is displayed because it possesses the marks of the Ten Powers, such that those who behold it can never tire of doing so; it acts as the sun for the world, illuminating the three periods of time;
it is the Sovereign Dharma King, whose every merit manifests from roots of goodness cultivated in the past; and it is [the object] for all Bodhisattvas in all...
The eons required to extol and praise [the Buddha] would be inexhaustible.
[Treatise: This section, from "At that time, the Tathāgata’s great compassion...
down to "...extol and praise [him] would be inexhaustible," consists of twenty-six and a half lines of scripture, clarifying how the Tathāgata manifests all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Regarding the section on "the infinite increase of all adornments that benefit sentient beings according to their faculties," this section is divided into two parts.

First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the Tathāgata was covered by great compassion" down to "born into the family of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture that clarify the Tathāgata’s manifestation of adornments and supernormal powers.
From the passage beginning with "causing the sentient beings of unspeakably many worlds to protect and benefit" down to the end of this section,
thirteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the virtues manifested by the Tathāgata; they reveal the Buddha’s sovereign mastery,
cause all sentient beings to give rise to the various bodhisattva practices, and fulfill the original vows regarding the sphere of the Buddha’s conduct.

[Sūtra] At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, having prepared such various offerings for the Tathāgata, together with hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya Tuṣita devaputras, joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One! Welcome, Sugata! Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! We pray only that you will look upon us with compassion."
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those dwelling in this palace, adorned himself with the adornments of a Buddha and manifested great majestic power.

This was for the sake of causing all living beings to give rise to great joy, for the sake of causing all bodhisattvas to develop profound awakening and understanding, and for the sake of increasing the desire-realm pleasures of all the devas of Tuṣita; thus the King of Tuṣita made offerings to him.
Because they serve [the Buddha] without weariness; because they resolve their minds upon the Buddha by taking immeasurable sentient beings as their object of contemplation;
because the roots of goodness and merit from planting the seeds of seeing the Buddha for immeasurable sentient beings are inexhaustible; because they are always able to give rise to pure faith;
because they see the Buddha and make offerings without seeking anything for themselves; because all their aspirations are pure; and because they diligently accumulate roots of goodness.
Because he never tires and because he has made the great vow to seek all-knowledge, he accepted the invitation of the Heavenly King and entered the Palace Adorned with All Jewels;
it was exactly the same in all worlds throughout the ten directions of this world-system.
[Treatise] Seventh: At that time, from the King of Tuṣita Heaven down to all worlds, it was likewise in every respect.
This section clarifies how the King of Tuṣita, having completed the preparations for the offering, invited the Buddha to enter his palace;
the portion concerning the Tathāgata’s acceptance of the invitation consists of thirteen lines of scripture, which clarify the King of Tuṣita’s preparation of the offering and his invitation.
The Buddha-Tathāgata, desiring to bring ultimate benefit to all sentient beings, accepted the invitation and joined with those of the ten directions to share in this portion.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Palace Adorned with All Jewels spontaneously manifested a wondrous and exquisite adornment surpassing all celestial ornaments;
nets of every kind of jewel surrounded and completely covered it, raining down everywhere all manner of supreme and sublime jewels.
Clouds of all kinds of ornaments rained down everywhere; clouds of all kinds of precious robes rained down everywhere; clouds of all kinds of sandalwood incense rained down everywhere;
clouds of all kinds of solid fragrances rained down everywhere; clouds of all kinds of precious ornamental canopies rained down everywhere;
clouds of inconceivable masses of flowers rained down everywhere; and inconceivable sounds of music and song issued forth everywhere.
He praised the Tathāgata’s omniscience as being entirely in accord with the sublime Dharma, and all such offerings surpassed those of the devas.
At that time, in the Tuṣita Palace, the music and songs of praise resounded incessantly;
through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they caused the mind of the King of Tuṣita to remain undisturbed, owing to his past roots of goodness.
Their faculties all attained fulfillment; immeasurable wholesome dharmas became increasingly firm and grew in pure faith;

they gave rise to great vigor and produced great joy; their pure and profound aspirations were awakened, and they resolved upon bodhicitta; their mindfulness of the Dharma was uninterrupted, and they maintained total retention without forgetting.
At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, immediately recollected the Buddhas of the past.
[The Sūtra says: "Having planted roots of goodness, he spoke these verses.

[The Commentary says: Regarding the eighth section, from "At that time, in the Palace Adorned with All Jewels" down to "he spoke these verses," this passage clarifies how the Tathāgata entered the palace and, through the permeation of the Buddha’s supreme virtues, caused the splendor of the palace's adornments to become even more magnificent.
The portion of the text concerning the offerings of the devas consists of thirteen lines and a half, which may be roughly divided into two sections:

first, from "At that time, all were adorned with jewels" down to "surpassing all the offerings of the devas," there are eight lines of scripture clarifying how the Tathāgata accepted the invitation and entered the hall;
through the fruit of the Buddha’s own roots of goodness, he manifested a splendor surpassing that of the devas.
The "Incomparable Pair" (Anupama-dvaya) refers to the excellence of the stage of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the stage of union (*yuganaddha*), which are like those of a Buddha; thus,

from the passage beginning with "At that time, in the Tuṣita Palace" down to "and spoke these verses," there are five and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the music and dance of the devas blazed forth without ceasing,
and how the devas joyfully spoke these verses— this clarifies the entry into the bliss of the Dharma (*dharmābhirati*).
[Sūtra] In the past there was a Tathāgata named Unobstructed Moon, the most excellent among all auspicious things;
he once entered this Adorned Hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Vast Wisdom, the most excellent among all auspicious things.
He once entered this Golden Hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Universal Eye, The most excellent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Lotus Hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Coral, The most preeminent among all auspicious things;
He once entered this Treasure Store Palace, And therefore this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Lion of Discourse, The most preeminent among all auspicious things.
He once entered this palace of the King of Mountains; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Sūryaprabha, the most excellent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this Palace of Many Flowers; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Buddha named Anantaprabha, The most excellent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Hall Adorned with Trees, And therefore this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Dharmadhvaja, The most excellent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this precious palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Jñānapradīpa, The most excellent among all that is auspicious.
He once entered this Gandhamādana hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Buddha named Guṇaprabha, The most excellent among all auspicious things;
He once entered this maṇi palace, Therefore, this place is the most auspicious.
[Commentary] The ninth section consists of twenty lines of verse praising ten Buddhas of the past who all entered this palace.

Regarding "Auspicious" (Śrī): it is called "Auspicious" because it is the gathering place of all virtues; it is called "Cloud" because it is augmented by manifold blessings. Regarding the "Golden-Colored Hall":
the hall possesses golden light, which also signifies that the Dharma-body is stainless. Regarding the "Lotus Hall":

the hall is adorned with lotuses of various colors, which also symbolizes that the Dharma-body is undefiled; this is the meaning of "lotus. As for "Mountain": [it refers to the mountain-like stability of the Dharma-body].
Regarding the "Palace of the King": this clarifies that the accumulation of merit is like Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains; it is not that the palace itself possesses mountains.

As the Sūtra says, "jewels" refers to the preciousness of virtue as the true jewel, rather than being concerned with gems and jade. Other meanings may be understood accordingly. There are three reasons why one must praise the former Tathāgatas:
first, the Deva-king Tuṣita reflects upon the power of his own past roots of goodness; second, [the distinction between] the ancient and the present; and third, [the continuity of] cause and effect.
The tracks of the path of all Buddhas of the past and present are universally pervasive;

the track of the path of the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa follows the ancient [tradition] without deviation, and is not the work of Māras, Brahmās, or Brahmins, so as to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith and enter [the path]. These ten Buddhas also achieve their names through their preparatory practices (*prayoga*) and subsequent conduct (*anuvartana*).
[Sūtra] Just as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven in this world, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, praised the past Buddhas with verses,
so too did the Kings of the Tuṣita Heavens in all worlds throughout the ten directions praise the merits of the Buddha in this same way.
[Treatise] The tenth section concludes both sutras by describing how the ten directions likewise praise the past Tathāgatas’ entry into this hall.
[Sutra] At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne within the treasury of maṇi jewels in the Hall Adorned with All Jewels.
Sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), his Dharma-body is pure and his wondrous functions are sovereign; he dwells in the same realm as the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Abiding in omniscience (*sarvajñā*), he enters into the same single nature as all Buddhas. With the Buddha-eye clearly discerning, he perceives all phenomena without obstruction.
Possessing great majestic power, he wanders universally throughout the Dharma-realm without ever resting, endowed with great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*).
He is able to travel everywhere to wherever there are sentient beings capable of being transformed, adorning his body with the unimpeded adornments of all Buddhas;
knowing the proper time, he preaches the Dharma for the assembly.
Inconceivable multitudes of bodhisattvas have gathered together from various lands in other directions; the assembly is pure, and their dharma-bodies are non-dual.
Without relying on anything, he was able to manifest the activities of a Buddha’s body at will; having sat upon this seat,
there spontaneously appeared within that palace immeasurable and innumerable extraordinary, exquisite, and magnificent articles of offering surpassing those of the devas—
namely, flower garlands, garments, ointments, powdered incense, precious parasols, banners, pennants, music, and songs of praise.

Each and every such offering was beyond measure or calculation; with a vast mind of reverence and respect, they made offerings to the Buddhas, and it was likewise so for all the Tuṣita heavens throughout the ten directions.
[Treatise] Section Eleven: From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "all were likewise," this passage clarifies how the Tathāgata entered the hall, ascended the seat, and sat down;

it demonstrates how the excellence of the Buddha’s virtue within the hall surpassed that of all the devas and the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, who all came to assemble there. At the end of this chapter, there are thirteen lines.

The first half of the sutra is roughly divided into two sections: 1. From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "preached the Dharma for the assembly," there are six lines and a half of the sutra clarifying the section on the Tathāgata sitting upon his seat and preaching the Dharma for the assembly. This is further divided into two parts. 2.
From "The unspeakably many bodhisattvas of the assembly" down to "all were likewise so," there are seven lines of the sutra clarifying the bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
The assembly hall where the Bodhisattvas gather is exquisitely adorned, surpassing all the heavens;
this magnificent array of clouds and the arrangement of seats are identical throughout the Tuṣita heavens of the ten directions, as has already been explained in the preceding section.

Regarding those who sit cross-legged upon the lion thrones, there are two meanings: first, it represents the dignified deportment of the world; second, it signifies the gathering of these ten [bodhisattvas] for the sake of transformation.

In this state, principle and phenomena are mutually penetrating; the essence of the Tathāgata’s seat is the inconceivable wisdom of the dharmadhātu-dependent origination, which abides nowhere. Great kindness and great compassion constitute the essence of this seat.

Because the nature of this wisdom of non-abiding is inherently all-pervasive and equal to space, it neither departs nor arrives, yet it manifests form-bodies in accordance with the number of sentient beings.
According to the distinctions among the faculties of sentient beings, they are tamed and delivered as appropriate, yet without any deliberate effort;
this is as the Sūtra says: "The Dharma-body is pure, and its wondrous functions are sovereign.

They dwell in the same realm as the Buddhas of the three periods of time and abide in omniscience; because the essence of wisdom has no interior, exterior, middle, or periphery, all Buddhas dwell together therein.
The realm is likewise so; those who enter the same single nature as all Buddhas possess the nature of no-nature, which is without entering or exiting.

All Buddhas are identical in this regard. Those with the clear and lucid Buddha-eye awaken to the fact that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, and are able to universally know all dharmas through wisdom. They possess great majestic power and travel everywhere throughout the ten directions.

That which has never ceased from its activity, yet uses the wisdom and insight that is unconditioned and non-reliant to shatter all false views and attachments until they are entirely extinguished, is called "sovereign power" (vīrya).

Because this wisdom is without interior or exterior and is omnipresent like space, it manifests forms in response to conditions without coming or going; this is called "wandering. That which is not mundane and not unreal is called... [the name of the state].

In the Dharma-realm, a single thought-moment encompasses the three periods of time; past and present, emotions are exhausted. Teaching and transforming sentient beings without end or beginning is called "never resting," clarifying that time does not shift.
One who possesses great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) has great wisdom that is non-dependent and formless, with a nature free from arising and ceasing—this is called "spiritual" (*śen*).
Wisdom that reaches everywhere without obstruction is called "penetration" (*tong*). It accords with conditions as they arise.
One who is able to go everywhere to those who can be transformed possesses wisdom that is without coming or going, center or periphery, front or back;
because all sentient beings throughout the ten directions see [the Buddha] according to their own resonance and response, and each sees him differently, this is called "going everywhere.

He is adorned with the unimpeded adornments of all Buddhas, which has two meanings: first, the adornment of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*); second, the adornment of the Buddhas...
The two types of merit—the primary retribution (*pratyātmika-vipāka*) and the environmental retribution (*bhājana-loka*)—adorn all the major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and minor marks (*anuvyañjana*).
Thus, the Tathāgata’s body is the primary retribution, while the land of the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-dhātu*) is the environmental retribution.

Through the excellence of his own karma, wisdom adorns both his own body and its environment; as the natural law (*dharmatā*) of wisdom, it inherently possesses boundless merits, such as the ninety-seven kinds.

The marks of a Great Being are merely covered by ignorance; that which is obtained as a result of maturation (*vipākaphala*) through benefiting sentient beings with loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity is the merit of the light of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).

Just as the Great Being possesses the primary marks of a Buddha, he likewise possesses secondary marks numbering as many as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury worlds (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*), which are infinite in extent. For now, I shall briefly cite one type as an example.

The merits of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are called the "King of Perfection," and all their benefits are fully set forth in the sūtras. Furthermore, the essence of wisdom that dwells without dependence—
being free from the grasping at self and other, or internal and external— possesses a body adorned with primary and secondary marks and a land of all-encompassing realms,
wherein all objects mutually contain one another, like the reflections in hundreds of thousands of bright mirrors.
The various realms of bodies and lands are mutually inclusive in layers upon layers of infinite depth;
these myriad objects are interpenetrated without end, like the jewel-net abode of Śakra, where the celestial retinues and the myriad images within the jewels are mutually inclusive.
There is no obstruction between body and environment: from the body emerge buddha-lands, and from the buddha-lands emerge clouds of bodies, all appearing together.

The manifestation of Buddha-activities is a single kind of sovereign mastery wherein all phenomena are thus within the realm of wisdom; therein, one does not speak of dharmas as being either sentient or insentient. As the Sūtra says:

"Skillfully knowing the proper time, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of the assembly. This means that having discerned whether the faculties [of beings] are mature or immature, he transforms and delivers them according to what is appropriate.
Question: What constitutes the Buddhas' knowledge of the proper and improper times regarding the minds of sentient beings?
It is said: Because the minds of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas and the minds of all sentient beings are fundamentally not different, they constitute a single mind and a single wisdom.
By this one knows that regarding both the opportune and non-opportune times, the Buddhas have awakened to and realized [this truth] and share it with sentient beings.
While sentient beings are deluded and claim it to be separate, all Buddhas, by means of the minds of all sentient beings...
Through wisdom, one attains perfect enlightenment; yet all sentient beings are deluded regarding the wisdom of the Buddhas and thus become sentient beings.

Even when they attain Buddhahood, they still appear as sentient beings because they were deluded regarding the principle. The Dharma gates taught by these Buddhas who were deluded regarding the principle are precisely for resolving the delusions within the minds of sentient beings.
Since these are not different, we know that the *Sutra on the Mind of Sentient Beings* states: [as cited above].
The statement that "unspeakably many bodhisattvas have gathered together from various lands in other directions" is made:

they are called "other directions" in reference to the distinctions among the myriad practices; they are called "various lands" because they tame sentient beings by adapting the Dharma to their faculties;
and they are said to have "gathered together" because they do not depart from the Tathāgata’s great, perfect, and wise illumination within this assembly.
Purity means the absence of mental consciousness; the non-duality of the *dharmakāya* means being of one essence with the Buddha, which is the equality of having no intrinsic nature.

It is without dependence, without attainment, and without realization, yet it is able to spontaneously manifest the activities of the Buddha-body through the wisdom of non-action, which is identical to the Buddha’s utility. Having sat upon this seat, one realizes these ten dedications.
The Dharma-realm is the fundamental source; that it manifests such extraordinary excellence is due to what is evoked by wisdom.
That it transcends all the heavens is due to the response of the retribution of wisdom, not because it is produced by sentient beings. The Master of the Treatise explains this in verse:
"The marks of retribution possessed by Bodhisattvas arise from their practice. The verse says: "The Bodhisattva takes patience as a hanging garland, and always wears shame and remorse as clothing."
The adornment of the precepts is their ointment and powdered incense; great compassion universally covering all is their canopy; the unmoving upright mind is their banner of meditative concentration;
and the banner of wisdom breaks through all false views. Skillful means dwelling eternally within the ocean of birth and death to benefit sentient beings is their music;
and the eloquent proclamation of the sublime Dharma through dhāraṇīs, whereby those who hear it attain liberation, is their song.
The above may be understood according to the text. This section contains an unspeakable number of bodhisattvas from other directions.
This section concerning the assembly of devas dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven consists of bodhisattvas totaling one hundred and eighteen times ten million billion in number.
As for the bodhisattvas who have come from other directions, they are unspeakably many. The devas are adorned with height.
The seats and palaces differ in color and type in one hundred and eighty-four ways;
there is one class consisting of a million billion Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, adorned by their own merit in infinite numbers.
This assembly is led by such great compassion, such wisdom, and such myriad practices, solely for the purpose of nurturing those who have first resolved to attain enlightenment.

Because the wisdom and great compassion born at the outset of the Buddha-family allow for mastery through habitual cultivation, time does not alter them, the Dharma does not change, and wisdom does not shift.
It is like bamboo or reeds that grow according to their original nature; there is no difference between the coarseness or subtlety of the beginning and the end.
It is also like a child who grows from infancy to adulthood—the greatness [of the final state] is no different from the greatness [of the initial potential].
This simply takes the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage as the expedient means for the path of cultivation;
the fruit of Buddhahood resides in the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

Furthermore, because within the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) each single abiding possesses the functional efficacy of all ten abidings, and because the ten practices, ten dedications, and ten stages are collectively fully contained within the ten abidings.

Therefore, it is just as when a divine dragon-horse king gives birth to a divine colt; born in that same land, the colt’s speed is similar to its father’s, though its power and utility have not yet reached those of its parents.
Likewise, a bodhisattva who has first resolved on enlightenment (prathamacittotpādika) mounts the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience and is born into the Buddha-family;
he possesses wisdom equal to the Buddha’s, yet only in terms of his spiritual powers and the strength of his supernormal faculties.

Because one has not yet matured through the long cultivation of the myriad practices of great compassion, although the merit of this cultivation is ultimately complete, the Dharma does not change and time does not shift.
In the end, nothing emerges that was not present at the moment of first generating the bodhicitta;

once the power and function of that effort are perfected, it is like the dragon girl who attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime without passing beyond a single kṣaṇa, and likewise, it is as when Sudhana attained the fruit of Buddhahood in one lifetime.
Regarding the meaning of "birth" (*jāti*) in your life, it is the attainment of non-birth (*anutpāda*). For now, there are eleven provisional designations for non-birth:
(1) the non-birth of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates; (2) the non-birth of the intrinsic nature of views; (3) the non-birth of emptiness; (4) the non-birth of self-nature (*svabhāva*);
(5) the non-birth of the non-transmigration of time and eons; (6) the non-birth of nirvana and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); (7) the sound of the teaching of the Dharma...

1. The non-arising of the silence of sound; 2. The non-arising of the eight wisdoms through discernment; 3. The non-arising of the nature of the supernatural powers and spiritual faculties, which is inherently all-pervasive;
4. The non-arising of manifesting before all sentient beings throughout the entirety of past and present kalpas, without departing from the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
Because there are these ten meanings of non-arising, it is called "one birth."
The intent of this sutra is that the attainment of bodhi occurs precisely at this stage;
for the dharmas of the ten practices, ten dedications, ten stages, and the eleventh stage serve as skillful means to support the initial aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood.

Because the desired fruit transcends all distinctions of before and after, these provisions (saṃbhāra) and the fruit of Buddhahood are simultaneous, acting as mutual essence and function to support one another; therefore, they are termed the "Adornment of Enlightened Practice" (bodhicaryā-vyūha).

The Sūtra states that by using the fruit to support practice, one ensures that practice is free from attachment; and by using practice to support the fruit, great compassion and great powers are accomplished.

Just as with the three vehicles, for Bodhisattvas who possess mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) but have not yet spoken of the Buddha-vehicle or the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the fruit of Buddhahood is projected as occurring after the final kalpa of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* beyond the eleventh stage. Thus, the three stages of worthiness (*tri-satkāya*) prior to the stages constitute [the preparatory path].

The provisions (*sambhāra*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the fruit of Buddhahood resides in the eleventh stage at the conclusion of the three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*).
Thus, the characteristics of these five stages in this teaching differ from those in the three vehicles (*triyāna*) by being their exact opposite;
this shall be further clarified later.
*The Combined Commentary on the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Forty-one.
