Chapter Twenty-four: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
[Commentary] To explain this chapter, there are three sections as previously stated. First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter:

it clarifies that the ten bodhisattvas, such as Vajradhvaja and others, each coming from different buddha-fields to the Tuṣita Heaven palace and arriving at the place of the Tathāgata, each manifested a magnificent jewel lion-throne and [applied] the ten methods of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Because it praises [the Buddha] through verses concerning cause and effect, it is titled the "Chapter on Verses of Praise" (*Gāthā-stotra-parivarta*).

Regarding the distinction from the "Buddha-fields," this chapter follows from the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*) and enters into the second section, the "Explanation of the Meaning" (*artha-vyākhyāna*), within the "Ten Dedications" (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). As for the purpose of this chapter's inclusion:

since this chapter intends to establish the dharma-gate of cause and effect within the Ten Dedications, this chapter must necessarily follow. Third, regarding the word-by-word commentary (*anuvyañjana-vyākhyāna*): [The text continues with the specific commentary on the verses.]
The exposition of the meaning is divided into two parts: first, a general outline of the intent of the sūtra; second, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first, the general outline of the intent of this chapter consists of a total of eleven sections arranged sequentially throughout the entire chapter.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, there was one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields.
They came from worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields to where the Buddha was.
Their names were Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva and Dṛḍhadhvaja Bodhisattva.
The lands from which the Bodhisattva Vīradhvaja, the Bodhisattva Prabhādhvaja, the Bodhisattva Jñānadhvaja, the Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja,
the Bodhisattva Vīryadhvaja, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, the Bodhisattva Jyotirdhvaja, and the Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja had come were called the World of Exquisite Jewels,
the World of Sublime Joy, the World of Exquisite Silver, the World of Exquisite Gold, and the World of Exquisite *Maṇi*.
In the world-systems of Nirmāṇa, Vajra, Padma, Utpala, Candana, and Gandha,
they each cultivated the pure conduct of brahmacarya in the presence of Buddhas, namely: the Buddha Anantadhvaja,
the Buddha Vātadhvaja, the Buddha Vimuktidhvaja, the Buddha Ācāradhvaja, the Buddha Prabhāsa-dhvaja, and the Buddha Nityadhvaja.

The Buddha Most Victorious Banner, the Buddha Sovereign Banner, the Buddha Brahma Banner, and the Buddha Banner of Contemplation—when those bodhisattvas arrived at the presence of the Buddhas, they prostrated at the Buddhas' feet;
then, by the spiritual power of the Buddhas, there were immediately manifested wonderful jeweled-treasury lion thrones, covered with jeweled nets that spread everywhere and filled the space.
Each of the assemblies of bodhisattvas, according to the direction from which they had come, sat upon their respective seats.
Upon it, he sat in the full lotus posture, his body emitting hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of pure light rays.
These immeasurable lights all arose from the jewel of the Bodhisattva’s pure mind, free from all faults and evils, and produced by his great vows;
they manifested the sovereign and pure dharmas of all Buddhas through the equanimity of all Bodhisattvas.
By the power of their vows, they are able to universally rescue and protect all sentient beings;

they are pleasing for all the world to behold, and those who see them do so not in vain, as all are brought to subdual. This assembly of bodhisattvas has fully accomplished immeasurable merits, namely:
traveling everywhere through all buddha-lands without obstruction, and beholding the pure Dharma that is free from dependence.
With a body of wisdom, they manifest infinite bodies that pervade the ten directions to serve all Buddhas;
they enter the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable dharmas of mastery of the Buddhas; they abide in the gates of infinite omniscience;
through the light of wisdom, they thoroughly understand all phenomena; within all phenomena, they attain fearlessness, and according to what they proclaim—
They possess inexhaustible eloquence that extends to the limits of the future; they open the gate of *dhāraṇī* through great wisdom;
their eye of wisdom is pure as they enter the profound realm of the Dharma; their sphere of wisdom is boundless and ultimately pure like space.
Just as the assembly of bodhisattvas in this world’s Tuṣita Heaven Palace has thus gathered, so too do those from the ten directions [assemble].
In every Tuṣita heaven palace, there were bodhisattvas bearing these same names who had gathered for this assembly;
the names of the Buddhas in the lands from which they came were likewise identical, without any difference.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of light rays from his two kneecaps, universally illuminating the ten directions throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
In all worlds, those bodhisattvas all behold these manifestations of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations;
likewise, these bodhisattvas also behold the manifestations of the spiritual transformations of all those Tathāgatas.

Thus, these bodhisattvas have all planted roots of goodness and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva together with the Tathāgata Vairocana in the past, and have fully realized and entered [this state].
The Buddhas possess sovereign and profound liberation; they have attained bodies that are non-different from the Dharma-realm and enter all lands without dwelling anywhere.
They behold immeasurable Buddhas and go to serve them all. Within a single thought-moment, they traverse the entire Dharma-realm with unimpeded sovereignty;
their minds and intentions are pure like priceless jewels—thus are the immeasurable and innumerable Tathāgatas.
May they always be protected and remembered, and may they be granted the power to reach the ultimate, supreme other shore;

may they always abide in pure mindfulness toward unsurpassed enlightenment, and in every thought-moment enter the sphere of all-knowledge. May they attain mastery and unimpeded penetration in entering the small within the large and the large within the small;
having attained the Buddha-body, may they dwell together with the Buddhas and obtain all-knowledge.
Born from omniscience, they are able to enter all the spheres traversed by all Tathāgatas;
they expound immeasurable gateways of wisdom and reach the further shore of the great wisdom of the Vajra Banner.
Having attained the vajra-samādhi and severed all doubts, they have acquired the sovereign supernormal powers of all Buddhas throughout all lands in the ten directions.
He teaches and tames hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless sentient beings;
though he is entirely unattached to any numerical reckoning, he is skillfully able to train in and accomplish ultimate skillful means, thereby establishing all dharmas.
Such are his hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakably inexhaustible, pure, and immeasurable merits throughout the three periods of time.
The assemblies of all the bodhisattvas gathered together at the place where the Buddha was; because of what was seen through that light, it was exactly the same at all the abodes of all the Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:

[Treatise] First, from the passage beginning "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha" down to the fifty-two lines of verse where he speaks in gāthās, this section of the sutra clarifies how the ten bodhisattvas, such as Vajradhvaja and others, assemble from the ten directions to manifest the non-duality of cause and fruit.
Within this section, the meaning is divided into ten parts; the first is: "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha."
From "Having arrived at the place where the Buddha was" down to this point is the section on the assembly of these various multitudes, divided into two parts.
First, from "Their names were" down to "Dharmadhvaja Bodhisattva," is the section listing the names of the ten bodhisattvas who came; this is further divided into three sub-sections.

Second, from "The lands from which they came" down to "the World of Wondrous Fragrance," is the section on the lands from which these bodhisattvas originated; this is divided into four sub-sections. Each [of the following sections]...

From "Having practiced the pure brahma-faring in the presence of the Buddha" down to "Observing the Banner-Buddha," there is a section of five [parts] concerning the names of the Buddhas whom he originally served.

From "The bodhisattvas therein" down to "Immeasurable Merit," there are eight lines of sūtra-text clarifying the section on the arriving bodhisattvas sitting upon transformed seats, emitting light, manifesting virtues, and bringing benefit; this constitutes the sixth part, namely:

From "down to being like empty space" there are seven lines of sutra text clarifying how the bodhisattvas who have come see the supportless, pure *dharmakāya*, and how their wisdom universally travels through the ten directions to serve the Buddhas with unimpeded mastery. This is divided into seven sections.
From "just as in this world" down to "there is no difference" clarifies that [the assembly] from all ten directions collectively concludes that they are identical to those who have come here.

Section Eight: The Gathering. At that time, from the World-Honored One’s descent [from the sky] down to the manifestation of his supernatural transformations, it is clearly shown how the Tathāgata emitted light that universally illumined the ten directions, so that the great assemblies on both sides could see one another. Section Nine: The Arrival of the Bodhisattvas. From "Thus the bodhisattvas...
down to "all gathered at the assembly," sixteen lines of scripture clarify the past causes of the bodhisattvas who had come.

The section on "Sharing the Buddha’s Roots of Goodness to the Ultimate Sovereignty of the Dharma" consists of ten parts, beginning from "Having seen what was manifested by the light at the Buddha’s abode" down to the two lines of verse that clarify the general conclusion.

The second part, the "Section on the Assembly of Bodhisattvas from the Ten Directions Being Identical to This World," is explained according to the text as follows, concerning these fifty-two lines of scripture:
[Insert detailed commentary here] ...Regarding this, in the fifty-two lines of scripture, approximately... [continue with specific analysis].
Establishing Ten Gates: 1. Clarifying the Dharma from which the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions have come;
2. Explaining the meaning of the names of the Bodhisattvas; 3. Explaining what the ten worlds symbolize; 4. Explaining the causes and effects of the ten Buddha names; 5.
Explaining the nature of the seats upon which the ten Bodhisattvas arrive at the Buddha’s abode to transform beings; 6. Explaining the bodies of the Bodhisattvas.
1. What dharma did the Seven Bodhisattvas of Radiance obtain that enabled them to manifest transformations at will throughout the ten directions?
2. What dharma does the radiance emitted by the Tathāgata Śakra signify? 3. From whom did the ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas who have come forth develop their resolve for enlightenment? 4.
How do they progress through the stages according to their respective positions, clarifying the causes and effects of their cultivation? 5. What is the dharma from which the bodhisattvas have come?

This scripture states that "each [bodhisattva] is accompanied by as many [beings] as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields" in order to clarify that the dharma-wisdom and the knowledge-and-vision of their advancement surpass those of the preceding stages. Thus, the *Ten Abodes* speaks of "hundreds," the *Ten Practices* of "thousands," and the *Ten Dedications* of "ten thousands";
all these come from worlds outside of lands numbering as many as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields.

Regarding "going to the place where the Buddha is," this clarifies that those who are deluded regarding the Dharma clouds are outside the world of wisdom; thus, their arrival is termed "coming to the place where the Buddha is.

As for the phrase "as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields," these are the numbers of both delusion and awakening. Second, concerning the meaning of the names of the Bodhisattvas listed below:
as for the name "Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva," the term "Bodhisattva" has already been explained previously. "Vajra" (Diamond) refers to... [text continues].

"Vajradhvaja" (Diamond Banner) clarifies the meaning of being firm and immovable. The Bodhisattvas of the ten preceding stages of practice are called "Forests," signifying that their practice provides vast and extensive shade and protection.

Therefore, the Bodhisattvas of this stage are designated by the title "Banner" to clarify that through the practice of great compassion, they are able to shatter all the afflictions of sentient beings while remaining within the great ocean of birth and death, and their own wisdom remains unshakable.
Because they are active, the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) clarify the meaning of humbling oneself through practice to harmonize with enemies;
the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) clarify the meaning of the mastery of destroying enemies through great wisdom that is firm and strong, following from compassion.

This refers to the Bodhisattva Firm Banner (*Dṛḍhadhvaja*), for whom this great compassion constitutes the essence of ethical discipline (*śīla*); and the Bodhisattva Courageous Banner (*Vikrāntadhvaja*), who refers to great compassion as patience (*kṣānti*).
As for the Bodhisattva Light Banner of Valiant Meaning, this refers to taking great compassion as the essence of diligence;
because he illuminates with wisdom throughout the night of birth and death, he is the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner.

This stage takes great wisdom as its essence, for within birth and death it is ever-luminous and constantly destroys darkness; thus it is the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, which takes meditative concentration as its essence.

"Sā" (Sa) signifies that he clearly employs great compassion and great wisdom to skillfully establish the net of the Dharma; it is called the "Jewel Banner" because his enlightened teaching is noble and precious, and thus is not like worldly treasures.
As for the Bodhisattva Vīryaketu (Inexhaustible Banner of Diligence), this stage is the seventh, the practice of skillful means (*upāya*).

He is well able to discern the faculties of others and engage in common activities with the world; though he dwells amidst the secular, he is not deluded, and though he shares the same environment as the dust of the world, he remains undefiled. This is diligence.
Regarding the meaning of the banner (*dhvaja*): the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja (Stainless Banner) is so named because he is the eighth perfection, that of the vow (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

Being himself free from birth and death, he benefits sentient beings by following his vows through wisdom; therefore, he is eternally stainless. Regarding the Bodhisattva Jyotirdhvaja (Star Banner), he is so named because he is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
Having attained the rank of a Dharma King, he possesses the excellence of differentiated wisdom and clarity, skillfully knowing the faculties of all beings, just like [the stars].

Regarding the teaching that all the constellations, both large and small, are luminous: the Bodhisattva Dharma-Dhvaja (Dharmadhvaja) is so named because at this stage he has skillfully established the *prajñāpāramitā* (perfection of wisdom);
since no one can destroy him, this is the meaning of "Dharma-Dhvaja. Thus, those mentioned above are the persons who are capable of practicing these deeds.
Third, as for the explanation of the name of the world: the land from which [the Buddha] comes is called the World of Wondrous Jewels (*Ratnavyūha*).
That the bright [wisdom] universally bestows the wondrous Dharma upon all sentient beings is the meaning of what is noble.

That the world is named "Wondrous Joy" (Sukhāvatī) clarifies that great compassion serves as the locus of the precepts; by dwelling in birth-and-death to benefit sentient beings, it causes them to attain great bliss.
The "wondrous silver world" clarifies that the essence of patience is accomplished through the principle-wisdom of the Dharmakāya, being like pure silver—supple, clear, and brilliant.
The Golden World signifies that through the clarity of diligence, one benefits the mundane without weariness and does not fail in the True Principle;
because the central virtue brings forth blessings, everything is golden. The World of Wondrous Maṇi signifies that the Dharma-nature is inherently pure and, while functioning, remains untainted;
because it takes sovereign mastery as its essential substance, it is wondrous. The World of Wondrous Vajra signifies the absence of intrinsic nature.
Subtle wisdom can destroy falsehood without being destroyed itself;
thus, the world of *Padma* (Wondrous Lotus) refers to the red lotus, clarifying that it is through great compassion that one can share its color and fragrance while remaining unstained.
The world of *Utpala* (Wondrous Blue Lotus) refers to the blue lotus; this eighth [world] represents the practice of following compassion with wisdom.
Being pure and unstained, like the color of a blue lotus that remains undefiled even when in the mud, this serves to symbolize the world of exquisite sandalwood;
it represents the fragrance of the Dharma preached by this Dharma Master as he attains his station.
The world of exquisite fragrance clarifies that at this stage, great wisdom and great compassion bring the merits of the stage to completion through non-reliant and effortless sublime wisdom.
Yet, filling the ten directions with wisdom that neither comes nor goes, the sound of the Dharma pervades everywhere;
because it has no form, it is called "Sublime Fragrance" rather than a specific class of forms, signifying its superiority over what preceded it which had traces.

Thus, the ten world-names above represent the dharmas within the practices of these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); therefore, the "World of Sublimity" refers to following along with birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The transformation and edification of sentient beings is the wondrous function of principle and wisdom. The worldly take lands, mountains, and rivers to be the world;

the wise and virtuous take the wondrous function of wisdom and virtue to be the world. Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the ten names of the Buddhas, and cause and effect, the Sūtra says:
"Each, in the presence of a Buddha, purely cultivates the Brahma-faring. This clarifies that one advances through the stages by cultivating preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

The "fruits" refer to the ten Buddhas mentioned below; that which is called the Buddha *Akṣayadhvaja* (Inexhaustible Banner) clarifies that the practice of giving within this stage of the Great Compassion of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) is inexhaustible, thereby constituting the name of the fruit of Buddhahood.

This giving is clarified in the following "Chapter on Dedication. The Buddha *Vāyudhvaja* (Wind Banner) clarifies that the trigram *Xun* represents wind, represents purity and whiteness, and represents speech.
It is red, it is the sun, it is light, and it is pure white; it is like the wind, which has no form or color, yet its fragrance and stench are all blown away so that everything is made pure.
Furthermore, Xun represents the rooster, which knows the time and crows; thus it symbolizes knowing the faculties [of sentient beings] and bestowing the teachings.
When it aligns with the Upper Trigram, the Gate of Heaven opens, signifying the flourishing of all virtues. Xun represents the beginning of the fullness of Yang, and it is fixed.
This is the time for discernment; it is the time to clarify the rules of the precepts.

Therefore, *Xun* (the trigram for wind) represents speech, the mouth, and the gateway of the face, capable of discussing all manner of goodness. It can transform the "small boy" (*chou*), for *chou* represents the young;
through the discourse of the multitude, it transforms the ignorant. By this one may know that the wind-banner of the Buddha is the wind of this *śīla-pāramitā*.
"Transformation Fruit" (Huàguǒ) is a title; "Buddha Victory Banner of Liberation" (Jiětuōzhāng Fó) refers to the fruit within the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).

Once the power of patience is perfected, there is no lack of liberation—this is the meaning of the West, where the trigram Dui represents inferiority. "Buddha Banner of Dignified Manner" (Wēiyízhāng Fó) is the Buddha-fruit presiding over the North;
it shares its name with "Buddha Wisdom of Dignified Manner" (Wēiyízhì Fó), who likewise presides over the North during the stage of Faith (*śraddhā*).
This constitutes the stage of the Teacher and Model (Śāstṛ-pada). Because one receives the ignorant with dignified and orderly deportment, one takes the restraint of conduct as the fruit;

thus, he is named the Buddha *Prabhāsa-lakṣaṇa-dhvaja*. Since this shares the same name as the Buddha *Prabhāsa-jñāna* of the northeastern direction in the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), it clarifies that the trigram *Kǎn* (Water) serves as the object to be remedied, *Chǒu* (Earth) represents the faculty of faith, and *Yín* (Wood) represents the initial realization of principle. This clearly demonstrates the metaphorical borrowing [of these symbols].
The square represents the Dharma; its primary direction is North (Chou), which corresponds to the mountain. The mountain is immovable, and immovability is stillness.
Stillness can give rise to illumination; this is the beginning of Zen. The beginning of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the blossoming of right wisdom.

By means of the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), one does not depart from the dharmas believed in during the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Upon those dharmas, one establishes [the mind); this is "illumination."
Because the essential substance of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) can give rise to the luminous wisdom that brings forth great compassion and benefits the mundane world,
it is similar to the Buddha Constant Banner (*Sadādhvaja*) and the Buddha Ultimate Wisdom of the Sixth [Stage] within the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Generally speaking,
the names of the Buddha-fruit established upon the *pāramitās* that ascend through the stages are collectively not separate from the fruit of what is believed within the ten levels of faith.
This is just like when Sudhana reached the fruit of Maitreya Buddha’s realization and was directed back to see Mañjuśrī;
this clearly shows that Mañjuśrī is the stage of the fruit of faith for the beginning of enlightenment. To initiate practice and progress, one does not depart from the original site.
Now, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva dwells on Mount Qingliang, which is in the northeast of this realm of Jambudvīpa, presiding over the trigram Gen.
This stage marks the beginning of enlightenment and the manifestation of wisdom; therefore, it is designated as the "Child Bodhisattva.

To speak in terms of ultimate reality, this is fundamentally the wondrous wisdom of the principle of non-substantiality (amūla-tattva) of the Buddhas of the ten directions; there is no path to Buddhahood that does not proceed through this gate.
All sentient beings possess this entirely, yet they remain deluded by the principle and confused by themselves, failing to perceive it. Were one to awaken to this principle...
The manifestation of discriminative thought is also clarified by means of meditative concentration; thus, *gen* (艮) signifies "stopping.

For all other cases, one should understand them by following this precedent and correlating their names with their respective positions. Fifth, regarding the substance of the seats from which the various Bodhisattvas come to transform beings, the Sūtra says:
"They magically create exquisite jewel lion-thrones, using the net of Dharma-jewels to benefit sentient beings through teaching and practice."
Therefore, a jeweled net completely covers the seat. Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), the substance of the seat is established by way of its fruition;

thus, it takes the "Jeweled Lotus Treasury" as its substance. Within the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the substance is established by way of attaining the Tathāgata’s wisdom and great compassion;
thus, it takes the "Vairocana Treasury" as its substance. This is precisely why the lion throne is designated as "Vairocana."
In the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*) within that treasury, the lion throne—which is purified through practice and free from defilement—takes the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*) as its essence.

In the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*), which clarify the place of great compassion within birth and death, the teaching and practice are universally comprehensive, encompassing all phenomena without being restricted to any single one;
therefore, the essence of the throne is designated simply as "jewel" (*ratna*), not limited to specific types of material, reflecting the nature of the teaching and practice.
Because they filter out sentient beings throughout the entire universe, their seats are covered by jeweled nets. Regarding the sixth, the Bodhisattvas’ bodily radiance:
this clarifies that Bodhisattvas in this stage dwell in the world through the practice of great compassion to benefit beings, and they illuminate sentient beings according to their wisdom;
thus, pure light constantly shines. Seventh, regarding what dharma the Bodhisattvas have attained to achieve mastery:
The scripture states: "Seeing the pure *dharmakāya* which has no basis, it manifests through the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) in immeasurable ways.
This clarifies that seeing the nature of phenomena as having no basis causes all ignorance to become a sublime function; thus, wisdom is able to transform beings everywhere without limit.
Regarding the eighth explanation of the places where the Tathāgata emits light and the dharmas they symbolize, this clarifies the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The emission of light from the lower wheel begins with faith; this clarifies that entering the stage of sainthood (ārya-bhūmi) begins with the toes, as in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
The emission of light from the insteps of the ten practices clarifies that one initiates conduct based on the Dharma-body of the noble nature (*ārya-dharmatā*).

As for the emission of light from above the knees during the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), it clarifies the manifestation of the light of the Dharma; the knees are so designated because they are the part of the human body used for sitting, rising, and turning.

This is the source of mastery in rolling up and unfolding [the dharmas]. It clarifies that this dharma-gate of the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is the great wisdom of liberation, untainted by defilement, which returns from the ultimate to the conventional;
it benefits sentient beings through compassion and vows, remaining eternally in *nirvāṇa* while dwelling in *saṃsāra*, and being unimpeded and sovereign between *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra*.
This stage is symbolized by the manifestation of light rays. This is the tenth ground (*bhūmi*).
The light between the eyebrows represents the fruit of the Middle Way. Regarding the nine clarities:
as for from whom all Bodhisattvas first resolve their minds, they take the beginningless discriminative ignorance within their own minds as the starting point of their resolve.
Because they realize that this beginningless ignorance is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, they immediately become equal in virtue to the Tathāgata Vairocana of the ten directions.
Because it is the root, if one is separated from this wisdom, there is no prospect of attaining Buddhahood, nor is there a day upon which one shall see the Buddha.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Such Bodhisattvas all share the same roots of goodness as Vairocana from the past;

they have clearly realized that their own ignorance is the essence of great wisdom, and all Buddhas share this wisdom. This concludes the ten clarifications regarding the cultivation of cause and effect according to the stages.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja is the practitioner; the World of Wondrous Jewels (Ratnavyūha) is the practice cultivated;
and the Buddha Akṣayadhvaja is the fruit of that practice. The remaining nine cases should be understood by analogy with this. Below follow ten sections of verse;
each section consists of ten lines, and each line constitutes one stanza. The dharmas described therein are as follows:
Regarding the gates for thoroughly regulating and governing within the ten stages of the *Pratipatti-pūrvaka-pratipatti* (the stage of dedication), these are fully contained within the text itself;

furthermore, adding further commentary would result in excessive textual proliferation and a sinking of the meaning, making the expressed dharma difficult to comprehend, so it shall be explained by way of summary. The remainder is fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa; by the power of his original great vows, he manifests the dharma of sovereign mastery.
This dharma is inconceivable; it is not within the sphere of the mind.
Only when wisdom reaches the other shore can one behold the realm of all Buddhas. The form-body (rūpakāya) is not the Buddha.
Sound is likewise thus; it does not exist apart from form and sound. The Buddha’s power of spiritual transformations cannot be known by those of little wisdom;
It is the true realm of all Buddhas, which can only be understood here by those who have long cultivated pure deeds.
Perfect Awakening has no place from which it comes, And there is nowhere to which it goes.
The pure and wondrous body of form is manifested through the power of spiritual faculties;
throughout immeasurable worlds, he manifests the body of a Tathāgata and extensively expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
His mind is free from attachment, his wisdom is boundless, and he thoroughly comprehends all phenomena, universally entering the Dharma-realm.
Manifesting the power of mastery over sentient beings and all phenomena,
they realize them all without obstruction and universally manifest all forms throughout every realm.
Those who seek all-knowledge and wish to swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment should, with a pure and wondrous mind, cultivate the practices of bodhi.
If there are those who see the Tathāgata’s Such majestic spiritual power, They should make offerings to the Most Victorious Honored One And not give rise to doubt.
[Treatise] From “The two Tathāgatas do not appear in the world” onwards, the following ten stanzas clarify how the Buddha reveals provisional means through reality.
[Section].
[Sūtra]: At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata is supreme and peerless; Profound and ineffable, Transcending the path of language.
Pure as space, O Lion among Men, observe how you, through the power of your sovereign supernormal faculties,
have transcended all conceptualization yet cause it to be seen.
For the sake of expounding the profound and subtle Dharma, the Guide has manifested this incomparable body for this very reason.
This is the Great Wisdom, the sphere traversed by all Buddhas.
Those who wish to understand it should always draw near to the Buddha, keeping their mental actions constantly pure.
By making offerings to all Tathāgatas without ever feeling weary or fatigued, one can enter the path of the Buddhas and possess inexhaustible merit.
Firmly abiding in the bodhicitta, one thus eliminates the net of doubt; contemplating the Buddha without weariness and penetrating all dharmas—such a person is a true son of the Buddha.
This person is able to understand the sovereign power of all Buddhas, as taught by those of vast wisdom, for the desire [for awakening] is the root of all dharmas.
One should give rise to supreme aspiration and resolve to seek unsurpassed enlightenment.
If there are those who revere the Buddha and keep in mind the Buddha’s grace, such persons shall never be separated from all Buddhas.
How could a person of wisdom, having seen or heard of the Buddha, fail to cultivate pure vows?
[Verse]: Treading the Path Traversed by the Buddha.
[Treatise]: Third, at that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja and others [utter] ten verses below this to praise the incomparable nature and marks of the Buddha’s body;
they emphasize that one must always draw near to and make offerings to him without weariness, for only when great vows are fulfilled can one tread upon this path.
The Section on the Path Traversed by the Buddha.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Valādhara-dhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as with clear and pure eyes, One perceives all forms because of the sun, So too is it with the pure mind."

Through the power of the Buddha, one sees the Tathāgata; Just as by the power of diligence, One can reach the very bottom of the ocean’s source, So too is the power of wisdom: It enables one to see immeasurable Buddhas.
Just as what is sown in a fertile field will surely grow, So too in this ground of pure mind Are born all the qualities of the Buddhas.
Just as a person who discovers a treasure trove is forever freed from the suffering of poverty, so too the Bodhisattva who attains the Buddha-dharma has a mind purified of defilement.
Just as the *gadhā* medicine can neutralize all poisons, so too the Buddha-dharma extinguishes the afflictions of all mental disturbances; it is the true and virtuous spiritual friend.
By the power of that which the Tathāgata has praised, one may hear the teachings of all Buddhas.
Even if one were to offer wealth and treasures to the Buddhas for countless eons, if one does not know the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha, this is not called a true gift.
[One should know] the immeasurable multitudes of physical marks and signs that adorn the Buddha’s body.
One cannot perceive the Buddha within the marks of form;
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is tranquil and eternally unmoving, yet he can manifest his body everywhere, Pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
Just as the realm of empty space is neither born nor extinguished, So too are all the Buddhas’ dharmas.
"Ultimately there is neither arising nor ceasing.
[Treatise: Fourth, at that time, the Bodhisattva Valāgraketu and others recited ten verses below to clarify the essentials of the Buddha and the Dharma:
that one can only perceive the Buddha through a pure mind and pure conduct; for conditioned phenomena are incapable of such realization.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Radiant Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“In all worlds, both human and celestial, Everywhere one beholds the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous form-body.
Just as the power of a single mind Is able to give rise to various kinds of minds.”
In this way, the body of one Buddha universally manifests as all Buddhas;
enlightenment is the non-dual dharma and likewise devoid of all marks. Yet, within the realm of dual dharmas, he manifests a body adorned with marks;
having realized that the nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, he arises like an illusion, his conduct being inexhaustible.
The Teacher thus manifests all Buddhas of the three times; his Dharma-body is entirely pure.
According to those who are to be transformed, he universally manifests sublime form-bodies.
The Tathāgata does not think, "I am creating such a body"; it is manifested spontaneously, never giving rise to discrimination.
The Dharma-realm is without differentiation and has no point of reliance;
yet within the world, it manifests infinite bodies. The Buddha-body is not a transformation, nor is it non-transformed;
within the untransformed Dharma, it displays transformed forms. Such perfect awakening is immeasurable.
The Dharma-realm is equal to empty space, Profound and vast, without limit or bottom;
The path of speech is entirely cut off, yet the Tathāgata has skillfully mastered it. He practices the Way in all places; In all lands within the Dharma-realm, his going is everywhere unimpeded.
[Treatise] The Bodhisattva Pañcaraśmiketu has ten verses clarifying how a single Buddha-body gives rise to many Buddha-bodies, like a magical manifestation; this is the section on "Arising.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
If one can believe and accept that the All-Knowing One is unimpeded,
and cultivates the practices of enlightenment with an immeasurable mind; manifesting infinite bodies throughout all lands,
yet those bodies do not abide in any place, nor do they dwell within any phenomena— [this is the state of] each and every Tathāgata.
Through the power of spiritual transformations, he manifests his body throughout inconceivable eons;
though the number of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time could be fully calculated,
the number of manifestations shown by the Tathāgata cannot be grasped— sometimes he shows one or two, and at other times an infinite number.
Universally manifesting throughout the lands of the ten directions, yet in reality there are not two kinds; just as the pure full moon appears universally in all waters,
and though its reflections are infinite, the original moon has never been two— so too this unimpeded wisdom,
having achieved equal and perfect enlightenment, universally manifests in all lands.
The Buddha-body is likewise non-dual; it is neither one nor two, nor is it infinite.
Yet, according to those who are to be transformed, he manifests infinite bodies. The Buddha-body is neither of the past nor of the future;
in a single thought-moment, he manifests birth, the attainment of enlightenment, and parinirvāṇa.
Like forms created by illusion, They are without birth and without arising; The Buddha-body is likewise, Manifesting without any birth.
[Commentary] Sixth: At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu and others [recite] ten verses below to clarify that the Buddha’s wisdom is without dependence.
Without action, without creation, neither internal nor external, yet able to manifest forms that are universally pervasive.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Buddha’s body is immeasurable, yet he can manifest a measurable form; according to what is appropriate for each, the Guide appears in such a way.
The Buddha’s body has no fixed location, yet it fills all places like space, which is without limit. Thus it is inconceivable, beyond the reach of the mind.
The mind does not arise within it; in the realm of all Buddhas, there is ultimately no arising or ceasing.
Like what is seen by one with cataracts, it is neither internal nor external.
One should know that the world’s perception of the Buddhas is likewise so; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Tathāgata appears in the world.
Sentient beings perceive that there is an emergence, yet in reality no one has arisen in the world. One cannot see the Buddha through lands, days, or nights;
nor through years, months, or a single kṣaṇa. One should know that it is entirely thus for all sentient beings who say:
"On such-and-such a day the Buddha attained the Way," or "The Tathāgata realized Bodhi."
In truth, he is not bound by days; the Tathāgata is free from conceptual construction.
He is not of the world, yet transcends all numerical reckoning. The Teachers of the three times all appear in this same way.
Just as the pure orb of the sun does not coexist with the darkness of night, yet one speaks of "a certain day," so too is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma.
All kalpas of the three periods of time / Are not conjoined with the Tathāgata; / Yet he speaks of the Buddhas of the three periods— / The Dharma of the Guides is thus.
[Commentary] Seventh: At that time, the ten verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva Ratnaketu" clarify what belongs to the Tathāgata.
Manifesting in accordance with what is produced by non-sentient things, one acts through wisdom without effort; sentient beings see this according to their own karma.

This section concerns the wisdom manifested through one's own practice of the path, as it corresponds to reality; therefore, "knowing at the proper time" (*kāla-jñatā*) is established because that which possesses time is a sentient being, for both long durations and short durations belong to sentient beings.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The bodies of all the Teachers are identical, and their meanings are likewise so;
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, they manifest in various ways according to what is appropriate. Behold the Honored Muni: His deeds are most extraordinary.
Pervading the entire realm of phenomena without exception, the Buddha-body is neither within nor without;
it appears through the power of spiritual mastery. Such is the nature of the Dharma of the Teacher:
according to the various classes of sentient beings and the karma accumulated in previous lives, he manifests in these diverse forms.
The manifestations appear each different; such is the body of all Buddhas.
Immeasurable and incalculable, they can only be excluded by the Great Awakened Honored One; none are able to conceive of them.
Just as my inconceivable mental karma cannot be grasped, so too is the Buddha inconceivable; he is not manifested by mental karma.
Just as inconceivable lands are seen in pure adornment, so too is the Buddha inconceivable, with no sublime mark that does not appear.
Just as all phenomena arise through a multitude of conditions, seeing the Buddha is likewise so;
it must depend upon various virtuous karmas, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
He is able to fulfill the hearts of sentient beings; such is the nature of all Buddhas' teachings.
Within all immeasurable lands, he fulfills every aspiration. When the Guide appears in the world, he universally responds throughout the ten directions by virtue of his power of vows.
[Treatise] 8. At that time, following the verse on Vīryadhvaja Bodhisattva, there are ten verses clarifying that the Buddha-body is neither internal nor external;
that the Buddhas of the ten directions are equal and possess no internal body, yet manifest divisions according to the karma of sentient beings.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata’s light of great wisdom Universally purifies all worlds. Once the worlds have been purified, He reveals all Buddha-dharmas.
Should there be anyone who wishes to see Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings,
Nothing fails to respond to their mind, yet in truth there is no place from which it comes.
By taking the Buddha as their object and maintaining focused mindfulness without ceasing, such a person shall behold the Buddha.
Their number shall equal that of their own thoughts, and they shall accomplish pure and white dharmas, becoming fully endowed with all merits; such a one, regarding omniscience—
With single-minded devotion, never forsaking the mind, the Teacher acts for the sake of sentient beings;
he expounds the Dharma as is appropriate, manifesting the most supreme body wherever there are those to be converted.

He realizes that both the Buddha-body and all things in the world are devoid of self; having awakened to this, he attains perfect enlightenment and further preaches it for the sake of sentient beings.
All these lions among men, with immeasurable powers of mastery, manifest bodies such as mindfulness and others, each distinct from the other.
Just as these bodies appear in the world, so too are the bodies of all Buddhas;
knowing their intrinsic nature is what is called being a Buddha—the Tathāgata who knows and sees universally.
Clearly understanding all phenomena—the Buddha-dharma and enlightenment—both are unattainable.
The Guide has neither coming nor going, nor does he abide anywhere. Far removed from all perversions, this is called Perfectly Complete Awakening.
[Treatise] Ninth: At that time, following the verse on the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, there are ten verses clarifying how the Tathāgata,

through a nature of wisdom that is mindless, thoughtless, and non-reliant, manifests without internal or external distinction throughout the ten directions, responding universally according to the faculties [of beings].
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata has no abode, yet he dwells universally in all lands; He goes to every realm and is seen everywhere.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, He manifests all bodies everywhere.
The attainment of enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, And likewise the parinirvāṇa—these are inconceivable for all Buddhas.
Who can conceive of the Buddha? Who can see the Perfectly Awakened One? Who can manifest the Most Victorious One?
All phenomena are suchness; The realm of the Buddhas is likewise so, Such that not even a single dharma exists.
Just as there is arising and ceasing in the intermediate state, sentient beings engage in false conceptualization.
For one who thoroughly realizes the nature of phenomena—that there is neither Buddha nor world—the Tathāgata appears everywhere to inspire faith and joy in sentient beings;
yet the essence of the Buddha cannot be apprehended, for even he has nothing to be seen.

If one can remain in the world detached from all clinging, with an unimpeded mind rejoicing and attaining awakening to the Dharma, then that which is manifested through supernormal power is what is called a Buddha.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of this chapter, there are three gates as previously stated. As for the first, explaining the title of the chapter: why is this chapter named "The Ten Dedications" (*Daśa-pariṇāmanā*)?

this clarifies how, within the state of sameness, there is a differentiation that causes one to advance upward. Thus, within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), as it is the foremost of practices, it is therefore—
In the country of Trayastriṃśa, there was a bhikṣu named Sudarśana who used a walking path within a forest to symbolize his ten practices.
He observed the faculties of beings with the eye of wisdom, the eye of insight, and the Dharma-eye to transform and guide them toward renunciation;
thus, that which is symbolized by the bhikṣu represents the ten practices, while the vast canopy provided by the multitude symbolizes that which is represented by the forest—these ten cycles.

In the section on the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is clarified that while the preceding two stages involve a predominance of the mind seeking transcendence and a deficiency in the practice of great compassion, the wisdom of all Buddhas attained at the initial moment of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) is called "dedication" because, within the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), its supramundane modes of action benefit sentient beings while remaining within the mundane world;
it is called "dedication" because it returns toward the truth (*tattva*) to enter the mundane world and benefit sentient beings. Therefore:
In this stage, the Dharma-teacher who represents the teaching is indicated by the name of the incense merchant, Blue Lotus;

this clarifies that the dharma-gate of these ten dedications is like the method of compounding incense, wherein various fragrances are combined into a single pellet to mutually benefit one another, thereby achieving a pervasive fragrance. The ten dedications are likewise thus.

Therefore, the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body—consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—is blended with the great kindness and great compassion, the various pāramitās, the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, and all the gates of nirvana and the afflictions of saṃsāra, together forming the true fragrance of a single Dharma-realm;
all of this takes the Great Vow as its primary source. For this reason:

This stage is called the "Stage of Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā-bhūmi*). The name of the elder, "Blue Lotus" (*utpala*), symbolizes that the practice of this stage is unstained by defilements and is the purity of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, "elder" clarifies that he dwells among the worldly while his wisdom excels that of ordinary people;
thus he is termed an "elder. "Blue lotus" clarifies that among all flowers, this flower is foremost in both color and fragrance.
This serves to manifest the practice-gates of the five stages. Why is this the first among these ten gates of dedication?
It is because this dharma-gate of the ten dedications, through the power of great vows, unifies compassion and wisdom, birth-and-death and nirvana, into the true sovereignty of a single dharma-realm;
thus it is able to support the fruits of Buddhahood of the preceding stages, enabling them to be fully endowed with the qualities of Samantabhadra.

Because the practice-gates (*caryāmukha*) are perfected, one also accomplishes the practice-gates of the subsequent stages—the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the eleventh stage—so that they may become habitual and sovereign.

This clarifies that the preceding ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten stages, and the eleventh stage are all, in their entirety, subsumed within this stage of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*);
for it is through these ten that the great categories of principle and wisdom, as well as great wisdom and great compassion, are perfectly integrated. By means of these ten...
The stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) encompasses everything from the preceding stages to the final ones, gathering them all together;
thus it symbolizes the blue lotus flower, whose color and fragrance are the most excellent among all flowers, surpassing all others.
Furthermore, it symbolizes that among all the three realms, the Tuṣita heaven is the most preeminent. Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three times in the world...

In this heaven, because the bodhicitta is fulfilled and one transforms the world, one ascends to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) and the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin);

these are so called because they delight in indulgence. Furthermore, ascending further to the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu) and Formless Realm (Ārūpyadhātu), these are so called because the mind is predominantly inclined toward tranquility.
Below these, the Yāma and Trāyastriṃśa heavens are places of attachment to pleasure, for the devas therein are not content. [The same applies to] the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājika).
The gods dwell on four sides and do not occupy a central position; therefore, this heaven is situated in the middle among the heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Furthermore, this heaven is the common dwelling place for those who have cultivated the three types of merit.

What are these three? First, the cultivation of generosity (dāna); second, the observance of ethical discipline (śīla); and third, the cultivation of meditative concentration (samādhi). Other gods do not cultivate these three.

Because merit is made equal and balanced, all [beings] receive it in abundance. Since they have cultivated the two merits of precepts and giving, other devas may be either excessively indulgent or excessively fond of tranquility;
therefore, the *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that those who desire to long for the bodhicitta will be reborn in this heaven.
For this reason, this heaven expounds these ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which here symbolize the Dharma.

Because it is superior, and because it lies midway between the lower realms of the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens and the higher realms of Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin—heavenly beings—this heaven is situated in the center of these five celestial abodes. Therefore, the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are taught;

they are taught in this heaven because they harmonize wisdom and compassion, bringing them into equilibrium and establishing one in the middle way. Thus, this location is used to symbolize the dharma-gate being expounded.
Furthermore, taking the merchant who sells incense, named Blue Lotus (*Utpala*), as the representation of the stage of Dharma (*dharmapada*), this meaning can be understood accordingly.
Therefore, it is called the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) to represent the ten *pāramitā* practices;

because they integrate the gates of the one and the many, and of the identical and the distinct, there are ten kinds of dedication to represent their inexhaustibility, which are blown forth by the wind of great vows.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.
Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were ten...
Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name, Vajradhvaja, appeared before him and all proclaimed in praise:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! You are indeed able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.
Noble son, this is the spiritual power of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within one million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions."
We collectively empower you through the power of the vows and the majestic spiritual authority of Tathāgata Vairocana from the past,
as well as by virtue of the purity of your own wisdom and the increasing excellence of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas;
thus we cause you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma, so that all bodhisattvas may attain pure fearlessness and be endowed with unimpededness.
Because of eloquence; because of entering the stage of unimpeded wisdom; because of abiding in the great mind of omniscience; because of accomplishing inexhaustible roots of goodness;

because of fulfilling the unimpeded pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*); because of entering the universal gateway of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); because of manifesting the spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
because of the uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness and wisdom regarding the past; and because of attaining the protection of all Buddhas for their faculties.
Because they extensively expound all dharmas through immeasurable gateways, because they hear and fully comprehend them so as to receive and uphold them without forgetting,
because they gather all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas, because they accomplish the aids to the supramundane path, because they do not sever the wisdom of omniscience,
because they develop great vows, because they interpret the true meaning, because they thoroughly understand the dharma-realm, and because they cause all bodhisattvas—
Because they have attained the three kinds of joy, because they cultivate all the roots of goodness that are equal to all Buddhas, and because they protect and maintain the lineage of all Tathāgatas—
namely, the exposition of the ten dedications of the Bodhisattvas— the Son of the Buddha, you should now,

by the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, expound this Dharma; for you shall receive the Buddha’s protective mindfulness, abide in the household of the Buddhas, and increase your emergence [from the world].
Because of their worldly merits, because they have attained the light of dhāraṇīs, because they have entered the unobstructed Buddha-dharma,
because their great radiance universally illumines the dharma-realm, because they have gathered the pure dharmas free from fault, because they abide in the sphere of vast wisdom,
and because they have attained the light of the unobstructed Dharma— at that time, all the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja immeasurable...
Wisdom; unimpeded eloquence and skillful means in discerning the meanings of words and phrases;
the light of the unobstructed Dharma; the Tathāgata’s body of equality; immeasurable and diverse pure vocal sounds;
the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable samādhi of excellent observation; the wisdom of dedication that cannot be destroyed by any roots of goodness; and contemplation.
He examines all phenomena and achieves skillful means, and possesses uninterrupted eloquence in expounding all phenomena in all places. Why is this?
It is because of the power of the roots of goodness from entering this samādhi. At that time, each of the Buddhas stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja with their right hand.
Having received the stroke of their hands, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja immediately arose from his meditative concentration and addressed [the assembly].

The bodhisattvas said: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses inconceivable great vows that fill the dharma-realm and are universally able to rescue and protect all sentient beings; that is to say, they cultivate and study the dedication of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."

The causes and conditions for this are: to enable future students of the Bodhisattva path to know the rules of conduct;

to enable them to understand the skillful means of samādhi so that their manifest wisdom may become clear and pure; to enable them to know the power of samādhi, which can bring about the mastery and clarity of discerning wisdom in preaching the Dharma;
and because the Dharma-standards of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are in accord with this. Therefore...
Regarding the two explanations for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the naming of this *samādhi* as "Wisdom-Light" (*jñānāloka*): why is it called Wisdom-Light *samādhi*?

It is because it is the gateway to the accomplishment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); without great wisdom, it would not be manifested. As revealed in the *Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika*), the Buddha-wisdom is made manifest and unified with one's own mind;
thus, through the *samādhi* of skillful means (*upāya*), it is non-active (*anabhisamskāra*) and thought-free (*acintya*), like purity.

When water is clear and bright, the sun, moon, and myriad phenomena naturally appear; likewise, within the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), the samādhi is named "Excellent Contemplation" (*susaṃkalpa*).
Thus, one clarifies the principle while following the distinctions of phenomena according to specific circumstances; this is called "Excellent Contemplation.
The samādhi entered through these ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) is named "Wisdom-Light" (*jñānāloka*); it is by means of wisdom that one practices compassion and clarifies the locus.
The mundane is unstained by this wisdom-light; there is nothing in the mundane that is not truly such.

Therefore, the Blue Lotus used by the Incense Merchant to represent it clarifies being unstained while remaining in the mundane. The Ten Abodes and Ten Practices, with the Bhikṣu as their primary emblem, clarify the merit of transcending the mundane.
This is all in accordance with the representations of Sudhana’s spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). For this reason:
Because this stage possesses the mastery of both compassion and wisdom, the samādhi is named the "Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.
Regarding the illumination of the distance and proximity of all Buddha-fields that come forth: "illumination" signifies that as one advances through the stages, wisdom increases and expands.

While the previous stage was described as [passing through] the dust-motes of ten thousand Buddha-fields, this stage is described as [passing through] the dust-motes of one hundred thousand Buddha-fields, signifying that the advancement surpasses the preceding four stages.
Regarding the enumeration of the Buddhas, the Sūtra states that in each of the ten directions there are as many Buddhas as there are atoms in one hundred thousand Buddha-fields.
This clarifies that the vast cultivation of the wisdom-activity is united with the functional power of the wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
As for the common names of the Buddhas: why do the Buddhas of the ten directions share the same names as the Bodhisattvas who have entered meditative absorption?
There are two meanings for the manifestation [of the Buddha] before the Vajradhvaja: first, as previously explained, it is the advancement toward the union of wisdom;

second, by means of the Buddha’s name and the Tathāgata’s body, he appears before the bodhisattva who has entered meditative absorption to clarify the stage of abiding, thereby severing doubts regarding self and others and establishing the Dharma-seal. Furthermore, since wisdom is already in accord, [the Buddha manifests].
1. Because the body is likewise non-dual; 2. To clarify that all Buddhas appear and offer praise; 3.

To clarify that through the empowerment of speech, the one entering samādhi is made firm in the seal of the Dharma and freed from delusion, and likewise causes those disciples who are to study it to sever their doubts;
4. Because since the bodies and wisdoms are identical, the teaching of the Dharma is also equal; 5. To clarify that all Buddhas collectively enter into the samādhi together.
Regarding what is called "collective empowerment" (*sādhāraṇādhiṣṭhāna*), there are two meanings: first, because one's own wisdom accords with and unites with the virtues of the Buddha;
second, because the Buddhas provide both wisdom and power as two conditions that come together, it is termed "empowerment.

Furthermore, although one has no doubts oneself, in order to sever the delusions of others, the Buddhas bestow the methods of the Dharma through empowerment. It is also said that there is the empowerment of the Buddhas.
1. The empowerment through the addition of the same name, because they are given the same name; 2. The empowerment through the manifestation of the body, because [the Buddha] appears before them;
3. The empowerment through the addition of verbal praise, because he praises them with words; 4. The empowerment through the power of Vairocana’s past vows; 5.
The empowerment through the ten kinds of dharmas, as fully detailed in the text itself; 6. The empowerment by the hands of the Buddhas of the ten directions being placed upon their heads.
Regarding the addition of the eight luminous Buddhas at the crown and their touching his head with their hands: for what reason do they touch his head?
It clarifies that the right hand is the instrument of action; it clarifies that the Buddhas receive him with their right hands to lead him out of meditative absorption and to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, it signifies that his own activity coincides with the activity of the Buddhas, and that he has received their approval.

Because it is the limit of phenomena (*dharmakoṭi*), there is the phenomenon of the limit of its own position within that very position. Ninth, the explanation of emerging from meditative absorption to address the assembly and praise the Dharma is fully contained within the scriptural text itself.
Tenth, the explanation of the correct teaching of the ten kinds of dedication is as found in the subsequent sections of the sūtra.
This concludes the commentary on the first section, comprising thirty-three lines of the sūtra.

[Sūtra] Son of the Buddha, how many kinds of dedication are there for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas? Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas...
There are ten kinds of dedication, which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have collectively expounded. What are these ten?

First, the dedication of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being. Second, the indestructible dedication. Third, the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
Fourth, the dedication reaching all places. Fifth, the dedication of inexhaustible merit.
Sixth is the dedication that gathers all roots of goodness into equality; seventh is the dedication that accords equally with all sentient beings;
eighth is the dedication characterized by suchness; ninth is the dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment;
tenth is the dedication of entering the immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Son of the Buddha, these are the dedications of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The ten kinds of dedication have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, will be taught by those of the future, and are being taught by those of the present.
