The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament Scripture, Fascicle Forty-four.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tōngxuán, a Layman of Fāngshān in Tàiyuán during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Treatise on the Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Five, Part Three: "The Dedication Equalizing All Buddhas.
[Treatise] The third dedication, "Equalizing All Buddhas," takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence, with the remaining nine perfections as its constituents.

In the section on the Manifestation of the Dharma (dharmavyañjana), it is the Elder Anuttarajaya in the Great Adorned Banner Aśoka Grove to the east of the delightful city where the youth Sudhana beheld him;
he is so named because the name is established based on the conduct practiced by the one who resides in the city called "Delightful" (Ramyā).
This is to clarify that those who have attained the Dharma and perfected patience see the city of Ramyāsthita.
The East represents illumination; patience (*kṣānti*) is the foremost of the practices of awakening and serves as the emblem for the positions of the Eastern constellations—Jue, Kang, Di, and Fang.

It presides over the source of all virtues. As Fang is the position of the Azure Dragon, presiding over auspiciousness and celebration, the East is thus taken as Yang, the beginning of the generation of all things.
Illumination and patience are the foremost of all practices because they give rise to manifold blessings. Therefore...
It is situated to the east of the city. Regarding the "Great Banner of Majestic Adornment" (*Mahāvyūha-dhvaja*): it signifies that patience remains unmoved even when confronted by adverse conditions;

this is the meaning of the "banner. Regarding the "Forest of Freedom from Sorrow" (*Aśoka-vana*): it clarifies that when patience brings practice to fulfillment, it is like a forest providing vast shade. It is called "Supreme Victory" (*Anuttara-jaya*):
among all practices, none surpasses patience, for among all practices, there is no practice that can be perfected without patience. Thus, [the rest follows].

The details are as explained in the sutra; the two meanings are as previously stated. Regarding the first major section, the intended meaning of this portion of the sutra is divided into ten subsections.
[Sutra]: "O Son of the Buddha, what is the dedication of all Buddhas for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas? O Son of the Buddha, this...
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in accordance with the path of dedication of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present,
and thus practices this path of dedication, they perceive all forms up to and including tactile objects and mental phenomena—
whether beautiful or ugly— without giving rise to attachment or aversion; their mind attains mastery, free from all faults, vast, pure, and filled with joy and gladness.
Delighting in being free from all sorrow and affliction, with a supple mind and serene faculties.

[Treatise] Question: How is it that from "how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates like all Buddhas" down to "the faculties are serene," there are five lines and a half of sūtra text that clarify training in the Buddha’s dedication so that the mind attains mastery?
The Section on Coolness.
[Sūtra] When the Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, have attained such peace and happiness, they further resolve their minds toward all Buddhas and form this thought and vow:
"By means of the roots of goodness I have now planted, may all Buddhas be happy."
It becomes further increased and more sublime—namely, the inconceivable bliss of the Buddha’s dwelling, which is without peer;
the immeasurable bliss of the Buddha’s samādhi; the bliss of great compassion; the boundless bliss of the liberation of all Buddhas;
and the most supreme, venerable, and sovereign bliss of vast, ultimate, and infinite [power].

The joy of power, the joy of detachment from all perceptions, the joy of tranquility, the joy of dwelling in unimpeded abiding, the joy of constant right concentration, and the joy of practicing non-dual conduct that is immutable. [Treatise]:
From "the two sons of the Buddha" down to "immutable joy," there are seven and a half lines of scripture; this refers to the bodhisattva.
The Section on Dedication to the Bliss of the Buddha.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has dedicated all roots of goodness to the Buddha, he further dedicates these roots of goodness to the Bodhisattvas, namely:
he vows that those whose aspirations are not yet fulfilled shall attain fulfillment, and those whose minds are not yet purified shall attain purification.
It causes those whose pure *pāramitās* are not yet fulfilled to attain fulfillment;

it establishes one in the adamantine mind of enlightenment (*vajrabodhicitta*) and brings about non-retrogression regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); it does not abandon great diligence and guards the gateway to enlightenment;
it enables all roots of goodness to flourish; and it causes sentient beings to relinquish pride, generate the bodhicitta, and fulfill their aspirations.
Abiding in all that in which Bodhisattvas abide, they obtain the sharp and keen faculties of a Bodhisattva, cultivate roots of goodness,
and realize *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
[Treatise] From "The three sons of the Buddha" down to "realizing *sarvajñā*," there are seven lines of sūtra text clarifying the dedication toward Bodhi.
The Section on the Vow for the Practice of Omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—
this is translated as "all-knowledge. [Sūtra] Child of the Buddha, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has thus dedicated all roots of goodness toward the state of a Bodhisattva,
he further dedicates them toward all sentient beings, vowing that all sentient beings shall possess every root of goodness, even the most minute.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, they see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and revere the Noble Sangha. All those roots of goodness become free from obstacles;

they maintain mindfulness of the Buddha’s perfection, mindfulness of the skillful means of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the venerability of the Sangha. Never being separated from the vision of the Buddha, their minds attain purity;
they obtain all Buddha-dharmas, accumulate immeasurable virtues, purify all supernormal powers, abandon doubts regarding the Dharma, and abide according to the teachings.
Just as one dedicates for the sake of sentient beings, so too is the dedication for the sake of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, may all sentient beings forever leave behind the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and all evil realms such as those of King Yama;
may they increase their aspiration for unsurpassed bodhicitta, and with single-minded diligence seek all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) forever.
By slandering the true Dharma of all Buddhas, one attains the peace and bliss of a Buddha, purifies body and mind, and realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

[Treatise: From "The four sons of the Buddha" down to "realizing all-knowledge," there are ten scriptural sections clarifying the dedication of merit to all sentient beings so that they may be freed from suffering.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, all the roots of goodness possessed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are initiated through great vows,
correctly initiated, accumulated, correctly accumulated, increased, correctly increased, and made entirely vast, complete, and fully perfected.

[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" down to "fully and completely filled," there are two lines of sūtra that clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s practice through the vastness and fulfillment of vows.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells within his home together with his wife and children, he has never for even a moment abandoned them.
With the mind of bodhicitta, one correctly contemplates the sphere of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); having crossed over oneself, one enables others to cross over so that they may attain the ultimate.
By means of skillful means, one transforms one’s own kin and retinue, causing them to enter the wisdom of a bodhisattva and bringing them to maturity and liberation.

Although dwelling together with them, the mind remains free from attachment; yet, out of original great compassion, one remains in the household life, acting in accordance with it through a heart of loving-kindness.
Wife and children do not constitute an obstacle to the bodhisattva’s pure path; although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva remains at home and engages in various worldly activities,
he never for a moment abandons the mind of omniscience— whether putting on clothes, consuming flavors, taking medicine,
rinsing the mouth, anointing the body, turning around, looking about, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Whether in speech or mental action, whether asleep or awake, in all such activities, his mind is constantly dedicated to the path of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
He maintains mindfulness and reflection, never abandoning them for even a moment.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, he abides in the immeasurable great vows of bodhi and, having gathered countless vast roots of goodness, he diligently cultivates all virtues.
Saving all beings so that they forever leave behind all pride and negligence, they resolutely proceed toward the ground of omniscience;
never giving rise to the intent to follow other paths, they constantly contemplate the bodhi of all Buddhas,
forever abandon all defiled phenomena, practice all that is to be learned by Bodhisattvas, and remain unobstructed on the path to omniscience.
Abiding on the stage of wisdom, they delight in recitation and study; through immeasurable knowledge, they gather all roots of goodness.
Their minds do not crave or delight in any worldly realm, nor are they stained by the actions they perform. With single-minded devotion, they receive and uphold the Buddha’s teachings.
Thus, while living as householders, these bodhisattvas universally gather roots of goodness, causing them to increase, and dedicate them to all Buddhas.

"Unsurpassed Bodhi. [Treatise] From "the six Buddha-sons" down to "dedicating toward the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas," eighteen lines and a half of scripture clarify the section on how the Bodhisattva,
by virtue of their fundamental great compassion, dwells in the mundane world without defilement or attachment.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, at that time, when a Bodhisattva gives even a single morsel or a single grain of food to an animal, they make this vow:
"May these beings abandon the animal realm; may they find benefit, peace, and happiness; may they attain ultimate liberation;

may they forever cross over the ocean of suffering, forever extinguish the sensation of suffering, forever eliminate the aggregate of suffering, forever sever the perception of suffering, and forever bring an end to the mass of suffering and the practice of suffering."
"May all those sentient beings abandon the root of suffering and all places of suffering.
Thus the Bodhisattva focuses his mind single-mindedly on all sentient beings, taking those roots of goodness as the foremost, and dedicates them toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
From the first moment the Bodhisattva generates the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), he universally gathers in all sentient beings and cultivates all roots of goodness.
By means of this dedication, they desire to cause others to forever leave behind the wilderness of birth and death, to attain the unimpeded bliss of all Tathāgatas,
to emerge from the ocean of afflictions, to cultivate the path of the Buddha-dharma, to be filled with universal loving-kindness, to possess vast power of compassion,

to cause all beings everywhere to obtain pure happiness, to protect their roots of goodness, to draw near to the Buddha-dharma, to exit the realm of Māra, to enter the realm of the Buddha, and to sever...
Planting the seeds of the Tathāgata in the world and abiding in the dharma of the equality of the three periods of time,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus dedicates all roots of goodness— those already accumulated, those yet to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated— and further reflects:
"Just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past practiced by honoring and making offerings to all Buddhas and delivering all sentient beings..."
To cause all beings to emerge forever from birth, they diligently cultivate all roots of goodness and dedicate them all without attachment—
namely, not relying on form, not clinging to sensation, being unerring in perception, not fabricating mental formations, and not grasping at consciousness;
they abandon the six sense bases, do not abide in worldly dharmas, and delight in supramundane states, knowing that all phenomena are like space and have no [intrinsic] location.
From the beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished; it possesses no reality and is free from all attachment.

It is far removed from all views of conceptual discrimination, remaining unmoving, unchanging, indestructible, and unimpaired. Abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is signless, devoid of signs, and yet is solely the single sign.
Thus deeply penetrating the nature of all phenomena, one constantly delights in practicing the roots of goodness of the universal gate, seeing them all clearly.
Just as all the assemblies of the Buddhas of the past dedicated their roots of goodness toward me, so too do I dedicate them.
Understanding this Dharma, realizing this Dharma, and relying upon this Dharma, I resolve my mind and practice without contradicting the characteristics of the Dharma.
I recognize that what is practiced is like an illusion, like a shadow, like the moon reflected in water, and like a reflection in a mirror.
[The Sutra says: "Manifested through the harmony and combination of causes and conditions, from the intermediate stage up to the ultimate ground of the Tathāgata.

[Treatise: From the section beginning with "the seven sons of the Buddha" down to "the ultimate ground of the Tathāgata," there are twenty-five lines and a half of scripture clarifying that by giving food to animals, one vows to forever leave behind all suffering and obtain a share of happiness.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further reflect:
"Just as the Buddhas of the past, when practicing the bodhisattva path, dedicated their various roots of goodness in this manner, so too shall it be for those of the future and the present;
I now likewise ought to resolve my mind in the same way as those Buddhas and dedicate all roots of goodness. This is the first.
Dedication that is superior dedication, most excellent dedication, supreme dedication, unsurpassed dedication,
peerless dedication, unequaled-with-the-equal dedication, incomparable dedication, matchless dedication, venerable dedication, sublime dedication,
impartial dedication, upright dedication, dedication of great merit, vast dedication, virtuous dedication, and pure dedication.
With pure dedication, he avoids evil dedication and does not follow after evil dedication.
Having thus correctly dedicated all roots of goodness, the bodhisattva accomplishes pure actions of body, speech, and mind;

he abides in the station of a bodhisattva free from all faults, cultivates wholesome deeds, remains free from the evils of body and speech, and is without blemish in his mind. He cultivates omniscience and dwells in a vast mind.
Knowing that all phenomena have no activity, abiding in supramundane dharmas, remaining unstained by mundane dharmas, discerning with wisdom, understanding immeasurable karmas,
accomplishing skillful means for the dedication of merit, and forever uprooting the foundation of all grasping— O Son of the Buddha,
this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s third dedication, which is equal to that of all Buddhas.

[Treatise] From "The Eight Disciples of the Buddha" down to the third section, "The Dedication of All Buddhas," there are fourteen lines of scripture clarifying the section on the dedication of all Bodhisattvas and all Buddhas.
[Sūtra] When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this dedication, they penetrate deeply into the activities of all Tathāgatas; they incline toward the supreme and wondrous merits of the Tathāgatas;
they enter the realm of profound and pure wisdom; they do not depart from the activities of all Bodhisattvas;
they are skillful in discerning subtle and clever expedient means; they enter the profound Dharma-realm; and they thoroughly understand the practice of Bodhisattvas.
Entering the lineage of the Buddhas in succession, they discern and understand all infinite and boundless phenomena through skillful means;
although they manifest their bodies within the world, their minds remain unattached to worldly dharmas.
[Treatise] From the nine bodhisattva-mahāsattvas down to the section on the mind being free from attachment, six passages from the sutra clarify the bodhisattva’s entry into the Buddha’s merit,
their profound penetration of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and their skillful knowledge of the sequence of bodhisattva practice.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses.
[Śāstra] Ten: From "At that time" onwards, this single line of sūtra clarifies the section on the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveying the assembly and speaking in verse.
[Sūtra] Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the method of dedication practiced by the Buddhas of the past,
and likewise study that which was practiced by all the Teachers of the future and present worlds.
They attain peace and happiness within all spheres of experience, and are praised by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
With vast, radiant, and pure eyes, I dedicate all these toward the various pleasures of the body-faculty of the Greatly Wise Bodhisattvas; likewise for the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue—
dedicating all such immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous joys to all the Most Victorious Ones.
All the various wholesome dharmas of all worlds, And those accomplished by all Tathāgatas—
I encompass them all therein without exception, Entirely rejoicing in them for the benefit of sentient beings.
With immeasurable kinds of worldly rejoicing, I dedicate this for the sake of sentient beings.
May all the happiness possessed by the lions among men be fully perfected for all living beings;
may every kind of happiness known and seen by all the Tathāgatas in all lands be attained by all sentient beings,
so that they may become great, brilliant lamps illuminating the world.
Whatever supreme and wondrous bliss the Bodhisattva attains, he dedicates it all to all living beings;
though he dedicates for the sake of all beings, he remains unattached to that dedication.
As the Bodhisattva practices this dedication, he gives rise to a mind of immeasurable great compassion.
Just as the virtues of dedication cultivated by the Buddha, may my own practice be fully perfected;
just as all the Victors have accomplished, may there be the subtle joy of the vehicle of omniscience,
as well as the immeasurable joy of the bodhisattva practices performed by me while in the world.
Manifesting entry into all realms for the sake of peaceful happiness, And constantly maintaining the joy of tranquility through the guarding of the sense faculties—
All of this is dedicated to all living beings, Universally causing them to cultivate and perfect supreme wisdom.
It is not that body, speech, and mind are themselves karma, Nor is there anything else apart from these.
By means of skillful expedients, they extinguish the darkness of delusion; thus cultivating and perfecting supreme wisdom, the bodhisattvas practice all manner of deeds.
Accumulating immeasurable and sublime merits, they accord with the Tathāgata and are born into the Buddha-family;
in tranquil stillness and without distraction, they correctly dedicate [their merit].
All sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions—
may I embrace them all and dedicate my roots of goodness to them, wishing that they may be fully endowed with peace and happiness;
I do not seek benefit for myself, but desire that all beings may be secure and blissful.
Never for a moment giving rise to a mind of conceptual proliferation, But contemplating that all phenomena are empty and selfless;
To all the infinite and most victorious ones of the ten directions, And to every true son of the Buddha whom I behold—
I dedicate all my roots of goodness to them, Vowing that they may swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
All sentient beings throughout the entire world, I shall embrace with an impartial mind, leaving none behind.
By means of all the virtuous deeds I have performed, May those beings swiftly attain Buddhahood.
The immeasurable and boundless great vows Proclaimed by the Unsurpassed Teacher—
May all the sons of the Buddhas be pure, And may their every heart’s desire be fulfilled.
Universally observing all worlds in the ten directions, May they bestow their merit upon them all;
May they all be endowed with sublime adornments— Thus do the Bodhisattvas train in dedication.
The mind does not weigh or measure dualistic phenomena, but constantly realizes that all dharmas are non-dual.
Whether phenomena are dual or non-dual, there is ultimately no attachment therein.
All the worlds throughout the ten directions are entirely the conceptual discriminations of sentient beings.
In the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nothing is apprehended; thus they thoroughly comprehend all perceptions.
Once the bodies of those bodhisattvas are purified, their minds become pure and free from blemish;
their verbal karma is already purified and devoid of faults—one should know that with a pure mind, there is no attachment.
With single-minded right mindfulness, I call to mind the Buddhas of the past, And likewise remember all the Teachers of the future,
as well as the Honored Ones among gods and humans in the present; I learn from them all the teachings they have proclaimed,
for all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess wisdom that is clear, penetrating, and unimpeded in mind.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he dedicates his accumulated merits toward enlightenment;
he is one of supreme wisdom, vast wisdom, non-deceptive wisdom, non-erroneous wisdom,
impartial and true wisdom, pure wisdom— the One of Most Excellent Wisdom speaks thus.
[Treatise] The forty-eight verses above, consisting of two lines per verse, have already elucidated the preceding dharmas in full detail;
there is no need for further explanation. As for the second part, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning:
why is this called "the dedication equal to all Buddhas"? This third dedication establishes the gateway of patience (*kṣānti-mukha*), clarifying the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because one vows that the three types of action (trikarma) shall be exactly as those of the Buddhas and that all the practices and vows of the Buddhas shall be fully realized,

it is said that "one dedicates equally to all Buddhas," so that one's vows and conduct become identical to those of the Buddhas. Furthermore, since it was previously stated that this is the "indestructible dedication" (akṣaya-pariṇāmanā),
the subsequent phrase "dedicating equally to all Buddhas" clarifies the sequential correspondence between them.
The fourth, the dedication reaching all places (*sarvatragatā-pariṇāmanā*), has the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) as its essence and the other nine perfections as its companions.

This is illustrated by the bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā whom Sudhana saw while staying in the city of Śūrpāraka—here called the City of Valor—within the Karṇikāra Forest; "Karṇikāra" means "time of strife. This clarifies this [dedication].
That the *bhikṣuṇī* can harmonize and resolve disputes represents the fourth dedication: the mark of performing the karma of diligence to benefit sentient beings.
That she is called a *bhikṣuṇī* clarifies her freedom from defilement and purity; that she is called a *śramaṇerikā* clarifies the gate of diligent practice through compassionate sound.
Taking freedom from defilement and compassion as the essence of this practice, she is titled "Lion’s Stretching," which clarifies that she has already attained [realization].
Having attained the four kinds of fearlessness through the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the "Lion" refers to the brilliance of wisdom and fearlessness.

"Stretching and extending" refers to the mastery of contraction and expansion. Through clarity, he employs pure great wisdom with heroic mastery to contract and expand as he preaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings;
he skillfully harmonizes and resolves strife, bringing all immeasurable sentient beings into subjection.
The details of what has been seen and heard differ extensively as explained in the sūtras; the intent here is to indicate that within this fourth dedication, one practices the conduct of diligence.
Because it manifests the characteristics of wisdom and compassion, undefiled compassion results in mastery in preaching the Dharma.

Compassion constantly follows the stream of suffering, while wisdom remains eternally undefiled—this is the meaning of the *maṇi* (jewel). Regarding the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the first is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are: first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena; second, the analytical knowledge of meaning; third, the analytical knowledge of eloquence; and fourth, the analytical knowledge of expression.

The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are: first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path that leads to the end of suffering. The two meanings are as previously stated. This section is the first long division [of the chapter].
The meaning of the sūtra consists of eight sections.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the dedication of all places of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?
"O Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates all roots of goodness, he forms this thought: 'May these roots of goodness...'"
The power of the faculties' merit reaches all places; it is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), reaching nowhere it does not go.
It reaches all things, all worlds, all sentient beings, all lands, all phenomena, all space, all three periods of time, all conditioned and unconditioned states, and all that exists.
May these roots of goodness, through the power of my speech and voice, likewise pervade all the abodes of the Tathāgatas;

may they make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time: may the vows of the Buddhas of the past be entirely fulfilled, may the Buddhas of the future be fully adorned, and may the Buddhas of the present, along with their lands, bodhimaṇḍas, and assemblies, fill all things everywhere.
By the great power of faith and understanding, by the unobstructed nature of vast wisdom,
and by the dedication of all roots of goodness, may these offerings— just like those of the various devas—
fill immeasurable and boundless worlds.
[Treatise] Question: How does a son of the Buddha dedicate roots of goodness so as to reach all places?

From this point downward, up to the section on "the infinite worlds," there are twelve lines of scripture that clarify how the roots of goodness cultivated by Bodhisattvas pervade the three periods of time like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), constituting the section on making offerings.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further form this thought:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, universally pervade all worlds of the various karmic origins throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm;
they pervade the unspeakably many world-systems of the ten directions, the unspeakably many Buddha-lands, the Buddha-realms, the various worlds, the immeasurable worlds, and the undivided [realms]."
In all such worlds— whether level, revolving, tilted, upright, or inverted—
he manifests his lifespan and displays various supernatural powers and transformations. Therein, by the power of his resolute conviction,
he appears in all those worlds for the sake of those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed.
For the sake of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, he universally reveals through the wisdom of all places the Tathāgata’s immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers;
his Dharma-body dwells everywhere without distinction, universally entering all dharma-realms as the Tathāgata-garbha body,
neither arising nor ceasing, manifesting throughout the world with skillful means to realize the reality of the Dharma.
Because their nature transcends all things, they attain the power of non-regression and non-obstruction;
because they are born into the lineage of the Tathāgata’s unobstructed vision and vast majestic virtue.

[Treatise] From "The two sons of the Buddha" down to "the lineage of vast and majestic power," twelve lines of scripture clarify that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is like the Dharmakāya’s universal pervasion, being without distinction and bringing about vast benefit.

Regarding the explanation of this section: "Just as with the world-systems, it is like the Flower Treasury World-System (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātujāla*)," which refers to the preceding [passage].
Virtue-Cloud calculated that three thousand great thousandfold world systems equal one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) number of world-oceans;
he further calculated that one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* number of world-oceans equals one world-nature (*loka-dhātu-prakṛti*);
and he further calculated that one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* number of world-natures equals one world-lineage (*loka-jāti*). He spoke of various worlds and of the multitudes [of worlds].
Birth is manifold, like the revolving of worlds: some revolve in a circular form, while others flow like rivers;
others, such as the sun and moon, have no fixed abode and are called "revolving" worlds.
A world situated on the side of Mount Sumeru, such as that of the Four Heavenly Kings, may be understood as an "upside-down" world; an inverted world is like a wasp's nest.
This is also as explained in the "Chapter on the Formation of the World" (*Lokadhātu-vyūha-parivarta*); what follows is provided in full according to the sutra.

[Sutra]: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with all the roots of goodness he has planted, vows that they shall become various exquisite flowers, various exquisite fragrant garlands, canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and lamps for these Tathāgatas."
And with all other various ornaments as offerings—whether to the image of the Buddha or to the stūpas and temples of the Buddha—it is all likewise.
By means of these roots of goodness, one dedicates them in this way:
namely, with undisturbed dedication, single-minded dedication, dedication from one's own intention, respectful dedication, immovable dedication, non-abiding dedication, and independent dedication.
They dedicate with a mind free of sentient beings, a mind free of agitation and rivalry, and a mind of tranquility. They further form this thought:

"Throughout all eons—past, future, and present—within the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained all-knowledge and realized the path to Bodhi under infinite names, each distinct from the others, in various ways."
At that time, those who manifest as Perfectly Enlightened Ones all abide with their life-span extending to the end of the future;

each one adorns their body with the adornments of the Dharma-realm. Their assemblies in the sites of enlightenment pervade the entire Dharma-realm and all lands, appearing at appropriate times to perform Buddha-works.
All such Buddhas, Tathāgatas, I universally dedicate through my roots of goodness.
I have previously made vows for countless incense canopies, countless incense banners, countless incense pennants,
countless incense curtains, countless incense nets, countless incense images, countless incense lights, countless incense flames,
countless incense clouds, countless incense seats, countless incense walking paths, countless incense dwellings, and countless incense worlds.
Countless incense mountains, countless incense oceans, countless incense rivers, countless incense trees, countless incense garments, countless incense lotuses, and countless incense palaces;
immeasurable flower canopies, and so forth, up to immeasurable flower palaces;
boundless garland canopies, and so forth, up to boundless garland palaces; and incomparable ointments... [and so on].
The extensive description of canopies of incense, up to and including incalculable palaces of unexcelled ointments;

the extensive description of canopies of powdered incense, up to and including incalculable palaces of powdered incense; the extensive description of canopies of garments, up to and including incalculable palaces of garments;
and the extensive description of canopies of jewels, up to and including inconceivable palaces of jewels.
From the canopies of light of measurable lamps, extensively described up to the palaces of light of immeasurable lamps;
from the canopies of unspeakably many ornaments, extensively described up to the palaces of unspeakably many ornaments;
and the unspeakably unspeakable numbers of mani-jewel canopies and unspeakably unspeakable numbers of mani-jewel banners—such as these.
Noble woman, there are mani-jewel banners, mani-jewel canopies, mani-jewel nets, mani-jewel images,
mani-jewel lights, mani-jewel flames, mani-jewel clouds, mani-jewel thrones,
mani-jewel walkways, mani-jewel abodes, mani-jewel lands, mani-jewel mountains, mani-jewel oceans, and mani-jewel rivers.
Noble women, jewel-trees, mani-jewel garments, mani-jewel lotuses, and mani-jewel palaces— all are unspeakably, unspeakably many.
Within each of these individual realms, there are likewise countless railings,
countless palaces, countless multi-storied pavilions, countless gates and portals, countless crescent-shaped arches, and countless defensive towers.
With countless windows and doors, countless pure jewels, and countless ornaments— using such various articles of offering as these—
he reverently made offerings to the aforementioned Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, praying that all worlds may attain purity,
that all sentient beings may achieve liberation, and abide in the stage of the Ten Powers regarding all phenomena.
Attaining the light of unimpeded Dharma, they cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with roots of goodness and to completely subdue their minds.
Equal to the realm of empty space, they travel to all lands without actually going anywhere; they enter all realms and bestow various wholesome dharmas.
They constantly behold the Buddhas, plant all roots of goodness, and accomplish the Mahāyāna, remaining unattached to all phenomena and becoming fully perfected.
Establishing all manner of virtues and immeasurable practices, they universally enter the boundless Dharma-realm of all phenomena and achieve the supernatural powers of all Buddhas,
attaining the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes. Just as the non-self universally encompasses all dharmas,
so too do my roots of goodness universally encompass all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, making offerings to them all without exception.
Furthermore, because it universally encompasses all immeasurable dharmas and is able to penetrate them all without obstruction;
because it universally encompasses all the assembly of bodhisattvas so that they ultimately share the same roots of goodness;

because it universally encompasses all bodhisattva practices, fulfilling them all through the power of original vows; and because it universally encompasses all bodhisattva teachings, understanding and realizing them with clarity.

Because all phenomena are unimpeded, they universally encompass the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas; because they accomplish immeasurable roots of goodness, they universally encompass the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas;
because they give rise to immeasurable resolve to fulfill all things, they universally encompass the samādhis, eloquence, and dhāraṇī-gates of bodhisattvas;
because they are well able to illuminate and realize the non-dual Dharma, they universally encompass [all these qualities].
Because all Buddhas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), manifest the great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) of the Tathāgatas,

they universally encompass all Buddhas of the three periods of time— whether descending to take birth, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma, taming sentient beings, or entering parinirvāṇa—

and because they have completely and pervasively honored and made offerings to them, they universally encompass all Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions, purifying them all to the ultimate degree.
Because they have reached the ultimate end, they universally encompass all vast eons, appearing within them to cultivate the bodhisattva practices without interruption;
because they universally encompass all realms of existence, they manifest birth therein in every way;
because they universally encompass all realms of sentient beings, they fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; [and] because they universally encompass all afflictions...

Because all habitual tendencies are rendered pure through skillful means; because all the infinite differences among the faculties of all sentient beings are universally gathered and fully understood;
because all the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings are universally gathered so that they may be freed from defilement and attain purity;
because all practices for transforming sentient beings are universally gathered, manifesting bodies according to what is appropriate for them; [and] because of universal gathering.

Because it causes all paths that correspond to sentient beings to enter the realm of all sentient beings, and because it universally encompasses the nature of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas and protects and sustains the teachings of all Buddhas.

[Treatise] From "The three sons of the Buddha" down to "because they protect and uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas," there are sixty-four lines of scripture clarifying the section on how Bodhisattvas,
through clouds of offerings numerous and inexhaustible like the *dharmatā*,
offer to Tathāgatas as numerous and boundless as the *dharmatā*, universally encompassing all roots of goodness.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, they employ the method of non-apprehension as their skillful means.
They do not differentiate between karma and its retribution, nor do they differentiate between retribution and karma.
Although there is no differentiation, they universally enter the Dharma-realm; although there is nothing performed, they constantly abide in roots of goodness; although there is nothing...
Arising [from this state], they diligently cultivate the supreme Dharma; without believing in any phenomena, they are able to enter deeply into them.
Without existing within phenomena, they fully know and see them. Whether things are created or uncreated, their nature cannot be known.

Although the nature of all phenomena is eternally non-existent and lacks self-mastery, they see all phenomena while seeing nothing at all. They universally know all things while knowing nothing at all. Thus does the Bodhisattva realize.

Having attained the ultimate realm, they know that all phenomena have dependent origination as their root; they perceive the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) where all phenomena are free from defilement.
They understand that the world is entirely like a magical transformation and clearly realize that sentient beings are but a single dharma, devoid of dual nature.
Without abandoning the sphere of karma, they skillfully manifest within the realm of conditioned existence through their expedient means.

Without destroying the characteristics of conditioned phenomena within the realm of the unconditioned, they demonstrate conditioned phenomena while not conceptualizing the characteristics of the unconditioned.

Thus observing all phenomena as ultimately quiescent, bodhisattvas accomplish all pure roots of goodness and give rise to the mind that seeks to rescue and protect sentient beings; their wisdom is clear and penetrating.
Always delighting in the practice of the ocean of all dharmas, having already fully accomplished supramundane merit by leaving behind the dharmas of ignorance and folly,
they no longer study mundane dharmas; having attained the eye of pure wisdom and being free from the cataracts of delusion, they cultivate the path of dedication through skillful means.
[Treatise] From "The four sons of the Buddha" down to "by means of skillful expedients,

one cultivates the path of dedication," sixteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on how Bodhisattvas cultivate dedication by taking non-apprehension as their expedient for cultivating all roots of goodness.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner so as to accord with the hearts of all Buddhas;
to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields; to teach and bring to maturity all sentient beings;
to fully receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas; to become the supreme field of merit for all sentient beings; and for the sake of all...
The merchant, a wise guide, acts as the sun-disk that purifies all worlds;
with each root of goodness, he pervades the entire dharma-realm, able to protect and rescue all sentient beings, causing them all to be purified and fully endowed with merit.
[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" down to "endowed with all merits," these six lines of scripture summarize the preceding section on the merit of making offerings. [Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha,
when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate in this manner, they are able to protect and sustain the lineage of all Buddhas.
They are able to bring all sentient beings to maturity; they are able to adorn and purify all buddha-fields; they are able to remain unimpeded by any karmic actions;
they are able to thoroughly understand all phenomena; they are able to contemplate all phenomena as non-dual; they are able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
they are able to realize the reality-limit that is free from desire; they are able to accomplish pure faith and understanding; and they are endowed with clear insight.
“Benefiting the faculties, O Son of the Buddha—this is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fourth dedication, ‘reaching all places.
[Treatise: From “O Son of the Buddha” below down to the fourth dedication, “reaching all places,” there are six lines of sūtra that clarify the general conclusion.
Thus far, the dedications for reaching all places have been explained, which cause the lineage of the Buddhas to remain uninterrupted and expand extensively.
The Section on Purifying Buddha-fields.
[Sūtra] When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dedication, they attain bodily action that reaches all places, because they are able to universally manifest in all worlds;
they attain verbal action that reaches all places within all worlds.
Because they expound the Dharma, they attain all places; because they uphold all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas through their mental karma, they attain all places;
because they travel everywhere in accordance with the minds of sentient beings through the supernormal power of the divine foot, they attain all places;
because they universally comprehend all phenomena through the realization of wisdom as it is, they attain all places; and because they possess dhāraṇī and eloquence, they attain all places.
Because he gladdens the minds of sentient beings according to their capacities, he reaches all places;
because he enters the Dharma-realm by universally entering all worlds within a single pore, he reaches all places;
because his body universally enters the bodies of all sentient beings within the body of a single sentient being, he reaches all places; and because he universally perceives every eon...
Because they constantly see all Tathāgatas throughout the kalpas, they attain the dedication to reaching all places and universally seeing them;
because in every single thought-moment all Buddhas appear before them, the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
are able to dedicate their roots of goodness by means of this dedication that reaches all places.

[Treatise] From the passage beginning with "The seven bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" down to "is able to dedicate roots of goodness in this manner," twelve and a half lines of scripture clarify that when one abides in this dedication,
one attains the distribution of bodily, vocal, and mental karma throughout all places in the ten directions.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.
[Śāstra] 8. From "At that time" onwards, this single line of sūtra clarifies the section in which the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveys the assembly and speaks in verse.
[Sūtra] Within and without, throughout all worlds, the Bodhisattva is entirely without attachment;
yet he does not abandon the work of benefiting sentient beings.
The Great Being practices such wisdom that all lands throughout the ten directions are entirely without support and without abode.
Not grasping at the various dharmas such as livelihood, nor falsely giving rise to any conceptual discriminations,
they universally encompass all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions without exception;
observing that their essential nature is non-existent, they skillfully dedicate [their merit] to reach all places.
Universally encompassing all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, One does not give rise to deluded thoughts therein,

just as with worldly dharmas; The Lamp Illuminating the World awakens thus to the various karmic practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas, Which are distinguished according to their superior, middling, and inferior grades.

Dedicating all roots of goodness to them, they follow the example of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who have reached the further shore; having fully accomplished their training under the Tathāgatas,
they always contemplate with sublime wisdom and are endowed with the most excellent dharmas among humans.
I universally dedicate all pure roots of goodness, Never abandoning the benefit of the deluded multitudes.
May I cause all sentient beings To become supreme lamps that illuminate the world;
Without ever making distinctions among sentient beings, Nor entertaining false conceptions regarding any phenomena.
Though they are unstained by attachment to the world, they do not abandon any sentient beings;

these Bodhisattvas always delight in the dharma of quiescence, yet through compliance with it they reach the realm of nirvāṇa without forsaking the path of sentient beings, thereby attaining such subtle and wondrous wisdom.
The Bodhisattva never discriminates between actions, nor does he grasp at any of their karmic fruits;

all worlds arise from conditions. Without departing from the view that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, he enters deeply into such realms and does not give rise to discrimination therein.
The Teacher who tames all sentient beings, Is clearly proficient in skillful dedication here.
[Commentary] The above consists of twenty-two lines of verse, with two lines forming each stanza, as fully contained within the text itself.
Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: what is meant by "dedication reaching all places"? In terms of its stages (*bhūmi*), there are eleven. First:
1. The Dharma-body pervades all places; 2. the two wisdom-bodies pervade all places; 3. the three great vows pervade all places; 4.
making offerings to all Buddhas pervades all places; 5. seeing, hearing, and receiving all Dharmas pervades all places;
6. universally manifesting form-bodies pervades all places; 7. awakening sentient beings pervades all places.

9. Abiding in all places without emerging from a single pore, reaching all locations; 10. Pervading the ten directions equally with the Dharma-realm, being without coming or going while reaching all locations;
11. Entering the body and mind of a single sentient being as equal to the body and mind of all sentient beings, reaching all locations;
12. Entering a single Buddha’s body and a single pore as equal to all Buddhas.
Dedication from the pores of the body to all places. Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of dedication:
first, dedicating unconditioned dharmas toward conditioned dharmas; second, dedicating conditioned dharmas toward unconditioned dharmas;
third, dedicating a single dharma toward many dharmas; fourth, dedicating many dharmas toward a single dharma; fifth, regarding all existent dharmas...
1. Dedication from non-existent dharmas; 2. dedication from non-existent dharmas toward existent dharmas;
3. dedication of worldly dharmas toward supramundane dharmas; 4. dedication of supramundane dharmas toward worldly dharmas; 5.
dedication by means of the non-existence of all intrinsic natures toward the dharma of dedication that exists; 6. dedication of all that exists... [and so forth].
Taking the Dharma as one's intrinsic nature, there is no dharma of dedication; this is for the sake of enabling those who would stagnate in existence or non-existence to attain mastery,
for the sake of being without obstruction regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, for the sake of attaining great supernormal powers so that no dharma can detain them,
and for the sake of making offerings to all Buddhas and transforming sentient beings, attaining mastery over the unity and multiplicity, the same and the different— this is done through sincerity.

The mind gives rise to great clouds of vows that completely envelop the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, manifesting various kinds of offerings to make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
because one vows that the merit and virtue of both oneself and others shall be perfected, it is therefore called the Dedication Reaching All Places.
Its great significance lies in cultivating and attaining the Dharma-body within the ten abodes and ten practices.
Wisdom and insight arise based on this Dharma; great vows and great compassion arise based on non-active wisdom and insight.
One gives rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and spiritual efficacy that do not stagnate in either defilement or purity, nor is the mind detained by the two dharmas of defilement and purity.
One enters the gate of mastery over supernormal powers, yet does not cling to the powers, nor cling to mastery; for the nature of all dharmas is inherently detached from supernormal powers.
Therefore, the fifth dedication, the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit, has the perfection of dhyāna as its essence;
it takes the lady Vasumitrā, whom the youth Sudhana beheld, as its practice; and it is the land where those who practice this reside.
The land is named "Perilous" and the city is named "Jewel Adornment. To praise his virtues:

in the center of his mind there is no discrimination, and he universally knows all dharmas. Sitting upright in a single body, he fills the entire Dharma-realm; within his own person, he manifests all lands.
His enlightened essence of dhyāna is omnipresent and sovereign; his enlightened dhyāna and wisdom are the non-dual union of essence and function, integrated with compassion.

Therefore, the city is named "Perilous" because it represents the convergence of true wisdom with the conventional; it is named "Adorned with Jewels" because it represents the convergence of the conventional essence with the self-luminosity of truth.
Here, tranquility and agitation are both fused, and wisdom and compassion are unimpeded; thus, one remains unstained by sensory objects.
For this reason, the city is called "Adorned with Jewels. As for the woman Vasumitrā, this is translated as "Friend of the World," meaning she is able to [benefit] worldly people.
For the sake of being a teacher and friend, she is also called a "Heavenly Friend," for she can act as a teacher and friend to all the devas.

Some call her "The One Who Exchanges Treasures," for by means of this woman’s skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*), she exchanges [worldly things] for the jewel of the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of sentient beings.
Her body is golden in color, and her eyes and hair are deep blue; whether one hears her preach the Dharma, or sees her even briefly, or grasps her hand, or sits with her—
The seat universally attains samādhi because it takes the essence of clarity-cultivation (míng-chán) as its substance;

since it pervades everywhere and accords with wisdom, the Way unites with those who perceive it, and all such perceivers are of the stream in which the essence of cultivation, wisdom, and compassion meet.

As for those of the stream of separate perception, they constantly face it yet do not behold its countenance; it is simply that concentration and wisdom accord, and wisdom and compassion merge, responding to and connecting with the faculties [of beings].

The worldly designation of him as "Woman" does not mean he is merely a woman. Within the fifth stage of the Ten Abidings, which governs the gate of dhyāna, the worldly elder is designated as "Liberation.

This clarifies that the conventional body is fundamentally true; because the bodies of sentient beings are originally the Buddha-land, the elder’s body contains the Buddha-land, making it clear that the bodies of sentient beings are likewise so. It is simply a matter of the characteristics of meditative contemplation.
One should immediately perceive that within the Ten Practices, the Elder Ratnacūḍa illustrates the gate of dhyāna by means of his own original residence—a ten-storied mansion with eight gates.
From the marketplace above, he leads those of the mundane world into the house; this illustrates that wisdom constitutes the essence of dhyāna, as it draws forth the mundane and guides its arising.
Therefore, it is said that leading them from the marketplace into the realm of wisdom is called "introduction."
Within the "Returning Home" section, specifically within the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), Vāsukī the Woman is taken as the gate of dhyāna.
This clarifies that the ten dedications take wisdom and compassion as the essence of dhyāna, using the woman to represent them and thereby manifest their form.

By employing this to symbolize the Dharma, one uses the mundane affairs of daily conduct to manifest wisdom following compassionate action; thus, while dwelling in the world, one remains unstained by defilement.

If you have not yet been defiled by them and have not yet awakened, you will be detained by worldly dust and karma; you must therefore cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, aspiring for supramundane insight.

If you have attained such insight and karma has perished, you must dwell amidst entanglements without being defiled, employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings and cause them all to attain liberation.
You must certainly know their faculties and guide them, never confusing or deluding sentient beings; this is essential.

Regarding the two meanings—relying on the faculties and receiving the medicine—they are as previously explained. To expand upon the meaning of this section of the sutra, it is divided into thirteen subsections.
[Sutra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva? O Son of the Buddha.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the roots of goodness arising from repenting and eliminating all heavy karmic obstructions;
the roots of goodness arising from prostrating in reverence to all Buddhas of the three periods of time; the roots of goodness arising from exhorting all Buddhas to preach the Dharma;
and the roots of goodness arising from hearing the Buddhas preach the Dharma, practicing with diligent effort, and awakening to the inconceivable, vast realm—
One gives rise to roots of goodness; one rejoices in all the roots of goodness belonging to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as those of all sentient beings.

The roots of goodness thus produced are inexhaustible alongside the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and the roots of goodness obtained by the diligent cultivation of all Bodhisattvas.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time attain equal and perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma.
Bodhisattvas fully know all the roots of goodness produced by those who, with a mind of sympathetic joy, turn the True Wheel of Dharma to subdue sentient beings;
they know [the deeds] of all Buddhas of the three periods of time— from their first aspiration, their cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, and their attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment,
up to their manifestation of entry into parinirvāṇa, and after their parinirvāṇa, the duration of the True Dharma remaining in the world until its final extinction— all such things as these.
A bodhisattva rejoices in all roots of goodness with such mindfulness as this: regarding the ineffable realms of all Buddhas,
their own realm, and even the unobstructed realm of Bodhi— regarding all these vast and immeasurable varieties of roots of goodness,
whatever has been accumulated, whatever has been resolved upon, whatever has been rejoiced in, and whatever has been perfected.
Whatever has been accomplished, whatever has been practiced, whatever has been attained, whatever has been realized,
whatever has been maintained, and whatever has been increased— all of these are dedicated toward adorning all buddha-fields,
just as in the past, throughout infinite eons, in all worlds, at all places where all Tathāgatas have practiced, namely, the immeasurable and...
The number of Buddha-worlds; that which is known by the wisdom of Buddhas, recognized by Bodhisattvas, and received by those of great resolve;
the flow and guidance of the pure karmic practices that adorn Buddha-fields; that which arises in accordance with sentient beings; that which is manifested through the spiritual power of Tathāgatas;
that which is accomplished by the pure karma of the appearance of Buddhas in the world; and that which is brought forth by the sublime conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—all these...
The Buddha attained enlightenment therein and manifested various sovereign spiritual powers; all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the future,
abiding pervasively throughout the Dharma-realm— those who shall attain the Way of the Buddha and obtain all pure,
adorned merit-fields— throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, boundless, limitless, uninterrupted, and inexhaustible— all [are likewise].
It is adorned with immeasurable, wondrous jewels born from the wisdom of the Tathāgata— namely, the adornment of all fragrances,
the adornment of all flowers, the adornment of all garments, the adornment of all treasuries of merit,
the adornment of the powers of all Buddhas, and the adornment of all Buddha-lands; it is the inconceivable capital city where the Tathāgata dwells.
These pure assemblies, who have shared karmic affinities for practicing together and dwell therein, shall attain perfect enlightenment in future ages;
that which all Buddhas have accomplished is not seen by the world, but can be perceived only by the pure eyes of Bodhisattvas.
These Bodhisattvas, possessing great majestic virtue and having planted roots of goodness in past lives, know that all phenomena are like illusions and like [dreams].
The Bodhisattva Universal Practice transforms all pure deeds, enters the inconceivable samādhi of mastery, and through skillful means performs the work of a Buddha.
He emits the radiance of a Buddha that universally illumines the world without limit;
all the present Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise adorn their worlds with immeasurable forms and immeasurable light.
All these forms are accomplished through merit; they consist of immeasurable fragrances, immeasurable jewels, immeasurable trees, countless adornments, countless palaces, and countless sounds.
In accordance with past conditions, various spiritual friends manifest all manner of meritorious adornments without end—namely, all adornments of fragrance and all adornments of garlands.
Adorned with all manner of powdered incense, adorned with all manner of jewels, adorned with all manner of banners,
adorned with all manner of precious silk streamers, adorned with all manner of precious railings, adorned with incalculable golden nets, adorned with incalculable rivers,
adorned with incalculable clouds and rains, and adorned with the playing of incalculable music of exquisite subtlety.
With such immeasurable and innumerable ornaments as these, they adorn all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm,
arising from the various karmas of the ten directions— all of which are known by the Buddhas and proclaimed by the Buddhas.
Within all those Buddha-lands, there are what are called adorned Buddha-lands and pure Buddha-lands.
The Buddha-lands of equality, the Buddha-lands of exquisite excellence, the Buddha-lands of majestic power, the Buddha-lands of vastness, the Buddha-lands of peace and happiness,
the Buddha-lands of indestructibility, the Buddha-lands of inexhaustibility, the Buddha-lands of immeasurability, the Buddha-lands of immovability,
the Buddha-lands of fearlessness, the Buddha-lands of radiance, the Buddha-lands free from opposition, the Buddha-lands of delightful beauty, and the Buddha-lands of universal illumination.
Adorned Buddha-fields, exquisite Buddha-fields, skillfully crafted Buddha-fields, foremost Buddha-fields, superior Buddha-fields,
distinguished Buddha-fields, most excellent Buddha-fields, supremely excellent Buddha-fields, sublime Buddha-fields, unsurpassed Buddha-fields,
peerless Buddha-fields, incomparable Buddha-fields, and Buddha-fields beyond analogy— thus, throughout the past, future, and present, [all are one].
All the adornments existing in all Buddha-fields, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dedicate by means of their own roots of goodness,
vowing that all the pure and adorned lands of all Buddhas of the past, future,
and present may entirely adorn a single world, just as those adornments exist in all those Buddha-fields.
All are fully accomplished, all are completely pure, all are gathered together, all are clearly manifest, all are exquisitely adorned, and all are maintained;
as it is for one world, so it is for all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm—all are likewise so.
All the various adornments of the buddha-lands of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are fully present in their entirety.

[Treatise] From "A single son of the Buddha" down to "are all fully complete," these sixty-one lines of scripture clarify the section on how all that a bodhisattva rejoices in and dedicates is entirely complete and perfect.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further dedicates his roots of goodness in this way, making this vow:
"May all the great Bodhisattvas in all the Buddha-fields that I cultivate fill them completely;
may those Bodhisattvas possess a true nature, penetrate with wisdom, be well able to distinguish all world-realms and realms of sentient beings, and enter deeply into the Dharma-realm."

Having abandoned delusion throughout the realm of empty space, he accomplished mindfulness of the Buddha and mindfulness of the Dharma; his true and inconceivable mindfulness of the Sangha was immeasurable and universally pervasive.
He also practiced mindfulness of the relinquishment of phenomena (*dharmaparityāga*). With the sun of perfect wisdom shining everywhere, he perceived all things without obstruction.
Born from the state of non-attainment, he gave rise to all Buddha-dharmas, becoming the sovereign lord of the most excellent roots of goodness for all beings.
Having generated the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, they abide in the power of the Tathāgatas and proceed toward *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

They destroy all demonic activities, purify the realm of sentient beings, and penetrate deeply into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Forever free from perversions, their roots of goodness and great vows are entirely unfailing.
Thus, such Bodhisattvas fill that land; born in such a place and possessing such virtues, they constantly perform the work of Buddhas.
Having attained the pure radiance of the Buddha’s Bodhi and being endowed with the wisdom of the Dharma-realm, they manifest supernatural powers such that a single body fills all dharma-realms.
Having attained great wisdom, they enter the sphere of action of all-knowledge;
they are well able to discern the words and meanings of the infinite and boundless dharma-realms, remaining entirely unattached to any world-system while yet being able to appear everywhere.

With a mind like empty space regarding all Buddha-fields, having no point of dependence yet able to discern the entire dharma-realm, they are skillfully able to enter and emerge from inconceivable and profound samādhis;
they proceed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), dwell in the lands of all Buddhas, and attain the powers of the Buddhas.
They reveal and expound incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) teachings without fear, in accordance with the three periods of time.
The roots of goodness of all Buddhas universally illumine the entire dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas;
they are able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, know incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) methods of language, and skillfully produce inconceivable and differentiated sounds.
They enter the supreme stage of the Buddha's own mastery and travel unhindered through all worlds in the ten directions.
Practicing in non-contention and relying on no fixed dharma, they cultivate and expand the mind of enlightenment through non-conceptualization;
possessing skillful wisdom, they thoroughly understand the meaning of words and phrases, and are able to reveal and expound them according to their proper sequence.
May such great bodhisattvas adorn that land, filling it and spreading throughout it, dwelling in accordance with the truth, and being thoroughly perfumed by cultivation.
Cultivating purity, supreme purity, and tranquil stillness within a single Buddha-field,
in every direction there are likewise countless, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, uncountable, ineffable,
inconceivable, unfathomable, unspeakable, and beyond-unspeakable numbers of great Bodhisattvas, pervading and filling it entirely.
In one location, it is likewise in all locations; as it is in one buddha-field, so it is in all buddha-fields throughout the entirety of space and the pervasiveness of the dharma-realm.
[Treatise] From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, up to "all Buddha-fields are likewise," there are thirty lines of scripture clarifying how Bodhisattvas,
by means of great vows, vow to fulfill the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas and adorn the lands of the ten directions.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of skillful means, dedicates all roots of goodness toward all buddha-fields;
by means of skillful means, dedicates them toward all bodhisattvas; by means of skillful means, dedicates them toward all Tathāgatas;
by means of skillful means, dedicates them toward the enlightenment of all Buddhas; and by means of skillful means, dedicates them toward all vast vows.
The skillful means of the path of departure; the skillful means of dedication to purify all realms of sentient beings;
the skillful means of dedication to always seeing the Buddhas appearing in all worlds; the skillful means of dedication to always seeing the Tathāgatas with immeasurable lifespans;
and the skillful means of dedication to always seeing all Buddhas pervading the entire Dharma-realm, turning the wheel of the Dharma without obstruction or regression.
The Dharma-Wheel.

[Treatise]: From "the three sons of the Buddha" down to "turning the unobstructed and non-retrogressive Dharma-wheel," seven lines of scripture clarify the section on the dedication of skillful means.

[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, they universally enter all buddha-lands and thereby purify all buddha-fields; they universally reach all realms of sentient beings and thereby purify all bodhisattvas;
they universally vow that all buddha-lands shall have Buddhas appear therein.
Therefore, the bodies of all Tathāgatas appear transcendentally throughout the entire dharma-realm and all Buddha-lands.

[Treatise] From "the four sons of the Buddha" down to "appear transcendentally," there are four and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on the purification of the Buddha-fields through vows,
wherein the Buddhas constantly appear transcendentally in all lands.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates [merit] through such incomparable dedications toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), his mind becomes vast like space, limitless, and enters the inconceivable.
He knows that all karma and its retributions are entirely quiescent; his mind is ever-equal, without boundary, and is able to penetrate everywhere.
"All Dharmadhātus. [Treatise]:

From "the five sons of the Buddha" down to "entering all dharmadhātus," three and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), wherein they know that the fruits of karma are quiescent.
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Forty-Four.
