The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya Scripture, Scroll Forty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
The Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Lay Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Treatise on the Sūtras*, Chapter Twenty-five on the Ten Dedications, Part Seven.
[Treatise]: The fifty-fifth [perfection] is the relinquishing of courtesans.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, all the women who constitute the inner palace retinue and attendants of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are of upright and beautiful countenance and fully endowed with talent; they are all skillful in conversation, laughter, song, and dance.
Adorning their bodies with various garments and various flowers and perfumes, those who behold them rejoice, never wearying of the sight—such are these jewels.
The hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of women were all born through the virtuous karma of the Bodhisattva;
they were autonomous according to their will, respectful and compliant without fail.

He bestowed them all as gifts upon those who came to beg, yet within this he felt no heart of affection, no heart of attachment, no heart of indulgence, no heart of bondage, no heart of grasping, and no heart of greedy defilement.

With a mind free from conceptual discrimination, a mind free from pursuit, a mind free from grasping at signs, and a mind free from longing or desire, the Bodhisattva at that time contemplates all roots of goodness for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain liberation;

he dedicates them for the sake of attaining the joy of the Buddha-dharma; he dedicates them so that within what is not solid, one may attain solidity; he dedicates them for the sake of attaining gold.
Because the mind is adamantine and indestructible; because it is dedicated toward entering the Buddha’s place of enlightenment; because it is dedicated toward reaching the further shore;
because it is dedicated toward attaining the unsurpassed bodhicitta; because it is dedicated toward being able to comprehend all phenomena through wisdom;
because it is dedicated toward giving birth to all roots of goodness; because it is dedicated toward entering the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
To the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, who dwell in such dharmas, are born into the family of the Tathāgatas,
increase the pure and supreme causes of all Buddhas, give birth to the most excellent path of omniscience, deeply enter the vast intellectual activities of Bodhisattvas,
extinguish all worldly defilements and afflictions, and are always able to provide offerings and gifts to the field of merit for the sake of all sentient beings.

Proclaiming the sublime Dharma with skillful means, establishing it so that they may practice all purifying conducts, and constantly and diligently gathering all roots of goodness—thereupon, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
namely, "May all sentient beings always attain the retinue of immeasurable samādhis; may the supreme concentrations of Bodhisattvas continue in an uninterrupted succession."
May all sentient beings always delight in seeing the Buddhas and enter the Samādhi of the Adornments of All Buddhas.
May all sentient beings accomplish the inconceivable meditative concentration of Bodhisattvas and sport with mastery in immeasurable supernormal powers.
May all sentient beings attain the samādhi of reality as it is and obtain an indestructible mind. May all sentient beings fully acquire the profound [wisdom] of Bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings attain mastery over profound samādhis among all meditative concentrations; may they achieve a mind of liberation and accomplish the retinue of all samādhis;
may all sentient beings become skillful in various samādhis and be able to fully grasp the characteristics of all samādhis; may all sentient beings attain the samādhi of supreme wisdom throughout...
May all sentient beings be able to study the various gateways of samādhi; may they attain the unimpeded samādhi and enter deep meditative absorption (dhyāna) without ever falling back.
May all sentient beings attain the non-attached samādhi, with minds constantly in right reception (samāpatti), not grasping at dualistic phenomena.
This is the excellence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when giving away all their inner palace retinues.
The dedication of the faculties is for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to obtain an indestructible and pure retinue;
for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to obtain the retinue of a bodhisattva;
for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to fully attain the qualities of the Buddha-dharma; and for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to fulfill the power of omniscience.
Therefore, it is because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to realize unsurpassed wisdom;
because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to obtain compliant retinues; because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to dwell together with fellow practitioners of the same resolve;
because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with all merit and wisdom; and because he wishes—
In order to cause all sentient beings to accomplish pure roots of goodness; in order to cause all sentient beings to obtain a harmonious retinue;
in order to cause all sentient beings to accomplish the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to accomplish sequential, rational eloquence for skillfully expounding the Buddhas.

Because it is an inexhaustible treasury of Dharma; because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to forever abandon all mundane roots of goodness and collectively cultivate supramundane, pure roots of goodness;
because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to fulfill their pure karma and accomplish all pure dharmas; because he wishes to cause all the Buddha-dharmas of all sentient beings to...
Because they manifest before all [beings] and universally adorn and purify them with the light of the Dharma.
[Treatise] Fifty-sixth: Giving away one’s beloved wife and children.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to give away his beloved wife and children, just as in the past...
At that time, Prince Sudāna— the Bodhisattva Manifesting Majestic Adornment King— and an immeasurable multitude of other bodhisattvas,
mounting the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), practiced all-encompassing giving to purely cultivate the bodhisattva path of generosity.
With a pure mind free from regret, they completely relinquished their most cherished possessions to seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having purified their profound aspiration and accomplished the practice for awakening, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who contemplate the bodhisattva path,
who are mindful of the Buddha and abide in the lineage of the Buddhas, having fulfilled such a mind of giving, resolutely seek the body of a Tathāgata;
they observe their own bodies as being bound to all things and lacking self-mastery, and with those very bodies, they universally embrace all beings.
Birth is like a jewel island that bestows upon all who are unsatisfied, causing them to be satisfied.
In this way, the Bodhisattva protects and attends to sentient beings, desiring to make himself the foremost stūpa so that all may give rise to joy;
desiring to produce a mind of equanimity toward the world; desiring to act as a cooling pond for sentient beings; and desiring to grant to the multitude...
Giving rise to the desire for all peace and happiness, acting as a great donor for sentient beings, possessing the wisdom of mastery that understands the practices performed by Bodhisattvas,
and being able to thus adorn oneself with such great vows, one proceeds toward omniscience; vowing to accomplish supreme wisdom as a field of merit,
universally mindful of sentient beings, constantly following and protecting them, and thereby accomplishing one's own benefit.

Increasing the light of wisdom that universally illumines the world, they constantly and diligently recollect the bodhisattva’s mind of giving and always delight in observing the realm of the Tathāgata.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with a mind liberated from bondage and attachment, gives away their wife and children, they dedicate the roots of goodness thus accumulated in this way: namely, "May all sentient beings abide..."
May the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest transformation bodies that pervade the entire Dharma-realm and turn the wheel of non-retrogression;
may all sentient beings attain a body free from attachment; may they travel throughout all Buddha-lands by the power of their vows;

may all sentient beings abandon hearts of love and hatred and sever the fetters of greed and anger; and may all sentient beings become children of the Buddhas, following the conduct of the Buddhas. May it be so! One.
May all sentient beings give rise to the mind of their own self toward all Buddhas that is indestructible;

may all sentient beings always be children of the Buddha, born through transformation from the Dharma; may all sentient beings attain the ultimate state and accomplish the sovereign wisdom of the Tathāgata;
may all sentient beings realize the Bodhi of the Buddha and forever be free from afflictions. May one...
May all sentient beings be able to fully expound the path to the Buddha’s bodhi and constantly delight in practicing the unsurpassed gift of Dharma;
may all sentient beings attain a mind of right concentration that cannot be destroyed by any conditions;
and may all sentient beings sit beneath the Bodhi tree, achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, and reveal to immeasurable sons of good family who are born from the transformation of the Dharma.
Sister, this is the dedication of the roots of goodness from a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s giving away of his wife and children,
performed for the sake of causing all sentient beings to fully realize unimpeded liberation and non-attached wisdom.
[Treatise] Fifty-seventh: The Gift of Dwelling Places.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas adorn their dwellings and various requisites and give them all away to whoever comes to beg, they practice the dharma of giving without attachment to the home, remaining far removed from all discursive thoughts and mental investigations associated with domestic life.
They feel revulsion toward household affairs and the means of livelihood; they are neither greedy for nor relish them, their minds being free from attachment.

Knowing that the household is easily ruined, their hearts are constantly weary of it and inclined toward renunciation. They find no delight whatsoever therein, desiring only to leave the home life to cultivate the bodhisattva practices and adorn themselves with the qualities of all Buddhas.
They relinquish everything entirely, their minds never experiencing regret, always acting for the sake of the Buddhas.
Whatever houses, wealth, or possessions they may have in any place, they give them all away in charity with a mind free from attachment.
Upon seeing those who come to beg, their hearts feel joy and celebration. At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these roots of goodness as follows:
"May all sentient beings renounce their wives and children and achieve the supreme bliss of leaving the household life."
May all sentient beings be liberated from the bonds of the household and enter the homeless life among the teachings of all Buddhas to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
May all sentient beings abandon the defilement of stinginess and delight in universal giving with a mind that never regresses.
May all sentient beings forever leave behind the ways of the household, possessing few desires and being content, without hoarding or accumulating anything. May all sentient beings emerge...
Dwelling in the household of worldly life within the family of the Tathāgata, may all sentient beings attain the unobstructed Dharma and eliminate the path of all obstacles.
May all sentient beings be free from attachment to their families; though appearing to dwell at home, may their minds be without clinging.
May all sentient beings be skillful in transforming and guiding others, never departing from the principles of the household while preaching the wisdom of the Buddha. May one...
May the bodies of all sentient beings, while currently dwelling in the household life, always abide in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom;
may all sentient beings, while on the ground of domestic life, abide on the ground of the Buddha, universally causing immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.
This is the dedication of roots of goodness by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva when giving a house, for the sake of sentient beings.
Because they have accomplished the various practices, vows, supernormal powers, and wisdom of a bodhisattva.
[Treatise] Fifty-eighth: Giving Gardens, Groves, Pavilions, and Terraces.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives various gardens, groves, pavilions, and terraces for the sake of play and happiness.
In this place of adornment, they form this thought: "I shall create beautiful gardens for all sentient beings;
I shall manifest the joy of the Dharma for all sentient beings; I shall bestow upon all sentient beings a mind of gladness;
I shall demonstrate boundless bliss and joy to all sentient beings; I shall open [the way] for all sentient beings."
Through this gate of pure dharmas, I shall cause all sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy;
I shall cause all sentient beings to attain the Bodhi of the Buddhas; I shall cause all sentient beings to fulfill their great vows;
I shall act toward all sentient beings like a compassionate father; and I shall cause all sentient beings to observe with wisdom. I shall...
"I shall provide all sentient beings with the necessities of life; toward all sentient beings, I shall be like a compassionate mother who nurtures all roots of goodness.

When a great bodhisattva, a son of the Buddha, practices these roots of goodness in this manner, they do not give rise to weariness or aversion toward wicked sentient beings, nor do they mistakenly conceive a mind of abandonment. Even if...
All sentient beings throughout the world are entirely unaware of his kindness;

yet from the very beginning, the Bodhisattva harbors no resentment toward them and does not give rise to even a single thought of seeking recompense. He desires only to extinguish their immeasurable suffering and affliction.

His mind regarding all worlds is like empty space, free from any defilement or attachment. Universally contemplating the true nature of all phenomena, he gives rise to great vows to bring about their cessation.
Never wearying of nor abandoning the suffering of sentient beings, with the great vehicle aspiration to extinguish all views, they cultivate the equal practices and vows of all bodhisattvas.
O Son of the Buddha, after the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has observed in this way, they gather all roots of goodness and dedicate them entirely, namely:
wishing that all sentient beings, in every thought-moment, may give birth to immeasurable wholesome dharmas and bring them to fulfillment.
With the aspiration for the unsurpassed grove, may all sentient beings attain the dharma of immovability; may they see all Buddhas and cause them all to rejoice.
May all sentient beings delight in the garden of the Dharma and obtain the sublime joy of the gardens of all Buddha-fields.
May all sentient beings attain a pure and wondrous mind and constantly behold the grove of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers. May all...
May all sentient beings attain the playful joy of the Buddhas and constantly engage in skillful play within the realm of wisdom.
May all sentient beings attain the joy of playful sport and universally travel to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment in all Buddha-fields.

May all sentient beings achieve the playful liberation of Bodhisattvas, performing the practices of a Bodhisattva throughout all future kalpas with a mind free from weariness. May all sentient beings...
Giving birth to the vast resolve that all Buddhas fill the Dharma-realm, dwelling in the gardens of the Buddhas,
and vowing that all sentient beings may travel everywhere to all Buddha-fields, making offerings to the Buddhas in each and every field;
and vowing that all sentient beings attain a mind of wholesome aspiration and purify and adorn all Buddha-fields— this is the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates the roots of goodness from giving away all gardens, groves, terraces,
and pavilions so that sentient beings may see all Buddhas and sport in all the Buddha-gardens.
[Treatise] The fifty-ninth: The Bestowal of the Vast Assembly of Offerings.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of immeasurable and innumerable vast assemblies of offerings—pure in every respect and approved by all Buddhas—he never harms or afflicts even a single sentient being.
Causing sentient beings to distance themselves from all evils, purify the three paths of action, and achieve wisdom;

establishing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of pure realms; accumulating immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of excellent articles for sustenance;
and giving rise to the extremely rare mind of bodhi to practice without limit.
He bestows gifts so that all sentient beings may abide in the path of purity—excellent in the beginning, middle, and end—and give rise to pure faith and understanding;
he causes hundreds of thousands of billions of immeasurable sentient beings to rejoice according to the inclinations of their hearts;

with great compassion, he rescues and protects all, serves and makes offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and practices the distribution [of merit] in order to accomplish the seeds of all Buddhas.

With a mind free from regret during the act of giving, increasing the faculty of faith and bringing the supreme practices to fulfillment, the Bodhisattva advances in every thought-moment in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this way, namely:
"May all sentient beings resolve upon the Great Vehicle and fully accomplish the Mahāyāna gift; may all sentient beings be able to..."
They practice great assemblies of giving— giving that is exhaustive, giving that is virtuous, the most excellent giving, the unsurpassed giving,
the most unsurpassed giving, the peerless giving, the giving that transcends all worlds, and the giving praised by all Buddhas.
They vow that all sentient beings shall become the foremost donors, striving to rescue beings from all evil realms and causing them all to enter unimpeded wisdom.
May the roots of goodness cultivated through the path of impartiality, in accordance with reality, attain non-differentiated realization of the wisdom that perceives its own object;
may all sentient beings dwell securely in the wisdom of all tranquil meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and enter the path of immortality;
may they perfect all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), wisdom, and courageous diligence, fulfill the adornments of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the Buddha-dharma, and reach the further shore forever.

May all sentient beings never grow weary in establishing great assemblies of giving, providing for and aiding all beings without rest, until they reach the ultimate, unsurpassed knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
May all sentient beings always diligently plant all roots of goodness and reach the further shore of immeasurable merit. May all sentient beings constantly receive the protection of the Buddhas...

The Buddha has praised those who act as great donors for the entire world, whose merit is fully perfected and who fill the Dharma-realm, illuminating the ten directions and bestowing unsurpassed bliss.

May all sentient beings establish great assemblies of giving, extensively gather roots of goodness, and universally embrace all beings so that they reach the other shore. May all sentient beings become supreme donors.
May all sentient beings abide in the Supreme Vehicle; may all sentient beings, through timely giving, forever leave behind untimely giving and fulfill the ultimate vow of great giving;
may all sentient beings accomplish virtuous giving and reach the further shore of the great giving of the Buddha-Mahāpuruṣas;
may all sentient beings ultimately and constantly practice the great adornment of giving, exhausting all [the virtues] of all Buddhas.
To serve all teachers by drawing near to them and making great offerings;
to vow that all sentient beings abide in pure giving, accumulate immeasurable merit equal to the Dharma-realm, and reach the other shore;

to vow that all sentient beings become great donors within all worlds, pledging to deliver all classes of beings and abide in the stage of the Tathāgata—this is the establishment of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The roots of goodness from this great assembly of offerings are dedicated so that sentient beings may practice the unsurpassed giving,

ultimately accomplishing the giving of a Buddha, the indestructible giving, the giving that makes offerings to all Buddhas, the giving free from malice and resentment, the giving that rescues sentient beings,
the giving that accomplishes all-knowledge, the giving that constantly beholds all Buddhas, the giving of excellent diligence, and the accomplishment of all bodhisattva merits.
Because of the vast bestowal of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
[Treatise] The sixtieth section: Bestowing All Requisites for Life.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give away all requisites for life, their minds are free from greed or stinginess.
Seeking no karmic reward and having no hope for worldly wealth or pleasure, they leave behind the mind of false conceptualization and skillfully contemplate the Dharma.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, they carefully examine the true nature of all phenomena and,
according to the various differences in the needs and aspirations of sentient beings, each distinct in its own way, they accomplish immeasurable means of livelihood.
All their adornments were exquisite and beautiful; they practiced boundless giving, bestowing all gifts, exhausting both internal and external possessions.
When practicing this giving, they increased the power of their aspiration and joy, attaining great merit and accomplishing the jewel of the mind.
They were always able to protect all sentient beings, causing them all to give rise to supreme vows, never once harboring a thought of seeking recompense.
All the roots of goodness [accrued by] all Buddhas of the three periods of time through the perfection of the knowledge of all modes—
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with these roots of goodness from this giving, dedicate them to sentient beings,
vowing that all sentient beings may be purified and disciplined, that all sentient beings may extinguish their afflictions, and that they may adorn and purify all Buddha-fields.
May all sentient beings, with a pure mind, pervade the entire dharma-realm in a single thought-moment;
may all sentient beings be filled with wisdom as vast as empty space and the dharma-realm;
may all sentient beings attain all-knowledge, universally enter the three periods of time, and subdue sentient beings, constantly turning the pure, non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma at all times.
May all sentient beings be endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, skillfully manifesting supernatural powers and expedient means to benefit living beings.

May all sentient beings be able to awaken to and enter the Bodhi of all Buddhas, and throughout all future kalpas, constantly proclaim the True Dharma within the worlds of the ten directions without ever ceasing, so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it. May one...
May all sentient beings, having cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva throughout immeasurable eons,
fully accomplish their vows. May all sentient beings, in all worlds— whether defiled or pure, small or large, coarse or subtle, inverted or upright,
adorned with a single ornament or with various ornaments— in as many worlds as can be described, throughout all ages...

Throughout all realms, may they cultivate the bodhisattva practices without exception; may all sentient beings, in every thought-moment, constantly perform all the buddha-activities of the three periods of time to teach and transform sentient beings toward omniscience.
[Treatise] Sixty-first: Bestowing all incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) things according to whatever sentient beings require.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva provides all that sentient beings require through such incalculable things as these, in order to ensure that the Dharma of the Buddha continues without interruption and that great compassion universally rescues all.
All sentient beings abide in great compassion and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva; they never violate the teachings of the Buddha.
Through skillful means, they practice all manner of virtues and do not sever the lineage of all Buddhas.

They grant whatever is requested without weariness or aversion, relinquishing everything without ever feeling regret in the interim, and always diligently dedicate their merit toward the path of omniscience.

At that time, beings of various forms, various destinies, and various types of fields of merit from the lands of the ten directions all gathered at the place where the Bodhisattva was, seeking various things.
Having seen them, the Bodhisattva universally accepted and embraced them all, his heart filled with joy as if seeing a virtuous friend;
with great compassion and pity, he resolved to fulfill their wishes, and his mind of renunciation increased without ceasing.
Without becoming weary or fatigued, he satisfies all their requests and causes them to be free from the suffering of poverty. At that time, the beggars rejoice greatly in their hearts;
they spread his fame further and further, praising his virtuous excellence until his reputation is widely distributed, and all come to seek refuge with him.
When the Bodhisattva sees this, he experiences immeasurable joy. Even if he were to receive the [sovereignty of] Indra for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas...
Śākyamuni experienced the bliss of the Yāma Heaven for countless kalpas; the bliss of the Tuṣita Heaven for immeasurable kalpas;
the bliss of the Sunirmita Heaven for boundless kalpas; the bliss of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven for incomparable kalpas;
the bliss of Brahmā King for incalculable kalpas; and the bliss of a Wheel-Turning King ruling over the three thousandfold world system for ineffable kalpas.
Even if one were to experience the bliss of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven for as many eons as there are atoms in thought, or the bliss of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven for unspeakable eons,
it could not equal that of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who, upon seeing a beggar approach, feels joy, love, delight, and exultation; whose faith increases, whose aspiration becomes pure,
whose faculties are harmonized and subdued, and whose resolute understanding reaches fulfillment, even progressing toward the enlightenment of all Buddhas.
O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate these roots of goodness for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
they dedicate them for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
they dedicate them for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain great benefit and profit; they dedicate them for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain complete purity.
Dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings to seek awakening; dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain equality;
dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain a virtuous and wholesome mind;
dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings to enter the Mahāyāna; dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings...

Because all who are born shall attain noble and virtuous wisdom, he dedicates [these roots of goodness] so that all sentient beings may fully possess the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
fulfill the ten powers, and manifest perfect enlightenment upon the vehicle. When the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
dedicate their various roots of goodness in this manner, their actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely liberated from [obstructions].
He is unattached and free from the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-principle, the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of a human, the notion of a youth,
the notion of a born being, the notion of an agent, the notion of an experiencer, the notion of existence, the notion of non-existence,
the notion of this world or the next world, the notion of dying here and being born there, the notion of permanence, and the notion of impermanence.
There is no perception of the three realms of existence, nor is there a perception of the non-existence of the three realms of existence;
it is neither perception nor non-perception. Likewise, there is dedication that is neither bound nor liberated; dedication that is neither karma nor the retribution of karma;
dedication that is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; dedication that is neither volition nor the state after having willed; and dedication that is neither mind nor non-mind.
When the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, dedicate their minds in this way, they do not cling to the internal, nor to the external;
they do not cling to the subject that perceives, nor to the object perceived; they do not cling to causes, nor to effects; they do not cling to phenomena (*dharma*), nor to non-phenomena (*adharma*);
they do not cling to thought, nor to non-thought; they do not cling to form (*rūpa*), nor to the arising of form, nor to the cessation of form.

They do not cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not cling to the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not cling to the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Son of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can thus remain unattached to these phenomena, they will not be bound by form, nor bound by the arising of form, nor bound by the cessation of form;
they will not be bound by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor bound by the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
If one is not bound by the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and if one is not bound to these phenomena, then one is likewise not liberated from them.
Why is this? Because there is not the slightest phenomenon—whether presently arising, already arisen, or yet to arise—that can be grasped or clung to.
The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are such that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). There is no intrinsic nature.

They are dissociated; they are neither one nor two, neither many nor immeasurable, neither small nor large, neither narrow nor broad, neither deep nor shallow, neither quiescent nor discursive proliferation, neither a locus nor a non-locus, neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither essence nor non-essence, neither existent nor non-existent.
When a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena in this way, it is "non-being."
Regarding the Dharma within the realm of speech, they conform to worldly conventions by establishing what is non-Dharma as Dharma;
they do not sever the paths of karma, do not abandon the bodhisattva practices, and never regress in their quest for omniscience.

They thoroughly understand that all karmic conditions are like dreams, sounds are like echoes, sentient beings are like shadows, and all phenomena are like illusions; yet, they also do not destroy the power of causes, conditions, and karma.
Knowing that the function of all karmas is vast and great, they understand that all phenomena are without action; they practice the path of non-action without ever ceasing for a moment.

O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in omniscience universally dedicates [all merit] to the nature of omniscience—whether in what is possible or impossible—dedicating it in every respect without ever regressing.
For what reason is it called dedication? Because it eternally crosses over the world and reaches the further shore, it is called dedication;

because it eternally emerges from all aggregates (skandhas) and reaches the further shore, it is called dedication; because it crosses over the path of language and reaches the further shore, it is called dedication;

because it leaves behind various perceptions and reaches the further shore, it is called dedication; because it eternally severs the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and [reaches the further shore]...
It is called dedication because it reaches the further shore and is forever free from a basis; it is called dedication because it reaches the further shore and is forever severed from all activity;
it is called dedication because it reaches the further shore and is forever emerged from all states of existence;

it is called dedication because it reaches the further shore and is forever relinquished of all grasping; it is called dedication because it reaches the further shore and is forever transcendent of worldly dharmas.
Because it leads to the other shore, it is called dedication. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they then abide in accordance with the Buddhas,
abide in accordance with the Dharma, abide in accordance with wisdom, abide in accordance with enlightenment,
abide in accordance with meaning, abide in accordance with dedication, abide in accordance with the objective realm, abide in accordance with practice, and abide in accordance with reality.
Abiding in the dwelling that accords with purity, when a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dedicates in this manner, they thereby penetrate all dharmas;
they thereby serve all Buddhas, such that there is not a single Buddha whom they do not serve, and not a single dharma that they do not honor; there is not a single dharma that can be destroyed.
The Dharma cannot be contravened; there is not a single thing to which one may become greedily attached, nor a single phenomenon from which one may feel aversion.

One does not perceive any internal or external phenomena as having even the slightest destruction; rather, the power of the path of causes and conditions is fully perfected, proceeding without cessation.
[Treatise] The above section on dedication contains sixty-one kinds of giving; within each kind of giving are ten great vows, totaling sixty-one vows.

Within these sixty-one vows are ten kinds of dedication, which manifest the relinquishing of all attachments and the accomplishment of all non-attachment, as well as the offering of the nature of non-action to the teachings and transformations of all Buddhas.
Because sentient beings practice inexhaustible conduct.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth dedication of all roots of goodness in accordance with firmness for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this dedication, they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Firm and non-retrogressive, they enter the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and cultivate all-knowledge;
they accord with the meaning of the Dharma, accord with the nature of phenomena, and accord with all firm roots of goodness.
They accord with all perfectly fulfilled great vows and possess the firm dharma that cannot be destroyed by any vajra. Among all phenomena, they attain mastery.
[Treatise] From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, this constitutes the sixth dedication of all roots of goodness in accordance with firmness (*anuloma-dṛḍha-sarvakuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*).
Below this, up to the attainment of mastery within all dharmas, there are six lines of sutra text that collectively conclude the merit of the preceding dedications.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveyed the ten directions, surveyed the assembly, and surveyed the dharma-realm; having done so,
he entered into the profound meaning of words and phrases, cultivated a vast and immeasurable mind,
universally covered the world with a heart of great compassion, and entered the lineage of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the merits of all Buddhas.
Having achieved the virtues of the sovereign power-body of all Buddhas, he observes the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings;
according to their roots of goodness that are ready for maturation, he manifests a form-body based upon the dharma-nature body. Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he spoke these verses:

[Treatise] From the passage beginning "At that time, Vajradhvaja... and below, there are six lines of scripture clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja observing the assembly and speaking verses in praise of the Dharma.
[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva manifests his body as a king, peerless among all worldly ranks.
His merit, majesty, and radiance surpass all; he universally brings benefit to all living beings.
His mind is pure and free from attachment; he is sovereign in the world and honored by all.
He proclaims the True Dharma to instruct humanity, causing all sentient beings everywhere to attain peace and security.
In this present life, he ascends the throne as a noble king; Constantly relying on the True Teaching, he turns the Wheel of Dharma.
By nature benevolent and compassionate, free from cruelty or tyranny, He is revered by the ten directions, all of whom submit to his transformation.
His wisdom and discernment are ever lucid, And his physical marks and talents are fully perfected.
Ruling over all lands, there are none who do not follow; Subduing the demonic armies, they cause them all to be utterly destroyed.
Firmly maintaining the pure precepts without transgression, They resolve their will with endurance, remaining unshakable.
Forever vowing to eliminate anger and resentment, They constantly delight in practicing all the Buddha-dharmas.
Food, drink, incense, garlands, and clothing; Carriages, horses, beds, mats, seats, and lamps—
The Bodhisattvas provide all these to aid and sustain others, Along with countless other varieties,
practicing giving for the sake of benefiting them, Causing their vast minds to be awakened.
Toward the Exalted One and all others, may their minds be pure and filled with joy;
may Bodhisattvas provide for everyone everywhere, relinquishing all that they possess, both internal and external,
so that their minds remain forever pure and never for a moment give way to narrow-mindedness.
Whether giving his head or his eyes, or giving his hands or his feet,
his skin, flesh, marrow, bones, and all other things— he relinquishes everything without a trace of stinginess in his heart.
Though the Bodhisattva dwells in the position of a great king, his lineage is noble and he is honored among men.
Opening his mouth and extending his tongue, he bestows it upon all living beings; his mind is joyful, free from sorrow or attachment.

By virtue of the merit of that gift of the tongue, he dedicates it to all sentient beings, universally praying that through these supreme causes and conditions, all may attain the broad and long tongue of a Tathāgata.

Whether giving away wife and children, or even a royal throne, or offering one’s own body as a servant, their minds remain pure and ever joyful. In all such matters, they are free from grief or regret;
whatever is sought according to desire, they bestow it all. They provide timely relief and succor without weariness or fatigue.
He is able to give away everything he possesses, universally satisfying all who come to him in search of gifts;

for the sake of hearing the Dharma, he gives even his own body. He practices various ascetic austerities seeking bodhi, and again, for the sake of sentient beings, he relinquishes everything, seeking supreme wisdom without ever turning back.
Having heard the True Dharma from the Buddha, he sacrificed his own body to serve as an attendant,
desiring to universally rescue all living beings and giving rise to immeasurable joy.
He beheld the World-Honored One, the Great Guide, who is able to bring vast benefit through a heart of compassion.
At that time, leaping for joy and giving rise to gladness, they listen to and receive the profound flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
All the roots of goodness possessed by these Bodhisattvas they dedicate entirely to all sentient beings,
universally protecting and shielding them without exception, so that they may forever be liberated and eternally dwell in peace and happiness.
Whatever retinues the Bodhisattvas possess—whether their physical forms are dignified and beautiful, or their eloquence and wisdom;
whether it be flower garlands, garments, or ointments—all such various adornments are fully complete.
These retinues are exceedingly rare, yet the Bodhisattvas are able to give them all away as gifts.
Dedicated solely to seeking perfect enlightenment to deliver all sentient beings, such a mind is never abandoned for even a moment.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus with clarity and carries out various kinds of vast deeds,
dedicating them all to all conscious beings, yet without giving rise to a mind of grasping or attachment.
The Bodhisattva relinquished that great royal throne, as well as his kingdom, cities, palaces,
towers, pavilions, and gardens; he gave away his servants and attendants without any stinginess,
wandering everywhere throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas to practice such giving.
Thereby they instruct and guide all living beings, causing them all to transcend and ascend to the shore beyond.

Though the immeasurable categories of beings differ from one another, when the Bodhisattvas see those gathered from the worlds of the ten directions, their hearts rejoice; according to whatever each lacks, they cause them to be fulfilled.
Just as the Buddhas of the three periods have dedicated [merit], so too does the Bodhisattva cultivate such karma;
following all that the Honored One, the Tamer of Men, has practiced, he reaches the further shore.
The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena: who is it that can enter this Dharma?
What is it that enters, and what is it that is entered? With such a mind of non-abiding in giving, the bodhisattva employs skillful wisdom in dedication;
the bodhisattva employs the method of dedication through skillful means, and the bodhisattva employs dedication toward the ultimate truth, remaining without attachment to any phenomena therein.
The mind does not discriminate among any karmas, nor is it stained by or attached to the fruits of karma.
Knowing that the nature of bodhi arises from conditions, one enters the profound dharma-realm without opposition.
There is no karma within the body, nor does one abide depending upon the mind.

Through wisdom, they realize the nature of non-action; though karma does not perish because of causes and conditions, the mind does not falsely grasp at past phenomena, nor does it crave or cling to future events, nor does it dwell upon the present.
Thus they thoroughly comprehend that the three periods of time are entirely empty and quiescent.
The Bodhisattva has already reached the further shore of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise transcended.
Having emerged from the worldly stream of birth and death, his mind is humble and ever-pure.
He contemplates with clarity the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and his own body.
Seeking awakening within each and every one of these, Their essential nature is ultimately unattainable;
One does not grasp at the mark of the permanence of phenomena, Nor does one cling to the mark of their annihilation.
The nature of phenomena is neither existent nor non-existent; The sequence of the principles of karma is never-ending.
Not dwelling upon any phenomena, One does not perceive sentient beings or enlightenment;
Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, Ultimately, nothing can be found.
If one can contemplate all phenomena in this way, Then it will be as the Buddhas have realized.
Although one seeks its nature, it cannot be found; yet the conduct of the Bodhisattvas is not in vain.
The Bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena arise from conditions and does not contradict any of the paths they practice.
They reveal and explain the traces of all karmic actions, desiring to bring all sentient beings to complete purity.
This is the path traversed by the wise, as taught by all Tathāgatas;
by reflecting in accordance with it, one enters the true meaning.
One spontaneously awakens and attains bodhi, realizing that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and likewise neither coming nor going.
Not dying here to be born there, this person awakens to and understands all Buddha-dharmas, thoroughly penetrating the true nature of all phenomena.
Without making distinctions regarding the dharma-nature, they know that dharmas are without self-nature and are non-discriminative; such a person skillfully enters the wisdom of all Buddhas.
The nature of phenomena pervades all places; all sentient beings and lands throughout the three periods of time exist therein without exception.
It has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended, yet it is fully realized by all Buddhas, who encompass it all without exception.
Although all phenomena of the three times are spoken of, such phenomena as these are entirely without intrinsic existence;
yet the nature of all phenomena pervades everything. The bodhisattva’s dedication is likewise so:
dedicating it thus to all sentient beings, they never regress within the world.

[Commentary] Now, as the prose sections above and below, as well as the eighty-two verses, fully contain their own textual meaning and do not require further explanation, I shall briefly explain the titles of the dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Regarding "Dedication that accords with all firm roots of goodness," the *Sūtra* says:
"O Son of the Buddha, when one dedicates in this manner, one immediately accords with the abiding of the Buddhas."

"Abiding in accordance with the Dharma, abiding in accordance with wisdom, and abiding in accordance with Bodhi" collectively clarify that one practices the *dānapāramitā* throughout the ocean of lands;

it is so named because one accomplishes the indestructible *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya*, and through the power of supernormal transformations, one expands great compassion and other such qualities practiced by the Buddhas.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it means practicing in accordance with principle, principle being in accordance with practice, and wisdom [being in accordance with both].
Following compassion with compassion and following wisdom with skillful means, one draws forth the ocean of wisdom through the power of vows, accomplishing the gateway of compassion.
This is called the "Discourse on the Dedication of Firm Roots in Accordance with Equanimity and Sovereignty. The Master of the Treatise says in verse:
"The Dharma-body and the wisdom of principle have no substantial nature; they are equal, pure, and unconditioned. Through skillful means and the power of vows, they are adorned."
He perfected the practice of majestic spiritual transformations, which are filled with the nature of phenomena that lack self-nature and arise from conditions;

he taught that what arises from conditions does not lose its unconditioned nature, and spoke of the arising of great clouds of vows through dedication. His various practices pervaded the boundless reaches of space without ever departing from the essence of conditions;
his wisdom of non-arising was like an echo or a shadow, filling the entire Dharma-realm. The essence of his wisdom was like a wish-fulfilling jewel, equal to that of Samantabhadra.
Dedicating these toward great vows, they are all without reality; yet though they lack reality, they do not abandon conditions. Although arising from conditions, their nature is without action.
The various practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas are like clouds; their wisdom neither comes nor goes, appearing like reflections.
Even if they were to teach and transform all sentient beings, it would be like a conjured person delivering an illusory multitude—much like the construction of palaces and houses in the world.
One must judge its manifestation by the accomplishment of its function; yet both the function and the essence of that function lack inherent self-nature.

When the work is completed and the task finished, it benefits others precisely through non-action. Even though palaces and halls possess the function of providing shelter and nourishment, they do not claim to be the ones who nurture.
This dedication of great vows is likewise so: although there is principle and wisdom, [they do not claim to act].
The merit of purifying afflictions does not arise from the power of dedicating [it] toward great vows that provide all-encompassing nurture and benefit;
rather, this dedication has been fully present since the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

However, it is spoken of in terms of the relative superiority or inferiority of progress, and also in terms of the breadth or brevity of the textual exposition; furthermore, it is discussed according to the principle that time does not deviate from its course.
This is a simultaneous exposition of all five stages; there is no sense of temporal sequence between the ancient and the modern.

The seventh [stage], the dedication that accords with all sentient beings, takes the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) as its essence and is governed by the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
While the first six perfections constitute the cultivation of the mind that transcends birth and death, this seventh has already [surpassed them].
The latter four pāramitās constitute skillful means and wisdom; by entering into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), they transform and teach sentient beings.

Therefore, among those who manifest the Dharma, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is taken as the spiritual friend for Sudhana in this seventh dedication, "Great Compassion that Accords with All Sentient Beings.
Consequently, in this new translation of the sutra, he is rendered as "Avalokiteśvara" (觀自在).

The Bodhisattva is not something to be relied upon [as a separate entity]. What was called "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" in the old translations refers to the fact that the worlds of the ten directions together constitute a single Buddha-land; there is no separate western direction nor a distinct Amitābha Tathāgata.

This is a provisional device established by the Tathāgata to guide those of lesser capacity with conditioned means, so that they may focus their minds on recitation, subdue their remaining evil thoughts, and follow their hearts.

Through the foundations of mindfulness, one attains the vision of transformation Buddhas, which accord with the measure of one’s own mind. Regarding various virtues, there have been erroneous interpretations claiming that in this Sahā world there is no Avalokiteśvara;
thus, this text amends the original version of the sutra to read "Avalokiteśvara. As for the term "Avalokiteśvara," it merely indicates practice through its name;
herein, it specifically manifests the contemplative observation of the signless wisdom and reality that transcend both the mundane and the supramundane.

Mastery is not the practice of mere clarity or compassion. These three dharmas—Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra—are the common practice of all Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the three periods of time.

Mañjuśrī presides over the principle of the wondrous wisdom of the Dharma-body; Samantabhadra is the wisdom-body that knows the faculties [of beings] and serves as the gateway for accomplishing the myriad practices.
Avalokiteśvara is the embodiment of great compassion; these three dharmas within the realm of birth and death constitute the virtue of a single person, and are named Vairocana.
All sentient beings collectively rely upon these three dharmas and thus designate him as a Buddha; if even one were lacking, he would not be so.
Now, this title follows the ancient tradition and does not rely on the new translation, yet it is based on the Sanskrit *Ālokiteśvara* (Light-World Lord).

The Bodhisattva Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara) uses the light of wisdom to teach and the light of conduct to manifest great compassion; equalizing his light with that of all sentient beings, he benefits them in every place.
Thus, he is named Mañjuśrī everywhere and Samantabhadra everywhere, and may also be called "Everywhere-Light World-Sound.
Now, the name Guanshiyin is established based on the manifestation of the response-body in accordance with the mind of right mindfulness.

The name cannot be taken as the dharma manifested by Avalokiteśvara. Regarding the meaning of the dharma manifested through the name "Avalokiteśvara," it signifies the sixth stage, the *prajñāpāramitā*;

it does not refer to the *upāyapāramitā*, which involves entering saṃsāra to act in common with sentient beings while never severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
The name "Nao" (惱) here is an error by the translator. Avalokiteśvara dwells on Potalaka, which means "Mountain of White Flowering Trees.
It is there that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva resides and preaches the *Maitrī-karuṇā-sūtra* for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
On this mountain there are many white flowering trees, and their blossoms are exceedingly fragrant. The sūtra says he "dwells on the mountain."
Regarding "the west is A": the west is gold and is the white tiger; it is the station of killing. Being clear regarding the station of killing, one presides over the gate of compassion.
When the Bodhisattva of the Right Course comes from the east, he does so by means of the station of wisdom. Reaching the section on "Wen," the commentary on the sutra says:

"O Son of the Buddha, what is the dedication that accords with all sentient beings for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva? and so forth. Having thus performed the dedication in accordance with all sentient beings...
Down to the verses, this long section is divided into twenty parts.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the dedication of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that accords with all sentient beings?
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in accordance with all roots of goodness he has accumulated—namely, even small virtues—dedicates them as follows:
Roots of goodness, great roots of goodness, extensive roots of goodness, manifold roots of goodness, immeasurable roots of goodness, various roots of goodness, roots of goodness as numerous as atoms,
incalculable roots of goodness, boundless roots of goodness, inconceivable roots of goodness, unfathomable roots of goodness,
roots of goodness within the realm of the Buddhas, roots of goodness within the realm of the Dharma, and roots of goodness within the realm of the Saṅgha— [he] thoroughly knows them.
The roots of goodness of the sphere of consciousness; the roots of goodness of the sphere of all sentient beings; the roots of goodness of the sphere of skillful means;
the roots of goodness of the sphere of cultivating all virtuous minds; the roots of goodness of the internal sphere; the roots of goodness of the external sphere;

the roots of goodness of the sphere of boundless factors conducive to enlightenment; and the ultimate establishment of the supreme resolve through the diligent cultivation of all roots of goodness of relinquishment.

The root of goodness of maintaining pure precepts and relinquishing everything; the root of goodness of enduring all things without fail; the root of goodness of constant diligence with a non-regressive mind;
the root of goodness of entering immeasurable samādhis through great skillful means; the root of goodness of skillfully observing with wisdom;
the root of goodness of knowing the distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings; and the root of goodness of accumulating boundless merit.
Diligently cultivating the roots of goodness of the bodhisattva’s career and practices, which universally cover and nourish all worlds.

[Treatise] From the first section, beginning with "From the initial son of the Buddha" down to "the roots of goodness of all worlds," there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify the stage where the bodhisattva personally accumulates the aforementioned thirty-two kinds of boundless roots of goodness.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices, dwells securely in, enters into, embraces, accumulates, prepares, understands,
purifies the mind regarding these roots of goodness, reveals them, and initiates them, he attains a mind of endurance, closes the gates to the evil destinies,
perfectly governs the sense faculties, is complete in dignified deportment, remains far removed from perversions, fulfills right practice, and becomes worthy of being a single [reliable witness].
They are worthy vessels for all the Buddha-dharmas; they act as fertile fields of merit for sentient beings; they are remembered by the Buddhas; they grow the roots of goodness of the Buddhas;
they abide in the vows and practices of the Buddhas; they perform the deeds of the Buddhas; they attain mastery over the mind; they equalize themselves with the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

they proceed toward the site of enlightenment of the Buddhas; they enter the powers of the Tathāgatas; they are endowed with the physical marks and signs of a Buddha; they transcend all worlds; they take no pleasure in rebirth in the heavens; and they do not crave wealth.
Delighting in non-attachment to all conditioned phenomena, they dedicate all roots of goodness as a treasury of merit for all sentient beings.
Abiding in the ultimate path, they universally cover all things; from within the path of falsehood, they extract sentient beings and cause them to dwell securely in all wholesome dharmas.
Pervading all realms without interruption or exhaustion, they open the way to omniscient bodhi.

At this gateway, they establish the banner of wisdom and adorn the Great Way, universally manifesting it to all worlds to eliminate defilements, skillfully taming the mind, and giving birth into the family of the Tathāgata.
They purify the Buddha-lineage, are fully endowed with merit, act as a great field of blessings, and serve as a reliance for the world.
They establish sentient beings so that all may become pure, and constantly and diligently cultivate all [virtuous qualities].
Roots of Goodness.

[Treatise]: From the second son of the Buddha down to "cultivating all roots of goodness," fourteen lines of scripture clarify how the Bodhisattva dedicates the roots of goodness from the thirty-two kinds of limitless fields of merit cultivated as described above.
The Section on the Treasury of Merit for All Sentient Beings.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates various roots of goodness through the power of the mind of pure aspiration and bodhicitta, they form this thought: "These roots of goodness are the accumulation of bodhicitta; these are bodhi..."
Whatever the mind contemplates is the bodhicitta; whatever the mind initiates is the bodhicitta; whatever the mind aspires to is the bodhicitta;

whatever the mind increases is the bodhicitta—all for the sake of compassion for all sentient beings, all for the sake of seeking all-knowledge, and all for the sake of accomplishing the ten powers of a Tathāgata. When one forms this thought, roots of goodness increase.
"Advancing forever without regressing.

[Treatise] From "The third son of the Buddha" down to "forever without regressing," there are six lines of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the aforementioned roots of goodness is accumulated through a compassionate heart that is non-conceptual (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and independent (*anāśrita*), never departing from the bodhicitta.
[The Portion for All Sentient Beings.

[Sūtra]: O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further reflects: "May I, by means of the fruit and retribution of these roots of goodness, cultivate the bodhisattva practices throughout all future kalpas, bestowing them all as gifts upon all sentient beings and dedicating them all toward that end."
I vow that for all sentient beings, universally and without exception, incalculable worlds shall be filled with precious gems;
incalculable worlds shall be filled with clothing; incalculable worlds shall be filled with exquisite fragrances;
incalculable worlds shall be filled with ornaments; and incalculable worlds shall be filled with immeasurable mani-jewels.
In incalculable worlds, exquisite flowers are abundant; in incalculable worlds, the finest flavors are abundant;
in incalculable worlds, wealth and goods are abundant; in incalculable worlds, couches and seats are abundant, covered with jeweled canopies and spread with exquisite fabrics;
in incalculable worlds, various ornaments and jeweled crowns are abundant—suppose there were a single person...
Throughout all kalpas of the future, they shall constantly come to seek these things and bestow them as gifts, never becoming weary or ceasing their efforts;
as they do for one person, so shall they do for all sentient beings.
[Treatise] From "The fourth son of the Buddha" down to "all are likewise," there are eleven and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how the Bodhisattva makes vows,
vowing that all the fruits of the boundless roots of goodness cultivated as described above shall,
throughout all future kalpas, cause all those aforementioned roots of goodness cultivated to be dedicated to all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
The worlds are filled with various jewels, which he bestows as an infinite portion upon all sentient beings.

[Sūtra] When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives in this manner, O Son of the Buddha, he has no mind of hypocrisy, no mind of expectation, no mind seeking fame, no mind of regret, and no mind of feverish distress;
he simply gives rise to the resolve to seek exclusively the path to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
With a mind that relinquishes everything, a mind of compassion for all sentient beings, and a mind that teaches and brings them to maturity,
causing them all to dwell securely in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
dedicate their roots of goodness in this way so that they may constantly practice giving throughout all future eons, dwelling in the knowledge of all modes.

[Treatise] From the fifth son of the Buddha onwards, down to the passage on "constantly practicing giving while abiding in the mind of omniscient wisdom," five and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva possesses no fivefold mind and constantly practices giving to accomplish the fivefold mind.
As detailed in the sutra itself, beginning with the "mind free from hypocrisy," these five sections conclude the preceding thirty [categories].
The two kinds of roots of goodness are concluded.
[Sūtra] The Buddha’s son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, further reflects:

"For the sake of even a single sentient being, I desire to cause the worlds of asaṃkhyeya to be filled with precious elephants, complete with seven limbs, of an extremely well-trained nature, standing upon golden pedestals."
With banners and golden nets covering them, adorned with various exquisite jewels, he gives them as a gift, vowing:
"May incalculable worlds be filled with precious horses, all adorned with the various ornaments of the king of dragon-horses.
He holds these and gives them as a gift, vowing: "May incalculable worlds be filled with celestial maidens..."
They are able to spread and play various kinds of wondrous music as an offering; they vow to fill incalculable worlds with men and women as an offering;
they vow to fill incalculable worlds with their own bodies as an offering; they resolve to generate the bodhicitta and offer it as an offering;
and they vow to fill incalculable worlds with their own heads, giving rise to heedfulness.
With a focused mind, one practices giving, wishing to fill incalculable worlds with one's own eyes and gives them away;
wishing to fill incalculable worlds with the flesh, blood, and marrow of one's own body, one gives them away with a heart free from attachment;
and wishing to fill incalculable worlds with sovereign kingship, one gives it away.
Among these, he holds them and gives them as a gift, vowing that the worlds of incalculable numbers (*asaṃkhyeya*) be filled with slaves and servants;

he holds them and gives them as a gift. A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of such various things, dwells in a vast mind of universal giving throughout all future eons, giving to a single sentient being, and as with one sentient being, so for all sentient beings.
He gives in this manner to all sentient beings throughout the realm of birth.
[Treatise] From the sixth son of the Buddha down to "gives in this manner," there are sixteen lines and a half of scripture clarifying that the Bodhisattva,
by means of such incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) elephants, horse-kings, female musicians, daughters, and his own person— these ten [gifts].
[He] constantly distributes all manner of incalculable things throughout incalculable eons.
[Sūtra]: O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path in a single world-system for as many eons as remain until the end of the future;
with such things as these, he gives to a single sentient being, and in this way provides for all sentient beings, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
Just as it is in one world, so it is likewise in all worlds throughout the entirety of space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm;
great compassion universally covers them all without ever ceasing, universally bestowing pity and providing whatever is required through offerings and support,
never allowing such practice to be interrupted by circumstances, nor even giving rise to weariness for the duration of a single finger-snap.

[The Sūtra says: “Mind. [The Commentary says: From the seventh son of the Buddha downward, until the passage stating that there is not even the duration of a finger-snap’s worth of a weary mind, there are six lines of sūtra-text clarifying how the Bodhisattva, through the ten kinds of giving mentioned above, brings infinite sentient beings to fulfillment.
Throughout infinite kalpas, there is not a single moment of weariness.
[Sūtra] When a Buddha-son, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practices giving in this manner, he gives rise to these thoughts:

namely, the mind of non-attachment, the mind of non-binding, the mind of liberation, the mind of great power, the profound mind, the well-gathered mind, the mind of non-grasping, and the mind of non-...

A mind that has well-tamed the notion of a self; a mind that is undistracted; a mind free from false conceptualization; a mind endowed with various true natures; a mind that does not seek karmic retribution;
a mind that thoroughly understands all phenomena; a mind abiding in the great dedication of merit; a mind that skillfully resolves all meanings;
a mind that establishes all sentient beings in unsurpassed wisdom; a mind that gives rise to the great light of the Dharma; and a mind that enters into oneness.
"The mind of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
[Treatise] From the eighth son of the Buddha down to "the mind of the knowledge of all-knowledge," there are six lines of scripture clarifying that the Bodhisattva,
by means of the aforementioned giving, acts as a donor through ten kinds of unattached and liberated minds.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates the roots of goodness he has accumulated in this manner in every moment of thought, saying:
"May all sentient beings have abundant wealth and treasures, lacking for nothing;
may all sentient beings achieve an inexhaustible treasury of great merit; may all sentient beings be fully endowed with all forms of peace and security."
May all sentient beings increase their bodhisattva-mahāsattva activities;
may all sentient beings fulfill the immeasurable, foremost, and supreme dharmas; may all sentient beings attain non-retrogression in the vehicle of omniscience;
may all sentient beings universally behold all Buddhas of the ten directions; may all sentient beings forever...
May all sentient beings be free from the defilements and dust of worldly afflictions and attain a pure and equanimous mind;
may all sentient beings leave behind all places of hardship and realize all-encompassing wisdom.
[Treatise] From the ninth son of the Buddha down to the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nine lines of sūtra clarify how the bodhisattva,
by means of the ten aforementioned infinite acts of giving, gives rise to ten infinite vows, vowing that all sentient beings may attain the portion of all-knowledge.
