Chapter Twenty-five on the Ten Dedications, Part Eight.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus dedicates [merit], they give rise to a heart of joy for the sake of causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and peace;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to obtain a mind of equanimity;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in a mind of renunciation; and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in all...
Because of the mind of giving, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of joyful giving;

because of the mind of giving, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving that forever leaves behind poverty; because of the mind of giving, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving all material wealth;
because of the mind of giving, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving immeasurable material wealth; for the sake of causing one...
Because all sentient beings dwell in the mind of universal giving—the immeasurable giving and the giving of all things;
because they wish to cause all sentient beings to dwell in the mind of uninterrupted giving throughout all future kalpas;

because they wish to cause all sentient beings to dwell in the mind of giving that relinquishes everything without regret or affliction; and because they wish to cause all sentient beings to dwell in the total relinquishment of all material resources.
Because of the mind of giving material things; because of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of conforming giving;
because of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of inclusive giving; because of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of vast giving;
and because of causing all sentient beings to abide in the mind of giving as offerings of immeasurable adorned requisites through renunciation.
In order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of unattached giving; in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of impartial giving;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving with the supreme power of a vajra;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in a mind of giving like the radiance of the sun; in order to cause all sentient beings—
Because they abide in the mind of the Tathāgata’s gift of wisdom; because they cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with the retinue of roots of goodness;
because they cause the roots of goodness and wisdom of all sentient beings to be constantly present before them;
because they cause all sentient beings to attain the perfection of an indestructible pure mind; and because they cause all sentient beings to achieve the supreme... [text ends]
Because of the supreme purity of their roots of goodness, they act to cause all sentient beings to awaken from the sleep of afflictions;
to cause all sentient beings to eliminate all doubts and delusions;
to cause all sentient beings to attain the pure merit of equal wisdom; and to cause the merits of all sentient beings to reach fulfillment.
Because it is full and cannot be destroyed; in order to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with the pure and immovable samādhi;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the indestructible knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*);
in order to cause all sentient beings to bring to completion the immeasurable, pure, and supernatural powers of a bodhisattva; in order to cause all sentient beings...

For the sake of cultivating and accumulating roots of goodness free from attachment; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to purify their minds through mindfulness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to give birth to pure and supreme roots of goodness;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to eliminate all obstacles to the Path created by Māras; for the sake of causing one...
Because all sentient beings are endowed with the dharmas of unimpeded, pure, and equal merit;
in order to cause all sentient beings to constantly mindfulness of all Buddhas with a vast mind without weariness or negligence;
in order to cause all sentient beings to always draw near to all Buddhas and diligently make offerings; and in order to cause all sentient beings to extensively open up all roots of goodness.

This gateway is able to universally fulfill all pure dharmas; it is for the sake of causing the immeasurable mind, the vast mind, and the most supreme mind of all sentient beings to be entirely purified;
it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to achieve a mind of pure and equal giving;
and it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to uphold the Śīla-pāramitā and other purities of all Buddhas.
In order to cause all sentient beings to attain the great perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) and remain forever without indolence;

in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in immeasurable concentrations (*samādhi*) and be able to give rise to various supernormal powers and wisdoms; in order to cause all sentient beings to know that all phenomena are without...
Because the essential nature is the *prajñāpāramitā*; in order to cause all sentient beings to fulfill the boundless pure realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*);
in order to cause all sentient beings to bring to completion all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*);
in order to cause all sentient beings to abide in impartial conduct, accumulate wholesome dharmas, and reach full perfection; in order to cause one...
Because they universally enter the spheres of all Buddhas and pervade them entirely;

because they cause the physical, verbal, and mental karma of all sentient beings to be universally purified; because they cause the karmic fruits and retributions of all sentient beings' wholesome deeds to be universally purified;
because they cause all sentient beings to thoroughly understand and realize all phenomena so that they may be universally purified; in order to cause one...
Because all sentient beings thoroughly understand the ultimate meaning and are universally purified;
because all sentient beings cultivate all supreme practices and are universally purified; because all sentient beings fulfill all great vows of bodhisattvas and are universally purified;
and because all sentient beings realize and attain all merit and wisdom and are universally purified.

Therefore, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to accomplish all roots of goodness of the same essence and dedicate them toward the birth of the vehicle of omniscience so that it may be universally perfected;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to adorn and purify all Buddha-lands so that they may be universally perfected;
and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to see all Buddhas without any attachment.
For the sake of fulfillment: in order to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with the adornments of merit consisting of the primary and secondary marks;
in order to cause all sentient beings to attain the sixty kinds of vocal qualities so that their speech is truthful and worthy of being believed and accepted;
and in order to cause them to fully perfect the Tathāgata’s unimpeded, wondrous voice adorned with hundreds of thousands of kinds of dharmas.
Therefore, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to achieve the unimpeded and impartial mind adorned with the ten powers;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to obtain the inexhaustible light of the Dharma and universal perfection of all eloquence of all Buddhas;
and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain the supreme, fearless lion’s roar of the Hero among Men.
In order to cause all sentient beings to attain all-knowledge and turn the irreversible, inexhaustible wheel of Dharma;
in order to cause all sentient beings to comprehend all phenomena and to reveal and expound them so that they are universally perfected;
in order to cause all sentient beings to cultivate pure, wholesome dharmas at the proper time so that they are universally perfected; in order to cause all sentient beings...
For the sake of purifying the birth, the accomplishment of the Teacher, and the unsurpassed Dharma-jewel;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to universally fulfill the single adornment, the immeasurable adornments, the great adornments, and the adornments of all Buddhas;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to equally enter and pervade all realms throughout the three periods of time; for the sake of causing all...
It is so that all sentient beings may be able to travel to all buddha-fields to hear and receive the true Dharma without exception;
so that they may bring about the benefit of wisdom for all sentient beings and be honored by the world as equals to the Buddhas;
so that all sentient beings may, through omniscience, know all phenomena and be universally perfected; and so that all sentient beings...
Because by practicing immovable karma, one attains the fruit of non-obstruction and universal perfection;
because it causes all sentient beings to have all their faculties attain supernatural powers so that they may know the faculties of all sentient beings;

because it causes all sentient beings to attain undifferentiated, equal wisdom through the universal purity of the single-marked Dharma; because it causes all... [to attain... for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings do not contradict the principle and are fully endowed with all roots of goodness;
because one desires to cause all sentient beings to clearly penetrate all the sovereign supernormal powers of all Bodhisattvas;

because one desires to cause all sentient beings to attain the inexhaustible merit of all Buddhas, whether in terms of fortune or wisdom, so that they may all be equal; because one desires to cause all sentient beings...
Because they give rise to the bodhicitta that understands all phenomena as being equal and of a single characteristic without exception;
because they cause all sentient beings to thoroughly comprehend the True Dharma so that it may become the supreme field of merit for the world;
because they cause all sentient beings to achieve impartial and pure great compassion so that it may serve as a field of great power for all donors; in order to cause one—
Because all sentient beings are foremost in firmness and cannot be thwarted or destroyed;
because all sentient beings will surely receive benefit upon seeing them and cannot be overcome or subdued; because all sentient beings shall bring the most supreme equanimity to full completion;
and because all sentient beings shall be able to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena and attain great fearlessness.
In order to cause all sentient beings to emit a single ray of light that universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions;
in order to cause all sentient beings to universally cultivate all the diligent practices of bodhisattvas without weariness or regression;
in order to cause all sentient beings to universally fulfill all vows of practice through a single vow of practice; in order to cause all...
It is so that all sentient beings may, through a single sublime voice, universally cause all who hear it to attain understanding;
so that all sentient beings may fully possess the pure mind of all bodhisattvas;
so that all sentient beings may everywhere encounter all spiritual friends and receive their guidance; and so that all sentient beings may cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.

Because of never ceasing to discipline sentient beings; because of causing all sentient beings to possess all sounds through sublime eloquence and to extensively expound the Dharma according to their capacities without interruption;
because of causing all sentient beings to be able to know all minds with a single mind through the equal dedication of all roots of goodness; because of causing all sentient beings to always...
Because they delight in accumulating all roots of goodness and establishing sentient beings in pure wisdom;
because they desire to cause all sentient beings to attain the body of pure merit and wisdom of omniscience;

because they desire to cause all sentient beings to skillfully know the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, observe them, and dedicate them so that they may be universally accomplished; because they desire to cause all sentient beings...
Because they have attained omniscience and achieved perfect enlightenment in universal perfection;
because they cause all sentient beings to attain the wisdom of perfected supernormal powers, such that by manifesting in one place, they manifest in all places;
and because they cause all sentient beings to attain the wisdom of universal adornment, such that by adorning and purifying one assembly, they adorn all assemblies.
It is for the sake of purification, so that all sentient beings may universally behold all buddha-lands within a single buddha-land;
and it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to adorn all buddha-lands with every kind of ornament—
inexpressible ornaments, immeasurable ornaments, and inexhaustible ornaments— pervading them everywhere.
Therefore, it is for the purpose of enabling all sentient beings to fully comprehend the profound meaning of all phenomena;
for the purpose of enabling all sentient beings to attain the supreme and foremost sovereign supernormal powers of all Tathāgatas;
for the purpose of enabling all sentient beings to attain the sovereign supernormal powers of all merits that are neither identical nor different; for the purpose of...
Because all sentient beings are endowed with all impartial roots of goodness so that they may universally receive the consecration of their crowns from all Buddhas;
and because it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to fully attain the pure body of wisdom, which is the most supreme and honored among all states of existence.
[Treatise] From the tenth son of the Buddha downward, because they are the most honored and supreme among all realms of existence,
one hundred and fifteen and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva, through the aforementioned two sections of limitless acts of giving,
universally gives rise to one hundred and ten kinds of vast and boundless [merit] for the sake of all limitless and diverse sentient beings.
One practices the aforementioned types of giving, vows, and dedications for the sake of the objects of focus and activities of sentient beings;

thus, the above is the summary. The thirty-two kinds of limitless roots of goodness mentioned previously, followed by the ten kinds of meritorious acts such as the giving of elephants and horses, along with great vows and dedications, are completed here for the sake of the realms of sentient beings and so forth.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus feel compassion and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, causing them all to become pure,
to remain far removed from stinginess and envy, to receive supreme and wondrous joys, and to possess great majestic virtue;

when they give rise to great faith and understanding, forever leaving behind anger and all obscurations and turbidities, their minds becoming pure, upright, gentle, and supple, free from flattery and crookedness— [this is called the perfection of patience].
With a firm and indestructible mind of equanimity toward those who wander in delusion and ignorance and those who practice the path of transcendence,
never regressing, they fully accomplish the power of pure dharmas; being free from affliction and loss, they skillfully dedicate their merit, constantly practicing right conduct,
subduing sentient beings, eliminating all unwholesome karma, and cultivating ascetic practices and all roots of goodness.
Furthermore, he exhorts sentient beings to practice so as to universally undergo all sufferings for the sake of all conscious beings;
with the eye of great wisdom, he observes all roots of goodness and knows that they are all characterized by wisdom,
skillfully dedicating them to all sentient beings in order to cause all sentient beings to dwell securely in the state of all pure merits, and for this purpose...
Because they are able to embrace all roots of goodness for all sentient beings by knowing the nature and meaning of all merits;
because they desire to universally purify all roots of goodness for all sentient beings;

because they desire to cause all sentient beings to plant various wholesome dharmas within the sphere of the field of merit with a mind free from regret; because they desire to cause all sentient beings...
Because they are able to universally embrace all sentient beings, causing each and every one to advance toward omniscience;
because they cause all sentient beings to universally gather all roots of goodness, ensuring each is conjoined with the practice of impartial dedication;
and because they dedicate these roots of goodness in this manner—namely, by vowing that all sentient beings shall reach ultimate...
May all sentient beings ultimately attain peace and security; may all sentient beings ultimately attain purity; may all sentient beings ultimately attain bliss;
may all sentient beings ultimately attain liberation; may all sentient beings ultimately attain equality;
may all sentient beings ultimately attain thorough understanding; may all sentient beings ultimately abide in all that is pure and wholesome.
I vow that all sentient beings may attain the unimpeded eye; I vow that all sentient beings may skillfully harmonize their minds;
I vow that all sentient beings may be endowed with the ten powers to subdue and transform all beings.

[Treatise] From the eleventh son of the Buddha down to "endowed with the ten powers to subdue sentient beings," twenty-three lines of scripture clarify the section on how Bodhisattvas enter suffering to act in concert with sentient beings out of compassion,
and receive them through great vows.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, he does not cling to karma, nor to its retribution;
he does not cling to the body, nor to material things; he does not cling to buddha-fields, nor to directions; he does not cling to sentient beings, nor to the absence of sentient beings;
he does not cling to all dharmas, nor to the absence of all dharmas.

[Treatise] From the twelfth son of the Buddha down to "not being attached to the absence of all dharmas," there are three lines of sutra text that clarify that although Bodhisattvas enter into suffering through the dedication of their vows and giving in order to benefit sentient beings,
their minds possess ten kinds of non-attachment.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they universally bestow these roots of goodness upon the world,
vowing that all sentient beings may fulfill the Buddha-wisdom, attain a pure mind, possess clear and lucid wisdom,
maintain inner tranquility, remain unmoved by external conditions, and cause the seeds of the Buddhas of the three periods of time to grow and flourish.

[Treatise] From the thirteenth "Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to the section on "Increasing and Accomplishing the Seed of the Buddhas of the Three Times," there are three scriptural passages clarifying how a bodhisattva, by means of all the aforementioned roots of goodness, vows that all sentient beings may obtain a portion of the seed of wisdom.
How does one enter the seed of the Buddha-wisdom? There are four dharmas: first, obtaining a pure mind; second, wisdom...
With wisdom clearly understanding the three inner states of mental tranquility and the four outer conditions of immovability, one thus cultivates and refines these qualities,
thereby increasing the seeds of the wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices such dedication, they transcend all...
None can surpass them; all the words of the entire world join in praising them, yet they cannot be fully extolled.
They universally cultivate all the practices of Bodhisattvas and are able to travel to all Buddha-lands, seeing all Buddhas without any obstruction.
Furthermore, through skillful means, they can universally behold the conduct of Bodhisattvas in all worlds.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they analyze the profound words and meanings of all dharmas and attain *dhāraṇī*,
expounding the sublime Dharma without interruption throughout all future kalpas. For the sake of sentient beings, in every thought-moment,
they universally manifest their bodies like reflections throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds, making offerings to all Buddhas and in every thought-moment purifying them to perfection.
They cause all ineffable and expressible Buddha-lands to be universally pervaded by the wisdom that practices the purification of Buddha-fields without ever becoming weary;
in every thought-moment, they cause ineffably ineffable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings to attain purity,
accomplishment, and equal fulfillment, diligently practicing within all those lands.
They embrace all *pāramitās* to bring sentient beings to maturity and accomplish pure karma, attaining unimpeded hearing.
In each and every Tathāgata’s turning of the wheel of Dharma throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-worlds,
they listen, receive, uphold, and diligently practice it, never giving rise to a single thought of abandonment, abiding in non-apprehension and non-reliance.
The Bodhisattvas Uncreated and Unattached, through their supernormal powers, in a single kṣaṇa— the brief duration of a finger-snap—
emanate bodies that travel everywhere to unspeakably many Buddha-worlds, where they appear simultaneously and identically with all the other bodhisattvas.

[Treatise] Section Fourteen: From "The Son of the Buddha" down to "Equal in View with All Bodhisattvas," seventeen lines and a half of scripture clarify the section on the praise of the supernatural powers, wisdom,
and *dhāraṇī* gates that transcend the world when a bodhisattva practices the aforementioned dedication.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva conduct in this manner, they are already able to fulfill immeasurable,
unspeakably unspeakable pure merits that cannot be fully exhausted even by recollection or praise;
how much more so when they attain unsurpassed bodhi, wherein all buddha-fields are equally pure and all sentient beings [are likewise purified].
Equally purified in all bodies; equally purified in all faculties; equally purified in all karmic fruits;
equally purified in all assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); equally purified in all perfected practices;
equally purified in the wisdom of skillful means regarding all dharmas; equally purified in all Tathāgatas...
"May this be dedicated toward the equal and pure realm of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of all Buddhas, which is equal and pure.

[Treatise] From the fifteenth "Son of the Buddha" down to "the equal and pure realm of supernatural powers," eight lines of scripture clarify that when a Bodhisattva practices such Bodhisattva conduct, their merit transcends all calculation.

How much more so for one who has attained unsurpassed bodhi? This section clarifies that even the retribution born of the practice of meritorious deeds is already infinite and transcends all calculation;
how much more so the principle and wisdom of effortless, sovereign bodhi—how could it possibly fail to be accomplished?
Regarding these merits and faults, through this section one comes to know the equality of dharmas and karma throughout the three periods of time.
Regarding their mutual non-contradiction, a brief explanation is provided according to the Sūtra, which states: "All Buddha-fields are equally pure;
all sentient beings are equally pure. This is spoken in terms of the wisdom of principle (*li-zhi*).
From "all faculties are equally pure" up to the four practices, the Sūtra generally clarifies that these are spoken in terms of the wisdom of principle.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner,
they attain the Dharma-gate of the pure joy of all merits and the infinite adornment of the perfection of merit. When dedicating in this way, sentient beings do not conflict with all lands,
all lands do not conflict with all sentient beings, and lands and sentient beings do not conflict with karma, nor does karma conflict [with them].

The lands do not conflict with sentient beings; sentient beings do not conflict with thought; thought does not conflict with mind; thought and mind do not conflict with objects; objects do not conflict with thought and mind;

karma does not conflict with retribution; retribution does not conflict with karma; karma does not conflict with the path of karma; the path of karma does not conflict with the dharma-nature of karma;

the dharma-nature does not conflict with characteristics; the characteristics of dharmas do not conflict with their nature; the arising of dharmas does not conflict with their nature; and the dharma-nature does not conflict [with its own nature].
The equality of birth-fields does not contradict the equality of sentient beings; the equality of sentient beings does not contradict the equality of birth-fields.
The equality of all sentient beings does not contradict the equality of all phenomena; the equality of all phenomena does not contradict the equality of all sentient beings.
The equality of the limit of detachment does not contradict the equality of the peaceful abiding of all sentient beings.
All sentient beings abide in equality; they do not deviate from the limit of detachment.
The past does not deviate from the future, the future does not deviate from the past, and the past and future do not deviate from the present. The present does not deviate from the past and future.
The equality of the worlds does not deviate from the equality of the Buddhas; the equality of the Buddhas does not deviate from the equality of the worlds. Thus, [it is] Bodhi...
The practice of the bodhisattva does not contradict omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and omniscience does not contradict the practice of the bodhisattva.

[Treatise] From the sixteenth section, "The Son of the Buddha," down to "does not contradict the practice of the bodhisattva," there are fifteen lines of scripture clarifying the section on the equality of the essence and characteristics of the dharmas of the three periods of time as seen by the bodhisattva. As the sutra says: "Sentient beings do not contradict..."
In all lands, there is no contradiction with the conditions of existence and the physical bodies of all sentient beings;
these similar lands arise from the karma of the mind. Thus, the distinctions in the minds of sentient beings are themselves the distinctions in the lands.

This is as fully explained in the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World": thought does not contradict the mind, because thought arises from the mind; therefore, thought is itself the mind. Other cases should be understood accordingly.
To know that karma does not contradict its retribution means that retribution arises from karma; retribution is the fruit of karma. The rest should be understood accordingly.
To know that as it is with karma, so it is with the paths of action (*karmapatha*) means that one’s future rebirth will be similar to the actions performed in the present life.

The rest should be understood accordingly. Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it does not contradict their characteristics: being without nature is the nature, and having no characteristics is the characteristic. Within this absence of nature, there are characteristics.

The true aspect (*dharmatā*) is the body, form, and sublime objects of the Tathāgata; that which sentient beings do not understand as being without intrinsic nature—the delusively conceptualized aspects such as devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, and animals—is each a karmic aspect produced by their own minds. Other instances should be understood by analogy with this.
This does not contradict the clarity of the nature, for that which is born is non-birth, and non-birth is birth; thus it is called a "field" (*kṣetra*).
"Equally, it does not contradict the equality of sentient beings"—this refers to the principle that there is neither purity nor defilement; the following cases are analogous.

"All sentient beings abide in equality and do not contradict the limit of freedom from desire": this clarifies that the realm in which sentient beings' retribution resides and the limit of liberation and nirvana are non-dual;
because the nature of reality and the limit of liberation are simultaneously non-dual in their essence.

The past does not conflict with the future; this collectively clarifies that the nature of the three periods of time is simultaneous and non-dual. Since the three periods of time have no substantial essence, they cannot be in conflict.

Other cases may be understood by analogy. The equality of the Buddha does not conflict with the equality of the Bodhisattva’s practice, for it is clarified that the Buddha’s wisdom and principle, as well as the Bodhisattva’s essence and function, are inseparable from the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they attain equality of karma, equality of retribution, equality of body,
equality of skillful means, equality of vows, equality of all sentient beings,
equality of all lands, equality of all practices, and equality of all-knowledge.
They equally attain the service of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they attain the making of offerings to all Bodhisattvas;
they attain the planting of all roots of goodness; they attain the fulfillment of all great vows; they attain the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings;
they attain the thorough knowledge of all karma; they attain the service and offering to all spiritual friends; they attain entry into all purities...
Purifying the assembly and the site of practice, attaining mastery over all true teachings, and bringing all pure dharmas to fulfillment— O Son of the Buddha,
this is the seventh dedication of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, which accords with and conforms to all sentient beings.
[Treatise] From the seventeenth "Son of the Buddha" down to the seventh "Conformity with All Sentient Beings," nine lines of scripture clarify that when a bodhisattva thus dedicates [merit],
they attain the equality of the dharma-realm, karma, lands, and the three periods of time;
having attained this, they serve all Buddhas and enter the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) within all pure assemblies.

The *Fen jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis) states: "When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva dedicates [merit] in this manner, they attain equality of karma, attain equality of retribution, and attain equality of the body.

Thus, through these ten dharmas of equality, illuminated by the power of dedication and the force of making vows, they adorn their own retribution and thereby obtain these fruits of the ten equalities."
[Sūtra] When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish this dedication, they are able to crush and destroy all Māras and enemies, extract the thorns of desire, and attain the joy of liberation.
Abiding in non-duality, possessing great majestic power, they rescue and protect sentient beings as kings of merit.
With unimpeded supernormal powers, they travel to all lands, enter the state of nirvana, and perfect all bodies.
The Bodhisattva practices all modes of conduct and vows, attaining mastery of mind and discerning knowledge of all phenomena;
they are able to manifest universally in all Buddha-fields, attain unimpeded ears to hear all sounds in every realm,
and possess the pure eye of wisdom to see all Buddhas, never for a moment forsaking any sphere of activity as they accomplish roots of goodness.
With a mind free from high and low regarding all phenomena, attaining non-attainment,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness equally in accordance with all sentient beings.

[Treatise] Section Eighteen: From "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to "Thus dedicating in accordance with all sentient beings," nine lines of scripture clarify the section on the accomplishment of the meritorious functions resulting from the aforementioned dedication, giving,
and vows, providing a general praise thereof.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.
[Śāstra] Section Nineteen: From "At that time" onwards, this single line of sūtra clarifies the section on the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja surveying the assembly and speaking in verse.
[Scripture] Whatever meritorious virtues a bodhisattva performs— whether subtle, vast, profound, or far-reaching—

even if practiced for but a single thought-moment— they are all able to dedicate toward the boundless requisites of life possessed by all bodhisattvas, which are manifold, abundant, and infinitely numerous.
With fragrant elephants and precious horses drawing chariots, with garments and rare treasures all most exquisite;
or with head, eyes, hands, and feet, or holding body, flesh, and marrow and bone—
reaching everywhere throughout immeasurable lands in the ten directions, universally bestowing upon all until they are fully satisfied.
All the merits cultivated throughout immeasurable eons are entirely dedicated toward the goal of rescuing and liberating all sentient beings; their minds never ultimately regress.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, Bodhisattvas constantly cultivate the supreme practice of dedication.
May all throughout the three realms attain peace and happiness, And may they all fully realize the unsurpassed fruit.
The Bodhisattva universally gives rise to vows of equality, Dedicating all accumulated pure karma to all living beings; Such a great vow shall never be forsaken.
The Bodhisattva’s power of aspiration is limitless and unobstructed, embracing all worlds in this manner;
thus they dedicate [merit] to all sentient beings, never for a moment giving rise to a discriminating mind.
May the wisdom of all beings be clear and lucid, and may their generosity and observance of precepts be entirely pure.
Practicing with diligence without slackening or ceasing, such great vows are never at rest;
the Bodhisattva dedicates these merits to reach the other shore, universally opening the pure and wondrous Dharma-gate,
with wisdom equal to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, discerning the true meaning to attain the ultimate.
The Bodhisattva has already mastered all modes of speech;
likewise, with various wisdoms, he teaches the Dharma according to principle without obstruction. Yet his mind does not cling therein;
he never creates duality regarding all phenomena, nor does he create non-duality.
Abandoning both duality and non-duality alike, one knows that all are merely the path of verbal expression;
one knows that all worlds are entirely equal, for there is nothing that is not the mind, speech, or all karma.
Sentient beings are like illusory transformations and lack any reality; all karmic retributions arise from this.
Whatever exists within all the worlds, The various fruits and retributions, each distinct, Are all without exception produced by the power of karma; If karma is extinguished, they are all exhausted.
The Bodhisattva observes all worlds, Seeing that the actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely equal.
They also cause sentient beings to abide in equanimity, Just like the peerless, Great Holy One.
The Bodhisattva’s virtuous deeds are entirely dedicated, Universally causing the physical forms of all beings to be pure,
And fully endowed with merit and skillful means, To become equal to the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men.
May the Bodhisattva’s benefit for all sentient beings— this ocean of merit—
be entirely dedicated so that his majestic radiance may especially transcend the world, and he may attain a body of heroic, fierce, and great power.
May all the merits cultivated through every practice cause the entire world to be universally purified.
The Buddhas are pure and without peer; the purity of sentient beings is likewise so.
Bodhisattvas attain skillfulness in meaning and are able to know the most supreme Dharma of all Buddhas.
By dedicating all such virtuous deeds, may they cause all beings to become equal to the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all phenomena are empty;
that in all worlds there is nothing whatsoever, neither creation nor a creator; that the karmic retribution of sentient beings is never lost;
and that while all phenomena are quiescent, they are not non-quiescent—thus remaining far removed from these two dualistic conceptualizations.
Knowing that all such discriminations are worldly views, they enter the state of right determination where discrimination is exhausted.
Such true children of the Buddha are born from the transformation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
being able to dedicate [merit] in this way, they completely eliminate all worldly doubts and delusions.
[Treatise] These twenty verses comprise forty-two lines in total; their meaning and phrasing are self-evident, so there is no need for further elaboration.
As for the second part, the word-by-word commentary: why is this called "the dedication that accords with all sentient beings"?
This is to clarify that the seventh *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) takes the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its primary focus, by means of the six *pāramitās*.
The power of wisdom cultivated within the honey enters the ocean of birth and death to act in concert with all sentient beings according to their respective capacities and types to benefit them;

therefore, it is called "Equal Accordance. This is as stated in the seventh stage, the Stage of Great Compassion, within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, where the laywoman Śroṇā said: "I have eighty-four thousand companions who act in concert with me."

That there are always *nayuta* [of beings] dwelling in this garden means, in broad terms, that they act in concert with all sentient beings' eighty-four thousand and unspeakably many afflictions; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this is the seventh stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) within this level, and that the Avalokiteśvara seen by Sudhana belongs to this very stage. As it says:
This section of dedication consists of twenty passages in total; the meanings of the remaining nineteen passages are self-evident and need not be further explained.
Within the representation of the dharmas, for example, in the seventh of the Ten Abodes, the upāsikā Śūradattā represents the stage of Great Compassion;
in the seventh of the Ten Practices, the stage represents the gateway of Great Compassion, which is fulfilled.

The King of the Foots transforms his own body to commit various transgressions and rebellious acts; he transforms his own body to seize and execute those who have committed such deeds, thereby quelling the evil and rebelliousness of sentient beings.
This seventh of the Ten Dedications is represented by Avalokiteśvara as the stage of compassion.

Indeed, the profound mystery of the Great Teaching is vast in its phrasing and expansive in its meaning; the names and phrases of its dharma-gates are clear and distinct, appearing exactly as they are.
The numbers ten by ten follow one another to form ten thousand, ten thousand, a thousand, and a thousand;

this sequence cannot be achieved by adding a small pond to the great ocean to bring about its depth, nor can a tiny lamp be lit to augment the light of the sun to assist its far-reaching illumination.
The meaning of this sutra is vast, its words complete, its principles exhaustive, and its phrasing abundant; thus, I shall briefly explain its general significance in a concise manner.
My wisdom is profound and hidden; I merely express this slight inclination, for it cannot be augmented by the dharma-characteristics of other sutras.

If one who practices with intent becomes stalled by these wondrous verses, they should know that principle arises from meditative concentration, and wisdom is clarified by principle. Compassion relies on vows to give rise to practice;
when vows are fulfilled, principle is manifested, wisdom becomes vast, and vows become expansive. Thus compassion is broadened, and the seeds of the Buddha are thereby born within the Dharma-realm.
By means of these conditions, all [practices] are collectively concluded as such; the remaining meanings will follow in later texts.
The eighth dedication, the Dedication of the Characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*), has the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) as its essence.

This stage is clarified as being equal to the eighth ground in that wisdom is preeminent; because aspiration induces the activity of wisdom and brings about great compassion, aspiration protects wisdom.

Because the essence of wisdom is pure, its beneficial transformation is not limited; it manifests as suchness within the Dharma, just as the youth Sudhana saw the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin in the eastern direction—this is his practice.

That he comes from the void to the Sahā world clarifies that the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena appears universally and pervasively, yet is without coming or going. Thus, Avalokiteśvara points to Samantagāmin in the eastern direction.
Furthermore, seeing [the sun] at the time of its rising represents the assembly with Avalokiteśvara; it signifies the fulfillment of vows, the arrival of compassion, and the perfection of wisdom.
Because compassion and wisdom must be brought to completion: the east symbolizes wisdom and the west symbolizes compassion.

The rising sun illuminating all represents springtime warmth giving rise to life, while the auspicious Azure Dragon symbolizes wisdom. The setting sun falling into obscurity represents autumn frost and the destructive White Tiger.
The eighth vow is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), which enters the realm of compassion to rescue sentient beings from the flow of suffering;

it clarifies the nature of the essence of protective wisdom, purifying it so that through the union of vows and compassion, one accomplishes the conduct of Samantabhadra. As one ascends through the stages of this practice, the two meanings—suchness (*tathatā*) and the path—are harmonized.

Regarding the meaning of the first long section of the sutra as previously explained, starting from the initial phrase "At that time... and so forth: [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the structure and intent of a Mahayana sutra, specifically addressing the relationship between the perfections, the stages of practice, and the realization of suchness.]
From this point down to the end of the verse, the long prose section is divided into ten parts.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva through the characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā)?

O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses clear and lucid right mindfulness; his mind is firmly established, he is far removed from delusion, and he practices with single-minded devotion."
With an unshakable profound resolve, they accomplish indestructible karma and proceed toward omniscience without ever turning back;

seeking the Great Vehicle with courageous fearlessness, they plant the roots of all virtues and bring universal peace to the world. They give rise to supreme wholesome roots, cultivate pure dharmas, increase great compassion, and perfect the jewel of the mind.
Constantly mindful of all Buddhas, they protect and uphold the True Dharma on the bodhisattva path.
With firm faith and joy, they accomplish immeasurable, pure, and wondrous roots of goodness;
they diligently cultivate all merits and wisdom to become teachers who discipline others, giving rise to all wholesome dharmas and dedicating them through the skillful means of wisdom.

At that time, with the eye of wisdom, the Bodhisattva universally observes all these roots of goodness, which are immeasurable and boundless; as for those various roots of goodness, at the time they were being cultivated—
Whether it be seeking conditions, or making preparations, or purifying, or entering, or exerting effort, or initiating practice, or attaining clear realization,
or being meticulous, or providing exposition— all such things involve various doors, various objects, various characteristics,
various matters, various divisions, various practices, various names, and various conceptual distinctions.
Born into various [realms], they cultivate therein all roots of goodness, which are established by a mind directed toward the vehicles of the ten directions;
they dedicate them all toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) in a single, non-dual manner.
By dedicating these roots of goodness in this way, they vow to attain an unimpeded bodily action and to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
May I attain pure and unimpeded verbal karma to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva; may I attain the fulfillment of unimpeded mental karma to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna;
may I attain the perfection of an unobstructed mind to purely cultivate all bodhisattva practices;
may I give rise to an immeasurable and vast mind of giving to provide for all boundless sentient beings; and may I [attain] regarding all phenomena...

May my mind attain mastery to expound the great light of the Dharma that nothing can obscure; may I attain clear penetration of all states of omniscience and resolve to awaken the bodhicitta to universally illuminate the world;
may I maintain constant right mindfulness of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, clearly visualizing the Tathāgata as ever present before me;
and may I abide in perfect, superior aspiration and resolve, remaining far removed from all demons and adversaries.
May I dwell securely in the wisdom of the Buddha’s ten powers, universally gathering in all sentient beings without ceasing;

may I attain samādhi to travel through all worlds while remaining unstained by the world; may I abide in all worlds without weariness, teaching and transforming sentient beings constantly and without rest;
and may I give rise to immeasurable wisdom born of reflection and skillful means to accomplish bodhi.
May I attain the inconceivable path of the Bodhisattvas and the wisdom that is never deluded regarding all directions, being able to discern all worlds;
may I attain the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations and the power of wisdom, being able to adorn and purify all lands in a single thought-moment;
may I attain the universal entry into the self-nature of all phenomena and see all worlds as entirely pure; may I attain...
May I give rise to non-discriminative wisdom and enter all lands within a single land;
may I manifest the adornments of all lands to transform and guide infinite and boundless sentient beings;
may I manifest the entire dharma-realm of infinite Buddha-lands within a single Buddha-land, and may it be so for all Buddha-lands as well; may I attain great spiritual mastery.
"Universal wisdom enables one to travel to all Buddha-lands.

[Treatise] First, from "At that time" onwards until "universal wisdom enables one to travel to all Buddha-lands," thirty-five lines of scripture clarify the Bodhisattva’s entry into this stage of dedication characterized by Suchness (*tathatā*), wherein they utilize what they have personally attained.
The Section on the Advancement of the Stage through the Further Dedication and Aspiration of Roots of Goodness toward their Objects.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of all roots of goodness, aspires to adorn all Buddha-fields;
he aspires to pervade all worlds; and he aspires to achieve the wisdom of observation as if it were his own body.
Thus dedicating, he does so for the sake of all sentient beings, namely:
may all sentient beings forever leave behind all realms of hell, animals, and the Lord of Death (Yama);
may all sentient beings eliminate all karmic obstacles; may all sentient beings attain a universal mind and impartial wisdom; and may all...
May all sentient beings gather together with equanimity toward both enemies and kin, bringing them all to peace and happiness;
may their wisdom be pure; may all sentient beings’ wisdom be perfected so that pure light shines everywhere;
may all sentient beings achieve the wisdom born of reflection and realize the true meaning; and may all sentient beings, through their pure resolve, seek enlightenment and attain the immeasurable.
[The Sūtra says: "May wisdom cause all sentient beings to be able to universally manifest the place of peaceful dwelling.

[The Commentary says: From the second section, "O Son of the Buddha," down to "manifesting the place of peaceful dwelling," there are ten lines of sūtra text clarifying the stage where the Bodhisattva contemplates the suffering of sentient beings in the evil realms as if it were his own body, vowing that they may swiftly attain liberation.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas constantly dedicate with a virtuous mind in this way:
so that all sentient beings may encounter the cool clouds and be drenched by the rain of Dharma; so that all sentient beings may always encounter the supreme field of merit as their objective sphere;
and so that all sentient beings may all be able to skillfully enter the treasury of the bodhicitta and protect themselves.
I uphold this for the sake of causing all sentient beings to leave behind all hindrances and entanglements and to dwell securely;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to obtain unimpeded knowledge of supernormal powers; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain bodies of mastery and manifest them universally;
and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to accomplish the most supreme knowledge of all modes and universally bring it forth.
Because their benefit never goes to waste; in order to universally gather all classes of sentient beings and cause them to become pure;
in order to enable all sentient beings to ultimately attain all-knowledge; and in order to cause the minds of all sentient beings to be unshakable and free from obstruction.

[Treatise] From the third son of the Buddha onwards, until the passage "because the mind is immovable and free from obstruction," there are ten sections of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* that clarify how the Bodhisattva,
through the aforementioned dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), brings about ten kinds of great benefits for sentient beings.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees delightful lands, gardens, groves, grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, famous incenses, superior garments, rare jewels, wealth, and various ornaments; or sees pleasant villages, towns, and settlements;
or sees the majestic power and sovereign authority of kings; or sees dwellings free from all clamor and distraction—having seen these things...
Through the wisdom of skillful means, they diligently cultivate and give rise to immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous merits;
for the sake of all sentient beings, they earnestly seek wholesome dharmas with a mind free from negligence, extensively gathering all manner of goodness like the great ocean;
with inexhaustible goodness, they universally cover all things and serve as the locus upon which all wholesome dharmas rely, skillfully dedicating all roots of goodness through expedient means.

Without conceptual discrimination, they reveal immeasurable varieties of roots of goodness; their wisdom constantly observes the minds of all sentient beings, and they perpetually recollect the sphere of roots of goodness.
They dedicate these roots of goodness to sentient beings with an equality equal to True Suchness (tathatā), without ceasing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dedicates these various roots of goodness in this way, namely: "May [all beings]..."

May all sentient beings attain the delightful vision of all Tathāgatas, seeing the true nature of phenomena as perfectly equal and without any grasping or attachment, and may their vows be completely purified.
May all sentient beings behold all Tathāgatas with great delight and provide perfect offerings.
May all sentient beings be reborn in the presence of all those who are utterly free from afflictions and most delightful.
May all sentient beings attain the vision of the delightful Dharma of all Buddhas in pure Buddha-fields;
may all sentient beings always delight in protecting and upholding all the delightful practices of Bodhisattvas;
may all sentient beings obtain the delightful eye of a spiritual friend that sees without obstruction; may all sentient beings always behold the One.
May all beloved and cherished things be free from opposition; may all sentient beings realize and diligently protect all beloved and cherished dharmas;
may all sentient beings attain pure radiance within all the delightful dharmas of the Buddhas;
and may all sentient beings cultivate the bodhisattva’s mind of total renunciation regarding all that is beloved and cherished.
May all sentient beings attain fearlessness and be able to expound all delightful and agreeable dharmas;
may all sentient beings attain the most delightful and profound samādhis of all bodhisattvas;
may all sentient beings attain the most delightful dhāraṇī-gates of all bodhisattvas; may all sentient beings attain [the qualities] of all bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings be able to manifest the most delightful and skillfully observed wisdom of a bodhisattva;

may all sentient beings be able to manifest the most delightful and sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); may all sentient beings be able to proclaim the most delightful, profound, and wondrous Dharma within the great assemblies of all Buddhas;
and may all sentient beings be able to use skillful means (*upāya*) to reveal, explain, and expound it.
May all sentient beings always be able to give rise to a most lovable and equal great compassion;

may all sentient beings, in every thought-moment, give rise to a most lovable and great bodhicitta, constantly causing their faculties to be joyful and delighted; may all sentient beings be able to enter into all that is most lovable...
May all sentient beings delight in the families of all Tathāgatas; may they attain the practice of delightful subduing to tame sentient beings without ceasing.
May all sentient beings attain the most delightful and inexhaustible eloquence of all Bodhisattvas to expound all dharmas. May all sentient beings, regarding that which is unspeakably unspeakable...
May they dwell for eons in all worlds that are lovely and delightful, teaching and transforming sentient beings with minds free from weariness;
may all sentient beings, through immeasurable skillful means, be able to universally awaken to and enter the most lovely and delightful Dharma-gates of the Buddhas;
may all sentient beings attain lovely and delightful unimpeded skillful means, knowing that all phenomena have no root.

May all sentient beings attain the limit of delightful freedom from desire; may they know that all phenomena are ultimately non-dual and sever all hindrances. May all sentient beings attain the limit of delightful freedom from desire;
may they know the equality and reality of all phenomena. May all sentient beings fully accomplish and perfect all the qualities of a bodhisattva.
May all sentient beings attain the adamantine treasury of diligence regarding the most delightful and non-conceptual Dharma, and accomplish the path to omniscience that is most delightful.
May all sentient beings be endowed with delightful and unimpeded roots of goodness to subdue all enemies of the afflictions. May all sentient beings attain the most delightful... one.
"Through the gate of all-knowledge, they universally manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment throughout the world.

[Treatise] From "The fourth son of the Buddha" down to "universally manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment throughout the world," forty-six lines and a half of scripture clarify that Bodhisattvas perceive superior and wondrous lands as well as all sublime objects through non-... (omission).
With a vast capacity and great vows, they vow that all sentient beings shall fully and universally attain birth therein, as well as share in the various benefits.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate such roots of goodness, they attain the light of wisdom.
Sustained by spiritual friends, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom shines upon their minds, forever extinguishing the darkness of delusion;
they diligently cultivate the True Dharma and enter into all activities of knowledge. Having skillfully studied the stages of wisdom, they disseminate roots of goodness that fill the Dharma-realm.
Through wisdom, they dedicate these roots toward the ultimate source of all bodhisattva virtues, and through wisdom, they penetrate deeply into the ocean of great skillful means.
"Accomplishing immeasurable and vast roots of goodness.

[Treatise] From the fifth "Son of the Buddha" down to "vast roots of goodness," five lines of scripture clarify the section on how the Bodhisattva increases his own roots of goodness by dedicating the aforementioned roots of goodness.
