The Monk Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou, Tang Dynasty, compiled the Sūtra and Treatises,
Volume Twenty-five, Part Nine, Chapter on the Ten Dedications. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this manner, namely, without attachment.
Not grasping at sentient beings in the world, their minds are pure and without dependence; they maintain right mindfulness of all phenomena and remain free from discriminatory views.

They do not abandon the sovereign wisdom of all Buddhas, do not contravene the gate of correct dedication of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, accord with all equal and true dharmas, and contemplate the indestructible, true marks of the Tathāgata.

They perceive no mark of a sentient being throughout the three periods of time; they accord well with the Buddha-way and skillfully expound the Dharma, profoundly understanding its meaning and entering the most supreme stage.
Having awakened to the true Dharma, their wisdom is perfected and their faith and joy are firm. Although they skillfully cultivate right action, they know that the nature of karma is empty;
they understand that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and they realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Contemplating all meanings and various practices according to worldly conventions without attachment, they eliminate all causes and conditions for clinging and know the principle of reality as it is.
They contemplate the nature of all phenomena as entirely quiescent and understand that all dharmas share one and the same true mark.
Knowing that the characteristics of all phenomena do not contradict one another, they dwell together with all bodhisattvas.
Practicing that path, they skillfully gather in sentient beings, leading them into the gate of dedication of all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present.
Their minds have no fear regarding any Buddha-dharma; with immeasurable minds, they cause all sentient beings to attain universal purity.
In the worlds of the ten directions, they do not give rise to grasping or the mind of "I" and "mine," and they remain undivided from all worldly realms.
They do not give rise to defiled attachment toward any sensory objects, but diligently cultivate all supramundane dharmas;
they have no grasping or reliance upon worldly things, and their right view regarding the profound and wondrous path is firm and stable.
Having abandoned all false views, they realize the true Dharma, which—like True Suchness (tathatā)—pervades all places without limit; the dedication of their roots of goodness is likewise so.
Thus, pervading all places without limit— just as *tathatā* (suchness) has reality as its nature— the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this;
understanding that all phenomena have reality as their nature— just as *tathatā* constantly maintains its original nature without change—
the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this, maintaining its original nature from beginning to end.
It is unchanging, just as True Suchness (tathatā) has the naturelessness of all phenomena as its nature;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so, for it realizes that all phenomena have naturelessness as their nature. It is like True Suchness, which has signlessness as its characteristic;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so, for it realizes that all phenomena have signlessness as their characteristic. It is like True Suchness, if there were...
Those who attain it never regress; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise. If there are those who attain it, they shall never regress from the Buddha-dharma.
Just as True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the sphere of practice for all Buddhas, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise the sphere of practice for all Tathāgatas.
Just as True Suchness is free from objective realms, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
The dedication of roots of goodness by taking the characteristics of the realms as one's objective field is likewise so;
it transcends the characteristics of objective fields to become the perfected objective field of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Just as True Suchness (tathatā) is able to establish [all things], the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so, for it is able to establish all sentient beings. Just as the nature of True Suchness is eternal...
The dedication of roots of goodness in accordance with reality is likewise thus: it continues without interruption throughout all future kalpas, just as true suchness cannot be measured;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus, equal to the realm of space and the minds of all sentient beings, such that none can measure it;
just as true suchness pervades all things, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus.
In this way, within a single kṣaṇa, they universally pervade the entire dharma-realm;
just as true thusness (tathatā) is eternally abiding and inexhaustible, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla-pariṇāmana) ultimately inexhaustible.
Just as true thusness has no counterpart, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness without counterpart, being able to universally fulfill all Buddha-dharmas without peer. Just as...
The dedication of roots of goodness that possess a firm essential nature is likewise firm in its essential nature, such that it cannot be thwarted by any afflictions or delusions.
Just as true thusness (*tathatā*) is indestructible, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
no sentient beings can damage it. Just as true thusness has illumination as its essence, so too are the roots of goodness.
Dedication is likewise thus: it has universal illumination as its nature.
Just as true suchness (*tathatā*) is omnipresent, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it is not non-existent anywhere.
Just as true suchness pervades all times, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness pervade all times. Just as...
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise always pure, just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is eternally pure;
while abiding in the world, its essence remains pure, just as *tathatā* is unimpeded regarding all phenomena.

The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise universally active throughout all things without obstruction, just as *tathatā* serves as the eye for all dharmas. The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise... [as before].
In this way, it is able to act as an eye for all sentient beings; just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is free from weariness, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
Just as one practices all the various bodhisattva deeds with constant freedom from weariness, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
just as the essence of *tathatā* is profoundly deep, so too is its nature profoundly deep. Just as...
Just as true thusness (tathatā) does not possess a single thing, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; one understands its nature to be without a single thing.
For example, just as the nature of true thusness is not something that appears, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
its essence is subtle and difficult to perceive. For example, just as true thusness is free from all defilements and obscurations, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
Thus, the eye of wisdom is pure and free from the cataracts of delusion;
just as the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is peerless, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness. It accomplishes all bodhisattva practices, being supreme and without equal;
just as the essence of *tathatā* is quiescent, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, for it is perfectly able to accord with quiescence.
The Dharma is like true thusness (tathatā) in having no root; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise able to enter all dharmas that have no root.
The dedication of roots of goodness is like true thusness in its boundless nature;
it likewise purifies sentient beings in numbers that are boundless. The dedication of roots of goodness is like true thusness in its nature of non-attachment.
Dedication is likewise thus: it is ultimately free from all attachments, just as true suchness (tathatā) is without obstruction;

the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus, extinguishing all worldly obstructions, just as true suchness is not within the sphere of worldly activity; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus, not belonging to any worldly realm.
The ability to practice is like the nature of true thusness (tathatā), which has no abiding; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise.

All of saṃsāra is not a place of abiding; just as the nature of true thusness is without action, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise, for all that is done is entirely relinquished. Just as the essence of true thusness is securely established, so too are the roots of goodness.

Dedication is likewise established in reality; just as True Suchness is in constant correspondence with all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness in constant correspondence with the hearing and cultivation [of the Dharma] by all bodhisattvas.
Just as True Suchness is eternally equal in nature within all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
In this way, practicing impartial conduct toward all worlds is like true thusness (tathatā) not being separate from all phenomena;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. Not abandoning the world until the end of the future is like true thusness, which is ultimately inexhaustible among all phenomena;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so, as it is dedicated toward all sentient beings.
Inexhaustibility is like True Suchness (tathatā), which is not in conflict with any phenomena;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise not in conflict with all Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time.
Just as True Suchness universally encompasses all phenomena, the dedication of roots of goodness likewise encompasses the roots of goodness of all sentient beings. Just as True Suchness is one...
The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise identical in its essential nature to all phenomena; it is of one and the same nature as the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Just as True Suchness is never separate from all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it encompasses and sustains all mundane and supramundane dharmas. Just as True Suchness cannot be eclipsed by anything, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.

Dedication is likewise such that no one in any world can obscure it; just as true thusness (tathatā) cannot be shaken, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla), which no demonic activities can disturb.
Just as the nature of true thusness is free from defilement and turbidity, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, in which there is no [failure] in practicing the bodhisattva path.
Just as defilements are like *tathatā* (suchness) in that they undergo no change, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it is likewise without change in its compassionate regard for sentient beings. Just as *tathatā* is inexhaustible, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it cannot be exhausted by any worldly phenomena. Just as the nature of *tathatā* is eternally awakened, so too are the roots of goodness.
Dedication is also like this: it is able to universally awaken one to all phenomena, just as true thusness (tathatā) cannot be destroyed;
the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this, giving rise to supreme aspirations toward all sentient beings that are never lost or destroyed.
Just as true thusness can provide great illumination, the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this, by means of the Great [Vehicle].
The light of wisdom illuminates all worlds; just as true suchness (*tathatā*) is ineffable, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*).
All that can be expressed in speech is beyond description, just as true suchness sustains all worlds, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness sustain them.
It is able to uphold all the practices of bodhisattvas, just as true suchness accords with the world.
The dedication of roots of goodness through verbal expression is likewise thus: it accords with all wisdom and verbal expression, just as true suchness pervades all phenomena.

The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus: it pervades all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, manifesting great supernormal powers and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, just as true suchness is without discrimination. The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise thus.
Dedication is likewise without discrimination regarding any world;
just as True Suchness pervades all bodies, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness pervade the infinite bodies within the lands of the ten directions.
Just as the essential nature of True Suchness is unborn, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness manifest birth through skillful means while remaining without [birth].
Just as that which is produced is like true thusness (tathatā), being omnipresent, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it manifests spiritual powers throughout all Buddha-lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time, being everywhere.
Just as true thusness pervades the night, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; throughout every night, it emits great radiance and performs [beneficial deeds].
The Buddha’s work is like true thusness (tathatā), which pervades the day;

the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this, causing all sentient beings during the day to see the Buddha’s spiritual transformations, expound the wheel of non-retrogression, and become free from defilement and pure, so that none pass by in vain.
Just as true thusness pervades the half-month and the full month, the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this.
Thus, by attaining skillful means regarding the successive seasons of all worlds, one knows all times within a single thought-moment;
just as *tathatā* (suchness) pervades the years and ages, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
Abiding for immeasurable eons, one clearly brings all faculties to maturity and causes them to be perfected; just as *tathatā* universally accomplishes all things.

The dedication of roots of goodness during the kalpa of destruction is likewise so; abiding through all kalpas, pure and unstained, one teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them all to become pure.
Just as True Suchness (tathatā) endures until the end of the future, the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so;
throughout the end of the future, one cultivates the various pure and wondrous practices of a bodhisattva, fulfilling great vows without fail.
Just as non-retrogression is like *tathatā* (suchness) pervading the three periods of time, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it causes all sentient beings to see the Buddhas of the three periods in a single instant, never for a single thought-moment being abandoned by them.
Just as *tathatā* pervades all places, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it transcends the triple world and is omnipresent.
They attain mastery over all things, just as True Suchness abides within both existence and non-existence; the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so.
They thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena of existence and non-existence are ultimately pure, just as the essential nature of True Suchness is pure;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so. By means of skillful means, they are able to gather the factors conducive to the Path and purify them.
The practice of all Bodhisattvas is like the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which is pure;
the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so, causing all Bodhisattvas to attain the pure mind of samādhi.
The dedication of roots of goodness, which are as stainless as the nature of True Suchness, is likewise so, remaining far removed from all defilements and fulfilling all purities.
A pure mind is like *tathatā* (suchness), being without self or what belongs to a self; the dedication of roots of goodness is also like this.
With a pure mind free from self and what belongs to a self, one fills the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
just as the essence and nature of *tathatā* are equal, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, whereby one attains the illumination of the equality of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Having realized all phenomena and being free from the cataracts of delusion—just as true thusness transcends all measure and number—the dedication of roots of goodness is likewise;

it dwells together with the great power-treasury of the vehicle of omniscience that transcends measure and number, giving rise to vast clouds of Dharma throughout all worlds in the ten directions. Just as true thusness abides in equanimity, so too does this [dedication] abide in peace.
The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this: it gives rise to all bodhisattva practices and dwells equally upon the path to omniscience.

Just as true thusness (tathatā) pervades the realms of all sentient beings, so too does the dedication of roots of goodness fulfill unimpeded knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), manifesting itself before all within the realm of sentient beings. Just as... [the simile continues].
Just as True Suchness is without discrimination and universally abides within the wisdom of all sounds, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it is likewise endowed with the wisdom of all speech and sounds, capable of universally manifesting various vocal expressions to instruct and reveal them to sentient beings.
Just as True Suchness is eternally free from the world, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, which is universal.
To cause sentient beings to forever transcend the world, just as the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is vast, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;

it is able to fully uphold the vast Buddha-dharma of the past, future, and present, never forgetting or losing it, and diligently cultivates all the practices of a bodhisattva, just as *tathatā* is without interruption or cessation. So too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it is like this: desiring to establish all sentient beings upon the ground of great wisdom, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva throughout all eons without interruption.
Just as the essential nature of true thusness (tathatā) is vast and pervasive throughout all phenomena, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It is like pure mindfulness and non-obstruction, universally encompassing all vast dharma-gates.
Just as True Suchness universally encompasses all categories of beings, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
just as one realizes wisdom of immeasurable varieties and cultivates the true, wondrous practices of a bodhisattva, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
just as True Suchness is free from grasping and attachment, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, being without grasping toward any phenomena and extinguishing all worldly [conceptions].
Taking up these intervals and causing them all to be purified—just as the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is immovable, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it abides in the perfect conduct and vows of Samantabhadra, ultimately immovable.
Just as *tathatā* is the realm of the Buddhas, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; it causes all sentient beings to fulfill all great [aspirations].
The realm of wisdom extinguishes the realm of afflictions and renders them entirely pure;

just as true suchness (*tathatā*) cannot be overcome, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pariṇāmanā*), for it cannot be overcome by any of the activities of Māras or the heterodox arguments of outsiders (*bāhyaka-tīrthika*).
Just as true suchness is neither something to be cultivated nor something not to be cultivated, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, they thus abandon all false conceptualizations and attachments, making no distinction between cultivation and non-cultivation;
just as true suchness has no retrogression or relinquishment, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
They constantly behold all Buddhas, resolve upon bodhicitta, and adorn themselves with great vows, never again retreating or abandoning them; just as true suchness universally encompasses all worlds.

The dedication of roots of goodness regarding the excellence of all vocal expressions is likewise able to attain the supernatural wisdom of all distinct vocal sounds and universally produce all manner of diverse speech; just as True Suchness has no expectations regarding any phenomena,
so too is the dedication of roots of goodness, causing all sentient beings to ride upon the vehicle of Samantabhadra.
Having attained liberation from all phenomena and being without craving or seeking, just as True Suchness abides in all stages (*bhūmi*), so too is the dedication of roots of goodness:
it causes all sentient beings to abandon worldly stages and abide in the stage of wisdom, adorning themselves with the practices of Samantabhadra.
Just as True Suchness is without interruption, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness.
It is likewise thus: regarding all phenomena, one attains fearlessness and expounds them everywhere according to the various sounds of sentient beings without interruption.
Just as True Suchness is free from all outflows (*āsrava*), so too is the dedication of roots of goodness;
it causes all sentient beings to accomplish the wisdom of the Dharma, to penetrate and understand all phenomena, and to fulfill the untainted merit of Bodhi.
Virtue is like true thusness (*tathatā*); there is not even the slightest phenomenon capable of corrupting or disturbing it so as to make even a fraction of it anything other than awakening.
The dedication of roots of goodness is also like this: it universally causes all phenomena to be awakened to;
its mind is immeasurable, pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is like true thusness: the past is not a beginning, the future is not an end, and the present is not—

The dedication of roots of goodness is likewise so: for the sake of all sentient beings, one constantly and ever-newly arouses the bodhicitta, universally wishing to make them pure and forever free from birth and death.

Just as true thusness (tathatā) makes no distinctions throughout the three periods of time, so too is the dedication of roots of goodness; in every present moment of thought, the mind is always awakened to the past.
The future shall all be utterly pure, just like true suchness (*tathatā*). The dedication of all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is likewise accomplished.
They give rise to all great vows and skillful means (*upāya*) to accomplish the vast wisdom of all Buddhas;
just as true suchness is ultimately pure and does not coexist with any afflictions (*kleśa*), so too are these roots of goodness.
Dedication is likewise able to extinguish all the afflictions of sentient beings and bring to fulfillment all pure wisdom.
[Treatise] From the sixth "Son of the Buddha" down to "bringing to fulfillment all pure wisdom," there are one hundred [verses].

The eighty-nine lines and a half of the sūtra clarify that all such dedications are performed with the non-substantiality and non-attachment of *tathatā* (suchness) as the constituent part of dedication.
The preceding one hundred and eighty-nine lines and a half of the sūtra clarify that, by taking *tathatā* as the essence of dedication,
one dedicates [merit] by means of *tathatā*, which pervades all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
It returns to pervade all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Why is this so?

It is because, by taking dedication as the skillful means, one gives rise to the great wisdom, great compassion, and the gate of the great *dhāraṇī* within the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) *tathatā*.
Through the power of the great spiritual path, one acts with great sovereign mastery in accordance with *tathatā*, yet remains eternally quiescent. If...

It is not like this: those who, through great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom, perform infinite dedications yet rely solely on the unconditioned True Suchness to purify their afflictions, are identical to the followers of the Two Vehicles who delight in quiescence, and to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles with the six supernormal powers who are born only in pure lands of a single direction.
They do not enter the true gate of the Dharma-realm, but dwell outside that gate upon the provisional vehicle.

Let us now set aside the station of the thatched hermitage; one should know that the various wisdoms filling the ten directions all arise through the power of great vows, and that the practice-gates of the perfect Dharma-realm are initiated by means of dedication.

Therefore, this net of teachings is established to receive those with whom there is a karmic affinity, so that they may clearly understand the rules and measures and follow in the footsteps [of the sages], causing students to reflect upon themselves.
This is one who achieves merit without error.
[Sūtra] When a Buddha-son, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dedicates in this manner, they attain the equality of all Buddha-fields because they universally adorn and purify all worlds;
they attain the equality of all sentient beings because they universally turn the wheel of the Dharma for them without obstruction.
Because of the Wheel of Dharma, they attain the equality of all bodhisattvas by universally giving rise to the vows for omniscience;
because of it, they attain the equality of all buddhas by observing that the essence of all buddhas is non-dual;

because of it, they attain the equality of all phenomena by universally knowing that the nature of all phenomena is unchanging; and because of it, they attain the equality of all worlds by skillfully understanding them through the wisdom of expedient means.
Because all paths of speech are transcended, they attain the equality of all bodhisattva practices;
because they dedicate all roots of goodness according to their respective kinds, they attain the equality of diligent cultivation of Buddha-works at all times, remaining uninterrupted at all times;
because they attain the equality of all karmic fruits, they remain entirely free from attachment to any mundane or supramundane roots of goodness.
Because it is ultimate, one attains the equality of the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas and manifests Buddha-activities in accordance with the world;
therefore, O Son of the Buddha, this is the eighth dedication of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
[Treatise] From the seventh son of the Buddha down to the eighth dedication of the aspect of *tathatā* (suchness),
there are eleven and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on the benefits obtained for oneself through dedicating according to the aforementioned aspects of *tathatā*.
[Sūtra] When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this dedication, they realize the gate of immeasurable pure dharmas;
they are able to let out the great lion’s roar of the Tathāgata with sovereign fearlessness, and through skillful means,
they teach and bring to maturity immeasurable bodhisattvas, never resting at any time, until they attain the single body of the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect body.
Pervading all worlds, they attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect voice;
with a single sound, they awaken all sentient beings, attaining the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect power;

within a single pore, they can universally contain all lands, attaining the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect spiritual penetrations; they place all sentient beings within a single atom, attaining the Buddha’s...
Possessing immeasurable and perfect liberation, they manifest within the body of a single sentient being all the realms of all Buddhas;
they attain the equanimous and right enlightenment of Buddhahood and the immeasurable, perfect samādhis of a Buddha; within a single samādhi, they can universally manifest all samādhis;
and they attain the immeasurable, perfect eloquence of a Buddha, such that by speaking a single phrase of Dharma, they exhaust the limits of the future.
To exhaustively eliminate all the doubts and delusions of all sentient beings, to cause them to attain the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect qualities,
to endow all beings with the ten powers of a Buddha, and to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment throughout the entire realm of sentient beings— O Son of the Buddha,
this is the dedication of all roots of goodness by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in accordance with the characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
[Treatise] Regarding the eighth bodhisattva-mahāsattva, from the point where the roots of goodness accord with the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) up to the dedication,
thirteen lines and a half of scripture clarify that once the aforementioned dedications have been performed, one attains the stage of being equal to the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.
[Śāstra] Ninth: From "At that time" onwards, one line of the sūtra clarifies the section on the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja speaking verses to praise the Dharma.
[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva’s aspiration and joy always abide securely; with firm right mindfulness, they are free from delusion and confusion.
Their mind is supple and ever-cool; they accumulate boundless meritorious practices.
The Bodhisattva is humble and compliant, without opposition; all their vows and aspirations are entirely pure.
Having attained the great radiance of wisdom, they are well able to illuminate all karmas.
Bodhisattvas contemplate the vastness of karma; its various distinctions are most rare and marvelous.
Resolving to practice without regression, they thereby benefit all living beings.
The various distinctions of karma are immeasurable in kind; the Bodhisattva diligently cultivates them all.
In accordance with sentient beings, he does not oppose their inclinations, universally causing their minds to be pure and filled with joy.
Having already ascended to the stage of the Honored One, the Tamer of Men, he is free from all feverish afflictions and his mind is unimpeded.
Thoroughly knowing both the phenomena and their meanings, they diligently practice for the benefit of all living beings.
Regarding the various, immeasurable, and innumerable types of virtuous deeds cultivated by Bodhisattvas, they understand all those distinctions;
for the sake of benefiting all living beings, they dedicate [the merit].
With sublime wisdom, they constantly observe the ultimate, vast, and true principle,
severing all bases of existence without exception. Just as that suchness is skillfully dedicated,
and just as suchness pervades all things, so too do they universally encompass all worlds.
The Bodhisattva dedicates with this mind, causing all sentient beings to be free from attachment;
the Bodhisattva’s power of aspiration pervades all things, just as True Suchness (tathatā) is nowhere not present;
whether seen or unseen, his mindfulness is all-encompassing, dedicating everything through his merit.
Abiding throughout the night, they likewise abide during the day; Abiding for half a month or a full month, they abide for years or even for kalpas.
Such is the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), and their practice is likewise so.
All that exists in the three periods of time and all buddha-fields, All sentient beings and all phenomena—[they abide within them all].
Abiding entirely therein yet abiding nowhere, they dedicate their practice in this way;
Just as the true nature (*tathatā*) is the primordial self-nature, so do Bodhisattvas give rise to the Great Mind;
Wherever true nature exists, there is nowhere it is not—thus do they dedicate their practice.
For example, just as true suchness is the fundamental nature,
wherein not a single dharma ever fails to obtain its own nature— this being the true nature—
so too is the dedication of karma like the characteristic of true suchness; so too is the karma like the nature of true suchness.
Just as the nature of *tathatā* is fundamentally real, so too is karma identical to *tathatā*.
Just as *tathatā* has no limits, so too is karma without bounds;
yet within it there is no bondage or attachment. Therefore, this karma attains purity.
Thus, these wise and true sons of the Buddha, with firm and unshakable resolve, have attained thorough mastery through their power of wisdom.
They enter the treasury of the Buddhas' skillful means and awaken to the true Dharma of the Dharma King; therein they are neither attached nor bound.

Thus, with a sovereign mind free from obstruction, one has never seen a single dharma arise that performs the activities of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. All phenomena in the world are like those appearances;
the characteristics of all dharmas are signless. To know such characteristics is to know the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva dwells in this inconceivable state, wherein conceptual thought can never reach its limit;
having entered this realm of the inconceivable, both thought and non-thought are utterly stilled.
Thus contemplating the nature of all phenomena, they thoroughly comprehend the distinctions among all karmic actions.
All grasping at a self is extinguished; abiding in merit, they are immovable.
All karmic fruits and retributions of the Bodhisattvas are sealed by inexhaustible wisdom.
Thus, the nature of the inexhaustible is itself exhausted; therefore, the means of the inexhaustible are extinguished.
The Bodhisattva contemplates that the mind does not exist externally, nor can it be found within;
knowing that the nature of the mind is non-existent, they realize that both self and phenomena are entirely detached and eternally quiescent.
Those sons of the Buddhas who know thus understand that the nature of all phenomena is forever empty and still.
There is not a single dharma that can be created; Like all Buddhas, they have awakened to non-self.
They understand that all worlds Are entirely equal in nature to True Suchness (tathatā).
Seeing this inconceivable characteristic, They are thus able to know the dharma of signlessness (animitta).
If one can abide in this profound Dharma, always delighting in the practice of the bodhisattva conduct,
desiring to benefit all living beings, adorned with great vows and never regressing—
this one transcends the world and does not give rise to the deluded discriminations of birth and death.

Thoroughly realizing that the mind is like an illusion, Diligently practicing all deeds to deliver sentient beings, The Bodhisattva, with right mindfulness, contemplates the world: All things arise from the conditions of karma.
Desiring to rescue and deliver them, they cultivate all practices, Universally gathering those of the three periods of time without exception.
Knowing fully the various differences among sentient beings, All of which are discriminated by perception and mental formations—
Observing these with complete clarity, Without destroying the nature of all phenomena,
The wise one knows the teachings of all Buddhas, And dedicates through such practice.
[Verse: Out of compassion for all sentient beings, May they engage in correct reflection upon the true Dharma.
[Treatise: From the tenth line below, fifty-eight stanzas clarify the preceding section on the Dharma through further versification.
Regarding the second part, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text, the remaining textual meanings are fully contained within the scripture itself, as in the eighth section.
The Sūtra says: "A single body pervades all worlds; one attains the immeasurable vocal resonance of a Buddha;
within a single pore, one can universally contain all lands; one attains the immeasurable supernormal powers of a Buddha and places all sentient beings within a single pore.
This refers to the ability to enter into suchness after the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and subsequent realization of the path (*darśanamārga*).
Knowing and seeing this, for the sake of ordinary persons who possess faith, I have briefly explained a small portion to open their eyes and minds;
it is not until one enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and through the wisdom of contemplation, achieves harmonious integration that one will see it directly. The Master spoke in verse:
"Thoroughly knowing the nature of the large and small pores, The lands of the ten directions have neither interior nor exterior; The realm of wisdom contains the lands of the ten directions."
The essential nature and characteristics of all lands are fundamentally illusory; the pure characteristics of the body of wisdom are unimpeded, and even the pores and atoms are likewise so.

The land arises from the mind through false conceptualization, yet the realm of non-deluded wisdom constantly encompasses it. When the mind of a sentient being is pure, there is no distinction between interior and exterior;
thus one realizes that the hairs on one's own body are also like this. With no discrimination in the mind, the sentiments of self and other become one.
Every mote of dust contains Buddha-fields; therefore, the Tathāgata teaches that dedication extensively arouses vows and practices, merging one's own and others' aspirations.
Wishing for others to obtain happiness, one shares the same resolve as oneself, purifying Buddha-lands through constant mutual interpenetration. By means of vast vows, one arouses great wisdom;
with the wisdom of identical essence, compassion fills the Dharma-realm. Through effortless, principle-wisdom, clouds of bodies arise, manifesting according to the various types of beings.

The manifestation of forms and sounds is likewise so. By means of the wisdom that realizes the identity of self and others, one manifests Buddha-lands within the bodies of sentient beings and turns the wheel of Dharma through the wisdom of sentient beings.

Because the minds of sentient beings are deluded and lack awakening, they do not realize that the wisdom of sentient beings is the wisdom of the Buddha, and that the wisdom of the Buddha is fundamentally the wisdom of sentient beings.
To those who are deluded, the wisdom of the Buddha appears as the state of sentient beings; to those who awaken, sentient beings are themselves the wisdom of the Buddha.
Having thus understood that the essence of this Buddha-wisdom is both identical and distinct, it is capable of serving as a refuge for sentient beings.
This concludes the explanation of the eighth dedication, the Dedication of the Characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The ninth is the Dedication of Unattached and Unbound Liberation. Its essence is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), and it is characterized by goodness...
The deity perceived by Vaiśravaṇa represents the practice of this stage. The city in which he resides is named Dhavalapati;
the deity is called Mahādeva. As for the name Dhavalapati, it means "City of the Gate of Existence" (Sadvāra-pura).

This constitutes the celestial and terrestrial coordinates of this realm, with the celestial gate being established as the "Gate of Heaven" (Dyau-dvāra). Thereafter, one successively perceives the Earth Deity.
These two positions clarify the harmonious union of the wisdom of these ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) with ultimate compassion.

The deity of the zenith represents the sublime wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), while the deity of the nadir represents great compassion that reaches its ultimate limit, supporting all things and nurturing all living beings;
thus, their position is like that of parents. The deity of the zenith manifests as an accumulation of immeasurable varieties of precious jewels.
As the mountain and earth deities emit light and cause the earth to quake, various precious objects and ornaments adorn it everywhere, purifying the land as a pure field (*kṣetra*).
Numerous treasuries spontaneously emerge, and the celestial and terrestrial deities nurture all beings according to their karma.

The virtue of thus saving sentient beings is vast; while its full manifestation is clarified only in the [final] text, I shall here briefly cite and synthesize the passages to express the underlying meaning of the Dharma.
This is intended so that later learners may easily perceive its meaning, not become confused regarding the teachings and practices, and not find their cultivation of the path arduous.
To illustrate this through metaphor: the nature of the deity named Mingzhijing (Wisdom-Purity) is like a mountain where the treasures of Dharma are fully present and the jewels of merit emerge;
it is like the earth, which nurtures and supports all things through pure great compassion, requiring no effort, for the essence of the earth is fundamentally and solely purity.
This soil is the ultimate purity of wisdom and compassion; thus, it is the adornment and purity of the Buddha-land.
This clarifies that divine wisdom and the virtue of responding to truth harmonize with heaven and earth to nurture all things. It is also the spiritual numen of heaven and earth;

it is the practice of the true and the conventional that a Bodhisattva, according to their stage, is capable of governing. This stage is manifested by celestial deities, signifying the ascent of clarity.
The progression of principle and wisdom is profound and subtle, like the numinous spirit of heaven that cannot be fathomed;

its divine efficacy brings all things into being through non-action—these two meanings are as previously stated. First, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" up until the conclusion of the verses, the long section is divided into seven parts.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perform the dedication of liberation that is unattached and unbound?
The Son of the Buddha replied: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva conceives a sense of reverence toward all roots of goodness;

that is to say, they conceive a sense of reverence toward the mind that emerges from birth and death, they conceive a sense of reverence toward the mind that gathers in all roots of goodness, and they conceive a sense of reverence toward the aspiration for them."

One should give rise to a mind of reverence for all roots of goodness; one should give rise to a mind of reverence for repenting of all past misdeeds; one should give rise to a mind of reverence for rejoicing in roots of goodness;
one should give rise to a mind of reverence for paying homage to all Buddhas; one should give rise to a mind of reverence for joining the palms in respectful salutation;
one should give rise to a mind of reverence for prostrating before stupas and shrines; and one should give rise to a mind of reverence for exhorting the Buddhas to preach the Dharma.
He respects these various roots of goodness, giving rise to respect for them all, and accords with them through patient acceptance (*anumodanā*).

[Treatise] Regarding the first son of the Buddha: from the passage "How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perform the dedication of liberation, unattached and unbound," down to "accordance with patient acceptance," there are eight scriptural sections that clarify the planting of roots of goodness within the causal stage.

The *Sūtra on the Ten Kinds of Respectful Attitudes* states: "When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of respect toward all roots of goodness, they do so by upholding ten kinds of intentions that are inexhaustible. These are as follows:

regarding the discourse and the dharmas presented therein, they give rise to a mind of respect for the emergence from birth and death—that is, emerging from the birth-and-death of the *pariccheda-ja* (segmented) realm within the Three Vehicles."
Because they attain the death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) out of weariness with birth-and-death and a longing for tranquility, they enter into the death of transformation;

this differs from the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in that their wisdom-born bodies pervade the ocean of lands, manifesting according to the faculties [of beings] without being of the nature of birth-and-death, even to the point of appearing identical to worldly phenomena yet not being of the nature of birth-and-death. Those who have entered the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) should regard them in this way.
Thus we know that if one discusses the wisdom of self-retribution, it is only when practice and realization are in accord that one can truly perceive it.

Because such [wisdom] gives rise to the nature of transcending birth and death, the mind conceives a sense of reverence. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One who conceives a sense of reverence for the mind that gathers all roots of goodness is practicing the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas;
one who conceives a sense of reverence for the mind that aspires to all roots of goodness... [is practicing the precept of benefiting sentient beings]. Ten.
One should develop a mind of respect for the impure goals sought by those with faith, as well as for the pure aspirations of those from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) onwards;
one must likewise develop a mind of respect for the repentance of past karmic transgressions, which constitutes the repentance of former deeds.
Below this, the meaning may be understood according to the text. Thus, by causing one to revere the cause, the fruit will not regress, like a ten-story pavilion.
The lower is firmly established while the upper remains; the preceding section concludes the causes for respect.
