The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Expanded and Vast Teachings, Scroll Fifty-three.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Lay Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, combining the various sutras into a single treatise,
Chapter Twenty-five, Part Twelve of the "Ten Dedications":
[Sutra] O Son of the Buddha, regarding all those buddha-fields, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, within a single buddha-field...
On the other hand, in a single direction, in a single location, within an area the size of a hair-tip, there are immeasurable, boundless,

and unspeakably numerous great bodhisattvas who all dwell fully pervaded by accomplished, pure wisdom. Just as it is in one direction, in one location, within an area the size of a hair-tip in a single buddha-field,
so it is throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive dharma-realm— in every single buddha-field, in every single direction.
In each and every location, even down to the measure of a single hair-tip, it is all likewise so;
this is the dedication of roots of goodness by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, universally wishing that all Buddha-lands be fully adorned with various kinds of wonderful jewels,
such as the Adornment of Jewels, and so forth, as extensively described, including the adornments of incense, flowers, and garlands.
The adornments of ointment incense, the adornments of burning incense, the adornments of powdered incense, the adornments of robes, the adornments of parasols,
the adornments of banners, the adornments of streamers, and the adornments of mani-jewels, arranged in succession, even increasing a hundredfold beyond this,
are all like the aforementioned jewel-adornments; thus it is explained in detail.
[Treatise] From the twenty-first "Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to the passage where it is extensively explained in eleven lines of scripture,

it clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s vow consists of manifesting in Bodhisattva bodies throughout all Buddha-fields and adorning them with jewels to an extent exceeding the previous by hundreds of thousands of times.
This section clarifies that the vow is to adorn the Buddha-fields with the Bodhisattva body.
Filling its interior, the subsequent passages conclude by stating that these adornments exceed the former by a hundredfold; one should dedicate these roots of goodness with this intent.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva takes the roots of goodness accumulated through the giving of Dharma and other practices to nurture a single..."
Dedication for the sake of severing all roots of goodness; dedication for the sake of adorning and purifying all Buddha-fields;
dedication for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment; dedication for the sake of causing the minds of all sentient beings to be pure and immovable;
dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings to enter the profound Buddha-dharma; dedication for the sake of causing all sentient beings...
He dedicates [the merit] so that all beings may attain the pure qualities that none can surpass;
he dedicates it so that all beings may attain indestructible power of purity;
he dedicates it so that all beings may attain inexhaustible power of wisdom to deliver all sentient beings and lead them into the Buddha-dharma; he dedicates it so that all beings...
They dedicate [their merit] so that all sentient beings may attain equal, immeasurable, and pure speech;
they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may attain the unimpeded eye and achieve wisdom that is equal to the entirety of space and pervades the Dharma-realm;
and they dedicate it so that all sentient beings may attain pure mindfulness and knowledge of all worlds throughout past kalpas.
I dedicate [these merits] so that all sentient beings may attain unimpeded great wisdom and be able to fully resolve and comprehend the treasury of all dharmas;
I dedicate so that all sentient beings may attain immeasurable great bodhi, pervading the entire dharma-realm without obstruction; I dedicate so that all sentient beings may attain equanimity...
One dedicates because of the equality and non-differentiation of roots of goodness that share the same essence;
one dedicates so that all sentient beings may attain the complete adornment of pure actions of body, speech, and mind endowed with all merits;
one dedicates so that all sentient beings may attain identity with the conduct of Samantabhadra; one dedicates so that all sentient beings may attain...
They dedicate [their merit] for the purpose of entering all Buddha-fields of equal essence and purity;
they dedicate it for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to fully observe all-knowledge and enter into its perfection;

they dedicate it for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to become entirely free from unequal roots of goodness; and they dedicate it for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain equality.
One dedicates for the sake of fulfilling all-knowledge through the successive stages of a profound mind free from differentiated marks;
one dedicates for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide securely in all pure dharmas;

one dedicates for the sake of causing all sentient beings to realize all-knowledge and attain the ultimate within a single thought-moment; one dedicates for the sake of causing all sentient beings to...

Having thus dedicated all roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the sons of the Buddha, dedicate them so as to attain the path of omniscience that is perfected and pure.
[Treatise] From the twenty-second section, "O Son of the Buddha," down to "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,

having universally dedicated all roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings," there are twenty-eight lines of scripture clarifying the section on the Bodhisattva’s general dedication of merit for the sake of all sentient beings.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, they dedicate them with the desire to universally fulfill and expound the power of all pure practices;
they dedicate them with the desire to accomplish the majesty of pure practices and attain an unspeakably unspeakable ocean of Dharma;
they dedicate them with the desire to possess within each and every ocean of Dharma the light of pure wisdom, equal to the infinite reaches of the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, they dedicate [their merit] with the desire to reveal, demonstrate, and expound the distinct meanings of all dharmas;

they dedicate it with the desire to accomplish the boundless and vast Samādhi of the Radiance of All Dharmas; they dedicate it with the desire to accord with the eloquence of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
and they dedicate it with the desire to accomplish the sovereign bodies of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Therefore, one dedicates [merit] for the sake of honoring all Buddhas and their delightful, unobstructed Dharma;
one dedicates it for the sake of fulfilling the mind of great compassion, to rescue and protect all sentient beings with never-receding persistence;
and one dedicates it desiring to accomplish inconceivable and diverse dharmas, unobstructed wisdom, a mind free from defilement, and the complete purity of the sense faculties.
They dedicate their merit for the sake of entering the dharma-assembly maṇḍalas of all congregations;

they dedicate their merit with the desire to constantly turn the equal, non-regressive wheel of Dharma in all such Buddha-lands—whether inverted or upright, coarse or subtle, vast or narrow, small or great, defiled or pure—and so forth;
they dedicate their merit with the desire to attain, in every thought-moment, fearlessness that is inexhaustible.
They dedicate [their merit] for the sake of manifesting and expounding the light of the sublime Dharma through all manner of eloquence;

they dedicate it for the sake of seeking all that is wholesome with joy, cultivating the arousal of the mind, and causing the faculties to become increasingly superior, so as to attain the great supernormal knowledge of all dharmas and exhaustively understand all phenomena;
and they dedicate it for the desire to personally approach and make offerings at all assemblies and sites of enlightenment.
He dedicates [the merit] for the purpose of expounding all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, so as to cause them all to rejoice.

[Treatise: The twenty-third section, from "Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness" down to "dedicates so as to cause them all to rejoice," consists of nineteen lines of scripture clarifying that the Bodhisattva, through the aforementioned dedication, desires only to cause the Dharma to be preached.
And they practice for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to peace and happiness, causing them to be perfected according to the extent of the Dharma-realm.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates these roots of goodness in this way:
that is to say, he dedicates by dwelling in the immeasurable dwellings of the Dharma-realm; he dedicates by dwelling in the immeasurable physical actions of the Dharma-realm; he dwells in...
One dedicates by abiding in the dedication of immeasurable verbal karma within the dharma-realm; one dedicates by abiding in the dedication of immeasurable mental karma within the dharma-realm;

one dedicates by abiding in the dedication to the equality of immeasurable forms within the dharma-realm; one dedicates by abiding in the dedication to the equality of immeasurable feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within the dharma-realm;
one dedicates by abiding in the dedication to the equality of immeasurable aggregates within the dharma-realm; one dedicates by abiding in the immeasurable dharma-realm.
The dedication through the equality of realms; the dedication through abiding in the equality of the immeasurable locations of the dharma-realm;

the dedication through abiding in the equality of the immeasurable internal aspects of the dharma-realm; the dedication through abiding in the equality of the immeasurable external aspects of the dharma-realm;

the dedication through abiding in the equality of the immeasurable arisings of the dharma-realm; and the dedication through abiding in the equality of the immeasurable profound resolve of the dharma-realm.
Dedication by abiding in the infinite skillful means of the dharma-realm;
dedication by abiding in the infinite faith and understanding of the dharma-realm; dedication by abiding in the infinite faculties of the dharma-realm;
dedication by abiding in the infinite equality of the beginning, middle, and end of the dharma-realm; dedication by abiding in the infinite karmic retributions of the dharma-realm.
They dedicate with equanimity by abiding in the equality of the infinite defilement and purity of the dharma-realm;

they dedicate with equanimity by abiding in the equality of the infinite sentient beings of the dharma-realm; they dedicate with equanimity by abiding in the equality of the infinite buddha-fields of the dharma-realm;
they dedicate with equanimity by abiding in the equality of the infinite dharmas of the dharma-realm; they dedicate with equanimity by abiding in the light of the infinite worlds of the dharma-realm.
They clarify the dedication of equality by abiding in the dedication of equality toward the infinite Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-realm;

they clarify the dedication of equality by abiding in the dedication of equality toward the infinite Bodhisattva practices and vows of the Dharma-realm; they clarify the dedication of equality by abiding in the dedication of equality toward the infinite Bodhisattva renunciations of the Dharma-realm;
and they clarify the dedication of equality by abiding in the dedication of equality toward the infinite Bodhisattva teachings and taming of beings of the Dharma-realm.
They dedicate equally by abiding in the dharma-realm; they dedicate with the equality of non-duality and infinity in the dharma-realm;
and they dedicate with the equality of the immeasurable assemblies of Tathāgatas and their sites of enlightenment within the dharma-realm.

[Treatise] From the twenty-fourth section, "The Son of the Buddha," down to "the Tathāgata’s assembly at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there are twenty-two lines of scripture clarifying the section on dedication:

how Bodhisattvas, through Dharma-giving adorned with great vows, transform sentient beings through vast aspirations, causing them all to abide in the equality of the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, it is the section on dedication.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure body of the Dharma-realm;
they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure speech of the Dharma-realm; they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure mind of the Dharma-realm;
and they abide in the infinite, equal, and pure conduct of all Bodhisattvas within the Dharma-realm.
May they dwell securely in the infinite, impartial, and pure assembly of the *dharmadhātu*;
may they dwell securely in the infinite, impartial *dharmadhātu* as they extensively expound all dharmas of pure wisdom for the sake of all bodhisattvas;

may they dwell securely in the infinite, impartial *dharmadhātu* as they are able to enter all worlds throughout the entirety of the *dharmadhātu* with their bodies; may they dwell securely in the infinite, impartial *dharmadhātu*.
O Son of the Buddha, one who illuminates all phenomena with equal radiance and purity, who is fearless, and who can, with a single voice, completely sever the web of doubts of all sentient beings;
who, according to their faculties and inclinations, causes them all to rejoice and abide in the supreme Dharma of the power of the knowledge of all modes,
the fearlessnesses, the masteries, the supernormal powers, and the vast merit of liberation— this, O Son of the Buddha, is what constitutes a Bodhisattva.
The Mahāsattva’s tenth dwelling: the immeasurable dedication equal to the Dharma-realm.

[Treatise] From the twenty-fifth "Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to the tenth "Dedication Equal to the Immeasurable Dharma-realm," there are eleven and a half lines of scripture that clarify how, when dedicating all roots of goodness as described above, one attains suchness.
These actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as the ten kinds of pure aspects of abiding in the dharma-realm,
are fully detailed in the text starting from the section "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, according to the specific descriptions therein.
[Sūtra] When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate all roots of goodness, such as the gift of Dharma, in this manner,
they fulfill the immeasurable and boundless bodhisattva practices and vows of Samantabhadra; they are able to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm,
equal to the extent of space, and cause all sentient beings to likewise fully achieve and perfect the boundless [vows].
With wisdom, they comprehend all phenomena; in every thought-moment, they see all Buddhas appearing in the world.

In every thought-moment, they see the infinite and boundless sovereign powers of all Buddhas—namely, the power of vast sovereignty, the power of unattached sovereignty, the power of unimpeded sovereignty, the power of inconceivable sovereignty, and the purification of all beings.
The power of mastery over birth; the power of mastery over establishing all worlds; the power of mastery over manifesting ineffable speech;
the power of mastery over manifesting at appropriate times; the power of mastery over non-regressive supernatural knowledges (*abhijñā*);

the power of mastery over expounding the entire infinite dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without exception; and the power of mastery over giving rise to the universal conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The power of mastery over the eye at its limit; the power of mastery in hearing, retaining, and upholding the true Dharma of immeasurable Buddhas through unimpeded ear-consciousness;
the power of mastery in which, sitting cross-legged in a single body, one pervades the infinite Dharma-realms of the ten directions without causing any crowding to sentient beings;
and the power of mastery in universally entering the infinite phenomena of the three periods of time through perfect wisdom.

Furthermore, they attain immeasurable purities: namely, the purity of all sentient beings, the purity of all Buddha-fields, the purity of all phenomena, the purity of the wisdom that universally knows all places, and the purity of boundless wisdom that pervades the realm of empty space;
they attain the wisdom of all distinct languages and sounds, responding universally to sentient beings through various modes of speech.
Purely emitting immeasurable, perfect light that universally illumines all boundless worlds;

pure in generating the wisdom of the practices of all Bodhisattvas throughout the three periods of time; and pure in the wisdom that enters, within a single thought-moment, the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, entering all boundless worlds to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
They have all performed what was to be done and attained such purity; they have all become fully endowed, all achieved accomplishment,
all undergone cultivation, all attained equanimity, all manifested before them, all known and seen, all entered into realization,
all observed, and all attained purity, reaching the further shore.
[Treatise] From the twenty-sixth Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva down to the arrival at the other shore,

there are twenty-four lines of sūtra explaining how the Bodhisattva dedicates roots of goodness— such as the aforementioned gift of Dharma— with the vow that all sentient beings may behold the Buddha,
enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and share in what the Buddha has attained. This concludes the section above.
This concludes the exposition of the ten gates of dedication.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways—namely, trembling, trembling everywhere, and so forth; rising, rising everywhere, and so forth; surging, surging everywhere, and so forth.

They leaped, quaked, and trembled everywhere; they roared, bellowed, and thundered everywhere; they struck and crashed everywhere—throughout all places—by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma.

There rained down celestial flowers, celestial garlands, celestial powdered incense, various celestial fragrances, celestial garments, celestial jewels, celestial ornaments, celestial maṇi-gems, and celestial aloeswood incense.
Celestial sandalwood incense, celestial exquisite parasols, various celestial banners, and multicolored celestial pennants;

the bodies of incalculable devas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of unspeakable devas, the wondrous sounds of the Dharma of inconceivable devas, and the sounds of devas praising the Buddha;
the joyful sounds of incalculable devas all acclaiming "Excellent!"—these were immeasurable incalculable hundreds of thousands.
Nayutas of devas reverently prostrated; countless sons of heaven constantly kept the Buddhas in mind, seeking the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata without ever forsaking them;
countless sons of heaven performed various musical performances, singing hymns of praise, and making offerings to the Tathāgata;
hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeyas of devas emitted great radiance, illuminating the entirety of empty space.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and all Buddha-fields, the infinite asankhyeya realms of the Buddhas appear;
the emanations of the Tathāgata surpass those of the devas, and just as this Dharma was taught here in the Tuṣita Heaven palace of this world,
it is likewise throughout the Tuṣita Heaven palaces in all worlds of the ten directions.

[Treatise] Section Thirteen: From "By the Buddha’s Spiritual Power" down to "In all worlds, even in the Tuṣita palaces, it is likewise so," there are sixteen lines of scripture clarifying the section on the Buddha’s majestic movement, the arising of offerings, and the earth shaking.
Within this section on the earthquake, the movement has three meanings: first, the movement caused by the majesty of the teaching; second, the [movement of] the great assembly...
Hearing the Dharma brings joy and delight, which moves the Buddha’s divine power so as to cause all the devas to manifest offerings.
This has two meanings: first, the teaching-gates of the Dharma attract and evoke offerings; second, the devas hear the Dharma with joy and thus manifest offerings.
Within these offerings, there are two further meanings: first, offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies; second, the devas singing praises, prostrating in reverence, and emitting light.
The equal offerings are as those made in worship; their number is to be known from the sutra.
Just as in all Buddha-fields there appear immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* realms of the Buddhas, so too do emanations of the Tathāgata appear, surpassing all devas.

This is because they manifest the qualities of the Dharma and accord with the realm of the Dharma being taught; thus, their appearance is not due to the offerings of the devas. In all worlds, [the Tushita...]
The celestial palaces of all the heavens were likewise entirely bound together; throughout the ten directions, they were all joined in this same manner.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a million buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there came to assemble from each direction bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a million buddha-fields, surrounding him on all sides.
Throughout the ten directions, they all spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to expound these great dedications.
O Son of the Buddha, we are all of one name, called Vajradhvaja (Diamond Banner).
We have all come from the world-system Vajraprabhā (Diamond Light) to this land from the presence of the Buddha Vajradhvaja. By the spiritual power of the Buddhas, all those worlds..."
The Dharma thus spoken, this assembly, its retinue, and the words, phrases, and meanings—all are likewise neither increased nor diminished.
We have all come from that land by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power to serve as witnesses for you, just as we who have come here to this assembly serve as witnesses for you.
This applies to all the Tuṣita palaces and jewel-adorned halls in every world throughout the ten directions.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas who came to act as witnesses was likewise so.

[Treatise] Fourteenth: At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power... down to "...was likewise so," there are ten lines of sutra text clarifying the section on the gathering of Bodhisattvas of identical names to act as witnesses. At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power...
Therefore, when each of the ten directions cites figures exceeding the number of atoms in a million Buddha-fields— referring to the hundred stages, the thousand practices,
and the hundred thousand positions— it indicates the magnitude of the expansion of the wisdom of ascending insight and knowledge.
Those who come from beyond the number of atoms in such a million worlds are said to be "outside" because they remain in delusion and fail to reach this level of ascending progress.

Regarding the realization and entry into the stage: it is said that bodhisattvas from as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a million worlds, all sharing the same name Vajradhvaja, have come to offer praise, exclaiming "Excellent! They praise the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja because their wisdom and their assembly of the Way are identical in name and substance;
thus, it clarifies that the present assembly of wisdom merges with that of antiquity, and it is also the realization of suchness.
Since all realms as numerous as atoms are entirely the wisdom of the vajra and free from delusion, the world is likewise named Vajraprabhā (Vajra Light).
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the entire assembly in the ten directions.
Having reached the Dharma-realm, he thoroughly understands both the words and their meanings; he expands his great mind and universally covers all sentient beings with great compassion;

he binds his mind in steadfast abiding within the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; he skillfully enters into all the meritorious dharmas of the Buddhas and accomplishes the sovereign bodies of all Buddhas;
and he contemplates the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings as well as all the roots of goodness they have planted.
Having fully discerned and known all faculties, he manifested a body of pure and wondrous form in accordance with the Dharma-body;
at that very moment, he spoke in verse.
[Treatise] Fifteenth: From "At that time" onwards, six lines and a half of scripture clarify the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
The verses spoken clearly extol the virtues of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja; as the text states, these may be understood from the words themselves.
Below this, there are ninety-four lines of verse, with two lines constituting a single stanza, as fully contained within the text.

Among them, the bestowal of prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) according to their respective stages, through which they gradually become Buddhas over the course of many eons, clarifies the progressive advancement of wisdom and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) through each stage.
Because it is vast, it is not limited by the extent of time—be it days, months, years, or kalpas, whether prolonged or brief;
rather, these are all names for the Buddha-fruit established in accordance with the stages of practice.
[Sūtra] The Bodhisattva accomplishes the wisdom of the Dharma and awakens to and understands the boundless gateways of the true Dharma.
The Teacher who guides through the light of the Dharma, The Bodhisattva who thoroughly understands the unimpeded,
true Dharma; The great guide of the Dharma who reveals the profound and rare teachings,
Leading immeasurable multitudes throughout the ten directions, Causing them all to dwell securely within the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattvas have already drunk from the ocean of the Buddha-dharma; Like clouds of Dharma, they rain universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The Sun of Dharma appears in the world, Proclaiming the sublime Dharma to benefit all living beings.
They are ever the rare masters who bestow the gift of Dharma, Thoroughly understanding the skillful means for entering the Dharma.
The light of the Dharma, pure and radiant, illuminates their minds; they preach the Dharma in the world with constant fearlessness.

Having well cultivated a mind of mastery over the Dharma, they are able to penetrate all Dharma-gates and achieve the ocean of profound and wondrous Dharmas, universally beating the Dharma drum for the sake of all sentient beings.
Proclaiming the profound and marvelous Dharma, Nurturing all virtues through the Dharma,
Possessing a mind of pure joy in the Dharma, He manifests the treasury of the Buddha-Dharma to the world.
Consecrated by the Kings of the Buddhas, He has perfected the body that is the treasury of the wisdom of dharmatā.
They are able to fully understand the true nature of phenomena;
Abiding securely in all wholesome dharmas, these Bodhisattvas practice the foremost giving.
Praised and delighted in by all Tathāgatas, their deeds are all approved by the Buddhas; By this, they achieve the state of the Honored One among Men.
The Bodhisattva accomplishes the wondrous Dharma-body, Personally born through transformation from the teachings of all Buddhas;
To benefit sentient beings, they act as a lamp of Dharma, Expounding immeasurable and most supreme teachings.
In accordance with their practice, they bestow the gift of the wondrous Dharma, And likewise observe those roots of goodness.
All the various virtues performed for the sake of sentient beings, I dedicate them all through wisdom.
All the meritorious qualities that bring about Buddhahood, I bestow them all as gifts upon all living beings.
May everyone attain complete purity And reach the further shore of the Buddha’s adornments.
The Buddha-fields of the ten directions are immeasurable, All fully endowed with immeasurable great adornments;
Such adornments are inconceivable, Yet all are used to adorn a single land.
May the pure wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata Cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with it.
Just like Samantabhadra, the true son of the Buddha, Self-adorned with all merits and accomplished in vast,
great supernormal powers, He travels throughout all worlds without exception,
Causing every single sentient being to practice the Bodhisattva path.
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as awakened by the Buddhas, Tathāgatas,
Be made entirely like Samantabhadra, fully practicing the supreme conduct.
May they possess all the various and distinct merits Accomplished by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Such merit is boundless; may all sentient beings fully perfect it.
May Bodhisattvas, endowed with sovereign power, go to study every place where learning is required.
Manifesting all great supernormal powers, they travel everywhere to the infinite lands of the ten directions.
In a single moment of thought, the Bodhisattva is able to behold countless Buddhas, equal in number to all sentient beings;
furthermore, within a single hair-tip, they fully encompass all phenomena and perceive them all clearly.
As for the immeasurable sentient beings in the world, the Bodhisattva is able to discern and know them all.
The Buddhas are as immeasurable as all sentient beings; with a great mind, I make offerings until they are all exhausted.

With various kinds of famous incense and supreme, wondrous flowers, with robes of many jewels and banners and canopies, I distribute them throughout the entire Dharma-realm, filling it completely, and resolve my mind to universally offer to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Within a single pore, one clearly beholds Buddhas as numerous as the inconceivable and immeasurable;
All pores are likewise thus. I universally prostrate to all the Lamps of the World, Bowing with reverence throughout my entire body To these infinite, most supreme ones.
Furthermore, with words one universally praises them, throughout all kalpas until the end of the future;
with offering requisites as numerous as all sentient beings,
one thus makes offerings to a single Tathāgata, and the same is true for all Tathāgatas.
Making offerings and praising all Tathāgatas throughout every single kalpa of that world—
may the number of kalpas in the world come to an end, yet the Bodhisattva’s offerings never cease;
through all the various kalpas of every world, they cultivate all practices for as many kalpas as there are.
To reverently make offerings to a single Tathāgata for the duration of all kalpas without weariness—
just as one would offer to a single Buddha for immeasurable kalpas, so too should one offer to all Buddhas;
nor should one discriminate regarding the number of these kalpas, nor should one give rise to fatigue or weariness toward those who receive the offerings.
The Dharma-realm is vast and without limit; the Bodhisattva observes it all with complete clarity.
Within this, great lotuses are spread everywhere, bestowing upon all sentient beings immeasurable Buddha-jewels.
Their flowers, fragrances, and colors are all perfect and complete; pure, adorned, and most subtle.

All that exists in the world is beyond compare; Taking these to offer to the Honored One among Men, Throughout as many infinite lands as there are sentient beings, Filling them all with exquisite jeweled canopies, I offer them all to a single Tathāgata; To offer to all Buddhas is likewise so.
With incomparable and most excellent unguents, never before seen in any world,
he makes this offering to the Teacher of Gods and Humans; with incense, burnt offerings, and exquisite flowers,
and with robes of various jewels and ornaments, for as many eons as there are sentient beings.
Thus making offerings to all the Most Victorious Ones, serving them with joy and without weariness—
equal in number to all sentient beings— those lamps illuminating the world accomplish great Bodhi in every moment;
they also praise and extol the Tamer of Men with boundless verses as they make their offerings.
To as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are sentient beings, I offer supreme and wondrous worship;
For as many immeasurable eons as there are sentient beings, I praise them thus, without end.
When making such offerings to all Buddhas, By the Buddha’s spiritual power, they pervade everywhere.
May I see all the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, Who dwell securely in the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—
In the past, future, and present. May all my roots of goodness Enable me to constantly practice the conduct of Samantabhadra,
And swiftly attain stable dwelling upon the ground of Samantabhadra.
As known and seen by all Tathāgatas, may all the infinite sentient beings in the world be fully endowed with the conduct of Samantabhadra, praised by the wise.
This is the practice of dedication cultivated together by the great beings of the ten directions.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have taught me this supreme practice of dedication;
throughout the ten directions of the world, there are none left out,
for they cause all sentient beings therein to attain awakening, making them always conform to the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Just as they practice giving through dedication, they likewise maintain the observance of precepts;
with diligence over a long period, they never retreat or falter. With patience and gentleness, their minds remain unshakable;
through meditative concentration, they hold the mind constantly on a single object. Through wisdom, they realize that objects are identical to samādhi.
They thoroughly penetrate the past, future, and present; there is no one in the world who can reach their limit.
The physical, mental, and verbal activities of these Bodhisattvas—all such deeds—are entirely pure.
Without exception in all their practices, they are equal to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Just as the dharma-realm is without discrimination, And all conceptual proliferation and attachment are forever exhausted;
Just as nirvāṇa is without obstruction, The mind is likewise always free from all grasping.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have already revealed All the dharmas of dedication possessed by the wise.
All various roots of goodness are dedicated; Therefore, one can accomplish the path of a Bodhisattva.

Sons of the Buddha who skillfully train in this dedication Fully fulfill immeasurable practices and vows, Gathering the entire Dharma-realm without exception; Therefore, one can accomplish the powers of the Sugata.
If one wishes to accomplish the vast and sublime conduct of a Bodhisattva as taught by the Buddha, one should properly abide in this dedication. These sons of the Buddhas are called Samantabhadra;
all sentient beings may indeed be counted, and the mental scope of the three periods of time may also be known.
Thus, O Samantabhadra, sons of all Buddhas, The limits of your merit can never be measured.
One might measure the void with a single hair, Or count the number of atoms in all lands;
Yet, O great sages, sons of all Buddhas, The conduct, dwelling, vows, and practices you maintain are beyond measure.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the word-by-word explanation: What is meant by "the immeasurable dedication equal to the Dharma-realm"? The explanation says:
Just as the Dharma-realm has no center or periphery, the mind of dedication has no center or periphery; just as the Dharma-realm has no agent, the mind of dedication has no agent;
just as the Dharma-realm has no coming or going, nor distance or proximity, the mind of dedication has no coming or going.
The wisdom of dedication that perceives the far and near *dharmadhātu* as being like space;
the inconceivable wisdom of dedication to the *dharmadhātu* which is itself inconceivable; the wisdom of dedication that has no basis in the *dharmadhātu*;
the wisdom of non-reliance, which is the common abode of all Buddhas throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*; and the dharma of the common abode of all Buddhas, which is without reliance.
The wisdom of dedication that is not encompassed by the three times or by any temporal divisions of arising and ceasing;
the wisdom of dedication in which the perfection of the dharma-realm and activities throughout the three times are present before one;
the dedication in which the activities of the three times are perfected and manifest before one; and the dedication with sovereign mastery over existence and non-existence within the dharma-realm.
This wisdom, being sovereign over existence and non-existence, is intended to cause both oneself and others to be unimpeded and sovereign, just like the *dharmadhātu*, as are all Buddhas.
For this reason, it is called the "Equal to the *Dharmadhātu* Infinite Dedication.
Its great purport is to cause all who have resolved for *bodhicitta* to become one with the *dharmadhātu*, such that all their virtuous functions are sovereign, perfect, vast, and without limit.
It is because it is limited by being free from the nature of large or small, and does not belong to the finite measures of one, two, three, hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, or millions;

it is a dharma of immeasurable limitlessness, encompassing the world, the supramundane, great wisdom, great compassion, joy, and equanimity, as well as the realm of dharmas and the realm of sentient beings.
If one does not dedicate in this manner, even if one seeks bodhi, one will only attain the two vehicles and dwell in quiescence.
Bodhisattvas who delight in being born in the Pure Land all dwell outside the gate; the three vehicles in the open space of the white ox-cart do not correspond to their lot.

These ten stages of dedication cause those of the three vehicles who have attained the supramundane mind to realize the nature of worldly birth and death as the self-nature of the Dharma-realm, and to give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Because it enables one to perceive that the nature of sentient beings is the dharma-realm wisdom, one attains the gate of impartial compassion and enters the mansion of universal radiance and perfect wisdom.
Thus, one does not allow them to dwell long in the grass huts or the illusory cities; this is precisely as the Layman Vimalakīrti described:

this single-period dharma-gate is a small portion of the *Saṃnipāta* teachings that causes those of the three vehicles to turn toward [the Great Vehicle], while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the revealed [truth].
The vehicle of the white ox of the ground briefly presents one portion of the treasure-place;
it is universally bestowed upon the gate of the Dharma-realm, the great wisdom of the Buddha-fruit of Universal Radiance, and the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices—this concludes the entirety.

Thus, within the sūtras of this division, the ten stages of Dedication serve to dedicate the great compassion, great wisdom, and the ten thousand [qualities] of the Dharma-body found within the ten Abidings and ten Practices.

One practices the adornment of merit for oneself and others; yet, due to obstructions, lack of true compassion and reverence, and narrow views, one’s compassion is not universal and the mind is not vast, failing to accord with the infinite *dharmadhātu*.

One should dedicate these [merits] so as to equalize and purify them, making them accord with the unimpeded, infinite, and sovereign nature of the *dharmadhātu*. If one does not do so, by means of the infinite...
To dedicate and make vows for the sake of all infinite sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, yet to dwell solely within the gate of reality and be reborn exclusively in the Pure Land—
failing to accord with the unimpeded equality of defilement and purity within the Dharma-realm, and failing to manifest the infinite, coessential great compassion—
is why the fruit of Buddhahood is not attained. Thus, these ten dedications correspond to the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten grounds.
The practice-gates of the eleven stages are all contained therein. Regarding this meaning, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are not further individually assigned;
rather, one takes the ten names for the Buddha-fruit within these stages and collectively designates them by the same name as "Wondrous Bodhisattva.
The names for the Bodhisattvas within the ten stages are identical to those of the Bodhisattvas in these ten stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The names Vajradhvaja and Garbha refer respectively to the Buddha-fruit of marvelous activity and the dharmas practiced therein; these are no different from this [Garbha stage].
However, because one has accumulated merit and the power of great compassion has reached fulfillment, it is called "Garbha" (Womb/Treasury).
It is not a separate dharma external to the stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Therefore, among the ten stages of Dedication in the life of Sudhana, the spiritual friends—
That is to say, the elder, the celestial deity of heaven, and the celestial deity of earth represent the ten stages (*bhūmi*); the nine night goddesses represent the stages of knowledge;
and the one [deity] represents the wife when the Tathāgata was a prince, signifying the position of exclusively cultivating great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

This clarifies the stages of wisdom cultivated through the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and the ten practices (*caryā*), while the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) use the power of vows to bring about universal integration and harmony.
Through the cultivation of the aggregates of the ten stages (*bhūmi*)—in which wisdom and compassion advance equally—one brings great wisdom and great compassion to profound and vast completion;
thus, these are symbolized by ten female figures. On the eleventh stage, compassion reaches fulfillment and the gateway of Samantabhadra’s conduct is realized;

this clarifies that compassion gives rise to wisdom, and thus the Buddha-mother Māyā is taken as the primary spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) at the beginning of the eleventh stage, capable of giving birth [to the realization].
All Buddhas take Māyā as their mother because she represents the stage of compassion (*karuṇā*), while the Buddha represents wisdom (*prajñā*);

since wisdom arises from compassion, it is said that "Māyā gives birth to the Buddha. Thus, one attains the Dharma-gate of illusory birth. This clarifies that the virtues of compassion and wisdom are perfected and the practices of Samantabhadra are fulfilled;
it thus elucidates the sequence of progressive cultivation. If established in this manner, even through a single practice...
At that time, those who advance together are like the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha in the second stage, the "Ocean Gate," among the Ten Stages of Sudhana;
he has accomplished the gate of compassion and wisdom for the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
For this reason, there are within it ten kings, such as the Asura King and others, which symbolize the practice of entering into birth and death. Furthermore, Sāgaramegha is this...

Because one can enter the great ocean of birth and death during the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and because the ocean of birth and death is itself the ocean of the Buddha, it is said that a Buddha appears and preaches the *Puyan jing* (Universal Eye Sūtra). The manifestation of the Ten Kings and others represents the mastery of the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*).
Furthermore, even the cases from the seventh stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—such as the laywoman Śuddhā (*Xiushu Youpoyi*) and others—are likewise established solely through this.
Furthermore, regarding the discussion on the increase and decrease of matured habitual tendencies, these five stages of the Dharma-gate do not, in total, transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa;
because they are established from beginning to end within that single moment, they possess no sense of temporal sequence.
The Sixth Assembly, held in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*).
Chapter Twenty-Six, Part One: "The Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*).
[Treatise] This chapter is explained through a fourfold analysis: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the reason for its inclusion.
The third section outlines the sequence of his advancement; the fourth follows the text for explanation. First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter:

why is it called the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmi-varga*)? The commentary states: it is because the universal radiance wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata constitutes the essence of the grounds. As the sūtra says:
"In this way, the Bodhisattva has already trodden upon the Tathāgata’s ground of universal radiance," which is the Great... [text continues].
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the differentiation of the four wisdoms and the omniscience regarding all aspects (*sarvākāra-sarvajña*) that has been explained;

it takes this as the essence of wisdom. Although Bodhisattvas have ascended through the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), they do not depart from this essence.
However, because the power of their path is not yet sufficient, they further cultivate it through the ten pāramitās and ten levels of progress, thereby perfecting that path.
The perfection of power is called the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, because each single *pāramitā* inherently contains these ten qualities, they are called the ten stages.
Within each set of ten, there are one hundred; yet since these hundreds do not deviate from the ten, they are called the ten stages.
This continues up to one thousand, ten thousand, one hundred thousand, ten million, one hundred million, one billion, and even up to ten times the unspeakable (*anabhilāpya*).
It is called the "Ten Grounds" because these ten numbers encompass the inexhaustible unity and multiplicity; thus, the dharma of these ten grounds pervades the cause,
and the ten objects of faith within the Ten Faiths are precisely the ten fruits of Buddhahood taught in the Hall of Universal Radiance,
beginning with the Buddha Immovable Wisdom as the first faith, and continuing through to the Buddha Unobstructed Wisdom.

The ten Wisdom Buddhas of Liberation constitute the fruits of what is to be believed; within the process of progressive cultivation, one passes through the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications.
Furthermore, by taking the ten wisdom-fruits from within the Ten Faiths, one establishes the substance of these Ten Grounds.
Among the ten Wisdom Buddhas, Immovable Wisdom Buddha serves as the foundation—this is Immovable Wisdom.
The Buddha takes the wisdom of universal radiance as his foundation; the wisdom of universal radiance takes the wisdom of non-abiding as its foundation;
and the wisdom of non-abiding takes all sentient beings as its foundation.
This is like when Sudhana visited Maitreya Bodhisattva, yet Maitreya caused Sudhana to see his very first spiritual friend, Mañjuśrī.
This is its meaning: even up to the fulfillment of the five stages, one does not depart from the Buddha-fruit of the initial faith.
Because this Dharma of the ten stages penetrates from beginning to end as a single, boundless gateway, it is titled the "Ten Stages" (Daśabhūmi).
"Stage" (*bhūmi*) has the sense of equal division; "one" (*eka*) refers to the sequence of progression through the shared and distinct levels. Thus it is.
This is indeed progress within non-progress and gradation within the absence of gradation. To speak briefly of the essence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):
if there were no "ten faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*) capable of believing that one's own mind is the initial fruit of Buddhahood, the ten stages themselves would not be established.
Therefore, without the initial mind of the ten faiths, neither the ten stages nor the fruit of Buddhahood in the eleventh stage can be realized.
Because of faith, from beginning to end, everything is entirely the fruit of immovable wisdom;

thus, one who can believe in their own mind is also the fruit of Buddhahood, that which is believed—the fruit of Buddhahood—is also the fruit of Buddhahood, and the body that practices is also the fruit of Buddhahood.
Only through such faith does true belief arise, for the cause and effect of what is practiced are ultimately no different from start to finish.

Because it is the Buddha of Moving Wisdom, this sutra contains the names of ten Buddhas for each of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications, representing the causes and effects of progressive cultivation according to their respective stages.

As for the ten grounds and the eleventh ground, they do not establish separate Buddha names; rather, they take the general names of the Buddha-fruit from within the ten dedications as their titles. Therefore, these follow the ten grounds and the eleventh ground.

The Ground merely takes up the sublime functioning of the integration of principle and wisdom and great compassion from within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), accumulating these so that the merit of one's virtuous conduct reaches maturity;
there is no other dharma. For this reason, the ten fruits of Buddhahood within the Ten Dedications are collectively named "Sublime" (*miao*) and "Luminous" (*ming*).
Having thus explained the Ten Dedications, the sublime functioning of the integration of principle and phenomena, as well as compassion and wisdom, has been harmonized.
Because the Dharma is thus established, this Tathāgata neither ascends to heaven, nor does the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven see him from afar;
there is no welcoming of the Buddha, nor the offering of worship. An ancient said: "In the tenth bhūmi, there is no welcoming of the Buddha nor the spreading of a seat.
This is because the text of the sutra has not yet reached its full conclusion; it is not that this [statement] fails to capture the intent of the sutra. It is simply...
As for the ritual procedures, they are like those in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* regarding the Great Vows and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion;

because these must be brought to fulfillment exactly as described therein, there is no need for such matters as the arrangement of seats. To clarify the ritual procedures, one follows the established methods of the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi and does not perform further distinct preparatory practices (*prayoga*), as the dharma-gates of the ten bhūmis rely solely upon the methods within the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

Taking Immovable Wisdom as the essence, the ten Buddhas of the ten months within the Ten Abodes, the ten Eye-Buddhas within the Ten Practices, and the ten Wondrous Buddhas within the Ten Transferences serve as the basis for the Immovable Wisdom Buddha of the Ten Faiths;

by adding further cultivation and progress to this, the Ten Grounds are understood to be identical to this—without departing from the original dharma. This is the second explanation of the arrival of the chapter.
The intention is to clarify that the explanation of the thirty minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) has been completed;
by means of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), one harmonizes and unifies principle (*li*), wisdom (*zhi*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the extensive arousal of great vows.

Having thus completed these, one relies solely on the preceding methods to accumulate the aggregates of practice through cultivation, thereby bringing those prior wisdoms and vows to fulfillment and causing great compassion to become profound and mature. Once this work is finished, [one enters the stages].
Since this chapter must be introduced here, Sudhana employs nine night goddesses, all of whom are female deities, to symbolize compassion;
he uses one Buddha as a wife during his time as a prince, named Gopā, to symbolize the joy of Dharma through the compassion of the ten bhūmis,
which delights all sentient beings, for these ten bhūmis are the accumulation of loving-kindness.
Because of the fulfillment of previous wisdom-vows, one attains the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) at the beginning of these ten grounds,
as it is said in the subsequent grounds, because of having attained the mind that seeks all Buddha-dharmas. Furthermore,

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are collectively called "treasuries" (*kośa*), which also symbolizes that these ten grounds are all based upon the dharmas prior to the grounds, by means of the thirty...

The seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) assist in perfecting the practice by fulfilling the great vows of aspiration, wisdom, compassion, and resolve prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva].
Because they encompass all virtues and bring them to completion as the effortless gateway to the qualities of all Buddhas, they are called a "treasury" (kośa).
A single bodhisattva alone is named Moon of Liberation; he has attained the Dharma within these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
Because it is the fruit of coolness (*śītalatā*), each [stage] has that which it symbolizes; reflect upon this and it will be understood.
Therefore, by means of this "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*), the aspiration, wisdom, compassion, and great vows prior to the stages are brought to completion.
Consequently, this chapter must appear here. Third, its progression is described through three gates: first, clarifying the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). One.
Riding upon the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*): 1. A detailed explanation of the similarities and differences [between the vehicles] according to the stages of progressive cultivation;

2. A re-statement of the locations where the Dharma was preached and the nature of the thrones; 3. An explanation of the similarities and differences between the Ten Grounds of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle, which has two parts:
first, the Ten Grounds of the Three Vehicles; second, the Ten Grounds of the One Vehicle. First, regarding the Ten Grounds of the Three Vehicles:

As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, although bodhisattvas—whether established as internal or external ordinary beings—cultivate the six pāramitās and become six kinds of human kings, if they cultivate the pāramitā of generosity (dāna), they become minor kings;
if they cultivate the pāramitā of ethical discipline (śīla), they become regional kings; and if they cultivate the pāramitā of patience (kṣānti), they become iron-wheel-turning kings.
By practicing the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) in Jambudvīpa, one becomes a copper-wheel-turning king (*tāmra-cakravartin*) ruling over two continents;
by practicing the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), one becomes a silver-wheel-turning king (*rūpya-cakravartin*) ruling over three continents;

and by practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), one attains the status of a gold-wheel-turning king (*suvarṇa-cakravartin*) ruling over the four continents, endowed with a thousand sons, through the two perfections of generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
These four gates of practice—faith, self-restraint, diligence, concentration, and wisdom—belong to the stage of the external ordinary person Bodhisattva.
The internal ordinary person stage consists of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences; within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), these are called the ten noble stages.
By cultivating the ten *pāramitās*, one attains the rank of the ten kinds of Heavenly Kings, governing the celestial realms above.

Starting from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as the primary stage, if one considers the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) for the severance of delusions within the three vehicles, those on the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) cultivate the six *pāramitās*.

By means of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they subdue the active manifestations of the five views and the five dull afflictions (*pañca-akuśala-mūla*), causing all existing afflictions to be temporarily suppressed and stilled—like a venomous snake charmed so that it cannot harm anything, remaining subdued and failing to arise. This is emptiness.
Contemplating the mind so as to realize that the fundamental nature of the mind and its objects is non-arising is called the Path of Seeing;
the Path of Cultivation involves entering quiescence through the contemplation of emptiness according to the Hīnayāna, whereby both body and cognition are entirely extinguished.

Although Bodhisattvas on the stages attain the three kinds of mind-made bodies, they do not follow emptiness into extinction because their wisdom remains; thus, they fail to fully comprehend the ground of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā-ālaya-bhūmi*).
Because the Tathāgata possesses fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he undergoes the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) beyond the three realms;
having already abandoned the death-and-rebirth of the segmented type (*prādeśika-cyuti*), he possesses the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). Regarding these:

in the first, second, and third stages, one attains the mind-made body of the bliss of *samāpatti*, because it clearly arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the application of correct wisdom and mindfulness. In the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one attains the [mind-made body] that realizes the self-nature of phenomena...
The nature of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is the luminous awareness of the self-nature of phenomena, arising according to its own nature.

Because it is attained in the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages as a co-emergent species that is without effort or volition, it is called the "mind-made body of luminous, effortless, spontaneous, and non-volitional arising.

Regarding the five views: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*); third, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); fourth, the adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and fifth, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Having seen these, the aforementioned five views are called the "proclivities of view" (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*); they can obstruct the Path of Seeing and act as afflictions for that Path.

For those of the Small Vehicle who cultivate the wisdom of emptiness to extinguish [afflictions], and for Bodhisattvas who realize that dharmas are empty and possess the practices of wisdom and compassion—whether they are born in a Pure Land or remain in the world to benefit sentient beings—they exercise mastery according to their inclinations. As for the five dull proclivities (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśaya*), [they are as follows]: 1. Proclivity of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) 2. Proclivity of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*) 3. Proclivity of ill-will (*pratigha-anuśaya*) 4. Proclivity of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*) 5. Proclivity of pride (*māna-anuśaya*) [The text continues: These five dull proclivities... [end of fragment].
These are: first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, pride; and fifth, doubt. Together with the preceding [five], they constitute the ten *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
These can obstruct the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and prevent one from acting in accordance with reality through subsequent engagement with specific phenomena.

Regarding these ten afflictions (*kleśas*), those of the Hīnayāna first abandon the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and subsequently abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation. As for the Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna, [they...]
All afflictions are harmonized through the various *pāramitās* according to principle, without interruption and without realization,
as has been explained above in the general overview of the provisional Mahāyāna teachings concerning the stages of a bodhisattva’s severance of delusions and attainment of fruits. Thus,
a bodhisattva of the ten stages cultivates the dharma of emptiness and non-arising, whereby the bodhisattva attains the ten kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) within the triple world.

Regarding the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) that occurs outside of karma, Bodhisattvas who have not yet fully understood this ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) still harbor a sense of weariness toward [saṃsāra] and their minds are predominantly inclined to seek the pure lands of the supramundane.
This is because they have not yet heard the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which reveals the fruit of Buddhahood within the One Vehicle;
or, even if they have heard it, they do not believe it, do not comply with it, do not realize it, and do not enter into it.
One might still take pleasure in the Pure Land being located in another direction and the fruit of Buddhahood occurring after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;

however, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Even if a bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās* for immeasurable kalpas, attains the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and cultivates various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), yet does not hear this *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, they are still called 'provisional'."

One who is called a bodhisattva but is not a true bodhisattva, even if they hear [this teaching], will not believe it, will not comply with it, will not realize it, and will not enter into it according to the Dharma.
This applies as a general rule to those who, like the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, are likewise unable to understand it.
Furthermore, it is said that even if there were a bodhisattva who read and recited the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, mastering them all thoroughly, and taught them to others...
To explain and master the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) is not yet difficult; rather, it is difficult to even briefly read this sutra.
This is because for those sentient beings of inferior capacity who have resolved their minds on Bodhi, it takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before they attain Buddhahood.

Thus, for non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles, this refers to the contemplation of the ten aspects of True Suchness (*daśa-tathatā*), or the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) from which they do not regress.
This is the stage where ignorance serves as the root; having resolved upon the mind through fundamental wisdom, one does not regress.

Prior to this, the time-periods, kalpas, determinate realities, pure lands, and defiled lands were entirely separated and situated in other directions, as those who indulge in longing for the former and aversion toward the latter established the various stages [of the three vehicles].
Second, regarding the ten stages of the One Vehicle: from the mind of the ten faiths, one immediately believes in the fundamental nature of one's own mind.
When ignorance (*avidyā*) is fully possessed by discerning vision, it becomes the Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna;

Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattvas such as Buddhamati and Ghoṣamati, and others, are the stage of this [realization]. By personally realizing that one’s own mind is primordial ignorance, one becomes Akṣobhyajñāna Mañjuśrī;
this is precisely the function of the wondrous wisdom of the intrinsic mind’s principle-wisdom within the *dharmadhātu*.
Having thus developed faith that the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices— the gateway of great wisdom and great compassion— is the very path one must traverse,
this serves as the basis for the faith described from the beginning of the sutra. It provides an analogy for the fruit of the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment,
as well as the ten Samantabhadras, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati-prabhāsa-rāja, and the assembly of fifty deities and spirits.

This is considered the gateway of faith established through manifest results: that the assembly of Bodhisattvas, devas, and others manifests entry into the Dharma and attains benefit because all such entries into the Dharma are identical to what the Buddha has attained;
thus, one clearly understands and follows from one's own mind that by transcending ignorance, one beholds Immovable Wisdom Buddha (Aksobhya-jñāna-buddha).
Therefore, faith is also the Buddha, and awakening is also the Buddha, for they are not different from the Buddha’s wisdom.

Because the essence and its function serve as the basis for progress and cultivation, when one gives rise to this faith, one universally perceives that the mental capacities of all sentient beings arise from the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Ordinary and sagely beings are of one substance and share the same wisdom; they possess no dual nature.
As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* regarding the Vow of the Celestial Maiden: "If these words are not false, may the three thousand..."
In that sutra, it is extensively explained that all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were entirely golden in color and possessed the marks of a great man, and at that time they made the vow:
"May all sentient beings be entirely golden in color and possess the marks of a great man. Furthermore, as stated in the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter of this same sutra:
"The various pleasures of sentient beings, as well as their wisdom regarding all skillful means, all depend upon [the Tathāgata]."
The *Buddhajñānapratiṣṭhāpana-sūtra* further states: "One should believe that within one's own mind, all Buddhas constantly appear in the world and turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
Having gained such faith, through the samādhi of skillful means, one gives rise to awakening and realizes the primordial wisdom that accords with the Buddhas;
this is called being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and becoming a true son of the Buddha. From this point onward...
The first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) abides where the Buddhas abide; that which is called the Tathāgata-nature is pure wisdom.
From this wisdom, one passes through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Within each of these positions, ten types of practitioners are assigned, corresponding to ten world-realms and ten lands. The fruits of Buddhahood resulting from these ten modes of practice are as explained previously.
Those who correspond to the stages of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices,
and the ten dedications are the practitioners within these present ten grounds— namely, the thirty-eight bodhisattvas beginning with Vajragarbha.
These thirty-seven are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*), which assist the compassion and wisdom cultivated during the preceding ten dedications.

The marvelous function of merit ultimately does not establish its own station; the Buddha-fruit is clarified through the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), wherein by the power of great vows, the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*) is perfected and the work of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is completed. In the ten *bhūmis*, it is merely brought to maturity through the power of auxiliary practices.
Upon reaching the eleventh stage, the Buddha-fruit is entirely as it was in the stage of the ten dedications. Thus says Vimukticandra.

The single Bodhisattva represents the person who requests the Dharma; he also represents the Dharma of liberation and cool refreshment within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). Thus, there are these thirty-eight Bodhisattvas.

While thirty-seven are collectively termed "Treasury" (*kośa*), the one individual is named Vimukticandra (Moon of Liberation), which specifically represents the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Those who possess such a mind are all deluded; it is not right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, in the severance of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), one should simply employ the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), the ten envelopments (*daśa-paryavasthāna*), and the ten latent tendencies (*daśānuśaya*) as the function of wisdom, rather than separately undergoing transformation outside the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Within the pores of a single hair and inside a minute speck of dust, the oceans of lands and all beings—ordinary and holy—dwell together like shadows;
how could there be any distinction between the interior and exterior of the triple world? Since even the unchanging is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be any differentiation?
As for delighting in transformations, it is solely through the power of the original vows of great compassion and the nature of the universal radiance-wisdom of the dharma-realm.

Because his nature is such that he adapts to the capacities of others to share in their radiance without distinction of place, and because he comes and goes [freely], he performs the Buddha-work by taking all worldly realms—including humans, devas, māras, and brahmās—as a single buddha-field;

The ten *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) are: first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); second, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*); third, sleep (*middha*); fourth, regret (*kaukṛtya*);
fifth, stinginess (*mātsarya*); sixth, envy (*īrṣyā*); seventh, restlessness (*auddhatya*); eighth, torpor (*styāna*); ninth, anger (*krodha*); and tenth, concealment (*mrakṣa*).

One who possesses penetrating wisdom and compassion employs these as an ocean of knowledge for the sake of the Buddhas’ vision and realization of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; therefore, they are like these flowers.
Within the ocean of the adorned realms, inside the state of Buddhahood, not only do Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages encompass the spheres of conversion and guidance;
rather, by means of the great power of their faith, they act as lords of the world, and through the vastness of their faith and understanding, they undergo vast births.
Furthermore, as described in the Vairocana Chapter, the capital city of King Priyadarśana-Sudhīra is not merely a mundane wheel-turning kingdom.
The royal city was named Flame Radiance (*Jvālāprabhā*), surrounded by a hundred trillion *nayuta* cities made of exquisite jewels.
Each measured seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, with ramparts of the seven precious substances as described in the sutra.
It was situated atop Mount Mahāmeru-puṣpaka, where thirty-seven thousand queens and court ladies resided, including twenty-five thousand.
