In the chapter on the Merits of the Radiance of the Minor Marks, the Dharma for the Repentance and Elimination of Faults as proclaimed by the Celestial Drum is taught:

one should repent and eliminate all karmic obstructions of body, speech, mind, and tongue through a number of virtuous acts equal to the total number of sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm. The devas asked: "How does one repent and eliminate them?
The Celestial Drum replied: "One should contemplate that karma does not come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below."
Together they accumulated [this merit] within their bodies and minds; even when sought throughout the ten directions, it was entirely unobtainable—and so on, as explained at length in the sutra.

When the Drum of Heaven thus preached the Dharma for the assembly of devas, the sons of the Tuṣita heaven in worlds as numerous as the atoms of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-fields attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Those who have attained the ten stages—namely, all these sons of the gods above—were all, in the past, practitioners of the ten faiths whose karma of the ten types of resolute belief served as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Having committed evil karma, they fell into the hells, but were then illuminated by the light of Vairocana, which caused them to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
There, they obtained the celestial drum that preaches the Dharma, and at once attained the ten stages and became free from [defilements].

The samādhi of the stainless is that which, through three lifetimes, attains the fruit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). If one has faith and understanding of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*) regarding karma, one attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime, as was the case with Sudhana.
The term "one lifetime" refers to the realization of the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharmatā*) upon entering the Path of Seeing;

it is a birth that occurs at no specific time within the total entry into the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, compared to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, this is the complete elimination of all contractions and distortions.

If one can believe in and practice even that which is difficult to accomplish due to the stagnation of principle, then this Dharma of the One Vehicle—its principle and wisdom being upright, neither carved nor pared down—reaches its own fundamental source. Thus, ignorance itself becomes the Immovable Wisdom Buddha;

all matters are naturally rectified, for it is by means of wisdom that one benefits beings, and this is precisely Buddhahood. Furthermore, one takes the vast and limitless compassionate vows of the Ten Dedications...
When the principle of integration is realized and the practice is vast, it accords with the wisdom-function that pervades the Dharma-realm;

yet, while fully engaged in practice, there is no agent, and while fully possessing the conduct, there is no dependence—this is because one is endowed with the conduct of Samantabhadra. For worldly beings who are greatly deluded, success is easily achieved and their merit is vast;

for those who do not believe and instead cultivate through crooked means over many eons, their work is difficult to complete and their merit is inferior, as they ultimately remain attached to their own emotions.

Those who have been born many times must still return to this teaching; as stated in this sutra, by giving rise to even a small measure of faith and joy, one obtains boundless and vast benefits, as fully described in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Minor Marks. This is explained through six gates.

First, regarding the cultivation of the ten kinds of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bala*) within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), it is said that among those [practitioners], there are some who commit evil karma.

Those who have fallen into the intermediate state of hell (*antarābhava*) yet possess the seed of faith and understanding: when the Bodhisattva Vairocana was in the Tuṣita Heaven, he emitted a light called "King of Banners" (*dhvajarāja-prabhā*).
This light shone upon the sentient beings in hell, causing them to leave suffering behind and be reborn in heaven.

There, celestial drums (*devadundubhi*) preached the Dharma, enabling them to attain the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and enter the *vimala-samādhi*. These are the three births through which they attained the fruit; these are the three births for attaining the fruit.
First, practicing the ten types of resolute understanding constitutes one birth; second, committing evil deeds and entering hell constitutes the second birth;
third, being illuminated by light and reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to attain the fruit of the Ten Stages constitutes the third birth.
This is the first gate of obtaining vast benefit with little effort. Second, the various devas attaining the fruit and the transformation of flowers from their pores.

When the clouds of offerings produced by Xinghua are presented to the Buddhas, and if there are sentient beings whose bodies are perfumed by their fragrance, all their karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished.
They shall attain the pure roots of goodness of the sovereign radiance of the Cloud-Standard of Incense.
This is the second gate: "Small Effort, Great Benefit. Third, if there are sentient beings who behold its benefit...
This lineage of the Pure Golden Net attains the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) through roots of goodness as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River;

this Wheel-Turning King transforms and teaches sentient beings within worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields—this is the third gate of "small effort, great benefit. Fourth, such pure gold...

When the net of the Wheel-Turning King’s crown emits the pure radiance from his maṇi-jewel topknot, if there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they all attain the tenth stage of a bodhisattva;
they achieve immeasurable wisdom-light and obtain the ten kinds of pure eyes, up to the ten kinds of pure minds, and so forth. This is the fourth function.

The *Fifth Sūtra on the Increasing Gate* states: "O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a person who took billions of nayutas of buddha-fields and ground them into atoms, with each atom representing one buddha-field.
Taking as many buddha-fields as there are such atoms and again grinding them into atoms, and then placing all these atoms in his right hand, he travels eastward past..."
If one were to drop a single mote of dust after every number of worlds equal to those motes of dust, and traveling thus toward the east until all such motes were exhausted—
doing likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir— if all the worlds in the ten directions,
both those upon which motes have been placed and those upon which they have not, were all gathered together to form a single Buddha-land; if there were such a thing...
If sentient beings, upon hearing this parable, are able to give rise to faith and understanding, you should know that this is even more rare and extraordinary.

The Buddha said, "Ratnapāṇi, it is just as you have said. If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing this parable, give rise to faith, I bestow upon them the prediction that they shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"One shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and obtain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata; this is the fifth gate of 'small effort yielding vast benefit.

The sixth sūtra says: 'O Ratnapāṇi, suppose there were a person who reduced as many great Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a thousand billion Buddha-fields—just as described above—into fine dust, and took these atoms...'"
Following the previous analogy, each [particle] is reduced one by one until they are gathered together to form a single Buddha-land,
which is then ground into dust; proceeding in this sequence and repeating this process eighty times,

all such vast Buddha-lands and their constituent atoms are seen entirely by the Bodhisattvas, through the power of their pure physical eyes resulting from karmic retribution, within a single thought-moment.
He is able to see clearly and behold as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten billion vast Buddha-fields,
shining with pure radiance like a crystal mirror throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields;
such is the power of the precious hands of this Universal Monarch of Pure Golden Nets, accomplished through the roots of goodness and the merit of his profound samādhi.
This concludes the sixth section on the gate of attaining vast benefit from a small effort. Thus it is clarified that this Dharma-gate of the sutra is infinite and boundless:
the mind of faith and understanding for a single thought-moment is infinite; that mind of purity is infinite;
the mind of making offerings to all Buddhas and benefiting all sentient beings is infinite; and the attainment of the vast and infinite through a single moment of correspondence is infinite.

The great benefit consists in clarity: because fundamental ignorance is [transformed] into the fundamental wisdom that arises from it, all roots of goodness become vast and limitless, for wisdom is non-reliant and equal to the *dharmadhātu*, and the roots of goodness one performs are likewise equal to the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, those who obtain such vast benefit upon hearing the Dharma in a single thought-moment do so precisely through this.
Because it gives rise to the seeds of faith and joy within the gates of the teachings, the general outline is as follows:

The Buddha who dwells in the womb, manifests birth, and appears to be born and pass away in this impure land of Sahā, provides the provisional teaching of guidance for sentient beings of inferior understanding;
this is precisely the teaching of the Three Vehicles. As this sutra states: "For the sake of sentient beings of inferior understanding, he emerges from the mother's womb."

This Flower Garland teaching, which manifests as the lotus-birth for sentient beings of superior faculties, was spoken by the Reward Buddha of Great Wisdom, the Universal Radiance of the Dharma Realm; it is not the body born of or passing away in a defiled land.
Therefore, it is taught for those of the highest of superior faculties. Although those who study the teachings of the Three Vehicles may cite this teaching, [it remains distinct].
One may understand the characteristics, practices, and stages of the three vehicles' teachings;

yet, if one's mental conception is not expansive and does not accord with the wisdom of the teaching, then taking this teaching gate to be identical to the teaching of the three vehicles' three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* would merely involve returning the provisional to the real. This indeed accords with the Sage’s intention.
How could one instead return the real to the provisional, thereby undermining the Sage’s exposition, deviating from the path, and losing the opportunity for advancement toward Buddhahood?
Even if one were to spend a hundred thousand million *trisaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it would still contravene the Sage’s intent;

for within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, these doctrines exist in their respective parts, yet because students are unable to comprehend them, the Buddha opened up this unsurpassed and correct exposition for those who are deluded, lest they instead give rise to obstructions—just as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "This sūtra is for those of the Mahāyāna."
That which is called the "Supreme Vehicle" refers to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles being [ultimately] the Mahāyāna;
thus, the Supreme Vehicle is the teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is a teaching that turns the Three Vehicles toward the One Vehicle.
By citing the Dragon Girl, it demonstrates that the reality of the principle of the Dharma-realm is timeless—that is, it is manifested within the span of a single kṣaṇa.
To achieve Buddhahood through three lifetimes is to shatter the emotional dust and kalpic attachments of the three vehicles;

conversely, it is called "transformation" when one takes the three vehicles' three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as the true [path], thereby turning the wondrous *vaidūrya* jewel-mirror of many lifetimes away from its clarity due to the thick veil of emotion, so that it resembles the dullness of copper or iron.
By means of the bright, pure, and true *Jambūnada* gold, one causes [the mind] to become like a discarded clod of earth.
The price [of this] is not the fault of the jewel; it is simply because those who distinguish between jewels and bribes have no merit.
This preceding section clarifies the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Ten Stages.

Practitioners need only select their teachings according to their practice—whether slow or swift—and must transcend worldly sentiments of "great" and "small," "self" and "other. Simply apply what corresponds to one's faculties, and that shall suffice.
Second, regarding the establishment of the sequence of progressive cultivation according to the stages, there are ten sections.

First is the section clarifying the cause for attaining the fruit within the ten kinds of faith; that is, taking the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom as the primary fruit of Buddhahood, and representing it through the ten bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī Bodhyagra, while the practitioner is represented by the Golden-Colored One.

The ten worlds, beginning with the World-Equivalent (*lokadhātu*), constitute the dharmas to be cultivated; the golden color symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while the remaining nine represent its various functions, making ten in total.
These correspond to the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which are the practice of the conditioned mind of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Because this involves the arising of faith within the colored mind, this is the assembly gathered in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance" at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*) during the second assembly.

Just as Sudhana’s vision of Mañjuśrī represents the stage of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*), it clarifies that the principle of one's own sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) pervades the beginning and end of both cause and fruit;
thus, secondly, from faith one first ascends the gate of the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit.
This corresponds to the third [stage], ascending the summit of Mount Sumeru to expound the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—the ten fruits of Buddhahood—the names of which are identical.
The moon represents the resultant dharmas of this stage; the ten Bodhisattvas, beginning with Prajñā, represent the practitioners who have entered this stage.
The ten worlds, all named "Flower," symbolize the blossoming of the flower of wisdom upon entering this stage, as the mind unfolds.
This signifies how Sudhana attained the power of recollection on Mount Sumerukalpa.
The "Gate of the Radiant Wisdom of All Buddhas" represents the Buddha’s wisdom of the first assembly and his abiding in the state where the Buddha dwells;

thus, this "Exalted Peak Mountain of the Ten Abodes" signifies the sublime wisdom within stillness. It corresponds to the trigram Gen (Mountain), to the mountain itself, to stillness, and to the gate-towers.
It represents the youthful and ignorant, as well as the initial ascent of light upon Mount Sumeru; this third stage is likewise identical to this.

Regarding those who have already abided in the gate of practice for the Buddha-wisdom, this refers to the fourth assembly, the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices in the Yāma Heaven Palace.
Within it, there are ten instances of the Buddha-fruit, all of which share the same name and are titled "Eye.
These are the fruits of practice in this stage; the ten [Bodhisattvas] such as Guṇakara (Virtue Forest) all share the common name "Forest."
The Bodhisattva represents the practitioner; the ten worlds are all named "Wisdom" because within the practices of this stage, they constitute the dharmas of wisdom and skillful means.
Thus, in the allegorical teachings, at the Country of the Three Eyes, one sees a bhikṣu walking back and forth beneath a grove of trees.
This represents the vastness and abundance of his practice, which nurtures and covers others like a forest; his walking back and forth represents his active cultivation of these practices.
Because there is no abiding, the "three eyes" represent the three eyes of the wisdom-eye (*jñāna-cakṣus*), the prajñā-eye, and the dharma-eye;

these two stages are called the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*). The Ten Practices (*daśa-carita*) correspond to the moon, and the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmana*) correspond to the eyes.

Regarding the ten names of the Buddhas mentioned above, they are all uniformly named "Wondrous" (*miao*); this signifies that the function of wondrous wisdom is perfected and the merit of advancement has matured, for the wondrous lies therein.

Each of these preceding points has its own symbolic significance; their names were not assigned arbitrarily. The fourth great vow is the inexhaustible gate wherein principle and phenomena, compassion and wisdom, are harmoniously integrated.
This corresponds to the fifth assembly, preached in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, which expounds the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Through these inexhaustible great vows, one integrates and unifies wisdom, principle, and great compassion, thereby fulfilling the practices of Samantabhadra and attaining the fruit of Buddhahood across ten kalpas.
The superior name is called "Exquisite" (*Miao*); this signifies the fruit of this stage for ten bodhisattvas.
The inferior names are all the same, called "Banner" (*Dhvaja*); this represents the practitioners of this stage. Ten worlds are named "Exquisite";
these signify the world of the practice of this stage, wherein the wondrous functions of the myriad practices—namely, wisdom, principle, compassion, vows, and merit—are taken as the worlds.
Therefore, as illustrated by Sudhana’s vision of the Elder Gandhahastin selling incense within the manifestation of the Dharma,
this stage of the path clarifies that one takes the inexhaustible variety of wisdom and the variety of vows and practices— arising from both principle and wisdom, as well as compassion and vows—
and blends them with the honey of dedication into a single pill of the incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

The wisdom that dwells without dependence pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it manifests physical bodies in accordance with the illnesses [of sentient beings] to subdue them, bestowing the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body while remaining unattached—just as the blue lotus possesses the foremost color and fragrance yet remains unattached.
It is the harmonious union of vows, wisdom, compassion, and the Dharma-body, comprising the ten pāramitās, the four means of integration, and the four immeasurables.
Seventeen: The Section on the Aids to the Path. The mundane and supramundane dharmas are combined into a single dharma, just as various fragrances are blended to form a single incense pellet.
Fifth: The Door of Cultivating and Accomplishing Virtues. Sixth: The Assembly in the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, where the Dharma-door of the Ten Stages is taught.
This clarifies that the dharmas of the ten stages consist solely in cultivating the aforementioned "turning over" (pariṇāmanā).
Regarding the dedication of dharmas so that virtuous conduct and merit may ripen and be fulfilled through the ten dedications: there is no other path for the practice of these vows than this.
Within the world of the Buddha-fruit, one simply adopts the sublime functions shared with the ten dedications;

they are not established separately, nor is there any need for the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven to see the Buddha approaching from afar and prepare a seat or welcome him, as this serves to clarify the ten [stages].
The dharmas within the Grounds (bhūmi) have already been explained according to the Ten Dedications (daśa-pariṇāmanā);
having concluded their integration, they differ only in terms of being "unripe" or "ripe," as there are no further distinct paths.

Therefore, the practice-entrances and contemplative wisdom of the tenth and eleventh grounds serve to reinforce the preceding fruits, just as the long leaves of a radish nourish its root; this is like the "Middle Way Wealth" symbolized by Sudhana.
He saw the night goddess named Vāsantī—translated here as "Mistress of Spring"—who presides over the city of Kapilavastu in the kingdom of Magadha.
This goddess presides over spring and oversees the growth of crops;
she is also called "Abiding in Fearlessness," meaning she serves as a refuge of fearlessness for all sentient beings. From her body, stars emerged, illuminating the multitude.

Born from each and every pore of his body, he manifests to transform and deliver countless beings in the evil realms who dwell in Kapilavastu—this city being called "Yellow" (Kapila)—in order to clarify that this city is located at the center of Jambudvīpa.

This signifies that the soil of the central palace is yellow, representing the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), the realization of the Middle Way, and the state of an Arhat, which is impartial and free from bias. Thus it is.
This night goddess who manifested the place where the Tathāgata attained enlightenment is, in essence, a goddess;

she represents how one who has attained wisdom transforms it into compassion. Because her wisdom is divine (*devī*), and because that wisdom is spiritual (*divya*)—being beyond non-contemplation and universally sustaining all existence—she symbolizes the first stage, the Joyful (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*). From the ninth [stage] onward...
From the time of this dedication until the ninth stage, they have all entered the rank of the divine; their enlightened advancement and wisdom-penetration bring infinite benefit to beings.
Because their wisdom spontaneously pervades all without the need for deliberate thought, I shall speak briefly here; the details are found in the subsequent texts.
As for all instances where Sudhana asks a spiritual friend about the duration of their resolve and how long they have been in the world, these are all...

This clarifies the accomplishment and cultivation of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), showing that although the kalpas one dwells in are vast and distant, the profundity of great compassion is such that even an eternity of wisdom is but a single moment.
This is as seen in the case of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, whose name and the teachings he expounds are titled the *Compassion Sūtra* (*Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka*).
Furthermore, it is as described in the seventh of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Knowledge [is attained] together with Bodhisattvas who have correctly entered the eighth stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Both the gates of compassion and wisdom within the seventh and eighth dedications must be thus harmonized from beginning to end before the meaning of the sūtra can be understood.
One must not see a single dharma as being able to fully realize the Buddha-mind; understand that these ten stages (*bhūmi*) are merely like the dharmas found within the ten dedications.

Because the aggregates are cultivated to perfection and compassion and wisdom fulfill former vows, this is the first stage, the Joyous Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), wherein one attains the mind that seeks the fulfillment of vows, as it is accomplished by relying on the previously mentioned ten minds of dedication and aspiration.

Regarding the sixth section, "The Gate of Infinite Freedom in Benefiting Sentient Beings through the Perfection of Virtue and the Completion of Practice," this is taught in the third dhyāna; it is the seventh assembly of the sūtra according to the Sanskrit original.
In the future, there will be one hundred trillion verses based on the *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-mūla-karman-sūtra*.
This sūtra explains that after the Tathāgata had transformed those of the three vehicles, he subsequently led the assembly of the three vehicles to the foot of the Bodhi tree to recount,
in their proper sequence, the various assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as they were originally preached when he first attained perfect enlightenment in the past.

Upon reaching the third dhyāna, as explained in the *Sūtra on the Original Karma of the Garland*, the stage of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) across the eleven stages constitutes the position of a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*). This stage is where the practices of Samantabhadra are fulfilled;

because the eleventh stage is that of the Tathāgata of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), this is considered "one life. It is like Sudhana, who, within the manifestation of dharmas through his practice, beheld the Buddhas.
Because Lady Māyā, the mother, practices this, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are clarified through the gate of accomplishing practice by means of wisdom following from compassion.
This refers to the Night Goddesses and the wife of the Tathāgata when he was a prince, named Gopā—translated here as "Guardian of the Ground.
These ten female attendants mature great compassion and guard the ground of great loving-kindness and compassion.

Just as in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) across the eleven stages, when the practice of compassion is perfected, wisdom arises from that compassion to extensively benefit sentient beings;

this is precisely what is symbolized by the Mother of Buddhas. "Mother" signifies compassion, which gives birth to great wisdom to transform and benefit sentient beings—referring to the ten spiritual friends within the stage of Equal Enlightenment. Therefore, it is said:
Because Māyā gave birth to the Buddha and the Buddha is wisdom, the seventh stage— the perfection of virtuous conduct and the final gate of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood—

is as explained in the eighth assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*) through the eleven chapters of the sutra. The first of these is the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśadhyāna-parivarta*),

followed by the ten supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the ten patiences (*kṣānti*), the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the lifespan of the Tathāgata, the dwelling places of bodhisattvas, and the [incomprehensibility of] the Buddha’s...

The "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks and Minor Characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Characteristics," the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," and the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" follow the format of the inquiries in the first assembly;

furthermore, there are ten chapters concerning the *Śikhin* (Crest) that have not yet been explained, as the extant texts are incomplete. All of these are to be understood through the symbolic teachings seen within Sudhana’s journey.
The conduct of the Bodhisattva Nala is explained as being identical to that of Sudhana, because both attain the fruit of Buddhahood within a single lifetime.
Consequently, within the pavilion, he manifests the conduct of three lifetimes, all of which are contained within the present. These three lifetimes are:
first, the lifetime of seeing the Path and practicing cultivation in the distant past; second, the present lifetime of attaining the perfection of the fruit; and third, the future lifetime.
The manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment and appearing in the world occurs entirely within the pavilion, as it is now manifest before us;
for past, future, and present cannot be apprehended. Nevertheless, the characteristics of the three births are not discarded, as they exist therein.
One knows them through wisdom for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions and benefiting others—this is precisely what constitutes the three births. If one were to consider...
In the True Treatise, there is no time when the bodhicitta is generated; there is no time of practicing or seeing the Path;
there is no time of attaining the fruit in the present life; and there is no time of manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment in the future.

Because the three periods of time and the mind-measure (cittamātra) lack intrinsic nature, because there is no establishment [of phenomena], and because there is no location or basis for dwelling, this is called the "time of becoming a Buddha. If one perceives this for oneself...

When the mind is capable of generating the bodhicitta, at the time one shall attain perfect enlightenment in the future, it is not called the "time of generating the mind" because of the arising and ceasing of emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā-vijñāna*).

For this reason, from the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood, all are inseparable from the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*), even unto the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct which is without beginning or end; this is the "Chapter on Leaving the World."

In sum, they do not depart from the Hall of Universal Radiance; this clarifies that cause and effect share the same root, for the ultimate goal of spiritual progress is the immovable Great Wisdom of Universal Radiance.

Since at that time [the goal] has no substance and wisdom has no dependence, Maitreya causes Sudhana to see his first friend, Mañjuśrī, once again—this immediately clarifies that the ultimate fruit does not shift from the cause, Sudhana.

The thought of seeing Mañjuśrī, hearing the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and personally seeing one’s own body enter the body of Samantabhadra clearly symbolizes that the cause of perfect enlightenment does not depart from the practice of the fruit;
it comprehensively clarifies the total convergence of cause and fruit, for the practices are fulfilled all at once.
Thus, this is the realm of wisdom, which is able to contain the vast capacities and mental measures of all sentient beings.

Since an eon (*kalpa*) is but a single moment and because the wisdom of the enlightened ones is devoid of emotionality, it does not depart from the Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalajñāna-buddha*) within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Because this [wisdom] has no prior, middle, or posterior limit, it is as stated in the verse by Mañjuśrī regarding the ten stages of faith:
"In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus one understands.
The third matter concerns the transcendence of all skillful means to achieve the ten powers;
this is the eighth gate of the constant practice of the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra, as explained in the ninth assembly within the "Chapter on Leaving the World.

This refers to dwelling constantly in the world to benefit sentient beings boundlessly, acting in accordance with the karmic conditions rather than in cooperation with worldly passions; this is precisely what is recalled within the practices symbolized by Sudhana.
When Mañjuśrī first encounters his friend, he hears the name of Samantabhadra and sees himself entering the body of Samantabhadra;
this is the completion of the attainment of the Buddha-fruit, wherein one constantly practices the conduct of Samantabhadra without beginning or end.

Practicing these deeds of Samantabhadra also clarifies that one does not depart from the fundamental, universally radiant wisdom that abides nowhere. An ancient commentator explained this as "reuniting with Samantabhadra."
The Dharma Hall of Radiance and the Three Assemblies of the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall are not to be considered as separate or redundant;

rather, their general principle is clarified by the fact that they are all subsumed within a single, universally radiant, non-abiding, great wisdom. This wisdom perfectly encompasses the three matters:

the cause of the initial aspiration for enlightenment, the fruit of Buddhahood, and the fulfillment of the practices of cultivation. At no time do these three ever depart from this wisdom, nor does it ever undergo transition.

Because the illumination based on wisdom gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) such that there are no traces of emotional views from beginning to end, the ninth is the "Gate of the Tathāgata’s Constant Fruit of Buddha-Wisdom, Neither Emerging Nor Submerging. This refers to the teaching of the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta Sūtra* within the tenth assembly;
for the dharmadhātu is the constant fruit of the Buddha. The tenth represents the communication of the six stages of people.
The gate of seeking and advancing through the Dharma refers to the location of the Great Stūpa at the eastern assembly of the City of Awakening (Ratnāvatī),
where Sudhana beheld Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the five stages of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) below him;
these ten gates above are a comprehensive reiteration from the time of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), intended to guide the student.

In order to facilitate the understanding of the meaning of the sutra, this section also briefly cites the sequence of the *dharmatā* (symbolic teachings) regarding Sudhana’s spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to harmonize them for easy comprehension.
Third, the re-statement of the locations where the Buddha preached the Dharma and the nature of his seats has three points of significance:
first, to describe the locations of the preaching and their underlying intentions; second, to describe the locations where light was emitted and their intentions.
Regarding the first section, which describes the location of the teaching and its underlying intention:
there are ten such locations and eleven underlying intentions. The first is the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree;
one occasion was at the banks of the Nairañjanā River, five *li* from the village of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa. This is the first.

The "Bull’s Roar Ground" is an araṇya (hermitage) where one attains the Way; according to worldly conventions, this is the method for transforming sentient beings, though the Buddha does not possess such [distinctions].
Even ascending to heaven is entirely a manifestation of the underlying principle.

If one considers the Tathāgata from the perspective of the essence of wisdom, it pervades the ten directions, eternally omnipresent without coming or going, yet manifests physical bodies in response to beings.
Therefore, this clarifies that there are worldly established dharmas which can be emulated and studied.
This section constitutes the second assembly, the "Gate of Exhorting Sentient Beings to Practice" wherein the Tathāgata cites his own fruits of realization.
According to the teachings of the ancient masters of old, it was located three *li* from the Bodhi tree; others say it was built by a dragon. It is difficult to determine which is correct.
Furthermore, as for the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*), it refers to the hall where the retributive abode of universal radiance wisdom is manifested.
The essence of this wisdom is vast and immeasurable. The retributive realm is infinite, layered upon layer, and pervades the entire Dharma-realm, just as was described at the beginning of the sutra.
Its ground is composed of solid diamond, and rows of jewel trees surround the palace.
The palaces, towers, and pavilions are all brilliantly radiant, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
this is the dwelling-place of the retribution-body of the essence of clear wisdom. It is omnipresent in all places, yet all places are contained within a single hair-tip.
One cannot restrict its location; therefore, when wisdom universally observes this dwelling, it likewise pervades the ten directions, being entirely infinite.

This is the realm. Here, in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*), he expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) to clarify that by citing the fruition, faith is established;

he further takes the fruit of wisdom obtained through retribution as the "house" and speaks of the Primordial Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Akṣobhya-jñāna-buddha*) therein to serve as the substance of faith for the stage of faith.
This clarifies that one's own mind is the Immovable Wisdom Buddha. Based on this, [he teaches that] there are no phenomena external to the mind.

Because one has accomplished faith, it is the abode of the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom; returning to faith in all that exists within one's own mind, one realizes that these various discriminations are the Tathāgata’s fundamental, universally radiant great wisdom, which is inherently unmoving.

It is only because of delusion regarding the source that movement occurs, not because of any inherent motion. In the third assembly, atop Mount Sumeru, the Ten Abodes were taught to signify entering into principle and attaining resonance.

Wisdom is not something that can be attained by a mind subject to arising and ceasing; it is like Mount Sumeru in the great ocean, rising eighty-four thousand yojanas high, which cannot be reached by the grasping of hands or feet.

Thus, when the eighty-four thousand mountains of defilement abide within the great ocean of afflictions, if one is without thought or volitional action regarding all phenomena, then the ocean of afflictions will dry up.
When the mountain of afflictions is exhausted, it becomes the mountain of all-knowledge; when the ocean of afflictions is exhausted, it becomes the ocean of nature.

If one gives rise to mental deliberation, all objects of attachment cause the mountain of afflictions to grow ever higher and the ocean of afflictions to grow ever deeper, such that one cannot reach the summit of wisdom’s clarity.
Therefore, taking meditative concentration as the means, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enters into skillful means.
In the Samādhi, it is taught that this Dharma-gate should be understood as follows: the extinction of thought is wisdom (*jñāna*), while present conceptualization is delusion.
When one clings to stillness, wisdom remains latent; when the mind is empty, wisdom manifests. This is the beginning of seeing the Path and the start of entering the family of Buddha-wisdom.
It is designated as transcending the mundane, surpassing the world, and attaining the summit of the mountain of wisdom, where one is equal to the heavens and possesses sovereign mastery. Furthermore—
Because the mountain-body consists of the stabilization of the mind through skillful means so that it does not wander, *Gen* (Mount Kan) is taken as the mountain and as "stopping";
this constitutes the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*). Having given birth to the Buddha-wisdom, one dwells in the dwelling of the Buddhas;

this clarifies that wisdom is generated based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), like Mount Sumeru. In the fourth assembly, held in the Yama Heaven palace, the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*) are taught; this is above [the Ten Abidings].
Dwelling in the celestial realm, one takes the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena as the essence of practice; thus, while remaining in the world, one is untainted.

Furthermore, this "heaven" is understood as the "time-element," meaning that the Bodhisattva, abiding in the knowledge of conduct, discerns whether the faculties of sentient beings are mature or immature, and what is the appropriate or inappropriate time [to act].
Thus, one does not engage in benefiting others recklessly, but knows which afflictions are increasing and which are decreasing, acting in accordance with those increases and decreases.
The manifestation of their maturation is known as the faculties that benefit sentient beings; this is called the Dharma of Time. Following the emptiness is called Dwelling in Emptiness.
In the fifth assembly, at Tuṣita Heaven, he taught the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).
This heaven is situated in the middle of the Desire Realm and is also called the Heaven of Joyful Contentment. He clarified the Dharma-gate of Dedication: not craving nirvāṇa and not craving birth.

Death is the constant abiding in saṃsāra; Nirvāṇa is the constant abiding [therein]. Because they are non-dual in nature and abide in the Middle Way, the other four heavens are all characterized by negligence.

Just as the gods of the Form Realm and Formless Realm possess pleasures and purity that cannot be reconciled with this, so too the fine garment of the Middle Way—though the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations may preach the Dharma of the ten stages—is nonetheless [defined] by this very station of the Middle Way.
Because the cultivation of the aggregates of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) has been perfected, the ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedications) are taught.

The emission of light from above the knees symbolizes mastery over contraction and expansion; since nothing arises except through the knees, it clarifies that the Great Vow and Great Compassion of the Wisdom-Reason (*jñāna-prajñā*) pervade and harmonize throughout the ten directions without obstruction.
Nothing is achieved except through the stage of the ten *pariṇāmanās*, just as the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) rely upon this.

Because it causes the accumulation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to ripen, and because there is no separate dharma, the sixth assembly at the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) expresses the ten stages (*bhūmi*) reaching the summit of the desire realm.

Furthermore, it signifies that [the Buddha] manifests in accordance with sentient beings and does not manifest through self-emanation; thus, this celestial abode is used to symbolize the wisdom that transforms others. Moreover, regarding this celestial abode:
This is where Māra Pāpīyān resides; it represents the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) that subdues the māras of the mind.

Because it brings about the perfection of the practice of great compassion, the seventh assembly is held in the third dhyāna heaven to signify the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct and the joy of the Dharma that benefits sentient beings;
this heaven is characterized solely by the movement of the joy of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-prīti*). The eighth assembly is held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-kuṭāgāra*).

The "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" and the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" clarify that when the Buddha appears and reaches the culmination of the path of progress and cultivation, he does not depart from his original place;
this clarifies that one does not depart from the single Universal Radiance Wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) as the basis for progress and cultivation.

To say that he "ascends to the heavens" is a metaphorical expression indicating that the advancement of the Dharma fundamentally does not depart from the single Universal Radiance Great Wisdom of the fundamental samādhi.
Although the Abiding in Radiance cultivates the practice of ascending progress, its fulfillment does not depart from the fundamental unmoving wisdom;
herein lies the Great Universal Function of the Ninth Assembly. Furthermore, it was preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance as the "Illumination of the Transcendence of Worldly Dharmas.
Because the Wisdom of Universal Radiance pervades the ten directions to universally benefit sentient beings, remaining unstained by any worldly phenomena, it is named "Transcending the World."
The wisdom of universal radiance is endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra; it constantly abides in the world without emerging or entering, and is thus called "transcending the world.
Because its essence of wisdom is eternally active yet without dependence, it is called "transcendent," not because of weary detachment.
That these three assemblies are all situated within the Hall of Universal Radiance clarifies that the causal practices and their fruits, as well as the universal radiance itself, are therein.
The Fulfillment is entirely one Great Wisdom of Universal Radiance, without beginning or end, and without dependence or abiding;

therefore, if sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta, they do not truly give rise to it unless they perceive this wisdom—it is only upon perceiving this wisdom that one is said to have given rise to the mind.
As for those who seek the Buddha outside of the mind, or who grasp at signs while seeking the Truth, they all [merely] provisionally...

Although one has performed wholesome deeds, they are not yet called "generating the mind of omniscience. Therefore, a sutra says: "Riding the vehicle of omniscience, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment.
Because one rides the vehicle of universal radiance and great wisdom, one does not depart from the site of enlightenment of universal radiance and great wisdom;
this is termed "arriving here. Thus, the generation of the mind and its ultimate fulfillment are not distinct. For this reason, it is called "generating the mind."

The initial mind is difficult to clarify, and this wisdom is difficult to believe; yet once one attains faith, one can enter [the path]. Thus, while it is easy to realize the "mind of realization" (*pramāṇa-citta*), it is difficult for the "mind of initial aspiration" (*praṇidhāna-citta*) to arise;
for when faith reaches its ultimate limit, one enters the stage of realization. One need only manifest it through the samādhi of skillful means, and the realm of wisdom will immediately appear.
The fact that these three assemblies are all held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vihāra*) clarifies the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is because the myriad practices throughout the beginning and end of cause and effect are of one and the same wisdom.

As previously described in the tenth assembly, in the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* preached at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, it is clarified that the *dharmadhātu* is not separate from the meaning of providing sustenance within the world;
thus, the groves of birth and death in the world are manifested as the very essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, this is the abode where the Tathāgata dwells.
In the multi-storied lecture hall, which encompasses the entire Dharma-realm, is the Lion Throne;
it is known only by those in the ten directions who are ready for deliverance, while those lost in delusion do not perceive it—namely, the five hundred śrāvakas and other sentient beings.
At the eleventh assembly, in the city of Āḍakavatī to the east, Mañjuśrī expounded the *Samantaprabhā* (Universal Radiance) for the great multitude.
Second: because the *Dharmadhātu-sūtra* gate and the spiritual friends such as Sudhana clearly show that Mañjuśrī is the leader for those who are deluded;
because all Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings collectively rely on this Dharma as their primary teacher;
and because he is the head of non-substantial wondrous wisdom, with Samantabhadra serving as the head of practice.
They all set out simultaneously, with no sequence of before or after. The above concludes the description of the location of the assembly and the intended meaning it symbolizes.
This section concerns the manifestation of light by the Tathāgata’s own person to represent the Dharma, which consists of ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

Second, regarding the description of the location where the light is emitted and its intended meaning: this refers to the manifestation of light representing the progressive advancement of practice, which consists of eleven [perfections]. First:
In the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata" within this assembly, light is emitted twice:

first, light from between his teeth is emitted to inform the multitudes in the ten directions that the Buddha has attained enlightenment, causing them all to assemble so that he may preach the Dharma of the causes and effects of Buddhahood;

second, light is emitted from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, universally illuminating the ten directions, known as the "Light of the Power and Wisdom of All Bodhisattvas. It shines throughout the ten directions.
Having illuminated the ten directions, the light entered the wheels beneath the Buddha’s feet; this clarifies that the fruit is raised by means of the cause and that the light enters into faith.
Furthermore, from within the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft, there emerged Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-lands, with Jinaśvara at their head;
this clarifies that the practices performed by the Tathāgata himself are all-pervasive, and clarifies the pervasiveness of the Buddha’s own self-realized practices.

Because the fruition and its function establish faith, this light enters the wheels beneath the soles of the feet; this light corresponds to the light emitted from between the eyebrows when the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are taught.
This is the fruit of the Buddha’s realization which is the object of faith, whereas that [light] is the light of the fruit resulting from one's own practice and spiritual progress.
Third, in the second assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from the wheels beneath his two feet.
This is the light that accomplishes the stage of faith within the Hall of Universal Radiance;
it is the light from the wheel-mark beneath the Buddha’s foot in the first assembly, now emitted to bring about the fruit of the ten stages of faith.

Therefore, the light of the ten faiths is explicitly taught, with the feet symbolizing the foundation and the wheels symbolizing perfection, thereby manifesting the accomplishment of the qualities and functions of the Buddha-fruit through the cultivation of faith.
Within the context of faith, it is because one has faith in the perfection of the Buddha-fruit that this is the case.

This is the beginning of entering the stages [of the bodhisattva], the commencement of ascending the noble path, the first birth into the family of the Buddhas, and the initial practice of the noble conduct;
thus it is symbolized here. This clarifies that the light is emitted from the toes of the feet to signify the entry into the noble state during the teaching of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).
First, in the fourth assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from the tops of his two feet to symbolize practicing according to the emptiness of phenomena;
thus, this light is explained as representing the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), clarifying that practice arises based on emptiness.

Sixth, in the fifth assembly, the Tathāgata emits light from his knees to symbolize the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*); it represents the mutual interpenetration of principle and phenomena, as well as wisdom and compassion, through great vows.
"Conjunction is like a person's knee, which is that by which extension and contraction occur. This explains the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
"Light" symbolizes the arousal of vows and the arising of compassion; it represents mastery over both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through wisdom and compassion.

In the sixth assembly, light was emitted from between the eyebrows, named "The Radiance of the Power of Bodhisattvas. This light is the same as that emitted from between the eyebrows in the first assembly.

The light is named "Bodhisattva Power-Wisdom Radiance. This cause and effect are analogous: the first is called "Power-Wisdom" (*balajñāna*) to signify fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while this is called "Power-Flame Radiance" (*balajvālābhāsa*) to signify that one's own realization has reached the source and is thus able to illuminate the conventional.

Just as within the Three Vehicles it is designated as "fundamental wisdom" when referring to the ultimate and as "subsequently attained wisdom" (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) when referring to the conventional, so it is here.
One who clearly realizes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is able to illumine the conventional; these two have no dual essence.

Although stages of advancement are established with distinctions of priority and sequence, the wisdom is not different, great compassion is not different, time is not different, and the practices of Samantabhadra are not different.
Because there is, in total, no shifting phenomenon, it is said that all immeasurable wisdoms are spoken of according to their specific functions, yet they do not deviate from the fundamental source.

When viewed through wisdom, it can be clearly perceived; when viewed through emotion, one immediately becomes deluded. Within the gate of great compassion, worldly conventions are drawn forth such that time, kalpas, and dharmas are each divided.
If great wisdom is applied to the ultimate truth, time and kalpas fundamentally have no basis for existence, whether long or short.

To speak of these in terms of the six characteristics—general and particular—the eighth [characteristic] is found in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Light of the Minor Marks" in the eighth assembly.
From his hand, he emits light that illuminates the suffering of the evil realms and clarifies the path; this is the light of Great Compassion that reaches out to embrace the mundane world.

Within the "Chapter on the Appearance [of Light]," the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows to anoint the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and emits light from his mouth to anoint the mouth of Samantabhadra.
This symbolizes the mutual interpenetration of wisdom and principle with the myriad practices to expound the virtues of the Buddha-fruit. This is the intended meaning.
It clarifies that Mañjuśrī represents principle (*tattva*) and wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*), while Samantabhadra represents knowledge (*jñāna*) and the intent behind the myriad practices.
This expresses the mutual penetration and intermingling of quiescent principle and active wisdom. Through their dialogue, the gateway to the Buddha-fruit is revealed:
Mañjuśrī is the formless *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, the fruit of wondrous wisdom that excellently discerns the correct from the erroneous; Samantabhadra is the great [body] of the Tathāgata...
The wisdom that pervades everywhere manifests in response to the physical body, knowing the sharpness or dullness of faculties and the fruits of conventional practice.

All Buddhas attain Buddhahood by means of these two dharmas; therefore, within this teaching, the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter causes these two dharmas to be harmonized and integrated, so that the fruit of Buddhahood is realized through the non-obstruction and perfect interfusion of principle and wisdom, the myriad practices, and the Dharma-realm.
The gate of Rong was thus illuminated by the radiance [of these teachings], causing them to engage in mutual inquiry and response so that later students might find the Dharma easy to understand.
The cause and effect of these three individuals—from their initial generation of faith until the final attainment of the fruit—are mutually pervasive in essence.
Contemplate this with wisdom and reason, and the substance and function of one’s own mind will become visible. In the first assembly, the Buddha-fruit is that which the Buddha himself has realized.
Therefore, these ten stages and the fruit of Buddhahood following the eleventh stage are accomplished through the practitioner’s own power;
for by thoroughly integrating the practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, one penetrates both clarity-wisdom (*prajñā*) and means-wisdom (*upāya*), and the myriad practices are fulfilled.
Thus, from the second assembly onward, this marks the conclusion of the practitioner’s own progressive advancement. This is the first [section].
The teaching on the ultimate conclusion, which has not yet been entrusted for circulation, also appears within this "Chapter on Manifestation," as clarified previously.
In the tenth chapter, "The Dharma-realm," light is again emitted from between the eyebrows, named "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times.

Because the three times are collectively one and the same time, the Dharma-realm is taken as the totality of the resultant essence, proceeding from faith, through the stages of abiding, practice, and dedication.
The ten stages, the eleventh stage, and the fruit of Buddhahood are collectively taken as the essence of the fruit, which is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Mañjuśrī represents the principle of the Dharma-realm, while Samantabhadra represents the wisdom of the Dharma-realm. The wondrous functioning of this principle and wisdom constitutes the single gateway of the Buddha.

Taking this one gateway as the means to transform the multitude of deluded beings, it is divided into two dharmas. Yet, if one follows their faculties and accords with worldly conventions, the dharma-gates are inexhaustible.
If one discusses the ultimate principle, it does not depart from the non-existence of phenomena; the unimpeded unity and multiplicity within this state is called Samantabhadra.
He first encounters the ignorant child to lead them to the subtle discernment of the correct and the false within the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature.

Entering the wisdom of non-arising, he is named Mañjuśrī, also known as the Youthful Bodhisattva, who can share in the limits of suffering, perform deeds for the benefit of living beings, and serve the Buddhas.
The family dharma is named Samantabhadra; the two persons who penetrate its essence are named Buddhas. Original self-mastery is named the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
From the beginning through to the end, this Dharma-realm as a whole constitutes the essence, with no other dharma existing apart from it.
This chapter represents the great totality of the cause and effect of all Buddhas, and is also the great path traversed by all the sages and worthies.

There is no path that does not issue forth from this; it is also the great palace wherein the Sovereign of All-Knowledge of one’s own mind dwells and contemplates, and it is named the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) because it is that upon which all sentient beings rely. Thus concludes the third section: the description of the place where the light is emitted and its underlying intent.
Regarding the fourth section—the description of the substance of the seat and its underlying intent—there are ten points concerning their similarities and differences.

Regarding the fact that the seat at the first assembly is made of *maṇi* jewels: from the perspective of its essential nature, the *dharmakāya* is inherently stainless, and thus it is called a "stainless jewel" (*vimala-ratna*).

Furthermore, the *buddhaphala-bodhi* (the enlightenment of the Buddha-fruit) takes the stainless *dharmakāya* as its essence, while the *saṃbhogakāya* obtained through retribution and the *nirmāṇakāya* constitute its wisdom-function; therefore, this clarifies the basis upon which they rely.

Because the essence gives rise to the function of wisdom, a *maṇi* jewel serves as the seat for the second assembly. Regarding the fact that the essence of the seat in the second assembly is a lotus-flower treasury, the intention is as follows:
it signifies that the second assembly, in terms of transforming and benefiting sentient beings, causes them to establish the seed of faith;
within that faith, it signifies the practice of abiding in the world without defilement; and it signifies that taking the benefit of beings without defilement as one’s merit is precisely the lotus.
For the third assembly of the treasury, the Lion Throne of Universal Radiance Treasury was established upon the Sublime Victory Hall of Śakra;

its hundreds of thousands of tiers symbolize the stages of entry from faith through skillful means, non-thought, and non-action, which are termed "establishment" because they are the tranquil samādhis.
By the power of this samādhi, one manifests the fundamental nature of the Tathāgata.
Through the creative arising of wisdom, one attains within the Buddha-family the name "Wisdom of Fearlessness" and the "Treasury of Universal Radiance Lion-Throne.
"Treasury" signifies that this stage enters the treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; "Lion" clarifies the fearlessness of wisdom;
and "Universal Radiance" signifies the realization of the Tathāgata’s original great wisdom of the universally radiant *dharmadhātu*.

The "hundred thousand tiers" represent the stages of cultivation through the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*). They signify transcending the mundane by surpassing hundreds of thousands of conceptual calculations and ignorance, and destroying hundreds of thousands of karmic obstructions.

Regarding the seat of the Buddha-fruit, it is not generally described in terms of tiers because there is no ascending or descending in cultivation, nor any gradations in the depth of awakening and delusion, or the superiority and inferiority of wisdom. Thus, within the ten abodes, for instance, the first alone already comprises a hundred [thousand].
The "thousand-tiered" level represents the stage of entering clarity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), marking the boundary of advancing in practice to transcend karmic obstacles.

In the fourth assembly, at the Yāma Heaven palace, a lion throne within a precious lotus treasury (*ratna-padmagarbha-siṃhāsana*) is manifested; this serves to symbolize the teaching of the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā-bhūmi*).
Regarding the sphere of practice, it is "unattached in the world," as symbolized by the lotus. As for the "lion," it follows the previous *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis.

As for those of the hundred-million-fold stage, because their advancement surpasses the former and their karma is superior, it is said that they "transformed" the seats rather than saying they "arranged" them.
This indicates that by entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata, their practiced deeds follow along with that wisdom and are transformed by wisdom;
thus, like a magical manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), it does not say they were "arranged," clarifying that practice proceeds from principle and transformation.

Therefore, in the fifth assembly at the Tuṣita Heaven palace, a lion throne of the maṇi-treasury is spread upon the dais, with one hundred trillion tiers representing the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Within these, by means of supramundane wisdom and insight, one abides in the world based on the fundamental Dharma-body;
relying on the essence of the fundamental Buddha-fruit as a seat for further advancement, one returns to the source.
By means of the power of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the force of vows, one perfects the body of reality (*dharmakāya*), which is the essence of compassion and wisdom, inherently stainless.

Because this dedication causes compassion and vows to be harmoniously integrated, such that essence and function are balanced, it is said that "a seat is spread" rather than "placed" or "magically created.
As for the "one hundred million billion tiers," these represent an advancement beyond the previous stage, thereby removing defilements.
Having purified the two obstacles, one accomplishes the unimpeded *dharmadhātu* and the wisdom of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-jñāna*).

Although the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) are cultivated simultaneously throughout the five stages, according to the teachings, the first two stages are distinguished by their superior resolve for transcendence (*lokottara-citta*), while their great compassion is inferior.

In these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), wisdom and compassion are harmonized through the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*), thereby attaining their proper place; thus, the sixth stage is associated with the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.

The reason the palace of the Sovereign Heavenly King (Śakra) is described only as the "Jewel-Treasury Hall" (*maṇi-garbha-vimāna*) and not as a throne-body is intended to signify that the throne is not easily attained.

While the Tuṣita Heaven possesses a jewel-throne, here— because it represents the Dharma-nature free from defilement and the great wisdom that constitutes the gateway of great compassion to nurture all sentient beings—
it is referred to only as a "hall" and not a "throne," thereby clarifying its reliance on the aforementioned dedication.
Because the Great Compassion Palace of the Dharma King nurtures all sentient beings without distinction as they progress upward, the seventh assembly is held in the third dhyāna.
The dharma-method of this assembly teaches practice for the future; furthermore, the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Practices" briefly enumerates those practices.
This "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Practices" consists of thirty-six chapters, which is but a brief enumeration; the full version shall appear in the future.
The eight million billion verses of the eighth and ninth assemblies, held together in the Hall of Universal Radiance, collectively do not depart from the single essence of wisdom—
the Universal Radiance— encompassing the ten levels of faith, the fruits of Buddhahood reached through progressive cultivation,
the "Chapter on Leaving the World," the constant practices of Samantabhadra, the ten concentrations, the ten supernatural powers, and so forth.
Because the cultivation and advancement through the five stages, the ten faiths, and so forth are accomplished by means of this, they are all subsumed within this wisdom;
this Wisdom of Universal Radiance is shared equally by all Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings. While the Buddhas have already realized it, sentient beings are deluded regarding it;

thus, although their essence and function are one and the same, their states of delusion and awakening differ. This is considered in relation to the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) within this teaching.

One who attains this single awakening immediately realizes the knowledge and vision of a Buddha. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, [the Buddha] reveals and awakens sentient beings to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, desiring to lead them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, even unto riding upon the vehicle of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā-yāna) directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Furthermore, this sutra says: "Riding upon the Tathāgata-vehicle, the inconceivable vehicle, the superior vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle."

As stated in the first fascicle, within the praise of the virtues of the bodhisattvas, it was said that having thoroughly understood the equal dharma of all Buddhas, they have already trodden the Tathāgata’s Ground of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-bhūmi*).
This wisdom of universal radiance is such that when sentient beings are deluded regarding this wisdom, it is "delusion";
when those who were deluded awaken to it, it becomes the wisdom of universal radiance, which is "awakening. For this reason, in the first assembly, the deities and spirits manifest [this truth].
Manifesting entry into the Dharma and attaining benefit therein means that the very entry is identical to what the Buddha has entered;
it is identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It serves as a model for sentient beings to enter the Dharma, so that later students may emulate it.

Therefore, the intention behind these three assemblies all being held in the Hall of Universal Radiance is to clarify that the five stages of ascent do not depart from this wisdom—neither in the awakening through understanding nor in the practice of cultivation.

When one is not separated from this wisdom, time and kalpas have no substantiality through which they can be transmuted; furthermore, this wisdom is not different from the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
By harmonizing and integrating compassion and vows through the dharma-gate of the ten dedications, sovereign spiritual powers are entirely contained within them.
Just as practicing the ten wholesome deeds with outflows for a single lifetime can still lead to rebirth in the heavens and the attainment of karmic retribution spiritual powers, so it is here.

If one achieves rebirth in the Pure Land through even ten recitations of the Buddha’s name, how much more so for one who resolves their mind based on wisdom, further augmenting this with the practices of compassion, vows, and the various *pāramitās*?
How could such a person fail to attain the essence of wisdom and sovereign supernatural powers after this single lifetime?
When considering the reality through the perspective of wisdom, even if one were to pass through infinite kalpas, it would originally not be otherwise.
To speak of "one lifetime" when referring to a single thought-moment means that time never extends, wisdom never diverges, and birth never truly occurs; for there is ultimately no birth.
One must not pursue the views of ordinary sentiment regarding the birth and extinction of phenomena. Rather, when one knows them through true wisdom, the myriad delusions will not cause confusion.
This is as in the Western Pure Land, where the sixteen contemplation gates all consist of forming mental images; once these images are perfected, [liberation is attained].

Since one has personally attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), how much more so for one who has realized the principle of wisdom (*jñāna*)—which is non-reliant, luminous, pure, and all-illuminating—and who understands that body and mind have no internal essence, such that both internal and external views have vanished. Such a person simply relies upon this principle of wisdom to expansively give rise to an ocean of great vows;
merging compassion and wisdom within a single moment, they manifest physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) to make offerings to the Buddhas and transform sentient beings. Furthermore...
The nature of non-creatorship is universally equal; it is without mind, without master, without self-nature, and without marks. Ordinary beings and sages are as one, abiding nowhere.
By means of the dharma of non-abiding, following the wisdom of non-abiding, one makes offerings to the Buddhas and benefits sentient beings.

Practicing in this way, what great spiritual powers and supernatural faculties could one not attain? Simply by relying on and training in the Chapter on the Ten Dedications, one will immediately obtain them.
In the tenth chapter, "The Dharma Realm," it is simply stated that his seat universally pervades the dharma realm; it does not mention tiers or levels.
It clarifies that the substance of the Buddha-fruit seat is made of *maṇi* jewels. From the first assembly through the fifth assembly, the substance of the seat is consistently this same *maṇi*.
This is because the substance of the Buddha-fruit is identical. The general meaning is that wisdom and compassion are not distinct from one another.
This single locus of universal luminous wisdom dwells in the world without defilement, no different from a single wondrous principle;
the *dharmakāya* and wisdom are one and the same. This autonomous and non-reliant entity functions without effort, reaching everywhere without moving, responding to things as they arise.
Only by harmonizing and fusing principle with wisdom can this be known. The above expresses the intended meaning merely to enable...
Because sentient beings perceive phenomena and understand the Dharma, they give rise to diligence in practice so that there may be no doubt; thus it is further elaborated at length.
Regarding the knowledge of the destination, the Master of the Verses says: "The wisdom of universal radiance is equal to space; while space is merely empty, this wisdom is sovereign.
From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, one relies on this [wisdom] to reach the ultimate, and finally returns to abide in this very place."

Because it is full, the three assemblies gather in the Hall of Radiance; cause and effect are harmonized as having no separate essence. According to the stages, one advances in the practice of the differentiated wisdom of cultivation;

according to that practice, the realms of distinct retribution differ. Yet these do not depart from fundamental wisdom, which is without arising or ceasing. Therefore, the Buddha sits upon the maṇi throne.
This meaning clarifies that within the five stages of the Buddha-fruit, all ascents and progressions are by means of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Because this fundamental wisdom of universal radiance constitutes both essence and function, the cause and effect from beginning to end are not separate from it.
Thus concludes the exposition on the meaning of the essence of the seat within the Hall of Universal Radiance.
