[Commentary] Regarding the fourth section, the word-by-word explanation of the meaning, this chapter of the sūtra is divided into four parts; the first is the introduction.
This is divided into two parts: the formal exposition of the three movements of the earth and the arising of offerings, and the recitation of verses in praise of the Dharma.

First, regarding the introductory section: from the initial words "At that time, the World-Honored One... down to "...because it is well-sealed by the seal of the wisdom of the dharma-realm," there are four segments of scripture which constitute the introductory section.
Second, from "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands... [and so forth].

From "As stated below, up to the thirty-ninth fascicle, after receiving, upholding, practicing, and cultivating [this teaching], one subsequently reaches the stage of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*)—this section constitutes the "Main Exposition" (*samyag-deśanā-vibhāga*).

Regarding the "Section on the Threefold Shaking of the Earth and the Offering" (*bhūmi-kampa-pūjā-vibhāga*), it begins from "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha" (*atha khalu buddhānubhāvena*) and extends down to "and spoke these verses" (*imā gāthā abhāṣata*).
Regarding the "Section on the Fourfold Recitation of Verses Praising the Dharma" (*catur-gāthā-dharma-stuti-vibhāga*), it begins from... [text continues].

From the passage "His mind is quiescent and ever-tamed" down to the end of the thirty-ninth fascicle, this constitutes the first section of the introduction, which is further divided into four parts. [Sūtra]:
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Maṇi-jewel Treasury Hall of the Palace of the King of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, together with a great...
The assembly of bodhisattvas was comprised of those who were all non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
having gathered from various worlds in the ten directions; they dwelt in the sphere inhabited by the wisdom of all bodhisattvas,
entered the domain accessed by the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, applied themselves with tireless diligence, and were well-able to manifest various kinds of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Performing all manner of deeds to teach and transform all sentient beings without missing the proper time;
fulfilling all the great vows of a bodhisattva by diligently practicing all conduct throughout all worlds, all eons, and all lands without even momentary rest;
and fully possessing the bodhisattva’s aids to the path of merit and wisdom to universally benefit sentient beings, remaining forever inexhaustible until reaching [the ultimate goal].
All Bodhisattvas have reached the ultimate shore of wisdom and skillful means;
they manifest entry into birth-and-death and nirvana without abandoning the cultivation of Bodhisattva practices;

they skillfully enter all Bodhisattva dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, samāpattis, supernormal powers, and clear wisdom; in all their activities, they attain mastery and obtain all that pertains to Bodhisattvas.

By means of sovereign spiritual power, in a single moment and without any movement, they are able to go to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas to serve as leaders of the multitudes;
they entreat the Buddhas to preach the Dharma, protect the wheel of the true Dharma of all Buddhas,
and with a vast mind, make offerings to and attend upon all Buddhas, constantly and diligently practicing all bodhisattva deeds.
In all the activities they undertake, their bodies appear universally throughout all worlds; their voices reach everywhere throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions;

their mental wisdom is unimpeded, allowing them to see all the merits of all bodhisattvas across the three periods of time, which they have fully cultivated and brought to perfection—such that even if one were to speak for unspeakable eons, one could never exhaustively describe them.

[Treatise] First, regarding the passage from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations" down to where it says "cannot be fully described," there are eighteen lines of scripture praising the resolve and virtue of the bodhisattvas who have come. To explain the meaning:

the phrase "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the palace of the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations" clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body manifests in accordance with its respective station.
Because it manifests, it relies on a locus to represent the Dharma; this shows that the Bodhisattva’s ten stages (bhūmi) culminate at the peak of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, because one practices the ten stages for the sake of sentient beings rather than seeking anything for oneself, it is called "other-transformation" (*paranirmita*).
Moreover, because at the conclusion of the ten stages one subdues the demons of mind and境 (objects of perception), attaining mastery, one enters the stage of detachment (*viveka*).

Because the stainless samādhi is naturally conjoined with the pure and clean dharmas; because it abides at the summit of the desire realm while constantly remaining in samādhi, neither dwelling in a mind of [mere] purity nor residing in the dhyāna realms;

and because it clarifies that the function of these ten stages culminates in the Dharma-cloud, which universally moistens all without being restricted by the opposition of defilement and purity, manifesting a form-body—therefore, these ten stages are taught here in this heaven. Thus it is said.
Therefore, regarding the verse on the benefits obtained by the Sovereign Heavenly King (Īśvara) in the first assembly, it says:

"The Buddha’s body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, universally responding to sentient beings and appearing before them all; through various gates of teaching, he constantly transforms and guides them, possessing mastery over the Dharma and able to bring about awakening.
Question: For what reason did the Tathāgata descend to this Heaven of Controlling Others’ Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin)? Why does [the text] not say so?
When the Heavenly King saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he prepared a seat, went out to welcome him, and offered verses of praise; in response, [the Buddha] said:

"In this stage, one simply practices according to the Dharma-gate of the previous Tuṣita Heaven Palace—namely, the methods of dedication, vows, conduct, compassion, and wisdom—and there is no other distinct method.
For this reason, I do not describe other matters, but rather continue to accumulate merit in accordance with my former ocean of vows."
When merit is perfected and wisdom is ultimate, there is no further need for ritual acts to manifest one's advancement; rather, they are harmonized simply by relying on the Dharma.

Furthermore, it was asked: "Why does one not proceed sequentially to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), but instead leap directly to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) when explaining the ten stages (bhūmis)?
He replied: "To clarify the ten stages, one must first follow the sequential order to harmonize principle and wisdom."

The compassionate vows ascend and descend, meeting and merging in their proper place; the ten dedications harmonize these vows, such that compassion and wisdom, principle and phenomena, are equally balanced.
Broad and narrow correspond to the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm, and equality toward sentient beings serves as the measure. To manifest the locus of the Dharma, one abides in the Middle Way;
returning to this central locus, one explains the meaning of the Middle Way. Thus, in the context of the ten dedications, one brings together compassion, vows, principle, and wisdom. That is to say:
In the desire realm, the Tuṣita Heaven is situated such that both above and below it there are two heavens; these are said to be the locations of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the middle [of these], within the upper limit of the desire realm and the lower limit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is explained that one is not restricted by either defilement or purity;

this clarifies the sovereign mastery of wisdom, principle, and great compassion. Furthermore, the dharma-gate of the eleventh stage, Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), is taught; in the third *dhyāna*, it is explained as manifesting benefit.
The practices of sentient beings fulfill the benefit of living beings through the joy of the Dharma, resembling the bliss of the third dhyāna;

the fourth dhyāna represents the pervasive and perfect wondrous function of the Buddha-fruit. Furthermore, the tenth bhūmi transcends the Heaven of Joy (Tuṣita), and the eleventh bhūmi transcends the second dhyāna.
This clarifies that because wisdom increases twofold at each stage, it surpasses the sequential order. "The Palace of the Maṇi Jewel Treasury" represents...
Because stainless great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) is able to encompass and nurture all beings, it is clarified that in this stage there is no grasping for one's own peace and happiness;
rather, with the sole intent to benefit sentient beings, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Therefore, being situated within the palace of the stainless jewel-treasury (*maṇiratnakośa*), together with a multitude of great bodhisattvas—namely, the thirty-seven [bodhisattvas] such as Vajragarbha—is manifested.
Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), the *Vimukticandra* (Moon of Liberation) clarifies each individual factor of enlightenment:
because their essential nature is all liberation, coolness, and bliss, that which is "clarified" (*prabhāsvara*) is itself the auxiliary path and the true path.

Having already completed the correct vision of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), the manifestation and maturation of the ten stages differ from those of the three vehicles; thus, it is the path of seeing of the ten stages.

The provisions prior to the stages (bhūmi) constitute this One Vehicle teaching because, from the very beginning, one relies upon the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom to give rise to faith and cultivate the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).
Consequently, one does not rely on the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to suppress manifest afflictions; rather, it is only at the tenth stage that one attains the *manomaya-kāya*.
Therefore, although this teaching speaks of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, [it does so from the perspective of ultimate reality].
Regarding the phrase "as well as mind and thought" (*manas-vijñāna*): this clarifies that one does not destroy conventional objects in order to achieve discriminative wisdom;

thus, it is not the same as suppressing afflictions to remain in birth-and-death or to be reborn in a pure land. Alternatively, it is said that the realm of the three thousandfold world-system constitutes the Buddha-realm;
therefore, within this teaching, even at the stage of the initial faith, one merely contemplates the infinite Buddha-realm where every dust mote contains the ten directions and every hair-pore.

Taking the dharma-realm as the object of faith and practice, rather than saying the trichiliocosm is the Buddha’s field of retribution—as stated in the "Chapter on the Excellence of the Head" (Xianshou pin)—this constitutes the gateway for aspiring to and practicing what is to be believed.
The "Chapter on the Merit of Resolving the Mind" (Faxin gongde pin) concerns the virtue of awakening and entering the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
As the Sūtra says: "All those bodhisattvas have attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."
Regarding those who do not regress, there are five types of bodhi: first, the bodhi of the Śrāvaka vehicle; second, the bodhi of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
third, the bodhi of the Bodhisattva consisting of the practice of emptiness and the six pāramitās;

fourth, the cultivation of the ten kinds of contemplation on the semblance of *tathatā* (suchness), the cultivation of the ten pāramitās, and the overcoming of the ten obstacles to *tathatā* and the twenty-two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The five bases for the awakening of the various types of ignorance consist of cultivating the ten pāramitās through the ten kinds of Tathāgata wisdom.

Taking incalculable eons as a single kṣaṇa-limit and harmonizing incalculable lifetimes into a single lifetime, the delusion and awakening of a single thought-moment is itself the Buddha-wisdom of awakening (*bodhi*).
This clarifies that, based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one generates the bodhicitta, as explained in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The treatise also contains this passage: "Based on fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi), there is non-awakening (a-bodhi)";

and it further states, "Because one awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening. This clarifies that non-awakening exists based upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom, while awakening exists based upon ignorance (avidyā).
Regarding this awakening, according to the faculties and spiritual lineages (gotra), there are these five types of distinctions among the dharmas of awakening.

This sutra is distinct from others; enlightenment is the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha-fruit, and the non-retrogressive bodhi as described in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

Some say one attains Buddhahood by transcending kalpas, while others say, "My statements that I practiced for immeasurable kalpas to attain the path of Buddhahood are all merely countless skillful means employed for the sake of indolent sentient beings. Or it is said that one must pass through [the stages].
The statement that one attains Buddhahood only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is all spoken according to worldly sentiment for the sake of the Three Vehicles;
it does not rely on the awakening of the mind through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). This teaching concerns the awakening of the mind through wisdom.

If discussed in terms of wisdom, one does not follow deluded sentiments, but takes immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* themselves as "no time. Based upon this "no time," [the duration] is provisionally established.

To establish that a single momentary limit encompasses the infinite three periods of time, and that the infinite kalpas of the three periods of time never transcend the limit of a single moment, the Sūtra says:
"Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going. Thus, throughout these three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, while there is the state of emotion (*qing*), there is no wisdom;
yet when subsumed by wisdom, emotion resides within wisdom. Although there is the state of emotion throughout immeasurable kalpas, it remains present within wisdom.

Within the wisdom of the limit of the moment (*kṣaṇakoṭi-jñāna*), if one grasps at the sentiment that wisdom is real while phenomena are empty, [one finds that] from the beginning they have always been non-existent;
since their essence has no beginning or end, there is never a time when they can shift. When comparing these two matters, one may only follow the reality and not the emptiness.
The Sūtra says, "They all come together from other worlds," because they come from the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) to achieve the ten stages of Bodhisattva (*daśa-bhūmi*).

Because [the Buddha] goes to other directions, yet within the nature of the *dharmadhātu* there are no distinct "other directions"—for it is only by virtue of not having reached a particular location that one names it an "other direction"—so it is for all stages (*bhūmi*).
As for abiding in the object of the wisdom of all Bodhisattvas, this refers collectively to the objects of the wisdom of Bodhisattvas in the five stages;
because they reach the object of the Buddha-wisdom within these ten stages, they enter into suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the place where wisdom enters: it is for the sake of relying on the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom to give rise to the mind and enter into the distinctions of practice-wisdom, thereby perfecting great compassion;

and for the sake of skillfully entering all bodhisattva meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), as described in the "Ten Samādhi" chapter—namely, the *samāpatti*, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), clear wisdom, and the *samādhi* of luminous clarity—which can give rise to the seals of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*) and the three types of supernormal power.
This refers to what is here called "right wisdom. Regarding *samādhi* and *prajñā*:

in a single moment of thought, without any movement, one is able to reach all places of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) because the nature of the seal of samādhi-wisdom is inherently pervasive, has no interior or exterior, is always conjoined with wisdom, and is without movement or distraction.
【Sūtra】Their names were: Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, Padmagarbha Bodhisattva, Guṇagarbha Bodhisattva,
Padmaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva,
Vimalacandragarbha Bodhisattva, Sarvaviṣayapratibhāsavyūhagarbha Bodhisattva, and Vairocana [Bodhisattva].
Bodhisattva Jñānagarbha, Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭagarbha, Bodhisattva Candanaguṇagarbha,
Bodhisattva Puṣpagaṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Kusumaguṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Utpalaguṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Devaguṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Puṇyagarbha,
Bodhisattva Asaṅgapariśuddhajñānaguṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Guṇagarbha, and Bodhisattva Nara.
Bodhisattva Extended Virtue Treasury, Bodhisattva Stainless Treasury, Bodhisattva Freedom from Defilement Treasury,
Bodhisattva Treasury Adorned with Various Eloquence, Bodhisattva Great Radiant Net Treasury, Bodhisattva Pure Majestic Virtue Radiance King Treasury,
Bodhisattva Golden Ornament Great Merit Radiance King Treasury, and Bodhisattva Treasury of Pure Virtue Adorned with All Marks.
The Bodhisattva Vajrajvālāguṇalakṣaṇavyūhagarbha, the Bodhisattva Prabhājvālāgarbha, the Bodhisattva Jyotiṣpatiprabhāvyūhagarbha,
the Bodhisattva Gaganāsaṅgajñānagarbha, the Bodhisattva Manojñāghoṣāsaṅgagarbha,
the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīguṇasarvasattvapraṇidhānadhāragarbha, and the Bodhisattva Sāgaravyūhagarbha.
The Bodhisattva Sumeru-guṇa-kośa, the Bodhisattva Viśuddha-sarva-guṇa-kośa, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-kośa, the Bodhisattva Buddha-guṇa-kośa,
the Bodhisattva Vimukti-candra, and other such bodhisattvas mahāsattvas— numberless, immeasurable, boundless,
incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas, with Vajragarbha Bodhisattva as their leader.
[Treatise] The second section, from "Their names were" down to "as their leader," consists of eighteen lines of scripture;
this is the section listing the names of the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the one named Vajragarbha Bodhisattva: wisdom is his vajra.
Because "Vajra" (Gang) can shatter all delusions; because "Treasury" (Zang) refers to the pervasive excellence of wisdom and virtue, he is named *Ratnagarbha*;
because the Bodhisattva *Padmagarbha* is clear regarding all practices and is unstained by either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; and because the Bodhisattva *Guṇagarbha* clarifies the multitude... [of dharmas].
Because his virtues are perfected, the Bodhisattva Padmaguṇagarbha clarifies the wisdom-virtue adorned by undefiled multitudes of practices;
the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha clarifies the illuminating function of great wisdom;
the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabhāsa-garbha (here translated as "the illuminating function of the sun") likewise clarifies this; and the Bodhisattva Vimalacandragarbha clarifies great compassion.
The Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation of the Treasury of Adornments is so named because his mind illuminates the mundane world and shatters the flames of affliction;
the Bodhisattva Vairocana-Jñānagarbha is so named because he clarifies that the two matters of merit and wisdom are all-pervasive;
and the Bodhisattva Kusumaguṇagarbha is so named because he clarifies this bodhi... [text fragment ends].
The Bodhisattva Sa-yu-de (Guṇasa) is named "Delightful Flower" because those who see his virtues find pleasure in him as one does in a flower;
the Bodhisattva U-p'o-lo-de-tsang (Utpalaguṇagarbha) takes the blue lotus as a metaphor, which can be understood through its underlying meaning;

and the Bodhisattva Hsing-su-wang-kuang-cao-tsang (Jyotiṣprabhāvyūhagarbha) is so named because he possesses clear and distinct knowledge of the sovereign, unimpeded, and differentiated [wisdoms]. Thus it is.

The various bodhisattvas understand this through the meaning of names; one may observe that in this section there are thirty-eight bodhisattvas, thirty-seven of whom share the same name, "Treasury" (Kośa).
This signifies the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
As for the single individual, Vimukticandra, he represents the factor of enlightenment among the thirty-seven that assists awakening.
Because he brings forth the fruit of pure, cool clarity; because he acts as the master who requests the Dharma for all bodhisattvas;
and because he causes the great assembly to hear the Dharma, practice it, and attain the bliss of cool clarity.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
Having entered this samādhi, immediately throughout the ten directions, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten billion buddha-fields,
there were ten billion buddhas— each named Vajragarbha— as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields.
Appearing before him, they spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha! You are indeed able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.

Son of Good Family, this is because all the Buddhas of ten billion Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions have collectively empowered you through the original power of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana."
By the power of your vows, by the power of your majestic spiritual authority, and also by the power of your own supreme wisdom,
you desire that I shall explain for all bodhisattvas the light of the inconceivable teachings of all Buddhas— namely, so that they may enter the stages of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*),
gather all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), skillfully discern all Buddha-dharmas, extensively know all phenomena (*dharma*), and be well-able to...
Because he teaches the Dharma, because his non-conceptual wisdom is purified, because he is untainted by any worldly phenomena, because his supramundane roots of goodness are purified,
because he has attained the sphere of inconceivable wisdom, and because he has attained the sphere of the wisdom of the Omniscient One; furthermore,
because he causes others to attain the beginning and end of the ten bodhisattva stages, he explains the distinctions of the ten bodhisattva stages according to reality.
Because they contemplate all Buddha-dharmas through their characteristics; because they cultivate the discernment of untainted dharmas;
because they skillfully adorn themselves with the light of great wisdom through excellent selection and observation; because they have skillfully entered the gateway of definitive knowledge;
because they sequentially expound fearlessness wherever they dwell; because they have attained the light of unimpeded eloquence; and because they abide in great eloquence.
Because of the excellence of their spiritual capacity and firm resolve, because they do not forget the bodhicitta through mindfulness,
because they bring all realms of sentient beings to maturity, and because they are able to reach all places to definitively awaken them— O son of good family,
you should now skillfully explain the distinctions of this dharma-gate, namely, that which is sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power and the illumination of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Furthermore, because they purify their own roots of goodness, because they universally purify the dharma-realm, because they universally gather in all sentient beings,
because they deeply enter the wisdom-body of the dharma-body, because they receive the empowerment of all Buddhas,
because they attain the most exalted body among all worlds, because they transcend all worldly paths, because they purify supramundane roots of goodness, and because they fulfill all-knowledge.
[Commentary] Third,

from the passage beginning "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" down to "because he fulfills the knowledge of all-knowledge," twenty-five lines of scripture clarify how Vajragarbha Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration together with the Buddhas who share his name.

All [the bodhisattvas] come before him to exhort and encourage him to preach the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). Within the section on entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the meaning is divided into four parts:

first, at that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva—this consists of one and a half lines of sūtra, totaling three phrases of scripture—which clarifies the section where Vajragarbha Bodhisattva enters meditative absorption; second, from "having entered this samādhi" onwards...
Upon arriving, two sets of verses appear before him clarifying the manifestation of Buddhas bearing the same name;

this section is divided into three parts, beginning with the words "Having spoken thus" and continuing down to "Because of being able to reach all places and definitively awaken others," which consists of sixteen lines of verse clarifying the entry into this samādhi through twenty-two causal conditions; this section is divided into four parts.
From "The man" onwards, there are five lines of scripture clarifying the section where the Buddhas of the ten directions exhort Vajragarbha Bodhisattva to preach the Dharma.
The scripture states: "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
This means that he took the wisdom of the Tathāgata as his faith and diligence, and performed his practice accordingly.
All Buddha-activities are entirely the Buddha’s spiritual power; because they are not performed by a self, they are called *samādhi*.
The great wisdom-light of the Bodhisattva is precisely the light of the Middle Way wisdom of the ten stages emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows;
it is also named the "Flame-Light of Bodhisattva Power," which was likewise emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows during the first assembly.
The light named "The Radiance of the Power and Wisdom of All Bodhisattvas" is, in its entirety,
the radiance of the Buddha’s wisdom at the conclusion of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Now, entering samādhi,

it is precisely this wisdom-samādhi that is described as the "Great Wisdom Radiance of the Bodhisattvas," which constitutes the bodhisattva’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Because of their practice, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are ten billion buddhas—each as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields—all sharing the same name, Vajragarbha.
The number ten billion signifies the perfection and inexhaustibility of the count; thus, "beyond worlds" refers to the stages from the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications.
The Buddha-fruit is external; now, this wisdom-virtue of the ten stages is established because the name of the Buddha-fruit manifests before one.

The reason it shares the same name as the Bodhisattva who has entered meditative concentration is to clarify that the wisdom of the one in concentration accords with and merges with the fundamental stage of the Buddha’s wisdom.
As for saying that the number is equal to the dust motes of ten billion Buddha-fields, this clarifies non-conceptualizing wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*).
Because the essence and function [of the Dharma] are all-pervasive, it is said that "ten billion Buddha-lands, as numerous as atoms, together bestow their empowerment.
This clarifies that when one’s stage reaches the source, one's own power merges with the power of the Buddhas; therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"It is also because of your superior power of wisdom, and because of the power of the original vows of the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. By means of this majesty...
"By the power of spiritual transformations" clarifies that the Dharma-gates of ascending these ten stages are all initiated by the great vows of all Buddhas within the ten dedications;
for without these ten great vows of dedication, this stage could not be spontaneously realized.
"By the power of majestic majesty" means that from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one always rides upon the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience through majestic power.
Because one ascends these ten stages through the power of this [wisdom], and because one does not depart from the Tathāgata’s activity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*),
if one did not rely on the Tathāgata’s vehicle of all-knowledge, how could one reach the position of these ten stages?

Since this wisdom penetrates from cause to fruit and is identical to the stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*), therefore, within this teaching, there are the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

Since the fruit of Buddhahood exists within each stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), there are sixty layers of the fruit of Buddhahood throughout the progression through the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the five stages (*pañca-vastu*). However, if one takes only those fruits that enter the [principal] stages, there are fifty layers of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Within these ten stages and the eleventh stage, the fruit of Buddhahood attained during the ten dedications is identical to its wondrous function.

The causes and conditions for the practice of penetration collectively comprise one hundred layers; through the ten *pāramitās* inherently possessed within the Buddha’s fundamental state, these manifest as ten layers of cause and effect.

This clarifies that practitioners all initiate their cultivation through the five stages upon this foundation of the Buddha’s original causes and effects, ascending and progressing by relying on that source. Thus, it is named the Dharma of the One Hundred and Ten Cities.
The "Gate" (dvāra) generally encompasses the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), wherein the Buddha-fruit is likewise named "Sublime" (*miao*).

This is because the dharmas of the tenth and eleventh stages do not establish a separate designation for the Buddha-fruit, as the dharmas of these two stages are identical to those of the ten stages of Dedication.
Regarding the ten *pāramitās* of the Buddha’s fundamental position, they are presented at the beginning of the first assembly as an exhortation by citing the fruit.

In the stage of cultivation, the Tathāgata is the fruit of Buddhahood; the names of the ten bodhisattvas above him are all identical, being titled "Universal" (Puxian), which clarifies that within the stage of the Buddha-fruit, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra follows the ten pāramitās, and thus their names differ according to those practices.
This is because it is the gate of causal practice for the fundamental cause of the Buddha. The forty classes of spirits and devas arise in emulation of this sequence.
In the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are distinct progressive cultivations of the ten *pāramitās*.
As one ascends through these stages of practice, they are also termed the ten distinct and universal [practices] of Samantabhadra. There are forty classes of spirit-deities;
with the ten *pāramitās* following the five stages of ascent and progression, there are thus fifty bodhisattvas.
The fifty causal practices of the Bodhisattva path and the ten resultant states of Buddhahood together constitute one hundred;

these are never separated from the fundamental resultant state of the Buddha and the fundamental ten practices of Samantabhadra, which form the "ten ones. Together with the forty [practices] and the fifty celestial deities, they constitute the fifty.
Within each of the six *pāramitās*, ten are subsumed, resulting in five hundred varieties of gates of differentiated wisdom, through which the myriad practices are perfected.
The Perfect Buddha also establishes a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) as the duration from the beginning to the end of his spiritual advancement;
for example, the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood in three births within a single moment.

Furthermore, in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, he takes the descent from heaven, birth, and entry into *nirvāṇa* as occurring within a single moment to serve as the temporal substance, for such is their primordial nature.
When one perceives that time passes, the mind follows after deluded thoughts. The above explains that,
by the power of the original vows and the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Arhat-Samyaksambuddha, this entire section—
explaining the causes and conditions for the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and the attainment of fruition— entirely relies upon the wisdom of Vairocana from the first assembly.
The ten powers, the forty practices of Samantabhadra, and the practices performed by the various devas and spirits—emulate these in your cultivation;
this is called "riding upon the Buddha’s spiritual power. This is due to the power of the Tathāgata’s vows and also because of your own superior power of wisdom.
The following twelve lines collectively present the purpose for entering samādhi; there are twenty-two causes and conditions, the meaning of which may be understood through the text.

In the fourth section, it is known that there are five types of *pañcavimśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* texts; this is the "Section on Exhortation" (*anuśaṃsā-vibhāga*) which contains ten causal conditions, as clarified in the text itself.
It says: "To fulfill all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) means: first, to fulfill fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); second, to fulfill discriminative wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*)."
[Sūtra] At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha a body that cannot be eclipsed,
unimpeded eloquence, pure wisdom of excellent discernment, the power of excellent recollection without forgetfulness,
clearly realized wisdom of excellent determination, wisdom that awakens all places, and the sovereign power of accomplishing the Way.

The Tathāgata’s fearlessness, his discernment and analytical wisdom regarding all dharmas as observed by one possessing omniscience, and his eloquence—these are endowed with the sublime adornments of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. Why is this?
Because he has attained such a dharma of samādhi; because it arises from his original vows; because of his well-purified profound resolve; and because of his well-purified wheel of wisdom.
Because they have well accumulated the aids to the path; because they have skillfully cultivated their tasks; because they keep in mind the immeasurable vessels of the Dharma;
because they know their pure faith and understanding; because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* free from error; and because they are well-sealed by the seal of wisdom regarding the *dharmadhātu*.

[Treatise] Fourth: From the passage beginning "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions" down to "because they are well-sealed by the seal of the wisdom of the dharma-realm," there are nine lines of sūtra text clarifying the section on how the Buddhas of the ten directions grant the ten powers to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, enabling him to preach the Dharma with mastery. Within this section on the empowerment and sustaining power granted by these Buddhas, the meaning is divided into three parts:
1. Explaining the ten kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas; 2. Explaining how the ten kinds of causal conditions enter this samādhi; 3.

Explaining the request of all Bodhisattvas for the preaching of the Dharma. First, from "At that time" down to "fully adorned," there are five lines and a half of sūtra text explaining how the Buddhas of the ten directions empower the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha with ten kinds of power.

This section is divided into two parts. Regarding the first, from "For what reason" onwards, there are four lines of scripture that clarify the presentation of ten types of causal conditions for entering this samādhi.
At the time of wishing to expound the dharmas of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), there are six kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) bestowed by all Buddhas:
(1) the empowerment of all Buddhas of the ten directions appearing before one with the same name; (2) the majestic spiritual power of the original vows of Vairocana.
1. The empowerment by the three Buddhas through the ten kinds of dharmic power bestowed upon Vajragarbha; 2. The empowerment by the four Buddhas through verbal praise; 3.
The empowerment by the various Buddhas each extending their right hand to stroke his head; 4. The empowerment by the Tathāgatas through the emission of light for consecration;
5. The request by the various Bodhisattvas for him to preach; 6. The first instance of the Tathāgata emitting light from his crown to exhort him to speak.
There are six kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in total: first, the second [chapter] "Liberation Moon" makes three requests; second, all the bodhisattvas join in the request;
third, all the Buddhas emit light to exhort [Vajragarbha] to speak; fourth, the fourfold request; fifth, the exhortation to speak;

and sixth, the section on the actual teaching, which begins from "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands" and continues until "the earth shook and offerings were raised."
Now, to correctly explain the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), we shall divide the first ground, the Joyful (*pramuditā*), into ten sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Having thus stroked his head, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha arose from samādhi and addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "The Buddhas..."
O Sons of the Buddha, what are these vows of the Bodhisattvas— which are well-determined, unadulterated, invisible, as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space,
extending to the end of the future, pervading all Buddha-fields, rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, guarded by all Buddhas,
and entering the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present? O Sons of the Buddha, what are they?

For the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the ground of wisdom for the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas’ ground of wisdom, there are ten stages which all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have spoken, will speak, and are now speaking; I also speak them in this way. What are these ten?

First, the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); second, the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*); third, the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*); fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

The fifth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; the sixth is the Ground Difficult to Conquer; the seventh is the Ground of Manifestation; the eighth is the Ground of Far-Going; the ninth is the Ground of Immovability;
the tenth is the Ground of Excellent Intelligence; and the eleventh is the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.

Son of the Buddha, these ten grounds of the bodhisattvas have been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—have been taught, will be taught, and are being taught now. Son of the Buddha, I do not see any buddha-field where [these] exist.

In this regard, why does the Tathāgata not speak of these ten stages? Because this is the supreme path toward enlightenment for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, and it is also a gateway to the light of the pure Dharma—namely, the detailed exposition of the various stages of the Bodhisattvas.
O Sons of the Buddha, this place is inconceivable; it is the wisdom realized by each respective Bodhisattva.

[Treatise] First, from the passage beginning "At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands" down to "the wisdom realized accordingly," there are sixteen and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section in which the Buddhas of the ten directions touch the crown of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva’s head with their hands,
causing him to arise and correctly expound the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
[Sūtra] At that time, after the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had spoken these names of the ten bodhisattva stages, he remained silent and did not further analyze them.
Then, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, having heard the names of the ten bodhisattva stages but not hearing their explanation, all felt a sense of longing and thirst, and thought to themselves:
"For what cause and for what reason does the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha speak only [the names]?"

The names of the ten stages of the bodhisattva were stated, but they were not explained. Then, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great assembly, questioned the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in verse:

Why does the one of pure awakening, endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and merit, speak of the various supreme and wondrous stages (*bhūmi*) with power, yet not explain them? All [beings] are entirely certain;
why do you, who are courageous and without timidity, speak the names of the stages but not unfold their wondrous meanings and principles?
This assembly all desires to hear; their minds are free from timidity. I pray that you will explain it in detail for them.
The gathering is entirely pure, free from indolence, and solemnly refined. They are steadfast and immovable, endowed with merit and wisdom.
Gazing at one another, they are all full of reverence; everyone looks up toward you with single-minded devotion.
[Verse: Like a bee longing for fine honey, like one parched with thirst yearning for nectar.
[Treatise: Second, from the point "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva... and below, there are five lines of prose followed by ten lines of verse.
These scriptures clarify that Vajragarbha Bodhisattva remained silent and did not preach the Dharma, while Vimukticandra [questioned him].
The Bodhisattva, knowing the minds of the assembly, requested on their behalf that the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages be expounded.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, possessed of great wisdom and fearlessness, having heard this being spoken,
spoke these verses for the sake of the sons of the Buddha, in order to gladden the hearts of the assembled multitude.
The deeds of the bodhisattva stages are the supreme foundation of all Buddhas.
They are revealed and explained as the foremost rarity, difficult to perceive, subtle, and hard to see. Transcending thought and surpassing the realm of the mind, they arise from the Buddha-realm;
those who hear them are utterly bewildered, yet they should hold their minds like a vajra.
With deep faith in the Buddha’s supreme wisdom, one knows that the mind-ground is without self.
To be able to hear this sublime Dharma is like painting in the sky, like the appearance of wind in the sky;
such discernment by the Sage’s wisdom is extremely difficult to perceive. I recollect the Buddha’s wisdom, most excellent and inconceivable.
[Verse: "In this world, there is no one capable of receiving [this teaching]; therefore, he remains silent and does not speak.

[Treatise: Third, at that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha—possessing great wisdom and fearlessness—concluded the prose section with these seven lines of verse, clarifying that the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha maintained his silence and did not speak.
[The Meaning of] This.
[Sūtra]: At that time, having heard this teaching, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, this assembly has now all gathered; their profound minds are well-purified, their reflections are well-cleansed, and they have well-cultivated all..."
Practicing virtue, they have accumulated the aids to the path; they are well able to draw near hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas and accomplish immeasurable roots of merit and goodness.
Having abandoned delusion and confusion, they are free from defilement. With deep resolve and faith, they do not follow the teachings of others within the Buddha-dharma.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You should now, by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound upon these bodhisattvas regarding the Tathāgata...
These most profound points can all be realized and known. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"May you explain the most peaceful state, The supreme conduct of the Bodhisattvas, And the differentiation of the various stages."
Purity of Wisdom and the Attainment of Perfect Enlightenment: This assembly is free from all defilements; Their resolve and understanding are entirely clear and pure.
Having served immeasurable Buddhas, They are able to know the meaning of this stage.
[Treatise] Fourth: At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra spoke the following verses, which comprise nine lines of scripture clarifying the general theme.
The Section on the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra’s Repeated Request for the Teaching of the Dharma.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O Son of the Buddha, although this assembly has gathered with pure and virtuous reflections, having abandoned folly and doubt, and though they do not follow the teachings of others regarding the profound Dharma, there are still others who are inferior."

"I perceive that when sentient beings hear this profound and inconceivable matter, they will mostly give rise to doubt and confusion, and will undergo various forms of decline and affliction throughout the long night [of saṃsāra].
Out of compassion for them, I therefore remain silent. At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Although this assembly is pure and possesses vast wisdom— profound, sharp, and capable of discernment—
and their minds are as immovable as the king of mountains, unshakeable like the great ocean; yet,
having not long practiced and not yet attained liberation, they act according to consciousness rather than according to true knowledge.
[Verse: "Hearing this, they will give rise to doubt and fall into evil realms; out of compassion for such as these, I do not speak.

[Treatise: Fifth, from this point onward, the long prose and nine lines of verse beginning with the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva clarify that the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva fears that those of inferior understanding who follow after consciousness will be unable to give rise to faith.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha once more, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, analyze and explain this inconceivable Dharma. Why is this?
When the Ten Grounds are taught, all Bodhisattvas ought to thus attain Buddhahood through the protective mindfulness of the Tathāgata, thereby giving rise to faith and acceptance."
Because they receive protection through being protected by [the Buddhas], they are able to give rise to heroic vigor within this stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*). Why is this?

Because this is the primary practice of Bodhisattvas, wherein all Buddha-dharmas are accomplished. It is, for example, like the writing of characters and numbers: everything is based upon the alphabet;
the alphabet is ultimate, and there is not even the slightest thing that is separate from the alphabet. Thus it is with the Buddha.
"O Son of the Buddha, all the teachings of the Buddhas take the ten stages (daśabhūmi) as their foundation;

by perfecting the cultivation of these ten stages, one attains omniscience (sarvajñatā). Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, please expound upon this for us, so that this person may surely be protected by the Tathāgata and come to have faith and acceptance.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! Please expound upon the practices of the stages for entering into enlightenment.
There is no Sovereign of Mastery throughout the ten directions who does not protect and mind this root of wisdom;
it is the ultimate abiding in wisdom from which all the Buddha-dharmas arise.
Just as letters and numbers are subsumed within the alphabet, So too are the Buddha-dharmas based upon the stages (*bhūmi*).

[Commentary] Sixth: At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra recited the following fourteen and a half verses of general praise, clarifying that this assembly was capable of hearing [the teaching]. If there are those who obtain to hear what the Buddha has...
"Please, out of compassion, speak on the section of being free from doubt.
[Sūtra] At that time, the assembly of great bodhisattvas simultaneously spoke in unison to Vajragarbha Bodhisattva,
addressing him in verse:
With supreme, stainless wisdom and boundless analytical eloquence, Proclaiming profound and beautiful words in accord with the ultimate truth,
Mindfully upholding pure conduct, And possessing the power of the ten strengths, the accumulation of merit, and the analytical skill of eloquence,
He expounds this most excellent stage, Where concentration, morality, and the assembly of the right mind prevail.
Free from conceit and wrong views, this assembly has no doubts.

We only wish to hear your excellent teaching, as one who thirsts longs for cool water, as the hungry thinks of delicious food, as the sick remembers a potent medicine, and as bees crave sweet honey; we are just like this—we pray to hear the Dharma of the Deathless.
Excellent, O One of Vast Wisdom! We pray that you will explain the entry into the stages, and the attainment of the ten powers, the unimpeded [knowledges], and all the practices of the Sugata.
[Treatise] Seventh: At that time, the assembly of great Bodhisattvas... (the following, including the verse, consists of six and a half lines of scripture).
Section on the Universal Invitation of the Great Assembly.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from between his eyebrows a pure radiance named Bodhisattva-Power-Flame-Luminosity,
with hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays of light as its retinue, universally illuminating all worlds in the ten directions, leaving none untouched.
The sufferings of the three evil realms were entirely brought to rest; furthermore, it illuminated all the assemblies of Tathāgatas, manifesting the inconceivable power of all Buddhas;
and it illuminated the bodies of Bodhisattvas empowered by all Buddhas throughout all worlds in the ten directions as they preached the Dharma.
Having performed these deeds, it formed a great cloud of radiant light in the space above.
When they were seated upon their jeweled pedestals, all the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise emitted from between their eyebrows a pure light;
the names, retinues, and functions of these lights were identical to those here.
Furthermore, this light illuminated this Sahā world—the Buddha, the great assembly, and the body and lion throne of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha—before vanishing into the space above.
In the center of the Great Radiance Cloud-Net Terrace within the Light Terrace, by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, he spoke these verses:
"The Buddha is unequaled, like space; The Ten Powers are immeasurable and supreme virtues."
The Supreme among humans, the Highest in the world, the Lion of the Śākyas—may he bestow his Dharma upon those sons of the Buddha;
may they, upholding the power of all Buddhas, open this most excellent treasury of the Dharma King.
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, may the vast wisdom and sublime practices of the various stages be analyzed and explained.
If one is empowered by the strength of the Sugata, One shall obtain the jewel of the Dharma and it will enter one’s heart.
The stages, stainless and in successive order, will be fulfilled, And one will likewise possess the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
Even while dwelling amidst the waters of the ocean or the fires at the end of an eon, Such a person is capable of receiving this Dharma and shall surely hear it.
Those who harbor doubts and do not believe shall never hear such a teaching as this;
therefore, one should explain the path of the superior wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Through entering, abiding, and progressing through successive cultivation, the wisdom of the Dharma arises from the sphere of practice for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.

[Treatise] Eighth: From "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, including the verses, there are twenty-one lines of scripture that clarify how the Tathāgatas of the worlds of the ten directions each emit light from between their eyebrows to drench the crown of the head of Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, mutually illuminating one another;
this light transforms into a platform, and from this light-platform, sounds emerge to exhort and explain the section on the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha surveyed the ten directions and, in order to increase the pure faith of the great assembly, spoke these verses:
“The path of the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, Is subtle and difficult to comprehend; It is beyond thought and free from all conceptualization.”
Seeking to see it, it cannot be found; it is neither born nor does it perish. By nature pure and eternally tranquil, it is free from defilement.
For those of wise intelligence, this is the sphere traversed by their wisdom: its self-nature is fundamentally empty and still, non-dual and inexhaustible.
Liberated from all realms of existence, one abides in the equality of nirvāṇa.
Neither beginning, middle, nor end; It cannot be expressed by words. Transcending the three periods of time, its characteristic is like space;
This quiescent realm is the practice of the Buddhas. Words cannot reach it, and its ground-like practice is likewise so;
Difficult to explain and difficult to receive, Wisdom arises within the Buddha’s sphere.
It is not a path of thought or mental activity, nor is it accessible through the gates of the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases. Wisdom knows it, yet the mind cannot reach it;
like the tracks of a bird in the sky, it is difficult to describe and difficult to demonstrate. Such is the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
the mind and intellect cannot comprehend them. Yet, through the power of compassion and aspiration, one gives rise to and enters the practice of these stages.
The mind that is perfected through successive stages, And the conduct of wisdom, are beyond the scope of deliberation.
This realm is difficult to see and difficult to know, and cannot be described; Yet, by the power of the Buddha, it is proclaimed.
You should respectfully receive this entry into the practice of such wisdom, Which could not be fully told even in hundreds of millions of eons; I now speak of it only briefly.
The true meaning is without remainder; wait with reverence for a single moment.
I shall speak the sublime Dharma in a subtle voice, relying on the power of the Buddha, employing analogies and corresponding words.
The infinite spiritual powers of all Buddhas enter my body; though this matter is difficult to proclaim, I shall now speak but a small portion of it.

[Treatise] Ninth: At that time, from the prose section beginning with "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" and continuing through thirteen lines of verse, it is explained that Vajragarbha Bodhisattva extols the profound Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) as transcending the realm of thought, intellect, and consciousness, being known only by wisdom and beyond the reach of words;
thus, empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of all Buddhas, he briefly explains but a small portion of it.
Within these nine sections, the general meaning is fully contained in ten points, which need not be further explained. These ten matters are:
first, the Buddhas touching [the crown of] his head to signify their approval and permission for him to teach; second, the general enumeration of the names of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);

third, remaining silent to await a request before proclaiming the Dharma, thereby clarifying that the Dharma is precious and should not be bestowed lightly upon unworthy recipients; fourth, the chapter on Vimukticandra.
1. Knowing the proper time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva requested three times; fearing that the vessels were inferior, he stopped three times. 2. The six great assemblies all joined in the request. 3.
It is clarified that those capable of hearing are empowered by all Buddhas, while those incapable do not hear from the very beginning.

4. It is clarified that sounds emerge from the light-terraces to exhort and explain. 5. It is clarified that the Buddha’s light performs the empowerment of the crown. 6. It is clarified regarding the vajra.
The Method for the Bodhisattva’s Departure: This profound teaching is difficult to explain; here, a brief summary of its essential meaning is provided.

It clarifies that the essence of these ten stages (*bhūmi*) serves as a mutual basis for the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and the eleventh stage.
Therefore, following the ten stages of faith, abodes, practices, and transferences, there are collectively the practice-gates of the ten stages. Next...
This is because one takes a single Tathāgata’s sovereign, unimpeded great wisdom as the companion, and practices with the ten *pāramitās* as the skillful means;
thus, it is entirely comprised within the ten *Samantabhadra-dharmas* of the first assembly.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said that the alphabet and so forth are used as metaphors for all written characters and numbers.
There is no dharma among all the Buddha-dharmas that is apart from the syllables; all are fundamentally based upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

This clarifies that the dharma of these ten stages penetrates both cause and fruit, being inseparable from the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*). Because one cultivates the wisdom of differentiation by means of the ten universal practices of Samantabhadra, one fulfills the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
Therefore, from the very beginning, within the exhortation to practice by taking up the fruit as the goal, [the light] is emitted from between the eyebrows.
The light from between [the Buddha’s brows] is named "Bodhisattva Power Wisdom Radiance"; it enters into the wheels on the soles of the Buddha’s feet to bring about the fulfillment of the ten faiths.

Now, returning to the Tathāgata’s brow, it emits a light named "Bodhisattva Power Flame Radiance" to drench the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, thereby enabling him to expound the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The radiance from the soles of the feet uses the fruit to produce the cause, generating faith; this is that light.
Having clearly explained that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the fruit of what is to be believed, [the Buddha] now once again emits the light of the fruit of the wisdom of the ten stages—
the initial object of belief— to empower the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, so that he may expound the practice of these ten stages.
That this light enters through the crown signifies that the ten stages are the middle-way wisdom among all bodhisattvas.

Because it is the summit of fruition and because it reaches the ultimate limit of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the Tathāgata-udaya-parivarta and the Dharmadhātu-parivarta both describe the emission of light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows;
this collectively clarifies that the locus where the light of wisdom—the essence of fruition—is perfected is therein.

Furthermore, the fact that the light enters through the crown of the head clarifies that, proceeding from the summit of wisdom, one practices compassion throughout the world, which is termed the "ten returns" (*daśāvartana*).

Because the great vows previously generated have been brought to fulfillment, this tenth stage clarifies the gateway of nurturing great compassion, whereby one accords with the fulfillment of those vows.
Therefore, the spiritual friends of Sudhana represent this through ten goddesses.
The eleventh stage clarifies the perfection of compassion, which universally benefits sentient beings through wisdom; it is represented by Māyā, the Mother of Buddhas, who gives birth to the Buddha.

To manifest this, one must skillfully grasp its essential meaning; only then can one know that the gateway to true faith and understanding has been perfected and the path of spiritual advancement is inexhaustible—a great teaching for which no other guide can be found.
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume 55.

The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament Scripture, Fascicle Fifty-Six.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan, Tang Dynasty.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, Collated Scripture and Combined Treatise, Chapter on the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmika), Part Four of Twenty-Six. [Treatise]:
From "The tenth son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings... down to the end of the scroll is the formal exposition.
The section on the characteristics of the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), is further divided into two parts: first, a general outline of this stage;
second, an explanation of the meaning according to the text. Regarding the general outline of this stage: within this Stage of Joy, it is broadly divided into twelve sections.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, well-cultivated various practices, well-accumulated the aids to the Path,
well-made offerings to all Buddhas, well-accumulated pure dharmas, been well-guided by spiritual friends, and whose deep mind is well-purified;
who establish vast aspirations and give rise to vast understanding, with compassion manifest before them, seeking the wisdom of a Buddha and desiring to attain the ten [powers].
For the sake of attaining power; for the sake of attaining great fearlessness; for the sake of attaining the equal Dharma of the Buddhas;
for the sake of being a savior for all the world; for the sake of purifying great compassion; for the sake of attaining non-remaining knowledge of the ten directions;
for the sake of purifying all Buddha-fields without obstruction; for the sake of knowing all three periods of time in a single thought-moment; and for the sake of turning the great wheel of Dharma.
Because they are fearless, O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind as this:

one that is headed by great compassion, characterized by the predominance of wisdom, embraced by skillful means, sustained by the most supreme and profound resolve, maintained by the Tathāgata’s powers, immeasurable, well-observed, discerning, courageous, powerful, and unimpeded;
one in which knowledge is manifest, which accords with spontaneous wisdom, and which is capable of receiving it.
All Buddha-dharmas are transformed through wisdom, as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, extending to the end of the future.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva first gives rise to such a mind, they immediately transcend the stage of ordinary beings and enter the rank of Bodhisattvas;
they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, such that no one can speak of any fault in their lineage, and they depart from worldly destinies to enter the state of transcendence.
The Bodhisattva who attains the path of the world, dwells in the Bodhisattva-dharma, enters into the equality of the three times,

and is certain to attain unsurpassed enlightenment within the lineage of the Tathāgatas— such a Bodhisattva dwelling in this dharma is said to dwell on the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
because of being in accord with the immovable.

[Treatise] First, regarding the "Son of the Buddha," the seventeen lines of scripture beginning with "If there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness" clarify the section on how one initially rises from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), gives rise to thirty kinds of vast aspirations and profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*),
enters the rank of a Bodhisattva, and is born into the family of the Tathāgata. Second, as for the explanation of the meaning according to the text, it begins from the scripture within this section.
It is said: "O Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, within this very section they shall give rise to thirty kinds of vast aspirations.
These are those who well cultivate all practices and well accumulate the aids to the Path—namely, the ten *pāramitās* and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharmas*).
From the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness, they constantly contemplate the body."

Contemplating emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature, one observes that feeling exists neither internally, nor externally, nor in between; one observes that the mind has no abiding place and that phenomena are without self.

Diligently practicing these contemplations is called the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*). When the mind accords with what is contemplated and attains the realization of the non-self of phenomena, it is called the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because one attains the non-self of phenomena through these, one acquires the five faculties (*indriya*), and by contemplating and penetrating the truth, one becomes non-regressive.

Regarding the five faculties (*indriya*) called "roots": because faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are established through non-retrogression from the cycle of birth and death, they are called "faculties" (*indriya*).
Because one acts accordingly without being defiled and does not associate with the passions, they are called "powers" (*bala*).

As for "power," just as with the preceding five faculties, when one does not retrogress toward sense objects and does not unite with the passions but instead associates with wisdom, it is called "power"; thus, one immediately attains [it].

One attains the seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of joy, the enlightenment factor of equanimity, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, and this mind, being in accordance with reality, is the enlightenment factor of concentration.
By attaining these seven factors of enlightenment, one obtains the eight factors of the noble path. As for the eightfold noble path:
Right view, right thought, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are these.
The commentary explains: entering the Buddha’s wisdom is called right view; observing phenomena with wisdom is called right thought;
practicing and advancing according to the dharmas of the five stages is called right effort; and constantly being united with wisdom rather than with worldly passions [is right mindfulness].

That which is called right mindfulness is the state in which the mind is without arising or ceasing, yet is able to give rise to the wisdom of all Buddhas and to manifest immeasurable great supernormal powers;
this is called right concentration. Being well able to discern between humans, non-Buddhists, the three vehicles, and the one vehicle;
between false views and right views; and between wrong determination and right determination, as well as wrong practice and right practice—this is called right speech.
Skillfully discerning all improper actions of oneself and others, and skillfully manifesting the Buddha’s wisdom and so forth as that which is equally shared by all sentient beings—
this is called Right Action. It causes all sentient beings, including humans, devas, non-Buddhists, the mundane world of birth and death,
and the liberation methods of the three vehicles that transcend the world, to all be dedicated toward the single fundamental [nature] of the Tathāgata.
The mind of all-encompassing wisdom is fundamentally free from emotional agitation; this is called right livelihood.

As the thirty kinds of vast aspirations and delights are fully elucidated in the sutra, once a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva, has first given rise to such a mind—as described in the five lines of scripture that follow—it is concluded that the bodhisattva is able to give rise to these thirty kinds of vast aspirations and delights. Having first given rise to such [a mind]...
"The mind immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings, enters the rank of Bodhisattvas, and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

This passage comprehensively subsumes the initial "Abiding in the First Resolve" from among the preceding ten abidings; it is identical here in the first "Stage of Joy" among these ten stages in that one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and becomes a true son of the Buddha.
This is clarified because they share the same vehicle, having the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their essence. Thus it is explained.
Within these five stages, the differentiated practices and differentiated wisdoms proceed simultaneously without beginning, end, or sequence;

thus they differ from the three vehicles, which follow dharmas according to emotional dispositions. Although the dharma-practices are extensive, they constitute a single Buddha-wisdom that seals all dharmas without sequence.
Therefore, these ten stages of the Dharma serve as the reverse formation of the preceding ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications.

Turning toward the Dharma does not mean that there is some separate dharma coming from elsewhere; it is like a radish, which grows leaves from its root and nourishes the root with those leaves. It is also like sowing grain: from the fruit the sprout is born, and when the sprout matures, the fruit is formed, returning once more to the original fruit.
