This clearly demonstrates that the fruit is not separate from the fruit within the cause. It is like a person who grows from birth until the age of thirty;
although they grow, one does not consider the state of being grown at birth to be "great," nor does a separate "greatness" arrive later.

Furthermore, from birth until old age, there is no sequence of before and after. Because wisdom acts as the precursor, it is not something grasped by the insentient; thus, there is no difference in terms of sequence.
Furthermore, in this Dharma-gate of the five stages of the One Vehicle, wisdom serves as the precursor because there is no before or after.

Although the teachings on the practices of these five stages distinguish between their progression, similarities, differences, and specific distinctions—establishing various levels of ascent and descent—these merely clarify the gradations within the single wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
They are not like the gradations perceived through ordinary emotional views; thus, by illuminating them with wisdom, they can be seen as such.
This refers to the case of the dragon girl, who attained Buddhahood within a single kṣaṇa through the practice of the three lives.

Those of the three vehicles who do not understand the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*—to reconcile provisional means with ultimate reality—instead claim that this is merely a sūtra of transformation and that one must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood.
This is the view held outside the outer gate of the Great Wisdom Mansion of the Dharma-realm.
Abiding for now in a grass hut, one merely attains the pleasure of escaping the coarse sufferings of the three realms;

yet, by obtaining the three kinds of mind-made bodies and dwelling outside the gate of the burning house, one provisionally establishes the three vehicles. Thus, there are carriages upon which to rely, for there is a distinction between the pure lands and the defiled lands;
consequently, one has not yet entered the Great Wisdom of the Dharma-realm where birth-and-death and nirvana are without dependence.

Because they abide [in this state], their wisdom and compassion are infinite; for the Buddha’s original retribution-body dwells in the palace of the Flower Treasury Ocean (*Gandavyūha-sāgara*), and because the ocean of sentient beings is itself the ocean of Buddhas, the wisdom of sentient beings is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Thus, within a single pore, all oceans of lands observed by wisdom—where ordinary beings and sages alike dwell—are universally perceived in a single kṣaṇa.

The ocean of infinite kalpas across the three periods of time has neither beginning nor end; it differs from the provisional teachings which fix the duration of kalpas and distinguish between pure and impure lands as absolute distinctions.

Therefore, regarding the dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in this sutra, one must not interpret it through the lens of the three vehicles—such as by claiming that afflictions are intentionally retained, or that through the power of vows one does not take birth in a pure land but remains in an impure realm to transform sentient beings with compassion—and so forth. One should instead understand it according to its true meaning.
None of these can be called the gate of the Great Abode of Universal Radiance and Great Wisdom within this Dharma-realm;

rather, one must reform the net-like views of the Three Vehicles, cause those with narrow vision to achieve perfect extinction, and eliminate the outflows of afflictions as well as the defiled and pure lands and their leaky bodies.
Only then can one be said to have entered the vastness of the Wisdom-body, and only then is it truly named the Immovable Vast Wisdom-body.
The Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is also characterized by immovability (*acalā-yoga*). It takes the Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*acala-jñāna-buddha*) of the Ten Faiths as its essence;
while names are established according to progress through the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications, upon reaching this stage, one returns to the original name.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise composes a verse: "Boundless wisdom and compassion constitute the Buddha's virtues; The Buddha accomplishes the ten [perfections] through wisdom and compassion."
The stages (bhūmis) further constitute the ten stages as the five successive positions of the preparatory gates; these do not depart from the wisdom and compassion arising from the ten stages.
Therefore, at the very first arousal of the mind in the Ten Abidings, one enters the wisdom of the ten stages.
Although the skillful means of the five positions differ, they serve only to mature the wisdom of the ten stages, just like a swift bird flying through space.
Without ceasing its movement, it reaches nowhere; likewise, as fish and dragons swim in water, they do not cease their constant swimming nor leave the water.
In this way, the distinctions among the practices of the five stages do not cease their differentiation, yet they do not depart from wisdom.
All distinctions of days, months, and years exist through the seal of the Dharma of wisdom, which has no separate essence. Wisdom is neither established nor destroyed.

Clearly understanding all stages, one eliminates habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and realizes that there is neither habit nor non-habit. Through the practice of compassion, one accomplishes the myriad practices and constantly gives rise to non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*).
This non-obstructive wisdom is the contemplative penetration of unobstructed causes; all that is accomplished through contemplative practice takes this natural, non-active wisdom as its essence.
It is also called "immovable wisdom" (*acala-jñāna*), for it is without dependence and cannot be moved. Thus is one established in peace.
Regarding the eleven matters that serve as the causal conditions for the gateway of advancement through the five stages, what are these eleven?
First, to ensure that those who have resolved to attain enlightenment do not become stagnant in a single dharma nor give rise to indolence or pride.

Second, to enable those who have resolved to attain enlightenment to acquire wisdom and practice all bodhisattva deeds. Third, to cause those who have resolved to attain enlightenment to give rise to wisdom through their vows.
1. From compassion, one causes those who practice loving-kindness and compassion to become firm and perfect; 2.

One causes those who have generated the bodhicitta to subdue their own habitual tendencies in accordance with worldly conventions, using the various pāramitās to advance toward the realm of wisdom and compassion; 3.

One causes those who have generated the bodhicitta to proceed from their respective stages through the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to counteract habitual afflictions, further cultivating the gateway of wisdom.
1. To distinguish and clarify the differences between the three vehicles, the one vehicle, and the various practices of humans and devas for those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta;
2. To cause those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta to know for themselves the conditions leading to the destination reached through their own practice; 3.

To cause those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta to understand the breadth and narrowness of the inclusion of beings within the three vehicles and the one vehicle, as well as the decrease and increase in merit and wisdom; 4. To clarify... [the tenth point].

The transformative manifestations of all Buddhas throughout past and present are always thus. Just as refined gold does not depart from its essential nature even as it undergoes the eleven refinements through which it becomes increasingly bright and pure, so too should one briefly explain the twelve gates of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The first gate, consisting of seventeen lines of scripture, has been concluded; the remainder will be clarified further below.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they achieve abundant joy, abundant pure faith,
abundant love and delight, abundant serenity, abundant jubilation, abundant exultation, abundant valor, abundant freedom from strife, abundant freedom from malice,
and abundant freedom from resentment. O Son of the Buddha, because this bodhisattva dwelling in this Stage of Joy recollects all Buddhas, they give rise to joy.
He gives rise to joy by recollecting the teachings of all Buddhas; he gives rise to joy by recollecting all Bodhisattvas;
he gives rise to joy by recollecting the practices of all Bodhisattvas; he gives rise to joy by recollecting the purification of all perfections (pāramitās);

he gives rise to joy by recollecting the excellence of the Bodhisattva stages; he gives rise to joy by recollecting the indestructibility of Bodhisattvas; and he gives rise to joy by recollecting the Tathāgatas.
He gives rise to a thought of joy for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings; he gives rise to a thought of joy because he can cause sentient beings to obtain benefit;

he gives rise to a thought of joy because he enters the wisdom and skillful means of all Tathāgatas. Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I give rise to a thought of joy because I am turning away from and departing from all worldly realms;
I give rise to a thought of joy because I draw near to all Buddhas; I give rise to a thought of joy because I distance myself [from the mundane]."
He gives rise to joy because he has departed from the stage of ordinary beings; he gives rise to joy because he draws near to the stage of wisdom;
he gives rise to joy because he has forever severed all evil destinies; he gives rise to joy because he acts as a place of reliance for all sentient beings;
he gives rise to joy because he beholds all Tathāgatas; he gives rise to joy because he is born within the realm of the Buddhas; he enters into all...
Because the Bodhisattva abides within the state of equality, he gives rise to joy; because he is far removed from all causes for fear, such as the bristling of body hair, he gives rise to joy.

Why is this? Because once this Bodhisattva has attained the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all fears are entirely eliminated—namely, the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of the miserable realms, and the fear of the majesty and power of great assemblies.

They attain eternal freedom from such fears and terrors. Why is this? Because this bodhisattva, having abandoned the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*), does not even cherish his own body, let alone material wealth; therefore, he has no fear of being unable to support himself.

He does not seek offerings from others, but devotes himself solely to giving and bestowing upon all sentient beings; therefore, he has no fear of ill repute. Thus, he remains far removed [from these fears].
Because I perceive that there is no notion of a self, I have no fear of death;
because I know for myself that once dead, I shall certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I have no fear of the evil realms;

and because my aspirations and joys are such that there is no one equal to me in all the world, let alone anyone superior, I have no fear regarding the majesty and power of the great assembly. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
[The Bodhisattva] remains far removed from such things as terror and the bristling of body hair.

[Treatise]: The second section, beginning with "The Buddha’s son, the Bodhisattva, having dwelled in the Stage of Joy," consists of twenty-five lines of scripture that clarify the stage of the Bodhisattva’s initial entry into the grounds (*bhūmi*). Within the explanation of this meaning, it is divided into five parts.
Section One: From "O Son of the Buddha, once the Bodhisattva has dwelt in the Stage of Joy" down to "having many [qualities] free from resentment," there are two and a half lines of scripture;
this section clarifies the Bodhisattva’s entry into the first Stage of Joy, the Section on Abundant Joy.
From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "he further forms this thought," there are five and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the formal exposition of this stage.
The Bodhisattva’s state of joy consists of ten kinds of joy. This section clarifies that joy arises from seeing, hearing, and recollecting the qualities of all Buddhas;

it is divided into three parts. From the passage beginning with "I have turned away from all worldly spheres" down to "For what reason?"—a span of six and a half lines of scripture—there are ten kinds of joy that clarify self-knowledge.
"Attaining the Buddha’s wisdom and forever departing from the source of suffering"—this section concerns entering the Dharma and thus constitutes the "Arising of Joy. It is divided into four parts.

From "Once this Bodhisattva has attained the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)" down to "For what reason?"—these two and a half lines of scripture clarify that having entered this Stage of Joy, one is able to depart from the five kinds of fear. This is divided into five parts. "This Bodhisattva, having... [and so forth].

From the passage beginning with "down to the occurrence of such things as the bristling of body hair," there are seven lines of sūtra that clearly explain the section on the objects of the five kinds of fears;
the twenty-five lines of sūtra above this are complete according to the text itself and need not be further explained.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, possesses a vast aspiration that cannot be thwarted or destroyed;

he further diligently cultivates all roots of goodness and brings them to fulfillment—namely, because his faith is predominant, because he has much pure faith, because his understanding is purified, because his faith is resolute, because he gives rise to pity and compassion, and because he accomplishes great loving-kindness. His mind...

Because they are free from weariness; because they are adorned with shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*); because they have achieved gentleness and flexibility; because they revere, obey, and honor the Buddha’s teachings and Dharma;
because they cultivate roots of goodness day and night without satiety; because they associate with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); because they always delight in the Dharma;
because they seek extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without satiety; and because they correctly contemplate the Dharma as it has been heard with their minds.
Because they are free from dependence and attachment, they do not crave gain, fame, or honor;

because they do not seek any material requisites for life, they give rise to a mind of reality that knows no satiety; because they seek the stage of omniscience, they seek the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-dharmas;
because they seek the perfections and the factors conducive to the path, they remain free from all guile.
Because he is free from deceit; because he acts according to his word; because he constantly guards truthful speech; because he does not defile the family of the Tathāgata;
because he does not abandon the bodhisattva precepts; because he gives rise to the mind of omniscience that is as immovable as the king of mountains;
because he does not abandon worldly affairs while accomplishing the supramundane path; and because he never tires of gathering the factors conducive to enlightenment. Constantly...
Because they seek the most supreme and excellent path, the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, who have accomplished such methods for purifying the stages,
are said to be "dwelling securely in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy. [Treatise] Third,
from the passage beginning "this Bodhisattva takes great compassion as the foremost" onwards, there are ten sections.

In the commentary on the one and a half lines of scripture clarifying entry into the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), which further explains the thirty-four kinds of vast aspirations and joys (*adhimukti*), the text is divided into three sections:

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, up to "cultivating all roots of goodness and attaining accomplishment," there is one and a half lines of scripture. This section clarifies further exhortation to diligently cultivate faith (*śraddhā*).
The section on advancing in the practice of awakening without weariness or indolence is divided into two parts.
From "Because faith is predominant" up to "the most excellent and supreme path," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture.

This section clarifies the stage of purifying this ground through the superior cultivation of thirty kinds of dharmas. It is further divided into three parts; from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, there is one [section].
The preceding section of fifteen and a half lines of scripture clarifies the stage of exhorting all to practice and abide;
as the scriptural text itself is complete, there is no need for further explanation.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they are able to accomplish such great vows,
such great valor, and such great activities— namely, by giving rise to vast, pure, and resolute understanding,
they reverently make offerings to all Buddhas with every kind of offering requisite, leaving none remaining, as vast as...
The ultimate reality of the Dharma-realm is like space; throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, it never ceases.

Furthermore, one makes great vows: to receive the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas, to embrace the Bodhi of all Buddhas, to protect the teachings of all Buddhas, and to uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas—vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space.
Throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, he never ceases; furthermore, he makes a great vow,
wishing that whenever a Buddha appears in any world— descending from the Tuṣita Heaven, passing away, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, being born, leaving home,
attaining enlightenment, teaching the Dharma, and manifesting parinirvāṇa— he shall go to each of those places to attend upon, serve, and honor them, becoming the foremost among the assembly.
They practice the True Dharma, turning it everywhere at once— vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space,
and without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future. Furthermore, they make great vows,
wishing that all bodhisattva practices be vast and immeasurable, indestructible and unmixed, encompassing all the pāramitās and purifying all [qualities].

He speaks as it truly is of all the bodhisattva practices—whether regarding the general characteristics, specific characteristics, common characteristics, distinct characteristics, the characteristic of formation, or the characteristic of disintegration—and teaches and transforms all beings, causing them to accept and practice these teachings so that their minds may increase and expand.
This continues until the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm, like space, throughout all kalpas of the future without cessation; furthermore, he makes great vows.

May I teach and transform all such beings within the realm of sentient beings—those with form and those without form, those with perception and those without perception, those with neither perception nor non-perception;
those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those bound to the three realms and entering the six destinies;
and all those comprised within name-and-form—causing them all to enter the Buddha-dharma and forever sever [the bonds of] birth.
May all beings in every world-realm be established upon the path to the wisdom of omniscience— vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space,
and continuing without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future; and may they further make great vows, wishing that all worlds—
whether vast or immeasurable, coarse or subtle, disordered, inverted, or upright, whether entering or traversing them— [may all be so].
Their movement is as diverse as the net of Indra, manifesting with clear and direct knowledge and vision of the infinite varieties throughout the ten directions;
it is as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and continues without rest through all kalpas until the end of the future.
Furthermore, they make great vows, wishing that all lands enter into a single land, and that a single land [enter into all lands].
They enter all lands and immeasurable Buddha-fields, which are universally and entirely pure, adorned with arrays of radiant light;
they are free from all afflictions and have accomplished the path of purity.
Immeasurable wisdom beings fill them, universally entering the vast realms of all Buddhas and manifesting according to the minds of sentient beings, causing all to rejoice.
Their joy is vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and continues without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future;
furthermore, they make great vows, wishing to share the same resolve and conduct as all bodhisattvas,
free from enmity or jealousy, to gather all roots of goodness, and to always assemble together with all bodhisattvas in a single, equal object of focus, never forsaking one another.

Free from the need for formal consultation (*prātimokṣa*), they are able to manifest various Buddha-bodies at will; according to their own minds, they are able to know the power, majesty, and wisdom of the realms of all Tathāgatas;

they attain non-retrogressive supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as they desire, traveling through all worlds, manifesting forms in all assemblies, universally entering all places of birth, and accomplishing the inconceivable Mahāyāna practice of a Bodhisattva.
Their practice is as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future; furthermore, they make great vows,
vowing to ride the non-retrogressive wheel to perform the bodhisattva deeds, so that their actions of body, speech, and mind shall never be in vain—
such that those who merely catch a glimpse of them will certainly be established in the Buddha-dharma, and those who briefly hear their voice will attain the reality.
As soon as wisdom gives rise to pure faith, one forever severs the afflictions, attaining a body like that of the Great King of Medicinal Trees and a body like that of a wish-fulfilling jewel.

One practices all bodhisattva deeds, as vast as the dharma-realm and ultimate as space, without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future. Furthermore, one makes great vows, wishing for [them] within a single...
Throughout all worlds, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without departing from a single hair-tip;
at every hair-tip, they manifest their initial birth, renunciation, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering *nirvāṇa*.
Having attained the realm of Buddhahood and the power of great wisdom, they accord with all things in every thought-moment.

He manifests the attainment of Buddhahood to sentient beings to enable them to attain quiescence; through a single awakening (ekabodhi), he knows that all dharma-realms are the very nature of nirvāṇa.
With a single voice, he preaches the Dharma so that the hearts of all sentient beings are filled with joy;
he demonstrates entry into Great Nirvāṇa while never ceasing the practices of a bodhisattva, and he reveals the ground of great wisdom to establish all dharmas.

By means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-abhijñā*), the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda-abhijñā*), and the supernormal power of illusion (*māyā-abhijñā*),

they exercise mastery over transformations that fill the entire dharma-realm— vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and continuing without cessation throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to such great vows and such great valor.
Such great activities, with these ten gates of vows as their foremost, fulfill one million asaṃkhyeya great vows.
[Śāstra] The fourth son of the Buddha, having dwelt in this Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), has fifty-eight lines below this.

In the commentary on the section of the *Sūtra* clarifying the arousal of the ten inexhaustible, vast vows upon abiding in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the explanation is divided into twelve segments:
1. From "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "such great functions," there is one and a half lines of sūtra text;
this is the general presentation of what this stage is capable of, serving as the section for the ten great vows. 2. "Namely" (*yad uta*). [End of segment]

From "down to there being no rest" for three and a half lines of verse, it clarifies the vow to offer all articles of worship to all Buddhas, as vast as the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, without interruption; this is divided into three parts.
Furthermore, from "having made the great vows" down to "there being no rest," there are three lines of verse that clarify the vow for all Buddha-dharmas.

The section on "Sustaining Without Rest" is divided into four parts. Furthermore, from "Having made the great vow" down to "without rest," there are four and a half lines of scripture clarifying the vow to go to all worlds where Buddhas appear, to pay them homage as their foremost attendant, and to receive and practice the true Dharma without rest.
This constitutes the fifth part. Again, from "Having made the great vow" onwards...

The section extending to "without ceasing" (p. 4, l. 5), comprising four and a half lines of scripture, elucidates the vast conduct of the Bodhisattva as being inseparable from the purification of the stages (*bhūmi*) through the various *pāramitās*.
It explains, according to reality, their general and specific characteristics, their similarities and differences, and their formation and dissolution;
furthermore, it concerns the stage of teaching and transforming sentient beings without cessation. This segment corresponds to the progression through the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*).
The establishment of the ten *pāramitās*, the ten bodhisattva practices, the ten worlds, and the ten names of the Buddhas constitutes, in total,
the accomplishment of names according to practice within a single *pāramitā*. Within these five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), there are five hundred [factors], as each *pāramitā* contains ten,
and within each of those tens there are one hundred, according to the similarities and differences of the additional practices (*adhikāra*) added to the five stages.
Above these are five hundred [assemblies], identical to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, devas, and others in the first gathering. Each single assembly has ten; each group of ten has one hundred;
and above the fifty assemblies are five hundred. Each occupies its respective position according to the Bodhisattvas, devas, and others of that rank;
their names and meanings signify the practice of the *pāramitās*. Furthermore, each of the four assemblies of Sudhana possesses five [qualities].
The "hundred" refers to the ten meanings being fully contained within one; this is called "totality. Their practices diverge in their paths;
this is called "distinction. One wisdom is non-dual; this is called "sameness. According to practice, retribution differs; this is called "difference.
Being able to accomplish distinct names is called "accomplishment. Cause and effect are fundamentally void; this is called "destruction. To act according to practice is called "practice."
Because they lack intrinsic nature, for instance, within a single *pāramitā* there are these six gates:
first, it can destroy the ten afflictive fetters such as stinginess and greed, which is termed "destruction"; second, it can accomplish virtuous fruits, which is termed "accomplishment";

third, although the various delusions are numerous, its relinquishment applies universally to many phenomena, which is termed "comprehensiveness"; fourth, it specifically brings about distinct results, which is termed... [the text continues].

To distinguish them, these five ultimately converge into a single wisdom, which is termed "sameness" (sāmānya). To counteract the six secondary afflictions (upakleśa), they are termed "difference" (viśeṣa).
These six aspects of phenomena are fully present within all phenomena; by entering into each individual phenomenon through the gateway of practice and observing it with wisdom, they become visible.
If these six meanings were absent from any single phenomenon, [the nature of reality could not be realized].

All of these are partial views. Furthermore, when one *pāramitā* is fully endowed with the ten *pāramitās*, it carries the meaning of relinquishment (*tyāga*) that universally encompasses all phenomena without exception; the other cases should be understood by analogy.

Sixth, from "having made the great vow" down to "without rest," there are five lines and a half of scripture clarifying the vow to transform all sentient beings within the three realms and four modes of birth.
This section, titled "The Chapter on Abiding in the Vast and Unceasing Wisdom of All-Knowledge," clarifies the method for teaching and transforming the three realms and four modes of birth.
For those in the desire realm whose minds are predominantly [distracted], it exhorts them to contemplate the suffering, emptiness, and impermanence of all phenomena;

by applying these antidotes to the evils of desire, they cultivate various wholesome dharmas, delight in pure meditative concentration (*śamatha*), purify the defilements of the mind, and become free from greed, hatred, and delusion.

When one who has broken through the karma of the desire realm by means of pride and possesses a mind largely characterized by the tranquility of the form realm dwells in the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the perception of stillness, they abide in the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) wholesome realm.
Through the skillful means of exhorting the cultivation of the ten *pāramitās*—kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity—they bring these skillful means to fulfillment.

By means of the gate of the great, effortless, and tranquil samādhi (*anabhisaṃskāra-mahāśānti-samādhi*), they transcend the perceptions of stillness and suppression, manifesting all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Thus is it accomplished.
By means of immeasurable wisdom in skillful expedients (*upāya*), they teach and transform sentient beings;

if those with a predominance of formless realm minds are to be taught through skillful means, they cultivate extensive learning and the wisdom of discernment regarding all worldly affairs, ensuring there is no confusion or stagnation.

With a body free from fixed distraction, they give rise to the power of great vows, accomplish the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and practice the one [path] in making offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Because one plants all seeds of the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) to transform all inexhaustible sentient beings so that they may all attain Buddhahood, one thus relies upon the faculties to initiate subduing [of the mind] and causes them all to reach the knowledge of omniscience.

"Knowledge" refers to the cultivation of differentiated wisdom within the fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*). Just as fundamental wisdom manifests differentiated wisdom by relying on non-conceptual concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*), so too does it proceed.
Wisdom arises through the application of fundamental wisdom when one practices contemplation;
alternatively, it is attained by relying on the learning of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have already reached such realization, rather than through unaided cultivation.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "having made the great vow" down to "without rest," there are four lines of scripture that clarify how, through wisdom, one clearly perceives the vastness and multiplicity of coarse and subtle worlds. The vow is thus established.
The delimited world of form is called "coarse," while the formless world is called "subtle. Those that dwell in disorder consist of various classes living in a jumble;
this is like the various mixed-dwelling worlds here in Jambudvīpa. Those that dwell askew are like the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Those that dwell inverted are like the nests of hornets and the like. Those that dwell upright can be easily understood. If one enters...
Those who "dwell" are like sentient beings living in the earth who only wish to enter and do not wish to leave.
Those who "practice" are like humans whose bodies harbor eighty-four thousand families of parasites; even when a person walks, stands, sits, or lies down, these parasites remain within.
Those who "depart" are like sentient beings dwelling in flowing water, which flows only in one direction. These are the distinctions of the Indra’s Net.

Just as the net of Indra’s celestial palace consists of successive layers of light and shadows that mutually contain one another, so too do these worlds dwell in successive layers within the Flower Treasury Adorned World (*Kusumatalagarbha-vyūha-loka*).

They coexist with the oceans of worlds of all sentient beings without their karmic activities obstructing one another; they dwell in mutual containment like Indra’s net, each appearing according to its own karma.
As the Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all aspects and all-knowledge" clarifies that the seeds of a Bodhisattva’s great compassion are perfected by the power of great vows;
through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), differentiated wisdom manifests; and through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), universal wisdom is perfected.
Know that all these arise based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); it is from this alone that the infinite gateways of wisdom emerge.
8. Furthermore, from "Having made the great vows" onwards, there are six lines of scripture that clarify the section on the mutual interpenetration and adornment of Buddha-lands through vows.
This segment clarifies entry into the realm of wisdom, wherein Buddha-fields appear to one another like reflections of light and shadow.
9. Furthermore, from "Having made the great vows" down to "without ceasing," there are seven lines of scripture that clarify...

10. "May all bodhisattvas practice with a single resolve, free from resentment and jealousy"—this section, extending from "having made the great vows" down to "without ever ceasing," consists of five lines and a half of scripture, clarifying the aspect of practicing the bodhisattva conduct by mounting the irreversible wheel, wherein the physical, verbal, and mental actions of those who see or hear [them] do not pass in vain.
11. "Having made the great vows... and so forth—[the following section continues].

The section from "without ceasing" up to ten lines of the sūtra clarifies the division on manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood and entry into nirvāṇa in accordance with the desires of sentient beings in all worlds;
the section from "O sons of the Buddha" below that, spanning approximately two lines of the sūtra,
clarifies the concluding summary of the ten great vows as the inexhaustible vow-division.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this great vow is accomplished through ten "exhaustive phrases" (*kṣaya-pada*). What are these ten? They are: the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings;
the exhaustion of the realm of worlds; the exhaustion of the realm of empty space; the exhaustion of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); the exhaustion of the realm of nirvāṇa;

the exhaustion of the realm of the appearance of Buddhas; the exhaustion of the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; the exhaustion of the realm of the mind’s objects of focus; and the exhaustion of the realm that is the object of entry for the Buddha’s wisdom.
My vow shall end only when the world-system ends, when the turning of the Dharma ends, when the turning of wisdom ends, and when the realm of beings ends;
my vow shall end only when the world-system, up to the turning of the Dharma, the turning of wisdom, and the realm of beings, have all ended.

Yet, because the realm of beings cannot be exhausted, and likewise the world-system, up to the turning of the Dharma, the turning of wisdom, and the realm of beings, cannot be exhausted, this [vow of mine]—
The great vows and roots of goodness are inexhaustible.

[Treatise] Regarding the fifth son of the Buddha, from "these great vows" onwards, there are seven and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how the aforementioned ten inexhaustible vows are accomplished through ten phrases of exhaustion. This section is divided into two parts.

From the passage beginning with "First, from the Buddha’s son" down to "the realm of sentient beings is exhausted and my vows are then exhausted," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify the ten phrases of exhaustion (*daśa-kṣaya-pada*).
This is divided into two parts: first, from "the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible" down to "there is no end," two lines of scripture clarify the part on the inexhaustibility of the vow;
second, it speaks of the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom.

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): it clarifies that the flow of sentient beings through the three realms, the flow of phenomena, and the flow of gnosis continue until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted;
only when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted do the bodhisattva’s vows and practices reach their end. Thus, as long as they are not exhausted, the vows and practices are not exhausted.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, once a bodhisattva has made such great vows, they attain a mind of benefit, a supple mind, a compliant mind, a tranquil mind, a subdued mind, a mind of cessation, a humble mind, a moistened mind, an unshakable mind, and an unturbid mind.

Having achieved pure faith, they possess the functional power of faith; they are able to believe in the original practices through which the Tathāgata entered [enlightenment], and they believe in them.
The accomplishment of all *pāramitās*; faith and entry into the sublime stages (*bhūmi*); the power of the perfection of faith; the confidence endowed with fearlessness;

the growth of the indestructible, uncommon Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); faith in the inconceivable Buddha-qualities; faith in the arising of the Buddha-realm, which is neither middle nor extreme;
faith in the sequential entry into the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata; and the exaltation of the accomplishment of the fruit.
To state it briefly: it is because of the power of the teaching that all bodhisattva practices, up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, are to be believed.

[Treatise] Following the sixth line, "The Buddha-son Bodhisattva, having made such great vows," there are eight lines of scripture that clarify the ten kinds of beneficial mental states and the ten kinds of functional applications of faith obtained after one has given rise to the ten inexhaustible vows; this is the section of detailed explanation.
The meaning is divided into three sections: first, it clarifies that after generating the ten great vows to their full extent, one attains ten kinds of supple minds;
second, it clarifies the attainment of ten kinds of faith; third, to state the essentials briefly, the final line summarizes the whole, which may be understood according to the text.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva further reflects: "The True Dharma of all Buddhas is thus profound, thus tranquil, thus extinguished, thus empty, thus signless, thus wishless, thus unstained, thus immeasurable, and thus vast;
yet the minds of ordinary beings fall into false views and are shrouded by ignorance."
Shrouded by the high banner of pride, they enter the net of craving and wander through the dense forest of flattery and deception, unable to emerge from it.
Their minds are associated with stinginess and envy; they do not relinquish the causes and conditions for rebirth in the various realms of existence, which they constantly create.
Through the accumulation of karma born of greed, hatred, and delusion, these increase day and night; driven by the wind of resentment, the fire of their consciousness blazes without ceasing.

Whatever karma one performs is associated with inversion; through the continuity of the flow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the flow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the flow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and the flow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), the seeds of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) arise within the field of the three realms.
Furthermore, the sprouts of suffering are produced, namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which arise together and do not exist apart from one another.

As this name-and-form increases, the village of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is produced. Within these, contact (*sparśa*) arises through mutual correspondence, and from contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises.

Therefore, with birth as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); with the increase of craving, there is grasping (*upādāna*); with the increase of grasping, there is becoming (*bhava*); with becoming as condition, there is birth;
and with birth as condition, there arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. Thus, for these sentient beings, this mass of suffering grows.

Within this, all is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*), without cognition, without awareness, without agency, and without experience—just like grass, wood, stones, or walls.
Just like a reflection, sentient beings neither perceive nor know [this].
When the Bodhisattva sees that sentient beings cannot escape from such a mass of suffering, he gives rise to the wisdom of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). He further reflects:
"I must rescue these sentient beings and establish them in the state of ultimate peace and happiness. Thus, he gives rise to great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
*Prabhāsa-jñāna* (Light-Intelligence).

[Treatise]: Regarding the seventh son of the Buddha, from the passage "this bodhisattva further thinks thus" onwards, seventeen lines and a half of scripture clarify the section on the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of reality, his compassion for the mundane, and his arousal of great loving-kindness and compassion in accordance with the conditions of delusion. This is the explanation of its meaning.
The middle section is divided into five parts. This first part is the "Gate of Contemplating Suffering to Accomplish Compassion" within the seventh stage of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
From the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" down to "thus vast and great," there are three lines of scripture;

this first section, which raises the theme that the Buddha’s True Dharma is exceedingly vast, is divided into two parts. The second part begins with "Yet the minds of ordinary beings fall into false views."

Regarding the fact that within the field of the three realms, the sprouts of suffering further arise, there are six lines of sutra text clarifying how the minds of ordinary beings fall into false views and give rise to the continuous succession of rebirth in miserable destinies; this is divided into three parts.

First, from "Thus it is" down to "these sentient beings grow within a mass of suffering," there are four lines of sutra text clarifying that the members of the twelve links of dependent origination constitute birth.

The section from "The four causal factors are all empty therein" down to "neither perceiving nor knowing" comprises two lines of scripture clarifying the section on sentient beings' ignorance of the emptiness and selflessness of the body.

The section from "the five bodhisattvas" down to "the wisdom of the light of great compassion" comprises three lines of scripture clarifying the section on perceiving the suffering of sentient beings and giving rise to compassionate pity. This entire segment consists of ten [sections].

The seven and a half lines of scripture are established as a summary through four analytical gates: first, the gate of presenting the essence to show delusion; second, the gate of ordinary beings deluding their own essence and thereby undergoing suffering;
third, the gate of the flow of existence without intrinsic nature due to a failure to understand dependent origination;

and fourth, the gate of Bodhisattvas attaining the truth and compassionately taking on birth for the sake of those in suffering. Regarding the first, the gate of presenting the essence to show delusion, it corresponds to the first three lines.

Thus, [the Buddha] raises up the True Dharma of all Buddhas—so profound, so tranquil, so quiescent, and so characterized by signlessness—and out of compassion for ordinary beings who do not awaken to it, being shrouded in the long night of ignorance and false views as they revolve in the stream of suffering.
It is asked: Since the essence of all sentient beings is itself the truth and their wisdom is equal to that of the Tathāgata, for what reason...

Question: From delusion arise all karmic sufferings. Answer: Because the essence of true suchness (tathatā) and wisdom-principle (jñāna) is entirely without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), this natureless wisdom-principle cannot know itself.
If it were able to know itself, it would not be called "without intrinsic nature. However, sentient beings follow conditions and flow along with their objects;
they do not know good or evil, and thus their karma varies according to the transformations of those objects. Or, due to the Buddha or a Bodhisattva...
For them, he explains the causes of suffering or how suffering arises from its own causes, so that they may develop revulsion and seek the path of right view that is not characterized by suffering.
As long as they have not yet developed revulsion toward the fruits of suffering, they will ultimately not believe the words of the Noble One;
they cannot know for themselves what is true or false, or what is suffering or happiness. They merely experience the arising of birth, yet feel no revulsion, no dread, and no burning distress.

If one’s awakening and understanding are not profound, and one does not diligently cultivate oneself by self-reproach and tireless effort to perform various meditative contemplations that enter the true gate of the Dharma-realm, one will ultimately never be able to exhaust the source of suffering. Second is the gate of ordinary beings who delude their own nature and thereby produce suffering:
as described below, when the minds of ordinary beings fall into false views and so forth, they come to dwell within the field of the three realms.

Furthermore, regarding the sutra passage on the "six modes of arising that produce the sprouts of suffering," within this section, there are eighteen kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*) experienced in birth;
these all arise based upon two types of affliction. What are these two? First, fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), which has been shrouded for a long night;
second, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which constantly flow and revolve following objects without ceasing. These two—

If one plants the seeds of ignorance, only upon attaining fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) does it become the functional application of wisdom; this is because it cannot be severed through the contemplation of emptiness of the three vehicles.
Therefore, according to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the Pure Land can only suppress the active manifestations of afflictions (*kleśa*);
they are not said to have "severed" the afflictions. Because they merely suppress them, they attain the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Bodhisattvas in the cycle of birth and death attain bodies born of the joy of their own will; yet they still possess both longing and aversion, and have not yet attained the universal radiance wisdom of the Dharma-realm regarding all Buddha-fields of self and others.

They have not yet attained the single ocean of wisdom identical with that of the Buddhas of the ten directions, nor have they forever severed the flow of all views—including false views, the grasping at self and other, and the rejection or acceptance of phenomena—remaining thus deluded by the two aforementioned types of ignorance.

To falsely give rise to aversion and abandonment, seeking to realize *tathatā* (suchness) and the characteristic of emptiness separately, is to be deluded regarding Great Wisdom. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"All afflictions and the various gates of worldly toil serve as the seeds of Buddhahood. It is said that for the One Vehicle Bodhisattvas, this ignorance and false view are realized and perfected into wisdom;
whereas for those of the Three Vehicles, they are suppressed in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), which is also described as "retaining afflictions to moisten [the roots of merit]."
These births are all not spoken of in accordance with wisdom; they differ from the One Vehicle.

Based upon the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*), there spontaneously exist gates of infinite great sovereign function, such as the ten Wisdom-Buddhas within the stage of the Ten Faiths, which take the Immovable Wisdom Buddha as their head. Thus, regarding this ignorance, false views, and all afflictions—

The fundamental [afflictions] are established; all other afflictions from those mentioned below arise from them and are collectively termed "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), because they exist in dependence upon the fundamental ones.
Just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is universally termed the cause of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), so too consciousness arises dependent on objects;
with the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) serving as the cause, the perception of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth within the six faculties constitutes the objective field for name-and-form.
The false view that grasps at names due to the seeds of consciousness regarding objects is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), as it is a cognition deluded regarding ultimate truth.

From the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), two kinds of false views arise; these two correspond to each of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and upon each faculty there are three [aspects].
For example, when the ear faculty hears a sound and recognizes it as such a sound, all of this arises from the seeds of name-and-form and consciousness.

The three types [of views] such as wrong view, as well as the eye, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties—collectively termed "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa)—together with consciousness, constitute the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
With name-and-form as the object and the faculties as the primary factors, consciousness acts as the grasper; this can be seen through reflection.
Therefore, this sutra states: "Not apart from this growth of name-and-form, the cluster of the six sense bases arises within it. Regarding these characteristics:
From birth arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises grasping; from grasping arises becoming; from becoming arise old age, death, and so forth.
Just as the two types of pride serve to increase ignorance, they enable the seeds of suffering to flourish and remain indestructible.
Therefore, a sutra says: "One who plants the banner of pride enters the net of craving, just like craving itself."
It acts as a moisture for ignorance, because it moistens the constant flow of birth and death; it results in an undesirable and unwanted body, just like flattery and deception;
it is a dense thicket of ignorance, because it is self-delusive, pervasive, and extensive; it is that which ordinary worldlings constantly practice without even a moment’s interruption;
and it is not an object of cultivated meditative concentration, being impossible to restrain, just like stinginess and envy.
These two types are considered eternal: ignorance and the further intensification of the causes for birth and death in the evil realms. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"When the mind is associated with stinginess and envy, it does not relinquish them and constantly creates the causal conditions for rebirth in the various destinies;
like greed, hatred, and delusion, this is the accumulation of karma. Ignorance is thus [the root]. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Greed, hatred, and delusion accumulate all [sufferings]."
Karma increases day and night, just as anger, resentment, and ignorance act as the causes for hatred; therefore, the Sūtra says:

"The fire of the mind-consciousness blazes unceasingly, fanned by the winds of anger and resentment. The flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of ignorance, and the flow of views—these are constant flows;
ignorance perpetually circulates without ceasing. Thus, these four flows are a great river that is eternally present.
If the flow does not cease, it forms a great ocean of suffering; if the mind is free of conceptual thought, all flows are suddenly exhausted.

When wisdom manifests, they immediately become the flow of Dharma. Thus, as the twelve links of existence mutually serve as both primary and secondary factors, there are twelve links upon each single link, totaling one hundred and forty-four links of existence that constitute the boundless cycle of birth and death.
The eighteen kinds of afflictions and ignorance above all take the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as their root;
these twelve links of existence take name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and false views as their basis.

If one seals them with the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the eighty-four thousand defilements are all collectively the ocean of wisdom-flow of the Dharma. Thus, ignorance and name-and-form face the five [aggregates].

The faculties consist of contact, sensation, perception, and mental formations, which are collectively governed by the mind’s intention and grasping. Thus, these nine conditions together arise to perceive objects;
this is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). These ten factors taken together are termed ignorance (*avidyā*) and collectively termed false view.
That which produces all afflictions, deludes the mind, and obscures objects is called ignorance. "Objects" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which consists of the six sense faculties.
Regarding the third gate, the flow of non-existence arising from ignorance of dependent origination, which follows from wrong views concerning objects:
this section clarifies the cause produced by delusion regarding reality and pursuit of the false. From the words "That which is called...

down to "the growth of the mass of suffering," these four lines of scripture explain that the so-called cause depends upon name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) to produce the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as their objective conditions.
Contact, by virtue of contact, is the cause for the six sense bases to take up [objects]; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises grasping; from grasping arises becoming;
because of becoming, there arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Within "name" (nāma) is contained "form" (rūpa), and within "form" is contained "name";

these two, name-and-form (nāmarūpa), exist together, and within them are included sound, odor, taste, and touch, as well as both informative form (vijñapti-rūpa) and non-informative form (avijñapti-rūpa).
However, when the mind, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness encounter objects and are stimulated to form delusions, these are all "contact" (*sparśa*).

Only the Tathāgata is unconditioned and possesses pure wisdom alone; he has no contact with phenomena. When sentient beings experience contact and sensation, they produce the afflictions of the three realms.
Śrāvakas, weary of birth and death, realize nirvana through contact and sensation. Bodhisattvas [realize] the Pure Land through contact and sensation.

There are two kinds of touch: pure and impure. A bodhisattva of the One Vehicle possesses the wisdom of the perfect integration of compassion and wisdom, yet has not yet attained mastery over such touches.
These various touches are observed through the illumination of wisdom, thereby accomplishing the function of wisdom. For this reason, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"One experiences all touches as if they were realized by wisdom. Furthermore, the fact that phenomena are fundamentally unborn and do not now perish clarifies the essence of dependent origination.
The self-nature is non-existent and is not a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing; that ordinary beings do not understand this is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

If one simply knows that the mind and its objects are fundamentally non-existent, then what arises is only the arising of phenomena, which is always the realm of wisdom and not a condition of arising and ceasing.
By observing with concentration and wisdom, understanding opens naturally. Fourth is the Bodhisattva’s Gate of Compassionate Action for Receiving and Delivering Beings, which proceeds from—
Within this, all is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self, up to the Wisdom of the Great Compassionate Radiance Sūtra in Five Practices.
Thus, from these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), all sentient beings arise;

through the eighteen kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*) mentioned previously, they transmigrate through birth and death, experiencing no suffering that they do not undergo. Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Pure Lands loathe [this cycle].

When the active manifestations of these [twelve links] are subdued and do not arise, the Bodhisattva of the One Vehicle achieves fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and gives rise to discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) to transform sentient beings, maintain wholesome dharmas, and realize *bodhi*.

This is because the mind and its mental factors differ in terms of delusion and awakening; it is not that the twelve links of existence are different from wisdom. As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: [text follows].
The same applies to this explanation as above regarding the eighteen kinds of afflictions.

Just as with false views and ignorance, when one first gives birth into the family of Tathāgata-wisdom at the initial stage of the ten abodes (the First Abode of Initial Resolve), even if one were capable of committing acts leading to the evil realms, false views have already been eliminated;
thus, while the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) are thin and subtle rather than exhausted, the eighteen kinds [of afflictions], including pride and so forth, are all likewise [diminished].

Because there are ten types [of afflictions], within the dharmas of the ten practices and ten dedications, ten methods of application are used to counteract them, gradually attenuating them until one reaches the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

Through the increasing clarity of correct wisdom, there remains only the attachment to dharmas that accompanies the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), yet there is no longer the unwholesome karma of habitual tendencies manifesting within the three realms—such as the five types: stinginess, envy, resentment, malice, and anger.

Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have already ceased; from the remaining stages up to the seventh, when compassion is perfected and wisdom is fulfilled, one then achieves the functional application of wisdom that accords with vows.

This may only be called "attaining the function of wisdom through afflictions" (*kleśa*), and cannot be called "severing afflictions," because the active manifestation of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) persists until the seventh stage, whereas the habitual tendencies of attachment to phenomena are only eliminated at the tenth stage.

There are two types of ignorance—the ignorance regarding the vastness of the primary marks (lakṣaṇa) as numerous as atoms, and the ignorance regarding the qualities of the secondary signs (anuvyañjana)—which are only seen to be exhausted upon reaching the final stage of practice at the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is as explained in the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* and the *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta*.

For this reason, the Tathāgata himself taught these two chapters of sūtra to clarify the two types of ignorance regarding the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, he clarified the subtle nature of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

The practice continues until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained, at which point it is finally exhausted. Based on this, the five stages (*pañca-vastu*) are established, with ten perfections (*pāramitā*) for each stage, totaling one hundred;

these are used to counteract [the afflictions]. Thus, the principles of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground are all similar in essence, establishing the different levels of the stages of practice and cultivation. In this way, the ten perfections across these five stages are all initially threefold.
The *pāramitās* serve to remedy the worldly path that follows from being entangled in afflictions, as illustrated by the first, second,

and third spiritual friends among Sudhana’s ten stages through the representation of three bhikṣus; subsequently, the latter three *pāramitās* serve to remedy the delusions pertaining to both the supramundane and the mundane,
as exemplified respectively by the elder Megha, the elder Vimukti, and the elder Sāgaradhvaja.

Following the manifestation of Kṣemadatta, the three pāramitās beginning with the pāramitā of skillful means (*upāya*)—namely, the pāramitās of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*)—are presented as the gates for entering the mundane world through supramundane means, thereby bringing mastery over compassion and wisdom;

these are manifested respectively by the female lay practitioner Śreṣṭhidāraka, the ascetic Ṛṣi, and the Brahmin practitioner of austerities. Following this, there are the mundane and supramundane [realms].
Because wisdom and compassion are sovereign, it is through the perfection of wisdom that one gives rise to compassion;
because one attains mastery by giving rise to compassion through wisdom, it is represented by the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja named Maitrāyaṇī. Wisdom is sovereign like a king;
having cultivated compassion within the seventh stage to give rise to wisdom, one now gives rise to compassion through wisdom within this tenth stage.
Therefore, she is the daughter of a king. She is "illuminated" by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*; through wisdom, she perfects compassion and thus attains mastery.

Consequently, this illumination clarifies the progressive cultivation of the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*). Within each stage, there are these four types of distinctions and similarities regarding their respective spheres of influence (*śakti-vibhāga*).
Only by further examining the specific distinctions and similarities among each of Sudhana’s spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) can one fully comprehend the understanding of these five stages.

The similarities and differences in practice follow from this Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). As mentioned above, there are four types of distinctions in the treatment of afflictions (*kleśa*) regarding these similarities and differences:
first, from the first stage to the third stage, one treats worldly defilements and accomplishes the habituation of the supramundane;
second, the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages treat the worldly wisdom within the supramundane that is not self-... [independent].
In practicing the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, one trains in compassion and wisdom that lack mastery within the mundane world;
therefore, during the eighth stage, the Buddhas provide three empowerments and seven kinds of exhortations to guard against this.
As is clearly explained in the eighth stage, the wisdom-pāramitā of the ninth and tenth stages serves as the remedy for the mundane.

Because he has attained mastery over compassion and wisdom, the third wife of the Tathāgata during his time as a prince, Gopā, represents that his great loving-kindness and great compassion are already perfected. This illustrates the meaning of the joy of the Dharma through compassion;
it is like the nine goddesses and one Buddha-wife encountered by Sudhana within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which serve to clarify this point.
Because this Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages nourishes the gate of great compassion, causing it to become perfect and sovereign, it is symbolized by a female deity;
yet even upon reaching that stage, the Bodhisattva’s altruistic practices of Samantabhadra are not yet fully mastered.
Thus, a general outline of the five stages of spiritual progression is presented in six points: first, the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), which clarify the initial birth into the Buddha-family.
First, it eliminates the active afflictions (*kleśa*). Second, it clarifies the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*) which treat the habitual delusions manifested in accordance with the world.

Third, it clarifies the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*) which give rise to the power of great vows, harmonizing wisdom and compassion to benefit sentient beings through the unimpeded integration of the mundane and the supramundane.

Fourth, it clarifies the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) which nurture the accumulated practice of compassion and wisdom until their function is perfected. Fifth, it clarifies the eleventh ground (*ekādaśabhūmi*).
The fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices refers to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Practices" and the sections following the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations.

The sixth clarifies the culmination of the stage of Buddhahood, namely the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata. As for the "Chapter on Leaving the World," it clarifies the progressive cultivation toward the fruit of Buddhahood;
thereafter, the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Constant Practice in the Dharma Realm" clarifies that throughout this entire scripture, from beginning to end, [the practice is consistently maintained].
Therefore, taking the *dharmadhātu* as its essence, through the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, all things are perfectly interfused;

there is not a single dharma that possesses temporal distinctions of before or after. When one illuminates this with wisdom, it can be seen that the various distinct stages and positions within these five ranks are all contained within the initial stage of the "Abiding in the First Thought of Enlightenment" (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), where they are universally sealed by the wisdom of vows, conduct, and compassion, thereby bringing them to perfection.
Because they are fulfilled, although the teachings have a sequence of before and after, the dharmas of aspiration, practice, compassion, and wisdom are simultaneous;
time does not differ from them, nor do the dharmas deviate from it. Therefore, those who resolve their minds for enlightenment should cultivate in this way and fulfill in this way.

Because they do not depart from the substance of the Tathāgata’s immovable wisdom, they are fulfilled; thus, within the single fruit of Buddhahood, wisdom and compassion are thoroughly realized from beginning to end.
Therefore, one universally perceives all sentient beings as the Buddha-land because there is no coming or going;

one teaches and transforms those sentient beings who are deluded regarding Tathāgata-wisdom so that they may rely upon their own fundamental nature; one causes all sentient beings to universally perceive all Buddhas within their own wisdom as being of one and the same wisdom;
and one ensures that they do not give rise to the notion of a separate Buddha apart from their own wisdom. Thus, [one causes] all...

Because sentient beings do not give rise to views of internal or external, distant or near regarding their own bodies, they are sealed with the single seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*) to shatter the perceptions of existence that involve magnitude, smallness, length, and shortness. Practicing in this way is precisely what ensures that the Buddha-seed within all sentient beings is never severed;
therefore, by teaching such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, one is able to ensure that the Dharma-seed endures.
They ceaselessly cause all sentient beings everywhere to see themselves as identical to the ocean of Buddha-wisdom and to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
for this reason, they are able to ensure that the lineage of the Sangha is never interrupted. Observing each thing in this manner, they cause the mind and its objects to correspond in such a way.
