A Combined Commentary on the Ten Stages Chapter, Part Twenty-six, Section Five.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in accordance with such great kindness and great compassion, with a mind of profound gravity...
When dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one has no begrudging attachment toward any object; seeking the Great Wisdom of a Buddha, one practices great renunciation (*mahātyāga*).

Whatever one possesses, all that can be given—namely, wealth, grain, granaries, gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and other such precious jewels, necklaces, ornaments for the body, elephants, and horses—is all capable of being bestowed.

Vehicles, slaves, servants, cities, towns, villages, gardens, groves, palaces, wives, concubines, men, women, internal and external retinues, as well as all other precious playthings, and even one's own head, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, marrow, and bones—all bodily parts—without sparing anything for the sake of seeking the vast wisdom of all Buddhas;
this is called a bodhisattva abiding in... [the stage of joy].
On the first stage, the Buddha-son Bodhisattva accomplishes great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).

Because he seeks further, without weariness, all mundane and supramundane beneficial matters for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings with this mind of great compassionate giving, he immediately achieves the mind of indefatigability.
Having achieved the mind of indefatigability, regarding all sūtras and śāstras...
The mind is free from timidity; because it is free from timidity, one immediately achieves mastery of the wisdom of all sūtras and śāstras.

Having attained this wisdom, one is well able to deliberate upon what should and should not be done. Toward all sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—one acts accordingly, according to their capacity, and in accordance with what they have practiced. Therefore, the bodhisattva attains worldly wisdom and becomes a master of the world.

Having known the proper time and the proper measure through wisdom, and being adorned with a sense of shame and dread of blame, they diligently cultivate the path that benefits both themselves and others.
Therefore, they achieve the adornment of shame and dread of blame; within this practice, they diligently cultivate renunciation, remaining non-regressive and unwavering to achieve steadfast power.
Having attained steadfast power, they diligently make offerings to the Buddhas and are able to practice the Buddha’s teachings exactly as they have been taught.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus accomplishes these ten dharmas that purify the stages— namely, faith, compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, equanimity, freedom from weariness,
knowledge of the sūtras and śāstras, skillful understanding of worldly dharmas, a sense of shame and dread of blame, firm strength, making offerings to all Buddhas,
and practicing according to the teachings— they become purified.

[Treatise] The eighth section, "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Son of the Buddha," and the subsequent twenty-one and a half lines of sūtra clarify the stage of entering the first bhūmi (*prathamā bhūmi*), specifically the section on practicing generosity in accordance with great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*). Within the commentary on this meaning, it is divided into four parts;
this is the eighth ground-characteristic within the first bhūmi, beginning from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding all that can be given, there is a passage of two and a half lines of sutra that clarifies the section on "all that can be relinquished," which is divided into two parts.
Specifically, from the point below [the title] down to "this is called the Bodhisattva abiding in the first stage,

accomplished in great giving," there is a passage of five and a half lines of sutra that clarifies how, within this stage, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-wisdom, one has no stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth.
Within this section, there are three types of giving: first, the giving of wealth and treasures; second, the giving of elephants, horses, wives, and children;
and third, the giving of one’s head, eyes, ears, body, and flesh.

O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva, having cultivated such compassion, is able to practice the Buddha’s teachings exactly as they were taught, ten sūtras clarify that the bodhisattva at this stage has attained perfection.
Having previously practiced giving, one attains ten kinds of benefits: first, clarifying the objective of great compassion and great giving;
second, clarifying that the purpose of what is given is to seek the True Dharma and to save sentient beings; third, seeking supramundane wisdom with a mind free from weariness;
fourth, possessing a mind free from timidity regarding all sūtras and śāstras; fifth, skillfully deliberating upon the superior, middling, and [inferior].
1. Inferior sentient beings practice according to their capacity, forming the portion of worldly wisdom; 2. adorning themselves with the sixfold sense of shame and remorse;
3. cultivating the path of self-benefit and benefiting others; 4. diligently practicing without retreat; 5. achieving firm and steadfast power; 6. making offerings to all Buddhas; 7.
being able to act in accordance with whatever is taught within the Buddha’s Dharma; 8. the four types of Buddha-sons; and finally, practicing in reliance upon the teachings.
Regarding practice, there are two and a half sections of sūtra that clearly summarize the accomplishment of the ten methods for purifying the stages (*bhūmi*), as fully detailed in the sūtra.
Within this section, as described above, [the practitioner] possesses faith, compassion, joy, and equanimity; is free from weariness; knows the various sūtras and śāstras;
is well-versed in worldly dharmas; possesses shame and remorse; has firm strength; and honors the Buddhas by means of their teachings.

Cultivation serves as the gateway to the Dharma for purifying the stages of practice; taking the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) as its essence, the other nine perfections serve as its companions.

[Sūtra] Having dwelled in this Stage of Joy, O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, by the power of his great vows, comes to see many Buddhas—namely, he sees many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of billions of Buddhas.
He reverently honored, respected, served, and made offerings to a thousand koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of nayutas of koṭis of Buddhas,
many hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, many thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas—
offering them all with a great mind and a profound mind robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
He offers all necessities of life as gifts and also makes offerings to the entire assembly of monks;

he dedicates these roots of goodness entirely toward unexcelled bodhi. O Son of the Buddha, because this bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, he achieves the method for maturing sentient beings.
He gathers in sentient beings through the first two means of integration—namely, giving and kind speech—and through the latter two methods of integration.
Relying solely on the power of faith and understanding, although their practice has not yet reached full mastery, among these ten *pāramitās* of the bodhisattva, the *dānapāramitā* is predominant;
it is not that they do not practice the other *pāramitās*, but rather they do so according to their strength and capacity.
Whatever the bodhisattva diligently cultivates—whether making offerings to the Buddhas or transforming sentient beings—all is accomplished through the cultivation of the pure stages (*bhūmi*).

All roots of goodness inherent in the Dharma are dedicated toward the stage of omniscience, becoming increasingly bright, pure, pliant, and perfected, so as to become serviceable at will, O Son of the Buddha.

Just as a skilled goldsmith refines gold by repeatedly placing it in the fire until it becomes increasingly bright, pure, pliant, and perfected, thereby becoming serviceable at will; so too does the Bodhisattva likewise make offerings to all...
The Buddha’s transformation of sentient beings consists entirely of cultivating the dharmas of the pure stages;

all roots of goodness therein are dedicated toward the stage of omniscience, becoming increasingly luminous, pure, harmonious, and supple, thereby achieving mastery and becoming fit for use according to one's will.

[Treatise] Ninth: Regarding the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva, Son of the Buddha, having dwelt in this Stage of Joy," there are eighteen lines and a half of scripture that clarify how, through the power of great vows, one comes to see many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings.
In the commentary on its meaning, it is divided into three sections: first, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "dedicating [merit] without... [the end].

Regarding the section on attaining supreme enlightenment, there are seven lines and a half of sūtra that clarify how, through the power of aspiration, one encounters hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and serves and makes offerings to them all;

this is divided into two parts. From "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) downwards, up to "as one wishes," there are seven lines of sūtra clarifying how one obtains superior benefits by making offerings to the Buddhas;
this is divided into three parts. From "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, again up to "as one... [the text continues].
The mind capable of being employed has four aspects, as clarified by a sutra using the analogy of a goldsmith refining gold by repeatedly casting it into fire;
this illustrates how a bodhisattva’s practice increases toward the higher stages. This section is fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in the First Ground should seek out and inquire of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and spiritual friends regarding the characteristics and the fruits attained within this ground, never becoming weary or satisfied, in order to accomplish the dharmas of this ground; furthermore,
they should likewise seek out and inquire of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends.
Question: Regarding the signs and the attainment of the fruit in the second bhūmi, one should seek and inquire about them with insatiable diligence in order to accomplish the dharmas of that stage;

likewise, one should also seek and inquire in this same manner regarding the signs and the attainment of the fruit in the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth bhūmis, desiring to accomplish those [dharmas].
Because it is the nature of the stages (*bhūmi*), this Bodhisattva skillfully knows the obstacles to the stages and their remedies; skillfully knows the formation and destruction of the stages;

skillfully knows the characteristics and fruits of the stages; skillfully knows the cultivation for attaining the stages; skillfully knows the purification of the dharmas of the stages; skillfully knows the progression from stage to stage;
skillfully knows what is possible and impossible regarding each stage; skillfully knows the superior wisdom of each stage; and skillfully knows the non-retrogression of each stage.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva thus skillfully understands the characteristics of the stages—
beginning with the thorough purification of all bodhisattva stages and proceeding until the entry into the stage of a Tathāgata— and initiates practice in the first stage without interruption,
continuing in this manner through to the tenth stage without any cessation, then, by means of the light of wisdom of these stages, they achieve the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
O sons of the Buddha, it is like a caravan leader who is skilled in expedient means and wishes to lead his merchants to a great city.
Before setting out, he first inquires about the merits and faults along the way, as well as whether the places for rest are safe or not.
Thereafter, he prepares the provisions for the journey and performs what is necessary. O sons of the Buddha, although that great caravan leader—

Before even setting out, he is able to know all matters of safety and danger within the journey; he skillfully employs wisdom to deliberate and observe, providing for all necessities so that there is no lack.

Leading the multitude of merchants until they reach that great city in safety, he ensures that both himself and the people are entirely freed from distress and affliction. Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Caravan Leader is likewise.
Abiding in the first stage (*bhūmi*), they skillfully know the obstacles to and the remedies for all stages,
up to skillfully knowing the purification of all bodhisattva stages and the transition into the stage of a Tathāgata; only then do they become fully endowed with the provisions of merit and wisdom,
and lead all sentient beings from the perilous wilderness of birth and death to safely reach the city of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), both body and...

Because sentient beings do not undergo hardships, a bodhisattva should always be untiring and diligently cultivate the sublime pure deeds of the various stages (*bhūmi*) until entering the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Son of the Buddha, this is called a brief explanation of the gate for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to enter the first bodhisattva stage;
were it explained extensively, it would involve immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas].
The Section on Distinctions.

[Treatise]: The following twenty-eight lines and a half of the sūtra, beginning with "The tenth son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva," clarify how a bodhisattva, upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), skillfully inquires into the successive stages of cultivation and the remedies for obstacles.
In the detailed explanation of the meaning, the section is divided into three parts:

First, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "accomplishing the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," there are fourteen lines of sūtra that clarify the causal and resultant aspects of how a bodhisattva, having already entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), further seeks this stage and the ten stages in order to enter the stage of the Tathāgata. Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "all... [the text continues].

Regarding the avoidance of suffering and affliction, six lines and a half of sūtra clarify this by using the analogy of a merchant leader traveling to a great city to illustrate how a bodhisattva inquires about the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*),
their security and peril, and the complete array of necessary provisions; this section,
from "The Three Sons of the Buddha" down to the distinctions of hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* [aeons], consists of seven lines and a half of sūtra clarifying the bodhisattva.
Practicing with skillful knowledge of the characteristics of the stages, their security and peril, they lead sentient beings to attain unimpeded liberation,
like a caravan leader. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this first stage, they mostly become kings of Jambudvīpa, noble and majestic.
They possess sovereign power to constantly protect the True Dharma and are able to gather in sentient beings through great giving.
They skillfully remove the defilements of stinginess and greed from sentient beings, always practicing great giving without exhaustion.

Whether it be giving, kind speech, purposeful action, or cooperation—whatever deeds they perform, none are apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.

The Bodhisattva who practices with non-conceptualization does not depart from the recollection of the bodhisattva conduct, does not depart from the recollection of the various perfections (*pāramitās*), does not depart from the recollection of the various stages (*bhūmis*), does not depart from the recollection of the powers (*bala*), does not depart from the recollection of the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), does not depart from the recollection of the unique buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and so on, up to not departing from the recollection of being fully endowed with all aspects of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*). Furthermore, he maintains the thought: "I shall..."
Among all sentient beings, he is the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite,
the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander, even unto being the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). Such a bodhisattva,
if desiring to leave the home life to practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, is then able to renounce his home, wife, and children.
Having renounced the five desires and left the household life to study the Path according to the Tathāgata’s teaching, and having already left the household life, they practice with diligent vigor;
in a single moment of thought, they attain one hundred samādhis, behold one hundred Buddhas, and know the spiritual powers of one hundred Buddhas;
they can shake one hundred Buddha-worlds, traverse one hundred Buddha-worlds, illumine one hundred Buddha-worlds, and bring one hundred Buddha-worlds to spiritual transformation.

Sentient beings are able to abide for a lifespan of a hundred kalpas, know the events of a hundred kalpas each in both the past and future limits, enter into a hundred dharma-gates, and manifest a hundred bodies;
within each body, they can manifest a hundred bodhisattvas as their retinue.
If, through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows, they manifest beyond these numbers, it may extend to hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Even in a thousand kalpas, or even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know [the extent of it].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] The eleventh section, "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Son of the Buddha," contains twenty and a half lines of scripture that clarify the stage of entering the position and receiving office for bodhisattvas.

The commentary explains that this constitutes the direct answer to the preceding question regarding the causes and effects of the first and tenth stages (*bhūmi*) of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Within this section, it is further divided into...
Second, from "The first [son of the Buddha] from the beginning" down to "the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvajñajñāna*), there are eight lines of sutra text.
Within this, there are five general points: (1) correctly presenting the fruit of the first stage; (2) clarifying the ability to protect and uphold the true Dharma;
(3) clarifying the practices to be performed; (4) clarifying the practice of gathering [beings]; and (5) clarifying that all actions are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Sangha, not departing from mindfulness of the five sciences, is endowed with the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*).

As for "in all aspects," it is because they accomplish the seed of great compassion through the assistance of application and great vows. Furthermore, the knowledge of all-knowledge has already been explained previously;

moreover, they give rise to a great aspiration and delight in cultivating both the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of distinctions, thereby extensively practicing the seed of great compassion.
That which arises from cultivation is like omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is manifested through meditative concentration;

therefore, differentiated knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) is accomplished only by relying on the instructions of a teacher and training under those who have already attained mastery. All of this exists in dependence upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Alternatively, for those individuals who attain clear understanding through progressively higher levels of contemplation based on their own faculties, they must still rely on the teacher’s instruction as a second factor.

Having reflected thus, he spoke the following verses, consisting of twelve lines of sūtra, which clarify that a bodhisattva in this stage is able to renounce home, wife, and children to practice the dharma of renunciation and attain the dharma-gate of beholding the realms of a hundred buddhas.
Within these twelve and a half lines of sūtra, there are eight main points: first, being capable of serving as a leader for sentient beings; second, ... [and so forth].
1. Capable of serving as a refuge for those seeking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and its distinctions; 2. Able to renounce the three *vidyās* that are difficult to abandon; 3.

Able to renounce the four *vidyās* and leave the household life to practice with diligence; 4. The five *vidyās* obtained through the attainment of *samādhi*; 5. The six *vidyās* consisting of the number of Buddhas seen through the support of merit; 6.
The seven *vidyās* consisting of the further expansion of seeing Buddhas through the power of vows; 7. The eight *vidyās* consisting of the repeated explanation.

The verse above states that "seeing many hundreds of Buddhas" refers to the cognitive realm of the Flower Treasury (*Kusumatalagarbha*), wherein a single Buddha-field ocean fuses with the oceans of all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, interpenetrating and pervading extensively.
These "many hundreds" do not refer merely to the hundred Buddhas limited by the Buddha-realm of a trichiliocosm; rather, they extend even to the pores of one's own body, pervading the entire Dharma.
The hundred [buddhas] of the realm of empty space cannot be understood through the hundred buddhas known by the ordinary mind;
therefore, these are many hundreds within the infinite realm of wisdom. They are merely established as dharmas for ascending progress according to the stages in order to clarify that progression.
However, regarding each individual buddha-realm, one must not harbor views of its center or its limits; one should simply attain [realization] for oneself.
When one contemplates the realm of the wisdom of the body as being without center or periphery, how can one argue that the Buddha-realm has limits or measures?

Seeing this, the dharmas of the first stage, the intermediate stages, the ten stages, and the Tathāgata stage are treated as a single ground. One universally cultivates the dharmas of the ten stages and the Buddha stage;
thus, within this, the cause and fruit are based on the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), wherein the Buddha-fruit is named "Sublime" (*praṇīta*) by means of the ten stages.

However, by accomplishing the great ocean of vows within the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and fulfilling those great vow-practices, one likewise does not depart from the practices of the Golden World, the Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and others within the initial stage of faith.
As a verse in a sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha, when such a wondrous jewel-mind first arises, one then transcends the ordinary."
Indeed, this station enters the sphere of practice of the Buddhas.
[Sūtra]: If a person accumulates manifold virtues and is fully endowed with pure, white dharmas; if they make offerings to the Honored One of Gods and Humans and follow the path of compassion;
if their faith and understanding are exceedingly vast and their aspiration and delight are likewise pure—
Seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, they have resolved upon this unsurpassed mind;
to purify the power of all-knowledge and the fearlessnesses, and to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas;
to rescue and gather the multitudes of sentient beings for the sake of attaining great compassion, and to turn the supreme wheel of Dharma, they adorn and purify the Buddha-lands.
Having generated this most supreme mind, one knows the three periods of time in a single thought-moment;
yet there is no discrimination regarding their various and differing times, as it is demonstrated to the world. To briefly explain the seeking of all the supreme merits of the Buddhas:
one generates a vast mind whose measure is equal to the realm of empty space.
Compassion precedes wisdom as its sovereign; skillful means act in mutual accord. With pure faith and understanding, the mind is like that of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable power.
Unobstructed knowledge manifests before one; awakening by oneself without depending on another, one becomes fully endowed with the state of a Tathāgata.
One who gives rise to this most supreme mind is a child of the Buddha, having just begun to be born.
With such a wondrous jewel-mind, one transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters the sphere traversed by the Buddhas.
Born into the family of the Tathāgatas, one’s lineage is free from blemish; equal to the Buddhas, one is certain to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
As soon as such a mind is generated, one immediately attains entry into the first bhūmi.
His resolve and delight are unshakable, like the king of great mountains;
Abounding in joy, love, and pleasure, as well as pure faith, With a mind of supreme courage and a heart of exultation, He is far removed from strife, impurity, harm, and malice;
Possessing a sense of shame and reverence, he is upright and sincere.
Guarding the sense faculties well, the peerless savior of the world— May I attain all wisdom here;
recollecting this, I give rise to joy. Having first entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), one immediately transcends the five fears:
Fear of lacking a livelihood, fear of death, fear of ill repute, Fear of the miserable realms, and fear of the majesty of others.
Because they do not crave attachment to "I" or to "mine," these sons of the Buddhas are far removed from all fears.
They constantly practice great loving-kindness and compassion; they always possess faith, reverence, shame, and dread of blame, and are fully endowed with merit.
Day and night they increase wholesome dharmas, delighting in the true benefit of the Dharma.
Not craving the experience of various desires, they contemplate the Dharma as they have heard it;

They remain far removed from attachment and do not greedily seek gain or offerings. Delighting only in the Buddha’s Bodhi, they single-mindedly seek the Buddha’s wisdom with diligent focus and no divergent thoughts.
They practice the pāramitās, remaining far removed from flattery, vanity, and deception.
Practicing according to what has been taught, dwelling within truthful speech, not defiling the family of the Buddhas, and not forsaking the bodhisattva precepts;
taking no pleasure in worldly affairs, constantly benefiting the world, and practicing virtue without weariness;
seeking further the ever-superior path—such is the delight in the Dharma.
In accordance with the meaning of merit, may I always give rise to the mind of great aspiration:
May I behold all Buddhas and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas; May I embrace the path of the Great Sages.
Constantly giving rise to such aspirations, may I practice the most supreme conduct, Bring all sentient beings to maturity, and adorn and purify the Buddha-fields.
In all Buddha-fields, the sons of the Buddhas completely fill them;
with equal and unified minds, their deeds are never in vain. At every single tip of a hair, they simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment.
Such great vows as these are immeasurable and boundless, as vast as space and as infinite as sentient beings.
The Dharma-realm and nirvāṇa, the appearance of Buddhas in the world, the realm of the Buddha’s mind,
that which is entered by the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and the exhaustion of the three turnings—
if those things have an end, only then shall my vow come to an end; as long as they are without end, so too shall my vow remain.
Having thus made this great vow, with a mind that is supple and well-disciplined, one is able to believe in the Buddha’s virtues and observe sentient beings.
Knowing that they arise from causes and conditions, one then gives rise to a mind of compassion, thinking:
"Such are these suffering sentient beings; I must now rescue and liberate them for their sake."
He practices various kinds of giving—his royal throne and precious jewels, even elephants, horses, chariots, his head, eyes, hands, and feet, and even the flesh and blood of his own body;
he is able to relinquish all these things with a heart free from sorrow or regret. He seeks out various scriptures and treatises, his mind never wearying of the task.
Skillfully understanding their meaning and intent, they are able to act in accordance with the ways of the world.
Adorned with a sense of shame and remorse, their practice becomes increasingly firm. They make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, honoring and respecting them;
thus they constantly cultivate these practices, without weariness day or night, so that their roots of goodness become ever more radiant and pure.
Just as fire refines true gold, so the Bodhisattva abiding herein purifies the ten stages;
their practice is free from obstruction, complete and uninterrupted.
Like a great caravan leader who, for the sake of the merchant folk, inquires about the paths’ dangers and ease to reach the great city in safety, [so does the Bodhisattva proceed].
One should know that the Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage is likewise thus: with valor and without obstruction, they proceed to the tenth stage.
Abiding within this first stage, they act as a great king of merit, transforming sentient beings through the Dharma;
with a compassionate heart free from harm, they rule over Jambudvīpa.
His transformative deeds reach everywhere, causing all to abide in great equanimity.
Seeking the most supreme path and desiring to achieve the wisdom of a Buddha, he renounced his own royal throne.
Able to practice with courageous diligence within the Buddha’s teaching, he then attained one hundred samādhis and beheld one hundred Buddhas.
He causes a hundred worlds to tremble, and his radiance and conduct are likewise;
he transforms the sentient beings of a hundred lands, causing them to enter into a hundred Dharma-gates;
he can know the events of a hundred eons, manifesting a hundred bodies and appearing with a hundred bodhisattvas as his retinue—such is the power of his sovereign vow.
Beyond these numbers, immeasurable, I have briefly described a small portion of the meaning of the stages;
if one were to analyze it extensively, even ten million eons would not suffice.
This supreme path of the Bodhisattvas, which benefits all living beings— thus have I now completed the teaching on the Dharma of the First Stage.
[Treatise] Twelfth: From "If a person has accumulated various virtues" onwards, there are forty-six lines and a half of sūtra verses that correspond to the preceding section on the Dharma.

These are fully contained within the text itself. As for the experience described in the sūtra regarding the entry into this First Bhūmi, it is because even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has just begun to be fully endowed with the capacity to generate vast vows and practices can enter [this stage]; therefore, it is not [the case that only those with long-standing cultivation can do so].

This is intended to clarify that the establishment of the teachings and the detailed explanation of the stages of practice—both its obstacles and its points of security and peril—arise from the preliminary understanding of the causal ground.
However, for one who has generated the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), these are all practiced simultaneously and instantaneously within a single moment of a single practice;
it is not necessary to practice them through a gradual sequence of stages by means of the categories of the general and the particular, the same and the different, or formation and disintegration.

The perfect fusion of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) can be seen within these three pairs of six characters. Within a single character, there are six aspects; this may be understood by analogy with the human body.

For instance, a single person’s body is complete with these six characteristics: the head, torso, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth. While their functions are distinct, they are entirely one body. This is the characteristic of particularity (*bhedalakṣaṇa*).

As for the characteristic of totality (*ekatvalakṣaṇa*), it is simply that all of these together constitute one body. Thus, the six characteristics are fully present within each individual character. The same principle may be applied accordingly to other cases.
The four great elements are the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). That they are all equally empty and without substance is called the common characteristic (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*).

Not discarding such commonality while possessing no distinct nature, yet having differences in function—such as head, body, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and tongue—is the characteristic of difference (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*).

That the head, body, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and tongue together constitute a single body is called the characteristic of formation (*abhinirvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*). It is merely according to [the principle of] non-existence...

The fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) lack intrinsic nature, lack substance, lack characteristics, and are without arising, without ceasing, without formation, and without destruction is called the "characteristic of disintegration.

Furthermore, all sentient beings are called the "universal characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); the distinction between the ignorant and the wise is called the "particular characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*);

that they all equally possess Buddha-wisdom is called the "common characteristic" (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*); and that they differ according to their retributive karma is called the "different characteristic" (*bhinna-lakṣaṇa*).

The arising of birth through the karma resulting from causes and conditions is called the characteristic of formation (*saṃsthāna-lakṣaṇa*). The mind having no basis and the substance of karma being without activity is called the characteristic of destruction (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the Reward-Buddhas (*vipākabuddha*) of the ten directions are called the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);

the distinctions between their bodies and lands adorned with various jewels are called the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); and the single Dharma-body, in which wisdom and principle are non-dual, is called the identical characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*).

Mutual knowledge following along with practice is called the "characteristic of difference" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); maturing sentient beings is called the "characteristic of fulfillment" (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*);

when both subject and object are absent, such that there is neither attainment nor realization, it is called the "characteristic of destruction" (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, encompassing all five stages within a single wisdom is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);

the progressive advancement of practice and understanding is called the "distinct characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); and that which is identical to the fundamental wisdom of the Buddhas is called the [ultimate] characteristic.

Cultivating the wisdom of identical characteristics (*sābhāsa*) is called the "distinctive characteristic" (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*); accomplishing universal Bodhisattva conduct (*samantabhadra-caryā*) to achieve great enlightenment is called the "accomplished characteristic" (*niṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*);
the essence of wisdom being without dependence and its function being without effort is called the "dissolving characteristic" (*vibhanga-lakṣaṇa*);

the differentiation of the long kalpas of the three periods of time is called the "individual characteristic" (*pratyeka-lakṣaṇa*); and universally observing all through wisdom within a single instant is called the "universal characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

The variation in length according to karma is called the "dissimilar characteristic" (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*); when attachment is extinguished and views are exhausted, such that there is no time of long or short, it is called the "similar characteristic" (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*).

When wisdom has no basis or dwelling, it is called the "characteristic of dissolution" (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*). Corresponding to the faculties and their objects is called the "characteristic of formation" (*saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*).

Taking the five and reversing them to the six, these characteristics of similarity and difference—along with all other dharmas—are to be understood by analogy with this example. Furthermore, clarify the single syllable.
Within this, there are six aspects of meaning that mutually function as both primary and secondary, and ten profound mysteries (*daśa-gambhīra-artha*), which are also subsumed here:

first, the gate of simultaneous complete correspondence; second, the gate of the unimpeded mastery over the vast and the narrow; third, the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion;
fourth, the gate of the sovereign interpenetration of all phenomena; fifth, the gate of the secret formation of both the hidden and the manifest; sixth...
The meaning [of this teaching] consists of: (1) the gate of the subtle mutual containment and establishment; (2) the gate of the realm of Indra’s net;

(3) the gate of generating understanding by relying on things to symbolize dharmas; (4) the gate of the ten worlds being perfectly interfused yet distinct; and (5) the gate of the principal and its attendants being perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues.
The Meaning of the Six Characteristics: Within this single character, there are the six characteristics; all characters and all phenomena possess these six characteristics.

One who perceives them well attains the gate of unimpeded wisdom and dhāraṇī, remaining unobstructed regarding all phenomena and cutting off attachment to existence, non-existence, permanence, or annihilation.

The phrase "these six characters— if even one is missing, then the principle and wisdom are not complete" means that because the contemplation within this first stage (*bhūmi*) universally penetrates all worldly dharmas, the various obstacles can be seen through the illumination of detachment from emotional attachments.

Second, regarding the explanation of the Second Ground, the Stainless (*vimalā*), five topical divisions (*pañca-dvāra*) shall be established for its analysis: first, explaining the title of the ground; second, clarifying which gate of practice is cultivated on this ground; third, illustrating the Dharma through Sudhana; fourth, clarifying what kind of liberation within the three realms is attained on this ground; and fifth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text. First, explaining the title of the ground: The *Bodhisattva-bhūmi* states: "Why is it called the 'Stainless Ground'? Because it is free from the stains of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Furthermore, as explained in the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya*, there are two kinds of stains: first, the stains of afflictions; second, the stains of ignorance. Among these, the stains of afflictions refer to the ten afflictions, such as attachment (*rāga*). The stains of ignorance refer to the ignorance that obstructs the realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). On this ground, because one has abandoned both the afflictions and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and because one has abandoned the ignorance that obstructs the realization of the true nature of phenomena, it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Moreover, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of holding to views as supreme (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the stains of holding precepts and vows as supreme (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the stains of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of eternity (*nitya-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of cessation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of causelessness (*ahetu-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of wrong cause (*viṣamahetu-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of no-action (*akriyā-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of nihilism (*vairāgya-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-causality (*ahetuka-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of non-result (*aphala-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-perception (*anupalambha-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-arising (*anutpāda-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of non-cessation (*anirodha-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-departure (*aniḥsaraṇa-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of non-liberation (*amokṣa-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-path (*amārga-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of wrong path (*kumārga-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-truth (*asatya-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false truth (*mithyāsatya-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-virtue (*akuśala-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false virtue (*mithyākuśala-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-purity (*aviśuddhi-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false purity (*mithyāviśuddhi-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-enlightenment (*abodhi-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false enlightenment (*mithyābodhi-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-nirvana (*anirvāṇa-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false nirvana (*mithyānirvāṇa-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-Buddha (*abuddha-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false Buddha (*mithyābuddha-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-Dharma (*adharmadṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false Dharma (*mithyādharma-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-Saṃgha (*asaṃgha-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false Saṃgha (*mithyāsaṃgha-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-preceptor (*ācārya-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false preceptor (*mithyācārya-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-upādhyāya (*upādhyāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false upādhyāya (*mithyopādhyāya-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-teacher (*śāstṛ-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false teacher (*mithyāśāstṛ-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "Stainless Ground. Furthermore, because one has abandoned the stains of the view of non-disciple (*śrāvaka-dṛṣṭi*) and the stains of the view of false disciple (*mithyāśrāv
Why is this stage named the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*)? This stage is so called because it counteracts the ten supreme wholesome precepts;
these supreme ten wholesome precepts are the nature-precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which are inherently stainless. Therefore, it is named the Stainless Stage.
Second, to clarify what practice-gate is cultivated in this stage: the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine [perfections] are secondary.
The *pāramitās* serve as companions. Regarding the representation of the Dharma through Sudhana and the Three Knowledges (*trividyā*):
in this stage, Sudhana’s spiritual friend is named the Night Goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā.

She is a female deity within the Bodhimaṇḍa who has attained the Bodhisattva liberation door called "The Joyful Play of Tranquil Meditative Concentration. All such night goddesses and river goddesses [are likewise represented].
The Sea Goddess and the Earth Goddess are always female deities who manifest the position of compassion; they signify that these ten stages (*bhūmi*) accumulate great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because they fulfill the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) through the vows of Samantabhadra, they are represented by goddesses and named "Night Goddess of Universal Virtue and Pure Light" (*Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā*).
This Night Goddess dwells constantly within the great cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) in order to fulfill the vow-practice of Samantabhadra.
Because she shatters the long-lasting darkness of all sentient beings during the night, her wisdom accords with reality and is thus titled "Divine" (Śrī).
This goddess within the Bodhimaṇḍa clarifies that the essence of the precepts (*śīla*) is the sublime principle of the Dharmakāya.
As for Sudhana’s attainment of the Bodhisattva liberation door of "Peaceful Meditation and Universal Pacing," it clarifies...

Because their inherent precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) pervade everywhere, equaling the Dharma-realm; because they act without acting while manifesting form-bodies (*rūpa-kāya*) and constantly dwelling in the world without being defiled by worldly dust;

and because their essence and function are eternally quiescent—wherein meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is the essence and spiritual movement is the function, and bliss is the bliss of the Dharma—those who dwell as spirits within the Bodhimanda are so named.
The supreme ten wholesome paths of action are the wondrous principle of the *dharmakāya*, which is the entirety of *bodhi*;
they are also the original teacher who inspired the night goddess Vāsantī to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

This is because it is clarified that all resolutions for enlightenment take this wondrous principle of *bodhi* as their essence. Fourth, it is explained what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained in this stage.
If one considers the unconditioned essence of Bodhi, then the three realms and six paths are universally and entirely liberation; this is the meaning of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

If, however, one discusses it according to specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), one who thoroughly knows the distinctions among the phenomena of the three realms understands that the essence of the precepts can cure the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
through the manifestation of the wondrous principle of Bodhi, one is able to contemplate desire alone.
Regarding the modes of activity of the afflictions within the realms, one first subdues the habitual tendencies of the afflictions of the desire realm through the sublime principle of bodhi.

Subsequently, within the three stages of the two realms of form and formlessness, one cultivates the eight dhyānas; only then does one clearly manifest the practice-gate of these two realms of form and formlessness.
If one does not cultivate in this distinct manner, but relies solely on the non-activity of bodhi, it will be unable to effect discernment.

Knowing the dharmas of conduct that defile the three realms, yet being unable to fully comprehend those dharmas of the three realms, one is no different from the śrāvakas and non-Buddhists because one lacks great wisdom.
Therefore, on this stage, one cultivates the precepts to subdue the afflictions of the desire realm;

on the [next] three stages, one cultivates the eight dhyānas to subdue the afflictions of the form and formless realms. On the first stage, it is clarified that this refers only to the initial resolve of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because those with great resolve joyfully seek the Great Dharma, they cultivate the eight dhyānas in the third stage;

this clarifies that while the dhyānas of the higher realms involve dwelling in meditation by calming thoughts through cessation (*śamatha*), the Bodhisattva does not cease his activity but dwells in natural quiescence (*svabhāva-śānti*) according to his essential nature.

Because he abandons that state of a mind stilled by cessation and dwells in natural quiescence according to principle, it is called *bodhi*. Generally, the dhyānas of the two upper realms are categorized as shallow according to their respective levels.

In the deep [attainments], there is the subduing of the perception of inhalation and exhalation through the mind, abiding in tranquility within the fourth dhyāna. Therein, inhalation and exhalation cease, and only pure, white, and wondrous forms appear before one. The three calamities of water, fire, and wind do not reach it because, through mindfulness, discursive thoughts have perished; since such karma no longer exists, only the karma of the form realm remains. Regarding the fifth [point], for those who explain the meaning according to the text: [The text continues: ...within this, the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness) is the most subtle among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). It is like the king of all sentient beings, and it is the basis upon which all other dharmas depend. Furthermore, it is the support for the continuity of birth and death. If one were to sever the *vijñāna*, then all other aggregates would perish immediately, just as when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases, the other faculties cannot remain. Therefore, it is said that the *vijñāna* is the most subtle and fundamental of all conditioned things. It is also the cause of the arising of all suffering. If one can understand the nature of this *vijñāna*, then one will be able to sever the root of birth and death. Thus, the Buddha taught that the *vijñāna* is the most profound and difficult to comprehend. One should contemplate it with diligence and not be negligent. This is the meaning of the fifth section. As for the sixth, the *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form): "Name" refers to the four non-material aggregates (*skandha*), and "form" refers to the material aggregate. Together they constitute the individual existence. Because they are the basis for the manifestation of all mental and physical states, they are called *nāmarūpa*. They are like the seed from which all future suffering grows. If one can abandon attachment to *nāmarūpa*, then one will not be bound by the cycle of rebirth. This is the meaning of the sixth section. As for the seventh, the *ṣaḍāyatana* (six sense bases): these are the six internal sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. They are the gateways through which objects enter and mental contact occurs. Because they are the foundation for the arising of craving and grasping, they are called the six sense bases. One should contemplate them as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self. By doing so, one can prevent the influx of afflictions. This is the meaning of the seventh section. As for the eighth, *sparśa* (contact): this is the coming together of the sense organ, the object, and consciousness, giving rise to a mental impression. It is the primary condition for the arising of feeling (*vedanā*). One should contemplate that contact is devoid of a permanent agent and arises only through the conjunction of conditions. By understanding this, one can transcend the cycle of sensation. This is the meaning of the eighth section. As for the ninth, *vedanā* (feeling): this is the experience of pleasure, pain, or neutrality resulting from contact. It is the root of craving. One should contemplate that feelings are fleeting and ultimately lead to suffering. By cultivating equanimity toward all feelings, one can sever the source of desire. This is the meaning of the ninth section. As for the tenth, *tṛṣṇā* (craving): this is the intense longing for objects of desire, existence, or non-existence. It is the fuel that drives the cycle of rebirth. One should contemplate that craving is like a raging fire that consumes the mind. By practicing the contemplation of impurity and the suffering of conditioned existence, one can extinguish the flames of craving. This is the meaning of the tenth section. As for the eleventh, *upādāna* (grasping): this is the firm adherence to views, precepts, sensual desires, and the doctrine of self. It is the cause of becoming. One should contemplate that grasping is like a heavy burden that drags one down into the abyss of saṃsāra. By abandoning all attachments, one can attain liberation. This is the meaning of the eleventh section. As for the twelfth, *bhava* (becoming): this is the karmic force that projects one into a new existence. It is the result of grasping. One should contemplate that becoming is like a wheel of fire that never comes to rest. By realizing the emptiness of all phenomena, one can cut off the flow of becoming. This is the meaning of the twelfth section. As for the thirteenth, *jāti* (birth): this is the manifestation of the five aggregates in a new life. It is the beginning of suffering. One should contemplate that birth is like a dream that brings forth all manner of delusions. By realizing the non-arising of all phenomena, one can transcend the state of birth. This is the meaning of the thirteenth section. As for the fourteenth, *jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death): this is the decay and dissolution of the aggregates. It is the end of suffering. One should contemplate that old age and death are like the fading of a lamp’s light. By attaining the wisdom of the cessation of suffering, one can reach the shore of nirvāṇa. This is the meaning of the fourteenth section. Thus, the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in detail to guide sentient beings toward the path of liberation. Those who practice accordingly shall surely attain the fruit of Arhatship. This concludes the explanation of the meaning according to the text. May all beings realize this truth and attain peace.
Furthermore, it is divided into two parts: first, a general outline of the meaning of the sūtra; second, an explanation of the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the general outline of the meaning of the sūtra: within this second bhūmi, it is broadly divided into six sections.
[Sūtra] When the bodhisattvas heard of this most supreme and subtle stage, their minds were entirely purified and they all rejoiced.
Rising from their seats, they leaped into the midst of the air and scattered exquisite flowers above;
simultaneously, they praised together: "Excellent, O Vajragarbha!"
The one of great wisdom and fearlessness has well explained this stage.

Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing that the minds of the assembly were pure and that they desired to hear all the characteristics of the practices belonging to the second stage, immediately requested Vajragarbha: "O One of Great Intelligence, please expound upon it."
The Sons of the Buddha all delight in hearing Of the second stage wherein they dwell.
[Commentary] Regarding the first section, "All Bodhisattvas having heard this," the following five lines of verse clarify the section on the Bodhisattvas’ joy upon hearing the Dharma.
Within the second section, the "Explanation of the Meaning according to the Text," the general purport of these initial five lines of verse is as follows:
1. When the Bodhisattva Saṃpraharṣaṇa heard the teaching on the dharmas of the first bhūmi, he rejoiced. 2. He scattered flowers and offered praise. 3.
Vimukticandra, knowing the assembly’s readiness, requested that the second bhūmi be taught. The meaning of these points is fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already cultivated the first stage and wishes to enter the second stage, they should give rise to ten kinds of profound resolve.
What are these ten? They are: the mind of rectitude, the mind of suppleness, the mind of capability, the mind of subduing, the mind of tranquility, and the mind of pure goodness."
With a mind free from distraction, a mind free from attachment, a vast mind, and a great mind—by means of these ten minds, the Bodhisattva enters the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*).
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stainless Stage, their very nature is to be naturally far removed from all killing;
they do not keep weapons or staves, harbor no resentment, and are endowed with a sense of shame, dread of blame, benevolence, and forgiveness toward all beings.
Sentient beings who possess life constantly give rise to thoughts of benefit and compassion;
such Bodhisattvas do not even harbor ill will or cause distress to sentient beings, let alone kill them while perceiving others as sentient beings.
Furthermore, they do not steal by nature; regarding their own resources, they always know moderation and sufficiency, and toward the property of others, they are compassionate and forgiving.
Desiring not to encroach upon or damage the property of others, and perceiving such things as belonging to another, he never gives rise to a mind of theft toward them;
he does not take even a blade of grass or a leaf if it is not given, let alone other articles of livelihood. By nature, he is free from sexual misconduct:
the Bodhisattva is content with his own wife and seeks not the wives of others; nor does he approach the wives or concubines of others, women protected by others, or the women of his own kin.

Even when betrothed by a matchmaker or protected by the Dharma, they do not give rise to a mind of lustful attachment; how much less would they engage in sexual intercourse, and how much less through improper means?
By nature they do not speak falsely; these Bodhisattvas always speak what is real, what is true, and what is timely—even in dreams they cannot bear to utter words of concealment.
They have no intention to do so, let alone commit it intentionally. By nature they are not double-tongued.
The Bodhisattva Jihva possesses no mind of divisiveness toward sentient beings and no mind of malice or harm;
he does not repeat these words to others for the sake of breaking them apart, nor does he repeat those words to this person for the sake of breaking this person apart.
He does not cause those who are not yet divided to be divided, nor does he increase or take pleasure in the division of those already divided; he does not delight in divisiveness.
One does not engage in divisive speech, nor does one utter divisive words, whether true or false; by nature,
one does not engage in harsh speech— namely, poisonous words, coarse words, words that cause suffering to others, words that incite resentment in others,
words spoken in one's presence or in one's absence, vile and base words, vulgar words, unpleasant words, words that displease the listener, or words of angry fury.
One should completely abandon all such speech as that which burns the heart, speech of enmity and resentment, speech of feverish affliction,
speech that is unlovely, speech that is unpleasant, speech that can harm one’s own body or the bodies of others; instead, one should always utter speech that is moistening,
gentle, pleasing to the mind, delightful to hear, joyful for those who hear it, and speech that enters well into the hearts of people like the wind.
In Athens, they say: "Speech that many love and delight in; speech that gladdens the body and mind;

speech that is not frivolous by nature. A bodhisattva always delights in speech that is well-considered, timely, truthful, meaningful, in accordance with the Dharma, logical, skillfully disciplined, and decisive after due deliberation according to the occasion—even when joking.
He constantly reflects with careful scrutiny; how much more so when it comes to uttering distracted words? By nature he is free from greed;
regarding the wealth and resources of others, he does not give rise to a covetous mind, nor does he desire or seek them. By nature he is free from malice;
toward all sentient beings, he constantly gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, and a mind of harmony.

With a mind that gathers itself, he forever abandons anger, resentment, malice, and the feverish afflictions of distress; he constantly contemplates acting in accordance with kindness, compassion, and beneficial aid.
Furthermore, being free from wrong views, the Bodhisattva abides in the right path, does not practice divination, and does not adopt evil precepts.

His mind and vision are upright, without deception or flattery, and he gives rise to resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Such is the son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Thus he protects and maintains the ten paths of wholesome action without interruption, and further reflects:
"All sentient beings who fall into the evil destinies do so because of the ten unwholesome actions;
therefore, I shall personally practice right conduct and also exhort others to practice right conduct. Why is this? Because if one cannot personally practice right conduct,"
"It is impossible for them to cause others to practice [in this way].

[Śāstra] The second section, beginning from "At that time," consists of forty-three lines of scripture that clarify the stage of having already practiced the first ground and desiring to proceed toward the second ground, specifically the portion concerning the abandonment of evil and the cultivation of good. This is divided into two parts.

First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha... down to "...by means of these ten minds one enters the Stainless Stage (vimalā-bhūmi)," there are four and a half lines of scripture clarifying how one cultivates the second stage by means of the ten minds.

Second, from the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva, the Son of the Buddha, having dwelt in the Stainless Stage... down to "...it is impossible for one to cause others to cultivate it," there are thirty [lines].

The *Aṣṭāṅgika-sūtra* clarifies that for a bodhisattva of the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), the activities of body, speech, and mind are well-disciplined and harmonious with the ten wholesome paths of action.
Possessing compassion, they fulfill the ten wholesome paths by being free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct in body; free from greed, hatred, and delusion in mind;
and free from false speech, frivolous talk, harsh speech, and divisive speech in speech—cultivating these ten wholesome paths as scattered virtues (*vyavakīrṇa-kuśala*) as in the desire realm.
The ten wholesome paths of action of the form realm and formless realm, together with the karma of cultivating meditative concentration, are reached only through the cessation of conceptualization.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further reflects: 'The ten unwholesome paths of action are the causes for rebirth in the hells, as animals, and as hungry ghosts;
the ten wholesome paths of action lead to rebirth among humans and devas, up to the Peak of Existence.'"

Furthermore, as for the cause of rebirth: when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are practiced with a narrow and inferior mind, out of fear of the three realms, and in the absence of great compassion, one understands them through hearing the voice of another; thus, they constitute the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

Moreover, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are cultivated to purity and are realized through self-awakening rather than through the instruction of another, [they constitute the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle].
Because they lack the skillful means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇopāya*) and because they have realized the profound law of dependent origination (*gambhīrapratītyasamutpāda*),

they establish themselves in the vehicle of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddhayāna*). Furthermore, because these superior ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) are cultivated with a purified mind that is vast and immeasurable,

because they are endowed with compassion (*anukampā*), because they are embraced by skillful means, because they give rise to great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), because they do not abandon sentient beings, and because they long for all [virtues]...
Because the Buddha’s great wisdom purifies all the bodhisattva stages, purifies and cultivates all the perfections (pāramitās),
