[Treatise] The section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" and extending for thirty-nine and a half lines of scripture clarifies the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), specifically the portion concerning the excellent maintenance of the ten supreme wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*). Within the explanation of its meaning, it is divided into three sections.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "In such a manner, the Bodhisattva should train in these skillful means," there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify this stage.
In this section concerning the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten paths of wholesome action, there are six points of intent:

(1) one contemplates that the ten unwholesome courses of action lead to rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals; (2) one contemplates that the ten wholesome courses of action result in birth within the three realms, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);

(3) these ten wholesome actions are practiced universally, and the Peak of Existence, including the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, is collectively termed "the Peak of Existence"; (4) the superior grade of the ten... [text continues].
Those who well fear suffering and cultivate the path to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle escape the conditioned existence of the three realms;

with their minds subdued, they exhaust the afflictions of the three realms and enter into transformative births and deaths, remaining in the meditative absorption of cessation for kalpas without awareness.
Those of the four superior grades of the ten wholesome paths who awaken to dependent origination but lack compassion accomplish the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; they likewise attain transformative births.
Because death constitutes a distinct root, one dedicates [the merit] toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and likewise passes through ten thousand *kalpas*.

By practicing the ten grades of superior wholesome deeds (*daśa-uttama-kuśala*), one cultivates vast vows, does not abandon sentient beings, and seeks the great wisdom of a Buddha to accomplish the conduct of a Bodhisattva.

By practicing the ten grades of supreme-superior wholesome deeds, one purifies all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, one accomplishes the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*). Thus it is named.
For those of the Supreme Vehicle who have already been reborn in the heavens or have transcended the world, there are these five kinds of ten paths of wholesome action.
O two sons of the Buddha, from this point downward, for the sake of the infinite multitudes within the great mass of suffering,
twenty-three lines of scripture clarify that each of the ten unwholesome paths of action has two kinds of cause and effect, as explained in the sutra.
Furthermore, within the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*), there are likewise three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—due to which the suffering experienced differs;
as the sūtra itself fully details these three. Therefore, after the Bodhisattva has formed such a thought, [the text] states that he causes others to abide therein.
Within this, two lines of the sūtra clarify that the Bodhisattva not only practices the ten wholesome actions himself, but also teaches others to practice the ten wholesome actions.

Regarding the classification of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) into superior and most superior grades: this clarifies that [the latter] arises from the mind through reliance on wisdom (*jñāna*).

Although the remaining three grades all involve departing from the karma of the triple world and attaining fruits beyond the triple world, they all arise from the mind through reliance on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

They gradually seek the Buddha-wisdom before entering the vows and practices of Samantabhadra. Thus, while the vows and practices of the Bodhisattvas among the Three Vehicles are extensive, they have not yet reached the stage of Buddha-wisdom.
Therefore, all have their limits; for instance, establishing a trichiliocosm as the Buddha’s field of retribution is based on this principle.
Consequently, this is entirely distinct from the practice of Samantabhadra within the wisdom of the Buddha.

While those of the Three Vehicles contemplate emptiness and the various gates of practice across the five stages—rejoicing in the principle and the ultimate reality—they do not yet rejoice in the gate of the Tathāgata’s *jñāna* (wisdom). However...

Furthermore, one must enter the vows and practices of Samantabhadra; the fruit of Buddhahood lies beyond the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). It is said that only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are completed does one finally arrive.
For those who do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they remain fundamentally outside the gate at the grass hut;
for them, the gate of the supreme ten wholesome paths and the One Vehicle takes the Tathāgata’s immovable wisdom in all places as the core of their faith.
Within the ten stages of abiding (*daśabhūmi*), one immediately enters the fruit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The five positions of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) all take the great wisdom of the Buddha-fruit as the means for accomplishing the gates of practice.

Thus, the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the eleventh ground take the Tathāgata’s universal radiance wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*) as their essence; this is the Buddha-fruit itself and the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Sharing the same substance, the essence of wisdom is perfectly luminous and transcends emotional views; therefore, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
For this reason, the *Lotus Sūtra* causes those of the three vehicles to turn back and return to the ocean of wisdom, using the dragon girl as its symbol.
This sūtra reveals the Buddha-gate instantaneously, just as is symbolized by Sudhana: although Sudhana traveled extensively among his spiritual friends, he never moved from his original place.

Although Maitreya was granted the merit of attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime before the Mother of Awakening (Prajñāpāramitā), he did not depart from the ocean of non-arising wisdom that is without thought-moments and devoid of before or after.
This is the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-yāna*), which exhausts all views throughout the past and present.
If one harbors notions of before and after, one does not enter the gate of Buddha-wisdom; such a person remains in a grass hut, staying outside the door.

The Master of the Treatise says in verse: All sentient beings possess the golden realm, Pure, stainless, and indestructible wisdom—the jewel of sovereign knowledge— Yet they dwell in poverty within their inner garments, Remaining outside the gate of liberation. A vast city of jewels stands at the crossroads;
Mañjuśrī guides them forward, Samantabhadra supports them, And a robust white ox of immense strength draws them along, Traveling everywhere in a single thought-moment.

Without expanding or contracting, such a precious vehicle cannot enter; they merely delight in the gate of diligent toil and stand before it, unaware that their own bodies abide eternally within, yet they constantly say, "I am not equal to them."

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further gives rise toward all sentient beings a mind of benefit, a mind of peace and happiness, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of gathering them in, a mind of protection, a mind of regarding them as oneself, a mind of regarding them as a teacher, and a mind of regarding them as a great teacher, thinking:
"Sentient beings are to be pitied; they have fallen into false views, evil wisdom, evil desires, and evil [states]."
"In the dense forest of the path, I should cause them to abide in right view and practice the path of reality. Furthermore, he thinks:
"All sentient beings, discriminating between self and other, mutually destroy one another; their strife and malice burn fiercely without ceasing.
I shall cause them to abide within unsurpassed great compassion. Furthermore, he thinks: "All sentient beings are greedy..."
Regarding those who are insatiable in grasping and seek only wealth and profit, sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood, [the Bodhisattva] thinks:

"I shall cause them to abide in the dharma of right livelihood, which consists of pure actions of body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings are constantly pursued by the three poisons and various afflictions;
because of these, they burn with fever and do not understand how to resolve to seek the skillful means for liberation. I shall cause them to eliminate these."
He extinguishes the great fires of all afflictions and establishes beings in the cool place of nirvana. Furthermore, he reflects:
"All sentient beings, being covered by the heavy darkness of ignorance, the thick film of false views, and entering the dense forest of the aggregates, have lost the light of wisdom;
wandering upon the perilous paths of the wilderness, they give rise to various evil views. I shall cause them to attain [liberation]."
With the unobstructed, pure eye of wisdom, he knows the true nature of all phenomena as they are, not following the teachings of others. Furthermore, he reflects:
"All sentient beings are within the perilous paths of birth and death; they are on the verge of falling into the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;
they have entered the net of evil views and are bewildered by the dense forest of ignorance, following false paths and wandering in delusion."
Their inverted conduct is like that of blind men without a guide; they do not follow the path of definitive deliverance, yet they claim it to be such.
They enter the realm of Māra and are seized by evil thieves; they comply with the mind of Māra and remain far removed from the Buddha’s intent.
"I shall pull them out from such perilous difficulties and establish them in the fearless city of omniscience. Furthermore, he thinks: "All sentient beings are [afflicted] by great..."
Submerged by the waves of cascading water, they are swept away by the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of ignorance, and the flood of views;
tossed about in the eddies of birth and death, drifting and whirling in the river of craving, rushing and surging with such force that they have no leisure for reflection;

pursued and never abandoned by thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty; seized within by the rākṣasa of the view of a self, they are led forever into the dense forest of lustful desire.
For those who dwell in the deep abyss of craving and attachment, rooted in the high mound of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"),

settled in the village of the six sense bases, without a savior or one capable of delivering them— for them I shall give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and provide relief through all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),
so that they may be free from calamity, leave behind defilement for tranquility, and abide upon the jewel-island of all-encompassing wisdom. Furthermore, he made this [vow]:
I contemplate all sentient beings dwelling in the prison of the world, beset by manifold sufferings and afflictions;

they constantly harbor love and hatred, giving rise to anxiety and fear, bound by the heavy shackles of craving and desire, and shrouded by the dense forest of ignorance, unable to emerge from within the three realms.
I shall cause them to forever leave behind the three realms of existence and abide in the unobstructed Great Nirvana.
Furthermore, he reflects thus: "All sentient beings are attached to a self; they do not seek liberation from the cave-dwelling of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Relying on the empty village of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they give rise to the four perversions (*viparyāsa*) and are afflicted by the four great poisonous snakes of the elements (*mahābhūta*).
They are slain by the hostile thieves of the five aggregates and undergo immeasurable suffering. I shall cause them to abide in the Supreme [Truth]."
The supreme state of non-attachment is that which is called the cessation of all obstacles and the realization of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, he reflects:
"The minds of all sentient beings are narrow and inferior; they do not practice the path of supreme omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Although they desire liberation, they take pleasure only in the vehicles of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. I shall cause them to abide in the vast Buddha-dharma and vast wisdom."
"O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva who thus upholds the precepts is well able to increase the mind of compassion.
[Treatise] From "The Fourth Son of the Buddha" onwards, thirty-nine and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on "arousing compassion for sentient beings" within the Second Bhūmi.
In the explanation of its meaning, it is divided into ten sections; the first is from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, comprising three... [lines].
The nineteen and a half lines of this sutra section contain ten types of compassionate minds toward sentient beings.

These ten types of mindfulness of the suffering paths of sentient beings aim to establish them within the ten types of happiness, as detailed in the sutra itself. Following that, there are another ten types [of thoughts], which further reflect:

"In this way, the two views of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), all arise based upon false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); therefore, they are designated [here]."

At its head, because the six realms and the three worlds arise from the dense forest of birth and death—rooted in ignorance, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), false views, unwholesome wisdom, and evil desires—it is designated as the foremost. If one understands that these various views have no inherent substance, then these very views are the *dharmadhātu*;
they arise through dependent origination, arising only as phenomena and appearing only as phenomena, shifting in accordance with wisdom.
All unwholesome paths within the three realms and six destinies arise collectively from these five views.
If one realizes this, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thereafter, all afflictions will never again arise.
Those who destroy the characteristics of these five views depart from worldly karma. Because of these five views, strife, contention, and hatred arise, just as [fire arises] from causes.
Greed gives rise to wrong livelihood, just as the three poisons do; from greed arise the karmas of anger and delusion, and when these evil karmas flourish, it is called "blazing.
Nirvana is cool and refreshing because karma has ceased and wisdom has manifested—this is bliss.

Furthermore, by citing the heavy darkness of ignorance and the veil of false views, it generally clarifies that many are obstructed by deluded karma; they are deluded regarding name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which thereby obstructs right wisdom.

Furthermore, the mention of falling into the hells, the realms of animals, and the realm of hungry ghosts clarifies that one falls into these hells due to the delusions and obstructions of the preceding [stages].

These are called the eighteen hells; the "eighteen" refer to the boiling cauldrons, the burning furnaces, the mountains of knives, the trees of swords, the dark abysses, the freezing ice, the fire chariots, the fire wheels, the iron nets, the copper pillars, the boiling excrement, the plucking out of tongues, the nailing of the body, the spitting of fire, and the drinking of molten copper.
The eighteen types of hells mentioned above, such as the City of the Fire of Ignorance and the River of Ashes, are experienced according to the evil karma produced by the mind.
As for those who enter the net of wrong views, this clarifies that sentient beings, deluded regarding the truth, falsely grasp at the body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

thus, through the views of extremes, adherence to precepts and rituals, views of grasping, and false views, they are perpetually ensnared in their own nets and revolve within the current of suffering.
Those who are deluded by the dense forest of ignorance—just as all sentient beings are deluded by the dense forest of ignorance—may be summarized in eighty-four thousand major categories.
Generally speaking, there is one fundamental delusion that is equal to space: to mistake [delusion] for the delusion of one's own self.
The Tathāgata’s Universal Radiance, the fundamental ocean of wisdom, is equal to the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space; this is the universal delusion.
Thus, because such ignorance extensively obscures fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), it is termed a "dense forest" (*gahana*).

Just as Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*) may become deluded regarding the path through ignorance, there are one hundred types of causes and effects associated with the progressive cultivation across the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*).
Within these five stages, each possesses ten kinds of *pāramitā* as the essential substance of their ascending practice; this is as in the case of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), from which—
After the ten stages of faith, one cultivates the samādhi of skillful means; this is the stage of the initial arousal of the mind within the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
Specifically, it refers to attaining the light of wisdom of all Buddhas through mindfulness, which is the fruit of correctly entering the stage of the initial arousal of the mind.
Entering the country of the Ocean Gate, one contemplates and cultivates the stage of purifying the ground; observing the ocean of all sentient beings is its purification.
The dharma-gate of attaining the universal eye within the ocean of the pure dharma-realm is the correct entry into the fruit of the stage of purifying the grounds (*bhūmi-viśodhana*).
Thus, these five stages consist of fifty dharma-gates, each possessing two kinds of cause and effect, totaling one hundred dharma-gates of progressive advancement.

Furthermore, from the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda-bhūmi*), one rides upon the wisdom of one’s own Buddha-nature and passes through these five stages to realize the vision of the truth (*satyadarśana*).
The gradual clarification further involves five causes and five effects; these are established based on the five fundamental stages, totaling ten, which comprise one hundred and ten dharma-gates.
All of these possess dharmas such as delusion, obstruction, and ignorance, as manifested in the conduct of Sudhana.
When one reaches those respective stages, they will be fully clarified; this is called "following" (anupūrva).
The delusion regarding the lack of mastery in advancing through the stages of cultivation persists until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained;
this refers to the "delusion regarding the vastness of calculation" and the "delusion regarding the vast magnitude of the proportions of the qualities of the marks and minor signs.

Only when the Buddha reaches the ultimate fruit does he fully comprehend them, as described by the Tathāgata himself in the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* and the *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parimāṇa-parivarta*.

In this way, within each stage of the path, the progressive cultivation and the delusions that act as obstacles are clarified through the correspondence with each of the spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra) represented by Sudhana, so that the practice may be fully understood and easily comprehended. Furthermore, there are ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths due to following deviant ways;
moreover, there are all sentient beings—humans, gods, Māras, Brahmās, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, those in Pure Lands, and Bodhisattvas.

All of these are heterodox paths; although their experiences of suffering and pleasure differ, they are all devoid of right view and practice inverted conduct, such as the four inversions and the eight inversions. This is like being blind and having no guide.

It clarifies that the Bodhisattva, observing delusion, gives rise to compassion and seeks the essential path for deliverance to benefit all beings. The subsequent sections can be understood accordingly, including the entry into the realm of Māra.
The "five māras" refers to the māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the celestial māra (*devaputra-māra*).

Being "seized by evil thieves" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) pursuing their respective objects and giving rise to various false views. To "follow the mind of Māra and distance oneself from the Buddha's intent" means that the faculties follow the transformations of their objects, thereby becoming deluded regarding one’s own Buddha-wisdom.
Therefore, I have extracted [beings] from such perilous difficulties and caused them to abide in the state of *amṛta* (the deathless).
"Fearing the city of omniscience" clarifies that by recollecting suffering and giving rise to compassion, one brings about the realization of fundamental wisdom.
Furthermore, the thought "all sentient beings are submerged by the waves of a great torrent" clarifies that they are submerged by the waters of craving.
"Entering the eddies of birth and death within the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of ignorance, and the flow of views" clarifies the general [condition].

"Because they are tossed about by the swirling currents of the river of craving, rushing and surging so violently that there is no leisure for observation" clarifies that the first four floods (āsravas) swiftly pursue objects,
giving rise to various deluded karmas; because there is no leisure to initiate contemplation and subdue them,
"they are followed and not abandoned by the perception of desire, the perception of ill-will, and the perception of harm" clarifies these three kinds of evil.
The demon of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) acts as a basis for the flow [of existence], seizing one within it so that one enters forever into the dense forest of craving and desire;
thus, it is explained that based on the body and so forth, the sixty-two views arise simultaneously with the five views.

Regarding these sixty-two views, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, four views arise for each of the five aggregates—making twenty in total—and twenty for each of the three time periods [past, present, and future].
Taken together, these constitute sixty views; when combined with the two views that the body itself is the self and that the body is distinct from the self, they total sixty-two views.

Furthermore, within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there are four such views: "form is the self," "the self is apart from form," "there is form within the self," and "there is a self within form.
Since each of the five aggregates possesses these four, all such views are based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Because that which arises is thus, this sutra says: "Without body and without vision, one attains the supreme body of a Buddha.
For those about to enter the dense forest of craving and desire, it clarifies that all birth and death arise from craving and desire;
because birth and death are so numerous, they are like a dense forest. In a single kṣaṇa, eight hundred births and deaths arise simultaneously, flowing and surging forth together.

"Without ceasing, at every moment, birth and cessation are simultaneous; for those who give rise to deep defilement and attachment toward what they crave, it clarifies that they deeply engage in the karma of the suffering of saṃsāra, revolving incessantly.

Regarding 'the primeval mound of *asmimāna* (the conceit of 'I am')': there are seven types of pride (*māna*), namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), the conceit of 'I am' (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*). 'Primeval mound' means—"
When pride (*māna*) is further augmented by pride-pride (*mānātimāna*), over-pride (*adhimāna*), and so forth, it is termed a "height" (*giri*).

Just as there may be high ground upon level earth, which is called a "plain" (*prastha*); and when the plain is higher still, it is a "mound" (*kūṭa*); and when the mound is higher still, it is a "height.

Thus, when the pride of self (*asmimāna*) is augmented by six further layers of pride, this constitutes a "heavy height. This definitively establishes the collection of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

"Those who fall" refers to the high mounds of pride upon which one further adds the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind to grasp at the objects of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), thereby increasing the causes of suffering.

The fourteen lines of scripture following this can be understood according to the text. These ten sections of scripture clarify the stage within this [level] where one contemplates suffering and gives rise to compassion for the purpose of providing protection and rescue.
