A Combined Commentary on the Ten Stages Sutra, Fascicle 26.6 [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stainless Stage (Vimalā-bhūmi), by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas, namely:
He beheld many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
Toward all these Buddhas, he served, honored, respected, and made offerings with a vast mind and a profound mind, providing them with robes, food, and other necessities.
He offers all requisites for life—food, drink, bedding, seats, medicine, and everything else—to provide for and make offerings to the entire community of monks.
He dedicates these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
With a heart of deep respect for all Buddhas, he further undertakes and practices the ten paths of wholesome action, continuing according to what he has received until he reaches *bodhi*.

He never forgets this until the end; for this bodhisattva has, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of eons, remained far removed from the stains of stinginess, envy, and broken precepts.
Thus, his generosity and observance of the precepts are pure and fulfilled. It is like genuine gold placed in alum stone and refined according to the proper method:
freed from all impurities, it becomes even more brilliant and pure. This bodhisattva, dwelling in this stage, is free from defilement.

The ground is likewise thus: because they have remained far removed from the stains of stinginess, envy, and breaking the precepts for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, their generosity and observance of the precepts are pure and fulfilled.
O Son of the Buddha, among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva excels in kind speech (*priyavāditā*);
among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), they excel in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). They do not fail to practice the others, but do so according to their capacity.
To this extent, the son of the Buddha is said to have briefly explained the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*), of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Abiding in this stage, he frequently becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) as a great Dharma-lord, fully endowed with the seven treasures and possessing sovereign power.
He is able to remove the stains of stinginess, greed, and immoral conduct from all sentient beings, and through skillful means, causes them to dwell securely in virtue.
Among the ten paths of wholesome action, he acts as a great donor, providing inexhaustible and universal gifts through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

All such deeds he performs are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the Sangha, and even never apart from mindfulness of the attainment of the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge. Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I..."
Among all sentient beings, he who aspires to be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished,
the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, and even the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge— such a bodhisattva,

if desiring to leave the home life to practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, is able to renounce his home, wife, children, and the five desires; having thus left the home life, [he proceeds].
Having diligently practiced with vigor, in a single moment of thought he attains a thousand samādhis,
beholds a thousand buddhas, and knows the spiritual powers of a thousand buddhas; he can shake a thousand worlds and even manifest a thousand bodies,
and within each body he can manifest a thousand bodhisattvas as his retinue, manifesting these through the sovereign power of the bodhisattva’s sublime vows.
Even after hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know [the number].
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] The fifth section, "The Son of the Buddha" and below, consists of thirty-one and a half lines of scripture that clarify the stage of "Correctly Entering the Second Ground, the Stainless," specifically the portion concerning "Attaining Vision of Many Buddhas.
Within the commentary on this meaning, it is clarified that the Bodhisattva of this ground, through the power of their vows, attains vision of many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
This section is further divided into ten sub-sections; the first is "The Son of the Buddha."

From "Furthermore, down to the *nāyuta* of Buddhas" to the end, there are three and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how Bodhisattvas in this stage, through the power of their vows, are able to see many Buddhas; this is divided into two parts.

From "In the presence of all those Buddhas" to "and also making offerings to the entire Saṅgha," there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the offering of the Three Minds and Five Matters to the Buddhas and the Saṅgha.
Regarding the division of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha herein: Vairocana is the Buddha Jewel, Mañjuśrī is the Dharma Jewel, and Samantabhadra’s practice is the Saṃgha Jewel.
These collectively encompass the Three Vehicles, the human and celestial realms, and the six paths of existence.
The Three Jewels are entirely contained within these three jewels, for all are accomplished through following the teachings of Samantabhadra’s conduct. Thus it is said.

From "The roots of goodness" down to "the purity and fulfillment of giving and ethical discipline," there are four lines of verse that clarify the section on the repeated reception of the ten wholesome precepts;
this clarifies that in the first bhūmi one also receives the supreme (uttarottara) ten wholesome precepts,
which are here further clarified through the analogy of refining gold, from "like true gold" down to "the purity and fulfillment of ethical discipline," consisting of three lines.
The first half of the sūtra clarifies the analogy of refining and polishing true gold, which becomes even more brilliant and pure when treated with alum;

this serves as a metaphor for the five sons of the Buddha and those below them, down to the phrase "according to their power and according to their portion. This section consists of two and a half lines of sūtra.
The second part, from the six sons of the Buddha down to "all modes" and "the knowledge of all-knowledge," consists of six [lines].
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* clarifies that for a bodhisattva in this stage, the reception of office (*abhiṣeka*) is as follows:
"All beings" refers to the fact that by cultivating all seeds through preparatory application (*prayoga*), one attains fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Furthermore, "wisdom" clarifies that through the application of fundamental wisdom, one accomplishes differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*); because fundamental wisdom manifests due to samādhi, so too does differentiated wisdom.
By means of the power of application (*prayoga*) that observes with fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), [the path] is cultivated;

yet if each individual does not [apply] the power of observation through application and the power of great vows, then fundamental wisdom will stagnate in quiescence, becoming identical to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, and thus it would be of no use.
(7) Furthermore, from the passage "having thought thus" down to "the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge," there is...
The two and a half lines of sūtra clarify that this stage of the bodhisattva knows for themselves the excellence of their own virtues; this is divided into eight sections, from "This bodhisattva...

down to "...takes them as his retinue. The four and a half lines of sūtra clarify that this bodhisattva is also able to renounce home, wife, and children to leave the household life, attaining one thousand samādhis and seeing one thousand Buddhas; this is divided into nine sections. If, by means of bodhi...

From "By the power of his sublime vows" (*sa viśiṣṭapraṇidhānabalena*) down to "unable to be counted," there are two lines of scripture that clarify how, through the power of superior vows, he beholds the Buddhas;

prior to this, the power of his dependent retribution (*niṣyanda-karma*) was divided into ten parts. From "At that time" (*tasmin samaye*) onwards clarifies the section on Vajragarbha’s recitation of verses.
【Sūtra】 Upright, gentle, and flexible, as well as capable, Tamed, tranquil, and purely virtuous;
swiftly giving rise to the vast mind that transcends birth and death— By means of these ten mental states, one enters and dwells in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*).
Having achieved the merit of ethical discipline (*śīla-guṇa*) therein, One stays far removed from taking life and does not cause harm or affliction.
They also abstain from stealing and sexual misconduct; they avoid lying, slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
They do not covet material wealth but are always compassionate. Following the right path with a straightforward mind, they are free from flattery and deceit.
Having abandoned treachery and pride, they are exceedingly gentle and supple. Relying on the teachings, they act accordingly and remain ever heedful.
In the hells and among animals they undergo manifold sufferings; As hungry ghosts, they are scorched by blazing, fierce flames.
All these result from the causes of their own transgressions. I shall leave them behind and dwell among those who practice the Dharma of reality;
There, I shall take birth at will, Even reaching the bliss of meditative concentration up to the Peak of Existence.
The paths of the Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Buddhas are all accomplished through the ten wholesome actions.
Reflecting thus, one remains heedful, personally upholding pure precepts and teaching others to protect them as well.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings undergoing manifold sufferings, one increases one’s great compassion even further.
Ordinary fools with perverted wisdom lack correct understanding; They constantly harbor resentment and engage in much contention.

Greedy for sense objects, they have no end to their desires; I should cause them to eliminate the three poisons and the great darkness of delusion that shrouds and covers them, So that they may enter the great perilous path of the net of false views.
Trapped within the cage of birth and death, bound by resentment, I shall cause them to destroy the thieves of Māra.
Swept away by the four currents, their minds submerged and drowning, The three realms burn like fire; suffering is immeasurable.
Regarding the aggregates as my dwelling, I abide within them; Desiring to deliver them, I diligently practice the Path.

If there are those whose resolve for liberation is inferior, who have abandoned the supreme wisdom of the Buddha—I desire to establish them in the Mahāyāna, causing them to exert diligent effort without weariness.
Bodhisattvas dwelling here gather merit; seeing immeasurable Buddhas, they make offerings to them all.
Cultivating goodness for billions of eons, it becomes even more radiant; Like refining true gold with excellent medicine, the Son of the Buddha abides here as a Wheel-Turning King.
Universally transforming sentient beings to practice the ten wholesome paths, He cultivates all virtuous dharmas to achieve the Ten Powers and save the world.
Desiring to renounce royal sovereignty and wealth, they immediately abandon the household life to rely upon the Buddha’s teaching.
With courageous diligence, in a single moment of thought, they attain a thousand samādhis and behold a thousand Buddhas.
All the various supernormal powers possessed by these Bodhisattvas on this stage can be manifested.
The deeds performed through the power of vows exceed even this; With immeasurable mastery, they deliver all living beings.
For those who benefit all worlds, the supreme practices of a bodhisattva are cultivated.
Thus have the merits of the second stage been expounded for the sake of the sons of the Buddha.
The sons of the Buddha, having heard of the practices of this stage, Whose bodhisattva realm is inconceivable, All felt reverence and joy in their hearts;
Scattering flowers into the air as an offering, they praised him, saying:
“Excellent, O Great Mountain King! With a heart of compassion, you take pity upon all sentient beings.”
The wise one has well explained the dharma of discipline; such are the characteristics of the practices in the second bhūmi.
These are the subtle and wondrous deeds of all bodhisattvas—truly without variation or distinction—for the sake of benefiting all living beings. Thus he has proclaimed this most pure teaching.
O you who are honored by all gods and humans, we pray that you will expound the wisdom-activities corresponding to the Dharma of the third stage;
may you, Great Sage, fully reveal according to their respective spheres the perfections of giving and ethical discipline,
as well as patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
When the Buddha had spoken of the path of skillful means and compassion, as well as his pure conduct and vows,
Vimukticandra again requested, saying: "O Great Being Vajragarbha, you who possess fearlessness,
please speak of the entry into the third bhūmi and its various qualities for those with gentle minds."
[Treatise] Following the sixth verse, there are forty-two verses that clarify the reiteration of the preceding dharmas and the request to explain the section on the third bhūmi.
Within the commentary on the meaning, this is divided into five sections.
First, from "Upright, gentle, and capable" down to "for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas," there are thirty verses that constitute the reiteration.
The first ten sections of the Dharma-gates consist of two lines per verse, as they are fully contained within the text itself.

From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, up to the characteristics of practice in the Second Bhūmi, there are four lines of verse clarifying the section on the Great Assembly hearing the Dharma and making offerings.
From "These subtle practices of all Bodhisattvas" onwards, up to "Please expound upon the Third Bhūmi," [is the third section].
The three verses clarify that the bodhisattvas, having heard the second stage, again requested the teaching on the dharmas of the third stage. This section is divided into four parts:
first, the various knowledges and activities corresponding to the dharma; second, down to the Buddha’s pure conduct and vows, all of which are explained as having three verses;
third, the section clarifying the collective request of the bodhisattvas; and fourth, the section beginning with Vimukticandra. Below this is...
The two verses clarify Vimukticandra’s renewed request to explain the section on the third bhūmi.
Regarding the third, the Radiant Bhūmi (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*), as one would previously explain the names of the bhūmis through five gates, why is it called the Radiant Bhūmi?
It is because the cultivation of the eight dhyāna-samādhis of the form and formless realms is perfected in this stage.

Because one thoroughly penetrates the mundane meditative bodies (*dhyāna*) of the form and formless realms, and through the mutual opposition of consciousness (*vijñāna*), clearly understands the afflictions (*kleśa*) that obstruct the three realms, causing wisdom to become increasingly bright and pure, it is therefore called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

From the first ground and the second ground, one has skillfully mastered the phenomena of the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) within the desire realm; on this third ground, one skillfully masters the form and formless realms.
Because one attains the wisdom-light that transcends the three realms through the dharma-gates of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, it is called the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākari*).

If one were merely to cultivate and purify the afflictions of the desire realm without cultivating the eight samādhis, one would still possess the obstructions of the two higher realms—the form and formless realms—and thus it would not be named the Ground of Radiance; for this ground involves the cultivation [and transcendence] of the karma of all three realms.
Because the hindrances are exhausted, it is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*), for through meditative concentration one is able to radiate the light of wisdom.
Second, as for what practice-gate is cultivated on this ground: it takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence, with the other nine perfections as its companions.

This clarifies that the karmic hindrances of the three realms are exhausted; thus, this patience is termed "the attainment of the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If, at the initial generation of the mind...
Abiding in the manifestation of the Buddha’s wisdom is called being born into the family of the Buddhas’ wisdom.
The ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences collectively constitute the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the general meaning.

If one speaks of the progressive cultivation of the coarse and the subtle, the three stages of the preliminary sages (*pūrvayoga*) are termed the "Patience of Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*), because they are subdued by the Buddha’s wisdom; this refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The second and third stages are called "conformity with the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages attain liberation from the three realms and the disappearance of worldly obstacles, at which point they are properly named "patience of non-arising"; the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages are termed "effortless patience of quiescence" (*anābhoga-nirodha-kṣānti*);
and the tenth stage is where compassion and wisdom are perfectly integrated, its rank equaling that of the Buddhas. Third, as for Sudhana’s representation of the Dharma:

In this stage, Sudhana beheld the night goddess Pramuditanayanajagadvirocanā not far from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury. Sudhana attained the liberation door of the Universal Joy Banner of Great Power.
This marks the first stage of entering the grounds, the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment; the second ground is the Stainless (vimalā).
The first stage is the essence of bodhi, serving as the essence of the precepts. The third stage is based upon the principle of bodhi and cultivates patience (*kṣānti*);
since patience is the foremost of practices, one is not far from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is through bodhi that the practice of patience is perfected.
Thus, one sits upon the lion throne within the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha-siṃhāsana*); the lotus symbolizes being unstained amidst conduct.

The son Mingyi (Subhūti) takes the principle of non-attachment as his banner; he is called "Observing Sentient Beings with Joyful Eyes" because he clarifies the practice of patience (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*) and cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The night goddess is explained as before. That Sudhana attained the liberation of the "Universal Joy Banner of Great Power" clarifies that he has emerged from the obstacles of the three realms, perfected the patience of the Dharma, and is such that greed, hatred, anger, resentment, and delusions cannot affect him.
Because it arises, the Dharma-patience (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*) manifests; because it possesses great power, it is the liberation of the Universal Joy Banner (*Samantaprītidhvaja*).

This clarifies that it is able to destroy the afflictions of both self and others, remains unshakable amidst all objects of experience, and achieves the joy of the Dharma regarding all things favorable or adverse.
Fourth, as for which realm among the three realms this stage attains liberation from: this...
Attaining liberation from the three realms serves as the antidote for the first two stages; these three stages successively serve as the antidotes for the upper two realms.

Since the eight dhyānas exhaust all obstacles of the three realms, one studies the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the fourth stage, the cultivation of the contemplation of the ten truths in the fifth stage, and the cultivation of the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in the sixth stage.
Because it is worldly wisdom within the supramundane, there are two meanings in the commentary on the text according to the fivefold method, as previously stated.
First, regarding the long division of the sūtra’s intent: within this *Prabhākārī-bhūmi*, it is divided into seven sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has purified the second bhūmi and wishes to enter the third bhūmi, they should give rise to ten kinds of profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*).

What are these ten? Namely: the resolve of purity, the resolve of abiding, the resolve of weary detachment, the resolve of freedom from craving, the resolve of non-retrogression, and the resolve of firmness..."
With a firm mind, a clear mind, a vigorous mind, a vast mind, and a great mind— by means of these ten minds,
the Bodhisattva enters the third stage. [Treatise] First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" down to "he enters the third stage," there is...
The *Pañcaskandhaka-sūtra* clarifies that from the second stage, one cultivates the third stage by giving rise to ten kinds of mental states, as detailed in the sūtra itself. [Sūtra]:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the third stage, they contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as..."
The true nature (*dharmatā*) is what is called impermanence, suffering, impurity, insecurity, decay, and non-abiding;
it arises and ceases moment by moment. It does not arise from a prior limit, nor does it go toward a future limit, nor does it abide in the present.

Furthermore, one contemplates that these phenomena are without rescue and without refuge, coexisting with grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; bound by love and hatred, sorrow and distress increase ever more.
There is no accumulation [of merit], yet the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion blaze unceasingly; entangled by manifold afflictions, they increase day and night.
Seeing that all is as unreal as an illusion, one develops a redoubled sense of weary detachment toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
One approaches the Buddha’s wisdom, seeing that the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable, peerless, immeasurable, difficult to attain, unmixed, and free from affliction.
Having reached the City of Fearlessness, they no longer retreat; they are able to rescue immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and hardship.

When Bodhisattvas thus perceive the immeasurable benefits of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and see the immeasurable faults and afflictions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), they give rise to ten kinds of compassionate concern for all sentient beings. What are these ten? They are as follows: seeing all sentient beings...
He gives rise to a heart of compassion seeing beings born alone and without support; he gives rise to a heart of compassion seeing all beings impoverished and destitute;

he gives rise to a heart of compassion seeing all beings burning with the fires of the three poisons; he gives rise to a heart of compassion seeing all beings imprisoned within the jails of the various realms of existence;
he gives rise to a heart of compassion seeing all beings constantly shrouded by the dense forest of afflictions.
He gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings are obstructed; he gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings do not observe things well;

he gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings lack the desire for wholesome dharmas; he gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings have lost all Buddha-dharmas;

he gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings follow the stream of birth and death; and he gives rise to a heart of compassion upon seeing that sentient beings have lost liberation.

To generate a mind of compassion through skillful means—this is the tenth [practice]. Thus, seeing that the realm of sentient beings is subject to immeasurable suffering and affliction, the bodhisattva exerts great diligence and reflects:
"I should rescue these sentient beings; I should liberate them; I should purify them; I should deliver them; I should establish them in a wholesome state;
I should cause them to abide securely; I should cause them to rejoice; and I should cause them to attain knowledge."
Seeing that they should be disciplined and brought to nirvana, the Bodhisattva thus becomes weary of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and feels compassion for all sentient beings.
Knowing that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) possesses supreme benefit, and desiring to rely upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata to rescue and deliver sentient beings, he reflects:
"These sentient beings have fallen into the great suffering of the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
Within this, by what skillful means can one rescue and deliver [beings] so that they may abide in the bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa?
He then reflects: "To deliver sentient beings and cause them to abide in nirvāṇa, one must not be separated from unimpeded wisdom of liberation;

unimpeded wisdom of liberation is not separate from the realization of all phenomena as they truly are; and the realization of all phenomena as they truly are is not separate from [the perfection of wisdom]."
The light of wisdom that practices non-action and non-arising does not depart from skill in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the decisive analytical knowledge (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
Skill in meditative concentration and decisive analytical knowledge do not depart from skill in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
Having thus observed and understood this, the bodhisattva redoubles their diligent seeking and cultivation of the True Dharma, desiring only to hear it day and night.

With joy in the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, relying on the Dharma, following the Dharma, understanding the Dharma, conforming to the Dharma, reaching the Dharma, abiding in the Dharma, and practicing the Dharma, the Bodhisattva thus diligently seeks the precious wealth of the Buddha-Dharma without any stinginess;

seeing no object as difficult to obtain or worthy of high esteem, they conceive the thought that those who can teach the Buddha-Dharma are difficult to encounter. Therefore, the Bodhisattva, regarding...
For the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, they are able to relinquish all internal and external wealth;
there is no act of reverence they cannot perform, no pride they cannot abandon, no service they cannot carry out, and no hardship they cannot endure.
If they hear a single verse of the Dharma never heard before, they give rise to great joy, which surpasses the attainment of the three thousand [great world systems].

If one were to fill a thousandfold world-system with precious jewels, yet upon hearing a single verse of the Dharma never heard before, give rise to great joy—this would surpass the attainment of the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King;

and if one obtains a single verse of the Dharma never heard before that can purify the Bodhisattva practice, this would surpass the attainment of the rank of Śakra or Brahmā for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Suppose someone were to say: "I possess a single phrase..."
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha can purify the bodhisattva practice; if you are now able to enter a great pit of fire and undergo extreme suffering, I shall give it to you.

At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself: "For the sake of purifying the bodhisattva practice through even a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, were the three thousandfold world-system filled with a great fire, I would still desire [to enter it]."
If one could personally receive [the Dharma] by casting oneself down from the realm of Brahmā, how much more so would one enter a small fire pit?
Yet, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, I must now endure all the various sufferings of the hells;
how much more so the minor afflictions of the human world? Thus, a bodhisattva exerts diligent effort in this way to seek the Buddha-dharma. Just as...
Having heard and observed this teaching, the bodhisattva practices it; once he has heard the Dharma, he collects his mind and dwells in a secluded place, reflecting:
"One attains the Buddha-dharma by practicing according to what has been taught; it cannot be purified through mere words alone."
[Treatise] From the second son of the Buddha down to the passage stating that purity is not achieved merely through verbal expression,
fifty-two lines and a half of scripture clarify the correct abiding in the third stage (*tṛtīyā bhūmi*). This involves beholding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*),
giving rise to compassion for all sentient beings, honoring the Dharma and respecting persons, and being able to enter a pit of fire to undergo suffering and joy for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
In the second section, the "Explanation of the Meaning According to the Text," there are five parts: 1.

From "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the third stage" down to "this constitutes the tenth," spanning nineteen lines of scripture, explains the contemplation of conditioned suffering and impermanence through ten kinds of compassion for sentient beings. 2. "The Bodhisattva perceives sentient beings in this way... [and so forth].

From the section beginning with "The realm of sentient beings" down to "the bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa," there are seven lines and a half of sūtra that clarify how a bodhisattva, mindful of delivering sentient beings, uses specific skillful means to establish them in what locations so that they may attain the bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa.
This is divided into three parts: from "Having formed this thought" down to "thus observing and knowing" constitutes five lines of sūtra.
This section clarifies the Bodhisattva’s contemplation regarding the ultimate destination for establishing sentient beings; it is four times greater than the True Dharma.

From here down to the passage on "observing and practicing," there are nineteen lines of scripture that clarify how a Bodhisattva, desiring to deliver sentient beings, redoubles their diligent cultivation and seeks the Dharma even at the cost of life, being able to enter a pit of great fire without suffering.
5. From this point downward, there are two lines of sūtra that clarify the stage of definitive practice, which is not merely verbal. It is as follows:
wishing to deliver sentient beings and cause them to abide in the bliss of nirvāṇa, one does not depart from unobstructed liberative wisdom;
this is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Furthermore, such true awakening is the light of the wisdom of non-action and non-arising, which is skillful in dhyāna.
The skillful wisdom of definitive observation and extensive learning—these five qualities are collectively the functional applications of the single fundamental wisdom.
When practitioners cultivate the meditative concentration of skillful means, these become manifest and visible; they increase manifold through diligent application to the True Dharma.
May those who practice with such devotion, who seek the teachings day and night, who delight in the Dharma, and whose clear intelligence is free from sorrow, attain this realization.
Therefore, those who delight in the Dharma are free from birth and death; those who rely on the Dharma rely on the wisdom of the Tathāgata; those who follow the Dharma accord with right liberation;
those who understand the Dharma understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); those who conform to the Dharma conform to right knowledge;
and those who reach the Dharma reach nirvāṇa themselves, yet are able to enter into saṃsāra to deliver sentient beings. Furthermore—
Because it causes one to reach nirvāṇa, those who abide in the Dharma abide within the wisdom of the Tathāgata; thus,

obtaining even a single verse of the Dharma is superior to obtaining the treasures of the great trichiliocosm and the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, which clarifies that worldly dharmas cannot escape birth and death—
the subsequent points should be understood accordingly.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Stage (prabhākari-bhūmi), they immediately depart from sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states;

with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and the joy and happiness born of seclusion, they dwell in the first dhyāna. Having stilled directed thought and sustained thought, with internal clarity and one-pointed mind, free from directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, they dwell in the second dhyāna.

Departing from joy, they dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; they dwell in the third dhyāna. Thus, they dwell having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of elation and dejection, experiencing neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and with purity of mindfulness through equanimity, they dwell in the fourth dhyāna.

The noble ones speak of dwelling in the third dhyāna, which possesses equanimity and mindfulness and is experienced as bliss, having abandoned pleasure and previously eliminated pain, with the extinction of joy and sorrow,
neither painful nor pleasant, pure in equanimity and mindfulness; and of dwelling in the fourth dhyāna, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance,
not attending to perceptions of diversity, entering the sphere of infinite space, and dwelling in the sphere of infinite space, transcending it.
Entering the sphere of infinite space, one dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness;
transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness;

transcending the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Yet, because it merely accords with the Dharma, one practices without any attachment or delight.

[Treatise] From the third "Son of the Buddha" downward, up to "and there is no attachment to what is enjoyed," ten and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on practicing the four *dhyānas* and eight *samādhis* of the form and formless realms in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) while dwelling in the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), without any attachment.
This is further divided into nine sections: 1. From "Son of the Buddha" downward, up to "joy born of seclusion."

One line and a half of the sutra constitute the section on abiding in the first dhyāna; from "having stilled vitarka and vicāra" down to "born of concentration, joy and bliss," there is one line of sutra.

The section on abiding in the second dhyāna consists of three parts; from "detached from joy, abiding in equanimity" down to "possessing mindfulness and clearly perceiving bliss while dwelling in equanimity," there are two lines of sutra.
This constitutes the section on abiding in the third dhyāna; from "abandoning pleasure" down to... [the fourth dhyāna].
There is one line of sutra concerning abiding in the fourth dhyāna; this is the section on abiding in the fourth dhyāna.
From "having transcended all perceptions of form" down to "abiding in the sphere of infinite space," there is one and a half lines of sutra;

this is the section on the concentration of the sphere of infinite space. From "having transcended the sphere of infinite space" up to "abiding in the sphere of infinite consciousness," there is one line.

The sutra passage concerning the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi) consists of seven sections, beginning with transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness and continuing down to abiding in the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).

The sutra passage concerning the concentration of the sphere of nothingness consists of eight sections, beginning with transcending the sphere of nothingness and continuing down to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). The sutra passage concerning the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
This concentration is the summit of the three realms; it merely accords with the Dharma and is thus without attachment. This mind is the concentration that is without support;

this is the essential body of the Dharma-realm concentration. For one who explains the meaning according to the text, it clarifies that upon reaching this Radiant Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), one attains the mind that transcends the three realms and enters the gate of the great non-active samādhi which is the very essence of the Dharma-realm. Although one practices the four [immeasurables],...

The eight dhyānas of meditative concentration always accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and have no basis; they are practiced solely to refine the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three realms so that wisdom may become clear and pure.
One should thus advance in cultivation. Therefore, it is like refining gold so that not even a *zhū* or two is lost;

in this way, through the successive refinement by means of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not lose even a *zhū* of the great, perfectly round, and luminous wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
By means of these eight kinds of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one refines and polishes them so that wisdom becomes increasingly clear and pure;
because the essence of the Dharma-body wisdom is fundamentally without increase or decrease, it is called the "Radiant Stage" (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*).

Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who attain these eight dhyānas transcend the suffering of the three realms and are born in the Pure Lands; those possessed of great compassion, however, retain their afflictions to moisten their rebirth, remaining in the world.
In the interim, when Śrāvakas and Arhats emerge from the eight dhyānas and enter the ninth dhyāna, they rely on the wisdom of emptiness to extinguish both body and cognition,
such that they are entirely non-existent; whereas the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle cultivate the eight dhyānas, thoroughly knowing that worldly phenomena have no intrinsic nature,
and because they realize the essence of the three realms is inherently without arising or ceasing, they give rise to the wondrous function of attaining all-knowledge.

Because one gives rise to great wisdom that knows worldly dharmas, it is called the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). It clarifies that on the first ground, one cultivates generosity (*dāna*) while abiding in the world;

on the second ground, one cultivates ethical discipline (*śīla*), clarifying the ability to purify the world; on the third ground, one cultivates the eight meditative absorptions (*aṣṭa-samādhi*), clarifying the attainment of supramundane [wisdom];
and on the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds, it clarifies the cultivation of supramundane and mundane wisdom within the midst of the supramundane; and on the seventh and eighth...
The ninth stage clarifies the cultivation of entering the world so that compassion and wisdom become perfectly integrated;

the tenth stage clarifies the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom and compassion to attain the state of Buddhahood. Therefore, although the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*) within the integration of principle and wisdom has no hierarchical gradations, these distinctions are established to counteract habitual tendencies, to harmonize and integrate the maturation of compassion and wisdom, and to cultivate the differentiated wisdom of the mundane and supramundane.
The stages are established according to their depth and breadth, providing a standard for others to emulate. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha,
this bodhisattva’s mind follows compassion— vast, immeasurable, non-dual, without enmity, without opposition, unobstructed, and free from affliction—
reaching everywhere throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, pervading all worlds.
Abiding in compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is likewise so.
[Treatise] From "The fourth son of the Buddha" down to "is likewise so," two and a half lines of scripture clarify that in this stage one cultivates the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*)—
compassion, joy, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— with great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) as the foremost part.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva attains immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). He can shake the great earth; he can manifest many bodies from one body, or one body from many bodies;
he can appear or disappear at will; he passes through stone walls and mountain barriers without obstruction, just as if through empty space;
he travels cross-legged through the air like a bird; and he enters the earth as if it were water, or walks upon it as if it were dry land.
The water is like the body of the earth, emitting smoke and flames like a great mass of fire, yet it rains down water again like a vast cloud.
Though the sun and moon possess great power in the sky, they can reach out with their hands to stroke and touch his body, exercising mastery even as far as the Brahma world.
This Bodhisattva’s divine ear is purified and surpasses that of humans; he hears all sounds of humans and devas, whether near or far.
If there are sounds at a distance, even those of mosquitoes, gnats, or flies, he is able to hear them all.
With the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), this bodhisattva knows the minds of other sentient beings as they truly are: he knows a mind with greed as it truly is a mind with greed;
he knows a mind free from greed as it truly is a mind free from greed; he knows a mind with hatred as it truly is a mind with hatred; he knows a mind free from hatred... [and so on].
A mind of delusion; a mind free from delusion; a mind with afflictions; a mind without afflictions; a small mind; a vast mind; a great mind; an immeasurable mind;
a contracted mind; a non-contracted mind; a distracted mind; a non-distracted mind; a concentrated mind; a non-concentrated mind; a liberated mind; a non-liberated mind;
a surpassable mind; an unsurpassable mind; a defiled mind; a non-defiled mind; a broad mind; a non-broad mind...
With a broad mind, he knows all things as they truly are. In this way, the bodhisattva uses the knowledge of others' minds to know the minds of sentient beings.
This bodhisattva recollects and knows infinite varieties of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), namely:
he recollects one life, two lives, three lives, four lives, and so on up to ten lives, twenty, thirty, and even a hundred lives, immeasurable hundreds of lives, and so forth.

Throughout a thousand births, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, eons of formation, eons of destruction, and immeasurable eons of both formation and destruction, I have existed in such-and-such a place, with such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage, such-and-such food, such-and-such a lifespan, such-and-such a duration of stay, and such-and-such experiences of suffering and pleasure; having died there, I was born in such-and-such a place. From...
He is able to recollect all such infinite distinctions of the past— dying in such-and-such a place and being born in this place, with such a form, such a complexion,
such a voice, and such speech. With his purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans,
this bodhisattva sees sentient beings as they are born and die, whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, and whether they go to happy or miserable realms, according to their karma.
And as for those beings who have accomplished evil conduct of body, accomplished evil conduct of speech, and accomplished evil conduct of mind;

who revile the noble ones, possess wrong views, and are possessed of the causes and conditions of the karma of wrong views—when their bodies break up at the end of life, they will inevitably fall into the evil destinies and be born in hell. If those beings have accomplished good conduct of body and accomplished good conduct of speech...

The Bodhisattva knows with his divine eye exactly as it is that those who have accomplished conduct, performed wholesome deeds, refrained from slandering the noble ones, and were endowed with right view— due to the causes and conditions of such right view—
will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn among the gods in the happy realms. Furthermore,
this Bodhisattva is able to enter and emerge from all dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis, yet he does not follow after their power.
Regarding rebirth, one is born therein solely by the power of the will and aspiration in accordance with those places that can fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
[Treatise] From "The fifth son of the Buddha" down to "born therein by the power of the will and aspiration," thirty-three lines of scripture clarify that while dwelling in this stage,
one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and achieves the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).

This section is further divided into six sub-sections: 1. From "O Son of the Buddha, once this bodhisattva has attained immeasurable supernormal powers" down to "up to the Brahma world," there are six lines of sūtra explaining the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*). 2. From "This bodhisattva...
down to "...are all able to hear," there are two lines of sūtra explaining the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). 3. [The third sub-section...]

1. From "This Bodhisattva" down to "knows the minds of sentient beings through the knowledge of others' minds," there are seven lines of sūtra clarifying the attainment of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
2. From "This Bodhisattva" down to "are all able to recollect," there are eight lines of sūtra clarifying the attainment of the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti).
3. From "This Bodhisattva" down to "all know as they truly are," there are seven [lines of sūtra].

The practice of the half-sūtra clarifies the attainment of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). This section above clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s mastery of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) is for the following reasons:
because his wisdom and compassion are not yet fully perfected; because he fulfills the practices of Samantabhadra; because he differs from the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Lands;

and because he differs from those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Consequently, he does not realize the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), as his wisdom exercises mastery in accordance with his conduct within birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus it is said:
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Though he practices the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), he does not exhaust his outflows (*āsrava*).

This refers to the passage from "this bodhisattva" downward, ending with "by the power of his vow, he is born therein," two lines of scripture which clarify the aspect of taking birth not by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas—
namely, they see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
and even up to many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas— and they serve, honor, respect, and make offerings to them all with a vast mind and a profound mind.
He offers all requisites for life—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal elixirs, and everything else—to them, and likewise makes offerings to the entire community of monks.
He dedicates these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In the presence of that Buddha, he listens to the Dharma with reverence; having heard it, he receives and upholds it, practicing according to his capacity. This Bodhisattva contemplates a single...
All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, existing only through causes and conditions.

Having first extinguished the bonds of views, and because one has not accumulated them over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, all bonds of desire, form, existence, and ignorance become thin and feeble;
thus, false greed, false hatred, and false delusion are all completely severed, and all roots of goodness are further increased.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like pure gold that has been skillfully refined and smelted; its weight does not diminish, yet it becomes increasingly bright and pure.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva dwelling in this Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*)—because he does not accumulate [unwholesome states]—completely eliminates false greed, false anger, and false delusion.
All his roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) become increasingly bright and pure; this is the patience (*kṣānti*) of this Bodhisattva.

The mind of humility, the mind of gentleness, the mind of harmony and compliance, the mind of joy and appreciation, the mind free from anger, the mind that is unshakable, the mind free from turbidity, the mind without pride or inferiority, the mind that does not expect recompense, the mind of gratitude, the mind free from flattery, the mind free from deception, and the mind free from treachery and perversity—all these are transformed into purity.

Among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva’s practice of beneficial conduct (*anugrahakarī pravṛtti*) is predominant; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), [the perfection of] skillful means is predominant.
In this stage, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) predominates; it is not that the others are not cultivated, but they are practiced according to one’s strength and capacity.

Son of the Buddha, this is called the Bodhisattva’s third stage, the Luminous (*Prabhākari*). When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he frequently becomes the King of the Thirty-three Heavens (*Trāyastriṃśa-rāja*).

By means of skillful means (*upāya*), he causes all sentient beings to abandon greed and desire, and practices giving (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial action (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*).

All actions performed by them are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and never apart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha, up to and including never being apart from mindfulness of the possession of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, they form this thought: "I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, and the supreme among all sentient beings."
As the support for the unsurpassed [enlightenment] up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), if one practices with diligent vigor,
in a single moment of thought one attains hundreds of thousands of samādhis, beholds hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, knows the spiritual powers of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
can shake hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, and even manifests hundreds of thousands of bodies, each body accompanied by hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.
If one were to manifest as a retinue through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows,
they would exceed these numbers even after hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, such that they could not be calculated or known.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to where it says "and spoke in verse," there are thirty-one lines of scripture that clarify the breadth and narrowness of the Buddhas seen by a bodhisattva in this stage, as well as their respective offices. Within this section, it is further divided into seven parts.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "practicing according to one's power," there are six and a half lines of scripture that clarify this stage.
The Bodhisattva, through the power of their vows, attains the vision of many Buddhas and performs offerings while hearing the Dharma. This section is divided into two parts. From "This Bodhisattva...

down to "...becomes even more luminous and pure," there are four lines of sutra text clarifying the contemplation of phenomena and the liberation from bondage. This section is divided into three parts.
From "O Son of the Buddha... down to "...becomes even more luminous and pure," there are three lines of sutra text clarifying the analogy of refining true gold to compare it with the Bodhisattva.
The section on the further clarification and purification of the preparatory knowledge of the *sādhūmī* stage is divided into four parts. From "This bodhisattva...

down to "...all become purified," there are three lines of sūtra that clarify the thirteen types of mental states that become further clarified and purified through patience and gentleness. This constitutes the fifth part.
From "This bodhisattva... down to "...according to his strength and according to his portion," there are two lines of sūtra that clarify the bodhisattva at this stage.

The section on the dharmas practiced by the Bodhisattvas from "the six classes of Buddha-sons" downward, ending with "unable to be numbered," consists of eleven and a half lines of scripture that clarify the quantity of Buddhas seen by Bodhisattvas in this stage based on their meditative concentration; this is divided into seven parts.
From "at that time" onward clarifies the section where Vajragarbha recites verses.
[Sūtra] With a mind that is pure, settled, and radiant; with a mind of weary detachment, free from greed, and free from harm;
with a firm, courageous, and vast mind—the wise enter the third stage by means of these.
Abiding here in the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), they contemplate all conditioned phenomena as suffering and impermanent.
Impure and decaying, they swiftly return to extinction; Lacking solidity, lacking stability, and devoid of coming or going.
View all conditioned phenomena as a grave illness, Enveloped by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
The fierce fires of the three poisons burn constantly, Without ceasing from beginningless time.
Disgusted with and detached from the three realms of existence, he does not crave them; He seeks exclusively for the Buddha-wisdom, without other thoughts.
It is unfathomable, inconceivable, and peerless; Immeasurable, boundless, and free from affliction.
Having seen this Buddha-wisdom, he takes pity on sentient beings, Who are solitary, without refuge, and without protection.
The three poisons burn fiercely, leaving them perpetually exhausted; dwelling in the prisons of existence, they constantly suffer, shrouded by afflictions and blind without eyes.

Their aspirations are base and inferior, they have lost the jewel of the Dharma, they follow along with birth and death, and they fear nirvana. I should rescue them through diligent and energetic effort.
Seeking to gain wisdom to benefit sentient beings, one should contemplate what skillful means will lead them to liberation;
never departing from the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom, one should further give rise to the thought that this wisdom arises from hearing.
Reflecting thus, one should exert oneself with diligence.
Day and night they listen and study without interruption; they hold only the True Dharma in the highest esteem.
Kingdoms, cities, wealth, shells, and various precious jewels, as well as wives, children, retinues, and royal thrones—all these the Bodhisattva is able to relinquish out of reverence for the Dharma.

To give away one's head, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, hands, feet, marrow, bones, heart, blood, and flesh—these things are not difficult to relinquish; rather, it is hearing the Dharma that is most difficult.
Suppose someone were to come and say to a bodhisattva: "Who is able to cast their body into a great mass of fire?"
I shall bestow upon you the jewel of the Buddha-dharma; having heard it, cast yourself into it without fear.

Even if the three thousandfold world-system were filled with fire, one would not find it difficult to cast one's body from the Brahma-world for the sake of seeking the Dharma—how much less so the various minor sufferings of the human realm?

From the first generation of the resolve for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, whatever sufferings of the Avīci hell may arise therein, one is able to endure them all for the sake of hearing the Dharma; how much more so the various sufferings of the human realm?
Having heard [the teaching], one reflects upon it correctly according to the principle, thereby attaining the four dhyānas and the formless absorptions.
The four immeasurables and five supernormal powers arise in succession; Without relying on their power, the Bodhisattva takes birth.
Abiding here, the Bodhisattva beholds many Buddhas, Makes offerings, hears the Dharma, and becomes firm in resolve.
Severing all false delusions, they become increasingly pure, Like refined gold whose essence never diminishes.
Dwelling here, one often acts as the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
transforming and guiding immeasurable hosts of devas to abandon greed and abide in the wholesome path. Single-mindedly and exclusively seeking the merits of the Buddha,
the Son of the Buddha dwelling here exerts diligent effort, becoming fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
Beholding hundreds of thousands of Buddhas with bodies adorned by the marks, And through the power of their vows, surpassing all these, they universally benefit all sentient beings;
Such is the supreme conduct of those Bodhisattvas. Thus have I explained the meaning of this third stage.
[Treatise] Seventh: Regarding the verses spoken herein, there are thirty-six lines of verse, with two lines constituting one stanza;
these restate the preceding dharmas as they appear in the text itself.

Fourth: Regarding the Blazing Wisdom Ground (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), before explaining this ground, five gates are established as previously [done for the other grounds]. First, the explanation of the name of this ground.

Why is this stage called the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*)? Because prior to this ground, one has cultivated the eight dhyānas of the higher realms and attained the wisdom that transcends the three realms;

therefore, it is named the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*). Here, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*), and as one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*), they become increasingly bright and pure; thus, it is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom. Prior to this ground, [wisdom] was produced by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It is named the Ground of Radiant Light (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). Because one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and because the wisdom that perceives their self-nature as being without support becomes exceptionally bright and pure, it is called "Flaming Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī*). Second, regarding what practice-gates are cultivated on this ground:
the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions. Third, [the meaning of] Sudhana’s representation: [is explained as follows].

Regarding the Dharma: within this stage, Sudhana beheld the night goddess Samantasattvatrāṇojaḥśrī, who had attained the bodhisattva liberation door of "Universally Manifesting in All Worlds to Discipline Sentient Beings.

The fact that this goddess resides within this assembly indicates that she is present together with the previously mentioned goddess Priyanetra, signifying her identity with the former [goddess] of the Vimalā-bhūmi.
Therefore, because the unconditioned nature of the Dharma-body is the essence of bodhi, and because the perfection of patience and the perfection of vigor are the practices of bodhi,
the Universal Virtue Pure Light (Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā) dwells within the site of enlightenment,
not far from the abode of the deity Joyful Eyes (Priyanetra). In this fourth stage, she universally rescues all sentient beings.
The Night Goddess is present within this assembly because she clarifies that the two stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are not separate from the myriad practices;

furthermore, she clarifies that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are auxiliary practices for attaining bodhi. Therefore, it is said that she is here in this assembly.

In this stage, she clarifies that by means of the essence of bodhi, one contemplates the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*) to accomplish mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).

Because of wisdom, one has already sought the supramundane bodhicitta in the preceding three stages; in these fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one cultivates mundane wisdom by means of that bodhicitta.
Therefore, it is said that within this assembly and at this stage, one beholds the Night Goddess Samantānugata (Universal Savior of Beings);
this clarifies that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness are present here.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time teach and transform all sentient beings through these skillful means for aiding the path.
From their initial aspiration until the attainment of ultimate wisdom, all Buddhas rely upon these very skillful means to further clarify and increase their various wisdoms.
Therefore, this spirit is named "Universally Saving All Sentient Beings with Sublime Virtue. "Sublime Virtue" (Miaode) elucidates the thirty [virtues].

The seventh stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), is so named because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) can manifest the sublime wisdom of both oneself and others.

Having previously cultivated generosity, ethical discipline, and patience during the first three stages to attain the supramundane mind, one now further refines it through these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
hence the name "Blazing Wisdom. It is the gateway of liberation that universally manifests throughout the world to tame all sentient beings.

This is to clarify that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) in this stage constitute the great path of training and subduing practiced in common by both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle;
therefore, they are named "Universally Manifesting the Liberation of All Sentient Beings through Subduing.
Each of these should be understood by classifying them according to the practices manifested by Sudhana; if it were not so, their meaning could not be fully realized.
The stages, positions, and gates of practice are fully elucidated from the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*).
Regarding which realm among the three realms one attains liberation in, if considered by way of general characteristics, one attains liberation from all three realms;

if considered by way of specific characteristics, it is explained that through the progressive advancement in this stage, one attains [liberation from] the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by means of cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

With the wisdom of the middle way, the mind of liberation is vast and the great intention is luminous and weighty; this serves as the remedy for the remaining habitual tendencies of the three realms that arose in the third bhūmi.
It clarifies the fifth bhūmi, wherein one cultivates the dhyāna-pāramitā and practices the contemplation of the ten truths (*daśa-satya*).

By attaining the supramundane states within both the higher realms and the desire realm, as well as mundane liberation within the world, all must be accomplished through the general and specific [aspects] of sameness.
This differs from the theories of formation and destruction; it is like the spirits of the "Joyful" (Pramuditā) stage first being born into the Buddha-family.
Because the *dāna-pāramitā* can nourish the holy path, the spirit is named "Lord of Spring," corresponding to the initial growth of spring.
As for the second stage, the "Stainless" (Vimalā), because the *śīla-pāramitā* takes the non-action of the Dharma-body as its essence, the spirit is named... [the name of the spirit follows].

The "Universal Virtue Pure Radiance" is the light of the precepts; it abides within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) because the Dharma-body is the essence of the site of enlightenment and the body is the essence of *bodhi*.
The third stage, the Ground of Radiant Light, has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence.
The deity is named Joyful Eye (*Priyanetra*), who observes sentient beings; because of patience, there is nothing that does not bring joy. Thus he departs.
The phrase "the site of enlightenment is not far" clarifies that patience takes the non-activity of the Dharma-body as its essence.

The fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī) Bhūmi, takes the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) as its essence; the name of the deity is "Universally Saving All Beings," because the perfection of diligence carries the meaning of universal salvation.
Furthermore, it serves to universally purify the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of the three realms that arose during the preceding three stages.

Therefore, those who dwell in this assembly clearly do not depart from the *dharmakāya*, nor from the practice of the patience of natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and the practice of vigor (*vīrya*).
Thus, by summarizing the names and the locations where they dwell, the sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*) is made easy to perceive;

reflect upon this and it will become clear. Furthermore, the fact that in the entry into the stages (*bhūmi-praveśa*), the spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) are frequently used as symbols of the Dharma indicates—

One enters the stages by means of noble wisdom; because it arises from the practice of blessings and is termed "divine" (śūnyatā), one should contemplate it through the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*)—namely, the principles of totality and particularity, sameness and difference, and formation and disintegration—in order to be free from delusion.

Regarding the second [section], the exegesis according to the text, there are two parts: first, the structural outline of the sūtra’s meaning; second, the word-by-word commentary. First, regarding the structural outline of the sūtra’s meaning:
Within this *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*, the text is divided into seven sections.
[Sūtra] Hearing of these vast practices, This delightful, profound, wondrous, and supreme stage,
The sons of the Buddha all felt courageous joy and great delight, Scattering various flowers everywhere as an offering to the Buddha.
When he preached such a sublime Dharma, the great earth and the waters of the ocean all trembled;
all the celestial maidens were filled with joy and together uttered wondrous sounds in praise.
The Sovereign King of Heaven rejoiced greatly and rained down mani-jewels as an offering to the Buddha.
Praising him, he said: "The Buddha has appeared for my sake, Expounding the supreme conduct of merit.

Thus, the meaning of the stages of the wise— Which is extremely difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of eons— I have now suddenly heard, This sublime Dharma sound of the Bodhisattva’s excellent practice."

I pray that you, O wise one, will further expound this path of certainty for the subsequent stages, which leaves nothing remaining and benefits all devas and humans. These sons of the Buddhas all long to hear it;
O Vīramati Vimukticandra, Son of the Buddha, please speak, O Vajragarbha!
From here, one enters the fourth stage; please proclaim all its characteristics.

[Treatise] From "The first son of the Buddha" onwards, there are twelve lines of verse clarifying the section where the great assembly, having heard of the preceding stage, rejoices and further requests the teaching of the subsequent stage.
Within the second part, the word-by-word commentary, it is further divided into two sections.

Once a son of the Buddha has heard this vast conduct, there follow eight verses on the "Exquisite Sound of the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Supreme Conduct," which clarify how the great assembly rejoices and makes offerings upon hearing the Dharma of the third bhūmi. This section is divided into two parts:
first, from the vow, there are four verses further expounding for the wise; these clarify the request for the Dharma of the fourth bhūmi.
The textual meaning of the preceding section on the gates is fully contained within the text itself; there is no need for further explanation.
As for the Great Lord Mahesvara King being described as "greatly rejoicing," it is because this heaven is the place where the Ten Stages are taught, and not because they are taught in other heavens.
This refers only to the lord of the place where the Dharma is preached.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has thoroughly purified the third stage and wishes to enter the fourth stage, the Radiant Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), they should practice ten gates of illumination of the Dharma.
What are these ten? Namely: observing the realm of sentient beings, observing the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), observing..."
Observing the world-realm, observing the space-realm, observing the consciousness-realm, observing the desire-realm, observing the form-realm, observing the formless-realm,
observing the realm of vast mental resolve and faith, and observing the realm of great mental resolve and faith—
by means of these ten gateways of dharma-luminosity, the bodhisattva enters the fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*) bhūmi.

[Treatise] Second: The section beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha... and extending for six and a half lines of scripture clarifies the entry into the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) through ten dharmas.
Within the detailed explanation of this meaning, it is divided into two parts:
first, from "At that time" down to "should cultivate the ten dharma-gates," there are two and a half lines of scripture clarifying the desire to enter the fourth stage.
The section on the examination of the names of the ten dharmas for which the Ground exhorts cultivation is divided into two parts.
What are these ten? Below this, there are four lines of scripture that constitute the actual enumeration of the names of the ten dharmas for examination.

Why are these ten dharmas enumerated so as to cause the Bodhisattva to clearly perceive them once again? It is because having attained supramundane wisdom in the previous three grounds, one now examines these ten once more.
Because the light of the Dharma brings supramundane wisdom back to reach the mundane so that it is identical with the supramundane.
