The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament, Scroll Fifty-nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty;
A Combined Commentary on the Ten Stages Sūtra, Fascicle 26-7.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), they are able to mature the Dharma through ten kinds of knowledge.
One attains the arising of those internal dharmas within the family of the Tathāgata. What are these ten? They are: first, because of non-retrogression from the profound resolve;
second, because of generating pure faith in the Triple Gem that is ultimately indestructible; third, because of contemplating the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);

fourth, because of contemplating the unarisen nature of the self-essence (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas; fifth, because of contemplating the formation and destruction of the world; sixth, because of contemplating that birth arises from causes and karma; [seventh,] because of contemplating birth and death...

Because of nirvāṇa; because of observing the karma of sentient beings and their lands; because of observing the past and future limits; and because of observing non-existence and exhaustion—these are the ten.
O sons of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this fourth stage, they observe the internal body as a body with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow;
they observe the external body as a body with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, removing... [worldly greed and sorrow].

With regard to the world, one observes with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to remove worldly greed and sorrow; observing the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally, one dwells contemplating the body as the body.

Observing feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally, one dwells contemplating feelings as feelings. Observing the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally, one dwells contemplating the mind as the mind.

Observing phenomena internally, externally, and both internally and externally, one dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to remove [worldly greed and sorrow].

Regarding worldly greed and anxiety: furthermore, this bodhisattva, for the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment;
and for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment;
and for the sake of producing unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy... [and applies right abandonment].

Having already generated the arousal of the mind and right practice, in order to cause all wholesome dharmas that have arisen to remain without loss and to cultivate them so they may increase and expand, he arouses the desire, exerts effort, and applies diligence through the arousal of the mind and right practice. Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire, accompanied by the factors of abandonment;
it relies on disenchantment, relies on detachment, relies on cessation, and is dedicated toward relinquishment. He practices with vigor...

He cultivates the basis for supernormal power consisting of concentration of intention, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation, which is accomplished through the formative forces of abandonment;

he relies upon disenchantment, relies upon detachment, relies upon cessation, and dedicates it toward equanimity. Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices the faculty of faith, relying upon disenchantment, relying upon detachment, relying upon cessation, and dedicating it toward equanimity;
he likewise practices the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, relying upon [the same].
Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices the power of faith by relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating [the merit] toward equanimity;

he likewise practices the powers of diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom by relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating [the merit] toward equanimity. Furthermore, this...
The Bodhisattva practices the awakening factor of mindfulness by relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward equanimity;

he likewise practices the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity by relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating them toward equanimity. Furthermore, this Bodhisattva...
Practicing right view by relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward equanimity;
practicing right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration by relying on disenchantment,
relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward equanimity— the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of such merits is for the sake of not abandoning even one [being].
Because of all sentient beings; because of being sustained by his original vows; because of having great compassion as the foremost; because of the accomplishment of great loving-kindness;
because of reflecting upon the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*); because of the accomplishment of adorning Buddha-fields;

because of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, unique Buddha-dharmas, marks and signs, and the complete perfection of the voice; he seeks the most supreme and excellent path.
Therefore, they accord with the profound liberation of the Buddhas as they have heard it, and they contemplate great wisdom and skillful means.

[Treatise] The third section, from "The Buddha-son, having dwelt in this Ground of Blazing Wisdom" onwards, consists of thirty-seven and a half lines of scripture that clarify the stage of cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Within the explanation of its meaning, it is divided into ten sections. First, the Buddha-son...

From here below, down to the passage "born into the family of the Tathāgata," there is one line and a half of sūtra that clarifies the section on attaining birth in the Buddha-family through ten kinds of wisdom.

As it is asked: just as in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*), is called "being born into the family of the Tathāgata," and the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) is also called "being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," so too at this fourth ground, it is called "being born."

Question: What is the distinction within the Tathāgata’s family? Answer: If one considers its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is a single essence without duality.
However, if one discusses its specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) regarding spiritual advancement, there are indeed degrees of depth and shallowness.

For instance, within the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), at the summit of Mount Sumeru, one clearly initiates the transformation of ordinary sentiment and first opens the Buddha-wisdom; this merely awakens one from delusion to understanding.
Because they have attained a portion of the cooling of afflictions, the fruit of Buddhahood is called the Moon; this is like the ten Buddhas of the ten months within the stage of the Ten Abodes.
Furthermore, as illustrated by the Dharma-expressions in the life of Sudhana, when he beheld the bhikṣu on Mount Meghaśrī, this merely manifested the Buddha’s wisdom and liberation.
His knowledge, virtue, and supernormal powers were not yet fully manifest, just as one born into the family of the Tathāgata at the first stage (bhūmi) possesses wisdom, yet it is not yet perfected.
The power of their spiritual penetrations allows them to emerge from the three realms; the wisdom by which they transform sentient beings is likewise according to what they themselves know.
Yet, they have not yet attained mastery over the unimpeded freedom of mundane and supramundane wisdom.
This is the fourth stage, wherein one is born into the family of the Buddhas and clearly understands both mundane and supramundane wisdom.

Because of wisdom, although one shares in the commonality of the divine nature (*devatā*) within the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is a distinction between the worldly and supramundane wisdom regarding depth;
this clarifies that in the preceding three stages, one merely cultivates the dhyānas of the two upper realms to attain the principle of a single detachment from the three realms.
In this stage, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*); thus the Sūtra says: "One attains those internal dharmas and gives rise [to them]."
Regarding the Dharma within the Tathāgata’s family, it clarifies that through the wisdom of reflective observation, one realizes that worldly wisdom has nothing in the mundane that is not true.
What are these two? From "What are the ten? down to "These are the ten," fourteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on the wisdom of this stage accomplished by means of ten dharmas.
These begin with what is called "the non-retrogression of the profound mind" regarding the Three Jewels.
"Because pure faith in the center is ultimately indestructible" means that these Three Jewels pervade all phenomena across the three realms and the three periods of time;
they are subsumed within the Three Jewels as a whole, for they are not like the Three Jewels conceived by worldly sentiment—this is called "the profound mind.

To contemplate that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) of the three realms is inherently devoid of self-nature is what constitutes the Buddha Jewel; it is to realize the identity and difference, the totality and particularity, of the phenomena of the three realms.

The formation and destruction [of the world] are called the Dharma Jewel; by means of the gate of self-practice, harmonizing the minds and intentions of sentient beings through skillful means to lead them toward the attainment of arhatship (*yathābhūta*) and the bliss of humans and devas is called the Saṃgha Jewel. Regarding the phrase "observing the formation and destruction of the world," the subsequent text states:
"Birth arises because of karma, and formation likewise occurs because of karma; however, with respect to the fundamental Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is no formation."

"Because destruction is not established, [one] contemplates birth-and-death and nirvana within the midst of destruction because sentient beings falsely perceive formation and destruction"—this clarifies that birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally and universally without intrinsic substance. "Because one contemplates the karma of sentient beings and their lands"—this clarifies that lands arise from karma;
since they were originally non-existent and now exist, one contemplates the prior limit and the subsequent limit.
Because the three periods of time are fundamentally non-existent and lack any characteristic of exhaustion, it is not said that there are many eons yet remain inexhaustible;

rather, it is simply stated that the three periods of time are fundamentally non-existent and have nothing that can be exhausted. This constitutes the tenth summary, which concludes the preceding ten dharmas.
Next, O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this fourth stage, there are six practices ranging from [the elimination of] worldly greed and anxiety.

The Sūtra clarifies the four applications of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) through the gate of contemplation regarding the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. Regarding the division of these four applications of mindfulness, first is the application of mindfulness of the body:

"To follow" (*anupaśyanā*) means to accord with. This clarifies skillfully following the internal body—the intestines, stomach, liver, gallbladder, heart, lungs, spleen, and kidneys—observing that within these five viscera and six receptacles there is no self, person, sovereign, or substantial characteristic. One who is diligent and courageous [should thus practice].
"Clearly and diligently observing without weariness" means that one who possesses mindfulness does not forget.

"Eliminating worldly greed and sorrow" means that by diligently observing the internal body and thoroughly knowing it to be without a master, one eliminates the afflictions of worldly greed and desire. Thus, one observes the external body through the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*).

"Anupa" (循) means to traverse the body (also translated as "following" or "skillfully"). "Mati" (意) refers to the thorough and circumambulatory observation of the external body’s skin, flesh, sinews, and bones.
The hair, body hair, nails, teeth, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, waist, and hips are entirely devoid of a sovereign self or the characteristics of a human body;
they all arise from false attachments and karma, and possess no real dharma. Where there is karma, there is existence; where there is no karma, there is non-existence.
One should contemplate that the essence of karma is fundamentally without basis, and realize that the body has no substance, so that the recipient of sensation vanishes, leaving nothing behind.
The great wisdom is perfectly luminous and entirely devoid of self, person, or recipient. Whether in motion or stillness, this abiding wisdom has no dependence on internal or external objects.

With a mind of diligent vigor, one knows as before how to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow; that is, by eliminating the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi), the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and false views (mithyādṛṣṭi), one contemplates greed and sorrow.
One contemplates the body internally and externally, surveying the body internally and externally in its entirety, seeing it as previously described.

Previously, it was advised to contemplate [the body] separately; now, one is to contemplate it as a whole: that its interior and exterior are without a master, like empty space, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended.
This is the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Following this, one contemplates internal and external feelings (*vedanā*) in their entirety, surveying them internally and externally, [seeing that] the nature of the subject who feels and the object felt—whether internal, external, or intermediate—is without any basis. Below this...

Having observed that the internal mind and external mind, as well as the knower and the known, have no place of abiding, one proceeds below this to observe that internal phenomena and external phenomena are devoid of self or person.
This above constitutes the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Next, from the fourth section down to the passage on "arousing the mind for correct practice," there are three and a half lines of scripture; this is the portion concerning the cultivation of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Fifth, this [section].
From the bodhisattvas down to those who dedicate toward equanimity, there are three scriptural passages clarifying the cultivation of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The passage on "cultivating the concentration of desire for the abandonment of formations" clarifies diligence and observation; the preceding four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) being undistracted constitutes this "concentration of desire.

Because it is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), it is called "abandonment of formations. Through diligent observation of the aforementioned four foundations of mindfulness, one abandons the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the practice of wrong views and so forth, as well as the practice of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness:

at this stage, one intensively cultivates and refines the afflictions of the desire realm; the afflictions of the two upper realms are further intensively cultivated through the dhyāna-pāramitā of five stages.

Of these, the first two stages refine the coarse [afflictions] by means of the essence of ethical discipline (*śīla*), while these four stages refine the subtle [afflictions] by means of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This constitutes the accomplishment of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) of the various devas and others in the desire realm are the retribution of the lower grade of the ten wholesome karmic paths;

this refers to one aspect of the dharma-nature wisdom-penetration (*dharmatā-jñāna-abhijñā*), which is so preeminent that it cannot be compared to the limited penetrations of the three realms or of the two vehicles and three vehicles.
Furthermore, when compared to subsequent stages, even these present stages are inferior, for although one performs contemplative practices, they are all [based on] principle.
Wisdom is its essence; it is for the sake of accomplishing differentiated wisdom and making it even more subtle;

it is for the sake of observing the dharmas of sentient beings so as to give rise to the fulfillment of original vows and achieve great compassion; it relies on those who practice aversion as an antidote to not grasping at unwholesome worldly dharmas;

it relies on those who practice detachment because their nature is inherently free from attachment; and it relies on those who practice cessation to extinguish all unwholesome dharmas so that they do not [arise].
Because they arise, those who dedicate [merit] toward equanimity reach the state of non-reliance; this clarifies that it is not a total abandonment, but rather reaching the wisdom of the open space.

Because they practice diligence to universally save all sentient beings, the practitioner of meditative concentration, contemplation, and severance focuses the mind single-mindedly without error. What follows below is as before, in six further sections.

From "down to" [the section on] dedicating toward equanimity (*upekṣā*), there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the cultivation of the five faculties—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—divided according to their bases.
These consist of aversion, detachment, cessation, and dedication toward equanimity;

as they take these four dharmas collectively as the essence of the antidote, this may be understood from the text itself. Seventh, from "furthermore" down to "dedication toward equanimity," there are two...
The next three and a half lines of scripture explain that the cultivation of the five powers (*pañca-balāni*) has as its essence reliance on disenchantment, cessation, and equanimity;

remaining unshakable regarding the objects of focus is what is termed "power. Furthermore, from the following section down to the dedication toward equanimity, there are three and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅgāni*) likewise has as its essence reliance on disenchantment, cessation, and equanimity. This explains [the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment].

Discerning and rectifying what is right and wrong is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Encouraging others toward self-benefit while remaining ever free from weariness is the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The manifestation of the joy of the Dharma, seeing those who come seeking [it] with delight and without satiety, is the awakening factor of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
"Relaxation" (*praśrabdhi*) means reliance and gladness; because the wisdom and insight that abide without dependence are constantly manifest, there is the radiance of the joy of the Dharma.

Because one is at ease in the world and is not wounded by sorrow or resentment, it is called the awakening factor of *praśrabdhi* (tranquility). By observing internally and externally, the mind eventually follows wisdom rather than revolving according to objects;

this is called the awakening factor of *samādhi* (concentration). When the view of self and body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is extinguished and the objects of self and other are eliminated, such that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena have no basis whatsoever, it is called the awakening factor of *upekṣā* (equanimity). When the views regarding mind and objects are extinguished and arise [in liberation], [this is the awakening factor of mindfulness].
Because wisdom arises alone without confusion, it is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The sections below are as previously explained.
Furthermore, from here down to the dedication toward equanimity (*upekṣā*), there are three scriptural passages clarifying the factors of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

These take disenchantment (*nirveda*), cessation (*nirodha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) as their essence. [The text] takes the eight wrong paths (*mithyāmārga*) as its basis, and by taking the eight wrong paths as the eight noble paths, the ten [perfections] are [attained].

After the Bodhisattva has cultivated such meritorious qualities as described above, down to skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), there are five lines and a half of sūtra that clarify the intent of performing the aforementioned contemplative practices for the sake of the ten dharmas. These take "not abandoning any sentient beings" as the primary principle, as clearly explained in the full text.
Furthermore, taking "the ten powers (*daśabala*) regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)" as the primary principle, they have already been clarified previously.
The "Fearless Ones" refers to the four fearlessnesses: first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows;
third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path to the exhaustion of suffering.
Such fourfold qualities are those whose faults cannot be challenged by humans, devas, or non-Buddhists. The "Unshared Buddha-dharmas" refers to the eighteen unshared dharmas.
1. His body is without error, because his bodily conduct is virtuous; 2. His speech is without error, because his vocal karma is virtuous; 3.
His mindfulness is without error, because he is free from distracted thoughts; 4. His mind is without differentiation, because he regards enemies and kin with equanimity; 5.

His mind is never unsettled, because it is the non-conceptual wisdom that is non-different from the *dharmadhātu*; 6. There is nothing he does not know, because there is nothing that is not clearly illuminated.
9. Because of thorough understanding, the seven types of desire do not diminish; he gives rise to births that are favorable and accord with the mental activities and desires of sentient beings.
10. Because of diligence, there is no loss; although his own path is fulfilled, he establishes the Dharma and benefits sentient beings without rest. 11.

Regarding "no decrease in mindfulness," it means he skillfully knows the faculties of all sentient beings, as well as the proper and improper times [for their guidance]. 12. Regarding "no retreat from concentration," it is because of the fundamental... [text ends]
Eleventh, because he is immovable, his wisdom does not diminish, for he skillfully discerns that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing;
twelfth, his knowledge and vision of liberation do not diminish, for his universal radiance of wisdom reaches everywhere without failure;
thirteenth, his physical actions follow the movement of wisdom, such that among the four modes of deportment, there is nothing that does not bring benefit to all sentient beings. 14.
Fifteenth, his verbal karma follows the movement of wisdom because he is free from frivolous talk;
sixteenth, his mental karma follows the movement of wisdom because he is forever free from perverse thoughts; seventeenth, his wisdom knows the unobstructed matters of the past;
eighteenth, his wisdom knows the unobstructed matters of the present; nineteenth, his wisdom knows...
Regarding these eighteen kinds of unhindered matters in future worlds, they belong exclusively to the Buddha and do not extend to lower fruits.

As for the marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*), there are ninety-seven major marks and [ninety-eight] secondary characteristics, as explained in the "Chapter on the Radiance of the Merit of Secondary Characteristics.
To provide but a single example: among the secondary characteristics of the hand, one named "Perfect King" (*Pūrṇarāja*) emits a light called "Name."
It has seven million *asaṃkhyeya* flames of blazing light as its retinue; yet, even taking up just one of its secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), it is inexhaustible.

Furthermore, there are major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) equal in number to the atoms within ten oceans of *kusumita-garbha* world-systems, each bodily mark adorned with various exquisite jewel-marks. This clarifies that the primary marks and the secondary marks are both inexhaustible.
Because the dharmadhātu of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) is equal in measure to space, its sounds are fully complete.
To speak of this in general terms, there are sixty kinds of Brahma-sounds (*brahma-svara*). If one distinguishes them according to their particulars, the Sūtra says:

"A vast and subtle sound pervades all lands, abiding for immeasurable eons in the pursuit of the most supreme and excellent path. This is precisely the dharma of the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva-phala*).
Because other dharmas do not transcend the gateway; because those who follow the profound liberation of the Buddha as it was heard conform to the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience;
and because those who contemplate great wisdom and skillful means are adept at following the inclinations of all sentient beings' faculties to lead them across suffering.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), they treat with remedies all instances of attachment, arising and ceasing, and conceptual observation toward the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)—which is primary—toward the notions of a person, a sentient being, a life-span, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields;
toward the notion of "mine," toward possessions, and toward objects of attachment. Thus, the Bodhisattva becomes detached from all such things. If this Bodhisattva perceives karma...

They completely abandon all afflictions censured by the Tathāgata and stained by them; yet, if they see an action as being in accord with the bodhisattva path and praised by the Tathāgata, they practice it entirely.

[Treatise] The fourth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," comprises one paragraph of five lines and a half of scripture that clarifies the division for counteracting the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Within this exegesis, it is divided into two parts: first, from "O Son of the Buddha, having dwelled in this Ground of Blazing Wisdom" down to "all are abandoned," there are three lines of scripture that clarify how this ground uses the objects of observation of the four applications of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) as the counteragent for the body.
With "view" as the primary factor, one universally contemplates the self, persons, sentient beings,
and so forth, as well as body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*), because one is thus able to become detached from all points of attachment. Second,

from "this bodhisattva" down to "all practice," there are two lines of scripture that clarify how this bodhisattva clearly perceives karma as that which is censured and praised by the Tathāgata, and [perceives] all sentient beings.
The path of karmic activity constantly flows through birth and death; this is what the Tathāgata has censured, and it should be remedied through contemplation.

If one uses contemplation to govern oneself such that no further karma arises, one should employ the skillful means of wisdom to engage in the activities of sentient beings in accordance with the cycle of birth and death, thereby delivering them.
This accords with the Bodhisattva path and is entirely praised by the Tathāgata.
Because they are able to practice.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, as this bodhisattva gives rise to skillful means and wisdom, they cultivate the path and the factors conducive to enlightenment;
in this way, they attain a moistened mind, a supple mind, a compliant mind, a beneficial mind, and a blissful mind, free from affliction.
A mind free from defilement; a mind seeking the most supreme and excellent dharmas; a mind seeking sublime wisdom; a mind that rescues all the world;
a mind of reverence for those of noble virtue that never transgresses their instructions; a mind that practices well whatever Dharma has been heard;
this bodhisattva’s mind that knows kindness and repays kindness; a mind that is extremely harmonious and gentle, dwelling in peace and happiness, upright, and supple.
Moving through the dense forest [of saṃsāra] without the conceit of self, well-receiving instruction, and grasping the intention of the teacher—
this bodhisattva thus achieves patience, thus achieves pliancy, and thus achieves tranquility.
When practicing the mental application that purifies the karma of the subsequent stage, having thus achieved patience, pliancy, and tranquility, they attain unceasing diligence.
Unadulterated diligence, non-retrogressive diligence, vast diligence, boundless diligence, blazing diligence, unequaled diligence, indestructible diligence,
diligence that brings all sentient beings to maturity, and diligence that skillfully discriminates between the path and what is not the path—
this is the bodhisattva’s purity of the mental realm, the non-forgetting of the profound resolve through awakening.
Their understanding becomes clear and sharp, their wholesome roots increase, they are freed from worldly defilements, and they sever all doubts;
endowed with clear discernment and suffused with joy, they are personally protected by the Buddhas, and their immeasurable aspirations and delights are all fully accomplished.

[Treatise] Fifth: This section of fifteen lines of scripture, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva, according to the skillful means he has aroused," clarifies the stage of attaining great benefit through the skillful means of prior contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna-upāya*).
Within the explanation of the "Section on Gentleness" (*mṛdu-bhāga*), the meaning is divided into four parts:
first, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva, according to the skillful means he has aroused" down to "he practices well with a mind."
There are four and a half lines of sūtra clarifying that in this stage, through practicing the path and its auxiliaries as described above, ten kinds of benefits for the mind are obtained.

This section on the mind is divided into two parts: first, from "Furthermore, this bodhisattva... down to "...obtains the intention of the teacher of the Dharma," which comprises approximately two lines of sūtra;
second, "Furthermore, he obtains ten kinds of minds," which concerns obtaining the intention of the teacher of the Dharma and being free from the dense forest of conduct.

3. Because it is clear and free from the obscuration of delusion and stagnation; this Bodhisattva—from here down to the passage on "diligence regarding what is the path and what is not the path"—is elucidated by five lines and a half of scripture.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage attains the ten patiences (*kṣānti*) and achieves the ten types of diligence (*vīrya*).
These ten types of diligence serve to make the current stage firm and stable, and they also bring about the subsequent [stages].

Because the stages (bhūmi) bring about correspondence, there are four [points]. From "the bodhisattva’s mental realm is purified" (*cittadhātu-viśuddhi*) downwards, up to "all are fully accomplished," there are three scriptural passages that clarify this stage:
the section clarifying that the bodhisattva’s mental realm is purified and receives the Buddha’s protective mindfulness;

and the section above that clarifies that by practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one attains profound, subtle, clear, sharp, and decisive realization and understanding regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
Because it is complete.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas;
that is to say, they see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas.
He reverently honored, respected, served, and made offerings to nayutas of buddhas, presenting them with all necessities of life—
robes, bedding, food, medicine, and everything required for sustenance— and likewise made offerings to the entire Sangha;
he dedicated all these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and paid homage at the feet of those buddhas.
Having heard the Dharma, they receive and uphold it, fully practicing it; furthermore, within those teachings of the Buddhas, they leave the household life to cultivate the Way.

They further refine their profound resolve and faith-understanding for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, causing all their roots of goodness to become increasingly bright and pure.
Son of the Buddha, it is like a goldsmith who refines true gold to fashion ornaments.
Just as all other gold cannot equal it, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in this stage:
all roots of goodness belonging to the lower stages cannot equal the roots of goodness belonging to this stage.
Like the pure circle of light of a maṇi jewel that emits radiance, which no other jewels can equal, it is entirely unaffected by conditions such as wind or rain.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is capable of destroying [obstacles] is likewise thus: dwelling on this level, he is beyond the reach of Bodhisattvas on lower levels;
all Māras and afflictions (*kleśa*) are utterly unable to destroy him. Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he predominantly practices "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*);
among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), he predominantly practices "diligence" (*vīrya*). He does not fail to cultivate the others, but does so according to his strength and capacity.
O Son of the Buddha, this is a brief explanation of the fourth stage, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he frequently becomes the King of the Suyāma Heaven. By means of skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*), he is able to eliminate the delusions of sentient beings, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), and establish them in right view.
All his activities—whether through giving (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), or cooperation (*samānārthatā*)—are likewise performed in this manner.

They are all never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and never apart from mindfulness of the Sangha, up to and including never being apart from mindfulness of the possession of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge. Furthermore, they form this thought:
"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, and even the sole one."

That which is the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge is the bodhisattva; if they exert diligent effort, in a single moment they attain entry into hundreds of millions of samādhis, behold hundreds of millions of buddhas, and come to know the spiritual powers of hundreds of millions of buddhas.
They are able to shake hundreds of millions of worlds and even manifest hundreds of millions of bodies, with each body having hundreds of millions of bodhisattvas as its retinue.
Furthermore, if one were to manifest through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows, it would exceed these numbers of hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas,
even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, such that they could not be calculated or known. At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva,
wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] Regarding the sixth stage, the Bodhisattva Son of the Buddha, having already dwelt in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the following thirty lines of scripture clarify the section on the expansion of the vision of the Buddhas. Within this passage, the meaning is divided into eight parts.
First, from "The Bodhisattva Son of the Buddha, having already dwelt in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom" down to "all the assemblies of monks," there are four and a half lines of scripture.
The section on "Clarifying through the Power of Vows" and "Seeing Many Buddhas and Making Offerings" is divided into two parts.

From the passage beginning with "By these roots of virtue" down to "becoming even more clear and pure," there are four lines of scripture that clarify seeing the Buddhas, serving them, and dwelling for many eons.

Within this, the section on "the further increase of clarity through deep-seated faith and understanding" is divided into three parts. From the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if a goldsmith... down to "...are completely unable [to do so]."
The *Ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā-sūtra* clarifies this through the analogy of a goldsmith refining pure gold to create ornaments that become increasingly bright and pure;

this is divided into four parts. From "This bodhisattva... down to the fourth stage, the *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*, there are two and a half lines of sūtra explaining the practices performed within this stage;
this is divided into five parts. From "The bodhisattva dwelling in this stage... down to [the end of the section], it is complete.
The *Sarvākāra* (All-aspect) [Sūtra] and the *Sarvajñajñāna* (Omniscient Wisdom) [Sūtra] can each be understood through four modes of practice.

These clarify the stage of the Bodhisattva’s reception of office (*abhiṣeka*). "In all aspects" clarifies the perfection of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) that constitutes the seed of omniscience.
"Omniscient wisdom" clarifies entering into both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*), which are both to be sought. Such is the basis for these [six].

Having again formed this thought, from "down to the basis of the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvajñajñāna*), there are two lines of sūtra that clarify that at this stage one is capable of being a teacher and leader for all sentient beings. From "this bodhisattva" down to "as his retinue," there are three lines of sūtra;
this describes entering samādhi through the power of one's own karmic retribution and beholding the Buddhas.

The "Manifestation of Power" (Vikurvaṇa) section is divided into eight parts. Regarding the passage beginning with "If by the power of vows," the following two lines of scripture clarify the division concerning how, through the power of vows, one perceives a vast number of Buddhas beyond the capacity for calculation.

[Sūtra] Having already purified the third stage, the Bodhisattva next contemplates the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, the realm of space, the realm of consciousness, and the three realms.
With a mind that understands and fully comprehends them, they are able to enter;
having ascended to the stage of Flaming Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), their power increases, and being born into the family of the Tathāgata, they never again regress.
With unshakable faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one contemplates that all phenomena are impermanent and without arising;
one contemplates the formation and destruction of worlds, karma, and the existence of birth;
one contemplates the limits of past and future regarding saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, and the buddha-fields, as well as their exhaustion. Practicing in this way, one is born into the family of the Buddhas.

Having attained this Dharma, his compassion increases; he further diligently cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness—the internal and external observation of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.
He dispels all worldly greed and sorrow, and the Bodhisattva practices the four right efforts, whereby unwholesome dharmas are eliminated and wholesome ones increase.
Having thoroughly cultivated the bases of supernormal power, the faculties, and the powers, and likewise the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path;
practicing those deeds for the sake of delivering sentient beings, protected by his original vows and headed by compassion;
seeking all-knowledge and a Buddha-land, he also contemplates the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
The four fearlessnesses and the unique qualities, the extraordinary marks and signs, the profound and beautiful voice,
as well as the place of liberation through the pursuit of the wondrous path;
and the great skillful means for practicing those [teachings] regarding the sixty-two views headed by the view of a self-body, including the immeasurable varieties of "I" and "mine."

All attachments to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth—all these afflictive activities censured by the Tathāgata within these four stages—are completely abandoned; for they are devoid of benefit.
The wise practice pure deeds, performing every action for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva practices with diligence and without indolence, Thereby attaining the ten mental states in their full perfection.
Seeking exclusively the Buddha-way without weariness, They aspire to receive their office to deliver sentient beings;
Reverently honoring the virtuous and practicing the Dharma, They recognize kindness, are easy to instruct, and are free from resentment or violence.
Having abandoned pride and left behind deceit, their minds become pliant and gentle; progressing with even greater diligence, they do not regress.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Blazing Wisdom Ground (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), their minds are pure and never lose the realization of awakening;
their certainty and goodness increase, and the stains of the net of doubt are entirely removed.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage are supreme among men; They make offerings to immeasurable *nayuta* Buddhas, hear the True Dharma, and likewise go forth into homelessness.
Irrepressible like refined gold, these Bodhisattvas dwelling here possess all virtues; Through wisdom and skillful means, they practice the Path.
Their minds do not regress before the various māras; like wondrous jewels that cannot be destroyed, they dwell here as many kings of the Yāma Heaven.
Sovereign over the Dharma and honored by the multitudes, they universally transform all living beings and eliminate evil views, single-mindedly seeking Buddha-wisdom and cultivating wholesome deeds.
The Bodhisattva exerts the power of diligent vigor, Attaining hundreds of millions of samādhis and the like;
Yet what is accomplished through the power of the wisdom of vows Exceeds these numbers beyond anyone’s ability to know.
Such is the fourth stage of the Bodhisattva, The pure and subtle path of practice.
[Verse]: Endowed with the meaning of merit and wisdom, I have already proclaimed this for the sake of the Buddha’s sons.

[Treatise]: Regarding the seventh bodhisattva who has already purified the third stage, there are thirty-four verses below that clarify the restatement (udāna) of the preceding section on the analysis of dharmas.
Within the explanation of the meaning, this is divided into two parts: first, the initial two verses praise [the stage].
The Bodhisattva, having already purified the dharmas of the third stage, is then able to enter the section on the fourth stage. This is divided into two parts:

first, from "Having ascended to the Stage of Flames and increased one's power" down to "I am a son of the Buddha," there are thirty-two verses that clarify the reiteration of the aforementioned dharmas;
second, regarding "the sixty-two views, with the view of a self as the foremost," this clarifies...

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises simultaneously with the sixty-two views; for this reason, one cultivates the contemplation of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vēdanā-citta-dharma*) to remedy it.
When one attains the state where there is no body, sensation, mind, or phenomena, all views are collectively absent, and there is only that which is seen by wisdom.

This is called awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and being born into the family of the Buddha; thus [is the nature of] the sixty-two views.
Regarding these, for each of the five aggregates there are three time periods; across these three time periods, one reckons four propositions:
first, "gone"; second, "not gone"; third, "both gone and not gone"; and fourth, "neither gone nor not gone.
Regarding the five aggregates of the future, one likewise reckons four propositions: first, "finite"; second, "infinite"; [and so forth].
Third, both finite and infinite; fourth, neither finite nor infinite. Regarding each of the present five aggregates (*skandha*), four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are respectively conceived:
first, eternal; second, impermanent; third, both eternal and impermanent; and fourth, neither eternal nor impermanent.
Upon these five aggregates, there are the three periods of time (*trikāla*); upon each of these three periods, there are likewise four [propositions].
Seeing one lifetime as having twenty-three lifetimes, each with twenty views, they total sixty;

these are collectively based on the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, making sixty-two views in total. Furthermore, for each of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there are four views.
Thus, one lifetime has twenty-three lifetimes, totaling sixty [views], which are the two views of annihilationism and eternalism combined.

62. If one regards all views through the gateway of the four foundations of mindfulness as collectively constituting the Buddha’s work, it is because the self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), being devoid of intrinsic nature, is in its entirety the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of this stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*), there are five gateways as previously explained; here, we shall first explain the name of this stage.

Why is this stage named the "Difficult to Conquer" (Durjayā) Bhūmi? It is so called because, through the perfection of dhyāna (dhyāna-pāramitā), one initiates roots of goodness and penetrates the worldly dharmas of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; since the lower stages cannot surpass it, it is named the Difficult to Conquer.
Second, as for what practice-gate is cultivated on this stage: this stage takes the perfection of dhyāna as its essence, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
Regarding the symbolic representation of Sudhana’s visit to the night goddess Śāntamukharatisagaravatī, who sits upon a lotus throne adorned with mani-banners:

when it says, "Not far from here," it means not departing from the essence of bodhi. It further states that Sudhana attained the bodhisattva liberation door called "The Great Adornment of Joy Arising in Every Thought-moment. This signifies that he does not depart from the substance of awakening.
Because he possesses the practice of the dhyāna-pāramitā, he is called "Ocean of the Sound of Tranquility," which clarifies that the essence of dhyāna is tranquility.
Furthermore, the "ocean of sound" signifies that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is capable of giving rise to the function of wisdom (*prajñā*).

As for his sitting upon a lotus throne adorned with mani-banners, the *maṇi* signifies the jewel of freedom from defilement, clarifying that meditative concentration is free from defilement; the "banner" (*dhvaja*) signifies...

The essential nature of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is fixed and does not move in accordance with objects; it clarifies that both the objective realm and the mind are inherently fixed in their own essence because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
As for "ornamentation," it refers to adorning the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*) through the meditative application of non-activity (*anabhisamskāra*).

As for "lotus," it symbolizes that practice is unstained, clarifying that the nature of practice is not different from non-active meditation, as both are without intrinsic nature. Thus, one attains Bodhi.
The liberation door of "the constant production of the adornment of great joy in every thought-moment" signifies the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Because the essence of dhyāna is identical to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "great. Constantly abiding within birth and death while constantly practicing the myriad practices is called "joy" (*prīti*);

because one finds no sorrow in the rapture of meditative concentration, it is termed "joy. Adorning wisdom with meditative stability is called "adornment" (*vyūha*); not being deluded regarding stillness and agitation is called... [non-delusion].

The explanation that this is called the "Difficult-to-Conquer" (*sudurjayā*) bhūmi is to clarify that because its essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) thoroughly understands that worldly phenomena lack the nature of either fixedness or distraction, it excels over both fixedness and distraction; thus, it is named the Difficult-to-Conquer.

Furthermore, because it has transcended the afflictions of the three realms yet does not realize nirvāṇa, neither the three realms nor nirvāṇa can destroy its wisdom of non-abiding. Therefore, [it is so named].
The night goddess named Durjayā signifies the state of wisdom and compassion that dwells without dependence amidst the long night of saṃsāra, thereby shattering the delusions of all sentient beings.
Thus, the name of this night goddess and the seat upon which she sits express the essential meaning of the Dharma:
the meditation on the indestructible, non-dependent, unconditioned, and natureless self-essence.
To manifest the myriad practices by arising from quiescence, Sudhana asked: "What is the activity of this gate of liberation?
What is its sphere of operation? By what means does it arise? And what does it observe? The Night Goddess replied:
"I have initiated a mind of pure and equanimous aspiration; I have initiated a mind free from all worldly dust and defilement."
I generate a mind of pure, firm, and indestructible aspiration, a mind that does not regress from the stage of non-retrogression,
and a mind that never turns back. Having thus generated such immeasurable states of mind as described in the sūtras,

for those whose minds predominantly dwell in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one should cause them to cultivate the meditative absorptions (*śamatha-samādhi*) until they reach the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because those who frequently practice the dhyānas of the form realm are led to enter the dhyāna of the Dharma-nature, which gives rise to objective conditions within the progressively higher stages;
because its wisdom and skillful means extensively deliver sentient beings with a vast function as infinite as space;
and because it does not cause one to cling to stillness or dwell in the bliss of meditative absorption—this Night Goddess, Sound-Ocean of Tranquility, sits upon a throne adorned with mani-banners.
The night goddess Padmāvatī is surrounded by a retinue of one million asaṃkhyeya deities;
this symbolizes that the essence of the Dharma-nature is non-active yet its pervasive substance is inexhaustible, and likewise the substance of practice is all-pervasive.
Thus, "one million" represents the greatest of large numbers, and "asaṃkhyeya" means incalculable. This clarifies the name through the perfection of quiescent function.
One may understand the meaning of this stage by reflecting upon the seat, the assembly dwelling together with one, the proximity or distance of the dwelling place, and the titles of the dharma-gates.

Fourth, regarding what kind of liberation from the three realms is attained at this stage: if considered according to their general characteristics, the three realms are identical in their liberation;

however, if considered according to their specific characteristics, this stage— [...is as follows: If one considers the three realms through their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), they are all equally liberated. If one considers them through their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), this stage—
Taking the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as its essence, it attains the liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the form and formless realms.
It is the fourth stage for the intensive subduing of the subtle afflictions of the desire realm; this stage is the intensive subduing of the subtle afflictions of the form and formless realms.
Since the liberations of the higher realms naturally entail liberation from the lower realms, this Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle constantly employs fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
To advance in practice, one takes non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) as the essence of dhyāna;

because this dhyāna transcends the meditative states of cessation and perception within the two higher realms, one attains the dhyāna of effortless spontaneity (*anabhisaṃskāra-dhyāna*) that accords with conditions through mastery over the Dharma-realm of principle and wisdom.

This clarifies that the progressively refined essence of wisdom in advancement does not depart from fundamental wisdom; this clarifies that the first four stages are further cultivated through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

The practice of the Desire Realm in the preceding stage is now intensified in this stage to employ the essence and function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to counteract the subtle afflictions of the higher realms.
Fifth, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text, there are two aspects as previously mentioned.
First, concerning the long division of the sūtra’s intent: this fifth stage is divided into fourteen sections.
[Sūtra] When the Bodhisattvas heard of this practice of the sublime ground, they attained realization of the Dharma and their hearts rejoiced.
Flowers rained from the sky as they praised him, saying: "Excellent! Great Being Vajragarbha!
Sovereign Lord of Devas and his celestial hosts, having heard the Dharma, leap for joy and abide in the void."
Universally emitting clouds of various wondrous lights, they made offerings to the Tathāgata, filling all with joy.
The celestial maidens played heavenly music and also praised the Buddha with words;
all this was through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattvas, and from within those sounds, these words were uttered:
The Buddha’s vows were made long ago; now they are fulfilled. The Way of the Buddha was sought long ago; now it is attained.
Śākyamuni Buddha has come to the celestial palace; one who benefits devas and humans is seen only after a long time.
The great ocean was still for a long duration; now it begins to stir. The Buddha’s light shone forth after a long duration.
Sentient beings have found peace and happiness only after a long time; The sound of Great Compassion is heard only after a long while.
You have reached the further shore of all merits; Arrogance and darkness have both been extinguished.
Utterly pure like space, You are unstained by worldly dharmas, just like a lotus flower.
The Great Muni has appeared in the world, like Mount Sumeru rising from the vast ocean;
Worshiping him can exhaust all suffering, and through worship one will surely attain the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This object of offering is peerless; therefore, with a joyful heart, worship the Buddha.
When these immeasurable goddesses had thus uttered these words of praise,
they all remained gazing up at the Tathāgata with reverence and hearts full of joy, dwelling in silence.
Then the Great Being Vimukticandra again requested the fearless Vajragarbha:
The characteristics of all practices in the fifth stage— I pray that the Son of the Buddha will proclaim them for us.
[Treatise] From the first line, "Having heard from the Bodhisattva these practices of this supreme stage," there follow nineteen verses of verse-text clarifying how the great assembly,
upon hearing the exposition of the Dharma-gate of the fourth stage, offered praise and joy, presented offerings, and requested further instruction.
Regarding the second section, the explanation of the meaning according to the text: within this verse, it is further divided into two parts.

First, from "After the Bodhisattvas had heard of these supreme stages of practice" down to "gazing up at the Tathāgata and remaining silent," seventeen verses clarify the section on the great assembly’s joy upon hearing the Dharma, their making of offerings, and their praise. Second, at that time...
The final two lines of the verse clarify how Vimukticandra requested the Dharma-gate of the fifth stage for the great assembly;
the meaning of the text within these verses is self-evident as one reads along.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has fully perfected the path practiced in the fourth stage and wishes to enter the fifth, the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*), they should enter it by means of ten kinds of pure equanimous minds. What are these ten? Namely, regarding the Buddhas of the past..."
The mind of equality and purity regarding the Dharma of the future; the mind of equality and purity regarding the Dharma of the present;

the mind of equality and purity regarding ethical discipline; the mind of equality and purity regarding the mind itself; the mind of equality and purity regarding the removal of views, doubt, and regret;
the mind of equality and purity regarding the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path; and the equality of the wisdom of cultivation and vision.
With a pure mind that observes all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as increasingly superior,
with a pure mind that teaches and transforms all sentient beings, and with a pure mind of equanimity—
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters the fifth bodhisattva stage by means of these ten kinds of pure minds of equanimity.

[Śāstra] Second: From the passage beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" down to "attaining entry into the fifth bodhisattva stage," there are ten lines of sūtra that clarify the section on entering the ground of the fifth stage by means of ten kinds of impartiality (*samatā-citta*). The commentary explains the meaning as follows:

"Just as the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path clarifies this stage, so too does the cultivation of the spontaneous [practice] resolve doubts regarding the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Thus, eight [points] are explained.

The local [stages] end with the tenth stage, while the initial mastery begins at the third stage. In these three stages, one remedies the coarse afflictions of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the two upper realms.

In these five stages, one further remedies the subtle afflictions of the meditative absorptions of the two upper realms; by means of this, one can eliminate the doubts regarding the correctness or incorrectness of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
In the sixth stage, one clearly attains mastery over supramundane and mundane wisdom, as in the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*).
The sixth bhūmi within this [set of ten] is exemplified by the bhikṣu Samudrareṇu;
because one attains mastery over supramundane and mundane wisdom at this sixth stage, it is represented by a bhikṣu.
Within this sixth bhūmi, it is further represented by the night goddess Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥprabhā to clarify the supramundane aspect.
In the city of the mind of worldly wisdom, there is no entry for the bandits of perverse thoughts;
all perverse notions are collectively transformed into the city of wisdom. This explains why the fifth stage is given the name "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjaya*):

because the application of meditative concentration, which is supramundane, effortless, and fundamentally quiescent, has been brought to completion. Thus, in the sixth stage, the "Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*), both mundane and supramundane phenomena...
Because the wisdom that fully understands has already reached its consummation, and because these ten stages accomplish compassion through wisdom,
they are represented by the night goddesses. Therefore, in this fifth stage, one eliminates doubts regarding the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and in the sixth stage,
one eliminates doubts regarding mundane and supramundane wisdom.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this fifth stage, because they have well cultivated the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),

because their profound mind is well purified, because they further seek the superior and victorious path, because they accord with suchness (*tathatā*), because they are sustained by the power of their vows,
and because they do not abandon compassion for all sentient beings, they accumulate the merit and wisdom that assist the path.

Therefore, because they practice with diligent effort without ceasing, because they give rise to skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), because they observe and illuminate the ever-higher stages (*bhūmi*),
because they receive the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, and because they are sustained by the power of mindfulness and wisdom, they attain a mind that does not regress.

[Treatise] From "The third son of the Buddha" onwards, up to "attaining the mind of non-retrogression," five lines and a half of sūtra clarify that one abides in the fifth stage by means of twelve kinds of dharmas; this may be understood according to the text.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows as they truly are: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering," "This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering," "This is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering," and "This is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

He skillfully knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), he skillfully knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he skillfully knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), he skillfully knows the truth of distinctions (*viśeṣa-satya*), and he skillfully knows the truth of establishment (*siddhi-satya*).

He thoroughly knows the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*), thoroughly knows the truth of birth (*utpāda-satya*), thoroughly knows the truth of the cessation and non-arising of suffering (*kṣaya-anutpāda-satya*), thoroughly knows the truth of the wisdom that enters the path (*mārga-praveśa-jñāna-satya*),

and thoroughly knows the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattva-bhūmi-krama-siddhi-satya*) up to the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom (*tathāgata-jñāna-siddhi-satya*).
Because this bodhisattva causes sentient beings to rejoice according to their mental inclinations, he knows conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and penetrates the single [truth].

One knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by means of the true nature (*dharmatā*); one knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*) by awakening to the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena;

one knows the truth of differentiation (*viśeṣa-satya*) by comprehending the distinctions among the various states (*avasthā*) of all phenomena; one knows the truth of establishment (*vyavasthāna-satya*) by skillfully discerning the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*);

one knows the truth of things (*vastu-satya*) by awakening to the suffering and affliction of body and mind; and one knows the truth of birth (*janman-satya*) by awakening to the continuity of rebirth in the various realms of existence (*gati*).
Because all feverish afflictions are ultimately extinguished, one knows the Truth of the Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*).
Because it gives rise to non-duality, one knows the Truth of the Knowledge of Entering the Path (*mārga-praveśa-jñāna-satya*).

Because it correctly awakens to all modes of activity (*sarva-caryākāra*), one knows the Truth of the successive accomplishment of all Bodhisattva stages up to the accomplishment of Tathāgata-knowledge, through the power of the knowledge of resolute faith (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*) and not otherwise.

[Treatise] From the fourth son of the Buddha down to "known by the power of ultimate wisdom," there are fourteen lines and a half of scripture that clarify the section on the skillful knowledge of the dharma-gate of the ten truths (*daśatattva*).
Within the commentary on this meaning, it is further divided into two parts: first, the son of the Buddha...

From "Having already attained" down to "the Bodhisattva well knows the ten kinds of dharma-gates of truth," there are six lines of verse that clarify this stage of the Bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the ten kinds of truth-dharma gates. This is divided into two parts:

from "this Bodhisattva, according to the mental inclinations of sentient beings" onwards, there are eight and a half lines of prose that explain the reasons for knowing the truths; this concludes the self-exegesis of the sutra. As it says:
In the first section, "skillfully knowing this Noble Truth of Suffering" differs from the three vehicles’ approach of wearying of suffering and aspiring toward purity before seeking the Noble Truths.
Rather, it means that because one realizes the very essence of all worldly sufferings is non-existent, suffering itself lacks the nature of extinction and the path lacks the nature of arising.
One should know that the essence of suffering is precisely non-arising and non-extinguishing, and is thus identical with the Noble Path.

Because there are two natures, it is said: "Having rightly known the Noble Truth of Suffering," and so forth. The four Noble Truths are collectively treated in this manner; the meanings of the subsequent truths are fully contained within the sūtra itself. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, once this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained such wisdom regarding the various truths, he knows them as they truly are. First, he knows that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Second, he knows that all conditioned phenomena are suffering. Third, he knows that all phenomena are empty and selfless. Fourth, he knows that Nirvāṇa is quiescent and extinguished. Fifth, he knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions. Sixth, he knows that all phenomena are devoid of a creator. Seventh, he knows that all phenomena are subject to change and transformation. Eighth, he knows that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, shadows, echoes, reflections, and magical displays. Ninth, he knows that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. Tenth, he knows that all phenomena are ultimately ungraspable. Having known these ten aspects, he further knows that all phenomena are neither born nor perish, neither come nor go, neither increase nor decrease, neither exist nor do not exist, and are beyond all conceptualization and verbal expression. This is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the truths. By means of this knowledge, he does not fall into the stage of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly attains the stage of a Bodhisattva. This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom of the truths. Because he possesses this wisdom, he is able to skillfully teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to enter the path of the Bodhisattvas. All conditioned phenomena are empty, false, deceptive, and delusive toward the foolish; at that time, the Bodhisattva increases his great compassion for all sentient beings and gives rise to the radiance of great loving-kindness.

[Treatise] From the fifth son of the Buddha down to the passage on "giving rise to the light of great compassion," two and a half lines of scripture clarify that the knowledge of the truths gives rise to a portion of great loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings. The commentary explains the meaning as follows:

Having clearly understood the knowledge of the truths, one knows conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as they truly are—illusory, false, and deceptive—and thus increases great compassion for the deluded and foolish.
The "light" is as it appears in the text; "truth" (*satya*) means reality or suchness. To know and see things as they truly are, without falsehood, is what is termed "truth.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having attained such power of wisdom, does not abandon any sentient being.
Constantly seeking the Buddha’s wisdom, one contemplates all conditioned phenomena as they truly are:

knowing that from the past limit, due to ignorance and craving, there arises the cycle of birth and death; that within the house of the aggregates, one cannot move toward liberation; that this increases the mass of suffering;
and that it is devoid of a self, a life-principle, a nourisher, or any entity that takes up a further body in future states of existence. It is free from these.
The self and what belongs to the self are likewise non-existent in the past and future; they are all utterly empty, false, and clung to through craving.
When these are completely severed and one attains liberation, one knows both existence and non-existence as they truly are.

[Treatise] From the sixth son of the Buddha down to the passage "all know according to reality," there are six lines and a half of scripture that clarify how one contemplates sentient beings through wisdom.

This explains the meaning by distinguishing between delusion regarding the truth and following after falsehood. It clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage contemplates all truths as being devoid of the characteristics of truth;
with wisdom that perceives no root, growth, beginning, or end, and no self or person, yet does not abandon anything.
Sentient beings skillfully understand that all sentient beings arise from the twelve links of dependent origination and dwell within the house of the five aggregates;
furthermore, they know that the essence of these conditions is devoid of a self or anything belonging to a self.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further reflect: "These ordinary worldlings, deluded and lacking wisdom, are truly to be pitied.

They have had countless bodies that have perished, are now perishing, and will continue to perish; yet, though they are thus utterly destroyed, they fail to conceive a sense of revulsion toward the body.
Instead, their suffering mechanisms increase ever further as they follow the current of birth and death."

They are unable to return from the house of the aggregates and seek no liberation; they do not know to fear or dread, yet they cannot extract the poisonous snakes of the four great elements, nor can they pull out the arrows of pride and views, nor extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor destroy the darkness of ignorance, nor dry up the great ocean of craving and desire;
they do not seek to enter [the path] under the Great Holy Teacher who possesses the Ten Powers.
The dense forest of the Māra’s intent causes one to be adrift and submerged by the waves of discursive thought within the ocean of birth and death.

[Treatise] From the seventh son of the Buddha down to "adrift by the waves," there are eight lines of scripture that clarify how Bodhisattvas contemplate sentient beings who, out of folly, drift along with suffering; this section is fully contained within the sutra itself.

It is simply that the speaker of the Dharma, with a mind of great compassion, praises them according to the text, knowing well the bonds of suffering and knowing well that the nature of those bonds is itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further reflects: 'These sentient beings undergo such [suffering]...'"
Suffering, solitary, impoverished, and oppressed, without rescue, without refuge, without an island, without shelter, without a guide, without eyes,
and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance— now, for the sake of all such sentient beings, I practice the dharmas of merit and wisdom that aid the path,
alone and single-mindedly, seeking no companion. By these merits, may all sentient beings attain ultimate purity.
Purifying [the mind] up until attaining the Tathāgata’s ten powers and unimpeded wisdom.

[Treatise]: From the eighth son of the Buddha down to "unimpeded wisdom," five lines and a half of scripture clarify how one arouses the resolve by single-mindedly exerting oneself for all sentient beings in their ultimate suffering, seeking no companion, and universally [applying] one's own merit.
[He] causes all sentient beings to attain the portion of the Tathāgata’s ten powers of wisdom, as detailed in the text itself.

[Sūtra]: O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with such wisdom, observes that all the roots of goodness he cultivates are for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, benefiting all sentient beings, and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
To have compassion for all sentient beings; to bring all sentient beings to maturity; to liberate all sentient beings; to embrace all sentient beings;
to cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction; to cause all sentient beings to universally attain purity;
to cause all sentient beings to be fully tamed; and to cause all sentient beings to enter parinirvāṇa.
[Treatise] The section beginning with "The ninth son of the Buddha" and extending for six lines of scripture clarifies how the Bodhisattva, through wisdom,
observes roots of goodness to rescue and protect all sentient beings, causing them to enter nirvana rather than seeking their own personal happiness;
this may be understood according to the text.

[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), they are called "those who possess mindfulness" because they do not forget any dharmas;

they are called "wise ones" because they are able to skillfully discern and understand them; they are called "those who follow the path" because they know the underlying intent of the sūtras and how their sequences are joined together;
they are called "those possessed of shame and remorse" because they protect themselves and protect others; and they are called "firm."

One who is steadfast is so called because they do not abandon their precepts; one who is awakened is so called because they are able to discern what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*);

one who follows wisdom is so called because they do not follow others; one who follows insight is so called because they skillfully know the distinctions between words that signify meaning and those that do not;
one who possesses supernormal powers is so called because they have skillfully cultivated meditative concentration; and one who possesses skillful means is so called because they are able...
Because he acts in accordance with the world, he is called "one who is never satiated"; because he skillfully accumulates merit and virtue, he is called "one who does not rest";
because he constantly seeks wisdom, he is called "one who is untiring"; because he gathers great compassion, he is called "one who diligently practices for the sake of others";
because he desires to lead all sentient beings into nirvana, he is called "one who seeks diligently without slackening."
One who seeks the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities is called "one who has resolved to practice";

one who accomplishes the adornment of Buddha-fields is called "one who diligently cultivates various wholesome deeds"; one who is able to fulfill the primary and secondary marks is called "one who constantly and diligently practices";
and one who seeks to adorn the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind is called "one of great reverence."
One who reveres the Dharma acts according to the teachings in the presence of all bodhisattva Dharma-teachers; therefore, they are called "those whose minds are without obstruction.
Because they constantly act within the world through great skillful means, they are called "those who day and night remain far removed from other [worldly] thoughts.
Because they always delight in teaching and transforming all sentient beings.

[Treatise] The section beginning with "The tenth son of the Buddha" consists of seventeen lines of scripture that clarify how a Bodhisattva dwelling in the fifth stage is able to skillfully know the analytical meaning of the various categories of phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*).

It explains that this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*) is fully endowed with and achieves the mundane and supramundane dharmas of self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as the adornment of the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind.
