Part 26.8 [Sūtra] When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice diligently in this manner, they transform and guide sentient beings through the giving of material gifts.

They teach and transform sentient beings through loving speech; they teach and transform sentient beings through beneficial conduct; they teach and transform sentient beings through collaborative action;

they teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting physical forms; they teach and transform sentient beings by expounding all dharmas; they teach and transform sentient beings by revealing the bodhisattva practices;

they teach and transform sentient beings by displaying the great majestic power of the Tathāgata; they teach and transform sentient beings by demonstrating the faults and afflictions of birth and death; and they teach and transform sentient beings by praising the Tathāgata.
They come to benefit sentient beings through wisdom and teach them by manifesting great supernormal powers;

they teach sentient beings through various skillful means and practices. O Son of the Buddha, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to thus diligently employ skillful means to teach sentient beings, their minds constantly continuous as they advance toward the wisdom of the Buddha, such that the roots of goodness they perform are inexhaustible.
[They] constantly and diligently cultivate and study the sublime dharmas of practice.

[Treatise]: From the section beginning with "The eleventh son of the Buddha" onwards, there are eight and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattvas of this stage, through generosity, kind speech, and shared conduct, are well able to teach and transform sentient beings, as well as seeking the supreme Dharma for themselves.

In the detailed explanation of the meaning, it is further divided into two sections. First, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards to "by means of various skillful means, he teaches and transforms sentient beings," there are six lines and a half of scripture that clarify the teaching and transformation of sentient beings through ten kinds of skillful means, such as giving and the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
These are distributed as follows: first, giving; second, the four methods of attraction; and subsequently, there are eight [categories] which together constitute [the remainder].

The ten aspects are self-evident in the text. From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, up to "constantly and diligently practicing the sublime methods of cultivation," there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the section on the perpetual continuity of teaching and transforming sentient beings; these are self-evident in the text.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not fail to study any of the worldly arts and crafts.
That is to say, they thoroughly master writing, arithmetic, calligraphy, seals and insignia, as well as various treatises on earth, water, fire, and wind.
Furthermore, they are skilled in medicinal prescriptions and the treatment of all illnesses, including epilepsy, insanity, emaciation, possession by malevolent spirits, and the effects of sorcery.
He was able to completely eliminate all poisons; he was highly skilled in the arts of writing, calligraphy, praise, chanting, song, dance, music, performance, laughter, and conversation.

Regarding the layout of kingdoms, cities, villages, towns, palaces, residences, gardens, groves, springs, streams, ponds, pools, grasses, trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs—whatever was arranged therein—all were placed with perfect appropriateness.
He possessed gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, pearls, *vaidūrya*, *musāragalva*, conch shells, jade, and coral.

He thoroughly knows the locations of all treasures and brings them forth to show them to others; he skillfully observes the sun, moon, and stars, the cries of birds, earthquakes, auspicious and inauspicious dreams at night, and the signs of fortune and misfortune on the body, without a single error.
He maintains the precepts, enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and possesses immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Whether it be the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) or any other worldly matters, he engages in them provided they do no harm to sentient beings.
For the sake of benefiting them, [the Buddhas] fully reveal and teach [these arts], gradually causing them to dwell securely in the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.

[Treatise]: From the twelfth section, "The Son of the Buddha," onwards, there is a passage of eleven and a half lines of scripture that clarifies how the Bodhisattvas of this stage skillfully understand the various worldly arts and crafts for the sake of sentient beings. Regarding the term "seals and insignia" (*mudrā*) mentioned in the text:

The *Mingxuan* (Clarifying the Profound) has not yet appeared; furthermore, regarding the binding of hand-seals (*mudrā*) as described in mantras and so forth, it follows the precedent of using jade for seals (*xi*) and copper, iron, or wood for official seals (*yin*). This clarifies the talismans and seals used by masters such as Nāgārjuna.

It speaks of earth, water, fire, and wind as the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*), yin and yang, awakening, wind, birds, emotions, and so forth—various other details are fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*),
by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas— namely, many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
and even up to many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas— to all of whom they pay homage, revere, serve, and make offerings of robes, food and drink, and bedding.
All medicinal decoctions and every necessity of life are offered as gifts, and they are also used to make offerings to the entire Saṅgha.
With these roots of goodness, one dedicates them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

one listens to the Dharma with reverence in the presence of the Buddhas, and having heard it, one receives and maintains it, practicing according to one's ability. Furthermore, within the teachings of those Buddhas, one goes forth into homelessness.
Having already left the household life, they further hear the Dharma and attain *dhāraṇī*, becoming Dharma-preachers who retain what they have heard.

Abiding in this stage for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* kalpas, all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
Son of the Buddha, it is like genuine gold that becomes increasingly polished and refined when ground and polished with *śukti* (mother-of-pearl).

Furthermore, the roots of goodness possessed by the Bodhisattvas on this ground become even more bright and pure; likewise, through the wisdom of skillful means, their contemplation and observation become increasingly bright and pure.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells on this Difficult-to-Conquer Ground (*Sudurjayā*), they accomplish merits through the wisdom of skillful means that cannot be matched by the roots of goodness of the lower grounds. O Son of the Buddha, it is like the sun, the moon, and the constellations of stars.
Just as the palace is sustained by the power of the wind of radiance and cannot be destroyed, nor can it be shaken by any other wind,
so too are all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas on this stage; they are observed through the wisdom of skillful means and cannot be destroyed,
nor can they be shaken by any of the roots of goodness of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or worldly beings.
Among the ten pāramitās of a bodhisattva, the dhyāna-pāramitā is predominant, though it is not that the others are not cultivated; rather, they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called a brief explanation of the fifth bodhisattva stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjaya).
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he mostly becomes a king of the Tuṣita heaven, exercising mastery over all sentient beings and subduing them.

All the wrong views of the various non-Buddhists that might cause sentient beings to dwell [in error], he instead establishes them within the True Dharma through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

All such actions performed are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha, and even extend to being never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all modes of omniscience. Furthermore, he acts in this way:
Thinking, "I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed,
and even the support for the knowledge of all-knowledge among all sentient beings," if this bodhisattva exerts diligent effort,
in a single moment of thought they attain ten billion samādhis, see ten billion buddhas, and know the spiritual powers of ten billion buddhas.
By his power, he is able to shake a thousand billion Buddha-worlds and even manifest a thousand billion bodies,
with each body manifesting a thousand billion bodhisattvas as its retinue; yet if one were to manifest through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows,
it would exceed these numbers, such that even in hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] From the thirteenth "Son of the Buddha" onwards, there is a section of thirty-two and a half lines of scripture that clarifies the extent of the Buddhas seen by the bodhisattvas of this stage, as well as their respective offices. Within this, there are eleven general points.
1. It clarifies that, by the power of his vows, he perceives a vast multitude of Buddhas; 2. It clarifies his making offerings; 3.
It clarifies his reverently listening to the Dharma and practicing according to his capacity; 4. It clarifies his leaving the household life, hearing the Dharma, and attaining dhāraṇī; 5.

It clarifies his dwelling in this stage while accumulating and cultivating a multitude of virtues; 6. It clarifies that, like genuine gold polished with mother-of-pearl, he becomes increasingly radiant.
1. Purity: The wholesome states of the lower stages cannot attain this. 2. The seventh illumination: Receiving the office [of consecration] as the King of Tuṣita Heaven. 3. The eighth illumination:
Entering into a thousand billion samādhis and manifesting a thousand billion deeds before a thousand billion Buddhas.
4. The ninth illumination: By the power of his vows, their number exceeds even that. 5. The tenth illumination: Vajragarbha speaks verses in praise of the Dharma, as in the text itself.
[End of Section].

[Sūtra]: Having purified the fourth stage of the bodhisattva, contemplating the equality of the Buddhas of the three periods, with a mind of precepts that eliminates doubt regarding the path and what is not the path—one observes in this way and enters the fifth stage.
The foundations of mindfulness are the bow, the faculties are the sharp arrows;
The right efforts are the horses, the divine bases are the chariot, and the five powers are the sturdy armor for destroying the enemy. Brave and unretreating, one enters the fifth stage;
shame and dread are the garments, the factors of enlightenment are the garland, Pure precepts are the incense, and meditative concentration is the unguent.
Adorned with the sublime ornaments of wisdom and skillful means, entering the forest of dhāraṇīs and the garden of samādhi;
with the wish-fulfilling gem as feet and right mindfulness as a neck, with compassion as eyes and wisdom as fangs,
he is a lion among men who roars the "selfless" roar, destroying the enemies of affliction and entering the fifth stage.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in this fifth stage further cultivates the supreme, pure path;

with resolve for the Buddha-dharma, they do not regress. Contemplating compassion without weariness, they accumulate the sublime merit of wisdom and virtue, diligently applying skillful means to observe the higher stages.
Empowered by the Buddha’s power, endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, they understand the Four Truths exactly as they are:

They thoroughly know the conventional truth and the ultimate truth; The truth of characteristics, the truth of differentiation, the truth of establishment, the truth of phenomena, And the truths of origination, cessation, and the path, Up to the Tathāgata’s unimpeded truth.
Although such contemplation of the truths is subtle and refined, one has not yet attained unimpeded, supreme liberation;
nevertheless, because it can generate great merit, it thus transcends worldly wisdom.
Having contemplated the truths, one now knows that conditioned phenomena are illusory in nature, lacking any solidity or reality.
Having attained the portion of the Buddha’s light of compassion, he seeks the Buddha-wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings.
He contemplates the prior and subsequent limits of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
within this mass of suffering where one wanders and turns back through the darkness of ignorance and the fetters of craving, there is no self, no person, and no life-span.
With craving and grasping as causes, one undergoes future suffering; though one seeks its limit, it cannot be found.
Drifting in delusion, there is no time for return. These beings are pitiable;
I should deliver them from the house of the aggregates, the realm of serpents, and the arrows of various views. The fire of the mind blazes fiercely, and the darkness of ignorance is heavy.
Distractedly drifting on the river of craving, one has no leisure for contemplation; Sinking and bobbing in the ocean of suffering, one lacks a clear guide.
Knowing this, one exerts diligent effort; All that is done is for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Such a person is called one possessed of mindfulness and wisdom, And even one who possesses awakening, understanding, and skillful means.
They practice merit and wisdom without weariness, honoring the learned without ever growing weary;
their lands and physical marks are all adorned, and all such things are for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to transform all the worlds;
they skillfully know the arts of writing, calculation, seals, and other such methods.
Furthermore, they are skilled in understanding all medicinal prescriptions, treating all manner of illnesses until every one is healed.
Their literary compositions, songs, and dances are all exquisite; their palaces, residences, gardens, and ponds are entirely peaceful and secure.
They reveal various treasures to people for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
The sun, moon, and stars, as well as earthquakes, and even the physical marks [of a Buddha], he observes;
the four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the supernormal powers—he manifests them all for the benefit of the world.
The wise one dwelling on this Difficult-to-Conquer stage makes offerings to nayutas of Buddhas and listens to their Dharma.
Just as fine jewels polish true gold, so all roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure;
like stars in the void, sustained by the power of the wind, they remain unharmed and unmoved;
and like a lotus that is not defiled by water, so does this Great Being conduct himself in the world.
Dwelling here, he mostly acts as the King of Tuṣita; He can crush the various false views of heterodox paths.
All the virtues he cultivates become the wisdom of a Buddha; May he attain the Ten Powers to save sentient beings.
He further practices great diligence, Immediately making offerings to billions of Buddhas.
The shaking of buddha-fields attained through meditative concentration is likewise so; what is accomplished through the power of vows exceeds even this.

Thus concludes the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), the most supreme and true path among men, which I have fully proclaimed for the sake of all sons of the Buddhas through various skillful means.
[Treatise] Section Fourteen: "The Fourth Bodhisattva Ground, Having Been Purified," and the subsequent passage consists of forty-four stanzas that repeat the preceding *dharmavibhāga*.

As the text itself fully contains [the details], the meaning is clear: the Difficult-to-Conquer Ground (*sudurjayā bhūmiḥ*) takes the essence of dhyāna as its antidote for the obstacles of tranquility and distraction within the three realms; it accords with the root of bodhi—the principle of non-conditioned dhyāna.

Transcending the triple world yet not remaining within it, free from the obstacles of craving for purity or aversion to defilement, one constantly dwells in tranquil meditation in accordance with principle;
through the mastery of concentration, one observes with discernment, possessing the wondrous skill of a master artisan for the sake of the world.
Regarding the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), it will now be explained by means of five gates as previously set forth.
As for the designation of this stage’s name: why is it called the "Stage of Presence"? It is because all mundane and supramundane wisdoms manifest before one;
because one skillfully contemplates the twelvefold dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); and because one attains thirteen samādhis.
Second, it clarifies what practices are cultivated on this stage: the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā* constitutes the essence, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions.

Third, it clarifies the symbolic meaning of Sudhana: in this stage, Sudhana beholds the night goddess named Sarvanagararakṣāsaṃbhavatejaḥpratiprabhā, who is seated within the assembly of the Tathāgata at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). All [the deities] are present there.
The Scripture on the Lion Throne of the Jewel-Radiant Mani King, Surrounded by Innumerable Night Goddesses,
Who Manifest Bodies with the Colors and Forms of All Sentient Beings and Bodies Universally Facing All Sentient Beings,
Attaining the Profound Sovereignty of the Wondrous Sound Liberation, Protecting All Cities, and Increasing Power and Majesty.
"O noble son, among all sentient beings who are asleep in the darkness of ignorance during the night of saṃsāra, I alone have awakened.
I cause all sentient beings to guard the city of the mind, to abandon the city of the triple world, and to dwell in the supreme Dharma-city of omniscience.
Know that this sixth stage is the dharma-gate thus cultivated, and that this Night-Governing Deity is [the one who reveals it]."
Fearing that practitioners might not understand the practices performed on these six stages, both the Dharma and the practice are manifested here.
Those dwelling in the Bodhimaṇḍa within the assembly of the Buddha clarify that practice has bodhi as its essence;
those seated upon the lion throne of all precious maṇi-kings clarify that it encompasses all distinctions.
Because wisdom constitutes the essence of the seat, the reliance on the fruit is likewise so; the *maṇi* jewel symbolizes wisdom that is free from the defilements of both self and others;
the "King" clarifies that wisdom possesses sovereignty; and "Lion" is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound, as one must observe and understand both cause and effect.
That she is surrounded by countless night goddesses symbolizes the pervasiveness of her practice; she manifests as one...
Regarding the "manifestation of physical forms corresponding to the physical forms of all sentient beings" and the "attainment of the liberation of profound, sovereign, and wondrous sound":
these clarify that at this stage, one possesses mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*) and is skilled in preaching the teachings;

thus, one should contemplate them through their names and meanings to perceive the general intent. At this stage, even when preaching the teachings, there is still concern that sentient beings may not understand.
Because of these practices, the Noble One cites both the teaching and the practice together to manifest them clearly for easy understanding; thus, one’s cultivation is free from error.

Regarding the sixth stage of the Ten Abidings, it clarifies the mundane wisdom within the supramundane, using the *bhikṣu* (monk) as its representative, because at this stage of the Ten Abidings, the mind seeking the supramundane predominates. This constitutes the tenth ground.
The middle section clarifies the cultivation of compassion, which pertains to the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*) and the subsequent stages; this is symbolized by female deities.

Following this precedent, one should understand its significance through the progressive advancement through the respective stages. Fourth, regarding what liberation from the realms is attained at this stage:
it encompasses the liberation from the three realms and the three vehicles as well as the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), specifically the mundane transcendence within the three realms.
Because one possesses mastery over the wisdom that liberates through worldly insight— clearly discerning the defilement and purity within the three realms,
as well as the defilement and purity regarding transcendence from the three realms— one enters into luminous purity and accords with the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When one accords with the patience of non-arising in accordance with principle, this is precisely the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), wherein one is well-versed in supramundane wisdom.

Entering worldly wisdom, one is able to follow the conduct of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings; not differing from the world, yet not destroying the seventh stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

One begins the practice at the eighth stage, completes the task at the ninth stage, and only at the tenth stage can one preach the Dharma with mastery, where compassion and wisdom are first perfected and mastery is attained.
If one were to grasp at a limited, partial non-arising, that would merely be the ten stages of abiding (*daśavihāra*).

When the mind is first awakened, it is already possessed of these [six aspects] in every single moment. Even if one discusses their beginning and end as being unchanging, although they are identical to those of ordinary beings, through immeasurable eons of accumulated cultivation, not even a hair’s breadth has shifted. One must contemplate this through the principle of the six aspects—totality and particularity.

If one merely pursues progressive advancement, one will deviate from its fundamental essence; therefore, there is no deficiency in original wisdom, for it fully comprehends all accumulated cultivation.
Ascending and descending without transition; principle and phenomena without deficiency; sameness and difference both equalized; wisdom and folly entirely distinct;
cause and effect non-dual—these five points explain the meaning according to the text. Regarding the two meanings, they are as previously stated.
First, concerning the long division of the sūtra’s intent: within this section on the sixth stage, the meaning is divided into nine subsections.
[Sūtra] Having heard these supreme practices, the Bodhisattvas’ hearts were filled with joy;
they rained down exquisite flowers, emitted pure light, and scattered precious jewels as offerings to the Tathāgata, praising his excellent teaching.
Hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts all rejoiced, together scattering various treasures from mid-air.
With flower garlands, necklaces, banners, and streamers, And precious canopies and fragrant ointments, they all made offerings to the Buddha.
The Sovereign Heavenly King and his retinue, their hearts filled with joy, Dwelt in mid-air, scattering jewels that formed clouds as offerings;
They praised, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, please proclaim this swiftly!"
Immeasurable celestial maidens dwelling in the air, together with musical sounds, sang praises of the Buddha;
within those voices, they all spoke these words: “The Buddha’s speech can eliminate the disease of afflictions;
the nature of phenomena is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of marks. It is just like empty space, beyond all discrimination.”
Transcending all attachments and severing the path of words— Truly real, equal, and eternally pure;
If one can penetrate the nature of all phenomena, The mind remains unmoved regarding existence or non-existence.
Diligently practicing to rescue the world— Such a person is a true son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth.
Bestowing gifts without grasping at any signs; Fundamentally severing all evils while firmly upholding the precepts;
Understanding that phenomena are non-harming, always possessing patience; Knowing the nature of phenomena to be detached, fully endowed with diligence;
Having exhausted all afflictions, entering into the various dhyānas; Skillfully penetrating the emptiness of nature and discerning all phenomena.
Endowed with the power of wisdom, you are able to provide universal relief; having extinguished all evils, you are praised as a Great Being (Mahāsattva).
After such millions of kinds of wondrous sounds have offered praise, they fall silent and gaze up at the Buddha.
Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha: "By what characteristics of practice does one enter the subsequent stage?"
[Commentary] The first section consists of eighteen verses, which may be divided into two parts:
first, seventeen verses clarifying the section on the great assembly’s joyful offerings and praises upon hearing the dharma-gate of the fifth stage;
second, the final single line clarifying the section where Vimukticandra further requests the subsequent stages. The scriptural text itself contains these details.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has fully perfected the fifth stage and wishes to enter the sixth, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they should contemplate ten dharmas of equality.
What are these ten? They are: because all dharmas are signless (*animitta*), they are equal; because they are without essence (*anātman*), they are equal..."
They are equal because they are non-arising; equal because they are non-ceasing; equal because they are primordially pure;
equal because they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); equal because they are without grasping or rejecting; equal because they are quiescent;

equal because they are like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, an echo, the moon reflected in water, an image in a mirror, a mirage, and a transformation; and equal with respect to existence and non-existence.
Because they are non-dual, they are equal; thus the bodhisattva contemplates the self-nature of all phenomena as pure, conforming to it without contradiction.

He enters the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), attaining the sharp and keen patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*), yet he has not yet attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

[Treatise] The second section, beginning with "At that time," consists of nine lines of scripture that clarify the stage of the "approach" (*pratipannaka*) for the final six stages by means of contemplating the ten equalities.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, having contemplated in this manner, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again takes great compassion as the foremost...

With compassion as the predominant factor, he contemplates the arising and ceasing of the world until great compassion is fulfilled. He reflects: "The birth of beings in the world arises entirely from attachment to a self;
if one is free from this attachment, there is no place for birth. Furthermore, he reflects: "Ordinary people lack wisdom and cling to a self;
constantly seeking existence or non-existence, they engage in improper reflection, give rise to deluded conduct, and walk upon wrong paths, thereby committing transgressions."
By performing meritorious deeds, deeds of the imperturbable, and by accumulating and increasing these various deeds, one plants the seed of the mind within them.

With outflows (*sāsrava*) and grasping (*upādāna*), there arises again future birth, aging, and death. That is to say, karma is the field, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the seed, it is covered by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), moistened by the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), irrigated by the sprinkling of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and increased by the net of views (*dṛṣṭi-jāla*). Thus, the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is produced. Name-and-form...

The growth [of craving] gives rise to the five faculties; from the mutual encounter of the faculties, contact arises; from the encounter of contact, feeling arises; following feeling, there arises the craving that seeks rebirth;

the increase of craving gives rise to grasping; the increase of grasping gives rise to becoming; once becoming has arisen, the arising of the five aggregates as a body within the various realms of existence is called birth;
once born, the deterioration and transformation is old age, and the final passing away is death; at the time of old age and death, various [sufferings] arise.
Because of the cause of burning affliction and because of burning affliction itself, sorrow, lamentation, and all manner of suffering gather together.
By reason of these conditions, there is gathering, yet there is no one who gathers; they cease spontaneously, and yet there is no one who ceases them.

In this way, the Bodhisattva contemplates the characteristics of dependent origination in accordance with reality. Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Non-comprehension is called ignorance (*avidyā*). The karma produced by this ignorance is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). The initial moment of mind upon which these formations depend is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Consciousness arises simultaneously with the four aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), which constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form constitutes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The conjunction of the three factors—the sense organ, the object, and consciousness—is contact (*sparśa*). Born together with contact is feeling (*vedanā*). Attachment to feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The intensification of craving is...
Grasping is the arising of outflow-tainted karma; from that karma arises the aggregates, which constitute birth; the maturation of the aggregates is aging; their disintegration is death;

at the time of death, the separation accompanied by delusion and attachment, with the chest constricted by distress, is sorrow; the weeping, wailing, and lamentation are grief; the affliction present in the five sense faculties is suffering (*duḥkha*);
that present in the mental faculty is anguish (*daurmanasya*); and the further increase of such anguish and suffering is despair (*upāyāsa*). Thus it is said.
This is merely the growth of the tree of suffering, devoid of self and what belongs to self, devoid of an agent and a recipient.
Furthermore, he reflects: "If there is an agent, then there is an action; if there is no agent, then there is no action.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), neither can be found. Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further reflects upon the three realms:
There is only this single mind, the Tathāgata, which, when analyzed here, explains that the twelve links of existence are all established based upon this one mind.
Why is this? Because craving arises together with the mind according to its objects; the mind is consciousness, while the objects are formations (*saṃskāra*).
Delusion regarding these formations is ignorance (*avidyā*). That which arises together with ignorance and the mind is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The increase of form is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases, when combined with their three divisions, constitute contact (*sparśa*). That which arises simultaneously with contact is sensation (*vedanā*). The lack of satiety regarding sensation is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The grasping and non-relinquishing of craving is clinging (*upādāna*). The arising of those various factors of existence is becoming (*bhava*). That which is produced from becoming is birth (*jāti*).
The maturing of birth is aging (*jarā*). The decay of aging is death (*maraṇa*). O Son of the Buddha, herein ignorance (*avidyā*) has two kinds of functions.
First, it causes sentient beings to become deluded regarding their objects of perception; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*).
Formations also have two kinds of functions: first, they can produce future retribution; second, they act as the cause for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Consciousness also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the continuity of existence (*bhava*); second, it acts as the cause for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form also has two kinds [of functions].
Karma has two functions: first, it mutually assists and completes [the process]; second, it acts as the generative cause for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The six sense bases also have two functions: first, each individually perceives its own respective object; second, they act as the generative cause for contact (*sparśa*).

Contact also has two functions: first, it is able to touch the object of cognition; second, it acts as the generative cause for feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling also has two functions: first, it is able to... [The text continues].

The appropriation (*upādāna*) of objects such as the beloved and the hated has two functions: first, it gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*); second, it acts as the cause for the arising of grasping (*upādāna*).
Craving also has two functions: first, it is attachment to desirable objects; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of grasping. Grasping also has two functions:

first, it causes the continuity of the various afflictions (*kleśa*); second, it acts as the cause for the arising of existence (*bhava*). Existence also has two functions: first, it is able to... [the text continues].
It causes birth within other realms of existence; furthermore, birth has two kinds of functions: first, it can give rise to the aggregates (*skandha*);
second, it acts as the cause for the arising of aging. Aging also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the faculties (*indriya*) to undergo transformation;
second, it acts as the cause for the arising of death. Death also has two kinds of functions: first, it can destroy the [aggregates]...

Because one does not perceive the two [factors] as they proceed, the continuity is not severed. O Son of the Buddha, herein, from "ignorance conditions volitional formations" up to "birth conditions aging and death," it is because ignorance through birth act as conditions that cause volitional formations through aging and death to be uninterrupted and to be assisted in their formation.
Therefore, when ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; and so on, up to when birth ceases, aging and death cease. This is because...

Because ignorance up to birth do not act as conditions for the cessation of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) up to old age and death—since they do not assist in their continuation—the Son of the Buddha, herein, when ignorance, craving, and grasping are not severed, this is the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*);
when the formative forces and existence (*bhava*) are not severed, this is the path of karma (*karma-mārga*);

and when the remaining factors are not severed, this is the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*). By discerning the cessation of these three paths through the analysis of the prior and subsequent limits, the three paths are thus severed.

The three paths are devoid of self and what belongs to self; they possess only arising and ceasing, like a bundle of reeds. Furthermore, "ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to observing the past;
"consciousness through feeling" refers to observing the present; "craving through existence" refers to observing the future. Thereafter, they proceed in continuous succession.
"The cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of volitional formations" refers to the observation of their sequential abandonment.

Next, the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are termed the three types of suffering (*triduḥkha*). Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth up to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) constitute the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and the remainder constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

When ignorance ceases, formations cease; this is the cessation of the three types of suffering. Furthermore, regarding "conditioned by ignorance, formations arise": through the causal condition of ignorance, various formations are produced; when ignorance ceases, formations cease.
Because there is no ignorance, there are also no volitional formations; the rest is likewise. Furthermore, that "ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to the bondage of birth;
that "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" refers to the cessation of bondage; the rest is likewise.

Furthermore, that "ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to conforming to the contemplation of non-existence; that "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" refers to conforming to exhaustion.
The contemplation of cessation and the others are likewise. O Son of the Buddha, these ten kinds of contemplations on dependent origination in both direct and reverse order consist of:
the continuity of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*); being subsumed within a single mind; the differentiation of one's own karma; mutual inseparability;
the uninterruptedness of the three paths; the contemplation of the past, present, and future; and the three types of suffering.
"Because of aggregation, because of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, because of being bound by arising and ceasing, and because of the contemplation of non-existence and exhaustion.

[Treatise] Third, from "this Bodhisattva" onwards until "because of the contemplation of non-existence and exhaustion," there are ten sections of scripture clarifying the division on the contemplation of the dependent origination of the twelve links in both reverse and forward order. Regarding the second part, the word-by-word commentary:
Regarding the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both direct and reverse order, there are ten sections of scripture as listed below:
first, within the initial section of the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha,
when this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has thus contemplated" and continuing with "Great Compassion as the foremost," the following fourteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the contemplation.

Regarding the arising and ceasing of the world, one should form this thought: "The birth of beings in the world all results from attachment to a self; if one is free from this attachment, there will be no place for birth.
Furthermore, it clarifies that because of the existence of a self, one constantly seeks existence and non-existence, and all various evil karmas and false paths arise from this.
As for "false paths," these refer to the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths. As for "evil conduct," it refers to...
The three evil destinies; as for those who practice meritorious deeds, these refer to the scattered wholesome merits from among humans up to the sixth heaven;

as for those who practice immovable deeds, these refer to the eight dhyānas of the form and formless realms. Furthermore, although those in the Small Vehicle who have attained the first three fruits and are subject to birth-and-death with distinct segments, and even those at the fourth fruit and the bodhisattvas in the Pure Land who are subject to birth-and-death through transformation, are exempt from coarse suffering, they still possess a portion [of it].
Both分段生死 (segmented birth and death) and 變易生死 (transformative birth and death) are called the false path, and are also called the accumulation and growth of immovable formations (*aniñjya-saṃskāra*).
The three evil realms are the accumulation and growth of evil karma; the desire realm is the accumulation and growth of conditioned wholesome karma;
the two upper realms are the accumulation and growth of the eight contaminated dhyānas; and the pure [states] of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise.

Earth-level Bodhisattvas accumulate and increase pure karma to form bodies of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bhava*); One-Vehicle Bodhisattvas accumulate and increase [karma] endowed with the Buddha’s compassion and wisdom.
Although both generally involve the twelve links of dependent origination, there are distinctions according to the vehicle and the conditions.
Specifically, for ordinary beings bound by all fetters within the triple world, the twelve links of dependent origination give rise to various evil karmas.

The followers of the Two Vehicles contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, thereby subduing active afflictions and attaining the pure land of conditioned outflows.
Bodhisattvas give birth in the pure land by practicing the four truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the gates of the six perfections.
One-Vehicle Bodhisattvas cultivate the ten *pāramitās* and the four means of integration through the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
The immeasurable thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the practice for assisting the path to awakening, which accomplishes all-encompassing omniscience;

vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, infinite and perfectly complete— the Buddha’s gateways to the Dharma of great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great wisdom, the fruit of Buddhahood—
thus constitute the Great Perfectly Luminous Universal [Wisdom], the unconditioned self-nature of dependent origination throughout the Dharma-realm.
The Wisdom of Radiance constantly takes the ocean of birth and death of all sentient beings as a single site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);

it constantly takes the dwelling places of sentient beings within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions and abides within a single pore. As for the nature of phenomena born of conditions, it is inherently non-existent from the beginning;
yet sentient beings recklessly conceptualize it, leading the sages to sigh in lamentation that they wander through birth and death in vain, lacking self-awakening and knowledge.

The Sage sighed with weariness at the great compassion [of those who protect], and therefore, O virtuous ones, you should accord with principle and contemplate well, abandoning all karma of arrogance;
thus you shall attain the cessation of the seeds of consciousness and the blossoming of the fruit of wisdom.

When the retribution of the three realms has perished, equal compassion descends upon the mundane world, acting in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings so as not to sink into the flow of death. Manifesting a form-body to benefit others according to their faculties, the Sūtra says:
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one plants the seeds of the mind; "planting" means sowing. Within the field of karma, one sows the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This constitutes "existence with grasping" (*sopādāna*) and "outflows" (*āsrava*). There are seven such outflows: first, views; second, the sense faculties;

third, forgetfulness; fourth, evil; fifth, intimacy; sixth, craving; and seventh, mindfulness. Furthermore, there arises future existence, birth in a future life, and [the suffering of] birth, old age, sickness, and death.
As stated below in the text itself: "Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance. "Enveloped" means that it covers and obscures one's own suchness-original wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*).
Because this wisdom lacks intrinsic nature and follows along with objective conditions, it becomes deluded. Consequently, suffering reaches its extreme.

When self-awakening removes this delusion, through the wisdom of awakening to non-self, ignorance itself ceases to exist. Thus, the delusion regarding the self becomes false, and the awakening to the self is established.
The nature of awakening through wisdom and that of delusion are fundamentally non-dual; both wisdom and delusion lack intrinsic nature and exist entirely in dependence upon conditions.
Because delusion and awakening thus arise from conditions, and because the fundamental wisdom is devoid of self-nature, it does not cognize itself as being either wisdom or non-wisdom;
rather, it arises in accordance with objects, and as one pursues objects, emotional attachments arise, giving rise to the view of a self.

When one has not yet reached the ultimate limit of suffering and, weary of suffering, seeks the Truth, yet does not believe or follow when a Sage transforms them because they have not themselves become weary of the source of suffering, there are two kinds of such arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*): first, the arousal of the mind out of weariness with the suffering of saṃsāra for a long time;
those who attain the fruit of either the Three Vehicles or the One Vehicle are called those who possess the "Noble Wisdom of Self-Awakening" (*svayambhū-āryajñāna*) and are also called Buddhas.

Wisdom is self-arising wisdom and teacherless wisdom; these two depend on a prior enlightened one who exhorts one to know the root of suffering before one can generate the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Regarding this generation of the resolve, there are these two types: if one says that the resolve must necessarily depend on a previous Buddha to be generated, then there is the fault of permanence, which is identical to the eternalist view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, as for the "prior enlightened one," whom would they take as their teacher? Who, in turn, would have been their teacher? Thus, it would lead to an infinite regress.

If one transmits and receives [the teaching] from one another without departing from the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), then if there were a primordial, eternal Buddha who served as the successive teacher, that ancient Buddha’s own essence would be inherently true and not subject to delusion.

In that case, it would be impossible to follow his ancient traces as the "true" [path], because true self-nature is eternally true and cannot follow along with birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, birth and death themselves are the eternal; birth and death are the Buddha.
Since the Buddha is eternally present, if sentient beings were fixedly subject to birth and death, then birth and death would themselves be eternal;
thus, they could not attain true realization. This is the view of annihilationism. Both of these [extremes] are incorrect, for they do not transcend the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
For all sentient beings, birth and death have no inherent nature; fundamentally there is no birth and death, yet they falsely conceptualize birth and death.
Fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death; because all Buddhas have no inherent nature from the beginning, in reality there is neither enlightenment (*bodhi*) nor nirvana.
Yet sentient beings delusively claim that the Buddhas possess enlightenment and nirvana.

If there are sentient beings who can know it thus, they are said to have "aroused the mind," they are called "Buddhas," and they are said to have "seen the Way," thereby being able to open [the path].
To realize that all sentient beings are those who have penetrated ignorance—wherein ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and even the Buddhas do not exist—is what is called "awakening.

It is simply by means of a wondrous wisdom that is without dependence, without dwelling, without substance, and without nature, which can respond to conditions like an echo and manifest form-bodies, that one is able to teach and transform sentient beings through this principle; this is called "great compassion," and therefore it is not [limited].

To have attainment and realization, to have joy and aversion, to have grasping and relinquishing, to have the ancient and the modern, and to have the true and the false—such is the way one generates the bodhicitta.
One generates the bodhicitta so as not to be shrouded by the ignorance of the long night.
Thus the Sūtra says: "The water of craving provides moisture," for birth arises because of craving; "the pride of self conceives and irrigates."
There are eight kinds of pride: first, pride; second, great pride; third, conceit-pride; fourth, the pride of "I am";
fifth, overweening pride; sixth, the pride of inferiority; seventh, false pride; and eighth, haughty pride.

As for the proliferation of the net of views, it refers to the five views and the sixty-two views, etc., which give rise to the sprout of name-and-form through the craving that arises from those various views.
The arising of form together with name is called "the growth of name-and-form," which gives rise to the five sense-faculties.

Because of name-and-form, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body encounter name-and-form to produce contact (*sparśa*); from contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises. The essence of the body-contact consists of eleven types:
roughness, smoothness, lightness, heaviness, cold, hunger, thirst, hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion. Eye-contact regarding forms consists of twenty-five types, beginning with blue...

Yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, high, low, regular, irregular, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, coarse, and fine—these are merely visible colors manifested in space.
Regarding sounds heard by the ear, there are eleven kinds:

those that are agreeable to the touch, those that are disagreeable to the touch, those that are neither, those caused by primary elements (*mahābhūta*), those not caused by primary elements, and those caused by both primary elements.

That which is commonly established by the world, that which is produced by what has been induced, that which is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and that which is included within authoritative speech (*āptavāda*) or not included within authoritative speech—this is it.
There are six kinds of odors: fragrant, foul, pleasant, unpleasant, neutral, and those arising from combination or transformation.
There are twelve kinds of tastes: bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, bland, agreeable, disagreeable, and so forth. They arise together with contact.

The mutual incompatibility and compatibility, the simultaneous arising and transformation, and that which is obtained upon the five sense-faculties and subsequently conceptualized by the mind—these are termed the sixty-five kinds of mental objects (*dharmas*).
When the mind gives rise to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in accordance with what appears within the five sense-faculties, it is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

Following contact, the sense-faculty of mind grasps [the object], which is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). To experience this feeling without letting it go is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). As craving increases, birth arises.
Grasping increases becoming; once becoming has arisen, it brings forth the six sense faculties.
Upon these, the sixty-five kinds of mental consciousness take various realms as their objects, forming the five aggregates of a body. Once born, its decay and transformation is called aging;
its final passing away is death. At the time of death, there arise various fevers and afflictions, extending even to sorrow, lamentation, and manifold sufferings.
All [phenomena] arise from these causes and conditions; having thus arisen, the subsequent one and a half lines of the sūtra clarify that dependent origination has no intrinsic substance.
One should contemplate that what is falsely called "birth and death" conforms to the nature of conditions.

Thus, one clearly understands that while the twelve links of dependent origination exist as objects of sentient beings' mental states (*citta*), they are non-existent in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). When one skillfully realizes this absence of inherent nature in conditions, birth and death themselves become non-arising.
The preceding section clarifies that because of attachment to a self, there are the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*);

however, by practicing the contemplation of non-self, one becomes free from the various false conditions of "mine-ness" (*mama-kāra*), for all things arise through dependent origination as the unconditioned nature of the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
In the second section, which consists of ten and a half lines of scripture, it clarifies the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of all sentient beings.

The arising of delusion regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is termed ignorance (*avidyā*). The karma produced by this and its fruit are the "formations" (*saṃskāra*), which serve as the basis for the initial mind, which is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Because one is deluded regarding the ultimate truth, it is called ignorance; that which is true becomes false, and both possess a basis and its retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Because there is this basis and retribution, there is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), through which the emotional consciousness grasps the false appearance of reality.

When the object and the aggregate of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, together with the six sense organs, arise simultaneously, this is called a "skandha" (aggregate). Because these aggregates do not disintegrate, it is termed the "karmic consciousness.
With the mind as the primary factor, the three elements—the sense organs, the objects, and the consciousness—conjoin to form the objective condition (*ālambana*).

Together they give rise to the four types of grasping (*upādāna*): the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serves as the object, while the emotional consciousness serves as the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), and feeling (*vedanā*) arises.

The conceptualization that follows is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). Being disturbed and deluded by discursive thought (*vitarka*) regarding pure gnosis is called the "aggregates" (*skandha*).
The conjunction of these three factors—the six sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness—is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

Because of these five aggregates, the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) exist simultaneously upon the six sense faculties, the mental objects, and consciousness; thus, the following twelve links of existence are fully present.
As stated in the sutra, the preceding section clarifies that delusion regarding the ultimate truth gives rise to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*),
and from these five aggregates, the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) arise together. In the third section,
seven and a half lines of scripture clarify that all that exists within the three realms is but the one mind, demonstrating that the twelve links of existence originate from this single mind.

Because one follows after objects and greed obscures the true mind, the deluded mind arises as false conceptualization. When this conceptualizing mind deviates from wisdom, its false discrimination becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*).
That which is discriminated by the deluded mind is consciousness; that which is conditioned by consciousness is mental formation (*saṃskāra*).

For one who is deluded regarding these formations, the object of perception is regarded as being truly existent; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Because the mind is ignorant, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) subsequently arises.
Form arises from the conjunction of name-and-form, the six sense faculties, and the deluded mind; these three things together produce contact (*sparśa*).
When this primary contact is associated with discrimination and grasping, it becomes sensation (*vedanā*). The rest is as fully detailed in the sūtra itself.

Thus, the mind, objects, the six faculties, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, old age, and death occur simultaneously without temporal sequence; their essence is devoid of before and after, yet the deluded falsely construct a sequence, thereby obscuring the Tathāgata.
Because the wisdom of suchness is fundamentally without an agent, the waves of various sufferings arise transversely, and the flow of suffering continues without ceasing.
Thus, the fourth section, consisting of fifteen and a half lines of scripture, clarifies that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) each have two kinds of functions:
first, due to ignorance, all sentient beings are caused to become deluded regarding the [nature of] non-existence.
The two [factors] that constitute the formation of cognition arise from delusion regarding the self-nature of the dharmadhātu;

because they serve as the conditions for the formation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), it is said that they act as the generative cause for volitional formations. Volitional formations also have two types of functions:

first, through delusion regarding the wisdom of the dharmadhātu, one clings to them and thereby brings about retribution in future lives; second, through false volitional formations, the seeds of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are produced. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Clouds act as the generative cause for consciousness, and consciousness likewise possesses two functions:
first, through delusion regarding the seeds of fundamental wisdom, it gives rise to the seeds of false consciousness, causing all karmic activities to continue in an uninterrupted succession;
second, through delusion regarding the subtle and wondrous merits—which are devoid of names and signs—of the fundamental, universally luminous wisdom, names and forms arise by means of consciousness.
This refers to the coarse name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that constitutes the karmic retribution of birth and death produced by various seeds. Name-and-form also has two types of functions:
first, because consciousness establishes name-and-form and name-and-form establishes consciousness, they are said to mutually assist one another's formation;
second, because of name-and-form, appearances manifest within the six sense bases, enabling the cognitive consciousnesses within those six bases to apprehend them.

The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) also have two kinds of functions: first, due to delusion regarding the essence that is signless, the principle of wisdom and its objects each follow their respective domains to separately grasp distinct objects such as form, sound, and so forth;

second, because the objects manifest before the six organs and the consciousness-mind confronts them, false emotion (*moha-citta*) arises. Therefore, it is said that they act as the productive cause for contact (*sparśa*). Contact also has two [functions].
The activity of *sparśa* (contact) is twofold: first, by being deluded regarding its object (*ālambana*), it produces various forms of joy and anger;
second, by giving rise to the seeds of *vedanā* (feeling) through contact with consciousness, it enables the experiencing of present objects and thereby brings about future results.

Furthermore, because one experiences present objects through feeling, it brings about the fruit of suffering in future existence. The activity of *vedanā* is also twofold: first, by being deluded regarding [the object]...
All phenomena are empty and are able to receive such matters as love and hatred; second, they act as the causal basis for the arising of craving.
The following is fully contained within the text itself. This section on dependent origination all begins with ignorance, which deludes the principle of reality (dharmatā).
The fifth section consists of four and a half lines of scripture, divided into two parts: first, "O Son of the Buddha, herein, ignorance conditions... [and so forth].

Having proceeded thus, because they descend to the level of mutual assistance and completion, there are two sets of verses that clarify how the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, are all collectively produced by delusion regarding fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Through the deluded mind, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is formed, which further assists and completes [the process].
Within each and every condition (*pratyaya*), there are twelve links; because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) mutually assist and complete one another, there are one hundred and forty [links].
Fourth, for each of the three worlds, there are one hundred and forty-four aggregates, totaling four hundred and thirty-two aggregates.

Due to delusion regarding fundamental true wisdom, they are termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Within ignorance, the five aggregates arise from the three factors of objects, the six sense faculties, and consciousness.
By means of the five aggregates confronting the six sense faculties as conditions, all contacts (*sparśa*) are produced. In total:
With the mental consciousness as the primary factor, following the faculties, objects, and cognitions, one is able to create various karmic conditions for birth and death;
even the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) arise from this.

As for the names and numbers of these eighty-four thousand afflictions, they are fully explained in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta*); one need only understand them through one's own consciousness.
The three factors—the mind, the faculties, and the objects—are of one nature. This "one nature" refers to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

By realizing the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature, the universal radiance of wisdom universally seals all objects; its wondrous function is eternally quiescent, and ignorance is transformed into wisdom, which is called the ocean of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience).
The two lines and a half of scripture beginning with "When the two types of ignorance have ceased" clarify the realization of ignorance being transformed [into wisdom].

The explanation of the conditions is complete according to the text itself. In the sixth section, there are three and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the non-interruption of the three factors—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—constitutes the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).
The non-interruption of two factors—the formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*)—constitutes the path of karma (*karma-mārga*).

The remaining portions, namely consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), and so forth, constitute the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*).

The past, future, and present—these three periods of time—and the afflictions of the three segments [of existence]: when these are severed, there are no longer the three periods of time nor the afflictions of the three segments.
Apart from self and what belongs to self (*ātman-ātmīya*), there is only arising and ceasing, like a bundle of reeds.

This clarifies that although there are conceptual distinctions and a semblance of arising and ceasing, upon investigation they are found to be empty and non-existent within. It is like a bundle of reeds and rushes: their characteristics [are mutually dependent].
Although each of the six sense faculties and their objects is individually empty and luminous, and although the Dharma-eye is constantly empty, this luminosity is what is observed and penetrated.
In the seventh section, there are two and a half lines of scripture which state: "Furthermore, regarding 'ignorance conditions volitional formations,' there are three periods of time.
Ignorance is the ignorance of the present thought-moment; that ignorance conditions volitional formations refers to the past as the object-condition."
Because it concerns the preceding object, the Sūtra says: "This is the contemplation of past consciousness up to feeling; this is the contemplation of the present as consciousness and feeling.
That which constitutes consciousness and feeling within the present moment serves to clarify consciousness and feeling;

this is the discernment and reception of present phenomena. Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there are two matters: because these pertain to the future within the present moment, craving has two matters; these pertain to the future within the present moment.
Within the process of perception (*saṃjñā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) and feeling (*vedanā*) arise first; subsequently, one conceives of them as real, which gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Thereafter, through this successive continuity, with ignorance (*avidyā*) as a condition, there arise formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness, feeling, and craving, whereby the fruits of karma and suffering across the three periods of time continue in an uninterrupted succession.
However, when ignorance ceases, then formations cease; and with the cessation of formations, consciousness, feeling, craving, and the rest of the twelve links likewise cease.

"The total cessation of the links of existence (bhavāṅga) is the abandonment through dependent observation" clarifies that the twelve links of dependent origination are severed only by means of observation;

thus, this section on the six characteristics comprehensively covers the eighth [topic]. Within this, there are one and a half lines of scripture that generally explain how the twelve links of existence collectively constitute the three types of suffering:
ignorance, volitional formations, and the six sense bases are the suffering of conditioned states (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), as they involve delusion regarding objects.
Because clinging does not cease, this is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). The two—contact and feeling—are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

It is explained that among all contacts, love and hatred arise, producing suffering; at the very moment one experiences contact through feeling, there is already suffering, which is further increased by attachment and aversion, making the suffering even more intense.
Therefore, the remainder is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Within the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), starting from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)...
Recognizing that craving gives rise to birth, old age, sickness, and death—this is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

One should simply contemplate that with the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*) cease, whereby the three types of suffering cease and the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) cease. The ninth section consists of five lines of sutra text and clarifies three stages:
the severance and arising of the conditions for the twelve links of existence. First, it clarifies that formations have ignorance as their condition.
In this arising of conditions, if there were no ignorance, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) would likewise not exist; it is also like the other [links].

That "ignorance conditions the formative forces" has the meaning of bondage and the meaning of arising. That "with the cessation of ignorance, the formative forces cease" has the meaning of the cessation of bondage and the meaning of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), for it is liberation.
Because it is associated with great wisdom, [it is said] "the three ignorances."

The practitioner who contemplates through conditions follows the contemplation of non-existence; by generating the power of contemplative practice, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as being non-existent in their own nature.
Thus, "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease," because one contemplates that the twelve factors of existence have no substantial reality.
The same applies to the others. Generally speaking, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, it is simply that ignorance does not exist.

That is to say, because the twelve links of dependent origination do not exist [independently], this tenth section—consisting of four and a half lines of scripture—clarifies that the continuous succession of the twelve factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) through ten types of forward and reverse contemplations is entirely subsumed within the single mind.

It is only due to the differences in the suffering and pleasure resulting from one's own karma that distinctions arise; yet these do not depart from the twelve factors of existence, remaining exactly as previously described.
That which is called the severance of the Way refers to the absence of these three: mind, objects, and ignorance. When these three are absent, all else is naturally absent.

If they are not severed, the three types of suffering—namely, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*)—will accumulate.

As for their severance, it is because through the absence of ignorance, the wondrous function of non-suffering is realized; this is due to the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*). The above constitutes the extended topical outline.
In the third section, ten types of forward and reverse contemplations on the twelve links of dependent origination are presented.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate all dependent originations through these ten aspects, they know that there is no self, no person, no life-span;
that their intrinsic nature is empty, and that there is neither an agent nor an experiencer. Thereby, they immediately attain the liberation of emptiness."
When the Gate of the Signless (*animitta-vimokṣa-mukha*) manifests before him, he contemplates that all links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are by their very nature extinguished and ultimately liberated;

not even the slightest dharma arises. At that moment, the Gate of the Signless manifests before him. Having thus entered emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the signless, he has no further aspirations or seeking, except for the foremost Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) with which he teaches and transforms sentient beings. At that moment, he attains the Gate of Wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*).

When the gates of liberation manifest before him, the bodhisattva thus cultivates the three gates of liberation: he is free from the notion of self and other, free from the notion of agent and recipient, and free from the notion of existence and non-existence.
[Treatise] From "The fourth son of the Buddha" down to "free from the notion of existence and non-existence," seven and a half lines of scripture clarify the contemplation.
Having realized that the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) lack intrinsic substance, one attains the stage of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa-bhāgīya*).

This section is broadly divided to clarify how, after performing the ten types of forward and reverse contemplations upon the twelve factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), one realizes that the nature of all dependent originations is inherently unborn, thereby bringing the three doors of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*) into manifestation. Regarding these three doors of liberation: first is the contemplation of the self-nature of the twelve links of dependent origination.
1. Because emptiness and non-action are both extinguished by their own nature and are ultimately liberated, one attains the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*). 2.

Because not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, one attains the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). 3. Having attained these two gates of emptiness and signlessness, there is no further aspiration or seeking;
there is only great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to reach ultimate completion.
Having attained liberation, he realizes the gate of liberation through wishlessness; the remainder is as fully detailed in the text itself.

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s great compassion increases further, and he practices with diligent effort so that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) which are not yet fulfilled may become complete.
Therefore, he forms this thought: 'All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) arise when there is conjunction.'"
Without conjunction there is no turning; when conditions assemble, there is turning, and when they do not assemble, there is no turning.
Thus I know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) abound in many faults and afflictions, and that this causal condition of conjunction must be severed.

Nevertheless, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment, one does not ultimately extinguish all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva observes in this way that conditioned phenomena are manifold.
All faults and evils lack intrinsic nature; being neither arising nor ceasing, one constantly gives rise to great compassion and does not abandon sentient beings.
Thus, one attains the manifestation of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is called the light of unobstructed wisdom.

Having thus accomplished this light of wisdom, although one cultivates the causal conditions of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one does not dwell within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); although one contemplates...
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are by nature quiescent, yet they do not abide in that quiescence because the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) have not yet been perfected.
[Treatise: From "The fifth son of the Buddha" down to "because they are perfected," ten and a half lines of scripture clarify this stage.

In this section concerning the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the three gates of liberation, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, and the further increase of great compassion through diligent cultivation, there is a further division into two parts. First, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva...
down to "...nor does he ultimately extinguish all conditioned phenomena," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify the contemplation of all conditioned things as being empty.
This impermanence is deeply loathsome; yet, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, one does not eternally extinguish all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

This section is divided into two parts. From the words "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva has thus [realized this]" down to "because they are not yet perfected," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattva contemplates conditioned phenomena as having many faults and evils, lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and yet constantly giving rise to great...
Regarding the attainment of the portion of the *prajñāpāramitā* of compassion, as the Sūtra says:

"For those who have not yet attained the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)," this clarifies that in this sixth stage, one has already attained the supramundane enlightenment of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
yet, having not yet attained the mastery of the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra through the perfection of mundane great compassion, one further reflects upon all things.
That conditioned phenomena arise through combination and transformation clarifies that when deluded mental states condition things, all dharmas are impermanent and subject to transformation;
when such delusion ceases, they accord with principle, meaning that the nature of all dharmas is inherently unarisen. This clarifies that when the mind arises, dharmas arise.
The following should be understood accordingly: as for "if conditions assemble, they transform; if they do not assemble, they do not transform," if there were no...

When ignorance conditions formative activity (*saṃskāra*), it revolves; when ignorance ceases, formative activity follows. When arising through wisdom, that which arises is only phenomena (*dharma*), for they are not subject to impermanence or transformation.
The following should be understood accordingly: conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) abound with many faults and afflictions;

whatever is produced by sentient consciousness is subject to the sufferings and ailments of birth, old age, sickness, death, and pain. If, however, one acts through wisdom and compassion, all [actions] are...
The conduct of Samantabhadra and so forth should be understood accordingly. Thus, one attains the manifestation of Prajñāpāramitā;
this transcends the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. This wisdom of the One Vehicle is the wisdom of the Buddha, the ultimate, unconditioned, and universally radiant wisdom.
It is called "all-pervading wisdom" because it benefits sentient beings according to their capacities, functioning spontaneously without effort.
Regarding the statement "it is not produced, yet it is spontaneously present," and so forth as fully detailed in the sūtra:

because the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) have not yet been perfected, one speaks of the "enlightenment of right awakening" (*samyaksambodhi*) being accomplished at the initial resolve, while the "enlightenment of subsequent practice" (*anupravartana-bodhi*) is fulfilled only at the completion of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain entry into the *samādhi* of emptiness and the *samādhi* of the self-nature of emptiness.
The samādhi of emptiness of the ultimate truth, the samādhi of the foremost emptiness, the samādhi of great emptiness, the samādhi of combined emptiness, the samādhi of arising emptiness,

the samādhi of emptiness that does not falsely discriminate according to reality, the samādhi of emptiness that does not abandon or depart, and the samādhi of emptiness that is free from both departure and non-departure—
by taking these ten gates of emptiness samādhi as his primary focus, this bodhisattva attains hundreds of thousands of emptiness samādhis.

All these samādhis manifest before him; thus, with these ten gates of signlessness and ten gates of wishlessness as the foremost, hundreds of thousands of gates of signlessness and wishlessness all manifest before him.
