[Treatise] From the sixth son of the Buddha down to the phrase "all appear before one," there are six lines and a half of scripture that clarify the attainment of the ten samādhis—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—in this Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). Regarding the samādhi of the self-nature of emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*):

it is called "samādhi" because it manifests spontaneously without being produced through effort, occurring naturally and effortlessly in accordance with the principle; "three" refers to its correctness; and "samādhi" refers to meditative concentration (*samāpatti*).

Furthermore, why is this called "Right Concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*)? It is because the number three is taken as "right. Generally, in the performance of ritual acts, the number three is established as the standard.
That which is obscured by emotional consciousness is termed "obscuration," while that in which right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) manifests is termed "three.
Moreover, "three" signifies "rightness. Why is this so? Because three is yang, it is right—just as the eleventh month is [the beginning of the yang cycle].
The first yang arises in the twelfth month; the second yang arises in the first month; the third yang arises in the first month.
Yi (the Tiger) is taken as wood and as the sun; the sun is fire. Since fire is produced in Yi, and the sun is taken as wisdom, the twelfth and first months are assigned to Gen.
Gen is divided into mountain, cessation, gate-towers, and the youngest son.

Because they represent the state of the spiritually immature, the Sages take them as symbols of the Dharma. In the first month, when the three yang lines have already arisen, fire is produced from the cessation of *gen* (艮).
This clarifies that from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) comes cessation, which gives rise to non-conceptual, correct wisdom.
Since this clarity is the gateway for entering the Path and awakening the mind, *gen* represents the spiritually immature; thus, it clarifies the mind of the spiritually immature.
Because *śamatha* (calm abiding) can give rise to the radiant light of the great sun of wisdom, it is called the "Third" [the correct]. "Mù" (昧) means concentration (*samādhi*).

When the five aggregates are in a state of profound stillness, right wisdom immediately manifests. Furthermore, the character for "stopping" (*zhǐ*) is the character for "correct" (*zhèng*), because when the one mind is present, its Way is correct;
thus, in this single place of stopping, there is no task that cannot be accomplished. This is the first meaning of emptiness. III.
The "Samādhi of Supreme Emptiness" is so called because it transcends all conditioned and impermanent dharmas;

it clarifies that which has newly surpassed the two upper realms and the meditative absorptions of cessation, and it also surpasses the pure and impure concentrations of the Three Vehicles—the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Pure Lands.
Furthermore, the fact that the myriad phenomena share a single nature is termed the "Samādhi of One Emptiness. The "Samādhi of Great Emptiness" transcends the mundane world.
The emptiness cognized by the mind transcends the three vehicles and abides in unconditioned emptiness.

Because one attains the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*), it is "emptiness in accord with samādhi," which clarifies that one is in harmony with all sentient and insentient beings—ordinary and sage—throughout the ten directions.
"Emptiness arising from samādhi" clarifies the sovereign mastery of quiescence and function. "Emptiness that does not falsely discriminate" clarifies the insentient.
The "samādhi of emptiness distinguished by consciousness" is manifested because it accords with what is seen according to individual faculties;

the "samādhi of emptiness that is not abandoned" is manifested because it remains far removed from faults and evils; the "samādhi of emptiness that both abandons and does not abandon" is manifested because it dwells in the world like a lotus in water.
Taking these three samādhis as the foremost, they are all inseparable from emptiness and wishlessness (*animitta*).
The three gates of samādhi characterized by wishlessness constitute its essence; from this, hundreds of thousands of samādhis all arise.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence, they further cultivate and bring to fulfillment the indestructible mind, the resolute mind, the purely virtuous mind, the profoundly deep mind, the non-retrogressive mind, the unceasing mind, and the vast mind.

The Bodhisattvas, sons of the Buddha, fully perfect these ten minds—the mind seeking infinite wisdom, the mind of skillful means, and the mind associated with wisdom—and thereby accord with the Bodhi of the Buddhas.
They do not fear heterodox arguments; they enter the stages of wisdom, leave behind the paths of the two vehicles, and advance toward the wisdom of the Buddhas.
No afflictions or demons can obstruct or destroy them, as they abide in the radiant light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom.

Within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they skillfully cultivate expedient means and wisdom, which are always in mutual accord with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
Constantly practicing without abandoning them, these sons of the Buddha, bodhisattvas dwelling in this stage of the Manifest (Abhimukhī),

attain the superior practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) and obtain the third kind of sharp and penetrating conformative patience (anulomikī kṣānti), because they [perceive] all dharmas as they truly are.
"Because they are mutually conformable and without contradiction.

[Treatise] From "The seventh son of the Buddha" down to "because they are mutually conformable and without contradiction," nine and a half lines of scripture clarify that while dwelling in this Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*),
one further cultivates the indestructible mind and enters the stage of the Buddha’s wisdom, section by section.

This consists of three sections: 1. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to "are all fully perfected," there are three and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on cultivating the ten kinds of infinite minds.

2. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, up to "constantly practicing without abandoning," there are four lines of scripture clarifying the section on conforming to the Buddha’s bodhi, fearing no heterodox arguments, and entering the stage of the Buddha’s wisdom. 3. The third section.

From the passage beginning with "The son [of the Buddha]" down to "because of being compliant and non-contradictory," there are two and a half lines of scripture that clarify the stage of the Bodhisattva abiding in this position who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and attains the portion of the "conformity-patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

The phrase "not fearing heterodox arguments" refers to the heterodox arguments of humans, devas, and non-Buddhists, as well as those of the three vehicles; "entering the ground of Buddha-wisdom" clarifies that this proceeds from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Because they enter the stage of the wisdom of differentiation, they leave behind the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

While the followers of the two vehicles sever afflictions (*kleśa*) to realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*), Bodhisattvas penetrate afflictions to accomplish the ocean of wisdom; thus it is said they "proceed toward Buddha-wisdom.

That no demonic afflictions (*kleśamāra*) can obstruct or destroy them clarifies that the demon of affliction is the cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). As for the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) and the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*)...
Birth and death are the fruit; the celestial Māras are the conditions for birth and death. The wisdom that abides in the Bodhisattva is the wisdom that accords with all worldly distinctions.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain the preeminence of the practice of Prajñāpāramitā;
this clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage [transcends] all conditions within the triple world.

Because one thoroughly attains the supramundane wisdom within the mundane through the contemplation of the arising phenomena in both their direct and reverse orders, it is called "increasing" (*vṛddhi*).
Regarding the third, "superior" (*adhimātra*) "pliant endurance" (*kṣānti*), according to the system of five endurances, this is the third, "pliant endurance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);
according to the system of ten endurances, it is the second, "pliant endurance. Within the five endurances of the three vehicles, the first is "subduing endurance" (*vinirdhava-kṣānti*).

Second, the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*); third, the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); fourth, the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*); fifth, the patience of cessation (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). As stated in the section on the ten stages within the Three Vehicles:

Bodhisattvas of the three levels of worthiness prior to the stages attain the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*); those of the fifth stage attain the patience of faith; those of the sixth stage attain the patience of conformity;

those of the eighth stage attain the patience of non-arising; and those of the tenth stage attain the patience of cessation. These ten types of patience are fully detailed in the subsequent text of the Sūtra. Thus it is.
In the teachings of the *Mahāyāna*, the ten *pāramitās* are cultivated throughout the five stages— the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), ten practices (*caryā*),
ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground— such that within each stage the ten *pāramitās* function as both primary and secondary factors.
Above these five stages, there are five hundred modes of practice, which are progressively refined and subtle, categorized through the six aspects of totality and particularity (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).

Regarding this meaning, when expressed in terms of time, days, months, and years, it is likewise so; just as in the net of Indra, the layers reflect one another, such that the one and the many, the same and the different, all remain without change.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, once a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī), by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas."
That is to say, seeing many hundreds of Buddhas, even up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas,
one serves, honors, respects, and praises them all with a vast mind and a profound mind; one offers all necessities of life— robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and so forth—
and also makes offerings to the entire Sangha, dedicating these roots of goodness [toward enlightenment].
Turning toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they reverently listen to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas;
having heard it, they receive and uphold it, attaining the light of wisdom of the *yathābhūta-samādhi* and practicing accordingly with mindfulness and without abandonment.
Furthermore, they obtain the sūtras of the profound Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas, [studying them] for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, and even for immeasurable hundreds [of kalpas].
The roots of goodness possessed throughout a thousand billion nayutas of kalpas become even more brilliant and pure,
just as genuine gold becomes increasingly bright and pure when repeatedly polished with lapis lazuli gems; likewise,

the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva on this stage become even more brilliant and pure through observation accompanied by skillful means and wisdom, and they become further tranquil and extinguished.
It is able to outshine others, just as moonlight illuminates the bodies of sentient beings, bringing them refreshing coolness,

and cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of wind-circles; likewise, all the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva on this stage can extinguish the blazing fires of affliction of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, and cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of demonic paths.
Among the ten pāramitās of a bodhisattva, the prajñāpāramitā is predominant; it is not that the others are not practiced, but they are cultivated according to one's strength and capacity.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the brief explanation of the sixth stage, the Stage of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Dwelling in this stage, the bodhisattva mostly becomes a Śubhakṛtsna Deva King, exercising mastery over all that pertains to the śrāvakas.

He is incapable of being defeated or discouraged by any challenges or objections; he causes sentient beings to eliminate their *asmimāna* (conceit of "I am") and to enter deeply into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

All his actions—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, up to and including mindfulness of the possession of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*). Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I shall, within..."
Among all sentient beings, this bodhisattva is the foremost, the most excellent, and even the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If such a bodhisattva practices with diligent vigor, in a single moment they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of samādhis, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas as their retinue;
through the mastery of their power of vows, they manifest even more than this.
This number could not be calculated even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] From the eighth son of the Buddha downwards, up to where it says "and then spoke in verse," there are twenty-seven and a half lines of scripture that clarify entering this stage and seeing the Buddhas, whether extensively or narrowly. This is divided approximately into six sections:
first, from the initial "son of the Buddha" down to "becoming even more bright and pure," there are nine lines of scripture clarifying seeing the Buddhas extensively through the power of vows.
The section on "Abundant Offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha" is divided into two parts. From the passage beginning with "Just as pure gold...

down to "cannot be destroyed by the four types of māras," approximately six and a half lines of scripture clarify the division that uses metaphors to illustrate the Dharma. This is further divided into three parts.
From the passage beginning with "These ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva... down to the sixth stage, the Abhimukhī-bhūmi, approximately two and a half lines of scripture clarify [this].
The section on the dharma-gates practiced by Bodhisattvas on this stage consists of four parts.
From "When a Bodhisattva has dwelt in this stage" down to "becoming the support for all-knowledge wisdom," six lines of scripture clarify this portion.

The section on the Bodhisattva’s empowerment and capacity to teach and transform all sentient beings consists of five parts. From "This Bodhisattva" down to the recitation of the verses, there are four [sections].
The *Caryā-melāpaka-pradīpa* clarifies that a bodhisattva in this stage perceives the Buddhas extensively through the power of samādhi.

[Sūtra] Having perfected the fifth bhūmi, the bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unborn, unceasing, and fundamentally pure;
they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and beyond grasping or rejecting.
The essential nature and characteristics are quiescent, like illusions and the like; existence and non-existence are non-dual, free from conceptual discrimination.

Contemplating in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in this way, one attains this wisdom and enters the sixth stage, where clear and sharp conformative patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) and wisdom are fully perfected, observing the marks of arising and ceasing in the world.
Through the power of delusion and darkness, the world arises; if delusion and darkness are extinguished, the world no longer exists.
Observing the true meaning of causes and conditions as empty, one does not destroy conventional designations or their functional harmony.
There is no agent, no recipient, and no conceptual thought; all conditioned phenomena arise everywhere like clouds.
Not knowing the ultimate truth is called ignorance; the volitional karma produced thereby, together with the arising of consciousness as the fruit of delusion, is called name-and-form.
In this way, up to the entire mass of suffering, one understands that the three realms depend upon the mind; the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so.
Birth and death are both produced by the mind; if the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted.
Ignorance produces two kinds [of results]: failing to understand conditions serves as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
In this way, it continues until old age and final death; from this, suffering arises without end.
With ignorance as a condition, it cannot be severed; when those conditions are exhausted, they all cease.
The factors of delusion, craving, and grasping are afflictions (*kleśa*); Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are karma; the rest are suffering (*duḥkha*).
From delusion up to the six sense bases is the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); The increase of contact and feeling is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
The remaining members of existence are the suffering of change; when selflessness is seen, the three sufferings cease.
Ignorance and formations belong to the past; consciousness through feeling evolve in the present.
Craving, grasping, and becoming produce future suffering; if these conditions are severed through contemplation, the limit of existence is exhausted.
With ignorance as a condition, this bondage arises; by attaining detachment from conditions, bondage is exhausted.
From causes, fruits arise; through detachment, they are severed. Contemplating this, one knows that their nature is empty.
Following along with ignorance, the various realms of existence (bhava) arise; if one does not follow along, the realms of existence are severed.

When this exists, that exists; non-existence is likewise so. Contemplating these ten aspects, the mind becomes detached from attachment to the continuity of the factors of existence, being gathered into a single state of mind.
One’s own karma is never absent, arising through the three paths, the three time periods, and the causes and conditions of the three types of suffering.
This process of bondage, arising and ceasing, proceeds toward inexhaustibility.
Thus universally observing the process of dependent origination— Without agent, without recipient, and without reality;
like an illusion, a dream, or a reflection, And like a fool chasing a mirage— By observing in this way, one enters into emptiness;
Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached, one attains signlessness.
Realizing their emptiness and falsity, they have no aspirations, except for compassion toward sentient beings;

this is the great being’s gate of practice for liberation. Increasingly deepening their great compassion, they seek the Buddha-dharma and understand that all conditioned phenomena arise from cooperation; their resolve is firm and determined as they diligently cultivate the Path.
The gate of the emptiness samādhi possesses hundreds of thousands [of aspects], and the same is true for signlessness and wishlessness;
the patience that accords with prajñā is all-surpassing, and the wisdom of liberation is brought to full perfection.
Furthermore, with a profound mind, one makes many offerings to the Buddhas and cultivates the Path within the Buddha’s teaching.
Having attained the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, their roots of goodness increase;
Like gold and lapis lazuli polished to brilliance, like the moon’s coolness pervading all things, Even when struck by the four winds, they cannot be destroyed.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage transcend the path of Māra, And likewise extinguish the fever of afflictions for all living beings.
In this stage, one mostly becomes a King of Transformation, Transforming and guiding sentient beings to eliminate their pride;
All that they do is sought for the sake of all-knowledge, Having completely transcended and surpassed the path of the śrāvakas.
The bodhisattvas of this stage apply themselves with diligent vigor, Attaining hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis.

There are also many immeasurable Buddhas, like the sun in the sky during the height of summer—profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive or know; neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas can comprehend them.
Such is the sixth stage of the bodhisattva, which I have now proclaimed for the sake of the Buddha’s sons.
[Treatise] The ninth section consists of forty-four stanzas that clarify the repetition (*geya*) of the preceding section on the Dharmadhātu; this has been explained in full according to the text.

The above section explains the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). This stage is characterized by the thorough mastery of conditions for generating wisdom pertaining to both the mundane and the supramundane.
The seventh stage, the Far-Reaching Stage (*Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), is [characterized] by the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
The honey-like perfection of the wisdom of compassion that enters into both mundane and supramundane knowledge.
Regarding the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), its five gates will now be explained as before. First, regarding the explanation of the name of the stage:
why is it called the Far-Reaching Stage? It is because on this stage one practices the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
Within the sixth stage, the three samādhis of emptiness manifest the gate of immeasurable, unconditioned wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*);
it is so named because one is able to enter the realms of immeasurable sentient beings, engage in the immeasurable karmic activities of teaching and transforming sentient beings,
and penetrate the immeasurable networks of worlds through unconditioned wisdom to enter into the conduct of all beings throughout all worlds, causing it to be universally pervasive everywhere.
The Ground of Far-Reaching Travel (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi) is so named because it enters into worldly conduct that is pervasive, universal, and vast.

Second, to clarify what gateways of practice are cultivated on this ground: on this ground, one cultivates the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), for by means of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one is able to enter the world and engage in the myriad practices identical to those of sentient beings.

However, because he does not depart from the world and does not follow birth and death, yet his great compassion increases, it is called the third perfection, the Perfection of Skillful Means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
To clarify the symbolic meaning of Sudhana: the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) whom Sudhana encounters here are those within the assembly of the Buddha;
this clarifies that while not departing from the essence of Bodhi, one practices all various deeds. Therefore, it is called "the blossoming of the tree flowers."
It symbolizes that upon the tree of wondrous wisdom free from signs, the flowers of Samantabhadra’s conduct have blossomed;
it is also the blossoming of the flowers of the conduct of ignorance of all sentient beings, for the purpose of causing them to become the flowers of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Thus, it represents the perfection of the seventh bhūmi, wherein worldly conduct is accomplished and the gateway of compassion is fulfilled; therefore, his body dwells amidst various jewels.
The lion throne composed of exquisite jewels within the tree-pavilion symbolizes that the various jewel-trees are the *adhiṣṭhāna* (retributive support) of the various practices.
The pavilion-shaped form formed by the jewel-trees clarifies the wisdom that accords with those practices.
The exquisite jewel lion throne symbolizes the practice of sublime, fearless activity. Thus, Sudhana attains the vastness of the Bodhisattva.

Regarding "joyful liberation": it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage accomplishes the practice of great compassion and is universally able to skillfully teach and transform sentient beings with joyful tirelessness; because they do not abide in either defilement or purity, it is called "liberation.
This is the teaching bestowed [upon them]; as this is the practice performed within the seventh stage, it is thus named.
The dwelling place serves as its symbolic representation. Regarding what liberation is attained within the four realms of existence and the three worlds:
this stage clarifies that one employs skillful means in all worldly activities to benefit sentient beings, yet remains unstained by worldly dharmas; this is the gate of liberation.
Furthermore, it is the "Gate of the Vast Joy of Bodhisattvas" attained by Sudhana, as the sutra says: "These seven..."
When the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*) are perfected through effort, one enters the practice of mastery over wisdom. Furthermore, it is said:
because in the first stage one seeks to fulfill all vows regarding the Buddha-dharma; because in the second stage one is free from the defilements of the mind;

because in the third stage one’s vows further increase and one attains the light of the Dharma; because in the fourth stage one enters the Path; and because in the fifth stage one accords with the world.
Because of what has been accomplished, the sixth stage is for entering the profound dharma-gate; the seventh stage is for the arising of all Buddha-dharmas;
and because in both cases the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are fully perfected.

Furthermore, it clarifies that from the first stage through the seventh stage, one achieves the application of wisdom (*jñānaprayoga*), whereas from the eighth stage through the tenth stage, one achieves non-application (*anābhoga*).

Because they involve effortful application (*sābhoga*), it is clear that everything prior to the seventh stage involves effortful application, while from the eighth stage onward, one attains effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
Fifth, regarding the interpretation of the meaning according to the text, there are two points as previously mentioned. First, concerning the long division of the sūtra’s intent:
within these seven stages, the text is divided into ten sections, beginning from "At this time, the hearts of the assembly of devas rejoiced."
Below are twenty-four lines of verse, divided into two sections.

[Sūtra] At that time, the hosts of devas were filled with joy; they scattered jewels that formed clouds abiding in the sky, universally emitting various wondrous sounds, and addressed the Most Victorious and Pure One.
Mastering the wisdom that realizes the ultimate truth, A lotus among hundreds of billions of men, unattached and perfected in merit;
To benefit all living beings, he expounds the profound practice.
The Lord of Devas, dwelling in the sky, Emitting great radiance that illuminates the Buddha’s body.
They also scattered clouds of the most supreme and wondrous incense; The wise ones who offer these gifts remove sorrow and affliction.
At that time, the hosts of devas were all filled with joy, And in unison they raised beautiful voices to offer praise:
"We have heard of the merits of this ground; We have thereby already obtained great and excellent benefit."
At that time, the celestial maidens were filled with joy in their hearts; competing with one another, they played thousands of kinds of musical instruments.
By the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, their voices together uttered these words:
"Your majestic demeanor is tranquil and most peerless; you are the World-Honored One who can tame those difficult to tame."
Having transcended all worlds, you traverse the world to reveal the sublime path;
though manifesting various and infinite bodies, you know that each body is devoid of intrinsic existence.
Skillfully employing words and speech to expound all dharmas, you do not grasp at the marks of letters or sounds.
They travel to hundreds of thousands of lands, making the highest offerings to the Buddhas;
their wisdom is sovereign and unattached, and they do not give rise to the notion of "my Buddha-field.
Though they diligently teach and transform all sentient beings, they harbor no thoughts of self or other.
Though you have already cultivated and perfected vast goodness, you do not give rise to attachment toward wholesome dharmas.
Seeing that all worlds are constantly ablaze with the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
you remain entirely free from all conceptualizations and exert the power of great compassion and diligence.
[Verse: All the devas and their daughters, having offered various kinds of worship and praise, all remained silent at the same time;
gazing up at the Honored One among Men, they wished to hear the Dharma.
[Treatise: First, from "the assembly of devas, their hearts filled with joy" down to "gazing up at the Honored One among Men, they wished to hear."
The Dharma consists of twenty-two verses clarifying the section on the great assembly’s joyful offerings upon hearing the sixth stage.

[Sūtra] At that time, Vimukticandra again requested, saying: “O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will proclaim for this great assembly—whose minds are pure—the various characteristics of the practices within the seventh stage.”
[Treatise] The second section, the division on the further request for the dharmas of the subsequent stages, is elucidated by the two lines of verse beginning with Vimukticandra.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva..."

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having fulfilled the practices of the sixth stage, desires to enter the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), they should cultivate ten kinds of paths arising from skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
What are these ten? They are: although they have well cultivated the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not abandon sentient beings due to their compassion;
although they have attained the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, they delight in the constant [practice of]...

While making offerings to the Buddha, although they have entered the gate of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, they diligently accumulate merit; although they are far removed from the triple world, they adorn the triple world;
although they have brought all flames of affliction to ultimate cessation, they are able to give rise to the flames of extinguishing greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings;
and although they know all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, shadows, and echoes.

Like a flame, like a magical creation, like the moon reflected in water, or like an image in a mirror, their intrinsic nature is non-dual, yet they perform immeasurable varieties of karmic actions according to the mind.
Although they know all lands to be like empty space, they are able to adorn Buddha-lands with pure and wondrous practices;
although they know the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is inherently bodiless, they [manifest] through the primary and secondary marks.
Adorning their bodies, although they know that the nature of the Buddhas' voices is empty, quiescent, and ineffable,
they are nevertheless able to produce various distinct pure sounds according to all sentient beings;

and while they follow the Buddhas in realizing that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment, they manifest through various characteristics and various [modes] in accordance with the mental inclinations and conceptual discriminations of sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva who has cultivated various practices throughout manifold eons, by means of these ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom, initiates sublime conduct and enters the seventh stage from the sixth stage. Having entered it, this conduct is constantly present before him;
this is called abiding in the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching) Bhūmi. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this seventh stage...
They enter the infinite realms of sentient beings; they enter the infinite activities of all Buddhas in teaching and transforming sentient beings;
they enter the infinite networks of worlds; they enter the infinite pure lands of all Buddhas; they enter the infinite varieties of differentiated dharmas;
they enter the infinite wisdom of the manifest enlightenment of all Buddhas; they enter the infinite number of eons; and they enter the infinite modes of awakening and comprehension of all Buddhas.
Worldly wisdom enters into the diverse faiths and understandings of immeasurable sentient beings;
it enters into the various names and physical forms manifested by immeasurable Buddhas; it enters into the differences in the desires, inclinations, and faculties of immeasurable sentient beings;
it enters into the immeasurable Buddhas’ speech and sounds that bring joy to sentient beings; and it enters into the immeasurable varieties of mental activities of sentient beings.
The Buddhas, through their vast and penetrating wisdom, cause [beings] to enter into the immeasurable faith and understanding of the Śrāvaka vehicle;

they cause them to enter into the immeasurable paths of wisdom taught by the Buddhas so as to inspire faith and understanding; they cause them to enter into the immeasurable accomplishments of the Pratyekabuddhas;
they cause them to enter into the immeasurable gateways of profound wisdom taught by the Buddhas; and they cause them to enter into the immeasurable skillful means and practices of the Bodhisattvas.
Having measured the matters compiled from the Mahāyāna teachings spoken by all the Buddhas so that the Bodhisattva may enter [this state],
the Bodhisattva forms this thought: "Such immeasurable realms of the Tathāgatas— even those which could not be known in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas—
I must fully accomplish as a Son of the Buddha with a mind that is effortless and non-conceptual."
This bodhisattva, through profound wisdom, observes in this manner and constantly and diligently cultivates the wisdom of skillful means, giving rise to the sublime path.
Abiding therein immovably, there is not a single thought-moment of rest or abandonment.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—even in sleep and dreams—they have never for a moment been associated with hindrances or obstructions. They never relinquish such contemplation. This bodhisattva...
In every thought-moment, the Bodhisattva is always able to fulfill the ten pāramitās. Why is this?
Because in every thought-moment they take great compassion as the foremost principle to practice the Buddha-dharma and advance toward Buddha-wisdom.
All roots of goodness are bestowed upon sentient beings for the sake of seeking Buddha-wisdom; this is called the dāna-pāramitā. It is capable of extinguishing the heat of all afflictions.
To have compassion as the foremost principle and not harm sentient beings is called the *śīla-pāramitā*.
To seek the supreme wholesome dharmas without ever becoming weary or satisfied is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
For the path of omniscience to be constantly present before one without ever being distracted is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. To be able to endure all phenomena is called the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Non-arising and non-ceasing is called the *prajñāpāramitā*. Being able to give birth to immeasurable wisdom is called the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*.
Being able to seek the most supreme and excellent wisdom is called the *praṇidhānapāramitā*.
Being unable to be thwarted or destroyed by any heterodox arguments or hosts of Māras is called the *balapāramitā*. To understand all things as they truly are is [the *jñānapāramitā*].

"O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma is called the Perfection of Wisdom. Within every thought-moment, Bodhisattvas fully attain these ten perfections, as well as the four means of attraction, the four bases of power, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the three gates of liberation;
in brief, even all factors conducive to awakening are completely perfected within every thought-moment."
[Treatise] Third: The section beginning with "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva...

contains fifty and a half lines of scripture that clarify the cultivation of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) by means of ten dharmas, as well as the dharma-section for entering the first dwelling of the seventh stage.
Regarding the second part, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning, this section is divided into three parts: first, "At that time, Vajra..."; [and so forth].
From the passage beginning with "Bodhisattva Vajragarbha" down to "dwelling in the seventh stage,
Dūraṃgamā," there are eighteen lines of scripture that clarify the cultivation of ten dharmas for entering the seventh stage. From the passage beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha,

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas" down to "accomplishing perfection through effortless mental application," there are fifteen sections of scripture that clarify the bodhisattva dwelling in the [seventh] stage.
The seventh stage consists of twenty types of entry into the realm of sentient beings and all dharma-gates for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

This section is divided into three parts for the sons of the Buddha. From the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva, by means of profound wisdom" down to "are all completely perfected," seventeen and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattvas at this stage practice the ten *pāramitās*, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all dharmas pertaining to bodhi, as stated in the sutra in the first section:

"Cultivating the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, while through compassion not abandoning any sentient being," this clarifies that while those of the Two Vehicles cultivate emptiness and their own delusions are already extinguished, they lack the compassion to benefit living beings; whereas the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land cultivate the dharma-gate of the three emptinesses for themselves...

Once delusions have been extinguished, they are reborn in a pure land according to their vows; only after achieving self-enlightenment through the Buddha’s teachings do they return to the defiled realm to benefit sentient beings through skillful means.

Thus, there are two obstacles—purity and defilement—and a coming and going between these two realms, as described in the sūtras of the Three Vehicles regarding bodhisattvas from other regions who come here to this Sahā world to hear the Dharma and then return to their own lands.
Thus, within this teaching of the One Vehicle, it is clarified that Bodhisattvas enter the Dharma from delusion, which is termed "assembling from other Buddha-fields.
Once awakened, they do not speak of returning to their original lands, clarifying that the body and the land are non-dual in nature.
Therefore, the meaning of these eighteen lines of scripture does not depart from the essence of the three emptinesses, taking them as the foundation for all practices.
This clarifies that prior to the sixth stage, one achieves supramundane perfection through the three emptinesses;
within the seventh stage, one fulfills practice through the three emptinesses because of the practice of mundane compassion. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"Although they have attained the equality of all Buddhas, they delight in constantly making offerings to the Buddhas. This clarifies that one reveres and honors [the Buddhas] by means of the equality of the natureless Dharmakāya.
"His conduct is all-pervasive and boundless; his luminous and quiescent function is unimpeded.
This clarifies that although he enters the gate of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, he diligently accumulates merit and virtue.
"Although he is far removed from the three realms, he adorns the three realms. This clarifies that while he is free from the karma of the three realms, he constantly takes birth within them.

Although those who practice wholesome conduct and transform sentient beings have ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions (*kleśa*), they are nevertheless able to give rise to the extinction of the flames of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings; this clarifies the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). The ten underlying tendencies are: first, greed; second, hatred;
third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, doubt; sixth, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); seventh, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); eighth... [and so forth].

The nine types of *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) and the ten types of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances), along with the ten *anuśaya* (latent proclivities) of the three realms, constitute the afflictions that delude one regarding the Four Truths and the Path of Cultivation; these total one hundred and thirty kinds of afflictions.

Specifically, there are ten kinds of afflictions for each of the Four Truths in the Desire Realm, totaling forty; when combined with the great afflictions common to the Path of Cultivation, they form this total.

The fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) consist of six: (1) greed, (2) hatred, (3) delusion, (4) pride, (5) the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and (6) the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

In total, there are forty-six afflictions in the desire realm. The remaining four—view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), precept-and-vow-grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—arise from the aforementioned six;
they are not fundamental because they originate from them. In the two higher realms, hatred is excluded from each, while the others remain as in the desire realm.
From the four truths of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are nine for each, totaling forty-two;
from the four truths of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are likewise nine for each, totaling forty-two; combined, there are one hundred and thirty types.

This extends up to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), which will be explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Minor Marks" (*anuvyañjana-parivarta*). Regarding the abandonment of afflictions within the Three Vehicles:
The five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-nīvaraṇa*) consist of wrong view, attachment to precepts and observances, and attachment to views; these five views serve as the sharp fetters.

Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt constitute the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-nīvaraṇa*). The five sharp fetters are afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), because as long as these various views have not been eliminated, the principle will not manifest before one.

The five dull fetters are afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The sharp fetters obstruct the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) because the various views have not yet perished and thus the truth does not appear before one.

The five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) obstruct the practitioner; although they arise repeatedly during the course of practice, even upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), greed, hatred, and delusion still persist as residual habits (*vāsanā*) because these have not yet been fully eradicated.

Thus, while a *srotāpanna* has completely severed the afflictions of the truths to be seen (*satya-darśana-heya*), a *sakṛdāgāmin* and an *anāgāmin* have not yet entirely eliminated the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Because Arhats have severed both types of afflictions—the afflictions of the truths to be seen (*darśana-heya*) and those of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—within the three realms, they are not reborn within them.

Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles, having subdued the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) and ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana*), cultivate the six *pāramitās* and are born in the Pure Lands;
these are also called the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) that exist separately above the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

The gods born from the *sāmbhoga-kāya* are named Maheśvara; they are also bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), yet because they have not yet completely severed the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), they possess the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):
first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); second, lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*); third, torpor (*middha*); fourth, regret (*kaukṛtya*);

fifth, stinginess (*mātsarya*); sixth, envy (*īrṣyā*); seventh, restlessness (*auddhatya*); eighth, dullness (*styāna*); ninth, anger (*krodha*); and tenth, concealment (*mrakṣa*). These ten envelopments correspond to the ten [fetters].

The arising of the outflows (*āsrava*) also acts as the cause for the production of the ten outflows, just as a bodhisattva of the One Vehicle, from the stage of the ten faiths, believes that their own discriminating mind arises from the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
from the initial mind of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*), it is identical to the first stage (*bhūmi*);

reaching the sixth abiding, it is identical to the sixth stage; and upon attaining entry into the samādhi of quiescent extinction, their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are equal to those of the ten abidings.

The sixth [bhūmi] among these is the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja. The general meaning is that the three stages previously mentioned—the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications—collectively take the sequential progression through the ten bhūmis as their essence. They collectively take the immovable wisdom of all Tathāgatas as their essence;
all afflictions are, by the power of meditative concentration, simultaneously eliminated through the power of non-conceptualizing wisdom.

The universal seal is identical with the essence of wisdom; throughout the three periods of past, present, and future, it is a single limit, devoid of any characteristics of shortness or length, or extension or contraction.

The following passage further clarifies this general meaning: if, within the span of a single thought-moment, one perceives one's own mind as having attained Buddhahood or not yet having attained Buddhahood, thereby creating distinctions of extended or contracted time and finite limits, one should know that such a person does not achieve realization.
Because the essence of the Tathāgata’s wisdom has not yet manifested before them, right view [remains incomplete]. The above clarifies the severance of afflictions. The Sūtra states:
"Although one knows that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams," as the text itself contains, "yet one performs immeasurable varieties of actions according to the mind.
This clarifies that by means of wisdom—which has no substantial body—one illusorily produces all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) in accordance with the immeasurable minds of sentient beings.
Although one knows that all lands are like empty space, one is able to adorn Buddha-lands with pure and wondrous conduct;

this clarifies that while karma is empty and the objective realm is tranquil, the retribution of compassion and wisdom adorns them. Compassion and wisdom have no basis, yet their manifested retribution appears like a shadow.
Although one knows that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is fundamentally bodiless, one adorns it with the primary and secondary marks.
The "body" refers to the Dharma-body, which is signless and purifies deluded karma;

when delusion perishes and karma is exhausted, the realm of wisdom—the environment and its inhabitants—manifests as auspicious signs like pure reflections of light, free from the attachments of existence or non-existence, such as the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*).

Although one follows all Buddhas in realizing that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment, one nevertheless accords with the mental inclinations and conceptual discriminations of sentient beings.
Those who practice various forms of cultivation through various characteristics, times, and kalpa-numbers clarify that the essence of the Dharma-body’s wisdom is without time,
without kalpas, and without the substance of the three periods of existence; yet, in accordance with the differences in the karma of all sentient beings,
there are distinctions of all times and kalpas, and thus they practice by discerning these distinctions of time and kalpa for the sake of sentient beings.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are as described: the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the three births, one birth, a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), and sixty *kalpas*, and so forth.
It is by means of these ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom that the Bodhisattva initiates superior practices.
Having clarified how one enters the seventh stage from the sixth stage based on the aforementioned ten dharmas, the following section is titled "Entering the Seventh Stage."
For one dwelling in the seventh stage, there are twenty kinds of dharma-gates of entry, as fully detailed in the text itself.
After this Bodhisattva has formed this thought, he relies upon the preceding outline of the text’s meaning, as fully presented in the sūtra itself.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha, is it only in this seventh stage that a bodhisattva fulfills all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), or can they also fulfill them in the other stages?
Vajragarbha replied: "O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva is able to fulfill them throughout all ten stages."
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are thus most excellent in the seventh stage. Why is this?

Because in this seventh stage, the practice of effortful application is fulfilled, and one attains entry into the practice of mastery over wisdom. Son of the Buddha, in the first stage, the Bodhisattva seeks all phenomena as objects of focus;
therefore, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment. In the second stage, they are free from the stains of the mind.
In the third bhūmi, because the vows increase further and one attains the light of the Dharma; in the fourth bhūmi, because one enters the Path;
in the fifth bhūmi, because one accords with worldly activities; in the sixth bhūmi, because one enters the profound gateways of the Dharma;

and in the seventh bhūmi, because one gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas—all these likewise fulfill the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Why is this? Because from the first bhūmi, the Bodhisattva...
Up to the seventh stage, one accomplishes the division of the effortful application of wisdom;
by the power of this, from the eighth stage through the tenth, the effortless practice is fully accomplished. O Son of the Buddha, it is like two worlds:
one is defiled and the other is purely pure. The space between these two is difficult to traverse, except for Bodhisattvas who possess [this power].
O Son of the Buddha, it is likewise with the stages of the Bodhisattvas: there are practices that are defiled and practices that are pure.
Between these two, it is difficult to pass beyond them, except for a Bodhisattva who possesses great power of aspiration, skillful means, and wisdom, who is then able to pass beyond them.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha, this is the seventh stage."
Regarding whether these are defiled practices or pure practices, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:

"O Son of the Buddha, from the first stage through the seventh stage, all the practices performed abandon the karma of afflictions because they are dedicated toward unexcelled enlightenment and because one partially attains the path of equality;
yet, they are not yet called 'practices that transcend afflictions. O Son of the Buddha, it is, for example,"
A Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) mounts the divine elephant-treasure and travels through the four continents;
though he knows there are those who are poor, destitute, and suffering, he is not defiled by their various afflictions. Yet, this is not yet called "transcending the human state.

If he relinquishes his royal body and is born in the Brahma-world, mounting a celestial palace, he beholds a thousand worlds and travels through a thousand worlds, manifesting himself as a Brahma-king.
Such radiance and majestic power is called "transcending the human state. It is the same for the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Buddha:
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, they ride upon the vehicle of the *pāramitās* as they travel through the world.
Knowing the faults and afflictions of all worlds, because they ride upon the correct path, they are not defiled by the faults of affliction; yet, they have not [yet]...

It is called "Transcending the Course of Afflictions. When one abandons all conditioned activities involving effort and enters the eighth stage from the seventh stage, riding upon the pure vehicle of the bodhisattva, one wanders through the world; knowing the faults of afflictions, one is no longer defiled by them.
This is then called "Transcending the Course of Afflictions," because one has attained the complete transcendence of all [afflictions]. O Son of the Buddha, this...
The Bodhisattva of the seventh stage has completely transcended the multitude of afflictions such as excessive greed;

dwelling in this stage, they are neither called one who possesses afflictions nor one who is free from afflictions. Why is this? Because all afflictions do not manifest, they are not called "possessing" them;
yet because their aspiration for the wisdom of the Tathāgata is not yet fulfilled, they are not called "free" from them. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...
Abiding in this seventh stage with a profoundly pure mind, he accomplishes physical action, accomplishes verbal action, and accomplishes mental action.
He has completely abandoned all unwholesome paths of action censured by the Tathāgata, and constantly and skillfully practices all wholesome actions praised by the Tathāgata.
Regarding all worldly scriptures and technical arts, such as the five [sciences]...
It is taught that within this stage, all things proceed spontaneously without relying on effort;
this Bodhisattva serves as a Great Teacher of Illumination within the trichiliocosm, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata and those from the eighth stage upward,

for no other Bodhisattvas can equal him in profound resolve, wondrous conduct, meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and liberations (*vimokṣa*).
All these are manifested before them, yet they are accomplished through cultivation rather than being obtained as a result of karmic maturation; in this stage,

the Bodhisattva fully cultivates the power of skillful means and wisdom, as well as all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), becoming increasingly superior and perfect in every moment of thought.

[Treatise] Fourth: From "At that time" onwards, there is a section consisting of forty-four and a half lines of scripture that clarifies the similarities and differences in the progression through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Within the analytical explanation of its meaning, it is divided into seven sections: 1.
From "At that time, Vimukticandra" down to "is also able to fulfill," comprising two and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the question posed by Vimukticandra.
The Fulfillment of All Factors of Enlightenment in the Various Grounds, divided into two parts. Vajragarbha Bodhisattva spoke as follows, down to the tenth ground of effortless practice;
there are ten scriptural passages that clarify the answers to the preceding questions regarding the distinctions between the understanding and practice of the various grounds up to the tenth.
This section on the distinctions between the understanding and practice of the various grounds is divided into three parts. "O Sons of the Buddha, it is as if there were two worlds."

From "Having already attained... down to "...is able to transcend," there are four and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how the bodhisattva of this stage, by the power of their vows, enters both defiled and pure practices without abiding in either. From "The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said...
down to "...transcending the human level," there are eight and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the use of analogies to illustrate this stage.
The two types of conduct—defiled and pure—are neither purely pure nor purely defiled; this is divided into five sections for the sons of the Buddha.
Bodhisattvas are likewise thus, from the point below [the description of] attaining all exhaustion and transcendence.

There are six sections of sutra text clarifying that the seventh stage consists of conduct with effort (*sābhoga-prayoga*), while the eighth stage consists of effortless conduct (*anābhoga-prayoga*). This seventh stage has already been explained.
The section from "down to not being called 'without'" consists of three and a half lines of scripture clarifying that this stage is neither called "having afflictions" nor "being without afflictions.
The section from "dividing into the seven Buddha-sons" and "the Bodhisattvas,

having dwelt in this seventh stage," down to "becoming even more excellently perfected," consists of nine and a half lines of scripture clarifying the mastery of worldly arts and becoming a Great Illuminating Teacher.
Within these forty-four and a half lines of scripture, from the very beginning when Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha, does the Bodhisattva fulfill all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) only in this seventh stage, or can they also fulfill them in the other stages?
[The answer is given] by way of the gate of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
In total, it is the single essence of the Tathāgata’s fundamental, universal radiance, great wisdom, and the unimpeded integration of quiescence and function—the very body of bodhi.
If one considers the progressive excellence of cultivation, there are fifty kinds of distinctions in the practice of bodhi within the gate of differentiated characteristics;
however, regarding its general essence and overall character, it is defined solely by the distinctions of the bodhi of these ten stages.
Regarding the general framework for spiritual advancement, within these ten stages (*bhūmi*), enlightenment as a whole takes five types of *bodhi* as its fundamental essence.
These five types of *bodhi* are: first, the *bodhi* of emptiness and signlessness; second, the *bodhi* of universal radiance and non-abiding wisdom;
third, the *bodhi* of great vows capable of giving rise to great wisdom and great compassion to extensively benefit sentient beings; [the remaining two are omitted in the source].
The four ways of generating bodhicitta are as follows: first, the bodhi of non-attachment through great compassion, which is able to follow along with both defilement and purity;

second, the bodhi of the five wisdoms; third, the bodhi of the perfection of myriad practices through compassion; and fourth, the bodhi of non-action. Now, "bodhi" is translated here as "awakening" (*jue*).

"Awakening" refers to the universal penetration of all phenomena without error. It is called "unsurpassed" because it pertains solely to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and not to the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). First.
The bodhi of emptiness and signlessness is attained in common by both the three vehicles and the one vehicle;

however, they differ in that [the former] possesses the practice of great compassionate vows while [the latter] lacks it, and in their breadth or narrowness, and their quiescent or active functions. In its fundamental essence, they both equally return to the signless.
The bodhi of the two universal radiances and non-abiding wisdom belongs solely to the one vehicle and not to the three vehicles; it is the one vehicle.
Regarding the mind of the ten stages of the bodhisattva, the wisdom of the first stage is called "abiding where the Buddhas abide" because one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
By means of this ground of wisdom, one advances in the cultivation of all practices;

according to the distinctions of wisdom and the distinctions of practice, through the deepening of habitual cultivation, the ten pāramitās are established as fifty successive levels of advancement, never departing from them.

The stage of wisdom known as "Universal Radiance and Abiding Without Dependence," which is attained by those of initial resolve, is such that when wisdom is without substance, there is likewise no transition, for it abides primordially as it is.
Because it is not something produced by the arbitrary activity of the mind, this clarifies that there is ultimately no distinction between the initial resolve and the ultimate state.
As for the statement that "this initial resolve is more difficult than previous resolves," it is because attaining this stage of wisdom is difficult; thus it is said in this sutra.
It is said that one has already trodden the Tathāgata’s Ground of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-bhūmi*),

for this Dharma-gate of the sutra takes this wisdom as the essential ground for the arousal of the bodhicitta and for practice; thus, the ocean of all various kinds of wisdom and the ocean of the ten thousand practices arise therein,
and through the three great vows, one can give rise to great wisdom, engender great compassion, and extensively benefit sentient beings— this is what "bodhi" means.
It clarifies that all phenomena do not arise from themselves, but rather that wisdom arises by relying on the great vow and accomplishes compassion;
nor do they arise from another, because both wisdom and the vow lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); nor do they arise from both together, because phenomena lack the nature of conjunction;
nor are they without cause, for wisdom must depend upon the vow to give rise to the practice of loving-kindness and compassion. Therefore, it is said that the seed of the Buddha [arises from this].
Because of these conditions, it is said that there is but one vehicle (*ekayāna*), yet it appears as three vehicles. Some may stagnate in quiescence, while others merely take birth in the Pure Lands.
This is because, through great compassion for sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, they give rise to vast vows to bring wisdom to fulfillment.

Or it is said that those who, by means of their vows, retain afflictions (*kleśa*) to remain in Sahā are those who have attained the Bodhi of signlessness and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

This is because they have not yet attained the wisdom of universal radiance; thus, although the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles possess vows and practices, they all aspire to attain buddhahood after many kalpas, which differs from this teaching where [enlightenment] occurs in a single moment without temporal duration.

Furthermore, even when the effortless wisdom of a bodhisattva in the eighth stage manifests before them, they still fear stagnation in quiescence, and therefore they guard against it with the eighth vow-pāramitā.

First, it is to cause one to recollect their original vows; second, it is because the Buddhas of the ten directions, through the three empowerments and seven exhortations, inspire them so that their wisdom does not stagnate in quiescence;
third, it is because within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) there are ten gates of great vows that give rise to wisdom;
fourth, by means of their great compassion, they are able to follow along with both defilement and purity, yet remain neither defiled nor impure—this clarifies the first six stages (*bhūmi*).
By practicing the six pāramitās, one attains supramundane, mundane, and both supramundane and mundane bodhi;
reaching this seventh stage, one employs this supramundane, mundane, and both supramundane and mundane bodhi to enter into worldly affairs in common with all ordinary beings,
accomplishing the practice of great compassion and carrying out the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Because they are perfected, although they appear identical to worldly defilements, their wisdom is by nature undefiled;

thus, they dwell in the world without attachment, just as a lotus flower, though constantly born in water, remains forever unsullied by it. Furthermore, because of their original vows, they remain in the world to benefit sentient beings;
since there is no self-clinging or craving for worldly pleasures within the essence of their wisdom, they take no delight in love, pride, arrogance, or the opulence esteemed by the world.

Furthermore, the essence of clear wisdom is without dependence or inherent nature; it can accord with great vows to dwell within the worldly stream, yet belongs neither to defilement nor purity, remaining therein with sovereign mastery.

Thus, this seventh stage dharma-gate is not within the reach of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), nor is it known by those bodhisattvas who practice the six *pāramitās* while still harboring joy in or aversion toward afflictions (*kleśa*).
As stated in the following passage regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of the bodhisattva...

Because they cannot know that which is beyond the reach of Śākyamuni, for the sake of realizing the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows; because they cannot follow the cycle of birth and death as they do, for the sake of fulfilling the practices of Samantabhadra and perfecting great compassion;
because they still harbor joy and aversion toward birth and death, and experience weariness, whereas they delight in being born in the Pure Land;

and because they have attained the bodhi of non-action through the perfection of the five wisdoms, compassion, and the myriad practices—if one considers this from the perspective of general characteristics:
Within the gate of identical characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the essence of wisdom is not different and time is also not different;

thus, from the very first thought-moment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one possesses them all in their entirety. If, however, one considers it through the gate of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), then during the ten stages, the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), and the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), one attains one portion of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom of identical essence, one portion of the Tathāgata’s practice of identical essence, and the turning [of the wheel] of all Tathāgatas.

Toward the gateway of the great vow, where compassion and wisdom are harmoniously perfected, from the first stage through the sixth stage, one nurtures and accomplishes the dharmas according to the three stages of the prior stage of worthiness; thereby, one emerges from the entanglements.
Although there is compassion, it is the aspiration that all sentient beings transcend the world—a compassion like that of the seventh stage which dwells eternally [in the cycle].
Just as a lotus in the world remains unsullied by water, it is clarified that birth and death are eternally quiescent;

from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, one has followed the teachings to give rise to faith and compliance, acting according to the nature of dharmas rather than through one's own limited power.
Thus, now upon reaching this seventh stage, as one is about to advance toward the supramundane mind of liberation, one only then begins to dwell amidst entanglements without being defiled.

Because he was newly established in the same customs as his fellow residents and took birth through the power of compassionate vows, he first entered the world through the gate of the three kinds of emptiness and non-action;
yet, as he practiced expedient means in concert with worldly entanglements, there still remained the dual latencies of non-action and action.

Since his conduct was still characterized by effort and his development was still unfolding, Sudhana—the personification of the Dharma—is called "Opening" (Kai) as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
One spreads the flowers of the tree of wisdom so that they bloom, causing the flowers of the ten thousand practices to flourish like the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
From this point onward, one enters the entanglements of the world; as the flowers of conduct unfold, one reaches the eighth and tenth stages, where compassion and wisdom are perfected.

One benefits sentient beings according to their needs through effortless action (*anābhoga*), until finally reaching the eleventh stage, where those benefited by one’s activity become equal [to the Buddha].
The Dharma-realm manifests physical bodies according to faculties and according to time; there is nothing it does not benefit, yet it acts without striving and responds without effort.
By means of the wisdom of universal radiance, it is not confined by spatial location and accords with the minds of sentient beings, manifesting forms according to objects without coming or going.
Thus, the wisdom of universal radiance is identical to the deluded minds of all sentient beings.
Because it is the single essence of nature, it is able to know the karmic actions performed by all sentient beings and manifest accordingly;
therefore, the Sūtra says that "in the first stage, one seeks all Buddha-dharmas.

This clarifies that the first stage is the stage of the three types of worthy ones (*tri-kalyāṇa-pudgala*) prior to the stages of application, wherein one establishes the model of the Buddha-fruit and vows to accomplish it.
It is not because one’s own practice is perfected; rather, it is because of the fulfillment of vows and the seeking of Bodhi.

Just as the models for the fruits of Buddhahood in the three vehicles appear after the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the model for the practice toward the fruit of Buddhahood in this sutra appears prior to the ten stages, extending even to the assembly of gods and spirits in the first chapter.
The statement that "all [attain] the second stage because they have removed the stains of the mind" clarifies what has been discussed above.

The aforementioned ten wholesome dharmas constitute the nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) of the Dharma-body, which purify all delusions. In the third stage (*bhūmi*), vows increase further, and one attains the radiance of the Dharma;
this clarifies that through the cultivation of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis of the two upper realms, one is called "pure and luminous wisdom" (*jñāna-prajñā-viśuddha-prabhāsa*).
Because one transcends the mental obstacles of the three realms and enters the ninth concentration (*samādhi*), one enters the fourth stage.

"The reason for the fifth stage is that it clarifies how, by cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as aids to the contemplation of bodhi, one causes the eye of wisdom to become clear and pure.

The reason for the sixth stage is that it accords with worldly activities; this clarifies how, through the gate of meditative concentration on the non-activity of the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm, one can accord with and penetrate all worldly arts and crafts, fully understanding them. The seventh stage is the entry into the profound dharma."
The "Gate" (Mukha) signifies that because wisdom and skillful means illuminate all mundane and supramundane phenomena, nothing remains unilluminated;
thus, the seventh stage gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas. It is explained that the seventh stage is able to enter the mundane and study the practices of Samantabhadra.
Although the preceding stages take universal radiance-wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*) as their essence, they all involve both learning and understanding.
There is a dharma-gate of practice with effort and aspiration for the higher stages; from the eighth stage through the tenth stage, all effortless practices (*anābhoga-caryā*) are fully accomplished.
At the beginning of the eighth stage, one first attains wisdom that is effortless; in the ninth stage, it is explained that there is mastery in teaching through the clarity of effortless wisdom;
and in the tenth stage, it is explained that there is effortless middle-way wisdom characterized by both compassion and wisdom.
Because it is the total fulfillment [of all practices] and because it is identical to the stage of Buddhahood, the seventh stage is the most preeminent. As the subsequent text states:
"Because the practice of effort (*prayoga*) is perfected," this clarifies that from the sixth stage onward, the wisdom of non-effort (*anābhoga*) gives rise to the myriad practices of effort;
thus, the conduct of Samantabhadra is perfected, reaching its fruition at the tenth stage within this very position.

Therefore, it is clarified that while the practice of the cause is difficult to initiate, the practice of the fruit is easy to accomplish; just as water entering a current flows spontaneously to the ocean, how much more so this practice, which does not fail to reach the sea?

This is the seventh stage of practice, identical to the conduct of the seventh dwelling within the ten dwellings, like the conduct of the laywoman Śreṣṭhī Viśākhā, who practiced the conduct of eighty-four thousand nayutas of sentient beings. I—
All are identical in this regard: just as the seventh stage of the Ten Practices (daśabhūmika) involves the King of Fulfillment manifesting his own transformation body to demonstrate acts of killing,
and just as in the seventh dedication of the Ten Dedications one sees Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to the west of Mount Vajra,
each of the practice-gates within this seventh stage follows the patterns of the practices and realizations prior to the stages.

In this manner, the three stages prior to the grounds—those of resolution, practice, and completion—are fully exhausted; within the ten grounds, one accumulates merit and perfects virtue, such that the fruition is identical to that which existed prior to the grounds.

Because the grounds prior to the [first] ground are the fruition, while the practices on the grounds are the cause, and because one emulates the fruition of the pre-ground stages, the Buddha-fruition established in the Mahāyāna differs from that of the three vehicles, which is attained after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. If a practitioner...
Thoroughly understand the intent of the teaching and do not engage in false interpretations.

When the Buddha-mind is correctly cultivated as the cause for the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), it simultaneously traverses all five stages—the ten abodes, the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds, and the eleventh ground.
Because wisdom and its object are non-dual, there is no shifting of time; sealed by the single Dharma-realm wisdom-seal, it transcends past and present.
Furthermore, if one relies on the principle of the six aspects (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*), then the fruit of the perfected cause of understanding is fully complete;
if one looks toward the arising of wisdom and the penetration of the fetters, then the merit of the initial stage of the "Abiding in the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) is supreme;

and if one takes great compassion as the foremost, then the seventh abiding, the seventh practice, the seventh dedication, and the seventh ground are superior, while all others proceed spontaneously (*anābhoga*).
Because it is fulfilled, as the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, it is like a world where one region is defiled and another region is purely pure;
between these two, it is difficult for anyone to pass through. This clarifies that the sixth stage is purely pure and the seventh stage is purely defiled;
in these two positions, one is obstructed by purity and defilement, making it difficult to pass beyond them. As stated in the subsequent passage: "Except for Bodhisattvas..."
From "The power of great skillful means, supernormal knowledges, and vows" onwards, the meaning is clarified by the text itself:

it clarifies that through great compassion and great wisdom—never departing from these two practices—one teaches and transforms all sentient beings, causing them to ultimately achieve Great Bodhi and possess the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
One manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) by means of applied wisdom (*prāyogika-jñāna*), and by means of fundamental wisdom...
Through the power of contemplative observation, the wisdom of differentiation is accomplished. Liberation Moon Bodhisattva asked:
"O Son of the Buddha, are the practices of a bodhisattva in this seventh stage defiled or are they pure? Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
"O Son of the Buddha, all the practices performed from the first stage through the seventh stage abandon the portion of afflictions and karma, and thus attain equanimity."

Although he has not yet surpassed the conduct of those still afflicted by defilements—as illustrated by the metaphor of the Wheel-Turning King—he does not depart from the human state, nor is he subject to the afflictions of poverty or hardship.

As the text clearly explains in detail, this is because he has attained the sublime wisdom of the three emptinesses and the fundamental gnosis within the sixth stage, further augmented by the power of his great vows and the mastery of his wisdom; thus, he does not depart from the human realm.
Abiding in a state unstained by worldly dharmas, one can participate in mundane affairs without being defiled or pure;

because wisdom has no basis, it does not undergo constant defilement, and because defilement has no basis, it cannot stain or purify. This is solely for the sake of the skillful means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) arising through dependent origination to benefit sentient beings.
At the eighth stage, the functions of integration reach their consummation in the practice of non-action; at the tenth stage, there is partial mastery.
If, at the end, the seven stages were extinguished, there would be no practice, no merit, and no fulfillment of the inexhaustible great compassion and great wisdom of Samantabhadra;

for this reason, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, in contrast to the seeds of the three vehicles that have emerged from entanglement, states that the category of afflictions (*kleśa*) is the seed of the Tathāgata.
Thus, it also says that a lotus blooming within fire is truly a marvel. This is the intended meaning.

Those who have already attained the sixth stage and previously emerged from the entanglements are said [to have reached this]; however, those who are still bound by all fetters cannot yet fully ascend this path.
