The remaining text is as fully detailed in the sūtra itself. "Dhyānas" refers to meditative absorption; "samādhis" refers to being free from dullness and agitation;
"samāpattis" refers to the correct reception of all phenomena through their correspondence with wisdom; thus, one attains supernatural powers and liberation.

"Liberation" refers to attaining mastery over the supernormal powers (abhijñā) through the conjunction of correct meditative absorption (samādhi) and the wisdom that realizes all phenomena; this is called liberation.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Combined Commentary*, Fascicle Sixty-One.

The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tōngxuán, a Layman of Fāngshān in Tàiyuán during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, Collating the Sūtras and Commentaries on the *Daśabhūmika*,
Fascicle 26 of 10. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he enters the Bodhisattva samādhi of Skillful Observation and Selection (*suvicaya*), and skillfully selects the meaning.
The Samādhi of Unfailing Supreme Wisdom; the Samādhi of Discerning the Treasury of Meanings; the Samādhi of Discerning Meanings as They Truly Are; the Samādhi of Firmly Abiding in the Solid Root;
the Samādhi of the Gateway of Wisdom and Supernatural Powers; the Samādhi of the Activity of the Dharma-realm;
the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Victorious Attainments; the Samādhi of the Gateway to the Various Treasuries of Meaning and to Saṃsāra and Nirvāṇa—[he] entered such as these.
By means of the gate of great wisdom and supernormal powers, and through hundreds of thousands of samādhis, this stage is purified; for this bodhisattva, having attained these samādhis,
has well-cultivated the skillful means of wisdom and, by the power of great compassion, transcends the stages of the two vehicles to attain the stage of investigative wisdom.
[Commentary] The section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" and extending for seven and a half lines of scripture clarifies the ten kinds of well-discriminating samādhis (*suvicita-samādhi*).

Within the analysis of its meaning, this is divided into two parts: first, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage" down to "purifying this stage," there are five and a half lines of scripture that clarify the attainment of the ten kinds of samādhis; second...
After this Bodhisattva has attained these samādhis, from the section down to the "Stage of Wisdom" (jñānabhūmi),

there are one and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the attainment of ten great samādhis and the surpassing of the stage of the Two Vehicles (dvayayāna). This should rather be stated as "surpassing the stage of the Three Vehicles" (triyāna),
yet because those who translated this sūtra were students of the Three Vehicles and did not properly understand the intent of the teaching, they merely said [the former].
It is said that they "surpass the two vehicles" rather than "surpass the three vehicles. If it were merely to surpass the two vehicles, as this verse in the sutra states:
"Among all the various classes of sentient beings in the world, few desire to seek the path of the śrāvaka;
those who seek the path of the pratyekabuddha are even fewer still; those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare. Yet, seeking the Mahāyāna is still considered easy."
It is extremely difficult to be able to believe this Dharma. If this stage merely transcends the Two Vehicles, then as for the meaning of these Four Vehicles, how can they be established?
How could the meanings of a single scripture be such that its preceding and succeeding sections do not cohere?
It is simply because those of the Three Vehicles have been misled by their own wisdom; it was titled with the "Holy Intent," yet later there were no gentlemen who thoroughly understood it.
Based on this statement, one should say that they "surpass the three vehicles" rather than "the two vehicles. The Sūtra states:

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they enter the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Investigation and Selection. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva in this stage enters the samādhis of skillful investigation and selection in their proper sequence:
"This is the dhyāna-concentration of the form realm; this is the dhyāna-concentration of the formless realm; this is the Śrāvaka [vehicle]; and so forth.
The *Pratyekabuddha* [samādhi] is the samādhi of well-discriminating the meaning of the fixed three vehicles or the fixed one vehicle;
it clarifies the well-discriminated meaning of the mundane and the supramundane, as well as what is the correct meaning and what is the erroneous meaning.

The *Parama-prajñā* (Supreme Wisdom) samādhi is the wisdom of the Buddha of the One Vehicle. Therefore, the *Arthagarbha* (Meaning-Treasury) samādhi is the treasury of the Small Vehicle, while this is the Great [Vehicle].
The Samādhi of the Correctly Discerning Meaning of the Vehicle-Treasury as the One Vehicle-Treasury is so called because it knows all phenomena as they truly are and does not falsely interpret them.
The Samādhi of Firmly Abiding in the Root is so called because it is non-retrogressive.

The Samādhi of the Gateway of Wisdom and Supernatural Powers is so called because by means of this wisdom, one can give rise to various gateways of supernatural powers. Regarding the Dharma... [text ends]
The Samādhi of the Real Nature of the Realms and Karma is so called because there is nothing—whether movement or stillness within the mind and its objects—that is not true.

The Tathāgata’s Victorious Samādhi is so called because, being without mind and without thought, wisdom accords with the teachings and transformations of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, yet remains free from the characteristics of coming and going.
The Samādhi of the Treasury of Various Meanings is so called because it encompasses all phenomena, such that there is nothing it does not penetrate, including both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Regarding the samādhi of nirvāṇa: it is clear that because the dharma of the eternal quiescence of nirvāṇa exists, there is birth and death;
yet because birth and death are taken as nirvāṇa, both are devoid of intrinsic nature. Because the quiescent and the active are one true reality, there is no self and no person.
Because wisdom can conform to worldly conventions to benefit all sentient beings, the following summary is complete in the text itself.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, because a bodhisattva dwelling in this stage practices the well-purified, immeasurable, signless conduct of body; practices the well-purified, immeasurable, signless conduct of speech;
and practices the well-purified, immeasurable, signless conduct of mind, they attain the light of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Liberation Moon Bodhisattva said: "O Son of the Buddha, all that [the bodhisattva] has possessed from the first stage onward..."

"Does the purification of one’s physical, verbal, and mental karma not surpass that of the followers of the Two Vehicles? Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied, "O Son of the Buddha, it does indeed surpass them;
however, this is solely due to the power of seeking all Buddha-dharmas through aspiration, and not yet by the power of observation through one's own wisdom.
Now, in this seventh stage, by virtue of the power of one's own wisdom, nothing can be reached by any of the followers of the Two Vehicles. It is, for example, like a king."
When a son is born into a royal family, he is produced by the Queen and is endowed with the marks of royalty;

as soon as he is born, he surpasses all the ministers, yet this is solely through the power of the king and not his own power. When he has grown up and perfected all arts and skills, he then surpasses everyone through his own power.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: at the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment, by means of their resolve...

Because they seek the Great Dharma, they transcend all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; now abiding in this stage, by the power of the wisdom of their own practice, they surpass all those of the two vehicles.

[Treatise] The section beginning with "The sixth son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... and extending for twelve and a half lines of scripture clarifies how all three types of action (trikarma) from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward surpass those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). In the detailed explanation of this meaning, it is divided into five sections.
First, the section from "O son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage" down to "the light of the dharma-patience" consists of two and a half lines of scripture.
The section explaining that the immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions of the bodhisattvas on this stage are all characterized by signless practice is divided into two parts:
from "Vimukticandra" downwards to "surpassing the three vehicles," which consists of two lines of verse; this is the section where Vimukticandra poses the question.
From "Vajragarbha" downwards to "that which cannot be reached by any of the three vehicles," there are two lines.
Half of this sutra consists of the section where Vajragarbha Bodhisattva answers the questions.

From "For example" (*tadyathā*) onwards, up to the two and a half lines of verse beginning with "By one's own power surpassing [others]," constitutes the fifth part, which clarifies the section on providing analogies through illustrative examples.
From "All bodhisattvas" onwards, up to the three lines of verse stating "surpassing all three vehicles," clarifies the stage of this *bodhi*.

"Sā" (薩) refers to the Bodhisattva’s own power surpassing the three vehicles (*triyāna*), as they have already surpassed those who, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, merely seek the Great Dharma.

The meaning of the above twelve and a half lines of scripture clarifies that the immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental karma of a Bodhisattva at this stage surpasses the three vehicles by their own power;
beyond the wisdom [of those vehicles], they cultivate emptiness while practicing only the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Furthermore—

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having suppressed the active manifestations of afflictions so that they do not arise, attain the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jarāmaraṇa*) in other directions—or as some say, in the "upper direction"—where there are pure lands of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

These three vehicles are all provisional establishments by the Tathāgata, established as skillful means to temporarily avoid coarse suffering; they are not like this teaching, which issues forth from wisdom.
The mind itself is this Sahā world, which is immediately the Pure Land, the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), and so forth, pervading all of space.
Purity and defilement are mutually contained; within a single atom are many lands, without any distinction of self or other, or coming and going.

When the assembly of translators failed to discern the Buddha’s intent, they erroneously inscribed "by imperial decree" (*shengzhi*) and titled it "Surpassing the Two Vehicles. Let later students not fall into such error.
Furthermore, it is clarified that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage, the pursuit of the Great Dharma and the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*) surpass [other vehicles],
but this is not due to one's own power (*svabala*). This seventh stage clarifies that one’s own power surpasses the three vehicles (*triyāna*),
as is self-evident from the text itself.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, they attain the profound seclusion of non-action while constantly engaging in the activities of body, speech, and mind.
They diligently seek the supreme path without ever abandoning it; therefore, although the Bodhisattva practices within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they do not realize [nirvana].
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha, from which stage does a Bodhisattva come to be able to enter cessation?"
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha said: "O Son of the Buddha, from the sixth bhūmi onward, bodhisattvas are able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
now, dwelling in this [seventh] bhūmi, they are able to enter it moment by moment and arise from it moment by moment, yet they do not realize [the ultimate limit].
For this reason, this bodhisattva is called one who has accomplished inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind, and who courses in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) without realizing it."

For example, suppose there is a person who boards a ship and enters the ocean; by the power of skillful means, they do not encounter the perils of the water. A bodhisattva at this stage is also like this:
boarding the ship of the *pāramitās*, they travel upon the ocean of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet by the power of their vows, they do not realize cessation (*nirvāṇa*).

[Treatise] The seventh section contains nine and a half lines of scripture that clarify this stage as being far removed from the practices of existence and non-existence, wherein one constantly practices the actions of body, speech, and mind, and constantly enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) without yet realizing it. In the commentary on the meaning, this is divided into five sections.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva... down to "...though he practices the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), he does not realize it," there are two parts.
The section on "Practicing Half a Sūtra" clarifies not abiding in non-practice while constantly practicing the three karmas and not realizing nirvāṇa; this is divided into two parts.

From "Vimukticandra" down to "is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation" constitutes one sūtra-section, which is the part where Vimukticandra raises questions, divided into three sections.
From "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said" down to "and does not realize [it]" comprises two lines.
The Sūtra clarifies that Bodhisattvas of this stage and those of the sixth stage are able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) without realizing it;

this is divided into four parts. From "This Bodhisattva... down to "...practicing at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without realizing it," one and a half lines of the Sūtra clarify that the three karmas of the Bodhisattvas of this stage are inconceivable and do not grasp at the realization of quiescence; this is divided into five parts. [The fifth part is] the simile.
For example, there is a passage of two and a half lines of scripture that clarifies the analogy of a person who has descended into the sea by boat and does not encounter the perils of the water;
this refers to Bodhisattvas from the sixth ground onward and those in the seventh ground who enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Their realization of cessation is neither like that of those in the four dhyānas or four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) of the upper realms who realize cessation through the suppression of conceptualization (*saṃjñā-vyupaśama*), nor is it like [the aforementioned].
The Arhats, weary of suffering, cultivate emptiness; following the extinction of the nature of emptiness, their compassion and wisdom do not arise.
Like the great void, they have nothing further to do, and even if a drum were struck upon their heads for an entire kalpa, they would not perceive it nor hear its sound.

Furthermore, there are those who use transformed fire to incinerate themselves and enter the death and rebirth of transformation; yet this is not like the Pratyekabuddhas who contemplate the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination.

In accordance with the contemplation of emptiness, compassion and wisdom do not arise; nor is it as in the provisional teachings, where bodhisattvas analyze phenomena to clarify emptiness and follow emptiness until the nature of reality is naturally non-arising.
By the power of their original vows and through the cultivation of the six perfections, coarse consciousness has already ceased while subtle consciousness still remains.
Because they follow the power of their vows, they are born in a Pure Land—or, as some say, in a Land of Retribution.
Above the realm of form, for those whose bodies have transcended the three realms, the mind has a basis of reliance and pure karma serves as the condition;

yet even in all such places of birth, there remains a basis of reliance. Within this One Vehicle, the mind of the sixth stage of the ten abodes is like that of the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, who sat cross-legged by the side of a walking path, detached from inhalation and exhalation, following [the breath].
The manifestations of his physical body appear as emanations like clouds, pervading the ocean of lands;
this refers to the gate of the infinite dharma-realm of the fundamental, universal radiance wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*), wherein the essence and function are inherently quiescent and limitless.
This differs from the three vehicles, where all emanated activities are based on places of rebirth resulting from karmic fruition and are thus subject to limitations. Thus it is said.
In the sixth stage of the Ten Stages, having already clarified the increase of power through guarding all cities, one is now able to guard the city of the mind;

it is not comprised of either meditative concentration or distraction, and the worldly affairs engaged in are those required for common purpose, as they do not arise from one's own [independent] karma.
The seventh stage is characterized by utility and development, initiating practice as in the three preceding emptinesses.
Therefore, Sudhana, in this stage, the spiritual friend is named Kapphiṇa (Flower-Blossoming Tree), who constantly develops the flowers of practice through the three emptinesses.
Thus, from the sixth stage onward, one is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation;

specifically, in the sixth of the ten dwellings (*daśavihāra*), one takes the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja as a model, following through the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

In each of the eleven stages, this general principle applies to every sixth mind. Even if one does not enter meditative absorption, it is simply explained that the Ocean Banner (*Sāgaradhvaja*) constitutes the essence;
the subsequent [minds] are the great functions within the Ocean Banner. The remaining meaning is self-evident from the sutra itself.
The preceding section clarifies the gate of not realizing *nirvāṇa*.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva, having attained such power of the wisdom of samādhi, manifests birth and death through great skillful means while constantly abiding in nirvāṇa;
though surrounded by a retinue, he always delights in solitude;
though taking birth within the three realms by the power of his vows, he is not defiled by worldly dharmas; and though eternally quiescent, by the power of skillful means—
Yet he returns to blaze intensely; though he does not burn, he accords with the Buddha’s wisdom while manifesting entry into the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
though he has attained the treasury of the Buddha-realm, he manifests abiding in the realm of Māra; though he transcends the path of Māra, he manifests the practice of Māra’s arts;
though he manifests conduct identical to that of non-Buddhists, he does not abandon the Buddha-dharma; and though he manifests compliance with all things...
While remaining in the world, he constantly practices all supramundane dharmas;
all his various adornments surpass those possessed by all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
[He] does not abandon the mind that delights in the Dharma.
[Treatise: The eighth section contains eleven lines of sūtra clarifying the stage of "demonstrating entry into all paths of saṃsāra through skillful means while abiding in the Buddha-dharma.
The commentary on its meaning states: "By means of the skillful means of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), one manifests ten kinds of demonstrations."
Manifesting a mind that transcends the world yet does not abandon the joy of the Dharma, as the Sūtra says:
"Although they accord with the Buddha-wisdom, they manifest entry into the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

This clarifies that after those of the Two Vehicles have attained their fruits, they become weary of the body of分段 (pudgala) birth produced by parents; they themselves transform it by fire and themselves [attain parinirvāṇa].
"Having burned his body, he enters the cycle of birth and death characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma-śarīra*); the remainder is self-evident from the text. Below, it says:
'The devas' refers to those in the desire realm, form realm, and formless realm. The *nāgas* are the various worldly dragons.
The *yakṣas*—this is translated as 'those who live in suffering,' or 'the observers,' or 'the swift ones. The *gandharvas*—this is called 'those who eat [fragrance]'."
*Gandharva* (sometimes called *Gandhāra*) means "Fragrance" or "Seeker of Fragrance"; these deities provide music and seek food.
*Asura* refers to those included within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*); this is translated as "Lacking Celestial Bliss.

*Garuda* is translated as "Voice of Sorrowful Pain," for they eat dragons that remain alive within their throats, producing sounds of sorrowful pain; they are also known as the Jewel-Winged Birds. *Kinnara* [is translated as "Slightly Human"].
This is called the "Doubtful Deity" (*Śaṅkā-deva*); because there are horns upon its head, people who see it wonder whether it is a human or a non-human (*amanuṣya*).

A *mahoraga* is translated here as "one who crawls on the chest and belly. This belongs to the same class as various animals and is akin to the dragons. The ancients called it the "Great Python Deity.
Regarding "humans and non-humans," "non-humans" refers to the class of ghosts (*preta*). As for Śakra, this is translated as "The Capable Lord" (*Indra*).
The Brahmā King is the sovereign of the first dhyāna. "Brahmā" means purity; because he has transcended the desire realm, he is called the Pure King.
This clarifies that bodhisattvas at this stage are able to universally identify with his kind and lead them to cultivate the merit and wisdom of bodhi without attachment or delight.
Therefore, it is said that they do not abandon their mind for the joy of the Dharma. The rest is self-evident in the text. Furthermore, it clarifies the self... [text ends].
After rejoicing, until the subsequent stage is fulfilled, one must diligently delight the mind in the Dharma. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom and dwells in the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*), by the power of their vows they are able to see many Buddhas—
namely, they see many hundreds of Buddhas, up to and including many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas.
In that Buddha-field, with a vast and superior mind, they made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise;
they bestowed all requisites for life—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and everything necessary for livelihood—and also made offerings to the entire Saṃgha.
They dedicated these roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, at that time...
Having respectfully listened to the Dharma taught by the Buddha, they receive and uphold it, attaining the light of wisdom from the samādhi of reality as it is.
They practice in accordance with this, being protected by all Buddhas as they constantly uphold the True Dharma.

They are always praised and rejoiced in by the Tathāgatas, and no challenges or difficulties posed by any of the followers of the two vehicles can cause them to retreat or be discouraged. Their patience regarding the Dharma for benefiting sentient beings is pure, just like space.
The roots of goodness accumulated over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas in this sutra become further increased and more excellent;
they are like pure gold interspersed and adorned with various wonderful jewels, which becomes even more excellent and its radiance doubled such that no other ornaments can equal it.
Likewise, all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva dwelling in this seventh stage also [become further increased and more excellent].
In this way, through the power of skillful means and wisdom, it becomes increasingly bright and pure, surpassing what can be attained by those of the two vehicles.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the light of the sun, which no light of the stars or moon can equal; it can completely dry up all the mud and mire upon the land of Jambudvīpa.
This Bodhisattva of the Stage of Far-Going is also like this, for none of the followers of the two vehicles can compare to them.
There is a Bodhisattva who is capable, indeed fully capable, of drying up the muddy quagmire of the cognitive delusions of all sentient beings;

among the ten *pāramitās*, this Bodhisattva’s *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) is predominant, though the others are not uncultivated, being practiced according to his strength and capacity.
Son of the Buddha, this is a brief explanation of the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā*). When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he...
He frequently acts as the King of the Heaven of Sovereign Mastery (*Īśāna-devendra*), skillfully teaching sentient beings the Dharma of realized wisdom so that they may enter into its realization.

Through all such activities—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—he never departs from mindfulness of the Buddha, nor does he ever depart from mindfulness of the perfection of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes. Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I shall, within..."
Among all sentient beings, this bodhisattva is the foremost, the most excellent, and even the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If such a bodhisattva exerts diligent vigor, in a single moment they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas as their retinue. If, by means of the bodhisattva...
Through the sovereign manifestation of his sublime power of vows, he displays [realms] exceeding this number,

such that even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas they could not be counted or known. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

[Treatise] The ninth section contains twenty-nine and a half lines of scripture that clarify how a bodhisattva in this stage perceives numerous Buddhas through the power of their vows and receives their office.
Within the explanation of this meaning, it is divided into five sections. First, from "O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva...
down to "...cannot be matched by other ornaments," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture that clarify this.
In this Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (Far-Reaching Ground), one attains the vision of many Buddhas and the offering of worship, whereby the hearing of the Dharma increases in excellence.

This section is divided into two parts: [1] the Bodhisattva dwelling in this seventh ground, down to the point where the mire of the cognitive afflictions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of all sentient beings is described;
[2] the five lines and a half of sūtra text clarifying that which the three vehicles do not surpass. This section begins with "This Bodhisattva... and extends down to the seventh [point].
In the *Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*, there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the gates of practice cultivated on this stage, divided into four parts.

From "When a bodhisattva has dwelt in this stage" down to "relying upon the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)," there are five lines of sūtra that clarify this section concerning the bodhisattva’s reception of office, their fitness to serve as a refuge for sentient beings, and their pursuit of wisdom. Regarding this bodhisattva:

Following the passage on "having aroused diligent effort," there are four and a half lines of scripture that clarify the measure of the dharmas, samādhis, and their associated retinues obtained through the power of one's own diligence and vows by a bodhisattva at this stage; they are illustrated by the metaphor of refined pure gold becoming increasingly bright and pure.
From the sixth stage onward, it is explained that [the bodhisattva] merely refines, polishes, and cleanses [the mind] to make it increasingly bright and pure.

This refers to the further cultivation of morality, concentration, wisdom, the four foundations of mindfulness, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth, to thoroughly purify the ground of gnosis;

it causes this ground to skillfully enter worldly expedient means, manifesting various forms of sentient beings' conduct and being able to teach and transform sentient beings through "acting in concert" with them;
thus it is explained as being adorned by the intermingling of various exquisite jewels, and is clarified by purity.
The wondrous wisdom adorns various multitudes of practices, and these various multitudes of practices adorn the ground of wisdom;
they mutually manifest and further increase its clarity and purity. The mind clarifies this ground by using universally radiant wisdom to adorn the myriad practices;
through practices that benefit sentient beings in the world, it gives rise to the sovereign function of wisdom, making wisdom even more luminous.
Therefore, when wisdom does not manifest in contrast to the myriad practices, that wisdom lacks a great master; this refers precisely to the Three Vehicles.
When the myriad practices do not proceed by means of wisdom, they are subject to limitations; these are the virtuous deeds of humans, devas, and non-Buddhists.
The remaining text is fully contained within the sutra itself.
[Sūtra] The Path of Samādhi of the Wisdom of the Ultimate Truth: Through the practice of the sixth stage, the mind becomes fulfilled;
Immediately, one accomplishes skillful means and wisdom. By this, the Bodhisattva enters the seventh stage;
Though clear regarding the three gates of liberation, they give rise to compassion; Though equal to the Tathāgatas, they diligently make offerings to the Buddhas.
Though contemplating emptiness, they accumulate merit; by this, the Bodhisattva ascends to the seventh stage.
Having transcended the triple world, they adorn it; extinguishing the fire of delusion, they kindle the flame of wisdom.
Knowing that all phenomena are non-dual, they diligently perform their tasks; realizing that all lands are empty, they delight in adorning the Buddha-fields.

Understanding that the body is immovable yet endowed with all marks, and realizing that the nature of sound is detached while skillfully expounding it, one enters into the distinctness of phenomena within a single thought-moment. By this, the wise ascend to the seventh stage;
observing these dharmas with clarity, they extensively bring benefit to the deluded masses.
Entering the realm of sentient beings without limit, The Buddha’s work of transformation is likewise immeasurable;
Regarding the lands, all phenomena, and the number of eons, He understands their desires, minds, and conduct, entering them all.
He preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles without end, Thus transforming and guiding all living beings.
The Bodhisattva diligently seeks the most supreme path; whether moving or resting, they do not abandon skillful means and wisdom.
Each and every action is dedicated toward the Buddha’s bodhi; in every thought-moment, they accomplish the pāramitās.
To resolve the mind and dedicate it is the perfection of giving; to extinguish delusions is the precept of morality; and non-harming is patience.
Seeking the good without weariness is the strategy for progress; Remaining unmoved within the Path is the cultivation of dhyāna;
Enduring non-arising is called prajñā; Dedication is skillful means, and the power of aspiring for vows is indestructible;
The wisdom that thoroughly understands—may all such things be fully perfected.
On the first stage, the objects of focus and merit are fulfilled; On the second, one is free from defilement;
on the third, disputes cease; On the fourth, one enters the Path; on the fifth, one acts in accordance with it; On the sixth, the light of the wisdom of non-arising shines forth;
On the seventh abiding, the merit of awakening is fulfilled, And all various great vows are fully perfected.
By this, all that is performed within the eighth stage is rendered completely pure;

the wisdom that arises here is difficult to surpass. It is like the space between two worlds, and like a noble universal monarch who is free from attachment; yet it is not yet called "complete transcendence."
When one dwells within the eighth stage of wisdom, Only then does one transcend the realm of the mind.
Like Brahmā observing the world while transcending the human station, Or like a lotus in water remaining unstained,
Though this stage transcends all multitudes of delusions, It is not called "having delusions," nor is it "without delusions."
Moving within this world without afflictions, they seek the wisdom of the Buddha with insatiable minds;
they are universally proficient in all worldly arts and crafts, as well as in scriptures, rhetoric, and treatises,
and have fully accomplished such practices as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The Bodhisattva cultivates and perfects the path of the seventh stage, Transcending all practices of the two vehicles.
Through wisdom, the vows of the first stage are fulfilled; Like a prince endowed with full power, he achieves profound depth and yet advances further on the path.
With each moment of mind, he remains in tranquil extinction, yet does not realize final cessation.
Just as one who boards a ship enters the great ocean, Though in the water, they are not drowned by it;
Possessing the merit of skillful means and wise conduct, None in all the world can comprehend them.
The mind that honors many Buddhas becomes increasingly clear, Like the radiant light adorned with exquisite jewels.
The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas on this stage is most luminous, Like the sun spreading its light to dry up the waters of craving.
Furthermore, they act as sovereign lords among the gods, Transforming and guiding all beings to cultivate right wisdom.
If, through the power of courageous diligence, They attain many samādhis and behold many Buddhas.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas, And even more than that through the mastery of the power of vows—
This is the Bodhisattva stage of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā), The pure path of skillful means and wisdom.
Neither the gods nor humans of all the worlds, Nor the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, can know it.
[Treatise] In the sixth section, there are forty-two verses that repeat the preceding *dharmaparyāya* as found in the full text.
Regarding the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), five gates will be explained; first, the explanation of the name of this stage is as follows:
Why is this stage named the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*)? It is because at this level, the Bodhisattva’s wisdom regarding worldly affairs requires no effort;

through divine wisdom, they contemplate without thinking and act without striving, while their wisdom spontaneously adapts and transforms all phenomena in infinite ways—therefore, it is called the Immovable Stage.
Second, as for what gate of practice is cultivated on this stage: on this stage, one practices the gate of vows (*praṇidhāna*).
The pāramitās serve to increase the wisdom of this stage; because the essence of wisdom is fundamentally pure, one brings forth practice through aspiration, becoming increasingly sovereign.

If one did not give rise to wisdom through aspiration, there would be the fear of returning to the level of the two vehicles; therefore, one uses aspiration to guard against it so as not to stagnate in purity.
Having reached this stage, it is in accordance with the Dharma that one receives the three empowerments and seven kinds of exhortations from all Buddhas, urging one to remember one's original vow.
May the wisdom of arising be generated; through its spontaneous activity, may vast compassion be able to arise, whereby one may accomplish the wisdom of non-action.
When the application of great compassion is perfected, one enters the seventh stage, which is characterized by effort and development within the worldly realm.
Having accomplished this stage of effort and development, one reaches the state of effortless non-development, wherein the application of wisdom is fulfilled and great compassion is perfected.

Therefore, it is still [discussed] later because good wisdom (*saddhī*) has not yet attained mastery; furthermore, because spontaneous wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) is further clarified without depending on deliberate mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Regarding the representation of the Dharma by Sudhana: that Sudhana sees spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) within this practice indicates that, in this stage, one accords with principle and enters true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), which is termed "effortless" (*anabhisaṃskāra*) in the eighth bhūmi.

Because it accords with the meaning within the assembly, it is said that "within this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), clear wisdom accords with the Middle Way," which is called the Middle Principle.
Because there is no distinction between self and other, nor between oneself and others, it is called the site of enlightenment.
This spiritual friend is titled "One Who Possesses the Power of Great Vow and Diligence to Rescue and Protect All Sentient Beings," clarifying that only at this stage can one truly respond to them.
His original vow to save sentient beings is infinite; this constitutes the manifestation of the seventh stage.

Because it is difficult to accomplish the practice of wisdom following compassion, at this stage, one practices compassion following wisdom to extensively and easily accomplish the salvation of beings.

Thus, the essence of wisdom pervades the ten directions, appearing in accordance with the breadth or narrowness of sentient beings, responding like an echo to a sound—acting spontaneously without a [discursive] mind.
Because all sounds are harmonized, her wisdom is beyond thought and equal to the realm of empty space;
she accords with the hearts of all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm according to their inclinations to benefit them, yet she is without the notion of "mine" and without an agent.
Therefore, by night, she is named Great Vow and Power of Diligence, who protects all sentient beings and sits pervasively manifesting herself everywhere.
The "Lion Throne within the Treasury of the King of Maṇis of All Palaces" signifies that great compassion universally covers all sentient beings, serving as the palace;
wisdom manifests in response to benefit living beings, serving as the hall; and wisdom being free from defilement or purity is the maṇi.
Because it universally saves sentient beings without effort regardless of whether they dwell in defilement or purity, it is called the "King. Therefore, it is universal.

The manifestation of the realm of the dharma-realm, covered above by a net of mani-jewels, symbolizes that the sphere of wisdom universally contains [all beings] and establishes teachings according to their faculties;
this is termed a "net. Because wisdom has no inherent substance yet can manifest all phenomena without a creator, it is called a "mani.
This clarifies that, regarding the fruit of reliance resulting from the benefit of sentient beings through the function of wisdom, one understands the cause by contemplating the effect.
Because the fruit is presented to encourage the cause, it is explained at length as in the sutra. This teaching on the eighth stage is the dharma to be practiced;
the night goddess is named Great Power of Vow and Diligence, who is the person practicing this path.
To clarify what kind of liberation is attained in this stage within the three realms, it is shown that one attains the pervasive application of wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings.

Throughout the cycle of existence, there is no attainment of liberation without merit; from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh, one practices both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In this eighth stage, these two modes of practice are brought to completion. As described in the *Bodhisattvacaryā*, the functions of this stage are finalized here.

It is only upon reaching the tenth stage that the ten powers (*daśabala*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and mastery are fully perfected, along with the five types of subsequent knowledge (*pañca-anvaya-jñāna*).

Regarding the explanation of the text and its meaning, there are two aspects as previously stated. As for the long-format structural analysis (*dīrgha-vibhāga*) of the intent of this sūtra, it divides these eight stages into twelve sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Heavenly King and his celestial host, having heard of this sublime practice, were all filled with joy.
Desiring to make offerings to the Tathāgata and to the countless great Bodhisattvas,
they rain down exquisite flowers, banners, and canopies; incense, garlands, necklaces,
and precious robes in immeasurable, boundless, and myriad varieties, all adorned with mani jewels.
The celestial maidens simultaneously played heavenly music, universally producing various wondrous sounds as an offering to the Buddha and his sons; together they spoke these words of praise:
"O Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, whom all who see you behold, out of compassion for sentient beings, you manifest your spiritual powers."
May these various celestial music of the devas universally emit sublime sounds so that all may hear them;
and within a single hair-tip, may hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of lands as numerous as atoms—
within such infinite Tathāgatas dwelling therein— expound the wondrous Dharma.
Within a single pore are immeasurable lands, Each with its four continents, great oceans, Sumeru, and Iron Ring Mountains; All are seen therein without any crowding.
Upon the tip of a single hair are the six realms of existence: The three evil paths, as well as humans and devas.
The hosts of nāgas, devas, and asuras each receive their retribution according to their own karma;
within all those buddha-fields, the Tathāgatas everywhere proclaim wondrous sounds that accord with the minds of all sentient beings, turning the most supreme and pure wheel of Dharma.
Within the lands are the various bodies of sentient beings, and within those bodies there are likewise various lands;
humans, devas, and all the realms of existence are each distinct. Having fully known them all, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for them.
Great lands may, according to his thought, transform into small ones; small lands, according to his thought, likewise transform into large ones.
Such supernatural powers are immeasurable; though the world speaks of them together, they cannot be fully exhausted.
Having universally emitted these wondrous sounds to praise the merits of the Tathāgata, the assembly remained silent with joy, gazing with single-minded devotion, desiring to hear his teaching.
[Treatise] The first section, from the time when the Heavenly King and his celestial host descended until they gazed with single-minded devotion desiring to hear the Dharma,
consists of twenty-two stanzas clarifying the portion on how the devas, upon hearing the Dharma, presented offerings and extolled the Buddha’s divine virtues.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vimukticandra again requested, saying: "Now this assembly is entirely tranquil;
we pray that you will explain, in due order, the various characteristics of the practices within the eighth stage.
[Śāstra] The second section, from "At that time, Vimukticandra" onwards, consists of two lines of verse clarifying the request to explain the division concerning the eighth stage.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying: "O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the seventh stage has well cultivated skillful means and wisdom, well purified all paths, well accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment,
is embraced by the power of great vows, is empowered by the power of the Tathāgatas, and is sustained by their own inherent power, they constantly remain mindful of the Tathāgata."
Through the power of coming forth, one attains the fearlessnesses and the unique Buddha-dharmas that are perfectly pure;
by means of profound mental reflection and awakening, one is able to accomplish great merit and wisdom, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion that do not abandon sentient beings.

One enters the path of immeasurable wisdom and realizes that all phenomena are from the beginning unborn, unarisen, signless, unformed, indestructible, inexhaustible, non-revolving, and have non-nature as their nature.
That which is equal throughout the beginning, middle, and end, free from all discrimination, the sphere entered by suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*),
devoid of all conceptualizations of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), without any grasping or attachment, like space— entering all phenomena as having the nature of space—
is called the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

[Treatise] Third: The section beginning with "At that time" and following consists of ten lines of scripture that clarify the stage of practicing the eighth ground and entering the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Second, as for the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text:

the scripture states, "Entering into the nature of all dharmas as being like space is called attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas. This clarifies [the progression] from the first ground up to the seventh.
The ground is that which accords with the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); it is only at the eighth ground that one attains this patience.

Prior to the eighth ground, both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are still subject to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and must be cultivated; it is upon reaching this eighth ground that these two modes of activity finally come to an end.
The remaining textual meanings are self-evident from the text itself.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, as soon as a Bodhisattva accomplishes this patience, they immediately enter the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā).
As a Bodhisattva of profound practice, they are difficult to know; they are indistinguishable [from the ultimate], free from all signs, all conceptualizations, and all attachments.
They are immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and are tranquil, being free from all clamor and contention.

The manifestation of cessation is like that of a bhikṣu who, possessing supernormal powers and having attained mastery over the mind, sequentially enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), whereby all movement of the mind, recollection, and conceptual discrimination entirely cease. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this:
abiding in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), he immediately relinquishes all effortful practices and attains the state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
In the Dharma-body, the activities of body, speech, and mind, as well as all mental exertions, cease and abide in the state of retributive action (*vipākakarma*).
It is like a person who, in a dream, sees his own body fallen into a great river; desiring to cross it, he exerts great vigor and employs great skillful means.
Because he exerts such vigor and employs such skillful means, he immediately awakens. Once awakened, all that was being done ceases. The Bodhisattva is also like this.
Seeing sentient beings within the four currents, you have generated great courage and initiated great diligence for the sake of their rescue and deliverance.
By means of that courageous diligence, you have reached this Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Having reached it, all functional efforts cease without exception, and the two modes of activity no longer manifest before you. Son of the Buddha, it is like being born into the Brahma world after having been in the desire realm.
All afflictions do not manifest; dwelling in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), it is likewise so that all activities of mind, thought, and consciousness do not manifest.
For this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, even the bodhisattva-mind, the Buddha-mind, the bodhi-mind, and the nirvana-mind do not arise, let alone the arising of a worldly mind.

[Treatise] Regarding the passage beginning with "The fourth son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, having accomplished this patience," there are seventeen lines of scripture that clarify the stage of the Bodhisattva entering the effortless (*anābhoga*) state. In explaining the meaning, this is divided into four sections.

The first section, from "The fourth son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva" down to "all have completely ceased," consists of five and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the entry into the eighth [stage].
The earth shakes, all conceptualizations cease, and quiescence manifests before him—states that even the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the two vehicles cannot reach.
From the point where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have descended to the level of practicing the two modes of activity, these do not manifest at all.

This section, spanning approximately eight lines of scripture, clarifies that from the first bhūmi onward, the power of skillful means reaches its consummation, such that the two modes of activity no longer manifest.

Third, from "The sons of the Buddha" down to "all do not manifest before him," two lines of scripture clarify the analogy of being born in the Brahma world where the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) do not manifest.

This is divided into four parts. From "This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" down to the end of one and a half lines of scripture clarifies that even the mind of a Bodhisattva, the mind of a Buddha, the mind of Bodhi, and the mind of Nirvāṇa do not yet manifest.
The *Fenjing* (Analysis Scripture) states that "that which cannot be reached by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas" refers to the Two Vehicles (Dviyāna).

This is because they are weary of existence (*bhava*) and realize non-existence (*abhāva*), thus differing from those who fulfill both the practices of existence and non-existence. They rely on the effortless (*anabhisaṃskāra*) function and depart from all clamor and contention;

they manifest within the state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*). Because their efforts regarding the two contentions of existence and non-existence are already fulfilled, and because they are free from contention, this is the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*).
Skillful means reach the sixth stage; the wisdom of the three emptinesses culminates in the seventh stage; great compassion fulfills all practices in the eighth stage.
Because effortless spontaneity and mastery of wisdom bring about great transformation for the benefit of sentient beings, there is no agent. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"For example, it is like a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with supernormal powers and has attained mastery over the mind. This is an analogy drawn from the Lesser Vehicle to illustrate the Greater Vehicle, as when a bhikṣu attains...

Emerging from the meditative absorptions of the three realms, they possess no mind belonging to the three realms; rather, by the power of pure meditative concentration, they emerge from the three realms and manifest supernormal powers through a wondrously pure mental faculty.
These powers are sixfold: first, the power of the body; second, the power of the divine ear; third, the power of the divine eye;

fourth, the power of recollecting past lives; fifth, the power of knowing the minds of others; and sixth, the power of the exhaustion of outflows. Such are the six supernormal powers of the two vehicles.
The number of names of the bodhisattvas in the Pure Land is similar [to those in other realms], yet they differ in their general application and scope:

the supernatural powers and transformations of those in the Two Vehicles cannot reach the Buddha-lands of other directions, whereas the supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas in the Pure Land enable them to travel to the Pure Lands of other directions.
Furthermore, the supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle encompass all sentient beings and lands throughout the ten directions within a single Buddha-field.

The three vehicles take the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows as their realization, whereas the bodhisattvas of the one vehicle, though free from all desires, do not take the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows as their realization.

The six supernormal powers of the three vehicles are all limited, while the ten supernormal powers of the one vehicle are limitless, as is clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernormal Powers" below. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "Though they practice the six supernormal powers, yet..."
Having exhausted all outflows through the mastery of wisdom, this differs from the three vehicles of the Lesser Fruit, as those three vehicles all involve coming and going;
as the sutras of the three vehicles say, "I wish to return to my native land," and so forth.

The supernatural powers possessed by the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle rely on the seal of the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*), whose nature is inherently pervasive and coextensive with the realm of empty space; thus, they manifest activities in response to objects without actually departing.
Regarding the nature of the Middle and the Extremes, the reason why Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle do not realize the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is that,

through the wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmasthāna-jñāna*), they do not perceive the nature of outflows; furthermore, because all phenomena— whether with or without outflows, involving grasping or relinquishing— are by their very nature the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*),
and because they possess mastery over wisdom and encompass universal conduct for the sake of sentient beings, they differ from those of the Three Vehicles.
Because there is still attachment and aversion, as well as grasping and rejecting, this present [teaching] uses the small to illustrate the great, as follows:
the analogy of a dream illustrates the dharmas from the first to the seventh bhūmi; these involve learning and cultivation, like the activities performed in a dream before awakening.
The eighth bhūmi is like having already awakened from the dream; therefore, all phenomena are entirely without functional utility, and one follows wisdom through wisdom itself.
As for the title "The King of Wisdom," the rest is clear from the text itself.

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, because of the power of the original vows of the Bodhisattvas on this stage, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, personally appear before them and bestow upon them the wisdom of the Tathāgata, causing them to enter the gateway of the stream of the Dharma, and speak these words: 'Excellent, excellent!'"
"Son of noble family, this patience is the foremost and accords with all the Buddha-dharmas.
However, son of noble family, you have not yet attained any of our ten powers, fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
You should apply yourself with diligent vigor to accomplish these dharmas; do not again abandon this gate of patience. Furthermore, son of noble family, although you..."
Although you have attained this liberation of quiescent extinction, ordinary beings have not yet realized it;
various afflictions manifest before them, and all manner of discursive thoughts constantly assail them. You should take pity on such sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family, you should recall your original vow to universally and greatly benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to...

One attains entry into the gate of inconceivable wisdom. Furthermore, son of good family, the dharma-nature of these phenomena remains eternally constant and unchanging whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear. It is not by virtue of attaining this dharma that the Buddhas are called Tathāgatas;
even all those of the two vehicles are able to attain this non-conceptual dharma. Furthermore, son of good family, you...

Observe that our physical forms are immeasurable, our wisdom is immeasurable, our buddha-lands are immeasurable, our skillful means are immeasurable, our radiance is immeasurable, and our pure voices are likewise immeasurable; you should now accomplish these matters as well.
Furthermore, son of good family, you have just now attained this one illumination of the Dharma, namely, that all phenomena are unborn and undifferentiated.

"Furthermore, son of good family, the light of the Tathāgata’s Dharma is immeasurable; its entries are immeasurable, its manifestations are immeasurable, and its revolutions are immeasurable, such that they cannot be fully known even in hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* eons. You should practice and bring this Dharma to fulfillment.
Moreover, son of good family, observe the immeasurable lands, the immeasurable sentient beings, and the immeasurable dharmas with their various differences throughout the ten directions."
Each and every one should, in accordance with reality, thoroughly penetrate these matters.

O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow upon this Bodhisattva such immeasurable gateways for the arising of wisdom, enabling him to give rise to immeasurable and boundless activities of differentiated wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, if the Buddhas did not grant this Bodhisattva these gateways for the arising of wisdom, he would at that very moment enter ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Having abandoned all activities for the benefit of sentient beings, because the Buddhas have bestowed such immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of wisdom,
the karmic activity of wisdom produced in a single thought-moment exceeds— by a factor of one hundred,
or even by a factor of hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta*— all the various practices cultivated from the first generation of the mind up to the seventh stage.

Furthermore, even one part in an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*), one part in a *kalā*, one part in a numerical calculation, one part in a metaphorical comparison, or even one part in a minute fraction (*upaniṣad*) does not equal it. Why is this?

O Son of the Buddha, whereas that bodhisattva previously practiced with a single body, now, dwelling in this stage, they attain immeasurable bodies, immeasurable voices, immeasurable wisdom, and immeasurable sensations.
They are born in immeasurable pure lands, transform immeasurable sentient beings, make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, enter immeasurable Dharma-gates, and possess immeasurable supernormal powers.

They preside over immeasurable assemblies and diverse sites of enlightenment, and they abide in immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions, accumulating all bodhisattva practices through the principle of immovability. O Son of the Buddha, it is like being aboard a ship.

Just as one who wishes to enter the great ocean must expend great effort and labor before reaching it, yet once having reached the sea, goes there simply by following the wind without relying on human power,
the distance traveled in a single day compares to the period before arrival such that even if one had spent a hundred years prior to reaching it,
one could not have covered that much ground; so too it is with the Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, who likewise accumulate [merit and wisdom].
Having gathered the vast provisions of roots of goodness and boarded the vessel of the Great Vehicle, they reach the ocean of bodhisattva conduct; in a single thought-moment,
through non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), they enter the realm of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajña-jñāna*),
a state that cannot be attained even after countless hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of eons spent in effortful practice.

[Treatise] Fifth: From the point "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, this section of the sūtra consists of forty and a half lines of scripture that clarify how a bodhisattva in this stage has entered the effortless (*anābhoga*) state.

Within the explanation of the meaning through the ten kinds of encouragement and empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by the Buddhas, the text is divided into twelve sections. First: from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "this patience" (*kṣānti*).

The section beginning with "The gate has five lines and a half of scripture" up to "the various Tathāgatas manifesting encouragement to practice the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of all Tathāgatas" is divided into two parts.
Furthermore, the section from "Moreover, son of good family" down to "you should take pity on such sentient beings" consists of two lines and a half of scripture;
this represents the encouragement and praise by the Buddhas for attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the mindfulness to deliver [beings] from afflictions.

The section on the categories of sentient beings with evil thoughts is divided into three parts. Furthermore, from "O son of good family, you should recollect" down to "the gateway of wisdom," there are two lines of scripture;
this constitutes the fourth part, which consists of the exhortations by all Buddhas to recollect one's original vows for the universal and great benefit of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, from "O son of good family" down to "attaining this non-conceptual dharma," [is the fifth part].
There are two and a half lines of sūtra clarifying the section on how all Buddhas exhort [beings] not to abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Five:
furthermore, "Son of Good Family, you should observe our physical marks," and so on, down to "accomplishing this matter";

these two and a half lines of sūtra constitute the section where all Buddhas provide encouragement to cultivate merit and wisdom and to preach the Dharma through the sound of their voices. Six: furthermore, "Son of Good Family... [and so forth].

From "The son [of noble family]" down to "having accomplished this dharma," there are three and a half lines of sūtra clarifying the section on the various Buddhas' exhortation to cultivate the immeasurable light of dharma (*dharmāloka*).
Furthermore, from "Moreover, son of noble family" down to "thoroughly penetrating those matters," there are two lines of sūtra;
these constitute the section on the various distinctions of the Buddhas' exhortations to cultivate and the thorough penetration of those matters as they truly are, as described above.

The twenty and a half lines of this sutra section contain three instances of "bestowal" (*pradāna*) and seven instances of "exhortation" (*codanā*). Regarding the three instances of bestowal: first, the manifestation of the bodies of all Buddhas;

second, the granting of wisdom; and third, the verbal praise "Excellent! Excellent! (*sādhu sādhu*) accompanied by the touching of the crown of the head (*mūrdhābhiṣeka*). Regarding the seven instances of exhortation:

these correspond to the seven sections as categorized in the preceding textual analysis. Section Eight begins from "O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones... and extends down to "the distinctions."

The section on the two types of wisdom-activity (*jñāna-karma*) explained by the sutras—wherein the Buddhas, through seven exhortations and three empowerments, cause the arising of differentiated activities—is divided into nine parts, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "Upāniṣad.

Furthermore, there are seven lines of sutra text explaining that once the gates of wisdom have been attained, they surpass and cannot be compared to the initial arousal of the mind; this constitutes the tenth part.

Why is this so? From the passage beginning with "Because of the nature of immovability" down to "The Bodhisattvas, O Son of the Buddha," there is a five-line sutra that clarifies the attainment of immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions;

and from the passage beginning with "Even if one were to spend a hundred years" down to "There is a three-line sutra that clarifies the use of analogies," it illustrates how traveling by ship upon the ocean surpasses [the journey] by a hundred years in speed.

From "dividing into twelve, O sons of the Buddha," down to "cannot reach," there are four lines of sūtra that clarify how one boards the vessel of the One Vehicle and reaches this sea of unconditioned practice.
Having thus divided [the stages], it exhorts the addition [of practice] from the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages;
at the very beginning of each stage, all Buddhas exhort, praise, empower, and cause the speaker of the Dharma to [proceed].

Because of the teaching of the Dharma, one arrives at this eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Through the three empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and seven exhortations, it clarifies that for one who practices for themselves, there is nothing attained through effort;
rather, in this stage, the wisdom of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatājñāna*) manifests spontaneously.
Because of the correspondence with the empowerment of all Buddhas and the Dharma, one is capable of receiving the vast Dharma of all Buddhas, just like the virtue of a worldly sovereign.

That the phoenix appears and the qilin responds is clearly the result of being moved by virtue. Thus, it is evident that when the wisdom of non-action manifests in this eighth stage, the response of all Buddhas of the ten directions occurs as a matter of natural law (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Good son, this patience is foremost in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas.
This clarifies that the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in this stage is not like that of the sixth stage.
Prior to the seventh stage, one possesses the "conformity-patience" (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*); therefore, this patience is the foremost in conforming to all Buddha-dharmas.
This clarifies that this non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the fundamental essence of the wisdom-nature of all Buddhas.

Good son, all that we possess—the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), such as the power regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*), and so forth, as well as the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)—are [all derived from this].

Regarding those qualities of the Buddha that you have not yet attained, I now clearly exhort you to advance toward them: the sovereign powers of the Tathāgata do not allow one to remain in a state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
As for the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): first, there is no error; second, there is no harsh or violent speech;
third, there is no loss of mindfulness; fourth, there is no lack of concentration; fifth, there is no perception of diversity; sixth, there is no... [incomplete source].
13. Discernment and relinquishment; 14. non-retrogression in aspiration; 15. non-retrogression in diligence; 16. non-retrogression in mindfulness;
17. non-retrogression in concentration; 18. non-retrogression in wisdom; 19. non-retrogression in liberation; 20.
all bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge; 21. all verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
15. Furthermore, all mental karma is preceded by wisdom and proceeds in accordance with wisdom;
16. knowing the past without attachment; 17. knowing the future without attachment; 18. knowing the present without attachment.
Regarding the four fearlessnesses: first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, [fearlessness regarding] the teaching...
The four fearlessnesses regarding the obstacles to the path and the path for the exhaustion of suffering have been clarified previously within the ten powers.

As for the passage beginning "Even though you have attained this liberation of quiescence," it exhorts one to keep in mind those sentient beings who have not yet attained it, and to fulfill one's original vow for universal and great benefit.
The subsequent section contains three general additions and seven specific exhortations, as clearly explained in the text itself. By means of these, [the Buddha’s] intent is made manifest.

Seventh, the activity of exhorting [beings] to give rise to immeasurable and differentiated wisdom is like the *kalā*—here translated as "vertically dividing a single hair on a person's body into one hundred parts, or even one-sixteenth part.
This refers to the sixteen *śu* (升) of the Western Regions being equivalent to one *dou* (斗); it signifies that the arising of wisdom in this stage ascends and progresses.
Because the dharmas of the preceding stage can only be compared to a small portion [of those in this stage], it is called "the stage of the near-attainment" (*upaniṣad*).

Here, *upa* means "near" and *niṣad* means "comparison. This indicates that the vastness of the wisdom arising from this stage and its benefit to sentient beings cannot be matched even by the benefits produced during hundreds of thousands of billions of incalculable eons on the preceding stage.
Because this slight, minute benefit serves to clarify the preceding stage by way of its inferior benefit,
and because this stage gives rise to the benefit of manifesting infinite transformation bodies, the remainder is self-evident in the text. The above section clarifies the three empowerments,
the seven exhortations, and the established rules for the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, the Ten Dedications, and the Ten Stages.

In the eighth stage, the Great Power (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) collectively clarifies that at the very first thought-moment of entering the Way in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;

at that time, all dharmas are fully provided for as a protection. Nevertheless, because dharmas must be established in a sequential order of ascending progress so as not to stagnate in various practices, this is taught so that those who have newly resolved their minds may know the proper measure and standard. Therefore, from...
Because they first give rise to the mind and establish great vows, their wisdom of great compassion ascends simultaneously with the Dharma-body.
Thus, although the teachings are presented sequentially, for the learner, the confusion and awakening, as well as the shallowness and depth of their wisdom, are revealed all at once;
for the realm of wisdom has no before or after.

Fascicle 26-11. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva dwells in this eighth stage, through the great skillful means and the wisdom arising from [that skillfulness], they give rise to no...

With the wisdom of functional application, he contemplates the objective domain of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), namely: he contemplates the formation of the world and the destruction of the world;

he knows as it truly is how long it takes for the world to form through the accumulation of karma, how long it takes for it to be destroyed through the exhaustion of karma, and for how long it remains formed, and for how long it remains destroyed. Furthermore, he knows the subtle and gross characteristics of the earth element.
He knows with the knowledge of the distinctions of immeasurable marks the small, large, and immeasurable marks of the elements of water, fire, and wind;

he knows with the knowledge of the distinctions of the subtle marks of atoms and the distinctions of their immeasurable varieties all the masses of atoms and the distinctions of those atoms within any world-system, exactly as they are, according to whatever world-system [is concerned].
He knows, exactly as they are, the number of atoms in the elements of earth, water, fire, and air; the number of atoms in all precious objects;
the number of atoms in the bodies of sentient beings; and the number of atoms in the bodies of lands.

He knows that the great bodies and small bodies of sentient beings are each composed of a certain number of atoms; he knows the bodies of hell-beings, the bodies of animals, and the bodies of hungry ghosts.
He knows that the bodies of asuras, devas, and humans are each composed of a certain number of atoms; he thus attains the wisdom that discerns the distinctions between atoms.
Furthermore, he knows the formation of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; he knows the destruction of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
and he knows the small characteristics, the great characteristics, the immeasurable characteristics, and the distinct characteristics of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Having attained such wisdom that discerns the distinctions of the three realms, O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva further gives rise to the light of wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings.
That is to say: they skillfully know the distinctions among the bodies of sentient beings; they skillfully differentiate the bodies of sentient beings;
and they skillfully observe the places of birth, manifesting their own bodies according to what is appropriate to teach, transform, and bring them to maturity. This Bodhisattva, within a single...
In accordance with the differences in the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm, he universally manifests birth by means of the light of wisdom;
likewise, in two, three, or even up to hundreds of thousands, or even unspeakably many trichiliocosms,
he universally manifests birth therein in accordance with the differences in the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings.
Because the Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, while his body remains unmoved within a single Buddha-field,
he manifests his body throughout the assemblies of unspeakably many Buddha-fields. Son of the Buddha, according to the various differences in the physical bodies,
minds, and inclinations of sentient beings, he manifests himself within those assemblies in the Buddha-lands.
As for the body, it means manifesting the form of a śramaṇa among the assembly of śramaṇas, the form of a brāhmaṇa among the assembly of brāhmaṇas,
and the form of a kṣatriya among the assembly of kṣatriyas; likewise, it manifests among the assemblies of vaiśyas,
śūdras, householders, the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods.

Among the hosts of the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, the Māras, the Brahmās, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha gods, he manifests forms according to each of their respective classes. Furthermore, for those who are to be delivered by the body of a śrāvaka, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka;
for those who are to be delivered by the body of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha; for those who are to be delivered by the body of a bodhisattva...

Those who are to be delivered by means of the Buddha’s own body, he manifests in the form of a Bodhisattva; those who are to be delivered by means of the Tathāgata’s body, he manifests in the form of a Tathāgata.

O Son of the Buddha, in this way, within all unspeakably many Buddha-lands, the Bodhisattva manifests his body in whatever manner corresponds to the differences in the faith and inclinations of sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva remains far removed from...
Abiding in equanimity regarding all conceptualizations of bodies, this bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings,

the body of the realm, the body of karmic retribution, the body of śrāvakas, the body of pratyekabuddhas, the body of bodhisattvas, the body of Tathāgatas, the body of wisdom, the body of Dharma, and the body of space.
This bodhisattva knows the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings and is able to transform the bodies of sentient beings into his own.
The body also manifests as the body of a buddha-field, the body of karmic retribution, and even the body of space;

furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, it can manifest the body of a buddha-field as its own body, and likewise manifest the body of sentient beings, the body of karmic retribution, and even the body of space.
Moreover, knowing the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, it can manifest the body of karmic retribution as its own body.
They also manifest as the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, and even the body of space.
Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, they are able to transform their own bodies into the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, and even the body of space;
according to the differing inclinations of those sentient beings, they manifest such forms within these bodies. This Bodhisattva knows the accumulation of sentient beings.
Furthermore, one knows the body of karma, the body of retribution, the body of afflictions, the form-body, and the formless-body;

one also knows the bodies of lands—those with small characteristics, large characteristics, immeasurable characteristics, defiled characteristics, pure characteristics, vast characteristics, inverted characteristics, upright characteristics, universally penetrating characteristics, and the distinctions of the square-lattice arrangement;
one knows the provisional designations for the body of karmic retribution; and one knows the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
One should know the conventional designations and distinctions of the Tathāgata’s body:

the bodhi-body, the vow-body, the transformation-body, the power-sustaining body, the body adorned with marks and signs, the body of majestic authority, the mind-born body, the merit-body, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body.

One should know that the wisdom-body possesses the characteristic of excellent deliberation, the characteristic of discernment according to reality, the characteristic of being subsumed by the practice of the fruit, and the characteristic of being both mundane and supramundane.
