The characteristics of temporal distinctions; the characteristics of the distinctions between the three vehicles; common and uncommon characteristics; the characteristics of transcendence and non-transcendence;
the characteristics of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); the characteristics of knowing the equality of the *dharmakāya*; the indestructible characteristics;

the characteristics of conventional designations according to time and worldly convention; the characteristics of the distinctions between sentient beings and non-sentient phenomena; and the characteristics of the distinctions between the Buddha-dharma, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha.

The characteristics of mutual knowledge, the characteristic of the immeasurable body of space, the characteristic of pervasiveness, the characteristic of formlessness, the characteristic of non-differentiation, the characteristic of boundlessness,
and the characteristic of the manifestation of the form-body.
[Śāstra] From the sixth son of the Buddha onwards, the following section of fifty-nine lines of scripture clarifies the Bodhisattva of this stage.

In the section explaining the meaning of the "Vast Mastery in Gathering Beings through Shared Activities" within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, based on the Bodhisattva’s own wisdom and virtue in skillfully knowing the distinctions,
formations, and disintegrations of all phenomena, the text is divided into eight parts. First, from the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha,
when a bodhisattva dwells in this eighth stage" down to "they know them all as they truly are," there are four lines of verse that clarify the observation through skillful wisdom.
The formation and destruction of the world through the causes of karma is divided into two parts.

Furthermore, from "having known the small and large characteristics of the earth element" down to "the specific characteristics," there are two lines of sūtra explaining the small and large specific characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind, which is divided into three parts.
From "knowing the subtle characteristics of atoms" down to "knowing the wisdom of the specific characteristics of atoms," there are seven lines.

The Sūtra clearly explains the distinct characteristics of atoms in four sections; furthermore, from "knowing the desire realm and the form realm" down to "the wisdom that contemplates the distinctions of the three realms," there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clearly explain the characteristics of the formation and destruction of the three realms in five sections.
From "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... down to "he manifests his body everywhere," there are eight and a half lines of sūtra that clearly explain [these matters].
6. Observing the differences in the bodies of sentient beings, the Bodhisattvas manifest bodies accordingly;
this section on "Manifesting the Body in Common Purpose" (*sabhāgatā-kāya-prakāśana*) consists of twelve lines of scripture from "O Sons of the Buddha" downwards. 7.
From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards until "this body manifests such forms," there are ten and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the Bodhisattvas in this stage abide in...
The section on the mastery over manifesting bodies—whether identical or distinct—within the state of non-conceptual mind consists of eight parts.

This Bodhisattva, having understood the gathering of sentient beings, and so forth, down to the manifestation of the marks of the form body, is clarified in twelve and a half lines of scripture as the section on the distinctions between the karma-result body (*vipākakāya*) and its characteristics.
The scripture states: "Observing the Omniscient One" refers to the objective realm of the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).

This is the wisdom of differentiation (*viśeṣajñāna*), which arises from the conceptualization of the sphere of activity of fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*). Regarding the observation of the characteristics of the world’s formation:

such as the initial formation of the world-system and the characteristics of the formation and destruction of the four seasons, of humans, of the heavens, of hells, of animals, and of hungry ghosts—all are formed by karma and all are destroyed by karma; they correspond according to their own kind and are not [otherwise].
Constantly and universally, within the midst of non-transmigration and non-change that is timeless, one perceives long life and short life;

the extension and contraction of birth and the myriad differences among classes of beings—whether they arise spontaneously or perish through external causes, or whether they occur simultaneously—all follow karma.

Yet, because these are not truly real, such periods of formation, destruction, abiding, and vacuity, as well as the extensions and contractions of time and the increases and decreases [of kalpas], are for the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly knows the small and great characteristics of the earth element:

he clearly understands that the small characteristic is a single atom, while the great characteristic is that a single atom has no inherent substance such that its breadth and narrowness are entirely equal;

furthermore, he knows how vast worlds and small worlds, with their distinctions of purity and impurity, are all established within a single pore and abide therein without being obstructed by their subtlety.
The layers are infinitely interpenetrating and unobstructed, like the Indra’s net where the ten directions mutually reflect one another; thus all are seen.

Regarding the characteristics of the elements of water, fire, wind, and space—both large and small—in this world system, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, it is said that the vessel-world is established with the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) at the very bottom;
its extent is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen hundred million [yojanas].
The thickness of the water wheel (*jala-maṇḍala*) above the yojana [foundation] is eleven hundred million, twenty-three thousand, four hundred and five yojanas.
For eight yojanas at the bottom, the water remains liquid; the remainder congeals to form gold. Thus, above this adamantine limit (*vajra-pṛthivī*), accumulated dust forms the world-systems.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The delusion of moisture (*sneha-vikalpa*) can produce the internal and external water elements."
The delusion of capability gives rise to the internal and external fire elements; the delusion of cutting and severing gives rise to the internal and external earth elements;

the delusion of agitation gives rise to the internal and external wind elements. That is to say: craving gives rise to the water element; the sense of "mine" and capability give rise to the fire element;
the dual grasping of subject and object gives rise to the earth element; and the conceptualization of self and other gives rise to the wind element.

When the craving for the element of wind arises, the mind of love perishes; thus the calamity of water does not reach one, the sense of "I" and "mine" perishes; thus the calamity of fire does not reach one, and discursive thought perishes; thus the calamity of wind does not reach one.

Because discursive thought is severed in the second dhyāna, the calamity of water does not reach it; because of the absence of discursive thought in the third dhyāna, the calamity of fire does not reach it;

and because of the absence of discursive thought in the fourth dhyāna, the calamity of wind does not reach it. This is because, due to the cessation of discursive thought, there is no inhalation or exhalation within, and no wind without.
Within, there is no capacity for or object of [affliction], and without, there is no calamity of fire; within, there is no craving of desire, and without, there is no calamity of water.
This is just like the sequence of the four dhyānas in the form realm. Furthermore, because of the intensification of craving of desire, one can produce the element of fire;
this is just as in the Lotus-Jewel Woman Hell, where because one grasps with a mind of craving, the craving of desire becomes intensified and thus turns into hot copper.
The suffering of being impaled upon pillars and the like involves being scorched by heat, fainting, and dying, only to be born again;
thus, in a single day, one undergoes thousands of births and ten thousands of deaths, a suffering that is without end.

All this arises from the transformations of craving, just as the fires of superior karma melt copper and the fierce winds of karma [operate], as described in the *Niraya Sūtra* and other texts. Such is the destruction of this state by karma.
The Bodhisattva is able to know and see all things exactly as they are. As the Sūtra says:

"In whatever world-system there may be, regarding the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, however many atoms (paramāṇu) each may possess—just as the great is formed by the accumulation of the small—one takes the *anuvyañjana-rajas* (the atom that penetrates gold, copper, iron, and the interstices of rabbit hair, wool, lice, nits, and seeds of grass)."

The measurement of wild barley in increments of seven times seven to determine the units of *aṅgula*, *hasta*, *ratni*, and *dhanus* is what is known by ordinary intellect, as described in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, the dimensions of this Jambudvīpa continent—its breadth and extent from south to north and east to west—are also as stated therein;
likewise, the bodies of humans and animals are measured according to their respective heights and lengths.

To calculate the number of dust particles on the bodies of humans and animals by comparing them to the method of accumulating dust in increments of seven times seven is merely the limited perception of ordinary beings.
Bodhisattvas at this stage perceive the bodies of all beings—humans, animals, and others—within the worlds and lands with their eye of wisdom;
they know the formation and destruction of the triple world, and as for the time during which the triple world is formed...
Regarding the major and minor marks, the Bodhisattva in this stage knows and perceives them through the power of wisdom.
Among the various groups, the Brāhmaṇas are of the pure lineage; the Kṣatriyas are of the royal lineage; the Vaiśyas are of the merchant lineage;
and the Śūdras are of the farmer lineage. As the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva knows the bodies of sentient beings," which refers to the body of karmic retribution.

Regarding the body of the land (*kṣetra-kāya*), there are cases where the bodies of sentient beings constitute the land, such as the eighty-four thousand types of parasites that dwell within the human body.
From this point downward, all ten bodies are capable of being either identical or distinct, each possessing its own sovereign mastery.

This Bodhisattva knows the bodies formed by the accumulation of karma by sentient beings, the specific karmic results they accumulate, and how these serve as the dominant conditions for obtaining their respective retribution-bodies.
Regarding these bodies: the body of afflictions refers to the bodies of the three realms; the form-body (*rūpakāya*) refers to the bodies of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and the formless-body refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Such bodies, whether large or small in their characteristics, can be known through wisdom.
Furthermore, one knows that the Tathāgata’s body includes the Bodhi-body and the Vow-body, for it is by means of the bodhicitta that vows are generated and the body is accomplished.
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests according to the needs of sentient beings; the body sustained by power (*balādhiṣṭhānakāya*) is sustained by the ten powers (*daśabala*);

the body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjanakāya*) is adorned by the myriad practices of merit and wisdom; the body of majestic power (*prabhāvavikramakāya*) manifests the subduing of all forms of pride;
the body born of intention (*manomayakāya*) accords with the desires and inclinations of sentient beings; and the body of merit (*puṇyakāya*)...
The Dharma-body is so called because it is endowed with adornments; the Wisdom-body is so called because it knows boundless phenomena;

the Knowledge-body is so called because it awakens to both one’s own wisdom and the wisdom of others. The characteristic of skillful deliberation is that it acts in accordance with what is known by wisdom, free from conceptualization.
The characteristic of discernment according to reality is that it gives rise to differentiated wisdom based upon fundamental wisdom.

Regarding the characteristic of being subsumed by the fruit of practice through the skillful discernment of meanings and characteristics: it is because the One Vehicle arises from the fruit of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as the vow and practice of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the characteristic of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane: it is because both the two types of wisdom—ultimate and conventional—are manifest before one.
Regarding the characteristic of the distinction between the three vehicles: while the two vehicles proceed toward quiescence, the Bodhisattva is born into...
The Pure Land, or matters such as "retaining delusions to moisten rebirth," are termed *sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa* (common characteristics), shared equally by the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.
That which is not such a characteristic—namely, possessing compassion versus lacking compassion—is termed *asādhāraṇa-lakṇa* (uncommon characteristics).

Furthermore, regarding common characteristics, ordinary beings and sages are of one essence, fully possessing the wisdom of the Tathāgata; however, because there are differences between delusion and awakening, these are termed uncommon characteristics.
The characteristic of renunciation refers to the Three Vehicles; that which is not the characteristic of renunciation refers to all ordinary beings who possess afflictions, which is the One Vehicle.

Apart from these two matters, the characteristic of those in training (*śaikṣa*) refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage, while the characteristic of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) refers to Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage onward. This is the knowledge of the equal characteristic of the *dharmakāya*.
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, their characteristics are indestructible; this refers to the objective realm attained as a result of wisdom.
Their characteristics differ according to time and provisional designations; this refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) which accords with the inclinations and desires of beings.

The distinction between the characteristics of sentient beings and non-sentient beings refers to the differentiation between the animate and the inanimate. The distinction between the dharmas of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha... [is the same].

Regarding distinct characteristics: the Śrāvaka Saṃgha, the Pratyekabuddha Saṃgha, the Bodhisattva Saṃgha of the Pure Lands, and the Bodhisattva Saṃgha of the One Vehicle are distinguished by their respective characteristics;

the Buddha likewise knows them accordingly, in accordance with their types. Because the immeasurable characteristics of the space-body arise from the Dharma-body, and because the infinite forms manifested through the wisdom that accords with practice are distinct, the pervasive characteristic constitutes the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body.

Because the all-pervading activity is itself all-pervasive, its color-form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is likewise pervasive; because those without form or distinct characteristics are identical in essence, they possess boundless characteristics;
because the realm of the wisdom of the Dharma-body is not limited by insentient matter, it manifests the characteristics of the form-body (*rūpakāya*);
and because the form-body is revealed as being without substance or dependence, manifesting through the sovereign power of wisdom. Thus ends [the preceding section].

As in the preceding analysis of the text, there are eight sections of scripture; where the text provides its own detailed explanation of these profound and hidden points, they are self-evident according to the words.
In general, this clarifies the function reached by the effortless wisdom of the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva has accomplished such bodily wisdom, they attain mastery over life, mastery over mind, mastery over wealth,
mastery over karma, mastery over birth, mastery over vows, mastery over resolve, mastery over supernormal powers,
mastery over wisdom, and mastery over the Dharma. Because they have attained these ten masteries, they are possessors of inconceivable wisdom and immeasurable wisdom.
This is the one of vast wisdom, the one whose wisdom cannot be destroyed.
Having entered thus and having accomplished thus, this bodhisattva attains a body-karma that is ultimately faultless, speech-karma that is faultless, and mind-karma that is faultless;
their body, speech, and mind-karma proceed in accordance with wisdom, and they are headed by great compassion, with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as their sovereign.
Being skillful and adept at discernment, having well-arisen great vows, and protected by the power of the Buddhas, they constantly and diligently cultivate the wisdom that benefits sentient beings.
Universally dwelling in infinite and diverse worlds, O Son of the Buddha, to state the essentials:
when Bodhisattvas abide in this Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), all actions of their body, speech, and mind are able to accumulate all the Buddha-dharmas.

[Treatise] From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, there are ten and a half lines of scripture that clarify this stage of the Bodhisattva regarding the section on the ten masteries over body, life, and wealth (*kāya-jīvita-bhoga-vaśitā*) and their freedom from fault. Within the exegesis, this is divided into three parts:

first, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "mastery over phenomena" (*dharma-vaśitā*), there are two and a half lines of scripture clarifying that this stage has already perfected suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the first half of the upper section, "Having attained the ten masteries" (*daśavaśitāprāpta*), it is divided into two parts.

From "Because he has attained these ten masteries" down to "the one whose wisdom cannot be destroyed," there is one and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the attainment of the four kinds of mastery over wisdom (*jñānavaśitā*).
From "This bodhisattva" down to "having accumulated all Buddha-dharmas," there are six and a half lines of sūtra that clarify this [mastery].
The Bodhisattva of this stage, by means of faultless actions of body, speech, and mind, accords with the *prajñāpāramitā* and is able to gather all dharmas.

As the *Sūtra on the Collection of All Dharmas* states: "Mastery over life" means that upon the essence of great wisdom—which is neither arising nor ceasing—one shares equally with all sentient beings in the mastery of undergoing birth and death. "Mastery over mind" means following non-thought (*amanasikāra*).
Because the tasks to be accomplished by wisdom are fulfilled, the remainder is self-evident according to the text.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they attain a firm abiding through the power of profound resolve, because all afflictions do not arise;

they attain a firm abiding through the power of superior resolve, because they do not depart from the Path; they attain a firm abiding through the power of great compassion, because they do not abandon...
They attain firm abiding in the power of great loving-kindness for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;

they attain firm abiding in the power of dhāraṇī for the sake of protecting all the world and not forgetting the Dharma; they attain firm abiding in the power of eloquence for the sake of skillfully observing and discerning all phenomena;
and they attain firm abiding in the power of supernormal faculties for the sake of traveling universally to boundless worlds.
Because he dwells by the power of great vows and does not abandon any of the deeds of a bodhisattva, he attains the power of the well-established *pāramitās* and accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas;
because he attains the power of the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*) manifest before him;
thus, this bodhisattva, having attained such power of knowledge, is able to manifest all manner of activities.
Among all matters, there is no fault or transgression.

[Treatise] Regarding the eighth son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva who dwells in this stage and below, down to the point where there is no fault or transgression among all matters—nine lines and a half of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva in this stage attains the portion of the ten powers (*daśabala*). As it says:

The Sūtra itself states: "The one who possesses all-aspect omniscience" (*sarvākāra-sarvajña-jñānin*). "All-aspect" (*sarvākāra*) clarifies that [the Buddha] has fully cultivated various types of knowledge through preparatory application (*prayoga*).

"Omniscient" (*sarvajña*) refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Alternatively, it is said that "the one who possesses all-aspect omniscience" clarifies that the differentiated wisdom (*viśeṣa-jñāna*) arises from the fundamental wisdom;
this indicates that by means of the fundamental [wisdom], which is effortless (*anābhoga*), [differentiated wisdom is produced].
"Because wisdom performs various manifold functions, because wisdom is non-dual, and because wisdom is manifest" clarifies that the aforementioned sovereign wisdom is now manifest.
"This Bodhisattva, from this point on, clarifies the attainment of the power of effortlessness":
because wisdom is devoid of subject and object, he is able to manifest all activities without fault.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this stage of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), because nothing can obstruct or destroy it.

It is called the Non-retrogressive Ground (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), because wisdom does not regress. It is called the Hard-to-Attain Ground (*durlabha-bhūmi*), because no one in all the worlds can fathom it.
It is called the Ground of the Youthful (*kumāra-bhūmi*), because it is free from all faults. It is called the Ground of Birth (*janma-bhūmi*), because one is born according to one's own aspiration.
It is called the Stage of Accomplishment (*niṣpanna-bhūmi*) because there is nothing further to be done; it is called the Ultimate Stage (*nisthā-bhūmi*) because wisdom is definitive;

it is called the Stage of Transformation (*nirmāṇa-bhūmi*) because it accords with the fulfillment of vows; it is called the Stage of Sustaining Power (*baladhāraṇa-bhūmi*) because others cannot shake it;
and it is called the Stage of Effortless Function (*anābhoga-bhūmi*) because it has already been previously accomplished.

[Treatise] The section beginning with "The ninth son of the Buddha" and extending for six and a half lines of scripture clarifies the ten names corresponding to the qualities of the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). The meaning of these grounds is self-evident from the scripture itself;
because no one in any world can fathom it, it is called the "Ground of Youthful Truth" (*kumāra-bhūmi*), clarifying that prior to the seventh ground there is both practice and development.
This is mundane wisdom; because this effortless wisdom manifests in the eighth stage, it is called the Stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi), as it is the first entry into true wisdom by a youth.

It is named the "Stage of Birth" (Janmabhūmi) because it is free from faults, clarifying that while there is still applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one has already severed the injury caused by the thorns of applied and sustained thought; thus it is called the "Stage of Birth" because [true wisdom] is born therein.
Because this occurs within non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), the remainder is self-evident according to the text.

[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, they enter the realm of the Buddhas; they are illuminated by the merits of the Buddhas, accord with the majestic deportment of the Buddhas, and the realm of the Buddhas manifests before them.
They are constantly protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas, and are honored by Brahmā, Śakra, the four Heavenly Kings, and the gods."

Vajra-holders constantly follow and guard them, never abandoning them; they possess the great samādhis that can manifest infinite varieties of bodies, each with great power, having attained supernormal powers as a result of their retribution, and exercising mastery over samādhi.
Wherever there are sentient beings capable of being transformed, they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment. Sons of the Buddha, such is the entry into the Mahāyāna.
They shall attain great supernormal powers and radiate great light; they shall enter the unobstructed dharma-realm and know the distinctions between worlds;
they shall manifest all great merits with sovereign mastery according to their will; they shall skillfully penetrate the past and future limits;
they shall universally subdue all paths of demonic and heterodox ways; and they shall deeply enter the sphere of activity traversed by the Tathāgatas throughout immeasurable lands.
Because they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and are able to attain the dharma of non-retrogression, they are said to dwell in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

[Treatise] The section beginning with "The tenth son of the Buddha" consists of ten and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the bodhisattvas of this stage enter the realm of the Buddhas and receive the protective mindfulness of the Buddhas, while being attended by Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Mārutas.
The section on "Subduing Māras and Abiding in the Immovable Stage" is divided into two parts. First, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva...

down to "...manifesting perfect enlightenment," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattvas of this stage enter the realm of the Buddhas, sustained by their own power, thereby invoking the constant attendance and service of Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.

This section is divided into two parts. First, from "The Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Buddha, having thus entered the assembly of the Mahāyāna" onwards, five lines of scripture clarify the entry into the effortless assembly of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the attainment of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) with sovereign mastery according to one's will.
Second, the passage "constantly being protected by the Tathāgatas" clarifies that all Buddhas do not fail to protect all sentient beings and that they gather their roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
The protection and mindfulness of such beings has three meanings: first, protecting and being mindful of sentient beings on the path of suffering who have not yet resolved their minds;
second, protecting and being mindful of those who have already resolved their minds and are still in training (śaikṣa) or have attained partial realization;

and third, protecting and being mindful of Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of effortless action (anābhoga), so that they may attain the sovereign mastery of a Buddha. Thus, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly attend upon them.
"Vai" (衛) also has three meanings: first, to protect and serve all sentient beings; second, to protect and serve those who have already resolved their minds [for enlightenment];
and third, to protect and serve those who have attained the wisdom of effortlessness as well as all Buddhas.
Furthermore, "service" (侍衛) has two meanings: first, protection through the nurturing care of great compassion; and second, the entry into the stages by Bodhisattvas who revere them.

Regarding the Dharma-attendants who possess great power as a retribution for their practice and have attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): prior to the seventh stage, these are supernormal powers of retribution born from cultivation;
they have not yet attained mastery. In this stage, there are supernormal powers of retribution born from effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which are vast and sovereign.
Prior to the seventh stage, the supernormal powers of retribution depend upon the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*).

In this stage, the retributive karma of birth, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and non-active wisdom (*anabhisamskāra-jñāna*) arise; because there is no longer the need for cultivation or effort, one emits great radiance.
Because all created obstacles have vanished, one emits light and naturally enters the unobstructed dharma-realm (*anāvaraṇa-dharmadhātu*).
Because all activities have ceased and one acts according to the function of wisdom, wisdom is without obstruction. The remainder is fully explained in the text itself.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, once a bodhisattva has dwelled in this Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), by the power of samādhi they constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas,
never abandoning them, serving and making offerings to them. In each and every kalpa and in each and every world,
this bodhisattva sees immeasurable hundreds of Buddhas, immeasurable thousands of Buddhas, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas.
He reverently honored, respected, served, and made offerings to all other Buddhas, dedicating every necessity of life to them.
From those Buddhas, he received the profound Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas and attained immeasurable clarities of Dharma, such as the distinctions between worlds.
When questioned or challenged regarding such matters as the distinctions between worlds, there was no one who could defeat him. Thus he passed through [this period].
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of kalpas, and even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas,

all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure, just as genuine gold fashioned into a precious crown placed upon the head of a noble cakravartin king of Jambudvīpa cannot be equaled by any of the ornaments of his ministers or subjects; such is the bodhisattva on this stage.
All roots of goodness are likewise thus; none can equal those of all the followers of the two vehicles, nor even those of Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage.
Because one dwells in this stage, the light of great wisdom universally extinguishes the dark ignorance of the afflictions of sentient beings and is well able to open wide the gates of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Great Lord of a thousand worlds...
Just as the Brahma King is able to universally exercise a heart of compassion and universally radiate light that fills a thousand worlds, so too is this bodhisattva;

he is able to radiate light that illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms within a million buddha-fields, causing all sentient beings to extinguish the fires of affliction and attain refreshing coolness.
Among the ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva, this is the pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
While the other pāramitās are not unpracticed, they are practiced only according to one's power and capacity;
this is called a brief explanation of the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. If explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable kalpas.
Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they mostly become Great Brahmā Kings.
The Lord, the most supreme sovereign of a thousand worlds, who skillfully explains all meanings and can bestow the path of the perfections upon śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
one who, when questioned regarding the distinctions of the world systems, is never able to be discouraged or defeated;
and whose every action—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—is never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha.
Not being separated from the mindfulness of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*), he further forms this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom the knowledge of all-knowledge relies.
If this bodhisattva, by exerting the power of great diligence, in a single moment of thought attains a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems...
There are samādhis as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, up to the manifestation of bodhisattvas as many as the atoms in ten million trichiliocosms as one's retinue;

yet through the sovereign power of the bodhisattva’s sublime vows, they may manifest even beyond these numbers, such that they could not be counted or known even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas. At that time, Vajra...
The Bodhisattva of the Storehouse, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

[Treatise] From the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, number eleven" onwards, there is a passage of thirty-two and a half lines of scripture that clarifies the vastness of the knowledge and vision of the Bodhisattvas in this stage, as well as their portion of receiving office. This may be divided into four sections: first, "O Son of the Buddha."

From "Because they are already well able to open and elucidate the gate of wisdom" onwards, there are thirteen lines and a half of sūtra that clarify how the Bodhisattvas of this stage see many Buddhas, followed by the section on the analogy of refining true gold into precious ornaments; this consists of two parts.
From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, up to "which cannot be exhausted," there are six lines and a half of sūtra that clarify the Bodhisattvas of this stage.
The section on the "Superiority of the Radiance, Practices, and Vow-Pāramitās" for the three types of Buddha-sons includes seven lines of scripture,
from those below them down to the "basis of the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvajñajñāna*), which clarify how Bodhisattvas in this stage receive their office,
practice the various pāramitās, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), never being separated from the Three Jewels.
Fourth, from this point downward, the text provides five lines and a half of sūtra explaining that the bodhisattvas in this stage,
by means of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) and the power of diligence, attain samādhis and manifest vast numbers of bodhisattva retinues through the power of their vows.
[Sūtra] On the seventh stage, one cultivates the wisdom of skillful means and thoroughly gathers the power of great vows that assist the path.
Furthermore, being sustained by the Honored One among Men, one ascends to the eighth stage in pursuit of supreme knowledge.
With accomplished merit, one is ever compassionate; wisdom is vast and equal to space.
Hearing the Dharma can give rise to the power of certainty; this is the patient acceptance of the unarisen and the cessation of phenomena.

Knowing that all dharmas have the characteristic of being unarisen and unoriginated—without formation, without destruction, and without the cycle of exhaustion—one departs from existence, attains equanimity, and cuts off discrimination. Transcending all mental activities, one abides like space.
Having accomplished patience that transcends conceptual proliferation, Profound, immovable, and eternally quiescent,
it cannot be known by any in the world. Completely free from attachment to the characteristics of the mind,
one dwells in this stage without discrimination, Just like a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation.
Like crossing a river in a dream, which vanishes upon awakening; Like being born in the Brahma heaven, where lower desires are severed.
Through the power of their original vows, they receive encouragement and guidance; Praising their superior patience, they confer empowerment, saying:
"The various teachings of our Buddhadharma— You have not yet attained them; you must now apply yourself with diligent progress."
Although you have already extinguished the fire of afflictions, The flames of delusion in the world still burn fiercely.
You should remember your original vow to deliver sentient beings, Causing them all to cultivate the causes that lead to liberation.
The true nature of phenomena is eternally constant and free from mental conception; Even those of the Two Vehicles can attain this.
It is not for this reason that you are the World-Honored One; rather, it is because of your profound and unimpeded wisdom that you are one who should be honored by gods and humans alike.
By bestowing this wisdom, you cause them to observe the boundless Buddha-dharmas so that they may all be fully accomplished, transcending all former practices in a single thought-moment.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage of wondrous wisdom, they attain vast and great supernormal powers.

In a single thought, their bodies manifest throughout the ten directions; like a ship entering the sea aided by the wind, their minds function effortlessly through the power of wisdom, fully knowing the formation and destruction of all lands.
The various elements, each distinct and diverse— small, large, and immeasurable— all are fully understood;
the four great elements of the three thousandfold world system, the bodies of sentient beings in the six realms of existence each being different,
as well as the number of atoms within all manner of jewels, are all observed by wisdom without exception.
The Bodhisattva is able to know all bodies, Assuming forms identical to theirs to transform sentient beings;
Though lands are infinite and of various distinctions, He manifests his form in them all without exception.
Just as the sun and moon dwell in the void, Their reflections appear in every body of water.
Abiding in the dharma-realm without movement, they manifest reflections according to the mind; likewise,
appearing differently according to the inclinations of each, they manifest their bodies within all assemblies—
whether as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or the body of a Buddha, there is none that is not manifested.
The bodies of sentient beings, lands, and karmic retribution, And the various bodies of the sages—the wisdom-dharmakāya and the space-body—are all equal in their characteristics.
Universally for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest these ten kinds of noble wisdom through universal observation; Furthermore, in accordance with compassion, they perform all manner of deeds.
All Buddha-dharmas are fully accomplished; Holding the precepts, one is as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Having achieved the ten powers, one is unshakable; No hosts of Māras can turn one back.
The Buddhas protect and mindfully remember you, and the Heavenly Kings pay homage; Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi constantly attends and guards you.
The merits of this stage are boundless; they could not be fully described even in billions of kalpas.
Furthermore, through the excellence of making offerings to the Buddhas, these virtues become ever more radiant.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this eighth stage, they frequently manifest as Brahma Kings, lords of a thousand worlds, adorned like the ornaments upon the crown of a king’s head.
He expounds the three vehicles without end; his compassionate light shines everywhere, dispelling all delusions.
In a single thought-moment, he attains samādhis as numerous as the atoms within a million worlds;
all his deeds are likewise so, yet through the power of his vows, his manifestations exceed even this.
The Eighth Bodhisattva Ground, the Immovable: I have already briefly explained this for you;
if one were to analyze it in detail according to its sequence, one could not exhaust it even in the course of a hundred million kalpas. [Commentary]:
From the section on the "skillful means and wisdom cultivated in the twelfth [chapter] of the Seventh Ground" down to "even in the course of a hundred million kalpas," [the meaning is as follows].
There are forty-four verses that fully explain the previously taught dharmas through repetition; these are complete according to the text itself.
Regarding the ninth stage, the Bhūmi of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), there will be an explanation according to the five gates as before. First, to explain the name of this stage:
for what reason is this ninth stage called "Excellent Intelligence"? This is because the practice of this ninth stage is identical to the tenth dwelling (*vihāra*).
The ninth stage, the Bodhisattva Abode of the Dharma Prince, is always paired with the ninth position among the five ranks and is identical to the rank of the Dharma Master;
because he thoroughly knows all dharmas, it is named the Stage of Good Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Second, to clarify what practice-gate is cultivated on this stage:

here, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is cultivated as the primary focus, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions. Third, to explain how Sudhana symbolizes the Dharma: Sudhana...
In Jambudvīpa there is a grove named Lumbinī, where a deity named Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha resides.
This "Jambudvīpa" refers to this continent; it is named after its groves because this continent derives its name from its forests.
This explains that the wisdom established as teaching at this stage is as vast and abundant as a forest, providing extensive shade and cover. Furthermore, it is said that within it...
The presence of groves and gardens illustrates that wisdom is layered and inexhaustible; thus it is named Lumbinī. Alternatively, it is called Rumminī;

"Rummi" is a feminine sound meaning "supreme joyous circular radiance. This clarifies that in this Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), the dharma-joy of wisdom is stainless and perfectly radiant.
By means of the perfect radiance of excellent wisdom, one destroys afflictions and attains [liberation].
Because of this joy, the spirit is named "Perfected Wondrous Virtue. He occupies the rank of Dharma Master of Radiant Wisdom because his wondrous wisdom is perfected.

He dwells in a pavilion adorned with jewel trees; these jewel trees represent the conduct of the Dharma Master, while the pavilion signifies that his wisdom is lofty and far-reaching, shining forth in successive layers without obstruction. Thus, he illuminates wisdom through the adornment of manifold practices.
By preaching the various teachings so that sentient beings may believe and submit, this Dharma Master is one whose practice and realization are complete.
Fourth, as for what kind of liberation is attained within the three realms: one attains the liberation of the perfection of wisdom.

Fifth, regarding the exegesis of the text according to its meaning, there are two points as previously stated. As for the long division of the sūtra’s intent, it is divided here at the stage of the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
In seven sections.
[Sūtra] When this eighth stage of the Bodhisattva was being taught, the Tathāgata manifested great supernormal powers,
shaking all the lands throughout the ten directions in inconceivable numbers of immeasurable billions.
The Unsurpassed Honored One of all knowledge and vision, His body universally radiates great light,
illuminating those immeasurable lands, Causing all sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Bodhisattvas Simultaneously leap up into the void and abide there.
With offerings surpassing those of all the heavens, they worship the Sovereign Lord Maheśvara,
the most supreme among speakers; with one mind and immeasurable joy,
each presenting various kinds of manifold offerings, they worship the ocean of profound merit.
Furthermore, there were ten million billion celestial maidens, Their bodies and minds filled with pervasive joy;
Each played countless varieties of musical instruments To make offerings to the Great Teacher among Men.
At that time, all the music played simultaneously, In hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of distinct ways.
All through the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata, they produce sublime sounds in praise:
"Tranquil, gentle, stainless, and free from harm; According to the stages they have entered, their minds are well-cultivated like space;
Reaching the ten directions, they extensively proclaim the Buddha-way to awaken all living beings."
In all places, whether in the heavens or among humans, he manifests incomparable and wondrous adornments;
born from the merit of the Tathāgata, he causes those who see him to delight in the Buddha’s wisdom.
Without leaving a single land, he reaches all beings, like the moon appearing everywhere to illuminate the world.
All sounds and mental conceptions are utterly extinguished, like an echo in a valley that does not fail to respond.
If there are sentient beings with inferior minds, for them he expounds the practice of the Śrāvakas;
if their minds are clear and sharp and they delight in the Pratyekabuddhas, then for them he teaches the path of the Middle Vehicle.
If there is one who possesses compassion and delights in benefiting others, for their sake he explains the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas;
if there is one with the most excellent mind of wisdom, then he reveals the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Just as a magician performs various feats, all of whose diverse forms and appearances are not real.
The illusory wisdom of the Bodhisattva is likewise; though it manifests all things, it is free from existence and non-existence.
Having thus offered millions of kinds of beautiful sounds in song and praise to the Buddha, he remained silent.
Vimukticandra then said: "Now this assembly is pure; I pray that you will speak of the practices of the Ninth Ground."

[Treatise] First, regarding the explanation of this Bodhisattva’s eighth stage, the following twenty-six verses clarify how the great assembly offers worship and praise upon hearing the teachings of the preceding stage, and requests the exposition of the dharma-gate of the ninth stage.
Second, as for the word-by-word commentary on these verses, they are further divided into two sections: the first consists of twenty...
The five verses of praise consist of two parts: the first section concerns the great assembly of the preceding stage rejoicing, making offerings, and extolling the Dharma;
the final verse of this section concerns the request for the subsequent stage. The meaning of these two sections of verses is self-evident from the text itself.
[Sūtra] At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
having already used such immeasurable wisdom to contemplate and investigate, desires to seek further the even more supreme tranquility and liberation,
they again cultivate the wisdom of the Tathāgata, enter the secret dharma of the Tathāgata, and contemplate the inconceivable Great [Vehicle]."

By means of the nature of wisdom, the purification of all dhāraṇīs and samādhi-gates, the possession of vast great supernormal powers, the entry into differentiated worlds, the cultivation of the powers, fearlessnesses,

and unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), and by following the turning of the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas, not abandoning great compassion, and through the power of his original vows, the son of the Buddha— the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—
enters the ninth bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī). Abiding in this Stage of Excellent Intelligence...
He knows, as they truly are, the courses of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena; the courses of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena;

the courses of mundane and supramundane phenomena; the courses of conceivable and inconceivable phenomena; the courses of determinate and indeterminate phenomena; the courses of the phenomena of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the courses of the phenomena of bodhisattvas; the courses of the phenomena of the stage of a Tathāgata; and the courses of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
By means of such wisdom, this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the forest of sentient beings' minds, the forest of afflictions,
the forest of karma, the forest of faculties, the forest of understandings, the forest of natures, the forest of inclinations, the forest of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the forest of rebirths,
the forest of the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the forest of the distinctions among the three groups of beings. This bodhisattva, like...

He truly knows the various characteristics of the minds of sentient beings, namely: the characteristic of arising in a mixture, the characteristic of rapid transformation, the characteristic of being subject to decay or non-decay, the characteristic of lacking form or substance, the characteristic of being without boundaries, the characteristic of purity, the characteristic of being stained or stainless, the characteristic of being bound or unbound, the characteristic of being produced by illusion, and the characteristic of arising according to the various realms of existence.
These hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and even immeasurable such [characteristics] are all like this.
He truly knows and further understands the various characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*), namely: the characteristic of long-term persistence; the characteristic of boundless origination;

the characteristic of arising simultaneously and not being abandoned; the characteristic of the single meaning of dormancy and manifestation; the characteristic of association with or dissociation from the mind;

the characteristic of persisting through rebirth in accordance with one's destiny; the characteristic of differentiation within the three realms; and the characteristic of love, view, delusion, and pride penetrating deeply like arrows.

He knows, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of faults, the characteristics of the uninterrupted causal conditions of the three types of karma, and so forth, up to eighty-four thousand [types], as well as the various characteristics of all karmas—namely, the characteristics of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral; the characteristics of being manifest or non-manifest;

the characteristics of arising simultaneously with the mind and not being separate from it; and the characteristics of having self-nature as their cause while perishing moment by moment in succession.

He knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of the non-loss of accumulated fruits; the characteristics of having retribution or being without retribution; the characteristics of receiving various retributions such as black-for-black;

the characteristics of the immeasurable fields; the characteristics of the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages; the characteristics of receiving results in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives;

and the characteristics of those who are in a vehicle or not in a vehicle, and those who are fixed or unfixed—briefly stated, even up to eighty-four thousand [teachings]. Furthermore, he knows the faculties of others as weak, middling, or superior.

The characteristics of the distinction between the prior limit and the posterior limit; the characteristics of non-distinction; the characteristics of superior, middling, and inferior; the characteristics of afflictions arising simultaneously and being inseparable;

the characteristics of vehicles and non-vehicles, and of the fixed and the unfixed; the characteristics of being fully matured and pliant; the characteristics of following the net of faculties, of lightness, transformation, and destruction;
the characteristics of supreme indestructibility; the characteristics of the distinction between regression and non-regression; and the distinct characteristics of remote, sequential, and co-arising.
He knows all characteristics, briefly stated from the eighty-four thousand down to their full extent, as they truly are;
furthermore, he knows the various dispositions—weak, middling, and superior—and the weak, middling, and superior inclinations, briefly stated from the eighty-four thousand down to their full extent;
and he knows the various characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely, those that arise simultaneously with a defiled mind and those that do not arise simultaneously with the mind.
The characteristics of association and dissociation with mental factors; the characteristic of persisting for a long duration; the characteristic of being unextractable from beginningless time;
the characteristic of being contrary to all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

the characteristic of the continuity of birth and bondage within the three realms; the characteristic of causing the succession of infinite mental states to manifest; and the characteristic of opening the gates to all sense bases.

The characteristics of being firm and difficult to cure; the characteristics of the accomplishment or non-accomplishment of places and locations; the characteristic of uprooting [defilements] solely by means of the Noble Path;

furthermore, knowing the various characteristics of taking birth—namely, the characteristic of taking birth according to karma, the characteristics of the distinctions among the six destinies, the distinctions between the realms of form and formlessness, and the distinctions between those with perception and those without perception; and [knowing that] karma is the field, moistened by the water of craving.
The characteristics of being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; the characteristic of consciousness acting as the seed to produce the sprout of future existence;

the characteristic of name-and-form arising simultaneously and inseparably; the characteristic of craving and seeking that continues existence; the characteristic of desire for sensation and desire for birth, characterized by beginningless attachment to pleasure;

the characteristic of falsely claiming to have transcended the three realms while still greedily seeking them; and furthermore, knowing the various characteristics of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), namely, the characteristics of the distinction between what is practiced and what is not.

The characteristic of perfuming according to the realms of rebirth; the characteristic of perfuming that follows the conduct of sentient beings; the characteristic of perfuming by karma and afflictions;
the characteristic of perfuming by the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the characteristic of perfuming that enters into subsequent existence; the characteristic of sequential perfuming;

the characteristic of perfuming that does not abandon the distant journey of uninterrupted afflictions; the characteristic of pervasive perfuming that is not real; and the perfuming resulting from seeing, hearing, and attending upon [the teachings].

Furthermore, one knows the characteristics of the habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*) of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas; as well as the characteristics of sentient beings who are fixed in the right [path],

fixed in the wrong [path], or undetermined— namely, the characteristic of being fixed in the right path through right view, the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong path through wrong view, the characteristic of being undetermined in both,

the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong path due to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the characteristic of being fixed in the right path due to the five faculties (*indriya*), the characteristic of being undetermined in both, and the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong path due to the eightfold wrong path.

The characteristic of the nature of right concentration is that one no longer engages in duality, being free from both the characteristic of indeterminate concentration and the characteristic of attachment to false dharmas and wrong concentration;
the characteristic of the noble path of right concentration is that one abandons both and is free from the characteristic of indeterminate concentration.

O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva who accords with such wisdom is said to dwell in the Stage of Good Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Having dwelt in this stage, they thoroughly understand the distinctions among the various conducts of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva is skillfully able to expound the Dharma of the śrāvakayāna,
the pratyekabuddhayāna, the bodhisattvayāna, and the dharmas of the Tathāgata-bhūmi. Because they practice in accordance with the wisdom that follows all spheres of conduct,

they are able to accord with the differences in the faculties, dispositions, inclinations, and understandings of sentient beings, as well as the distinctions between their various realms of rebirth, receiving [the teachings] accordingly.
For those bound by the latent tendencies of karma and the slumber of afflictions that have arisen, he teaches the Dharma so that they may develop faith and understanding,
increase their wisdom, and each attain liberation through their respective vehicles.

[Treatise] The second section consists of sixty-one and a half lines of sūtra text, which clarifies the stage of cultivating entry into the nine grounds (*navabhūmi-praveśa-bhāvanā*) and the stage of knowing the distinctions among all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-viśeṣa-jñāna*) upon correctly abiding in the minds of the nine grounds. Within the word-by-word commentary, this is divided into fourteen sections:
1. From "At that time" (*atha khalu*) down to the ninth ground, *Sādhumatī*, there are six and a half lines of sūtra text; this is the section on "entering" (*praveśa*).

The ninth stage (*bhūmi*) is divided into two parts. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "the practice of unconditioned phenomena" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma-caryā*), there are four lines of sūtra that clarify the dwelling in the ninth stage and the knowledge of the ten kinds of practices of all sentient beings; this section is divided into three.
From "This Bodhisattva" down to "the dense forest of distinctions," there are three lines of sūtra that clarify how the Bodhisattva in this stage knows the one [truth].
The eleven types of thickets of all sentient beings are divided into four parts.

From "this Bodhisattva knows them as they truly are" down to "knows them all as they truly are," there are four lines of sutra text clarifying that the Bodhisattva in this stage penetrates the distinctions between ten types of characteristics.
Furthermore, from "knowing all afflictions" down to "knowing all eighty-four thousand [afflictions] as they truly are," there are five parts.
There are four and a half lines of scripture clarifying that a bodhisattva in this stage knows the characteristics of the eighty-four thousand afflictions as they truly are;

furthermore, from "knowing all karmas" down to "eighty-four thousand," there are five lines of scripture clarifying that a bodhisattva in this stage knows the various characteristics of karma up to eighty-four thousand, knowing them as they truly are.
"Dividing into seven" and "furthermore knowing the various faculties" (*indriya*) down to "even eighty-four thousand [faculties],
he knows them all as they truly are" consists of four and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how a bodhisattva at this stage knows the distinct characteristics of the various faculties. Furthermore,
"knowing the various inclinations" (*adhimukti*) consists of one and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how a bodhisattva at this stage knows the distinctions among the various inclinations.

From "up to eighty-four thousand divisions" and "furthermore, having known the various characteristics of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)" down to "only by means of the Noble Path can they be uprooted," the *Ṣaḍākāra-sūtra* clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the various types of characteristics of the latent dispositions.

From "furthermore, having known the various characteristics of taking birth" down to "the characteristic of falsely claiming to have transcended the three realms while still greedily seeking [existence]," [the sūtra clarifies the characteristics of birth].
The *Pañcagatika-sūtra* clarifies this stage where the Bodhisattva knows the various characteristics of taking birth; this constitutes the eleventh section.

Furthermore, from "knowing the various characteristics of habitual tendencies" down to "the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s perfuming," the *Pañcagatika-sūtra* clarifies this stage where the Bodhisattva knows the various characteristics of habitual tendencies;
this constitutes the twelfth section. Moreover, [the sūtra] explains that the Bodhisattva knows the beings who are fixed in the right determination (*samyaktvaniyata*).

From "Furthermore" (*yǐxià*) down to "both abandon the indeterminate characteristics" (*èjù shě bùding xiàng*), four and a half lines of scripture clarify that at this stage, the Bodhisattva knows the distinction between the certain and the false;
this constitutes section thirteen. From "O Sons of the Buddha" (*fózi yǐxià*) down to "causing them to attain liberation" (*lìng dé jiětuō*), two lines of scripture provide the general conclusion;
this constitutes section fourteen, which concerns knowing the distinctions among various dharmas. O Sons of the Buddha.
From this point downward, there are four lines and a half of sūtra that clarify the section on obtaining benefit according to one's faculties through the four vehicles of Dharma.
Furthermore, from the first section of the initial six lines and a half of sūtra, it says:
"By means of such immeasurable wisdom, they contemplate and investigate, desiring to further seek a more supreme, tranquil liberation."

This clarifies that in the eighth stage, one enters the principle of wisdom (*jñāna*) with effortlessness, proceeding toward the sublime advancement of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-fruit—the great function of the ten powers and four fearlessnesses—which is characterized by the quiescence of effortlessness; thus, one further cultivates the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This clarifies that because one has not yet attained mastery over the Buddha’s functional activities during the cultivation of the eighth and ninth stages, one enters the secret of the Tathāgata.
The Dharma transcends conceptual deliberation and the cultivation of objects of knowledge; it does not form mental constructs, yet universally responds to all phenomena without ceasing.
Thus, to observe the nature of inconceivable great wisdom is the fundamental, universally radiant great wisdom.
"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to the essence of luminous wisdom. This nature has no fixed basis or abode, yet it manifests great function in accordance with the faculties and objects of perception.
Regarding the purification of the gates of *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*: by means of non-abiding wisdom, one universally responds to sentient beings to accomplish great function;

this is the meaning of "right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*) and "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*). Thus, one possesses great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): because wisdom responds to faculties, it is called "supernormal" (*śa*);
because its essence pervades the ten directions without going, it is called "pervasion" (*tong*); furthermore, because wisdom has no fixed abode, it is called... [the name of the power].
As for its being "divine" (*śen*): to possess knowledge and vision equal to oneself and others is called "penetration" (*tong*);

furthermore, because the nature of wisdom possesses great power while remaining formless, it is called "divine," and because it lacks self-nature yet possesses manifold names, it is called "penetration.
Furthermore, because it possesses knowledge and vision while being free from birth and death, it is called "divine"; it is equal to the *dharmadhātu* and unifies both the one and the many.

That which is called "penetration" and below is self-evident according to the text. The above constitutes the second section of the cultivation of the ninth stage, the portion concerning abiding in the ninth stage.

In this section, the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Stage of Good Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), he knows, as they truly are, the dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. This clarifies the practice.
In this stage, one becomes a great Dharma teacher who thoroughly knows the mental activities of all sentient beings—
whether they are wholesome or unwholesome— as well as those that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, which are termed neutral (*avyākṛta*). Just as there are four kinds of unwholesomeness,

there are thirteen kinds of wholesomeness (*kuśala*), consisting of natural wholesomeness (*svabhāva-kuśala*), associated wholesomeness (*samprayoga-kuśala*), derivative wholesomeness (*pṛṣṭha-kuśala*), and ultimate wholesomeness (*paramārtha-kuśala*).

There are two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states—those that are associated, follow along, initiate, are ultimate, acquired at birth, skillful means, manifest, beneficial, engaging, remedial, tranquil, and of uniform outflow—as found among the eight consciousnesses:
the five consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and so forth are non-obscured neutral; the sixth mental consciousness is obscured and determinate; and the seventh is the grasping [consciousness].
The eighth consciousness, which is obscured and indeterminate, is called the *ālayavijñāna*. It is unobscured and indeterminate;

however, because it serves as the seed for the grasping consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*)—which is associated with outflows—and acts as the cause for rebirth in future lives, it is like a vessel containing seeds.

Furthermore, there are four types of indeterminate [consciousness]: those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), transformation (*nairmāṇika*), and maturation (*vipākaja*), just as in the world.
Whether one possesses dignified deportment or lacks it, and whether one is skilled in crafts or not, all such states involve the loss of right mindfulness;
this is just like learning worldly magical transformations. Such states are dissociated from right mindfulness.

Just as karma performed in the present world results in a body of ripening in a future life, so too does death correspond to a single moment of non-awakening when receiving rebirth. Furthermore, there are four types of indeterminate intrinsic natures.
Corresponding to the elicitation of the ultimate truth, these four types of indeterminate states constitute the supramundane path; such are the dharmas of practice.
In this stage, the Bodhisattva fully knows that dharmas of the three realms are with outflows (*sāsrava*), while dharmas that transcend the three realms are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Among those without outflows, the dharmas of the three vehicles that transcend the three realms are without outflows, as is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the Buddha.
Universal Radiant Wisdom is the practice of the dharma that is untainted and belongs to both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The three vehicles are the practice of the supramundane dharma; ordinary beings are the practice of the mundane dharma;

and the One Vehicle is neither mundane nor supramundane, for it is able to accord with the world while possessing the practices of Samantabhadra—thus it is the dharma of the conceivable and the inconceivable.

All that belongs to the three realms is a conceptually conceivable phenomenon (*cintya-dharma*). Furthermore, the supramundane paths of the three vehicles are all conceivable because they involve something attained (*upalabdha*).

Therefore, the cognitive realm of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is inconceivable (*acintya*), for it is without attainment; it is the state of infinite great mastery wherein stillness and activity are inseparable.
Regarding the fixed and unfixed phenomena: these refer to the four dhyānas of the form realm and the four [formless attainments] of the formless realm.
Dhyāna is a dharma of concentration; it is not a dharma of fixed concentration because it is not true concentration and because it possesses arising and ceasing.

The supramundane concentration of extinction of the Three Vehicles is a dharma of concentration; it is not a dharma of fixed concentration because it all involves the dharmas of grasping and abandoning.

The Dhyāna of the Dharmadhātu in the One Vehicle is a dharma of concentration; it is not a dharma of fixed concentration because it is the sovereign freedom of quiescence and function. All ordinary beings...

Now, the Dharma is an indeterminate dharma, whereas the Dharma of all Buddhas is a determinate dharma; therefore, all ordinary beings and sages lack a determinate nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), as they have no basis for reliance.

As for the Dharma of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they weary of suffering and its accumulation, cultivate cessation and the path, realize dependent origination, and enter the nature of non-arising.
Having abandoned compassion and wisdom, they transcend the worldly bonds of conditions. Therefore...
The practitioner of the dharma of *bodhisattva* conduct practices the six *pāramitās* while retaining delusions and taking birth in the Pure Land;
the practitioner of the dharma of the *tathāgata* stage possesses universal radiant wisdom, which serves as the ground for all sentient beings and for the three vehicles and the one vehicle;
and the practitioner of conditioned dharmas consists of the humans and devas of the triple world and those practicing the three vehicles.

Because those born of the outflow-free (anāsrava) are collectively categorized as conditioned formations (saṃskāra), and because the pure and impure minds persist, the unconditioned dharma-practice belongs exclusively to the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Thus ends the preceding section of four lines of scripture, which concludes the analysis of the ten kinds of dharma-practice.
Third, regarding the section on this bodhisattva’s knowledge of the ten kinds of dense forests of all sentient beings, the scripture says:
This Bodhisattva, through such wisdom, knows the "dense forest" of sentient beings' minds as it truly is.

This refers collectively to the vast multitude of afflictions, which are like a dense forest, all arising from the mind; when there is no mind, the dense forest of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is extinguished.
Because great wisdom is like a forest that can universally shelter and protect all sentient beings, the "dense forest of afflictions" refers to delusion.
The self-nature of the *dharmadhātu* gives rise to all the dense forests of afflictions, numbering as many as the atoms within the world-systems of the space-element;

thus, one clearly perceives that afflictions are vast and their obscurations are like a dense forest. Once the realm of realized wisdom is reached, it becomes a dense forest of the merits of the ten thousand practices.
Therefore, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) can be known through the roots of karma, the faculties, the lineages, and the inclinations.
The "dense forest" (*gahana*) consists of seven [afflictions]: first, desire for sensory enjoyment; second, aversion; third, malice; fourth, craving; fifth, pride;
sixth, ignorance; and seventh, views and doubt. These seven types constantly delude and obscure [the mind], and are thus called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*).
Because they delude the infinite objects of the mind and obstruct the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhi-jñāna*), they are termed the "dense forest. Regarding the "dense forest of rebirth":
Regarding the dense forest of habitual tendencies that arise simultaneously with eight hundred births and cessations at a single kṣaṇa-limit:

as established in the sūtras, the ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and ten stages (*bhūmi*) are all considered a portion of the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmipūrva*).

One is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; while one suddenly severs the coarse afflictions (*dausthulya-kleśa*) of the three realms, one gradually treats the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) on the grounds (*bhūmi*) from the first stage onward.

On the first stage, one clearly contemplates the phenomena of the world; on the second stage, one uses the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) to remedy the afflictions and habitual tendencies of the desire realm;

on the third stage, one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis to remedy the afflictions and habitual tendencies of the two upper realms; on the fourth stage, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata;

on the fifth stage, one cultivates the gateways to all worldly arts and crafts; on the sixth stage, wisdom emerges from the entanglements and becomes fully perfected; and on the seventh stage, one enters [the path].
The skillful means for benefiting sentient beings consist of the wisdom of the eighth bhūmi, which manifests effortlessly; the practices of the ninth bhūmi, which are spontaneously accomplished;
and the Buddha-activity of the tenth bhūmi, where merit is perfected—all of which are skillful means for treating habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the "dense forest" of distinctions among the three aggregates: based on the three unwholesome roots, there are sixteen kinds of dense forests; when expanded, these are eighty-four thousand.

The sixteen kinds of "thousands and the inexhaustible" are: the three unwholesome roots, the three poisons, the three stumps, the three impurities, the three burnings, the three arrows, the three evil conducts, the three abandonments, the three fetters, the three possessions, the three fevers, the three afflictions, the three disputes, the three blazing fires, the three thickets, and the three obstructions;
these are all collectively made to have greed, hatred, and delusion as their essence.
The various afflictions (*kleśa*)—as clarified by the three preceding lines of the sūtra—are categorized as the "thicket of afflictions" (*gahana-kleśa*).
When it says, "this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the various characteristics of the minds of sentient beings," this refers to them collectively.

Specifically, "the characteristic of arising in a mixed manner" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*) taking on diverse objects; "the characteristic of rapid transformation" refers to their arising and ceasing in impermanence, moment by moment.
Regarding the characteristics of abiding, destruction, and non-destruction: the impermanence of the world is what the mind grasps as the characteristic of destruction.

Since the characteristics of the world are not established, there is no destruction; truth and falsity are identical herein, which is the characteristic of the equality of the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding the characteristic of formlessness: it is like the mind’s thought of emptiness, acting as emptiness and perceiving the characteristic of boundlessness.
Regarding those who cultivate the perception of boundless purity, they know such phenomena of defilement and purity, bondage and non-bondage, exactly as they are;

they know them all truly and accurately, even unto the immeasurable. Just as in the twelve links of dependent origination, from "self-love," "grasping," and "existence" downward refers to their destruction, this passage clarifies that a Bodhisattva in this stage knows various mental perceptions exactly as they are.
One knows these marks through wisdom.

[Treatise] Regarding the five lines and four and a half characters of the sūtra that further explain the various characteristics of all afflictions, they are stated collectively as follows:
Regarding what is called the "aspect of long-term accompaniment," it means that all afflictions have no beginning or end, as they constantly accompany the object-condition (*ālambana*) of ignorance.
Regarding the "aspect of boundless origination," it is because *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) is designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of being the object-condition of the mind;
when that mind takes an object, feeling (*vedanā*) arises simultaneously with it, and the mental perception (*saṃjñā*) remains bound to the object-condition of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The seeds thus planted ripen as the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination; the waves of existence cease not.

With name-and-form as the object and the mind as the recipient, perception and volition act as the driving forces. The *manas* clings to consciousness, giving rise to craving, hatred, and delusion within the field of fundamental karma.
Therein, the seeds of consciousness are sown, producing various sprouts and crops—approximately eighty-four thousand types—which are innate and never abandoned. Such is the nature of things.
Regarding the previously explained single meaning of "sleeping" and "arising": the "sleeping afflictions" (anuśaya) are the seven types mentioned before;

the "arising afflictions" (paryavasthāna) are those that manifest as active karma, namely the ten latent tendencies (daśānuśaya) and the ten envelopments (daśa-paryavasthāna). Among these ten latent tendencies, six—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), extreme views (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi), false views (mithyā-dṛṣṭi), views regarding precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), and grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa)—are obstacles to the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga); four—namely, greed (rāga), hatred (dveṣa), delusion (moha), and pride (māna)—are [obstacles to the Path of Cultivation].

Although the practice of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) occurs after the path of seeing (darśanamārga), afflictions of the path of cultivation arise until they are eliminated at the third stage (bhūmi).
Those of the path of seeing are eliminated at the sixth stage. At the seventh stage, one encounters the Buddha’s compassionate wisdom and practices for the benefit of sentient beings.

From the first and second stages upward, the ten superior wholesome deeds (daśakuśala) remedy the delusions of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). At the third stage, one cultivates the four dhyānas and the eight [liberations].

Because one attains a mind that transcends the three realms by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which remedies the afflictions of the two upper realms, and because one is fully endowed with supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*) as the six stages (*bhūmi*), the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), and the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) manifest before one, there are no longer afflictions of the path of seeing from the seventh stage onward.
