which universally illuminate the animal realms of the ten directions and extinguish the suffering of sentient beings.

From the center of his navel wheel, he emitted ten million asaṃkhyeya rays of light that universally illuminated the realms of King Yama throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings;

from his left and right flanks, he emitted ten million asaṃkhyeya rays of light that universally illuminated all human realms throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings; and from his two hands, he emitted ten million asaṃkhyeya rays of light...
From his two shoulders, he emitted ten million *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light that illuminated all the palaces of the devas and asuras throughout the ten directions;
from the back of his neck, he emitted ten million *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light that universally illuminated the bodies of all the śrāvakas throughout the ten directions; and from his mouth...
A hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light universally illuminate the bodies of all Bodhisattvas from their initial generation of the mind up to the ninth stage throughout the ten directions.

From between their two eyebrows, they emit a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light that universally illuminate the ten directions, causing the palaces of Māra to become entirely invisible for those Bodhisattvas who have received their office. From the crowns of their heads, they emit a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya*...
As many rays of light as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems universally illumined all worlds in the ten directions;
they circled to the right ten times around the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and abiding in mid-air,
they formed a network of light called "Blazing Radiance," initiating various kinds of offerings to worship the Buddha and the other Bodhisattvas.
Compared to this, all the offerings made by Bodhisattvas from their first generation of the mind up to the ninth stage do not equal even one hundredth part;

they cannot even be reached by calculation, number, or analogy. Furthermore, from his net of light, he causes a rain of various exquisite incenses, flower garlands, robes, banners, pennants, and precious canopies to fall before each and every assembly of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions.
Various ornaments such as mani-jewels serve as offerings, all produced from supramundane roots of goodness and surpassing all worldly realms.

If there are sentient beings who see and know this, they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. O Son of the Buddha, this great radiance performs [these deeds] in such a manner.

When these acts of offering were completed, he again circumambulated the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of every single Buddha throughout all worlds in the ten directions ten times;
having done so, he entered through the soles of the feet of all the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas knew that in such-and-such a world, a certain Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was able to practice such vast conduct.

When the Bodhisattva attained the position of consecration, at that time, the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the ten directions—immeasurable, boundless, and including those up to the ninth stage—all came to surround him, paying respect and making offerings.

As they observed him with single-mindedness and correct contemplation, each of those bodhisattvas immediately attained ten thousand samādhis. At that very moment, all those who were to receive their own consecrations throughout the ten directions...

From within the mark of excellence on the chest known as the Adamantine Adornment (*vajra-alaṃkāra*), all these bodhisattvas emit a great light named "Able to Destroy the Enemies of Māra," accompanied by a retinue of one million *asaṃkhyeya* lights.
This light universally illumines the ten directions and manifests immeasurable supernatural transformations;
having performed these deeds, it enters into this adamantine adornment of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Once that light has entered into the mark of virtue upon his majestic chest, it causes all the power of this bodhisattva’s wisdom to increase by more than a hundred thousandfold.
[Treatise] The third section, consisting of sixty-eight and a half lines of scripture, clarifies that the bodhisattva of this stage sits upon a lotus flower.
Section Two: The Seat for the Great Dharma Master Receiving the Great Position of a Buddha of the Ten Stages.
Explaining the Meaning According to the Text. Within this section, it is further divided into ten parts.

First, from the beginning—"At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva..."—down to "receiving the position," there are seven lines of scripture clarifying how the bodhisattva of this stage proceeds from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*)...
In the ninth stage, having fulfilled the practice of great merit, wisdom, and great compassion, one enters the realm of sentient beings and enters the sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas.

This section is divided into two parts. From the words "O Son of the Buddha" down to "bestowing the supreme position of omniscience," there are eight and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattva of this stage attains thirteen samādhis and all other samādhis, which then manifest before them.

This is divided into three parts: first, from "When this samādhi manifests before one" down to "serving as its retinue," there are eight lines of sūtra that clarify how the bodhisattva in this stage, through the power of samādhi and the ripening of merit, causes a lotus flower to emerge;

once these Bodhisattvas have sat upon their lotus seats, their voices universally fill the worlds of the ten directions, and all things naturally tremble.

The light of the merit from his chest radiates universally throughout the ten directions and enters this Bodhisattva’s chest-merit,
causing its power to increase by more than a hundred thousandfold. This first section, consisting of seven lines of scripture,
clarifies how one cultivates the practices that assist the Path through the progressively purified dharmas from the first stage to the ninth stage, observing all phenomena and cultivating merit.
Virtue, wisdom, and the extensive practice of great compassion are all for the sake of accomplishing this ground of fundamental wisdom and compassion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Because one reaches the fulfillment of this stage, it is clarified that, from the very beginning, one takes the ground of the wisdom and compassion of all Buddhas as the five stages of cultivation;
thus, from the initial stage of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), one has already reached this ground of the wisdom of all Buddhas. Therefore, from the beginning...
There are five kinds of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and these five types of initial generation of the mind do not depart from a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

What are the five? First, the initial generation of the mind at the first stage of the *daśabhūmi* (Ten Abidings); second, the initial generation of the mind at the second stage of the *daśacaryā* (Ten Practices); third, the initial generation of the mind at the third stage of the *daśapariṇāmanā* (Ten Dedications);

fourth, the initial generation of the mind at the fourth stage of the *daśabhūmi* (Ten Grounds); and fifth, the initial generation of the mind at the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*). Thus, the initial generation of the mind in these five stages is entirely...

Because the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*) does not differ from the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), it constitutes the essence of wisdom that is without beginning or end.

These five kinds of initial arousal of the mind are all without beginning or end because they are not objects of perception for insentient consciousness or its subject-object duality, and because they are not encompassed by time, days, months, or years; thus, these five stages are all aroused simultaneously—just as one is ten.
Abiding in the initial resolve, one immediately uses that stillness of mind—undisturbed—to manifest the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is like the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī on Mount Sumeru attaining the gate of the light of wisdom through mindfulness of all Buddhas;
"mountain" signifies stillness. Thus, from the very first moment of leaving the stage of ordinary beings, by keeping the mind still and undisturbed, the Buddha-wisdom manifests.
Entering the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-ground is called the first dwelling of initial resolve. Second, regarding the ten practices:

initial resolve clarifies that one practices within the wisdom of all Buddhas without defilement. This is illustrated by the monk Sudeva of the Three-Eyed Country, who practiced walking meditation in the forest;
his walking meditation in the forest represents practice without defilement, while his walking meditation in the forest represents practice without abiding.
The three eyes represent the Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Wisdom-eye.
Having personally attained these three eyes of Tathāgata-wisdom, one further benefits all sentient beings by practicing without attachment. This is the first of the thirty dedications:
"At the initial arousal of the mind, [he was] the merchant of incense named Blue Lotus. This clarifies that he blended various incenses and sold them as a merchant of incense.

Dwelling therein, one clarifies the ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) to give rise to the gates of infinite great vows, harmonizing compassion and wisdom so that the *dharmakāya* may proceed with uniform equality;
thus, the blue lotus signifies being unstained by any exquisite colors or fragrances.
At the beginning of the forty stages, one first gives rise to the mind [of awakening] to cultivate and nurture great loving-kindness and great compassion, which then increase and become preeminent.
The Night Goddess Vasanti—here translated as "Spring-Birth Mistress"—represents the Lord of Great Compassion, for she causes the sprouts of bodhicitta to arise in sentient beings.

This is the eleventh stage. Because at the initial arousal of the mind, effortless and spontaneous great compassion first manifests, taking the birth of all Buddhas from Queen Māyā as its primary example, it clarifies that [this stage] proceeds from...

Because the wisdom born of compassion teaches and transforms sentient beings, as described above regarding the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, these five kinds of direct and reverse [contemplations] are all fully present within the initial mind at once, without any sequence or temporal limits.
Since they take the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* as their essence, the distinctions of before and after, or ancient and modern, cannot be spoken of. This section consists of seven [points].
The passage from "The practice of the sutra clarifies the perfection" through "the great wisdom and great compassion of the past and present, ancient and modern,

are fulfilled in the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings" explains that because the Buddha’s practices are complete, he reaches the station of the Great Dharma King and enters the dense forest of the birth and death of sentient beings;
this constitutes the second section, which contains eight and a half lines of scripture clarifying how the bodhisattva of this stage enters into this position.
One immediately attains ten kinds of samādhis and all samādhis; among them, the first is the "Stainless Samādhi" (*vimala-samādhi*), which is defined as right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

It is called the Stainless Samādhi because this stage is entirely free from the stains of the unevenness in the functions of compassion and wisdom regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—specifically, the distinction between defilement and purity.
It differs from the three vehicles, which abandon saṃsāra and grasp at nirvāṇa, and thus lack such purity.

Because it is free from the defilement of earth-dust, it is also distinct from the bodhisattvas of the lower stages who have not yet attained mastery over the myriad practices of wisdom, compassion, saṃsāra, and nirvāṇa due to their remaining stains.
Because the bodhisattvas of this stage are free from such stains, it is called the "Stainless Samādhi" (Vimalā).
By means of the seal of the non-conceptualizing wisdom of the dharma-realm, they seal all objective spheres so that there is nothing that is not an object of wisdom. Furthermore...

Because it is free from the obstacles of subject and object, birth and death, nirvana and samsara, defilement and purity, and so forth, it is called the Samādhi Free from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*).

Furthermore, the word "three" (*san*) signifies "correct" (*zheng*); since "correct" clarifies that single cessation (*śamatha*) is itself the character for "correct," it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of this stage, by means of the nature of the great universal radiance-wisdom which is inherently non-reliant, is termed "cessation," and constantly illuminates all phenomena with this wisdom.
The object of this state is called the Samādhi of Perfect Clarity. "Samādhi" (determinacy) refers to the generation of wisdom through discernment, such that one is no longer deluded by various views;
thus it is termed "samādhi. Its clarity arises from the first stage (*bhūmi*), where one cultivates various skillful means and factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Upon reaching this stage, all performed practices and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are absent; therefore, it is named the "Stainless Samādhi" (*vimala-samādhi*). It is also called the "Third [Stage]."
"Obscuration" refers to right reception (*samāpatti*); this stage is clarified by the fact that, through non-abiding and effortlessness, wisdom spontaneously pervades all.

Therefore, it is called the "Stainless Samādhi" (*vimala-samādhi*). Because this clarifies how effortless wisdom spontaneously and universally pervades, one enters the "Samādhi of the Differentiation of the Dharma-realm," which is the effortless, spontaneous application of wisdom in accordance with circumstances.

Because giving is the wisdom of differentiation, its manifest function does not depart from the essence; because it does not depart from the fundamental wisdom of non-action, it adorns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Regarding the samādhi of "all kinds of flower-light": it refers to reaching everywhere among the various places where Buddhas attain enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma, wherein one’s bodily conduct and the adornments of various jewels are present. Regarding the samādhi of "all kinds of flower-light": [it is so called because...]
The Samādhi of Illumination is so called because its light from the practice of samādhi illuminates all sentient beings.
The Samādhi of the Ocean Treasury is so called because it contains and stores all dharmas; it is like the ocean, which possesses ten virtues, serving as a metaphor for this state.

The Samādhi of the Ocean Seal is so called because the seal of the great ocean of wisdom—whose self-nature is perfect, bright, clear, and stainless—imprints all realms of the three periods of time, causing them to appear therein.
Among these, the Samādhi of the Vast and Great Space Realm clarifies that the essence of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness illuminates its own nature as being infinite and all-pervasive;

the Samādhi of Contemplating the Self-Nature of All Dharmas clarifies that through the contemplation of wisdom, one realizes that all dharmas lack self-nature and other-nature, and are thus sovereign;
and the Samādhi of Knowing the Mental Activities of All Sentient Beings [clarifies... [Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.]
Because he knows the faculties through wisdom and delivers beings according to those faculties,
the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas clarifies that this Samādhi Free from Defilement and the Samādhi of Essential Nature share the same single body and characteristic as all Buddhas.
From this point onward, the Bodhisattva has countless samādhis such as these manifest before him.

One who has attained skillfulness regarding the entry into and emergence from all these samādhis is one who can manifest many bodies from a single body and enter a single body from many bodies; who can emerge while entering and enter while emerging;
and who, within a single samādhi, discerns the mental activities and conduct of many sentient beings, as well as the spheres of many samādhis, and teaches many.
For sentient beings, there is no loss of opportunity; the final samādhi is named "Receiving All Supreme Positions.

This is the fulfillment of the wisdom of the ten stages and the completion of practice, wherein great compassion is equal, effortless, and spontaneous as it dwells in the world to benefit sentient beings.
Such numerous samādhis all arise from the Dharma-body and the Dharma-realm, which are by nature the unconditioned.

Because it arises from the Samādhi of Unobstructed Functioning of Radiant Wisdom and Quiescence, this samādhi is not the domain of those who practice tranquility within the three vehicles, nor those seeking liberation from the three realms, nor those who delight in being born in pure lands.
It is the realization of all ignorance that immediately becomes great wisdom; it is [the realization] of the bodies, lands, and atoms of all sentient beings.

This encompasses the realm of all those who dwell in the Buddha-lands; this Samādhi of Great Wisdom, which is quiescent yet active and without dependence, is the King of the inexhaustible treasury of the essence and function of the fundamental wisdom of all Buddhas.
It can manifest transformations according to the infinite mental dispositions of all sentient beings without missing the proper time, yet it has no agent. Thus, this third samādhi is present.
From the passage below "at a former time" to the end of the seven and a half lines of scripture, it clarifies the bodhisattva who receives the office (*abhiṣeka*).
Regarding the birth of the flower as a retribution, the *Sūtra* states: "When this samādhi manifests before one, a great lotus flower suddenly emerges.

This is the bodhisattva receiving the office, whose own practices of compassion and wisdom are fulfilled; through the convergence of dharmas and the application of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he benefits sentient beings."
This is the body of the final samādhi among the ten stages, obtained as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*).

Regarding the statement that "the quantity of its flowers is equal to one million three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems": one thousand sets of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*) constitute one small thousandfold world system;

one thousand small thousandfold world systems constitute one medium thousandfold world system; and one thousand medium thousandfold world systems constitute one great thousandfold world system. It is now said that [the quantity] is equal to this.
Regarding the phrase "a million three-thousandfold world systems," this clearly indicates the designation of an immeasurably vast extent.

The subsequent descriptions of adornments are as detailed in the sūtra itself. As for the statement in the sūtra, "arising from supramundane roots of goodness," this refers not to the pure lands that transcend the triple world, nor to the wholesome qualities of bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles who have transformed their birth-and-death through the *parinirmita* (transformation) mode of existence.
Because it cannot be known by the sense faculties, this knowledge that all phenomena are formed of an illusory nature constantly emits light that universally illumines the Dharma-realm.
This corresponds to the cause and fruit of the roots of goodness, like a lotus flower whose stem is made of *vaiḍūrya* maṇi jewels.
Regarding "vai," it means "light"; thus, the luminous *vaiḍūrya* represents the clarity of the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body.
Because it is pure, the light of that maṇi jewel is pure and stainless; it resembles lapis lazuli but is not composed of lapis lazuli, being made solely of maṇi.
It serves as the stem for the lotus flower, wherein "stem" refers to the retributive fruit of the nature of the dharmakāya and jñānakāya being free from stain.
Because the essence of the dharmakāya and jñānakāya acts as the foundation for all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), it is now described according to this retributive fruit.
The birth of the lotus is further accomplished as a reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) because its intrinsic nature is the purity of the Dharma-body’s wisdom.
Therefore, it has a stem made of radiant, pure *maṇi* jewels and a pericarp of *candana-rāja* sandalwood;

this clarifies that it arises from the roots of goodness of the fivefold Dharma-body—namely, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—and is produced by means of the Dharma.

The body is able to produce the fragrance of the fivefold dharma-body, consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth; now, by relying on this retributive fruit, these qualities mutually support one another in succession.
That the calyx is made of agate represents the factors that assist bodhi; it is the retribution for the roots of goodness of the myriad practices.
Obtaining this, which is a red-colored jewel, signifies the manifestation of the bodhi of principle and wisdom through the myriad practices, as well as their adornment.
Because the fivefold Dharma-body mutually supports and inspires one another, they are described in sequence. As for the leaves being made of Jāmbūnada gold:
this gold is luminous, pure, and supple; it is born from the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion.

Since "compassion" (maitrī-karuṇā) carries the meaning of providing shelter and protection, its flowers always possess immeasurable radiance. This represents the light of the Dharma of wisdom, which benefits sentient beings through skillful means.
That which has treasuries of various jewels produced from its roots; that which completely binds this ground and is covered by nets of jewels produced from the containment of all virtues;
that which is well-arranged as a net of teaching to filter all sentient beings;
and that which has as its retinue lotuses as numerous as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms, produced from the roots of goodness—this is the first practice, pervading everywhere.

All practices, all modes of conduct, and the roots of goodness arising from the universal single practice—these constitute the roots of goodness through which the sovereign mastery of the ten thousand practices arises as the primary and attendant manifestations.
These aforementioned flowers were manifested before the Tathāgata in the Hall of Universal Radiance when the Ten Faiths were first taught;
the assembly of retinues is [manifested] from within the ūrṇā-hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows.
The preceding section raised the fruit to encourage practice; this is the fourth [section], the fruit at the conclusion of the practice.
From "At that time" onwards, the three lines of scripture clarify that the size of the seats occupied by the Bodhisattvas of this stage is commensurate with their stature.

Those seated upon the Flower-King (Padmarāja) represent the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while the Bodhisattvas who are the retinue seated upon the various flower-seats represent the differentiated wisdom (*prabheda-jñāna*).
The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," spanning five lines of scripture,
clarifies that when this stage of Bodhisattva’s wisdom, compassion, and myriad practices are all-pervasive,
they move the assembly to offer offerings as described in the text itself. The sixth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," spanning twenty-four and a half lines, [describes the same].
The Sūtra clarifies that when a Bodhisattva in this stage sits upon his seat and emits light to relieve suffering, he does so according to a sequence based on the parts of his body.

First, light from beneath his feet illuminates the sufferings of the great hells; this clarifies that what is beneath the feet is the ultimate practice one treads upon for the sake of relieving suffering.
Next, light from both knees illuminates the sufferings of animals, clarifying that these are what one treads upon next.
Following the exhaustion of the knees, light is emitted from within the navel-cakra, illuminating the realm of King Yama.
Those whose suffering is like that of the great hells and who are not governed by a king, due to their extremely intense evil karma, go directly to the miserable destinies;
those in the minor hells who are governed by a king are those whose navels are the locus where the accumulation of various impurities resides and where birth and death are partitioned.
The ultimate limit of delusion regarding reality and the source of birth and death correspond to the two lunar stations of Xū (戌) and Hài (亥), which are assigned to the Qian hexagram;
this signifies that the light emitted from within [the heart] illuminates all phenomena of birth and death. The light emitted from the left and right flanks illuminates the realm of human suffering;
"flank" (*xiè*) refers to the place of grasping and supporting, clarifying that humans are beings who can be gathered and sustained. Therefore, [light is emitted from] both hands.
He emits light from his crown that illuminates the devas and asuras in order to attract and guide them;

he emits light from both shoulders to illuminate those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, signifying their delight in hearing the Dharma and their ability to combat the afflictions; he emits light from near his ears to signify that one attains the fruit through hearing the Dharma;
and he emits light from his neck and back to illuminate those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, signifying their lack of delight in hearing the Dharma and their turning away from it.
The light emitted from the face is because the Buddha possesses knowledge and vision; the light emitted from between the eyebrows is because he has received the teaching;

the light emitted from the crown of the head is because it is the fruit of the Middle Way in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and the light [emitted from other parts] is because it is the ultimate fruit of a Buddha. The remainder is as fully detailed in the text itself.
Seventh, "O Son of the Buddha," and so forth, comprises two and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the Bodhisattvas in this stage emit light as described above.

Having completed the offerings of light and the deeds performed, [the light] circumambulated the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of every Buddha in all worlds of the ten directions ten times, and then entered from beneath the feet of the Tathāgatas. The "ten circumambulations" signify the perfection of the ten dharmas;
that the light enters beneath the Buddhas' feet signifies the returning of the fruit to the cause. This is the meaning.
From within the Hall of Universal Radiance, the Tathāgata rose and emitted light from the wheels on the soles of his two feet to perfect the ten levels of faith;
next, for the ten abodes, he emitted light from the tips of his toes; next, for the ten practices, he emitted light from the tops of his feet;
next, for the ten dedications, he emitted light from his knees; and next, for the ten grounds, he emitted light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The light emitted from within now reaches here; the perfection of the fruit at the end of the ten stages of the path is not different from the dharma of initial faith.

Time does not shift, the dharma does not change, and the fruit does not differ. For this reason, the light that marks the completion of the ten stages returns through the soles of the Buddha’s feet, clarifying that the fruit is identical to the cause and thus not different, and illuminating the Tathāgata as the dharma that is to be believed.

To show that the fruit is identical to the cause, the Bodhisattva advances in practice by realizing that the cause is identical to the fruit; therefore, at these stages of the ten bhūmis, one returns to the cause from the fruit.
For this reason, the light enters beneath the feet of all Buddhas. This also clarifies that because their practice is fulfilled, it enters the wheels upon the Buddha’s feet;
since the feet are the locus of practice, the following three sections may contain ten lines of scripture as they appear in the text.
[End of Section].

[Sūtra]: At that time, all Buddhas of the ten directions emitted from between their eyebrows a pure light named "Augmenting All-Knowledge and Supernatural Powers," with countless lights as its retinue, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Circling ten times to the right around the realm, he manifested the vast and sovereign power of the Tathāgata to awaken hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas;
he caused all buddha-fields to tremble universally, extinguished the sufferings of all evil realms,
eclipsed all the palaces of Māras, and revealed the paths where all Buddhas attain enlightenment.
The majesty and splendor of this assembly were thus universally illumined, pervading all worlds throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm;
having done so, they came to this assembly of Bodhisattvas, circumambulated it to the right, and manifested various kinds of magnificent adornments.
Having displayed these things, [the light] entered from the crown of the great Bodhisattva’s head, and his retinue’s radiance likewise [entered].
Each enters the crown of those bodhisattvas; at that moment, this bodhisattva attains a million samādhis previously unattained, which is called "having attained the rank of consecration.
He enters the realm of the Buddhas, becomes fully endowed with the ten powers, and is reckoned among the number of Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the crown prince born to a Wheel-Turning Sage King, whose mother is the principal queen and whose physical marks are complete.
Having fully equipped the Wheel-Turning King, he caused this crown prince to sit upon a magnificent golden throne on the precious white elephant;

he spread out great canopies, raised great banners and streamers, burned incense, scattered flowers, and played various musical instruments. Taking the waters of the four great oceans, he placed them within a golden vase;
the King held this vase and poured the water over the crown of the prince’s head. At that moment, he was named as having received the royal position and ascended [to it].

Just as a Kṣatriya king, upon receiving consecration, is immediately able to fulfill the practice of the ten paths of wholesome action and is also named a Wheel-Turning Sage King, so too is it for a Bodhisattva who receives office:
because the water of the Buddhas' wisdom is poured upon his crown, he is said to have received office;
and because he is endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, he is reckoned among the number of Buddhas. O Son of the Buddha, this is called Bodhi.
When the Bodhisattva accepts the office of Great Wisdom, by virtue of this office of Great Wisdom,

they are able to perform immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of difficult practices and increase immeasurable wisdom and merit; this is called "Abiding in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma."

[Treatise] The fourth section consists of twenty-two and a half lines of scripture that clarify how all Buddhas of the ten directions collectively emit the light of wisdom to confer empowerment and authorize [the Bodhisattva] to share in the rank of a Buddha. In the commentary on this meaning, it is divided into four parts:
first, from "At that time, all Buddhas of the ten directions" down to "falling within the number of Buddhas," there are twelve lines of scripture.
This section clarifies how Bodhisattvas in this stage receive their office and are consecrated by the Buddhas of the ten directions; it is divided into two parts.

First, regarding the Buddha-sons: from the passage "like a wheel-turning sage king" down to "also may be called a wheel-turning sage king," there are six lines of scripture that clarify the example of a wheel-turning king receiving the office of crown prince and taking water from the four great oceans to pour over his head.

The section on the "Crowning Metaphor" is divided into three parts. The passage beginning with "The empowerment of the Bodhisattva is likewise" and ending with "having fallen into the number of Buddhas" consists of approximately two lines of scripture that clarify the Bodhisattva’s reception of empowerment.
By means of the water of the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) of all Buddhas and their radiance, they are consecrated upon the crown of the head and thus enter the number of Buddhas.
This is divided into four sections. The passage beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha" and ending with the name... [is as follows].

The section on the "Virtuous Increase of the Wisdom-Light Consecration and the Practice of Receiving Office," which concludes the three types of practice for those dwelling securely in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), has been explained above.
These four segments of scripture clarify that when the wisdom of the ten stages is perfected, it accords with the Buddhas;

thus, the Buddhas emit light and confer consecration so that their wisdom may be equalized with the Buddhas' wisdom, and so that they may be sealed by the marks of the Buddha-fruit wisdom. Furthermore...
It initiates and increases the eleven stages and brings the sublime wisdom of the Buddha to maturity;
thus, these ten stages first manifest the Buddha-wisdom, while the eleventh stage attains mastery over it. The remainder is as fully detailed in the text itself.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), they know, as it truly is, the accumulation of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the accumulation of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the accumulation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),

the accumulation of the world-realm (*lokadhātu*), the accumulation of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the accumulation of the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), the accumulation of the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*),

the accumulation of the sentient-being realm (*sattvadhātu*), the accumulation of the consciousness-realm (*vijñānadhātu*), the accumulation of the space-realm (*ākāśadhātu*), and the accumulation of the nirvāṇa-realm (*nirvāṇadhātu*). This Bodhisattva knows these, as they truly are.
He knows the accumulation of the conduct of various views and afflictions; he knows the accumulation of the formation and destruction of worlds;

he knows the accumulation of the conduct of śrāvakas, the accumulation of the conduct of pratyekabuddhas, and the accumulation of the conduct of bodhisattvas; he knows the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, form-body, and dharma-body;

he knows the accumulation of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes and the wisdom of omniscience; he demonstrates the attainment of awakening, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the entry into the discernment of all phenomena.
To summarize the essential points of the collection on definitive knowledge: O Son of the Buddha, by means of such supreme and superior awakened wisdom,
this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows, as they truly are, the transformation of sentient beings’ karma, the transformation of afflictions,

the transformation of views, the transformation of worlds, the transformation of the dharma-realm, the transformation of śrāvakas, the transformation of pratyekabuddhas, and the transformation of bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata transforms all conceptualization and non-conceptualization; he knows all such things as they truly are, and he knows them as they truly are:

the Buddha-holding, Dharma-holding, Saṃgha-holding, karma-holding, affliction-holding, time-holding, vow-holding, offering-holding, practice-holding, eon-holding, and wisdom-holding—all such things he knows as they truly are. Furthermore, he knows the Buddhas as they truly are.
They enter into subtle wisdom, namely: subtle wisdom regarding the practice of cultivation, subtle wisdom regarding the end of life, subtle wisdom regarding rebirth,

subtle wisdom regarding leaving the household life, subtle wisdom regarding the manifestation of supernormal powers, subtle wisdom regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment, subtle wisdom regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma,
subtle wisdom regarding the duration of the lifespan, subtle wisdom regarding the parinirvāṇa, and subtle wisdom regarding the endurance of the teaching.
He knows such subtle wisdom as these exactly as they are; furthermore, he enters the secret realms of the Tathāgata, namely:
the secret of the body, the secret of speech, and the secret of the mind; the secret of deliberating upon the proper and improper time; the secret of bestowing predictions upon bodhisattvas;
the secret of gathering in sentient beings; the secret of the various vehicles; and the secret of the differences in the faculties and conduct of all sentient beings.
He knows as they truly are such things as the secrets of karmic actions, the secrets of attaining awakening, and the secrets of practice; furthermore,
he knows the wisdom of all Buddhas regarding the entry into eons— namely, how one eon enters incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
incalculable eons enter one eon, numbered eons enter unnumbered eons, and unnumbered eons enter numbered eons, even within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
Entering eon after eon; entering a single thought-moment as an eon; entering that which is neither an eon nor a non-eon; entering an eon with a Buddha as an eon without a Buddha;
entering an eon without a Buddha as an eon with a Buddha; entering past and future eons as the present eon; entering the present eon as past and future eons;
entering past eons as future eons; and entering future eons as past eons.
They know as they truly are such things as the entry of long eons into short eons and the entry of short eons into long eons.

Furthermore, they know the various wisdoms of entry possessed by the Tathāgata, namely: the wisdom of entering the path of a single hair, the wisdom of entering atoms, the wisdom of entering the lands and bodies of perfect enlightenment, the wisdom of entering the bodies of sentient beings and attaining perfect enlightenment, the wisdom of entering the minds of sentient beings and attaining perfect enlightenment, and the wisdom of entering the conduct of sentient beings.
The entrance into the wisdom of perfect enlightenment that accords with all places; the entrance into the wisdom of perfect enlightenment that manifests universal conduct;

the entrance into the wisdom that manifests conduct in accordance with the flow [of samsara] and conduct against the flow; the entrance into the wisdom that manifests the conceivable and the inconceivable, and the knowledge of what is understood and what is not understood in the world;
and the entrance into the wisdom of the śrāvakas, the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas, and the practices of the bodhisattvas.
The wisdom of the Tathāgatas’ practice and the wisdom possessed by all Buddhas— vast and immeasurable as it may be—
this Bodhisattva of this stage is able to enter into it.
[Śāstra] The fifth section consists of thirty-six and a half lines of sūtra text, clarifying that the Bodhisattva of this stage enters into the vast.
Regarding the section on the detailed analytical knowledge that thoroughly understands the various aspects of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), it is divided into eight parts: 1.

From "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "knowing all origination," there are eight lines of verse that clarify the knowledge of all aspects of the Truth of Origination within this Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
2. From "O Son of the Buddha" down to "all are known as they truly are," there are three and a half lines.
The Sūtra clarifies that Bodhisattvas at this stage truly know ten kinds of transformative methods, divided into three parts;

furthermore, from "having truly known" down to "all are truly known," two lines of sūtra clarify that Bodhisattvas at this stage truly know ten kinds of sustaining methods, divided into four parts; furthermore, from "having truly known" down to "such as these are all truly known..."
The four lines and a half of sūtra beginning with "He knows" clarify that the Bodhisattva in this stage knows the ten kinds of subtle wisdom of the Tathāgata;

this constitutes the fifth [topic]. Furthermore, the four lines of sūtra beginning from "Having entered the secret place of the Tathāgata" down to "knows all as they truly are" clarify that the Bodhisattva in this stage knows the ten kinds of secrets of the Tathāgata; this constitutes the sixth [topic]. Moreover, he knows all Buddhas...

From "He knows all as it truly is" down to this point, seven lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva of this stage knows the Tathāgata’s phases of entering and emerging from the *kalpas* of regression and progression. Furthermore,

from "He knows all that the Tathāgata enters" down to "the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Tathāgata’s wisdom," six and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva of this stage enters the thirteen [abodes].

The section on the "Wisdom of All Modes" (sarvākārajñatā) is divided into eight parts. From the passage beginning with "the sons of the Buddha and below" down to "are all able to enter," one and a half lines of scripture clarify that Bodhisattvas at this stage are able to enter the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata. Within the first segment of eight lines of scripture, it states:
"One knows the origin of the desire realm as it truly is. This is because the five aggregates are the common object of delusion within the three realms.
Based on the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) that follow upon the four truths, there is the ignorance that is deluded regarding the truths;

since each truth possesses all ten [afflictions], there are forty instances of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding this suffering and origin, through the cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga*), in the two upper realms—excluding hatred (*dveṣa*)—there are thirty-six in each.
These constitute the suffering and origin of the conditioned dhyāna realms; these are the dhyānas of the two upper realms.

All [of these] are obtained through the cessation and subduing of mental attention (*manasikāra*); therefore, because they are comprised within the outflows (*āsrava*) of the triple world, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) eliminates the arising of thoughts and the coming and going within the triple world.
These one hundred and twenty-eight kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*) common to the triple world constitute the general substance of the six realms of existence.
When categorized by means of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), [they are fully accounted for].
Regarding the causes and conditions of illumination, there are a total of eighty-four thousand and an incalculable number of accumulations;
as previously assigned for the stages prior to the eighth and ninth grounds, they should be understood accordingly. As for the Form Realm and Formless Realm, they may be known from the above.

As for the accumulation within the Dharma-realm, it is explained that when a single thought-moment accords with true wisdom, the aforementioned eighty-four thousand and the incalculable [defilements] manifest as such.

The teaching on the gates of all afflictions (*kleśa*) as the total accumulation of the ocean of wisdom—the aggregate of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation within the great wisdom of the entire *dharmadhātu*—is called the "Ocean of All Various Wisdoms.

As for the accumulation of the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), this refers to all the afflictions existing within the three realms; these are likewise subdued through the three vehicles, whereby one attains transformation.
The ease of birth and death and the bodies produced at will all arise from the accumulation of conditioned phenomena within the three realms;
therefore, the accumulation of the unconditioned consists solely of the Tathāgata’s omniscience and all various kinds of differentiated wisdom.
Since all else is conditioned, the accumulation of the realm of sentient beings and the accumulation of the realm of emptiness and nirvāṇa are to be correctly distinguished as such.
Arising from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they gather the various distinct cognitions of the realm of sentient beings, the realm of space, and the realm of nirvāṇa;

these bodhisattvas know, as it truly is, the accumulation of views and afflictions, namely the five views—such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—as well as the sixty-two views, which have already been explained in the preceding stage. Regarding the accumulation of the formation and destruction of worlds, they know the three [worlds].
He fully knows the formation, the abiding, and the destruction of a thousand great trichiliocosms and all worlds in the ten directions throughout various kalpas;
those who gather through the practice of the Śrāvakas observe the Four Noble Truths to become weary of the suffering of the triple world and to rejoice in the bliss of Nirvāṇa,
and they further contemplate all worldly phenomena as suffering, empty, impermanent, and impure.
All that is pleasurable is subject to decay and extinction; the accumulation of various karmic fruits results in suffering that is never severed, like the gathering of waves.
Unwholesome dharmas increase, giving rise to birth, old age, sickness, and death. The thirty-six constituents together form the body.
One cultivates the two hundred and fifty precepts to purify the suffering of the desire realm, cultivates the eight dhyānas of the two higher realms, and thereby understands those higher realms.

All karma is impermanent. Upon entering the ninth dhyāna, one transcends the perception of the three realms and enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), wherein both body and cognition are exhausted, and there is tranquil extinction and non-cognition.
As stated in the subsequent passage of this sutra: "For example, when a bhikṣu has entered the attainment of cessation, even if a drum is struck upon his head, he no longer hears the sound.
Furthermore, there are śrāvakas who have escaped the three realms and whose minds are weary of and averse to them.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* both state that those with fragmented bodies (分段身) burn their bodies with fire and enter into the birth-and-death of transformation (變易生死).

Śrāvakas of the two vehicles and Bodhisattvas in the Pure Land suppress active afflictions (*saṃmukhībhava-kleśa*) through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), thereby attaining the birth-and-death of transformation;
this is not achieved by severing afflictions, for they have not yet fully understood ignorance (*avidyā*) as the root.
Because of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one falsely perceives ignorance as being substantially real; thus, false aversion arises.

Through this mind of aversion, one achieves transcendence of the segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*) within the triple world and attains the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). Abiding in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), one no longer receives a body within the triple world in future lives.
It is as if an illusory fire were to burn the body; as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* itself: [The text continues with the citation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.]

All these involve the wearying of saṃsāra and abiding in nirvāṇa, gathering the practices of pratyekabuddhas; the gathering of these consists of the practice of the twelve links of dependent origination.
These four truths and twelve links of dependent origination are mutually integrated across the three vehicles to form nine vehicles, as previously described.
Even the bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle cultivate these same four truths and twelve links of dependent origination within the sequence of these ten stages.

Next, regarding the Dharma to be cultivated: these various methods of cultivation—such as the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Mind-Only View, and the Path of Seeing—are each distinct.
As for the collection of Bodhisattva practices, it is the Great Compassion of the Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the entanglements;

they cultivate the Six Pāramitās and the two aspects of compassion, taking birth in the Pure Land, and only when their path is perfected do they return to the world to teach and transform sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva, relying on the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of enlightenment, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Cultivating great compassion and non-attachment to the triple world, they transform sentient beings.

This is the establishment of all practices by relying on the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and effortlessness (*anabhisaṃskāra*)—and it is also the bodhi of the three vehicles.

The gates of practice and the spheres of activity cultivated through the skillful means and applications of the Bodhisattvas consist merely of taking the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system as a single Buddha-field.
This *Ekayāna* sūtra concerns itself solely with the ten *pāramitās*, the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination,
and the four foundations of mindfulness, all of which are cultivated by generating the mind [of awakening] within the sphere of the Tathāgata’s fundamental, universally radiant wisdom.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four means of integration, the four immeasurables, and all auxiliary paths to awakening take the fundamental wisdom of one’s own mind as their essence.
Because this wisdom is non-reliant and limitless, the gates of practice performed through it and their resulting fruits are both non-reliant and limitless.
Thus, the bodies and lands of self and others manifest in infinite, overlapping interpenetration, because this wisdom is limitless and unimpeded.
Because all bodies and lands, self and others, are like illusions and shadows and are entirely without obstruction, all practiced deeds have wisdom as their essence.
This is the collection of the bodhisattva practices of the three vehicles and the one vehicle;
such practices as the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage—these skillful means of practice constitute the bodhisattva path of the one vehicle.
The collection of the Tathāgata’s powers and fearlessnesses through the accumulation of practices consists of the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.

As for the "collection of the form-body and dharma-body," the ten powers and fearlessnesses constitute the form-body; the inexhaustible major marks and minor characteristics of a great man constitute the dharma-body.
This collection of the dharma-body is such that there is no principle to be attained or realized, neither bondage nor liberation, neither arising nor ceasing.
This refers to the impurity of defilements. Regarding "all types," this means that the seeds of perfumed cultivation are established through the five stages of application (*prayoga*).

Because all sentient beings, in accordance with the application of the five aggregates, immediately produce the seeds of ignorance and various karmas, the Bodhisattva’s application in the five stages establishes the seeds of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). The term "knowledge of all modes" denotes clarity.

The wisdom of differentiation arises from the fundamental wisdom that is without support, abiding, or fabrication; this is called the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) in the context of the Three Vehicles.
In the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), wisdom is directly the fundamental, perfect luminosity, which simultaneously encompasses the three periods of time without distinction of before or after.
At the moment of attaining *bodhi*, it is the wisdom that turns the wheel of Dharma; the twelvefold teachings spoken by the Gatherer (*saṃgha*) are the entry into all [truths].

Regarding the accumulation of the wisdom that definitively discerns phenomena: by means of adamantine, unimpeded wisdom, one skillfully discerns supramundane phenomena such that there is nothing not clearly understood and nothing not definitively determined; all is free from error.
To state the essentials, summarizing the general outline: "The knower of all who knows all accumulations" clarifies that there is nothing known exhaustively. This.
This concludes the first section, which ends with the knowledge of all *saṃudaya* (origination). The second section, consisting of three and a half lines of scripture, states:
"By means of such progressively superior awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*), one knows the transformation of the karma of sentient beings as it truly is.
This clarifies that all sentient beings, through the karma created by their own afflictions (*kleśa*), transform their own forms as well as the lands where they dwell, each according to themselves.
He knows, exactly as they are, that all the forms he assumes, the lands in which he dwells, and all his enjoyments arise from nothing other than karma;
furthermore, he knows that those who experience much suffering due to stinginess, greed, hatred, attachment, or aversion receive these results first.

He knows that all sentient beings ride upon the transformations of their various karmas, and he knows exactly which afflictions cause others to fall into the realms of rebirth through their conjunction with them.
He fully knows how the causes and effects of the various paths correspond to one another. Those who are transformed by views do so through the five views and the sixty-two views;
conditioned by name-and-form, they give rise to grasping and produce various bodies of afflictions.
Those who transform worlds do so through the various karmas of their own minds, producing the various forms of all worlds. Furthermore, regarding that which is...

Regarding the transformation of the world, one further takes hold of it; those who transform through the dharmadhātu of the various karmas of birth-by-transformation all produce various objective realms from their own inherently pure wisdom.

As for the transformations of the śrāvakas, they arise according to the power of right mindfulness induced by untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), such as the eighteen transformations; the same applies to the pratyekabuddhas. This collectively clarifies the correct [nature] of the two vehicles.
The transformations of the Bodhisattva’s emanations, which function universally according to the power of liberation, the power of mental intention, and the powers of the various *pāramitās*,
the power of the vow of great compassion, and the power of one’s own knowledge and vision of liberation,

manifest various bodies and various activities through the power of the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body) that accords with such intentions. As for the emanations of the Tathāgata, they arise from the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) Great [Wisdom].
Wisdom universally responds to all things because it is eternally pervasive; thus, it is both discriminative and non-discriminative.
As for "transforming," it means that by means of the dharma of non-discrimination within discrimination, it brings about the awakening and liberation of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, at the very moment of correct discrimination, there is the transformation of non-discrimination. The following is the summary. The above concludes the section on knowing all transformations. Part One.
The three sections and two and a half lines of sūtra clarify that Bodhisattvas in this stage are constantly able to maintain these ten immeasurable dharmas;
because they maintain each one without confusion or loss, they possess the "Buddha-retention" (buddhadhāraṇī), knowing all dharmas maintained by the Buddha;

they possess the "Dharma-retention" (dharmadhāraṇī), knowing the sequence of the dharmas; and they possess the "Saṃgha-retention" (saṃghadhāraṇī), knowing that the nature and essence of all combinations and dispersals are without separation or interval.

The "karma-sustaining" [knowledge] is because it knows the similarities and differences among the karma of sentient beings; the "affliction-sustaining" [knowledge] is because it knows the characteristics of afflictions;

the "time-sustaining" [knowledge] is because it knows that the beginningless past and the kalpas of the three periods of time—whether identical or different, general or specific—do not undergo transmigration. From here on, the remaining cases should be understood accordingly.
The above concludes the knowledge of the various sustainings. Fourth, there is the section on "knowing as it truly is the ten subtle wisdoms of the Tathāgata."
There are four and a half lines of sūtra clarifying that the Tathāgata, by means of non-reliant, non-abiding, and effortless wisdom (*anāśrita-apratiṣṭhita-anābhoga-jñāna*),
spontaneously and universally knows all phenomena; thus, throughout the ten stages— namely, the time of practice, death, rebirth, renunciation, the manifestation of supernormal powers,
the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the duration of his lifespan, the parinirvāṇa, and the endurance of the teaching— he remains [omniscient].
Without forming a thought regarding phenomena, he constantly and universally knows them; without moving from the present moment, he thoroughly knows the events of the three periods of time.

Thus concludes the section on subtle knowledge. Furthermore, there are four scriptural passages concerning entry into such secret places, which constitute entry into the Tathāgata’s ten inexhaustible secret places.
Regarding the "secret of the body": it manifests within the pores of the body's atoms.
Infinite lands, infinite bodies, and infinite manifestations of attaining Buddhahood and manifesting Parinirvāṇa;
infinite vocal karma and speech—these ten matters, simultaneous yet distinct, are sovereign throughout the ten directions.
All of these are the Tathāgata’s universal radiance-wisdom, like a perfect mirror that pervades the realm of empty space, responding universally and spontaneously at once.
All things that are manifested can be made to appear through non-action; the above concludes the secret knowledge [of the sixth].
Furthermore, there is the knowledge of all Buddhas regarding their entry into eons (*kalpa*), which consists of seven lines of verse:

"Entering an *asaṃkhyeya* eon in a single thought-moment, and entering a single thought-moment in an *asaṃkhyeya* eon. The following is as fully detailed in the sūtra itself regarding such long and short, many and few eons.

Regarding the principle of mutual interpenetration (*xiāngrùfǎ*): because both principle and wisdom are devoid of intrinsic nature, the lengthening or shortening of the faculties of sentient beings corresponds to the lengthening or shortening of eons (*kalpa*).

Through the skillful means of wisdom, the Tathāgata simultaneously and instantaneously manifests all realms of karmic activity; within this single, unified wisdom, each perceives its own manifestation according to its karma.
By clarifying the distinctions and non-distinctions of causal karma and temporal divisions, he shatters the deluded attachments regarding fixed time and eons.

The attachment to length and shortness is like that of an insentient being; when wisdom and so forth arise simultaneously, there are no characteristics of extension or contraction, nor any limitations of kalpas, years, months, days, or time.
Thus ends the section on knowing the characteristics of the entry into kalpas (7).

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of the various entries of the Tathāgata, six lines and a half of sūtra clarify that the Bodhisattva at this stage knows the thirteen kinds of entry of the Tathāgata.
Wisdom refers to the wisdom of the "hair-path" practitioner (*mārgajñatā*), which is the wisdom that enters into sentient beings of indeterminate nature to give rise to skillful means;

it is the wisdom that causes them to attain right faith; it is the wisdom that enters into those with the nature of subtle particles; it is the wisdom that enters into the paths of subtle sentient beings to be born together with them, inducing the arising of wisdom so they may attain the abodes of humans and devas and dwell in the roots of goodness of a Buddha; it is the wisdom of the perfectly awakened body that enters into the bodies of buddha-fields.
This refers to the wisdom that manifests the attainment of Buddhahood and entry into parinirvāṇa within the body of the Buddha and even inside its pores;
it is the wisdom of perfect enlightenment within the bodies of sentient beings, which consists of the skillful practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to awaken sentient beings.
It is also the wisdom of perfect enlightenment within the minds of sentient beings, because the minds of sentient beings are identical to the mind of the Tathāgata.
Because the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings as being of one essence and engages them according to their karma, he enters the wisdom that accords with all places;
because he awakens them within all six realms of existence according to their faculties, he enters the wisdom that manifests universal conduct;
and because [he understands] the conduct of all sentient beings and the ninety-five [heterodox paths]...
Because all non-Buddhists employ the wisdom of "sameness of purpose" (*sāmānyārtha-jñāna*), they enter into and manifest the wisdom of "contrary conduct.

By manifesting as an evil Māra to afflict and delude practitioners, or by practicing what appears to be a non-path, they bring benefit to sentient beings without exception—such as manifesting as King Ajātaśatru to carry out the murder of his father and mother—causing them to gain faith and attain the Way. This is the entry into the manifestation of inconceivable karma.

Whether the wise who understand or do not understand the conceivable world cause the world to know that this is the inconceivable noble practice, or cause the world to be unable to understand it as being either ordinary or noble—the rest may be inferred accordingly, as is fully provided in the sūtra itself.
Thus ends the entry into the Tathāgata’s wisdom. From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards is one and a half lines.
The sutra concludes that bodhisattvas in this stage are fully able to enter the vast and immeasurable wisdom of all buddhas.
[Sutra] O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they immediately attain the inconceivable liberation of a bodhisattva.
The liberation of unobstructedness, the liberation of pure observation, the liberation of universal illumination, the liberation of the Tathāgata-garbha,
the liberation of conforming to the unimpeded wheel, the liberation of penetrating the three periods of time, the liberation of the treasury of the dharma-realm, the liberation of the wheel of light,
and the liberation of the realm without remainder— headed by these ten, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeyas [of such liberations].
All gates of liberation are attained within this tenth stage; likewise,
they fully accomplish immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gateways of samādhi, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gateways of dhāraṇī,
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya gateways of supernatural powers.
[Treatise] The sixth section consists of seven and a half lines of scripture that clarify the meaning of the ten great liberations attained by a Bodhisattva at this stage.
Within this section, four categories of phenomena are presented: first, the ten kinds of inconceivable liberations;
second, the total enumeration of hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya liberations; third, the simultaneous presentation of the three [qualities] obtained; and fourth, [the specific details].
The four categories of these [supernormal powers] are presented together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other *abhijñās*, all of which are fully detailed according to the text.
