[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva penetrates such wisdom and accords with immeasurable bodhi.

It is taught that through the power of skillful mindfulness, one is able in a single moment to settle, receive, gather, and maintain all the immeasurable great lights of Dharma, the great illuminations of Dharma, and the great rains of Dharma belonging to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is like the great rain poured down by the Naga King Sāgara, which cannot be contained anywhere except within the great ocean.
Just as one who is unable to settle, receive, gather, or uphold [the teachings], so too it is with the great Dharma-lamp, the great Dharma-illumination,
and the great Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury. With the sole exception of Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage,
all other sentient beings— including Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even Bodhisattvas up to the ninth stage— are unable to settle, receive, or [uphold it].
Sons of the Buddha, it is as follows: for example, the great ocean can settle, receive, gather, and sustain the great rain poured down by a single great nāga king;

and even if two, three, or even an infinite number of nāga kings were to pour down their rains all at once in a single moment, the ocean can still settle, receive, gather, and sustain them all. Why is this? Because...
Because it is an immeasurably vast vessel, the Bodhisattva dwelling on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) is likewise able to settle,
receive, gather, and uphold the light of the Buddha’s Dharma, the illumination of the Dharma, and the rain of the Dharma— whether two, three,
or even immeasurable teachings— in a single moment of thought, expounding them all at once; for this reason, this ground is named "Dharma."

The Bodhisattva Megha-vimukti-candra said, "O Son of the Buddha, how many Tathāgatas can a Bodhisattva of this stage receive, uphold, and maintain the great Dharma-luminosity, the great Dharma-illumination, and the great Dharma-rain within a single thought-moment?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied, "O Son of the Buddha, this cannot be known by means of calculation; I shall speak a parable for you."
Son, it is as if in each of the ten directions there were worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields;
and in those worlds, every single sentient being had attained the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining,
being upheld by the Buddhas, and was foremost in erudition among the assembly of śrāvakas, like [the disciples] under the Great Vajra Lotus-Top Buddha.

The Victorious Bhikṣu said: "Suppose one sentient being were to receive the teachings that all other beings have received, and then another were to receive them again—Son of the Buddha, what do you think?
Are the teachings received by these sentient beings finite or infinite? Bodhisattva Vimukticandra replied:
"Their number is exceedingly great, immeasurable and boundless. Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "Son of the Buddha..."
I shall explain this for you so that you may attain understanding: O Son of the Buddha, regarding the Bodhisattva on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*),
in a single moment of thought before one Buddha, the great dharma-lights, great dharma-illuminations, and great dharma-showers that are established, received, gathered, and maintained—
the treasury of the dharmas of the three times— surpass all the dharmas heard and retained by all sentient beings in as many worlds as there were previously.
A hundredth part does not equal it, nor can even a metaphorical comparison reach it. Just as at the place of one Buddha,
so it is at the places of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions as previously described, and even more than that number— immeasurable and boundless—
at each and every one of those Tathāgatas, there is the light of Dharma, the illumination of Dharma, the rain of Dharma, and the Dharma of the three periods of time.
Because they are able to settle, receive, gather, and uphold all the *dharmas*, this stage is named "Dharma Cloud" (*dharmameghā*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas of this stage, by the power of their own vows, raise great clouds of compassion and thunder the great Dharma;
taking penetrating clarity and fearlessness as lightning flashes, and merit and wisdom as dense clouds, they manifest various bodies, moving to and fro everywhere.

In a single moment of thought, they universally proclaim the Great Dharma throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of lands in the ten directions,
subduing the hosts of Māra; furthermore, exceeding even this number,

they rain down the nectar of immortality upon all sentient beings according to their inclinations throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of lands.
Because it rains down to extinguish all the dust and flames of the afflictions of sentient beings, this stage is called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).

Child of the Buddha, on this stage, a Bodhisattva manifests Buddha-activities within a single world—from descending from Tuṣita heaven until entering parinirvāṇa—in accordance with the minds of the sentient beings who are to be saved;
and likewise in two, three, or even as many worlds as there are motes of dust.
Furthermore, extending beyond this to as many lands as there are atoms in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds, it is likewise in all of them;
for this reason, this stage is named the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā).

[Treatise] The seventh section consists of forty-five and a half lines of sūtra explaining that the Bodhisattvas of this stage, within a single moment of thought, are able to receive all the light of the Buddhadharma of the ten directions and can fully comprehend them;
furthermore, within the exegesis of the "Mastery in Raining Down the Dharma throughout the Ten Directions," it is divided into eight sections. First, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards...

They are unable to uphold the eight-and-a-half-fascicle *Sūtra* that clarifies this stage, wherein it is explained that the Bodhisattva of this stage is capable of upholding the great Dharma-light and the great Dharma-illumination of all Buddhas, yet is unable to do so for the other two vehicles or Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage;
and it further employs the analogy of the rain falling from the Sāgara Dragon. This section is divided into two parts, beginning from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "named the Cloud of Dharma."

There are six lines and a half of sūtra that clarify the analogy of the great ocean being able to receive the rain poured down by all the great nāga kings, as well as the section clarifying that a bodhisattva at this stage is capable of receiving all dharmas and can expound them all simultaneously in a single moment of thought;
this is divided into three parts. From the passage beginning with "Vimukticandra" down to "the great rain of Dharma," there are two lines of sūtra that clarify [this].
Vimukticandra asked: "In a single moment of thought, how many portions of the Tathāgata’s illumination of the Dharma can a Bodhisattva of this stage receive and uphold?
Following this question, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva provides an answer down to the point where he offers a simile;
one and a half lines of scripture clarify how much of the Buddha’s teaching on all phenomena is received by a Bodhisattva of this stage, using the division of immeasurable numbers as a calculation.
From "The five sons of the Buddha" down to "even analogies cannot reach it," there are eleven and a half lines of scripture;
this is the first analogy, vast and beyond compare, illustrating the extent of the Dharma-illumination attained by Bodhisattvas at this stage.
It is divided into six parts: from "In the presence of one Buddha" down to "named the Cloud of Dharma."
There are seven lines of verse clarifying that the rain of the Buddha-dharma received by Bodhisattvas at this stage exceeds the previous metaphors;
these are the "Sons of the Buddha," from this stage of the Bodhisattva down to the one named Dharanidhara (Cloud of Dharma).

There are eight lines of verse clarifying that the Bodhisattvas at this stage, through the power of their own vows and vast compassion, bring great benefit to others. These are the "Sons of the Buddha."

From this point downward, reaching as far as the stage named Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā*), four and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Bodhisattva in this stage is able to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven palace into the worlds of the ten directions, surpassing the previous analogy of atoms by a factor of two.
As stated in the first section regarding the "Great Dharma-Illumination" (*mahā-dharmāvabhāsa*): "In the worlds of the ten directions, there are no supramundane dharmas that are not [illuminated]..."

"Because of the total knowledge and total understanding that exhausts [all things], the Great Dharma shines" means that one is able to illuminate the faculties and karmas of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions with the sun of wisdom, such that they are always as if before one's eyes; that among all sentient beings, whether good or evil, there is none who does not see it.
"The Great Dharma rain falls" means that one is able to accord with the faculties of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, one by one.

Because the Dharma rains equally upon all at that time, all such vast Buddha-activities in these states can be stabilized and received by the bodhisattvas, just as the great ocean receives the rain of the Sāgara Dragon King.
"Sāgara" is named for the great ocean he rains upon; this dragon's rain falls only upon the sea, and only the sea can receive it.
Just as the Dharma-rain of all Buddhas in the ten directions can be received in a single thought-moment by a Bodhisattva of this stage alone—as detailed in the text below—[the Sūtra says]:
"O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas on this stage is clear and penetrating, and their supernormal powers are sovereign; according to their mental inclinations, they are able to..."
They can transform a narrow world into a vast world and a vast world into a narrow world; they can transform a defiled world into a pure world and a pure world into a defiled world;
they can transform worlds that are disordered, sequential, inverted, or upright.
Thus, they are able to mutually transform all such infinite worlds, or, according to their mental intention, place an entire world within a single atom.
The characteristics of all mountains, rivers, and dust motes within the realms, such as Mount Sumeru, remain as they were; the world is not diminished.
Alternatively, one may place two, three, or even unspeakably many worlds, including Mount Sumeru and all its mountains and rivers, within a single minute particle of dust;
yet the substance and characteristics of that minute particle remain as they were, while the worlds therein are all clearly manifested.
Or, according to their mental inclinations, they manifest the adornments of two worlds up to unspeakably many worlds within a single world;
or, within the adornments of a single world, they manifest two worlds up to unspeakably many worlds;
or, according to their mental inclinations, they place the sentient beings of unspeakably many worlds into a single [world].
In some worlds, they may, according to their mental resolve, place the sentient beings of a single world into unspeakably many worlds without causing them any harm;
or, according to their mental resolve, they may manifest within a single pore all the adorned phenomena of the realms of all Buddhas;
or, according to their mental resolve, they may manifest unspeakable eons within a single thought-moment.
From each body, as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, he manifests that same number of hands;
in each hand, he holds flower caskets, incense boxes, garlands, canopies, banners, and streamers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, pervading the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas.
Furthermore, from each body, he again manifests that same number of heads, and from each head, he again manifests that same number [of eyes].
With tongues as numerous as atoms, they praise the Buddha’s merits throughout the ten directions in every moment of thought;

or, according to their mental inclinations, within a single thought-instant, they universally manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment through to parinirvāṇa, as well as the adornments of the lands throughout the ten directions;
or they manifest their bodies pervading the three periods of time, and within those bodies there are immeasurable...
The Buddha and the adornments of his buddha-field, as well as the formation and destruction of worlds, are all manifested without exception.
Or, from within a single pore of his own body, he emits all winds without causing any harm or affliction to sentient beings.
Or, according to his mental resolve, he transforms boundless worlds into a single great ocean, within the waters of which a great lotus flower appears, radiant with light.

Magnificently adorned, it completely covers immeasurable and boundless worlds; therein it manifests the magnificent array of the great Bodhi tree, even manifesting the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Or, upon its body, it manifests all the radiances of the ten directions—light from *maṇi* jewels, the sun, the moon, the stars, clouds, lightning, and so forth—such that there is nothing that does not appear. Or...
By exhaling breath from the mouth, one can move the infinite worlds of the ten directions without causing sentient beings to have any thought of alarm or fear;

or one may manifest the wind, fire, and water calamities of the ten directions; or, according to the inclinations of sentient beings' minds, manifest a physical body fully endowed with majestic adornments;
or manifest the body of a Buddha within one's own body, or [manifest] within a Buddha...
Manifesting his own body within his own body, or manifesting his own land within the body of a Buddha, or manifesting the body of a Buddha within his own land—

O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva on this stage of the Cloud of Dharma can manifest such things, as well as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sovereign spiritual powers.
[Treatise] The eighth section consists of thirty-five and a half lines of sūtra that clarify this stage of the bodhisattva’s power of recollection (*anusmṛti-bala*),
wherein the vast and the subtle, the large and the small, and the one and the many interpenetrate through the mastery of universal transformation. Within the commentary on this meaning,

it is explained that for a bodhisattva on this Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), by the power of their mental recollection, the vast and the subtle, self and other, and the one and the many, mutually interpenetrate.
The interpenetration of the large and the small, and the sovereign power of spiritual penetrations and virtues, are all accomplished according to the thoughts of one’s own mind.
Thus, the activities and spheres of experience of all sentient beings are all produced by the retributive karma of one’s own mind.
Whether it be humans, devas, hells, animals, hungry ghosts, or the fruits of good and evil retribution—all are created solely by the mind. Such is the tenth stage of the Bodhisattva.

By the power of the great wisdom of the unconditioned Dharma-body, Śākyamuni, in accordance with whatever thoughts arise in the minds [of beings], knows and perceives all things throughout the ten directions simultaneously and with sovereign ease;
for the sake of non-delusion, he takes universal radiance-wisdom as his essence.

Because this essence of wisdom is without dependence, it accords with the nature of reality, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, equal in measure to empty space, and completely filling the ten directions.
The world is accomplished through the great function of the wisdom of non-nature, which is recollected by means of the wisdom of non-forgetfulness;

it is accomplished through the possession of the wisdom of the general and the particular, which performs both the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and destruction simultaneously;

it is accomplished through the sovereign wisdom of the broad and the narrow, the large and the small, whose transformative activity is unimpeded; and it is accomplished through the wisdom of the same essence as all sentient beings, which is able to transform all things.
The realms of sentient beings are entirely pure lands; through the wisdom of the non-duality of self and other, one manifests many bodies from a single body and a single body from many bodies;

through the wisdom that perceives the dharmadhātu as neither large nor small and free from all measure, one can contain vast Buddha-fields within a single pore; and through the wisdom that is equal to space, boundless and without direction—
In a single thought-moment, they manifest throughout the ten directions without coming or going; through the wisdom that is like an echo, they respond to all beings according to their needs;
through the wisdom of perfected merit and virtue, they constantly dwell in sublime lands while always residing together with all sentient beings.
Were it not for the power of the sages' sustaining grace, sentient beings...

One does not see that although the power of wisdom and the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of a Bodhisattva on these ten stages are equal in nature to space, space is vast and useless, whereas the wisdom of one on these ten stages fills all of space.
This wisdom has no substantial essence and no creator; it is like space itself, yet by the power of recollection, it pervades space according to its fruit.
Layer upon layer, its pervasive transformation is inexhaustible, like a wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel;
though its nature is devoid of subject and object and involves no deliberate activity, it assumes the same color as all surrounding objects. The rest is self-evident in the text.

[Sūtra] At that time, the various bodhisattvas in the assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, the four world-protecting kings, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā, the Śuddhāvāsa deities, Maheśvara, and all the sons of the gods, all had this thought:
"If the power of the supernatural knowledges and wisdom of a bodhisattva can be such as this, what then must the Buddha be like? At that time—
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, this great assembly has heard of the bodhisattvas' power of supernatural penetrations and wisdom, yet they have fallen into a web of doubt.
It would be well, O Benevolent One, if you would sever their doubts by briefly manifesting the manifestations of a bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual powers. At that time, the golden...
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha immediately entered the samādhi called "The Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands.
As he entered this samādhi, all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly each saw their own bodies within the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha;
therein they clearly beheld all the various kinds of magnificent adornments of the trichiliocosm. After [a period of time]...
Even if one were to speak for a hundred million kalpas, one could not exhaustively describe it. Furthermore, within that [realm], he saw a Bodhi tree;
its trunk was ten thousand *trichiliocosms* in circumference and a hundred thousand *trichiliocosms* in height, and the shade cast by its branches and leaves was likewise so.
Corresponding to the dimensions of the tree, there was a lion throne, upon which sat a Buddha named Sarvajñābhijña.

The King and the entire great assembly all saw that Buddha seated beneath the Bodhi tree upon a lion throne, adorned with various marks and signs such that even if one were to speak of them for a hundred million eons, they could not be exhausted.

After the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had manifested such great supernormal powers, he caused the members of the assembly to each return to their original places; at that time, the great assembly attained [realization].
Never having conceived a thought of wonder, they remained silent, gazing with single-minded devotion toward Vajragarbha.

[Treatise] The ninth section, consisting of eighteen and a half lines of scripture, clarifies that when this great assembly heard of the supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages and gave rise to doubt,
the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered the Samādhi of Essential Nature (*tattva-svabhāva*) and manifested the supernatural powers of a Buddha.

The Section on Dispelling Doubts for the Assembly and Explaining the Meaning consists of ten matters within this section: first, the great assembly harbors doubts; second, Vimukticandra makes a request; third, Vajragarbha enters meditative absorption;

fourth, the realm manifested within that absorption; fifth, the great assembly sees for themselves; sixth, they see [the realm] within the body of Vajragarbha; seventh, the manifestation of the excellence of the Bodhi tree;
eighth, [the manifestation of] the excellence of the lion throne; ninth, the manifestation of the excellence of the assembly; and tenth, the manifestation of the excellence of the Dharma.
3. Especially Exalted: Beneath seven trees, there is a Buddha seated upon a lion throne named Sarvajñānābhijñārāja;
the eightfold assembly beholds the Buddha. 4. Eight: Vajragarbha Bodhisattva suspends his supernatural powers;

the tenfold assembly each sees their own bodies returned to their original places, attaining a state never before experienced, which is the essential nature of all buddha-fields. 5. Three: [End of section].

That which is obscure is precisely the unconditioned Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). As for the Bodhi tree, it is established by virtue of the retribution obtained through the practice of the Dharma-nature body.
Thus, the Buddha beneath the tree is titled "The All-Knowing Sovereign of Penetration," which signifies the sovereign great wisdom within the unconditioned Dharma-nature.
These three dharmas are, in their essence, eternally thus for all sentient beings; it is only because...
Because it is not manifested through one's own preparatory effort, the rest is fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, this samādhi is most rare and possesses great power; what is its name? Vajragarbha replied: "This samādhi..."
It is named "The Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands. Furthermore, he asked: "What is the sphere of this samādhi? He replied:

"O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva cultivates this samādhi, according to what his mind contemplates, he can manifest within his own body as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in the sands of the Ganges River;
moreover, he surpasses these numbers, dwelling as a son of the Buddha in immeasurable and boundless [realms]."
Because this Bodhisattva on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma attains such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great samādhis,
his physical body and physical karma, his speech and verbal karma, and his mind and mental karma are unfathomable. He possesses mastery over supernatural powers,
observes the realms of the three periods of time and the realms of samādhi, and sports within all gates of liberation and the manifestations of his transformative power.

The deeds performed through supernormal power and the deeds performed through light are, in brief, such that even all the activities from lifting a foot to setting it down cannot be known by Bodhisattvas from the stage of the Son of the Dharma (Dharmaputra) up to those dwelling on the Stage of Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī).
O Son of the Buddha, the entire range of the Bodhisattva on this Cloud of Dharma Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi) is, in brief, thus; were it to be explained in detail, it would require—
Even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one could not exhaustively describe it. Liberation Moon Bodhisattva said:
"Son of the Buddha, if the sphere of a bodhisattva’s supernormal powers is such as this, what then is the power of a Buddha’s supernormal powers?
Vajragarbha replied: "Son of the Buddha, it is like a person who takes a single clod of earth from the four continents and says:"
"Between the soil of the great earth of infinite worlds and the soil of this world, which is more? My observation of your question is likewise so:
how can the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is boundless and peerless, be compared by measure with that of a bodhisattva?

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if one were to take a tiny amount of soil from the four continents while the remainder is immeasurable; such is the supernatural wisdom of this Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.
Wisdom has, throughout immeasurable eons, spoken but of a small portion; how much more so regarding the stage of the Tathāgata!
O Son of the Buddha, I shall now cite examples for you as proof, so that you may come to know the realm of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, suppose that in each of the ten directions there were Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms in boundless worlds, and in each of those lands, such [a number] were attained...
Bodhisattvas on the stages fill [the world] like a forest of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp;

yet the wisdom produced by all those bodhisattvas through practicing the bodhisattva path for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas does not equal even one hundredth part of the sphere of wisdom of a single Tathāgata, nor can it reach even a fraction (upaniṣad) thereof.

[Treatise] The tenth section consists of twenty-seven lines of sūtra that clarify the power of the wisdom and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the bodhisattvas on this stage, which cannot be known by those on lower stages and cannot be compared even to the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
In explaining the meaning of this section, there are approximately eleven topics: first, Vimukticandra asks for the name of the samādhi; second, Vajra... [and so forth].
1. Vajragarbha Bodhisattva’s correct response regarding the name of the samādhi; 2. A further inquiry concerning the realm of the samādhi; 3. Vajragarbha’s correct response; 4.
The correct explanation of the general characteristics of the attainment of the samādhi on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*); 5.

An elucidation of how the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the three karmas of a Bodhisattva on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma are unknown to those on lower stages; 6. An elucidation of a brief exposition of the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.

9. Regarding the extensive explanation of the spheres of experience (*viṣaya*), it is difficult to measure even in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas; Candravimala asked how the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*) is. 10.
Vajragarbha raised a clod of earth as a metaphor for the amount of soil in the four continents; the disparity is difficult to compare. 11.

Vajragarbha correctly explained that because the power of the path of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi-mārga-bala*) is already difficult to proclaim, how much more so is the spiritual power of the Tathāgata?
It may be said that eleven examples are provided to clarify the underlying intent within this passage, as they are fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, such wisdom of this Bodhisattva is no different from the body, speech, and mental activities of a Tathāgata;
he does not abandon the power of the various samādhis of a Bodhisattva, and for countless kalpas he serves and makes offerings to all Buddhas."
Throughout a single eon, he makes offerings to all Buddhas with every kind of requisite for worship;

empowered by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, his light of wisdom becomes even more preeminent, skillfully resolving all challenges posed within the dharma-realm such that no one can defeat him for hundreds of thousands of billions of eons.
Son of the Buddha, it is as if a master goldsmith, using the most exquisite...
Just as ornaments made of pure gold are inlaid with great *maṇi* jewels, which the Sovereign Heavenly King himself wears and adorns upon his body—
such that no other celestial beings' ornaments can equal them— so too it is for the Bodhisattvas on this stage:
from the first stage up to the ninth, all the wisdom and conduct of those Bodhisattvas cannot be equaled by others.
The light of wisdom of a Bodhisattva who has reached this stage can cause sentient beings to enter even into the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*);

no other light of wisdom can do so. O Son of the Buddha, it is like the light of the celestial king Maheśvara, which can cause the bodies and minds of sentient beings to become cool and refreshing, a state that no other light can attain. This stage is likewise.
The light of the bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise; it enables all sentient beings to attain coolness and even to abide in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The light of wisdom of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas up to the ninth stage cannot reach it.
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already been able to dwell securely therein.

With such wisdom, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, further explain for them the knowledge of the three periods of time, the knowledge of the distinctions within the dharma-realm, the knowledge that pervades all worlds, the knowledge that illuminates all worlds, and the knowledge of compassionate mindfulness toward all sentient beings;
to state it in brief, they even explain the attainment of the knowledge of all-knowledge. Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva—
The perfection of wisdom is the most preeminent among the other perfections; it is not that the other perfections are not practiced.
O Son of the Buddha, this is a brief explanation of the tenth stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).
If it were to be explained in detail, even an immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* of kalpas would not suffice. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he mostly manifests as Maheśvara.
The Deva King Rāvaṇa possesses mastery over the Dharma and is able to bestow upon sentient beings—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas—the practices of the pāramitās.
Within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), there is no one who can defeat him in debate regarding any difficult questions.

All his activities—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, and so on, up to being never apart from [mindfulness of the Dharma].

Being endowed with mindfulness, he further forms this thought: "I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto the one who is the basis for the knowledge of all modes and all-knowledge.

If he applies himself with diligent vigor, in a single moment of thought, he attains [realizations] as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
From their samādhis up to manifesting as many bodhisattvas as atoms in those [lands] as their retinues—
if one were to manifest through the sovereign power of the bodhisattvas' sublime vows, it would exceed this number; namely, in terms of their practice,
their adornments, their faith and understanding, their activities, their bodies, their speech, their radiance, their faculties, and their spiritual transformations.
Whether regarding their voices or their spheres of activity, they cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* eons.

[Treatise] The tenth section contains thirty-five and a half lines of scripture clarifying that the physical, verbal, and mental karma of a Bodhisattva in this stage is no different from that of a Tathāgata,
and that they do not abandon the various samādhis of a Bodhisattva while serving and making offerings for incalculable eons.
The section on the meaning of "nurturing all Buddhas" contains approximately twenty Dharma-gates within this division:
(1) non-differentiation from the body, speech, and mind activities of the Tathāgatas; (2) not abandoning the power of the various samādhis of the Bodhisattvas;
(3) serving and making offerings to all Buddhas throughout incalculable eons; (4) [being sustained] by the spiritual power of all Buddhas...
1. Wisdom increases further and becomes more excellent; 2. One is well able to explain all difficult questions regarding the dharma-realm;
3. Like pure gold inlaid with mani jewels, one forms a celestial jewel crown; 4.
The garments worn by the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereignty surpass those of other gods; 5. The correct exposition of this stage surpasses that of the lower stages.

Ninth, just as Maheśvara is able to cause the minds of sentient beings to attain coolness, this serves as a metaphor to clarify that the Bodhisattvas of this stage are able to cause all sentient beings to attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), which neither the twelve vehicles nor the Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage can equal.
Eleventh, for the Bodhisattvas of this stage, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, further expound [the Dharma] on their behalf.

10. It explains ten gates of wisdom; 12. It clarifies that for the bodhisattva practicing on this stage, the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) is primary while the other nine are its companions;
13. It briefly explains the general outline of this stage, as a detailed exposition would be difficult to exhaust;
14. It illustrates how the bodhisattva of this stage receives office and becomes the celestial king Maheśvara.
Fifth, it is explained that at this stage, the Bodhisattva is well able to extensively practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
sixteenth, they are never separated from mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; seventeenth, they are mindful of their own capacity to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings;
eighteenth, they personally and diligently cultivate further; nineteenth, in a single thought-moment, they attain ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands.
If one adds the power of supreme vow-force to twenty times a hundred billion *samādhis*, it exceeds the previous number;
the meaning of the text is fully contained within the words themselves. As for Maheśvara, this is translated as "Great Sovereign" (*Mahā-īśvara*);
he is the ultimate pinnacle of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) within the great trichiliocosm, possessing sovereign divine powers, spiritual penetrations, and wisdom beyond compare.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, when these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva appear in succession before him, he is then able to enter into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
It is like the Lake Anavatapta from which four great rivers flow;
their currents spread throughout Jambudvīpa, never being exhausted, but rather increasing further until they enter the ocean and fill it completely. Thus spoke the Buddha.

O Son of the Buddha, it is the same for the Bodhisattva: from the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) flows the water of roots of goodness and great vows, which fills sentient beings through the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) without end;
furthermore, it continues to increase until it enters the ocean of omniscience (sarvajñatā), filling it completely.
O Son of the Buddha, the ten stages (daśabhūmi) of the Bodhisattva possess distinctions because they are based upon the Buddha-wisdom. Just as...
Because the great earth has ten mountain kings, what are these ten? They are as follows:

the Snowy Mountain King, the Fragrant Mountain King, the Vidyādhara Mountain King, the Ṛṣigiri Mountain King, the Yugandhara Mountain King, the Aśvakarṇa Mountain King, the Nimindhara Mountain King, the Cakravāḍa Mountain King, the Ketumatī Mountain King, and the Sumeru Mountain King. Thus spoke the Buddha.
Child, just as all medicinal herbs are contained within the King of Snowy Mountains and can never be exhausted by taking them, so too is it with the Bodhisattva’s stage of Joy;
all the worldly scriptures, arts, literature, verses, and incantations are contained therein and can never be exhausted by explaining them.
Son of the Buddha, just as all manner of fragrances gather upon the King of Fragrant Mountains...
In this regard, the stage of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*) where Bodhisattvas dwell is likewise inexhaustible;

all the bodhisattva precepts, practices, and dignified conducts are fully contained therein and can never be fully described. O Son of the Buddha, it is like Mount Vaidūrya, the king of mountains, which is composed entirely of pure jewels;
all manner of precious gems are contained within it and can never be fully extracted. So too is it with the stage of the Bodhisattvas.

Abiding in the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) is likewise thus: all worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis are contained therein, and their explanation is inexhaustible.

O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Mountain King of Divine Seers (*ṛṣi-giri-rāja*), composed entirely of precious jewels, wherein divine seers possessing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) all dwell without end; such is the station of the Bodhisattva’s Radiance.
The Ground of Wisdom is likewise thus: within all paths, the most excellent wisdoms are all contained therein, and they can never be fully described.

Son of the Buddha, just as Mount Yugandhara, the king of mountains, is composed entirely of jewels and where great yakṣas dwell without end, so too is it with the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of the Difficult-to-Conquer Ground; it is exactly like this in every respect.
The sovereign supernormal powers of mastery are all contained therein and can never be fully described.

O Son of the Buddha, just as the King of Mountains, Aśvakarṇa, is composed entirely of jewels such that all manner of fruits are found within it and can never be exhausted, so too is the Bodhisattva’s stage of Presence (Abhimukhī):
the principle of dependent origination and the realization of the fruits of the Śrāvakas are all contained within it.
It cannot be fully described, just as the king of mountains, Nimiṃdhara, is composed entirely of precious jewels and inhabited by powerful nāga deities without end;
likewise, the Bodhisattva’s stage of Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā) is also thus, wherein skillful means, wisdom,
and the realization of the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood all reside, and cannot be fully described, just like the king of mountains, Khadiraka.
All the hosts of sovereigns composed of pure jewels dwell therein without end; likewise, the bodhisattvas’ dwelling on the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi) is also thus.
All the distinctions of the sovereign practices of these bodhisattvas and their worlds are contained therein, and could never be fully described.
It is like Mount Meru, the king of mountains, composed of pure jewels, where the great and powerful asuras reside.
Just as the kings of the nāgas all dwell within it without end, so too is it with the bodhisattva’s stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*):
the wisdom and practices regarding the arising and ceasing of all worlds are all contained therein and can never be fully described.
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, composed entirely of precious jewels, wherein the gods of great majesty and power all dwell without end.

The Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) where Bodhisattvas abide is likewise so: the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Tathāgata, as well as all Buddha-activities, are entirely contained therein; their exposition through questions and answers is inexhaustible.

O Son of the Buddha, just as these ten kings of mountains all exist within the great ocean yet receive distinct names, so too are the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva likewise situated together [within the same reality].
Within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), [the stages] receive their names according to their specific distinctions.

[Treatise: The twelfth section contains forty-two and a half lines of scripture that clarify the ten similes of the ten great mountain kings of Lake Anavatapta, explaining the meaning of the wisdom practiced through the sequential skillful means of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
This section consists of twelve sub-sections of scripture, each with its own natural divisions; there is no need for further structural analysis.

First, it cites the analogy of Lake Anavatapta: from the initial mind of the ten stages, the Bodhisattva flows forth the water of roots of goodness and great vows from the bodhicitta, filling sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) without end.
They increase further and further until they enter the ocean of omniscience; from the first production of the thought of enlightenment,
they dwell within the water of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and great vows, bringing sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction and fulfilling the ocean of omniscience,
never departing from the essential nature of the water of wisdom and great vows at the initial moment, thereby perfecting it through that original essence of water.

Furthermore, to expand upon this, the metaphor of the great earth possessing ten mountain kings is raised to clarify that from the ground of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, ten kinds of progressive cultivation arise;
because they do not depart from the essence of the ground of wisdom, they gradually become higher and more excellent.

Thus, just as the five stages and five layers of the ten dharmas do not depart from the Tathāgata’s ground of universal radiance and omniscience, these five layers of tenfold progressive cultivations likewise arise therefrom.
Thus, these five stages, each consisting of ten successive practices, constitute a single moment, a single limit, and a single thought-moment,
devoid of the sequence of the three periods of time; because they take the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their essence,
they are like the waters of Lake Anavatapta flowing into the great ocean, emerging from the land of Jambudvīpa as the ten great mountain kings.
By departing from the substance of the ground and illuminating it with meditative concentration and wisdom, one can see that even at the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, one attains Buddhahood;
this serves as a model for understanding through such representation. It is based on this that the ten levels of faith are explained;

these are spoken of within the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsabhavana*), which refers to the fruit of manifest clarity born of retribution (*vipākaja*) arising from universal radiance-wisdom. Because the cultivation of the cause is fulfilled, one does not depart from it.
By virtue of this wisdom, the ten kings of mountains are illustrated by the analogy of the king of snowy mountains for the first stage;

the meaning of this is self-evident according to the scriptural text, and the subsequent stages are to be understood by analogy. Next is the king of fragrant mountains, and next is the king of Vaidūrya mountains.
*Vaidūrya* means "various" (*vividha*) and *dāri* means "to hold"; thus, it is said that this mountain can hold various kinds of treasures.

Because of its flowers and fruits, it is likened to the third stage; the meaning of this is self-evident according to the scriptural text. Regarding "dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti": how is this so?

As for dhyāna, it is simply called "samādhi" because it accords with the essence [of the mind]. This clarifies that when consciousness and perception (*saṃjñā*) do not function, it is like the sun not yet having risen;
the character *mei* (昧) signifies that consciousness and perception are in a state of obscurity, and only then does right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) manifest.
Regarding the three [periods], it is precisely because the three yang lines arise from the eleventh month to the first month that the third is taken as the "correct" (zheng).

When the three yang lines arise, wisdom (*jñāna*) becomes manifest; since wisdom is the correct, the non-arising of the five aggregates and the sudden cessation of worldly sentiments are termed "samādhi" (*mèi*).
Because one can manifest correct wisdom from this state, it is called "samādhi. Furthermore, "one stilling" (*yī zhǐ*) constitutes [this].
Regarding the term *samāpatti* (equipoise): it clarifies that within the obscurity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one is able to manifest right wisdom;
thus, it is called *samāpatti* because it is right wisdom. Because the right wisdom manifests such that the five aggregates no longer exist, it is termed "liberation.

While all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are generally referred to as the "Great Body Samādhi" (*mahā-kāya-samādhi*), this passage specifically cites its practice. The "Mountain King of the Immortals" (*ṛṣi-giri-rāja*) represents the fourth stage (*bhūmi*).
The meaning is as explained in the sutra: regarding "Mount Gandhamādana," *ganda* means "pair" (*dva*) in this language, and *mādana* means "holding the vidyās.
This mountain is held by yakṣas and great deities who possess the vidyās;

because those on the fifth bhūmi attain both supramundane and mundane wisdom and supernormal powers, and are able to master and maintain all the vidyās in their entirety, it is called Mount Aśvakarṇa.

The King represents the stages of the six grounds as detailed in the sutra itself. Mount Nimindhara—here called "Holding the Borders"—represents the Ground of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*), for it can sustain all the various practices of biased views among sentient beings, and because it sustains the entirety of the three realms and the six destinies.
Mount Cakravāḍa—translated here as "Wheel-Encircling"—encircles the great trichiliocosm.
It clarifies that in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), practice without effort is spontaneously perfected. Regarding *Ketumati*: *ketu* means "banner" and *mati* means "wisdom";
thus, it refers to the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). It is situated on Mount Sumeru within the four continents of Jambudvīpa and amidst the great ocean.
This clarifies that in the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*), the wisdom of the Middle Way is fulfilled, universally encompassing all phenomena.
"Because of the three realms," and so forth—the following one and a half lines of scripture clarify the summary conclusion regarding the distinctions among the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

It clarifies that within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they receive distinct names based on their differentiation; it clarifies that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is non-dual from the stage of the initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) through the tenth stage and the Buddha-stage, yet receives distinct names due to the differentiation of its wisdom. Thus ends the twelfth [section].
Each section corresponds exactly to the meaning of the stages as expressed in the sutra text, which the sutra itself explains in sequence.
[Sutra] O Son of the Buddha, for example, the great ocean receives the name "great ocean" by virtue of ten characteristics that cannot be altered or taken away. What are these ten?
First, it becomes progressively deeper; second, it does not accept corpses; third, any other water that enters into it loses its own identity.
1. Its fundamental name is "Universal Sameness. 2. It is a single flavor. 3. It contains immeasurable precious treasures. 4. None can reach its bottom. 5. It is vast and immeasurable. 6.
It is the dwelling place of great bodies. 7. The tides do not exceed their limits. 8. It universally receives great rains without overflowing. The practice of a bodhisattva is likewise;
for these ten characteristics, the bodhisattva’s practice is called "unshakeable and unassailable."
What are these ten? They are as follows: first, the Ground of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*), because it gives birth to great vows that become progressively deeper;

second, the Ground of Purity (*Vimalā-bhūmi*), because one does not accept any corpse of broken precepts; third, the Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*), because one abandons worldly conventional designations;

fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), because one attains a single flavor with the merits of the Buddha; fifth, the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*), because it gives birth to immeasurable skillful means and spiritual powers.
Because it penetrates all the various precious jewels produced in the world; because on the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhī) it observes the profound principle of dependent origination;

because on the Ground of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā) it possesses the excellent observation of vast awakened wisdom; because on the Ground of Immovability (Acalā) it manifests vast and magnificent adornments;
and because on the Ground of Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī) it attains profound liberation and acts within the world with knowledge of things as they truly are, without transgressing their limits.
Therefore, on the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one is able to receive the great rain of the Dharma-light from all Buddhas and Tathāgatas without ever being satiated.
[Treatise] The thirteenth section consists of fourteen lines of scripture that clarify the ten qualities of the great ocean as a metaphor for the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
In explaining the meaning of the "Advancement" (*abhyudgama*) section, it is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the ten [qualities] of the ocean.
Regarding the ten virtues of entrusting oneself to the ocean as the second virtue: these represent the Dharma by illustrating the distinctions in the wisdom of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

As for the textual meaning of the progressive cultivation therein, it is fully detailed in the text itself; since each stage is complete with its own ten dharmas, there is no need for further sub-sectioning.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were a great maṇi jewel possessing ten qualities that surpass all other jewels.
What are these ten? First, it originates from the great ocean; second, it is refined by a skilled artisan; third, it is perfect and without flaw;
fourth, it is pure and free from defilement; fifth, it is transparent both inside and out; sixth, it is skillfully perforated; seventh, it is strung...
Eighth, they place eight strands of precious thread atop high banners of lapis lazuli; ninth, they universally radiate all manner of various lights;
tenth, they are able to rain down various precious objects according to the King’s will, fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings according to their hearts.
Son of the Buddha, you should know that Bodhisattvas likewise possess ten such matters by which they transcend all other sages. What are they?
These constitute the eleven [qualities]: first, generating the mind of omniscience; second, maintaining the pure and clear practice of the precepts and dhūtas;
third, the perfection and absence of deficiency in all dhyānas and samādhis; fourth, the purity of the path of practice, free from all defilements;
fifth, the internal and external clarity of skillful means and supernormal powers; sixth, the wisdom of dependent origination, which is well able to penetrate through [all things].
Seventh, it is threaded with the various threads of skillful means and wisdom; eighth, it is placed atop the high banner of sovereignty;

ninth, observing the conduct of sentient beings, it emits the light of hearing and retention; tenth, having received the office of Buddha-wisdom and entered the number of Buddhas, it is able to extensively perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the accumulation of all kinds and all aspects of omniscient merit.
In the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Bodhisattva’s Practice," it is said that if sentient beings have not planted roots of goodness, they cannot hear this.
Liberation Moon Bodhisattva asked: "Upon hearing this dharma-gate, how much merit is obtained? Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
"The merit obtained from hearing this dharma-gate is equal to the merit accumulated by all-knowledge (sarvajñā). Why is this? It is because there is no merit for those who do not hear it."
If one can believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, and recite this dharma-gate of merit, how much more so if one applies oneself with diligence and practices according to the teaching!
Therefore, you should know that it is only by hearing this dharma-gate of the merit of gathering all-knowledge that one can believe,
understand, receive, uphold, and cultivate it, and subsequently reach the stage of all-knowledge.
[Treatise] The fourteenth section contains twenty and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how the *maṇi* jewel possesses ten kinds of nature by which it surpasses all other jewels;
this serves as a metaphor for how the ten stages (*bhūmi*) surpass all other noble ones (*ārya*). In the detailed explanation of the meaning, this is divided into six sections.
First, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "fulfilling their vows," there are six lines of sūtra that clarify the presentation of the *maṇi* jewel.

The jewels have ten kinds of natures; from "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, up to "extensively performing the work of a Buddha," there are seven and a half lines of scripture that clarify the sequence of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as exemplified in the sixth stage:

"skillfully knowing the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, and skillfully knowing the fundamental essence and characteristics of the causes and conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death. This is identical [to what was explained previously].
The analogy given for the sixth stage—of skillfully examining the dependent origination of birth and death until reaching its bottom—is like a drill;
the seventh stage is like a thread made of various kinds of skillful wisdom, which can follow along with birth and death without being defiled by any impurities.

On the eighth stage, the myriad practices are employed at will throughout the realms of all sentient beings, knowing that they are eternally without intrinsic nature and are as immovable as Mount Sumeru.

From "The Banner" (*dhvaja*) onwards, as found in the text itself, there are two lines of sūtra from "O Sons of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) down to "cannot be heard," which praise the difficulty of hearing this chapter.

From "Vimukticandra" (*Vimukticandra*) onwards, there is one line of sūtra, which constitutes the question by Vimukticandra regarding how much merit is obtained by hearing this Dharma. From "Vajragarbha" (*Vajragarbha*) onwards, until... [text continues].
Such merit is clarified by one and a half lines of sūtra, wherein Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replies:
"The merit accumulated by all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā) is like that of one who has heard this Dharma. It clarifies that the portion of the Buddha’s merit is divided into six parts.
Why is this? From here down to the stage of all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā-bhūmi), three and a half lines of sūtra clarify that it is as if one has heard this Dharma.

Regarding the section on the arising of doubt concerning the vastness of merit: if one who hears the Dharma possesses merit equal to that of the Buddha—namely, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) attained by the All-Knowing One (*sarvajña*)—why is this explained? It is because faith and understanding arise only through hearing this Dharma;
thus, hearing it for the first time is the foremost of all [instances of] omniscience. Therefore, the merit of the initial cause of faith is compared [to the Buddha’s].
The fruit is identical in essence to the cause, clarifying that there is no fruit apart from the cause; just as there is no sprout apart from the fruit, and no fruit apart from the sprout.
To clarify that the mind of faith takes the fruit as the cause, it is as stated regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths:
within the Great Wisdom Hall of the Tathāgata’s Universal Radiance Dharma-realm, ten Wisdom Buddhas are spoken of, with Immovable Wisdom Buddha serving as the [first].

First, take faith as the root; because the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom and the ten Buddhas of Wisdom are the wisdom-fruits of one’s own mind, they are ultimately fulfilled and never depart from this wisdom.
Other meanings are self-evident in the text itself. The intent is clear:
just as a seed is the cause for the production of its fruit, fundamental wisdom is like the seed, while differentiated wisdom is the fruit.
This preparatory application is like a fruit upon a sprout, for these two types of wisdom each possess boundless merit.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the nature of phenomena is thus, worlds in each of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields, shook in six ways and eighteen modes—namely, shaking, universal shaking, and so forth; rising, universal rising, and so forth.
They quaked, quaked universally, surged, surged universally, surged universally; they trembled, trembled universally, trembled universally; they roared, roared universally, roared universally;

they crashed, crashed universally, crashed universally; they struck, struck universally, struck universally. A rain of celestial flowers, celestial garlands, celestial garments, and various precious ornaments for adorning the body fell, along with banners, streamers, and silk canopies, while celestial music was played, its sounds harmonious and elegant, all sounding forth at once.

Having thus praised all the merits contained within the Stage of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), this Dharma was expounded in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven in this world; likewise, it was so in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were ten billion...
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field have come to this assembly and spoken thus: "Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha!
You have well expounded this Dharma. We are all likewise named Vajragarbha;
the worlds in which we dwell are each distinct, yet they are all named Vajraguṇa, and the Buddhas therein are all named Vajradhvaja. We currently reside in our own respective worlds."
All here have received the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority to proclaim this Dharma;
the assembly is entirely equal in its words, phrases, and meanings, with no increase or decrease from what is here spoken.
All have come to this assembly through the Buddha’s spiritual power to serve as witnesses for you, just as we have now entered this world, so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
In this same manner, he proceeded to bear witness. At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva surveyed the entire assembly in the ten directions, which pervaded the entire dharma-realm;

desiring to praise and inspire the mind set upon the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*), desiring to manifest the realm of the bodhisattvas, desiring to purify the power of the bodhisattva’s practices, desiring to explain the path for grasping all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), and desiring to eliminate...
To extinguish all worldly defilements and desires, to bestow the desire for all-knowledge, to manifest the adornment of inconceivable wisdom,
and to reveal all the merits of the bodhisattvas— desiring thus to further open up and clarify the meaning of this stage—
he spoke these verses, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power:

[Treatise] The fifteenth section consists of twenty-two and a half lines of scripture, which clearly explains the sixfold and eighteen-fold earthquake of the great earth resulting from this Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages, as well as the offering of worship and the arrival of the Vajragarbha Bodhisattvas from the ten directions to witness the Dharma.
This section is further divided into three parts: first, "At that time... [and so forth].

From "By the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "In all worlds likewise," there are eight lines of verse clarifying the section on the Dharma’s majesty shaking the earth and the heavens raining down various flowers as an offering.
From "At that time" down to "and went to bear witness," there are nine lines of verse clarifying how the Bodhisattvas named Vajragarbha from the ten directions all came together.

The section on realization is divided into three parts. First, from "At that time, Vajragarbha... down to "...and spoke these verses," there are six lines of scripture clarifying the observation of sentient beings and the objective dharmas, followed by the section on the intent to speak the verses, which says:
"Outside of worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields."
Those who come to this assembly clearly understand, through the vastness and abundance of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the fundamental essence,

that the measure of distance and number is equivalent to the dust motes of ten billion lands; having thus comprehended all these matters, they possess the clear and doubtless wisdom of the Dharma regarding the beginning,
end, cause, and effect of the ten stages for those newly entering them, and they harmonize the fundamental fruit-dharmas of the ten stages with their initial state.

Because the wisdom of a bodhisattva who has entered these ten stages is non-dual, they realize the inferiority of the preceding nine stages and enter the vast and great wisdom of the tenth stage; thus, by distinguishing the distance and proximity of phenomena and their relative abundance, it is also clarified that the Dharma taught by Vajragarbha is non-dual and identical with that of all Buddhas of the ten directions. As for "beyond the world": [The text continues: ...it refers to the state where one transcends the mundane realm. Furthermore, because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, it is called "non-dual. Because he has severed the two obstacles of afflictions and cognizable objects, it is called "unobstructed. Because he has exhausted the two types of habitual tendencies, it is called "pure. Because he has attained mastery over the two kinds of transformation, it is called "sovereign. Because he has perfected the two types of benefit—benefiting oneself and benefiting others—it is called "fulfilled. Because he has realized the two types of equality—the equality of phenomena and the equality of sentient beings—it is called "equal. Because he has attained the two types of liberation—the liberation of mind and the liberation of wisdom—it is called "liberated. Because he has manifested the two types of bodies—the Dharma-body and the form-body—it is called "manifest. Because he has attained the two types of knowledge—the knowledge of things as they are and the knowledge of all modes—it is called "knowledge. Because he has perfected the two types of vows—the vow to save sentient beings and the vow to purify lands—it is called "vow. Because he has attained the two types of power—the power of fearlessness and the power of unimpeded eloquence—it is called "power. Because he has attained the two types of sovereignty—the sovereignty over all dharmas and the sovereignty over all activities—it is called "sovereignty. Because he has attained the two types of bliss—the bliss of tranquility and the bliss of great compassion—it is called "bliss. Because he has attained the two types of permanence—the permanence of the Dharma-nature and the permanence of the continuity of emanations—it is called "permanent. Because he has attained the two types of self—the self of the true nature and the self of the universal manifestation—it is called "self. Because he has attained the two types of purity—the purity of the Dharma-realm and the purity of the adornment of lands—it is called "pure. Because he has attained the two types of eternity—the eternity of the unconditioned and the eternity of the continuous flow of transformation—it is called "eternal. Because he has attained the two types of bliss—the bliss of the cessation of suffering and the bliss of the fulfillment of desires—it is called "blissful. Because he has attained the two types of self—the self of the ultimate reality and the self of the sovereign master—it is called "at ease. Because he has attained the two types of purity—the purity of the intrinsic nature and the purity of the manifest function—it is called "pure. Because he has attained the two types of permanence—the permanence of the unchanging essence and the permanence of the unceasing activity—it is called "permanent. Because he has attained the two types of self—the self of the great emptiness and the self of the great compassion—it is called "self. Because he has attained the two types of purity—the purity of the Dharma-body and the purity of the form-body—it is called "pure. Because he has attained the two types of permanence—the permanence of the Dharma-nature and the permanence of the continuity of the teaching—it is called "permanent. Because he has attained the two types of self—the self of the ultimate truth and the self of the conventional truth—it is called "self. Because he has attained the two types of purity—the purity of the internal realization and the purity of the external manifestation—it is called "pure. Because he has attained the two types of permanence—the permanence of the unconditioned and the permanence of the conditioned continuity—it is called "permanent. Because he has attained the two types of self—the self of the great wisdom and the self of the great skillful means—it is called "self. Because he has attained the two types of purity—the purity of the Dharma-realm and the purity of the lands and assemblies—it is called "pure. Because he has attained the two types of permanence—the permanence of the unarisen and the permanence of the unceasing—it is called "permanent. Because he has attained the two types of self—the self of the great liberation and the self of the great empowerment—it is called "self. [Sūtra]: "His mind is tranquil and ever-disciplined; Equanimous and unimpeded like space, Free from all defilements, he abides in the Path. Listen now to this supreme practice."
Having cultivated all manner of virtues for hundreds of billions of eons, making offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they have resolved upon the Great Mind, diligently upholding the precepts and always remaining gentle and patient; they are fully endowed with shame, modesty, merit, and wisdom.
Aspiring to seek the Buddha’s wisdom, they cultivate vast insight; Vowing to attain the Ten Powers, they give rise to the Great Mind.
They make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, And purify every land throughout all realms.
Thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are equal, They give rise to the Great Mind for the benefit of sentient beings.
Abiding in the first stage, one gives rise to this mind, Forever leaving behind all evils and always remaining joyful.
Through the power of aspiration, one extensively cultivates all wholesome dharmas;

Out of compassion, one enters the subsequent stages, Perfecting ethical discipline and learning while keeping sentient beings in mind. Washing away all defilements, the mind becomes luminous and pure.
Observing the fires of the three poisons in the world, those of vast understanding proceed to the third stage;
seeing that all within the three realms of existence are impermanent, like an arrow piercing the body with burning pain,
they grow weary of the conditioned and seek the Buddha-dharma— those of vast wisdom proceed to the stage of Radiance.

Endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, they attain the knowledge of the Path; They make offerings to hundreds of thousands of immeasurable Buddhas and constantly contemplate their most supreme merits. Such persons enter the stage that is difficult to conquer;
With wisdom and skillful means, they skillfully observe and manifest in various ways to save sentient beings.
Furthermore, making offerings to the Ten-Powered, Unsurpassed Honored One, they enter the Ground of Manifestation of Non-arising.
Though difficult for the world to know, they are able to know it; they do not grasp at a self and are free from the existence or non-existence of dharmas.
Since the nature of phenomena is fundamentally quiescent, they turn in accordance with conditions. Having attained this subtle and wondrous state, they advance toward the Seventh Ground.
With wisdom, skillful means, and a vast mind, Difficult to practice, difficult to subdue, and difficult to comprehend,
Though having realized cessation, you diligently cultivate it; Able to proceed to the immovable stage like space,
The Buddha exhorts you to arise from cessation And extensively perform the various activities of wisdom.
Possessing the ten masteries, he observes the world and thereby ascends to the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
With subtle wisdom, he contemplates the dense forest of sentient beings' mental activities, karma, and afflictions;
desiring to transform them so they may enter the Path, he expounds the sublime treasury of the ultimate meaning of all Buddhas.
Practicing the stages in succession and endowed with all virtues, up to the ninth stage, they accumulate merit and wisdom,
constantly seeking the supreme Dharma of all Buddhas. Having received the Buddha’s water of wisdom poured upon their crowns,
they attain countless samādhis and also thoroughly understand the workings of karma.
The final samādhi is named "Receiving the Empowerment. Abiding in the vast realm, forever unmoving— When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, A great jewel lotus suddenly appears;
its size matches that [of the bodhisattva], And he sits within it, surrounded by the sons of the Buddha, all observing together.
He emits hundreds of thousands of billions of great rays of light, which extinguish the suffering of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, from the crown of his head he emits light that enters universally into the assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it abides everywhere in mid-air, forming a net of light. Having made offerings to the Buddhas, the light re-enters through the soles of his feet.
At that moment, all the Buddhas fully understood; This Son of the Buddha had ascended to his office.

The Bodhisattvas from the ten directions came to observe him; The Great Being receiving his office extended light, Which illuminated all the Buddhas, And from between their brows they too emitted light, Shining everywhere as it entered through the crown of his head.
The worlds of the ten directions all tremble, and the sufferings of all hells are extinguished;
at that time, the Buddhas confer their offices upon him, just as the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning King receives his station.
If one is thus graced by the Buddhas with consecration, this is called ascending to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
Wisdom increases without limit, awakening all worlds: The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm;
The realm of phenomena, the realm of worlds, and the realm of sentient beings— Whether finite or infinite, including even empty space— All such things are thoroughly penetrated.
With great power in all transformative activities, And through the subtle wisdom empowered by all Buddhas,

his renouncing the world, his attaining the Perfect Path, His turning the sublime Wheel of Dharma, and his entry into Nirvāṇa.
Even the dharmas of tranquil liberation and those not yet spoken, they are able to comprehend them all.
The Bodhisattva dwelling on this Stage of the Cloud of Dharma is fully endowed with the power of mindfulness to uphold the Buddha-dharma;

All the infinite sentient beings of the ten directions Have attained the power of hearing and retaining the Buddha-dharma;

By the majestic power of their past wisdom and vows, In a single thought-moment, they pervade all lands of the ten directions.

and bodhisattvas of this stage who make offerings to the Buddha throughout all the lands of the ten directions.

In a single thought-moment, immeasurable samādhis are attained; The Buddhas perceived therein are likewise so.

[Treatise] This chapter clarifies the names of the ten samādhis as spoken by the Buddha himself, and the applications of the ten samādhis as explained by Samantabhadra.
The Buddha’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is the essence (*tattva*), and Samantabhadra’s differentiated wisdom (*vicitra-jñāna*) is its function (*vṛtti*);

To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed according to five sections: first, explaining the purpose of this assembly;

The General Meaning of the Eleven Chapters: An Exegesis of the Text Based on the Five Sciences, Part One. Regarding the explanation of the purpose for the assembly’s arrival:
from within this Hall of Universal Radiance of Great Wisdom, one gives rise to faith;

through the wisdom of immovability as the basis for ascending practice, one proceeds through the ten stages and the eleventh stage until the path is perfected and conduct is complete, reaching the fruit of Buddhahood without ever departing from the source.

Because wisdom is such, this assembly must come to clarify that the cause does not shift; for time does not shift, wisdom does not shift, and practice does not shift, as cause and effect are of one essence.
Thus, it leads Sudhana to see Maitreya, and Maitreya in turn causes him to see Mañjuśrī again and enter the body of Samantabhadra—this is it.
Second, the explanation of why this assembly is taught: what is it that is to be explained?
Therefore, I shall again set forth the origins of how the World-Honored One first attained Buddhahood in the kingdom of Magadha. As the Sūtra says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in the forest of Āraṇya-dharma;

having just attained perfect enlightenment, he entered the Samādhi of the Limit of the Kṣaṇa in the Hall of Universal Radiance. This clarifies his initial attainment of Buddhahood and the forty-nine days [that followed].
The Dharma wheels turned throughout his life and his descent from heaven do not, in total, exceed a single kṣaṇa; they neither shift nor migrate.
Fearing that future sentient beings might lose their original intent and give rise to false notions of change and transition, it is necessary to recount them again to clarify the beginning and end:
there is no time at which they can shift. This clarifies that the three bodies of all Buddhas and all sentient beings are thus.

In total, this is a single body that does not migrate; from the initial stage of faith through the progression of practice across the five positions, it never shifts from its original time, months, years, days, hours, nor from the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom-dharma.

Therefore, the third section clarifies for what causes and conditions this *Ekādaśa-parivarta-sūtra* is taught here in the Hall of Universal Radiance. The commentary states: "It is for the sake of clarification."

In the first assembly at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Buddha first attained perfect awakening; this was the Buddha’s exhortation to practice by citing his own initial fruit of attainment.
In the second assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantāloka-prāsāda*), he clarified that this is the retributive dwelling where the Tathāgata’s great wisdom itself resides.
He spoke of ten Wisdom Buddhas, with Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalamati*) as the foremost, so that [beings] might cultivate faith and diligence.
At this gate, those who have first resolved to attain Bodhicitta are made to arise from this Great Wisdom Mansion of Universal Radiance;

they advance in practice with faith until, ultimately, they do not depart from the Tathāgata’s original wisdom, original conduct, and original time, thereby restoring themselves as original Buddhas where all matters remain as they were.
Therefore, following these ten stages (*bhūmi*), these ten [perfections] are taught within the locus of the original mind of faith.
The first chapter of this sutra employs the elucidation of cause and effect based on the world, time, days, months, and years, as it relies entirely upon the fundamental source;
therefore, eleven chapters of the sutra are expounded herein. These eleven chapters collectively clarify all the realms encountered at the moment of attaining Buddhahood;
that is to say, they clarify that those who are able to give rise to the bodhicitta will themselves become Buddhas, without exception.
Because the Buddha Vairocana was present in the first assembly, one practices by following his example exactly as it was in the original;

In the "Chapter on Transcending the World," Samantabhadra constantly practices these three matters; they are all the single essence of the Tathāgata’s Universal Radiance Wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), comprising both cause and effect.

These are entirely the single function of Universal Radiance Wisdom throughout the beginning and end of cause and effect, and across all times, seasons, years, and months; there is no temporal substance whatsoever. Thus it is said.

Alternatively, because the distant and near kalpas of the three periods of time interpenetrate one another in nine temporal dimensions, they are layered without obstruction. Therefore, [it is said to be so].
It does not depart from the wisdom of universal radiance, for there is nothing that is not sealed by it from beginningless time and no end;

because there is no finality that is not thoroughly penetrated, the ocean of kalpas across the three periods of time is all one single moment. Thus, even the causes and effects of the five stages do not transcend this fixed essence.

Because the Sūtra expounds the wisdom of Bodhi as being without beginning or end and occurring all at once, it is not like the limited perceptions of ordinary beings which possess temporal sequence.
