seeing one's own body enter the body of Samantabhadra is the very pattern of what was taught here in the Hall of Universal Radiance regarding the ten stages of faith.
Now, having reached the fruit of Buddhahood, one does not depart from those causes.

Regarding the stage of fulfilling the conduct of Samantabhadra after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) clarifies that the conduct of Samantabhadra subsequent to the fruit of Buddhahood is all-pervasive.
As for the statement that one observes everywhere yet does not see Samantabhadra nor the seat upon which he sits:

this clarifies that from the very beginning—through the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*)—one has been riding upon the vehicle of Samantabhadra’s own conduct.
Advancing through many stages of seeking, one attains the Tathāgata’s liberation, compassion, and wisdom, and the supramundane mind;

by practicing these concurrently, one perfects the path of the Buddha’s sovereign, effortless mastery. Having seen for oneself that this pervades all, one enters the conduct of Samantabhadra and all samādhis following the fruit of Buddhahood in the tenth stage.
These are purely skillful entries into the mundane world, free from seeking even supramundane Buddhas.

Because it is the fruit, one simultaneously cultivates both compassion and wisdom; the supramundane Buddha-fruit samādhi is sought through three ways, yet none are seen—this is purely great compassion, for there is no practice for self-benefit, as they do not meet [in that regard].
Because the practices of Samantabhadra prior to the Buddha-fruit of the ten stages possess the mind for both self-benefit and benefiting others, one seeks mundane and supramundane liberation.

Therefore, because one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra on the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*) without seeking one's own liberation, it consists purely of conduct for the benefit of sentient beings;

and because from the stages prior to the eleventh, the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) has already been manifested and the path of self-liberation fully perfected such that there is nothing further to be sought, on the eleventh stage one acts solely for the sake of benefiting others.
Because all sentient beings lack the accumulation of their own merit, they seek the conduct of Samantabhadra for self-benefit and benefiting others prior to the tenth stage,
yet they have not yet attained the conduct of Samantabhadra within the eleventh stage; for this reason,
although the great assembly searched everywhere, they were ultimately unable to see the body or the seat of Samantabhadra.
Examine this with careful scrutiny and contemplate it with wisdom; the remainder is fully contained within the text itself.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, where is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra now? The Buddha said:
"Universal Eye, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is currently present here in this assembly at the site of enlightenment, attending upon me and dwelling here."

At that time, while remaining utterly unmoving, Samantacakṣus and the other bodhisattvas again surveyed the assembly at the site of enlightenment, searching everywhere, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we have still not been able to see the body or the seat of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
The Buddha said: "It is so, sons of good family. For what reason are you unable to see him?"
Good son, because the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is profoundly deep and ineffable, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra has attained the gate of boundless wisdom,
entered the Lion’s Boundless Prowess Samādhi, and acquired supreme sovereign power. He enters the realm of pure non-obstruction,
gives rise to the ten powers of a Tathāgata, takes the treasury of the Dharma-realm as his body, and is shared by all Tathāgatas.
That which is protected and remembered by him can, in a single moment of thought, fully realize and enter the non-differentiated wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
for this reason, you are unable to see it.
[Treatise] Fifth: From "At that time, Universal Eye" down to "for this reason, you are unable to see it."
The eleventh section of the sutra clarifies that when the bodhisattvas enter the power of samādhi and desire to see Samantabhadra, they search everywhere but cannot find him.
The Tathāgata then explains to them that the resolve and virtue of Samantabhadra are exceedingly profound, and that you are unable to see him. Why is it that you do not see Samantabhadra?
This is to clarify that for bodhisattvas of the ten stages, it is because their supramundane wisdom and the predominance of their great compassion [are so vast].
There is a samādhi that is entirely supramundane wisdom and compassion; because of this, one does not see Samantabhadra.
This is the practice-gate of the eleventh stage, which is constantly in the world yet the supramundane mind has perished, and its tranquil function is sovereign.
Because it is not associated with supramundane samādhis, one does not see [him]. In explaining the meaning of this, it is divided into four sections: first, "At that time, Universal Eye..."

From "The Bodhisattva [Samantabhadra] has already descended" down to "Where is he now? there is one line and a half of sūtra text clarifying the section on the location of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra within the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) chapter;

this is divided into two parts. From the words "The Buddha said" down to "There is no movement from the beginning," there is one line and a half of sūtra text clarifying the section where the Tathāgata reveals the location of Samantabhadra; this is divided into three parts. At that time, Puyan and all the bodhisattvas...

From "The Bodhisattva [Saṃkusumitarājendra]... down to "his body and seat," there are two and a half lines of sūtra explaining how Samantacakṣus and the other bodhisattvas repeatedly observed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva yet were still unable to see him; this is divided into four parts. From "The Buddha said, 'It is thus...
down to "...they could not even see his ears," there are six lines of sūtra explaining how the Tathāgata praised Samantabhadra for the sake of Samantacakṣus and the others.
The resolve and virtue of the worthy Bodhisattva have penetrated deeply into the Lion’s Unfurling Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*), which you are unable to perceive.

As the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* states, "entering the Lion’s Unfurling Samādhi" clarifies that one has entered the fruit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and that the Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*) practices are entirely a samādhi of fearless mastery.
It clarifies that through boundless conceptions, one acts in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings.
"Brilliant Great Function" (Ming Dàyòng) means that because [this function] arises from the Truth itself, it does not depend on thought; thus, "Lion" (Shīzǐ) signifies fearless mastery.

"Exertion" (Fènxùn) signifies that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva constantly and universally manifests pervasive activity throughout the ten directions, always acting in accordance with the ten worlds, such that there is not a single sentient being who is not universally saved, nor any whose faculties are capable of being benefited who is ever missed.
Because it occurs at the opportune moment, it is called the "Lion’s Leaping Samādhi.
Just as a lion leaps forth all at once, causing every hair on its body to vibrate simultaneously, so too does Samantabhadra Bodhisattva constantly abide in the ocean of samādhi of great function.

Relying on wisdom, he universally manifests his activity at all times, equalizing his conduct with that of all sentient beings. Because he never misses the proper time and does not depend on discursive thought, his great functions are all-pervasive.

Because of benefiting sentient beings without rest, because from the beginningless past until now it is a single thought-moment, and because there is no distinction between past and present, the Dharma thus functions;
therefore, the mind’s great function is luminous while remaining eternally quiescent—this is the meaning of "valiant prowess" (*vikrīḍita*).
One who has attained supreme sovereign function employs it universally and constantly within that great function to benefit sentient beings; this is entirely samādhi and nothing else.

Regarding the differences in cessation: because there is a supramundane mind during the stages of ascent prior to the ten bhūmis, "entering the realm of pure non-obstruction" clarifies that the measure of Samantabhadra’s wisdom is equal to space;

because it is rootless and cannot be fully known, "the difference in non-practice for the sake of benefiting others" clarifies that this gives rise to the ten kinds of power of a Tathāgata. These are the ten powers of a Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Furthermore, the arising of Samantabhadra’s conduct and the teaching of sentient beings to attain Buddhahood and the ten powers all originate from the power of Samantabhadra’s vows.

Regarding the taking of the Dharma-realm treasury as one’s body: because the body of fundamental wisdom and the body of differentiated wisdom are by nature universally pervasive, their measure is equal to the mental activities of all sentient beings; they contain and encompass everything, and thus all are Buddhas.
Thus, within a single pore, the lands of the ordinary and the holy throughout the ten directions are universally contained without exception;
for since wisdom has no interior, exterior, or intermediate dimensions, it is fundamentally such as this.

That which is collectively protected and remembered by all Tathāgatas is because they share the same fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and because it constitutes their great activity; thus, within one—

In a mere moment, one is able to realize and enter the wisdom of non-differentiation. This clarifies the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s skillful means of manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment within the realms of sentient beings throughout the ten directions to deliver them; it also clarifies such matters as manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
Furthermore, when discussed from the perspective of the essence of non-differentiating wisdom, even infinite eons are, in total, but a single moment.
If all sentient beings, in a single thought-moment, were to create for themselves the perception of birth and death throughout inexhaustible kalpas,
yet through the clear contemplation of penetrating wisdom and principle, they were to regard those inexhaustible kalpas as a single thought-moment due to non-differentiating wisdom—
by being thus in accord, they would simultaneously achieve buddhahood together with all Buddhas of the past, present, and future.

The Buddha, therefore, seals [all things] with the seal of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because the essence of the three periods of time is fundamentally equal and lacks the limits of priority or posteriority.

He clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages still possess a mind directed toward transcendence and remain deluded regarding the conduct of entering the entanglements (*saṃyojana*) in the eleventh stage;
thus, those who cannot yet see [the ultimate reality] are caused to advance so that the Bodhisattva may preserve their own power and not become stagnant.
Because it pertains to the ten preceding stages, the remainder is self-evident in the text. Regarding the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (Lion’s Play Samādhi):
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it universally accords with the thoughts and activities of all sentient beings to bring them to maturity;

this great function is effortless (*anābhoga*), which is the meaning of "playful exertion" (*vijṛmbhita*) and the meaning of "samādhi. When discussed in terms of its great function, there is nothing separate from it.
Because of their cessation.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, having heard the Tathāgata speak of the pure merits of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and his attainment of ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis,
used the power of those samādhis to observe everywhere, thirsting with longing to see Samantabhadra.
Even the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla could not see the rest of the assembly of all those bodhisattvas, nor did he perceive the time [of their presence].
Then, the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus arose from samādhi and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I entered ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis seeking to see Samantabhadra, yet in the end I was unable to see his body, nor his bodily actions, speech, or..."
Vocal action, mind, mental action, the seat, and the dwelling place—all these are not seen. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, son of good family! You should know that this is all due to the power of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s abiding in inconceivable liberation.
What do you think, Universal Eye? Is there anyone who can describe the various illusory manifestations within the words and letters of an illusion?"
When asked about his dwelling place, he did not answer, saying, "No. The Buddha said, "O Universal Eye, even the illusory marks within an illusion cannot be described;
how much less so the realm of the secret body, the realm of the secret speech, and the realm of the secret mind of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra?
How could one enter or perceive them therein? Why is this? Because the realm of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is profoundly deep."
Inconceivable and immeasurable, exceeding all measure— to state the essential point— Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by means of adamantine wisdom,
universally enters the Dharma-realm; he acts nowhere and dwells nowhere in any world,
knowing that the bodies of all sentient beings are fundamentally no-bodies, without coming or going, attaining sovereignty that is inexhaustible and without distinction.
His supernormal powers are without dependence, without fabrication, and without fluctuation, reaching the ultimate limit of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Noble son, if there are those who behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, or serve him, or hear his name, or contemplate him, or bring him to mind,
or give rise to faith and understanding, or diligently observe him, or first set out toward him, or correctly seek him—
If one seeks to give rise to vows that continue without interruption, all shall obtain benefit and none shall pass in vain.
At that time, Universal Eye and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas conceived a yearning for the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to behold him, and spoke these words:
"Homage to all Buddhas! Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra! Thus they recited this three times.
Prostrating with the head in reverence, the Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*) and the entire assembly, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, you should further prostrate and reverently entreat Samantabhadra. You should also, with single-minded devotion, observe the ten directions and imagine the body of Samantabhadra standing before you.
Contemplating in this way, you should cultivate deep faith and understanding that pervades the entire Dharma-realm."
Renouncing all [defilements] and vowing to share the same conduct and vows as Samantabhadra, one enters the non-dual reality of the Dharma-body, which manifests universally throughout all worlds.
Fully knowing the differences in the faculties of sentient beings, one gathers the path of Samantabhadra in all places.
If one can give rise to such a great vow, then one shall behold the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
At that time, Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus), upon hearing these words of the Buddha, together with all the bodhisattvas, prostrated at once and entreated to behold the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
[Treatise] Sixth: From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "entreated to behold the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra."

The *Sādhana-triṃśad-dvāra-sūtra* clarifies the section on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas thrice invoking the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and earnestly entreating him to appear. Within this section, it is further divided into seven parts:
first, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to "nor did they see any [existence]."
The three and a half lines of sutra clarify that the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus sought Samantabhadra through ten thousand unspeakable samādhis but was unable to see him;

this is divided into two parts. From "the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus" down to "could not see him at all," there are three lines of sutra clarifying that the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus arose from samādhi and informed the Buddha that he had not seen Samantabhadra.
The virtuous Bodhisattva’s actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as his seat, are divided into three. The Buddha said: "Thus it is," and so on, down to the ultimate limit;

there are eleven lines of scripture clarifying that the Buddha, for the sake of Universal Eye (Samantadarśin), praised the profundity of Samantabhadra’s three activities, which cannot be characterized by the samādhis of "emerging" or "entering," nor by the aspect of "seeing. Fourth, "Good sons... and so forth.

From the passage "down to no one passes in vain" (*na vṛthā gacchati*), there are three and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the Buddha’s praise of the benefits of seeing, hearing, approaching, and serving Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, which do not pass in vain. This section is divided into five parts.

From "At that time, Universal Eye" (*atha khalu Samantanetra*) down to "prostrating with his head in reverence" (*śirasā vanditvā*), for approximately three lines of sūtra, it clarifies Universal Eye and the other bodhisattvas.
All were thirsting with longing for Samantabhadra; they thrice uttered "Namo" and prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground. This section is divided into six parts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Puyan (Universal Eye) and so forth, down to the passage "you shall immediately behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

These six and a half lines of scripture clarify that the Buddha further exhorted the great assembly, including Puyan, to pay even greater homage and to contemplate the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in order to seek out Samantabhadra.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the virtuous Bodhisattva, as if facing him in person," down to "he attained the vision of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva"—
this one and a half lines of scripture clarify the Universal Eye and how the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, following the exhortation, further paid homage to Samantabhadra.
This concludes the section on knowing the proper time to manifest his own body, which comprises thirty-two lines [of verse].

The seventh section of the sutra clarifies that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva cannot be seen by the Bodhisattvas such as Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) because they have not attained the samādhi through which one perceives the three karmas, the seat, and the realm of Samantabhadra. Therefore,

it employs various illusory manifestations within the context of illusory spells and letters as metaphors for his dwelling place, thereby elucidating that the essence of illusory spells and letters is utterly non-existent.
As for the locus, that which is sought cannot be attained by seeking within the locus of entering and emerging from samādhi.

One must instead transcend that stillness and the arising-and-ceasing of thoughts; rather, one gives rise to the perception of clarity and awareness. When this perception moves and functions, its own essence is all-pervasive;
it functions while remaining eternally quiescent, not because it is further extinguished. It is for this reason that Samantabhadra, through adamantine wisdom, universally enters the Dharma-realm.

In all worlds, there is nowhere to travel and nowhere to abide; one knows that the bodies of all sentient beings are all non-bodies, without coming or going, attaining unceasing and inexhaustible, undifferentiated, sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

This clarifies that "spirit" (*shen*) refers to acting in accordance with things; it is called "spirit" because it is not non-reflective, not unsettled, not disordered, and neither comes nor goes, but acts spontaneously.
Wisdom pervades all, benefiting sentient beings with mastery; knowing their faculties and manifesting accordingly is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*).
When the three karmas of body, speech, and mind act in such a way that there is no distinction between meditative absorption and distraction, this is truly called the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Regarding his seat, just as the substance of the seat of a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground is described as merely having a magnitude equal to a trichiliocosm, so too is this [seat] of Samantabhadra.

Because the dimensions of the seat are equal to the void and the entire *dharmadhātu* of the Great Lotus Treasury, it is clearly known that the scope of the wisdom of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) is still separated from this by such a distance.
To ascend to this station from here, one must enter and emerge from as many unspeakable gates of samādhi as are appropriate;
yet, because there are still obstacles consisting of limitations regarding quiescence and activity, one has not yet attained the Tenth Ground.
Because Samantabhadra Bodhisattva attains great mastery only after the stage of fruition,

he manifests his body and expounds the matters of the thirteen samādhi realms only after one has made the threefold request for Samantabhadra and undergone the threefold advancement, yet still gives rise to conceptual thoughts.

The underlying intent is to reprove those at the ten stages (*bhūmi*) who still harbor a seeking mind for transcendence and whose habitual tendencies remain within the worldly realm of birth and death.

Because they have not yet attained equality with the Tathāgatas in their mastery over all functions throughout the ten directions, and because they still harbor conceptualizations regarding the teachings of the Tathāgata, they remain subject to the defiled habitual tendencies within those ten stages.

This clarifies that while the bodhisattvas of the ten stages take the conventional and ultimate truths as their objects, they still possess residual habitual afflictions that transcend the mundane world; thus, the above intent is to clarify that the bodhisattvas of the ten stages take the ultimate truth as their object.

Because the two habits of the mundane have not yet been extinguished and the two habits of stillness and distraction have not yet been exhausted, there remains the habit of entering and emerging from various samādhis;

thus, one has not yet attained constant entry [into them]. Although saṃsāra is like the nature of space—having no agent yet being eternally omnipresent and not contained within limits—it takes all sentient beings and their objective realms as its essence. This is Samantabhadra.
This wisdom is like empty space; it serves as the essential body for the birth of all sentient beings. When sentient beings are deluded regarding this wisdom, it is called ignorance.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, in accordance with those deluded phenomena, manifests physical bodies throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Because this wisdom has no substantial body and is like empty space—neither a product of fabrication nor subject to coming or going—it is without departure.
This coming is neither birth nor cessation; it merely employs an ocean of wisdom equal to empty space to awaken the deluded at all places.

Since this wisdom has no substance or form and can manifest the great function that accords with the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, how could one seek it through the entry and exit of samādhis by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages? How then could it be seen?
Therefore, the Tathāgata has taught the bodhisattvas that if one seeks the essential nature or characteristics of illusory spells and letters, nothing can be found;
yet even the mind that performs the illusion cannot be found—how, then, could those illusory characteristics be sought?
Thus, by means of entering and emerging from samādhi and seeking the mind, one seeks the non-reliant, virtuous great function of Samantabhadra.

The body of skillful wisdom is ultimately unattainable; therefore, the Tathāgata instructs all bodhisattvas to first give rise to the thought [of seeking it] and reverently perform three prostrations to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Only then, through the power of supernormal faculties, does he manifest his body according to what is appropriate.
This body of clear wisdom cannot be sought within the locus of samādhi, for as the essence of wisdom, it dwells nowhere and relies on nothing.
If one conceives thoughts, recollections, or aspirations, they will manifest accordingly through transformation, for there is no fixed place or basis upon which they rely;
they are like echoes in a valley, being merely sounds that respond to objects. If one seeks them with desire, no location can be found where they exist.
The Buddha said: "The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is now present here in this assembly at the site of enlightenment, attending me and dwelling in the first [stage]."
That which is immovable is clarified by the fact that the nature of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is inherently without dependence;

it is therefore called "the present site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because it serves as the antidote to all views and aggregates of grasping at existence, it is called the "assembly" (*parṣad*), being identical in essence to the great function of all Buddhas of the ten directions through the unimpeded universal radiance of wisdom (*samantaprabhāsa-jñāna*) in its general and specific aspects, its similarities and differences.
Therefore, the ocean of wisdom with its boundless distinctions functions simultaneously and equally, yet it does not shift from the essence of fundamental wisdom;

this non-abiding wisdom is called "intimately approaching me" because one abides in the initial state of immovability. Thus, the expression "namo" clarifies that one takes refuge and follows with faith.
In terms of the dharma, "south" (nam) signifies departure (*niḥsaraṇa*); within departure there is emptiness (*śūnya*), and because it is empty and non-existent, [it is so named].
This clarifies that *li* (separation) constitutes the sun; *li* presides over the mind. Because one penetrates the principle of voidness through the mind, the wisdom of the mind becomes luminous;
therefore, it is said "Namo" (Homage). To take refuge means to faithfully accord with the principle of the wisdom of voidness.
For this reason, the significance of Sudhana’s seeking friends in the south is likewise so, as is the significance of the Dragon Girl’s attaining Buddhahood in the south.

If one merely realizes the principle of emptiness and non-existence, the ten directions are all to the south; if one clings to all phenomena as being truly existent, the ten directions are all to the north.
Thus, the rest is fully contained within the text itself.
