A Combined Commentary on the Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-seven, Part Two: The Ten Determinations.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by means of the power of his liberation and supernormal faculties, acted according to what was appropriate for each.
He manifests a physical body so that all those bodhisattvas may see Samantabhadra approaching the Tathāgata;
they also see him seated upon a lotus throne amidst this entire assembly of bodhisattvas;
they also see him coming in successive succession from the presence of all Buddhas in all other worlds; and they also see him teaching the Dharma in the presence of all those Buddhas.
He expounded all the practices of the bodhisattvas, revealed the path to the knowledge of all modes of knowing (*sarvajñajñāna*),

elucidated all the spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) of the bodhisattvas, distinguished all the majestic virtues (*tejas*) of the bodhisattvas, and manifested all the Buddhas of the three periods of time. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*) and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, seeing this miraculous transformation, their hearts leaped with joy.
Filled with great joy, all prostrated themselves; they conceived a heart of deep respect for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as if seeing all the Buddhas of the ten directions.

At that time, by the great majestic power of the Buddha, the power of the faith and understanding of the bodhisattvas, and the power of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s original vows, there naturally rained down ten thousand kinds of clouds, namely, various flowers.
There were clouds of various garlands, clouds of various fragrances, clouds of various powdered incenses, clouds of various canopies, clouds of various garments,
clouds of various ornaments, clouds of various precious jewels, clouds of various burning incenses, and clouds of various silken fabrics;
unspeakable worlds shook in six ways, and celestial music was played, its sound heard from afar.
It can be said that the world emits a great radiance, and that light shines universally upon unspeakable worlds,
causing the three evil realms to be entirely extinguished; it purifies unspeakable worlds, causing unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas to enter the conduct of Samantabhadra,
unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas to accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra, and unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas [to abide] in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
"May they all fully attain and realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Treatise] From "At that time" (seventh) down to "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," there are nineteen and a half lines of scripture.
This is the section where Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifests his body for the sake of the assembly. For what reason is it possible to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva?
Because one perceives through the maintenance of mental recollection, and because the substance is turned toward function, this is the body of Samantabhadra.
Since it clarifies that all mental recollections constitute the function of the Buddha, universally perceiving all sentient beings is likewise the function of the Buddha.
In the explanation of the meaning, there are three sections: first, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... down to "...manifesting one...".
The section from "All Buddhas of the three periods of time" to "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifests his body according to the needs of beings" consists of seven lines of scripture,

clarifying the second part [of the manifestation]. At that time, from "Universal Eye" down to "all Buddhas," there are two and a half lines of scripture clarifying how the great assembly of bodhisattvas rejoiced upon seeing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, as if they were seeing all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
From the section "Dividing into three" down to "Samyak-saṃbodhi," there are ten chapters of sutra that clarify the power of faith and understanding of all Bodhisattvas;
the cloud-offerings arising from the original vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; the light of universal illumination;
the pacification of the three evil realms; and the entry of all Bodhisattvas into the practices of Samantabhadra, according to their respective capacities.
Because one sees [the Buddha] as soon as he manifests his body, if one seeks him by causing the mind to enter or exit samādhi, one will not find him.

Seeing that there is no entering or exiting, one realizes that wisdom cannot be sought through the entering or exiting of samādhi; therefore, unless one’s station coincides with the Way and wisdom accords spontaneously, it will not be realized.
To see through conceptual thought is merely to see the manifestation of the body according to conditions; only after this can one finally realize its fundamental source.

Regarding the body, the remaining meanings are fully contained within the text itself; the intent clarifies that the wisdom of non-abiding is the great essence of Samantabhadra, while manifesting bodies according to need is the great function of Samantabhadra.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is one who dwells in great majestic power;
who dwells in the peerless; who dwells in the faultless; who dwells in non-retrogression; who dwells in equanimity;
who dwells in the indestructible; who dwells in all differentiated dharmas; who dwells in all undifferentiated dharmas; who dwells in all..."
"Regarding those sentient beings who dwell with skillful minds, and who abide in the samādhi of liberation through mastery over all dharmas," the Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Universal Eye!
It is as you have said. The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra possesses incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) pure merits, namely:
the merit of peerless adornment, the merit of immeasurable jewels, and the inconceivable ocean."
The merit of immeasurable marks; the merit of boundless clouds; the merit of infinite limits; the merit of being beyond praise;
the merit of inexhaustible dharmas; the merit that is ineffable; the merit of all Buddhas; the merit of praising and extolling which can never be exhausted.

[Treatise] Eighth: From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye" down to the nine lines and a half of scripture praising his inexhaustible merit, it is clarified that the Bodhisattva Universal Eye praises the ten kinds of vast abodes of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra by means of ten kinds of abiding dharmas.
This section explains the meaning, clarifying how Universal Eye praises the ten kinds of vast [qualities] of Samantabhadra.
The Tathāgata Mahāvihārin praised the ten vast and great merits of Samantabhadra; the meaning of this praise is as expressed in the text.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:

"Samantabhadra, you should explain the ten great samādhis for the sake of Universal Eye and the assembly of bodhisattvas here, so that they may enter them well and bring to fulfillment the qualities of Samantabhadra."

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice and vow to expound these ten great samādhis, thereby causing the bodhisattvas of the past to have already attained liberation, the bodhisattvas of the present to now attain liberation, and the bodhisattvas of the future to surely attain liberation. What are these ten?
First is the Great Samādhi of Universal Radiance; second is the Great Samādhi of Sublime Radiance; third...
1. The Great Samādhi of Successively Traveling to All Buddha-fields; 2. The Great Samādhi of Practicing with a Pure and Profound Mind;
3. The Great Samādhi of Knowing the Treasury of Past Adornments; 4. The Great Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom; 5.
The Great Samādhi of Thoroughly Understanding the Buddha-Adornments of All Worlds; 6. [The Great Samādhi of] Sentient Beings...
Ninth is the Great Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm; tenth is the Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel.
These ten great samādhis can be skillfully entered by the great bodhisattvas;
they have been taught, will be taught, and are currently being taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. If bodhisattvas cherish, revere, and practice them...
One who is untiring shall attain accomplishment; such a person is called a Buddha, is called a Tathāgata, and is also called one who has attained the Ten Powers.
He is called a Teacher, a Great Teacher, All-Knowing, All-Seeing, Abiding in Non-obstruction, Penetrating All Objects, and Master of All Dharmas.
This Bodhisattva here universally enters all worlds, yet remains unattached to those worlds;
universally enters all realms of sentient beings, yet grasps nothing among sentient beings; universally enters all bodies, yet encounters no obstruction regarding bodies;
and universally enters the entire dharma-realm, knowing that the dharma-realm is boundless, while drawing near to the three periods of time.
Clearly perceiving all Buddhas, skillfully expounding all Buddha-dharmas, thoroughly understanding all syllables, mastering all conventional designations,
accomplishing the pure path of all bodhisattvas, abiding in all the distinct practices of bodhisattvas,
universally attaining the wisdom of all three periods of time within a single thought-moment, universally knowing all phenomena of the three periods of time, and universally expounding them.
The universal turning of the non-retrogressive wheel of all Buddhas; the universal realization of all paths to enlightenment throughout each of the past, future, and present ages;

and within each of these paths to enlightenment, the universal comprehension of everything taught by all Buddhas—this is the gateway to the Dharma-characteristics of all Bodhisattvas, the gateway to the wisdom-awakening of all Bodhisattvas, and the gateway to all modes of being.
The gate of the banner of unsurpassed wisdom; the gate of the various practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
the gate of fierce and sharp supernormal powers and vows; the gate of all dhāraṇīs and eloquence; the gate of the distinctions among all phenomena of the three periods of time;
the gate of the manifestations of all Buddhas; and the gate of establishing all sentient beings in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). By means of these...
The Buddha’s spiritual power adorns and purifies all gateways to the worlds. If a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they attain the power of the dharma-realm without exhaustion;
they attain the practice of space without obstruction; they attain the rank of Dharma King with immeasurable sovereignty;
and like those in the world who receive their office through consecration, they attain boundless wisdom, universal penetration, and vastness.
With the ten powers fully perfected, they possess a mind free from contention and enter the limit of quiescence;

with great compassion and fearlessness like that of a lion, they are heroes of wisdom who kindle the bright lamp of the True Dharma. Their every merit is beyond praise, inconceivable even to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Having attained the wisdom of the Dharmadhātu, they abide in the immovable limit while yet being able to plant seeds in accordance with worldly convention.
They extensively expound the various teachings while abiding in the signless; they skillfully enter into the characteristics of phenomena and attain the treasury of self-nature purity.
Born into the pure family of the Tathāgatas, they skillfully open various distinct Dharma-gates and, through wisdom, realize that all things are non-existent.
Knowing the proper time, they constantly practice the gift of Dharma to awaken all beings; such are called the wise who universally gather in and sustain all sentient beings.

Having purified [themselves] through the wisdom of skillful means, they manifest the attainment of the Buddha-way while constantly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva without cessation or exhaustion.
They enter the sphere of the skillful means of all-knowledge and manifest various kinds of vast supernormal powers.
Therefore, Samantabhadra, you should now analyze and explain in detail the ten great samādhis of all bodhisattvas.
This assembly all wishes to hear it.

[Treatise] Ninth: At that time, from the passage where the Tathāgata addresses Samantabhadra Bodhisattva down to "all joyfully wish to hear," there are forty-five lines of scripture clarifying the command for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to expound the ten kinds of samādhi sections.
In the explanation of the meaning, it is divided into eight sections: 1. From "At that time, the Tathāgata...
down to "...shall attain liberation," there are four and a half lines of scripture clarifying the Buddha’s instruction for Samantabhadra to explain the ten great samādhis. 2. From "What are the ten?
down to "the Great Unobstructed Wheel Samādhi," there are six lines of scripture clarifying what the Tathāgata first [taught].
The self-proclamation of the names of the thirteen samādhis is divided into three parts.

Following these ten great samādhis, down to what is to be explained and what is currently being explained, there is one and a half lines of sūtra that clarify how these samādhis are collectively taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The reason for dividing the names of these samādhis as "self-proclaimed by the Tathāgata" is to clarify that the Tathāgata is the [source] of these samādhis.
The passage beginning with "The body causes Samantabhadra to explain the function of samādhi" clarifies that Samantabhadra is the functional application (*yòng*) of this samādhi;

it clarifies that within the stage of the Buddha-fruit, both essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*) are perfected. Thus, in terms of essence, he is called the Buddha, while in terms of function, he is Samantabhadra.
In this stage, essence and function are unified and operate with sovereign mastery. 4. From "If all bodhisattvas... down to "...is also named."
Regarding the mastery over all dharmas (*sarvadharma-vaśitā*), there are four and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the Buddha’s praise:
if one hears this samādhi and joyfully practices it, this is called attaining the stage of mastery over the Buddhas.

From the passage beginning with "this bodhisattva" down to "universally understanding all that the Buddhas have spoken," there are nine and a half lines of sūtra that clarify that those who cultivate and study this samādhi attain [mastery].
Section Six: The Skillful Turning of the Buddha’s Dharma Wheel through Non-attachment to All Phenomena and Sovereignty.

This concludes the section on the characteristics of the dharmas of all bodhisattvas. From here down to the section on Adorning and Purifying All Worlds, there are five lines and a half of scripture explaining how the Buddha praises the cultivation of these thirteen samādhis and how one can enter ten kinds of dharma-gates. Section Seven: If a bodhi... [text continues]

After the Bodhisattva had entered this samādhi, there are twelve and a half lines of sūtra from the passage "down to manifesting various kinds of great supernatural powers" which clarify the Buddha’s praise:

that if one enters this samādhi, one attains the utility of great skillful means (*mahopāyakauśalya*) to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood without abandoning the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices. This is divided into eight sections; therefore, from "henceforth" down to "all together vow."

I have heard that there is a passage of one line and a half in the sutra which clarifies how the Tathāgata exhorted Samantabhadra to explain this thirteenth chapter on the "Mastery of the Merits and Functions of Samādhi. The words and meanings therein are as clear as the sutra itself.

Following this "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," the intent of the eleven subsequent chapters of the sutra is to demonstrate how the supramundane wisdom of great compassion attained within the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is actualized in the world.
It is through the perfection and mastery of the wisdom of great compassion that one achieves the fulfillment of the practices of Samantabhadra;

by means of supramundane compassion and wisdom, one abides in the state of Buddhahood, while the wisdom and compassion of worldly differentiation constitute the conduct of Samantabhadra and the path of the Bodhisattva.
This continues until the conclusion of the two verses at the end of the "Chapter on Manifestation."
Tenth: From "At that time" below, there are ten sections of scripture that correctly explain the functional efficacy of the ten kinds of samādhis;
their textual arrangement is listed as follows.
[Sūtra]: At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, receiving the intent of the Tathāgata, surveyed the assembly of bodhisattvas such as Universal Eye and others...
He addressed him, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Samādhi of Universal Radiance for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses ten kinds of inexhaustible dharmas. What are these ten? They are: the inexhaustibility of the wisdom of the appearance of all Buddhas;
the inexhaustibility of the wisdom of the transformation of sentient beings; the inexhaustibility of the wisdom of worlds being like reflections; and the [inexhaustibility of] the profound..."

O Son of the Buddha, you possess inexhaustible wisdom in entering the dharma-realm; inexhaustible wisdom in skillfully gathering all bodhisattvas; inexhaustible wisdom in the non-retrogression of bodhisattvas;
inexhaustible wisdom in skillfully contemplating the meaning of all dharmas; inexhaustible wisdom in the power of the mind that skillfully maintains [the teachings];
inexhaustible wisdom in abiding in the vast mind of enlightenment; and inexhaustible wisdom in the power of the vow for omniscience regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
These are called the ten inexhaustible dharmas of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to ten kinds of boundless minds.
What are the ten? They are: giving rise to the boundless mind to deliver and liberate all sentient beings;
giving rise to the boundless mind to serve all Buddhas; giving rise to the boundless mind to make offerings to all Buddhas...
The boundless mind that resolves to universally behold all Buddhas; the boundless mind that resolves to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas without forgetting them;
the boundless mind that resolves to manifest the immeasurable spiritual transformations of all Buddhas;
the boundless mind that resolves never to abandon any bodhisattva practice in order to attain the powers of a Buddha; and the boundless mind that resolves to universally enter into all-knowledge.
The boundless mind that resolves to enter the inconceivable, vast realm of the Buddhas by proclaiming all Buddha-dharmas within subtle spheres;
the boundless mind that resolves to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas by giving rise to profound aspiration for the eloquence of the Buddhas;
and the boundless mind that resolves to manifest various sovereign bodies and enter the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas.
"O sons of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses ten kinds of wisdom regarding the distinctions of entering samādhi with an infinite mind.
What are these ten? They are as follows: entering meditative concentration in the east and arising in the west; entering meditative concentration in the west and arising in the east;

entering meditative concentration in the south and arising in the north; entering meditative concentration in the north and arising in the south; and entering meditative concentration in the northeast [and arising in the southwest]."
Entering meditative absorption in the southwest and arising in the southwest; entering meditative absorption in the northeast and arising in the northwest;

entering meditative absorption in the southeast and arising in the southeast; entering meditative absorption in the northwest and arising below; entering meditative absorption above and arising above;
entering meditative absorption below and arising [above]—these, O Son of the Buddha, are the ten [powers] of this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
What are the ten kinds of skillful wisdom for entering the great samādhis? O Sons of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva takes the trichiliocosm as a single lotus flower and manifests his body so as to pervade this lotus,
sitting cross-legged upon it, within that body he further manifests a trichiliocosm containing ten billion sets of four continents.

In each of the four continents (*cāturmahādvīpaka*), he manifests ten billion bodies; each body enters ten billion times ten billion triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
Within those worlds, in each of the four continents, he manifests ten billion times ten billion bodhisattvas practicing the path.
Each of these bodhisattvas’ practices gives rise to ten billion times ten billion resolute understandings (*niścayajñāna*); each resolute understanding...

He causes ten billion times ten billion faculties to be perfected, such that each individual faculty accomplishes the non-retrogressive karma of the Dharma of ten billion times ten billion Bodhisattvas.
Yet, the bodies he manifests are neither one nor many; whether entering or emerging from meditative concentration, there is no confusion whatsoever.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the Asura King Rāhu, whose original body is seven hundred yojanas long, yet his manifested form is... [longer].
Extending sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* out of the great ocean, his body emerges to stand exactly level with Mount Sumeru.
Son of the Buddha, although that Asura King transforms his body to a length of sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas*, he does not destroy the characteristics of his original form;
all his aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) remain entirely as they were, and his mind remains undisturbed.

Without confusion, they do not conceive the thought that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is anything other than themselves, nor do they perceive their own essential body as being other than themselves.
Their original bodies of birth constantly experience all manner of bliss, while their transformation bodies perpetually manifest various sovereign supernatural powers and majestic might.
O Son of the Buddha, even the Asura Kings—who possess greed, hatred, and delusion, and are fully endowed with pride—are still able to manifest such transformations.
How much more so for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who can deeply penetrate that mental phenomena are like illusions,
that all worlds are entirely like dreams, that the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is like reflected images, that all worlds are like transformations,
and that all speech and sounds are like echoes; seeing the dharmas as they truly are by means of the dharmas as they truly are.
Yet, for his own person, he knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure; he thoroughly understands that body and mind have no substantial reality;
his body dwells universally in immeasurable realms; and by means of the vast radiance of the Buddha’s wisdom, he purely cultivates all practices of enlightenment.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, he transcends the world and goes far beyond it.
Free from the world, they cannot be deluded or eclipsed by it.

Son of the Buddha, it is just as when a bhikṣu observes his own internal body and dwells in the contemplation of impurity, clearly seeing that the body is entirely impure; so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
dwelling in this samādhi, he observes the dharma-body and sees all worlds universally entering into his own body, within which [he abides].
Clearly seeing all worlds and worldly dharmas, yet being entirely unattached to those worlds and worldly dharmas—
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the first skillful wisdom of the Great Samādhi of Universal Radiance of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

[Treatise] Regarding the first, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-samādhi*), there are four sections: 1. Explaining the name of the samādhi; 2. Clarifying the essence and function of the samādhi;
3. Presenting the sphere of the samādhi; 4. Explaining the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the explanation of the name:
why is it called the "Samādhi of Universal Radiance"? *Sam* means "correct" (*samyak*), and *mā* means...

In samādhi, when the consciousness-mind does not manifest, it is called "obscuration"; when correct wisdom is all-pervasive, it is called "universal illumination"; when delusion is shattered and confusion eliminated, it is called "light";
and because there is nothing the Dharma does not penetrate, it is called "clarity. Regarding the essence and function of these two types of clarity within samādhi:
the clarity of this samādhi takes the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya as its essence, while the ten kinds of [non-conceptual]... [are its function].
With the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) as its function, for this reason the Buddha himself spoke of the name of the samādhi, and Samantabhadra spoke of the function of the samādhi.
Regarding the three types of knowledge that illustrate the sphere of the samādhi:
within these first three samādhis, the sphere is briefly illustrated by taking the trichiliocosm as a single lotus flower, and manifesting one's body so as to pervade this lotus.
Upon the flower, he sat in the full lotus posture; within his body, there further appeared a trichiliocosm, wherein were ten billion sets of four continents.
In each set of four continents, there appeared ten billion bodies, and each body entered ten billion, ten billion trichiliocosms. Within those worlds, in each set of four continents...
Throughout the world, there appear ten billion upon ten billion bodhisattvas practicing their cultivation;
each bodhisattva’s practice gives rise to ten billion upon ten billion resolute understandings, causing ten billion upon ten billion root-natures to become perfected.
Each root-nature accomplishes ten billion upon ten billion non-retrogressive karmas of the bodhisattva-dharma; yet the bodies they manifest are neither one nor many.
Entering and emerging from meditative concentration without any confusion—in this manner, each subsequent stage increases twofold in breadth, as fully described in the sutras.
This is the realm of the first three samādhis; the intent is to clarify that body and land interpenetrate one another in layers upon layers, pervading everywhere in vastness and infinity.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text, I shall briefly cite it here.
1. Regarding the ten meanings: first, the meaning of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva expounding this samādhi by receiving the Tathāgata’s mandate, rather than through his own power;
second, the repeated mention of the name of the samādhi; third, the mention of the bodhisattva’s ten kinds of inexhaustible wisdom;
fourth, the clarification that such a bodhisattva is able to give rise to ten kinds of boundless minds; fifth, the clarification that this bodhisattva possesses [these qualities].
10. Entering the Ten Kinds of Samādhi; 6. Clarifying the Skillful Wisdom of Entering the Ten Kinds of Samādhi; 7.
Raising the Analogy of Rāhu, King of the Asuras, Manifesting a Transformation Body Without Abandoning His Original Form;
8. Clarifying that Bodhisattvas Profoundly Penetrate the Mind-Dharma as Being Like an Illusion; 9. Clarifying that a Bhikṣu Contemplates the Impurity of the Internal Body Without Destruction.
The body remains as it was before; this is the metaphor for the ten enlightenments.
When a Bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, they observe the Dharma-body and perceive all worlds and worldly phenomena universally entering into that body.

As practiced above, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance takes the fundamental wisdom of observing the Dharma-body as its essence and the ten inexhaustible wisdoms as its function, thereby giving rise to the ten [powers].

Taking the boundless mind as the practice to be cultivated, one attains the power of mastery over the similarities and differences of samādhis through the ten kinds of wisdom that enter into the distinctions of samādhi; by means of the ten kinds of skillful wisdom that enter into samādhi,
one causes the body of samādhi to manifest within a single or multiple Buddha-fields and sentient-being fields, never abandoning one's own current body while constantly remaining as such.
Therefore, once again within his own body, he manifests immeasurable bodies to deliver sentient beings and to make offerings to all Buddhas, as stated in the subsequent text:
"Abiding in this samādhi, he contemplates the Dharma-body and sees all worlds universally entering into his body;
therein he clearly perceives all worlds and all worldly phenomena within all worlds and all worldly phenomena."
All are without attachment because the nature of the Dharma-body itself has no internal, external, large, small, middle, or peripheral dimensions;
because the Dharma is seen as such; and because the Dharma is thus without attachment.

This is because that which appears from the signless realm of the Dharma-body—both the world and worldly phenomena—is of the nature of shadows and illusions. Therefore, regarding the world and worldly...
Because all dharmas are the Dharma-body, of a single flavor, and without dual characteristics, all retributive objects are like reflections, layered upon one another without obstruction.

This is like Rāhu, the king of the asuras; "Rāhu" is interpreted as "clouding" (hūn-yún) because his brilliance can eclipse the light of the sun, causing distress to the world. "Asura" means "no heaven" (wú tiān), for they are not gods.
Because it is a sublime play, the transformative activities therein are as clearly explained in the Sūtra itself.
[Sūtra]: "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of Sublime Radiance?
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to enter into as many great trichiliocosms as there are atoms in a great trichiliocosm."
In each and every world-system, he manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm;
from each body, he emits rays of light as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm; from each ray of light, he manifests colors as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm;
and each color illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm.
In each and every world-system, they discipline as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm;
these bodhisattvas fully know the various differences among all such worlds, namely:

the defilement of worlds, the purity of worlds, the causes of worlds, the establishment of worlds, the common abodes of worlds, the radiance and color of worlds, and the coming and going within worlds.
In this way, all these bodhisattvas fully know the bodhisattvas and enter all these worlds;
yet they also all enter the bodies of the bodhisattvas, and nevertheless, the various worlds do not become confused, nor are the various phenomena destroyed or extinguished.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising sun circling Mount Sumeru and illuminating the mountains of the seven treasures; those mountains of the seven treasures and their jewels...
Throughout the mountain ranges, light and shadow appear with distinct clarity;

every solar reflection upon the precious mountains is manifested within the shadows of the mountain ranges, and likewise, every solar reflection within the shadows of the seven mountain ranges is fully manifested within the shadows upon the mountains.
In this manner, they are successively reflected one upon another. Some say that the solar reflections emerge from the seven precious mountains, while others say...
The shadows of the sun appear among the seven mountains; some say the shadows enter the seven precious mountains, while others say they enter the intervals between the seven mountains.
Yet these solar shadows reflect one another without limit; their essential nature is neither existent nor non-existent.
They do not abide within the mountains, yet they do not depart from them; they do not abide within the waters, yet they do not depart from them. Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in this wondrous, luminous, and vast samādhi, he does not destroy the established characteristics of worlds nor extinguish the intrinsic nature of all worldly phenomena; he does not abide within worlds, nor does he abide outside of worlds.
He makes no conceptual distinctions regarding any worlds, yet he contemplates them without destroying their characteristics.

All phenomena have a single characteristic, which is the absence of characteristics; they do not destroy the intrinsic nature of phenomena, but abide in the nature of suchness, never departing from it.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a master illusionist who, being well-versed in the arts of illusion, stands at a crossroads and performs various illusory feats:
within a single day, or even in a brief moment, he may manifest a full day, or manifest a night, or again manifest...
For seven days and nights, half a month, one month, one year, or a hundred years— according to his desire— he is able to manifest cities, towns, villages,
springs, streams, rivers, oceans, suns, moons, clouds, rain, palaces, mansions, and all such things, none of which are not fully complete;
yet he does not allow these manifestations to persist for years so as to damage their fundamental nature, nor does he do so for even a single day.

Just as the illusory manifestations of days, months, and years do not destroy the clear appearance of the original time, nor does the original time perish because it is fundamentally extremely brief, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
having entered this wondrous, luminous, and vast samādhi, they manifest incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds within a single world; yet each of those incalculable worlds—
All are fully endowed with the great oceans, mountains, cities, towns, villages, gardens, groves, houses,

and dwellings of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, as well as the various celestial palaces of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, all adorned in every way.
Regarding the small chiliocosms, the medium chiliocosms, and the great trichiliocosms; the karmic actions and their retributions; death here and birth there;

all the temporal cycles within the world—moments, days and nights, half-months, months, years, centuries, eons of formation, eons of destruction, defiled lands, pure lands, vast lands, and narrow lands—and all that exists therein...

The Buddha has appeared in the world; his buddha-field is pure, and he is surrounded on all sides by an assembly of bodhisattvas who possess sovereign supernormal powers and transform sentient beings.
In every direction and location throughout those lands, immeasurable multitudes of people completely fill them.
Sentient beings of diverse forms and various destinies—immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable—come, go, and abide therein in the past, future, and present.
The manifestation of such things as the production of immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous jewels from the power of pure karma—all these are fully displayed within a single world-system.
Bodhisattvas here see them all clearly; they enter them universally, observe them universally, contemplate them universally, and comprehend them universally.
Through inexhaustible wisdom, they know them all as they truly are, yet they do not allow this one world-system to be destroyed by the multiplicity of those worlds.
The realms do not perish because this world is one; why? Because the Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*).

This is called "entering the dharma of no life-force and no activity. As for the one who "abides in the dharma of non-self," it is because the Bodhisattva diligently practices the dharma of non-contention (*araṇa-dharma*) within all worlds. Thus is the Bodhisattva... [like]...
Because they truly see that all bodies arise from conditions, they are called those who abide in the dharma of no sentient beings (*niḥsattva*).
Because Bodhisattvas know that all phenomena of arising and ceasing are produced from causes, they are called those who abide in the dharma of no person (*niḥpudgala*).
Because Bodhisattvas know that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is equal, they are called those who abide in the absence of mind-born beings (*manomaya*) and *mānava*.

Regarding the "Dharma of Abiding": because the Bodhisattva knows that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent, this is called "abiding in the dharma of quiescence. Regarding the "Dharma of Non-conceptualization":
because the Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas have a single characteristic, this is called "abiding in the dharma of non-conceptualization. Regarding the "Dharma of the Inconceivable":
because the Bodhisattva knows that the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is devoid of any various distinctions among dharmas, this is called "abiding in the inconceivable dharma. The Bodhisattva...
Because the Bodhisattva diligently cultivates all skillful means to thoroughly subdue sentient beings, he is called one who dwells in the Dharma of Great Compassion.
O Son of the Buddha, in this way, the Bodhisattva is able to cause incalculable worlds to enter into a single world;
he knows the various distinctions among countless sentient beings, sees countless Bodhisattvas each setting forth on their respective paths, and contemplates countless Buddhas.
In every place where those Tathāgatas appear and proclaim the Dharma, those Bodhisattvas are able to receive it all;
they also see themselves practicing therein. Yet, without leaving this place, they see themselves there, and without leaving that place, they see themselves here.
There is no distinction between that body and this body, for they have entered the Dharma-realm; thus, they are constantly diligent.
Observing without rest and never abandoning wisdom because it is non-retrogressive, it is like a master illusionist who,
while performing various illusions in a certain place, does not destroy the original ground by means of the illusory ground,
nor does he destroy the original day by means of the illusory day. In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise manifests lands where there are no lands.
In what appears as a land, there is no land; in what appears as sentient beings, there are no sentient beings; in what appears as non-sentient beings, there are sentient beings;
in the formless, form appears; and in form, the formless appears. From the beginning there is no confusion, and in the end there is no confusion.
From the outset, the Bodhisattva understands that all worldly phenomena are likewise identical to illusions and transformations, and thus knows that dharmas are illusory.
Therefore, one knows that wisdom is illusory; because one knows that wisdom is illusory, one knows that karma is illusory.
Having realized that both wisdom and karma are illusory, one gives rise to illusory wisdom and contemplates all karma as being like a worldly illusion.
It does not manifest its illusions outside of space, nor does it have a location outside of those illusions. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: they do not [seek] outside of empty space.
They enter into the world, yet they do not enter into anything outside the world; they enter into empty space. Why?
Because there is no distinction between empty space and the world. Abiding in the world, they also abide in empty space.
Within a single moment of thought, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to perceive and cultivate all the various distinct and wondrously adorned activities of the world within that empty space.
They are fully able to comprehend the formation and destruction of countless worlds, and they know the sequential succession of all kalpas;
they can manifest countless kalpas within a single thought-moment without causing that single thought-moment to become vast.
These Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas attain inconceivable liberation and illusory wisdom, reaching the further shore and dwelling at the limit of illusion, entering the illusion of the world.
He repeatedly contemplates that all phenomena are entirely like illusions and does not contradict the illusory world;
exhausting his illusory wisdom, he understands that the three periods of time are no different from an illusion. Having decisively attained thorough penetration, his mind has no boundaries.
Just as the Tathāgatas dwell in illusory wisdom with an equanimous mind, so too do the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know all worlds to be entirely...
Like an illusion, it is entirely unattached in all places and free from the notion of "mine.
Just as a magician who performs various illusory feats does not dwell together with those illusions, yet is not deluded by them, so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
knowing all phenomena, he reaches the other shore and his mind does not conceive of a self that can act.
Entering into phenomena and yet not being confused regarding phenomena— this is the second sublime light,
the great samādhi of skillful wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

[Treatise] Regarding the second, the Samādhi of Sublime Radiance (*prabhāsvara-samādhi*): within this section, there are four points. First, the explanation of the name of the samādhi is as previously stated.
Second, the essence and function of the samādhi will be clarified below. Third, the realm of the samādhi of triple illumination.
Fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. First, regarding the explanation of the name: it is for the purpose of illuminating the essence of the Dharma-body’s principle and wisdom.

First, the purity by which it manifests wondrous light establishes its name; second, the explanation of the essence and function of this samādhi clarifies that this samādhi takes fundamental wisdom as its essence and illusory wisdom as its function;

third, the clarification of the realm of this samādhi refers to entering into as many three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems as there are atoms within a three-thousandfold great thousand-world system.
Within each and every world-system, he further manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm;
furthermore, from each individual body, he emits rays of light as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm, as described in detail in the sutra.
Moreover, within the bodies of these bodhisattvas, they can manifest all the lands of both the noble ones and ordinary beings, mutually illuminating one another in layers of depth.
The mutual entry of these characteristics and so forth constitute the sphere of this samādhi, as fully described in the sūtra.

Regarding the word-by-word commentary, it is further divided into two parts: first, a general outline of the sūtra’s meaning; second, the word-by-word explanation. Regarding the general outline of the sūtra’s meaning:
within this section, the text is divided into ten subsections. The first is the single line beginning with "O Son of the Buddha... [and so on].
This section of the sutra, in which Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addresses the assembly and reiterates the name of the samādhi, is divided into two parts.

From the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... down to "...various phenomena are neither destroyed nor extinguished," there are eleven lines of scripture that clarify entering the realm of samādhi.
Within this, the vastness and narrowness of bodies and lands are illuminated and manifested, mutually interpenetrating like layered reflections of light and shadow.

The Section on Non-confusion has three parts. "O Sons of the Buddha, it is as if the sun has risen" down to "nor does it ever depart from the water" consists of eight lines of scripture that clarify how the seven-jeweled mountains, the great ocean waters, and the spaces between the mountains are manifested through the light of the sun, with these solar reflections mutually illuminating one another so that the images are layered upon layers without end. This is the Section on the Simile of Light and Reflection.
Fourth, the Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, from the lowest level down to those who never abandon [the practice], have five kinds of conduct explained in the sutras.
It clarifies that such Bodhisattvas abide in the Samādhi of Wondrous Light and Vastness; they do not destroy worldly appearances, nor do they destroy true nature.
They do not dwell in either, and they do not destroy either. This is divided into five sections for the Buddha-sons. For example, it is like a master illusionist who has already...

From the passage below stating that "down to this very day it has not perished," there are seven lines of sutra text clarifying how a magician creates illusions of days, months, years, and varying durations of time without destroying the actual day; this is divided into six sections.
From the passage below "the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas" down to "without destroying those many worlds," there are seventeen lines of sutra text clarifying that the Bodhisattva enters this Sublime Light.
The Great Samādhi that enables multiple worlds to enter one another without mutual obstruction is divided into seven parts.

Why is this? From the passage below, ending with "this is called abiding in the dharma of great compassion," there are eleven lines of scripture clarifying that when a bodhisattva abides in the dharma of non-self, there is no obstruction regarding the bodies and minds within the spheres of self and others among all phenomena.

Regarding the section on "Obstruction," from the passage beginning with "O Son of the Buddha" down to "because there is no regression," six lines and a half of scripture clarify that this Bodhisattva enters a single world-system through incalculable world-systems;
skillfully knows the distinctions among countless sentient beings and the distinctions in the Bodhisattva’s own modes of entry;
and perceives the Buddhas appearing everywhere, manifesting their own bodies within each of those [world-systems].

Regarding the various practices cultivated by a single Buddha, although the bodies [of Buddhas] have no coming or going between one another, they can manifest identity and difference with sovereign mastery, divided into nine parts.

From the passage beginning "Just as a magician... down to the end where it says "not confused," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify the analogy of the magician for the Bodhisattva.
This section on the "Metaphor of Illusion Produced by Real Wisdom" is divided into ten parts, wherein the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands.

"Because all-knowledge is an illusion," and so forth, down to the end of the twenty and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the section on attaining mastery over the gate of the illusion of wisdom by entering this wondrous *Mahā-ābhāsvara-samādhi*. Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text:

this section shows that the nature of fundamental, unconditioned wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) is inherently all-pervasive, and through the wisdom that manifests like a reflection, it reveals all phenomena.
The objects of perception interpenetrate self and other, and unity and multiplicity are sovereign through fundamental wisdom;
thus, many enter into one like reflections of wisdom, while one manifests as many objects, each with distinct bodily forms and characteristics.
That which serves as the cause for the world is the cultivation of the present life serving as the cause for future lives; that which establishes the world clarifies the various individual worlds.
Because they establish the laws [of nature], sentient beings dwell together in the world. Within a single world, there are many types of sentient beings who dwell together.
Regarding the luminous world, some sentient beings dwell within the light of the Buddha;
thus, the sun, moon, and stars, as well as kings and other beings among humanity, are transformations produced by their collective karma, their refined radiance ascending upward.
Furthermore, there are devas who dwell therein and those who come and go; as they move through the air, this Bodhisattva fully knows them all.
Regarding the "eight classes of spirits," their names have already been explained in the First Assembly. As for the term *pudgala* (person):
it clarifies that one who repeatedly takes up [existence] (*saṃskāra*) pursues evil dharmas and moves toward the fruit of suffering. This is the dharma of the *maṇava* (young brahmin).
The method for instructing the youth [Śāriputra] is fully contained within the sutra itself.
[Sutra]: "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of Supernatural Power that Proceeds Sequentially and Universally to All Buddha-lands?
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva passes beyond countless worlds to the east, and furthermore..."
Passing through as many worlds as there are atoms in those worlds, he enters this samādhi within all those worlds—entering it for a single kṣaṇa, or for a muhūrta, or in continuous succession;
entering it during the first watch of the day, or the middle watch of the day, or the last watch of the day; or entering it during the first watch of the night, or the middle watch of the night.
They may enter at that time, or during the latter part of the night; they may enter for one day,
or five days, or half a month, or one month, or one year, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, or ten million years,
or a hundred thousand times ten million years, or a hundred thousand nayutas of ten million years.
They may enter for one eon, or enter for a hundred eons, or enter for a hundred thousand eons,
or enter for a hundred thousand nayuta koṭis of eons, or enter for incalculable eons, or enter for immeasurable eons, or enter for boundless eons,
or enter for incomparable eons, or enter for uncountable eons, or enter for ineffable eons, or enter for inconceivable eons.
Whether entering for immeasurable eons, unspeakable eons, or unspeakably-unspeakable eons—
whether long or short, whether phenomena or time— and despite these various differences, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to a discriminating mind toward them;
they are without attachment, do not create duality, do not create non-duality, do not create universality, and do not create particularity, even while remaining detached.

By means of this discernment and through the skillful application of supernatural powers, he arises from samādhi regarding all phenomena without forgetting or losing them, reaching the ultimate state.
It is like the sun-son deity who travels around, illuminating without ceasing day or night:
the rising of the sun is called day, and its setting is called night; yet day does not arise, nor does night perish. So it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Countless worlds enter the samādhi of supernormal powers; having entered this samādhi, they clearly perceive those countless worlds, and it is likewise for all such realms.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s third sequential supernormal power of great samādhi and skillful wisdom, which universally visits all Buddha-lands.
[Treatise] Regarding the third [topic], the Samādhi of Supernatural Power for Traveling Universally to All Buddha-lands, there are three sections within this passage:
first, explaining the name of the samādhi; second, explaining the essence and function of the samādhi; and third, explaining the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the name: why is it called "Supernatural Power for Traveling Universally to All Buddha-lands"?

The penetration of samādhi constitutes this samādhi: because the rational nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) is all-pervasive, the essence of the functional wisdom (*jñāna-prayoga-svabhāva*) is all-pervasive;
because the essence of the functional wisdom is all-pervasive, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are all-pervasive.

This clarifies that, regarding the all-pervasiveness of the essence of the rational wisdom, the movement and stillness of responding to objects through illusion-like wisdom are eternally without coming, based upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Going to and returning from one another, extending and contracting, it is by these that the name is established; thus it is called the "Samādhi of Supernatural Power for Traveling Universally to All Buddha-lands.

Second, regarding the essence and function of this samādhi: the essence of this samādhi is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), and its function is the arising of illusion-like wisdom (*māyopama-jñāna*) based upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
This illusion-like wisdom is like an echo in an empty valley responding to external objects.
Because the perfected sound (*niṣpanna-śabda*) has no intrinsic nature of its own, these two types of wisdom take the Dharma as their essence;
they possess only virtuous functions and lack any objective support. Since the minds of all sentient beings are fundamentally thus, wisdom itself lacks self-nature and cannot cognize itself;
it follows objects and thereby becomes deluded. Therefore, one must illuminate this delusion by means of the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

The explanation based on the fundamental [text] is as follows: regarding the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is established as the essence of *śamatha*; regarding the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is established as the essence and function of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This clarifies that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can give rise to insight (*vipaśyanā*), and that contemplation can initiate wisdom.

Regarding the third section, the word-by-word commentary, there are two points as previously stated. As for the long division of the sutra’s meaning within this passage, it is divided into four sections: first, "O Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*).
From here down to the "Samādhi of Supernatural Powers," there is one and a half lines of sūtra that clarify Samantabhadra’s reiteration of the name of this samādhi.

This is divided into two parts: first, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "this bodhisattva," there are sixteen and a half lines of sūtra clarifying the entry into samādhi, wherein [the bodhisattva] possesses mastery over the prolongation and contraction [of time], is free from discrimination, and does not forget any phenomena.

The section on "Loss" (the third) consists of three and a half lines of scripture, which clarifies the analogy of the Sun Deity (Sūryadevaputra) shining over the four continents without arising or ceasing throughout day and night; this constitutes the fourth division.

From the words "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, up to "skillful wisdom," there is one and a half lines of scripture that clarifies the comprehensive summary of all that has been mentioned above.
The section on the names of these samādhis has been concluded above; the meaning of the text is self-evident and need not be further explained.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s samādhi of the practice of the pure profound mind?

O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the number of the bodies of all Buddhas to be equal to the number of sentient beings, and beholds immeasurable Buddhas exceeding [the sands of] the Ganges."
With as many atoms as there are in world-systems of the *saṃkhyeya* [countless],
he made offerings to each and every one of those Tathāgatas with all kinds of exquisite fragrances, with all kinds of exquisite flowers,
and with all kinds of canopies as vast as *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields— offerings that surpass all worlds.
They made offerings with every kind of most excellent and sublime ornament throughout the realms; they made offerings by scattering all manner of various jewels;
they made offerings by adorning the walking paths with every variety of ornamental implement;
they made offerings with all the countless, most excellent treasuries of maṇi-jewels, which had flowed forth through the Buddha’s spiritual power.
They offer as gifts to all Buddha-fields various supreme and wondrous articles of worship that surpass the finest flavors and foods of the heavens;
by means of their supernormal powers, they universally gather these to present as offerings.

At the presence of each and every Tathāgata, they pay homage with reverence and respect, prostrating themselves with their heads to the ground and casting their entire bodies upon the earth to inquire about the Buddha-Dharma.
They praise the equality of the Buddhas, extol the vast merits of all Buddhas, and enter into the great compassion entered by all Buddhas.
Attaining the unimpeded power of the equality of the Buddhas, they diligently seek the sublime Dharma from all Buddhas in a single thought-moment;
yet, regarding such phenomena as the appearance of Buddhas in the world or their entry into parinirvāṇa, they find nothing at all to be apprehended.

Just as a distracted mind cognizes its object, yet when the mind arises one does not know from what object it arises, and when the mind ceases one does not know at what object it ceases—so too it is with this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; he never discriminates between the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world and the marks of his parinirvāṇa.
Son of the Buddha, it is like a mirage in midday: it does not arise from clouds, nor does it arise from a pond.
It arises neither on land nor in water; it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither good nor evil, neither clear nor turbid.
It is unfit for drinking or rinsing, yet cannot be defiled. It has no substance, yet is not without substance; it has no taste, yet is not without taste.
Through the power of causes and conditions, it manifests the appearance of water, perceived by consciousness; from afar it resembles water, and thus the notion of water arises.
If one conceives of approaching it, the original thought ceases of its own accord; this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this.
One cannot perceive the appearance of a Tathāgata arising in the world, nor the marks of his parinirvāṇa.

Whether Buddhas possess marks or are markless, these are all merely the conceptual discriminations of the mind of ideation. Son of the Buddha, this samādhi is called "The Practice of the Pure Profound Mind."

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has entered this samādhi and emerged from it, they do not lose [what was perceived]. It is, for example, like a person who awakens from sleep and remembers the events of a dream;
although the objects of the dream do not exist at the time of waking, they are able to recollect them and their mind does not forget.
In the same way, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters this samādhi, they see the Buddhas and hear [the Dharma].
Arising from meditative concentration, they maintain the Dharma without forgetting it;

by means of this Dharma, they enlighten all assemblies in the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and adorn all Buddha-lands. They fully comprehend infinite meanings and purposes, and all dharma-gates are likewise purified.
Kindling the great torch of wisdom, they perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas, endowed with fearlessness and eloquence.
To exhaustively reveal and expound the profound treasury of the Dharma constitutes the fourth skillful wisdom of the great samādhi of the pure deep mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Regarding the fourth, the Samādhi of the Practice of the Pure Deep Mind, there are three sections as previously explained.
As for the explanation of the name of this samādhi: why is it called the "Samādhi of the Practice of the Pure Deep Mind"?
It is because the Bodhisattva, having already cultivated the wisdom of emptiness and signlessness, has attained a body that conforms to the principle of wisdom—a body that is all-pervasive.

The body of prior primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), which is all-pervasive, is honored through the application of skillful means and a profound mind with ten types of offerings—such as incense, flowers, and canopies—made toward all Buddhas as they appear.
Because the *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya* are unconditioned and free from conceptualization, this is how their name is established. Second, the explanation of the essence and function of *samādhi*:
Taking the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* as its essence, it gives rise to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to perform the ten kinds of offerings as numerous as sentient beings;
this constitutes its function. Regarding the three points following the textual exegesis, the two meanings are as previously stated.
As for the long sectioning of the sutra’s intent within this passage, it is divided into four sections: first, the one line of sutra beginning with "O Son of the Buddha... [and so forth].
The section clarifying Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s reiteration of the name of the samādhi:

"O Sons of the Buddha, from this bodhisattva downward, until the point where he does not discriminate between the appearance of Tathāgatas in the world and their nirvāṇa," consists of eighteen lines and a half of sūtra text.

This explains the offering of ten things—such as incense, flowers, and canopies—to Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings. This section is divided into three parts concerning the Sons of the Buddha.

From "Just as the mirage in the midday sun" down to "all are what is discriminated by the mind's perceptions," there are seven lines of sutra text that clarify the analogy of the midday mirage to illustrate how Bodhisattvas know the appearance and parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
From "These four sons of the Buddha, having attained this samādhi" down to "skillful wisdom," there are ten lines of sutra text that clarify entering [the state of] the three [bodies].
Regarding the section on "forgetting like a dream yet not forgetting what was seen in the realm [of experience], and providing excellent explanations for others," this is divided into two parts.
As for the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the meaning is as the text itself.

However, for those who enter contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), they must first properly attain the appropriate state by entering the concentration of non-thought and no-mind (*acittaka-samādhi*), realizing the principle of the *dharmakāya* and conforming to the nature of space; only then may one proceed.

Fundamental wisdom arises through skillful means, giving rise to wisdom that initiates offerings; the mind must attain mastery in its functioning so that it acts in accordance with the principle of reality (*tattva*).
If one merely cultivates the dharma-body of emptiness and signlessness, one will be unable to give rise to the function of wisdom.
If one only single-mindedly gives rise to conceptualizations and fails to perceive the signless dharma-body, then this is purely conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
The sequential application of these ten concentrations is fully elucidated within each respective scriptural passage.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of the Past?
O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to know the appearance of the Buddhas of the past, namely, the succession of kalpas."
The sequence of all lands within the intermediate [realms], the sequence of kalpas within the sequence of lands, the sequence of the appearance of Buddhas within the sequence of kalpas,
the sequence of the teaching of the Dharma within the sequence of the appearance of Buddhas, the sequence of various inclinations of mind within the sequence of the teaching of the Dharma,
the sequence of the faculties within the sequence of inclinations of mind, and the sequence of discipline within the sequence of the faculties.

Within the sequence of subduing, there is the sequence of the lifespans of all Buddhas; within the sequence of lifespans, one knows the sequence of the numerical quantities of years numbering in the hundreds of millions (*koṭi*) and trillions (*nayuta*).
O Son of the Buddha, because this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained such infinite sequential knowledge, he then knows the past Buddhas, he then knows the past lands, and he then knows the past.
Through this Dharma-gate, one knows all past kalpas; one knows all past dharmas; one knows all past minds;
one knows all past understandings; one knows all past sentient beings; one knows all past afflictions; one knows all past rituals;
and one knows all past purities. O Son of the Buddha, this samādhi is named [the Samādhi of Knowing the Past].
The Pure Treasury of the Past is able, within a single thought-moment, to enter into a hundred kalpas; it can enter into a thousand kalpas; it can enter into a hundred thousand kalpas;
it can enter into a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas; it can enter into incalculable kalpas; it can enter into immeasurable kalpas; it can enter into boundless kalpas;
it can enter into incomparable kalpas; it can enter into uncountable kalpas; it can enter into [uncountable] kalpas...
They can enter eons that are calculable, they can enter inconceivable eons, they can enter immeasurable eons, they can enter ineffable eons, and they can enter ineffably ineffable eons.

O Son of the Buddha, when those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter this samādhi, they do not extinguish the present, nor do they take the past as an object. O Son of the Buddha, from this [samādhi], those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas...
From this samādhi, one also attains, purifies, accomplishes, enters, realizes, fulfills, and maintains the ten kinds of inconceivable consecration-dharmas received from the Tathāgata.
One also understands with equal clarity the purity of the three wheels. What are these ten?
First, eloquence that does not contradict the meaning; second, inexhaustible preaching of the Dharma; third, instruction... [text fragment ends]
Fourth, his speech is without error; fifth, his eloquence is uninterrupted; sixth, his mind is free from fear;
seventh, his words are invariably truthful; eighth, he is the refuge for all sentient beings; ninth, he delivers those within the three realms; tenth, his roots of goodness are supreme;
and tenth, he is the sublime Dharma that tames and guides. Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of consecration methods. If a bodhisattva enters these three...

Emerging from that samādhi without interval, he immediately attains these ten kinds of dharmas in a single thought-moment, just as when the kalala enters the womb and consciousness takes birth in an instant.

Son of the Buddha, it is the same for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: arising from this concentration in the presence of the Tathāgata, he attains these ten dharmas in a single thought-moment. This, O Son of the Buddha, is called the [first] stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Fifth is the skillful wisdom that knows the Great Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of the Past.
[Treatise] Regarding the fifth, the knowledge of the Great Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of the Past, there are three gates as explained previously.
As for the explanation of the name of this samādhi: why is it called the "Great Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments of the Past"?
When this Bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they are able to know the kalpas and lands in which the Buddhas of the past appeared, as well as the Dharma-gates through which those Buddhas appeared;
by adorning their own mind with these, they perfect fundamental wisdom and possess discriminative wisdom, thereby attaining the name of the aforementioned samādhi and performing offerings within it.
Within this concentration, one must understand the kalpas, lands, and the appearance of the Buddhas.
Regarding the second section, the sequential dharma-gate for explaining the essence and function of samādhi:

its essence is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and its function is the wisdom that knows the distinctions of the sequence of eons and lands. The following is as in the text. Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text:

as for the "three wheels," these are supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and direct instruction (*samyag-deśanā*). These three wheels are pure; this clarifies them.

He has attained the supernormal powers of clarity, possesses excellent memory and non-forgetfulness, and skillfully expounds all dharmas like one who is in the *kalala* stage—this is translated as "thin curd"—meaning that at the initial moment of conception, it is like thin curd; the rest is self-evident from the text.
