the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan, Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Treatise on the Sūtras*, Chapter Twenty-seven on the Ten Determinations, Part Four.
[Sūtra] “O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm? “O Son of the Buddha, this—”
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the samādhi called "Sovereignty over the Dharma-Dhātu" within their own sense bases,
from the eye base up to the mind base, they naturally become able to know all worlds,
know the phenomena of all worlds, know all world-systems, know billions of nayutas of world-systems, and know the [A]... [world-systems].
In as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, one knows that in all those worlds Buddhas have appeared,
and that the assemblies of bodhisattvas completely fill them; they are radiant, pure, virtuous, and free from impurity,
adorned with vast arrays of various kinds of jewels, and therein the bodhisattvas may remain for a single kalpa.
A hundred eons, a thousand eons, ten billion eons, a hundred thousand billion nayutas of eons,
incalculable eons, immeasurable eons, boundless eons, incomparable eons, uncountable eons, ineffable eons,
inconceivable eons, unfathomable eons, unspeakable eons, unspeakably unspeakable eons, and unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
For as many eons as there are atoms, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices without ever ceasing; furthermore, throughout such immeasurable eons,
they abide in this samādhi, both entering and arising from it, perfecting worlds, taming sentient beings, thoroughly comprehending the dharma-realm,
universally knowing the three periods of time, expounding all dharmas, and manifesting various kinds of great supernormal powers.

Through skillful means that are unattached and unimpeded, because they have attained mastery over the dharma-realm, they skillfully discern the eye, skillfully discern the ear, skillfully discern the nose, skillfully discern the tongue, skillfully discern the body, and skillfully discern the mind;
thus, they skillfully discern all such various distinctions and differences to their ultimate limit. In this way, the bodhisattva possesses thorough knowledge.
Having seen this, they are able to give rise to ten trillion dhāraṇī-dharma-lights; accomplish ten trillion pure practices;
obtain ten trillion perfections of the sense faculties; attain ten trillion supernormal powers; enter ten trillion samādhis;
accomplish ten trillion spiritual powers; and cultivate and perfect ten trillion strengths.
With a thousand billion profound intentions, they exercise ten trillion powers of sustenance; they manifest ten trillion divine transformations;
they are fully endowed with ten trillion unimpeded perfections of bodhisattvas; they have accumulated ten trillion bodhisattva aids to the path;
they illuminate ten trillion bodhisattva treasuries; they expound ten trillion bodhisattva skillful means; and they elucidate ten trillion meanings.
They accomplish ten thousand koṭis of vows; they give rise to ten thousand koṭis of dedications; they purify ten thousand koṭis of bodhisattva stages;
they clarify ten thousand koṭis of Dharma gates; they reveal ten thousand koṭis of teachings; they cultivate ten thousand koṭis of expositions.
Furthermore, these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the pure sons of the Buddha, possess immeasurable further merits.
Boundless merit, incomparable merit, incalculable merit, ineffable merit, inconceivable merit,
immeasurable merit, unspeakable merit, and inexhaustible merit— O Son of the Buddha,
this bodhisattva has already perfected, accumulated, and fully realized all such merits.
Their adornments are all purified, all translucent, all embraced, all capable of being produced,
all worthy of praise, all made firm, and all fully accomplished. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi,
they are attended by as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten thousand asaṃkhyeya Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, each bearing distinct names.
Furthermore, for each and every name thus received, there are ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field,
with Buddhas each distinct from one another; as it is in the east, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir— thus,
Buddhas as numerous as atoms appear before him, manifesting the pure lands of all Buddhas and preaching the immeasurable bodies of all Buddhas.
He spoke of the inconceivable eyes of all Buddhas; he spoke of the immeasurable ears of all Buddhas; he spoke of the pure noses of all Buddhas;
he spoke of the pure tongues of all Buddhas; he spoke of the non-abiding minds of all Buddhas;

he spoke of the unsurpassed supernatural powers of the Tathāgatas, causing them to cultivate the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgatas and to attain the pure sounds of the Tathāgatas, opening [the way for them].
He demonstrates the Tathāgata’s wheel of non-retrogression; he reveals the Tathāgata’s boundless assemblies and causes them to enter the Tathāgata’s boundless secrets;
he praises all the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata and causes them to enter the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma;
he proclaims the Tathāgata’s lineage throughout the three periods of time; he manifests the Tathāgata’s immeasurable physical forms; and he expounds upon the Tathāgata’s protection.
The method of mindfulness expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma-sound of the Tathāgata;
it elucidates all Buddha-worlds, proclaims the samādhis of all Buddhas, and manifests the successive assemblies of all Buddhas.

It protects and upholds the inconceivable Dharma of all Buddhas, explaining that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and clarifying that the nature of all phenomena is without movement or change. It opens...
It reveals all unsurpassed wheels of Dharma, extols the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgatas, causes [beings] to enter all clouds of samādhis,
and enables them to know that their minds are like illusions and transformations, boundless and inexhaustible. When a son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
dwells in this Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharmadhātu, in each of the ten directions there are ten thousand asaṃkhyeyas...
In each of the names of as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field,
there are simultaneously ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields of atoms of Buddhas who protect and sustain this Bodhisattva, causing this Bodhisattva to attain a boundless body,
causing this Bodhisattva to attain an unobstructed mind, and causing this Bodhisattva to attain non-forgetfulness regarding all dharmas.
The Bodhisattva attains decisive wisdom regarding all phenomena, causing this Bodhisattva to become increasingly acute and capable of receiving and comprehending all phenomena;
causing this Bodhisattva to clearly understand all phenomena and to possess sharp faculties, becoming skilled in all dharmas of supernormal power; [causing] this Bodhisattva’s sphere of activity...
Moving unimpeded throughout the dharma-realm without ever resting, they cause this bodhisattva to attain unobstructed wisdom that is ultimately pure;
they cause this bodhisattva, by means of supernormal powers, to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood in all worlds.
O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they attain ten kinds of oceans. What are these ten? They are as follows: namely, they attain...
Because they behold the ocean of all Buddhas, they attain the ocean of sentient beings, as they are able to fully subdue them;

because they are able to fully comprehend the ocean of all dharmas through wisdom, they attain the ocean of all lands, as they travel to them all by means of non-substantial and unconditioned spiritual powers;
because all their practices are completely perfected, they attain the ocean of merit; and because they are able to expand [their influence], they attain the ocean of spiritual powers.
Because he manifests [teachings] to bring about awakening; because he thoroughly knows the various differences within the ocean of all faculties;
because he knows the ocean of all minds, understanding the infinite variety of the different mental states of all sentient beings;

because he attains the ocean of all practices, being able to fulfill them entirely through the power of his vows; because he attains the ocean of all vows, causing them all to be accomplished and eternally purified—[this is] the Buddha.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained these ten kinds of oceans, they further attain ten kinds of supreme excellence.
What are these ten? First, they are the foremost among all sentient beings;
second, they are the most distinguished among all devas; third, they possess the ultimate sovereignty among all Brahmā kings; fourth...
1. They are unstained by and unattached to all worldly realms; 2. They cannot be eclipsed by anything in any world;
3. All Māras are unable to confuse or disturb them; 4. They enter universally into all states of existence without obstruction;
5. They know that wherever they take birth, it is not substantial; 6. They attain mastery over all Buddha-dharmas. Ten.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained these ten kinds of excellence, they further attain ten kinds of powers with which they cultivate various practices within the realm of sentient beings. What are these ten?
First is the power of valor, for the sake of subduing the world; second is the power of diligence, because it never regresses.
Thus, the third is the power of non-attachment, because it is free from all defilements; the fourth is the power of tranquility, because there is no contention regarding any phenomena (*dharma*);
the fifth is the power of following and reversing, because the mind has mastery over all phenomena;
the sixth is the power of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), because one attains mastery over all meanings; and the seventh is the power of non-obstruction, because wisdom is vast and great.
The eighth is the power of fearlessness, because it is able to expound all dharmas; the ninth is the power of eloquence, because it is able to maintain all dharmas;

the tenth is the power of revelation, because wisdom is boundless. O Son of the Buddha, these ten kinds of powers are the power of vastness, the most supreme power, the power that cannot be overcome, the immeasurable power, the power of excellent accumulation, the immovable power, and the firm power.

The power of wisdom, the power of accomplishment, the power of supreme concentration, the power of purity, the power of extreme purity, the power of the Dharma-body, the power of the light of the Dharma,
the power of the lamp of the Dharma, the power of the Dharma-gates, the power of being indestructible, the power of extreme valor, the power of the Great Man,
the power of the practice of the Good Man, the power of attaining perfect enlightenment, and the power of the roots of goodness accumulated in the past— abiding in these.
The power of immeasurable roots of goodness; the power of abiding in the power of the Tathāgata; the power of mental reflection; the power of increasing the joy of bodhisattvas;

the power of giving birth to the pure faith of bodhisattvas; the power of increasing the courageous vigor of bodhisattvas; the power born of the bodhicitta; the power of the pure and profound resolve of bodhisattvas;
the power of the supreme and profound resolve of bodhisattvas; and the power of the perfuming of the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas.
The power of perfected habituation, the power of all dharmas, the power of the body of non-obstruction, the power of entering skillful means,
the power of the pure and wondrous Dharma, the power of abiding in great majesty such that no world can shake it,
and the power that no sentient being can eclipse— O Son of the Buddha, regarding these immeasurable [powers] of this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
The qualities of merit can produce, can accomplish, can bring to perfection, can illuminate, can fulfill,
can universally fulfill, can expand, can solidify, can increase, can purify, and can universally purify the limits of this bodhisattva’s merit,
the limits of wisdom, the limits of practice, the limits of the Dharma-gate, and the limits of mastery.
Regarding the limit of asceticism, the limit of accomplishment, the limit of purity, the limit of renunciation, and the limit of mastery over phenomena—there is no one capable of describing them.
These are the spheres obtained, accomplished, entered, and manifested by this bodhisattva; these are their observations, their realizations, their purifications, and their full understandings.
All the established gateways to all dharmas cannot be fully expounded even in unspeakable eons; yet, O Son of the Buddha,
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi is able to thoroughly know that which is innumerable,
immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, unspeakable, unspeakably unspeakable, and unspeakably unspeakably unspeakable.
Regarding all samādhis, the objective spheres (*viṣaya*) of each individual samādhi are immeasurable and vast.
Within those objective spheres, whether entering, arising from, or abiding in them, there are their respective characteristics,
manifestations, spheres of activity, outflows, intrinsic natures, cessations, and modes of transcendence— all such things [are fully known].
The Buddha-son sees this as being like the four great rivers flowing from the palace of the Great Nāga King Anavatapta;
they are unturbid, unmixed, and free from impurity, their radiant color pure like space.
On each of the four sides of that lake there is a single mouth, and from each mouth flows out one river: from the mouth of the elephant flows the Gaṅgā River, and from the lion... [the Siṃha].
From the mouths [of the deities] issued the Sītā River; from the mouth of the Ox issued the Sindhu River;

and from the mouth of the Horse issued the Vakṣu River. As these four great rivers flowed forth, silver sand issued from the mouth of the Gaṅgā, diamond sand issued from the mouth of the Sītā, golden sand issued from the mouth of the Sindhu, and [iron sand] issued from the mouth of the Vakṣu.
Emerging from the mouth of the Gaṅgā River, it takes on the color of lapis lazuli; from the mouth of the Sītā River, the color of white silver;
from the mouth of the Sindhu River, the color of golden yellow; and from the mouth of the Vakṣu River, the color of lapis lazuli.
Each river mouth is one yojana wide. Once these four great rivers have flowed out, they each encircle the great lake seven times.
Flowing in four directions according to their respective quarters, surging and rushing toward the great ocean, these rivers wind around each [continent],
where there are *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses formed of celestial jewels;
they emit wondrous fragrances, possess exquisite and pure colors, and feature various petals and various stalks.
The filaments are composed entirely of various jewels that are naturally translucent and all emit light, illuminating one another.

The circumference of this Lake Anavatapta is fifty yojanas; its bottom is covered everywhere with exquisite sand made of various jewels, adorned with diverse mani-gems, and its banks are embellished by immeasurable wonderful treasures, while the sublime fragrance of sandalwood is scattered throughout.
Within it, blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), as well as various other precious flowers, completely fill the space;
when a gentle breeze blows, their fragrance permeates far and wide.

Flower groves and jeweled trees surround it on all sides, and when the sun rises, everything within and without the ponds and rivers is universally illuminated, with the reflections of all things merging and connecting in a continuous stream.

Thus, within this radiant web of light, all such things—whether distant or near, high or low, broad or narrow, coarse or fine, even down to the smallest single grain of sand or mote of dust—all possess the penetrating brilliance of exquisite jewels.
Within every one of these, the reflection of the solar disc appears; moreover, they mutually reflect one another’s images in this manner. Such is the multitude of things.
Reflections neither increase nor decrease; they neither conjoin nor disperse, yet all are clearly perceived according to their original substance.
O Son of the Buddha, it is just as the four great rivers flow from the four mouths of Lake Anavatapta and enter the great ocean;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who flows forth from the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) through all practices until finally entering into omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
Just as the ocean is filled by the great river Gaṅgā, which flows from the silver-colored mouth of an elephant with its silver sands,
so too is it with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: through the eloquence of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*), they proclaim all the doors of meaning taught by all Tathāgatas,
giving rise to all pure and white dharmas (*śukladharma*), and ultimately entering the ocean of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) like the great river Sītā.
Just as the Vajrasandhi Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva flows forth from the golden-colored lion’s mouth,
so too does [this Bodhisattva] likewise use the eloquence of the Dharma to preach the Buddha’s vajra-words for the sake of all sentient beings;
he draws forth vajra-wisdom and ultimately enters the ocean of unimpeded wisdom, just as the Sindhu Great River flows forth from the mouth of a golden ox.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvarṇasāra likewise, through such eloquent discourse and skillful means in accordance with dependent origination,
awakens sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice, be tamed, and reach maturity, until they ultimately enter the ocean of skillful means of dependent origination—
just as the great river Vārakī flows from the horse-mouth of Vaiḍūrya-colored Mount Sumeru, carrying water of the hue of vaiḍūrya.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāradvatīputra likewise rains down hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable Dharma teachings with inexhaustible eloquence,
so that all who hear them are thoroughly saturated and ultimately enter the ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma,
just as the four great rivers, following and encircling Lake Anavatapta, flow into the ocean from the four directions. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: they accomplish bodily actions that accord with [wisdom], verbal actions that accord with [wisdom], and mental actions that accord with [wisdom];
they accomplish bodily actions preceded by wisdom, verbal actions preceded by wisdom, and mental actions preceded by wisdom.
These flow forth in the four directions and ultimately enter the ocean of all-knowledge. Son of the Buddha, what is called a "Bodhisattva"?
The sons of the Buddha from the four directions— those who have attained awakening by seeing all Buddhas,
who hear all dharmas and uphold them without forgetting, who fulfill all practices of the pāramitās, and who preach the Dharma with great compassion to satisfy sentient beings—
are like the four great rivers surrounding a great lake, amidst which grow blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), and white lotuses (kumuda).
Just as the pond of lotuses is entirely filled with fragrant *puṇḍarīka* flowers, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
within the heart of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they never abandon sentient beings, but through teaching the Dharma and subduing them, cause them all to be perfected in immeasurable samādhis;
they behold the Buddha-lands adorned and pure, like the Great Lake Anavatapta surrounded by jewel trees.

The Mahāsattva is also like this: manifesting the adornments surrounding a Buddha-land to lead all sentient beings toward Bodhi, just as the Great Lake Anavatapta is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, pure and free from turbidity;
so too is the Bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, its measure boundless and filled with roots of goodness.
Just as the great lake Anavatapta is full, pure, and free from turbidity, with its shores adorned by immeasurable jewels and filled everywhere with the fragrance of sandalwood,

so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: the shore of the great vow of the bodhicitta is adorned with hundreds of thousands of billions of the ten kinds of wisdom-jewels, and it scatters everywhere the sublime fragrances of all manner of virtues.
Just as the bottom of the Great Lake Anavatapta is adorned with a bed of golden sand interspersed with various mani-jewels,

so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise adorned, having observed all things with subtle wisdom and being arrayed with the various jewels of the inconceivable Bodhisattva liberations; thus he attains the unimpeded light of all dharmas and abides therein.
Just as the Naga King Anavatapta dwells in all profound skillful means and is forever free from all the torments of the naga realm,
so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forever free from all worldly grief and affliction;
though manifesting birth, he remains untainted, like the four great rivers that provide moisture.
Just as water, having moistened all the lands of Jambudvīpa, enters the great ocean, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
using the rivers of the four kinds of wisdom, moisten devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas,
causing them all to enter the great ocean of the wisdom of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by means of the four powers.
What are the four adornments? First, the river of the wisdom of vows, which protects and subdues all sentient beings without ever ceasing.

Second, the river of the wisdom of the pāramitās, which cultivates bodhisattva practices to benefit sentient beings, continuing inexhaustibly through the past, future, and present, until finally entering the ocean of the wisdom of all Buddhas. Third, the samādhi of the bodhisattva.
Fourth, they are adorned with the samādhis of the countless rivers of wisdom; they behold all Buddhas and enter the ocean of all Buddhas.
Possessing the great compassion of the river of wisdom and the sovereign power of great kindness, they universally rescue sentient beings, gathering them in through skillful means without ceasing.
They cultivate the gateway of secret meritorious virtues until they ultimately enter the great ocean of the ten powers, just like the four great rivers.
Just as the waters that flow forth from Lake Anavatapta enter the great ocean and are ultimately inexhaustible, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:
through the power of their great vows, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices with sovereign knowledge and vision that is without end, ultimately entering the ocean of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Just as the four great rivers enter the great ocean and nothing can obstruct them, so it is with these Bodhisattvas.
Just as that which obstructs prevents entry, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

they constantly and diligently cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, accomplishing all light of wisdom, abiding in all the Buddha-dharmas of enlightenment, and entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata without obstruction.
It is like the four great rivers rushing into the ocean; even after passing through successive kalpas, there is no [diminution].

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who does not grow weary is likewise thus: through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, they cultivate the bodhisattva conduct throughout all future kalpas and enter the ocean of the Tathāgatas without ever becoming weary. O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the sun rises:
within the Heatless Lake, there are sands of gold, silver, diamond, lapis lazuli, and all other various kinds of jewels.

All things possess shadows that manifest within it; likewise, all precious substances such as golden sand also manifest their reflections to one another, mutually reflecting and penetrating each other without any obstruction. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:
dwelling in this samādhi, they see within every single pore of their own body that which is unspeakably many.
It can be said that as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are atoms in a Buddha-field also behold all the lands,
sites of enlightenment, and assemblies of that Buddha; at each Buddha’s presence, they listen to the Dharma, receive and uphold it, believe and understand it, and make offerings to it,
each for unspeakably unspeakable billions of nayutas of kalpas, yet they do not perceive the length or brevity of the duration of those times or assemblies.
Furthermore, there is no constriction; why is this? Because they enter the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) with a subtle and wondrous mind;
because they enter the unequalled differentiation of karmic fruits; because they enter the sphere of inconceivable samādhi; because they enter the sphere of inconceivable contemplation;
because they enter the sphere of the sovereign power of all Buddhas; and because they have attained the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Therefore, they attain the great supernormal transformations of all Buddhas; they attain the ten powers of all Tathāgatas, which are difficult to obtain and difficult to know;
they enter the perfected realm of the practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; and they attain the tireless supernormal power of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, although these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to enter and emerge from meditative concentration in a single thought-moment, they also...

Without abandoning long-term abiding in meditative concentration, they remain free from attachment; though they have no basis for dwelling within sensory objects, they do not relinquish any focal point of observation.
Though they skillfully enter the limit of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), they manifest the spiritual powers of a Buddha to benefit all sentient beings without ever becoming weary.
Though they equally enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they do not perceive its limits. Though they are without...
Though their dwelling has no fixed location, they constantly enter the path to omniscience;
by the power of transformation, they universally enter among immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings, fully adorning all worlds.

Although they are free from the inverted discriminations of the world and have transcended all grounds of conceptualization, they do not abandon the various marks [of phenomena]. Though they are able to...
Endowed with skillful means and ultimately pure, although they do not differentiate the various stages of a bodhisattva, they have already skillfully entered them all, O Son of the Buddha.
Just as space can contain all things yet is free from existence and non-existence, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; though he universally enters all worlds, he remains detached from them.
Although he diligently delivers all sentient beings through worldly perceptions, he remains free from the notion of sentient beings;
although he deeply understands all phenomena, he remains free from the notion of phenomena; although he delights in beholding all Buddhas, he remains free from the notion of Buddhas;
although he skillfully enters various samādhis, he knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like space, remaining unstained and unattached; although by means of the non-...
With boundless eloquence, they expound inexhaustible verses of Dharma, yet their minds always abide in the dharma that is free from words and letters;

though they delight in contemplating the ineffable dharma, they constantly manifest pure sounds; though they dwell at the limit of all dharmas beyond speech, they constantly manifest various forms and appearances;
and while teaching and transforming sentient beings, they know that all dharmas are ultimately [empty].
Although they diligently cultivate great compassion to deliver sentient beings, they know that the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible and undispersed;
although they thoroughly understand that the dharma-realm is eternally abiding and unchanging, they never cease to tame sentient beings through the three wheels;
and although they always dwell securely where the Tathāgatas dwell, their wisdom is pure and their minds are free from fear or discrimination.
Expounding various dharmas and turning the wheel of Dharma without ever ceasing— O Son of the Buddha,
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s ninth skillful wisdom of the great samādhi of mastery over the dharma-realm.
[Treatise] Regarding the ninth, the Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm:
this clarifies that this Bodhisattva enters samādhi within each and every pore of their own body, naturally able to know all worldly realms and the dharmas of the world;
furthermore, they fully and exhaustively know all worldly dharmas within the space-realm of the ten directions, even up to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The great assembly also all know this completely. Why is this? Because wisdom accords with the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
because wisdom has no center, boundary, magnitude, or measure; because it is like empty space; and because the essential nature of wisdom is luminous and pure.
Within a single pore, the space has no measure of magnitude or smallness; being equal to the realm of empty space, one is able to universally know the ten directions.
All realms of the world cannot be measured or known through emotional consciousness;

they can only be realized after the cessation of thought through the skillful means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Only when the wisdom of principle and phenomena (*li-shi*) manifests before one can one truly qualify for this.

This is because it is the state where concentration is exhausted and conceptualization has vanished, being without thought and without mind, and is only attained by the seal of non-active wisdom (*anabhisamskāra-jñāna*); therefore, it is called the Self-Nature of the Dharma-Dhātu.
In this samādhi, one does not dwell upon mental objects but acts with the spontaneous wisdom of universal knowledge; therefore, it is called the "Self-Abiding Dharma-Dhātu. This sutra states:
"It is like the space within a hole bored by an insect in a mustard seed; it suffers no diminution. It can be perceived through the wisdom that is free from thought;
those who perceive it through the wisdom of conceptual thought deviate from it. When the views of self and body are exhausted, the ten directions are equal in measure to the body."
Because the single nature has no interior or exterior, the moment the mind clings to it, there is separation.
Regarding the four rivers flowing from the palace of the Great Dragon King Anavatapta: according to the sutras, atop Mount Gandhamādana there is Lake Anavatapta;
from the four sides of that lake, one river flows out from each direction. From the eastern side, the Sītā River flows from the mouth of a lion, and it issues forth vajra [gold].
To the east, it enters the country of China; then it enters the South Sea.
To the south, the Gaṅgā River flows from the elephant’s mouth with silver sands, entering South India and then the South Sea.
To the west, the Sindhu River flows from the bull’s mouth with golden sands, entering the country of Sindh and then the West Sea. To the north, the Vakṣu...
The river flows from the mouth of the Vaiḍūrya Horse; its sands are of lapis lazuli. It enters the kingdom of Pārasīka and then flows into the Northern Sea.
Its pool is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with each of its four mouths measuring one yojana.
Within it, the *Dharmaparyāya* is clearly elucidated. There are *utpala* flowers—translated as "blue lotuses"—and *padma* flowers.
"Flower" (puṣpa) is here translated as "red lotus. The *kumuda* flower is here translated as "small white flower";
when its petals have not yet opened, they are tightly clustered, and thus it is named *puṇḍarīka*. This is translated as the "hundred-petaled white lotus.
As for the Dragon King Anavatapta: "An" means "non-existent," and "Avatapta" [means "heated"].
This refers to "torment. It means that this dragon has forever departed from the torment within the dragon realm;
regarding the internal meaning of the text, the representation of the Dharma is presented exactly as in the sutra itself.
[Sutra] "O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel? O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva..."
When Mahāsattvas enter this samādhi, they abide in unimpeded bodily action, unimpeded verbal action, and unimpeded mental action; they abide in unimpeded buddha-fields,
attain unimpeded wisdom for maturing sentient beings, acquire unimpeded wisdom for disciplining sentient beings,
emit unimpeded light, manifest unimpeded nets of light, and display unimpeded, vast transformations.

They turn the pure wheel of Dharma with unimpeded transformation; they attain the unobstructed mastery of Bodhisattvas; they universally enter the powers of all Buddhas and universally abide in the wisdom of all Buddhas;
they perform the deeds of Buddhas, purify what is purified by Buddhas, and manifest the spiritual powers of Buddhas to bring joy to the Buddhas;
they practice the conduct of Tathāgatas, abide in the path of Tathāgatas, and constantly draw near to immeasurable Buddhas, acting as the servants of all Buddhas.
Inheriting the lineage of all Buddhas, these sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having dwelled in this samādhi, contemplate omniscience in its totality,
contemplate omniscience in its particulars, conform to omniscience, manifest omniscience, take omniscience as their object of focus,
and perceive omniscience in its totality and perceive omniscience in its particulars.
Regarding Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s vast vows, vast mind, vast conduct, vast destination, vast entry, vast radiance, vast manifestation,
vast protective mindfulness, and vast transformations— vastly continuing the Way without retrogression,
without ceasing, without substitution, without weariness, without abandonment, without distraction, and without confusion, ever progressing forward;

Why is it that they are constantly continuous? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished great vows among all dharmas, set forth the Great Vehicle, and entered the ocean of great skillful means of the Buddha-dharma;

by the power of their supreme vows, they possess mastery in all the practices performed by bodhisattvas, as their wisdom clearly illuminates them, and they are fully endowed with the supernormal powers and transformations of a bodhisattva.
He is well able to protect and mind all sentient beings, just as all Buddhas of the past, future, and present protect them;
he constantly gives rise to great compassion for all beings and accomplishes the Tathāgata’s unchanging Dharma.
Son of the Buddha, it is as if someone were to place a maṇi jewel within a dyed garment; although the maṇi jewel takes on the color of the garment, it does not abandon its own nature.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Svabhāva is likewise thus: he accomplishes wisdom as his heart-jewel, and while observing that all-encompassing omniscience is universally and clearly manifest, he does not abandon the various practices of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has made the great vow to benefit all sentient beings and to deliver all sentient beings from suffering.
They serve all Buddhas, purify all worlds, and bring comfort to sentient beings;
they enter deeply into the ocean of Dharma to purify the realms of sentient beings, manifesting great sovereign power to bestow gifts upon them and universally illuminating the world.

They enter the boundless dharma-gate of illusory transformations, remaining non-retrogressive and unswerving, without weariness or satiety. O Son of the Buddha, it is as if space were to support all things.

Whether the world is forming or abiding, it is without weariness, without fatigue, without exhaustion, without decay, without dispersal, without destruction, without change, without alteration, and without differentiation;
it does not abandon its own nature. Why is this? Because such is the natural law of the nature of space.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise establishes immeasurable great vows to deliver all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is free from weariness. Son of the Buddha, it is like Nirvana:

regarding the immeasurable sentient beings of the past, future, and present who attain parinirvāṇa therein, one never becomes weary. Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure;
this is called Nirvana. How could there be weariness within that? The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, desiring— [to continue the practice].
How can one give rise to a mind of weariness when manifesting in the world to deliver all sentient beings and cause them to transcend [suffering]?
O Son of the Buddha, just as a Sarvajña (Omniscient One) never grows weary in causing all Bodhisattvas of the past,
future, and present to be born— both those already born and those yet to be born— within the family of the Buddhas, and even until they achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are non-dual, and because there is no attachment to any phenomena (*dharma*).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise; with a mind of equanimity abiding in all-knowledge, how could they have a mind of weariness or exhaustion?
Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has a lotus flower, and that flower is vast.
It extends to the furthest reaches of the ten directions, adorned with unspeakable numbers of petals, unspeakable jewels, and unspeakable fragrances.
Each of those unspeakable jewels further manifests various kinds of precious gems—pure, exquisite, and perfectly well-arranged.
These flowers constantly emit light of manifold colors, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.
A net of pure gold, unimpeded, covers its surface; precious bells sway gently, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds.
These sounds expound the Dharma of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). This great lotus is born from the arising of all roots of goodness and the pure adornments of a Tathāgata;
it is a manifestation of auspiciousness and spiritual power, appearing with ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* [petals].
It is the accomplishment of the wondrous path of the Bodhisattva Viśuddhaguṇa; it is the outflow of the mind of omniscience;
within it, the reflections of the Buddhas of the ten directions appear. The world gazes upon it as if it were a stupa;
among sentient beings, there are none who see it and do not pay homage. It arises from the true Dharma that thoroughly understands illusion; all worlds cannot be [otherwise] than this.
It was as if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva were sitting cross-legged upon this flower, his body in size perfectly proportioned to the flower;

empowered by the spiritual authority of all Buddhas, from each and every pore of the Bodhisattva’s body there issued forth hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of light rays, as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields, and each of these light rays...
There appeared mani-jewels, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands;
these jewels were all named Universal Radiance Treasury, adorned with various colors and forms, accomplished through immeasurable merits,
and formed a lattice-work of various gems and flowers that completely covered them above, scattering hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas [of flowers].
His supreme, wondrous fragrance and infinite colors and forms were adorned in various ways; furthermore, inconceivable canopies of jewel-adornments appeared, covering him from above.

Within each and every mani-jewel, there appeared millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of palaces, as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields; within each and every palace, there appeared millions of billions of nayutas.
Upon each lion throne— equal in number to the atoms within unspeakably many buddha-fields—
there appeared hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of unspeakably many buddha-field atomic particles of light; and from each ray of light,
there appeared hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of unspeakably many buddha-field atomic particles of colored forms.
From his physical form, there appeared wheels of light as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields;
from each wheel of light, there appeared *vairocana* mani-jewel flowers as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields;
and from each flower, there appeared [lotuses] as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas...

It is said that there are as many platforms as there are atoms in a buddha-field; on each platform appear as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields;
each Buddha manifests as many miraculous transformations as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields;
and each miraculous transformation purifies as many hundreds of billions of nayutas of unspeakably many [buddha-fields].
Within each of the multitudes of sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there appear hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of buddhas,

as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field; each of these sovereign buddhas rains down hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, and each of these buddha-dharmas possesses a hundred...
In each and every sūtra among the number of sūtras equal to the atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields,
there are explained as many dharma-gates as there are atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields;
and within each and every dharma-gate, there are as many vajra-wisdoms as there are atoms within unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields.
The various verbal expressions for the distinctions of the wheels of Dharma he enters are each separately expounded; in each wheel of Dharma,
he brings to maturity as many realms of sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, and within each realm of sentient beings,
there are as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields who [abide] in the Buddha-dharma.
Having attained mastery therein, these sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling in this samādhi, manifest such realms of supernatural power and immeasurable transformations;
they know them all to be like illusions and remain unstained by attachment.

They abide within the unobstructed limit of the Tathāgata lineage—the true mark of the dharmadhātu, which is the self-nature of phenomena that is pure and beyond verbal expression, and which is infinite.
Without going or coming, neither prior nor posterior, profoundly deep and bottomless, it is attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One enters it by means of wisdom through one's own self, not through awakening by another. The mind is neither deluded nor discursive;
it is praised by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Flowing forth from the power of all Buddhas, it enters the realm of all Buddhas.

With a nature as it truly is, they realize it through the eye of direct perception; with the eye of wisdom, they see universally; having accomplished the Buddha-eye, they serve as bright lamps for the world.
Moving within the sphere of objects known by the eye of knowledge, they extensively reveal subtle and wondrous Dharma gates.
Having perfected the bodhicitta, they are superior beings who encounter no obstacles regarding any realm of experience. Entering the lineage of wisdom, they give birth to all forms of gnosis.
Having transcended the phenomena of birth within the world, they manifest births through supernormal powers and transformations, employing skillful means to discipline and subdue beings;

all such things are nothing other than the merit of their skillful mastery. Their resolve and desires are entirely pure, most subtle and exquisite, and they are fully endowed with perfect wisdom as vast as space.
They are well able to observe the realm of the noble ones through the power of their faith, practice, and vows.

Firm and immovable, its virtues inexhaustible, it is praised by the world; it is the treasury beheld by all Buddhas, the locus of great enlightenment, and the ocean of omniscience where all wondrous jewels are gathered. Like a lotus for the great wise ones, it is pure by nature;
all sentient beings who behold it give rise to joy, all obtain benefit, and the light of wisdom shines everywhere.
They behold immeasurable Buddhas and purify all dharmas; their conduct is tranquil, and they attain ultimate non-obstruction regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
Constantly employing skillful means, they abide within the merit and practice of the Buddha’s bodhi and are born therein.

Possessing the wisdom of a Bodhisattva and serving as leaders among Bodhisattvas, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas alike; through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, they accomplish the Buddha-dharma body.
The power of mindfulness is inconceivable; though focused on a single object, it is without an object of perception.
Its activity is vast, signless, and unimpeded, equal to the dharma-realm, immeasurable and boundless.
The enlightenment realized is like space, without limits and free from all attachment, universally bringing benefit to all worlds, flowing forth from the ocean of roots of goodness of omniscience.
Having fully mastered immeasurable realms and perfectly accomplished the dharma of pure giving, they abide in the bodhisattva mind and purify the bodhisattva lineage.
They are able to accord with and give rise to the enlightenment of all Buddhas;
they attain skillfulness in all Buddha-dharmas, possess subtle and wondrous conduct, and achieve firm strength. The sovereign majestic power of all Buddhas is difficult for sentient beings to hear.
The Bodhisattvas fully know how to enter the gate of non-duality and abide in the dharma of signlessness;

although they have forever relinquished all signs, they are able to extensively expound all manner of dharmas. According to the inclinations, desires, and understandings of sentient beings, they bring them all to subdual and cause them all to rejoice.
Taking the dharma-realm as their body, they are free from discrimination; the realm of their wisdom is inexhaustible.
Their resolve is ever courageous and their mind is always equanimous; they perceive the ultimate limit of the merits of all Buddhas,
comprehend the sequential distinctions of all kalpas, reveal all dharmas, cause all Buddha-lands to abide in purity,
manifest the radiance of all true teachings, and demonstrate all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present.
The dwelling place of a Bodhisattva is a bright lamp for the world; it gives rise to all roots of goodness and brings about eternal departure from the mundane world.
One is constantly born into the presence of Buddhas and attains the Buddha-wisdom that is foremost in clarity.

All Buddhas together sustain and protect such a one, who has already entered the ranks of future Buddhas. Born from the company of virtuous friends, all their aspirations and pursuits are free from deficiency.

Not failing to fulfill [their vows], they possess great majestic power and abide in the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*). Whatever they have heard, they are able to explain well and reveal it to others.
Through the roots of goodness from hearing the Dharma, they abide in the wheel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Their minds encounter no obstacles regarding all phenomena;

they do not abandon various practices and remain free from all conceptual discrimination. Their minds are unmoving and thoughtless regarding all phenomena, and having attained the eye of wisdom, they extinguish all...

He is able to illuminate all Buddha-dharmas within the darkness of ignorance; he enters into all realms of existence without destroying them, thoroughly understanding that the spheres of all existences have been devoid of movement from the very beginning.

Although his physical, verbal, and mental actions are all boundless, and although he follows worldly conventions to expound various and immeasurable syllables, he never deviates from being free of words.
Through the method of letters, they enter deeply into the ocean of the Buddhas, knowing that all phenomena possess only provisional names.
They are neither bound nor attached to any objective realms, understanding that all phenomena are empty and non-existent. All practices they cultivate arise from the Dharma-realm;

like space, they are signless and formless. Having entered deeply into the Dharma-realm, they expound the teaching in accordance with it, giving rise to one [insight] within a single gateway of objects.
With all-knowledge, they contemplate the stage of the ten powers; through wisdom they train in wisdom, taking wisdom as a bridge to reach *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
With the eye of wisdom, they see phenomena without obstruction, skillfully entering all stages and knowing their various meanings.

They attain complete clarity regarding every single dharma-gate, and there are no great vows that they do not fulfill. O Son of the Buddha, it is by means of this that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva opens [the way].
This demonstrates the non-differentiated nature of all Tathāgatas; this is the gateway of unimpeded skillful means; this can give birth to the assemblies of Bodhisattvas;
this Dharma is exclusively the domain of samādhi; this can cause one to courageously enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
this can reveal and manifest the gateways of all samādhis; this can universally enter all lands without obstruction; this can discipline...
They subdue all sentient beings; they are able to abide in the limit of non-sentience; they are able to reveal and demonstrate all Buddha-dharmas;

they have no attainment whatsoever regarding objective spheres. Although they constantly expound and reveal [the Dharma] at all times, they remain forever far removed from conceptualization and discrimination.
Although they know that all dharmas are devoid of activity, they are able to manifest all manner of activities.
Although karma knows that all Buddhas possess no dual characteristics, it is able to manifest all Buddhas;

although it knows they are formless, it expounds upon forms; although it knows there is no sensation, it expounds upon sensations; although it knows there is no perception, it expounds upon perceptions;
although it knows there are no mental formations, it expounds upon mental formations; and although it knows there is no consciousness, it expounds upon consciousness.
All consciousnesses constantly use the wheel of Dharma to reveal and instruct all beings; though they know that phenomena are unborn, they perpetually turn the wheel of Dharma;
though they know that phenomena are without distinction, they expound various gates of differentiation;

though they know that all phenomena have neither arising nor ceasing, they describe all characteristics of arising and ceasing; and though they know that all phenomena are neither coarse nor subtle, they speak of all phenomena.
Although they know that all phenomena are without coarse or subtle characteristics, they are able to proclaim the most supreme Dharma;
although they know that all phenomena are ineffable, they are able to expound pure speech;
although they know that all phenomena have neither interior nor exterior, they speak of all internal and external phenomena; and although they know that all phenomena cannot be fully comprehended...
And yet, they speak of various kinds of wisdom and observation; though they know that all phenomena lack true reality, they proclaim the true path to liberation;
though they know that all phenomena are ultimately inexhaustible, they are able to expound the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*);
though they know that all phenomena are without conflict or contention, they nevertheless do not deny the distinctions between self and other; though they know all phenomena...

Ultimately having no teacher, yet always revering all teachers and elders; though knowing that all dharmas are realized without depending on another, yet always revering all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); though knowing that all dharmas do not turn, yet turning the wheel of Dharma;
though knowing that all dharmas have no arising, yet demonstrating various causes and conditions; and though knowing that all dharmas have no prior limit, yet extensively expounding them.
Although he knows that all phenomena have no future limit, he extensively teaches regarding the future;
although he knows that all phenomena have no middle limit, he extensively teaches regarding the present; although he knows that all phenomena have no agent, he speaks of various actions;
although he knows that all phenomena have no causes and conditions, he speaks of various accumulated causes; although he knows that all phenomena have no... [existence].
They teach by means of analogy the paths of equality and inequality; though they know all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, they definitively expound the dharmas of the three periods of time;
though they know all phenomena have no basis, they teach that one attains liberation by relying on wholesome dharmas;
though they know dharmas have no body, they extensively expound the Dharma-body; though they know the Buddhas of the three periods of time have no...
While abiding in the limitlessness [of reality], they are able to expound that there is but a single Buddha; though they know that dharmas have no form, they manifest various forms;
though they know that dharmas are invisible, they extensively explain all views; though they know that dharmas are signless, they speak of various signs;
though they know that all dharmas have no objective sphere, they extensively proclaim the sphere of wisdom; though they know that all dharmas have no...
The Buddha speaks of the various distinctions of the fruits of practice despite there being no distinction;

he speaks of the various modes of purification for transcendence despite knowing that all phenomena have no transcendence; he speaks of all phenomena of cyclic existence despite knowing that all phenomena are primordially abiding;
and he constantly and extensively explains the dharma of illumination despite knowing that all phenomena have no illumination.
When a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enters this wheel of wisdom of the samādhi of great majestic power,
he is then able to realize all buddha-dharmas, enter into all buddha-dharmas, accomplish them, perfect them,
accumulate them, purify them, abide in them, and thoroughly comprehend them in relation to all phenomena.
In accordance with their intrinsic nature, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not form such thoughts as:

"there are so many bodhisattvas," "so many bodhisattva-dharmas," "the culmination of so many bodhisattvas," "the culmination of so many illusions," "the culmination of so many transformations," "the accomplishment of so many supernormal powers," "the accomplishment of so much wisdom," "so much reflection," or "so much realization."

Why is it that they enter various destinies and various realms? Because the nature of this bodhisattva samādhi is such, its extent is such, and it is such that it is boundless and supremely excellent.
This samādhi possesses various realms, various powers, and various profound penetrations;
namely, it enters the gates of ineffable wisdom and enters the various adornments that are free from conceptual discrimination.
They enter boundless and supreme *pāramitās*; they enter countless meditative concentrations; they enter hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of ineffably vast wisdoms;
they enter the vision of the boundless, sublime treasury of Buddhas; they enter realms without cessation;
they enter pure faith, understanding, and the factors conducive to enlightenment; they enter the great supernormal powers of sharp faculties; and they enter their respective spheres of activity.
Entering the unimpeded mind; entering the eye of equality that beholds all Buddhas; entering the accumulation of the supreme vows and practices of Samantabhadra;
entering the body of the wondrous wisdom of Nārāyaṇa; entering the ocean of wisdom of all Tathāgatas; entering the arousal of immeasurable kinds of spiritual transformations within one’s own stage;
entering the birth of the inexhaustible gates of wisdom of all Buddhas; and entering and abiding in the manifest realm of all Buddhas.

The entrance into the sovereign wisdom of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva through the purification of the realms and sense-bases; the entrance into the incomparable universal gate of wisdom that reveals all things;
the entrance into the universally known subtle states of the entire dharma-realm; the entrance into the subtle states of the entire dharma-realm as they are universally manifested;
the entrance into the light of all supreme wisdom; the entrance into the limit of all sovereignty; and the entrance into all eloquence.
The entrance into the limit of the Dharma-gates; the entrance into the wisdom-body that pervades the entire Dharma-realm; the entrance into the accomplishment of the universal path in all places;
the entrance into the skillful abiding in all differentiated samādhis; and the knowledge of the minds of all Buddhas.
