Chapter Twenty-seven, Part Five: The Ten Determinations.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the conduct of Samantabhadra, enters ten billion unspeakable samādhis in every thought-moment;
yet he does not perceive the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra nor the adornments of the Buddha-realm of the past. Why is this?
Because he knows that all phenomena are ultimately inexhaustible, and because he knows that all Buddha-fields are boundless.
Because they know that the realms of all sentient beings are inconceivable; because they know that the past has no beginning; because they know that the future is without end;
because they know that the present is as boundless as empty space pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
because they know that the spheres of activity of all Buddhas are inconceivable; because they know that the practices of all Bodhisattvas are innumerable; [and] because they know all Buddhas...
The realm spoken of by eloquence is ineffable because it is boundless; one should know that all phenomena which are objects of the illusory mind are immeasurable.

O Son of the Buddha, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel grants everything sought and satisfies the minds of seekers without end, yet the power of the jewel is never exhausted, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Thus, entering this samādhi, one knows that the mind is like an illusion, giving rise to the realm of all phenomena, which is pervasive, inexhaustible, and unceasing.

Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes the unimpeded conduct and wisdom of Samantabhadra, observing immeasurable and vast illusory manifestations as being like reflections, neither increasing nor decreasing.
For example, just as the individual minds of ordinary beings— those already arisen, those presently arising, and those yet to arise—
are boundless, uninterrupted, and inexhaustible, with their mental flow continuing in succession without end in an inconceivable manner;
so too it is for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who enters this Samādhi of the Universal Door of Illusion, which is boundless and immeasurable.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly realized the infinite dharmas of the universal gate of illusion of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the dragon kings Nanda, Upananda, Mānasvin, and other great dragons send down rain;
the drops are as large as axle-trees and are without limit. Although they rain in such a manner, the clouds are never exhausted. This is the effortless power of these dragons.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viṣayāvatī is likewise thus: dwelling in this samādhi, he enters the gates of all the samādhis of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,

the gates of wisdom, the gates of Dharma, the gates of beholding all Buddhas, the gates of proceeding to all directions, the gates of mastery of mind, the gates of empowerment, the gates of miraculous transformations,
the gates of supernormal powers, the gates of illusory manifestations, and the gate of the illusory nature of all phenomena— things that are ineffable.

The gate of being filled with unspeakably many bodhisattvas; the gate of approaching unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field; the gate of entering unspeakably unspeakable, vast nets of illusion;
the gate of knowing unspeakably unspeakable distinctions of vast Buddha-fields; and the knowledge of unspeakably unspeakable...
The gate of knowing the existence and non-existence of the nature of things; the gate of knowing the mental conceptions of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings;
the gate of knowing the distinctions between unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas and eons;
the gate of knowing the formation and destruction of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds; and the gate of knowing unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields that are inverted or upright.
Within a single thought-moment, they know all things as they truly are. Thus entering [this state], it is without limit and without end;

it is without weariness or aversion, uninterrupted and unceasing, without retreat and without loss. Among all phenomena, they do not abide in improper places, but constantly engage in right reflection.
Neither sinking nor agitated, they seek all-knowledge and never abandon it for the sake of all Buddha-fields.
The Lamp Illuminating the World turns the wheel of Dharma, ineffably ineffable; through sublime eloquence, he interrogates the Tathāgata without end;
he demonstrates the path to Buddhahood without limit; he tames sentient beings, never abandoning them;
he constantly and diligently cultivates the practices and vows of Samantabhadra without ever resting; and he manifests immeasurable, ineffable [deeds].
It is unspeakable that the body of form-characteristics has no interruption. Why is this?
It is like a burning fire which, following whatever conditions are present, continues to blaze without ceasing for as long as those conditions persist. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:

they observe the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the world-realm as being like empty space, without limit or boundary, even unto the point of being able to [perceive] within a single...
In the space of a single thought, he went to as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields;

at each and every buddha-field, he entered into unspeakably unspeakable varieties of all-knowledge teachings, causing unspeakably unspeakable realms of sentient beings to leave the household life for the sake of the Way, diligently cultivate roots of goodness, and reach ultimate purity. He caused them not to...
Bodhisattvas who are neither expressible nor inexpressible, having attained certainty regarding those whose vows of Samantabhadra’s conduct were previously uncertain,
dwell securely in the gateway of Samantabhadra’s wisdom; through immeasurable skillful means, they enter into unspeakably unspeakable eons of the vast distinctions of formation,
abiding, and destruction throughout the three times, within those unspeakably unspeakable periods of formation, abiding, and destruction.
The distinctions of the world arise from such great compassion and great vows as to subdue all immeasurable sentient beings without exception.

Why is this? Because these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, desiring to deliver all sentient beings, cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, give rise to the wisdom of Samantabhadra, and fulfill all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should, regarding such types, such spheres, such majestic powers, such vastness,
such immeasurability, such inconceivability, such universal illumination, such Buddhas dwelling manifest before them,
such protection and mindfulness by all Tathāgatas, and such fulfillment of their former vows— [should practice accordingly].
With roots of goodness such as these, they diligently cultivate the samādhi of an unimpeded and immovable mind; free from all feverish afflictions and without weariness, their minds do not regress.
Establishing profound resolve and joy, they are courageous and fearless, conforming to the sphere of samādhi and entering the ground of inconceivable wisdom.
They do not rely on words and letters, do not cling to the world, and do not grasp at any phenomena.

Without giving rise to conceptual discrimination, one should not be stained by worldly affairs; without discriminating among objective spheres, one should simply abide in the wisdom regarding all phenomena and not engage in mental weighing.

That is to say: drawing near to omniscience, awakening to the Bodhi of the Buddhas, accomplishing the light of the Dharma, bestowing roots of goodness upon all sentient beings, and pulling sentient beings out from within the realm of Māra.

Having entered the realm of the Buddha-dharma, one should not abandon the great vow, but diligently contemplate the path of transcendence, expand and purify the sphere of reality, and accomplish the various perfections (*pāramitās*).
One should engender deep faith and understanding toward all Buddhas, constantly observe the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), and never for a moment forsake this practice.
One should know that one's own self and the nature of all phenomena are universally equal, and one should clearly understand this.
One should demonstrate to the world the wisdom and skillful means that accord with the Dharma, always exerting oneself without rest;
one should manifest one's own meager roots of goodness and diligently increase them; one should diligently increase the roots of goodness in others;
one should personally cultivate the path to omniscience; one should diligently increase the bodhisattva realm; and one should delight in drawing near to spiritual friends.
One should dwell together with fellow practitioners; one should not discriminate regarding the Buddha; one should not abandon mindfulness;
one should always abide peacefully in the equal dharma-realm; one should know that all consciousnesses are like illusions; one should know that all worldly conditioned activities are like dreams;
one should know that the manifestation of the Buddhas through the power of their vows is like reflected images; and one should know all vast [phenomena].
One should know that great undertakings are like transformations; one should know that all speech is like an echo; one should contemplate all phenomena as being entirely like illusions;
one should know that all phenomena of arising and ceasing are like sounds; one should know that all Buddha-fields to which one goes are devoid of intrinsic nature;
and one should inquire after the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata without ever becoming weary. One should act in this way.
Awakening all the worlds, he diligently instructs and exhorts them without ever abandoning them;
knowing the proper time to subdue all sentient beings, he expounds the Dharma without ceasing.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the conduct of Samantabhadra in this way, they thus fulfill the bodhisattva realm and thus penetrate the path of transcendence.
One should thus uphold the Dharma; thus observe the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time; thus contemplate the gateway to all-knowledge;
thus reflect upon the unchanging Dharma; thus purify one’s superior aspiration; thus believe and resolve in all Tathāgatas; thus understand the vast power of the Buddhas;
thus become definitively established in an unobstructed mind; and thus gather [all beings].
When all sentient beings, sons of the Buddha, and Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter this Great Wisdom Samādhi in which the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra abides,
there are in each of the ten directions unspeakably unspeakable numbers of lands,
and in each of those lands there are names of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

Each and every name is manifested before by as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, who grant the power of mindfulness of the Tathāgata so that the realm of the Tathāgata is not forgotten;
they grant the ultimate wisdom regarding all phenomena so that one may enter into omniscience; and they grant the decisive wisdom that knows the various meanings of all phenomena.
To uphold all Buddha-dharmas and enter into unimpededness; to lead others toward supreme Buddha-enlightenment and cause them to enter into omniscience;
to awaken to the dharma-realm and cause the ultimate wisdom of Bodhisattvas to attain the radiance of all dharmas, free from all darkness;
and to cause the non-retrogressive wisdom of Bodhisattvas to know the skillful means of timing and non-timing in order to discipline sentient beings.
They grant birth and the unimpeded eloquence of bodhisattvas, causing them to realize boundless dharmas and preach them inexhaustibly;

they grant the power of supernatural transformations, causing them to manifest unspeakably unspeakable numbers of distinct bodies with infinite physical forms of various different kinds to awaken sentient beings; and they grant perfect speech and sound, causing them to manifest unspeakably unspeakable...
By expounding various sounds and diverse言辞 (words and phrases) to awaken sentient beings, he possesses the power that is never in vain;
such that all sentient beings who see his form or hear his Dharma shall all achieve fulfillment without their efforts being in vain.
O Son of the Buddha, because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus fulfills the practices of Samantabhadra, he attains the power of the Tathāgata and emerges with purity.
Having departed from the path and perfected all-knowledge, with unimpeded eloquence, supernormal powers, and transformations, they ultimately subdue all sentient beings;
endowed with the majestic power of a Buddha, they purify the conduct of Samantabhadra and abide in the path of Samantabhadra until the end of the future.
For the sake of subduing all sentient beings, they turn the subtle and wondrous wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas. Why is this so, O Son of the Buddha?
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished such sublime great vows and bodhisattva practices,
they become Dharma-teachers for all the world, suns of Dharma for all the world, moons of wisdom for all the world,
and Sumeru kings of mountains for all the world— loftily towering, firm, and immovable.
Thus, they become boundless oceans of wisdom for all the world; they become bright lamps of the True Dharma for all the world, shining universally upon the infinite without interruption;
they reveal boundless pure merits to all sentient beings, causing them all to dwell securely in roots of virtue and merit;
and they cultivate universally in accordance with the great vows of omniscience.
The noble one’s vast conduct is always able to inspire and encourage immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the unspeakably,
unspeakably vast Samādhi of Conduct; O Greatly Sovereign Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has attained such wisdom,
realized such dharmas, dwells with thorough clarity and insight into such dharmas, and has acquired such supernormal powers to abide as he does.
In this realm, he manifests such spiritual transformations and exerts such supernatural powers; he constantly dwells in great compassion, always benefiting sentient beings,
revealing to them the secure and correct path, establishing the great banner of light of merit and wisdom,
realizing inconceivable liberation, abiding in the liberation of omniscience, and reaching the further shore of the liberation of all Buddhas— thus training without ceasing.
Having already attained mastery in the gate of skillful means for inconceivable liberation, they enter the gate of the distinctions of the Dharma-realm without confusion.
They sport with sovereign ease in the Samādhi of Samantabhadra, which is unspeakably unspeakable;
they dwell in the lion-like leaping wisdom, their mental activity being unimpeded. Their minds constantly abide in ten great treasuries of Dharma. What are these ten? Namely:
Abiding in the recollection of all Buddhas; abiding in the recollection of all Buddha-dharmas; abiding in the great compassion that tames all sentient beings;
abiding in the wisdom that manifests inconceivable, pure buddha-fields; abiding in the definitive understanding that penetrates deeply into the realm of all Buddhas;
and abiding in the equality of the enlightenment of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, which is unimpeded.
Abiding in the limit of non-attachment; abiding in the signless nature of all phenomena; abiding in the roots of goodness that are equal to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
abiding in the wisdom that precedes the non-differentiated body, speech, and mental actions within the *dharmadhātu* of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present;
and observing all Buddhas of the three times as they take birth, renounce the world, proceed to the site of enlightenment, and attain [awakening].
The turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Perfectly Awakened One and his entry into parinirvāṇa are all contained within the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
O Son of the Buddha, these ten great Dharma-treasuries are vast, immeasurable, incalculable, incomparable, inconceivable, ineffable, inexhaustible, and difficult to endure;
they cannot be fully described by any worldly wisdom. O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already reached them.
Having realized the purity of all the practices of Samantabhadra and reached the other shore, with vast resolve and power, he reveals to sentient beings immeasurable roots of goodness;
he increases the power of all bodhisattvas, fulfills all bodhisattva merits in every thought-moment,
accomplishes all bodhisattva practices, and receives and upholds all the Buddha-dhāraṇī dharmas.

Although all Buddhas abide eternally in the true suchness (tathatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they manifest in accordance with all worldly conventions to discipline and transform all sentient beings. Why is this?
Because, O Son of the Buddha, it is by virtue of this samādhi that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas attain all [qualities] through abiding in the Dharma of this samādhi.
The Buddha has attained the vast wisdom that skillfully explains all extensive dharmas; he has attained the sovereign eloquence of mastery over all dharmas;
he has attained the most excellent, pure, and fearless state supreme among all worlds; he has attained entry into the wisdom of all samādhis;
he has attained all the skillful means of bodhisattvas; and he has attained the gateways of light of all dharmas, reaching to comfort all the world.
Knowing the Dharma’s further shore, he understands the proper and improper times for all sentient beings;
he illuminates all places throughout the worlds of the ten directions, enabling all sentient beings to attain supreme wisdom and acting as the unsurpassed teacher of all worlds.
Abiding in all meritorious virtues, he reveals the pure samādhi to all sentient beings, causing them to enter the most sublime wisdom. Why is this so?
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in this manner, they benefit sentient beings, increase their great compassion,
draw near to spiritual friends, behold all Buddhas, comprehend all phenomena,
travel to all lands, enter all directions, enter all worlds, awaken to the equality of all phenomena, and come to know.
The equality of all Buddhas is the abiding in the equality of omniscience; within this Dharma, one performs such karma and no other karma.

One abides with a mind that is not yet satisfied, a mind that is undistracted, a mind that is single-pointed, a mind that is diligently cultivated, a mind that is resolute, and a mind that is unchanging. Thus one reflects and thus one acts.
In this way, the ultimate sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, have no discrepancy between their words and their deeds;

they act as they speak. Why is this? For example, just as a diamond receives its name because it is indestructible and there is never a time when it is separated from that indestructibility, so too do the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas receive their designation through all their various practices.

A name can never at any time be separated from the phenomena it denotes; for example, once "fine color" is established as the name for genuine gold, that name can never be separated from the fine color.

In the same way, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva receives their name through various wholesome deeds, and that name can never at any time be separated from those wholesome deeds. It is like the Son of the Sun Deity (Sūryadevaputra) who...
He obtained his name from the "Wheel of Radiance" (Prabhā-maṇḍala), and there was never a time when he was separated from that Wheel of Radiance.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise so named because of the light of wisdom; there is never a time when he is separated from the light of wisdom.
It is, for example, like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, which stands far above the great ocean with its four jeweled peaks, rising loftily high.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Never-Abandoning-the-Four-Peaks is likewise;

by means of all his roots of goodness, he remains in the world, towering far above others, and thus he receives his name "Never-Abandoning" because there is never a time when he abandons those roots of goodness.
It is like the great earth, which receives its name because it supports all things, and there is never a time when it ceases to do so.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśeṣamati is also like this: he receives his name because he delivers all beings, yet there is never a time when he abandons great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Just as the great ocean receives its name because it contains all waters, yet there is never a time when it abandons water, so too the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva receives his name through these great [elements].

Having attained a name through his vows, he never for a moment abandons them; his vow to deliver sentient beings is like that of a military general who, having mastered the arts of combat, attains a reputation and never at any time forsakes that skill.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having mastered such a samādhi, attains its name and so forth.
Until they achieve the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), they never abandon this practice;

like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) who governs the four continents, they constantly and diligently protect all sentient beings, ensuring they do not die untimely deaths and that they always experience happiness.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering these various great samādhis, they constantly and diligently transform and deliver [beings].
Just as when seeds are sown in the earth, they can eventually cause stems and leaves to grow until ultimate purity is attained,
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who practices the conduct of Samantabhadra,
thereby enabling the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings to increase. It is like a great cloud during the heat of summer.

Just as a great rain falls and causes all seeds to grow, so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enter such great samādhis and cultivate the bodhisattva practice, raining down the great Dharma-rain until all sentient beings are brought to ultimate purity,
ultimate nirvāṇa, ultimate peace, and ultimate fulfillment.
Having reached the ultimate shore and attained ultimate joy, they have severed all doubt and serve as the ultimate field of merit for all sentient beings.
They cause the meritorious deeds of giving to become entirely pure; they cause them all to abide in the path of non-retrogression; they cause them to equally attain the wisdom of omniscience;
they cause them all to achieve liberation from the three realms; and they cause them all to attain ultimate knowledge. They cause them all...
To attain the ultimate Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas and to establish all sentient beings in the state of omniscience. Why is this?

Because when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish this Dharma, their wisdom becomes clear and they enter the gateway of the Dharma-realm, thereby purifying the inconceivable and immeasurable practices of Bodhisattvas;
that is to say, they purify all forms of knowledge in order to seek omniscience.
One can purify sentient beings because they bring them to subdual; one can purify buddha-fields because of constant dedication; one can purify all dharmas because of universal comprehension;
one can purify fearlessness because of being free from timidity; one can purify unimpeded eloquence because of skillful exposition;
one can purify *dhāraṇī* because of attaining mastery over all dharmas; and one can purify the practice of constant association.
Because they behold all Buddhas appearing in the world, the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, dwelling in this samādhi,
attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakably unspeakable pure merits.
Because they have attained mastery over such realms of samādhi and because they are empowered by all Buddhas, their own virtues...
Because it flows from the faculties and powers; because it enters the stage of wisdom with great majesty;
because of the guiding power of spiritual friends; because it subdues all the powers of Māra; because of the power of the purity of shared roots of goodness;
because of the power of the aspiration for vast vows; and because of the power of the fulfillment of planted roots of goodness, it transcends all worlds and is inexhaustible.

Because the merit of this is peerless in power, O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi attains ten kinds of dharmas that are identical to those of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten? They are: attaining the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and manifold adornments identical to those of all Buddhas;
being able to emit a pure great network of light rays identical to those of all Buddhas; [and] the spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*)... [identical to those of all Buddhas].
They possess supernormal powers and transformations to discipline sentient beings, identical to the Buddhas; they possess pure and perfect voices, identical to the Buddhas;
they manifest pure Buddha-lands according to the karma of sentient beings, identical to the Buddhas;

they are able to grasp and retain all the languages of all sentient beings without forgetting or losing them, identical to the Buddhas; and they possess inexhaustible eloquence, following [the needs of others] like the Buddhas.
They turn the wheel of Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings, causing wisdom to arise;
they possess the great lion’s roar of all Buddhas, being without fear or dread; they awaken the multitudes with immeasurable teachings, equaling all Buddhas;

and in a single thought-moment, through great supernormal powers, they universally enter the three periods of time, equaling all Buddhas as they are able to manifest everything for all sentient beings.
The Buddha’s adornments, the majestic power of all Buddhas, and the realm of all Buddhas are identical to those of the Buddhas themselves.

[Treatise] The tenth is the Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel. This is, for example, like the thousand-spoked diamond wheel of a Wheel-Turning King, whose hub, spokes, rim, and linchpin are all perfectly complete and radiant;
it destroys the cycle of birth and death and manifests the perfection of this Bodhisattva’s wisdom.
Because the compassionate myriad practices, spiritual powers, and the strength of the Way have filled the realm of sentient beings, severing their delusions and bringing all to complete fulfillment;
one clearly realizes that the fruit of Buddhahood has already been attained within oneself. The wisdom, compassion, vows, and practices of a Bodhisattva never cease;

without departing from a single thought-moment, they fulfill three periods of kalpas, and without leaving a single pore, they pervade the ten directions, the Dharma-realm, and the realm of sentient beings.
Because the clouds of compassion and wisdom simultaneously and universally cover all, it is therefore called the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel.

As for the Dragon King Mānasa: *māna* means "mind" and *sa* means "compassion"; this refers to the fact that when this dragon king raises clouds and sends down rain, it arises from a heart of compassion.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, since these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained such dharmas as are identical to those of all Tathāgatas, for what reason are they not called 'Buddhas'? For what reason are they not called 'Possessors of the Ten Powers'?
For what reason are they not called 'Omniscient Ones' (*sarvajña*)? And for what reason are they not called 'Those who have attained Bodhi within all dharmas'?"
Therefore, it cannot be called the Universal Eye. Why is it not called the unimpeded vision within all objects?
Why is it not called the awakening to all phenomena? Why is it not called dwelling non-dually with the Buddhas of the three periods of time?
Why is it not called dwelling in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)? Why is the cultivation of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra still not yet at rest?
Therefore, they are unable to reach the ultimate limit of the dharma-realm and relinquish the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Puyan Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, son of the Buddha!

As you have said, if these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are identical to all Buddhas, for what reason are they not called 'Buddhas,' and why are they unable to relinquish the bodhisattva path? Son of the Buddha..."
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already been able to cultivate the various practices and vows of all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, entering the realm of wisdom;
thus they are called a Buddha. Because they practice the bodhisattva path in the presence of the Tathāgata without rest, they are called a bodhisattva.
Because they have fully entered all the powers (*bala*) of the Tathāgata, they are called one who possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*), even though they have not yet [fully] attained them.
To practice the conduct of Samantabhadra with tenfold vigor without ceasing is called a bodhisattva;

to know all dharmas and be able to expound them is called omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Although one can expound all dharmas, to skillfully contemplate each and every dharma without ever resting is called a bodhisattva who knows that all dharmas are without dual characteristics. This is...
It is called "Awakening" because it skillfully observes the path that differentiates all phenomena within the non-duality of duality and non-duality, progressing ever further without rest;
it is called a "Bodhisattva" because they have already clearly perceived the realm of the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*);
and although they have attained the realm of the Universal Eye, it continues to increase in every thought-moment without ceasing.
Resting is defined as the Bodhisattva’s ability to clearly illuminate all phenomena, free from all obscurations of darkness;
this is called unimpeded vision (*anāvaraṇa-darśana*). One who constantly and diligently recollects unimpeded vision is said to have already attained the eye of wisdom of all Buddhas;
this is further described as awakening to all phenomena and beholding the eye of the perfectly awakened wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
Heedlessness is termed "the Bodhisattva dwelling where the Buddha dwells. To be called one who dwells non-dually with the Buddha is to be sustained by the Buddha.
To cultivate all forms of wisdom is termed "the Bodhisattva constantly contemplating the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all worlds.
This is what is meant by "dwelling in the reality-limit. Although they constantly observe the reality-limit of all phenomena, they do not...
To enter into realization without abandoning or forsaking it is called the Bodhisattva’s state of neither coming nor going, where distinctions such as similarity or difference are forever stilled;
this is called the resting of vows. When the vast cultivation of these vows is perfected and non-regressive, it is called the "unresting" of the Samantabhadra vows.
This is the thorough understanding that the *dharmadhātu* is without limit or boundary.

That all phenomena are of one mark, which is the markless, is called the ultimate *dharmadhātu*. Although a Bodhisattva abandons the path of a bodhisattva, they know that the *dharmadhātu* has no limits;
yet, knowing all its various distinct marks, they give rise to great compassion and deliver all sentient beings until the end of the future, without weariness.
This is called the Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*) Bodhisattva, O Son of the Buddha.
For example, it is like the elephant king Elāpattra, who dwells in a cave of seven treasures on Mount Suvarṇakukṣi;
the perimeter of that cave is entirely encircled by railings of the seven treasures, with rows of precious tāla trees standing in succession, and a net of pure gold covers it from above.
The elephant’s body is as pure white as jade or snow, and atop it stands a golden banner adorned with golden tassels.
His trunk was covered with a net of jewels, and jeweled bells hung down from it. He possessed the seven limbs of perfection and was endowed with six tusks;
he was upright, full, and pleasing to behold, causing all who saw him to rejoice. He was well-trained, gentle, and compliant, his mind free of any contrary intent.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, desired to travel abroad, the Elephant King immediately understood his intention and, vanishing his form within a jeweled cave, proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Before the Lord of the Śākyas, by means of his supernormal powers, he manifested various transformations so that his body came to have thirty-three heads;
on each head were produced six tusks, on each tusk seven ponds, within each pond seven lotuses,
and within each lotus seven celestial maidens, who all simultaneously performed hundreds of thousands of divine musical performances.
At that time, Śakra, riding upon this precious elephant, departed from the Vaijayanta Palace and proceeded to a flower garden where *pundarīka* lotuses were everywhere in abundance.
Having arrived at the flower garden, Śakra descended from the elephant and entered the Palace Adorned with All Jewels,
where he enjoyed various pleasures accompanied by a retinue of countless celestial maidens who sang and played music.
At that time, the Elephant King again used his supernormal powers to conceal his elephant form and manifest as a celestial being;
together with the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens and their various court ladies, he enjoyed himself and sported within the Puṇḍarīka Lotus Garden.
His manifested physical appearance, radiance, garments, movements, comings and goings, speech, laughter, and manner of gazing were all identical to those of the gods, without any difference.
There is no one capable of distinguishing whether this is an elephant or a celestial being, for the elephant and the deity are mutually similar. O Son of the Buddha,
that elephant king Airāvaṇa, without undergoing any transformation while within the seven-jeweled cave on Mount Kāñcanaparvata,
ascends to the realm of the Thirty-three Gods and manifests various kinds of things worthy of offering out of a desire to make offerings to Śakra Devendra.
Delighting in the objects of experience, they receive celestial bliss no different from that of the devas. So too it is with the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:
they cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as well as various samādhis to serve as ornaments of manifold jewels;
they take the seven factors of enlightenment as the body of the Bodhisattva, and the light they emit as its net, thereby establishing the Great Dharma.
The great Dharma-bell rings from the banner; Great Compassion is its cave, and firm Great Vows are its tusks.
With wisdom and fearlessness like a lion, the dharma-scarf is bound upon its head. It reveals the secrets and reaches the further shore of the practices and vows of all Bodhisattvas.
Desiring to establish itself upon the seat of enlightenment, it attains All-Knowledge and Supreme Perfect Awakening, increasing [the benefit] universally.
The noble and vast practice of vows is non-retrogressive, unceasing, uninterrupted, and never forsaken; through the vigor of great compassion,
it delivers all suffering beings until the end of the future, never abandoning the path of Samantabhadra, manifesting the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment,
manifesting unspeakably unspeakable gateways to the realization of perfect enlightenment, and manifesting unspeakably unspeakable turnings of the wheel of Dharma.
They manifest gates of dwelling in the profound mind, unspeakably unspeakable;
they manifest gates of the transformation of nirvana in unspeakably unspeakable vast lands;
they manifest birth in unspeakably unspeakable diverse worlds to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra; and they manifest unspeakably unspeakable Tathāgatas within the unspeakable...
He speaks of attaining supreme perfect enlightenment beneath bodhi trees in unspeakably vast lands,
surrounded by assemblies of unspeakably many bodhisattvas; or of attaining perfect enlightenment by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra in a single thought-moment,
or in a brief instant, or at one time, or in a single day, or in a half-month, or...
For one month, or for one year, or for countless years, or for one kalpa— and thus even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—
they cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and attain perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, they act as the foremost leaders within all Buddha-fields,
drawing near to the Buddhas, prostrating, making offerings, inquiring, and observing that all things are like illusions.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas purify the realms and cultivate immeasurable bodhisattva practices,
immeasurable wisdoms, various miraculous transformations, various majestic virtues, various forms of knowledge, various spheres of experience, various supernormal powers,
various masteries, various liberations, various illuminations of the Dharma, and various methods for teaching and subduing sentient beings.
One's own essence is not extinguished, yet through the power of practice and vows, one manifests in this way in all places.
Why is this? It is because one desires to subdue all sentient beings through the sovereign spiritual powers of Samantabhadra;
to cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to attain purity; to cause them to forever sever the wheel of birth and death; and to adorn and purify the vast expanse.
Because they traverse all worlds; because they constantly behold all Tathāgatas; because they enter deeply into the stream of all Buddha-dharmas;
because they recollect the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they recollect all Buddha-dharmas and the Dharma-body of the ten directions;
because they universally cultivate all bodhisattva practices to bring them to fulfillment; and because they enter the stream of Samantabhadra to attain mastery.
"O Son of the Buddha, because of his omniscience, you should observe this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:

he does not abandon the conduct of Samantabhadra nor interrupt the path of the Bodhisattvas; seeing all Buddhas and realizing omniscience, he enjoys the mastery of all-knowledge dharmas, just as the elephant king Airāvaṇa, without abandoning his elephant body, goes to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to be honored by the gods."

Riding upon the experience of celestial bliss, engaging in divine play, serving the Lord of Devas, and sporting with celestial maidens, they enjoy themselves without any distinction from the other gods.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise:
not abandoning the various practices of Samantabhadra’s Great Vehicle, never retreating from his vows, attaining the sovereignty of a Buddha, and being endowed with all-knowledge.
Having realized the Buddha’s liberation, they are unobstructed and unhindered, achieving purity; they are unstained by any lands and free from discrimination regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Although they know that all phenomena are universally equal and devoid of dual characteristics, they constantly and clearly perceive all Buddha-lands.
Though they have already become identical to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they continue to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.

O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who abide in such vast dharmas of the Samantabhadra vows and practices with an uninterrupted continuity of conduct should know that the minds of these people have attained purity.
O Sons of the Buddha, this is the tenth, the Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel, the supreme mind and vast wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. O Sons of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva...
The Ten Great Samādhi Wheels of the Universal Worthy Conduct wherein the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells.

[Treatise] Chapter Eleven: At that time, from the point where the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*) addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*), continuing until the end of the forty-third fascicle, it clarifies how the Bodhisattva Universal Eye questioned the Bodhisattva Universal Worthy regarding such bodhisattvas.
Why is he not called "Buddha" nor "One Possessing the Ten Powers," but rather named "Airāvaṇa Elephant King Dwelling on Mount Kāñcanaparvata"?
*Airāvaṇa* is translated here as "Fragrant Leaves" (*Gandhaparṇa*);
it is so named because there are many fragrant leaf trees near his jeweled cave. Furthermore, he can manifest thirty-three heads, each with six tusks.
Upon each tusk, seven ponds are manifested; within each pond, seven lotus flowers are manifested.
Taking one of these manifested lotuses, whose leaves are fragrant and pure, he uses it as his name. He dwells on the flank of the foremost Golden Mountain;
knowing when Śakra intends to go on a journey, he sinks here and emerges in the heavens to escort Śakra to his garden.
When going out for excursions, he transforms his own body to resemble that of a celestial being;
when returning to the palace, he transforms back into the body of an elephant to escort Śakra back to the palace, and then vanishes from the heavens to emerge from within a precious cave.
This illustration clarifies that although this bodhisattva has already attained the rank of Buddhahood, he does not abandon the practice of skillful means, just like that king of elephants.
Although he is able to manifest his body as a deva, he never loses his fundamental status as an elephant; the remaining extensive meanings are fully detailed in the text of the sutra.

The above ten concentrations consist of eleven sections of text, clarifying that from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment through the attainment of Buddhahood, from birth to entry into nirvana, all are fundamentally embodied within this single moment (*kṣaṇa*), extending even back to antiquity.
Now, because all Buddhas likewise attain Buddhahood simultaneously as a whole, for sentient beings, the extension or brevity of their lives—
when considered in relation to the Truth— is without beginning or end. Furthermore, it clarifies that these eleven chapters of this single assembly collectively elucidate the path of Samantabhadra,
the unimpeded expedient practice leading to the fruit of Buddhahood according to each stage, just as from the stage of the Ten Faiths onward, one mounts the fundamental [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.

The arising of wisdom, the practice of the vows of Samantabhadra, the teaching and transforming of sentient beings, and the refinement of one's own wisdom until it becomes pure and clear—just as the metaphor of refining true gold through the ten stages of smelting—all these do not depart from the essence of this samādhi.
Now that one has reached the eleventh bhūmi and beyond, the polishing of one's own wisdom is complete; thereupon, one consists entirely of benefiting sentient beings.

Because this is the practice of Samantabhadra, these ten chapters on meditative concentration synthesize the time from the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and the beginningless past up until the moment all Buddhas attain Buddhahood;
they show that the kalpas do not pass, that the fruit of Buddhahood and the skillful means of Samantabhadra’s practice have neither beginning nor end,
and that while his physical and mental activities fill the ten directions throughout the kalpas, he does not depart from a single pore, nor does he leave the present moment.
Because there is no transmigration, all ages of the past, present, and future throughout the kalpas are entirely encompassed by these ten stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Sentient beings are deluded and falsely perceive them as being extended or abbreviated; yet when they resolve their delusion and return to the source, these ten stages of concentration are the fundamental essence—the eternal Way that is neither extended nor abbreviated, which has been thus from the beginning.

Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Supernatural Powers [Śāstra] In explaining this chapter, there are two sections for analysis: first, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion; second, the word-by-word commentary on the text. 1. Explanation of the Purpose for Its Inclusion:
This is to clarify that while the preceding chapter was the "Ten Samādhis," this chapter clarifies how to give rise to functional activity through those samādhis.

Regarding the ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) [mentioned] in the second section, the "Explanation of the Meaning According to the Text," this clarifies that there are indeed ten kinds of supernormal powers.
These ten powers are detailed as follows, as clearly explained in the text.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the Bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What are the ten?

Sons of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know the distinctions among the minds of sentient beings within a single trichiliocosm. That is to say, they know wholesome minds, unwholesome..."

Wholesome mind, expansive mind, narrow mind, great mind, small mind, mind that accords with birth and death, mind that turns away from birth and death, the mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha,
the mind of a bodhisattva, the conduct of a śrāvaka, the conduct of a pratyekabuddha, the conduct of a bodhisattva,
the mind of a deva, the mind of a nāga, the mind of a yakṣa, the mind of a gandharva, the mind of an asura, the mind of a garuḍa, the mind of a kiṃnara...
The mind of a *rākṣasa*, the mind of a *mahoraga*, the mind of a human, the mind of a non-human, the mind of those in hell, the mind of animals,
the mind of those in the realm of King Yama, the mind of hungry ghosts, and the minds of sentient beings in various states of adversity— thus,
he discerns and knows all such immeasurable varieties of the minds of diverse sentient beings. As with one world, so it is with a hundred worlds and a thousand worlds.
To know the minds of all sentient beings within hundreds of thousands of worlds, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds,
and even within as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—
this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s first supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*).

[Treatise] The first section consists of thirteen and a half lines of scripture, which clarify the total enumeration of the ten types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and present the great function of the first among them, the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*).
As for King Yama, this is called "The Obstructer" (*Yama*), meaning he obstructs and restrains;
it is so named because he restrains and exhorts transgressors so that they may be freed from suffering.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal power of the unimpeded, pure divine eye, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields: the deaths and births of sentient beings in good and evil realms;
their marks of merit and their marks of transgression; whether they are handsome or ugly, defiled or pure—such are the various categories he beholds.
Immeasurable sentient beings, namely: the assembly of devas, the assembly of nāgas, the assembly of yakṣas, the assembly of gandharvas,
the assembly of asuras, the assembly of garuḍas, the assembly of kiṃnaras, the assembly of mahoragas, the assembly of humans, the assembly of non-humans,
the assembly of sentient beings with subtle bodies, the assembly of sentient beings with vast bodies, the assembly of the small, and the assembly of the great— such various assemblies.

Born among the multitude, with unimpeded vision they clearly perceive everything: according to the karma accumulated, according to the suffering and pleasure experienced, according to the mind, according to conceptualization, according to views, according to speech, according to causes, according to karma, according to objects of perception, and according to that which arises—they see all of these without error.
This is called the second unimpeded power of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The Supernormal Power of the Knowledge of the Celestial Eye.
[Treatise] The second section contains eleven lines of scripture clarifying the great function of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the celestial eye.
[Sutra] O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to know his own self and...
The past lives of all sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—

namely, that they were born in such-and-such a place, with such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage, such-and-such food and drink, and such-and-such suffering and happiness over the course of kalpas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields— [he knows].

Since beginningless time, within the various realms of existence, they have grown and increased through causes and conditions, succeeding one another in a continuous succession of samsara without interruption—
manifesting in various categories, various lands, various destinies of birth,
various forms, various karmic actions, various fetters and afflictions, various mental states, and various causal conditions for the distinctions of rebirth.
He fully understands all these matters and further recollects that in as many eons as there are atoms in those Buddha-fields,
within as many worlds as there are atoms in those Buddha-fields, there were as many Buddhas as there are atoms in those Buddha-fields;
for each and every Buddha, he knows their names, how they appeared in the world, their assemblies, and their parents.
The attendant [should say]: "In this manner, such śrāvakas— these two most excellent great disciples—
having gone forth in such a city, attained supreme perfect enlightenment beneath such a bodhi tree,
sat upon such a seat in such a place, and expounded such various sūtras, thereby benefiting so many sentient beings."

I am able to recollect all such things as the duration of my life during that time, the various Buddha-deeds I performed, and how I entered parinirvāṇa by relying on the realm of nirvana without remainder;
furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, the length of time for which the Dharma remained, and so forth—all this I can remember.
Moreover, I can recollect the names of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably, unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Each and every name has as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;

from their initial aspiration, through their making of vows, their practice, their making offerings to all Buddhas, their taming of sentient beings, their assemblies, their preaching of the Dharma, the duration of their lifespans, their supernatural transformations,
and even until their entry into *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and the duration of the Dharma’s abiding after their *parinirvāṇa*.
To be able to know all the various ways in which stūpas and temples were constructed and adorned over the long or short term, causing all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness—
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s third supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), the wisdom of knowing past lives throughout the kalpas of the past.

[Treatise] The third section, consisting of twenty-four and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the great function of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*).
[Sutra] O Son of the Buddha, by means of the knowledge that knows all kalpas extending to the end of the future, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva realizes the unconditioned...
He speaks of all the kalpas within as many world-systems as there are atoms in an unspeakable number of Buddha-fields;
and within each kalpa, he speaks of all the lifespans, deaths, births, and the continuity of existence for all sentient beings, as well as their karmic actions and their fruits and retributions—
whether wholesome or unwholesome, whether leading to liberation or not, whether determinate or indeterminate, and whether fixed in error or fixed in correctness.
Whether wholesome roots are accompanied by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) or not accompanied by latent tendencies;
whether wholesome roots are complete or incomplete; whether wholesome roots are grasped or not grasped; whether wholesome roots are accumulated or not accumulated;
or whether unwholesome dharmas are accumulated or not accumulated—in this manner, it is one.
They are able to fully comprehend all of this; furthermore, they know that throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
extending to the end of the future, there are unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas as numerous as the atoms in Buddha-fields,
and in each and every kalpa, there are unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, with the name of each and every one of them.

There are Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields; for each and every one of these Tathāgatas, from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment,
their arising of vows, their establishment of practices, their making of offerings, their teaching and transforming of sentient beings, their assemblies, their preaching of the Dharma,
the duration of their lifespans, their supernormal powers and transformations, and even until their entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and the period following their *parinirvāṇa*.

To be able to fully know such matters as the duration for which the Dharma will abide, the construction of stupas and temples, and their various adornments that cause all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness—
this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fourth supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*),
the wisdom that knows the kalpas extending to the end of the future.

[Treatise] The fourth section, consisting of eighteen lines of scripture, clearly elucidates the great function of the supernormal knowledge of the intellect (*jñāna-abhijñā*) that extends through all kalpas until the end of the future.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes the unimpeded, pure, perfect, and vast divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
With penetrating intelligence free from obscurations, they have realized and mastered all things without hindrance;

they are fully accomplished in the mastery of hearing or not hearing any sound whatsoever according to their own will. O Son of the Buddha, in the eastern direction there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
that which has been spoken, shown, revealed, expounded, and established by all those Buddhas—
Regarding all those dharmas that are for the purpose of conversion, for subduing, for recollection, and for discernment— those which are profound, vast, diverse in their distinctions,
characterized by immeasurable skillful means and immeasurable ingenuity, and utterly pure— they are able to receive and uphold them all;
furthermore, within them, whether it be the meaning or the phrasing, whether it be for a single person or a great assembly, they accord with their respective languages and their respective wisdoms.
With wisdom, they are able to comprehend, manifest, discipline, and master all things— according to their spheres of activity,
their bases, and their paths of emergence— retaining them all without forgetting, losing, interrupting, or regressing, and without confusion or delusion;
they explain them to others so that they may attain realization, never failing to preserve even a single word or a single phrase.
Just as it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir;
this is called the fifth unimpeded, pure supernormal power of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s divine ear-knowledge.
[Treatise] The fifth section, comprising thirteen and a half lines of scripture, elucidates the great function of the supernormal power of the perfected divine ear.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in the supernormal power of non-substantiality and the supernormal power of non-action, which are equal.

The bodhisattva hears the names of all Buddhas in all worlds, however far away, through these [powers]: the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), the power of vast supernormal knowledge, the power of immeasurable supernormal knowledge, the power of non-reliant supernormal knowledge, the power of supernormal knowledge according to thought, the power of arising supernormal knowledge, the power of non-arising supernormal knowledge, the power of non-retrogressive supernormal knowledge, the power of uninterrupted supernormal knowledge, the power of indestructible supernormal knowledge, the power of increasing supernormal knowledge, and the power of supernormal knowledge that goes wherever it is directed. Upon hearing these names of the Buddhas, this bodhisattva...
This refers to the names of all Buddhas in countless worlds, immeasurable worlds, and even in worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
having heard their names, one immediately perceives oneself present before those Buddhas in those various worlds,
which may be upright or inverted, each with its own distinct form, location, and particular characteristics.
In infinite, unimpeded, and diverse buddha-lands, across various eons and with immeasurable merits individually adorning them,
those respective Tathāgatas appear therein, manifesting supernatural transformations and proclaiming their names;
though these are immeasurable, innumerable, and each distinct, this bodhisattva, upon hearing the names of all those Tathāgatas, remains unmoved from his original place.
He saw his own body at the place of that Buddha, paying homage, showing respect, serving, and making offerings; he inquired about the Dharma of Bodhisattvas and entered the wisdom of the Buddhas,
fully comprehending all Buddha-lands, sites of enlightenment, assemblies, and the teachings therein,
reaching the ultimate point without any grasping or attachment— thus for as many unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields as there are atoms of dust.

For many eons, he has universally reached the ten directions without actually going anywhere; yet he visits lands, beholds Buddhas, listens to the Dharma, and requests the Way without interruption, without cessation, without rest, and without weariness.
He cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva and fulfills his great vows, making them all complete and never regressing, so as to ensure that the vast lineage of the Tathāgata shall not perish.

Because it is severed, this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s sixth dwelling: the supernormal knowledge of proceeding to all Buddha-fields through the wisdom of the absence of intrinsic nature and the absence of activity.
[Treatise] This sixth section consists of twenty and a half lines of scripture, clarifying the arising of the supernormal knowledge that dwells in the absence of intrinsic nature.
The Thirteenth Great Function of Supernormal Power:
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, by means of the wisdom that skillfully discerns the vocal sounds of all sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows the various languages of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields."
The speech referred to here includes the speech of sages, the speech of non-sages, the speech of devas, the speech of nāgas,
the speech of yakṣas, the speech of gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans,
even down to the speech of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings— each expressing its own various meanings.
He is able to fully comprehend all such distinctions; according to whichever world this bodhisattva enters,
he can know all the inclinations and dispositions of the sentient beings therein, and he utters speech in accordance with those dispositions so that they all understand it without any doubt,
just as when the sun rises and shines universally upon all forms, enabling those with eyes to see them all.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhādarśana is likewise; through the wisdom that skillfully distinguishes all speech, he penetrates the clouds of all speech and causes all those in the world who possess intelligence to fully understand every word.
This is called the seventh [perfection] of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: skillfully distinguishing all speech.
