[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya physical bodies as adornments.

With wisdom they know that all phenomena are far removed from the marks of form, being without marks of differentiation, without marks of variety, without marks of measurelessness, without marks of conceptualization, and without marks of blue, yellow, red, or white.
In this way, the Bodhisattva enters the Dharma-realm and is able to manifest their body in various colors, namely: boundless color, immeasurable color, pure color, and adorned color.
Resplendent color; universally pervasive color; incomparable color; universally illuminating color; surpassing color; non-opposing color;
endowed with all marks color; free from all evils color; of great majestic power color; worthy of reverence color; inexhaustible color;
manifold and wondrous color; extremely sublime and dignified color; immeasurable color; well-guarded color; able to bring to maturity color; conforming to transformation color.

This is the form that is unobstructed; the form that is profoundly transparent; the form that is free from defilement and turbidity; the form that is utterly pure and serene; the form of great heroic vigor;
the form of inconceivable skillful means; the form that is indestructible; the form free from blemish and obscuration; the form free from hindrance and darkness;
the form well-established; the form of sublime adornment; the form with all marks perfectly dignified; the form with various secondary characteristics; the form of great majesty.
The color of noble form; the color of wondrous realms; the color of well-polished brilliance; the color of pure and profound resolve;

the color of blazing and magnificent radiance; the color of supreme vastness; the color of uninterrupted continuity; the color of non-reliance; the color of peerless comparison; the color that fills unspeakable Buddha-fields;
the color of increasing growth; the color of firm and sustaining grasp; the color of supreme merit; the color that accords with all...
The mind delights in form; it is the purity of form, the understanding of the accumulation of forms, the skillful mastery of manifold exquisite forms,
the certainty regarding forms, the absence of obstruction in forms, the luminous clarity of space-like forms, the pure and delightful forms,

the forms free from all dust and defilement, the immeasurable forms, the forms of wondrous vision, the forms of universal vision, the forms manifested according to the occasion, the tranquil forms, and the forms free from craving.
The color of a true field of merit; the color capable of producing tranquility; the color free from all fears; the color free from the conduct of ignorance; the color of wisdom and valor;
the color of physical marks that are unimpeded; the color of universal wandering; the color of a mind that has no dependence;
the color arisen from great loving-kindness; the color manifested by great compassion; the color of impartial renunciation; and the color endowed with merit.
The color of infinite forms recollected according to one’s mind; the color of a treasury of jewels of exquisite hues; the color of light; the color of beings’ faith and delight;
the color of the manifestation of omniscience; the color of eyes of joy; the foremost color adorned with all kinds of jewels;
the color that has no location; the color of sovereign manifestation; the color of various supernatural powers; the color of being born into the family of the Tathāgata; surpassing all metaphors.
The metaphorical forms that pervade the Dharma-realm; the forms to which all multitudes of beings go; the forms of various kinds; the forms of accomplishment; the forms of transcendence;
the forms of majestic deportment according to those to be converted; the forms that one never tires of beholding; the forms of various pure luminosities;
the forms capable of emitting countless nets of light; the forms of unspeakably many varieties of radiant light; and the inconceivable fragrant lights.
The color of the light of the solar disc that transcends the three realms and is immeasurable; the color of the manifestation of the incomparable lunar body;
the color of immeasurable, lovely clouds of flowers; the color of the adornment of various clouds of lotus garlands that arise;
the color of the fragrant flames that surpass all worlds and universally perfume; and the color from which the treasury of all Tathāgatas arises.
Form is ineffable, yet it is revealed, elucidated, and expounded through sound; it manifests all dharmas and is endowed with all the practices of Samantabhadra.

O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have deeply entered such a formless dharma-realm are able to manifest these various bodies of form, causing those to be transformed to see them, causing those to be transformed to remember them, and turning the wheel of Dharma for those to be transformed.

The Wheel of Dharma follows those to be converted according to their timing and according to their characteristics; it causes those to be converted to draw near, it causes those to be converted to attain awakening,
it gives rise to various supernormal powers for the sake of those to be converted, it manifests various forms of mastery for the sake of those to be converted,
and it bestows various efficacious deeds upon those to be converted— this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s [practice] for the purpose of liberation.
"For the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently cultivates and accomplishes the eighth [stage]: the wisdom, supernormal powers, and physical bodies of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

[Treatise] This section concerning the eighth [stage] consists of forty-one lines of scripture that clarify the great function of the wisdom and supernormal powers for manifesting the adornments of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* physical bodies.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, by means of the wisdom that knows all phenomena, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understands that all phenomena are without names and without lineage;
they neither come nor go; they are neither different nor not different; neither manifold nor not manifold; neither dual nor non-dual;
they are without self and without peer; they are neither born nor extinguished; they are unmoving and indestructible.
It is truly non-existent and not false; it is one mark, which is markless; it is neither non-existence nor existence; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma;
it does not follow the conventional, yet it is not that it does not follow the conventional; it is neither karma nor non-karma; it is neither retribution nor non-retribution;
it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither the ultimate truth nor not the ultimate truth; it is neither the path nor non-path; it is neither transcendence nor non-transcendence.
This bodhisattva does not grasp at that which is neither non-measure nor immeasurable, neither mundane nor supramundane, neither born from causes nor not born from causes,
neither determinate nor indeterminate, neither accomplished nor unaccomplished, neither emerging nor non-emerging,
neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized, and neither conformable to reason nor non-conformable to reason.
While not abiding in conventional truth, they do not differentiate among phenomena nor establish verbal designations; they accord with the nature of quiescence and do not abandon any vows.
Seeing the meaning and knowing the Dharma, they spread the clouds of Dharma and pour down the rain of Dharma.
Although they know that the true mark is ineffable, they employ inexhaustible eloquence through skillful means to follow both the letter and the meaning.
He expounds the teachings in successive order, having attained skillful mastery in the verbal expression and discourse regarding all phenomena;
his great loving-kindness and great compassion are entirely purified, enabling him to produce words from within all wordless dharmas.

In accordance with and without contradiction to both the phenomena and their meanings, he explains that all dharmas arise from conditions; thus, although there is verbal expression, there is nothing [ultimately] expressed.
They manifest inexhaustible eloquence in expounding all dharmas, analytically establishing, developing, and guiding them so that the nature of all phenomena is fully revealed;
they sever the net of doubts for all beings until it is entirely purified.

While gathering in sentient beings, they do not abandon ultimate reality, and they never regress from the non-dual dharma, constantly able to expound the unimpeded gates of Dharma through manifold wonders.
The sound follows the minds of sentient beings, universally raining down the rain of Dharma without missing its proper time;
this is called the ninth supernormal power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the wisdom of all dharmas.
[Treatise] This ninth section, consisting of twenty-two and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the supernormal power of the wisdom of all dharmas.
This great function clarifies how, based on the fundamental wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*),
all differentiated wisdoms arise. [Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal power of the wisdom of the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena in every thought-moment, yet does not retreat from the Bodhisattva path nor abandon the Bodhisattva [vows].
In their practice, they do not abandon the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion; they cultivate the *pāramitās* without ever resting; they observe all Buddha-lands without weariness;
they do not abandon the vow to deliver sentient beings; they do not cease the turning of the wheel of Dharma; they do not neglect the activity of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
they do not abandon the practice of making offerings to all Buddhas; and they do not relinquish all dharmas themselves.
At the gateway, they do not abandon the constant vision of all Buddhas; they do not abandon the constant hearing of all Dharmas;
they know that all Dharmas are equal, unimpeded, and sovereign; they achieve all supreme vows pertaining to the Buddha-dharmas and bring them to full completion;
they thoroughly understand the distinctions between all lands; they enter the lineage of the Buddhas and reach the further shore; and they are able, in each and every [place]...
In all worlds, this bodhisattva studies all dharmas and realizes that dharmas are without marks; he understands that all dharmas arise from conditions and possess no intrinsic nature.
Nevertheless, he expounds various dharmas through skillful means according to worldly conventions.

Although his mind dwells nowhere amidst these dharmas, he accords with the faculties, inclinations, and desires of sentient beings, teaching them various dharmas through skillful means. This is the dwelling of the bodhisattva.
At the time of samādhi, according to the inclination of his mind, he may abide for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas,
or ten billion kalpas, or a hundred billion kalpas, or a thousand billion kalpas, or a hundred thousand billion kalpas,
or ten million nayutas of kalpas, or a hundred nayutas of kalpas, or a thousand nayutas of kalpas.
For ten billion kalpas, or perhaps for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of billions of kalpas, or for incalculable kalpas, or for immeasurable kalpas,
and even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, the bodhisattva enters this samādhi of the extinction of all phenomena;
although he remains for such a duration of kalpas, his body does not disintegrate, nor does it become emaciated.
This transformation is neither seen nor unseen, neither extinguished nor destroyed, neither weary nor lax, and it is inexhaustible.
Although it performs no action whatsoever regarding either existence or non-existence, it is nonetheless able to accomplish all the deeds of a bodhisattva;
that is to say, it never abandons any sentient being, but constantly teaches and tames them without ever missing the proper time, causing them all to grow and flourish.
The Buddha-dharma attains complete perfection within the bodhisattva practices; desiring to benefit all sentient beings, his supernormal powers and transformations never cease.
Like light or a shadow, they manifest everywhere, yet he remains unmoving and tranquil within samādhi.
This is the wisdom and supernormal power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who enters the samādhi of the extinction of all phenomena.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in these ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
they cannot be conceived by any gods or humans, they cannot be conceived by any sentient beings, they cannot be conceived by any Śrāvakas, any Pratyekabuddhas,
or any other assembly of Bodhisattvas; thus, the physical actions (*kāyakarman*) of this Bodhisattva are entirely inconceivable.
His verbal karma is inconceivable, his mental karma is inconceivable, his mastery over samādhi is inconceivable, and the sphere of his wisdom is inconceivable.
Except for the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have attained such supernormal powers, no one else is able to describe, extol, or praise the merits of this son of the Buddha. This is what it means.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of supernormal powers; if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these supernormal powers, they fully attain the supernormal power of unimpeded knowledge throughout all three periods of time.

[Treatise] The tenth section, consisting of thirty-five and a half lines of scripture, clarifies the great function of the supernormal power of wisdom (*jñāna-abhijñā*) through the *sarvadharma-kṣaya-samādhi*.

This section clarifies that within the principle of the quiescent extinction of the *dharmatā*, one constantly gives rise to the great functions of great wisdom and great compassion to benefit sentient beings;
thus, the nature [of these powers] is perfected. All ten of these supernormal powers mentioned above are inconceivable.
The Dharma-gate of the infinite, tranquil function arising from the great sovereign wisdom of non-action, unimpeded, and limitless—
which enters the realm of the Indra-net in its manifold layers of sovereignty— cannot be conceptualized as the limited views of the three vehicles.
For example, Aniruddha, with my divine eye, I see the trichiliocosm as if looking at [an object in] my hand.

The *āmala* fruit in the palm [of the hand] and so forth are like the provisional teachings of the Bodhisattvas, who perceive the coming and going between their own and others' Buddha-lands as having limits;
therefore, this refers to the Dharma-body, which is limitless and without interior, exterior, or middle. The Wisdom-body is likewise, being universally limitless.
Because it functions through the重重 (repeatedly layered) great manifestations within the Indra-net, it is generally defined according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The All-Knowing Heaven is not like the divine powers of sight and hearing possessed by those in the higher realms of the world, nor like the supernormal powers of the Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Pure Lands of the Three Vehicles; for, abiding in a body of supernormal power that is devoid of intrinsic nature,
it never departs from its original location while [simultaneously] pervading all Buddha-lands and all lands of sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

All manifest sovereign bodies as well as from their pores; the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and consciousness are entirely one body and one nature, like the Indra’s net where all images mutually contain one another, devoid of the nature of coming, going, self, or other.
These ten penetrations are thus all-pervasive and thus thoroughly penetrating; this is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Because one uses wisdom to penetrate universally and knows all things by virtue of their being of the same nature as oneself, it is called "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*);
it is not because of coming and going or seeing others. These ten concentrations, ten supernatural powers, and ten patiences are the final stages of the ten grounds;
they are skillful means for entering into birth and death to benefit sentient beings, and they are also the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences.

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*), as well as the five positions (*pañcasthāna*) where these are cultivated in common, along with their remaining meanings, are fully contained within the scriptural text itself.

**Chapter Twenty-nine: The Chapter on the Ten Patiences (*Daśakṣānti-varga*)** [Treatise] In order to explain this chapter, it is divided into three sections: first, the explanation of the title of the chapter; second, the explanation of the purpose for its inclusion.
Third, the explanation of the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter:

it clarifies that this chapter encompasses the gate of practice for ascending from one’s own stage starting from the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), and it also encompasses the skillful means for accomplishing the practice of benefiting sentient beings after attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.

It establishes its name based on the patience (*kṣānti*) that accords with such practice. If, according to the provisional teachings, one considers the stages prior to the Bodhisattva grounds (*bhūmi*):

It is only upon entering the path of seeing on the stages of the *kṣānti* (patience) that one truly enters into accordance with the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena).

However, if one considers the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) to be accessible from the initial mind of the ten stages, then attaining the "gate of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas through mindfulness" is called "being born into the family of Buddha-wisdom," and it is also called "attaining the *ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*" (patience following the sound), which is likewise termed "accordance with the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. This is merely because the names differ according to the specific practice. For now, let us leave it at that.

Regarding the initial stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one is born into the family of the Buddha’s wisdom; this is designated as the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) that accords with the Buddha’s correct wisdom.
Within the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), it is designated as the "patience of non-arising" that acts in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom.

Within the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), by means of the integration of principle and wisdom, one gives rise to the gate of great compassion through infinite great vows, thereby harmonizing and fusing with principle.

Great wisdom and great compassion cause [the practitioner] to become balanced and harmonious; this is called the "harmonious integration" (*saṃbheda*) of great vows, great compassion, and great wisdom—the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in both quiescence and activity.
This is the practice that accords with the patient acceptance of non-arising prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

From the first stage through the third stage, taking these three preceding stages as a whole, one practices by synthesizing them into a single method; this is called the cultivation and nourishment of wisdom and compassion.

Through the fulfillment of habitual practice, based on the first stage (*bhūmi*) and the preceding ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), and ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), one’s great vows are perfected.
One gives rise to the resolve to constantly remain within birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to protect sentient beings; for this reason, it is also called "conformity-patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Upon reaching the eighth stage, one attains "non-arising patience" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thus, the youth Sudhana thoroughly understands the first stage.
The consciousness is named *Vasanta-dhṛti*; this means "Lord of the Sprouting of Crops in Spring.

It is also named "Abiding in Fearlessness," which clarifies that it is the lord who presides over the sprouts of the Bodhi-mind first generated by sentient beings, and it is also named "Lord who Acts as a Refuge for Sentient Beings to Render Them Fearless. This is the vow of the Bodhisattva prior to the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Because one practices within the realm of sentient beings through the power [of the first stage], on the second stage one clearly cultivates the ten superior and supreme precepts of good conduct to eliminate the afflictions and habitual tendencies of the desire realm so that they become non-attached;
on the third stage one cultivates the eight dhyānas and nine samāpattis of the higher realms to ensure non-attachment to the realm of dhyāna.
This is called conforming to the benefit of principle and wisdom while nurturing great compassion for the sake of the mundane, thereby following the path of non-attachment.

The patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*) is clearly elucidated in the fourth stage, where one is further clarified as being born into the family of the Buddha (*jinakula*) and remaining undefiled by the three realms (*tridhātu*).

In the fifth stage, through the gateway of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one generates skillful wisdom (*kauśalyajñāna*) and cultivates worldly arts and crafts. In the sixth stage, having cultivated both worldly and supramundane wisdom, one brings an end to the meditative absorptions;
the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) manifest before one, which is termed the patience of cessation (*nirodhakṣānti*). In the seventh stage, it is constant...

Abiding in birth and death, one practices until the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) is perfected; having brought to an end the effortful practice of the bodhisattva path, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In the ninth stage, through the rank of Dharma Master, one clarifies the teaching of the Dharma and attains mastery in its application.

In the tenth stage, the Buddha-activity reaches its partial completion. Once the conduct of Samantabhadra is fulfilled in the eleventh stage, that which follows consists purely of the state of the Perfectly Enlightened Tathāgata.

Apart from the Bodhisattva’s skillful means for saving sentient beings, these ten kinds of patience (kṣānti)—if discussed in terms of advancement through the ten stages (bhūmi)—yield one patience per stage;
the same applies to the ten concentrations (samādhi) and the ten supernormal powers (abhijñā).

Furthermore, regarding the stages of endurance, these are established as the titles of chapters within the practices of Samantabhadra; they also correspond to the positions of progressive cultivation according to each stage.

The merit of cultivation establishes names according to one's practice; this is titled the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (10). Regarding the intent behind the second chapter, the "Explanatory Chapter":
since the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) have already been discussed previously, this [chapter] treats the powers in relation to patience (*kṣānti*).

If there were no divine wisdom and penetration, one would merely achieve the "Patience of Subjugation" (*vinaya-kṣānti*), and the "Dharma-patience" (*dharma-kṣānti*) would not arise. Therefore, this chapter must follow; it concerns the accomplishment of patience prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the "pervasion" within the eleven stages: because pervasion constitutes patience (*kṣānti*), these ten concentrations (*samādhi*), ten penetrations (*abhijñā*), and ten patiences are the functional manifestations of a single virtue.
Third, as for the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the following ten sections clarify the ten kinds of patience.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of patience for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If one attains these patiences, one reaches the stage of all bodhisattvas’ unimpeded patience, wherein all Buddha-dharmas are unimpeded and inexhaustible.
What are the ten? They are: patience toward sounds, conformative patience, and patience toward the non-arising [of phenomena]."

The patience of phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*), the patience like an illusion, the patience like a flame, the patience like a dream, the patience like an echo, the patience like a shadow, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space—these ten kinds of patience have been taught by the Buddhas of the three times, are being taught now, and will be taught in the future.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience toward sounds? It is when, upon hearing the Dharma spoken by all Buddhas, one is not startled.

To be without fear or dread, to have deep faith and realization, to delight in and incline toward it, to recollect it with single-mindedness, and to cultivate and abide therein—this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s first patience regarding sounds. Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s patience of conformity?
It refers to reflecting upon and examining all phenomena, perceiving them as equal and non-contradictory, and understanding them through such conformity.
To cause the mind to be pure, correctly established, cultivated, entered into, and perfected—this is called the second conformative patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon arising, nor does he perceive even the slightest phenomenon ceasing. Why is this?
Therefore, if there is no arising, there is no ceasing; if there is no ceasing, there is no exhaustion; if there is no exhaustion, there is freedom from defilement;
if there is freedom from defilement, there is no differentiation; if there is no differentiation, there is no location; if there is no location, there is tranquility;
if there is tranquility, there is freedom from desire; if there is freedom from desire, there is non-action; if there is non-action, there is wishlessness.
Where there is no aspiration, there is no abiding; where there is no abiding, there is neither going nor coming.

This is called the third *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s *māyopama-kṣānti* (patience like an illusion)?
Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are entirely like illusions, arising from causes and conditions.
Within a single dharma, they understand many dharmas; within many dharmas, they understand a single dharma.

Having realized that all dharmas are like illusions, these Bodhisattvas thoroughly comprehend lands, thoroughly comprehend sentient beings, thoroughly comprehend the dharma-realm, thoroughly comprehend the equality of the world, thoroughly comprehend the equality of the appearance of Buddhas, and thoroughly comprehend the equality of the three periods of time, thereby accomplishing various supernatural powers and transformations.
Transformation is like an illusion: it is not an elephant, not a horse, not a chariot, not infantry; it is not male, not female, not a boy, not a girl;
it is not a tree, not a leaf, not a flower, not a fruit; it is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind;
it is not day, not night; it is not the sun, not the moon; it is not a half-month, not a month, not a year, not a hundred years, nor even one [moment].
Eons are neither many nor few, neither fixed nor chaotic, neither pure nor mixed, neither one nor different, neither broad nor narrow, neither much nor little,
neither measurable nor immeasurable, neither coarse nor subtle, and they are not any of these various kinds of things. Yet,
while the illusion is not the variety and the variety is not the illusion, it is through illusion that these various distinctions are manifested.
It is likewise for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who contemplates all worlds as being like illusions—
namely, the world of karma, the world of afflictions, the world of lands, the world of phenomena, the world of time, the world of destinies, the world of formation,
the world of destruction, the world of movement, and the world of conditioned activity. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates even a single [world] in this way.
When all worlds are like an illusion, one does not see the birth of sentient beings, nor the death of sentient beings;
one does not see the arising of lands, nor the perishing of lands; one does not see the arising of phenomena, nor the perishing of phenomena;

one does not see anything in the past that can be conceptualized, nor any activity occurring in the future, nor even the dwelling of a single thought-moment in the present—thus one does not engage in observation.
Enlightenment does not discriminate regarding enlightenment; it does not see the appearance of a Buddha, nor does it see the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha;
it does not see abiding in great vows, nor does it see entering the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*). It does not emerge from the nature of equality.

Although a bodhisattva accomplishes buddha-lands, he knows that lands have no differentiation; although he accomplishes the realm of sentient beings, he knows that sentient beings have no differentiation.
Universally observing the dharma-realm, they abide peacefully in the nature of phenomena, serene and unmoving;

though they realize the equality of the three periods of time, they do not contradict the differentiation of dharmas across the three periods; though they have perfected the aggregates and sense-bases, they have forever severed their underlying basis;
though they deliver sentient beings, they understand that the dharma-realm is equal and devoid of any manifold distinctions; though they know all dharmas to be remote...
Transcending words and beyond verbal expression, yet constantly preaching the Dharma with inexhaustible eloquence;
though not grasping at the task of transforming sentient beings, yet never abandoning great compassion to deliver all;
turning the wheel of Dharma while revealing past causes and conditions, yet knowing that the nature of causes and conditions is without movement or change—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The fourth is the patience like an illusion. O Son of the Buddha, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the patience like a mirage?
O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all worlds are identical to a mirage.

Just as a mirage has no location—being neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent, neither annihilated nor eternal, and neither a single color nor a variety of colors—[so too are all worlds].
The various forms are neither with form nor without form; they are merely displayed in accordance with worldly conventional discourse.

When a bodhisattva thus observes and understands all phenomena as they truly are, realizing them directly and bringing them to full perfection, this is called the fifth patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, "Patience Like a Mirage.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience "Like a Dream"?
Son, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all worlds are like dreams; for example, as a dream is neither the world nor apart from the world,
neither the desire realm, the form realm, nor the formless realm, neither arising nor passing away,
neither defiled nor pure, yet it manifests appearances— so too does the bodhisattva mahāsattva know all worlds.
Because they are all identical to dreams and without change; because their intrinsic nature is like a dream; because attachment to them is like a dream;

because their nature is free from [inherent existence] like a dream; because their fundamental nature is like a dream; because they appear like a dream; because they are undifferentiated from a dream;
because they are conceptualized through the imagination of a dream; and because they are like the state upon waking from a dream—this is called the sixth [ground] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
"O Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s acceptance of [all things] as being like a dream?

O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the Buddha preach the Dharma and contemplates the nature of all phenomena; through cultivation and study, they achieve perfection and reach the other shore.
They know that all sounds are identical to echoes, neither coming nor going, and thus manifest them in this way. O Son of the Buddha, this is it."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the voice of the Tathāgata does not emerge from within, nor does it emerge from without, nor does it emerge from both within and without.

Although he understands that this voice is neither internal, nor external, nor emerging from both internal and external, he is nevertheless able to manifest skillful names and phrases to provide perfect exposition.
It is, for example, like an echo arising from conditions, which accords with the Dharma.
The nature [of this teaching] is without contradiction, such that all sentient beings may understand it according to their own kind and thereby engage in practice;

just as Śacī, the wife of Śakra and daughter of an Asura, produced a thousand kinds of sounds from a single voice without even thinking, "Let these be uttered," so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: he enters the realm of non-conceptualization.
Having attained mastery over sounds that accord with the various types of beings, this Bodhisattva constantly turns the wheel of Dharma throughout boundless worlds.
Skillfully observing all sentient beings, he proclaims the teaching with his broad and long tongue;
his voice is unimpeded, pervading the lands of the ten directions, so that each hears the Dharma according to what is appropriate for them, though he knows that sound has no arising.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who universally manifests voices knows that there is nothing spoken, yet extensively expounds all dharmas;

with a sublime and impartial voice, beings each understand according to their own kind, and through wisdom, he is able to fully comprehend this—this is called the seventh patience of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, "Patience Like an Echo.
Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s patience like a shadow? Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva is not born in the world, nor does he pass away from the world; he is not within the world, nor is he outside the world;
he does not traverse the world, nor does he not traverse the world; he is not identical with the world, nor is he different from the world;
he does not go to the world, nor does he not go to the world; he does not abide in the world.
They do not abide in the world, yet they are neither of the world nor beyond the world; they do not practice the bodhisattva path, yet they do not abandon their great vows;
they are neither real nor unreal. Although they constantly practice all Buddha-dharmas, they are able to accomplish all worldly affairs;
they do not follow the current of the world, nor do they abide in the current of dharmas—just like the sun, the moon, or a man.
The reflections of a woman’s house, mountains, forests, rivers, springs, and other such things appear within oil, water, the body, precious jewels, bright mirrors, and other pure objects;
yet these reflections are neither identical to nor different from the oil and so forth, neither separate from nor joined with them.
They do not float away in flowing streams, nor do they sink into ponds or wells, even though they manifest therein.
Within it there is no attachment whatsoever; yet all sentient beings know that such reflections appear in this place, and they also know that such reflections do not exist in that place.
Although distant and near objects both manifest as reflections, the reflection does not possess the proximity or distance of the object itself.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, being able to know his own body and the bodies of others as one.
All things are the domain of wisdom; one does not conceive of them as dual, such as the distinction between self and other.
Rather, within their own lands and in the lands of others, they manifest all various differences simultaneously and universally.
Just as roots, sprouts, stalks, nodes, branches, and leaves do not exist within a seed, yet such things can arise from it, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
To skillfully employ expedient means to discern the two aspects within the non-dual Dharma and to penetrate them with unimpeded mastery—
this is called the eighth "patience like a shadow" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieves this patience,
although they do not travel to the lands of the ten directions, they are able to manifest universally in all buddha-fields, yet they do not depart from this [very place].

Without reaching that state, they universally manifest like reflections, acting without obstruction so that all sentient beings perceive their differentiated bodies as having the same solid characteristics as those of the mundane world.
Yet this differentiation is itself non-differentiation; there is no obstruction between difference and non-difference.
This Bodhisattva is born from the lineage of the Tathāgata, and thus their body, speech, and mind are pure.
Because they are unimpeded, they are able to obtain a body of pure, boundless forms and marks.
Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s acceptance of the illusory nature of things? Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all worlds are entirely like illusions;
that is to say, the mental activities of all sentient beings are like illusions, arising from the perceptions of their own conceptualizations. All [things] are thus.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the world arise from the transformation of conceptualization; all suffering and pleasure arise from the false grasping of the transformation of inversion;
all unreal phenomena in the world appear through the transformation of verbal expression; and all afflictions arise from the transformation of conceptual thought and mental perception.
Furthermore, there is the transformation of pure discipline which appears through non-conceptualization.

Because they do not undergo transformation throughout the three periods of time due to the equality of non-arising; because they transform through the vast cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s power of vows;
because they manifest through the skillful means of the Tathāgata’s great compassion;

and because they manifest through the turning of the wheel of Dharma, which is the teaching of wisdom, fearlessness, and eloquence—thus do Bodhisattvas understand and realize the mundane and supramundane manifestations.
He knows the vast, he knows the boundless, he knows things as they are, he knows sovereignty, he knows reality, and he knows that which is not false.
He cannot be shaken by what can be seen; though he acts in accordance with the world, he is never corrupted or destroyed.

For example, like a magical transformation, it does not arise from the mind, nor does it arise from mental factors, nor does it arise from karma, nor does it receive karmic retribution; it is neither born in the world nor does it perish in the world.
It cannot be followed; it cannot be grasped or touched; it does not abide for long, nor does it abide for a moment;
it does not move within the world, nor is it apart from the world; it is not bound exclusively to one direction, nor is it universally attached to all directions;

it is neither finite nor infinite; it is neither weary nor ceasing, yet it is not without weariness or cessation; it is neither ordinary nor noble; it is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither born nor dead.
Wisdom is neither folly nor view, neither non-view nor reliance on the mundane world; it does not enter the dharma-realm, nor is it cleverness or dullness;
it is neither grasping nor non-grasping, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, and neither existence nor non-existence.
When a bodhisattva practices such skillful means in the world, cultivating the bodhisattva path and thoroughly understanding worldly phenomena, they manifest divided bodies.
Manifesting transformations, they do not cling to the world nor grasp at a self; regarding the world and the body, they make no discriminations.
They do not abide in the world, yet they do not depart from the world; they do not abide in phenomena (*dharma*), yet they do not depart from phenomena.

By virtue of their original vows, they do not abandon a single realm of sentient beings, nor do they fail to discipline even the smallest number of sentient beings; they do not discriminate among phenomena, yet it is not that they do not discriminate.
The Dharma-knowledge realizes that the nature of all phenomena has neither coming nor going; though they are non-existent, they fulfill the Buddha-dharmas.

One understands that phenomena are like illusions, being neither existent nor non-existent. Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus dwells in the patience of the illusory-like, they are able to fully satisfy the path to the Bodhi of all Buddhas and benefit sentient beings; this is called Bodhi.
O Mahāsattva, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva achieves this ninth stage, the "patience regarding the illusory nature" (*nirmāṇa-kṣānti*), whatever they do is entirely like an illusion.

For example, just as an illusory being has no place of dependence or abiding in any Buddha-field, no grasping or attachment toward any world, and gives rise to no conceptual discrimination regarding any Buddha-dharma, yet proceeds toward Buddhahood; so too does this Bodhisattva.
Awakening is free from weariness; they cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, remaining free from all inversions. Though they have no body, they manifest all bodies;
though they have no dwelling place, they abide in all lands; though they have no form, they universally manifest all forms;

though they do not cling to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they clearly illumine the equality and perfection of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). O Son of the Buddha, such is this bodhisattva.
The Mahāsattva who has no basis in any phenomena is called "liberated"; one who has completely abandoned all faults is called "tamed";
one who is immovable and non-reverting, universally entering the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, is called "possessed of supernormal powers";
one who has attained skillfulness regarding the dharma of non-arising is called "non-retrogressive"; and one who is endowed with all powers... [is called] "heroic."
That which cannot be obstructed even by the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) is called "unimpeded.

Son of the Buddha, what is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like space? Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands that all dharma-realms are like space because they are signless;
that all worlds are like space because they are unarisen; and [that] all dharmas...
Just as space is non-dual, so too are the practices of all sentient beings like space because they have no place to go;
all Buddhas are like space because they are without discrimination; all powers of the Buddhas are like space because they are without distinction;
and all meditative concentrations are like space because they are equal throughout the three periods of time—thus it is said to be one.
Because all phenomena are like space and are ineffable, and because the bodies of all Buddhas are like space—
unattached and unimpeded— the Bodhisattva, by means of such space-like skillful means, realizes that all phenomena are utterly non-existent. O Son of the Buddha,
when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva realizes all phenomena through this space-like patience and wisdom, at that time...
He attains a body like space through his bodily karma; he attains speech like space through his verbal karma; and he attains a mind like space through his mental karma.
Just as all phenomena rely upon space, which neither arises nor perishes, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
all phenomena of his body neither arise nor perish. Just as space cannot be destroyed, so it is with the Bodhisattva.

The Mahāsattva is also like this: his wisdom and various powers are indestructible, just as space is the support for all worlds yet has no support itself; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this:
he is the support for all dharmas yet has no support himself. Just as space is without birth and without cessation, so too is he.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who can sustain all that arises and ceases in the world:
there is no direction and no attainment, yet they can demonstrate direction and attainment, causing the practice of the world to be universally pure.
Just as empty space has no cardinal points or corners, yet can manifest infinite directions and corners, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: they have no karma.

Without retribution, they are able to manifest various karmic rewards; just as empty space neither moves nor dwells, yet can manifest all manner of dignified postures, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
neither moving nor dwelling, yet able to discern all conditioned activities. Just as empty space is neither form nor non-form, yet can manifest them, [so it is with the Bodhisattva].
In the same way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, though possessing various forms, is neither a worldly form nor a supramundane form,
yet is able to manifest all forms. Just as space is neither distant nor near,
yet can endure for a long time and manifest all things, so too the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither distant nor near.
It is able to abide for a long time, manifesting all the practices performed by Bodhisattvas; it is like space, which is neither pure nor defiled, yet not separate from purity and defilement.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he is neither obstructed nor unobstructed, yet not separate from obstruction and non-obstruction.
It is like space, wherein all worlds appear before it, yet it does not manifest all worlds.
Previously, for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, all these dharmas likewise appeared before him,
yet they did not appear before any [limited] dharmas; just as space universally enters into all things without boundary,
so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally enters into all dharmas, yet the mind of the Bodhisattva has no boundary.

Why is this? Because that which is performed by a Bodhisattva is like space; that is to say, all their practices, all their purifications, and all their accomplishments are entirely equal, of one substance, one flavor, and one measure, as pure as space and pervading all places.
Thus they realize and know that all dharmas, within all dharmas, possess no differentiation.
They have distinguishedly purified all Buddha-lands; they have perfected all bodies that are without dependence;
they have understood all directions without any confusion; they are endowed with all powers that cannot be destroyed;
they have fulfilled all boundless merits; they have reached the station of all profound dharmas; they have penetrated the path of all pāramitās; and they universally sit upon a single...
The adamantine seat universally emits all sounds according to the various types of beings, turning the wheel of Dharma for all worlds without ever missing the proper time;
this is called the tenth "patience like space" of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes this patience, they attain a body that does not come because it has no going, and they attain a body that is unborn.

Because there is no cessation, one attains the immovable body; because there is no destruction, one attains the non-substantial body; because one is free from falsehood, one attains the single-characteristic body;
because it is signless, one attains the immeasurable body; because the powers of a Buddha are immeasurable, one attains the equal body;
because it accords with the nature of suchness, one attains the undifferentiated body; and because one contemplates the three periods of time equally, one attains the body that reaches all places.
Because the pure eyes illuminate all things equally and without obstruction, one attains the body that reaches the limit of desirelessness;

because one knows that all phenomena have neither union nor dispersion, one attains the body of infinite space; because the treasury of merit is inexhaustible like space, one attains the body of uninterrupted and inexhaustible eloquence equal to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
and because one knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are but a single characteristic, which is the absence of self-nature.
Because their nature is like empty space, they attain a body of immeasurable and unobstructed sound;
because it is like empty space, they attain a body of all-encompassing, skillful, and pure bodhisattva conduct that is unimpeded in all places;
because it is like empty space, they attain a body of the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas that continues in succession without interruption.
Because they have severed [all attachments] like space, they attain a body that manifests within all buddha-fields as immeasurable buddha-fields;
because they are free from all craving and attachment like the boundlessness of space, they attain a body that ceaselessly manifests all sovereign dharmas;
because they are like the boundless ocean of space, they attain a body of indestructible, firm power.
Because they sustain all worlds like space, they attain bodies with faculties as sharp and clear as vajra, which are as firm and indestructible as space;
because no conflagration at the end of any eon can burn them, they attain bodies possessing the power to sustain all worlds;
and because their power of wisdom is like space, O Son of the Buddha, these are called the ten [qualities] of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as there may be people in the world Who hear of a place where a treasure-trove lies;
Because it can be obtained, their hearts give rise to great joy— In this same way, those of great wisdom, The true sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas."
Hearing the teachings of all Buddhas, Their profound and quiescent characteristics— When hearing this deep Dharma, their minds find peace;
Neither startled nor terrified, Nor do they give rise to fear.
The Great Being seeking Bodhi, Upon hearing this vast sound, His mind is pure and able to endure it.
Free from doubt regarding this, they reflect to themselves: "By hearing this profound and subtle Dharma, we shall attain all-knowledge and become great teachers of gods and humans.
Upon hearing these words, the bodhisattvas' hearts were filled with great joy; they gave rise to a firm resolve, vowing to seek all the Buddha-dharmas.
Because they delight in bodhi, their minds gradually become subdued; they cause faith to increase further and remain without contradiction or slander toward the Dharma.
Therefore, upon hearing this sound, their minds attain endurance, abiding steadfastly without wavering as they practice the bodhisattva conduct in pursuit of bodhi.
Dedicatedly practicing that path with diligence and without turning back,
not abandoning the yoke of all virtues for the sake of seeking awakening, his mind is free from fear; hearing the Dharma,
he increases his valor and makes offerings to the Buddha to bring him joy, like a person of great merit who discovers a treasury of pure gold.
Just as one fashions ornaments from the materials appropriate for personal wear, so too is it with the Bodhisattva:

hearing this profound meaning, they contemplate it and increase the ocean of their wisdom. By practicing in accordance with the Dharma, they understand that when phenomena exist, they are in accord with reality;
they also understand that when phenomena do not exist, they are likewise in accord with reality. They follow those phenomena in this very way.
Thus knowing all phenomena, one accomplishes a pure mind; with clear penetration and great joy, one knows that phenomena arise from conditions.
Diligently practicing with valor, one contemplates all phenomena with equanimity and realizes their intrinsic nature.
Not contradicting the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, one universally awakens to all phenomena.
Their resolve and joy are ever firm as they adorn and purify the Buddha-bodhi.
Unshakable as Mount Sumeru, they seek perfect enlightenment with a single mind. Having aroused the intent of diligence, they further cultivate the path of samādhi;
Practicing with effort for immeasurable kalpas, they never once fall back or lose their way— This is the Dharma entered by Bodhisattvas.

This is the sphere of action of the Buddhas; one who can thoroughly understand this, whose mind is free from weariness or indolence as described by the Peerless One, observes all phenomena with equanimity.
Through the patience that is not uneven, one accomplishes the wisdom of equanimity; by following what the Buddha has taught, one perfects this gateway of patience.
One understands according to the Dharma, yet does not conceptualize phenomena.
All the sons of the gods within the Heaven of the Thirty-three share a single vessel for their food;
though what they eat differs for each, and the food they consume is of various kinds, it does not come from the ten directions, but arises according to the karma they have cultivated.
Just as [the reflection] naturally exists within the vessel, so too is the Bodhisattva.
He observes that all phenomena arise entirely from causes and conditions; because they are unarisen, they do not cease; because they do not cease, they are inexhaustible;
and because they are inexhaustible, they are undefiled. Regarding the phenomena of worldly transformation, he thoroughly understands them to be without transformation.
Where there is no difference, there is no location; where there is no location, that is quiescence.
With a mind free from defilement and attachment, one vows to deliver all living beings.

Focusing single-mindedly on all phenomena, never allowing for distraction or agitation, one employs skillful means in the world with a heart of compassionate resolve, diligently seeking the Ten Powers.
Dwelling in the world yet not abiding therein, Neither going nor coming, Skillfully expounding the Dharma through expedient means—this patience is supreme.
Realizing that phenomena are inexhaustible, Entering the true realm of reality (dharmadhātu), yet truly there is no entering;
The Bodhisattva abiding in this patience Universally beholds all Tathāgatas.
Simultaneously receiving the prophecy is called "assuming the office of a Buddha.

Thoroughly understanding that the phenomena of the three periods of time possess the characteristic of quiescent purity, one is able to transform sentient beings, establishing them upon the paths of goodness.
All the various phenomena of the world are entirely like illusions; if one can know them thus, [one attains this state].
That mind is unmoving; all karmas arise from the mind. Therefore, it is said that the mind is like an illusion.
If one is free from this discrimination, one universally extinguishes all realms of existence.
It is like a skilled illusionist who manifests all manner of forms, causing the multitude to greedily delight in them, yet ultimately nothing is to be found.
The world is also thus: All things are like illusions. Lacking intrinsic nature and without arising, they manifest in various ways To deliver all sentient beings.
They cause them to know that phenomena are like illusions; Sentient beings are no different from illusions.
Realizing that within illusion there are no sentient beings, [One sees] sentient beings and their lands [as such].
All phenomena existing throughout the three periods of time, without exception, are entirely like illusions—
such as the forms of men and women created by illusion, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep,
houses, ponds, springs, groves, flowers, fruits, and the like. These illusory things have no cognition, nor do they have any place of abiding.
Ultimately characterized by quiescence, they appear only in accordance with conceptual discrimination.
When Bodhisattvas can thus universally perceive all worlds—whether existent or non-existent—all phenomena are understood to be entirely like illusions.
Sentient beings and their lands are produced by various types of karma; they enter into the limit of illusion.
Being without dependence or attachment therein, they thus attain skillfulness; dwelling in the state of cessation, free from conceptual proliferation, they abide on the ground of non-obstruction.
Universally manifesting great majestic power, these courageous sons of the Buddha enter in accordance with the wondrous Dharma.
Skillfully observing all perceptions, they [sever] the entanglements within the world.
All perceptions are like a mirage, causing sentient beings to have perverted understandings. The Bodhisattva skillfully knows perceptions and abandons all perversions.
Sentient beings are each distinct, their forms and types not of one kind;
he realizes that they are all merely perceptions, none of which possess true reality—so it is with all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
All are shrouded by conceptualization; if one abandons inverted views, then the worldly notion of the world is extinguished.
The world is like a mirage; because of the distinctions in conceptualization, one knows the world abides in conceptualization.
Free from the two inversions, it is like a shimmering heat-mirage which the world perceives as water.
Water is truly non-existent; the wise should not seek it. Sentient beings are likewise so;

the realms of worldly existence are all non-existent. Like a mirage that dwells upon perception, the sphere of the unimpeded mind is free from all perceptions and free from all conceptual proliferation—yet those who are deluded remain attached to perceptions.

Causing all to attain liberation, Far removed from the mind of pride, Eliminating worldly perceptions and abiding in the place where the finite and infinite are exhausted— This is the skillful means of the bodhisattva.
The bodhisattva understands that all worldly phenomena are like dreams; Neither having a location nor lacking a location, Their essential nature is eternally quiescent.
All phenomena are without discrimination; like a dream, they do not differ from the mind. All worlds throughout the three periods of time are exactly thus:
the nature of a dream is without arising or ceasing, and it has no location or direction.
The triple world is entirely thus; when the seer’s mind is liberated, the dream does not exist within the world.
Not abiding in the non-worldly, these two are not discriminated; one thus enters the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
Just as various diverse appearances are seen within a dream, so too is the world; it is no different from a dream.
For one who dwells in the meditative absorption on dreams, they understand that the entire world is like a dream.
Neither identical nor different, neither one nor manifold;
The karmic defilements and purities of sentient beings and all lands— All such things he fully understands.
The practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas And their various great vows, He clearly perceives them all as being like dreams.
Not different from the world, yet realizing that the world is entirely empty and quiescent;
not destroying worldly phenomena, which are like what is seen in a dream—such as forms of long and short and so forth—this is called the patience regarding dreams.
By means of this, one understands worldly phenomena and swiftly accomplishes unimpeded wisdom, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
Practicing such conduct, one gives birth to vast understanding; skillfully knowing the nature of all phenomena, the mind has no attachment to them.
Regarding all the various sounds in every world—neither internal nor external—one realizes them all to be like echoes, just as when one hears various echoes.
The mind does not give rise to discrimination; when a Bodhisattva hears sounds, their mind is likewise.
Beholding all the Tathāgatas and listening to the sound of their preaching of the Dharma—though they hear the immeasurable exposition of the sūtras, they remain unattached.
Like an echo, there is no place from which it comes; so too are the sounds that are heard.
They are able to discern phenomena without contradicting the nature of reality; they thoroughly understand all sounds yet do not discriminate among them.
Knowing that all sounds are empty and quiescent, they universally produce pure voices while realizing that phenomena do not reside in words.
Skillfully entering the realm of wordlessness, they are nevertheless able to manifest verbal teachings.
Like an echo pervading the world, they fully understand the path of speech;
possessing all qualities of sound, they know the nature of sound to be empty and quiescent.
Using worldly sounds and voices, they demonstrate that all phenomena are like conceptual distinctions; their voices reach everywhere, awakening all living beings.
When a bodhisattva attains this patience, they purify their voice to transform the world. Skillfully explaining the three periods of time, they remain unattached to the world.
Desiring to benefit the world, they single-mindedly seek awakening and constantly enter into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding that [nature], they are free from discrimination, universally observing all worlds.
Quiescent and without intrinsic nature, yet constantly acting for the benefit of others;
practicing with an unshakable mind, neither dwelling in the world nor departing from it;
having no dependence upon the world, as no locus of dependence can be found; thoroughly understanding the nature of the world, one remains unstained by that nature.
Though not relying on the world, he transforms the world to bring it across to liberation;
he thoroughly knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena in the world, yet realizes that phenomena are non-dual.
Without duality and without attachment, his mind does not depart from the world, nor does it dwell within the world, for he is not outside the world.
Cultivating all-knowledge is like a reflection in water; it is neither internal nor external.
When a Bodhisattva seeks enlightenment, they realize that the world is not the mundane world. They do not dwell within the world, yet they transcend it;
since the world cannot be described, it exists neither internally nor externally, appearing in the world like a shadow.
Entering this profound meaning, they are free from defilement and entirely lucid. Without abandoning their original vow, they universally illuminate the lamp of wisdom.
Throughout the boundless reaches of the world, their wisdom enters all things with perfect equanimity.
They universally transform all living beings, causing them to relinquish all attachments, as they contemplate the most profound Dharma.
Benefiting the multitudes of sentient beings, they enter into wisdom from this point on. Practicing all paths, the Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena;
understanding them clearly as being entirely like illusions, they perform illusory deeds, never ultimately abandoning them.
In accordance with the mastery of transformation, they cultivate the path to Bodhi.
All phenomena are like illusions, and the bodhisattva’s practice is likewise.
All worlds and immeasurable karmas are equally like illusions; ultimately they abide in quiescence.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are also like illusions, for they have cultivated all practices through their original vows.
Manifesting as a Tathāgata through transformation, the Buddha, with great compassion, delivers sentient beings;
yet this deliverance is also like a transformation. By the power of transformation he preaches the Dharma; knowing that all worlds are like transformations, he does not discriminate among them.
Though the transformative deeds are various and distinct, they all arise from the differences in karma.
Cultivating the conduct of enlightenment, one adorns the treasury of emanations.
With immeasurable virtuous adornments, one creates worlds according to karma. The dharma of emanation is free from conceptualization;
nor does one conceptualize phenomena—both of these are utterly quiescent. Such is the bodhisattva’s practice: the ocean of emanations is realized through wisdom.
The nature of transformation seals the world; transformation is not a phenomenon of arising and ceasing. Wisdom is also like this.
The tenth patience is the clear contemplation that sentient beings and all phenomena are by nature quiescent, like space, having no location.
Having attained this wisdom that is like space, one is forever free from all grasping and attachment.
Just as space is devoid of variety and encounters no obstruction in the world, so too is the power of the patience of emptiness accomplished;
it is like space, without exhaustion. Its sphere of activity is like the void; one does not form conceptual distinctions regarding emptiness.
Space has no intrinsic nature, yet it is neither annihilated nor subject to cessation, nor does it possess various distinctions.
The power of wisdom is likewise thus: Just as space has no beginning, And likewise has no middle or end, its measure cannot be grasped;
So too is the wisdom of the Bodhisattva. Observing the nature of phenomena in this way, all are like space: Without arising and without cessation—this is what the Bodhisattva attains.
Abiding personally in the dharma that is like space, one further preaches it for the sake of sentient beings.
Subduing all Māras is entirely through the skillful means of patience (*kṣānti*). The various distinctions of worldly characteristics are all empty and devoid of marks;
entering the state where there are no marks, all characteristics are entirely equal, being realized through this single skillful means.
Universally entering all worlds, This means knowing the phenomena of the three periods of time.
Their wisdom and their voices, As well as the bodies of the Bodhisattvas, Are equal in nature to empty space;
All are utterly quiescent. These ten kinds of patience Are what the Sons of the Buddha practice.
With his mind well-established, he extensively teaches for the sake of sentient beings;
having trained well in this, he achieves great power—the power of the Dharma and the power of wisdom.
As a skillful means for awakening, he penetrates this gateway of patience, achieves unimpeded knowledge, and transcends all multitudes.
Turning the unsurpassed wheel, the measure of the vast practices they have cultivated cannot be grasped;
only the ocean of wisdom of the Tamer of Men can discern and know them.
Having abandoned self to practice and entered the profound nature of phenomena, their minds dwell eternally in the deep Dharma, and thus they bestow it upon all living beings.
The number of sentient beings and the atoms of all lands may still be known;

But the limit of the Bodhisattvas’ various merits can never be measured. The Bodhisattvas are able to accomplish these ten kinds of patience, wisdom, and conduct; Sentient beings are unable to fathom them.
[Treatise] From the tenth section downward, there is a verse that serves as a recapitulation of the ten stages of patience (*kṣānti*) mentioned previously.

Thus, the first "Patience with Sound" (*śabdakṣānti*) is collectively assigned to the initial stage among the five positions: namely, the beginning of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the beginning of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the beginning of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the beginning of the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*). Similarly, the second "Conformity Patience" (*anulomikī kṣānti*) corresponds to the [beginning of] the ten abodes... [and so forth].
The second dwelling, the ten practices, the second practice, the ten dedications, the second dedication, the ten stages, the second stage,

the eleventh stage, and the second position— thus, each is sequentially assigned to its corresponding position. However, because they differ in the degree of mastery and ripening resulting from the habitual cultivation of progressive effort,
there is such a thing as the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the patience regarding illusions (*māyopama-kṣānti*).

The patience like a flame, the patience like a dream, the patience like an echo, the patience like a shadow, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space—all are to be individually correlated with and cultivated through the five stages as described above;
furthermore, since each stage possesses ten types of patience, the remaining meanings are self-evident within the text. Thus, the practices of the eleven stages are fulfilled.

Chapter Thirty: The *Asaṃkhyeya* (Incalculable) Chapter.
[Treatise] To explain this chapter, four sections are established: first, explaining the intent of the chapter’s arrival;

second, explaining the master who poses the questions; third, explaining the master who expounds the Dharma; and fourth, explaining the meaning according to the text. First, regarding the intent of the chapter’s arrival:

it clarifies that the preceding three chapters on the Ten Concentrations (*samādhi*), the Ten Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā*), and the Ten Endurances (*kṣānti*) encompass the entirety of cause and effect from beginning to end, from origin to conclusion.

At the moment of transition between kṣaṇas, one has already perfected the dharma-patience of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-dharma-kṣānti*) and fully realized the causes and fruits, the teachings and practices, and the skillful means (*upāya*) bestowed by all Buddhas.
The fruition of these practices mutually support one another from beginning to end without interruption;
they do not depart from the time of a single kṣaṇa. As stated in the *Ratna-rāja-sūtra*: "Within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), there are ninety kṣaṇas; one kṣaṇa passes through nine..."

Although there are a hundred such births and cessations within these three periods of time, because the fruit of Buddhahood and the skillful means of Samantabhadra’s practice do not undergo temporal transition, one takes only the *kṣaṇa* (moment) as the measure; thus, the name "birth and cessation" is not established.

Even when discussing birth and cessation, they are merely posited within a single *kṣaṇa* without any further duration of length or shortness. From this point downward, it extends to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata."
This clarifies the gate of the vast and sovereign practices of the three karmas within the state of Buddhahood:

first, the "Asaṃkhyeya" chapter clarifies the vast sovereignty of the Tathāgata’s mental karma; second, the "Tathāgata’s Lifespan" chapter clarifies the vast sovereignty of the Tathāgata’s life-force;
and third, the "Bodhisattva Abodes" chapter clarifies the vast sovereignty of the Tathāgata’s conduct in gathering and sustaining sentient beings.
Chapter One: "The Permanently Abiding Sovereign Four Buddhas' Inconceivable Dharma" explains the vast sovereignty of the Buddha’s three karmas and their divine virtues;
Chapter Five: "The Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" explains the vast sovereignty of the adornments obtained through the retribution of the Buddha’s bodily karma;
Chapter Six: "The Merits of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance" explains [the Buddha’s three karmas].
The merits manifested by the Dharma-body are vast and sovereign; according to the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra*, these are assigned to the third dhyāna.
It is taught that the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Samādhi* consists of one hundred trillion verses, of which this "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" (*Samantabhadracaryā-prakaraṇa*) is a summary.
This corresponds to the seventh assembly and is titled the "Chapter on the Buddhāvataṃsaka Samādhi," the seventh being the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra."
The eighth chapter, "The Manifestation of the Eight Tathāgatas," elucidates the Buddha’s three karmas,
the pervasiveness of his enlightened conduct, and his vast, sovereign mastery.
These eight chapters of the sutra collectively extol the Buddha’s fruition, conduct, wisdom, virtues, the efficacy of his three karmas, and their adornments.
Because the marks of his majestic retribution are vast and sovereign, following this chapter, two explanations are required for the Dharma Lord who poses the questions:
first, he is a Bodhisattva named *Cittarāja* (Mind-King); this clarifies that after attaining the mind and achieving patience, one is termed a "King" due to mastery over mental karma.
Third, regarding the Lord who expounds the Dharma: for what reason does the Tathāgata [speak] in this chapter?
This explains that the vastness of these numerical methods is beyond the reach of the wisdom of those in lower stages and can only be fully realized by a Buddha;
therefore, these two delusions regarding the fruit of Buddhahood are not understood until one reaches the perfection of specific knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).

These two chapters—the "Chapter on Incalculable Qualities" (*asaṃkhyeya-varga*) and the "Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Minor Marks" (*anuvyañjana-prabhā-guṇa-varga*)—were spoken by the Tathāgata himself, while the remaining five were [spoken by others].
Each stage is explained according to its respective level; the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths explain the Dharma of the Ten Faiths, namely Mañjuśrī, Buddhamati, and others.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abidings explain the Dharma of the Ten Abidings, namely Dharmamati, Vasumati, and others.
One should understand other cases by analogy with this. This chapter does not reach the fruit of the Wisdom of Distinction, which belongs to the Perfect Buddha.
As for the position that it is the Tathāgata himself who speaks, the subject of the inquiry is indeed the Tathāgata.
Because his mental wisdom is sovereign, he is called "King," which signifies the mastery of mind; only one with such mastery is capable of posing the questions.
Since these are all the sovereign mind of the Buddha, when he establishes the teachings, he causes those who study them to emulate him; thus, he speaks of "practice" so as to make it universal.

The virtuous lord accomplishes patience through his conduct and governs as a sovereign by means of it; furthermore, these various dharmas culminate in the fruit of Buddhahood once wisdom is perfected.
Because this wisdom is all-pervasive, he knows spontaneously without the need for applied effort or deliberate attention, for this is what the Buddha himself has declared.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Cittarāja addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, proclaim the *asaṃkhyeya*, the immeasurable, the boundless, the unequaled, the uncountable, the incomparable, the inconceivable, the unfathomable, the ineffable, the unspeakably unspeakable.
World-Honored One, what is meant by 'asaṃkhyeya' up to 'unspeakably unspeakable'?"
"Is it unspeakable? The Buddha addressed Mind-King Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You now ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, because you desire to cause all the worlds to enter into the meaning of the quantities known by the Buddha.
Son of good family, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you. At that time, Mind-King...
