Holding [them] as one, the paths are distinct; the distinct paths are one inversion;
the inversions are one *samaya*; the *samayas* are one *vidūra*;
the *vidūras* are one *khepara*; the *kheparas* are one investigation; the investigations are one...
One *viśva* makes one *viśvāhva*; one *viśvāhva* makes one *sudarśana*; one *sudarśana* makes one *sudarśanīya*;
one *sudarśanīya* makes one *nirarbuda*; one *nirarbuda* makes one *ahuli*;
one *ahuli* makes one *ahulika*; one *ahulika* makes one *utkala*; one *utkala* makes one *utkalaka*; one *utkalaka* makes one *ahulpuluha*.
One *pu-ha-li* makes one *ha-li*; three *ha-li* make one *sa-ha-li*; three *sa-ha-li* make one *xi-lu-ga*;
one *xi-lu-ga*, two *xi-lu-ga*, and three *xi-lu-ga* make one *da-la-bu-tuo*; one *da-la-bu-tuo*, two *da-la-bu-tuo*, and three *da-la-bu-tuo* make one *he-lu-na*;
one *he-lu-na*, two *he-lu-na*, and three *he-lu-na* make one *mo-lu-tuo*; one *mo-lu-tuo*, two *mo-lu-tuo*, and three *mo-lu-tuo*... [and so on].
One *rudha* makes one *samudra*; one *samudra* makes one *kṣaya*;
one *kṣaya* makes one *mahāmahā*; one *mahāmahā* makes one *vinirbhoga*;
one *vinirbhoga* makes one *vigata-māna*; one *vigata-māna* makes one *acala*.
One *acala* constitutes one *paramāṇu*; one *paramāṇu-paramāṇu* constitutes one *amatra*;
one *amatra-amatra* constitutes one *bhamatra*; one *bhamatra-bhamatra* constitutes one *gamatra*;
one *gamatra-gamatra* constitutes one *namatra*; [one *namatra-namatra* constitutes one...]*namatra*.
One *tṛā-nama* makes one *tṛā-vima*; one *vima* makes one *vima-vima*;
one *vima-vima* makes one *vima-bhrama*; one *bhrama* makes one *bhrama-bhrama*;
one *bhrama-bhrama* makes one *śiva-ma*; one *śiva*...
One *mātrāśiva-mātrā* makes one *īla*; one *īla* makes one *vīla*; one *vīla* makes one *tīla*;
one *tīla* makes one *gīla*; one *gīla* makes one *sūbura*;
one *sūbura* makes one *nīla*; one *nīla* makes one... [nīla].
One *kīla* makes one *kīlakīla*; one *kīlakīla* makes one *sūkṣma*;
one *sūkṣma* makes one *piḍa*; one *piḍa* makes one *miḍa*; one *miḍa* makes one *saraṭa*;
one *saraṭa* makes one *meruda*; one *meruda* makes one *keruda*; one *keruda*...
One *ta-khi-lu-ta* makes one *mo-du-lo*; one *mo-du-lo* makes one *sa-mo-lo*;
one *sa-mo-lo* makes one *a-ye-sa*; one *a-ye-sa* makes one *ka-ma-lo*;
one *ka-ma-lo* makes one *mo-ka-po*; one *mo-ka-po* makes one *mo-ka-po*. One *mo-ka-po* [makes one... *mo-ka-po*.
One *atara*, one *atara*, one *atara* constitutes one *hiruśa*;
one *hiruśa*, one *hiruśa*, one *hiruśa* constitutes one *veruva*;
one *karava*, one *karava*, one *karava* constitutes one *hahaba*; one *hahaba*, one *hahaba*, one *hahaba* constitutes one *vibha*.
Vipara-vipara makes one nāvara; nāvara-nāvara makes one mālara; mālara-mālara makes one sāvara;
sāvara-sāvara makes one milapu; milapu-milapu makes one cāmala; cāmala—cāmala.
One *cāmara* makes one *dhāmara*; one *dhāmara* makes one *palamata*;
one *palamata* makes one *vigaṃma*; one *vigaṃma* makes one *upabaddha*;
one *upabaddha* makes one *vyākhyāna*; one *vyākhyāna* makes one *vyākhyāna*.
One *akṣaya* (inexhaustible) is said to be one *akṣayākṣaya* (inexhaustible-inexhaustible); one *akṣayākṣaya* is one *upapatti* (birth);
one *upapatti* is one *anātman* (selflessness); one *anātman* is one *apantata* (limitless); one *apantata* is one *utpala* (blue lotus);
one *utpala* is one *utpalotpala*; one *utpalotpala* is one *padma* (lotus); one *padma* is one *padmapadma*. One *padmapadma* is one...
Saṃkhyeya, saṃkhyeya, saṃkhyeya makes one *gati*; *gati*, *gati*, *gati* makes one *prati*; *prati*, *prati*, *prati* makes one *asaṃkhyeya*;
*asaṃkhyeya*, *asaṃkhyeya*, *asaṃkhyeya* makes one *asaṃkhyeyāvarta*; *asaṃkhyeyāvarta*, *asaṃkhyeyāvarta*, *asaṃkhyeyāvarta* makes one *aprameya*;
*aprameya*, *aprameya*, *aprameya* makes one *aprameyāvarta*; *aprameyāvarta*, *aprameyāvarta*, *aprameyāvarta*.
One "boundless" (*ananta*) consists of boundless, boundless, boundless; one "boundless-turning" (*anantāvarta*) consists of boundless-turning, boundless-turning, boundless-turning;
one "unequaled" (*asama*) consists of unequaled, unequaled, unequaled; one "unequaled-turning" (*asamāvarta*) consists of unequaled-turning, unequaled-turning, unequaled-turning;

one "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) consists of incalculable, incalculable, incalculable; one "incalculable-turning" (*asaṃkhyeyāvarta*) consists of incalculable-turning, incalculable-turning... [incalculable-turning].
One *saṃkhyeya-parivarta* is made into one *asaṃkhyeya*; one *asaṃkhyeya* is made into one *asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*; one *asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* is made into one *acintya*;
one *acintya* is made into one *acintya-parivarta*; one *acintya-parivarta* is made into one *aprameya*.
One immeasurable is a single immeasurable-turn; one immeasurable-turn is a single immeasurable-turn-immeasurable-turn;
one immeasurable-turn-immeasurable-turn is a single unspeakable-unspeakable-unspeakable; one unspeakable-unspeakable-unspeakable is a single unspeakable-turn-unspeakable-turn-unspeakable-turn;
one unspeakable-turn-unspeakable-turn-unspeakable-turn is a single unspeakable-unspeakable-unspeakable, which is again an unspeakable-unspeakable-unspeakable.
At that time, when [the eons] were unspeakably unspeakable times more, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Citta-rāja:
"Unspeakably unspeakable, They fill all that is unspeakable."
Throughout unspeakable eons, one could not exhaustively describe what is unspeakable;
All unspeakable Buddha-fields are ground and pulverized into fine dust, And within a single mote of dust, there are unspeakable lands; As it is with one, so it is with all.
These unspeakable Buddha-fields are reduced to atoms in a single thought-moment;
unspeakably many such moments continue this reduction. This continues thus throughout unspeakable eons, yet these atoms contain unspeakable fields;
to describe these fields as being composed of atoms is even more difficult to express.
By means of the method of incalculable calculation, one counts eons in this manner;
by using the number of these atoms to count eons— wherein each atom represents unspeakably many eons throughout the ten directions—
one might praise a single Samantabhadra, yet none could ever exhaust the measure of his merit.
Within the space of a single minute hair-tip, there are unspeakably many Samantabhadras;
it is the same for every hair-tip. Thus, even throughout the entire Dharma-realm, the number of lands contained within a single hair-tip is immeasurable and unspeakable.
Upon every single hair-tip throughout the full extent of empty space, all lands are likewise so;
within those lands upon each hair-tip, there are immeasurable varieties of distinct abodes,
with unspeakably many different types of lands and unspeakably many similar types of lands.
Upon every tip of a hair, which is itself ineffable, There are unspeakably many pure lands with unspeakably diverse adornments; With unspeakably various wonders,
each and every one ineffable, Within each and every such hair-tip, They proclaim the names of unspeakably many Buddhas.
In each and every name there are Tathāgatas, all of whom are unspeakably unspeakable;
within the bodies of each and every Buddha, they manifest unspeakably many pores,
and within each and every one of those pores, they manifest unspeakably many varieties of forms and colors.
From all the pores, which are themselves ineffable, Ineffable rays of light are emitted;
Within each and every one of those lights, Ineffable lotus flowers appear;
Within each and every one of those lotuses, There are ineffable numbers of petals.
Within the petals of unspeakably many flowers, each manifests unspeakable forms and appearances;
within those unspeakable forms, there further appear unspeakably many petals.
Within those petals, unspeakable light radiates forth; within that light, unspeakable forms and appearances are revealed.
Within these unspeakable forms, each manifests unspeakable rays of light;
within each unspeakable ray of light, unspeakable moons appear; from each of those unspeakable moons, again unspeakable moons appear;
and within those unspeakable moons, each manifests unspeakable rays of light.
Within each and every one of those rays of light, there further appear unspeakably unspeakable numbers of suns;
within each and every one of those suns, there appear unspeakably unspeakable varieties of colors;
and within each and every one of those colors, there again appear unspeakably unspeakable rays of light.
Within each and every one of those rays of light, there appear unspeakably many lion thrones,
with unspeakably many ornaments for each; within the unspeakably many lights of each ray,
there are unspeakably many sublime colors, and within those colors, unspeakably many pure lights.
Within each of those pure lights, various wondrous radiances appear;
these lights again manifest diverse rays of light, beyond description and beyond the power of speech.
Within such various radiances, there appear exquisite jewels, each as vast as Mount Sumeru.
Within each and every ray of light appear jewels that are unspeakably unspeakable;
Just as a single exquisite jewel on Mount Sumeru manifests unspeakably many buddha-lands,
so too do all the jewels on Mount Sumeru, without exception, manifest lands in this same way.
If a single buddha-field were ground into dust, and the color and form of each particle of that dust were unspeakable;
if all those fields were further reduced to dust, and each particle possessed such characteristics as to be unspeakably unspeakable—
then from all such various particles of dust, unspeakable rays of light would emerge.
The Buddhas appearing within the light are unspeakable; The Dharma taught by those Buddhas is unspeakable;
The sublime verses within that Dharma are unspeakable; The understanding gained from hearing those verses is unspeakable;
The realization attained in every thought-moment is unspeakable; The manifestation of the ultimate truth is unspeakable.
Manifesting all future Buddhas, They constantly expound the Dharma without end;
Each and every Buddha-dharma is unspeakable, Its various purities are unspeakable,
Its sublime vocal sounds are unspeakable, And its turning of the wheel of the true Dharma is unspeakable.
Within each and every wheel of Dharma, he expounds sūtras that are unspeakable;
Within each and every sūtra, he analyzes dharma-gates that are unspeakable;
Within each and every dharma-gate, he further explains all dharmas that are unspeakable.
Within each and every one of those dharmas, they subdue sentient beings in ways that are ineffable;
or again, at the tip of a single hair, they dwell for ineffable eons,
and as it is at the tip of one hair, so it is for all others— the number of eons they dwell is exactly thus.
That mind is unimpeded and unspeakable; The manifestations of the Buddhas are unspeakable.
Each and every manifested Tathāgata Further manifests further emanations that are unspeakable.
The Dharma-body of those Buddhas is unspeakable; The divided bodies of those Buddhas are unspeakable.
Adorned with immeasurable, ineffable [qualities], He proceeds to ineffable worlds throughout the ten directions;
He travels through ineffable lands, Observes ineffable sentient beings, and purifies ineffable sentient beings; He tames ineffable sentient beings.
Those various adornments are unspeakable; those various spiritual powers are unspeakable;
those various masteries are unspeakable; those various miraculous transformations are unspeakable;
all their supernormal faculties are unspeakable; and all their spheres of experience are unspeakable.
All empowerments are unspeakable; The worlds in which they abide are unspeakable;
The pure true reality is unspeakable; The expounding of the sūtras is unspeakable.
Within each and every one of those sūtras, The teaching of the dharma-gates is unspeakable.
Within each and every dharma-gate, it is further taught that all dharmas are ineffable;
within each and every such dharma, whatever is determinate is ineffable;
and within each and every determination, the taming of sentient beings is ineffable.
Inexpressible similar phenomena; inexpressible similar minds;
inexpressible dissimilar phenomena; inexpressible dissimilar minds;
inexpressible dissimilar faculties; inexpressible dissimilar speech.
In every thought-moment, throughout all places where they act, The taming of sentient beings is unspeakable;
All their spiritual transformations are unspeakable; All their manifestations are unspeakable;
Within them, the passing of time and eons is unspeakable; Within them, their various distinctions are unspeakable.
The Bodhisattvas are able to analyze and explain them all; even those most skilled in calculation cannot discern them.

Within the space of a single hair-tip, there are lands of great and small extent, lands that are defiled or pure, coarse or subtle—all such things are unspeakable, yet each can be clearly understood and distinguished.
If a single land were ground into dust, The number of those particles would be immeasurable and unspeakable;
If lands as infinite as the count of such particles Were all to come together and gather upon a single hair-tip,
These unspeakably many lands Would gather upon that hair-tip without any crowding.
Without causing even a hair-tip to expand, all those lands gather together within it;
the forms and characteristics of all these lands remain as they were, without confusion,
such that one land does not disturb another— this is true for all lands.
The realm of space is without limit; He causes every hair-tip to be filled with it.
Within all such lands upon those hair-tips, A Bodhisattva can describe them all in a single thought-moment.
Into a single minute pore, Inexpressible numbers of lands enter in succession.
The pores can contain all those lands, and all those lands can enter every pore;
the number of eons for this is ineffable, the number of eons for their containment is ineffable.
While they abide in these rows, no one is able to describe all those eons.
Thus having embraced and abided therein, the objects of experience are unspeakable;
the skillful means for entering them are unspeakable; what is done after having entered is unspeakable;
the clarity of the mental faculty is unspeakable; and wandering through the various directions is unspeakable.
Their courageous diligence is unspeakable; Their sovereign spiritual transformations are unspeakable;
All their contemplations are unspeakable; All their great vows are unspeakable;
All their spheres of experience are unspeakable; Their universal penetration of all things is unspeakable.
The purity of physical action is ineffable; The purity of verbal action is ineffable;
The purity of mental action is ineffable; The purity of resolute faith is ineffable;
The purity of sublime wisdom is ineffable; The purity of sublime discernment is ineffable.
The realization of all true marks is inexpressible; The severing of all doubts is inexpressible;
Transcending birth and death is inexpressible; Ascending to the stage of certainty is inexpressible;
Profound samādhi is inexpressible; Thoroughly penetrating all things is inexpressible.
All sentient beings are unspeakable; All buddha-fields are unspeakable.
Knowing the bodies of sentient beings is unspeakable; Knowing their mental inclinations is unspeakable;
Knowing their karmic fruits is unspeakable; Knowing their mental dispositions is unspeakable.
Knowing that their categories are ineffable; knowing that their spiritual lineages are ineffable;
knowing that their assumption of bodies is ineffable; knowing that their places of birth are ineffable;
knowing that their actual birth is ineffable; and knowing that once born, they are ineffable.
Knowing their understanding is inexpressible, Knowing their inclinations are inexpressible,
Knowing their speech is inexpressible, And knowing their activities are inexpressible—
Such is the great compassion of the Bodhisattva, Which benefits all worlds.
Universally manifesting their bodies is unspeakable; Entering all Buddha-fields is unspeakable;
Beholding all Bodhisattvas is unspeakable; Generating wisdom is unspeakable;
Inquiring about the True Dharma is unspeakable; Expounding the Buddha’s teachings is unspeakable.
Manifesting various bodies is unspeakable; Traveling to all lands is unspeakable;
Displaying spiritual powers is unspeakable; Pervading the ten directions is unspeakable;
Appearing as emanations everywhere is unspeakable; Attending upon all Buddhas is unspeakable.
Inconceivable offerings are prepared; Inconceivable varieties of infinite, pure, and wondrous jewels; Inconceivable supreme lotus flowers;
Inconceivable most excellent fragrant garlands— These inconceivable offerings are made to the Tathāgata.
Pure faith is unspeakable; supreme realization is unspeakable;
Exalted aspiration is unspeakable; revering all Buddhas is unspeakable;
Practicing generosity is unspeakable; their minds of the past are unspeakable.
Giving whatever is requested is unspeakable; Giving everything entirely is unspeakable.
Pure observance of the precepts is unspeakable; Purity of mind and intention is unspeakable.
Praising all Buddhas is unspeakable; Delighting in the True Dharma is unspeakable.
The accomplishment of all patiences is ineffable; The patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena is ineffable.
Being fully endowed with tranquility is ineffable; Abiding in the stage of tranquility is ineffable.
Arousing great diligence is ineffable; That mind is past and ineffable.
The non-retrogressive mind is ineffable; The unshakable mind is ineffable.
The treasury of all concentrations is ineffable; The contemplation of all phenomena is ineffable.
Abiding in tranquility within meditative absorption is ineffable; Thoroughly penetrating all dhyānas is ineffable.
The penetration of wisdom is ineffable; Mastery over samādhi is ineffable;
Thoroughly understanding all phenomena is ineffable; Clearly beholding all Buddhas is ineffable;
Cultivating immeasurable practices is ineffable; Generating vast vows is ineffable.
The profound realm is ineffable; The pure Dharma-gate is ineffable;
The power of the Bodhisattvas' Dharma is ineffable; The abiding of the Bodhisattvas' Dharma is ineffable;
Their various right mindfulnesses are ineffable; Those various Dharma-realms are ineffable.
The cultivation of the wisdom of skillful means is ineffable; the study of profound wisdom is ineffable;
immeasurable wisdom is ineffable; ultimate wisdom is ineffable;
the wisdom regarding all phenomena is ineffable; that pure wheel of Dharma is ineffable.
That great cloud of Dharma is unspeakable; That great rain of Dharma is unspeakable;
Those various spiritual powers are unspeakable; Those various skillful means are unspeakable;
The entry into the wisdom of empty stillness is unspeakable; The continuous succession of every thought-moment is unspeakable.
The immeasurable gateways of practice are unspeakable; Moment by moment, they constantly abide in unspeakable oceans of Buddha-fields. They are able to travel to all of them, which are unspeakable;
The distinctions among those fields are unspeakable, And their various purities are unspeakable.
The distinctions of adornments are unspeakable; The boundless forms and signs are unspeakable;
The various interminglings are unspeakable; The various exquisite beauties are unspeakable;
The pure buddha-fields are unspeakable; The defiled worlds are unspeakable.
He thoroughly knows that sentient beings are ineffable; He knows their spiritual lineages are ineffable;
He knows their karmic retributions are ineffable; He knows their mental activities are ineffable;
He knows their faculties and natures are ineffable; He knows their understandings and aspirations are ineffable.
The defilement and purification [of beings] are ineffable; Contemplation and subduing are ineffable;
Mastery over transformations is ineffable; Manifesting various bodies is ineffable;
Cultivating diligence is ineffable; Liberating sentient beings is ineffable.
Manifesting inconceivable miraculous transformations, Emitting inconceivable great rays of light,
With inconceivable varieties of colors and forms, Purifying inconceivable sentient beings,
From every single inconceivable pore, Emitting inconceivable nets of light.
The manifestation of colors through the net of light is unspeakable; The universal illumination of Buddha-fields is unspeakable;
Courageous valor and fearlessness are unspeakable; Skillful means are unspeakable;
The taming of sentient beings is unspeakable; Causing them to emerge from birth and death is unspeakable.
The purity of physical action is unspeakable; The purity of verbal action is unspeakable;
The boundless mental action is unspeakable; The supreme and wondrous conduct is unspeakable;
The accomplishment of the jewel of wisdom is unspeakable; The profound entry into the dharma-realm is unspeakable.
The Bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī is ineffable; Skillfully practicing and learning is ineffable.
The voice of the wise is ineffable; The purity of that voice is ineffable.
Right mindfulness and reality are ineffable; Awakening sentient beings is ineffable.
The perfection of majestic deportment is unspeakable; Pure cultivation is unspeakable;
The accomplishment of fearlessness is unspeakable; The subduing of the world is unspeakable;
The assembly of the Buddha-sons is unspeakable; And pure, supreme conduct is unspeakable.
Praising all Buddhas is unspeakable; Eulogizing them inexhaustibly is unspeakable.
The Guides of the World are unspeakable; Expounding their praises is unspeakable.
Those Bodhisattvas are unspeakable; Their pure merits are unspeakable.
The limits of those [realms] are unspeakable; One who can abide therein is unspeakably abiding;
The wisdom of abiding therein is unspeakable; Abiding through all kalpas is beyond description;
Rejoicing in all Buddhas is unspeakable; The equality of wisdom is unspeakable.
Skillfully entering all dharmas is ineffable; Being unimpeded regarding dharmas is ineffable;
The three times being like space is ineffable; Wisdom regarding the three times is ineffable;
Thoroughly penetrating the three times is ineffable; Abiding in wisdom is ineffable.
The sublime and wondrous conduct is unspeakable; The immeasurable great vows are unspeakable;
The pure great vows are unspeakable; The accomplishment of bodhi is unspeakable;
The bodhi of all Buddhas is unspeakable; The generation of wisdom is unspeakable.
The discernment of meanings and principles is ineffable; Knowing that all phenomena are ineffable is ineffable;
Adorning and purifying Buddha-fields is ineffable; Practicing the various powers is ineffable;
Cultivating them over a long period is ineffable; Awakening and understanding in a single thought-moment is ineffable.
The sovereign mastery of all Buddhas is unspeakable; The extensive exposition of the True Dharma is unspeakable;
Their various supernormal powers are unspeakable; Their manifestation in the world is unspeakable;
The pure wheel of Dharma is unspeakable; Their courageous ability to turn it is unspeakable.
Expounding various [teachings] that are unspeakable; Out of compassion for the world, throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons, One might praise unspeakable merits until unspeakable eons have passed;
Yet these unspeakable virtues would be difficult to exhaust.
Inexpressible Tathāgatas, with inexpressible tongues, Praise the Buddha’s inexpressible virtues;
Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions Were to simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment, They could not exhaust them in inexpressible eons.
Within that, a single Buddha can universally manifest all unspeakably many bodies;
within one such unspeakable body, he manifests unspeakably many heads;
within one such unspeakable head, he manifests unspeakably many tongues.
Within this ineffable [reality], there is one tongue, Manifesting sounds that are themselves ineffable;
Within this ineffable [reality], there is one sound, Which abides for incalculable eons.
As it is with one, so it is with all Buddhas; As it is with one, so it is with all bodies.
As one, so are all heads; as one, so are all tongues; as one, so are all voices.
Even if one were to praise the Buddha for unspeakable eons, those eons might come to an end, but the praise of the Buddha’s merits can never be exhausted.
Within a single atom, there are entirely present Inexpressible lotus worlds;
In each and every lotus world, The Tathāgata Bhadraśrī is inexpressibly many,
Pervading the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), Including all the atoms contained therein.
Whether worlds are forming, abiding, or decaying, their number is immeasurable and beyond description;
Within the space of a single atom, there are infinite boundaries, Where immeasurable lands universally enter;
the distinctions of the ten directions are beyond description, And the classifications of the ocean of lands are beyond description.
In each and every land there is a Tathāgata, Whose lifespan in kalpas is unspeakable;
The conduct of all Buddhas is unspeakable, And the profound, wondrous Dharma is unspeakable;
Their supernormal powers and great strength are unspeakable, And their unobstructed wisdom is unspeakable.
Entering into the pores is unspeakable; The causes and conditions of the pores are unspeakable;
Accomplishing the ten powers is unspeakable; Awakening to bodhi is unspeakable;
Entering the pure dharma-realm is unspeakable; Attaining the treasury of profound wisdom is unspeakable.
The various quantities are unspeakable, yet he fully knows them all as they are;
The various shapes and measures are unspeakable, yet there is nothing therein he does not thoroughly penetrate;
The various samādhis are unspeakable, yet he is able to abide within them throughout entire kalpas.
Before unspeakably many Buddhas, they have practiced with unspeakable purity;
they have attained unspeakable minds of unimpeded wisdom; they travel to the ten directions manifesting unspeakable spiritual powers; their conduct is boundless and unspeakable.
They travel to unspeakably many lands; Their thorough realization of all Buddhas is unspeakable;
Their courageous and fierce diligence is unspeakable; Their wisdom and penetration are unspeakable.
Regarding phenomena, they neither act nor do not act; Their entry into all realms is unspeakable.
Inexpressible great kalpas cannot be fully described; Constantly roaming the ten directions with inexpressible skillful means;
Inexpressible wisdom of reality, Inexpressible wisdom of spiritual powers, Manifesting in every thought-moment in ways that are inexpressible.
Regarding the ineffable teachings of all Buddhas, one understands each and every one as ineffable;
one may realize awakening in a single moment, or enter it at various times.
Within a single pore there are ineffable Buddha-fields, and within a single atom there are ineffable Buddha-fields.

Thus they travel to all Buddha-fields, Beholding the unspeakable Tathāgatas and attaining the unspeakable single reality; Skillfully entering the unspeakable lineage of Buddhas and the unspeakable Buddha-lands,
They are able to go to them all and achieve enlightenment.
The lands, sentient beings, and all Buddhas— Their essential natures and distinctions cannot be described;
Thus, throughout the three periods of time without limit, The Bodhisattva clearly perceives them all.
[Commentary] Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the meaning according to the text: one *lakṣa* makes one *koṭi*. One *lakṣa*...

This "one *koṭi*" (one hundred million) is here called one *zhì* (ten trillion). Furthermore, according to the calculation system of the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) of this land, there are twenty-three numerical units in total:

one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand, hundred thousand, million, ten million, hundred million, billion, ten billion, hundred billion, *zhì*, *jīng*, *gāi*, *zǐ*, *rǎng*, *gōu*, *jiàn*, *zhèng*, and *zài*. From the unit *rǎng* onward, there are three grades of numbers.
Regarding the calculation of these numbers: those of the lower grade consist of ten times ten variations; those of the middle grade consist of ten thousand times ten thousand variations;
and those of the superior grade consist of one billion times one billion variations. Now, this "Asaṃkhyeya" chapter employs the superior method of calculation;

thus, it states that "one hundred thousand times one hundred thousand makes one koṭi," and "koṭi times koṭi" corresponds here to a *rāja* (壤). A *nayuta* corresponds to a *gāva* (溝), and a *vimbara*... [text ends].
*Bāra* corresponds here to *zhèng* (correct), *lái* (to come), and *zìshìyǐqù* (from this point onward).
The names of the various regions all end here. *Míjiā* and *píjiā* are both pronounced with the rising tone (*shēng*).

*Jīn* (pronounced *jūlíng*) *jiémó*, *suōpó* (pronounced with the rising tone), *luó* (pronounced *láng'ǎo*), *píkēdàn* (pronounced *dānduōgān*), *yīluótuó* (*yī* pronounced *yúxī*), and *āmó* (pronounced *mò'ǎo*).
*Bo* (pú mò fǎn), *bì* (pú jì fǎn), *sū* (sū mò fǎn), *pì* (pǔ jì fǎn), *mí* (mò jì fǎn), *tú* (zhái jiā fǎn). These terms above signify vastness and magnitude;

although they are immeasurable and difficult to measure, their intended meaning clarifies that the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the vows and practices of Samantabhadra, and the three karmas are so expansive that no worldly calculation can reach them. This is fully detailed in the verses below.
Having clarified this, based on the great numbers, there are one hundred and twenty great numbers;
reaching from the "unspeakable-unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*) multiplication up to one final cycle, a verse says:
"The unspeakable-unspeakable fills all that is unspeakable-unspeakable; throughout unspeakable-unspeakable eons, one could not exhaustively speak of the unspeakable-unspeakable."
It is said that all Buddha-fields are completely ground and pulverized into fine dust; within a single mote of dust, there are unspeakably many fields, and as it is for one, so it is for all.

These unspeakably many Buddha-fields are pulverized into dust in a single thought-moment, and in every thought-moment they are likewise pulverized; this continues thus throughout unspeakably many eons. This dust—
This land is unspeakable; to describe this land by means of its atoms is even more difficult.

By means of the method of unspeakable calculation, one counts unspeakable eons (*kalpa*) through the number of these atoms. For every single atom, there are unspeakably many such eons throughout the ten directions.
To praise a single Samantabhadra for that many eons would never be able to exhaust the measure of his merit; thus is the intention of the Tathāgata made clear.
Because the merit of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices transcends all measurement and calculation,
this chapter describes the Samantabhadra vows and practices within the stage of Buddhahood as being immeasurable like space, incomparable to the atoms of lands, infinite and infinitely layered,
and infinitely and infinitely vast, as fully detailed in the sutra itself; such many eons constitute a single land.

Since such infinite Tathāgatas and the practices of Samantabhadra are inexhaustible within a single kṣaṇa, according to the questions posed in the second assembly mentioned previously, there should be ten "Summit" chapters (*śikhara-parivarta*) in total; however, the text has not yet reached them.

Chapter Thirty-one: On the Lifespan [Śāstra] In explaining this chapter, three sections will be established: first, the purpose for which the chapter was composed; second, the identity of the teacher who expounded the doctrine; and third, a word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.
Regarding the first, the purpose for which the chapter was composed: it clarifies that the preceding chapter has already explained the *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable).
This alone is sufficient; there are two interpretations regarding the "Lord who expounds the teaching. Regarding the Lord who expounds this chapter:

one interpretation holds that it is Heart-King Bodhisattva (*Cittarāja-bodhisattva*) who speaks, clarifying the Buddha’s lifespan. This is because the Buddha’s lifespan takes the Heart-King as its essence, and the Heart-King represents mastery over life-force (*jīvita-vaśitā*);
thus, it clarifies that the life-force of the Tathāgata’s Heart-King extends or shortens according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Briefly, regarding the mastery over things and the fact that the Tathāgata has no lifespan and neither length nor brevity:

third, as for the explanation of the meaning according to the text, this chapter of the sutra clarifies the long and short duration of the Buddha’s lifespan by establishing graded stages for those who have not yet awakened,
so that they may know the inexhaustible lifespan of the Tathāgata— using the few to reveal the many, and using the short to reveal the long.
If it were not thus, how could one know the lifespan of the Buddha? In reality, the Tathāgata has no nature of long or short life, nor does he have birth or cessation.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is like fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*):
it is without birth or cessation, and without going or coming. Thus, it is represented by the life-span of ten Buddhas to signify its inexhaustibility.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Cittarāja, amidst the great assembly, addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, one kalpa in the Sahā world, the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha, constitutes a single day and night in the Sukhāvatī world, the buddha-field of Amitābha Buddha;
and one kalpa in the Sukhāvatī world constitutes [a day and night] in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja."
One kalpa in the world-system of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa-dhvaja in the realm of Dhātu-vajra-dṛḍha constitutes one day and night in the world of Kāṣāya-dhvaja;
one kalpa in the world of Kāṣāya-dhvaja constitutes one day and night in the world-system of the Tathāgata Padma-vikāśana-suvijaya-prabha in the realm of Avaivartika-ghoṣa-cakra;
and one kalpa in the world of Avaivartika-ghoṣa-cakra constitutes one day and night in the world of Vimalā under the Tathāgata Dharma-dhvaja.
One eon in the world-system Vimalā (Free from Defilement) is one day and night in the Buddha-field of the Lion Buddha in the world-system Supradīpa (Good Lamp);
one eon in the world-system Supradīpa is one day and night in the Buddha-field of Prabhāgarbha (Treasury of Light) in the world-system Suvimalaprabhā (Excellent Radiance);
and one eon in the world-system Suvimalaprabhā is [one day and night] in the world-system Duratikrama (Difficult to Surpass).
One eon in the Buddha-field of the Lotus-Blossomed Radiance of the Dharmadhātu is a single day and night in the world-system of the Buddha Sarvābhijñāprabhāsa of the Adorned Wisdom world;
one eon in the Adorned Wisdom world is a single day and night in the Buddha-field of Candraprajña of the Mirror-Radiance world.
O Son of the Buddha, in this manner, proceeding through a sequence until one reaches the final world beyond a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds,
one *kalpa* constitutes one day and night in the world-system of the Victorious Lotus (*Śrīpadma*) within the Buddha-field of Worthy Victory (*Bhadrajaya*).
Within that realm, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and all his fellow great Bodhisattvas fill it completely.
Chapter Thirty-Two: The Abodes of Bodhisattvas.

[Treatise] To explain this chapter, three sections will be established: first, explaining the purpose for which this chapter has come; second, identifying the master who preaches the Dharma; and third, explaining the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first, explaining the purpose for which this chapter has come: previously, there was the Tathāgata’s lifespan and abiding.
Throughout this kalpa, the Buddha, by means of the bodhisattva practices, has extensively gathered and transformed beings within the oceans of worlds and human realms;
as it is thus in this direction, so it is in the lands of the ten directions and throughout Jambudvīpa.

While these dwelling places have their specific bases, his transformative activities are not restricted, reaching everywhere without exception. In essence, his body contains all buddha-fields, and a single hair-pore accommodates the entire dharma-realm.

The multitude [of beings] at the moment of a single instant responds to the ten directions, appearing everywhere with equal presence; their physical bodies are universally seen according to their faculties.
This clarifies the realm of a Bodhisattva’s sustaining power (*dhāraṇī*) and transformative guidance (*pariṇāmana*). This chapter must be explained through two interpretations:

first, regarding the master who expounds the Dharma, it clarifies the Bodhisattva’s practice of sustaining power and transformative guidance; second, it concerns the sovereign mastery of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) that accords with wisdom.
Because of this practice, it causes the Bodhisattva Mind-King to expound this chapter on the "Abodes," which generally clarifies that wisdom-activity arises in accordance with one's own mind-king;
having clarified that through the practices of Samantabhadra one achieves patience by following along [with these practices], all subsequent stages are called the Mind-King,
which possesses mastery over the world and does not conflict with phenomena.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Citta-rāja addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in the eastern direction there is a place called Mount Ṛṣigiri. Since ancient times, the assemblies of bodhisattvas have dwelt therein.
Currently, there is a bodhisattva named Vajravīra who resides there with a retinue of three hundred bodhisattvas."
They constantly dwell therein and expound the Dharma. To the south, there is a place called Mount Śikhin;

since ancient times, the assembly of bodhisattvas has resided there. There currently dwells a bodhisattva named Dharmamati, who, together with a retinue of five hundred bodhisattvas, constantly dwells therein and expounds the Dharma. To the west...
There is a place called Vajrajvālāparvata, where from time immemorial the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt;
there currently resides a bodhisattva named Vīryaparākramo-vaiśāradyacaryā, together with a retinue of three hundred bodhisattvas, who constantly expound the Dharma therein.
To the north, there is a place called Gandhamādana-parvata, where from time immemorial...

Among those bodhisattvas who dwell therein, there is currently a bodhisattva named Gandhahastin who, together with a retinue of three thousand bodhisattvas, constantly expounds the Dharma within that place.
To the northeast, there is a location called Mount Qingliang (Clear Cool), where since ancient times various bodhisattvas have dwelt; there is currently a bodhisattva...
The name "Sa" refers to Mañjuśrī, who, together with his retinue of ten thousand bodhisattvas, constantly dwells therein and expounds the Dharma.
Within that ocean of Dharma, there is a place called Vajra Mountain, where various bodhisattvas have resided since ancient times;
currently, there is a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata who dwells there with his own retinue of bodhisattvas.
One thousand two hundred members of the assembly of bodhisattvas always dwell therein and expound the Dharma.
To the southeast there is a place called Mount Cetiya, where since ancient times various assemblies of bodhisattvas have resided;
there currently dwells a bodhisattva named Deva-mukuṭa, together with his retinue of one thousand bodhisattvas, who always remain therein.
While he was preaching the Dharma, in the southwestern direction there is a place called Mount Radiance (*Prabhāsa-giri*), where from time immemorial various bodhisattvas have dwelt.

There currently resides a bodhisattva named Bhadrajyotis, together with a retinue of three thousand bodhisattvas, who constantly preach the Dharma therein. In the northwestern direction there is a place called Fragrance...
In this Wind Mountain, from ancient times until now, various bodhisattvas have dwelt and resided therein.
There currently resides a bodhisattva named Fragrant Light (*Gandhaprabhāsa*), who, together with his retinue of five thousand bodhisattvas, constantly expounds the Dharma within it.
Furthermore, within the Great Ocean, there is another dwelling place called the Adorned Cave (*Vyūha-guhā*), where, from ancient times until now, various bodhisattvas...
The assembly of bodhisattvas dwells therein. To the south of Vaiśālī, there is a dwelling place named Suvastumūla, where since ancient times the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt.
In the city of Mathurā, there is a dwelling place named Pūrṇaguhā, where since ancient times the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt. In the city of Kujinana, there is one...
There is a dwelling place called the Dharma Seat (*dharmāsana*), where from time immemorial the assembly of bodhisattvas has resided.
In the City of the Pure Other Shore (*viśuddhapārapura*), there is a dwelling place called the Mucilinda Cave, where from time immemorial the assembly of bodhisattvas has resided.
In the country of Mālava, there is a dwelling place established by the Unobstructed Dragon King (*anāvaraṇa-nāgarāja*).

Since ancient times, the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt therein; in the country of Kāmpilya, there is a dwelling place named Birth of Compassion where, since ancient times, the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt.
In the country of China, there is a dwelling place named Nārāyaṇa Cave where, since ancient times, the assembly of bodhisattvas has dwelt.
In the kingdom of Śūla, there is a dwelling place named Ox-Head Mountain (*Gośīrṣa-parvata*), where from ancient times various bodhisattvas have resided.
In the kingdom of Kāśmīra, there is a dwelling place named Succession (*Anupūrva*), where from ancient times various bodhisattvas have resided.
In the city of Vardhamāna-pramoda, there is a dwelling place named Venerable (*Bhadanta*).

Since ancient times, the assembly of bodhisattvas has resided within these caves. In the country of Āmrapālī, there is a dwelling place named Vision of the Radiance of a Hundred Million Treasuries (*Koṭigarbhaprabhādarśana*), where since ancient times the assembly of bodhisattvas has resided.
In the country of Gandhāra, there is a dwelling place named Śambhala Cave, where since ancient times the bodhisattvas...
The assembly dwelt therein.

[Treatise] Regarding the threefold explanation of the text according to its meaning: "Caitika Mountain" (Zhiti Shan) is translated here as "Pure Faith," for those who see this mountain are able to give rise to pure faith.
"Vaiśālī City" (Pisheshali Cheng) is translated here as "Extensive" (Guangbo), as it is located in Central India.

Because it is most vast, it is also called the City of Vaiśālī (Broad and Pure). The city of Mādurā is translated here as the City of Peacocks (*mayūra-pura*) and is also called the City of the Secret Canopy (*guhya-ātapatra*);
both names were established based on ancient events. The city of Koṭiñjaya is also called Koṭinagara.
*Koṭi* means "great basin. In that great basin, water was stored like a pond, and it was always situated by the side of this basin.
He frequently preached the *Jingjing jing* (Sūtra on Protecting Purity) and the *Yangsheng jing* (Sūtra on Nourishing Life) for the sake of others.
His later disciples all took their teacher’s dharma-name as their surname; thus, the city is named after him. The *Zhenlinduo* (眞隣陀) Cave—this is translated as "Liberation"—is the name of a dragon.
*Linduo* (隣陀) means "place"; because there was a dragon in this place who heard the Dharma and attained [realization], it is so called.
Because of liberation, it is named [after that]; Ma-lan-ta (Mālava) country—untranslated; Gan-pu-che (Kamboja) country—untranslated;

Chen-kan (Cīna), also called Chih-na, or also called Chen-tan; this is translated as "contemplation" (*cintā*), for because the people of this country engage in much contemplation and deliberation, it is named after this—it is this land of Han. Nara-yen (Nārāyaṇa); this means...
Jianlao (Kashgar): The full name is *Kharaśūtra*, though this region uses an abbreviated form, simply calling it Shule.
Kāśmīra: Formerly called Jibin; this translates as "Who has entered?
In the past, before this country was established, there was a great dragon lake that no one dared to approach. Later, there was a *rākṣasa*...
When the Han Emperor saw that the terrain was so excellent it was suitable for human habitation, he requested from the Dragon enough space for one knee. The Dragon granted this;
the Arhat then manifested his supernatural power to enlarge his knee until it gradually filled the pond. Believing the Dragon's word, the Emperor relinquished the land and departed.
The Arhat then used his divine power to dry up the water so that the common people might dwell there, and he established [the settlement].
Regarding the name of the residence, everyone said, "If it were not for our holy master, who could have entered this place?

For this reason, the name was established based on these words. This country is located within the borders of North India, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, which is translated as "Holder of the Earth" (Chí-dì).
Because many sages and saints dwell in this country, it is not subject to other kingdoms.
Because it was subject to harm, it is also said that *gandha* means "fragrance" and *dhara* means "pervasive" (*prabhūta*).

This refers to the fact that within this country, fragrant scents grow in great abundance and pervade everywhere. It lies between the two regions of North India and South India, in the middle of Central India.
The Śambhala Cave is so named because the *śampāka* tree (a fragrant flower tree) grows in great numbers near its vicinity.
This chapter, titled "The Tree," primarily elucidates the Bodhisattva’s practice of sustaining and maintaining the Three Jewels so that they remain uninterrupted in the nurturing of sentient beings;
it cites this single Jambudvīpa as a representative of all lands in the ten directions and all Jambudvīpas, with the entire principle being applied accordingly.
Above this, the assembly at the Buddha-flower [World] in the Third Dhyāna Heaven is added to constitute the seventh [chapter].
