Because one initiates the practice of great sovereign power within the three realms through the skillful means of the ten pāramitās, one achieves each [mark] upon the nine grades of afflictions.
The practice of the ten *pāramitās* accomplishes the ninety kinds of marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) serve as superior aids to clarify the skillful means (*upāya*), they accomplish the seven kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

By means of these seven factors of enlightenment and the skillful means of the path consisting of the ten *pāramitās*, the nine grades of afflictions are transformed into the two wisdoms of the conventional and the ultimate.
The perfection of great compassion consists of ten modes of practice established upon a single grade of affliction, which result in ten types of manifested signs;
these ninety factors are correlated with the ten *pāramitās*. Seven factors are correlated with the seven limbs of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

The signs corresponding to the atoms within the ten Flower Treasury worlds (*padmakośa-lokadhātu*) correlate with the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, as well as the three karmas and the universal pervasiveness of the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Question: From which teaching does this emerge? Answer: All the dharma-gates contained in this sutra emerge solely from its own teaching;
no other sutras can accord with these gates of this teaching. What is meant by "its own teaching"? Answer:
It is because Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s own practice; he causes his own practice to explain the marks obtained through the fruition of that very practice.

Because the wise practitioner does not depart from the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, nor from the seven factors of enlightenment and the ten pāramitās, one understands the teaching through names, understands practice through the teaching, and understands the subduing of delusions through practice. When delusions are extinguished, retribution is perfected;
thus, that which arises from cause and effect is itself the teaching. One must not attempt to cite other provisional teachings or the practice-gates of the three vehicles as examples for this.

Regarding the retributive fruits obtained from what has been cultivated, one may understand their meaning by following the sequence of the light rays emitted, the names of the Bodhisattvas, and even the names of their seats as presented in the preceding chapters.

For the practitioner who acts as a Buddha and acts as Samantabhadra, the gates of wisdom and compassion are accomplished without departing from the afflictions of the three realms and nine stages; such is the nature of all retribution.

The causes and conditions of birth are further established within the nine grades of afflictions of the three realms, whereby one accomplishes the practice of sublime wisdom, attains the practice of mastery beyond the three realms, and secures the karmic retribution of excellence that transcends the three realms. By inferring from this, the intention of the Buddha can be clearly understood;
this is precisely the teaching of the Sūtra. All subsequent characteristics are based upon these three types of action, two types of wisdom, and seven [factors].

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) take the ten *pāramitās* as their essence; furthermore, the seven factors of enlightenment and nine *pāramitās* together constitute a single *jñāna-pāramitā*.
With the *jñāna-pāramitā* as the fruit of Buddhahood, the seven factors of enlightenment and nine *pāramitās* serve as the practice;
thus, as a karmic reward, one attains the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and the ten lotuses.
The marks of a great person, as numerous as the atoms within the Flower Treasury World, represent the perfection of the Great Compassion of Discriminative Wisdom (*vibhāga-jñāna*).
Because these are obtained as the retribution for the practices of Samantabhadra throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the meanings of the two preceding explanations are mutually inclusive.
Hereafter, all the various marks arise from the Great Compassionate function of Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), following upon Discriminative Wisdom.

The retribution-born [marks] are self-evident according to the text, as the Sūtra says: "The *kaṇṭhapuṣpa* is accomplished. This intends to clarify that the three lines on the neck are accomplished by means of the three folds of the neck.
It is said that in the Western Regions there is the *kaṇṭhapuṣpa* fruit, which is red and formed with three lines;
by comparing it to this, the phrase "Mount Meru concealing clouds" clarifies the Tathāgata’s mark of the great man consisting of the upper right auxiliary tooth.
The flames rise as high as Mount Sumeru.
[From] the *Tathāgata-anuvyañjana-prabhā-guṇa-parivarta*, Chapter Thirty-Five.
[Commentary: To explain this chapter, four sections are established: first, an explanation of the title; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion.
Third, the explanation of the Lord of the Dharma; fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. First, the explanation of the title of the chapter:

Why is it named "The Merit of the Light of the Minor Marks"? This clarifies that the preceding chapter already explained the ocean of the ten marks of the body, wherein the body is adorned by as many oceans of marks as there are atoms in ten lotus-treasury worlds. This present chapter concerns that Buddha...
Because the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) within the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) possess the merit of being devoid of intrinsic nature;

because the light is established by means of the principle and wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that accords with the practice and its fruition, thereby accomplishing the marks of a Great Man;

and because the name of this chapter is established on this basis—namely, that the light of the fruition-marks is accomplished through the sublime principle of wisdom which, in accordance with practice, destroys the afflictions—this is the second explanation of the chapter.
The purpose of this section is to clarify that the marks of the Great Beings mentioned in the preceding chapter arise as karmic retribution based on the Tathāgata’s practice;

therefore, it is entrusted to Samantabhadra to explain them. Since the conduct of Samantabhadra is the conduct of all Buddhas, these secondary signs (anuvyañjana) and their radiant light clarify the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya—which is without intrinsic nature—and the merit of practicing in accordance with that [wisdom], which is without substance or characteristics.

Because light is able to greatly benefit sentient beings, it returns by means of formlessness and lack of substantial nature to illuminate those with whom it has a karmic connection, just as the sound of the formless celestial drum preaches the Dharma to bring about liberation; therefore, this chapter must appear here.

Nevertheless, although principle and practice are non-dual and constitute a single essence, they cannot be conflated when considering the differences in the fruits realized and the benefits bestowed upon others.
There is no third explanation for the primary teacher of the doctrine; it clarifies that the fruit of such wondrous principle is the Jewel Hand.
Because it signifies the meaning of "guiding and receiving," this chapter is established to symbolize how the wondrous wisdom-nature light of the Dharmakāya guides and receives all sentient beings.
Why does the Tathāgata himself speak this chapter? It is to clarify that the Tathāgata himself speaks it.

Within the fruit of Buddhahood, there are two delusions: first, the delusion regarding the vastness of the numerical categories of phenomena; second, the delusion regarding the merit of the minor marks and radiant light.
These two stages of phenomena are not within the reach of the wisdom of bodhisattvas; they become manifest only when the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected.
This is because the *dharmakāya* of principle-wisdom serves merely as the non-reliant substance for practice and the condition for penetrating delusion; thus, within the midst of that practice—
The manifestation of the signs of merit belongs to the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices;

being the fruition born of the retribution for Samantabhadra’s own practice, it is further caused by Samantabhadra himself to describe the ultimate fruit of the retribution for his own practice. The *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* concerns the vastness of numerical dharmas;
the *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta* concerns the essence of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body, which is without intrinsic nature and without dependence.
Because of these merits, both of these dharmas are not attained through conditioned practice; they are not reached by the conduct of Samantabhadra, but rather take that conduct as their basis.
They are the dharmas pertaining to the final stage when the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected through the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself explained the dharma-gate of his own stage from within that very stage, for the sake of those who follow.
Because scholars are not deluded by this, this chapter clarifies that within the principle of the formless nature of the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body,

all dharmas that benefit sentient beings are manifested through the resonance of the luminous celestial drum— a thing without physical form or substance— which preaches the wondrous, signless principle of the Dharma-body; by this,
one immediately ascends to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) through the merit of being free from defilement, and thus it is not otherwise.

Because the characteristics of the lower stages are brought into harmony with the great vows, wisdom, compassion, and the myriad practices, and because this is spoken by the Tathāgata from his own station,
although the fruit of practice and the fruit of wisdom are not distinct, the stages are distinguished according to the Dharma so that the principles are made clear.
This enables those who have resolved their minds to practice to understand them without confusion, clarifying the meaning of the Dharmakāya and its faculties.

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) does not belong to that which is produced through the cultivation of conditioned practices; it consists solely of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
One must rely upon this fundamental wisdom, blending it with the power of Samantabhadra’s great vows and dedicating [the merit] through cultivation and study.

One should always take fundamental wisdom as the essence of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Although the ten *pāramitās* are added to this Dharma-body and fundamental wisdom, [they do not constitute its essence].
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four means of integration, and the four immeasurables constitute the practices for accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings.
However, as the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* is devoid of intrinsic nature, it cannot undergo arising or ceasing;
rather, it can serve as the cause for all various practices and vows to result in liberation—free from defilement, free from affliction, and free from the karma of the three realms.

The essence of this is that within this chapter it is clarified how the merit of these secondary marks (anuvyañjana) functions in accordance with practice, never failing its own fruit, and extensively benefiting sentient beings; for this is the constant Buddha-fruit of all bodhisattva practices.
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself has spoken thus: if one lacks the fruit of such wisdom and virtue, all sentient beings are impermanent.
Just as the essence of empty space serves as the very essence of all that exists, yet empty space itself does not belong to the realm of cultivation or birth;
regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the fourfold sequence of the text, this section is divided into thirteen parts.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a secondary mark (anuvyañjana) named King Paripūrṇa. From within this secondary mark issues a great radiance called Blazing, which has seven million asaṃkhyeya rays of light as its retinue."
[Treatise] First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "and [became] his retinue," there are three lines of scripture clarifying the essence and function of the raised light.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, when I was a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, I emitted a great light named 'Light Banner' (Prabhāketu)."
King, ten times as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field were illuminated; those beings in the hells within those worlds who encountered this light found their manifold sufferings stilled.
They attained ten kinds of purity in their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and likewise experienced joy, leaping for gladness, and celebration.
At the end of their lives there, they were reborn in the Tuṣita heaven, where they possessed celestial palaces.
There is a drum named "Exceedingly Delightful"; once those devas have been born there, this drum emits a sound and addresses them, saying:
"O sons of the gods, because you were not heedless in mind, you planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgata;
having previously attended upon many spiritual friends, through the great majestic power of Vairocana, you passed away from that life and were reborn here in this heaven."
[Treatise] From the second section on the sons of the Buddha down to the point where they pass away from there and are reborn in this heaven,

eight lines of scripture clarify the section concerning the causes for the proclamation by the celestial drum and the benefits obtained by those in hell when the Tathāgata dwells in Tuṣita Heaven, emitting the wondrous light of the non-conditioned purity of the principle and wisdom of the Dharma-body.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet are named King Universal Illumination.
Among these are secondary marks (anuvyañjana) named King Perfection, which constantly emit forty kinds of light rays.
Among them is one ray named Pure Virtue, which can illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms within a hundred million nayutas of Buddha-fields, according to the various karmas of sentient beings.

He causes all those who indulge in various sensual pleasures to mature, and all sentient beings in the extreme suffering of the Avīci Hell who encounter this light die and are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. Once reborn there, they hear the sound of celestial drums proclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent, O sons of the gods! The Bodhisattva Vairocana has entered the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement."
At that time, when they were thus paying homage, the sons of the gods heard the sound of the celestial drum exhorting them in this way, and they all conceived this thought:
"How marvelous! How rare! What cause has produced this subtle and wondrous sound? Then the celestial drum addressed the sons of the gods, saying:
"The sound I have produced is accomplished through the power of various roots of goodness. Sons of the gods, listen as I speak of myself."
Yet they do not cling to a self, nor do they cling to what belongs to a self; all Buddhas are likewise thus.
They themselves declare, "I am a Buddha," yet they do not cling to a self, nor do they cling to what belongs to a self.

O sons of the gods, just as my voice does not come from the east, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below, so too is the attainment of Buddhahood through karmic retribution—not coming from any such direction.
The sons of the gods who have come from the ten directions—just as you yourselves were once in hell, neither the hell nor the body came from the ten directions;
rather, they arose solely because you were bound by the delusions of inverted, evil karma and ignorance, thus taking birth in a hellish body.
This has no fundamental basis and no place of origin. Sons of the gods, it is through the power of the majesty of the Bodhisattva Vairocana that he emits [these rays].
This great radiance does not come from the ten directions; likewise, O sons of gods, my sound of the celestial drum also does not come from the ten directions.
It arises solely through the power of the roots of goodness of samādhi and the majestic power of the Prajñāpāramitā, producing such pure sounds and manifesting such various forms of mastery.
"O Son of Heaven, it is like this: for example, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, possesses the most exquisite palaces and various musical instruments of the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
yet these musical instruments do not come from the ten directions. My celestial drum-sound is likewise: it does not come from the ten directions.
O Sons of Heaven, it is as if all worlds, numbering as many as the atoms in a hundred billion nayuta buddha-fields, were ground to dust."
"O sons of the gods, although I preach the Dharma to as many sentient beings as there are motes of dust,
according to their inclinations, so that they may be greatly gladdened, I feel no weariness toward them,
no discouragement, no pride, and no negligence; and the Bodhisattva Vairocana, while abiding in the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement, is likewise."
From within a single secondary mark on the palm of his right hand, he emitted a ray of light that manifested immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers;

even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas could not understand them, let alone ordinary beings. O sons of the gods, you should go to where that bodhisattva is, attend upon him, and make offerings to him;
do not again become greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires, nor be attached to the five desires themselves.
"O sons of the gods, it is as if the fire at the end of an eon burns Mount Sumeru until nothing remains;
likewise, when the mind is entangled by craving, one can never give rise to the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha.
O sons of the gods, you should recognize kindness and repay it. O sons of the gods, there are sentient beings who do not know [this]..."

"Those who fail to repay their debts of gratitude often meet with untimely deaths and are reborn in the hells. O sons of the gods, in the past you were within those hells when this light shone upon your bodies;
having abandoned that place, you have been born here. You should now swiftly dedicate yourselves toward the increase of your roots of goodness.
"O sons of the gods, just as my celestial drum is neither male nor female, yet is able to produce immeasurable and boundless [sounds],"
O sons of gods and daughters of gods, this inconceivable matter is likewise for you: though neither male nor female, you are able to enjoy various sublime palaces and groves.

Just as my celestial drum is neither born nor extinguished, so too are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—neither born nor extinguished. You should know that if you can awaken to and understand this, it is so.
Then he enters the Samādhi of the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom.

[Treatise] Regarding the third son of the Buddha, from the passage beginning with "beneath the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet" down to "entering the Samādhi of the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom," forty-two and a half lines of scripture clarify how sentient beings in the evil realms receive the benefit of the light.
The Section on the Celestial Drum Preaching the Dharma, Arising from the Retribution of Abandonment.
[Sūtra] At that time, having heard this sound, the sons of the gods attained what they had never experienced before;
they immediately all manifested ten thousand clouds of flowers, ten thousand clouds of incense, ten thousand clouds of music, ten thousand clouds of banners, and ten thousand clouds of canopies.
Having performed these transformations of clouds of songs and praises, they proceeded together to the palace where the Bodhisattva Vairocana resided;
there, with palms joined in reverence, they stood to one side, desiring to behold him, yet they were unable to see him.

[Treatise] Regarding the fourth period, from the passage "When the sons of the gods heard this sound" down to "yet they could not see him," there are four lines and a half of scripture that clarify how the sons of the gods arose to make offerings and proceeded to their celestial palaces,
yet were unable to see the Vairocana Bodhisattva portion.
[Sūtra] At that time, a son of heaven spoke these words: "The Bodhisattva Vairocana has passed away from here and been born into the human world in the household of King Śuddhodana;
riding upon a sandalwood palatial pavilion, he has entered the womb of Queen Māyā."

[Treatise] In the fifth period, from the devaputras below down to Māyādevī’s womb, there are two sets of sūtra passages that clarify how the devaputras inform the assembly of devas regarding the portion of bodhisattvas who take birth in the human realm.
[Sūtra] At that time, the sons of the gods, observing with their divine eyes that the Bodhisattva’s body was dwelling in the human world within the house of King Śuddhodana,
and seeing that the Brahmā and Kāmadhātu gods were attending upon and making offerings to him, all the hosts of sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"If we do not go to where the Bodhisattva is to inquire after his well-being, or even for a single moment give rise to attachment toward this celestial palace..."
When it is time for them to descend, each of these sons of the gods, together with a retinue of ten nayutas, desires to go down to Jambudvīpa.
At that time, a voice issues from the celestial drum, proclaiming: "O sons of the gods, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not pass away from this life to be reborn there;
rather, by means of their supernormal powers, they act in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, causing them [to perceive the descent]."

Just as you have now seen these sons of the gods, who are able to produce sounds despite not being objects of visual perception, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who enters the *vimala-samādhi* (Stainless Samādhi).
He is likewise not an object of visual perception, yet he can manifest birth in various places.
Free from conceptual discrimination, having eliminated pride, and being without attachment, O sons of the gods, you should all resolve to [attain] Arhatship.
With a mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they purify their intentions and abide in virtuous deportment; they repent of and eliminate all karmic obstructions,
afflictive obstructions, retributive obstructions, and obstructions to vision, using bodies as numerous as the sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm,
heads as numerous as the sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, and tongues as numerous as the sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm.

[The text] states: "Equal in number to the sentient beings of the realms, one performs wholesome bodily actions, wholesome verbal actions, and wholesome mental actions, thereby repenting and eliminating all obstacles, faults, and evils.
[Treatise]: At the sixth stage, the sons of the gods, having observed with their divine eyes down to the point of repenting and eliminating all [faults],...

Regarding the fifteen and a half lines of scripture on the faults of hindrances, it clarifies that when the various devaputras wished to go to the human realm to make offerings to the Drum-Sound (Dundubhisvara),
[the Buddha] told them that the essence of Vairocana Bodhisattva neither comes nor goes, and exhorted them to resolve upon bodhicitta and repent to eliminate their faults and evils.
This constitutes the section on the elimination of faults and evils.
[Sūtra] At that time, having heard these words, the sons of the gods attained a state never before experienced and, with great joy, asked him:
"How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva repent and eliminate all faults and evils?
Then, by the power of the roots of goodness from the bodhisattva’s samādhi, the celestial drum emitted a voice and declared: "Sons of the gods, the bodhisattva knows that all karmas..."
It does not come from the east, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below;
yet it gathers together and dwells within the mind, arising solely from inversion and having no place of abode. Thus, the Bodhisattva clearly perceives this with certainty, free from doubt.
O sons of the gods, as I, the celestial drum, speak of karma, speak of its retribution, speak of conduct, and speak of precepts—so too do I speak.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas likewise delight in speaking of and teach all samādhis.
I speak of "I" and "mine," and sentient beings speak of greed, hatred, delusion, and various karmas; yet in reality, there is no self and nothing that belongs to a self.
All the karmic actions performed and the retributions of the six realms of existence cannot be found anywhere throughout the ten directions when sought. O sons of the gods, it is like this:
My voice is neither born nor extinguished; the various devas who have committed evil do not hear other sounds, but hear only the sound that awakens them regarding the hells.
All karmic actions are likewise neither born nor extinguished; according to what is cultivated, one receives its retribution.
O sons of the gods, the sounds produced by my celestial drum cannot be [exhausted] throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Exhaustively and without interruption, neither coming nor going can be apprehended. O sons of the gods, if there were coming and going, there would be the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
yet no Buddha ever teaches a doctrine of annihilationism or eternalism, except as a skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity.
O sons of the gods, it is like my voice, which in immeasurable worlds accords with sentient beings.
The minds of all were likewise enabled to hear [the teachings] of all Buddhas; furthermore, according to the inclinations of sentient beings, they were all enabled to see them.

It was as if there were a vaidūrya mirror named "Able to Illuminate," pure and translucent, equal in size to ten worlds, wherein all mountains, rivers, and all multitudes within immeasurable and boundless lands were clearly reflected.
All images, from those born as humans down to those in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, appear therein.
What do you think, sons of the gods? Can it be said that those images come into the mirror or go out from the mirror?
They replied, "No, sons of the gods. All karmas are likewise; although they are able to produce [results], [they do not come or go]."
"O sons of the gods, all virtuous karmic fruits have no place from which they come or to which they go.
Just as a magician deceives the eyes of men with illusions, you should know that all karma is likewise so. To know it thus is true repentance;
all evil deeds will thereby become completely purified."

[Treatise] Seventh: From "At that time, the celestial drum... down to "...all sinful evils are entirely purified," there are twenty-seven lines of scripture which clarify how the celestial drum preaches for the sake of the devaputras the section on the Bodhisattva’s repentance and elimination of evil, and the realization of the non-arising of karma.

[Sūtra] When this Dharma was being taught, among the worlds numbering as many as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, the devaputras of the Tuṣita heaven attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) devaputras of the six desire realms (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara*) resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This applied to all [the devas] within the six desire heavens.
The celestial maidens all relinquished their female bodies and gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi.
At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard this exposition of Samantabhadra’s vast and great dedication, attained the ten stages;

they obtained the samādhi adorned with all powers and, through purifying the three karmas to the extent of the number of sentient beings, repented and eliminated all heavy obstructions. Thereupon, they immediately beheld hundreds of thousands [of Buddhas].
Upon each of the seven-jeweled lotuses, as numerous as the atoms within billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, there sat a bodhisattva in the full lotus posture, emitting great rays of light.
From every single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) of those bodhisattvas, they emitted rays of light equal in number to all sentient beings;
within those rays of light sat Buddhas, as numerous as all sentient beings, seated in the full lotus posture.
He preached the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings, yet he had not yet manifested even a fraction of the power of the *vimala-samādhi* (Stainless Samādhi).

[Treatise] From the passage "When this Dharma was being taught for the eighth time" down to "even a fraction of the power of the *vimala-samādhi*," there are eleven lines and a half of scripture clarifying the section on how the devaputras and devakanyās obtained benefits.

[Sūtra] At that time, those devaputras, with the aforementioned various flowers, further manifested from every single pore of their bodies clouds of exquisite flowers equal in number to all sentient beings, as an offering to Vairocana Tathāgata.
Holding them, they scattered them over the Buddha, and they all came to rest upon the body of the Buddha. Those clouds of fragrance rained down universally throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields.

If there are sentient beings in worlds as numerous as motes of dust who have their bodies perfumed by this fragrance, their bodies will experience peace and bliss, just like a bhikṣu who has entered the fourth dhyāna; all their karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished.

Furthermore, if there are those who hear it, those sentient beings—who possess five hundred internal afflictions regarding form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and likewise five hundred external ones—[shall be liberated].

There are twenty-one thousand types of afflictions for those whose conduct is dominated by desire, twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct is dominated by anger, twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct is dominated by delusion, and twenty-one thousand for those whose conduct is characterized by equal parts of these.
Having understood that all such things are entirely false and illusory, and having known this, one accomplishes the pure roots of goodness of the Sovereign Radiance of Fragrant Banner Clouds. If...

There are sentient beings who, upon seeing his canopy, plant roots of goodness equal to those of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) adorned with a pure golden net—roots as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River.
[Treatise] Ninth: At that time, from those various devaputras down to the roots of goodness as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are ten.

The *Dvayāvatāra-sūtra* clarifies that when the various devaputras presented offerings of incense and flowers to the Buddha, any sentient beings who smelled the fragrance had their eighty-four thousand afflictions completely purified.
They accomplished the pure roots of goodness of the "Sovereign Radiance of the Incense Banner Cloud.
Furthermore, if any sentient beings saw those canopies, they planted the seeds for becoming a Cakravartin King of the Golden Net. A single [instance of this]...
[This is] a portion of the roots of goodness as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

[Sūtra]: O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this position of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), they teach and transform sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-fields.

[Treatise] The tenth section, from "The Buddha-son Bodhisattva, having attained this rank of Cakravartin King" down to "teaching and transforming sentient beings," consists of one and a half lines of scripture that clarify the extent of the sphere of influence and the scope of the conversion effected by the Golden Net Cakravartin King.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, it is as if, in the world-system of the Tathāgata Candraprabha, which is like a clear mirror, there are always immeasurable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās from various worlds who manifest their bodies to come and listen to the Dharma.
He extensively expounds upon the accounts of his past lives (*jātaka*) without a single moment’s interruption. If there are sentient beings...
Those who hear the name of this Buddha will surely attain rebirth in that Buddha’s land.

[Treatise] The eleventh section, "Buddha-Son," beginning from the passage "For example, like the world of the bright mirror" down to "will surely attain rebirth in that Buddha’s land," consists of four lines of scripture that clearly cite the analogy of the Tathāgata Candraprabha (Moon-Wisdom) to demonstrate the benefits gained by hearing his name.
[Section].
[Sūtra]: It is likewise for a Bodhisattva who dwells securely in the station of a Wheel-Turning King with a Pure Golden Net;
if anyone should even momentarily encounter its radiance, they will necessarily attain the tenth stage of a Bodhisattva through the power of the roots of goodness previously cultivated.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, just as one who has attained the first dhyāna, though not yet having reached the end of their life,
sees the palaces existing in the Brahma-heaven and experiences the bliss of the Brahma-world, so it is for all who have attained the various dhyānas. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
dwelling in the rank of a Universal Monarch of the Pure Golden Net, emits the pure radiance from his maṇi-crest, if there are sentient beings...
All those born who encounter this light attain the tenth stage of a bodhisattva;
they achieve immeasurable radiance of wisdom, obtain ten kinds of pure eyes, and so forth up to ten kinds of pure minds;
they are endowed with immeasurable and profound samādhis, and thus accomplish such pure fleshly eyes.

[Treatise] Section twelve, from "The Bodhisattva abides securely" down to "accomplishing such pure fleshly eyes," consists of nine lines of scripture clarifying that if one encounters the light of this Golden Net Universal Monarch,
one immediately attains a portion of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The Remainder of the Thirty-fifth Chapter: "The Merit of the Radiance of the Buddha’s Minor Marks."
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were someone who took billions of nayutas of buddha-fields and ground them into atoms;
then, taking one atom as a single buddha-field, they again ground that many buddha-fields into atoms.
Taking all these atoms and placing them in the left hand, they travel eastward for as many worlds as there are atoms, setting down a single atom."
If one were to travel east until reaching the end of these atoms, and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—
and if all the worlds in the ten directions, whether those upon which atoms have been placed or those not so placed, were all combined to form a single Buddha-field—
what do you think, Ratnapāṇi? Would such a Buddha-field be vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable?
Mati replied, "No, it is not so. Such a buddha-field is vast, immeasurable, rare, extraordinary, and inconceivable.
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this parable, can give rise to faith and understanding, you should know that they are even more rare, extraordinary, and marvelous.
The Buddha said, "Precious Hand, it is so, it is so, just as you have said. If there are good sons or..."
To those women who hear this parable and give rise to faith, I grant this prediction:
they shall certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall obtain the Tathāgata’s supreme jewel-hand of wisdom.
Furthermore, suppose there were someone who reduced as many vast Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a thousand billion Buddha-fields—such as those described above—into fine dust.
Taking these minute particles of dust and exhausting them one by one according to the previous analogy, until they are integrated to form a single Buddha-field,
which is then again ground into dust; proceeding in this sequence and succession for as many as eighty such cycles— within a single thought-moment,
the pure physical eye of a Bodhisattva perceives all the minute particles of dust existing within all such vast Buddha-fields resulting from the karmic retribution of their deeds.
Within it, he was able to see clearly and behold as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten billion vast Buddha-fields,
their pure radiance illuminating worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields;
such were the pure golden nets of the Universal Monarch Ratnapāṇi, all of which were accomplished through the roots of goodness and the merit of his profound samādhi.

First, it explains the cause from which the light comes; second, it explains by what causes and conditions those who are touched by the light [attain realization];

third, it explains from what cause the celestial drum is able to preach the Dharma. Regarding the first—explaining the cause from which the light comes—it arises from the Tathāgata’s own essential nature, the fundamentally pure *dharmakāya*, which has no basis for abiding.

Because it arises from the merit of the naturally pure nature of wisdom and is able to accomplish the primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) while being without any basis of dependence, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Secondary Signs. This radiance is shared equally by all sentient beings;

yet, if it is not assisted, uplifted, and manifested through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, it cannot be made manifest. Thus, the practices and vows of Samantabhadra are necessary for its revelation.
If one does not rely on this essence of radiance, one cannot achieve the great function of the Dharma-realm which is without eyes;
for this reason, this sutra is titled the *Sutra on the Mutual Adornment of Enlightenment and Practice*. Having reached the perfection of these two practices, each then manifests its own merit.
The marks of the Great Man in the preceding chapter were accomplished through the practice of Samantabhadra, and now they cause Samantabhadra himself to manifest them.

Therefore, it is said that the light of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) in this chapter is the light of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Buddha’s own fruition—the unconditioned *dharmakāya*—which abides nowhere.
This light is the Buddha’s own teaching; we grasp the meaning of the sūtra solely by relying on the Teacher.

Within the description of these lights, the light of the secondary marks is immeasurable; now, based on this chapter, I shall briefly cite three examples. First, I shall cite [the example of] the Tathāgata...

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses a secondary mark (anuvyañjana) named King Paripūrṇa, who dwells in the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that is without support and without intrinsic nature, yet is able to illuminate all things with sovereignty;
this is called King Paripūrṇa. To specifically illustrate the specific functions within this light, it is said:
"From within this secondary mark, a great radiance issues forth, named Blazing. This radiance possesses specific functions that are able to..."
"Shattering the delusions with seven million *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light as their retinue" means that these lights accord with the faculties of beings, numbering seven hundred;
this total number refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). By extinguishing the sufferings of the six realms, they constitute seven hundred;
"hundred" is the primary unit of counting. They cause all beings to give rise to the ten stages of the path within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
For this reason, the essence of this light is the fruit of Buddhahood; all that is reached by its radiance relies upon the source.

Furthermore, regarding those practitioners prior to the eighth stage who have developed their practice, it is said there are seven million; "ten thousand practices" and "asamkhyeya" clarify that the essence of light is complete and its roots are omnipresent.
Next, it mentions the Tuṣita Heaven to illustrate the time when he was a Bodhisattva and emitted a great light.
The King of the Banner of Renowned Names illuminated worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields;
the sentient beings in the hells there obtained relief from all their sufferings and attained the purification of the ten faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

They cast off their hellish bodies and were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where they heard the sound of celestial drums preaching the Dharma, attained the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement, and ascended to the tenth stage of the Bodhisattva path.

The light of clarity illuminates past causes: those who, while practicing with the power of the ten stages of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-vimokṣa*), lacked inherent diligence and thus gave rise to evil destinies through negligence, encounter this light so that their suffering ceases and their three karmas (*tri-karma*) return to their original state. Regarding this clarity, there are three births that bring about fruition:
in the first birth, one cultivates the ten stages of faith and understanding, yet the mind is not focused and one commits various evil deeds; in the second birth, one dwells in an evil destiny.
In the midst of the hells, three times they were touched by the radiance of light, their suffering ceased, and they were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven;
there, the sound of the celestial drum proclaimed the Dharma, and they attained the fruit of the tenth stage. These constitute three births.

Furthermore, if within this teaching one relies on wisdom to resolve the mind, seeking with diligence and without indolence, cultivating the samādhi of skillful means and entering the Buddha’s wisdom, one will be born as a Tathāgata.

One who becomes a true son of the Buddha is already said to have attained Buddhahood. Just as the crown prince born of the primary consort of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) possesses the marks of a wheel-turning monarch;
though he has not yet ascended the throne, he is the true seed of that king, and in essence there is no difference between them.

Likewise, a bodhisattva at the first stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), having newly arisen from the seed of faith, cultivates the samādhi of skillful means, whereby right wisdom is spontaneously manifested.

Although one born into the family of the Tathāgata has not yet attained the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), they occupy the rank of a Buddha; for their seed of true wisdom is no different from that of a Buddha.

From this point onward, through the cultivation and refinement of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) during this single lifetime, one enters into birth by transformation (*nirmāṇa-upapatti*) in accordance with right knowledge, attaining mastery over supernormal powers.
This is like a person who, throughout a single lifetime, cultivates the conditioned ten paths of wholesome action through the activities of body, speech, and mind.

If even those who merely cultivate goodness can attain rebirth in the heavens and acquire celestial supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), how much more so for one in whom right wisdom is manifest, who realizes the Dharma-body, and who, being free from the intention to commit evil, specializes in learning compassion—how could such a person not enter the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?

If one were to discuss this directly according to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), then throughout both birth-and-death and nirvana, all is considered transformation; awakening to wisdom is precisely this.
The Buddha does not define supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as such because they are provisional skillful means (*upāya*) for benefiting sentient beings.

If one takes only the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), that is true awakening; all other supernormal powers, from the descent from Tuṣita to the attainment of Buddhahood, are subsumed under the category of practice (*caryā*).
Now, reaching this chapter, it clarifies the perfection of awakening and practice. Regarding the two kinds of light before the Buddha, the first is named "Perfect."

Regarding the first name of King Pūrṇa, "Light Banner" (Prabhāketu): this refers to the great function of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha-fruit, which is perfectly luminous and destroys delusions.
Without this light of fundamental wisdom, there is no period for attaining Buddhahood through any practice of the path.
Second, the name "Perfectly Full" (Pūrṇa) refers to the thousand-spoked wheel-light beneath his feet; this clarifies that he has attained the Bodhisattva stage and ascended.
The light of the intensified practice serves as the feet because it represents the conduct that has been practiced;

its constant emission of forty kinds of light accomplishes the four stages prior to the grounds—namely, the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
Among these, there is one light that, according to the various desires and inclinations of all beings within the six realms of existence, causes them all to reach maturity, and so forth.
Those in the Avīci Hell who undergo uninterrupted suffering and encounter this light will all be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

Through the resonance of the celestial drum preaching the Dharma and the repentance that eliminates all delusions, they attain the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement or the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom.
One ray of light is the light that arouses faith according to the faculties of the six realms of existence; the other three are... [as previously described].

The light of the fulfillment of the fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the paths of practice—consisting of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*)—constitutes the stage of the three sages prior to the stages (*pūrvayoga*).
This marks the completion of the perfect integration of compassion, wisdom, vows, and practice.

The ten stages merely bring to fruition the merit previously established during the ten dedications prior to them; there is no separate stage [beyond them]. For this reason, they emit only forty rays of light.
The fruit of fifty [rays] being without specific function represents the Buddha’s own station, as it does not belong to the stage of practice;

thus, the light from beneath his feet clarifies the stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, and ten dedications of aspiration and conduct. As for the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), they are established in terms of the Dharma;
because the preceding vows have reached fulfillment, a single minor mark of excellence (*anuvyañjana*) radiates light from the palm of his right hand.
The manifestation of immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers signifies the act of drawing in and receiving others;

since "hand" (hasta) carries the meaning of "receiving," this [manifestation] is appropriate as a skillful means (upāya) for engaging with all that is practiced within the three realms of the mundane world.
Because it is not something known by mundane devas and humans, nor by those of the three vehicles, these three types of light are cited here to encompass all that exists within the world.

Regarding the reason why those who were touched by the light—other than the many others not discussed here—were [liberated], the intent of the sutra clarifies that it was because they possessed faith in previous lives.
As the sutra says: "In the past, you drew near to many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This clarifies that although they had previously planted the seeds of faith, even though they committed evil karma and were born in hell, [they were liberated] because [of that prior faith].
If the seeds of faith exist within one’s body and the suffering of that body has subsided, one can immediately resolve to give up the body to be reborn in heaven.
Even if the seeds of faith from previous lives were absent, should the light illuminate the body, one would neither perceive nor know [the truth].
As for how the Drum of the Threefold Knowledge (*trividyā*) preaches the Dharma, it is due to causes and conditions; as the sutra says: "It is solely by means of the Samādhi of Vairocana."
By the power of [the Buddha’s] strength, by the majestic power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and by the power of three general conditions, this sound is heard:
first, the power of the *samādhi* of the Bodhisattva Vairocana; second, the wondrous wisdom of effortless mastery within the *samādhi* of the absence of intrinsic nature;
and third, the fact that sentient beings have previously heard of this absence of intrinsic nature.

Only those who possess the seeds of the Dharmakāya and great wisdom are worthy of hearing such a wondrous sound; by having their delusions removed, they attain the Way, as in the case of the Vimala-samādhi.
This is the wondrous principle of non-substantiality, whose essence is without center or periphery, equal to the nature of space.
Its nature is inherently stainless and possesses infinite wisdom and insight. It is naturally devoid of "mine-ness" and need not be sought through external means.
This refers to the Bodhisattva Rūpāvabhāsa entering the Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means (ananta-upāya-samādhi), which is clearly manifested through the power of meditative concentration.
It is also like Sudhana attaining the "Light of Wisdom that Recollects All Buddhas" atop Mount Supratiṣṭha.
In both cases, these represent the initial manifestation of the mind of the Ten Abodes; therefore, they are presented in this chapter.
Because the middle does not depart from the fulfillment of the initial stage, it returns to the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-prāsāda*) to explain the ten stages of faith;

by explaining these eleven chapters, the gates of the eleven stages and the fruit of Buddhahood are manifested. This signifies that one achieves the fruit without departing from a single thought-moment and without being separated by even a moment of time.
Thus, the *upāya-samādhi* (convenient samādhi) is the spontaneous liberation within the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
However, when one naturally neither gathers nor restrains the mind, allowing it to settle of its own accord, all delusions are spontaneously purified and the Way manifests of itself;

only then can one employ action and function without losing the underlying principle. Yet, it is through the vows and practices of Samantabhadra that the great function of compassion and wisdom is perfected—the gate of the non-active *dharmadhātu* dependent origination—exactly as in the aforementioned cultivation of the five stages.
The practitioner is such a person. As the Sūtra says: "Regarding form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, there are five hundred afflictions within and five hundred afflictions without.
Those with a predominance of hatred have twenty-one thousand types; those with a predominance of greed have twenty-one thousand types;
those with a predominance of delusion have twenty-one thousand types; and those with equal parts [of all three] likewise."
The twenty-one thousand [types of craving] and above total eighty-four thousand;

as with form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, each possesses five aggregates, and together with the ten underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*), the faculty of mind (*manas*) serves as the primary factor.

Thus, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch constitute the external, while sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the mind constitute the internal. Just as the internal and external mental objects (*viṣaya*) come together to form conditions (*pratyaya*).
All are capable of generating the ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) regarding form, sound, odor, taste, touch, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the mind;

these internal and external factors mutually interpenetrate, each consisting of ten such types. Thus, each of these ten internal and external afflictions can individually give rise to the ten latent afflictions.
Consequently, there are five hundred afflictions for each of the internal and external objects of perception, arising from the delusion of the mind.

The internal and external mutually support one another: the five internal aggregates constitute the cause of the objective realm, while the five external objects give rise to the subjective perceiver.
Through these two conditions—the internal and external, the perceiver and the perceived—the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) arise and do not cease;

thus, up to eighty-four thousand [afflictions] emerge. These ten underlying tendencies are all produced by the five aggregates, and within each underlying tendency there are one hundred [sub-afflictions].

Taking the five aggregates within the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*), these five aggregates form the ten afflictions. Within each aggregate there are one hundred [sub-aggregates], thus totaling five hundred within the five aggregates.
Taking these five aggregates as the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), within these five sense objects there are another five hundred.

Combining the sense objects and the aggregates as internal and external, they together constitute one thousand. When assigned to the seven consciousnesses (*sapta-vijñāna*), they comprise seven thousand divisions.
Three periods of seven times three is twenty-one; when multiplied by two thousand one hundred, it becomes twenty-one thousand.

This is based on those who predominantly possess greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as those with equal proportions of these three, each having twenty-one thousand, totaling eighty-four thousand. The remainder is fully detailed in the text itself.
Regarding the ten fetters (*daśa-āsrava*), as each possesses the five internal and external aggregates and the ten fetters mutually intersect, there are one hundred [factors].
Each of the one hundred and ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) possesses the five aggregates (*skandha*), resulting in five hundred [factors].

Because the internal mind takes external objects as its conditions, they act as mutual primary and secondary factors; thus, with five hundred each for the internal and external, they collectively form one thousand.

Due to the functioning of the *manas* and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) as causes and effects, there are seven thousand afflictive phenomena (*kleśa-dharma*), following the previous analogy of three times seven.

Twenty-one [recitations] shall likewise amount to twenty-one thousand; if one calculates according to this Dharma-gate taught by the Devadundubhi, the wisdom of the principle of non-arising and the methods for confessing and purifying transgressions are most excellent and sublime.

Those who cultivate the path and resolve to attain Bodhicitta should maintain these recitations, apply their attention, and emulate them in their practice through the skillful means of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Through diligent effort and contemplative observation, one returns to this very stage of attaining Buddhahood in a single moment (*kṣaṇa-buddhatva*).
Within it, the sequence for the integration of the Dharma-gates is fully contained as in this chapter.

Just as all the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) encountered by Sudhana said, "I have already set my mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how should I be taught to study Bodhi? [so too is the path herein].
The path of the Bodhisattva clarifies that bodhi is without seeking, without cultivation, and without the three periods of time; therefore, one seeks only its practice.
This light of the merit of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) serves only as illumination for the practice, causing the practice to be without dependence and without cultivation.
All who have resolved their minds first cultivate the samādhi of skillful means (upāya), by which it is manifested.

From within this principle, one should precisely apply the preparatory practice (*prayoga*); therefore, it is called "the gate of using the fruit to establish the cause" and "the gate of the cause being identical to the fruit.
Because there is no separate practice apart from the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), one takes the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*) as the means of cultivation.
Thus, seeking only the Bodhisattva path is itself the practice of bodhi; this clarifies that there is no [bodhi] apart from the practice.
Because this has been attained, one sets forth the practices of Samantabhadra; yet because these are not yet perfected, one seeks the Bodhisattva path.

Since awakening is devoid of the three periods of time and does not emerge from even a single kṣaṇa, such that all myriad practices are simultaneously perfected, it is called the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

This directly addresses the realm of wisdom where the three periods of time and obstacles such as extension or brevity are undifferentiated—a perspective that ordinary beings and those of the three vehicles fail to perceive.
The three incalculable eons and infinite eons are the gateway of the non-transmigration of the realm of wisdom within this teaching;

because the essence is thus and the Dharma is thus, it is not brought about by the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of a Buddha. Those of the three vehicles, with their conceptual views, claim it is the supernatural power of a Buddha;
they are deluded regarding the fact that the true Dharma is originally thus within this Hall of Universal Radiance.
The eleven chapters of this Dharma encompass the entire section; throughout the infinite past and present, they have never shifted by even a hair’s breadth or a single thought.
One must thus believe, understand, and practice them; this is called awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, for it is through this that one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Therefore, one should know that the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the two levels of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimalā-bodhi*), all depend upon the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences.
Toward the Dharma, one thus achieves completion.
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra.
[Commentary] To explain this chapter, it shall be analyzed by means of four sections: first, the explanation of the title of the chapter; second, the explanation of the chapter... [text continues].

The intent of the coming [of this chapter] is explained through three interpretations; the fourth is the word-by-word commentary on the meaning. First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter:

why is it named the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra"? It is to clarify that from the first assembly at the Bodhimaṇḍa, the Tathāgata represents the fruit of Buddhahood—just as the ten [Buddhas] do—while Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, devas, and others below him represent the Buddha’s [causal] practices.

Because of the practice of Samantabhadra, from the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance, the ten wisdoms of the Tathāgatas—such as Immovable Wisdom and Unobstructed Wisdom—are taught to establish the ten stages of faith.

This clarifies that one's own mind is the Immovable Wisdom Buddha, which is the fundamental fruit of one’s own mind; the same applies to the other nine. Mañjuśrī, Chief of Enlightenment, [is the first].
The ten bodhisattvas beginning with Muxiu (Netrādhipa) represent the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct within one's own person;
the ten names of the Buddhas and the ten names of the bodhisattvas corresponding respectively to the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten stages,
and the eleventh stage— and even the infinite names of the Buddhas and the infinite names of the bodhisattvas— are all [contained within] oneself.
One personally cultivates the fruit of Buddhahood within one's own mind through the practices of Samantabhadra until reaching this "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra.

Herein, there is the fruit of Buddhahood within one's own mind and the practices of Samantabhadra within one's own mind. It is only in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" that the manifestation of one's own Buddha-fruit is clarified;
it is here that the essence and function of the principle-wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*) finally reach their consummation. Thus concludes this "Chapter on the Appearance [of the Tathāgata]."
The Tathāgata in the center emits light from between his eyebrows to moisten the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and light from his mouth to moisten the mouth of Samantabhadra,
so that the Dharma-body of their intrinsic wisdom and principle— Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra— may engage in mutual question and answer.
Only through this can the realm of the Tathāgata’s manifestation clarify the sublime wisdom of one’s own intrinsic principle and wisdom, [revealing] Samantabhadra.

The *Caryā-sāgara* (Ocean of Practices) and the *Buddhatva-pratipatti* (Progress toward the Fruit of Buddhahood), which encompass the beginning, end, fulfillment, entrustment, and circulation [of the teaching], are also contained within the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta* (Chapter on Manifestation).
The *Lokātīta-parivarta* (Chapter on Transcending the World) concerns the eternal path following the fruit of Buddhahood, which is the practice of Samantabhadra without beginning or end.

The *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* (Chapter on the Dharma-realm) concerns the eternal path of the Buddha; since the Dharma-realm is suchness (*tathatā*), it is also based on the meaning of the practice of Samantabhadra following the fruit of Buddhahood.
The "Chapter on Benefiting the World" represents the fulfillment of one's own path of practice;
it consists purely of benefiting the world because there is no worldly realm to be abandoned and no supramundane realm to be attained.

Since its fundamental purpose is to constantly benefit sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra, other meanings will be clarified further in subsequent chapters. This chapter comprehensively encompasses the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

From the arrival at the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) up to its conclusion, the names of the chapters are established based on the beginning and end, cause and effect, and the fundamental and derivative aspects.

Roughly speaking, from this assembly’s ten concentrations (*daśa-samādhi*) through the eleven subsequent chapters of the sutra, they are collectively subsumed under the essence of the ten concentrations;
from beginning to end, they do not transcend the limit of a single *kṣaṇa*. Therefore, this chapter elucidates the internal state of the Buddha-fruit (*buddha-phala*).

The second [point], explaining the purpose of this chapter, is as follows: The preceding chapter elucidated the light of the ultimate nature-wisdom (*dharmatā-jñāna*) that brings benefit to sentient beings;
this chapter elucidates how the practices of Samantabhadra can likewise benefit beings. If there is wisdom but no practice, that wisdom remains incomplete when engaging with the mundane world;
if there is practice but no wisdom, [the practice lacks its guiding principle]. Thus, [this chapter is established] because one has personally fulfilled the practices of Samantabhadra.
Because wisdom cannot emerge from the mundane through mere conduct, it is only when the essence of principle and conduct are thoroughly penetrated that the gate of non-dual mastery is perfected;
for this reason, this chapter must appear. Regarding the master who expounds the teaching:
why is Samantabhadra the master who expounds this chapter? It is because the gate of conduct in this chapter is the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practice.
Therefore, it is returned to Samantabhadra himself to explain that Samantabhadra is the function of the wondrous principle of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya;

for if these two dharmas were to proceed alone, they would not be perfect. Thus, first the light of the nature-wisdom of the Dharmakāya is presented, followed by the explanation of Samantabhadra’s practice.
Fourth, regarding the exegesis according to the text: this chapter of the sutra is divided into [the following sections]:
Section Fifteen.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra again addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:

"O Sons of the Buddha, what has been expounded just now is merely a brief explanation of a small portion of the Tathāgata’s realm, taught in accordance with what is appropriate for the faculties and capacities of sentient beings."

Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of sentient beings who, due to ignorance, commit evil deeds, conceive of "self" and "what belongs to self," are attached to the body, and are possessed by inversions, doubts, false views, and conceptual discriminations;
being constantly bound by these fetters, they follow the stream of birth and death and remain far removed from the path of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Buddhas appear in the world.

[Treatise] First, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... down to "...appeared in the world," there are five lines and a half of scripture that clarify how sentient beings are far removed from the Buddha-way before the Buddha appears in the world.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text of the "Section on the Partial Exposition of the Realm" mentioned in the preceding chapter, it is as previously stated: the aforementioned ten bodies.
The "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" and the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks" are brief summaries of a small portion [of the teaching].

Because those with false views are constantly bound by the fetters of afflictions and are always in association with them, they remain far removed from the path of the Tathāgata; it is not said that [the path] appears for them.

If one possesses right view, what would appear and what would submerge? What would be established and what would perish? What would be the Brahma-state? What would be purity? If one attains for oneself—
When the mind is thus equal, neither defiled nor pure, this is the emergence of a Buddha. As for those bound by fetters, there are the fetters of the six sense bases:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. As for wrong views, they are the so-called eightfold wrongness:

wrong mindfulness, wrong livelihood, wrong intention, wrong diligence, wrong concentration, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong wisdom. As for reckoning in terms of "I" and "mine," these are the [views of] self and what pertains to a self.
Regarding those who possess the two views and are subject to delusion and doubt— those who hold the four inversions, reckoning the impermanent as permanent,
the selfless as self, the unsatisfactory as satisfying, and the impure as pure— the Tathāgata manifests his appearance for the sake of such beings,
briefly explaining a small portion of the sphere of merit; yet in reality, the Tathāgata neither appears nor disappears, being solely in accord with the Way.

This wisdom realm naturally accords with itself; one does not form views of birth, arising, or cessation regarding the Buddhas, but simply uses the two gates of meditative concentration to purify the defilements of the mind.
When the view of self and extremes has subsided, wisdom manifests in accordance with reality.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes such a great fault as when bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of anger toward other bodhisattvas.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of malice toward other bodhisattvas, they immediately bring about one million gates of obstruction."

[Treatise] From the second "Son of the Buddha" down to the passage on "accomplishing one million gates of obstacles," there are two and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra perceives sentient beings as having great transgressions and evils, yet never sees even a single transgression or evil;
whereas if he sees even a single instance of anger in a Bodhisattva, it constitutes one million gates of obstacles.
[Sūtra] What are the one million obstacles? They are: the obstacle of not seeing bodhi; the obstacle of not hearing the true Dharma; the obstacle of being born in impure worlds;
the obstacle of being born in the various evil destinies; the obstacle of being born in places of difficulty; the obstacle of having many illnesses;
the obstacle of being frequently slandered and reviled; the obstacle of being born in realms of dullness and stupidity; the obstacle of losing right mindfulness; and the obstacle of lacking wisdom.
Obstructing the eye, obstructing the ear, obstructing the nose, obstructing the tongue, obstructing the body, and obstructing the mind; obstructing evil associates and obstructing evil companions;

obstructing the delight in practicing the Hīnayāna and obstructing the delight in associating with the vulgar; obstructing faith and delight in those of great majesty and virtue, and obstructing the delight in dwelling together with those who have abandoned right view;
obstructing birth in non-Buddhist paths and obstructing birth within the realm of Māra; and obstructing separation from the Buddha.
The obstacle to the true teaching; the obstacle to not seeing virtuous friends; the obstacle to the hindrance of wholesome roots; the obstacle to the increase of unwholesome dharmas;
the obstacle to being born in inferior states; the obstacle to being born in border regions; the obstacle to being born into a family of evil people; the obstacle to being born among evil deities;
and the obstacles to being born among evil nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.
The obstacles among the mahoragas and evil rākṣasas: the obstacle of not delighting in the Buddha-dharma; the obstacle of practicing the teachings of the ignorant;

the obstacle of being attached to the Hīnayāna; the obstacle of not delighting in the Mahāyāna; the obstacle of having a nature prone to fear and terror; the obstacle of the mind being constantly afflicted by anxiety and distress;

the obstacle of craving and attachment to birth and death; the obstacle of not being single-minded toward the Buddha-dharma; and the obstacle of not rejoicing in seeing or hearing the sovereign supernormal powers of the Buddha.

The obstacles to obtaining the faculties of a bodhisattva; the obstacles to the non-arising of a bodhisattva’s pure conduct; the obstacles to the regression or cowardice of a bodhisattva’s profound resolve;
the obstacles to the non-arising of a bodhisattva’s great vows; the obstacles to the non-awakening of the mind of omniscience; the obstacles of indolence regarding bodhisattva practice;
the obstacles to the inability to purify all karmic hindrances; the obstacles to the inability to gather great merit; and the obstacle of the lack of clarity in the power of wisdom.

The obstacle of attachment to gain; the obstacle of severing the vast wisdom; the obstacle of failing to maintain the various practices of a bodhisattva; the obstacle of delighting in slandering the words of omniscience;
the obstacle of distancing oneself from the bodhi of all Buddhas; the obstacle of delighting in dwelling within the realm of Māras;

the obstacle of not single-mindedly cultivating the realm of the Buddhas; the obstacle of not resolutely generating the great vows of a bodhisattva; and the obstacle of not delighting in associating with bodhisattvas.

The obstacle of dwelling together; the obstacle of not seeking the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva; the obstacle of a nature characterized by excessive views and doubt; the obstacle of a mind that is constantly dull and dark;
the obstacle of being unable to practice the impartial giving of a bodhisattva, which gives rise to the obstacle of non-renunciation;

the obstacle of being unable to maintain the precepts of the Tathāgata, which gives rise to the obstacle of breaking the precepts; and the obstacle of being unable to enter the gate of patience, which gives rise to the obstacles of delusion, affliction, harm, and anger.

Because they are unable to practice the great vigor of a bodhisattva, there arises the obscuration of indolence; because they are unable to attain the various samādhis, there arises the obscuration of distraction;

because they do not cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there arises the obscuration of faulty wisdom; there is the obscuration of lack of skill regarding what is possible and what is impossible;
there is the obscuration of lack of skillful means regarding the deliverance of sentient beings; and [the obscuration] regarding the wisdom of a bodhisattva.

The inability to observe within the middle obstructs the dharma of a bodhisattva’s renunciation; the failure to comprehend it obstructs the non-attainment of the ten kinds of vast eyes of a bodhisattva.
Thus, the eyes are like those of one born blind; the ears do not hear the unobstructed dharma, thus the mouth is like that of a mute sheep;
the physical marks and signs are incomplete, thus the faculty of the nose is destroyed; and there is an obstruction to the inability to discern and understand.

Because of engaging in the speech of sentient beings, one achieves the obstruction of the tongue faculty; because of treating sentient beings with contempt, one achieves the obstruction of the body faculty;

because the mind is frequently deranged and turbulent, one achieves the obstruction of the mental faculty; because one does not maintain the three types of restraint, one achieves the obstruction of physical karma;
because one constantly gives rise to the four kinds of faults, one achieves the obstruction of verbal karma; and because one frequently generates greed, hatred, and wrong views.
Therefore, it accomplishes the obstacle of mental karma; it is a thief that seeks the Dharma while obstructing the mind; it severs the obstacle to the bodhisattva’s sphere of activity;
it causes the mind to give rise to cowardice and timidity within the bodhisattva’s courageous Dharma; it causes the mind to give rise to indolence within the bodhisattva’s path of renunciation;
it causes the mind to give rise to cessation within the bodhisattva’s gateway of the light of wisdom; and it obstructs the bodhisattva’s mindfulness.
The obstacle of inferiority arising from within one's own power, which prevents one from upholding the Tathāgata’s teachings;
the obstacle that prevents one from approaching the Bodhisattva’s path of transcendence (*niyāma*); the obstacle that prevents one from cultivating the Bodhisattva’s path of non-destruction;

the obstacle that hinders conformity with the correct station (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of the two vehicles; and the obstacle that distances one from the lineage (*gotra*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time. Buddha.
If a son or a bodhisattva gives rise to even a single thought of anger toward other bodhisattvas, they will bring about as many as one million such gates of obstruction.
[Treatise] Third:
What are these one million gates of obstruction? From here down to "bringing about as many as one hundred... [as previously mentioned].
The "Forty-Four Sections on the Ten Thousand Obstacles" (*Wàn zhàng mén sìshí sì xíng jīng*) clearly enumerates one hundred obstacles to manifest them as the foremost among the million obstacles.
Below this, the text explains these one hundred obstacles to serve as the heads of the million obstacles,
thereby preventing practitioners from giving rise to even a single thought of anger toward other bodhisattvas, as stated in the sutra itself.
Those who cultivate the Way must be extremely cautious, as described above. When first initiating the mind for the cultivation of the Way, one must not harbor thoughts of loss or extinction;
only when the Way is perfected will one realize that emotions and perceptions are empty. If one harbors the view of self while seeking the Way, it will ultimately be incompatible with it.

One must rely on those of wisdom to subdue one's own arrogance, and only when the heart of reverence reaches its depths can one employ the two gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
One must thoroughly discern the meditative concentrations and wisdom cultivated by those in the two upper realms, śrāvakas, non-Buddhists, and bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings;

only by knowing these one by one can one recognize the True Dharma. Only then will the mind be free from the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox as one seeks the gateway of differentiated wisdom.
Through the power of great vows, one should expand great compassion and accomplish the practices of Samantabhadra; otherwise, it would be like seeking the Dharma with the intent of a thief.

One who skillfully disciplines the mind must guard against the arrogance that increases toward others; if a Bodhisattva gives rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment, they shall enter a hundred thousand doors of obstruction.

As the sutras clearly explain, having encountered the calamities of evil spirits, malevolent ghosts, and the like, one may gain a single portion of the mind seeking the Way, yet its supportive power will be thwarted by an uncontrollable rage. Therefore, all who have resolved their minds [upon enlightenment] should exercise vigilance.

One should treat this with Dharma-like humility and reverence, focusing the mind single-mindedly on seeking it; furthermore, one must constantly recite and uphold this "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" to guard the three karmas and bring them into accord with truth.
[Sūtra] Why is this? O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes a greater transgression or evil than that of the Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the passage from "As for those who give rise to anger toward other bodhisattvas" [in the *Śāstra*]:

the section beginning with "The fourth, why is this? and ending with "those who give rise to anger" consists of one and a half lines of scripture that summarizes the preceding portion concerning not giving rise to anger toward other bodhisattvas.
[Sūtra] Therefore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices should diligently cultivate ten kinds of dharmas.
What are these ten? They are: not abandoning any sentient being; conceiving the thought of a Tathāgata toward all bodhisattvas;
never slandering any Buddha-dharma; and knowing that all buddha-lands are inexhaustible.
