To exhaustively practice the bodhisattva deeds while generating deep faith and joy; not to abandon the mind of enlightenment that is equal to space and the dharma-realm;
to contemplate enlightenment and enter the powers of the Tathāgata; to diligently cultivate unimpeded eloquence to teach and transform sentient beings without weariness;
and to dwell in all worlds with a mind free from attachment—these, O sons of the Buddha, are the ten [qualities].
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells securely in these ten dharmas, they are able to fulfill ten kinds of purity.
What are the ten? They are: the purity of penetrating the profound Dharma; the purity of attending upon spiritual friends; the purity of protecting and upholding all Buddha-dharmas;
the purity of thoroughly understanding the realm of empty space; the purity of deeply entering the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); and the purity of contemplation... [and so forth].

The purity of boundless mind, the purity of roots of goodness shared with all bodhisattvas, the purity of non-attachment to all eons, the purity of observing the three periods of time, and the purity of practicing all Buddha-dharmas—these are the ten.
Sons of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in these ten dharmas, they become fully endowed with ten kinds of vast wisdom. What are they?
These constitute the ten, namely: the wisdom that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings; the wisdom that knows the karmic retributions of all sentient beings;
the wisdom that knows all Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom that knows the profound and secret principles of all Buddha-dharmas;
the wisdom that knows all dharani-doors; the wisdom that knows all phonemes and eloquence; and the wisdom that knows the languages of all sentient beings.
The wisdom of skillfulness in vocal expression and eloquence; the wisdom of universally manifesting one’s body in all worlds;
the wisdom of universally manifesting one’s reflection in all assemblies; and the wisdom of possessing all-knowledge in all places of rebirth—these, O Son of the Buddha, are the ten.
Once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in these ten wisdoms, they then attain entry into the ten [stages].
The ten kinds of universal entry are as follows: first, all worlds enter into a single hair-pore;
second, a single hair-pore enters into all worlds; third, the bodies of all sentient beings enter into a single body; fourth, a single body enters into the bodies of all sentient beings;
fifth, unspeakable eons enter into a single thought-moment; sixth, a single thought-moment enters into unspeakable eons; seventh, all Buddha-dharmas enter into... [the text continues].
One dharma enters all Buddha-dharmas; the unspeakable realm enters one place; one place enters the unspeakable realm; unspeakable faculties enter one faculty;
one faculty enters unspeakable faculties; all faculties enter that which is neither faculty nor non-faculty;
that which is neither faculty nor non-faculty enters all faculties; all perceptions enter one perception; and one perception enters all.
One should contemplate that all speech and sounds enter into a single sound, and a single sound enters into all speech and sounds;
that all three periods of time enter into one period, and one period enters into all three periods of time. This is the tenth [stage], O Son of the Buddha.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has observed in this way, they abide in ten kinds of supreme and wondrous minds. What are these ten? Namely, they abide in...

The sublime state of mind that dwells in the non-linguistic nature of all worldly languages; the sublime state of mind that dwells in the mental conceptions of all sentient beings without any basis for dependence;
the sublime state of mind that dwells in the ultimate realm of empty space; the sublime state of mind that dwells in the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
the sublime state of mind that dwells in all the profound and secret Buddha-dharmas; and the sublime state of mind that dwells in the profoundly deep, undifferentiated Dharma.
The sublime mental abiding that eliminates all doubts; the sublime mental abiding in which all worlds are equal and without distinction;
the sublime mental abiding in the equality of the Buddhas of the three times;
the sublime mental abiding in the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas—these, O Son of the Buddha, are the ten sublime mental abidings in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell.
Once the supreme and wondrous mind has been attained, one obtains ten kinds of skillful knowledge regarding the Buddha-dharma.

What are these ten? They are: skillful knowledge that thoroughly understands the profound Buddha-dharma; skillful knowledge that gives rise to the vast Buddha-dharma; skillful knowledge that proclaims the various Buddha-dharmas;
skillful knowledge that realizes and enters the equal Buddha-dharma; and skillful knowledge that clearly comprehends the distinctions of the Buddhas...
The wisdom of skill in the Dharma that realizes the non-differentiation of the Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom of skill in the Dharma that deeply penetrates the adornments of the Buddha-dharmas;
the wisdom of skill in the Dharma that enters the Buddha-dharmas through a single means; the wisdom of skill in the Dharma that enters the Buddha-dharmas through immeasurable means;
and the wisdom of skill in the non-differentiation of infinite Buddha-dharmas—by means of one's own mind and one's own power, within a single...

The skillful wisdom that never regresses from all Buddha-dharmas constitutes the tenth; O sons of the Buddha, once Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have heard this teaching, they should all resolve their minds upon it, reverently receive and uphold it.

[Treatise] Therefore, all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, down to the sons of the Buddha who are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, should resolve their minds to respectfully receive and uphold these six sections of ten dharmas; as the meaning of the sūtra text itself clarifies:
(1) All Bodhisattvas who wish to swiftly fulfill the various Bodhisattva practices should diligently cultivate ten dharmas, and thus they will be able to...
By fulfilling the ten aspects of purity (1), one can fulfill the ten aspects of vast wisdom (2);
by [fulfilling] the ten aspects of universal entry (3), one attains the ten kinds of skillful knowledge (4).
Above, there are ten sections of scripture, as it is said in the sutra: "Knowing all sentient beings..."
To give rise to the wisdom that practices the mind is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Because one is personally without mind and the obstructions between self and other are severed, one's own mind and the minds of all sentient beings are of one essence and non-dual.
Since it is by means of this that one can know the minds of all sentient beings—and because one's own mind and the minds of sentient beings are non-dual—one even comes to know all Buddha-dharmas.
The wisdom of the profound and secret principle is likewise so, because one’s own mind has no distinction between self and other minds;

thus, the principle of sages and ordinary beings is identical and their essence is the same. Because the principle of sages and ordinary beings is identical and their essence is the same, the mental phenomena of both sages and ordinary beings are fully known.

Because the minds of sages and ordinary beings share one and the same principle, the body has no interior or exterior, and all views have no interior or exterior; therefore, there is nothing [to be seen].
The peripheral worlds and the realm of empty space are equal; one’s own mind and the realm of empty space are equal.

Thus, there is neither large nor small, neither far nor near, nor any intermediate point. Since one’s own mind has no large or small, far or near, nor any intermediate point, wisdom is eternally pervasive throughout the worlds of the ten directions without coming or going. Since wisdom is eternally pervasive throughout the worlds of the ten directions...
Being without coming or going, one is able to manifest physical bodies according to the faculties of beings with mastery;

being able to manifest physical bodies according to the faculties with mastery, one possesses mastery in preaching the Dharma according to those faculties; and one possesses mastery in the mutual interpenetration of the single body and the manifold bodies.
All the various dharmas of mastery below this are likewise practiced through the power of the nature of meditative concentration and wisdom.
This spontaneous integration is not known by the deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing;
thus, it is the nature of correct wisdom itself—free from mind, thought, and deluded imagination—which is inherently all-pervasive and devoid of coming or going.

For the sake of teaching and transforming all sentient beings at all times and according to their faculties, it manifests and performs all manner of activities equal to those of sentient beings, yet there is no agent.
Because it has no location and functions according to the nature of wisdom, it is like an echo responding to a sound;
because it has no agent and does not come or go, all that follows should be understood and cultivated through this wisdom.
[Sūtra] Why is it that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who uphold this Dharma attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with little effort and swiftly,
becoming fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, which are equal to those of all Buddhas of the three periods of time?

[Treatise] 11. From "For what reason? down to "equal to the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods," there are two and a half lines of sūtra that clarify the section on how, by hearing this Dharma and being exhorted to reverently accept and uphold it, one can swiftly attain Buddhahood through minimal effort.
[Sūtra] At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma,
worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.
There fell clouds of all kinds of flowers surpassing those of the devas, clouds of incense, clouds of powdered incense, clouds of robes, canopies, banners, pennants, mani jewels, and so forth.
Raining down clouds of all manner of ornaments; raining down clouds of various celestial musicians; raining down clouds of all Bodhisattvas;
raining down clouds of the unspeakable physical marks and signs of the Tathāgatas; raining down clouds of unspeakable praises of "Excellent! to the Tathāgatas;
raining down clouds of the Tathāgatas' voices filling the entire Dharma-realm; raining down clouds of unspeakable adornments of worlds.
The clouds and rains of increasing enlightenment are unspeakable; the clouds and rains of radiant illumination are unspeakable;

the clouds of supernatural power and the preaching of the Dharma are likewise unspeakable. Within the Bodhisattva palaces beneath the Bodhi trees at the sites of enlightenment in this world’s four continents, one beholds the Tathāgata attaining equal and perfect awakening and expounding this Dharma throughout all the ten directions.
The entire world is likewise in this way.

[Treatise] Twelfth: From "At that time, by the Buddha's supernatural power" down to "In all worlds it is likewise so," these eleven lines of scripture clarify how the majestic influence of the True Dharma causes the earth to shake in six ways and causes the heavens to arise.
The section on the method for making offerings like clouds contains three meanings regarding the arising of offerings as if the earth were shaking: first, the inspiration of the Dharma’s majesty;
second, the joy experienced by the bodhisattvas upon hearing the Dharma; and third, as the sutra says, "Because the Dharma is thus.
The sutra further states that those who receive and uphold this Dharma will swiftly attain Bodhi with little effort—this refers to the wisdom of non-thought and non-reliance in a single moment.
Manifestation is itself bodhi.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the Dharma is thus, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions,
there came ten times the number of atoms in a buddha-field of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Arriving in this land, they filled the ten directions and spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to expound this profound Dharma of the prediction and the greatest vows of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha, we are all named Samantabhadra, and each has come from the world-system called Universal Victory to this land from the presence of the Tathāgata Universal Banner Sovereign."
It is entirely through the Buddha’s spiritual power that this Dharma is expounded in all places;

such is this assembly, and such are these teachings—all are equal, without increase or decrease. We have all come to this site of enlightenment by virtue of the Buddha’s majesty and power to bear witness for you.
In this site of enlightenment, we are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.
And they come to bear witness that it is likewise in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

[Treatise] Thirteenth: From the passage beginning with "At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power" down to "it is likewise in all worlds throughout the ten directions," there are ten lines and a half of scripture clarifying the universal pervasiveness in all places within the world-system of Universal Victory (*Samantavijaya*).

The virtuous Bodhisattvas have all come together to bear witness. For instance, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, who come to this land and fill the ten directions;
this is because they praise the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices.
The expression "Excellent! Excellent! is a praise for the difficulty of encountering the teaching of the Dharma;

that the Son of the Buddha is able to expound this profound Dharma of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the greatest vows of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas clarifies that the practices and vows of Samantabhadra—the fruit of the Dharma in which wisdom, principle, and great compassion are perfected—have reached their consummation. Because these fruits have reached their end, it is the profound prediction bestowed by the Buddha.
Because of the Dharma, we clarify the practice of the Great Compassion of the Dharmakāya and Jñānakāya;

since within every atom are contained the inexhaustible practices of the Buddhas and Samantabhadra, we are called "Profound Sons of the Buddha. We all share the same name, Samantabhadra, clarifying that our Dharma-practice is non-dual.
Because this name is identical, each of us comes from the world *Samantavijaya* (Universal Victory), from the presence of the Tathāgata *Samudgata-vaijayanta-vaśavartin* (Universal Banner Sovereign).
Those who come and those to whom they come abide in a path of humility and harmony; this is called the World of Universal Victory (*Samantavijaya*).

Because it can shatter the arrogance of oneself and others as well as all afflictions, it is named the Universal Banner (*Samantadhvaja*). "Banner" signifies that the enlightened mind does not follow after objects;
because wisdom, compassion, and practice are layered and all-pervasive, it is called the Universal Victory Banner. Although one dwells within birth and death, one is not defiled by them.
All are called "self-abiding"; this Buddha’s world is named "Following the Causes and Effects of Practice.

Those who come to this land clarify that they have reached the ultimate limit of the stages of advancement within this Dharma. Because of the Buddha's spiritual power, he expounds this Dharma in all places;
whereas previously it was clarified that his physical actions (*kāyakarman*) are all-pervasive, here it is clarified that his verbal actions (*vākkarman*) are likewise universal.
The following may be understood according to the text.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and through the power of his own roots of goodness,
surveyed the ten directions as far as the Dharma-realm, desiring to reveal the bodhisattva practices and proclaim the realm of the Tathāgata’s awakening.
I wish to speak of the realm of great vows; I wish to speak of the number of eons in all worlds; I wish to clarify how all Buddhas appear according to the time;
I wish to speak of how the Tathāgata appears for those sentient beings whose faculties have matured so that they may make offerings;

I wish to clarify that the merit of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is never in vain; I wish to clarify that the roots of goodness one has planted will inevitably yield their fruit; I wish to clarify his great majesty.
The Bodhisattva Virtue manifests forms for all sentient beings and preaches the Dharma to cause them to attain awakening, and then speaks these verses.

[Treatise] Fourteenth: From the passage beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" onwards, there are seven lines of scripture clarifying the section on Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s observation of the assembly and his intent in reciting the verses, as the scripture intends to reveal the bodhisattva practices.
The conduct of Samantabhadra is intended to explain the realm of the Tathāgata’s bodhi;
the fundamental wisdom of the dharma-body’s lack of intrinsic nature is intended to explain the realm of great vows;
and the arousal of the vow of great compassion by Samantabhadra is intended to explain the number of kalpas in all worlds, as stated in the verse below: "One kalpa enters into all [kalpas]."
That all kalpas enter into one kalpa and one thought-moment enters into all kalpas is intended to clarify that the merit of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is not in vain;
it clarifies that [the Buddha] responds to capacities without missing the proper time; it clarifies that the roots of goodness planted will inevitably yield their fruit;
and it clarifies that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas respond to sentient beings according to their capacities so that they obtain benefit, thereby manifesting great majestic power.
The Bodhisattva Virtue manifests forms and preaches the Dharma for all sentient beings;

this clarifies that while the principle of wisdom is omnipresent and devoid of coming or going, he manifests physical bodies in accordance with [the capacities of beings] and bestows the Dharma according to their faculties. These ten matters above are all explained individually and in detail within the following verses.
[Sūtra] You all should rejoice and cast off all hindrances; with single-minded reverence, listen to the vows and practices of the Bodhisattvas.
I shall explain in due order how those supreme lions among men, the Bodhisattvas of the past, practiced their conduct, as well as the number of kalpas involved.
The world, together with all its karmas, and the Peerless Honored One—such as these past Buddhas have arisen therein.
Great vows emerge in the world: "How may I eliminate the various sufferings and afflictions for the sake of sentient beings?
Thus, the conduct of all the Lions of Debaters is fulfilled in its continuity.

Having attained the Buddha’s impartial Dharma, the realm of omniscience, I behold all the Lions among Men of the past eons, Who emit great nets of radiant light, universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Reflecting thus, I make this vow: "May I become a lamp for the world, Fully endowed with the merits of a Buddha."
Possessing the ten powers and omniscience, I shall fully rescue and liberate all sentient beings from the blazing fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
causing them to extinguish the sufferings of the evil realms. Having made such a vow with firm and irreversible resolve,
I shall fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and attain the ten unhindered powers.
Having made such a vow, he practiced without retreat or fear; whatever he did was never in vain, and thus he is named the Lion of Treatises.
Within a single Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas appear in the world;
I shall now explain their Universal Eye in successive order, just as it is within that Bhadrakalpa.
So too it is for immeasurable eons; those future buddha-practices, I shall explain in detail.
As it is with one buddha-field system, so it is with immeasurable fields.
I now declare the various practices of the future Lords of Ten Powers, as they arise in succession throughout the world, according to their vows and their names.
According to the prediction they have received, according to their lifespan, according to the true Dharma they practice while single-mindedly seeking the unobstructed path,
according to the sentient beings they transform, according to how long the true Dharma remains in the world,
according to the Buddha-fields they purify, according to sentient beings and the wheel of Dharma, and according to whether it is the proper or improper time for preaching.
Gradually purifying all sentient beings according to their respective karmas— whether their practices, inclinations,
and understandings be superior, middling, or inferior— he transforms them to cultivate [the path].
Entering into such wisdom, he practices the most supreme conduct, constantly performing the deeds of Samantabhadra to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
With unimpeded physical action, And speech that is entirely pure, The mental conduct is likewise;

Throughout the three times, there is nothing otherwise. The Bodhisattva practices in this way, Ultimately traversing the path of Samantabhadra, Giving birth to the sun of pure wisdom That universally illumines the entire Dharma-realm Throughout all kalpas of future ages.
The lands are ineffable, yet in a single thought-moment they are all fully known;
those practitioners who are free from conceptual discrimination can enter this most supreme stage.
I shall now briefly explain these dharmas of the bodhisattvas; their wisdom is boundless, for they have penetrated the realm of the Buddhas.
All have skillfully entered; their conduct is non-regressive. Endowed with the wisdom of Samantabhadra, they fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra.
They enter into incomparable knowledge. I shall now describe their conduct within a single atom:
How all worlds are seen therein—if sentient beings should hear this, [they shall likewise attain such realization].
With a deluded mind, one becomes insane; Just as within a single atom, so it is with all atoms.
The entire world enters therein; Such is the inconceivable. Within each and every atom are the phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
The realms and lands are all immeasurable, And one is able to discern and know them all.
Within each and every atom, there are immeasurable kinds of Buddha-fields;

all these various types, being immeasurable, are known within each single one. All that exists within the Dharma-realm—its various distinct characteristics and the differences among the various realms of existence—one is able to discern and know them all, having deeply entered subtle wisdom.
They can discern all worlds and explain with complete clarity how all kalpas are formed and destroyed;
they know the long and short durations of all kalpas, and that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment. They can distinguish all practices, whether they are identical or different;
they enter deeply into all worlds, both those that are vast and those that are not.
In one body, infinite lands; in one land, infinite bodies.
All the various worlds existing throughout the ten directions, with their vast and immeasurable characteristics—all these he is able to know.
Within all three periods of time, regarding the infinite lands, he possesses profound and perfect wisdom.
He fully understands their formation and destruction throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
such things as their arising or their dissolution are ineffable, yet those of virtuous character understand them all profoundly.
Whether there be various lands adorned with diverse terrains, or likewise the various realms of existence, these arise from the purity of karma.
There are some worlds that are defiled in infinite ways; these arise from the karmic responses of sentient beings, all according to their actions.
There are immeasurable and boundless lands, yet one knows them to be a single land;
thus one enters into all such lands, their number being unknowable, throughout all worlds.
They enter entirely into a single land, yet the worlds do not become one; nor is there any confusion therein.
There are worlds turned upward or downward, some high and others low—all these they can discern and know through the perceptions of sentient beings.
Vast and expansive are these various worlds, immeasurable and without limit.

Knowing that the manifold is one, And knowing that the one is manifold— Samantabhadra and all sons of the Buddhas, By means of the wisdom of Samantabhadra, Can thoroughly know the number of all lands; Their number is without limit.
They know the transformations of all worlds, The transformations of lands, the transformations of beings, The transformations of phenomena, and the transformations of all Buddhas.
All are ultimately perfected; throughout all worlds, The various and diverse adornments of subtle and vast lands Arise entirely from karma.

Innumerable sons of the Buddha, who have skillfully trained in entering the Dharma-realm, Possess sovereign power through their supernormal faculties, Pervading everywhere throughout the ten directions.
Even if one were to spend eons as numerous as all sentient beings speaking the names of those worlds, one could not exhaust them, save for the revelation of the Buddha.
Even if one spent immeasurable eons speaking the various names of worlds and Tathāgatas, they could never be fully told; how much more so, then, the most supreme wisdom?
The Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time arises from the dharma-realm;
it fills the stage of the Tathāgata with pure and unimpeded mindfulness, and with boundless, unobstructed wisdom.
By discerning and expounding the dharma-realm, one reaches the further shore, transcending all worlds of phenomena—both vast and subtle.
Adorned by their cultivation, they are able to know all in a single thought.
Among them, those lions among men cultivate the various practices of a Buddha, attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and manifest all manner of masteries.
Thus, throughout the future world, for immeasurable eons in succession, there shall be these Honored Ones among Men.
The Bodhisattvas are able to know all practices and vows, all realms, and thus diligently practice them therein to attain perfect enlightenment.
They also know the assemblies, lifespans, and the way they transform sentient beings;
by means of these various Dharma-gates, they turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
The Bodhisattva, knowing thus, dwells in the stage of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
with wisdom fully clear, they give birth to all Buddhas encompassed within the present age.
Entering deeply into all Buddha-lands and penetrating the Dharma-realm, [they dwell] within those various worlds.
All Buddhas of the present have attained mastery over the Dharma;
their discourse is unimpeded, and they likewise know those assemblies, the power of their pure lands, and their manifestations.
Throughout immeasurable billions of eons, the World-Honored One, the Subduer of Men, has constantly contemplated these matters with all his majestic spiritual power.
The inexhaustible treasury of wisdom, capable of knowing all things;
Giving birth to unimpeded eyes, and unimpeded ears, nose, and body; With unimpeded, broad, and long tongues, able to bring joy to all beings;
Possessing the most supreme and unimpeded mind, vast and universally pure; Wisdom completely filling [all realms].

Fully knowing the dharmas of the three periods of time, skillfully training in all transformations— the transformation of lands, the transformation of beings, the transformation of worlds, and the transformation of discipline— they have reached the ultimate shore of transformation.
The various distinctions in the world all arise from abiding in conceptualization; entering the Buddha’s wisdom of skillful means, they understand them all with complete clarity.
The assemblies are unspeakably many, yet for each one he manifests his body; He causes all to see the Tathāgata liberating boundless multitudes.
The profound wisdom of all Buddhas is like the sun rising upon all lands in the world;
It appears everywhere without ceasing, thoroughly penetrating all worlds.
Provisional names have no reality; sentient beings and the world are like dreams and like reflections of light.
Regarding all worldly phenomena, one does not give rise to discriminatory views. One who has well departed from discrimination does not even perceive discrimination.
Immeasurable and incalculable eons— to understand them is but a single thought-moment.
Knowing that thought is also without thought, one thus perceives the world:
In a single thought-moment, one completely transcends immeasurable lands; Though passing through immeasurable eons, one does not move from one's original place.
Unspeakable eons are but a mere instant; Do not perceive length or brevity.
Ultimately, momentary phenomena—the mind abides in the world, and the world abides in the mind.
Herein, do not falsely give rise to the dualistic discrimination of "two" or "not-two.
Sentient beings, worlds, eons, all Buddhas, and the Buddha-dharma—all are like illusions; the Dharma-realm is entirely equal.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, he manifests infinite bodies; Knowing that the body arises from conditions, he is ultimately unattached.
Relying on non-dual wisdom, he appears as a Lion among Men;
He is not attached to the dharma of non-duality, Knowing that non-duality is not dual, And thoroughly understanding all worlds.

Like a flame, like a shadow and light, Like an echo, and likewise like a dream, Like an illusion, and like a magical transformation— Thus one enters in accordance with The sphere of action of all Buddhas.
Having accomplished the wisdom of Samantabhadra, One shines universally throughout the profound Dharma-realm;
All attachments to sentient beings and lands Are completely relinquished and abandoned.
They give rise to the mind of great compassion, universally purifying all worlds.
Bodhisattvas always maintain right mindfulness of the lion-like wondrous Dharma, which is as pure as space.
Seeing that the world is constantly deluded and inverted, they resolve to rescue and deliver all beings; their conduct is entirely pure.
Pervading the entire realm of phenomena, The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Whether the Buddha-dharma or worldly dharmas— If one sees their true reality, There is no distinction whatsoever.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body treasury Pervasively enters into the world; Though it exists within the world, It remains unattached to the world.
Just as reflections in pure water have no coming or going, so should one know that the Dharmakāya pervades the world.
Thus, free from defilement and attachment, body and world are both pure, serene like space;
all things are without birth, and one knows the body to be inexhaustible.
Without arising and without cessation, neither permanent nor impermanent,
he manifests to all the worlds to eliminate all false views and reveal right view.
The nature of phenomena has no coming or going and is unattached to "self" or "what belongs to self," just as a skilled illusionist manifests various things.
Coming from nowhere and departing to nowhere, The nature of illusion is neither finite nor infinite.
Amidst that great assembly, He manifests both the finite and the infinite.
With this mind of tranquil concentration, One cultivates all roots of goodness, Giving birth to all Buddhas.
Neither finite nor infinite, yet both finite and infinite— All these are but deluded perceptions.
Thoroughly understanding all realms of existence, They do not cling to the finite or the infinite.
The profound Dharma of the Buddhas is vast, deep, and quiescent; With profound and immeasurable wisdom, They know the depths of all realms of existence.
The Bodhisattva is free from delusion; their pure mind is constantly continuous. Skillfully employing the power of supernatural faculties, they deliver immeasurable sentient beings:
those who are not yet at peace, they cause to find peace; those who are already at peace, they lead to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Thus pervading the entire Dharma-realm, their minds are without attachment and do not dwell even in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Not entering into nirvāṇa, they thus pervade the entire world; awakening all living beings—whether categorized as phenomena or as sentient beings—they understand them thoroughly yet remain unattached. They rain down the rain of Dharma everywhere, saturating all worlds;
throughout all realms, in every thought-moment, they achieve perfect enlightenment.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, they never experience regression; they fully understand all the various bodies in the world.
Knowing the nature of the body in this way, they attain the body of all Buddhas.
They universally know all sentient beings, as well as all kalpas and all buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, which are boundless.
There is no ocean of wisdom they do not enter; the bodies of sentient beings are immeasurable. For each and every one, they manifest their own body;
the Buddha-body is without limit. The wise perceive them all clearly; in a single thought-moment, they know how all Tathāgatas appear.
Even if one were to spend immeasurable eons extolling this, it could never be fully described.
The Buddhas are able to manifest their bodies and enter parinirvāṇa in every place; within a single thought-moment, they produce immeasurable śarīras, each distinct from the others.
Thus, in future ages, those who seek the fruit of Buddhahood and possess the immeasurable bodhicitta—the Buddha knows them all with decisive wisdom throughout the three periods of time.
All the Tathāgatas know them all; Thus they discern and know the names of those dwelling in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
The immeasurable stages of conduct, They enter the sphere of wisdom, their wheel never regressing.
With subtle, vast, and great wisdom, They penetrate deeply into the realm of the Tathāgatas.
Having entered, one does not regress; this is called the wisdom of Samantabhadra.
The Most Victorious One enters all Buddha-realms, practicing without regression.
Attaining unsurpassed enlightenment and an immeasurable, boundless mind, the various distinct karmas are all accumulated through conceptualization.

He understands all things with equanimity—whether they are defiled or undefiled, the minds of those in training, the minds of those beyond training, and all inexpressible states of mind. In every moment of thought, he knows them all:
he realizes they are neither one nor two, neither defiled nor pure, and likewise free from confusion; for they all arise from their own conceptual perceptions.
Thus clearly seeing all sentient beings, Whose mental conceptions arise differently, giving rise to various worlds— By such skillful means, they cultivate the most supreme practices;
Born through transformation from the Buddha-dharma, they are named Samantabhadra. Yet all sentient beings give rise to these delusions.
The perceptions of the various realms of good and evil— From these, one is either born in heaven Or else falls into hell.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the world: It arises from the karma of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Because false conceptualization is boundless, The worlds are likewise immeasurable. All lands and realms Are manifested by the net of perception.
By means of the skillful method of the net of illusion, one is able to enter [all realms] in a single thought-moment.

It is likewise for the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Though worldly perceptions differ, one can equally enter the objective sphere of each and every faculty; all immeasurable eyes enter into the various distinctions of natures.
Immeasurable and ineffable, what is seen is without distinction;
Nor is there any confusion, as each follows their own karma And experiences its respective retribution. The power of Samantabhadra is immeasurable;
he fully knows them all— The entire sphere of all eyes; Great wisdom is able to enter it all.
Thus all these worlds can be discerned and known; likewise, one practices all deeds without ever turning back.

The Buddha’s teachings, the teachings on sentient beings, and the teachings on lands—such teachings of the three periods of time, of every variety, are all fully understood, both in the past and in the future.
The future contains the present; the three times see one another.
Each and every one is clearly understood in such infinite ways, awakening all worlds. The limit of the skillful means of the All-Knowing One cannot be found.

[Treatise] Fifteenth: Correctly Expounding the Meaning of the Verses. This section of verses consists of one hundred and twenty-one lines, all of which simultaneously and universally eulogize the preceding ten Dharmas of Radiance (*dharmāloka*).

Because the conduct of Samantabhadra has reached its ultimate consummation—wherein cause and effect, wisdom and principle, and compassion and vows are all perfected—the meaning is as clarified within the verses themselves.
Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle Seventy-Seven.

Chapter Thirty-Seven, Part One: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
[Treatise] In order to explain this chapter, four sections are established: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion.
Third, explaining the reason why the Tathāgata emits light to empower Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; fourth, interpreting the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter: Why is it titled "The Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata"?

It is because, following the second assembly held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsabhavana*), the ten levels of faith were taught, with the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Acalajñāna*) presiding over the first level of faith. Next, [the text] begins...

The nine Buddhas other than the Buddha of Obstructing Wisdom (*Āvaraṇajñāna*) represent the progressive cultivation within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Furthermore, because the single wisdom (*ekajñāna*) is endowed with ten kinds of wisdom, names are established according to their respective functions.
From within these ten stages of faith, one advances in practice without departing from the essence of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*);

by giving rise to the vows and practices of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one cultivates differentiated wisdom (*viśeṣa-jñāna*) and achieves great loving-kindness and compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*).
Reaching the fulfillment of this stage is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

This clarifies that while the initial appearance at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in the first assembly was the appearance of Vairocana Buddha as having newly attained perfect awakening, the appearance in this chapter is the appearance resulting from the fulfillment of the stages of practice, realization, wisdom, and compassion as a bodhisattva advances through the five stages; therefore, it is called "appearance" (*udbhava*).
The present chapter is also like Sudhana’s vision of the youth Kalyāṇakārin and the maiden Guṇavatī; this signifies that the two practices of wisdom and compassion are fulfilled.
Consequently, one sees the Tathāgata Maitreya, which signifies the meaning of the appearance of a Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Tathāgata empowers these two persons with light, and through their dialogue, he explains the gateway to the appearance of a Tathāgata. Mañjuśrī represents [this].
Manifesting fundamental wisdom is Samantabhadra, who is the gate of accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings through discriminative wisdom.

Second, regarding the purpose of this chapter: it clarifies that within the preceding five stages, the three dharmas of Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Buddha-fruit have already been fully explained;
this chapter clarifies that the practice of the Buddha-fruit is now perfected, and thus this chapter must follow. Third, [it explains] the Tathāgata’s emission of light.

Regarding the source of the light added to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra: the light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows clarifies that this is the light of the Buddha’s Middle Way and the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhaphala-jñāna*).

Its being poured upon the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head clarifies that the wisdom-virtue of the Buddha-fruit is supreme and exalted, thereby causing Mañjuśrī to initiate the inquiry into the gateway of the Buddha-fruit. The Tathāgata emits light from his mouth to pour upon the mouth of Samantabhadra.
This clarifies that because Samantabhadra is the wisdom of differentiation (*vibhāga-jñāna*) and desires to fulfill the preaching of the Dharma, he asks:

"For what reason does the Tathāgata not himself speak this chapter? The answer is: He emits light and bestows empowerment upon these two, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, in order to manifest the Dharma so that future students may understand it easily; it is not that the Tathāgata himself is incapable of doing so.

Question: What is meant by the "manifesting dharma" (*vijñapti*)? Answer: It is explained that Mañjuśrī is the manifestation of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* as fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is the manifestation of the Buddha’s progressive cultivation as the wisdom of differentiation (*praveśa-viśeṣa-jñāna*).
It is only when one reaches this stage and both fundamental wisdom and the wisdom of differentiation are equally perfected and complete that one is first designated as a Tathāgata who has emerged.

The manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* (the body of appearance) is based on the fact that within the self-nature of the *dharmakāya*— which is inherently pure and stainless— one can manifest one's own essence as the luminous,
pure primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) that is free from dependence. When this wisdom of individual differentiation is spoken of as being in accord with the wisdom and virtue of the Buddhas of the past,
present, and future, it is precisely because one’s own practiced realization and conduct have become the perfection of the Buddha’s awakened practice.
Therefore, because the Tathāgata emits light and bestows empowerment through the establishment of the Dharma-ordinance,

it is clear that for all Bodhisattvas, when the fruit is perfected and merit is completed, the Dharma is always thus; for the light emitted by the Buddha permits one to reach the stage of Buddhahood, and since the Dharma is not erroneous,
it clarifies that such Dharmakāya fundamental wisdom differentiates and benefits sentient beings, such that the myriad practices are all fully prepared and complete.
The circle and square represent the manifestation of one’s own Tathāgata; Mañjuśrī represents the manifestation of the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*);
Samantabhadra is the preacher of the Dharma; and the Buddha is the fruit. This can be understood by reflecting upon it; the general meaning is clear.

Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the gates of wisdom and practice that accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood, and they further cause the preaching of the Dharma of the Buddha’s manifestation. The Buddha [is the fruit].
This fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is in its essential nature ineffable; all that is expressed in words is discriminative wisdom (*pravicaya-jñāna*).

The appearance of Vairocana Buddha in the first assembly at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) clarifies that this first assembly at the site of enlightenment is not for the purpose of the Tathāgata Vairocana emitting light to establish the Dharma for those who have newly resolved to attain awakening and are practicing.

Because the modes [of these two] clearly manifest the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya and the diverse practices for benefiting sentient beings as being fully perfected, these two individuals are said to be exactly like the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas appearing in the present.
Thus, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the common dharma of all Buddhas of the past and present. For those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, from the very beginning...
Since the initial arousal of the mind of faith, one has traversed all these practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; it is only now that they reach fulfillment.
Thus, this progressive cultivation never departs from the essence of the ten wisdoms of the Immovable Wisdom Buddha within the original faith.
Therefore, it is clarified that at this time, through immovable wisdom, immovable practice, and immovable capacity, one can universally traverse the ten directions.
Without moving from one, one enters many; without moving from many, one enters one; without moving from the small, one enters the large;

and so on, as clarified in the sutras. This is for the purpose of realizing that the body, mind, principle, and wisdom are without intrinsic nature and without dependence, such that emotional consciousness and its attachments perish and the Dharma-assembly is eternally thus.
By means of these five stages of ascending progress, one either ascends to the heavens to manifest the Dharma, or the body pervades the ten directions.
Thus, at the very moment of its final completion, it does not depart from the essence of the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) within the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*).
Therefore, this dharma that has already reached the culmination of its own fruition does not depart from the place where faith is taught—
the Universal Radiance Hall— and the teaching remains as when Sudhana arrived before Maitreya Tathāgata and again beheld Mañjuśrī, his initial friend of faith.
Fearing that later students might become confused regarding the Dharma, [the text] uses Sudhana’s journey to represent each point so that it may be easily understood;
the general meaning can be known by relying on this. Furthermore, according to this single scripture, there are three conclusions:
the two types of cause and fruit, and the eternal path. First, from the initial Bodhimaṇḍa to Vairocana...
The *Pǐn* (Chapters) consists of six chapters; this sutra is the cause and fruit within the Buddha’s own five stages (*pañca-avasthā*).

It features fifty assemblies, including the Bodhisattva Ten Universal Samantabhadra, Ocean Moon Light Great Radiance, and the Divine Beings (*deva*), which constitute the second: the five stages of the bodhisattva who has resolved upon faith (*śraddhā-cittotpādaka*).
Regarding the cause and fruit of these six stages—including the stage of faith—from the second assembly onwards, [it is taught] throughout the *Pǔ*...

From the "Chapter on Proclaiming the Names of Buddhas" in the *Prabhāsa-kuṭa* assembly down to the eighth assembly, the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" in the *Samantāvabhāsa-kuṭa*, there are thirty-two chapters of sutra that clarify the cause and effect of a bodhisattva’s initial resolve (*cittotpāda*).
Within these thirty-two chapters, the "Chapter on the Buddha-flower Samādhi" in the third dhyāna is yet to come; this is what is to be cultivated here.

In the sequence of adding practice within the stages of practice, from Mañjuśrī to the Great Stūpa, he expounds the *Sūtra-gate of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma-realm* to transform Sudhana, causing him to seek southward after fifty-three sublime friends. This clearly uses the practice to exhort the cultivation of the five stages;
it serves as a manifestation of the cause and fruit that conclude the [entire] work. However, fearing that [the reader] might merely grasp the teaching, [the text] speaks only of the doctrine.
The practice of returning to the confusion of delusion is resolved by means of Sudhana; these fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are those who have already set out in practice.

By seeking instruction from each one and progressing upward, they serve as models for the five stages of advancement for those who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), ensuring that their practice does not become lost. The intent behind this is explained in the text.

To explain these two kinds of eternal paths: as stated in the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* and the *Lokātīta-parivarta*, regarding the path of transcendence, one constantly benefits sentient beings within the eternally true *dharmadhātu*, which is not false. This eternally true *dharmadhātu* is the eternal path because it is the fruit of Buddhahood;
thus, constantly benefiting the world and sentient beings without seeking self-interest is the universality of the Buddha’s eternal path.
The "Noble Practice" (*Bhadra-caryā*) is also called the threefold completion of cause and effect within this sutra, representing the two types of eternal paths.

As found from the second assembly through the eighth assembly in the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter, it clarifies the advancement through the five stages by a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind.
The first completion and the entrustment for circulation are both clarified in this chapter; thus, this chapter elucidates the progressive ascent through the five stages.

At the conclusion of the "Fruition Perfection" (Guoyuan), there were those who sought at the end of the "Dharmadhātu Chapter" (Fajiepin) for an entrustment (*parindanā*) and a mandate for circulation;

this was because they had not yet grasped the intended meaning of the scripture. This is because the "Dharmadhātu Chapter" comprehensively encompasses the entire body of the teaching, as well as the great essence of the non-duality of stillness and function throughout the three periods of time and across all past and present—there being no distinction between beginning and end or temporal divisions—and it is not something established through deliberate effort (*prayoga*).

Setting aside the causal conditions and motivations, this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" serves solely to guide Bodhisattvas who have awakened the mind by means of the Vehicle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-yāna*), leading deluded followers to this point.
It is precisely because the practice of the five stages of the sūtra has reached maturity through diligent cultivation that the matters of circulation and entrustment are now discussed.
As for the fundamental nature of the Dharma-realm itself, it is inherently free from delusion.
The nature itself does not awaken; it has neither emergence nor disappearance, neither formation nor destruction, and neither flow nor penetration.
This intent for the entrustment and circulation is taught at the conclusion of the stage of applied effort for the sake of ordinary beings who have not yet awakened;
therefore, it does not follow after the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta. Whereas the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" directly discusses the fruit at the culmination of the merits of all Buddhas.

This is self-continuing and requires no further entrustment; as stated in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," from the Tathāgata’s lion throne up to the dharmadhātu itself, there is no boundary—this clarifies the ultimate fruition.

Just as the "Tathāgatotpatti-parivarta" clarifies that for those with faith, it is only through the power of completing the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) across the five stages that one finally attains the pure reality and first ascends to the stage of fruition.
Having completed the two practices and perfected the circular path, he then speaks of the entrustment and circulation, clarifying that the fruition is initially fulfilled;

thus, the Way of the Human is the Dharma-realm, which is not measured by the limits of past and present, or beginning and end. To circulate this Dharma is called "circulation," which is precisely the Chapter on the Dharma-realm.
This constitutes personally fulfilling the merit of the Dharma-realm and constantly exhorting the multitude through the practice of the Dharma-realm.
To emulate and study through skillful means (*upāya*) is what is called "entrusting and circulating through skillful means.

These skillful means are precisely the methods within the five stages (*pañca-vastu*): namely, the various *pāramitās*, the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), great vows, great wisdom, and great compassion. All the teachings of the Buddhas are exactly like this.
Only then can it be accomplished. Fourth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: within this chapter, the text is divided into two sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a great radiance named "The Emergence of the Tathāgata."
He manifests as his retinue immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of light rays,
which universally illuminate all worlds throughout the ten directions, the entirety of space and the dharma-realm; they circumambulate them ten times to the right,
manifesting the Tathāgata’s infinite sovereignty and awakening countless multitudes of bodhisattvas, while shaking all worlds in the ten directions.
Having eliminated all suffering of the evil realms within the world-systems, eclipsed all the palaces of the Māras,
manifested all the Tathāgatas sitting upon the seat of enlightenment and attaining perfect awakening, and displayed all the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment— having performed these deeds—
he came and circumambulated the assembly of Bodhisattvas to the right, entering the Tathāgata-nature-arising Wondrous Virtue.
When the Bodhisattva reached the summit, the entire great assembly in this *maṇḍala* leaped for joy with body and mind, giving rise to great rapture, and thought:
"How truly marvelous and rare! Now that the Tathāgata has emitted such a great radiance, he must surely proclaim the most profound Great Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta, born of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), on his lotus throne, bared one shoulder...
With his right shoulder bared and kneeling on his right knee, he joined his palms with a single-minded focus toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
The Great Wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment gives rise to virtue; Universally penetrating all realms, he has reached the further shore.
Equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, Therefore, I now pay homage to you with reverence.
Having already ascended to the shore of the signless realm, you manifest a body adorned with wondrous marks and emit a thousand stainless rays of light,
which utterly destroy the hosts of Māra throughout all worlds in the ten directions, causing them all to tremble without exception.
Never having terrified a single sentient being—such is the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata.
The nature of space and the realm of phenomena are equal;
having been able to abide thus, he causes all living beings, infinite in number, to extinguish evil and remove their manifold defilements.
Having practiced asceticism with diligent effort for countless eons, he has accomplished the path to supreme enlightenment;
his wisdom is unimpeded regarding all realms of experience, and he shares the same nature as all Buddhas.
The Guide emits this great radiance, shaking all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Having already manifested immeasurable powers of supernatural transformation, you have returned once more to enter my body.
Having skillfully trained in the definitive Dharma, immeasurable bodhisattvas have all gathered here, causing me to resolve to inquire about the Dharma; therefore, I now entreat the King of Dharma.
Now this assembly is entirely pure, Able to skillfully deliver all the worlds;
Their wisdom is boundless and free from attachment— Such noble and excellent ones have all gathered here.
To the Honored One, the World’s Teacher, Whose wisdom and diligence are both immeasurable.
Now, with your radiance illuminating the great assembly, I pray that you allow me to inquire about the unsurpassed Dharma.
Who is it that can truly and fully expound upon the profound realm of the Great Sage?
Who is the eldest son of the Tathāgata’s Dharma? O Honored Guide of the World, I pray that you reveal this to us.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately emitted from his mouth a great radiance named "Unobstructed and Fearless," with hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light as its retinue,
universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions, as vast as empty space and equal to the Dharma-realm.
It circled to the right ten times, manifesting the various sovereign powers of the Tathāgata and awakening immeasurable beings.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas caused all worlds throughout the ten directions to tremble, extinguished all suffering in the various evil realms,
eclipsed all the palaces of the Māras, and manifested all the Tathāgatas sitting upon the seat of enlightenment and attaining perfect awakening,
as well as all the assemblies at their sites of enlightenment; having performed these deeds, they came and circumambulated [the Buddha] to the right.
The assembly of bodhisattvas entered the mouth of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.

Once their light had entered, the body and lion throne of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, as well as those of all the other bodhisattvas, surpassed their former state by a hundredfold—except for the lion throne of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotra-vyuha-guṇa asked the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:
The Mahāsattva said: "O Son of the Buddha, this great and wondrous manifestation of supernormal powers displayed by the Buddha causes all Bodhisattvas to give rise to joy;
it is inconceivable and nothing in the world can equal it. What auspicious sign is this? The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra replied:
"O Son of the Buddha, in the past I have seen various Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas manifesting such [powers]."
With great supernormal transformations, he then preached the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Appearance. As I reflect upon it, at this present moment, he shall preach that Dharma.
When these words were spoken, the entire great earth shook in its entirety, and immeasurable lights of inquiry into the Dharma emerged.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nature-Arising Sublime Virtue addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, O Bodhisattva..."
"Sāgaramati, how should one understand the manner in which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, appear?
I pray that you will explain this for me, O Son of the Buddha! This entire assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas has long cultivated pure deeds;
they have perfected mindfulness and wisdom, have reached the ultimate shore of great adornment, and are endowed with all [virtues]."
The Buddhas, whose conduct of dignified demeanor consists of right mindfulness of all Buddhas never forgotten, who observe all sentient beings with great compassion,
who have definitively realized the spheres of supernatural power of the great Bodhisattvas, who have obtained the empowerment of the Buddhas' spiritual might,
and who are able to receive the wondrous Dharma of all Tathāgatas— possessing such immeasurable merits as these— all have now arrived.
"O Son of the Buddha, you have already served and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas;
you have accomplished the supreme and wondrous practices of a Bodhisattva and attained mastery over all gates of samādhi.
You have entered the secret realm of all Buddhas, understood all Buddha-dharmas, severed all doubts and delusions, and are empowered by the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas."
Furthermore, knowing the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings, he preaches the true Dharma of liberation according to their preferences;
in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom, he expounds the Buddha-dharma and reaches the further shore. Possessing such immeasurable merits as these, well done, Son of the Buddha!
Pray, speak of the appearance of the Dharmakāya, its marks, speech, sounds, mind, and mental objects of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Regarding the practices performed within the realms, the attainment of the Way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma,
and even the manifestation of entry into parinirvāṇa— may you please explain all such matters as these, including the roots of goodness produced through seeing,
hearing, and drawing near. At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-vyūha-śrī, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and spoke in verse:
Excellent is your unimpeded great wisdom; Excellent is your awakening to the boundless realm of equality.
I pray that you will speak of the immeasurable virtues of the Buddhas, So that the sons of the Buddha, having heard them, may all rejoice.
How do Bodhisattvas accord with and enter [the truth] As the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world?
Please explain what are the spheres of body, speech, and mind, as well as their respective domains of activity;
how do the Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment? How does the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma?
And how does the Sugata pass into parinirvāṇa? Having heard this, the great assembly rejoices in their hearts.

If there are those who see the Buddha, the Great Dharma King, and draw near to him so that all roots of goodness increase, pray tell of that treasury of merits: what do sentient beings obtain upon seeing him?
Or if they should hear the name of the Tathāgata, whether he is in the present world or has entered parinirvāṇa.
Having conceived deep faith in that treasury of merit, what benefits are there? Please proclaim this!
All these bodhisattvas join their palms and gaze up at the Tathāgata, as well as at you, O Ocean of Great Merit;
O Purifier of Sentient Beings, please speak for them.
May you expound the meaning corresponding to the sublime Dharma through causes, conditions, and parables;
may sentient beings, having heard it, give rise to the Great Mind, their doubts exhausted and their wisdom purified like space.
May they behold the adorned bodies manifested by all Buddhas throughout every land.
May you, with wondrous voice and parables, reveal the Bodhi of the Buddha;
just as in those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lands throughout the ten directions over immeasurable *kalpas*,
the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered here today is likewise difficult for all of them to behold.

All these bodhisattvas, with deep reverence, have conceived a longing thirst for the subtle and wondrous meaning; may you, with a pure mind, fully expound it. The great assembly said: "O Son of the Buddha, this place is inconceivable; that is to say, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has appeared through immeasurable dharmas.
Why is this? It is not by means of a single condition nor by means of a single matter that the appearance of a Tathāgata is accomplished;
rather, it is accomplished through ten immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya matters."
What is "that which has gone"? It is that which is formed by the bodhicitta that, throughout immeasurable past eons, embraced all sentient beings;
it is formed by the pure and sublime aspirations throughout immeasurable past eons;

it is formed by the great loving-kindness and great compassion that, throughout immeasurable past eons, rescued and protected all sentient beings; and it is formed by the continuous succession of practices and vows throughout immeasurable past eons.
Because it was accomplished through past immeasurable cultivation of merit and wisdom with a mind never weary;
because it was accomplished through past immeasurable offerings to the Buddhas and the transformation of sentient beings;
because it was accomplished through past immeasurable paths of pure wisdom and skillful means; because it was accomplished through past immeasurable treasuries of pure merit. Past...

Because it is accomplished through the wisdom of the path of immeasurable adornments; because it is accomplished through the immeasurable penetration of the meaning of the Dharma in the past—O Son of the Buddha, in this way, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* gateways of the Dharma are fully perfected in the Tathāgata.
[Treatise] First, from the beginning— "At that time, the World-Honored One," etc.— down to "O Son of the Buddha,
in this way immeasurable asaṃkhyeya dharma-gates are perfected in the Tathāgata," there are one hundred and a half lines of sūtra, including verses,
which clarify how the Tathāgata emits light and empowers Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra to expound the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta* accordingly.

The commentary on the text is divided into five sections. First, from the initial passage "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from between his eyebrows a light of the white tuft-mark" down to "and spoke these verses," there are twelve and a half lines of sūtra text clarifying the section where the Buddha emits light to bathe Mañjuśrī’s crown so that he may inquire about the Dharma. Second, twenty lines of verse clarify Mañjuśrī.

[as follows]... down to the thirty-five lines of verse, which clarify how the Tathāgata’s emitted light entered everywhere.

consisting of twenty verses. The Fifth Section: The Repeated Verses on the Ten Dharmas of the Appearance of the Tathāgata, as Previously Requested for Explanation, by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra...
From the passage below— "O Son of the Buddha, in this way immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* dharma-gates are perfected in the Tathāgata"—
down to the section where Samantabhadra informs the assembly that the appearance of a Tathāgata is accomplished through ten immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* matters;
these five preceding sections constitute the textual account of the Buddha’s light empowering Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

In their mutual dialogue, they explain that the appearance of the Buddha involves the radiation of light and the bestowal of empowerment; this has already been fully set forth in the preceding section.
Within the general meaning that expresses the Dharma, it clarifies the methods for ascending in practice, the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya*, and the wisdom of differentiation.

Because the compassionate practice that perfects the ten directions reaches its ultimate consummation, it is called the "Appearance of the Tathāgata. Therefore, light is emitted and empowerment is bestowed upon Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
The two [bodhisattvas] clearly manifest the principle and wisdom as essence and function, thoroughly penetrating them. Mañjuśrī is the manifestation of the Tathāgata;
he is the subtle principle of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the gateway to the fundamental wisdom.
Samantabhadra is the gateway to the differentiated wisdom, the myriad practices, and the great compassion of all Buddhas of the ten directions. Now, the five [aspects] are clarified.
Having progressed through the stages and reached this level, these two dharmas are perfected; this is called the manifestation of one’s own Buddha.
Therefore, light is emitted from between the eyebrows to consecrate the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, causing him to inquire about the dharma-gate of the ultimate summit of one’s own Buddhahood.
Light is emitted from the mouth, which is the light of teaching, causing him to explain the distinctions of the myriad practices that constitute the ultimate summit of one’s own Buddhahood.
Because the Dharma is perfected through wisdom and compassion throughout the ten directions, these two persons are used to symbolize the teaching so that students may understand it easily;
it is not that the Tathāgata himself was unable to explain it. Furthermore, this represents that fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) transcends the reach of words.
This chapter of the sutra clarifies that within the Dharmakāya, fundamental wisdom and its differentiated wisdoms, as well as compassion and the myriad practices, are all perfected.
Therefore, from the first through the eleventh stages, the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of these levels bring the cultivation of both the ultimate and conventional truths to completion;
their meaning is self-evident from the text itself. Second, "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if, for example, within a trichiliocosm...
and so forth; the following ten sections of scripture clarify the realm of the Tathāgata’s manifestation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as taught by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, as well as its...
The practice of the ten matters is explained within this section.
Among the ten gates of the Tathāgata’s manifestation, there are ten scriptural passages that describe how the Tathāgata’s manifestation involves hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya matters.
The first of these clarifies the Tathāgata’s ten immeasurable manifestations.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the trichiliocosm were not accomplished by a single condition nor by a single event, but was only brought into being through immeasurable conditions and immeasurable events. These are as follows:
the rising and spreading of great clouds, the falling of torrential rain, and the successive support provided by four kinds of wind-circles. What are these four? The first is named "Able to Support."
Because it can sustain great waters, it is called "The Able Sustainer"; because it can dissolve great waters, it is called "The Able Dissolver";
because it establishes all locations, it is called "The Establisher"; and because its skillful arrangement of adornments is universally excellent, it is called "The Adornment.
All of these arise through the collective karma of sentient beings and the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattvas, causing [all things] therein to...

Sentient beings each receive and enjoy [the world] according to what is appropriate for them. O Son of the Buddha, through such immeasurable causes and conditions as these, the trichiliocosm is thus established.

Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): there is no one who creates it, no one who makes it, no one who knows it, and no one who brings it into existence; yet that world is nonetheless accomplished, and the Tathāgata likewise appears therein.
Furthermore, it is not through a single condition nor by a single matter that accomplishment is attained;
rather, it is through immeasurable causes and conditions and immeasurable modes of phenomena that accomplishment is achieved. These are as follows:

having previously heard, listened to, and upheld the great Dharma-cloud rain from past Buddhas, one is thereby able to give rise to the four kinds of great wisdom-wind wheels of the Tathāgata. What are these four?
First is the great wisdom wind-wheel of the dhāraṇī of mindful retention, which can sustain the great dharma-cloud rains of all Tathāgatas;
second is the great wisdom wind-wheel of the production of śamatha and vipaśyanā, which can exhaust and dry up all afflictions;
third is the great wisdom wind-wheel of skillful dedication, which can bring all roots of goodness to fulfillment.
Fourth, there is the great wind-wheel of the adornment of birth and the differentiation of stainlessness,
which causes the roots of goodness of all sentient beings previously transformed to be purified and perfected, by virtue of the power of the Tathāgata’s untainted roots of goodness. Thus,

although the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through which the Tathāgata attains such equal and perfect enlightenment is without arising and without action, the sons of the Buddha nevertheless achieve accomplishment.
This is the first mark of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like when a trichiliocosm is about to be formed:
a great cloud sends down rain called "The Great Deluge," which no region can receive and no ground can sustain, except for the great earth.

When a thousandfold world-system is about to be formed, it is likewise with the Buddha-sons, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who raise a great cloud of Dharma and rain down a great rain of Dharma called "The Accomplishment of the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

This cannot be received nor can it be sustained by those of the two vehicles whose mental dispositions are narrow and inferior; it can only be sustained by the power of the mental continuum of the great Bodhisattvas.
This, O Son of the Buddha, is the second sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, for example, by the power of karma, great clouds send down rain that comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
in the same way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise [manifests] through all the bodhi-...
By the power of their roots of goodness, they raise great clouds of Dharma and rain down great showers of Dharma; yet these come from nowhere and go nowhere.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the third sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like a great cloud that sends down a great rain over the trichiliocosm.
No sentient being in all the worlds is able to know their number; were one to attempt to calculate them, it would only cause one to go mad.
Only Maheśvara, the Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm, by the power of the roots of goodness cultivated in the past, understands them without exception, down to a single drop.
Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise thus, as he brings forth the Great Dharma.
The great rain of the Dharma-cloud falls upon all sentient beings; it is something that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know.

Should they attempt to fathom it, their minds would surely become deranged. Only Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the lords of all worlds, can—by virtue of the power of the wisdom cultivated in the past—clearly comprehend even a single word or phrase as it enters the minds of sentient beings.
"O Sons of the Buddha, this is the fourth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it thus. Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha, it is like when a great cloud sends down rain:

there are great clouds and rains called 'able to extinguish,' which can extinguish the calamity of fire; and there are great clouds and rains called 'able to produce,' which can produce the great waters."
There is a great rain-cloud named "Able to Cease" that can cease the great waters; there is a great rain-cloud named "Able to Accomplish" that can accomplish all kinds of mani-jewels;
and there is a great rain-cloud named "Discrimination" that can discriminate the three-thousandfold world-system.
Son of the Buddha, the appearance of a Tathāgata is also like this: he raises a great cloud of Dharma and rains down the great Dharma-rain.
The rain of Dharma includes a great rain of Dharma called "Able to Extinguish," which can extinguish all the afflictions of sentient beings;
a great rain of Dharma called "Able to Arouse," which can arouse all the roots of goodness in sentient beings;
a great rain of Dharma called "Able to Cease," which can cease all the delusions of view in sentient beings; and a great rain of Dharma called "Able to Accomplish," which can accomplish...
O Son of the Buddha, the great rain of the Dharma of all wisdom and Dharma-jewels is called "Discriminating the Various Inclinations of the Minds of All Sentient Beings";
this is the fifth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like a great cloud raining water of a single flavor, yet according to its...
The manifestation of the Tathāgatas, who rain down immeasurable varieties [of teachings], is likewise so:
they rain the single-flavored water of the Dharma of great compassion, preaching the Dharma through immeasurable distinctions according to what is appropriate.

O Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth sign of the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: for example—
When the trichiliocosm was first formed, the palaces of the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) were formed first;
next, the palaces of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) were formed; and finally, the dwelling places of humans and other sentient beings were formed.
Son of the Buddha, the appearance of a Tathāgata is likewise: first, the wisdom of the various practices of bodhisattvas arises; next, that of the pratyekabuddhas arises.

The wisdom of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) subsequently gives rise to the roots of goodness of the śrāvakas; the wisdom of all conditioned phenomena subsequently gives rise to the conditioned roots of goodness of other sentient beings.

O Son of the Buddha, it is like a great cloud raining water of a single flavor, yet the palaces that arise are of various different kinds according to the differences in the roots of goodness of sentient beings; likewise, the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata is of a single flavor.
"O Son of the Buddha, the rain of Dharma varies according to the capacities of sentient beings;
this, O Son of the Buddha, is the seventh sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like when the world is first about to be formed: a great body of water arises, filling the trichiliocosm and giving rise to great..."
There was a lotus named "The Jewel Adornment of the Merits of the Tathāgata’s Appearance," which covered the surface of the water and radiated light throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

At that time, Maheśvara, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others, having seen this flower, knew with certainty that in this eon there would be so many Buddhas appearing in the world. O Son of the Buddha, at that time, within it...
There is a wind-circle named "Pure Radiance" (*śubha-vimala-prabhā*) that can form the palaces of the various devas of the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
There is a wind-circle named "Adornment of Pure Light" (*vimala-prabha-alaṃkāra*) that can form the palaces of the various devas of the Desire Realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
