There is a wind-circle named "Impenetrable and Unbreakable" (*dṛḍha-sāndra-abhedya*) that can form the great and small Cakravāḍa mountains as well as the Vajra mountains. There is a wind-circle named...
There is a wind-circle named "Immovable" that is capable of forming Sumeru, the King of Mountains, as well as the ten great mountain kings. What are these ten? They are:
Mount Khadiraka, Ṛṣigiri, Māleya, Mahāmāleya, Yugandhara, Nimindhara, Cakravāḍa, and Mahācakravāḍa.
In the mountains of Gandhamādana and Himavat, there is a wind-circle named "Abiding" (*Pratiṣṭhāna*) which can form the great earth;
there is a wind-circle named "Adornment" (*Vyūha*) which can form the palaces of the terrestrial devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of the gandharvas;
and there is a wind-circle named "Inexhaustible Treasury" (*Akṣayakośa*) which can form all the great oceans of the trichiliocosm.
There is a wind-circle named Universal Radiance Treasury (*Samantaprabhā-garbha*) that can produce all the mani-jewels of the trichiliocosm;
there is a wind-circle named Firm Root (*Dṛḍhamūla*) that can produce all the wish-fulfilling trees.

O Son of the Buddha, the water of a single flavor rained down by the great clouds makes no distinction, yet because the roots of goodness of sentient beings differ, the wind-circles [manifest accordingly].
Just as the world-systems differ due to the differences among the wind-circles, O Son of the Buddha, the appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise so.

Endowed with all roots of goodness and merit, he emits the light of supreme great wisdom called "The Incessant Lineage of the Tathāgatas," which is the inconceivable wisdom that universally illumines all worlds in the ten directions and is one with all Bodhisattvas.
All Tathāgatas shall receive the prediction of consecration and shall attain perfect enlightenment, appearing in the world.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Tathāgata appears, there is again a light of supreme great wisdom called "Pure and Stainless," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s untainted and inexhaustible wisdom;
there is also a light of supreme great wisdom called "Universal Illumination," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s universal entry.
Furthermore, there is the light of supreme great wisdom called "Holding the Buddha-lineage," which is capable of accomplishing the Tathāgata’s power that is unshakable;

furthermore, there is the light of supreme great wisdom called "Transcending the Indestructible," which is capable of accomplishing the Tathāgata’s fearless and indestructible wisdom; furthermore, there is the light of supreme great wisdom called "One."
All supernormal powers can accomplish all the unshared dharmas of a Tathāgata and the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom called "Birth of Transformations," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s wisdom that ensures the roots of goodness produced through seeing, hearing, and drawing near to him are never lost or destroyed.
Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom called "Universal Accordance," which can accomplish...
He comes with a body of inexhaustible merit and wisdom to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named "Ultimate Naming," which is able to accomplish the profound and wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata;
according to what it awakens others to, it ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed. Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named...
Various adornments can perfect the Tathāgata’s marks and signs that grace his body, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.

Furthermore, there is the light of supreme great wisdom called "Indestructible," which can perfect the Tathāgata’s sublime lifespan—equal to the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space—which is inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s great compassion is of a single flavor...

Water is without discrimination; yet, because the desires and inclinations of all sentient beings differ and their faculties are each distinct, it gives rise to various great wisdom-wind-circles that cause all Bodhisattvas to accomplish the dharma of the appearance of the Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha, within the wheel of great wisdom in which all Tathāgatas share a single essence, various radiances of wisdom are born. The Buddha—
"O sons, you should know that from a single flavor of liberation, the Tathāgata brings forth immeasurable and inconceivable varieties of merit.
Sentient beings may think, 'This was created by the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata,' but, O sons of the Buddha, this was not created by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Sons of the Buddha, it is because there is not even a single bodhisattva who has not previously planted roots of goodness in the presence of a Buddha."
It is impossible for the faculties to attain even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
rather, it is solely by the power of the majestic virtue of all Buddhas that sentient beings are enabled to possess the merits of a Buddha.

Yet the Buddha-Tathāgata is without discrimination, without formation, without destruction, without an agent, and without any act of doing. O Son of the Buddha, this is the emergence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Manifesting the eighth sign, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand it in this way:

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, just as four wind-wheels arise based upon space and are able to support the water-wheel—what are these four? First is named Abiding (Sthita), second is named Constantly Abiding (Nityasthita), third is named Ultimate (Paryanta), and fourth is named Solid (Dṛḍha)—these four wind-wheels are able to support the water-wheel, and the water-wheel is able to...

It upholds the great earth so that it does not disintegrate; therefore, it is said that the earth wheel rests upon the water wheel, the water wheel rests upon the wind wheel, and the wind wheel rests upon space.
Space has no support, yet though it has no support, it enables the trichiliocosm to abide securely.
Son of the Buddha, the appearance of a Tathāgata is likewise so: he rests upon unimpeded wisdom.
The radiance of the Buddha gives rise to four kinds of great wisdom wind-circles that can sustain the roots of goodness of all sentient beings.
What are these four? They are: the great wisdom wind-circle that universally gathers in sentient beings and causes them all to rejoice;

the great wisdom wind-circle that establishes the True Dharma and causes all sentient beings to give rise to love and joy; and the great wisdom wind-circle that protects the roots of goodness of all sentient beings.
The wind-circle of great wisdom, endowed with all skillful means and penetrating the untainted realm—this wind-circle of great wisdom constitutes the four sons of the Buddhas.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess great loving-kindness that rescues and protects all sentient beings, and great compassion that delivers all sentient beings;
their great loving-kindness and great compassion universally bestow benefit, for this great loving-kindness and great compassion rely upon great skillful means.
Skillful in great skillful means, they rely on the appearance of the Tathāgata; the appearance of the Tathāgata relies on the light of unimpeded wisdom;
the light of unimpeded wisdom has no basis. O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth sign of the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: [the analogy follows].
Just as when the trichiliocosm has been fully formed, it brings benefit to immeasurable and diverse sentient beings—
namely, aquatic beings who find benefit in water, terrestrial beings who find benefit in land, beings in palaces who find benefit in palaces,
and beings in space who find benefit in space— so too does the appearance of a Tathāgata [bring benefit].
Furthermore, there are these various ways of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings: those who experience joy upon seeing the Buddha obtain the benefit of joy;

those who abide in pure precepts obtain the benefit of pure precepts; those who abide in the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) obtain the benefit of noble, supramundane, and great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
and those who abide in the light of the Dharma-gates obtain the benefit of the non-destruction of cause and effect. They abide...
Those who possess the light of non-existence attain the indestructible benefit of all dharmas; therefore it is said that the appearance of the Tathāgata benefits all immeasurable sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, this is the tenth mark of the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, son of the Buddha, should know it thus. Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
To know the appearance of the Tathāgata is to know immeasurable knowledge; because he accomplishes immeasurable practices, one knows his vast knowledge;

because it pervades the ten directions, one knows his knowledge is without coming or going; because he is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing, one knows his knowledge is without activity or object of action;
because he is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, one knows he is without body; because he is like empty space, one knows...
Knowing equality because one knows that all sentient beings are without self; knowing inexhaustibility because one knows it pervades all lands without end;
knowing non-retrogression because one knows it continues without interruption through the limits of the future;
knowing indestructibility because one knows the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no counterpart; and knowing non-duality because one knows that equal observation is itself non-existence.
Because of this, it is known that all sentient beings obtain benefit, for their original vows have been dedicated and fulfilled with mastery.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
The Great Hero endowed with the ten powers is most unsurpassed;
like space, his realm is peerless, vast, and immeasurable. His merit is foremost, transcending the world;
the merit of the one with ten powers is boundless, beyond the reach of thought or mental calculation.
The lion among men has but a single Dharma-gate, which sentient beings cannot know even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Even if the lands of the ten directions were ground into dust and someone could calculate their number, they would still be unable to describe,
even in thousands of millions of billions of eons, the measure of merit within a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata.
It is like a person holding a measuring rod to measure empty space, followed by another who calculates its dimensions;
yet the limits of empty space cannot be found. The realm of the Tathāgata is also like this:
there may be those who, in a single instant, fully know the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Even if one were to pass through eons as numerous as all sentient beings, one could not know the nature of a single thought-moment of the Buddha;
just as the Dharma-realm pervades all yet cannot be seen or grasped as "all," so too is the sphere of the Ten Powers: it pervades all, yet is not "all."
Suchness is free from delusion and eternally quiescent; Without birth and without cessation, it is universally pervasive.
The realm of all Buddhas is likewise so; Its essential nature is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
It is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet not a limit; It is present throughout the three periods of time, yet not universal.
The realm of the Teacher is likewise: pervasive throughout the three times, it is entirely unimpeded.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unconditioned and immutable, like space which is fundamentally pure.
The purity of the nature of all Buddhas is also thus; this original nature is neither a "nature" nor a "non-nature," transcending both existence and non-existence.
The nature of phenomena does not reside in verbal expression; it is beyond speech, free from discourse, and eternally quiescent.
The nature of the realm of the Ten Powers is likewise so.
One who can discern all literary expressions knows that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent, like a bird flying through the sky leaving no trace behind.
By the power of his original vows, he manifests a form-body, Causing all to behold the Tathāgata’s great spiritual transformations.
If there are those who wish to know the realm of the Buddha, They should purify their minds like space,
Remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all grasping, So that the mind may proceed everywhere without obstruction.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, listen well: I shall clarify the realm of the Buddha through a few similes.
The merit of the Ten Powers is immeasurable; for the sake of awakening sentient beings, I now briefly describe the spheres of the physical, vocal, and mental actions manifested by the Guide.
The turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma and the parinirvāṇa— I shall now describe all these roots of goodness through analogies.
Just as when the world is first established, It cannot be formed by a single cause or condition;
Through immeasurable powers and various causes and conditions, This trichiliocosm is brought into being.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise; Only through immeasurable merit is it accomplished.
While the thoughts of beings as numerous as motes of dust in a buddha-field might still be known, The cause for the arising of the Ten Powers cannot be fathomed.
It is like the clouds at the beginning of an eon pouring down rain, Which gives rise to the four kinds of great wind-circles.
Through the roots of goodness of sentient beings and the power of the Bodhisattvas, these three thousandfold worlds are each established in peace;

the Dharma-clouds of the Ten Powers are likewise so. Arising from the wind-wheel of wisdom and the pure mind, they universally guide all those sentient beings toward whom they have previously directed their aspirations, leading them to achieve the unsurpassed fruit.
Just as there is a great rain called the "Vast Downpour," Which no place can contain except at the time when the world is about to be formed; So too is the appearance of a Tathāgata:
With the power of the great wind in the pure void, he universally rains down the Dharma-rain, filling the entire Dharma-realm.
All those with inferior intentions are unable to uphold it; Only those with pure and vast minds can do so.
Just as when great rain pours down from the sky, It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
The agent and the recipient are likewise non-existent, Yet it naturally and universally saturates all.
The Dharma rain of the Ten Powers is likewise: Without going, without coming, and without fabrication;
With past conduct as its cause, it is the power of the Bodhisattvas. All those of great resolve listen and receive it;
Just as when empty clouds pour down a great rain, No one is able to count its drops.
Except for the Sovereign Kings of the Three Thousand Worlds,
who possess the power of merit and fully comprehend the Dharma-rain of the Sugata; even so, no sentient beings are able to fathom it,
except for those who are masters of the world, who perceive it clearly as if looking at a jewel in the palm of their hand.
Just as empty clouds pour down great rain, which can extinguish, arise, and sever all things,
and bring every precious treasure to completion; so too is the Dharma-rain of the Ten Powers,
which discerns all that exists within the three thousandfold world-system, extinguishing delusions, giving rise to goodness, and severing all views.
All the jewels of omniscience are brought to fulfillment; The mental inclinations of sentient beings are all discerned.
Just as rain of a single flavor falls from the sky, Yet according to what it rains upon, each is different— How could there be any distinction in the nature of that rain?
Rather, it differs according to the objects; such is the nature of phenomena.
The Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is neither one nor many; it is equal, tranquil, and free from discrimination.
Yet, according to the various differences among those to be converted, it naturally manifests such infinite forms.
Just as when the world is first formed, the palaces of the gods in the Form Realm are established first.
Next come the gods of the desire realm, then the human abodes; the palace of the gandharvas is the last to be formed.

The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise: first he initiates boundless bodhisattva practices, next he transforms the pratyekabuddhas who delight in tranquility, then the assembly of śrāvakas, and finally all sentient beings.
When the devas first beheld the auspicious omen of the lotus, they knew that a Buddha was about to be born;
with joyful water stirred by the power of the wind, the palaces, mountains, and rivers were all established.
Through the Tathāgata’s great radiance of past roots of goodness, he skillfully distinguished the bodhisattvas and bestowed upon them their predictions.
The essence of all wheels of wisdom is entirely pure, Each capable of revealing the teachings of all Buddhas.
Just as a forest exists depending upon the earth, And the earth remains unbroken by depending upon water;
The wheel of water depends upon wind, and wind depends upon space, Yet that empty space has no dependence whatsoever.
All Buddha-dharmas rely upon compassion; Compassion, in turn, is established upon skillful means.
Skillful means rely upon wisdom, and wisdom relies upon insight; The body of unimpeded wisdom has no dependence.
Just as once the world is fully established, All sentient beings obtain its benefit.
Those dwelling on earth or in water, and those who inhabit the sky—whether two-legged or four-legged—all receive benefit.
Such is the appearance of the Dharma King: all sentient beings obtain its advantage;
whoever sees, hears, or draws near to him shall have all their delusions and afflictions extinguished.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is a boundless Dharma, Which the deluded of the world are unable to know;
Desiring to awaken all sentient beings, He provides metaphors for that which is beyond metaphor.
[Commentary] The second section clarifies that the appearance of the Tathāgata possesses ten kinds of immeasurable bodies.
[Sūtra] "O Sons of the Buddha, how should Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas perceive the body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should perceive the body of the Tathāgata in immeasurable places. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not [perceive him] in terms of a single dharma, a single matter, a single body, a single land, or a single assembly."
O Sons of the Buddha, it is as if one were to see the Tathāgata appearing everywhere;
for example, just as space pervades all places—whether material or immaterial—yet neither arrives there nor fails to arrive. Why is this?
Because space has no body, the body of the Tathāgata is likewise pervasive in all places, pervasive among all sentient beings, and pervasive in all phenomena.
It pervades all lands, neither arriving nor not arriving. Why? Because the body of the Tathāgata is no-body;

yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests that body. Son of the Buddha, this is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, Son of the Buddha, it is like space: vast and expansive, non-material, and yet...
Just as space can manifest all forms yet remains without discrimination or conceptual proliferation,
so too is the body of the Tathāgata; because it universally illuminates with the light of wisdom,
it causes all mundane and supramundane roots of goodness and karmic deeds of all sentient beings to reach fulfillment, while the body of the Tathāgata itself remains without discrimination.
It is without conceptual proliferation. Why? Because from the very beginning, all attachments and all conceptual proliferations have been forever severed.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the second characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, immeasurable sentient beings all obtain [light].

Beneficiality refers to destroying darkness and creating light, transforming moisture into dryness, causing grasses and trees to grow, ripening grain crops, clearing the void, and causing lotus flowers to bloom.
For those who travel, it reveals the Path; for those who dwell, it enables their tasks. Why is this?
Because the solar disc universally radiates immeasurable light. Son of the Buddha, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise; with its immeasurable...

Their activities universally benefit all sentient beings: namely, extinguishing evil and generating goodness, breaking ignorance to produce wisdom, rescuing and protecting through great kindness, and delivering them through great compassion;
causing their faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment to increase; inspiring deep faith and causing them to abandon turbid minds;
enabling them to perceive the indestructibility of cause and effect; granting them the divine eye to see the places of death and rebirth; and ensuring their minds are free from obstruction.

It destroys the roots of goodness, causes wisdom to be cultivated and clarified, causes the flower of awakening to blossom, and causes those who have resolved their minds to fulfill their original practices.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s vast sun-body of great wisdom emits immeasurable light that shines everywhere.
Son of the Buddha, this is the third mark of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should view it in this way. Furthermore:

O Son of the Buddha, it is as if when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, it first illuminates all the great kings of mountains such as Sumeru, next it illuminates the Black Mountains, and then it illuminates the high plateaus; thereafter, it shines universally upon the entire earth.

The sun does not form the thought, "I shall first illuminate this and later illuminate that"; rather, because the mountains and lands have elevations and depressions, its illumination occurs in such a sequence.

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past and future are likewise endowed with the wheel of wisdom that encompasses the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), constantly emitting the unimpeded light of wisdom.
This light first illuminates the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and other great mountain-kings;

next, it illuminates the Pratyekabuddhas; then, it illuminates the Śrāvakas; and finally, it illuminates those sentient beings who possess determined roots of goodness, according to the capacity of their minds and faculties.

Having manifested vast wisdom, it then universally illumines all sentient beings, even those fixed in the wrong path, reaching them all to serve as the causal conditions for their future benefit and to bring them to maturity. Thus, the sun of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom does not form such a thought:
"I shall first illumine the great practices of Bodhisattvas, and only later illumine sentient beings fixed in the wrong path."
It merely emits light that shines equally and universally, without obstruction, hindrance, or discrimination.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the sun and moon, which appear according to the season and illuminate great mountains and deep valleys without partiality;
the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise, shining universally upon all things without discrimination, yet its wisdom accords with the differing faculties and desires of sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha, that the radiance has various differences—this is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body.
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising sun:
although beings born blind, because they lack the faculty of sight, have never seen it, even though they have not seen it, they are nonetheless benefited by the sunlight."
Therefore, from this we know that by utilizing various garments and food and drink according to the seasons of day and night, one keeps the body harmonious and free from all ailments;

likewise, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is also thus. Those who lack faith and understanding, who violate the precepts and hold wrong views, and who live by wrong livelihood—such as those born blind who lack the eye of faith—do not see the sun of the Buddhas’ wisdom.
Although the wheel itself is not seen, the sun-disk of the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise benefited by that sun of wisdom. Why is this?
Because through the Buddha’s majestic power, all physical suffering, as well as the afflictions and the causes of future suffering belonging to those sentient beings, are completely extinguished.
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata possesses a light named "Accumulation of All Meritorious Qualities," and there is a radiance...
There is a light named Universally Illuminating All Existence; a light named Pure Sovereign Illumination;
a light named Emanating Great Sublime Sounds; a light named Universally Understanding All Languages and Dharmas to Delight Others;
a light named Clearly Manifesting the Sovereign Realm that Permanently Severs All Doubt; and a light named Non-Abiding Wisdom.
There is a light named Sovereign Universal Illumination; a light named Sovereign Wisdom that Permanently Severs All Proliferation;
a light named Producing Wondrous Sounds According to What is Appropriate; and a light named Producing the Adornment of Pure Sovereign Sound to Mature Sentient Beings in Buddha-lands.
O Son of the Buddha, from each and every pore of the Tathāgata, thousands of such lights are emitted.

Five hundred rays of light universally illumined the lower directions, and five hundred rays of light universally illumined the upper directions, reaching the various assemblies of bodhisattvas at the abodes of various Buddhas within various lands.
When those bodhisattvas beheld these lights, they all simultaneously attained the realm of the Tathāgata: ten heads, ten eyes, ten ears, ten noses, ten tongues, ten bodies, and ten hands.

To the full extent that the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) are all completely purified, those bodhisattvas who have previously accomplished the various stages (*bhūmi*) and stations (*sthāna*) perceive that light becoming even more pure;
all their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) reach full maturity as they proceed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Those dwelling in the two vehicles (*dvyāyānika*) extinguish all defilements, while for a certain portion of sentient beings born blind, their bodies—once [the light reaches them]—[are likewise transformed].

With a joyful mind that is also pure, supple, tamed, and capable of cultivating mindfulness and wisdom, all sentient beings throughout the various realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals attain happiness and liberation from all sufferings; at the end of their lives, they are all reborn in the heavens or among humans.
O Son of the Buddha, those sentient beings do not perceive or know by what causes and conditions, or by what spiritual power, this occurs.
Having been born here, those who were blind from birth thought to themselves, "I am Brahmā; I am created by Brahmā.
At that time, the Tathāgata, dwelling in the Samādhi of Universal Sovereignty, emitted sixty kinds of wondrous sounds and addressed them, saying:
"You are not Brahmā, nor are you created by Brahmā, nor are you made by Śakra or the World-Protectors; all of you are [the products of]..."
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, when those sentient beings heard these words,
they all knew their past lives by the Buddha’s supernatural power and gave rise to a heart of great joy. Because of this joy, there spontaneously emerged clouds of *utpala* flowers,
clouds of incense, clouds of music, clouds of robes, clouds of canopies, clouds of banners, clouds of pennants, clouds of powdered incense, clouds of jewels, and half-lion standards.
Clouds of moon-pavilions, clouds of songs and hymns of praise, and clouds of various adornments all make offerings to the Tathāgata with a heart of reverence.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings have attained the pure eye; the Tathāgata bestows upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Son of the Buddha, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom benefits living beings in this way.
Causing blind sentient beings to attain the full maturation of roots of goodness—O Son of the Buddha, this is the fifth mark of the Tathāgata’s body;

all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, for example, the lunar disc possesses four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities. What are these four? First, it eclipses the light of all the stars.
The second is that it manifests waxing and waning in accordance with the passage of time. The third is that its reflection appears without exception within the clear waters of Jambudvīpa.
The fourth is that all who behold it perceive it as being directly before them, yet this lunar orb is devoid of discrimination and devoid of conceptual proliferation.
O Son of the Buddha, the moon of the Tathāgata’s body is likewise; it possesses four such wonders.

Furthermore, what are the four extraordinary qualities? They are as follows: first, although he eclipses all the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—both those in training and those beyond training—and manifests a lifespan that is long or short according to what is appropriate for them, the body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases;
yet, within the vessel of bodhi among all sentient beings in every world who possess a pure mind, his reflection does not fail to appear.
All sentient beings who behold [the Buddha] each think that the Tathāgata appears before them alone, preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations,
enabling them to attain liberation according to their respective stages, and manifesting a Buddha-body according to what is required for their transformation;
yet the body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation, and all the benefits he brings about reach ultimate fulfillment.
Sons of the Buddha, this is the sixth mark of the Tathāgata’s body; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way.

Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha, it is as if the Great Brahmā King of the trichiliocosm, by means of a slight expedient, were to universally manifest his body throughout the great trichiliocosm so that all sentient beings see the Brahmā King present before them.
Furthermore, this Brahma King does not divide his body, nor does he possess various bodies. Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgatas are likewise:
they are without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation; they do not divide their bodies, nor do they possess various bodies.
Yet, in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, they manifest their bodies, without forming the thought, "I shall manifest so many bodies. Sons of the Buddha!
This is the seventh mark of the Tathāgata’s body; all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way.

Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like a king of physicians who is well-versed in various medicines and incantations, such that there is no medicinal application in Jambudvīpa he does not fully master.
Moreover, by the power of his roots of goodness from past lives and the power of great vidyā-mantras, he provides prescriptions for them.
Because of this, there was no illness among those sentient beings who saw him that was not cured. Knowing that his life was about to end, that Great King of Physicians thought to himself:
"After my death, all sentient beings will have no one to rely upon. I should now manifest a skillful means.
At that time, the King of Physicians prepared medicine and anointed his body, sustaining it with the power of clear mantras so that after his death, his body would not decay.
It is neither scattered, nor withered, nor parched; its deportment, vision, and hearing are no different from before, and all those it treats are completely cured.
Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Physicians, is also like this:
having refined medicinal dharmas for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, he has attained accomplishment and mastered everything through cultivation and study.
Through the power of the great vidyā-mantra of skillful means, they have all reached the other shore;

they are well able to eliminate the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings and abide for immeasurable kalpas. Their bodies are pure, free from discursive thought and free from movement or activity;
yet their buddha-works never cease. When sentient beings behold them, the diseases of their various afflictions [are likewise extinguished].
All are completely extinguished, O Son of the Buddha; this is the eighth mark of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Combined Commentary*, Scroll 78.
Phonetic Transcriptions: Tàn (dǎng làn qiè) Guì (xī wěi qiè) Zào (xiān dào qiè) Kuò (kǔ guō qiè) Cǔn (cuò běn qiè) Hù (hù yīn) Wěi (yú zhuī qiè) Jǐ (qí jǐ qiè) Bèi (bó hǎi qiè) Zhǔ (zhī yù qiè)
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament, Scroll Seventy-Nine.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Fangshan, Taiyuan, during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, Collating the Sūtras and Commentaries, Chapter Thirty-Seven, Part Two: “The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
[Sūtra] Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were in the great ocean a great maṇi-jewel named “Gatherer of All Radiance.”
If there are sentient beings who touch the light of the Vairocana-treasury, they all become the same color as it;

if there are those who see it, their eyes attain purity. Wherever that light shines, it rains down maṇi jewels called "Peaceful Bliss," causing all sentient beings to be free from suffering and to become harmonious and well-adjusted. O Son of the Buddha, the bodies of all Tathāgatas are also like this.

This great treasury of jewels, the great storehouse of wisdom containing all merits, is such that if any sentient beings touch the jewel of the Buddha’s body and its light of wisdom, they will become identical in color to the Buddha’s body. Those who behold it will have their Dharma-eye purified.
Wherever this light shines, it causes all sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of poverty and, ultimately, to be fully endowed with the bliss of the Buddha’s bodhi.

Sons of the Buddha, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and free from conceptual proliferation, yet it is able to universally perform great Buddha-works for all sentient beings.
Sons of the Buddha, this is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way.
Furthermore, sons of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean, which contains the great *maṇi* jewel of sovereign power.

The king was named Sarvalokavyūhagarbhasampannaśatasahasraguṇasamanvāgata, who, wherever he resided, caused all calamities and afflictions of sentient beings to be eliminated and their aspirations to be fulfilled.
Yet, this sovereign wish-fulfilling jewel-king cannot be seen by sentient beings of meager merit; the Sovereign Wish-Fulfilling Jewel-King of the Tathāgata’s body is likewise so.

This is called that which causes all sentient beings to be entirely filled with joy; whether they behold his body, hear his name, or praise his virtues, it causes them all to forever leave behind the suffering and afflictions of birth and death.

Even if all sentient beings in all worlds were to simultaneously focus their minds on desiring to see the Tathāgata, he would cause them all to see him and fulfill all their aspirations. O Son of the Buddha, the Buddha-body is not...
This is visible only to sentient beings of meager merit, with the sole exception of those who are to be tamed by the sovereign spiritual power (*vaśitā-ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.
If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha’s body, plant roots of goodness and even reach maturity—for the sake of such maturation—he causes them to see the body of the Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, this is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body. All [characteristics] are thus.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should view it in this way: because that mind is immeasurable and pervades the ten directions;
because its activity is unimpeded like space; because it universally enters the dharma-realm; because it abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); because it is without arising or ceasing;
because it dwells equally throughout the three periods of time; and because it abides in vows that extend to the very end of existence.
Because they purify all worlds and adorn each and every Buddha-body, at that time the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
Just as empty space pervades the ten directions— Whether it be form or non-form, existence or non-existence,
the bodies of sentient beings or their lands throughout the three periods of time—
So too does the true body of all Buddhas universally exist without limit; There is nowhere in the entire dharma-realm that it does not pervade.
Invisible and ungraspable, yet manifesting forms to transform sentient beings;
Like space, which cannot be grasped, they cause all beings to perform various deeds, Without thinking, "What am I doing now? or "Why do I act? For whom do I act?"
The physical actions of all Buddhas are likewise: they cause all living beings everywhere to cultivate wholesome dharmas, yet the Tathāgata never makes any discrimination.
Regarding my various deeds here now, it is like the rising of the sun over Jambudvīpa; its radiance destroys all darkness without exception.
As the mountains, trees, ponds, lotuses, and all things upon the earth—every variety of being—receive benefit, so too does the sun of the Buddhas rise:
it causes the wholesome deeds of beings in the realms of humans and devas to grow;
it forever dispels the darkness of ignorance to attain the light of wisdom, and one constantly experiences honor, dignity, and every happiness.

Just as when the sun’s light appears, it first illuminates the King of Mountains, then the other mountains, and finally the high plateaus and the great earth, yet the sun never engages in discrimination;
so too is the radiance of the Sugata: it first illuminates the Bodhisattvas, then the Pratyekabuddhas.
Later, he illuminates the śrāvakas and sentient beings, yet the Buddha is fundamentally free from any movement of thought.
Just as one born blind does not see the sun, the sunlight nonetheless benefits them by enabling them to know the seasons and partake of food and drink,
forever freeing them from various afflictions so that their bodies are at peace.
Sentient beings lacking faith do not see the Buddha, yet the Buddha still brings about their benefit and welfare;
by hearing his name or being touched by his light, they may thereby attain even Bodhi.
Just as the pure moon in the void can outshine the multitude of stars and manifest its waxing and waning.
In all waters his reflection appears; To all who gaze upon him, he stands before them.
The Tathāgata, like a pure moon, is likewise so: He can obscure other vehicles and manifest both long and short.
Appearing universally in the water of the pure minds of devas and humans, All believe that he stands right before them.

Just as the Brahmā King, dwelling in his own palace, Universally manifests in all the Brahmā realms of the trichiliocosm, And all humans and devas are able to see him, Yet he does not actually divide his body to go there;
The manifestation of the Buddhas’ bodies is likewise: There is nowhere throughout the ten directions that they do not pervade.
His body is infinite and beyond measure; it neither divides itself nor makes distinctions.
Like a king of physicians skilled in medical arts, whoever beholds him is healed of all illness.
Even if their life has already come to an end, by applying medicine to their bodies, he causes them to perform all tasks just as before.

The Supreme King of Physicians is likewise so: Endowed with skillful means and omniscience, Through his past sublime conduct, he manifests the Buddha-body; Sentient beings who behold him find their afflictions extinguished.
It is like a sovereign jewel within the ocean, Which universally radiates immeasurable rays of light.
Sentient beings who touch it become the same color as it; likewise, those who see it have their eyes purified.

This Sovereign of Supreme Jewels is also thus: those who touch its light all become the same color, and those who obtain the sight of it have their five eyes opened, destroying the darkness of all defilements and abiding on the stage of a Buddha.
Just as the wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel satisfies every request that arises,
yet beings with little merit cannot see it— for the king of jewels possesses no discrimination—
so too is the Sugata, the king of jewels; he completely fulfills all desired pleasures and aspirations.
Sentient beings lacking faith do not see the Buddha; it is not that the Sugata has abandoned them in his mind.
[Treatise] Third, it clarifies that when the Tathāgata appears, there are ten immeasurable sounds.
[Sūtra] "O Sons of the Buddha, how should Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas understand the voice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know that the voice of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere, because it pervades all immeasurable sounds.
They should know that the voice of the Tathāgata brings joy to all according to their mental inclinations, for it clarifies the teaching of the Dharma."
Because it is fully understood, one should know that the Tathāgata’s voice causes all beings to rejoice according to their faith and understanding, and brings their minds to a state of cool clarity;

therefore, one should know the Tathāgata’s voice. Because its transformation does not miss the proper time, and there is no one who hears what they ought to hear, one should know the Tathāgata’s voice.
Because it is without arising or ceasing, like an echo, one should know the Tathāgata’s voice. Because it has no master, one should know the Tathāgata’s voice.
One should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is profound because it arises from the cultivation of all karmas;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is difficult to measure because it is produced from the dharmadhātu, which is free from crookedness;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is uninterrupted because it universally enters the dharmadhātu; one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is unchanging until...

Because it is ultimate, O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is neither measurable nor immeasurable, neither having a master nor lacking a master, and neither indicative nor non-indicative. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha, for example, when the world is about to be destroyed, sounds emerge spontaneously without a master or a creator; what are these four kinds of sounds?
First: "You should know that the bliss of the first dhyāna is free from all desires and evils, transcending the sentient beings of the desire realm;
having heard this, they naturally attain the accomplishment of the first dhyāna, cast off their bodies of the desire realm, and are reborn in the Brahma Heaven. Second:
"You should know that the bliss of the second dhyāna is without vitarka and vicāra, transcending the sentient beings of the Brahma Heaven; having heard this,"
Spontaneously attaining the accomplishment of the second dhyāna, they relinquish their bodies as Brahmā gods and are born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Third:

"You all should know that the bliss of the second dhyāna is free from fault; surpassing the beings of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, upon hearing this, they spontaneously attain the accomplishment of the third dhyāna, relinquish their bodies as Ābhāsvara gods, and are born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. Fourth: "You all should know..."

Upon hearing that the fourth dhyāna is tranquil and transcends the beings of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, they spontaneously achieve the fourth dhyāna, relinquish their bodies in the Śubhakṛtsna realm, and are born in the Bṛhatphala Heaven. These are the four sons of the Buddha. These various sounds have no master and no creator;
they arise solely from the power of the various wholesome karmas of sentient beings. Sons of the Buddha, the voice of the Tathāgata is likewise.

Furthermore, being thus without owner, without agent, and without conceptual differentiation—neither entering nor exiting—it issues forth from the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom these four kinds of vast sounds. What are the four? First:
"You should all know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely suffering; namely, the suffering of hell-beings, the suffering of animals, and the suffering of hungry ghosts."
The suffering of lacking merit; the suffering of attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self"; the suffering of performing various unwholesome deeds;

and the suffering of desiring rebirth among humans or devas—[thinking] one should plant roots of goodness to be born among humans or devas and leave behind places of adversity—when sentient beings hear this, they abandon their perversions, cultivate various wholesome practices, leave behind places of adversity, and are born among humans or devas. Second: "You should all know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)..."
All sufferings burn fiercely like glowing iron balls; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to decay.
Nirvāṇa is tranquil, unconditioned, and blissful, far removed from this burning and extinguishing all feverish afflictions.

Upon hearing this, sentient beings diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and attain the "patience that accords with the sound" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) within the Śrāvaka vehicle. Third, you should know that as for the Śrāvaka vehicle:
"Those whose wisdom is narrow and inferior due to relying on the words of others have another superior vehicle called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, which is realized without a teacher;
you should study this. Those who delight in the superior path, having heard these sounds, shall abandon the Śrāvaka path and cultivate the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
Fourth: You should know that beyond the stage of the two vehicles, there is a further superior path called the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva [Vehicle]."
Its practice accords with the six *pāramitās*, it does not interrupt the bodhisattva conduct, and it does not abandon the bodhicitta.

Abiding amidst immeasurable births and deaths without weariness, it surpasses the two vehicles and is called the Great Vehicle, the foremost vehicle, the superior vehicle, the most excellent vehicle, the highest vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle, and the vehicle that benefits all sentient beings. If there are sentient beings who have faith and understanding...

Those with vast and sharp faculties who have planted roots of goodness in the past, who are empowered by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, and who possess superior aspiration and a longing for the fruit of Buddhahood—having heard this sound, they resolve upon bodhicitta.

O Son of the Buddha, the voice of the Tathāgata does not issue from the body, nor does it issue from the mind, yet it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, this is [the power of the Buddha’s voice].
The Tathāgata’s voice possesses the foremost mark; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like an echo, which arises due to mountains, valleys, and sounds;
it has no form and cannot be seen, nor does it possess discrimination, yet it can follow all speech. The Tathāgata’s voice is likewise.
This has no form and cannot be seen; it has no location, yet it is not without location.
It appears only in accordance with the inclinations and understandings of sentient beings. Its nature is ultimately beyond words, beyond demonstration, and cannot be proclaimed.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the second characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way. Furthermore:
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great Dharma drum of the devas called "Awakening.
When the sons of the gods act with negligence, a voice issues from the void, proclaiming: "You should all know that all sensual pleasures are impermanent, false, and inverted;
they perish in an instant and merely deceive the foolish, causing them to become attached. Do not [be negligent]!"
If one is heedless or acts with heedlessness, one will fall into the various evil realms, and later regret will be of no avail.

When the gods who were heedless heard this sound, they gave rise to great anxiety and fear; abandoning all sensual pleasures within their own palaces, they went to the place of the Heavenly King to seek the Dharma and practice the Path.
O Son of the Buddha, that sound of the celestial drum has no master, no creator, no arising, and no ceasing, yet it is able to benefit [beings].
O infinite sentient beings, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise; desiring to awaken those who are heedless, he produces immeasurable sounds of wondrous Dharma, namely:

the sound of non-attachment, the sound of non-heedlessness, the sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, the sound of non-self, the sound of impurity, the sound of cessation, the sound of nirvāṇa, and the sound of immeasurable spontaneous wisdom.
The sound that cannot be destroyed is the bodhisattva practice; the sound that reaches all places is the stage of the Tathāgata’s effortless wisdom.
By means of this sound, he awakens beings throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Having heard this sound, countless sentient beings all give rise to joy and diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas, each seeking liberation through their own respective vehicle—namely, some practicing...

Whether they practice the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or cultivate the unsurpassed Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the voice of the Tathāgata does not abide in any location and is beyond verbal expression.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the third characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice;
all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it thus. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the Sovereign King of the Gods (Śakra) possesses—
There is a celestial maiden named Sukhavaktra (Excellent Mouth). From within her mouth, she utters a single sound, and that sound is in harmony with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music.
Within each of these musical instruments, there are again hundreds of thousands of distinct tones.
O Son of the Buddha, you should know that from this single voice from the mouth of that maiden Sukhavaktra, such immeasurable sounds as these are produced. Thus it is.

Coming forth is likewise so: from within a single sound, immeasurable voices are produced, which reach all places according to the differences in the mental inclinations of sentient beings, causing them all to attain understanding. O Son of the Buddha, this is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice;
all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know it thus. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Great Brahmā King.
Abiding in the Brahma palace, he utters the voice of Brahmā; there is not one among the entire assembly of Brahmās who does not hear it, yet that sound does not go beyond the assembly.
All the Brahmā deities conceive this thought: "The Great Brahmā King is speaking to me alone.
The sublime voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: the entire assembly at the site of enlightenment hears it, yet its sound [does not go beyond].
It does not issue from outside the assembly. Why? Because those whose faculties are not yet mature should not hear it. Those who hear this sound all think:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks to me alone. O Son of the Buddha, the voice of the Tathāgata neither issues forth nor abides, yet it is able to accomplish all tasks.
This is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice. All Bodhisattvas...

O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, you should understand it in this way: Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like various waters which are all of one single taste, yet appear different according to the vessels they enter; these waters have no thoughts and no discrimination.
The speech and sounds of the Tathāgata are likewise of only one taste—namely, the taste of liberation—and appear different according to the diverse mental vessels of sentient beings.
Though there are immeasurable distinctions, it is without thought or deliberation, and likewise without conceptual discrimination.
Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know it thus.
Furthermore, Son of the Buddha, it is like the dragon king Anavatapta, who raises great dense clouds that pervade Jambudvīpa and universally pours down sweet rain upon the hundred grains.
The crops all grow and flourish, and all rivers, streams, springs, and ponds become completely full.

These great rains do not issue from the body or mind of the Dragon King, yet they are able to provide manifold benefits to sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is also like this:
he raises the cloud of great compassion throughout the realms of the ten directions and universally rains down the unsurpassed nectar of immortality.
The rain of Dharma causes all sentient beings to give rise to joy, increases their wholesome dharmas, and brings fulfillment to all vehicles.
O Sons of the Buddha, the voice of the Tathāgata does not come from without nor does it emerge from within, yet it is able to benefit all sentient beings;
this is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Dragon King Manasvin, who when he intends to send down rain, does not do so immediately;
first, he raises a great cloud that covers the void and remains suspended for seven days, waiting until all sentient beings have finished their labors. Why is this?
Because that Great Dragon King possesses a heart of compassion and does not wish to disturb or trouble sentient beings. After the seven days...
Just as the sun first sends down a fine, subtle rain that universally moistens the great earth, so too is it with the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
When he is about to send down the rain of Dharma, he does not do so immediately; first, he raises the clouds of Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Desiring to ensure that their minds are free from alarm and fear, he waits until they have matured, and only then does he universally pour down the nectar-like rain of Dharma and proclaim it.
"O Son of the Buddha, the profound, subtle, and excellent Dharma gradually brings them to fulfillment in the unsurpassed flavor of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes;
this is the eighth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if in the ocean there were a great nāga king named Mahāvyūha."
When it rains upon the great ocean, it may rain ten kinds of adorned showers, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand kinds of adorned showers.

O Son of the Buddha, the water itself makes no distinction; it is solely through the inconceivable power of the Dragon King that these adornments are produced, ranging from hundreds to thousands of immeasurable varieties. The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are likewise so.
When preaching the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, he may do so using ten distinct types of sounds,
or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or eighty-four thousand sounds; he may even use eighty-four thousand modes of practice,
or up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sounds, each speaking the Dharma individually so that they may hear it.
All of them give rise to joy through the Tathāgata’s voice, which is without discrimination.

Yet, because all Buddhas are perfectly pure within the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they are able to produce various sounds according to what is appropriate for the faculties of sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, [shared by] all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

It should be understood in this way. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the Dragon King Sāgara, wishing to manifest the sovereign power of a great dragon king to benefit sentient beings and cause them all to rejoice, raises a vast web of clouds from the four continents up to the realm of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, completely covering everything;
the colors and forms of these clouds are of infinite variety. Or...
The color of Jāmbūnada gold light, or the color of Vaiḍūrya light, or the color of white silver light, or the color of sapphire light,
or the color of musāragalva light, or the color of agate light, or the color of supreme treasury light,
or the color of red pearl light, or the color of immeasurable fragrance light, or...

The radiance of stainless garments, the radiance of pure water, or the radiance of various ornaments—such clouds and nets spread everywhere in all directions. Having thus spread, they emit lightning of various colors:
namely, from clouds of Jāmbūnada gold, lightning of vaidūrya color issues forth; from clouds of vaidūrya color, lightning of gold color issues forth.
From clouds the color of silver lightning, lightning the color of beryl emerges; from clouds the color of beryl, lightning the color of silver emerges;
from clouds the color of musāragalva, lightning the color of agate emerges; from clouds the color of agate, lightning the color of musāragalva emerges;
from clouds the color of the *jaya-kośa* jewel, lightning the color of red pearls emerges; from clouds the color of red pearls...
From it issued clouds of the color of lightning-light from the jewel-treasury of supreme excellence;

clouds of the color of stainless garments issued from lightning-light of the color of immeasurable fragrances; clouds of the color of stainless garments issued from lightning-light of the color of pure water;
clouds of the color of various ornaments issued from lightning-light of the color of various ornaments; and lightning-light of the color of pure water issued forth.
From clouds of various colors, flashes of lightning of a single color emerged; from clouds of a single color, flashes of lightning of various colors emerged.

Furthermore, from within those clouds, various sounds of thunder issued forth, causing all sentient beings to rejoice according to their own minds—sounds such as the singing of celestial maidens, the music of the devas, or the singing of nāga maidens.
Some were like the singing voices of gandharva maidens, some like the singing voices of kinnara maidens, some like the sound of the great earth quaking,
some like the sound of ocean waves and tides, some like the roar of the king of beasts,
and some like the warbling of beautiful birds; having produced these and other immeasurable varieties of sounds like thunder, they then arose once more.

A cool breeze causes the hearts of all sentient beings to feel joy, after which various rains descend to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable beings, from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations down to the earth. The rain that falls in each place is different;
specifically, in the great ocean, clear, cool water falls, known as "Uninterrupted," while in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations...
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there falls rain consisting of various musical instruments such as flutes and pipes, called "Exquisite";
in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), there falls rain of great maṇi jewels, called "Emitting Great Radiance";
in the Tuṣita Heaven, there falls rain of great ornaments, called "Hanging Topknots"; and in the Yāma Heaven, there falls rain of great, wondrous flowers, called "Various Ornaments."
A rain of various wonderful fragrances named "Delightful" falls upon the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
a rain of celestial jewel-garments named "Covering" falls upon the palaces of the Dragon Kings; a rain of red pearls named "Emerging Radiance" falls upon the palaces of the Asuras;
and a rain of various flowers named "Opening" falls upon Uttarakuru in the north.
The distribution throughout the remaining three continents is likewise entirely so; yet, according to their respective locations, the rain that falls differs.
Although that Dragon King’s mind is impartial and free from distinctions between self and other, the rain varies because of the differences in the roots of goodness of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, is also like this, wishing to...

To teach and transform sentient beings through the True Dharma, one first spreads clouds of the body that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting in various ways according to their inclinations and desires.
That is to say: for some sentient beings, one manifests clouds of birth-bodies;
for some, clouds of transformation-bodies; for some, clouds of bodies sustained by power; for some, clouds of form-bodies; or for others...
He manifests clouds of bodies endowed with the primary and secondary marks; or for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests clouds of bodies of merit;
or for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests clouds of bodies of wisdom; or for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests clouds of indestructible bodies of the powers;

or for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests clouds of fearless bodies; or for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests clouds of bodies of the dharma-realm. O Son of the Buddha, by means of suchness, the Tathāgata...
These immeasurable clouds of light universally cover all worlds throughout the ten directions,
manifesting various kinds of radiant lightning according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings; that is to say,
for some beings they manifest radiant lightning named "Reaching Everywhere," and for other beings they manifest radiant lightning named "Boundless Light."
For some sentient beings, he manifests a lightning-flash of light called "Entering the Secret Dharma of the Buddha";

for some sentient beings, he manifests a lightning-flash of light called "Manifestation of Reflected Light"; for some sentient beings, he manifests a lightning-flash of light called "Radiance of Illumination";
and for some sentient beings, he manifests a lightning-flash of light called "Entering the Inexhaustible Dharani Gate."
For some sentient beings, he manifests a ray of light named "Right Mindfulness Without Distraction";

for some sentient beings, he manifests a ray of light named "Ultimate Indestructibility"; for some sentient beings, he manifests a ray of light named "Entering Accordantly with All Realms of Existence";
and for some sentient beings, he manifests a ray of light named "Fulfilling All Wishes," causing them all to rejoice.
O Son of the Buddha, after the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has manifested such immeasurable flashes of lightening,
he further produces immeasurable thunderous sounds of samādhi according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings— namely,
the thunderous sound of the samādhi of "Skillfully Awakened Wisdom," the thunderous sound of the samādhi of "Vast and Stainless Ocean," and the samādhi of "Mastery over All Dharmas."
The Samādhi of the Thunderous Vajra Wheel, the Samādhi of the Thunderous Sumeru Banner, the Samādhi of the Thunderous Ocean Seal, the Samādhi of the Thunderous Sun Lamp,
the Samādhi of the Thunderous Inexhaustible Treasury, and the Samādhi of the Thunderous Indestructible Power of Liberation—
these and other such immeasurable varieties emerge from the cloud-like bodies of the Buddha-sons, the Tathāgatas.
The thunderous sound of samādhi is about to descend as the rain of Dharma; first, it manifests auspicious signs to awaken sentient beings.

That is to say, from the unobstructed mind of great compassion, there appears the Great Wisdom Wind-wheel of the Tathāgata, which is named "Able to Cause All Sentient Beings to Give Rise to Inconceivable Joy and Delight. Once this sign has appeared, all bodhisattvas and all...

Once the bodies and minds of all sentient beings have attained refreshing coolness, they are then rained upon by the great cloud of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, the great cloud of great compassion, and the great inconceivable cloud with an inconceivable rain of the vast Dharma, causing the bodies and minds of all sentient beings to become pure.
This is what is called raining down the great Dharma-rain for Bodhisattvas seated at the site of enlightenment; it is named the "Dharma."
For Bodhisattvas in their final body, who are without distinction of realm, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called "The Play of Bodhisattvas:
The Secret Teaching of the Tathāgata. For Bodhisattvas bound to one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), he rains down a great rain of Dharma called "Pure Universal Radiance.
For Bodhisattvas who have received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he rains down a great rain of Dharma called "Adorned with the Ornamentations of the Tathāgata."

For Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages of patience (*kṣānti*), they rain down the great Dharma rain called "The Blooming Wisdom Flower of the Jewel of Merit," practicing the Bodhisattva conduct of great compassion without interruption.

For Bodhisattvas who dwell in and aspire toward the stages, they rain down the great Dharma rain called "Entering the Profound Gate of Manifesting Transformations," practicing the Bodhisattva conduct without rest or weariness.
For Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds on enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*), [the rain is likewise bestowed].
He rains down a great rain of Dharma called "The Arising of the Tathāgata’s Practice of Great Compassion to Rescue and Protect Sentient Beings" for those seeking the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

He rains down a great rain of Dharma called "Deeply Understanding the Law of Dependent Origination to Attain the Fruit of Indestructible Liberation by Remaining Far Removed from the Two Extremes" for those seeking the Śrāvaka Vehicle. He rains down a great rain of Dharma called "By Means of Great Wisdom."
The sword that severs all enemies of affliction rains down the great Dharma rain for sentient beings— both those whose roots of goodness are accumulated and those who are not yet determined—
named "Able to Accomplish Various Dharma Gates," giving rise to great joy. O Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgatas,
following the minds of sentient beings, rain down such vast Dharma rains as these, filling all infinite realms.
"O Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses a mind that is impartial and is without stinginess regarding the Dharma;
yet, because the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings differ, the rain of Dharma he showers forth appears to have distinctions.
This is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way. Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha, you should know as follows:"
There are ten kinds of immeasurable sounds. What are these ten? They are as follows: they are immeasurable like the realm of empty space because they reach all places;
they are immeasurable like the dharma-realm because there is nowhere they do not pervade;

they are immeasurable like the realm of sentient beings because they cause all minds to rejoice; they are immeasurable like all karmas because they explain their retributions; they are [immeasurable] like afflictions...
Because they cause all that is immeasurable to be completely extinguished; because they enable beings to hear according to their own immeasurable speech and sounds through understanding;
because they universally observe and deliver immeasurable beings according to their desires and inclinations; because they are as immeasurable as the three periods of time and have no boundaries;
because they are as immeasurable as wisdom in discerning all things; and because they are as immeasurable as the Buddha-realm in entering the Buddha-dharma.
"O Son of the Buddha, you should know that the voice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
is endowed with such incalculable and immeasurable qualities as these for all Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
When the trichiliocosm is about to be destroyed, the power of the merit of sentient beings causes a voice to proclaim:
"The fourth dhyāna is tranquil and free from all suffering. Having heard this, they all become detached from desire.
In the same way, the World-Honored One of Ten Powers emits a sublime sound that pervades the entire dharma-realm.
For them, he preaches that all conditioned phenomena are suffering and impermanent, enabling them to forever cross the ocean of birth and death.
Just as within the deep mountains and vast valleys, every sound is echoed back;
though the echo can follow the words of others, it ultimately possesses no discrimination.
The speech and sound of the One Possessing Ten Powers are likewise thus;
according to the ripening of their faculties, he manifests for them so that they may be tamed and filled with joy.
He does not think, "I am now able to expound this," just as there is a celestial drum named "Awakening" that constantly resounds with the sound of the Dharma in the sky.
He admonishes those heedless devaputras, causing them to hear and thereby become free from attachment;
the Dharma drum of the One of Ten Powers is likewise, emitting various wondrous sounds that awaken all living beings, causing them all to realize the fruit of Bodhi.
The Sovereign Heavenly King has a precious lady who skillfully plays all manner of music from her mouth;

from a single sound she can produce hundreds of thousands of tones, and within each of those sounds there are likewise hundreds of thousands of voices of the Sugatas. From a single sound, she produces every sound.
According to their differing dispositions and desires, each is made to hear [the teaching] so that they sever their afflictions.
Just as when the Brahmā King utters a single sound, he is able to cause all the Brahmā hosts to rejoice;
yet the sound reaches only the Brahmās and does not go outside, and each one says, "I alone have heard it."
The Brahma King of Ten Powers is likewise; though he utters but a single sound, it fills the entire Dharma-realm.
It reaches the assembled multitude without traveling far, yet because they lack faith, they are unable to receive it.
Just as all waters share the same nature, their eight meritorious qualities and flavors are without distinction.
As the ground and the vessel differ for each, they are thus made various and distinct;

the voice of the Omniscient is likewise so: the nature of phenomena is of a single flavor and without discrimination, yet according to the differing conduct of sentient beings, it causes what is heard to be various and distinct.
Just as the great Nāga King Anavatapta Pours down rain that universally moistens Jambudvīpa,
Causing all grasses and trees to grow, Yet without it issuing from his body or mind—
So too is the wondrous voice of the Buddhas: It rains everywhere throughout the Dharma-realm, filling it completely.
It can cause the arising of goodness and the extinction of all evils; it cannot be obtained from either within or without.

It is like the Dragon King Manasvin, who raises clouds for seven days without first raining, waiting until all sentient beings have finished their labors, and only then lets fall the rain to bring about benefit.

The exposition of the Ten Powers is likewise: first transforming sentient beings to bring them to maturity, and only then preaching the profound Dharma, so that those who hear it shall not be struck with fear.
Like a great dragon in the ocean, he pours down the ten kinds of rain of adornment.
Whether they be a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand kinds, though water is of a single taste, its manifestations are distinct;

ultimate eloquence is likewise so. Whether one expounds ten, twenty, or various dharma-gates—be they a hundred, a thousand, or even immeasurable—one does not give rise to the thought that there are any differences between them.
The most supreme Dragon King Sāgara raises clouds that universally cover the four continents;
though it rains differently in every place, the dragon’s mind harbors no dual thoughts.
So too is the Buddha, the Dharma King: the cloud-body of his great compassion pervades the ten directions.
For all those practicing the path, the rains are each different, yet toward all things there is no discrimination.
[Treatise] Fourth: It is explained that when the Tathāgata appears, he possesses ten immeasurable minds.
[Sūtra] "O Sons of the Buddha, how should the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Sons of the Buddha, the mind, intellect, and consciousness of the Tathāgata are all unapprehendable; one should know the mind of the Tathāgata only by means of its immeasurable wisdom.
Just as space is the support for all things, yet space itself has no support, so it is with the Tathāgata."
Wisdom is likewise so: it serves as the basis for all mundane and supramundane wisdoms, yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata has no basis.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the dharma-realm, which constantly gives rise to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The liberation of the Bodhisattva is such that the Dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases;
the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise, constantly producing all manner of mundane and supramundane wisdoms, yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
Son of the Buddha, this is the second characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way. Furthermore—
O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean whose waters flow secretly through the lands of the four continents and the eighty billion minor islands;
there is no one who digs a well who does not obtain water, yet that great ocean makes no discrimination, thinking, "I am producing this water.
The ocean-water of the Buddha's wisdom is likewise: it flows into the hearts of all sentient beings, and if...
When sentient beings observe their objects and cultivate the Dharma-gates, they attain wisdom that is pure, clear, and lucid;
yet the Tathāgata’s wisdom is equal, non-dual, and without discrimination. It is only because the mental activities of sentient beings differ that the wisdom they obtain varies from one to another.
Son of the Buddha, this is the third characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind. All Bodhisattva-mahasattvas...

Bodhisattvas should understand it in this way. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean, which possesses four precious jewels endowed with immeasurable virtues that are able to produce all the treasures within the sea.
If these jewels were not present in the great ocean, not even a single treasure could be found. What are these four? First is the Jewel of Accumulation; second is the Inexhaustible Treasury.
The third is named Far-Removed-from-Blazing, and the fourth is named Endowed-with-Adornments;
these four precious jewels are not seen by any ordinary beings, nāgas, or devas. Why is this?

Because the Nāga King Sāgara places these precious jewels, which are magnificent and perfectly symmetrical, in a deep and secret location within his palace. O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha...
The ocean of great wisdom of the Awakened One is likewise thus; within it there are four great jewels of wisdom that are fully endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom.

Because of these, one is able to produce the jewels of wisdom for all sentient beings, for those in the stages of training and no-more-training among śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and for all bodhisattvas.
What are the four? They are: non-attachment, skillful means, [the power of vows, and] the power of great compassion.
The great wisdom-jewel that skillfully discriminates between conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;

the great wisdom-jewel that distinguishes and explains immeasurable teachings without violating the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); the great wisdom-jewel that knows the timely and the untimely without ever erring;
and the great wisdom-jewel [of the Tathāgatas]. If within the ocean of the great wisdom of all Tathāgatas these four jewels were absent, there would not be even a single sentient being.
It is impossible for one who has entered the Mahāyāna not to attain these four jewels of wisdom. Why?
Because these four jewels of wisdom are placed within the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
they are impartial, upright, pure, and exquisite, universally benefiting the assembly of all bodhisattvas so that they may all obtain the radiance of wisdom. O Buddha!
Sons of the Buddha, this is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, sons of the Buddha, it is as if there were four great jewels of blazing radiance spread across the floor of the great ocean;
their nature is extremely fierce and hot, and they are constantly able to drink up and contract the immeasurable waters poured into it by the hundred rivers. Therefore, the great ocean does not...

There are four [jewels] that increase and decrease. What are the four? First is named Sūryagarbha (Sun-Treasury); second is named Ardratā-vigata (Free from Moisture); third is named Jvālārcis (Flame-Light);

and fourth is named Aśeṣa-kṣaya (Exhaustion Without Remainder). Son of the Buddha, if these four jewels were not in the great ocean, everything from the four continents up to the Peak of Existence would all be submerged and swept away. Son of the Buddha, this great jewel Sūryagarbha emits light.
When the light touches the seawater, it all transforms into milk; when the light of the Great Jewel of Separation from Moisture touches that milk, it all transforms into curd;
