when the light of the Great Jewel of Flame-Brightness touches that curd, it all transforms into clarified butter (*ghṛta*) without exception;
and when the light of the Great Jewel touches that clarified butter, it transforms into the finest cream (*sarpis*), blazing like fire until it is entirely consumed without remainder.

Sons of the Buddha, the great ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise endowed with four kinds of great jewels of wisdom that possess immeasurable majesty, virtue, and radiance.
When the light of these wisdom-jewels touches the bodhisattvas, it causes them to attain even the great wisdom of a Tathāgata.
What are these four? They are: the extinguishing of all waves of distracted wholesome states; [the remaining three are omitted in the source fragment].
The jewel of great wisdom that eliminates all attachment to phenomena; the jewel of great wisdom whose light of insight shines universally;
the jewel of great wisdom equal to the Tathāgata, which is boundless and effortless;

O Sons of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattvas cultivate all the factors conducive to enlightenment, they give rise to immeasurable waves of miscellaneous wholesome roots, [surpassing] all the gods of the world.
That which neither humans nor asuras can destroy, the Tathāgata— by means of the light of the great wisdom-jewel that extinguishes all waves of distracted goodness—
touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to abandon all waves of distracted goodness and to maintain one-pointedness of mind,
abiding in samādhi; furthermore, by means of the light of the great wisdom-jewel that removes all craving for dharmas, he touches those bodhisattvas.
Sāgaramegha caused them to abandon their attachment to the flavor of samādhi and gave rise to vast supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Furthermore, with the light of wisdom that universally illuminates the jewel-light of great wisdom, he touched those bodhisattvas, causing them to abandon the vast supernormal powers they had produced and to abide in the practice of the function of great luminosity.
This was by means of the boundless, effortless jewel-light of great wisdom that is equal to the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s contact with great light causes those Bodhisattvas to relinquish the practice of the great luminous effort that has arisen, until they attain the Tathāgata’s stage of equality and bring all effort to rest without remainder.

Sons of the Buddha, if there were not this great illumination and contact from these four jewels of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it would be impossible for even a single Bodhisattva to attain the stage of a Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha! It is not possible.
Sons of the Buddha, this is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha, just as everything from the surface of the water up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception—
including all the great trichiliocosms therein and the abodes of sentient beings in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness— none of them arise without depending upon space.
Why does it abide in emptiness? Because empty space is all-pervasive. Although that empty space universally contains the three realms, it is without discrimination.

Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is also like this: whether it be the wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, the wisdom of conditioned practices, or the wisdom of unconditioned practices—all of these rely upon suchness.
The arising of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the abiding of the Tathāgata’s wisdom: why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom pervades all things.
Although it universally encompasses immeasurable wisdom, it is free from discrimination. Son of the Buddha, this is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind;
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it thus. Furthermore, son of the Buddha, on the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a medicinal herb.

The king of trees is named "Inexhaustible Root. That medicinal tree’s root grows from one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas below, reaching down to the adamantine ground and the limit of the water-circle.
When that king of medicinal trees produces its roots, it causes all the roots of every tree in Jambudvīpa to grow;
when it produces its trunk, it causes all the trunks of every tree in Jambudvīpa to grow; and likewise for its branches, leaves, and flowers.
The fruits are all likewise so; this medicinal king-tree’s root can produce the trunk, and the trunk can produce the root, yet the root has no end, and is thus called the "Inexhaustible Root.
O Son of the Buddha, that medicinal king-tree causes growth in all places, yet it cannot provide the benefit of growth in two locations: namely, the deep pits of hell and the water-circle.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, just as that tree is never weary of or indifferent toward them from the very beginning,
so too is the Great Medicine King Tree of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom; with its roots consisting of vast compassionate vows—

vows made in the past to accomplish all wholesome dharmas of wisdom and to universally cover all realms of sentient beings while eliminating the sufferings of all evil destinies— it likewise flourishes.
Born from the lineage of the true wisdom of all Tathāgatas, it has skillful means as its sturdy and immovable trunk;
the various *pāramitās* of wisdom that pervade the *dharmadhātu* as its branches;
meditative concentrations, liberations, and the great *samādhis* as its leaves; and the *dhāraṇīs*, eloquence, and factors of enlightenment as its...
With the ultimate, unchanging liberation of all Buddhas as its fruit, O Son of the Buddha, why is the great medicinal king-tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom called the "Inexhaustible Root"?
Because it is ultimately without rest, and because it does not sever the bodhisattva practices.
Bodhisattva practices are the Tathāgata-nature, and the Tathāgata-nature is bodhisattva practice; therefore—
It is named the Tathāgata Buddha-Son of Inexhaustible Roots, a Great Medicinal King Tree of Wisdom.
When its roots grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to produce the root of great compassion that never abandons sentient beings;
when its trunk grows, it causes all bodhisattvas to increase their firm and resolute vigor and profound resolve; when its branches grow, it causes all bodhisattvas...

When the branches of all the pāramitās increase in this Bodhisattva, the leaves that arise cause all bodhisattvas to grow the leaves of pure ethical discipline, dhūta practices, merit, fewness of desires, and contentment;
when the flowers arise, they cause all bodhisattvas to possess the flowers of the marks and signs adorned by all roots of goodness; when the fruits arise, they cause all bodhisattvas to attain...
O Sons of the Buddha, from the patience of non-arising up to the fruit of the patience of the Tathāgata’s consecration,

the great medicinal king-tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom can only fail to provide growth and benefit in two places: namely, those of the two vehicles who have fallen into the vast and deep pit of the unconditioned,
and those sentient beings who have destroyed their roots of goodness and are submerged in great false views and craving, being unfit vessels for the Dharma.

...of water; likewise, O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata has never been subject to exhaustion or abandonment, because it is well-established in its faculties and arises without cessation.

O Son of the Buddha, this is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like, for example, a trichiliocosm...

"Son of the Buddha, when the kalpa-ending conflagration arises and burns away all grasses, trees, and forests, even up to the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, leaving nothing behind and blazing intensely—suppose someone were to take dry grass in their hand and throw it into that fire;
what do you think? Would it not burn? He replied, "No, Son of the Buddha, it would not. "Son of the Buddha, as for that [grass]..."

Just as one might throw grass into a fire and it may fail to burn, so too there is no place where the Tathāgata’s wisdom fails to discern all sentient beings, all lands, all kalpas, and all dharmas throughout the three periods of time; to say that he does not know them is impossible. Why?
Because his wisdom is impartial and he has attained complete and clear penetration. O Son of the Buddha, this is the mind of the Tathāgata.
The eighth characteristic: Sons of the Buddha, you should know that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should understand it in this way.
Furthermore, for example, when the world-system is destroyed by the calamity of wind, there arises a great wind named "Disperser" (*Vikiraṇa*) which can destroy the three-thousandfold world-system;

it reduces the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) and all else to fine powder. Furthermore, there is another great wind named "Obstructor" (*Pratibandha*) which surrounds the [world-system] on all sides.
In a trichiliocosm, the winds that scatter and destroy obstacles cannot reach other world-systems.
O Son of the Buddha, if it were not for these great obstructing winds, there would be no world-system in the ten directions that would not be destroyed.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise so: he possesses a wind of great wisdom called "The Able to Extinguish," which is able to extinguish all great bodhisattvas.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions of bodhisattvas possess a wind of great wisdom called "Skillful Sustenance.
This wind skillfully sustains those bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature, preventing the wheel of the wind of great wisdom from severing all their habitual tendencies of the afflictions.
O Son of the Buddha, if it were not for the Tathāgata’s wind of skillful sustaining wisdom, immeasurable bodhisattvas would all fall to the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
By means of this wisdom, all bodhisattvas transcend the stages of the two vehicles and abide securely in the ultimate position of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, there is no place to which the Tathāgata’s wisdom does not reach. Why is this? Because there is not a single sentient being who is not...
They possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet because of their deluded thoughts, inversions, and attachments, they do not realize it.
If they were free from deluded thoughts, then omniscience, spontaneous wisdom, and unimpeded wisdom would manifest before them.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a great scripture whose size equals the three-thousandfold world system, inscribed within that very three-thousandfold world system.
All matters were completely exhausted as follows: the events within Mount Mahācakravāḍa were transcribed in a volume equal to Mount Mahācakravāḍa;
the events within the great earth were transcribed in a volume equal to the great earth; the events within a medium chiliocosm were transcribed in a volume equal to a medium chiliocosm;
and the events within a small chiliocosm were transcribed in a volume equal to a small chiliocosm. Thus it was.
Whether it be the four continents, the great oceans, Mount Sumeru, the palaces of the earth-dwelling devas, the palaces of the sky-dwelling devas of the desire realm,
the palaces of the form realm, or the palaces of the formless realm— if one were to write down each of these, their total measure would be equal to this great sutra scroll;
and though its measure is equal to the great trichiliocosm, it remains entirely contained within [this single volume].
Within a single atom, as it is in one atom, so it is in all atoms.
At that time, there was a person of clear and penetrating wisdom who, having fully attained the pure divine eye, saw this sutra scroll within the atom.
Seeing that it provided no benefit whatsoever to sentient beings, he thought: "I shall now, by the power of diligence, shatter that [atom]."

Having formed the thought, "I shall bring forth this sutra scroll from within this minute atom to benefit all sentient beings," he immediately employs skillful means to break that atom and produce this sutra scroll, so that all sentient beings may universally obtain benefit.
Just as it is with one atom, so it should be known to be the same for all atoms. Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise thus.
Immeasurable and unimpeded, it is universally capable of benefiting all sentient beings and is fully present within the bodies of all beings;
yet, because ordinary, ignorant people cling to deluded thoughts, they do not know, do not perceive, and thus fail to obtain its benefit.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure eye of wisdom, surveyed all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm and spoke these words:
How marvelous, how marvelous! How is it that these sentient beings, though possessing the wisdom of the Tathāgata, are so deluded and confused that they neither know nor see it?

I shall instruct them in the Noble Path so that they may forever leave behind false imaginings and attachments, and within their own bodies perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, no different from that of a Buddha; thus I shall teach those sentient beings to practice.
By practicing the noble path, one causes the abandonment of false conceptualization;

having abandoned false conceptualization, one realizes the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata and brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings. Son of the Buddha, this is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind.
Sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it in this way. Sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should [apply] such as these...

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses: "The immeasurable, unimpeded, inconceivable, and vastly expansive knowledge of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—[knowing] the mind [of all beings].
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, desiring to elucidate this meaning further, spoke in verse:
If you wish to know the mind of all Buddhas, You should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddha. The Buddha’s wisdom has no place of dependence;
like space, it has nothing upon which to rely. The various pleasures of sentient beings, As well as all the wisdoms of skillful means, All depend upon the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Buddha’s wisdom has no point of support, Neither that of the śrāvakas nor that of the pratyekabuddhas.
And the liberations of all Buddhas All rely upon the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases;
The Buddha-wisdom is likewise so. It gives birth to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*);
Without increase and without decrease, Without arising and without exhaustion. Like water flowing secretly through the earth, One never fails to find it when seeking.
Without thought and without exhaustion, its power pervades the ten directions; the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise so.
It resides within the minds of sentient beings; if one practices with diligence, one will swiftly attain the radiance of wisdom.
Just as a dragon possesses four jewels that produce all manner of treasures, yet keeps them in a deep and secret place.
Ordinary people are unable to perceive it; the Buddha’s four wisdoms are likewise.
It gives birth to all-encompassing knowledge that others cannot perceive, except for the great Bodhisattvas.
Just as the ocean possesses four treasures that can drink all waters, causing the sea not to overflow, yet remaining without increase or decrease.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: it stills the waves and removes attachment to phenomena;

vast and without limit, it gives birth to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. From the lower realms up to the Peak of Existence, throughout the desire, form, and formless realms, all things rely upon space; yet space makes no distinctions between Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The wisdom of the assembly of Bodhisattvas All relies upon the Buddha-wisdom. Buddha-wisdom is non-conceptual.

On the Snowy Mountains there is a king of medicines Named "Inexhaustible Root," Which can produce all trees—roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Buddha-wisdom is also like this; From within such seeds it is produced.
Having already attained awakening, one further gives rise to the practices of a bodhisattva.
It is like a person holding dry grass and placing it within the conflagration at the end of an eon; even a diamond would be consumed by the flames.
There is no principle by which this—whether the kalpas and lands of the three periods of time, or the sentient beings therein—would not be burned. Yet that grass might somehow remain unburned.
There is nothing this Buddha does not know. There is a wind named "Dissolution" that can destroy a great trichiliocosm;
yet if there were no other wind to stop it, it would destroy immeasurable realms. The wind of Great Wisdom is likewise:
it extinguishes the delusions of all bodhisattvas, while a distinct wind of skillful means causes them to abide in the stage of the Tathāgata.
Suppose there were a great sutra scroll, equal in size to the three-thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust;

and as it is with this one mote, so it is with all motes. Suppose there were a wise person with pure eyes who clearly saw it all, and by breaking open the dust, brought forth the scrolls to universally benefit all sentient beings. The Buddha’s wisdom is also like this.
Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, it is bound by deluded thoughts; neither awakening nor knowing,
the Great Compassion of the Buddhas causes them to eliminate these delusions, thus appearing to bring benefit to all Bodhisattvas.
[Treatise] The fifth [section] clarifies that the appearance of the Tathāgata possesses ten immeasurable spheres.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva know the sphere of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows all worldly spheres through unobstructed and unhindered wisdom."
The realm is the realm of the Tathāgata: the realm of knowing all three periods of time, the realm of all lands, the realm of all phenomena,
the realm of all sentient beings, the realm of non-differentiation in true suchness, the realm of non-obstruction in the dharma-realm,
the realm of the limit of reality which is boundless, the realm of space which is immeasurable, and the realm that is no realm.
The realm is the realm of the Tathāgata; O Son of the Buddha, just as the realms of all worlds are immeasurable, so too are the realms of the Tathāgata immeasurable.
Just as the realms of the three periods of time are immeasurable, so too are the realms of the Tathāgata immeasurable.
Even as the realm of the "non-realm" is immeasurable, so too are the realms of the Tathāgata immeasurable. It is thus.

In all realms and in all places, there is no realm of the Tathāgata; and as it is with these, so too in all places there is no realm of the Buddha-son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. One should know that the realm of the mind is the realm of the Tathāgata.
Just as the realm of the mind is immeasurable, boundless, unbound, and unfreed, so too the realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless.
There is bondage, yet no liberation. Why? Because through such and such conceptualizations and discriminations, there arise such and such immeasurable manifestations.
Son of the Buddha, it is like a great dragon king who sends down rain according to his will; that rain does not emerge from within, nor does it emerge from without.
The realm of the Tathāgata is also like this: it follows such conceptualizations and discriminations.
Thus, there are such immeasurable manifestations appearing throughout the ten directions, yet they all have no place of origin.
Sons of the Buddha, just as the waters of the great ocean are all produced by the mental power of the dragon kings, so too is the ocean of all-knowledge of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
it is likewise produced from the great vows of the Tathāgatas in the past. Sons of the Buddha, this is the ocean of all-knowledge.
It is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and ineffable; nevertheless, I shall now briefly provide a simile—listen attentively, O Son of the Buddha!
In this Jambudvīpa, there are two thousand five hundred rivers that flow into the great ocean; in Aparagoyānī to the west, there are five thousand rivers that flow into the great ocean;
and in Pūrvavideha to the east, there are seven thousand five hundred [rivers that flow into the great ocean].
A hundred rivers flow into the great ocean; from the northern continent of Uttarakuru, ten thousand rivers flow into the great ocean.
Son of the Buddha, regarding these twenty-five thousand rivers that flow continuously and without interruption into the great ocean across these four continents—what do you think?
Is this water much or not? He replied: "It is very much, Son of the Buddha. Furthermore, there is the Dragon King Daśaraśmi.
The water rained by the Dragon King Hundred Radiances into the great ocean was twice as much as before; the water rained by the Dragon King Great Ornament,
the Dragon King Mānasa, the Dragon King Thunder-Resounding, the Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda, the Dragon King Immeasurable Radiance,
the Dragon King Continuous Torrent, the Dragon King Great Victory, and the Dragon King Great Exertion into the great ocean was again twice as much as that.

The eighty billion great dragon kings, such as the Dragon King Swift Dragon (Kṣipra-nāgarāja) and others, each rained down upon the great ocean, with each succeeding one exceeding the previous by tenfold.
Furthermore, the son of the Dragon King Sāgara, named Jambūdhvaja, rained water into the great ocean that was again tenfold more than before.
Moreover, the water from within the palace of the Dragon King Ten Radiant Lights (Daśaprabha) flowed into the great ocean, increasing it yet further.
The water flowing from the palace of the Dragon King Hundredfold Radiance into the great ocean exceeds the former by many times; furthermore,
it exceeds even more the waters of the Dragon Kings Great Adornment, Mānasa, Thunder-Resonance,
Nanda and Upananda, Immeasurable Radiance, Continuous Downpour, Great Victory, and Great Agility.
In the palaces of these eighty billion great dragon kings, such as the Dragon King [Sāgara], there are waters that flow into the great ocean, each successively exceeding the previous one in volume.

Furthermore, the water from the palace of the Prince of the Sāgara Dragon King, Yāman-dhvaja, which flows into the great ocean, exceeds even that by a further multiple. O Son of the Buddha, the Sāgara Dragon King...
The king pours forth more ocean water than before, doubling its previous amount; from within the palace of the Nāga King Sāgara, water surges out into the sea, again doubling what was before.
The water that issues forth is the color of dark lapis lazuli, and it gushes out at specific times;
for this reason, the tides of the great ocean do not miss their appointed time. Son of the Buddha, such is the great ocean: its waters are immeasurable, and it contains manifold jewels.
"The sentient beings to be measured are immeasurable, and the great earth upon which they rely is likewise immeasurable. Son of the Buddha, what do you think?
Is that great ocean immeasurable? He replied, "Indeed it is immeasurable; it cannot serve as a metaphor.
"Son of the Buddha, this immeasurability of the great ocean does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, of the immeasurability of the Tathāgata’s ocean of wisdom."
Not even a fraction, not even a *upaniṣad*-part thereof can compare to it; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, I employ metaphors according to their mentalities.

However, the realm of the Buddha cannot be reached by metaphor. O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know that the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable, because from the first generation of the mind of awakening, he has practiced all bodhisattva deeds without interruption. Thus should it be known.
It should be known as an immeasurable mass of jewels because it ensures that the seeds of the Three Jewels and all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are never interrupted;
it should be known as the immeasurable sustenance enjoyed by all *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who dwell therein;
and it should be known as the immeasurable ground of abiding for all bodhisattvas, from the initial Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the ultimate Stage of Non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇā-bhūmi*).

Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who wish to enter immeasurable wisdom for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings should understand the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this manner. At that time,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
Just as the realm of the mind is immeasurable, so too is the realm of all Buddhas;
just as the realm of the mind arises from the intellect, one should observe the Buddha-realm in this same way.
Just as a dragon does not leave its original place, yet pours down great rain through the power of its mind.
Although the rain has no place from which it comes or to which it goes, it fills and saturates all according to the mind of the dragon;
so too is the Muni of Ten Powers: coming from nowhere and going nowhere, he manifests his body for those with pure hearts, equal in measure to the Dharma-realm and entering into every pore.
As the ocean’s rare treasures are immeasurable, so too are sentient beings and the great earth.
The nature of water is of a single flavor, equal and without distinction; those born within it each receive benefit.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: all that exists therein is immeasurable.
Those who dwell on the stages of those in training and those beyond training all obtain benefit therein.
