Chapter Thirty-Seven, Part Three: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
[Treatise] Sixth: It is explained that the appearance of the Tathāgata involves ten immeasurable practices.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, how should Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know that unimpeded conduct is the conduct of the Tathāgata; they should know that the conduct of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the conduct of the Tathāgata.
Sons of the Buddha, just as True Suchness is not born in the past limit, does not move in the future limit, and does not exist in the present...
The undertaking of the Tathāgata’s practice is likewise thus: it is neither born, nor moved, nor arisen.

O Son of the Buddha, just as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is neither measurable nor immeasurable because it is formless, so too the Tathāgata’s practice is neither measurable nor immeasurable because it is formless.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like a bird flying through the void; even after a hundred years have passed, there is no distinction between the places it has traversed and those it has not.
All are immeasurable. Why? Because the realm of empty space is without limit; the conduct of the Tathāgata is likewise.

Suppose there were someone who, for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, were to analyze and expound upon what has been taught and what has not yet been taught—they would all remain immeasurable.
Why? Because the conduct of the Tathāgata is without limit. O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha...

The Perfectly Awakened One dwells in unimpeded conduct; though having no fixed abode, he is able to universally manifest his activities for all sentient beings so that, upon seeing them, they may transcend all paths of obstruction.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the King of Golden-Winged Birds, who flies through the void and soars about without departing, observing with his pure eyes all the nāgas within the ocean.
The Palace, exerting heroic power with its left and right wings, churns the waters of the ocean until they are split apart on both sides;
it then seizes those male and female nāgas whose lives are about to end.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the King of Garuḍas, abides in unimpeded conduct and, with his pure Buddha-eye, observes all within the palaces throughout the dharma-realm.
If there are any sentient beings who have previously planted roots of goodness that have reached maturity, the Tathāgata exerts his ten powerful forces with heroic vigor;

using the two wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā, he stirs up the great ocean of the waters of birth and death, causing its two sides to part so that he may scoop them up and place them within the Buddha-dharma,
enabling them to sever all false conceptualizations and frivolous disputations and to dwell in the non-conceptual state of the Tathāgata.
O sons of the Buddha who practice without obstruction, you are like the sun and moon, which travel alone through the void without equal, benefiting sentient beings.
They do not form such thoughts as, "From where have I come, or to what place have I arrived? The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also thus:
their nature is fundamentally quiescent and free from discrimination, yet they manifest travel throughout the entire Dharma-realm, desiring to bring benefit to others.
Benefiting all sentient beings, they perform the deeds of the Buddhas without ceasing;
they do not give rise to such conceptual proliferation or discrimination as "I have come from here" or "I am going there.

O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should perceive and know the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through such immeasurable skillful means and immeasurable characteristics of nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:

"Just as true thusness (tathatā) is neither born nor extinguished, Without location and impossible to see, So too is the practice of the Great Benefactor (mahārthakara): It transcends the three times and is immeasurable."
The Dharma-realm is neither a realm nor a non-realm; it is neither finite nor infinite.

The practice of those of great merit is likewise: being neither finite nor infinite, they have no body, just as a bird flying for billions of years leaves no trace between the beginning and end of space, which remains equal and undifferentiated.
Throughout myriad kalpas, you have expounded the conduct of the Tathāgata; what has been said and what remains unsaid is immeasurable.
Like a garuḍa in the sky surveying the great ocean, you cleave the waters to seize the male and female nāgas;
so too, the One of Ten Powers can uproot those with virtuous roots, causing them to emerge from the sea of existence and eliminate all delusions.
Just as the sun and moon travel through space, Illuminating all things without discrimination,
So the World-Honored One traverses the Dharma-realm, Teaching and transforming sentient beings without a single stirring thought.
[Treatise] The seventh [section] clarifies that the appearance of the Tathāgata involves ten immeasurable accomplishments of perfect enlightenment.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, how should the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas understand the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has attained perfect enlightenment?
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know that when the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he does not observe any objective referents;
he is equal toward all phenomena, free from doubt, non-dual, signless, without activity, and without cessation.
Immeasurable and boundless, far removed from the two extremes and abiding in the Middle Way, transcending all written characters and verbal expressions, he knows the mental activities,
conduct, faculties, dispositions, inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings— to speak briefly, in a single thought-moment,
he fully knows all phenomena of the three periods of time. Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean...
Because it can manifest the forms and features of all sentient beings within the four continents, it is collectively described as the great ocean;
the Bodhi of the Buddhas is likewise so, universally manifesting the mental activities, faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings, yet manifesting nothing at all.
Therefore, it is called the Bodhi of the Buddhas. O Sons of the Buddha, the Bodhi of the Buddhas...
O Sons of the Buddha, that which cannot be proclaimed by any written characters, cannot be reached by any sounds, and cannot be expressed by any speech,
is revealed through skillful means according to what is appropriate. When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attains perfect enlightenment,
he acquires bodies equal in measure to all sentient beings, and he acquires bodies equal in measure to all phenomena.

They attain bodies equal in measure to all lands; they attain bodies equal in measure to all three periods of time; they attain bodies equal in measure to all Buddhas; they attain bodies equal in measure to all languages;
they attain bodies equal in measure to True Suchness (*tathatā*); they attain bodies equal in measure to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
they attain bodies equal in measure to the realm of empty space; they attain bodies equal in measure to the unobstructed realm; and they attain all vows.
Equal in measure to the body, one attains all conditioned phenomena; equal in measure to the body, one attains the realm of quiescent nirvana.
Son of the Buddha, as with the body thus attained, so too are speech and mind.

Having thus attained these immeasurable and innumerable purities of the three spheres, when the Son of the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body a single...
All sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment, and even until all sentient beings are seen universally entering nirvana, they are all of one single nature—namely, the nature of non-nature.

What kind of nature is this? It is the nature of signlessness, the inexhaustible nature, the nature of non-arising, the nature of non-ceasing, the nature of non-self, the nature of non-non-self, the nature of non-sentient-being, and the nature of non-non-sentient-being. There is no [such thing as] a nature.
The nature of enlightenment is non-existent; the nature of the dharma-realm is non-existent; the nature of space is likewise non-existent, and there is also no nature of attaining perfect awakening.
Because one knows that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, one attains omniscience. With great compassion continuously flowing, one rescues and delivers sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, it is like space: whether all worlds are formed or destroyed, space is always without increase or decrease. Why is this?
Because space is unarisen, the Bodhi of all Buddhas is likewise; whether one attains perfect enlightenment or does not attain perfect enlightenment, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because Bodhi is without marks and without non-marks, being neither one nor manifold.
Son of the Buddha, suppose there were someone who could manifest as many minds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each of those minds were further manifested...

"If one were to manifest Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—all of whom are without color, form, or marks—and continue doing so for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges without ceasing, O Son of the Buddha, what do you think? How many such emanated Tathāgatas would that person’s transformative mind have produced?
The Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotrasamudgataruciraguṇa replied, "As I understand the meaning of what you have said, sir,"
"Transformation and non-transformation are equal and without distinction; why then do you ask how many there are? Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replied, "Excellent, excellent, Son of the Buddha!

As you have said, even if all sentient beings were to attain perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment, they would be equal to those who do not attain perfect enlightenment, for there is no difference between them. Why is this? Because *bodhi* (enlightenment) is without marks (*animitta*)."

Therefore, if there are no marks, there is neither increase nor decrease. Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus realize perfect enlightenment as being identical to bodhi—of one mark and markless.

When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he enters the samādhi of the wisdom of excellent awakening through the skillful means of the single mark; having entered it, he abides within the vast body of the single perfect enlightenment.
Manifesting bodies equal in number to all sentient beings, he dwells within each body as a single, vast body of a Perfectly Enlightened One;
and all those vast bodies of Perfectly Enlightened Ones are likewise so.

O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable gateways to Perfect Enlightenment; therefore, you should know that the bodies manifested by the Tathāgata are limitless, for they are without measure.
Because it is immeasurable, the body of the Tathāgata is said to be equal to the realms of infinite sentient beings.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know that within a single pore of the Tathāgata’s body there are as many bodies of Buddhas as there are sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the body of the Tathāgata who has attained perfect enlightenment is ultimately without arising or ceasing; thus, from a single pore, it pervades everywhere.
One should know that it is likewise with every single pore of the entire dharma-realm; there is not even the slightest space that is empty and devoid of the Buddha’s body.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, reaches everywhere.

According to their capacities and according to their powers, he manifests equal and right enlightenment upon the lion throne beneath the bodhi tree at the site of awakening by means of various bodies.
O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know that their own minds are constantly and at every moment endowed with the perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this very mind.
Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings; in each, there is the Tathāgata attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, vast and all-pervading.
Abiding neither in existence nor in non-existence, neither ceasing nor interrupted, and entering without rest into the inconceivable gateway of skillful means—
O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should thus know how the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
The Perfectly Awakened One thoroughly knows all phenomena:
non-dual, free from duality, entirely equal, and naturally pure like space; he makes no distinction between self and non-self.
Just as the bodies of sentient beings appear within the ocean-seal, for this reason he is called the Great Ocean.
Bodhi universally seals all mental activities; therefore, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*).

Just as the world undergoes formation and destruction, yet space neither increases nor decreases, so too do all Buddhas appear in the world, while bodhi remains a single characteristic, eternally without characteristics.
Just as when a person uses a mind of transformation to manifest a Buddha, the nature of that which is manifested and that which is not manifested is no different;
so too, when all sentient beings attain Bodhi, there is neither increase nor decrease in those who have attained it or those who have not.
The Buddha possesses a samādhi named "Good Awakening"; beneath the Bodhi tree, he enters this meditative concentration.
He emits immeasurable light upon all sentient beings, awakening the multitudes like the blossoming of lotuses.

Just as there are thoughts, faculties, and desires within the minds of all beings throughout the kalpas and lands of the three periods of time, he manifests bodies equal in number to them; for this reason, the Perfectly Awakened One is named Immeasurable.
[Treatise] The eighth [section] clarifies that the appearance of the Tathāgata involves ten immeasurable turnings of the wheel of Dharma.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understand the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
"O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus: by means of the power of mastery over the mind, the Tathāgata..."
He turns the wheel of Dharma by turning without arising, because he knows that all phenomena are eternally without arising;
he turns the wheel of Dharma by severing what is to be severed through the three turnings, because he knows that all phenomena are free from extreme views;
he turns the wheel of Dharma by transcending the limit of desire and the non-limit, because he enters the limit of emptiness of all phenomena; he turns the wheel of Dharma without verbal expression.
Because one knows that all phenomena are inexpressible, one turns the wheel of Dharma through ultimate quiescence;
because one knows that all phenomena have the nature of nirvāṇa, one turns the wheel of Dharma by means of all letters and all speech;
because the voice of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere, one turns the wheel of Dharma knowing that sound is like an echo; and one thoroughly understands the reality of all phenomena.
Because of its intrinsic nature, it produces all sounds within a single sound while turning the wheel of Dharma;

because it is ultimately without a master, it turns the wheel of Dharma without omission or exhaustion; and because it is unattached internally or externally, O Son of the Buddha, it is like all written characters and spoken languages, which could not be exhausted even if spoken throughout all future eons—the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Buddha is likewise in every respect.
The establishment and manifestation of syllables proceeds without rest and without exhaustion, O Son of the Buddha.
The Wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata enters entirely into all languages and syllables, yet it abides nowhere.
It is like written characters, which universally enter into all things, all speech, all calculations, and all mundane and supramundane domains, yet they abide nowhere.

The voice of the Tathāgata is also like this: it universally enters into all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, all karmas, and all retributions, yet it abides nowhere. The various languages of all sentient beings are none other than the wheel of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. Why is this?
Son of the Buddha, because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of speech and sound is itself the wheel of the Dharma.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand the Tathāgata’s turning of the wheel of Dharma in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to know the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata should know the source from which the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma arises.
What is the source from which the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma arises? O Son of the Buddha, it is that the Tathāgata, in accordance with all...
The mental activities, desires, and inclinations of sentient beings are of infinite variety; accordingly, the turning of the wheel of Dharma issues forth in various sounds.
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses a samādhi called "Ultimate Unimpeded Fearlessness.
Having entered this samādhi, from each and every body and each and every mouth of his perfectly awakened state, he emits [voices] equal in number to all sentient beings.
Within each and every sound of his speech, all sounds are fully contained; though they turn the wheel of Dharma with distinct differences, they cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
One who knows how to turn the wheel of Dharma in this way should be known as one who accords with all Buddha-dharmas.
If one does not know it thus, they do not accord with the Buddhas' sons, the Bodhisattvas.
Mahāsattvas should understand that the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma because it universally enters the infinite realms of sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
The Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma does not turn; In the three times, there is neither arising nor attainment.
Just as letters have no time of exhaustion, So too is the wheel of Dharma of the One of Ten Powers.
As letters universally enter yet nowhere arrive, So too is the wheel of Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment.
Entering all speech and sounds yet entering nothing, He is able to cause all sentient beings to rejoice.
The Buddha has a samādhi named "Ultimate," Having entered this concentration, he then preaches the Dharma.
All sentient beings are without limit; He universally emits his voice to bring them to awakening and understanding.
Within each and every sound, they further manifest immeasurable voices, each distinct;
sovereign in the world, they are free from discrimination, causing all to hear according to their inclinations.
These syllables do not emerge from within or without, nor are they lost or destroyed, nor do they accumulate.
Yet he turns the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; such sovereign mastery is most extraordinary.
[Treatise] The ninth section clarifies that the appearance of the Tathāgata involves ten immeasurable entries into nirvāṇa.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understand the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?

O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to know the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata must thoroughly understand that the fundamental self-nature is like the nirvāṇa of True Suchness (tathatā);
the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also thus, like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
The parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also like this; as is the nirvāṇa of the dharma-realm, so is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;
as is the nirvāṇa of space, so is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; as is the nirvāṇa of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), so is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;
as is the nirvāṇa of the limit of detachment from desire, so is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; as is the signless (*animitta*).
The limit of nirvāṇa is such that the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also thus; the limit of my own nature is such that the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also thus;
the limit of the nature of all dharmas is such that the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also thus;
the limit of true thusness (tathatā) is such that the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also thus. Why is this? Because nirvāṇa is without birth and without emergence.
Therefore, if a phenomenon is without arising and without emergence, it is likewise without cessation.
O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not speak of the ultimate *parinirvāṇa* of the Tathāgatas for the sake of Bodhisattvas, nor does he manifest such an event to them.
Why is this? It is because he desires to cause them to see that all Tathāgatas abide eternally before them, and within a single thought-moment, to see the past and the future as one.
The physical marks and signs of all Buddhas are perfectly complete, just as they are in the present; yet one does not give rise to thoughts of duality or non-duality.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are forever free from all conceptual attachments and perceptions.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world in order to inspire joy in sentient beings and to cause them to feel longing and devotion.
The Tathāgata manifests parinirvāṇa, yet in reality, the Tathāgata neither appears in the world nor enters nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata eternally abides in the pure Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and manifests parinirvāṇa in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising sun that shines universally upon the world; its reflection appears without exception in all vessels of clear water, pervading every location.
Yet there is no coming or going; should a single vessel break, the reflection no longer appears. Son of the Buddha, what do you think?
Is it the fault of the sun that the reflection does not appear? He replied, "No, it is not. It is simply because the vessel is broken; the sun is not at fault.
Son of the Buddha, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: it universally manifests throughout the Dharma-realm without before or after for all sentient beings.
In the vessel of a pure mind, there is no Buddha who does not appear; when the vessel of the mind is constantly pure, one always beholds the Buddha-body.

If the mind is turbid and the vessel is broken, then one cannot see the Buddha. Son of good family, if there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata then manifests nirvāṇa for them;
yet in reality, the Tathāgata is neither born nor passes away, and there is no such thing as his extinction.
"O Son of the Buddha, it is like the element of fire, which performs the functions of fire throughout all worlds; yet at times, the fire may be extinguished in one particular place.
What do you think? Is the fire in all worlds extinguished? He replied, "No, Son of the Buddha.
"In the same way, O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, likewise performs the deeds of a Buddha in all worlds."

When a Buddha has completed his work in a single world-system and manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*, how could it be that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, in all world-systems have likewise entered final extinction?
Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha in this way.
Furthermore, Son of the Buddha, it is like a master illusionist who is highly proficient in the arts of illusion.

By the power of illusory arts, he manifests illusory bodies in all the lands, cities, towns, and villages throughout the trichiliocosm, and through the power of illusion, he remains for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; yet in other places, having completed his illusory displays, he conceals his body and does not appear.
Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Does that great master of illusions conceal his body in only one place?
"If he does not manifest, does he then become hidden and extinguished in all places? He replied, "No, Son of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; he thoroughly knows immeasurable wisdom, skillful means, and various illusory arts.
He universally manifests his body throughout the entire Dharma-realm, maintaining it so that it remains eternally present until the end of the future. Or, in a single location, according to..."

When the Tathāgata has completed the tasks to be performed for the minds of sentient beings, he manifests *nirvāṇa*. How could it be said that because he manifests entry into *nirvāṇa* in one place, he has entered final extinction everywhere?
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should understand the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha in this way.
Furthermore, sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests *nirvāṇa*...
At that time, he entered the Immovable Samādhi (*acalā-samādhi*).

Having entered this samādhi, from each and every body he emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great rays of light. From each ray of light emerged incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lotus flowers;
each lotus flower had unspeakably many exquisite jewel stamens, and within each stamen there was a lion.
Upon each and every seat, there is a Tathāgata sitting in the full lotus posture; the number of these Buddha-bodies is exactly equal to the number of all sentient beings.
Each is adorned with supreme and wondrous merits, having arisen from the power of their original vows.
If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured, upon seeing these Buddha-bodies, they will all receive transformation and guidance. Yet, as for those Buddhas...
The Buddha’s body abides ultimately for the sake of all future time, skillfully transforming and delivering all sentient beings without ever missing the proper moment.
O Son of the Buddha, the body of the Tathāgata has no fixed location; it is neither real nor unreal.
It appears solely through the power of the original vows of all Buddhas, manifesting whenever sentient beings are capable of being delivered. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it in this way.
O sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, abides in the great parinirvāṇa within the immeasurable,

unimpeded, ultimate realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the realm of empty space (ākāśadhātu), suchness (tathatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-arising and non-ceasing, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Yet, for the sake of all sentient beings, by virtue of maintaining his original vows, he manifests at appropriate times without cessation, never abandoning any being.
At that time, when all lands and all phenomena were produced, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"As the sun extends its light across the Dharma-realm, When the vessel is broken and the water leaks away, the reflection perishes accordingly."
The sun of supreme wisdom is likewise: for sentient beings lacking faith, it appears as nirvāṇa;

like fire in the world, it performs the functions of fire. In one city or town, it may at times cease, yet for the Supreme among Men, who pervades the entire dharma-realm, he manifests the end of his life once his work of transformation is complete.
The illusionist manifests his body in all lands, yet vanishes once his task is complete;
the Tathāgata’s transformation is likewise so. The Buddha possesses a samādhi named "Immovable"; having finished transforming sentient beings, he enters this concentration.
In a single thought, the body emits immeasurable light; from that light emerge lotus flowers, and upon each flower is a Buddha.
These Buddha-bodies are as infinite as the Dharma-realm, visible only to sentient beings who possess merit.
Thus, each and every one of these countless bodies is fully endowed with a complete lifespan and magnificent adornments.

As the nature of non-arising is the appearance of a Buddha, And as the nature of non-extinction is the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha, All words and metaphors are utterly severed; The Accomplisher of All Meanings is without equal.
[Commentary] The tenth section clarifies that the manifestation of the Tathāgata involves ten immeasurable ways of seeing, hearing, and drawing near.
[Sūtra] "O Son of the Buddha, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understand the roots of goodness planted through seeing,
hearing, and attending upon the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha? O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know that all roots of goodness planted through seeing,
hearing, and attending upon the Tathāgata are never in vain, for they give rise to inexhaustible wisdom and lead to liberation."
Because it transcends all obstacles and difficulties; because it is certain to reach the ultimate goal; because it is free from falsehood and deception; because all vows are fulfilled;

because it does not exhaust conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*); because it accords with unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*); because it gives birth to the wisdom of all Buddhas; because it extends to the end of the future;
because it accomplishes all supreme practices in every way; and because it reaches the stage of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna-bhūmi*).—The Buddha.
Son, it is like a man who eats a small piece of diamond; it is never digested, but must pass through his body and emerge outside.
Why? Because a diamond does not coexist with the impurities of the fleshly body.
Likewise, even a small root of goodness planted in the presence of the Tathāgata must likewise pass through the entire body of afflictions and all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Why is this? Because these few roots of goodness do not coexist with the afflictions of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a heap of dry grass as large as Mount Sumeru, and a single mustard seed’s worth of fire were cast into it;
it would surely burn them all away. Why? Because fire has the power to burn. This is so in the presence of the Tathāgata.
Planting even a small root of goodness is likewise so: it will surely burn away all afflictions and ultimately lead to the attainment of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Why is this? Because the nature of this small root of goodness is ultimately consummate.
Son of the Buddha, it is like a king of medicinal trees on Mount Himavat called Sudarśana; if anyone sees it, their eyes attain purity, and if they hear of it...
If there are those who hear it, their ears will attain purity; if there are those who smell it, their noses will attain purity; if there are those who taste it, their tongues will attain purity;

if there are those who touch it, their bodies will attain purity. Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, if any sentient being takes even a particle of earth from that ground, it will likewise bring about the benefit of curing illness. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Medicine, is also like this.
This is able to bring about every benefit for sentient beings: if there are those who behold the Tathāgata’s form-body, their eyes attain purity;
if there are those who hear the Tathāgata’s name, their ears attain purity; if there are those who smell the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s precepts, their noses attain purity;
if there are those who taste the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, their tongues attain purity and become broad and long.
The tongue understands the dharma of speech; if there are those who encounter the light of the Tathāgata, their bodies attain purity and ultimately achieve the unsurpassed Dharma-body.
If one gives rise to mindfulness of the Tathāgata, one attains the purity of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who make offerings to the lands traversed by the Tathāgata, as well as to his stūpas and temples, they too shall be endowed with goodness.
"O Sons of the Buddha, having eradicated the roots of all afflictions and attained the bliss of the noble ones, I now tell you:

even if there are sentient beings who, upon seeing or hearing the Buddha, are shrouded by karmic obstacles such that they do not give rise to faith or joy, yet plant roots of goodness, those will not go to waste;
they shall ultimately enter into parinirvāṇa. O Sons of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should act accordingly."
Thus it is known that all roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, and attending upon the Tathāgata are entirely free from all unwholesome dharmas and fully endowed with wholesome dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, although the Tathāgata uses all manner of parables to explain various matters, there is no parable capable of explaining this Dharma.
Why is this? Because the path of the mind and intellect is cut off; it is inconceivable. Thus, the Buddhas...
Bodhisattvas merely provide parables to gladden the minds of sentient beings; this is not the ultimate teaching.

O Son of the Buddha, this dharma-gate is called "The Secret Place of the Tathāgata," "That Which No World Can Know," "Entering the Seal of the Tathāgata," "Opening the Gate of Great Wisdom," "Manifesting the Lineage of the Tathāgata," and "Accomplishment."
Because it is the name of all Bodhisattvas, it is called "that which cannot be destroyed by any in the world";
because it is entirely in accord with the realm of the Tathāgata, it is called "that which can purify the realms of all sentient beings";
because it expounds the inconceivable, ultimate Dharma of the fundamental true nature of the Tathāgata, O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate is not taught by the Tathāgata for other sentient beings.
This Dharma-gate is taught solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas who are intent upon the Mahāyāna, and solely for those Bodhisattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle;
it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the Sons of the Buddha.
It is, for example, like the seven treasures possessed by a Cakravartin King; it is because of these treasures that the Cakravartin is manifested, and these treasures [belong] to him.
It shall not fall into the hands of other beings, except for the crown prince born of the first queen who is fully endowed with the marks of a noble universal monarch (*cakravartin*);

if such a king lacks this son possessed of all virtues, then after the king’s death, these various jewels will all vanish and perish within seven days. Son of the Buddha, this sutra-treasure is likewise.

In this way, it shall not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for those true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata, who plant the roots of goodness that produce the marks of the Tathāgata, and who are the sons of the Buddha.

Son of the Buddha, if there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. Why is this? Because all followers of the two vehicles do not hear this sutra. What [could they understand]?
How much more so for those who uphold, recite, copy, analyze, and explain it—only bodhisattvas are capable of such things.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this Dharma-gate, they should rejoice greatly and receive it with reverence, honoring and upholding it upon their heads.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has faith and delight in this sutra will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas,
practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma),
yet had not heard this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty; or perhaps having heard it at some time, did not believe it, did not understand it, and did not accord with it.
One who enters [this state] but cannot [attain it] is not called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.
However, if one hears this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom, and having heard it,
believes, understands, accords with, and awakens to its realization, you should know that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgata and accords with the realm of all Tathāgatas.
Possessing the realm of all bodhisattva dharmas, abiding in the sphere of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), remaining far removed from all worldly dharmas,
giving birth to all that is practiced by the Tathāgatas, penetrating the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of all bodhisattvas,
possessing mastery over the Buddhas with a mind free of doubt, dwelling in the teacherless Dharma, and entering deeply into the unimpeded realm of the Tathāgata.
O sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have heard this Dharma, they are able to know immeasurable dharmas through the wisdom of equality;
they are able to leave behind all conceptual discrimination with a straightforward mind; they are able to manifestly behold all Buddhas through the joy of supreme aspiration;
they are able to enter the realm of equalized space through the power of mental attention; and they are able to [attain] sovereign mindfulness.
By practicing the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one is able to perfect all merits through the power of wisdom;
by means of spontaneous knowledge (*svayambhū-jñāna*), one is able to leave behind all worldly defilements; by means of the bodhicitta, one is able to enter the net of all ten directions;
by means of great observation, one is able to know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time share a single essential nature; and by means of roots of goodness...
The wisdom of dedication universally enters such dharmas; it enters without entering and does not take any single dharma as an object of attachment.

It constantly contemplates all dharmas through a single dharma. Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas accomplish such merit, they attain teacherless, spontaneous wisdom with little exertion of effort. At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this further, said:
This meaning is expressed in verse:
The merit obtained from seeing, hearing, and making offerings to all Tathāgatas is immeasurable;
within the realm of conditioned existence, it shall never be exhausted. One must extinguish the afflictions and leave behind all suffering.
Just as when a person swallows a small piece of *vajra*, it will not be digested until it finally comes out;
so too, by making offerings to the merits of the One of Ten Powers (*daśabala*), one extinguishes delusions and will surely attain *vajra*-wisdom.
Like a heap of dry grass equal to Mount Sumeru, even if cast into a fire the size of a mustard seed, it will all be completely consumed.
Even a small merit from making offerings to the Buddhas will surely sever the afflictions and lead to Nirvana.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a medicine named Sudarśana; seeing, hearing, smelling, or touching it cures all ailments.
Likewise, if one sees or hears the One of Ten Powers, one attains supreme merit and reaches the wisdom of a Buddha.

[Treatise] Thus, as explained above, for each of the ten immeasurable qualities of the Tathāgata’s appearance, there are ten similes, as fully clarified in the Sūtra. Regarding the mountain named *Khadira*: this is its original name;
*Nimindhara* means "Holding the Edge" (*chíbiān shān*); *Mucilinda* means "Liberation" (*jiětuō*), and this refers to liberation.
The abode of the nāgas, the *upaniṣad* portion, has already been explained above. Or, *mūsala*, which is translated here as "purple-colored jewel.
Thus, the foregoing comprises one hundred parables illustrating the appearance of the Tathāgata, his body, mind, wisdom, and the ten immeasurable matters of his sphere of activity (*viṣaya*).
All these are non-parables used as parables; they provide a brief indication of but a small portion thereof.
Because the path of mind and intellect is severed, it rests in the inconceivable; because it is without nature and without action, it rests in the function of infinite sovereignty.

Therefore, it cannot be expressed by words, measures, or metaphors. Thus, within this chapter on the entrustment and circulation, it is said that this Dharma-gate shall not fall into the hands of other beings—those who delight in the study of the two vehicles, the three vehicles, the śrāvakas, or the pratyekabuddhas.

Those who realize joy, emptiness, and non-self, and vow to be born in the Pure Land, are "other sentient beings," because they have not yet turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle] and remain within the cycle of *pariṇāmi-ja* (transformative) birth and death;

they are thus categorized as "other sentient beings. If there are ordinary persons with the great mind (*mahācitta*) or those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], they are entrusted by the Buddha and are termed "circulation" (*pravacana*). Even if one were to [attain] the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*) in this Dharma...
The Bodhisattva himself has declared that if there were no ordinary beings who delight in learning [this teaching], it would not be called an entrustment, nor would it be called its circulation.
It is made clear that this sutra is entrusted to ordinary beings and to those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment], so that they may take delight in learning it;

having learned it, they realize and enter [the truth], which is called its circulation. It is not entrusted to those already born into the Buddha-family who have entered the stages from the tenth bhūmi upward.
The *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha* states that after the tenth stage, Bodhisattvas enter the realm of the Buddhas; their numbers in the ten directions and in this land are difficult to measure.
Why, then, would the Tathāgata need to worry that there are none who will believe and delight in it, or none who will propagate it?

Therefore, one should know that entrusting [the teaching] to ordinary beings of great resolve and those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds toward enlightenment, causing them to awaken and enter [the path], is what is called "entrustment."
Regarding the entrustment for circulation, it is not entrusted to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above;
the intent of the sutra is solely to speak this Dharma-gate for the sake of Bodhisattvas who are heading toward the Inconceivable Vehicle.

It clarifies that ordinary beings who turn their minds toward the One Vehicle awaken to and enter the Dharma-realm vehicle and the Inconceivable Vehicle, enabling them to progress through the ten faiths and ten abidings.
Therefore, it is further illustrated by the analogy of the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch who possesses the marks of royalty;
after the king’s death, his seven treasures do not disperse or perish because this son is capable of governing the king’s rightful position.
O Son of the Buddha, if such a son did not exist, these various treasures would all be dispersed and vanish within seven days after the king’s death. This is the meaning of this sutra.

This precious jewel is likewise such that it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King—those born into the family of the Tathāgata who have planted roots of goodness for the marks of a Tathāgata.

If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-door would soon perish; therefore, it is clearly known that it serves only to cause ordinary persons to give rise to [the aspiration for enlightenment].
The mind realizes and enters [this truth] because it is not entrusted to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above;

for if one were to discuss the number of those Bodhisattvas who have already entered the stages and first attained the Way, it would still not compare to the number of atoms in an ocean of worlds—so why need one worry that there is no one to propagate it?
The meaning is clear: even if there are only sages constantly preaching it and no ordinary beings, [the Dharma will continue].

Delighting in the cultivation of awakening and entry, one realizes that phenomena are inherently extinguished; thus it is said there are no ordinary beings who practice, and that the teaching of extinction is itself non-arising and non-ceasing.

As the *Sūtra* says: "Except for those true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata, plant the seeds of the Tathāgata’s marks, and possess all roots of goodness"—this clarifies that the Tathāgata takes the wisdom of liberation as his family, which is like a single thought-moment of non-thought.
When all views regarding body and mind have perished, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s sublime principle of non-substantiality and correct wisdom;

therefore, this is called the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve, within the ten stages. This constitutes being born for the first time into the Buddha-family. Furthermore, at the fourth stage, when the phenomena of the three realms are exhausted, it is also called being born for the first time into the Buddha-family.
At the eighth stage, when the first portion of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) manifests before one, it is likewise so called.
This is called being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s non-arising patience, as previously explained.

Those who plant the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata perceive all phenomena as having non-nature as their nature and non-characteristic as their characteristic; they do not destroy characteristics, yet they are without characteristics.
Because the characteristics of the object of wisdom are inherently true, this is called planting the marks of a Tathāgata and clarifying the wisdom of one's own mind.
The realm is neither arising, abiding, nor ceasing; this is the mark of the Tathāgata.
It clarifies that the wisdom of one's own mind and the wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings are of a single nature and lack inherent existence;

they are of a single characteristic and lack characteristics, without interior, exterior, or middle, like the realm of empty space. Thus, it can manifest shadow-like bodies according to the dispositions, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings.
Birth has no place of origin and cessation has no place of departure; realizing that the mind and its objects are like an illusion is the mark of a Tathāgata.
Those who realize such a Dharma are born into the family of the Buddhas and plant the seeds of the marks of a Tathāgata.
Those who plant the seeds of all roots of goodness clarify their cultivation and study of the Tathāgata’s true wisdom-seed. Thus, when ordinary beings hear this Dharma...
Cultivating and studying such true wisdom-seeds of the Tathāgata is called the non-interruption of the Buddha-seed;
this is termed the entrustment and circulation. Therefore, one should know that this teaching is not entrusted to bodhisattvas who have merely entered the stages and attained the Way.
As the Sūtra says: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six [perfections]..."
Even if one practices the various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) through the perfections (pāramitā),
if one has not heard this Dharma-door of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty, or having heard it at some time, does not believe it, does not understand it,

does not comply with it, and does not enter into it, such a person cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata. Such is the case for a bodhisattva.

This refers to those within the provisional teachings who contemplate emptiness and non-self, and though they rejoice in transcending the world, they practice the six *pāramitās* with a mind that loathes suffering and seeks to attain a pure land. They do not realize that their own ignorance is the root of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
thus, these bodhisattvas cultivate pure conduct, contemplate emptiness and non-self, and with a mind loathing suffering, give rise to the aspiration for liberation through acceptance and rejection.

All this lies in the fact that the two views persist constantly; it is not like this teaching, which relies on wisdom to resolve the mind, realizing that the fundamental nature of one's own mind and its objects is one.

Since there is no thought of longing or aversion, and no distinction between purity and impurity, the realm of sentient beings is the realm of the Tathāgata, and the mind of sentient beings is the mind of the Tathāgata—just as is explained in this chapter.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma, each of the ten directions experienced eighteen kinds of earth tremors—namely, six types of movements:
the east surged while the west subsided; the west surged while the east subsided; the south surged while the north subsided; the north surged while the south subsided;

the periphery surged while the center subsided; and the center surged while the periphery subsided. Each of these occurred in worlds as numerous as ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas in each direction.
The movements—namely, moving, moving everywhere, moving equally everywhere; rising, rising everywhere, rising equally everywhere; leaping up, leaping up everywhere, leaping up equally everywhere;
shaking, shaking everywhere, shaking equally everywhere; roaring, roaring everywhere, roaring equally everywhere;

and striking, striking everywhere, striking equally everywhere—caused a rain of all manner of celestial flower-clouds, parasol-clouds, banner-clouds, pennant-clouds, incense-clouds, and garland-clouds to fall.
Clouds of scented ointments, clouds of ornaments, clouds of great radiance from mani-jewels, clouds of the praises of all bodhisattvas,
clouds of the various distinct bodies of unspeakably many bodhisattvas, clouds of the manifestation of perfect enlightenment,
clouds that purify inconceivable worlds, and clouds of the Tathāgata’s speech and sounds— these four [kinds of clouds] fill the boundless Dharma-realm.
The Tathāgata’s supernatural power in the world is such that he manifests these displays, causing all bodhisattvas to rejoice greatly;

throughout all worlds in the ten directions, it is likewise so. At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were respectively eighty [unspeakable... each.
One may say that as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, all named Samantabhadra, appear before him and speak these words:

"Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able, through the majestic power of the Buddhas and in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), to expound the inconceivable Dharma of the appearance of the Tathāgatas.
Son of the Buddha, we [are the ones who have come] from the ten directions... [The text continues with the number eighty.]
It may be said that as many Buddhas as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields—all bearing the same name—have all taught this Dharma just as I have taught it;
likewise, all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions teach it in this same way.
Son of the Buddha, within this assembly now, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in one hundred thousand Buddha-fields have attained all the [qualities] of Bodhisattvas.
We have all been granted the prediction that we shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a single lifetime;
and as for the sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms within a Buddha-field, who have resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
we have likewise granted them the prediction that in a future age, after the passage of kalpas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields, they shall attain it.
In every kalpa, they shall all attain Buddhahood, sharing the same name: Buddha Viśeṣagati.

We, in order that future bodhisattvas may hear this Dharma, shall together protect and uphold it throughout these four continents, for the sake of the sentient beings to be saved, and throughout the ten directions across hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of countless, immeasurable, and even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of dharma-realms.
All sentient beings to be delivered throughout all worlds, equal to space, are likewise thus. At that time,
by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, by the power of Vairocana’s original vows, by the nature of phenomena, by the power of roots of goodness,
because the Tathāgata gives rise to wisdom without missing a single thought, and because the Tathāgata responds to conditions without failing the proper time, [he acts] according to the occasion.
In order to awaken all bodhisattvas; because their past deeds are never lost or destroyed; so that they may attain the vast conduct of Samantabhadra;

and to manifest the sovereignty of omniscience—beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are respectively ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands...
Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms within billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, have come here, filling all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions.
They manifest the vast adornments of bodhisattvas, radiate great nets of light, shake all worlds in the ten directions,
shatter all the palaces of Māras, and extinguish the sufferings of all evil realms.

Manifesting the majestic power of all Tathāgatas, singing praises of the infinite and diverse qualities of the Tathāgata, universally raining down all manner of various rains, manifesting infinite and diverse bodies, and receiving the infinite teachings of the Buddhas, they each spoke these words through the Buddha’s spiritual power:
"Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to expound this Tathāgata..."
"O Sons of the Buddha, we who are all named Samantabhadra are of an indestructible nature;
we have each come here from the world-system of Universal Radiance, from the presence of the Tathāgata Universal Banner Sovereignty.
In all those places as well, this very Dharma is being taught—with these same words, these same meanings, these same explanations, and these same certainties, exactly as it is here."
"Neither increasing nor decreasing, we have all come to this place by the Buddha's spiritual power, having attained the Dharma of the Tathāgata, to bear witness for you.
Just as I have come here, so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions—equal to empty space and pervading the Dharma-realm—in every one of the four continents.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual strength, contemplated...
He observed that the great assembly of bodhisattvas desired to further clarify the vast majesty and power of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world,

that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is indestructible, and that immeasurable roots of goodness are never in vain. He saw that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is invariably endowed with all supreme qualities,
and that they are perfectly able to observe the minds of all sentient beings, teaching the Dharma according to their needs without fail.
At that time, there arose from the immeasurable light of the Dharma of all Bodhisattvas, the sovereign adornments of all Buddhas, and the single,
undifferentiated body of all Tathāgatas— arising from their primordial great practice— the following verses:
The various deeds performed by all Tathāgatas cannot be matched by any worldly analogy;
in order to lead sentient beings to awakening and understanding, they manifest this subtle, secret, and profound Dharma through analogies that are not truly analogies—
a teaching difficult to hear even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
Only those who have been tamed by diligence and wisdom shall hear this secret and profound meaning.
Those who, upon hearing this Dharma, give rise to joy, have in the past made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
they are sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas and are constantly honored and praised by humans and devas.
This is the supreme wealth that transcends the world; This can deliver all classes of beings;
This can give birth to the pure path. You all should uphold it and not be negligent.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement in this chapter that the earth shakes in six ways with eighteen characteristics, this refers to the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra."

The direct statement that there are six kinds of earthquakes clarifies the essence of the direct speech; this chapter clarifies the Dharmakāya, the principle-wisdom (*prajñā*), and the conduct of Samantabhadra, wherein compassion and wisdom are perfected.
Because it manifests the universal movement throughout the ten directions, even the offering of worship is likewise perfected, as it says:
"In each of the ten directions, beyond eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas..."

Beyond world-systems as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, there are respectively eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, all sharing the same name, Samantabhadra. They all manifest their bodies and come to bear witness, praising these and other such matters;
all these instances are measured by the number eighty, and the names of these Buddhas are all the same: Samantabhadra.

It is clarified that the Eightfold Noble Path is the practice traversed by the Buddha; because he established his name as "Buddha" through these very practices, this clarifies that the Eightfold Noble Path’s awakening and conduct are both perfectly complete and pervasive throughout the ten directions.

Therefore, there are Buddhas equal in number to the atoms within eighty unspeakable *nayuta* of Buddha-fields who all share the same name, Samantabhadra, for their awakening and conduct are thus perfected.

This assembly is fulfilled by taking the Eightfold Noble Path as its essence; herein, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields attain all supernatural powers and samādhis, and all receive the prediction of enlightenment in one lifetime.
This clarifies that while they have personally practiced and attained the fruit, this is also the assembly of those being transformed, and thus they likewise receive the prediction in one lifetime.
"One-life" (ekajāti) is so named because one does not perceive births across the three periods of time; this is the meaning of "one-life.
This [state] universally subsumes the fundamental single-body-marks of both ordinary beings and sages, being without any distinct or differing nature.

One who enters this stage through a single kṣaṇa of birth is called "one-life," for they no longer perceive the nature of birth across the three periods of time. Such is the reality of dharmas; all other views are... [omitted].
Furthermore, I have also bestowed predictions upon as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a Buddha-field who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
that in a future age, after passing through as many incalculable eons as there are atoms in a Buddha-field,
they shall all attain Buddhahood with the same name, "Excellence of Realm," within a single moment. This clarifies that [this occurs] precisely in one instant.
When samādhi manifests and the ocean of true wisdom appears before one, the delusions of boundless kalpas are extinguished all at once;
the liberation of mind and object is called "Buddha" and is a supreme realm. It is not like the entanglements of ordinary sentiment where such delusions persist.
To think that this liberation is achieved through the gradual accumulation of practice over kalpas is merely to give rise to conceptual speculation; one will not yet attain Buddhahood.
"Within the True Dharma, it has never been thus," and so forth, clarifies that the sentient beings saved within these four continents are vast and numerous;

"in summary, the ten directions are the same as this," and so forth, [describes] how beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms of ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, there are respectively ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions...

The arrival of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten trillion buddha-fields, filling the ten directions, clarifies that they have come from all quarters to universally witness the practice of Samantabhadra and the Dharma of Samantabhadra; thus it is said:
"We are all named Samantabhadra, each having come from the presence of the Buddha Universal Banner Sovereign in the world Universal Radiance."

The arrival [of these beings] clarifies that they all arise from the fundamental nature of the *dharmakāya*, which is intrinsically pure; this is termed the "Universal Banner" (*Samantadhvaja*) of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-jñāna*).

From this wisdom, there arise various wisdoms and various practices equal in number to the *dharmadhātu*, the realm of empty space, and the multitude of sentient beings—namely, the practices of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, it is said that they come from the world-system of Universal Radiance on the Universal Banner.
Because the Buddha has come, the remaining meanings are fully clarified according to the sutra.

All of these are based on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to constitute the world, while based on discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*) to constitute Samantabhadra. This Dharma-gate of this chapter is revealed through the total integration of awakening, practice, compassion, and fulfillment.
Thus, it is for the purpose of clarifying how one practices as Samantabhadra within the fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Because of the wisdom of differentiation, the Buddha is titled Samantabhadra; thus, it is collectively expressed that all practices are performed through Buddha-wisdom.
Since the Eightfold Noble Path and the Ten Pāramitās do not depart from fundamental wisdom and pervade all conduct, they are cited as a number:
namely, the total of eighty unspeakable *nayuta* Buddha-lands as numerous as atoms of dust.
This is a symbolic teaching; this instruction is spoken for those of great resolve, not for those of inferior understanding who would recklessly engage in forced interpretations.

One must deeply penetrate the meaning of the beginning and end, the preceding and following, and the general and specific, as well as the similarities and differences within the texts according to their respective stages.
This chapter concerns the completion of the five stages through one's own spiritual cultivation, wherein both principle and wisdom, as well as the myriad practices, have reached their consummation.
The completion of Great Compassion is precisely this: the gate of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world to benefit sentient beings without attachment.
This chapter is like the great ocean, the ultimate limit of the vastness of the rivers of the five stages of application flowing into it;
this chapter is like Mount Sumeru, the king of all jewel mountains, unsurpassed in height; this chapter is like the great earth.
Because compassion nurtures all sentient beings, this chapter is like empty space;

because the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body pervade the entire Dharma-realm, it is like a perfectly pure mani-jewel mirror whose dimensions encompass all worlds throughout the ten directions, wherein all forms and images appear without obstruction. This Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s manifestation is likewise so.
Furthermore, because the wondrous principle of the Dharmakāya is formless and shapeless, the Great Perfectly Round Mirror of Wisdom— fundamentally pure and universally luminous—
manifests throughout the ten directions all the karmic actions of sentient beings, the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices, and the bodies and lands of all Buddhas,
all of which abide therein with complete sovereignty. Therefore, those who resolve to attain Bodhicitta should have faith in this.
One should know that within one’s own mind and the minds of all sentient beings, there exists in total such sovereign wisdom and virtue of a Tathāgata;
because one has confidence that this is identical to the Buddha-body and will soon be realized, as stated in this chapter:
"The measure [of the sūtra] is equal to a trichiliocosm, yet its scrolls are contained within a single minute atom; it is likewise with all atoms."
This is intended to cause one to believe and know that all subtle sentient beings possess an ocean-like collection of the Tathāgata’s four wisdoms within their very atoms;
that those who break open these atoms to reveal the scrolls of scripture clarify that once a Bodhisattva has attained this for themselves,
they see that all sentient beings equally possess it, and that through the wisdom of skillful means, they abide within the ocean of birth and death.

By employing skillful means through bodily actions that arise within the midst of sentient beings as numerous as they are, he leads them to open their minds and awaken to the realm of his own wisdom, which is no different from that of a Buddha.
Therefore, it is said: "Breaking these atoms, this sutra scroll is revealed. As the sutra says:
"Just as the waters of the great ocean flow secretly beneath the lands of the four continents and the eighty billion small islands, there is no one who can dig them up."
The analogy of "not failing to obtain water" clarifies that all sentient beings possess the power of self-observation; there is no one who cannot attain the ocean-like mind of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that in every thought-moment their own minds are always the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.
This is to clarify that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas do not differ from this very mind in their attainment of enlightenment.

Because he has attained perfect enlightenment, it is further stated below that "the minds of all sentient beings are entirely like this; all possess the Tathāgata who has attained perfect enlightenment.

This clarifies that the intrinsic nature of the minds of both ordinary beings and sages is pure and without distinction; there is only the difference between delusion and awakening, separated by not even a hair’s breadth.
If, for even a single thought-moment, deluded thoughts do not arise, one attains a state where mind and objects are swept away, and the nature itself is unborn and non-extinguishing.
Because attaining non-realization is itself the attainment of perfect enlightenment, one benefits sentient beings extensively through this very dharma; this is the practice of Samantabhadra.

Because the principle of the non-substantiality of mind uses wondrous wisdom to discern the causes and effects of the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, humans, devas, and the karmic retributions of the evil realms, it is named Mañjuśrī.
Through the wisdom that accords with distinctions, he knows the faculties of beings and brings them to maturity without fail.
Resting is named Samantabhadra; rescuing and protecting all sentient beings with great compassion is named Avalokiteśvara.
To cultivate and study these three minds simultaneously is named Vairocana. When the mind’s habitual tendencies are perfected, it is named Sovereignty (*vibhutva*).
When there is no phenomenon that is not clear, it is named Unobstructed Wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*), which universally accords with the capacities [of beings] throughout the ten directions.

That which is without coming or going is called spiritual penetration (*abhijñā*). Cultivating this from the beginning until it becomes habitual, one attains the realization that throughout many kalpas, wisdom is "non-transmigratory.

This totality is not difficult; why needlessly fail to practice? If one studies yet does not attain it, it is like a person of superior merit who, though surpassing humans and devas, fails to believe and does not cultivate—how can their suffering ever end? This is the great purport: the appearance of the Tathāgata Buddha.
The gateway of the fruit—the wondrous principle of Mañjuśrī and the wondrous practice of Samantabhadra—is shared equally by all sentient beings;

it is neither of the past nor of the present, for its nature is inherently one. May future students believe and practice this with profound sincerity, knowing that it is not remote and need not give rise to self-doubt.
As the verse in this chapter says: "Just as the bodies of sentient beings appear within the ocean-seal [samādhi]..."
This explains that because it universally seals all mental activities within the great ocean of bodhi, it is called the "Rightly Awakened Mind.
Bodhi is the wondrous principle of the mindless nature, devoid of essence or characteristics, and beyond attainment or realization;
one who penetrates this dharma is called "Sublime Wisdom. By means of this sublime wisdom of bodhi, one universally seals all perverse thoughts.
The nature of phenomena is inherently unborn; this is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). The Master of the Treatise states in verse:
"The golden realm of all sentient beings—pure, stainless, and possessing indestructible wisdom—is like a priceless jewel within a garment.
Yet they remain outside the gate, enduring perpetual poverty. The vast jeweled vehicle stands at the crossroads, and Mañjuśrī leads [them home]."
Guided by Samantabhadra, he mounts a robust white ox of immense strength that traverses all realms in a single thought without expanding or contracting.

Yet, such a precious vehicle cannot enter him; he merely delights in the gate of diligent toil and stands before it, unaware that his own body is always within, sending forth constant words of "I am not yet capable."

In general, one must always have confidence that all conceptualizations regarding the spheres of one’s own body, speech, and mind, and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), arise from the conceptualizations regarding the spheres of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind.

They are all without substance, without intrinsic nature, and devoid of self or person; they are merely the unconditioned self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*, arising through conditions, fundamentally rootless.
One should know and observe in this way that the nature of the dharmadhātu, which can be found within the locus of planting [seeds], has no interior, exterior, or middle.
Observing oneself and others as being of one and the same essence—being without self and without "mine"—one practices thus through the power of concentration and wisdom.
Having realized this for oneself, one observes the suffering of sentient beings, thereby accomplishing both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Just as the vast practices and vows of Samantabhadra correspond to the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*) of this sutra, this chapter harmonizes them through explicit text.
Manjushri reveals the dharma-gate of fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), while Samantabhadra represents the non-action of the myriad practices within that fundamental [wisdom].
Since fundamental wisdom is the Buddha, the self-characteristics of its essence and function are explained through a dialogue concerning fundamental wisdom.
The gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood clarifies fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is accomplished through these two practices.
This fundamental wisdom is inherently devoid of arising or ceasing, as it is manifested through the two dharmas of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Because this [wisdom] causes that which was manifested—the cause—to speak of itself, the Buddha himself is without arising or ceasing. Thus, it is clarified that the cause is [such].
It is said that because there is no agent for the fruit, these three dharmas are sovereign, perfect, and pervasive;
thus they are called the appearance of a Buddha in the world. This clarifies that which acts without acting and acts while not acting.
