The Treatise composed by Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Sūtra collated and combined with the Treatise by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty.
[Treatise] The ninth assembly was preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-prāsāda*), expounding the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*).
Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part One: Leaving the World.

[Treatise] In order to explain this chapter, it shall be treated according to five sections: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;

third, an explanation of the reasons why the initial attainment of Perfect Enlightenment is described; fourth, an explanation of the reason for the identity of the teacher who expounds the Dharma; and fifth...
Explanation of the Text and Meaning: First, regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter:
it is named the "Chapter on Leaving the World" because the preceding chapter was titled "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," and this chapter is therefore titled "Attaining Departure from the World.
This title has two meanings: first, looking toward the Master who expounds the Dharma, he teaches and benefits sentient beings; this is *li* (benefit).

Chapter on Benefiting the World: The title "Benefiting" is used here in conjunction with "Beneficial Action. Second, regarding sentient beings who hear the Dharma and remain unstained while living in the world, this refers to the Chapter on Leaving the World;
thus, these two meanings—concerning the master who preaches the Dharma and those who derive benefit—are explained comprehensively.
Second, as for the purpose of the chapter’s introduction: it clarifies that the preceding chapter marks the conclusion of the advancement through the five stages.
The fruit of Buddhahood has been realized and the practices of awakening are already fulfilled; this chapter is the constant practice of Samantabhadra.
Since the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, it has been taught all at once and simultaneously.

It is the common practice of all Buddhas of the past and present, extending even from the Hall of Universal Radiance where the Dharma of the ten levels of faith, the ten concentrations, the ten supernormal powers, and the ten patiences were taught for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Such as the *Tathāgata-āyus-pramāṇa*, the *Bodhisattva-vihāra*, the *Buddha-acintya*, the *Tathāgata-daśa-kāya-lakṣaṇa-sāgara*,
the *Tathāgata-anuvyañjana-prabhā-guṇa*, the *Samantabhadra-caryā*, and the *Tathāgata-prādurbhāva-lokottara-dharmadhātu-parivarta*—
these fourteen chapters of the sutra, up to forty chapters, were not [previously known] among gods or humans.
By means of the Samādhi of Leaving the Boundary of a Single Instant, the Wisdom of Universal Radiance simultaneously seals all and simultaneously speaks of them in unison;
thus, from these various assemblies up to the ascent to heaven, it is stated that they do not depart from the Hall of Universal Radiance where he first attained Perfect Enlightenment.
This clarifies that the beginning and end of perfect penetration are such that time and phenomena do not shift. Therefore, this chapter must be included here, as explained in three ways.
Regarding the purpose of describing the origins of the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment: why does the beginning of this chapter describe the time and place of his first becoming a Buddha?

The meaning of the scripture’s statement, “At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) for the Dharma of Araṇya, in the Hall of Universal Radiance,” up to “having fully perfected his wondrous realization,” is to clarify this point.

These ten concentrations, as well as the five stages beginning with the "Chapter on Transcending the World," all involve progress from beginning to end by means of this essence of Samantabhadra’s practice as the vehicle for advancement.
Furthermore, the intent of the forty chapters is that, although they are distinct, they are collectively not separate from the essence of the ten concentrations of Universal Radiance Wisdom;
they are taught simultaneously and without temporal sequence, being the same throughout the ten directions.
Regarding this ascent to heaven, it is simply said that one does not depart from the Bodhimanda in the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala*).

As stated in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśasamādhi-parivarta*), eleven chapters of the sutra are taught in a single assembly at the beginning of the "Ten Samādhis. This is also the same as in the present chapter;
as previously described, it further states: "At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha... until his wondrous enlightenment was fully perfected."

The "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" elucidates how these samādhis, being without before or after, universally encompass the beginning and end of this entire scripture as well as the three periods of time;
therefore, the "Chapter on Leaving the World" describes it by means of its two thousand dharma-gates, which universally encompass the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice,
the causes and fruits of Buddhahood, and the eternally abiding Way throughout the past, present, and future.
This illumination refers to the moment when, upon first attaining perfect enlightenment, one simultaneously uses the wisdom of universal radiance to instantaneously imprint the human realm,
the heavens, and the worlds of the ten directions all at once, without sequence— just as a perfect mirror suddenly reflects all other mirrors.
This teaching is sudden because it immediately presents the realm of wisdom for those of great capacity, and is not like the mental conceptions of those with inferior understanding.
Because consciousness is that which is known, Buddhahood is attained in a single thought-moment, and the teaching is also expounded in a single thought-moment;
this is because it refers to the essence of wisdom, which is not encompassed by the temporal divisions of the three periods, nor by years, months, days, or the measures of the conceptual mind.

Fourth, as for the reason why the master who expounds the Dharma is [described]: why is it that in this chapter, it is again the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra who is made to speak? This clarifies these two thousand [verses].

This Dharma gate is that which Samantabhadra constantly practices; therefore, he causes Samantabhadra himself to speak of his own practice so that all who hear the Dharma may emulate and learn from it, thereby practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra.
This continues even until the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood and entering Nirvana, as all of these are the conduct of Samantabhadra.
If one considers this through the wisdom of the fundamental Dharmakāya, [it is all Samantabhadra’s practice].

The Buddha-body possesses no merit of arising or ceasing; because it is discussed in terms of discerning wisdom (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) as being entirely subsumed within the practices of Samantabhadra, the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter clarifies that one's own awakening and practice are perfected.

Thus, all Buddhas of the ten directions share the same name, Samantabhadra, to demonstrate that within the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications, there is only a single portion of the awakened mind.
Being able to remedy one portion of the coarse afflictions among all afflictions, they attain a portion of compassion and mercy;
although they tread upon one portion of the tracks of Samantabhadra’s conduct, because they have not yet fully perfected the entirety of Samantabhadra’s conduct,

the Buddha-fruit according to their respective stages is merely designated by names such as Moon, Eye, or Wondrous, until the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter clarifies that their awakening and conduct are equal.
Because it is perfectly complete, it is for this reason that Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within an unspeakable number of Buddha-fields all share the same name, Samantabhadra.
This clarifies that fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) fully accomplishes the function of differentiated wisdom (prajñapti-jñāna), and because its function is perfected, it receives this name.

Since the essence subsumes the function, this is established by naming it according to its function. Now, the reason this chapter has Samantabhadra speak is likewise because of the fundamental [wisdom].
Wisdom is established through its function and named accordingly. If we consider it from the perspective of initial resolve and faith-understanding (*adhimukti*), then function follows the source;
the source is Samantabhadra, and function follows fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Thus, the world is named "Golden," and the Buddha-fruit is titled "Immovable.
The person capable of awakening to this is called Mañjuśrī. When one’s own practice reaches the fruit of Buddhahood and the realization of conduct is perfected, one then takes that very root as...
Because the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) issues forth from its function, it is named Samantabhadra;

because the practices performed are likewise named Samantabhadra, as stated in this chapter, "Samantabhadra" refers to Samantabhadra in terms of the function arising from the fundamental. Furthermore, the Samantabhadra mentioned in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter is also like this:
the Samantabhadra in the first assembly is the Samantabhadra of the self-practice of Vairocana Tathāgata. The ten [practices]...

From the "Chapter on Samādhi" onwards, it is explained that Samantabhadra is an ordinary being who, having ascended through the stages from the Ten Faiths and Ten Abidings until the path is perfected, manifests the practice of Samantabhadra.

It clarifies that from the Ten Faiths up to the Ten Grounds, one employs [this practice] so as to immediately establish the Fundamental Wisdom (mūla-jñāna) from the very beginning, thereby bringing it to full completion.
From the Ten Grounds toward the Eleventh Ground, one proceeds by means of this Fundamental Wisdom.
To accomplish the wisdom of differentiation and exclusively benefit sentient beings, it is said that from the "Ten Samādhis" onward, it is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra who does so.
Therefore, when the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" was taught, those bodhisattvas who had already ascended to the ten stages (daśabhūmi) sought Samantabhadra again and again yet could not find him;
this clarifies that although they had realized fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna), its application had not yet reached full completion. Thus, the Tathāgata...
It causes the thought to arise that one must see Samantabhadra as if he were right before one’s eyes; this clarifies that one uses this very Samantabhadra exclusively.
Because one follows from function by means of the conceptualization of wisdom, the *Samantabhadracaryā-prakaraṇa* (Chapter on the Manifestation) has Mañjuśrī question Samantabhadra.
This clarifies that one follows from function by means of the essence; as it is said in this chapter, Samantabhadra is the principal, [and thus] one follows from the essence.

Because Samantabhadra’s merit is similar to that of Samantabhadra in the first assembly of the Primordial Tathāgata, all the Dharma-gates taught in the first assembly were caused to be preached by Samantabhadra. Thus, it is a case of the essence following its function.
In the second assembly, Samantabhadra’s wisdom-function follows from the essence; this continues up through the tenth stage, where the function always follows the essence. Furthermore—
Causing the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to be perfected and made luminously clear, one subsequently abandons the bliss of samādhi and nirvāṇa at the conclusion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Because these are like a dense forest of afflictions (*kleśa*), one is then enabled to possess the great function of Samantabhadra;

only then can one be called one who has established the teaching universally, being sovereign within the midst of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus is the practice established through the realm of wisdom, and so forth.
At one time, for this reason, the ten concentrations and this chapter collectively provide a general account of the beginning and end of attaining true and perfect enlightenment at the Bodhimaṇḍa.
Any practitioner who has resolved their mind [on awakening] must deeply grasp the intended meaning; only then will they be fit to cultivate the path.

One must not merely seek through many previous lives only to find no correspondence, but should instead, by the power of concentration and wisdom, contemplate and illuminate the true nature of the object of focus.
Regarding worldly states where the mind and its objects are predominantly defiled or pure, one employs the Dharma of the equality of essence and function—wisdom and principle—to treat them.
For those with excessive mental scattering and agitation, one treats them with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For those who excessively delight in quiescence, one treats them with compassion and wisdom through the power of the equal Dharma-body and the dedication of great vows. This is precisely as practiced in the five stages of cultivation described in this sutra.
The practice of governing by Dharma reaches its ultimate consummation; yet, if one’s own wisdom is insufficient, one must seek out a skilled master.

It is not possible to remain complacent and achieve nothing of benefit. One should know that this Dharma-preacher is the embodiment of the fruit of Buddhahood, who—after attaining realization—manifests through the body according to its function.
He is Samantabhadra, who explains the eternal Way from beginning to end; his two thousand types of Dharma-activities encompass the ten thousand.
In the practice of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one relinquishes the seventh stage; there is both practice and the development of wisdom-purity that is effortless.

In the tenth stage, one relinquishes the dense forest of *nirvāṇa*-samādhi. When the practice of Samantabhadra is perfected and one enters into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to fulfill great compassion, only then does one attain mastery.
Fifth, regarding the word-by-word commentary on the meaning: this single chapter comprises seven fascicles of scripture.
The long version is divided into ten sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the Bodhimaṇḍa in the forest retreat, seated upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne in the Samantaprabhā Hall;
his wondrous enlightenment was fully perfected, the two paths were forever severed, and he had attained the state of non-attainment.
The Dharma of marks abides in the Buddha-abode; having attained the equanimity of a Buddha, one reaches the state of non-obstruction, the unshakeable Dharma, and the unimpeded range of activity.
Established in the inconceivable, one universally perceives the bodies of the three periods of time, which are eternally pervasive throughout all lands.
Wisdom is eternally clear and penetrating regarding all dharmas, comprehending all practices and exhausting all doubts. One’s body is such that no one can fathom it. All.
The wisdom sought by bodhisattvas and others reaches the ultimate, non-dual shore of Buddhahood;

it is fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s equal liberation, realizes the Buddha’s ground of equality that is without center or periphery, and extends throughout the entire realm of phenomena, equal to the realm of empty space.

[Treatise] First: From "At that time, the World-Honored One... down to "...the entire dharma-realm and space-realm," there are eight lines of scripture clarifying the praise of the dharma-gate attained by the Buddha upon his enlightenment;
this constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*) of this chapter. Regarding the phrase "wondrous realization is fully perfected" within the praise of virtues:
it means that the nature of the principle of effortless wisdom is inherently all-pervasive, and thus the two [types of] practice are eternally...
"Exhaustion" means severing the dualistic views of permanence and annihilation, existence and non-existence.

"Reaching the dharma of signlessness" means that the realm of wisdom is like an illusion, and the mind and its objects have no master. "Abiding where the Buddhas abide" means that the Buddha has no abode;

"attaining the equality of the Buddhas" means that great wisdom is all-pervasive, knowing the faculties and benefits without distinction between self and other. "Arriving at the place of no obstructions" means that the noble and the ordinary are one.

The essence of the dharmas that are sovereign in both the general and the particular, and which cannot be turned back, means that their essence and function are sovereign and lack any nature that can be altered.

That their sphere of activity is unimpeded means that the function of wisdom is all-pervasive and nothing serves as an obstruction. Thus, they are established as "inconceivable," meaning that delusion has vanished and one acts in accordance with wisdom.
To universally perceive the three periods of time means that the seal of wisdom encompasses past, present, and future without extension or contraction. Their bodies are eternal...
"Pervading all lands" means that internal and external views have vanished and the notions of large and small are exhausted;
the mind is like empty space, and the essence of wisdom is inherently pervasive. The manifestation of the form-body is not a matter of coming or going.
"Wisdom is eternally clear and penetrating regarding all phenomena" praises the Tathāgata’s differentiated wisdom, which fulfills all practices and exhausts all doubts, such that none can surpass it.
The Tathāgata’s merit and function in his final incarnation are praised by all Bodhisattvas who seek such wisdom as being exhaustive in meaning,
complete in conduct, pervasive in presence, omniscient in affairs, perfect in wisdom,
effortless in spontaneity, and free from contraction or expansion; responding universally throughout the ten directions without mind, intellect, or consciousness.
The virtues sought are based on non-abiding; with a single voice, he proclaims universally, yet they awaken according to their individual faculties, as their wisdoms differ accordingly.
The following is self-evident from the text itself.
[Sūtra] Together with Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields...
All of them shall, within a single lifetime, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they have each come together from various lands in other directions,
fully endowed with the skillful means and wisdom of bodhisattvas— namely, being well able to observe all sentient beings and, through the power of skillful means,
bringing them to subdual and causing them to abide in the Dharma of bodhisattvas, being well able to...
Observing all worlds, they universally visit them through the power of skillful means;

they are well able to observe the realm of nirvana, contemplating and deliberating upon it while practicing sublime conduct that is forever free from all conceptual proliferation and discrimination, without interruption.
They are well able to gather in and sustain all sentient beings, skillfully entering immeasurable methods of skillful means, and knowing all...
Sentient beings are empty and non-existent, yet they do not destroy the fruits of their karma;
they skillfully know the minds of sentient beings and are able to master all the various distinctions of the faculties, objects, and skillful means.

They uphold the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time, attaining personal realization and subsequently explaining it to others. They are well-established in all immeasurable mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their true nature.
Having thoroughly observed all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena and knowing them to be non-dual,
one is able in a single thought-moment to attain all the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; in every thought-moment,
one can manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, causing all sentient beings to resolve their minds for awakening and achieve the Way, within the mind of even a single sentient being.

Through conditions, they fully know the spheres of all sentient beings; though they have entered the ground of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, they do not abandon the bodhisattva practices or the various deeds they perform. With wisdom and skillful means, they act without deliberate effort;

for each and every sentient being, they abide for immeasurable eons, appearing only with difficulty even in incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), as they turn the wheel of the true Dharma and subdue them.
Sentient beings shall not have labored in vain; they have already fully perfected the pure vows and practices of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such immeasurable merit cannot be exhausted even if all Tathāgatas were to speak of it for boundless eons.
[Treatise] The second section, from "inexpressible hundreds of thousands of billions" down to "cannot be fully described," consists of twenty-one lines of scripture;
this is the portion praising the perfection of the supreme virtues of the great assembly of bodhisattvas.

【Sūtra】Their names were: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantavikurvita Bodhisattva, Samantamati Bodhisattva, Samantadarśin Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantāvalokita Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva, Samantadhvaja Bodhisattva, and Samantabuddhivikrīḍita Bodhisattva.
Such as these, numbering ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-fields of atoms...
They have fully accomplished as many vows as there are atoms in the universe; their profound mind of Samantabhadra’s practices and great vows are all already perfected.
They are able to go to every place where all Buddhas appear in the world to request them to turn the wheel of Dharma.

They are well able to receive and uphold the Buddha-eye of all Buddhas, ensuring that the lineage of all Buddhas is never interrupted. They skillfully know the predictions of enlightenment bestowed by all Buddhas upon their appearance in the world.
In successive order, they manifest their names, lands, and the attainment of perfect enlightenment; they turn the wheel of Dharma in Buddha-less worlds and manifest as Buddhas,
enabling all defiled sentient beings to become entirely pure, extinguishing all karmic obstacles of bodhisattvas,
and entering the unimpeded, pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

[Treatise] The third section, beginning with "The third is named... and extending to "...enters the unimpeded, pure Dharma-realm," consists of ten lines of scripture clarifying the enumeration of the Bodhisattvas' names and the section on their praise of virtues.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra entered the vast samādhi named "Adornment of Buddha-Flowers.

When he entered this samādhi, all worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways and eighteen manners, and a great sound issued forth which was heard by all; only then did he arise from that samādhi.

[Treatise] Fourth: From the passage beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra... down to "...thereafter he arose from samādhi," three and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on Samantabhadra entering meditative absorption, the eighteen signs by which the great earth trembles, and Samantabhadra’s emergence from samādhi.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantamati, knowing that the assembly had gathered, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, we pray that you will expound for us: what constitutes a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? What constitutes their extraordinary conception?
What constitutes their practice? What constitutes their spiritual friends? What constitutes their diligent application of energy? And how does the mind attain peace?"

What is meant by "concealment"? What is meant by "accomplishing sentient beings"? What is meant by "precepts"? What is meant by "knowing for oneself that one has received the prediction [of enlightenment]"?
What is meant by "entering the state of a bodhisattva"? What is meant by "entering the state of a Tathāgata"? What is meant by "entering the mental activities of sentient beings"?
What is meant by "entering worlds"? What is meant by "entering eons"? What is meant by "expounding the three periods of time"? What is meant by "knowledge"?
What is the generation of a mind free from weariness throughout the three periods of time?
What is differentiated wisdom? What is dhāraṇī? What is the manifestation of a Buddha? What is the generation of the mind of Samantabhadra?
What is the Dharma of awaiting [the opportunity] as Samantabhadra? For what reason does one give rise to great compassion? What are the causes and conditions for generating the bodhicitta?
Regarding the cultivation of a mind of reverence toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): what is purity? What are the various *pāramitās*?
What is the realization through wisdom (*jñānānubodha*)? What is direct realization (*adhigama*)? What are the powers (*bala*)? What is equanimity (*samatā*)?
What are the phrases concerning the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma (*buddhadharmatattvārtha-pada*)? What is the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*)? And what is its upholding (*dhāraṇa*)?
What is eloquence? What is mastery? What is the nature of non-attachment?
What is the impartial mind? What is the arising of wisdom? What is transformation? What is the sustaining power?
What is the attainment of great consolation? What is the profound entry into the Buddha-dharma? What is reliance? What is...?
What is the arousal of a fearless mind? What is the arousal of a mind free from doubt?
What is the inconceivable? What is skill in esoteric speech? What is skill in analytical wisdom? What is the entry into samādhi? What is universal penetration?
What are the gates of liberation? What are the supernormal powers? What are the clear insights? What is...?
What is liberation? What are the groves? What are the palaces? What are the delights?
What is the adornment? What is the arousal of the unshakable mind? What is the non-abandonment of the profound and great mind?
What is observation? What is the preaching of the Dharma? What is purity? What is the seal? What is wisdom?
What is the illumination? What is the peerless dwelling? What is the mind that is not inferior? What is the superior mind like a mountain?
What is the ocean-like wisdom that enters unsurpassed bodhi? What is the dwelling like a jewel?
What is the arousal of the Mahāyāna vow-mind like a diamond? What is the great initiation?
Regarding the ultimate great matter: what is indestructible faith? What is the bestowal of prophecy?
What is the dedication of roots of goodness? What is the attainment of wisdom? What is the arousal of the boundless and vast mind?
What is the hidden treasury? What is ethical discipline (*vinaya*)? What is mastery? What is unimpeded function?
What is the unimpeded function for the sake of sentient beings? What is the unimpeded function regarding buddha-fields? What is the unimpeded function regarding dharmas?
What is the unimpeded function regarding bodies? What is the unimpeded function regarding vows? What is the unimpeded function regarding spheres of activity?
What is the unimpeded function regarding wisdom? What is the unimpeded function regarding supernormal powers? What is [the unimpeded function]...?
Regarding the unimpeded function of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*): what is the unimpeded function of power? What is playfulness (*vikrīḍita*)?
What is the domain (*gocara*)? What is power (*bala*)? What is fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*)? What are the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)?
What is activity (*karman*)? What is the body (*kāya*)? What is bodily action (*kāyakarman*)? What is the body? What is speech (*vāc*)?
What is the purification of verbal action? What is its protection? What is the accomplishment of the great task? What is the mind?
What is the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*)? What is the pervasive mind?
What are the faculties (*indriya*)? What is the profound mind? What is the superior profound mind? What is diligent cultivation? What is decisiveness?

What is the certainty of understanding? What is the entry into the certainty of understanding the world-realm (*loka-dhātu*)? What is the entry into the certainty of understanding the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*)?
What are habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)? What is grasping (*upādāna*)? What is cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? What is the accomplishment of the Buddha-qualities (*buddha-dharma*)?
What is the retrogression from the path of the Buddha-qualities? What is the path of separation from birth (*jāti-vigama-mārga*)? What is certainty (*niścaya*)?
What is the Dharma? What is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharmas? What is the designation for a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa)?
What is the path? What is the immeasurable path? What is the path of assistance?
What is the path of cultivation? What is the path of adornment? What are the feet? What are the hands? What is the belly? What is the treasury?
What is the mind? What is the armor? What are the weapons? What is the head? What are the eyes?
What are the ears? What is the nose? What is the tongue? What is the body?
What is the mental faculty (*manas*)? What is walking? What is standing? What is sitting? What is lying down? What is...?
What is the place of abiding? What is the sphere of activity? What is observation? What is universal observation?
What is the display of prowess? What is the lion’s roar? What is pure giving? What is pure ethical discipline? What is pure patience?
What is pure diligence? What is pure... [meditative concentration]...? What is pure... [wisdom]...?
What is pure concentration? What is pure wisdom? What is pure loving-kindness? What is pure compassion?
What is pure sympathetic joy? What is pure equanimity? What is the meaning? What is the Dharma?
What are the requisites for merit? What are the requisites for wisdom? What is illumination?
What is the seeking of the Dharma? What is the clear understanding of the Dharma? What is the practice of the Dharma? What is Māra? What are the deeds of Māra?
What is the relinquishing of the deeds of Māra? What is seeing the Buddha? What are the deeds of the Buddha?
What are the deeds of pride? What are the deeds of wisdom? What is being encompassed by Māra?
What is it that is sustained by the Buddha? What is it that is sustained by the Dharma? What is the activity performed while dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven?
For what reason does he pass away from the Tuṣita Palace? For what reason does he manifest dwelling in the womb? What is the manifestation of the subtle transition?
For what reason does he manifest birth? For what reason does he manifest a smile? For what reason does he manifest walking seven steps?

For what reason do you manifest as a youth? For what reason do you manifest dwelling within the inner palace? For what reason do you manifest renouncing the household life? For what reason do you demonstrate the practice of austerities?
How do you proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)? How do you sit upon the site of enlightenment? What are the extraordinary signs at the time of sitting upon the site of enlightenment?
For what reason do you manifest the subduing of Māra? What constitutes the attainment of the powers of a Tathāgata? And how do you turn the wheel of the Dharma?
For what reason does the wheel turn? For what reason are pure and white dharmas obtained? For what reason do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas manifest parinirvāṇa?
Excellent, Son of the Buddha! We pray that you will expound such dharmas as these.
[Treatise] Fifth: From "At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantamati" down to "O Son of the Buddha, please expound such dharmas as these," there are seventy-two lines and a half of scripture.

This section clarifies that the Bodhisattva Samantamati has two hundred questions, which collectively inquire about all the dharma-gates and practices from the initial generation of the bodhicitta up to the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.
[The Aspect of the Perceived.
[Sūtra] At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the various bodhisattvas, including Samantamati, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of reliance for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are as follows: taking the bodhicitta as one's reliance, never..."
Because of the danger of forgetfulness, they rely on spiritual friends; because of the necessity of being in harmony as one, they rely on roots of goodness;
because of the need for cultivation and growth, they rely on the perfections; because of the requirement for complete practice, they rely on all dharmas;
because of the ultimate need for renunciation, they rely on great vows; and because of the need to increase awakening, they rely on all practices.
Because all things are universally accomplished, they rely upon all bodhisattvas; because their wisdom is identical, they rely upon the Buddhas;

because their faith is pure, they rely upon all Tathāgatas; and because the instructions of their compassionate fathers are uninterrupted, they rely upon them—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall become like [the Buddhas].
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have come to the locus of the unsurpassed great wisdom possess ten kinds of extraordinary conceptions.
What are these ten? They are: the conception of all roots of goodness as one’s own roots of goodness;
the conception of all roots of goodness as seeds of enlightenment; the conception of all sentient beings as vessels for enlightenment; and [the conception] of the One...
One should always resolve to give rise to the perception of self-mastery regarding all phenomena; give rise to the perception of renunciation regarding all conditioned formations;

give rise to the perception of one's own practice regarding all dharmas; give rise to the perception of the Buddha-dharma regarding all teachings; give rise to the perception of the path of speech regarding all modes of expression;
give rise to the perception of a compassionate father regarding all Buddhas; and give rise to the perception of non-duality regarding all Tathāgatas. This is called...
10. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain unsurpassed skillful conceptualization.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the practice of bringing all sentient beings to full maturity;
the practice of seeking all dharmas to study and cultivate them all; and the practice of all roots of goodness to cause them all to...
Because they cause all samādhis to increase, their practice of single-mindedness is undisturbed; because they cause all wisdom-practices to be fully understood, there is nothing they cannot know;
because they cause all practices of cultivation to be perfected, there is nothing they cannot cultivate;

because they cause all practices regarding Buddha-fields to be completely adorned, and because they cause all practices toward spiritual friends to consist of respectful service and offerings, they revere all Tathāgatas.
Because they have inherited all spiritual powers and act with mastery over transformations, this constitutes the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom and conduct.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of spiritual friends for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: those who cause one to abide in the bodhicitta, and who are well-versed in...
A spiritual friend causes one to give rise to roots of goodness; a spiritual friend causes one to practice all the *pāramitās*; a spiritual friend causes one to explain all phenomena;
a spiritual friend causes one to bring all sentient beings to maturity; a spiritual friend causes one to attain definitive eloquence;
a spiritual friend causes one not to cling to any world; a spiritual friend causes one [to dwell] throughout all eons.
The spiritual friend who causes one to practice without weariness; the spiritual friend who establishes one in the conduct of Samantabhadra;

the spiritual friend who causes one to enter the wisdom of all Buddhas; the spiritual friend who enters [the path]—these are the ten. O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of diligent vigor for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows:
the diligent vigor of teaching and transforming all sentient beings; the diligent vigor of the profound...
The diligent effort to enter into all phenomena; the diligent effort to adorn and purify all worlds;
the diligent effort to practice all that is to be learned by Bodhisattvas; the diligent effort to eliminate the evils of all sentient beings;
the diligent effort to bring to rest the sufferings of all three evil realms; the diligent effort to crush and destroy all Māras; the diligent effort to vow to become one.
To act as the eye of purification for all sentient beings with diligent vigor; to make offerings to all Buddhas with diligent vigor;
to cause all Tathāgatas to be fully delighted with diligent vigor—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed perfection of vigor, O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Bodhisattvas have ten ways of attaining peace and security. What are these ten? They are: first, abiding in the bodhicitta themselves and also causing others to abide in the bodhicitta, whereby they attain peace and security;
second, personally attaining ultimate freedom from anger and contention and also causing others to be free from anger and contention, whereby they attain peace and security;
third, personally departing from the dharmas of the foolish and ordinary, and also causing others to depart from the dharmas of the foolish and ordinary...
The mind attains peace and security: one diligently cultivates the roots of goodness oneself and also causes others to diligently cultivate the roots of goodness;
the mind attains peace and security: one abides in the path of the *pāramitās* oneself and also causes others to abide in the path of the *pāramitās*; the mind attains peace and security:

one is born into the family of the Buddhas oneself and shall also cause others to be born into the family of the Buddhas; the mind attains peace and security: one enters deeply into the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* oneself...

One personally enters the reality of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and causes others to enter it as well, so that their minds attain peace and security;
one does not oneself disparage any of the Buddha-dharmas, and causes others not to disparage them either, so that their minds attain peace and security;
and one personally fulfills the vow for omniscient awakening (*sarvajñatā-bodhicitta*), and causes others to fulfill that vow as well.

Attaining peace and security for oneself by deeply entering the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, and causing others to enter the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas so that their minds attain peace and security—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the peace and security of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten [qualities].
What are the ten ways of maturing sentient beings? They are: maturing sentient beings through generosity; maturing sentient beings through the form-body (*rūpakāya*);
maturing sentient beings through teaching the Dharma; maturing sentient beings through practicing together with them (*sahacaryā*);
maturing sentient beings through non-attachment; maturing sentient beings by revealing the bodhisattva practices; and maturing sentient beings through blazing...
They manifest in all worlds to bring sentient beings to maturity; they manifest the great majestic power of the Buddha-dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity;
they bring sentient beings to maturity through various supernatural transformations; and they bring sentient beings to maturity through various subtle, secret, and skillful means.
These, O Son of the Buddha, are the ten ways by which Bodhisattvas bring the realm of sentient beings to maturity.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of precepts. What are the ten? They are: the precept of not abandoning the bodhicitta;
the precept of remaining far removed from the stages of the two vehicles; the precept of observing and benefiting all sentient beings;

the precept of causing all sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-dharma; the precept of practicing all that is to be learned by bodhisattvas; and the precept of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena.
The precept of dedicating all roots of goodness toward supreme enlightenment; the precept of non-attachment to the bodies of all Tathāgatas;
the precept of contemplating all phenomena as being free from grasping and attachment; and the precept of the restraint of the sense faculties—these constitute the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the unsurpassed, vast, and great precept-pāramitā of the Tathāgata, O Son of the Buddha. Thus it is for the Bodhisattva.

Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of methods for receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); by these, bodhisattvas know for themselves that they have received the prediction. What are the ten? They are as follows:

(1) by generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) with a sublime intention, they know for themselves that they have received the prediction; (2) they know for themselves that they have received the prediction because they never weary of or abandon the practices of all bodhisattvas;

(3) they know for themselves that they have received the prediction because they resolve to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout all kalpas; (4) they know for themselves that they have received the prediction because they cultivate... [and so forth].

One knows for oneself that one has received the prediction of enlightenment regarding all Buddha-dharmas; one has deep and single-minded faith in all the Buddha-teachings and knows for oneself that one has received the prediction;
one cultivates all roots of goodness and knows for oneself that they have all been brought to fulfillment;

one knows for oneself that one has received the prediction to establish all sentient beings in the Bodhi of the Buddhas; and one knows for oneself that one has received the prediction of non-dual harmony with all spiritual friends.
Receiving the prediction [of enlightenment] by conceiving of all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as Tathāgatas;

receiving the prediction by knowing for oneself that one constantly and diligently guards the original vow for Bodhi—these are the ten. Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of entries by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into the state of bodhisattvas.
What are these ten? They are: entering the original vow, entering practice, entering the accumulations, and entering all... [the dharmas].

The entry into the perfections, the entry into accomplishment, the entry into vows, the entry into various understandings, the entry into the adornment of Buddha-fields, the entry into mastery of spiritual powers, and the entry into the manifestation of taking birth—these are the ten entries of the Bodhisattvas.

By means of these, the sons of the Buddhas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, universally enter all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time. What are the ten entries by which they enter into all Tathāgatas?
These constitute the ten, namely: entering infinite perfect enlightenment; entering infinite turning of the wheel of Dharma;
entering infinite skillful means; entering infinite differentiated voices; entering infinite taming of sentient beings; entering infinite sovereign spiritual powers;
entering infinite variously differentiated bodies; entering infinite samādhis; and entering the infinite... [etc.]
Entering the manifestation of nirvana through power and fearlessness is the tenth; these are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas universally enter the three periods of time.
Furthermore, sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten ways of entering the conduct of sentient beings.
What are the ten? They are: entering the past conduct of all sentient beings; entering the future [conduct] of all sentient beings... [and so forth].
They enter into the present conduct of all sentient beings; they enter into the wholesome conduct of all sentient beings;
they enter into the unwholesome conduct of all sentient beings; they enter into the mental conduct of all sentient beings; they enter into the conduct of the faculties of all sentient beings;

they enter into the conduct of the inclinations of all sentient beings; they enter into the conduct of the afflictions and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings; they enter into all sentient beings...

To act at the proper time or the improper time for the purpose of teaching, transforming, and subduing sentient beings—this is the tenth practice of a bodhisattva by which they universally enter into all the activities of sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters worlds. What are these ten? They are:
entering defiled worlds; entering pure worlds; entering small worlds; entering large worlds; [entering...]

Entering worlds within atoms, entering subtle worlds, entering inverted worlds, entering upright worlds, entering worlds where Buddhas exist, and entering worlds where no Buddhas exist—these are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas universally enter all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of entry into eons (*kalpa*). What are these ten? They are as follows:
That is to say: entering past eons, entering future eons, entering present eons; entering countable eons, entering uncountable eons;
entering countable eons as uncountable eons, entering uncountable eons as countable eons;
entering all eons as non-eons, entering non-eons as all eons; and entering all eons as one.
Mindfulness is the tenth; by these, the Bodhisattvas universally enter all kalpas.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas speak of the three periods of time. What are the ten? They are: speaking of the past within the past;
speaking of the future within the past; speaking of the present within the past; speaking of the past within the future; [and so on].
The future world speaks of the present world; the future world speaks of the inexhaustible present world;
the present world speaks of the past world; the present world speaks of the future world; the present world speaks of equality;

the present world speaks of the three periods of time as being a single thought-moment—these are the ten bodhisattvas who thus universally proclaim the Buddhas and Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the three periods of time.
There are ten kinds of knowledge regarding the three periods of time. What are these ten? They are: knowledge of all established arrangements;
knowledge of all languages; knowledge of all discourses; knowledge of all conventions; knowledge of all designations; knowledge of all regulations; knowledge of conventional names;
knowledge of the inexhaustible; knowledge of cessation; and knowledge of the emptiness of all things. These are the ten. By means of these, the bodhisattva universally...
Knowing all phenomena of the three periods of time, the Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, give rise to ten kinds of tireless minds.
What are these ten? They are: the tireless mind in making offerings to all Buddhas; the tireless mind in attending upon all spiritual friends;
the tireless mind in seeking all dharmas; and the tireless mind in hearing the true Dharma.
With a mind free from weariness, they proclaim the True Dharma; with a mind free from weariness, they teach and discipline all sentient beings;
with a mind free from weariness, they establish all sentient beings in the Bodhi of the Buddha;
with a mind free from weariness, they practice the bodhisattva conduct in each and every world for unspeakably unspeakable eons; and with a mind free from weariness, they travel throughout.
The mind that observes and contemplates all Buddha-dharmas without weariness regarding any world—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, great wisdom of non-weariness.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of distinct wisdom for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows:

That is to say: the wisdom that knows the distinctions among sentient beings; the wisdom that knows the distinctions among their faculties; the wisdom that knows the distinctions among karmic retributions;
the wisdom that knows the distinctions among modes of rebirth; the wisdom that knows the distinctions among world-systems; the wisdom that knows the distinctions among the dharma-realm;

the wisdom that knows the distinctions among all Buddhas; the wisdom that knows the distinctions among all dharmas; the wisdom that knows the distinctions among the three periods of time; and the wisdom that knows all languages.
The wisdom that discerns the distinctions of the Path is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and great wisdom of distinctions.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of dhāraṇīs. What are the ten? They are as follows:
the dhāraṇī of retaining what is heard, because it upholds all dharmas without forgetting them; the dhāraṇī of cultivation... [and so forth].
The *dhāraṇī* of Contemplating All Dharmas as They Truly Are, because it skillfully contemplates all dharmas;
the *dhāraṇī* of Reflection, because it thoroughly understands the nature of all dharmas; the *dhāraṇī* of Dharma Radiance, because it illuminates the inconceivable dharmas of all Buddhas;
and the *dhāraṇī* of Samādhi, because it hears the True Dharma at the presence of all present Buddhas with an undistracted mind. Perfect.
The *Ghoṣa-dhāraṇī*, because it brings about the thorough understanding of inconceivable sounds and languages;

the *Triyadhva-dhāraṇī*, because it expounds the inconceivable teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; the *Nānā-pratibhāna-dhāraṇī*, because it expounds the boundless teachings of the Buddhas;
and the *Anāvaraṇa-śrotra-janana-dhāraṇī*, which is that which has been taught by unspeakable numbers of Buddhas.
Because they are able to hear all dharmas, and because they abide in the *dhāraṇī* of all Buddha-dharmas through the powers and fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas wish to attain these dharmas, they should diligently practice and study them.
O Son of the Buddha, what are the ten kinds of Buddhas spoken of by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas? They are as follows: the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha of Vows, and the Buddha of Action.

The Buddha of Retribution, the Buddha of Abiding, the Buddha of Nirvāṇa, the Buddha of the Dharma-realm, the Buddha of Mind, the Buddha of Samādhi, the Buddha of Original Nature, the Buddha of Following Joy—these are the ten Buddhas.
O Sons of the Buddha, what are the ten kinds of Samantabhadra-minds that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva generates? What are the ten? They are:

generating the mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings; generating the mind of great compassion (*karuṇā*) to take on [the suffering of others]...
Because all sentient beings suffer, they give rise to the mind of universal giving, relinquishing all that they possess;
because they take the aspiration for omniscience as their primary focus, they give rise to the mind adorned with merit, joyfully seeking all Buddha-dharmas;
because they train in all bodhisattva practices, they give rise to the adamantine mind, never forgetting or losing it throughout all births.
One should resolve upon a mind like the ocean, because all pure and white dharmas flow into it; one should resolve upon a mind like the king of great mountains, because one endures all evil words;
one should resolve upon a mind of peace and security, because one bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
one should resolve upon a mind of the ultimate perfection of *prajñā*, because one skillfully contemplates that all phenomena are non-existent. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in this mind, they will swiftly achieve the skillful wisdom of Samantabhadra.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of Samantabhadra practices for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the practice of vowing to abide through all future kalpas;
and the practice of vowing to make offerings to and honor all Buddhas of the future. This is the Samantabhadra practice.
Through the practice of the Dharma-vow, may all sentient beings be established in the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
through the practice of the Dharma-vow, may all roots of goodness be accumulated; through the practice of the Dharma-vow, may one enter into all pāramitās;
through the practice of the Dharma-vow, may all bodhisattva practices be fulfilled; and through the practice of the Dharma-vow, may all worlds be adorned.
The Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna: may I be born in all Buddha-fields; the Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna:
may I skillfully observe all phenomena; the Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna: may I attain unsurpassed bodhi in all Buddha-lands. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas diligently cultivate these dharmas, they will swiftly bring the Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna to fulfillment.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate sentient beings and give rise to great compassion.
What are these ten? They are: contemplating that sentient beings are without refuge or protector and giving rise to great compassion;

contemplating that the nature of sentient beings is unruly and giving rise to great compassion; contemplating that sentient beings are impoverished and lack roots of goodness and giving rise to great compassion; [contemplating...]

Observing that sentient beings have been asleep through the long night, he gives rise to great compassion; observing that sentient beings practice unwholesome dharmas, he gives rise to great compassion;
observing that sentient beings are bound by the fetters of desire, he gives rise to great compassion;

observing that sentient beings are submerged in the sea of birth and death, he gives rise to great compassion; observing that sentient beings are perpetually afflicted by the suffering of illness, he gives rise to great compassion.
Observing that sentient beings lack the desire for wholesome dharmas, they give rise to great compassion;
observing that sentient beings have lost all Buddha-dharmas, they give rise to great compassion. These are the ten [ways] by which Bodhisattvas constantly observe sentient beings with this mind.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten causes and conditions for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva to resolve upon Bodhicitta. What are these ten? They are as follows: namely, for the sake of teaching...
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of transforming and subduing all sentient beings; one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of eliminating the mass of suffering of all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing complete peace and happiness upon all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of severing the ignorance of all sentient beings; one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing [wisdom] upon all sentient beings...
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom; one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of reverently making offerings to all Buddhas;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of following the Tathāgata’s instructions so as to please the Buddhas;

one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of beholding the physical marks and signs of all Buddhas’ form bodies; and one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of entering the vast wisdom of all Buddhas.
The bodhicitta is generated for the sake of manifesting the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas; this is the tenth, O Sons of the Buddha.

If a Bodhisattva generates the unsurpassed bodhicitta for the sake of entering into the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), when they approach and make offerings to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they should give rise to ten kinds of mind. What are these ten? Namely, they should give rise to [the mind of] providing...

With a mind of service, a joyful mind, a mind free from opposition, a compliant mind, a mind free from seeking anything else, a one-pointed mind, a mind sharing the same roots of goodness, a mind sharing the same vows, a mind like that of a Tathāgata, and a mind sharing the same perfect conduct—these are the ten.
Sons of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to such minds, they will attain ten kinds of purity. What are these ten? Namely:
The profound mind is pure because it reaches ultimate perfection without impairment;
the form-body is pure because it manifests itself according to what is appropriate; the voice is pure because it thoroughly understands all languages;
eloquence is pure because it skillfully expounds the infinite teachings of the Buddhas; and wisdom is pure because it abandons all darkness of ignorance.

Birth is pure because of the mastery of a bodhisattva’s powers; the retinue is pure because it accomplishes the roots of goodness shared by sentient beings from past lives; retribution is pure because all karmic obstructions are eliminated;
great vows are pure because they are non-dual in nature with those of all other bodhisattvas; and conduct is pure through the vehicle of Samantabhadra.
And because of renunciation, these constitute the ten. O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pāramitās for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are as follows: the dāna-pāramitā, because of relinquishing all that one possesses;
the śīla-pāramitā, because of purifying the Buddha-precepts; the kṣānti-pāramitā, because of abiding in the Buddha-forbearance; the vīrya-pāramitā, [because of... the first...
The perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) because all actions are non-regressive; the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) because of contemplating a single object of focus;
the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*) because of observing all phenomena as they truly are;

the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) because of fulfilling all the great vows of Samantabhadra; and the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) because of manifesting all sovereign functions.
Therefore, because the Dharma-pāramitā universally enters into all the Buddha-dharmas, it is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of wisdom through which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas awaken in accordance with reality. What are the ten? They are as follows: [the wisdom of] all worlds...
The wisdom that discerns the immeasurable distinctions of all sentient beings;
the inconceivable wisdom that discerns the entry of all phenomena into one and the entry of one into the manifold; the vast wisdom that discerns the entire realm of phenomena;
the ultimate wisdom that discerns the entire realm of space; and the wisdom that discerns the entry of all worlds into the past.
Worldly wisdom that perceives all worlds entering the future; wisdom that perceives all worlds entering the present;
wisdom that perceives that the infinite vows and practices of all Tathāgatas are all brought to fulfillment within a single wisdom;
wisdom that perceives that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained liberation through a single identical practice; wisdom that perceives...

These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the light of mastery over all dharmas, their vows will all be fulfilled, and in a single thought-moment, they will be able to comprehend all Buddha-dharmas and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of realization and knowledge. What are the ten? They are: first, knowing one...
One knows all phenomena through a single characteristic; one knows all phenomena through infinite characteristics; one knows all phenomena in a single thought-moment;
one knows the mental activities of all sentient beings without obstruction; one knows the equality of the faculties of all sentient beings;

one knows the habitual tendencies of the afflictions of all sentient beings; one knows the underlying propensities of the minds of all sentient beings; and one knows the virtues of all sentient beings.
They know all unwholesome practices; they know the sovereign dwelling and transformations of the vows and practices of all bodhisattvas;
and they know that all Tathāgatas are endowed with the ten powers and have attained equal and perfect enlightenment—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain skillful means regarding all dharmas.
