Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Commentary on the Sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-Eight: "Leaving the World," Part Three.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of non-dejected minds that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas generate. What are these ten? O Buddha...
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought: "I shall subdue all Māras, the Lord of Heaven, and their retinues"—this is the first mind that is not inferior.

Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I shall utterly destroy all non-Buddhists and their false teachings"—this is the second mind that is not inferior. Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I shall..."
To use kind words and skillful analogies for all sentient beings so as to cause them all to rejoice is the third mind free from inferiority.
Furthermore, to think, "I shall fully accomplish all the practices of the *pāramitās* throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)" is the fourth mind free from inferiority.
Furthermore, to think, "I shall accumulate the treasury of all merit" is...
This is the fifth mind that is free from inferiority. Furthermore, one forms this thought: "Unsurpassed Bodhi is vast and difficult to accomplish;
I shall practice it so that it is fully perfected. This is the sixth mind that is free from inferiority. Furthermore, one forms this thought:
"I shall, by means of unsurpassed teaching and unsurpassed discipline, teach and discipline all sentient beings. This is...

Seventh, the mind free from inferiority further reflects: "In all worlds, which are diverse and different, I shall attain equal and perfect enlightenment with infinite bodies"—this is the eighth mind free from inferiority. Furthermore, it reflects:
"When I am practicing the bodhisattva path, if there should be sentient beings who come to beg from me for their hands, feet, ears, noses, blood, or flesh..."
Whether it be one's marrow, wife, children, elephants, horses, or even the royal throne—one is able to relinquish all such things without giving rise to a single thought of regret or remorse.

Seeking only to benefit all sentient beings and not for the sake of seeking karmic retribution, taking great compassion as the foremost and great kindness as the ultimate—this is the ninth mind that is free from inferiority. Furthermore, one forms this thought: three...
All the Buddhas of all worlds, all the Buddha-dharmas, all sentient beings,
all lands, all mundane realms, all that pertains to the three periods of time, the entire realm of empty space, the entire realm of dharmas,
the entire realm of linguistic designations, and the entire realm of quiescent nirvana— all such various phenomena as these, I shall [attain]...
By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, one fully knows, fully awakens to, fully sees, fully realizes, fully cultivates, and fully abandons;
yet within this, there is no discrimination, freedom from discrimination, no manifold distinctions, no merit, and no objective sphere.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither one nor two. Through non-dual wisdom, one knows all dualities; through signless wisdom, one knows.
One knows all marks through non-conceptualizing wisdom; one knows all conceptualizations through non-differentiating wisdom;
one knows all distinctions through non-discriminating wisdom; one knows all worlds through non-worldly wisdom;
one knows all times through non-temporal wisdom; and one knows all sentient beings through non-sentient wisdom.
With non-attached wisdom, they know all attachments; with wisdom that dwells nowhere, they know all dwelling places;
with wisdom free from defilement, they know all defilements; with inexhaustible wisdom, they know all exhaustion;

and with wisdom that reaches the ultimate realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they manifest their bodies in all worlds; and with wisdom that transcends speech and sound, they demonstrate the ineffable.

Regarding speech and sound: by means of the wisdom of a single self-nature, one enters into the absence of self-nature; by means of the wisdom of a single objective realm, one manifests various objective realms.
Knowing that all phenomena are inexpressible, yet manifesting great sovereign speech, one realizes the stage of omniscience.
For the sake of teaching and taming all sentient beings, one manifests great spiritual powers throughout all worlds.
Mastery of transformations is the tenth [quality] of the mind free from inferiority. Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of minds free from inferiority that a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates;
if bodhisattvas abide in these minds, they will attain all the most supreme dharmas of a Buddha that are free from inferiority.

Son of the Buddha, regarding the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*... [of the bodhisattva mahāsattva]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.)
There are ten kinds of mountain-like superior resolve regarding the three types of enlightenment. What are these ten?
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly applies his mind and diligently cultivates all dharmas of omniscience, this is the first mountain-like superior resolve.
Constantly contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty and unattainable is the second mountain-like superior resolve.
May I, throughout immeasurable kalpas, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate all pure and white dharmas;
because I abide in all pure and white dharmas, may I know and see the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata—this is the third mountain-like superior mind.
For the sake of seeking all Buddha-dharmas, may I honor and serve all spiritual friends with an impartial mind, without any divergent aspirations.

The fourth is the superior mind like a mountain, which, with a heart that steals not the Dharma, gives rise only to reverence and unprecedented resolve, being able to relinquish all that one possesses; even if sentient beings should revile,
slander, beat, strike, butcher, or maim their bodies, or even take their lives, they are able to endure all such things without ever [retaliating] because of them.
Even when agitated thoughts arise or thoughts of anger and malice arise, he does not retreat or abandon his great compassion and vast vows, but causes them to increase further without ceasing.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva has achieved the renunciation of all phenomena as they truly are, and because he has attained the patience and gentleness of all Tathāgatas and possesses mastery over them. This is the [first].
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Pañcaśaila, possessing a superior mind, has accomplished superior great merits, namely: superior merit of the devas,
superior merit of humans, superior merit of physical form, superior merit of power, superior merit of retinue,
superior merit of desire, superior merit of royal sovereignty, and superior merit of mastery.
Although they have accomplished such superior merits of virtue, superior merits of merit, and superior merits of wisdom,
they ultimately do not give rise to attachment toward them— namely, they do not cling to flavors, they do not cling to desires, they do not cling to wealth,
and they do not cling to retinues; rather, they deeply delight in the Dharma, following the Dharma, abiding in the Dharma, and proceeding toward the Dharma.
Previously, by following the Dharma to its ultimate conclusion, they took the Dharma as their reliance, the Dharma as their refuge, the Dharma as their protection, and the Dharma as their shelter;
they guarded the Dharma, delighted in the Dharma, sought the Dharma, and contemplated the Dharma.
Sons of the Buddha, although these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas fully experience various kinds of Dharma-joy, they always remain far removed from the realms of Māra. Why is this? Because...
In the past, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gave rise to this thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to forever leave the realm of all Māras and abide in the realm of the Buddhas. This is the sixth mountain-like superior mind.
Having already sought unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for immeasurable [eons], the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—

Having practiced the bodhisattva path with diligent effort for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) without ever flagging, one still thinks, "I have only now first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and am practicing the bodhisattva conduct. Thus, one is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid.
Although it is possible to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single thought-moment, [one remains thus] for the sake of sentient beings.
Therefore, practicing the bodhisattva path for immeasurable eons without rest—this is the seventh mountain-like superior mind.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the natures of all sentient beings are not harmonious or virtuous;

they are difficult to tame and difficult to liberate, and they are unable to recognize or repay kindness. For this reason, he generates a great vow for their sake, desiring that they all attain [liberation].
Having mastery over mind and thought, acting without obstruction, abandoning evil thoughts, and not giving rise to afflictions toward others—this is the eighth.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mountain-like Superiority thinks thus:
"It is not another who causes me to resolve upon bodhicitta, nor do I wait for others to assist me in my practice; I myself have resolved upon the mind and gathered this."
I vow to exhort myself to follow the Buddha-dharma until the end of all future kalpas, practicing the bodhisattva path to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, as I now cultivate the bodhisattva practices, I shall purify my own mind and purify the minds of others;
I shall know my own realm and know the realms of others, and I shall fully share in the realm of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Equanimity is the ninth mountain-like superior mind. A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this way:
there is not a single dharma by which one cultivates the bodhisattva practice; there is not a single dharma by which one fulfills the bodhisattva practice;
there is not a single dharma by which one teaches and tames all sentient beings; and there is not a single dharma by which one makes offerings to and reveres all Buddhas.
There is not a single dharma that has been, is being, or will be realized in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

there is not a single dharma that has been, is being, or will be taught. Both the speaker and the dharma are unattainable, yet one does not abandon the vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva seeks all [dharmas].
Since all phenomena are non-apprehensible, it is in this way that one gives rise to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, although there is no apprehension of phenomena, one diligently cultivates superior wholesome karma;
through pure antidotes, wisdom becomes perfected and increases in every moment until everything is fully complete. One’s mind does not tremble, does not fear, and does not shrink back from this.
If all phenomena are entirely quiescent, what purpose do I have in seeking the path of unsurpassed bodhi?

This is the tenth mountain-like superior mind. O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of mountain-like superior minds of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If any Bodhisattvas...
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the sons of the Buddha, dwell therein, they attain the sovereign mind of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom, which is like the king of mountains.
There are ten ways in which they enter the ocean-like wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are these ten? They are as follows: first, entering all the infinite realms of sentient beings; this is the first. As it is said: [and so forth].
The ocean-like wisdom that enters all worlds without giving rise to discrimination is the second.
The ocean-like wisdom that knows all realms of space to be immeasurable and unimpeded, universally entering the entire network of diverse worlds throughout the ten directions, is the third.
The ocean-like wisdom through which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas skillfully enter the Dharma-realm—namely, non-obstruction—is [the fourth].
Because they enter into the non-interruption, the non-permanence, the immeasurability, the non-arising, the non-cessation, and the totality [of phenomena],
and because they fully comprehend them all, this is the fourth [quality]. It is like the oceanic wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
who [knows] the roots of goodness accumulated by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Dharma-preachers, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all ordinary beings of the past, future, and present.
Regarding all roots of goodness that the Buddhas of the three periods of time— past, present, and future— have accumulated, are currently accumulating,
or will accumulate for the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and regarding all roots of goodness from the teachings preached, being preached,
or yet to be preached by those Buddhas of the three periods of time to discipline and transform all sentient beings— he understands them all completely.
To know with deep faith, to rejoice with sympathetic joy, and to aspire to cultivate [the path] without ever becoming weary or satisfied— this is the fifth [attribute].
Just as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ocean-like Wisdom enters unspeakable numbers of past kalpas in every moment of thought,
wherein in a single kalpa there may be ten billion Buddhas appearing in the world, or a thousand billion Buddhas appearing in the world, or a hundred thousand billion Buddhas appearing in the world.
Whether they be countless, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, uncountable, inexpressible, inconceivable,
unfathomable, unspeakable, or even unspeakably unspeakable— beyond all calculation—
the appearance in the world of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as well as the sounds of their bodhimaṇḍas and assemblies.

Hearing the Bodhisattva preach the Dharma, he clearly perceives all things—how all sentient beings are tamed, the lengthening or shortening of their lifespans, and how long the Dharma remains—just as he sees one eon; all other eons are likewise so.
Furthermore, in those eons where no Buddha appears, he sees that among all sentient beings, there are those who plant various roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

They also fully comprehend the faculties [of beings], and they fully comprehend whether there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured such that they shall see a Buddha in a future age.
Thus observing incalculable, incalculable eons of the past without ever becoming weary of mind—
this is the sixth way in which the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ocean-like Wisdom enters the future and contemplates.
He examines and discerns all kalpas—immeasurable and boundless—knowing which kalpas have a Buddha and which kalpas have no Buddha;

in which kalpas how many Tathāgatas appear in the world, what the name of each individual Tathāgata is, in what world they dwell, what the name of that world is, how many sentient beings they deliver, and for how long their lifespan lasts. He observes in this manner throughout the entirety of the future.
To fully comprehend all things as being inexhaustible and never to feel weary or satisfied—this is the seventh [quality].
Just as the ocean is vast, so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samudramati enter into the present world, observing and contemplating it;

in every single thought-moment, he universally perceives that throughout the infinite varieties of unspeakable worlds in the ten directions, there are Buddhas who have already attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
Now, whether already accomplished, currently accomplishing, or yet to come, he shall proceed to the site of enlightenment and sit beneath the Bodhi tree upon auspicious grass;
there he shall subdue the armies of Māra and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having arisen from this, he shall enter cities and towns, ascend to celestial palaces, preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, turn the great wheel of the Dharma, manifest supernatural powers, and discipline sentient beings, and so forth.
Having entrusted the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and relinquished his life-span to enter parinirvāṇa,
and having entered nirvāṇa, he causes the collection of the Dharma-piṭaka to abide long in the world; he adorns the Buddha-stūpas with various offerings,
and also beholds all sentient beings in that world who encounter the Buddha, hear the Dharma, receive and uphold it, recite it, and contemplate it with mindfulness.
Only by increasing wisdom and understanding does one observe in this way, pervading the ten directions without error regarding the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands that all Buddhas are entirely like dreams, yet is able to go to the abodes of all Buddhas to pay homage and make offerings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva is not attached to their own self, nor are they attached to [other] phenomena.
The Buddha is not attached to the world, nor to the assembly, nor to the preaching of the Dharma, nor to the enumeration of kalpas;
yet, seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, observing the worlds, and entering into the various kalpas, he never feels weariness or satiety. This is the eighth [quality].
Thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ocean-like Wisdom makes offerings during each and every one of the unspeakably unspeakable kalpas.
They reverently pay homage to unspeakably unspeakable and immeasurable Buddhas by manifesting their own bodies to pass away from this life and be reborn there,
making offerings with all manner of transcendent requisites beyond the triple world; they likewise make offerings to the Bodhisattvas,
Śrāvakas, and the entire great assembly, and after each and every Tathāgata has entered Parinirvāṇa, they offer supreme requisites for worship.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, with inconceivable minds, minds that seek no recompense,

ultimate minds, and minds of great benefit, for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, honor and benefit all Buddhas throughout unspeakably unspeakable kalpas by tending the *śarīra* relics and extensively practicing acts of giving to satisfy sentient beings.
To protect and uphold the True Dharma for sentient beings, and to reveal and expound it— this is the ninth [practice].
It is like the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ocean-like Wisdom (Sāgarajñāna), who, in the presence of all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, and all Dharma-preachers,
single-mindedly and exclusively seeks the Dharma taught by Bodhisattvas, the Dharma studied by Bodhisattvas, the Dharma instructed by Bodhisattvas, and the practice of Bodhisattvas.
The Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Purity, the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Maturation, the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Discipline, the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Equanimity,
the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Renunciation, and the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Dhāraṇī— having attained these dharmas, one upholds, recites, analyzes,
and explains them without weariness, causing immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to all-knowledge within the Buddha-dharma.
When a Bodhisattva enters the true mark of the corresponding mind and attains non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they remain without weariness for unspeakably unspeakable eons;
this is the tenth [quality], O son of the Buddha, whose wisdom is like the ocean. These are the ten ways in which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters into *anuttara* [samyak-saṃbodhi].
The *samyaksaṃbodhi* is like the ocean of wisdom; if bodhisattvas abide in this Dharma, they will attain the great ocean of unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of jewel-like abidings for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. What are these ten? Sons of the Buddha, [the Bodhisattvas... (Note:

The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Mahāyāna sūtra, likely the *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*, specifically the section on the "Ten Jewel-like Abidings" (*daśa-ratnākara-vihārāḥ*). The translation reflects the available portion.)
The Bodhisattva is able to travel to the abodes of countless Tathāgatas in immeasurable worlds to behold them, pay homage, serve them, and make offerings;

this is the first jewel-like dwelling. In the presence of inconceivable Tathāgatas, he listens to the True Dharma, receives and upholds it, recollects it without forgetting, and through analytical reflection, his awakened wisdom increases; such is [the second jewel-like dwelling].

To fill the ten directions is the second jewel-like dwelling. To pass away from this world-system and manifest birth in other places without being confused regarding the Buddha-dharma is the third jewel-like dwelling.

To know that all dharmas arise from a single dharma, and to be able to analyze and expound each of them individually through the ultimate various meanings of all dharmas, is [the fourth jewel-like dwelling].

Since all these are of one meaning, this constitutes the fourth [jewel-like dwelling]: knowing weariness with and detachment from afflictions, knowing the cessation of afflictions, knowing the protection against afflictions, and knowing the eradication of afflictions;
practicing the bodhisattva path without prematurely realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet ultimately reaching the further shore of that limit;
possessing skillful means and being well-trained in what is to be learned, so as to fulfill former vows.
All practices are brought to fulfillment and the body never grows weary; this is the fifth jewel-like dwelling.
One knows that all mental constructions of sentient beings have no location, yet one speaks of various directions and places.
Although there is no conceptualization and no deliberate activity, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, one engages in practice and manifests existence.
To act in this way is the sixth jewel-like dwelling: knowing that all dharmas are of one single nature—namely, the nature of non-nature;
having no diverse natures, no immeasurable natures, no calculable natures, and no weighable natures; being without color and without marks;
such that whether as one or as many, they are all unapprehendable—and thus decisively and definitively knowing this to be the Dharma of all Buddhas.
"This is the dharma of bodhisattvas; this is the dharma of pratyekabuddhas; this is the dharma of śrāvakas;
this is the dharma of ordinary beings; this is wholesome dharma; this is unwholesome dharma; this is mundane dharma;
this is supramundane dharma; this is faulty dharma; this is faultless dharma; this is contaminated dharma; this is uncontaminated."
That "this is a conditioned phenomenon" and "this is an unconditioned phenomenon," up to this point, constitutes the seventh [jewel-like dwelling].
Just as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnasthita seeks the Buddha and finds him unapprehendable, seeks the Bodhisattva and finds him unapprehendable, seeks the Dharma and finds it unapprehendable,
and seeks sentient beings and finds them unapprehendable, yet he does not abandon the training and subduing of sentient beings, causing them to achieve perfection in all phenomena.

What is the "Abiding Like a Jewel" called Right Awakening Vow? It is because the bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully observes and knows the conceptual discriminations of all sentient beings, and knowing the spheres of all sentient beings, employs skillful means to transform and guide them so that they may attain nirvāṇa.
Desiring to fulfill the vow to transform sentient beings, he ardently practices the bodhisattva path; this is the eighth Abiding Like a Jewel.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all skillful means for teaching the Dharma and manifesting nirvāṇa in order to deliver sentient beings are established by the mind’s perception; they are neither inverted nor false. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that all phenomena are equal throughout the three periods of time, remaining as suchness, unmoving, and identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Dwelling therein, he does not perceive even a single sentient being who has been transformed, is being transformed, or will be transformed;
yet he also personally realizes that there is nothing to be practiced and that not even the slightest dharma can be found that either arises or ceases.
Nevertheless, by relying on all dharmas, he ensures that his vows do not go in vain. This is the ninth jewel-like dwelling of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. In this regard:
In the presence of each of the inconceivable and immeasurable Buddhas, they hear the teachings on the bestowal of predictions—
unspeakably unspeakable in number— with various names and different kalpas, from a single kalpa up to unspeakably unspeakable kalpas;
hearing this constantly in such a manner, they practice it upon hearing, remaining without alarm, without fear, without delusion, and without confusion, knowing it as it truly is.
Because the wisdom that comes forth is inconceivable; because the Tathāgata bestows a prediction of enlightenment based on non-duality; because of the superior power of one’s own conduct and vows;

and because one causes those to be transformed according to their needs to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thereby fulfilling all vows throughout the entire Dharma-realm—this is the tenth, the "Jewel-Abiding" stage. Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
Sā, regarding the ten kinds of jewel-like abodes in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall obtain the jewel of the unsurpassed great wisdom of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, what are the ten kinds of adamantine Mahāyāna vows that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva generates? What are the ten? O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva forms this thought: "All dharmas are without limit and cannot be exhausted;
I shall, by means of the wisdom that exhausts the three periods of time, universally awaken to them all without exception.
This is the first adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought: "Within the space of a single hair-tip..."
"There are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, let alone all those within the entire dharma-realm;
I shall bring them all to extinction through supreme nirvāṇa. This is the second adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, he reflects: "The worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable, boundless, and without limit; they cannot..."
"I shall adorn all such worlds as these with the most supreme adornments of the Buddha-fields;
that all such adornments are entirely real—this is the third Vajra-like Mahāyāna vow-mind of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless; there is no..."
"The limits [of these beings] cannot be exhausted; I shall dedicate all roots of goodness toward that supreme wisdom so as to illuminate them.
This is the fourth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, he reflects: "All Buddhas are immeasurable, boundless, and without limit; they cannot..."
"I shall exhaustively dedicate the roots of goodness I have planted as offerings so that they may reach everywhere without deficiency;
only then shall I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This is the fifth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees all Buddhas and hears what they...
When preaching the Dharma, one gives rise to great joy, being unattached to one's own body and unattached to the Buddha-body.

One understands that the Tathāgata’s body is neither real nor false, neither existent nor non-existent, neither having a nature nor lacking a nature, neither form nor formless, neither with marks nor markless, neither arising nor ceasing;
it truly has nothing at all, yet it is not subject to destruction. Why is this? Because it cannot be apprehended as a single [entity].
Because they sever all essential natures and characteristics yet still grasp at them, this is the sixth Vajra-like Mahāyāna vow-mind.
O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may be reviled, slandered, beaten, or tortured by sentient beings;
or their hands and feet may be severed, their ears and noses cut off, their eyes plucked out, or their heads decapitated. All such things they are able to endure.
Enduring all things, they never give rise to thoughts of anger or malice because of them;
throughout unspeakably, unspeakably many incalculable eons, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices to gather in and sustain sentient beings, never ceasing or abandoning them. Why is this?

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have already skillfully observed that all phenomena lack dual characteristics; their minds are neither disturbed nor distracted, and they are able to relinquish themselves.
Because one endures suffering with the body, this is the seventh adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas form this thought: "In future ages, kalpas shall be immeasurable, boundless, without limit, and inexhaustible;
I shall, throughout those kalpas, practice the Bodhisattva path in a single world-system to transform and guide sentient beings."

Even if a single world-system were to arise, and all world-systems throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space were likewise to do so, his mind would not be startled, nor terrified, nor afraid. Why?

Because for a Bodhisattva, the nature of the Dharma is such that he must practice for the sake of all sentient beings. This is the eighth Vow-mind of the Great Vehicle, which is like a diamond. Buddha.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reflects thus: "Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi has the mind as its root.
If the mind is pure, one can fulfill all roots of goodness and will certainly attain mastery over the Buddha's bodhi.
If one wishes to realize Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, it is accomplished immediately according to one's wish. If he so desires...
I am also capable of attaining the one-sided path that severs all conditions for grasping and abides therein;
yet I do not sever them, because I desire to reach the ultimate Buddha-bodhi. Nor do I immediately realize unsurpassed bodhi. Why?
Because I wish to fulfill my original vow by practicing the bodhisattva conduct throughout all worlds to transform sentient beings. This is the ninth [simile], like gold.
O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have resolved their minds upon the Great Vehicle know that the Buddha cannot be apprehended,
enlightenment cannot be apprehended, the Bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, all phenomena cannot be apprehended, sentient beings cannot be apprehended,
the mind cannot be apprehended, practice cannot be apprehended, the past cannot be apprehended, the future cannot be apprehended, and the present cannot be apprehended.

The Bodhisattva thus abides in a state of tranquility, a profound abiding, an abiding in cessation, an abiding in non-contention, an abiding in the ineffable, an abiding in non-duality, an abiding in the peerless,

an abiding in self-nature, an abiding in accordance with reality, an abiding in liberation, an abiding in nirvāṇa, and an abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet even so, they do not abandon anything.

All great vows consist in not abandoning the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), not abandoning the bodhisattva practices, not abandoning the teaching and transforming of sentient beings, not abandoning the perfections (*pāramitā*), not abandoning the subduing of sentient beings, not abandoning the service of all Buddhas, not abandoning the exposition of all dharmas, and not abandoning the adornment of world-systems. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has generated...

Because of his great vows, although he has thoroughly realized the characteristics of all phenomena, his heart of great compassion increases even further, and he fully practices immeasurable merits. Toward all sentient beings, his mind never abandons them. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are non-existent; ordinary beings encounter delusion and neither know nor perceive this, so I shall cause them all to attain it.
I have attained awakening and clearly and distinctly illumined the nature of all phenomena. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas abide in quiescent extinction yet, with a heart of great compassion, teach the Dharma and transform sentient beings throughout the worlds without ever ceasing;
how could I now abandon great compassion? Furthermore, I previously gave rise to a vast vow-mind and resolved to bring benefit.
May all sentient beings give rise to the mind that accumulates all roots of goodness; may they give rise to the mind that dwells securely in skillful dedication;
may they give rise to the mind that produces profound wisdom; may they give rise to the mind that embraces all sentient beings;
may they give rise to the mind of equality toward all sentient beings; and may they speak words of truth, free from falsehood and deception, vowing to [benefit] all sentient beings.

"I vow that the lineage of all Buddhas shall never be interrupted; until all sentient beings have attained liberation, realized perfect enlightenment, and fully perfected the Buddha-dharma, my great vow remains unfulfilled. How could I wish to abandon great compassion?
This is the tenth, the adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind. O Son of the Buddha, this is what constitutes a Bodhisattva.
Mahāsattvas give rise to ten kinds of adamantine Mahāyāna vows of aspiration.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s adamantine nature, the supreme great supernormal power, and wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of great undertakings. What are the ten? O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas... [perform] these undertakings.
To think in this way, "I shall offer worship and respect to all Buddhas," is the first great arousal of the spirit.
Furthermore, to think, "I shall nurture all the roots of goodness possessed by all Bodhisattvas," is the second great arousal of the spirit.
Furthermore, to think, "I shall adorn [the realms] after the parinirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas," [is the third].

One should make offerings to the Buddha-stūpas with all kinds of flowers, all kinds of garlands, all kinds of incense, all kinds of unguents, all kinds of powdered incense, all kinds of robes, all kinds of parasols, all kinds of banners, and all kinds of pennants;
to uphold and protect that Buddha’s True Dharma is the third great undertaking. Furthermore, one should form this thought: "I shall teach, transform, and discipline [sentient beings]."
To subdue all sentient beings and cause them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the fourth great undertaking.
Furthermore, one should think: "I shall adorn all worlds with the unsurpassed adornments of the Buddha-fields"—this is the fifth great undertaking. Furthermore, one should think: "I shall resolve..."

With a heart of great compassion, for the sake of even a single sentient being, one practices the bodhisattva path in every world throughout each and every kalpa until the end of the future, just as one would for that one being, so it is for all sentient beings;
causing them all to attain the unsurpassed bodhi of Buddhahood without giving rise to even a single thought of weariness or indolence— this is the sixth great arousal [of the mind].
Furthermore, he gives rise to this thought: "Those Tathāgatas are immeasurable and boundless;
I shall, for the duration of an inconceivable kalpa, honor and make offerings to a single Tathāgata, and as I do toward one Tathāgata, so shall I do toward all Tathāgatas.
This is the seventh great undertaking of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, he gives rise to this thought: "Those..."
After the parinirvāṇa of each of the Tathāgatas, I shall erect for the relics of each and every one of them a precious stūpa,
vast and high in measure equal to unspeakable world-systems; likewise, I shall create images of the Buddhas in the same manner,
and for inconceivable kalpas, I shall [honor them] with all kinds of jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, incense, flowers, and robes.
To make offerings without giving rise to even a single thought of weariness; for the sake of accomplishing the Buddha-dharma; for the sake of making offerings to all Buddhas;

for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings; and for the sake of protecting, upholding, revealing, and expounding the True Dharma—this is the eighth great undertaking of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Furthermore, he thinks: "I shall, by means of this merit..."
Having established the roots for unsurpassed bodhi and attained entry into the stage of all Tathāgatas, they become equal in essence with all Tathāgatas;
this is the ninth great undertaking. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought:
"Once I have attained perfect enlightenment, I shall expound the True Dharma throughout all worlds for unspeakable eons, manifesting [my presence]."
With inconceivable and sovereign supernormal powers of body, speech, and mind, they do not give rise to weariness and never depart from the True Dharma.
This is because they are sustained by the power of the Buddha; because they diligently practice great vows for the sake of all sentient beings;

because they take great loving-kindness as their primary motivation; because they bring great compassion to ultimate fulfillment; because they have realized the dharma of signlessness; because they abide in truthful speech; and because they have personally realized all dharmas.
Because all things are quiescent, one knows that all sentient beings are entirely ungraspable; yet, because this does not contradict the workings of karma,

because it is of one essence with the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because it pervades the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, because it penetrates the signlessness of all dharmas,
and because it accomplishes the non-arising and non-ceasing [of reality] while being fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas— therefore, by means of these...
To subdue sentient beings through the power of great vows and perform the great work of a Buddha without rest—this is the tenth great undertaking of a Son of the Buddha.
These are the ten kinds of great undertakings of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
if Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will not sever their bodhisattva conduct and will become fully endowed with the unsurpassed, great wisdom of the Tathāgata, O Son of the Buddha.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of ultimate great undertakings. What are these ten? They are: the ultimate great undertaking of reverently making offerings to all Tathāgatas;
the ultimate great undertaking of being able to rescue and protect all sentient beings according to their needs;
the ultimate great undertaking of single-mindedly seeking all Buddha-dharmas; and the ultimate great undertaking of accumulating all roots of goodness... [and so forth].
The ultimate great task of contemplating all Buddha-dharmas; the ultimate great task of fulfilling all vows;
the ultimate great task of accomplishing all bodhisattva practices; the ultimate great task of serving all spiritual friends;
the ultimate great task of proceeding to the abodes of all Tathāgatas in all worlds; the ultimate great task of hearing [the Dharma].
To accomplish the ultimate great task of upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the ultimate task of the great wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of indestructible faith for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? Namely, regarding the first...
Unbreakable faith in all Buddhas; unbreakable faith in all Buddha-dharmas; unbreakable faith in all noble Saṅgha; unbreakable faith in all Bodhisattvas;
unbreakable faith in all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); unbreakable faith in all sentient beings;
unbreakable faith in all the great vows of Bodhisattvas; unbreakable faith in all bodhi...
Unwavering faith in the practice of the perfections; unwavering faith in reverently making offerings to all Buddhas;
and unwavering faith in the bodhisattvas’ skillful, secret expedient means for teaching and disciplining all sentient beings—these are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain unwavering faith in the supreme, great wisdom of all Buddhas.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). What are the ten? They are: receiving the prediction through having profound internal understanding;
receiving the prediction through being able to give rise to all bodhisattva roots of goodness in accordance with that understanding; receiving the prediction through practicing vast conduct;
receiving the prediction through being manifest; receiving the prediction through not being manifest; and receiving the prediction through realizing enlightenment by means of one’s own mind.
Receiving the prediction [of enlightenment] upon attaining realization; receiving the prediction upon achieving patience; receiving the prediction upon teaching and disciplining sentient beings;
receiving the prediction upon reaching the ultimate end of all kalpas; and receiving the prediction upon attaining mastery over all bodhisattva practices—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall receive the prediction from all Buddhas.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dedication of roots of goodness by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to dedicate all their roots of goodness.

What are these ten? They are: dedicating my roots of goodness so that they may be identical with those of spiritual friends, praying that they be accomplished in this way and not otherwise; dedicating my roots of goodness so that they may be identical with the minds of spiritual friends.
May I achieve such accomplishment and not another, through my roots of goodness being identical to the conduct of spiritual friends;
may I achieve such accomplishment and not another, through my roots of goodness being identical to the roots of goodness of spiritual friends;
may I achieve such accomplishment and not another, through my roots of goodness being equal to those of spiritual friends. May I achieve such accomplishment and not another.
By means of my roots of goodness, may I achieve such accomplishment as that of the spiritual friend; may there be no other accomplishment.
By means of my roots of goodness, may I achieve such accomplishment as the purity of the spiritual friend; may there be no other accomplishment.

By means of my roots of goodness, may I achieve such accomplishment as the dwelling place of the spiritual friend; may there be no other accomplishment. By means of my roots of goodness, may I [achieve such accomplishment as] the spiritual friend...

The perfection of knowledge is accomplished in this way; do not seek accomplishment elsewhere. Because my roots of goodness are identical to those of spiritual friends, they are accomplished in this way;

do not seek accomplishment elsewhere. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme dedication of roots of goodness to the Buddhas. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten ways of attaining [this].
What are the ten kinds of wisdom? They are: the wisdom of attaining mastery over giving; the wisdom of gaining profound understanding of all Buddha-dharmas;
the wisdom of entering the boundless knowledge of the Tathāgatas; the wisdom of being able to sever doubts regarding all questions and answers;
the wisdom of entering into the meaning of the wise; and the wisdom of profoundly understanding all Tathāgatas.
Through skillful mastery of speech and sound within all Buddha-dharmas, they attain wisdom and profound understanding;
having planted even a small root of goodness before the Buddhas, they are certain to fulfill all pure and white dharmas.

They obtain the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata and achieve the wisdom that accomplishes the inconceivable dwelling of a Bodhisattva; through this wisdom, they are able to travel to all places in a single thought-moment.
One may say that attaining the wisdom-awakening of a Buddha-field, awakening to the bodhi of all Buddhas, entering all dharma-realms,
hearing and retaining all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas, deeply penetrating the various adorned speech and sounds of all Tathāgatas,
and attaining wisdom— these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they shall attain the unsurpassed [wisdom] of all Buddhas.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sons of the Buddhas who have realized wisdom, have ten ways of generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind. What are these ten? They are:
generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind toward all Buddhas; generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating the realm of all sentient beings;
generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating all lands... [one]... generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating all phenomena.
One should give rise to an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating all worlds and the entire dharma-realm;

one should give rise to an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating that all phenomena are like empty space; one should give rise to an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind by contemplating the vast practices of all bodhisattvas;
and one should give rise to an immeasurable [vast mind] by maintaining right mindfulness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
With a vast and expansive mind, one contemplates the inconceivable karmic retributions of all actions;
with a vast and expansive mind, one resolves to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields; with a vast and expansive mind, one resolves to enter universally into the great assemblies of all Buddhas;
with a vast and expansive mind, one observes the wondrous voices of all Tathāgatas.
The immeasurably vast and expansive mind is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas abide in these minds, they will attain the ocean of immeasurable, boundless, and vast wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of treasuries.
What are the ten? They are: knowing that all dharmas are the treasury for initiating meritorious conduct;
Knowing all dharmas is the treasury of right reflection; knowing all dharmas is the treasury of the illumination of *dhāraṇīs*;
knowing all dharmas is the treasury of eloquence for expounding the teachings; knowing all dharmas is the treasury of the unspeakable, well-awakened reality;
knowing the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas is the treasury of observation and manifestation; knowing all...
The Dharma is the treasury that skillfully gives birth to equanimity; it is the treasury of knowing all dharmas and constantly beholding all Buddhas;
it is the treasury of thoroughly understanding that all inconceivable eons are like illusory abodes;
it is the treasury of generating joyful pure faith toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide therein...
By this Dharma, one attains the treasury of the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas and is able to fully subdue all sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of discipline (*vinaya*). What are the ten? They are:
the discipline of not giving rise to slander toward any of the Buddha-dharmas; the discipline of having a mind of faith and joy toward all Buddhas...
The discipline that can be destroyed; the discipline of respect and reverence toward all Buddhas;

the discipline of never abandoning affection and delight for all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); the discipline of not giving rise to thoughts of [the path of] Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas regarding any [beings];
and the discipline of remaining far removed from all retreats from the Bodhisattva path and not giving rise to any...
The discipline of not harming the minds of sentient beings; the discipline of bringing all roots of goodness to ultimate completion;
the discipline of being able to subdue all māras; and the discipline of bringing all pāramitās to fulfillment—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the discipline of supreme great wisdom, O Buddha.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of mastery. What are the ten? They are:
mastery over life, because they abide for the duration of unspeakable eons; mastery over mind, because their wisdom can enter into incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) samādhis;
and mastery over requisites, because they are able to adorn all worlds with immeasurable ornaments.
Mastery over karma, because one experiences retribution according to the appropriate time;
mastery over birth, because one manifests birth in all worlds; mastery over resolve, because one perceives Buddhas filling all worlds;
mastery over vows, because one attains perfect enlightenment in various lands at will and at any time; and mastery over spiritual power, because one manifests all great miraculous powers.
Because they manifest infinite dharma-gates through mastery over transformations;
because they manifest the ten powers and fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata and attain perfect enlightenment within every thought-moment through mastery over wisdom—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the fulfillment of all Buddhas’ pāramitās, wisdom, spiritual powers, and bodhi.
Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the sons of the Tathāgata, possess ten kinds of unimpeded functions. What are these ten? They are: the unimpeded function regarding sentient beings;

the unimpeded function regarding buddha-lands; the unimpeded function regarding dharmas; the unimpeded function regarding bodies; the unimpeded function regarding vows; the unimpeded function regarding spheres of activity;
the unimpeded function regarding wisdom; the unimpeded function regarding supernormal powers; and the unimpeded function regarding spiritual might.
The Unimpeded Power of Action; O Son of the Buddha, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s unimpeded power of action regarding sentient beings?
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded power of action regarding sentient beings for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. What are these ten? They are:
the unimpeded power of knowing that all sentient beings are without the nature of a sentient being; the unimpeded power of knowing all sentient beings... [and so forth].
Merely by conceiving of the unimpeded function of that which is held, one preaches the Dharma for all sentient beings without ever missing the proper time;
through the unimpeded function of universal transformation, one manifests throughout all realms of sentient beings;

through the unimpeded function of placement, one places all sentient beings within a single pore without any crowding; and through the unimpeded function, one manifests all other directions for the sake of all sentient beings.

He employs the unimpeded function of causing the entire world to see him; he employs the unimpeded function of manifesting the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protecting Devas for the sake of all sentient beings;
he employs the unimpeded function of manifesting the tranquil deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas for the sake of all sentient beings;
and he employs the unimpeded function of manifesting the conduct of bodhisattvas for the sake of all sentient beings.

Manifesting to all sentient beings the physical marks and signs of the Buddha’s form-body, the power of all-knowledge, and the realization of perfect enlightenment—this is the tenth unimpeded function of the Buddhas.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding the lands of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
the unimpeded function of making all lands into a single land; the unimpeded function of entering all lands into one [land]; and so forth.
The unimpeded function of the pores that knows all lands are inexhaustible; the unimpeded function of a single body sitting cross-legged that fills all lands;
the unimpeded function of manifesting all lands within a single body;
the unimpeded function of shaking all lands without causing sentient beings to feel fear; and the unimpeded function of adorning [all lands] with the ornaments of every land.
The unimpeded application of adorning a single buddha-field, using the adornments of one field to adorn all fields;
the unimpeded application of manifesting a single Tathāgata and a single assembly throughout all buddha-fields for the sake of sentient beings;
and the unimpeded application of pervading all small, medium, large, broad, deep, upward-facing, downward-facing, sideways, and upright fields within every field.
To universally demonstrate to all sentient beings the infinite varieties of the nets of all directions through unimpeded function—this is the tenth.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are as follows:
knowing that all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon, and that a single phenomenon enters into all phenomena, yet without contradicting sentient beings.
The unimpeded function of mental liberation arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*, whereby one explains all phenomena for others and causes them all to attain awakening;
the unimpeded function of knowing that all phenomena are free from words, whereby one enables sentient beings to all gain entry into realization;
and the unimpeded function of knowing that all phenomena enter into a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), whereby one is able to expound upon immeasurable characteristics of phenomena.
The unimpeded function of knowing all phenomena as being beyond verbal expression, enabling one to teach infinite Dharma-gates to others;
the unimpeded function of skillfully turning the universal wheel of syllables regarding all phenomena;

the unimpeded function of entering a single Dharma-gate through all phenomena without contradiction, such that even if one were to speak for unspeakable eons, there would be no exhaustion; the unimpeded function of using a single...
The unimpeded function by which all dharmas enter into the Buddha-dharma, causing all sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding;

the unimpeded function by which one knows that all dharmas have no limit; the unimpeded function by which one knows that all dharmas have no boundary of obstruction, being like an illusory net with immeasurable distinctions, which can never be exhausted even if explained for sentient beings throughout immeasurable eons—this is it.
O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions of the body. What are these ten? They are:
the unimpeded function of entering the bodies of all sentient beings into one’s own body; the unimpeded function of entering one’s own body into the bodies of all sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of entering the bodies of all Buddhas into the body of a single Buddha; [and the unimpeded function of entering] the body of a single Buddha...
Entering the unimpeded function of the bodies of all Buddhas; entering all lands into one's own body with unimpeded function;
filling all phenomena of the three periods of time with a single body to manifest to sentient beings with unimpeded function; manifesting boundless bodies from within a single body;
entering samādhi with unimpeded function; and manifesting from within a single body as many bodies as there are sentient beings to achieve perfect enlightenment.
To realize unimpeded function in the bodies of all sentient beings; to manifest the body of a single sentient being within the bodies of all sentient beings;
to manifest the bodies of all sentient beings within the body of a single sentient being; to manifest the Dharma-body through the unimpeded function in the bodies of all sentient beings;
and to manifest the bodies of all sentient beings within the Dharma-body—these are the ten.
