Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty.
The Treatise composed by Li Tongxuan, Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan of the Tang Dynasty;
the Sūtra-collation and Treatise-compilation by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Monastery in Fuzhou of the Tang Dynasty;
Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part Four: On Leaving the World.
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded applications of the vows of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:

the unimpeded application of making all the vows of all Bodhisattvas one’s own vow; the unimpeded application of manifesting the attainment of self-enlightenment through the power of the vows of all Buddhas to attain Bodhi;
[the unimpeded application of] attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi oneself according to the beings to be transformed...
The unimpeded function of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the unimpeded function of not interrupting great vows throughout all infinite eons;
the unimpeded function of distancing oneself from the body of consciousness and adhering to the body of wisdom; the unimpeded function of manifesting all bodies through the power of sovereign vows;
the unimpeded function of relinquishing one's own body to fulfill the vows of others; and the unimpeded function of universally teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
Having been born, they do not abandon their great vows; they employ unimpeded power throughout all eons to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, yet their great vows remain uninterrupted.

They employ unimpeded power to manifest perfect enlightenment within a single pore, and by the power of their vows, they pervade all buddha-fields, acting for the sake of each and every sentient being throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds.

This is the manifestation of unimpeded function: by proclaiming a single phrase of the Dharma, it pervades the entire dharma-realm, raising great clouds of the True Dharma, flashing the lightning of liberation, thundering the roar of the true Dharma, and raining down the flavor of ambrosia;
through the power of great vows, it saturates all realms of sentient beings—this unimpeded function constitutes the tenth [stage] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, O Son of the Buddha.
There are ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding objective realms. What are these ten? They are:

the unimpeded function of abiding in the realm of the Dharma-dhātu while not abandoning the realm of sentient beings; the unimpeded function of abiding in the realm of the Buddhas while not abandoning the realm of Māras;
the unimpeded function of abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa while not abandoning the realm of saṃsāra; and entering into all [realms].
Abiding in the realm of wisdom without severing the realm of the bodhisattva lineage through the unimpeded function;
abiding in the realm of tranquility without abandoning the realm of distraction through the unimpeded function;

abiding in the realm that is without going or coming, without conceptual proliferation, without characteristics, without essence, and beyond verbal expression—like the realm of space—yet without abandoning the playful activity for all sentient beings.
The unimpeded function of abiding in the realm of the powers and liberations while not abandoning the realms of all locations;
the unimpeded function of entering the realm of the limit of non-sentient beings while not abandoning the unimpeded function of teaching and transforming all sentient beings;
and the unimpeded function of abiding in the realm of meditative concentration, liberation, supernormal power, clear wisdom, and tranquility while—

The unimpeded function of manifesting birth in all worlds; the unimpeded function of dwelling in the realm of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment adorned by all his practices while manifesting the tranquil deportment of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—these are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions of wisdom for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are they?
The ten are: the unimpeded function of inexhaustible eloquence; the unimpeded function of never forgetting any *dhāraṇīs*;
the unimpeded function of definitively knowing and definitively explaining the faculties of all sentient beings;

the unimpeded function of knowing, in a single thought-moment, the mental activities of all sentient beings through unimpeded wisdom; and the unimpeded function of knowing all... [the text continues].

The unimpeded function of administering medicine according to the needs of sentient beings—whether they desire pleasure, possess latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), habitual perfusions (*vāsanā*), or the diseases of afflictions—and the unimpeded function of entering the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata in a single thought-moment; the unimpeded function of knowing all eons of the three periods of time and the sentient beings therein through unimpeded wisdom;
and the manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment in every thought-moment to reveal it to sentient beings.
There is the unimpeded application of severing [delusions] regarding one sentient being while knowing the karma of all sentient beings;
there is the unimpeded application of understanding the speech of all sentient beings through the sound of one sentient being. These are the ten.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded applications of the supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? Namely, regarding...
Manifesting the body of all worlds within a single body without obstruction;
hearing and receiving the teachings spoken in the assemblies of all Buddhas within the assembly of a single Buddha without obstruction;
accomplishing ineffable, unsurpassed enlightenment within the mental thought of a single sentient being and awakening the minds of all sentient beings without obstruction; [using] a single voice...
The unimpeded function of manifesting the diverse sounds and languages of all worlds so that all sentient beings may each attain understanding;

the unimpeded function of manifesting within a single thought-moment all the various distinctions of karmic fruits throughout all kalpas of the past, so that all sentient beings may fully know and see them;
and the manifestation of vast Buddha-fields from within a single atom, immeasurable...
The unimpeded function of majestic adornment that causes all worlds to be fully adorned; the unimpeded function of universal entry into all three periods of time;
the unimpeded function of emitting the great light of Dharma that manifests the bodhi, sentient beings, practices, and vows of all Buddhas;
and the skillful protection of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras.

The ten powers of the Tathāgata, the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas, and the unimpeded functions of garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas— these constitute the ten.
If bodhisattvas attain these unimpeded functions, they are able to universally enter all Buddha-dharmas, O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
There are ten kinds of unimpeded applications of spiritual power. What are these ten? They are: the unimpeded application of placing unspeakably many worlds within a single atom;
the unimpeded application of manifesting within a single atom all Buddha-fields equal in extent to the Dharma-realm;
and the unimpeded application of placing the waters of all great oceans within a single pore while traveling back and forth through the worlds of the ten directions.
Yet, they do not disturb or afflict sentient beings, remaining unimpeded;
they manifest all manner of supernatural powers within their own bodies inside unspeakable worlds without obstruction;
and with a single hair, they bind together countless Diamond Ring Mountains (*vajraparvata*) and travel through all worlds, never causing sentient beings to give rise to a heart of fear.

The unimpeded function of making an unspeakable number of eons into a single eon and a single eon into an unspeakable number of eons, manifesting therein the distinctions of formation and destruction without causing sentient beings any fear;

the unimpeded function of manifesting the various calamities of water, fire, and wind throughout all worlds to bring about transformation and decay without distressing sentient beings; the unimpeded function of all...
When the three calamities destroy the world-system, they are able to protect and sustain all the necessities of life for all sentient beings, ensuring nothing is damaged or lacking;

with unimpeded power, they can hold inconceivable world-systems in a single hand and cast them beyond unspeakable world-systems without causing sentient beings any sense of alarm or fear; with unimpeded power, they can explain that all lands are identical to empty space.

To cause all sentient beings to fully attain realization through unimpeded function—this is the tenth. O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions of the power of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are: the unimpeded function of the power of sentient beings, because of teaching, transforming, and taming them without ever abandoning them;
the unimpeded function of the power of buddha-fields, because of manifesting unspeakably many adornments...
The unimpeded function of the power of adornment, because it is majestic and solemn; the unimpeded function of the power of the Dharma, because it causes all bodies to enter the bodyless state;
the unimpeded function of the power of the eons, because its cultivation is uninterrupted; the unimpeded function of the power of the Buddha, because it awakens those who are asleep;

the unimpeded function of the power of practice, because it encompasses all bodhisattva practices; and the unimpeded function of the power of the Tathāgata, because it delivers and liberates [beings].
Because of all sentient beings, there is the unimpeded function of the power of no-teacher; because of self-awakening to all dharmas, there is the unimpeded function of the power of all-knowledge;
because of attaining perfect awakening through all-knowledge, there is the unimpeded function of the power of great compassion;

because of not abandoning any sentient being, [there is the unimpeded function of the power of great compassion]. These, O Son of the Buddha, are called the ten [powers] of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Regarding the cultivation of these unimpeded functions: if one attains these ten unimpeded functions, then whether one wishes to realize or not realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it will be according to one's will without obstruction. Even after attaining perfect enlightenment, one does not cease practicing the bodhisattva conduct.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have made great vows to enter the infinite and unimpeded.
Because they skillfully manifest through the gateway of means, O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of playful mastery (*vikrīḍita*). What are these ten? They are as follows:
to manifest the body of a buddha-field (*kṣetra-kāya*) by means of the body of a sentient being, yet without destroying the body of the sentient being—this is the playful mastery of a Bodhisattva;
to manifest the body of a sentient being by means of the body of a buddha-field, yet without destroying the body of the buddha-field—this is the playful mastery of a Bodhisattva.
This bodhisattva sports within the body of a Buddha, manifesting the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas without diminishing the body of a Tathāgata;
this bodhisattva sports within the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, manifesting the body of a Tathāgata without increasing the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
this bodhisattva sports within the body of bodhisattva conduct, manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

To have a body yet not sever the body of bodhisattva practice; to manifest a body that sports in the attainment of perfect enlightenment while manifesting a body that cultivates bodhisattva practice, yet without diminishing the body of the attainment of *bodhi*;
to manifest a body within the realm of *nirvāṇa* while sporting in the cycle of birth and death, yet without being attached to birth and death—this is the bodhisattva’s sport in birth.
Manifesting the realm of death and nirvana, yet not ultimately entering into nirvana;
this is the bodhisattva’s play, wherein they enter samādhi and manifest all activities—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—without ever abandoning the meditative absorption of samādhi.
This is the bodhisattva’s play, wherein they hear the Dharma from a single Buddha and receive and uphold it, their body remaining unmoving, yet by means of [their] three...

By the power of their profound concentration, within the assemblies of unspeakably many Buddhas, they each manifest their own bodies—neither dividing themselves nor arising from meditative equipoise—and hear the Dharma, receiving and upholding it in an uninterrupted succession.
Thus, in every thought-moment, from each body of samādhi, they produce unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodies of samādhi; in this manner, they proceed through all [the assemblies].
Eons may yet be exhausted, but the body of a bodhisattva’s samādhi cannot be exhausted; this is the bodhisattva’s play, which constitutes the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom-play.
Disciples of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of spheres. What are the ten? They are as follows: namely, manifesting...
To manifest the gateway of the boundless realm of phenomena so that sentient beings may enter it is the bodhisattva’s sphere;
to manifest the infinite, wondrous adornments of all worlds so that sentient beings may enter them is the bodhisattva’s sphere;
to transform and proceed to all realms of sentient beings, awakening them through every skillful means, is the bodhisattva’s sphere; from the body of the Tathāgata, [to bring forth] Bodhi...
To manifest the body of a Tathāgata from the body of a Bodhisattva is the domain of a Bodhisattva;
to manifest world-systems within the realm of empty space and to manifest the realm of empty space within world-systems is the domain of a Bodhisattva;

to manifest the realm of nirvāṇa within the realm of saṃsāra and to manifest the realm of saṃsāra within the realm of nirvāṇa is the domain of a Bodhisattva; [to do so] regarding the speech of a single sentient being...
To produce all Buddha-dharma speech from within words is the bodhisattva’s realm;

to manifest as a single body with boundless bodies, and to manifest as all distinct bodies from a single body, is the bodhisattva’s realm; to fill the entire dharma-realm with a single body is the bodhisattva’s realm;
and to cause all sentient beings to generate [the aspiration for enlightenment] within a single thought-moment is the bodhisattva’s realm.
The manifestation of infinite bodies from each bodhicitta and the attainment of perfect enlightenment—this is the realm of the bodhisattva; this constitutes the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the realm of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of power. What are the ten? They are: the power of profound resolve; the power of... [and so forth].
Because it is intermingled with all worldly conditions, it is the power of superior resolve (*adhyāśaya-bala*) that does not abandon any Buddha-dharma;

because whatever is undertaken is brought to completion, it is the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*); because it understands all mental activities, it is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-bala*); because it fulfills all that is sought, it is the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*);
because it remains uninterrupted until the end of the future, it is the power of practice (*caryā-bala*); and because it is able to give birth [to all], it is the power of the vehicle (*yāna-bala*).

The power of spiritual transformations, by not abandoning the Great Vehicle while engaging with all vehicles, manifests within each and every pore all pure worlds and the appearance of all Tathāgatas in the world;

the power of awakening, by causing all sentient beings to resolve to attain Buddhahood without interruption; and the power of turning the wheel of Dharma, by proclaiming a single phrase of the teaching.
Because they accord with the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings, these constitute the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the supreme, all-encompassing ten powers of omniscience of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of fearlessness for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to hear and retain everything.

In all verbal discourse, one should maintain this reflection: "Suppose there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings coming from the ten directions to question me regarding hundreds of thousands of great dharmas; I would not perceive even the slightest sign of difficulty in answering those questions.
Because I perceive no such difficulty, my mind attains fearlessness, ultimately reaching the shore of that great fearlessness, according to their [needs]."
Question: To be able to respond to all inquiries, severing their doubts without any timidity—this is the first fearlessness of a Bodhisattva.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has received the Tathāgata’s consecration and possesses unimpeded eloquence, reaching the ultimate further shore by revealing the secrets of all written characters, words, and sounds, they form this thought: "Suppose there were a multitude..."
Innumerable and boundless beings come from the ten directions to question me regarding immeasurable dharmas.

In those questions, I do not perceive even the slightest sign of difficulty in answering; because I see no such difficulty, my mind attains fearlessness, reaching the ultimate shore of great fearlessness.
According to whatever they ask, I am able to provide a response that severs their doubts and perplexities, leaving them without any dread.
This fearlessness is the second [source of] fearlessness for the Bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are empty;

they are devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self; they are without action and without an agent; they are without a knower, without a life-principle, without a nourisher, and without a person (pudgala);
they are free from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and have forever transcended all views. With a mind like space, he acts in this way.
Reflecting that one does not perceive even the slightest mark of any sentient being capable of harming or vexing the bodhisattva’s actions of body, speech, or mind—why is this?
Because the bodhisattva has distanced himself from "I" and "mine," he does not perceive even the slightest mark of affliction in any phenomena.
Since he does not perceive such things, his mind attains fearlessness; having reached the ultimate shore of great fearlessness, he is firm, courageous, and indestructible.

This is the third fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is protected by spiritual power, sustained by the power of the Buddha, and abides in the majestic deportment of the Buddha, their conduct is true and without change. They form this thought:
"I do not see even the slightest aspect of my deportment that would cause sentient beings to give rise to a sense of reproach. Because they do not see such a thing, their mind...
To attain fearlessness and preach the Dharma with stability and security amidst the great assembly is the fourth fearlessness of a Bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely pure, bright white, gentle, and free from all evils, they reflect thus:
"I do not perceive even the slightest portion of my own actions of body, speech, or mind that is worthy of censure."

Because they do not perceive the characteristics of blame, their minds attain fearlessness; they are able to cause sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-dharma—this is the fifth fearlessness of a bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is constantly attended and guarded by the Vajrapāṇis, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
All Tathāgatas protect and do not abandon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who forms this thought:
"I do not see any Māras, non-Buddhists, or sentient beings with [wrong] views who can come to obstruct even a small portion of my practice of the Bodhisattva path.
Because he does not see them, his mind attains fearlessness, and having reached the ultimate shore of that great fearlessness, he gives rise to a heart of joy.
To practice the bodhisattva conduct is the sixth fearlessness of a bodhisattva.

Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already achieved the first faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) such that the mind is free from forgetfulness, he is approved by the Buddhas. He forms this thought:
"Regarding the words, phrases, and dharmas of the path to awakening taught by the Tathāgata, I do not perceive even the slightest portion within them that could be forgotten."
Because they have lost the characteristics of [delusion] through non-perception, their minds attain fearlessness;
they uphold the true Dharma of all Tathāgatas and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva—this is the seventh fearlessness of a bodhisattva.

O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has fully mastered wisdom and skillful means, has attained the ultimate perfection of all bodhisattva powers, and constantly and diligently teaches and transforms all beings.
Sentient beings constantly bind their aspirational minds to the Bodhi of the Buddha;
yet, out of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of maturing them, they manifest birth within a defiled world of afflictions.

They appear with noble lineage, a perfect retinue, and all desires fulfilled according to their hearts' wishes, experiencing joy and happiness. Nevertheless, they reflect: "Although I am gathered here with this retinue..."
If one sees minor signs and becomes attached to them, thereby abandoning my cultivation of dhyāna, samādhi, liberation, and all dhāraṇīs and eloquence—the dharmas of the bodhisattva path—why is this?
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained mastery over all dharmas and reached the other shore;
while cultivating the bodhisattva practice, they vow never to sever it, seeing nothing in the world that [could cause such attachment].
Because they do not perceive that which could delude the Bodhisattva path within a single realm, their minds attain fearlessness and they reach the ultimate shore of great fearlessness;
through the power of their great vows, they manifest birth in all worlds—this is the eighth fearlessness of the Bodhisattva.
Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never forgets the *saṃbhāra* (provisions).
The *vibhava-citta* (the mind of awakening) mounts the Great Vehicle and practices the conduct of a bodhisattva;
by the power of the great mind of omniscience, it manifests all the tranquil deportments of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, while forming this thought:
"I do not perceive within myself even the slightest sign of seeking deliverance through the two vehicles. Because such signs are not perceived, the mind attains fearlessness.
That supreme, great, and fearless shore which can universally manifest all vehicles and paths, the ultimate fulfillment of the equal Mahāyāna—
this is the ninth fearlessness of the Bodhisattva. O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has accomplished all pure and white dharmas,
is endowed with roots of goodness, and has perfected supernatural powers, they ultimately abide in the state of all Buddhas.
Having fulfilled all bodhisattva practices and received the consecration of omniscience from all Buddhas,
they constantly transform sentient beings while practicing the bodhisattva path, maintaining this thought:
"I do not see a single sentient being who should be matured whom I am unable to mature through the manifestation of the sovereign power of all Buddhas."
Because they do not perceive [any duality], their minds attain fearlessness, reaching the ultimate shore of great fearlessness;

they do not sever the bodhisattva practices nor abandon the bodhisattva vows. According to the needs of all sentient beings to be transformed, they manifest the realm of the Buddha to deliver and transform them.
This is the tenth fearlessness of a Buddha-son; these are the ten kinds of fearlessness of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Fearlessness: If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they attain the supreme, great fearlessness of all Buddhas, yet they do not abandon the fearlessness of Bodhisattvas.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of uncommon dharmas of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten?
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas naturally practice the six perfections without being taught by others.
The pāramitās consist of always delighting in great giving without generating stinginess; constantly maintaining pure precepts without any transgression;
being fully endowed with patience such that the mind is unshakable; possessing great vigor that never regresses; skillfully entering the various dhyānas without ever becoming distracted;
and adeptly cultivating wisdom to completely eliminate all evil views—this is the foremost [practice], which follows spontaneously without depending on the instruction of others.
Following the path of the *pāramitās*, the sons of the Buddha—the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—cultivate the six perfections and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
They are able to universally embrace all sentient beings by means of material wealth and the Dharma, practicing generosity;

they maintain right mindfulness before them, speak with gentle countenance and loving words, and with a joyful heart, reveal the meaning as it truly is, causing others to attain awakening to the Bodhi of all Buddhas.

To be without hatred or partiality and to benefit all equally is the second unique quality of a Buddha-son, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: to diligently gather in sentient beings by following the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) without relying on the instruction of others.

This skillful dedication consists of dedicating without seeking karmic rewards, dedicating in accordance with the Bodhi of the Buddhas, and not being attached to any worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Dedicating samādhi for the benefit of all sentient beings, and dedicating it so as not to sever the wisdom of the Tathāgata—this is the third [dedication].
Without relying on the instruction of others, for the sake of all sentient beings, they initiate roots of goodness and seek the Buddha’s wisdom and the uncommon dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reaches the ultimate consummation of skillful means.

With a mind like the shore, he constantly looks back upon all sentient beings; he does not weary of the mundane realms of the foolish and ordinary, nor does he delight in the path of renunciation of the two vehicles.

Unattached to his own happiness, he exerts himself only in transforming and delivering others. He is skillfully able to enter and emerge from meditative concentrations and liberations, attaining complete mastery over all samādhis.
As he comes and goes through birth and death, it is as if he were wandering through a garden, never for a moment ceasing.
They give rise to a mind of weariness and fatigue; they may dwell in the palaces of Māra, or manifest their bodies within all places of birth—whether as Śakra, Brahmā, or the lords of the world.
They may even go forth among the assemblies of non-Buddhists, yet they remain forever far removed from all false views.
Furthermore, regarding all worldly literature, incantations, scripts, seals, mathematics, and even [their] wandering...
They manifest all methods of drama, song, and dance with such exquisite skill that none are lacking; at times they manifest as beautiful women whose wisdom and talent are foremost in the world.

Regarding all mundane and supramundane dharmas, they are able to inquire and explain, and through their questions and answers, they resolve all doubts to the ultimate degree; they are likewise thoroughly proficient in all matters, both mundane and supramundane.
Having reached the further shore, all sentient beings constantly come to gaze upon him; though he manifests the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he does not lose the mind of the Mahāyāna;

though in every thought-moment he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment, he does not cease his bodhisattva practices—this is the fourth unique [quality], the skillful means of reaching the ultimate further shore without depending on the instruction of another.
O sons of the Dharma, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas skillfully know the path that unifies skillful means and reality; they possess mastery over wisdom and reach the ultimate, which is to say:
they abide in nirvāṇa yet manifest birth and death; they know there are no sentient beings yet diligently practice teaching and transforming others;
they abide in ultimate quiescence yet manifest the arising of afflictions; and they dwell in the single, firm, and dense Dharmakāya of wisdom.
While universally manifesting the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings, he constantly enters deep meditative concentration yet displays the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;

he is eternally far removed from the three realms yet does not abandon sentient beings; he ever delights in the joy of the Dharma yet manifests the presence of court ladies, singing, and playful merriment;
and though his body is adorned with all the marks and signs of excellence, he displays the forms of the ugly, the poor, and the lowly.
Constantly accumulating all manner of virtues and being free from all faults and evils, they manifest birth in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
yet, although they have already reached the further shore of the Buddha's wisdom, they do not abandon the bodhisattva’s body of wisdom.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such immeasurable wisdom, even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know it, let alone any ordinary person.
To protect all sentient beings is the fifth unshared quality of the Buddhas, wherein both the provisional and the ultimate are practiced simultaneously without depending on the instruction of others.
O Son of the Buddha, the physical, verbal, and mental actions of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva follow wisdom and are entirely pure;

that is to say, they are fully endowed with great compassion and forever free from the intent to kill, up to being fully endowed with right understanding and devoid of false views. This is the [fifth].
Sixth, the uncommon quality of acting in accordance with wisdom through body, speech, and mind without relying on the instruction of others:
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is fully endowed with great compassion and does not abandon sentient beings;

for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he undergoes all manner of sufferings—namely, the sufferings of hell, the sufferings of animals, and the sufferings of hungry ghosts—without ever giving rise to weariness. Only...
To single-mindedly deliver all sentient beings without ever being stained by the realms of the five desires, and to always be diligent in extinguishing all sufferings—
this is the seventh unique quality of arising great compassion without depending on the instruction of others. O Son of the Buddha,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is always one whom the Brahma Kings, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings delight to behold.
All sentient beings behold [the Bodhisattva] without ever being satiated. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has practiced pure conduct for a vast period of time and is free from all faults; therefore, sentient beings never tire of seeing him.
This is the eighth unshared quality (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Buddha-son, Bodhisattva: that all sentient beings delight in beholding him without depending on the instruction of others.
The Mahāsattva, having adorned himself with the great vow for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and possessing firm resolve and aspiration,
does not ultimately lose the mind of omniscience— the clear, pure, and wondrous jewel— even while dwelling in the perilous places of ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. Son of the Buddha,
it is like a jewel named "Pure Adornment" which, even when placed in the midst of mud and mire, does not change its radiant color and is able to clarify the turbidity [of the water].
Just as water is entirely clear and pure, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
although they may dwell in places that are turbid and defiled by the foolish and ignorant, they never lose or destroy the jewel-like mind seeking the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

Rather, they are able to cause those evil sentient beings to distance themselves from the impurities of false views and afflictions, enabling them to seek the jewel of the pure mind that seeks all-knowledge.

This is the ninth uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*): by not relying on the instruction of others, even when dwelling in places of great hardship, one does not lose the jewel of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta-ratna*).
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes the wisdom of the realm of self-awakening;

having realized it spontaneously without a teacher, he attains ultimate mastery and reaches the further shore. With the stainless Dharma-diadem crowning his head, he nevertheless remains [dependent] upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
To abandon intimacy with worldly associates and always delight in honoring all Tathāgatas—this is the tenth.

To attain the supreme Dharma without being taught by others, never to be separated from spiritual friends, and never to abandon the respect for the Buddha’s unshared qualities—O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of unshared qualities of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; if Bodhisattvas abide in them, they shall then attain [them].
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of activities that constitute the unsurpassed, vast, and unique qualities of the Tathāgata.
What are these ten? They are: the activity of all worlds, because they are able to completely adorn and purify them;

the activity of all Buddhas, because they are able to make offerings to them all; the activity of all Bodhisattvas, because they plant roots of goodness in common with them; [the activity] of all sentient beings...
Because all karmic actions are capable of transforming and teaching; because all future karmic actions are gathered throughout the limits of the future;
because all karmic actions of spiritual power do not leave a single world but reach everywhere throughout all worlds;

and because they are karmic actions of all-encompassing radiance—they emit rays of light of boundless colors, within each ray of which there is a lotus seat, upon each of which sits a bodhisattva in meditative concentration.
The karma of ensuring that the lineage of all Three Jewels is never interrupted, because he manifests sitting in the full lotus posture;

the karma of protecting and upholding the teachings of all Buddhas after their parinirvāṇa; the karma of all transformations, because he teaches the Dharma and transforms all sentient beings in all worlds;
and the karma of all empowerments, because in a single thought-moment, he accords with the minds of all sentient beings.
Because they manifest whatever is desired so that all vows may be completely fulfilled, this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and vast karma of a Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of bodies of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the non-coming body, which does not [come] into any world;...
It is the body that does not depart because it takes birth; it is the unreal body because it cannot be found anywhere in all worlds;
it is the non-illusory body because it is found exactly as it is in all worlds; it is the inexhaustible body because it demonstrates the world through the principle of reality as it is;
it is the firm body because it remains uninterrupted until the end of the future; and it is the indestructible body because no demons can destroy it.
The body that moves cannot be moved by any demons or non-Buddhists; the body endowed with marks manifests the pure marks of a hundred merits;

the markless body is because the ultimate nature of all phenomena is entirely without marks; the universally-reaching body is because it is one and the same as the bodies of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they shall attain the unsurpassed state of a Tathāgata.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of bodily karma of an inexhaustible body. What are the ten? They are:
first, the bodily karma of filling all worlds with one’s body; second, the bodily karma of being able to manifest one’s body before all sentient beings;
third, the bodily karma of being able to take birth in all realms of existence; fourth, the bodily karma of wandering through all worlds.
The bodily action of proceeding to the assemblies of all Buddhas; the bodily action of being able to universally cover all worlds with a single hand;
the bodily action of being able to grind the Vajra-encircling mountains of all worlds with a single hand until they are crushed like fine dust;
and the bodily action of manifesting within one's own body the formation and destruction of all Buddha-fields to show them to sentient beings.
The bodily karma of containing the bodies of all realms of sentient beings within a single body;
the bodily karma of universally manifesting all pure Buddha-fields within one’s own body so that all sentient beings therein attain enlightenment—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed Buddha-karma of the Tathāgata and be able to awaken all sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas further possess ten kinds of bodies. What are these ten? They are:
the body of the various *pāramitās*, because they practice them all correctly; the body of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), because they do not abandon any sentient beings;

the body of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because they undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without weariness; and the body of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), because they rescue and protect [them].
The merit body, for the sake of all sentient beings; the wisdom body, because it benefits all sentient beings;
the dharma body, because it is of one nature with the bodies of all Buddhas; the skillful means body, because it manifests before all places;
the spiritual power body, because it displays all miraculous transformations; and the bodhi body, which accords with...
Because they attain perfect enlightenment according to the appropriate time, this constitutes the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall obtain the Tathāgata’s body of supreme great wisdom. O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of speech for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: gentle speech, because it causes all sentient beings to be at peace; nectar-like speech...
Because they cause all sentient beings to become entirely cool, they do not speak deceptively; because all their speech is in accordance with reality, it is truthful speech;
because they do not utter false words even in dreams, it is vast speech; because all Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings revere them, it is profound speech;
because they reveal the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is steadfast speech; because they preach the Dharma without... [omission].
Because it is exhaustive, it is speech that is upright; because its utterances are easy to understand, it is speech that manifests in various ways according to the occasion;
because it awakens all sentient beings, it is speech that causes them to comprehend according to their inclinations. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous speech. O Son of the Buddha, such is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
There are ten ways to purify verbal karma. What are these ten? They are: purifying verbal karma by delighting in hearing the voice of the Tathāgata;
purifying verbal karma by delighting in hearing the explanation of the merits of bodhisattvas;
purifying verbal karma by not speaking words that all sentient beings do not wish to hear; and purifying verbal karma by truly distancing oneself from the four faults of speech.
To purify verbal karma by joyfully leaping for joy and praising the Tathāgata; to purify verbal karma by loudly extolling the Buddha’s qualities as they truly are at the stūpas of the Tathāgata;
to purify verbal karma by bestowing the Dharma upon sentient beings with a profoundly pure mind;
to purify verbal karma by praising the Tathāgata with music and song; and to purify verbal karma by listening to the True Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas.

Sons of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies their verbal karma through these ten matters—purifying verbal karma by not begrudging body or life, and relinquishing the body to serve all bodhisattvas and Dharma masters in order to receive the sublime Dharma—then they shall obtain ten kinds of protection. What are these ten? They are as follows:
The celestial kings at their head, with all the hosts of devas providing protection; the dragon kings at their head, with all the hosts of nāgas providing protection;
the yakṣa kings at their head, the gandharva kings at their head, the asura kings at their head, the garuḍa kings at their head, the kiṃnara kings at their head, and the mahoraga kings at their head.
With Brahmā King as their leader, each [of these protectors] shall guard the Dharma-kingship of the Tathāgata together with their own respective retinues;
and with the Dharma-kings as their leaders, all Dharma-preachers shall likewise be fully guarded. These are the ten, O sons of the Buddha.
Once Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have obtained this protection, they are able to accomplish ten kinds of great deeds. What are these ten? They are as follows: first—
May all sentient beings be made to rejoice; may they be able to travel to all worlds;
may all their faculties be fully understood; may all their inclinations be purified; may all afflictions be severed and eliminated;
may all habitual tendencies be abandoned; may all desires and pleasures be made bright and pure; and may all their profound intentions...
To cause all dharmadhātus to increase, to cause them all to pervade all nirvāṇas, and to cause all to clearly perceive them—this is the tenth.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of mind for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows:
the earth-like mind, because it can sustain and nourish the roots of goodness of all sentient beings; the ocean-like mind, the first...
Because all the immeasurable and boundless waters of the Dharma of the great wisdom of all Buddhas flow into it, his mind is like Sumeru, the king of mountains;
because he places all sentient beings in the state of the most supreme mundane and supramundane roots of goodness, his mind is like the king of maṇi jewels;
because he delights in purity and is free from all defilement, his mind is like a diamond; and because he penetrates all things with certainty, his mind is like a vajra.
Because it is the Dharma, its mind is like the Diamond Ring Mountains (Vajra-maṇḍala-parvata), for no demons or externalists can shake it;

because it is the mind, it is like a lotus flower, for no worldly dharmas can defile it; because it is the mind, it is like the Udumbara flower, for it is difficult to encounter throughout all kalpas;
because it is the mind, it is like the pure sun, for it destroys the obscurations of darkness; because it is the mind, it is like space, for it is immeasurable. This is what is meant by...
Tenth: If bodhisattvas abide within these, they attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, and pure mind.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of resolve generated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
the resolve to think, "I shall deliver all sentient beings"; and the resolve to think, "I shall cause all sentient beings to sever and eliminate their afflictions."
I resolve to cause all sentient beings to eliminate their habitual tendencies; I resolve to sever all doubts and delusions;
I resolve to extinguish the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings;
I resolve to eliminate the hardships and calamities of all evil realms; I resolve to reverently accord with all Tathāgatas; I resolve to...
The mind that resolves to well-train in all that is to be learned by all bodhisattvas;
the mind that resolves to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment by all Buddhas upon every single tip of a hair-pore throughout all worlds;
the mind that resolves to beat the unsurpassed Dharma drum in all worlds so that all sentient beings may attain awakening according to their faculties and inclinations—these constitute the ten. If...
When all Bodhisattvas abide therein, they attain the Tathāgata’s supreme mind of great undertaking.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pervasive minds of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. What are the ten? They are:
the pervasive mind of all space, because the resolve of the mind is vast; the pervasive mind of all dharma-realms, because it enters deeply into the...
Because it is boundless, it universally knows the minds of all three periods of time in a single thought-moment;

because it is universal, it clearly understands the minds of all Buddhas appearing in the world—from entering the womb, birth, renunciation, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, to entering parinirvāṇa;
because it is universal, it knows the faculties, desires, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings; thus it is universal with respect to all wisdom.

The universal mind of wisdom, which understands the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through its conformity to it; the universal mind of non-arising, which knows the distinctions within the net of illusions;
the universal mind of non-obstruction, which does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of any phenomena;
the universal mind of sovereignty, which does not dwell upon its own mind or the minds of others; [all this is accomplished] in a single thought-moment.

Because they manifest the attainment of Buddhahood everywhere, these constitute the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain immeasurable and unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas, universally adorning them.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of faculties for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
the faculty of joy, because their faith in seeing all Buddhas is indestructible; the faculty of aspiration... [and so forth].

Because they hear the Buddha-dharma and fully awaken to and understand it, they possess the non-retrogressive faculty; because all their activities are brought to ultimate completion, they possess the stable faculty;
because they do not interrupt any bodhisattva practice, they possess the subtle faculty; because they enter the subtle principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they possess the faculty of non-resting;
and because they bring all matters concerning sentient beings to ultimate fulfillment, they possess the adamantine faculty of realization.
Because it is the nature of all phenomena, it is the Root of Vajra Radiance; because it universally illumines the spheres of all Buddhas, it is the Root of Non-differentiation;
because all Tathāgatas share a single body, it is the Root of Unobstructed Limits;
and because it penetrates deeply into the ten powers of the Tathāgata, these constitute the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they shall attain the unsurpassed state of a Tathāgata.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sons of the Buddha who possess the perfection of great wisdom, have ten kinds of profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*).

What are these ten? They are: the profound resolve that is unstained by any worldly phenomena; the profound resolve that is not mixed with the paths of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*);

the profound resolve that thoroughly understands the bodhi of all Buddhas; the profound resolve that accords with the path of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*); the profound resolve that... [is not... (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end.)
The profound mind that cannot be shaken by any demons or non-Buddhists; the profound mind that purely cultivates the perfect wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
the profound mind that upholds all teachings as they are heard; the profound mind that is unattached to any place of rebirth;
the profound mind that is fully endowed with all subtle wisdom; and the profound mind that cultivates all Buddha-dharmas—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they attain the supreme purity of the profound mind of omniscience, O Son of the Buddha.
What are the ten kinds of superior profound minds of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas? They are as follows:
the superior profound mind of non-retrogression, because of accumulating all roots of goodness; the superior profound mind free from doubt and confusion;... [and so forth].
Because they understand the secret language of all Tathāgatas; because they correctly uphold that which flows from the superior, profound resolve, great vows, and great practices;
because they possess the most excellent, superior, profound resolve that penetrates deeply into all Buddha-dharmas;

because they possess the sovereign, superior, profound resolve that exercises mastery over all Buddha-dharmas; and because they possess the expansive, superior, profound resolve that universally enters into various dharma-gates.
The superior, dominant profound mind that accomplishes all deeds; the superior, dominant profound mind that adorns all samādhis, supernormal powers, and transformations;
the superior, dominant profound mind that dwells securely by upholding original vows;
and the superior, dominant profound mind that matures all sentient beings without rest—these are the ten. If any...
When Bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they attain the supreme, pure, and exalted deep resolve of all Buddhas.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of diligent cultivation for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
diligent cultivation of giving by relinquishing everything without seeking reward; and diligent cultivation of the precepts through the practice of *dhūta* austerities and fewness of desires.

Contentment is practiced because there is no deception; patience is diligently cultivated to abandon the notions of self and other, so that all evils are ultimately never produced and the mind of malice or harm never arises;

vigor is diligently applied to the actions of body, speech, and mind so that they are never distracted, and all that is undertaken never regresses until reaching the ultimate goal; meditative concentration is diligently cultivated so that liberation and samādhi manifest.
He diligently cultivates supernormal powers because he is free from all desires, afflictions, strife, and their attendants;

he diligently cultivates wisdom because he tirelessly accumulates and gathers all merits through practice; he diligently cultivates great loving-kindness because he knows that all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature;
and he diligently cultivates great compassion because he knows the emptiness of all phenomena and universally undergoes suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without weariness.

Because of weariness [with saṃsāra], one awakens to the ten powers of the Tathāgata; through diligent cultivation, one attains unimpeded thorough understanding and manifests them for the sake of sentient beings;
because of diligent cultivation, one does not regress from the wheel of Dharma and turns it until it reaches the minds of all sentient beings—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata; they are the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who practice with diligence.
Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). What are the ten? They are: first, the most supreme resolute conviction, because they plant and honor roots of goodness;
second, the resolute conviction of adornment, because they give rise to various kinds of adornments;

third, the vast resolute conviction, because their minds are never narrow or inferior; fourth, the resolute conviction of quiescence, because they are able to enter the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, the resolve of universal certainty is such that there is nowhere it does not reach;
the resolve of capability and certainty is able to receive the empowerment of the Buddha's power; the resolve of firmness and certainty crushes all demonic activities;
the resolve of clear discernment thoroughly understands all karmic retributions; and the resolve of manifestation appears before one, manifesting supernatural powers at will.

Therefore, it is the definitive understanding that perpetuates and upholds all that has been predicted by the Buddhas; it is the sovereign definitive understanding that attains Buddhahood at will and at any time.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the supreme definitive understanding of the Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of definitive understanding through which they know all things.
What are the ten aspects of the world? They are: knowing how all worlds enter into one world;
knowing how one world enters into all worlds; knowing that all worlds are pervaded by the body of a single Tathāgata and a single lotus seat;
knowing that all worlds are like empty space; and knowing that all worlds are endowed with the adornments of the Buddha.
He thoroughly knows that all worlds are filled with bodhisattvas; he knows that all worlds enter into a single pore;
he knows that all worlds enter into the body of a single sentient being; he knows that all worlds are completely pervaded by a single Buddha’s bodhi-tree and a single Buddha’s site of enlightenment;
and he knows how to cause a single sound to universally pervade all worlds, bringing benefit to all sentient beings.

To understand each [realm] individually and give rise to joy—this is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and definitive resolve regarding the Buddha-fields.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of definitive resolves by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know the realm of sentient beings. What are the ten? They are: knowing all sentient beings...
Knowing that the nature of the realms is without substantial reality, one knows that all realms of sentient beings entirely enter the body of a single sentient being;
one knows that all realms of sentient beings entirely enter the body of a bodhisattva; one knows that all realms of sentient beings entirely enter the Tathāgatagarbha;
and one knows that the body of a single sentient being universally enters all realms of sentient beings, such that all realms of sentient beings are capable of serving [as the basis for awakening].
The Buddhas, as vessels of the Dharma, know the realms of all sentient beings and manifest the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors according to their desires;
they know the realms of all sentient beings and manifest the tranquil deportment of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas according to their desires;
they know the realms of all sentient beings and manifest the bodies adorned with the merits of Bodhisattvas. They know all sentient beings...
To manifest the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of a Tathāgata, as well as his tranquil deportment (*īryāpatha*), within the realm of sentient beings in order to awaken them—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great majestic power and definitive understanding.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows: namely, the bodhicitta.

The habitual tendencies of roots of goodness; the habitual tendencies of teaching and transforming sentient beings; the habitual tendencies of seeing Buddhas; the habitual tendencies of taking birth in pure worlds;
the habitual tendencies of practice; the habitual tendencies of vows; the habitual tendencies of the perfections;
the habitual tendencies of contemplating the equality of all phenomena; and the habitual tendencies of the distinctions among various realms—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in them...

This Dharma is eternally free from all habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśa-vāsanā*), attaining the Tathāgata’s great wisdom—the wisdom of the non-habitual tendency regarding habitual tendencies.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of "grasping" by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not sever the various bodhisattva practices.
What are these ten? They are: first, grasping for the sake of ultimately teaching and transforming the entire realm of sentient beings; grasping for the sake of one... [and so forth].
They take up the practice of the Bodhisattva path for the sake of the ultimate adornment and purification of all worlds;

they take up the roots of goodness for the sake of accumulating the merits of the Buddhas' marks and signs; they take up great compassion for the sake of extinguishing the suffering of all sentient beings;
they take up great loving-kindness for the sake of bestowing upon all sentient beings the bliss of omniscience; and they take up the accumulation of the perfections.
Because of the various adornments of a bodhisattva, they take up skillful means; because they manifest in all places, they take up awakening;

because they attain unimpeded knowledge, briefly stated, a bodhisattva takes up all dharmas and manifests them everywhere through clear wisdom. These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these takings, they will then be able to...
Without interrupting the practices of all bodhisattvas, they attain the unsurpassed, non-apprehensible Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of cultivation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the cultivation of the various pāramitās; the cultivation of training;

the cultivation of wisdom; the cultivation of meaning; the cultivation of the Dharma; the cultivation of renunciation; the cultivation of manifestation; the cultivation of diligent and tireless practice; and the cultivation of accomplishment.
The Samyaksaṃbuddhas cultivate and turn the wheel of the Dharma; this is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas dwell therein, they attain unsurpassed cultivation and cultivate all dharmas.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of accomplishments of the Buddha-dharma for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are:
not being separated from spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to accomplish the Buddha-dharma; having deep faith in the Buddha...

Accomplishing the Buddha-dharma through speech; accomplishing the Buddha-dharma by not slandering the True Dharma; accomplishing the Buddha-dharma by dedicating immeasurable and inexhaustible roots of goodness;
accomplishing the Buddha-dharma by having faith and understanding in the boundless realm of the Tathāgata;
accomplishing the Buddha-dharma by knowing the realm of all worlds; and accomplishing the Buddha-dharma by not abandoning the realm of the Dharmadhātu.
To remain far removed from the realms of all Māras and achieve the Buddha-dharma of right mindfulness; to achieve the Buddha-dharma of the realm of all Buddhas;
to achieve the Buddha-dharma of joyfully seeking the realm of the Tathāgata’s ten powers—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom, O Son of the Buddha.
Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of retrogression from the Buddha-dharma that should be avoided. What are these ten? They are: retrogression from the Buddha-dharma through disparaging spiritual friends;
retrogression from the Buddha-dharma through fearing the suffering of birth and death; retrogression from the Buddha-dharma through wearying of the practice of the bodhisattva path;
retrogression from the Buddha-dharma through not delighting in dwelling in the world; and retrogression through attachment to meditative absorption...
Losing the Buddha-dharma by clinging to roots of goodness; losing the Buddha-dharma by slandering the True Dharma;
losing the Buddha-dharma by severing the bodhisattva practice; losing the Buddha-dharma by delighting in the path of the two vehicles;
losing the Buddha-dharma by harboring resentment toward other bodhisattvas—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas remain far removed from these dharmas, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of detachment.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the children of the Buddha born upon the path of birth, have ten kinds of paths that transcend birth. What are these ten?
They are as follows: first, giving rise to the *prajñāpāramitā* while constantly observing all sentient beings;
second, distancing oneself from all views while liberating all sentient beings bound by views; third, not dwelling upon any mental signs (*nimitta*).
Not abandoning sentient beings who cling to all signs is the third. Transcending the three realms while constantly remaining in all worlds is the fourth.
Being forever free from afflictions while dwelling together with all sentient beings is the fifth.
Attaining the dharma of detachment from desire while constantly using great compassion to pity all sentient beings who cling to desire is the sixth.
Sixth, although always delighting in tranquility, constantly manifesting all retinues; this is the seventh.
Being free from birth and death in the world, yet arising here and there to practice the bodhisattva path; this is the eighth.
Remaining unstained by any worldly phenomena, yet not ceasing any worldly activities; this is the ninth. Although the enlightenment of all Buddhas has already appeared before them...
Not abandoning any of the bodhisattva’s vows and practices—these, O sons of the Buddha, are the ten paths of non-arising for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
These lead to transcendence from the world; they are not shared with the world and are unmixed with the practices of the two vehicles.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the bodhisattva’s definitive dharma.

The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
