Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Commentary on the Scripture*, Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part Five:
"The Chapter on Transcending the World.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of definitive dharmas for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are as follows:
They are certain to be born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas; they are certain to abide within the sphere of all Buddhas;

they have certain knowledge of the deeds to be performed by Bodhisattvas; they are certain to dwell securely in the perfections (pāramitās); they are certain to gain entry into the assemblies of the Tathāgatas;
they are certain to be able to manifest the nature of the Tathāgata’s lineage; and they are certain to dwell securely in the powers of the Tathāgata.

They enter deeply into the Buddha’s bodhi, being certain that they are of one and the same body with all Tathāgatas, and certain that there is no duality between them and the dwelling place of all Tathāgatas.
These are the ten [qualities]. O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give birth to the path of the Buddha-dharma.
What are these ten? They are: following and relying upon spiritual friends; this is the giving birth to the Buddha-dharma.
Because they share the same path and have planted roots of goodness, their profound mind of faith and understanding is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma;
because they know the sovereign power of the Buddhas, they make great vows, which is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma;

because their minds are vast and expansive, they endure their own roots of goodness, which is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma; and because they know that karma is never lost, they practice through all kalpas without weariness.
The path of generating the Buddha-dharma is that which extends to the end of the future;

it is the manifestation of this path of generating the Buddha-dharma in incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya*) in order to bring sentient beings to maturity. It is the non-interruption of bodhisattva practices because it increases great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
It is the path of generating the Buddha-dharma through immeasurable minds, wherein in a single thought-moment one pervades all of space.

Because it is the realm of space, this supreme practice is the fundamental path for giving birth to the Buddha-dharma; because there is no loss or destruction in what is practiced, it is the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

It is the path for giving birth to the Buddha-dharma that causes all sentient beings to joyfully resolve upon bodhicitta, for it is sustained by all wholesome dharmas. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain [them].
The names of the Great Beings—the Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—are tenfold. What are these ten?
They are as follows: they are called *bodhisattva* because they are born from the wisdom of enlightenment;
they are called *mahāsattva* because they dwell securely in the Great Vehicle; they are called *agrasattva* because they realize the foremost Dharma.
He is named Victorious Being (*Vijayasattva*) because he awakens to the supreme Dharma; he is named Most Excellent Being (*Varasattva*) because his wisdom is most excellent;
he is named Superior Being (*Agrasattva*) because he gives rise to superior diligence; he is named Unsurpassed Being (*Anuttarasattva*) because he reveals the unsurpassed Dharma;
he is named Powerful Being (*Balasattva*) because he extensively knows the ten powers; he is named Peerless Being (*Asamasattva*) because he is peerless in the world.
Because there is nothing comparable to it, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya-sattva*); because one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), this constitutes the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas obtain these titles, they then accomplish the Bodhisattva path. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of paths for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are as follows: first, the path of the Bodhisattva is the path of not abandoning solitude.
1. Because of the bodhicitta, these two paths constitute the bodhisattva path; because they give rise to wisdom and skillful means, these three paths constitute the bodhisattva path;
because one practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without attachment to the triple world, these four practices constitute the bodhisattva path;
and because one confesses and removes karmic obstacles, rejoices in merit, reverently honors, entreats the Tathāgata, and skillfully dedicates [merit], [these five] constitute the bodhisattva path.

Because they are without rest, the five faculties are the path of the bodhisattva; because they abide in pure faith, are firm and immovable, and give rise to great vigor until their task is accomplished;

because they are consistently right mindfulness without divergent objects of focus, skillfully knowing the methods for entering and emerging from samādhi, and being well able to discern the realm of wisdom, the six supernormal powers are the path of the bodhisattva, namely:
With the divine eye, they see all forms within all worlds and know the deaths and births of all beings as they pass from this life to another;
with the divine ear, they hear the teachings of all Buddhas, receive and uphold them, and remember them, extensively expounding them for sentient beings according to their faculties;
with the knowledge of others' minds, they can know the minds of others with mastery and without obstruction; and through the recollection of past lives, they remember and know the past.

Because they increase roots of goodness throughout all kalpas, they possess the supernormal power of the psychic faculties (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), manifesting in various ways according to the needs of all beings to be converted so as to cause them to delight in the Dharma;
because they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna*), they initiate the bodhisattva practice without interruption.
These seven recollections are the path of the bodhisattva, namely: recollection of the Buddha, wherein one perceives within a single pore [the entire universe].
One should be mindful of the Buddha because he awakens the minds of all sentient beings;

one should be mindful of the Dharma without departing from it, as one personally receives the sublime Dharma within the assemblies of all Tathāgatas and explains it according to the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all beings so that they may realize and enter it;
and one should be mindful of the Saṅgha, constantly and continuously perceiving them without rest in all things.

One reflects on renunciation by seeing the Bodhisattvas of the world; one reflects on ethical discipline by understanding all the Bodhisattva practices of renunciation and increasing the mind of vast generosity;
one reflects on the heavens by constantly recollecting the Bodhisattvas in their final birth in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; and one reflects on the assembly [of the Sangha].
Because they give rise to wisdom and skillful means to teach, transform, and subdue all beings universally and without interruption,
they accord with the Eightfold Noble Path to Bodhi; this is the path of the bodhisattva, namely, practicing the path of right view by remaining far removed from all false views,
giving rise to right intention by abandoning the mind of deluded discrimination and always acceding with all-knowledge, and constantly practicing...
With right speech, one is free from the four faults of speech because it accords with the words of the Noble Ones; with right action, one constantly practices to transform and subdue sentient beings;

one abides in right livelihood through the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), contentment, and correct deportment, following the conduct conducive to Bodhi and the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), thereby forever abandoning all faults; and with right diligence, one zealously cultivates all the practices of a bodhisattva.
Through ascetic practice, they enter the ten powers of the Buddha because their minds are free from obstruction;
their minds are always in right mindfulness because they are able to remember and maintain all sounds and speech;

their minds are always in right concentration because they eliminate worldly distraction and enter the inconceivable gates of liberation of Bodhisattvas, wherein all samādhis are produced within a single samādhi; thus they enter the ninth stage.

Furthermore, this concentration is the path of a bodhisattva, which is characterized by freedom from desire, ill will, and harm; it consists of preaching the Dharma through all vocal actions without obstruction;

it involves the cessation of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) while employing the discursive thought and investigation of omniscience to teach and transform sentient beings;
it entails abandoning attachment and aversion while beholding all Buddhas with great joy; and it consists of transcending worldly pleasure while conforming to supramundane Bodhi.
The path of the bodhisattva proceeds from this immovability into the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*) without abandoning rebirth in the realms of desire or form;

and while abiding in the meditative attainment that extinguishes all perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), one does not cease the conduct of a bodhisattva. Thus, one trains in the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha, which constitute the bodhisattva path:
namely, the wisdom of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), and the wisdom of knowing the past and future of all sentient beings.

The wisdom that thoroughly knows the causes and effects of present karma; the wisdom that skillfully teaches the Dharma according to the needs of all sentient beings by discerning their superior, middling, and inferior faculties;
the wisdom that skillfully knows the various and immeasurable natures of all sentient beings;

the wisdom that skillfully knows the distinctions among the soft, middling, and superior understandings of all sentient beings and the skillful means to lead them into the Dharma; and this [wisdom] pervades all worlds as one.
In all lands, throughout all three periods of time and all kalpas, they universally manifest the physical forms and majestic deportment of Tathāgatas,
yet they do not abandon the practices of Bodhisattvas. With wisdom, they thoroughly know all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis— whether defiled or pure—
and at both the proper and improper times, through skillful means, they give rise to the wisdom of the liberation-gates of all Bodhisattvas, knowing all things.

The wisdom that knows the distinctions of sentient beings dying here and being born there within the various realms of existence; the wisdom that, in a single thought-moment, fully knows the number of all kalpas throughout the three periods of time;
the wisdom that thoroughly understands the inclinations, latent tendencies, afflictions, and habitual patterns of all sentient beings, as well as their cessation;
and yet not abandoning the practices of a bodhisattva—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas...
Then one attains the unsurpassed path of skillful means of all Tathāgatas.
Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess immeasurable paths, immeasurable auxiliary paths, immeasurable paths of cultivation, and immeasurable paths of adornment.
Son of the Buddha, what are the ten kinds of immeasurable paths of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas? They are as follows: first, because space is immeasurable.
The bodhisattva path is also immeasurable because the dharma-realm is boundless; the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible;
the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable because the worlds are limitless; the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable because the number of eons cannot be exhausted;
and the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable because the linguistic dharmas of all sentient beings are without end.
Because the measure is infinite, the bodhisattva path is also infinite; because the body of the Tathāgata is infinite, the bodhisattva path is also infinite;
because the Buddha’s voice is infinite, the bodhisattva path is also infinite; because the power of the Tathāgata is infinite, the bodhisattva path is also infinite;
because the wisdom of omniscience is infinite, the bodhisattva path is also infinite. These are the ten.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of immeasurable aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa*). They are as follows:
the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas aiding the path is like the realm of empty space; the boundless assembly of bodhisattvas aiding the path is like the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
the inexhaustible assembly of bodhisattvas aiding the path is like the realm of sentient beings; [and it is] like the world-systems...
The Bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the Path is boundless, as infinite as the number of kalpas, such that it cannot be fully described.

The Bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the Path is likewise such that all the worlds together could not exhaustively describe it. Just as the modes of speech and expression of sentient beings are immeasurable, so too the wisdom produced by the Bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the Path in knowing these modes of speech and expression is immeasurable. It is like the body of a Tathāgata, which has no end.
The aids to the path gathered by these bodhisattvas are immeasurable, pervading all sentient beings, all lands, all worlds, and all eons;

they are as immeasurable as the Buddha’s voice. Because a single sound uttered by a bodhisattva pervades the entire dharma-realm such that there is not a single sentient being who does not hear and know it, the aids to the path thus gathered are likewise immeasurable, just as the Buddha’s powers are immeasurable.
Bodhisattvas, receiving the power of the Tathāgata, accumulate the aids to the path (bodhipakṣa) in an immeasurable way;
just as the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) is immeasurable, so too is the accumulation of the aids to the path by Bodhisattvas immeasurable. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten [qualities].

What are the ten kinds of immeasurable cultivation of the path? They are as follows: 1. Cultivating the absence of coming and going, because the actions of body, speech, and mind are without movement; 2.
Cultivating non-increase and non-decrease, because they accord with their original nature; 3. Cultivating neither existence nor non-existence, because they lack intrinsic nature; 4.
Cultivating them as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, like an echo, like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage, and like water.
The Middle Way is cultivated because it is free from all attachments; it is cultivated as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and effortlessness;

it is cultivated as clear vision because one gathers merit without ceasing while observing the three realms; it is cultivated as ineffable, beyond speech, and detached from verbal expression because it is far removed from the establishment of conventional designations and conceptual constructs;
it is cultivated as the indestructible dharma-realm because wisdom manifests the direct knowledge of all phenomena.
1. By cultivating the non-destruction of the reality-limit (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*) through entering universally into the reality-limit and the limit of space;
2. By cultivating vast wisdom through the inexhaustible power of all activities to be performed; 3.

By abiding in the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), cultivating equanimity through the direct perception of all phenomena without doubt—these are the ten. If any...
When Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they attain the Tathāgata’s omniscience and unsurpassed skill in means as sons of the Buddha.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of paths of adornment for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten?

Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not depart from the desire realm, yet they enter the meditative concentrations, liberations, and various samādhis of the form realm and the formless realm.
Furthermore, not being reborn there because of this is the first adornment of the path;
the manifestation of wisdom entering the path of the śrāvaka without using that path to seek liberation is the second adornment of the path;
and the manifestation of wisdom entering the path of the pratyekabuddha while giving rise to great compassion without ceasing is the third adornment.

Although the Path of Adornment is surrounded by a retinue of humans and devas, and attended by hundreds of thousands of maidens singing and dancing, he never for a moment abandons dhyāna, liberation, and the various samādhis; this is the fourth adornment of the path.
He experiences all sensual pleasures together with all sentient beings in mutual enjoyment, never for even a single thought-moment departing from them.

The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Equanimity is the fifth path of adornment; having already reached the further shore of all worlds, they are entirely unattached to any worldly dharmas, yet they do not abandon the practice of delivering sentient beings—this is the sixth path of adornment;
abiding in the right path, right knowledge, and right view, they are able to manifest entry into all deviant paths.
Not grasping at things as real and not clinging to them as pure, causing those sentient beings to distance themselves from false dharmas— this is the seventh adornment of the path.
Constantly and skillfully guarding and upholding the Tathāgata’s pure body, speech, and mental karma so that there are no faults,
and desiring to transform sentient beings who have transgressed the precepts by manifesting the conduct of all ordinary fools, even though one has already perfected purity...

The Bodhisattva abiding in pure merit proceeds toward and manifests birth in all the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and various perilous and impoverished states, causing those sentient beings to attain liberation; yet in reality, the Bodhisattva is not born in those realms.
This is the eighth path of adornment, which is the wisdom that attains inexhaustibility without depending on the instruction of others.
His radiance universally illuminates all Buddha-dharmas; sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, he shares the same Dharma-body as all Buddhas.
He accomplishes all firm, great-person, luminous, and pure secret dharmas;
he abides in all equal vehicles, and the realms of all Buddhas appear before him, fully endowed with everything.
The light of worldly wisdom illuminates all realms of sentient beings, enabling him to act as a Dharma-preacher for them, demonstrating the pursuit of the True Dharma without ever resting.
Although he is in truth the unsurpassed teacher of sentient beings, he demonstrates respect for his *ācāryas* and *upādhyāyas*.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
The Bodhisattva path manifests in accordance with what is appropriate; this is the ninth adornment.
Having perfected the roots of goodness and brought all practices to their ultimate consummation, they receive the collective empowerment of all Tathāgatas.
Reaching the further shore of mastery over all dharmas, they are crowned with the diadem of unimpeded dharma. Their bodies pervade all worlds, appearing everywhere.
The Tathāgata’s unimpeded body is sovereign over all phenomena, reaching the supreme pinnacle;
he turns the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma, having already perfected all the dharmas of mastery belonging to Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests birth in all lands, sharing the same realm as the Buddhas of the three periods of time without ever ceasing.
The Bodhisattva’s practice does not abandon the Bodhisattva-dharma; it does not slacken in the Bodhisattva-activity;
it does not depart from the Bodhisattva-path; it does not relax the Bodhisattva-observance; it does not sever the Bodhisattva’s acquisitions; it does not cease the Bodhisattva’s skillful means;

it does not terminate the Bodhisattva’s performed deeds; it does not grow weary of the Bodhisattva’s generative utility; and it does not stop the Bodhisattva’s power of sustaining. Why is this? Because...

Because the Bodhisattva desires to swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, observes the gateway to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and cultivates the practices of a Bodhisattva without rest—this is the tenth adornment of the path.

If Bodhisattvas abide in this dharma, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great adornment of the path, and yet they do not abandon the Bodhisattva path. O Son of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has ten kinds of feet. What are these ten? They are: the foot of ethical discipline, because he brings all his sublime great vows to complete fulfillment;
the foot of diligence, because he gathers all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) without ever falling back;

the foot of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because he causes sentient beings to rejoice according to their inclinations; the foot of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), because he travels from one Buddha-field to another without leaving the first.
The fulfillment of the profound mind through visiting all buddha-fields; the fulfillment of vows through seeking all supreme dharmas;
the fulfillment of firm resolve through bringing all undertakings to ultimate completion; the fulfillment of compliance through not contradicting the instructions of all venerable ones;

the fulfillment of delighting in the Dharma through tirelessly hearing, retaining, and upholding all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas; and the fulfillment of the rain of Dharma through expounding it for the sake of the multitude without ceasing.
Because they are free from cowardice, they practice the perfection of conduct; because they have distanced themselves from all evils, this constitutes the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and most supreme feet, by which a single step can reach every world-system.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of hands. What are they?
The ten are as follows: the hand of profound faith, because it resolutely accepts and ultimately upholds all that the Buddha has taught;
the hand of generosity, because it satisfies the desires of those who come seeking by providing whatever they wish;

the hand of greeting with a welcoming mind, because it extends the right palm to receive and guide others; and the hand of making offerings to all Buddhas, because it accumulates a multitude of merits without weariness.
Therefore, they possess the hand of extensive learning and skillfulness that completely severs all doubts of sentient beings;

the hand that causes them to transcend the three realms and bestows upon sentient beings the means to pull them out from the mire of desire; the hand that establishes them on the further shore by rescuing drowning beings from within the four violent torrents;
the hand that does not begrudge the True Dharma, fully revealing all sublime teachings; and the hand that skillfully employs all treatises.
Because they use the medicine of wisdom in their hands to extinguish the diseases of body and mind, they constantly hold the hand of the jewel of wisdom;
because they open the light of the Dharma to shatter the darkness of afflictions—this constitutes the ten.

If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed hand of the Tathāgata that universally covers all worlds throughout the ten directions. O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds [of such hands].
What are the ten qualities of the belly? They are: the belly free from flattery and crookedness, because the mind is pure; the belly free from illusion and hypocrisy, because the nature is upright;
the belly that is not false, because it is without treachery or partiality; the belly that does not deceive or plunder, because it has no greed for any object;
the belly that severs afflictions, because it is endowed with wisdom; the belly of a pure mind, because it is free from all evils; and [the belly that] contemplates...
The belly that contemplates food and drink according to the Dharma as it truly is; the belly that observes non-action and awakens to dependent origination;
the belly that awakens to all paths of renunciation; the belly that thoroughly matures the profound mind; the belly that is free from the defilement of all extreme views;
and the belly that causes all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-belly—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these...
By this dharma, one attains the unsurpassed and vast belly of the Tathāgata, which is able to contain all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of treasuries for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows:

the treasury of the Bodhisattva that does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, because it reveals the immeasurable majesty and virtue of the Buddha-dharma; the treasury of the Bodhisattva that increases the seeds of the Dharma...
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is so called because it gives birth to the vast radiance of wisdom; it sustains the lineage of the Saṃgha by enabling beings to enter the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
it awakens those sentient beings established in right concentration by skillfully responding to the proper time without exceeding even a single thought-moment;
and it brings to ultimate maturity those sentient beings who are not yet fixed, acting as the cause for their liberation.
Because its continuity is without interruption, it gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings fixed in error;
this is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it causes all future causes to be fully accomplished. It is the cause that fulfills the ten powers of a Buddha and is indestructible;
this is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it possesses the invincible roots of goodness that subdue the armies of Māra. It is the most supreme, fearless Great Lion’s Roar.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is so called because it causes all sentient beings to rejoice; it is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka because it attains the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
it is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka because its wisdom universally enters all places, thereby fully and clearly knowing all sentient beings, all lands, all phenomena, and all Buddhas;
it is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka because within a single thought-moment, it perceives all things with perfect clarity.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these ten dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed storehouse of great wisdom, which is rooted in invincible roots of goodness.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of mind possessed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:

the mind of diligent effort, because all that is undertaken is brought to ultimate completion; and the mind of indefatigability, for the purpose of accumulating the marks and signs of physical perfection.
Because of the practice of merit, the mind of great courage and strength shatters all the armies of Māra;
because of the practice according to reality, the mind eliminates all afflictions; because of the non-retrogressive mind, it never ceases until reaching Bodhi;
because of the naturally pure mind, it knows the mind is unmoving and unattached; and it knows the minds of sentient beings according to their understandings and desires.

The mind that causes beings to renounce [samsara] and enter the Buddha-dharma; the Great Brahma-abiding mind that knows the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings and protects them without employing other vehicles;
the mind of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action that perceives the marks of the triple world without grasping or attachment;
and the mind adorned with the supreme treasury of the *svastika* mark, as firm as a vajra, for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because even if as many Māras as there are come, they cannot move a single hair [of his body], this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s treasury of the light of supreme great wisdom and mind.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of donning armor for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: donning the armor of great loving-kindness to rescue and protect all beings; one...
They don the armor of great compassion for the sake of all sentient beings; they don the armor of great vows because they endure all sufferings;
they don the armor of dedication because they bring all actions to ultimate completion; they don the armor of merit because they establish all the adornments of the Buddhas;
and they don the armor of the perfections because they benefit all sentient beings and deliver them across [to liberation].
Because they contain all conscious beings, they don the armor of wisdom; because they extinguish the darkness of afflictions of all sentient beings, they don the armor of skillful means;
because they give rise to roots of goodness through the universal gate, they don the armor of the firm and undistracted mind of omniscience;
because they do not delight in other vehicles, they don the armor of single-minded determination; because they are free from doubt and confusion regarding all phenomena, this is [the armor].
10. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they are clad in the unsurpassed armor of the Tathāgata and are able to utterly subdue all Māra armies.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of weapons for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows:
Generosity is the weapon of the Bodhisattva, for it shatters all stinginess; ethical discipline is...
The armor of the bodhisattva is equanimity, because it abandons all transgressions; wisdom is the armor of the bodhisattva, because it cuts off all conceptual discrimination;

right livelihood is the armor of the bodhisattva, because it remains far removed from all wrong livelihood; and skillful means is the armor of the bodhisattva... [because it extinguishes all afflictions].
Because weapons are manifested in all places, it is briefly stated that all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion are the weapons of a bodhisattva;

for by means of the gateway of afflictions, they deliver sentient beings. Birth and death are the weapons of a bodhisattva, for they do not sever their bodhisattva practice while teaching and transforming sentient beings.
To speak the Dharma as it truly is is the weapon of a bodhisattva, for it is able to shatter [ignorance].
Because all attachments are [transcended], omniscience is the weapon of the bodhisattva; because they do not abandon the gateways of bodhisattva practice, these constitute the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they are able to eliminate all the afflictions and fetters accumulated by sentient beings throughout the long night.
Son of the Buddha, what are the ten kinds of heads possessed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
There are ten: first, the head of nirvāṇa, because its crown cannot be seen; second, the head of veneration, because it is honored by all gods and humans;

third, the head of vast resolve, because it is the most supreme within the trichiliocosm; fourth, the head of the foremost roots of goodness, because it is worshipped by all sentient beings of the three realms;
and fifth, the head that bears sentient beings, because it is endowed with the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head.

The head of signs, because it does not disparage others; the head that is eternally supreme in all places; the head of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because it nurtures all dharmas of merit;
the head of skillful means and wisdom in conjunction, because it universally manifests bodies identical to all classes of beings;
the head of teaching and transforming all sentient beings, because it takes all sentient beings as its disciples; and the head of guarding.
It is the foremost protector of the Buddha-dharma eye, for it ensures that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed; this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the foremost, unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of eyes: namely, the fleshly eye, which sees all forms; the divine eye, which sees one... [and so forth].
Because it encompasses the minds of all sentient beings, it is the Wisdom Eye; because it perceives the faculties and spheres of all sentient beings, it is the Dharma Eye;
because it perceives the true reality of all phenomena, it is the Buddha Eye; because it knows and perceives all phenomena, it is the Knowledge Eye;
because it perceives the radiance of the Buddhas, it is the Radiance Eye; because it perceives nirvana, it is the Eye that Transcends Birth and Death; thus it is unimpeded.
Because that which is seen by the eye is unobstructed, the eye of omniscience sees the universal gateway of the dharma-realm; this is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will obtain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great eye of wisdom.
Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of ears. What are the ten? They are: hearing sounds of praise and eliminating [attachment];... [text continues]
Upon hearing disparaging sounds, they sever their hatred; upon hearing the teachings of the Two Vehicles, they do not cling to them nor seek them;

upon hearing of the Bodhisattva path, they rejoice and leap for joy; upon hearing of the various places of suffering and difficulty such as the hells, they give rise to great compassion and make vast vows;
and upon hearing the description of the superior and wondrous matters of humans and devas, they know that all these are impermanent phenomena. Upon hearing [of] existence...
Praising the merits of all Buddhas, they apply themselves with diligent vigor to swiftly bring them to full completion;
hearing the teachings on the six perfections, the four means of attraction, and other such dharmas, they resolve to practice and vow to reach the further shore;

hearing all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they know them all to be like echoes, thereby entering the ineffable and profound, wondrous meanings. From the moment they first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas...
Up until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they constantly hear the True Dharma without even a moment’s rest, yet they never abandon the work of transforming sentient beings;
this is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas accomplish these qualities, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom-ear.
Disciples of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of noses. What are the ten? Namely, hearing all...
He does not perceive foul odors as foul, nor does he perceive various fragrant scents as fragrant;
hearing both fragrance and stench, his mind remains equanimous, abiding in *upekṣā* (equanimity) where there is neither fragrance nor stench.

If he hears the fragrance or stench of sentient beings' clothing, bedding, or their own limbs, he is able to know their conduct characterized by greed, hatred, delusion, or their equal proportions. If he hears...
All the fragrances of hidden treasures, grasses, trees, and so forth, are clearly discerned as if facing them directly before one’s eyes.
If they smell the fragrance of sentient beings from the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, they know all the past deeds those beings have performed.
If they smell the fragrance of the giving, ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom of the various śrāvakas, they abide in the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
They cause [beings] to be moved by reverence when they hear the fragrance of all bodhisattva practices, entering the stage of the Tathāgata through impartial wisdom;
and when they hear the fragrance of the realm of the wisdom of all Buddhas, they do not abandon the various bodhisattva practices. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they shall obtain the immeasurable and boundless pure nose of a Tathāgata, O Son of the Buddha. Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has ten kinds of tongues. What are these ten? They are: the tongue that reveals and expounds the inexhaustible conduct of sentient beings;
the tongue that reveals and expounds inexhaustible Dharma-gates; the tongue that praises the inexhaustible merits of all Buddhas;
the tongue that eloquently articulates inexhaustible speech and eloquence; the tongue that elucidates the aids to the path of the Mahāyāna; and the tongue that universally covers the ten directions.
The tongue that universally illumines all Buddha-fields like space; the tongue that causes all sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding;
the tongue that causes all Buddhas to rejoice; the tongue that subdues all Māras and externalists;
the tongue that eradicates all afflictions of birth and death and leads one to Nirvāṇa—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they shall then attain the state of a Tathāgata.
The Buddha-Son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, possesses ten kinds of bodies that universally cover all Buddha-lands and are unsurpassed.
What are these ten? They are: first, a human body, for the purpose of teaching and transforming all people;

second, a non-human body, for the purpose of teaching and transforming those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; third, a celestial body, for the purpose of teaching and transforming those in the desire realm and the form realm.

Because of sentient beings of the formless realm, he manifests the body of one in training (*śaikṣa*) by way of the stage of training; because of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he manifests the body of an arhat;
because of the stage of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the body of a solitary realizer to teach and transform them so they may enter that stage;

because of the Great Vehicle, he manifests the body of a bodhisattva to bring it to fulfillment; because of the consecration with the water of wisdom, he manifests the body born of intention; and because of skillful means, he brings forth these manifestations.
The untainted Dharma-body manifests for all sentient beings through effortless spontaneity; this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas accomplish these qualities, they shall attain the unsurpassed body of a Tathāgata. Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of intentions of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are as follows: the preeminent intention that initiates all roots of goodness.
The root-mind is securely established because it is firm and immovable in its deep faith; the penetrating mind understands in accordance with the Buddha-dharma;
the internalizing mind knows the inclinations and joys of all sentient beings; the undisturbed mind is unmixed with any afflictions;
and the luminously pure mind cannot be defiled by adventitious dust. Thus, when observing the minds of sentient beings, there is not a single one...
Because mindfulness does not fail at the proper time; because one skillfully discriminates what is to be done so that the mind never gives rise to transgression in a single instance;

because one closely guards the sense faculties so that the mind is subdued and prevented from wandering; and because one skillfully enters samādhi so that the mind deeply enters the Buddha-samādhis, being free from "I" and "mine"—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain all the [qualities] of the Buddhas.
O sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: the practice of hearing the Dharma, because of loving and delighting in the Dharma;
the practice of expounding the Dharma, because of benefiting sentient beings; the practice of departing from greed, anger, delusion, and fear, because of taming one’s own mind;
the practice of the desire realm, because of teaching and transforming sentient beings in the desire realm; [the practice of] the form and formless realms...

The practice of the *dhātu-samādhi* (element-concentration) is for the sake of swiftly turning back [from worldly existence]; the practice directed toward the meaning of the Dharma is for the sake of swiftly attaining wisdom;

the practice in all places of birth is for the sake of freely teaching and transforming sentient beings; the practice in all Buddha-fields is for the sake of prostrating to and making offerings to all Buddhas;
the practice of *nirvāṇa* is for the sake of not severing the continuity of *saṃsāra*; and the practice of fulfilling all Buddha-dharmas is for the sake of bringing them to completion.
Because they do not abandon the practice of the Bodhisattva-dharma, this constitutes the ten [qualities].
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s practice of neither coming nor going. Disciples of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of abidings for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: the abiding in the bodhicitta, because it is never forgotten; the abiding in the pāramitās, because one does not grow weary of providing assistance...
One dwells in the path because it causes the Dharma to abide and increases wisdom; one dwells in the araṇya because it leads to the realization of great dhyāna-concentration;
one dwells in the dhūta practices, contentment, and the four noble lineages because they accord with omniscience; one dwells in deep faith because it bears the burden of the True Dharma;
one dwells in proximity to the Tathāgata because it involves training in the Buddha’s deportment; and one dwells in the arising of supernormal powers.
Because they fulfill great wisdom, they attain the patient endurance of fulfillment and receive the prediction of enlightenment;
because they dwell at the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they are endowed with the powers, the fearlessnesses, and all Buddha-dharmas. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme dwelling of omniscience. Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of sitting. What are the ten?
The so-called Wheel-Turning King’s seat is for the sake of promoting the ten paths of wholesome action;

the Four Heavenly Kings’ seat is for the sake of establishing the Buddha-dharma with sovereign mastery over all worlds; Śakra’s seat is for the sake of acting as the supreme lord for all sentient beings;
Brahmā’s seat is for the sake of attaining mastery over the minds of oneself and others; the Lion’s seat is for the sake of being able to preach the Dharma; and the Seat of the True Dharma.
The seat of dhāraṇī and eloquence, because it reveals and teaches through the power of retention and skillful speech; the seat of firm resolve, because it brings the vow to ultimate fulfillment;
the seat of great loving-kindness, because it causes all wicked sentient beings to rejoice; the seat of great compassion, because it endures all suffering without weariness;
the seat of the vajra, because it subdues all māras and non-Buddhists—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in them...
By this dharma, one attains the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata. There are ten kinds of reclining for the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

What are the ten? They are: first, reclining in tranquility, because the body and mind are serene; second, reclining in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because of practicing according to reality;
third, reclining in samādhi, because the body and mind are supple; fourth, reclining as Brahmā, because of not afflicting oneself or others.
One sleeps with virtuous karma because there is no regret; one sleeps with right faith because it cannot be shaken; one sleeps on the right path because of awakening by spiritual friends;
one sleeps with sublime vows because of skillful dedication; one sleeps having completed all tasks because what was to be done has been accomplished;
one sleeps having relinquished all effort because of total mastery. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide...
Abiding by these dharmas, one attains the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Great Dharma-bed and is able to awaken all sentient beings.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten places of abiding. What are the ten? They are:
taking great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as their place of abiding, because their minds are impartial toward all sentient beings; taking great compassion (*karuṇā*) as their place of abiding...
Because one does not disparage those who have not yet trained, one takes great joy (*muditā*) as one's dwelling place;

because one is free from all sorrow and affliction, one takes great equanimity (*upekṣā*) as one's dwelling place; because one is equal toward the conditioned and the unconditioned, one takes all the perfections (*pāramitā*) as one's dwelling place;
because the bodhicitta is primary, one takes all forms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as one's dwelling place; [and] because of goodness...
Because of skillful observation, they take signlessness as their place of abiding; because they do not depart from the state of correctness, they take wishlessness as their place of abiding;

because they observe the taking of birth, they take mindfulness and wisdom as their place of abiding; because the dharma of patience is fulfilled, they take the equality of all phenomena as their place of abiding;
and because they receive the prediction of enlightenment, [they take this as their place of abiding]. These are the ten. If any...
When Bodhisattvas dwell securely in this Dharma, they attain the supreme, unimpeded dwelling-place of the Tathāgatas, O Son of the Buddha.

There are ten kinds of spheres of activity for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are: taking right mindfulness as their sphere of activity, because they fulfill the foundations of mindfulness;
taking all realms of existence as their sphere of activity, because they perfectly awaken to the course of the Dharma.
They take wisdom as their sphere of activity because they thereby gain the Buddha’s joy; they take the perfections as their sphere of activity because they thereby fulfill the knowledge of all modes;
they take the four means of attraction as their sphere of activity because they thereby transform sentient beings;
they take birth and death as their sphere of activity because they thereby accumulate roots of goodness; and they engage in casual conversation and play with all sentient beings.
They take the spheres of activity as their domain in order to teach and transform beings according to their needs so that they may forever be liberated;

they take supernormal powers as their domain in order to know the faculties and realms of all sentient beings; they take skillful means as their domain because they are in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and they take the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as their domain in order to accomplish all-knowledge without interruption.
Because it is the practice of a bodhisattva, these constitute the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of observation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
the observation of knowing all karmas, because of seeing them in their subtle details; the observation of knowing all realms of existence...
Because they do not grasp at sentient beings, they observe and understand all faculties; because they understand that there are no faculties, they observe all phenomena;
because they do not destroy the dharma-realm, they observe and see the Buddha-dharma; because they diligently cultivate the Buddha-eye, they observe and attain wisdom;
because they expound the Dharma according to reality, they observe the patience of non-arising; because they definitively comprehend the Buddha-dharma, they observe the stage of non-retrogression.
Because it extinguishes all afflictions and transcends the three realms and the stages of the two vehicles;
because it is the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) that observes all Buddha-dharmas with sovereign immovability;

and because it is the samādhi of excellent awakening-wisdom that observes the performance of Buddha-deeds throughout all ten directions—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the state of a Tathāgata.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sons of the Buddha, possess ten kinds of universal observation.
What are these ten? They are: universally observing all who come seeking by fulfilling their wishes with a non-contradictory mind;
universally observing all sentient beings who violate the precepts and establishing them within the pure precepts of the Tathāgata; universally observing... [the rest of the sentence continues].
Because they establish sentient beings with harmful intent within the Tathāgata’s power of patience;
because they universally observe all indolent sentient beings and exhort them to be diligent so that they do not abandon their burden of the Great Vehicle;

because they universally observe all sentient beings with distracted minds and cause them to abide on the ground of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, free from distraction and agitation; [and] because they universally observe all sentient beings with evil wisdom...
He universally contemplates all as spiritual friends of equality in order to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt and destroy views of existence;
he universally contemplates all teachings he hears in order to swiftly attain the realization of the supreme meaning;
he universally contemplates all infinite sentient beings in order to never abandon the power of great compassion; he universally contemplates all...
Because they swiftly achieve all the teachings of the Buddhas and attain all-encompassing wisdom—this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom that universally observes.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of "exertion" (*visphūrjana*) for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are: the exertion of the bull king, which eclipses...

Because he is for the sake of the great assembly of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, he is the "Exertion of the Elephant King," for his mind is well-tamed and supple as he bears the burden of all sentient beings;
he is the "Exertion of the Dragon King," for he raises the great dense clouds of the Dharma,

flashes the lightning of liberation, thunders the roar of the meaning of reality as it is, and brings down the rain of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, and the three [doors of liberation].
Because he obscures the rain of ambrosia, the Great King of Golden-Winged Garuḍas exerts his prowess to exhaust the waters of craving,
shatter the eggshell of ignorance, and seize the various venomous dragons of affliction, causing them to emerge from the great ocean of suffering in birth and death;
because he is the Great Lion King, he exerts his prowess and dwells in fearlessness, using the great wisdom of equanimity as his weapon to subdue all Māras and external adversaries.
Because he is courageous and valiant, he is able to destroy all enemies that are the afflictions within the great battle-array of birth and death;
because he possesses the valor of great wisdom, he knows the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, as well as dependent origination, and is able to freely reveal all dharmas;
and because he possesses the valor of *dhāraṇī*, by the power of mindfulness and wisdom he upholds the Dharma without forgetting it, acting according to the faculties of sentient beings.
Because he proclaims [the Dharma], his eloquence is vigorous, unimpeded, and swift, discerning all things so that everyone may receive benefit and their minds be filled with joy;
thus the Tathāgata’s vigor brings to full completion all the dharmas that assist the path to omniscience.
Through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, whatever is to be attained is entirely attained, and whatever is to be realized is entirely realized.
Because they awaken while seated upon the lion throne, subduing the hosts of Māra and attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, sovereign, and powerful mastery of all Buddhas over all phenomena.
Son of the Buddha, what are the ten kinds of lion’s roar of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas? What are they?
It consists of ten aspects, namely: the Great Lion’s Roar of Bodhicitta, which is the proclamation, "I shall certainly attain perfect, complete enlightenment";

and the Great Lion’s Roar of Great Compassion, which is the resolve, "I shall cause all sentient beings who have not crossed over to cross over, those who have not been liberated to be liberated, those who have not been established in peace to be established in peace, and those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa. Furthermore, [the resolve] that "I shall cause the Buddhas..."
That the lineage of the Dharma and the Saṅgha shall never be severed is the Great Lion’s Roar that repays the grace of the Tathāgata;
"I shall purify all Buddha-fields" is the ultimate, firm vow, the Great Lion’s Roar;
"I shall eliminate all evil realms and places of hardship" is the Great Lion’s Roar of upholding pure precepts; "I shall bring all to fulfillment..."
"The physical, verbal, and mental marks and signs of adornment of all Buddhas" is the great lion’s roar of insatiable seeking of merit;
"I shall bring to full completion all the wisdom possessed by all Buddhas" is the great lion’s roar of insatiable seeking of knowledge;
"I shall eliminate all Māras and all demonic activities" is the great lion’s roar of practicing correct conduct to sever all afflictions.
The Great Lion’s Roar: "I shall thoroughly realize that all phenomena are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, and without person;
they are empty, signless, wishless, pure as space, and are the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas"—this is the Great Lion’s Roar.
It is the Bodhisattva in their final birth who causes all Buddha-lands to tremble and makes them entirely pure.
At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings all came to offer praise and entreaty, saying: "We pray only that the Bodhisattva may manifest birth by means of the dharma of non-arising.
The Bodhisattva then, with the unimpeded eye of wisdom, universally surveyed all sentient beings in the world and perceived that none were his equal;
he immediately manifested his birth within the royal palace, took seven steps by himself, and let out the great lion's roar.
"I shall forever exhaust the limits of birth and death; I am the most supreme and foremost in the world"—this is the Great Lion’s Roar spoken according to reality.
This is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they attain the unsurpassed Great Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure giving for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are they?
There are ten kinds, namely: giving with equanimity because one does not discriminate among sentient beings; giving according to their wishes because one fulfills their aspirations;
giving without confusion because it causes them to obtain benefit; giving as is appropriate because one knows the superior, middling, and inferior capacities;
giving without dwelling upon it because one seeks no karmic retribution; giving with an open hand because the mind has no lingering attachment; and giving everything because it is ultimately pure.
The gift dedicated toward enlightenment because it is free from both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
the gift for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings because it is never abandoned until the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);

and the gift of the threefold purity because one observes the giver, the recipient, and the gift with right mindfulness as being like space. These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will then attain suchness.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who come to the unsurpassed, pure, and vast giving possess ten kinds of pure precepts. What are these ten? They are:
the pure precept of body, because it guards against the three evil deeds of the body; the pure precept of speech, because it is free from the four faults of speech;
the pure precept of mind, because it is forever free from greed, hatred, and false views; and the precept of not breaking anything... [all vows].
The pure precept of training serves as a sovereign lord among all humans and devas; the pure precept of guarding the bodhicitta does not delight in the Lesser Vehicle;
the pure precept of guarding what was ordained by the Tathāgata gives rise to great dread even toward the most subtle of transgressions;
and the pure precept of secret protection rescues those sentient beings who have violated the precepts.
Therefore, the pure precept of not committing any evil because of the vow to cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
the pure precept of distancing oneself from all views of existence because of non-attachment to precepts;

and the pure precept of protecting all sentient beings because of the arousal of great compassion—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
The supreme, faultless, and pure precepts: Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the children of the Buddha, possess ten kinds of pure patience (*kṣānti*).
What are these ten? They are: (1) the pure patience of accepting verbal abuse and insults, for the sake of protecting all sentient beings;

(2) the pure patience of accepting blades and staves, for the sake of skillfully protecting oneself and others; (3) the pure patience of not giving rise to anger or malice, for the sake of [keeping] one’s mind...

Because it is unshakeable, pure patience does not reproach the lowly; because it is supreme, pure patience is capable of great forbearance; because it is expansive, pure patience provides a refuge for all and rescues them;

because it relinquishes one’s own life, pure patience remains far removed from pride; because it does not slight those who have not yet studied, pure patience does not become angry when reviled or harmed;
because it observes things as being like illusions, pure patience does not retaliate even when offenses are committed; because it does not perceive a self...

Because it is not dependent on others, it is the patience of purity regarding secondary afflictions; because it is detached from all objective spheres, it is the patience that accords with the bodhisattva’s true wisdom;
because it knows all phenomena to be unborn and pure, it is the patience that enters the sphere of omniscience without relying on the instruction of others.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain [the state] of all Buddhas without reliance on others.
He realizes the supreme Dharma-patience. O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure diligence. What are these ten?
They are: first, pure diligence of body, because they serve, make offerings to, and honor all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, teachers, and venerable fields of merit without ever regressing;
second, pure diligence of speech, because they [apply it] to whatever Dharma they have heard...
Because he tirelessly and extensively praises the Buddha’s merits for others;

because his pure intention and vigor enable him to skillfully enter and emerge from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and various samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity without rest;
and because his upright mind and pure vigor are free from deception, flattery, crookedness, and hypocrisy, as he exerts himself in all practices without ever turning back.
With a superior and increasingly pure mind, one exerts diligence with a constant resolve to seek ever-higher wisdom;
because of the vow to be endowed with all pure and white dharmas, this pure diligence is not in vain.
It encompasses generosity, ethical discipline, patience, learning, and heedfulness, continuing without interruption until reaching bodhi. Thus, it subdues all māras through entirely pure diligence.
Because it can eliminate all afflictions, entanglements, and hindrances—namely greed, hatred, delusion, and false views—it brings to fulfillment the light of wisdom.
This pure diligence ensures that whatever actions are undertaken are thoroughly examined and brought to ultimate completion so as to leave no cause for regret.
Because it attains all the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), this pure diligence is neither coming nor going.
Having attained knowledge as it truly is, they enter the gate of the Dharma-realm; body, speech, and mind are all entirely equal.

Because they thoroughly understand characteristics and the absence of characteristics and are without attachment, they accomplish the pure diligence of the light of the Dharma. Transcending all stages, they receive the Buddha’s consecration.
With an outflow-free body, they manifest death, birth, renunciation, the attainment of enlightenment, teaching the Dharma, and final nirvana, thus becoming fully endowed with these qualities.

Because these are the deeds of Samantabhadra, they constitute the ten [perfections]. If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, and pure vigor.
*The Compendium on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Eighty-five.
