The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Adornment, Scroll Eighty-Six.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tōngxuǎn, a Lay Elder of Fāngshān in Tàiyuán during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Commentary on the Scripture*, Chapter Thirty-Eight: On Leaving the World, Part Six.
[Sūtra] Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure dhyāna for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? They are as follows:

The pure dhyāna of always delighting in leaving the household life, because it relinquishes all possessions; the pure dhyāna of manifesting and teaching the right path, because it provides true and virtuous spiritual friends;
the pure dhyāna of dwelling in an araṇya and enduring wind, rain, and so forth, because it is free from the notions of "self" and "mine";
and the pure dhyāna of being free from the clamor of worldly beings, because one always delights in tranquility, whereby the activities of the mind become harmonious and supple.
Dhyāna is pure because it guards the sense faculties, whereby the mind and wisdom are tranquil and purified;
dhyāna is pure because it is the skillful means for awakening to the Path, as it cannot be disturbed by any sounds or the thorns of meditative absorption;

dhyāna is pure because it is free from attachment to flavors, as it observes all things through direct realization; dhyāna is pure because it initiates supernormal clarity without abandoning the desire realm; [dhyāna] knows...
Because they possess mastery over the faculties and natures of all sentient beings, they sport freely in pure dhyāna;
because they enter the Buddha-samādhi and realize non-self, these constitute the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, and pure dhyāna.
Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure wisdom. What are the ten?
That which is called the pure wisdom that knows all causes, because it does not destroy the ripening of karmic results;

the pure wisdom that knows all conditions, because it neither conflicts with nor clings to them; the pure wisdom that knows neither annihilation nor permanence, because it thoroughly understands dependent origination as it truly is;
the pure wisdom that uproots all views, because it neither grasps at nor rejects the marks of sentient beings; and the contemplation of all...
Because the pure wisdom that understands the mental activities of sentient beings to be like illusions, there is vast eloquence;
because the pure wisdom that discriminates all phenomena through unimpeded questioning and answering, it is something that no māras, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas can know;
because the pure wisdom deeply penetrates the knowledge of all Tathāgatas, one beholds the subtle and wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas.

The wisdom of the view of self-existence [is pure] because it perceives that the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is pure; the wisdom of purity perceives that all phenomena are entirely quiescent;
the wisdom of purity perceives that all lands are identical to empty space; the wisdom of pure discernment knows that all marks are unimpeded;
the total retention, eloquence, and skillful means of the perfection of wisdom are purified so as to cause one to attain all supreme knowledge. One.

Because they attain the wisdom of vajra-knowledge corresponding to mindfulness, the wisdom of the equality and purity of all phenomena, and the most supreme wisdom regarding all phenomena—these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s great unobstructed wisdom.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure compassion for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are they?
The ten are: the pure compassion of equanimity, because it universally gathers all sentient beings without discrimination;

the pure compassion of benefit, because it causes all who encounter its actions to rejoice; the pure compassion of identifying with others, because it ultimately causes all to emerge from birth and death;
the pure compassion of not abandoning the world, because the mind constantly takes it as an object of mindfulness while accumulating roots of goodness.
Therefore, they possess the pure compassion that reaches liberation, which causes all sentient beings to eliminate every affliction;
the pure compassion that gives birth to bodhi, which causes all sentient beings to resolve to seek the mind of omniscience;
the pure compassion that is unimpeded in the world, which emits great radiance to shine equally and universally upon all; and the pure compassion that fills all of space.

The loving-kindness that rescues and protects sentient beings because it reaches everywhere; the pure loving-kindness with an object (*sālambana*) because it realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) and the true dharma;
and the pure loving-kindness without an object (*anālambana*) because it enters the bodhisattva’s state of non-arising—these are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure loving-kindness.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure compassion. What are the ten? They are: pure compassion that is peerless, because it arises from a solitary resolve;
pure compassion free from weariness, because one undergoes suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without considering it a toil;
and pure compassion in taking birth in difficult circumstances, for the sake of liberating sentient beings. [The remaining types include] pure compassion in the happy realms... [and so forth].
Pure compassion that manifests impermanence through the taking of birth; pure compassion that does not abandon its great vow throughout kalpas for the sake of sentient beings fixed in error;
pure compassion that does not cling to one's own happiness because it universally bestows joy upon all sentient beings;
pure compassion that seeks no reward for its kindness because it cultivates the purity of its own mind; and pure compassion that can eliminate perversions by teaching according to reality.
Because they are real dharmas, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas know that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is pure, free from defilement, and free from feverish affliction;
yet, due to adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), sentient beings undergo manifold sufferings.

Having known this, they give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings, and for the sake of those whose nature is pure, they preach the stainless, pure, and luminous Dharma. Thus it is said: "Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas... [and so forth].
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are like the tracks of birds in the sky;

because sentient beings are obscured by the cataracts of ignorance and cannot perceive them clearly, he contemplates them and gives rise to great compassion. This is called true wisdom, for its purpose is to reveal the Dharma of Nirvāṇa to them.
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and vast [wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the children of the Buddhas who possess pure compassion, have ten kinds of pure joy. What are these ten? They are:
the pure joy of generating the bodhicitta; the pure joy of relinquishing all possessions;

the pure joy of not despising those who break the precepts, but instead teaching and bringing them to maturity; and the pure joy of being able to endure and vow to [save] sentient beings who commit evil.

The pure joy of liberation through sacrificing one’s body in the search for the Dharma, without giving rise to regret; the pure joy of personally renouncing sensual pleasures and always delighting in the joy of the Dharma;
the pure joy of causing all sentient beings to renounce the joy of material resources and always delight in the joy of the Dharma;
and the pure joy of seeing all Buddhas, reverently making offerings to them without ever feeling satiated, which is equal to the Dharma-realm.
Purity of joy consists of causing all sentient beings to love and delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and the mastery of samādhis;
entering and emerging from them with a pure and joyful mind; practicing the equipment for joy; following the bodhisattva path; performing all ascetic practices;
and realizing the Sage’s (*muni*) tranquility, immovability, and unsurpassed concentration and wisdom—this purity of joy is the tenth. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas...
Then one attains the unsurpassed, vast, and pure joy of the Tathāgata. Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure relinquishment (*śuddha-tyāga*).
What are these ten? They are: the pure relinquishment that does not give rise to attachment when all sentient beings show respect and make offerings;
the pure relinquishment that does not give rise to anger when all sentient beings treat them with contempt or insult.

Constantly acting within the world, they are not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas; with pure equanimity (*upekṣā*), they wait for the proper time to transform those sentient beings who are vessels of the Dharma, yet they harbor no resentment toward those who are not vessels, maintaining pure equanimity.
They do not seek the dharmas of the two vehicles—whether those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—maintaining pure equanimity.
Their minds are always far removed from all sensual pleasures and dharmas that accord with the afflictions, remaining pure.
He abandons and renounces with purity the disparagement of the two vehicles, the weariness with and desire for departure from birth and death,

all worldly speech, speech that is not Nirvāṇa, speech that is not free from desire, speech that does not accord with principle, speech that disturbs others, the speech of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— in brief,
he completely distances himself from and renounces with purity all speech that constitutes an obstacle to the Bodhisattva path; or there may be...
There are sentient beings whose faculties have already matured and who have given rise to mindfulness and wisdom, yet they do not know the supreme Dharma;

they await the proper time before being transformed, and [the Bodhisattva] relinquishes them for the sake of their purification. Alternatively, there may be sentient beings whom the Bodhisattva has already taught in the past, but who can only be tamed upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood;
these too he relinquishes for the sake of their purification while awaiting the proper time. Regarding these two types, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

To have no sense of high or low, no grasping or rejecting, to remain far removed from all various forms of conceptual discrimination, to dwell constantly in right concentration, to enter into the Dharma as it truly is, and for the mind to attain patient endurance and pure equanimity—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure equanimity. O Son of the Buddha, such is the equanimity of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

The term *sat* has ten meanings. What are these ten? They are: (1) the meaning of being "much-heard" (*bahuśruta*), because of firm practice; (2) the meaning of "skillfulness in the Dharma," because of discerning investigation;

(3) the meaning of "emptiness," because of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); (4) the meaning of "tranquility," because of being free from the clamor and bustle of sentient beings;
(5) the meaning of "ineffability," because of not clinging to any language; (6) the meaning of "reality as it is" (*yathābhūta*), because of thoroughly penetrating the three [natures].
Because the world is equal, it is the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*; because all phenomena are of one taste, it is the meaning of *tathatā*;
because all Tathāgatas enter into accordance with it, it is the meaning of the *bhūtakoṭi*; because it is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is, it is the meaning of *mahāparinirvāṇa*;
and because one extinguishes all suffering while cultivating the various practices of a bodhisattva, these are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these...
The Dharma thus attains the supreme meaning of omniscience. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dharmas for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. What are these ten? They are:

the dharma of reality, because one practices according to what has been taught; the dharma of detachment from grasping, because one is entirely free from both the grasper and the grasped; the dharma of non-contention, because there is no contention with any delusions;

the dharma of quiescence, because it extinguishes and eliminates all... [one]... *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end. The final phrase "滅除一" likely refers to the cessation of a specific category of afflictions or conceptualizations.)*
Because it cuts through all feverish afflictions, it is the Dharma of detachment from desire; because all craving is severed, it is the Dharma of non-conceptuality;
because the conceptualization of objective referents has forever ceased, it is the Dharma of non-arising; because it is like space and immovable, it is the Unconditioned Dharma;

because it is free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is the Dharma of primordial nature; because its own-being is unstained and pure, it is the Dharma of intrinsic nature; [it is] the relinquishing of all *upādāna*.
The Dharma of Nirvana is able to give rise to all bodhisattva practices because their cultivation is uninterrupted; this is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide in these, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and vast Dharma.
Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of requisites for merit for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows: exhorting sentient beings...
Arousing the bodhicitta is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit, because it ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not interrupted;
practicing the ten kinds of dedication is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit, because it eliminates all unwholesome dharmas and accumulates all wholesome dharmas;
and being guided by wisdom is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit, because it transcends the triple world.
Because of merit, his mind is free from weariness; this is a bodhisattva’s auxiliary of merit, for it brings about the ultimate liberation of all sentient beings.
Because he relinquishes all internal and external possessions without exception; this is a bodhisattva’s auxiliary of merit, for he is unattached to any object.
Because he exerts unremitting diligence to fulfill the primary and secondary marks; this is a bodhisattva’s [auxiliary of merit].
Because he practices great giving without limit by opening the doors of the requisites for merit, he dedicates all roots of goodness— whether superior, middling, or inferior—
to the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta, never disparaging them. Because these requisites for merit of the Bodhisattva are conjoined with skillful means,
he gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings who are of wrong determination, inferior, or unwholesome.
Not harboring thoughts of contempt or disdain is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit,
because they constantly give rise to the great person’s heart of vast vows; reverently making offerings to all Tathāgatas and regarding all bodhisattvas as Tathāgatas,
causing all sentient beings to experience joy, is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit, as it maintains their original aspiration with extreme firmness.

Because it is firm, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has accumulated roots of goodness over incalculable eons, even though supreme enlightenment is as if held in the palm of his hand, he gives it all away to all sentient beings;
his mind is free from sorrow or affliction and free from regret. His mind is vast, equal to the realm of empty space—this is the bodhisattva’s merit that aids the path.
Because they fully give rise to great wisdom and realize the Great Dharma, these constitute the ten.

If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will be fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and vast accumulation of merit. Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of requisites for wisdom for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
What are the ten? They are: drawing near to those who are learned and truly virtuous; knowing... (the text continues).
To recognize [the teacher], to honor, provide offerings, respect, and prostrate to them, and to comply with all their various instructions without contradicting them—this is the first.
Because one is entirely upright and free from falsehood or pretension, one is forever free from arrogance and constantly practices humility and reverence;
one’s actions of body, speech, and mind are without coarseness, being gentle, compliant, sincere, and straightforward—this is the second. Such a person is fit to become a Buddha.

Because they are vessels of the Dharma, their mindfulness and wisdom follow awakening without ever becoming distracted; they possess a sense of shame and remorse, are gentle and supple, and their minds remain unshakable.
They constantly recollect the six remembrances (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), constantly practice the six respects (*ṣaṭ-gaurava*), and always abide in accordance with the six firm dharmas.

These constitute the three [qualities] together with the ten kinds of knowledge as skillful means; thus they delight in the Dharma and delight in its meaning, taking the Dharma as their joy, and they always delight in hearing it without ceasing.

To be weary of and renounce worldly discourse and worldly talk, to single-mindedly listen to and receive supramundane teachings, and to distance oneself from the Hīnayāna while entering the wisdom of the Mahāyāna—these are the four.
Because of recollecting with one-pointed mind and being free from distraction, one single-mindedly bears the burden of the six *pāramitās*;
having already matured the practice of the four *brahma-vihāras*, one follows the luminous Dharma and practices it all well.
Those of wise and sagacious conduct all diligently inquire and seek instruction; they distance themselves from the evil realms and turn toward the auspicious paths;
their minds always delight in right mindfulness and observation, subduing their own emotions and guarding the intentions of others—this is the fifth firm practice.
Because they practice true conduct, they always delight in renunciation, do not cling to the three realms of existence, constantly awaken their own minds, and harbor no ill will toward the Saṃgha.
Having cut off the three types of delusion and purified the three karmas, one decisively realizes that the intrinsic nature of the mind is such;

this constitutes the six [perfections] which can purify the minds of oneself and others. Therefore, one contemplates the five aggregates as being like illusory phenomena, the elements as being like venomous snakes, the sense bases as being like an empty village, and all dharmas as being like illusions, mirages, the moon reflected in water, dreams, and shadows.
Like an echo, like a reflection, like a painting in the sky, like a whirling firebrand, like the colors of a rainbow or lightning, and like the light of the sun and moon— without marks, without form,
neither permanent nor annihilated, neither coming nor going, and abiding nowhere— observing in this way, one knows that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation;
this is the seventh [knowledge] by which a bodhisattva knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent.
When the Mahāsattvas hear that all phenomena are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, without persons;
without mind and without objects; without greed, hatred, and delusion; without body and without things; without master and without dependence;
without attachment and without activity—when they hear that all such things are non-existent and entirely return to quiescent extinction—they believe deeply, without doubt, and do not slander this.

It is for eight reasons that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, being able to achieve perfect understanding, skillfully disciplines the sense faculties, practices according to the principle, and constantly abides in śamatha and vipaśyanā;
their mind is tranquil, all mental fluctuations are entirely non-arising, and there is no self, no person, no agent, and no action;
they do not conceive the notion of a self, nor do they conceive the notion of "mine"; they are free from all wounds and blemishes.
There are no scars, nor is there any patience attained therein; the actions of body, speech, and mind neither come nor go.
There is no diligence and no valor. One contemplates all sentient beings and all phenomena with a mind that is entirely equal and without abiding.
It is neither this shore nor the other shore; it is free from the nature of "this" and "that," coming from nowhere and going nowhere.
Furthermore, when departing, one always uses wisdom to contemplate in this way; this is the ninth stage of reaching the shore of analytical characteristics.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives the dharma of dependent origination, they perceive the purity of dharmas. Because they perceive the purity of dharmas, they perceive the purity of the buddha-lands.
Because they perceive the purity of the buddha-lands, they perceive the purity of empty space. Because they perceive the purity of empty space...
Because of purity, one sees the purity of the dharma-realm; because of seeing the purity of the dharma-realm, one sees the purity of wisdom.
These are the ten practices for accumulating all-knowledge, O Son of the Buddha. These are the ten aids to wisdom for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall attain all the dharmas of the Tathāgata.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of sufficiency in clear insight (*vidyā-vaśitā*) that constitute an unobstructed, pure, and subtle accumulation of wisdom.
What are these ten? They are: the sufficiency of clear insight in skillfully discerning all phenomena; the sufficiency of clear insight in non-attachment to all phenomena;

the sufficiency of clear insight in being free from inverted views; the sufficiency of clear insight in illuminating the sense faculties with the light of wisdom; and the sufficiency of clear insight in skillfully initiating right [effort].

The power of energy (*vīrya-bala*); the power of wisdom regarding the truths (*satya-jñāna-bala*), which thoroughly penetrates the true nature of reality; the power of wisdom regarding the cessation of afflictions and karma (*kleśa-karma-nirodha-bala*), which accomplishes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);

the power of wisdom regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-bala*), which universally observes all things; the power of wisdom regarding the recollection of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-bala*), which is pure regarding the limits of the past;
the power of wisdom regarding the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā-bala*), which severs all outflows of sentient beings—these are the ten. If any...
When Bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they attain the supreme great light of the Tathāgata regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the Dharma. What are the ten? They are:

seeking the Dharma with a straightforward mind, because they are free from flattery and deception; seeking the Dharma with diligence, because they are far removed from indolence and pride; and seeking the Dharma with single-minded devotion...
One seeks the Dharma because one does not begrudge body or life for the sake of eliminating the afflictions of all sentient beings;

one seeks the Dharma not for the sake of fame, profit, or honor, but for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, both oneself and others; one seeks the Dharma not merely for self-benefit, but for the sake of entering into wisdom;
one seeks the Dharma because one takes no pleasure in mere words and letters, but for the sake of transcending birth and death; and one seeks the Dharma because one does not crave worldly pleasures.

To seek the Dharma for the sake of delivering sentient beings and generating the bodhicitta; to seek the Dharma for the sake of severing the doubts of all sentient beings so that they may be free from hesitation;
to seek the Dharma for the sake of fulfilling the Buddha-dharmas and taking no pleasure in other vehicles—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the great wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas without depending on the instruction of others.
O Wisdom-son, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of clearly understood dharmas. What are the ten? They are as follows:
conforming to worldly conventions to cultivate and grow roots of goodness is the clearly understood dharma of naive ordinary beings;

attaining unimpeded and indestructible faith and awakening to the self-nature of dharmas is the clearly understood dharma of those who follow by faith; and diligently practicing the dharmas in accordance with them... [is the clearly understood dharma of those who follow by Dharma].
The Dharma-abiding person clearly understands the Dharma by being far removed from the eightfold wrong path and turning toward the eightfold right path;

this is the clear understanding of the eighth person. The one who has eliminated the various fetters, severed the outflows of birth and death, and perceives the true truths is the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) who clearly understands the Dharma.
The one who contemplates the defects in sensory flavors and knows there is no further coming and going is the *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) who clearly understands the Dharma.

One who does not delight in the three realms, seeks the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*), and does not give rise to even a single thought of attachment toward the phenomena of rebirth—this is an *anāgāmin*.

One who clearly understands the nature of phenomena, attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), achieves the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the nine meditative concentrations (*navasamādhi*), and the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*)—this is an *arhat*.
Such a person clearly understands the nature of phenomena and delights in contemplating the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of conditions.
With a mind that is always tranquil, contented, and free from worldly affairs, they realize the causes through their own self-awakening without depending on others.

They achieve various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom; as pratyekabuddhas, they clearly understand the wisdom of the Dharma, their faculties are sharp and keen, and they constantly delight in delivering all sentient beings.
They diligently cultivate the dharmas of merit and wisdom that assist the path, as taught by the Tathāgata.
There are ten powers and fearlessnesses, fully endowed with all merits; this Bodhisattva person clearly understands these dharmas—these are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom and clear understanding of the dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are as follows:
That is to say: the practice of the Dharma by revering and honoring all spiritual friends; the practice of the Dharma by being constantly awakened by the devas;

the practice of the Dharma by always maintaining a sense of shame and remorse before the Buddhas; the practice of the Dharma by having compassion for sentient beings and not abandoning the cycle of birth and death;
the practice of the Dharma by seeing every task through to completion with an unshakable mind; and the practice of the Dharma by following [the path] with single-minded mindfulness.
The practice of the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind, diligently training and practicing the Dharma;
the practice of distancing oneself from false views while earnestly seeking the path of the True Dharma; the practice of crushing all Māras, afflictions, and karma;

the practice of knowing the superior and inferior capacities of the faculties of all sentient beings and teaching the Dharma accordingly so that they may abide on the stage of Buddhahood; and the practice of dwelling securely in the infinite.
The practice of the Dharma that extinguishes afflictions throughout the vast dharma-realm and purifies the body constitutes the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata. Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of māras for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

What are these ten? They are as follows: the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), because it gives rise to all forms of grasping; the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*)... [text continues]... because it gives rise to all forms of grasping.
The demon of constant defilement; the demon of karma, which can create obstacles; the demon of the mind, which gives rise to arrogance; the demon of death, which abandons the place of birth;

the demon of celestial beings (*devaputra-māra*), who are self-indulgent and haughty; the demon of roots of goodness, which constantly clings and grasps; the demon of meditative absorption (*samādhi-māra*), which long relishes its flavor;
the demon of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra-māra*), which gives rise to a mind of attachment; and the demon of the wisdom of the Dharma of Bodhi, which has no desire to relinquish it.
Therefore, these are the ten [factors] by which a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should employ skillful means to swiftly seek to distance themselves from them.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of demonic activities for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. What are the ten? They are as follows:

forgetting the bodhicitta while cultivating various roots of goodness is a demonic activity; giving with a malicious mind, maintaining ethical discipline with an angry mind, and abandoning those of evil character are [demonic activities].
To despise, treat with contempt, distract, or revile those who are lazy or possess poor wisdom is the work of Māra.
To give rise to stinginess regarding the profound Dharma; to fail to teach it to those who are capable of being transformed;

or to forcefully preach it to those who are not vessels for the Dharma even when receiving wealth, profit, honor, and offerings—these are the works of Māra. Furthermore, to take no pleasure in hearing the various *pāramitās* is the work of Māra.
Even if one hears the teachings, one does not practice them; or though one practices, one frequently gives rise to indolence.

Because of this indolence, one’s resolve is narrow and inferior, and one does not seek the unsurpassed, great Bodhi. This is the work of Māra: staying far from virtuous friends and drawing near to evil friends;
delighting in seeking the two vehicles while having no joy in taking birth; aspiring to nirvāṇa and seeking the stillness of detachment.
These are the works of Māra: to give rise to a mind of anger toward a bodhisattva and to glare at them with evil eyes; to seek out their faults and misdeeds and proclaim their transgressions;
to cut off all the wealth, profit, and offerings they receive—these are the works of Māra. To slander the true Dharma and take no pleasure in hearing it;
even if one happens to hear it, to immediately give rise to disparagement; and upon seeing someone preaching the Dharma, to fail to show respect.

To claim that one’s own teachings are correct while asserting all other teachings are entirely false is a work of Māra; to delight in studying worldly treatises, to be skillful in composing elegant phrases, to expound the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles while concealing the profound Dharma, or to transmit sublime meanings to those who are unworthy, thereby causing them to distance themselves from Bodhi and dwell upon deviant paths—these are works of Māra.

Furthermore, for those who have already attained liberation and established themselves in peace, to constantly delight in associating with such persons [while neglecting others] is also a work of Māra.
To offer worship yet refuse to draw near to or transform those who have not attained liberation or peace;
to increase the work of Māra and cultivate pride, lacking reverence for sentient beings and frequently inflicting harm upon them;
to seek neither the True Dharma nor authentic wisdom, with a mind so corrupt and evil that it is difficult to enlighten—this is the work of Māra.
These are the ten things that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should swiftly distance themselves from while diligently seeking the work of a Buddha.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of abandoning demonic activities for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are the ten? They are:
abandoning demonic activity by drawing near to spiritual friends and reverently making offerings to them; and abandoning demonic activity by not exalting oneself and not praising oneself.
To have faith and understanding in the profound Dharma of the Buddha without slandering it is to abandon the deeds of Māra; never to forget the mind of omniscience is to abandon the deeds of Māra;
to diligently cultivate sublime practices with constant heedfulness is to abandon the deeds of Māra;
to constantly seek all the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is to abandon the deeds of Māra; and to constantly expound the Dharma with a mind free from weariness is to abandon the deeds of Māra.
Taking refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions and conceiving the thought of their providing protection;
abandoning the deeds of Māra by faithfully accepting and recollecting the empowerment of the spiritual power of all Buddhas;

abandoning the deeds of Māra by planting roots of goodness identical to those of all Bodhisattvas in a state of equality and non-duality—these are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, [they shall abandon the deeds of Māra].
Thus, one is able to transcend all paths of Māra. O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of vision of the Buddhas. What are these ten? They are:
the unattached vision of the Buddhas who abide in the world and attain perfect enlightenment;

the vision of the Buddhas who manifest through vows; the vision of deep faith in the Buddhas of karmic retribution; the conforming vision of the Buddhas who maintain and sustain the teachings; and the vision of profound entry into the Buddhas of *nirvāṇa*.
Seeing the Buddha of the Dharma-realm who reaches everywhere; seeing the Buddha of the Mind who dwells in peace; seeing the Buddha of Samādhi who is immeasurable and without dependence;
seeing the Buddha of Original Nature who is clearly manifest; seeing the Buddha of Following Joy who universally receives—all these constitute the ten.
If Bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they will constantly behold the unsurpassed Tathāgata. O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten [qualities].
What are the ten kinds of Buddha-activities? They are as follows: first, to provide guidance according to the proper time, which is a Buddha-activity for causing correct practice;
second, to cause one to see [the Buddha] within dreams, which is a Buddha-activity for awakening past roots of goodness;

third, to expound for others sūtras never heard before, which is a Buddha-activity for generating wisdom and severing doubt; fourth, to teach the Dharma of transcendence to those entangled by the fetters of remorse... [and so forth].

This is the Buddha’s work to cause beings to leave behind doubt. If there are sentient beings who give rise to a mind of stinginess, up to a mind of evil wisdom, the mind of the two vehicles, a harmful mind, a mind of doubt, a distracted and agitated mind, or a mind of pride—then for their sake, he manifests the Tathāgata’s body adorned with all its marks.
This is the Buddha’s work to cause the growth of past roots of goodness, for the True Dharma is difficult to encounter.
At that time, he extensively expounds the Dharma so that, upon hearing it, they may attain the wisdom of dhāraṇī and the wisdom of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
universally benefiting immeasurable sentient beings. Because his resolute belief (*adhimukti*) in the Buddha’s deeds is pure, should any demonic activity arise,
he is able to employ skillful means to manifest sounds such as those of the realm of empty space, using the teaching that does not harm or afflict others as an antidote to cause them—
When the various māras hear this, their majestic radiance is extinguished;
for the Buddha’s vocation, aspiration, and sublime majesty are so great that his mind is constantly and uninterruptedly self-guarded, never allowing them to enter the fixed stage of the two vehicles.
If there are sentient beings whose faculties and natures are not yet mature, he will ultimately not speak of the realm of liberation; this is the work of the Buddha’s original vow.
Therefore, having detached from all bonds of birth and death and outflows, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva in an uninterrupted succession.
With a heart of great compassion, they gather in sentient beings, causing them to initiate practice and attain ultimate liberation.
Because they do not sever the Buddha-work by practicing the bodhisattva path, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly realizes that both themselves and all sentient beings are originally quiescent.
Without being startled or terrified by cessation, one diligently cultivates merit and wisdom without ever feeling weary or satisfied;

though knowing that all phenomena are devoid of agency, one does not abandon the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; though forever free from desire regarding all sensory objects, one constantly delights in beholding and serving the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas;
and though knowing that entry into the Dharma does not depend on another, one plants [the seeds of realization].
Employing various skillful means to seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), although they know that all lands are like empty space, they always delight in adorning all Buddha-fields;
although they constantly observe that there is no person and no self, they teach and transform sentient beings without weariness or fatigue;
and although they are fundamentally unmoving within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they manifest various transformations through the power of their supernormal knowledges and wisdom.
Although he has already perfected the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), he practices the bodhisattva path without rest;
although he knows that all phenomena are ineffable, he turns the pure wheel of Dharma to gladden the minds of sentient beings;
although he can manifest the spiritual powers of all Buddhas, he does not weary of or abandon the bodhisattva body; and although he manifests entry into great parinirvāṇa, yet...
Manifesting birth in all places and being able to thus practice the dharma of the simultaneous exercise of skillful means and reality—this is the work of a Buddha;
this is the tenth. If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the unsurpassed, teacherless, and vast activity that does not depend on the instruction of others.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of prideful activities. What are these ten? They are as follows:
To fail to show respect toward one's teachers, preceptors, parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas— those who abide in the right path,
those who are directed toward the right path, and those who are fields of merit— is the karma of pride. Or, there may be a Dharma teacher who has attained the most excellent vehicle of the Dharma,
who understands the essential path of the Mahāyāna, who has acquired dhāraṇīs, and who expounds the vast teachings of the sūtras, yet [the listener] lacks [faith].
To give rise to a mind of arrogance while resting, and to lack reverence for the Dharma being taught, is an act of pride.
To hear the sublime Dharma being preached in an assembly and refuse to praise it so as to cause others to believe and accept it, is an act of pride.
To be fond of giving rise to overweening pride, exalting oneself and disparaging others, failing to see one's own faults and unaware of one's own shortcomings, is an act of pride.
To delight in giving rise to the pride of superiority; to fail to praise those who possess virtue when one ought to do so; to feel no joy when seeing others offer praise;

these are the karmic activities of pride. To see a Dharma master preaching the Dharma for others, and knowing it to be the Dharma, the Vinaya, the truth, and the word of the Buddha, yet—out of a desire to disparage that person—also disparage the Dharma, personally giving rise to slander and causing others to slander it as well.
The karma of pride consists of seeking a high seat for oneself while claiming to be a Dharma teacher who ought to receive offerings, yet refusing to perform manual labor;
it consists of failing to rise to greet those who are senior or long-practiced, and being unwilling to serve them;
it consists of frowning with displeasure upon seeing virtuous people, using harsh and rude speech, and watching for their faults; and it consists of [disdain] toward those who are wise.
Those who know the Dharma are unwilling to draw near to, revere, or make offerings to [such persons], nor do they wish to inquire of them:

"What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What should be done? What should not be done? By performing what kind of karma will one obtain various benefits and peace and happiness throughout the long night?
Swallowed by ignorance, stubbornness, and pride, they will ultimately never [attain these].
To perceive the path of transcendence as a basis for pride is an act of arrogance. Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose minds are shrouded by pride;
even when Buddhas appear in the world, they are unable to draw near, pay respect, or make offerings. They do not give rise to new roots of goodness and cause old ones to perish.

They speak what should not be spoken and engage in disputes where there should be none. In the future, they will surely fall into perilous and deep pits, from which they shall not emerge for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

If one encounters a Buddha, how much more so if one hears the Dharma? Yet, it is solely because they have previously resolved upon bodhicitta that they eventually awaken on their own to this karmic arrogance.
This constitutes the tenth [type of arrogance]. If Bodhisattvas distance themselves from this karmic arrogance, they will attain ten kinds of karmic wisdom. What are these ten? They are:
the karmic wisdom of believing and understanding that karmic retribution is inexhaustible and that cause and effect are unalterable; and the karmic wisdom of not abandoning the bodhicitta.

Constantly recollecting all Buddhas is the work of wisdom; reverently making offerings to and honoring spiritual friends with a mind of respect, never becoming weary or indolent, is the work of wisdom;
delighting in the Dharma and delighting in its meaning without ever being satisfied is the work of wisdom;

remaining far removed from wrong thoughts and diligently cultivating right mindfulness is the work of wisdom; being free from pride toward all sentient beings and regarding all bodhisattvas as [one's own teachers] is the work of wisdom.

To regard and cherish the True Dharma as one’s own body, to honor the Tathāgata as one protects one’s own life, and to conceive the thought of all practitioners as Buddhas—this is the activity of wisdom.
To ensure that the actions of body, speech, and mind are free from all unwholesomeness, to praise the noble and holy ones, and to accord with Bodhi—this is the activity of wisdom.
To not destroy dependent origination, to be free from all false views, and to shatter darkness to attain illumination—this is the activity of wisdom.
Illuminating all phenomena is the activity of wisdom. The ten kinds of dedication consist of: practicing in accordance with the various *pāramitās*;
conceiving of skillful means as a compassionate mother; conceiving of them as a compassionate father; entering the house of Bodhi with a pure mind;

and [cultivating] such factors conducive to the path as generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), merit, and wisdom. This is the activity of wisdom.
Constantly and diligently accumulating [merit] without weariness is the activity of wisdom. If there is an activity praised by the Buddha that can destroy the demons, afflictions, and strife;
that can free one from all hindrances, coverings, and fetters; that can teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings;
that can accord with wisdom and embrace the True Dharma; and that can adorn and purify the Buddha-fields—[this is it]. It can give rise to...
To give rise to supernormal powers and clear insights, cultivating them all with diligence and without ever flagging or retreating—this is the activity of wisdom. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme and great wisdom-activity of all skillful means.
Disciples of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of things by which they are held fast by Māra. What are the ten? They are as follows:
It is held by the māra of indolence; it is held by the māra of narrow-minded aspiration; it is held by the māra of being satisfied with little practice;
it is held by the māra of accepting only one thing and nothing else; it is held by the māra of failing to generate great vows;
it is held by the māra of delighting in dwelling in cessation and severing afflictions; and it is held by the māra of seeking the eternal cessation of birth and death.
Abandoning the bodhisattva practice is being held by Māra; failing to transform sentient beings is being held by Māra;

harboring doubt and slandering the True Dharma is being held by Māra—these are the ten. If bodhisattvas can renounce these states of being held by Māra, they will attain ten kinds of being held by the Buddhas.
What are the ten? They are: first, the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The mind is sustained by the Buddha; throughout successive lives, one maintains the bodhicitta so as not to forget it.

Sustained by the Buddha, one recognizes all demonic activities and is able to swiftly depart from them. Sustained by the Buddha, upon hearing of the various *pāramitās*, one practices according to what has been taught.
Sustained by the Buddha, one understands the suffering of birth and death yet does not feel weary or loathing toward it. Sustained by the Buddha, one contemplates the profound...

Attaining immeasurable fruits through the profound Dharma and being sustained by the Buddha; preaching the teachings of the Two Vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings while not personally realizing the liberation of those vehicles and being sustained by the Buddha;

delighting in observing unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) while not dwelling within them, and not giving rise to dualistic conceptions regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned and being sustained by the Buddha;
reaching the realm of non-arising (*anutpāda*) while manifesting there to receive [rebirth].
Being sustained by the Buddhas, although they have realized all-knowledge, they engage in the conduct of a bodhisattva and do not sever the lineage of bodhisattvas;
being sustained by the Buddhas—this is the tenth. If bodhisattvas dwell therein, they will obtain the power of the supreme sustenance of all Buddhas.
Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of dharmas by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained. What are they?

These constitute the ten, namely: knowing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are subsumed under the dharma of impermanence; knowing that all conditioned phenomena are subsumed under the dharma of suffering;
knowing that all conditioned phenomena are subsumed under the dharma of selflessness; knowing that all phenomena are subsumed under the dharma of the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*;
and knowing that all phenomena are subsumed under the dharma that arises from conditions and does not arise in the absence of conditions.
By maintaining the knowledge that improper mental attention gives rise to ignorance, and because ignorance arises, [the links] up to old age and death arise;
by the cessation of improper mental attention, ignorance ceases, and because ignorance ceases, [the links] up to old age and death cease. This is what is encompassed by the Dharma.

By maintaining the knowledge of the three doors of liberation, one gives birth to the Śrāvaka vehicle; by realizing the dharma of non-contention (*araṇā*), one gives birth to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Upheld by the vehicle of the factors of enlightenment, one knows the six *pāramitās* and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) as giving rise to the Mahāyāna;
upheld by the knowledge that encompasses all lands, all phenomena, all sentient beings, and all worlds, one knows this as the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom;
upheld by the knowledge that severs all conceptualization, relinquishes all grasping, and remains free from the limits of past and future, one accords with *nirvāṇa*.
Being sustained by the Dharma of the *paryaṅka* (the cross-legged posture) constitutes the tenth. If Bodhisattvas dwell therein, they will obtain the sustenance of the supreme Dharma of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of activities performed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
What are these ten? They are: preaching for the sake of the sons of gods in the desire realm so that they may cultivate renunciation;
The Dharma teaching states that all sovereign powers are impermanent and all pleasures shall eventually fade away;
he exhorts those devas to resolve upon Bodhicitta—this is the first deed performed.

For the devas of the Form Realm, he explains the entry into and emergence from the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; yet if they develop attachment therein, through that attachment their bodies arise once more.
When he sees those who hold wrong views, ignorance, and so forth, he explains to them wisdom as it truly is.

If they give rise to perverted perceptions toward all phenomena, whether material or immaterial, regarding them as pure, he explains to them that they are impure and entirely impermanent, exhorting them to resolve upon Bodhicitta;
this is the second task performed by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling [in this stage].
In the Tuṣita Heaven, he enters a samādhi called "Adorned Body Emitting Light," which radiates light that universally illumines the trichiliocosm.
According to the inclinations of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma using various voices. Upon hearing this, the faith of sentient beings becomes pure;
at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he exhorts them to resolve upon Bodhicitta. This is [the second].

Regarding the third activity performed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: while in the Tuṣita Heaven, they see all the Bodhisattvas within the Tuṣita Heavens of the ten directions with their unobstructed eyes;

those Bodhisattvas likewise see them, and having seen one another, they discourse upon the sublime Dharma concerning the descent into the mother’s womb, the initial birth, the renunciation of the world, and the journey to the path of enlightenment.
Adorning the site with great majesty, he further manifests the practices performed throughout his past lives;

by virtue of those practices, he accomplishes all the merits of this great wisdom. Without leaving his original place, he is able to manifest such matters as these—this is the fourth activity performed by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, pervading the ten directions.
All the assemblies of bodhisattvas from the Tuṣita Heaven palace gathered together, respectfully surrounding him.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, desiring to fulfill the aspirations of those bodhisattvas and cause them to give rise to joy, expounded the Dharma-gates according to the stages in which those bodhisattvas should abide, their practices, their abandonments, their cultivations, and their realizations. Those [bodhisattvas...]

Having heard the Dharma teaching, the bodhisattvas were all greatly rejoiced at having attained what they had never experienced before; each returned to their own native land and the palaces where they dwell.
This is the fifth deed performed by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven:
when he desired to disrupt and confuse the Bodhisattva’s work, Māra Pāpīyān, the lord of the desire realm, approached the Bodhisattva surrounded by his retinue.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, in order to subdue the armies of Māra, dwelt in the gateway of wisdom consisting of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) encompassed by the adamantine path.
He taught the Dharma using both gentle and harsh speech, so that Māra Pāpīyān could find no opportunity.
When Māra saw the sovereign power (*vibhūti-prabhāva*) of the Bodhisattva, he was struck with awe.
The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the sixth task to be performed.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven perceives that the various devaputras of the desire realm do not delight in hearing the Dharma, the Bodhisattva then emits a great sound, proclaiming everywhere: "Today, the Bodhisattva shall manifest a rare event within the palace."
"If you wish to see him, you should go quickly. When the sons of the gods heard these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of them all gathered together.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, seeing that the assembly of devas had all arrived, manifested various rare wonders within the palace for them.
Having never before seen or heard of such things, those sons of the gods were filled with wonder upon beholding them.
They were all filled with great joy, their minds intoxicated and submerged in it; then, amidst that pleasure, they raised their voices and declared:
"O virtuous ones! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering;
all dharmas are without self; and nirvāṇa is tranquil extinction. Furthermore, they proclaimed: "You should all cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva."

When they are about to perfect the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), those devaputras who hear this sound of the Dharma feel sorrowful lamentation and admiration, giving rise to world-weariness;

there are none among them who do not resolve to attain Bodhicitta. This is the seventh task performed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, who, without leaving their original place, are able to travel to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.
All Buddhas behold all Tathāgatas, drawing near to them, prostrating before them, and reverently listening to the Dharma.

At that time, because the Buddhas desire to cause the Bodhisattvas to obtain the supreme method of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), they expound for them the names of the Bodhisattva stages and all spiritual powers (*abhijñā*).

By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*), they become fully endowed with all supreme merits and enter into the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
This is the eighth stage, the stage of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has performed his duties.

Residing in the Tuṣita Heaven, in order to make offerings to all Tathāgatas, he employs great supernormal powers to manifest various kinds of offering articles—excellent and delightful—that pervade all worlds throughout the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. Therein, he makes offerings to the Buddhas within those worlds.
Countless sentient beings who witness this offering all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this is the ninth deed performed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven,
wherein they manifest various forms throughout all worlds in the ten directions, issuing forth immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates that are like illusions and shadows.

With various marks, various physical forms, various modes of conduct, various activities, various skillful means, various similes, and various discourses, they cause all sentient beings to rejoice according to their inclinations;
this is the tenth activity performed by the Buddha-sons. These, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, are the ten kinds of activities performed while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
If Bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will then be able to descend to be born in the human realm hereafter.
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, ten things are manifested. What are the ten?
Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great light from the soles of his feet.
The light is named "Adornment of Peace and Bliss. It universally illumines all evil realms and beings in distress throughout the trichiliocosm;
no sentient being who touches this light fails to be liberated from suffering and attain peace and bliss.
Having attained peace and bliss, they all know that a wondrous Great Being is about to appear in the world. This is the first manifestation shown by the Buddha.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven to take birth, he emits a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows,

named "Awakening Universal Illumination," which shines throughout the trichiliocosm and illuminates the bodies of all those Bodhisattvas who were his fellow practitioners in past lives; having been touched by this light, those Bodhisattvas all come to know [him].
When the Bodhisattva is about to descend to be born, each [of the devas] brings forth immeasurable offerings and approaches the Bodhisattva to present them;

this is the second matter manifested. O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a great radiance from his right palm called "Pure Realm," which is fully capable of...

He purifies all the three thousandfold world-systems. Within them, if there are any Pratyekabuddhas who have attained the outflow-free state and perceive this light, they immediately relinquish their life-span;
if they do not perceive it, by the power of the radiance, they are transported to other worlds elsewhere. All Māras, all non-Buddhists, and all sentient beings with views likewise [experience this].
They are transferred to other world-systems, with the sole exception of those sentient beings sustained by the spiritual power of the Buddhas or who are emanations;

this is the third matter manifested. Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits from his two knees a great radiance called "Pure Adornment," which universally illumines all the devas.
From the Heaven of the World-Protectors (*Lokapāla*) below up to the Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsa*) above, there was nowhere he did not pervade.
All those devas knew that the Bodhisattva was about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven; filled with longing, they were moved by sorrow, lamentation, and distress.
Each holding various flower garlands, garments, unguents, powdered incense, banners, canopies, and musical instruments, they went to the Bodhisattva’s abode to pay him respectful homage.
The fourth manifested matter is that which follows the offerings until the descent [into the womb] and even unto nirvana. O Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a great radiance from within the heart-treasury adorned with the *svastika* and vajra,
named "Inconquerable Banner," which universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, there were ten billion Vajrapāṇi spirits who all gathered together to follow and attend upon him from his initial descent until his parinirvāṇa; this is the fifth matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven, he emitted light from every single pore of his body.

The great radiance named "Discerning Sentient Beings" universally illumines all great trichiliocosms and pervasively touches the bodies of all bodhisattvas, as well as all devas, worldlings, and other bodhisattvas. These bodhisattvas all form this thought:
"I should dwell here to make offerings to the Tathāgata and to transform sentient beings. This is the sixth manifested phenomenon.

O Sons of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven, he emits from within the Great Maṇi Jewel Treasury Palace a great radiance called "Excellently Abiding Observation.
This light illuminates the royal palace where this Bodhisattva is to take birth. Once the light has shone, all other Bodhisattvas likewise follow him down to Jambudvīpa.
If he manifests birth in a household, a village, or a city for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings,
this is the seventh matter of manifestation. Son of the Buddha,
when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, from the celestial palaces, great towers, and various adornments, he emits—
A great radiance named "Pure Adornment of All Palaces" shone forth from the womb of the Bodhisattva’s mother.
Having illuminated it, this light caused the Bodhisattva’s mother to be peaceful, secure, and joyful, and brought her to the full accomplishment of all merits.
Within her womb, there spontaneously appeared a vast and lofty pavilion, adorned with great *maṇi* jewels, for the purpose of providing her with peace.
Because he dwells in the body of a bodhisattva, this is the eighth manifested matter.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great radiance from beneath his two feet called "Well-Established.
If there are sons of gods or Brahmā gods whose lives are nearing their end, upon being touched by the light, they all attain the prolongation of their lifespan.
Making offerings to the Bodhisattva from his initial descent into birth until his parinirvāṇa is the ninth matter manifested;
O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven,
he emits a great light from his secondary marks (anuvyañjana) called "Adorned by the Sun and Moon," manifesting the various deeds of the Bodhisattva at which time all humans and devas—
Some see the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven; some see him entering the womb; some see his initial birth; some see his renunciation;
some see his attainment of enlightenment; some see his subduing of Māra; some see his turning of the wheel of Dharma;
and some see his entry into Nirvāṇa—this is the tenth matter of manifestation. O Son of the Buddha, regarding the body, the seat, and the palace of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
Within the pavilion, they emit millions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, all manifesting the various deeds of Bodhisattvas.
Having manifested these deeds, because they are fully endowed with all dharmas of merit, they descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born among humans.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten things by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas manifest dwelling in the womb. What are they?

O sons of the Buddha, for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to bring to maturity those sentient beings of small minds and inferior understanding, and so as not to cause them to give rise to such thoughts as, "This bodhisattva was born spontaneously by transformation;
his wisdom and roots of goodness were not acquired through cultivation," the bodhisattva manifests dwelling in the womb. This is the first matter of the bodhisattva.
The Mahāsattva manifests entry into the womb in order to mature the roots of goodness of his parents, his kinsmen, and those sentient beings who were his companions in previous lives.
Why is this? Because they must all see him entering the womb in order to mature all their various roots of goodness.
This is the second matter. When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the mother’s womb, he does so with right mindfulness and right awareness.
Knowing that there is no delusion, once dwelling in the mother’s womb, his mind is always in right mindfulness and never confused;

this is the third matter. While the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is in the mother’s womb, he constantly expounds the Dharma, and the great Bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings from the worlds of the ten directions all come to assemble, causing them all to obtain immeasurable spiritual powers.
That the Bodhisattva Pratyutpanna-jñāna (邊智慧) achieves such superior function of eloquence while dwelling in the womb is the fourth matter.

That the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while in his mother’s womb, assembles a great congregation and, by the power of his original vows, teaches and transforms all the assembly of bodhisattvas is the fifth matter. That the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains buddhahood among human beings...
He should manifest being in the mother’s womb by means of the most excellent human birth; this is the sixth matter.

While the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is in the mother’s womb, the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm all see the Bodhisattva as one sees the reflection of one’s own face in a clear mirror. At that time, the great-minded devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas...
The asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others all approach the Bodhisattva to pay respectful homage and make offerings;

this is the seventh matter. Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is in his mother’s womb, all other Bodhisattvas in other worlds who are in their final birth and dwelling in their mothers’ wombs all come together to assemble and speak with him.
The Dharma-door of the Great Assembly, titled "The Vast Treasury of Wisdom," is the eighth matter.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is in his mother’s womb, he enters the Samādhi of the Stainless Treasury.

By the power of this samādhi, within the mother’s womb he manifests a great palace, adorned with various ornaments, all of which are exquisitely beautiful, such that even the Tuṣita Heaven palace cannot compare to it, and causes...
The mother’s body is peaceful, secure, and free from ailment; this is the ninth matter.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the mother’s womb, by means of great majestic power, he manifests articles of offering called the "Pure Treasury that Opens Great Merit," which pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Tathāgatas. All those Tathāgatas then expound the Dharma for him.
The Dharma-realm treasury, the dwelling place of infinite Bodhisattvas, is the tenth matter, O Son of the Buddha.

These are the ten matters by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas manifest their dwelling in the womb; if Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand these dharmas, they are able to manifest extremely subtle modes of conduct.
