The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament Scripture, Scroll Eighty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the commentary composed by Li Tōngxuán, a Lay Elder of Fāngshān in Tàiyuán during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, *The Combined Commentary on the Scripture*, Chapter Thirty-Eight: "Leaving the World," Part Seven.
[Sūtra] O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of extremely subtle approaches for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten? What are they?
That is to say: while in the mother’s womb, he manifests the initial generation of the bodhicitta up to the stage of empowerment;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven; while in the mother’s womb, he manifests his initial birth; while in the mother’s womb, he manifests the stage of childhood;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests residing in the royal palace; and while in the mother’s womb, he manifests his departure.
While dwelling in the mother’s womb, he manifests the practice of austerities, his departure for the site of enlightenment, and his attainment of perfect awakening;
while dwelling in the mother’s womb, he manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma; while dwelling in the mother’s womb, he manifests parinirvāṇa;
and while dwelling in the mother’s womb, he manifests the great subtlety—namely, all the practices of bodhisattvas and the immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas.
"O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten subtle modes of conduct for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas while in the mother’s womb.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the subtle mode of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of birth. What are the ten? They are as follows: namely, being far removed from..."
Born with ignorance yet possessing right mindfulness and right awareness, he emits a great net of light that universally illumines the three-thousandfold world system;
born into his final existence, he shall not undergo further rebirth; born into non-arising and non-origination, he knows the three realms to be like an illusion;
born manifesting his body everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he attains the three bodies of the wisdom of all-knowledge; and born emitting a single...
The light of all Buddhas universally awakens the bodies of all sentient beings; they enter the body of the Samādhi of Great Wisdom Observation.

When the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Buddha, are born, they cause all Buddha-fields to tremble, liberate all sentient beings, eliminate all evil realms, and eclipse all Māras; immeasurable Bodhisattvas all gather together.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest birth for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, it is by means of ten matters that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest a smile and make a vow within their own minds.
What are these ten? They are as follows: the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects, "All the world is submerged in desire."
Having realized that no one else but myself is capable of providing such rescue and deliverance, he smiled with a serene countenance and made a vow within his mind, further reflecting:
"The entire world is blinded by afflictions; it is only I who now possess perfect wisdom.
Having realized this, he smiled with a serene countenance and made a vow within his mind, again reflecting: "By means of this body of provisional names, I shall now [act]."
"Therefore, one shall attain the unsurpassed Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, which fills the three periods of time.

Having known this, he smiled with a joyful countenance and made a vow within his own mind. At that time, the Bodhisattva, surveying all the Brahmās and even all the Maheśvaras throughout the ten directions with his unobstructed eye, thought to himself: "All these sentient beings each claim for themselves—"
Having known this through the power of great wisdom, the Bodhisattva, with a joyful and smiling mind, makes a vow within his heart.
At that time, the Bodhisattva observes all sentient beings who have long planted roots of goodness but now have all fallen away;

having known this, he, with a joyful and smiling mind, makes a vow within his heart. The Bodhisattva observes that although the seeds sown in the world are few, the fruits obtained are exceedingly many.
Having known this, he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his own mind.

The Bodhisattva perceives that all sentient beings who receive the Buddha’s instruction will certainly obtain benefit; having known this, he smiles with a joyful countenance and makes a vow within his own mind.
The Bodhisattva perceives that those Bodhisattvas of the past who practiced together with him became attached to other matters and failed to attain the vast merit of the Buddha-dharma.
Having known this, the Bodhisattva, with a joyful and smiling countenance, made a vow within his own mind.

The Bodhisattva observed that the various devas and humans who had gathered together in the past world were still present until now in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), unable to abandon it and yet never growing weary of it.
Having known this, the Bodhisattva, with a joyful and smiling countenance, made a vow within his own mind. At that time, for their sake...
Touched by the light of all Tathāgatas, he felt redoubled joy and serenity, smiling with a heart that made a vow to himself;

this is the tenth. Sons of the Buddha, for the sake of taming sentient beings, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests the walking of seven steps for ten reasons. What are these ten? Namely, to manifest the Bodhisattva...
By the power [of his merit], he took seven steps to manifest the bestowal of the seven riches; he took seven steps to fulfill the vows of the earth deities;

he took seven steps to manifest the sign of transcending the three realms; he took seven steps to manifest that the supreme conduct of a Bodhisattva surpasses the gait of the elephant king, the ox king, and the lion king; he took seven steps to manifest the sign of the vajra-ground.
Therefore, he took seven steps to manifest his desire to bestow courageous power upon sentient beings; he took seven steps to manifest his practice of the seven jewels of awakening;
he took seven steps to manifest that the Dharma he had attained was not derived from the instruction of another;
he took seven steps to manifest his supreme and peerless excellence within the world. These, O sons of the Buddha, constitute the ten [reasons] for taking seven steps.
Bodhisattvas manifest in this way for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten reasons why Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas manifest in the stage of childhood. What are these ten? They are:
to manifest mastery over all worldly arts, such as writing, calculation, diagrams, and seals; and thus they dwell in the stage of childhood. To manifest...
He dwells in the stage of a youth to manifest mastery over all worldly occupations, such as elephants, horses, chariots, bows, arrows, swords, and halberds;
he dwells in the stage of a youth to manifest mastery over all worldly matters, such as writing, literature, debate, gambling, and games;
and he dwells in the stage of a youth to manifest the complete departure from all faults of body, speech, and mind.
The stage of the Son is the gateway for manifesting entry into meditative absorption and abiding in *nirvāṇa*, because it pervades immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions;
the stage of the Youth is for manifesting a power that surpasses all devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, world-protectors, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
He dwells in the stage of a youth to manifest the physical marks and majestic radiance of a bodhisattva, which surpass those of all Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors;
he dwells in the stage of a youth to cause sentient beings who are attached to sensual pleasures to rejoice in the Dharma;
and he dwells in the stage of a youth out of reverence for the True Dharma, diligently making offerings to the Buddhas throughout all worlds in the ten directions.
Abiding in the stage of a youth (*kumārabhūmi*), they manifest the reception of the Buddha’s empowerment and the illumination of the Dharma;

thus, abiding in the stage of a youth constitutes the manifestation of the stage of a youth for the ten sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Having manifested the stage of a youth, they abide in the royal palace for ten reasons.
What are these ten? Namely, it is to bring to maturity the roots of goodness of those sentient beings who were their companions in previous lives.
Therefore, he dwells in the royal palace to manifest the power of the Bodhisattva’s roots of goodness;
he dwells in the royal palace to demonstrate to gods and humans who are attached to objects of pleasure the great majestic power and enjoyments of the Bodhisattva;
he dwells in the royal palace to accord with the inclinations of sentient beings in the five turbidities; and he dwells in the royal palace to manifest the great majestic power of the Bodhisattva.

He dwells in the royal palace because he is able to enter samādhi within the inner chambers; he dwells in the royal palace in order to fulfill the aspirations of those sentient beings who shared his vows in past lives;
he dwells in the royal palace because he wishes to fulfill the desires of his parents, kinsmen, and retinue;
and he dwells in the royal palace because he intends to offer music and the sublime sound of the Dharma as an offering to all Tathāgatas.
Manifesting in the royal palace, he dwells within it to demonstrate the subtle samādhi; from his initial attainment of Buddhahood until his parinirvāṇa, he manifests all these stages.
He manifests in the royal palace in order to accord with and protect the teachings of all Buddhas.
Manifesting in the royal palace is the manner in which a bodhisattva in their final birth acts. Having thus manifested dwelling in the royal palace, he thereafter—
For ten reasons, the renunciant sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, manifest the act of leaving the home life. What are these ten? They are:
they manifest leaving the home life out of weariness with domestic life; they manifest leaving the home life so as to cause sentient beings attached to the household to abandon it;
they manifest leaving the home life to accord with and delight in the path of the Noble Ones; they manifest [leaving the home life] to proclaim...
He manifests renunciation to extol the merit of leaving the household life; he manifests renunciation to demonstrate the permanent departure from the two extreme views;
he manifests renunciation to cause sentient beings to abandon the desire for pleasure and the attachment to self;
he manifests renunciation to first display the signs of transcending the three realms; and he manifests renunciation to demonstrate sovereignty that is not subject to another.
They manifest leaving the household life in order to reveal that they shall attain the Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessnesses;
they manifest leaving the household life because it is the final bodhisattva dharma that ought to be so.
These are the ten reasons why Bodhisattvas, sons of the Buddha, Mahāsattvas, manifest the practice of asceticism for the sake of taming sentient beings. What are these ten?

The ten are as follows: he manifests the practice of asceticism in order to bring to maturity those beings of inferior understanding; he manifests the practice of asceticism in order to uproot the wrong views of beings;
he manifests the practice of asceticism so that beings who do not believe in karmic retribution may perceive it;
he manifests the practice of asceticism because it is the natural law of conforming to a world of defilement; and he manifests the practice of asceticism to demonstrate his capacity for endurance.
He manifests the practice of asceticism because he has toiled and diligently cultivated the Path; he manifests the practice of asceticism so that sentient beings may joyfully seek the Dharma;
he manifests the practice of asceticism because sentient beings are attached to sensual pleasures and self-indulgence;
and he manifests the practice of asceticism to demonstrate the excellence of the Bodhisattva’s undertaking of practices, such that even in his final birth he does not abandon diligent vigor.
To cause sentient beings to delight in the dharma of tranquility and increase their roots of goodness, they manifest the practice of asceticism;
because the faculties of gods and worldlings are not yet mature, they manifest the practice of asceticism while awaiting the time for them to reach maturity.

These are the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas use these skillful means to discipline all sentient beings. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva proceeds to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
There are ten kinds of matters. What are these ten? They are: when approaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), illuminating all worlds;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, shaking all worlds; when approaching the site of enlightenment, universally manifesting one's body in all worlds;
and when approaching the site of enlightenment, awakening all bodhisattvas and all those who were fellow-practitioners in past lives.
When sentient beings approach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he manifests all the adornments of the site of enlightenment;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, he manifests various physical postures and the manifold adornments of the Bodhi tree according to the desires of the minds of those sentient beings;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, he causes them to see all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; and when approaching the site of enlightenment, he lifts his foot.
With every step he takes, he constantly enters samādhi; in every thought-moment he attains Buddhahood without interruption.

When he proceeds to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and all the various kings, each unaware of the others, present all manner of sublime and wondrous offerings.

When approaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one uses unimpeded wisdom to universally observe all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva in all worlds and attain perfect awakening; this is the tenth [practice] by which bodhisattvas thus teach and transform sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, there are ten matters. What are these ten? They are:
That is to say: at the time of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, they cause all worlds to tremble in various ways;

at the time of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, they illuminate all worlds with equality; at the time of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, they eliminate the sufferings of all evil destinies;
at the time of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, they cause all worlds to be composed of vajra; and at the time of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, they universally manifest all Buddhas.
When the Tathāgata sits upon the lion throne at the site of enlightenment, his mind is like space, free from all discrimination;

when he sits at the site of enlightenment, he manifests physical postures and deportment according to what is appropriate for beings; when he sits at the site of enlightenment, he dwells in accordance with the adamantine samādhi;
when he sits at the site of enlightenment, he occupies a pure and wondrous place sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas.
At the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the power of one’s own roots of goodness is able to empower all sentient beings; this is the tenth.
O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, there are ten kinds of extraordinary and unprecedented events.
What are these ten? O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, all the Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions...
They all appeared before him, raising their right hands and praising him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, O Unsurpassed Guide!

This is the first unprecedented event. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all Tathāgatas protect and keep him in mind and bestow upon him their majestic power; this is the second unprecedented event for a Bodhisattva."

When the Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all the bodhisattvas who were his companions in previous lives come to surround him and reverently make offerings with various kinds of ornaments; this is the third unprecedented event.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, all the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and insentient things in all worlds bend toward him.
The body bowing low and its shadow turning toward the site of enlightenment—this is the fourth unprecedented event.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they enter a samādhi called "Observation of the Dharma-realm.
By the power of this samādhi, all the practices of the Bodhisattva are brought to complete fulfillment; this is the fifth unprecedented event of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

When the Bodhisattva sat at the site of enlightenment, he attained a dhāraṇī named Supreme Stainless Wondrous Light Ocean-Treasury, which is able to receive the great cloud-like Dharma rain of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; this is the sixth unprecedented event.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, by the power of his majestic virtue, he produces supreme and wondrous offerings that pervade all worlds.
Making offerings to the Buddhas throughout the realms is the seventh unprecedented event.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), abiding in supreme wisdom, they fully perceive and understand the faculties, intentions, and mental activities of all sentient beings;
this is the eighth unprecedented event. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they enter a samādhi named "Excellence" (*Sādhu*).
To realize that the power of this samādhi can cause one’s body to fill all worlds throughout the three periods of time and the entirety of the realm of empty space—
this is the ninth unprecedented event. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment,
they attain the stainless radiance and unimpeded great wisdom, whereby their physical actions universally enter the three periods of time— this is the tenth unprecedented event.
There are, O sons of the Buddha, ten kinds of extraordinary and unprecedented events that occur when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Sons of the Buddha, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates ten meanings while sitting at the site of enlightenment that he manifests the subduing of Māra.
What are these ten? They are: [to teach] for the sake of sentient beings in the defiled age who delight in combat and desire...

He manifests the subduing of Māra in order to reveal the power of a bodhisattva’s majestic virtue; he manifests the subduing of Māra in order to sever the doubts of gods and worldlings who harbor them;
he manifests the subduing of Māra in order to teach and discipline the hosts of Māra’s armies;

and he manifests the subduing of Māra in order to cause those among the gods and worldlings who delight in military arrays to gather together to witness it, thereby bringing their minds under discipline.
The manifestation of the subduing of Māra is for the purpose of demonstrating that all the powers possessed by Bodhisattvas are such that none in the world can oppose them;

the manifestation of the subduing of Māra is for the purpose of inspiring courageous strength in all sentient beings; the manifestation of the subduing of Māra is out of compassion for all sentient beings of the final age;
and the manifestation of the subduing of Māra is for the purpose of demonstrating that even at the site of enlightenment, [the path] remains...
There are ten reasons why he manifests the subduing of Māra: first, because there are hosts of Māras who come to harass him, and only thereafter can he transcend the realm of Māra;
second, to demonstrate that the functioning of afflictions and karma is weak and inferior, while the power of the roots of great compassion and goodness is preeminent;
third, to manifest the subduing of Māra in accordance with the practices of the turbid and evil world; [and so forth]. These constitute the ten.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of powers by which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas accomplish the power of a Tathāgata. What are these ten? They are:
the accomplishment of the power of a Tathāgata by transcending all Māras, afflictions, and karma;

the accomplishment of the power of a Tathāgata by being fully endowed with all bodhisattva practices and sporting in all bodhisattva samādhi-doors; the accomplishment of the power of a Tathāgata by being fully endowed with all bodhisattva... [text continues]
Because of his vast meditative concentration, he attains the power of a Tathāgata; because he has perfected all pure factors conducive to enlightenment, he attains the power of a Tathāgata;
because he has attained the light of wisdom regarding all phenomena through skillful reflection and discernment, he attains the power of a Tathāgata;
because his body pervades all worlds, he attains the power of a Tathāgata; and as for the sounds of the speech he utters, they are all...

Because his mind is equal to that of all sentient beings, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata; because he is able to empower all things through his supernormal powers, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata;

because his physical, verbal, and mental karma are equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time without any difference, and because he comprehends the dharmas of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment, he achieves the power of a Tathāgata;
and because he has attained the samādhi of excellent awakening, he is endowed with the qualities of a Tathāgata.
The ten powers (daśabala) refer to the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, up to the power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñānabala);
by means of these, one becomes a Tathāgata’s power, and these constitute the ten. If Bodhisattvas are endowed with these ten powers, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
O Son of the Buddha, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha turns the great wheel of Dharma, there are ten matters. What are these ten?
First, they are fully endowed with the wisdom of the four kinds of fearlessness; second, they give rise to the four analytical eloquences and accordant voices;
third, they are skillfully able to expound the characteristics of the four noble truths; fourth, they accord with the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas;
fifth, they are able to cause the minds of sentient beings to be filled with pure faith; and sixth, all their speech is never in vain.
Seventh, they are empowered by the sustaining force of the great compassionate vow to extract the poisonous arrows of suffering from all sentient beings;
eighth, they emit sounds that pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions; ninth, they preach the Dharma without interruption for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*);
tenth, whatever Dharma they teach is capable of giving rise to the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, the path, meditative concentrations, and liberations.
The sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgatas, turn the wheel of Dharma through such immeasurable varieties of phenomena as the liberation from samādhis.

Sons of the Buddha, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, turns the wheel of Dharma, he plants seeds of pure, white dharmas within the minds of sentient beings so that they do not go in vain. What are these ten? They are as follows: the past...
By the power of his vows, being sustained by great compassion, not abandoning sentient beings,
and preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations through mastery of wisdom; by never missing the appropriate time, by speaking without falsehood according to what is suitable,
by thoroughly understanding through the knowledge of the three times, and because his body is most excellent and peerless— his speech is [spontaneous].
Because they cannot be measured, their wisdom is sovereign, and whatever they utter brings complete awakening; this is the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has performed the work of a Buddha, he manifests parinirvāṇa by contemplating ten kinds of meanings.
What are these ten? They are: to show that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are truly impermanent; to show all conditioned things... [and so forth].
Because it is not a state of true security, he demonstrates that Great Nirvāṇa is the place of security, free from fear;
because humans and devas delight in attachment to the physical body, he manifests the physical body as a teaching on impermanence so that they may aspire to abide in the pure Dharma-body;
and because the power of impermanence cannot be overturned, he demonstrates that all conditioned phenomena do not abide according to one's will and are not autonomous.

Therefore, they demonstrate that all three realms of existence are like illusions and transformations, lacking any solidity; they demonstrate that the nature of nirvāṇa is ultimately solid and indestructible;
and they demonstrate that while all phenomena are without birth or arising, they possess the characteristics of aggregation, dispersion, and destruction.
O Son of the Buddha, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have completed their buddha-work, fulfilled their vows, and turned the wheel of Dharma, [they manifest these things].

Having already brought to maturity all those who were to be transformed and delivered, and having caused all the bodhisattvas to receive their honorable titles and attain their predictions of enlightenment,
it is the natural law that one enters the unchanging Great Parinirvāṇa. O Son of the Buddha, for these ten reasons,
the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifests parinirvāṇa.

[Treatise] Sixth: At that time, after Samantabhadra Bodhisattva had finished addressing Samantamati Bodhisattva and the others, down to the end of the two thousand answers in the fifty-ninth fascicle, it says:

"O Son of the Buddha, for the sake of contemplating ten meanings, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifests parinirvāṇa. This section contains two thousand answers by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
In each of the teachings he answers, there are ten dharmas; as each passage is self-evident, there is no need for further explanation.
Simply practicing according to what has been taught constitutes the section on "Correct Exposition."
[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate is named "The Vast and Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas," which is proclaimed by immeasurable Buddhas together.
It enables the wise to comprehend immeasurable meanings and gives rise to joy in all; it causes the great vows and great practices of all bodhisattvas to continue in succession.
O Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma and, having heard it, believe in it...
Having understood and understood, one who practices will certainly and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

Because they practice according to what has been taught. Son of the Buddha, if bodhisattvas do not act according to what has been taught, you should know that such persons are forever separated from the *buddha-bodhi*. Therefore, a bodhisattva should act according to what has been taught. Son of the Buddha, this...
The Chapter on the Dharma-Door of Transcending the World, Which Is the Definitive Meaning of the Sphere of All Bodhisattva Meritorious Practices,
Universally Entering All Dharmas, Universally Producing All-Knowledge, Surpassing All Worlds, Departing from the Paths of the Two Vehicles,
Not Shared with Any Sentient Beings, Fully Illuminating All Dharma-Gates, and Increasing the World-Transcending Roots of Goodness in Beings.
One should respect it, listen to it, recite and uphold it, contemplate it, aspire to it, and practice it;
if one can do so, know that such a person will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary] From "The seventh son of the Buddha" down to "perfect enlightenment" (samyak-saṃbodhi), there are twelve and a half lines of scripture;
this constitutes the section on the entrustment and circulation of this Dharma-gate.

[Sūtra] When this chapter was being taught, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of this Dharma-gate, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds in the ten directions all shook violently and were universally illumined by a great light.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Son of the Buddha! You have been able to teach [this]."

This is the chapter on the "Dharma Gate of the Universal Entry into All Buddha-Dharmas and Supramundane Dharmas," which is the definitive meaning of the sphere of meritorious conduct for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha, you have already well studied this Dharma and well expounded this Dharma;
we all, through our majestic power, shall protect and uphold this Dharma, and we Buddhas all rejoice in it, just as we Buddhas do.

We rejoice in you; all Buddhas likewise do so. O Son of the Buddha, we Buddhas, with one mind, shall protect and uphold this sutra, so that all bodhisattvas of the present and future who have not yet heard it may hear it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions.
The entire assembly, extending to the limits of the Dharma-realm, spoke in verse.

[Treatise]: When this chapter was being expounded—the section from "At that time" down to the eleven lines of verse—it clarifies how the majesty of the Dharma shook the earth, and how the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before him to praise the Dharma spoken by Samantabhadra.
Together we shall protect this portion of the Dharma.

[Sūtra] Having practiced asceticism for immeasurable eons, born from the true Dharma of immeasurable Buddhas, you have established immeasurable multitudes in Bodhi; hear me speak of those peerless practices.

Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, he abandoned attachment; He extensively delivers all living beings without forming conceptual thoughts, and his mind has no reliance on the merit of Buddhahood. I shall now describe those supreme and wondrous practices:
They transcend the three realms, māras, afflictions, and karma, And are endowed with the most excellent conduct of noble merit.
With all delusions extinguished, his mind is tranquil; I now describe the path he has traveled.

Forever free from the illusions and deceptions of the world, he manifests various transformations for the sake of sentient beings, appearing through the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind to display manifold phenomena. I shall speak of his capabilities to bring joy to the multitude.

Seeing all sentient beings oppressed and constrained by birth, old age, death, afflictions, and calamities, he desires to liberate them and teaches them to resolve their minds on awakening. One should listen to and receive his meritorious conduct:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
One who constantly practices for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas—listen, O Benevolent One, to that person’s merit!
For billions of kalpas they seek Bodhi, never begrudging their own body or life;
wishing only to benefit all living beings and not themselves—I shall now describe that practice of loving-kindness and compassion.
[Verse: For immeasurable billions of kalpas he has expounded his virtues; though it were but a single drop from the ocean, they would not be considered few.
His merit is peerless and beyond analogy; by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall now briefly describe it.
[Treatise: The ninth section, beginning with "Having practiced asceticism for immeasurable kalpas," consists of sixteen lines of verse.
All praised the vast and incomparable merit of those who have resolved to attain great bodhicitta and practice compassion and vows.
[Sūtra] Their minds are neither elated nor depressed; seeking the Way without weariness, they cause all sentient beings to...

Abiding in the wholesome, increasing the pure dharmas, and benefiting all universally through wisdom—like a tree, a river, a spring, and also like the great earth, they are the support for all. The Bodhisattva is like a lotus:
compassion is the root, peace is the stalk, wisdom is the medicinal herb, and the aggregate of ethical discipline is the fragrant purity.
The Buddha emits the radiance of the Dharma, Causing it to blossom fully; Those who behold it find joy, as they do not cling to the waters of conditioned existence.
The Bodhisattva’s wondrous tree of Dharma Is born from the ground of an upright mind, With faith as its seed and compassion as its roots;
Wisdom constitutes its trunk, And skillful means its branches and boughs.
The five perfections are its dense foliage; meditative concentration is its leaf and supernormal powers its flower.
All-knowledge is its fruit, and supreme power is its creeper. It hangs its shade, covering the three realms.
The Bodhisattva, the Lion King, has the pure white Dharma as his body, the Four Truths as his feet, and right mindfulness as his neck.

With eyes of loving-kindness and wisdom as his crest, and the silken band of liberation bound upon his crown, he roars the Dharma like a lion in the valley of ultimate emptiness, terrifying all the māras. This Bodhisattva acts as a caravan leader;
he beholds all sentient beings throughout the wilderness of saṃsāra, in the perilous and evil places of affliction, seized by the bandits of Māra.
For those blinded by ignorance who have lost the right path, he shows the straight and upright way, leading them to the City of Fearlessness.
Seeing sentient beings afflicted by the diseases of the three poisons and various sufferings,
tormented throughout the long night, he gives rise to great compassion and extensively expounds the gates of remedial practice.
Eighty-four thousand kinds [of teachings] extinguish all suffering and affliction.

The Bodhisattva, as a Dharma King, transforms sentient beings through the right path, causing them to distance themselves from evil and cultivate goodness, while single-mindedly seeking the merits of the Buddhas.
At the abodes of all Buddhas, he receives the consecration and the noble prediction, extensively bestowing the wealth of the sages upon all.
The Bodhisattva turns the wheel of Dharma, a treasure of the factors of enlightenment, just as the Buddha turned it:
with the precepts as its hub and samādhi as its rim, adorned with wisdom and having insight as its sword;
having already destroyed the thieves of affliction and likewise annihilated the host of Māra’s enemies, all those of the various non-Buddhist paths cannot help but scatter upon seeing it.
The Bodhisattva’s ocean of wisdom is deep and vast, without limit or shore;
Filled with the flavor of the True Dharma and replete with the jewels of the factors of enlightenment, This great mind has no boundless bank;
all-knowledge is its tide, which sentient beings cannot fathom. To describe it would be inexhaustible—the Bodhisattva is Mount Sumeru.
Transcending the world, he stands at the peak of supernormal powers and samādhi; his great mind is settled and immovable.
If there are those who draw near to him, they share in his wisdom and appearance.
Far removed from all objective realms, there is nothing he does not perceive. The Bodhisattva is like a diamond, resolutely seeking all-knowledge.
With faith and ascetic practice, firm and immovable, their minds are fearless as they benefit all living beings; all Māras and afflictions are utterly destroyed.
The Bodhisattva’s great compassion is like heavy, dense clouds, with the three types of supernormal knowledge flashing like lightning.
With the thunderous voice of the divine feet, he universally employs the four analytical eloquences;
raining down the water of the eightfold merit, he moistens and saturates all beings, causing them to eliminate the heat of afflictions.
The Bodhisattva’s city of the True Dharma takes Prajñā as its walls, shame and remorse as its deep moats, and wisdom as its defensive ramparts.
He widely opens the gates of liberation, Constantly guarding with right mindfulness. The Four Truths are the level royal road;
The six supernormal powers are his gathered weapons. Furthermore, he erects the great banner of Dharma;
Throughout all its circumference, the hosts of Māras within the three realms of existence Are utterly unable to enter. This is the Bodhisattva Garuḍa.
With the wish-fulfilling gem as its firm feet, And skillful means and valor as its wings, With compassion and clarity as its bright eyes, It dwells upon the tree of omniscience.
Surveying the great ocean of the three realms of existence, It seizes gods, humans, and nāgas, And establishes them on the shore of nirvāṇa.
The sun of the Bodhisattva’s True Dharma Has appeared in the world.
The wheel of the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline, Moving with the swiftness of the bases of supernormal power,
Illuminating with the light of wisdom, increasing the medicinal herbs of the faculties and powers, Extinguishing the darkness of the afflictions, And drying up the ocean of craving and desire—
The moon of the Bodhisattva’s light of wisdom, Taking the dharma-realm as its wheel, Traverses the ultimate emptiness.
There is nothing in the world not seen within the consciousness-mind of the three realms;
At all times, amidst the stars of the two vehicles, there is increase and decrease, yet none can equal him.
The Bodhisattva, the Great Dharma King, his body adorned with merit, Complete in all the marks and signs, is gazed upon by gods and humans alike.
With the pure eyes of skillful means and the vajra of wisdom, you have attained mastery over all phenomena;
through the Way, you transform all living beings. You are a Bodhisattva, a Great Brahmā King, who transcends the three realms of existence with sovereign ease;
karma and delusions are entirely severed. Possessing both compassion and equanimity, there is nothing you do not embody as you manifest your body in every place.
Awakening through the sound of the Dharma, Within those three realms, He uproots the foundations of all false views.
The Bodhisattva Sovereign Deity Transcends the ground of birth and death; His sphere of experience is ever pure, His wisdom never regresses.
Having severed the paths of the lesser vehicles, He receives the rites of consecration.
Endowed with merit and wisdom, his fame is heard everywhere. The Bodhisattva’s mind of wisdom is as pure as space;

It is without intrinsic nature and has no place of dependence. Nothing whatsoever can be apprehended therein, yet he possesses great sovereign power And is able to accomplish the affairs of the world, Being himself possessed of pure conduct.
Causing sentient beings to be likewise, The Bodhisattva’s ground of skillful means benefits all beings;
The Bodhisattva’s water of compassion washes away all afflictions.
The Bodhisattva’s fire of wisdom burns the fuel of delusive habits; The Bodhisattva’s wind of non-abiding travels through the three realms of emptiness.
The Bodhisattva is like a precious jewel, capable of rescuing those in poverty and distress;
The Bodhisattva is like a vajra, able to shatter inverted views; The Bodhisattva is like a garland, adorning the bodies within the three realms of existence;
The Bodhisattva is like a mani-gem, increasing all virtuous practices; The virtues of the Bodhisattva are like flowers.
Constantly generating the factors of enlightenment, The Bodhisattva’s vows are like a garland, Perpetually bound upon the heads of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva’s fragrance of pure precepts, Firmly maintained without violation, And the Bodhisattva’s incense of wisdom, Pervade the entire triple world.
The Bodhisattva’s power is like a canopy, Able to shield one from the dust of afflictions.
The Bodhisattva’s wisdom is like a banner, capable of crushing the enemy of self-conceit;
adorned with the silk of sublime conduct, wisdom is its ornament, while shame and modesty serve as its clothing, universally covering all living beings.
The Bodhisattva’s unimpeded vehicle covers them as they emerge from the triple world; the Bodhisattva is a great elephant of mighty power.

With a mind well-tamed, the Bodhisattva is a horse of supernormal power; leaping across all realms of existence, the Bodhisattva is a dragon of Dharma-teaching, raining down universally upon the minds of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva is the *udumbara* flower, difficult to encounter in this world; the Bodhisattva is a great heroic general who utterly subdues all demons.
The Bodhisattva turns the wheel of Dharma just as the Buddha has turned it; The lamp of the Bodhisattva destroys the darkness so that sentient beings may see the right path.
The river of the Bodhisattva’s merit flows constantly in accordance with the right path;
The bridge of the Bodhisattva’s diligence widely delivers all classes of beings, Through great wisdom and vast vows.
Together they construct a sturdy ship to ferry all sentient beings across, establishing them upon the shore of Bodhi.
They are the pleasure garden where Bodhisattvas sport; they bring true joy to sentient beings.
Adorned with the flowers of liberation, they are the palace of wisdom for Bodhisattvas; like wondrous medicine, they eliminate the disease of afflictions.
The Bodhisattva is like the Snowy Mountain, producing the medicinal herbs of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva is equal to the Buddha in awakening all sentient beings; what else could the Buddha-mind be?
Just as the Perfectly Awakened One awakens the world, coming as the Buddha has come, so too does the Bodhisattva come, just like the All-Knowing One.
Entering the universal gate through wisdom, the Bodhisattva skillfully guides all living beings;
the Bodhisattva naturally awakens to the realm of omniscience.
The Bodhisattva’s immeasurable power cannot be destroyed by the world; with fearless wisdom, the Bodhisattva knows both sentient beings and phenomena.

All the various worlds, with their diverse forms and characteristics, their sounds and names— He is able to discern and know them all. Though detached from name and form, he manifests manifold appearances.
None among all sentient beings can fathom his way. Such are his meritorious qualities.
The Bodhisattva has fully accomplished [this], realizing that all natures are devoid of inherent nature;
Unattached to existence or non-existence, such is the All-Knowing One. Inexhaustible and without dependence, I shall now expound this to bring joy to all sentient beings.
Though he knows the characteristics of all phenomena, they are like illusions, entirely empty and quiescent.

By means of a heart of compassionate vows and the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, they manifest various and immeasurable miraculous transformations. You should all listen to and receive these merits:
that within a single body they can manifest immeasurable and diverse bodies, yet remain without mind and without objective realm.
Universally responding to all beings, Within a single sound, he fully expounds All manner of speech and sounds;
According to their kind, he can manifest The linguistic conventions of all sentient beings.
Having forever left behind the body of afflictions, He manifests a body of sovereign mastery; Knowing that phenomena are ineffable, He nevertheless delivers various teachings.
Their minds are eternally quiescent, pure as space; yet they universally adorn lands and manifest before all beings.
Without attachment to a body, they are able to manifest bodies throughout all worlds, taking birth according to what is appropriate, even while being born in all places.

Nor do they dwell in the taking of birth; knowing the body to be like empty space, they manifest boundless bodhisattva bodies according to the various inclinations of beings, appearing everywhere in all places.
They constantly and reverently make offerings to the Most Victorious among Two-Legged Beings with incense, flowers, various musical performances, banners, pennants, and precious canopies.
Always with a profound and pure mind, they make offerings to all Buddhas; never leaving the assembly of a single Buddha, they are universally present at the abodes of all Buddhas.
Within those great assemblies, they pose difficult questions and listen to the Dharma;
hearing the Dharma, they enter samādhi, through each and every immeasurable gateway, and their emergence from concentration is likewise so.
Manifesting inexhaustibly through wisdom and skillful means, they realize that all worlds are like illusions yet are able to manifest within the world.
Appearing as boundless illusory phenomena, they display various forms, as well as minds and speech;
though entering into the web of conceptualizations, they are forever free from attachment.
Some manifest the initial arousal of the mind to benefit the world; Others manifest long-term cultivation that is vast and boundless.

Through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, Meditative concentration, and wisdom—the four sublime abodes, the four means of attraction, and so forth— All supreme dharmas, they manifest the completion of their practice.
Having attained patience, they are free from conceptual discrimination; some manifest as bound to one more birth.
Some receive empowerment from the Buddhas, while others manifest in the form of śrāvakas or again as pratyekabuddhas.
They enter parinirvāṇa in various places yet do not abandon the practice of bodhi. Some manifest as Śakra, and some manifest as Brahmā.
Sometimes surrounded by celestial maidens, sometimes dwelling alone in silent retreat;
sometimes appearing as a bhikṣu to tranquilly discipline his mind; sometimes appearing as a sovereign king to govern the laws of the world;
sometimes appearing as a woman skilled in arts, sometimes appearing to practice asceticism, or sometimes appearing to enjoy the five desires.
Sometimes he manifests entering the various dhyānas; sometimes he manifests his initial birth.

Whether as a child, an old man, or one facing death—if anyone should attempt to conceive of him through thought, their mind will be filled with doubt and driven to madness. Sometimes he appears in celestial palaces;
sometimes he manifests the descent of his spirit. He manifests entering or dwelling in the womb, attaining Buddhahood, and turning the wheel of Dharma.
Sometimes he is born, sometimes he enters nirvana; Sometimes he appears entering a school, Or among palace ladies, or leaving the world to practice dhyāna;
Sometimes he sits beneath the Bodhi tree, Spontaneously attaining perfect enlightenment;
Or he manifests turning the wheel of Dharma, Or manifesting first seeking the Way, Or manifesting as the body of a Buddha.
Reclining in meditation within immeasurable lands, some cultivate the path of non-retrogression;
Accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, they enter deeply for countless eons, all reaching the further shore.
Immeasurable eons are a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is immeasurable eons; All eons are not eons, yet for the sake of the world, they manifest as eons.
Without coming or accumulation, they accomplish the affairs of all kalpas. Within a single mote of dust, they universally see all Buddhas;
throughout all places in the ten directions, there is nowhere that lands, sentient beings, and dharmas do not exist—all these they see in succession, throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Ultimately inexhaustible, the Bodhisattva knows that sentient beings are vast and boundless.
Within the body of a single sentient being, there arise immeasurable causes and conditions; just as one knows the immeasurable within the one, so it is for all.
According to what they have realized, he teaches those who have not yet learned.
He fully knows the faculties of sentient beings—superior, middling, and inferior—and their differences;

he also knows the shifting of faculties, what is suitable for transformation and what is not, and how one faculty relates to all others through the power of successive causes and conditions, with their subtle and distinct variations.
He knows them in their proper sequence without error, and furthermore, he knows their inclinations and understandings.
He knows all habitual tendencies of the afflictions, as well as the past, future, and present;
having fully realized all mental activities and understood that all formations neither come nor go, and having known their nature,
he preaches the unsurpassed Dharma regarding both defiled and pure formations, understanding them all in their various aspects.
Attaining enlightenment in a single thought, one accomplishes all-knowledge;
Abiding in the Buddha’s inconceivable mind of ultimate wisdom, one can know everything in a single thought.
Through the power of the Bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom, having attained mastery over its functioning, One is able, within a single moment of thought, to [perceive]...

They travel to boundless lands; thus they proceed with such swiftness that throughout countless eons there is nowhere they do not pervade, yet without moving even a single hair’s breadth. It is like a skilled artisan manifesting various forms;
though one seeks them within that illusion, there are no forms, nor are there any that are not forms.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: through the illusion of skillful means and wisdom, they manifest all manner of forms that fill the world.
Just as the pure sun and moon, bright and clear, reside in the void and their reflections appear in all waters without being mixed with the water, so too is the Bodhisattva’s pure wheel of Dharma.
Know that it is likewise so: the water of the mind manifests in the world, yet remains unmixed with worldly things.
Just as when a person is in a dream, performing all manner of deeds, though many billions of years pass, not even a single night has ended;
so too the Bodhisattva, abiding in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), manifests all activities.
Though immeasurable eons may reach their end, the wisdom of a single thought-moment is inexhaustible.
Just as within mountain valleys and amidst palaces, all manner of sounds echo in response, yet in reality there is no discrimination,
so too the Bodhisattva abiding in the nature of phenomena can, through sovereign wisdom, extensively produce voices that accord with the various types of beings.
Furthermore, there is no discrimination therein; it is like seeing a mirage and perceiving it as water, running toward it but unable to drink, only to find one's thirst increasing all the more.
One should know that the afflictive minds of sentient beings are likewise. The Bodhisattva gives rise to compassion and rescues them, causing them to transcend [suffering].

Contemplate form as a mass of foam, Sensation as a bubble upon the water, Perception as a mirage in the heat, Formations as the core of a plantain tree, And consciousness as a magical illusion that manifests various phenomena.
Knowing the aggregates thus, the wise have no attachments; All sense bases are entirely empty and quiescent.
Like the movement of a mechanical device, the nature of all realms is eternally free [from self]; they falsely appear in the world.
The Bodhisattva dwells in reality, the ultimate truth of quiescence;
he extensively proclaims these various teachings, yet his mind has no point of reliance—neither coming nor going, and likewise, no abiding.
The causes of afflictions, karma, and suffering—these three constantly circulate.
Dependent origination is neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor false; Entering the Middle Way in this manner, one speaks without attachment.
Able, within a single thought-moment, to universally manifest the minds of the three periods of time, Throughout the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Regarding all various matters, you accord with the threefold discipline; You expound the three liberations and establish the path of the three vehicles.

You have accomplished all-knowledge and thoroughly understood what is possible and impossible, As well as all karmas, faculties, elements, analytical knowledges, meditative concentrations, And the paths leading to all destinations.
Possessing the recollection of past lives and the divine eye, they have eliminated all delusions;

They know the ten powers of a Buddha, yet have not yet achieved them; They thoroughly understand the emptiness of all phenomena, yet constantly seek the sublime Dharma without merging with afflictions;
They do not exhaust their outflows, yet possess broad knowledge of the path to liberation.
And by means of this, they deliver sentient beings; herein they attain fearlessness. They do not abandon the cultivation of all practices, nor do they err or deviate from the Path.
Furthermore, they do not lose right mindfulness; their diligence, aspiration, samādhi, and wisdom do not diminish.
The three clusters are all purified, and they clearly penetrate all three periods of time.
Greatly compassionate toward all sentient beings, Unobstructed in every respect, By entering this Dharma-gate, one accomplishes such conduct;

I shall now describe a small portion of it. The meaning of its adornment with merit is exhausted only after incalculable eons, And even speaking of that conduct would be inexhaustible; I now speak but a small fraction of it.
Like a single mote of dust upon the great earth, they abide in reliance upon the Buddha’s wisdom.
Giving rise to thoughts of wonder, they practice the most supreme conduct; endowed with great compassion, they diligently bring peace and security to all sentient beings.
Abiding firmly within pure precepts, they possess the practices for receiving the various prophecies.
Able to enter the Buddha’s merits, The conduct of sentient beings, and the lands, Knowing all kalpas and worlds without thought of weariness;
Possessing the *dhāraṇī* of discerning wisdom, Thoroughly penetrating the true meaning, their contemplation and teaching are peerless;
To the tranquil and perfectly awakened ones, I resolve to give rise to the mind of Samantabhadra.
And by cultivating their practices and vows, through the power of the causes and conditions of compassion, with a pure intention directed toward the Path, they practice the pāramitās;
through ultimate conforming wisdom, they realize the mastery of the power of knowledge and achieve unsurpassed bodhi;
having perfected equalizing wisdom, they expound the most supreme Dharma.
Able to maintain [the teachings] and endowed with sublime eloquence, they attain the station of the Dharma King;
far removed from all attachments, they preach with an equanimous mind. Giving birth to wisdom, through transformation they attain enlightenment and abide throughout all kalpas.
The wise experience great rejoicing as they penetrate deeply and rely [upon this].
Fearless and free from doubt, they have thoroughly realized the inconceivable. Skillful and subtle, they discern well and enter skillfully into all samādhis.
Universally perceiving the realm of wisdom, they have perfected all liberations.
They sport with the various supernormal powers and clear insights, forever free from all fetters; they roam at will through groves and gardens.
With pure dharmas as his palace, all conditioned phenomena are a source of joy;
manifesting immeasurable adornments while remaining unmoved in the world, he observes with a profound mind. With wondrous eloquence, he can expound the seal of pure bodhi;
the light of his wisdom illuminates all, and his dwelling is beyond compare.
Their minds are not inferior; their resolve is like a great mountain. Planting roots of virtue like a deep ocean, they dwell securely in the Dharma as it truly is.
Clad in the armor of their vow, they initiate the Great Task that none can ultimately destroy.
Having received the prophecy of enlightenment, they abide in a vast mind.
The secret treasury is inexhaustible; awakening to all phenomena, worldly wisdom is entirely sovereign, its wondrous function unimpeded.
Throughout all realms of sentient beings and all various dharmas, bodies, vows, and spheres—along with wisdom, spiritual powers, and the like—they manifest throughout the world.
Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of playful manifestations and spheres of activity, sovereign power that cannot be restrained,
fearlessness, and the unshared qualities— all adorned by every karma; through the attainment of the protection of all bodies,
bodily actions, speech, and the purification of speech, ten kinds of tasks are accomplished.
When the Bodhisattva’s mind first arises, and when that mind becomes all-pervasive, the various faculties are free from distraction and attain supreme mastery.
With a profound mind and an ever-increasing resolve, they remain far removed from flattery and deception;
possessing various kinds of definitive understanding, they enter universally into the world and abandon the habitual tendencies of those afflictions.
Having taken up this most excellent path, skillfully cultivating it to completion, one attains all-knowledge, leaves behind decline,
enters the stage of certainty, and definitively realizes nirvāṇa. One gives birth to the path of the Buddha-dharmas,
achieves the title of merit, and perfects the path, the immeasurable paths, and even the path of adornment.
Successively and well-established, entirely free from attachment; with hands, feet, and internal organs made of vajra, armored in compassion;
fully equipped with various weapons, having wisdom as the head and clear insight as the eyes, the conduct of awakening as the ears, and pure precepts as the nose.
Extinguishing darkness without obstruction, with eloquence as his tongue, a body that reaches everywhere, and supreme wisdom as his mind;
whether walking, staying, or practicing various deeds, seated upon the lion throne at the site of enlightenment, or reclining in the Brahma-posture in the sky;
in all his conduct and observations, he universally illumines the realm of the Tathāgata.

Universally observing the conduct of sentient beings, Displaying prowess and letting forth lion’s roars, Free from greed, practicing pure giving, abandoning pride, and upholding pure precepts; Without anger, always patient; Without indolence, ever diligent;
attaining mastery in meditative concentration; With wisdom that has no object of action, Rescuing with compassion and never wearying in pity.
Delighting in the Dharma, they abandon afflictions; amidst all sensory objects, they know both the meaning and the Dharma.
Their merit is fully perfected, and their wisdom is like a sharp sword.
Universally illuminating their joy in hearing much, they clearly understand the direction toward the Dharma. Knowing Māra and the paths of Māra, they vow to abandon them all.
Beholding the Buddhas and their buddha-activities, they resolve to embrace them all; free from pride, they cultivate wisdom and are not held by the power of Māra.
Sustained by the Buddhas and likewise upheld by the Dharma, they manifest dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, then manifest the end of that life, and demonstrate abiding in the mother’s womb.
He also manifests subtle movements, appearing to be born and smiling; he likewise manifests walking seven steps and demonstrating the mastery of all arts and crafts;
he also shows himself dwelling in the deep palace, leaving home, practicing austerities, and proceeding to the site of enlightenment;
there, sitting upright, he emits radiance and awakens all living beings.
Having subdued Māra and attained perfect enlightenment, he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
all that he manifested has now come to an end as he enters Great Parinirvāṇa. The practices of those Bodhisattvas were cultivated for immeasurable eons, vast and boundless;
I shall now describe but a small portion of them, even though it may lead countless beings [to liberation].
Abiding securely in the Buddha’s virtues, in sentient beings, and in all phenomena, they are ultimately without grasping;
thus fulfilling such practice, they sport with the various supernormal powers. They place myriad buddha-fields upon the tip of a hair and pass through billions of eons;
holding infinite fields in their palms, they travel everywhere without weariness of body.
Returning, they place them back in their original locations, yet sentient beings do not perceive it.
The Bodhisattva, by means of all manner of various adornments of the lands, places them within a single pore, yet truly causes everyone to see them.
Furthermore, with a single pore, he universally contains all oceans; the great oceans neither increase nor decrease.
Sentient beings do not cause harm; The immeasurable Iron Ring Mountains Are grasped by hand and ground into dust.
One mote of dust is placed in each world-system; When all these motes of dust have been exhausted, Those world-systems of dust are again ground into dust.
Such motes of dust may be known, But the wisdom of the Bodhisattva is difficult to measure.
From within a single pore, he emits immeasurable rays of light— The radiance of the sun, moon, and stars,
the light of mani jewels and fire, And the splendor of all the devas— all these are eclipsed and obscured.
He extinguishes the suffering of all evil realms and preaches the unsurpassed Dharma for all the worlds.
With various distinct sounds, the Bodhisattva, by means of a single voice, is able to expound them all;
he definitively analyzes and explains all the teachings of the Buddhas, causing all living beings who hear them to rejoice greatly.
He establishes all kalpas of the past within the future and the present.
The future and present kalpas are turned back and placed within the past; the burning, formation, and abiding of immeasurable lands,
as well as all worlds throughout the ten directions— past, future, and present— are all contained within a single pore,
such that there is no Buddha in any of the ten directions who does not abide within his body.
Clearly manifesting and deeply understanding the laws of transformation, you skillfully respond to the minds of sentient beings by manifesting various bodies,
yet remain entirely unattached. You may manifest the bodies of all sentient beings within the six realms of existence,
the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, or the bodies of the hosts of devas and humans.
The bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, The bodies of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
Or manifesting the bodies of bodhisattvas practicing for all-knowledge, Skillfully entering the soft, middling, and superior [capacities],
Manifesting the attainment of enlightenment within the various nets of sentient beings' perceptions, As well as throughout all Buddha-fields, They thoroughly understand these nets of perception.
Having attained mastery over thought, they manifest the practice of the bodhisattva path;
they display all manner of skillful means and such vast, divine transformations.
Such realms as these cannot be known by anyone in the world; though they manifest, there is nothing manifested, yet they ultimately increase further and further.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, you cause them to practice the path of truth. Your body, speech, and mind are equal to space;
pure precepts serve as your ointment and perfume. Your various deeds are your garments, and the Dharma-ribbon adorns your pure topknot.
The jewel of omniscience is your crown; there is no merit that does not pervade all.
The Bodhisattva is a Wheel-Turning King: Consecration is his accession to the throne; the Perfections are his wheels;
the various supernormal powers are his state elephants; his feet are his horses; wisdom is his great jewel; sublime conduct is his court ladies;
the four means of integration are his lord of the treasury; and skillful means is his commander-in-chief.
Samādhi is the city wall; emptiness and stillness are the palace. Compassion is the armor, wisdom the sword, mindfulness the bow, and clear insight the sharp arrow.
The canopy of supernormal power is raised high, and the banner of wisdom is erected far aloft.
With the power of patience unshakable, one directly breaks the army of Māra; Dhāraṇī serves as the level ground.
The various activities are its river; pure wisdom is its spring; sublime insight forms its groves;
and emptiness is its clear, limpid pool. The factors of enlightenment are its lotus blossoms; spiritual powers serve as its natural adornment;
samādhi is its constant delight; reflection is its courtly lady; and the nectar of immortality is its choice food.
Taking the flavor of liberation as their drink, they sport within the three vehicles.
These bodhisattvas’ practices are subtle and ever-increasing; through cultivation over immeasurable eons, their minds never grow weary or satisfied.
They make offerings to all Buddhas, purify all buddha-fields, and cause all sentient beings everywhere—
Abiding in omniscience, one could know the number of all atoms in every land;
One could measure the entirety of the realm of empty space with a single grain of sand;
One could count and know every thought-moment of the minds of all sentient beings; Yet the virtues of the Buddha-sons can never be fully told.
Desiring to be endowed with these merits and all supreme, wondrous dharmas;

desiring to cause all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and dwell in constant peace and happiness; and desiring to make one’s own body, speech, and mind entirely equal to those of all Buddhas—one should generate the vajra-mind and train in this practice of merit.

[Treatise] The tenth section, beginning with "His mind is neither high nor low," consists of five-word verses extending to the end of the scroll, totaling two hundred and seventy-five and a half verses.
Through various parables, these verses illustrate the great compassion and benefits bestowed by the Bodhisattvas, as well as the dharma-gates they cultivate.
As detailed in the Sūtra itself, each point is clearly explained; indeed, all who give rise to the bodhicitta [partake of this].

One should reverently recite and uphold this with the crown of one's head to adorn the actions of body, speech, and mind, thereby perfecting the gateway of the great wisdom, great compassion, and vows of the Dharma-body to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood—the Great Function of Samantabhadra. This "Chapter on Transcending the World" follows the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood;
it is the eternal practice of Samantabhadra, which universally seals the ten directions without rest, just as [the preceding chapters were] good.
Just as Sudhana saw the Tathāgata Maitreya, and the Tathāgata Maitreya in turn caused him to see Mañjuśrī and hear the name of Samantabhadra;
and just as Sudhana gave rise to immeasurable clouds of the ten great vows and only then saw himself enter the body of Samantabhadra—
this chapter is identical to that.
