[Treatise] The tenth assembly expounds the gateway of the Dharma-realm at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part One [Treatise]:
This chapter will be explained through a sixfold analysis: first, an explanation of the title of the chapter; second, an explanation of the purpose for its inclusion;

third, an explanation of the place where the Tathāgata resides; fourth, an explanation of the master who preaches the Dharma; fifth, an explanation of those assembled; and sixth, an explanation of the teaching itself.
**General Explanation of the Six Sections According to the Text:** 1. **Explanation of the Title of the Chapter:** Why is this chapter titled "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātupraveśa*)?
Those who clearly understand and delight [in the truth] transition from delusion to initial realization; thus, it is called "entering.

The nature of the realm of body and mind is inherently without dependence; thus, it is called "Dharma. It penetrates both the one and the many, as well as the provisional and the real, such that the barriers between right and wrong vanish.
It is called a "realm" (*dhātu*) because it is purely conjoined with wisdom and is not an object of deluded consciousness; thus it is called the "Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, because one realizes that the seeds of ignorance and consciousness are purely the functioning of wisdom and are not subsumed under delusion—this being the sphere of non-reliant wisdom—it is called the Dharma-realm.
Moreover, because the essence of wisdom is without dependence or spatial direction, it universally perceives both the ultimate and conventional truths.
In sum, within the inconceivable pores of the body, the motes of dust interlace with myriad forms and boundless realms;

the Buddha-fields are layered upon one another, and the wisdom of the Buddhas and the minds of ordinary beings share the same essence. When objects and images interpenetrate one another, this is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, within a single mote of dust, all lands are universally contained;
there is no void that is not pervaded and no land that is not encompassed. The retributive realms are layered without decay, for all phenomena are devoid of self-nature.

Thoroughly penetrating principle and reaching into phenomena without falsehood is called the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, with a single wondrous sound heard throughout the ocean of lands, with the measure of a single fine hair equaling the boundless, and with the disappearance of views of large and small and the realization that self and others share the same essence—where consciousness ceases, emotion is extinguished, and wisdom penetrates without obstruction—this is called "entering the *dharmadhātu*.
This is designated as the universal name based on the realm of wisdom; do not rely on [other] designations.

Regarding the intent of the arrival of this "Chapter on the Two Explanations" as perceived by the consciousness of the fleshly eye: it clarifies that previously there was the manifestation of one's own Tathāgata;
furthermore, it clarifies that the mind being unstained is called "transcending the world. This is purely the Dharma-realm, the realm without falsehood;
for this reason, this chapter has come forth. This chapter is the [foundation] for the attainment of enlightenment by all Buddhas.
The constant fruit of one’s own wisdom is without beginning and without end; it is also the substance of the aforementioned five stages of progressive cultivation.
Because one has reached the fulfillment of this habitual practice, the spontaneous application of wisdom returns to the fundamental Dharma of the source.
Third, regarding the explanation of the place where the Tathāgata dwells: [the questioner] asks, "For what reason do the beginnings of all the preceding assemblies state 'No'?"
Apart from the Bodhimaṇḍa, the Universal Radiance Hall (Samantāvabhāsa-maṇḍala-maṇḍapa) is where three assemblies coexist;

yet, why is this Dharma-realm assembly not the same as the previous ones? Why, when it is said, "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park," does it not directly state [the location]? Answer: It is for the purpose of clarifying that the previous [assembly] was... [the Universal Radiance Hall].

In the Hall of Radiance (*Prabhāsvaramaṇḍala*), the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are taught, followed by the five stages beginning with the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

These six positions are gates for ascending the Path; because they involve progressive cultivation that does not depart from the essence of Bodhi, it is said that one does not leave the site of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*).

However, fearing that this might lose the fundamental intent of the Sūtra—that the Tathāgata’s realization of perfect enlightenment is the very essence itself—it is necessary to re-examine this point.
The narrative that the three assemblies were together in the Hall of Universal Radiance clarifies that the cultivation of the five stages of clear faith and progress has already concluded.
This does not depart from the fundamental essence of immovable wisdom within the Hall of Universal Radiance;

because it is the realm of wisdom rather than a state of deluded sentiment, time likewise does not shift. At this very moment of a single *kṣaṇa*, this Dharma-realm assembly is directly stated to be in Śrāvastī.

The explanation of the prior stages of advancement in the Bahuputraka Garden has concluded. This assembly clarifies that one’s own attainment of Buddhahood is fulfilled through the practice of delivering sentient beings;
therefore, appearing again in human realms, cities, and gardens, he further transforms those of the two vehicles—śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—as well as bodhisattvas of the pure lands.
Thus, it is established that [the Buddha-body] is purely of the nature of the sovereign *dharmadhātu*.

The five stages of bodhi and the practices to be cultivated are without distinction; the wisdom of Samantabhadra’s vows and conduct to be studied is, in its entirety, the fulfillment of the Buddha-fruit and the completion of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Constantly pervading the ten directions to benefit sentient beings, there is no need for further reconciliation of the Dharma.
This direct statement is like the Jeta Grove, where all rivers flow into the ocean and lose their individual names.
It is not that the Dharma-realm lacks a name; rather, it differs from the previous five stages in its mode of ascending progress and harmonious integration.
As for the city of Śrāvastī—formerly called She-wei (Śravasti) or Shi-luo-fa (Śrāvastī)—this means "Good Path" (Sudharmā) or "Renowned Things" (Śravaṇa).
This is because the people in this city were fond of studying the Way and its Virtue (moral conduct), and [the fame of their learning] was heard by other countries.
In that country there were many people; therefore, based on the moral character of its inhabitants, the name of the land was established.

As for "Jetavana" (Śrīvaśavati), "jet" means to go, to cross over, or to proceed swiftly. Because the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, resided in this grove, all sentient beings who went to the Buddha’s presence would swiftly attain liberation. This is because the Buddha delivers sentient beings in great abundance.
Thus, names are established based on these reasons. As for "Grove" (*vana*), it is because this garden contains groves;
furthermore, because the Tathāgata’s practices extensively cover all beings with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) like a canopy, his Buddha-practices are called a "grove.

Because a grove serves as a canopy that provides the sense of coolness, the Dharma-realm—being cool—shelters sentient beings from the heat of their afflictions, causing them to become pure and refreshed.
Because it was cool, it is called the Jetavana. As for the naming of the monastery garden at the time of its establishment:
it was named after the donor, being established by Prince Jeta who planted the grove and the Elder Sudatta who provided the grounds;

furthermore, because the Elder relieved the destitute and bestowed gifts upon the orphaned and the aged, it is also called the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Now, it is designated according to the Tathāgata.

The wisdom and virtue that universally encompass and extensively benefit all beings is called the Jetavana Garden; in this region it is termed a "temple" (saṅghārāma), while in that region it is termed a "garden" (udyāna).

If the essence and function of the dharma-realm, as well as its objects and wisdom, are universally contained therein—taking the infinite realm of wisdom of the dharma-realm as the Jetavana Garden, rather than what is seen by the physical eye or the consciousness of emotional ignorance—then it pervades every dust-mote and world-system.
Within this garden, there are four masters who preach the Dharma;
these masters of the Dharma are also the Tathāgata Vairocana at the site of enlightenment in the past,
the Buddhas self-attained by all Bodhisattvas within the five stages of the Dharma, the Buddhas to be realized by the future Tathāgata Maitreya, and also the three [Buddhas].

Because all Buddhas of the past and present throughout the world are the essence of wisdom within the Dharma-realm, they are free from the emotional perceptions of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—or of extension and contraction;
because there are no new or old, nor created or destroyed Buddhas within the Dharma-realm;

and because through the vision of the Dharma-realm one perceives all sentient beings from their first aspiration for Bodhicitta until their attainment of Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma and delivering them.

When sentient beings enter nirvana, they do not shift from the Dharma-realm; for while there are differences in substance, function, and temporal duration, these are merely differences perceived through the deluded views of ordinary beings.

Within the wisdom of the Dharma-realm, all Buddhas of the three periods of time who have attained Buddhahood and all sentient beings who attain Buddhahood abide together in a single moment, within a single minute particle, as one Dharma-body and one wisdom.

Wisdom, the single sound of speech, liberation, supernormal power, the inconceivable, and the realm of retribution—all these are a single lotus seat, layered upon layer, unimpeded and without obstruction. This is what is seen by the eye of wisdom in its true reality;
it cannot be grasped by the deluded sentiments known by the fleshly eye. If there are those who can thus truly believe and understand this, they shall—
Knowing that this person has awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, sat upon the site of enlightenment, and attained the wisdom of the Tathāgata—
because they are able to believe that the bodies and minds of self and others are collectively the single substance and function of the Great Wisdom of the Dharma-realm—

they can expound the teachings within this Dharma-realm. Regarding the essence of these teachings, eleven items are cited as examples, with the supernatural power of the Tathāgata serving as the enabling capacity.
First, the teaching-body is defined as the phenomena manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power;
second, it is defined by the inconceivable, for the sounds and dharma-gates manifested are not produced by the faculties of speech, mind, or thought;
third, empty space is the teaching-body, for the realms of all manifested phenomena are like empty space; fourth, light is the teaching-body.
1. Because this light from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows universally illuminates the dharma-realm of the three periods of time, manifesting all dharmas;

thus, the five sense objects constitute the essence of the teaching, as each individual object contains the nature of the others and encompasses the dharmas of the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
2. Because the fruit of the Buddha’s retribution constitutes the essence of the teaching, manifesting the past.
1. Because it is adorned by the dharma-gates practiced through past karma; 2. Because its teaching-essence consists of the *dharmatā*, as there is no body or mind to be realized or cultivated;
3. Because its teaching-essence consists of the names and titles of Bodhisattvas, for each individual name is established based on the dharmas they practice;
4. Because its teaching consists of the numerical categories of Bodhisattvas and so forth.

The essence is arrayed as five hundred bodhisattvas—five hundred each of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī—whose identical names symbolize that within the realm of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the causes and fruits of the five stages are simultaneously perfected in both unity and multiplicity.

Tenth, the teaching-essence is universal radiance, for it manifests transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions, responding to faculties all at once. Thus, the teaching-essence of this exposition of the Dharma is immeasurable.

Regarding the infinite [qualities], it is appropriate to cite ten; if we consider the person who is able to hear and receive the teaching, they are defined by six factors corresponding to the six sense bases—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and by contact, feeling, and non-attachment.
Thus, the one who hears and receives the teaching is not solely the faculty of the ear that listens.
Regarding the meaning of the assembly gathered here: at the beginning of this assembly, there were one hundred and forty-two bodhisattvas, with Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī as the two leaders.
The remaining one hundred and forty bodhisattvas all share names in groups of ten;
collectively, they are called "five hundred. As the Sūtra says: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, five hundred."
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states: "All these bodhisattvas have fully accomplished the practices of Samantabhadra.

Thus, these five hundred bodhisattvas all take Mañjuśrī as the essence of the fundamental wisdom manifested as the *dharmakāya*, and Samantabhadra as the great function of the wisdom of differentiation. In this manner, there are one hundred and forty-two bodhisattvas.
How is the number five hundred established? From the Bodhisattva Self-Crowned (Svayambhū) downward, there are one hundred bodhisattvas;
these are the practices of the ten *pāramitās* within the fundamental essence of the fruit of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Within each of these ten, the ten are mutually contained, and within each of those ten, a hundred are contained. This constitutes the great function of all the myriad practices of all sentient beings within the equality of the Dharma-realm.
From the Bodhisattva Ten Heavenly Crowns (*Daśadivyamukuṭa*) downward, these are the fruits of practice within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

From the initial [stage] of the ten Banner-Bodhisattvas— such as Sunlight-Flame Banner (*Sūryaprabhājvālāketu*) and so forth— through the ten Powers (*daśabala*), the ten Treasuries (*daśakośa*), and the ten Eyes (*daśacakṣus*),

Dedicating [merit] throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one integrates and harmonizes the wisdom and principle (*jñāna-tattva*) with great vows and great compassion within each of the forty-two practices of the Bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
By cultivating the practices of the forty minds, each *pāramitā* contains ten, and within each of those ten there are a hundred; thus, within the forty minds, four hundred [practices] are perfected.
Furthermore, within the fundamental fruit of the Dharma-realm, the hundred *pāramitās* become five hundred, all of which take Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī as their essence.
Among these, by means of the forty-two noble practices (*ārya-caryā*), four hundred *pāramitā-gates* reach this stage of the fundamental fruit of the Dharma-realm;

Because the practice and its fruit coincide in entering the *dharmadhātu*, they are called the "Five Hundred.

This clarifies that within the forty stages of mind (*cittotpāda*), although one progresses toward the Buddha-fruit, there is no fundamental fruit of progress or practice within the root *dharmadhātu*.

Therefore, from the Bodhisattva Ten Heavens onwards, the "Heavenly Crown" serves as the fundamental practice and fruit within the *dharmadhātu*; this crown is the ornament upon the summit of the head.
The Adorned Dharma-realm (*vyūha-dharmadhātu*) is the fruit of the fundamental Buddha and the pinnacle of the myriad practices;

therefore, one should know it through the meaning of its name and that which it adorns. The names of this sutra, the adornments, the dwelling places, and the number of the assembly are all *dharmaparyāyas*;

These are manifested as an assembly that neither hears nor sees this inconceivable spiritual power of the dharma-realm. Thus, the meanings of these five assemblies shall be explained according to the text.

The term "Bodhisattva" has six intended meanings (*abhiprāya*): First, from the beginning up to the one hundred and forty-second [verse], the two Bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, as well as the Buddha, collectively encompass the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) and the cause and fruit of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The Bodhisattva who shares this same name, Dhvaja (Banner), refers to those among the ten wisdom-Bodhisattvas—such as Dharmamati and the others—who reside within the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
When they reach this fruit of the non-conceptual Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are designated as "Banners.

This is because their initial resolve and the wisdom of the Ten Abodes have already crushed and destroyed the afflictions; thus, upon reaching this fruit-stage of the Dharma-realm, they are called "Banners. Third.

from among the ten practices, because the ten forest-dwelling bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakusuma and others, have reached this fruit of the *dharmadhātu*, they are designated as "Vīryas" (*vīrya*).

Thus, because their *vidyās* possess the power of manifold virtuous practices and are able to accomplish the practice of the fruit of the *dharmadhātu*, [they follow] fourthly, below which there are ten identical [mantras].

Upon reaching this fruit of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-phala), they are designated as the Ten Treasuries.

By means of those Ten Dedications, they overturn biased views through dedication, harmonizing principle and wisdom with compassion and vows; thus, they are able to accomplish all virtues upon reaching this Dharma-realm.

Within the fruit of the *dhātu*, they are designated as the "Five Treasuries" (*pañca-kośa*). From the fifth stage downward, the ten bodhisattvas such as Susamaya and others share the common name "Eye" (*cakṣus*).
These thirty-seven treasury-bodhisattvas, including Vajragarbha and others from the ten stages, are designated as "Eyes" upon reaching this fruit of the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, because those [stages] of the ten grounds contain and preserve the multitude [of qualities], they are so named.

[Sutra]: These bodhisattvas have all fully accomplished the sphere of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows, which is unimpeded and universally pervades all buddha-fields;
they manifest bodies infinitely to attend upon all Tathāgatas; their pure eyes are...

It is unimpeded in manifesting the miraculous transformations of all Buddhas; it is infinite in its reach, as it constantly and universally attends all Tathāgatas who have attained perfect enlightenment;
its radiance is boundless, for it universally illuminates the ocean of all true dharmas with the light of wisdom;
its teaching of the Dharma is inexhaustible, for its pure eloquence remains undiminished throughout boundless eons; it is equal to space.

Because the sphere of wisdom is entirely pure, there is no basis for dependence; because one manifests a form-body according to the minds of sentient beings, the cataracts of ignorance are eliminated;

because one realizes that the realm of sentient beings is devoid of a self-entity of "sentient beings," it is equal to empty space; and because the wisdom equal to space illuminates the dharma-realm with a great net of light.

Their minds are tranquil like space; having forever severed doubt and confusion regarding all Buddhas, they enter with deep faith into the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.

The Section on Requesting the Dharma.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, took great compassion as his body, great compassion as his gate, and great compassion as his head;
employing the dharma of great compassion as his skillful means, he pervaded all of space and entered the Lion’s [Roar Samādhi].
Upon entering this Samādhi of Frequent Stretching, all worlds were universally adorned and purified.
At that time, this Great Adorned Pavilion suddenly became vast and boundless;

its floor was of vajra, its roof covered with the King of Jewels, and immeasurable jewel-flowers and various maṇis were scattered throughout it, filling every place, while its walls were made of lapis lazuli.
The pillars were composed of various jewels and adorned with great radiant *maṇi* gems; *Jāmbūnada* gold and *cintāmaṇi-rāja* jewels were placed all around upon them as ornaments.
High towers were connected by projecting galleries, the rafters and eaves supporting one another, and windows and doors reflecting each other’s light.
The stairs, courtyards, balconies, and railings were all fully provided, everything being adorned with exquisite jewels.
Its precious ornaments were all fashioned into the forms of humans and devas, firm, exquisite, and foremost in the world;
nets of *maṇi* jewels covered them from above. At the sides of every gate, banners and streamers were erected, all emitting light that pervaded the entire dharma-realm.
Outside the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the steps, railings, and balustrades were immeasurable and beyond description, none of which failed to be adorned.
[It is] made of mani-jewels. [Treatise]:

From "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to "made of mani-jewels," thirteen lines of scripture clarify how the Tathāgata, by the power of samādhi, manifests the adornments of the fruits of retribution from his past practices throughout the ten directions.
The *Sūtra on the Vast and Extensive Division of the Great Adornment Pavilion* states: "Lion" signifies fearlessness;
"stretching out the limbs" signifies being at ease and free from fatigue. This clarifies that through non-action (*anābhoga*), spontaneous wisdom (*jñāna*) is sovereign;
without striving, it responds to infinite phenomena, which are spontaneously accomplished. Because it is perfected without effort, it is as previously explained regarding entry into this [state].
The phrase "the pavilions adorned by the Samādhi of Frequent Stretching suddenly become vast and boundless" means that they are expansive and wide;
it signifies that these pavilions suddenly become as broad and spacious as the dharma-realm and empty space. This clarifies that the realm of the Tathāgata is eternally and inherently boundless.
When sentient beings, whether deluded or awakened, attain resonance with it in a single thought-moment, there is no phenomenon that is not [encompassed].
Because it is equal [to all], the mind is like space, pervading and containing the entire Dharma-realm;
thus it is said that it suddenly becomes vast and expansive, without boundaries. This is intended to guide future followers rather than the assembly present here.
"The ground is of vajra" means that it is formed as the fruition of the Dharmakāya’s realization. Within it, immeasurable jewel flowers and various maṇi gems are scattered everywhere.
That it is situated in fullness is the result produced by the totality and particulars of various practices;
that its pillars are made of lapis lazuli is the retributive accomplishment of upholding compassionate vows with a stainless, pure mind;

that it is composed of various jewels is the manifestation of the adornments upon the pillars being complete with all treasures, signifying that within a single pure mind one upholds the myriad practices without wavering.
That which is adorned with great radiant *maṇi* jewels arises from the manifestation of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Jāmbūnada gold—gold that is supple, luminous, and pure, far surpassing ordinary gold—arises from the mind’s manifestation of gentleness, humility, and compliance.
The wish-fulfilling jewel kings (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*) placed all around as ornaments arise from fundamental wisdom.
Arising from the realization of the wisdom of differentiation and the practice of the ten thousand differentiated practices, one dwells with sovereign non-obstruction to benefit all sentient beings;
this is the manifestation of birth in a perilous tower that extends far and wide. "Perilous" (*wei*) means high; "far-reaching" (*jiong*) means distant;

"extending" (*dai*) refers to being adorned and reflected by various jewels. Taken collectively, this describes a jeweled tower that is both high and far-reaching, its adornments reflecting one another to pervade the Dharma-realm.
Within that realm, numerous jeweled towers adorn one another, mutually reflecting and penetrating each other;

"by the towers" refers to the side galleries extending from them, where the rafters and eaves support one another—meaning they are joined in continuous succession. It is said that each fills the entire dharma-realm.

Regarding the phrase "windows and lattices reflect one another," this clarifies that the doors and windows atop the jeweled pavilions are transparently bright and pure, without obstruction. As for "steps, courtyards, balconies, and railings," these refer to the tiered levels.
The steps lead down to a level ground paved with jewels; the stairs above are bordered by railings made of jeweled planks, and above the railings are eaves supported by jeweled poles.
This is what is meant in the *Lou deng fu* (Rhapsody on Ascending the Tower): "Leaning against the eaves and railings to gaze afar.

All these various elements being fully provided signifies that the ten thousand treasures are complete and solemnly arrayed. Generally speaking, the pavilion (*ge*) is formed through the response of differentiated wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*), while the tower (*lou*) is formed through [the response of] the totality.
Fundamental wisdom gives rise to the function of contemplative observation, transcending all realms and the physical forms produced by karmic retribution, such as those of humans or devas.
[Sūtra] At that time, furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the Jeta Grove suddenly became vast and expansive, beyond measure.
He spoke of Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, all equal in magnitude, adorned with an intermingling of every kind of exquisite jewel;
unspeakable jewels were spread across their ground, with incalculable jewels forming their walls, and jeweled *tāla* trees adorning the sides of the paths;
therein, moreover, were immeasurable fragrant rivers, filled with scented water, flowing with turbulent currents.
All swirling currents of precious flowers turn to the right as they flow, spontaneously producing the inconceivable sounds of the Buddha-dharma.
Inconceivable *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, in full bloom, spread across the surface of the water.
Various jewel-flower trees are planted in rows along the banks, and inconceivable pavilions and terraces stand in successive order upon the shore, adorned with *maṇi* jewels.
It was completely covered by jeweled nets; incalculable jewels emitted great radiance, and incalculable jewels adorned the ground.
Various exquisite incenses were burned, their fragrance wafting in dense clouds. Furthermore, immeasurable varieties of jeweled banners were erected, namely:
jeweled incense banners, jeweled robe banners, jeweled pennant banners, jeweled silk banners, jeweled flower banners, jeweled necklace banners, and jeweled... [banners].
The banner of garlands, the banner of precious bells, the banner of maṇi-jewel canopies, the great maṇi-jewel banner, the maṇi-jewel banner of pervasive illumination,
the maṇi-king banner that utters the sounds of the names of all Tathāgatas, the lion maṇi-king banner,
the maṇi-king banner that expounds the ocean of the past deeds of all Tathāgatas, and the banner that manifests the reflections of the entire dharma-realm.
Like the banner of the maṇi-king, it is arrayed and adorned, pervading the ten directions.

[Treatise] Ten: From "At that time, furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power" down to "arrayed and adorned, pervading the ten directions," sixteen lines of scripture clarify that the Jeta Grove was suddenly adorned by the Buddha’s spiritual power.
The magnificent, vast, and all-pervading ground of distributed jewels throughout the ten directions is the retribution for practices performed to adorn and benefit humans and devas;
the jeweled nets are the practice of teaching; the jeweled walls are the practice of morality; the jeweled trees are the practice of providing shelter for sentient beings;
the jeweled banners are the practice of dedication; and the jeweled rivers are the practice of compassion—each and every one is thus.
Because it is the retribution accomplished through the various practices of conventional wisdom,
[the Sūtra says]: At that time, within the void above the Jeta Grove, there appeared inconceivable clouds of celestial palaces,
innumerable clouds of fragrant trees, unspeakable clouds of Mount Sumerus, and unspeakable clouds of musical performances, all emitting exquisite sounds.
Inconceivable clouds of jewel lotuses and inconceivable clouds of jewel thrones were spread out,
upon which bodhisattvas sat, praising the Tathāgata’s virtues with celestial robes; there were inconceivable clouds of mani-jewels in the forms of various heavenly kings,
inconceivable clouds of white pearls, and inconceivable clouds of red pearl pavilions and ornaments.
It may be said that clouds of adamantine, solid *maṇi*-jewels raining down abide in the void, surrounding and pervading it entirely as an adornment.
[Treatise] From "At that eleventh time, in the Jeta Grove" down to "as an adornment," seven lines of scripture clarify this.
[This is] the portion on the Adornment of Space through the Tathāgata’s past roots of goodness and the power of his own majesty.
[Sūtra]: Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness are inconceivable; because the Tathāgata’s pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) are inconceivable;
because the Tathāgata’s majestic power is inconceivable; and because the Tathāgata is able, by means of a single body, to manifest transformations at will throughout the entire [universe].
Because all worlds are inconceivable, the Tathāgata is able, through his supernormal powers, to cause all Buddhas and the adornments of all Buddha-lands to enter into his own body;
because they are inconceivable, the Tathāgata is able to universally manifest the images of the entire Dharma-realm within a single minute atom;
because they are inconceivable, the Tathāgata is able to manifest [all things] within a single pore.
Because all Buddhas of the past are inconceivable, the Tathāgata emits from each and every ray of light such that they are able to universally illumine all worlds;

this is inconceivable. Because the Tathāgata is able to produce from within a single pore clouds of emanations as numerous as the atoms of all Buddha-fields, filling all Buddha-lands; this is inconceivable.
Therefore, because the Tathāgata is able to universally manifest within a single pore all the inconceivable eons of formation, abiding, and destruction of all worlds in the ten directions—
just as one sees the pure and adorned Buddha-lands here in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden—
all worlds throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space in the ten directions are likewise so manifested.
He saw what is called the vision of the Tathāgata’s body dwelling in the Jeta Grove, with the assembly of bodhisattvas completely filling it.

[Treatise] Why? From here down to "the assembly of bodhisattvas completely fills it," there are fourteen lines of scripture that clarify the praise of the Tathāgata’s sovereign adornment of supernatural power and the perfection of the great assembly, concluding the section as a whole.
The ten directions were likewise so.
[Sūtra] He saw clouds raining down all manner of adornments; he saw clouds raining down the radiant light of all jewels;
he saw clouds raining down all mani-jewels; he saw clouds raining down all manner of ornamental canopies that completely covered the Buddhas.
Clouds of Buddha-fields were seen raining down all celestial bodies; clouds of flowers were seen raining down everywhere; clouds of trees laden with garments were seen raining down everywhere;
clouds of precious garlands and necklaces were seen raining down in continuous succession, pervading the entire great earth;
clouds of all manner of ornaments were seen raining down everywhere; and clouds of all things were seen raining down everywhere.
One sees clouds of various fragrances in the forms of sentient beings raining down everywhere a continuous succession of subtle and exquisite nets of jewel-flowers;
one sees clouds of all celestial maidens holding precious banners and pennants circling and moving back and forth through the void, raining down everywhere;
and one sees clouds raining down everywhere all kinds of precious lotus flowers, from the midst of whose petals there naturally...
[He saw] clouds of various musical sounds emerging, and clouds raining down everywhere to adorn all the lion thrones with jeweled nets and pendants.
[Treatise: From "thirteen, having seen the clouds raining down all manner of adornments" down to "and thus serving as adornments."

There are eleven lines of sūtra clarifying the section on the adornment of the void and the jeweled ground by clouds of rain from jewels falling through the void of the ten directions. [Sūtra] At that time,
to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, across the oceans of worlds, there was a world...
In the realm named Golden Lamp Cloud Banner, there is a Buddha named Vairocana Supreme Virtue King.

Among that Buddha’s assembly, there is a bodhisattva named Vairocana-Vow-Light who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, comes toward the Buddha’s abode.
By the power of the Buddha, they all manifest various clouds, namely: clouds of celestial flowers, clouds of celestial...
Clouds of incense, clouds of powdered incense, clouds of celestial garlands, clouds of jewels, clouds of ornaments,
clouds of precious parasols, clouds of exquisite robes, and clouds of precious banners and pennants— these clouds of all manner of wonderful jewels and adornments filled the void.
Having reached the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and, in the eastern direction, manifested a jeweled pavilion.
Adorned with a pavilion and seated upon a lion throne within a universally illuminating jewel lotus treasury, his body was covered by a net of wish-fulfilling jewels;

together with his retinue, he sat in the full lotus posture. To the south, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, there is a world named Vajragarbha, where the Buddha is named Samantaprabha.
In that assembly of the Buddha Jina-garbha-rāja, there was a bodhisattva named Akṣayavīrya-rāja, who,
together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, came toward the place where the Buddha was staying, carrying nets of all kinds of precious incense,
carrying necklaces of all kinds of precious jewels, carrying bands of all kinds of precious flowers, and carrying bands of all kinds of precious garlands.
Wearing vajra-garlands, holding nets of all kinds of maṇi-jewels, wearing sashes of all kinds of jewels,
wearing sashes of all kinds of precious garlands, and wearing sashes of all kinds of supreme radiant maṇis—
adorned with lion-maṇi-jewel garlands and pervading all oceans of worlds through their spiritual power— they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he immediately manifested in the southern direction a pavilion adorned with *maṇi* jewels that illuminates the entire world, as well as a lion throne within a treasury of lotuses that shines throughout the ten directions;
there, covered by a net of all kinds of precious flowers, he sat cross-legged together with his retinue. To the west, beyond unspeakably many Buddha-fields...
Beyond worlds as numerous as atoms of dust, there is a world named Maṇiratnapradīpa-Sumerudhvaja; its Buddha is named Dharmadhātujñānapradīpa.

Among that Buddha’s assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Samantavijayānuttaratejorāja, who, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of dust in an ocean of worlds, came toward the place where the Buddha was, all manifesting through their spiritual powers.
There were clouds of various kinds of ointment incense and burning incense as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
clouds of fragrant waters of various colors as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
and clouds of *maṇi* jewel-kings with radiance equal to the dust of all the great earths, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Clouds of Sumeru mountains adorned with various wheels of light-flames as numerous as the atoms in unspeakable Buddha-fields;
clouds of Sumeru mountains adorned with various colored Vajra-treasury mani-kings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakable Buddha-fields;
[clouds of] Jāmbūnada gold as numerous as the atoms in unspeakable Buddha-fields that universally illumine all worlds.
Inexpressibly many clouds of Sumeru mountains of jewel-treasures of the Dharma-realm, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
inexpressibly many clouds of Sumeru mountains of mani-jewel kings manifesting the marks and signs of all Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
inexpressibly many clouds of... manifesting one... [as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields].

In the *Tathāgata-pūrvayoga-nidāna-sarvabodhisattvacaryā-pratipatti-maṇirājā-sumeru-megha*, which describes the conduct practiced by all bodhisattvas, there appeared clouds of *maṇi-rāja* Sumeru mountains as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields. These clouds manifested all Buddhas seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Having filled the entire Dharma-realm and arrived before the Buddhas, they prostrated themselves at the Buddhas' feet.
In the western direction, he manifested a pavilion of all-fragrant kings, covered above by a net of genuine jewels;
he also manifested a lion throne within a treasury of precious lotuses, bearing the banner of Indra’s shadow, and covered it with a net of mani-jewels of exquisite color.
Adorning his head with a crown of precious mind-kings, he sat cross-legged together with his retinue.
To the north, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, there is a world named Jewel-Raiment Radiant Banner.
Its Buddha is named Great Radiance Illumining the Dharmadhātu of Space.

Within that Buddha’s assembly, there is a bodhisattva named King of the Unobstructed Supreme Treasury, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, has come toward the Buddha.
By means of his spiritual power, he manifested clouds of all kinds of precious robes, namely: clouds of yellow precious radiant robes;
clouds of robes perfumed with various fragrances; clouds of sun-bannered *maṇi* king robes; clouds of blazing golden *maṇi* robes;
clouds of robes of all precious light-flames; and clouds of exquisite *maṇi* robes bearing the images of all the stars.

Having arrived at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and, from the northern direction, manifested an ocean of mani jewels consisting of clouds of white-jade-lustrous mani garments,
clouds of light universally illuminating with supreme brilliance, clouds of mani garments with blazing majesty,
and clouds of mani garments that adorn the ocean-like expanse, filling all of space.
Adorned with pavilions and lion thrones within a *vaiḍūrya* jewel lotus treasury, their bodies were covered by nets of *maṇi* jewels of lion-like majesty;
with pure jewel-kings as crest-jewels, they sat cross-legged together with their retinues,
having passed beyond world-oceans of Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms in an inexpressible number of worlds in the northeast.
In the external world-system named All-Joyful Pure Radiance Net, there is a Buddha named Unobstructed Eye.
Among that Buddha’s assembly is a Bodhisattva named Moon King Who Manifests the Vows of the Dharma Realm.

May he, together with as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, come toward the place where the Buddha is; and may they all, by means of their spiritual powers, manifest clouds of precious pavilions and clouds of incense pavilions.
Clouds of incense pavilions, clouds of flower pavilions, clouds of sandalwood pavilions, clouds of vajra pavilions,
clouds of maṇi pavilions, clouds of gold pavilions, clouds of robe pavilions, and clouds of lotus pavilions completely covered all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Having reached the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and then manifested in the northeast.
He manifested a great maṇi pavilion that serves as a gateway to all dharma realms, along with an incomparable lion throne made of the king of fragrances and the lotus treasury;
his body was covered by a net of maṇi flowers, he wore a crown of the king of maṇis from the treasury of wondrous jewels,
and together with his retinue, he sat in the full lotus posture in the southeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields.
Beyond the ocean of world-systems, there is a world named Fragrant Cloud Adorned Banner; its Buddha is named Dragon Sovereign King.

Within that Buddha’s assembly, there is a bodhisattva named Dharma-Wisdom Radiant Flame King, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, comes toward the place where the Buddha is.
All of them, by means of their spiritual powers, manifest clouds of golden, perfect radiance and immeasurable jewels.
The Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa-paripūrṇa-prabhā-megha; the cloud of light from the uṣṇīṣa of various jewel colors;
the cloud of light from the lotus-treasury; the cloud of light from the branches of various jewel trees;
the cloud of light from the crown protuberance of the Tathāgata; and the cloud of light from the color of Jāmbūnada gold.
Clouds of the perfect radiance of the sun and clouds of the perfect radiance of the moon and stars completely filled the void;
having reached the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, in the southeastern direction,
miraculously manifested a most supreme jewel-radiant pavilion of Vairocana and a lion throne of vajra-maṇi lotus-treasury, ablaze with the light of various jewels.
A net of mani-jewel kings covered his body, and together with his retinue, he sat in the full lotus posture.
To the southwest, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, there is a world named Sunlight Mani Treasury;
the Buddha there is named Universal Illumination of All Dharmas Wisdom Moon King. Within that Buddha’s assembly, there is a bodhisattva named Destroyer.
The King of Wisdom Banners, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, came toward the Buddha’s abode.
From all his pores issued forth clouds of flower-flames equal to the realm of empty space,
clouds of fragrance-flames, clouds of jewel-flames, clouds of vajra-flames, clouds of incense-burning flames, clouds of lightning-light flames, and Vairocana-maṇi jewels.
Clouds of flames of all-golden light, clouds of flames from the supreme treasury of maṇi-kings, and clouds of flames from the oceans of light of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time—
all these emerged one by one from his pores and pervaded the realm of empty space. Having reached the presence of the Buddha,
they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, in the southwestern direction, manifested a light that universally appears throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
He was seated upon a lion throne within a great pavilion of mani-jewel nets and a treasury of fragrant lamps and flaming lotuses;

it was covered above by a net of *vimalagarbha* (stainless-treasury) mani-jewels and adorned with a crown of *sarvasattvābhinirhāranirghoṣa* (the sound of the setting-forth of all sentient beings) mani-kings.
Together with his retinue, he sat in the full lotus posture in the northwest direction, beyond worlds as numerous as the unspeakable.
Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field, there is a world named Vairocana-vow-maṇi-king-treasury;

its Buddha is named Universal Radiance Supreme Sumeru King. Within that Buddha’s assembly, there is a bodhisattva named Vow-Wisdom-Radiant Banner, who, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, came toward the place where the Buddha was.
In every moment of thought, from all the marks and signs of excellence, all the pores, and all the limbs and members of the body,
there emerge clouds of the forms of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, clouds of the forms of all Bodhisattvas, clouds of the forms of the assemblies of all Tathāgatas,
clouds of the forms of the emanated bodies of all Tathāgatas, and clouds of the forms of the birth-stories of all Tathāgatas.
Clouds of the forms of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, clouds of the forms of the bodhimaṇḍas of all Tathāgatas,
clouds of the forms of the miraculous transformations of all Tathāgatas, clouds of the forms of all lords of the world,
and clouds of the forms of all pure buddha-fields filled the void; having reached the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet.
Then, in the northwest direction, he manifested a pavilion adorned with mani-jewels that universally illumines the ten directions,
as well as a lion throne within a treasury of precious lotuses that universally illumines the world;
covering his body with a net of invincible radiant pearls and wearing a crown of mani-jewels of universal light, he sat cross-legged together with his retinue.
