The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya, Scroll Eighty-Nine.
The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Layman of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty,
combining the various editions of the sutra for the *Entry into the Dharma Realm*, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Two.
[Sutra] Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields in the direction below, across the oceans of worlds, there is a world named...
The Tathāgata named Sarvatathāgataparipūrṇaprabhāsamantāvabhāsa has the title Gaganāsaṅgalakṣaṇajñānadhvajendra.

Within that Buddha’s assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Sarvāvaraṇavikiraṇavegajñānarāja, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, came toward the place where the Buddha was; from all his pores, he issued forth the proclamation of all assemblies.
From the ocean of birth, there issued forth clouds of sounds of speech that proclaimed the ocean of skillful means for the practice of all Bodhisattvas throughout the three periods of time;
from it issued forth clouds of sounds proclaiming the ocean of skillful means for the vows undertaken by all Bodhisattvas;

from it issued forth clouds of sounds proclaiming the ocean of skillful means for fulfilling and purifying all the *pāramitās* of all Bodhisattvas; from it issued forth clouds of sounds proclaiming one...
Clouds of sound proclaiming the fulfillment of all bodhisattva practices throughout all lands; clouds of sound proclaiming the sovereign power of accomplishing all bodhisattvas;

clouds of sound proclaiming the sovereign power of all Tathāgatas approaching the site of enlightenment, defeating the hosts of Māra, and attaining perfect awakening; clouds of sound proclaiming all Tathāgatas turning the wheel of Dharma.

From the gateway of the sūtras, clouds of sounds from the ocean of names issued forth, proclaiming the ocean of skillful means of the Dharma for teaching and taming all sentient beings according to their needs;

clouds of sounds from the ocean of skillful means issued forth, proclaiming how, at all times, in accordance with roots of goodness and the power of vows, all sentient beings may universally realize wisdom;
having reached the presence of the Buddha, these clouds paid homage by bowing their heads.
The Buddha’s feet immediately manifested below as the forms of the palaces of all Tathāgatas, adorned with various jewels, along with towers, pavilions,
and lion thrones within a treasury of all precious lotuses; there, wearing a *maṇi* jewel crown that universally manifests the reflections of the site of enlightenment,
he sat cross-legged together with his retinue, above which were unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, there is a world named *Akṣayabuddhagotravyāhāra*.

The Buddha there is named *Samantajñānacakra-prabhāsvara-svara*. Among that Buddha’s assembly, there is a bodhisattva named *Dharmadhātuvibhaktapraṇidhāna*, who, together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, set out from that site of enlightenment and comes toward this Sahā world.
Within all the marks and signs of excellence, all the pores, all the limbs and members, all the ornaments,
and all the garments of Śākyamuni Buddha, there appear the Buddhas of the past, such as Vairocana,
as well as all the Buddhas of the future— both those who have already received their prediction and those who have not— manifesting therein.

In all lands throughout the ten directions, he also manifests the ocean of past deeds of all Buddhas together with their assemblies as they practiced the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), including all those who received their gifts;

he likewise manifests the ocean of past deeds as they practiced the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); and he also manifests the ocean of past deeds as they practiced the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
There also appear oceans of past deeds in which, though his limbs were severed as if by honey, his mind remained undisturbed;
there also appear oceans of past deeds in which he manifested the courageous and non-retrogressive perfection of vigor through his past conduct;

there also appear oceans of past deeds in which he attained accomplishment by seeking the ocean of the dhyāna-perfection of all Tathāgatas in the past; and there also appear [oceans of past deeds] in which he sought all... in the past.
The ocean of past events concerning the Dharma accomplished by the wheel of Dharma turned by the Buddha, the arousal of the courageous mind, and the relinquishment of all things;
the ocean of past events concerning the joy of beholding all Buddhas of the past, the joy of practicing all bodhisattva paths, and the joy of transforming all realms of sentient beings;
and the ocean of past events concerning all the great vows of bodhisattvas previously made—these were all manifested.
The ocean of past fundamental events concerning the pure adornments also appears;
the ocean of past fundamental events concerning the courageous purity of the perfection of power achieved by bodhisattvas also appears;

and the ocean of past fundamental events concerning the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom cultivated by all bodhisattvas also appears—all such oceans of fundamental events are entirely pervasive and vast.
Having reached the Buddha’s abode within the Great Dharma Realm, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately manifested above him a pavilion adorned with all vajra-treasuries,
as well as a lion throne of the lotus treasury of the indranīla-vajra-king.
Covering his body with a net of all-jewel-luminous maṇi-kings, he proceeded to expound upon the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
The King of Maṇi Jewels, named Crest-Jewel (Cūḍāmaṇi), together with his retinue, sat cross-legged.

[Treatise: Fourteenth, from "At that time, having passed beyond unspeakable Buddha-fields in the east" down to "together with his retinue, sat cross-legged," there are ten sections of scripture clarifying the assembly of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions.
Within the luminous Dharma-realm, the fruits of Buddhahood are ineffable; they equal the number of atoms in Buddha-fields.
These original practices answer the previous questions of the Bodhisattvas; they are all the inexhaustible and all-pervading practices of one’s own Buddhahood.
For this reason, the world is named Vajra-Lamp-Cloud-Banner. "Vajra-Lamp-Cloud-Banner" refers to the great compassion that rains down the light of all dharmas for all Buddhas.
All arise from this Vajra-wisdom and initiate the practice of great compassion; because they shatter the afflictions of all sentient beings, they are called "Banners.
The Buddha’s name, Vairocana King of Supreme Virtue, is the fruit within these practices.
The Bodhisattva is also named Vairocana Light of Vows; this clarifies that the fruit follows one's former vows.
Because he practices great compassion, the King clearly manifests the various sovereign and unimpeded states of the Buddha-fruit in accordance with his conduct;
because these arise from adamantine wisdom, and because the name of this fruit accords with such practice,
he comes together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields, so that their words and deeds may be fulfilled and all bodhisattvas may assemble here for this Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that they "come. This clarifies that within the *dānapāramitā*, the primary and auxiliary practices are fulfilled;
that all the bodhisattvas who come have their bodies adorned with jeweled nets clarifies that the practice of the teaching is fulfilled.
Below this, the nine directions are collectively arranged in sequence according to the ten *pāramitās*; in total, these constitute the supreme pinnacle of the Vajra-wisdom of a single Buddha.
The distinctions between identity and difference should be understood by following this same pattern; the details below are self-evident according to the text.

This merely explains the general meaning of the sūtra, as the specific dharma-gates are fully contained within the sūtra itself. The above six sections constitute the response to the previous forty questions posed on two occasions.
The subsequent sections likewise respond to the five preceding inquiries concerning the Buddha’s samādhi and supernormal powers.

The Buddha’s response regarding the sequence of realms concerns the assembly of Bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions; this refers to the physical bodies resulting from past cultivation within the environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).

It answers the previous inquiry concerning the various stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten *pāramitās* cultivated as causes, clarifying that because their practice is perfected, their adorned bodies are likewise perfected.
The ten Buddha-lands and the ten names of the Buddhas represent the practices that were performed.
The ten Buddhas of the middle causal stage are all titled "Kings," clarifying that the Buddha-fruit possesses mastery over wisdom;
the Bodhisattvas are all covered by nets, clarifying that they are fully endowed with the net of the teaching.
[Sūtra] Thus, all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, together with their retinues, are born from the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
With the eye of pure wisdom, they see the Buddhas of the three periods of time and universally hear the ocean of sūtras of the wheel of Dharma turned by all the Tathāgatas;
having thus attained the further shore of mastery over all Bodhisattvas.
In every thought-moment, they manifest great spiritual transformations, drawing near to all Tathāgatas;
with a single body, they fill all worlds and appear universally within the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas.
Within a single atom, they manifest the realms of all worlds, teaching and bringing all sentient beings to maturity without ever missing the proper time. From a single pore, they emit...
They know that the sounds of the Dharma spoken by all Tathāgatas are like illusions;
they know that all Buddhas are like reflections; they know that birth in all realms of existence is like a dream;
they know that all karmic retributions are like images in a mirror; they know that the arising of all births is like a mirage; they know all worlds...
All realms are like transformations; they have accomplished the Tathāgata’s ten powers, fearlessnesses, and heroic mastery, and are able to roar the lion’s roar.
They have entered deeply into the great ocean of inexhaustible eloquence and attained the ocean of the speech of all sentient beings.
Possessing the wisdom of all dharmas, their conduct within the dharma-realm of empty space is unimpeded; they know all dharmas without obstruction—this is all bodhi.
The spheres of his supernormal powers are entirely purified; with courageous and diligent effort, he subdues the armies of Māra.
Constantly using wisdom, he thoroughly understands the three periods of time and knows that all phenomena are like empty space—without conflict and without grasping.
Although he exerts himself with diligence, he knows that omniscience ultimately comes from nowhere; although he contemplates objective spheres, he knows...
All that exists is entirely ungraspable; by means of skillful wisdom, one enters the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
by means of the wisdom of equality, one enters all lands; by the power of mastery, one causes all worlds to enter into one another;
one takes birth in every place within all worlds; and one perceives the various forms and characteristics of all worlds within the most subtle realms.
They manifest vast buddha-fields within vast realms and manifest subtle buddha-fields within a single buddha-field;
in a single moment of thought, they receive the empowerment of the majestic spiritual power of all buddhas, seeing throughout the ten directions without confusion;
in an instant, they are able to travel to them all—such bodhisattvas as these fill the Jeta Grove, all through the majestic power of the Tathāgata.
The Power of the Divine.
[Treatise] Fifteen: Thus, all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, down to the very last, are entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata;
there are thirty-five lines of scripture praising the aforementioned Bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions.
The functions of virtue are further divided into those that repay the benefactors above and those adorned by supernatural powers.
First, the adornment of the pavilions is described; next, the pervasive adornment of the jeweled ground; next, the adornment of space;

and finally, the adornment of the physical forms of the bodhisattvas from the ten directions who have gathered there. Each and every adornment is transparently interpenetrating and mutually inclusive.

As for the mutual interpenetration and unimpeded mastery of each and every aspect of the bodies, lands, and adornments of the ocean-like assemblies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions—
wherein the essence is profoundly layered— it is simply because the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* constitutes their essence,

and the myriad phenomena obtained through the retribution of the differentiated wisdoms naturally accord with this principle; thus, even when all Tathāgatas manifest all manner of supernormal powers, they do not depart from this.
Because wisdom gives rise to its great function, there is nothing that is not sovereign, nothing that does not interpenetrate, and nothing that is not luminously pure.
Such wisdom is accomplished only through the harmonious cultivation and advancement of the five aforementioned stages; therefore, it cannot be attained by practicing a single dharma alone.
One may practice many dharmas without departing from the one, but one must not cling to the one as being self-sufficient. This is so.
The Jeta Grove and the adornments of all lands throughout the dharma-realm do not depart from two factors:
first, they are accomplished through the wisdom, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and various practices cultivated in the past;

second, they are adorned by the inconceivable supernormal powers of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as clearly explained in the sutra itself. This answers the preceding question regarding the various bodhisattvas.
Forty Questions.
[Sūtra]: At that time, the foremost great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Revata, Subhūti, Aniruddha, Nanda, Kapphiṇa, Kātyāyana, and Pūrṇa—...
All those great śrāvakas in the Jeta Grove were entirely unable to see the Tathāgata’s supernormal power,
the Tathāgata’s majestic adornment, the Tathāgata’s sphere of activity, the Tathāgata’s playful manifestations, the Tathāgata’s miraculous transformations, the Tathāgata’s supreme excellence,
the Tathāgata’s wondrous conduct, the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue, the Tathāgata’s sustaining presence, nor did they see the Tathāgata’s pure buddha-field. They were likewise unable to perceive them.

The inconceivable realm of the Bodhisattvas; the great assembly of Bodhisattvas; the Bodhisattvas who universally enter, the Bodhisattvas who universally arrive, and the Bodhisattvas who universally approach;
the miraculous transformations of the Bodhisattvas; the Bodhisattvas’ playful sport; the retinues of the Bodhisattvas;

the locations of the Bodhisattvas; the adornments of the Bodhisattvas’ lion thrones; the palaces of the Bodhisattvas; the dwellings of the Bodhisattvas; and the samādhis into which the Bodhisattvas enter.
In this regard, a bodhisattva observes the bodhisattvas who are poised, the bodhisattvas who are courageous, the bodhisattvas who offer worship,
the bodhisattvas who receive predictions of enlightenment, the bodhisattvas who bring beings to maturity, the bodhisattvas who are valiant, the bodhisattvas whose dharma-body is pure,

the bodhisattvas whose wisdom-body is perfected, the bodhisattvas who manifest through their vow-bodies, the bodhisattvas who have accomplished their form-bodies, and those who are endowed with all the primary marks.

The Bodhisattva Pure Radiance, the Bodhisattva Adorned with the Colors of Constant Light, the Bodhisattva Emitting Great Webs of Light, the Bodhisattva Raising Clouds of Transformations, and the Bodhisattva Whose Body Pervades the Ten Directions—all such matters as these, which consist of the perfection of all practices, were not seen at all by the Śrāvakas and great disciples.
Why is this? Because their roots of goodness are not the same; fundamentally, they have not...

Because they have not cultivated the roots of goodness for the mastery of seeing the Buddhas; because from the beginning they have not praised the pure merits of all Buddha-fields in the worlds of the ten directions;
because from the beginning they have not extolled the various supernatural transformations of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
and because from the beginning they have not resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while amidst the流转 (saṃsāra) of birth and death.
Originally, they did not cause others to abide in the bodhicitta; originally, they were unable to ensure that the lineage of the Tathāgatas would not be severed;
originally, they did not embrace all sentient beings; originally, they did not exhort others to practice the bodhisattva pāramitās;
and originally, while wandering through the flow of saṃsāra, they did not urge sentient beings to seek the supreme eye of great wisdom.

Therefore, they have fundamentally not cultivated the roots of goodness that give rise to all-knowledge; they have fundamentally not perfected the roots of goodness for the appearance of Tathāgatas in the world;
they have fundamentally not attained the supernatural powers and wisdom for purifying Buddha-fields;

they have fundamentally not attained the objects of knowledge known by the eyes of Bodhisattvas; and they have fundamentally not sought the roots of goodness of the uncommon awakening that transcends the world.
Because it is fundamental, it does not originate from the arousal of any of the great vows of bodhisattvas; because it is fundamental, it is not produced through the empowerment of the Tathāgatas;
because it is fundamental, it does not know that all phenomena are like illusions or that bodhisattvas are like dreams;
because it is fundamental, it does not attain the vast joy of the great bodhisattvas—all such things are the sphere of the wisdom-eye of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

It is not shared with any of the followers of the two vehicles; for this reason, the great śrāvakas are unable to see it, unable to know it, unable to hear it, unable to enter it, unable to attain it, unable to recollect it, unable to observe it, unable to deliberate upon it, unable to contemplate it, and unable to discern it.
Therefore, although they were within the Jeta Grove, they did not see it.
Furthermore, because the great śrāvakas lack such roots of goodness, lack such an eye of wisdom,
lack such samādhi, lack such liberation, lack such supernormal powers, lack such majestic virtue,
lack such power, and lack such mastery, they do not possess the various great miraculous transformations of the Tathāgata.
Because there is no such dwelling place and because there is no such objective realm, one is therefore unable to know it, unable to see it, unable to enter it,
unable to realize it, unable to abide in it, unable to understand it, unable to examine it, unable to endure it,
unable to approach it, and unable to traverse it; furthermore, one is unable to extensively expound it for others.
They explain, praise, manifest, guide, encourage, direct them toward, cause them to practice, cause them to abide in, and cause them to realize [the truth].
Why is this? Because the great disciples have attained liberation by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
they have accomplished the path of the śrāvakas, fulfilled the conduct of the śrāvakas, and abide in the fruit of the śrāvakas within the truth of non-existence (*abhāva-satya*).

Having attained definitive knowledge, they dwell eternally in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is ultimately quiescent; yet, being devoid of great compassion, they abandon sentient beings and remain intent on their own affairs.

Regarding that wisdom, they are unable to accumulate it, unable to practice it, unable to abide in it, unable to aspire toward it, unable to accomplish it, unable to purify it, unable to enter it, and unable to penetrate it.
Because they were unable to know, see, or realize it, although they were within the Jeta Grove, they did not witness such a vast and great miraculous manifestation of the Tathāgata.
[Treatise] 16. At that time, the foremost great śrāvakas, from Śāriputra downward, did not even see it.
Thus, the extensive great supernormal transformations are clarified in fifty lines of sūtra as above.

Just as the śrāvakas lack such seeds of roots of goodness, so too those in the assembly of bodhisattvas—vast as an ocean—who were in the Jetavana Grove adorned by the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations and the magnificent, expansive buddha-field, did not see them at all because they lacked such roots from previous lives. This concludes the second section: the explanation of the assembly of śrāvakas.
As for the name Śāriputra, it was given because his mother’s eyes were as clear and sharp as those of the śāri bird;
since her eyes resembled the appearance of that bird, he was named after her. As for Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this is translated as "Bean-clan" (Cai-shu-shi);
he was so named because his mother’s clan name was Maudgalya, and she was a descendant of the Mount Mung bean (lu-dou shan). Thus, [he is called] Mahā...
Kāśyapa is so called because his body was golden in color and he could drink the rays of the sun;
he is also said to be a descendant of the Rishi Pītavasana (Drinking Light). Mahākāśyapa means "Great Kāśyapa.
Līpāda means "Offering" (Pūjaka) in this language. Subhūti means "Well-Appeared" (Sujanman). Aniruddha means "Unextinguished" (Aniruddha). Nanda means...
Pramudita-Kapphiṇa—translated here as "Yellow"—is a descendant of the ancient Sage Yellow-Head (Kapila).
Kātyāyana refers to one who belongs to a particular lineage; because he is of this progeny, he is called "Extended" (Kātyāyana), with "Extended" signifying lineage.
Pūrṇa is so named after his mother, Maitrāyaṇī; thus, he takes her name. These ten great śrāvakas manifest as if they do not hear.
Because they do not see the Tathāgata’s inconceivable transformations within the dharma-realm, which cause those who delight in inferior teachings to seek the Great Vehicle;
for the five hundred śrāvakas and the world-protectors mentioned previously were already those who possessed the seeds and were able to follow the Buddha’s practice.

[Sūtra] O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were hundreds of thousands of billions of immeasurable hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges River—naked, tormented by hunger and thirst, their entire bodies scorched, and being pounced upon and pecked at by crows, vultures, jackals, and wolves. Driven by thirst, they seek water to drink;
yet though they dwell by the river’s edge, they do not see the river. Even if some should see it, they see it as parched and dry. Why is this? Because [the karma] is profound and thick.
Because they are shrouded by karmic obstructions, those great śrāvakas are likewise; although they dwell within the Jeta Grove, they do not see the Tathāgata’s vast and great supernormal powers.

This is because the cataracts of ignorance regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) cover their eyes, and because they have never planted the roots of goodness on the ground of omniscience. It is, for example, as if there were a person in a great...
While sleeping soundly within the assembly, he suddenly dreamed that on the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the Great City of Sudarśana where Śakra dwells, the palaces, gardens,
and groves were adorned with every kind of splendor; hundreds of thousands of millions of devas and devīs scattered celestial flowers everywhere until they covered the ground,
while various trees of fine garments produced exquisite robes and various flowering trees blossomed in full bloom.
The "Exquisite Flowers" refers to the music trees that play celestial music, while the celestial maidens sing with beautiful voices.
Within this, immeasurable devas sport and enjoy themselves; those people see for themselves that they are wearing celestial garments and dwell, stay, and move about throughout that place.
Yet, among all the people in that great assembly, although they are in the same location, they neither know nor see [the others]. Why is this?
Therefore, what is seen in a dream cannot be seen by that great assembly; likewise, all bodhisattvas and the kings of the world are also thus.

Because they have long accumulated the power of roots of goodness, because they have made the vast vow for omniscience, because they have studied the merits of all Buddhas, and because they have practiced the path adorned by bodhisattvas, they fulfill [the vision].
Because they have perfected the dharmas of omniscient wisdom; because they have fulfilled all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra;
because they have entered all the stages of bodhisattva wisdom; because they sport in all the samādhis in which bodhisattvas dwell;
and because they have already attained unobstructed observation of the entire sphere of bodhisattva wisdom—for these reasons, they see the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, in his entirety.

All the great disciples among the śrāvakas are unable to see or know these inconceivable, sovereign, and miraculous transformations, because they lack the pure eye of a bodhisattva. It is, for example, like the Snowy Mountains, which abound with various medicinal herbs;
while a skilled physician may go there and be able to distinguish them all, the hunters and herdsmen who dwell constantly on that mountain do not see them.
This medicine is likewise so: through the power of mastery possessed by Bodhisattvas who enter the realm of wisdom, they are able to see the vast and great spiritual transformations of the Tathāgata.

Yet the Great Disciples, seeking only their own benefit and not desiring to benefit others, seeking only their own peace and not desiring to bring peace to others, do not know or see [these things] even while staying in the forest—just as there are various [treasures] within the earth that remain unknown.
The treasure store was completely filled with all kinds of rare and extraordinary jewels. There was a man, wise, discerning, and skilled in distinguishing all hidden treasures;

he also possessed great power of merit and virtue, enabling him to take whatever he desired with sovereign ease to support his parents, provide for his relatives, and relieve the elderly, the sick, and the destitute, distributing his bounty to all without exception.
Just as a person who possesses wisdom but lacks merit, though they may reach the location of a treasure storehouse, does not know it, does not see it, and thus gains no benefit from it—
so too it is with these great bodhisattvas: possessing the eye of pure wisdom, they are able to enter the inconceivable and profound realm of the Tathāgata,
they are able to see the Buddha’s spiritual power, they are able to enter the various Dharma-gates, and they are able to traverse through samādhis.

The ocean is able to make offerings to all Buddhas, is able to awaken sentient beings through the True Dharma, and is able to gather in sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Even the great *śrāvakas* cannot perceive the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, nor can they see the assembly of bodhisattvas;
it is like a blind person who, having reached a great island of jewels, is unable to [perceive them] whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Just as one who cannot see all the various jewels is unable to gather them or enjoy their use because they are unseen, so it is with these great disciples:
although they were in the grove in the presence of the World-Honored One, they did not see the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual power, nor did they see the great assembly of bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because there was no unimpeded purity of bodhisattvas [present for them to perceive].
The eye cannot gradually enter the Dharma-realm because it perceives the Tathāgata’s power of mastery.
It is like a person who has obtained a pure eye called "Stainless Radiance," such that no dark forms whatsoever can act as an obstruction;
at that time, even in the darkness of night, while standing amidst a multitude of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of people, that person may walk about.
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no aspect of those people’s physical form or deportment that this person with clear vision does not fully perceive;
yet, while that person with clear vision perceives their every movement and gesture, those people cannot see him at all.
The Buddha is also like this: having achieved the eye of wisdom, pure and unimpeded, he clearly perceives everything in all worlds. Its...
Manifesting a great assembly of bodhisattvas surrounded by miraculous transformations, he was such that none of the great disciples could see him;
it was as if a bhikṣu were in the midst of a great multitude, having entered into a *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) meditative absorption—
namely, the totality of earth, the totality of water, the totality of fire, the totality of wind, the totality of blue, and the totality of yellow.
The universal concentration of red, the universal concentration of white, the universal concentration of the heavens, the universal concentration of the bodies of various sentient beings,
the universal concentration of all vocal sounds and languages, and the universal concentration of all objects of focus—
those who enter these concentrations perceive their respective objects, while the rest of the great assembly cannot see them at all, except for those who themselves abide in this samādhi.
The inconceivable realm of the Buddhas manifested by the Tathāgata is likewise so. When a Bodhisattva perceives it fully, a Śrāvaka cannot observe it.

It is, for example, like a person who applies a medicine for invisibility to their eyes and, while in a great assembly, comes and goes, sits and stands, such that no one can see them, yet they are able to perceive all matters within the assembly. You should know this regarding the Tathāgata.

It is likewise thus: transcending the world, one universally perceives the world in a manner that cannot be seen by any Śrāvakas, except for those great Bodhisattvas who are oriented toward the realm of omniscience. It is like when a person is born, two deities always follow them:
the first is called the "Co-natal" deity, and the second is called the "Same-name" deity; these deities constantly see the person, but the person does not see the deities.

It should be understood that the Tathāgata is likewise in this regard: when he manifests great supernormal powers within the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, all the great śrāvakas are unable to see them.
This is, for example, like a bhikṣu who has attained mastery over the mind and enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
therein, the functions of the six sense faculties all cease to operate, and he neither knows nor perceives any speech, because he is sustained by the power of meditative concentration.

It is likewise for all śrāvakas who have not yet entered parinirvāṇa: although they dwell within the Jeta Grove and possess their six sense faculties, they do not know, see, understand, or enter into the various activities of the Tathāgata’s sovereign assembly of bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because the realm of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and vast, difficult to perceive and difficult to know.
Inconceivable and immeasurable, transcending all worlds, it is beyond thought and indestructible;

it is not the domain of any of the followers of the two vehicles. Therefore, such matters as the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual power, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the Jeta Grove pervading all pure worlds—none of these were known or seen by the great śrāvakas.
Because they were not suitable vessels.

[Treatise: Seventeen sons of the Buddha—beginning with the ten billion immeasurable hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges River and extending down to all the Great Śrāvakas—were entirely unable to know or see [this], because they were not suitable vessels. This is explained in seventy-four lines and a half of scripture.
There are ten similes that illustrate how the śrāvakas present in the assembly lack the vast roots of merit for enlightenment;
they neither know nor see the Tathāgata’s sovereign power. These ten similes from the sutra text are self-evident.
In this way, the śrāvakas appear as if they do not hear or see the sphere of the Tathāgata’s transformative spiritual powers, whereas the bodhisattvas do.
The assembly of the ocean-like multitude causes those who are truly śrāvakas but possess the seed of turning their minds toward the Great Vow, Great Wisdom,
and Great Compassion of the Tathāgata to remain perpetually within birth and death to extensively benefit all sentient beings.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Vairocanapraṇidhānaraśmi, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“You all should observe The inconceivable path of the Buddha Within this Jeta Grove.”

Manifesting the power of supernormal feats through the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata, the countless worlds that appear therein are bewildering and cannot be comprehended. The profound and wondrous Dharma of the Dharma King is immeasurable and inconceivable;
the various supernormal feats he manifests cannot be fathomed by anyone in the world.
Because he has realized that all phenomena are signless, he is therefore called a Buddha;

yet his adornment of marks is so vast that it cannot be fully extolled. Now, within this grove, he manifests great supernormal powers, profound and boundless, such that words cannot describe them; behold his great majestic virtue!
Innumerable hosts of bodhisattvas from all the lands of the ten directions have come to behold the World-Honored One.
Your vows are entirely fulfilled; your conduct is without obstruction.
None throughout all the worlds can fathom you—not any pratyekabuddhas, nor even those great śrāvakas.
None at all can know the sphere of the Bodhisattva’s practice; The Bodhisattva’s great wisdom has completely perfected all the stages.

Highly erecting the banner of valor, difficult to crush and difficult to move, These beings of great renown possess the power of immeasurable samādhis, And manifest all manner of supernatural transformations.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Indestructible Vigor King, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse: "The Dharma-realm is completely filled. [He then continued: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Indestructible Vigor King, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, observed the ten directions and spoke these verses:"
Behold these sons of the Buddhas, treasuries of wisdom and merit, who have perfected the practice of enlightenment and bring peace and security to all worlds.

Their minds are fundamentally luminous and penetrating; they skillfully enter into various samādhis, their wisdom is boundless, and their spheres of experience are immeasurable—just as they are now in this Jeta Grove.
Adorned in every way, the assembly of bodhisattvas gathers like clouds; they dwell in proximity to the Tathāgata.

Behold this immeasurable ocean-like multitude who have come from the ten directions to sit upon jeweled lotus thrones—neither coming nor dwelling, without dependence and free from conceptual proliferation.
With a stainless mind free from obstruction, they reach the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm;
establishing the banner of wisdom, firm and unshakable, they know the nature of phenomena to be without transformation,
yet manifest transformative deeds throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions, simultaneously proceeding to the abodes of all Buddhas.
Yet he does not divide his body; behold the Lion of the Śākyas!
By the power of his sovereign supernormal faculties, he is able to cause the assembly of Bodhisattvas to gather together all at once.
Although all the teachings of the Buddhas are entirely equal within the Dharma-realm, they differ according to verbal expression; this assembly has fully realized this.
The Buddhas always abide peacefully at the limit of equality within the Dharma-realm; they expound the teachings of diverse dharmas with inexhaustible words and phrases.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Victorious Unsurpassed Majestic Virtue King, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and...
He spoke in verse:

"Behold the Unsurpassed One, whose vast wisdom is perfected; well-versed in what is timely and untimely, he expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitude. He subdues all non-Buddhists and all heterodox disputants."
Universally following the minds of sentient beings, He manifests supernormal powers for their sake.
Perfect Awakening is neither finite nor infinite; Whether finite or infinite, The Muni has completely transcended them both.
Like the sun in the void, Shining upon all places, The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise.
Thoroughly understanding the phenomena of the three times, like the moon on the fifteenth night, its orb without decrease or defect;
so too is the Tathāgata, with all pure qualities (śukla-dharma) fully perfected.
Like the sun moving through the sky without ceasing for even a moment, so too is the Tathāgata, his miraculous transformations (ṛddhi-prātihārya) perpetually continuous.
Just as the lands of the ten directions / Are unimpeded within space, / So too does the Lamp of the World manifest transformations / Within the world.
/ Just as the earth of the world / Is that upon which all living beings rely, / So too is the Wheel of Dharma of the Lamp of the World / Their reliance. / Just like a fierce and swift wind,
His conduct is without obstruction, and the Buddha-dharma is likewise.
Swiftly pervading the world like a great wheel of water, the wheel of wisdom is also thus— the support upon which the Buddhas of the three times rely.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Unobstructed Supreme Treasury, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as a great mountain of jewels Benefits all sentient beings, So too is the wisdom of the Buddha."
Universally benefiting the world, like the waters of the great ocean, Pure, clear, and free from defilement—seeing the Buddha is likewise so; He is able to remove all thirst and craving.
Just as Mount Sumeru emerges from the great ocean, The Lamp of the World is also thus, having emerged from the ocean of Dharma.
Just as the ocean possesses a multitude of jewels, Satisfying all who seek them, So too is the teacherless wisdom:
All who see it are awakened. The Tathāgata’s profound wisdom Is immeasurable and beyond counting;
Therefore, his supernormal powers Manifest in ways inconceivable, Like those of a skilled illusionist.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: manifesting various phenomena, it displays all powers of mastery like a wish-fulfilling gem that can satisfy every desire.
The Supreme Victor is also thus, fulfilling all pure vows; like a brilliant, pure jewel, he illuminates all things everywhere.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it universally illumines the minds of all living beings.
Just as a jewel with eight facets reflects all directions equally, so too is the unimpeded lamp;
it universally illumines the dharma-realm, like the water-purifying pearl that can cleanse all turbid waters. Seeing the Buddha is also like this.
At that time, when all the sense faculties were completely purified,
the Bodhisattva King of the Moon of Vows Manifesting in the Dharma Realm, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
Just as the sapphire jewel can turn all colors blue, so too do those who behold the Buddha all resolve to practice the path to enlightenment.
Within each and every atom, the Buddha manifests his supernormal powers,
causing immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas to become entirely pure through his profound and subtle power.
The realm of the Bodhisattvas is boundless and unknowable; the world cannot fathom the manifestations of the Tathāgata.
Adorned with pure marks, they universally enter the Dharma-realm, bringing all Bodhisattvas to fulfillment within inconceivable Buddha-lands, wherein they attain perfect enlightenment.
All the bodhisattvas and the lords of the world fill [the space];
the Unsurpassed Honored One Śākyamuni possesses complete mastery over all dharmas. He manifests the power of supernatural transformations;
the various practices of the bodhisattvas are boundless and immeasurable, infinite and inexhaustible—this is the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.

For their sake, he manifests all things; the Son of the Buddha trains well therein. Having accomplished the profound realms of phenomena and attained unimpeded wisdom, he clearly understands all dharmas.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata, he turns the wheel of Dharma for the multitudes; his miraculous transformations pervade everywhere, causing the entire world to become pure.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is perfected, and his sphere of activity is likewise pure; he is like a great dragon king who universally relieves all living beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Radiant Flame of Dharma-Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
It is said:
The Tathāgatas of the three times and their great śrāvaka disciples are all unable to know the matter of the Buddha’s lifting and setting down his feet;
nor can any of the pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, or present worlds.
They do not even know the manner in which the Tathāgata lifts and sets down his feet; how much less can ordinary beings,
bound by the fetters of afflictions and with their consciousnesses shrouded by ignorance, know the unimpeded wisdom of the Teacher,
the Perfectly Awakened One, which transcends the path of language and whose measure is unfathomable?
Who is able to know and see, like the light of the bright moon, the limits of the Buddha’s supernormal powers? None can fathom their boundaries;

one cannot perceive their end or limit. Even if one were to contemplate, for the duration of immeasurable eons, each of his various skillful means and the transformations manifested in every thought-moment, one could never fully comprehend them.
Contemplating omniscience, the inconceivable Dharma— the limits of each and every gateway of skillful means cannot be found.
If one should give rise to vast vows regarding this Dharma, then for such a person, knowing and seeing this realm will not be difficult; they shall practice with courageous diligence.
The great ocean of the inconceivable Dharma— With a mind free from all obstructions, Entering this gateway of skillful means,
their minds are already tamed; Their aspirations are vast and wide, And they shall attain the supreme state of Great Bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner King Who Destroys All Māra Armies, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The wisdom-body is not a body; It is unimpeded and inconceivable. Should anyone attempt to conceive of it, It would be like trying to grasp space.
Incomparable to all, arising from inconceivable karma, this pure body is uniquely and wondrously adorned;
unattached to the three realms, its radiance illuminates the entire dharma-realm,
making it utterly pure, opening the gate of the Buddha’s bodhi, and giving birth to manifold wisdoms.
Just as the sun in the world universally radiates the light of wisdom, Far removed from all dust and defilement, it extinguishes every obstacle;
It purifies all realms within the three worlds, Forever cutting off the flow of birth and death.
Accomplishing the path of the Bodhisattva, It gives rise to unsurpassed enlightenment, Manifesting infinite forms.

This form has no basis; though its manifestations are immeasurable, in a single moment of inconceivable awakening, one can realize all phenomena. How could one wish to measure the limits of the Tathāgata’s wisdom?
In a single thought-moment, one fully and clearly penetrates all phenomena of the three periods of time.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha’s wisdom is inexhaustible and indestructible.
The wise should thus single-mindedly contemplate the Bodhi of the Buddha; this contemplation is inconceivable. In contemplating it, it cannot be grasped;
Bodhi cannot be described, for it transcends the path of language. All Buddhas are born from this.
This Dharma is difficult to conceive.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Banner of Light of Vow-Knowledge, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
If one can skillfully observe the inexhaustible ocean of bodhi, Then one will be free from deluded thoughts and resolutely uphold the Dharma.
If one attains a resolute mind, Then one can cultivate wondrous conduct, meditative stillness, and self-reflection.
Forever severing all doubts and suspicions, The mind will never grow weary.
Furthermore, being free from indolence, they progress ever further in their cultivation;
having fully perfected the faith and wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas, they cause them to increase in every thought-moment.
Always delighting in and constantly observing the dharma that is neither attained nor relied upon, they have practiced these meritorious deeds for immeasurable billions of kalpas.
Dedicating everything toward the path sought by all Buddhas, though remaining within birth and death,
their minds are free from attachment; they dwell securely in the teachings of the Buddhas,
and regarding all that exists in the world— the aggregates, the elements, and all such phenomena— they relinquish them all.
Dedicated solely to seeking the Buddha’s virtues, Ordinary beings are entangled in delusive confusion, Constantly wandering through the world.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is unimpeded; He rescues them and brings them to liberation. The Bodhisattva’s practice is difficult to extol;
The entire world cannot conceive of it. It universally eliminates all suffering And bestows happiness upon all living beings.
Having already attained the wisdom of Bodhi, he further takes pity on all living beings; with light illuminating the world, he delivers all multitudes.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrasāravīryaprajñārāja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions.
And he spoke in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, the name of a Buddha is difficult to hear; how much more so to draw near him and forever sever all doubts?
The Tathāgata is the lamp of the world, who has fully realized all dharmas."
Universally producing merit throughout the three periods of time, Causing all beings to become completely pure;
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is praised by all, Constantly gazed upon for billions of eons without ever wearying of the mind.
If there are sons of the Buddha Who contemplate the Buddha’s wondrous form-body, They will surely abandon all attachments to existence.
Dedicating [merit] to the path of Bodhi, the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body constantly utters a vast sound;

with unimpeded eloquence, he opens the gate of the Buddha’s Bodhi. He awakens all sentient beings to the immeasurable and inconceivable, causing them to enter the gate of wisdom and bestowing upon them the prediction of Bodhi.
The Tathāgata has appeared in the world as the great field of merit for the world; he universally guides all sentient beings, causing them to accumulate meritorious deeds.

If one makes offerings to the Buddha, one will forever eliminate the fear of the evil realms and extinguish all suffering, achieving a body of wisdom. This is so if one beholds the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
One who can give rise to the vast and great mind will constantly encounter the Buddhas; their power of wisdom will increase.
If they see the most excellent among men, they will resolutely direct their intent toward Bodhi; such a person can know for themselves that they shall surely attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Supernatural Power of Vow-Knowledge Discerning the Differentiations of the Dharma Realm, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“Śākyamuni, the Unsurpassed Honored One, Possessing all merits and virtues, The hearts of those who behold him are purified.”
Dedicated to great wisdom and the great compassion of the Tathāgata,
you have appeared in the world for the sake of all living beings to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Since the Tathāgata has undergone diligent suffering for the sake of sentient beings throughout incalculable eons, how can the worlds ever repay the kindness of this Great Teacher?
Rather than seeking liberation by abandoning the Tathāgata, I would prefer to undergo the sufferings of the evil realms for immeasurable eons;

rather than seeking peace and happiness by abandoning the Buddha, I would prefer to undergo all manner of suffering on behalf of all sentient beings; rather than remaining in the various evil destinies...
If one constantly hears the name of the Buddha, one would not wish to be born even in the good realms;
if for a moment one does not hear the Buddha, it would be better to be born in the various hells.

Throughout each and every incalculable eon, one would never seek to escape the evil destinies by remaining far removed from the Buddha. For what reason would one wish to dwell for long in all the various evil paths?
Because by seeing the Tathāgata, wisdom increases; If one sees the Buddha, all suffering is extinguished. One can enter the realm of great wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
If one sees the Buddha, all obstacles are abandoned, And inexhaustible merit is nurtured.
Having accomplished the path to enlightenment, the Tathāgata is able to forever sever the doubts of all sentient beings;
according to what their minds desire, he causes them all to be fully satisfied.
[Treatise] The eighteenth section clarifies the part where the Bodhisattva Vairocana and the other ten Bodhisattvas speak in verse. Below this...
There were ten bodhisattvas who had all come from the ten directions; each spoke a single verse, each according to his own name, and each praised his own dharma.

All these practices of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas follow the names of the bodhisattvas, and the meaning expressed by those names can be seen in their verses, as in the first case of the Bodhisattva Vairocanapraṇidhānaraśmi, who represents the seed.
The various radiances are precisely the light of the vows of the Buddha-fruit; this refers to the practices within the stage of the Bodhisattva of the Buddha-fruit.

From the beginning, there is a general praise that causes all observers to perceive the realm of the Tathāgata in the Jeta Grove. Following this, the next nine sections represent the specific details within that general summary;
each corresponds to the name of a Bodhisattva, and their meanings are to be understood according to the dharmas praised in the verses, such as "Indestructible."
The King of Diligence further recited the meaning of indestructible diligence; from "the King of Mastery" downward, it should be understood accordingly.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra universally surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas with equanimity.
The skillful means of the dharma-realm equal to the skillful means of the realm of empty space; equal to the realm of sentient beings; equal to the three periods of time; equal to all eons;
equal to the karma of all sentient beings; equal to the desires of all sentient beings; equal to the understandings of all sentient beings;
equal to the faculties of all sentient beings; equal to the times for maturing all sentient beings; and equal to the light of all dharmas.
[The Sūtra says: "By means of ten dharma-phrases, the Shadow Skillful Means [Bodhisattva] develops, reveals, illuminates, and expounds this Lion’s Stretching Samādhi for all bodhisattvas.
[Treatise: Section nineteen begins from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... and extends down to "the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi," comprising six lines.
The Sūtra clarifies that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, by means of ten kinds of all-encompassing gates of skillful means, intends to expound the section on the Lion’s Stretch Samādhi. [Sūtra]:
What are these ten? They are as follows: expounding the ability to manifest all Buddha-fields within the Dharma-realm, even down to a single atom...
The dharma-phrase of the sequential emergence of all Buddhas within the realms of dust, the dharma-phrase of the sequential formation and destruction of all lands,
the dharma-phrase of the proclamation that can manifest throughout all Buddha-fields equal to the realm of empty space, praising the merits of the Tathāgata for as long as all future kalpas endure,
and the dharma-phrase of the proclamation that can manifest the Tathāgatas within all Buddha-fields equal to the realm of empty space.
The Dharma-phrase expounding the gate of attaining perfect enlightenment, immeasurable and boundless, transcending the world;
the Dharma-phrase expounding that which can manifest Buddhas sitting at the site of enlightenment amidst assemblies of Bodhisattvas in all Buddha-fields equal to the realm of empty space;
and the manifestation from every pore, moment by moment, of transformation bodies as numerous as all Buddhas of the three periods of time, filling the Dharma-realm.
The discourse on the Dharma-phrase of the realms can cause a single body to fill all oceans of lands throughout the ten directions, manifesting them with equal clarity;
the discourse on the Dharma-phrase can cause the spiritual transformations of all Buddhas of the three periods of time to appear universally within all objective spheres;
the discourse on the Dharma-phrase can cause all things of the three periods of time to appear universally within every atom of all Buddha-fields.
The Dharma-expositions that, throughout immeasurable eons, proclaim the various spiritual transformations of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field;

the Dharma-expositions that cause all pores to produce the sounds of the ocean of great vows of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, continuing until the end of future eons to develop and guide all Bodhisattvas;
and the Dharma-expositions that cause the dimensions of the Buddha’s lion throne to become equal [to the universe].
O Son of the Buddha, these ten, beginning with the equality and non-differentiation of the adornments of the dharma-realm, the assemblies of bodhisattvas, and the sites of enlightenment,
turn various subtle and wondrous wheels of Dharma throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
[Treatise]: From "What are the ten? down to "O Son of the Buddha, these ten are the foremost," there are eighteen lines of scripture;
this constitutes the section on the ten kinds of ineffable dharma-words.
[Sūtra] There are ten times the number of dharma-phrases as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, all of which are the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, relied upon the Buddha’s spiritual power to contemplate the Tathāgata,
to contemplate the assembly, to contemplate the inconceivable spheres of all Buddhas, and to contemplate the boundless samādhis of all Buddhas.
He observed the inconceivable oceans of worlds; he observed the inconceivable wisdom of the illusory nature of phenomena;
he observed that all inconceivable Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely equal;
and he observed all immeasurable and boundless modes of expression, speaking these verses:
[Treatise] The twenty-first [section], comprising ten dharma-phrases as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable Buddha-fields, concludes the general summary.
The following six lines of scripture constitute the section on the verses spoken by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva regarding the realm of the Buddha’s contemplation.
[Scripture] Within each and every pore, there are oceans of lands as numerous as atoms; in all of them, Tathāgatas sit, surrounded by assemblies of Bodhisattvas.
Within each and every pore, there are immeasurable oceans of lands where Buddhas occupy their seats of enlightenment;
thus it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, within each and every pore.
Buddhas as numerous as atoms in all lands, surrounded by assemblies of bodhisattvas, preach the conduct of Samantabhadra.
A single Buddha sits within one land, yet fills the realms of the ten directions. Clouds of immeasurable bodhisattvas all gather at his abode;
their number is like the atoms in billions of lands—the ocean of merit of these bodhisattvas.
All together rose from within the assembly, filling the realms of the ten directions; Abiding entirely in the conduct of Samantabhadra, they all roamed the ocean of the Dharma-realm.
Universally manifesting in all lands, they entered equally into the assemblies of all Buddhas;
Sitting peacefully in every land, they listened to and heard all teachings, Within each and every realm.
Having cultivated all practices for billions of eons, these are the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas;
Universally illuminating the ocean of Dharma, they enter the ocean of great vows, Abiding on the ground of the Buddha’s realm.
Thoroughly comprehending the conduct of Samantabhadra, they give birth to all Buddha-dharmas; Possessing the ocean of Buddha-merits, they extensively manifest miraculous powers.
Bodies like clouds, numbering as many as atoms, fill all lands; they rain down the nectar of the Dharma everywhere, causing all beings to abide in the Buddha-way.
[Commentary]: Within these ten verses, the meaning of the ten previously mentioned inexhaustible phrases is reiterated to clarify the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The essential nature is unimpeded, with the one and the many interpenetrating and the large and the small mutually entering;
within every pore and every minute atom, all oceans of Buddha-fields are contained, and each and every realm is mutually inclusive without obstruction. As the verse says:
"Within each and every pore, Oceans of lands as numerous as atoms All have Tathāgatas seated, Each accompanied by assemblies of Bodhisattvas," as it is stated in the Sūtra.
The above twenty-one sections of the sūtra clarify how the Tathāgata, through the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*,
causes those who have advanced through the five stages to enter the dharma-gate of Samantabhadra’s ten thousand practices, which are inherently perfect within the nature of the dharmadhātu.
Since there is fundamentally no need for a formal conjunction of these Samantabhadra practices, from this point onward, the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows.

The gate called "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times," which causes all bodhisattvas to enter and abide in the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi—these twenty-one sections above constitute the assembly within the dharma-realm of Samantabhadra’s differentiated wisdom and unimpeded conduct.
Having reached fulfillment, he then causes Samantabhadra to speak verses in praise of the Dharma; thereafter, he emits light from between his eyebrows.
Having clarified that the fundamental dharmakāya-primal wisdom of universal radiance is identical with the unimpeded,
sovereign distinctions and similarities within the dharma-realm, and that the gates of Samantabhadra’s practice— the essence and function of principle and wisdom— converge simultaneously,

Mañjuśrī is then commanded to speak verses in praise of the Dharma; for through the two bodies of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, the two wisdoms of the conventional and the ultimate become one, and the dharma-realm is leveled.

In this Dharma-gate of the eternally abiding equality, within this Dharmadhātu, there are two aspects: essence and function. If there were no Samantabhadra, the wisdom of differentiation would not proceed;
thus, in the state of quiescence, there would be no compassionate activity. If there were no Mañjuśrī, the practice of Samantabhadra would not exist, for it would then be conditioned and impermanent.
Therefore, through the Dharma-gates of these two persons, the essence and function of the single Dharmadhātu are established as one.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is summarized thus: that which is called a "Buddha" is simply the wisdom that dwells nowhere within the essence and function of these two persons;

it is said that those who dwell where the Buddha dwells, the Buddha dwells in non-dwelling—namely, the wisdom that dwells nowhere within the essence and function of the myriad practices of the principle and wisdom of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Thus, one attains the name of Buddha. For this reason, the preceding section on Samantabhadra is the "Gate of Revealing Principle through Practice," while the subsequent section on Mañjuśrī is the "Gate of Manifesting Practice through Principle.
In establishing the teachings through verbal expression, the names have a sequence;

yet, regarding the *dharmadhātu*, these two dharmas mutually support one another as fundamentally one body and its function. Therefore, by means of the Tathāgata, conditions are raised to manifest the Dharma—this is the Teacher.
The *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (Lion’s Stretching Samādhi) belongs to the gate of Samantabhadra, while the light from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows belongs to the gate of Mañjuśrī.
Since this light is manifested by the wondrous wisdom of the Dharmakāya and arises from the fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*),

whereas the *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* functions within the sphere of the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), it is only when these two are of one essence that the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is fully realized.
The gate of mastery symbolizes the self-nature of fundamental wisdom, which is beyond words; its functioning through verbal expression is that which is gathered by Samantabhadra.
If these three dharmas are practiced separately, this constitutes the cycle of birth and death for humans and devas;

even if one attains the Way, such a person is called "blind-eyed" or "dwarfish," for they merely dwell in a grass hut and do not enter the gate of the great mansion of the Dharma-realm. Thus says the Master.

The *Subhūṣita-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Subhūṣita) refers to the stage within the five positions where cultivation has reached completion, where principle and wisdom have merged and fused, and where the exhaustion of preparatory effort has suddenly vanished.

It is filled with the joy of the Dharma, no longer belonging to progressive advancement, and is characterized by the universal pervasion of spontaneous wisdom and the manifestation of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Without acting, the realm of wisdom is applied; without striving, the Buddha-fields mutually interpenetrate to the ultimate degree.
The minute is not made small, yet it exhausts the oceans of Buddha-fields within; the vast is not made large, yet it extends throughout the ten directions, all contained within a single hair-tip.
This is the free exercise of the ocean of wisdom, manifesting jewel-adorned lands in mutual interpenetration, which is called "bending and stretching.
To accord with principle such that bodies and realms—whether one or many—are mutually inclusive is termed the samādhi of "bending."

"Stretching forth" signifies comfort, joy, and the absence of fatigue; it clarifies that through the causal conditions for advancement in the preceding five stages, one has integrated conditioned and unconditioned phenomena through mental attention (*manasikāra*).

It clarifies that this *dharmadhātu* is already perfected in its advancement, such that wisdom functions spontaneously and all phenomena are self-accomplished, free from the fatigue of intentional effort. Therefore, below this point, the hair-tuft between the eyebrows is emitted.
The mark of radiance is named "The Door of Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times.
This reveals the door of mastery in practice through the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, and belongs to Mañjuśrī;

that is, it subsequently employs verses spoken by Mañjuśrī to praise the light of the Dharma, so that this Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra may act in unison through the union of wisdom and means, and thus the fruit of Buddhahood is spontaneously perfected.

However, the essence of the principle-wisdom (*prajñā*) and the substance of the phenomena-wisdom (*jñāna*)—the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*—cannot be pursued through mere paper, bamboo, or silk, nor through recorded transcriptions, nor through preceding and succeeding names and phrases.

These names and phrases cannot be grasped all at once; rather, one should simply take up the principle-wisdom to know its general and specific aspects, its similarities and differences, and its formation and disintegration.
Nevertheless, for those whose deluded minds are first being awakened, one must first practice various wholesome deeds.
Thus, by means of the gateway of manifesting principle, the cause is the clarity of wisdom and principle, as in the ten *pāramitās*:
nine *pāramitās* are practice, while the *jñāna-pāramitā* alone is the fruit; the remaining nine *pāramitās* serve as the skillful means for manifesting the essence and function of wisdom.
For this reason, prior to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practices is first elucidated.
Within the present chapter, the Buddha, through his light, simultaneously bestows empowerment upon Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra,
unifying them as a single entity of wisdom and practice, essence and function. First, he causes them to manifest the great functioning of the Dharma-realm through the assembly of Samantabhadra,
entering the gate of the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s yawn samādhi) and sealing it with that samādhi.

Because of this practice, next is the light between the eyebrows named "The Door of Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times," which causes all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi.
This clarifies that the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya and the manifesting wisdom of differentiation are one in essence and function;
only then is it called "entering the door of the Dharma-realm. Therefore, the preceding [sections] comprise twenty-one [lights].
The "Section on Practice" (*duàn jīng*) is the gate of non-attachment through which practice accords with principle; therein, Samantabhadra is the principal figure and Mañjuśrī is his companion.

The subsequent "Gate of the Tathāgata Emitting Light from between His Brows Named 'Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm of the Three Times'" is the gate of the perfect fusion and unimpeded freedom through which principle accords with practice. In this [gate], Mañjuśrī is the principal figure and Samantabhadra is his companion.
When the companions are thus integrated with their principal [object], it is only then that they are called "sovereignty over the Dharma-realm. From the passage beginning, "At that time,

the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all Bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Great Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Lion-Stretch," down to "not departing from this Jeta Grove at the place of the Tathāgata," this is designated as the "Perfection of Practice through the Convergence of Principle."
This section on the gate of unhindered mastery is further divided into six parts.

[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Tathāgata’s Great Samādhi of the Lion’s Stretch and Yawn, emitted a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows; the light was named "Universally Illuminating the Three Times."
The Dharma-realm gate, with as many rays of light as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields,
universally illumines all oceans of worlds and all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions. At that time, the assembly of Bodhisattvas in the Jeta Grove all saw,
within every single atom of every Buddha-field throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, each containing—
In as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in all Buddha-lands— possessing various names, various colors, various purities, various abodes, and various forms— in all such lands,
there were great Bodhisattvas seated upon lion thrones at sites of enlightenment, having attained perfect awakening, surrounded by assemblies of Bodhisattvas before and behind them.
He saw [the Buddha] surrounded by the lords of the world as he performed offerings;
or he saw him within great assemblies in unspeakably many buddha-fields, emitting sublime sounds that filled the dharma-realm as he turned the wheel of the true Dharma;
or he saw him in the palaces of devas, the palaces of nāgas, the palaces of yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.
Within the palaces of the *mahoragas*, humans, non-humans, and others, or in human realms such as villages,
towns, settlements, royal capitals, and great cities, they manifest various lineages, various names, various bodies, various marks, and various radiances;
they abide in various modes of deportment, enter various *samādhis*, and display various supernatural transformations, sometimes by their own power...
With various sounds and voices, they cause various bodhisattvas within various great assemblies to speak various dharmas using various modes of expression;

likewise, the bodhisattva assemblies in this gathering behold such profound samādhi and great supernormal powers of these Buddhas and Tathāgatas, pervading the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Throughout all directions— east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below— within the oceans of lands, these abide according to the mental conceptions of sentient beings.
From the beginningless past until the present, within every land, every body of a sentient being, and every path of empty space,
in each and every location the size of a single hair-tip, there are as many buddha-lands as there are atoms.
The various arisings of karma abide in their proper sequence, and all possess bodhimandas with assemblies of bodhisattvas;
all likewise perceive the Buddha’s spiritual power, which does not destroy the three periods of time nor destroy the world.

It manifests its reflections within the minds of all sentient beings, and according to the inclinations of the hearts of all sentient beings, it issues forth sublime sounds that universally enter all assemblies.
He manifests universally before all sentient beings; while his physical forms differ, his wisdom is without distinction.
According to their needs, he reveals the Buddha-dharma to teach and transform all sentient beings without ever ceasing.
Those who behold this buddha-power are all those whom the Tathāgata Vairocana sustained through his roots of goodness in the past.
Some were previously gathered through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); some were matured through seeing, hearing, remembering, or associating with [the Buddha];
some were previously instructed to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
some had planted roots of goodness together with various Buddhas in the past; and some had previously employed the skillful means of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-kuśala*).
Through skillful means of teaching and maturing them, they all enter the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and profound samādhi;
they attain great supernormal powers that pervade the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space,
whether entering the Dharma-body, the form-body, the practices accomplished in the past, the perfection of the various pāramitās, or the various adornments.
Whether entering the wheel of pure conduct, or entering the various bodhisattva stages, or entering the power of attaining perfect enlightenment,
or entering the great supernormal transformations of the non-differentiated samādhis in which Buddhas dwell, or entering the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and wisdom,
or entering the ocean of the Buddha’s unimpeded eloquence— those bodhisattvas, by means of various understandings, various paths, various gates, and various...

They enter into such oceans of the spiritual transformations of Buddhas— equal in number to the atoms within ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields— as well as their various principles, various conformities, various wisdoms, various aids to the path, various skillful means, and various samādhis.
Through these and other such doors of skillful means, they enter.

When the son [of the Buddha] enters the Samādhi of Bending and Stretching and emits from the white tuft between his eyebrows a light called "The Door of Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm of the Three Times," this light is the fundamental, universal radiance-wisdom within the Dharmatā-body.

When this wisdom manifests before one, one perceives the three times—past, present, and future—as a single entity throughout the long duration of time; even the birth and death of infinite kalpas are seen as such.
Without shifting from the present, realizing that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature and becoming a great ocean of wisdom, one attains the coolness of all phenomena;

then, by means of sentient beings, one gives rise to discerning wisdom to know their faculties and benefit them, pervading the entire ocean of lands without rest—this is called the conduct of Samantabhadra.
This refers to the attainment of unspeakably many gates of samādhi for the purpose of teaching and transforming others, as described in the subsequent text of the sutra.
The gates of infinite sentient beings are fully detailed as explained in the sutra; they are self-evident according to the text.
