The section on the names of the samādhis entered [by the Bodhisattvas], consisting of sixty-six lines of the main exposition from the *Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa-parivarta* within the ocean of miraculous transformations of the samādhi that fills the dharma-realm in every thought-moment, states:
[Sūtra] All those bodhisattvas were fully endowed with great wisdom, supernormal powers, clarity, and mastery, and they dwelt in all...

The Ground [of the Bodhisattva] universally contemplates all things with vast wisdom; from the seed-nature of all wisdoms, the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is constantly present before them.
Having attained the pure eye of wisdom free from the cataracts of delusion, they act as guides for all sentient beings.
Abiding in the equality of the Buddhas, they are without discrimination regarding all phenomena; they thoroughly penetrate the objective realm and understand all worlds.
The intermediate states are all quiescent and devoid of any place of dependence;

they universally visit all Buddha-lands without attachment, are able to observe all phenomena without abiding, and enter everywhere into the palaces of the sublime Dharma without coming from anywhere.
They teach and transform all worlds, universally manifesting peace and security for the sake of sentient beings.

Abiding in wisdom and liberation as their sphere of activity, they constantly dwell in the body of gnosis at the limit of detachment, transcending the ocean of all existences and manifesting the true reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
With the light of wisdom fully perfected, they universally perceive all phenomena; dwelling in samādhi, they are firm and immovable.
Toward all sentient beings, they constantly give rise to great compassion, knowing that all dharma-gates are entirely like illusions. All sentient beings...
All births are like dreams; all Tathāgatas are like reflections; all speech and sounds are like echoes; all phenomena are like magical transformations.
They are well-able to accumulate sublime practices and vows, their wisdom is perfected and pure, they possess skillful means, and their minds are profoundly tranquil.
They have skillfully entered the realm of all dhāraṇīs and are endowed with samādhi.
Possessing power and valor, they are without fear; having attained the eye of clear wisdom, they abide at the limit of the *dharmadhātu* and reach the state where all phenomena are non-apprehendable.
They cultivate the boundless great ocean of wisdom and reach the ultimate further shore of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), being sustained by the perfection of wisdom.
Through the perfection of supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāramitā*), they universally enter the world, relying on the three...

Through the perfection of wisdom, they attain mastery over the mind; through non-erroneous knowledge, they know all meanings; through skillful analytical knowledge, they reveal the treasury of the Dharma;
through the knowledge of manifest realization, they explain and interpret words and phrases; through the power of great vows, they preach the Dharma inexhaustibly;
through fearlessness, they constantly roar the lion’s roar as a Great Teacher; and with purity, they always delight in contemplating the phenomena that have no basis.

With the Dharma-eye, he universally observes all things; with the moon of pure wisdom, he illuminates the formation and destruction of the world; with the light of wisdom, he shines upon the true reality.
His merit and wisdom are like a mountain of adamant, beyond the reach of any analogy. Skillfully observing all phenomena, his faculty of wisdom increases;
through courageous and fierce diligence, he subdues all Māras, possessing the majestic radiance of immeasurable wisdom.
His body blazes forth, transcending all worlds; he has attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena and is well able to realize the limit of exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
Abiding at the universal limit, he enters the limit of true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The wisdom of the contemplation of signlessness is constantly present before him.
Skillfully accomplishing all bodhisattva practices, he knows all objective realms through non-dual wisdom and perceives them universally.
He has traveled to all realms of existence throughout the entire world; his lamp of wisdom is perfected in all Buddha-lands;
he is free from the darkness and obstructions of all phenomena; he radiates pure Dharma-light that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions;
he is the true field of merit for all the world; whether seen or heard, his vows are all fulfilled; his merit is vast and high, surpassing all the world; he is courageous and valiant.
Fearless in crushing all non-Buddhists, he proclaims the subtle and wondrous sound throughout all lands; he perceives all Buddhas everywhere with a mind never weary or satiated.
Having attained mastery over the Buddha-dharma body, he manifests bodies according to those who should be transformed.
Having attained mastery such that a single body fills all Buddha-lands, he travels by means of pure supernormal powers and the great ship of wisdom wherever he goes.

Unimpeded wisdom is perfectly fulfilled and pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it is like the rising sun that universally illuminates the world, manifesting forms and images according to the minds of sentient beings.
It knows the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all beings, entering the non-contentious realm of all dharmas.
It knows the nature of all phenomena is without birth or arising, enabling the free mutual entry of the small and the great, and bringing definitive understanding.
The profound realm of the Buddha-ground is explained through inexhaustible phrases; within a single phrase, one expounds the ocean of all *sūtras*.
Having attained the great wisdom of the *dhāraṇī*-body, whatever is received and upheld is never forgotten.
In a single thought-moment, one can recall events of immeasurable eons; in a single thought-moment, one fully knows all sentient beings of the three periods of time.
He constantly gives birth to wisdom and, by means of all *dhāraṇī* gates, expounds the boundless ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma;
he perpetually turns the pure wheel of Dharma that never regresses, causing all sentient beings to give rise to wisdom and attain the realm of the Buddhas.
Through the light of wisdom, they enter the profound *samādhi* of "Excellent Vision" (*Sudarśana*) and penetrate the unobstructed limit of all phenomena within a single [instant].

The sovereign wisdom of all dharmas is pure and adorned in all spheres; it universally enters all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions, reaching every single location without exception. Within each and every atom, it manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
within the nature of formlessness, it manifests all forms. It universally enters every direction from within a single direction. All these Bodhisattvas are thus endowed with such [qualities].
These beings, who are treasuries of boundless merit, wisdom, and virtue, are constantly praised by all Buddhas;

though one were to speak of their virtues with various words, they could never be exhausted. There is not one among them who does not dwell within the Jeta Grove, having deeply entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s virtues and beholding everywhere the illumination of the Buddha’s radiance.

[Treatise] Third: From "All those bodhisattvas were fully endowed with great supernormal powers" down to "they all saw the light of the Buddha’s radiance," fifty-three lines and a half of scripture clarify the section on the virtues gained by the bodhisattvas through the benefit of the Buddha’s radiance.
[Sūtra] At that time, the bodhisattvas, having attained the light of the inconceivable True Dharma, were filled with great joy in their hearts.
Each of them manifested various clouds of great adornments from within their own bodies, the decorative ornaments of the pavilions, their lion thrones,
and all objects throughout the entire Jeta Grove, filling all the ten directions.
The Dharma-realm is that which, in every moment of thought, emits great clouds of light that fill the ten directions and are able to awaken all sentient beings;

it produces clouds of all kinds of mani-jewel bells that fill the ten directions and emit subtle, wondrous sounds praising and extolling all the merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; it produces clouds of all kinds of musical instruments that fill [the ten directions]...
Within sounds that fill the ten directions, they expound the karmic retributions of all sentient beings;
clouds of the various vows, practices, and physical forms of all bodhisattvas emerge, filling the ten directions as they proclaim the great vows of all bodhisattvas;
clouds of the sovereign transformations of all Tathāgatas emerge, filling the ten directions as they manifest the teachings of all Buddhas.
From the sounds and voices of their speech, there issued forth clouds of the bodies of all Bodhisattvas, adorned with the primary and secondary marks, filling the ten directions;

they proclaimed the successive manifestations of all Tathāgatas in all lands; they brought forth clouds of the bodhimandas of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, filling the ten directions; and they manifested the adornments of the merits of all Tathāgatas attaining perfect enlightenment.
The clouds of all dragon kings fill the ten directions, raining down all manner of fragrances;
the clouds of the bodies of all world-protectors fill the ten directions, proclaiming the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
the clouds of all jewel-adorned, pure Buddha-fields fill the ten directions, manifesting the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma by all Tathāgatas—all these bodhisattvas...
Because they have attained the light of the inconceivable Dharma, the Dharma should manifest in this way through such clouds of great miraculous transformations and adornments,
as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority,
wishing to proclaim once more these various miraculous events within the Jeta Grove, surveyed the ten directions.
[The Treatise] states:

From "At that time, all the bodhisattvas... down to the verses, twenty-one and a half lines of scripture clarify how the various samādhis and supernormal powers attained by the bodhisattvas manifested clouds of transformations to adorn the Jeta Grove.
[And] the divisions of the lands of the ten directions.

[Sūtra]: "You should contemplate this Jeta Grove, Where, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, All manner of adornments are manifested boundlessly, Filling the entirety of the dharma-realm in the ten directions."
Within the spheres of their thrones and other realms, all the lands of the ten directions—
with their infinite varieties of great adornments— appear with distinct forms and images.
From the pores of the Buddha-sons emerge clouds of variously adorned jewel-flames.
And emitting the subtle, wondrous voice of the Tathāgata, it pervades all lands throughout the ten directions;
within the flowers of the jewel-trees, a wondrous body appears— its physical form and marks like those of Brahmā,
rising from meditative concentration and walking with gait and deportment ever serene.
Within each and every pore of the Tathāgata, inconceivable transformation bodies constantly appear;
all are like the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, adorned with various marks and signs of excellence.
From the midst of all the adornments in the sky above the Jeta Grove, a wondrous sound issues forth:
Universally proclaiming all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time who have accomplished the ocean of all merits;
from the various jewel trees within the Jeta Grove, there likewise issue forth immeasurable, wondrous sounds,
expounding the various differences within the oceans of karma of all sentient beings.
All the various realms within the forest appear before all the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
each one manifests great supernormal powers, as numerous as the atoms within the oceans of lands of the ten directions,
and as numerous as the atoms within all the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions.
They all enter the pores of the Tathāgata, And are seen manifesting their successive adornments;
All these adornments appear as Buddhas, Equal in number to all sentient beings throughout the world.
Each one emits great rays of light, Transforming the multitudes of beings according to their needs.
Clouds of incense, flames, various flowers, and jewel treasuries— every kind of magnificent adornment,
vast and equal to space, pervading all lands throughout the ten directions;
and all the wondrous sites of enlightenment belonging to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Within the realm of this grove, every form and image appears clearly;
all the sons of the Buddhas, Samantabhadra, who have adorned lands for oceans of hundreds of thousands of kalpas—
numbering as infinite as sentient beings— all behold them within these woods.
[Treatise] 5. You should contemplate this Jeta Grove... down to "there is none in this grove who does not see" [the following].
The twenty-six verses of clear prose and verse by Mañjuśrī reiterate the aforementioned Dharma as clearly as the text itself.
The above clarifies that all the bodhisattvas illuminated by the Buddha’s light, having received that illumination, entered the *pralambana-samādhi* (the samādhi of stretching and bending).
The skillful means of the realm of the Worthy (Bhadra) are simply all samādhis; they are collectively the gate of expedient practice.
This is because the realm of Samantabhadra is entirely accomplished through the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body.
[Sūtra] At that time, because those bodhisattvas were illuminated by the light of the Buddha’s samādhi, they immediately entered such a samādhi;
each and every one attained gates of great compassion as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields,
benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and from every single pore upon their bodies, there issued forth unspeakably many Buddhas.
From each of the light rays, as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, there emanate bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many buddha-fields.
Their physical forms and characteristics are like those of the lords of the world; they appear before all sentient beings, pervading and filling the dharma-realm in the ten directions.
Through various skillful means, they teach, transform, and subdue them—some appearing in unspeakable [forms].
They may manifest as the gates of impermanence for celestial palaces as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field;
or they may manifest as the gates of birth and rebirth for all sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many buddha-fields;

or they may manifest as the gates of the spiritual practices of all bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many buddha-fields; or they may manifest as the gates of dreamscapes as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many buddha-fields; or...
They may manifest gates of the great vows of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields;

or they may manifest gates of shaking worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields; or they may manifest gates of discerning worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields;
or they may manifest gates of appearing in birth within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields; or...
They manifest gates of the *dānapāramitā* as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;

or they manifest gates of the *śīlapāramitā* consisting of the various ascetic practices and meritorious deeds cultivated by all Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
or they manifest gates of the *kṣāntipāramitā* consisting of the severing of limbs, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Some gates manifest the practice of the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor) as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
some manifest the gates of all Bodhisattvas practicing various *samādhis*, meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and liberations as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
and some manifest the light of wisdom that perfects the path of the Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.

Some gates manifest as seeking the Buddha-dharma with such diligence that for the sake of a single word or a single phrase, they relinquish countless bodies and lives, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields;

some gates manifest as drawing near to all Buddhas and inquiring about all dharmas with a mind free from weariness, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields; some gates manifest as... [unspeakably many buddha-fields].

Equal in number to the atoms of dust, according to the seasons and inclinations of sentient beings, he goes to their respective places and, through skillful means, brings them to maturity, leading them to abide in the gate of the light of the ocean of all-knowledge;

or he manifests, in numbers equal to the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields, the gate of the power of merit and wisdom that subdues all Māras and restrains all non-Buddhists; or he manifests, in unspeakably many Buddha-fields...
They manifest the gate of wisdom that knows all arts and crafts in numbers as vast as atoms;
or they manifest the gate of wisdom that discerns the differences among all sentient beings in numbers as vast as the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields;

or they manifest the gate of wisdom that discerns the differences among all phenomena in numbers as vast as the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields; or they manifest [the gate of wisdom] in numbers as vast as the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
The gate of wisdom that knows the differences in the mental inclinations of all sentient beings;
or manifests the gate of wisdom that knows the faculties, conduct, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
or manifests the gate of wisdom that knows the various karmas of all sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; or manifests...
One may speak of gates for awakening all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field; by means of such inconceivable numbers of expedient gates,
as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, one proceeds to the dwellings of all sentient beings to bring them to maturity—
namely, by going to celestial palaces, or to the palaces of nāgas, or to the abodes of yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras.
Whether they go to the palaces of the *rākṣasas*, *garuḍas*, *kiṃnaras*, or *mahoragas*; or to the palace of the Brahma King;
or to the palace of a human king; or to the palace of Yama, the Lord of Death;
or to the abodes of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings—they gather all beings through equal great compassion, equal great vows, equal wisdom, and equal skillful means.
Among those born [in this world], some are tamed upon seeing [the Buddha], some are tamed upon hearing [his teaching],
some are tamed by mindfulness, some are tamed by hearing his voice, some are tamed by hearing his name, some are tamed by seeing his halo,
and some are tamed by seeing his net of light; thus it is according to the various beings.
Whatever places sentient beings find joy in, they all go there so that they may obtain benefit. O Son of the Buddha, within this Jeta Grove, all these bodhisattvas,
for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, sometimes manifest themselves in various exquisitely adorned palaces,
and sometimes appear dwelling in their own towers and pavilions upon jeweled lion thrones amidst the assemblies at sites of enlightenment.
They surround him on all sides so that he is seen throughout the ten directions, yet they do not leave this Jeta Grove where the Tathāgata resides.
O Son of the Buddha, these bodhisattvas sometimes manifest clouds of immeasurable transformation bodies, or they manifest their own bodies as solitary and peerless;
that is to say, some manifest the body of a śramaṇa, some manifest the body of a brāhmaṇa, or...
Manifesting as a body practicing austerities, or a body of full vigor, or a body of a king of physicians,
or a body of a merchant leader, or a body of one living by pure means, or a body of a musician, or a body serving the various devas,
or a body of a craftsman or technician, he approaches all sentient beings in villages, camps, cities, royal capitals, and market towns, according to their needs.
According to what is appropriate, through various forms, various modes of conduct, various voices, various discourses, and various dwellings,
they practice the bodhisattva path throughout all worlds like the net of Indra; or they explain all the crafts and occupations of the world,
or they explain the lamp of wisdom that illuminates the world, or they explain a single [teaching].
Whether they manifest the adornments of the karmic power of all sentient beings, or explain the establishment of the various vehicles and stages in the lands of the ten directions,
or describe the realms of all phenomena illuminated by the lamp of wisdom to teach and bring all sentient beings to maturity—
they do so without ever departing from this Jeta Grove, the abode of the Tathāgata.

[Treatise] 6. At that time, from the passage "those bodhisattvas" down to "not departing from the Jeta Grove," the sixty-three lines of scripture clarify that because the bodhisattvas are illuminated by the light of the Buddha’s samādhi,
they attain the aforementioned samādhis, as well as infinite great compassion, infinite supernormal powers, and infinite benefit for sentient beings.

From the section on "The Arising of Parts" onwards, these twenty-seven segments of the sūtra collectively clarify the conclusion of the previous answers to the forty dharma-gates questioned by the assembly of bodhisattvas.
This Dharma-realm Dharma-gate reveals the essence of wisdom as sovereign;
it manifests through the power of wisdom itself without relying on the spoken words of the Tathāgata, and furthermore, it causes Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra to [fulfill] their original...

The section from "The Lord himself proclaims the practice of the fundamental fruit so that it may be easily understood" up to "therefore one does not lose the essence and function of the teaching" constitutes the beginning,
end, and perfect completion of this entire sutra, which is subsumed under the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. Second, the section from "At that time,
the youth Mañjuśrī" down to the very end of the sutra is attributed to Mañjuśrī.

The youth proceeded south from the Sudharmā-terrace to the realm of Jambudvīpa to manifest the practice of benefiting beings, so that those who would later resolve their minds for enlightenment might not be confused regarding their conduct and might easily attain understanding.
From the passage beginning "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" onwards is titled the "Gate of Manifesting Practice to Benefit Beings in the World. Prior to this teaching, it was simply stated:

From the passage "Mañjuśrī, the Youthful One, does not speak" (*mañjuśrīr na vadati kumārabhūtaḥ*) onwards, [the text] enters the mundane realm to transform and benefit sentient beings through practice and establishment.

Thus, he is named "The Youthful One. Prior to this, [the text] generally summarizes the fruit of Buddhahood within the Universal Radiance Wisdom (*samantaprabha-jñāna*), establishing the modes of transformation by means of the stages of the Bodhisattvas—beginning with "Awakening Head" (*bodhimukha*) and so forth—within the ranks of the noble ones. These are the various Bodhisattvas of the five positions, beginning with Awakening Head.
All are universally transformed without fixed direction, manifesting freely whether hidden or apparent. Mañjuśrī is the foremost of those who inspire faith;

from this point downward, because he enters the mundane world from within the essence of the Dharma-realm to initiate the transformation of the ignorant, his name is established based on the conduct he practices, and he is thus titled Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Through his wondrous wisdom, he transforms the ignorant and leads them into the Buddha-wisdom.

Because wisdom is born within the Buddha-family, this is the primordial dharma-body and the manifestation of fundamental wisdom—the principle of non-substantiality—of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is therefore the wondrous wisdom.

Thus, all Buddhas of the three periods of time are first born into the Buddha-family from this, and from this they accomplish the great vows and practices of Samantabhadra. For what reason is it so named?

Regarding those who have already established the gates of practice for the sake of attaining worldly benefit and birth, the preceding sections merely spoke of ascending to heaven to signify the accomplishment of their practice;
the various devas had not yet gone among humans to transform and benefit them within the secular world.

From this "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" chapter onward, in the remaining one and a half fascicles of the sutra, there are only Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and World Rulers who have already attained the Way, but none who remain in the secular state as ordinary people.

Now, as for entering this Dharma-gate: from the passage where the youth Mañjuśrī descends from the Well-Abiding Pavilion (*Susthitālaya*) onwards, he enters the human realm to engage with those of ordinary capacity and transform commoners, enabling them to realize the principles of this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, he causes the youth Sudhana to seek out fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to represent the five [stages].
Within the three types of dharmakāya as cause and effect, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra (*viśeṣa-jñāna*) operate;
the wisdom that abides in neither of these two is called "Buddha. Because these three dharmas are fully possessed, one is named "Buddha.
Because these three dharmas pervade the five stages from beginning to end, acting as cause and effect, they are called the "Vehicle" (*yāna*).
The Tathāgata-vehicle proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and is also called the vehicle of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-yāna);
because the Dharma-realm takes these three types of cause and effect as its essence and function, the causes and effects of the five preceding stages are likewise so.
In total, these three dharmas constitute the cause and effect. This Buddha, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and the fifty...
The practice of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) constitutes cause and effect, yet for [the Buddha] himself there is no cause and effect;

this is because within the state of one’s own Buddhahood, there is nothing to be cultivated and nothing to be practiced. It is merely for the sake of those practicing within the five stages that the points where the impure and pure habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are treated and matured are designated as "cause" and "effect.
However, as for the Dharma-body, the wisdom of principle, and the myriad practices, they are inherently [perfected].

Although there is no [intrinsic] cause and effect, the names "Tathāgata cause" and "Tathāgata effect" are established based on the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) within the five stages that counteract afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Thus, Mañjuśrī traveled to the city of Bodhimaṇḍa among humans to teach according to their faculties,
causing Sudhana to initiate the stage of preparatory practice, seek out fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and thereby accomplish one hundred and ten causes.
The "Fruit Dharma-gate" is so named because it prevents students from becoming confused regarding the practices of the five stages, making them easy to understand;
because it serves as a model for practice for those who have subsequently resolved to attain Bodhicitta;
and because it provides students with a pattern for accomplishing practice so that they do not lose their way. Furthermore, there is another underlying intention. Up to this point...
Below, we shall clarify the section on "descending to the mundane realm to benefit sentient beings and accomplish practice.
Within this section, from the passage concerning Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta down to the end of the sutra, the text is divided into three long sections.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī emerged from the Well-Situated Pavilion (Susthitakūṭāgāra) together with immeasurable fellow-practicing bodhisattvas,
the various vajra-spirits who constantly attend and guard him, the various body-host spirits who universally make offerings to all Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings,
the foot-traveling spirits who have long made firm vows to always follow him, and the Lord of Delighting in Hearing the Sublime Dharma.
The Earth Deity, Constantly Cultivating Great Compassion; the Water Deity, Sovereign of Illuminating Wisdom; the Fire Deity, Sovereign of the Maṇi Crown;
the Wind Deity, Sovereign of Thorough Mastery of All Rituals in the Ten Directions; the Directional Deity, Diligently Devoted to Eradicating the Darkness of Ignorance;
the Night Deity, Single-minded and Untiring in Proclaiming the Buddha-Sun; and the Day Deity, Adorning the Dharma Realm.
The Lord of All Space, the Deity of Space, universally delivers sentient beings across the ocean of all existences;

the Lord of the Ocean, constantly and diligently accumulates the roots of goodness conducive to the path toward omniscience; the Lord of Mountains, as lofty as a mountain, constantly and diligently protects the bodhicitta of all sentient beings;
and the Lord of the Capital City, constantly and diligently guards the wisdom of all-knowledge.
The great nāga kings constantly and diligently protect the unsurpassed city of Dharma for all sentient beings;
the yakṣa kings always cause sentient beings to increase in joy; the gandharva kings constantly and diligently eliminate the realms of hungry ghosts;
the kumbhāṇḍa kings ever vow to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of existence; and the garuḍa kings...
May they attain the accomplishment of the bodies of all Tathāgatas, transcending the world; may the Asura Kings, upon seeing the Buddha, rejoice and bow with reverence;
may the Mahoraga Kings, ever weary of birth and death, constantly delight in seeing the Buddha;
may the great Heavenly Kings honor the Buddha, praising and making offerings to him; and may the great Brahmā Kings and Mañjuśrī likewise [be so].
The assembly of bodhisattvas, adorned with such merits, emerged from their respective abodes and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
They circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right for immeasurable times and made various offerings with all manner of ritual requisites.

Having completed these offerings, they took their leave and traveled south toward the human realm. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, beheld Mañjuśrī.
The Bodhisattva Li (Vīrya) and the assembly of bodhisattvas, adorned with their retinues, departed from the Jeta Grove and traveled southward through the human realms.
As they proceeded, he thought to himself: "I shall now go to the south together with Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, surrounded by six thousand bhikṣus, emerged from his own dwelling and came forth to meet them.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the World-Honored One in full, the World-Honored One granted his permission.
He circumambulated him three times to the right, took his leave, and departed for the place where Mañjuśrī was. These six thousand bhikṣus were those with whom Śāriputra had lived together;
they had not long since gone forth [into the homeless life], namely: the bhikṣu Sāgarabuddhi, the bhikṣu Sujāta, the bhikṣu Puṇyaprabha, and the bhikṣu Mahā...
The novice bhikṣu Vidyudgati, the bhikṣu Viśuddhacāritra, the bhikṛṣideva, the bhikṣu Jñānaketu, the bhikṣu Brahmajaya, the bhikṣu Śāntamati,
and others such as these, numbering six thousand in all— each of whom had previously made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas,
deeply planted roots of goodness, possessed vast power of understanding, a clear and penetrating eye of faith, a broad and expansive mind, and profound insight.

The Buddha’s realm is the thorough realization of the fundamental nature of all phenomena; his constant delight in diligently seeking the merits of all Buddhas for the benefit of sentient beings is entirely accomplished through the teaching and transformation of Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, while walking along the path, observed the bhikṣus and addressed Sāgarabuddhi, saying: "Sāgarabuddhi, you should observe Mañjuśrī."
The body of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is pure and adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; no devas or humans can conceive of it—you should observe it.
The halo of Mañjuśrī is brilliantly penetrating, causing immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy—you should observe it.
The net of light adorning Mañjuśrī eliminates the immeasurable sufferings of sentient beings—you should observe it.
"O one who causes you distress, you should observe that this assembly of Mañjuśrī is entirely composed of bodhisattvas who have been sustained by their past roots of goodness;
you should observe that the path traversed by Mañjuśrī, eight paces to the left and right, is level and adorned; you should observe the place where Mañjuśrī dwells, ten..."
A constant site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) follows and revolves [with him]; you should observe the path traversed by Mañjuśrī, which is fully adorned with immeasurable merit.
On both sides, great hidden treasuries of various kinds of rare jewels emerge spontaneously;
you should observe the roots of goodness resulting from Mañjuśrī’s past offerings to the Buddhas.
Observe how Mañjuśrī causes clouds of ornaments to flow from between all the trees as a treasury of adornments;
observe how he pays homage and offers worship by bowing his head to the lords of all worlds who rain down clouds of offerings;
and observe how, when all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are about to preach the Dharma, they all emit light from the white tuft of hair between their eyebrows.
A light came and illuminated his body, entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra praised, extolled, revealed, and expounded for the bhikṣus how the youth Mañjuśrī was thus adorned with such immeasurable merits.
Having heard this teaching, those bhikṣus became pure in mind and attained faith and understanding.
With firm resolve, they could not contain their joy; their entire bodies leaped for joy, their physical forms became supple and soft, and their faculties were filled with delight.

All sorrow and suffering were eliminated, and all defilements and obstructions were utterly exhausted. They constantly beheld all Buddhas, deeply sought the True Dharma, and possessed the faculties of a Bodhisattva.

Attaining the power of a Bodhisattva, the great compassion and great vows all arose spontaneously within them. They entered the profound realm of the various perfections throughout the ten directions.
With the ocean of Buddhas ever appearing before him and having conceived deep faith and joy in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"I pray that the Great Master will lead us to the presence of that Sage.
Then Śāriputra immediately accompanied them to that place, and upon arrival, he said: "Virtuous ones, these bhikṣus wish to obtain..."

At that time, having beheld the youth Mañjuśrī surrounded by immeasurable sovereign bodhisattvas and his great assembly, he turned to look at the bhikṣus like an elephant king. Then the bhikṣus prostrated at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and spoke these words:
"We now behold, revere, and pay homage to him, as well as to all others who are present."
"By these roots of goodness, may the noble Mañjuśrī, the preceptor Śāriputra, and the World-Honored One Śākyamuni all bear witness:
just as you possess such a physical body, such a voice, such marks and signs, and such sovereign mastery, may I likewise fully attain them all. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family accomplishes ten kinds of practices for approaching the Mahāyāna, they will be able to swiftly enter the stage of the Tathāgata, let alone the stage of a bodhisattva. What are these ten? They are:
accumulating all roots of goodness with a mind free from weariness; beholding all Buddhas and serving and making offerings to them with a devoted heart..."
A mind free from weariness in seeking all Buddha-dharmas; a mind free from weariness in practicing all *pāramitās*;
a mind free from weariness in accomplishing all Bodhisattva samādhis; a mind free from weariness in sequentially entering all three periods of time;
a mind free from weariness in universally adorning and purifying the Buddha-fields of the ten directions; and a mind free from weariness in teaching and taming sentient beings.
The mind of all sentient beings is free from weariness; throughout all lands and for all eons, they accomplish the practices of a bodhisattva with a mind free from weariness.

For the sake of bringing even a single sentient being to maturity, they practice as many perfections as there are atoms in all Buddha-lands, thereby accomplishing all the powers of a Tathāgata. In this manner, they proceed until all beings have been brought to maturity.

If a bhikṣu, or a son or daughter of good family, accomplishes deep faith and gives rise to these ten kinds of tireless minds regarding the realm of sentient beings and the accomplishment of all the powers of a Tathāgata,
they will be able to nurture all roots of goodness, abandon all realms of birth and death, and transcend the lineage of all worldly beings.
Having avoided falling into the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one is born into the family of all Tathāgatas;
one gives rise to all Bodhisattva vows, trains in the cultivation of all Tathāgata merits, and accomplishes all Bodhisattva practices.
Attaining the powers of a Tathāgata, one subdues all Māras and heterodox teachers, is able to eliminate all afflictions, enters the stages of the Bodhisattvas, and draws near [to Buddhahood].
When the bhikṣus heard this Dharma at the stage of the Tathāgata-ground, they attained a samādhi called "Unobstructed Eye that Sees the Realm of All Buddhas.

Because they had attained this samādhi, they saw all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, as well as all their respective sites of enlightenment and assemblies; they also clearly saw those [realms] in the ten directions.
They also see all sentient beings in every realm of existence throughout the world;
they see all the various distinctions within the worlds of the ten directions; they see all the atoms within all those worlds;
and they also see all the palaces where the sentient beings in those worlds dwell, adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Hearing the various sounds and voices of those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as they expound all dharmas, he fully understands their phrasing and explanations;
he is also able to observe the faculties, minds, and desires of all sentient beings in those worlds;
he is also able to recollect the ten successive births before and after of all sentient beings in those worlds; and he is also able to recollect those worlds.

Within this world-system, they are also able to recollect the events of ten eons each in the past and future, as well as the ten past lives of those Tathāgatas, their ten attainments of perfect enlightenment,
their ten turnings of the wheel of Dharma, their ten kinds of supernormal powers, their ten kinds of teaching the Dharma, their ten kinds of instruction,
and their ten kinds of eloquence; furthermore, they immediately achieve ten thousand bodhicittas and ten thousand samādhis.

All one thousand *pāramitās* were completely purified; they attained the perfect radiance of great wisdom, the ten supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and dwelt in the bodhisattva mind—supple, subtle, firm, and immovable.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus to dwell in the conduct of Samantabhadra. Having dwelt in the conduct of Samantabhadra, they entered the ocean of great vows.
The ocean of great vows has already been accomplished; because the ocean of great vows has been accomplished, the mind is pure;

because the mind is pure, the body is pure; because the body is pure, the body is light and agile; because the body is pure, light, and agile, one attains great supernormal powers (abhijñā) without regression;
because one has attained these supernormal powers, one does not depart from the presence at the feet of Mañjuśrī.
He manifests his body before all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and fully accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas.
[Treatise] The first section begins from the passage "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, from the Well-Abiding Pavilion...
down to the beginning of the sixty-second fascicle: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī exhorted the bhikṣus."

Having already set forth the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this section of the sutra is titled "The Gateway of Entering the World from Its Very Foundation and Traveling Through It. Within this gateway, it is divided into two parts:
first, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta" down to "taking his leave and traveling south toward the human realm," there is [the first part].
The twenty and a half lines of sūtra clarify the departure from the Buddha toward the human realm by the Bodhisattvas traveling together and the assembly of constant attendants;
this is divided into two parts. From "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra...
down to "accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas," there are eighty-six and a half lines of sūtra clarifying the six [disciples] beginning with Śāriputra.
One thousand bhikṣus followed Mañjuśrī southward, and while on the road, they attained the realization of this Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle.

Regarding the sequential explanation of the meaning: first, from the beginning—"At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī emerged from the Sudharmā Pavilion"—this clarifies that he manifests the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) by means of his own *dharmakāya* as the pavilion.
Because they give rise to the wisdom of differentiation within [the realm of] the Middle to benefit sentient beings, they are called "Bodhisattvas of Immeasurable Shared Practice.

Because they accomplish the auxiliary paths and serve as wings and followers to jointly teach and transform sentient beings, they are the lords and companions of the ten thousand practices who constantly attend and guard them.
Regarding the phrase "all the Vajra Deities who serve as guardians," this refers to all the deities who act as attendants; among these deities, according to...
There are two meanings: first, the names are established based on the specific virtues of the various deities' conduct;
second, they are designated according to the distinctions in Mañjuśrī’s virtues and practices to signify his role as a retinue for protection and guardianship.
This section includes the bodhisattvas, the divine beings, and the thirty-two assemblies, along with the six thousand bhikṣus mentioned later.
The assembly considers these to be the forty-two kinds of expedient practices for accomplishing the great ocean of wisdom and liberation for sentient beings.
The first Vajra Deity is the universal radiance-wisdom within the Dharma-body;
because this wisdom manifests, it is called a "deity" (deva), and because it universally serves as the body of offerings for all sentient beings, the assembly of deities represents reverence.

The meaning is that because he has extensively manifested clouds of transformation bodies throughout the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas and guide sentient beings, he receives a body that is upright, well-proportioned, and adorned;
the foot-stepping spirits represent his tireless practice in diligently teaching and transforming sentient beings; and the wind spirits with mani-jewel crowns signify his pure and stainless wisdom.
It is able to establish the meaning of the teachings; like the wind, its essence can blow apart and disperse all things, yet it can also sustain, support, and cause all things to grow.
However, it has no inherent nature of its own, which is represented by the crown free from defilement.
Like the image of the Dharma-body, its wisdom is able to expound the net of teachings to disperse and destroy afflictions; as for purity and defilement, it itself has nothing to rely upon.
Because the trigram Xun represents wind and instruction, the remaining details are as fully set forth in the sutra itself.
As for the hungry ghosts removed by the King of Kumbhāṇḍas: they have large bags hanging down like winter melons and sit in a squatting posture.
They carry these on their shoulders; this imagery symbolizes the Dharma, representing how great compassion descends into the mundane world to bear the burden of sentient beings without complaint.
The weary King of the Mahoragas belongs to the class of great serpents that travel on their bellies;
taking this as a symbolic representation of the Dharma, his movement upon chest and belly signifies the meaning of reverence. He is the guardian deity of the saṃghārāma.

Other [deities] are to be understood according to their names, with their meanings expressed in accordance with this principle. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas emerge from their own abodes.
"Abiding" means following the faculties to engage with the mundane world. "Circumambulating the Tathāgata immeasurable times" refers to reverently following his conduct;
"circumambulation" proceeds from the south, through the east, to the north. These two—Śāriputra and the other six thousand bhikṣus—followed Mañjuśrī as they traveled south.
This section is further divided into seven parts: first, at that time, the Venerable Śāriputra... [text continues].

From "Ānanda, [Śāriputra]... down to "...all of whom were accomplished through the teaching and transformation by Mañjuśrī," there are thirteen lines and a half of scripture that clarify how Śāriputra and six thousand bhikṣus followed Mañjuśrī southward;
this section is divided into two parts. First, from "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra... down to "...the light from the ūrṇā-kośa mark."

Light comes to illuminate his body, entering from the crown of his head; there are sixteen lines of scripture clarifying how Śāriputra exhorted the bhikṣus to observe the ten kinds of auspicious signs adorning Mañjuśrī’s body as he traveled along the road, and how the road was divided into three parts.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had already descended to this place, whereupon these bhikṣus made their aspiration.
There are ten lines and a half of sutra text concerning the attainment of an audience [with Mañjuśrī], clarifying Śāriputra’s praise of Mañjuśrī’s ten immeasurable virtues.
All the assembly of bhikṣus wished to see Mañjuśrī, so Śāriputra made his request to Mañjuśrī in four sections. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva... [and so forth].

[The section] "May I fully attain all [perfections]" consists of six and a half lines of scripture clarifying the part where six thousand bhikṣus prostrate to Mañjuśrī, make their own great vows, and request the Buddha to bear witness; this is divided into five parts.
Then, from the passage where Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addresses the bhikṣus, down to "entering the stage of the Tathāgata," there are eighteen [sections].
In the *Caryā-sūtra*, it is clearly explained that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva taught the ten kinds of practices free from weariness to the bhikṣus;
by practicing these, one does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles but enters the stage of the Tathāgata. This section has six parts.

After the bhikṣus heard this Dharma, [the text] continues down to the point where they abide in the bodhicitta with firm and unshakable resolve; there are sixteen lines of the sūtra clarifying these six points.

When the thousand bhikṣus heard Mañjuśrī’s exposition of the Dharma, they attained the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Eye and each obtained ten gates of liberation regarding the ten dharmas within all phenomena. [The text] is divided into seven parts.
At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had exhorted the bhikṣus, down to the end of the fascicle, there are six lines of scripture in which Mañjuśrī speaks again.

Exhorting the bhikṣus to abide in the practices of Samantabhadra, they immediately attained non-separation from the feet of Mañjuśrī and manifested themselves before the Buddhas of the ten directions, fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas. Regarding the analysis of the text and its meaning according to the divisions:
six thousand bhikṣus manifested their faith and entered the stages (*bhūmi*), because they possessed the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), and the ten practices (*caryā*).
Because the ten dedications, the ten stages, and the path of the eleventh stage are all attained simultaneously, it is said that six thousand [beings] surround him from before and behind.
With Śāriputra as the leader and the rest as his companions, this illustrates the leader and companions proceeding together, clearly demonstrating the advancement toward seeking the True Dharma.
"Emerging from one's own dwelling place" means emerging from the state of the śrāvakas and those of provisional capacity.

Because he had seen [the Buddha] and sought the Great Bodhi of the Dharma-realm, he circumambulated the Buddha three times. Circumambulating the Buddha three times was in accordance with the Buddha’s true teaching;

all three circumambulations were performed by keeping the right side toward him. Starting from the south, one proceeds east, then north, then west, and finally returns to the west—these three circuits constitute the ritual of circumambulation by the right.
Nowadays, people instead walk counter-clockwise (leftward); [this text describes] six thousand such [circuits].
This bhikṣu Śāriputra has been a fellow resident in the monastic life for no long time, yet he is not a mere arhat;
he possesses the seeds from previous lives, making it easy for him to arouse the mind [for awakening]. As the Sūtra says:

"Six thousand bhikṣus have all made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, deeply planting roots of goodness, possessing vast power of understanding, and having clear and penetrating faculties of faith. This clarifies that they had previously planted the seeds of faith.
Śāriputra, having now planted the seeds of faith, has matured; he exhorts the bhikṣus to contemplate the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī’s circle of merit, which is brilliantly penetrating.
This is the constant radiance of a pure mind, a net of light that causes all who see it to rejoice.
This is the perfection of the Dharma-net, clarifying the light of his teachings as they adorn his body for all who behold him.
Because he has extinguished suffering, the eight paces traveled by Mañjuśrī on his left and right are level and adorned;

this clarifies that his body and mind are always accompanied by the Eightfold Noble Path. That the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) pervade all ten directions indicates that his transformative practice is constantly fulfilling the ten directions.
When the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the Dharma, they emit light from between their eyebrows.

Regarding "consecrating the crown of Mañjuśrī," this clarifies that Mañjuśrī is the crown of the dharmakāya— the signless wisdom— in which the Buddhas of the ten directions first receive their initial resolve for enlightenment.
Since all Buddhas, upon their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, enter this wisdom and are thereby born into the Buddha-family,
all sentient beings who first generate the bodhicitta likewise do so by means of this dharmakāya.
The essence of signless wisdom is possessed by all sentient beings from the very beginning;
yet it can only be clearly manifested through the skillful means of samādhi. Thus, the trees are adorned with jewels, arising as the fruit of the retribution for past practices.
When the six thousand bhikṣus observed Mañjuśrī and the ten kinds of tireless dharmas they heard, they immediately attained [the realization of] non-existence.
Regarding the Samādhi of Obstructing the Eye: one attains the bright and pure eye of signless wisdom within the Dharma-body;

because grasping has perished and views have subsided, the eye of wisdom is perfectly penetrating—it is not the fleshly eye. Thus, the five views, such as the view of a self and extremes, vanish, and the Dharma becomes self-evident.

That is to say, when obstructions are exhausted throughout the ten directions, at the very beginning, within each and every phenomenon, one clarifies ten dharmas to manifest the power of this samādhi.
At the beginning of its inception, it clarifies the subsequent exhortation to the vows and practices of Samantabhadra, whereby all vidyās are fully realized.

This concludes the above section on the six thousand bhikṣus who resolved their minds [on enlightenment]. The following section clarifies those who have attained awakening and, having become conditions for the benefit of beings—such as Śāriputra—manifest as śrāvakas;
this has already been described above. The remaining meanings herein can be understood accordingly.
The meaning is as provided in the text itself.
