Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Four: Entering the Dharma Realm.
[Sūtra] At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
he gradually traveled south through the human realms until he reached the east of the City of Bliss (*Sukhāvatī-pura*).
There he stayed within the Śāla grove of the Banner of Adornment (*Vyūha-dhvaja*), a great reliquary stūpa where former Buddhas had once dwelt to teach and transform sentient beings.
This place is also where, in times past, the World-Honored One practiced the bodhisattva path and was able to relinquish immeasurable things that are difficult to give up;
for this reason, the fame of this grove is heard throughout immeasurable buddha-fields.
This place is constantly frequented by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
When people were making offerings, Mañjuśrī, together with his retinue, arrived at this place;
he immediately preached the *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm* there, with one hundred trillion nayutas of sūtras as its retinue.
While he was preaching this sūtra, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nāgas within the great ocean.
Having heard this Dharma, they developed a profound weariness with the dragon realm and sought the path of the Buddha;
they all cast off their dragon bodies and were reborn among gods and humans. Furthermore, ten thousand dragons attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings were each brought to discipline within the three vehicles. This was the occasion at the City of Blessings.
People heard that the youth Mañjuśrī was at the Great Stūpa in the Śāla Grove of the Adorned Banner.
[Treatise] The second stage of the gradual journey southward involved traveling through the human realm until reaching the east of the City of Bliss;

this is where Mañjuśrī entered the secular world to preach the *Sūtra on the Gate of Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm*, located specifically to the east of the City of Bliss in the Śāla Grove.

The Śāla Grove is the location of the Great Stūpa. Furthermore, this section—from "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus" down to "the location of the Great Stūpa in the Śāla Grove"—consists of fifteen and a half lines of scripture, which is further divided into two parts:
first, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva" down to "people."

Regarding the offerings made by non-humans, there are seven lines and a half of explicit text in the sutra concerning Mañjuśrī’s journey to the human realm to reach those who are fit vessels for his transformative influence; in two sections, Mañjuśrī, together with his retinue,
descends as far as the great stūpa, as detailed in eight lines of text where Mañjuśrī expounds the Universal [Dharma].
The Section on Gaining Benefit by Hearing the Dharma through the *Dharmadhātu-prakāśa-sūtra* Gate.
At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve upon bodhicitta, he summarized the preceding teachings and gradually traveled south, passing through the human world.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva guides others toward illumination by using separation as the means to illumination; "passing through the human world" refers to this process.
It clarifies that the great compassion of the Bodhisattva acts as an uninvited friend, guiding and transforming beings according to their faculties. As for the name "City of Blessings" (Puṇyavatī):
it is established based on the fact that many people there cultivate merit; it is also named so because it is the place where the Noble One resides, serving as a banner of merit and virtue.
Regarding the term "Banner," there are two meanings: first, that past Buddhas once practiced the difficult act of renunciation at this very site.

It is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*) because it destroys that which is clung to. Second, this place is adorned with ancient Buddha-stūpas and shrines, as well as forests that are dense, towering, and sublime;
because these great stūpas and shrines are renowned throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and their fame is heard afar, they are called "great.
Furthermore, from the perspective of the Dharma-realm gate, there is no seeing of inside, outside, or middle, and thus it is called "nameless."
Regarding its greatness: because the physical image of the Honored One is enshrined within it, it cannot be destroyed;
thus it is called a *stūpa* (塔) or a temple (*caitya*), and is also called a banner (*dhvaja*).

A Brahmin monk said that because one can hear the drum beaten at the southern side of this stūpa-temple but not from the northern side, it is known as "Great" (*Mahā*) in the world. *Sāla* means "towering"; [it is frequented by] devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.

Having finished the *vyākaraṇa*, the following clarifies that Mañjuśrī and his retinue—consisting of six thousand assemblies of Bodhisattvas, devas, and humans who are constantly offered worship by the eight classes of beings, including gods and nāgas—expound the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*.
This is because it is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is luminously penetrating, all-pervasive, and conforms to the faculties [of beings] everywhere. (100)
"Ten million billion nayutas" refers here to the *gāthā* (verses); its general meaning is that the *sūtra* is an "unspeakable" [number], which serves as its retinue.
This clarifies that the wisdom of differentiation (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) is all-pervasive, bestowing benefit according to the faculties [of beings].

*Sūtra* is translated here as "long prose" (*dīrgha-pada*). When this sūtra was being preached, [the passage] beginning with "in the great ocean" below clarifies that immeasurable nāgas heard the Dharma and were all... [enlightened].
Having cast off their dragon bodies, ten thousand dragons were born among gods and humans;
they gave rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta and attained non-retrogression, while countless sentient beings were each tamed within the three vehicles.

Having clearly understood the Dharma-gate of attaining one’s own root-nature according to the wisdom that follows distinctions based on individual faculties, the above clarifies the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*.
The gate of providing relief and benefit according to their faculties is fully detailed in the sutra itself.
[Sutra]: A great assembly of immeasurable numbers came out from the city to visit him.
At that time, there was an upāsaka named Mahāmati who was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred upāsakas, namely the upāsaka Sudatta and others.
The upāsaka Sudatta, the upāsaka Puṇyaraśmi, the upāsaka Yaśas, the upāsaka Yaśodatta, the upāsaka Candraprabha, the upāsaka Sumati, the upāsaka Mahāmati,
the upāsaka Bhadrapāla, and the upāsaka Bhadraśreṣṭhin— these five hundred upāsakas together came to visit him.
The youth Mañjuśrī prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her three times to the right, and withdrew to sit to one side.

There were also five hundred upāsikās, namely: the upāsikā Mahāmati, the upāsikā Suprabhā, the upāsikā Suvapuṣā, the upāsikā Ruciragātrā, the upāsikā Bhadrā, the upāsikā Bhadraguṇā, and the upāsikā Bhadraprabhā.
The upāsikā Dhvajaprabhā, the upāsikā Guṇaprabhā, the upāsikā Sunetra,
and five hundred other such upāsikās came to the place where the youth Mañjuśrī was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
and withdrew to sit on one side. There were also five hundred youths, namely the youth Sudhana and...
The youth Cāritramati, the youth Śīlamati, the youth Vinayamati, the youth Parākramamati, the youth Sumati, the youth Prajñāmati,
the youth Bodhimati, the youth Sunayanamati, the youth Subāhumati, and the youth Suprabhamati—
these five hundred youths approached the place where the youth Mañjuśrī was, prostrated themselves before him, and...
Having circumambulated him three times to the right, they withdrew and sat to one side. There were also five hundred young maidens, namely:

the maiden Bhadrikā, the maiden Mahāprājñā, the maiden Kalyāṇakīrti, the maiden Surūpā, the maiden Dṛḍhamati, the maiden Kalyāṇaguṇā, the maiden Guṇavatī, the maiden Brahmadattā, the maiden Guṇaprabhā, and the maiden Suprabhā.
In this manner, five hundred maidens came to the place where the youth Mañjuśrī was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
and withdrew to sit on one side. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, knowing that the people of Puṇyavatī had all assembled,
manifested a body of sovereign power according to their inclinations, its majestic radiance so brilliant that it eclipsed the entire multitude.
By means of sovereign great kindness, he caused him to be cooled; by means of sovereign great compassion, he gave rise to the mind to preach the Dharma;
by means of sovereign wisdom, he knew the inclinations of his mind; and by means of vast eloquence, he was about to preach the Dharma for him.
Furthermore, at that time, he observed the causes and conditions by which Sudhana received his name, knowing that when this youth first entered the womb...
Within his residence, seven-storied towers made of the seven precious gems spontaneously appeared;

beneath these towers were seven hidden treasuries, and upon the ground above these treasuries, the earth split open of its own accord, producing sprouts of the seven precious gems—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate.
After the youth Sudhana had been in the womb for ten months, he was subsequently born with a physical form...
Its parts were perfectly proportioned and complete; its seven great treasuries, each measuring seven cubits in length, breadth, and height, emerged from the earth, radiating brilliant light.
Furthermore, within the house, five hundred precious vessels appeared spontaneously, naturally filled with various items:
namely, diamond vessels containing all kinds of incense, and within those incense vessels...
Various garments were placed in beautiful jade vessels; various foods and drinks of superior flavor were filled in mani-vessels;
various extraordinary and precious jewels were filled in gold vessels; silver was filled in silver vessels; gold and silver were filled in gold and silver vessels;
lapis lazuli and mani-jewels were filled in crystal vessels; and mother-of-pearl was filled in mother-of-pearl vessels.
Vessels made of *vaidūrya* and agate appeared spontaneously, filled to the brim with pearls; vessels made of pearls appeared, filled to the brim with agate;
vessels made of *agnimaṇi* appeared, filled to the brim with *udakamaṇi*; and vessels made of *udakamaṇi* appeared, filled to the brim with *agnimaṇi*.
Such five hundred precious vessels as these appeared naturally, and there fell a rain of various jewels and all manner of wealth.
Because he caused all the treasuries to be completely filled, his parents, kinsmen, and skilled physiognomists together named this boy Sudhana (Good Wealth).
Furthermore, it was known that this youth had already made offerings to past Buddhas,
deeply planted roots of goodness, possessed vast faith and understanding, and always delighted in drawing near to spiritual friends through the actions of his body, speech, and mind.
Free from all faults, they purify the bodhisattva path and seek omniscience to become vessels for the Buddha-dharma;
their minds are as pure as space, dedicating themselves toward enlightenment without any obstruction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, having thus observed the youth Sudhana, comforted and instructed him, and expounded for him the teachings of all Buddhas.
The Dharma refers to the teaching on the dharma accumulated by all Buddhas; the teaching on the continuity of all Buddhas; the teaching on the sequence of all Buddhas;
the teaching on the purity of the assemblies of all Buddhas; the teaching on the turning of the wheel of Dharma and the guidance of all Buddhas;
the teaching on the physical marks and signs of the form bodies of all Buddhas; and the teaching on the accomplishment of the dharma bodies of all Buddhas.
He taught the Dharma of the eloquence and speech of all Buddhas, the Dharma of the radiance and illumination of all Buddhas,
and the Dharma of the equality and non-duality of all Buddhas. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī,
having taught this Dharma to the youth Sudhana and the great assembly, earnestly exhorted and encouraged them, increasing their spiritual power and causing them to rejoice.
Having generated the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and caused [beings] to recollect their past roots of goodness,
and having performed these deeds, he then preached the Dharma to sentient beings at that very spot according to their needs before departing.
At that time, the youth Sudhana heard from Mañjuśrī such various merits of the Buddha as these.
With a mind diligently seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he followed Mañjuśrī and spoke these verses:
The three realms of existence are its city walls; Pride and arrogance are its ramparts; The various destinies are its gates.
With the waters of craving as its moat, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, the fire of greed and hatred blazing fiercely, Māra acts as its sovereign. The childish rely upon it for their dwelling;
with craving as its fetters and deceitful guile as its reins, their eyes obscured by doubt, they enter upon various false paths.
Because of stinginess, envy, and arrogance, one enters the three evil realms; or else, falling into the various states of existence, one suffers the pains of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The sun of wondrous wisdom is pure, and the wheel of perfect great compassion can dry up the ocean of afflictions.
I pray that you will deign to look upon me with a moment’s observation—O moon of wondrous wisdom, pure and serene.
Great Compassionate One, stainless wheel, who bestows peace upon all; May you deign to look upon me, Sovereign of the entire realm of phenomena.
With the Jewel of Dharma as your guide, you traverse the sky without obstruction;
May you deign to instruct me, Great Caravan Leader of merit and wisdom, Who courageously seeks awakening.
Universally benefiting all living beings, I pray you will grant me your protection.
Clad in the armor of patience, holding the sword of wisdom in hand, You freely subdue the armies of Māra; I pray you will pull me out and rescue me.
Dwelling upon the summit of the Sumeru of Dharma, The Maiden of Samādhi constantly attends you in reverence, While the Asuras of delusion are extinguished.
O Śakra, may you look upon me—this fool dwelling in the three realms of existence.
O Benevolent One, you who have fully tamed the causes of delusion, karma, and the destinies of rebirth, show me the path like a lamp.
May I abandon all evil realms and follow the pure paths of virtue; O You who transcend all worlds, reveal to me the gate of liberation.
The world clings to inversions, conceiving notions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity; with the eye of wisdom, you are able to leave them all behind.

O you who have attained liberation from the self, who well know the paths of error and correctness, whose discerning mind is without fear, and who have reached definitive certainty— show me the path to Bodhi, and let me abide in the ground of the Buddha’s right view.
The Buddha is a tree of merit, long-standing; He rains down the lotus of the Buddha’s sublime Dharma. To me he shows the path to Bodhi.
Buddhas of the past, future, and present Pervade every place without exception. Like the sun appearing in the world, Tell me the way for my sake.
You well know all karmic actions And have deeply penetrated the practices of all vehicles.

The person of wisdom and resolve shows me the Mahāyāna: May its wheels be great compassion, its hub the vow, its axle faith, and its pins patience; Adorned with the jewels of merit, may I be mounted upon this vehicle.
With the vast casket of dhāraṇī, the canopy adorned by loving-kindness, And the bells of eloquence ringing out their sound—may I be borne by this.
May I mount this vehicle: Pure conduct as its seat-cushion, Samādhi as its maidservants, The Dharma drum vibrating with wondrous sound— I pray you grant me this vehicle.
The four means of attraction, an inexhaustible treasury, Adorned with the jewels of merit, Shame and remorse as its reins and harness— I pray you grant me this vehicle.
Constantly turning the wheel of giving, Perpetually anointing oneself with the fragrance of pure precepts, Adorned firmly with patience—may you cause me to mount this vehicle;
With dhyāna and samādhi as its boxwood seat, And wisdom and skillful means as its yoke, taming those who do not regress— May you cause me to mount this vehicle; The great vow is its pure wheel.
The power of firm dhāraṇī, accomplished through wisdom, Causes me to mount this vehicle, whose universal practice is thoroughly refined;
With compassion as its slow-turning wheels, it moves toward all things without fear.
May I mount this vehicle, Firm as a diamond and skillful like an illusion.
Completely unobstructed, may I be carried by this vehicle; vast and utterly pure, it universally bestows happiness upon all sentient beings.
Equal to space and the dharma-realm, may I be carried by this vehicle to purify the wheel of karma and afflictions, sever the suffering of saṃsāra, and destroy Māras and non-Buddhists.
May I be borne upon this vehicle, with wisdom filling the ten directions;
may its adornments pervade the entire Dharma-realm, universally satisfying the vows for all sentient beings.
May I be borne upon this vehicle, pure as space, with attachment and views entirely extinguished; may I benefit all multitudes. May I be borne upon this vehicle.
May the power of my vows proceed with swiftness, And may my mind dwell in the security of meditative concentration.
May I carry all sentient beings upon this vehicle, Like the earth, which does not waver, And like water, which universally benefits;
Thus carrying all beings, May I carry them upon this vehicle, The wheel of the four means of attraction, perfectly fulfilled.
Holder of the pure light, such a sun of wisdom, I pray you show me so that I may see you—
you who have already entered the station of the Dharma King, who have already donned the crown of the Wisdom King, and who have already bound the silken ribbon of the sublime Dharma;
may you look upon me with compassion.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned to look at Sudhana like an elephant king and spoke these words to him:

"Excellent, excellent, noble son! You have already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and now wish to draw near to various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to inquire about the conduct of bodhisattvas and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva, noble son."
"Approaching and making offerings to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) is the primary causal condition for possessing all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
Therefore, do not give rise to weariness or aversion toward this. Sudhana said: "I pray that the Noble One will explain to me extensively:
how should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct? How should a bodhisattva cultivate the bodhisattva conduct? How should a bodhisattva proceed toward the bodhisattva conduct?"
How should one practice the bodhisattva conduct? How should one purify the bodhisattva conduct? How should one enter the bodhisattva conduct?
How should one accomplish the bodhisattva conduct? How should one accord with the bodhisattva conduct?
How should one recollect the bodhisattva conduct? How should one expand the bodhisattva conduct? How should one [fulfill] the conduct of Samantabhadra?
"May you swiftly attain full perfection. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke these verses to the youth Sudhana:
"Excellent, O treasury of merit! That you have come to my presence And given rise to a heart of great compassion."
Diligently seeking supreme enlightenment, having already made vast vows,
To eliminate the suffering of sentient beings for the sake of all worlds, One practices the bodhisattva path.
If there are bodhisattvas who do not weary of the sufferings of birth and death, They will possess the path of Samantabhadra, Which none can ever destroy.
O you of auspicious light and auspicious power, O abode of merit and ocean of pure merit!
May you cultivate the universal vow for the sake of all sentient beings. You behold the boundless limits;
you hear the Dharma from all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, upholding it without forgetfulness. Within the realms of the ten directions...
Universally beholding immeasurable Buddhas, you have accomplished an ocean of all vows;
Fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva, you have skillfully entered the ocean of expedient means;

Abiding securely in the Bodhi of the Buddhas, you are able to follow and learn from the Teachers, destined to attain all-encompassing wisdom. You pervade all lands throughout kalpas as numerous as atoms.
You have practiced the conduct of Samantabhadra And accomplished the path to enlightenment.
Throughout immeasurable lands and boundless oceans of kalpas, You have practiced the conduct of Samantabhadra And brought all great vows to fulfillment.
These immeasurable sentient beings, Hearing of your vows, rejoice And all resolve their minds upon Bodhi.
"May I learn the vehicle of Samantabhadra.
At that time, having spoken these verses, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the youth Sudhana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! You have already resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek awakening."
O son of good family who practices the bodhisattva path, if there are sentient beings who are able to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this matter is difficult;
yet once they have resolved their minds, to seek the bodhisattva practice is twice as difficult.

Son of good family, if you wish to accomplish the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), you should resolutely seek a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Son of good family, [you must] seek...
Do not give rise to weariness toward spiritual friends; do not give rise to complacency regarding spiritual friends.
You should comply with all the instructions of spiritual friends. Regarding the skillful means of spiritual friends, do not look for faults.
Son of good family, to the south of here there is a land called Supriya. In that land, there is a mountain named...
On that mountain of Wondrous Peak, there is a bhikṣu named Meghaśrī. You should go to him and ask:
"How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct? How does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva conduct? And so on, until:
"How does a bodhisattva swiftly attain the full perfection of the conduct of Samantabhadra? The bhikṣu Meghaśrī shall explain this for you.
[Treatise] Third: The Section on Distinguishing the Faculties and Dharmas to Accomplish Practice.

From the departure of the immeasurable multitude from the city until the end of the sutra, this section describes how Mañjuśrī observes Sudhana and his followers, and how they travel south to Mount Megha-dhvaja, proceeding sequentially to seek out the fifty-three spiritual friends for the sake of goodness.

Regarding the section on the "Gate of Progressing in Practice through the Cause and Effect of the Five Stages of Knowledge," it is stated that this is the "Gate of Discerning the Faculties and Dharmas to Accomplish Practice" so that future generations may emulate it and perfect their conduct. Within this segment, it is further divided into two parts:
the first begins from "A great assembly of immeasurable numbers emerged from the city" and extends down to "At that time, Mañjuśrī... [and so forth].
The second section, comprising ninety-four and a half lines of scripture, clarifies how Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turns like an elephant king;

it describes how the fourfold assembly gathered at Puṇyavatī City, and how Mañjuśrī, according to their various inclinations and requests, taught them the Dharma so that they might attain refreshing clarity.
It further distinguishes the contemplation of Sudhana’s investigation of cause and effect, exhorting him to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

At that time, Mañjuśrī turned like an elephant king; from this point until the end of the sutra is titled "Knowing the Faculties and Bestowing the Dharma to Enable Practice," which gives rise to the gate for later students.
Within the first section from the beginning, the ninety-four and a half lines of scripture are divided into six parts: first, the immeasurable great assembly emerges from the city.
From "They came to where he was" down to "the five hundred maidens," there are twenty-one lines and a half of scripture;

this constitutes the second section, "The Gathering of the Great Assembly. From "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to "dedicating [merit] toward bodhi without obstruction," there are twenty-five lines of scripture, which clearly describe the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
The section on observing the reasons for Sudhana’s name and praising his past roots of goodness and their fruition in this present life is divided into three parts.
At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had thus observed the youth Sudhana—
beginning from the passage below [the previous section] down to the six and a half lines of scripture stating that "all Buddhas possess the non-dual Dharma"— Mañjuśrī [spoke].
The section on knowing Sudhana’s faculties and preaching the Dharma for him is divided into four parts.

First, from "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī" down to "and then departed," there are four and a half lines of sūtra text clarifying the section where Mañjuśrī, having preached the Dharma for Sudhana and the great assembly, departs. Fifth, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" onwards...

Upon arriving, he spoke in verse; two and a half lines of scripture clarify that after Sudhana had heard the Dharma and given rise to faith, he diligently sought unsurpassed bodhi and addressed Mañjuśrī in verse to express his own lamentation regarding the suffering wheel of the three realms of existence and to request instruction on the Dharma.
This section consists of six parts; within the verses, thirty-four lines of verse clarify Sudhana’s own [lamentation].
"Alas, the root of suffering"—this section on requesting the Dharma for the benefit of oneself and others consists of thirty-four verses.
Of these, the first four verses express lamentation over the causes of the suffering of birth and death;
the remaining thirty verses are the praise of the virtues of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the request for the Dharma-gate. As for the explanation of the meaning according to the text:
As in the first section, although the *Sūtra on the Gathering of the Fourfold Assembly* states that "immeasurable great assemblies" emerged from the city,

when their number is specified, it mentions only five hundred; this clarifies that the count is established according to those capable of generating the bodhicitta through the five stages and ten pāramitās,
rather than being calculated by the number of individuals, because within the practice of the five stages...
The ten pāramitās mutually possess one hundred aspects, because within each one there are ten.
For example, when the dāna-pāramitā is primary, the other nine are its companions; when the śīla-pāramitā is primary, the other nine are its companions;
when the kṣānti-pāramitā is primary, the other nine are its companions; and all others follow this pattern. Thus, these one hundred pāramitās—within [each]...
The ten abodes, ten practices, ten dedications, ten stages, and the eleventh stage of ascending progress—

these are established as five hundred distinct names according to the varying degrees of depth in treating the habitual tendencies of delusions during the path of vision and subsequent practice. However,

if one considers the conduct of Samantabhadra as encompassing the entirety of the Dharma-realm within the inexhaustible ocean of lands, then there are unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands, as numerous as atoms.
Regarding the various *pāramitās*, for now we shall briefly consider that within each of the five stages there are one hundred *pāramitās*, totaling five hundred per stage;
as previously mentioned, the ten thousand nāgas who all resolved upon *bodhicitta* clarify the perfection of the ten thousand practices (*daśasahasra-caryā*).
"Sudatta" means "One Who Gives Generously"; "Anāthapiṇḍada" is also called "The Provider for the Destitute."
Vasudatta means "Bestower of Wealth" in this language, and is also called "One Who Practices Virtuous Giving.
Thus, these four assemblies, together with ten thousand nāgas, gave rise to the bodhicitta. The total number of assemblies was five:
the assembly of nāgas, the five hundred upāsakas, and the five hundred upāsikās—all of whom were householders with pure and profound faith. [The assembly of] youths...

Sons and daughters who are all under twenty years of age, whose years have not yet reached the prime of manhood (*wèiguān*), and who are untainted by worldly desires—such men and women of pure faith—are called *tóngzǐ* (male novices) and *tóngnǚ* (female novices).
Those of tender age who have newly initiated their original resolve to enter the stream of the Dharma and receive its teachings are called *tóngzǐ* and *tóngnǚ*.
"Tóng" (child) refers to one who has just begun to receive instruction; it is established as "tóng" based on their residence in the village and their age.
Though she had not lived long, she established her will and virtue among the villagers; she was known as "Child" (Tongzi), yet in years she was senior to others.
Because she possessed pure and faithful confidence, she was simply called a "Pure Faith Layman" (Qingxinshi) or "Pure Faith Laywoman" (Qingxinnu). Those listed above are merely followers of names;
the meaning lies in the virtues they have cultivated. Alternatively, names may be established based on physical appearance, such as the "Laywoman of Great Wisdom" (Dazhi Jushi Nu).

The father’s title was Jñānaguṇa; other names should be understood by analogy with this. The Sūtra says, "His majestic light blazes forth," which clarifies that Mañjuśrī’s physical radiance is so brilliant and intense that it outshines the entire assembly. This is as described when Mañjuśrī examined the name and circumstances of Sudhana:
at the very moment of his initial entry into the womb, seven [treasures] spontaneously appeared within his residence.
As for the "Jewel Pavilion," this refers to the fruit realized from causes; it cannot arise as a retribution without a cause.

It clarifies that the faith of previous lives—the ability to believe that one's own mind is fully endowed with the pure and stainless *dharmakāya*, as well as the universally radiant wisdom that abides nowhere—serves as the seed of faith, which is termed the "womb. This is like the "Universal Radiance" within the stage of faith.
The Venerable One says that the "Golden World" refers to the pure, stainless *dharmakāya* of the Wisdom of Immovability;
the "Universal Radiance Wisdom" is titled the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom because its fundamental nature is inherently incapable of being moved.
That which is currently called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) was, in past lives, the conviction in this very mind as being non-existent.
The clarity and the ignorance of all sentient beings together constitute the seed of the pure wisdom of the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas.
This seed of faith is called the "womb" (garbha). Born from this womb of faith within the world, one obtains the ten precious pavilions as a karmic reward.
This womb of faith is accomplished through the power of contemplative observation by means of wisdom.
The seven treasures and the seven hidden treasuries correspond respectively to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhipākṣikadharma*);
the subsequent instances of the number seven follow this same pattern. Dwelling in the womb for ten months signifies practicing the ten *pāramitās* within the stage of faith;
the completion of the worldly period signifies the birth of supramundane wisdom. That his physical form and limbs were perfectly proportioned signifies...
Because it is accomplished through the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path, there are naturally five hundred precious vessels within the dwelling,
filled spontaneously with all manner of various objects. Within these precious vessels,

the intermingling reflections that adorn them clarify the five stages of practice and the ten *pāramitās* within the seeds of faith planted in previous lives regarding the Buddha’s causes and effects.

The five hundred practices, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—whether identical or distinct—the beginning and end of the myriad practices, and cause and effect, are all entirely contained within that which is attained through faith.

This is what is realized in this present life. By means of this faith, one can once again give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) without departing from the Dharma-gate of the "One Hundred and Ten Cities" in a single lifetime; it is instantaneously and completely sealed within the locus of faith, thereby perfecting the hundred [virtues].
The tenfold Dharma-gate does not depart from the Śāla grove, yet his body travels everywhere through all lands;

this is solely because the dust contains the nature of the Dharma-realm, which is naturally so, and because wisdom encompasses the three periods of time—past, present, and future—in a single thought-moment.

This is explained according to the actual reality of the Dharma-realm and does not rely on the false imaginings of ordinary sentiment; other meanings will be clarified below as they correspond to the text.
Having explained the names by way of their causes, the section on explaining the causes by way of their retributions is concluded. The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, this youth has already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, deeply planted roots of goodness, and possesses vast faith and understanding.

This clarifies that the seeds of faith planted in previous lives have now reached full maturity in this life. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva—namely, the one who is the accumulation of all Buddhas—[spoke].

The Dharma clarifies the accumulation of the ten *pāramitās*, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the stages of application (*prayoga*) of the five paths, and the one hundred and ten city-like dharma-gates.
Regarding these one hundred and ten city-like dharma-gates, within the five paths there are fifty points of cause and effect for cultivation. That is to say:
Just as in the previous ten abodes, the ten Bodhisattvas of Wisdom are identical to the ten Buddhas of the fruition stage who share the name "Moon";
so too, in these ten practices, there are the ten Forest Bodhisattvas and the ten Eye Buddhas;
in the ten dedications, there are the ten Banner Bodhisattvas and the ten Wondrous Buddhas; and likewise for the ten stages and the eleventh stage, all are based upon this.
Within the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the causes and fruits of the Bodhisattva and the Buddha constitute these five stages.
Each of these fifty layers of cause and fruit further possesses the causes and fruits of progressive cultivation, thus dividing into one hundred.

These do not depart from the fundamental essence of the *dharmadhātu*, which is the constant reality of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; therein, the ten *pāramitās* constitute one hundred and ten. This begins from the first stage, the ten abodes (*vihāra*).
Within this, one manifests the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* through the *upāya-samādhi*, mounts the vehicle of the *dharmadhātu*, and practices the conduct of Samantabhadra.
By means of these, one establishes the sequential stages for treating the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of delusion;
this constitutes the tenth stage of ascending and descending through the hundredfold causes and effects for the purpose of treating the habitual tendencies of delusion.
The cause and effect of this pāramitā—namely, wisdom, compassion, and vows—is the ever-present conduct of Samantabhadra within the essence of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
It serves as the track for all who have resolved to attain bodhicitta to tread upon;
therefore, it is called the "Tathāgata Vehicle," by which one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment, for from the very first resolution of the mind, one mounts the dharma-realm.

Because Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the gates of essence and function, principle and wisdom, and great compassionate vows and practices, they constitute the very essence and function of the fundamental site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The following fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) encountered by Sudhana represent the practical manifestations (*ākāra*) of the preceding five stages.

It is clarified that while the preceding five stages only spoke of their respective dharmas, there was a fear that one might become confused regarding their actual practice; therefore, [the subsequent section] follows.
This Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, wishing to cause Sudhana to arouse the manner of seeking the Dharma,
again clarifies the modes of practice within the five stages of the bodhisattva path so that future learners may emulate them; thus,
he establishes these fifty-three individuals as a hundred and ten layers of the gates of cause and effect, thereby elucidating the Dharma.
Within the essence of the *dhātu*, Mañjuśrī is established as the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Dharmakāya Buddha, and Samantabhadra as the wisdom of differentiation (*prabheda-jñāna*).
Maitreya Buddha is the fruit of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) within this principle of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Through these three dharmas, the gate of the sovereign and unimpeded functioning of the single essence of the *dharmadhātu* is formed, pervading the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) and the five [wisdoms].
Ten bodhisattvas serve as the causes and effects, just as previously described; within the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, the ten *pāramitās* constitute the practice to be mounted.
As one advances through the five stages (*pañca-vastu*), there are fifty successive layers of *pāramitās*, each of which possesses both cause and effect.
Thus, within each of these fifty spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), there are two sets of fifty.
Within this, there are one hundred methods for penetrating the Dharma-realm; therein, the ten *pāramitās* are fundamentally and eternally practiced as one hundred and ten.
Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya—the fruit of Buddhahood—these three dharmas are, in fact, but a single Dharma-realm.
This is the gate of sovereign mastery in the great function of the fruition of non-effort, which serves solely to clarify the cause-and-effect relationship for all Bodhisattvas of superior progress.
The merit of supreme advancement is such that it inherently lacks cause and effect;
it is like a sovereign who possesses no formal ranks, yet through his majestic power and sovereign authority, he establishes ranks for all his officials according to their respective merits.
Question: For what reason is Maitreya Buddha taken here as the fruit of Buddhahood, rather than Vairocana?
The Tathāgata Vairocana provides the answer regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, clarifying that Vairocana is the fruit already realized, while Maitreya is the future fruit of Buddhahood.

This is because they are identical in their accordant realization; as the Buddha Vairocana first generated the bodhicitta in a single thought-moment, he attained the future fruit of Maitreya Buddha, and thus they are in perfect correspondence.
Within the Maitreya Pavilion, the time-intervals and days and months of the three periods of time are all unified as one;
thus, it is clarified that by means of the seal of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna-mudrā*), the three periods—past, present, and future—are marked as being without before or after. As the Sūtra says:
"The accumulated Dharma explains the continuous Dharma of all Buddhas, even unto the sequential Dharma of all Buddhas"—all of which has been explained above.
The assembly of all Buddhas is purified by the light of the Dharma, for all the assemblies of the Buddhas are of one and the same purity;
thus, the bodies, lands, and assemblies do not obstruct one another, but rather interpenetrate one another in infinite layers.
As for the thirty-four verses that follow, the first four verses are a self-praise [by the author].
"Birth and death proceed from the three realms of existence as their primary cause; the various sufferings of saṃsāra—birth, old age, and so forth—ceaselessly arise.
The following thirty verses clarify Sudhana’s praise of Mañjuśrī’s virtues and his request for the Dharma.

Regarding "the city-walls of the three realms of existence," this clarifies that Sudhana praises himself for dwelling within the three realms of existence, firmly established therein and unable to escape, as if residing within a city-walled fortress.

There are three types of existence (*bhava*): existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, and existence in the formless realm. All sentient beings within these three bodies of existence are unable to escape them.
Regarding pride (*māna*): "haughtiness" (*kaura*) refers to improper conduct; "conceit" (*māna*) refers to looking down upon others. Furthermore, there are seven types of pride:

pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), overweening pride (*abhimāna*), pride of self (*asmimāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*). These belong to those who wander through the various realms of rebirth (*gati*).

That is to say: there are the destinies of wrong views and the destinies of [wrong] precepts; furthermore, there are three destinies: the destiny of false certainty, the destiny of uncertainty, and the destiny of right certainty.
Furthermore, there are four evil destinies; furthermore, there are the five destinies of humans and devas and the ten wholesome destinies; furthermore, there are two destinies:

the supramundane destiny of the Two Vehicles who weary of suffering, and the destiny of the Pure Lands of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas; furthermore, there is the destiny of the One Vehicle Bodhisattva, in whom wisdom and compassion are perfectly integrated and who has not yet [entered parinirvāṇa].
Regarding the various realms of existence such as these, they are all gateways through which one enters according to one’s good or evil deeds;
the water of craving serves as their moat, for craving can moisten and nourish birth and death like a moat.

The deluded are able to be confused regarding the True Dharma, and are thus called "deluded ordinary beings" (*bālapṛthagjana*). There are eighty-four thousand [afflictions], and the Ten Stages Bodhisattvas...
There are twenty-two types of ignorance regarding the stages of existence; if categorized according to the five stages, there are one hundred and ten types of ignorance.
Once these are understood, they result in one hundred and ten types of liberation.
For those whose fires of greed and hatred are blazing intensely, the afflictions of the three realms take greed as the head of the ten fetters (*daśa-kaṣāya*) and hatred as the retinue of anger.

Ignorance acts as a general covering, while conceit acts as a light [obscuration]. Thinking lightly of oneself and disparaging others, doubt—conjoined with the five views—is able to obstruct the Noble Path;
together they constitute the causes and conditions of birth and death. When doubt ceases and views subside, wisdom then manifests before one.
Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), doubt and the five views are able to obstruct the Noble Path, while greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit are able to obstruct cultivation.

If a practitioner of the Path does not govern their conduct with the Path while practicing, they will instead revolve within birth and death, flowing according to karma and failing to attain self-mastery.
Now, this sutra briefly explains these two gates of greed and anger; the remaining eight are treated as general examples to illustrate their meaning.
This is because, due to these two obstacles of greed and anger, all roots of goodness fail to arise. Thus it is said:
The blazing fire refers to the King Māra as sovereign, namely the four māras: the skandha-māra, the kleśa-māra, the devaputra-māra, and the maraṇa-māra.
Those who dwell relying upon ignorance are called "the ignorant," meaning that they are shrouded and obstructed so that the mind is not clear.
Greed is the fetter; because of prior greed, anger arises, and because of this greed, attachment arises.

Those who bind themselves with fetters and shackles are those bound by the ropes used for criminals; those who use flattery and deception as reins are clearly those attached to falsehood because they are being controlled.
Those whose eyes are covered by doubt are those who, having conceived doubt regarding the right path, enter into various false paths;
those who conceive doubt regarding the wisdom that realizes the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) are themselves on a false path.
Regarding the phrase "born of stinginess, jealousy, and arrogance": there are five bases for stinginess:
dwelling in one's home, attachment to wealth and goods, lack of joy in praising the virtues of others, being miserly regarding the Dharma, and lack of joy in giving to others—these are the five.

As for jealousy, it is to harbor resentment toward those who surpass oneself. Arrogance (*māna*) is self-indulgence; because one does not observe propriety, it is called arrogance. Extravagance (*mada*) is a lack of frugality. Thus it is said.

Attachment, aversion, pride, envy, and stinginess constitute the five fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the lower realms; attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, pride, and ignorance pertain to both the upper and lower realms.
These ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and five fetters, along with the four maras, cause one to enter the three evil destinies and undergo the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Those who transcend these become "supramundane" (*lokottara*) and are no longer [bound by] the aforementioned [defilements], O Sudhana.

Having concluded the lamentation on the causes and conditions of the suffering of birth and death within the three realms, the following thirty verses praise his virtues and request the Dharma, as is clear from the text itself.
Thus, the afflictions of the three realms are treated: the first and second stages treat the delusions of the lower realm;
the third stage treats the delusions of the two upper realms; the fourth stage transcends the three realms; the fifth stage practices worldly arts; and the sixth stage [practices] the world...
The supramundane wisdom is perfected in the seventh stage; entering into birth-and-death and the three realms and six paths of existence, one practices great compassion.

In the eighth stage, non-effortful wisdom and compassion are perfected. In the ninth and tenth stages, the Buddha-activities are finally fulfilled. In the eleventh stage, the conduct of Samantabhadra is universalized.
In the twelfth stage, one's merit is equal to the Dharma-realm, and the union of principle and wisdom is eternally constant. These are the regulations for the Ten Abodes.
One portion is similar in its functional application to the practice-gates of these Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), yet they differ in their progressive advancement.

The Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*) discuss only the practice-gate of non-defilement, while within the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), compassion and vows are harmonized and integrated, as fully manifested in the fifty-three Good Friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and clearly elucidated in that specific stage.
The second [section] concerns Mañjuśrī’s knowledge of faculties and the bestowal of the Dharma.

To cause them to perfect their practice and give rise [to realization], five sections are established within this gate for subsequent learners: first, clarifying that faith has already been generated;
second, clarifying the gathering of holy beings; third, clarifying the exhortation of holy beings to draw near to virtuous friends;
fourth, clarifying Sudhana’s inquiry as to how one studies the bodhisattva path; and fifth, clarifying Mañjuśrī’s instruction regarding the destination of practice.
First, clarifying that those who have already generated the mind of faith are as the Sūtra says: "Good son, you have already generated the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This refers to the Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of the Bodhi-mind through faith;

it is only by means of the practice of *samādhi* that they are able to manifest the principle, and when the characteristics of their practice are revealed and their karma is exhausted, they become purely luminous. Second, clarifying the inclusion of these noble ones.
Regarding the recipient, the Sūtra states: "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king. This signifies the meaning of "receiving" (or "embracing").

Just as the Great Sage’s unimpeded wisdom is perfect and its form is all-pervasive, appearing in accordance with the faculties [of beings] and facing them, he does not turn his back on any sentient being.
At such a time, all sentient beings who are to see him according to their needs all face him directly; yet at that moment, each of those sentient beings does not perceive one another.

Knowing that it was merely the Noble One who had been speaking exclusively to me, [I now understand] what is called Mañjuśrī’s "seeing" of Sudhana—that is, his turning like a king of elephants—which signifies the discernment of faculties, the bestowing of attention, and the gathering in for the sake of the Dharma.

Thus, the Noble One, possessing the three types of knowledge (*trividyā*), exhorted me to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). As the Sūtra says: "Good son, draw near to and make offerings to all those who possess true knowledge."
Consciousness is the primary causal condition for the perfection of all-knowledge; therefore, do not give rise to weariness or aversion toward it.
This all-knowledge is the bodhicitta; because it is non-apprehensible, it manifests as fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Taking non-apprehensibility as its essence, it illuminates and manifests the myriad phenomena as its function. Thus spoke Simhabhadra of the Four Clarities when requesting the Dharma.
The sutra says: "How does one train in the bodhisattva path? There are eleven questions regarding the request for the bodhisattva path. Question:
Why is it said only that one "seeks the bodhisattva path," and not that one "trains in the bodhicitta"? Answer:
Because bodhi is non-attainable, non-cultivable, non-trainable, and non-practicable; therefore, one only seeks the bodhisattva path.
To study the bodhisattva practices while the bodhicitta is naturally and constantly manifest is like one who has attained the "Gate of Recollecting the Wisdom-Light of All Buddhas" atop Mount Sumeru.
This uses a concrete object to symbolize the Dharma: *gen* (艮) represents the mountain, and *gen* also signifies cessation.
By restraining the mind through cessation so that deluded thoughts do not arise, right wisdom appears before one; this is called "recollection."

Because one contemplates with right wisdom so as to accord with the signless, wondrous principle of all Buddhas, this signless right wisdom manifests before one, universally illuminating the mind and its objects;
thus, the five views—of self, of phenomena, of permanence, of annihilation, and of extremes—are entirely extinguished.
All phenomena become empty and tranquil, and as views vanish and karma ceases, it is called "Radiance. Therefore, it is said that one recollects the gate of the radiant wisdom of all Buddhas.
This clarifies that samādhi and dhyāna are skillful means (*upāya*) capable of manifesting the two gates of essence and function of the principle and wisdom;
they are perfectly complete and sovereign, even unto the unspeakable samādhis, all of which are the practice for manifesting right gnosis (*samyagjñāna*).
Thus, among the ten pāramitās, only the gnosis pāramitā (*jñānapāramitā*) is characterized by effortless sovereignty (*anābhoga-vaśitā*).
The remaining nine pāramitās are the auxiliary practices that manifest this fruit.

From the initial generation of the bodhicitta, they mutually interpenetrate one another in groups of ten, like refining pure gold until it becomes increasingly bright and clear. This brings about the accomplishment of various adornments;
when wisdom is perfected and practice is complete, one enters the Indra’s Net Dharma-gate, at which point one may truly be said to have fulfilled the merit of the Dharma-realm.
Spontaneously, from the first stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one takes as the essence the non-functioning, non-cultivation,
and non-action of *bodhicitta* while seeking to study and practice all the inexhaustible gates of conduct of Samantabhadra;
thus, by merely seeking the Bodhisattva path and learning the Bodhisattva practices, the effortless awakening manifests through its own accord as one practices these practices.
Within this, there is always the assistance of the dhyāna-pāramitā to manifest its essence and function, so that wisdom and principle may become increasingly clear, autonomous, and sovereign.

Thus, in the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*), one employs the preparatory skillful means of the samādhi of non-thought and non-action to assist in manifesting bodhi;
for bodhi has no substance and no nature, and serves as the basis of non-abiding for all conditioned phenomena.

Based on these conditions, one seeks the various practices of a bodhisattva; since these practices are identical to bodhi and lack inherent nature, if one were to cultivate bodhi separately from practice, that would be the bodhi of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the contemplation of emptiness—thus it would not be the One Vehicle.
Rather, it is the bodhi of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, which is the sovereign unity of wisdom and principle, the myriad practices, and compassionate vows.
This is because the Tathāgata spoke to bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;

they are dharmas of arising and ceasing," using the provisional teaching bodhisattvas' cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness through analytical dharma to destroy the existence of the triple world.
Since the Tathāgata has not yet clarified for them that the various existences of the triple world are themselves bodhi, he speaks thus. This is by means of this One Vehicle reality.
The teaching for Bodhisattvas is that they should seek only the Bodhisattva path and practice only the Bodhisattva conduct;

this is because enlightenment (*bodhi*) is the function of the principle of wisdom, wherein essence and function are fully encompassed as one, not to be sought separately. If one were to seek enlightenment separately, then essence and function would become distinct, and dualistic views would persist;
thus, it would not be called "riding the inconceivable vehicle. For this reason, one seeks only the Bodhisattva path.

There is no separate enlightenment, for enlightenment is luminosity; it is without seeking, without the arousal of the thought of awakening, without practice, without location, without question, without answer, without attainment, and without realization. It practices all practices and fulfills the path of Samantabhadra;
being without practice and without cultivation, this is the great function of enlightenment in its perfection. Therefore, one seeks only the Bodhisattva path and studies the Bodhisattva conduct.
Therefore, it can be said that at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the five clarifications on Mañjuśrī’s instruction on the destination of practice, the Sūtra says: "Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a mountain named Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). Within that mountain there is..."

The bhikṣu named Meghaśrī is this very person. Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of faculties (*indriya*) and the Dharma, so as to bring about their practice and give rise to the gateway for future students, the section from the end of the sutra is divided into eight long segments:
first, from the passage "At that time, Mañjuśrī turned like an elephant king" down to "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva... [and so on].

After the Bodhisattva had spoken these verses, twenty-two lines of verse from the sutra further clarify how Mañjuśrī exhorted Sudhana to draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and skillfully enter the ten stages (daśabhūmi). This is the gateway for entering the principle through meditative concentration and accords with the truth;
it is the wisdom attained by the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa through the recollection of all Buddhas.
The Gate of the Radiance of Wisdom proceeds downward from this point to the royal daughter, the maiden Maitrīcaryā;
these ten spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are all spiritual friends within the stages of the Ten Abidings (daśabhūmi). From this Mount Sumeru Peak downward, seven gates are established:
first, the gate of entering the Ten Abidings through faith, wherein one realizes principle and accords with truth by means of meditative concentration.
The "Ten Abodes" chapter is the second gate, which is the initiation of all practices based upon the truth;

this includes the bhikṣu Sudarśana and the nine others, totaling ten spiritual friends. The "Ten Practices" chapter is the third gate, which is the harmonious integration of wisdom, principle, great compassion, vows, and practices;
this includes the merchant Vāsavadattā, Utpalabhūti, and the others, totaling ten spiritual friends.
This "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" is the gateway for cultivating compassion and wisdom through the four aggregates to achieve virtue;

it comprises the night goddess Vāsantī and the following nine spiritual friends, totaling ten. This "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" is the gateway for completing the five compassions, giving rise to wisdom, and attaining Buddhahood;
it comprises the Buddha’s mother, Lady Māyā, and the following nine spiritual friends, totaling ten.
The "Knowledge" (Jñāna) section comprises ten chapters from the "Ten Determinations" (Daśa-niścaya) downward;

this is the sixth gate of the fulfillment of practice, which is the fruit of Buddhahood, namely the Tathāgata Maitreya. The "Appearance of the Tathāgata" (Tathāgatotpatti-sambhava) chapter is the seventh gate of the effortless, great function of mastery over the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), wherein all things interpenetrate like Indra’s net in perfect harmony; it is the unconditioned Dharma-realm.
The "Great Function" is this Chapter on the Dharma Realm; it clarifies how the entire Dharma Realm is encompassed and subsumed.

Thus, these fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) give rise to these gates of practice as skillful means, so that those who later resolve to attain Bodhicitta may recognize these five stages and advance through the gates of practice with ease.
Although the preceding sections discussed the Dharma, there was concern that practitioners might become confused regarding its application.
Therefore, to cause Sudhana to once again initiate the gateway of practice and to represent this so that students may not fall into error, first,

from the entry into the Ten Abodes through faith, within the section on "The Gateway of Unifying with Principle and Accordance with Truth through Meditative Concentration," there is the passage beginning from "At that time,
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king" down to "I vow to learn the vehicle of Samantabhadra," including the verses.
The twenty-two lines of this section are divided into four parts: first, from "At that time,

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva turned like an elephant king" down to "therefore, do not become weary or disheartened here," there are five lines of scripture which clearly show Mañjuśrī praising Sudhana’s aspiration for bodhicitta and exhorting him to draw near to the virtuous.
The section on "Do not give rise to weariness regarding knowledge" is divided into two parts.

From the words "Sudhana said" down to "How can the conduct of Samantabhadra be swiftly brought to fulfillment," there are five lines and a half of sūtra that clarify Sudhana’s eleven questions concerning the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
This section is further divided into three parts. From the words "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva... onwards, there may be approximately one [section].
In the *Caryā-melāpaka-pradīpa*, Mañjuśrī speaks in verse to praise Sudhana’s section. It is divided into four parts to correctly present these verses.
The verse says: "If there are bodhisattvas who do not weary of the suffering of saṃsāra, they will possess the path of Samantabhadra, which none can destroy.
This clarifies that taking the suffering of saṃsāra as bodhi is itself indestructible; if one were to depart from birth [and death], [the path would be destroyed].
When practicing the bodhisattva path and generating the bodhicitta, one encounters that which is to be destroyed. Why is this?

It is because one is destroyed by the duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and by the two obstacles of defilement and purity; furthermore, one is destroyed by the dualistic views of right and wrong, and by the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
It is also said: "If one enters the ocean of skillful means and dwells securely in the Buddha’s bodhi, one shall be able to follow and learn from the Teacher."
To become an omniscient one, it is only by means of the ocean of great vows, great compassion, and myriad practices as skillful expedients that one can abide securely in the bodhi of a Buddha.
If one is not clear regarding even a single dharma among all dharmas, or does not practice even a single practice among all practices, then the bodhicitta will not be perfected;
for bodhicitta is without obstruction and without intrinsic substance.
Within the single nature and the single practice, if there is grasping and rejecting, there is obstruction.
Grasping and rejecting are simply because the ocean-seal wisdom of the universally radiant *dharmadhātu* penetrates all things without exception.
By seeking only the fulfillment of bodhisattva practices, the bodhicitta becomes perfected; for bodhisattva practices and bodhicitta are not one thing and another—they are identical.
Because there is neither conjunction nor dispersion, and because both [birth-and-death and nirvana] are unattainable; because one thus practices the bodhisattva conduct;

because both birth-and-death and nirvana are unattainable—meaning that while abiding in nirvana within birth-and-death—one thus cultivates all bodhisattva practices, increasing great loving-kindness and great compassion, fulfilling great vows, and following the path of Samantabhadra.

The remainder is clear from the text itself. Furthermore, regarding the first section—entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) through faith and the gateway of attaining the principle and conforming to the truth via meditative concentration—from the passage "At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had spoken these verses" up to "the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī shall explain it for you," there are twelve and a half lines of scripture, which are divided into five sections. First:
From "At that time" onwards, there are two and a half lines of scripture clearly explaining Mañjuśrī’s praise of Sudhana for being able to resolve upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta;

this is divided into two parts. From "Good son" onwards, up to "it is even more difficult," there are two lines of scripture clearly explaining the praise of Sudhana’s seeking of spiritual friends as being even more difficult; this is divided into three parts. Good son... [end of section].

From "Furthermore, down to 'one should resolutely seek a true spiritual friend'"— this section of one line of scripture clarifies the stage of seeking all-knowledge by resolutely seeking a true spiritual friend. From "Good son, furthermore, down to 'do not look for faults'"—
this section of two and a half lines of scripture clarifies Mañjuśrī’s instruction to Sudhana regarding the vision of a spiritual friend.

"Be insatiable in your quest for knowledge; do not look for faults"—this section, as found in the text itself, consists of five dharmas spanning four and a half lines of scripture from "Good sons" down to "the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī shall expound for you. These five dharmas are:
first, indicating the direction where the spiritual friend resides; second, indicating the land where the spiritual friend resides; third, indicating... [text continues].
1. Regarding the location where the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) resides; 2. Regarding the establishment of the name of the spiritual friend based on their virtues; 3.
Regarding the demonstration of the spiritual friend’s capacity for moral cultivation and their ability to expound the Dharma; 4. Showing the direction of the spiritual friend’s residence:
why is one directed toward the south? This is to clarify that by entrusting oneself to a specific quarter, one symbolizes the Dharma, taking the south as the representation.
Li (the trigram Li) represents brightness because its central line is empty; because its center is empty, Li is brightness, it is the sun, and it is the nine heavens.
Within the human body, it corresponds to the head and the eyes, and to the heart.

Because the heart penetrates the void and wisdom is like the self-brightness of the sun, Li is taken as a symbol to represent this Way. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "It brilliantly refines all ritual forms throughout the ten directions."
The "Principal Directions" and "Divine Directions" refer to the Dharma. It merely takes these as its methods; yet the Great Image is directionless.

Just as the sun moves through the sky and its brilliance adorns the earth, so does wisdom move through space and its brilliance adorns all things—there is nothing it does not know, nothing it does not illuminate.
To grasp this single method, the ten directions become one undifferentiated whole. Second, it shows the land where the spiritual friend dwells.
In the south there is a land called Sukhavatī (Supreme Bliss); because its luminous wisdom and principle are void and capable of purifying afflictions, it is named Sukhavatī.
Third, it indicates the dwelling place of the spiritual friend: in that land there is a mountain named Sumeru (Wondrous Peak);
because non-conceptual, pure dhyāna is designated as the mountain, and the manifestation of the wisdom of empty mind is designated as the wondrous principle of purity, it is so named.

The clarity of wisdom and the power of insight that can destroy delusions are termed "peaks" (*feng*). *Gen* is taken as "mountain," "stopping," "the young and ignorant," "the little boy," and "gate-towers.
Stopping is taken as the initial illumination; because the three yang lines represent the beginning of generation, it corresponds to the first month.
When one line stops below, it forms the character for "correct" (*zheng*); thus, the first yang arises in the eleventh month, and the second yang arises in the twelfth month.
The second yang-line arises in the first month, and the third yang-line arises [therein]; therefore, it is taken as the first month.
Because the third yang-line arises, the third is taken as the "correct" (zheng). Furthermore, the place where the three yang-lines arise is the birth of fire in the branch of Yin.
Fire is taken as the day; the day is born in Yin. Since this is the place where the light first arises, it is named "the youthful and ignorant" (tóngméng) and "the little boy" (xiǎonán).
Because of its position, it is taken as a representation and symbolized by means of the Dharma.
As for Mañjuśrī’s residence on Mount Qingliang in the northeast, this takes the Bodhimaṇḍa in Magadha as being in the northeast;
this mountain is to the northeast of that Bodhimaṇḍa in Jambudvīpa, and it is the king of all mountains in this Jambudvīpa.
Because *Gen* (Mountains) is the sovereign element, ten thousand bodhisattvas dwell within it; this is Mañjuśrī, the companion who perfects the ten thousand practices.

Thus, taking Mañjuśrī as the sovereign, he serves as the teacher who initiates all Buddhas with the wondrous wisdom of the fundamental gnosis of the Dharmakāya; consequently, Mañjuśrī is present everywhere.
Mañjuśrī, all sentient beings likewise possess this inherently; they all enter the primordial noble wisdom through this Dharma.
Having been born into the family of the Buddhas, they share the same wisdom, liberation, knowledge, and vision as all Buddhas.
From this point onward, they study the wisdom of differentiation, give rise to vows and practices, and achieve great compassion, being called Samantabhadra.
The practice of the Dharma-realm is likewise. Therefore, the Tathāgata takes the image of the world’s phenomena as a means to manifest the Dharma so that it may be easily understood.
Thus, he takes Mount Wondrous Peak in the Land of Supreme Bliss as the image to clarify the place where the three Yang lines arise.

He uses Gen (Mount) to signify cessation; through cessation, the initial arising is clarified. Because it clarifies the initial arising, it is called "the youthful and ignorant" (tóngméng). Furthermore—
Because Mañjuśrī is the one who initiates the awakening from ignorance and enters the state of sainthood, he is titled the "Youthful Bodhisattva.
This name was established based on his transformative activity; for he inspires all sentient beings to enter the sublime wisdom of the principle of signlessness (*animitta*).
Thus, it clarifies that through the samādhi of skillful means, he manifests fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is the initial arising of all things.
It is because it is the abode of the wisdom of all Buddhas that this name is established.

By means of these symbolic images to represent the Dharma, the student first employs a mind free from discursive thought, tranquil and unmoving like the king of mountains; thus, the wondrous principle of formlessness and wisdom manifests within one's own mind.
Through the wisdom of one’s own mind, liberation and coolness are attained; it does not require the physical body to actually ascend the mountain.
Therefore, on the summit of Mount Sumeru, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are taught; as one ascends through these ten stages toward the fruit of Buddhahood, each is designated by the name "Moon.

Similarly, at this Wondrous Peak Mountain, the ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), beginning with the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, represent those who have first attained the cool bliss of the Dharma from the stage of ordinary beings. This clarifies the application of Sudhana’s practice.

To clarify the ten stages of dwelling (*daśavihāra*), the term "Wondrous Peak Mountain" is used to signify that it is only through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that one can manifest the fundamental wisdom of one's own mind.
Just as all Buddhas perceive that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), without characteristics (*animitta*),
without dependence, and without beginning or end, when one accords with this Dharma, it is called "dwelling in what the Buddhas dwell."

Only then can one see that past karma has been extinguished and the noble wisdom flows forth; having mastered the various types of knowledge within the Middle Way, one accomplishes the infinite Great Function of Samantabhadra throughout the Dharma-realm, extensively transforming all sentient beings of the boundless Dharma-realm so that they may all enter the cognitive vision of fundamental wisdom.
Therefore, those of ordinary mind who are beginners should first enter the mountains to delight in stillness.
First, training the concentrated mind to manifest right wisdom is also a skillful means (*upāya*) and may be named the "Exquisite Peak Mountain of the Land of Supreme Bliss.
Second, because the mind leaves behind mundane objects to delight in cultivating tranquility, it also carries the meaning of "supreme bliss.

Third, while employing various skillful means to benefit sentient beings for ordinary people, one simply does not abide within them. Fourth, regarding the raising of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

One who establishes virtue and is named "Cloud of Virtue" (Guṇamegha) is so called in the sense that a cloud of virtue can rain down the Dharma, sprinkling and moistening sentient beings to enable them to attain refreshing coolness.

A *bhikṣu* is translated here as "Extinction of Dispute" (*kṣayavivāda*); because one extinguishes the disputes of afflictions—such as existence and non-existence, right and wrong—it is called the "Extinction of Dispute.
This is because [one] is able, through the five views such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the two views of existence and non-existence...

Because they obstruct the Path, one must first still them through the samādhi of non-recollection and non-thought; only then will correct wisdom manifest. Thus it is said that "quarreling is extinguished.
Mount Miaofeng symbolizes the bhikṣu’s practice of samādhi: when wisdom manifests, concentration is attained, and when tranquility is lost, function becomes sovereign.
Only then can he preach the teachings to nourish the ignorant; therefore, he is named "Cloud of Virtue" (Guṇamegha) and resides in Gen.
To clarify the stage of "enveloping" (mōng-wei) for the purpose of ceasing [suffering], this is the beginning of moistening birth and opening the light of wisdom.
Taking the virtue of the Bhikṣu Megha as a model, he dwells upon the summit of the mountain to manifest the Dharma;

it clarifies that this stage begins with ordinary beings of faithful mind, and through the practice of samādhi, one awakens to enter the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*), becoming the first of the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) until reaching the "Dharma-Summit" (*dharmakūṭa*), whereupon one accords with the signless (*animitta*).

The assembly of sublime wisdom is called the Sublime Peak (*Sumeru*); because it can expound the teachings through sublime wisdom to nourish and benefit all sentient beings, it is named Cloud of Virtue (*Guṇamegha*).
By practicing such skillful means, one manifests one’s own mind so that correct wisdom appears before one.
Thus, the significance of Mount Sumeru and the monk Cloud of Virtue is entirely contained within oneself, even unto Mañjuśrī.

The fruit of Samantabhadra’s Buddhahood is entirely inherent; through the power of expedient means (*upāya*), samādhi, and the manifestation of wisdom and principle, one performs deeds to benefit sentient beings.
To practice these deeds is itself Suchness (*tathatā*). As clearly elucidated in the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta*, these five stages of the gate of practice are established.
These gates of practice for the expedient cultivation of the five stages are all based upon the Dharma.

Taking the Buddha-fruit of the *dhātu* as its essence, because the fundamental wisdom of the universal radiance of the *dharmadhātu* is endowed with the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra as its great function,
it remains unchanged from beginning to end, from root to branch. Through the stages established according to the process of cultivation—
ranging from initial application to full maturity— the dharma-gate of the one hundred and ten cities is collectively subsumed within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Within this [text], there are six gates: the practice of the *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), their general and specific aspects, their similarities and differences, and their formation and disintegration.

By illuminating these with wisdom, one may perceive the meaning of the "one hundred and ten cities," as previously explained regarding the eastern part of Puṇyavatī City. Fifth, it raises the question of the moral virtue and capabilities of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This spiritual friend is capable of explaining and demonstrating the application of the bodhisattva practices and the gateway to the five stages of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
therefore, Mañjuśrī directed Sudhana to ask the bhikṣu Meghaśrī: "How should one learn the bodhisattva practices?
How should one cultivate the bodhisattva practices? and so forth, up to: "How can one quickly [master] the conduct of Samantabhadra?"
The Bhikṣu Paripūrṇa-guṇamegha shall explain this for you: this is the initial mind that enters the Ten Abodes, known as the "Abode of the First Aspiration.
