In order to accomplish all the various practices of the Buddhas; in order to desire to attain all the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the Buddhas;
in order to desire to be endowed with all the powers (*bala*) of the Buddhas; in order to desire to obtain all the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of the Buddhas;
in order to desire to hear all the Buddha-dharmas; in order to desire to receive all the Buddha-dharmas; in order to desire to uphold all the Buddha-dharmas; in order to desire...
It is for the sake of understanding all Buddha-dharmas; for the sake of wishing to protect all Buddha-dharmas;
for the sake of wishing to be of one essence with the assembly of all bodhisattvas; for the sake of wishing to be equal and without distinction from the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas;
for the sake of wishing to fulfill all bodhisattva pāramitās; and for the sake of wishing to accomplish all bodhisattva [practices].
Because it is that which is practiced; because one desires to bring forth all the pure vows of bodhisattvas;
because one desires to obtain the treasury of majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas;
because one desires to obtain the great light of inexhaustible wisdom, the dharma-treasury of all bodhisattvas; and because one desires to obtain the vast treasury of all bodhisattva samādhis.
In order to accomplish the immeasurable and innumerable treasury of supernatural powers (*abhijñā-kośa*) of all bodhisattvas;
in order to teach and discipline all sentient beings through the treasury of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-kośa*) so that they may all ultimately reach the final limit;
in order to manifest the treasury of miraculous transformations (*vikurvaṇa-kośa*); and in order to attain mastery over all treasuries of sovereignty through one's own mind.
Therefore, desiring to enter the treasury of purity and being adorned with all marks,
O Noble One, I now, with such a mind, such an intention, such a delight, such a desire, such a longing, such a reflection,
such a reverence, such a means, such a culmination, and such humility, approach the Noble One.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to instruct and exhort the assembly of bodhisattvas; he is capable of elucidating through skillful means what has been attained,
showing them the path, providing them with ferries and bridges, and bestowing upon them the Dharma-gates so as to eliminate delusion and confusion,
uproot the arrows of hesitation, sever the net of doubt, illuminate the dense forest of the mind, wash away the turbidity of mental defilements, and cause the mind to become pure and white.
Purify the mind; straighten the mind; sever crookedness from the mind; bring the mind to rest within birth and death; liberate the mind from unwholesome states;
cause the mind to be released from its attachments at the points of attachment; cause the mind to move away from the realm of defiled craving;

cause the mind to swiftly enter the sphere of omniscience; cause it to quickly reach the city of the Unsurpassed Dharma; cause it to abide in great compassion; and cause it to abide in great loving-kindness.
Entering the bodhisattva conduct, causing the cultivation of the gates of samādhi, causing entry into the stage of realization,
causing the contemplation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), causing the increase of power, and causing the practice of conduct—
may the Noble One please proclaim for me how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path, so that by practicing accordingly, one may swiftly attain purity.
When he quickly attained clear understanding, the Elder Suvimalavikrāntagāmin, through the power of his past roots of goodness, the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha,

and the mindful power of the youth Mañjuśrī, immediately entered a bodhisattva samādhi-door called the "Infinite Revolving Dhāraṇī that Universally Encompasses All Buddha-fields. Having entered this samādhi, he attained a purified body.

Within his body appeared the various manifestations of light and adornments of the assemblies and sites of enlightenment belonging to ten times the number of atoms in ten Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, as well as all the supernatural transformations, past practices,
great vows, auxiliary dharmas for the path, and pure adornments of renunciation performed by those Buddhas.

The manifestations of all Buddhas attaining perfect enlightenment, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma, and teaching and transforming sentient beings—all such things appear within his body without any obstruction.
These various forms and various sequences abide as they originally were, without being confused or disordered; namely, various lands, various assemblies, and various paths.
In various adorned settings, the Buddhas therein manifest diverse supernatural powers, establish diverse vehicles and paths, and demonstrate diverse gates of vows;

some perform buddha-works while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven within a single world, while others perform buddha-works after descending from the Tuṣita Heaven in a single world; likewise, some abide in the womb, while others undergo birth.
Whether dwelling in palaces or having renounced the world, whether proceeding to the site of enlightenment or defeating the armies of Māra,
whether surrounded by the respectful attendance of devas and nāgas, whether exhorted by the lords of the world to preach the Dharma,

whether turning the wheel of the Dharma, whether entering parinirvāṇa, whether distributing the relics, or whether erecting stūpas and temples— those Tathāgatas, amidst various assemblies and in various worlds...
Among all sentient beings— possessing various destinies, various lineages, various desires, various karmic actions, various languages, various faculties and natures,
and various afflictions, latent tendencies, and habitual propensities—
he may dwell in a subtle place of enlightenment, or in a vast place of enlightenment, or in a place of enlightenment measuring one yojana, or in a place measuring ten [yojanas].

A site for the path of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) measuring a *yojana*, or sites for the path of practice measuring as many *yojanas* as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
by means of various supernormal powers, various modes of speech, various sounds, various Dharma-gates,
various gates of dhāraṇī, various gates of eloquence, various oceans of noble truths, and various forms of fearlessness.
The Great Lion’s Roar proclaims the various roots of goodness and various recollections of all sentient beings,
bestows various predictions of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas, and speaks of the various dharmas of the Buddhas;
Sudhana was able to hear and receive all such utterances from those Tathāgatas, and he also beheld the inconceivable samādhis and miraculous transformations of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
At that time, the householder Vimokṣa rose from samādhi and addressed the youth Sudhana, saying:
"Good son, I have entered and emerged from the Tathāgata’s liberation door of unimpeded adornment.

Good son, when I enter and emerge from this liberation door, I immediately see the World-Honored One, the Dragon Sovereign King, in the world-system Jāmbūnada-golden Radiance in the eastern direction."
I saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocanagarbha, surrounded by a great assembly at his site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), with the Bodhisattva Vairocanagarbha as the principal;

and I saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantagandha in the world-system of Swift Power (Kṣiprabala) in the southern direction, surrounded by a great assembly at his site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Cittarāja as the principal; and I saw the western...
He saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sumerupradīpa of the world-system Gandhavabhāsa,
surrounded by his assembly at the site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Asaṅgamati as the leader; he also saw the Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha Abhedyavajra of the world-system Kāṣāyadhvaja in the northern direction, surrounded by his assembly at the site of enlightenment.

He saw the Bodhisattva Vīravajrapada as the leader; furthermore, he saw in the northeast the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Anupalambhadhātunetra, surrounded by his assembly at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), with the Bodhisattva Anupalambhasuvikurvaṇa as the leader; furthermore, he saw in the southeast...
He saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Gandhadīpa in the world Gandhārciḥprabhasvara, surrounded by his assembly at the site of enlightenment,
with the Bodhisattva Vajrajvālāmati as the chief; and he also saw the Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha Dharmadhātucakravarti in the world Prajñāsūryaviśvāvabhāsa in the southwestern direction, surrounded by his assembly at the site of enlightenment.
He saw him surrounded by the Bodhisattva Sarvavikurvāṇadhvaja as his chief;

furthermore, he saw in the northwest direction, in the world-system Samantaviśuddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvabuddharatnottaradhvaja, surrounded by his assembly at the site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Dharmadhvajarāja as his chief; and he also saw the Buddha above.
He saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Infinite Wisdom Light Perfect Banner, appearing in succession,
surrounded by a great assembly at his place of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Dharma-realm Gate Banner King as the chief;
furthermore, he saw the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Unobstructed Wisdom Banner in the Buddha-world Radiance below.
Surrounded by a great assembly at the site of enlightenment, with the Bodhisattva Sarvalokadhātvanabhibhūtarājendra as their leader, [the Buddha said]:
"Good son, I see such Tathāgatas as these—numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions.
Those Tathāgatas do not come here, nor do I go there; yet, if I wish to see the world Sukhāvatī..."
Tathāgata Amitābha will appear to me at will; if you wish to see Tathāgata Vajraprabha in the world of Candana,
Tathāgata Ratnaprabha in the world of Sugandha, Tathāgata Ratnapadmaprabha in the world of Padma,
Tathāgata Śāntiprabha in the world of Suvarṇa, or Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the world of Abhirati, [you shall see them].
I saw all such Tathāgatas as the Tathāgata Siṃha of the world Suviśuddhasthita,
the Tathāgata Candrabuddhi of the world Ādarśaprabhā, and the Tathāgata Vairocana of the world Ratnasiṃhavicitravyūha;
yet those Tathāgatas did not come here, nor did my body go to them, for I knew all Buddhas and...
I know my own mind to be entirely like a dream; I know all Buddhas to be like reflections.
Knowing my own mind to be like water, I know all the physical forms and characteristics of all Buddhas, as well as my own mind, to be entirely like illusions.
Knowing all Buddhas and my own mind to be entirely like echoes—I thus know, thus recollect, that all the Buddhas I behold arise from this.
"Good son, you should know that when Bodhisattvas cultivate all Buddha-dharmas, purify all Buddha-fields, accumulate sublime practices,
and subdue sentient beings; when they give rise to great vows, enter the gate of inconceivable liberation,
attain the sovereign play of omniscience, realize the Bodhi of the Buddhas, and manifest great supernormal powers to travel everywhere throughout the ten directions."
Through subtle wisdom, one universally enters all kalpas; all such things arise entirely from one's own mind.

Therefore, son of good family, you should support your own mind with wholesome dharmas, moisten your own mind with the water of the Dharma, purify your own mind regarding sense objects, strengthen your own mind with diligence, and broaden your own mind with patience.
One’s own mind should be realized as pure through wisdom; one’s own mind should be made clear and sharp through wisdom;
one’s own mind should be developed through the sovereign power of the Buddha; one’s own mind should be made vast through the equanimity of the Buddha;
one’s own mind should be examined through the ten powers of the Buddha. Noble son, I [know] only this liberation of the Tathāgata’s unimpeded adornment.
Entering and exiting through the gates like all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they have attained unimpeded wisdom, abide in unimpeded conduct,
and have realized the Samādhi of Constantly Seeing All Buddhas, the Samādhi of Not Abiding in the Limit of Nirvāṇa, and the Samādhi of Thorough Penetration into the Universal Gate realm.
They are entirely equal regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time, and are able to skillfully manifest divided bodies throughout all lands.
Abiding in the state of equality of all Buddhas, the realms of the ten directions appear before them entirely; they observe with wisdom such that nothing is not clearly understood.

Within their own bodies, all worlds in their formation and destruction appear completely, yet they do not give rise to the notion of duality regarding their own bodies and those worlds. How could I possibly know or describe such sublime conduct?
"Noble son, from here go south to the edge of Jambudvīpa; there is a land named Mālikāra where there is a bhikṣu named Sāgaradhvaja.
Go to him and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the elder Vimokṣa, circumambulated him to the right, and gazed upon him.
One should examine, extol, praise, contemplate, long for, and look up to [the spiritual friend] with tears of sorrow streaming down;

one should mindfully recollect them with a single-minded focus, rely upon the spiritual friend, attend to the spiritual friend, and revere the spiritual friend. Through the spiritual friend, one perceives all-knowledge;
one does not give rise to opposition toward the spiritual friend, has no flattery or deception in one’s heart toward the spiritual friend, and always follows the spiritual friend with the mind.
Following the spiritual friends, he conceived of them as compassionate mothers because they cause him to abandon all unbeneficial dharmas;
he conceived of them as compassionate fathers because they give birth to all wholesome dharmas. Having spoken thus, he took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of entering the proper stage (*dharmaparyāya*), from the passage beginning "At that time, the youth Sudhana...

down to "...Sons of good family, I only know this liberation-gate of the Tathāgata’s unimpeded adornment, and how I enter and emerge from it," there are one hundred and forty and a half lines of scripture. Within this section, ten gates are established.
1. Contemplating the superior progress of the Dharma bestowed by Samprajanya; 2. Traveling gradually for twelve years until reaching the city of Vanavāsin;
3. Seeking liberation from the elder Vimokṣaka; 4. Having seen him, paying homage and formally presenting one's request; 5.
The elder Vimokṣaka immediately entering the Bodhisattva-samādhi and manifesting his body throughout the ten directions.
In each of the ten Buddha-fields, he answered Sudhana’s request and led him to enter the six liberations.

The Elder then arose from his meditative concentration and, through verbal explanation, described the ten Buddha-realms within that concentration and the great assembly at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Seventh, the liberation of the manifestation of all Buddhas before one according to the mind’s recollection; eighth, the mental recollection of the absence of [intrinsic nature].
9. Seeing the body of the Buddha as like a shadow, with no interior or exterior between the nine consciousnesses; 10. Reaching everywhere throughout the ten directions without coming or going.
"Good sons, I have attained entry into and emergence from this liberation door of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Adornment.
This concludes the section on the names of the samādhis correctly revealed and the mastery of entering and emerging. From here below is the ascent.
Regarding the phrase "proceeding to the preceding stage," it clarifies that one who practices through gradual progression does not abide in the preceding dharmas.
The phrase "twelve years" refers to the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha dwelling in the country of Samudramukha for twelve years, as mentioned previously;
this illustrates that one directly contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as the supramundane liberation.
Because this bhikṣu seeks supramundane liberation and regards the ocean of birth and death as the Buddha-body,
Sudhana has come here to the city of Dhanyākara and traveled through it for twelve years in succession to clarify the practice within the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination;
thus, he takes the twelve links of dependent origination as the very substance of his meditative concentration.
The Elder Vimukta is a worldly layman who, while manifesting in the secular world, practices the true path;
he is truly named "Liberation" because, like the bhikṣu Sāgara-megha, he does not dwell in saṃsāra but contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination to give rise to the supramundane mind.
This Elder Vimukta, amidst the dharmas of the twelve links of dependent origination, abides within saṃsāra without destroying dependent origination.
Because it is based on dependent origination, it is said that "he wandered for twelve years"; this signifies the meaning of non-abiding.
It signifies the meaning of the non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; it signifies the meaning of the absence of emergence or disappearance between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

If one considers this in terms of the general application of wisdom, its essence consists of the ten pāramitās; however, in terms of the specific application to the stages, it is explained through the mastery of both common and distinct [practices].
This fifth gate of the dhyāna-pāramitā is the dhyāna of the non-constructive nature of the dharma-dhātu itself;

because all that arises through conditions is by its very nature detached, there is no mental object whatsoever that is not this forest of dhyāna-concentration—the unimpeded liberation of the dharma-dhātu.
Therefore, the city is named "Abiding Forest," for all mental objects are active yet without utility.

Because the nature abides in itself, the seeker observes its superior progression and attains the vision of liberation. "The elder" clarifies that by means of the ultimate (paramārtha), one accords with the conventional (saṃvṛti);
the very essence of the ultimate and the conventional is inherently liberated. Having seen this, one prostrates with the five limbs;

this signifies that the ultimate and the conventional are without dependence and that the five stages are unified. It also clarifies the total meditative concentration (samādhi) of the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination.
The fact that the forest [of trees] also joins their palms signifies the non-duality of the ultimate and conventional truths.
The above section explains how meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are darkly united; the following section further articulates the petitioner’s request through speech.

Below this, the entry into *samādhi* and the manifestation of ten Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions clarifies that the essence of concentration is all-pervasive, complete, and perfect; thus, "ten" is used as the number representing perfection. Furthermore...

Below this, the ten Tathāgatas and their leading Bodhisattvas seen within meditative concentration are the Buddha-fruit and practices manifested from the very stage [of the practitioner] through this samādhi;
furthermore, as for seeing the various Buddhas by recollecting them according to one's thoughts,
it is because one’s own mind corresponds to the true Buddha, such that all that is recollected is the realm of the Buddha, with nothing else remaining.
It also clarifies that one's own mind is the Buddha and that all thoughts are collectively the Buddha; the rest is self-evident from the text.
This is the fifth stage, the "Abode Endowed with Skillful Means," which takes the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as its essence and the other nine perfections as its companions.

If considered within the context of the cognitive realm (*jñāna-viṣaya*), these five stages are cultivated concurrently; if considered according to their specific stages, they specifically treat the True and the Conventional through tranquility (*śamatha*).

The second section clarifies that all worldly mental states and objects are collectively *dhyāna*. It does so by taking the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the five aggregates (*skandha*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and unifying them within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; thus, through the spontaneous functioning of *dhyāna*, it reveals the meditative gate of non-constructive dependent origination.
The second part explains the advancement to the preceding stage, beginning from the passage "Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... down to the point of taking leave.
The departure consists of sixteen lines of verse, which may be divided into four sections: first, extolling the virtues of the previous [teacher];
second, indicating the location and realm of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, mentioning the name of the spiritual friend;

and fourth, Sudhana’s respectful longing for his good friend, weeping as he takes his leave. Regarding the first section, "extolling the virtues of the previous," this clarifies the qualities of the Elder Vimokṣa.
Extending virtue to the preceding stage, there are ten kinds of excellence by which the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) exhort Sudhana to advance in his practice.
Second, regarding the journey southward as previously explained in the first stage:

reaching the borders of Jambudvīpa clarifies that this stage, the Abiding in the Correct Mind (*samyaktva-nyāma*), is the attainment of supramundane and mundane wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Because it marks the ultimate limit, it is called the "limit of Jambudvīpa. This indicates that one has attained the mundane and supramundane mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), yet has not yet attained the perfect great compassion of entering the secular world to act in common with those bound by afflictions;

therefore, it is represented by the *bhikṣu*, who manifests the signs of having transcended the secular within the world. The subsequent stage clarifies the perfection of the great compassion of entering the secular world.
This was expressed by means of the upāsikā Pūrṇamanorathā. There is a land named Mālikāra—which has not yet been translated from the Sanskrit original—where there was a bhikṣu named Sāgaradhvaja.

He was so called because his clarity of virtue and wisdom was like the ocean, and he was able to destroy the karma and delusions of sentient beings; "dhvaja" (banner) carries the meaning of "to crush and destroy."
