Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Eight: Entering the Dharma Realm.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of Entering Properly into the Stage, from the passage "At that time, Sudhana...
down to "...I only know this one gate of liberation," this segment is divided into thirteen sections:
1) Contemplating the superior progress based on the instruction of the spiritual friend; 2) Gradually traveling south to the place where the ocean tide reaches; 3) Seeing...
1. The Universal Adornment Garden is adorned with various jewels; 2. Sudhana enters the garden and searches everywhere for the laywoman Pañcadarśanā;
3. He approaches her; 4. He pays homage and prostrates to her, formally presenting his request;
5. The laywoman Viśvā tells him the Dharma she herself practices; 6. Sudhana says: "Noble One..."

1. How long has it been since [the Bodhisattva] first resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta? 2. Sudhana the youth asks: "O Noble One, how long will it be before you shall attain unsurpassed bodhi? 3.
The laywoman Śrīprabhā gives the correct answer regarding the causes and conditions for the duration of her attainment of Buddhahood.
4. Sudhana requests that she explain the name of the dharma-door of liberation. 5. [The laywoman explains] how it is named.
13. The laywoman Śūradattā correctly answered her name as "Banner of Peace and Freedom from Sorrow.
She said, "I know only this single gate of liberation," and so forth, thereby deferring her own virtues and promoting others. This is like a garden or a palace adorned with various jewels;
all such things being adorned with many jewels symbolizes that one's conduct and vows are vast and exhaustive throughout the entire Buddha-realm.
Because of the realm of birth, his physical support and environment are magnificently adorned, vast and limitless; his countenance is upright and handsome, and he is graced with various ornaments.
He manifests a mind of loving-kindness and compassion to benefit things and aid living beings; he is disciplined, gentle, and harmonious, embodying the Way and selflessness.

There is no among the ten *pāramitās* that he does not practice in accordance with them. He serves and makes offerings to the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions everywhere. That which he has thus inspired is the Right [Dharma].
Her appearance and deportment are so admirable that those who behold her are freed from delusion;
revered by devas and humans, she manifests the conduct of great compassion by appearing in a female body while possessing no female mind.

All her adornments, as well as her palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, and pools, are born of the retribution of the myriad practices of compassion and wisdom. As previously indicated in brief, all her ornaments are likewise produced through such merit.
The Sūtra itself clarifies that the meaning of this stage is the extensive adornment of the retribution for the practice of compassion through the skillful means of the *pāramitās*.
As the Sūtra states: "Good son, any sentient beings who behold me shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies that to reach this stage, one must necessarily cultivate [the path] to its ultimate extent.

When the three liberations of emptiness, mundane wisdom, and supramundane wisdom manifest before one, and one accomplishes vast practices of compassion, only then does one arrive at the gateway of skillful means for entering the cycle of birth and death.

Upon realizing that the nature of birth and death is fundamentally of one essence with the ocean of the Buddha’s merit and wisdom, one attains the liberation gate of the "Banner of Peace and Security Free from Sorrow. Only then is one said to dwell in the stage of Non-retrogression.

Although they know emptiness and non-self, they still harbor fear regarding birth and death; not having yet entered the banner of peace and security free from sorrow, they constantly abide in a state of regression.

Even if they do not regress, ordinary beings will eventually fall back, while those who become followers of the Two Vehicles or are born in the Pure Lands take pleasure in their respective fruits of joy.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddhas of the ten directions all come to my presence upon their precious thrones.
"Preach the Dharma for me to demonstrate the union of compassion and wisdom; this stage clarifies the gateway of accomplishing non-effortful wisdom through compassion.
In the tenth stage, the Princess Maitrīcaryā (Compassionate Conduct) clarifies the gateway of attaining mastery over compassion through wisdom.
King Siṃhadhvaja represents the mastery of non-effortful wisdom within these ten stages of abiding, while the princess represents the absence of [self-concern].
The compassion of the stained [stage] reaches its fulfillment at the tenth stage, the Abode of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), because wisdom and compassion are perfected;
thus, the tenth ground is the gateway for accumulating great compassion and accomplishing practice, symbolized by nine goddesses and one wife of a Tathāgata.

The eleventh ground is the perfection of the practice of great compassion; it is the gateway to attaining Buddhahood through the arising of wisdom from compassion, which is represented by Māyā’s birth.
The Buddha represents this through these eleven stages. Within these ten stages, the ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) have collectively fulfilled the fruit of Buddhahood;

because they possess the practices of Samantabhadra, they universally manifest as benevolent gentlemen among the people of the world—acting as teachers of youths, householders, elders, and even as boys and girls—conducting themselves like ordinary persons. This clarifies that the fruit has reached its ultimate limit.

Because the practices are universal, they are generally categorized by the arousal of the mind through wisdom; from the very first stage of the Initial Arousing of the Mind (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), compassion and wisdom arise simultaneously.
Taking the fundamental wisdom of the supramundane path as the starting point, five stages (*pañca-vihāra*) and fifty practice-gates (*caryā-mukha*) are established.
By means of these, one distinguishes between the mature and the immature, as well as the common and the distinct, through these fifty *pāramitās* across the five stages.

The middle five stages involve refining and tempering [the practitioner] to distinguish the breadth and narrowness of their wisdom and compassion, as well as the degree of their maturity, their transcendence of the world versus remaining within its entanglements,

their movement with or against the flow, and the differences in the quantity and quality of their merit and wisdom. This causes those who have resolved to attain enlightenment not to dwell in complacency with any single dharma—
whether three, four, ten, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand— but intentionally impels them to advance further until they reach the infinite.
Because it is as vast as the Dharma-realm, five stages are established therein; within each of the fifty layers, both the practices of wisdom and compassion are fully present.
These fifty *pāramitās* interpenetrate one another, resulting in approximately five hundred gates of *pāramitā*.
They function as mutual primary and secondary factors, perfecting this compassionate wisdom whose mental capacity encompasses both the mundane and the supramundane.

The gates of the narrow and the broad, the mature and the immature, have now been clarified. Regarding the six meanings of totality and particularity, identity and difference, and formation and disintegration:
these ten gates of dwelling and the ten *pāramitās* are established as ten dharmas based directly upon the reality-body (*dharmadhātu*) of the Dharma;

through their perfect fusion and mutual interpenetration, they form one hundred dharma-gates. By means of this initial arousal of the bodhicitta, one practices the fundamental causal conduct of the Buddha.
Taking this as the model for practice, one proceeds from this fundamental model through five stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and refinement;

only then does one come to rely upon the original model. Although there are distinctions between the raw and the refined resulting from this refinement, wisdom and compassion do not differ from the initial resolve.

Furthermore, the sun, moon, time, and seasons do not undergo any transition, because with respect to the mind of awakening generated through wisdom, there is originally no division of the three periods of time.
This upāsikā represents the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), which consists of both mundane and supramundane dharmas;

she is named "Fulfilling Vows" (*Pūrṇamanoratha*) to indicate that she causes those with a preponderance of supramundane intent to rely upon the fulfillment of their original vows, and that she gives rise to the practice of compassion by loving saṃsāra as an object of affection in order to deliver sentient beings. Thus, she is taken [as a symbol] by means of the name "Fulfilling Vows."
Because his resolve to nurture and raise his descendants is tireless, he manifests as the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā (Great Compassion) to nurture all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
Whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous, he never abandons them; he never gives rise to a thought of failing to save them.
He transforms into various bodies, never forsaking even a single sentient being by so much as a hair’s breadth, and constantly appears before each one.

Because he instructs and exhorts all sentient beings in various ways to bring them to maturity, this stage—concerning the turning back of the supramundane mind of the sixth bhūmi—is characterized by frequently not severing the craving for birth-and-death while still employing the habit of affection to deliver sentient beings.
It is symbolized by the *upāsikā* (laywoman), and is therefore called "with practice and with development. In the tenth, the *abhiṣeka* (consecration) stage, by means of one...
The differentiation of non-active wisdom is accomplished through the arising of compassion from that wisdom, such that there is no longer any habitual tendency toward attachment;

this is represented by the Lion Banner King’s daughter, the maiden Maitrāyaṇī. This is the meaning of the maturation of wisdom and compassion through their cultivation and harmonious integration within the stage of the tenth bhūmi.
As I have stated above, I have eighty-four thousand nayutas of fellow-practitioners as my retinue.

She constantly dwells in this garden, clearly manifesting that she moves in concert with the eighty-four thousand nayutas of afflictions that constitute the gardens of sentient beings, thereby guiding and drawing them in.

When Sudhana asked the upāsikā how long it had been since she first resolved upon bodhicitta, her intention was to clarify that for one seeking liberation, there is no duration of time; once the resolve is made, it is immediately present throughout the three periods of time.

At one time, because there is no distinction of long or short within the essence of liberation, the inquiry regarding the duration of the arousal of the mind within the practice of great compassion intends to clarify that the profundity of great kindness and great compassion corresponds to the duration of the world-ages (*kalpa*) in which the realm of sentient beings abides.
Since the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the vows and practices of great compassion are likewise inexhaustible; this is what is meant by the subsequent question concerning "long."

The intention of attaining Buddhahood is likewise; taking thirty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] as a measure, it has already been surpassed, for the intention known only to a Buddha is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, the first three bhikṣus attained the supramundane mind—this is the first ten;
up to the bhikṣu Samudrareṇuvatsa, he attained both the mundane and supramundane minds—this is the twentieth.
This concludes the seventh stage, entering worldly conduct through compassion; this is the thirtieth [chapter]. It clarifies the duration and proximity of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
*Kukila*—the Sanskrit original has not yet been translated—is the Vairocana-maṇi-ratna, which means the "Stainless Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of Pervasive Radiance.
The *ratnatāla* tree is shaped like the *tāla* palm of this region.

With the *aruna* incense made of exquisite jewels—here translated as "red"—and the Buddha *Varuṇa*—here translated as "Water God"—there is a liberation named "Free from Sorrow, Banner of Peace and Security.
This has two meanings: first, it refers to teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they may be freed from sorrow;
this is the banner of peace and security for Bodhisattvas. As long as sentient beings have not yet escaped birth and death...
Because the Bodhisattva does not seek personal peace and security, he manifests as two types of bodhisattvas.

Although they have realized that the nature of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is empty, they still harbor fear toward birth and death; thus, they have not yet attained ultimate peace and freedom from sorrow.

If they can enter into birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, realizing that birth and death, sentient beings, and the one who teaches and transforms are all, in their totality, the practice of *nirvāṇa*, [they attain it].

Emerging without cessation is called the Banner of Peaceful Security Free from Sorrow; thus, among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), this is the seventh, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-bhūmi*).

Here, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions. In terms of the gate of wisdom, these five stages collectively counteract [defilements];
in terms of the gate of the stages themselves, they specifically counteract the predominance of mundane and supramundane minds and the deficiency of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because it causes compassion and wisdom to reach fulfillment, the second section—inferring virtues and ascending to the preceding stage—consists of sixteen and a half lines of scripture, beginning from "Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
and ending with "taking leave and departing. Regarding the meaning of the text within this section, it is divided into five gates:
first, inferring virtues in the past to cause them to excel and advance; second, demonstrating excellence... [and so forth].
1. The place of knowledge is named "Ocean Tide. 2. He reveals the name of that land as "Narasū. 3. He utters the name of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
4. He prostrates, sheds tears, takes his leave, and departs. These tears signify the profound depth of great compassion (mahākaruṇā);
they also signify the utmost sincerity and gravity of one who reveres the Dharma and honors people; furthermore, they signify the sovereign manifestation of wisdom and compassion.
Grieving for the common world and lamenting those in the realms of suffering, the Noble Mind’s vast salvation and compassionate sighs are difficult to surpass.
To the south lies a place by the ocean tide; that this place shares the same name as the previous stage, "Ocean Tide," signifies the convergence of compassion and wisdom.
It indicates that the gateway of compassion from the preceding stage is elevated and integrated with the essence of wisdom, thereby bringing forth the eighth vow-pāramitā.

The wisdom of initiating activity is conjoined with the gate of compassion. If wisdom does not give rise to great vows and practice, there is no way for compassion to function as it inclines toward tranquility.
Therefore, within the ten stages, upon reaching the eighth stage, the Buddhas bestow three empowerments and offer seven exhortations, causing one to remember their original vows;
only then can great compassion arise. For this reason, these two positions are both named "Ocean."
Tidings of clarity arise through the eighth vow, the *pāramitā* of which unifies compassion and wisdom into a single essence;

only then does one attain effortless great function (*anabhoga-mahopayoga*), acting extensively for the benefit of others without thought, just as the ocean tide surges with vast waves yet acts without intention.
Thus, the Bodhisattva of this stage employs effortless wisdom to transform all classes of beings, knowing their faculties and never missing the opportune moment.
For this reason, both stages share the name "Ocean Tide. In this assembly, wisdom and compassion are non-dual. The name of the land is Nārasu, which means "not indolent.

This is the eighth stage, entering the wisdom of effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Its original designation is "Wisdom Pervading Everywhere," for it gives rise to benefit for sentient beings without laziness or weariness;
the mind of indolence and sloth is absent from this stage, which is among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The pattern of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) arises from this point; from its initial trace until the eighth stage, it converges with its original pattern.

Within this, a portion corresponds to the eighth stage among the ten stages, where the great function and the non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) become one, and the sphere of the Buddha becomes fully perfected.
The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" marks the point of completion, as it is the fulfillment of the *dharmadhātu*.

This chapter constitutes the source and origin; because the fundamental wisdom is eternally thus and its great function is effortless, those who first resolve upon the Great Bodhicitta originally rely on the essence of the Wisdom of Sound and Light of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). When the merit of this resolution matures, it is simply the primordial Dharma-realm itself.
However, based on the maturation or immaturity, and the extensiveness or narrowness of wisdom and compassion, the stages and sequence are clarified herein. The name of the Immortal is *Vī*.
"Kṣemadatta" (Mugosha) means "One Whose Utterance Is Fearful. His wisdom-eye is increased and clarified, and he excels at crushing heterodox treatises.
Because his speech accords with reality and causes opponents to cease their arguments, he is named "One Whose Utterance Is Fearful.
Sudhana wept and shed tears as he contemplated ten difficult matters, as fully explained in the sutra.
The eighth station, the Abode of the Ocean Tide, is where the Rishi Vimuktaśa resides as a youthful prince (*kumārabhūta*).

[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, reflecting in accordance with the true teaching of the Bodhisattvas, reflecting in accordance with the pure conduct of the Bodhisattvas, gave rise to an increase in the power of Bodhisattva merit, and his mind produced clear vision of all Buddhas. His mind produced...
The mind that gives birth to all Buddhas; the mind that causes all great vows to increase and grow; the mind that universally perceives all phenomena throughout the ten directions;
the mind that clearly illuminates the true nature of all phenomena; the mind that universally disperses all obstacles;
the mind that observes the dharma-realm without darkness; the mind adorned with the jewel of pure intention; and the mind that subdues all [adversaries].
The minds of the various Māras gradually wandered until they reached the country of Nalasura, where they searched everywhere for Vimalakṣa.
There they saw a great forest adorned with incalculable trees: namely, various leafy trees spreading their branches wide and lush;
various flowering trees in full, brilliant bloom; and various fruit trees, ripening in succession.
Jeweled trees rain down *maṇi* fruits; great *candana* trees stand in rows everywhere; various *agaru* trees constantly emit fine fragrances;
delightful-scented trees are adorned with exquisite perfumes; *pāṭala* trees surround them on all four sides; *nyagrodha* trees rise up tall and majestic;
*jāmbūnada* trees constantly rain down sweet fruits; and *utpala* and *padma* flowers [abound].
The ponds were adorned with *mālatī* flowers. At that time, the youth Sudhana saw the seer sitting on a grass mat beneath a sandalwood tree, surrounded by ten thousand disciples.
Some wore deerskins, some wore tree bark, and others had woven grass for clothing;
their topknots hung down over their foreheads as they encircled him. Having seen this, Sudhana approached his presence.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, he spoke these words: "I have now encountered a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
A spiritual friend is the gateway to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), for they enable me to enter the path of reality.
A spiritual friend is the vehicle to all-knowledge, for they enable me to reach the stage of the Tathāgata. Thus [he praised] the spiritual friend.
Thus, a spiritual friend is a ship heading toward omniscience, for they enable me to reach the island of the jewels of wisdom;
a spiritual friend is a torch heading toward omniscience, for they enable me to give birth to the light of the ten powers;
a spiritual friend is a path heading toward omniscience, for they enable me to enter the city of nirvana; a spiritual friend is...
Thus, a spiritual friend is one who leads toward the lamp of omniscience, enabling me to perceive the even and uneven paths;
a spiritual friend is one who leads toward the bridge to omniscience, enabling me to cross over dangerous and evil places;
a spiritual friend is one who leads toward the canopy of omniscience, enabling me to give rise to the coolness of great compassion. A spiritual friend...

"Thus, because he leads me toward the eye of omniscience so that I may see the gateway to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), a spiritual friend is one who leads me toward the tide of omniscience so that I may become fulfilled by the waters of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Having spoken these words, he rose from the ground, circumambulated him immeasurable times, joined his palms, stood before him, and said: "Noble One, I have already set forth [upon the path]..."
"Having set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva-practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva-path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, Vimalagupta looked toward his assembly and said: "Good son, this youth has already resolved [upon enlightenment]."
O son of good family with the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: this youth universally bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
this youth universally grants benefit to all sentient beings; this youth constantly contemplates the ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas;
this youth desires to drink the nectar-rain of the Dharma; this youth...
This youth wishes to fathom the vast ocean of all dharmas; this youth wishes to cause sentient beings to abide within the ocean of wisdom;
this youth wishes to universally give rise to vast clouds of compassion; this youth wishes to universally rain down the vast rain of Dharma;
this youth wishes to universally illuminate the world with the moon of wisdom; this youth wishes to extinguish the afflictions of the world.

"O you who are afflicted by the heat of poison, when this youth desires to cause all the roots of goodness in sentient beings to grow, the assembly of sages, having heard these words, each scattered various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers upon Sudhana, prostrated themselves before him, circumambulated him with reverence, and spoke thus:
'Now this youth shall surely protect and deliver all sentient beings; he shall surely...'"
One shall extinguish the sufferings of all hells; one must surely sever forever the path of animals;
one must surely depart from the realm of King Yama; one must surely close the gates to all places of difficulty; one must surely dry up the oceans of craving and desire;

one must cause sentient beings to eternally extinguish the aggregate of suffering; one must surely and forever shatter the darkness of ignorance; and one must surely and forever sever greedy attachment.
The world must surely be encircled by the great wheel-boundary mountains of merit; the world must surely be revealed by the great jewel Sumeru of wisdom.

A sun of pure knowledge shall certainly appear, and the Dharma-treasury of roots of goodness shall certainly be opened and shown, so that the world may clearly discern the treacherous from the easy. At that time, Vimalaghoṣa addressed the assembly of seers, saying: "Excellent!"
"If a man is able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he will surely accomplish the path to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This son of good family has already given rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
he shall purify the ground of all Buddha-qualities. At that time, Vimalacakra addressed the youth Sudhana, saying: "Excellent!"
"Son of noble family, I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation called 'Incomparable Banner. Sudhana said, "Noble one, what is the sphere of the liberation 'Incomparable Banner'?
At that moment, the seer Vimala extended his right hand, stroked Sudhana’s head, and took Sudhana’s hand;
immediately, Sudhana saw himself traveling to as many Buddha-fields in the ten directions as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
He went to the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, where he beheld those Buddha-fields and their assemblies,
as well as the various adornments of the marks and signs of those Buddhas; he also heard those Buddhas preaching the Dharma according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings,
thoroughly penetrating every single word and phrase, receiving and upholding them each distinctly without any confusion.
I also know that those Buddhas purify all vows through various understandings; I also know that those Buddhas accomplish all powers through pure vows;
I also see those Buddhas manifesting physical forms according to the minds of sentient beings;
I also see the various colors of those Buddhas’ great networks of light, which are pure, perfect, and complete; and I also know the unimpeded wisdom of those Buddhas.
Furthermore, by the power of the great light of wisdom, one sees one’s own body before the Buddhas for the duration of a day and night,
or seven days and nights, a half-month, a month, a year, ten years, a hundred years, a thousand years, or even ten million years;
or for an ayuta of ten million years, a nayuta of ten million years, or for half an eon, or one eon, a hundred eons, or a thousand eons.
For kalpas numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions, even up to as many as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,

at that time the youth Sudhana was illuminated by the light of the wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s liberation called "Inconquerable Banner," whereby he attained the light of the Samādhi of the Vairocana Treasury;
and he was illuminated by the light of the Samādhi of the liberation of inexhaustible wisdom.
One attains the light of the *dhāraṇī* of universally encompassing all directions because it is illuminated by the light of the *dhāraṇī-gate* of the vajra-wheel;
one attains the light of the samādhi of the mind of extremely pure wisdom because it is illuminated by the light of the *prajñāpāramitā* of the treasury of universal-gate adornments;
and one attains the light of the Buddha’s samādhi of the space-treasury wheel because it is [illuminated] as one.
Because the light of the Samādhi of the Dharma-Wheel of All Buddhas shone upon him, he attained the light of the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Wisdom of the Three Times.
At that time, the seer released Sudhana’s hand, and Sudhana the youth immediately saw himself returned to his original place.
Then the seer said to Sudhana, "Noble son, do you remember? Sudhana replied, "Yes, I do."
"O noble son, this is the power of the holy spiritual friend, the words of the Rishi. I know only this Bodhisattva liberation called 'Incomparable Banner.

As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have accomplished all supreme samādhis and attained mastery at all times, who in a single thought-moment give birth to the immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas—"

Adorned with the lamp of the Buddha’s wisdom, it illuminates the world universally; in a single thought-moment, it enters the realms of the three periods of time and manifests various forms throughout the lands of the ten directions.

Its wisdom-body enters all dharma-realms and appears before sentient beings according to their minds, observing their faculties and conduct to bring them benefit. It emits pure light that is most lovely and delightful.
How could I know or describe his meritorious conduct, his supreme vows, his adornment of the buddha-field,
the sphere of his wisdom, the range of his samādhis, his miraculous transformations, his playful mastery of liberation,
the distinctions of his physical marks, the purity of his voice, or the radiance of his wisdom? Good son, here in the south...
There is a village named Iṣāyā where there is a brahmin named Śrīghoṣa;
go to him and ask how a bodhisattva learns the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with deep reverence, took his leave, and traveled south.
[Treatise] Regarding the section on the Dharma-gate of the primary entry into the respective stage, from the initial passage "At that time, the youth Sudhana...
down to "I have attained the liberation-door of the Invincible Banner," this portion of the text is divided into thirteen sections: 1.
Instruction and contemplation for further advancement; 2. Gradual travel to the country of Nalasa; 3. The cycle...
1. A thorough investigation of Viśvāmitra’s four visions; 2. A great forest adorned with incalculable trees; 3.
Five visions of the rishi sitting on grass beneath a sandalwood tree while leading ten thousand disciples; 4. The extension of his request; 5. The rishi’s praise of Sudhana; 6.
The rishi’s instruction to Sudhana regarding the Dharma-gate; 7. [The rishi’s] commendation of Sudhana; 8. The rishi’s revelation of the Dharma-gate to Sudhana.

4. Sudhana sees the Buddhas and attains benefit; 5. The Rishi releases [him].
"Good Wealth’s hand has returned to its original place. (13) "I know only this liberation called 'Incomparable Banner'";

the following sections concern the recommendation of virtues and the advancement [of the stages]. As for the *pāṭala* tree, it resembles the *qiū* tree of this region and possesses a very fragrant scent;
its flowers are purple. The *nyagrodha* tree has leaves resembling those of the persimmon tree of this region, and its fruit resembles the *pí* (chestnut/jujube).
The *pazi* (a type of fruit) bears its stem like a persimmon; among all trees, its species is most resilient to age and reaches the greatest height.
Leading ten thousand followers and fully possessing the myriad practices, one asks: "For what reason is this stage called 'seeing the immortals' (*xianren*)?
The answer is: "There are two meanings. First, it signifies that wisdom is pure, as an immortal is pure; it clarifies that this stage is free from effort."
Wisdom manifests as unstained, like a seer; through the second [aspect], wisdom manifests without effort.
By means of the practice of great compassion, one is able to engage with those on various paths through common activities to bring forth sentient beings.

Their dwelling place is adorned with forest trees, clearly shaded to benefit all things, and adorned with ponds and lotuses, clearly manifesting a compassionate abiding in the world without defilement—like a seer beneath a sandalwood tree.

Spreading grass to sit upon symbolizes the tree of wisdom; its spreading shade represents the pervasive fragrance of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Spreading grass to sit demonstrates the wisdom that is effortless in its ability to effectively subdue greed and disorder, clarifying the characteristics of few desires.
The deer skin and grass garments show the practice of few desires and contentment. As for the topknot and hanging locks of hair, they signify the absence of... [the text here is incomplete].
The perfection of the wisdom of merit is thus; those who surround him from before and behind clarify the principal and its attendants, and the perfection of the ten thousand practices.

When Sudhana saw this, he approached his location and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, which clarifies the etiquette of revering the Dharma and honoring the person, and further signifies that the objects of the five sensory realms all return to the ground of wisdom. He then uttered words of praise, saying: "O True and Good Knower!"

One who recognizes a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) possesses wisdom that is effortless (*anābhoga*), for it is inherently real; thus, there is the liberation of the "Unsurpassed Banner" (*Anabhibhū-dhvaja*).
This clarifies that in this stage, the ground of effortless wisdom is spontaneously all-pervasive, benefiting all sentient beings and crushing afflictions without interruption.
Because lower stages cannot equal it, it is called the "Unsurpassed Banner. The Rishi [so named] did so because...
The act of rubbing Sudhana’s head with the hand signifies offering consolation; the act of taking Sudhana’s hand by the hand signifies guidance and reception.

Sudhana’s own vision of his body proceeding to worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields, and arriving at the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields, clarifies that the realm of wisdom is all-pervasive. Generally...

In the eighth stage among the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the eighth dwelling among the ten dwellings (*vihāra*), one must all receive the empowerment, exhortation, and sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas and noble ones;
likewise, in the tenth dwelling of empowerment and the tenth Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one must collectively receive the empowerment and sustaining power of all Buddhas.
Therefore, if one were not so sustained, one might at times stagnate in quiescence or fail to attain full realization.
Because it is the realm of the Buddha, none can advance upon it of their own accord; for from the very beginning, they have not reached the realm of the Buddha’s effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
Thus, the vision of the Buddha’s realm is explained in detail according to the Sūtra. "Ayuta" is a number of ten billion in this land;
"nayuta" is a number of one hundred million in this land. [The text continues: "The sages released Sudhana’s hand."
Vasumitra then saw himself return to his original place; through the empowerment of the power of wisdom, he entered the Dharma.
Having attained the Dharma, he remained constantly so by his own power. Even though the Noble One withdrew his empowerment, there was no difference in what was seen.
Thus, just as one who has crossed to the shore in a boat cannot carry the boat along with them, this is the illumination of the Stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūmi).

At the very beginning, when the novice enters the realm of the effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) of reality, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) serves as the primary factor and the other nine perfections act as its companions.

This stage clarifies that while the effortless wisdom manifests, there is a danger of becoming stagnant in quiescence; therefore, one employs the gateway of great vows to activate the functional application of that wisdom.
Furthermore, it causes one to recollect the original vow to extensively deliver all sentient beings. Such is the progression of these stages.
Because the Dharma prevents [the mind] from becoming stagnant, it is through the gate of wisdom that all stages are universally cultivated.

Regarding the gate of specific stages, this stage corresponds to the seventh stage (*saptamī-bhūmi*) in its compassionate activity, and to the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) in its effortless light of wisdom.
Through the arousal of the eighth *pāramitā* of vows, it causes wisdom and compassion to function with sovereign mastery. This is the first [stage] of advancing by means of the excellence of virtue.
From the passage beginning with "In this way, as for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" down to the point where he takes his leave and travels southward, there are twelve and a half lines of scripture.

Regarding the meaning within this section, it may be divided into six gates: first, extolling the virtues of those who preceded him; second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);

third, citing the name of the village, Iṣāna; fourth, indicating the name of the spiritual friend, Jina; [fifth, describing the encounter with the spiritual friend]; and sixth, [describing the reception of the teaching].
The fifth [section] consists of five exhortations to inquire about the dharma-gate of practice; the sixth is the ritual salutation and departure, traveling southward as previously explained.
Regarding the name of the village in the south, *Īśāna*, this means "Long and Straight" (*Chang-zhi*);

it signifies that this spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) gathers and transforms beings by extending their straight path, free from all flattery and deception, and is therefore named the Brahmin "Long and Straight."
This is translated as "Pure" (*viśuddha*). It is named "Victorious Heat" (*Jvalanārcis*) to signify that this spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is unstained and tranquil;
it signifies that he has overcome the heat of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) and demonstrates the blazing intensity of a supreme fire.

This is the ninth stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*), wherein one attains mastery over the Dharma. It clarifies the ninth power: the perfection of the power of the Dharma (*dharma-bala-pāramitā*).

He manifested the practice of "five-fold heat-torment" (pañca-ūṣma-tāpana) common to non-Buddhists (tīrthika) in order to attract and guide misguided followers toward correct wisdom; by demonstrating that his attainment of knowledge was equal to theirs,
he caused those who followed false views and practiced asceticism in vain to all believe and submit— details of which are provided in the text below.
In the ninth, the village of Īśāna, dwells the Dharma Prince Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
[Sūtra] At that time, because the Bodhisattva Sudhana was illuminated by the liberation of the Invincible Banner (*Ajitadhvaja*), he abided in the inconceivable spiritual powers of all Buddhas;
he realized the inconceivable liberation and supernatural knowledges of a Bodhisattva, and attained the wisdom of a Bodhisattva.
The light of wisdom of the inconceivable samādhi, which attains the cultivation of samādhi-wisdom at all times;
the light of wisdom of samādhi that thoroughly understands that all objective realms abide based upon conceptualization;
the light of wisdom of the supreme excellence of all worlds, which manifests its body in all places and teaches non-existence through ultimate wisdom.
Through the two kinds of non-conceptual, equal dharmas, they universally illumine all objects with clear and pure wisdom;
whatever teachings they hear, they are able to endure and accept them with pure faith and understanding; they are definitively and clearly aware of the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
their minds never abandon the sublime conduct of a bodhisattva; they seek all-knowledge without ever regressing; and they diligently obtain the light of wisdom of the ten powers.
Seeking the sublime Dharma with never-ceasing devotion, they enter the realm of the Buddhas through correct practice;
they give rise to the infinite adornments of Bodhisattvas and bring all boundless great vows to complete purity. With inexhaustible wisdom, they know the web of infinite worlds;
with a heart free from cowardice, they deliver an ocean of immeasurable sentient beings and fully comprehend the boundless practices of all Bodhisattvas.
He perceives the various distinctions within infinite worlds; he perceives the various adornments of infinite worlds;
he enters the subtle realms of infinite worlds; he knows the various names of infinite worlds;
he knows the various languages of infinite worlds; he knows the various inclinations of infinite sentient beings; and he beholds infinite sentient beings.
He perceived the various practices for maturing infinite sentient beings; he perceived the distinctions in the thoughts of infinite sentient beings;
and he gradually traveled toward the village of Īśāna, where he saw the ascetic Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa performing various austerities in his quest for omniscience.
On all four sides were masses of fire like great mountains, and in their midst stood a mountain of blades, steep and towering.
When he had ascended to the summit of that mountain and cast himself into the fire, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet,
stood with palms joined, and spoke these words: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path."
"Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction, I pray that you will speak for me.
The Brahmin said, "Good son, if you can now ascend this mountain of blades and cast yourself into this mass of fire, all the practices of the Bodhisattvas will become completely purified.

At that time, Sudhana the youth thought to himself: "It is difficult to obtain a human body; it is difficult to be free from calamities; it is difficult to attain freedom from calamity; it is difficult to attain [this state]."
Pure dharmas are difficult to encounter; meeting a Buddha is difficult; possessing all the sense-faculties is difficult; hearing the Buddha-dharma is difficult; meeting virtuous people is difficult;

encountering true spiritual friends is difficult; receiving correct instruction according to the principle is difficult; attaining right livelihood is difficult; and practicing in accordance with the Dharma is difficult.
Is this not the work of Māra, or one sent by Māra? Is this not a member of Māra’s wicked faction, falsely manifesting as a Bodhisattva or a good person?

"Desiring to manifest as a scholar while wishing to create obstacles for me in my roots of goodness—obstacles difficult to overcome and obstacles to my life-span—and seeking to hinder my practice of the path to omniscience by dragging me into the various evil realms;
desiring to obstruct my Dharma-gate and my Buddha-Dharma"—when he had this thought, ten thousand Brahmās in the midst of the void spoke these words: "Good son, do not [do so]!"
One should neither form such thoughts nor fail to form them: "Now this noble one has attained the radiance of the Vajrajvālā-samādhi;
he exerts great vigor to deliver all sentient beings with a mind that never retreats;
he desires to exhaust the ocean of all craving, to sever the net of all false views, to burn the firewood of all afflictions, and to illuminate the dense forest of all delusions."
I wish to sever all fear of old age and death, to destroy all obstacles of the three periods of time, and to radiate the light of all dharmas.
O son of good family, many of us Brahmā-devas are deeply attached to false views;
we all consider ourselves to be the Sovereign, the Creator, and the most supreme within the world. We see that the Brahmins perform the austerity of being scorched by the five fires, and...

No longer finding joy in their palaces or attachment to the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and finding no flavor (*rasa*) therein, they all came together to the place where the brahmin was.

At that time, the brahmin, by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), manifested great ascetic practices and preached the Dharma for them, enabling them to extinguish all views (*sarvadṛṣṭi*), eliminate all pride (*māna*), abide in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), and practice great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Thus they were inspired.
With a vast mind, he has resolved upon Bodhicitta; he constantly beholds all Buddhas and perpetually hears the sublime Dharma.
His mind is unimpeded in all places. Furthermore, ten thousand māras in the void scattered celestial maṇi jewels over the brāhmaṇa and addressed Sudhana, saying:
"Good son, when this brāhmaṇa was performing the austerity of the five fires..."
The radiance of his fire eclipsed all the ornaments and adornments of my own palace, making them appear like a mass of ink;

it caused me to feel no attachment or delight therein. I, together with my retinue, came to where he was, and this brahmin preached the Dharma for me, so that I and countless other sons and daughters of the gods were all established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there were furthermore ten thousand kings of the *Īśvara* devas who,
from within the void, each scattered celestial flowers and spoke these words: "Good son, when this brāhmaṇa scorched his body with the five fires,
the radiance of that fire eclipsed all the palaces and various ornaments of our own abodes, making them appear as if— "
"May the gathering of ink cause me not to give rise to attachment therein; may I, together with my retinue, come to that place.

May this Brahmin preach the Dharma for me, so that I may attain mastery over my mind, mastery over afflictions, mastery over rebirth, and mastery over all karmic obstructions. Regarding all [these matters]...
They have attained mastery over samādhi, mastery over ornaments, mastery over the span of life, and even mastery over all the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, ten thousand kings of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, performing celestial music in the void as an offering of reverence, spoke these words: "O noble son..."
"Son, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated my palace, its various ornaments, and all the court ladies.
It enabled us to no longer experience sensual pleasures nor seek them, making our bodies and minds supple and gentle.
Thereupon, I came to his side together with the assembly. At that time, the brahmin preached the Dharma for me, which was able to—"
Our minds have attained purity; our minds have attained clarity; our minds have attained pure goodness; our minds have attained suppleness;
our minds have given rise to joy, even unto the attainment of a body purified by the ten powers.
We have produced immeasurable bodies, even unto the attainment of the Buddha-body, the Buddha-speech, the Buddha-voice, and the Buddha-mind, fully accomplishing all-knowledge wisdom. Furthermore...
Ten thousand *Tuṣita* kings, sons of gods, goddesses, and immeasurable retinues rained down various wonderful incenses from the midst of the sky,
paid homage with prostrated respect, and spoke these words: "O son of good family, when this brahmin scorched himself with the five fires,
it caused us gods and our retinues to have no attachment to the pleasures within our own palaces."
They went to where he was and heard his preaching of the Dharma, which enabled us to become free from craving for sensory realms,
to possess few desires and be content, to give rise to joy in our hearts and a sense of fulfillment, to produce all roots of goodness, to resolve upon Bodhicitta,
and even to bring all Buddha-dharmas to perfection. Furthermore, ten thousand Trāyastriṃśa devas, together with their retinues of devaputras and devakanyās, came forward.
Thereafter, they surrounded him in the void, raining down celestial *māndārava* flowers as an offering of reverence and spoke these words:
"O son of good family, when this brahmin was performing the 'five-fold heat-torment' (*pañcatapana*), we gods were no longer attached to the pleasures of celestial music;
together we went to his place. At that time, the brahmin taught us everything."

"All phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay; may this cause me to renounce all sensual pleasures, cause me to sever arrogance and negligence, and cause me to love and delight in unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, noble son, when I beheld this brahmin, the summit of Mount Sumeru shook in six ways; we were terrified and all resolved our minds upon bodhi with firm resolve."
Furthermore, ten thousand nāga kings—namely, the nāga king Elāpattra, the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, and others—rained black sandalwood from the midst of the sky;
immeasurable nāga maidens played celestial music and rained down exquisite celestial flowers and celestial perfumes as they paid respectful homage, saying these words: "O son of good family..."

Son, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five heats, the radiance of that fire illuminated all the palaces of the nāgas, causing the nāga hosts to be freed from the fear of hot sand and the fear of the garuḍas; their anger was extinguished, their bodies attained coolness, and their minds became free from defilement.
Hearing the Dharma, they gained faith and understanding, came to loathe the nāga realm, and with a sincere heart repented and sought purification.
From the obstruction of karma up to the arousal of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the abiding in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
there were ten thousand yakṣa kings in the sky who, with various offerings, reverently made offerings to this brāhmaṇa and to Sudhana,
saying these words: "O noble son, this brāhmaṇa [who has practiced] the five heats..."
When my body is being roasted, may I and my retinue all give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings;

may all rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others likewise give rise to a compassionate heart. Because of this compassionate heart, may they cause no harm or affliction to any sentient beings, but instead come to see me.
May I and they, together with one another, feel no attachment or delight in our own palaces.
When we came to where he was, the brahmin immediately preached the Dharma to us according to our needs, so that all of us attained peace and happiness of body and mind.
Furthermore, he caused immeasurable yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Then, ten thousand gandharva kings spoke these words from the midst of the sky:

"Noble son, when this brahmin performed the 'five-fold heat-torment' (pañcatapana), the radiance of that fire illuminated my palace and caused all of us to experience inconceivable and immeasurable bliss. For this reason, we came to his presence.
This brahmin preached the Dharma for us, enabling us to [attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having attained non-retrogression from enlightenment, ten thousand asura kings emerged from the great ocean and stood in the sky.
Bending their right knees, they joined their palms in homage before him and spoke these words:
"O Son of Good Family, when this brahmin scorched himself with the five fires, all our asura palaces, the great ocean, and the great earth were entirely..."
This earthquake causes us to abandon arrogance and heedlessness;

therefore, we have come to his presence to hear the Dharma from him, so that we may cast off flattery and deception, abide upon the stage of patience, remain firm and unshakable, and perfect the ten powers.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand *garuḍa* kings, with the King Endowed with Courageous Strength as their leader, who manifested themselves as young disciples of non-Buddhist paths.
Manifesting in the midst of empty space, he uttered these words: "Good sons, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated my palace;
everything shook and we were all struck with terror. Therefore, we came to his presence.
At that time, the brahmin immediately preached the Dharma to us according to our needs, instructing us to practice."
Practicing great loving-kindness, extolling great compassion, crossing the ocean of birth and death, and rescuing sentient beings from the mire of desire;
praising the bodhicitta, giving rise to the wisdom of skillful means, and taming sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.
Furthermore, ten thousand kinnara kings proclaimed these words in the void: "O noble son, this brahmin [endures] the five heats..."
When our bodies were being roasted, from the many *tāla* trees, jeweled bell-nets, jeweled silk streamers, musical trees, exquisite jewel-trees,
and various musical instruments within the palaces where we resided, there spontaneously issued forth the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma,
the sound of the assembly of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and the sound of those seeking unsurpassed bodhi, saying: "In such-and-such a direction..."
In such-and-such a land, there is such-and-such a bodhisattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta;

in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a land, there is such-and-such a bodhisattva practicing asceticism, capable of relinquishing what is difficult to relinquish, up to the point of purifying all conduct for omniscience;

in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a land, there is such-and-such a bodhisattva proceeding to the site of enlightenment; and so on, until in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a land, there is such-and-such a Tathāgata who, having completed his buddha-work...
And as for parinirvāṇa, noble son, suppose there were someone who ground all the grasses and trees of Jambudvīpa into fine dust;
the limit of the number of those atoms could be known, but the names of the bodhisattvas,

the names of the Tathāgatas, the great vows they have made, and the practices they have cultivated, which are proclaimed by the precious tārā trees and even the musical instruments within my palace, are without end.
"O sons of good family who are able to know its limits, we were filled with great joy upon hearing the sound of the Buddha,
the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; we have come to this place, whereupon the Brahmin immediately preached the Dharma to us as was appropriate,
causing myself and immeasurable other sentient beings to [resolve] for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having attained non-retrogression, there were furthermore immeasurable devas of the desire realm who, from within the void, venerated and made offerings with exquisite ritual implements,
proclaiming these words: "O son of good family, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires,
the light of that fire illuminated all the hells, such as Avīci, causing all the sufferings experienced therein to cease entirely."
Because we saw this light of fire, pure faith arose in our hearts; by virtue of that faith, when our lives there ended, we were reborn among the devas.
Out of gratitude, we have come to this place to pay homage and gaze upon you with never-tiring devotion.
At that time, O Brahmin, please teach us the Dharma so that immeasurable sentient beings may resolve to attain Bodhicitta. Then, the virtuous one—
Upon hearing this Dharma, the youth Sudhana was filled with great joy;

he conceived a heart of true spiritual friendship toward the brahmin, prostrated himself at his feet in reverence, and proclaimed these words: "I have given rise to unwholesome thoughts toward the Great Sage, my spiritual friend;
I only pray that the Holy One will grant me forgiveness for my transgression. At that moment, the brahmin [accepted] Sudhana.
And he spoke these verses:
"If there are bodhisattvas who follow the instructions of spiritual friends, Free from all doubt and fear,
dwelling with an unshakable mind— Know that such persons as these Will surely attain vast and great benefit."
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained the ultimate state of unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, the youth Sudhana ascended a mountain of blades and threw himself into a mass of fire;

before he had even reached the middle, he attained the Bodhisattva samādhi of "Excellent Abiding," and upon merely touching the flames, he further attained the Bodhisattva supernatural power of "Tranquil Joy."
Maitrīdatta said, "How marvelous! Noble One, when my body touches such a mountain of blades and this great mass of fire, it is peaceful and blissful.
Then the Brahmin told Maitrīdatta, "Son of good family, I have attained only this Bodhisattva liberation of the Inexhaustible Wheel (*akṣayacakra-vimokṣa*).
As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who possess the flaming radiance of great merit capable of incinerating [all afflictions]..."
May all sentient beings be free from all delusions of view without remainder, never regressing; may they possess an inexhaustible mind, a mind free from indolence, and a mind free from cowardice;
may they give rise to a vajra-treasury Nārāyaṇa-like mind and swiftly cultivate all practices without a mind of sluggishness;
and may their vows be like the wind-wheel, universally sustaining all things, so that their great vows of diligence never regress.
"How can I know or describe the conduct and virtues of that son of good family?
"In this southern direction there is a city named Siṃhavijṛmbhita, where there is a young girl named Maitrāyaṇī.
Go to her and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path. At that time, Sudhana prostrated at her feet and circumambulated her countless times.
After circumambulating several times, he took his leave and departed.

the youth Sudhana" down to "I have only attained this liberation of the inexhaustible wheel," this segment of the sutra is divided into twenty parts.

2. Recalling the instructions of the spiritual friend and proceeding gradually toward the south; 3.

Below the wheel is the virtue of advancing through investigation as described above. When the Brahmin demonstrates this practice, all sentient beings perceive the gates of practice according to their own respective differences.

Within the symbolic dharma, the "knife mountain" represents the stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmaputra*), whose essence is the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) and wisdom; it constitutes the realization of birth and death for the practitioner.
In suffering, one sees only the nature of the Dharma-realm; liberation must be attained through the absence of fear, for only then can one exercise sovereign power.
The flames are the radiance of vajra-wisdom and are also called the Vajra-samādhi.
As the aforementioned devas have already explained, this Dragon King Ena-vara was in his past life damaged by his violation of the precepts.
Because this extremely foul-smelling tree grew upon his head, he was named accordingly. Nanda means "Joy" (in Chinese), and *upā* means "pure faith.
This clarifies that because this dragon heard the Dharma and rejoiced with faith and delight, he attained the liberation of the Bodhisattva’s Inexhaustible Wheel.
This intends to clarify that one who dwells as a Dharma Prince attains the rank of a Dharma Master.

The single practice follows the diverse inclinations and desires of sentient beings, such that each perceives the teaching of the Dharma and the gateways of practice as having inexhaustible distinctions;
because it clearly accords with the faculties of sentient beings and brings them to fulfillment, it is called the "Inexhaustible Wheel.

This is the stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra-vihāra*), which takes the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) as its primary focus and the other nine perfections as its companions. Within the gateway of wisdom, it is categorized by five [aspects].

Regarding the stage that penetrates and governs through the gate of governing by stage: herein, one practices the governance of the teaching to overcome the obstacle of lack of mastery over the Dharma, thereby attaining mastery identical to that of the ninth stage among the ten stages.
From this point, one proceeds through the practice of the resultant conduct until reaching the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*), where the merit ripens;
this is modeled after the fundamental fruit within the ten abidings, which takes the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, the Great Universal Radiance Wisdom, as its primary substance.
Using the second section, "The Gate of Advancing through Merit," it is divided approximately into four parts: first, advancing through merit;
second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), stating that there is a city in the south named Siṃhavikrīḍita;
third, mentioning the name of the spiritual friend, who is the maiden Maitrāyaṇī; and fourth, prostrating at the feet of the Brahmin Jvalanānta and taking one's leave.
As for departing toward the south, the meaning is as previously explained in the first section regarding the name of the city, "Lion’s Leap" (*Siṃhavikrīḍita*).

This is the city inhabited by King Siṃhadhvaja; that king was the father of the girl Maitrāyaṇī. He represented mastery over wisdom as a king, while his practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) pervaded all things as his daughter.
This illustrates how compassion arises from wisdom, remaining within the defilements of birth and death yet remaining untainted by them.

Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of non-defilement and so forth have been exhausted, as clarified by the account of the laywoman Śreṣṭhī (Hushu) in the preceding seventh stage, the habitual tendency of affection for sentient beings is preserved to function as the gateway of compassion. Since the habitual tendency of love for saving sentient beings has not yet been severed, she is titled a *upāsikā*;
by means of this, she fulfills the practice of great compassion within the eighth stage through effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
This constitutes the perfection of clarity, as wisdom arises from compassion;

since in this stage compassion arises from wisdom, she is the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja and remains a maiden, signifying that in this stage she spontaneously benefits sentient beings without the taint of habitual attachment.

[Treatise] The tenth is the stage of the Empowerment of the Princess Maitrīcaryā in the City of Siṃhavijṛmbhita.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana gave rise to a mind of supreme reverence toward his spiritual friends;

he developed a vast and pure understanding, constantly mindful of the Mahāyāna and single-mindedly seeking the wisdom of the Buddhas, vowing to behold all Buddhas and contemplate the realm of phenomena.
Unobstructed wisdom is constantly present before him, definitively knowing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena:
the limit of eternal abiding, the limit of all moments across the three periods of time, the limit like empty space, the limit of non-duality,
the limit of non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena, the limit of unobstruction regarding all meanings, the limit of non-destruction throughout all eons, and the [limit] of all Tathāgatas...
Reaching the limit of limits within the minds of all Buddhas, they are free from discrimination, having shattered the web of conceptualizations and abandoned all attachments.
They do not grasp at the assemblies or the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of the Buddhas, nor do they grasp at the pure lands of the Buddhas.
They know that all sentient beings are entirely without self, that all sounds are like echoes, and that all forms are like reflections. Gradually...
Next, traveling south, he reached the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita and searched everywhere for the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
He heard that this maiden was the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, accompanied by five hundred maidens as her attendants,
and was dwelling in the Vairocanagarbha Palace upon a throne of golden-threaded netting and celestial garments with legs of nāgavijaya sandalwood, where she was preaching the sublime Dharma.
Having heard this, Sudhana went to the gate of the royal palace seeking to see that girl.
He saw a vast multitude of people entering the palace and asked them, "Where are you all going now?
They all replied, "We wish to go to the maiden Maitrāyaṇī to hear the sublime Dharma. Sudhana the youth then thought to himself: "Since this gate of the royal palace..."
Without limit or obstruction, I too should enter the chamber of Vairocana’s treasury where Sudhana has entered;
having entered, I see that its floor is of crystal, its pillars of lapis lazuli, its walls of diamond, and its enclosures of Jāmbūnada gold.
It has hundreds of thousands of rays of light for windows and is adorned with incalculable maṇi jewels and treasure-store maṇis.
The perimeter of the mirror was adorned with the most supreme maṇi jewels of the world as its ornamentation;
it was covered above by countless jeweled nets, from which thousands of golden bells produced wondrous sounds.
It was thus decorated with such inconceivable varieties of precious jewels. The skin of the maiden Maitrāyaṇī was golden, her eyes were deep purple, and her hair was dark blue.

The youth Nīla was preaching the Dharma with a Brahma-like voice; having seen this, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and standing before him with palms joined, spoke these words:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how they should cultivate them."
"O Bodhisattva, I have heard that the Noble One is skilled in providing instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, the maiden Maitrāyaṇī said to Sudhana, "Noble son, you should observe the adornments of my palace. Sudhana prostrated himself and surveyed it everywhere;
he saw within every wall, within every pillar, within every mirror, and within every image.
Within each form, within each mani-jewel, within each ornamental accessory, within each golden bell, within each jewel tree,
within each precious image, and within each precious necklace, one clearly sees all the Tathāgatas of the Dharma-realm—
from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, through their cultivation of bodhisattva practices, to the fulfillment of their great vows and their complete perfection.

The accomplishment of the merits of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma, and even the manifestation of entry into nirvana—all such images appeared without exception, just as all reflections of the sun, moon, and stars appear throughout the void within clear water.
All of this was due to the power of the roots of goodness cultivated by the maiden Maitrāyaṇī in her past lives. At that time...
The youth Sudhana, recollecting the marks of all the Buddhas he had beheld, joined his palms and gazed up at the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
At that time, the maiden said to Sudhana: "Noble son, this is the gate of the Universal Adornment of Prajñāpāramitā.
I obtained this Dharma from as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in thirty-six Ganges Rivers; it was attained by those Tathāgatas."
Each through different approaches, they have caused me to enter this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā;
what one Buddha has expounded, another does not repeat. Sudhana said, "Noble Lady, what is the scope of this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā?
The maiden replied, "Son of good family, I have entered this Prajñāpāramitā."
When one contemplates, observes, recollects, and discerns the gateway of universal adornment in accordance with its direction, one attains the dharani of the universal gateway,
wherein one hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* dharani gateways all manifest before one— namely, the dharani gateway of Buddha-fields,
the dharani gateway of Buddhas, the dharani gateway of dharmas, and the dharani gateway of sentient beings.
