I know only this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā, as do the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

The mind of this Bodhisattva is vast and equal to the realm of empty space; entering the Dharma-realm, his merit is fully perfected as he dwells in supramundane dharmas and remains far removed from worldly conduct.
His eye of wisdom is free from obscuration as he universally contemplates the Dharma-realm;
his heart of wisdom is as vast as empty space, clearly perceiving all objective realms. He has attained the stage of non-obstruction and the treasury of great radiance, being well able to...
They discern the meaning of all phenomena, act within the world without being stained by worldly dharmas, benefit the world, and cannot be destroyed by the world.
They serve as a universal refuge for all worlds, universally know the mental activities of all sentient beings, and preach the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate.
At all times they attain constant mastery; how then could I possibly know [them]?
"O son of good family who can expound those meritorious practices, there is a land to the south here called Trimukha.
There dwells a bhikṣu named Sudarśana; go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and remained full of longing and devotion.
He gazed upon [the teacher] with reverence, took his leave, and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of the primary entry into the respective stage (*bhūmi*), the meaning of the sūtra text is divided into twenty-one sections:
1. Generating a mind of respect toward the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); 2. Mindfulness of the excellence of the teaching; 3. Gradual progression to the south...
1. Traveling the four directions, he arrives at the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhitā; 2. He seeks out the maiden Maitrāyaṇī; 3.
He hears that the maiden belongs to a lineage of royal descent; 4. Five hundred maidens serve as her attendants; 5. He observes the palace where the maiden dwells;
6. He observes the seat upon which the maiden sits; 7. Having heard this, Sudhana proceeds to visit her.
1. After entering, Sudhana beheld the girl and her environment, adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
2. Having seen this, Sudhana formally presented his request. 3. The girl directed Sudhana to observe the results of her environment and her dwelling, so that he might know the causes of her conduct.
4. Having observed them, Sudhana joined his palms and gazed up at the girl Maitrāyaṇī.
15. The maiden *Dārikā* told Sudhana that the name of her dharma-gate is the "Gate of the Universal Adornment of Prajñāpāramitā.
16. The maiden recounted the number of Buddhas she had seen while practicing this dharma-gate:
it was as many as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers, and the names of those Buddhas were all different. 17. The maiden *Prabhāvatī* received this dharma-gate from all those Buddhas.
18. Each enters by means of different gateways, yet the eighteen Buddhas speak it all at once without repeating it. 19. Sudhana said:
"I ask about the scope of this Dharma-gate. 20. At the very moment he raised the observation of the Dharma-gate he had practiced, he attained the Universal Dhāraṇī-gate;
the number of these dhāraṇī-dharma-gates was one million asaṃkhyeya.
Its total number is one hundred and eighteen; twenty-one. I know only this "Gate of Universal Adornment" of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Hereafter, it clarifies the progressive advancement through successive stages for those who travel southward, excelling in their spiritual progress.
Upon reaching the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita, one searches everywhere for the girl Maitrāyaṇī; this is the assembly of wisdom.

Compassion has no dual nature. Hearing that this young girl is the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja and that five hundred maidens serve as her attendants, one clearly understands that within these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), specifically the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-bhūmi*), the two gates of wisdom and compassion universally encompass all five stages.
Since the cultivation throughout these ten stages follows this path alone and there is no other way, she is called "The Teacher" (*Śāstrī*).
The five hundred attendants of the daughter of King Sūtradhvaja who have already heard the Dharma are those practicing within this very stage.
Belief in this single stage encompasses all five stages; when wisdom and compassion are both integrated in this manner, it is only then called the "Ten Abodes.
One should know that these are named the "Abodes" because they abide where the Buddhas abide. This is because, within this stage, one relies upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The realm of retribution is, in its entirety, identical in both name and substance to the realm attained as the fruit of Buddhahood;

it fully possesses the Buddha-realm of Indra’s net where all things interpenetrate, with the bodies and lands of the Buddhas containing one another in infinite layers, and time, seasons, years, and months being entirely without extension or contraction.
Each and every gate is individually complete with all infinite Dharma-gates, just as described in the sutra text.
That which naturally possesses and causes one to skillfully observe is the palace where the maiden Maitrīcaryā dwells, named the Vairocanagarbha Palace;

this is precisely because the fruition of Buddhahood, which encompasses all virtues, and the treasury of practices across the five stages—the gates of the Buddha’s cause and effect—are all contained within this stage.
Thus, it is like the dragon-victory sandalwood pedestal with its golden thread netting from heaven.

Regarding the phrase "preaching the sublime Dharma while seated upon the seat of robes," this clarifies that he sits upon the throne of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) with a body of great compassion for the sake of Nāgārjuna.
He preaches the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body— consisting of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—
and covers and protects all sentient beings with the white and pure net of his teaching, thereby guiding them.
Having heard this from Seat-Sudhana, he went to the gate of the royal palace to seek an audience with that lady. He saw immeasurable multitudes entering the palace;

this clarified that this Hall of Wisdom and Palace of Compassion is a place entered in common by all sentient beings and a capital city inhabited in common by Bodhisattvas of the five stages. Sudhana asked them, "Where are you all going now?"
He went to Samudrareṇu and reported to him, saying, "We wish to go to the maiden Maitrīyaśas to hear and receive the sublime Dharma.
Samudrareṇu replied, "This is clear and beyond doubt. Sudhana the youth then thought to himself, "Since there are no obstacles at this royal palace gate, I too should enter.
Having thus resolved with faith, he entered; having entered, he beheld Vairocana.
As for that Treasury Hall, it is because the wisdom, compassion, and myriad practices of one's own mind and the causal wisdom and compassion of the five stages enter into union simultaneously.
Regarding the floor being made of *sphatika* (crystal), this indicates that this jewel resembles crystal;

although there are differences such as red, white, crimson, and azure, it is categorized simply by its clarity and purity. The pillars are made of *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli) obtained as a reward for the Dharmakāya, signifying purity.
The walls are composed of the vajra that sustains and maintains the myriad virtues, signifying the protection of pure wisdom;
the perimeter walls are made of Jambūnada gold, symbolizing the external adornment of pure precepts;

the windows and casements consist of hundreds of thousands of light rays, representing the retribution-obtained illumination of the mundane through the light of the Teachings; and it is adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) maṇi jewels.

That which is adorned all around by the mani-mirror of the treasury born from the retribution of pure conduct free from defilements arises from the manifestation of the fundamental wisdom that gives rise to the wisdom of differentiation to illuminate the faculties of sentient beings.

That which is embellished with the most supreme worldly mani-jewels arises from the retribution of worldly conduct that is untainted by impure practices. It is further adorned with countless nets of jewels.
The net spread over its top signifies the establishment of the net of teachings to bind those born through retribution;

the hundreds of thousands of golden bells atop it that produce wondrous sounds clarify that the sound of preaching the Dharma pervades the ten directions for those born through retribution. What follows clarifies the adornment of the primary retribution:
the fact that the girl Maitrīcaryā has skin the color of gold clarifies that the Dharma-body is pure and white in mind.

Those born of retribution free from defilement are golden in color; these Arhats and Bodhisattvas are all golden-hued, with eyes and hair entirely deep blue, for they illuminate and protect sentient beings through pure wisdom. As for their Brahma-voice, it is clear and resonant, heard throughout the ten directions.
To cause Sudhana to contemplate their *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (retributive environment), he clearly understands that by perceiving the fruit, one recognizes its cause.
This Dharma-gate is such that within each and every mirror, all the realms of the Buddhas manifest in mutual inclusion,

as described in detail in the sutra: "This Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā was sought and attained by me from the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers"—
this clarifies the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences.
In order to encompass the thirty [stages], those who seek and attain this Dharma from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of six Ganges Rivers comprehensively include the six stages:
the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), the eleventh ground, and the practice of the fruit of Buddhahood;

for all these practices are entirely contained within the dharmas of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), thereby establishing the dharmas of those preceding and succeeding six stages. This is because, during the prior stage of faith, one merely has faith and has not yet realized it.

Because one has truly entered and abides in the stages, the gates of cause and effect and practice for the ten stages and the eleventh stage merely rely upon the dharmas of the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences;

having already perfected the gates of wisdom, compassion, vows, and practice through the harmonization of principle and phenomena, one follows and emulates these throughout the ten stages and the eleventh stage to become thoroughly proficient, as there are no further new dharmas. Therefore, [the teaching] concludes with the preceding ten stages.
Within the eleven stages, there is no establishment of the names of the ten Buddha-fruit titles according to their respective positions;

furthermore, there is neither the matter of seeing the Buddhas approaching from afar nor the ritual of welcoming the Buddhas. The meaning of observing the text according to its progression—whether ascending or descending—is naturally revealed therein.

For this reason, within this tenth stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), the two practices of wisdom and compassion comprehensively encompass the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten... [transferences].

Because the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmana*), wisdom (*jñāna*), compassion (*karuṇā*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), and practices (*caryā*) are all contained within it, it is said that the thirty teachings are, despite the traces of their sequential arrangement in words, one dharma in terms of wisdom, compassion, vows, and practice; they are one time, whether measured by years, months, days, or kalpas.
This applies even to the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā-citta*), as well as the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*). This is one.
Because within this state there is not a single phenomenon— whether universal or particular, identical or different, forming or decaying—
that does not exist therein; thus, according to the text of this section, it causes the youth Sudhana to contemplate the adorned realm,
wherein he beholds [all things] within each wall, each pillar, each mirror, each mark, each form, and even within a single...
Within a single jewel garland, one sees all the Tathāgatas of the entire Dharma-realm: from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, through their cultivation of bodhisattva practices,
the fulfillment of great vows, and the perfection of merit, up to their attainment of equal and right enlightenment,
their turning of the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and even their manifestation of entry into *nirvāṇa*— such images are all seen without exception, as clearly as reflections in water.
One perceives all the various images within space—such as the stars, the sun, and the moon—as extensively described in the sutras.
By means of this realm, one clarifies that a single stage encompasses all stages; because the days, months, seasons, and kalpas do not shift or change, it is said:
"I sought this Dharma-gate from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers; it was taught once, never again."

One must understand that all these are received [by the Bodhisattva]; for these three sets of ten dharmas—the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*)—are collectively contained within a single abode among the ten abodes.
Furthermore, there are thirty dharma-gates within wisdom and likewise thirty dharma-gates within compassion; these also constitute the teachings of thirty-six Ganges-sands of Buddhas.
Furthermore, because each and every stage contains practice-gates that pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
because the metaphor of the sands of the Ganges is used to briefly illustrate this sense of pervasiveness; because one stage is taken to encompass all six stages;
because it signifies that all wisdom and liberation are not separate from the three emptinesses and the six pāramitās; and because within each stage there are six positions.
"Because each of the six stages possesses inexhaustible practices and vows," and so forth,
[the text] cites one hundred and eighteen *dhāraṇī* gates to clarify that this single stage universally encompasses the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages,
and the eleventh stage; thus, the causes and fruits do not transcend these one hundred and eighteen gates in total.
Because they are gathered and subsumed in this way, the one hundred and eighteen great *dhāraṇī* gates do not transcend the practice of the ten *pāramitās*.

Within these, they intersect with one another to form one hundred *pāramitās*. These one hundred *pāramitās*, in turn, do not transcend the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which serve as their mutual companions and supports to constitute the six sublime stages: the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten levels of sagehood (*daśārya*).
Together, they are called the "Gate of Universal Adornment" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, sought from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers;

this number of Ganges Rivers is cited because it represents the smallest numerical unit within this sutra, thereby clarifying that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the initial resolve encompass all sixty factors across the six positions. Thus, [the lower numbers] are excluded.
Even those at the stage of the Ten Faiths have not yet entered the [true] stages; contemplate this deeply and subtly, and you will understand the general meaning.

It is clear that each of these three levels of the Sages—the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications—each contains the Ten Grounds, the Eleventh Ground, and the Ground of Wondrous Enlightenment.
This is because the gateway of the Dharma-realm universally encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; thus, there is but one wisdom, one compassion, and one liberation.
One eon, one year, one month, one day, and one moment are without before or after, and there is no distinction between them;
yet, because various conventional dharmas are established according to worldly distinctions, one must ultimately not form views of extension or contraction, length or brevity.
This is just as when the youth Sudhana first gave rise to a mind of supreme reverence toward his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
With vast and pure understanding, one constantly recollects the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), single-mindedly seeking Buddha-wisdom and vowing to behold all Buddhas.

One contemplates the wisdom that is unimpeded within the *dharmadhātu*, such that this wisdom is always present before one. It is not appropriate to say that one "single-mindedly recollects the Mahāyāna" alone;

for this sutra is the gateway to the *dharmadhātu* and the fruit of Buddhahood, which is incomparable to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Furthermore, it is distinct from the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, as for establishing the fruit of Buddhahood subsequent to the stages (*bhūmi*), this too cannot be established through comparison;

how then can it be said that one "single-mindedly contemplates the Mahāyāna" by using the Great to compare with the Small? All the resolve for awakening (*cittotpāda*) within this Dharma-gate is based on the resolve for the fruit of Buddhahood;
all realms of mental measure, vows, practices, wisdom, and compassion are not to be understood through comparison. They cannot be so.

To compare the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) with the delusive gateways of the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna), thereby causing one to lose the intended meaning of the sutra and falsely transmit the teachings, is the erroneous statement of a translator who did not understand the text. As it should be stated hereafter:

"Exclusively seeking the Buddha-vehicle, the vehicle of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-yāna*), the inconceivable vehicle, and the vehicle of the Buddha-fruit (*buddha-phala-yāna*)," using the term "Buddha-fruit" for Mañjuśrī.
Because one enters the Samantabhadra-dharmadhātu at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, there is no distinction between beginning and end, nor any differentiation of time and kalpas;
it transcends the measure of the conceptual mind and is directly wisdom itself. The rest is as stated in the sūtra.

This stage of the "Consecration" (Abhiṣeka) takes the Perfection of Wisdom as its primary quality, with the other nine perfections as its companions. In this stage, wisdom governs the practice throughout both the preceding and subsequent phases.

Regarding the question of the obstacles to entering the gate of non-duality through mastery over the sequence of the perfection of wisdom and compassion—namely, the obstacles of differentiation and the inequality of wisdom and compassion—it is asked:
"In this stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), since wisdom and compassion are already perfected, why is it not symbolized by a Buddha?
Why, instead, is it symbolized by a princess? The answer is: To clarify that within these ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), a single stage is itself the ten.
The bhikṣu Deven, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, the bhikṣu Susthita, and the bhikṣu Sāgaranāgarāja—
all these abide in the stage of supramundane liberation prior to Buddhahood; Maitreya, the laywoman Śrīmati,
the householder Viśākha, the seer Akṣamālā, and the brahmin Jvalanāntaratejas— all these are the fruit of Buddhahood.
The central circular assembly represents the Bodhisattva path, wherein all positions are mutually inclusive and subsumed within one another.

1. Gradually traveling on foot, he arrives at the country of Trayanī. 2. He searches for the bhikṣu Sudarśana three times. 3.

The bhikṣu named Sudarśana is so called because he clearly perceives the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, and the Insight-eye;
he clearly perceives all phenomena and the dispositions of the faculties of all sentient beings, teaching and transforming them at the appropriate time to bring them to liberation.
Thus, he is named Sudarśana. As for "bhikṣu," this name signifies one who extinguishes disputes; he is able to transform the afflictions, views, and disputes of sentient beings.
Therefore it is said: A bhikṣu asks why, at the beginning of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), one first sees a bhikṣu?
The answer is that this is to clarify that all practices performed by a bodhisattva are intended to cause all sentient beings to be without contention, free from defilement, and transcend the world;
thus they are the foremost of practices. Since all must be undefiled and transcendental, one first sees a bhikṣu to clarify the mind.
Only by departing from the world is one capable of dwelling among the laity to share their radiance and benefit sentient beings; therefore, what follows below clarifies the worldly order.
Walking back and forth in the grove signifies that one’s practice is as vast and manifold as a forest, providing shelter through its roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
This illustrates how conduct is fully perfected; thus, walking back and forth in the grove signifies entering [into the path].

That his skin is golden in color signifies that his wisdom is pure and his mind is settled; that it is white and stainless signifies that his compassion benefits all beings—a reward summoned by his karmic retribution.
The yellow complexion is the retribution for meritorious virtue. The three lines on the neck are produced as the retribution for never speaking falsely.
The broad and level forehead is the retribution for wide and profound wisdom.
Eyes long and wide like blue lotuses are obtained as the retribution for wisdom and compassion. The lips and mouth are crimson and pure like the *bimba* fruit.

The fruit is the bright red color, which is the color of the South. The South is *Li* (the trigram for fire); *Li* is the sun, it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is the mind, and it is the gateway to the Dharma.

Taking wisdom as the sun and the mouth as the gateway for preaching the Dharma, the retribution produced by that which can express the True Dharma through the mouth of the sun of wisdom is [manifested].
The *svastika* marked upon the chest signifies the purity of the activity of wisdom.

His arms are slender and long; this is the retributive karma produced by reaching out to assist others in becoming virtuous. His fingers are webbed;

The karmic fruits arising from turning the wheel of Dharma to benefit sentient beings are thus extensively praised for their merit, all as clarified in the sutras.
These are all the practices of wisdom—internal cultivation and external adornment—the causes of manifold blessings that are never discarded in vain.
Clearly knowing the cause and recognizing the fruit, there are immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.

thus, the Earth Goddess Treasury of Immovability manifests various treasuries of jewels, for this is the practice of meditative concentration capable of manifesting the treasury of wisdom; and the Space Goddess Universal Radiance adorns space.

This clarifies that by observing all phenomena with correct wisdom, one adorns the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and gives rise to differentiated knowledge and performs differentiated practices;
because these do not depart from the emptiness of phenomena, one accomplishes the ocean of merit and the divine rain of *maṇi* jewels.
This clarifies that through the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s great vows, one accomplishes the virtue of great compassion and universally rains down the jewels of the Dharma to benefit all beings.
That the Sumeru Mountain deity prostrates with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, bows low, and joins his palms in reverence illustrates conduct characterized by humility,
freedom from pride, and respect. That the Unobstructed Power Wind-deity rains down exquisite fragrant flowers illustrates speech that is gentle,
humble and respectful, selfless, harmonious and pleasing, free from harshness or malice, timely, and non-false.

Beneficial speech, speech in accordance with the Dharma, words of praise, and all words of universal goodness are entirely due to the wind-god of unimpeded power raining down exquisite fragrant flowers;
those who hear them become fully endowed with the fragrant flowers of precept, concentration, and wisdom.
Therefore, the *Book of Changes* says that *Xun* (the trigram for wind) represents speech and that wind moves across the earth; through this one may clearly perceive the enlightened ruler.
Your ritual propriety and refined speech are modeled upon and learned from the Way to perfect benevolent virtue; thus it is said that wind moves across the earth.
"Earth" refers to *Kun*; as *Kun* represents the multitude, they model themselves on the words and teachings of the noble person (*junzi*), and thus there is something worthy of observation.

This scripture takes correct wisdom as its essence, with the divine mouth issuing forth the words of the correct teaching; these sounds of speech are the "wind," which emerges in harmony with the Way.
The words of the ritual state: "The Night Goddess Spring Harmony adorns her body and prostrates herself with her whole being.

This clarifies that she is compassionate, harmonious, and joyful, and dwells constantly within the night of birth and death, causing all sentient beings who see her to rejoice and give rise to roots of goodness;
thus she is named the Night Goddess Spring Harmony Adorning Her Body and Prostrating Herself.

"Earth" signifies the adornment of the vows and practices of great kindness and great compassion, casting oneself into the realm of birth and death to teach and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;

it clarifies that the Lord of Constant Awakening, the Day-Spirit, who holds the mani-banner that universally illuminates all directions and dwells in space emitting great radiance, is the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena that illumines all sentient beings.
Because he causes liberation through the perfection of discriminating wisdom, when the youth Sudhana went to the place of the bhikṣu and made his request,
[the bhikṣu] stated that he had already generated the unsurpassed bodhicitta; this clarifies that at the first stage, in the presence of the friend Mañjuśrī,
he had already generated bodhicitta and realized the essence of bodhi, which is without practice and without cultivation.
Seeking without attainment and without realization—seeking the Bodhisattva path in this way is precisely not departing from the bodhicitta.
Merely seeking the Bodhisattva path is the fulfillment of the bodhicitta; because the essence of Bodhi is fundamentally unconditioned and manifest, it cannot be sought through effort.

Seeking constantly, seeking in manifestation, having already sought, and seeking for manifestation—because there is no such conceptualization regarding the arousal of bodhicitta, it is called "already aroused."

"Because I have first resolved upon supreme perfect enlightenment and because I have brought forth this mind of the three periods of time, I am called 'one who has already resolved upon supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Bhikṣu replied to Sudhana: 'My years are few and my time since leaving home is recent;
yet, having begun from the very first birth of the wisdom of all Buddhas within the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmi), I practice this conduct—this is what is meant by 'years'.'"
Having left home at a young age, he was also close to this "Ten Practices" (daśa-caryā) gate. The listing of names before and after these practices occurred simultaneously;

the same applies to the "Ten Dedications" (daśa-pariṇāmanā). These three dharmas are practiced simultaneously because the realm of wisdom does not transcend a single kṣaṇa-limit, encompassing all six stages—from faith through the ten bhūmis to the eleventh bhūmi—at once. Furthermore, this begins from the very first arousal of the mind (prathama-cittotpāda).
Because one does not perceive the prior or posterior limits of birth and old age, it is called "leaving home at a young age.
Furthermore, the phrase "those who have drawn near to me in this life" clarifies that one does not perceive the beginning, end, or middle of birth.

The statement "having purified the Brahma-conduct in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers" clarifies the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) through thirty [eons].

The wisdom that harmonizes the Dharma through both skillful means and compassion consists of these thirty factors; because the causes and effects of the Buddha’s stages mutually interpenetrate wisdom and compassion without end, they are called the "thirty.
Because they do not depart from the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path, they are called the "thirty-eight.
Having purified the Brahma-conduct under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, the aforementioned Girl Maitrīcaryā is thus said to have practiced for "thirty-six" [kalpas].
The sands of the Ganges represent the practices of the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*) and the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

The phrase "before thirty-eight Ganges-sands of Buddhas" refers to the superior progress toward the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). These thirty-eight Ganges-sands of Buddhas encompass the positions of the three stages of worthiness;
within the Eightfold Noble Path, they constitute the cause and fruit of the Buddha. This collectively clarifies the occasion of the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
When right knowledge manifests and ignorance is destroyed, immeasurable evil karmas are extinguished and immeasurable wisdom manifests;

this is called being equal in number to the sands of the Ganges. Therefore, one may purify the Brahma-faring for a single day and night, or for seven days and nights, or even before a Buddha for half a month, a month, a year, or a hundred years.

"Reaching until unspeakable years and even until the completion of unspeakable kalpas, one fulfills the six pāramitās"—this clarifies that the fulfillment of the six pāramitās pertains to the supramundane path.

As for the remaining four skillful means, the pāramitās of aspiration, power, and wisdom, these involve entering saṃsāra to accomplish the practice of great compassion; therefore, this bhikṣu speaks only of the six perfections.

Regarding the practice, it is not merely called the ten pāramitās; one also perceives that Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, his preaching of the Dharma, his remaining in the world, and his entry into parinirvāṇa, as well as each of his various teachings.
One who can perceive all these differences is within the realm of clear wisdom.

Although worldly conventions distinguish between them, this wisdom does not undergo even a hair’s breadth of temporal transition. Thus, from the days, months, years, and kalpas above, it is clear that time does not shift.
Furthermore, it says: "O son of good family, when I practice walking meditation, within a single thought-moment, all the ten directions appear before me;
even all unspeakably many Buddha-fields appear as entirely adorned and purified; even the diverse practices of unspeakably many sentient beings appear before me;
and this is because, through the power of accomplishing the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra, [all this occurs] in a single thought-moment."

Receiving the teachings of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Tathāgatas, as extensively described in the sūtras—this section clarifies that the distant and the near are mutually inclusive and immutable, which cannot be fully detailed; in short, it does not depart from the meaning of "a single thought-moment.

This intends to clarify that the essence of the wisdom-body (*dharmakāya*) manifested through the practice of walking meditation is without dependence; because this wisdom is without dependence, it is without interior or exterior.
Because wisdom has no interior or exterior, the ten directions are not distant and this direction is not near;

because the essence of wisdom is neither distant nor near, it is like empty space, clearly illuminating the ten directions. It gives rise to practice according to vows to benefit sentient beings in accordance with their faculties;
it neither departs nor arrives, yet manifests form-bodies in response, like the sun appearing within all waters. By means of this wisdom—
Because objects, time, days, years, and kalpas are by nature devoid of transition, when a single thought of delusion ceases, many kalpas of past and present do not shift by even a hair’s breadth;
distant and near objects do not exist outside of the dust of the senses. May wisdom be empowered by vows;

for vows are the king of wisdom, and through the practice of compassion and supernatural powers, the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct arises entirely from the empowerment of vows. Wisdom is like that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...

Although Bodhisattvas possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because they lack the great vow to benefit sentient beings, their powers are like a single firefly compared to a hundred thousand suns when set against the supernormal powers of Samantabhadra’s conduct and vows. The remaining meaning is clear from the sutra itself.
As for the name of this dharma-gate, "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation Gate of the Lamp that Follows Accordance," it clarifies that the Bodhisattva is, in himself, a Tathāgata.

The liberation door called "The Lamp of Bodhisattvas Following Accordance" is the universal luminous wisdom that accords with the various practices of all beings, giving rise to differentiated wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings, constantly causing them to manifest enlightenment without rest.

This is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as the primary element within the joyous conduct, with the other nine perfections acting as its companions, as they are all integrated within a single path among the gates of wisdom.
Within the gate of cultivating various practices according to stages, one cultivates the supramundane practice of the six *pāramitās*.
This first gate of the ten practices takes the gate of the *jñāna-pāramitā* from among the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) as its basis;

it universally seals all Buddha-realms and sentient-being realms throughout the three periods of time, because all inexhaustible eons are subsumed within a single moment, and because [all things] do not emerge outside of the tip of a hair. The following sections are to be understood by this analogy.

However, from the beginning to the end, it is thus throughout. Within the second section, "The Gate of Advancing by Inferring Virtue," there are twenty-one and a half lines of scripture, ranging from "From all the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" downward to "took their leave and departed. Regarding the textual meaning within this, it is roughly divided into five sections:
first, inferring virtue and advancing; second, indicating the location and land of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); third... [and so forth].

4. He indicates the dwelling place of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), which is on an island in the river. 5. He states the name of the spiritual friend, calling him "Lord of Sovereignty" (Īśvarapati).
6. He prostrates, pays his respects, takes his leave, and departs toward the south. The meaning of the term "South" is as explained previously.
As for the land named "Renowned" (Yaśasvin): it is named according to its teacher; because the teacher possesses renown, the land is called Renowned.
Dwelling upon the riverbanks symbolizes that the precepts are like rivers which must inevitably enter the ocean of wisdom.

Thus, the "youth" signifies that the precepts are pure and undefiled; he is called a youth because he has already entered from the fruit of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body wisdom into the mundane to benefit beings, and having emerged into the supramundane, he leads sentient beings while remaining within the bonds of existence.
The name is established because of sovereign mastery.
