[Treatise] The second is the youth Jñānaśrī, Lord of Sovereignty in the Land of Renown, who presides over the practice of Beneficial Action.
[Sūtra] At that time, having received the instructions of the bhikṣu Sudarśana, the youth Sudhana memorized, recited, contemplated,
and practiced them until they were clear and certain; having attained realization and entry into that dharma-gate,
surrounded by hosts of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, he traveled toward the country of Yaśovatī to seek everywhere for the youth Īśvaraghoṣa.
Devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others in the sky addressed Sudhana, saying: "Good son, this boy is now on the sandbank of the river.
At that time, Sudhana went to where he was and saw the boy surrounded by ten thousand other boys, playing by piling up sand.
Having seen him, Sudhana prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him countless times.
Circumambulating him and joining his palms in reverence, he withdrew to one side and said:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I pray that you will explain this for me. The Lord of Mastery replied: "Good son, in the past, I once..."

"Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, through the study of the arts of writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seals, one immediately attains entry into the Dharma-gate of the wisdom of all crafts and supernormal powers.
Son of good family, by means of this Dharma-gate, I have come to know the worldly dharmas of writing, arithmetic, calculation, seals, elements, and bases;
furthermore, I am able to cure wind-disorders, epilepsy, consumption, emaciation, and afflictions caused by malevolent spirits."
He is able to cure all such various illnesses; he is also skilled at establishing cities, towns, villages, gardens, groves, terraces, towers, palaces, and dwellings of every kind;

he is adept at refining various elixirs of the immortals and managing all occupations such as agriculture, farming, and commerce, ensuring that all matters of acquisition and rejection, advancement and retreat, find their proper place; furthermore, he is skilled in discernment.

He knows the physical characteristics of sentient beings—whether they perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds, whether they will be born in the higher realms or the lower realms—and he fully understands such matters as:
"This person should attain the path of the Śrāvaka vehicle; this person should attain the path of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
this person should enter the stage of omniscience. Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to study these teachings and increases their resolve.
"O son of good family, who has attained ultimate purity, I am also able to know the bodhisattva method of calculation:
one hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi; a koṭi multiplied by a koṭi constitutes one ayuta; an ayuta multiplied by an ayuta constitutes one nayuta;
a nayuta multiplied by a nayuta constitutes one bimbara; and a bimbara [multiplied by a bimbara constitutes...]"
One *bimbara* makes one *kaṅkara*; [and so on as extensively explained] up to:
one *utpala* makes one *padma*; one *padma* makes one *saṃkhyeya*; one *saṃkhyeya* makes one *gati*; one *gati* makes one *upama*;
one *upama* makes one *asaṃkhyeya*; and one *asaṃkhyeya* makes one *asaṃkhyeyaparivarta*.
Countless revolutions, countless revolutions, constitute one immeasurable; immeasurable, immeasurable, constitute one immeasurable revolution;
immeasurable revolutions, immeasurable revolutions, constitute one boundless; boundless, boundless, boundless, constitute one boundless revolution;

boundless revolutions, boundless revolutions, constitute one incomparable; incomparable, incomparable, incomparable, constitute one incomparable revolution; incomparable revolutions, [incomparable revolutions].
One asaṃkhyeya-parivarta becomes one asaṃkhyeya; one asaṃkhyeya-parivarta becomes one asaṃkhyeya-parivarta;
one asaṃkhyeya-parivarta becomes one aprameya; one aprameya becomes one aprameya-parivarta;
one aprameya-parivarta becomes one aprameya-parivarta; one aprameya-parivarta becomes one acintya.
One "inconceivable" is equal to one "turn of the inconceivable";
one "turn of the inconceivable" is equal to one "immeasurable"; one "immeasurable" is equal to one "turn of the immeasurable";
one "turn of the immeasurable" is equal to one "unspeakable"; one "unspeakable" is equal to one "turn of the unspeakable."
An unspeakable number of revolutions of an unspeakable number of revolutions constitutes one "unspeakably-unspeakable.
Furthermore, an unspeakable number of these "unspeakably-unspeakables" constitutes one "unspeakably-unspeakable revolution.
Noble son, by means of this bodhisattva method of calculation, I can calculate a vast heap of sand extending for immeasurable yojanas and know exactly the number of individual grains within it.
They are also able to calculate and know all the various distinctions and sequential arrangements of all worlds in the eastern direction;
it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
They are also able to calculate and know the breadth, narrowness, magnitude, and names of all worlds throughout the ten directions, as well as the names of all eons contained therein.
The names of all Buddhas, the names of all dharmas, the names of all sentient beings, the names of all karmas, and the names of all Bodhisattvas—all these truths I fully understand.
Good son, I only know this Dharma-gate of the Light of Wisdom of Great Supernatural Powers of All Crafts; as for how the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to know all things, I do not know.
One is able to know the number of all sentient beings; one is able to know the number of categories of all phenomena; one is able to know the number of distinctions among all phenomena;
one is able to know the number of all three periods of time; one is able to know the number of names of all sentient beings;
one is able to know the number of names of all phenomena; one is able to know the number of all Tathāgatas; and one is able to know the names of all Buddhas.
I am able to know the number of all bodhisattvas; I am able to know the names of all bodhisattvas.

But how could I possibly describe their merits, demonstrate their practices, reveal their realms, praise their supreme powers, explain their aspirations, proclaim their aids to the path, manifest their great vows, extol their wondrous conduct, expound their various perfections, or elaborate upon their purity?
"O son of good family, Purifying the Radiance of Supreme Wisdom, there is a great city in this southern direction called Samudrapratishṭhāna.
There dwells an upāsikā named Gopā; go to her and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
When the youth Sudhana heard these words, the hairs on his entire body stood on end.
Standing there, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, having attained a rare and precious heart of faith and delight; he accomplished a vast mind for the benefit of sentient beings;
he was able to clearly perceive the successive appearances of all Buddhas; he was able to penetrate the profound wisdom of the pure wheel of Dharma;
he manifested his body in accordance with all realms of existence; and he thoroughly understood the state of equality throughout the three periods of time.

He prostrated at his feet before the Great Ocean of Inexhaustible Merit Born from the Realms, which radiates the sovereign light of great wisdom and opens all the bolts of the cities of the three realms of existence;
having circumambulated him countless times and gazed upon him with earnest devotion, he took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Gate of Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage:

from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Dharma-gate of the Light of Great Supernatural Wisdom of All Crafts," this section is divided into seven subsections:
1. Receiving the Teaching, Mindful Retention, and Advancement; 2. Being Surrounded by Multitudes of Devas, Nāgas, and Yakṣas.
1. Circumambulating three times toward the country of Śrāvastī, he searched everywhere for the youth Indragomin;
the Four Heavenly Kings revealed his location to him. 2. Sudhana then went to that place and saw him surrounded by ten thousand youths.
3. They were playing at gathering sand; having seen this, Sudhana prostrated himself and requested the Dharma he sought. 4. Indragomin.
The Lord told Sudhana that among the dharmas to be practiced, there are approximately ten categories: first, writing; second, calculation and arithmetic;
third, seals, including hand-seals (*mudrā*) and symbolic seals (*mantra-mudrā*); fourth, the realms, referring to the world-systems;
fifth, locations, meaning the dwelling places of sentient beings within those world-systems; sixth, medical treatment; seventh, craftsmanship; and eighth, training and refinement.
The nine stages of the elixir of immortality and the ten stages of the farmers and merchants know the world-transcending faculties of sentient beings;

these are equal to the methods of calculation explained previously in the "Asaṃkhyeya" chapter, and this [chapter] is likewise as that. This is the practice of a Bodhisattva, which is known through the calculation of dharmas;
the Buddha’s wisdom and the perfection of his wisdom-eye know it naturally, without requiring [such calculation].

The algorithms and other matters are as clear in the text itself. This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) acting as the primary factor within the practice of benefiting others, with the remaining nine perfections acting as its companions.
If one considers the dharma-gate of the cognitive domain, a single stage universally cultivates all ten practices;
however, if one considers the specific stages, within this practice of benefiting others, it includes writing, arithmetic, calculation, sealing, agriculture, commerce, and the arts of physiognomy.

Only that which is supramundane is called the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*). Within the first ten stages (*bhūmi*), the essence of the precepts consists solely of the Dharma-body, the Dharma-nature, and the principle of wisdom;
this is like the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha contemplating the ocean of birth and death—the twelve links of dependent origination—as the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
In the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the essence of the precepts is like the "Ocean-Master" skillfully entering the ocean of birth and death. As in the [Daśabhūmika]...
In this letter, it is stated that practicing meritorious deeds out of fear of transgression constitutes the essence of the precepts (*śīla*) for the mundane level;

whereas in the *Daśabhūmika*, cultivating great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) constitutes the essence of the precepts. Thus, the night goddess Priyadarśanā (Joyful Vision) who observes sentient beings is on the Buddha’s right side—left representing wisdom (*prajñā*) and right representing compassion (*karuṇā*). Furthermore, her act of observing sentient beings with joy is precisely the manifestation of loving-kindness and compassion.
The name is used to designate the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), which varies according to the different levels of advancement through the five stages.

Through the penetration of wisdom, all five stages within a single stage are fully present. Herein, regarding the ten wholesome spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) from both superior and inferior perspectives, when discussed in terms of their practical essence, matters such as worldly arts, medical prescriptions, and offerings are as explained in detail in the sutras. Second, the inference of virtue.

Regarding the seventeen lines of scripture from "The advancement [of those] like the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" down to "having taken leave, they departed," the meaning of the text is summarized in five sections:
first, inferring the advancement of their virtues; second, indicating the dwelling place and location of the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra);
third, citing the name of the city where the spiritual friends reside, namely Samudrapratiṣṭhita; fourth, citing... [text truncated].
The name of this virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) is Upāsikā Pañcavimala-pratipatti; having paid her respects and taken her leave, she departed.
The city is named Sāgarāvasthita, which signifies that this upāsikā can contain all virtues like the ocean.

The name of the upāsikā is Pañcavimala-pratipatti, which clarifies that the name was established based on her virtues, signifying that this upāsikā abides in the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Within the *pāramitās*, one possesses the ten *pāramitās*: by being able to constantly practice great renunciation, one possesses the *dāna-pāramitā*;
by wearing plain clothing and maintaining purity, it is called the *śīla-pāramitā*; by having disheveled hair and a ruined appearance, it is named the *kṣānti-pāramitā*;

by the mind never harmonizing with worldly things, it is named the *vīrya-pāramitā*; and by using wisdom and compassion to benefit the mundane world without being joined with consciousness, it is named the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
Having attained meditative concentration, one realizes the Buddha-fruit; this supramundane sublime wisdom is called "wisdom.

Constantly dwelling within birth and death to guide and receive sentient beings, while the mind remains free from feminine karma yet manifests the acceptance of a female body to clarify the practice of great compassion—this is called "skillful means.

Constantly following original vows to deliver beings throughout the six realms is called the "great vow. Fearlessly facing birth and death while constantly turning the Dharma wheel—this is called "power."
The wheel is called "power" because it arises illusorily in accordance with wisdom to constantly perform Buddha-activities throughout all oceans of lands; this is called "wisdom.
Being thus endowed with these ten pāramitās, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) is what is meant by being "endowed with excellence.
When Sudhana heard this, the hairs on his entire body stood on end; this was because he was filled with joy and wonder at hearing the name "Endowment."
Third is the Upāsikā Adhipati Anulomacāriṇī of the City Dwelling in the Sea.

[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated and reflected upon the instructions of the spiritual friend, which were like a vast ocean that never tires of receiving the great rain from the clouds;
he thought to himself: "The instructions of the spiritual friend are like the springtime."
The instruction of a spiritual friend is like the root and sprout of all wholesome dharmas; it is like the full moon, for wherever its light reaches, it brings refreshing coolness to all.
The instruction of a spiritual friend is like the snowy mountains in summer, able to remove the heat and thirst of all wild beasts.
The instruction of a spiritual friend is like the sun over a fragrant pond, able to cause the lotuses of all wholesome minds to bloom. The instruction of a spiritual friend is like...
The instruction of the spiritual friend is like a great jewel island, filled with various treasures of the Dharma within the mind;

the instruction of the spiritual friend is like the Jambu tree, accumulating the flowers and fruits of all merit and wisdom; the instruction of the spiritual friend is like a great dragon appearing in the void, sporting with sovereign ease;
the instruction of the spiritual friend is like Mount Sumeru, where the thirty-three gods dwell amidst immeasurable wholesome dharmas.
Abiding in the instructions of the spiritual friend, he was like Śakra surrounded by his assembly, such that none could obscure him or overcome him as he subdued the demonic hosts of rival paths.
Reflecting thus, he traveled by stages until he reached the city of Samudravetāḍī, searching everywhere for this upāsikā.
Then all the people there said to him, "O son of good family, this upāsikā..."
Having heard that the laywoman was residing within a house in this city, Sudhana went immediately to her gate and stood there with palms joined.
The house was vast and extensively adorned, surrounded on all sides by walls made of various jewels; each of its four sides had a gate decorated with precious gems.
Once Sudhana had entered, he saw the laywoman seated upon a jeweled throne, in the prime of her youth.
He was handsome, upright, and pleasing to behold; he wore plain garments and let his hair hang down, and his body was without necklaces or ornaments.

His physical marks, majestic virtue, and radiant light were such that none could equal them except for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Within his residence, ten billion seats were spread out, surpassing all that exists among humans and devas;
these were all accomplished through the karmic power of the Bodhisattva. Within the house, there were no ordinary clothes.
Regarding food, drink, and all other necessities of life, one should simply place a small vessel before them; furthermore, ten thousand young maidens—
whose deportment and physical appearance are like those of celestial nymphs, whose bodies are adorned with exquisite jewel ornaments,
and whose voices are so beautiful that all who hear them rejoice— should constantly remain by their side, attending to, gazing upon, and contemplating them.
Observing them, they bowed their heads and submitted to their instructions. From the bodies of those maidens issued a wondrous fragrance that perfumed everything universally.
Any sentient beings who encountered this fragrance all became non-regressive;

they were free from thoughts of anger or harm, free from thoughts of resentment or enmity, free from thoughts of stinginess or jealousy, free from thoughts of flattery or deception, free from thoughts of treachery or crookedness, and free from thoughts of hatred or attachment—they were without anger.

With a mind free from anger, a mind free from inferiority, and a mind free from arrogance, he gave rise to a mind of equanimity, cultivated a mind of great compassion, and developed a mind intent on benefiting others;

dwelling in a mind of restraint, he was free from the heart of greedy seeking. Those who heard his voice were filled with joy and exultation, and those who beheld his body were all freed from defilement and attachment.
At that time, having seen the laywoman Guṇavatī, Sudhana prostrated himself before her.
With deep respect, they circumambulated him, stood with palms joined, and said:

"Noble One, we have already set our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet we do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
We have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction; we pray that you will explain this to us. He then replied:
"Good son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
Within this single small vessel, I can produce all kinds of delicious food and drink according to the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings, filling them all to satiety.
Even if there be a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, a hundred million, or a billion sentient beings..."
Whether it be a hundred million sentient beings, a thousand million sentient beings, a hundred thousand million nayutas of sentient beings, or even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings;
or even if there were as many sentient beings as the atoms in Jambudvīpa, as many as the atoms in one four-continent world system,
a small thousand-world system, a medium thousand-world system, a great trichiliocosm, or even up to the unspeakably unspeakable...

Suppose one were to provide food and drink for as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, satisfying all those sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions according to their desires; yet such food and drink would never be exhausted, nor would it diminish.
Such food and drink, such various superior flavors, various seats, and various garments—[all likewise inexhaustible].
Various bedding and seats, various vehicles, various flowers, various garlands, various incenses,
various unguents, various burning incenses, various powdered incenses, various precious jewels, various necklaces, various banners, various pennants, various parasols,
and various supreme and exquisite articles of daily life— all these shall be made fully available according to their wishes and inclinations.
Furthermore, son of good family, suppose that in a single world-system in the eastern direction, all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having eaten my food,
were to realize the fruits of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha and abide in their final bodies; and as it is in one world-system, so it is in a hundred world-systems,
a thousand world-systems, a hundred-thousand world-systems, a billion world-systems, ten billion world-systems, and a hundred billion world-systems.
A hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, a hundred thousand nayutas of world-systems, worlds as numerous as the atoms in Jambudvīpa,
worlds as numerous as the atoms in a single four-continent system (cāturdvīpaka), worlds as numerous as the atoms in a small thousandfold world-system (sāhasra-lokadhātu),
worlds as numerous as the atoms in a medium two-thousandfold world-system (dvisāhasra-lokadhātu), and worlds as numerous as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasra-lokadhātu).

Furthermore, throughout as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have eaten my food shall all realize the fruits of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha and abide in their final bodies;
and it is likewise so in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. Moreover, son of good family:
In all worlds from one world in the eastern direction up to as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
all those bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth, having eaten my food, sit beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment,
subdue the armies of Māra, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as in the eastern direction, so too in the southern direction.
"In the northwest, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, it is likewise so. Good son, do you see these ten thousand maidens who are my retinue?
She replied, "I have already seen them. The upāsikā said, "Good son, these ten thousand maidens are the leaders;
such a retinue of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas are all equal to me."
They share the same conduct, the same aspirations, the same roots of goodness, the same path of renunciation, the same pure understanding, the same pure mindfulness, the same pure inclinations,
the same immeasurable awakening, the same attainment of the faculties, the same vast mind, the same sphere of activity,
the same principle, the same meaning, the same clear comprehension of the Dharma, the same pure physical form, the same immeasurable power, the same supreme diligence, and the same correctness.
Their Dharma-sounds are identical; their voices accord with the various species of beings; their purity is identical as the foremost sound; they equally praise immeasurable pure merits;
their pure karma is identical; their pure retribution is identical; their great loving-kindness is identical in its universal pervasiveness in rescuing and protecting all;

their great compassion is identical in its universal pervasiveness in bringing sentient beings to maturity; and their pure bodily actions are identical, arising in accordance with conditions to cause all who see them to rejoice.
They are identical in the purity of their verbal karma as they proclaim the transformation of the Dharma through worldly speech;
they are identical in attending the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas; they are identical in traveling to all Buddha-fields to make offerings to all Buddhas;

they are identical in being able to manifest and behold all Dharma-gates; and they are identical in dwelling in the stages of pure conduct of Bodhisattvas. Noble son, these ten thousand maidens are able to...
From this vessel, in a single instant, one takes superior food and drink that reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all bodhisattvas in their final births,
śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even extends to all those in the realm of hungry ghosts, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
Son of good family, these ten thousand women, by means of this vessel of mine, can likewise satisfy the celestial food of the gods in the heavens, and so forth.
"O son of good family, wait but a moment; you shall see for yourself how human food is provided in abundance among humans.
When these words were spoken, Sudhana saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates—all invited by the original vows of the laywoman (upāsikā).
Once they had gathered, she spread out seats and had them sit; according to their needs, she bestowed food and drink upon them, causing all to be fully satisfied.
Sudhana said to her, "Noble daughter, I have only known this liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, their all-encompassing virtues are like the great ocean—profound and inexhaustible;
they are like space—vast and boundless; they are like the wish-fulfilling gem—fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings; they are like a great city—"
All their requests were granted; they gathered all manner of treasures like Mount Sumeru, and they constantly stored up the wealth of the Dharma like a vast treasury.
Like a bright lamp, they dispelled all darkness; like a lofty parasol, they universally sheltered all living beings.
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Good son, in the south there is a city named Mahodaya; therein [resides...]
"The lay devotee is named Mingzhi (Wisdom-Light); go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him without weariness, and then took his leave and departed.

[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation-gate of the inexhaustible treasury of merit," this segment is divided into twenty sections:
(1) the section on the vastness of the spiritual friend’s instruction, which is like the great ocean; and (2) the section on contemplation and advancement.
2. Gradually traveling south, he arrives at the city of Samudrapratisthāna; 3. He searches for his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); 4.
The people inform him of the friend's location within the city; 5. Sudhana approaches the gate and stands with palms joined in reverence;
6. The description of the resultant environment: her residence is vast and adorned in various ways; 7. Having entered, Sudhana sees the laywoman (upāsikā) seated upon a jewel throne.
8. Seated there, he beheld her principal body, whose appearance and deportment were most venerable. 9. He saw within her residence ten billion exquisite seats spread out. 10.
He saw a small vessel placed before the seats, with ten thousand young maidens acting as attendants;
there were no other garments, food, or drink to be found. 11. Having seen this, Sudhana paid his respects and extended his homage.
12. He requested the twelve upāsikās to inform him of the dharma-gate he was to cultivate, which is named "The Bodhisattva’s Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit.
13. Because it is like a small vessel, it is fully endowed with all kinds of delicious foods and drinks required by sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the six realms of existence.
14. Upon eating, both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas realize realization.
15. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas in their final existence who are bound to only one more birth, having eaten, all attain Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree.
16. He raises up a multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* companions whose three karmas are identical.
17. Sudhana sees immeasurable sentient beings emerging from the four gates.
18. Entering [the assembly], whatever food was requested according to their wishes and whatever was required, all were completely filled.
19. He proclaimed, "I know only this gate to the treasury of a bodhisattva’s merit. 20. By extolling his virtue, he advanced to accomplish the subsequent practice.
As for the ten thousand maidens, they were fully endowed with the ten thousand practices; as for entering through the four gates, these are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
The fact that food and drink offered from a single small vessel can satisfy infinite sentient beings without exception clarifies that although the vessel’s capacity is small,
when applied through the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* and entered into the gateway of the *Indra-jāla*, the small contains the inexhaustible.
Furthermore, by adding the vast power of aspiration of the *dharmadhātu*-wisdom, even a morsel of food as large as a single atom [can fulfill all].
It causes all sentient beings born throughout the ten directions to eat their fill, yet from the beginning not even a hair’s breadth is diminished;
for a single atom of food is equal in measure to the Dharma-realm, being without interior, exterior, middle, or boundary, and thus unobstructed.
Therefore, this Dharma-door is named "The Bodhisattva’s Treasury of Merit," clarifying that the vow for giving is vast and great. This is the third [absence].
In the practice of counteracting adverse conduct, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine perfections as its companions.

From the perspective of wisdom (*jñāna*), these ten practices are cultivated throughout the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*). From the perspective of the stages themselves, patience constitutes their essence;

for when patience serves as the small vessel, there is no practice that is not fully perfected, and through humility, nothing is not beneficial. Second, regarding the advancement by inferring one's own virtues, from... [text continues].
Regarding the passage from "As the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...having taken their leave, they departed," there are eight and a half lines of scripture.

Within this, the meaning is summarized according to four sections: first, the exhortation to advance by virtue of one's qualities; second, the indication of the location and the city where the spiritual friends reside;
third, the mention of the city’s name, Mahāvyūha, and the names of the spiritual friends, Prajñākūṭa and Vidyuddeva; and fourth, [the description of] the assembly hall.
The gentleman Sudhana prostrated, took his leave, and departed. As for the city named Mahāvyūha (Great Array), its name was established based on the teachings of the Master:

because the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) greatly expands benefit, the city was so named. As for the layman named Sumati (Intelligent Wisdom), his name was established based on the fourth practice, "Unyielding Conduct":
seeing that sentient beings have faculties that can be benefited, he looked up into the void; this "void" is precisely the [spiritual] wealth.

Because they bestow [the Dharma] together with the Dharma, they are called "Luminous Wisdom" (*prajñā-jyotis*). This is the "Abiding in Noble Birth" (*janma-udbhava*) among the ten abidings, and the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) among the ten stages.
Having attained supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), it manifests before them; as their karma within the three realms is exhausted, they shall be born into the family of the Buddhas.

Therefore, among these ten practices, they are called "Luminous Wisdom Laymen" (*prajñā-jyotis-gṛhapati*). They are called "laymen" (*gṛha*) because they dwell in the household and abide in the mundane world while cherishing the Way to benefit living beings.
The youth.
Fourth, the wise layman (gṛhapati) named Adhikara, who presides over the great city of Mahābhiṣaṇa and whose conduct is unyielding.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, having attained the light of liberation known as the inexhaustible treasury of merit and adornment, [proceeded further].
Contemplating that ocean of merit, observing that space of merit, proceeding toward that mass of merit,
ascending that mountain of merit, gathering that treasury of merit, entering that abyss of merit, roaming that pool of merit, purifying that wheel of merit,
beholding that storehouse of merit, entering that gate of merit, traversing that path of merit, and practicing [them].
With his seeds of merit gradually maturing, he traveled to the city of Mahāsaṃbhava and searched everywhere for the wise householder.
He conceived a thirsting longing for the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and his mind was perfumed by that spiritual friend.
His resolve toward the spiritual friend became firm, and through skillful means, he sought to see all spiritual friends with an irreversible mind, vowing to serve them.
These spiritual friends have minds free from weariness; they know that by relying on spiritual friends one can fulfill all virtues,
they know that by relying on spiritual friends one can generate all blessings, they know that by relying on spiritual friends one can increase all practices,
and they know that by relying on spiritual friends one is able to serve them spontaneously without being taught by others.
When all spiritual friends contemplate in this way, they cause their roots of goodness to grow, purify their profound resolve, increase their faculty-nature,
augment their fundamental virtues, strengthen their great vows, broaden their great compassion, draw near to all-knowledge,
fulfill the path of Samantabhadra, illuminate the true Dharma of all Buddhas, and increase the radiance of the Tathāgata’s ten powers. At that time, the goodness—
Vasudatta saw that householder within the city, at a marketplace crossroads upon a terrace of the seven precious gems, seated on a throne adorned with countless jewels.
That throne was exquisite and pure, its body made of mani-gems and its feet of diamond and sapphire;
it was interlaced with jeweled cords, embellished with five hundred wonderful gems, and spread with celestial fabrics.
They raised celestial banners and streamers, spread great jeweled nets, and set up great jeweled canopies.
Using Jāmbūnada gold for the covers and Vaiḍūrya gems for the poles, they had people hold them to shade [the Buddha] above.

With the pure and pristine feathers of the king of geese as fans, they fanned him while burning various wonderful incenses and raining down various celestial flowers on his left and right at all times.
He played five hundred musical instruments, their sounds exquisite and surpassing those of the celestial musicians; all sentient beings who heard them were filled with joy.
Ten thousand attendants surrounded him before and behind; his physical form was upright and majestic, pleasing for all to behold, adorned with celestial ornaments.
He was peerless and most excellent among gods and humans, having fully accomplished the resolve of a bodhisattva.
Desiring to share with the householder his former roots of goodness, [the youth] stood in attendance, gazing upon him and receiving his instructions.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying: "Noble One, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to emerge from all sufferings and hardships; for the sake of..."
For the sake of the ultimate peace and happiness of all sentient beings; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide upon the island of the Dharma-jewel; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to dry up the river of craving;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to give rise to great compassion; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abandon [all attachments]...
Out of desire for love, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to thirst for and yearn after the Buddha’s wisdom;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to emerge from the wilderness of birth and death; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to delight in the merits of all Buddhas;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to exit the city of the triple world; and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to enter the city of omniscience.

"Therefore, you have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet you do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path to become a place of refuge for all sentient beings.
The householder said: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! It is well that you have been able to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
O sons of good family, those who give rise to the thought of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—the threefold bodhicitta—are difficult to find.
If one can give rise to this thought, such a person is then able to seek the practices of a bodhisattva;

they will encounter spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) without ever becoming weary, they will attend upon spiritual friends without ever feeling exhausted, and they will make offerings to spiritual friends without ever growing fatigued.

One serves spiritual friends without weariness, never giving rise to sorrow or distress; one seeks spiritual friends without ever turning back; one cherishes spiritual friends without ever abandoning them;
one attends to spiritual friends without even a moment’s rest; one gazes upon spiritual friends without ceasing for an instant;
one practices the teachings of spiritual friends without ever becoming indolent; and one receives the mind of spiritual friends as one's own.
"Without error, son of good family, do you see these people in my assembly? Sudhana replied, "Yes, I see them, householder.

The householder said, "Son of good family, I have caused them to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, to be born into the family of the Tathāgata, to increase their pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), and to dwell securely in the immeasurable *pāramitās*."
By training in the ten powers of a Buddha, one leaves behind the seeds of the mundane world and dwells in the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
one abandons the cycle of birth and death, turns the wheel of the True Dharma, and extinguishes the three evil destinies to abide in the path of the True Dharma.

Just as all Bodhisattvas are able to protect and deliver all sentient beings, O son of good family, I have attained the liberation door called "The Treasury of Merit Born According to One’s Wishes," such that whatever may be required is entirely provided.
He fulfills their wishes— namely, clothing, necklaces, elephants, horses, chariots, flowers, incense, banners, parasols, food, drink,
medicinal decoctions, houses, dwellings, couches, seats, lamps, slaves, cattle, sheep, and various attendants—
all such articles of daily life and whatever else they require, he causes them all to be fully provided; and even for them, he expounds the true and wondrous Dharma.
"Good son of the Dharma, wait but a moment; you shall see for yourself.

When these words were spoken, immeasurable sentient beings from various locations, various worlds, various lands, and various cities—each with distinct forms and different desires—arrived together in an infinite number through the power of the Bodhisattva’s past vows.
At that time, each person according to their desire made their requests. Then the householder, knowing that the assembly had gathered, focused his mind for a moment and looked up into the void;
whatever they required descended from the sky, and the entire assembly was fully satisfied.
Thereafter, he further preached various teachings for them, specifically for those who had been satisfied by obtaining excellent food.

It is the teaching on the various practices for accumulating merit that lead away from poverty; the practice of knowing all dharmas; the practice of accomplishing the food of dharma-joy and the delight of dhyāna;
the practice of cultivating and perfecting the primary and secondary marks; the practice of increasing and accomplishing the conduct that is difficult to subdue;
the practice of being well-able to comprehend the unsurpassed food; and the practice of accomplishing inexhaustible great majestic power to subdue Māra and his enemies.
To those who have obtained excellent drink and are fully satisfied, he preaches the Dharma so that they may renounce attachment to birth and death and enter the flavor of the Buddha-dharma;
to those who seek to obtain various supreme flavors, he preaches the Dharma so that they may all attain the mark of the supreme flavor of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
and to those who have obtained vehicles and are fully satisfied, he proclaims for them the various... [seeds].
He causes all who encounter these various Dharma-gates to board the Mahāyāna vehicle;

for those who lack clothing, he provides them with the teaching so that they may obtain the raiment of pure shame and modesty, up to and including the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous color—there is nothing among these that he does not fully provide.
Thereafter, he preaches the Dharma to each according to their needs, and once they have heard the Dharma, they return.
Having returned to his own place, the householder then revealed to the youth Sudhana the inconceivable realm of liberation of a bodhisattva and said to him:
"Son of good family, I know only this door of liberation called the 'Treasury of Merit Arising According to One's Wishes.
As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have achieved the jewel-hand that universally covers all ten directions..."
Throughout the lands and realms, by the power of mastery, he rains down all manner of requisites for life—
namely, various kinds of precious jewels, various kinds of necklaces, various kinds of jeweled crowns, various kinds of garments,
various kinds of music, various kinds of flowers, various kinds of perfumes, various kinds of powdered incense, and various kinds of burning incense.
Various jeweled canopies of diverse colors and various banners and streamers fill all the dwellings of sentient beings as well as the assembly grounds and *bodhimaṇḍas* of all Tathāgatas;
whether for the sake of maturing all sentient beings or for the sake of making offerings to all Buddhas,
how could I, O Good Man, know or speak of those merits, sovereign spiritual powers, and masteries?
"To the south of here, there is a great city named Siṃhala. There dwells an elder named Dharmadhara-śikhin;
you should go to him and ask how a bodhisattva learns the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with reverence and respect, as if honoring a disciple, he thought thus: "By this..."

Householder, may you protect and mind me, enabling me to see the path to omniscience; may my affectionate regard for spiritual friends be uninterrupted; may my vision of spiritual friends be unbreakable and respectful;
may my mind always be able to comply with the instructions of spiritual friends; may I have firm and resolute faith in the words of spiritual friends;
may I constantly give rise to a profound heart in serving spiritual friends; and may I prostrate at their feet and circumambulate them without end.
Having measured the circumference [of the site] and gazed upon it with earnest devotion, he took his leave and departed.

[Treatise: Within the first section on the Dharma-gate of entering the proper state, from the passage beginning "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this liberation-door of the treasury of merit arising according to one's wishes," in this segment:
The Meaning is divided into ten sections: 1. Contemplating and advancing according to the teachings bestowed by the spiritual friend; 2.
Proceeding gradually until reaching the city of Mahāvyūha and seeking out the layman Vimalakīrti; 3. Developing a yearning and reverent aspiration for the spiritual friend; 4.
Recalling that one should serve all spiritual friends with a mind free from weariness; 5. Beholding him...
1. The layman was in the city, at a jeweled terrace on a street in the marketplace, seated upon a throne adorned with countless jewels.
2. Sudhana requested what he sought from the layman. 3. The layman praised him for being able to resolve upon the great bodhicitta and seek the path of a bodhisattva.
4. The layman showed Sudhana the multitude who were able to resolve upon the great bodhicitta. 5. Nine.
The householder told Sudhana that the dharma-gate he had practiced is called the "Liberation Gate of the Treasury of Merit Born According to One's Wishes.
Whatever was required was entirely fulfilled. He waited for the assembly to gather and demonstrated his method of giving;
looking up into the void, whatever was needed descended from the sky, filling everything completely, and then he preached the Dharma for them.

After [the passage] "The Dharma proceeds from me; I know only this door of liberation, the treasury of merit produced according to one's will," the following describes the laywoman’s advancement to the preceding stage by inferring her virtues.

By means of a small vessel, she clarifies the gate of patience, abandoning arrogance, indolence, and haughtiness as she offers food and drink. This fills the interior of this stage, manifesting a mind of diligence.
By practicing the contemplation of emptiness with a mind that is supple and constant, one eliminates afflictions and attains the mind of unsurpassed wisdom.
All reliance upon the True Dharma and the roots of goodness for rebirth as humans or devas are contained therein. The householder says:
"Born into the family of the Tathāgata" refers to the Pure Dharma; this stage is the fourth, the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*), and it is also among the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
In the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), the karma of the three realms is exhausted and one is born into the family of the Tathāgata; however, worldly wisdom and compassion are not yet perfected.
During the fifth stage and within the sixth stage, one practices and studies the two types of knowledge—conventional and ultimate—and finally attains the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
With the three gates of liberation manifest before them, they spontaneously exercise supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to transform and teach throughout the ten directions.
Thereafter, from the seventh dwelling and the seventh stage onward, one enters the mundane world and performs deeds identical to those of ordinary beings, practicing the gateway of great compassion.
In the eighth stage, one partially attains effortlessness; in the tenth stage, the power of a Buddha is finally perfected;
and in the eleventh stage, one spontaneously benefits sentient beings. Therefore, regarding this upward gazing at the void, it is the practice of diligence that is cultivated throughout all [stages].
All karmic suffering is completely severed; all Buddha-dharmas, as well as the merits of humans and devas, are entirely contained therein.

By practicing only the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and penetrating the gate of the quiescence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), all afflictions naturally cease to appear, and all clear wisdom naturally manifests before one.
This has been stated according to the essential points; the extensive meaning is self-evident in the sūtras themselves.

The fourth is the practice of being unyielding, which takes diligence as its primary element and the other nine as its companions. Within the gate of wisdom, these ten practices are identical across the five stages.
Within the gate of the stages, they are distinguished by the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena, the understanding of dependent origination, and liberation as supreme;
they counteract the residual habits of the three realms, manifest the dharmakāya-wisdom, and bring about birth into the family of the Tathāgata at the initial moment of the first stage.
In the fourth stage, one initiates the Buddha-wisdom and is born into the family of the Tathāgata;

in the eighth stage, the wisdom that is free from effort manifests, purifying the delusions of the three realms and bringing forth the Buddha-wisdom, whereby one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s effortless wisdom;
and in the tenth stage, through wisdom and compassion that universally save, one receives the rank of a Buddha—this, too, is birth.
In the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the stages are established according to this very model; these ten abodes (*vihāra*) represent the progressive advancement of the ten stages.

Unlike the provisional teachings where the fruit of Buddhahood occurs after the ten stages, and where the forty mental grounds of the three vehicles constitute the stage of application (*prayoga-mārga*) while the ten stages constitute the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), in this *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the ten abodes constitute the path of vision.

The ten stages of practice (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and the eleven stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the preparatory cultivation (*prayoga*) for the sake of making [the practice] habitual and proficient.

Therefore, the fruit of Buddhahood first manifests at the beginning; this is because, through the compassionate vows of Samantabhadra, the great function of wisdom and compassion is made habitual, proficient, and sovereign, and because the light of the fundamental, universal radiance-wisdom (*mūla-samantaprabhā-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata himself manifests. Thus, from beginning to end, it is fundamentally [one].
In the end, because there is no differentiation of time, duration, or measure, it is spoken of according to reality by means of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya;
this is not the same as what is understood through the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles. Therefore, one must observe all things in relation to the source.

Ultimately, when the habitual tendencies for the Buddha-fruit are perfected and the practices of Samantabhadra are fulfilled, one simply employs a single approach for the sake of teaching and transforming others.
To all sentient beings, he practices eternally and constantly from beginning to end, without start or finish, and without formation or destruction;
his perpetual vocation is simply to manifest through wisdom throughout the ten directions and within all six realms of existence to benefit living beings.
From the moment he first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment and gives rise to faith to practice, he generates such faith and joy, and he generates such a vow.

May I give rise to such a resolve and seek to perceive such a path: from the first moment of generating the bodhicitta, through the power of meditative concentration and contemplation, may I realize union with the Dharma-body and manifest the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance. May I clearly know that the nature of the ocean of birth and death for all myself and others is inherently liberated;
yet, solely for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, I shall lead them to dissolve their delusions and depart from the suffering of false conceptualization.
Therefore, one does not perceive whether one’s own self attains Buddhahood or does not attain Buddhahood.

If one gives rise to the thought of plotting to achieve Buddhahood, know that such a person is far removed from the Buddha-way. If, however, one relies solely on the power of the natureless Dharmakāya—wherein self and other are detached from inherent nature, free from arising and ceasing—one gives rise to the power of skillful means, the power of great vows, and the power of great compassion.

The gate is without action, yet it acts to give rise to infinite vows and aspirations, teaching and transforming all sentient beings within the dharma-realm who lack inherent nature, causing them to awaken from delusion and realize the principle that their own minds are devoid of inherent nature.
When one is bound by the attachments of false conceptualization, one neither speaks of attaining Buddhahood nor speaks of not attaining Buddhahood; one must not harbor such thoughts or plans.

The reality of the situation is as follows: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* establishes five stages of the teaching solely to attract and guide those who have not attained what they claim to have attained, who have not reached what they claim to have reached, and who, though not yet fulfilled, claim to be fulfilled—those who are mired in the obstacles of defilement and purity regarding the path to Bodhi and the practices of a Bodhisattva, harboring a mind of complacency and the notion that there is rest.
Thus, it establishes fifty successive layers of cause and effect.

The one hundred and ten successive dharma-gates prevent stagnation and ensure that the mind of cessation and relinquishment does not persist, thereby fulfilling the vows of Samantabhadra and reaching the ultimate state of inexhaustibility.

Thus, within the second section, the "Gate of Advancing by Recommending Virtue," the fifteen and a half lines of scripture from "Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed" are categorized and divided.
Regarding the five gates: first, "Advancing by Inference through Virtue" refers to the section beginning with "Just as all Bodhisattvas... and so forth.
Second, "Indicating the Location of the Spiritual Friend" refers to the South, as explained previously.
Third, "Indicating the City Where the Spiritual Friend Resides": the city is named Siṃhala (Lion Palace); this name is established based on the Teacher, for the Lion represents fearlessness.
Yi-ming explains that within this fifth stage, the Practice Free from Delusion and Confusion, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) serves as the palace.

There is an elder named Dharmaratna-śekhara who represents the fact that the meditative practice performed by this elder is the sovereign and unimpeded functioning of the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
This meditation universally encompasses the practices of the ten *pāramitās*, and the Eightfold Noble Path is entirely contained therein.
He descended to the house where the elder resided; that residence consisted of ten-story pavilions and had eight gates.

This signifies that the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) universally encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which is why it is called the "Crest of the Dharma-Jewel" (*Dharmaratna-śikhara*). It represents the gathering of all stages [of practice] and the reaching of the summit of the Dharma (*dharmakoṭi*).
Having performed the fivefold prostration, he took his leave.
