Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Eleven: Entering the Dharma Realm.
[Treatise] The fifth master, Ratnaśikhin, the Elder of Siṃhala City, presides over the practice of departing from delusion and confusion.
[Sūtra] At that time, having heard this liberation from the householder Sumati, the youth Sudhana traveled through that ocean of merit,
cultivated that field of merit, gazed upon that mountain of merit, proceeded toward that ford of merit, and opened that [gate of merit].

Observing that treasury of merit, purifying that wheel of merit, savoring that mass of merit, generating that power of merit, and increasing that force of merit, he proceeded by stages toward the city of Siṃhapura.
Searching everywhere, he saw the elder Ratnaśikhin in the marketplace; he immediately approached him, prostrated at his feet, and paid homage.

Circumambulating him countless times, he stood with palms joined and said: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Excellent, Noble One! I pray that you will explain to me the path of all bodhisattvas, so that by means of this path I may proceed."
At that time, the Universal Knower took Sudhana by the hand and led him to his residence, showing him the house and saying these words: "Noble son, look now at my home.
Then Sudhana saw that the house was pure and radiant, fashioned of true gold, with walls of white silver and a palace of crystal, and adorned with sapphire-blue lapis lazuli.
The pavilions were fashioned with exquisite gems of mother-of-pearl as their pillars, adorned throughout with hundreds of thousands of varieties of jewels.
Lion thrones were made of red pearl-maṇi, canopies of maṇi, and nets of pearls covered them from above.
A pool of agate jewels was filled with fragrant water, and immeasurable jewel trees stood in rows all around. That residence was vast and spacious, consisting of ten stories.
Having entered through the eight gates, Sudhana observed them in succession: he saw that on the lowest level, all kinds of food and drink were being given;
on the second level, various precious garments were being given; on the third level, all manner of precious ornaments were being bestowed;
on the fourth level, beautiful maidens as well as all sorts of exquisite and rare jewels were being given; and so on up to the fifth level...
Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage gathered like clouds, expounding all dharmas to benefit the world and accomplishing all *dhāraṇī* gates,
all seals of samādhi, and the practices of samādhi through the light of wisdom. There, on the sixth level,
they saw bodhisattvas who had all already accomplished profound wisdom, clearly understanding and penetrating the nature of all phenomena, and were fully perfected.
In the inconceivable and wondrously adorned site of enlightenment, they gathered together within the gate of unimpeded conduct—
the samādhi of the vast dhāraṇī that is free from obstacles— to analyze and reveal the gates of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
namely: the *prajñāpāramitā* of the treasury of tranquility, and the wisdom that skillfully discriminates all sentient beings.

The gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Immovable," the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Light of Detachment," the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Inconquerable Treasury," the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Illuminating the Wheel of Sentient Beings," the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Oceanic Treasury," and the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Eye’s Renunciation and Attainment."
The gate of the *pāramitās* that enters the inexhaustible treasury; the gate of the *pāramitās* that is the ocean of all skillful means;
the gate of the *pāramitās* that enters the ocean of all worlds; the gate of the *pāramitās* of unimpeded eloquence;
the gate of the *pāramitās* that accords with sentient beings; and the gate of the *pāramitās* that is unobstructed.

The *prajñāpāramitā* gate of "Radiant Light," the *prajñāpāramitā* gate of "Constantly Contemplating Past Conditions to Spread the Clouds of Dharma," and such hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* *prajñāpāramitā* gates as these were seen on the seventh tier; there,
various bodhisattvas had attained the patience like an echo (*pratibhāsa-kṣānti*), and through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), they discerned and observed them, thereby emerging.

Free from all [obstructions], they are able to hear and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas. Upon seeing the eighth level, they see immeasurable bodhisattvas gathered therein, all of whom have attained supernatural powers and never fall back.
They are able to use a single voice to pervade the lands of the ten directions;

their bodies appear universally in all places of practice, reaching throughout the entire dharma-realm without exception. They enter the realm of the Buddhas everywhere and behold the Buddhas everywhere.
One’s body appears as the foremost among all the assemblies of Buddhas, expounding the Dharma;
one sees the ninth tier where the assembly of Bodhisattvas bound to one more birth is gathered; one sees the tenth tier filled with all Tathāgatas;
from the first generation of the mind of awakening, one cultivates the Bodhisattva practices, transcends birth and death, and brings them to full completion.
"By means of his vows and supernatural powers, he purifies Buddha-fields, assembles the congregations at the sites of enlightenment, turns the wheel of the true Dharma, and subdues sentient beings;
may all such things be clearly seen. At that time, having witnessed these events, Sudhana said:
"Noble One, by what cause and condition has this pure assembly been brought about? What roots of goodness were planted to obtain such a retribution? The elder replied:
"O noble son, I recall that in the past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there was a world named Perfectly Adorned.
There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Boundless Light Universally Adorning the Dharma Realm reigned, his ten titles being fully perfected.
When that Buddha entered the city, I played musical instruments and burned a single pellet of incense for him."
I dedicate these merits from this offering toward three goals: namely, to be forever free from all poverty and suffering;
to always behold the Buddhas and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); and to constantly hear the True Dharma.
It is by virtue of obtaining such rewards that, O son of good family, I know only this bodhisattva liberation door of the immeasurable jewel-treasury of merit, as do the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
They attain the inconceivable treasure-trove of merit and enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s body, which is non-conceptual; they receive the supreme cloud of Dharma, which is non-conceptual;
they cultivate the implements of merit, which are non-conceptual; they fully bring forth the net of Samantabhadra’s conduct, which is non-conceptual;
they enter the realm of samādhi, which is non-conceptual; and they abide in the roots of goodness of Bodhisattvas, which are non-conceptual.
The Tathāgata dwells in the realization of non-discrimination, abides in the equality of the three periods of time, and dwells in the realm of the universal eye of non-discrimination;
he never grows weary throughout all kalpas. How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Veṇuvana (Roots of Bamboo), and in that land there is a city named...
He said, "Within the Universal Gate there is an elder named Universal Eye; go to him and ask how a bodhisattva learns the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and then took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate for entering the actual stage, from the passage beginning "At that time, Sudhana...
down to "...I only know this Bodhisattva liberation-door of the Treasury of Immeasurable Merit," the meaning is divided into ten sections: 1.
Increasing the ocean of merit through the instructions of the spiritual friend; 2. Progressing gradually toward the south...
1. He proceeded toward the city of Siṃhapura and searched throughout its three circuits. 2.
He saw the elder Ratnacūḍa in the marketplace and paid him fourfold homage, formally presenting his request. 3. The elder took Sudhana by the hand and led him to his residence. 4.
He had Sudhana observe his dwelling, which was composed of various jewels, having ten stories and eight gates. 5. [He observed] the seven... [of that dwelling].
1. Sudhana, having observed this, inquires about the causes for his cultivation; 2. the Elder explains the causes he cultivated in the past; 3.
he further sets forth the dedication toward the three places; 4. [the section on] advancing by inferring virtue. Regarding the exegesis following the text:

one searches everywhere for the Elder Ratnaśikhin’s clear and universal observation that the mind and its objects are empty, and that there are three types of meditative concentration involving distraction.
The gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that is without reliance, without attainment, and without realization is seen within the marketplace as the clarity of stillness amidst chaos;

if one looks toward the "Elder Liberation" within the Ten Abodes, it represents entering *samādhi* and clarifying the gate of the body containing Buddha-lands, which signifies the initial establishment of the essence of concentration.
This concentration within the Ten Practices clarifies the constant nature of the essence of practice.

Dwelling in the marketplace of birth and death to gather and transform sentient beings without failing the essence of meditative concentration—because movement and function are both quiescent and the nature is inherently detached—one immediately proceeds to pay homage; this signifies swiftly attaining that essence of concentration without delay.
Below, the formal presentation of the request follows: "Grasping the hand of Sudhana" refers to being guided and received, as he is about to go to his dwelling place.
"Showing him his house and causing Sudhana to observe it" is intended to make known the underlying cause.
"The house is pure, radiant, and composed of true gold" refers to the stages, taking *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) as the primary factor and the other nine *pāramitās* as its companions;
it clarifies that the essence of concentration is pure and stainless, and that its karmic fruition is manifested as a house made of radiant true gold.
The walls made of white silver signify that the essence of dhyāna constitutes the precepts (*śīla*), for the precepts have the meaning of protection.

The palace made of *sphaṭika* signifies that the essence of dhyāna manifests wisdom (*prajñā*) and accomplishes patience (*kṣānti*); this jewel resembles water in its brilliant purity, yet it possesses various colors.
The multi-storied pavilions made of deep blue *vaiḍūrya* signify that one practices diligence (*vīrya*) by means of the essence of dhyāna.
The contemplative observation becomes even more luminous, pure, and clean. The pillars are made of exquisite *śukti* gems, for through meditation (*dhyāna*), one practices and maintains all dharmas.
Hereafter, the remaining ornaments are arranged in succession according to the order of the ten *pāramitās*;
the ten-story pavilion likewise corresponds to these ten *pāramitās*, starting from the bottom.
Arranging them upward, there is naturally a sequence. As for the opening of the eight gates, each side has two gates, totaling eight across the four directions;

this clarifies the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path. The tenth layer clarifies the tenth *jñāna-pāramitā* (Wisdom Perfection), the perfect realization of the causes and effects of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, fulfilled in a single thought-moment, and the teaching and transforming of sentient beings.
Entering into *nirvāṇa*, all are fundamentally without movement; this is because, within the realm of wisdom, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently thus.
Below this, within the nine successive layers, they are sequentially assigned: first to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), second to morality (*śīla*), and third to patience (*kṣānti*).

These are all established through the manifestation of the Dharma by means of karmic retribution arising from practice, as taught to Sudhana regarding his original cause, wherein he said: "I recall the past..."
In kalpas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, there was a world named Paripūrṇavyūha, where the Buddha was named Anantaprabhā-dharmadhātu-samanta-vyūha-rāja.
When that Buddha entered the city, I played musical instruments and burned a single pellet of incense as an offering;
by dedicating this merit toward three specific goals, I obtained this karmic fruit: my dwelling house is like...

This clarifies that the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has been attained; the statement that the number of Buddha-fields within the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*) serves as the measure indicates that this concentration transcends the dust of delusion.
Because one’s own wisdom enters this dhyāna-gate of the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), it signifies the manifestation of wisdom that transcends the dust of delusion.
Furthermore, the expression "the sound of joy arising from skillful teaching" signifies that wisdom arises from the cause of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, regarding the "fixed incense," it refers to burning but a single pellet;
when the fivefold Dharma-body is fully prepared and dedicated toward the three places, one enters this Samādhi-gate of Unobstructed Quiescence and Function.

Thus, one can forever be free from poverty, constantly see all Buddhas and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and perpetually hear the True Dharma—these are the three places. As the Sūtra states in detail: "I alone..."
One who knows this bodhisattva’s liberation door of the immeasurable treasure-store of merit understands the samādhi door of unimpeded application to tranquil activity;

it is able to encompass both merit and wisdom, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the four means of attraction and the four immeasurables, all of which are contained within it.
For this reason, this elder is named Ratnaśikhin (Jewel-Crest), signifying this practice of following along.
The gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) collectively encompass the principles of the Dharma; all other details are fully contained within the text itself.

This section constitutes the fifth [stage], the practice of being free from delusion and confusion (*moha-vikṣepa*), which takes the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) as its primary focus and the other nine perfections as its companions.

In terms of the gates of wisdom (*jñāna*), this stage shares the same antidotes as the various positions; within these positions, this specific stage serves as the antidote for mundane and supramundane distraction regarding meditative concentration.

The obstacle to non-sovereignty is as follows: this ten-story pavilion of the elder subsumes the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the eleventh stage, and the fruit of Buddhahood, encompassing them all because it takes as its essence the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) meditation that is without dependence and without intrinsic nature.
Thus, within the essence of this meditation—which is itself without dependence and without dwelling—the ten perfections (*pāramitā*)...
Taking the *pāramitās* as its adornments, the Master of the Treatise explains it in verse:
The garden of meditation has non-activity as its intrinsic nature; Universal luminosity wisdom is its great mansion. The pavilions are adorned with diverse contemplations;
The food of Dharma is given to satisfy all beings. The precious robes of pure precepts are always worn universally; Vigor and compassion [are its ornaments].

The mind serves as the court lady; the meditative mind skillfully masters worldly knowledge on the fifth stage. Bodhisattvas dwelling in the clarity of penetration abide in the prajñā of cessation on the sixth stage.
On the seventh stage, they dwell in the skillful means of saṃsāra without effort. On the eighth stage, they exercise mastery of function.
On the ninth stage, they dwell as Dharma Kings for one more birth. Within the tenth stage, the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected. Such is the sequence.

Yet, in practicing and studying, one ultimately does not abide in the beginning, middle, or end; by means of these various dharmas, one benefits all sentient beings and attains both the primary and secondary retributions therein.
This is a brief explanation of the general outline; the detailed meaning is as clarified in the text itself, showing that within a single practice, ten practices are practiced simultaneously.
The beginning has no end; all cases are thus. Second, regarding the section on the advancement of merit, from the passage "As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
down to "took their leave and departed," there are ten and a half lines of scripture.
Within this, it is divided into six sections: first, advancing merit; second, indicating the location of spiritual friends, namely the South; third... [and so forth].
1. Indicating the name of the land of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra): Vīrapura. 2. Indicating the name of the city where the spiritual friend resides:
Samantamukha. 3. Indicating the name of the spiritual friend: Samantanetra. 4. Paying respects and departing. Regarding the exegesis of the text according to its phrasing:
this is to promote the virtues [of the teacher] so that Sudhana may advance. Within the section praising these virtues, there are eight lines of verse, as follows:

The station name "Fujine" (Vine Root) clearly signifies the sixth [station], the Good Spiritual Friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Because the *prajñā* is profound and solid, it penetrates to the source of all sentient beings;
just as a vine root is deep and firm, penetrating the great earth down to the water's edge, it takes the sense of being "solid, real, and piercing through" as its metaphor.
This is because the wisdom-observation (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*) penetrates both mundane and supramundane phenomena, reaching their very source and bottom.
The city named "Universal Gate" (Pumen) is so called because it is known everywhere through the universal eye (*samantacakṣus*) that comprehends all phenomena; it is named after its presiding lord.

The elder is named "Universal Eye" (*Samantacakṣus*) because his wisdom surpasses that of humans and devas, such that there is nothing in the mundane or supramundane realms he does not know universally.
From this point on, the text encourages one to go and visit him, as is fully detailed in the original scripture.
Sixth, in the country of Veṇuvana, the elder Samantanetra presides over the practice of "Universal Manifestation.
[Sūtra] At that time, having heard this liberation from the elder Ratnaśikhin, the youth Sudhana entered deeply into the immeasurable knowledge and vision of all Buddhas,
dwelt in the immeasurable superior practices of Bodhisattvas, and thoroughly mastered the immeasurable [qualities] of Bodhisattvas.
Through skillful means, they seek the immeasurable Dharma-gates of Bodhisattvas; they purify the immeasurable faith and understanding of Bodhisattvas;
they clarify the immeasurable faculties of Bodhisattvas; they achieve the immeasurable aspirations of Bodhisattvas; they penetrate the immeasurable gateways of practice of Bodhisattvas;
they increase the immeasurable power of vows of Bodhisattvas; and they establish the immeasurable banner of invincibility of Bodhisattvas.

With his wisdom, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra illuminated the Dharma of Bodhisattvas and proceeded by stages until he reached the kingdom of Veṇu-mūla. There, he inquired and sought out the location of that city;

though he encountered many hardships, he did not shrink from toil and suffering. With nothing but right mindfulness of the instructions of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), vowing always to stay close to, serve, and make offerings to him, he thoroughly restrained all his faculties and remained free from all negligence. Only then was he able to see Samantabhadra.
The city gates and walls were surrounded by hundreds of thousands of villages; its battlements were lofty and steep, and its streets were broad and level.
Seeing the Elder approaching, he went before him, prostrated himself, joined his palms, and stood, saying:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train."
"How does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva path? The elder replied, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have already been able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family, I know all the various ailments of sentient beings—those caused by wind, bile, phlegm, heat, malevolent spirits, sorcery, and even injuries from water or fire."
I am able to cure all such various diseases that arise through skillful means.
Son of good family, whenever sentient beings of the ten directions who are afflicted by illness come to me, I treat them all so that they may recover.
Furthermore, I bathe their bodies with fragrant water and adorn them with fragrant flowers, necklaces, and various fine garments and superior robes.
He provides them with food, drink, and material wealth until all are fully satisfied and lack for nothing; thereafter, he teaches each according to their needs:

to those with excessive desire, he teaches the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); to those with excessive anger, he teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*);

to those with excessive delusion, he teaches the discernment of the various characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); and to those whose [defilements] are equally distributed, he reveals [the appropriate practice] for them.
They reveal the sublime Dharma-door in order to cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta;

they extol the merits of all Buddhas in order to cause them to give rise to great compassion; they demonstrate the immeasurable suffering and affliction of saṃsāra in order to cause them to increase their merit;
they praise the cultivation of immeasurable merit and wisdom in order to cause them to make great vows.
May they praise the subduing of all sentient beings so that they may cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra;
may they speak of how Bodhisattvas dwell throughout all lands and all eons to cultivate the net of all practices;

may they extol and praise the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) so that they may be endowed with the marks and signs of a Buddha; and may they cause them to attain the pure body of a Buddha, which is able to pervade everywhere.
He extols and praises the *śīla-pāramitā* because he desires to cause them to attain the Buddha’s pure and inconceivable body;
he extols and praises the *kṣānti-pāramitā* because he desires to cause them to obtain the Tathāgata’s invincible body;
he extols and praises the *vīrya-pāramitā* because he desires to cause them to attain...
One praises and extols the dhyāna-pāramitā in order to cause the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body;
one praises and extols the prajñā-pāramitā in order to cause the manifestation of the Buddha-Bhagavān’s pure form-body (rūpa-kāya);
and one praises and extols the upāya-pāramitā in order to cause its manifestation.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they abide through all kalpas praising and extolling the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*);
desiring to manifest pure bodies that transcend all buddha-fields, they praise and extoll the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*);
and desiring to manifest pure bodies that bring joy to all according to the minds of sentient beings, they praise and extoll [the perfection of knowledge].

The perfection of wisdom, desiring that they obtain a body that is ultimately pure and sublime, extols and praises the eternal departure from all unwholesome dharmas; having thus bestowed these gifts, each is sent back.
Good son, I also well know the essential methods for compounding all fragrances, namely: the peerless fragrance *Sindhuvara* and the pungent fragrance *Kṣāntivāra*.

There are fragrances such as Anuttama-gandha (Incomparable Fragrance), Bodhi-gandha (Enlightenment Fragrance), Aruṇavati-gandha, Kālāguru-candana-gandha (Black Aged Sandalwood Fragrance), Uragasāra-candana-gandha (Snake-Heart Sandalwood Fragrance), and Akṣobhya-indriya-gandha (Fragrance that Stabilizes the Faculties). I fully know the methods for preparing and blending these fragrances.
Furthermore, O son of good family, I take these fragrances to make offerings so that I may universally behold all Buddhas.

All their aspirations were fulfilled, namely: the aspiration to rescue and protect all sentient beings, the aspiration to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, and the aspiration to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, son of good family, when this incense was burned, from each and every piece of incense there issued forth immeasurable fragrances that pervaded the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm of the ten directions. Or...
They serve as fragrant palaces or fragrant halls; likewise, there are fragrant railings, fragrant walls, fragrant parapets,

fragrant doors and windows, fragrant multi-storied pavilions, fragrant crescent-shaped ornaments, fragrant canopies, fragrant banners, fragrant pennants, fragrant curtains, fragrant nets, fragrant images,
fragrant ornaments, fragrant radiances, and fragrant clouds and rains, filling every place as a magnificent adornment.
"Good man, I know only this Dharma-gate for causing all sentient beings to universally behold all Buddhas and rejoice.

As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who are like great medicinal kings—if they are seen, heard, remembered, dwelt with, followed, approached, or if their names are invoked—all obtain benefit; none pass by in vain. If there are sentient beings..."
Having encountered them even for a moment, they cause all afflictions to be extinguished; they enter the Buddha-dharma and leave behind all aggregates of suffering;
they forever stifle all fears of birth and death and reach the state of omniscience where there is nothing to fear;
they shatter the great mountain of old age and death and abide in the bliss of equanimous, tranquil extinction. How could I possibly know or describe this?
"O son of noble family, Guṇakāra, to the south of here there is a great city named Tālaketu.
In it dwells a king named Analaṃkāra. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana paid homage at the feet of Samantanetra, circumambulated him countless times, and gazed upon him with profound reverence.
He took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of entering the specific stage correctly:
from the passage beginning with "At that time" down to "I only know this Gate of Universal Joy in Beholding All Buddhas for the Sake of All Sentient Beings," this segment is divided as follows.
This consists of eight sections: 1. The instruction of the spiritual friend Samyaksmṛti on contemplation and advancement; 2.
Traveling to the country of Vaṃśa-mūla to inquire about and seek out the city of Samantamukha; 3. Seeing the elder on the road and formally presenting one's request;
4. The elder bestowing upon Sudhana the matters to be practiced. There are four such matters to be practiced: first, skillful cultivation...

1. The twofold excellent teaching on the remedies for the various afflictions; 2. The Dharma-gate of the faculties through the excellent harmonization of all fragrances as offerings to universally behold all Buddhas;
3. Advancing by inferring virtues. Regarding the interpretation of the text according to its phrasing: the city walls consist of battlements (*citi*) that are lofty and steep;

the highest of these double-tiered battlements are called *citi*, while the layered tiers themselves are called *dīrghikā*. The height of the city is called *unnata* (lofty), and its difficulty of ascent is called *viṣama* (steep).
This good spiritual friend abides in the sixth stage of practice; because his wisdom is inexhaustible, layered, and most exalted, it is difficult to enter.
That "broad and level highway" refers to the wisdom of the three emptinesses, which is vast and boundless.

Regarding "worldly and world-transcending wisdom that is all-pervasive," it refers to the treatment of all ailments: the worldly ailment of the disharmony of the four great elements is treated with medicinal decoctions.
Treating the disease of afflictions through the five contemplations for settling the mind and the ten *pāramitās* is like properly blending various incenses;
with the fragrance of the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body, it universally perfumes according to the faculties.
From the appearance of the Buddha, all such matters are explained by means of phenomena to illustrate the Dharma; both the phenomena and the Dharma encompass both the mundane and the supramundane.

The two meanings regarding the world are as follows: in the sixth stage, the Stage of Right Mind (Ṣaṣṭha-samyakcitta-vihāra) among the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmika*), the monk Sāgaradhvaja enters the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and emanates clouds of transformations from his body that pervade everywhere to benefit beings;

this illustrates the gate of the unimpeded union of wisdom and quiescence within the sixth stage. Now, herein, within the sixth stage of the Ten Practices (*Daśaprakāra-caryā*), the Practice of the Manifestation of Wisdom (*Prajñā-suvyakti-caryā*), this is cited.
By employing this tranquility exclusively, one achieves the accomplishment of the conduct of body, speech, and mind that is characterized by stillness.

As described above, those who can truly cure the diseases of sentient beings possess such practice as a manifestation of the Dharma. For those with wind disorders (*vāta*) who have many discursive thoughts, they should use counting the breaths (*gaṇanā*) as an antidote to draw the mind inward and bring it to rest.
Through these skillful means, the mind focused on the object of observation becomes calm and compliant, manifesting the concentration of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*).

The application of wisdom through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) benefits and transforms all beings: for those with jaundice, which symbolizes an abundance of desire (*rāga*), one applies the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);
for those with phlegm-fever, which symbolizes an abundance of ignorance (*moha*), one applies the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

and for those with demonic afflictions, which symbolize grasping at exquisite forms and failing to leave behind the karmic activities of Māra and celestial retributions, one applies the supernormal power of the Dharma.

The contemplation of emptiness that neutralizes poisonous spirits represents the ability of all thoughts of grasping to give rise to all afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), harmful karma, and the karma of craving—craving being likened to water and hatred to fire.

Such maladies can all be counteracted by this practice, just as various fragrances are blended together. Furthermore, the actual existence of such practices that manifest the Dharma clarifies wisdom and skillful exposition.

Teaching the incense [of morality] so that it may perfume and purify all evil attachments and karmic actions: just as various evil karmas produce a foul odor, so does conduct in accordance with wisdom produce fragrance.
This refers to the Sindhu River—*sindhu* meaning "bank"—which issues from the mouth of the Golden Ox in the western direction of Lake Anavatapta;
this clearly illustrates the great river flowing into the country of Sindhu. *Pāra* means "bank. This clarifies [the meaning].
This fragrance emerges from the banks of this river to represent the sixth stage, the Good Manifestation (Sudṛśa), wherein the three emptinesses, wisdom,
and the four unhindered analytical knowledges are perfected. Just as those great pools surge forth with four rivers that moisten the earth and eventually form the great ocean,
so too do all the fragrances of the fivefold Dharma-body— precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation— all arise.
If there are sentient beings therein who hear [this teaching] and enter into faith, they shall all attain liberation and transcend to the other shore.
The sūtra mentions one of these rivers; the remaining three may be understood by analogy with this. Regarding the *alunabhadī* fragrance: this is translated as "fragrance";
its bright red color represents red as the primary color of the south, and it also signifies that the element of fire (*tejas*) is empty and non-substantial.
It is the sun, it is the light, and it is the mind; because it is free from the mind of phenomena (*dharmacitta*), "free" (*li*) is like "adorned" (*li*).

In this stage, the three emptinesses, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the radiant light of signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*) adorn the mental states of all sentient beings, so that they all attain the fragrance of the liberation of wisdom.
Regarding the "Uragasāra candana," *uraga* is the name for a snake, and *candana* is sandalwood.
"Tán" refers to the *candana* (sandalwood) tree. This snake is most venomous and constantly suffers from the heat of its own poison;

when it coils around this sandalwood tree, the poisonous vapors are immediately stilled. Likewise, if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing it said that both mind and objects are empty—lacking intrinsic essence, lacking location, and such that not a single dharma can be apprehended—believe and enter into this "fragrance," they will realize all things.
The poisonous heat of the afflictions is naturally purified, and its remaining fragrance can be understood according to its name.

In this way, the fragrance of these eight kinds of wisdom perfumes the seeds of consciousness of sentient beings with wrong views, causing them to rely on the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path and enter the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Good son, I know only this [method] for causing all sentient beings to universally behold all [realities].
The "Buddha’s Gate of Joy" clarifies, as above, the wisdom that counteracts all phenomena and develops the wisdom of all Buddhas;
through skillful means, it causes all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom so that they may all rejoice. Below this, it clarifies the advancement by attributing virtue to others;
this is called the sixth stage within the "Good Manifestation Practice," wherein one relies on a spiritual friend through the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The first [perfection] is the principal, while the other nine are its companions. If categorized by way of the gates of wisdom (*jñāna*), all stages are identical in their remedial function.

If categorized by way of the gates of the stages, they remedy the obstacles to the mastery of conduct and the mastery of the quiescent application of body, speech, and mind, thereby bringing conduct to fulfillment and ensuring that the activities of body, speech, and mind become purely immaculate.
Thus, in the second section, "Advancing through the Deduction of Qualities," it says: "As for the bodhisattvas..."
From the following section down to the point where he takes his leave and departs, there are nine lines and a half of sūtra text, which may be divided into four sections:
first, an exhortation to advance by virtue of one's merit; second, an indication of the location and the name of the city where the spiritual friend resides, namely, Tāladhvaja;
third, the mention of the king’s name, Anikṣiptadhura; and fourth, the respectful salutation and departure from the city named Tāladhvaja.
This is translated here as "Luminous Purity" (*vimalaprabhā*), a name established based on the primary teacher of the transformation.
Because during the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-Attachment (*asaṅga*), he skillfully enters the world with supramundane luminous and pure wisdom to act as a lord of compassion;

because he thoroughly knows the faculties of beings and manifests emanation bodies to engage in common activities, never failing to receive and guide sentient beings; and because he never tires of benefiting living beings, the King is named "Insatiable."
The practice of the cause leads to the realization of the fruit; the remainder is as detailed in the text itself.
Seventh, King Anantaprabha of the city of Tāladhvaja presides over the practice of non-attachment.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana recalled and reflected upon the instructions of the spiritual friends, mindful of how spiritual friends are able to...
Thinking, "They embrace me, they protect me, and they cause me not to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," one gives rise to a mind of joy,
a mind of pure faith, a vast mind, a serene mind, a leaping mind, a celebratory mind,
a sublime mind, a tranquil mind, an adorned mind, a non-attached mind, and an unimpeded mind.

With a mind of equanimity, a mind of mastery, a mind dwelling in the Dharma, a mind that travels everywhere to the Buddha-fields, a mind beholding the adornments of the Buddhas, and a mind never abandoning the Ten Powers, he proceeded gradually through various kingdoms, villages, towns, and settlements until he reached the city of Tāladhvaja.
There he asked where King Anala was; the people replied, "This king is currently at..."
Seated upon the lion throne in the central hall, he proclaimed the Dharma and transformed beings; those who could be disciplined, he disciplined;

those who could be gathered, he gathered; he punished their evils and adjudicated their disputes; he comforted the orphaned and the weak, causing them all to forever sever killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
He further caused them to prohibit false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter, and led them to remain far removed from greed.
While he was harboring anger and wrong views, Sudhana the youth, following the words of the people, immediately went to visit him;
from afar he saw that king seated upon a Nārāyaṇa-vajra throne, with incalculable jewels forming its legs, adorned with immeasurable precious images,
covered above by a lattice of golden cords, and wearing a crown of wish-fulfilling maṇi gems.
His head was adorned with Jāmbūnada gold in the shape of a crescent moon; his forehead was adorned with indranīla mani jewels;
he wore ear-rings of precious mani jewels hanging down from both sides; his neck was adorned with a necklace of priceless mani jewels;
his arms were adorned with armlets of exquisite celestial mani jewels; and he had a parasol made of Jāmbūnada gold.
Various jewels were interspersed to form the spokes, while great lapis lazuli gems formed the shaft;

mani-jewels of radiant flavor formed the hub, and bells made of diverse gems constantly produced exquisite sounds. Emitting great light that pervaded the ten directions, such a jeweled canopy covered him from above.
King Anala possessed great power and majesty, capable of subduing all other hosts.
There was no one capable of opposing him; with ten thousand ministers surrounding him before and behind, they jointly administered the affairs of state.
Furthermore, in his presence were one hundred thousand fierce soldiers, hideous in appearance and clad in coarse, shabby garments;
brandishing weapons, baring their arms and glaring with rage, there were countless sentient beings who were struck with terror upon seeing them.
Whether they violate the king’s commands, steal the property of others, take the lives of others, violate the wives of others, give rise to false views, harbor malice and resentment,
or conceive greed and envy— committing such various evil deeds as these— they are bound with the fivefold fetters and brought before the king,
to be punished according to their offenses by having their hands and feet cut off, or their ears and noses severed.
Some have their eyes gouged out, some have their heads severed, some have their skin flayed, some have their bodies dismembered;
some are boiled in boiling water, some are burned with fire, and some are driven up high mountains and pushed over to fall.
Having seen such immeasurable tortures and the sounds of wailing and crying out—just as in the Saṃghāta and Mahāprajāpatī (Mahāpātāla) hells—Sudhana perceived them and spoke thus:
I reflect that for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I seek the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva;

yet now this king destroys all wholesome dharmas and commits great sinful karma, oppressing and afflicting sentient beings even unto taking their lives, without ever regarding or fearing the evil realms of the future.
How can I, wishing to seek the Dharma here, give rise to great compassion and rescue and protect these beings?
While he was forming this thought, a deva in the sky addressed him, saying: "Son of good family, you should remember the instruction of the spiritual friend, the Elder Universal Eye.
Sudhana looked up and said to him: "I constantly remember it; I do not dare to forget it for a moment. The deva said:
"Son of good family, do not weary of or distance yourself from the words of the spiritual friend, nor from the spiritual friend himself."
This one can lead you to a place of safety free from danger and hardship. Son of good family, the bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillful means is inconceivable;
his wisdom of gathering in sentient beings is inconceivable; his wisdom of mindful protection of sentient beings is inconceivable;
his wisdom of bringing sentient beings to maturity is inconceivable; and his wisdom of guarding sentient beings is inconceivable.
"The inconceivable wisdom that liberates sentient beings; the inconceivable wisdom that disciplines sentient beings.
Having heard these words, the youth Sudhana immediately went to the king's presence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know [how to fulfill] the bodhi..."
"How should one train in the bodhisattva conduct? How should one cultivate the bodhisattva path? "I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will explain this to me. At that time, King Anala, having finished attending to his royal affairs, took Sudhana by the hand and led him into the palace.
He invited him to sit together and said, "Good son, you should observe the palace in which I dwell."
As soon as Vaiśravaṇa spoke these words, he surveyed everywhere and saw that the palace was vast beyond compare, composed entirely of exquisite jewels.
It was surrounded on all sides by walls made of the seven precious substances, with hundreds of thousands of towers and pavilions made of various gems, all exquisitely adorned and most beautiful.
An inconceivable net of mani-jewels covered it from above. Ten billion...
The handmaidens were upright and peerless; their deportment and movements were all worthy of admiration. Whatever they undertook was without exception skillful and ingenious;
they rose before [the king] and retired after him, serving his every wish with a gentle mind. At that time, King Anala said to Sudhana: "Son of good family, what do you think?
If I had truly committed such evil deeds as these, how could I have obtained such [a reward]?"
The retribution is such, the physical body is such, the retinue is such, the wealth and abundance are such, and the sovereignty is such.
Good son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation of being like an illusion.
Good son, all the sentient beings in this land of mine mostly practice killing, stealing, and even wrong views; by other means, it is impossible to cause them to abandon their evil karma.
"Good son, for the sake of taming those sentient beings, I manifest as an evil person who commits various sinful deeds and undergoes all manner of suffering.
When all those sentient beings who have committed evil see this, their hearts are filled with terror, they develop a sense of weary detachment, and they feel a sense of trepidation;
thus they sever all the evil karma they have created and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

"O son of good family with the mind of *samyaksambodhi*, it is by means of such skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*) that I cause all sentient beings to abandon the ten unwholesome actions and abide in the ten paths of wholesome conduct,
attaining ultimate happiness, ultimate peace, and ultimately dwelling upon the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
O son of good family, my body, speech, and mind have never once harmed or afflicted even a single sentient being."

"Good son, as for my mind, I would rather undergo the suffering of the Avīci hell in the future than give rise to a single thought of causing harm to even a mosquito or an ant, let alone a human being.
A human is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) capable of producing all wholesome dharmas. Good son, I have attained only this liberation that is like an illusion."
All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and know that all realms of existence are entirely like illusions;
that all practices of Bodhisattvas are entirely like transformations (*nirmāṇa*); that all worlds are entirely like shadows; and that all phenomena are entirely like dreams.
They enter the unimpeded Dharma-gate of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and practice the "Indra's Net" of all deeds through non-attachment.
Their unimpeded wisdom operates within the sphere of objects, universally entering all samādhis of equality and having attained mastery over dhāraṇīs;

how then could I know or speak of their meritorious conduct? Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Surasmitā and a king named Mahāprabha; go to him and ask: how should a bodhisattva study awakening?

While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivating the bodhisattva path, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the king’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and then took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the gateway of entering the actual stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to...
"I have only attained this liberation that is like an illusion. This section of the sutra is divided into fourteen sections:
(1) Mindfully recollecting the spiritual friend and advancing; (2) proceeding to the city of Tālāvatī; (3) asking the people where the king is located;
(4) the people answering that he is currently in the main hall; (5) Sudhana approaching and seeing the king from afar.
1. The Vajra-throne of Nārāyaṇa; 2. King Ṣaḍdarśana reports on the Palace Adorned with a Body; 3. All manner of precious jewels; 4.
King Ṣaḍdarśana’s instruments of torture for punishing evil, which are so agonizing and unbearable; 5. Sudhana’s mind gives rise to doubt; 6.
A deity in the sky informs him to follow the words of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to eliminate his doubt; 7. Sudhana’s doubt being eliminated, he proceeds to visit [the next teacher].
11. The king prostrates and formally presents his request. 12. The king takes Sudhana by the hand and leads him into the palace to observe the realms of karmic retribution;

he manifests his own body undergoing various sufferings as the result of evil karma created through the liberation-door of "illusory-like" manifestation, causing real sentient beings to feel awe and fear so that they may give rise to all manner of wholesome roots.

13. Generating the Bodhicitta: The king personally applied himself to his conduct, constantly ensuring that toward even a single mosquito or ant, he did not give rise to a thought of causing suffering or harm, much less toward human beings. 14. Advancing through Virtue:
King Anala—translated here as "Insatiable"—is like the seventh stage of the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmika).
The stage of compassion is represented by the laywoman Śreṣṭhadattā. This seventh of the ten practices, the practice of compassion, is represented by King Aśoka;

it serves to govern the conduct of those who do evil, transforming their own created evils into self-inflicted discipline so as to cause sentient beings to truly weary of the world, cultivate virtue, and achieve the path to Bodhi. This is the seventh dedication.

With Avalokiteśvara presiding over the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), and with the Night Goddess named Kāñcanaprabhāśrī presiding [over it], all such names are specific designations for the accomplishment of compassion according to each respective stage. The rest is clearly explained in detail in the sutra.
This is the spiritual friend of the seventh stage, the Unattached Practice (Asaṅga-caryā), by means of the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).
The first [perfection] is the principal, while the other nine are its companions. In terms of the gateway of wisdom, all stages universally remedy [defilements];

in terms of the gateway of the specific stages, they remedy the lack of mastery over the two modes of defiled and pure conduct within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), thereby enabling one to attain mastery through great wisdom and great compassion while abiding within that very cycle.
Second, regarding the progression through the excellence of qualities, from among the various bodhisattvas...
From the point where he finally takes his leave and departs, there are eight lines and a half of sūtra text, which may be divided into four sections: first, extolling his virtues and his advancement;

second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend and the city where he dwells, named *Prabhāsa* (Wonderful Light); third, citing the name of the spiritual friend-king, *Mahāprabha* (Great Light);
and fourth, prostrating and taking leave. Regarding the statement in the sūtra that "the city is named *Prabhāsa*":

This is identical to the eighth dwelling of the eighth stage; the wondrous function of effortless wisdom is the sovereign of the perfected discriminative wisdom within its own fundamental state, and that which is named "Great Light" is called the fundamental wisdom. All other details are fully contained within the text itself.
Combined Commentary on the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Ninety-Eight.

the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Layman of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, combining the sutras and treatises, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Twelve of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*).
[Treatise] Eighth: The Practice Difficult to Attain of King Mahāprabha in the City of Wonderful Light.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded right mindfulness, contemplated the dharma-gate of illusory wisdom attained by that king;
he reflected upon that king’s liberation as being like an illusion and observed that king’s illusory nature of phenomena.
He gave rise to illusory vows to purify illusory dharmas, and universally manifested various illusory transformations throughout all illusory periods of the three times.
Thus reflecting, he traveled by stages, whether through human cities, towns, and villages, or across wildernesses, rocky gorges, and perilous terrains;
yet he never grew weary and never rested until he finally reached the Great City of Wondrous Light.
There he asked the people, "Where is the Great City of Wondrous Light? and everyone replied, "The City of Wondrous Light is now..."
"This city is the dwelling place of King Mahāprabha. At that time, the youth Sudhana, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, thought to himself:

"My spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is in this city; I shall now certainly behold him in person, hear of the practices performed by the bodhisattvas, hear of the gateways to the essential liberation of the bodhisattvas, and hear of the bodhisattvas..."
Having heard of the Dharma realized by all Bodhisattvas, having heard of the inconceivable merit of all Bodhisattvas,
having heard of the inconceivable mastery of all Bodhisattvas, having heard of the inconceivable equanimity of all Bodhisattvas, having heard of the inconceivable valor of all Bodhisattvas,
and having heard of the vast and pure inconceivable realm of all Bodhisattvas, he formed this thought and entered the Light of Subtlety.
The city beheld this great city, constructed of the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate—
and surrounded by seven tiers of deep moats made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight virtues,
their bottoms strewn with golden sand and covered everywhere with blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).
Above it, seven rows of precious tāla trees stand in succession, and seven kinds of vajra-walls serve as its enclosure,
each surrounding it individually: namely, the Lion-Radiance Vajra-wall, the Unsurpassable Vajra-wall,
the Indestructible Vajra-wall, the Irreparable Vajra-wall, the Firm and Unobstructed Vajra-wall, and the Supreme Vajra-wall.

The Vajra-walls of the Wondrous Net Treasury and the Vajra-walls of Dustless Purity are all adorned with countless exquisite mani-jewels interspersed and arrayed; various kinds of precious gems form the battlements.
The city is ten yojanas in length and breadth, eight sides in circumference, with eight gates opening on all sides, all extensively embellished with the seven treasures and lapis lazuli.
Its ground is made of jewels, adorned in various ways, and is most delightful. Within that city, there are ten billion streets;
between each street, there dwell immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings.
There are countless Jambūnada-gold pavilions, covered above by nets of vaidūrya and maṇi jewels, as well as countless silver pavilions.
A lattice of red pearl *maṇi* jewels covered its upper part; countless lapis lazuli pavilions were covered by a lattice of exquisite treasury *maṇi* jewels;
countless crystal pavilions were covered by a lattice of stainless treasury *maṇi*-king jewels;
and countless pavilions of light-illuminating world-*maṇi* jewels were covered by a *maṇi*-king sun-treasury.
A net of countless emerald-blue (*indranīla*) maṇi-jewel pavilions covered its top;
a net of countless ocean-of-beings maṇi-king pavilions of wondrous-light maṇi-kings covered its top;
a net of countless vajra-jewel pavilions of invincible-banner maṇi-kings covered its top.
It was covered above by countless black sandalwood pavilions and nets of celestial *mandārava* flowers;
it was covered above by countless peerless kings of fragrance pavilions and various nets of flowers;
furthermore, that city possessed countless nets of *maṇi* jewels, countless nets of precious bells, countless nets of celestial incense, and countless celestial flowers.

It was completely covered by nets of countless precious images, canopies of countless precious garments, canopies of countless precious parasols, canopies of countless precious pavilions, and canopies of countless precious flower garlands; everywhere within it were erected precious parasols, banners, and streamers.
In the center of this city was a pavilion named Treasury of the True Dharma, adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels.
Its majestic radiance was brilliant and magnificent, peerless and unsurpassed; those sentient beings who beheld it could never tire of the sight.

King Mahāprabha constantly dwelt within that place. At that time, the youth Sudhana felt no attachment whatsoever toward any of these precious objects, from the various wonderful things down to the six sensory realms of men and women; he focused his mind solely on the ultimate Dharma.

With a heart longing to see spiritual friends, he gradually traveled until he beheld King Mahāprabha sitting upon a vast and magnificent lion throne of *cintāmaṇi* jewel lotus-wombs at a crossroads not far from his residence;
its legs were made of dark-blue lapis lazuli, it was draped with canopies of golden silk, and adorned with nets of various jewels.
With exquisite celestial garments serving as his mattress, the king sat upon it in the full lotus posture.
His body was adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a Great Man and eighty secondary signs;

he was like a mountain of pure gold, his radiance blazing intensely, like the sun in a clear sky, his majestic light shining brilliantly like the full moon, bringing coolness to all who beheld him, like the Brahmā King.
Abiding among the Brahma-multitude, his ocean-like qualities and Dharma-treasures are boundless;
he is adorned with the forest of marks and signs like the Snowy Mountains; he is like a great cloud that can thunder forth the Dharma to awaken all beings;
he is like space, manifesting various Dharma-gates like the stars and constellations; and like Mount Sumeru, the four colors appear everywhere.
The ocean of the minds of sentient beings is likewise like a treasure island, filled with various jewels of wisdom.

Before the royal throne, there were heaps of precious gems—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, maṇi-jewels, pearls, coral, amber, conch shells, and jade—as well as garments, necklaces, and various foods and drinks, all filling the space in infinite and boundless variety. Furthermore, he saw...
There were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite jewel chariots; hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial musical performances;

hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial incenses; and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of medicinal decoctions and requisites for the sick—all such things were entirely rare and excellent.
There were also immeasurable milch cows with hooves and horns of golden color, and immeasurable thousands of billions of beautiful women.
With the most exquisite sandalwood, he anointed his body; adorned with celestial robes and necklaces, he was thoroughly proficient in all sixty-four arts.
He was well-versed in all worldly customs and etiquette, bestowing gifts according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
In cities, villages, and at the crossroads of every road, he established all manner of life-sustaining necessities at every single station.
On both sides, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who bestowed these various things upon sentient beings for the purpose of universally gathering them in,
for the purpose of causing sentient beings to rejoice, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to leap with joy, for the purpose of purifying the minds of sentient beings,
for the purpose of bringing coolness to sentient beings, for the purpose of extinguishing the afflictions of sentient beings, and for the purpose of...
In order that sentient beings may know all principles and meanings; in order to cause sentient beings to enter the path of omniscience; in order to cause sentient beings to abandon hostile minds;
in order to cause sentient beings to leave behind the evils of body and speech; in order to cause sentient beings to uproot all false views;

and in order to cause sentient beings to purify all paths of action—at that time, the youth Sudhana... [fifth]...
