He prostrated himself on the ground, bowed at his feet, and circumambulated him to the right for countless times. Standing with palms joined, he addressed him, saying:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well-able [to explain this]."

"Please instruct me and explain this for my sake," he requested. The King of the Dharma replied, "Son of good family, I have purely cultivated the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion;

I have fulfilled the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Banner of Great Compassion. Son of good family, I have questioned and deliberated upon this Dharma, and have contemplated and observed it before immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas."
O son of noble family who cultivates adornment, I take this Dharma as my king; I instruct with this Dharma; I gather in with this Dharma;
I follow after the world with this Dharma; I lead sentient beings by means of this Dharma; I cause sentient beings to practice by means of this Dharma;
I cause sentient beings to enter [the path] by means of this Dharma; and I bestow upon sentient beings this very method.
He then uses these teachings to infuse sentient beings with habitual tendencies; he uses these teachings to cause sentient beings to initiate practice;

he uses these teachings to cause sentient beings to dwell in the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; he uses these teachings to cause sentient beings to dwell in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), taking loving-kindness as primary and becoming fully endowed with the power of loving-kindness;
and in this way, he causes them to abide in a mind of benefit, a mind of peace and happiness, and a mind of compassion (*anukampā*).
With a heart of compassion, I embrace all beings; with a heart that protects them, I never abandon them;
with a heart that uproots the suffering of sentient beings without rest, I shall, by these means, cause all beings to attain ultimate happiness and constant joy.

May their bodies be free from all suffering and their minds attain cool clarity. May they sever the craving for birth and death, delight in the joy of the True Dharma, wash away the defilements of affliction, and shatter evil.
Karmic obstacles are severed; the flow of birth and death enters the true ocean of Dharma; all realms of existence are cut off;
one seeks all-encompassing wisdom and purifies the ocean of the mind, giving rise to indestructible faith.

Good son, I have already dwelled in this practice of the Banner of Great Compassion, able to transform and teach the world through the True Dharma. Good son, all sentient beings within my land [regard] me as...

"Free from fear, noble son! If there are sentient beings who, impoverished and destitute, come to me with requests, I open my storehouses and let them take whatever they desire, saying to them: 'Commit no evil; do not harm sentient beings;
do not give rise to various views; do not produce attachments. You who are poor and lacking, if you have anything you require, you should [take it]. "
"Come to me and to the crossroads; all manner of things are there in full abundance. Take whatever you desire according to your wish, and do not harbor any doubt or difficulty.
Good son, all the sentient beings dwelling in this city of *Prabhāsa* are bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
According to their respective inclinations, what they perceive differs: some see this city as being small in scale, while others see..."
This city is vast in its dimensions; some see its ground as consisting of earth and sand, while others see it adorned with various jewels.
Some see walls made of heaped-up earth, while others see it surrounded on all sides by walls of precious gems.
Some see its ground strewn with many tiles and stones, uneven and undulating, while others see it interspersed with immeasurable great maṇi-jewels.

The level ground was adorned like the palm of a hand; some saw houses made of wood and earth, while others saw palaces, various multi-storied pavilions, courtyards, windows, balconies, railings, and doors—all of which were nothing other than wondrous jewels.

Good son, if there are sentient beings whose minds are pure, who have planted roots of goodness in the past, and who have made offerings to the Buddhas and resolved their hearts upon [the path], [they shall see these things].

Those who are directed toward the path of omniscience and take omniscience as their ultimate goal, as well as those whom I previously gathered in while practicing the bodhisattva conduct in the past, see this city as adorned with various jewels and pure; all others see it as defiled.
Son of good family, when all sentient beings within this land delight in committing various evils during the age of the five corruptions, my heart feels compassion for them.
Desiring to rescue and protect [beings], one enters the gate of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi of conforming to the world, which has great compassion as its foremost quality.

When entering this samādhi, all the fears, mental afflictions, harmful intentions, hostile intentions, and contentious intentions of those sentient beings are entirely extinguished of their own accord. Why is this? Because one has entered the Bodhisattva’s great compassion.
Because the Dharma of the Samādhi of Following the World as the Foremost is thus, son of good family, wait but a moment and you shall see it for yourself.
At that time, King Mahāprabha entered this samādhi, and the city—both inside and out—trembled in six ways;
from all such things as the jeweled ground, jeweled walls, jeweled halls, jeweled palaces, towers, pavilions, balconies, staircases, and windows, there issued forth [sounds].
With voices of sublime resonance, they all bowed their bodies in reverent salutation toward the king.
All the inhabitants within the city of Wondrous Light simultaneously leaped for joy and rushed together to where the king was, casting their entire bodies to the ground.

From the villages, camps, towns, and cities, the entire multitude came to see the king, greeting him with joy and reverence. Even the birds and beasts dwelling near the king’s presence [beheld one another]...
Beholding [the King], they gave rise to hearts of compassion and all turned before the King to pay respectful homage.

All the mountains, plains, grasses, and trees turned toward the King to offer salutations. The ponds, pools, springs, wells, rivers, and oceans all surged and overflowed, flowing and pouring forth before the King.
Ten thousand dragon kings raised great clouds of incense, flashing lightning and rolling thunder, raining down fine [fragrant] mist.

There were ten thousand celestial kings of the fine rain, namely the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the King of the Yāma Heaven, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, the King of the Sunirmita Heaven, and the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, who served as the leaders.
In the midst of the void, they performed various musical performances; countless celestial maidens sang praises in song, and they rained down countless flowers.
Countless clouds of incense, countless clouds of jewel garlands, countless clouds of jewel robes, countless clouds of jewel parasols,
countless clouds of jewel banners, and countless clouds of jewel pennants adorned the void as offerings to that king,
the great elephant king Airāvaṇa; by his power of mastery, he spread these throughout the sky.
Adorned with countless great jewel lotuses, hanging with innumerable jewel tassels, innumerable jewel silk ribbons, innumerable jewel garlands,
innumerable jewel ornaments, innumerable jewel flowers, and innumerable jewel perfumes— all of various wondrous and marvelous kinds—
as well as innumerable celestial maidens singing various songs of praise; furthermore, within Jambudvīpa, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions more.
Hundreds of millions of rākṣasa kings, yakṣa kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, and piśāca kings— whether dwelling in the great ocean or inhabiting the land—
who had been drinking blood, eating flesh, and harming sentient beings, all gave rise to a heart of compassion and resolved to act for their benefit.

With clear awareness of the future life and no longer committing any evil deeds, they paid homage with reverence and joined palms, prostrating themselves before the King as if he were Jambudvīpa itself.

"In the remaining three continents, and even throughout the trichiliocosm, and even throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds in the ten directions—all sentient beings who are poisonous and evil are likewise [transformed].
At that time, King Mahāprabha arose from samādhi and said to Sudhana: "Son of good family, I know only this bodhisattva..."

The samādhi-door of "Great Compassion as the Foremost, Accordant with the World," because it is like the high canopy of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose heart of compassion universally shades all sentient beings;
because it is like the practice of the lower, middle, and upper stages, wherein all practices are performed with equality;
because it is like the great earth, which is able to sustain all sentient beings through a heart of compassion; and because it is like the full moon of merit.
Because its radiance manifests equally throughout the world, it is a pure sun; because it illuminates all objects of knowledge with the light of wisdom, it is a bright lamp;
because it can destroy all darkness within the minds of sentient beings, it is a water-clearing jewel;
and because it can purify the turbidity of flattery and deception within the minds of all sentient beings, it is a wish-fulfilling gem.
Because they are able to fully satisfy the heart's desires of all sentient beings,
they act as great winds that swiftly cause sentient beings to practice samādhi and enter the great city of omniscience; how then could I know their conduct,
describe their virtues, weigh that mountain of merit, or gaze upon those stars of their qualities?
He contemplates that wind-circle of great vows which enables entry into those profound Dharma-gates,
manifests that ocean of adornments, elucidates those practices of Samantabhadra, reveals those caverns of samādhi,
and praises those clouds of great compassion. Good son, here in the south there is a royal capital named...
"In the city of Sālagrāma, there dwells an upāsikā named Acalā; go to her and inquire how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, Sudhana paid homage at the feet of King Anala, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with deep reverence, and taking his leave, departed.

[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva samādhi-door of Great Compassion as the Foremost, which accords with the World," this segment of the sūtra is divided into fifteen sections:
1) Contemplating the instruction of the Good Spiritual Friend; 2) Ascending... [and so forth].
1. He proceeds; 2. he gradually travels through human settlements, cities, and towns; 3. thereafter, he eventually reaches the great city of Suprabha;
4. he asks people for the location of his dwelling; 5. all the people reply, "This very city is it"; 6.
upon hearing where the city is located, Sudhana rejoices with leaping joy. This clarifies Sudhana’s entry into the great city of Suprabha.

Regarding what was seen: based on the realm of karmic retribution adorned with various jewels, Sudhana beheld the aforementioned sublime realms and the six sensory objects of men and women, yet he felt no attachment to them; rather, he focused his mind single-mindedly on contemplating the ultimate Dharma.
Ninth, as he traveled gradually, he saw the place where King Mahāprabha resided. Ninth, he saw the king’s reliance [upon that place].
2. The Adornment of the Reward Body’s Seat; 3. The Ten Good Wealthy Sons Prostrate Themselves at His Feet; 4. The Formal Presentation of What Is Sought; 5.
The King Declares to Good Wealthy Son the Practice He Performs, Named the Bodhisattva Practice of the Banner of Great Compassion;
6. In the City of Sublime Light, What Is Seen According to One’s Mind Varies Between Pure and Impure; 7. The King.
When he entered the samādhi gate of "Entering the World in Accordance with Great Compassion as the Foremost," the entire palace ground adorned with jewels as a karmic reward shook in six ways;
the trees bowed their heads, springs surged forth, and the myriad subjects, devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits all paid homage.
Yakṣas and rākṣasas all gave rise to hearts of compassion, and among the kings of the eight classes of beings, there was none who did not pay him the highest respect.
All gave rise to joy and cultivated roots of goodness; through the power of this samādhi, which takes great compassion as its foremost principle, such is the nature of the Dharma.
Fifteenth, [the text] extols his virtues and causes Sudhana to advance. Regarding the sequential explanation of the meaning according to the text:
he gradually travels on, whether reaching human realms, cities, towns, villages, wildernesses, crags, or valleys, and finally arrives at the Wondrous [City].

The phrase "illuminating the great city" clarifies that through the practice of universal observation and contemplation, one treats the preceding stage where wisdom is inferior and great compassion is not yet perfected;
by training in this, one brings wisdom and compassion to equilibrium. Only when wisdom and compassion are mastered does one reach the eighth stage, the city of effortless and wondrous activity.
Therefore, asking the multitude, "Where is the City of Wondrous Light now? clarifies this by means of...
The power of contemplative observation, wherein wisdom and compassion are equal, is such that one does not even recognize it oneself;
therefore, one must inquire of those who have long resided there to manifest the station of non-attainment where wisdom and compassion are difficult to harmonize.

When the multitude all replied, "As for the City of Wondrous Light, this very city is the dwelling place of King Great Radiance," this clarifies that Sudhana has attained a state of realization in accord with wisdom.
Having entered the gate of the Sovereign of Compassion, which is like that of a king, Sudhana rejoices; this is his entry into the joy of the Dharma.
Having formed such thoughts, he further reflects within himself that he will surely hear even more sublime teachings concerning the conduct of Bodhisattvas.

Having thus formed these ten kinds of reflections, he enters the City of Wondrous Light (*Prabhākarī*). This concludes the cultivation of worldly compassion and mercy within the seventh stage of practice mentioned previously.

This practice enters the eighth city of Effortless Wisdom, named the City of Entering Sublime Radiance. Having attained clear and penetrating wisdom and expanded great compassion, one enters this city;
what is seen therein—the jeweled-adorned ground, trees, palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, and so forth—is all clearly entered through this gateway of practice.
In terms of wisdom, compassion, and the manifestation of retribution, these arise as a single, non-futile occurrence.

All of these— namely, the Palace of Compassion, the Hall of Wisdom, the Tower of Contemplative Pity, the Various Wisdom Pavilions, the Flower-Pathways of the Dharma-nature, the Moats of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment,
and the Water of the Eightfold Noble Path— are surrounded by the trees of Bodhisattva conduct and the protection of the bodily,

verbal, and mental actions of all sentient beings, which serve as its walls; this corresponds exactly to the battlements described at the beginning of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, where it says, "This is the wall."
Looking up at the openings, they are all adorned with jewels; these seven layers are formed as the fruition of the seven *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* (aids to enlightenment).
The number seven is applied here in this manner throughout. The city is ten *yojanas* in length and breadth;
as for a *yojana*, according to the twelfth fascicle of the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, it is calculated that seven atoms of dust form a single window.
Seven particles of dust from a window-pane form one particle of a rabbit-hair tip; seven particles of a rabbit-hair tip form one particle of a sheep’s wool-tip;
seven particles of a sheep’s wool-tip form one particle of a cow’s hair-tip; seven particles of a cow’s hair-tip form one nit;
seven nits form one louse; seven lice form one mustard seed; seven mustard seeds form one [barley grain].
Seven barley grains make one finger-joint (*aṅgula*); seven finger-joints make half a *śukti*;
two and a half *śuktis* make one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits make one bow (*dhanus*); five bows make one *daṇḍa*;
twenty *daṇḍas* are called one *krośa*; eighty *krośas* make one *yojana*. These measurements are calculated according to the standard *śukti* of this region.
Two *li* and eighty paces constitute one *krośa*; eight *krośas* make one *yojana*. One *yojana* equals seventeen *li*.
If this city measures ten *yojanas*, it would total one hundred and seventy *li* from east to west and south to north.
According to the calculation that there are one billion crossroads within the city...
Within each of these paths, there dwell immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings;

this cannot be contained within the small *yojana* measurements of this world. Rather, it takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as the great city—since one is ten—the essence and function are thoroughly integrated.
Within the ten wisdoms, the wisdom of differentiation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) serves as the thoroughfare.
Within one, there are a hundred million functions of both identity and difference, extending even to the inexhaustible;

the Eightfold Noble Path constitutes eight gates, and four times eight makes thirty-two, clarifying the ten *pāramitās*, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the branches of the Eightfold Noble Path.

Together, these constitute the progressive cultivation of the ten abodes (*bhūmis*), the ten practices (*caryās*), and the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanas*), harmonizing and perfectly integrating the two practices of wisdom and compassion, thereby causing them to be fully realized.

The Sovereign designates fundamental wisdom as the "King of Great Radiance. According to the faculties, dispositions, and capacities of sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—it is seen as the "City of Wondrous Light," which varies in its breadth and narrowness and differs in its purity and impurity.

All the precious adornments of the city, the ground, the trees, and the palaces are collectively categorized according to wisdom, compassion, and the manifestation of retribution; these are fully detailed in the text itself.
In the city there is a pavilion named King of Great Radiance of the Treasury of True Dharma, where the Sovereign of Fundamental Wisdom constantly dwells;
this is the objective realm that is the retribution of differentiated wisdom.
Not far from the pavilion where the Sovereign of Great Radiance resides, Sudhana saw him sitting at a crossroads upon a wish-fulfilling jewel throne.

The "Noble Lotus-Womb Vastly Adorned Lion Throne" clarifies that the four wisdoms, the four immeasurables, and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) serve as the four crossroads for guiding and receiving sentient beings.
This set of four crossroads comprises many paths, even up to hundreds of thousands in total, through which the great road passes from north, south, east, and west;
thus it is called the "four crossroads. This single set of four crossroads encompasses all such pathways.

Because he gathers [beings] at this single crossroads, and because he brings forth rebirth according to their inclinations so that all may be stainless, he takes the wish-fulfilling, stain-free jewel as his seat;
because his conduct is untainted, the lotus and lapis lazuli are called the feet of the seat.
The bright wisdom that accords with the ten thousand practices, being luminous, pure, and unobstructed, is represented by the canopy of golden silk, signifying that wisdom accords with [the world].
Compassion contains and nurtures all sentient beings; the net of jewels symbolizes the wondrous teaching-net that rewards their birth.
The celestial robes serve as a cushion and mattress, for wisdom that is non-reliant constitutes the substance of the seat. A cushion and mattress are those with variegated patterns;
because wisdom that is non-reliant is fully endowed with the literary elegance of the four types of unimpeded eloquence, it draws in and guides sentient beings. Thus...
The King sits cross-legged upon this [lotus] with the two activities of wisdom and compassion interpenetrating in mastery— the twenty-eight marks of a great man—
clarifies that although wisdom and compassion have already been cultivated during the two stages of the Ten Abodes and the Ten Practices,
they are not yet perfected during the Ten Dedications; because these [marks] are not yet complete, it clarifies that this refers to the stage of the Three Virtuous Persons (the Ten Dedications).
Only when [the conditions] are fully perfected does one become a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) possessing the thirty-two marks;

therefore, this refers to the meaning of the convergence of the similarities and differences, as well as the general and specific aspects of the various stages, within the immovable state of the cognitive domain of wisdom. One must by no means employ arbitrary extensions or contractions based on personal sentiment, for that would utterly fail the intent of the Sūtra.

If this scriptural teaching were taken to mean that a Golden-Wheel King possesses [only] the secondary marks (anuvyañjana), it would be a complete deficiency in understanding the meaning of the Sūtra.
Regarding the Cakravartin King Golden Net as described in the "Chapter on the Merits of Radiance":
this Cakravartin King transforms and guides sentient beings within worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
Whenever this king emits the pure radiance from his maṇi-ornamented topknot, any sentient being who encounters this light attains [liberation].

When a Bodhisattva completes the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they attain immeasurable light of wisdom, the ten kinds of pure eyes, the ten kinds of pure intentions, and the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
These secondary marks are shared with the Brahmā kings of the higher realms who likewise possess such worldly excellence;
therefore, they are not identical to the thirty-two major marks and eighty secondary marks attained upon the completion of the stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*).
For instance, kings such as Mūrdhagata were wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*) who, upon attempting to surpass Śakra, lost their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and fell back into decline;
these belong to the level of the minor golden-wheel-turning kings over the four continents within the Three Vehicles.
They likewise possess the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, fully endowed with the marks of merit, yet they differ among themselves in these ten ways.

The King of Great Central Radiance is a king of men whose sphere of conversion and transformation completely fills hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds in the ten directions, manifesting everywhere to universally support and guide beings; thus,

unlike the Golden Wheel-Turning King among the three vehicles who converts only the people of the four continents but does not reach the various heavens, this is the eighth difficulty within these ten practices.
He has attained the conduct of a king of men who gathers and transforms the boundless realms of the ten directions, as well as the celestial kings of the upper realms;
there are none among the six paths of humans and devas whom he does not universally encompass.

Because he has attained the Buddha-wisdom, the following praises his two karmas of merit and wisdom as clearly explained in the text. As the Sūtra says: "It is also like space, manifesting various Dharma-gates like stars."
The "Elephant" refers to the enlightened ruler who, through the principles of the directions, establishes the laws of the quarters; this is precisely the Eight Trigrams and the Nine Palaces.

Above, the image of *Qian* (Heaven) encompasses the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the twelve double-hours (*shi*), the celestial stems and earthly branches, the sun, moon, five planets, and all the arrayed constellations, all of which possess fixed laws.
Thus, the worldly kings take these as models to bestow virtue and issue mandates.
The Buddha took [the throne] to symbolize his preaching of the Dharma; the rest is fully detailed in the text itself.
That various kinds of rare jewels filled the streets before the king’s throne were the objects bestowed by the king, as extensively explained in the sutra.
That the king’s body was like a mountain of gold refers to the color of an Arhat; through the inner illumination of pure wisdom, he practiced compassion to bless all beings.
This is what is evoked [by the power of the vow]. A woman of upright appearance possesses all sixty-four skills (though these are not detailed here).

I, who have purely cultivated the Bodhisattva practice of the Banner of Great Compassion, clearly understand that from the first of the ten practices up to the sixth practice, one cultivates the gateway to supramundane wisdom;
from the seventh practice up to this eighth practice, one continues the prior cultivation of worldly [wisdom].
The practice of wisdom arising from compassion reaches this eighth stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). Here, the wisdom of effortlessness (*anābhoga-jñāna*) manifests;
with great compassion as its primary guide, wisdom follows by shattering delusions, and is thus named the "Banner" (*dhvaja*).

From this point onward, up to the tenth stage of practice, one universally practices the conduct of great compassion toward even the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), continuing through the ninety stages.
"I have personally received all six types of non-Buddhist practitioners as my disciples; this is because I have fulfilled the practice of one final [birth] while amidst various false views.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* says: "If you fall into the same state as those six teachers of the non-Buddhists, only then may you accept the food.
The King said: "In the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, I have questioned them regarding this Dharma, contemplated it, observed it, and cultivated it."

The "Adornment of Practice" resolves the doubts of Sudhana. Why is it that in the eighth of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the stage of the Youthful (*kumārabhūta*), one prostrates oneself with the five limbs upon seeing the seer Vimalacitra, and yet here, in this eighth practice (*caryā*), one also prostrates with the five limbs upon seeing King Mahāprabha?
The intention is to clarify that in this stage, the cultivation of compassion reaches the level of wisdom.
The five stages in their entirety are universally encompassed by this [symbol], because it represents the universal pervasiveness of wisdom and compassion; thus, it is used as the symbol.
Within these five stages, the eighth stage clarifies that the bodhisattva’s practice is perfected.
From this eighth stage onward, one cultivates the ten kinds of power and mastery of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, within these five stages, the tenth stage is entirely the wave of wisdom.
Because the *pāramitā* is the primary element and the other nine are its companions, from this point onward, the subsequent stages are spontaneously accomplished. Here,
King Mahāprabha enters the Bodhisattva samādhi headed by Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), manifesting the functional activity of the compassionate mind he practices to benefit others with mastery,
so that future learners may emulate him to clarify non-reliant wisdom and enter equality.
The minds of sentient beings are of the same substance as it, having no distinct nature; both the animate and the inanimate are all of the same substance.

Because of the karma experienced upon entering this samādhi, all sentient beings, as well as the forests and gushing springs, all flow toward it, all bend their branches, and all prostrate themselves; the yakṣas and rākṣasas all cease [their hostilities].
With wisdom and clarity, he accords with all sentient beings, sharing their karmic activities; his single nature is non-dual.
Just as when a worldly sovereign possesses compassion for people, dragons and spirits submit, phoenixes gather and fish glide—how much more so would humans not look up to him in devotion?
How much more so for this Great Radiance King, whose wisdom penetrates the true source and whose conduct is equal to the Dharma?

Taking the mind of universal compassion as primary, one’s spirit unites with all sentient beings and shares the same radiance as all things, serving as the fundamental source of the myriad existences.
It is like a *maṇi* jewel that assumes the colors of objects while its own original color remains unchanged;

it is like sacred wisdom that is without self-mind, yet takes the minds of all things as its own mind, such that no object is at variance with it. This clarifies the great mind of compassionate love based on the realization of the single essence.
Because he manifests a physical body in response to beings so as to cause them to attain illumination, the mountains, plains, grasses, and trees all turn toward the King to pay him homage;
the ponds, pools, springs, wells, rivers, and seas all overflow and flow forth before the King.
This is because the realm of wisdom and the Great Compassion of the Dharma accord with one another in this way. If sentient beings...
The objects transformed by consciousness cannot be produced by sentient beings; for instance, within the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), all environments perform the work of a Buddha.

Sudhana praised this woman with a single verse for her cultivation of the three qualities: precept, patience, and diligence.
The practice of attaining a body that illuminates the world with radiance is like the sutra’s detailed explanation;
by means of the laywoman entering meditative absorption to manifest the *sarvadharmāparitṛpti-samādhi-mukha*, she causes Sudhana to see it as clearly explained in the text.
As for the *amogha-cakra-samādhi*, one must study it because both worldly and world-transcending [qualities] are fully perfected therein, such that the wisdom of the ten powers is attained.
As for the Wheel Samādhi, it is because the wheel of the Buddha’s differentiated wisdom has been perfected;

as for the Samādhi Door of the Inexhaustible Treasury of the Buddha-seed, it is because there is nothing that wisdom does not encompass and no transformation that is ever interrupted. These three samādhis constitute the general [principle], while the ten thousand samādhis are the particulars.
This clarifies the teaching door of the Indra’s Net, wherein the one and the many are mutually inclusive and enter into one another with sovereign mastery.
Pushing downward from this stage, virtue ascends; herein lies the ninth stage of the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-caryā*).

In this stage, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is predominant, with the other nine perfections acting as its companions. From the perspective of the gates of wisdom, these stages collectively remedy all obstacles;

from the perspective of the specific stages, they specifically remedy the obstacle of lacking mastery over the teaching of the Dharma, thereby enabling the attainment of such mastery. This is the second instance of virtue being pushed upward.
From the passage beginning with "Furthermore, following the manner of the various bodhisattvas" down to "taking his leave and departing," there are fifteen and a half lines of scripture.
Within this, four sections may be distinguished: first, extolling his virtues so that Sudhana may advance;

second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend and citing the name of the city, namely Puṇḍravardhana; third, citing the name of the spiritual friend; and fourth, describing his conduct as he sets out.
The heterodox teacher outside the house was named Viśvāmitra. Regarding the literal explanation of the text:
the city is named Anāthapiṇḍada; *anātha* means "joy" (*nanda*) and *piṇḍada* means "birth" (*sara*).

This signifies that this city gives rise to immeasurable joy, bliss, and other such matters, indicating that this spiritual friend’s perfection of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is equal to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Having already perfected the fruit of Buddhahood and universally practiced all deeds, he should manifest his body everywhere according to what is seen;
entering those halls and gates to bring forth birth and benefit the common people, causing them all to rejoice, the city is therefore named "Birth of Immeasurable Joy and Bliss.

Those who leave the home life and follow external paths are called "Universal Practitioners" (*vairācārin*); because their wisdom is equal to the fruit of Buddhahood, they are termed "those who have left the home life."
To transform those of heterodox currents by manifesting in conformity with their false views is called being an "externalist" (tīrthika);

to perform deeds that benefit sentient beings and to fully engage in the affairs of the three vehicles is called "universal conduct" (sarvatraga). To remain untainted amidst such conduct is to be a "renunciant" (pravrajita).

Within the practices of a bodhisattva, to transform the heterodox and not the orthodox is called being an "externalist"; to remain untainted while dwelling in such conduct is called being a "renunciant."
From householders up to the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners, I have acted for them all; the meaning of the "South" is as explained previously.
In the tenth [chapter], at the city of Duḥsara, I went forth as the leader of the Pāśupata non-Buddhists, practicing the "True Conduct."
[Sūtra] At that time, after the youth Sudhana had heard the Dharma from the laywoman Acalā, he devotedly recollected all her instructions, receiving them with faith and reflecting upon them.
Gradually traveling through various kingdoms and towns, he reached the city of Tuṣāra;
at sunset, he entered that city, passing through its marketplaces, shops, and neighborhoods.
Searching everywhere along the roadsides, he eventually found the Universal Wandering Heretic (Parivrājaka) to the east of the city. There was a mountain there named Śubhavatu;
at the hour of midnight, Sudhana saw the summit of this mountain—its grasses, trees, and rocky peaks—radiating a brilliant light like the rising sun.
Having witnessed this, he was filled with great joy and thought to himself: "I shall surely find [him] here."
The spiritual friend then departed from the city and ascended that mountain, where he beheld the non-Buddhist practitioner upon a level area of the peak, walking slowly in circumambulation.
His physical marks were perfect and his majestic radiance was so brilliant that even the Great Brahmā King could not surpass it;
he was surrounded by ten thousand hosts of Brahmās. The spiritual friend approached him, prostrated with his head at his feet, and circumambulated him.
Having circumambulated him immeasurable times, he joined his palms before him and spoke these words:

"Noble One, I have previously set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. Viśvāmitra replied:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! I have already established myself in the bodhisattva practice that reaches all places;
I have already accomplished the samādhi-door of universally observing the world; I have already accomplished the power of spiritual transformations that are non-dependent and effortless;
and I have accomplished the universal gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Noble son, throughout all the various directions in the world..."
All various forms, various modes of conduct and understanding, and various deaths and births in all realms of existence— namely, the realm of devas,
the realm of nāgas, the realm of yakṣas, the realm of gandharvas, the realm of asuras, the realm of garuḍas, the realm of kiṃnaras, the realm of mahoragas,
the hells, the animal realm, the realm of Yama, and the realms of humans and non-humans— in all such realms, they may dwell.
Among all such sentient beings— whether they hold various views, or have faith in the Two Vehicles, or further believe in and delight in the path of the Mahāyāna—
I benefit them through various skillful means and various gateways of wisdom. That is to say,
I may expound for them all the various arts and crafts of the world so that they may become fully proficient in all clever techniques and dhāraṇīs.
The Bhikṣuṇī Jñānāvatī sometimes expounded the skillful means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to cause them to fulfill the path to omniscience;
sometimes she expounded the various *pāramitās* to cause them to dedicate [their merit] toward the stage of omniscience;
sometimes she praised the great bodhicitta to prevent them from losing the resolve for the unsurpassed path; or sometimes she praised the practices of the bodhisattvas to cause them...

They fulfill their vows to purify buddha-fields and deliver sentient beings; or they expound upon how the commission of various evil deeds leads to the reception of manifold bitter retributions such as those in the hells, causing them to develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward unwholesome karma;
or they expound upon the various roots of goodness consisting of offerings made to the Buddhas, which definitively result in the fruit of omniscience, causing them to give rise to joy.
With a mind that either praises and explains all the merits of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas to cause them to delight in the Buddha-body and seek omniscience;
or praises and explains the majestic power of the Buddhas to cause them to aspire to and delight in the indestructible body of a Buddha;
or praises and explains the sovereign body of a Buddha to cause them to seek the great majesty of a Tathāgata that cannot be eclipsed.
Furthermore, virtuous son, within this city of Tuṣāra, in every location and among all classes of people—
whether men or women— I employ skillful means to manifest myself in forms identical to theirs and preach the Dharma to them as appropriate.
Yet none of these sentient beings can know who I am or from where I have come.

Furthermore, son of good family, just as you have benefited sentient beings in this city, so too shall you benefit all the multitudes wherever they dwell—in cities, towns, and villages throughout Jambudvīpa—causing those who hear you to practice according to reality.
Son of good family, within Jambudvīpa there are ninety-six groups, each giving rise to divergent views; yet...
I have skillfully tamed those who give rise to attachment to a self within all these realms, causing them to abandon every form of view;
as it is in Jambudvīpa, so it is in the other four continents; as it is in the four continents, so it is in the trichiliocosm;
and as it is in the trichiliocosm, so it is in the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions.

"O sons of noble family, throughout the oceans of sentient beings, I manifest various physical bodies through various skillful means and various Dharma gates, according to the inclinations of the minds of those beings, and I preach the Dharma for them with various voices and sounds so that they may obtain benefit.
I only know this Bodhisattva practice of reaching all places; as for the [practices] of all other Bodhisattvas..."
The body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is equal in number to all sentient beings; he attains a body that is indistinguishable from that of all beings.
By means of his transformation bodies, he enters universally into all realms of existence, manifesting birth in every place and appearing before all sentient beings.
With pure radiance, he illuminates the world, dwelling through all kalpas by means of unimpeded vows.
They have attained peerless practices like the net of Indra; they constantly and diligently benefit all sentient beings while dwelling together with them without attachment;
they are entirely equal throughout the three periods of time; they universally illuminate everything with the wisdom of non-self;
and they observe all things with the treasury of great compassion. How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
"Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Vast, where there is a merchant chief named Utpalabhūti who sells incense.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave.
And he departed.

[Treatise] Within the first "Dharma-gate of Entering Properly into the Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva practice of reaching all places," there are five general sections; the first is "Single-minded Goodness."
1. The progressive advancement of knowledge and contemplation; 2. Traveling gradually to seek out a virtuous friend; 3.

Seeing [the teacher] walking on a mountain peak and level ground—the mountain peak represents wisdom (*jñāna*) and the level ground represents the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), signifying that great wisdom is not separate from the Dharma-body, yet it appears similar to false views;
4. Approaching to pay respects and formally presenting one's request; 5. Practicing wholesome conduct universally.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text of the dharma practiced by the friend Sudhana: "Outsiders" (*bāhyaka*) refers to those who practice everywhere;
because Bodhisattvas transform the heterodox but do not transform the orthodox, they are called "outsiders.

All that they cultivate and advance toward has not yet reached the ultimate wondrous practice of the principle and wisdom of the single-vehicle *dharmadhātu*, wherein the one and the many, identity and difference, and body and land are mutually interpenetrated with sovereign mastery.
In the worlds of the ten directions, there are gateways as numerous as Indra’s net, all of which belong to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Such are the ones who penetrate both the mundane and the sacred, leading others through the skillful means of common practice; they are called "omnipresent non-Buddhists" (*sarvatraga-tīrthika*).
Those such as Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi are also of this class. They conceal their true nature and act in accordance with the various types among the masses.
Beings merely receive its benefits, never knowing who is right and who is wrong. Such an activity constantly pervades the ten directions, manifesting at all times;

it follows form like a shadow and responds to sound like an echo. It is not a substance that comes or goes, yet through the penetration of wisdom into all phenomena, it constantly manifests a physical body in response, as stated in the subsequent text: "I have already accomplished universal observation."
Having already accomplished the gateways of worldly samādhis, having already accomplished the supernormal powers of non-reliance,
and having accomplished the universal gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā*, I universally benefit sentient beings throughout all various locations,
forms, and dispositions in the world; even while remaining in the world, I pervade all realms of existence.
When he constantly acts for the benefit of others, the multitude of people do not know from where he comes, nor do they feel doubt or wonder;

unaware and unperceiving, they do not know what kind of person this stream of being is. Because his conduct pervades all places where sentient beings dwell, this is the tenth true practice of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Here, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions. This...
The stage of *sthiti* (abiding) functions to remove the obstacle of lack of mastery while acting within the cycle of birth and death, thereby enabling one to attain mastery;
the remaining broad meaning is as in the preceding text. These ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) are the model for entering the Dharma-gate wherein the Buddha dwells;

these ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are the pattern for the conduct of Samantabhadra; the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are formed by emulating these; and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are based upon these ten abidings and ten practices.
Practicing with harmony and integration through the power of compassion and vows, one gives rise to wisdom and arouses pity so as not to fall into partiality;
one cultivates both supramundane *nirvāṇa* and the two obstacles of defilement and purity, ensuring they constantly abide within the ocean of all birth-and-death throughout the ten directions,
relying on the self-nature *dharmadhātu* and the universal Bodhisattva practices of the Buddha-fruit, which are eternally pervasive like Indra’s net.
Because it is a gateway of unimpeded access to the realm of the net, these ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are established.

They harmonize wisdom and compassion, as well as worldly and world-transcending states, so that all may be integrated and reconciled. Because they rely on fundamental mastery, those who exclusively cultivate meditative practices seeking world-transcendence are brought into harmony;
by giving rise to immeasurable conceptions, they activate the function of great wisdom, ensuring there is no fixed distraction. Thus, they are established.
The ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) cause the bodhisattvas who are training through provisional means not to unilaterally and falsely seek a Buddha’s pure land elsewhere;

they establish the ten dedications so that one may constantly abide in the body of tranquil concentration and perpetually pervade all of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to gather and transform sentient beings;
they give rise to the ten dedications so that one’s thoughts encompass the ten directions and all things equally.

The stream of sentient beings’ perceptions, conceptions, volitions, and recollections, though flickering and shifting, becomes the function of wisdom, giving rise to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
It causes even a field of merit as small as a mustard seed to pervade the ten directions and fill the entire Dharma-realm, giving rise to the ten dedications.
It causes all worldly views and even the most minute supernatural powers to become universal.
The Worthy One extensively brings forth the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), causing those in the eighth abode and eighth stage to increase their wisdom;
he causes Bodhisattvas to recollect their great vows and, through skillful means, to give rise to great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*) for the universal benefit of sentient beings.
Abiding not within mere pure wisdom, he brings forth the ten dedications, causing Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds to give rise to the Great [Vehicle] of the Tathāgata.
May one be endowed with the merits of a Buddha and give rise to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) as extensively explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (*Daśabhūmika-vyākhyāna*).

If one lacks these ten gates of dedication, all those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment] will collectively abide in the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and no bodhisattva will attain the equipment for becoming a Buddha or fulfill the conduct of Samantabhadra.
A bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) relies upon these three dharmas with excellence...
Through the power of aspiration, one resolves the mind and relies solely on the three aforementioned dharmas of application to progress until the merit is perfected and the Way is fulfilled.
Just as at the initial resolution of the mind, one does not shift through time, days, months, or years;
it is like Maitreya pointing back to Mañjuśrī, clarifying that the fruit does not depart from the cause. Thereupon, one sees oneself enter into the body of Samantabhadra.
The illumination of Samantabhadra’s conduct is likewise not separate from the internal cause; thus Maitreya said:
"When I descend to Jambudvīpa in the future, you and Mañjuśrī shall come again to see me. This shows that the future world and the present time do not shift.

This is discussed according to the reality of wisdom (*jñāna*), and is not the same as the deluded transformations of emotional consciousness or false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that perceive many kalpas within a single vehicle.

The practice of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) occurs at the very beginning of the stage of initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*). Furthermore, it is said that the trichiliocosm constitutes the Buddha’s field of retribution, yet this has not yet reached the infinite realm of the Dharma-dhātu;
thus, from the section on the "Gate of Mutual Interpenetration Without Obstruction" onwards, one advances through the virtues of the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).

Within this advancement through the virtues of the Ten Stages of Dedication, Sudhana encounters the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the Ten Stages of Dedication, proceeding from the advancement through virtues according to the various Bodhisattvas.
From "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" down to "having taken his leave and departed," all sections below this follow the same pattern as the five gates mentioned above.
Specifically: first, it extols the virtues [of the previous teacher] to cause Sudhana to advance;

second, it indicates the location and name of the country where the spiritual friend resides, which is called Vast and Great (Vipula); third, it mentions the name of the spiritual friend, namely the Incense Merchant named Utpalabhūti.

In the section where Roca and Padma offer four exhortations for Sudhana to go and inquire, and five expressions of reverence before departing, the commentary on the text explains the meaning as follows:

among the praises of their virtues, the phrase "abiding through unimpeded vows in all kalpas and attaining unimpeded practices like a net of Indra" refers precisely to the skillful means of vow and practice within the Ten Stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).
Furthermore, this is combined with the Dharma-gate of "Skillfully Knowing All Fragrances."
Blending incense and medicinal herbs to be sold as a means of manifesting dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one unifies the conceptualizations and discriminations of wisdom and compassion,
nirvana and the defiled-pure, and the general and the particular, into a single pellet of the incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and liberation-knowledge-and-vision.
Just as these blended perfumes— combining various fragrances into a single pellet— are mutually interpenetrating, so too are all phenomena unified.
All that provides benefit is devoid of self-nature, yet it does not lose its own virtue; identity and difference are each established in themselves.

This refers to the merchant who sells incense, symbolizing the Blue Lotus of the tenth dedication (*daśama-pariṇāmanā*). It signifies the harmonious integration of principle and wisdom, great compassion and great vows, and the mastery over the general and particular aspects of the ten thousand practices, all unified as a single pill because there is no attachment to their meaning. As for the meaning of the "South," it is as explained previously regarding the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).
The first explanation is as follows: The land is called "Vast" because it extensively gives rise to great vows and initiates boundless practice to universally embrace all classes of beings.
Thus, these vows are the wind for the myriad practices, causing them to proceed boundlessly.
Furthermore, these vows are the wind of wisdom, causing all thoughts and conceptions to become the sovereign function of great wisdom and supernormal powers. These vows are...
The wind that induces the blooming of all samādhis and concentrations purifies sentient beings who are mired in defilement,
causing them to have no dependence and to attain non-reliant wisdom; because its quiescent function is sovereign and pervades all sentient beings,

it is like the "Peak of Wondrous Height" (*Sumeru*) used to symbolize signless wisdom at the beginning of the Ten Abodes, and like the "Land of Three Eyes" compared [to the sun] at the beginning of the Ten Practices.
The appearance of the Buddha Kūṭāgāraśikharābhyudgata-rāja at the beginning of the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) represents the initial emergence from the bonds of affliction;

his meeting with the Elder Ghoṣila at the head of the ten dedications represents the harmonious integration of wisdom and compassion, and the unification of the myriad practices, nirvāṇa, and saṃsāra.

These are the underlying intentions according to the respective stages, which should be examined in detail. These fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) all represent the progressive advancement of practice.

One must certainly understand this destination and not practice it falsely. This "Selling Incense" represents the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), which harmonize and integrate the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) through great vows.
It is the gate of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) where wisdom and principle, as well as compassion, enter into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) without any obstruction;
its name is "Blue Lotus," signifying conduct that is unstained by birth-and-death and unstained by nirvana.
Abiding in duality and non-duality, yet remaining undefiled therein like a blue lotus,
which necessarily grows from within the mud and turbid water yet remains unstained by the nature of that mud and water— its color and fragrance being supreme— so too, O Bodhisattva,
through the power of dedicating this great vow, you shall dwell within the mud of birth and death before finally accomplishing Buddhahood within the Dharma-realm.
The fruit of Samantabhadra’s myriad practices is the retribution of merit whose color and fragrance are supreme, such that none can surpass it;
among all flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent in color and fragrance.

Just as among all practices, the ten dedications harmonize birth-and-death and nirvana, unifying wisdom, compassion, and the myriad practices into a single Dharma-realm to transform all sentient beings.
It causes all to be free from suffering and to manifest the fragrance of great wisdom; this is superior because it surpasses all others who seek transcendence separately.
Therefore, it is represented by the merchant Qinglianhuhexiang (Blue Lotus Flower Combined Fragrance) so that it may be easily understood.
The first of the ten spiritual friends on the thirtieth stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is the Elder Mahāgovinda, the Merchant of Incense,
whose dedication is "Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings."
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, following the instructions of his spiritual friends, disregarded his own body and life;
he was not attached to wealth and treasures, did not delight in crowds of people, did not indulge in the five desires, did not long for his kinsmen, and did not value royal rank.
He aspired only to transform and deliver all sentient beings, to adorn and purify the lands of all Buddhas, and to make offerings to all Buddhas.
May I realize and know the true nature of all phenomena; may I cultivate and accumulate the great ocean of all bodhisattva merits;
may I practice all meritorious deeds without ever regressing; may I constantly perform the practices of a bodhisattva throughout all kalpas by the power of great vows;
and may I universally enter the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas.
I only pray that you will enter a single gate of samādhi and universally manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of all gates of samādhi;
I only pray that you will see all Buddhas within a single pore of a Buddha’s body without ever feeling weary or satisfied;
I only pray that you will attain the light of wisdom of all dharmas and be able to uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, single-mindedly seeking these qualities of all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva, traveling by stages through various lands, arrived at the great kingdom and went to the householder’s residence.
He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, desiring to seek the equal wisdom of all Buddhas and desiring to fulfill the aspirations of all Buddhas."
With immeasurable great vows, they desire to purify the most supreme form-bodies of all Buddhas; they desire to see the pure dharma-bodies of all Buddhas;
they desire to know the vast wisdom-bodies of all Buddhas; they desire to purify and cultivate all bodhisattva practices;
they desire to illuminate all bodhisattva samādhis; they desire to dwell securely in all bodhisattva dhāraṇīs; they desire to eliminate...

Having extinguished all obstacles and desiring to travel throughout all worlds of the ten directions, yet not yet knowing how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice or how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path in order to give birth to the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), the elder said:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are indeed able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"O son of good family who has set his mind on *samyak-saṃbodhi*, I am skilled in discerning all fragrances and I also know the methods for blending all fragrances—
namely, all incenses, all burning incenses, all unguents, and all powdered incenses. Furthermore,
I know the origins from which all such kings of fragrance arise, and I am also well-versed in the fragrances of the devas."
Furthermore, he skillfully distinguishes all the various fragrances belonging to nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth;
as well as fragrances that cure various diseases, fragrances that sever all evils, fragrances that produce joy,
fragrances that increase afflictions, fragrances that extinguish afflictions, and fragrances that cause delight in conditioned existence.
The incense that inspires weary detachment toward the conditioned; the incense that relinquishes all arrogance and negligence; the incense that arouses the mind to recollect the Buddha;
the incense that realizes and understands the Dharma-gates; the incense enjoyed by the noble ones; the incense of the various distinctions of all bodhisattvas;
the incense of all the stages of the bodhisattvas—incenses such as these arise, manifest, appear, and are accomplished, pure and secure.
I have fully realized all such things as the spheres of skillful means, majestic power, functional activities, and their fundamental basis.
Good son, in the human world there is a fragrance called "Elephant Treasury" (*hastigarbha*), which arises from the fighting of dragons;

if one pellet is burned, it immediately gives rise to a great cloud of fragrance that completely covers the royal capital, and for seven days it rains down fine fragrant rain. If this rain touches the body, [it brings about purification].
Their bodies will be golden in color; even the garments they wear and the palaces and towers they inhabit will all be golden.

If the wind carries these into the palaces and beings smell them, for seven days and seven nights they will be filled with joy, their bodies and minds will be blissful, and they will be free from all illness.
They will not harm one another, and they will be free from all sorrow and suffering, without alarm, fear, agitation, or anger.

"Seeing that their minds are directed toward one another with compassion and their intentions are pure, I know this and preach the Dharma for them so that they may resolutely resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son, on Mount Malaya there is a sandalwood incense called 'Ox-head' (*gośīrṣa*); if one anoints one's body with it, even if one enters a pit of fire, the fire cannot burn them. Good son.
In the ocean of the sons [of the gods], there is a fragrance named Invincible (*anabhibhūta*).
If it is used to anoint drums and various conch shells, when their sounds are produced, all enemy armies will spontaneously retreat and disperse.

Noble son, from the side of Lake Anavatapta emerges the aloeswood fragrance named Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*). If one burns even a single pellet of this fragrance, as small as a sesame seed, its scent...
The fragrance pervades the realm of Jambudvīpa; all sentient beings who hear it are freed from all transgressions, and their precept-qualities become pure.
Good son, on Mount Himavat there is a fragrance named Aruṇa. If there are sentient beings who smell this fragrance, their minds will certainly be freed from all defiled attachments.
When I preach the Dharma for them, there are none who do not attain the Vimala Samādhi (Stainless Samādhi). Good son...
In the realm of the Rākṣasas, there is an incense named Ocean-Treasury (*sāgaragarbha*). This incense is used exclusively by the Cakravartin kings;

if one pellet is burned and its fragrance wafts forth, the king and his fourfold army will all soar through the void. Good son, in the Heaven of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), there is an incense named Pure Adornment (*viśuddhavyūha*);
if one pellet is burned and its fragrance wafts forth, it causes the minds of all the devas to become universally pure.
"O son of good family, when one recollects the Buddha, there is a fragrance in the Suyāma Heaven called Viśuddhagarbha.
If one burns a single pellet of it to fumigate the air, the hosts of the Suyāma Heaven will all gather like clouds at the abode of that Heavenly King to listen to the Dharma together.
O son of good family, in the Tuṣita Heaven there is a fragrance called Sindhava, which [is used] at the seat of a Bodhisattva bound to one more birth."

If one burns a single pellet from the former [incense], it will give rise to a great cloud of fragrance that pervades the entire Dharma-realm, universally raining down all manner of offering articles to make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Good son, there is a fragrance called "Captivating the Mind" (*Manohara*);
if one burns a single pellet of it, for seven days it will universally rain down all kinds of ornamental articles. Good son...
I, Subhūti, know only this method of harmonizing incense; as for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who have distanced themselves from all evil habitual tendencies,
who are unstained by worldly desires, who have forever severed the afflictions and the snares of Māra,
who have transcended all realms of existence, who adorn themselves with the fragrance of wisdom, and who are entirely free from attachment to the world— all these they have fully accomplished.
Their precepts are pure through non-attachment; their wisdom and conduct are free from attachment;
they are without attachment toward any object whatsoever. Their minds are equanimous, unattached, and independent.
How could I know their wondrous conduct, describe their merits, reveal their gates of pure precepts, demonstrate their faultless deeds, or discern their freedom from defilement?
"O son of good family who practices virtue of body, speech, and mind, to the south of here there is a great city named Kūṭāgāra.
Within it dwells a mariner named Vaira. Go to him and ask: 'How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and gazed upon him with deep reverence.
He took his leave and departed.

[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the "Dharma-gate of Entering Properly into the Stage," from the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana" down to "I only know this method of harmonizing incense," five gates are established within this segment; the same applies to all subsequent stages.
Following this model: first, reflecting upon the instructions of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) with right mindfulness;
second, gradually proceeding on the journey to the place where the elder resides; third, paying respect by prostrating at his feet; fourth, formally expressing one's request;

fifth, the elder explaining his own practice and bestowing it upon Sudhana. Regarding the word-by-word commentary on the text, starting from "At that time, the youth Sudhana... [the narrative continues].
Below this, there are ten gates of aspiration that clarify the entry into dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

This is the progressive advancement of one who traverses the stages by means of aspirations that harmonize all aspects of the ultimate and conventional, the defiled and the pure, and the non-obstruction of wisdom and compassion.
"Reaching the vast land" refers to generating wisdom through aspiration, initiating inexhaustible practices, and guiding sentient beings. This continues up to the tenth [aspiration].
Within every single atom of the lands as numerous as the atoms in the ten directions, there are inexhaustible Buddha-dharmas and physical manifestations that guide and receive sentient beings;
it is thus throughout all the lands and atoms of the ten directions. Like a celestial net of Indra, these realms are layered and inexhaustible because his vows and practices are vast.
Therefore, the name of this land is "Vast" (Guangda), which is now being formally explained in the fourth section.
Within the section on the requested gate, the elder replied: "I am skilled at discerning all fragrances; this has two meanings:
first, truly knowing all worldly fragrances; second, using fragrance to symbolize the Dharma.

Regarding the first, truly knowing all fragrances, this refers to the 'totality of all fragrances to be known' mentioned in the sutra—namely, incense for burning, for smearing, and for powdering—which are the specific enumerations of the 'kings of fragrance' that emerge."
The section below "Having dwelt [there]" concerns the various fragrances produced by the categories of karma arising from birth;
the section below "These are" indicates that there are five kinds of fragrance among humans, one kind among rākṣasas, and four kinds among devas, totaling ten kinds of fragrance.
Their functions are fully detailed in the sūtra itself. These aforementioned fragrances are used to symbolize the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
Illuminating the nature of incense as being without dependence, it can give rise to all that is wholesome and extinguish all that is evil;

illuminating great vows as being without dependence, it can produce immeasurable roots of goodness. Thus, one raises clouds of immeasurable great wisdom and rains down the rain of immeasurable pure dharmas;
one practices immeasurable acts of great compassion and transforms immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to attain the extinction of suffering and to give rise to...
If the Great Being had not possessed a great vow, he would not have been able to give rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).

Even if one were to cultivate liberation, it would all result in the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). In the human world there is a fragrance called "Elephant Treasury" (*hastigarbha*); this fragrance is produced from the combat of dragons.
If a single pellet of it is burned, it raises a great cloud of incense that completely covers the royal capital, and for seven days it rains down a fine rain of fragrance.
If it were to smear the body such that the body becomes golden in color, this signifies that at the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment within the stage of the Ten Abodes,
one raises great clouds of vows with the fragrance of the seven factors of awakening, extensively gives rise to compassionate practices to universally cover all sentient beings,
and seeks all-encompassing wisdom; furthermore, with the dragon of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one battles against the afflictions of the twelve links of existence until piercing through to the void.
Boundless wisdom-fire blazes forth, and the incense of great wisdom arises; clouds of compassion form, raining down the rain of pure dharmas upon sentient beings.
Those who are moistened by it attain perfect enlightenment at the very moment they first resolve their minds.

Even the garments they wear, as well as the palaces and towers, all become golden in color, clarifying that through the arousal of great vows and the dedication of merit, all worldly things [are transformed].
Because the union of patience, compassion, contemplation, and wisdom pervades the entire dharma-realm with sovereign purity,
if sentient beings are blown into the palace by the wind and inhale it, for seven days and seven nights they shall be free from all sorrow and suffering;
they shall not be startled, terrified, distracted, or angry, but shall face one another with a mind of loving-kindness and pure intention— this is the progressive transformation of clarity.
Upon hearing this, they all likewise rejoice, giving rise to the gates of great vows and awakening the seven factors of enlightenment. Having understood this, I preach the Dharma for them;

that is to say, one who wishes to exhort sentient beings to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment must first exhort them to generate vast vows, dedicate their merit, and give rise to a heart of firm and sincere resolve. First, one lays out the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the seven...

Only those whose awakening and conduct are as pure as flowers are worthy of hearing the path of the Most True One; thus, if you practice with such exhortation, there will be no failure among ten thousand attempts.
As for Mount Malaya: this mountain is located within the borders of South India, in the kingdom of Malayagiri.
This kingdom derives its name from this mountain. This mountain produces much white sandalwood incense; indeed, it is from this mountain that sandalwood incense originates.

It is called "ox-head" (gokhura) when used as an ointment for the body; even if one enters a pit of fire, the fire cannot burn them. This clarifies the stage of dwelling in the ground (*bhūmi-vihāra*).

By generating the power of great vows and the power of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and by means of the principle of the non-substantiality of the *dharmakāya* through the ten supreme wholesome dharmas, one perfects the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*) and uses it as an ointment for the body.
Thus dedicated, one enters the pit of the fires of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)—the fires of greed, anger, and attachment.
Fire cannot burn or harm the incense in the ocean called "Invincible" (*anabhibhūta*);
if it is applied to drums and various conch shells, when their sound is produced, all enemy armies will spontaneously retreat and disperse.

This illustrates that one who dwells in the practice of patience achieves it through the *dharma-kṣānti*, and thus returns into the ocean of birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings by means of forbearance.
The mind hears all sounds of good and evil; when evil, perverse enemies are struck, they naturally retreat and disperse.
On the shores of Lake Anavatapta there is a type of agalloch incense called Padmagarbha;

a single pellet of this incense, as small as a sesame seed, if burned, will cause its fragrance to pervade the entire realm of Jambudvīpa, and all sentient beings who smell it shall be freed from [afflictions].
All transgressions and precepts are purified, and the light of clarity arises; dwelling in the Noble Abode, one penetrates the karma of the three realms without obstruction.
Constantly born into the family of the Buddhas, stainless and pure, this corresponds to the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), from which one emerges from the karma of the three realms.
By means of the mind of the four great vows, one returns to enter the great pool of the four currents of birth and death to transform and teach sentient beings.
All sentient beings submerged in birth and death are entirely free from defiled attachment;

they are like lotus blossoms in a treasury, proclaiming the subtle and wondrous fragrance of the Dharma that pervasively perfumes the ten directions. Those who hear it have their transgressions extinguished and their categories of precepts purified.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a fragrance named Aruṇa, which is a scarlet scent capable of dyeing cloth crimson. If sentient beings smell this fragrance, [they shall likewise be purified].
Those whose minds are resolute and free from all defiled attachments are those who fully possess the skillful means of abiding in the gate of the dhyāna-pāramitā;
they dedicate their great vows toward saṃsāra so that all sentient beings may cultivate and become habituated to the dhyāna-pāramitā, thereby attaining entry into the stainless samādhi.
By means of the Himalayas, this represents the essence of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), which is inherently pure and stainless.

Because it is the essence of defilement, within the realm of the rākṣasas there is a fragrance called "Ocean Treasury" (*sāgaragarbha*). This fragrance is used exclusively by a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*);
if one pellet is burned and its smoke wafts forth, the king and his fourfold army all ascend into the air.

This clearly symbolizes that by means of the sixth stage, the Abode of the Correct Mind (*samyakcittavihāra*), one employs the wisdom of the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*) to transform the rākṣasa-like afflictions and re-enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The ocean, by means of the wheel-turning king of *prajñā*, burns with the incense of the treasury of the wisdom-ocean and perfumes the kings of birth-and-death;

the four kinds of *māra* all ascend into the emptiness of phenomena. This concludes the general representation of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), wherein the vows and practices of the ten abodes and ten conducts are harmonized and fused, allowing for mastery over the two wisdoms of birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*, as well as the two gates of compassion and wisdom.
Based upon this, one cultivates the principle of the non-conceptual dependent origination of the self-nature of the dharma-realm;
this is symbolized by incense, ointments, and blended perfumes, so that learners may easily understand it—let them know that all cases are to be understood in this manner.
If, within the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten stages, there were no power of dedication and great vows, one would merely attain the [fruits] of the two vehicles.
Since there is no one who can achieve Buddhahood through a fixed path, there are practitioners who must thoroughly master the proper ritual procedures.
They must clearly contemplate the meaning of the teachings through the six aspects (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*): the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and disintegration.

From the perspective of "I alone know this," those who harmonize the dharma of incense clarify the wisdom that harmonizes the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—as well as wisdom, compassion, vows, and practice, and the relationship between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and defilement and purity.
The fragrance of the Sovereign of Purity and the name of the Blue Lotus have already been used to represent this;

what follows is an inference of virtues leading to further advancement, the remaining meanings of which are self-evident from the text. Second, regarding the inference of virtues that causes Sudhana to advance, the section from "Just as all Bodhisattvas...
down to "having taken his leave and departed" consists of ten lines of scripture, which are divided into five sections. First, the inference...
1. The advancement of virtue; 2. Indicating the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); 3. Naming the city and the pavilion where the spiritual friend resides;
4. Naming the boatman, Vasiṣṭha; 5. Prostrating and departing. Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: "In the south" is explained as before.
Regarding the name of the city, "Pavilion": this is near the South Sea; the ground is low and damp, and the people...
They mostly dwell in multi-storied pavilions, which are also established according to the wisdom of differentiation;

within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the myriad phenomena are harmonized through their totality, particulars, similarities, and differences, arranged in successive layers to form the names of the cities.

The ship’s captain Vāsava—here translated as "Svairaprabha" (Self-Mastery Radiance)—has attained self-mastery within the ocean of birth and death; he is the one who, within these Ten Dedications, is capable of...
Entering the ocean of birth and death, one practices great compassion as the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).

Within the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), one contemplates the ocean of birth and death and the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*) as the nature that is inherently pure; because this is fundamentally nothing other than Buddha-wisdom, it is taken as the essence of the precepts.

Within the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), one clarifies the two skillful methods: the method of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and the method of calculation (*gaṇanālakṣaṇa*), as well as worldly arts and crafts for the benefit of others.

Sentient beings take this as the essence of their precepts; these ten dedications enter the conventional from the ultimate to lead sentient beings through the sea of birth and death, taking the practice of compassion and kindness as the essence of their precepts.
Thus, in these three stages of cultivating the precepts, there are both similarities and differences in the methods of advancement.
As for the "ship's captain," the Master takes great compassion as the essence of his precepts and abides eternally therein.

Because he dwells within the ocean of birth and death to ferry sentient beings across through coming and going, as clearly explained in the section on praising his virtues regarding the essential meaning:
"He is fully accomplished in the precept of non-attachment, like a boatman who ferries people across without remaining on this shore and without remaining on the other shore."
