[Treatise] The second pavilion-city is that of the boatman Vaśira, whose lord is the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmana*).

[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, facing the city of Lokeśvararāja, surveyed the roads—observing whether the paths were high or low, whether they were level or rugged, whether they were pure or defiled, and whether they were winding or straight. Proceeding gradually, he reflected:
"I shall draw near to that spiritual friend; for a spiritual friend is one who has accomplished the practice of all bodhisattvas."
The cause for accomplishing the practice of the path of the Bodhisattvas; the cause for accomplishing the practice of the path of the perfections (*pāramitā*);

the cause for accomplishing the practice of the path of gathering in sentient beings; the cause for accomplishing the practice of the path of universally entering the dharma-realm without obstruction;
the cause for accomplishing the practice of the path that causes all sentient beings to eliminate false wisdom; the cause for accomplishing the practice that causes all—

The cause for sentient beings to leave behind arrogance is the practice that brings accomplishment; the cause for extinguishing the afflictions of all sentient beings is the practice that brings accomplishment;
the cause for causing all sentient beings to abandon all views is the practice that brings accomplishment;
the cause for pulling out all the thorns of evil for all sentient beings is the practice that brings accomplishment.
What is the causal path for all sentient beings to reach the city of omniscience?
It is because one obtains all wholesome dharmas from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and by the power of the spiritual friend, one attains the path to omniscience.
A spiritual friend is difficult to see and difficult to encounter. Reflecting thus, he gradually traveled on until he reached that city, where he saw the shipmaster.

Outside the city gate, on the seashore, he was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and an immeasurable multitude of other beings who were expounding the Dharma of the great ocean as a skillful means to reveal the ocean of the Buddha’s merits.
Having seen this, Sudhana went to him, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and with palms joined before him, spoke these words: "Noble One, I have..."
"Previously, I gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I did not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices or how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me.
The boatman replied, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have already been able to give rise to the *anuttara*..."
The mind of *samyaksambodhi* can now further inquire into the cause for generating great wisdom, the cause for severing all causes of birth-and-death suffering,
the cause for proceeding to the great jewel-island of omniscience, the cause for accomplishing the indestructible Mahāyāna,

the cause for remaining far removed from the fear of birth-and-death characteristic of the two vehicles while dwelling in various tranquil samādhis, and the cause for riding the chariot of great vows throughout the [universe].
The cause for the pure path of unimpeded practice of the bodhisattva conduct in all places; the cause for the pure path of indestructible wisdom adorned by the bodhisattva conduct;
the cause for the pure path of universally observing all phenomena throughout the ten directions without obstruction;
the cause for the pure path of swiftly entering the ocean of all-knowledge; O virtuous son.
"Son, I am here on this city's seashore path, a son of good family who purely cultivates the bodhisattva practice of the banner of great compassion.
Observing the impoverished beings within Jambudvīpa, for their benefit I practice various austerities;
according to their wishes, I cause them all to be fulfilled. First, I satisfy their minds with worldly things, and then I bestow the wealth of the Dharma upon them."
To cause joy; to cause the cultivation of meritorious conduct; to cause the arising of the path of wisdom; to cause the increase of the power of roots of goodness;

to cause the arousal of the bodhicitta; to cause the purification of the vow for enlightenment; to cause the strengthening of the power of great compassion; to cause the cultivation of the path that can extinguish birth and death;

to cause the arising of practice that does not weary of birth and death; to cause the gathering in of the ocean of all sentient beings; to cause the cultivation of the ocean of all merits; to cause illumination.
I cause all oceans of phenomena to be seen, I cause [beings] to enter all oceans of Buddhas, and I cause them to enter the ocean of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Noble son, dwelling here, I contemplate in this way, attend to in this way, and thus benefit all sentient beings.
Noble son, I know all the jewel-islands, all the jewel-places, and all the jewels within the ocean.
I know all varieties of jewels; I know the purification of all jewels, the drilling of all jewels, the extraction of all jewels, and the fashioning of all jewels.
I know all jewel vessels, all uses of jewels, all realms of jewels, and all radiances of jewels.
I know all the abodes of the nāga palaces, all the abodes of the yakṣas, and all the abodes of the bhūtas.

He skillfully maneuvers and avoids all dangers within the palace; he also skillfully distinguishes the eddies and whirlpools, the depth and shallowness, the distance and proximity of the waves, and the various differences in the quality of the water’s color.

He also skillfully distinguishes the movements and degrees of the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the lengthening and shortening of days and nights, mornings and evenings, and the passage of time measured by the clepsydra.
Furthermore, he knows whether the ship’s iron and wood are strong or brittle, and understands its mechanical workings.
Whether the water was rough or smooth, whether the river was large or small, and whether the wind was favorable or adverse—all such signs of safety and danger were clearly understood by me.
Thus, I would proceed when it was appropriate to proceed and stop when it was appropriate to stop.
Good son, having accomplished such wisdom, I am constantly able to benefit all sentient beings. Good son, with my excellent ship, I transport various groups of merchants.

I lead them along the path of peace and security, further teaching the Dharma to gladden them and guide them to the Isle of Jewels, where I provide them with all manner of treasures until they are fully satisfied. Thereafter, I lead them back to Jambudvīpa.
Good son, I have traveled back and forth with such great ships, yet never once has even one been damaged. If there are sentient beings who behold my body or hear [my voice]...
My Dharma causes them to never again fear the ocean of birth and death; it ensures they will certainly enter the ocean of all-knowledge;
it enables them to exhaust the ocean of all cravings and desires; it allows them to illuminate the ocean of the three periods of time with the light of wisdom;
it enables them to end the ocean of suffering of all sentient beings; it purifies the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings; and it swiftly adorns and purifies the ocean of all buddha-lands.

I am able to travel to the great oceans of the ten directions, universally knowing the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings, universally comprehending the ocean of the conduct of all sentient beings, and universally acceding to the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings. Good son, I have only attained this practice of the Banner of Great Compassion; if there are those who see me, hear me, dwell with me, or remember me, they shall all— [The text continues: ...attain the same as I have attained. Furthermore, good son, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other practices of the banner of great compassion that I have not yet attained. Why is this? Because my life span is short and my wisdom is shallow. Good son, you should not think that I alone have attained these practices of the banner of great compassion. Why is this? O Amoghasiddhi, like all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, you are well able to traverse the great ocean of birth and death;

you are unstained by the ocean of all afflictions; you are able to abandon the ocean of all false views; you are able to contemplate the ocean of the nature of all phenomena; you are able to gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction;

you are already well-established in the ocean of omniscience; you are able to extinguish... [one]... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a liturgical or dhāraṇī text. The final character "一" (one) likely refers to the first of a series of afflictions or obstacles to be extinguished.)
He is able to dwell with equanimity throughout the ocean of all sentient beings' attachments; he is able to cross the ocean of sentient beings by means of his supernormal powers;
and he is able to discipline the ocean of sentient beings according to the proper time. How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Sukhāvatī, and within it there is an elder named Anuttara.
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and wept tears of sorrow;
seeking the spiritual friend with a heart that never grew weary, he took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of entering the actual stage, from the passage beginning "At that time, Sudhana...
down to "...if there are those who see me, hear me, dwell with me, or remember me,
all [their encounters] shall not be in vain," this segment is divided into five sections, the first of which is "Recollection of the Good."
1. Knowledge, teaching, reflection, and spiritual advancement; 2. Gradually traveling on foot to reach that city; 3.
Seeing the shipmaster standing outside the city gate on the seashore; 4. Paying homage with palms joined and expressing one's request; 5.
The shipmaster bestows upon Sudhana the Dharma-door of his own practice. Regarding the exegesis of the text according to its phrasing: "seeing the shipmaster."
Outside the city gate, on the seashore, he dwells surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and other great multitudes;

this has two meanings: first, it is a literal reality, for he acts as a guide for merchants entering the sea and seekers of jewels, as the perils of the ocean cannot be known except through noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*);
second, it is a symbolic dharma (*dharma-pratibimba*), signifying that one personally attains the true gateway and emerges from the entanglements (*saṃyojana*).
Free from suffering, he brings his vows and practices to fruition, forming a great ocean of compassion that constantly stands upon the shore of birth and death to draw in and guide sentient beings.
The hundred thousand merchants represent the perfection of the precepts (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the fulfillment of the myriad practices;
the immeasurable multitude represents the universal completion of all deeds. As the Sūtra says: "Because one proceeds toward the great jewel island of omniscience."
Regarding the accomplishment of the cause of the indestructible Mahāyāna: "Mahā" means great and "Yāna" means vehicle; the teaching thus expounded is collectively termed the Mahāyāna teaching.
It is far removed from the fear of the two vehicles regarding birth and death, and it abides in the samādhi of tranquility.
This passage praises Sudhana, clarifying that he is able to abide in the samādhi of tranquility while circulating within the realm of birth and death.

Because he returns to benefit sentient beings without departing, O son of good family, I know all the jewel-islands, all the jewel-places, all categories of jewels, all species of jewels, and all vessels for jewels within this ocean; such things truly exist.
This wisdom is that which is known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); regarding all worldly phenomena and their conventional designations, I know everything within the ocean.

The "Jewel Island" refers to the island of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) that clearly penetrates all things. The "abode of all jewels" refers to the skillful discernment of the faculties (*indriya*) of the worthy and capable—whether they be sharp or dull.
The "categories of all jewels" refers to the skillful knowledge of the distinctions between those who practice in common and those who practice differently.

The "seeds of all jewels" refers to the skillful knowledge of the differences between the Great and Small Vehicles (*mahāyāna* and *hīnayāna*). My knowing "all jewel vessels" refers to knowing the assemblies.

I know that for those born with great or small capacities, what Dharma should be used to bring them to maturity; that all jewel-like applications of the Dharma should be accorded to their faculties so that they may perform their respective functions;
that the realm of all jewels consists of the realms of the Three Vehicles, the One Vehicle, and the Triple Gem;
and that the light of all jewels consists of the lights of wisdom—both great and small—of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.
That which purifies all jewels consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten perfections, and the skillful means of the five contemplations for settling the mind;
this is the skillful means for purifying the jewel of omniscience. That which drills through all jewels consists of the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

That which brings forth all jewels consists of being skillfully able to establish teachings according to the faculties [of beings], thereby causing the jewel of manifest wisdom to appear; thus it produces everything.

"Jewels" refers to the fact that through signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*), one gives rise to discerning wisdom (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*), and by means of the wind of great vows, one raises the clouds of great compassion to rain down all manner of jewel-showers to transform all sentient beings.
By harmonizing the mind and its objects so that they have no dependence, the jewels of omniscience (*sarvajña*) naturally manifest themselves;
therefore, those who dwell in the difficult places of the dragon palaces are like bodhisattvas in a pure land, for they are like dragons.

The yakṣa who possesses a portion of compassion and the power of traveling through space with a partial mastery is a metaphor for the śrāvaka, who can empty the three poisons and also attain supernormal powers.
The "difficult place" of the rākṣasa palace is a metaphor for the pratyekabuddha dwelling in the ocean of nirvāṇa;
because they can empty ignorance, yet the seeds of the all-knowledge of all Buddhas do not manifest before them, such states are difficult.
All [of these] are dedicated through the power of aspiration so that, remaining together within birth and death, they do not harm ignorance;

they penetrate the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and, by grasping ignorance, attain the Buddha’s seed-wisdom (*tathāgata-jñāna*). This is the gate of mastery over dependent origination within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), called "the dedication of all to avoid all calamities.
Furthermore, it skillfully discerns the depth and shallowness of the whirlpools: namely, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).
The depth or shallowness of karma corresponds to the distance of the waves; the extent of emotional consciousness, thoughts, and攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects) corresponds to the amount of water.
The quality of the water’s color—whether good or bad—corresponds to the nature of the loving heart, whether wholesome or unwholesome.

Furthermore, one clearly discerns the movements, cycles, and quantities of the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the lengthening and shortening of days and nights, morning and evening, and the passage of time measured by the dial and water-clock. This is to be thoroughly clear regarding worldly affairs and to understand the profound phenomena of yin and yang.

One thoroughly knows the orbital movements and degrees of the five planets, the timing of wind-risings, the measurement of the *ghatikā* and *nāḍī*, and the lengthening or shortening of the four seasons. Within the manifest Dharma,
one clearly understands the rules for the progressive cultivation of the five stages, the distinctions between the three vehicles,

the methods for turning according to the gates of practice and the faculties of practitioners, the principles of the times when maturity leads to liberation, and the many days, months, years, and kalpas that have passed.

He was able to know all these things from a young age: whether the iron and wood of the ship were strong or brittle, whether its mechanisms were stiff or smooth, the size of the waters, and whether the winds were favorable or adverse.

There was no sign of safety or peril that he did not clearly understand. Truly knowing these matters as metaphors for the Dharma, he clearly understood those of the three vehicles who had turned their minds [toward enlightenment] and those who had not, and who were capable of entering into birth and death.

Incapable of entering the realm of birth and death, those whose faculties have matured or not yet matured within the One Vehicle possess, in the sixth dwelling and sixth stage (*bhūmi*), the wisdom of the three emptinesses that brings about the manifestation of cessation; their minds attain transcendence from birth and death while they are amidst birth and death.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh dwelling and seventh stage, while abiding in the transcendence of birth and death, constantly remain within birth and death.

In the eighth stage of death and the eighth stage of abiding, one attains the manifestation of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The bodhisattva’s effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) manifests, spontaneously benefiting sentient beings.

In the ninth stage and the ninth ground, one studies the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*), four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the tenth stage, where a portion of the Tathāgata’s world-transcending wisdom and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) becomes equal and perfect. One then dwells in the position of the Buddha’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

In the eleventh chapter, "The Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata," the study of Samantabhadra’s wondrous practices of supernormal powers concludes with the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra.
Within this, the fruition of Buddhahood—the three dharmas of Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Tathāgata—consists of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya and its differentiated wisdoms;
thus, the great compassion of principle and wisdom is fulfilled in accordance with the vows previously made.
In the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) employs the practices of Samantabhadra to transform sentient beings;

in this One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), such sequential progression is taught through conventional names and terminology. Yet, such advancement does not transcend the single moment of the ultimate limit (*kṣaṇa-paryanta*).

Thus, while in the Three Vehicles the cause precedes the fruit and the path is fulfilled over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, in this One Vehicle the realization of the Path (*darśana-mārga*) occurs at the very beginning.

Within the stage of the Initial Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), the causal practices of application (*prayoga*) exist throughout the ten stages of practice (*daśa-pratipatti*), the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten bhūmis, and the eleventh bhūmi.
Thus, one is able to fully know the safety and danger, the roughness and smoothness of this ship made of iron and wood;

furthermore, one knows the dullness or swiftness of the faculties, when to stop and when to pause, and even the five methods of cessation (*pañca-nivāraṇa*) within the teachings of the three vehicles as well as those of humans and devas.
When the mind observes that the faculties are mature, one should act immediately to cause them to advance within the Dharma of the Single Vehicle.

Because the nature of birth and death and the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) serve as the great function of wisdom for the sake of the Dharma-activity, the general meaning below is likewise so.
"Good son, I shall take a fine ship to transport the multitude of merchants to the path of peace and security," and so forth.

Leading them to the Treasure Island and providing them with all manner of rare jewels until they are fully satisfied, and then escorting them back to Jambudvīpa—this matter symbolizes the Dharma taught herein:
from the initial stage of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), one attains the fundamental wisdom of a Buddha;
from that point onward, throughout all subsequent stages, the sublime Dharma is expounded for them until the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
The jewel of the path of the wisdom of all-knowledge has already been filled within the eleventh stage;

one shall now return it to its original place within the ocean of birth and death where one formerly resided. With this jewel of the wisdom of all-knowledge thus obtained, one shall extensively benefit inexhaustible sentient beings.
This clarifies that such a statement is made in terms of the advancement of practice, so as to make it easy to understand.
Furthermore, one does not emerge from the ocean of birth and death to become a great jewel island; the rest is fully detailed in the text itself.
All of these are explained in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), relying on phenomena to manifest the Dharma so that understanding may arise. This is the second [point]:
the indestructible dedication to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The ship’s captain says: "I shall take this great ship to and fro throughout the beginningless [past], without ceasing."

Regarding the first, "that which is indestructible": if there are sentient beings who see my body or hear my Dharma, causing them to never again fear the ocean of birth and death and ensuring they will certainly enter the ocean of omniscience—this is the meaning of the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).

With the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as the primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions, this is explained in terms of the various stages within the gateway of wisdom.
In the section on the "Gate of Universal Treatment According to Stages," one achieves the precept of Great Compassion because, like a mariner upon the ocean,
one constantly comes and goes without ever being born within the ocean of birth and death; thus, having accomplished the practice of the Banner of Great Compassion,
the following passage— beginning from "Just as all Bodhisattvas..."— pushes forward these virtues to promote Sudhana’s further advancement.
Taking his leave and departing is presented in ten lines of verse, which may be roughly divided into five sections: first, advancing by virtue of merit;
second, indicating the location of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, citing the name of the city where the spiritual friend resides, called "Delightful" (*Ramaṇīya*);
fourth, citing the name of the spiritual friend, called "Unsurpassed Victory" (*Anuttarajaya*); and fifth, paying respects and taking leave, including the name of the city.
"Delightful" (Kāmadhara) is so named because this elder was skilled in clearly adjudicating the various affairs of human beings and could further preach the supramundane Dharma;
because sentient beings delighted in him, they would not leave him, and thus the city was called Delightful and the elder was titled Unsurpassed Victor (Anuttarajaya).
This is the entrance to the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā); among all practices, patience is preeminent.

Furthermore, because his virtue and artistry surpass those of the world, he is called "Unsurpassed. Regarding the superior excellence of his practices, this refers to what was previously stated in the section praising his virtues.
Third, the "Delightful City" (Ratnāvatī), the Unsurpassed Elder Lord, and so forth—all these are dedicated by the Buddhas.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana gave rise to a mind of great loving-kindness that is all-pervasive, a mind of great compassion that is moistening and nourishing,
which continues without interruption; he was adorned with the two kinds of merit and wisdom, abandoned all defilements of affliction, realized the equality of dharmas,
maintained a mind free from high or low, extracted the thorns of unwholesomeness, extinguished all obstacles, and took firm diligence as his foundation.
With the profound moats and ditches of samādhi as its gardens, it uses the sunlight of wisdom to shatter the darkness of ignorance,
the wind of skillful means to open the flowers of insight, and the unimpeded vows to fill the entire Dharma-realm;

with a mind constantly manifesting entry into the city of omniscience, one thus seeks the path of a bodhisattva, gradually traversing it until reaching the interior of that city, where one beholds the non-existent.
Upaśānta was in the city’s eastern quarter, within the Great Adornment Banner Aśoka Grove, surrounded by immeasurable merchants and hundreds of thousands of householders.
While he adjudicated various human affairs, he taught them the Dharma so that they might forever uproot all conceit of self,
become free from "I" and "mine," relinquish their accumulated possessions, and attain a mind purified of the stains of stinginess and envy.

Purified and free from all defilements, he attained the power of pure faith; he constantly delighted in seeing the Buddha, upheld the Buddha-dharma, gave rise to the power of a bodhisattva, initiated bodhisattva practices, entered the samādhis of a bodhisattva, attained the wisdom of a bodhisattva, dwelt in the right mindfulness of a bodhisattva, and increased the bodhisattva’s aspiration.
At that time, the youth Sudhana observed that elder preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
Having already cast his body to the ground to prostrate at his feet, he rose after a long while and said: "Noble One, I am Sudhana; I am Sudhana.
I am solely seeking the conduct of a bodhisattva. How does a bodhisattva learn the conduct of a bodhisattva?
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the path of a bodhisattva? By practicing and learning in this way, may I always be able to transform and deliver all sentient beings."
From birth, they are always able to behold all Buddhas face-to-face, constantly hear all Buddha-dharmas,
always maintain and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, and always enter all dharma-gates. They enter all lands to study the bodhisattva practices,
abide through all kalpas cultivating the bodhisattva path, are able to know the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas, and are able to receive [the teachings of] one...
When he was being protected by the mindfulness of all Tathāgatas and was able to attain the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, that elder said to Sudhana:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have already been able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family, I have accomplished the bodhisattva practice-door of reaching all places, which is without dependence and without effort."
“O son of good family, what is the bodhisattva practice door of reaching all places through the power of supernormal knowledges?
O son of good family, within this trichiliocosm, among all sentient beings of the desire realm—
namely, all those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all those in the Suyāma Heaven, and all those in the Tuṣita Heaven...”
All the gods of the Heaven of Skillful Transformations, all the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations,
all the gods of Māra, and all other beings— gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— in all their dwellings, such as villages, camps, cities, and towns; all these sentient beings.
In the midst [of this], he preached the Dharma to cause them to abandon what is contrary to the Dharma, to cause disputes to cease, to cause strife to be eliminated,
to cause contention to stop, to cause the bonds of enmity to be broken, to cause fetters to be untied, to cause them to emerge from prison,
to cause them to be freed from fear, and to cause all evil karmas— from killing up to wrong views— and all things that ought not to be done, to be prohibited, so as to bring them into compliance.
They practice all wholesome dharmas and cause others to study all arts and crafts, thereby bringing benefit to the world.
They analyze various treatises for them to inspire joy and gradually bring them to maturity.
To those who follow non-Buddhist paths, they explain superior wisdom to sever their various views and lead them into the Buddha-dharma, even up to the Brahma-heavens of the form realm.
"O Deva, I likewise preach for them the supreme Dharma— just as in this trichiliocosm,
and even throughout worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields—
I preach the Buddha-dharma, the Bodhisattva-dharma, the Śrāvaka-dharma, and the Pratyekabuddha-dharma; I speak of the hells and I speak of the earth."
He speaks of the beings in hell; he speaks of the path leading to hell; he speaks of animals; he speaks of the distinctions among animals; he speaks of the suffering experienced by animals;
he speaks of the path leading to the animal realm; he speaks of the world of Yama; he speaks of the suffering in the world of Yama;
he speaks of the path leading to the world of Yama; he speaks of the heavenly worlds; he speaks of the bliss in the heavenly worlds; he speaks of the path leading to the heavenly worlds.

The intermediate path discourse, the discourse on the human world, and the discourse on the suffering and happiness of the human world were taught as a means to reveal the merits of Bodhisattvas, to cause the abandonment of the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra, to cause the knowledge and vision of the sublime merits of those who possess all-knowledge, to cause the understanding that beings within the various realms of existence suffer due to delusion, and to... [cause them to... provide the translation.
Knowing and seeing the dharma of non-obstruction, he acts out of a desire to reveal the causes for the arising of all worlds,
a desire to reveal that the cessation of all worlds is bliss, in order to cause sentient beings to abandon all conceptual attachments,
to cause them to realize the Buddha’s reliance on the non-dependent, to cause the wheel of all afflictions to be forever extinguished, and to enable them to turn the wheel of the Tathāgata.

I have preached this Dharma wheel for the sake of sentient beings. Noble son, I only know this pure dharma-door of practicing the bodhisattva path that reaches all places, as well as the power of spiritual penetrations that are non-reliant and non-active.
As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are fully endowed with all sovereign spiritual penetrations and are able to travel everywhere to all buddha-fields—[I do not know their ways].

Having attained the stage of the Universal Eye, they hear all sounds and speech, universally enter into all dharmas, possess sovereign wisdom free from conflict, and are peerlessly courageous. With a broad and long tongue, they emit impartial sounds;
their bodies are wondrously beautiful, identical to those of all bodhisattvas and ultimately non-dual and indistinguishable from those of all Tathāgatas, as their bodies of wisdom are vast and great.
She universally enters the realms of the three periods of time, boundless and equal to empty space;
how could I possibly know or describe her meritorious conduct? Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Sūna.
In that land there is a city named Kaliṅgavana, where there is a bhikṣuṇī named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā. Go to her.

Question: When a bodhisattva trains in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path, how does Sudhana, having prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him countless times with earnest gazing and reverence, take his leave and depart?
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of correctly entering the respective stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time,

the youth Sudhana" down to "the power of the unconditioned and non-reliant spiritual penetrations for purifying the Dharma-gate of practicing the Bodhisattva path in all places," five gates are established within this section: 1) the thought of advancing through the instructions of a spiritual friend.

Second, he gradually traveled on until he reached that city; third, he saw the unsurpassed and eminent elder Śreṣṭhin in the Aśoka Grove to the east of the city, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and householders;
fourth, he threw himself to the ground, paid his respects, and rose again; fifth, he formally presented his request, and the unsurpassed Śreṣṭhin then bestowed upon him his own [robe].
Regarding the sequential explanation of the meaning according to the text of the *Caryā-dharmaparyāya*:

"Gradually passing through until reaching within that city" refers to ascending and entering the stage, which is called the "inner vision of the unsurpassed excellence. "Being in the eastern part of the city" clarifies that generating birth through wisdom is designated as the "east";
not abiding in one's original position represents wisdom, and by conforming to the mundane world to lead sentient beings, it illuminates the stage of generating birth.
Furthermore, the West symbolizes compassion; as illustrated below, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva resides on the western slope of Vajra Mountain to represent the station of compassion.
This is because all these Buddhas who dedicate [merit] are awakened ones (*buddha*).
As for the lunar mansion *Jiǎo* (Horn), it is the mansion of the East; since *Jiǎo* presides over the assembly of monks, nuns, and Daoists, as well as all those who perform good deeds.
The gate is popularly written as "this" (此), but it should be "this awakening" (此覺) according to its intended meaning and affiliation.
Since it serves as the gateway for all manner of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*), "corner" (*jiao*) represents the Gate of Heaven (*deva-dvāra*), which is the source of all wholesome qualities.

Because this is located to the east of the city, the wise conduct of Samantabhadra is represented by the East, signifying that he is the foremost among those who give rise to all wholesome qualities. The great compassionate conduct of Avalokiteśvara is represented by the West.
The West is associated with Metal; Metal is the White Tiger, presiding over autumn and presiding over killing. It is governed by Compassion. As this sutra states:
"Clearly practicing the rituals of the ten directions, one presides over the deities of the directions. Furthermore, the deities of the directions revolve according to the directions.

This meaning clarifies that one revolves according to the methods of the directions in order to deliver sentient beings. However, in reality, the nature of the Great Image (Mahānimitta) is inherently...
Formless and ethereally fused, it leaves no trace; yet, in accordance with directions, it manifests the Dharma, and as the Dharma follows conditions, it is differentiated.
Thus, the sages bestowed their teachings upon the entanglements of the mundane world, using the very things and events found within those mundane conditions to manifest the Dharma.
For instance, the principle beyond words cannot be used to lead the ignorant, and the true source devoid of forms cannot benefit the common folk; therefore, one employs directional conventions.

Those who mark the corners [of the site] to represent the adherence to dharmas do not benefit the mundane world or enlighten the deluded; those who abandon them, however, lose the opportunity for the present.

Now, to benefit the mundane world and enlighten the deluded, this eastern side of the city is established as the place to lead the deluded toward clarity and give rise to all manner of wholesome virtues.
Furthermore, the chamber is designated as the Green Dragon (*Nāga*), a position of worldly merit and fortune. As for the "Forest of No Sorrow" (*Aśoka-vana*), this refers to its presiding deity.
The perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is fulfilled through patience because it practices without sorrow; thus, it is called a "forest" (*vana*).

Because this elder’s practice extends throughout the ten directions, providing broad shade for all classes of beings according to their forms, and because his practice is so vast that it covers them all, it is a "forest.
Furthermore, because he transforms others so that they are free from sorrow, it is the "Forest of No-Sorrow. [There were] immeasurable merchants, numbering in the hundreds...
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by a thousand householders (*gṛhapati*)," this is a symbolic representation of those to be converted:
it signifies using ignorance to transform into wisdom, wisdom to transform into ignorance, and evil to transform into goodness.

Furthermore, they are called "householders" because, like merchants, they constantly dwell within birth and death (*saṃsāra*) while practicing benevolent virtue to transform and benefit all classes of beings. This is an explanation based on their conduct as Sudhana observes the elder.
Having preached the Dharma for the assembly, he threw his body to the ground to symbolize the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
In general, this represents returning to the conventional from the ultimate truth (*tathatā*), taking great compassion and skillful patience as the ground.

Furthermore, his saying "I am Sudhana, I am Sudhana" signifies the profound depth of his quest for the Dharma; it also clarifies that by realizing non-self (*anātman*), he has perfected patience. Below this...
The Elder told Sudhana: "The practice you are engaged in is called 'the Bodhisattva Practice that Accomplishes All Places.
This clarifies how, like all Buddhas, one dedicates [merit] toward all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, such that there is no place where one's activity does not pervade.
As will be clearly explained in the following text, this is like the progression from the first to the third stage (*vihāra*) within the *Daśabhūmika*."
Seeing the three bhikṣus manifesting the practice of supramundane dharmas from within the mundane world— from their initial dedication onward—
seeing these three elders as being of purely secular origin, such as the incense merchant, the boatman, and Anuttarajaya,
clarifies that entering the mundane from the ultimate truth is called "dedication" (pariṇāmanā). This is the spiritual friend for the "Dedication Equal to All Buddhas," characterized by patience.

With the *pāramitās* as the primary factors and the other nine as their companions, from the perspective of the gates of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*), they universally remedy [defilements] across all stages;

from the perspective of the gates of the stages (*bhūmi-mukha*), they remedy the obstacle of non-sovereignty regarding patience (*kṣānti*) within the ocean of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), thereby enabling the attainment of mastery over the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
While the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) clarify the cultivation of supramundane patience that transcends suffering, this present stage clarifies the entry into the mundane world.
In the middle section on "Accomplishing the Patience of Benefiting through Compassion," within this dedication, there are ten lines from the passage beginning with "Just as all bodhisattvas...

down to "...took their leave and departed," which describe how, when those who come to beg for his body, flesh, hands, feet, kingdom, city, wife, or children, he feels no weariness or resentment, but rather experiences an ever-increasing joy. This constitutes the second section: "Advancing by Recommending Virtue."
The first half of the sutra is divided into five sections: (1) inferring her virtuous progress; (2) indicating the country where the spiritual friend resides;
(3) indicating the name of the city where the spiritual friend dwells; (4) citing the name of the spiritual friend; and (5) paying respects and taking leave.
Regarding the name of the city, *Kalingavana*: this is translated as "Mutual Strife," because of these bhikṣuṇīs.
Their rank is identical to the fourth of the ten abodes and the fourth of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Having emerged from the entanglements of the triple world and been born into the family of the Tathāgata, they accomplish untainted compassion by returning to the mundane from the absolute.

The Bhikṣu Ming represents the meaning of transcending the mundane, while the Bhikṣuṇī Ciyin Ming represents the practice of dedication. These ranks and dharma-gates do not manifest as male or female; rather, they employ these forms to symbolize the underlying Dharma.
Speaking in terms of reality, because this nun is the dharma of this stage, she manifests the entry into the conventional by means of the ultimate;
thus, she reconciles the ultimate and the conventional, and because she has resolved the dualistic disputes of defilement and purity, she abides in the wisdom of the *dharmatā*.

While remaining conventional, she is eternally ultimate and untainted with compassion, for she has extinguished the combative disputes of the two views regarding the existence or non-existence, and defilement or purity, of the ultimate and the conventional. Thus, she accomplishes the second [stage].
The fourth is the practice of diligence in the dedication of giving that reaches all places through loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
This city is named "Forest of Strife" because it clarifies that the practice of loving-kindness is pervasive, all-encompassing, and provides vast shelter; thus it is called a "forest.

Furthermore, it is so named because this bhikṣuṇī’s karmic retribution resulted in a multitude of magnificent jewel-trees, which are so numerous that they are called a "forest. The name of the country is Śūṇa.
This name "Valiant" (*vīra*) signifies the meaning of diligence; this constitutes the fourth perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
These teachings all rely upon bases and rely upon events to manifest the Dharma, for the event is itself the Dharma.
The name "Lion’s Stretch" (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*) is established based on her virtuous conduct; like a lion’s stretch, it clarifies that she is filled with the joy of compassion.
The meaning of the Dharma-joy of traveling throughout the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings without weariness is like the physical and mental comfort and delight of a person;
it signifies that although the bhikṣuṇī travels throughout the ten directions, she harmonizes disputes and her mind remains eternally transcendent from the mundane.
This clarifies that within the dedication [of merit], she dwells amidst entanglements without defilement due to her compassion.
The fourth is the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, who presides over the city of Kaliṅavana and dedicates her roots of goodness to reaching all places.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana traveled by stages until he reached that kingdom and city, where he searched everywhere for her.
There were immeasurable people who all said to her, "O son of good family,
this bhikṣuṇī is teaching the Dharma for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings within the Jyotiṣka Garden, which was donated by King Prasenajit.
At that time, Sudhana approached that garden and, after observing it thoroughly, saw a great tree therein named...
It was shaped like a full moon and resembled a multi-storied pavilion, emitting a great radiance that illuminated one yojana.
There was seen a leafy tree named Universal Canopy (*Samantacchadana*), its form like a parasol, emitting a deep blue light like lapis lazuli.

There was also seen a flowering tree named Flower Treasury (*Kusumagarbha*), as tall and vast as the King of Snow Mountains, raining down a multitude of exquisite flowers without end, just as [the Buddha did].

In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is further seen a Pārijātaka tree, as well as a tree of amṛta fruit shaped like a mountain of gold, which constantly emits radiance and is fully endowed with all kinds of fruits.
Furthermore, there is seen a mani-jewel tree named Vairocana-garbha; its form is peerless, and the heart-king maṇi-jewel is situated at its very center.
It is universally adorned with *maṇi* jewels of unsurpassed *asaṃkhyeya* colors and forms;

furthermore, there are clothing trees called "Pure," from which various colored garments hang down in magnificent array; there are also musical trees called "Joyous," whose sounds are exquisite and surpass all celestial music;
and there are fragrance trees called "Universal Adornment," which constantly emit wondrous scents that permeate everywhere.
In the gardens unimpeded in the ten directions, there are further springs, streams, ponds, and lakes, all adorned with the seven precious gems.
Black sandalwood mud accumulates within them, while exquisite golden sand is spread across their bottoms.
They are filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues, and are strewn with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses.
Lotuses of exquisite fragrance completely covered its surface, and immeasurable jewel trees stood in rows all around.
Beneath each jewel tree were spread lion thrones, adorned with various kinds of wonderful jewels. Celestial robes were laid out, permeated with sublime fragrances;
precious silk streamers hung down, and jeweled canopies were draped above. Nets of Jambū-river gold covered them entirely, and as precious bells swayed gently, they emitted wondrous sounds.
In some instances, beneath the trees, there were lion thrones spread with lotus-treasury jewels;
in others, lion thrones spread with fragrance-king maṇi-treasuries; in others, lion thrones spread with dragon-adorned maṇi-king treasuries;
and in others, lion thrones spread with jewel-lion-cluster maṇi-king treasuries.
In some places there were lion-thrones made of the Vairocana-maṇi-rāja-garbha spread beneath trees;
in other places there were one hundred thousand lion-thrones made of the Vairocana-maṇi-rāja-garbha spread beneath trees.
Each individual throne was surrounded on all sides by one hundred thousand precious lion-thrones, each of which was fully adorned with immeasurable ornaments.
This great garden was adorned so that various jewels filled it everywhere, like a jewel-island in the great ocean.
Kāliṅga cloth was spread upon its ground—soft, exquisite, and capable of producing a pleasant touch; when one stepped on it, the foot sank, and when lifted, it returned to its original state.
Countless birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds, and the excellent, sublime adornments of the precious sandalwood groves were of every wonderful variety.

Flowers rain down perpetually and inexhaustibly, like the garden of various flowers belonging to Śakra; the incomparable king of fragrances universally perfumes all, like the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) belonging to Śakra;

the trees of music and the precious *tāla* trees with their nets of many jewel-bells produce wondrous sounds, like the songs produced by the goddesses of beautiful speech belonging to Maheśvara; and all things are as one would wish.
Various exquisite garments hung from the trees as adornments, like the great ocean with its immeasurable colors;

hundreds of thousands of pavilions were adorned with myriad jewels, like the Great City of Sudarśana in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; precious canopies extended far and wide, like the peaks of Mount Sumeru;
and their radiance shone everywhere, like the palace of Brahmā. At that time, the youth Sudhana beheld this great garden.
These immeasurable merits and various adornments are all produced by the accomplishment of the supramundane roots of goodness resulting from the karmic retribution of a bodhisattva;
they flow from the merit of making offerings to all Buddhas, such that no one in any world can equal them.
All of this arises from the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, who has realized that all phenomena are like illusions and has gathered vast, pure qualities.

Accomplished through the merit and wholesome karma [of this bhikṣuṇī], the gods, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, as well as immeasurable sentient beings of the trichiliocosm, all enter this garden without it becoming cramped. Why is this?
It is because of the inconceivable power of the spiritual majesty (*anubhāva*) of this bhikṣuṇī. At that time, Sudhana saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā seated everywhere throughout the [garden].

Beneath all the precious trees were great lion thrones; his physical form was upright and majestic, his deportment tranquil, and his sense faculties well-disciplined like those of a great elephant king.
His mind was free from defilement and turbidity, like a pure pool; he universally fulfilled all requests, like a wish-fulfilling jewel;
he was unstained by worldly dharmas, like a lotus flower; his mind was fearless, like a lion king; and he protected and maintained purity.

The precepts are unshakable like Mount Sumeru; they bring a mind of refreshing coolness to those who behold them, like a king of wondrous fragrances that can eliminate the heat of afflictions in sentient beings;
they cause all sufferings to be extinguished upon being seen, like the exquisite sandalwood incense from the Snowy Mountains;
they ensure that seeing them is never in vain, like the King of Medicines, Sudarśana; and they are like the deity Vāruṇa.
She causes all the sprouts of the roots of goodness in the multitude to grow, like a fertile and rich field.
Though she sits upon each seat in a different assembly, the Dharma-gates she teaches are likewise distinct.
In some instances, she is seen seated amidst a host of Śuddhāvāsa devas, with the son of Maheśvara as their leader; for these bhikṣuṇīs, she teaches a Dharma-gate named "Inexhaustible Understanding."
Alternatively, he may see her seated, surrounded by a host of Brahma devas with the Brahma King as their leader, who delight in her;
this bhikṣuṇī is preaching for them a Dharma gate called the "Pure Wheel of Speech with Universally Distinct Sounds.
Or he may see her seated, surrounded by sons and daughters of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, with the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartins as their leader.
And as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī teaches them the Dharma-door called "The Pure Mind of a Bodhisattva.

Or, seeing her seated in the midst of a retinue of gods and goddesses of the Heaven of Excellent Transformations, with the King of the Heaven of Excellent Transformations as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī teaches them the Dharma-door called "The Excellent Adornment of All Dharmas. Or, seeing her situated...
Seated amidst the sons and daughters of the gods of Tuṣita Heaven, surrounded by them with the King of Tuṣita as their leader,
this bhikṣuṇī was preaching a Dharma-gate called "The Revolving Treasury of the Mind. Or,
seeing her seated amidst the sons and daughters of the gods of Suyāma Heaven, surrounded by them with the King of Suyāma as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī...
He saw that bhikṣuṇī seated there, teaching a Dharma gate called "Boundless Adornment," surrounded by the sons and daughters of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
with Śakra Devānām Indra as their leader; or he saw her seated there,
teaching a Dharma gate called "The Gate of Disenchantment," surrounded by the Dragon King Śataraśmi, the Dragon King Nanda, and others.
Surrounded by the dragon kings Pāṇḍaka, Manasvin, Elāpattra, Anavatapta, and others,
as well as their sons and daughters— with the dragon king Sāgara as their leader—
this bhikṣuṇī taught them a Dharma gate called "The Radiant Adornment of the Buddha’s Realm of Supernatural Power."

In some instances, she saw her seated, surrounded by a host of yakṣas with the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader, as this bhikṣuṇī was expounding for them a dharma-gate called "The Treasury that Protects and Saves All Sentient Beings.
In other instances, she saw her seated, surrounded by a host of gandharvas with the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra as their leader; this bhikṣuṇī...

In some places, he saw her seated on a throne, surrounded by a host of asuras with the asura king Rāhu at their head, teaching them a dharma-gate called "Inexhaustible Joy. In other places, he saw her seated on a throne,
surrounded by a host of garuḍas, teaching them a dharma-gate called "The Gate of Wisdom for Swift Adornment of the Dharma Realm."
With the Garuḍa King Jeta as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī taught them a Dharma door called "Terrorizing the Ocean of All Existences.

Or, seeing her seated and surrounded by a host of kiṃnaras, with the Great Tree Kiṃnara King as their leader, this bhikṣuṇī taught them a Dharma door called "The Radiance of the Buddha’s Conduct. Or...
In some instances, he saw her seated, surrounded by a host of mahoragas, with the mahoraga king Amra as their leader;
this bhikṣuṇī was preaching for them a Dharma gate called "Arousing the Mind of Joy in the Buddha.
In other instances, he saw her seated, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of men and women; this bhikṣuṇī was preaching for them...
There was a dharma gate called "Superior Conduct" or "The Seat of Vision," surrounded by a host of rākṣasas who constantly seize vital energy, with the Great Tree Rākṣasa King as their leader;
this bhikṣuṇī was preaching this dharma gate for them, which is called "Generating a Mind of Compassion.
Alternatively, she was seen seated, surrounded by a host of sentient beings who take pleasure in and believe in the Śrāvaka vehicle.
This bhikṣuṇī was preaching a dharma-gate called "Victorious Wisdom Radiance" while seated amidst a retinue of beings who were devoted to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
or she was seen seated amidst a retinue of beings who were devoted to the Mahāyāna, preaching a dharma-gate called "The Vast Radiance of the Buddha's Virtues. This bhikṣuṇī...

He saw the bhikṣuṇī seated upon a throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds on enlightenment, preaching a dharma-gate called the "Gate of the Radiant Wisdom of the Samādhi of Universal Doors.
Or he saw her seated upon a throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas of the second stage, preaching a dharma-gate called the "Gathering of the Vows of All Buddhas. This bhikṣuṇī...
In some places, he saw her seated on a throne surrounded by bodhisattvas of the third stage, this bhikṣuṇī preaching a dharma-gate called "The Stainless Wheel.
In some places, he saw her seated on a throne surrounded by bodhisattvas of the fourth stage, this bhikṣuṇī preaching a dharma-gate called "Tranquil Adornment.
In some places, he saw her seated on a throne surrounded by bodhisattvas of the fifth stage, this bhikṣuṇī preaching a dharma-gate called "Arising."
In some instances, she was seen seated on a throne surrounded by bodhisattvas of the fifth stage, all of whom were within the sphere of omniscience;
for them, this bhikṣuṇī preached the dharma-gate named "Exquisite Flower Treasury.
In other instances, she was seen seated on a throne surrounded by bodhisattvas of the sixth stage; for them, this bhikṣuṇī preached the dharma-gate named "Vairocana Treasury."
Sometimes he saw her seated on the seventh stage, surrounded by all the bodhisattvas, preaching for them a dharma-door called "The Stage of Universal Adornment.

Or he saw her seated on the eighth stage, surrounded by all the bodhisattvas, preaching for them a dharma-door called "The Body of the Sphere of the Entire Dharmadhātu. Or he saw her seated on the ninth... [text continues]
In some instances, she was seen sitting on her seat, surrounded by Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage, preaching a dharma-gate called "The Adornment of the Power of Non-Apprehension.

In other instances, she was seen sitting on her seat, surrounded by Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, preaching a dharma-gate called "The Unobstructed Wheel. Or she was seen sitting on her seat, surrounded by Vajrapāṇi deities.
Surrounding this bhikṣuṇī, they were expounding a dharma-gate called "The Adamantine Wisdom Adornment of Nārāyaṇa.
Sudhana saw all the sentient beings in all these realms who had been matured and tamed, and who were capable of being vessels for the Dharma;
they all entered this grove and sat down, surrounding their teacher at their respective seats.

The bhikṣuṇī Subhāṣitā taught the Dharma to the sons of the Buddha according to their respective inclinations, capacities, and distinctions, causing them to attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why was this?
Because this bhikṣuṇī had entered the *prajñāpāramitā* door called "The Universal Eye that Abandons and Attains," which explains the *prajñāpāramitā* of all Buddha-dharmas.
The gate of the honeyed door of the differentiation of the dharma-realm; the gate of the perfection of wisdom that shatters all wheels of obstruction;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom that gives birth to the wholesome minds of all sentient beings;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom of sublime adornment; the gate of the perfection of wisdom of the unobstructed treasury of reality; the gate of the dharma...
The *dharmaparyāya* gate of the perfection of wisdom of the fulfillment of realms, the *dharmaparyāya* gate of the heart-treasury of the perfection of wisdom,
and the *dharmaparyāya* gate of the universal source-treasury of the perfection of wisdom— headed by these ten *dharmaparyāya* gates of the perfection of wisdom,
they enter countless millions of such *dharmaparyāya* gates of the perfection of wisdom. All the bodhisattvas within this Sunlight Garden [do so].
And all those sentient beings were those whom the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā had first exhorted to resolve their minds upon,
to receive and uphold the True Dharma, and to contemplate and practice for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
thereby attaining non-retrogression; at that time, Sudhana saw the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā within such a grove and such a seat.
Thus she practiced walking meditation, thus was the assembly gathered, thus were her supernormal powers, and thus was her eloquence.
Furthermore, hearing this inconceivable Dharma-door and the vast cloud of Dharma that moistened her heart, she then gave rise to this thought:

"I shall circumambulate [the Buddha] to the right for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of times. At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated the garden and the assembly.
The noble youth Sudhana, having seen his own body and all the trees within the grove circumambulate this bhikṣuṇī to the right for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of times,
stood with palms joined and said: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Although I have awakened the bodhicitta, I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct or how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction, I pray that you will explain this to me.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Noble son, I have attained liberation named 'Accomplishment of All-Knowledge' (Sarvajñatā-samudgata). Sudhana asked, "Noble One, for what reason is it called 'Accomplishment'?"
The bhikṣuṇī Sarvajñā said, "Noble son, this light of wisdom universally illumines all phenomena of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment.
Sudhana said, "Noble one, what is the scope of this light of wisdom?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "Noble son, by entering this gate of the light of wisdom, I am able to give birth to all phenomena."
By means of this Samādhirāja-samādhi, he attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and proceeds to the Tuṣita palaces in all worlds of the ten directions.
Before each of the bodhisattvas bound to one more birth, he manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
each of these bodies performs acts of worship as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
That is to say, manifesting the bodies of celestial kings up to the bodies of human kings, I hold aloft clouds of flowers, clouds of garlands, burning incense, unguents,
and powdered incense; as well as robes, necklaces, banners, streamers, silk canopies, jeweled nets, jeweled curtains,
jeweled treasuries, and jeweled lamps— all such articles of adornment I hold and offer for worship, just as [I have done] before.
The manner in which Bodhisattvas dwelling in the Tuṣita palace [manifest]— whether dwelling in the womb, being born, remaining at home, leaving the home life,

proceeding to the site of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of the true Dharma, or entering into nirvāṇa— and likewise, whether they dwell in the palaces of devas, the palaces of nāgas,
or even the palaces of humans during those intervening periods— in each and every one of those instances, [the Tathāgata manifests in such a way].

Whosoever comes to me, I shall honor them all in this same manner. If there are sentient beings who know that I thus make offerings to the Buddha, they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there are sentient beings who come to my presence, I shall immediately preach the *prajñāpāramitā* for them. Good son, I have seen one—
Because they clearly perceive all sentient beings with the eye of wisdom, they do not differentiate the characteristics of sentient beings;

because their minds have no attachments, they hear all speech without differentiating the characteristics of speech; because they thoroughly realize the Dharma-body, they see all Tathāgatas without differentiating the characteristics of Tathāgatas;
because they maintain all wheels of Dharma, they do not differentiate the characteristics of the wheels of Dharma; thus they awaken to the Dharma.

By virtue of its intrinsic nature, one realizes all phenomena in a single thought-moment without discriminating the characteristics of those phenomena, for one knows that all phenomena are like illusions.
"Good son, I know only this liberation that accomplishes all-knowledge.

As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, their minds are free from discrimination as they universally know all phenomena; sitting upright in a single body, they fill the entire Dharma-realm. Regarding themselves...
Within his own body he manifests all lands, and in a single thought-moment he reaches the abodes of all Buddhas;
within his own body he universally displays the spiritual powers of all Buddhas; with a single hair he lifts up unspeakably many Buddha-worlds;
and within a single pore of his own body, he manifests the formation and destruction of unspeakable worlds in a single thought-moment. Is this not so?
It can be said that unspeakably many sentient beings dwell together within a single thought-moment, entering into unspeakably many kalpas;
how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Good son, to the south of here is a land called Dangerous Obstacles (Khaṇḍa). In this land is a city named Jewel Adornment (Ratnavyūha). Within it...
"There is a woman named Vasumitrā; go to her and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then Sudhana, the youth, prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her countless times, gazed upon her with deep reverence, and having taken his leave, departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of correctly entering the specific stage, from the passage "At that time, the youth Sudhana...
down to "...I only know this liberation-door of accomplishing all-knowledge," this segment is divided into five sections:
1) proceeding gradually to that kingdom and city; 2) searching everywhere for this bhikṣu.
1. The bhikṣuṇī informs the three groups of people of the bhikṣuṇī’s location. 2.
Sudhana goes to that Sunlight Garden (Sūryaprabha-udyāna) of King Prasenajit and observes all the secondary requisites (upabhoga-pariṣkāra) belonging to the bhikṣuṇī.
3. Sudhana joins his palms in reverence and requests what he seeks; the bhikṣuṇī bestows upon Sudhana the method for his own practice, as in the fourth [chapter].
When Sudhana went to King Suprabha’s Sunlight Garden (Sūryaprabha-udyāna) and observed it, he saw thirteen kinds of adornments within the secondary environment and the assembly of the bhikṣuṇī:
first, the adornment of jewel trees; second, the adornment of flowing springs, ponds, and flowers made of the seven jewels;
third, the adornment of lion thrones beneath the jewel trees; fourth, the adornment of various jewels... [and so forth].
1. Adorned by five forests on the ground that rain down flowers and incense; 2. Adorned by six trees of musical instruments and various jewel bells whose sounds resonate in harmony;
3. Adorned by seven celestial garments; 4. Adorned by eight hundred thousand jeweled pavilions and adorned by jeweled canopies;
5. Adorned by radiance like the peaks of Mount Sumeru; 6. Adorned by palaces. Ten.
1. A praise of the merits possessed by the bhikṣuṇī, the supramundane roots of goodness arising from making offerings to all Buddhas;
2. A praise of the bhikṣuṇī’s resolve and virtue; 3. A praise of the pervasive manifestation of her three karmas and their functional applications, which are not in vain for those who behold them;
4. An elucidation of the great assembly surrounding her; from this point downward, thirty types of assemblies are all clarified.

This bhikṣuṇī encompasses the practice of nurturing sentient beings; she bestows the Dharma according to their individual faculties, each case being distinct, continuing until the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*) and the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) that borders upon the rank of the Buddha.
Throughout this process, she universally gathers and transforms all assemblies, clarifying how a single stage pervades the practices of all five stages.
Thus, every single stage is likewise so; in this manner, the pervasive Dharma is practiced in successive layers throughout the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
One refines [the mind] by means of the fifty-three dharmas and the one hundred and ten city-dharmas;

only then is it called the inexhaustible, sovereign dharma of the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and disintegration. Within each and every stage, all stages are universally present.
This is to reveal that a single dharma pervades many dharmas, because a single stage pervades all practices, thereby revealing the many dharmas.
Because one enters into a single dharma, the five stages and five hundred dharma-gates are established;

because one enters into a single dharma, it is clarified that the general is not different from the particular and the particular is not different from the general, like the mutual interpenetration of the net of Indra.

That which was previously given as alms by King Prasenajit represents this teaching: it clarifies that the three dharmas of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), patience (*kṣānti*), and compassion (*maitrī*) are gathered together in a single assembly.
The bhikṣu’s renunciation of ornaments is patience; the śrāmaṇerī is compassion; King Arthasiddhi is wisdom and clarity.
Through the power of dedication, these enter the mundane world to practice the conduct of vigor.
Patience, wisdom, and compassion are harmoniously united to encompass the practices of the five stages as a single dharma-realm essence and function; thus, this is the Dharma of the Lion’s Stretch.
Within the gateway of the *dhātu*, because there is the joy of the Dharma, one proceeds with diligence from this point;

by means of these three dharmas—patience (*kṣānti*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and compassion (*maitrī*)—one reaches the seventh and eighth stages of the *pariṇāmanā*. It is only upon seeing Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on the path of correct progress that these [qualities] finally become equalized.
In the latter two stages, one cultivates the functioning of the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*); it is not that the first three [stages] lack them.
This wisdom, patience, and compassion are spoken of here in terms of their relative superiority and inferiority as they progress upward: the Elder represents superior wisdom with much compassion;
the Nun represents a compassionate mind that dwells in the world without defilement; the Maiden represents being stained yet remaining untainted;
and the Pārijātaka tree—translated as "Pervasive Fragrance"—refers to a tree whose roots, trunk, branches, and leaves all emit a pervasive fragrance.
The various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—this refers to the practice of universally perfuming the dharma-realm. Kālinī cloth is translated here as "fine cotton cloth.
Varuṇa is translated here as "Water-Heaven. The ten gates of Prajñā, such as Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) and Abandonment and Attainment (Tyāgaprāpti), are fully explained in the sutra.
These are the dharmas spoken by the bhikṣuṇīs; thus there are countless millions of such Prajñās.
Regarding the Sunlight Garden (Sūryaprabha-udyāna): it takes patience, wisdom, and loving-kindness as the substance of the garden.
Sudhana stands with palms joined and makes his request without performing a prostration; yet he circumambulates all the trees in the garden to the right.

This signifies that the various trees are born from the retribution of practice, illustrating that the garden of manifold practices is fully endowed with the dharmas of patience, wisdom, loving-kindness, and samādhi.
The three practices are perfected and surrounded by conduct; because this is a dharma worthy of reverence, there is no separate prostration.
It is surrounded by various trees to clarify the entry into the wisdom of patience and the three practices of compassion.
Thus, the meaning of diligence in this stage is that when Sudhana requests the bhikṣuṇī for the Dharma-name "Accomplisher of All-Knowledge," it refers to this.
Within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the wisdom of patience, compassion, and all differentiated wisdoms are fully generated from these three dharmas.

By means of these, the assembly to be gathered and transformed proceeds until the stage after the tenth bhūmi, where the wisdom of the vajra, supernatural powers, and the excellence of wealth [are attained].
Furthermore, [the youth] Sudhana asked: "What is the sphere of this dharma-gate? As the sutra says: "O son of good family, I..."
Entering this gate of the light of wisdom, one attains the King of Samādhis that gives birth to all dharmas.
By means of this samādhi, one obtains the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*). The following sections clarify the activities, functions, and spheres of this dharma-gate as fully explained in the sutra.
In brief, the great function arises from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), giving rise to the great utility of the wisdom of patience (*kṣānti-jñāna*), compassion, and the myriad practices.
Because this is called the realm of the *dharmadhātu* within the gateway of differentiated teachings, practicing in accordance with this mode is termed Avalokiteśvara;
he is also named Samantagāmin Bodhisattva because his non-effortful wisdom and compassion are equal.
Therefore, in the seventh dedication, Avalokiteśvara and Samantagāmin assemble together in one place.
And he saw that this good man, seeing all sentient beings, does not discriminate the marks of sentient beings because he sees with the clarity of the eye of wisdom;

even when hearing words and sounds, he is entirely without attachment to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, because he sees with the eye of wisdom and knows with the eye of Dharma. From here on, his virtues are further extolled to cause Sudhana to advance.
The second section, beginning with "As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas," and so forth, is the advancement through the excellence of others.
Within this section on advancement, there are eleven lines of scripture divided into five gates: first, the advancement through the excellence of others;
second, the indication of the location and the country where the spiritual friends reside; third, the mention of the name of the city where they dwell, which is Ratnavyūha (Jewel Adornment).
Fifth, regarding the respectful departure for the South: as previously described, the name of the southern land is "Perilous.
This woman practices the dharma-door of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). Among those who extol her virtues, she sits upright alone, yet fills the entire Dharma-realm;
within her own body, she manifests all lands and the realms of both good and evil.

In sum, because the essence of the Dharma-realm meditation universally encompasses and contains all practices, universally gathers in all sentient beings, and universally engages in the same activities as them, it thoroughly fills all realms throughout the ten directions.
Thus, when people of the world see his seemingly defiled conduct, they find it difficult to believe upon seeing or hearing of it;
for this reason, the name of the country is "Perilous Difficulty" (Kṣema-durghaṭa), and the name of the city is "Jewel Adornment" (Ratnavyūha), both of which are difficult to see or hear.

Faith is called the "perilous faith" because one awakens and enters through it; when both mind and objects are found to be ineffable, delusions are eliminated, birth and death are forever ended, and one attains one's own supernormal powers—this is called the "jewel-adornment.
It clarifies that for those of the Two Vehicles and for Bodhisattvas who have emerged from entanglements, this state is characterized by detachment and non-action, and is thus named "liberation.
Within these ten dedications, this is the fifth dedication, which dedicates the practice of emerging from entanglements.
Fifth, within the state of pure and undefiled meditative absorption, she enters into the world to engage in mundane affairs and universally practice for the benefit of sentient beings;
even when manifesting the performance of defiled dharmas, she has never had a single thought of a defiled mind, and is thus called "Female.
Yet in her essential reality, she is neither male nor female, because she takes up the wondrous wisdom of the fundamentally true nature of reality.
The essence of compassion is like that of a woman; it does not arise from worldly sentiments such as the perception of male or female.
If one were to give rise to perceptions of male or female based on worldly sentiments, one would likewise fail to perceive this Dharma-gate.

This refers to the Bodhisattva who, through the application of wondrous wisdom, gives rise to the practice of compassion; in silent accord with worldly conduct, they pervade the ten directions, manifesting physical bodies in response to beings.

One should establish an edification within this station to demonstrate that the Bodhisattva possesses such virtues: abiding in reality yet not realizing it, remaining unstained while amidst the bonds of existence, and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Who is right and who is wrong? This is not a matter for worldly sentiment or intellectual calculation, nor is it something practiced by the ignorant and deluded of the world.
It is only those whose wisdom penetrates the true source and whose conduct is equal to the Dharma-realm who can understand this.
Is it not because one who possesses the faculty of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) in accordance with the profound response and is fully equipped with worldly conventions alone can truly realize this Way?
As for the woman Pāpamitrī (Pobanmi), this is translated as "Worldly Friend" (*Lokamitra*) or "Heavenly Friend," so called because she acts as a teacher and friend to all gods and humans;
alternatively, it is said that she exchanged jewels for wealth, or that she manifested worldly acts of sexual passion in order to exchange them for matters of wealth.
All these worldly practices are difficult to comprehend; throughout the three realms and the six destinies—among humans, devas, and those in the hells—there is no conduct that is not present herein.
This is a state of being unstained yet stained, accessible only through the wisdom of Samantabhadra.
