The Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the Commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Lay Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, combining the sutras and treatises, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Fifteen of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Lokadhātupraveśa*).
[Treatise] Fifth: The Country of Perilous Difficulties; the Lady Vāsantī and the Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, illuminated by the light of great wisdom, contemplated and observed with his mind;

he beheld the nature of all phenomena, attained the dharanī-door of comprehending all sounds and voices, attained the dharanī-door of upholding all wheels of the Dharma, and attained the power of great compassion that serves as a refuge for all sentient beings. He then entered into contemplation.
They attain the gate of the radiant light of the principles and meanings of all phenomena; they fulfill pure vows that pervade the Dharma-realm;
they obtain the radiant wisdom of all phenomena that universally illuminates the ten directions; they acquire sovereign power to universally adorn all worlds;
and they initiate the complete vows of all bodhisattva activities, gradually traveling to lands of peril and difficulty.
In the city of Ratnavyūha, people searched everywhere for the woman Vasumitrā.
There were those in the city who did not know of this woman’s merit and wisdom, and they thought to themselves: "This youth has tranquil faculties and clear wisdom;
he is neither deluded nor distracted. He gazes steadily at her for a full *krośa* without weariness or fatigue, remaining free from attachment and without blinking."
The point of his instantaneous mind is unmoving; it is profound and vast like the great ocean.
One should not harbor thoughts of craving or attachment toward this woman, Vasumitrā; one should not give rise to perverted views, nor conceive notions of purity or desire.
This youth is not one who practices the ways of Māra, nor does he enter the realm of Māra, nor is he submerged in sensual desire.
Since you, who are not bound by Māra and do not engage in what should not be done, have already achieved this, for what purpose do you seek this woman?
Among those present, one who had previously known that this woman possessed wisdom said to Sudhana: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
That you are now able to investigate and search for the lady Vasumitrā shows that you have already attained it."
O son of good family who possesses vast and excellent benefit, you should resolutely seek the state of Buddhahood;
you should resolutely desire to act as a refuge for all sentient beings; you should resolutely desire to extract the poisonous arrows of craving from all sentient beings;
and you should resolutely desire to shatter all notions of purity regarding female forms held by all sentient beings. O son of good family, Vāsuki...
When the girl Madhūrikā was residing in her own home, north of the marketplace within this city,
the youth Sudhana heard these words; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he went to her gate and beheld her residence—
vast, magnificent, and adorned with jeweled walls, jeweled trees, and jeweled moats, each surrounded by tenfold enclosures, and within those jeweled moats, fragrances...

The waters were full and golden sands covered the ground; celestial jewel flowers—blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*)—completely covered the surface of the water.
Palaces and towers were distributed everywhere, with gates, portals, and windows facing one another in regular succession.
All were provided with jeweled nets and bells, and banners and streamers were placed throughout, adorned with immeasurable rare and wonderful treasures.
It was adorned with lapis lazuli for its ground, interspersed with various jewels, and perfumed with the burning of aloeswood and the application of sandalwood paste.
Suspended were many jeweled bells that produced melodic sounds when stirred by the wind, and celestial flowers were scattered everywhere across the ground.
Its manifold splendors and beauties are beyond description; hundreds of thousands of treasuries of rare gems and ten great gardens served as its adornments.
At that time, Sudhana saw this woman, whose countenance was upright and dignified, whose physical features were perfect, and whose skin was golden;
her eyes and hair were deep blue, and she was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor delicate—none among the humans or devas of the desire realm could compare to her.
Her voice was exquisite and beautiful, surpassing all the Brahma worlds, and she possessed the complete range of distinct vocalizations of all sentient beings.
They do not merely understand, but penetrate deeply the meanings of words; they are skilled in eloquent discourse and have attained the wisdom of illusion.
They enter the gate of skillful means, their bodies adorned with necklaces of various jewels and all manner of ornaments, and they wear upon their heads crowns made of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* gems.
Furthermore, they are surrounded by immeasurable retinues, all of whom share the same roots of goodness, the same conduct, and the same vows and merit.

When the Great Treasury of Virtue was complete and inexhaustible, the woman Vasumitrā emitted from her body a vast radiance that universally illuminated all the palaces within the residence; those who encountered this light attained physical coolness.
At that time, Sudhana went before her, prostrated at her feet, stood with palms joined, and said: "Noble One, I have already previously..."
Having resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I did not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice or how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Hearing that the Noble One was well able to provide instruction, I prayed, "May you explain this to me.
He then replied, "Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'The Limit Beyond Greed' (*vītarāgakoṭi*); according to it—"
If there are those who desire to see me in bodily form, whether they be devas, and I appear to them in the form of a celestial maiden with a radiance so sublime and peerless;
likewise, even down to humans and non-humans, should they behold me, I immediately manifest as a human or non-human female according to their inclinations, enabling them all to see me.
If there are sentient beings who, being entangled by sensual desires, come to me...
If there are those for whom I preach the Dharma, having heard it, they will become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Unattached Realm.
If there are sentient beings who see me even for a moment, they will become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Joyful Delight.
If there are sentient beings who speak with me even for a moment, they will become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Unobstructed Sound.
If there are sentient beings who briefly take hold of my hand, they will be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universally Visiting All Buddha-fields.
If there are sentient beings who briefly ascend my seat, they will be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Liberation.
If there are sentient beings who briefly gaze upon me, they will be freed from desire and attain...
If there are sentient beings who see my stretching of the limbs, they will become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Subduing Non-Buddhists.

If there are sentient beings who see my blinking of the eyes, they will become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of the Buddha-realm. If there are sentient beings who embrace me, then...
By being free from desire, one attains the Bodhisattva samādhi of "Constantly Never Abandoning All Sentient Beings.
If there are sentient beings who kiss my lips, they shall become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva samādhi of "Increasing the Treasury of Merit for All Sentient Beings.
Any sentient beings who draw near to me shall all dwell in the attainment of the limit of freedom from desire and enter it.

When the Bodhisattva’s stage of omniscience manifested before him through the liberation of unimpeded understanding, Sudhana said, "Noble One, what roots of goodness did you plant and what meritorious deeds did you cultivate to achieve such sovereign mastery?
He replied, "Good son, I remember that in the past there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Uccagāmin. His royal capital was called Supratiṣṭhita."
O son, when that Tathāgata of Exalted Conduct, out of compassion for sentient beings, entered the royal city and stepped upon its threshold,
the entire city shook; it suddenly became vast and expansive, adorned with various jewels,
with immeasurable lights reflecting and penetrating one another, and various precious flowers strewn across the ground, while celestial music played simultaneously from all sides.
All the heavens were filled with deities reaching to the void. "Good son, at that time I was the wife of a householder named Śrīmatī.
Witnessing the Buddha’s supernatural power, my mind attained awakening; I then went with my husband to where the Buddha was and made an offering of a single precious coin.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī was the attendant to the Buddha and served me."
"Son of good family, I have taught the Dharma so that beings may resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

I know only this bodhisattva liberation of the 'limit of freedom from desire. As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished infinite wisdom of skillful means, whose treasury is vast and whose sphere of activity is incomparable—how could I possibly know or speak of them?"
"To the south of here, there is a city named Supāraga where a householder named Vīradatta resides.
He constantly makes offerings at the sandalwood-seat stūpa of the Buddha.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path. At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him.
Having circumambulated him countless times with profound reverence and gazing upon him, he took his leave and departed.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of entering the specific stage:
from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva liberation door of the limit of being free from desire," this segment concerns—
1. Establishing the five gates and contemplating the instructions of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for advancement;
2. Gradually traveling to the perilous country of the City Adorned with Jewels; 3. Searching everywhere for the woman Vasumitrā; 4.
Finding her within her own home, north of the marketplace inside that city; 5. Having seen her, paying homage and respect.
I shall now set forth the requested points and explain the liberation of Sudhana at the Limit Beyond Greed (*rāgānta-vigata*).
Regarding the interpretation of the text: Sudhana dwells in his own home to the north of the marketplace. This is because the profusion of birth and death is likened to a marketplace;
the north is the position of *khan* (the trigram for water), and *khan* is the northern direction, presiding over black.

This is also the station of all deluded and ignorant sentient beings. When Bodhisattvas dwell in this marketplace of the ocean of craving within the stream of delusion, they engage in the same practices as others to bring them forth [to awakening], causing them to realize that they have been dwelling in their own home all along.
This is because the ocean of birth and death of sentient beings is the very residence of the Bodhisattva; out of great compassion, the Bodhisattva dwells within it.
Within the house of birth and death for sentient beings, he delivers and liberates them, accomplishing the conduct of Samantabhadra and perfecting immeasurable merit.
As the sutra says: "The youth Sudhana went to his gate and saw that his residence was vast, magnificent, and beautiful," and so forth, describing in detail the adornments.
This is the first instance of seeing his *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as karmic retribution). Next, at that time...
Sudhana beheld this woman, whose countenance was upright and majestic, even unto her golden skin;
having thus seen her primary retribution (*vipāka*) as well as her various artistic skills— as detailed below in the sutra— it was then that Sudhana approached her,
made his formal request for what he sought, and received from her the instructions on the practice to be undertaken.
The liberation of the Bodhisattva Dharma is called "the limit of being free from desire. By means of this liberation, he manifests his body according to their inclinations and desires;
those seen within the ten directions and the three realms perceive him differently, as is fully explained in the sutra. Furthermore, the sutra says:
"If there are sentient beings who even briefly behold me, they immediately become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Joy."
It clarifies that those with faith cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and delight their minds in the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*).
Therefore, if there are sentient beings who even briefly converse with me, they will become free from greed and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Sound.

This clarifies that wisdom arises from concentration, realizing that sound has no intrinsic substance. Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who grasp my hand, they will likewise be freed from greed.
To wish to attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universally Visiting All Buddha-fields is the meaning of "guiding and receiving.
As for the following, "descending to the seat" is the meaning of the increase of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*). "Briefly beholding me" is the meaning of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
"Stretching and yawning" is the meaning of the joy of the Dharma. "Winking the eyes" is the seeing of the truth and entering the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom. "Embracing me" [is the meaning of...]
"Those who embrace and do not abandon sentient beings" means the sense of receiving instruction and preaching the Dharma.
"Those who kiss my lips" means that all who draw near to me, one by one, shall attain the limit of freedom from greed and enter the stage of a bodhisattva’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
This refers to the fact that among all those who draw near, none do so in vain; they all obtain the gateway to omniscience.
It clarifies that those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have emerged from the entanglements merely seek liberation from suffering;

they have not yet entered the gate of "identical activity" (*sāmānyārtha*) for the sake of delivering sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death through great compassion. They have not reached the station of the Sovereign of Wisdom of Mastery over the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which remains untainted amidst defilement and purity, which is the universal radiance of wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) beyond dependence, and which spontaneously benefits all living beings throughout the ten directions.
Only when there is neither bondage nor liberation can one be said to have eternally departed from the limit of desire.

To loathe [saṃsāra] and emerge from its entanglements, yet to lack the practice of great compassion and for wisdom not to be ultimate—because there remains something upon which to rely—one’s cultivation of the path should not be satisfied with attaining even a single portion of the mind characterized by signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, and the liberation of emptiness; rather, one should cultivate wisdom and compassion and give rise to them.
Vowing to deliver all sentient beings, one studies the wisdom of differentiation; exhausting the phenomena of the three realms, there is nothing that is not known.
Clearly employing the affairs of the three realms, they are immediately realized as the Dharma-realm, skillfully illuminating both self and others.

Through the formation of the twelve links of dependent origination, one attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), perceiving that boundless eons and the present are non-dual. One seeks no other place for a separate supramundane liberation.
Nirvana is characterized by the seal of non-action and non-reliance; the fundamental nature of the dharmas of the triple world is solely the Dharma of the Buddhas.

Since the fundamental nature of the Dharma is thus, there is no separate seeking or conceptualization. When one perfectly realizes the dharma-gates of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, they will naturally correspond to one another.
This lady Vasumitrā is the fifth dedication in this assembly, the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit."

The gate is so named because it equalizes birth and death through practice, causing the views of right and wrong to vanish; because within the Dharma-realm meditation gate, both true and conventional truths, as well as the two defilements, are simultaneously exhausted;
because its nature is equal to the Dharma-realm and its wisdom pervades existence and non-existence; because there is neither practice nor non-practice, and neither birth nor non-benefit;
and because it summons manifold merit and virtue, it is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. Sudhana said, "Noble One, what is the lineage of this gate?"
"What roots of goodness did I cultivate, and what merits did I perform, before giving away my daughter and speaking to Sudhana of my own past causes?
When the Tathāgata Viśuddhacāritra appeared in the world, I was the wife of a householder;
through the gift of precious coins and the encouragement of Mañjuśrī to resolve upon great bodhicitta, by these causes and conditions I attained this liberation. This much I know."
Regarding liberation through reaching the limit of freedom from desire: it clarifies the past causes by which one relinquishes what is most highly valued—namely, wealth and money.
This is the text on "freedom from desire. Mañjuśrī exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*); this is "freedom from desire.

Just as with a single precious coin, though the gift given is not large, because the mind holds it in high esteem, one is able to relinquish much; it is no different from this, and thus it is inexhaustible.
The dedication of the treasury of merit also takes the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as its essence. It clarifies that all dharmas are like precious coins in the sense of universal penetration.

In terms of the gate of wisdom, it universally remedies [obstructions] across all stages; in terms of the gate of specific stages, it specifically remedies the obstruction within the fifth dedication, which consists of the inability to exercise mastery over entering birth-and-death with supramundane *dhyāna*, and over the interpenetration of the true and conventional, the defiled and the pure.

Because it treats the obstacle of lacking mastery in conduct toward all sentient beings so as to bring about such mastery, the second section, "Inference of Virtue and Advancement," contains six lines of scripture from "As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "...took their leave and departed.
This is divided into five gates: first, inference of virtue and advancement; second, indicating the location and the name of the city.
1. Skillfully ferrying across; 2. The name of the lay friend (kalyāṇamitra), Vṛṣṭika; 3.
The activities performed by the lay friend, namely making offerings at the sandalwood stūpa and its pedestal; 4. Paying respects, taking leave, and departing.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: as for "Southern" and "City named Suvastu," these refer to this elder’s skillful ferrying across.

Regarding why this lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*) is named Viśvantara—this translates as "The All-Encompassing"—it is because this lay practitioner’s wisdom is vast and all-encompassing, encompassing all dharma-gates of the ten directions. His full name is *Siddhārtha*, which is translated as "Maitreya" (慈氏).
This clarifies that by means of the sixth supramundane wisdom, he dwells in the mundane world while practicing compassion through skillful means.
Because benefiting sentient beings is accomplished through practice,
the sixth is the City of Skillful Crossing, where the householder lord Viśvāmitra practices the dedication of all firm roots of goodness in accordance with the truth.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana traveled by stages until he reached the city of Supratiṣṭhita.
He went to the house of the lay devotee, prostrated at his feet, and stood with palms joined, saying:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one should cultivate it."
“I have heard, O Noble One, that you are well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me.
The householder replied, “Son of good family, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called ‘The Limit of Non-Parinirvāṇa. Son of good family, I do not give rise to the thought:
‘Such a Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa,’ nor do I think: ‘Such a Tathāgata is currently entering parinirvāṇa,’ nor do I think: ‘Such a Tathāgata...’”
"In the future, when I enter parinirvāṇa, I shall know that throughout all worlds in the ten directions, no Buddha-Tathāgata ever truly enters parinirvāṇa;
it is only for the sake of taming sentient beings that they manifest such an appearance.
Son of good family, when I opened the door of the Tathāgata’s stūpa containing the sandalwood throne, I attained a samādhi named 'The Inexhaustibility of the Buddha-seed.'"
"Son, in every moment of thought I enter this samādhi, and in every moment of thought I know all infinite and supreme matters.
Sudhana said, "What is the sphere of this samādhi? The householder replied, "Noble son, as I enter this samādhi, I see, in their proper sequence, all the Buddhas of this world, namely: Kāśyapa..."
With Buddhas such as Śākyamuni Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Vipaśyin Buddha,
Viśvabhū Buddha, Puṣya Buddha, Anuttarajaya Buddha, and Anuttarapadma Buddha as their leaders, they were able, in a single moment of thought,
to see one hundred buddhas, to see one thousand buddhas, to see one hundred thousand buddhas, and to see [innumerable] buddhas.
One sees one hundred million Buddhas, one thousand million Buddhas, one hundred thousand million Buddhas, *ayuta* million Buddhas, *nayuta* million Buddhas,
and even as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds; in this manner, one sees all such [Buddhas] in succession,
and also sees those Buddhas at the time they first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, planted various roots of goodness, attained supreme supernormal powers, and achieved greatness.
May I practice the sublime conduct, fulfill the perfections, enter the bodhisattva stages, attain pure patience, subdue the armies of Māra,
achieve perfect enlightenment, purify my buddha-field, be surrounded by an assembly of followers, emit great light, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma,
and manifest various supernatural transformations— all these I am able to uphold, all these I am able to remember, and all these I am able to observe.
Examining and discerning, one sees that all Buddhas of the future, such as Maitreya Buddha, and all Buddhas of the present, such as Vairocana Buddha, are likewise entirely so;

and all Buddhas of the three periods of time throughout this world and the worlds of the ten directions, along with their assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, are likewise entirely so. This is excellent.

"Good man, I have only attained this liberation of the limit of non-extinction attained by Bodhisattvas, such that all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the wisdom of a single thought-moment, universally know the three periods of time; with a single thought-moment, they enter all samādhis;
the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom constantly illuminates their minds; they are without discrimination regarding all phenomena, and they fully comprehend all Buddhas."
All are entirely equal; the Tathāgata, myself, and all sentient beings are one without duality.

Knowing that the self-nature of all phenomena is pure, free from thought, and free from movement, I am able to universally enter all worlds, remain apart from all conceptual discrimination, abide in the seal of the Buddha-dharma, and fully awaken all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm. How then could I [be otherwise]?
"O son of good family, you who are able to know and speak of those meritorious deeds, there is a mountain to the south named Potalaka.
There dwells a bodhisattva named Avalokiteśvara; go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path. Then he spoke these verses:
Upon the ocean there is a mountain where many sages and worthies dwell; composed of various jewels, it is utterly pure.
Flowering trees and fruit-bearing groves fill it everywhere, and springs, streams, ponds, and pools are all fully present.
The heroic being Avalokiteśvara dwells upon this mountain for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
"You should go and inquire about all these virtues; he will show you the great skillful means.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and took his leave to depart.

[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of entering the proper stage, from the passage beginning "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva’s liberation, the limit of the non-extinction of all Buddhas," five topical headings are established:
1) the gradual journey to the city of Suprabha; 2) arriving at the house of the householder.
Prostrating at his feet and standing with palms joined three times, he formally presented his request.
The four laymen then correctly expounded for Sudhana the Dharma of his practice—the gateway to liberation called "The Limit of Non-Nirvāṇa.
Fifth, regarding the offering of the sandalwood throne and stupa that appeared before him, the Sūtra says: "I opened the sandalwood throne, the stupa of the Tathāgata."
The samādhi attained at this stage, named "The Inexhaustibility of the Buddha-seed," clarifies that the discriminative minds of all sentient beings are all seeds of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
they are identical to the seeds of the wisdom of all Buddhas and possess no characteristics such as arising or ceasing.
This corresponds to the sixth dwelling among the Ten Dwellings (*daśavihāra*), the sixth stage among the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), and the [sixth] among the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*).

The sixth practice consists of dedicating the wisdom-gate of the sixth supramundane stage among the ten abodes and ten practices toward the conduct of benefiting sentient beings through wisdom while remaining within the entanglements of the mundane world; therefore, one assumes the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) to transform worldly society.
One establishes a single shrine room (*stūpa-śālā*) and places a sandalwood seat (*candana-pīṭha*) therein, but does not install a physical image, thereby manifesting the [sixth] stage.

The six gates of wisdom penetrate the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*). By means of this stupa-base, one makes offerings to all Buddhas as they appear before one, clarifying that the dharma of signlessness is devoid of views regarding the three periods of time—past, present, and future.
This is because the wisdom of one’s own Buddha and the wisdom of all Buddhas are identical in their signless essence, being of a single limit (*ekānta*) for all sentient beings.
Birth, too, is fundamentally of one limit with the wisdom of all Buddhas;

for the sake of all sentient beings, he preaches such a Dharma so that all sentient beings may open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Therefore, the city is named "Good Crossing," and the lay devotee is named "Inclusion," because he includes all Buddhas and all sentient beings.

Because wisdom is of a single essence and is neither born nor extinguished, and since the wisdom of all Buddhas possesses this nature of non-arising and non-extinction, all sentient beings likewise do not arise or perish. By virtue of this Dharma, one attains the state of all Buddhas who do not enter nirvana.
This meaning clarifies that, just as the formless [reality] upon the seat is the Buddha, Sudhana said: "These three..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "What is the state of indistinctness?": the following is the householder’s answer concerning the number of Buddhas seen upon entering this samādhi.
He sees all the Buddhas of this world-system and other directions throughout the three periods of time; the total number of Buddhas seen is fully explained in the sutra.

The underlying meaning clarifies that all Buddhas and sentient beings possess the characteristic of being without birth or extinction, and that these are skillfully manifested through the metaphor of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel.
The sandalwood throne-stūpa serves as a guide and representation, leading all sentient beings to realize that the characteristics of their own mind-nature are wisdom.
Like the sandalwood throne-stūpa, [the nature] is originally without marks; it is the primordial Buddha.

When one clearly realizes that both nature and marks are non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, then realizing marks is like an illusion and realizing nature is like space. When wisdom has no place of reliance or abiding, how could there be birth?
The cessation of this is the dedication that accords with all firm roots of goodness, taking the *prajñāpāramitā* as its essence and the other nine perfections as its companions.
This remedies the obstacle to mastery in practicing great compassion while moving within *saṃsāra* regarding supramundane wisdom, thereby enabling the attainment of mastery.
Thus, in the second stage of "Advancing by Inferring Virtue," one proceeds from suchness...
The passage concerning the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas’ departure after taking their leave, along with the fourteen lines of verse, is divided into five sections:
(1) praising his virtues and describing his advancement; (2) indicating the location of the spiritual friend; (3) citing the name of the mountain, Potalaka;
(4) citing the name of the spiritual friend, Avalokiteśvara, whose formal title is Guanshiyin; and (5) [the conclusion].
Having paid respects and taken leave, I shall now explain the meaning of the text. Regarding the name of the mountain, *Potalaka*:
this is translated as "Mountain of the White Flowering Tree. This is because white flowering trees grow abundantly on this mountain, and their fragrance is so potent that its scent reaches afar.
This serves to clarify that this holy being practices the gateway of compassion (*karuṇā*) by taking the most humble and lowly state as his conduct.

"Flower" (*puṣpa*) signifies the blossoming of the myriad practices; thus, this compassion, humility, gentleness, and joy constitute the blossoming flower of the practice of teaching and transforming others.
"Incense" (*gandha*) refers to its fragrance wafting far to permeate all sentient beings, causing all who hear its name to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
The reason the name "Avalokiteśvara" is cited as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is because the older translation referred to him as "Guanshiyin."
In the correct Sanskrit, he is called Avalokiteśvara. This means that with the light of his compassion, he illuminates the world and rescues those who hear of his suffering as soon as they do so.

As for the notion that he only rescues those who wait until they have recited his name, the intent is to cause them to turn their minds toward exclusively focusing on wholesome dharmas, so that they may give rise to the resolve and make the roots of their merit and virtue firm and deep.
Question: Since Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara) already possesses compassion, why must he necessarily be called Guangshiyin (Avalokiteśvara)?
The voice replied: "In general, all Bodhisattvas establish their names based on their practice, and their practice is manifested through their names; thus they indicate their respective stages.

Although all Bodhisattvas possess both wisdom and the two gates [of means], here, because one must manifest the essential progression through name and practice, we employ the name to represent the Dharma.
Thus, this seventh dedication—'Conforming to All Sentient Beings'—is established as the stage of accomplishing worldly compassion."
The "Gate of Compassion" uses the name Avalokiteśvara as a designation for compassion to serve as a marker for the stage of practice, thereby causing one to advance.
As for "Avalokiteśvara," it clarifies the meaning of attaining supramundane *prajñā* through contemplative observation;

because he is "sovereign" (*īśvara*), it serves to represent the observation of worldly suffering, thus signifying the gate of compassion. This is not like the name "Guanshiyin" (Avalokitasvara) found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The middle [section] states that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva comes from the presence of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja in the East;
furthermore, other sutras state that Avalokiteśvara is in the presence of Amitābha Buddha in the West.

All of these are the Tathāgata’s intentional skillful means for expressing the dharma and establishing names. The meaning is that the East represents wisdom (*prajñā*) and the West represents compassion (*karuṇā*).

This indicates that while the Dharma is ultimately without spatial location, it is conventionally designated by the east as the time when spring’s yang energy emerges and the sun rises to shine universally upon the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
Among these, the seven stars of the eastern quarter—Jie, Fang, Xin, and so forth—are all positions of manifold goodness, signifying the gateway of wisdom.
The seven lunar mansions of the western quarter—Ang, Bi, Shen, and so forth—preside over the White Tiger and signify the principle of autumnal killing; Ang, in particular, represents this.
Since the administration of justice primarily involves punishing evil, it was made presided over by Avalokiteśvara; yet in reality, this is but one region of the Buddha-land.
Since a single atom contains the entire Dharma-realm, how could there be spatial locations where self and other exist in mutual obstruction?
Thus, there is no separate Buddha. Former masters who translated the scriptures, relying on the teachings of the Three Vehicles, claimed that Avalokiteśvara does not exist in this land.
To designate Avalokiteśvara as the title for this is not [to say] that he has actually attained the realm and wisdom of the Dharmadhātu-Vairocana Tathāgata;
rather, within the "Gate of Unifying the Three and Entering the One" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, these three dharmas are fully present:
Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva represent the signless wisdom of the Dharmakāya and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Mañjuśrī represents the primary subject of practice, signifying that one initiates diverse activities from fundamental wisdom;
Samantabhadra represents great compassion, signifying that one constantly remains within the flow of suffering without seeking personal escape;
and Avalokiteśvara represents these three dharmas as the conduct practiced by a single individual, signifying that they are brought to full completion and universal pervasion.
To teach and transform the entire realm of sentient beings without exception is named Vairocana Buddha;

this clarifies that Mañjuśrī is omnipresent, Samantabhadra is omnipresent, Avalokiteśvara is omnipresent, and Vairocana is omnipresent, pervading even within every atom in infinite layers. This is a brief explanation.
The phrase "like a mountain upon the sea where many sages and saints dwell" refers specifically to the Southern Sea, which also symbolizes the sea of birth and death;
other meanings are clearly explained in the full text. It further takes compassion as its spring and flowing stream.
The seventh is the dedication of Potalaka Mountain, presided over by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, which accords with all sentient beings.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana single-mindedly contemplated the instructions of that householder regarding entry into the understanding of that bodhisattva.
Having escaped [from that state], he attains the power of recollection characteristic of those bodhisattvas; he remembers the sequence of the appearance of those Buddhas,
he recalls the continuous succession of those Buddhas, he maintains the sequence of the names of those Buddhas,
he contemplates the sublime Dharma taught by those Buddhas, he knows that those Buddhas are fully adorned, and he realizes that those Buddhas have attained perfect enlightenment.
Those Buddhas, traveling by means of their inconceivable activities, gradually proceeded until they reached that mountain;

searching everywhere, they beheld this Great Bodhisattva on the western face, within a rocky valley where spring waters glistened, the forest was lush, and fragrant, soft grasses were spread upon the ground in a clockwise pattern.
There, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) upon a diamond-jewel stone.

Seated in the lotus posture, immeasurable bodhisattvas all sat upon precious stones, respectfully surrounding him as he proclaimed the Dharma of Great Compassion so that they might gather in and sustain all sentient beings. Upon seeing this, Sudhana leaped for joy;
with palms joined, he gazed intently without blinking for a moment, thinking: "A spiritual friend is indeed a Tathāgata, for they know well [the way to lead others]."
The wise know that a spiritual friend is a cloud of all dharmas; a spiritual friend is a treasury of all merits; a spiritual friend is difficult to encounter;
a spiritual friend is the cause for the jewels of the ten powers; a spiritual friend is an inexhaustible torch of wisdom;
a spiritual friend is the sprout of the roots of merit; a spiritual friend is the gateway to all-knowledge; a spiritual friend is an ocean of wisdom.
The spiritual friend who is a guide, being an instrument for the path toward omniscience, immediately proceeded to where the great bodhisattva was.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara saw Sudhana from afar and addressed him, saying: "Welcome! You have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind to universally gather in all sentient beings;
you have given rise to an upright mind, single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-dharma, with profound and heavy great compassion to rescue and protect them."

The continuous manifestation before them of all the wondrous practices of Samantabhadra; the fulfillment and purification of the profound mind of great vows through diligent seeking of the Buddha-dharma;
the ability to receive and accumulate roots of goodness with never-ceasing satisfaction; compliance with spiritual friends and non-contradiction of their instructions;
and the maturation of a mind born from the ocean of the merit and wisdom of Mañjuśrī—these were all attained.
Having attained the vast samādhi through the power of the Buddha, he single-mindedly sought the profound and wondrous Dharma;
constantly beholding all Buddhas, he gave rise to great joy. His wisdom was pure like space;

having himself attained clarity, he further explained it for others, dwelling securely in the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Avalokiteśvara...
The Bodhisattva Vaśitā circumambulated the venerable one countless times, joined his palms, and stood before him, saying:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices or how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me."
The Bodhisattva said, "Excellent, excellent, noble son! You have already been able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Noble son, I have already accomplished the liberation door of the bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion.
Noble son, by means of this liberation door of the bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion, I impartially teach and transform all sentient beings."

"O son of good family, my continuity is unbroken; dwelling in this gateway of the practice of great compassion, I am always present before all Tathāgatas and universally manifest before all sentient beings.
I gather in sentient beings through generosity, or through kind words, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation; or I gather them by manifesting a physical body."
To sentient beings, he may manifest various inconceivable nets of pure light of diverse colors to gather them in;
or by means of voice, or through dignified demeanor, or by preaching the Dharma, or by manifesting supernatural transformations, he causes their minds to awaken so that they attain maturity;
or he manifests a form identical to theirs and dwells together with them to bring them to maturity, O son of good family.
May I, practicing this gateway of great compassion, always protect and deliver all sentient beings;
may all sentient beings be free from the fear of treacherous paths, free from the fear of burning affliction, free from the fear of delusion, free from the fear of bondage,

free from the fear of slaughter, free from the fear of poverty, free from the fear of inability to survive, free from the fear of ill repute, free from the fear of death, and free from the fear of the great...

May all beings be free from the fear of the masses, the fear of the evil realms, the fear of darkness, the fear of transmigration, the fear of separation from loved ones, the fear of encountering enemies, the fear of physical affliction, the fear of mental affliction, and the fear of sorrow and lamentation. Furthermore, I make this vow:
may all sentient beings, whether they think of me, recite my name, or behold my body, all attain liberation from these fears.
"O son of good family who fears nothing, by these skillful means I have caused all sentient beings to be free from fear;
I then further instruct them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* so that they never again fall back.
Son of good family, I have attained only this gate of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion; as for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have already purified [themselves]..."
Having established all the vows of Samantabhadra, one constantly practices all the deeds of Samantabhadra;
one constantly performs all wholesome dharmas, constantly enters all samādhis, and constantly dwells throughout all infinite kalpas.

One constantly knows all phenomena of the three periods of time, constantly visits all infinite lands, constantly pacifies the evils of all sentient beings, and constantly causes all sentient beings to flourish.
"Since Śubhavyūha constantly cuts off the stream of birth and death for sentient beings, how could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
At that time, there was a bodhisattva from the east named Samantagāmin who came through the air to the summit of the Cakravāḍa mountains in this Sahā world.
He pressed the earth with his foot, and the entire Sahā world shook in six ways.

All were adorned with various jewels. The Bodhisattva Samantagāmin emitted a radiance from his body that eclipsed all the light of the sun, moon, stars, lightning, the eight classes of supernatural beings (deva-nāga-aṣṭakula), Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors; their lights appeared like a mass of ink.
This light shone universally upon all the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the abode of King Yama, causing the manifold sufferings of those in the evil destinies [to cease].
They all extinguish afflictions and do not give rise to sorrow or grief, remaining entirely free from them;

furthermore, throughout all Buddha-lands, they cause a universal rain of all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, garments, banners, and canopies—such ornaments as these—to be offered to the Buddhas.
Moreover, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings' hearts, they manifest themselves universally within all palaces.
He caused all who saw his body to feel complete joy, and then he approached the place where Avalokiteśvara was.
At that time, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said to Sudhana: "Noble son, did you see the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin coming to this assembly?
He replied, "I have seen him. Avalokiteśvara said, "Noble son, you should go and ask the Bodhisattva how one should learn the Bodhi [of a Bodhisattva]."
[The Bodhisattva] practices the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivates the bodhisattva path.

[Treatise: Within the first dharma-gate for correctly entering the specific stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this dharma-gate of the practice of great compassion," five gates are established based on a single thought-moment.

Following the instructions of his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) regarding the two gradual stages of contemplation and advancement, Sudhana traveled to that mountain, searching for this great bodhisattva everywhere.

Third, he saw the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara seated in the full lotus posture upon a diamond-precious stone within the rocky valleys on its western face. Fourth, having seen him, Sudhana gazed upon him with joy.

Avalokiteśvara saw Sudhana from afar and praised him; Sudhana prostrated at his feet and requested that Avalokiteśvara explain the gate of liberation consisting of the practice of great compassion. Regarding the commentary on the meaning of the text:

as in the case of the fifth [visit], the woman Bhṛkuṭī, she received him by means of a lion’s stretch, thereby manifesting the conduct of compassion, as well as her reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) marks and her sphere of experience.
His dwelling is adorned with all manner of jewels; he reaches the ultimate limit of great compassion through the sixth and seventh dedications of merit.

Rather than seeking his own karmic reward, he dwells among sentient beings to benefit them, residing in the impure realms of the world where mountain crags, valleys, springs, and streams shimmer with clarity, and where forests are lush and verdant, and fragrant grasses, soft and supple, spread across the ground in a clockwise direction—such is the abode of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattvas, immeasurable in number, sit upon vajra-jewels; this signifies their dwelling place.
The rocky ravines signify perilous paths and the evil realms (*apāya*). The glistening, translucent mountain streams signify compassion.
The lush, verdant forests signify the dense shade of a compassionate heart. The fragrant herbs, soft and supple, signify the fragrance of gentle speech and sublime teachings.

The ground being spread out to the right in a clockwise direction to delight the hearts of people symbolizes that sentient beings are transformed in accordance with [the Buddha's] teaching, spreading the ground of compassion so that they have a place of refuge.

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva sitting upon a vajra-stone symbolizes that through the application of vajra-wisdom, his compassionate conduct is firm, solid, and profound, remaining unshakable. His sitting in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) signifies the union of wisdom and compassion.
The infinite Bodhisattvas, including Ch’e (Chenrezig), were all seated upon precious stones; their compassionate conduct was firm and profound.

When Sudhana gazed at them with eyes that did not blink for a moment, it was because he revered the Dharma and honored these noble beings, seeing them with a heart of loving-kindness and free from any other thought.
Sudhana’s praise of their virtues is clearly explained in detail in the sutra. Sudhana then proceeded to the abode of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva...
When Samantabhadra saw Sudhana from afar, he immediately said, "Welcome," along with various words of praise;

that he spoke these words before even offering his salutation demonstrates the profound depth of his great compassion, which first offers consolation and praise, and only then performs prostrations, circumambulations, and presents his request.
Thus, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva bestowed upon Sudhana the practice and realization of Great Compassion.

The seventh stage of the seventh dwelling, the Illumination of the Doors of Liberation (*vimokṣamukha-āloka-pariṇāmanā*), involves cultivating supramundane compassion within the seventh ground to bring about the practice of mundane compassion.
Upon reaching this station, the Bodhisattva fulfills the seventh "Equal Accordance with All Sentient Beings" dedication;
thus, the wisdom that enters the mundane world also functions within this practice, as indicated in the following text.
Although his station is in the east, there is a bodhisattva named Samyaktva-naya (Rightly Directed). When he arrives and is seen, he dwells together with those in the assembly;
this signifies that the bodhisattvas at this stage enter into worldly conduct while manifesting both compassion and wisdom in equal measure.
Next, the subsequent passage of the sutra’s reconciliation states: "Good son, I dwell in this gate of the practice of great compassion, always present among all..."
The Buddha-Tathāgata universally manifests before all sentient beings and gathers them in through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), as explained at length in the sutras;

this intends to clarify that he does not depart from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) while manifesting form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) throughout the worlds of the ten directions to benefit beings with compassion.
Below this, there is a detailed explanation of the vows made by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva himself to benefit sentient beings.

The practice for serving living beings is explained in detail below. From "I have only attained this gate of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion" onwards is the section on deferring to virtue and advancing upward.
This is the gate of dedication that accords with all sentient beings, where the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.
Regarding the various stages within the gate of wisdom, these universally remedy [defilements] across all positions. As for the specific positions:

Within the gates, the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*) treat the obstacle of not attaining mastery while dwelling in the mundane world despite having transcended it through great compassion;
they cause one to attain such mastery. Second, regarding the advancement through the inference of virtues, from the passage beginning "Just as all bodhisattvas...
down to "cultivating the bodhisattva path," there are eighteen and a half lines of scripture divided into five sections. The first is the advancement through the inference of virtues.
1. Indicating the location of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); 2. Stating the name of the spiritual friend as the "Right Path" (samyak-gati); 3.
Repeatedly praising the spiritual friend’s radiant majesty, supernatural powers, and universal transformation; 4. Exhorting one to go and inquire. Question:
For what purpose is it not stated that he takes his leave and departs? Answer: Because [the instruction is given] within this assembly of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The vision of the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin represents that the two stages of wisdom (*jñāna*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are here simultaneously fulfilled.
It signifies that the culmination of compassion is the very wisdom of ignorance itself becoming luminous; because the essence of compassion and wisdom is non-dual, he does not depart.
Furthermore, it clarifies that from the Lion-Stretching Bhikṣuṇī, who cultivated compassion to give rise to wisdom, this proceeds through the eighth dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The Earth Deity of the Tenth Dedication Ground immediately transforms wisdom into compassion; this celestial deity is wisdom, while the Earth Deity is compassion.

When wisdom and compassion are unified as a single essence, they constitute the practice of Samantabhadra. This union of wisdom and compassion is the true body of the Arhat, pervading the divine nature;
it is called the "Deity of Heaven and Earth" and is not a worldly ghost or spirit. This is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

It is said that in the eastern direction there is a Bodhisattva named Samantagāmin (Correctly Proceeding). He is called "Correctly Proceeding" because he possesses right wisdom and is free from error.
His coming from space signifies that the essence of wisdom has no dependence and lacks form or substance;
his spirit is omnipresent, and from the self-nature of true emptiness, he manifests an illusory body to benefit sentient beings in response to conditions, echoing their needs in a single kṣaṇa.
The nature of the ten directions has no coming or going; because illusory images manifest through emptiness, it is said that they "come from emptiness.
That which is called the East symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*). That which is called the South symbolizes the Dharma as being void, luminous, and detached.
Within detachment there is voidness, which constitutes luminosity, correctness, and the sun. "Detachment" (*li*) means to be adorned. It is by means of luminosity that it adorns the earth.
The north is Kan (Water), which is black; Zi represents the culmination of yin, and Gui represents the end of yin.

To turn one’s back on the black and follow the light, to turn away from the heterodox and follow the correct—this is the position of the initial opening of enlightenment. Therefore, one proceeds to the south.
Now, reaching the eighth, the Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness, this clarifies that the east is wisdom, Zhen (Thunder), thunder, and sound.
Sound is the Azure Dragon; it represents spring and birth, merit, and auspiciousness. It is born in the Tiger (Yin) position and emerges from the Rabbit (Mao).
One determines right and wrong in the Dragon (Chen) and Snake (Si) positions. By the time one reaches the Horse (Wu), all belong to the Yang positions;
Wu is the culmination of Yang, and Wei is the end of Yang. From Wei through the Ox (Chou) are the Yin positions. By means of this, the eighth wisdom increases in clarity.

The dedication of the aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*) takes the eastern direction as its basis, because it is the illumination of wisdom that shines upon the myriad heterodoxies;
it enters into birth and death to shake all existing things so that clarity may arise; it teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may realize True Suchness;
it illuminates the path of the foolish to bring about the virtue of a gentleman; it destroys the path of the sycophantic and heterodox to establish correct wisdom; and it illuminates all things.
Because it gives rise to all that is wholesome, it causes the various roots of goodness to grow;

because it accomplishes pure, stainless, auspicious merit and virtue, the East symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*) and the West symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*). By means of these two positions, it clarifies the equality of compassion and wisdom.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin came from the East and was seen at a certain place west of the White Flower Mountain (*Sita-puṣpa-parvata*), thereby clarifying the significance of the East.
"Manifesting wisdom externally and manifesting compassion externally—this is the true path of Avalokiteśvara. Compassion and wisdom are two aspects of a single reality;
from this point onward, one proceeds from wisdom to practice compassion. That which follows is the spirit of Heaven and Earth.

Therefore, it is clear that practicing wisdom from within compassion results in a limited practice that does not reach its end, whereas practicing compassion from within wisdom results in a vast and limitless practice."
As it was previously stated, when the wisdom and compassion of the ten stages are perfected, in the eleventh stage, compassion again serves as the essence and wisdom as the function;

thus, Māyā is compassion and the birth of the Buddha is wisdom. In this manner, every successive stage of advancement possesses its own underlying significance, whether considered collectively or individually, in terms of identity or difference, just as the directions of east, west, south, and north each manifest their own distinct characteristics.

To seek out and dispel delusion while illuminating the Way, one should represent this by heading south; if one seeks to manifest wisdom and compassion for the benefit of the common people, one should represent this by heading east or west.
As for Avalokiteśvara being located to the west of Mount Baihua: "white" corresponds to the position of Metal;

the west is white, representing the position of Metal, which presides over the rank of General. The east corresponds to the position of Wood; it presides over the color green and represents the aspect of physical form (*lakṣaṇa*).
The positions correspond to their functions: the phase of birth presides over life, while the phase of decline presides over death.
The Tathāgata, in accordance with worldly conventions, established these gateways of the Dharma so that they might be easily understood by the world;

thus, he placed the gateway of great compassion at the site of slaughter to rescue those from suffering, and placed the gateway of great wisdom at the site of springtime birth in the east to symbolize wisdom.
To give rise to manifold virtues and enable them to easily attain their purpose is as the Master Lao said: "The General of the Front ranks on the right; the General of the Left ranks on the left.
This clarifies that the Superior is luminous and endowed with compassion, fearing the reckless taking of life. Yet, in reality, the Great Image is indeterminate;
how could it have a fixed shape that can be grasped? It is merely by summarizing the Law that names are established and its principles set forth.
Nevertheless, the path of wisdom and compassion fulfills the ten directions through a single dharma and practices all myriad deeds through a single practice.

Although the establishment of dharmas according to worldly conventions is not without its basis—just as worldly arrangements exist—it is nonetheless the application of means according to specific circumstances.
Therefore, this sutra states that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said: "In the eastern direction, there is a bodhisattva..."
Named "Rightly Entering" (*samyak-prasthāna*), this represents the great function of the eighth stage of non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which illuminates the great night of the world;
therefore, its position is identical to that of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten stages, and the eleventh stage.
While there are differences in the progression, maturation, and the direct or reverse order of these stages, this Bodhisattva Rightly Entering has come from the void to this Sahā world.

When the summit of the Cakravāḍa mountain range surrounding the world is pressed down with a toe, causing this Sahā world to quake in six ways, it signifies that wisdom can shatter darkness, such that the delusions of sentient beings are extinguished and objective realms vanish and disperse. As wisdom manifests, delusion perishes;
since the objective realm of the great earth—which is the retribution for deluded karma—also vanishes and disperses, the earth quakes. "Quake" means to disperse.
It is also like when meditative concentration manifests before one: delusion perishes and wisdom responds, and as objects are exhausted, they vanish.
Pressing the earth with a toe is the sphere of action of wisdom; it symbolizes that when the wisdom of dharma-emptiness arises and manifests, all attachments are dispersed.
Mount Cakravāḍa represents the objects of attachment grasped by delusion—having no basis, the objects grasped by wisdom manifest through the method of dhyāna-contemplation.
When clarity cannot be measured by the conceptualizing mind and all things are adorned with various jewels, then delusion vanishes and objects cease;
as one accords with the purity of wisdom and merit, all virtues immediately manifest, emitting bodily radiance that eclipses the sun,
moon, stars, lightning, and the light of the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four world-protecting kings.
All these radiances are like a mass of ink; yet their light universally illumines all hells and the animal realm.

Just as the lights of the three realms are all produced by tainted karma following the mind of arising and ceasing, and are born of merit that has not yet transcended arising and ceasing, so too all my own tainted karmic fruits have both self and other; the karma obtained by others exists exactly as it truly is.

The wisdom-light of great compassion—characterized by rationality, the untainted, non-self, and non-action, and possessing the purity of the *dharmatā* through its spontaneous nature—is beyond the reach of the mundane world;
it is without obstruction, boundaries, or limits, penetrating the ten directions and pervading the six realms of existence.
Therefore, the subsequent practices of wisdom and compassion are fully elucidated as they appear in the sūtras.
The Eighth: The Dedication of the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin, Lord of the Aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, respectfully receiving his instruction, immediately went to where that bodhisattva was.
He prostrated at his feet, stood with palms joined, and said: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."

Although I have conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The Bodhisattva Samantagambhīravikramin said:
"Noble son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Universal Gateway Swift Movement'. Sudhana said: "Noble One, regarding this..."
"By which Buddha was this Dharma-gate obtained? From what buddha-field did it come? How far is it from here? And how long has it been since it set out? He replied:

"Good son, these matters are difficult to know; they cannot be understood by any in the world—gods, humans, asuras, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—but only by those bodhisattvas who are courageous, diligent, tireless, and undaunted."

“O Noble One,” said Sudhana, “I have been embraced by all spiritual friends, am mindful of all Buddhas, am endowed with roots of goodness, possess pure aspiration, have attained the faculties of a bodhisattva, and have the eye of wisdom; thus I am able to hear, retain, understand, and explain [the Dharma].
By the power of the Buddha and the power of the spiritual friend, I am able to believe and accept it. I pray that you will instruct me on the correct path.”

The Bodhisattva said, "Good son, I have come from the world-system called Wondrous Treasury (Prabhāsvara-kośa) in the eastern direction, from the presence of the Buddha Universal Victorious Birth (Samantavijaya-janman).
I obtained this Dharma-gate from that Buddha and set out from there;

an unspeakably unspeakable number of kalpas, as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields, have already passed. Within each and every thought-moment, I have raised [this teaching] unspeakably unspeakable times."
At every step, equal in number to the atoms within a Buddha-field, I pass through as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds;
into each and every one of those Buddha-fields I enter universally, reaching the abodes of those Buddhas and making offerings with sublime articles of worship.
All these articles of offering are produced by the unsurpassed mind and sealed by the unconditioned Dharma.
"O son of good family, whom all bodhisattvas praise, I have universally seen all sentient beings in that world;

I know their minds and I know their faculties. According to their inclinations and understandings, I manifest my body and preach the Dharma, or emit light, or bestow wealth and treasures—teaching and taming them through various skillful means without ceasing."
Just as it is from the east, so it is likewise from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Good son, I have attained only this bodhisattva liberation of "Universal Swift Movement," which enables one to quickly reach all places;
yet it does not equal the sphere of wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who universally reach everywhere throughout the ten directions.
I have skillfully distributed my body in its various manifestations so that it pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
I reach all paths and enter all lands, knowing all dharmas and arriving at all worlds. I impartially expound all dharma-gates, simultaneously illuminating all sentient beings.
Toward all Buddhas, I give rise to no discrimination, and in all places, I am without obstruction. And I—
"How can one know and speak of those meritorious deeds? "Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Dvāravatī, and within it dwells a deity named Mahādeva.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path. Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him countless times.
Having gazed upon [the Buddha] with utmost reverence and courtesy, he took his leave and departed.
