[Commentary] First, within the Dharma-gate of entering the specific stage, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana... and so forth.
I have only known this liberation door of the light of the Dharma that destroys the darkness of delusion for all sentient beings;
herein, five gates are established: first, contemplating the instructions of a spiritual friend to advance upward;
second, gradually traveling until reaching that city, entering through the eastern gate and standing there for no long time before seeing the sun set; third, by...

Eighth, regarding the supreme condition of mindfulness of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): Sudhana saw the Night Goddess Abhimukhī in the midst of space, seated upon a lion throne within a precious pavilion and a fragrant lotus treasury.
Her body was golden in color, her eyes and hair were deep blue, and her appearance was dignified and beautiful.
Sudhana prostrated himself on the ground before the Night Goddess’s feet and made his request.
Regarding what was sought, after having beheld the Night Goddess, he further established six points:

first, seeing that the Night Goddess’s physical form was upright and handsome, her skin golden in color, and her eyes and hair deep blue; second, seeing that the Night Goddess wore crimson robes, a Brahma-crown, and jeweled necklaces;
third, seeing that the constellations and celestial bodies were vividly manifest upon her body; fourth, seeing each and every one of the Night Goddess’s hairs...
From every pore, she manifested the transformation and deliverance of immeasurable sentient beings, bestowing the Dharma according to their faculties;

some were born in the heavens or among humans, while others attained the distinct fruits of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. The Night Goddess, endowed with the five kinds of vision, further manifested various masteries of the Bodhisattva samādhis.
Sudhana prostrated himself upon the ground, bowed at the feet of the Night Goddess, and with palms joined, made his request.
The dharma-gate sought here, its realm, its physical dimensions, and its pores, are the body of the *dharmadhātu* itself;
it is the ultimate limit of the realm of the *dharmadhātu*. It causes practitioners to emulate and learn from it until the ten stages are perfected.
Even when one has fully grasped the model, the learner has only attained a portion of it, for it is a portion within the whole. Therefore...

The realm of wisdom and the timing do not shift; thus, while [the progression] is entirely based on the advancement through stages, it is further divided into seventeen sections within the petitions for what is sought:
first, Sudhana’s aspiration to rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to obtain the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha's merits;
second, the night goddesses’ praise of Sudhana and their bestowing of the dharmas they themselves have practiced.
1. The title of the Dharma-gate is "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation of Radiant Light that Shatters the Ignorance and Darkness of All Sentient Beings.
2. From "Good sons" onwards, and from "I, toward sentient beings of evil wisdom" onwards, [the text] sets forth the practice of his own great compassion.
3. The night goddesses speak twenty-one verses, describing their own [experiences].

1. Knowing this Dharma, he exhorts Sudhana to practice and study it, leading him to enter [the path]. 2. Sudhana asks the Night Goddess how long it has been since she first resolved her mind [on enlightenment].
3. He further asks the Night Goddess how long it has been since she attained this Dharma-door. 4.

From a past world-system as many eons ago as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, he cites the number of eons since she first resolved her mind. 5. [He describes] the duration of those eons since she first resolved her mind.
10. Listing the name of the kalpa, "Tranquil Light" (*Śāntaprabha*); 11. Listing the names of ten worlds, "Birth of Wondrous Jewels" (*Prabhūtaratnasaṃbhava*);

12. Listing the four continents named "Jewel Moon Lamp Light" (*Ratnacandrapradīpa*); 13. Listing the city named "Lotus Light" (*Padmaprabhā*) and its king, "Good Dharma Deliverance" (*Saddharmataraṇa*);
14. Listing that to the east of the city there is a great Bodhi tree, beneath which is a Buddha named "One" (*Eka*).
14. Sarvadharmanirghoṣarāja attained perfect awakening; [this is] the fourteenth section. There was a night goddess named Vimalacandraprabhā who announced that a Buddha had appeared in the world;
[this is] the fifteenth section. Having been a queen named Dharmamaticandrā under that Buddha, she made offerings and resolved upon bodhicitta;
for as many eons as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, she did not give rise to evil.

For eighty eons, as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru, he constantly experienced peace and happiness while cultivating roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; yet his Bodhisattva roots of goodness were not yet fulfilled.
Furthermore, sixteen times ten thousand eons prior to the Bhadrakalpa, there was an eon named Aśoka and a world named Vimalā.
Within this light, five hundred Buddhas appeared. I was then the daughter of an elder named Radiant Wisdom-Light;
that original night goddess was born in the city of King Wondrous Banner and served as a night goddess there.
She came again, shaking my residence, emitting light and manifesting signs, and praised all the merits of the Tathāgata Sublime Eye, acting as her own guide.

I was led to the presence of the Buddha; as soon as I beheld the Buddha, I attained a samādhi called "The Radiant Wheel of Wisdom that Arises from Seeing Buddhas and Taming Sentient Beings across the Three Times.

By the power of attaining this samādhi, I gained the recollection of as many eons as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, and I heard [the Dharma] in the presence of all the Buddhas who appeared during those eons.

Having heard the sublime Dharma, by virtue of hearing that sublime Dharma, one immediately attains this liberation of the light of the Dharma that destroys the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings.
Having attained this liberation, one immediately sees one’s own body pervading worlds as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields.
This clarifies how long it has been since the initial arousal of the bodhicitta: eighty-one Mount Sumerus have already passed.
Passing through kalpas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, and further through ten thousand kalpas— among which were kalpas as numerous as the atoms in one Mount Sumeru—
this was the period of past resolve. Then, for kalpas as numerous as the atoms in eighty Mount Sumerus, plus another ten thousand kalpas,
he cultivated various roots of goodness in the presence of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and only then did he attain the samādhi named "Beholding the Buddhas and Taming Sentient Beings."
Furthermore, through the wheel of light of worldly wisdom, by recollecting the kalpas of the past, he beheld Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within Mount Sumeru;

it was by hearing the sublime Dharma practiced by those Buddhas that he attained this liberation door of the light of the Dharma which shatters the darkness of ignorance in all sentient beings, attaining it precisely during these recollections of the kalpas.

This Dharma-gate of the Light of the Dharma for Dispelling the Darkness of Ignorance of All Sentient Beings reveals that the time since this realization was attained spans eighty-two *sumeru*-mountain-microdust numbers of *kalpas*, plus ten thousand additional *kalpas*. Throughout all those *kalpas*,
she has constantly practiced the bodhisattva path in a female body, clearly cultivating a profound and deep heart of great compassion over such vast and long-lasting eons.

By means of the final recollection, the kalpas of the three periods of time are encompassed within a single thought-moment, such that all are universally pervaded within that one thought-moment; this constitutes many kalpas within a single thought-moment.

Universally pervading the ten directions from the perspective of wisdom, it is as if first taking up worlds as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field of the past, and within each of those worlds, one makes offerings to and serves every Buddha; next, one takes up a hundred [worlds].
Throughout kalpas numbering as many atoms as there are in a buddha-field, and further through thousands, hundreds of thousands, and unspeakably many buddha-fields of atoms,
they go everywhere to serve and attend upon the Buddhas, receiving and upholding all the Dharma-gates they teach;
gradually increasing and expanding, they pervade the dharma-realm of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas and bringing peace and happiness to all beings.
Sentient beings, this is the first stage; beginning with one hundred, it extends throughout all dharma-realms and inexhaustible Buddha-fields in the ten directions.

This differs from the three vehicles, which speak only of "one hundred Buddhas" rather than "the atoms of one hundred Buddha-fields" or "unspeakably many Buddha-field atoms of worlds," and so forth. The remaining details are fully clarified in the sutra as intended.

To manifest worldly conduct with profound and deep compassion, without seeking a mind for transcendence even throughout the exhaustion of kalpas—this is the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Here, the *kalyāṇamitra* takes the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as primary, with the other nine perfections as its companions.

This clarifies the gate of entering the secular world while sharing in its entanglements to nurture great compassion, thereby bringing the perfection of giving to full completion. May [beings] attain it.

Because she perfected the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), she was frequently reborn without being separated from a female body, signifying that she lacked the marks of transcending the world;
she constantly dwelt among the worldly masses. Within these ten stages, this generally clarifies the gate of dwelling in the world to nurture great compassion.

These ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) lack the appearance of renunciants; they are all goddesses who speak of the causal roots from which her original aspiration for Bodhi arose over many lifetimes.

The time of conceiving the mind [of enlightenment] is also represented by a female body, signifying that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the practice of nurturing great compassion as one enters the realm of sentient beings.
This is because a woman represents compassion, which can nurture children and grandchildren without weariness;
it is used to clarify that the Bodhisattva nurtures sentient beings. Second, regarding the progression of virtue, from "As for all... [and so forth].
From the point where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes his leave and departs, there are fifteen and a half lines of prose and ten lines of verse;
within this, five topical gates are established: first, the advancement through the stages of virtue;
second, the indication of the location where the spiritual friend resides, stating: "In this Jambudvīpa, within the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha."
There is a night goddess named Samantabhadra-vimalaprabhā; Sudhana spoke verses to praise the virtues of the night goddess Vāsantī.
Having finished speaking these verses, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the night goddess and took his leave to depart.
This night goddess Samantabhadra-vimalaprabhā was King Vāsantī in a past kalpa.
Furthermore, during that time, the Teacher who awakened him at night acted as his guide and instructor for eighty-two *sumeru*-dust-particle numbers of kalpas,
plus another ten thousand kalpas, as previously described; this does not refer to the South,
but specifically to the Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha, which signifies the stage of cultivation.
Because the compassion that dwells within birth and death does not depart from the essence of bodhi, there exists separately the practice of worldly compassion;
thus, Jambudvīpa and the kingdom of Magadha being within the site of worldly bodhi indicates that this world is contained within the site of bodhi,
clarifying that the practice of worldly compassion is internal to the bodhicitta.
The practices one performs are not separate from [the ultimate]; the manifestation of the conduct of great loving-kindness and great compassion is one with the essence of awakening.
Clarifying that the fruit acts as the cause, cause and effect are one. As Sudhana, in his praise of the Night Goddess, says in verse:
"Having remained for many kalpas in the evil realms, I have finally been able to see and hear the Dharma; I should receive it with joy, for it extinguishes affliction."
Because of affliction, it is clarified that the essential practice of great compassion requires dwelling in the ocean of suffering within birth and death for many kalpas without weariness;

only by practicing the path of compassion can its accomplishment be attained. Thus, it is clarified that the practice of the supramundane path manifests immediate results in a single thought-moment, and the practice of great compassion is not limited by the number of kalpas. The rest is as detailed in the text.

The two matters—the many eons from the perspective of the conventional and the single thought-moment from the perspective of the ultimate—are harmonized and integrated within the self-nature without obstruction;
thus, within a single thought-moment there are many eons, and within many eons there is a single thought-moment, because the essences of the ultimate and the conventional do not obstruct one another.
The second night goddess, Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā, presides over the Vimalā Bhūmi.

[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana thoroughly understood the Bodhisattva-piṭaka produced by the initial aspiration for enlightenment of that night goddess Vaśaṃvartī, the Bodhisattva vows she had issued, the Bodhisattva perfections she had purified, and the Bodhi... [she had entered].
Having cultivated the bodhisattva practices on all stages, traversing the path of renunciation, possessing the ocean of light of omniscience,

with a mind that universally rescues sentient beings and clouds of great compassion that pervade everywhere, he was able to constantly give rise to the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra throughout all buddha-fields until the end of the future;
gradually traveling on, he arrived at the place of the night goddess Samantaśrī-vimalaprabhā and prostrated at her feet.
Circumambulating her countless times, he joined his palms before her and spoke these words:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva stages, how a bodhisattva gives birth to the bodhisattva stages, or how a bodhisattva accomplishes the bodhisattva stages. The night goddess replied, "Excellent!"

"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have already been able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and now you further inquire about the cultivation, emergence, and accomplishment of the bodhisattva stages.
Son of good family, there are ten dharmas through which a bodhisattva accomplishes the fulfillment of the bodhisattva practice. What are these ten? First, attaining pure..."
First, to constantly perceive all Buddhas; second, to attain the pure eye that constantly contemplates the marks and signs that adorn all Buddhas;

third, to know the ocean of immeasurable and boundless merits of all Tathāgatas; fourth, to know the ocean of the light of the Dharma of immeasurable Buddhas, which is equal to the Dharma-realm; fifth, to know each and every hair-pore of all Tathāgatas.
Sixth, they emit oceans of great light as numerous as all sentient beings, benefiting all infinite beings; seventh,
they see from every single pore of all Tathāgatas the emergence of oceans of flaming light rays of every precious color,
which in every thought-moment manifest oceans of all Buddhas' transformations, filling the Dharma-realm and reaching its ultimate limit.

Eighth, attaining the Buddha’s voice that turns the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time through an ocean of vocal sounds identical to those of all sentient beings; ninth, knowing the infinite ocean of names of all Buddhas;
tenth, knowing the inconceivable and sovereign power of all Buddhas to discipline and transform sentient beings. Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to fulfill all the practices of a bodhisattva.
Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called "The Joyful Wandering in Tranquil Meditative Concentration, Universally Seeing All Buddhas of the Three Times.
Through it, I see those Buddhas, their pure lands, their places of enlightenment, their assemblies, their supernatural powers, their names, and their preaching of the Dharma.
They clearly perceive all the various differences in lifespan, speech, and physical marks, yet remain free from attachment.
Why is this? Because they know that the Tathāgatas do not pass away into eternal extinction; they do not come, for their essential nature is unborn;
they are not subject to birth, for the Dharma-body is equal; they do not perish, for they possess no characteristic of arising; and they do not truly abide, for they are like illusory phenomena.
Because it does not falsely benefit sentient beings; because it does not involve migrating through or transcending birth and death; because its nature is not destroyed, being eternal and unchanging;
because it is a single mark, entirely free from verbal expression; and because it is signless, as the nature of marks is fundamentally empty.
Son of good family, when I thus realized all Tathāgatas, I attained the Bodhisattva’s joy of tranquil meditative concentration and the liberation of universal wandering.
With clear understanding and mastery of the gates of liberation, he increases his contemplation and investigation, becoming firm and adorned with stability.
He does not give rise to any false conceptualizations or discriminations, but with great compassion protects all sentient beings.
With a single, unmoving mind, he cultivates the first dhyāna, stilling all mental karma and gathering in all sentient beings through the power of his wisdom; his joy is exultant and courageous.
Cultivating the second dhyāna, they contemplate the inherent nature of all sentient beings as weary of birth and death;
cultivating the third dhyāna, they are able to extinguish all the suffering and feverish afflictions of all sentient beings;
cultivating the fourth dhyāna, they increase and perfect the vows for all-knowledge, give rise to the ocean of all samādhis, and enter the gates of the ocean of liberation of all bodhisattvas.
Sporting in all supernatural powers and accomplishing all transformations, they enter the Dharma-realm universally through pure wisdom.
Good son, when I cultivated this liberation, I brought sentient beings to maturity through various skillful means;
that is to say, for those lay beings who were heedless, I caused them to conceive thoughts of impurity, thoughts of loathsomeness, thoughts of weariness, and thoughts of oppression.

One should cultivate the perception of bondage, the perception of the rākṣasa, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of emptiness, the perception of non-arising, the perception of lack of autonomy, and the perception of old age, sickness, and death.
One should not give rise to attachment or delight in the five desires for oneself, nor should one encourage sentient beings to cling to sensual pleasures;
rather, one should dwell solely in the joy of the Dharma, departing from the household life to enter the homeless state. If there are sentient beings...

Dwelling in seclusion, I have stilled all evil sounds; during the quiet hours of the night, I have expounded the profound Dharma, provided conditions for its practice, opened the gate of renunciation, and shown the path of correctness.

I have acted as a light to remove the veil of darkness, extinguish fear, praise the vocation of renunciation, and extol the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and spiritual friends who possess every merit.

He also praised the practice of drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore, son of good family, when I was cultivating liberation, I caused all sentient beings not to give rise to unrighteous greed, not to produce perverse discrimination, and not to commit various sinful deeds; those already committed, I caused them all to cease, and those not yet arisen, I caused them to refrain from.
If they had not yet produced wholesome dharmas, had not practiced the *pāramitās*, or had not sought after all [virtues], I caused them to do so.
I cause those whose wisdom has not yet arisen, who have not yet generated great compassion, and who have not yet performed the karma of humans or devas, to be born [in such states];
and for those already so born, I cause them to increase. I provide such favorable conditions for the Path as to lead them even to the accomplishment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Good son, I have attained only this Bodhisattva liberation door of "Peaceful Meditation and Joyful Universal Striding. As for...
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, being fully endowed with all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, thoroughly comprehend the entire boundless Dharma-realm;
they are constantly able to increase all roots of goodness, perceive the power of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, abide in the realm of all Tathāgatas,
and dwell perpetually within birth and death with minds free from hindrance, swiftly fulfilling all [aspirations].
Their wisdom-vow enables them to travel to all worlds, to behold all Buddhas,
to universally hear and receive all Buddha-dharmas, to shatter the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings,
and to produce the light of all-encompassing wisdom within the great night of birth and death; how could I possibly know or describe their merit?
"Virtuous son, not far from here, on the right side of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there is a night goddess named Joyful Eyes Observing Sentient Beings.
Go to her and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the night goddess Universal Virtue Pure Light, wishing to reiterate the meaning of this liberation for the sake of Sudhana, [spoke as follows].
The youth spoke in verse:
“If one possesses a mind of faith and understanding, One sees all the Buddhas of the three times.
That person’s eyes are pure, and they can enter the ocean of all Buddhas. Behold the bodies of the Buddhas, Adorned with pure marks.”
With the power of spiritual penetration in a single thought, you pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Tathāgata Vairocana attained perfect enlightenment at the site of awakening; throughout all realms of reality, he turns the pure wheel of Dharma.
The Tathāgata knows the nature of phenomena—tranquil, extinguished, and without duality—his body adorned with the marks of purity.
Universally manifesting throughout all worlds, the Buddha’s body is inconceivable; it completely fills the entire Dharma-realm.
Every single land is universally seen, and there is nothing that is not seen.
The Buddha’s body is eternally radiant, equal in number to the atoms within all lands, possessing various pure colors, pervading the Dharma-realm in every thought-moment.
From a single pore of the Tathāgata, He emits inconceivable light, Universally illuminating all living beings And causing their afflictions to be extinguished.

From a single pore of the Tathāgata, He produces inexhaustible emanations That pervade the entire Dharma-realm, Eliminating the suffering of sentient beings. The Buddha utters a single wondrous sound;
Causing all beings to understand according to their kind, He rains down the vast and great Dharma everywhere, Causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
In the past, when the Buddha cultivated various practices, He already took me under his care; Therefore, I am able to see the Tathāgata.
I see universally all lands, And all Buddhas appearing in the world, Their number equaling that of all sentient beings.
The various realms of liberation are not something I can know;
that all bodhisattvas enter into a single pore of the Buddha—such wondrous liberation is not something I can know.
Nearby there is a night goddess named Joyful Eyes Who Observes; you should go to her.
Question: When that Bodhisattva was traveling,
the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

[Treatise] First, the Dharma-gate of Correct Entry into the Appropriate Stage, from the passage beginning "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I have only attained this Bodhisattva liberation-door of the Universal Gait of the Joy of Tranquil Samādhi.
Within this section, five gates are established: 1) contemplating the advancement based on the instructions of the spiritual friend; 2) gradual progression; [and so forth].
Wandering on, he went to the abode of the night goddess Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā, where he paid his respects and requested her to explain various dharmas for the sake of Sudhana.

The fourth night goddess explained her own dharma-gate called "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation of Peaceful Meditation Joyfully Wandering Everywhere" and bestowed it upon Sudhana. The fifth night goddess correctly expounded this dharma.

This gate universally perceives all Buddhas of the three periods of time, their lands, their sites of enlightenment, and their assemblies, as well as their protection and salvation of all sentient beings.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning according to the text: the name of this dharma-gate is "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation Gate of the Joy of Tranquil Meditative Concentration and Universal Striding.
This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), taking the Dharma-body as ethical discipline.

The essence is itself the nature of all objective realms because it is inherently meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); thus, the meditative concentration of the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is itself wisdom that is universally pervasive.
Because this wisdom is universally pervasive, one wanders everywhere. Constantly abiding in birth and death, one practices great compassion to nurture one's own being;
within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one possesses the conduct of a bodhisattva, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
This is called the Bodhisattva liberation gate of "The Joyful Universal Striding in Tranquil Samādhi.
Within the clarity of birth and death, one is also able to fully possess the joy of the Dharma of Bodhi; furthermore, one can universally practice the path of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, this illumination of the Bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion within the Bodhimanda of one's own mind is named "Universal Virtue" (Samantaguṇa).
As for the Night-Spirit Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*): because her wisdom and compassion pervade everywhere to illuminate the long night of sentient beings, she is named "Pure Light.

Her compassionate nurturing of the mundane world is termed "Virtue" (*guṇa*), while her wisdom—which does not function through self-aggrandizement but operates universally—is termed "Spirit" (*devī*).
Thus, through this dhyāna, one takes bodhi as the essence and practices the unimpeded Dharma-realm of great tranquility.
Because the great compassionate mind is pervasive in both its quiescence and its activity, the names of the four dhyānas are established according to its functional efficacy. As the Sūtra says:

"To distinguish, comprehend, accomplish, increase, contemplate, investigate, and firmly adorn [the mind], so that no deluded thoughts or discriminations arise, and with great compassion to rescue and protect all sentient beings, one practices with a single unmoving mind."
The practitioner of dhyāna, through the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya, correctly contemplates and brings all sentient beings across; this is not called delusive thought.

Because they do not contemplate unwholesome dharmas, and because all objects of discernment and focus within the principle of the Dharma-nature benefit living beings by relying upon wisdom, they establish the gateway of great compassion. Since they are untainted by worldly habits, it is not called [delusive thought].
Regarding "stopping all mental karma" and "the power of wisdom that gathers all sentient beings with courageous vigor and a joyful heart":
stopping all mental karma refers to a partial compassion that is not universal;
"a joyful heart" refers to the practice of the Bodhisattva of this second stage through the *dharmatā* of *bodhi*.
Because it is the joy of the Dharma that gathers and transforms all sentient beings through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it is called the Second Dhyāna.
Those who cultivate the Third Dhyāna contemplate that the self-nature of all sentient beings is free from birth and death;
they clearly perceive that all sentient beings share the same *bodhi*-nature and are by their very essence liberated, taking this as the substance of dhyāna, and do not [rely on external objects].
Because one perceives that only one’s own body possesses the essence of dhyāna, yet all sentient beings collectively possess the liberation of the essence of dhyāna, one cultivates the third dhyāna.
As the Sūtra says: "All sentient beings naturally weary of and seek to leave birth and death by cultivating the third dhyāna.
This "naturally wearying of and seeking to leave birth and death" is an error of the translator; it should read: "all sentient beings [possess this capacity]."

Because their nature is inherently free from birth and death, they cultivate the third dhyāna to completely extinguish all the suffering and feverish afflictions of sentient beings, and they cultivate the fourth dhyāna.
These bodhisattvas of the Single Vehicle, from the moment they first resolve their minds, ride upon the fundamental wisdom-vehicle of the Tathāgata’s bodhicitta;
they practice the conduct of great compassion within the ocean of birth and death, observing and penetrating the nature of sentient beings.
The fundamental source and ultimate depth are one with the Tathāgata’s essence and function of bodhi,
an ocean of wisdom whose skillful means constantly employ the sun of dharma-realm wisdom to dispel the darkness of ignorance for all sentient beings during the night of non-attainment.
This differs from the three vehicles of the past, which separately seek the fruit of personal purity and bliss, yet have never truly [attained it].
Because one attains the ultimate fruit of all happiness, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is preached; it brings together the three vehicles into one, for all return to this Dharma.
Hereafter, all practices for benefiting sentient beings are fully elucidated according to the sūtra.
This is the upholding of the supreme ten wholesome precepts, taking the essence of Bodhi as the substance of the precepts, and dwelling within the site of Bodhi.
The Night Deity (Rātridevatā) manifested the precept-body by taking the bodhicitta and the perfection of great compassion as its essence;
the Ten Dedications took the ship’s captain as the precept-body; the Ten Practices took the celestial youth Śilpabhijña as the precept-body;
and within the Ten Abodes, the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha contemplated that the self-nature of the twelve links of dependent origination is inherently pure.
Regarding the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*): within this second stage (*bhūmi*), one takes the Night Goddess Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā in the Bodhimanda as the essence of the precepts.
This clarifies that within awakening, wisdom abides in the world by taking the cultivation of the gate of compassion as the essence of the precepts;
this is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who, within the second stage, Vimalā, [establishes] the wave of the precepts.

Taking the *pāramitās* as its essence and the other nine [perfections] as its companions, it remedies the obstacle to exercising mastery while dwelling within the ocean of birth and death through the practice of compassion;
thus, it clarifies the harmonious integration of the two states of non-mastery—bodhi and saṃsāra—thereby causing one to attain mastery.
Within this stage, one contemplates the three realms through the essence of bodhi.
The nature of arising and ceasing is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) contemplation. Second, regarding the progression through the advancement of virtues:
from the passage beginning with "As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... down to "having taken their leave and departed," there are twenty-four lines of prose and verse.
Within this, five gates are established: first, advancing Sudhana by first extolling his virtues; second, indicating the [virtues]; [and so forth].

The section on Knowledge states: Not far from here, to the right of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there is a night goddess named Priyadarśanā-sattva-avalokana-samanta-śubha-vimala-prabhā. She again spoke verses to Sudhana.
Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the goddess Samanta-śubha-vimala-prabhā. He took his leave and departed. The commentary says: "Not far from here..."
"Not far" clarifies that with bodhi as the second [stage], the third perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is situated within the Bodhimaṇḍa;
because this practice of patience likewise takes bodhi as its object, it is said to be "not far from here. Regarding "to the right of the Bodhimaṇḍa":
the left represents the position of wisdom (*prajñā*), while the right represents the position of compassion (*karuṇā*). This clarifies [the meaning].

One practices patience through the arousal of bodhicitta; for without patience there is no compassion. This clarifies that because one possesses patience, one is able to practice loving-kindness and compassion.

There is a night goddess named *Priyanayanā-sattvāvalokanī*, whose name signifies "loving-kindness within patience" (*priya-nayanā*) and "observing sentient beings without abandoning them" (*sattvāvalokanī*). Furthermore, she observes their faculties and gathers them [in the Dharma].

The deity named "Observer of Sentient Beings" (Sattvāvalokana-rātri-devaputra), whose former station was that of taking bodhicitta as the essence of his precepts, has purified all desire for existence within the three realms.
He has stilled the distracted mind of the lower realm and desires the pure mind that delights in the meditative bliss of the two upper realms.
In this third stage, the Radiant Ground (Prabhākari-bhūmi), by practicing the eight dhyānas, he is able to become identical with those meditations.

The nature of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) that is still subject to defilement is similar to that of the desire realm; the nature that is free from such defilement is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

It is named "Night" because its wisdom accords with reality (*yathābhūta*), and it is termed "Divine" (*deva*) because it possesses sovereign power in teaching and transforming sentient beings within the three realms.
Furthermore, it is clarified that at this stage, one individually subdues the habitual tendencies of desire within each of the three realms through wisdom.
Causing them to attain purity, one observes the common and distinct characteristics within the three realms; this is named the night goddess *Sattvāvalokanī*.
In the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*), one is born into the family of all Buddhas. In the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), one practices worldly arts and skills.

In the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*), the meditative concentrations of the three gates of liberation and the extinction of suffering manifest, and one attains mastery over the supernormal power of tranquil activity, pervading the ten directions to gather and transform sentient beings.
Having been born here, one attains mastery over both the supramundane and the mundane; therefore, from the seventh stage onward, one enters into mastery over the mundane.
As there is such a scope of influence within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), so it is with the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) and the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).

Those who attain liberation within the intermediate stage enter the world and, upon reaching the seventh stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), advance to the level of the sages;

they then behold Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva of Right Course. Upon returning to the world during the ninth and tenth stages of dedication, their wisdom-penetrations become divine, sustaining the realm of sentient beings through the nine stages (*bhūmi*). The maiden Gopā was the wife of the Tathāgata when he was formerly a prince; she represents the fulfillment of the dharma-joy of compassion through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

yet, one must still rely upon the recollection of original vows and the empowerment of the Buddha to achieve clear realization. At the ninth and tenth stages, one begins to study the ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) of a Buddha.

[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, revering the instructions of the spiritual friend and acting upon the words of the spiritual friend, formed this thought:
"A spiritual friend is difficult to see and difficult to encounter; seeing a spiritual friend causes the mind to become undistracted;
seeing a spiritual friend shatters the mountains of obstacles; seeing a spiritual friend enters the ocean of great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings. Seeing the spiritual friend...
Having gained knowledge, he attained the light of wisdom that universally illumines the dharma-realm; seeing spiritual friends, he was able to practice the path to all-knowledge;
seeing spiritual friends, he was able to behold everywhere the oceans of Buddhas in the ten directions;

seeing spiritual friends, he attained the vision of all Buddhas turning the wheel of Dharma, which he remembered without forgetting. Having formed this thought, he resolved to go to the presence of Priyadarśana.

The night goddess Praśāntarutasarvasattvasaṃtoṣaṇī observed the youth Sudhana and empowered him so that he might know how to approach spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to give rise to all roots of goodness and bring them to growth and maturity; that is to say,

she caused him to know that approaching spiritual friends enables one to cultivate the requisites for awakening, and she caused him to know that approaching spiritual friends enables one to arouse a courageous mind.
It makes known that approaching spiritual friends can perform indestructible deeds; it makes known that approaching spiritual friends can attain invincible power;
it makes known that approaching spiritual friends can enter boundless regions;
it makes known that approaching spiritual friends can practice for a long duration; it makes known that approaching spiritual friends can accomplish boundless activities.
Approaching spiritual friends enables one to practice immeasurable paths; it should be known that approaching spiritual friends enables one to swiftly attain power and travel to all lands;
it should be known that approaching spiritual friends enables one to reach everywhere throughout the ten directions without leaving one's original place.
At that time, the youth Sudhana suddenly gave rise to this thought: "By approaching spiritual friends, one is able to be courageous and fierce."
By associating with spiritual friends, one can diligently cultivate the path to omniscience; by associating with spiritual friends, one can swiftly give birth to the ocean of great vows;
by associating with spiritual friends, one can endure boundless suffering for all sentient beings throughout all future eons;
and by associating with spiritual friends, one can don the armor of great diligence to preach the Dharma within a single atom.
Their voice pervades the Dharma-realm; by attending upon spiritual friends, they are able to swiftly travel to all oceans of directions;
by attending upon spiritual friends, they cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout all future eons within a single pore-path;
by attending upon spiritual friends, they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva in every thought-moment, ultimately abiding securely on the ground of omniscience.
By associating with spiritual friends, one is able to enter the paths of adornment through the sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
by associating with spiritual friends, one is able to constantly and universally enter the gates of all dharma-realms;

by associating with spiritual friends, while always taking the dharma-realm as one's object and never wavering from it, one is able to travel everywhere to the lands of the ten directions. At that time, Sudhana...
Having formed this thought, the youth went to where the night goddess Joyful Eyes Who Observes Sentient Beings was;
he saw that night goddess seated upon a lion throne within the lotus-treasury at the site of the Tathāgata’s assembly,
having entered the liberation of the Universal Banner of Great Power and Joy, from every single pore of her body emitting immeasurable kinds of transformations.
Bodies like clouds, according to what is appropriate for each, preach the Dharma with sublime voices, universally gathering all immeasurable sentient beings,
causing them all to rejoice and obtain benefit; that is to say, they emit immeasurable clouds of transformation bodies that fill all worlds throughout the ten directions,
preaching the various bodhisattva practices of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) in all matters.
Without attachment to any sentient beings, they universally bestow upon them an equal mind, free from contempt or arrogance.
They give away both internal and external things, being able to relinquish what is difficult to part with.

Producing clouds of immeasurable transformation bodies as numerous as all sentient beings, they fill the Dharma-realm and appear before all beings to preach the upholding of pure precepts without transgression, and the cultivation of all...
He was fully endowed with all ascetic practices; he had no dependence on any worldly things and no attachment to any sensory objects.
He spoke of the coming and going within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); he spoke of the prosperity and decline, and the suffering and pleasure, of gods and humans.
He spoke of all sensory objects as being impure; he spoke of all phenomena (*dharma*) as being impermanent; and he spoke of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as being suffering.
Being flavorless, they cause all worlds to abandon perversions and dwell within the realm of the Buddhas; upholding the precepts of the Tathāgata, they thus expound various modes of conduct.
The fragrance of these precepts universally perfumes all, causing all sentient beings to reach full maturity.
Furthermore, they manifest clouds of various bodies equal in number to all sentient beings, proclaiming the ability to endure all sufferings, namely, those such as being cut and dismembered.
Though beaten with whips and canes, reviled, or insulted, their minds remain serene, unmoved, and undisturbed; amidst all activities they are neither humble nor haughty;
toward all sentient beings they do not give rise to pride; they dwell securely in patient endurance regarding the nature of all phenomena.
They proclaim that the bodhicitta is inexhaustible; because the mind is inexhaustible, wisdom is also inexhaustible, universally severing the [afflictions] of all sentient beings.
By speaking of the afflictions, they cause sentient beings to feel weary of their base, ugly, and incomplete bodies;
by praising the pure, wondrous, and unsurpassed bodies of the Tathāgatas, they cause them to give rise to joyful aspiration. Through such skillful means, they bring sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, they manifest clouds of various bodies equal in number to the realms of sentient beings, according to the inclinations of the minds of those beings.
It speaks of the courageous diligence that cultivates the dharmas that assist the path to all-knowledge; the courageous diligence that subdues the enmity of Māra;
the courageous diligence that gives rise to the bodhicitta without wavering or retreating;
the courageous diligence that delivers all sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death; and the courageous diligence that eradicates all the hardships and calamities of the evil realms.
Vigorous effort that destroys the mountain of ignorance; courageous vigor that makes offerings to all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, without ever becoming weary;
courageous vigor that upholds the Dharma wheels of all Buddhas; courageous vigor that shatters and disperses all mountains of obstacles;
and courageous vigor that teaches and brings all sentient beings to maturity.
With such skillful means, he matures sentient beings by diligently purifying all Buddha-fields;
furthermore, he manifests various clouds of infinite bodies and, through diverse expedients, causes the hearts of all sentient beings to rejoice,

To preach the unsurpassed, pure Brahma-conduct is to explain that the desire realm is the domain of Māra, thereby instilling fear;
it is to manifest the lack of delight in worldly sensual pleasures and the dwelling in the joy of the Dharma;

it is to cause them, in successive order, to enter the various dhyānas and samādhis, to contemplate and observe so as to eliminate all existing afflictions, and furthermore, to expound upon these matters for them.

All the Bodhisattvas, through the sovereign play of the miraculous manifestations of the ocean of samādhis, cause all sentient beings to rejoice and find delight, freeing them from all sorrow and fear;
their minds are purified, their faculties are sharp and keen, and they cherish the Dharma, cultivating and increasing it.
Furthermore, they emit clouds of various bodies equal in number to the realms of sentient beings to travel throughout the ten directions and preach the Dharma for them.
Making offerings to the Buddhas and spiritual teachers and true friends of virtue within their lands;
upholding all the wheels of Dharma of the Buddhas with diligent and tireless effort; expounding upon and praising the ocean of all Tathāgatas;
observing the ocean of all dharma-gates; revealing the essential natures and characteristics of all dharmas; and elucidating all the samādhis.

Opening the gates of the profound, they exhaust the ocean of doubts of all sentient beings within the realm of wisdom; manifesting the vajra of wisdom, they shatter the mountains of views of all sentient beings;
ascending the sun-disk of wisdom, they destroy the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice and attain all-knowledge.
Furthermore, they emit clouds of various bodies equal in number to the realms of sentient beings, universally visiting all places.
Before sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma with various words and phrases according to what is appropriate for them;

he may speak of worldly supernatural powers and merit, or he may speak of how the three realms are all terrifying, causing them to cease performing worldly karmic actions, to leave the place of the three realms, and to emerge from the dense forest of existence; or he may praise the path of omniscience, causing them to transcend it.

Transcending the stages of the two vehicles, he may preach for them the non-abiding in saṃsāra and the non-abiding in nirvāṇa, so as to prevent them from becoming attached to the conditioned or the unconditioned;
or he may preach for them dwelling in celestial palaces up to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), so as to cause them to rejoice and resolve upon bodhicitta.
Through such skillful means, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them all ultimately to attain everything.
Furthermore, Wisdom produces clouds of bodies as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, universally approaching the presence of all sentient beings.
In every thought-moment, it manifests all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; in every thought-moment, it manifests pure great vows that fill the Dharma-realm;
in every thought-moment, it manifests the adornment and purification of all oceans of worlds; in every thought-moment, it manifests offerings.
They nourish the ocean of all Tathāgatas; in every thought-moment they manifest entry into the ocean of all dharma-gates;
in every thought-moment they manifest entry into oceans of worlds as numerous as the atoms within all world-oceans;

in every thought-moment they manifest the pure cultivation of the path to omniscience throughout all lands for as many eons as lie in the future; and in every thought-moment they manifest entry into the powers of the Tathāgata.
In every thought-moment, he demonstrates the ocean of skillful means for entering all three periods of time;

in every thought-moment, he demonstrates traveling to all lands and manifesting various supernatural transformations; in every thought-moment, he demonstrates all the practices and vows of the bodhisattvas, causing all sentient beings to abide in omniscience.
Such deeds are performed constantly without rest, and furthermore, they manifest as many as all...
With clouds of bodies corresponding to the mental activities of sentient beings, they go before all sentient beings and teach the methods for bodhisattvas to assemble all-knowledge and aid the path:

the power of non-retrogression, the power of uninterrupted continuity, and being unstained by the phenomena of birth and death.
The power of exertion to shatter all hosts of Māras; the power to remain far removed from all defilements of affliction;

the power to shake all Buddha-lands, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy; the power to shatter all... [the text continues].

The practice of *sajñāna* (true wisdom) consists of: teaching the wisdom of entering the ocean of all sentient beings' realms; teaching the wisdom of entering the ocean of all sentient beings' minds;

teaching the wisdom of delivering all sentient beings without ever missing the proper time; and teaching the utterance of the sounds of the entire dharma-realm.
The Wisdom of Teaching that, in every thought-moment, pervades the ocean of all dharma-realms; the Wisdom of Teaching that, in every thought-moment, knows the destruction of all oceans of worlds;
the Wisdom of Teaching that, in every thought-moment, knows the distinctions in the formation, abiding, and adornment of all oceans of worlds;

and the Wisdom of Teaching that, in every thought-moment, possesses the mastery to approach and make offerings to all Tathāgatas and listen to the turning of the Wheel of Dharma—thus it is manifested.
The perfection of wisdom causes all sentient beings to experience great joy, harmony, and gladness;

Just as it is taught that the various perfections of a bodhisattva mature sentient beings, so too does he proclaim all the diverse practices of bodhisattvas for the sake of benefiting them.

It fully reveals all practices, all essential natures, all principles, all purities,
and all associated matters as the perfection of the vow of conduct; it fully reveals the essential nature,

and all the associated matters of the perfection of skillful means; and he reveals all the requisites, all the essential natures,
all the accomplishments, all the purifications, and all the locations of the perfection of wisdom.
All that increases, all that penetrates deeply, all that is luminous, all that is revealed, all modes of reasoning, all associated matters, all forms of discernment,
all aspects of practice, all associated dharmas, all encompassed dharmas, the objects of knowledge,
the karma of what is known, the buddha-fields as they are known, the eons as they are known, and the worlds as they are known.
They know the appearance of the Buddhas; they know what is known by the Buddhas; they know the bodhisattvas; they know the minds of the bodhisattvas; they know the stages of the bodhisattvas;
they know the requisites of the bodhisattvas; they know the setting forth of the bodhisattvas; they know the dedications of the bodhisattvas; they know the great vows of the bodhisattvas;

The principles of the Dharma, such as these, reveal all realms corresponding to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in order to bring sentient beings to maturity.
