Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, combining the sutras and treatises,
Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Twenty-two of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*).
[Treatise] In the seventh assembly of Buddhas, the Night Goddess Sarvarthasiddhi-vikāśita-sarva-druma-kusuma-nirghoṣā presides over the Stage of Far-reaching Practice (*Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*).
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, having entered the bodhisattva liberation door of the Profound and Sovereign Wondrous Sound and having advanced in his practice,
went to the presence of the night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamkusumitābhijñā. He saw her body within a pavilion of various precious fragrant trees,
seated upon a lion throne composed of exquisite jewels, together with ten million night goddesses.
While circumambulating him, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet and, joining his palms before him, spoke these words:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor how one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
I pray that you will deign to show me compassion and explain this for me."

The Night Goddess said: "Good son, when the sun has set in this Sahā world and the lotuses have closed, and when all the people have finished their excursions and sightseeing, I see that among all those beings—whether on mountains, by waters, in cities, or in wildernesses—they all resolve to return to their respective dwellings; I then secretly [protect them]."
I protect them so that they may attain the right path and reach their destination, dwelling in peace and happiness night and day.

Good son, if there are sentient beings in the prime of youth who, intoxicated by their fine appearance, are arrogant, heedless, and self-indulgent in the five desires, I manifest for them the signs of old age, sickness, and death to inspire terror within them, causing them to abandon all evils. Furthermore, I praise various roots of goodness to lead them to cultivate them.
For those who are stingy, he praises generosity; for those who violate the precepts, he extols pure morality;
for those with anger, he teaches them to abide in great compassion; for those harboring malice, he causes them to practice patience; for those who are indolent, he inspires diligence;

for those whose minds are distracted, he leads them to cultivate meditative concentration; for those dwelling in wrong wisdom, he causes them to study Prajñā; and for those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle...

May those who dwell in the Great Vehicle yet are attached to the various realms of existence within the triple world be established in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

May those sentient beings whose merit and wisdom are meager, who are oppressed by their afflictions and karma, and who encounter many obstacles, be established in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
May those sentient beings whose minds are obscure and who lack wisdom [be established in the perfection of wisdom].
"O son of good family who abides in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom, I have already accomplished the Bodhisattva liberation door called 'The Radiance of Vast Great Joy Arising.
" Sudhana said, "O Noble One, what is the scope of this liberation door?
The night goddess replied, "Son of good family, one who enters this liberation is able to know the Tathāgata’s skillful means for universally gathering in all sentient beings."
What is the wisdom that universally encompasses all? Good son, it is because all the various pleasures experienced by all sentient beings are due to the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue;
because they accord with the Tathāgata’s teaching; because they practice according to the Tathāgata’s words; because they study the Tathāgata’s conduct;
because they obtain the power of the Tathāgata’s protection; because they cultivate the path sealed by the Tathāgata; and because they plant the roots of goodness practiced by the Tathāgata.

Therefore, it is because of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, because of the illumination of the sun-like light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and because of the encompassing power of the Tathāgata’s nature-purity karma. How is this known?
Son of good family, when I entered this liberation of the "Light of the Vast Joy of Arising" and recollected the past of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana...
He clearly beheld the entire ocean of bodhisattva practices cultivated in the past. Noble son, when the World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva,
he saw all sentient beings clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," dwelling in the dark chamber of ignorance, entering the dense forest of various views,
bound by craving and attachment, destroyed by anger, disordered by folly, entangled by stinginess and jealousy, [and wandering] in birth and death.
Having seen that those in saṃsāra suffer from poverty and hardship and fail to encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he gives rise to great compassion to benefit sentient beings.
That is to say, he arouses the aspiration to provide all wonderful jewels and requisites to gather in sentient beings;
he vows that all sentient beings shall be fully endowed with the necessities of life and lack nothing in their hearts. In this one...
In all affairs, one should be free from a mind of attachment; toward all objects of experience, one should have no mind of greedy defilement;
toward all possessions, one should have no mind of stinginess; toward all karmic rewards, one should have no mind of expectation; toward all glory and excellence, one should have no mind of envy;
toward all causes and conditions, one should have no mind of delusion; and one should give rise to a mind that contemplates the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
He gives rise to the mind that seeks to rescue and protect all sentient beings; he gives rise to the mind that enters deeply into the whirlpools of all dharmas;

he gives rise to the mind that abides in great equanimity and loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; he gives rise to the mind that practices skillful means and great compassion toward all sentient beings;
he gives rise to the mind that acts as a great Dharma-canopy to universally cover all sentient beings; he gives rise to [the mind] that shatters [ignorance] with the vajra-pestle of great wisdom.
The arising of the mind that shatters the mountain of afflictive obstructions for all sentient beings; the arising of the mind that causes all sentient beings to increase in joy and happiness;

the arising of the mind that vows for all sentient beings to attain ultimate peace and bliss; the arising of the mind that rains down all manner of wealth and treasures according to the desires of sentient beings;
and the arising of the mind that brings all sentient beings to maturity through impartial skillful means. May [all sentient beings]...
Having given rise to a mind of contentment regarding the noble riches and a resolve that all sentient beings may ultimately attain the fruit of the ten powers of wisdom,
and having thus generated such a mind, he attained the power of a bodhisattva and manifested great spiritual transformations throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
Before all sentient beings, he rained down all manner of necessities for life, fulfilling their every desire.
Their intent is to cause all beings to rejoice, so that they feel no regret, no stinginess, and remain uninterrupted and unceasing; by these skillful means,
they universally gather in and transform sentient beings, bringing them all to maturity so that they may emerge from the hardships of birth and death, without seeking any reward,
and purifying the jewel-like minds of all sentient beings so that the single root of goodness common to all Buddhas may arise and increase.
The Bodhisattva Ocean of the Merit of All-Knowledge thus matures all sentient beings in every thought-moment,
purifies all Buddha-lands in every thought-moment, universally enters all dharma-realms in every thought-moment, pervades the entire realm of empty space in every thought-moment,
universally enters all three periods of time in every thought-moment, and accomplishes the taming of all multitudes in every thought-moment.
They give birth to wisdom that constantly turns the wheel of the Dharma in every thought-moment; they constantly benefit sentient beings through the path of omniscience in every thought-moment;

they universally manifest the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment before all various classes of beings throughout all worlds until the end of the kalpas in every thought-moment; and they universally [manifest] throughout all worlds in every...
Throughout all kalpas while practicing the bodhisattva path, they do not give rise to dualistic conceptions regarding:
the universal entry into all vast oceans of world-systems; the various boundaries within all types of world-systems; the various adornments of world-systems;
the various essential natures of world-systems; the various shapes of world-systems; and the various distributions of world-systems.
In some worlds, there is defilement combined with purity; in some worlds, there is purity combined with defilement;
in some worlds, there is exclusively impurity; and in some worlds, there is exclusively purity. Some are small and some are large; some are coarse and some are subtle;
some are upright and some are tilted; some are inverted and some are face-up. Within all such worlds, moment by moment...
Practicing all the bodhisattva deeds, entering the bodhisattva stage, manifesting the power of a bodhisattva,
and also manifesting the bodies of all Buddhas of the three periods of time so that all sentient beings may universally perceive and know them according to their own minds— O son of good family,
when the Tathāgata Vairocana was thus practicing the bodhisattva deeds in past ages, he saw that sentient beings were not cultivating merit and lacked...
Possessing wisdom, yet obscured by the cataracts of ignorance regarding self and what belongs to self, one enters into improper reflection and various false views;

failing to recognize cause and effect, one follows karma that accords with afflictions and falls into the deep pits of the perilous cycle of birth and death, fully experiencing all manner of immeasurable sufferings.
Arising a heart of great compassion, one fully cultivates all the *pāramitās* for the sake of sentient beings.
They extol and praise firm roots of goodness to cause them to dwell securely, far removed from the suffering of poverty within birth and death;
they diligently cultivate the dharmas that aid the path of merit and wisdom; they explain for them various gateways of cause and effect; they explain that karmic retribution is never inconsistent;
they explain the points of realization regarding the Dharma; and they explain the inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings.
He taught that one should ensure the continuity of all lands where beings are born, protect all seeds of the Buddhas,
and cause all teachings of the Buddhas to be preserved while abandoning all evils. Furthermore,
he praised the dharmas that assist the path toward omniscience so that all sentient beings might give rise to joy in their hearts, practice the gift of Dharma, and universally gather in all beings.
It initiates the conduct of omniscience, causes the great bodhisattvas to practice the path of the perfections,
causes the ocean of all roots of goodness for attaining omniscience to increase, causes all noble riches to be fulfilled,
causes them to enter the gate of the Buddha’s mastery, causes them to grasp immeasurable skillful means, and causes them to behold reality as it is.
The Youth Sudhana, who was empowered by majesty to abide in the wisdom of a bodhisattva, said:
"Noble One, how long has it been since you first resolved your mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? The Night Goddess replied:

"Son of Good Family, this matter is difficult to believe, difficult to know, difficult to understand, difficult to enter, and difficult to explain; it is beyond all worldly beings as well as those of the two vehicles."
It cannot be known, except by those protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas, embraced by virtuous friends, who have gathered supreme merit,
whose aspiration is pure, who possess no inferior mind, no defiled mind, and no deceitful mind, whose minds have attained the light of wisdom that shines universally,
who have resolved to bring universal benefit to all sentient beings, and for whom all afflictions and all Māras have no power.
It is able to destroy [deluded] thoughts; it necessarily accomplishes the mind of omniscience; its mind takes no pleasure in any of the joys of birth and death;
it is able to seek the wondrous bliss of all Buddhas; it is able to extinguish the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings;
it is able to cultivate the ocean of all Buddha-merits; it is able to contemplate the true nature of all phenomena; and it is able to possess all pure faith and understanding.
One who has transcended the torrential flood of all birth and death; who is able to enter the ocean of wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
who is able to reach with certainty the unsurpassed city of Dharma; who is able to courageously enter the realm of the Tathāgatas;

who is able to swiftly proceed to the stages of the Buddhas; who is able to immediately accomplish all powers of wisdom; and who has attained ultimate perfection in the Ten Powers—such a person, regarding...
This is able to sustain, to enter, and to comprehend. Why is this? Because this is the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which even all bodhisattvas cannot know, let alone other sentient beings.
Nevertheless, I now, by the Buddha's majestic power, desire to cause those sentient beings who are ready for conversion to become compliant and to quickly purify their minds;
I desire to cause the minds of those sentient beings who cultivate roots of goodness to attain peace.

"O Sovereign, I shall explain to you according to your questions. Then, the night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamantabhadranirghoṣā, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, contemplated the realm of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and spoke in verse:

O Son of the Buddha, regarding that which you have asked—the profound realm of the Buddhas—though one were to speak of it for eons as numerous as the atoms of inconceivable lands, it could not be exhausted.
Such sentient beings as these, who are not shrouded by greed, hatred, delusion, pride, or confusion, are able to know the wondrous Dharma of the Buddha; they do not abide in stinginess or envy.

Those whose minds are turbid with flattery and deception, And who are shrouded by afflictions and karma— They cannot know the Buddha’s realm, which does not cling To the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, nor to the conception of a self.
Only those who have overturned views and perceptions can know what the Buddha has awakened to: The Buddha’s realm is tranquil, Pure by nature, and free from conceptual discrimination.
Those who are not attached to any state of existence can know this nature of phenomena. Born into the family of the Buddhas, they are protected by the Buddhas;
as upholders of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas, they are the domain of the eye of wisdom.
They draw near to spiritual friends, delight in pure and white dharmas, and diligently seek the powers of all Buddhas.
Hearing this Dharma with joy, their minds are pure and free from discrimination;
like the great void, the lamp of wisdom destroys all darkness—this is their sphere of activity.
With a mind of great compassion that universally covers all worlds, they regard all things as equal—this is their sphere of activity.
With a joyful mind free from attachment, they are able to relinquish everything; giving impartially to all sentient beings is their sphere of activity.

With a pure mind free from all evils, ultimately without regret, and practicing in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings—this is their sphere of activity. They thoroughly understand the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
As well as all seeds of karma, their minds are without agitation or confusion; this is their domain.
With courageous and diligent application, they abide with a non-regressing mind; diligently cultivating all-knowledge, this is their domain.
With a mind tranquil, abiding in samādhi, Ultimately cool and free from the fever of affliction,
Having cultivated the causes for the ocean of all-knowledge,
This liberated one has realized the true nature of all things And deeply entered the gateways of the boundless realm of phenomena.
Universally delivering all living beings without exception— this is the liberation of those who are lamps of wisdom,
who thoroughly understand the true nature of sentient beings. Unattached to the ocean of all existences,
appearing everywhere like reflections within the water of the mind— this is the liberation of those who follow the right path.
Born from the seeds of skillful means and vows of all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
Exerting diligent practice throughout all kalpas and lands— This is the liberation of Samantabhadra:
Universally entering the gates of the entire Dharma-realm, He beholds all the oceans of lands in the ten directions.
I also see within them the formation and destruction of kalpas, yet my mind remains ultimately free from discrimination.
Within every single atom of the entire dharma-realm, I see the Tathāgatas sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment,
realizing bodhi and transforming all beings— this is the liberation of the unimpeded eye.
Throughout oceans of immeasurable great kalpas, you have attended upon and made offerings to spiritual friends;
for the sake of benefiting all living beings, you sought the True Dharma, and having heard it, you have remembered it without any loss.
The vast realm of Vairocana is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Relying on the Buddha’s power, I shall speak for you, so that your profound mind may become even more pure.

Good son, in the distant past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, there was an ocean of worlds named Universal Radiance of True Gold Mani Mountains. Within that ocean of worlds, a Buddha appeared named Universal Illumination.
"O son of noble family, King of Tranquil Majesty of the Wisdom Mountain of the Dharma Realm, when that Buddha was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he purified that ocean of world-systems.
Within that ocean of world-systems, there are world-system seeds as numerous as the atoms of those worlds;
within each world-system seed, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms of those worlds, and in every single world, there is likewise [a Tathāgata]."
Each and every Thus-Come One appearing in the world has taught as many sūtras as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds;

in each and every sūtra, they bestow predictions of enlightenment upon as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, manifesting various spiritual powers and expounding various dharma-gates to deliver immeasurable sentient beings. Good son, that Universal Radiance True Gold Maṇi...
Within the ocean of world-systems of the mountain, there is a world-lineage named Universal Ornament Banner.
Within this world-lineage, there is a world named Universal Radiance of All Jewel Colors, which has as its substance a king of *maṇi* jewels that manifests the reflections of all emanation-buddhas;
it is shaped like a celestial city and has as its substance a king of *maṇi* jewels that manifests the reflections of the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Tathāgatas.
At its lower limit, it rests upon an ocean of all kinds of jewel-flowers where the pure and the impure are intermingled.

Within this world-system, there are as many sets of four continents (cāturdvīpaka) as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru; among them, one set of four continents stands at the center, named Sarvaratnaparvatadhvaja.
Each of these four continents is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and each possesses its own [central mountain].
Within Jambudvīpa, there was a royal capital named Cloud-Lamp Adorned with Firm and Wondrous Jewels,
surrounded by ten thousand great cities. At a time when the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa was ten thousand years,
there was a king therein named Universal Sound of All Dharmas Perfect Canopy, who had five hundred ministers, sixty thousand court ladies, and seven hundred [sons].
The prince and all those other princes were handsome, brave, and strong, possessing great majestic power.
At that time, the king’s majesty extended throughout Jambudvīpa, and there were no enemies. When the kalpa of that world was nearing its end, the five corruptions arose;
the lifespan of all people became short, their wealth and resources diminished, and they were mostly coarse and ugly in appearance.

Suffering will abound and happiness will not be cultivated; people will exclusively commit evil deeds, quarreling with one another, mutually insulting and disparaging each other, alienating the families of others, and envying their prosperity.
Following their own whims and biased views, they will greedily seek what is contrary to the Dharma.

Due to these causes and conditions, wind and rain will not come at the proper times, the crops will fail to ripen, and all gardens, forests, grasses, and trees will wither away, leaving the people impoverished and destitute.

Various pestilential diseases rushed forth in all directions; finding no one to rely upon, they all came together to surround the great royal capital from its immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of quadrillions of sides. They raised their voices in loud cries;
some lifted their hands, some joined their palms, some struck their heads against the ground, some beat their breasts with their hands, some knelt and wailed long and loud, and some leaped about.
With bodies emitting loud cries, hair disheveled, rags worn and tattered, skin cracked and withered, and countenances devoid of luster, they addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, Great King! We are now impoverished, orphaned, and destitute; tormented by hunger, thirst, cold, and disease, we are emaciated and overwhelmed by manifold sufferings.
Our lives will soon come to an end, yet we have no refuge, no protector, and no one to whom we may appeal."
Having now come to take refuge in the Great King, I perceive in the Great King benevolence and wisdom; in the presence of the Great King,
I obtain peace and happiness, I obtain what is beloved, I obtain my livelihood, I obtain protection,
I obtain a treasure-store, I encounter a bridge, I meet a road, I find a raft, I see a jewel-island, and I obtain wealth and profit.
At that time, as the Great King ascended to the celestial palace and contemplated this thought, he heard these words.

Having attained a million *asaṃkhyeya* gates of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he focused his mind in contemplation and uttered ten kinds of words of great compassion. What are these ten? They are: "Alas!
Sentient beings have fallen into the bottomless great pit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). How shall I swiftly exert myself to rescue them and cause them to attain [liberation]?"
Abiding on the stage of omniscience, [he thought]: "Alas! Sentient beings are oppressed by various afflictions;
how shall I act as their protector and cause them to dwell securely in all wholesome deeds? Alas!
Sentient beings are terrified by birth, old age, sickness, and death; how shall I act as their refuge so that they may forever attain peace of body and mind?"
How lamentable! Sentient beings are constantly oppressed by the various fears of the world;

how shall I provide them with aid so that they may abide in the path to all-knowledge? How lamentable! Sentient beings lack the eye of wisdom and are perpetually shrouded by the views of selfhood and doubt;
how shall I employ skillful means to enable them to pluck out the cataracts of their deluded views?
Alas! Sentient beings are constantly deluded by the darkness of ignorance; how shall I act as a bright torch for them, so that they may illuminate and behold the city of omniscience?
Alas! Sentient beings are constantly defiled by stinginess, envy, flattery, and deception;
how shall I enlighten and awaken them, so that they may realize the pure Dharma-body? Alas! Sentient beings...
While growing up, they were swept away and submerged in the great ocean of birth and death;
how shall I universally transport and deliver them so that they may reach the further shore of supreme enlightenment? Alas for sentient beings, whose faculties are stubborn and difficult to subdue;
how shall I act as their charioteer to cause them to be fully endowed with the spiritual powers of all Buddhas? Alas for sentient beings, who are like those born blind!
"The blind do not see the road; how shall I act as their guide to lead them so that they may enter the gateway of all-knowledge?
Having spoken these words, he beat the drum to proclaim: "I now universally bestow upon all sentient beings whatever they require, ensuring they are fully satisfied.
Immediately, he issued an edict throughout the great and small cities and all the settlements within Jambudvīpa.
They opened all their treasuries and brought forth various items, placing them at the crossroads—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *maṇi* gems, and other jewels;
clothing, food, drink, flowers, incense, necklaces, palaces, houses, couches, and bedding.
They erected great *maṇi* jewel banners of radiant light, the touch of which brought peace and security to all bodies, and they also bestowed [remedies] for all illnesses.
For the sake of medicinal decoctions, he opened various treasuries and bestowed upon others all kinds of precious vessels filled with diverse jewels,
vajra-vessels filled with various fragrances, and precious incense-bowls; likewise, he gave all manner of clothing, palanquins, carriages, banners, pennants, and silk canopies—
all such articles of daily life— and he also gave away all villages, camps, cities, and towns, as well as mountains.

He was able to relinquish everything—marshes, forests, groves, wife, children, kinsmen, and retinue, as well as his royal throne, head, eyes, ears, nose, lips, tongue, teeth, hands, feet, skin, flesh, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, and all internal and external possessions—including his firm and wondrous jewels.
To the east of the city of Cloud-Lamp Adorned with Jewels, there was a gate named Radiance of the Mani Mountain; outside that gate was...
The site of this sacrificial assembly was vast, pure, and level, free from pits, ravines, thorns, or gravel;

everything there was composed of exquisite jewels. It was strewn with various precious flowers and perfumed with sublime incenses, while precious lamps were lit and clouds of every fragrance filled the void.
Countless jewel trees stood in orderly rows, and immeasurable nets of flowers [hung above].
A net of immeasurable incense covered its surface, and hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of musical instruments constantly produced exquisite sounds;
all these were adorned with wonderful jewels and were entirely the fruit of the pure karma of bodhisattvas.
Within that assembly, lion thrones were arranged, with ground made of ten kinds of jewels and railings of ten kinds of jewels.
Various jewel trees surround it on all sides, with adamantine jewel wheels supporting them from below.
Images of nāgas made of every kind of jewel together uphold it, adorned with various precious objects. Banners and streamers are arranged in alternating rows, and a multitude of nets covers it above.
Immeasurable precious incense constantly emits clouds of fragrance, and various precious garments are distributed everywhere.
A thousand kinds of musical instruments constantly played beautiful melodies, and above them were spread precious canopies that perpetually emitted immeasurable light from jewel-flames,
as brilliant and pure as Jāmbūnada gold. These were covered with jeweled nets from which hung various tassels and necklaces of maṇi-jewel bands,
with various jeweled bells arranged all around, constantly producing sublime sounds to exhort all sentient beings to practice.
When performing virtuous deeds, that great king sat upon a lion throne, his form upright and endowed with the marks of a great man;
he wore a crown of wondrous jewels emitting light, possessed a body like Nārāyaṇa that could not be destroyed, and every limb was perfectly complete.
Born into a lineage of kings who were universally virtuous and excellent, he attained mastery over both wealth and the Dharma, as well as eloquence.
With unimpeded eloquence and clear, penetrating wisdom, he governed the kingdom such that no one disobeyed his commands.
At that time, immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings from various lands,
various clans, various physical forms, various garments, various languages, and various desires all came together here to Jambudvīpa.
He observed that all those kings said, "This king is one of great wisdom, a Sumeru of merit, and a moon of virtue.
When the King dwelt in the vast practice of giving according to the vows of a bodhisattva,
he beheld those who came to beg and gave rise to a heart of compassion, a heart of joy, a heart of respect, a heart of friendship, a heart of vastness, and a continuous heart.
A mind of diligence arose; a mind of non-retrogression arose; a mind of renunciation arose; a mind of universality arose.

Good son, at that time, when the king saw those beggars, his heart was filled with great joy for a brief moment—such as even the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the King of the Yāma Heaven, or the King of the Tuṣita Heaven could not achieve in the course of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The pleasure he experiences cannot equal the pleasure experienced by the Celestial King Subhakṛtsna over countless eons;
nor the pleasure experienced by the Celestial King Śubha over immeasurable eons; nor the Brahma-pleasure experienced by the Great Brahma King over boundless eons;
nor the celestial pleasure experienced by the Celestial King Ābhāsvara over inconceivable eons; nor [the pleasure experienced by] the Celestial King Śuddhāvāsa...
The celestial pleasures experienced throughout inexhaustible kalpas cannot equal the bliss of tranquility attained by the Kings of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens for unspeakable kalpas.
Son of Good Family, it is as if there were a person, kind, benevolent, filial, and fraternal, who, encountering the calamities of the world,
suddenly lost his parents, wife, children, brothers, and sisters amidst the wilderness and on the roads, and then [met them] again...
When encountering [the Buddha], serving him, and gazing upon him, his heart never grew weary or satiated;
at that time, when the Great King saw those who came to seek [refuge], his mind was likewise filled with joy.

Good son, at that time, because of that spiritual friend, the King’s aspiration for the Bodhi of the Buddha increased, his faculties were perfected, and his faith became pure, joyful, and complete. Why is this?
This bodhisattva diligently cultivates all practices, seeking omniscience; they vow to benefit all sentient beings,
vow to attain the immeasurable, wondrous bliss of Bodhi, abandon all unwholesome states of mind, constantly delight in accumulating all roots of goodness,
always vow to rescue and protect all sentient beings, and constantly delight in observing the path to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Delighting in the practice of the Dharma of omniscience, fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings, entering the great ocean of the merits of all Buddhas,
shattering the mountains of all demonic activities and the obstructions of delusion, following the teachings and practices of all Tathāgatas, and traversing the unobstructed path of omniscience,
they have already deeply entered the stream of omniscience and the stream of all dharmas, remaining ever constant.
Now, manifesting great vows that are inexhaustible, dwelling as a Great Being in the dharma of a Great Man,
accumulating the treasury of all universal gates of goodness, remaining detached from all attachments, and being unstained by the spheres of all worldly realms;
knowing the nature of all phenomena to be like space, one conceives the thought of [the beggar] as an only son, as one's father and mother, and as a field of merit.

One should conceive the thought that [the recipient] is difficult to encounter, the thought of gratitude and benefit, the thought of firm resolve, the thought of the teacher, and the thought of the Buddha.

Without discriminating based on location, without selecting based on lineage, and without choosing based on physical appearance, one should grant everything universally and impartially to whoever arrives according to their desire, with a heart of great compassion, free from hindrance, so as to satisfy them all.
To those who seek food and drink, one should give food and drink; to those who seek... [and so forth].
To those seeking clothing, he gives clothing; to those seeking incense and flowers, he gives incense and flowers; to those seeking garlands and parasols, he gives garlands and parasols;

[he gives] banners, pennants, necklaces, palaces, gardens, elephants, horses, chariots, seats, bedding, gold, silver, mani-jewels, all manner of precious objects, all treasuries, as well as his retinue, cities, towns, and villages.
While he was thus bestowing [these gifts] universally upon all sentient beings, there was in this assembly a daughter of a householder named Ratnaprabhā, who was accompanied by sixty young maidens.

She was upright and exquisite, a sight pleasing to all people; her skin was golden, her eyes and hair were deep blue, her body emitted a wondrous fragrance, and her mouth produced the sound of Brahma-vocalization. She was adorned with most excellent precious garments and was always possessed of a sense of shame.
Possessing a sense of shame and right mindfulness so that they are undisturbed, they are endowed with dignified deportment and show reverence to their teachers and elders.
They constantly mindfully practice profound and wondrous conduct, and they remember and do not forget the teachings they have heard.

Their past roots of goodness flow and moisten their hearts, making them pure and vast like space, dwelling in equanimity toward all sentient beings. They constantly behold all Buddhas and seek the wisdom of omniscience at the time of the Jewel Light.
The woman approached the king from no great distance, joined her palms in homage, prostrated herself, and thought to herself: "I have gained a great benefit!

I have gained a great benefit! I have now met a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Toward this king, I shall conceive the notion of him as my Great Teacher, the notion of him as a spiritual friend, the notion of his possessing compassion, and the notion of his being able to sustain me. With a mind upright and straight, I give rise to great joy and release my body."

Adorning themselves with necklaces, they offered them to that king and made this vow: "May this Great King now serve as a place of reliance for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings shrouded in ignorance. May I, in the future, likewise be so;
may I possess the same knowledge as this Great King, the same vehicle upon which he rides, the same path he cultivates, the same physical marks he possesses, and all the same wealth and property."
"May I, in the future, fully attain such [qualities] as gathering infinite and inexhaustible assemblies that are difficult to surpass and difficult to destroy;
wherever I am born, may I be reborn accordingly. At that time, the Great King, knowing that this young girl had conceived such a resolve, addressed her, saying:
"Young girl, whatever you desire, I shall grant it all to you. Everything I currently possess—"
When she had relinquished [her body] so that all sentient beings might universally attain fulfillment, the maiden Ratnaprabhā’s faith became pure and she gave rise to great joy;
she then praised the King with these verses:
In the past, before this great king had appeared in this city, all was utterly joyless, like the realm of hungry ghosts.

Sentient beings slaughtered one another; they practiced theft, indulged in sexual license, spoke with double-tongued deceit and untruths, uttered meaningless and harsh words, and greedily coveted the wealth of others.
Those who harbor malice and poisonous intent, Who hold wrong views and engage in unwholesome conduct, At the end of their lives fall into evil realms.
By such beings as these, Enveloped by ignorance and delusion, And abiding in inverted views, The heavens do not send down rain;
Because there is no timely rain, The hundred grains all fail to grow.
The grasses and trees are all withered and parched, And the springs and streams have likewise run dry.
Before the Great King arose in this world, Rivers and ponds were all dried up; In the gardens and groves, there were many skeletons, Appearing from afar like a desolate wilderness.
Now that the Great King has ascended the precious throne, He extensively delivers all living beings; Massive clouds of oil-like rain cover the eight directions.
A universal rain falls, filling all things; the Great King oversees the common people.
All violence and cruelty are severed, and judicial punishments are brought to rest. The solitary and the orphaned are all secure and at peace.
In the past, sentient beings each harmed one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh; now they have all given rise to a heart of compassion.
In former times, sentient beings were poor and lacked clothing; they sheltered themselves with grass, emaciated by hunger like hungry ghosts.
Now that the Great King has appeared in the world, non-glutinous rice grows spontaneously and exquisite garments emerge from the trees.
Men and women are all finely adorned, whereas in the past they vied for meager gains.
In times past, people unlawfully oppressed and plundered one another; now, everyone is abundantly provided for.
In former times, people committed evil deeds, giving rise to improper greed and lust; they variously assaulted and coerced the wives of others and young maidens.
Now, when seeing other women who are upright, beautiful, and finely adorned, [they do not covet them].
Yet his mind is free from attachment, like the gods of the Heaven of Contentment. In former times, sentient beings spoke falsely and untruthfully;
their speech was contrary to the Dharma and devoid of benefit, being crooked and intended only to win over others' minds.
Today, all classes of living beings have completely abandoned such evil speech, for their minds have become supple and gentle.

His speech is likewise harmonious and gentle. All sentient beings of the past who practiced various kinds of heterodox dharmas—be they cattle, sheep, dogs, or swine—now join their palms in reverent salutation. Having heard the King’s True Dharma, they have awakened and abandoned their false views;
they clearly understand that the retribution of suffering and pleasure all arises from causes and conditions.
The Great King utters wondrous sounds, and all who hear them rejoice. His voice, equal to that of Brahmā and Śakra, cannot be rivaled by any other.
The Great King’s many precious canopies hang suspended in the midst of space;
they are supported by shafts of lapis lazuli and covered with nets of maṇi jewels, from which golden bells naturally produce [melodious sounds].
With a harmonious and elegant voice, the Tathāgata proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma, extinguishing the delusions of sentient beings.

Furthermore, he extensively expounds upon all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions and within all kalpas, as well as the Tathāgatas together with their retinues; he likewise speaks in succession concerning the past lands of the ten directions.

And all the Tathāgatas within those lands emit subtle and wondrous sounds that pervade the entire Jambudvīpa, extensively expounding upon the various distinctions of karma for humans, devas, and others.
Having heard this, sentient beings come to know their own store of karmic seeds; they abandon evil and diligently practice cultivation.
Dedicating this toward the Bodhi of the Buddha, The father of the king was Pure Radiance, And the mother of the king was Lotus Light.
When the five turbidities appeared, He occupied the throne and ruled the world. At that time there was a vast garden, Within which were five hundred ponds;
Each was surrounded by a thousand trees, And each was completely covered with flowers.
Upon the banks of that pond, he constructed a hall with a thousand pillars; its railings and other ornaments were all fully prepared without exception.
When evil dharmas arose in the final age, no rain fell for many years, and the ponds and streams all dried up.
The grasses and trees were all withered and parched, seven days before the king was born.
First, auspicious and miraculous signs appeared, which all who saw them took to heart. "The Savior of the World shall now emerge!
Then, in the middle of the night, the great earth shook in six ways.
There was a precious lotus pond, its radiance like that of the sun appearing; within five hundred such ponds, waters of merit were filled to the brim.
Withered trees all sprout branches, Their flowers and leaves flourish and grow lush.
The waters of the ponds, now full to the brim, flow and spread everywhere, Pervading the entire land of Jambudvīpa;
There is nowhere they do not moisten and saturate— Whether medicinal herbs or various trees, Or the sprouts and crops of the hundred grains, With their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
All shall flourish and prosper; the ditches, pits, and mounds—every such place on the earth, whether high or low—shall all become level and even.
All impurities, such as thorns, gravel, and pebbles, shall in a single thought-moment be transformed into various precious jewels.
When sentient beings saw this, they rejoiced and offered praise, all saying:
"We have gained a great benefit, like a thirsty man drinking sweet water.
At that time, King Prabhāsa, together with his immeasurable retinue, prepared the royal carriage and traveled to observe the various gardens within the five hundred ponds.
There is a pond named *Ananda*; upon the pond is a Dharma hall where the father-king resides.
The former king said to his consort: "I recall that seven nights ago, at midnight, the earth shook and a light appeared here.
At that time, within that flower pond, a thousand-petaled lotus emerged."
His radiance is like a thousand suns, reaching upward to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
With a diamond for its stalk and Jambu-river gold for its pedestal, it has various jewels for its petals and exquisite fragrance for its filaments and anthers.
Upon that flower, the King is born, sitting upright in the full lotus posture, adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
Revered by the celestial deities, the former kings were filled with great joy;
entering the pond, he stroked his infant son and held him up to present him to the Queen.
"Your son should rejoice!"—at that moment, treasuries of jewels all sprang forth, and jewel-trees produced exquisite garments; heavenly music played beautiful sounds, filling the entirety of space.
All sentient beings were filled with great joy; With palms joined, they cried out, "How marvelous!

Well done, O Protector of the World! At that time, the King emitted a radiance from his body That shone universally upon all things, Causing the darkness throughout the four continents to vanish And all illnesses to be extinguished, including those of the yakṣas and piśācas.
Poisonous insects and various evil beasts that seek to harm people will all hide away of their own accord.
Their ill repute will vanish and their good fortune will be lost; they will be beset by calamities and diseases.
Thus, all such manifold sufferings shall cease, and everyone will rejoice. Toward all classes of sentient beings, they will look upon one another as parents.

Leaving behind evil, he gives rise to a heart of compassion; Dedicated solely to seeking all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), He closes off the various evil realms and reveals the path for humans and devas. Proclaiming omniscience, he delivers and liberates all living beings.
We, having beheld the Great King, have universally obtained excellent benefit— We who were without refuge and without a destination.
"May all beings be entirely at peace.

At that time, the maiden Ratnaprabhā, having praised King Sarvadharmanirghoṣasamantavyūha with these verses, circumambulated him countless times, joined her palms in prostration, bowed with deep reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side. Then, that great king—
He addressed the young woman, saying: "Excellent, young woman! That you are able to believe in and know the merits of others is truly rare.
Young woman, all sentient beings are unable to believe in or know the merits of others. All sentient beings do not know how to repay kindness;
they lack wisdom, their minds are turbid and distracted, their natures are not clear, and they fundamentally lack resolve and strength."
Furthermore, those who have regressed from such practice neither believe in nor understand the merits, supernatural powers, and wisdom possessed by Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas. O maiden,
since you now resolutely seek to attain Bodhi and are able to know such merits of a Bodhisattva,
your merit in having been born here in Jambudvīpa and having resolved upon a courageous mind to universally gather in all sentient beings is immeasurable.

"Even if it were to be wasted, it would still bring about such merit. After the King of Praise had finished praising the girl, he personally handed a priceless precious robe to the maiden Ratnaprabhā and her retinue, saying to each one: "Put on this robe.
At that time, all the maidens knelt with both knees upon the ground, received the robes with both hands, placed them upon their heads, and then put them on.

Having put on their garments, they circumambulated the king to the right; from among all those precious robes, the light of all the stars emerged everywhere, and when the multitude saw this, they all said:
"These women are all exceedingly beautiful, adorned like the stars of a clear night sky.
Good son, who could this King Sarvadharmanirghoṣaparipūrṇacchattra have been other than [the Buddha]?"
The present Vairocana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is he; King Prabhāpāla is King Śuddhodana;
Lady Padmaprabhā is Lady Māyā; and the maiden Ratnaprabhā is none other than my own self.
Those beings gathered by that king at that time through the four methods of attraction are all those present in this assembly.
These bodhisattvas have all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
or they dwell in the first through the tenth stages (*bhūmi*), possessing various great vows, accumulating various aids to the path, cultivating various sublime practices,
being equipped with various adornments, attaining various supernormal powers, and abiding in various liberations within this assembly.
While dwelling within the palaces of various sublime dharmas, at that time the Night Goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasukhasaṃvāsā,
wishing to reiterate the meaning of this liberation for the sake of the youth Sudhana, spoke these verses:
I possess vast eyes that see universally throughout the ten directions;

Within the ocean of all world-systems, I see those wandering through the cycle of the five destinies, And I also see those Buddhas sitting beneath the Bodhi trees, Their spiritual powers pervading the ten directions as they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. I possess pure ears.
I hear all sounds everywhere, and I also hear the Buddhas preaching the Dharma; with joy, I accept them with faith.
I possess the knowledge of others' minds, which is non-dual and unobstructed; within a single thought-moment, I can fully comprehend the ocean of all minds.
I have attained the knowledge of past lives, by which I am able to know all kalpas.
I clearly understand the distinctions between myself and others; in a single thought-moment, I know the eons as numerous as the atoms within oceans of lands.
I remember all those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the various classes of sentient beings within the five realms of existence;
I recall those Buddhas from the time they first resolved upon the aspiration for enlightenment, up until their cultivation of all spiritual practices.

Each and every one is perfectly complete; I also know those Buddhas, Who, having accomplished the path to enlightenment, Turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of all beings through various skillful means.
I also know the ocean of all vehicles belonging to those Buddhas, The duration for which their True Dharma remains, And the number of sentient beings they deliver.
Throughout immeasurable eons, I have practiced this dharma-gate; I now speak it for you, O Son of the Buddha, and you should learn it.
Good son, I know only this bodhisattva liberation gate called "The Radiance of Vast Great Joy Arising."
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas draw near to and make offerings to all Buddhas; they enter the great ocean of vows for omniscience and fulfill the ocean of all Buddhas' vows.
Attaining courageous wisdom, they universally enter the ocean of all Bodhisattva stages from within a single Bodhisattva stage.
Attaining pure vows, they universally enter all Bodhisattva practices from within a single Bodhisattva practice.

Having attained mastery over the ocean of practices, you have universally entered the ocean of all bodhisattva liberation-gates through a single bodhisattva liberation-gate; how then could I know or describe those meritorious deeds?
Good son, within this site of enlightenment there is a night goddess named Great Vow and Power of Diligence Who Protects All Sentient Beings; go to her.
When he asked the Bodhisattva, "How does one teach and transform sentient beings so that they may proceed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
how does one adorn and purify all Buddha-fields; how does one serve all Tathāgatas; and how does one practice all Buddha-dharmas?
the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and paid him profound homage.
He gazed upon [the teacher] with reverence, took his leave, and departed.

[Treatise: Within the first section on the Dharma-gate of entering the proper stage, from the passage beginning "At that time, the youth Sudhana" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva’s liberation gate of the light of great joy born of vastness," the text is divided into long sections.

Divided into five sections: (1) "At that time, the youth Sudhana... down to "...I pray you, out of compassion, explain this for me," consisting of seven lines of sūtra, clarifies the section where Sudhana arrives at the place of the night goddess and formally presents his request;
(2) "The night goddess said, 'O son of good family... down to "...the Bodhisattva’s birth of the light of vast great joy and understanding."
The section on the liberation door consisting of fifteen lines and a half of sūtra text clarifies the portion where the Night Goddess bestows upon Sudhana the method for his own practice;

this is divided into three parts. From Sudhana’s words, "O Great Sage," down to "causing him to abide securely in the wisdom of a bodhisattva," there are sixty-six lines of sūtra text clarifying the fourth part:
the section on Sudhana entering the realm of this dharma-door. This is divided into four parts. Sudhana... [text continues].
The youth said, "O Noble One, how long has it been since you gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta?
Thereafter, nineteen lines of prose clarify the intent to speak of the duration of his resolve and the difficulty of its being believed;
twenty-nine lines of verse follow as a restatement of the preceding dharma, which is profound and difficult to believe, intended for those of superior faculties capable of hearing it.

As the sutra clearly explains in detail, from the passage beginning with "In the distant past, there were five good sons" down to "I only know this Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the vast light of great joy and birth," there are eight and a half pages of scripture.

This constitutes the answer to the previous question asked by Sudhana regarding the length of time since he first resolved his mind toward enlightenment (*cittotpāda*); it is explained according to the text within the commentary on the meaning.
"Good son, in ages past... and so forth, which consists of approximately four sections:

first, citing eons as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds to answer the previous question regarding the duration since he first resolved his mind; second, citing the name of the ocean of worlds, Universal Radiance True Gold Mani Mountain;
third, citing the appearance of a Buddha within that ocean of worlds named Universal... [The text continues with the names of the Buddhas and their lands].

In the ocean of worlds within the world-system of King of the Tranquil Majesty of the Mountain of Wisdom Illumining the Dharma-realm, there are world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a world; in each world-system, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in a world;
and in every single world, a Tathāgata appears, and so forth—this concludes the specific enumeration below.

Within it, there was a Jambudvīpa containing a royal capital named Cloud-Lamp Adorned with Firm and Wondrous Jewels, surrounded by ten thousand great cities. The lifespan of its people was ten thousand years.
Therein dwelt a king named Perfect Canopy of the Sound of All Dharmas, who had five hundred ministers, sixty thousand court ladies, and seven hundred princes. At that time...
There was a daughter of an elder named Ratnaprabhā, who, together with sixty young maidens—whose bodies were golden in color and whose eyes and hair were deep blue—was present.
In the subsequent passage, the King exhorted the young maiden Ratnaprabhā to believe in and recognize the merits of others;
he then personally bestowed precious garments upon her. Once she had put on the garments, at that...
From within the precious robes, the light of all the stars and constellations was universally emitted.
At that time, the King Universal Sound of All Dharmas Perfect Canopy was none other than the present Tathāgata Vairocana; the King Radiant Light was King Śuddhodana;
Lady Lotus was Lady Māyā; and the maiden Jewel Light was none other than myself.

Therefore, these beings who are gathered by the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) constitute the answer to Sudhana’s question regarding how long it has been since he first resolved upon the unsurpassed, great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
This clarifies the practice of cultivating the conduct of great compassion on the seventh stage;
for were it not for this, one could not give rise to a vast mind that is unrestricted by the number of eons, reaching to the very limit of birth and death, and equalizing the three periods of time.

Just as one might take the atoms within an ocean of worlds and set the duration of time equal to the measure of incalculable eons, reaching the limit of the afflictions and sufferings of all sentient beings, only then can one truly extol the practice of great compassion in this stage; thus, the "dusts of an ocean of worlds" is used as a metaphorical comparison.
If one were to use worldly phenomena to represent the gates of cultivation, those who observe events to understand the Dharma would cite the entire world.

"Numbering as many as the atoms in an ocean of realms" means that, in direct terms, there is no time at which they can be limited. Cultivating the practice of great compassion means severing the mind of limitation.

There is an ocean of worlds named "Universal Radiance True Gold Mani Mountain," which signifies arising from the wisdom of universal radiance to cultivate the practice of great compassion; from the very beginning, it has had no starting point.
The ultimate pure gold symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The *maṇi* jewel symbolizes this wisdom being stainless.

The mountain symbolizes this Wisdom of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhājñāna*), which, while dwelling within birth and death, benefits all sentient beings with purity and freedom from defilement, remaining as immovable as a mountain.
To realize this wisdom is called the appearance of a Buddha; it is called the Wisdom that Universally Illuminates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Wisdom Mountain" (Huishan) signifies that which is based upon the universal radiance of wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) to establish the Buddha’s name.
"Lamp" refers to the wisdom that illuminates further and further without interruption or exhaustion. "Mountain" signifies not being moved by external objects, as well as the meaning of rising high;
its essence performs no action, which is the meaning of quiescence. When wisdom manifests and afflictions and karma perish, this is the King of Majestic Virtue. This is the self.
Therefore, it is said that the name of that Buddha was King of the Tranquil Majesty of the Wisdom Mountain Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm.
Noble son, when that Buddha was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he purified that ocean of worlds by initiating bodhisattva practices through fundamental wisdom,
adorning his own karmic retribution so as to cause all worlds, numbering as many as the atoms within them, to become pure and serene.

It clarifies that within every world-system there is a Tathāgata appearing in the world; that the universal light-intelligence universally seals all world-systems such that there is not one where a Tathāgata does not appear in the world;
and so on, down to all the four continents below, which are entirely sealed by the seal of universal light-intelligence without exception, even extending to universally sealing everything.
The ocean of the minds of sentient beings is like the sun in the sky; when the water is clear, the sun appears.
Down to the King of the Dharma-realm as the capital city, it is governed by the King of Wisdom.

The king is named "Perfect Canopy of the Sound of All Dharmas," which clarifies the simultaneous practice of both compassion and wisdom. The five stages of expedient practice are the ministers, numbering five hundred.
The minister practices the Dharma of compassion within the six realms of existence; because he takes joy in this as his court ladies, it is said there are sixty thousand court ladies.
The seven hundred princes represent the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

From "down to" and below, when the evil age arises and human lifespans are short, with suffering abounding and joy scarce—this is the place where one practices compassion. The sixty maidens symbolize the six realms of existence.
The practice of wisdom and compassion is synthesized as follows in the subsequent text:
"At that time, was the Universal Monarch Sarvadharmanirghoṣasamantaprabha anyone else? He was none other than the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairocana.
King Prabhāpāla was King Śuddhodana. Queen Padmavati was Queen Māyā. The youth Ratnaprabha..."
"The 'Woman' refers to my own body, which is manifested by the Great Intention (*mahāmanas*), and which practices the conduct of Great Wisdom, Great Compassion, and Great Mercy.
Being endowed with these three dharmas, the Master of the Treatise says in verse: The Universal Radiant Wisdom is named Buddha; In accordance with the Original Vow, she is named Father;
Nurturing all living beings with compassion, she is named Lady; Delighting in the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings, she is named Maiden. [All that follows below...]
The oceans of worlds and the clusters of lands, all numbering as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds, are entirely the sphere of transformation for these four types of gathering;
with infinite wisdom and compassion, one should practice in this manner.

Within the ocean of the dharma-realm, the measures of distance, proximity, length, and brevity cannot be grasped; thus, this sutra clarifies that phenomena are identical to principle by citing such kalpas.
In the ocean-like world-systems, kingdoms, and cities that extend throughout the ten directions, vast and infinite, Tathāgatas appear everywhere within those lands.
Their kings practice various deeds to save living beings, children, princesses, queens who seek the Dharma, and court ladies.
These women inform the Great Kings of the sufferings of the wicked people of the age; their accounts are indeed true. Furthermore, they employ this Dharma to manifest this [teaching].

This section, which provides an analogy by citing the methods and patterns for practicing the *upāya-pāramitā* on the seventh stage, conveys the general meaning of the preceding sutra passages and verses:
it causes one to cultivate great compassion within the secular world without establishing the marks of renunciation;
taking Vairocana Buddha as the presiding object of reliance thus signifies the seventh stage.
This gate of compassion universally encompasses the five stages, reaching all the way to the ultimate ocean of the Buddha’s fruition;
therefore, from its beginning to its end, it is no different from the universal luminous wisdom (*samantābhāsa-jñāna*).

It does not establish ten stages for a single Buddha’s universal assembly, nor does it involve the progressive advancement of a hundred Buddhas as was the case previously during the stage of the three emptinesses of *prajñā* emerging from entanglements; therein, both the King and...
The female who leaves the household life to become a bhikṣuṇī is represented here by a layperson;

even if one were to consider the Buddha Vairocana as the fruit of Buddhahood, he too possesses a "secular body," adorned with flower crowns, necklaces, bracelets, and armlets, and does not bear the appearance of one who has left the household life.
Thus, this seventh position, the Gate of Compassion, [is compared] with the five preceding ones...

Within this stage, although the practices are identical, because there is a distinction between the supramundane and the worldly manifestations, one is made to recognize the superiority of progress, as well as the commonalities and differences between the general and the specific.
This is the seventh stage, the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā bhūmi*). Why is it called the Stage of Far-Going?
It is because the practice of great compassion within the mundane world cultivated on this stage reaches far through the oceans of worlds in the ten directions.
The practice of penetrating all phenomena of heaven, earth, and the hells does not seek anything for oneself;
rather, it takes the single thought of the supramundane mind as its core, with the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*) as the primary factor and the other nine as its companions.

This serves to remedy the two minds of worldly defilement and purity, and the obstacle of lacking mastery while dwelling in birth and death through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), thereby enabling one to attain mastery up to the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva path.
One attains partial mastery over the ten powers of a Buddha, yet mastery is not yet fully realized until the tenth stage;
from the sixth stage onward, one has not yet attained mastery within the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Because the two types of karma—defiled and pure—have not yet been extinguished, it is only from the seventh stage onward that one attains mastery within the four means of attraction. Therefore, this stage serves as the antidote to defilement.

"Because I have purified the two obstacles and entered into the practice of untainted purity and compassion, I know only this Bodhisattva liberation of the 'Radiance of Vast Great Joy'—for it is only at this stage that the dharmas of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are finally perfected.
This is the second section on advancing by inferring [the qualities of others], beginning from the passage: "As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... and so forth.
Upon taking leave to depart, three points are established: first, to recommend virtue for advancement;
second, that within this *bodhimaṇḍa* there is a night goddess named Mahāpraṇidhānavīryaparākrama who protects all sentient beings;
third, to pay respects and take leave, stating that "bodhimaṇḍa" is used instead of "bodhi" because this eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā*), is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*).
Wisdom manifests all phenomena as universally gathered, such that there is no "bodhicitta" [to be attained];

because it neither speaks of having already generated, nor will generate, nor is currently generating, nor of being detached or non-detached from it, it simply refers to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as the place where non-effortful wisdom dwells within the Middle Way.
For this reason, Sudhana likewise does not say, "I have already generated the bodhicitta," and so forth; thus, the night goddess is named Mahā-... (Great).
Those who wish to rescue and protect all sentient beings through the power of diligence do so by fulfilling the practices of wisdom and compassion;
they act spontaneously and effortlessly, driven by the wind of their original vows to benefit others.

Because they benefit living beings with a single stroke of the wind of the *pāramitā* of original vows without ceasing, all Buddhas provide seven exhortations and three empowerments to cause them to teach and transform sentient beings.
Because it establishes its name through the presence of rest, it is called "The Power of Great Vow-Energy that Protects and Saves All Sentient Beings.
