who is destined to attain Buddhahood within this trichiliocosm during the Bhadrakalpa— all of these were his [disciples].
Just as she was my mother here in this trichiliocosm, so too, throughout all kalpas and within all the infinite worlds of the ten directions in this ocean of worlds,
for all those who practice the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra in order to transform all sentient beings,
I saw myself becoming their mother. At that time, the youth Sudhana said to Māyā:
The Lady Ya said, "Great Sage, how much time has passed since you attained this *vimokṣa-sūtra*?

He replied, "Good son, it was in a past age beyond the reach of inconceivable numbers of kalpas—beyond what can be known by the supernormal powers, divine eye, or insight of Bodhisattvas in their final birth.
At that time, there was a kalpa named Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*) and a world named Meru-guṇa. Although it contained various mountains and five [continents]..."
In that realm, which was composed of various jewels, pure and adorned, free from all impurities and evils, there were a thousand billion sets of four continents.
Among them was a set of four continents named Lion Banner (*Siṃhadhvaja*). Within it were eight billion royal cities, and among them was a royal city named Sovereign Banner (*Vaiśravaṇadhvaja*).
Therein resided a wheel-turning king named Great Majestic Virtue (*Mahātejas*); that king—
To the north of the city was a site of enlightenment named Full Moon Radiance (*Pūrṇacandraprabhā*). The deity of that site of enlightenment was named Compassionate Virtue (*Maitraguṇa*).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Stainless Banner (*Vimaladhvaja*) who sat at the site of enlightenment, about to achieve perfect awakening.

An evil Māra named Golden Light (*Suvarṇaprabha*), together with his retinue of immeasurable hosts, came to the bodhisattva’s location; he possessed great majestic power and was on the verge of transforming [the world].

The Wheel-Turning Sage King, having attained the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties, manifested an army many times greater in number than before to surround the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). All the māras were struck with terror and fled in all directions.
When that bodhisattva was about to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the deity of the site of enlightenment, seeing this event, rejoiced immeasurably and then—
That king conceived the thought that she was his son, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and made this vow:
"In whatever place this Wheel-Turning King may be born, until he attains Buddhahood, may I always be his mother.
Having made this vow, she further made offerings to ten nayutas of Buddhas at this very site of enlightenment. Son of good family, what do you think of her?
Is the deity of this site of enlightenment anyone other than myself? The Wheel-Turning King was none other than the present World-Honored One, Vairocana.

Since I first made my vow before him, this Buddha, the World-Honored One, has been born in every realm throughout all lands in the ten directions, planting various roots of goodness, practicing the bodhisattva path, and bringing beings to maturity through his teachings.
For all sentient beings, even unto those manifesting in their final bodies, I appear in every thought-moment throughout all worlds,
manifesting the miraculous transformations of a Bodhisattva’s birth, always being their son while they are my mother. Good son, in the past and present,
when the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions were about to attain Buddhahood, they all emitted a great light from the center of their navels.
"Radiant light has come to illumine my body, as well as the palaces, mansions, and dwellings where I reside; he shall be my mother in my final birth.
Noble son, I know only this Bodhisattva liberation door of the illusory wisdom of great vows.
How can the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, with their treasury of great compassion, constantly teach and transform sentient beings without ever becoming weary, possessing such mastery?"
"Within each and every pore, he manifests the immeasurable spiritual transformations of all Buddhas; how could I now possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
Good son, in this world, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is a king named Samprajanya.
That king has a daughter named Devendraprabhā. Go to her and ask: 'How should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva path?'"
While practicing the bodhisattva path, the youth Sudhana respectfully received his instructions, prostrated with his head at his feet,
circumambulated him countless times, and then withdrew while looking back with longing and veneration.
[Treatise] Regarding the first section, the Dharma-gate of correctly entering the respective stage, the passage beginning from "At that time, the youth Sudhana...
and extending down to "attaining the wisdom of the realm of the Buddhas' vision" is divided into eleven sections. The first section, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana...

down to "attaining the wisdom of the realm of the Buddhas' vision," consists of one and a half lines of scripture and clarifies the stage of Sudhana’s ascending entry into the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).

From "Having formed this thought" down to "having formed this thought," there are eleven and a half lines of scripture clarifying the section on Sudhana’s praise of Māyādevī’s physical form and its sovereign characteristics; this is divided into three parts.
From "There was a city-lord goddess named Ratnanetra" down to "he shall certainly attain Buddhahood," there are thirty-six lines of scripture.
The section on the City-Ruling Goddess Vijayā explaining to Sudhana the Dharma-door of Governing the City of the Mind is divided into four parts.

First, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the goddess of the body-host" down to "because she beholds the appearance of all Buddhas arising in all lands," there are fourteen and a half lines of scripture that clarify how the goddess of the body-host praises the body of Lady Māyā; then, Lady Māyā emits light from her ear-ornament.
When the light entered the body of Sudhana, there were five stages; at that time, there was a rākṣasa king named Sunetra who guarded the Bodhisattva Hall, and so on, down to this being the tenth:
the Rākṣasa King Vidyutprabha, who spoke to Sudhana regarding the ten kinds of methods for approaching spiritual friends.
From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, down to the point where it says, "At the time these words were spoken," there were ten [sections].
The *Ekallavīrā-caryā-sūtra* clarifies how the Rākṣasa King taught the thirteen samādhis to Sudhana, enabling him to always remain in close proximity to spiritual friends;
this section consists of seven [sub-sections]. Sudhana the youth looked up into the sky and then descended [to reflect upon] the inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous merits of the Tathāgata;
this portion consists of twenty-seven lines of scripture clarifying Sudhana’s [realization].
He saw the Rākṣasa King expounding for him the method of paying homage to the ten directions and seeking spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
he further expounded for him the method of contemplating the body and mind as being like a dream and like an illusion.

Having seen the lotus, the seat, and the pavilion-adornments of Lady Māyā, the above three classes of goddesses constitute the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvaprayoga*) for entering this eleventh stage.
There are three [points]: first, skillfully guarding the city of the mind; second, skillfully knowing that the nature of sound pervades the ten directions;

third, the rākṣasa king named "Guardian of the Dharma Hall," who—by means of thirteen gates of samādhi and by contemplating body and mind as being like dreams and illusions—protects the meaning of the Dharma-realm hall. As for the rākṣasa king, this is translated as "The King Who Is To Be Feared."
The Sovereign (Vasavartinī) observes and protects the Dharma Hall of body and mind through samādhi, so that deluded, heterodox, and evil ghosts may be dispersed.
Thus, the light emitted from Māyā’s ear-ornament enters the body of Sudhana to clarify the entry into the Samādhi of the Light of the Teaching;
the ear primarily governs sound. By means of these three dharmas, one attains the correct [realization] only after completing the preliminary expedients for the eleventh stage.

Entering the Gate of the Eleven Stages (8): At that time, having seen such a seat and descended [into it] because he had attained the accomplishment of the body of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kāya*), there are thirty-one lines and a half of scripture explaining how Sudhana saw Māyādevī’s illusory form-body (*māyā-rūpa-kāya*) pervading before all sentient beings throughout the ten directions. Part Nine: At that time...

After the youth Sudhana had seen Lady Māyā, [the text] down to the passage "How should one learn the bodhisattva conduct so as to achieve its fulfillment" contains thirty-seven and a half lines of scripture clarifying that Lady Māyā manifested a body surpassing all forms and colors,
pervading the entire ocean of worlds; Sudhana likewise manifested an equal number of bodies before her, joining his palms in reverence.
Homage to the section on requesting what is sought and attaining entry into the various gates of samādhi. It is answered in ten parts, beginning with:
"O Son of the Buddha, I have already accomplished the liberation of the illusory wisdom of the great vows of a bodhisattva," and continuing down to:

"As for those who practice the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra to transform all sentient beings, I manifest my own body and become their mother. Therein it says: "I manifest my own body and become their mother."
Chapter One Hundred Seven: A General Explanation of the Section on Māyā’s Response to Sudhana’s Questions Regarding the Dharma-Gate;
Part Eleven. At that time, the youth Sudhana said to Lady Māyā: "How long has it been since you realized this liberation? [The text continues] down to:
"I only know this Bodhisattva liberation gate called 'the illusory birth through the wisdom of great vows. (Two sections.)
The seventeen and a half lines of scripture clearly answer Sudhana’s question regarding how long it has been since he attained this liberation.
To explain the meaning according to the text: within the general characteristics of Lady Māyā, she is established through three dharmas;

within her specific characteristics, she attains her name through practice-gates that equal the number of Buddhas and the number of sentient beings. As for these three dharmas, the first is "equality."
First, it takes as its essence the wondrous principle of the *dharmakāya*, which is the self-nature purity of all Buddhas and sentient beings, equal and signless;
second, it takes as its essence the universally luminous, effortless, and non-reliant wisdom within the principle of equality that is common to all Buddhas and sentient beings;
third, it takes as its essence the effortless wisdom of principle and phenomena that is equal to all Buddhas and sentient beings.

Within this, there is the nature of non-action that nurtures all sentient beings; through great kindness and great compassion, one benefits others, being fundamentally of one body with all sentient beings.
Having transcended the distinction between self and other, one constantly acts for their benefit without seeking gratitude in return.
This is the natural state of the True Heaven, shared by all sentient beings; if one practices according to these three dharmas, then even though—
However, although this is common to all sentient beings, those who are deluded regarding it must employ the gates of skillful means (*upāya*) to initiate and clarify it before they can attain it.
What are these skillful means? These skillful means consist of ten great gates of vows; one should practice and study them according to these vows.
First, at the moment of initial resolve, one should give rise to great vows of compassion equal in number to all sentient beings. All [vows] are...
First, I vow to deliver all sentient beings from the sufferings of the triple world and cause them all to attain Buddhahood;
second, I vow to serve, revere, and make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions, never allowing such service to be in vain;
third, I vow that wherever I am born within all worlds, should there be those whose virtue or arts surpass my own, I shall serve and study under them.
Although he studies all arts, his wisdom surpasses that of humans and devas; he never gives rise to arrogance, but always makes great loving-kindness and great compassion his priority.
He constantly employs the four foundations of mindfulness to treat illnesses according to their specific conditions and establishes the four right efforts.
His fifth vow is to always keep the seven factors of enlightenment foremost in his mind, thereby increasing all correct wisdom and illuminating the ten directions.
Second, may the ocean of great wisdom be generated through conditions; sixth, may the Eightfold Noble Path be constantly practiced;

seventh, may it be ever-present without beginning or end; eighth, may the Eightfold Noble Path manifest within myself and abide eternally in the world to benefit humans, devas, and all sentient beings of the six realms; ninth, I do not seek other pure lands elsewhere.

He perceives the gateway to the entire dharma-realm and deeply understands that defilement and purity both fundamentally arise from delusion, while based upon the True [Dharmadhātu], they are fundamentally non-existent.
He clearly knows the principles of the eight vows and the practice-gates of the five stages of a bodhisattva;

within the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage, he thoroughly understands the skillful means, various samādhis, and the dharmas for benefiting humans and devas.
In a single thought-moment, they pervade everywhere and thoroughly know the destinies [of beings], practicing the stages in succession;

through the nine vows, they constantly mind the wind-wheel of their original vow to uphold fundamental wisdom, and by drumming forth the boundless practices of the *pāramitās*, they manifest physical bodies corresponding to the ten directions to guide and lead all sentient beings according to their faculties. Through the tenth vow, they constantly employ the body of great compassion.

To give rise to all-knowledge that pervades the entire dharma-realm according to principle, with great wisdom shining universally so as not to omit a single thing, and to provide impartial and universal sustenance—this is the practice accomplished by the body of Lady Māyā. If a practitioner would cultivate it, they should do so in this way;
for there is not a single Buddha who has not been born from the ocean of great vows and the wisdom of great compassion. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
It is said that because all vows made while practicing the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra arise from me, this wisdom of the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*) arises from compassion.
All practices of great loving-kindness and great compassion prior to the tenth stage arise through fundamental vows and from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Upon reaching the eleventh stage, all cultivation and development are brought to completion, and everything is purely [of this nature].
Great compassion constitutes the essence of the Dharma-realm; through this compassion, wisdom arises, and illusory bodies are manifested in numbers equal to those of all sentient beings.

These bodies constantly act for their benefit without ever ceasing, and this is what is meant by "being born as a Buddha. It does not require the attainment of the thirty-two marks or even the ninety-seven marks;
rather, at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), a portion of true wisdom and compassion arise simultaneously. Although...
Not yet having attained the dharma of mastery over transformation and change, because they know and see the Truth as one, they practice in this way and awaken to it in this way;
only then can they be called "attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the mind.

This is also called "showing, awakening, and enlightening sentient beings with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," desiring to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From here, [the teaching proceeds] from Queen Māyā...

Following the initial gate of the eleven stages of the Human Manifestation (*nṛtya*), the subsequent nine spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) collectively clarify that [the Bodhisattva] takes great compassion as his mother;

all proceed from the conduct of this mother, generating compassion through the illusion of wisdom (*jñāna-māyā*). Thus, compassion and wisdom pervade the ten directions, universally manifesting without creating stages or sequential antidotes.
Thereafter, although these spiritual friends also say, "I alone... [the meaning remains as previously explained].
Knowing that this dharma-gate cannot be known by others clarifies that within the identical [nature], the distinct is contained, expressing the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra;
it pervades all according to conventional reality, unlike those prior to the ten stages who are obstructed and fail to reach it.
These eleven stages merely manifest the fulfillment of the practices of the eleven stages of cultivation; thus, the eleven stages of Samantabhadra are revealed.

His virtue pervades everywhere and encompasses the mundane world; seeking nothing beyond it, from the time of the Lord of Heaven’s Light (Indrāgnidatta) onwards, he was entirely one with the common worldly stream.
He did not manifest divine marks or extraordinary features, but was in every respect identical to ordinary people. There was only his benefit to others through the Dharma.
It is explained that prior to the ten stages (bhūmi), this is the practice of compassion and wisdom—the Dharma-gate of the self-transcending holy path.
The first stage is the gateway of entering the secular world to save living beings through the practice of great compassion;

it signifies that the path of transcendence is perfected and there is no further need to seek liberation. It is characterized solely by a mind that is free from the duality of defilement and purity, wherein one boards the ship of the Dharma-nature, raises the sail of great compassion, and employs great wisdom as the helmsman to be driven by the winds of original vows across the waves.

Constantly traversing the ocean of birth and death with the net of *pāramitā*, they scoop up all sentient beings who are caught in the nets of attachment and establish them upon the shore of the universally radiant wisdom.
They perpetually give rise to the merit of the myriad practices dwelling in illusion within the unimpeded jewel-hall of the *dharmadhātu*,
just like the tower-palace where Maitreya dwells, or as Sudhana obtained the *pāramitā* [of skillful means].
Kṣitigarbha (Cakravartin) explained to him the method for seeking a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), instructing Sudhana to universally prostrate toward the ten directions,
to contemplate all objective realms with right mindfulness, to travel throughout the ten directions with courageous mastery,

and to observe his own body and mind as being like a dream, an illusion, and a shadow while seeking a spiritual friend. At that time, Sudhana received and practiced these instructions, and immediately beheld [the spiritual friend].

The vision of a great jewel lotus emerging from the earth clarifies that those who seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) throughout the ten directions should seek the Dharma with earnest sincerity within and without their own body and mind; it clarifies that there is no inherent nature whatsoever that can be called the *dharmakāya*.

Furthermore, it causes one to contemplate the body and the mind as being like dreams and shadows, thereby leading to the realization of their characteristics and the realization of their nature. Through the realization of characteristics, one realizes the nature.
When the shadow-like manifestations are identical and non-dual, one enters the gate of the illusory birth of wisdom; this is the vision of Lady Māyā.

As for the initial sight of the lotus emerging from the earth: the self-nature pure *dharmakāya* is the substance of the "earth," and because all myriad practices arise from it as lotuses, the "vajra" constitutes the stem, which is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The wisdom that discerns all differentiated practices arises from the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya;
even if such a realm of adornment exists, it is likewise a *niṣyanda-phala* (retributive reward) based upon this [Dharmakāya], for there is ultimately no separate cause and effect of retribution.
"Wondrous treasury of jewels" refers to the *niṣyanda-phala* born of the nurturing and containment of compassion. "Māṇi-jewels as leaves" signifies conduct free from defilement.

That which is born of retribution has the Jewel King of Radiance as its pedestal, for it is that which is born of the retribution of the sovereign power of manifesting and illuminating through fundamental wisdom.

That which has the colors and fragrances of various jewels as its filaments is born of the retribution of the fragrances of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
That which is covered above by countless jewel nets is... [due to]... [the retribution of... (The sentence is incomplete in the source text).

It is able to bestow the net of teachings as a retribution for [past] births. As for the multi-storied pavilions above, they are called "the treasury that universally encompasses the dharma-realm of the ten directions" because they are produced as a retribution for the pervasive net of teachings through great wisdom that covers all.
As for their wondrous and exquisite adornment, it is due to the adornment of the retribution of sublime conduct. As for the ground being made of diamond, it is the retribution of the Dharma-body.
As for its birth, it has thousands of pillars arranged in rows, meaning there are tens of millions of rows.
That everything is made of maṇi jewels means that within every row there is no defilement.
That the walls are made of Jāmbūnada gold is the retribution born of gentleness and patience. That jeweled necklaces hang down on all four sides represents the four [reliances].
The practice of gathering [beings] through the bestowal of compassion is the response to the birth of sentient beings. From this point downward, one should understand according to these examples;

as the teachings are vast and the text is extensive, they cannot be described in full detail. Hereafter, regarding the manifestation of Māyādevī’s body pervading the entire Dharma-realm, her bodies that perform activities identical to those of all sentient beings, and her production of the bodies of all Tathāgatas, it is as stated in the text itself.
