[Treatise]: When the youth Sudhana questioned Lady Māyā regarding this liberation, how long had she possessed it?

Māyā replied: "O noble son, in ages past, beyond the reach of inconceivable time—beyond what can be known by the supernormal powers or the divine eye of Bodhisattvas in their final birth, and knowable only by a Buddha—it cannot be understood through temporal divisions nor measured by the number of kalpas;
it must necessarily be realized through the seal of Buddha-wisdom in profound accord."
If one were to exhaust all measures of past and present to see the beginning and end of when a deceased person first attained the mind and received the Dharma,
even if one were to compare it to the number of atoms in infinitely many *kṣetras*, there would be no way to fully enumerate it;
even if one were to continue this process through infinitely many such infinite *kṣetra*-dusts, the count could still not be reached.
One may count all deaths and reckon them to their end, yet only when wisdom is manifest does one know that they cannot be calculated by numerical methods;

for even if one were to calculate the distance from beginning to end using mathematical algorithms, exhausting kalpas both finite and infinite, one could never find the limit of the space within a single pore.
This is because space has no measure of duration; it is by means of this immeasurability that time is attained. Thus it is said:
The Mañjuśrī-gāthā states: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding.
Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the ten powers.
This is the great measure of a Bodhisattva in their final body. At that time, the eon is named Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*), signifying that the Dharma-body constitutes the substance of the eon.
The world named Sumeru takes immovable wisdom as its essential substance;
although it contains various mountains and the intermingling of the five destinies, that land is composed of various jewels, pure and adorned, devoid of all defilement and evil.
This is because when one's own mind is pure, all objective realms are pure; all phenomena are without stain, and thus purity and impurity are created by the mind.

The second vision is that one’s own mind perceives impurity; it clarifies that great compassion universally encompasses the five destinies and that great wisdom is untainted by dualistic views of purity and impurity, and is thus called "Adorned with Myriad Jewels.

The mention of a thousand billion sets of four continents clarifies the stage of benefiting sentient beings through the ten thousand practices. The mention of a single set of four continents named Lion Banner clarifies great wisdom.
Pervading the ten directions within a single realm, there were eight billion royal cities.

Among them was a city named Sovereign Banner (*Svayambhūdhvaja*), which illuminated the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path and the Ten Perfections (*daśapāramitā*). It was a place where wisdom dwells and moves;

it was called the Abode of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), and its king was named Great Majestic Virtue (*Mahātejas*). This king possessed mastery over wisdom and was capable of subduing [all afflictions].
Birth and death are inherently indestructible. To the north of that royal city is a bodhimanda named Full Moon Radiance.

As for "to the north of the city," the north represents the position of *khan* (the pit); it is the station where the Master, the Sovereign of Wisdom, dwells and governs, the place for subduing delusion.
It is called a bodhimanda because it can cure the afflictions of attachment; thus it is named Full Moon Radiance. The deity of that bodhimanda is named Compassion (*Maitrī*).
Virtue consists of transforming delusion through wisdom and taking compassion as its essence.
There was a bodhisattva named Vimaladhvaja whose practice arose from the dharmakāya and whose nature was inherently stainless.
As he sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), on the verge of attaining perfect awakening, an evil Māra named Suvarṇaprabha appeared together with his retinue of immeasurable hosts.

When that wheel-turning king of great majesty reached the Bodhisattva’s abode, he had already attained the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*) and manifested a host of soldiers many times greater in number than before, surrounding the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). All the māras were struck with terror and fled in all directions.
This signifies that the evil māra named Golden Light (*Suvarṇaprabha*) is, within the realm of the wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), of one mark with both the provisional and the real.
The Bodhisattva Always Free from Defilement has not yet clarified that the mind and its objects are equal;

he must rely on the King of All-Knowledge to clearly contemplate the principle that the mind and its objects are fundamentally non-dual. When one realizes that the mind and its objects are like illusions and all realms arise from illusory wisdom, one is no longer deluded by objects.
Since all delusory thoughts and mental demons are in truth nothing but the Dharma-realm, they are all Buddha-activities. This is called... [the name].
The scattering [of the assembly] from the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) refers to the joy of the compassionate deities, which is the bliss of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*).

That the deities of the site of practice conceive of that king as a son clarifies that the destruction of views arises through wisdom (*jñāna*), while the transformation of the world through practice arises through compassion (*karuṇā*).

This demonstrates that the wisdom of this stage is born from compassion; thus, one regards wisdom as a son. Furthermore, "the union with the wheel-turning king" refers to the *vimala* (stainless) stage.

"Rocana is the deity of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, and my own body is it"—this clarifies that [the Buddha], fearing people might not understand his meaning, has relied upon phenomena and images to make it easy to comprehend. Ultimately, there can be no objects existing separately outside the mind;
it merely clarifies that the mind has no interior, exterior, or middle, and that all dharmas—self and other—are of one essence, being neither one nor many.
He merely uses the obscurity of the Dharma and its difficulty of manifestation as a pretext to clarify it through events, so that those with wisdom may attain understanding through parables.
Furthermore, all who first resolve upon the unsurpassed Great Bodhicitta must first give rise to great vows and great compassion to teach and transform sentient beings;
only then do they seek the essential means of liberation and practice deeds for the benefit of sentient beings. This applies even unto the stage of actual practice.
Fulfilling this Dharma without wavering in resolve—this is how all Buddhas are: for they were first born from the practice of great compassion and vows.

Thus, when the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions are about to attain Buddhahood, they all emit great light during their fasts to illuminate my body, my palace, and my residence. This is the Wisdom of the Palace of Compassion.
The Palace nurtures it as its dwelling; the ocean of birth and death is its home.

Within this place where the body is purified by light, at the moment all sentient beings are born and grow, this location is the treasury where living beings are conceived and developed. It is like the root and crown of a tree:
from there, the trunk, branches, and twigs grow upward, while the roots extend downward into the earth—situated between the forces of Yin and Yang.

The primordial beginning of the occurrence at the limit is like the *jiǎzǐ* (gengzi) sexagenary cycle, wherein *shù* (wushu) serves as the *tiānkuí* (celestial leader), generating yang on the left and yin on the right.
The radiance emitted within the ritual space now represents the primordial beginning of receiving birth, corresponding to the image of the *tiānkuí*.
It marks the commencement of the arising of compassion and the source of the generation of great wisdom; thus, it is just as with human birth, which likewise begins from this point.
That which is born and gradually grows from childhood also arises from the wheel of the fast (*upavāsa-cakra*), where the vital energy (*prāṇa*) circulates through the upper and lower parts;
this is the nature of growth. This location is the primordial source of the initial reception of vital energy, and it is from here that light is emitted.
It is the position of *Dhanu* (the Bow), the juncture between beginning and end, the source of growth—this is precisely within the fast. Furthermore, it symbolizes the locus.

Within the interval between wisdom and compassion, the perfection of wisdom is the *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair) between the eyebrows; the perfection of great compassion is the *ūṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance).
Therefore, this is the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), the gate of Samantabhadra abiding in the world to benefit sentient beings.

It remedies the obstacles of the tenth stage—namely, the lack of mastery in supramundane conditions for benefiting sentient beings and the lack of vastness in one's conduct—just as [the previous stages remedy their respective hindrances].

In the Chapter on Concentration (*Samādhi-paṭala*), when the various Bodhisattvas seek and search for Samantabhadra and do not see him, this refers to the primary leadership and governance of the ocean-gate of the *pāramitās* within the Dharma-realm through the practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) amidst great wisdom.
It is further stated that all Buddhas of the three periods of time take compassion as their initial birth; without compassion for benefiting sentient beings, there would be weariness with birth.

Death is precisely the point at which those of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the Pure Land—those who have subsequently turned their minds toward the stream that can eventually attain the true fixed nature—will be reborn;
it will take many kalpas before they can return [to the path]. The rest is self-evident in the sutra itself. I know only this:
for the Bodhisattva of Great Vows, Wisdom-Illusion, and Liberation, when clearly investigating the advancement of virtue, there are three gates, the first of which demonstrates the spiritual friend.
It is said that in the Heaven of the Thirty-three there are two kings named Samprajanya; the three daughters of these kings are named Devendraprabhā.
Go and ask them about the conduct of a bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path.
The second is the daughter of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven’s King of Right Mindfulness, named Sovereign Light of the Heavenly Lord;
she masters wisdom and compassion and possesses the gateway of right mindfulness toward all phenomena, which is never lost and ever-present.
[Sūtra] At that time, Sudhana went to the celestial palace, saw that goddess, prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her, and standing before her with palms joined, said:

"Noble Lady, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard, Noble Lady..."
"You are well able to guide and instruct; I pray that you will speak for me. The goddess replied, "Noble son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Pure Adornment of Unimpeded Mindfulness.
Noble son, by the power of this liberation, I remember that in the past there was a most excellent eon named Blue Lotus (*utpala*).
In that eon, I made offerings to as many [Buddhas] as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
I have personally attended, protected, and made offerings to all those Buddhas, Tathāgatas,

from the time they first left home until they dwelt in their mothers’ wombs as Bodhisattvas, at the time of their birth, when they took seven steps, when they uttered the Great Lion’s Roar, and while they remained in the palace during their youth. I constructed monasteries for them and provided all necessary articles.

At the time of sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, attaining perfect enlightenment, turning the wheel of the true Dharma, and manifesting the miraculous transformations of a Buddha to teach, transform, and subdue sentient beings—I clearly remember all such deeds from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the exhaustion of the Dharma, without exception;
they are ever present before me, held in mindfulness without being forgotten. Furthermore, I remember...
In a past kalpa named *Sudhara*, I made offerings to Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers.
Furthermore, in a past kalpa named *Guna-vyuha*, I made offerings to Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms within a single Buddha-world.
Moreover, in a kalpa named *Anupalabdhi*, I made offerings to eighty-four billion [Buddhas].
During another kalpa named Good Light, ten thousand nayutas of Buddha-Tathāgatas appeared, and I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa.

During another kalpa named Immeasurable Light, I made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in twenty Ganges Rivers. During another kalpa named Supreme Virtue, I made offerings to them as well.
In another kalpa named "Good Compassion," I made offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River.
In another kalpa named "Supreme Roaming," I made offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in eighty Ganges Rivers.
In another kalpa named "Wondrous Moon," I made offerings to [as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in] seven...
"O son of good family, in this manner I have recollected ten times as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have never abandoned those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
From all those Tathāgatas, I heard this Bodhisattva liberation called 'Pure Adornment of Unobstructed Mindfulness,' which I have received, upheld, practiced, and never forgotten."

I have clearly recollected, vividly manifested before me, maintained, and practiced in accordance with all the deeds performed by the Tathāgatas throughout all previous eons— from their initial stage as bodhisattvas until the exhaustion of the Dharma— by means of the power of my liberation of pure adornment,
never once becoming weary or negligent. Noble son, I know only this liberation of the purity of unimpeded mindfulness.
All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have emerged from the night of birth-and-death with brilliant clarity, forever departing from the darkness of delusion;
they never fall into昏沉 (torpor) or 睡眠 (drowsiness), their minds are free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and their physical conduct is tranquil and light.

They possess pure awakening regarding the nature of all phenomena, have accomplished the ten powers (*daśabala*), and enlighten all sentient beings. How could I, O son of good family, know or speak of their meritorious conduct?
"In the city of Kapilavastu, there is a teacher of youths named Viśvāmitra; go to him and ask how a bodhisattva learns the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana, filled with joy and exultation because he had heard the Dharma, his inconceivable roots of goodness naturally increased and expanded;
he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave.
He withdrew and departed. [Treatise]:

The king was named *Samprajanya* (Right Mindfulness). His wisdom was pure and sovereign, like that of a celestial king. "Right Mindfulness" signifies that his pure wisdom is free from discursive thought (*amanasikāra*) yet sovereign;
he acts in accordance with principle without deliberate effort, and thus all affairs are accomplished spontaneously. This clarifies the tenth [chapter].
The pure wisdom of the first bhūmi manifests spontaneously within the stage of the ten abodes; it is merely called the "Heavenly Son of Right Mindfulness.

When asked about his brahmacarya, he does not yet mention having a daughter. Upon reaching this eleventh bhūmi, he is called a "King," and it is further stated that he has a daughter, clarifying that compassion arises from wisdom.
The daughter named "Light of the Heavenly Lord" symbolizes non-conceptualizing wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*).
The nature of great compassion within is untainted, functioning at will for the benefit of sentient beings. This stage represents the perfection of wisdom, whose activity is without before or after.
It takes the celestial realm as its locus; yet, while manifesting divine transformations freely within the midst of birth and death, it is not confined to any specific location.
I respectfully state my aspiration: may I attain the Bodhisattva liberation named "Unobstructed Recollection."
One who clarifies unimpeded mindfulness attains the unimpeded wisdom of the three periods of time. In a single thought-moment, they seal the past, present, and future;

they universally know in a single thought-moment the duration of the birth-and-death kalpas of all sentient beings across the ancient and modern eras and the future, as well as the duration of the kalpas in which all Buddhas of the three periods attain enlightenment.
Through the wisdom of non-delusive thought, they understand everything clearly and perfectly, as if it were manifest before them right now.
Since all phenomena manifesting before one are fundamentally thus, this clarifies the wisdom of right mindfulness that is free from deluded thoughts.
Within this, regarding the number of Buddhas throughout all kalpas— whether one makes offerings to many Buddhas or few across those kalpas,
such fluctuations being indefinite— it is the universal wisdom of non-thought within a single thought-moment.
To make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time in their full number—this is the state wherein there is neither long nor short, yet within the long and the short.
It is the realm of the great perfect wisdom that is fundamentally timeless; the Dharma is naturally thus, not produced through cultivation.

Those who cultivate merely reflect upon themselves, realizing the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby transforming delusion into wisdom. Since this wisdom has nothing to be cultivated, one simply attains liberation through self-understanding.
Deluded regarding the truth, there is nothing that can be acted upon, nor is there the nature of the three periods of time or of antiquity and modernity;
this is the second stage of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*) of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Following the second stage of the eleven stages of spiritual friends, this section generally clarifies the body of practice for gathering and benefiting sentient beings through the pervasive and all-encompassing application of unimpeded wisdom within right mindfulness.
In this world-system, as well as in all worlds throughout the ten directions, the six realms of existence and so forth are likewise universally born from the ocean of Māyā’s great compassion;
they take as their essence the wisdom of non-action through right mindfulness.

This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) within the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), because it is the gate through which compassion arises from wisdom; thus, the woman is named Devendrābhā (Light of the Lord of Devas).
Third, the section on the master Viśvāmitra, the youth of Kapilavastu, who pervades the ten directions and serves as a teacher and model for the world.

[Sūtra] Descending from the celestial palace, he gradually proceeded toward that city and arrived at the place of Viśvāmitra; prostrating at his feet, circumambulating him, and joining his palms, he paid his respects with reverence.

Respectfully standing to one side, he said to him: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. Viśvāmitra replied: "Good son, this..."
There is a youth named Śāriputra who studies the bodhisattva’s knowledge of characters; you should question him, and he will explain it for you.
[Treatise] The city of Kapilavastu—this is translated as "Yellow City. "Yellow" refers to the middle [region].

Because his complexion was naturally bright, he served as a teacher for this youth; he did not depart from the path of the Middle Way, yet he governed according to secular classics, much like the lineage of Confucius in this land.
He was a manifest master of the world, a gateway like that of Confucius. His head was shaped like a roof eave turned downward, and he dwelt in the secular world practicing the way of humility.
He manifested the Dharma through his physical form, resembling Mount Niqiu in appearance—just like that mountain.
To claim that the names "upper," "middle," and "lower" arose because they were not caused by Mount Tai and were merely conventional designations born of sacrificial rites is incorrect.
Those of the Kong clan are sages; they have no fixed name and no fixed nature. Their name and clan were established based on their virtue, rather than being derived from a common secular surname.

It was based on their virtue that they possessed the quality of breadth and clarity, and thus they took "Kong" as their clan name. "Kong" signifies breadth; through their conduct, they transformed the ignorant.

He is named Qiu. "Qiu" is a designation for a mountain. Since the hexagram Gen represents the mountain, the young male, and the state of childhood ignorance, this name was established based on his transformative conduct;
thus he is named Qiu. Furthermore, because his virtue transcends the mundane, he is named Qiu;
and because his supreme virtue is so dignified and stable that it possesses a nature impervious to being shaken or moved, he is named Qiu from birth.
That which is in Yanzhou is the division of Gen; it presides over the transformation of young boys and the position of the "ignorant and childlike" (dunmong).
Yanzhou above corresponds to the Asterism Jiao (The Horn), which is the Gate of Heaven and presides over the gate of all virtues.
It also presides over monks, nuns, and Daoist priests, who are born by riding upon the energy of Jiao. This is not something that ordinary worldly people can embody; therefore, Sudhana arrived there.
That this friend, Samantabhadra, did not speak further but instead sent Sudhana to the place of Viśvāmitra follows the correct method of a teacher:
one does not personally instruct in every matter, but entrusts them to an assistant teacher; matters that cannot be decided are referred to the primary master for guidance.
Thus, virtue is never solitary, for it must have its neighbors; by supporting and completing one another, their transformative influence is carried out.
The fourth is the gate of the wisdom of the characters that pervade the ten directions, belonging to the youth Sudhana-kumāra, Master of All Arts.
[Sūtra] At that time, Sudhana went to his place, prostrated with his head at his feet in reverence, and standing to one side, said:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know the bodhisattva..."
"How does one study the bodhisattva practices? How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? I heard these words and said, "I pray that the Noble One will instruct me well;
please explain this to me. At that time, the youth replied to Sudhana, "Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Skillfully Knowing All Arts.
I constantly chant and uphold these phonemes (*akṣara*). When I chant the letter *A*, I enter into *parinirvāṇa*..."
If one recites the syllable *ta*, there is an entrance into the Prajñāpāramitā gateway called "Entering the Non-differentiated Realm through the Power of Bodhisattvas.
When one recites the syllable *pa*, there is an entrance into the Prajñāpāramitā gateway called "The Gateway of Boundless Differentiation.
When one recites the syllable *cha*, there is an entrance into the Prajñāpāramitā gateway called "Universally Illuminating the Dharma-realm."
The gate named "Universal Wheel Severing Distinctions" is entered when pronouncing the syllable *na*;
the gate named "Attaining the Supportless and Unsurpassed" is entered when pronouncing the syllable *ra*;
the gate named "Stainless Detachment from Reliance" is entered when pronouncing the syllable *ta* (light tone); and the gate named "Non-retrogressive Skillful Means" is entered...
When pronouncing the syllable *ba* (pó), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Vajra-Field" (*vajramaṇḍala*).
When pronouncing the syllable *ca* (chà), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Universal Wheel" (*samantacakra*).
When pronouncing the syllable *sa* (shā), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Ocean-Treasury" (*sāgaragarbha*). When pronouncing the syllable *va* (fú), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā...
The gate of the *pāramitā* called "Universal Birth and Abiding" is entered when pronouncing the syllable *Ṭa*;

the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Perfect Radiance" is entered when pronouncing the syllable *Cha*; the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Accumulation of Distinctions" is entered when pronouncing the syllable *Ṭha*;
and the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Universal Illumination" is entered [when pronouncing the syllable *Ta*].
When pronouncing the syllable *ka* to pacify afflictions, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Cloud of Non-Differentiation.
When pronouncing the syllable *sa* (suǒ-ě), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Pouring Down a Great Rain.

When pronouncing the syllable *ma*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Great Currents Turbulently Rushing with All Peaks Standing Side by Side. When pronouncing the syllable *ga* (upper tone)...

When pronouncing the syllable *kha*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Establishment. When pronouncing the syllable *tha* (pronounced as *thā*), one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Treasury of the Equality of True Suchness" (*tathatā*).

When pronouncing the syllable *ṣa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Purity of Entering the Ocean of the World. When pronouncing the syllable *sa*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā... [text continues]

The gate of the honey-door is named "Adornment of Mindfulness of All Buddhas"; when pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, one enters the Prajñāpāramitā door named "Observation and Discernment of All Multitudes of Dharmas.

When pronouncing the syllable *śa* (with the retroflex *ṣa*), one enters the Prajñāpāramitā door named "Light of the Wheel of the Teachings of All Buddhas in Accordance with Reality. When pronouncing the syllable *kī*, one enters the Prajñāpāramitā door...
When pronouncing the syllable *kṣa* (pronounced as *chǔ-wo*), one enters the gate of the *pāramitā* called the Treasury of Wisdom Cultivated on the Ground;
when pronouncing the syllable *sa* (pronounced as *sū-hē*, with the first tone), one enters the gate of the *pāramitā* called the Treasury that Quells the Ocean of All Karmas;
when pronouncing the syllable *ha* (pronounced as *huài*), one enters the gate of the *pāramitā* called Purifying All Obscurations of Delusion and Opening the Pure Radiance.

When the syllable *ha-la-ta* (upper tone) is chanted, the gate of the pāramitās called "Gate of Worldly Wisdom" enters the gate of the prajñāpāramitā called "Wisdom Wheel of the Realm of Birth and Death.

When the syllable *ba* (with the *pu-wo* rhyme) is chanted, the gate of the pāramitās called "Perfect Adornment of the Palace of All-Knowledge" enters [the gate of the prajñāpāramitā]. When the syllable *cha* (upper tone) is chanted...
When pronouncing the syllable *va*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of Expedient Means for Cultivation," in which each [practice] is individually perfected.
When pronouncing the syllable *bha* (pronounced with the *sū-hk* reversal), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Manifestly Beholding All Buddhas Throughout the Ten Directions.
When pronouncing the syllable *ha* (both *ha-bha* pronounced in the rising tone), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Observing the One."
When he skillfully gathers all sentient beings who lack conditions and causes them to give birth to the power of non-obstruction,
he enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Practicing Entry into the Ocean of All Meritorious Qualities" while pronouncing the syllable *Sra* (pronounced with the seventh tone).
When he pronounces the syllable *Ga*, he enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Firm Ocean-Treasury that Sustains All Dharma Clouds."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*, one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universally Beholding All Buddhas of the Ten Directions According to One’s Vows.
When pronouncing the syllable *ṇa* (pronounced as *nǚ kě*), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Observing the Syllable-Wheel with Its Inexhaustible Billions of Characters.
When pronouncing the syllable *sphā* (pronounced as *sū hē*), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Transformation."
When pronouncing the syllable *sa* (as before), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Radiant Wheel of Unimpeded Eloquence Pervading the Vast Treasury.
When pronouncing the syllable *ya* (pronounced as *yī* and *gě*), one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Proclaiming the Realm of All Buddha-Dharmas.
When pronouncing the syllable *śca* (pronounced as *shì* and *zhě*), [one enters a gate of Prajñāpāramitā].
Entering the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Universal Roar of the Dharma-Thunder throughout the Realm of All Sentient Beings" when pronouncing the syllable *ca*;
entering the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Awakening Sentient Beings through the Dharma of Non-Self" when pronouncing the syllable *ṭha*;
and entering the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Excellent Treasury of the Distinctions of All Dharma-Wheels."
"Good man, when I chant these syllables, these forty-two gateways to the *prajñāpāramitā* serve as the foremost entry into immeasurable and incalculable gateways to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Good man, I know only this liberation of the Bodhisattva Skillful in All Arts (*sarva-śilpa-jña*). As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are able to [manifest] all worldly and..."

Regarding the worldly arts of skillful means, he has reached the further shore through the penetration of wisdom; he comprehensively masters various distant regions and diverse crafts without omission.
He possesses profound understanding in writing and mathematics, and is skilled in medical prescriptions and incantations for effectively curing all manner of ailments.
There are sentient beings possessed by ghosts and demons, those afflicted by resentment, curses, or malignant stars, those pursued by wandering corpses, and those suffering from epilepsy.
He is able to cure all manner of ailments, such as emaciation and wasting, restoring them to full health.

Furthermore, he is skilled in discerning gold, silver, pearls, shells, coral, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, tridacna, kīcaka, and all other treasures, including their origins, their various classifications, and their respective values;
he also knows the villages, camps, towns, small and large cities, and palaces.

Whether it be gardens, groves, adorned springs, marshes, or any place inhabited by multitudes of people, the Bodhisattvas are able to provide protection and guidance for them according to their respective locations.

Furthermore, they skillfully observe celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography, human physiognomy and its auspicious or inauspicious signs, the cries of birds and beasts, clouds, mists, and seasonal climates, as well as the abundance or scarcity of crops and the security or instability of nations; there is no worldly art or craft that they do not master.

Having thoroughly trained in the fundamental source and being able to distinguish the supramundane Dharma by clarifying its names and defining its meanings, one observes its essential characteristics and practices accordingly.

When wisdom enters therein, one becomes free from doubt, free from hindrance, free from ignorance, free from dullness, free from sorrow and affliction, free from sinking, and free from anything that is not directly realized. How then could I possibly know or describe their merit?
"Virtuous son, in this kingdom of Magadha there is a village; within it is a city named Pāṭaliputra, where there dwells a female lay practitioner (upāsikā) named Bhadrāśrī.
Go to her and inquire: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva?
At that time, the youth Sudhana bowed his head in respectful salutation at the feet of Viditajñāna and circumambulated him.
After circumambulating countless times with longing and reverence, he took his leave.
[Treatise] Viśvāmitra said: "There was a youth here named Śilpakaṃḍa who studied the letters of the Bodhisattva;
the wise one is Viśvāmitra, the teacher, and the youth is the student. Their names were established according to their teachings, just as 'Kong' [Confucius] is in this land."
Among the disciples of the Master Kṛṣṇa (the Buddha), such as Yān Huí (Yan Hui), Sudhana paid his respects and inquired about what he sought.
The youth said, "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Skillfully Knowing All Arts. I constantly chant and maintain these syllables.
When I chant the letter *A*—which here signifies 'non-arising'—I enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called 'Bodhisattva.'"

The power of penetrating the non-differentiated realm and clearly realizing the gate of emptiness of all phenomena is the bodhisattva’s power to sever all obstructions and enter into effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) that pervades the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings. When pronouncing the syllable *Ta*,
one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Realm of Boundless Differentiation," which illuminates all modes of existence (*bhava*).
This wisdom of differentiation is the practice of Samantabhadra that universally knows the principles, practices, understandings,
and appropriate means for transforming all sentient beings within the three realms and six paths; thus, with the forty-two *prajñāpāramitā* gates as its primary elements,
it is called the "Matrices of Syllables" (*akṣara-mātṛkā*) that enter into immeasurable and innumerable *prajñāpāramitās*.
The gates are self-evident according to the text.
Fifth is the Gate of the Noble and Victorious Upāsikā Master of All Worldly Correct and Erroneous, Auspicious and Inauspicious Matters,
and Various Arts and Techniques, who Proclaims All and Thoroughly Understands Them for the Benefit of Sentient Beings.
[Sūtra] Approaching the village town, he went to where Bhadrajyotis was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and with palms joined in reverence, stood to one side and said:

"Noble One, I have previously set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard, Noble One..."
"You are well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me. Wensheng replied, "Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'The Unreliant Site of Enlightenment.
Having realized it myself, I further explain it to others. I have also attained the inexhaustible samādhi.
It is not that the dharmas of that samādhi are either exhaustible or inexhaustible; rather, it is because it can give birth to the nature of all-knowledge and the eye of wisdom."
Because the ear is inexhaustible, it can give rise to the nature of all-knowledge;
because the nose is inexhaustible, it can give rise to the nature of all-knowledge; because the tongue is inexhaustible, it can give rise to the nature of all-knowledge;
because the body is inexhaustible, it can give rise to the nature of all-knowledge; because the mind is inexhaustible...
Because it is inexhaustible, it can further give rise to the inexhaustible waves of merit of the nature of all-knowledge;
because it is inexhaustible, it can further give rise to the inexhaustible light of wisdom of the nature of all-knowledge;

because it is inexhaustible, it can further give rise to the inexhaustible swift supernatural powers of the nature of all-knowledge. "Good son, I know only this liberation of the 'Place of Enlightenment Without Dependence.'"
How could I possibly know or fully describe the unattached conduct of all the merits of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas like you?
Son of good family, to the south there is a city named Kṣemavatī; there dwells an elder named Dṛḍhamukti.
You should go and ask him: "How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the laywoman Bhadrottamā, circumambulated her countless times, and with longing and veneration, took his leave and traveled south.
[Treatise] The laywoman Bhadrottamā was one who clearly understood the medical arts and various worldly crafts; there were no mundane or supramundane matters she did not master.

She provided for the well-being of beings and nourished life, such that there was no method she did not understand. While dwelling amidst the secular world, she used skillful means to benefit sentient beings. Or...

He composed extensive expositions on worldly divination and profound prognostication for those who had not yet attained realization; he acted as a skilled physician with excellent medicines to rescue the world from its unrest;
he distinguished precious objects to determine their authenticity and edited terminology to explain the meaning of the texts.

His extraordinary talents and unique wisdom were universally illuminating, such that he could subdue all malevolent spirits and demonic influences; his mind was equal to the ocean of wisdom of Samantabhadra.

The Dharma-body Buddha of the sublime fruit, personally transforming all spirits and myriad beings, reaches everywhere without limit, pervades every land without exception, performs every deed without exception, and saves every being without exception;
out of compassion, she manifests in a female body, her wisdom is all-enlightening, and she is named Śrīmatī (Wise and Victorious). The city gate of the Dhyāna-pāramitā is called Potalaka. This...
It is called "Joy" (Kṣema) because it increases virtue; it is named after its quality of greatly benefiting many people and increasing auspicious matters.
The *kīcaka* jewel is like the whorl of hair on a lion’s tail. Regarding the "place of practice without reliance" (*anāśraya-maṇḍala*):
the Dharma has no place of reliance, and the body likewise has no reliance, as it pervades the myriad practices. Because these practices have no intrinsic substance, it is located in South India.
Sixth, in the southern city of Pṛthu-kṣetra, the elder Dṛḍha-vimukti presides over the world;
his gate of liberation is the purity of mindfulness toward those who do not exist.
[Sūtra] Having arrived at that city, he went to the elder’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and with palms joined in reverence, stood to one side.

He stood up and addressed him in white words: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva-practice, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva-path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The elder replied: "Son of good family, I have attained the bodhisattva-understanding..."

This liberation is called "Pure Adornment of Unattached Mindfulness. Since I attained this liberation, I have diligently sought the True Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions without ceasing. Good son, I know only this liberation of the Pure Adornment of Unattached Mindfulness;
as for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the great lion-like fearlessness, I do not know them.
"O son of noble family, how could I know or describe the conduct and virtues of one who roars while abiding in a vast accumulation of merit and wisdom?
However, within this very city there is an elder named Moon of Excellence (*Candrasūrya*). In that elder's residence there is always a radiance;
go to him and ask: 'How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Dṛḍhamati, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave to depart.
[Treatise] There is a city in the south named Kṣemavatī. It is so named because this spiritual friend provides sustenance through the moisture of wisdom and virtue;
as people there increase in goodness and their virtues become profound, it was established with that name. Thus, the elder’s name is Dṛḍhamati (Firm Resolve).
The liberated one clearly seeks the Dharma without indolence, as he himself said: "At that time, Sudhana went to him, paid his respects, and requested what he sought.
The elder said: 'I have attained the adornment of non-attached, pure mindfulness;
this is the sixth, the adornment of the wisdom of signless prajñā. It is such that regarding the mindfulness of all phenomena, it is itself without attachment.'"
Also: The seventh is the Gate of the Radiance of Pure Wisdom, presided over by the Elder Sun-Moon (Candrasūrya) in the city of Pūrṇakalpa.
[Sūtra] He approached the place where Sun-Moon was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, joined his palms in reverence, stood to one side, and said to him: "O Noble One..."
"I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will explain this to me.
Miochandra replied, "Son of good family, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Pure Wisdom' (*viśuddha-jñāna*)."
"O son of noble family Prabhāsa, I know only this liberation of the light of wisdom.
As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have realized immeasurable dharma-gates of liberation, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Son of noble family, to the south of here there is a city named Utpala; in it dwells a householder named Ajitasena."
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Candracchattra, circumambulated him countless times, and with longing and reverence, took his leave, saying:
[Treatise] In this city there was an elder named Moon of Wonder (Candraprabha). Herein, it clarifies the sixth gate of signless wisdom within the assembly of elders;

because the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) constitutes its single essence, it elucidates the gate of the threefold emptiness and signlessness of the sixth stage prior to the ten stages. This is the supramundane liberation.
Within the eleven stages subsequent to the Ground (bhūmi), there is the gate of wisdom of the threefold emptiness and cessation;

this is where, in the world, the seventh perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) is accomplished. It is non-dual and of one essence with great compassion, for it is born from the illusory wisdom of the Mother of Great Compassion.
This final stage occurs within the seventh and eighth positions among the ten abodes (vihāra) and ten grounds (bhūmi).
One must understand that within these eleven stages, the sixth and seventh stages are harmonized into a single essence; such is the nature of the process of advancement.
When Sudhana went to pay his respects, prostrate, and request what he sought from the Elder Moon of Wondrous Radiance (Candracchattra), the Elder said:
"I know only this liberation called 'Pure Wisdom Light'. This was stated by the Elder Moon of Wondrous Radiance.
The virtue established here is named "Luminosity of Compassionate Wisdom" (maitrī-karuṇā-jñāna-prabhā), which signifies the destruction of delusions;

it is so named because it destroys the delusions of worldly sentient beings through compassion that benefits others. This clarifies that the three voids, compassion, and pure wisdom are collectively a single unity in which essence and function are perfected.
Eighth, in the southern city of Janmanagara, the elder Anīkajita attained the gate of the inexhaustible mark within the dharma of signlessness.
[Sūtra] He gradually proceeded toward that city, arrived at the elder’s residence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and with palms joined in reverence, stood to one side.

He stood up and addressed him in white words: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The Elder replied: "Good son, I have attained the bodhisattva understanding..."

"Good son, my liberation is called 'the mark of inexhaustibility. Having realized this bodhisattva liberation, I see immeasurable Buddhas and attain an inexhaustible treasury. Good son, I know only this liberation of the mark of inexhaustibility;
as for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained infinite wisdom and unimpeded eloquence, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?"
"Noble son, to the south of this city there is a village named Dharma. In that village there is a brahmin named Paramaśānta;
go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Anābhibhū, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave with deep longing and reverence.
[He] departed.

[Treatise]: Regarding the "South," according to the first interpretation, there is a city named "Birth" (*Janma*), which symbolizes the eighth vow, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), because it gives birth to all dharmas and various practices.
The elder’s name, "Invincible Army" (*Ajitasena*), symbolizes victory over all.

Because he was beset by the demonic armies of ignorance, pride, birth-and-death, and false views—all of which are like wicked thieves—he, the virtuous youth Sudhana, went to pay his respects and inquire about what he sought.
The elder replied: "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Inexhaustible Appearance.
This clarifies that all mental objects and states are, in their totality, the appearance of the Tathāgata; within a single pore, they are produced moment after moment."
Within the principle of the exhaustion of all marks and the absence of thought, how could there be any mark of exhaustion produced by the illusion of wisdom?
This is the ninth gate: the Gate of the Sincere Vow of the Brahmin Lord Most Tranquil in the Dharma Village to the South of the City of Birth.

[Sūtra] Gradually traveling south, he arrived at that village and saw Most Tranquil (Sāntamati). He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and with palms joined in reverence, stood to one side and said:

"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva-practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva-path."
"I have heard that the Holy One is skilled in providing instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me.
The Brahmin replied, "Son of good family, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Speech of Sincere Vows.
Because of this speech, bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future never regress from their pursuit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor have they ever done so."
There is no present falling back and no future falling back. Good son, because I abide in speech of sincere vows, whatever I do according to my will is never not fulfilled.
Good son, I know only this liberation of the speech of sincere vows;
as for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are never at variance in their conduct with the speech of sincere vows, whose words are always sincere and never false—I do not know them.
"How could I possibly know or speak of the birth of these causes for immeasurable, false merits?
Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Sumanāmukha. There is a boy there named Śrīsaṃbhava and a girl named Guṇavatī.
Go to them and ask: How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate it?"

When the Bodhisattva was on his way, the youth Sudhana, out of reverence for the Dharma, prostrated at the feet of the brahmin, circumambulated him countless times, and departed with longing and veneration.
[Treatise] To the south of this city there is a village named Dharmavardhana, inhabited by many people; it is called a settlement.
That which is designated as "Dharma" by virtue of having no intrinsic nature is taken here as "quiescence. Within this name, there is a Brahmin whose personal name is Most Quiescent (*Paramaśānta*);
both his clan name and his given name are entirely quiescent. This represents the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
Whether conforming to worldly convention or transcending it, the assembly is not noisy; this is called the mastery of power and function. Sudhana went to visit him and arrived.
I respectfully prostrate and request that which is sought, saying: "May I attain the Bodhisattva liberation named 'The Words of Sincere Aspiration'.
Here, "sincere" (*satya*) means reality; it clarifies that the basis of one's aspiration is truthful and free from false speech.

This is the speech of a person of faith, spoken according to the heart's vow, relying on truth and devoid of deception; the substance of the speech is true, and that which is aspired for is likewise so.
Because all are real, the names, phrases, and syllables, as well as sounds, expressions, and all that is spoken, are entirely real by nature.
This constitutes liberation; this is the station of the Dharma Master. Representing the dharma-realm as a village, all verbal discourse is itself the true person and the Dharma;
everything is thus. This represents the fact that speech is not false.
The tenth is the Gate of the City of Virtuous Birth, Adorned with Flowers of Sublime Intent, where the youth Śrīsaṃbhava and the maiden Guṇavatī dwell, having perfected wisdom and compassion,
abiding in the world through the gate of illusory manifestation. [Sūtra] At that time,
the youth Sudhana proceeded gradually to the south until he reached the city of Adorned with Flowers of Sublime Intent and beheld Śrīsaṃbhava.
The virtuous boy and the virtuous girl prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and then, with palms joined before him, spoke these words:

"Noble One, we have already set our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet we do not know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practices, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path. We only pray that you, out of compassion, will [instruct us]."
While I was proclaiming this, the boys and girls said to Sudhana: "Noble son, we have realized the bodhisattva liberation called 'Abiding as an Illusion.
Because we have attained this liberation, we see that all worlds abide as illusions, being produced by causes and conditions;
we see that all sentient beings abide as illusions, arising from karma and afflictions."
The world is entirely an illusory abode, for it arises through the successive conditions of ignorance, craving, and so forth;

all phenomena are entirely an illusory abode, for they are produced by various illusory conditions such as the view of self; all three periods of time are entirely an illusory abode, for they are produced by the inverted cognition of the view of self and so forth;
and all sentient beings experience birth and death, aging, sickness, and death, as well as sorrow, lamentation, and suffering.

All afflictions are illusory abodes, for they are produced by false conceptualization; all lands are illusory abodes, for they are manifested by the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, the inversion of views, and ignorance; all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are illusory abodes, for they are constituted by the conceptualization of wisdom and abandonment;
and all bodhisattvas are illusory abodes, for they are able to self-discipline and transform sentient beings.

Because it is accomplished through the dharmas of the vows and practices for birth, all the assemblies of bodhisattvas, their transformations, their taming activities, and all their deeds are "abiding in illusion," being accomplished by the illusion of vow and wisdom.
Noble son, the self-nature of illusory objects is inconceivable. Noble son, we two can only know this liberation of abiding in illusion as it truly is.
"How can we know or describe the meritorious conduct of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have skillfully entered the illusory net of boundless phenomena?
At that time, after the boys and girls had spoken of their own liberations,
they used the power of inconceivable roots of goodness to make Sudhana’s body supple, radiant, and lustrous, and addressed him, saying:

[Treatise] In this southern region there is a city named Supuṣpamukha (Wonderful Flower Gate), which symbolizes the fulfillment of the ten dharmas of the eleventh stage because the flowers of wondrous wisdom and conduct are all perfectly complete.
Therein dwells a youth named Śrīsaṃbhava (Birth of Virtue) and a maiden named Guṇavatī (Possessing Virtue);
because their two practices of wisdom and compassion are equal and balanced without precedence or succession, they are called "Children" (kumāra).

The son and the maiden possessed wisdom and compassion in equal measure; though dwelling in the world, they were free from thoughts of the five desires because they resided in the "illusory abode" (*māyā-vihāra*).
Sudhana went to them, prostrated, paid his respects, and requested what he sought, saying:
"We have realized the Bodhisattva liberation called 'Illusory Abode. Regarding both the realm of the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings..."

Born from the illusion of wisdom, one dwells within the realm of illusion, which is neither real nor unreal. Where there is no consciousness or emotion, both the subjective mind and its objects vanish;
nature and characteristics are unimpeded due to the merit of wisdom. Thus, illusory bodies and lands arise as layers upon layers, like Indra’s net.
Bodies and environments, realms and appearances, interpenetrate one another in all ten directions, free from obstruction.

The wisdom that penetrates the worlds of the ten directions is, in its essence, thoroughly pervasive, without beginning or end, and unifies past and present within a single nature that abides eternally.
It has no place of reliance within the world, for it clarifies that the nature of worldly phenomena is inherently detached from dependent origination;
that suchness is a false provisional designation; that the essence of delusion is fundamentally non-existent; and that the true is without abiding. Thus, wisdom has no reliance.

Because it is like empty space, and because both wisdom and retribution-born bodies are all illusory abodes; because existence and non-existence are sovereign as they accord with the function of wisdom;

and because although the essence of wisdom is identical to emptiness, it does not abide in quiescence—thus the body of wisdom is immeasurable and pervades the ten directions equally, its nature being without coming or going, like the marks of light and shadow;
and because body and land are layered and interpenetrating, without large or small. As the Sūtra says: "The realm of illusion."
The self-nature is inconceivable.
*The Combined Commentary on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha*, Fascicle 115.
