Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty.
The Treatise composed by Li Tongxuan, Elder of Fangshan in Taiyuan of the Tang Dynasty;
the Sūtra collated and the Treatise combined by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou of the Tang Dynasty;
Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Three through Eleven: Entering the Dharma Realm.
[Sūtra] "Good son, the bodhicitta accomplishes such immeasurable merits. To state the essentials:
you should know that it is equal to all the merits of all Buddha-dharmas. Why is this?
Because all bodhisattva practices are born from the bodhicitta, and the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are born from the bodhicitta."

Therefore, noble son, if there are those who resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they have already given birth to immeasurable merit and are universally able to encompass the path to all-knowledge.
Noble son, it is as if there were a person who obtained the medicine of fearlessness and became free from five terrors. What are these five? Namely: fire cannot burn them, nor can poison [harm them].
It cannot be pierced by swords, it cannot be harmed by water, it cannot be swept away by waves, and it cannot be smoked out by fire.

In the same way, O son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has obtained the medicine of the bodhicitta of omniscience is not burned by the fire of greed, not struck by the poison of anger, not wounded by the sword of delusion, not swept away by the currents of existence, and cannot be harmed by the smoke of discursive thought and mental examination. Son of good family, it is like this: [the simile continues].
Just as a person who has obtained the medicine of liberation will never encounter untimely calamities, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
having obtained the medicine of the wisdom of liberation that is the bodhicitta, they are forever free from all untimely calamities of birth and death.
Good son, it is like a person who holds the mahā-aṅgada medicine; when a venomous snake merely smells its scent, it immediately flees far away. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: by holding the great *āṅgīra* medicine of the bodhicitta, all poisonous snakes of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) that smell its scent are entirely dispersed and extinguished. Good son, it is as if there were a person holding the "Invincible" (*anabhibhūta*) medicine;
no enemy whatsoever is able to overcome them. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: by holding the bodhi...
The resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is the supreme medicine that cannot be surpassed; it is capable of subduing all the armies of Māra.
Good son, it is just as if there were a person who, by holding the *vighuṣṭa* medicine, could cause poisoned arrows to fall away of their own accord.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by holding the *vighuṣṭa* medicine of the resolve for enlightenment, causes the arrows of greed, hatred, delusion, and all false views to fall away spontaneously.
However, O fallen son of good family, it is like a person who holds the *sudarśana* medicine, which can eliminate all existing diseases;
so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva, who holds the *sudarśana* king of medicines that is the bodhicitta, and thereby completely eliminates all diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Son of good family, it is as if there were a medicinal tree named *saṃdhāna*, which, when taken—
If its bark is applied to a sore, the sore is immediately healed; yet, as the tree bark is taken, it grows back again, never being exhausted.
In the same way, the Tree of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā-vṛkṣa*) born from the Bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:
if anyone beholds it and gives rise to faith, the sores of their afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are entirely eliminated by the Tree of All-Knowledge.
From the beginning, there is no harm done to it. Good son, it is like a medicinal tree named Rootless (Amūla), by whose power all the trees of Jambudvīpa grow;
so too is the Bodhicitta-tree of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for by its power all the wholesome dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and all bodhisattvas increase.
"Noble son, it is like a medicine named Ālambā; when applied to the body, both the body and the mind become fully capable.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtains the Ālambā medicine of the bodhicitta, their body and mind likewise cause the increase of wholesome dharmas. Noble son, it is like a person who obtains the medicine of mindfulness."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who remembers and maintains all that he has heard without forgetting possesses the wondrous medicine of the power of mindfulness of the bodhicitta;
he is able to hear and maintain all Buddha-dharmas without ever losing them. Good son, it is like a medicine named Mahāpadma:
whoever consumes it dwells for the duration of a kalpa. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who consumes the bodhicitta is likewise.
The great medicinal lotus is likewise so; it grants mastery over life for incalculable eons, O son of good family.
For example, if a person were to take a medicine that renders one invisible, neither humans nor non-humans would be able to see them.

In the same way, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes up the wondrous medicine of invisibility that is the bodhicitta, none of the māras can see them. Son of good family, it is like this:

In the ocean there is a jewel named "Universal Gatherer of All Treasures. If this jewel were present, even if the kalpa-fire were to burn and consume the world, it would be impossible for this ocean to diminish by even a single drop. It is the same with the bodhicitta-jewel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
as long as it abides within the great ocean of the bodhisattva’s vows and is constantly recollected and maintained without being allowed to regress, [the ocean of the Dharma will never dry up].
It is impossible for one who has lost the capacity to destroy even a single root of goodness of a bodhisattva;
if their resolve were to regress, all wholesome dharmas would immediately vanish and be extinguished. Good son, it is as if there were a mani jewel named "Great Radiance";
whoever adorns their body with a necklace of this jewel will outshine all other precious ornaments, such that the light of all those things no longer appears.
The jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this:
it adorns their body and outshines all the jewel-like ornaments of the minds of those of the two vehicles, leaving them entirely without luster.
Good son, just as the water-purifying pearl can clear turbid water, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, for it can purify the one [vehicle].

Son of good family, all afflictions are turbid like impurities; it is just as if there were a person who, having obtained the *jalamdhara* jewel, fastened it to his body and entered the great ocean, remaining unharmed by the water.
In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise obtains the wondrous jewel that dwells in the water of the bodhicitta; entering the ocean of all saṃsāra, he never sinks. Son of good family!
For example, suppose there is a person who obtains a dragon-jewel and enters a dragon palace; no dragons or snakes can cause him harm.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who obtains the great dragon-jewel of the bodhicitta cannot be harmed by the dragons and snakes of the afflictions when entering the desire realm. Good son, it is like Śakra wearing a maṇi crown.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva also outshines all other hosts of devas by wearing the great vow-jewel crown of the bodhicitta.
Son of good family, it is like a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) and thereby eliminates all the suffering of poverty; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this.
This son of good family, having attained the wish-fulfilling jewel of the bodhicitta, is far removed from all fear of wrong livelihood.
For example, just as someone who obtains a sun-crystal gem holds it toward the sunlight and fire is produced, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
having obtained the wisdom-sun jewel of bodhicitta, he holds it toward the light of wisdom and wisdom is produced.
Fire, son of good family, it is just as if there were a person who obtained a moon-essence gem (*candrakānta-maṇi*) and, holding it toward the light of the moon, produced water.
In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains the moon-essence jewel of the bodhicitta;
holding this jewel of the mind, they reflect upon the light of dedication and produce the water of all roots of goodness and vows. Son of good family, it is just as with a dragon king...
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who wears the crown of the wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewel upon his head is likewise freed from all fear of enemies.
Son of good family, it is like a precious gem named "Treasury of Adornments for All Worlds"; whoever obtains it, [is never again separated from it].
It causes all that they desire to be completely fulfilled, yet this precious jewel suffers no diminution.
The jewel of the bodhicitta is also like this: if anyone obtains it, it causes all their aspirations to be fully satisfied, yet the bodhicitta suffers no diminution.
Noble son, it is as if a wheel-turning monarch possesses a maṇi jewel which he places within his palace.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Emitting Great Radiance to Destroy All Darkness likewise dwells in the desire realm by means of the great maṇi-jewel of the bodhicitta;
therefore, the light of great wisdom completely destroys the dark ignorance of all realms of existence.
Son of good family, it is like this: if there is anyone touched by the radiance of a great sapphire maṇi-jewel...
In the same way, the jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this:
when observing all phenomena and dedicating their roots of goodness, there is nothing that does not become identical to the color of bodhicitta.

Son of good family, it is as if a vaidūrya jewel were to remain amidst impurities for hundreds of thousands of years; because its nature is fundamentally pure, it is not defiled by foul odors or filth.

The jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: even while dwelling within the desire realm for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it is not defiled by the faults and afflictions of the desire realm, because its nature is as pure as the dharmadhātu.
Son of good family, it is like a jewel named Pure Radiance (*viśuddhaprabhā*), which is able to completely outshine the colors of all other jewels; so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The jewel of the bodhicitta is likewise able to completely eclipse all the merits of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, O son of good family.
For example, there is a jewel named "Flame" that can utterly extinguish all darkness;
in the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s jewel of bodhicitta can extinguish all the darkness of ignorance.
Good son, it is as if there were a priceless jewel in the ocean that a merchant acquires and boards upon a ship to bring into the city;
among all other kinds of *maṇi* jewels numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, none can equal its radiance, color, or value.
The jewel of the bodhicitta is likewise: dwelling within the great ocean of birth and death, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva mounts the vessel of the Great Vow.
The ship, with its profound mind continuing in succession, carries them to enter the city of liberation; no merit of the two vehicles can equal it.
Son of good family, it is like a precious jewel named Sovereign King (*Vajrarāja*) located on Jambudvīpa, forty thousand *yojanas* from the orbs of the sun and moon;
all the adornments within the palaces of the sun and moon are fully reflected in its shadow.

In the same way, the jewel of the pure merit of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has resolved upon the mind of enlightenment likewise abides within the cycle of birth and death, illuminating the emptiness of the dharma-realm; the sun and moon of Buddha-wisdom and all merits appear therein.
Good son, it is like a precious gem named Sovereign King (*Vaiśrāvaṇarāja*), in the places illuminated by the light of the sun and moon, all manner of treasures appear.
The value of all such things as clothing and other objects cannot compare with that of the sovereign jewel of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva;

it is likewise with all the meritorious virtues—whether mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows—of all devas and humans, and of those of the two vehicles, throughout the three times wherever the light of omniscience shines. Good son, none can equal them.
In the ocean there is a treasure called "Ocean Treasury" (Sāgaragarbha) which universally manifests all manner of adornments within the sea;
likewise, the Bodhicitta jewel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to universally manifest all the adornments of the ocean of omniscience.
Son of good family, it is like the Jāmbūnada gold of the heavens, which, with the sole exception of the great Mani-jewel of the Mind-King, surpasses all other things.

Nothing else can equal it; likewise, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), nothing else can equal it, except for the great jewel-king of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
Son of good family, it is as if there were a person skilled in the methods of taming dragons who attains mastery over all dragons; so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
This is the method for taming dragons through the attainment of the bodhicitta; one attains mastery over all the dragons of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Good son, it is like a valiant warrior clad in armor and wielding weapons whom no enemy can subdue;
likewise, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, clad in the armor and wielding the weapons of the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), [cannot be overcome] by any karma.
No delusions, evil ones, or enemies are able to subdue it. Son of good family, it is like the black sandalwood incense of the heavens:
if one *zhu* is burned, its fragrance pervades a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*).
The total value of all the precious jewels that fill a three-thousandfold world system cannot equal it. The incense of the bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this.
The merit of this single thought universally perfumes the Dharma-realm; the merits of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot compare to it.

Good son, just as white sandalwood, when applied to the body, can completely eliminate all feverish afflictions and cause both body and mind to attain universal coolness, so too is the fragrance of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
This is able to eliminate all the feverish afflictions of false conceptualization, greed, hatred, delusion, and other such defilements, causing one to be fully endowed with the coolness of wisdom.
Good son, it is like Mount Sumeru: if anyone approaches it, they immediately become the same color as the mountain.
The mountain of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this; if anyone approaches it, they all attain the same state.
O son of good family Sarvajñatāvarṇa, it is just as, for example, the fragrance of the bark of the pārijātaka tree cannot be matched by any of the fragrances of flowers such as the vārṣika,
campaka, or sumana found within Jambudvīpa; likewise, the Bodhicitta-tree of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also thus.
The fragrance of the merit of these great vows that have been made cannot be equaled by any of the fragrances of the untainted precepts,
concentrations, wisdoms, liberations, or the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to those of the two vehicles, O son of good family. For example,
although the pārijātaka tree has not yet blossomed, one should know that it is the source from which immeasurable flowers will arise.
In the same way, the Bodhicitta-tree of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, though it has not yet blossomed with the flowers of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
should be known as the source from which the Bodhi-flowers of countless devas and humans arise. Son of good family, for example,
if one were to perfume a garment with the fragrance of the Pārijātaka flower for a single day, it would surpass the scent of the Campaka, the Paribhadra, and other such flowers.
"Good son, although the *sumana* flower may be perfumed for a thousand years, its fragrance cannot equal that of the bodhicitta-flower of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
It is likewise with this: the fragrance of the various merits perfumed throughout a single lifetime pervades all the abodes of the Buddhas in the ten directions;
it cannot be matched by the fragrance of the untainted (*anāsrava*) merits of all those of the two vehicles, even if they were perfumed for hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
Just as on an island in the ocean there grows a coconut tree whose roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers,
and fruits are constantly utilized by all sentient beings without a moment’s rest, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s tree of the bodhicitta;
from its initial arousal of the heart of compassionate vows until the attainment of Buddhahood and the duration of the True Dharma in the world, it constantly benefits [beings].
Benefiting all the world without interruption, son of good family, it is as if there were a medicinal extract named *harītaka*;
if someone were to obtain even one *liang* of it, it could transform a thousand *liang* of copper entirely into pure gold, yet those thousand *liang* of copper could not transform this medicine.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of the wisdom of dedication through the bodhicitta, likewise [transforms all].
Medicine universally transforms all dharmas such as karma and afflictions, causing them all to become the marks of omniscience;

it is not karma or afflictions that can transform the mind. Good son, just as a small fire blazes ever more fiercely as it consumes whatever it burns, so too is the fire of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
its flame of wisdom increases in accordance with whatever it takes as an object of focus.
"Good son, it is like this: for example, when one lamp is lit to ignite hundreds of thousands of lamps, that original single lamp neither diminishes nor is exhausted.

In the same way, the lamp of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise universally ignites the lamps of the wisdom of all Buddhas of the three times, yet its own lamp of mind neither diminishes nor is exhausted.
Good son, it is like this: for example, when a single lamp enters a dark room..."
Just as a lamp can completely destroy the darkness of hundreds or thousands of years, so too is the lamp of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva;

entering within the chamber of the hearts of sentient beings, it is able to utterly eliminate the various obscurations of darkness consisting of karma and afflictions throughout unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*. Good son, for example, a lamp wick [burns] according to its size.
And just as its radiance shines forth and its light never ceases when fresh oil is added, so too is the lamp of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

with the great vow as its wick, it illuminates the Dharma-realm; with the oil of great compassion, it teaches and transforms sentient beings, adorns the buddha-fields, and performs the works of a Buddha without rest. Son of good family, it is like, for example, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin [heaven].

Just as the celestial crown of Jambūnada gold worn by the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereignty (Īśvara) cannot be rivaled by any of the ornaments of the gods in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
the great vow-crown of the bodhicitta cannot be rivaled by the merits of any ordinary person or follower of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Noble son, he is like a lion king.
When the lion roars, the lion cubs who hear it all increase in courage and vigor; other beasts, upon hearing it, immediately flee and hide.
You should know that the roar of the Lion-King Buddha’s Bodhicitta is likewise:
when Bodhisattvas hear it, their merits increase, while those who cling to acquisitions all retreat and scatter. Son of Good Family, it is as if someone were to take a lion’s whisker...
When the string of a musical instrument that produces joy is played, all the other strings snap.
In the same way, son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes the body of the Tathāgata’s lion-like *pāramitā* and the pillar of the bodhicitta as the string of the Dharma-joy;
once its sound is struck, all the strings of the five desires and the merits of the two vehicles are completely severed and extinguished.
For example, suppose someone were to collect various kinds of milk, such as that of cattle and sheep, until they filled the great ocean,
and then were to cast a single drop of lion’s milk into it, causing all of it to turn sour and spoil while passing through unimpeded;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who places the lion-like milk of the Tathāgata’s bodhicitta into the afflictions and karma of immeasurable kalpas.

Within the great ocean of the milk of affliction, they cause it all to be destroyed and utterly vanish, passing through directly without obstruction and never dwelling in the liberation of the two vehicles.
Good son, it is just as, for example, a kalaviṅka bird within its egg possesses great power that no other birds can equal; so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva within saṃsāra.
The power of the merit of great compassion arising from the production of the bodhicitta is such that no śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha can equal it.
Son of good family, it is like the prince of the garuḍa birds: when he is first born, his eyes are clear and sharp and his flight is powerful and swift;
though all other birds have been fully grown for a long time, none can equal him. So too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, he thus generates the bodhicitta as a prince of the Buddha, with pure wisdom and courageous great compassion, which no follower of the two vehicles can equal, even after practicing the path for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Good son, it is like a strong man who, grasping a sharp spear, pierces through solid and dense armor directly and without obstruction; so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, by thus grasping the sharp and swift spear of bodhicitta, one is able to pierce through the dense armor of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all false views, penetrating them entirely without obstruction.

Son of good family, it is like a powerful hero, a great nāga, who, when manifesting his majestic wrath, inevitably develops a boil upon his forehead; as long as that boil has not yet healed, throughout Jambudvīpa—
In the same way, no sentient being is able to subdue a bodhisattva mahāsattva;

if they give rise to great compassion, they will certainly produce the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and as long as they have not abandoned that mind, no māras or followers of māra in all the worlds can cause them harm.
Good son, it is like a master archer who has many disciples; although they have not yet become proficient in their training...
Just as that teacher’s mastery of arts and his wisdom, skillful means, and ingenuity surpass those of all other people,
so too it is with a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening: although they have not yet become habituated to the practices of omniscience,
their vows, wisdom, understanding, and aspirations cannot be matched by any ordinary worldlings or followers of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a person learning archery who first steadies his feet and afterwards practices the technique;
so too it is for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, wishing to learn the path of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, must first dwell securely in the bodhicitta and thereafter practice all the Buddha-dharmas.
Son of good family, it is like a magician who, about to perform a magical feat, [first prepares his materials].
First, one must give rise to the intention and maintain the illusory methods; thereafter, all that is performed will be fully accomplished. It is the same for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:
when they are about to manifest the supernatural illusions of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they must first give rise to the intention and resolve for Bodhicitta;
only then will everything be fully accomplished. Son of good family, it is like the art of illusion.
The mark of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who manifests form within the formless is likewise so:
although it has no form and cannot be seen, it is nevertheless able to universally manifest various adornments of merit throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Good son, it is like a cat or a wildcat; as soon as it sees a mouse, the mouse immediately enters its hole and dares not come out again.
It is likewise with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta:

when they momentarily observe all afflictions and karmic actions with the eye of wisdom, these immediately flee and hide, never to arise again. Good son, it is as if there were a person wearing ornaments of Jambu-river gold;
they outshine everything else, making it appear like a heap of ink. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this.

This ornament of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) outshines all the ornaments of merit belonging to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, rendering them entirely devoid of luster.

Son of good family, just as even a small portion of the power of a fine magnet can attract and break apart iron hooks and chains, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has generated the resolve for enlightenment; if they give rise to even a single...
Mindfulness is fully capable of destroying all the hooks and shackles of views, desire, and ignorance.
Son of good family, it is just as when iron encounters a magnet: as soon as it sees it, the iron disperses and no longer remains.
In the same way, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to the bodhicitta, all karmas, afflictions, and even the liberation of the two vehicles disperse the moment they briefly behold it.
"Furthermore, cessation is without abiding. Good son, it is like a person who has skillfully entered the great ocean;
no aquatic creatures can cause him harm, even if he enters the mouth of a makara fish, he will not be swallowed by it.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having resolved upon the bodhicitta and entered the ocean of birth and death, all karmas and afflictions..."
Afflictions cannot cause harm; even if one enters the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one will not be obstructed by them.
Son of good family, it is just as if a person were to drink the nectar-essence of ambrosia (*amṛta-rasa*);
no other things can cause him harm. In the same way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise drinks the nectar-dharma of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
One does not fall to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas because one is endowed with the power of vast compassion and vows.
Good son, it is like a person who obtains añjana medicine and applies it to their eyes; though they walk among people, they are not seen by others.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having obtained the añjana medicine of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), they are able to...
By means of skillful means, they enter the realm of Māra, yet all Māras are unable to see them.

Good son, it is as if there were a person who, by relying upon a king, would not fear other people; so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, for by relying on the king of great power that is the bodhicitta, he does not fear the obstacles of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) or the perils of the evil realms. Good son, it is as if there were...
Just as a person dwelling within water does not fear being burned by fire, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
dwelling in the water of the roots of goodness of the bodhicitta, they do not fear the fire of the wisdom of liberation of the two vehicles.
Son of Good Family, it is just as if a person were to rely upon a fierce general and thus have no fear of any enemies; so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
In this way, noble son, just as the Great General Vajrapāṇi, relying on the Bodhicitta, is fearless toward all enemies of evil conduct,
so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; wielding the vajra-pestle of the Bodhicitta, he likewise subdues all māras.
"O son of noble family from the non-Buddhist paths, it is like a person who takes an elixir of longevity and remains perpetually robust, neither aging nor wasting away.
In the same way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva takes the elixir of longevity that is the bodhicitta;
throughout incalculable eons, he cultivates the bodhisattva practices with a mind free from weariness and free from attachment. O son of noble family, it is as if there were..."
Just as one preparing medicinal decoctions must first take high-quality, pure water, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
wishing to cultivate all the practices and vows of a Bodhisattva, one must first give rise to the bodhicitta.
Son of good family, just as a person protecting their body first protects the life-faculty, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who likewise protects and sustains [it].
The Buddha-dharma likewise requires that one first protect the bodhicitta. Good son, it is like a person whose life-faculty has been severed;

they can no longer benefit their parents or kinsmen. In the same way, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who abandons the bodhicitta cannot benefit all sentient beings and cannot accomplish the merits of the Buddhas. Good son...
Son, it is like the great ocean, which nothing can destroy; the ocean of the bodhicitta is likewise, for it cannot be destroyed by the karma, afflictions, or the minds of those of the two vehicles.
Son of good family, it is like the light of the sun, which the radiance of the stars cannot eclipse;
the sun of the bodhicitta is likewise, for it cannot be eclipsed by the light of the untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) of all those of the two vehicles.
Good son, just as a prince, immediately upon birth, is respected by great ministers because of the sovereignty of his lineage,
so too is it with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: having resolved upon bodhicitta within the Buddha-dharma,
he is immediately respected by the elders who have long practiced the holy life, as well as by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because of the mastery of great compassion, good son, it is just as when a prince, though still young in years, is saluted by all the great ministers;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Although he has only recently resolved to attain enlightenment and is practicing the Bodhisattva path, those of the Two Vehicles who are long-standing elders should all salute him. Good son, it is just as when a prince, even though [regarding] all...
Among his ministers and attendants, he has not yet attained mastery, yet he already possesses the marks of a king;

because of the supreme excellence of his birth, he does not stand as an equal among all his ministers and attendants. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, although he has not yet attained mastery over all karma and afflictions, is nonetheless fully endowed with the marks of enlightenment and does not stand as an equal among all those of the two [vehicles].
Because their lineage is supreme, they ride upon equality. Good son, it is like a pure and wondrous maṇi jewel that appears impure because the eye is clouded by cataracts;
the bodhicitta jewel of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is just the same—it is called impure by those who lack wisdom and have no faith. Good son, it is like a medicine that is empowered by mantras.
If there are sentient beings who see, hear, dwell with, or even merely remember this medicinal herb of the bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—
which causes all illnesses to be completely extinguished upon being seen, heard, or dwelt with; which is sustained by all roots of goodness,
wisdom, skillful means, and the vows and knowledge of the Bodhisattvas— then all their afflictions [shall likewise be extinguished].
All illnesses are completely eliminated. Good son, it is like a person who constantly holds ambrosia (amṛta) in their possession;
their body will ultimately never change or decay. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this:

if they constantly recollect and maintain the ambrosia of the bodhicitta, the body of their vows and wisdom will ultimately never decay. Good son, it is like a wooden mechanical man; if there is no...
Just as a wedge, once its body is separated, cannot move, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
if they lack the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), their actions will be dispersed and they will be unable to accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas.

Good son, it is like the Cakravartin King who possesses a precious sandalwood called "Elephant-Treasury" (*gajagarbha*); if this king of incense is burned, the fourfold army will all ascend into the air.
The incense of the bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśa is likewise:
if one gives rise to this intention, it causes all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva to forever transcend the triple world and proceed within the unconditioned space of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Good son, it is as if a vajra is produced only from a source of vajras or a source of gold, and not from the sources of other jewels.
The diamond of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise so:
it arises solely from the diamond of great compassion that protects sentient beings, and from the ground of the supreme realm of omniscience;
it does not arise from the roots of merit of other sentient beings. Good son, it is like a tree called "Rootless" which does not grow from a root.

Yet its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all lush and flourishing. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s tree of the bodhicitta has no root that can be apprehended, yet it is able to nurture the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), great vows, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*);
these spread wide and cast a dense shade, universally covering the world. Good son, it is like a diamond (*vajra*), which is not inferior or base.
Just as an ordinary vessel or a broken vessel can hold [water], yet cannot contain it except in a complete and exquisite vessel, so too is the vajra of bodhicitta:
it cannot be contained within the vessels of inferior beings who are characterized by stinginess, envy, violation of precepts, laziness, distracted mindfulness, and lack of wisdom;
nor can it be held by those who have fallen away from their sublime resolve or who possess scattered thoughts and evil perceptions.
That which can be contained and supported within the vessel of birth is only the precious vessel of the Bodhisattva’s profound mind.
Good son, for example, just as a diamond can pierce all manner of jewels, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta; it can completely penetrate all the jewels of the Dharma.
Good son, for example, just as a diamond can destroy all mountains, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta...

Furthermore, it is able to utterly destroy all mountains of false views. Son of good family, for example, although a diamond may be broken and no longer whole, it still surpasses all other jewels; the diamond of the bodhicitta is also like this:
even if one’s resolve is weak and it suffers some slight impairment, it still excels all the merits of the two vehicles. Son of good family, for example...
Just as a vajra, even if it has cracks or flaws, is still able to destroy all poverty, so too is the vajra of the bodhicitta;
even if it has cracks or flaws and does not advance in various practices, it is still able to abandon all of birth and death.
Noble son, just as a small vajra is capable of destroying all things, so too is the vajra of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, entering even a limited sphere of experience thus shatters all ignorance and afflictions.
Good son, for example, a diamond cannot be obtained by ordinary people; the diamond of the bodhicitta is likewise not obtainable by sentient beings of inferior intent.
Good son, for example, a person who does not recognize jewels does not know the power of a diamond.
If its function is not understood, the vajra of bodhicitta is likewise so; if one does not know the Dharma, one does not understand its power and cannot utilize it.
Noble son, for example, just as no one can destroy a vajra, the vajra of bodhicitta is likewise so;
no phenomena whatsoever can destroy it. Noble son, it is like a vajra-pestle.
None of the great strongmen were able to hold it, except for one possessing the power of Mahānārāyaṇa;
likewise, none of those in the two vehicles were able to hold it, except for a Bodhisattva’s vast causal conditions, firm, and wholesome power.
Son of good family, it is like a vajra, which no object whatsoever can destroy.
It can universally destroy all things, yet its essential nature suffers no diminution; the bodhicitta is likewise thus.

Throughout the countless eons of the three periods of time, it universally teaches and transforms sentient beings, performing those ascetic practices that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to do, yet it never experiences weariness or exhaustion.
O son of good family, it is like a diamond which nothing else can support, but which only the diamond-ground can support;
the bodhicitta is likewise, for neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas can support it, except for those who are heading toward sarvajñatā.
O son of good family, it is like a diamond vessel that has no flaws or defects, used for holding...
Just as water never leaks through to enter the earth, so too is the adamantine vessel of the bodhicitta;
it holds the water of roots of goodness and never allows it to leak away into the various realms of existence.
Noble son, just as the vajra-limit can support the great earth and prevent it from sinking, so too does the bodhicitta support all [the qualities] of a bodhisattva.
One’s practice and vows shall not cause one to fall or sink into the triple world, O son of good family.
For example, just as a diamond remains long in water without rotting or becoming wet, so too is the bodhicitta;

throughout all kalpas, while remaining within the waters of birth-and-death, karma, and delusion, it is neither destroyed nor transformed. Son of good family, for example, just as a diamond [is unaffected] by all fires...
It is likewise impossible for any of the fires of the afflictions (*kleśa*) within all of saṃsāra to burn or heat the bodhicitta.
Son of good family, it is like the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*) within the trichiliocosm,
which can support the Buddhas as they sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), subdue all Māras, and attain [awakening].
Just as the seat of a Perfectly Awakened One cannot be occupied by any other being, so too is the seat of the bodhicitta;

it can sustain all the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, all the pāramitās, all the patiences, and all the stages (bhūmis), as well as the dedication of merit, the reception of predictions, and the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening.
It sustains the making of offerings to all Buddhas, the hearing of the Dharma, and the practice of all other mental states.
If those who cannot maintain the bodhicitta of a son of good family were to achieve such immeasurable, boundless,

and even unspeakably unspeakable supreme merits, then any sentient being who gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* would likewise obtain such supreme dharmas of merit. Therefore, son of good family, you have obtained [them].
It is well that you have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and sought the bodhisattva conduct;
having attained such great merit, O son of good family, regarding your question as to how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path,
O son of good family, you may enter this Great Vairocana-Adorned Treasury.

By observing thoroughly throughout the towers and pavilions, one is able to understand that they have studied the bodhisattva practices and, having completed their study, have accomplished immeasurable merit.
[Treatise] Sixth: From the passage "At that time, the youth Sudhana joined his palms in reverence" until the end of this fascicle.
This section clarifies how Sudhana proclaims his own aspiration for great bodhicitta; it explains the inconceivable power and efficacy of the roots of merit of bodhicitta as praised by Maitreya,
and clarifies that all supernatural powers, spiritual faculties, and the myriad practices of a bodhisattva have bodhicitta as their root,
thereby extinguishing birth and death, cutting off the flow of suffering, and purifying the eighty-four thousand [afflictions].
The gateway of afflictions reveals that the ocean of all-knowledge is entirely rooted in the bodhicitta;

as the text extensively praises, because the bodhicitta is without dependence, without abiding, and has no intrinsic nature such that arising and ceasing can be apprehended, the afflictions manifesting before one are naturally purified, and the ocean of wisdom immediately appears. Because this wisdom manifests, various skillful means [arise].
The myriad practices of supernatural powers are accomplished through wisdom; because the bodhicitta is without dependence, wisdom is likewise without dependence.
Because wisdom is without dependence, all that is performed has no performer upon whom one can rely or dwell.
Thus, the karma of birth and death perishes, and only the mastery of wisdom remains. The myriad practices of great compassion arise from wisdom, yet the essence of wisdom is non-existent.
Relying on the myriad practices, benefiting sentient beings like a magical transformation; the power of the spiritual path is like the moon in the sky, appearing universally in all waters.
The essence of wisdom does not depart, nor do the "waters" of the sentient beings' minds come toward it. According to the purity of their own karma, wisdom shares the same substance as that purity;
yet, according to the depth or shallowness of that purity, the manifestations of wisdom differ. It is neither this nor that. If one wishes to see the [Buddhas] of the ten directions...

The ocean of wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata is merely the manifestation of Buddha-wisdom through the purification of the karmic conditions of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
When one seeks only superior external objects, one's own Dharma becomes obscured and fails to realize that each phenomenon is perfected by its own merit;
thus, one does not diminish one's own progress and does not contravene the holy intent. This is like the five stages possessed by each of Sudhana’s spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The Bodhisattva’s practice of skillful means does not cling to other dharmas nor to one's own mind; it has no fixed basis or dwelling place.

It simply causes the mind to be vast, benefiting many through skillful samādhi, so that all sentient beings may be freed from suffering, and further causes one's own mind to reach the ultimate reality of dharmas, as well as causing [other] sentient beings to do the same.
If they have not all equally attained the benefit for sentient beings through the dharmas and practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions—
even if they do not know or understand the dharma of a single sentient being— they cannot be called Buddhas who have perfected wisdom,
nor can they be called Mahāsattvas.
[Sūtra] At that time, the youth Sudhana, having respectfully circumambulated Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva to the right, addressed him, saying:
"I pray only that the Great Sage will open the door of this pavilion so that I may enter.
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva went before the pavilion and snapped his fingers; the door opened immediately, and he commanded Sudhana to enter. Sudhana’s heart was filled with joy.
Having entered, he closed the door again and saw that the pavilions were vast and immeasurable, equal to space;

their ground was composed of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels, as were their incalculable palaces, incalculable gates and portals, incalculable windows, incalculable staircases, incalculable railings, and incalculable pathways—all fashioned from the seven treasures. Incalculable...
There were *asaṃkhyeya* banners, *asaṃkhyeya* standards, and *asaṃkhyeya* canopies arranged all around;
*asaṃkhyeya* garlands of various jewels, *asaṃkhyeya* garlands of pearls, *asaṃkhyeya* garlands of red pearls, and *asaṃkhyeya* garlands of lion-pearls hung down everywhere;
there were also *asaṃkhyeya* half-moons, *asaṃkhyeya* silk ribbons, and *asaṃkhyeya* [ornaments].
It was adorned with precious jewel-nets; incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel-bells, stirred by the wind, produced melodic sounds;
incalculable varieties of celestial flowers were scattered; incalculable celestial jewel-garlands and bands were suspended;
incalculable censers of various jewels were arrayed; incalculable fine gold dust rained down; incalculable jewel-mirrors were hung; and incalculable jewel-lamps were lit.
He spread out incalculable precious robes, arranged incalculable precious canopies, and set up incalculable precious thrones;

upon these thrones were spread incalculable precious silken cloths. There were incalculable images of Jambūnada gold boys and girls, incalculable images of various forms made of diverse jewels, and incalculable images of bodhisattvas made of exquisite jewels, filling every place in incalculable numbers.

Flocks of birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds; it was adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) precious *utpala* flowers, incalculable precious *padma* flowers, incalculable precious *kumuda* flowers, and incalculable precious *puṇḍarīka* flowers;
incalculable precious trees stood in successive rows, and incalculable *maṇi* jewels radiated great light.
He clearly perceived these and other such immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) ornaments as his adornments.
Furthermore, he saw within them hundreds of thousands of exquisite pavilions, each individually adorned exactly as described above;
they were vast, magnificent, and beautiful, all situated in space without obstructing one another, nor was there any confusion among them. Within one of these, the youth Sudhana—
Standing in the center, he saw all places; in every single location, he saw them all in this same way.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, beholding such various and inconceivable realms of sovereign mastery within the Vairocana-Adorned Treasury Pavilion, gave rise to great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
His body and mind became supple and soft, free from all conceptualizations, with the exception of one.
With all obstacles severed and all delusions extinguished, what he sees is never forgotten, what he hears he can remember, and what he contemplates is not confused;

he enters the gate of unimpeded liberation. Universally directing his mind, universally beholding all, and universally prostrating himself, as soon as he has begun his salutation, through the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, he perceives his own body pervading all [the Buddhas].
Within the towers and pavilions, one clearly beholds various inconceivable realms of sovereign mastery; that is to say,
one may see Maitreya Bodhisattva at the time he first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta— seeing his name, his clan,
and how he was awakened by such a virtuous friend as to plant such roots of goodness, and dwelling for such a lifespan.
In this manner, throughout such eons, encountering such Buddhas, dwelling in such adorned lands, practicing such conduct, and making such vows—
those Tathāgatas, their assemblies, and their lifespans, lasting for such durations of time—
he clearly beheld them all as he drew near to serve and make offerings to them; or he saw Maitreya first attain the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind.
Since that time, he has been known as Maitreya; some have seen him cultivating various sublime practices to bring all the *pāramitās* to fulfillment,
some have seen him attain the stages of patience (*kṣānti*), some have seen him dwell in the spiritual levels (*bhūmi*), some have seen him achieve the purification of a buddha-field,

and some have seen him protect and uphold the True Teaching of the Tathāgata as a great Dharma Master who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at such-and-such a time, in such-and-such a place, and in such-and-such a manner.
Whether it was the Tathāgata receiving the prediction of unsurpassed bodhi, or seeing Maitreya as a wheel-turning monarch exhorting all sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action;
or acting as a world-protector to benefit sentient beings; or acting as Śakra Devendra to rebuke the five desires;
or acting as King Yama to praise non-heedlessness; or acting as the King of Tuṣita Heaven to extol...

He extolled the merits of Bodhisattvas throughout their lifetimes; or, as the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, he manifested the various transformations and adornments of Bodhisattvas for the assembly of devas;
or, as the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he expounded all the teachings of the Buddhas for the assembly of devas;
or, appearing as a Māra king, he taught that all phenomena are entirely impermanent; or, as Brahmā...

The King spoke of the immeasurable joy and bliss of the various dhyānas; or, as an asura king, he entered the great ocean of wisdom and, realizing that all phenomena are like illusions, constantly preached the Dharma for his assembly to sever all pride and arrogance;
or again, he was seen dwelling in the realm of Yama, emitting great light to rescue those suffering in the hells; or he was seen among the hungry ghosts.
He sees himself bestowing food and drink upon those in the realm of hungry ghosts to relieve their hunger and thirst;

or he sees himself employing various skillful means to tame sentient beings who are in the paths of animals; or he sees himself preaching the Dharma to the assemblies of the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings (Lokapālas);
or he sees himself preaching the Dharma to the assemblies of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; or he sees himself [preaching] to the assemblies of the King of the Yāma Heaven.
He may be seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of the King of Tuṣita Heaven; or he may be seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of the King of Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
or he may be seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of the King of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
or he may be seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of the Great Brahmā King; or he may be seen preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Dragon Kings.
Sometimes he is seen preaching the Dharma for an assembly of yakṣa and rākṣasa kings;
sometimes he is seen preaching the Dharma for an assembly of gandharva and kiṃnara kings; sometimes he is seen preaching the Dharma for an assembly of asura and dhānava kings;
and sometimes he is seen preaching the Dharma for an assembly of garuḍa and mahoraga kings.
He may see the Dharma being taught for the sake of all other assemblies of humans and non-humans;
or he may see it being taught for an assembly of śrāvakas; or he may see it being taught for an assembly of pratyekabuddhas;
or he may see it being expounded for the assembly of bodhisattvas, from those who have first resolved their minds up to those bound by only one more birth and those who have received the empowerment.
He may see the preaching of the Dharma praising all the merits of the first through the tenth stages;
or he may see the praise of the fulfillment of all the *pāramitās*; or he may see the praise of entering the various gates of patience (*kṣānti*);

or he may see the praise of the various great gates of *samādhi*; or he may see the praise of the profound gates of liberation; or he may see the praise of the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Within the sphere of samādhi and supernormal powers, one may see the praise and exposition of the various practices of bodhisattvas;

or see the praise and exposition of their great vows; or see them praising and expounding to fellow-practicing bodhisattvas the various worldly means of livelihood, crafts, and skillful methods for benefiting sentient beings;
or see them praising and expounding to bodhisattvas in their final birth the empowerment of all Buddhas.

At the crown of one's head, one may see Maitreya for hundreds or thousands of years walking back and forth, reciting, reading, and copying sutra scrolls, diligently seeking and investigating, and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude;
or entering various dhyānas and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); or entering the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and the various liberations (*vimokṣa*);
or entering samādhi, manifesting various supernatural transformations through the power of skillful means; or seeing various bodhisattvas entering [these states].
From each and every pore of their bodies, they emit clouds of all manner of transformation-bodies through the samādhi of transformation:
some see clouds of celestial hosts emerging, some see clouds of nāga hosts emerging,
and some see clouds of yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, asuras, garuḍas, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors emerging.
Some clouds of bodies appear as universal monarchs, minor kings, princes, ministers, officials, elders, and householders;
some clouds of bodies appear as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas; some clouds of bodies appear as all sentient beings;
and some clouds of bodies appear emitting sublime sounds that praise the various Dharma-gates of the bodhisattvas, namely, praising and expounding upon Bodhi.
The gateway of the merits of the mind: praising and explaining the merits of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *jñānapāramitā*;

praising and explaining all the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*), the samādhis, the *samāpattis*, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the clear knowledges (*vidyā*), the dhāraṇīs, the eloquence (*pratibhāna*), the truths (*satya*), the wisdoms (*jñāna*), tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), liberation (*vimukti*), the conditions (*pratyaya*), the supports (*niśraya*), and the preaching of the Dharma.

He praises and explains the gateways of all such merits as the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
the vehicles of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas; the stages, the patiences, the practices, and the vows.
Or else, within these, he beholds the Tathāgatas surrounded by great assemblies.
He also clearly beheld the birthplaces, lineages, physical forms, lifespans, names of lands and eons, titles, teachings, benefits, and the duration of the remaining of those Buddhas’ doctrines;
he saw all their various differences, including their respective sites of enlightenment and their assemblies, all with perfect clarity.
Furthermore, within those pavilions inside the Treasury of Adornments, he saw a particular pavilion that was lofty, vast, and magnificently decorated.
Supreme and peerless, within which he fully beholds the three thousandfold world system with its ten billion sets of four continents and ten billion Tuṣita heavens;
in each of these, Maitreya Bodhisattva descends in spirit to be born, with Śakra and Brahmā supporting and upholding his head as he takes seven steps,
surveys the ten directions, utters the Great Lion’s Roar, and manifests as a youth dwelling therein.
Residing in palaces, sporting in gardens, renouncing the world for the sake of omniscience, practicing asceticism, accepting the milk-rice offering, proceeding to the site of enlightenment,
subduing the various Māras, attaining equal and perfect awakening, contemplating the Bodhi tree, being exhorted by the Brahmā King to turn the wheel of the true Dharma,
ascending to celestial palaces to expound the Dharma, the number of kalpas, the span of his life, the assemblies, and the adornments thereof.

The purification of buddha-lands, the practices and vows cultivated therein, the skillful means for teaching and maturing sentient beings, the distribution of relics, and the preservation of the Dharma teachings are all distinct.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Combined Commentary*, Fascicle 118.

Xiè (xiān jié qiè). Mí (měi wéi qiè). Dǎo (dōu hǎo qiè). Pào (zhèng mào qiè). Āo (wǔ dào qiè).
The Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s New Flower Ornament Scripture, Scroll One Hundred Nineteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Tang Dynasty;
the commentary composed by Li Tongxuan, a Layman of Fangshan in Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty;
