By the power of spiritual friends, one attains this ultimate, pure Dharma-body, which is equal throughout the three periods of time;
furthermore, one attains the pure, unsurpassed Form-body that transcends all worlds, manifesting forms according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings,
entering all lands, pervading all places, and extensively displaying supernatural powers within all worlds so that they may behold it.
There is none who does not rejoice. Good son, you should observe this body of mine: this body of mine has been accomplished over an ocean of boundless eons;
it is difficult to see and difficult to hear even in immeasurable thousands of billions of nayutas of eons.

Good son, if there are sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, or those who have planted only a few roots of goodness—whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas—[they too shall rejoice].
They would not even be able to hear my name, much less see my body.
Good son, if there are sentient beings who hear my name, they shall no longer regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether they see me, touch me, welcome me, escort me, follow me for a moment, or even see or hear me in a dream—all such instances are likewise [efficacious].
There are some sentient beings who, by recollecting me for a single day and night, attain maturity; or those who attain maturity by recollecting me for seven days and nights,
half a month, one month, half a year, one year, one hundred years, one thousand years, one eon, one hundred eons,
or even for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Whether in one lifetime, a hundred lifetimes, or even for as many lifetimes as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
those who bring me to mind and thereby reach maturity— whether they see me emitting great rays of light or see me shaking the Buddha-fields,
whether they feel fear or feel joy— all of them attain maturity. Son of good family, by means of such [power] I...
These gates of skillful means, as numerous as the atoms within these Buddha-fields, cause all sentient beings to attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son, if there are sentient beings who see or hear of my pure land, they will certainly be born within this pure land. If there are sentient beings who see or hear of me...
"O son of good family, one who purifies the body will surely be born within my pure body; you should now observe this pure body of mine.

At that time, the youth Sudhana observed the marks and signs, the limbs and joints, and every single pore of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s body, and found that within each and every pore there were unspeakably unspeakable oceans of Buddha-fields, and within each ocean of Buddha-fields...
One sees the Buddhas appearing in the world, surrounded by a great assembly of Bodhisattvas;
furthermore, one sees all those oceans of lands established in various ways, with various shapes, various adornments, and various great mountains encircling them on all sides;
various colored clouds cover the void, and in such a manner, various Buddhas appear and expound various teachings.
Seeing that these various activities were each distinct, he further saw Samantabhadra, within each and every ocean of world-systems,
manifesting clouds of Buddha-emanations as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings,
leading them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the youth Sudhana again saw himself...
While dwelling within the body of Samantabhadra, he teaches and transforms sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions; furthermore,
compared to the light of wisdom and roots of goodness obtained by the youth Sudhana through his attendance upon as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a Buddha-field,
that which was obtained by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva exceeds it such that the former does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part.
Even a hundred thousandth part, or even a hundred thousand-billionth part, or even by means of calculation or analogy, cannot reach it.
All the oceans of Buddha-lands that the youth Sudhana entered from his first generation of the mind until he beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—
in that interval— all are now contained within a single pore of Samantabhadra.
He recollected the oceans of Buddha-fields entered [by the Bodhisattva], which exceeded by unspeakably unspeakable times the number of atoms in a Buddha-field as previously described;

as it was for one pore, so it was for all pores. As the youth Sudhana took a single step within the field of a pore of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, he passed beyond a number of Buddha-fields equal to the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

Even if one were to travel through as many worlds as there are in this manner for as long as all future kalpas, one would still be unable to know the limits of the successive oceans of lands within a single pore—

the ocean of lands, the treasury of oceans of lands, the distinctions of oceans of lands, the universal entry into oceans of lands, the formation of oceans of lands, the destruction of oceans of lands,
and the adornments of oceans of lands— nor would one be able to know the succession of oceans of Buddhas, the treasury of oceans of Buddhas, or the [oceans of Buddhas].
The limits of the oceans of Buddhas— their differentiation, their universal entry, their arising, and their cessation— cannot be known;
nor can the limits of the oceans of Bodhisattva assemblies— their sequence, their treasury, their differentiation, their universal entry, their gathering, and their dispersal— be known.
The limits of all such oceans as these— the knowledge of how to enter the realms of sentient beings, the knowledge of the faculties of sentient beings,
the wisdom for teaching and taming all sentient beings, the profound mastery in which Bodhisattvas dwell, and the various stages and paths entered by Bodhisattvas—
were all contained within a single pore of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s body; and within a single pore, Sudhana spent an eon.
Practicing in this manner for one eon, and even continuing in this way for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
they do not pass away from this land to appear in that land; rather, in every moment of thought, they pervade the boundless oceans of lands,
teaching and transforming sentient beings, causing them to incline toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the youth Sudhana attained, in due order, the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
he became equal to Samantabhadra, equal to all Buddhas, and attained equality in body, which fills all world-systems; equality in conduct; equality in perfect enlightenment;
equality in supernormal powers; equality in the wheel of Dharma; equality in eloquence; equality in speech; equality in voice; and equality in power.
Their fearlessness, their dwelling as equal to the Buddhas, their great compassion, and their inconceivable liberation and mastery were all entirely equal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra spoke these verses:

[Treatise] Ninth: At that time, having received the instructions of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, this section ending with the verse clarifies how Sudhana, having already attained the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime from Maitreya, universally sealed the Dharma-gates of the one hundred and ten cities;
he was now like a diamond within the initial stage of faith.
Before the lion throne of Tathāgata Vairocana at the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Treasury of Wisdom, upon a seat of lotuses made of all kinds of jewels,
one gives rise to ten kinds of vast minds equal to the expanse of space. By traversing these through the *Vidyādhara-piṭaka*,
one reaches the city of Maitreya after passing through one hundred and ten cities, attaining the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime, never departing from the initial mind of faith.
Within the sublime principle of the Vajragarbha-jñāna-bodhi of Tathāgata Vairocana, having attained accomplishment,
one gives rise within that very sublime principle of the Vajragarbha-jñāna-bodhi to the constant and universal Samantabhadra practices that perfectly encompass the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
From this point onward, Sudhana practices the Bodhisattva path within the body of Samantabhadra.

After Samantabhadra placed his hand upon the crown of the head of the youth Sudhana, he clarified that within the Dharma-realm, the fruit of Buddhahood is eternal and the characteristics of the eternal practices of Samantabhadra are likewise so;
only by being in accord with these can one attain the ancient fruits already perfected by all Buddhas and the ancient practices of Samantabhadra.
This extends through the lineage up to Maitreya Bodhisattva, clarifying that within this absence of the three periods of time, there is but a single birth.

The birth that marks the initial entry into the stage of Buddhahood through the practices of the paths of seeing and cultivation is the birth of descending from the divine realm to take birth in the world;
this is the birth of one who will attain Buddhahood in the future. This is encompassed by the Dharma-gate of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).

Likewise, Sudhana’s present life is the birth in which the practice of the path of seeing is fulfilled, while his future birth is what clarifies the birth of attaining Buddhahood. It is by means of this [sixfold analysis] that it is so understood.

The fruit of Buddhahood attained in a future lifetime, the fundamental Vajragarbha-wisdom, the sublime principle of Bodhi, the fruit obtained by Vairocana Tathāgata, the primordial practice of Samantabhadra—these are inherently one and complete.
The three periods of time and all of antiquity and modernity are non-dual; time does not shift, yet sameness and difference are sovereign within the *Indra-jāla* of the Dharma-realm.
The Dharma-gate of the Unobstructed Net is divided here into six sections based on this single stage of Maitreya:

first, the section clarifying the raising of the cause through the fruit to arouse faith; second, the section clarifying the application of practice after having attained faith to accord with cultivation;

third, the section of practicing the application to accord with the fruit; fourth, the section of correlating the fruit already acceded to with the cause; fifth, returning to rely upon... [text truncated].

The Gate of the Perfect Interfusion of Original Causes; the Gate of the Non-duality and Simultaneity of Beginning and End within Cause and Effect in the Ultimate Dharma-realm—by harmonizing these six gates, their underlying intent can be perceived.
This section, spanning ten pages of scripture below, clarifies how Sudhana, in the presence of the Bodhisattva Maitreya, makes a supreme entry into the fruition of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

The Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Adornments of Unforgetting Mindfulness, which attains all realms of the three periods of time within the sphere of wisdom and returns as a seal upon the one hundred and ten cities;
entering at the stage of the first stage of faith, without departing from the limit of a single kṣaṇa,
with causes perfected and fruits fulfilled, one arrives before the Lion Throne of Vairocana Tathāgata at the Bodhimanda of Vajragarbha.
Arising upon a seat of the treasury of all jewel lotuses, vast as the realm of empty space, one gives rise to the ten kinds of great mind;
only then does one initiate the constant practice of Samantabhadra for the fruit of Buddhahood within the Dharma-realm.

Within this stage, amidst dust-motes as numerous as those in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra simultaneously touches the crown of Sudhana’s head within each and every mote, thereby manifesting the Buddha.
The fruition of the dharma-realm is the fulfillment of conduct; the fulfillment of conduct does not depart from the time of the cause, nor does wisdom differ from it.
Thus, one sees spiritual friends as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, and even sees the lands within the limbs, joints, and pores of Samantabhadra’s body.
Through the wisdom that enters the realm of the dharma-realm by means of illumination, the net of practices—whether one or many—is of infinite, layered profundity.
The gates of obstruction and non-obstruction, exhaustion and inexhaustibility, and the constant nature of benefiting sentient beings are explained in detail according to the text itself.
This treatise briefly sets forth the intended meaning within the sutra; therefore, the full text cannot be recorded here in its entirety.
Within this section, it is divided into ten parts: first, at that time, the youth Sudhana, relying upon the Bodhisattva Maitreya...
After the Bodhisattva’s instruction, from the passage down to "dwelling together with longing desire to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva," thirty-three and a half lines of scripture clarify how Sudhana,
through the superior practice of Maitreya Bodhisattva, enters the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime,
thereby returning to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) within his initial mind of faith— the Palace of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā-vimāna)— as the realm of wisdom.

The Dharma-realm is eternally thus, its quiescence and function being unimpeded; the realm of the Indra-net, wherein the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices for the fruit of Buddhahood is eternally perfected.

A passage from the sutra states: "Proceeding by stages, he traveled through one hundred and ten cities until he reached the country of Universal Gate (Samantamukha)," because all Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings are of one and the same [nature].
Because the single dharma-realm and its lands have no distinct substance, the passage concerning the traveling through one hundred and ten cities clarifies that,
at one time, he universally seals all previously practiced dharmas as being without before or after; thus, by contemplating and observing with a single mind and vowing to see Mañjuśrī,
he immediately beheld spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm.
This clarifies that the wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body perceives all things universally and without exception as non-different from the essence of Mañjuśrī;

this explains the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the number of atoms in these three thousandfold world-systems, the meaning of the sequence of the general characteristics of the initial enumeration of the *dharmadhātu* in the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) clarifies the three thousandfold worlds within a single pore.
The great trichiliocosm extends throughout the ten directions, each part being equal; it is an inconceivable skillful means for entering the Dharma-realm, beyond all calculation.
Next, within this Vajragarbha Bodhimaṇḍa, before the lion throne of the Tathāgata Vairocana, [the assembly] arose upon seats of all kinds of precious lotuses, as vast as the realm of empty space.

The mind is clarified by means of the fundamental faith; within that faith, one gives rise to the gate of Samantabhadra’s constant practice—the realm of the Indra’s net of the entire dharma-realm—which is the essence of the Buddha-fruit Bodhi, the Vajra-Wisdom Treasury, and undefiled Great Compassion.

From this point downward, the subsequent sections follow this same principle as explained extensively in the text. This clarifies the comprehensive inclusion of all that has been cultivated and practiced.
By clarifying the causes and effects of these phenomena and returning them to their fundamental mode, the Dharma is established in this way to bring about awakening and understanding.
To practice accordingly, observing and penetrating each and every thing as one's own mind, so that one’s realization accords with reality—this is the great intent of all the sages and worthies.

This intent clarifies that one does not depart from the essence of Bodhi within the initial mind of faith; by cultivating the fundamental wisdom, one fulfills the various levels of discriminative wisdom until it is universal.
The ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct, filled with the virtues that pervade the dust-motes and lands of the ten directions in successive layers, is the fulfillment of one’s own practice;

yet this cause and effect does not transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa. Constantly using this Dharma to transform sentient beings, it never ceases within the limit of a single kṣaṇa, free from any thought of beginning or end. This clarifies the Vairocana-Samantabhadra Dharmadhātu.
Without beginning or end, the great perfect wisdom constantly and universally seals all;
its constant activity is free from arising or ceasing, and there is no matter of rest or abandonment. This is eternally so throughout the ten directions.
Within this very Vajragarbha Bodhimanda, before the lion throne of the Tathāgata Vairocana, [he sat] upon a seat of all-jeweled lotus-treasury.
Having generated the vast mind that rises up like the realm of empty space, down to the point where the youth Sudhana generates such a mind,
there are eight lines of scripture clarifying how, within the initial mind of faith, Sudhana gives rise to the great functioning of Samantabhadra’s Dharma-realm—
wherein cause and effect are simultaneous and unimpeded— within the essence of Bodhi, the Vajra-Wisdom Treasury of the Dharma-realm.

This is divided according to the meaning of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) and comprises three sections: first, from "By the power of his own roots of goodness and the empowerment of the Tathāgata, through the shared roots of goodness of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" onwards;

second, from "Furthermore, having seen ten kinds of signs of light" onwards; third, up to this point, which constitutes eleven lines of scripture for the purpose of clarifying the section on Sudhana’s vision of ten kinds of auspicious omens;
and fourth, from "Furthermore, having seen ten kinds of signs of light" onwards, up to this point.
The seventeen lines of sūtra text following "For this reason" clarify the section on Sudhana seeing ten kinds of light, which is divided into five periods.

From the passage beginning with "After Sudhana the youth had seen these signs of the ten kinds of light" down to "increasing the great Dharma and accomplishing all-knowledge," fifty-seven lines of sūtra text clarify the section on Sudhana seeing the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra within the [lotus] pond.
He came forward and sat upon a lion throne of precious lotuses in the midst of the great assembly;
and he saw that within every single pore of Samantabhadra’s body, the vast Dharma-realm was divided into six parts.
At that time, having witnessed such sovereign spiritual powers of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Sudhana the youth descended into the divine play of all Tathāgatas.
In total, there are twenty-three lines of scripture clarifying how Sudhana again contemplates the body of Samantabhadra and sees all Buddhas of the ten directions—
humans, devas, and those in the hells— all contained within the pores of his skin. This section is divided into seven parts, beginning from "Sudhana the youth,
having seen the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra in this manner" down to "Sudhana the youth, having already obtained this."

The thirteen and a half lines of scripture clarify the section on the Bodhisattva Sudhana attaining the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the perfection of wisdom that pervades all phenomena;

from the passage where Samantabhadra Bodhisattva extends his right hand to stroke the crown of Sudhana’s head down to the dharma-gates he attained, these are all identical. The fourteen lines of scripture clarify Samantabhadra in this very realm.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī touched the crown of Sudhana’s head and bestowed upon him the Dharma-gates he had attained;

likewise, at that very moment, Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas throughout all the atoms of all worlds in the ten directions simultaneously touched the crown of Sudhana’s head and bestowed upon him the Dharma-gates he had attained—all in this same manner.
Thus it was divided into nine parts. At that time, the Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed Sudhana:
Having spoken thus, [the text] continues down to: "O son of good family, you should observe this pure body of mine,
which contains sixty sections of sūtra-texts clearly explaining how the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra spoke to Sudhana, declaring that for the sake of sentient beings seeking the path of liberation,
he has practiced the two paths of merit and wisdom for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields."

When the Bodhisattva practices seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he seeks it through his own body, flesh, hands, feet, liver, gallbladder, royal throne, wealth, treasures, and even the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)—seeking all-knowledge for the sake of benefiting sentient beings through these gateways without even a moment’s interruption;
this is divided into ten [sections]. At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated the physical marks, secondary characteristics, and every limb and joint of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

From "Within a single pore" down to the end of the verse, thirty-nine lines of scripture clarify the Dharma-gate of the realm of the marks and signs of the pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s body as perceived by Sudhana.
The ocean of Buddha-lands entered in a single thought-moment exceeds, by incalculable times incalculable, the number of atoms in a Buddha-land described previously; this constitutes one pore.
In this way, all the pores are likewise extensive, as clearly explained in the sutra itself.

[Sutra] "You should all eliminate the defilements of delusion And listen with single-minded focus and without distraction To my discourse on how the Tathāgata is endowed with all perfections And the true path of universal liberation."
The Transcendent, Tamed, Gentle, and Supreme Hero, Whose mind is pure as space,
Constantly radiating the great light of the sun of wisdom, Universally causing all sentient beings to extinguish the darkness of ignorance—
Such a Tathāgata is difficult to encounter or hear; Only now, after immeasurable billions of kalpas, have you met him.
Like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age, one should thus listen to the Buddha’s virtues;
In accordance with the various activities of the world, he is like a conjured being manifesting myriad deeds,
Solely to delight the minds of sentient beings, never giving rise to conceptual discrimination or thought.
At that time, having heard this teaching, all the bodhisattvas were filled with single-minded longing and yearning, wishing only to hear of the true merits of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
They all thought: "The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra has fully cultivated all practices;
his essential nature is pure, and all his words are entirely non-void. He is praised by all Tathāgatas. Thus they reflected.

Having already conceived a profound sense of longing and reverence, at that time the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra—adorned with the full perfection of merit and wisdom, like a lotus flower unsullied by any dust or defilement of the triple world—addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Listen attentively!
I now wish to describe a single drop from the ocean of the Buddha’s merits. He then spoke in verse:
The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as space, Pervading the minds of all sentient beings.
He fully understands all the delusions of the world, Without giving rise to various discriminatory thoughts;
In a single thought-moment, he knows all phenomena of the three periods of time, And likewise comprehends the faculties of all beings.
Just as a skillful master illusionist Manifests boundless phenomena in every thought-moment,
According to the various mental activities of sentient beings And the power of their past karma and vows,
Causing what they see to differ for each, Yet the Buddha is fundamentally free from any movement of thought.
In some places, one may see the Buddha seated, filling all worlds throughout the ten directions;
yet there are those whose minds are not pure, who do not see the Buddha for immeasurable eons.
But those with faith and understanding, free from pride, shall see the Tathāgata as soon as they resolve their minds toward him.
Some, possessing a defiled mind of flattery and deception, may search for him through billions of eons yet never encounter him;
others may hear the Buddha’s voice in every place, its exquisite melody gladdening the heart.
Yet there are those who, for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, fail to hear it because their minds are impure.

In some places, one sees great Bodhisattvas of pure virtue, Filling the three thousandfold world-systems, all fully perfected in the conduct of Samantabhadra; The Tathāgata sits majestically amidst them.
Or one sees this realm, wondrous beyond compare, Adorned and purified by the Buddha over immeasurable eons.
The most supreme Honored One, Vairocana, awakened to Bodhi therein;
Or one may see the sublime and wondrous Lotus Realm, Where the Tathāgata Bhadraśrī resides,
surrounded by an infinite assembly of bodhisattvas, All of whom diligently cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.
Some see the Buddha Amitāyus surrounded by Avalokiteśvara and others,
all of whom have already attained the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), filling the worlds of the ten directions;
some see this trichiliocosm adorned in various ways, like the world of Abhirati.
The Tathāgata Akṣobhya dwells therein, as do the bodhisattvas such as Gandhahastin;
or he is seen by Mahāyaśas Candrabuddhi together with the bodhisattva Vajradhvaja and others,
abiding in a wondrously adorned realm like a perfect mirror, pervading the pure lands throughout the ten directions.
In some places, one sees the World-Honored One, Sūryagarbha, dwelling in the pure land of Excellent Radiance,
surrounded by consecrated bodhisattvas who pervade the ten directions as they preach the Dharma;
or one sees the Buddha Vajrajvālā, together with the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu.
They travel throughout all vast lands, preaching the Dharma to eliminate the cataracts of sentient beings.
At the tip of every single hair, there are unspeakable numbers of Buddhas endowed with the thirty-two marks,
surrounded by assemblies of Bodhisattvas, delivering various teachings to save living beings.
Some behold within a single pore a vast realm, fully adorned, wherein dwell infinite Tathāgatas; it is filled with pure sons of the Buddha.
Others see within a single atom all the buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas completely fill [the realms], having cultivated all practices throughout unspeakable eons.
Some see, within the space of a single hair-tip, infinite oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust and sand,
each arising from various karmic causes and distinct from one another, where Vairocana turns the wheel of Dharma.
Some see worlds that are impure, while others see those composed of pure jewels;
they see the Tathāgatas dwelling for immeasurable eons, even until their parinirvāṇa—
manifesting all such things throughout the worlds of the ten directions in various, inconceivable ways.
In accordance with the mental faculties, wisdom, and karma of all sentient beings, there is none whom he does not transform and purify.
Such is the Unsurpassed Great Teacher, who fills the lands throughout the ten directions and manifests various supernormal powers; I shall speak of but a small portion—listen now!
Some see Śākyamuni having already attained the Way of Buddhahood after inconceivable kalpas;
some see him now just beginning as a bodhisattva, benefiting all sentient beings throughout the ten directions;
others see this Lion of the Śākyas making offerings to various Buddhas and practicing the Path.
Sometimes one sees the Most Victorious Honored One among men, manifesting various powers and miraculous feats;
sometimes one sees him practicing generosity or maintaining ethical discipline, or patience, diligence, or the meditative concentrations;
through wisdom, skillful means, vows, power, and knowledge, he manifests all things in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
Some see them having reached the ultimate perfection; some see them dwelling in the stages, dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and the wisdom of supernormal powers—thus they manifest everything without exception.
Some see them practicing for immeasurable eons, abiding in the bodhisattva stage of endurance.
Some manifest dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression; some manifest the water of the Dharma being poured over their crowns.
Some manifest the bodies of Brahmā, Śakra, or the World-Protectors;
some manifest the various forms and marks of Kṣatriyas and Brahmins, adorned with all manner of splendor, just as a magician manifests a multitude of images.
Sometimes he manifests the initial descent of his spirit from Tuṣita; sometimes he is seen receiving consorts within the palace;
or he is seen renouncing all worldly glory and pleasure, leaving home and secular life to practice the Way.
Sometimes he is seen being born, or seen passing away; or he is seen leaving home to study various practices.
Some see him seated beneath the Bodhi tree, subduing the hosts of Māra and attaining perfect enlightenment;
some see the Buddha having just entered parinirvāṇa; some see stūpas arising throughout the world;
or they see images of the Buddha installed within those stūpas—manifesting in this way because he knows the proper time.
Or one may see the Tathāgata Amitāyus bestowing the noble prediction upon the bodhisattvas, so that they become unsurpassed Great Teachers;
or see them successively dwelling in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Or one may see him, after performing buddha-works for immeasurable billions of kalpas, enter parinirvāṇa.
Some see him now first attaining enlightenment; some see him correctly practicing various sublime deeds;

they see the Tathāgata, the pure moon, dwelling in the Brahma world, the palace of Māra, the palace of the Vaśavartin gods, and the Nirmāṇarati heaven, manifesting all manner of supernatural transformations.
Some see him dwelling in the Tuṣita Palace, surrounded by immeasurable devas;
for their sake he preaches the Dharma to bring them joy, and they all together resolve their minds to make offerings to the Buddha.
Or some see him residing in the Yāma Heaven, or in the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa, the World-Protectors, the Nāgas, and the spirits.
In all these celestial palaces, there is not one that does not manifest his image;
at the abode of the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, he scattered flowers and spread his hair as an offering.
From this, he fully realized the profound and wondrous Dharma, and constantly uses this path to transform all living beings.
Some see the Buddha entering nirvana; some see him first attaining bodhi;
some see him remaining for immeasurable eons; and some see him passing into extinction in an instant.
His physical form, its radiance, and his lifespan, as well as his wisdom, his bodhi, and his nirvana—[all these are seen].
The bodies manifested through majestic deportance for the sake of the assembly— each and every one of these is infinite;
some manifest their bodies as exceedingly vast, like the great jewel mountain Sumeru,
while others are seen sitting cross-legged, unmoving, filling boundless worlds.
Some see a halo extending one fathom; some see it spanning thousands, tens of thousands, or millions of yojanas;
some see it illuminating immeasurable lands; some see it filling all buddha-fields.
Some see the Buddha’s lifespan as eighty years; others see it lasting hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, or millions of years.
Or dwelling for inconceivable eons, thus successively doubling beyond this,

the Buddha’s wisdom penetrates all with purity and unimpededness; in a single thought-moment, he universally knows that the phenomena of the three periods of time all arise from the causes and conditions of mind and consciousness—
subject to arising and ceasing, impermanent, and devoid of self-nature.
In a single world-system he attains perfect enlightenment, and in all world-systems he likewise attains it;
in every one of them, and in each of those, it is the same. According to the minds of sentient beings, he manifests everywhere;
the Tathāgata abides in the unsurpassed path, accomplishing the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
Endowed with wisdom that is unimpeded, you turn the wheel of Dharma of twelve aspects;

you thoroughly understand suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. You discern the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, possessing unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena, meanings, definitions, and phrasing; by means of these four analytical knowledges, you expound them extensively.
All phenomena are selfless and devoid of marks; The nature of karma neither arises nor perishes.
Completely detached like space, The Buddha distinguishes them through skillful means.
Thus does the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma, Universally shaking all lands throughout the ten directions.
The palaces, mountains, and rivers all tremble, yet no sentient beings are caused to feel alarm or fear.
Thus he universally proclaims this vast sound, causing all to understand according to their faculties and inclinations;
he causes them all to resolve their minds to eliminate the stains of delusion, while the Buddha has never given rise to such a thought.
Some hear of giving, morality, patience, diligence, Meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, and knowledge;
Or they hear of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, With various sounds and words each distinct;
Or they hear of the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts, The bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of awakening.
The various recollections, supernormal powers, tranquility, insight, and so forth— The immeasurable skillful means and all dharma-gates;
To the dragons, spirits, the eight classes of beings, humans, non-humans, And the hosts of devas such as Brahmā, Śakra, and the World-Protectors—
The Buddha preaches the Dharma for them with a single voice, Causing each to understand according to their own kind.
If there are those with greed, hatred, and delusion, With anger, concealment, stinginess, envy, pride, and flattery—
The eighty-four thousand diverse afflictions— May they all hear the teaching of their respective remedies.
If they have not yet fully cultivated pure and white dharmas, May they be made to hear the exposition of the ten precepts.
Having already been able to practice giving and subdue others, they cause them to hear the sound of quiescent nirvāṇa.
If there are those whose resolve is inferior and who lack compassion, who loathe birth and death and seek only their own liberation,
they cause them to hear the teaching on the three gates of liberation, so that they may emerge from suffering and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
If there are those who possess little desire by nature, who loathe and turn away from the three realms of existence, and seek tranquility—
cause them to hear the teaching on dependent origination so that they may attain liberation by means of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
If there are those with pure and expansive minds, who are fully endowed with the virtues of generosity and ethical discipline...
Approaching the Tathāgata who is endowed with compassion, they cause him to hear the sound of the Mahāyāna being preached;
in some lands they hear the One Vehicle, or two, or three, or four, or five,
and so on until there is no limit— all these are the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.

Nirvāṇa is quiescent and has never been otherwise; though there are distinctions in the excellence or inferiority of wisdom and practice, it is like the nature of space, which is one and the same, yet the birds flying within it differ according to how far they travel.
The Buddha-nature and its voice are likewise: they pervade the entirety of the realm of space.
According to the differences in the mental capacities and wisdom of sentient beings, What they hear and what they see each vary.
Because the Buddha cultivated all practices in the past, He can manifest wondrous sounds according to their inclinations;
Without a mind that discriminates between this and that, He considers not: "To whom do I speak, and to whom do I not speak?"
The Tathāgata’s face emits a great light; The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates he teaches are likewise complete.
It universally illuminates the world to eliminate afflictions, Possessing pure merit and wisdom, ever in accord with the three worlds.
Just as space is free from defilement and attachment, yet manifests for the sake of sentient beings by displaying the sufferings of birth,

old age, sickness, and death; likewise, though he displays dwelling in the world and remaining throughout his lifespan in accordance with worldly ways, his essential nature is pure, identical to space.
All lands are without limit, and the faculties and desires of sentient beings are likewise immeasurable;
with the eye of wisdom, the Tathāgata clearly perceives them all, manifesting the Buddha-way according to those who are to be transformed.
Throughout the entirety of empty space and the ten directions, amidst all the assemblies of humans and devas—
According to their various forms and characteristics, the Buddha manifests his body in the same way.
Whether he appears before an assembly of śramaṇas, with shaven hair and beard, wearing the kāṣāya robe,
holding the robes and bowl, and guarding the sense faculties, he causes them to rejoice and brings their afflictions to rest.
When he associates with brahmins, he manifests for them a gaunt body,
holding a staff and carrying a water-pot, ever pure; endowed with wisdom and skill in discourse,
he satisfies himself by exhaling the old and inhaling the new— drinking wind and dew as no different from food.
Whether sitting or standing, he remains unmoving; manifesting such ascetic practices, he subdues the heterodox paths.

Or, upholding those precepts as a teacher of the world, he is thoroughly proficient in medical arts and various treatises, mathematics, astronomy, geography, and the signs of all things—including the auspicious and inauspicious omens pertaining to the body—of which there is nothing he does not understand.
They enter deeply into the various dhyānas and liberations, samādhis, supernormal powers, and the practice of wisdom;
through discourse, chanting, and shared play, they employ skillful means to establish all beings on the Buddha-way.
Some manifest noble robes to adorn their bodies, wearing flower crowns upon their heads and shaded by lofty canopies.
Surrounded by the fourfold army in front and behind, he proclaims his majesty to the assembly to subdue minor kings;
sometimes he acts as a judge to hear lawsuits and decide legal cases, skillfully understanding all worldly affairs of administration.
Whether granting or taking away, he is clear and discerning in all matters, causing everyone to rejoice and submit.
Sometimes he acts as a great minister, solely providing counsel and support;
skillfully governing the various kings, he maintains the laws and benefits all quarters of the world with universal reach, yet no sentient beings can comprehend him.
Sometimes he becomes a minor king among the many petty rulers, or he becomes a flying Wheel-Turning Emperor.
He causes all the princes and the assembly of court ladies to be fully transformed by his teaching, beyond the reach of comprehension;
sometimes he becomes one of the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, ruling over the dragons, yakṣas, and others,
preaching the Dharma for their assemblies and causing them all to rejoice greatly.

Sometimes he acts as the Great Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, dwelling in the Sudharma Hall and the Nandana Grove, wearing a flower crown upon his head and preaching the wondrous Dharma; the various devas gaze up at him in reverence, unable to fathom him.
Or he dwells in the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, or Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens, or in the abode of Māra, the Lord of the World.
Dwelling in palaces of mani jewels, they preach the practice of truth to subdue beings;
or, within the assemblies of the Brahma heavens, they teach the four immeasurables and the paths of dhyāna,
causing all to rejoice before departing, such that no one knows the signs of their coming or going.

Or he may go as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where he preaches for them the jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), as well as other immeasurable noble virtues; thereafter he departs.
Those who lack knowledge do not perceive this, which is seen by the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom: all the sentient beings therein.
By means of all boundless gates of skillful expedients, He teaches and transforms beings in various ways to bring them to fulfillment.
Just as a master illusionist, skilled in illusory arts, Manifests all manner of illusory phenomena,
So too does the Buddha transform sentient beings, Appearing to them in all kinds of forms.
Just as the pure moon in the sky, Causes all sentient beings in the world to see its waxing and waning,
And reflects its image in all rivers and ponds;
So too does the Tathāgata’s wisdom-moon appear in the world, Displaying increase and decrease through skillful means.
The water of the Bodhisattva’s mind manifests their reflections; the Śrāvakas, like stars, possess no radiance or color.
Just as the great ocean is filled with jewels, pure, unsullied, and immeasurable, all sentient beings throughout the four continents appear as their images within it.
The ocean of the Buddha’s bodily merits is likewise: stainless, unclouded, and without limit.
Within it, the reflections of all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of phenomena appear;
just as the pure sun emits a thousand rays, it illuminates the ten directions without moving from its original place.
The radiance of the Buddha-sun is likewise: Neither going nor coming, it dispels the darkness of the world.

Just as a dragon king sends down a great rain, Which issues neither from his body nor from his mind, Yet is able to moisten and saturate everywhere, Washing away the scorching heat and bringing refreshing coolness.

The Dharma rain of the Tathāgata is likewise; though it does not issue from the body or mind of the Buddha, it can awaken all sentient beings, universally causing them to extinguish the fires of the three poisons.
The pure and wondrous Dharma-body of the Tathāgata has no equal throughout the entire triple world.
By means of supramundane paths of language, its nature is neither existent nor non-existent;

thus, while having no basis, it does not fail to abide, and while there is nothing it does not reach, it does not depart—like a painting in the sky or what is seen in a dream. One should contemplate the body of the Buddha in this way.
All phenomena within the three realms, whether existent or non-existent, cannot serve as metaphors for the Buddha;
just as among the birds and beasts of the mountains and forests, none dwell by relying upon space,
so too are the distinctions of the Buddha’s body like the infinite colors of the mani-jewels in the great ocean.
The Tathāgata is neither form nor non-form; He manifests according to conditions, yet dwells nowhere.

Space, true suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), Nirvāṇa, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and quiescence— Only such true dharmas as these Can be used to reveal the Tathāgata.
The atoms in all lands may be counted, The waters in the great oceans may be drunk up, Space may be measured and the wind bound; But none can fully describe the Buddha’s virtues.
If there are those who hear this ocean of merit And give rise to a heart of joy, faith, and understanding—
Whatever has been thus extolled shall all be attained; Be careful not to harbor doubts or suspicions regarding this.

[Treatise] From the tenth verse, beginning with the eight-line stanza down to the end of the sutra, the section clarifying the vast and immeasurable merit of Samantabhadra’s praise of the Tathāgata’s fruition of the Dharma-realm and his benefit for sentient beings is divided within the verses as follows:

In the first of the three sections, eight lines of verse clarify Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s exhortation for the assembly to listen attentively to his discourse on the division concerning the Buddha’s own qualities.
This is divided into two parts: first, six lines of scripture clarify the assembly’s joyful desire to hear;
second, the verses briefly set forth a small portion of the Tathāgata’s qualities, the intent of which is fully contained within the verse text itself.
The Combined Commentary on the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s New Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle 120.
